Initially created: 2025-12-17T20:47:41.691+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: The ancestors of the Jīn dynasty
originated from the Mòhé clan.
The Mòhé were originally called Wùjí.
Wùjí
was the land of the ancient Sùshèn.
During the Yuán Wèi period,
the Wùjí had seven tribes: namely the Sùmò部,
the Bódū部,
the Ānchēgǔ部,
the Fúniè部,
the Hàoshì部,
the Hēishuǐ部,
and the Báishān部.
During the Suí dynasty, they were called Mòhé,
and all seven tribes shared this name.
In the early Táng dynasty,
there were the Hēishuǐ Mòhé and Sùmò Mòhé,
while the other five tribes were unheard of.
The Sùmò Mòhé initially attached themselves to Gāolì,
bearing the surname Dà.
When Lǐ Jì defeated Gāolì,
the Sùmò Mòhé took refuge in Dōngmóu Shān.
Later, they became Bóhǎi,
proclaimed themselves kings,
and ruled for more than ten generations.
They had written characters, rites and music, official government, and an administrative system.
They had five capitals, fifteen prefectures, and sixty-two sub-prefectures.
The Hēishuǐ Mòhé resided in the land of Sùshèn,
bordered the sea to the east,
and adjoined Gāolì to the south.
They were also allied with Gāolì.
They once assisted Gāolì with a force of one hundred and fifty thousand troops to resist Táng Tàizōng,
but were defeated at Ānshì.
During the Kāiyuán era,
they came to court,
and the Hēishuǐ Prefecture was established.
Their tribal chiefs were appointed as Dūdū and Cìshǐ,
and a Zhǎngshǐ was placed to oversee them.
The Dūdū was granted the surname Lǐ
and the given name Xiànchéng,
and was appointed commander of the Hēishuǐ region (Hēishuǐ Jīnglüèshǐ).
Thereafter, Bóhǎi grew strong,
and the Hēishuǐ became subject to them,
whereupon their tribute ceased.
During the Five Dynasties period,
the Qìdān seized all of Bóhǎi's territory,
and the Hēishuǐ Mòhé became vassals of the Qìdān.
Those in the south were registered by the Qìdān
and called Shú Nǚzhí;
those in the north were not registered by the Qìdān
and called Shēng Nǚzhí.
The land of the Shēng Nǚzhí included the Húntóng Jiāng and Chángbái Shān.
The Húntóng Jiāng was also called Hēilóng Jiāng,
which is
what is meant by "Báishān, Hēishuǐ."
Indeed.
The given name of the founding ancestor of the Jīn dynasty was Hánpǔ.
He initially came from Gāolì,
already over sixty years old.
His elder brother, Āgǔnǎi, was fond of Buddhism
and remained in Gāolì, refusing to leave,
saying:
"In later generations, there will certainly be those among our descendants who can reunite;
I cannot depart."
He alone went with his younger brother Bǎohuólǐ.
The founding ancestor lived by the Púgàn river in the Wányán部,
while Bǎohuólǐ lived in Yélǎn.
Later, Húshímén returned to Tàizǔ with the Hésūguǎn people
and claimed that his ancestor had separated from his two brothers and left,
evidently referring to himself as a descendant of Āgǔnǎi.
Shítǔmén and Dígǔnǎi
were descendants of Bǎohuólǐ.
When Tàizǔ defeated the Liáo forces on the border
and captured Yélǜ Xièshí,
he then dispatched Liáng Fú and Wòdálà
to issue a proclamation to the Bóhǎi people, saying:
"The Nǚzhí and Bóhǎi are originally one family."
Indeed, in their early days, they were all among the seven tribes of Wùjí.
When the founding ancestor arrived at the Wányán部
and had resided there for a long time,
the people of his tribe once killed a person from another clan.
Because of this, the two clans became hostile,
and their feuding could not be resolved.
The people of the Wányán部 said to the founding ancestor:
"If you can resolve this enmity for our tribe
and prevent the two clans from killing each other,
our tribe has a virtuous woman,
sixty years old and unmarried,
whom we will give to you in marriage,
and you shall remain one of our tribe."
The founding ancestor replied:
"Agreed."
Then he went to persuade them, saying:
"If killing one person does not resolve the feud,
the damage will only increase.
Why not just punish the one who instigated the disturbance,
and let our tribe compensate you with goods,
so that you can avoid fighting and also gain profit?"
The offended party agreed.
So an agreement was made, stating:
"Whenever someone causes death or injury,
their family shall be levied one person, ten pairs of horses, ten brood cows, and six taels of gold.
These shall be given to the family of the killed or injured person,
and the two sides shall then be reconciled,
and private feuds shall not be allowed."
They replied:
"We will scrupulously adhere to the agreement."
The custom among the Nǚzhí
of compensating thirty horses and oxen for a killing began from this point.
After the compensation was paid as agreed,
the tribesmen trusted and submitted to him,
thanking him with one blue ox
and also promising to give him the sixty-year-old woman.
The founding ancestor then took the blue ox as a betrothal gift and married her,
also acquiring her wealth and property.
Later, she bore two sons,
the elder named Wūlǔ,
the younger named Wòlǔ,
and one daughter named Zhùsībǎn,
thus becoming people of the Wányán部.
In the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was posthumously honored with the title Jǐngyuán Huángdì,
and his temple name was Shǐzǔ.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng,
his tomb was named Guānglíng.
In the fifth year,
his posthumous title was augmented to Shǐzǔ Yìxiàn Jǐngyuán Huángdì.
His son was Dé Dì,
whose given name was Wūlǔ.
In the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was posthumously honored as Dé Huángdì.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng,
his tomb was named Xīlíng.
In the fifth year,
his posthumous title was augmented to Yuānmù Xuándé Huángdì.
His son was Ān Dì,
whose given name was Báihǎi.
In the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was posthumously honored as Ān Huángdì.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng,
his tomb was named Jiànlíng.
In the fifth year,
his posthumous title was augmented to Héjìng Qìng'ān Huángdì.
His son was Xiànzǔ,
whose given name was Suíkě.
The old customs of Hēishuǐ involved no permanent dwellings;
they dug pits in the ground by mountains and waters,
placed beams of wood over them,
and covered them with earth.
In summer, they moved with water and grass, residing outdoors;
in winter, they moved into these pits,
their movements being inconstant.
Xiànzǔ then moved to Hǎigǔshuǐ,
cultivated the land, planted crops,
and first built houses
with a structured roof and framework.
People called this place Nàgélǐ.
"Nàgélǐ"
means
"dwelling" in Hàn language.
From then on, they settled permanently by the Ānchūhǔshuǐ.
In the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was posthumously honored with the title Dìngzhāo Huángdì,
and his temple name was Xiànzǔ.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng,
his tomb was named Huīlíng.
In the fifth year,
his posthumous title was augmented to Xiànzǔ Chúnliè Dìngzhāo Huángdì.
His son was Zhāozǔ,
whose given name was Shílǔ,
a man of resolute and straightforward character.
The Shēng Nǚzhí had no written agreements,
no regulations,
and could not be controlled.
Zhāozǔ wanted to establish some rules,
but all his paternal uncles and tribesmen were displeased,
and wished to bury him alive.
He had already been seized when
his paternal uncle Xièlǐhū, knowing that the tribesmen were about to kill Zhāozǔ,
said:
"My brother's son
is a virtuous man
who will surely be able to carry on the family and
pacify the tribesmen.
How can these people simply want to bury him alive?"
He immediately went,
drew his bow, and shot an arrow into the crowd.
Those holding Zhāozǔ scattered and fled,
and Zhāozǔ was thus saved.
Zhāozǔ (昭祖) gradually governed with codified laws,
and his tribes gradually grew strong.
The Liáo (遼) appointed him the official Tìyǐn (惕隱).
The various tribes, however, still clung to old customs
and refused to adopt the codified laws.
Zhāozǔ (昭祖) displayed his military might as far as Qīnglǐng (青嶺) and Báishān (白山).
He appeased those who submitted
and campaigned against those who did not,
entering the lands of Sūbīn (蘇濱) and Yēlǎn (耶懶).
Everywhere he went, he achieved victories.
On his return, he passed through Púyànshuǐ (僕鷰水).
"Púyàn" (僕鷰)
in Hàn (漢) language means "foul sore."
Zhāozǔ (昭祖) disliked the place name,
and although he was exhausted,
he refused to stop.
He traveled to Gūlǐdiàn (姑里甸)
and fell ill.
By night,
he slept in a village house.
Robbers arrived,
so he set off again in the middle of the night,
stopping at Bīlàjì (逼剌紀) village.
That evening,
he died.
While carrying the coffin,
they encountered bandits on the road,
who seized the coffin and made off with it.
The tribesmen pursued the bandits and fought them,
recovering the coffin.
Púhǔ (蒲虎) of the Jiāgǔ (加古) tribe again came to attack them.
As he was about to catch up,
Púhǔ (蒲虎) asked a passerby:
"How far is Shílǔ’s (石魯) coffin from here?"
The person replied:
"It's far away,
you won't catch up if you pursue it."
Púhǔ (蒲虎) then stopped.
Thus, they were able to return and bury him.
The customs of the Shēng Nǚzhēn (生女直) were such that
by Zhāozǔ’s (昭祖) time, codified laws were gradually adopted,
and the people largely listened.
However, they still had no written script,
no official administration,
and no knowledge of months or new and full moons,
which made it impossible to ascertain the length of their lives.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì (天會)
he was posthumously granted the title Emperor Chéngxiāng (成襄),
with the temple name Zhāozǔ (昭祖).
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng (皇統),
his tomb was named Ānlíng (安陵).
In the fifth year,
his posthumous title was augmented to Emperor Zhāozǔ Wǔhuì Chéngxiāng (昭祖武惠成襄).
His son was Jǐngzǔ (景祖),
whose given name was Wūgǔnǎi (烏古廼).
He was born in the Xīnyǒu (辛酉) year, the first year of Tàipíng (太平) of the Liáo (遼).
From the first ancestor to this point,
six generations had passed.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) gradually brought the various tribes under his control.
From those of Báishān (白山), Yēhuǐ (耶悔), Tǒngmén (統門), Yēlǎn (耶懶), and Tǔgǔlún (土骨論),
to the chiefs of the Wǔguó (五國),
all obeyed his commands.
At this time,
some border people of the Liáo (遼) fled and joined him.
When the Liáo (遼) used troops to relocate the people of Tiělè (鐵勒) and Wūyě (烏惹),
many Tiělè (鐵勒) and Wūyě (烏惹) people refused to move
and also fled to him.
The Liáo (遼) sent Hélǔlínyá (曷魯林牙) with troops to demand the return of the escaped people.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) feared that Liáo (遼) troops would penetrate deep into his territory,
gaining full knowledge of the mountains, rivers, and all difficult and easy roads,
and perhaps plotting against him.
So, he stopped them with a strategy, saying:
"If troops penetrate deeply,
the various tribes will surely be alarmed and disturbed,
and unforeseen trouble will arise.
The fugitives also cannot be recovered,
which is not a good plan."
Hélǔ (曷魯) thought this was reasonable,
so he stopped his army.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) then went with Hélǔ (曷魯) to search for them himself.
At this time,
although neighboring tribes generally submitted,
Shíxiǎn (石顯) of the Wūlíndá (烏林答) tribe at Háilǎnshuǐ (孩懶水) still resisted and refused to submit.
They attacked him but
could not defeat him.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) informed the Liáo (遼) ruler of his plan,
and the Liáo (遼) ruler sent an envoy to rebuke Shíxiǎn (石顯).
Shíxiǎn (石顯) then sent his son, Pózhūkān (婆諸刊), to court.
The Liáo (遼) ruler generously rewarded him and sent him back.
Later, Shíxiǎn (石顯) and Pózhūkān (婆諸刊) went to meet the Liáo (遼) ruler during the spring hunt.
The Liáo (遼) ruler then detained Shíxiǎn (石顯) at the border
and sent Pózhūkān (婆諸刊) back to his tribe.
This was Jǐngzǔ’s (景祖) scheme.
Subsequently, Báyǐmén (拔乙門), the Jìdùshǐ (節度使) of the Púniè (蒲聶) tribe of the Wǔguó (五國), rebelled against the Liáo (遼),
blocking the eagle-tribute route.
The Liáo (遼) people were about to punish him,
and first sent Tónggàn (同幹) to convey the imperial decree.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) said:
"He can be taken by strategy.
If we use force,
he will flee to difficult terrain for protection,
and it will not be pacified in a year or two."
The Liáo (遼) people agreed with him.
This was because Jǐngzǔ (景祖) ultimately feared Liáo (遼) troops entering his territory,
so he claimed the credit himself.
Thereupon, Jǐngzǔ (景祖) feigned friendship with Báyǐmén (拔乙門),
offering his wife and children as hostages.
He then ambushed and captured him,
presenting him to the Liáo (遼) ruler.
The Liáo (遼) ruler received him in his sleeping quarters,
feasted and rewarded him exceptionally,
appointing him Jìdùshǐ (節度使) of the Shēng Nǚzhēn (生女直) tribes.
The Liáo (遼) people called a Jìdùshǐ (節度使) a Tàishī (太師),
and the Jīn (金) people’s designation of
"Dūtàishī" (都太師)
began from this.
The Liáo (遼) ruler intended to engrave a seal and give it to him.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) was unwilling to be registered under the Liáo (遼),
and declined, saying:
"Please wait for another day."
The Liáo (遼) ruler still wanted to give it to him,
and sent an envoy.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) tricked the envoy by having his tribesmen spread rumors, saying:
"If our lord accepts the seal and is registered,
the tribesmen will surely kill him."
He used this to reject it,
and the Liáo (遼) envoy then returned.
Once he became Jìdùshǐ (節度使),
he had officials and subordinates,
and his organizational structure gradually took shape.
The Shēng Nǚzhēn (生女直) previously had no iron.
Neighboring countries had those who came to sell armor and helmets.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) spent all his wealth, paying high prices to trade for them,
and also instructed his brothers and kinsmen to purchase them all.
After acquiring much iron,
he used it to repair bows and arrows,
and prepare weapons and equipment.
His military strength gradually grew,
and the number of those willing to join him, before and after, was large.
The Púchá (蒲察) tribe of Wòyǐnmǐnshuǐ (斡泯水), the Wányán (完顏) tribe of Tàishén Tèbǎoshuǐ (泰神忒保水), the Wēndíhén (溫迪痕) tribe of Tǒngménshuǐ (統門水), and the Wányán (完顏) tribe of Shényǐnshuǐ (神隱水),
all successively came to submit.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) was magnanimous,
capable of accommodating others,
and throughout his life showed no signs of joy or anger.
He shared his wealth with others,
distributed food, and gave away clothes,
without any吝惜.
If someone offended him,
he would not bear a grudge.
Earlier,
there were some who rebelled and left.
He sent people to persuade and entice them.
The rebels said:
"Your lord
is a Huóluó (活羅).
A Huóluó (活羅), I can capture it.
How could I possibly submit to a Huóluó (活羅)?"
"Huóluó" (活羅)
in Hàn (漢) language means "cígū" (慈烏) (literally 'compassionate crow', likely referring to a type of bird of prey or scavenger).
It is found in the north,
shaped like a large chicken.
It is good at pecking things.
When it sees sores on the backs of horses, cattle, or camels,
it pecks at their backs to eat from them.
Horses and cattle often die.
If it is hungry and cannot find food,
it will even eat sand and stones.
Jǐngzǔ (景祖) was fond of wine and women,
and ate and drank excessively.
People at the time called him Huóluó (活羅),
so they used this to mock him,
but he did not take it to heart.
Later, those who mocked him were overwhelmed and surrendered.
He generously rewarded them and sent them back.
There were those from Hélǎnshuǐ (曷懶水) who led their people to surrender.
He recorded their years and names,
then sent them away immediately,
allowing them to return to their former state.
People thus trusted and submitted to him even more.
In the eighth year of Xiányōng of the Liáo dynasty,
the Wǔguó Mòliǎn 部 Xièyě bójǐn rebelled against Liáo,
blocking the eagle route.
Jǐngzǔ attacked them,
and Xièyě came to resist.
Jǐngzǔ donned heavy armor
and led his troops in a fierce battle.
Xièyě's army was defeated
and fled to Bálǐmài Luò.
It was then the tenth month,
and the ice suddenly melted,
making it impossible for Xièyě's army to camp.
All his troops dispersed.
Jǐngzǔ then withdrew his forces.
On the way, they encountered fleeing rebels
who blocked their path through dangerous terrain.
They fought day and night,
and by the time they reached their own部, they were exhausted.
Jǐngzǔ immediately went to see Dálǔgǔ, a Liáo frontier general,
and reported his success in defeating Xièyě.
As he traveled to Láiliúshuǐ,
before meeting Dálǔgǔ,
his illness recurred and worsened.
He died at home
at the age of fifty-four.
In the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was posthumously granted the title Huìhuán Huángdì,
and his temple name was Jǐngzǔ.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng,
his tomb was named Dìnglíng.
In the fifth year,
his posthumous title was augmented to Jǐngzǔ Yīngliè Huìhuán Huángdì.
His second son inherited the position of Jiédùshǐ,
who was Shìzǔ,
whose personal name was Hélǐbō.
According to the customs of the Nǚzhēn people,
when a son came of age, he would live separately.
Jǐngzǔ had nine sons.
His primary consort, of the Tángkuò clan, gave birth to Hézhě,
followed by Shìzǔ,
then Hésūn,
then Sùzōng,
and then Mùzōng.
When it was time for them to live separately,
Jǐngzǔ said:
"Hézhě is gentle and mild,
suitable for managing household affairs.
Hélǐbō has great capacity and knowledge;
there is nothing he cannot accomplish.
Hésūn is also a gentle and kind person."
So he ordered Hézhě to live with Shìzǔ,
and Hésūn to live with Sùzōng.
After Jǐngzǔ's death,
Shìzǔ succeeded him.
After Shìzǔ's death,
Sùzōng succeeded him.
After Sùzōng's death,
Mùzōng succeeded him.
Mùzōng in turn passed the succession to Shìzǔ's son,
and eventually Tàizǔ
ascended the great throne.
Shìzǔ
was born in the eighth year of Chóngxī, the Jǐmǎo year, of the Liáo dynasty.
In the tenth year of Xiányōng of the Liáo dynasty,
he inherited the position of Jiédùshǐ.
Báhéi, Jǐngzǔ's half-brother, harbored rebellious intentions.
Shìzǔ, fearing he would cause trouble,
treated him with extra care,
not allowing him to command troops,
but only to be a部zhǎng.
Báhéi then instigated Huánmó, Sǎndá, Wūchūn, and Wōmóuhǎn to rebel,
and sowed discord among the various部s, making them disloyal to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ still wished to appease him;
the details are in the biographies of Báhéi and Huánmó, etc.
Shìzǔ once bought ninety suits of armor from the blacksmith Wūbùtún of the Jiāgǔ部.
Wūchūn wanted to use this as a pretext for war.
Shìzǔ returned the armor to him;
the details are in the biography of Wūchūn.
There were rumors circulating in the部, saying:
"If you wish to live, attach yourselves to Báhéi;
if you wish to die, attach yourselves to Hélǐbō and Pōlàshū."
Shìzǔ heard this
and became suspicious,
but had no way to discern the truth.
So he pretended to prepare for a journey,
as if he intended to go somewhere.
Secretly, he sent people to spread rumors, saying:
"Bandits are coming!"
Those among the部who heard this did not know whether it was true or false.
Some sought refuge in Báhéi's residence,
while others sought refuge in Shìzǔ's residence.
Thus, Shìzǔ fully understood the loyalties and dispositions of his brothers and their subordinates.
After several years,
Wūchūn came to attack,
and Shìzǔ resisted him.
It was then mid-October,
and heavy rain fell for days and nights.
Ice slush covered the ground,
preventing Wūchūn from advancing.
Later, he regretted it, saying:
"This is Heaven's will."
Then he led his troops away.
Wūchūn stayed at Zǐbùnǎi's house in Ālǐ'ǎi Village,
while besieging his brother Shèngkūn with troops in Húbù Village.
After the troops retreated,
Shèngkūn apprehended his brother Zǐbùnǎi
and requested permission from Shìzǔ to execute him,
also asking for his family to be spared from slaughter.
This was granted.
Huánmó and Sǎndá also raised an army,
and Sùzōng was sent to resist them.
At this time,
Wūchūn's army was in the north,
and Huánmó's army was in the south,
their power was very formidable.
Shìzǔ instructed Sùzōng:
"If peace is possible, make peace;
otherwise, fight a decisive battle."
Sùzōng's army was defeated.
Just then, Wūchūn, due to the prolonged rain, withdrew.
Shìzǔ then led a detachment of his army across Shěhěnshuǐ
and through Tiēgéshuǐ,
destroying the homes of Huánmó and Sǎndá.
The next day,
a thick fog obscured everything,
and they lost their way,
only realizing it when they reached Póduōtǔshuǐ.
He immediately returned to the area between Shěhěn and Tiēgé,
climbed a high mound to look around,
and saw six horsemen approaching.
He shouted loudly
and galloped to attack them.
Shìzǔ shot one man dead
and captured five alive.
When questioned,
they revealed that they were Bǔhuī and Sāgǔ, who had been sent to assist Huánmó and Sǎndá.
Shìzǔ went to the residences of Huánmó and Sǎndá,
burned down their homes,
and killed about a hundred people.
The old general Zhǔbǎo also died there.
By the time Shìzǔ returned
and met with Sùzōng,
Sùzōng's army had been defeated again.
Shìzǔ rebuked Sùzōng for his defeat.
He sent someone to negotiate for peace.
Huánmó and Sǎndá said:
"Give us Yínggē's big red horse and Cíbùshī's purple-bay horse,
and we will make peace."
Both horses were famous Nǚzhēn steeds,
so the request was refused.
Huánpō and Sàndá convened a grand assembly of various tribes to attack.
Passing the Péimǎn tribe,
because they were allied with Shìzǔ,
they set fire to and burned it.
The Púchá tribe's Shāzhī Bójǐn and Húbǔdá Bójǐn sent Āxǐ to report the distress.
Shìzǔ instructed him to feign compliance to save himself,
saying:
"When we fight, distinguish yourselves with flags and drums."
Shìzǔ went to resist Huánpō's forces.
As he was about to depart,
a messenger reported:
"Báhēi was eating at his beloved concubine's father's house,
a piece of meat stuck in his throat,
and he died."
So, he sent Sùzōng to seek aid from Liáo,
and then led his troops out.
He sent Cíbùshī to gather the soldiers of Hǎigū and his brothers,
but soon learned that Hǎigū and his brothers had defected to Huánpō.
Wishing to consolidate their forces,
he went straight to Hǎigū.
A scout reported:
"The enemy has arrived."
About to battle,
Shìzǔ admonished Cíbùshī, saying:
"You will form the vanguard at Tuōhuògǎi Yuán.
Wait until I raise the flag three times
and beat the drum three times,
then abandon the flags and fight decisively.
Life and death hang on this day;
life is not to be grudged."
He had Péimǎn Húxǐ lead a large purple-chestnut horse as a spare,
and galloped to the formation.
At that time, Huánpō and Sàndá were powerful,
and Shìzǔ's military officers were fearful before the battle,
all standing rigid, pale with terror.
Shìzǔ appeared calm as usual,
and said no words of blame or reproach,
but only ordered the soldiers to remove their armor and rest briefly,
to wash their faces with water,
and to drink some water.
After a moment,
he exhorted and encouraged them,
and the army's morale revived.
Then he dismissed the crowd and privately led Mùzōng aside,
holding his hand and secretly saying to him:
"Regarding today's events,
if we win, that is well.
But if by any chance we do not win,
I will surely not survive.
You, mounted on your horse, observe from afar,
do not participate in the battle.
If I die,
do not collect my bones,
do not cling to relatives,
but immediately gallop to inform your brother Pōlàshū,
register with Liáo and receive an official seal,
and beg for troops to avenge this enmity."
After speaking,
he bared his sleeves,
did not wear armor,
but used a padded robe with dangling lapels to protect his front and back heart,
sheathed his bow, held his sword,
raised the flag three times,
beat the drum three times,
abandoned the flags, and engaged in close combat,
personally serving as the army's vanguard,
charging into the enemy's formation,
with the troops following him.
Cíbùshī attacked fiercely from the rear,
utterly defeating them.
Taking advantage of the victory, they pursued them
from Ābùwān to Běiàidiàn.
The dead lay like fallen hemp plants,
and the broken Tuōshuǐ river turned red with blood.
They captured all the abandoned chariots, armor, horses, cattle, and military provisions.
Shìzǔ said:
"Today's victory,
were it not for Heaven, could not have been achieved to this extent;
we can also be content.
Even if we let them go,
the spirit of the defeated army will not revive for generations."
Then he led his army back.
Shìzǔ observed the battlefield where he had charged,
which had become a wide road,
about thirty paces wide.
He had personally killed nine men,
who lay piled on top of each other,
and everyone found it extraordinary.
From then on, Huánpō and Sàndá could not regroup.
Soon after,
they each came with their respective tribes to surrender;
it was the seventh year of Dà'ān of Liáo.
Initially,
during the rebellion of Huánpō and his brothers, Bùshùlǔ Bù Bǔhuī and Púchá Bù Sāgǔchū came to assist him.
By this time,
they were invited,
but refused to reconcile.
Shílǔ, one of Bǔhuī's partisans, then killed Bǔhuī and surrendered.
Sāgǔchū pursued the fleeing rebels,
and a person by the roadside secretly shot him,
hitting him in the mouth, and he died.
From then on, all the old tribes submitted.
During Jǐngzǔ's time,
the people of the Wòlè tribe, Bēinǎi, came to submit.
By this time,
they had other intentions.
Coincidentally, his house caught fire,
and he falsely accused Huāndū of arson.
Shìzǔ demanded compensation as agreed.
Bēinǎi felt uneasy,
and consequently allied with Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn to raise an army.
Shìzǔ sent Sùzōng to fight,
defeated them,
and captured Bēinǎi.
Shìzǔ presented him to Liáo.
Làpēi and Máshǎn plundered the Yějū Nǚzhēn
and seized horses grazing by the Láiliú River.
Shìzǔ attacked them,
suffering four wounds,
but recovered after a long time.
Làpēi and others again seized Mùzōng's horses
and formed alliances with various tribes.
Shìzǔ again attacked them.
Làpēi and others feigned surrender,
so he turned back.
Làpēi obtained one hundred and seventeen soldiers from Gūlǐdiàn,
and occupied Mùléngshuǐ, defending its strategic points.
Shíxiǎnzǐ Pózhūkān was also among them.
Shìzǔ besieged and conquered it,
capturing all the Gūlǐdiàn soldiers.
Máshǎn fled.
Then, he captured Làpēi and Pózhūkān,

After this,
he again requested them,
and the Liáo people gave them to him,

Huāndū utterly defeated Wūchūn and others at Xiétuī.
Gùshí and Báshí were all captured.
Shìzǔ personally led his forces and joined Huāndū's army east of the ridge;
all the armies arrived.
At this time,
Wūchūn had already died earlier.
Wōmóuhǎn requested reconciliation from Liáo.
After peace was made,
he attacked again.
So, the army advanced and besieged him.
Wōmóuhǎn abandoned the city and fled.
They broke into his city,
captured all its inhabitants,
and distributed them among the various armies according to their merits.
When the city was first breached,
they discussed whether to execute or spare the chief, Chángshēng.
Everyone knelt,
and the Liáo envoy was present.
Suddenly, a man wearing a long saber rushed forward, very close,
and said to Shìzǔ:
"Do not kill me."
The Liáo envoy and those around him all fled and hid.
Shìzǔ's expression did not change in the slightest.
He grasped the man's hand,
and said to him:
"I will not kill you."
Then he punished those around him who had hidden,
saying:
"How dare you abandon your positions?"
After the punishment,
he then slowly ordered the one who had rushed forward to be seized and killed.
His courage and ability to subdue people were like this.
Shī returned,
fell ill,
and became critical.
Yuán's wife, Nálǎnshì, wept ceaselessly.
Shìzǔ said:
"Do not cry.
You will only outlive me by one year."
Sùzōng asked about posthumous affairs.
He said:
"You will only outlive me by three years."
Sùzōng left,
and said to others:
"My elder brother, even at this point,
does not speak kindly to me."
Then he knelt on the ground and wept.
Soon after, he called Mùzōng and said:
"Wūyǎshù is gentle and kind.
If you are to manage the Qìdān affairs,
Āgǔdá can do it."
He passed away on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the eighth year of Dà'ān of Liáo.
He reigned for nineteen years,
and was fifty-four years old.
The next year,
Nálǎnshì passed away.
The year after that,
Sùzōng passed away.
When Sùzōng was critically ill,
he sighed:
"My elder brother was truly full of wisdom!"
Shìzǔ was naturally grave,
and possessed wisdom and discernment.
Once he saw something, he would surely recognize it.
What he heard briefly, he did not forget.
He did not shiver in severe cold,
nor did he look back in motion or at rest.
Before every battle, he never wore armor,
but first divined victory or defeat through dream omens.
Once, while drunk, he rode a donkey into the inner chambers.
The next day, seeing the donkey's hoof prints,
he asked and learned of it.
From then on, he never drank alcohol again.
At the beginning of his reign,
both internal and external factions mutinied,
forming alliances to become bandits.
and transformed weakness into strength.
After defeating Huánhè, Sàndá, Wūchūn, and Wōmóuhǎn,
his foundation grew great from then on.

His younger brother by the same mother, Pōlàshū, inherited the position of Jìdùshǐ.
He was Jǐngzǔ's fourth son,
and was Sùzōng.
He was born in the *rénwǔ* year, the eleventh year of Chóngxī of Liáo.

Initially,
Yǎdá was Guóxiàng.
Yǎdá was
the father of Huánhè and Sàndá.
Jǐngzǔ requested him from Yǎdá with money and horses,

Sùzōng was quick-witted and eloquent from a young age.
During his elder brother's time,
he served as Guóxiàng,

At that time,
his uncle Báhēi had rebellious intentions.
And when Huánhè, Sàndá, Wūchūn, Wōmóuhǎn, Shíxiǎn and his son, Lāpēi, and Máchan caused trouble,
during the military campaigns,
Sùzōng frequently led a front.
He was especially adept at understanding the Liáo people's national policies and human sentiments.
Whenever there were Liáo affairs,

Whenever they reported matters to Liáo officials,

Often, the interpreter would garble them.
Sùzōng wanted to explain things directly and thoroughly himself,

The interpreter was confused,
and, left with no choice,
brought him forward,

He then used grass, wood, tiles, and stones as counters,
counting out each matter and presenting it.
The listening officials were all astonished,
and when asked why,
he replied with humble words:
"I am rustic and uncultured,
hence I do this."
The officials believed it to be true,
and no longer doubted him,
thus all his petitions were successful.
In the battle against Huánhè and Sàndá,
the tribal member Sàihǎn died,

One day,
he suddenly placed the blunt side of a sword on Sùzōng's neck and said:

What if I slit your throat to repay that?"
After a long time,
when his brother's coffin arrived,
he became enraged and attacked Xíbuchū,

He attacked Sùzōng at his home,

He then attacked Huāndū,
who, armored, resisted him inside the room.
Unable to enter,
Huóluó took his door curtain and left,

Bēinǎi lured Wūchūn's troops to cross the mountain pass,

Shìzǔ said:

He ordered Sùzōng, Xiéliè, and Cíbùshī to fight them.
Sùzōng dismounted,

then the spirits shall witness today's events."
After speaking, he bowed twice.
Then he lit a fire with bundled tinder.
A moment later,
a strong wind rose from behind,
making the fire burn even more fiercely.
It was the eighth month at that time,
and all the green grass was burned,
smoke and flames reaching the sky.
Our army charged with the smoke,
and utterly defeated them.
Then Bēinǎi was captured,
imprisoned, and offered to Liáo.
Huóluó was also captured.
Sùzōng pardoned his crime,
and employed him at his side,
later indeed gaining from his service.
In the eighth year of Dà'ān,
he inherited the throne from the position of Guóxiàng.
At that time,

He was summoned but

Mùzōng

Bàtè fled,

Āshū and Máodǔlù of the Hégé liè tribe raised troops and caused trouble.

At that time, Āgěbǎn and Shílǔ of the Hégéliè tribe, living near Táo wēn shuǐ and Túlónggǔ shuǐ, blocked the hawk road of the Five Nations
and captured and killed the Liáo envoys sent to catch hawks.
The Liáo emperor decreed Mùzōng to suppress them.
Āgěbǎn and others held strategic positions and set up stockades.
As it was very cold,
skilled archers with strong bows and sharp arrows were recruited to attack them.
After several days,
their city was entered,
and several surviving Liáo envoys were released

Liúkě and Zhàdū of the Wūgǔlún tribe at the confluence of Tǒngmén and Húnchǔn Shuǐ, and Díkùdé of the Wūgǔlún tribe at Sūbīn Shuǐ, raised an army in Mǐlǐmí Shíhǎn Chéng.

In the eighth month,

Shítǔmén's army then joined Màndūhē's,

In the last years of Mùzōng,
Āshū made Dájì incite the border people,
but the Hélǎndiàn people seized and delivered him.
Mùzōng sent Shíshìhuān to pacify and win over Hélǎndiàn,
but before he departed,
Mùzōng died.
It was then that he was dispatched.
Before this,
Gāolí had established good relations,
but later, there were some rifts.
Gāolí envoys came to request discussions,
but when the envoys arrived in Gāolí,
they were refused entry.
The people of Wǔshuǐ submitted to Gāolí,
seizing fourteen Tuánliànshǐ (militia commanders).
The details are found in the biography of Gāolí.
In the second year (1104), jiǎshēn,
Gāolí again came to attack,
and Shíshìhuān again defeated them.
Gāolí again requested peace,
and the fourteen Tuánliànshǐ previously captured were all sent back.
Shíshìhuān pacified the border people and returned.
The people of Sūbīnshuǐ did not obey orders,
so Wòdài and others were sent to Huóluōhǎi Chuān
to summon the officials and issue pronouncements.
Wòhuòbójǐn of the Hánguó tribe in Sūbīnshuǐ did not come.
Wòzhǔnbù and Zhídébù arrived,
but then fled again.
Wūtǎ encountered the two tribes at Mǎjì Lǐng,
seized them, and brought them back.
Then Wòhuò was attacked
and captured.
Wòdài advanced to Běiqínhǎi,
attacked and captured Hóngtèchéng,
then returned.
In the fourth year (1106), bǐngxū,
Gāolí sent Hēihuānfāngshí to congratulate him on his succession,
and Bēilǔ was sent to respond.
Gāolí promised to return those who had fled and were there,
so Āguā and Shèngkūn were sent to receive them.
Gāolí broke the agreement,
killed the two envoys,
built nine cities in Hélǎndiàn,
and came to attack with tens of thousands of troops.
Wòsài defeated them.
Wòlǔ also built nine cities,
facing Gāolí's nine cities.
Gāolí came to attack again,
and Wòsài again defeated them.
Gāolí agreed to return the fugitives,
withdraw the army from the nine cities,
and restore the previously encroached territory.
In the ninth month,
the troops were disbanded.
In the seventh year (1109), jǐchǒu,
the harvest failed,
so fines for robbers were reduced,
and the poor were relieved.
In the eleventh year (1113), guǐsì,
Kāngzōng died
at the age of fifty-three.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì (1137),
he was posthumously honored with the title Gōngjiǎn Huángdì.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng (1144),
his tomb was designated Qiáolíng.
In the fifth year (1145),
he was additionally honored with the title Kāngzōng Xiànmǐn Gōngjiǎn Huángdì.
Appraisal: At the beginning of the Jīn dynasty,
the three brothers
were also insignificant.
Xīzōng posthumously honored the ancestors as emperors,
and established temples for Shǐzǔ, Jǐngzǔ, and Shìzǔ,
to be worshipped perpetually.
Shǐzǔ married a sixty-year-old woman and had two sons and one daughter;
was this not heaven's will?
Jǐngzǔ did not accept Liáo registers or Liáo seals,
but took Yǎdá's
"Guóxiàng" (Chancellor)
to give to his son.
After Shìzǔ defeated Huánhē and Sàndá,
Liáo's government declined daily,
yet he entrusted Tàizǔ to Mùzōng.
Were his considerations not deep and far-reaching?
Collation Notes
Tàizǔ, styled Yìnggānxīngyùn Zhāodédìnggōng Rénmíngzhuāngxiào Dàshèngwǔyuán Huángdì,
taboo name Mín,
original taboo name Āgǔdǎ,
was the second son of Shìzǔ.
His mother was Yìjiǎn Huánghòu Nálǎnshì.
During the reign of Liáo Dàozōng, five-colored clouds frequently appeared in the east,
large like two thousand *hú* (bushels) of granaries.
Sītiān Kǒngzhìhé secretly told people:
"Below them, an extraordinary person will be born,
who will accomplish extraordinary things.
Heaven gives omens;
it is not something human power can achieve."
On the first day of the seventh month of the fourth year of Xiányōng (1068), wùshēn,
Tàizǔ was born.
As a child, when playing with other children,
his strength surpassed several of them;
his demeanor was upright and serious,
and Shìzǔ especially loved him.
When Shìzǔ fought Lápēi and Máchan at Yěquèshuǐ,
Shìzǔ was wounded four times,
and gravely ill.
He sat Tàizǔ on his knee,
stroked his hair and caressed him,
saying:
"When this child grows up,
what more do I have to worry about?"
At the age of ten,
he loved bows and arrows.
As soon as he reached adulthood,
he was skilled at archery.
One day,
a Liáo envoy sat in the residence,
and looking around, saw Tàizǔ holding a bow and arrow.
He asked him to shoot at a flock of birds,
and all three consecutive shots hit.
The Liáo envoy said with astonishment:
"What a remarkable man!"
Tàizǔ once feasted at the home of Huólíhǎn of the Hèshíliè tribe.
Strolling outside the gate,
he looked south at a high mound,
and asked the crowd to shoot at it;
none could reach it.
Tàizǔ's single shot went beyond it,
estimated to have traveled over three hundred and twenty paces.
The imperial clansman Màndūhē was best at long-distance archery,
but even he was still a hundred paces short.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
a shooting monument was erected to commemorate it.
When Shìzǔ campaigned against Bǔhuī,
Tàizǔ, through Cíbùshī, requested to accompany him.
Shìzǔ did not allow it, but secretly admired him.
After Wūchūn died,
Wōmóuhǎn requested peace.
After requesting peace,
he attacked again,
and then besieged his city.
Tàizǔ, at twenty-three,
wore a short cuirass,
removed his helmet,
and rode his horse unarmored,
going around the siege to give orders to the various armies.
Those in the city recognized him by sight.
The valiant warrior Tàiyù rode a swift horse, holding a spear, and sallied out of the city,
charging to stab Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ had no time to prepare,
but his maternal uncle Huólàhú galloped out between them,
struck Tàiyù,
breaking his spear,
and stabbing his horse.
Tàiyù barely escaped.
He once went out of the camp with Shāhútài to kill and plunder,
without letting Shìzǔ know.
When returning,
the enemy pursued them with a large force.
He rode alone through a narrow alley,
lost his way,
and the pursuers became more urgent.
He came across a high bank as tall as a man,
and his horse leaped over it,
whereupon the pursuers turned back.
Shìzǔ fell ill.
Tàizǔ went to Liáo Tǒngjūn Sī on business.
As he was about to leave,
Shìzǔ admonished him, saying:
"You must finish this matter quickly.
If you return before the middle of the fifth month,
then I may still live to see you."
Tàizǔ went to see Hélǔ Sāogǔ Tǒngjūn.
Having completed his business,
he returned home one day before Shìzǔ passed away.
When Shìzǔ saw Tàizǔ arrive,
and that all the requested matters had been accomplished as desired,
he was extremely pleased.
He took Tàizǔ's hand,
embraced his neck and caressed him,
saying to Mùzōng:
"Wūyǎshù is gentle and kind,
but only this son is capable of settling the Qìdān affairs."
Mùzōng also held Tàizǔ in high regard,
always going out and coming in together.
When Tàizǔ returned from a distant journey,
Mùzōng would personally go out to welcome him.
Shìzǔ had already captured Làpéi,
but MáChǎn still occupied Zhíwū Kǎishuǐ.
Sùzōng sent Tàizǔ to first capture MáChǎn's family members,
then Kāngzōng arrived at Zhíwū Kǎishuǐ and besieged him.
Tàizǔ joined the army,
personally captured MáChǎn,
and presented his severed head to Liáo.
The Liáo ruler appointed Tàizǔ as Xiángwěn,
and also appointed Mùzōng, Cíbùshī, and Huāndū all as Xiángwěn.
After a long time,
he led a detached force to attack the Níyí Bānggǔ tribe's Báhēi and Bōlìkāi,
using Dátú'ā as a guide.
They marched by night along the Shuài Shuǐ and attacked them,
capturing their wives and children.
Earlier,
Bátè of the Wēndū tribe had killed Bágé of the Tángkuò tribe.
Mùzōng ordered Tàizǔ to attack him.
Tàizǔ came to take his leave,
and said to Mùzōng:
"Last night I saw an auspicious red omen;
this expedition is certain to defeat the enemy."
So he departed.
That year there was heavy snow,
and it was very cold.
With the troops of the Wūgǔlún tribe, he passed through Mòlín Xiāng along the Túwēn Shuǐ,
and overtook Bátè between Āsī Wēnshān and Běiluò,
killing him.
When the army returned,
Mùzōng personally welcomed Tàizǔ at Àijiàn Cūn.
Sāigǎi, as Dūtǒng, attacked Liúkě;
Màndūhē and Shítǔmén attacked Díkùdé.
Sāigǎi discussed with his officers;
some wanted to first pacify the border tribes' castles,
others wanted to directly attack Liúkě City.
The debate could not be settled,
so they wished for Tàizǔ to come to the army.
Mùzōng sent Tàizǔ,
saying:
"There must be something suspicious.
The only troops not yet dispatched are seventy armored soldiers;
I give them all to you."
Màndūhē was below Mǐlǐmí Shíhǎn City;
Shítǔmén had not yet arrived.
The locals wanted to seize Màndūhē and hand him over to the enemy.
An envoy came to report the emergency,
meeting Tàizǔ at Xiédūi Diàn.
Tàizǔ said:
"All the national troops are here.
If the enemy gains control over Màndūhē first,
what good will it do to eradicate them later?"
So he divided forty armored soldiers to him.
Tàizǔ went with thirty men to Sāigǎi's army.
On the way, he met someone who said:
"The enemy has already occupied the southern road of Péngnì Lǐng."
The multitude wanted to go via Shāpiān Lǐng,
but Tàizǔ said:
"Are you afraid of the enemy?"
After crossing Péngnì Lǐng,
they did not see the enemy.
Soon after, they heard that the enemy was guarding Shāpiān Lǐng to resist them.
When they reached Sāigǎi's army,
they attacked vigorously that night,
breaking their forces by dawn.
At this time, Liúkě and Wùtǎ were both in Liáo.
After defeating Liúkě,
they returned to attack Wùtǎ City,
and the people in the city surrendered it.
Originally,
when Tàizǔ passed Péngnì Lǐng
and went below Wùtǎ City,
some of his cavalry fell behind.
The people of Wùtǎ City attacked them and stole a cauldron.
Tàizǔ stopped his horse and called out to them, saying:
"Do not take my cooking utensils."
The person rudely replied:
"Since you can come here,
why worry about not having food?"
Tàizǔ pointed with his whip and said:
"After I defeat Liúkě,
I will take it from you."
Now,
that person held the cauldron and came forward, saying:
"Who among us slaves would dare to damage the Xiángwěn's utensil?"
He sent Pújiānú to recruit Zhàdū.
Zhàdū surrendered,
and was released.
Mùzōng was about to attack Xiāo Hǎilǐ,
and recruited over a thousand soldiers.
The Nǚzhēn army had never before reached a thousand.
At this point,
Tàizǔ's courage doubled,
saying:
"With these armored troops,
what cannot be accomplished?"
Hǎilǐ came to fight,
joining with the Liáo troops,
but then he stopped the Liáo people and fought himself.
The Bóhǎi Liúshǒu offered armor to Tàizǔ,
but Tàizǔ did not accept it.
Mùzōng asked why he did not accept.
He replied:
"If I fight wearing their armor,
then victory in battle would be attributed to them."
In Mùzōng's later years,
he ordered that no tribes were allowed to arbitrarily issue identification plaques for fast postal service to report matters.
Orders became unified from this point,
all initiated by Tàizǔ.
In Kāngzōng's seventh year,
the harvest failed,
and many people wandered as refugees;
the strong turned to banditry.
Huāndū and others wanted to severely enforce the law,
decreeing that all bandits should be executed.
Tàizǔ said:
"To kill people for property
is wrong.
Property
is what people produce."
So he reduced the law for compensating banditry to three times the amount.
Many people in the populace were in arrears,
selling their wives and children but still unable to repay.
Kāngzōng discussed this with his officials.
Tàizǔ, in the outer court, tied a piece of silk to the end of a staff,
waved it to his followers,
and declared:
"Now the poor cannot sustain themselves,
selling their wives and children to repay debts.
The love for one's flesh and blood
is common to all human hearts.
From now on, do not collect for three years;
after three years, gradually work towards it."
All listened to his command,
and those who heard were moved to tears.
From then on, people near and far became devoted to him.
In the *guǐsì* year, in the tenth month,
Kāngzōng dreamed of chasing a wolf,
repeatedly shooting but failing to hit it.
Tàizǔ stepped forward and shot it.
The next morning,
he asked his advisors about his dream.
They all said:
"It is auspicious.
It is a sign that the elder brother cannot obtain something, but the younger brother will."
In that month,
Kāngzōng passed away,
and Tàizǔ succeeded him as Dū Bó Jíliè.
The Liáo envoy, Āxībǎo, came
and said:
"Why was the mourning not reported?"
Tàizǔ said:
"If there is mourning, you cannot offer condolences,
and yet you make it a crime?"
Another day,
Āxībǎo came again,
riding directly to Kāngzōng's burial place,
inspecting the horses given as funerary gifts,
intending to take them.
Tàizǔ was enraged and was about to kill him,
but Zōngxióng remonstrated and stopped him.
Afterward, the Liáo decree was long in coming.
The Liáo ruler was fond of hunting,
addicted to alcohol, negligent in government affairs,
and memorials from all directions were often not attended to.
After Gēshíliè Āshū fled to Liáo,
Mùzōng took his city and his people.
Unable to return,
he secretly conspired with his cousin Yínzhúkě, CíLǐhǎn, and Húndū Púsù, a resident of Nánjiāng, intending to flee together to Gāolì.
When the plot was discovered,
Tàizǔ sent Jiágǔ Sāhē to capture them.
However, Yínzhúkě and CíLǐhǎn were captured first by the Liáo garrison,
and Húndū Púsù had already fled.
Sāhē took their wives and children and returned.
In the second year, *jiǎwǔ*,
in the sixth month,
Tàizǔ arrived in Jiāngxī.
Envoys from the Liáo court came to deliver the order to assume the *jiédù* (military governor) position.
Initially,
the Liáo court would annually dispatch envoys to purchase famous falcons,
"Hǎidōngqīng,"
by the sea.
Their route passed through the territory,
and the envoys were greedy and abusive,
demanding without limit.
Both public and private sectors suffered from this.
Kāngzōng had previously used the non-return of Āshū as a reason
to somewhat reject their envoys.
When Tàizǔ succeeded to the *jiédù* position,
he also sent Pújiānú to demand Āshū.
Thus, these two matters were often brought up,
eventually leading to the destruction of the Liáo before stopping.
By this time,
he again sent imperial kinsmen Xíɡǔnǎi and Wányán Yínzhúkě to demand Āshū.
When Xíɡǔnǎi and others returned,
they fully reported on the arrogance, extravagance, and decline of the Liáo emperor.
Thereupon, he summoned civil and military officials and elders,
informed them of the plan to attack Liáo,
and instructed them to prepare defenses for strategic points,
build castles,
and repair weapons,
awaiting further orders.
When the Liáo Tǒngjūn Sī (Overall Military Command) heard of this,
they sent *jiédùshǐ* Gēlái to inquire about the situation,
saying:
"Do you harbor other intentions?
Repairing armaments
and strengthening defenses,
against whom are these preparations for?"
Tàizǔ replied:
"Establishing defenses for self-protection,
what else is there to ask?"
The Liáo court again sent Āxībǎo to question him.
Tàizǔ said to him:
"We are a small state,
serving a great state and not daring to neglect propriety.
But the great state does not extend its virtue and benevolence,
instead sheltering fugitives.
To treat a smaller state in this manner,
how can one not feel disappointment?
If Āshū is returned to us,
we request to continue with tributary rituals.
Should we be left with no choice,
how can we stand idly by and be controlled?"
When Āxībǎo returned,
the Liáo people began to prepare,
ordering *tǒngjūn* Xiāo Tàbùyě to mobilize various armies to Níngjiāng Zhōu.
When Tàizǔ heard of this,
he sent Púɡuālálà to again demand Āshū,
actually to observe their situation.
Púɡuālálà returned and reported:
"The Liáo troops are many,
their number unknown."
Tàizǔ said:
"They have just begun to mobilize troops;
how could they assemble so quickly?"
He again sent Húshābǎo,
who returned and reported:
"There are only troops from the Sìyuàn Tǒngjūn Sī, the Níngjiāng Zhōu army, and eight hundred Bóhǎi men."
Tàizǔ said:
"It is indeed as I said."
He told his generals and aides:
"The Liáo people know I am about to raise an army,
and they are assembling troops from various routes to prepare against me.
I must strike first to control them,
and not be controlled by others."
Everyone said:
"Good."
Then he went to see Xuānjìng Huánghòu
and informed her of the plan to attack Liáo.
The Empress said:
"You inherit from your father and brothers to establish the state and family.
Act when you see fit.
I am old,
do not cause me sorrow.
You surely will not come to that."
Tàizǔ was moved to tears.
He presented a cup for a toast to her longevity.
Immediately, he led the Empress and his generals out the gate,
raised a cup facing east,
and prayed to Huang Tiān Hòu Tǔ (Heaven and Earth)
about the Liáo people's wild abandon,
their refusal to return Āshū,
and his intention to use military force.
After pouring the libation,
the Empress ordered Tàizǔ to sit properly,
and he drank with his officials and subordinates,
issuing commands to various tribes.
He sent Pólúhuǒ to levy troops from Yílǎn Lù Díɡǔnǎi.
Wòlǔɡǔ and Ālú were to pacify the Nǚzhēn of Wòhū and Jísài two routes, who were registered with Liáo.
Shíbùdié went to Wándǔ Lù to capture the Liáo falconry official Dálúɡǔ Bù Fùshǐ Cíliè and the Bóhǎi noble Dàjiānú from Níngjiāng Zhōu.
Then Dálúɡǔ Bù Shílǐɡuǎn came to report, saying:
"I heard you are raising an army to attack Liáo.
Which side should my tribe follow?"
Tàizǔ said:
"Although my army is small,
it is the old country,
and neighboring yours, so you should naturally follow me.
If you fear the Liáo people,
then go to them yourselves."
In the ninth month,
Tàizǔ advanced his army to Níngjiāng Zhōu,
encamping at Liáohuì Chéng.
Pólúhuǒ's levy of troops was late,
so he was punished with a beating,
and a supervisor was again dispatched.
Troops from all routes assembled at Láiliú Shuǐ,
totaling two thousand five hundred men.
He proclaimed the crimes of Liáo,
declaring to Heaven and Earth:
"For generations, we have served the Liáo state,
diligently performing our duties and presenting tribute.
We pacified the rebellions of Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn,
and defeated the forces of Xiāo Hǎilǐ.
Our merits were not recognized,
instead, insults and aggression were inflicted upon us.
The criminal Āshū
was repeatedly requested but not returned.
Now we are going to punish Liáo for its crimes.
May Heaven and Earth grant us protection."
Then he ordered his generals to pass around a cudgel and swear an oath, saying:
"You all, with one heart and all your strength,
those who achieve merit,
slaves and retainers will become free commoners,
commoners will be granted official positions,
those who already have positions will be promoted,
with rewards varying according to the importance of their merit.
Should anyone violate this oath,
they will die by the cudgel,
and their families will not be pardoned."
The army encamped in the land of Tánɡkuò Dàiwòjiǎ.
The various armies performed divination by shooting arrows,
and stood armored.
A light, like a fierce fire,
rose from people's feet and on top of spears and halberds.
People considered this an auspicious sign for war.
The next day,
they encamped at Zházhǐ Shuǐ,
and the light appeared as before.
As they approached the Liáo border,
he first sent Zōngɡàn to oversee the soldiers in leveling the trenches.
After crossing,
they encountered Bóhǎi troops attacking our left wing, Qīmóukè.
Our forces, being few, fell back,
and the enemy troops advanced directly towards the central army.
Xiéyě rode out to fight,
with Zhédiè leading the charge.
Tàizǔ said:
"This battle must not be taken lightly."
He sent Zōngɡàn to stop them.
Zōngɡàn galloped out in front of Xiéyě,
pulled back Zhédiè's horse,
and Xiéyě then returned with them.
The enemy pursued them.
Yélǜ Xièshí fell from his horse,
and the Liáo people advanced to rescue him.
Tàizǔ shot the rescuer dead,
and also shot Xièshí, hitting him.
A rider charged forward,
and Tàizǔ shot him again,
the arrow piercing through his chest.
Xièshí pulled out the arrow and fled.
Tàizǔ pursued and shot him,
hitting him in the back,
the arrow sinking halfway in.
He stumbled and died.
They captured his horse.
Zōngɡàn and several horsemen plunged into the Liáo army.
Tàizǔ rescued him,
fighting without his helmet.
Someone shot him from the side,
an arrow brushing against his forehead.
Tàizǔ looked and saw the shooter,
killing him with a single arrow.
He told his officers and soldiers:
"Do not stop until the enemy is annihilated."
The troops followed him,
their courage redoubled.
The enemy fled in a great rout,
seventeen or eighteen out of ten dying from trampling.
Sāɡǎi was on another route,
and could not join the battle.
Someone was sent to inform him of the victory,
and Xièshí's horse was bestowed upon him.
Sāɡǎi sent his sons Zōnghàn and Wányán Xīyǐn to congratulate him,
and to also acclaim him as Emperor,
thus urging him to ascend the throne.
Tàizǔ said:
"To claim a great title after just one victory,
how shallow would that appear to others."
The army advanced to Níngjiāngzhōu,
and the various armies filled the moats to attack the city.
The people of Níngjiāng came out from the east gate,
and Wēndíhén Ātúhǎn intercepted and attacked them,
annihilating them all.
On the first day of the tenth month,
they captured the city,
and obtained the Defender-in-chief, Dàyàoshīnú.
He was secretly released
to persuade the Liáo people to surrender.
The Tiělí部 came to offer submission.
Next, at Láiliúchéng,
the captives were bestowed upon the generals and soldiers.
Bóhǎi Liángfú and Wòdálá were summoned and made to feign defection,
and they persuaded their fellow villagers, saying:
"The Nǚzhēn and Bóhǎi were originally of one family.
I raise an army to punish the guilty,
not to indiscriminately harm the innocent."
Wányán Lóushì was sent to persuade the Nǚzhēn registered under the Liáo to surrender.
When the army returned,
they visited Xuānjìng Huánghòu,
and distributed the spoils to the imperial clan elders.
The property of Shílǐ Guǎn was given to the generals and soldiers.
Initially, all circuits were ordered to organize three hundred households into a móukè,
and ten móukè into a mèng'ān.
Chóuwò and others were rewarded for pacifying the Chánmóushuǐ Nǚzhēn.
The chieftain Húsūlǔ of Bīegǔ surrendered with his city.
In the eleventh month,
Liáo Dūtǒng Xiāo Jiūlǐ and Fùdūtǒng Tàbùyě led an army of one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry to rendezvous north of the Yāzihé.
Tàizǔ personally led an attack against them.
Before reaching the Yāzihé,
it was already night.
Tàizǔ was just about to sleep
when someone seemed to support his head three times.
He awoke and rose,
saying:
"Divine spirits are warning me."
He immediately ordered drums beaten and signal fires lit, and set off.
At dawn, they reached the river.
The Liáo soldiers were just destroying the ice bridge.
Ten strong warriors were selected to attack and drive them away.
The main army followed,
and successfully landed on the bank.
Of the three thousand seven hundred armored soldiers,
only one-third had arrived.
Soon after, they encountered the enemy at Chūhédiàn.
A great wind arose,
dust and sand obscured the sky.
They attacked, utilizing the wind's momentum,
and the Liáo army collapsed.
They pursued them to Wòlúnluò,
killing and capturing an countless number of heads, captives, chariots, horses, armor, weapons, and treasures.
These were liberally bestowed upon the officials, subordinates, generals, and soldiers.
Feasting and celebration lasted for a full day.
The Liáo people had once said that if the Nǚzhēn army reached ten thousand, they would be invincible.
It was at this time that they finally numbered ten thousand.
Wòlǔgǔ defeated the Liáo army,
and beheaded their Jiédùshǐ, Tàbùyě.
Púhuī and others attacked Bīnzhōu,
and captured it.
Wùrěchúgǔshì came to surrender.
Liáo general Chìgǒuer fought at Bīnzhōu,
and Púhuī and Húnhù defeated him.
King Huílíbǎo of Tiělí surrendered with his tribe.
Wúdǔbǔ and Púchá again defeated Chìgǒuer and Xiāo Yǐxuē's army east of Xiángzhōu.
The two circuits of Wòhū and Jísāi surrendered.
Wòlǔgǔ defeated the Liáo army west of Xiánzhōu,
and beheaded the Tǒngjūn Shílóu on the battlefield.
Wányán Lóushì captured Xiánzhōu.
In this month,
Wúqǐmǎi, Sāgǎi, Cíbùshī, along with their officials, subordinates, and generals, urged him to ascend the throne,
wishing to respectfully offer the exalted title on the first day of the New Year.
Tàizǔ refused.
Ālíhégmán, Pújiānú, Zōnghán, and others stepped forward and said:
"Now that great deeds have been accomplished,
if you do not assume a title,
there will be no way to secure the hearts of all under heaven."
Tàizǔ said:
"I will consider it."
On the Rénshēn day, the first day of the first month of the first year of Shōuguó,
the assembled officials presented the exalted title.
On this day,
he ascended the imperial throne.
The Emperor said:
"The Liáo took 'iron' as their name,
for its hardness.
Although iron is hard,
it eventually changes and decays.
Only gold does not change and does not decay.
The color of gold is white,
and the Wányán tribe favors white."
Thus, the state was named Dàjīn (Great Gold),
and the era name was changed to Shōuguó.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
the Emperor personally led an attack on Huánglóngfǔ,
advancing to Yìzhōu.
The people of the prefecture fled to garrison Huánglóng,
and the remaining populace was brought back.
Liáo dispatched Dūtǒng Yēlǜ Élíwǎn, Zuǒfùtǒng Xiāo Yǐxuē, Yòufùtǒng Yēlǜ Zhāngnú, and Dūjiān Xiāo Xièfóliú,
with two hundred thousand cavalry and seventy thousand infantry to guard the border.
Lóushì and Yínzhúkě were left to guard Huánglóng.
The Emperor led the troops towards Dálǔgǔchéng,
then camped west of Níngjiāngzhōu.
A Liáo envoy, Sēngjiānú, came to discuss peace.
The state letter addressed the Emperor by name
and moreover demanded that he become a tributary state.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
the army advanced.
A perfectly round ball of fire
fell from the sky.
The Emperor said:
"This is an auspicious omen;
it is surely heaven's aid."
He poured white water and bowed,
and all the generals and soldiers rejoiced.
They pressed closer to Dálǔgǔchéng.
The Emperor ascended a height and gazed upon the Liáo army, which resembled continuous clouds and dense bushes.
He turned to his attendants and said:
"The Liáo soldiers are divided in heart and timid in spirit;
though numerous, they are not to be feared."
He then proceeded to a high mound to form an array.
Zōngxióng, with the right wing, first charged the Liáo left army,
and the left army retreated.
The left wing emerged from behind their array,
and the Liáo right army fought with all their might.
Lóushì and Yínzhúkě charged into their main formation.
They broke through the array nine times,
each time fighting their way out.
Zōnghán requested to assist them with the central army.
The Emperor sent Zōnggàn to create a diversion.
Zōngxióng had already gained an advantage,
attacking the Liáo right army,
and the Liáo army was then defeated.
Taking advantage of the victory, they pursued them
to their camp.
As night had fallen,
they surrounded it.
At dawn,
the Liáo army broke through the encirclement and fled.
They were pursued north to Ālóugāng.
All the Liáo infantry were annihilated,
and several thousand farming tools were obtained and distributed to the various armies.
In this campaign,
the Liáo people had intended to set up military farms,
and both fight and defend,
hence their farming tools were also captured.
In the second month,
the army returned.
On the Xīnwèi day, the first day of the third month,
they hunted at Liáohuìchéng.
In the fourth month,
Liáo's Yēlǜ Zhāngnú arrived with a state letter.
The Emperor, deeming the letter's tone disrespectful,
detained five of their people,
sending only Zhāngnú back with a reply,
the letter also being similarly worded.
On the Gēngwǔ day, the first day of the fifth month,
they avoided the summer heat in the nearby suburbs.
On the Jiǎxū day,
they worshipped heaven and shot willows.
According to custom,
on the fifth day of the fifth month, the fifteenth day of the seventh month, and the ninth day of the ninth month, they worshipped heaven and shot willows.
This was done annually.
On the Jǐhài day, the first day of the sixth month,
Liáo's Yēlǜ Zhāngnú again arrived with a state letter,
still addressing the Emperor by name.
The Emperor also addressed the Liáo ruler by name in his reply,
and furthermore admonished him to surrender.
On the Wùchén day of the seventh month,
his younger brother Wúqǐmǎi was appointed Ānbānbójíliè,
State Chancellor Sāgǎi was appointed Guólúnbójíliè,
Cíbùshī was appointed Āmǎibójíliè,
and his younger brother Xiéyě was appointed Guólúnbójíliè.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Liáo envoy Cílà arrived with a letter,
and was detained.
The Jiǔbǎixī encampment came to surrender.
On the Wùxū day of the eighth month,
the Emperor personally led an expedition to Huánglóngfǔ.
Upon reaching the Húntóngjiāng,
there were no boats.
The Emperor ordered one person to go ahead,
and riding a reddish-white horse, he directly waded across,
saying:
"Follow where my whip points."
The armies followed him,
the water reaching the horses' bellies.
Later, boatmen were sent to measure the crossing point,
but its depth could not be found.
In the second year of Tiānjuàn of Xīzōng,
Huánglóngfǔ was made Jìzhōu,
and the army was called Lìshè,
due to Tàizǔ having crossed it.
In the ninth month,
Huánglóngfǔ was conquered.
Cílà was sent back,
and then the army returned.
Upon reaching the river,
they crossed directly as before.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
they arrived back from Huánglóngfǔ.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
a yellow dragon appeared in the sky.
On the day Guǐsì,
Sāgǎi, the Guólùn Bójíliè, was made Guólùn Hūlǔ Bójíliè,
and Ālíhèmǎn was made Guólùn Yǐshì Bójíliè.
In the eleventh month,
the Liáo ruler, hearing of the capture of Huánglóngfǔ,
was greatly alarmed.
He personally led seventy myriad troops to the gate.
The Fùmǎ, Xiāo Tèmò, and the Línyá, Xiāo Chálà, led fifty thousand cavalry and forty myriad infantry to Wòlínluò.
The emperor personally led the defense.
On the day Jǐhài of the twelfth month,
the army halted at Yáolà,
and all the generals met to deliberate.
They all said:
"The Liáo army numbers seventy myriad,
and its vanguard is not easily resisted.
Our army has come from afar,
both men and horses are exhausted,
so it is advisable to halt here,
dig deep trenches and build high ramparts to await them."
The emperor agreed.
Dígǔnǎi and Yínzhúkě were sent to guard Dálǔgǔ.
On the day Dīngwèi,
the emperor personally went to scout the Liáo army with cavalry,
and captured those overseeing provisions.
He learned that the Liáo ruler had returned west two days prior
due to Zhāngnú's rebellion.
On this day,
the emperor returned to Shújiéluò,
where a light appeared on the tip of his spear.
On the day Wùshēn,
the generals said:
"Now that the Liáo ruler has returned,
we can pursue and attack him while he is off guard."
The emperor said:
"If we do not meet the enemy when they come to fight,
but pursue them when they depart,
do you wish to take this as courage?"
All were struck with awe and shame,
and expressed their willingness to exert themselves.
The emperor again said:
"If you truly wish to pursue the enemy,
make preparations and go,
do not trouble yourselves with provisions.
If we defeat the enemy,
what will we not obtain?"
All leaped with enthusiasm,
and pursued the Liáo ruler to Hùbùdágāng.
In this campaign,
the troops numbered only two myriad.
The emperor said:
"They are numerous, we are few;
the troops must not be divided.
Their central army appears strongest,
and the Liáo ruler must be there.
If we defeat their central army,
we can achieve our goal."
He ordered the right wing to engage first.
After several skirmishes,
the left wing joined and attacked.
The Liáo army suffered a great rout.
Our forces charged them,
breaking through their center.
The Liáo army was utterly defeated,
with dead bodies stretching for over a hundred *lǐ*.
We captured carriages, canopies, tents, weapons, and military supplies,
as well as countless other treasures, horses, and cattle.
In this battle,
Xiéyě brandished his spear and killed several tens of people.
Ālíběn was surrounded,
Wēndíhǎndíhūdié led four *móukè* of soldiers to rescue him.
Wányán Méngguā suffered several wounds on his body,
but fought relentlessly,
and all were deemed to have rendered the greatest service.
Xiāo Tèmò and others burned their camps and fled.
Then the army returned.
Jiágǔ Sāhē captured Kāizhōu.
Pólúhuǒ took Tèlínchéng,
and Cílihǎn surrendered.
In the first month, on the day Wùzǐ, of the second year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Since the defeat of the Liáo army,
many from all directions have come to surrender,
and they should be treated with leniency and care.
From now on, officials and common people of the Qìdān, Xī, Hàn, Bóhǎi, the Nǚzhēn registered under Liáo, Shìwéi, Dálǔgǔ, Wùrě, Tiělí tribes,
who have surrendered or been captured by the army,
or who have escaped and returned,
shall not be considered guilty.
Their chieftains shall retain their offices,
and be allowed to reside wherever suitable."
In the intercalary month,
Gāo Yǒngchāng occupied Dōngjīng
and sent Tàbùyě to request aid.
Gāolí sent envoys to congratulate on the victory,
and also to request Bǎozhōu.
An imperial edict permitted them to take it themselves.
In the second month, on the day Jǐsì,
an imperial edict stated:
"Because of the recent bad harvests,
the common people struggled for food,
and many attached themselves to powerful families,
becoming slaves.
Also, those who committed crimes,
but could not afford compensation,
and thus became slaves by forfeiting their persons;
or those who privately agreed to a deadline,
to be redeemed by another person,
and became slaves if the deadline passed—
all shall be allowed to redeem one person by two to become commoners.
If the original agreement was for one person to redeem,
then the original agreement shall be followed."
In the fourth month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
Wòlǔ was put in charge of all internal and external armies.
He, along with Púchá and Dígǔnǎi, met Wòlǔgǔ, the Dūtǒng of Xiánzhōulù, to suppress Gāo Yǒngchāng.
Húshābǔ and others were killed.
In the fifth month,
Wòlǔ and others defeated Yǒngchāng.
Tàbùyě captured Yǒngchāng and presented him,
and he was executed in the army.
The prefectures and counties of Dōngjīng and the Nánlù Nǚzhēn associated with Liáo all surrendered.
An imperial edict abolished Liáo laws,
reduced taxes,
and established *méng'ān* and *móukè* as per the system of this dynasty.
Wòlǔ was made Nánlù Dūtǒng and Diébójíliè.
Ādúhǎn defeated sixty thousand Liáo troops at Zhàosànchéng.
In the ninth month, on the day Jǐhài,
the emperor hunted in the nearby suburbs.
On the day Yǐsì,
Wòlǔ, the Nánlù Dūtǒng, came to meet at Pólúmǎishuǐ.
Golden tallies were first created.
On the first day of the twelfth month, Gēngshēn,
Ānbān Bójíliè Wúqǐmǎi and all the officials presented the honorific title "Dàshèng Huángdì,"
and changed the next year to Tiānfǔ Yuánnián.
In the first month of Tiānfǔ Yuánnián,
Kāizhōu rebelled.
Jiágǔ Sāhē and others suppressed it.
Guólùn Bójíliè Xiéyě took Táizhōu with one myriad soldiers.
In the fourth month,
Yēlǜ Niēlí, the Liáo Qínjìn Guówáng, came to attack.
Dígǔnǎi, Lóushì, and Pólúhuǒ led two myriad soldiers,
and joined Wòlǔgǔ, the Dūtǒng of Xiánzhōulù, to attack him.
In the fifth month, on the day Dīngsì,
an imperial edict declared that from the capture of Níngjiāngzhōu onwards, those of the same surname who married
would be flogged and separated.
In the seventh month, on the day Wùshēn,
Wányán Wòlún was appointed to govern Dōngjīng affairs.
In the eighth month, on the day Guǐhài,
Gāolí sent envoys to request Bǎozhōu.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Wòlǔgǔ and others defeated Yēlǜ Niēlí's army at Jílízīshān,
and captured Xiǎnzhōu.
Qián, Yì, Háo, Huī, Chéng, Chuān, Huì and other prefectures all surrendered.
In this month,
Mǎ Zhèng, the Dēngzhōufángyùshǐ of Sòng, came with a national letter,
which roughly stated:
"In the region of the rising sun,
a sage has indeed been born.
I have heard that in your campaign against Liáo,
you have repeatedly defeated strong enemies.
If, after conquering Liáo,
the Hàn territories that fell into Qìdān hands during the Five Dynasties period
could be granted to our humble state."
In the first month, on the day Gēngyín, of the second year,
Zhāng Chóng, the Liáo Shuāngzhōujiédùshǐ, surrendered.
Sǎndù was sent to Sòng in reply,
and the letter said:
"Regarding the requested territory,
we shall now jointly attack Sòng,
and whoever obtains it will possess it."
In the second month, on the first day, Guǐchǒu,
the Liáo envoy Yēlǜ Núgē and others came to negotiate peace.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Bójǐn Dígǔnǎi and Lóushì came to visit.
The emperor, seeing that the Liáo ruler was recently in Zhōngjīng
and yet they dared to come casually,
flogged them all.
Hégǎolǐbǎo, Shuānggǔ and others reported that
Xiánzhōu Dūtǒng Wòlǔgǔ knew the Liáo ruler was in Zhōngjīng but did not advance to attack,
that fodder and grain were abundant but not truthfully reported,
and that he took many captives, wealth, and livestock obtained during the attack on Xiǎnzhōu for himself.
On the *Guǐwèi* day of the third month, the first day of the lunar month,
Shégē was ordered to act as *Dūzhǒng* and to try and judge him.
Wòlǔgǔ was found guilty of being part of a surrendered *móukè*.
On the *Rénchén* day,
the Liáo envoy Yēlǜ Núgē arrived with a state letter.
On the *Gēngzǐ* day,
based on Lóushì’s statement that Huánglóng Fǔ was remote and distant,
and should be heavily garrisoned,
an order was given to combine all roads' *móukè*,
and Lóushì was made *Wànhù* to guard it.
On the *Xīnsì* day of the fourth month,
a Liáo envoy arrived with a state letter.
On the *Bǐngshēn* day of the fifth month,
Hútūgǔn was ordered to go to Liáo.
On the *Jiǎyín* day of the sixth month,
an edict was issued to officials to forbid people from abusing hired commoners,
or charging double for their ransom.
On the *Jiǎxū* day,
over 800 households from the Liáo prefectures of Tōng, Qí, Shuāng, and Liáo came to surrender.
They were ordered to be distributed among various tribes,
and settled in fertile lands.
On the *Guǐwèi* day of the seventh month,
an edict stated:
"The impoverished people of the six *móukè* from Pǐlǐ Shuǐlù, Wányán Shùlǐgǔ, Bóhǎi Dàjiānú, and others,
were previously given official grain
and settled in fishing and hunting grounds.
Now that a long time has passed,
their numbers are unknown.
Their figures should be reported."
Hútūgǔn returned from Liáo.
Yēlǜ Núgē again arrived with a state letter.
On the *Bǐngshēn* day,
Hútūgǔn went to Liáo.
Two hundred Liáo households came to surrender
and were settled in Tàizhōu.
An edict was issued to send Ālǐgǔ, Lǐjiānú, and Tèlǐdǐ to persuade those who had not yet surrendered.
An edict was also sent to the *bójǐn* Cíliè of the Dálǔgǔ tribe:
"All newly surrendered people
should be well cared for and comforted.
Let all who come settle down comfortably as they please,
and be given official grain.
Do not disturb them lightly."
In the eighth month,
Hútūgǔn returned from Liáo.
Yēlǜ Núgē and Tūdié again arrived with state letters.
On the *Wùzǐ* day of the ninth month,
an edict stated:
"For state letters and edicts,
those skilled in writing should be chosen to compose them.
Let all regions seek out learned and talented scholars
and urge them to come to the capital."
On the *Gēngxū* day, the first day of the lunar month of the intercalary month,
the surrendered generals Huòshí and Hán Qìnghé were made *qiānhù*.
Xiāo Bǎo and Yǐ Xīn from the Nine Hundred Xī tribe,
Élíyě from the northern tribe,
the Hàn Chinese Wáng Liù'ér and Wáng Bólóng,
Qìdān Tèmò, Gāo Cóngyòu, and others,
each led their followers to surrender.
Liáo Yēlǜ Núgē arrived with a state letter.
On the *Guǐwèi* day of the tenth month,
Zhāng Yìnggǔ and Liú Zhòngliáng, who had surrendered from Lónghuà Zhōu, were made *qiānhù*.
On the *Yǐwèi* day,
the Xiánzhōu *Dūtǒng Sī* reported
that the Hàn Chinese Lǐ Xiàogōng and Bóhǎi Èr Gē had led their followers to surrender.
They were ordered to be made *qiānhù* with their respective divisions.
On the *Jiǎchén* day of the twelfth month,
the *Bójǐn* Shùbèi was sent to inform Gāolì about the pacified Liáo territory.
Yēlǜ Núgē arrived with a state letter.
Liáo Yìzhōu *Jiédù Shǐ* Liú Hóng surrendered with three thousand households and captured Liáo scouts,
and was made *qiānhù*.
The two thousand rebels of Chuānzhōu, who had surrendered and then rebelled again,
were defeated by Gēshíliè Zhàolǐ.
In the first month of the third year, on the *Jiǎyín* day,
five people from Dōngjīng who were hostages, including Yǒngjí, formed a group and rebelled.
The matter was discovered,
their ringleaders were executed,
and the rest were flogged one hundred times,
and half of their families' assets in the army were confiscated.
An edict was issued to Wòlún, who was in charge of Dōngjīng affairs,
stating that any future offenders would be treated likewise.
On the *Bǐngchén* day,
an edict was issued to Biēgǔ Bójǐn Chóuwò:
"The Húlúgǔ and Diébāhé two tribes have sent their intentions.
You may have had previous conflicts,
but from now on, do not disturb each other."
In the third month,
Yēlǜ Núgē arrived with a state letter.
On the *Bǐngzǐ* day, the first day of the lunar month of the fourth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *Rénxū* day of the fifth month,
an edict was issued to the Xiánzhōu Lù *Dūtǒng Sī*:
"Before the war began,
the Nǚzhí households from Hésūguǎn and Huípàlǐ, whether registered or unregistered with Liáo,
who committed crimes and were exiled to the border or fled into Liáo,
are all originally our people.
Being far away in a foreign land,
I greatly pity them.
Now that peace has been negotiated,
they should be sought out and brought back.
You are to clearly instruct the *qiānhù* and *móukè* of all routes
to thoroughly inquire about their official titles, names, and places of origin,
and record them for submission."
On the *Xīnmǎo* day of the sixth month,
Liáo sent Grand Tutor Xíníliè and others to present a document and seal.
The emperor pointed out several discrepancies in the document and returned it.
Sǎndǔ returned from Sòng.
The Sòng envoys Mǎ Zhèng and his son Mǎ Hóng came to offer tribute.
Sǎndǔ accepted the title of Sòng *Tuánliàn Shǐ*,
which angered the emperor.
He was flogged and the title was revoked.
The Sòng envoys returned,
and *Bójǐn* Cíliè, Hélǔ, and others were again sent to Sòng.
On the *Xīnhài* day of the seventh month,
Liáo people Yáng Xúnqīng and Luó Zǐwéi each led their followers to surrender,
and were ordered to be made *móukè* with their respective divisions.
On the *Jǐchǒu* day of the eighth month,
Nǚzhí script was promulgated.
In the ninth month,
because the Liáo envoy for the ceremonial investiture was late,
an edict was issued for armies of all routes to cross the river and encamp.
In the eleventh month,
Xíníliè and others again arrived with a state letter.
Gāolì increased the height of the Great Wall in Gélǎndiàn by three *chǐ*.
Húlàgǔ and Xí Xiǎn were ordered to strengthen their garrisons.
In the second month of the fourth year,
Cíliè and Hélǔ returned from Sòng.
〔一０〕Sòng envoys Zhào Liángsì and Wáng Huī came to discuss the territories of Yānjīng and Xījīng.
〔一一〕
On the *Jiǎchén* day of the third month,
the emperor said to his ministers:
"The Liáo people have been repeatedly defeated,
and their envoys seek peace,
but only use empty words
as a tactic to delay our army.
We should discuss launching an attack.
Let the Xiánzhōu Lù *Tǒngjūn Sī* prepare the army and repair weapons,
and report the numbers."
On the *Xīnyǒu* day,
an edict was issued to the Xiánzhōu Lù *Dūtǒng Sī*:
"As the peace negotiations with the Liáo state have come to nothing,
I will advance the army on the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month."
Shégē was ordered to leave one thousand soldiers to guard,
and Shémǔ was to bring the remaining troops to rendezvous at Húnhé.
Liáo Xíníliè arrived with a state letter.
On the *Yǐwèi* day of the fourth month,
the emperor personally led the campaign against Liáo.
The Liáo envoy Xíníliè and the Sòng envoy Zhào Liángsì and others accompanied him.
On the *jiǎchén* day of the fifth month,
the army encamped west of the Húnhé River.
Shǐ Zōngxióng was dispatched to advance rapidly to Shàngjīng.
A surrendered man, Mǎ Yǐ, was sent to hold an imperial edict to persuade the people in the city.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
upon arriving at Shàngjīng,
an imperial edict was issued to officials and commoners, stating:
"The Lord of Liáo has lost the Way,
and both high and low are resentful.
Since We raised Our army,
We have attacked and captured cities and towns that, relying on their fortifications, refused to submit;
We have comforted and taken care of those who surrendered.
You must have heard of this.
Now, regarding the peace negotiations with your country,
We have been repeatedly deceived.
We do not wish for the people of the world to suffer in misery for long,
and thus We have decided to advance and suppress.
Previously, We sent Zōngxióng and others to successively call upon and persuade you,
but you still did not listen.
If We attack now,
the city will be broken.
Moreover, in accordance with the principle of righteous punitive expeditions,
We do not wish to harm the people.
Therefore, We publicly issue this clear edict
to inform you of the good fortune and disaster.
You should consider it carefully."
The people of Shàngjīng relied on their defenses and stored provisions, planning for a firm defense.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
an immediate order was given to advance and attack.
The Emperor said to Xíníliè, Zhào Liángsì, and others:
"You can observe Our use of troops
to determine your course of action."
The Emperor personally oversaw the city,
urging the generals, officers, and various armies to advance with drums and shouts.
From dawn until *sì* (9-11 a.m.),
Shé Mǔ, with his subordinate troops, was the first to ascend.
They captured the outer city,
and the Rear-guard Tàbùyě surrendered the city.
Zhào Liángsì and others offered wine cups for a toast,
all shouting "Long live!"
On that day,
an amnesty was granted to the officials and commoners of Shàngjīng.
An imperial edict was sent to the Liáo Deputy Commander Yú Dǔ.
On the *rénxū* day,
the army encamped at Wòhēhé River.
Zōnggàn led the assembled officials in remonstrating, saying:
"The distance is great, and the weather is hot;
the army and horses are exhausted.
If we penetrate deep into enemy territory,
provisions will run out,
and we fear there will be future difficulties."
The Emperor agreed to this,
and thus the army returned to the capital,
ordering a detachment to attack Qìngzhōu.
Yú Dǔ ambushed Shé Mǔ at the Liáohé River.
Wányán Bèidá and Wūtǎ and others fought and repelled him.
Wányán Tèhǔ died there.
On the *guǐmǎo* day of the seventh month,
the Emperor returned from campaigning against Liáo.
In the ninth month,
the Zúiwēi water department's Shílǐgǔdá and others killed Bóyǐn Chóuwò and Púhūdá, and rebelled.
On the *wùchén* day, the first day of the tenth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *wùyín* day,
Wòlǔ was ordered to divide the troops of Húlàgǔ and Wūchūn to suppress Shílǐgǔdá.
In the eleventh month,
