Tāshībù, with his father Yǎozhù, and Sìxǐ, with his wife, forced their way out of the gate,
reaching Guīdé on the *gēngwǔ* day.
The emperor was enraged by the two men
and had them both executed in the marketplace.
On the *yǐhài* day,
Yílà Niángǔ, Right Commissioner of the Privy Council and Administrator of the Bureau of Close Attendants, was sent to Xúzhōu
to survey the terrain
and inspect the actual conditions of the granaries.
Bái Huá went to Dèngzhōu to summon troops.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day of the second month,
Zhāng Huán of Yúshān killed Grand Marshal Wányán Hūtǔ.
Provincial Administrator Hūxiéhǔ personally led troops to suppress him.
He met the pacification commissioner Yán Lù and executed Zhāng Huán,
then returned.
Grain within the city was requisitioned.
Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, who was serving as the Administrator of Guīdé Prefecture, was appointed Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs and acting Chancellor.
Four hundred and fifty soldiers of the Loyal and Filial Army, led by Grand Marshal Guānnú, were kept.
More than two hundred and eighty soldiers led by Commandant Mǎ Yòng were kept.
The remaining troops were dispatched to Sù, Xú, and Chén prefectures to obtain provisions.
On the *yǐchǒu* day of the third month,
Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān requested that all the garrison troops be disbanded and sent out of the city to find food.
Guānnú secretly plotted with Guóyòng'ān
to invite the Emperor to Hǎizhōu,
but this was not followed.
Cài Marshal Wūgǔlún Hào arrived in Guīdé with over four hundred *hú* of grain.
He submitted a memorial requesting the Emperor's presence.
The Emperor dispatched Scholar Wūgǔlún Púxiān to convey his intention to proceed to Cài to the people of that prefecture.
On the *wùchén* day,
Guānnú incited a rebellion with the Loyal and Filial Army,
attacking and killing Mǎ Yòng.
Then, he killed Lǐ Xī, Assistant Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs; Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, Chancellor; and Túdān Chánglè, Grand Inspector.
More than three hundred officials, from the Right Minister downwards, were also killed.
The Emperor pardoned Guānnú,
and publicized Nǚlǔhuān's crimes.
Guānnú was made Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs and acting Chancellor.
Zhāng Tiāngāng, a Langzhong of the Right and Left Bureaus, was made Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and acting Chancellor.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Guānnú was formally appointed Chancellor,
and concurrently Deputy Left Grand Marshal.
Guānnú ordered the Emperor to reside in the Zhàobì Hall,
and none of the close ministers dared to make a report or reply.
The Emperor wept daily and said:
"Since ancient times, there has been no country that did not perish, and no ruler who did not die.
But I regret that I did not know how to employ people,
which led to me being imprisoned by this slave."
Thereupon, he conspired with Sòng Guī, Director of the Inner Bureau, and others to execute Guānnú.
In the summer, on the *rénwǔ* day of the fourth month,
Wányán Hūxiéhǔ, Provincial Administrator of Xúzhōu, apprehended Wáng Déquán and his son and executed them,
along with their associates Wáng Lín, Yáng Guī, and Xiémǎo Yánshòu.
He summoned the Director of Records, Shāng Yǔ, and employed him.
Yán Lù, Pacification Commissioner of Yúshān, rebelled and defected to Liánshuǐ.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Lǐ Shùn'ér, Commandant of Chénzhōu, killed Niángé Nūshēn, Provincial Administrator, and Liú Tiānqǐ, Pacification Commissioner,
and sent a surrender message to Cuī Lì.
Zhāng Jùnmín and Lǐ Qí fled to Biànjīng.
Wáng Bì returned to Guīdé.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Cuī Lì brought Wáng Cóngkè, Prince of Liáng, Wáng Shǒuchún, Prince of Jīng, and over five hundred male and female members of the imperial clan to Qīngchéng.
All were killed in the calamity.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the two palaces were moved north.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Yílà Yuàn, Jiedushi of Dèngzhōu, rebelled with his city,
and along with Báihuá, fled into Sòng territory.
On the *jǐmǎo* day of the sixth month,
Guānnú and his associates Ālǐhé and Báijìn were all executed.
The Emperor ascended the Shuāngmén Gate,
pardoned the Loyal and Filial Army,
to stabilize the wavering.
He then decided to relocate to Cài,
and issued an edict commanding Cài, Xī, Chén, and Yǐng to send troops to escort him.
Wūlíndá Hútǔ, Resident Administrator of Zhōngjīng and acting Chancellor, abandoned the city and fled to Cài.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Zhōngjīng fell,
and Qiáng Shēn, Resident Administrator and General Commander of Expedient Affairs, died.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Wányán Hūxiéhǔ, Provincial Administrator of Xúzhōu, was summoned to the imperial traveling court.
Mòniǎ Yùdiǎn was appointed acting Provincial Administrator,
and Guō Ēn was made General Commander and Jiedushi.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
the Emperor departed Guīdé,
leaving Grand Marshal Wáng Bì to defend it.
On the *rénchén* day,
he arrived at Bózhōu.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Wáng Jìn, Jiedushi of Bózhōu, and Wáng Bīn, Assistant Jiedushi, were ordered to conscript civilians to transport iron armor and dried provisions.
Zhāng Tiāngāng, acting Chancellor, was left to oversee this,
and to promote meritorious officers and soldiers.
Wáng Yìshēn, Prince of Línzī Commandery, rebelled, occupying the Wàngkǒu Stockade at Língbì.
The Emperor dispatched Nǚxīliè Wán, a Close Attendant and Director, to lead troops from Xú and Sù to suppress him.
Wáng Yìshēn was defeated and fled to Liánshuǐ,
entering Sòng territory.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
Cuī Fùgē of the Bózhōu Garrison killed Wáng Bīn, the defending official, and others.
Zhāng Tiāngāng, by expedient authority, granted Fùgē the title of Jiedushi,
and suspended the transport of iron armor and dried provisions.
The people of the prefecture then settled down.
On the *jǐhài* day,
the Emperor entered Càizhōu.
An edict was issued to the Department of State Affairs to write a letter summoning Wǔ Xiān to gather his troops and come to reinforce.
Mòniǎ Yùdiǎn, Provincial Administrator of Xúzhōu, proceeded to Càizhōu.
Sàibù, who had been reinstated as Left Prime Minister *zhi shi*, was appointed acting Provincial Administrator.
On the *guǐmǎo* day, the first day of the seventh month,
a partial amnesty was granted within Càizhōu territory for all miscellaneous crimes below death penalty.
Officials, soldiers, and common people universally received two ranks of promotion.
Those who had already handled affairs were further promoted one rank.
Gate restrictions were relaxed,
and all goods were circulated,
which benefited the people of Cài.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Wūgǔlún Hào was made Censor-in-Chief,
retaining his title as General Commander.
Zhāng Tiāngāng was made Imperial Censor,
still acting as Chancellor.
Wányán Yàoshī was made Jiedushi of the Zhènnán Army,
and concurrently Inspector of Càizhōu territory.
On the *wùshēn* day,
Wūgǔlún Púxiān, Langzhong of the Right and Left Bureaus, concurrently held the post of Administrator of Xīzhōu,
acting as Right Supervising Commissioner of the Grand Marshal's office,
and carrying out the affairs of the Grand Marshal's headquarters.
Lóushì, Grand Marshal of the Expeditionary Army and acting General Commander, was assigned to the Bureau of Military Affairs.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
unmarried women were selected to serve in the palace.
Several had already been obtained.
Due to the remonstrance of Hūxiéhǔ, the Right Minister,
one who understood writing was kept,
and the rest were allowed to go free.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Wèi Fán was dispatched to conscript Wǔ Xiān's troops.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Púxiān Shílǔ, Imperial Guard, arrived from Biàn with the imperial portraits of the ancestors.
An imperial order instructed the authorities to enshrine them in the Qiányuán Temple.
Púchá Shìdá, former Imperial Censor, and Bǎsāhé, Western Grand Marshal,
returned from Biàn.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Wǔ Xiān coerced his officers and soldiers,
and plotted to take Jīnzhōu from the Sòng. When they reached Xīshuǐ, the army dispersed.
Lú Zhī, acting Minister of the Six Ministries, and Shí Jiè, Vice Minister, plotted to return to Càizhōu.
Xiān pursued Zhī but could not catch him,
so he killed Jiè.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
regulations were established for rewards for submitting horses,
and also for punishments for requisitioning horses.
Mòniǎ Yùdiǎn, assigned to the Bureau of Military Affairs and acting Chancellor, was put in charge of these matters.
Envoys were dispatched to various circuits
to select troops to assemble at Cài.
On the *jǐsì* day,
Púchá Shìdá was made Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel,
and acting Minister of the Six Ministries.
On the *jiǎxū* day of the twelfth month,
all civilian men were conscripted for defense.
Robust women were selected and dressed in men’s clothes and hats
to transport large stones.
The Emperor personally went out to console the troops.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Dà Yuán army breached the Liàn Jiāng,
and the Sòng army breached the Chái Tán, entering the Rǔ Shuǐ.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
the Dà Yuán army broke through the outer wall.
Gāo Lágē, the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of Sùzhōu, was killed in battle.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Commander-in-Chief Bóshùlǔ Lóushì and Palace Guard Commander Wùlíndá Hútǔ were both given temporary authority as Councilors.
Duwèi Wányán Chénglín was appointed Marshal of the Eastern Front
and temporary Commander-in-Chief.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
the Dà Yuán army destroyed the western wall.
The Emperor said to his attendants:
“I have been a high-ranking official for ten years,
Crown Prince for ten years,
and sovereign for ten years.
I know I have committed no great errors or wickedness,
so I have no regrets about dying.
My only regret is that the ancestral lineage has lasted over a hundred years,
but will end with me.
To be like the ancient depraved and tyrannical rulers who lost their states,
this alone causes me distress.”
He also said:
“In ancient times, there was no state that did not perish.
The rulers of perished states were often imprisoned,
or captured and presented,
or disgraced in the court,
or confined in desolate valleys.
I will certainly not come to such a pass.
You gentlemen observe,
my resolve is firm.”
Duwèi Wáng Àishí died in battle.
Artillery Commander-in-Chief Wáng Ruì killed Marshal Jiágǔ Dānggē
and, with thirty men, surrendered to Dà Yuán.
On the *gēngyín* day,
imperial utensils were awarded to the warriors.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the Emperor, in disguise, led troops out of the eastern gate at night, planning to escape.
They reached the stockade but could not proceed,
fought, and returned.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
fifty imperial horses
and one hundred and fifty official horses were slaughtered to reward the generals and soldiers.
In the first month of the third year, on the *rényín* day,
the god of Chái Tán was enfeoffed as Hùguó Língyìng Wáng.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
close attendants were assigned to guard the four city gates.
On the *wùshēn* day,
that night,
the Emperor assembled his officials
and abdicated in favor of Eastern Front Marshal Chénglín.
Chénglín firmly declined.
The imperial edict stated:
“How could I have chosen to entrust this to you by any other means?
My body is too fat and heavy,
making it inconvenient to ride and charge on horseback.
You are usually agile and possess military strategy.
If by some chance you can escape,
the imperial lineage will not be cut off.
This is my wish.”
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Chénglín ascended the imperial throne.
All the officials offered congratulations.
After the ceremony, he promptly went out to resist the enemy,
but the Sòng banner had already been raised on the southern side.
A moment later,
shouts from all four sides shook heaven and earth.
The guards on the southern side abandoned the gate,
the main army entered,
and engaged in street fighting with the city troops.
The city troops could not resist.
The Emperor hanged himself in the Yōulán Xuān.
The Last Emperor retreated to defend the inner city.
Hearing of the Emperor’s death,
he led his ministers to weep,
and bestowed the posthumous title Āizōng.
Before the weeping and offerings were finished,
the city fell.
The imperial guards set fire to it.
Fèngyù Jiàngshān collected Āizōng’s bones and buried them by the Rǔ Shuǐ.
The Last Emperor was harmed by the chaotic soldiers,
and the Jīn dynasty perished.
The encomium states: When Jīn first rose,
nothing in the world was stronger.
Tàizǔ and Tàizōng exerted their might over the Central Plains,
generally intending to emulate the early precedent of Liáo,
establishing the states of Chǔ and Qí,
then abandoning them.
The Sòng people were not competitive,
and thus lost their old territories.
Xīzōng and Hǎilíng resorted to tyrannical policies,
causing discontent in the Central Plains,
and the Jīn dynasty was nearly lost.
Heaven, weary of the northern and southern wars,
gave birth to Shìzōng,
who replaced tyranny with benevolence,
and brought peace to the people.
Thus, the Jīn dynasty lasted over a hundred years,
because the policies of Dàdìng effectively united the hearts of the people,
and thereby achieved its success.
Zhāngzōng aimed to refine governance,
but corrupt policies grew daily,
exactions were endless,
the people’s strength gradually exhausted.
Míngchāng and Chéng'ān marked the peak and beginning of decline.
As for Wèishào,
the institutions were greatly damaged,
and signs of demise were already apparent.
Xuānzōng moved south,
abandoning his roots,
relying on lingering might externally,
engaging in continuous wars with Sòng and Xià,
and internally leading to exhaustion,
hastening its own collapse.
There was nothing worthy of note in Āizōng’s reign.
The imperial Yuán’s merits and virtues grew daily,
heaven and men inclined towards it.
Like the rising sun and extinguishing torch,
it was a natural progression of events.
Though they strove to sustain themselves
and preserve the state amidst ruin,
their strength was exhausted, and they perished.
This is indeed pitiable.
Nevertheless,
according to ritual,
“the sovereign dies for the altars of soil and grain,”
and Āizōng had no shame in this.
Collation Notes
Imperial Annals, Volume 19: Supplement
Jǐngxuan Huángdì, personal name Zōngjùn,
originally named Shéngguǒ,
was Tàizǔ’s second son.
His mother was Empress Shèngmù Tángguō Shì,
Tàizǔ’s primary consort.
Zōngjùn was the most legitimate among all the sons.
In the fifth year of Tiānfǔ,
Hūlǔ Bójíliè Gǎo commanded all armies to take Zhōngjīng.
The Emperor separately led a Házhá Měng’ān,
receiving a golden tablet.
After conquering Zhōngjīng,
he and Gǎo together attacked the Liáo ruler at Yuānyang Luò.
The Liáo ruler fled to Yīnshān.
Gěng Shǒuzhōng attempted to relieve Xījīng.
The Emperor and Zōnghàn, among others, attacked and repelled him.
South of Xījīng city was a stupa.
The enemy first occupied it,
shooting down,
causing many casualties among the soldiers.
The Emperor said:
“First take this,
then Xījīng can be captured.”
Afterward, they attacked the stupa,
captured it,
and then took Xījīng.
When Tàizǔ died,
the Emperor and his elder brother Zōnggàn led the imperial clan and ministers to enthrone Tàizōng.
In the second year of Tiānhuì,
he passed away.
When Xīzōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously honored with the full title Jǐngxuan Huángdì
and temple name Huīzōng,
and reburied at Xīnglíng.
After Hǎilíng usurped the throne and enthroned himself,
he demoted Xīzōng to Dōnghūn Wáng,
and demoted the Emperor to Fēng Wáng.
Shìzōng later restored Xīzōng’s temple name and posthumous title,
and honored the Emperor as Jǐngxuan Huángdì.
His sons were Hālá, Chángshèng, and Zhālá.
Hālá became Xīzōng.
Ruìzōng Lìdé Xiǎnrén Qǐshèng Guǎngyùn Wǔwǔ Jiǎnsù Huángdì, personal name Zōngyáo,
initially named Zōngfǔ,
originally named Élí Sòng.
During Dàdìng, he was posthumously honored with the full title,
and his current personal name was posthumously adopted.
He was imposing and dignified;
people looked upon him with awe.
He was magnanimous by nature,
generous,
and valued honesty.
When Tàizǔ campaigned in all directions,
all his sons commanded armies,
but the Emperor often remained in the imperial tent.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ,
when Tàizǔ personally led an expedition,
Tàizōng remained to guard Huánglóng Fǔ.
Ānfúgē incited newly surrendered people to rebel.
The Emperor and Wūgǔnǎi suppressed them.
Nánlù Jūnshuài Húshítá was disgraced due to corruption.
The Emperor went to investigate the matter,
and all praised his fairness.
In the fifth year of Tiānhuì,
Zōngwàng passed away.
The Emperor was made Right Deputy Grand Marshal,
stationing troops in Yānjīng.
In the eleventh month,
he dispatched his generals to attack Sòng.
The Emperor departed from Héjiān,
conquering lands in Zī and Qīng.
In the sixth year, first month, Sòng's Mǎ Kuò arrived at Lè'ān with 200,000 troops.
The Emperor led his army to attack and defeat them.
Hearing that the Sòng ruler was in Yángzhōu,
and as spring plowing was in full swing,
he left a large army to cultivate fields along the river and returned,
stationing his army in Shānxī.
In the second month,
Yílàgǔ defeated Sòng's Tái Zōngjùn and Sòng Zhōng's 50,000 troops at Dàmíng.
The next day, he defeated them again,
capturing Zōngjùn and Zhōng before returning.
People from Jìzhōu launched a night attack on Zhàolǐ's camp.
Zhàolǐ defeated them.
The Sòng ruler sent a memorial requesting peace,
but secretly wrote to entice the Qìdān and Hàn people.
An edict was issued to attack Sòng.
The Emperor departed from Hébĕi,
received the surrender of Huázhōu,
took Kāidé Fǔ,
attacked Dàmíng Fǔ,
and captured it.
Hébĕi was pacified.
Initially,
when attacking Sòng,
the generals from Hébĕi and Hédōng were undecided.
Some wished to first pacify Hébĕi,
while others wished to first pacify Shǎnxī.
Tàizōng adopted both strategies.
Then Zōnghàn arrived to meet at Pú.
After Hébĕi was pacified,
Tàizōng then took Dōngpíng and Xúzhōu,
obtaining all the gold and silks transported by the Sòng people from Jiānghuái and stored in the Xúzhōu official treasury.
These were distributed among the various armies,
and Liú Yù subsequently surrendered Jìnán.
He sent Bálísu and others to raid the Sòng ruler in Yángzhōu.
When the Sòng ruler heard of this,
by the time Bálísu reached Yángzhōu,
he had already crossed the river the previous evening.
The Sòng ruler then demoted himself, removing his imperial title,
and again sent a letter requesting the preservation of his state.
The details are in the biography of Zōnghàn.
Afterwards, Zōngbì pursued the Sòng ruler.
The Sòng ruler crossed the river,
entered Hángzhōu,
then fled into the sea,
whereupon Zōngbì returned.
At this point,
the cities and towns in Shǎnxī that Lóushì had subjugated repeatedly rebelled.
Zōnghàn and others said:
"Previously, in suppressing Sòng,
we divided the western army to join the eastern army.
However, the military strength of the five circuits of Shǎnxī is formidable;
we should combine our forces to attack and capture them.
Now Tǎlǎn has pacified Jiāngběi.
Zōngbì should first go to Luòyáng with 20,000 elite troops.
In the eighth month, we should go to Shǎnxī.
Either Zōngbì should lead the expedition,
or one of Zōngfǔ, Zōnggàn, or Xīyǐn should go."
The Emperor said:
"Lóushì, whenever he went, always achieved his objectives.
Now, to exclusively campaign in Shǎnxī,
is he perhaps weary of war and saving himself?
You all should exert yourselves!"
Consequently, an edict ordered the Emperor to go.
At this time,
Sòng's Zhāng Jùn's forces took Shǎnxī.
The Emperor arrived at Luòshuǐ to prepare his troops.
Zhāng Jùn had 60,000 cavalry
and 120,000 infantry encamped at Fùpíng.
The Emperor arrived at Fùpíng.
Lóushì commanded the left wing,
Zōngbì commanded the right wing.
The two armies advanced simultaneously.
From noon until dusk,
after six engagements,
they shattered the enemy.
Yàozhōu and Fèngxiáng Fǔ both surrendered.
They then took Jīng and Wèi two prefectures.
They defeated Sòng's Commissioner of Military Affairs Liú Ní's army at Wǎtíng,
and Yuánzhōu surrendered.
Sālǐhē broke through Déshùn Jūn's Jìngbiān fort.
Sòng's Jīngyuán Circuit Commander Zhāng Zhōngfú and Prefect of Zhènróng Jūn Lǐ Yànqí surrendered the city.
Sòng's Qínfèng Circuit Military Commissioner Wú Jiè's army was stationed on the border of Lǒngzhōu.
Recruitment and Pacification Commissioner Mǎ Wǔ attacked and repulsed them,
then captured a county and returned.
The Emperor advanced and received the surrender of three forts including Gānquán,
took Bǎochuān City,
defeated Sòng's Xīhé Circuit Deputy Military Commissioner's 30,000 troops,
captured over a thousand horses,
captured two forts including Ānxī,
and Xīzhōu surrendered.
He dispatched Left Wing Commander Ālúbǔ
and Right Wing Commander Zōngbì to pacify and recruit the cities and towns that had not yet surrendered.
Thus they gained Gǒng, Táo, Hé, Lè, Xīníng, Lán, Kuò, Jīshí, and other prefectures,
as well as Dìngyuǎn, Hézhèng, Gānyù, Níngtáo, Ānlǒng and other walled garrisons,
and over forty garrisons and native-Han encampments.
Consequently, the Jīngyuán and Xīhé circuits were both pacified.
Sālǐhē took Qìngyáng Fǔ,
and Mù Wěi surrendered Huánzhōu.
After pacifying the five circuits of Shǎnxī,
he selected 6,000 cavalry
and had Sālǐhē station them at strategic points.
Thereupon, the army returned,
and with Zōnghàn, he paid homage at the capital.
Xīzōng was appointed Ānbǎn Bójíliè,
and the Emperor was made Left Deputy Grand Marshal.
In the thirteenth year,
he passed away while traveling in Guīzhōu,
aged forty.
He was interred in Ruìlíng,
posthumously enfeoffed as Lù Wáng,
and given the posthumous title Xiāngmù.
In the sixth year of Huángtǒng,
he was promoted to Jìguó Wáng.
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Tàishī and Shàngzhùguó,
and re-enfeoffed as Xǔ Wáng.
Upon Shìzōng's ascension,
he was posthumously granted the honorable posthumous title Lìdé Xiǎnrén Qǐshèng Guǎngyùn Wénwǔ Jiǎnsù Huángdì,
and his temple name was Ruìzōng.
In the second year,
he was re-interred at Dàfángshān,
and his tomb was named Jǐnglíng.
Xiǎnzōng Tǐdào Hóngrén Yīngwén Ruìdé Guāngxiào Huángdì,
whose personal name was Yǔngōng,
originally named Hútǔwǎ,
was the second son of Shìzōng.
His mother was Empress Míngdé, of the Wūlíndá clan.
He was born in the bìngyín year of the sixth year of Huángtǒng.
He was majestic in physique and appearance,
filial, fraternal, cautious, and magnanimous.
In the eleventh month of the first year of Dàdìng,
Shìzōng ascended the throne in Dōngjīng.
In the yǐyǒu year,
he was enfeoffed as Chǔ Wáng,
and officials were appointed to his establishment.
In the twelfth month,
he accompanied Shìzōng to Zhōngdū.
In the second year, fourth month, on the jǐmǎo day,
he was given the name Yǔndí.
In the fifth month, on the rényín day,
he was appointed Crown Prince.
Shìzōng said to him:
"In ritual, the son of the principal wife is honored,
which is why I establish you.
Be friendly towards your brothers,
and treat all officials with decorum.
Do not let your position as heir make you arrogant.
Diligently pursue your studies daily.
Unless summoned,
there is no need to attend me at meals."
The Emperor submitted a memorial to express his gratitude.
He devoted himself to study,
discussing with the various scholarly officials in Chénghuá Diàn.
In his leisure, he read books,
forgetting fatigue even late into the night.
The next day, he would invariably present any difficult characters to the scholarly officials for verification and correction.
In the ninth month, on the gēngzǐ day,
an edict ordered the three Grand Masters of the Eastern Palace to address the Crown Prince by name,
while the Junior Masters and below were to address him as "your subject."
In the eleventh month, on the gēngzǐ day,
on his birthday,
all officials offered congratulations at Chénghuá Diàn.
Shìzōng bestowed upon him court robes and a fine horse,
and hosted a banquet in Rénzhèng Diàn,
with members of the imperial clan and all officials attending.
Thereafter, on his birthdays,
Shìzōng would either visit the Eastern Palace
or host a banquet in the inner palace,
making it a regular annual practice.
In the twelfth month, on the xīnmǎo day,
he memorialized:
"During the congratulatory rituals at the Eastern Palace,
imperial princes and first-rank imperial kinsmen all bow facing north,
while I merely return a bow.
I humbly implore Your Majesty's gracious consent for me to return their bows,
so as to cultivate the way of close kinship and friendly affection."
Shìzōng approved,
making it a fixed regulation.
Shìzōng heard that the scholar Zhèng Sōng
was virtuous. Sōng had previously retired from the position of Assistant Prefect of Bózhōu with the title of Defense Commissioner.
He was reinstated as Left Assistant Tutor
and was granted an imperial decree exempting him from court attendance,
ordering him to assist the Crown Prince in his studies.
Sōng considered himself a friend and tutor.
The Emperor once looked at Sōng and told him to fetch a belt.
Sōng replied,
"Your servant is honored with the title of Tutor;
I dare not obey such a command."
The Emperor's expression changed, and he praised him,
thereafter treating him with even greater respect.
Whenever he went hunting and caught a deer,
he would always share it with him.
In the ninth month of the fourth year,
he took Consort Túshàn into his household,
performing the personal迎禮 (qīnyíng lǐ) ceremony.
According to custom,
for the grand imperial procession (dàjià lúbù), the Son of Heaven rode in a jade carriage (yùlù),
while the Crown Prince's procession (huángtàizǐ lúbù) rode in a golden carriage (jīnlù).
In the sixth year,
Shìzōng traveled from Xījīng back to the capital.
The ritual officials did not know that the Crown Prince had his own golden carriage (jīnlù) for his procession,
so they requested that the Crown Prince join the grand imperial procession (dàjià) and ride in a supplementary carriage,
traveling in front of the Son of Heaven.
The Emperor doubted that this was proper,
and after carefully reviewing the old codes,
the ritual officials realized their mistake.
Thereupon, Lǐ Bāngzhí, a Secretary in the Ministry of Rites, and Lǐ Shān, an Assistant Secretary, were demoted one rank.
Wǔ Zhīcái, a Junior Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Zhāng Zǐyǔ, a Recorder of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Doctor Zhāng Jǔ were demoted two ranks.
A short while later,
the ritual officials debated whether, when receiving the imperial decree and making an obeisance at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
he should wear his usual court robes
and ride a horse.
Shìzōng said,
"This is no different from the rites for external officials who offer obeisance at various temples,
which Hǎilíng did on a whim.
How can it be taken as a model?
For a grand imperial decree and the triennial extended ancestral sacrifice (sānsuì xiáxiǎng), ancient rites should be used.
Confucius said: 'Rather than extravagance,
it is better to be frugal in rites.' This should not be treated so casually."
He further said,
"Although Right Chancellor Sū Bǎohéng is a Hàn person and not well-versed in classics and histories,
and Administrator Shí Jū is well-versed in classics and histories but does not speak up,
since the ritual officials were already demoted the other day,
do they still not fear?
Let them present the ancient rituals and rites,
and I will choose and implement them."
After a long time,
when about to confer the imperial decree and seal upon the Crown Prince,
the ceremonial procedures prescribed preparing imperial regalia and announcing it at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The Emperor said,
"When I received the honored title and made my obeisance,
I followed the precedent of Emperor Zhēnzōng of the former Sòng dynasty,
wearing ordinary court robes and riding a horse.
Yet the Crown Prince is to use full ceremonial rites.
The inconsistency is inappropriate
and utterly meaningless."
He said to Right Chancellor Liángbì and Left Chancellor Shǒudào,
"This is due to your negligence."
Liángbì and others apologized, saying,
"Your servants' foolish foresight did not extend to this."
The Emperor again said,
"This is due to the civil officials' adherence to old ways."
In the tenth month, jiǎshēn day, of that year,
the extended ancestral sacrifice (xiáxiǎng) was performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and the second offering (yàxiàn) ceremony was conducted.
In the seventh year,
the Emperor fell ill,
and decreed Left Chancellor Shǒudào to attend to his medicine.
He moved to the Línfāng Hall in the Qiónglín Garden for recuperation.
In the first month, jiǎxū day, of the eighth year,
he was renamed Yǔngōng.
On the gēngchén day,
he received the imperial decree and seal of the Crown Prince,
and the Emperor submitted a memorial to express thanks.
In the fifth month of the ninth year,
Shìzōng ordered to escape the summer heat at Cǎoluò.
Suí Wáng Wéigōng accompanied him,
and all those who were to accompany them were given travel expenses.
The Emperor memorialized, saying,
"To go far from the imperial court
and exclusively seek a cool place
is not something a loyal subject should find peace in.
I wish to cancel the trip."
Shìzōng said,
"Your body is weak.
The area behind the mountains is cool and high,
so I ordered you to go."
On the dīngchǒu day,
the hundred officials bid farewell north of the capital city,
bowing twice,
and the Emperor returned their bows.
In that month,
the hundred officials received an imperial decree to prepare memorials inquiring about his well-being.
In the sixth month,
the hundred officials inquired about his well-being as before.
In the eighth month, yǐyǒu day,
he arrived back from Cǎoluò,
and the hundred officials welcomed him north of the capital city,
following the farewell ceremony.
On the bǐngxū day,
he had an audience.
Shìzōng said,
"My son and I have been separated for the summer;
I have missed you greatly."
In the ninth month,
it was decreed that the Crown Prince's provisions should not be disbursed monthly,
but an annual sum of fifty million (cash) be provided.
In the eighth month of the tenth year,
the Emperor was in the Jīngyán (classics lecture) at Chénghuá Hall.
Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince) Shòuwáng Shuǎng remarked,
"Your Highness is not yet very proficient in the court language.
Why not dismiss the Hàn officials around you
and use only Nǚzhēn people?"
The Emperor said,
"How can I casually dismiss the tutors (yùdé), assistant tutors (zànshàn), and attendant officials?"
Shuǎng then bowed and withdrew.
The Emperor said,
"The four palace officials are called 'tutors' (yùdé) and 'assistant tutors' (zànshàn);
their purpose is clear,
yet he wishes to dismiss them.
This is due to lack of learning."
An envoy returned from Shāndōng.
The Emperor asked what hardships the common people were enduring.
The envoy replied,
"The difficulty of obtaining money is the greatest hardship.
Official treasuries are full of money, some even piled in the open,
yet the common people have no money,
and this causes their suffering."
The Emperor said,
"If it is stored in empty rooms,
what good is its abundance?"
He said to Hùbù Shàngshū (Minister of Revenue) Zhāng Zhòngyú,
"The Son of Heaven stores wealth for the whole empire;
why must it be exclusively in the state treasury?"
He then memorialized, saying,
"Money in the state treasury
is no different from copper ore in the wilderness.
I beg that it be put into circulation
so that both public and private sectors may benefit."
Shìzōng approved and accepted this,
and decreed the relevant officials to discuss its implementation.
In the eleventh month, dīnghài day, of the eleventh year,
there was a ceremony at the Yuánqiū (Round Mound).
The Emperor performed the second offering (yàxiàn) ceremony.
In the fifth month of the twelfth year,
Shìzōng heard that Húlà, the Defense Commissioner of Dézhōu, was plotting rebellion.
He then said,
"I have always been exceptionally devoted to the principle of kinship,
yet he dares to act like this."
The Emperor slowly memorialized, saying,
"Uncle Húlà's nature is wild and reckless,
addicted to entertainment,
and without an heir.
Suddenly, there is such a wild scheme.
I hope you will further investigate and verify it."
In the tenth month, jǐwèi day,
the extended ancestral sacrifice (xiáxiǎng) was performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and the Emperor officiated the ritual on behalf of the Emperor.
In the tenth month of the thirteenth year,
he received an imperial decree to hunt in Bǎozhōu and Dìngzhōu with Zhào Wáng Wéizhōng and Cái Wáng Wéigōng.
In the eleventh month, jiǎwǔ day,
he returned to the capital.
In the fourth month, yǐhài day, of the fourteenth year,
Shìzōng held court in the Chuígǒng Hall,
with the Emperor and various princes attending.
Shìzōng discussed the relations between brothers and their wives.
Shìzōng said,
"To listen to a wife's words and quarrel with one's brothers is truly deplorable."
The Emperor replied,
"The poem 'Sīqí' says: 'Set an example for your wife,
and extend it to your brothers,
to govern your family and state.'
Your servants are foolish;
we wish to encourage each other and cultivate this virtue."
He then cited the meaning of 'chángdì huā ěr' (cherry blossoms) implying mutual support
and 'jílíng' (wagtail) signifying urgent help in times of difficulty,
expressing his intention in writing
to admonish his brothers.
In the fifteenth year,
Shìzōng decreed that officials of the fifth rank and above should express their gratitude by presenting themselves to the Crown Prince.
In the fifth month, jiǎchén day, of the seventeenth year,
while attending a banquet in the Chángwǔ Hall,
Dian Shi Ling (Director of Food Service) Niè Hé presented porridge.
As the Emperor was about to eat,
there was a spider in the porridge bowl.
Niè Hé was terrified and at a loss,
but the Emperor calmly said,
"A spider spins its web and floats in the air,
it just happened to fall in here.
How can it be your fault?"
In the tenth month, jǐmǎo day,
the extended ancestral sacrifice (xiáxiǎng) was performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and he officiated the ritual on behalf of the Emperor.
In the fourth month of the nineteenth year, on the day Wùshēn,
there was a ritual at the Tàimiào,
and he temporarily performed the sacrificial rites.
On the day Dīngsì,
Zhānshì Wūlíndá Yuàn came in to express gratitude.
The Emperor ordered a fútóu and yāodài to be brought,
and the officials in attendance requested,
"This is the courtesy shown to a prime minister or a teacher."
The Emperor said,
"Yuàn has served Bìxià for a long time,
so I show him this special respect."
They all said,
"This is beyond what we, your subjects, can achieve."
In the eleventh month,
Empress Míngdé was reburied at Kūnhòulíng.
The Emperor walked alongside the hearse,
and encountered a great wind and snow.
His attendants offered rain gear,
but the Emperor refused it.
By the time they reached the resting place,
his clothes were completely soaked,
and all who witnessed it shed tears.
Although Hǎilíng had been demoted to a commoner,
Zōnggàn was still referred to as Emperor Míngsù.
Those who debated the matter considered this incomplete,
so the Emperor submitted a memorial to discuss it thoroughly.
Shìzōng graciously accepted it.
Thereupon, Zōnggàn's imperial title was removed,
and he was demoted and enfeoffed as Liáowáng.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Shìzōng was about to visit Shàngjīng.
He decreed that the Emperor should guard the country,
and made
the "Seal of Guardianship"
to bestow upon him.
Regarding sending envoys, performing sacrifices, officials above the fifth rank, and matters of significant importance or harm, envoys were to be dispatched to report swiftly.
For officials below the sixth rank and other routine matters,
he was permitted to make decisions.
Every three days, he would receive memorials from the Shàngshūshěng in the Jíxiándiàn.
Officials in the capital were to attend in court dress on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month to pay their respects.
While the imperial carriage was on the road,
an envoy was sent every twenty days to inquire about his well-being.
Once he reached Shàngjīng,
an inquiry about his well-being was made every thirty days.
Shìzōng said,
"This imperial tour might last one or two years,
so you shall guard the country.
It is like a farmer tending his fields,
or a merchant pursuing profits;
as long as you can uphold your father's legacy,
you will be considered a worthy son."
The Emperor replied,
"I have been in the Dōnggōng for over twenty years,
and have made many mistakes,
yet Bìxià has never blamed me because of Empress Míngdé.
I am truly foolish
and unable to bear this heavy responsibility.
I beg to accompany you."
Shìzōng said,
"All people raise their sons hoping for support in their old age.
I will leave the Tàiwèi, the two Zuǒchéng, and Cānzhèng to assist you.
They are all veteran officials of the state,
with whom you can consult.
Moreover, state affairs are not difficult;
just be fair and just in your intentions,
and do not listen to slander and evil.
After a month, you will become proficient in state affairs."
The Emperor tearfully insisted on declining,
and those around him were moved.
In the third month,
Shìzōng went to Shàngjīng,
and the Emperor guarded the country, remaining in the Zhōngdū.
Initially,
when the Emperor was in the Dōnggōng,
he would sometimes stroll in the Fāngyuàn with his eunuchs.
The eunuchs entered and exited the forbidden palace
without ever being restricted.
When these people saw the Emperor guarding the country,
each became pleased with himself.
The Emperor, knowing this,
said to his eunuchs,
"Previously, when I was in the Dōnggōng, I did not personally attend to state affairs,
and spoke with you all daily.
Now that I am guarding the country,
you may only enter when summoned."
In the fifth month,
Shìzōng arrived in Shàngjīng
and issued an imperial edict stating:
"I arrived in Liáoyáng on the eighth day of the previous month,
and reached Shàngjīng on the second day of this month.
The next day, I offered sacrifices at Qìngyuánmiào.
To inspect the regions and observe the people
is an ancient system.
Your responsibility in guarding the country is heavy.
As the summer heat is intense,
you should take even greater care of yourself,
lest you cause me worry."
The Emperor said to Túndān Kèníng,
"The imperial carriage is on tour,
and state affairs have been entrusted to me.
Criminal cases are the most serious,
for upon them depend people's lives and deaths.
Whenever there is something to discuss,
we must strive for utmost impartiality.
Until the sovereign returns to the capital,
let no matter be neglected."
From then on,
whenever a criminal case was reported,
the Emperor personally reviewed it,
summoning the Dūshì to meticulously correct any errors,
working tirelessly from dawn to dusk,
and sometimes granting them food.
A close attendant reported that lotuses were blooming in the Yáochí pool,
and suggested holding a banquet.
The Emperor said,
"The Sagely Sovereign is on his eastern tour,
and has commanded me to guard the country.
How dare I indulge in banquets and neglect my duties?
Picking a few flowers will suffice."
In the seventh month,
he dispatched his son, Jīnyuánjùnwáng Mádágé, to present a memorial inquiring about Shìzōng's well-being
and requesting his return to the capital.
In the eleventh month, on the day Rén'yín,
the Emperor went on a winter hunt.
On the day Xīnhài,
he returned to the capital.
In the first month of the twenty-fifth year, on the first day, Yǐyǒu,
the Emperor exempted all officials from the congratulatory ceremonies.
he deeply maintained humility and restraint.
His palace officials did not have to perform the court prostration,
and did not need to stand in attendance when presenting memorials,
and the ceremonies for the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month were exempted.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, capital officials were to wear court attire and pay their respects,
but this was also suspended and exempted.
At this time,
when officials were due to offer congratulations,
he also refused to accept them.
On the day Jiǎyín,
the Emperor went to Chūnshuǐ.
In the second month, on the day Gēngshēn,
he returned to the capital.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
he dispatched his son, Jīnyuánjùnwáng Mádágé, to present a memorial congratulating Shìzōng on Wànchūnjié.
In the fourth month,
after a long period without rain,
the Emperor personally prayed,
and on that very day, sufficient rain fell.
In the sixth month, on the day of Jiǎyín,
Dì fell ill.
On the day of Gēngshēn,
he passed away in Chénghuá Diàn.
Shìzōng returned from Shàngjīng,
and when he reached Tiānpíngshān Hǎoshuǐchuān,
upon hearing the news of the demise,
he set up an altar and performed a libation south of the temporary palace,
weeping uncontrollably for a long time.
Princes, officials, imperial clan members, noblewomen, and imperial guards all gathered to mourn.
Shìzōng cried aloud as he returned to the palace.
By the time he arrived in Zhōngdū,
he had set up altars and wept for Dì seven times in total.
Shìzōng appointed Bīn Wáng Yǒngchéng as the Zhōngdū Liúshǒu [resident commander]
to escort the coffin.
He dispatched Téng Wáng Fǔ Chángshǐ Zàixīng and Yùyuàn Tōngjìn Ālìlà to protect Jīnyuán Jùnwáng,
and sent Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ Tángguō Dǐng to offer sacrifices.
An imperial edict ordered Fēi Túshānlì and the imperial grandsons to wear mourning attire according to the Hàn system.
Dì had been the heir apparent for a long time,
and his benevolence and virtue were deeply felt by the people.
Three times a day, people would come to weep and mourn.
The imperial guards and soldiers all vied to enter and mourn,
prostrating themselves and weeping beneath Chénghuá Diàn,
their cries resounding like thunder.
The common people of Zhōngdū set up altars at market entrances and street corners to mourn.
On the first day of the seventh month, Rénwǔ,
he was posthumously granted the title Xuānxào Tàizǐ.
In the ninth month, on the day of Gēngyín,
he was temporarily interred in Xīchūn Diàn in the Southern Garden.
On the day of Jǐyǒu,
Shìzōng arrived from Shàngjīng.
Before entering the city gates,
he first went to Xīchūn Diàn to offer a libation,
weeping deeply for a long time.
By the time of the funeral,
he had personally visited six times.
Dì served Shìzōng,
and whenever the emperor went on an imperial tour to Xījīng,
Liángxíng,
or visited imperial tombs, offered sacrifices at ancestral temples,
paid respects at Yǎnqìng Gōng,
hunted or inspected crops,
performed sacrifices to Heaven, or shot arrows at willows,
he was never far from his side.
When the emperor performed rites at Yuánqiū,
or personally offered sacrifices at Tàimiào,
Dì would perform the second libation.
If the emperor did not personally offer sacrifices, Dì would act on his behalf.
When there was a great national celebration, he would lead all officials in submitting a congratulatory memorial.
On New Year's Day and Wànchūnjié, he would lead the ranks of officials in offering felicitations.
In the tenth month of winter, on the first day of Gēngxū,
the prime minister and others paid their respects at Qìnghé Diàn.
Tàiwèi Wányán Shǒudào offered felicitations,
and Shìzōng lamented mournfully for a long time.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Jiǎshēn,
the imperial hearse departed, and
Shìzōng performed a roadside sacrifice west of the capital city.
On the day of Gēngyín,
he was buried in Dàfángshān.
Shìzōng wished to bestow an imperial title upon Dì [the deceased prince],
and he consulted his ministers.
Hànlín Xiūzhuàn Zhào Kě replied:
“Táng Gāozōng posthumously bestowed the title Xiàojìng Huángdì on Prince Hóng.”
Zuǒ Chéng Zhāng Rǔbì said:
“This indeed originated from Wǔhòu.”
Thus, the matter was dropped.
Instead, a temple was built behind Yǎnqìng Gōng,
with three offerings for sacrifices
and the use of Dēnggē music.
In the twenty-sixth year,
his son Jǐng was established as the Imperial Grandson.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Shìzōng passed away.
The Imperial Grandson ascended the throne,
known as Zhāngzōng.
In the fifth month, on the day of Jiǎwǔ,
he was posthumously honored with the title Tǐdào Hóngrén Yīngwén Ruìdé Guāngxiào Huángdì,
and his temple name was Xiǎnzōng.
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
he was interred in the Tàimiào,
and his mausoleum was named Yùlíng.
Dì's nature was benevolent and kind,
and he could not bear to inflict punishment or death.
When Liáng Tán'ér stole gold and silver leaves,
he pitied his aged mother.
When Lǐ Fúxìng stole silk pieces,
it coincided with the completion of the rites at Kūnhòu Líng.
When Jiālìng Běnbǎ stole silverware,
it coincided with Wànchūnjié.
In all these cases, he found ways to spare their lives.
For those who lost property,
he ordered restitution but did not impose punishment.
Upon hearing of famine in various regions,
he would immediately report it [to the emperor],
and increased relief and sustenance.
During hunting excursions and imperial tours, he would inquire about the hardships of the people wherever he went.
He treated ministers with respect
and loved his brothers.
When Míngdé Huánghòu was buried in Kūnhòu Líng,
all the imperial consorts were interred with her.
When the funeral procession departed from Pánníng Gōng,
Zhào Wáng Wéizhōng's mother's carriage departed first,
and he ordered the bearer of the yellow canopy to go ahead.
Dì called out to the canopy bearer, but there was no response.
Shǎofǔjiān Zhāng Jǐnyán wanted to report this incident,
but Dì stopped him.
He once wrote an inscription for the Zhòngguāng Throne,
and also carved a maxim for his seat on a small jade tablet,
[一一]and also carved it on the back of the tablet,
all of which contained profound principles.
He was most skilled at archery but did not exhaust animals.
Once, he was ordered to pay respects at an imperial tomb,
and he hunted beforehand.
He shot one deer and obtained it,
then immediately ordered the hunt to stop,
saying:
“It is sufficient for the sacrificial rites;
why kill more?”
It is said that his love for life was his inherent nature.
A eulogy says: Liáo Wáng Gǎo captured Zhōngjīng,
and Zōnghàn and Zōngwàng both followed.
Jǐngxūan separately led the Hézhá Mèng'ān.
Hézhá Mèng'ān
was Tàizǔ's Mèng'ān.
Zōnghàn requested the enthronement of Xīzōng;
Zōnggàn dared not object,
and Tàizōng could not refuse.
His righteousness was just,
and his reasoning was sound.
The old histories state that Ruìzōng was generous and fond of bestowing favors.
Xīzōng did not live to the end of his years,
and Hǎilíng died violently.
From that time onward,
those who attained the great position were all his descendants,
which has its reasons.
Xiǎnzōng was filial and fraternal, diligent and harmonious.
He spent twenty-five years in the Eastern Palace [as Crown Prince]
and was not known to have committed any faults.
He understood the emperor's intentions and guided people,
and people in all directions secretly benefited from his kindness.
Heaven did not grant him a long life,
what a pity!
Collation Notes
Annals 1: Astronomical phenomena, sun and moon eclipses, halos, auroras, cloud formations;
moon and five planets' transits and celestial anomalies.
From Fúxī's observation of the heavens and earth,
Huángdì's welcoming of the sun and calculation of its movements,
Zhònglí's ordering of heaven and earth,
Yáo's calendrical observations of the sun, moon, and stars,
Shùn's regulation of the Seven Regulators,
King Wǔ of Zhōu's consultation with Jīzǐ,
the exposition of the Great Plan,
and the coordination of the Five Records,
the way of observing the heavens was perfected.
The Yì says:
“Heaven displays images to reveal auspicious and inauspicious signs,
and the sages imitate them.”
Thus, Kǒngzǐ, based on the history of Lǔ, compiled the Chūnqiū,
recording anomalies in the sun, stars, wind, rain, frost, hail, thunder, and lightning, but not common occurrences,
thereby elucidating the way of Heaven and verifying human affairs.
From Qín and Hàn onwards,
times of good governance were few,
Yīn and Yáng deviated,
and celestial phenomena were in disarray;
no dynasty was without such occurrences.
In the 119 years of the Jīn dynasty,
there were 42 solar eclipses,
and the number of anomalies in stars, wind, rain, frost, hail, and thunder is unknown.
Among the nine rulers of Jīn,
none was wiser than Shìzōng.
Within 29 years,
there were still eleven solar eclipses,
and four or five solar prominences and虹貫 hóngguàn [halo phenomena].
However, throughout the Jīn dynasty,
auspicious clouds surrounding the sun occurred three times,
all during Shìzōng's reign.
After Xī and Hé,
the Hàn had Sīmǎ,
and the Táng had Yuán and Lǐ,
all of whom hereditary managed astronomical offices,
hence their explanations were detailed.
Moreover, the six directions form a single entity,
and the methods of astronomical calculation showed no discrepancies.
Jīn and Sòng stood in opposition,
and both countries established calendars,
with differences in their methods,
and the selection of astronomers also varied in quality.
Now, by imperial decree, the Jīn Shǐ is being compiled.
For the astronomical section,
each record follows its original,
specifically using the Chūnqiū as a standard.

Collation Notes
Monograph 2: Calendrical System 1 - Calculating Qi and Shuo - Calculating Gua and Hou - Calculating Sun's Position - Calculating Sundial and Clepsydra
In ancient times, the sages, by following the Way of Heaven, bestowed upon men the seasons,
thereby regulating the myriad crafts and making the various governments prosperous.
The methods of calculation and inference have a long history.
From the Tàichū era of the Hàn dynasty until the former Sòng dynasty,
those who compiled calendars were no less than seventy families.
Generally, after a hundred years or several decades,
they would usually change the calendar once.
This is because the waxing and waning, advancement and retreat of the Sun, Moon, and five planets,
along with the movement of the heavens,
are extremely irregular.
Humans then create instruments to observe them,
to make them regular;
but accumulating small discrepancies into large ones inevitably leads to errors.
The Jīn dynasty ruled for over a hundred years,
but its calendar was changed only once.
In the fifth year of Tiānhuì,
Yáng Jí of the Sītiān first created the Dàmíng calendar.
In the fifteenth year, in the spring, on the first day of the first month,
it was first promulgated.
Its method
used 383,768,657 as the calendar epoch and
5230 as the day divisor.
However, its origin
could not be thoroughly investigated;
some said it was based on the Sòng Jìyuán calendar, with additions and subtractions.
In the third month of the Wùyín year of Zhènglóng, on the day Xīnyǒu,
the Sītiān reported that there should be a solar eclipse,
but
there was none.
In the fifth month of the Guǐsì year of Dàdìng, on the day Rénchén,
there was a solar eclipse;
in the eleventh month of the Jiǎwǔ year, on the day Jiǎshēn,
there was a solar eclipse,
and the predicted times were all earlier than the actual.
In the ninth month of the Dīngyǒu year, on the day Dīngyǒu,
the eclipse was later than the actual.
From this, the predictions gradually diverged,
so Emperor Shìzōng ordered Zhào Zhīwēi of the Sītiānjiān to revise the Dàmíng calendar.
The calendar was completed in the eleventh year.
At that time, Yēlǜ Lǚ, a Hanlin attendant, also created the Yǐwèi calendar.
In the eleventh month of the twenty-first year, at the full moon,
there was a lunar eclipse.
So, the Shangshěng ordered the Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng Rèn Zhōngjié, along with the Sītiān calendrical officials, to verify the exact time in moments, minutes, and seconds,
and compare the accuracy of Zhīwēi's, Lǚ's, and the currently used calendar.
Zhīwēi's calendar was found to be more accurate,
so it was adopted.
In the early years of Míngchāng,
the Sītiān again improved the new calendar.
Zhāng Xíngjiǎn, a Lǐbù Lángzhōng, said:
"Please wait for another solar eclipse in the future,
re-verify it without error,
and then use it."
The matter was thus shelved.
Therefore, throughout the Jīn dynasty,
only Zhīwēi's calendar was used.
Our dynasty initially also used it,
but later changed to the Shòushí calendar.
Its records are now preserved in the Tàishǐ (Grand Historian's Office),
collected and recorded
to form the Calendrical Monograph.
Calculating Qi and Shuo, Part 1
Extended Epoch: From the Yuánjiǎzǐ to the present Dàdìng Gēngzǐ,
88,639,656 years have passed.
Day divisor: 5230 parts.
Annual constant: 1,910,224 parts.
Total remainder: 27,424 parts.
New moon constant: 154,445 parts.
Total intercalary remainder: 56,884 parts.
Year constant: 365 days,
with a remainder of 1274 parts.
New moon constant: 29 days,
with a remainder of 2775 parts.
Qi constant: 15 days,
with a remainder of 1142 parts,
60 seconds.
Full moon constant: 14 days,
with a remainder of 4002 parts,
45 seconds.
Quarter moon constant: 7 days,
with a remainder of 2001 parts,
22.5 seconds.
Obscuration limit: 4087 parts,
30 seconds.
New moon deficit: 2455 parts.
Cycle circumference: 313,080 parts.
Epoch divisor: 60.
Second mother: 90.
To find the Winter Solstice of the first month:
Set the accumulated years since the Yuánjiǎzǐ.
Multiply it by the annual constant to get the total accumulated parts.
Subtract the cycle circumference until it's less than one.
The remainder, divided by the day divisor, gives the number of days,
and the non-remainder gives the fractional parts.
Assign it to the Jiǎzǐ calculation as the greater and smaller remainders of the desired Winter Solstice of the first month.
To find the next Qi:
Set the greater and smaller remainders of the Winter Solstice of the first month.
Add the Qi constant cumulatively.
If the seconds exceed the second mother, carry over to parts;
if parts exceed the day divisor, carry over to days.
This gives the day, remainder, and seconds of the next Qi.
To find the standard new moon of the first month:
Subtract the new moon constant from the total accumulated parts.
The remainder is the intercalary remainder,
which is subtracted from the total accumulated parts to get the new moon accumulated parts.
Subtract the cycle circumference until it's less than one.
The remainder, divided by the day divisor, gives the number of days,
and the non-remainder gives the fractional parts.
This is the greater and smaller remainders of the desired standard new moon of the first month.
To find the quarter moon, full moon, and next new moon:
Set the greater and smaller remainders of the standard new moon of the first month.
Add the quarter moon constant cumulatively.
This gives the standard days and fractional seconds for each quarter moon, full moon, and next new moon.
To find the day of obscuration:
Set the smaller remainder of the Qi with obscuration.
If it is above the obscuration limit, then it is a Qi with obscuration.
Multiply it by the second mother,
include its seconds,
and subtract 477,556 from it.
If the remainder is a multiple of 6,856,
the result, combined with the greater remainder of the Qi,
is called the day of obscuration.
To find the day of extinction:
Place the fractional remainder of the Moon's disappearance.
(The fractional remainder of the synodic month that is less than a full synodic month.
)Multiply it by six.
As in 1/491.
Add the result to the integral remainder of the synodic month.
This is called the "Disappearance Day" (miè rì).
Calculating the Guà and Hòu.
Hòu Cè: Five.
Remainder: three hundred eighty.
Seconds: eighty.
Guà Cè: Six.
Remainder: four hundred fifty-seven.
Seconds: six.
Zhēn Cè: Three.
Remainder: two hundred twenty-eight.
Seconds: forty-eight.
Second denominator: ninety.
Chén Fǎ: two thousand six hundred fifteen.
Half Chén Fǎ: one thousand three hundred seven and a half.
Kè Fǎ: three hundred thirteen.
Seconds: eighty.
Chén Kè: eight.
One hundred four divisions.
Seconds: sixty.
Half Chén Kè: four.
Fifty-two divisions.
Seconds: thirty.
Second denominator: one hundred.
To find the seventy-two Hòu.
Place the integral and fractional remainders of the Zhōngqì.
Call this the "initial hòu" (chū hòu).
Add the Hòu Cè cumulatively to it.
This gives the subsequent hòu and the final hòu.
To find the sixty-four Guà.
Place the integral and fractional remainders of the Zhōngqì.
Call this the "Duke Guà" (gōng guà).
Add the Guà Cè cumulatively to it.
This gives the "Ruler Guà" (pì guà).
Add to it again.
This gives the "Marquis Inner Guà" (hóu nèi guà).
Add the Zhēn Cè to it.
This gives the beginning of the Jiéqì,
which is the "Marquis Outer Guà" (hóu wài guà).
Add the Zhēn Cè to it again.
This gives the "Grandee Guà" (dàfū guà).
Add the Guà Cè to it again.
This is the "Minister Guà" (qīng guà).
To find the "Earth King on Duty" (Tǔ Wáng Yòngshì).
Subtract the integral and fractional remainders of the four seasonal Zhōngqì using the Zhēn Cè.
This is the day when the Earth King is on duty.
To find Fālǐan.
Place the fractional remainder.
Multiply it by six.
As in 1/Chén Fǎ, this is the chén.
If it is not exact,
divide by the Kè Fǎ for the kè.
Calculated from Zǐ Zhèng (midnight).
This gives the chén, kè, and fēn of the added time.
(If half Chén Fǎ is added,
this is called the beginning of the Zǐ Kè.
