In general, for the Moon's motion in its conjunctions/oppositions: in winter, it enters the *yīnlì* (yin calendar);
in summer, it enters the *yánglì* (yang calendar);
the Moon travels along the *Qīngdào* (Green Path).
(After the Winter Solstice and Summer Solstice,
the half-conjunction of the *Qīngdào* is in the mansion of the Spring Equinox,
east of the ecliptic.
After the Beginning of Winter and Beginning of Summer,
〔三０〕the half-conjunction of the *Qīngdào* is in the mansion of the Beginning of Spring,
southeast of the ecliptic.
The same applies to the opposite mansions.)
In winter, it enters the *yánglì* (yang calendar);
in summer, it enters the *yīnlì* (yin calendar);
the Moon travels along the *Báidào* (White Path).
(After the Winter Solstice and Summer Solstice,
the half-conjunction of the *Báidào* is in the mansion of the Autumn Equinox,
west of the ecliptic.
After the Beginning of Winter and Beginning of Summer,
the half-conjunction of the *Báidào* is in the mansion of the Beginning of Autumn,
northwest of the ecliptic.
The same applies to the opposite mansions.)
In spring, it enters the *yánglì* (yang calendar);
in autumn, it enters the *yīnlì* (yin calendar);
the Moon travels along the *Zhūdào* (Vermilion Path).
(After the Spring Equinox and Autumn Equinox,
the half-conjunction of the *Zhūdào* is in the mansion of the Summer Solstice,
south of the ecliptic.
After the Beginning of Spring and Beginning of Autumn,
the half-conjunction of the *Zhūdào* is in the mansion of the Beginning of Summer,
southwest of the ecliptic.
The same applies to the opposite mansions.)
In spring, it enters the *yīnlì* (yin calendar);
in autumn, it enters the *yánglì* (yang calendar);
the Moon travels along the *Hēidào* (Black Path).
(After the Spring Equinox and Autumn Equinox,
the half-conjunction of the *Hēidào* is in the mansion of the Winter Solstice,
north of the ecliptic.
After the Beginning of Spring and Beginning of Autumn,
the half-conjunction of the *Hēidào* is in the mansion of the Beginning of Winter,
northeast of the ecliptic.
The same applies to the opposite mansions.)
The four seasons separated form the eight nodes.
When they reach the conjunctions of *yīn* and *yáng*,
they all meet with the ecliptic.
Therefore, the Moon's motion has Nine Paths.
For each, take its entered initial and final limit degrees and minutes/seconds.
Subtract one hundred and one degrees.
Multiply the remainder by the entered initial and final limit degrees and minutes.
Halve it and move the decimal place to get minutes.
When minutes reach one hundred, it becomes one degree.
This is called the *yuèdào yǔ huángdào fànchā* (Moon's path and ecliptic general difference).
Generally, for the Sun, inside the equator is *yīn*,
outside is *yáng*.
For the Moon, inside the ecliptic is *yīn*,
outside is *yáng*.
Thus, when the Moon is in true conjunction/opposition,
entering the mansions after the Summer Solstice is called the "same name" (同名).
Entering the mansions after the Winter Solstice is called the "different name" (異名).
For those in the "same name" category,
place the *yuèxíng yǔ huángdào fànchā* (Moon's motion and ecliptic general difference).
Multiply by nine and divide by eight.
This is the *dìngchā* (fixed difference).
After the half-conjunction and before the true conjunction/opposition,
subtract the difference.
After the true conjunction/opposition and before the half-conjunction,
add the difference.
(This addition/subtraction results in a six-degree difference.
When "same,"
it is like the difference between the ecliptic and equator intersecting with the same name.
If the comparison gradually varies,
then it changes differently depending on the location of the conjunction/opposition.)
Still, take the true conjunction/opposition degrees from the Autumn Equinox degrees.
Multiply by the *dìngchā* (fixed difference).
As one of a quadrant,
the result is the *yuèdào yǔ chìdào dìngchā* (Moon's path and equator fixed difference).
What was previously added becomes subtracted,
and what was subtracted becomes added.
For those in the "different name" category,
place the *yuèxíng yǔ huángdào fànchā* (Moon's motion and ecliptic general difference).
Multiply by seven and divide by eight.
〔三一〕This is the *dìngchā* (fixed difference).
After the half-conjunction and before the true conjunction/opposition,
add the difference.
After the true conjunction/opposition and before the half-conjunction,
subtract the difference.
(This addition/subtraction results in a six-degree difference.
When "different,"
it is like the difference between the ecliptic and equator intersecting with different names.
If the comparison gradually becomes similar,
then it changes inconsistently depending on the location of the conjunction/opposition.)
Still, take the true conjunction/opposition degrees from the Spring Equinox degrees.
Multiply by the *dìngchā* (fixed difference).
As one of a quadrant,
the result is the *yuèdào yǔ chìdào dìngchā* (Moon's path and equator fixed difference).
〔三二〕What was previously added becomes subtracted,
and what was subtracted becomes added.
Add or subtract each from the accumulated ecliptic lunar mansion degrees.
This yields the *jiǔdào xiùjīdù* (accumulated Nine Paths lunar mansion degrees).
Subtract the accumulated Nine Paths degrees of the previous mansion from this.
This gives the Nine Paths degrees and minutes for that mansion.
(The minutes are rounded to *tàibànshǎo* (excess, half, or deficit).
〔三三〕Regarding spring, summer, autumn, and winter, the mansion degrees where the Sun is located during the four seasons are taken as correct.)
Calculating the lunar distance from the Nine Paths mansions at true conjunction/opposition plus-time
Take the ecliptic daily degrees and minutes at true conjunction/opposition plus-time.
Subtract one hundred and one degrees.
Multiply the remainder by the true conjunction/opposition degrees and minutes.
Halve it and move the decimal place to get minutes.
When minutes reach one hundred, it becomes one degree.
This is called the *yuèdào yǔ huángdào fànchā* (Moon's path and ecliptic general difference).
For those in the "same name" category,
place the *yuèxíng yǔ huángdào fànchā* (Moon's motion and ecliptic general difference).
Multiply by nine and divide by eight.
This is the *dìngchā* (fixed difference),
to be added.
Still, take the true conjunction/opposition degrees from the Autumn Equinox degrees.
Multiply by the *dìngchā* (fixed difference).
As one of a quadrant,
the result is the *yuèdào yǔ chìdào dìngchā* (Moon's path and equator fixed difference),
to be subtracted.
For those in the "different name" category,
place the *yuèxíng yǔ huángdào fànchā* (Moon's motion and ecliptic general difference).
Multiply by seven and divide by eight.
This is the *dìngchā* (fixed difference),
to be subtracted.
Still, take the true conjunction/opposition degrees from the Spring Equinox degrees.
Multiply by the *dìngchā* (fixed difference).
As one of a quadrant,
the result is the *yuèdào yǔ chìdào dìngchā* (Moon's path and equator fixed difference),
to be added.
Place the ecliptic lunar degrees and minutes at true conjunction/opposition plus-time.
Add or subtract the two differences from it.
This then becomes the *zhèngjiāo jiāshí yuèlí jiǔdào xiùdù jí fēn* (true conjunction/opposition plus-time lunar distance from the Nine Paths mansions degrees and minutes).
Calculating the lunar position degrees at the *dìngshuò xiánwàng jiāshí* (fixed new moon, quarter, and full moon plus-times)
Place the Sun's position in the ecliptic lunar mansions at the *dìngshuò jiāshí* (fixed new moon plus-time).
Generally, at the *héshuò jiāshí* (new moon conjunction plus-time),
the Moon's motion is hidden beneath the Sun,
at the same degree as the Sun.
This is the *jiāshí yuèlí xiùcì* (plus-time lunar distance from the mansion position).
For each, add the *xiánwàngdù jí fēnmiǎo* (quarter and full moon degrees and minutes/seconds)
to the Sun's position in the ecliptic lunar mansions at its respective *xiánwàng jiāshí* (quarter and full moon plus-time).
Subtract the full mansion positions.
Name it as before.

This yields the *dìngshuò xiánwàng jiāshí yuè suǒzài huángdào xiùdù jí fēnmiǎo* (fixed new moon, quarter, and full moon plus-time lunar position in the ecliptic lunar mansion degrees, minutes, and seconds).
Calculating the Nine Paths lunar degrees at the *dìngshuò xiánwàng jiāshí* (fixed new moon, quarter, and full moon plus-times)
For each, take the lunar distance from the ecliptic lunar mansions degrees and minutes/seconds at the *dìngshuò xiánwàng jiāshí* (fixed new moon, quarter, and full moon plus-time).
Add the accumulated ecliptic degrees after the true conjunction/opposition of the previous mansion.
〔三四〕This is the *dìngshuò xiánwàng jiāshí zhèngjiāo hòu huángdào jīdù* (fixed new moon, quarter, and full moon plus-time accumulated ecliptic degrees after true conjunction/opposition).
Calculate the accumulated Nine Paths degrees as before.
Subtract the accumulated Nine Paths degrees of the previous mansion.

The remainder is the *dìngshuò xiánwàng jiāshí jiǔdào yuèlí xiùdù jí fēnmiǎo* (fixed new moon, quarter, and full moon plus-time Nine Paths lunar distance from the mansions degrees, minutes, and seconds).
(At the *héshuò jiāshí* (new moon conjunction plus-time),
if it is not a true conjunction/opposition,
then the Sun is on the ecliptic,
and the Moon is on the Nine Paths.
The entered mansion degrees,
although varying slightly,
if their two poles are examined,
should correspond to the standard.
Thus it is said: "The Moon's motion is hidden beneath the Sun,
at the same degree as the Sun,"
meaning it is the *jiāshí jiǔdào yuèdù* (plus-time Nine Paths lunar degrees).
For calculating the lunar degrees at dawn, dusk, and midnight,
all follow the preceding method.)
Step Six: Calculating Conjunctions and Oppositions
Conjunction/Opposition termination minutes: one hundred forty-two thousand three hundred nineteen.
Seconds: nine thousand three hundred sixty-eight.
The **jiāo zhōng** day: twenty-seventh day,
remainder one thousand one hundred nine parts,
and nine thousand three hundred sixty-eight seconds.
The **jiāo zhōng** day: thirteenth,
remainder three thousand one hundred sixty-nine,
and nine thousand six hundred eighty-four seconds.
The **jiāo shuò** day: second,
remainder one thousand six hundred sixty-five,
and six hundred thirty-two seconds.
The **jiāo wàng** day: fourteenth,
remainder four thousand two,
and five thousand seconds.
Second denominator: ten thousand.
The **jiāo zhōng** [degree]: three hundred sixty-three degrees,
seventy-nine parts,
thirty-six seconds.
The **jiāo zhōng** [degree]: one hundred eighty-one degrees,
eighty-nine parts,
sixty-eight seconds.
The **jiāo xiàng** [degree]: ninety degrees,
ninety-four parts,
eighty-four seconds.
Half **jiāo xiàng**: forty-five degrees,
forty-seven parts,
forty-two seconds.
Solar eclipse maximum limit: two thousand four hundred.
Fixed method: two hundred forty-eight.
Solar eclipse maximum posterior limit: three thousand one hundred.
Fixed method: three hundred twenty.
Lunar eclipse limit: five thousand one hundred.
Lunar eclipse maximum limit:
Fixed method: three hundred forty.
one thousand seven hundred.
Set the integral of the **tiān zhèng shuò**,
divide by the **jiāo zhōng** parts.
If there is a remainder,
use the day method as one [unit],
this is the day.
What is less than a day is the remainder.
This is the **tiān zhèng** eleventh month **jīng shuò** additional time entering **jiāo** general day and remainder seconds.
Add the **jiāo shuò** to this,
to get the next **shuò**.
Add the **jiāo wàng** to this,
to get the next **wàng**.
Adding the **jiāo wàng** again
also yields the next **shuò**.
Each is the **shuò** or **wàng** entry into **jiāo** general day and remainder seconds.
To find the fixed **shuò** daily midnight entry into **jiāo**
Set each general day and remainder seconds for entry into **jiāo**,
subtract the **jīng shuò** and **wàng** small remainders.
This is the fixed **shuò** and **wàng** midnight entry into **jiāo** general day and remainder seconds.
If the fixed **shuò** and **wàng** advance or retreat,
the **jiāo** day also advances or retreats.
Otherwise, the **jīng** is taken as the fixed.
For a large month, add two days.
For a small month, add one day.
For all others, add four thousand one hundred twenty seconds and six hundred thirty-two.
This is the next **shuò** midnight entry into **jiāo**.
Accumulate by adding one day.
When it reaches the **jiāo zhōng** day and remainder seconds, subtract it.
This is the daily midnight entry into **jiāo** general day and remainder seconds.
To find the fixed **shuò wàng** additional time entry into **jiāo**
Set the **jīng shuò** and **wàng** additional time entry into **jiāo** general day and remainder seconds.
Using the fixed numbers for entry into **qì** and entry into **zhuǎn tiǎo nuò**,
subtract **tiǎo** and add **nuò**.
This is the fixed **shuò wàng** additional time entry into **jiāo** general day and remainder seconds.
To find the fixed **shuò wàng** additional time entry into **jiāo** accumulated degrees and **yīn yáng** calendar
Set the fixed **shuò** and **wàng** additional time entry into **jiāo** general day.
Multiply it by the day method.
The remainder within,
advance two places.
Using thirty-nine thousand one hundred twenty-one as one [unit] gives degrees.
What is less is converted backwards to parts and seconds.
This is the fixed **shuò** and **wàng** additional time lunar motion entry into **jiāo** accumulated degrees.
Using the fixed **shuò** and **wàng** additional time entry into **zhuǎn chí jí** degrees,
subtract **chí** and add **jí**.
This is the lunar motion entry into **jiāo** fixed accumulated degrees.
If it is below the **jiāo zhōng** degree,
it enters the **yáng lì** accumulated degrees.
If it is above,
subtract it.
The remainder is the entry into **yīn lì** accumulated degrees.
(For daily midnight,
calculate according to this.)
Observe the moon's entry into **yīn yáng lì** accumulated degrees and parts.
If it is below the **jiāo xiàng**,
it is the lesser **xiàng**.
If it is above,
subtract the **jiāo zhōng** from it again.
The remainder is the greater **xiàng**.
Place the entered greater or lesser **xiàng** degree above.
List the **jiāo xiàng** degree below.
Subtract and multiply them.
Double and move the decimal place to get parts.
One hundred parts make a degree.
Use this to subtract from the entered greater or lesser **xiàng** degree and parts.
The remainder is then subtracted from and multiplied by the **jiāo zhōng** degree.
Multiply by eight.
Divide by one hundred ten to get parts.
One hundred parts make a degree.
This gives the moon's departure from the ecliptic degree.
To find the **shuò wàng** additional time entry into **jiāo** constant day and fixed day
Set the **shuò wàng** entry into **jiāo** general day.
Using the fixed numbers for entry into **qì tiǎo nuò**,
subtract **tiǎo** and add **nuò**.
This is the entry into **jiāo** constant day.
Also, set the fixed numbers for entry into **zhuǎn tiǎo nuò**.
Advance one place.
One hundred twenty-seven as one [unit].
The resulting **tiǎo** subtracted and **nuò** added to the entry into **jiāo** constant day,
is the entry into **jiāo** fixed day
To find the entry into **jiāo yīn yáng lì** parts before and after the **jiāo**
Observe the entry into **jiāo** fixed day.
If it is below the **jiāo zhōng**,
it is the **yáng lì**.
If it is above,
subtract it.
It is the **yīn lì**.
If it is around one day,
(convert days to parts using the day method.)
It is the parts after the **jiāo**.
If it is around thirteen days,
subtract the **jiāo zhōng** from it again.
It is the parts before the **jiāo**.
To find the fixed remainder of the maximum extent of solar and lunar eclipses
Set the **shuò** and **wàng** entry into **qì** and entry into **zhuǎn tiǎo nuò** fixed numbers.
Add those with the same name, subtract those with different names.
Multiply by one thousand three hundred thirty-seven.
Divide by the fixed **shuò** and **wàng** additional time entry into **zhuǎn** calculation of the external **zhuǎn** fixed parts.
The result,
subtract **tiǎo** and add **nuò** to the **jīng shuò** and **wàng** small remainder.
This is the general remainder.
For a solar eclipse: observe the general remainder. If it is below half the method,
it is the middle anterior parts.
If it is above half the method,
subtract half the method.
It is the middle posterior parts.
Set the middle anterior and posterior parts.
Subtract and multiply by half the method.
Double it.
Divide by ten thousand to get parts.
This is called the time difference.
For middle anterior,
subtract the time difference from the general remainder to get the fixed remainder.
Subtract half the method again.
The remainder is the parts before noon.
For middle posterior,
add the time difference to the general remainder to get the fixed remainder.
Subtract half the method.
It is the parts after noon.
For a lunar eclipse: observe the general remainder. If it is after sunset and before midnight,
if it is below three-quarters of the day method,
subtract half the method.
It is the parts before **yǒu**.
If it is above three-quarters,
subtract the day method again.
The remainder is the parts after **yǒu**.
Also, observe the general remainder. If it is after midnight and before sunrise,
if it is below one-quarter of the day method,
it is the parts before **mǎo**.
If it is above one-quarter,
subtract half the method again.
The remainder is the parts after **mǎo**.
For these parts before and after **mǎo** and **yǒu**,
multiply them by themselves.
Multiply by four.
Move the decimal place back.
Divide by ten thousand to get parts.
Add this to the general remainder.
It is the fixed remainder.
Set each fixed remainder.
Calculate using the method of **fā liǎn** additional time.
This gives the **chén kè** of the solar or lunar eclipse maximum.
To find the solar and lunar eclipse maximum daily motion accumulated degrees
Set the fixed **shuò** and **wàng** eclipse maximum large and small remainders.
The remainder after subtracting them from the **jīng shuò** and **wàng** large and small remainders
is used to add or subtract the **jīng shuò** and **wàng** entry into **qì** daily small remainder.
(For **jīng shuò** and **wàng** day, if less, add; if more, subtract.)
This is the eclipse maximum entry into **qì**.
Add this to its accumulated amount within the **qì**.
This is the eclipse maximum middle accumulated amount.
Also, set the eclipse maximum entry into **qì** small remainder.
Multiply by the daily gain and loss rate for the entered **qì**
Add or subtract this from its daily **yíng suō** accumulated amount.
Add for **yíng**, subtract for **suō** from the eclipse maximum middle accumulated amount.
This is the eclipse maximum daily motion accumulated degrees and parts.
To find the **qì** difference
Set the accumulated degrees and minutes of the Sun's daily motion on the day of the solar eclipse maximum.
If it reaches the mean limit, subtract it.
If the remainder is below the quadrant,
it is the first limit.
If above,
subtract it again from the mean limit
to get the last limit.
In both cases, multiply the value by itself,
advance two decimal places,
and multiply by one four hundred seventy-eighth (1/478).
The result
is subtracted from one thousand seven hundred forty-four (1744).
The remainder is the *qìchā* number (氣差數).
Multiply it by the minutes before or after noon.
Divide by half the daytime minutes.
The result
is the constant number to be subtracted.
(If it is not enough to subtract,
subtract it in reverse
to get the constant number.
What should be added is subtracted;
what should be subtracted is added.)
After the spring equinox,
the *yánglì* (陽曆) subtracts,
the *yīnlì* (陰曆) adds.
After the autumn equinox,
the *yánglì* adds,
the *yīnlì* subtracts.
(Two days and two thousand one hundred minutes before the spring equinox and after the autumn equinox constitute the *dìngqì* (定氣).
Perform addition and subtraction here.)
To find the *kèchā* (刻差):
Set the accumulated degrees and minutes of the Sun's daily motion on the day of the solar eclipse maximum.
If it reaches the mean limit, subtract it.
Subtract the remainder from the mean limit, and multiply the result by itself.
Advance two decimal places,
and multiply by one four hundred seventy-eighth (1/478).
The result
is the *kèchā* number.
Multiply it by the minutes before or after noon.
Divide by one-fourth (1/4) of the day's method.
The result is the constant number.
(If it is above the number,
double the number,
then subtract the obtained number from it to get the constant number,
and apply addition or subtraction accordingly.)
After the winter solstice,
before noon: *yáng* adds, *yīn* subtracts;
after noon: *yáng* subtracts, *yīn* adds.
After the summer solstice,
before noon: *yáng* subtracts, *yīn* adds;
after noon: *yáng* adds, *yīn* subtracts.
To find the constant minutes before and after the conjunction for a solar eclipse [四二]
The two constant numbers for *qìchā* and *kèchā*:
If they have the same sign, add them;
if they have different signs, subtract them.
This gives the eclipse difference.
Apply addition or subtraction to the minutes before and after the conjunction
to get the constant minutes before and after the conjunction.
Observe the constant minutes before and after.
If it is in *yánglì*,
there is no eclipse.
If it is in *yīnlì*,
there is an eclipse.
If the *yīnlì* before the conjunction is not enough to subtract,
subtract it in reverse
(reverse subtract the eclipse difference)
to get the *yánglì* after the conjunction.
If the *yīnlì* after the conjunction is not enough to subtract,
subtract it in reverse
to get the *yánglì* before the conjunction;
then there is no eclipse.
If the *yánglì* before the conjunction is not enough to subtract, [四三]
subtract it in reverse
to get the *yīnlì* after the conjunction.
If the *yánglì* after the conjunction
is not enough to subtract,
subtract it in reverse
to get the *yīnlì* before the conjunction; [四四]
then there will be an eclipse on that day.
To find the magnitude of a solar eclipse:
Observe the constant minutes before and after the conjunction.
If it is below two thousand four hundred (2400),
it is the "minutes before totality".
Divide by two hundred forty-eight (248) to get the "major part" (大分).
If it is above two thousand four hundred (2400),
subtract it again from five thousand five hundred (5500).
(If it is not enough to subtract, there is no eclipse.)
This is the "minutes after totality".
Divide by three hundred twenty (320) to get the "major part".
If there is a remainder,
divide it further to get "seconds".
This gives the minutes and seconds of the solar eclipse.
To find the magnitude of a lunar eclipse:
Observe the minutes before and after the conjunction
(without using the *qìchā* and *kèchā* differences).
If it is below one thousand seven hundred (1700),
it is a total eclipse.
If it is above,
subtract it again from five thousand one hundred (5100).
(If it is not enough to subtract, there is no eclipse.)
Divide the remainder by three hundred forty (340) to get the "major part".
If there is a remainder,
divide it further to get "seconds".
This is the minutes and seconds of the lunar eclipse.
If the conjunction minutes are below the totality limit,
subtract them again from the totality limit,
and also divide by three hundred forty (340),
to get the "major part within totality".
To find the "constant duration minutes" (定用分) for a solar eclipse:
Set the "major part" of the solar eclipse.
Subtract it from thirty (30) minutes and multiply the result by itself.
Then multiply by two thousand four hundred fifty (2450).
Divide this by the "constant minutes" (定分) obtained from the outer rotation calculation (外轉算) when the constant new moon (定朔) enters the rotation calculation (轉算). [四五]
The result
is the "constant duration minutes".
Subtract the "constant remainder" (定餘)
to get the minutes for the first contact (*chūkúi* 初虧).
Add the "constant remainder"
to get the minutes for the last contact (*fùyuán* 復圓).
Calculate each using the "addition of time method for expansion and contraction" (*fāliǎn jiāshí fǎ* 發歛加時法).
This gives the *chénkè* (辰刻) for the three limits of the solar eclipse.
To find the "constant duration minutes" for a lunar eclipse:
Set the "major part" of the lunar eclipse.
Subtract it from thirty-five (35) minutes and multiply the result by itself.
Then multiply by two thousand one hundred (2100).
Divide this by the "constant minutes" obtained from the outer rotation calculation when the constant full moon (定望) enters the rotation [四六] calculation.
The result
is the "constant duration minutes".
Add or subtract the "constant remainder"
to get the minutes for the first contact and last contact.
Calculate each using the "addition of time method for expansion and contraction".
This gives the *chénkè* for the three limits of the lunar eclipse.
For a total lunar eclipse:
Subtract the "major part within totality" from fifteen (15) and multiply the result by itself.
Then multiply by four thousand two hundred (4200).
Divide this by the "constant minutes" obtained from the outer rotation [四七] calculation when the constant full moon enters the rotation calculation.
The result
is the "minutes within totality" (既內分).
Subtract this from the "constant duration minutes"
to get the "minutes outside totality" (既外分).
Set the "constant remainder" of the lunar eclipse, subtract the "constant duration minutes"
to get the first contact.
Then add the "minutes outside totality"
to get the totality (*shíjì* 食既).
Then add the "minutes within totality"
to get the maximum eclipse (*shíshèn* 食甚).
(This is also the "constant remainder minutes".)
Add the "minutes within totality" again
to get the regaining of light (*shēngguāng* 生光).
Then add the "minutes outside totality" again
to get the last contact.
Calculate each using the "addition of time method for expansion and contraction".
This gives the *chénkè* for the five limits of the lunar eclipse.
To find the *gēngdiǎn* (更點) for a lunar eclipse:
Set the *chénfēn* (晨分) of the day when the maximum eclipse occurs.
Double it.
Divide by five to get the *gēngfǎ* (更法).
Divide the *gēngfǎ* by five again
to get the *diǎnfǎ* (點法). [四八]
Then set the various minutes for the beginning and end of the lunar eclipse.
If above *hūnfēn* (昏分), subtract *hūnfēn*.
If below *chénfēn*, add *chénfēn*.
If it does not reach the *gēngfǎ*, it is the first *gēng*.
If it does not reach the *diǎnfǎ*, it is the first *diǎn*.
Calculate sequentially according to the method,
and you will get the number of *gēng* and *diǎn* for each.
To find the direction of a solar eclipse:
If the eclipse is before totality:
The first contact is in the southwest,
the maximum eclipse is in the due south,
and the last contact is in the southeast.
If the eclipse is after totality:
The first contact is in the northwest,
the maximum eclipse is in the due north,
and the last contact is in the northeast.
If the eclipse is eight parts (8/10) or more,
it all begins in the due west
and ends in the due east.
(This is based on the location at due noon.)
To find the direction of a lunar eclipse:
If the moon is in *yánglì*: The first contact begins in the northeast,
the maximum eclipse is in the due north,
and the last contact is in the northwest.
If the moon is in *yīnlì*: The first contact begins in the southeast,
the maximum eclipse is in the due south,
and the last contact is in the southwest.
If the eclipse is eight parts (8/10) or more,
it all begins in the due east
and ends in the due west.
(This is also based on the location at due noon.) [四九] To find the visible magnitude of a solar or lunar eclipse during sunrise or sunset
Subtract the very small remainder of each eclipse
from the difference between sunrise and sunset;
the remainder is the "eclipse-band difference" (dàishíchā).
Multiply this by the portion eaten,
and divide by the full "fixed-use portion."
(For a total lunar eclipse,
subtract the eclipse-band difference from the portion within totality,
multiply the remainder by the portion eaten,
and divide by the portion outside totality.
If it is insufficient to subtract,
it is an eclipse-band visible at sunrise or sunset.)
Subtract this from the portion eaten,
which is the portion of the sun or moon's eclipse-band seen at sunrise or sunset.
(If the greatest eclipse occurs during the day,
dawn is the gradual ingress,
and dusk is the egress.
If the greatest eclipse occurs at night,
dawn is the egress,
and dusk is the gradual ingress.)
To find the xìu-subdivision (sùcì) of the greatest eclipse of the sun and moon:
Set the accumulated degrees of the daily motion of the sun and moon at the greatest eclipse.
(At full moon, add an additional half-circumference.)
Add the degrees of the ecliptic for the day at the winter solstice of the Tiānzhèng (天正) calendar plus the time correction.
Sum them and name the result.
Subtract the ecliptic xìu-subdivision from this,
and you will obtain the xìu-degrees and minutes for the greatest eclipse of the sun and moon.
