Set the general accumulated minutes.
Subtract the circumferential ratio of each planet from it.
If there is a remainder,
it is the accumulated minutes before conjunction.
Then subtract the circumferential ratio again,
and the remainder is the accumulated minutes after conjunction.
Divide by the daily method (rìfǎ).
If it is insufficient, carry over as minutes and seconds.
This is the accumulated minutes and mean star of that planet's mean conjunction after the winter solstice of the Tiānzhèng calendar.
(When named as days,
it is called accumulated minutes.
When named as degrees,
it is called mean star.)
Add the segment days cumulatively to the accumulated minutes,
which gives the accumulated minutes for all segments.
Add the mean degrees cumulatively to the mean star,
this gives the mean star for all segments.
To find the entry into the calendar for the mean conjunction and all segments of the Five Planets:
Set the previous general accumulated minutes.
Add the accumulated minutes after conjunction for each planet.
Subtract the calendar ratio from it.
If there is a remainder,
divide by that planet's calendar degree method to get degrees.
If it is insufficient, carry over as minutes and seconds.
This is the entry into the calendar in degrees, minutes, and seconds for that planet's mean conjunction.
Add the limit degrees of all segments cumulatively,
which gives the entry into the calendar for all segments.
To find the increase/decrease difference for the mean conjunction and all segments of the Five Planets:
Set the entry into the calendar in degrees, minutes, and seconds for that planet's segment.
If it is below or equal to the calendar mean,
it is an increase.
If it is above,
subtract the calendar mean.
The remainder is a decrease.
Divide this by that planet's calendar calculation interval to get the calculation number.
The remainder is the degrees and minutes within the calculation interval.
Set the calculation number outside the calculation.
Multiply it by the increase/decrease rate below that calculation number.
Divide by the calendar calculation interval to get minutes.
Add or subtract this to the accumulated increase/decrease degrees below it.
This is the fixed increase/decrease difference for that planet's segment.
To find the fixed accumulated minutes for the mean conjunction and all segments of the Five Planets:
Set the mean accumulated minutes for that planet's segment.
Add or subtract the fixed increase/decrease difference (add for increase, subtract for decrease).
This is the fixed accumulated days and minutes for that segment.
Add the Tiānzhèng winter solstice grand remainder and fractional minutes.
If it reaches 60 of the jìfǎ (紀法), subtract it.
The remainder,
if any, is the fixed day and the added time in minutes and seconds.
If it is insufficient, assign the Jiǎzǐ (甲子) cycle outside the calculation.
This gives the day's stem and branch.
To find the month and day of the Five Planets and all segments:
Set the fixed accumulated days and minutes for each segment.
Add the Tiānzhèng intercalary days and minutes.
Divide by the suòcè (朔策) (new moon interval) and fractional minutes to get the number of months.
The remainder,
if any, is the number of days and minutes elapsed in the current month.
Assign the number of months outside the 11th month of the Tiānzhèng calendar.
This gives the number of days and minutes after the new moon for that segment.
The distance to the day's stem and branch gives the month and day of the local fixed new moon.
To find the corrected star position for the mean conjunction and all segments of the Five Planets with time correction:
Set the mean star.
Add or subtract the fixed increase/decrease difference (add for increase, subtract for decrease).
(For Venus, double it,
for Mercury, triple it,
and then add or subtract.)
Add the degrees of the ecliptic for the day at the winter solstice of the Tiānzhèng calendar plus the time correction.
Name it according to the xìu-subdivision,
which gives the xìu-degrees and minutes and seconds of that planet's segment at the corrected time.
To find the fixed star position at midnight before the first day of each segment of the Five Planets
Each segment's initial daily rate
is multiplied by its segment's constant accumulated days, then added to hours and minutes.
Divide by one hundred.
Then, subtract the segment's fixed daily increment of hours and minutes for the stars.
This gives the initial daily fixed star position in *sùdù* for that segment, at midnight before dawn.
To find the daily rate and *dù* rate for all segments:
For each segment, the interval between its daily *chén* and the next segment's daily *chén* is its daily rate.
Subtract the *sù* position at midnight of the current segment from that of the next segment;
the remainder is the *dù* rate.
To find the parallel divisions for all segments:
Take each segment's *dù* rate, including *fēn* and *miǎo*.
Divide it by the segment's daily rate.
This gives the segment's parallel *dù*, *fēn*, and *miǎo*.
To find the total difference and daily difference for all segments:
Subtract the preceding parallel division from the succeeding one in the current segment;
the remainder is the general difference for that segment.
(For example, to find the general difference for Júpiter's *cìjí*,
subtract the parallel divisions for *shùnjí* and *shùnchí*;
the remainder is the *cìjí* general difference.
All others follow this pattern.)
Double this and shift the decimal place to get the increment/decrement difference.
Add or subtract this from the segment's parallel division
to get the initial and final daily motion divisions.
(If the former is greater than the latter,
add for the initial,
subtract for the final.
If the former is less than the latter,
subtract for the initial,
add for the final.)
Double the increment/decrement difference to get the total difference.
Divide it by (daily rate minus one)
to get the daily difference.
To find the increment/decrement difference for preceding and succeeding *fúchí* and *tuì* segments:
For preceding *fú*,
take the initial daily motion division of the succeeding segment,
add half of its daily difference,
to get the final daily motion division.
For succeeding *fú*,
take the final daily motion division of the preceding segment,
add half of its daily difference,
to get the initial daily motion division.
Subtract this from the *fú* segment's parallel division;
the remainder is the increment/decrement difference.
For preceding *chí*,
take the final daily motion division of the preceding segment,
subtract double its daily difference,
to get the initial daily motion division.
For succeeding *chí*,
take the initial daily motion division of the succeeding segment,
subtract double its daily difference,
to get the final daily motion division.
Subtract this from the *chí* segment's parallel division;
the remainder is the increment/decrement difference.
(This applies to the *chí* segments near the preceding and succeeding stationary points.)
For the three stars, Mùxīng (Júpiter), Huǒxīng (Mars), and Tǔxīng (Saturn), when retrograding,
multiply the parallel division by six,
shift the decimal place one position,
to get the increment/decrement difference.
For Jīnxīng (Vénus)'s preceding and succeeding *fú* and *tuì*,
multiply the parallel division by three,
halve it and shift the decimal place,
to get the increment/decrement difference.
For preceding *tuì*,
take the initial daily motion division of the succeeding segment,
subtract its daily difference,
to get the final daily motion division.
For succeeding *tuì*,
take the final daily motion division of the preceding segment,
subtract its daily difference,
to get the initial daily motion division.
Subtract this from the current segment's parallel division;
the remainder is the increment/decrement difference.
For Shuǐxīng (Mércury),
half the parallel division is the increment/decrement difference.
In all cases, add or subtract the increment/decrement difference from the parallel division
to get the initial and final daily motion divisions.
(If the former is greater than the latter,
add to the initial, subtract from the final;
if the former is less than the latter,
subtract from the initial, add to the final.)
Then, double the increment/decrement difference to get the total difference.
Divide it by (daily rate minus one)
to get the daily difference.
To find the *sù* position of the stars at midnight before dawn each day:
Take the initial daily motion division of each segment.
Adjust it cumulatively by the daily difference (add or subtract).
(If the latter is less, subtract;
if the latter is more, add.)
This gives the daily motion in *dù*, *fēn*, and *miǎo*.
Then, add or subtract in order,
remove full *sù* positions,
to get the *sù* position of the star at midnight before dawn each day.
(The difference between the final daily motion of the preceding segment and the initial daily motion of the succeeding segment
should preferably not exceed one or two daily differences.
If it exceeds the daily difference by several multiples,
or is inverted and illogical,
one should adjust the increment/decrement difference of the preceding and succeeding sections slightly by addition or subtraction
[七一] to make it logical,
and then use it.
If both preceding and succeeding parallel divisions are either both greater or both lesser,
then record them as flat.
If the *miǎo* of the total difference
is less than one *fēn*,
also record it as flat.
If it is illogical but becomes logical when recorded as flat,
also record it as flat.)
To find the conjunction (*pínghé*) and appearance/occultation (*jiànfú*) and entry into qi (*rùqì*) for the five planets:
Set the accumulated constant.
Divide it by the *qìcè* and the reduction *fēn*.
This gives the *qì* number.
Any remainder gives the days, *fēn*, and *miǎo* for entry into *qì*.
When computed from the *tiānzhèng dōngzhì* outside the calculation,
this is the sought *pínghé*, *fújiàn*, and entry into *qì* days, *fēn*, and *miǎo*.
To find the motion difference (*xíngchā*) for the five planets' *pínghé* and *jiànfú*:
Subtract each segment's initial daily star motion division from its solar daily motion division;
the remainder is the *xíngchā*.
If Jīnxīng is retrograding,
and Shuǐxīng is in retrograde conjunction,
add them together to get the *xíngchā*.
If Shuǐxīng is occulted in the evening and appears in the morning,
directly use the solar daily motion division as the *xíngchā*.
To find the general accumulated constant (*fánjī*) for the five planets' *dìnghé*, *dìngjiàn*, and *dìngfú*:
For the three stars, Mùxīng, Huǒxīng, and Tǔxīng,
their *pínghé* morning-rapid evening-occultation accumulated constants
are directly their *dìnghé*, *dìngjiàn*, and *dìngfú* general accumulated constants.
For the two stars, Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng,
take their segment's *yíngsuōchā*.
(Double for Shuǐxīng.)
Divide each by the *xíngchā*.
This gives the days;
any remainder is reduced and converted to *fēn* and *miǎo*.
If it is in *pínghé* evening-appearance morning-occultation,
subtract *yíng* and add *suō*;
if it is in retrograde conjunction evening-occultation morning-appearance,
add *yíng* and subtract *suō*.
In all cases, add or subtract the constant accumulated
to get the *dìnghé*, *dìngjiàn*, and *dìngfú* general accumulated constant.
To find the fixed star position (*dìngxīng*) for the five planets' *dìnghé* and accumulated constant:
For the three stars, Mùxīng, Huǒxīng, and Tǔxīng,
divide their *pínghé xíngchā* by their daily solar *yíngsuōchā*.
This gives the days of difference from conjunction.
Subtract the solar *yíngsuōchā* from this.
This gives the *dù* of difference from conjunction.
If the day is in an *yínglì* period,
subtract the days of difference and *dù* of difference.
If it is in a *suō* period,
add them.
Add or subtract this from the star's *dìnghé fánjī*
to get the *dìnghé dìngjī dìngxīng*.
For Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng's direct conjunction and retrograde conjunction,
[七二] divide their *pínghé* and *tuìhé xíngchā* [七三] by their daily solar *yíngsuōchā*.
This gives the days of difference from conjunction.
Add or subtract the solar *yíngsuōchā* in order.
This gives the *dù* of difference from conjunction.
If direct motion is in an *yínglì* period,
add the days of difference and *dù* of difference;
if in a *suō* period,
subtract them.
If retrograde motion is in an *yínglì* period,
subtract the days of difference,
add the *dù* of difference;
if in a *suō* period,
add the days of difference,
subtract the *dù* of difference.
In all cases, add or subtract this from the star's *dìnghé* and *zàidìnghé fánjī*
to get the *dìnghé* and *zàidìnghé dìngjī dìngxīng*.
Add the *dōngzhì dàyú* and reduction *fēn* to the accumulated constant.
Remove full cycles according to the *jìfǎ*,
name it,
and this gives the *dìnghé rìchén*.
Add the *dōngzhì* adjusted time ecliptic daily *dù* to the fixed star position.
Remove full *sù* positions,
and this gives the *sù* position of the *dìnghé*.
(The *yíngsuō* for its direct and retrograde positions
is the solar *yíngsuō*.)
To find the accumulated constant days for Mùxīng, Huǒxīng, and Tǔxīng's *dìngjiàn* and *dìngfú*:
Take each star's *dìngjiànfú fánjī*.
Add for morning, subtract for evening, the *xiàngxiàn* days, *fēn*, and *miǎo*.
(Half of the *zhōngxiàn* is the *xiàngxiàn*.)
[七四] If below the *zhōngxiàn*,
multiply by itself.
If above,
subtract from the *suìzhōu* days, *fēn*, and *miǎo*.
The remainder is also multiplied by itself.
For every seventy-five, count as one.
[七五] The result
is multiplied by the star's *fújiàn* *dù*.
Divide by fifteen.
This is the difference.
The difference, divided by its segment's *xíngchā*,
gives the days.
Any remainder is reduced and converted to *fēn* and *miǎo*.
Add for appearance (*jiàn*), subtract for occultation (*fú*), from the general accumulated constant to get the fixed accumulated constant.
[七六] Add the name as before,
and this gives the *rìchén*.
To find Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng's *dìngjiànfú dìngjī rì* [七七]
Each calculates the daily difference of concealment and appearance,
removing the daily solar eccentricity difference
to obtain the day.
If it is concealed in the morning and appears in the evening,
and the sun is in the ascending calendar,
add it.
If it is in the descending,
subtract it.
If it is concealed in the evening and appears in the morning,
and the sun is in the ascending calendar,
subtract it.
If it is in the descending,
add it.
Add or subtract the accumulated stellar latitude to obtain the constant accumulation.
Observe the constant accumulation:
if it is below the middle limit,
it is after the winter solstice.
If above,
subtract it from the full circle;
the remainder is after the summer solstice.
For either period after the solstices,
if it is below the quadrant,
multiply it by itself.
If above,
subtract it from the middle limit,
and also multiply it by itself.
Divide each by the given method
to get the fen.
(After the winter solstice, morning appearance/evening concealment,
use eighteen as the divisor.
After the winter solstice, evening appearance/morning concealment,
and after the summer solstice, morning appearance/evening concealment,
use seventy-five as the divisor.
) Multiply by the degrees of concealment and appearance,
divide by fifteen,
to get the difference.
If the difference is a full daily difference,
divide by it to get the day.
If not full, convert to fen and miao.
Add or subtract the constant accumulation to get the fixed accumulation.
(After the winter solstice, morning appearance and evening concealment,
add it;
evening appearance and morning concealment,
subtract it.
After the winter solstice, morning appearance and evening concealment,
subtract it;
evening appearance and morning concealment,
add it.)
Add the given value as before,
then you get the fixed days and chen of appearance and concealment.
As for Mercury:
it is swift in the evening.
If it is from the beginning of the Great Heat qi to the ninth day and thirty-five fen of the Beginning of Winter qi,
it is not visible.
It is stationary in the morning.
If it is from the beginning of the Great Cold qi to the ninth day and thirty-five fen of the Beginning of Summer qi,
it does not appear in the morning in spring,
and does not appear in the evening in autumn.
This was also known in ancient times.
Húnyí
In ancient times, there were three schools of thought regarding the heavens:
one was Gàitiān,
the second Xuānyè,
and the third Húntiān.
During the reign of Hàn Língdì,
Cài Yǒng presented a memorial from Shuòfāng,
stating that
"the Xuānyè school
completely lacked masters and methods";
the mathematical methods of Zhōubì were fully extant,
but when tested against celestial phenomena, there were many discrepancies;
only Húntiān was close,
most accurately capturing its essence.
The bronze instrument at the Grand Astronomer's platform in recent times is an example.
It stood eight chi high, spherical in form, embodying the shapes of heaven and earth,
to rectify the positions of the ecliptic and equator,
to calculate the degrees of the sun and moon,
to compute the speeds of the five planets,
and to observe the shifts of the qi and weather.
Its precision and profound subtlety
made it indispensable for a hundred generations.
However, as the tradition was passed down through a long period,
and many makers contributed,
there were varying degrees of success and failure in observation and prediction.
Zhāng Héng's creation was called the Língxiàn,
but its transmission was lost in history.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, the government possessed the instrument
but not the original book,
hence earlier records also lacked it.
Wú Zhōngchángshì Wáng Fān said:
"The Húntiānyí
was the old instrument of Xīhé,
called Jīhéng."
Passed down through generations,
its evolution was inconsistent.
During the Tàipíng Xīngguó era of the Sòng dynasty,
Zhāng Sīxùn of Shǔ first created its model,
constructing it within the palace.
It was completed after more than a year.
An imperial edict ordered it to be placed below the drum tower east of the Wénmíng Diàn,
and inscribed "Tàipíng Húnyí."
After Sīxùn's death,
the Jīhéng broke down,
and no one again knew its method of construction.
During the Jǐngdé era,
astronomical official Hán Xiǎnfú imitated the methods of Liú Yào, Kǒng Tǐng, and Cháo Chóng.
It was too simplistic.
During the Jǐngyòu era,
Dōngguān Zhèng Shū Yìjiǎn then used the methods of Táng's Liáng Lìngzàn and the monk Yīxíng,
which were quite detailed and complete,
but also too intricate and difficult to use.
During the Yuányòu era,
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Sū Sòng and Zhāowén Guǎn Xiàolǐ Shěn Kuò were ordered to thoroughly review and finalize the essential methods of the Húnyí.
They then memorialized to appoint Lìbù Gōudāngguān Hán Gōnglián,
who was proficient in the Jiǔzhāng Gōugǔ method,
and constantly used it to verify celestial degrees against the methods of Zhāng Héng, Wáng Fān, the monk Yīxíng, Liáng Lìngzàn, and Zhāng Sīxùn.
The general framework could be investigated.
If the instruments were constructed according to mathematical calculations,
it could also be accomplished.
They requested to set up a bureau and dispatch officials to manufacture it.
An edict was issued as requested.
They memorialized Zhèngzhōu Yuánwǔ Zhǔbù Wáng Yǎnlán,
and Táishǐ Jú officials Zhōu Rìyán, Yú Tàigǔ, and Zhāng Zhòngxuān,
to supervise the construction together.
After the system was completed,
an edict ordered it to be placed in the Jíyīng Diàn,
collectively called Húntiānyí.
When Gōnglián was about to build the instrument,
he first compiled a scroll entitled Jiǔzhāng Gōugǔ Yàncè Húntiān Shū,
which was stored in the palace.
It is now lost,
hence the world knows nothing of it.
The old Húnyí,
which mapped the heavens and squared the earth,
with its mechanism hidden inside,
displaying the celestial paths above,
and then the movements of the sun, moon, and five planets,
to observe the advance and retreat of cold and heat,
like Zhāng Héng's Húntiān and Kāiyuán Shuǐyùn Tóng Húnyí,
was such an instrument.
Over time, it no longer aligned,
and became impractical to use.
Gōnglián's design consisted of three rotating rings:
one was the Liùhéyí,
placed vertically within the terrestrial sphere,
which was the celestial meridian ring,
connected to the terrestrial sphere,
its body immovable;
the second was the Sānchényí,
placed inside the Liùhéyí;
the third was the Sìyóuyí,
placed inside the Sānchényí.
Four dragon pillars were erected beneath the terrestrial sphere,
and an Áoyún was placed beneath the Liùhéyí.
Below the four dragon pillars, a cross-shaped water pedestal was set up,
with channels dug to convey water to level the height.
A separate Tiāncháng Dānhuán was set inside the Liùhéyí,
and two Dānhuán, the ecliptic and the equator, were also set
inside the Sānchényí.
They intersected east and west, rotating with the celestial movement,
to observe the movement of the constellations.
Additionally, four Xiànghuán were made,
attached to the Sānchényí,
connected to the Tiānyùn Huán.
The two intersections of the ecliptic and equator formed two vertical 直距 (zhíjù) placed inside the Sìyóuyí.
The north end was attached to the terrestrial sphere of the Liùhéyí above,
to rectify the degree of the north pole above the horizon.
The south end was attached to the terrestrial sphere of the Liùhéyí below,
to rectify the degree of the south pole below the horizon.
This was the general form of the Húnyí.
A Wàngtǒng was placed between the zhíjù,
with an axle set at the middle of the tube,
attached to the zhíjù,
allowing it to rotate up and down.
The tube always pointed to the sun.
The sun's body was always in the aperture of the tube.
As the heavens moved one cycle westward,
the sun moved one degree eastward.
It was also used to observe the degrees of stars in the four directions,
all based on the designs of Lǐ Chúnfèng, Kǒng Tǐng, Hán Xiǎnfú, and Shū Yìjiǎn.
On the Sānchényí, a Tiānyùn Huán was set,
operated by water power.
The method of water power began with Hàn's Zhāng Héng,
was perfected by Táng's Liáng Lìngzàn and the monk Yīxíng,
and then revived by Zhāng Sīxùn during Tàipíng Xīngguó.
Gōnglián now further revised and rectified its design,
setting up the Tiānyùn Huán,
with supporting mechanisms like Tiānzhù Guānzhóu below to move the Húnyí above.
This was the new design.
The old system of the armillary sphere,
what Zhāng Hēng called "placed in a secret chamber,"
was used to calculate the movements of the seven luminaries,
to gauge the times of twilight and dawn for the calendar,
to verify the twenty-four solar terms,
and to examine the clepsydra's divisions of day and night;
nothing was superior to the armillary sphere.
The Suí Zhì states that in the Liáng imperial library there was one made during the Yuánjiā period of the Sòng dynasty.
It was made of wood,
spherical in shape like a ball,
and its entire body was covered with the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the star colors of the three schools, the ecliptic and celestial equator, the Milky Way, etc.
A separate horizontal ring was placed around its exterior,
dividing it into upper and lower halves,
to represent the Earth.
During the Kāiyuán period,
an imperial decree ordered the monk Yī Xíng and Liáng Lìngzàn to construct a new bronze armillary sphere.
It represented the spherical heavens,
on which were clearly arranged the stellar mansions and their celestial degrees.
Water was injected to drive wheels, causing it to rotate by itself.
It completed one rotation in a day and a night.
Separately, the Sun, Moon, and five planets were placed to circulate,
entwined on the outside of the heavens,
allowing them to move.
Each time the heavens rotated one circuit to the west,
the Sun moved exactly one degree to the east,
and the Moon moved thirteen degrees with a remainder.
In total, after twenty-nine rotations, the Sun and Moon met;
after three hundred sixty-five rotations, the Sun completed one circuit.
A wooden case was also placed to serve as the horizon,
with half of the sphere above ground
and half below ground.
Two wooden figurines were also set up in front of the horizon,
with bells and drums, so that the wooden figures would automatically strike them to report the time divisions.
[七八]It was named the "Water-Powered Armillary Sphere, Overhead View."
Once completed,
it was ordered to be placed in the Wǔchéng Diàn.
The Sòng Grand Historian's Bureau originally had no armillary sphere.
During the Tàipíng Xīngguó period,
Zhāng Sīxùn followed the method of Kāiyuán,
but above, he used a cover as the purple palace,
and at the sides, as the celestial degrees,
and turned it east and west.
This was a new invention.
Gōng Lián then modified and created it based on the Suí Zhì.
Above, it listed the twenty-eight lunar mansions and their celestial degrees,
as well as the inner and outer official stars of the Zǐwēi Yuán,
to observe the revolutions of the seven luminaries.
It was contained within a liùhé yí (celestial sphere) and tiānjīng dìhún (celestial warp and terrestrial weft).
It was likewise carried on a wooden case.
A central axis ran through it,
exiting the armillary sphere to the north and south,
longer to the south and shorter to the north.
The dìhún was on the surface of the wooden case,
placed horizontally,
to represent the Earth.
The tiānjīng and dìhún were connected,
placed vertically,
half above ground
and half concealed underground,
to represent the heavens.
The northern end of its central axis passed through the upper bar of the tiānjīng,
its tip level with the bar,
protruding thirty-five degrees slightly less beyond the case,
to represent the North Pole above ground.
The southern end also passed through the tiānjīng and exited beyond the lower bar,
entering the case thirty-five degrees slightly less,
to represent the South Pole below ground.
Teeth were made along the celestial equator,
four hundred seventy-eight teeth to engage the celestial wheel.
As the mechanical wheels and terrestrial hub rotated precisely east and west,
the culminating stars at twilight and dawn corresponded to their degrees,
and the solstices, equinoxes, and solar terms were also accurately verified.
Wáng Fān said:
"In the method of the armillary sphere,
the Earth should be inside the heavens,
but its arrangement is inconvenient.
Therefore, by reversing its form,
with the Earth as the outer shell,
it is no different to those who understand it.
Though its appearance is strange and its form peculiar, it aligns with principle,
and can be called ingeniously clever."
Now, the dìhún is also outside the armillary sphere,
which is likely based on Wáng Fān's design.
Below it was Zhāng Sīxùn's old design,
with a pivot wheel and axles,
driven by water power,
to directly make mechanical figures shake bells, strike gongs, and beat drums.
Statues of the twelve deities representing the time divisions were placed on the wheel.
When the beginning and middle of an hour arrived,
they would hold plaques, circulate, and emerge,
reporting the corresponding number of divisions to determine the length of day and night.
In winter, when water froze,
and rotation became slow and difficult,
mercury was used instead.
The one now made by Gōng Lián
was placed together on a single stand.
The stand had two compartments:
the armillary sphere (húnyí) was placed on top,
and the armillary sphere (húnxiàng) was placed inside.
Water was used to power its rotation,
and the pivots, gears, and axles were concealed below.
Inside, there were five layers of geared wheels for day and night time divisions.
The first layer was called the celestial wheel,
used to turn the teeth along the celestial equator of the armillary sphere.
The second layer was called the tooth-engaging wheel,
on which teeth were fixed,
rotating with the central wheel of the celestial pillar,
to drive the upper and lower four wheels.
The third layer was called the hour-and-quarter bell and drum wheel,
on which were fixed the teeth for the beginning and middle of each hour and the hundred quarters,
to strike bells, beat drums, and shake chimes.
The fourth layer was called the hour-beginning and hour-middle time-keeping deities wheel,
on which were fixed the twelve deities for the beginning of each hour and the twelve deities for the middle of each hour.
The fifth layer was called the quarter-reporting time-keeping deities wheel,
on which were fixed the hundred quarter-keeping deities.
All these five wheels were mounted on a single axis,
bound above by a celestial restraint,
and supported below by an iron pestle-and-mortar.
In front, it was covered by a five-layered wooden cabinet,
slightly increasing the differences from the old design.
To the north of the five wheels,
a pivot wheel was also set up sideways.
This wheel had seventy-two spokes forming thirty-six sections,
bound by three rims,
clamping and holding thirty-six water vessels.
A single iron pivot axle ran horizontally through the hub,
with the axle protruding north and south as the terrestrial hub,
driving the terrestrial wheel.
When the central wheel of the celestial pillar moved,
the mechanical wheels moved the armillary sphere (húnxiàng),
and above, moved the armillary sphere (húntiānyí).
To the left of the pivot wheel, a celestial pool (tiānchí) and a water-leveling pot (píngshuǐhú) were also installed.
The píngshuǐhú received water from the tiānchí,
and injected it into the water-receiving vessels,
to drive the pivot wheel.
The water-receiving vessels emptied into the water-discharge vessels.
Through a northern opening below the vessels, water was led into the lower water-lifting vessels,
which, by means of the lower water-lifting wheel, transported water into the upper water-lifting vessels.
Inside the upper vessels, the upper water-lifting wheel and the river cart (héchē) rotated together with the upper and lower wheels,
transporting water into the celestial river (tiānhé).
The tiānhé then flowed back into the tiānchí,
completing a cycle every day and night, starting anew.
These were the two instruments, the húnyí and húnxiàng, made by Gōng Lián, which served three purposes,
collectively named the Húntiānyí.
When Jīn captured Biàn,
all were transported to Yān.

The celestial wheels, the teeth along the celestial equator, the driving wheels, the suspended images, the bells, drums, time-keeping deities, clepsydra reports, celestial pool, and water vessels, etc., were all abandoned and destroyed over time.
Only the bronze húnyí was placed on the observation platform of the Grand Historian's Bureau.
However, the distance from Biàn to Yān was over a thousand *lǐ*, and the terrain elevation differed,
so when observing the Polaris through the sighting tube, there was a slight discrepancy;
it had to be lowered four degrees to be visible.
In the eighth month of autumn, Míngchāng sixth year (1195 CE),
a great storm occurred,
with thunder and lightning striking.
A dragon rose from beneath the *áo* (turtle) cloud-and-water pedestal of the húnyí,
and the platform suddenly split in the middle and collapsed.
The húnyí fell down from the platform.
Officials were immediately ordered to repair it,
and it was re-placed on the platform.
During the Zhēnyòu Southern Crossing (1213-1217 CE),
it was decided to melt down the húnyí to cast other objects.
Unwilling to dismantle it,
and finding it difficult to transport it whole,
it was eventually abandoned.
During the Xīngdìng period (1217-1222 CE),
officials of the Directorate of Astronomy reported to the court
that there was no húnyí on the platform and an insufficient number of observers.
They suggested
that instruments should be cast and more students recruited
so that all observations and examinations could be fully carried out.
Xuān Zōng summoned Yáng Yúnyì, the Minister of Rites, and asked him.
Yúnyì replied:
"The state has always had very strict prohibitions on bronze.
Even if all public and private holdings were used,
it might not be enough.
Currently, resources are urgently needed,
and financial means are insufficient.
It is truly not feasible."
Another day,
the emperor mentioned it again.
Therefore, only a few additional observers were appointed,
and the proposal to cast instruments was dropped.
Initially,
when Zhāng Xíngjiǎn was Minister of Rites and concurrently Supervisor of the Directorate of Astronomy,
he once made two clepsydra, the Liánhuā Lòu and Xīngwán Lòu, and presented them.
Zhāng Zōng ordered the Liánhuā Lòu to be placed in the imperial palace,
and the Xīngwán Lòu to be used when the imperial carriage was on tour.
During the Zhēnyòu Southern Crossing,
both clepsydra were moved to Biàn.
When Biàn fell, they were destroyed and abandoned,
and their design could no longer be traced.
Collation Notes
Zhi, Lines 4 and 5
The vital essences of the Five Phases,
in heaven, are the five planets;
on earth, they are the five materials;
in humans, they are the Five Constants and Five Affairs.
The five planets are recorded in astronomical treatises,
and this has been true throughout all dynasties.
Their physical forms are on earth,
their temperaments are in humans.
Auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, each according to its category,
are the interactions between heaven and earth.
Therefore, throughout the dynasties, there have also been treatises on the Five Phases.
Since the Hàn dynasties,
scholars like Xiàhóu Shèng and his followers
specialized in the Five Phases of the Great Plan as their study.
Historians often adopted their theories,
so that whenever a certain omen of auspiciousness or inauspiciousness was mentioned,
it was linked to the success or failure of a certain affair,
and correlated with the Five Phases.
To say that it is entirely so
risks being forced and strained;
to say that it is not so,
"Respectful [conduct],
timely rain falls,"
and
"Confused [conduct],
wind blows"
— such statements
Jīzǐ already spoke of.
The Jīn dynasty was unable to unify all under heaven,
and for celestial phenomena and disasters, there was still the theory of stellar fields.
Auspiciousness and inauspiciousness of the Five Phases appearing within the realm could not be attributed elsewhere.
So, they compiled what the historians had recorded,
following the method of previous histories,
to compose the Treatise on the Five Phases.
As for the interactions of the Five Constants and Five Affairs,
it is not necessary to rigidly adhere to the Hàn scholars' examples.
Initially,
when the Jīn arose,
and pacified various tribes,
there were often auspicious and unusual occurrences.
Therefore, whenever Shìzǔ fought the enemy,
he would often use dreams to divine victory or defeat.
When Wūchūn's troops reached Sūsùhǎidiàn,
Shìzǔ said:
"I had an unusual dream last night;
I should not personally engage in battle.
If the left army fights bravely, we shall win."
Soon after, he and Sùzōng and others attacked them,
and the enemy was utterly defeated.
When Tàizǔ was born,
there were often five-colored clouds in the shape of a granary of two thousand hú [of grain] or a sword,
frequently seen in the east.
Kǒng Zhìhé, the Liáo court astrologer, said:
"An extraordinary person will be born beneath it,
who will accomplish extraordinary deeds.
Heaven announces it with an omen,
it is not something human effort can achieve."
At Wēndū Bùbátèpàn,
Mùzōng sent Tàizǔ to subdue him.
Upon departure,
he reported:
"Last night I saw a red auspicious omen;
we will surely conquer upon going."
So, he fought Bàtè
and killed him.
When Mùzōng attacked Āshū,
between chén and sì hours,
suddenly a violent rainstorm darkened the sky,
and thunder and lightning encircled Āshū's residence.
That evening, there was a huge fire, roaring like thunder,
which fell into Āshū's city,
and they subsequently captured it.
Tàizǔ once went to Níngjiāng,
and dreamed that Wòdài's threshing ground was burnt,
destroyed in an instant.
Upon waking, he was greatly distressed and immediately rode back.
Wòdài had already fallen ill,
and did not rise the next day.
When Wòsài attacked Gāolì,
Tàizǔ, while lying down, had a dream,
and immediately rose, saying:
"Today, news of victory will surely arrive."
He then prepared a feast on the polo field to await it.
Two deer crossed the water and came,
and were captured.
Tàizǔ said:
"This is an auspicious omen."
Before he finished speaking,
the victory report arrived,
and everyone was greatly astonished.
Another day, the army was at Níngjiāng,
stationed on a high mound.
Sāgǎi looked up and saw Tàizǔ's body like a towering pine,
and the horse he rode was as large as a hill.
Tàizǔ also saw Sāgǎi's person and horse as extraordinary.
Sāgǎi then reported what he had seen.
Tàizǔ happily said:
"This is a lucky omen."
He then raised his wine and poured a libation, saying:
"When we achieve success in the future,
we shall recognize this place."
When the army reached the land of Tángkuò Dàiwòjiǎ,
the troops stood in their armor,
and a light emanated from their feet and spears.
The next day,
when they arrived at Zházhǐshuǐ,
the light reappeared as before.
In the first year of Shōuguó,
the Emperor was in Níngjiāngzhōu,
and a perfectly round light
fell from the sky.
On the day jǐmǎo of the eighth month,
a yellow dragon appeared in the sky.
On the day dīngwèi of the twelfth month,
the Emperor awaited the return of the Liáo army at Shújiélán,
and a light reappeared at the tip of his spear.
In the third month of the sixth year of Tiānfǔ,
when the army attacked Xījīng,
a fire like a dipper
fell into the city.
That month,
the city surrendered but then rebelled again.
On the day xīnmǎo of the fourth month,
it was taken.
In the second year of Tàizōng's Tiānhuì era,
in Hélǎnyílùgǔ, continuous rain damaged the crops,
and they were also eaten by locusts.
In autumn,
Tàizhōu suffered from floods,
damaging the crops.
In the seventh month of the third year,
wild silkworms in Jǐnzhōu made cocoons.
In the ninth month,
Guǎngníngfǔ presented auspicious grain.
In the tenth month of the fourth year,
Zhōngjīng presented auspicious grain.
In the winter of the sixth year,
Yílǎnlù suffered from famine.
On the day bǐngshēn of the seventh month of the ninth year,
the Emperor was at the West Tower attending to government affairs.
He heard that the white magpie presented by Xiánzhōu had a suddenly unusual sound.
The Emperor rose to look
and saw outside the East Tower a luminous image, majestically rising about fifty zhàng high,
with red clouds supporting it from below,
like what the world calls a Buddha.
He then knelt respectfully in devotion,
and after a long while, it disappeared.
In the winter of the tenth year,
Yílǎn, Hélǎn, and other circuits suffered from famine.
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year of Xīzōng's Tiānhuì era,
sweet dew fell in Xióngyuèxiàn, Lúzhōu.
On the day xīnsì of the seventh month of the fifteenth year,
officials presented a four-legged sparrow.
On the night of bǐngxū,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In the summer of the first year of Tiānjuàn,
a dragon was seen in the wild waters of Xīzhōu
for three days.
Initially,
a dark dragon was seen on the water's surface,
which disappeared after a long time.
The next day,
a golden dragon was seen,
its claws holding an infant.
The infant was played with by the dragon
without any sign of fear,
remaining so for three days.
Also seen was a person,
riding a white horse,
wearing a red robe and jade belt,
like a young official.
In front of the horse were six toads.
It disappeared after three [shí] hours.
The people of the commandery competed to go and see it.
On the day dīngyǒu of the seventh month,
the Ànchūhǔhé overflowed,
destroying people's homes.
On the day dīngchǒu of the twelfth month of the third year,
there was an earthquake.
In the autumn of the first year of Huángtǒng,
there were locusts.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
the Jīgǔ Hall caught fire.
In the second month of the second year,
there was famine in Xīhé Lù.
In the third month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
there was heavy snow.
In autumn,
Yān, the two eastern and western Jīng, Hédōng, Héběi, Shāndōng, Biàn, and Píngzhōu had abundant harvests.
In the third year,
Shǎnxī suffered a drought.
In the fifth month, on the day Dīngsì,
Jīngzhào Fǔ presented auspicious wheat as tribute.
In the seventh month, on the day Bǐngyín,
Tàiyuán presented a xièzhì and auspicious wheat.
In the first month of the fourth year, on the day Yǐchǒu,
Shǎnxī presented auspicious grain,
with twelve stalks,
and one plant having seven ears.
In the tenth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
there was an earthquake.
In the intercalary month of the fifth year, on the day Wùyín,
Dàmíng Fǔ presented a cow that gave birth to a qílín.
On the day Rénchén,
Huáizhōu presented auspicious grain.
In the eleventh month of the seventh year,
Wányán Bǐngdé presented a three-horned ox.
In the fourth month of the ninth year, on the night Rénshēn,
there was a great storm,
and thunder and lightning struck and damaged the chīwěi of the imperial sleeping chambers.
There was fire that entered the Emperor's sleeping chambers,
burning the curtains and drapes.
The Emperor was frightened,
and moved to another palace.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
there was a dragon at Yúlín Hé in Lìzhōu.
A great wind damaged sixteen or seventeen tenths of civilian houses and official residences;
wood, tiles, people, and livestock were all swept away more than ten lǐ,
and hundreds were killed or injured.
Shímò Lǐ, who was the Tongzhī Zhōushì, was crushed to death.
In the twelfth month of the second year of Tiāndé of Hǎilíng,
wild people collecting coal
found an exotic fragrance.
In the fifth month of the third year of Zhēnyuán, on the day Guǐchǒu,
there was a disaster in the great palace of Nánjīng.
In the twelfth month of the third year, on the day Jǐchǒu,
it rained,
and trees were covered in ice.
In the sixth month of the second year of Zhènglóng, on the day Rénchén,
locusts flew into the capital.
In autumn,
Zhōngdū, Shāndōng, and Hédōng suffered from locusts.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year, on the day Gēngyín,
frost clung to the trees.
In the second month of the fifth year, on the day Xīnwèi,
Hédōng and Shǎnxī experienced earthquakes.
Zhenróng, Déshùn and other garrisons experienced a great wind,
which damaged houses,
and many civilians were crushed to death.
Hǎilíng asked Sī Tiān Mǎ Guìzhōng and others:
"Why is there an earthquake?"
Guìzhōng and others replied:
"It is caused by the oppression of yīn by fúyáng."
He further asked:
"Why is there a great wind with the earthquake?"
They replied:
"When the earth loses its nature,
then the ground quakes.
Wind acts as a command;
if the ruler is strict and urgent, there will be calamities of fierce winds affecting things."
In the sixth month of the sixth year, on the day Rénxū,
a great wind damaged the chīwěi of the Chéngtiān Mén.
In this year,
Shìzōng was in mourning for Empress Zhēnyì,
in Liáoyáng.
One day, as he was about to sleep,
a red light illuminated his room,
and a yellow dragon appeared above the room.
Also, at night, a large star flowed into his residence.
In the eighth month,
clouds and mist came again from the west,
and a yellow dragon appeared within them;
everyone saw it.
At this time,
Línhuáng Fǔ heard the sound of chariots and horses in the sky.
Looking up, they saw wind and clouds, vast and indistinct,
with divine spirits, soldiers, and armor covering the sky,
moving from north to south.
There were also voices urging them to proceed quickly.
Not long after,
Hǎilíng issued an edict to launch a southern campaign.
In the second year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng, on the Xīnmǎo day of the intercalary second month,
sixteen positions in the Shénlóng Diàn burned,
and the fire spread to the Tàihé and Hòudé Diàn.
In the third year, in the third month, on the Bǐngshēn day,
locusts plagued the eight lù south of Zhōngdū.
In the fourth year, in the third month, on the night of the Gēngzǐ day,
there was an earthquake in Jīngshī.
In the seventh month, on the Xīnchǒu day,
there was a great wind, thunder, and rain,
which uprooted trees.
In the territory of Línhuáng Fǔ, rice and millet grew spontaneously.
Lánzhōu presented two white rabbits.
In the eighth month,
Yǒngxīng presented auspicious grain,
with different stalks but the same ear.
Locusts from the eight lù south of Zhōngdū flew into Jīngjī.
In the eleventh month, on the Xīnchǒu day,
the Shàngshū Shěng caught fire.
That year
was a bumper harvest.
In the fifth year, in the sixth month, on the Wùzǐ day,
Hénán Fǔ presented thirteen stalks of *zhīcǎo*,
found on a rock in Zhītián,
and offered them to the Tàimiào.
In the sixth month, on the Jiǎchén day,
*zhī* grew on a pillar in the Dà'ān Diàn,
its color like jade.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
there was an earthquake in Jīngshī,
with a sound coming from the northwest,
rumbling like thunder,
and white hair grew from the ground.
In the seventh month, on the Wùshēn day,
there was another earthquake.
In the eleventh month, on the Guǐyǒu day,
there was a great fog,
making daytime dark.
In the seventh year, in the ninth month, on the Gēngchén day,
there was an earthquake.
In the eighth year, in the fifth month, on the Jiǎzǐ day,
there was a great wind at Běiwàng Diàn,
with rain and hail,
ten *lǐ* wide
and sixty *lǐ* long.
In the sixth month,
the Hé river burst its banks at Lǐgù Dù,
and the water entered Cáozhōu.
In the tenth year, in the first month,
Dèngzhōu presented *zhīcǎo*.
In the eleventh year, in the sixth month, on the Wùshēn day,
hail fell for over thirty *lǐ* in the Bìlǐ Hǎishuǐ territory of the Xīnán Lù Zhāotǎo Sī,
the smaller ones like chicken eggs.
The largest one
was three *chǐ* wide
and over a *zhàng* long,
and only disappeared after four or five days.
In the twelfth year, in the third month, on the Gēngyín day,
it rained soil.
In the fourth month,
there was a drought.
In the thirteenth year, in the first month,
the Shàngshū Shěng reported:
"Zhāng Xiàoshàn of Wǎnpíng had a son named Hédé.
On the dawn of the third month of Dàdìng twelve, he died of illness,
but revived by evening,
claiming to be Xǐ'ér, the son of Wáng Jiàn, originally from Liángxiāng.
Xǐ'ér had died three years prior.
Wáng Jiàn tested him with family matters,
and he could relate them in detail.
This is clearly a case of a soul returning to a borrowed corpse,
and we propose to hand him over to Wáng Jiàn as his son."
The Emperor said:
"If this is so, then cunning and opportunistic individuals will compete to produce fraud and deceit,
disrupting human relations."
He only allowed him to be returned to Xiàoshàn.
In the eighth month, on the Dīngchǒu day,
candidates for the *jìnshì* examination were tested at Mǐnzhōng Sì.
At midnight, music was suddenly heard rising from the East Pagoda,
reaching the palace in the west.
Examining officials Wányán Púniē, Lǐ Yàn, and others
believed it signaled the dawn of a literary era
and an omen of finding worthy talents.
In the fourteenth year, in the eighth month, on the first day, Dīngsì,
at Cǐcí Lǐshé,
at noon,
a white dragon appeared in a small creek east of the imperial tent,
and then ascended on thunder clouds,
its tail still dragging on the ground,
and after a long while, it went north.
In the sixteenth year, in the third month, on the Wùshēn day,
beans rained in the territory of Línhuáng.
Their shape was sharp at the top and red,
and when eaten, their taste was quite bitter.
In the fifth month, on the Wùshēn day,
the Nánjīng palace caught fire.
That year,
Zhōngdū, Héběi, Shāndōng, Shǎnxī, Hédōng, Liáodōng, and other ten lù suffered from drought and locusts.
In the seventeenth year, in the seventh month,
there was heavy rain.
The Hūtuó and Lúgōu rivers overflowed,
and the Hé river burst its banks at Báigōu.
In the twentieth year, in the fourth month, on the Jǐhài day,
the gate of Tàiníng Gōng caught fire.
In the fifth month, on the Bǐngyín day,
there was an earthquake in Jīngshī,
and black and white hair grew from the ground.
In the seventh month,
there was a drought.
In autumn,
the Hé river burst its banks at Wèizhōu.
In the twenty-second year, in the fifth month,
locust nymphs appeared in Qìngdū,
spreading over ten *lǐ*.
One night, a great wind blew,
and all the locusts disappeared.
In the twenty-third year, in the first month, on the Xīnsì day,
the lamp mountain in Guǎnglè Yuán burned,
and the fire spread to the Xīchūn Diàn.
In the third month, on the Yǐyǒu day,
there was dust and soil rain.
In the fourth month, on the Gēngzǐ day, it was also like this.
In the fifth month, on the Dīnghài day,
there was hail,
and white hair grew from the ground.
In the twenty-fourth year, in the first month, on the first day, Xīnmǎo,
Xúzhōu presented eighteen stalks of *zhī*.
Zhēndìng presented two stalks of auspicious grain,
with different stalks but the same ear.
In the twenty-sixth year, in the first month, on the Gēngchén day,
Hénán Fǔ presented three stalks of *zhī*.
In autumn,
the Hé river burst its banks,
destroying the city wall of Wèizhōu.
In the twenty-seventh year, in the fourth month, on the Xīnchǒu day,
there was a slight earthquake in Jīngshī.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng of Zhāngzōng, in the fifth month, on the Dīngwèi day,
white hair grew from the ground.
In the fifth month,
the Hé river overflowed at Cáozhōu.
In the twelfth month,
Mìzhōu presented one white quail and one white pheasant.
Héjiān Fǔ presented auspicious grain.
That winter, there was no snow.
In the first year of Míngchāng (明昌), first month,
Huáizhōu (懷州), Héjiān (河間), and other places presented *zhīcǎo* (芝草) and auspicious grains.
Second month,
white hair grew from the ground.
Sixth month, on the *gēngzǐ* (庚子) day,
the Director of Riverworks presented a strange egg.
Summer,
there was a drought.
Seventh month,
persistent rain damaged the crops.
In the second year, fifth month,
Huán (桓) and Fǔ (撫) prefectures suffered from drought.
Autumn,
Shāndōng (山東) and Héběi (河北) experienced drought,
and famine.
In the third year, autumn,
in Suídé (綏德), destructive insects were born.
There was a drought.
In the fourth year, third month,
Dǒng Shīzhōng (董師中), the Censor-in-chief, reported:
"Recently, Venus was seen in broad daylight,
there was an earthquake in the capital,
and a red aura appeared in the north,
only dissipating at dawn.
These are signs from Heaven,
hopefully to warn and awaken the Sagely Sovereign."
The Emperor asked:
"From where did you obtain what you said about the celestial phenomena?"
Shīzhōng (師中) replied:
"Former Investigating Censor Chén Yuánshēng (陳元升) obtained it from a long-serving official of the Directorate of Astronomy."
The Emperor said:
"It is indeed a crime for officials of the Directorate of Astronomy not to report such matters,
but it is even more improper to speak of them to others.
I wish to decree that from now on, if the Directorate of Astronomy has important matters and does not report them, the long-serving officials may speak of them.
How about that?"
Shīzhōng (師中) replied:
"Excellent."
Fifth month,
there was continuous heavy rain,
and officials were ordered to pray for clear weather.
Sixth month,
the river burst its banks in Wèizhōu (衞州),
and Wèi (魏), Qīng (清), and Cāng (滄) were all affected.
This year,
Héběi (河北), Shāndōng (山東), Nánjīng (南京), and Shǎnxī (陝西) circuits had a great harvest.
In Xíng (邢), Míng (洺), Shēn (深), Jì (冀) and the sixteen *móukè* (謀克) territories of the western Héběi (河北) Circuit,
wild silkworms spun cocoons.
Eleventh month, on the *rénwǔ* (壬午) day,
there was hoarfrost on trees.
In the fifth year, seventh month, on the *bǐngxū* (丙戌) day,
it was the Tiānshòu (天壽) Festival.
Prior to this, there had been continuous overcast and rainy days,
but on this day, the weather cleared,
and a dragon was seen dragging its tail in the clouds before the palace hall.
Eighth month,
the river breached the old dike at Yángwǔ (陽武),
flooding Fēngqiū (封丘) and extending eastward.
In the sixth year, second month, on the *dīngchǒu* (丁丑) day,
there was an earthquake in the capital,
heavy hail,
darkness at midday,
and a strong wind.
The earthquake caused the right *chīwěi* (鴟尾) of the Yìngtiānmén (應天門) gate to collapse.
Sixth year, eighth month,
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning.
A dragon rose from the *áofū* (鰲趺) (tortoise pedestal) of the armillary sphere,
the platform suddenly split in the middle and was destroyed,
and the instrument fell beneath the platform.
In the first year of Chéng'ān (承安), fifth month,
there had been no rain since the first month,
but it rained in this month.
Sixth month,
a civilian from Píngjìn (平晉) County, Lì Tōng's (利通) family, had silkworms that spontaneously formed a cotton cloth,
seven *chǐ* (尺) one *cùn* (寸) five *fēn* (分) long,
and four *chǐ* (尺) nine *cùn* (寸) wide.
In the second year,
there was no rain from the first month to the fourth month.
Sixth month, on the *bǐngwǔ* (丙午) day,
there was hail.
In the fourth year, third month, on the *wùwǔ* (戊午) day,
there was hail.
Fifth month,
there was a drought.
In the fifth year, fifth month, on the *gēngchén* (庚辰) day,
there was an earthquake.
Tenth month, on the *gēngzǐ* (庚zǐ) day,
the sky had been overcast for a long time,
and on this day the clouds were yellow and there was wind and haze.
On the morning of the *guǐmǎo* (癸卯) day,
hoarfrost attached to trees,
and remained so until sunset.
In the second year of Tàihé (泰和), eighth month, on the *bǐngshēn* (丙申) day,
at Gǔshān Shíshèngtái (鼓山石聖臺) in Wǔ'ān (武安) County, Cízhōu (磁州),
ten large birds gathered on the platform.
Their feathers were brilliantly multi-colored,
mostly red and yellow patterns,
with russet crests and chicken-like necks.
Their tails were broad and long,
resembling a carp's tail but longer,
and they were taller than a person.
Nine smaller young birds,
also four or five *chǐ* (尺) tall, attended by their side.
Tens of thousands of other birds, of various shapes and colors,
some flying, some crouching,
some walking, some standing,
all formed ranks,
with their heads all facing forward as if bowing in audience.
They first came from the southeast,
their momentum like continuous clouds,
their sound like rumbling thunder,
shaking the trees and forests.
Herdsmen were terrified,
and immediately drove their cattle and struck objects to frighten them,
but the birds were utterly unmoved.
Suddenly, large birds like eagles and ospreys angrily flew to attack them.
The people were even more frightened,
and ran to inform the county officials,
who all believed them to be phoenixes.
Artisans were ordered to paint their image and present it.
They remained for two days and then departed to the northwest.
Upon inspecting the site,
there were droppings over several *qǐng* (頃),
each of different colors.
Thousands of birds were left behind,
unable to leave for several days.
What they had eaten were all giant carp,
the largest over ten *chǐ* (尺) long,
and fish bones covered the ground.
Zhāngzōng (章宗) reported this event to the ancestral temple
and issued an imperial edict to the empire.
Third year, fourth month,
there was a drought.
Tenth month, on the *jǐhài* (己亥) day,
there was a strong wind.
Fourth year, first month, on the *rénshēn* (壬申) day,
there was overcast fog,
and hoarfrost on trees.
Third month, on the *dīngmǎo* (丁卯) day,
there was a strong wind,
destroying the *chīwěi* (鴟尾) of the Xuānyángmén (宣陽門) gate.
Fourth month,
there was a drought.
On the *rénxū* (壬戌) day,
the Duānmén (端門) gate of Wànnínggōng (萬寧宮) suffered a fire.
Eleventh month, on the *dīngmǎo* (丁卯) day,
it was overcast.
Hoarfrost on trees lasted for three days in total.
〔一０〕Fifth year, summer,
there was a drought.
Eighth year, intercalary fourth month, on the *jiǎwǔ* (甲午) day,
there was hail.
〔一一〕Hénán (河南) Circuit suffered from locusts.
Sixth month, on the *wùzǐ* (戊子) day,
flying locusts entered the capital region.
Eighth month, on the *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day,
a tiger appeared outside the Yángchūnmén (陽春門) gate.
The imperial carriage went out, and the tiger was shot and captured.
At this time, there was also a children's rhyme that said:
"The Yìshuǐ (易水) flows,
the Biànshuǐ (汴水) flows,
a hundred years pass quickly, and then rest, rest.
Both families dwell well,
front and back, all will remain."
By the middle of Zhēnyòu (貞祐) reign,
the entire nation relocated to Biàn (汴).
In the first year of Dà'ān of Wèi Shàowáng,
the Yellow River in the Xú and Pī regions cleared for over five hundred *lǐ*.
an edict regarding this matter was issued to all corners of the realm.
Yáng Guī, a man from Líntáo, submitted a memorial, saying:
"The nature of the river is originally turbid,
but now it has turned clear.
This means the water has lost its nature.
Just as heaven moves and earth is still,
if that which should move becomes still,
and that which should be still moves,
For nearly two years,
Its being an ominous omen is clear.
Moreover, the proverb says: 'When the Yellow River clears,
a sage is born.'
Even if a sage were to be born,
I fear it would not be today.
It also says: 'When the Yellow River clears,
a *zhūhóu* becomes Son of Heaven.'
One should properly be cautious and fearful,
to avert disaster and change.
To boast of it to the four directions,
your subject does not understand."
The prime minister considered it seditious talk
and proposed to execute him.
Fearing that this would block the path of speech,
an edict was issued to Dàxīng Fǔ to send him back to his native jurisdiction under escort.
On the *bǐngshēn* day of the eleventh month,
Píngyáng experienced an earthquake,
with sounds coming from the northwest.
On the night of *wùxū*,
it shook again.
From this time on, tremors resumed,
particularly severe in Fúshān Xiàn.
Seventeen or eighteen out of ten urban buildings and private residences collapsed,
and a total of two to three thousand people died.
On the *yǐyǒu* day of the second month of the second year,
a great earthquake occurred,
with rumbling sounds.
From the sixth month, seventh month, until the last day of the ninth month,
the tremors were continuous.
In the eleventh month,
fire emerged from a channel in front of the residence of a civilian named Zhōu Xiūwǔ in the capital,
two *chǐ* high,
burning his plank bridge.
About ten days later,
fire emerged from a stone crevice beneath the banner pole of the Dàbēi Gé,
two to three *chǐ* high.
It would extinguish if someone approached,
lasting for over ten days in total.
From then on, the capital city saw two or three dozen conflagrations every night.
In the fourth month of this year,
Shāndōng and Héběi experienced a great drought.
By the sixth month,
rain became incessant,
and a *dǒu* of rice in the common market reached over a thousand cash.
On the night of the *yǐhài* day of the second month of the third year,
a great wind came from the northwest,
unroofing houses and snapping trees,
blowing down and breaking the gate of Qīngyímén.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the third month,
the Dàbēi Gé suffered a disaster,
spreading fire to over ten thousand households.
The fire did not cease for five days.
Shāndōng, Héběi, and Hédōng circuits experienced a great drought.
In this year,
a man named Hǎo Zàn went to the Provincial Secretariat, saying:
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
heavenly anomalies have been repeatedly seen.
Fire has burned ten thousand homes,
wind has broken gate passes.
These are not minor abnormalities.
It is appropriate to abdicate and yield to one of virtue."
The authorities asked:
"Are you suffering from madness?"
Zàn loudly declared:
"I am not mad,
but I am planning for the sake of the state.
All the prime ministers are not competent."
He shouted loudly in front of the Provincial Secretariat every day,
for half a month in total.
The Emperor was enraged
and had him secretly executed.
On the *xīnwèi* day, *wèi* hour, of the seventh month of the first year of Chóngqìng,
a wind came from the east,
blowing a piece of silk several tens of *zhàng* high,
twisting like a dragon,
which fell inside the Gǒngchén Mén.
In this year,
Hédōng, Shǎnxī, Shāndōng, and Nánjīng circuits suffered drought.
In the second month of the second year,
the list of successful *jìnshì* candidates was released.
There was a mad monk who publicly declared:
"Kill the Son of Heaven."
He was sought but his whereabouts unknown.
In this year,
Hédōng and Shǎnxī experienced a great drought,
and a *dǒu* of rice in Jīngzhào reached eight thousand cash.
In the first year of Zhìníng,
white flowers bloomed on the bamboo in Xuānzōng's former garden in Zhāngdé,
like egret vines.
Purple clouds covered the city for several days,
and soon after, he succeeded to the great inheritance.
In the seventh month,
due to drought in Hédōng, Shǎnxī, and other places,
Gāo Zhuāngcì, the Minister of Works, was sent to pray for rain at the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Rivers.
By then, there was sufficient rain.
At that time, a *dǒu* of rice could reach twelve thousand cash.
On the *guǐsì* day of the eighth month,
Wèi Shàowáng was assassinated.
On this day,
the seawater did not tide.
The Bǎochí Salt Administration feared a loss in revenue
and prayed, but received no response.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day of the ninth month,
the tide came when Xuānzōng ascended the throne.
Initially,
when Wèi Wáng ascended the throne, he changed the era name to Dà'ān.
In the fourth year, he changed it to Chóngqìng,
and then again to Zhìníng.
Someone remarked:
"The three era names, 'Dà'ān', 'Chóngqìng', and 'Zhìníng' (至寧, meaning 'ultimate peace'), imply that ultimate peace has arrived."
Soon after, the upheaval of Hú Shāhǔ occurred.
On the night of the *wùzǐ* day of the eighth month of the first year of Zhēnyòu of Xuānzōng,
just before dawn,
there was a great dark fog,
making it impossible to see when walking slowly,
only dispersing between *chén* and *sì* hours.
On the *yǐmǎo* day of the twelfth month,
it rained,
and trees were covered in ice.
At that time, there was a children's rhyme in Wèizhōu:
"Clinging together in winter,
splitting for half a year.
During the Cold Food Festival,
no human trace."
In the first month of the following year,
Mongol troops broke Wèi,
and it became ruins.
In the sixth month of the second year,
the Cháobái Hé overflowed,
carrying the iron-clad gate of Gǔběikǒu pass to Lǎo Wáng Gǔ.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the Bǎozhèn Gé in Nánjīng suffered a disaster.
On the *rénxū* day,
when the Emperor was at Yícūn,
a yellow dragon was seen in the northwest.
In winter,
the Yellow River from the border of Shǎnzōu to Bāliǔshù in Wèizhōu
was clear for over ten days,
with even the smallest fish visible.
On the *jǐyǒu* day of the twelfth month,
it rained,
and trees were covered in ice.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the second month of the third year,
there was a great wind,
and the owl-tail ornament of the Lóngdé Diàn was damaged.
On the *wùchén* day of the third month,
there was a great wind,
and haze.
In the fourth month,
there had been no rain since the previous winter
until this month.
In the fifth month,
Hénán experienced a great locust plague.
in the capital city, people were startled and chased after wolves in the middle of the night,
which only subsided after more than a month.
On the evening of the *bǐngshēn* day of the tenth month,
there was a misty vapor in the northwest like piled earth,
only dispersing at the second watch.
At dawn on the *jǐwèi* day of the first month of the fourth year,
black fog filled all four directions,
only dispersing at *sì* hour.
This spring,
people in Héshuò resorted to cannibalism.
In the fifth month,
Hénán and Shǎnxī experienced a great locust plague.
Fèngxiáng, Fúfēng, Qíshān, and Méixiàn suffered damage to wheat from insects.
In the seventh month,
there was a drought.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
flying locusts passed over the capital.
In the third month of Xīngdìng (興定)元年's first year (1212),
there were locusts in the palace.
In the fourth month,
Dānzhōu (單州) suffered hail damage to its crops.
Chénzhōu (陳州) and Shāngshuǐ (商水) County presented auspicious wheat,
with one stalk bearing four ears.
Kāifēng (開封) Prefecture presented auspicious wheat,
with one stalk bearing three ears, and two stalks bearing four ears.
On the Yǐchǒu (乙丑) day of the fifth month,
Hénán (河南) experienced a great wind,
which blew away the prefectural gates and offices.
Yánzhōu (延州) and Yuánwǔ (原武) County suffered hail damage to their crops.
On the Guǐmǎo (癸卯) day of the seventh month,
auspicious grain sprouted on the Grand Altar of the Earth,
with one stalk bearing fifteen ears.
In autumn,
there was continuous rain.
In the tenth month,
Bīnzhōu (邠州) presented a white rabbit.
Dānzhōu (丹州) presented auspicious grain,
with different fields bearing the same type of ear.
In the fourth month of the second year (1213),
there were locusts in various commanderies of Hénán (河南).
In the fifth month,
Qín (秦) and Shǎn (陝) suffered harm from wolves.
In the sixth month,
there was a drought.
In that year,
the capital repeatedly caught fire,
so Yáng Yúnyì (楊雲翼), the President of the Board of Rites, was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
In the spring of the third year (1214),
the Board of Civil Office caught fire.
On the Guǐwèi (癸未) day of the fourth month,
a black wind arose in Shǎnyòu (陝右) in broad daylight,
with a sound like thunder.
The earth in that area greatly shook,
especially in Píngliáng (平涼), Zhènróng (鎮戎), and Déshùn (德順).
Houses collapsed,
and the dead numbered in the tens of thousands,
with livestock casualties double that.
In summer,
there was a drought.
On the Rénshēn (壬申) day of the twelfth month,
it rained,
and trees were covered in ice.
At the second watch on the Wùchén (戊辰) day of the first month of the fourth year (1215) [一五],
the heavens rumbled with sound.
On the Rénzǐ (壬子) day,
it was dark at midday,
and after a while, there was great thunder, wind, and rain.
On the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day of the fourth month,
a strong wind blew the Hénán (河南) Prefecture office more than a hundred paces,
its doors, archives, gates, and keys opened,
and documents were scattered,
their whereabouts unknown.
In the sixth month,
there was a drought.
In the seventh month,
Hénán (河南) experienced severe floods,
especially in Táng (唐) and Dèng (鄧).
On the Guǐyǒu (癸酉) day of the twelfth month,
there was a fire.
In that year,
in Huázhōu (華州)'s Wèinán (渭南) County, a commoner named Péi Déníng (裴德寧) was felling a tree,
and when he split it, he found a red
"Tài" (太)
character inside,
with its surface having grown together again.
Officials reported that this event was quite similar to the auspicious wood with the inscription
"Tiānxià Tàipíng" (天下太平)
found in Chéngdū (成都) during the Dàlì (大曆) reign of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
and was therefore a harbinger of peace.
They requested that it be submitted to the imperial archives.
In the third month of the fifth year (1216),
due to drought,
an edict was issued to the court and provinces,
〔一六〕 and officials were commanded to pray.
On the Rén Yín (壬寅) day of the eleventh month,
Xiàngguó (相國) Temple in the capital caught fire.
On the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day of the twelfth month,
frost adhered to trees.
Before this,
there was a children's rhyme that said:
"Green mountains turn,
the turning mountains are green.
All is delayed,
for young people."
This was meant to say that at that time, all people were soldiers,
moving through mountains and valleys,
fighting incessantly,
until they grew old.
In the fourth month of Yuánguāng (元光)元年's first year (1222),
the imperial domain suffered drought.
In the tenth month,
the Emperor hunted in the near suburbs,
and caught a white rabbit.
The courtiers considered it an auspicious sign.
The next day,
he went to the private palace,
placed a bell around the rabbit's neck,
and was about to release it.
The rabbit was startled and leapt continuously,
suddenly dying on the table.
At noon on the Xīnyǒu (辛酉) day of the first month of the second year (1223),
more than a thousand cranes flew in the palace courtyard,
departing after a short while.

At this time, there were frequent omens and strange occurrences.
Within two years,
a tiger entered Zhèng (鄭) Gate in broad daylight;
there were foxes and wolves in the Board of Civil Office and the palace;
ghosts cried at night on the imperial carriage road;
magpies were startled at night,

In the twelfth month,
Xuānzōng (宣宗) died.
On the Wùwǔ (戊午) day of the first month of Āizōng (哀宗)'s Zhèngdà (正大)元年's first year (1224),
the Emperor first held court.
He honored the Empress Dowager as Rénshèng Gōng Huáng Tàihòu (仁聖宮皇太后),
and the Grand Imperial Consort as Císhèng Gōng Huáng Tàihòu (慈聖宮皇太后).
On that day,
a great wind blew off the tiles of Duānmén (端門),
and it was so hazy that the sun could not be seen;
a yellow qi filled the sky.
Rénshèng (仁聖) also dreamed that tens of thousands of beggars followed her,
and she was disturbed by this.
A diviner said:
"The Empress is the mother of all under heaven;
when the common people are poor,
to whom will they appeal?"
Thereupon, an edict was issued to the capital to provide porridge and medicinal ice to respond to this,
which people considered an omen of Rénchén (壬辰) and Guǐsì (癸巳) years.
Also, there was a man dressed in sackcloth,
who looked towards Chéngtiān (承天) Gate and laughed three times,
and cried three times.
Officials detained and questioned him.
The man said:
"My first laughter was
to laugh that in this great empire, there are no capable ministers or generals.
My later crying was
to grieve that the ancestral homeland has been destroyed to such an extent."
Officials considered this seditious talk
and sentenced him to severe punishment.
The Emperor said:
"Recent edicts have allowed common scholars to speak directly,
and even if it involves satire, no punishment is imposed.
Moreover, this man's words also have reason,
he just shouldn't have cried and laughed below the palace gate."
So, he was merely beaten with a staff.
On the Jiǎshēn (甲申) day of the first month of the second year (1225),
there was an omen of yellow and black.
In the fourth month,
there was a drought.
The imperial domain experienced heavy rain and hail.
In the spring of the third year (1226),
there was intense cold.
On the Yǐchǒu (乙丑) day of the third month,
a fire emerged from the Board of Civil Office,
as large as a bushel measure,
moving and turning.
People were all startled and avoided it,
and it extinguished after some time.
In the fourth month,
there were drought and locusts.
In the sixth month,
Jīngdōng (京東) experienced hail,

On that day,
wind and frost destroyed all the grain.
In the spring of the fifth year (1228),
there was intense cold.
In the second month,
there was thunder and snow,
and all the blossoming trees withered.
In the fourth month,
Zhèngzhōu (鄭州) experienced heavy rain and hail,

The imperial domain suffered drought.
In the eighth month,
a voice was heard on the imperial throne saying:

It was sought but not found.

resembling the old Wèizhōu (衞州) city,
with its temples and pagodas clearly visible,
and it disappeared after several days.

In the ninth month, on the night of the *xīnchǒu* day,
the Emperor moved to Cài.
He departed from Guīdé,
and for several days there was a torrential downpour,
with the flat ground submerged several *chǐ* deep,
and soldiers drowned.
When he reached Cài, the weather finally cleared,
but then there was a severe drought for several months.
Those who understood the signs considered it inauspicious.
Originally,
a year or two before Nánjīng fell,
there was a monk in the marketplace, whose origin was unknown,
who carried a cloth bag filled with dates
and daily distributed them to the market people without end;
wherever he went, scores of children followed him.
There was also a man who picked up broken tiles from the street
and then smashed them with a stone.
People all thought he was mad
and did not understand his meaning,
but later they realized
that his intention was probably to make people disperse early,
as the state was about to crumble like tiles.

Monograph Five: Geography, Part One: Shàngjīng Lù, Xiánpíng Lù, Dōngjīng Lù, Běijīng Lù, Xījīng Lù, Zhōngdū Lù
As for the territory and borders of Jīn:
to the east, it extended to the lands of the various wild peoples of Jílǐmí Wùdì Gǎi;
to the north, from over three thousand *lǐ* north of Púyǔ Lù,
the territory of Huǒlǔhuǒtuántuó Mòkè served as the border.
Turning right, it entered the boundary moat excavated by Pólúhuǒ of Tàizhōu and proceeded west,
passing through Línhuáng and Jīnshān,
spanning north of Qìng, Huán, Fǔ, Chāng, and Jìng Zhōu,
extending beyond Tiānshān,
encompassing Dōngshèng,
connecting with Xīxià,
crossing the Yellow River,
and then westward through Jiāzhōu and Mǐzhī Zhài,
beyond Líntáofǔ, Huìzhōu, and Jīshí,
intermingling with the lands of the uncivilized Qiāng.
Then, from the south of the Jīshí Mountains, it turned left eastward,
crossing Tǎozhōu,
passing over Yánchuānbǎo,
following the Wèi River to the north of Dàsànguān,
and along the mountains into Jīngzhào,
encompassing Shāngzhōu.
To the south, it extended forty *lǐ* southwest of Táng and Dèng,
taking the middle course of the Huái River as its boundary,
thus forming the border with Sòng.
Adopting the system of Liáo,
five capitals were established,
and fourteen Commanderies-in-Chief were set up,
making a total of nineteen Circuits.
Within these, there were nine scattered Prefectures,
thirty-six Military Governors,
twenty-two Defense Commanderies,
seventy-three Governorates,
sixteen Military Districts,
and six hundred thirty-two counties.
Later, all Military Districts were promoted to Prefectures,
and some castles, fortified villages, and towns were promoted to counties.
Thus, the Jīn had a total of one hundred seventy-nine Capital Prefectures and Prefectures,
the number of counties increased by fifty-one compared to the old system,
one hundred twenty-two castles, fortified villages, forts, and passes,
and four hundred eighty-eight towns.
Although there were establishments and abolishments during the perilous times of Zhēnyòu and Xīngdìng,
after returning to Dàyuán,
some were retained.
Therefore, all that can be verified is fully recorded,
and what is not recorded is omitted.
Shàngjīng Lù,
which is the land of Hǎigǔ,
was the old territory of Jīn.
The national language
for "Jīn"
is
"Ànchūhǔ."
Since the Ànchūhǔ River originates here,
it was named Jīnyuán,
and the dynastic title was derived from this.
In the early days of the dynasty, it was called the Interior.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn, it was named Shàngjīng.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán under Hǎilíng,
the capital was moved to Yān,
the title of Shàngjīng was abolished,
and it was merely called Huìníngfǔ.
Calling it "the capital" was deemed a violation of regulations.
In the seventh month of the thirteenth year of Dàdìng,
it was restored as Shàngjīng.
Its mountains include Chángbái, Qīnglǐng, Mǎjìlǐng, and Wándūlǔ.
Its rivers include the Ànchūhǔ River, Húntóngjiāng, Láiliúhé, Sòngwǎjiāng, and Yāzǐhé.
It had one Prefecture,
governing four Military Governors,
one Defense Commandery,
six counties,
and one town.
It formerly had Huìpíng Zhōu,

〔三七〕During the Liáo dynasty, it was originally the pastureland for the twenty tribal groups of the Qìdān.
During Hǎilíng's Zhènglóng reign,
Déchāngjūn was established,
subordinate to Shàngjīng.
In Dàdìng 25th year, it was abolished.
In Chéng'ān 3rd year, it was re-established in Chángchūn county.
The former Tàizhōu was made Jīn'ān county
and subordinated to it.
(North to the border: 400 *lǐ*.
South to Yìzhōu: 800 *lǐ*.
East to Zhàozhōu: 350 *lǐ*.)

Nineteen forts:
Chángchūn (Liáo's Chángchūnzhōu Sháoyángjūn.
In Tiāndé 2nd year, it was downgraded to a county,
subordinate to Zhàozhōu.
In Chéng'ān 3rd year, it became subordinate to this prefecture.
Has the Tàlǔgǔ River and Yāzǐ River.
Has Bìlíbù Spring.)
Border forts.
In Dàdìng 21st year, 3rd month,
Shìzōng, observing that the nineteen forts of the Dōngběilù Zhāotǎosī were within Tàizhōu's territory,
and the twenty-four forts previously established in the Línhuánglù were unevenly distributed,
sent Púchá Zhāngjiānú and others, who were Dàlǐsī Zhí, to inspect their placement.
Thereupon, from Dálǐdài Shíbǎozǐ in the northeast to the Hèwǔhé area,
and from Hèwǔhéfǎozǐ to Sālǐnǎi in the Línhuánglù,
forts and garrisons were set up in a straight line.
Píngshì Yīlà Mǐn said:
"Where the forts are established in the northeast and Línhuáng,
the soil is barren and firewood is scarce.
The relocated people should temporarily follow the water and grass to live,
and after the able-bodied men are dispatched to build,
moats should be dug to prepare for border defense."
The emperor ordered that in areas without water and grass, officials should build houses,
and all the forts in Línhuánglù should be garrisoned by released commoners.
The provincial council proposed:
"The twenty-four forts in Línhuánglù,
each fort housing thirty households,
totaling 720,
if construction is completed,
officials will provide one year's food."
The emperor, due to the famine, temporarily suspended this,
ordering only the digging of moats for preparation.
In the 4th month,
Lìbù Lángzhōng Xīhú Shīhǎi was sent to plan the moats.
They were soon filled and blocked by sand and snow,
rendering them ineffective for defense.
So, it was proposed:
"Two hundred and fifty forts can be built.
Each fort requires three hundred laborers per day,
and it can be completed in one month.
Food is also sufficiently prepared.
This can be a long-term plan for border defense.
The land of the nine forts in Tàizhōu and five forts in Línhuáng is saline and barren.
Officials can build houses outside.
For the nineteen forts west of Sālǐnǎi,
where the old garrisons have few barracks,
over thirty thousand pieces of official timber from the Dàyánluò
can be obtained, and timber can be sought from the nearby ridges of Zhídōngbǎo.
Officials will construct one rafter of a house for each family to accommodate them."

Zhōngdū Lù (Central Capital Circuit)
In the first year of Huitong of the Liao dynasty, it became Nánjīng (Southern Capital).
In the first year of Kaitai, it was named Yānjīng (Yan Capital).
In the first year of Zhēnyuán of Hǎilíng, it was designated as the capital.
As Yān was the name of a feudal state,
it was deemed inappropriate as a capital city's name.
Therefore, it was changed to Zhōngdū.
One Prefecture.
Oversees three Jiézhèn (military commands),
nine Cìjùn (prefectures governed by an inspector),
a plan for the palace and institutional layout of Yānchéng was first drawn up.
In the third month,
Zhāng Hào and others were ordered to expand Yānchéng.
There were thirteen city gates.
To the east were Shīrén, Xuānyào, and Yángchūn.
To the south were Jǐngfēng, Fēngyí, and Duānlǐ.
To the west were Lìzé, Hàohuá, and Zhāngyì.
To the north were Huìchéng, Tōngxuán, Chóngzhì, and Guāngtài.
Hào and others used timber from Tányuán in Zhēndìng Fǔ
to construct palaces and sixteen Liángwèi (cool retreats).
Yìngtiānmén had eleven bays.
There were towers on its left and right.
Inside the gate were the Left and Right Xiánglóng Mén,
and Rìhuá and Yuèhuá Mén.
The front hall was called Dà'ān.
There were Left and Right Yèmén.
The eastern corridor of the inner hall was Fūdémén.
To the northeast of Dà'ān Diàn was the Dōnggōng (Eastern Palace).
To the due north were three gates.
The central one was Cuìyīng,
the residence of the Empress Dowager.
To the west was Huìtōng Mén.
North of this gate was Chéngmíng Mén.
Further north was Zhāoqìng Mén.
To the east was Jíxǐ Mén.
The Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) was outside it.
Its east and west gates were the Left and Right Jiāhuì Mén.
The gate had two towers,
and was located behind the rear gate of Dà'ān Diàn.
