Chief Military Commissionerate (Zǒngguǎnfǔ),
Yínghǎi Jūn.
During the Sòng dynasty, it was Héjiān Jùn and Yínghǎi Jūn.
In Tiānhuì seventh year (1129), a Zǒngguǎnfǔ was established.
During the Zhènglóng period, it was elevated to a second-class Fǔ,
and the Yíngzhōu Yínghǎi Jūn Jiedu Envoy was appointed concurrently as Zǒngguǎn,
and a Zhuǎnyùn Sī was established.
Later, the Zǒngguǎnfǔ was re-established,
and the Tíxíng Sī for Héběi Dōngxī Dàmíng and other circuits.
(It produces seamless cotton, Cāng salt, lìn mats, Málián flowers, Xiāngfùzǐ, Qián prawns and crabs, and dried fish.

It has one prefecture (fǔ),

Collation Notes
Gazetteer Eight Rivers and Canals: Yellow River, Cao Canal, Lugou River, Hutuo River, Zhang River
Yellow River.
After the Jīn Dynasty first conquered the Sòng Dynasty,
the two rivers were entirely given to Liú Yù.
When Yù perished,
the river then entirely entered Jīn territory.
For several decades,
it would either breach or be dammed,
shifting without a fixed course.
The Jīn people established officials and assigned subordinates
to manage these affairs.
Along the river, there were twenty-five _sào_ in total,
six in Hé'nán and
nineteen in Héběi.
Each _sào_ had one _sǎn xún hé guān_ (scattered river patrol official) assigned.
The five _sào_ of Xióngwǔ, Xíngzé, Yuánwǔ, Yángwǔ, and Yánjīn also managed the Bìanhé River,
with one _huáng biàn dū xún hé guān_ (Yellow and Bian Rivers chief patrol official) assigned at Héyīn to supervise them.
The four _sào_ of Huáizhōu, Mèngjīn, Mèngzhōu, and those north of the city also managed the Qìnshuǐ River,
with one _huáng qìn dū xún hé guān_ (Yellow and Qin Rivers chief patrol official) assigned at Huáizhōu to oversee them.
The four _sào_ of Chóngfú above and below, Wèinán, and Qíshàng belonged to the _Wèinán dū xún hé guān_ (Weinan chief river patrol official),
who resided in Xīnxiāng.
The four _sào_ of Wǔchéng, Báimǎ, Shūchéng, and Jiàochéng belonged to the _Jùn Huá dū xún hé guān_ (Junhua chief river patrol official),
who resided in Jiàochéng.
The _Cáodiàn dū xún hé guān_ (Caodian chief river patrol official) oversaw the four _sào_ of Dōngmíng, Xījiā, Mènghuá, and Língchéng.
The _Cáojì dū xún hé guān_ (Caoji chief river patrol official) was in charge of the four _sào_ of Dìngtáo, Jìběi, Hánshān, and Jīnshān.
Thus, there were six _dū xún hé guān_ in total.
Later, an additional _Chóngfú shàng xià sào dū xún hé guān_ (Chongfu Upper and Lower Saos chief river patrol official) was specially established, who also served as the commander of Shíqiáo.
All _xún hé guān_ (river patrol officials)
were selected by the _Dūshuǐ Jiān_ (Directorate of Waterways) for their integrity.
They commanded 12,000 _sào_ soldiers,
and annually used over 1.113 million bundles of firewood,
over 1.837 million bundles of hay.
The wood for stakes was not included in this count.
This was the system for river defense.
In the sixth month of Dàdìng 8 (1168),
the river breached at Lǐgùdù,
and the water flooded Cáozhōu city,
diverting its flow into the territory of Shānzhōu.
In the first month of Dàdìng 9 (1169),
the imperial court dispatched Liáng Sù, the _Dūshuǐ Jiān_ (Director of Waterways), to inspect it.
Zōng Yán, a member of the imperial clan and _Hénán Tǒngjūn Shǐ_ (Military Commissioner of Henan), said:
“The reason the Yellow River overflows
is that the riverbed has accumulated silt,
and thus cannot contain the water.
Although Cáo and Shān are now suffering from this calamity,
these two prefectures originally relied on water resources for their livelihood,
and the damage to farmland is minimal.
If we now wish to restore the river to its old course,
it would not only incur enormous labor costs,
but also be extremely difficult to succeed.
Even if it could be dammed,
should there be heavy rains on another day,
it would still breach,
and the river calamity in Shāndōng would then be incomparable to that in Cáo and Shān.
Moreover, launching such a large project in several prefectures along the river
would cause unrest among the people,
and I fear the Sòng people might seize the opportunity to create border troubles.”
And Sù also said:
“The new river carries six parts of the water,
while the old river carries four parts.
If we now block the new river,
the two flows will merge back into one.
If it swells and overflows,
a breach to the south would harm Nánjīng,
while a breach to the north would harm both Shāndōng and Héběi.
It would be more convenient to build a dike south of Lǐgùdù to prevent overflows.”
The _Shàngshū Shěng_ (Department of State Affairs) reported this,
and the Emperor approved it.
In the third month of Dàdìng 10 (1170),
Zōng was appointed _Cānzhī Zhèngshì_ (Policy Advisor),
and the Emperor instructed him, saying:
“When you were _Hénán Tǒngjūn_ (Military Commissioner of Henan) previously,
you spoke about the advantages and disadvantages of the Yellow River dikes and _sào_,
which greatly pleased me.
I often think that whenever the common people are subjected to levies and labor services,
officials conspire to exploit them.
If we do not plan early and instead impose urgent collections,
the people will incur ten times the expense.
However, the collected materials
may be stored for years,
until they rot and become unusable,
rendering hundreds of thousands of _cái_ (wealth units) of our people
into discarded waste.
This harm is not small.
Since you are now participating in state affairs,
you must reform all such abuses
and implement what is beneficial.”
In Dàdìng 11 (1171),
the river breached at Wángcūn,
and the border areas of Mèng and Wèi Prefectures in Nánjīng were greatly affected.
In the first month of Dàdìng 12 (1172),
the _Shàngshū Shěng_ (Department of State Affairs) reported:
“The inspecting officials say that
the water is flowing southeast,
and its momentum is very great.
It is possible to build new dikes from Guǎngwǔshān in Héyīn eastward along the river,
to Yuánwǔ, Yángwǔ, Dōngmíng counties, and Mèng and Wèi Prefectures.
11,000 laborers are to be employed daily,
with a projected completion in sixty days.”

An imperial edict was issued to dispatch Zhāng Jiǔsī, _Tàifǔ Shàojiān_ (Vice Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices), and Gēsīliè Miáo (also known as Ābǔsūn), _Tóngzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì_ (Associate Administrator of the Southern Capital’s Garrison), to supervise the work.
In the third month of Dàdìng 13 (1173),
at the request of the _Shàngshū Shěng_ (Department of State Affairs) to repair the dikes of Mèngjīn, Xíngzé, and Chóngfú _sào_ to prepare for floods,
the Emperor ordered the eight _sào_ from Xióngwǔ downwards to proceed accordingly.
In the seventh month of autumn, Dàdìng 17 (1177),
there was heavy rain,
and the river breached at Báigōu.
In the twelfth month,
the _Shàngshū Shěng_ (Department of State Affairs) reported:
“To repair and build the river dikes,
11,500 laborers are to be employed daily,
with completion in sixty days.”
An edict was issued for Dàdìng 18 (1178) on the first day of the second month to mobilize military laborers from within 600 _lǐ_,
and also half of the officials' manpower;
the rest were to be civilian laborers.

Zhāng Dàjié, _Shàngshū Gōngbù Lángzhōng_ (Director of the Board of Works), and Gāo Sū, _Tóngzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì_ (Associate Administrator of the Southern Capital’s Garrison), were to supervise the work.
Previously,
from Chénqiáozhèn in Xiángfú County eastward to Pángāng in Chénliú,
the Yellow River dike, over forty _lǐ_ long, had been managed by county officials.
The officials of Nánjīng requested
the special establishment of a _sào_ official.
In the ninth month of Dàdìng 19 (1179),
one _jīng sào xún hé guān_ (capital _sào_ river patrol official) was established.
In Dàdìng 20 (1180),
the river breached at Wèizhōu and Yánjīn Jīngdōng _sào_,
inundating as far as Guīdé Fǔ.
Shímò Huī, _Nánjīng Fù Liúshǒu_ (Vice Administrator of the Southern Capital’s Garrison), an inspecting official, said:
“The river water, due to the torrential rains this autumn, surged violently
and thus abandoned its old course,
its momentum increasingly moving southward.”
The chief ministers reported this.
Thereupon, new dikes were built from below Wèizhōu _sào_ connecting to the north and south banks of Guīdé Fǔ to defend against the raging torrent.
The estimated labor was over 1.796 million units,
with over 24,000 laborers employed daily,
projected to be completed in seventy days.
Consequently, one _xún hé guān_ (river patrol official) was established at Guīdé Fǔ,
with 200 _sào_ soldiers,
and an edict was issued to exempt the frequently employed labor areas from this year’s taxes.
In the tenth month of Dàdìng 21 (1181),
as the river shifted to its old course,
an order was given to build dikes in preparation.
In the eighth month of Dàdìng 26 (1186),
the river breached the Wèizhōu dike,
destroying its city.
The Emperor ordered Wáng Jì, _Hùbù Shìláng_ (Vice Minister of Revenue), and Wáng Rújiā, _Dūshuǐ Shàojiān_ (Vice Director of Waterways), to rush there by courier to plan for defense.
However, Jì did not rescue the afflicted people;
instead, he focused on gathering people to fish and seize government property,
which caused great resentment among the people.
The Emperor heard this and disliked it.
Subsequently,
the river’s floodwaters reached Dàmíng.
The Emperor then dispatched Liú Wěi, _Hùbù Shàngshū_ (Minister of Revenue), to manage the affairs of the Board of Works,
to plan as appropriate,
and demoted Jì to _Càizhōu Fángyù Shǐ_ (Defense Commissioner of Caizhou).
In the tenth month of winter,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
“I have heard that the deceased Sòng Dynasty stationed one person for every step of river defense;
we can increase the number of river defense troops.”
Another day,
he again said:
“I have recently heard that when the river overflows,
those people who suffer from it
lose all their property.
Why are officials again dispatched to the disaster-stricken circuits for _tuīpái_ (levying additional taxes)?”
Zhāng Rǔlín, _Yòuchéng_ (Right Chancellor), said:
“Those being _tuīpái_ now are not in the disaster-stricken areas.”
The Emperor said:
“Even so,
they must be in neighboring circuits.
Since they live near the water,
how could there be no one startled or forced to relocate?
When their property is assessed,
how could there be any surplus?
What is the point of _tuīpái_ then?”
In the eleventh month,
he again said to his chief ministers:
“Before the river breached at Wèizhōu, there were those who spoke of it;
after it breached,
why did the officials not inform me?”
He ordered an inquiry into the reason.
In the first month of spring, Dàdìng 27 (1187),
the _Shàngshū Shěng_ (Department of State Affairs) reported:
“The Sacred Empress Temple in Héyīn County, Zhèngzhōu,
in previous eras, when the river water caused calamity,
prayers were often answered,
and it was granted additional honorary titles and temple plaques.
Now, due to prayers,
the river flows peacefully;
we request additional commendations.”
The Emperor granted their request,
and specially added the title Zhāoyìng Shùnjì Shènghòu,
and named the temple Língdé Shànlì zhī Miào.
In the second month,
Zhāng Jù, the Magistrate of Xīnxiāng county in Wèizhōu; Tángkuò Tánggǔchū, the Assistant Magistrate; and Wēndūn Wēihē, the Chief Clerk,
were all commended for their successful efforts in rescuing and protecting the city when the Héshuǐ river flooded and blocked it.
All were promoted and rewarded in varying degrees.
The Yùshǐtái memorialized:
"Heretofore, officials in the Jīng, Fǔ, Zhōu, and Xiàn along the river have overlooked and paid no heed to the damage and breaches in the river defenses within their jurisdiction.
If the senior and junior officials of the Jīng, Fǔ, Zhōu, and Xiàn along the river were all to be officially responsible for river defense in their titles,
and if during their tenure they devise effective plans that can ward off great disasters,
or if their vigilance is lax, leading to neglect and calamity,
then a report should be submitted to the throne at the appropriate time,
to deliberate rewards and punishments."
The Emperor adopted this proposal,
and further ordered that each year, when the river was about to overflow,
an official from the Gōngbù should be dispatched to inspect the riverbanks.
Thus, the senior and junior officials of the Nánjīng Fǔ and its affiliated counties Yánjīn, Fēngqiū, Xiángfú, Kāifēng, Chénliú, Zuòchéng, Shíxiàn, and Chángyuán;
Guīdé Fǔ and its affiliated counties Sòngchéng, Nínglíng, and Yúchéng;
Hénán Fǔ and Mèngjīn;
Hézhōng Fǔ and Hédōng;
Huáizhōu's Hénèi and Wǔzhì;
Tóngzhōu's Cháoyì;
Wèizhōu's Jí, Xīnxiāng, and Huòjiā;
Xúzhōu's Péngchéng, Xiāo, and Fēng;
Mèngzhōu's Héyáng and Wēn;
Zhèngzhōu's Héyīn, Xíngzé, Yuánwǔ, and Fànshuǐ;
Jùnzhōu's Wèi;
Shǎnzhōu's Wénxiāng, Húchéng, and Língbǎo;
Cáozhōu' Jìyīn;
Huázhōu's Báimǎ;
Suīzhōu's Xiāngyì;
Téngzhōu's Pèi;
Shànzhōu's Shànfù;
Jiězhōu's Pínglù;
Kāizhōu's Púyáng;
Jìzhōu's Jiāxiáng, Jīnxiāng, and Yùnchéng;
the four Fǔ and sixteen Zhōu were all made responsible for supervising river defenses,
and the magistrates and their assistants of the forty-four Xiàn were all made responsible for managing river defenses.
Initially,
Wèizhōu was damaged by river floods,
so an order was given to reinforce and build Sūmén,
and relocate the prefectural seat.
By the twenty-eighth year,
the water had receded,
and residents gradually returned,
but none were happy about the relocation.
Thus, Dàlǐ Shǎoqīng Kāng Yuánbì was sent to investigate.
Yuánbì returned and memorialized:
"A great many residents of the old prefecture have returned to their livelihoods.
Furthermore, the courier station along the southern envoy route is located there.
Previously, there were no flood preparations,
which is why it suffered damage.
If only the thin and damaged sections of its dikes are repaired,
it can be secured without worry.
Compared to relocating the seat,
the savings would be several times over.
It would be better to heed the people's wishes
and repair the old city."
So the prefecture was not relocated.
An imperial edict was also issued that from now on, any river defense officials who were negligent or unprepared
would be severely punished.
In the fifth month of the twenty-ninth year,
the river overflowed north of the small dike in Cáozhōu.
In the sixth month,
the Emperor issued an edict to the relevant authorities, saying:
"I heard that on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month the river overflowed,
yet the report received is so delayed.
Water affairs are most urgent;
the work cannot be delayed.
Even a slight delay,
and it will be difficult to secure."
In the twelfth month,
the Gōngbù reported:
"The construction of river dikes required over six million eight hundred thousand laborers.
Aside from the soldiers and laborers already employed for dike construction,
there were over four million three hundred thousand laborers that needed to be supplied by the populace."
An imperial edict was then issued, ordering Zhōu and Fǔ within five hundred lǐ of the work sites to dispatch laborers,
and in areas where laborers were not dispatched, to levy payment for hired labor uniformly,
assessed according to property and resources.
For each laborer, in addition to one hundred and fifty wén in wages,
fifty wén in official funds and
one and a half shèng of rice were to be paid daily.
It was also ordered that Dàlíngshòu, a member of the imperial clan serving as Jiédùshǐ of Zhānghuà Jūn and Dūshuǐ Shàojiān, should lead five hundred men to circulate and maintain order.
Previously,
the Hénán Lù Tíxíngsī had stated:
"Many residents along the river are impoverished and have fled,
presumably due to the onerous and heavy labor service for river defenses.
We believe that to guard against floods,
nothing is needed but dikes and fascines.
If earthwork is calculated realistically,
and firewood, straw, piles, and stakes are levied in a timely manner,
what difficulty could there be?
This spring, when building dikes, the Dūshuǐ Jiān initially estimated that earth would be taken from very nearby,
but when construction began, it was several times further,
causing laborers, fearing they would not meet the deadline,
to buy earth at exorbitant prices,
sometimes up to a thousand guàn for a single work team.
Moreover, Xǔzhōu was initially assessed for over one hundred eighty thousand bundles of firewood and straw,
and then later another forty-four thousand were allocated.
These are all materials needed every year,
and if uniformly levied during the agricultural off-season, they would be easy to deliver.
From now on, when dike and fascine construction begins,
we request that the supervising agency accurately calculate,
assess the amount of materials needed for one year,
and either convert this number into taxes,
or implement government purchase,
to be delivered in three installments during the winter months, which would be more convenient."
An imperial edict ordered the Shàngshūshěng to deliberate and report.
In the first month of spring in the first year of Míngchāng,
the Shàngshūshěng memorialized:
"Your ministers believe that,
from now on, whenever public works are undertaken,
the distance for transporting earth and the height of the embankment to be built should first be measured,
the work quota and deadline should be set,
and publicly posted so that people know in advance,
without increasing labor.
As for all materials needed for river defense,
the Dūshuǐ Jiān should be entrusted, before the eighth month each year,
to first register the actual deficit beyond existing stored materials,
and the amount of spring work for the following year,
and report it to the Zhuǎnyùnsī for planning and arrangement,
to be delivered in installments during the three winter months.
If water conditions are unstable,
with sudden and dangerous floods in summer and autumn,
then materials from neighboring fascine divisions should be used for defense.
If insufficient,
then they should be purchased from nearby Zhōu and Xiàn.
However, considering the muddy and difficult roads for households to transport materials,
it is better to simply convert it within their taxes to other goods,
with an increased price,
paid by the officials.
Violators shall be punished according to the law.
Furthermore, a principal official from the relevant Tíxíngsī should be ordered to rush by post horse to supervise and investigate.
This way, the work will be orderly,
and the river will not be unprepared."
The Emperor approved this.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year,
the Shàngshūshěng memorialized:
"Wáng Rǔjiā, Jiédùshǐ of Hépíng Jūn, and others stated, 'On the south bank of the great river, there are old distributary river mouths.
If they can be dredged,
they would sufficiently relieve the force of the water.
And north of the long dike, there may also be places where water can be collected and drained.
We request that an official be appointed to inspect them.
North of the Jìběi fascine, a crescent dike should be built.'
Your ministers believe that this proposal should be followed.
The officials of the supervising agency are appointed to this post because of their familiarity with river defenses,
so they should be sent to inspect together with Rǔjiā and others,
to avoid differing opinions.
If it is indeed impossible to open and drain channels north and south of the great river,
then the crescent dike should be built as proposed."
The Emperor adopted this.
In the twelfth month,
an imperial edict ordered officials of the Dūshuǐ Jiān to supervise the construction of the Huánghé dikes,
and also ordered Dàmíng Fǔ to dispatch a Zhèng Qiānhù and
two hundred armored soldiers to maintain order and manage affairs.
In the first month of spring in the fifth year,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
"The Dūshuǐjiānchéng Tián Lì, together with officials of his directorate, discussed the advantages and disadvantages of the Yellow River.
He once submitted a memorial stating:
'In previous dynasties, whenever the ancient embankment breached to the south,
the water often flowed through the Nán Qīnghé and Běi Qīnghé.
South of the Nán Qīnghé, there are several dry river channels,
and the river water flowing through them reaches seven or eight tenths of its capacity.
The Běi Qīnghé is the old course of the Jǐshuǐ,
and can only accommodate two or three tenths.
Now, the river water tends northward,
eroding the long embankment in more than ten places,
and outside the embankment, there are often accumulated waters.
It is feared that it will be difficult to reinforce and repair the long embankment or construct moon embankments according to the original plan.
It is feasible to breach the river at Qiángcūn on the north bank, allowing it to flow into the old course of the Liángshān Luò,
and thus restore the division into the Nán Qīnghé and Běi Qīnghé.
However, the old embankment of the Běi Qīnghé has deteriorated over the years,
so a time limit should be set for its reinforcement and reconstruction into a large embankment.
Moreover, many military households cultivating land reside in the old course of Liángshān,
and they should also be relocated.
Currently, it is proposed to first breach the embankment at Wángcūn and Yícūn on the south bank to divert water,
so that the long embankment can be secured.
For now, it is advisable to maintain the status quo.
If the water cannot be diverted,
then proceed with the aforementioned breach,
dividing it into four channels,
and manage the water situation as appropriate once it is observed.'"
The Shàngshūshěng noted that Lì's statements regarding the advantages and disadvantages differed from the assessment made by Liú Wěi and others in the second year of Míngchāng,
and when Fēng Déyú, the proponent of the suggestion, was made to confront Lì,
there were also disagreements.
The matter was sent to the Gōngbù for deliberation.
It was further stated:
"If a sudden breach were made at Qiángcūn,
there are over twenty prefectures and counties bordering the Běi Qīnghé,
with embankments extending over a thousand *lǐ* on both sides.
Their defenses have always been inadequately maintained,
and it is feared that the military households stationed there would also be difficult to relocate quickly.
This year, a breach should first be made in the embankment of Yánjīn County on the south bank to discharge water.
The long embankment on the north bank, from Báimǎ downwards
to Dìngtáo upwards,
should all be reinforced and protected,
so as to prevent future calamities.
If the three *sào* embankments east of Dìngtáo are to be abandoned, then they need not be repaired.
Only breach the old blocked river mouth,
and guide the accumulated water eastward and southward,
flowing between the Zhāngbiāo and Báitǎ rivers north of the embankment.
Military households affected by the water can be relocated,
and those settled in sections of the old course of Liángshān Luò
should also be resettled in advance."
The prime ministers reported:
"If we were to immediately follow Lì's proposal,
we fear that once the change is made,
the advantages and disadvantages would be significant.
We recently summoned Wáng Rǔjiā, Jìedùshǐ of Hépíngjūn, to deliberate.
First, dispatch two capable officials from the Xíng Hù Gōngbù to re-inspect it.
If their findings agree, then immediately calculate the actual labor and materials needed, and allocate laborers based on the distances of the prefectures and counties.
The officials overseeing the spring works will then serve as the flood defenders for the current year,
and also discuss long-term solutions with the officials of the directorate."
An imperial edict appointed Lǐ Jìngyì, Zhī Dàmíngfǔ Shì, a member of the imperial clan, and Shàngshū Hùbù Lángzhōng, to serve as Xíng Hù Gōngbù Shì,
and Xū Chíguó, Cānzhī Zhèngshì, as Dū Tíkòng.

It was further reported that Lǐ Xiànkě, Dézhōu Fángyùshǐ, and Jiāo Xù, Shàngshū Hùbù Lángzhōng, were dispatched to Shāndōng to construct and protect city embankments in the prefectures and counties affected by water,
and to also organize laborers to repair the old embankments along both banks of the Běi Qīnghé where they exist,
and to also instruct them to study river defense plans.
Another day,
the emperor handed a scroll by Sòng Yán Shìliáng detailing the advantages and disadvantages of the Yellow River to Cānzhī Zhèngshì Mǎ Qí, saying:
"Some of what this book says is useful.
I bestow it upon you."
In the second month,
the emperor instructed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Shǒu Zhēn, saying:
"Wáng Rǔjiā and Tián Lì are solely responsible for river defense.
This is a matter of great importance to the state.
I recently asked if they had inspected the south bank.
They replied, 'Not yet.'
I then asked if a breach could be made on the south bank.
They again said, 'Cannot know.'
Moreover, the water has been trending northward for a long time.
Planning should have begun last year.
Are they not performing their duties as required?
You are to issue an imperial edict ordering them to diligently reinforce and protect,
without any lapses in preparation,
and to thoroughly study long-term solutions.
Should there be any slight negligence,
they shall be punished accordingly."
In the third month,
the Xíngshěng, together with officials from the Xíng Hù Gōngbù and Dūshuǐjiān, each reported on the advantages and disadvantages of river defense.
The Dūshuǐjiān originally proposed to divert the river flow at Wángcūn and Yícūn on the south bank.
However, recently the water current at the Yícūn embankment has slowed somewhat,
while at Wángcūn, the bank several *lǐ* upstream is being eroded in a swirling motion,
making it possible to open a breach and create a single river channel,
without affecting any cities, towns, or villages.
It was also proposed to breach the river at Qiángcūn on the north bank,
to again divide it into the two Qīnghé rivers flowing into the old course of Liángshān.
The small embankments on both banks of the Běi Qīnghé have always been incomplete;
a large embankment should be built later.
The Shàngshūshěng stated:
"Given the force of the Yellow River's water,
if a breach were made at Qiángcūn,
the fertile lands of the Shāndōng prefectures and counties, and various salt fields, would surely be submerged.
Even if the damaged embankments were repaired,
and still could not fully contain the water,
the labor would be immense,
and the people of Shāndōng would be exhausted for no benefit,
but rather harmed.
Furthermore, the long embankment has already been reinforced,
and the proposal to breach the river into the Liángshān Luò has been shelved,
as water has been diverted on the south bank.
Cities and towns along the water's path have been encouraged to build protective city embankments.
The previously repaired old embankments of the Qīnghé have been abandoned.
Dūshuǐjiānchéng Tián Lì stated that the three *sào* embankments east of Dìngtáo should be abandoned and not repaired,
only saying: 'Breach the old blocked river mouth to guide the accumulated water into the Zhāngbiāo and Báitǎ rivers north of the embankment,
and all military households cultivating land in the path of the water must be relocated.'
Our view is that
wooden barriers should only be constructed in front of the embankment as a precaution.
The residents living there should not be relocated for now.
When the water overflows in summer and autumn,
they can be temporarily evacuated,
and return to their livelihoods when the water recedes.
This is also what the Hù Gōngbù said."
The emperor said:
"The places are so far apart.
How can one fully know the advantages and disadvantages there?
Only by entrusting the Xíngshěng to plan with utmost care will it be acceptable."
In the fourth month,
regarding Tián Lì's statements on river defense,
the emperor issued an edict to Cānzhī Zhèngshì Chíguó, saying:
"This matter
not only holds you responsible,
but requires you and others to plan wholeheartedly,
so as not to trouble my mind.
As Lì stated,
building the embankment requires 200,000 laborers,
working 50 days a year,
which can be completed in five years.
This is an immense undertaking,
unprecedented in ancient times.
Moreover, whether it can be completed is unknown,
and even if it could,
it is feared it would be difficult to implement.
Relocating 4,000 military households is not difficult,
but if the water breaches specifically there,
its destination is still unknown.
Should there be a collapse and outflow,
how would it be contained?
If two breaches were made on the south bank,
causing the water to flow southward,
its force might be partially diffused.
However, I have not personally observed the topography of the water,
making it difficult to formulate detailed plans,
and the same applies to you.
The Chéngxiàng and Zuǒchéng are not familiar with this;
you should gather all officials to deliberate thoroughly before proceeding."
All officials agreed:
"What Lì proposed—abandoning the long embankment,
not constructing a new one,
and letting the river flow into the old course of Liángshān,
allowing the Nán Qīnghé and Běi Qīnghé to flow separately—
is a long-term plan to save costs and relieve the people.
However, we believe that the Yellow River's water forces are extraordinary,
constantly changing and unpredictable,
and cannot be managed or directed by human effort.
Furthermore, the Liángshān Luò has silted up to a high level,
and the Běi Qīnghé is too narrow to contain it.
Moreover, there are numerous peasant homes and wells in the prefectures and counties it passes through.
If the great river flows northward into the Qīnghé,
Shāndōng will surely suffer.
Lì also requested that the Dūshuǐjiān be permitted to issue directives to the zhōufǔ and yùnsī,
to have exclusive control over expenditures,
and to be entrusted with responsibility,
with everything treated as urgent as military affairs,
and further overseen by the Zhízhèng.
However, officials of the directorate have already been augmented,
and many local supervisory positions have been concurrently held by chief officials of prefectures along the river,
and their subordinates have been ordered to manage river defense.
For any negligence or slowness, there are already laws for sentencing and punishing them as in military affairs.
Therefore, nothing Lì proposed is usable."
His proposal was thus shelved.
In the eighth month,
due to the river breaching the old embankment at Yángwǔ,
inundating Fēngqiū and areas to the east,
the Shàngshūshěng reported that
officials of the Dūshuǐjiān and Xíngbù had failed to provide adequate protection.
An imperial edict ordered Gāo Xù, Tóngzhī Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ, and Nǚxīliè Yì (nicknamed Hánjiānú), Wǔwèijūn Fù Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ, to go together to plan measures.
The Shàngshūshěng reported:
"Officials of the Dūshuǐjiān had committed offenses previously,
and had already been warned
to constantly and diligently secure and protect.
Now, Wáng Rǔjiā and others have paid scant attention.
Upon seeing the water tending southward,
they did not plan in advance.
Despite repeated reports from the Liúshǒusī,
they procrastinated,
leading to harm to the people.
This constitutes a deliberate violation of imperial decrees,
and they deserve to be severely punished for their private crimes."
An edict ordered Rǔjiā and others to each be demoted by two ranks,
receive seventy strokes with a rod, and be dismissed from their posts.
The Emperor said to his Grand Counselors:
“Lǐ Yù’s report on the river breach
suggested sending a high-ranking official
to comfort the people’s hearts,
and his words are correct.
In the past, when there was a concern about a breach north of the Yellow River,
and plans were made for embankments and defenses,
we even established a moving secretariat (xíngshěng).
How much more so now, when it is rampant and causing harm,
should we not just dispatch minor officials?
I fear it will disappoint the populace.
From the perspective of the state,
although the land of Shāndōng is more important than Hénán,
yet the people are all our children;
why should there be a distinction between one and the other?”
So he ordered Cānzhī Zhèngshì Mǎ Qí to go,
and allowed him to act according to circumstances (biànyí cóngshì).
The Emperor said:
“Lǐ Yù cannot be considered blameless.
Although officials of the Dūshuǐ Jiān are not under the jurisdiction of the Tíxíng Sī,
if he had, by expediency, gathered the people with the Liúshǒu Sī to secure and protect,
or submitted a report to the shěngbù,
why could he not have let Us know?
He merely exaggerated the water situation without any planning,
and after the breach had occurred,
he just went with Wáng Rújiā to inspect it and returned,
without having implemented any measures.
When asked about the month the Wángcūn River mouth was dredged,
he replied ‘at the end of the fourth month,’
but in reality it was the sixth month.
He doesn’t even know the month and day;
should an official of the Tíxíng Sī be like this?”
Soon after, Hùbù Yuánwàiláng Hé Gé was ordered to provide relief to the flood-affected people.
At that time, Xíngshěng Cānzhī Zhèngshì Xū Chíguó and Mǎ Qí reported:
“We have arrived at Guānglù Cūn and inspected the embankment mouth.
Because the river water is overflowing,
and the embankment has collapsed,
we have to go more than ten *lǐ* away to get earth.
Moreover, the top of the embankment is narrow,
only a few steps wide,
making it impossible for human power to be applied effectively.
Even if we exert our utmost effort to complete it temporarily,
it will eventually be destroyed again.
And the middle section is silted up,
with varying ground levels,
preventing the flow from being discharged.
Furthermore, when the water recedes,
new sandbanks will also be difficult to dredge.
As for the four embankments of Mènghuá and others, and the Mèngyáng Embankment Road,
along the eastern bank of the Biàn River,
we can only exert full effort to repair and protect
where work can be done.
We plan to start the work during the slack season for farming,
and complete it by the time the ground freezes.
Then the capital city will not be harmed.”
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Mǎ Qí said:
“The number of external officials of the Dūshuǐ Jiān is excessive and redundant.
They rely on each other for every matter,
or even seek credit,
leading to confused and inconsistent discussions,
thereby neglecting official duties.
I propose abolishing the Dūshuǐ Jiān clerks
and establishing two Guōdàng officials.
Furthermore, historically, the selection of Dū and Sàn Xúnhé officials
was solely by recommendation from the supervising officials,
all from various offices.
Some were old or infirm,
avoiding the burdens of warehouses,
and resorted to bribery and influence-peddling,
resulting in many being unqualified.
I propose elevating Dū Xúnhé to rank from seven,
selected from those qualified to be county magistrates and deemed upright,
while Sàn Xúnhé remains as before,
also selected from various offices and upright officials recommended by chéngbù,
all to be under sixty years of age, energetic, and capable.
After one year in office,
the Tíxíng Sī will investigate;
if found unqualified,
they shall be immediately dismissed.
If they manage the defense effectively,
causing the river to flow safely,
upon completion of their term,
they shall be recommended by their own directorate and the Tíxíng Sī,
and granted promotion or demotion accordingly.
All Sīshǐ Fù of the Héqiáo Sī are also proposed to be selected and appointed in the same manner.”
Subsequently, Xū Chíguó also made a similar statement,
and their request was granted.
In the intercalary tenth month,
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Shǒuzhēn said:
“Mǎ Qí’s plans for river defenses
have not yet shown the number of works.
Added to the cumulative projects over the years,
the people’s strength will be exhausted.
Now Chíguó is also ill;
I request that another capable person be sent to discuss this.”
The Emperor said:
“If the embankment and rescue efforts can succeed,
then we certainly dare not begrudge resources.
But I fear that resources will be depleted and strength exhausted,
and what is built will be destroyed again.
How can we withstand such repeated hardship?”
The Grand Counselors replied:
“If we exert our full effort to secure and protect,
even if there is harm, it will be minor.
If we are indifferent and neglectful,
then the harm will be much greater.”
The Emperor said:
“Will this not lead to banditry?”
Shǒuzhēn replied:
“The Sòng dynasty, when repairing river breaches,
also sometimes led to banditry.
However, it mostly arose from famine and scarcity.
Now, times are peaceful and the years are bountiful,
and there are few labor assignments,
so it may not reach that point.
Moreover, river defense work
is a matter of course.
Those assigned to work now are still manageable.
As for levying straw and firewood,
regardless of whether they have it or not,
if urged to deliver with urgency, they will sell their property to obtain it,
which I fear will further distress the people.”
The Emperor said:
“Laborers must be conscripted from nearby areas.
If they are transferred from far away,
the people will suffer even more hardships,
but just providing relief should suffice.
However, we must wait for Mǎ Qí to arrive before discussing this.”
On the *gēngchén* day,
Qí returned from the xíngshěng.
Upon an audience,
he reported:
“The Mèngyáng River embankment and the Biàn River embankment have been filled and repaired,
and the water cannot threaten Biànchéng.
From now on, the river's current tends northward.
Next year, at the beginning of spring, we plan to dredge and open a channel in the middle,
to relieve the danger on both the north and south banks.
In total, the project is estimated to require over eight million seven hundred thousand laborers,
and work can begin at the end of the first month.
Your servant requests to go to the river earlier to supervise again.”
The Emperor sent what he said to the Shàngshū Shěng,
and officials responsible for inspecting river embankments and guarding against floods were punished to varying degrees.
Another day,
when the Shàngshū Shěng presented matters,
the Emperor brought up the river defense issue,
and Mǎ Qí reported:
“Your servant dares not be less than fully devoted,
but I fear that my wisdom and strength may be insufficient.
If another official were dispatched to make observations,
perhaps there would be an extraordinary plan,
which is yet unknown.
If his strategy happens to be the same as mine,
then when the work begins,
it would still somewhat alleviate the court's concerns.”
The Emperor agreed.
He ordered Hànlín Dàizhì Àotún Zhōngxiào to act as Shàngshū Hùbù Shìláng and Tàifǔ Shǎojiān Wēn Fǎng to act as Shàngshū Gōngbù Shìláng,
to handle the affairs of the Hùbù and Gōngbù,
and to manage the river defenses.
He also instructed them, saying:
“You two are both known to Us,
which is why We entrust you,
hoping you will fulfill Our expectations.
If there are any mistakes,
We will not tolerate you.”
In the seventh month of Chéng'ān first year,
an imperial edict stated that from now on, officials of prefectures, sub-prefectures, and counties along the river, even if appointed by other departments, should not leave any positions vacant.
In the ninth month of Tàihé second year,
an imperial edict was given to officials of the Yùshǐ Tái:
“The advantages and disadvantages of river defense are not initially your concern,
but Yùshǐ Tái officials question everything;
those that should be investigated should also be investigated.”
In the second month of the fifth year,
based on Cuī Shǒuzhēn’s report,
“The Yellow River is critically dangerous,
and although straw and materials are said to be offset by taxes,
it happens no less than five or six times a year,
sometimes under the name of ‘harmonious purchase’ (hé mǎi),
yet the price is never returned,”
an imperial edict ordered Yòu Sānbù Sīzhèng Guō Xiè and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Mèng Zhù to investigate and report.
Xiè and others reported:
“In Dàmíng Fǔ, Zhèngzhōu, and other places, since Chéng'ān second year,
the levied straw and materials for which no payment has been made
amount to over 219,000 strings of cash.”

So it was ordered that the available cash from various places be used by capable officials, together with upright and strong officials from various prefectures and counties, to compensate everyone one by one,
and subsequently the Ànchá Sī was ordered to investigate.
On the *rénshēn* day of the eleventh month, Zhēnyòu third year, of Xuānzōng,
In the fourth month of the third year,
Yánzhǎn Tiānzé, the Cìshǐ of Dānzhōu, stated:
"The method of defense
is to breach the great river and make it flow north through the territories of Dézhōu, Bózhōu, Guānzhōu, and Cāngzhōu.
Its old embankment is still clearly present,
so the labor will not be strenuous,
and as water flows downwards, there will certainly be no danger of floods.
However, those who oppose this will either argue that it harms the national interest by damaging the salt fields of Cāngzhōu,
or they will explain that it will inundate the fertile fields north of the river.
I have often heard elders by the river say that
when the water spreads out,
it becomes too shallow to cross on horseback
and too deep to navigate by boat.
This is a major strategy for defense.
If it is said that it will inundate people's fields,
then after the river shifts,
it will silt up into fertile soil,
perfectly suitable for cultivation,
yielding double the usual harvest.
What greater benefit could there be?
If this plan is missed,
then the troops and provisions along the Hénán route will be insufficient,
and the people of Héběi and Shāndōng will all scatter."
An imperial edict ordered discussions on this.
In the third month of the fourth year,
Wēnsā Kěxǐ, the Cìshǐ of Yánzhōu, stated:
"In recent times, the river has departed from its old course,
flowing southeast from Wèizhōu,
passing through Xúzhōu and Pīzhōu to the sea.
Because of this,
the land of Hénán has become narrow.
I have secretly observed that the river west of Xīnxiāng Xiàn can be breached to flow northeast.
To its south, there is an old embankment,
so the water cannot overflow.
It flows for over fifty *lǐ* and merges with the Qīnghé.
It then enters the sea via Jùnzhōu, Dàmíng, Guānzhōu, Qīngzhōu, and Liǔkǒu.
This is the river's old course,
and it all has old embankments.
Repairing the gaps will suffice.
In this way, the Shāndōng and Dàmíng routes,
etc., will all be in Hénán,
and Héběi's various commanderies will also gain half of it.
In retreat, it will be sufficient for defensive preparations;
in advance, it will be sufficient to strengthen the foundation for recovery."
He further stated:
"The residents of the south bank
have already been registered as river laborers to repair and construct river dams
and build garrison houses.
They are also made to transport fodder and grain.
Their taxes and corvée are heavy,
double that of other places.
The summer and autumn taxes
are not even discussed yet.
I request a reduction for those whose burdens are slightly lighter,
to ease the people's strength."
The matter was sent to the Shàngshūshěng,
where the prime ministers stated:
"The river has flowed southeast for a long time.
If it is breached all at once,
we fear that the old course will not contain it,
and it will overflow,
dividing into several rivers
that cannot be reunited.
If the water divides, it becomes shallow and narrow, easy to cross.
It will freeze in cold weather,
making defense even more difficult.
This is highly inadvisable."
An imperial edict merely ordered a suitable reduction of the taxes and corvée of the residents of the counties and commanderies on the south bank.
In the fourth month of the summer of the fifth year,
an imperial decree was issued to the Shūmìyuàn:
In strategic locations along the river,
stone embankments should be built,
and "scattering star piles" (撒星樁) and "horse-trapping pits" (陷馬塹) should be set up to prepare for the enemy.
Regarding the transport canal,
the Jīn capital was in Yān,
fifty *lǐ* east of the Lùshuǐ.
Therefore, sluice gates were built to regulate the various waters of the Gāoliánghé and Báilíantán,
to facilitate the transport of grain from Shāndōng and Héběi.
In all cities along the river in various circuits,
granaries were established to store the taxes from neighboring commanderies.
For example, Línqīng and Lìtíng in Ēnzhōu;
Jiānglíng and Dōngguāng in Jǐngzhōu;
Xīngjì and Huìchuān in Qīngzhōu;
and Wǔqiáng in Xiànzhōu and Shēnzhōu.
These six prefectures and various counties were all locations for granaries.
were the old Yellow River flowing through the territories of Huázhōu, Dàmíng, Ēnzhōu, Jǐngzhōu, Cāngzhōu, and Huìchuān;
the Zhāngshuǐ, which became the Yùhé to the northeast,
then conveyed provisions from Sūmén, Huòjiā, Xīnxiāng, Wèizhōu, Jùnzhōu, Líyáng, Wèixiàn, Zhāngdé, Cízhōu, and Míngzhōu;
the Héngshuǐ then passed through Shēnzhōu and met the Hūtuó,
bringing provisions from Xiànzhōu and Qīngzhōu.
All these converged at Xìn'ān Hǎirán,
flowed upstream to Tōngzhōu,
and from Tōngzhōu entered the sluice gates,
reaching the capital after more than ten days.
Other rivers, such as the Jùmǎhé in Bàzhōu,
the Shāhé in Xióngzhōu,
and the Běiqīnghé in Shāndōng,
were all routes for transport.
However, upstream from Tōngzhōu,
the terrain was steep and the water did not stay,
so it easily became shallow.
Boats would get stuck and could not move,
hence land transport was often employed,
which people found quite arduous.
During the reign of Shìzōng,
those who spoke out requested the opening of the Lúgōujīnkǒu to facilitate grain transport.
Many people were conscripted for several years,
but it ultimately met with no success.
The matter is documented in the section on the Lúgōuhé.
only carts were used for transport.
The system was as follows:
Spring transport began when the ice melted
and ended with the summer rains.
Autumn transport began in the eighth month
and ended when the ice froze.
When a convoy was about to depart,
people were assembled,
and the loaded grain was sealed and marked.
It was first delivered to the unloading point,
and accepted if it matched the sealed sample.
All convoy boats were to be repaired three days before the scheduled departure.
One convoy was loaded per day,
and departed three days after loading was completed.
Distances were calculated and limits set for upstream and downstream travel.
Upon reaching the designated granary,
three days were allowed for unloading,
and another three days for giving and receiving payment.
The transport fees were as follows:
For water transport, salt cost 48 *wén* per *shí* per 100 *lǐ*;
rice 50 *wén*, 1 *fēn*, 2 *lí*, 7 *háo*;
millet 40 *wén*, 1 *fēn*, 3 *háo*;
and money 1 *wén*, 7 *fēn*, 2 *lí*, 8 *háo* per *guàn*.
For land transport, the wages were:
rice 112 *wén*, 1 *fēn*, 5 *háo* per *shí* per 100 *lǐ*;
millet 57 *wén*, 6 *fēn*, 8 *lí*, 4 *háo*;
and money 3 *wén*, 9 *lí*, 6 *háo* per *guàn*.
For other goods, for every 100 *jīn* transported 100 *lǐ*:
on flat roads, it was 131 *wén*, 5 *fēn* in spring and winter,
and 157 *wén*, 8 *fēn* in summer and autumn;
on mountain roads, it was 149 *wén* in spring and winter,
and 201 *wén* in summer and autumn.
For the fees collected by the Sīyuànwù,
it was 90 *wén*, 3 *fēn* in spring and winter,
and 114 *wén* in summer and autumn.
For common households that leased official boats for grain transport,
the fees were set at a rate of ten parts.
In the first year, 2 parts were deducted;
in the second year, 1 part, 8 *lí*;
in the third year, 1 part, 7 *lí*;
in the fourth year, 1 part, 5 *lí*;
and for five years or more, 1 part.
Initially,
in the eighth month of the fourth year of Dàdìng under Shìzōng,
due to a great harvest in Shāndōng,
an imperial edict ordered the transfer of its grain to replenish the capital.
In the tenth month,
the emperor went out to the nearby suburbs
and saw that the canal was silted up.
He summoned officials and asked for the reason.
The responsible official stated that it was due to the Hùbù's failure to plan for it.
The emperor summoned Cáo Wàngzhī, the Hùbù Shìláng,
and reprimanded him, saying:
"There is a river, yet you did not dredge it,
causing the common people to suffer greatly with land transport.
The fault lies with you.
I do not wish to punish you immediately;
you should exert all your strength to make the transport canal passable."
In the first month of the fifth year,
the Shàngshūshěng reported
that tens of thousands of laborers could be conscripted.
The emperor said:
"It is spring, and the people should not be burdened.
Order the palace secretariat's households, the princely retinue of the Eastern Palace, and military laborers within 500 *lǐ*
to dredge and repair it."
In the twenty-first year,
as the capital's reserves were low in the eighth month,
an imperial edict ordered over a million *shí* of grain from the six commanderies along the river, including Ēnzhōu and Xiànzhōu, to be transported to Tōngzhōu,
and then carted into the capital.
In the fourth month of the third year of Míngchāng,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
"Liáodōng and Běijīnglù have always been rich in rice and grain.
It is advisable to transport them by sea to Shāndōng.

Yesterday, after inspecting the coastal areas near Dōngjīng, it was found that from Dàwù Qīngkǒu, including Xiánpíng and Tóngshànguǎn, granaries could be established to store grain and facilitate grain transport.
If Shāndōng and Héběi suffer from famine,
it can then be transported to provide relief."
The decree was approved.
In the fifth year of Chéng'ān,
the prefectures and counties along the river were ordered
to pay 200,000 *shí* of soybeans as tribute,
and transport them to the capital.
After inspection of quality, the cost of raising horses would be paid from their salaries.
Additionally, 100,000 *shí* of wheat were to be transported,
each paid in its original form.
Then, Tián Lì, the Dūshuǐjiān Chéng, was ordered to inspect the grain transport routes.
In the first year of Tàihé,
the Shàngshūshěng, considering that the six granaries managed by the Jǐngzhōu grain transport office
received annual taxes of no less than sixty thousand *shí*,
and that the farthest counties from the collection points were no less than two hundred *lǐ* away,
with officials taking bribes and causing delays,
the people suffered immensely.
Even when officials were nearby to supervise, the situation remained the same.
Therefore, one Censor Yùshǐ was appointed to patrol and investigate.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor arrived in Bàzhōu.
Because the old grain transport canal was shallow and obstructed,
an imperial edict was issued to the Shàngshūshěng to dispatch six thousand soldiers and laborers from Shāndōng, Héběi, Hédōng, Zhōngdū, and Běijīng
to re-excavate it.
For those whose *túntián* land was encroached upon,
the officials would provide equivalent compensation.
For private land, a higher price would be paid.
In the sixth year,
the Shàngshūshěng observed that officials in prefectures and counties through which the grain transport canals passed
considered it none of their concern,
often leading to shallow and stagnant waterways,
which allowed *gānghù* to exploit the situation by claiming the waters were too shallow for full loads,
resulting in numerous corrupt practices.
Consequently, a new system was established:
all officials in prefectures and counties through which the grain transport canals passed
would have the title
“Tíkòng Cáohé Shì” (Supervisor of Grain Transport Affairs) for prefectural officials,
and
“Guǎngōu Cáohé Shì” (Manager of Grain Transport Affairs) for county officials,
to ensure the timely inspection of grain transport
and the protection of dikes and embankments.
There were three prefectures: Dàxīng, Dàmíng, Zhāngdé.
Twelve zhou: Ēn, Jǐng, Cāng, Qīng, Xiàn, Shēn, Wèi, Jùn, Huá, Cí, Míng, Tōng.
Thirty-three counties:
In the twelfth month,
a patrol official for the Tōngjìhé was newly established,
forming one office with the Tiānjīnhé,
jointly managing the sluices and embankments of the grain transport canal,
named simply the Tiānjīnhé Patrol Official,
subordinate to the Dūshuǐjiān.
In the sixth month of the eighth year,
Zhāng Xíngxìn, the Cìshǐ of Tōngzhōu, stated,
“It takes over ten days for a boat to pass through the sluice from Tōngzhōu and reach the capital,
but the government only provides expenses for five days' journey,”
so the allowance was increased.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu,
after relocating to Biàn,
as Chén and Yǐng prefectures were near water,
there was a desire to borrow civilian boats for grain transport,
but it was inconvenient.
Therefore, a Tíjǔ official was established, following the model of the Guānzhōu grain transport office,
to recruit and register boatmen,
and officials from the Hùbù were ordered to patrol and supervise them.
In the fourth year,
following the advice of Yòuchéng Hóu Zhì,
the Qìnshuǐ was opened to facilitate provisions transport.
The Emperor also considered the hardship of transporting supplies to the capital,
and ordered the use of imperial oxen and official carts
to assist with the effort.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of Xīngdìng,
the Emperor instructed the Crown Prince,
“An official escorting grain to the Central Capital
must be carefully chosen.
Should there be any mishap,
the officials of the Shūmìyuàn will also be held accountable.
The boats should be those with two prows and sterns, made by Máohuāniǎn,
and banners should be displayed as if transporting troops,
to prevent the enemy from knowing it is grain.”
The Xīnxī Hángshěng Bǎhúlǔ said,
“Shǎnxī annually transports grain to assist Guāndōng,
and the people's strength is greatly exhausted.
If boats were to enter the river from the Wèi and proceed downstream,
it could relieve the people's burden.”
Therefore, strict vigilance was ordered,
and if there was an alert,
all boats were to be moored on the south bank.
At that time, the imperial court supplied military provisions to Pī, Xú, Sù, and Sì,
with counties in Jīngdōng transporting over one hundred thousand *shí* annually,
which greatly distressed the people.
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
a Tōngjì Granary was established in Guīdé Fǔ,
with a Dūjiān official
to receive grain from the eastern commanderies.
Lǐ Fùhēng, Jìdùshǐ of Dìngguó Jūn, said:
“The imperial residence in Hénán
and grain cannot be too much.
In recent years,
whenever there has been a slight shortage,
we have relied on Shǎnxī.
Shǎnxī's land is fertile, and its harvests are abundant;
an aid of one hundred thousand *shí* is not difficult.
However, the cost of transport by cart
first consumes half of it.
How can the people bear it?
It would be advisable to build twenty large boats,
which could cross into the river from Dàqìng Guān,
reach Húchéng to the east,
and return within a few days,
with only about one hundred polemen.
If each boat could carry three hundred and fifty *hú*,
then one hundred people could transport seven thousand *hú* in a few days.
From summer to autumn, over thirty million *hú* could be transported,
The Emperor agreed.
At that time, a granary Dūjiān and a Jiānzhīnà (Superintendent of Receipts and Disbursements) were also established at Tóngjùn Zhèn in Língbì County,
as the Chángzhígōu was being opened,
intending to transport grain by boat from Wàn'ānhú into the Biàn and then to the Sì,
to store the grain.
Lúgōu Hé.
In the tenth year of Dàdìng,
there was a discussion about digging the Lúgōu to connect the capital to grain transport routes.
The Emperor joyfully said,
“If this is done,
goods from all routes can directly reach the capital,
what greater benefit could there be?”
He ordered a calculation,
which indicated that laborers within a thousand *lǐ* of the area would be employed.
The Emperor ordered that disaster-stricken areas be exempted,
and officials' attendants assist in the labor.
Later,
an edict was issued to the Zǎichén, saying,
“Shāndōng suffers from famine this year,
and initiating public works will hinder farming.
How can there be no resentment?
Opening the canal was originally for the benefit of the people,
but instead it causes resentment;
this is unacceptable.
It should be temporarily suspended.”
In the twelfth month of the eleventh year,
the provincial officials memorialized to reopen it.
From Jīnkǒu, it would be dredged to the north of the capital city, entering the moat,
and then eastward to the north of Tōngzhōu,
entering the Lùshuǐ.
The work was estimated to take eighty days.
In the third month of the twelfth year,
the Emperor sent people to review it,
and they returned reporting
“it would only take fifty days.”
The Emperor summoned the Zǎichén and reprimanded them, saying,
“The remaining thirty days would only hinder farming and waste labor.
Why did you not consider this?”
When the canal was completed,
due to the high and steep terrain,
the water was turbid.
Being steep, the current rushed and swirled, eroding the banks and causing collapses.
Being turbid, mud and silt accumulated and blocked the channel,
and accumulated debris made it shallow,
unable to bear boats.
Thereafter,
the Emperor said to the Zǎichén,
“Dividing the Lúgōu into a grain transport canal
has not yet shown results.
If it could indeed be made to work,
all goods from the southern routes would reach the capital,
and prices would fall.”
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Fùmǎ Yuán Zhōng said,
“I request that those familiar with river courses
inspect the area.”
Ultimately, it could not be made to work and was abandoned.
In the fifth month of the twenty-fifth year,
Before this,
it had broken at Xiǎntōng Zhài,
and an imperial edict had dispatched laborers from within three hundred *lǐ* of Zhōngdū to repair it.
Now it broke again,
and the imperial court feared wasting labor and materials,
so they ordered that it not be repaired for the time being.
In the third month of the twenty-seventh year,
the Zǎichén stated,
“The sluice below Jīnkǒu at Mèngjiā Shān
is over one hundred and forty *chǐ* higher than the capital city.
It is guarded only by *shèliáng jūn* (archers guarding provisions),
which may not be reliable.
Should there be a sudden flood,
or if people act maliciously,
the harm would be considerable.
If it were permanently blocked,
all the irrigated rice fields would become dry land,
but planting grain and wheat there would not be a waste of land.
Otherwise,
a double sluice should be built,
and also *sǎoguān* (sweep official) offices
and *sǎobīng* (sweep soldier) quarters should be established on the banks,
so that there might be no cause for concern.”
The Emperor approved their words
and sent an envoy to block it.
In the summer, on the *bǐngzǐ* day of the fourth month,
an imperial edict enfeoffed the water god of Lúgōu as Ānpíng Hóu.
In the fifth month of the twenty-eighth year,
an imperial edict ordered that a stone bridge be built at Lúgōuhé,
a vital ford for travelers.
Before it could be carried out, Shìzōng died.
In the sixth month of the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng of Zhāngzōng,
since crossing the river was difficult due to its swift currents,
an imperial edict commanded the construction of boats.
Later, it was again ordered that a stone bridge be built instead.
It was completed in the third month of the third year of Míngchāng,
and an imperial decree named it Guǎnglì.
Officials proposed that, as it was a route taken by the imperial carriage
and a vital road for merchants and travelers,
the government should build eastern and western corridors
for people to reside in.
The emperor said:
"Why is that necessary?
The common people should build them themselves."
Zuǒchéng Shǒuzhēn said:
"I only fear that they will be occupied by powerful gentry.
Moreover, many profit-seeking people stop on the east bank.
If the government builds them, both the east and west banks will be satisfactory,
The emperor then agreed.
In the sixth month,
the Lúgōu dikes burst.
An imperial edict ordered them to be quickly blocked
to prevent flooding and harm.
Yòushíyí Lù Duó submitted a memorial, stating
that the water should be diverted to follow its natural course,
and it was unnecessary to repair the old dike below Xuántóngkǒu and above Dīngcūn.
The emperor ordered the prime ministers to discuss it,
and then commanded Gōngbù Shàngshū Xū Chízhuó and Lù Duó to jointly inspect the dike and road.
Hūtuóhé.
In the sixth month of the eighth year of Dàdìng,
the Hūtuó river breached its banks at Zhēndìng.
It was ordered that twenty-eight thousand laborers from Héběi Xīlù, Héjiān, Tàiyuán, and Jìzhōu be dispatched
to repair and complete its dikes.
In the second month of the tenth year,
two river patrol officials were newly established for the Hūtuó river.
In the seventeenth year,
the Hūtuó river burst its banks at Báimǎgāng.
Officials reported this,
and an imperial edict dispatched envoys to reinforce the blockage,
mobilizing laborers within five hundred *lǐ* of Zhēndìng.
The work began on the first day of the second month of the eighteenth year.
Tóngzhī Zhēndìng Yǐn Gǔshāhǔ and Tóngzhī Héběi Xīlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Xú Wěi were commanded to supervise it.
Zhānghé.
In the first month of spring of the twentieth year of Dàdìng,
an imperial edict ordered officials to repair the Zhānghé sluices.
All necessary labor and materials were to be provided by the government,
so as not to disturb the people.
In the sixth month of the second year of Míngchāng,
both the Zhānghé and Lúgōu dikes burst.
An imperial edict ordered them to be quickly blocked.
On the *guǐwèi* day of the first month of spring of the fourth year,
officials reported that the repair of the Zhānghé dikes and revetments was estimated to require over three hundred eighty thousand laborers.
An imperial edict ordered that, following the precedent of the Lúgōu river,
people affected by the flood and lacking food be recruited as laborers,
with the government providing money and rice.
If insufficient, people affected by the water were to be conscripted,
and paid as above.
Collated Notes
Records, Volume 9, Rituals 1, Suburb Sacrifices
When the Jīn people entered Biàn,
the Sòng dynasty had enjoyed long peace,
and its institutions, rituals, and music were brilliantly complete.
The Jīn people collected all their maps and records,
and carried their imperial carriages, ritual objects, and honor guards north.
At that time, they were engaged in military affairs,
and had no leisure to discuss these matters.
Later,
they established the imperial ancestral temple in Huìníng,
and all matters were started from scratch.
During the Huángtǒng period,
Xīzōng toured to Xīzhēn.
He first rode in the imperial golden carriage,
led the honor guard,
and displayed the drums and wind instruments.
The sight and sound were strikingly new.
The rituals for the imperial ancestral temple and court assemblies were also carried out successively.
Subsequently, Hǎilíng, with his wolfish ambition,
desired to annex Jiāngnán.
He then ordered officials to repair the former palace in Biàn
and restore the ancestral temples and altars of state,
and brought all the former Sòng ritual vessels back.
Outwardly, he was warlike;
inwardly, he indulged in desires.
As his policies had already erred,
how could he discuss rituals and music?
After Shìzōng rose to power,
he again recovered the former Sòng ritual vessels that had been moved, and brought them back.
He then ordered officials to compare and examine the historical evolution of the former Táng and Sòng institutions,
established the
"Xiángdìng Suǒ"
to discuss rituals,
and set up the
"Xiángjiào Suǒ"
to review music.
These were overseen by a prime minister knowledgeable in scholarship.
For every appropriate detail of an affair and every regulated aspect of an object,
after reporting it to the emperor, they were then compiled.
The book was completed in the early Míngchāng period,
totaling over four hundred volumes,
named *Jīn Zuǎnxīu Zálù*.
All matters, names, and numbers,
branched out and extended,
strung together like pearls and arranged like a chessboard,
were orderly and clear,
brilliant as vermilion.
It also included diagrams for auspicious and inauspicious rituals: thirteen sections of the imperial equipage for grand funerals,
and nine sections of the lesser imperial equipage for suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices.
And it ordered the Shàngshū Zuǒyòusī, Chūnguān, Bīngcáo, and Tàichángsì to each keep a copy,
its intention being profoundly far-reaching.
At that time,
the realm was prosperous and peaceful,
and the people and things were moderately well-off.
It was indeed this foundation that sustained it for several hundred years.
Alas,
how true it is that ritual is for governing the state!
And what about the transforming influence of Guānju and Línzhǐ,
whose lasting customs and thoughts affected later generations?
How significant they were!
When Xuānzōng moved south,
the territory daily shrank.
Just as the rising sun, but only a burning torch,
Cài couldn't flow eastward, and the last embers died out.
The scattered and lost maps and records were nowhere to be found,
and what Prime Minister Hán Qǐxiān and others discussed,
as well as what Ritual Official Zhāng Wěi and his son Zhāng Xíngjiǎn privately wrote from public records,
were also lost to transmission.
Therefore, among existing books,
only several volumes of collected rituals remain.
Those stored in the imperial archives were also incomplete and fragmented.
Therefore, we merely compiled the rituals for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temple sacrifices, various deity worships, court audiences, and assemblies into this book,
while inauspicious rituals were omitted.
Indeed, since the successive assassinations by Xīzōng, Hǎilíng, and Wèishàowáng,
although it was said
that "thirteen sections of the imperial equipage are for grand funerals,"
whether they were actually carried out or not,
cannot be verified.
Therefore, the funeral rites of Xuānxiào, though they exist,
are also not recorded again.
Alas,
although Confucius did not abandon the "sacrifice of the live sheep at the new moon announcement,"
the incompleteness of historical texts must also be handled with caution.
Thus, the Ritual Records are compiled.
Southern and Northern Suburban Sacrifices.
The Jīn's suburban sacrifices were based on their custom of bowing to Heaven.
Later,
when Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he announced sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
which involved setting up altars and performing sacrifices.
After Tiāndé,
the system of Southern and Northern Suburban Sacrifices began.
During Dàdìng and Míngchāng, these rituals became increasingly complete.
The Southern Suburban Altar
was outside the Fēngyímén gate,
at the *sì* (southeast) position relative to the imperial palace.
It was a round altar of three tiers,
each with twelve steps,
arranged according to the earthly branches.
There were three enclosing walls,
with three gates on each of the four sides.
The fasting palace was to the northeast,
and the storehouse to the south.
Both the altar and the enclosing walls were plastered with red earth.
The Northern Suburban Square Mound
was outside the Tōngxuánmén gate,
at the *hài* (northwest) position relative to the imperial palace.
It was a square altar of three tiers,
with four main steps at the *zǐ*, *wǔ*, *mǎo*, and *yǒu* (north, south, east, west) positions.
There were three square enclosing walls,
also with three gates on each of the four sides.
The Altar for Worshipping the Morning Sun was called Dàmíng,
located southeast of the Shīrénmén gate,
at the *mǎo* (east) position relative to the imperial palace.
The system of gates and enclosing walls was the same as that of the Square Mound.
The Altar for Worshipping the Evening Moon was called Yèmíng,
located northwest of the Zhāngyìmén gate,
at the *yǒu* (west) position relative to the imperial palace.
The ground was dug out to form a depression,
and the altar was built within it.
Heavenly August Supreme Emperor (Hàotiān Shàngdì) and Imperial Earth Goddess (Huángdì Qí) were always jointly sacrificed to at the Round Mound on the winter solstice.
The Imperial Earth Goddess was sacrificed to at the Square Mound on the summer solstice.
The morning sun was worshipped in the eastern suburbs on the spring equinox.
The evening moon was worshipped in the western suburbs on the autumn equinox.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng, the suburban sacrifice was first performed.
The Emperor ordered the grand councilors to deliberate on the ceremony of accompanying the sacrifice.
The Left Executive Assistant, Shí Jū, reported,
"According to the Lǐjì, 'All things are rooted in Heaven,
and humans are rooted in their ancestors.
This is why ancestors are associated with Shàngdì.'
Indeed, the one who accompanies [the sacrifice]
is the host to the spirit.
Those who come from outside have no master and do not stop.
Therefore, by extending the sacrifice to ancestral progenitors, they are honored.
Since the Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn dynasties,
one ancestor has always been paired with Heaven.
It was not until Táng Gāozōng
that Gāozǔ and Tàizōng were first grandly paired.
In the early Chuígǒng period,
Gāozōng was also added,
thus establishing the ritual of three ancestors being simultaneously paired.
During the Sòng dynasty,
three emperors were also once paired;
later, the Board of Rites submitted a deliberation,
believing that when facing Heaven and Earth,
there should not be two masters for the spirits.
Consequently, only Tàizǔ was paired.
Your servant believes that the winter solstice suburban sacrifice should follow ancient rites."
The Emperor said,
"The Táng and Sòng dynasties' practice of using private relatives
does not conform to ancient custom
and is not worthy of being imitated.
Now, only
Tàizǔ should be paired."
He further told the grand councilors,
"The ritual of bowing to Heaven in Our country is very important.
Now, your proposal to construct an altar according to ancient regulations
is also appropriate.
Our state has supplanted the rulers of Liáo and Sòng,
occupying the rightful position under Heaven.
How can the suburban sacrifice not be performed?"
Then, in the eighth month, an edict was issued saying:
"Among all national affairs, none is greater than sacrifice;
among all sacrifices, none is greater than that to Heaven.
This practice has been followed since ancient times,
and the old regulations are all extant.
We contemplate how Tàizǔ established the Mandate
and illuminated the peaceful plans of Our dynasty,
possessing all states,
for five cycles until now.
While adapting to the times in formulating regulations,
there have been embellishments to the national appearance;
however, in tracing the root and upholding tradition,
We have not yet found leisure to personally perform the suburban sacrifice.
Moreover, as the blessings of Heaven increasingly arrive and the harvest is repeatedly abundant,
how can We not elaborate on this grand tradition and clearly manifest the great repayment?
Choosing the day of the sun's maximum rise,
We shall personally offer sacrifice at the round altar.
We are pleased to join with Our officials
to plan this glorious event.
On the seventeenth day of the eleventh month of this year, the service shall be held at the Southern Suburb.
We instruct you, officials in charge,
to each fulfill your duties,
assisting Us in this sacrifice,
none daring to be irreverent."
Then, on the day before,
he visited all the ancestors,
informing them of the suburban sacrifice.
On that day,
the imperial carriage and retinue were prepared,
and he personally went to the suburban altar to perform the rites.
Ritual Procedures:
Fasting: The Táng system was used.
For major sacrifices,
scattered fasting was observed for four days,
and concentrated fasting for three days.
For moderate sacrifices,
scattered fasting for two days,
and concentrated fasting for one day.
When the Emperor personally performed the sacrifice,
seven days beforehand,
the Acting Grand Commandant would administer an oath to the assistant and final offering officials, imperial princes, and accompanying imperial relatives at the palace.
Imperial relatives aged fifteen and above,
even if their official rank did not reach the seventh grade, also assisted in the sacrifice and took the oath.
An oath was also administered to all officials at the Department of State Affairs.
The Acting Grand Commandant faced south,
the Minister of Education faced north,
the Censor supervising the sacrifice stood to the west,
and the Erudite of Rites stood to the east,
all facing each other.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies and the Minister of Imperial Feasts stood behind the Minister of Education,
in a second row, facing north.

The Directorate of Astronomy, Assistant Minister of Imperial Feasts, Director and Assistant Director of the Grand Ancestral Temple, Director and Assistant Director of Grand Music, Director and Assistant Director of Imperial Provision, Director of Imperial Wine, Director of Storehouse and Sacrifices, Assistant Director of Suburban Sacrifices, Controller of Ritual Vessels, Grand Prayer Master, Usher of Rites, Harmonizer of Music, and all other executive officials stood in a second row, ascending from the west, facing north.
The Ritual Official in charge handed the oath text to the Acting Grand Commandant,
who then administered the oath, saying:
"On this such and such year, with such and such cyclical characters,
such and such month,
such and such day,
such and such cyclical characters,
the Emperor is performing the sacrifice at the Southern Suburb.
Let each fulfill their duties.
Should anyone be disrespectful,
the state has its constant punishments."
The Ritual Official in charge announced,
"Officials of the seventh rank and below, all withdraw."
On the day before the concentrated fasting,
the Palace Steward set up the imperial seat in the Dà'ān Diàn,
facing south in the center.
East and west rooms were set up beside the imperial seat,
and an imperial canopy was set up inside the room,
with curtains hung below the pillars.
Three days before the sacrifice,
the small resting place was arranged.
One day before the sacrifice,
prayer cushions were set up,
as well as the Emperor's plaque position, the Emperor's blessing-drinking position,
and yellow mats,
from where the jade chariot descended to where the imperial sedan ascended.
On the day of concentrated fasting,
the Communicating Chamberlains led officials of the fifth rank and above, both civil and military,
to take their places according to the ritual.
All guards and attendants,
dressed in their respective uniforms and accoutrements,
with their pendants fastened,
all proceeded to the palace gate to receive the Emperor.
Two *ke* (approximately 30 minutes) after sunrise,
the Chief of the Palace reported
"All is ready outside."
The Emperor donned his formal robes and crown,
fastened his pendants,
and exited in his imperial sedan,
with警蹕 (clear the way) and imperial guards as per regular ceremony.
The Emperor took his seat on the imperial throne,
sitting facing east.
The Communicating Chamberlain conveyed the command,
and all officials above and below the hall prostrated themselves.
When finished,
they faced west,
and the Chamberlain announced
"Each await further orders."
After about one *ke* (15 minutes),
the Chief of the Palace knelt and reported:
"Your servant such and such says,
I request Your Majesty to descend and proceed to the fasting chamber."
He prostrated himself,
rose,
and returned to his attendant position.
The Emperor descended from his seat,
entered the room,
and all officials withdrew.
All executive officials stayed overnight in the main chamber,
attending to their duties as usual,
but did not mourn for the deceased or inquire about the sick,
nor did they approve documents involving punishments or executions,
nor did they pass judgment on criminals,
nor did they engage in any unclean matters.
On the day of concentrated fasting,
only matters related to the sacrifice were carried out;
all others were prohibited.
If there was a deficiency after fasting,
it was handled by a temporary substitute.
Arrangements: Five days before the sacrifice,
the Directorate of Imperial Equipage and the Palace Steward arranged the fasting palace.
The officials in charge set up the escorts and guards' stations to the east and west of the palace.
They also set up the accompanying imperial princes' stations slightly south of the east of the palace,
facing west, with seniority to the north,
and descendants of the imperial clan positioned behind them.

They also set up the stations for the Minister of Education, the assistant, the final offering official, and the executive officials who would carry out the rituals, to the west of the outer enclosed gate on the south of the altar,
facing east, with seniority to the north,
in a second row but different positions.
They also set up the 'Room of Heavenly Names'
to the east of the outer enclosed gate on the south of the altar,
facing west.
The Grand Rite Commissioner's station was behind it,
all facing west.
They also set up a large mat-covered shed to the northwest outside the altar,
to park chariots and palanquins to guard against wind and snow.
Three days before the sacrifice,
the Palace Steward set up the grand resting place north of the path inside the outer eastern enclosed gate,
facing south.
They also set up the small resting place north of the卯 (mǎo) steps below the altar,
facing south.
The officials in charge set up a food tent north of the central eastern enclosed gate,
facing south.
Guards were stationed,
each dressed in their uniforms and accoutrements,
guarding the enclosed gates,
two guards at each gate.
The Director of Suburban Sacrifices led his subordinates
to sweep and clean the altar, both above and below, and inside and outside the enclosure.
Then, the pyre position was made,
to the east of the eastern gate of the southern central enclosure,
at the巳 (sì) position on the altar.
A burial pit was also made,
at the戌 (xū) position inside the central enclosure.
the Tàiyùe Lìng
led his subordinates to set up the ascending song music on the altar, slightly to the south,
facing north.
The jade chimes were to the west of the central steps,
the metal bells to the east of the central steps.
One Zhù
was slightly to the north in front of the bells, one Yǔ
slightly to the north in front of the chimes,
facing each other east and west. The singers followed next,
with other musicians each positioned behind the suspended instruments.
The qín and sè zithers were in front,
gourd and bamboo instruments behind,
on the first tier below the altar.
All were arranged in staggered double rows,
facing north.
Also, the Gōngxuàn Yuè
orchestra was set up outside the outer gate of the southern enclosure. The Bāyì
eight-row dance and two other dances were performed in front of the music.
Also, Cǎicí Yuè was set up in front of Yìngtiān Mén.
One day before the sacrifice, the Fènglǐ Láng
ascended and set up the Emperor's plaque position on the altar, between the Chén and Sì directions,
facing north.
Also, the Emperor's "drinking blessings" position was set up to its left, slightly set back,
facing north.
He also led the Lǐzhí Guān to set up the Assistant Final Libation position to the northeast of the Mǎo steps,
facing west, with the northernmost being the highest rank.
The Sītú was positioned to the east of the Mǎo steps,
south of the path, facing west.
The Lǐbù Shàngshū, Tàicháng Qīng, Guānglù Qīng, and Lǐbù Shìláng were each positioned next in order,
followed by the Tàicháng Chéng and Guānglù Chéng.
Also, the Dàlǐ Shǐ was positioned to the left of the previous group, slightly set back,
facing west.
Also, the sub-offering officials, the Sītiān Jiān, and the Dúcè Zhōngshū Shìláng were positioned north of the path of the central enclosure gate,
facing west.
The Jiāoshè Lìng, Lǐnxī Lìng, Tàiguān Lìng, and Liángyùn Lìng were positioned behind them.
Also, the Jiāoshè Chéng, Tàizhù, Fènglǐ Láng, and other attending officials below them were positioned behind them,
all facing west,
in staggered double rows.
