Also, the civil and military officials participating in the sacrifice, from first to fifth rank, were positioned south of the path inside the central enclosure gate,
facing west,
all standing in double rows.
Also, the assisting intoners, scribes, and fasting officials were positioned north of the path outside the eastern enclosure gate,
facing west.
Also, the imperial clan members attending the sacrifice were positioned south of the path,
facing west.
Civil and military officials participating in the sacrifice from sixth to ninth rank
were positioned again to their south,
all facing west,
in staggered double rows,
each according to their rank.
Also, two Jiānjì Yùshǐ
were positioned, one to the southwest of the central steps,
and one to the northwest of the northern steps,
both facing east.
Also, two Jiānlǐ Bóshì
were positioned, one to the southeast of the central steps,
and one to the northeast of the northern steps,
both facing west.
Also, the Tàiyùe Lìng was positioned slightly to the east between the instrument stands,
facing west.
The Xiélǜ Láng was positioned to the west of the instrument stands,
facing east.
Also, the Fènglǐ Láng was positioned south of the altar, slightly to the east,
facing west.
The officiants followed next.
The Sīzūn was positioned at the place for pouring libations,
both facing north.
Also, the sacrificial animal display board was set up outside the eastern gate of the outer enclosure,
facing west.
The ritual food display board was slightly to the west of its north,
facing south.
To the east of the sacrificial animal display board
was the position for the sacrificial animals.
The Tàishǐ and Tàizhù were each positioned behind the sacrificial animals,
both facing west.
Also, the Lǐbù Shàngshū, Tàicháng Qīng, and Guānglù Qīng were positioned south of the sacrificial animal display board, slightly to the north,
facing west.
The Tàicháng Chéng, Guānglù Chéng, and Tàiguān Lìng were positioned behind them.
The Jiānjì Yùshǐ and Jiānlǐ Bóshì were positioned slightly set back to the west of the Lǐbù Shàngshū's position,
facing north.
The Lǐnxī Lìng's position was to the southwest of the sacrificial animal position,
facing north.
Also, ritual foods were arranged on tables in front of the ritual food display board.
At three kè after the Wèi hour,
when the foods were arranged,
also, the Lǐbù Shàngshū, Tàicháng Qīng, and Guānglù Qīng were positioned slightly to the east in front of the tables,
with the northernmost being the highest rank,
facing west.
The Tàicháng Chéng, Guānglù Chéng, and Tàiguān Lìng were positioned behind them,
facing west.
Also, the Jiānjì Yùshǐ and Jiānlǐ Bóshì were positioned slightly to the west in front of the tables,
with the northernmost being the highest rank,
facing east.
Also, exotic treasures and auspicious omens were set up to the northwest of the Gōngxuàn Yuè,
with the Tàifǔ Shǎojiān positioned behind the treasures.
Annual tributes from various prefectures were positioned to the northeast of the Gōngxuàn Yuè,
with the Hùbù Lángzhōng positioned behind them.
The Emperor's eight treasures were positioned to the southwest of the Gōngxuàn Yuè,
with eight Fúbǎo Láng each behind a treasure.
Treasures from vanquished and destroyed nations were positioned to the southeast of the Gōngxuàn Yuè,
with the Shǎofǔ Shǎojiān positioned behind them.
Also, the Dàyuè Lìng was positioned slightly to the east of the north of the Gōngxuàn Yuè,
with two Xiélǜ Láng to the south of the Dàyuè Lìng,
facing each other east and west.
The Sītiān Jiān,
at two kè after the Wèi hour,
together with the Jiāoshè Lìng, ascended and set up the spirit seats for Hàotiān Shàngdì and Huángdì Qí on the altar, in the northern direction, facing south,
with the Huángdì Qí's position slightly set back to the east,
and all mats made of dry straw.
The Tàizǔ's accompanying seat was positioned in the eastern direction, facing west,
with mats made of rush.
The spirit seats for the Wǔfāng Dì, the Sun, the Moon, Shénzhōu Dìqí, Tiānhuáng Dàdì, and Běijí were on the first tier of the altar,
and all mats were of dry straw.
Fifty-four seats for inner officials, five spirits, five officials, and twenty-nine seats for the Yuèzhèn Hǎidú were on the second tier of the altar.
One hundred fifty-eight seats for middle officials, and twenty-one seats for Kūnlún and the mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes were on the third tier of the altar.
One hundred six seats for outer officials, and thirty seats for hills, mounds, plains, and wetlands were inside the inner enclosure.
Three hundred sixty seats for all the stars were outside the inner enclosure.
All mats were made of sedge.
Spirit seat plaques were each set up at the head of the seats.
Ceremonial jade for the spirits was also set up.
After the purification announcement was completed,
the spirit seats on the altar and on the first tier were temporarily removed.
They would be re-established at five kè before the Chǒu hour on the day of the sacrifice.
The Fènglǐ Láng, together with the Sīzūn and other attending officials, set up eleven Biān baskets to the left of each of the Heaven, Earth, and accompanying deity positions,
and eleven Dòu vessels to their right.
All were arranged in three rows.
Three Dēng vessels were placed between the Biān and Dòu.
One Fǔ and one Guǐ were in front of the Dēng,
the Fǔ on the left,
the Guǐ on the right.
Each was placed upon a mat in front of the spirit seat.
Also, for the Heaven and Earth positions, two Tàizūn, two Zhùzūn, two Xīzūn, and two Shānlèi were set up for each.
In the southeastern corner of the altar, for the accompanying deity position, two Zhùzūn, two Xīzūn, and two Xiàngzūn were set up,
to the east of the wine vessels for the Heaven and Earth positions,
all facing north, with the westernmost being the highest rank,
all with stands,
and ladles added,
serving as the libation pouring places.
Also, for the Heaven and Earth positions, two Xiàngzūn, two Húzūn, and four Shānlèi were set up for each.
These were on the altar, to the south of the central steps,
facing north, with the westernmost being the highest rank.
For the accompanying deity position, two Húzūn and four Shānlèi were to the north of the Yǒu steps,
facing east, with the northernmost being the highest rank,
all with stands.
They were set up but not used for pouring,
and to their left was pure water,
and to their right was dark wine.
Also, for the Wǔfāng Dì, the Sun, the Moon,
Shénzhōu Dìqí, Tiānhuáng Dàdì, and Běijí,
all on the first tier had eight Biān baskets to their left and eight Dòu vessels to their right,
with Dēng vessels between the Biān and Dòu,
one Fǔ and one Guǐ in front of the Dēng,
and one Jué cup stand in front of the spirit seat.
For the fifty-four seats of inner officials on the second tier,
five spirits, five officials, and twenty-nine seats for the Yuèzhèn Hǎidú,
each seat had two Biān, two Dòu, one Fǔ, one Guǐ, one Zǔ, and one Jué cup stand.
For the one hundred fifty-eight seats of middle officials on the third tier,
Kūnlún and the twenty-one seats for mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
and the one hundred six seats for inner and outer officials within the inner enclosure,
the thirty seats for hills, mounds, plains, and wetlands,
and the three hundred sixty seats for all the stars outside the inner enclosure,
each position had two Biān, two Dòu, one Fǔ, one Guǐ, one Zǔ, and one Jué cup.
Also, for each position on the first tier, two Tàizūn and two Zhùzūn were set up,
all with stands and ladles added.
For each position on the second tier, two Shānzūn were set up,
for each position on the third tier, two Shènzūn,
and for each category inside and outside the inner enclosure, two Gàizūn were set up,
all with ladles added.
From the second tier downwards, all used Páojié cups.
These were first washed and wiped clean,
and placed at the vessel positions.
Their vessel positions were all to the left of the spirit seats.
All sacrificial vessels were placed upon mats,
and Biāndòu each had a cloth cover.
Also, for Heaven, Earth, and the accompanying deity, one Biān, one Dòu, one Fǔ, one Guǐ, four Zǔ, and one Máoxuè Dòu vessel were set up for each,
and for each spirit seat on the first tier, two Zǔ,
inside the ritual food canopy.
Furthermore, the 皇帝 xǐ (rinsing vessel) was set up at mǎo bìxià,
north of the path,
facing south.
The guàn xǐ (washing basin) was on the east,
the jué xǐ (cup rinsing vessel) on the west.
The yí (ewer) was on the east,
the jīn (towel) on the west.
A fěi (basket) was placed to the south,
containing a jade cup stand.
Furthermore, the position for the yà zhōng xiàn xǐ was set up to the east of the xiǎo cì,
facing south.
The guàn xǐ was on the east,
the jué xǐ on the west,
with a scoop added.
A fěi was on the west,
placed to the south,
with a towel added.
Furthermore, the positions for the dì yī děng fēn xiàn guān guàn xǐ jué xǐ,
and the dì èr děng fēn xiàn guān guàn xǐ were set up,
each to the left of its respective chén bì dào.
The léi (wine vessel) was to the left of the xǐ,
the fěi to the right of the xǐ,
all facing inwards.
The persons holding the léi and fěi stood behind them.
The Tài fǔ jiān and Shǎo fǔ jiān, two kè after wèi on the day before the sacrifice,
led their subordinates to ascend the altar and arrange the jade and silk offerings.
For Hào Tiān Shàng Dì, a dark green bì and dark green silk were used;
for Huáng Dì Qí, a yellow cóng and yellow silk;
for the coordinating deities, dark green silk;
for Huáng Dì, a yellow cóng;
for Qīng Dì, a green guī;
for Chì Dì, a red zhāng;
for Dà Míng, a green guī and bì;
for Bái Dì, a white hú;
for Hēi Dì, a dark xuán huáng;
for Běi Jí, a green guī and bì;
for Tiān Huáng Dà Dì, a dark xuán guī and bì;
for Shén Zhōu Dì Qí, two dark colored guī with a base.
All were placed in boxes.
The silk offerings for the Wǔ Dì each followed their directional color.
All silk offerings were displayed in fěi.
After setup,
they waited for the announcement of purification to be completed, then temporarily removed them,
and set them up again on the day of the sacrifice.
Five kè before chǒu on the day of the sacrifice,
the Lǐ bù set up the zhù (prayer tablet) and cè (memorial tablet) to the right of the deities' seats,
all placed on àn (tables).
The Tài cháng qīng lit the lamps and performed the燎 (liáo) (burning).
The Hù bù láng zhōng set up the annual tribute from the various zhōu to the northeast of the gōng xuàn,
with gold in the front row,
jade and silk next,
and other items in the following rows,
all placed on xí (mats),
standing behind the annual tribute,
facing north.
The Tài fǔ jiān and Shǎo fǔ jiān set up exotic treasures and auspicious omens to the west of the gōng xuàn,
facing north,
with the ruì (auspicious omens) in front,
medium and lesser ones next,
all placed on xí,
standing behind the treasures,
facing north.
The Shǎo fǔ shǎo jiān set up spoils from conquered nations and destroyed treasures to the southeast of the gōng xuàn,
all placed on xí,
standing behind the treasures,
facing north.
The Fú bǎo láng set up the Bā Bǎo (Eight Treasures) to the southwest of the gōng xuàn,
each separately placed to the south of the treasures,
all facing north.

The Sī tiān jiān, Tài fǔ jiān, Shǎo fǔ jiān, Jiāo shè lìng, and Fèng lǐ láng ascended to set up the seats for Hào Tiān Shàng Dì, Huáng Dì Qí, the coordinating deities, and the dì yī děng deities on the altar,
and also set up the jade and silk offerings,
each at its proper place.
The Tài zhù took the burial jade and added it to the silk offerings,
placing the jade for worshipping the deities in front of each deity's seat,
then withdrew.
The Guāng lù qīng led his subordinates to fill the sacrificial vessels.
For Hào Tiān Shàng Dì, Huáng Dì Qí, and the coordinating deities, each position had three rows of biān (bamboo containers),
with the rightmost being superior.
Shaped salt was in front,
dried fish, qióu (dried meat), and ěr (pastry) next.
In the second row, chestnuts were in front,
dried peaches, dried apricots, and dried dates next.
In the third row, dried water caltrops were in front,
dried gorgon fruit, dried chestnuts, and dried venison next.
Three rows of dòu (wooden vessels),
with the leftmost being superior.
Celery pickles were in front,
bamboo shoot pickles and mallow pickles next.
In the second row, leek pickles were in front,
turnip pickles, fish paste, and rabbit paste next.
In the third row, pork ribs were in front,
pickled meat, fermented grain paste, and venison paste next.
Fǔ (square vessels) for hulled millet,
guǐ (round vessels) for foxtail millet,
and dēng (vessels) for all dà gēng (grand broth).
For the ten positions of the dì yī děng on the altar,
each position had three rows of biān,
with the rightmost being superior.
Shaped salt was in front,
dried fish next.
In the second row, dried apricots were in front,
peaches and dates next.
In the third row, dried water caltrops were in front,
chestnuts and dried venison next.
Three rows of dòu, with the leftmost being superior.
Celery pickles were in front,
bamboo shoot pickles next.
In the second row, turnip pickles were in front,
leek pickles and fish paste next.
In the third row, pork ribs were in front,
pickled meat and venison paste next.
〔一二〕Fǔ for hulled millet,
guǐ for foxtail millet,
and dēng for dà gēng.
For the dì èr and dì sān děng, each position had two biān,
dried venison and dried dates.
Two dòu,
venison paste and turnip pickles.
Zǔ (cutting boards),
one section of lamb.
Inside the nèi wěi and outside the nèi wěi, each position had biān with dried venison,
dòu with venison paste,
and zǔ with one section of lamb.
The Liáng yùn lìng led his subordinates to fill the zūn (wine vessels) and léi.
For Hào Tiān Shàng Dì and Huáng Dì Qí, the dà zūn was superior,
filled with fàn qí (clear wine);
the zhù zūn next,
filled with lǐ qí (sweet wine);
the xī zūn next,
filled with àng qí (foaming wine);
the xiàng zūn next,
filled with tí qí (rich wine);
the hú zūn next,
filled with shěn qí (deep-colored wine);
the shān léi was inferior,
filled with sān jiǔ (three wines).
For the coordinating deities, the zhù zūn was superior,
filled with fàn qí;
the xī zūn next,
filled with lǐ qí;
the xiàng zūn next,
filled with àng qí;
the hú zūn next,
filled with tí qí;
the shān léi was inferior,
filled with sān jiǔ.
For the dì yī děng, each position had a dà zūn filled with fàn qí,
and a zhù zūn filled with lǐ qí.
For the dì èr děng, the shān zūn was filled with tí qí.
For the dì sān děng and inside the nèi wěi, the shèn zūn was filled with fàn qí.
For outside the nèi wěi and the multitudinous stars,
the gài zūn was filled with sān jiǔ.
**Inspecting the Sacrificial Animals and Vessels**: The day before the sacrifice, at eight *kè* in the afternoon,
all pedestrians are prohibited within two hundred paces of the altar.
Two *kè* before *wèi*,
the *Jiāoshè Lìngchéng* (郊社令丞) leads his subordinates to sweep the area above and below the altar.
The *Sīzūn* (司尊) and *Fèng Lǐláng* (奉禮郎) lead the ritual attendants to bring in the sacrificial vessels,
setting them in their places.
The *Sītiānjian* (司天監) sets up the spirit tablets.
The *Tàifǔjiān* (太府監) and *Shàofǔjiān* (少府監) arrange the jade and silks in the baskets.
Three *kè* before *wèi*,
the *Lǐzhíguān* (禮直官) guides the *Lǐnxī Lìng* (廪犧令) and all the *Tàizhù* (太祝) and *Zhùshǐ* (祝史) to bring the sacrificial animals to their positions.

Then the *Lǐzhíguān*'s assistant separately guides the *Lǐbù Shàngshū* (禮部尚書), *Tàicháng Qīng* (太常卿), *Guānglù Qīng* (光祿卿), *Lǐbù Shìláng* (禮部侍郎), *Tàicháng Céng* (太常丞), *Jiānjì Yùshǐ* (監祭御史), *Jiānlǐ Bóshì* (監禮博士), *Lǐnxī Lìng*, *Tàiguān Lìng* (太官令), and *Tàiguān Céng* (太官丞) to the sacrificial animal inspection area outside the east gate of the inner enclosure.
After standing in position,
they guide the *Lǐbù Shàngshū*, *Shìláng*, *Tàicháng Céng*, and the *Jiānjì Yùshǐ*, *Jiānlǐ Bóshì* to ascend from the *mǎo* (卯) steps.
They inspect the washing and cleansing.
All attendants report that it is clean.
When everything is complete,
they descend and return to their original positions.
The *Lǐzhíguān* moves forward slightly and says:
"The cleansing is complete.
Please inspect the sacrificial animals."
The *Lǐbù Shàngshū*, *Shìláng*, and *Tàicháng Qīng*, *Céng* move forward slightly,
inspect the animals,
then retreat
and return to their original positions.
Next, they guide the *Guānglù Qīng*, *Céng* to circulate around the animals once.
The *Guānglù Qīng* retreats.
The *Guānglù Céng* turns to the west and bows, saying,
"Ready."
Then he returns to his position.
Next, they guide the *Lǐnxī Lìng* to circulate around the animals once.
He turns to the west and bows, saying,
"Sufficient."
Then they guide all the *Zhùshǐ* to circulate around the animals once.
The leading one turns to the west and bows, saying,
"Fat."
When finished,
all return to their positions.
The *Lǐzhíguān* moves forward slightly and says,
"Please inspect the food offerings."
Then he guides the *Lǐbù Shàngshū* and those below him to their respective positions.
After standing in position,
they inspect the food offerings.
When finished,
the *Lǐzhíguān* guides the *Lǐbù Shàngshū*, *Shìláng*, and *Tàicháng Qīng*, *Céng* to return to their fasting quarters.
The remaining officials, the *Lǐnxī Lìng* and all the *Tàizhù*, *Zhùshǐ*, then lead the animals in sequence
and hand them over to the *Tàiguān Lìng*, *Céng*.
Next, they guide the *Guānglù Qīng*, *Céng*, *Jiānjì*, and *Jiānlǐ*
to inspect the tripods and cauldrons.
After checking the washing and cleansing,
they return to their fasting quarters.
One *kè* after *bū*,
the *Tàiguān Lìng* leads the butchers to slaughter the animals with *luándāo* (鸞刀).
Each *Zhùshǐ* collects hair and blood, filling the *dòu* (豆) vessels,
and places them under the offering canopy.
Then they cook the animals.
The *Zhùshǐ* then collects the buried blood and stores it in plates.
**Presenting Jade and Silks**: Five *kè* before *chǒu* on the day of the sacrifice,
the *Sītú* (司徒) and all the accompanying officials below the **Assistant Final Presenter**
who are to perform duties or attend,
each put on their robes and take their places.
The *Sītiānjian* again sets up the spirit tablets on the altar and the first tier.
The *Tàifǔjiān* and *Shàofǔjiān* arrange the jade and silks.
The *Tàicháng Qīng* and *Jiāoshè Lìngchéng* light the candles for the bonfire.
The *Guānglù Qīng*, *Céng* fills the *biāndòu* (籩豆), *fǔguǐ* (簠簋), *zūn léi* (尊罍).
After the *Jiānjì* and *Jiānlǐ* inspect them,
they remove the cloths and covers.
The *Dàyuè Lìng* (大樂令) leads the musicians to array themselves within the palace orchestra.
The civil dance with eight rows of dancers stands behind the banner in front of the orchestra.
The martial dance with eight rows of dancers stands with four rows on each side of the palace orchestra.
The dance leaders, holding banners, are in front.
Then they guide the *dēnggē* (登歌) musicians to ascend by the *mǎo* (卯) steps.
Each takes their position.
Singers, drummers, and string players sit,
wind instrument players stand.
The *Fèng Lǐláng*'s assistant enters first and takes position.

The remaining *Lǐzhíguān* and assistants separately guide the **Assistant Presenting Officials**, the *Jiānjì Yùshǐ*, *Jiānlǐ Bóshì*, various ritual attendants, and the *Tàizhù*, *Zhùshǐ*, *Zhāiláng* (齋郎), **Assistant Offerers**, **Vessel Holders**, and other officials
to enter through the east gate of the middle enclosure.
They stand in double rows, facing north, moving west, to the south of the altar.
The *Fèng Lǐláng*'s assistant announces,
"Bow."
The **Assistant Presenting Officials** and all below them bow twice.
When finished,
the *Fèng Lǐ* assistant says,
"To your positions."
The assistants and *Lǐzhíguān* separately guide the *Jiānjì Yùshǐ* and *Jiānlǐ Bóshì*
to inspect above and below the altar,
correcting anything not in accordance with the rites.
They then retreat and return to their positions.
The *Lǐzhíguān* guides the *Sītú* to enter and take his position,
standing facing west.
The *Lǐzhíguān* guides the *Bóshì*.
The *Bóshì* guides the **Assistant Presenter**
to enter through the side gate of the east enclosure and take his position,
standing facing west.
Then the *Lǐzhíguān* guides the **Final Presenter**
to a position next to his.
One *kè* before dawn on the day of the sacrifice,
the *Tōngshì Shèrén* (通事舍人) guides the *Shìzhōng* (侍中) to the fasting hall.
He kneels and reports,
"Requesting the middle-level readiness."
He bows deeply,
then rises.
A moment later,
he kneels and reports,
"Outer preparations complete."
After the *Shàngniǎn* (尚輦) brings forth the sedan chair,
he kneels and states,
"Your humble servant,
[name], requests Your Majesty to descend from the throne and ascend the sedan chair."
When the Emperor arrives at the Grand Temporary Abode,
he kneels and states,
"Your humble servant,
[name], requests Your Majesty to descend from the sedan chair."
The Emperor enters the Temporary Abode
and takes his place outside the Grand Temporary Abode.
At dawn,
he proceeds before the Temporary Abode and kneels, reporting,
"Requesting the middle-level readiness."
A moment later,
he again reports,
"Outer preparations complete."
When finished,
the *Tàicháng Qīng* kneels before the Temporary Abode and states,
"Your humble servant,
[name], requests Your Majesty to proceed with the ceremony."
He bows deeply,
then rises.
All跪奏 (kneeling reports)
follow this procedure.
The Emperor exits the Temporary Abode,
then he is led to the gate of the middle enclosure.
The *Diànzhōngjiān* (殿中監) presents the *dàguī* (大圭).
The *Tàicháng Qīng* reports,
"Please take up the *dàguī*."
Entering through the main gate,
the Emperor takes his place in the Small Temporary Abode,
standing facing west.
The *Tàicháng Qīng* and the *Bóshì* stand in position on either side.
Then he reports,
"The officials have respectfully completed preparations.
Please proceed with the ceremony."
**Inviting the Deities**: Six *chéng* (成) of music,
then the music stops.
Another *Tàicháng Qīng* official
then ascends to burn incense and bury the blood.
When finished,
he reports,
"Bow."
When finished,
waiting for the *Shìzhōng* to ascend the altar,
he requests to proceed to the hand-washing position.
[一三] Upon arriving at the position,
he reports,
"Please tuck in the *dàguī* and wash hands."
When finished,
he reports,
"Please wipe hands."
The Emperor wipes his hands.
When finished,
he reports,
"Please take up the *dàguī*."
Then he is led to the altar.
The *Diànzhōngjiān* presents the *zhènguī* (鎮圭).
Then he reports,
"Please tuck in the *dàguī* and take up the *zhènguī*."
The Emperor takes up the *zhènguī*
and proceeds before the spirit throne of *Hàotiān Shàngdì* (昊天上帝).
He reports,
"Please kneel
and place the *zhènguī*."
The Emperor places it.
When finished,
he takes up the *dàguī*.
He bows deeply,
then rises.
The *Shìzhōng* presents the jade and silks.
Then he reports,
"Please tuck in the *dàguī*, kneel, and present the jade and silks."
When finished,
he reports,
"Please take up the *dàguī*."
He bows deeply,
then rises.
He retreats slightly,
then reports again,
"Please bow twice."
He proceeds to *Huángdìqí* (皇地祇) and the accompanying deities' positions.
The placing of the *zhènguī* and jade and silks
is all done in accordance with the ritual.
[一四] For the accompanying deities' positions, only the request to place the *zhènguī* and silks is made.
After the presentation of the jade and silks is complete,
the Emperor returns to the board position.
Then he reports,
"Please return to the Small Temporary Abode and release the *dàguī*."
The Emperor enters the Small Temporary Abode,
then stands slightly to the east of the south side of the Small Temporary Abode,
to wait.
When the Huángdì is about to present the ceremonial silk to the accompanying deities,
the assistant leads the first-rank presenting officials separately to the washing station.
They insert their hú, wash their hands, dry their hands, and hold their hú.
Each ascends via their respective steps,
but not via the wǔ bì.
Arriving before the deity,
they insert their hú,
kneel,
and the tài zhù presents them with a jade bi.
After the offering is made,
they prostrate,
and rise.
They bow twice.
After this is done,
each descends via their original steps,
and returns to their position.
Initially,
when the presenting officials are about to descend,
the lǐ zhí guān leads the zhù shǐ, zhāi láng, and those assisting with the offering to bow twice.
Each zhù shǐ carries a dǒu of mao xuè and enters,
each ascending via their respective steps.
The zhù shǐ meet and take them on the壇 (tán).
After the offering is made,
they withdraw and stand by the zūn.
Presenting cooked food: After presenting the jade bi,
they descend and return to the xiǎo cì.
The relevant officials first arrange three niú dǐng, three yáng dǐng, three shǐ dǐng, and three yú dǐng,
each to the right of the huò.
The tài guān lìng chéng leads the food presenters to the spot,
using ladles to lift beef, mutton, pork, and fish,
filling the dǐng from their respective huò.
The beef, mutton, and pork all include one shoulder, one arm, one shank, one knuckle, one scapula, and one entire spine,
two long ribs, two short ribs, and two substitute ribs,
totaling eleven parts.
〔一五〕The beef and pork each weigh thirty jīn,
the mutton fifteen jīn,
and the fish fifteen pieces weighing fifteen jīn.
After filling,
they leave.
Two zhù shǐ use a jiōng to lift one dǐng each,
the niú dǐng in front,
the yú dǐng next.
The relevant officials follow with ladles,
arranging each at the food curtain position for each deity.
For the accompanying sacrifices on the壇 (tán) of the first rank, the Wǔfāng Dì, Dàmíng, Yèmíng, Tiānhuáng Dàdì, Shénzhōu Dìqí, and Běijí,
the parts of the mutton and pork are all the same.
The guāng lù qīng leads the zhù shǐ, zhāi láng, and tài guān lìng chéng to use ladles to lift beef, mutton, pork, and fish onto the zǔ.
The shoulder, arm, and shank are at the upper end,
the knuckle and scapula at the lower end,
the spine and ribs in the middle.
The fish is placed horizontally,
with its head towards the honored position,
arranged after the dǐng is removed.
The guāng lù qīng chéng and tài guān lìng chéng fill the biān, dòu, fǔ, and guǐ.
The biān are filled with fěn cí,
the dòu with sǎn shí,
the fǔ with rice,
and the guǐ with millet.
After the Huángdì returns to the xiǎo cì,
the music stops.
The lǐ zhí guān leads the Sītú out to the food curtain area,
along with the zhāi láng who present the biān, dòu, fǔ, guǐ, and zǔ.
Each presents the food for Tiān, Dì, and the accompanying deities.
The Sītú leads the tài guān lìng to enter the main gate of the inner wěi in order.
The music begins,
and they wait below the壇 (tán).
The zhù shǐ advance to remove the mao xuè dòu,
descending from the mǎo bì,
and exiting in sequence.
After this is done,
the Sītú and the zhāi láng who present the biān, dòu, fǔ, guǐ, and zǔ,
offer the food for Hào Tiān Shàngdì and Huáng Dìqí,
ascending from the wǔ bì.
The tài guān lìng chéng and the zhāi láng who present the biān, dòu, fǔ, guǐ, and zǔ,
offer the food for the accompanying deities and the first-rank divine positions,
ascending from the mǎo bì.
The respective tài zhù meet them along the path between the壇 (tán) and the steps.
At the position of Hào Tiān Shàngdì,
the Sītú inserts his hú, kneels facing north, and presents the offerings.
The fěn cí biān are placed before the qiú ěr,
the sǎn shí dòu before the tǎn hǎi,
the fǔ to the left and the guǐ to the right,
all before the dēng.
The niú zǔ is before the dòu,
followed by the yáng shǐ yú zǔ,
with the right side being superior.
The Sītú prostrates,
and rises.
After the food presenters have completed their offerings,
they all take out their hú and return to their positions,
bowing once.
The Sītú then proceeds to the position of Huáng Dìqí to present offerings,
all according to the above ritual.
The accompanying deities are also served in the same manner.
The Sītú and those who presented the food for Tiān, Dì, and the accompanying deities descend in sequence.
The tài guān lìng leads the presentation of food for the first-rank divine positions,
each at its own place,
all according to the previous ritual.
When all is complete,
the music stops.
The Sītú, tài guān lìng, and others all return to their positions.
After this,
the shì zhōng ascends from the mǎo bì,
stands at the zūn for pouring wine for Hào Tiān Shàngdì,
and waits.
The tài cháng qīng then prostrates in front in sequence,
kneels and announces,
"Requesting the Huángdì to proceed to the washing station,"
prostrates,
and rises.
The Huángdì emerges from the xiǎo cì.
The diàn zhōng jiān presents the dà guī,
then announces,
"Requesting to hold the dà guī."
Upon reaching the washing station,
it is announced,
"Requesting to insert the dà guī and wash hands."
The Huángdì washes hands.
After this,
it is announced,
"Requesting to dry hands."
The Huángdì dries hands.
After this,
it is announced,
"Requesting to hold the dà guī."
Then, they proceed to the jué washing station.
Upon reaching the station,
it is announced,
"Requesting to insert the dà guī and receive the jué,"
and then announced,
"Requesting to wash the jué."
The Huángdì washes the jué.
After this,
it is announced,
"Requesting to wipe the jué."
The Huángdì wipes the jué.
After this,
it is announced,
"Requesting to hold the dà guī,"
and the jué is handed to the jué-bearing official.
The Huángdì proceeds to the zūn for pouring wine for Hào Tiān Shàngdì,
holding the jué.
The liáng yùn lìng raises the shì zhōng, who kneels to pour the fàn qí from the tài zūn.
After pouring,
the Huángdì hands the jué to the shì zhōng.
The Huángdì then proceeds to the divine seat of Hào Tiān Shàngdì.
The shì zhōng advances the jué.
It is then announced,
"Requesting to insert the dà guī,
kneel, hold the jué, and offer three libations of wine."
After this,
it is announced,
"Requesting to set down the jué."
After setting down the jué,
it is announced,
"Requesting to hold the dà guī."
They prostrate,
and rise.
It is then announced,
"Requesting to retreat slightly,"
and they stand and wait.
The zhōng shū shì láng reads the memorial inscription.
After this,
it is announced,
"Requesting to bow twice."
They proceed to the position of Huáng Dìqí and the accompanying deities,
all according to the above ritual.
After the offering is complete,
the Huángdì returns to the bǎn wèi.
It is then announced,
"Requesting to return to the xiǎo cì,
and release the dà guī."
The Huángdì enters the xiǎo cì.
The tài cháng qīng stands southeast of the xiǎo cì.
The ritual director guides the Bóshì,
the Bóshì guides the Yàxiàn,
to the hand-washing station.
They tuck their hu in, wash their hands, and wipe their hands.
After this,
they proceed to the wine cup washing station.
They tuck their hu in, wash the wine cups, and wipe the wine cups.
After this,
they hand the wine cups to the attendant.
Holding their hu, they ascend from the máo bì [eastern steps]
to the place where wine is poured for Hào Tiān Shàng Dì,
and stand facing west.
The attendant hands them the wine cups.
They then tuck their hu in and hold the wine cups.
The person holding the zūn lifts the excellent brew and instructs them to kneel and pour the lǐqí from the zūn.
After pouring,
they again hand the wine cups to the attendant.
Holding their hu, they proceed to the shrine of Hào Tiān Shàng Dì.
Initially,
when the Yàxiàn reaches the hand-washing station,
the civil dance retires,
the martial dance advances,
and the music begins.
The Yàxiàn proceeds to the shrine of Hào Tiān Shàng Dì,
tucks their hu in and kneels.
The attendant hands them the wine cups.
They then hold the wine cups and perform three libations,
place the wine cups,
hold their hu,
prostrate themselves,
rise,
retreat slightly,
and bow twice.
Next, they proceed to Huáng Dì Qí and the accompanying deities' positions,
performing everything as in the above ritual.
After the offering is complete,
they descend and return to their original positions.
The ritual director guides the Bóshì,
the Bóshì guides the Zhōngxiàn,
to the hand-washing station.
They wash their hands,
wash the wine cups,
ascend the altar, and make offerings,
all as in the above ritual.
Initially,
when the Zhōngxiàn is about to ascend the altar,
the ritual director guides the first-class assistant offering officials to the hand-washing station.
They tuck their hu in,
wash their hands,
and wipe their hands.
Holding their hu,
they each ascend by their respective steps,
but not by the wǔ bì [southern steps],
to the place where wine is poured for the deities.
[一六] The attendant hands them the wine cups,
and they pour the fànqí.
After this,
they hand the wine cups to the attendant.
Together, they proceed to the shrine,
tuck their hu in and kneel.
The attendant hands them the wine cups.
They then hold the wine cups and perform three libations,
place the wine cups,
hold their hu,
prostrate themselves,
rise,
retreat slightly,
and bow twice.
After this,
each is guided back to their original position.
Initially,
when the first-class assistant offering officials are about to ascend,
the ceremonial guide leads the second-class, third-class, and all the attendant officials within and outside the inner precinct [內壝內外衆星位分獻] [一七] to their respective hand-washing stations.
They tuck their hu in, wash their hands, wipe their hands, pour wine, make offerings, and bow,
all in accordance with the above ritual.
The Zhùshǐ and Zhāiláng assist in making offerings in turn.
After this,
each returns to their original position.
All the Tài Zhù each advance and remove one biān and one dòu.
They slightly move them from their original places,
and the music begins.
When the removal is complete,
the music stops.
Initially,
after the Zhōngxiàn ritual is completed,
and they descend and return to their original position,
the Tài Cháng Qīng then advances to the front in turn, prostrates himself,
and kneels to report,
"Requesting His Majesty to proceed to the position for receiving blessings."
His Majesty exits his position,
and the Diàn Zhōng Jiān presents the dàguī.
[一八] He then reports,
"Requesting to hold the wine cups,
perform three libations,"
and then reports,
"Requesting to taste the wine."
His Majesty tastes the wine.
After this,
he hands the wine cups to the Shìzhōng.
He then reports,
"Requesting to receive the blessed meat."
The Shìzhōng again presents the wine and wine cups.
He then reports,
"Requesting to receive the wine cups and drink the blessings."
His Majesty drinks the blessings.
After this,
he reports,
"Requesting to hold the dàguī."
He prostrates himself,
and rises.
He then reports,
"Requesting to bow twice."
After this,
he is guided back to his original position,
stands facing west,
and waits for the music for sending off the deities to stop.
He then reports,
"Requesting to proceed to the position for observing the burning pyre."
Upon reaching the position,
he stands facing south,
and waits for the fire to be half consumed by the pyre.
He then kneels and reports,
"Your humble servant, [official title and name], respectfully reports that the ritual is complete."
His Majesty returns to the great temporary lodging,
exits outside the middle precinct gate,
and he reports,
"Requesting to release the dàguī."
His Majesty enters the great temporary lodging.
Initially,
after the Zhōngxiàn ritual is completed,
the Sītú, Shìzhōng, and Tài Zhù each ascend from the máo bì [eastern steps].
The Tài Zhù carries the blessed meat platter forward.
They remove blessed meat from the altars of Heaven, Earth, and the accompanying deities and place it on the platter,
taking the second joint of the front leg in all cases.
They also place glutinous millet and millet rice together in one biān,
and present them to stand behind the Sītú and Shìzhōng,
facing north.
While His Majesty is at the position for receiving blessings,
the Tài Cháng Qīng reports,
"Requesting His Majesty to tuck in the dàguī and taste the wine."
After this,
the Sītú then presents the blessed meat platter.
His Majesty receives the blessed meat.
After this,
the ritual official reports and praises, saying,
"Granting blessed meat."
The praiser calls out,
"Bow twice."
All those present bow twice.
The deities are sent off,
and the music stops after one movement.
After His Majesty has entered the great temporary lodging,
he changes into the tōngtiānguān and jiàngshābáo,
ascends the imperial carriage,
proceeds to the fasting palace,
and rides the jīnlù.
The Tōngshì Shèrén guides the Ménxià Shìláng to kneel before the imperial carriage and report,
stating,
"Your humble servant, [official title and name], requests the imperial carriage to depart."
Upon reaching the place where the attendant officials mount their horses,
he then kneels and reports,
"Your humble servant, [official title and name], requests the imperial carriage to pause briefly,
and orders the attendant officials to mount their horses."
The Shìzhōng states,
"The imperial command is approved,"
and then withdraws,
transmitting the command, saying,
"Attendant officials, mount your horses."
After the attendant officials have mounted their horses,
he then kneels and reports,
stating,
"Your humble servant, [official title and name], requests an order for the chariot's right attendant to ascend."
After the Qiānniú Jiāngjūn has ascended,
he kneels and reports, stating,
"Your humble servant, [official title and name], requests the imperial carriage to depart."
As the imperial carriage moves,
the twelve teams of front, middle, and rear imperial orchestras all perform in unison.
The attendant officials who are to participate in the ritual and sacrifice first proceed to the Yìngtiānmén to welcome him,
and bow twice.
The Dà Yuèlìng first proceeds outside the Yìngtiānmén,
preparing to play music as prescribed.
After this,
a day is chosen to offer congratulations.
In the first year of Chéng'ān,
when preparing for the suburban sacrifice,
the ritual officials stated:
"The jade for honoring the spirits should be genuine jade,
and the jade for burning should be secondary jade.
Formerly, in the eleventh year of Dàdìng,
the jade for Heaven and Earth were both replaced with secondary jade.
Your ministers suspect that this was not entirely appropriate.
Ritual values substance;
those who cannot maintain it dare not offer it.
If genuine jade were burned,
for regular sacrifices, there might be times when it is lacking,
which would, in turn, violate the ritual system.
If we follow the practices of recent times and the ceremonies of our present dynasty,
using genuine jade to honor the spirits
and secondary jade for burning and burying
would be appropriate according to ritual.
In recent suburban sacrifices,
the Tiānhuáng Dàdì was elevated from the second rank,
and Běijí to the first rank.
Previously, the eight preceding deities each had jade for ritual offerings and jade for burning,
but these two deities still lack them.
According to the 'Diǎnrù' section of the Zhōulǐ, it states, 'Use guī and bì jades to sacrifice to the sun, moon, and stars.'
In recent rituals, for the nine palace noble spirits and the Dàhuǒ star position,
the theory of the Zhōulǐ is still used.
Therefore, for the Tiānhuáng Dàdì and Běijí,
it is certainly appropriate to use jade for honoring the spirits and jade for burning."
The Emperor ordered that both should use genuine jade.
The provincial ministers then further reported:
"In previous suburban sacrifices,
Heaven, Earth, and the accompanying deities each used one calf.
The Five Directional Emperors, Sun, Moon, Shénzhōu, Tiānhuáng Dàdì, and Běijí—ten positions in total—are all major sacrifices,
and should also use calves.
At that time, sheep were merely used as substitutes.
For the accompanying deities from the second rank downwards, sheep and pigs were divided and butchered for offerings.
We secretly believe that for the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the numerous biāndòu vessels are to prepare items for yin and yang,
while the scarcity of dǐngzǔ vessels indicates that human culinary offerings cannot adequately express their virtue,
thus emphasizing simplicity.
Therefore, the positions of Heaven, Earth, Sun, Moon, and stars all used one zǔ vessel.
Previously, the first-rank deity positions exclusively used two zǔ vessels,
which seems inconsistent.
Now, the first-rank deity positions should each use one calf,
the other positions should offer sheep and pigs as divided,
and for the morning sacrifice in the Tàimiào, twelve calves should be used."
The Emperor followed this.
Collation Notes
Treatise Ten: Ritual Two: Fāngqiū Ceremony, Morning Sun and Evening Moon Ceremony, Gāoméi
Fāngqiū Ceremony.
Fasting and Purification: Three days before the sacrifice, at dawn,
the officials in charge shall arrange the positions of the officiating officials from the third offering downwards in the Shàngshūshěng.
The chief officiant faces south,
the supervising censor for the sacrifice is to the west,
facing east,
the supervising erudite of rituals is to the east,
facing west,
both ascending northwards.
The Sìtú (Assistant), the second, and final officiants are to the south,
facing north.
Next are the Guānglù Qīng and Tàicháng Qīng,
then the first-rank assisting officiants and the Sìtiānjiàn,
then the second-rank assisting officiants, Guānglùchéng, Jiāoshèlìng, Dàyuèlìng, Liángyùnlìng, Lǐnxīlìng, and Sìzūnyí,
then the inside and outside assisting officiants within the inner enclosure, Tàizhùguān, Fènglǐláng, Xiélǜláng, and various attendants.
They take their positions
and stand still.
Next, the Lǐzhíguān guides the chief officiant to his position.
The chief officiant reads the oath:
"On such and such a day in the fifth month of this year, at the summer solstice,
we will sacrifice to the Huángdìqí at Fāngqiū.
All substitute officials
shall perform their duties.
Should anyone be disrespectful,
the state has its standing penalties."
After reading,
the Lǐzhíguān announces,
"Officials of the seventh rank and below withdraw first."
The remaining officials bow in response.
When finished,
they withdraw.
For two days of scattered fasting,
they lodge in their principal dwellings
and conduct affairs as usual.
The prohibitions of fasting are all as for the suburban sacrifice.
The guards at the enclosure gates and the Dàyuè workers
all observe a night of pure fasting.
The officiating officials practice the ceremony at the sacrificial site in advance.
Arrangements: Three days before the sacrifice,
the relevant department sets up the positions for the officiating and attendant officials from the third officiant downwards outside the east gate of the outer enclosure,
south of the road,
facing north,
ascending westwards,
according to the suitability of the ground.
They also set up a food tent outside the east gate of the inner enclosure,
north of the road, facing south.
Two days before the sacrifice,
the relevant department sets up guards,
each wearing their uniform,
to guard the enclosure gates,
two people per gate.
The Dàyuèlìng leads his subordinates
to set up the music for the ascending song on the altar,
as for the suburban sacrifice.
The Jiāoshèlìng leads his subordinates
to sweep the area above and below the altar,
and digs a burial pit at the rén direction outside the inner enclosure.
One day before the sacrifice,
the Sìtiānjiàn and Jiāoshèlìng, each wearing their uniform,
lead their subordinates
to set up the divine seat of the Huángdìqí on the north side of the altar,
facing south,
with a mat of straw.
They also set up the accompanying deity seats to the east,
facing west,
with mats of rush.
They also set up the divine seat of the Shénzhōu Dìqí on the southeastern part of the first tier of the altar,
with a mat of straw.
They also set up twenty-nine seats for the Five Spirits, Five Officials, Yuèzhèn, and Hǎidú between the second-tier steps,
each according to its direction.
They also set up twenty-one seats for Kūnlún, mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes inside the inner enclosure,
and thirty seats for hills, mounds, plains, and wetlands outside the inner enclosure,
all with mats of rush.
They also set up divine tablet boards,
each at the head of its seat.
West of the Zǐ Steps:
the Water Spirit Xuánmíng, Běiyuè, Běizhèn, Běihǎi, and Běidú are on the second tier of the altar.
Běishān, Běilín, Běichuān, and Běizé are inside the inner enclosure.
Běiqiū, Běilíng, Běifén, Běiyǎn, Běiyuán, and Běixí are outside the inner enclosure.
All are arranged in a single row,
with the east as the superior position.
North of the Mǎo Steps:
the Wood Spirit Gōumáng,
Dōngyuè, Chángbáishān, Dōngzhèn, Dōnghǎi, and Dōngdú are on the second tier of the altar.
Dōngshān, Dōnglín, Dōngchuān, and Dōngzé are inside the inner enclosure.
Dōngqiū, Dōnglíng, Dōngfén, Dōngyǎn, Dōngyuán, and Dōngxí are outside the inner enclosure.
All are arranged in a single row,
with the south as the superior position.
East of the Wǔ Steps:
the Shénzhōu Dìqí is on the first tier of the altar.
The Fire Spirit Zhùróng,
Nányuè, Nánzhèn, Nánhǎi, and Nándú are on the second tier of the altar.
Nánshān, Nánlín, Nánchuān, and Nánzé are inside the inner enclosure.
Nánqiū, Nánlíng, Nánfén, Nányǎn, Nányuán, and Nánxí are outside the inner enclosure.
All are arranged in a single row,
with the west as the superior position.
West of the Wǔ Steps:
the Earth Spirit Hòutǔ, Zhōngyuè, and Zhōngzhèn are on the second tier of the altar.
Zhōngshān, Zhōnglín, Zhōngchuān, and Zhōngzé are inside the inner enclosure.
Zhōngqiū, Zhōnglíng, Zhōngfén, Zhōngyǎn, Zhōngyuán, and Zhōngxí are outside the inner enclosure.
All are arranged in a single row,
with the south as the superior position.
South of the Yǒu Steps:
the Metal Spirit Rùshōu, Xīyuè, Xīzhèn, Xīhǎi, and Xīdú are on the second tier of the altar.
Kūnlún, Xīshān, Xīlín, Xīchuān, and Xīzé are inside the inner enclosure.
Xīqiū, Xīlíng, Xīfén, Xīyǎn, Xīyuán, and Xīxí are outside the inner enclosure.
All are arranged in a single row,
with the north as the superior position.
For the divine seats of the Huángdìqí, the accompanying deities, and the Shénzhōu Dìqí,
along with the jade for honoring the spirits,
once set up,
they shall be temporarily removed after the announcement of purification,
and reset early on the day of the sacrifice.
The divine seats from the second rank downwards
shall be set up and not removed.
The Fènglǐláng and Lǐzhíguān also set up the positions for the three officiants slightly north of the east of the Mǎo Steps,
facing west.
The Sìtú is positioned east of the Mǎo Steps,
south of the road,
facing west.
The Tàicháng Qīng and Guānglù Qīng's positions are next.

The Guānglùchéng, Jiāoshèlìng, Tàiguānlìng, and Lǐnxīlìng's positions are further to their east.
Each rank has different positions in multiple rows,
all facing west and ascending northwards.
They also set up the Tàizhù, Fènglǐláng, and various attendants outside the east gate of the inner enclosure, south of the road,

facing north.

The Tàicháng Qīng, Guānglù Qīng, and Tàiguān Lìng were positioned to the east,

The jiānjì and jiānlǐ were positioned to the west,

The Sīzūn and Fènglǐ Láng, leading their subordinates,

For the accompanying deities, two xīzūn, two húzūn, and four shānléi were

For the Shénzhōu Dìqí, eight biān were to their left and eight dòu to their right.

One fǔ and one guǐ were in front of the dēng.
One jué diàn was
in front of the spirit seat.
Furthermore, for the second-rank deities, each position had two biān, two dòu, one fǔ, one guǐ, one zǔ, and one jué diàn.
For each deity inside and outside the inner enclosure, there was one biān, one dòu, one fǔ, one guǐ, one zǔ, and one jué diàn.
All arrangements and displays were the same as above.
Additionally, for the Shénzhōu Dìqí, two tàizūn and two zhùzūn were set up,
all with diàn.
For the second-rank deities, each direction had two shānzūn.
Inside the inner enclosure, each direction had two shènzūn.
Outside the inner enclosure, each direction had two gàizūn.
All had a ladle and added.
Additionally, for the main and accompanying deities, one biān, one dòu, one fǔ, one guǐ, three zǔ, and one máoxuè dòu, as well as one zǔ for the Shénzhōu Dìqí, were set up,
each inside a provision tent.
Furthermore, two washing vessels were set up to the east of the *mǎo* steps on the altar,
facing north.
The guànxǐ was to the east,
and the juéxǐ was to the west,
both with a léi and a ladle added.
A fěi was to the west of the washing vessels,
arranged to the south,

The fěi for the juéxǐ was filled with gourd cups,

Additionally, positions for the first-rank presenting officials' guànxǐ and juéxǐ were set up,

The léi was to the left of the washing vessel,
and the fěi was to the right of the washing vessel,

The bearers of the léi and fěi were positioned behind them.
On the day of the sacrifice, five *kè* before *chǒu*,

The seat for the Shénzhōu Dìqí was set up for the first-rank.
Additionally, jade and silk offerings were set up.
For the Huángdìqí, yellow zōng jade was used.
For the Shénzhōu Dìqí, two guī with a base were used.
All were placed in boxes.
The silk for the main and accompanying deities was yellow.
The silk for the Shénzhōu Dìqí was dark-colored.
The silk for the Five Deities, Five Officials, Yuèzhèn and Hǎidú followed their respective directional colors.
All were displayed in baskets.
The dàzhù took the buried jade and placed it on the silk,
and the jade for worshiping the spirits was placed in front of each spirit seat.
The Guānglù Qīng, leading his subordinates,
entered to fill the biān and dòu for the main and accompanying deities.
The three rows of biān had the rightmost as the highest.
The three rows of dòu had the leftmost as the highest.
Their contents were all as in the Suburban Sacrifice.
The dēng were filled with dàgēng.
The xíng were filled with hégēng.
Additionally, the provisions for the first-rank accompanying deity, the Shénzhōu Dìqí, were set up.
The three rows of biān had the rightmost as the highest.
The three rows of dòu had the leftmost as the highest.
Their contents were all as in the Suburban Sacrifice.
The dēng were filled with dàgēng.
The fǔ were filled with millet.
The guǐ were filled with broomcorn millet.
For each second-rank position,
two biān were to the left,
with chestnuts in front,

Two dòu were to the right,
with jīngzū in front,

The fǔ were filled with millet.
The guǐ were filled with broomcorn millet.
The zǔ contained
one sheep and one pig.
For each position inside and outside the inner enclosure,
one biān was to the left,
with dried venison.
One dòu was to the right,
with cured venison.
The fǔ contained millet.
The guǐ contained broomcorn millet.
The zǔ contained lamb.
The Liángyùn Lìng, leading his subordinates,
entered to fill the wine zūn.
For the Huángdìqí, the tàizūn was highest,
filled with fànqí.
The zhùzūn was next,

The xīzūn was next,
filled with āngqí.
The xiàngzūn was next,
filled with tíqí.
The húzūn was next,
filled with chénqí.
The shānléi was lowest,
filled with the three wines.
For the accompanying deities,
the zhùzūn was highest,
filled with fànqí.
The xīzūn was next,
filled with lǐqí.
The xiàngzūn was next,
filled with āngqí.
The húzūn was next,
filled with tíqí.
The shānléi was lowest,

Next, the wine zūn for the first-rank accompanying deity, the Shénzhōu Dìqí, were filled.
The tàizūn was highest,

The zhùzūn was next,

For the second-rank,

Inside the inner enclosure,

The Tàicháng Qīng set up candles in front of the spirit seats.
Inspection of the Sacrificial Animals and Vessels: On the day before the sacrifice, at eight *kè* in the afternoon,
within two hundred *bù* of the altar, passage is forbidden to travelers.
Two *kè* before *wèi* (3-5 PM),
the *Jiāoshèlìng* (Director of Suburban and Altar Rites) leads his subordinates
to sweep clean the area above and below the altar.
*Sīzūn* (Supervisor of Wine Vessels) and *Fènglǐláng* (Gentleman for Presenting Rites),
leading the officials in charge of duties, enter with the sacrificial vessels
and arrange them in their positions.
The *Jiāoshèlìng* displays the jade and silk offerings in the *fěi* (basket).
Three *kè* before *wèi*,
the *Lǐnxīlìng* (Director of Sacrificial Animals) and the *Zhūtài Zhù*, *Zhùshǐ* (Chief Augurs and Prayer Scribes),
bring the sacrificial animals to the inspection area.
The *Lǐzhíguān* (Officials on Duty for Rites) and *Zànzhě* (Assistants) separately lead the *Tàichángqīng* (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices),
*Guānglùqīng* (Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainment) and *chéng* (assistant),
*Jiānlǐ* (Supervisor of Rites), *Jì* (Supervisor of Sacrifices),
and *Tàiguānlìng* (Director of the Court of Imperial Banquets) to the inspection area for sacrificial animals outside the east gate of the inner enclosure (*wěi*).
The inspection of washing and purification, announcement of cleanliness, and inspection of sacrificial foods
are all the same as for the suburban sacrifice (*Jiāosì*).
When all is complete,
the *Lǐnxīlìng*, *Zhūtài Zhù*, and *Zhùshǐ* in turn lead the sacrificial animals to the area
and hand them over to the *Tàiguānlìng*.
Next, they lead the *Guānglùqīng* and those below him to the area,
inspect the cauldrons and cooking vessels,
and oversee the washing and cleaning.
Then they return to their fasting place.
One *kè* after *bū* (3-5 PM),
the *Tàiguānlìng* leads the butchers to slaughter the animals with *luándāo* (knives with bells).
The *Zhùshǐ* each take hair and blood,
place them in *dòu* (stemmed vessels),
and set them within the food curtain.
Then they cook the animals.
The *Zhùshǐ* also take the buried blood and store it in a platter.
Presenting Jade and Silk: On the day of the sacrifice, five *kè* before *chǒu* (1-3 AM),
the *Xiànguān* (Presenting Officials) and other officiating officials
each don their respective attire.
The *Yǒusī* (Officials in Charge) set up the spirit tablets,
display the jade and silk offerings,
fill the *biāndòu* (bamboo and wooden vessels), *fǔguǐ* (rectangular and round sacrificial vessels), *zūn* (wine vessels), and *léi* (jars),
and await the *Jiānjì* (Supervisor of Sacrifices) and *Jiānlǐ* (Supervisor of Rites) to inspect the area above and below the altar.
Then they remove the covers.
The *Dàyuèlìng* (Director of Grand Music) leads the musicians,
along with the *Fènglǐláng* and *Zànzhě*, to enter first.
The *Lǐzhíguān* and *Zànzhě* separately lead the *Fēnfèngguān* (Sub-Presenting Officials) and those below them,
the *Jiānjì*, *Jiānlǐ*, *Zhūdà Zhù* (Chief Augurs), *Zhùshǐ*, *Zhāiláng* (Fasting Grooms), and those in charge of duties,
to enter from the east gate of the southern enclosure.
They stand facing north,
in double rows,
to the south of the altar,
with the west side as the superior position,
and take their places.
The *Fènglǐláng* prompts,
"Bow!"
The *Xiànguān* and all below them bow twice.
After this,
they are led in turn to their respective positions above and below the altar steps.
Next, the *Jiānjì* and *Jiānlǐ* are led to inspect the area above and below the altar.
After this,
they retire to their original positions.
The *Lǐzhíguān* separately leads the *Sānxiànguān* (Third Presenting Officials) and other officiating officials to their positions.
All officiating officials enter from the east gate of the southern enclosure.
The *Lǐzhíguān* advances to stand to the left of the *Chūxiàn* (First Presenter),
and announces,
"The officials in charge have respectfully prepared everything;
we request to proceed with the ceremony."
He then retires to his original position.
The *Xiélǜláng* (Gentleman for Harmonizing Pitchpipes) raises his *hù* (tablet) high.
The flag-bearer raises the flag.
They bow,
and rise.
The musicians strike the *gǔ* (drums) and *zhù* (wooden box),
and the *Kūnníng* (Quiet of Earth) music begins,
in eight sections.
The flag is lowered,
the *yǔ* (tiger-shaped percussion instrument) is struck,
and the music stops.
They await the *Tàichángqīng* to bury the blood.
After this,
the *Fènglǐláng* prompts,
"Bow!"
All those present bow twice.
He then prompts,
"All officials in charge, proceed to your positions!"
The *Lǐzhíguān* leads the officials in charge to their respective positions to wait.
The *Tàizhù* (Chief Augur) kneels and takes the jade and silk offerings from the *fěi*,
and stands by the *zūn*.
The *Zhūwèi Tàizhù* (Chief Augurs in all positions) also each take jade and silk offerings and stand by the *zūn*.
The *Lǐzhíguān* leads the *Chūxiàn* to the hand-washing position,
and the *Sùníng* (Solemn Peace) music begins.
Upon reaching the position,
he stands facing north,
and the music stops.
He tucks his *hù* (tablet) into his belt,
washes his hands,
dries his hands,
holds his *hù*,
and proceeds to the altar.
The *Sùníng* music begins.
Whenever the *Chūxiàn* ascends or descends,
the *Sùníng* music is played.
He ascends from the *mǎo* (east) steps,
and upon reaching the altar,
the music stops.
He proceeds to before the spirit seat of *Huángdìqí* (Imperial Earth Deity),
stands facing north,
and the *Jìngníng* (Tranquil Peace) music begins.
He tucks his *hù* into his belt,
and kneels.
The *Tàizhù* places the jade on the silk,
kneels facing west, and presents it to the *Chūxiàn*.
The *Chūxiàn* receives the jade and silk, presents them,
holds his *hù*,
bows low,
rises,
bows twice.
After this,
the music stops.
Next, he proceeds to before the spirit seat of the *Pèiwèi* (Associate Deities),
stands facing east,
and the *Yìníng* (Abundant Peace) music begins.
He presents the silk as in the above ceremony,
and the music stops.
He descends from the *mǎo* (east) steps,
the music begins,
he returns to his position,
and the music stops.
As the *Chūxiàn* is about to present the silk to the *Pèiwèi*,
the *Zànzhě* leads the *Dìyīděng Fēnfèngguān* (First-Class Sub-Presenting Officials) to the hand-washing position,
where they tuck their *hù* into their belts,
wash their hands,
dry their hands,
hold their *hù*,
and proceed via the *mǎo* steps to before the spirit seat of *Shénzhōudìqí* (Deities of the Divine Continent and Earth).
They tuck their *hù* into their belts,
and kneel.
The *Tàizhù* presents the jade and silk offerings to the *Fēnfèngguān*.
The *Fēnfèngguān* receives the jade and silk offerings,
presents them,
holds their *hù*,
bows low,
rises,
bows twice.
After this,
they retire.
Initially,
as the *Dìyī Fēnfèngguān* (First Sub-Presenting Official) is about to ascend,
the *Zànzhě* leads the *Dì'èr Fēnfèngguān* (Second Sub-Presenting Official) to the hand-washing position,
where they wash their hands,
dry their hands,
hold their *hù*,
and each ascend via their respective steps,
but not via the *wǔ* (south) steps,
to before the spirit seat of the *Shǒuwèi* (Foremost Deity),
and present the silk as in the above ceremony.
The remaining *Zhùshǐ* and *Zhāiláng* assist in presenting the offerings. After this,
they are each led back to their positions.
As the *Chūxiàn*'s presentation of the silk is about to conclude,
the *Zhùshǐ* present the *máoxuè dòu* (vessels of hair and blood),
each ascending via the *wǔ* steps.
The *Zhūtài Zhù* receive them on the altar,
and advance to present them before the spirit seats of the main and associate deities.
The *Tàizhù* and *Zhùshǐ* then both retire,
and stand by the *zūn*.
Presenting Cooked Food: After the *Chūxiàn* has ascended and presented the jade and silk offerings,
the *Yǒusī* first arrange two ox cauldrons, two sheep cauldrons, and two pig cauldrons for the deities,
each to the right of the cooking vessel.
The *Tàiguān* leads the food presenters to the area,
and uses a *bǐ* (spoon/ladle) to lift the ox, sheep, and pig meat
from the cooking vessels and place it into each cauldron.
For the ox, sheep, and pig, each has one shoulder, arm, foreleg, shank, shoulder blade, main spine, transverse spine, long rib, short rib, and substitute rib,
all with two bones combined,
〔一０〕 of them.
The *Zhùshǐ* each use a *jiōng* (lifting bar) to jointly lift the cauldrons,
the *Yǒusī* follow, holding *bǐ*,
and arrange them within the food curtain.
The *zǔ* (meat platters) for the accompanying sacrifices are filled with lamb,
and then arranged within the food curtain.
The Guānglù Qīng (Minister of the Imperial Regalia) filled the biāndòu and fúguǐ.
the dòu were filled with ground grain food;
the fú were filled with millet;
and the guǐ were filled with glutinous millet.
After filling,
the rings of the dǐng were removed.
Spoons were added to the dǐng.
The Tàiguān Lìng (Director of Imperial Banquets) used spoons to lift the beef, mutton, and pork,
placing them on the zǔ (meat stands).
The biān were filled with powdered rice cakes;
the gizzards and hocks were at the lower end;
and the spine and ribs were in the middle.
After the first presenter returned to his position,
the music stopped.
The Lǐzhíguān (Official in Charge of Rites) led the Sītú (Minister of Education) out to the offering area,
together presenting the biāndòu, fúguǐ, and zǔ.
The Zhāiláng (fasting attendants) each held the offerings for the Huángdìqí (Imperial Earth God) and the assisting deities,
ascending from the mǎo-rank steps.
All the Tàizhù (Grand Prayer Officials) greeted them on the altar.
The Sītú proceeded to the front of the Huángdìqí's spirit seat,
inserted his hù (tablet),
presented the biāndòu and fúguǐ,
then presented the zǔ.
He knelt facing north to lay them down.
After completion,
he held his hù,
bowed low,
rose,
placed the biān in front of the qiú'ěr (dried provisions and pastries),
the dòu in front of the tán hǎi (pickled minced meat and fish),
the fúguǐ in front of the dēng (food vessels),
and the zǔ in front of the biān.
kneeling and laying them down facing east in front of their spirit seats,
all in accordance with the aforementioned ceremony.
Each descended from the mǎo-rank steps
and returned to their position.
The Tàiguān Lìng, along with the Zhāiláng, then presented the offerings for the Shénzhōu Dìqí (Earth God of the Divine Land),
ascending from the mǎo-rank steps.
The Tàizhù greeted them in the path between the altar steps,
laying them down in front of the spirit seats,
in front of the biān.
the music stopped.
The Tàiguān Lìng and the offering presenters descended from the mǎo-rank steps
and returned to their positions.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Chūxiànguān (First Presenter) to the hand-washing station,
and the music began.
Upon reaching the station,
the music stopped.
He stood facing north,
inserted his hù,
washed his hands,
dried his hands,
held his hù,
proceeded to the cup-washing station,
and upon reaching the station,
stood facing north,
inserted his hù,
washed his cup,
and wiped his cup before handing it to the attendant.
He held his hù
and proceeded to the altar.
The music began.
He ascended from the mǎo-rank steps
to the altar,
and the music stopped.
He proceeded to the Huángdìqí's wine vessel area,
standing facing west.
The attendant handed the cup to the Chūxiàn.
The Chūxiàn inserted his hù
and held the cup.
The Sīzūn (Officer in Charge of Wine Vessels) lifted the lid.
The Liángyùn Lìng (Director of Fine Brews) knelt to pour the fànqí (clear wine with floating scum) from the Tàizūn (Grand Wine Vessel).
the Chūxiàn handed the cup to the attendant,
held his hù,
proceeded to the front of the Huángdìqí's spirit seat,
stood facing north,
inserted his hù,
and knelt.
The attendant handed the cup to the Chūxiàn.
The Chūxiàn held the cup,
made three libations onto the máojū (straw mat),
laid down the cup,
(For all three presenters, after laying down the cup,
the attendant received it and rose.) held his hù,
bowed low,
rose,
retreated slightly,
knelt,
and the music stopped.
The Jǔzhùguān (Official who Presents the Prayer) knelt
and presented the prayer tablet.
The prayer was read.
The Tàizhù knelt facing east,
and after the prayer was read,
bowed low
and rose.
The Jǔzhù placed the tablet on the altar table,
bowed twice,
and rose.
Next, he proceeded to the assisting deities' wine vessel area.
The attendant handed the cup to the Chūxiàn.
The Chūxiàn inserted his hù
The Sīzūn lifted the lid.
The Liángyùn Lìng knelt to pour the fànqí from the Zhùzūn (Adorned Wine Vessel).
The music played the Tàicù gōng bǎo níng melody.
The Chūxiàn handed the cup to the attendant,
held his hù,
proceeded to the front of the assisting deities' spirit seats,
stood facing east,
inserted his hù,
and knelt.
The attendant handed the cup to the Chūxiàn.
The Chūxiàn held the cup,

He laid down the cup,

Ceremony for Worshipping the Morning Sun and Evening Moon.
Fasting and purification, arrangements, inspection of sacrificial vessels, presentation of jade and silk, presentation of cooked food—
these procedures were all like those of the Grand Sacrifices.
For Worshipping the Morning Sun, the jade used was a green *bì* disk;
for Worshipping the Evening Moon, a white *bì* disk.
The silks were all the same color as the jade.
Each sacrifice used one sheep and one pig.
The official in charge acted as the three offering officials and the Minister of Education.
Regarding the Emperor personally performing the Worshipping the Morning Sun,
in the early Jīn Dynasty, the native rituals were used.
In the first month of Tianhui 4th year (1126),
the Worshipping the Morning Sun was first performed at the Qiányuán Hall,
after which congratulations were received.
In Tianjuan 2nd year (1139),
the ceremony for Worshipping the Morning Sun on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month was established.
The Emperor wore boots and a robe,
and the hundred officials wore regular attire.
The official in charge set up a stove table and imperial cushions at the steps in front of the hall used for the ceremony.
Cushions for the hundred officials were set up outside the hall gate,
all facing the sun.
The Xuanhui Commissioner announced and guided the Emperor to his position,
facing south,
bowed twice,
offered incense,
and bowed twice again.
All chamberlains responded with announcements.
The officials outside the hall gate bowed in attendance as per usual ceremony.
In Dàdìng 2nd year (1162),
it was abolished due to lack of historical precedent.
In Dàdìng 15th year (1175),
those who spoke on affairs said that for the current New Year's Day and Wànchūn Festival,
the official in charge should be ordered to establish the ritual of bowing to the sun.
The official in charge cited the Han and Tang Dynasties' Worshipping the Morning Sun at the vernal equinox,
with ascending smoke and presentation of jade, like the ceremony at the Yuánqiū altar.
Also, according to the Tang Kaiyuan Rituals,
a position for the Great Bright Spirit was set up facing south,
and the Emperor faced north.
There was no system of bowing to the sun while facing south.
Now, by imperial decree, the sun is bowed to on the first day of the lunar month.
It is appropriate to follow ancient custom and bow facing east in front of the hall.
An imperial edict ordered to temporarily follow facing south.
On that day,
officials were first led to stand outside the hall gate.
Attendant officials stood in rows to the left and right of the dew terrace in front of the hall.
The Emperor bowed at the incense table on the dew terrace as per the above ceremony.
In Dàdìng 18th year (1178),
the Emperor bowed to the sun at the Rénzhèng Hall,
and the ritual of facing east was first implemented.
The Emperor exited the hall,
a position was set up facing east,
the Xuanhui Commissioner announced
“Bow,”
the Emperor bowed twice,
offered incense,
and when finished,
bowed twice again.
Officials all bowed in attendance,
and performed their greetings according to their rank,
as per usual ceremony.
Gāoméi.
In Míngchāng 6th year (1195),
Emperor Zhāngzōng had no sons.
Ministers of the Department of State Affairs proposed to perform the Gāoméi sacrifice.
A坛 was then built at the southeast end outside the Jǐngfēng Gate,
at the *mǎo-chén* (east-southeast) location relative to the palace gate,
facing the Yuánqiū altar east and west.
The altar was constructed according to the design of the Northern Suburb Altar.
Annually, on the vernal equinox, sacrifices were offered to Qīngdì, Fúxīshì, and Nǚwāshì,
a total of three deities.
On the altar, they faced south,
with the most honored to the west.
Jiāngyuán and Jiǎndí were located on the second tier of the altar,
facing east,
with the most honored to the north.
On the day before, at *wèi* (around 1-3 PM), three *kè* (quarter-hours) before the end of the *wèi* period,
the spirit tablets were arranged,
sacrificial vessels inspected,
and the imperial bow, arrows, and quiver were displayed to the right of the upper and lower spirit tablets.
The fasting and purification, presentation of jade and silk, and presentation of cooked food
were all according to the Grand Sacrifice ceremony.
For Qīngdì, the silk and jade were both green;
for the others, there was no jade.
Each deity's sacrifice used one sheep and one pig.
The official in charge acted as the three offering officials and the Minister of Education.
When the ceremony was complete,
the consecrated meat was presented,
double the amount of meat for other sacrifices.
The official presenting the consecrated meat wore a bow, arrows, and quiver when presenting.
The Emperor ordered the empresses, consorts, and concubines to all hold bows and arrows and shoot facing east.
Then, they were ordered to drink the ritual wine and partake of the consecrated meat in order.
Collation Notes
Records, Volume 11, Rituals, Part 3: Imperial Ancestral Temple,
Dì and Xiá sacrifices, Morning and Evening Offerings, Seasonal Offering Ceremonies.
In the early Jīn dynasty, there were no imperial ancestral temples.
In the ninth month of Tiānfǔ seventh year (1123),
Tàizǔ was buried southwest of the imperial city in Shàngjīng.
A Níngshéndiàn was built above his tomb
for seasonal offerings and sacrifices.
From then on, temples were established in all capitals,
but only those in the capital were called Tàimiào.
In Tiānhuì sixth year (1128),
the two Sòng emperors visiting Tàizǔ's temple
is an example of this.
Sometimes, existing Liáo temples were used,
where imperial portraits were placed,
and these were also called temples.
In Tiānjuàn third year (1140),
when Xīzōng visited Yān and received his honorific title,
he personally offered sacrifices and gave thanks,
which is an example of this.
In Huángtǒng third year (1143),
the Tàimiào was first established.
In the eighth year (1148),
the Tàimiào was completed,
which was the temple in Shàngjīng.
In the early Zhēnyuán period (1153-1155),
Hǎilíng moved the capital to Yān.
He then expanded the old temple
and moved the spirit tablets of the imperial ancestors to the new capital.
On the dīngmǎo day of the eleventh month of the third year (1155),
they were enshrined in the Tàimiào.
During the Zhènglóng period (1156-1161),
palaces and buildings were constructed in Nánjīng,
and ancestral temples were re-established.
This continued after the move south.
The system for these temples
is not recorded in the official histories.
However, general information can be gleaned from biographies and miscellaneous records,
which are appended here.
The temple in Biànjīng
was east of the imperial road south of the palace.
The hall's layout
was a single building with four sloping roofs.
Its northern part was partitioned for the spirit chambers,
and in front was a common corridor.
It had twenty-six bays from east to west,
forming twenty-five sections.
Each section was a chamber.
At each end of the temple, one section was left empty as an antechamber,
leaving twenty-three middle sections as eleven chambers.
Starting from the west, three sections formed one chamber,
which was the temple for Shǐzǔ.
It included the five ancestral spirit tablets of Dé Dì, Ān Dì, Xiànzǔ, Zhāozǔ, and Jǐngzǔ.
The rest were two sections per chamber.
(Some say:
"Only the second and third chambers had two sections,
the rest had only one section per chamber,
totaling seventeen sections.")
The chamber for Shìzǔ included Sùzōng,
the chamber for Mùzōng included Kāngzōng,
the rest had no inclusions.
Each chamber had one door and one window,
the door on the left,
the window on the right,
both facing south.
The stone niches were against the west wall of each chamber,
facing east.
There were six niches for Shǐzǔ,
five facing south and one facing east.
The second and third each had two niches.
The rest were one niche per chamber,
totaling eighteen niches.
On sacrifice days, the spirit tablets were brought out from beneath the north wall,
facing south.
For the dì and xiá sacrifices, all spirit tablets were brought out.
Shǐzǔ faced east,
while the other spirits faced north and south according to their zhāomù order,
arranged from east to west.
Outside the chamber doors was a common corridor.
The hall had two steps,
and three flights of stairs.
In front were two well pavilions.
Outside, there were four layers of double walls.
There were gates on the south, east, and west.
At the corners of the inner wall were towers.
The south gate had five doors,
the others three.
Northeast outside the middle wall
was the Cèbǎodiàn.
A Tàicháng official inspected its seals seasonally,
which was called diǎnbǎo (inspecting the treasures).
South of the inner wall was the Dàcì.
Southeast was the Shénpáo.
The temple gate was flanked by two side corridors,
each with twenty-five bays,
serving as quarters for the zhāiláng and attendants.
Outside the southwest wall
was the temple office.
The spirit gate had twenty-four halberds on display,
planted with wooden supports.
Beneath the halberds were palm-shaped boards,
painted with two green dragons,
with five-foot-long five-colored ribbons hanging down.
They were hung above the halberds the day before a sacrifice,
and stored away after the sacrifice.
Chamber order.
In Dàdìng twelfth year (1172),
a discussion arose about building a separate temple for Mǐnzōng.
The ritual officials cited the precedents of Jìn Huì, Huái, Táng Zhōngzōng, and Hòutáng Zhuāngzōng being enshrined.
If these precedents were followed,
Wǔlíng Huángdì, being without a successor, should also be enshrined.
However, Zhōngzōng's enshrinement
initially involved an empty chamber,
and eventually led to an increase to nine chambers.
Huì and Huái's enshrinement involved moving the two temples of Yùzhāng and Yǐngchuān.
Zhuāngzōng's enshrinement involved transferring one chamber of Yìzǔ.
The current system of the Tàimiào,
excluding the transferred temples,
is seven generations and eleven chambers.
If Wǔlíng were to be enshrined,
another temple would have to be transferred.
Xúnzǐ said:
"He who possesses the world serves seven generations."
If collateral relatives like brothers are accommodated,
and ancestors are removed,
then an emperor may not be able to serve seven generations.
Upon reviewing the ancestral temple's generational order,
from Ruìzōng up to Shǐzǔ,
there are seven generations in total,
with no other temples available for transfer.
The Jìn History states:
"Temples are limited by the number of spirit tablets they can accommodate,
not by a fixed number."
The Eastern Jìn and Táng dynasties both followed this system,
thus increasing to eleven chambers.
Emperor Kāng, upon inheriting the throne,
designated his brothers as one chamber,
thus not moving distant temples but enshrining Emperor Chéng.
The Táng treated Emperors Jìng, Wén, and Wǔ as belonging to the same generation,
adding two chambers in the eastern part of the Tàimiào,
setting it at nine generations and eleven chambers.
The current Tàimiào has already reached this number.
If the principle of "not constrained by a fixed number" is adopted,
increasing to twelve chambers
would be acceptable.
However, the temple system is already established,
and to deliberate on further expansion
is a very serious matter.
Moreover, it might also entail changing the zhāomù order of Emperor Ruìzōng's spirit chamber.
The Spring and Autumn Annals' principle states that close kinship should not harm the reverence for the esteemed.
The Hàn History states:
"Fathers and sons do not sit together,
but a grandson can follow his grandfather."
If Wǔlíng is enshrined,
the Tàimiào would be expanded to twelve chambers.
According to the Spring and Autumn Annals' principle of honoring the esteemed,
Wǔlíng should be in the eleventh chamber,
and participate in the dì and xiá sacrifices.
According to the principle of a grandson following his grandfather,
he should be below Tàizōng,
and occupy the zhāo position,
and also be called a zōng.
However, the previously enshrined Ruìzōng is already in the eleventh chamber.
Throughout successive xiá sacrifices,
Ruìzōng is in the mù position,
opposite Tàizōng's zhāo position.
If the spirit chamber and zhāomù order are to be changed,
it is not something that officials dare to lightly discuss.
It should be left to the sacred judgment.
In the fourth month of the nineteenth year (1179),
Mǐnzōng was enshrined in the dì sacrifice,
and the Tàimiào was consequently expanded to twelve chambers.
In the twenty-ninth year (1189),
when Shìzōng was about to be enshrined,
officials stated:
"The Tàimiào has twelve chambers.
From Shǐzǔ to Xīzōng, although it represents eight generations,
Shìzōng and Xīzōng were brothers,
and one was not the successor of the other.
Following the precedent of Jìn Chéngdì,
it only accounts for seven generations.
If Shìzōng and Xiǎnzōng are specially enshrined, it would then be nine generations."
Therefore, in the fifth month, Xiànzǔ and Zhāozǔ were removed, and Shìzōng, Míngdé Huánghòu, and Xiǎnzōng were enshrined in the temple.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
Xuānzōng moved south.
All ancestral temple and altar sacrifices were entrusted to Zhōngdū.
Since Mǒliǎn Jìnzhōng abandoned the city and fled south,
the ritual of regular visits ceased entirely.
In the fourth year (1216),
the ritual officials stated:
"Ancestral temples and altars are the great affairs of the state.
Now that Your Majesty is sojourning in the auxiliary capital,
the spirit tablets of the successive emperors have been moved here.
It is fitting to reconstruct the Grand Ancestral Temple and the Altars of Land and Grain
to offer the seasonal sacrifices.
According to the temple system in Zhōngdū,
from the Founding Ancestor to Zhāngzōng, there were twelve chambers.
However, the current temple has only eleven chambers.
If we were to build an additional one, it would be difficult to complete quickly.
Moreover, the times are full of difficulties,
so rituals should adapt to changes.
We now propose to temporarily enthrone Sùzōng's spirit tablet with that of Shìzǔ,
and the spirit tablets from the Founding Ancestor downwards shall be respectfully placed in their respective chambers."
The spirit tablets were made of chestnut wood,
following the Táng system,
which was established in the ninth year of Huángtǒng (1149).
For the tablet chamber (Shìshì),
the sides, top, and bottom were all made of stone.
The door faced east,
made of wood for the panels,
painted vermillion.
Inside the chamber was a cushion.
After placing the tablets,
the emperor's tablet was on the left,
covered with a yellow silk scarf,
and the empress's tablet was on the right,
covered with a red silk scarf.
The screens (fǔyǐ) were made of paper,
with a wooden frame,
and two feet resembling standing screens.
They were covered with three strips of red silk,
embroidered with fifty-four golden axes,
lined with red silk,
placed over the screens,
with the plain half hanging behind.
They were placed beneath the north wall,
facing south,
with an altar-table (jīyán) set in front for the spirit tablets to rest on.
There were five mats,
each five feet five inches long,
and two feet five inches wide.
Wǎn mats (rush mats) had
white borders.
They were made of sedge (lìn),
edged with red silk,
embroidered with white orchid patterns and cloud motifs,
and covered again with red silk lining.
Two for each position.
Sāo mats (braided mats) had
painted borders.
They were made of blue rush woven with five-colored wool,
edged with red silk,
painted with algae patterns and cloud motifs,
also lined with red silk.
