Two for each position,
placed on top of the wǎn mats.
Cì mats (secondary mats) had
embroidered borders.
They were made of light bamboo (jūn),
also called peach branch mats,
edged with red gauze,
embroidered with iron-colored axes,
and lined with red silk.
Two for each position,
placed on top of the sāo mats.
Two tiger mats;
the larger one was the same length,
but one foot wider.
It was a cushion made of tiger skin,
padded,
edged with red silk embroidered with golden axes.
There was also a smaller tiger skin cushion,
made in the same way as the three mats.
When it was warm, peach branch cì mats were used.
When it was cold, the peach branch mats were removed and tiger skin cushions were added.
For the summer and autumn sacrifices,
peach branch cì mats were used.
In the two winter months,
the peach branch mats were removed and small tiger skin cushions were added on top of the sāo mats.
In the twelfth month (làdōng),
two large tiger skin cushions were further added on top of the sāo mats,
and the two small tiger skin cushions were moved on top of the large cushions.
There were curved tables with three legs
and straight tables with two legs,
each one foot five inches long,
painted with vermillion lacquer.
A curved table was placed in front of the emperor's tablet,
and a straight table was placed behind it.
Dì and Xiá Sacrifices.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng (1171),
the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) memorialized on the rituals of the dì and xiá sacrifices, stating:
"The 'Lǐ Wěi' (Apocrypha of Rites) says, 'A xiá sacrifice every three years,
a dì sacrifice every five years.'
During the Kāiyuán era of Táng,
the Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng) debated,
and the dì and xiá rites were both considered grand sacrifices (yīnjì).
Xiá means to share food in the ancestral temple,
and dì refers to arranging by seniority.
They express the former rulers' compassion for their descendants
and complete the filial piety of the many successors towards their parents.
Different from regular sacrifices,
they are performed at specific times.
Sacrifices should not be too frequent,
as frequency leads to irreverence.
They should not be too infrequent,
as infrequency leads to negligence.
Therefore, kings emulate the ways of heaven
to establish ritual codes.
Zhēng and Cháng sacrifices (seasonal) symbolize the seasons,
and dì and xiá symbolize leap months.
With two leap months in five years,
the way of heaven is perfected.
The ancestral temple emulates this,
making these two grand sacrifices.
Since the Zhōu Dynasty,
this ritual has been used.
Since the ninth year of Dàdìng (1169), the xiá rite has been performed.
If we discuss the dì sacrifice,
it should be performed eighteen months after the xiá, in the first month of summer."
An imperial edict commanded that
"a xiá sacrifice in the winter of the third year, and a dì sacrifice in the summer of the fifth year"
be made permanent rites.
It was also stated:
"During the time of Hǎilíng,
envoys were sent only in the second and tenth months each year for two sacrifices,
with a xiá sacrifice every three years.
According to Táng rites, seasonal sacrifices were offered in the Grand Ancestral Temple in the first month of each season,
and a là sacrifice in the last month of winter,
totaling five sacrifices per year.
If we follow Hǎilíng's system of only two sacrifices per year,
it is not the ritual of a Son of Heaven.
It is appropriate to follow the classic rites of five sacrifices per year."
This was adopted.
On the day of the sacrifice, all spirit tablets were brought out into the front corridor,
arranged according to zhāomù order.
Meritorious officials whose portraits were painted (yīngtú gōngchén) were accorded secondary sacrifices in the temple courtyard,
each paired with the emperor they served,
in order of their rank.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) served as the second libationer (yàxiàn),
and princes (qīnwáng) as the final libationer (zhōngxiàn),
or sometimes princes were used for both.
Or the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) as the second libationer,
and the Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglù Qīng) as the final libationer.
In that month, the regular seasonal sacrifice was suspended.
The ceremony details are missing.
Morning Sacrifice Ceremony.
In the eleventh month of the eleventh year of Dàdìng (1171),
the day before the suburban sacrifice (jiāosì),
a morning sacrifice was offered at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Fasting and abstinence were observed as for the imperial suburban sacrifice.
Three days before the sacrifice,
the Director of the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào Lìng), leading his subordinates,
swept inside and outside the temple.
The Inspection Department (Diǎnjiǎn Sī) marked out an area in front of the temple
and set up guards and banners.
The Department of Imperial Households (Shàngshè) set up eleven preparation tents (zhuànmán) to the west of the Southern Spirit Gate,
facing south,
with the west as the superior position.
The Director of the Palace Administration (Diànzhōng Jiān), leading the Department of Imperial Households,
arranged the Grand Secondary Hall (Dàcì Diàn).
A Small Secondary Hall (Xiǎocì) was also set up below the eastern steps (zùjiē),
slightly to the south,
facing west.
The emperor's kneeling mat position was also set up in the main hall,
with the tablet position slightly to the west.
Yellow felt mats (huángdào rù) were also laid inside and outside the temple gate,
from the imperial chariot (yùlù) to the sedan chair ascent point,
and also from the Grand Secondary Hall to the Eastern Spirit Gate.
One position for the Seven Sacrifices (Qī Sī) was also set up below the main hall, north of the transversal street,
west of the western street,
facing east.
The positions for meritorious officials accorded secondary sacrifices were below the main hall, east of the path,
south of the transversal street,
facing west,
with the north being the superior position.
Two days before,
the Dàlè Lìng (Grand Director of Music) arranged the ceremonial suspended instruments (gōngxuán zhī lè) in the courtyard.
In each of the four directions, three sets of biānzhōng (bell-chimes) and three sets of biānqìng (stone-chimes) were set up.
In the east, the biānzhōng started from the north,
with the biānqìng interspersed,
facing east.
In the west, the biānqìng started from the north,
with the biānzhōng interspersed,
facing west.
In the south, the biānqìng started from the west,
with the biānzhōng interspersed.
In the north, the biānzhōng started from the west,
with the biānqìng interspersed.
All faced north.
Twelve special qìng (stone chimes), large bells, and bózhōng (flat bells) were set up,
within the area of the suspended instruments,
each according to its celestial position.
Lùgǔ (road drums) and lùtáo (road rattles) were erected within the northern section,
on either side of the path.
One Jìngǔ (advance drum)
was positioned slightly south behind them.
Jiàngǔ (standing drums), pígǔ (military drums), and yìnggǔ (responsive drums) were placed at the four corners;
the jiàngǔ in the center,
the pígǔ on the left,
and the yìnggǔ on the right.
A zhù (percussion instrument) and a yú (tiger-shaped scraper) were placed within the suspended instrument area;
one zhù was on the east side of the path,
and one yú was on the west side of the path.
Dance markers (wǔbiǎo) were erected between the cuánzhuì (rows of dancers).
The dēnggē zhī lè (ascending song music) instruments were set up between the front pillars of the hall;
one jīnzhōng (metal bell) was on the east,
one yùqìng (jade chime) was on the west,
both facing north.
One zhù was slightly west to the north of the jīnzhōng,
and one yú was slightly east to the north of the yùqìng.
Two bófǔ (clappers),
one to the north of the zhù,
and one to the north of the yú,
faced each other east and west.
Qín (zithers) and sè (lutes) were placed in front.
Those made of gourd and bamboo were set up between the steps,
in double rows facing north.
All the musicians were positioned behind the suspended instruments.
One day before,
the Tàimiào Lìng (Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple) opened the chambers.
The Fènglǐ Láng (Ritual Attendant Official) led his subordinates
to set up the divine tablets (shénwèi) beneath the northern wall inside each chamber.

Each tablet had one fǔyǐ (screen with axe patterns), one guānxí (rush mat), two sāoxí (hemp mats), two cìxí (secondary mats), one purple silk thick cushion, one purple silk covered cushion, one qǔjī (curved armrest), and one zhíjī (straight armrest).
An emperor's tablet (huángdì bǎnwèi) was also set up inside the door of the eastern hall section,
facing west.
A yìnfúwèi (position for receiving blessings) was also set up in the eastern wing,
facing west.
An yàzhōngxiànwèi (position for the assistant final presenter) was also set up slightly east to the north of the transverse street below the hall,
facing west.
The positions for the assisting princes, imperial clan members, and envoys were behind the yàzhōngxiàn.
The positions for the assisting imperial clan members were south of the transverse street,
facing west.
The officials for presenting the zàn (libation cup), presenting the zànpán (libation basin), presenting the wine cup, and presenting the jué (wine cup) were further to their south.
The officials for presenting the yí (ewer), pán (basin), jīn (cloth), and fěi (basket) were behind them.
The officials for offering sacrifices to the Seven Altars (qīshì xiànguān) were south of the officials presenting the jué.
The officials assisting with the libations, reading the祝 (zhù - prayer), presenting the léixǐ (ewer-basin), juéxǐ (cup-basin), etc., were behind them.
The Sīzūnyí Guān (Officer in Charge of Sacrificial Vessels) was south of the qīshì xiànguān.
The yàzhōngxiàn, Sīléixǐ, Juéxǐ, Fèngjuéjiǔ Guān, etc., were further to their south.
All faced west,
with the northernmost as the highest rank.
The Dàlǐ Shǐ (Grand Master of Ceremonies) was slightly south to the west of the western steps,
facing the yàzhōngxiàn.
The Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant), Sītú (Minister of Education), and assisting prime ministers were south of the Dàlǐ Shǐ.
The Shìzhōng (Palace Attendants) and Zhízhèng Guān (Executive Officials) were further to their south.

The Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites), Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices), Tàipú Qīng (Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud), Guānglù Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments), and meritorious officials offering sacrifices were to the west.

The Jǔcè (Officials for Presenting Tablets), Guānglù Chéng (Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments), and Tàicháng Bóshì (Academicians of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) were further to their west.
The officials assisting meritorious officials with libations, léixǐ, juéxǐ, etc., were behind the meritorious officials offering sacrifices.
Two positions for the Jiānjì Yùshǐ (Censors Supervising Sacrifices) were set up below the western steps,
both facing east,
with the northernmost as the highest rank.

The Fènglǐ Láng, Tàimiào Lìng, Tàiguān Lìng (Director of the Court of Imperial Supplicants), Tàizhù (Grand Prayer Official), Gōngwéi Lìng (Director of the Palace Gates), and Zhùshǐ (Prayer Scribes) were south of the yàxiàn (secondary presenter), zhōngxiàn (final presenter), and Fèngjuéjiǔ Guān.

The officials for presenting biāndòu (bamboo and wooden vessels), fǔguǐ (rectangular and round vessels), and the sacrificial animals (jiànzǔ zhāiláng) were further south of the Tàizhù and Fènglǐ Láng.
The Tàimiào Chéng (Assistant Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple) and Tàiguān Chéng (Assistant Director of the Court of Imperial Supplicants) were each behind their respective directors.
Two Xiélǜ Láng (Officials for Regulating Music) were positioned,
one between the front pillars of the hall,
and one to the northwest of the ceremonial suspended instruments,
both facing east.
The Dàlè Lìng was north of the dēnggē music area.
The Dàsīlè (Grand Director of Music) was north of the ceremonial suspended instruments.
The Liángyùn Lìng (Director of Fine Brews) was at the place where the zūn (wine vessels) were poured.
All faced north.
Positions for assisting civil and military officials (zhùjì wénwǔ qúnguān) were also set up south of the transverse street,
facing east, with the northernmost as the highest rank.
The Guānglù Qīng set up the sacrificial animals (chénshēng) to the east of the transverse street outside the eastern divine gate,
facing west,
with the southernmost as the highest rank.
The Lǐnxī Lìng (Director of the Imperial Stables) was positioned southwest of the sacrificial animals,
facing north.
All the Tàizhù were east of the sacrificial animals,
each behind a sacrificial animal.
The Zhùshǐ each accompanied them from behind,
all facing west.
The Lǐbù Shàngshū inspected the sacrificial animals (shěngshēng) slightly north in front of the sacrificial animals.
The Yùshǐ (Censor) was positioned west of the Lǐbù Shàngshū.
Both faced south.
The Lǐbù led its subordinates
to set up the prayer tablet table (zhùcè àn) to the right outside the chamber door.
The Sīzūnyí led his subordinates
to set up the zūnyí (sacrificial vessels) positions to the left of the chamber door.

Each position had one jiǎyí (wine vessel), one huángyí (yellow wine vessel), two xīzūn (ox-shaped vessels), two xiàngzūn (elephant-shaped vessels), two zhùzūn (decorated vessels), and two shānléi (mountain-shaped jars).
Each was supplied with a spoon (sháo), a lid (xiá), and a stand (diàn) for pouring.
Zàn pán jué diàn (libation basins, wine cups, and stands) were also placed in baskets (fěi),
and positioned at the place of the ancestral zūnyí.
Two húzūn (pot-shaped vessels), two tàizūn (grand vessels), and four shānléi were also set up,
each with a diàn and xiá,
between the steps below the hall,
facing north with the westernmost as the highest rank.
These were set up but not poured from.
For each of the meritorious officials of the Seven Altars, two húzūn were set up to the left of their seat.
All had lids and stands inside.
Pouring vessels had spoons.
All were placed on mats.
The Fènglǐ Láng set out the sacrificial utensils:
four guǐ in front of each position,
followed by four fǔ,
then six dēng (stemmed vessels),
then six xíng (bowls for soup),
with biāndòu at the back.
On the left were twelve biān,
on the right were twelve dòu (bean-shaped vessels).
All were washed and arranged,
placed on mats.
The biāndòu were covered with cloths,
covering the contents.
One biān, one dòu, one fǔ, one guǐ, and four zǔ (stands for sacrificial meat)
were set up inside the food curtain of each chamber.
Two yùxǐ (imperial basins) were also set up to the east of the eastern steps.
The yàzhōngxiàn léixǐ (ewer-basin for the assistant final presenter) was set up southeast below the eastern transverse street,
facing north.
The léi (ewer) was east of the xǐ (basin),
the fěi (basket) west of the xǐ,
facing south,
filled with cloths.
The yàzhōngxiàn juéxǐ (cup-basin for the assistant final presenter) was set up west of the léixǐ.
The léi was east of the xǐ,
the fěi west of the xǐ,
facing south,
filled with cloths, jué, and diàn.
Officials holding the cloths, ewers, and baskets were positioned behind them.
Five *kè* before the *chǒu* hour on the day of the sacrifice,
the Tàicháng Qīng led the officiants
to place candles in front of the divine tablets and outside the doors.
The Guānglù Qīng led his subordinates
to fill the biāndòu.
The contents of the biān were:

dried fish (yúshū), roasted millet cakes (qiú'ěr), rice cakes (fěncí), dried dates (gānzǎo), shaped salt (xíngyán), deer jerky (lùpú), hazelnuts (zhēnshí), dried persimmons (gānjù), peaches (táo), water caltrops (líng), gorgon fruit (qiàn), and chestnuts (lì),
arranged in order.
The contents of the dòu were:

celery pickles (qínzū), bamboo shoot pickles (sǔnzū), mallow pickles (kuízū), turnip green pickles (jīngzū), chive pickles (jiǔzū), fermented gruel (yíshí), fish paste (yúhǎi), rabbit paste (tùhǎi), pounded pork (túnpāi), deer paste (lùní), thick meat sauce (tánhǎi), and mixed grain porridge (sǎnshí),
arranged in order.
The xíng were filled with clear soup (gēng),
with added vegetables (máohuá).
The dēng were filled with rich soup (dàgēng).
The fǔ were filled with rice and millet (dàoliáng).
The guǐ were filled with broomcorn millet and foxtail millet (shǔjì).
Millet (liáng) was placed before rice (dào),
and foxtail millet (jì) before broomcorn millet (shǔ).
The Liángyùn Lìng entered to fill the zūnyí.
The jiǎyí and huángyí were filled with fragrant black millet wine (yùchàng).
Except for the xīzūn, xiàngzūn, and zhùzūn, which were filled with clear water (xuánjiǔ),
all others were filled with wine,
(using fragrant medicinal wine).
Each was supplied with a diàn, sháo, and xiá.
Among the zūn and léi below the hall—
the húzūn, tàizūn, and shānléi—
except for the uppermost shānléi being filled with xuánjiǔ,
all others were filled with wine,
supplied with xiá and diàn.
The Tàimiào Lìng led his subordinates
to set up the mats and cushions for the meritorious officials of the Seven Altars in their respective places.
Each position had one guānxí and one bìxiāo rù (green silk cushion).
Each also had a bǎnwèi set up in front of their seat,
as well as two biāndòu, two fǔguǐ, and one bólì (bowl).
At each position, two húzūn were set up to the right of the divine seat,
facing north.
The xuánjiǔ was to the west.
The Director of the Imperial Cellar (Liángyùn Lìng) filled the wine vessels (zūn) with ritual wine as usual,
adding a ladle (sháo) and a scoop (zhù),
and placing the goblet (jué) beneath the wine vessel,
with a stand (diàn) added.
The Minister of Imperial Banquets (Guānglù Qīng) prepared the food offerings.
To the left were two bamboo containers (biān),
with chestnuts (lì) in front,
and dried venison (lùfǔ) next.
To the right were two wooden sacrificial vessels (dòu),
with fermented greens (jīngzū) in front,
and minced venison (lùní) next.
The sacrificial table (zǔ) was filled with cooked lamb (yángshú),
and the rectangular (fǔ) and round (guǐ) grain vessels were filled with millet (shǔ) and broomcorn millet (jì).
The Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào Lìng) also set up seven sacrificial pyres (liáochái)
and dug a burial pit (yìkǎn) to the north outside the West Divine Gate (Xīshénmén).
The Director of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Jiān) displayed exotic treasures (yìbǎo), auspicious rarities (jiāruì), and treasures from conquered nations (fáguó zhī bǎo).
The Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) displayed the annual tributes from various prefectures,
with gold (jīn) in the front row,
jade (yù) and silk (bó) next,
and the rest at the back,
all to the north of the palace enclosure (gōngxuán),
facing east and west,
each laid out on a mat (xí).
For all objects offered to the spirits (shén), if something was unavailable at the time, it was replaced with a seasonal item.
Inspection of Sacrificial Animals (Shěngshēng Qì): The day before, after the hour of wěi (1-3 PM),
access to the temple grounds (miàosuǒ) was restricted to pedestrians.
The Director of Sacrificial Vessels (Sīzūn Yí), the Ceremonial Aide (Fènglǐ Láng), and the officiants (zhíshìzhě)
ascended from the west steps to await.
A moment later,
the various Chief Diviners (Zhū Tàizhù) and the Director of Sacrificial Animals (Lǐnxī Lìng)
brought the sacrificial animals into position.

The Attending Officer of Rituals (Lǐzhí Guān) and the Usher (Zànzhě) led the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) and the Vice Minister of Imperial Banquets (Guānglù Qīngcéng) to the animal inspection platform,
where they stood steady.
The Attending Officer of Rituals led the Minister of Rites.
The Usher led the Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ)
to enter and ascend the west steps,
inspecting the washing and cleansing thoroughly.
When finished,
all officiants raised their voices and declared:
"Clean!"
They all descended,
returned to the animal inspection platform,
and the Attending Officer of Rituals stepped slightly forward, saying:
"The declaration of cleanliness is complete.
Please proceed with the animal inspection."
Next, he led the Minister of Rites and the Vice Minister (Shìláng) slightly forward.
After the animal inspection was completed,
they withdrew to their original positions.
Next, he led the Minister of Imperial Banquets and the Vice Minister out of their ranks,
to circulate around the animals once.
The Vice Minister of Imperial Banquets faced west and declared:
"Plump!"
and declared:
"Prepared!"
The Director of Sacrificial Animals, leading the various Chief Diviners, circulated around the animals once,
faced west, bowed, and declared:
"Fat!"
The Attending Officer of Rituals stepped slightly forward, saying:
"The animal inspection is complete.
Please proceed to the food inspection platform."
He led the Minister of Rites and others to their respective positions,
where they stood steady.
After the Imperial Censor completed the inspection of the food preparations,
the Attending Officer of Rituals declared
"Food inspection completed!"
and all returned to their fasting quarters (zhāisuǒ).
The Minister of Imperial Banquets, the Vice Minister, the Chief Diviners, and the Director of Sacrificial Animals successively led the sacrificial animals
to the Director of the Imperial Household (Tàiguān Lìng).
The Attending Officer of Rituals led the Minister of Rites
to inspect the tripods (dǐng) and cauldrons (huò),
and to oversee the washing and rinsing.
When finished,
they returned to their fasting quarters.
An hour and a quarter after sunset,
the Director of the Imperial Household, leading the butchers (zǎirén),
took up the luan knives (luándāo) and slaughtered the animals.
The ritual officers (zhùshǐ) each took hair and blood,
placing them together in one sacrificial vessel (dòu) for each altar,
and then proceeded to cook the animals.
The ritual officers washed the livers in aromatic wine (yùchàng),
and then took liver and fat,
placing them together in one sacrificial vessel for each altar,
and all returned to the food preparation area.
Imperial Procession (Luánjià Chūgōng): The day before,
the responsible officials set up the grand imperial procession (dàjià lǔbù) outside the Gate of Heavenly Response (Yìngtiānmén).
The Director of Imperial Carriages (Shàngniǎn) brought the jade chariot (yùlù) inside the Gate of Heavenly Response,
facing south.
On that day, at dawn,
the attendant ministers (shìchén), imperial guards (zhíwèi), and processional officers (dǎojiàguān)
stood in ranks on either side in front of the Hall of Fasting (Zhìzhāidiàn), awaiting.
The Secretariat Aide (Tōngshì Shèrén) led the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) to bow prostrate,
then kneel,
and announce:
"Request 'middle strictness' (zhōngyán)."
The Emperor wore the Heaven-connecting Crown (Tōngtiān Guān) and crimson gauze robes (jiàngshāpáo).
A moment later,
the Palace Attendant announced:
"Outer preparations complete (wàibàn)."
The Emperor emerged from the fasting chamber,
ascended the imperial seat,
and after the assembled officials paid their respects,
the Director of Imperial Carriages advanced the sedan chair (yú).
The Palace Attendant announced:
"Request His Majesty to ascend the sedan chair."
The Emperor rode the sedan chair,
with imperial guards clearing the way with calls (jǐngbì) as per usual ceremony.
The Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Qīng) first proceeded to the jade chariot,
smoothed his robes and ascended,
standing upright and holding the reins.
The processional officers led the way.
When the Emperor arrived at the jade chariot inside the Gate of Heavenly Response,
the Palace Attendant advanced to the front of the sedan chair,
announcing:
"Request His Majesty to descend from the sedan chair and ascend the chariot."
The Emperor ascended the chariot.
The Minister of the Imperial Stud stood and offered the chariot straps (suī).
The processional officers divided into left and right, guiding on foot,
with the foremost
(yú) as the senior.
The Palace Attendant of the Department of the Imperial Secretariat (Ménxià Shìláng) advanced to the front of the chariot,
announcing:
"Request the imperial chariot to proceed and depart."
After the announcement,
he bowed prostrate,
rose,
and returned to his position.
The imperial guards and ceremonial objects halted inside the Gate of Heavenly Response.
When the imperial chariot moved,
the cry of
"Clear the way!"
was raised.
Upon reaching the Gate of Heavenly Response,
the Palace Attendant of the Department of the Imperial Secretariat announced:
"Request the imperial chariot to pause briefly,
and command the attendant ministers to mount their horses."
The Palace Attendant received the imperial decree and withdrew,
declaring:
"By imperial command."
The Palace Attendant of the Department of the Imperial Secretariat withdrew,
transmitted the command,
declaring:
"Attendant ministers, mount your horses!"
The Usher (Zànzhě) relayed the command:
"Command the attendant ministers to mount their horses!"
The processional officers divided to the left and right, leading the way.
The Palace Attendant of the Department of the Imperial Secretariat announced:
"Request the imperial chariot to proceed and depart."
When the imperial chariot moved,
the cry of
"Clear the way!"
was raised, but no drums or wind instruments were sounded.
Approaching the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào),
the Attending Officer of Rituals and the Usher each led the officiating officials (xiǎngguān).
The Secretariat Aide separately led the accompanying officials, imperial kinsmen, and descendants (cóngxiǎng qúnguān, zōngshì zǐsūn),
outside the temple gate,
standing in ranks to welcome the procession.
When the imperial chariot reached the temple gate,
it turned around to face south.
The Palace Attendant, in front of the chariot, announced:
"Your servant, the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), so-and-so, states:
Request His Majesty to descend from the chariot
and enter the temple gate on foot."
The Emperor descended from the chariot.
The processional officers led the way.
The Emperor entered the temple gate on foot,
moving slightly to the east.
The Palace Attendant announced:
"Request His Majesty to ascend the sedan chair."
The Director of Imperial Carriages presented the sedan chair,
with imperial guards in attendance as per usual ceremony.
The Emperor rode the sedan chair to the Grand Abode (Dàcì).
The Palace Attendant announced:
"Request His Majesty to descend from the sedan chair
and enter the Grand Abode."
The Emperor entered the abode.
The curtain was lowered.
Parasols, fans, and imperial guards were arranged as per usual ceremony.
The Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Qīng) and the Erudites of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Bóshì) stood separately to the left and right of the Grand Abode.
The processional officers proceeded to their positions in the temple courtyard,
standing and awaiting.
Morning Libation (Chénguàn): Five quarters before the hour of chǒu (1-3 AM) on the day of the sacrifice,
the officiating officials and assisting sacrificial officials
each donned their respective robes.
The Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Director of the Imperial Cellar, leading their subordinates,
entered to fill the wine vessels (zūnléi).
The Minister of Imperial Banquets, the Director of the Imperial Household, and the food servers filled the bamboo containers (biāndòu) and grain vessels (fǔguǐ),
and removed their lids.
The Ceremonial Aide and the Usher entered first
and took their positions.

The Usher led the Imperial Censors (Yùshǐ), the Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple, the Chief Diviners, the Director of the Palace Women (Gōngwéi Lìng), the ritual officers, and the officiants,
all entering from the east side gate,
and taking their positions.
At two *kè* before dawn,
the official-in-charge of ceremonies led the officials of the Tàicháng Sì, along with the Tàizhù and Gōngwéi Lìng, to ascend the hall.
They opened the room of the ancestral spirit tablets.
The Tàizhù and Gōngwéi Lìng brought out the spirit tablets of the Emperor and Empress,
and set them on the seat.
In sequence,
the spirit tablets of the successive chambers were each set before the embroidered screen within,
and positioned.
The *zànzhě* led the Yùshǐ, Tàimiào Lìng, Gōngwéi Lìng, Tàizhù, Zhùshǐ, and the officials of the Tàicháng,
to stand between the steps,
once again facing north.
The Fènglǐ Láng in the hall intoned,
"Offer the spirit tablets!"
When this was done,
the Fènglǐ said,
"Bow twice!"
The *zànzhě* relayed this,
and all from the Yùshǐ down bowed twice.
When this was done,
each returned to their position.
The Dà Yuè Lìng led two dance workers in,
and they took their positions.
The official-in-charge of ceremonies and the *zànzhě* each led the offering officials.
The Tōngshì Shèrén separately led the assisting civil and military officials and members of the imperial clan to enter and take their positions.
The Fúbǎo Láng presented the imperial seal,
placing it north of the ceremonial bells and drums.
The Emperor entered the main resting area.
A short while later,
the Shìzhōng announced,
"Request 'middle strictness'!"
The Emperor put on his *gǔnmiǎn* ceremonial robes.
The Shìzhōng announced,
"External preparations complete!"
The Tàicháng Qīng prostrated himself,
knelt,
and announced,
"Your servant, Tàicháng Qīng [Name], humbly states,
requesting the Emperor to proceed."
He prostrated himself,
and rose.
The curtain was rolled up,
and the Emperor emerged from the resting area.
The Tàicháng Qīng and Tàicháng Bóshì led the way,
with umbrellas, fans, and guards as in normal ceremony.
The Dàlǐ Shǐ followed behind.
Upon reaching outside the east divine gate,
the Diànzhōng Jiān knelt and presented the *zhènguī*.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to hold the *guī*!"
The Emperor held the *zhènguī*.
The umbrellas, fans, and guards remained outside the gate,
while close attendants followed in.
The Xiélǜ Láng knelt, prostrated himself, raised his banner,
and rose.
The artisans beat the drums and struck the *zhù*,
and the Chāngníng music of the ceremonial bells and drums began.
Upon reaching the foot of the eastern steps,
the banner was lowered,
the *yǔ* was struck,
and the music stopped.
Ascending from the eastern steps,
the *dēnggē* music began.
The left and right attendants, according to their numbers, ascended to their designated positions on the platform,
stood facing west,
and the music stopped.
The leading officials positioned themselves to the left and right as attendants.
The Tàicháng Qīng advanced and announced,
"Request to bow twice!"
The Emperor bowed twice.
The Fènglǐ said,
"All officials bow twice!"
The *zànzhě* relayed this,
and all those in position bowed twice.
The Fènglǐ then intoned,
"All functionaries, take your positions!"
The official-in-charge of ceremonies and the *zànzhě* separately led the functionaries to their positions above and below the hall.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request the Emperor to proceed to the *léixǐ* position!"
The *dēnggē* music began.
Upon reaching the eastern steps,
the music stopped.
Descending from the eastern steps,
the music of the ceremonial bells and drums began.
Upon reaching the washing position,
the music stopped.
The internal attendant knelt and took the *yí*,
rose,
and poured water.
Another internal attendant knelt and took the *pán*,
rose,
and received the water.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to tuck in the *zhènguī*!"
The Emperor tucked in the *zhènguī*,
washed his hands.
When this was done,
an internal attendant knelt and took a towel from the basket,
rose,
and presented it.
He wiped his hands.
When this was done,
the official presenting the *zàn* and *pán* knelt and presented the *zàn*.
The Emperor received the *zàn*.
An internal attendant presented the *yí* and poured water.
Another internal attendant knelt and presented the *pán* to receive the water.
The washing of the *zàn* was completed.
An internal attendant knelt and presented a towel.
The Emperor wiped the *zàn*.
When this was done,
an internal attendant laid down the *pán* and *yí*,
and also laid down the towel in the basket.
The official presenting the *zàn* and *pán* received the *zàn* with the *pán*.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to hold the *zhènguī*!"
He led the way.
The Emperor ascended the hall.
The music of the ceremonial bells and drums began.
Upon reaching the foot of the eastern steps,
the music stopped.
The Emperor ascended from the eastern steps.
The *dēnggē* music began.
The Tàicháng Qīng led the way,
proceeding to the *zuōzūn* position of the founding ancestor.
The music stopped.
The official presenting the *zàn* and *pán* filled the *zàn* with *chàng*.
The one holding the *zūn* raised it.
The Shìzhōng knelt and poured the *yùchàng*.
When this was done,
the Tàicháng Qīng led the way,
entering to stand before the spirit tablet of the founding ancestor in the room,
facing north.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to tuck in the *zhènguī*!"
He knelt.
The official presenting the *zàn* and *pán* knelt facing west,
handing the *zàn* to the official presenting the *zàn*.
The official presenting the *zàn* knelt facing west and presented the *zàn*.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to hold the *zàn* and perform the *guàn* offering of *chàng* on the ground!"
The Emperor held the *zàn* and performed the *guàn* offering of *chàng* on the ground.
When this was done,
he handed the *zàn* to the official presenting the *zàn* and *pán*.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to hold the *zhènguī*!"
He prostrated himself,
rose,
and led the way out of the door.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to bow twice!"
The Emperor bowed twice.
The Tàicháng Qīng led the way to the next position,
proceeding as in the previous ceremony.
The *guàn* offering was completed.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to return to the designated platform position!"
The *dēnggē* music began.
Upon reaching the platform position, he stood facing west.
The music stopped.
The Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to return to the small resting area!"
He led the Emperor.
The *dēnggē* music began.
Descending from the eastern steps,
the *dēnggē* music stopped.
The music of the ceremonial bells and drums began.
Approaching the small resting area,
the Tàicháng Qīng announced,
"Request to release the *zhènguī*!"
The Diànzhōng Jiān knelt and received the *zhènguī*.
The Emperor entered the small resting area.
The curtain was lowered.
The music stopped.
A short while later,
the ceremonial bells and drums played the melody of Lái Níng,
with *huángzhōng* as the fundamental tone (*gōng*),
*dàlǚ* as the second tone (*jué*),
*tàicù* as the third tone (*zhǐ*),
and *yìngzhōng* as the fifth tone (*yǔ*).
The Rénfēng Dàoxià dance was performed,
stopping after nine iterations.
*Huángzhōng* was played three times.
*Dàlǚ*, *tàicù*, and *yìngzhōng* were each played twice.
The Lái Níng melody was used to send off the spirits.
Initially,
when the dawn libation was about to be completed,
the zhùshǐ (祝史) each held containers of毛血 (máoxiě) and肝膋 (gānlíao).
First, outside the Southern Divine Gate,
the zhāiláng (齋郎) held braziers, charcoal, xiāo (蕭) (artemisia), háo (蒿) (wormwood), shǔ (黍) (millet), and jì (稷) (panicled millet),
each standing behind the gānlíao.
After the Huángdì (皇帝) completed the dawn libation,
the solemn music performed six movements,
and everyone entered through the main gate,
ascending the Grand Staircase.
The zhū Tàizhù (諸太祝) on the stairs each received the máoxiě and gānlíao,
advancing to offer them before the divine seats.
The zhùshǐ stood at the position of the zūn (尊) (wine vessel),
and the zhāiláng placed the brazier to the left outside the chamber door.
The xiāo, háo, shǔ, and jì were each placed beneath the charcoal.
The zhāiláng descended the Western Staircase,
and the zhū Tàizhù each took liver to roast in the brazier,
then returned to the zūn's position.
When the cooked offerings were presented: the Huángdì ascended for libations,
the Tàiguān Lìng (太官令) led the servers,
who presented the dishes outside the Southern Divine Gate within the various offering tents,
with the west being the place of honor.
The Lǐzhígān (禮直官) led the Sītú (司徒) out to the offering area,
and with the jiànzǔ zhāiláng (薦俎齋郎) holding the sacrificial vessels,
and the jiànbīndòu fúguǐ guān (薦籩豆簠簋官) holding the bīndòu (籩豆) and fúguǐ (簠簋),
the Lǐzhígān and Tàiguān Lìng led them in order through the main gate,
and the Gōngxuán Fēngníng (宮縣豐寧) music played.
(The removal of the dòu (豆) (containers) was done universally.
) Upon reaching the Grand Staircase,
the music ceased.
The zhùshǐ together advanced to remove the máoxiě dòu,
descended the Western Staircase,
and exited.
When the dishes ascended,
the zhū Tàizhù received them on the stairs,
each setting them before the divine seats.
First, the beef was offered,
next the mutton,
then the pork and fish.
The Lǐzhígān led the Sītú and those below him,
descending the Western Staircase,
and returned to their positions.
The zhū Tàizhù each took xiāo, háo, shǔ, and jì, dipped them in fat,
and burned them in the brazier.
After completion,
they returned to the zūn's position.
The zànzhě (贊者) led the Jǔcè Guān (舉冊官) to ascend the Western Staircase,
proceeding to the right of the Shǐzǔ (始祖) (First Ancestor) seat,
to advance and place the zhùcè (祝冊) (prayer tablet) to the west of the bǎnwèi (版位) (tablet position).
After placing it,
they stood near the south of the zhùcè desk.
The Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) knelt and reported,
"Please proceed to the léixǐ (罍洗) position."
The curtain rolled up,
and they came out in sequence,
and the Gōngxuán music played.
The Diànzhōng Jiān (殿中監) knelt and presented the zhènguī (鎮圭) (ceremonial jade tablet),
the Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please take the zhènguī,"
and led the way,
proceeding to the léixǐ position,
where the music ceased.
Washing hands,
and washing the ceremonial cups,
were both according to the ritual of the dawn libation.
After washing,
the Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please take the zhènguī,"
and led the way,
ascending the hall,
the Gōngxuán music played,
until below the zuòjiē (阼階) (Eastern Staircase),
where the music ceased.
Ascending the zuòjiē,
the Dēnggē (登歌) music played.
The Tàicháng Qīng led the way,
proceeding to the Shǐzǔ seat's zūnyí (尊彝) (vessel) area,
the Dēnggē music played,
until reaching the zūnyí area,
where the Dēnggē music ceased,
the Gōngxuán played the Dàyuán (大元) music,
and the Civil Dance entered.
The Fèngjué Guān (奉爵官) touched the zūn with the ceremonial cup,
the person holding the zūn lifted it,
the Shìzhōng (侍中) knelt and poured the fànqí (泛齊) (wine) from the xīzūn (犧尊) (sacrificial vessel).
After completion,
the Tàicháng Qīng led the way,
entering before the divine seat in the Shǐzǔ chamber,
standing facing north.
The Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please tuck in the zhènguī,"
and knelt.
The Fèngjué Guān handed the ceremonial cup to the Jìnjuéjiǔ Guān (進爵酒官).
The Jìnjuéjiǔ Guān knelt, facing west, and presented the ceremonial cup,
the Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please hold the ceremonial cup and perform three libations of wine."
Three libations of wine were poured onto the máojū (茅苴) (straw mat),
after completion,
the ceremonial cup was handed to the Jìnjuéjiǔ Guān,
the Jìnjuéjiǔ Guān handed the ceremonial cup to the Fèngjué Guān.
The Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please take the zhènguī,"
and rose.
Leading the way,
they exited the chamber.
The Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please stand briefly,"
and the music ceased.
The Jǔcè Guān advanced to hold up the zhùcè,
the Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) tucked in his hù (笏) (tablet) and knelt to read the prayer,
after the Jǔzhù Guān (舉祝官) had held up and set down the tablet,
he first proceeded to the next position.
The Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please bow twice,"
after bowing twice,
the Tàicháng Qīng led the way,
proceeding to the next position to perform the ritual,
both according to the previous ceremony.
After the libations and offerings were completed,
the Tàicháng Qīng led the way back to the bǎnwèi,
the Dēnggē music played,
until they stood still, facing west at the position,
and the music ceased.
The Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please return to the xiǎocì (小次) (smaller waiting area),"
the Dēnggē music played.
Descending the zuòjiē,
the Dēnggē music ceased,
the Gōngxuán music played.
Approaching the xiǎocì,
the Tàicháng Qīng reported,
"Please release the zhènguī,"
the Diànzhōng Jiān knelt to receive the zhènguī.
Entering the xiǎocì,
the curtain lowered,
the music ceased,
the Civil Dance withdrew,
the Martial Dance entered,
the Gōngxuán played the Sùníng (肅寧) music,
performing the Dance of Accomplishment and Stability,
the dancers stood still,
the music ceased.
After the Huángdì completed the libations and offerings,
and was about to proceed to the xiǎocì,
the Lǐzhígān led the Bóshì (博士),
the Bóshì led the Yàxiàn (亞獻) (Secondary Offeror),
to the guànxǐ (盥洗) (washing) position,
standing facing north,
tucking in the guī (圭) (jade tablet),
washing hands,
wiping hands,
and holding the guī.
Proceeding to the juéxǐ (爵洗) (cup washing) position,
standing facing north,
tucking in the guī,
washing the cup,
wiping the cup and handing it to the attendant,
holding the guī.
Ascending the Western Staircase,
proceeding to the Shǐzǔ seat's zūnyí area,
standing facing west.
The Gōngxuán music played.
The attendant handed the cup to the Yàxiàn,
the Yàxiàn tucked in the guī,
held the cup,
the person holding the zūn lifted it,
the Tàiguān Lìng poured the lǐqí (醴齊) (sweet wine) from the xiàngzūn (象尊) (elephant vessel),
after completion,
proceeding before the Shǐzǔ divine seat,
tucking in the guī,
and kneeling.
The attendant handed the cup to the Yàxiàn,
the Yàxiàn held the cup and offered wine.
Three libations of wine were poured onto the máojū,
the cup was placed,
holding the guī,
bowing low,
rising,
retreating slightly,
bowing twice,
after completion,
the Bóshì led the way,
the Yàxiàn proceeded to the next position to perform the ritual,
both according to the previous ceremony.
After the ritual was completed,
the music ceased.
For the Zhōngxiàn (終獻) (Final Offeror), besides wearing his original attire and holding the hù,
the rest was according to the ceremony of the Yàxiàn.
The offering officials for the Seven Ancestral Shrines and meritorious ministers completed the rites.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Qīng 太常卿) knelt and reported,
“Please proceed to the position for receiving blessings (Yǐnfú Wèi 飲福位).”
〔一０〕The curtain was rolled up,
and the emperor exited to the secondary hall.
The palace orchestra (gōngxuán 宮縣) began to play.
The Director of the Palace (Diànzhōng Jiān 殿中監) knelt and presented the imperial scepter (zhènguī 鎮圭).
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“Please, Your Majesty, take the imperial scepter.”
He led the way
to the foot of the eastern steps (zuòjiē 阼階),
and the music ceased.
Ascending from the eastern steps,
the ascending song (dēnggē 登歌) began to play.
As the emperor was about to reach the position for receiving blessings,
the music ceased.
Previously,
after the emperor had completed the offering,
the Grand Invoker (Tàizhù 太祝) divided the meat from the three sacrificial animals before the spirit tablets,
taking the second bone of the front leg from each and placing it on a sacrificial stand (zǔ 俎).
He also took millet and grain (shǔjì 黍稷) rice in a bamboo ritual vessel (biān 籩) and placed them together in one biān.
He also poured the finest sacrificial wine (shàngzūn 上尊) and placed it together in one zūn (尊, wine vessel).
Then, the official in charge of ceremonies (lǐzhíguān 禮直官) led the Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) to ascend from the western steps,
walk east,
and stand between the front pillars before the eastern steps,
facing north.
When the emperor arrived at the position for receiving blessings,
he stood facing west.
The ascending song "Auspicious Peace" (Fúníng zhī Yuè 福寧之樂) began to play.
The Grand Invoker poured the blessed wine into a goblet (jué 爵)
and presented it to the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中).
The Palace Attendant received the goblet and held it, standing.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“Please, Your Majesty, bow twice.”
After this was done,
he reported,
“Please insert the scepter (jìn guī 搢圭),”
and knelt.
The Palace Attendant knelt, facing north, and presented the goblet.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“Please take the goblet.”
The emperor performed three libations into the sand pit.
Then he reported,
“Please sip the wine.”
The emperor sipped the wine.
After this was done,
he handed the goblet to the Palace Attendant.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“Please receive the blessed meat (zuò 胙).”
The Grand Invoker handed the biān with millet and grain rice to the Minister of Education.
The Minister of Education knelt and presented it.
The emperor received it and handed it to his attendants.
The Grand Invoker then knelt and handed the sacrificial stand (zǔ 俎) with the blessed meat to the Minister of Education.
After the Minister of Education received the zǔ, he knelt and presented it.
The emperor received it and handed it to his attendants.
The official in charge of ceremonies led the Minister of Education to withdraw and stand.
The Palace Attendant again knelt and presented the goblet of wine.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“Please, Your Majesty, receive the goblet and drink the blessing.”
After drinking the blessing,
the Palace Attendant received the empty goblet and rose,
handing it to the Grand Invoker.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“Please hold the scepter.”
The emperor bowed low,
then rose.
He then reported,
“Please, Your Majesty, bow twice.”
After bowing twice,
the music ceased.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies led the way.
The emperor returned to his designated standing position (bǎnwèi 版位).
The ascending song began to play.
Once he reached his position,
the music ceased.
The Grand Invokers each came forward to remove the biān and dòu (豆, sacrificial vessels).
The ascending song "Abundant Peace" (Fēngníng zhī Yuè 豐寧之樂) began to play.
Once the removal was complete,
the music ceased.
The Minister of Rites (Fènglǐ 奉禮) announced:
“The distribution of blessed meat has been performed.
The assistant sacrificial officials bow twice.”
The announcers relayed the order.
All officials in position bowed twice.
The palace orchestra's "Come and Be Peaceful" (Láiníng zhī Yuè 來寧之樂) began to play,
stopping after one section.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“The rites are concluded.”
He led the way forward.
The emperor descended from the eastern steps.
The ascending song ceased.
The palace orchestra began to play.
They exited the gate.
The palace orchestra ceased.
Umbrellas, fans, staffs, and guards were arranged as usual.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies reported,
“Please release the imperial scepter.”
The Director of the Palace knelt and received the imperial scepter.
The emperor returned to the grand secondary hall (dàcì 大次).

The Palace Attendant for General Affairs (Tōngshì Shèrén 通事舍人), the official in charge of ceremonies, and the announcers each led the offering officials (xiǎngguān 享官), the imperial clan's descendants (zōngshì zǐsūn 宗室子孫), and the accompanying officials (cóngxiǎng qúnguān 從享羣官)
to exit in order.
They also led the officials guiding the imperial carriage to wait outside the East Spirit Gate (Dōngshén Mén 東神門), before the grand secondary hall.
The procession leading the way was as when they arrived.
The announcer led the censors (yùshǐ 御史) and those below them back to their official positions,
where they stood firm.
The Minister of Rites announced,
“Bow twice.”
All bowed twice.
The announcer led the artisans (gōngrén 工人) and dancers (wǔrén 舞人) to exit in order.

The Grand Ritual Commissioner (Dàlǐ Shǐ 大禮使) led the various ritual officials, the Director of the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào Lìng 太廟令), the Grand Invoker, and the Director of the Palace Women (Gōngwéi Lìng 宮闈令)
to ascend and house the spirit tablets as usual.
When the rites were concluded,
the official in charge of ceremonies led the Grand Ritual Commissioner and those below him to descend from the western steps,
reach the cross street (héngjiē 橫街),
bow twice, and withdraw.
The祝冊 (zhùcè, sacrificial prayer scrolls) were stored in a casket (kuì 匱).
The seven ancestral shrines and meritorious ministers were offered separate sacrifices,
following the rites of the joint seasonal offering (xiáxiǎng 祫享).
This was the seasonal offering (shíxiǎng 時享).
The responsible officials (yǒusī 有司) carried out the duties.
Beforehand,
the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Sì 太常寺) submitted a report to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù 禮部),
which informed the Hanlin Academy (Xuéshì Yuàn 學士院) and the Directorate of Astronomy (Sītiān Tái 司天臺)
to select an auspicious day.
On that day, they reported it to the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Seven days beforehand,
they received the oath and injunctions at the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng 尚書省).
At dawn on that day,
the official in charge of ceremonies set up the position boards beneath the main hall (dūtáng 都堂),
following the established oath and injunction diagram.
The official in charge of ceremonies led the three offering officials (sānxiànguān 三獻官),
along with the officials who were to perform the duties (yìngxíngshì zhíshìguān 等),
each to their respective positions,
where they stood firm.
The announcer called,
“Bow with hands clasped” (yī 揖).
All officials in position bowed with clasped hands.
After this was done,
the official in charge of ceremonies presented the oath document to the first offering official (chūxiànguān 初獻官).
The first offering official inserted his ceremonial tablet (hù 笏) into his belt
and read the oath document:
“On such and such a month, such and such a day,
the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào 太廟) is offered sacrifices in early spring.
Each shall perform their duties.
Should one be disrespectful in their service,
the state has its established punishments.”
After reading,
he held his ceremonial tablet.
Officials of the seventh rank and below withdrew first.
The remaining officials bowed in response before withdrawing.
During the four days of "scattered purification" (sànzhāi 散齋), affairs were conducted as usual,
and one lodged in the main sleeping quarters.
However, mourning visits, inquiries about illness, making music, judging and signing documents for executions, punishing criminals, and participating in anything impure or evil were forbidden.
During "concentrated purification" (zhìzhāi 致齋),
which lasted three days at one's own office,
only sacrificial duties were allowed to be performed;
all others were prohibited.
One day was spent at the place of offering.
If one was already purified but absent,
a substitute would perform the duties.
Three days beforehand,
the Ministry of War (Bīngbù 兵部) would arrange for guards to be stationed
at the four gates of the temple.
One day beforehand,
pedestrians were prohibited from passing.
The Bureau of Imperial Carriages and Attendants (Yíluán Sī 儀鸞司) set up eleven sacrificial canopies (zhuànmàn 饌幔) to the west outside the South Spirit Gate (Nánshén Mén 南神門),
facing south.
They also set up two positions for the Seven Sacrificial Lords of Fate and Households (Qī Sì Sīmìng Hù 七祀司命、戶) north of the cross street,
west of the road,
facing east.
They also set up the lodging quarters for the various officials (qúnguān zhāisù cì 羣官齋宿次) in the east and west side rooms of the temple gate.
Two days prior,
the Dàlèjú (Bureau of Grand Music) set up the Dēnggē music on the hall.
The Tàimiàolìng (Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple) led his subordinates
to sweep and clean the inside and outside of the temple hall gates.
Inside the room, the spirit tablets were laid out beneath the northern wall,
facing south, towards the door.
Tables were set on the mat.
Two kneeling mats were also set for the Sānxiàn Guān (Three Presenting Officials).
(One was inside the room,
one was outside the room.)
After the Xuéshìyuàn (Hanlin Academy) had drafted the invocation text,
it was sent to the Tōngjìnsī (Office of Memorials and Communications) for imperial endorsement,
then delivered to the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites),
and placed on the invocation table.
After the Cíyìjú (Bureau of Sacrifices) had washed and cleaned the sacrificial vessels and zūn yí (wine vessels),
they were arranged according to ritual.
Inside the room were two Nèitàizūn (Inner Grand Zūn) and two Shānlěi (Mountain Léi).
Five Xīzūn (Sacrificial Animal Zūn), five Xiàngzūn (Elephant Zūn), one Jīyí (Chicken Yí), and one Niǎoyí (Bird Yí) were placed to the left outside the room,
with the charcoal brazier slightly in front.
Two Zhùzūn (Pig Zūn) and two Xīzūn (Sacrificial Animal Zūn) were placed on the hall,
and two Xiàngzūn (Elephant Zūn) and six Húzūn (Pot Zūn) were placed below.
All faced north, with the west side as superior,
covered with ,
all arranged but not yet filled with wine.
The Léixǐ position for the presenting official was also set.
The Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) set the invocation table to the right outside the room.
The Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals) set up the position boards and the Shěngshēngwèi (Animal Inspection Post),
according to form.
The day before,
all the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) and the Lǐnxīlìng (Director of the Bureau of Sacrificial Animals) brought the sacrificial animals outside the Dōngshénmén (Eastern Spirit Gate).
The Sīzūnyí (Officials in Charge of Zūn Yí), the Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals), and the Zhíshì (Attendants) all entered,
ascended from the western steps,
and waited.
The Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals) led the Tàichángqīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices),
and the Zànzhě (Ushers) led the Yùshǐ (Censors),
ascending from the western steps,
and inspected the washing and cleaning everywhere.
[一一]The Zhízūnzhě (Vessel Bearers) announced the cleanliness.
When finished,
they were led down to the Shěngshēngwèi (Animal Inspection Post).
The Lǐnxīlìng (Director of the Bureau of Sacrificial Animals) stepped forward slightly,
said,
"Please inspect the sacrificial animals,"
and then retreated to his position.
The Tàichángqīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) inspected the animals,
and the Lǐnxīlìng (Director of the Bureau of Sacrificial Animals) and the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) circulated among the animals, announcing their readiness,
all according to the suburban sacrifice ritual.
When completed,
the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) and the Lǐnxīlìng (Director of the Bureau of Sacrificial Animals) led the animals in sequence to ,
and handed them over to the Tàiguānlìng (Director of the Bureau of Imperial Food).
The Zànzhě (Ushers) led the Guānglùqīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments) to ,
requested an inspection of the tripods and cauldrons,
and re-inspected the washing and cleaning.
The Zànzhě (Ushers) led the Yùshǐ (Censors) to ,
inspected the prepared dishes.
When finished,
they, along with the Tàichángqīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) and others, each returned to their fasting places.
The Tàiguānlìng (Director of the Bureau of Imperial Food) led the butchers to cut the animals with the luándāo (phoenix knife).
The Zhùshǐ (Ritual Scribes) each took hair and blood,
filling one dòu (vessel) per room.
They also took liver and fat, filling one dòu (vessel) with these,
placed them at the food preparation area,
and then cooked the animals.
The Guānglùqīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments) led his subordinates
to fill the sacrificial vessels.
The Liángyùnlìng (Director of the Bureau of Imperial Brews) entered to fill the zūn yí (wine vessels).
On the day of the sacrifice, at dawn,
all officials wore their respective rank attire.

The Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals) and Zànzhě (Ushers) first led the Yùshǐ (Censors), Bóshì (Erudites), Tàimiàolìng (Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple), Tàiguānlìng (Director of the Bureau of Imperial Food), Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests), Zhùshǐ (Ritual Scribes), Sīzūnyí (Officials in Charge of Zūn Yí), and Zhíléifěiguān (Officials holding Léi and Fěi baskets), etc.,
to enter through the Sānmén (Southern Gate),
standing between the steps,
facing north, with the west side as superior.
They stood still.
The Fènglǐ (Officer of Ceremonies) said,
"Bow twice."
The Zànzhě (Ushers) relayed the command.
All bowed twice.
When finished,
the Zànzhě (Ushers) led the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) and the Gōngwéilìng (Director of the Palace Gates and Inner Apartments),
ascending from the western steps,
to the Shǐzǔshì (Chamber of the First Ancestor),
opened the Shìshì (Spirit-tablet Repository),
and the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) brought out the Dìzhǔ (Emperor's spirit tablet),
while the Gōngwéilìng (Director of the Palace Gates and Inner Apartments) brought out the Hòuzhǔ (Empress's spirit tablet),
and placed them on the seats.
(The Dìzhǔ was to the west,
the Hòuzhǔ was to the east.)
The Zànzhě (Ushers) led the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) and the Gōngwéilìng (Director of the Palace Gates and Inner Apartments),
descending from the western steps,
and both returned to their positions.
The Fènglǐ (Officer of Ceremonies) said,
"Bow twice."
The Zànzhě (Ushers) relayed the command.
All officials in position bowed twice.
When finished,
they all took their positions for duty.
The Dàlèlìng (Director of Grand Music) led the musicians in.
The Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals) and Zànzhě (Ushers) separately led the Sānxiàn Guān (Three Presenting Officials) and all other officials,
all entering through the Sānnándōngpiānmén (Southern East Side Gate),
to the cross street of the temple courtyard.
The Sānxiàn Guān (Three Presenting Officials) were in the center,
facing north, with the west side as superior.
The Zhíshìguān (Attendant Officials) and all other officials who were to perform duties,
according to rank,
stood in double rows.
The Fènglǐ (Officer of Ceremonies) said,
"Bow."
The Zànzhě (Ushers) relayed the command.
All officials in position who faced north bowed twice.
(Those who had bowed earlier did not bow.)
After bowing,
the Zànzhě (Ushers) led the Sānxiàn Guān (Three Presenting Officials) to their positions facing west, below the eastern steps of the temple hall.
The remaining Zhíshìguān (Attendant Officials) and all other officials
all took their places.
When completed,
the Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals) went before the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official),
[一二]said,
"Please begin the ceremony."
The Xiélǜláng (Master of Music) knelt,
bowed low,
rose,
and the music began.
The Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals) led the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official) to the Guànxǐwèi (Washing and Cleansing Post),
stood facing north,
and the music stopped.
He tucked his hù (tablet) in his belt,
washed his hands,
wiped his hands,
and held his hù (tablet).
He went to the Juéxǐwèi (Cup-washing Post),
stood facing north,
tucked his hù (tablet) in his belt,
washed the zàn (libation cup),
wiped the zàn (libation cup),
handed the zàn (libation cup) to the attendant,
held his hù (tablet),
ascended the hall,
and the music began.
He reached the position of the zūn yí (wine vessels) in the Shǐzǔshì (Chamber of the First Ancestor),
stood facing west,
and the music stopped.
The attendant presented the zàn (libation cup) to the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official).
The Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official) tucked his hù (tablet) in his belt,
[一三]and held the zàn (libation cup).
The Zhízūnzhě (Vessel Bearers) lifted the .
The Tàiguānlìng (Director of the Bureau of Imperial Food) poured the yùchàng (sacrificial wine).
When finished,
the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official) handed the zàn (libation cup) to the attendant,
held his hù (tablet),
went before the spirit tablets in the Shǐzǔshì (Chamber of the First Ancestor),
the music began,
stood facing north,
tucked his hù (tablet) in his belt,
and knelt.
The attendant handed the zàn (libation cup) to the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official).
The Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official) held the zàn (libation cup),
poured the chāng (sacrificial wine) on the ground for libation.
When finished,
he handed the zàn (libation cup) to the attendant,
held his hù (tablet),
bowed low,
rose,
went out of the door,
faced north,
bowed twice.
When finished,
the music stopped.
The ritual was performed for each chamber
as described above.
The Lǐzhíguān (Director of Rituals) led the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official) down to his position.
Before the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official) ascended to perform the libation,
the Zhùshǐ (Ritual Scribes) each presented the hair, blood, liver, and fat dòu (vessels),
and the Zhāiláng (Fasting Youth) presented the charcoal brazier, xiāohāo (southernwood and mugwort), and shǔjì (millet and panicled millet) fěi (baskets),
each waiting inside the food preparation curtain.
After the Chūxiànguān (First Presenting Official) completed the morning libation,
they entered in sequence through the Zhèngmén (Main Gate),
ascending from the Tàijiē (Grand Steps).
All the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) received the hair, blood, liver, and fat dòu (vessels) on the steps,
and all entered to place them before the spirit seats.
The charcoal brazier, xiāohāo (southernwood and mugwort) fěi (baskets) brought by the Zhāiláng (Fasting Youth)
were all placed to the left outside the room,
and they, along with the Zhùshǐ (Ritual Scribes), descended from the western steps and exited.
All the Zhūtài Zhù (Grand Sacrificial Priests) took the liver and fat,
washed them in the yùchàng (sacrificial wine),
and roasted them over the charcoal brazier.
When finished,
they returned to the zūn (vessel) area.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the officials set up eleven lamb tripods and eleven pig tripods for the spirits,
each to the right of a *huò* (cauldron).
After the first presenter ascended and performed the libation,
the *Guānglù Qīng* led the fasting attendants to the [proper place],
and with a spoon, lifted lamb from the *huò*,
filling one tripod.
The shoulder, foreleg, shank, buttock, flank, one main backbone, one transverse backbone, one long rib, one short rib, and one substitute rib [were included],
all with two bones side by side.
Next, pork was lifted like the lamb,
filling one tripod.
For each chamber, there was one lamb tripod and one pig tripod,
all set with lids.
The fasting attendants jointly lifted [the tripods],
entered the *huò* chamber,
and placed them in front of the food curtain.
〔一四〕The fasting attendants removed the lids,
placed them to the right of the tripods,
and removed the [inner vessels].
The *Guānglù Qīng* led the *Tàiguān Lìng*,
and with a spoon, lifted lamb,
placing it on one *zǔ* (sacrificial stand).
The shoulder, foreleg, and shank were at the upper end,
the buttock and flank at the lower end,
and the backbone and ribs in the middle.
Next, pork was lifted like the lamb,
each placed on one *zǔ*.
For each chamber, there was one lamb *zǔ* and one pig *zǔ*.
The fasting attendants immediately took the lids and lifted the tripods, first withdrawing them,
placing them before the spirits,
and when finished,
returned to the place of the food curtain.
The *Lǐzhígān* led the *Sītú* out to the front of the food curtain,
standing there to wait.
The *Guānglù Qīng* led his subordinates,
filling the *biān* (bamboo baskets) with powdered cakes,
filling the *dòu* (wooden platters) with minced food,
filling the *fǔ* (square wooden vessels) with millet,
and filling the *guǐ* (round wooden vessels) with panicled millet.
After the first presenter completed the libation,
and returned to his position,
the *Zhùshǐ* jointly advanced to remove the *dòu* containing hair and blood,
descending from the west steps to exit.
The *Lǐzhígān* led the *Sītú*,
commanding the officials who presented *biān*, *dòu*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ*, and the fasting attendants who carried the *zǔ*,
each carrying *biān*, *dòu*, *fǔ*, *guǐ*, and lamb and pig *zǔ* respectively.
They advanced in order for each chamber,
standing outside the south spirit gate to wait,
the lamb *zǔ* in front,
the pig *zǔ* next,
and the *biān*, *dòu*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* next after that.
Entering through the main gate,
the music began.
They ascended from the grand steps,
and all the *Tàizhù* welcomed and guided them on the steps,
where the music stopped.
Each was placed before a spirit's position,
and when finished,
the *Lǐzhígān* led the *Sītú* and those below him,
descending from the west steps,
the music began,
and they returned to their positions,
where the music stopped.
All the *Tàizhù* each took mugwort, artemisia, millet, and panicled millet, dipped them in fat,
and burned them on the charcoal brazier,
then returned to the place of the wine vessels.
The *Lǐzhígān* led the first presenter to the *léixǐ* (ablution basin) position,
the music began,
and upon reaching the position,
he stood facing north,
and the music stopped.
He inserted his *hù* (tablet) [into his belt],
washed his hands,
wiped his hands,
and held his *hù*.
He proceeded to the *juéxǐ* (cup washing) position,
stood facing north,
inserted his *hù*,
washed his *jué* (cup),
wiped his *jué*,
handed the *jué* to the attendant,
held his *hù*,
ascended the hall,
the music began,
and proceeded to the wine vessel dispensing place in the chamber of the First Ancestor,
standing facing west,
and the music stopped.
The attendant handed the *jué* to the first presenter.
The first presenter inserted his *hù* and held the *jué*,
the attendant lifted the [wine vessel lid],
and the *Tàiguān Lìng* poured the *fànqí* (filtered wine) from the *xīzūn* (sacrificial vessel decorated with a rhinoceros).
When finished,
he next proceeded to the wine vessel dispensing place in the Second Chamber,
following the above procedure.
He proceeded to the front of the spirit position of the First Ancestor,
the music began,
stood facing north,
inserted his *hù* and knelt,
the attendant handed the *jué* to the first presenter,
the first presenter held the *jué*,
made three libations of wine onto the bundle of cogon grass,
placed the *jué* down,
held his *hù*,
bowed low,
rose,
exited outside the chamber door,
stood facing north,
and the music stopped.
The herald led the *Tàizhù* to outside the chamber door,
facing east,
inserted his *hù*,
and knelt to read the prayer.
〔一五〕After reading,
he held his *hù*,
and rose.
Next, he proceeded to the Second Chamber.
Next, he proceeded to each chamber to perform the rites,
all according to the above procedure.
The first presenter descended the steps,
the music began,
returned to his position,
and the music stopped.
The *Lǐzhígān* next led the second presenter to the ablution position,
stood facing north,
inserted his *hù*,
washed his hands,
wiped his hands,
and held his *hù*.
He proceeded to the *juéxǐ* position,
stood facing north,
inserted his *hù*,
washed his *jué*,
wiped his *jué* and handed it to the attendant officer.
He held his *hù*,
ascended the hall,
proceeded to the wine vessel dispensing place of the First Ancestor,
stood facing west,
the attendant handed the *jué* to the second presenter.
The second presenter inserted his *hù*,
held the *jué*,
the wine vessel attendant lifted the [wine vessel lid],
and the *Tàiguān Lìng* poured the *lǐqí* (sweet wine) from the *xiàngzūn* (sacrificial vessel decorated with an elephant).
When finished,
he next proceeded to the wine vessel dispensing place in the Second Chamber,
following the above procedure.
He proceeded to the front of the spirit position of the First Ancestor,
the music began,
stood facing north,
inserted his *hù*,
knelt,
the attendant handed the *jué* to the second presenter.
The second presenter held the *jué*,
made three libations of wine onto the bundle of cogon grass,
placed the *jué* down,
held his *hù*,
bowed low,
rose,
exited outside the door,
bowed twice facing north,
and when finished,
the music stopped.
Next, he proceeded to each chamber to perform the rites,
all according to the above procedure.
He descended the steps,
the music began,
returned to his position,
and the music stopped.
The *Lǐzhígān* next led the final presenter to the ablution [position], and to ascend the hall to perform the rites,
all according to the procedure for the second presenter,
descending and returning to his position.
Next, the Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù) was led to remove the bamboo containers (biāndòu).
(Slightly shifting from their original position.)
Music started.
When the removal was complete,
music stopped.
All returned to their places.
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) said,
"Bestow the sacrificial meat (zuò)."
The Announcer (Zànzhě) relayed,
"Bestow the sacrificial meat,
bow twice."
Those in attendance all bowed twice.
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) led the Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù) and the Director of the Palace Quarters (Gōngwéilìng) to respectfully carry the spirit tablets (shénzhǔ).
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù) tucked his tablet (hù) into his belt,
placed the Imperial spirit tablet (dìzhǔ) into the casket (kuì),
and carried it into the spirit tablet chamber (shìshì).
He held his tablet (hù),
then retired to his position.
Next, the Director of the Palace Quarters (Gōngwéilìng) was led to place the Empress's spirit tablet (hòuzhǔ) into the casket (kuì),
〔一六〕and carried it into the spirit tablet chamber (shìshì).
All procedures were as above.
He retired to his position.
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) and the Announcer (Zànzhě) led the officiating officials (xíngshì guān) and attending officials (zhíshì guān) to their respective places.
The Ritual Attendant (Fènglǐ) said,
"Bow twice."
The Announcer (Zànzhě) relayed,
and all officials in attendance bowed twice.
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) and the Announcer (Zànzhě) led the officials (bǎiguān) out in sequence.
The Director of Grand Music (Dàyuèlìng) led his artisans out in sequence.
The Director of the Imperial Kitchen (Tàiguānlìng) led his subordinates
to remove the ritual food offerings.
Next, the Supervising Censor for Sacrifices (Jiānjì Yùshǐ) was led to the hall to monitor the complete removal.
Upon completion,
they returned to the purification chamber (zhāisuǒ).
The Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiàolìng) closed the doors and descended.
The Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng) stored the sacrificial prayers (zhùbǎn) in the casket (kuì).
〔一七〕The Minister of Banquets (Guānglù) respectfully presented the sacrificial meat (zuò).
The Supervising Censor for Sacrifices (Jiānjì Yùshǐ) took his position to inspect it.
The Minister of Banquets (Guānglùqīng) bowed twice towards the palace gate (wàngquè),
then retired.
For the Seven Sacrifices (Qīshì),
the summer Stove (Xiàzào) and Central Dwelling (Zhōngliú),
the autumn Gate (Qiūmén) and Road (Lì),
and the winter Path (Dōngxíng),
the sacrificial vessels were arranged,
and wine and food offerings were placed inside.
Awaiting the final offering (zhōngxiàn), which was about to be presented,
the offering official performed the rites,
and read the prayer text.
Each year, in the first month of the four seasons (sìmèngyuè), and during the Lā festival (là), there were five offerings.
〔一八〕All followed the above procedures.
Collation Notes (Jiàokānjì)

Treatise 12, Rites 4: Ceremonies of Reporting and Announcing (Zòugào Yí); Ceremony for the Emperor's Respectful Thanks (Huángdì Gōngxiè Yí); Ceremony for the Empress's Respectful Thanks (Huánghòu Gōngxiè Yí); Ceremony for the Crown Prince's Respectful Thanks (Huángtàizǐ Gōngxiè Yí); Presenting New Harvests (Jiànxīn); Meritorious Officials Enjoying Concurrent Sacrifices (Gōngchén Pèixiǎng); Displaying Treasures and Jades (Chénshè Bǎoyù); Miscellaneous Ceremonies (Záyí)
Ceremonies of Reporting and Announcing (Zòugào Yí).

When the Emperor ascended the throne, reached adulthood (jiāyuánfú), received an honorary title (shòuzūnhào), took an empress, conferred titles by imperial mandate (cèméng), made inspection tours (xúnshòu), embarked on military campaigns (zhēngfá), performed sacrifices to heaven and earth (fēngsì), requested a posthumous title (qǐngshì), or constructed and repaired ancestral temples (yíngxiū miàonèi),
whenever there were major national events, they were announced.
Sometimes to one chamber,
sometimes to all, including the original temple (yuánmiào).
All followed the one-offering rite (yīxiànlǐ),
using prayers (zhù) and silk (bì).
After the Huángtǒng era,

whenever the Emperor received an honorary title (shòuzūnhào), enfeoffed the Empress and Crown Prince (cèhuánghòu Tàizǐ), performed the Dì and Xiá sacrifices (dìxiá), was enshrined in the ancestral temple (shēngfù), had spirit tablets peacefully installed (fèng'ān), or moved (fèngqiān), etc., all such matters were announced.
For suburban sacrifices (jiāosì), the chamber for the co-sacrificed deity (pèidì zhīshì) was announced.
On the 17th day of the 3rd month of Dàdìng 14 (1174),
an edict was issued to change the Emperor's personal name.
Grand Councilor of the Left (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng) Liángbì was ordered to announce to Heaven and Earth (tiāndì).
Píngzhāng Shǒudào was ordered to announce to the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào).
Grand Councilor of the Left (Zuǒ Chéng) Shí Jū was ordered to announce to Empress Zhāodé's Temple (Zhāodé Huánghòu Miào).
Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) Zhāng Jǐngrén was ordered to announce to the Altars of Soil and Grain (Shèjì).
Officials were also dispatched to offer sacrifices and announcements to the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè).
Two days prior,
the Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiàolìng) cleaned the inside and outside of the temple.
The posts for the announcing officials and their subordinates (gàoguān yǐxià cìsuǒ) were arranged.
The day before,
the officiating officials (xíngshì guān) went to the place of sacrifice (sìsuǒ) for purification and fasting (qīngzhāi).
Three *kè* (1 *kè* = 15 minutes) before the announcing day,
the Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) led the Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiàolìng) and his subordinates
into the hall to open the chamber doors,
clean and spread the mats,
and set up small tables (jǐ) below the northern wall (běiyǒngxià),
following the seasonal offering ceremony (shíxiángyí).
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) led the sacrificing officials (sìjì guān) to arrange the baskets of silk (bìfěi) to the left of the chamber doors
and the sacrificial prayers (zhùbǎn) on the table to the right of the chamber doors.
And the incense table and sacrificial vessels were set up,
all covered with mats.
For each position, to the left was a bamboo container (biān) filled with dried venison (lùfǔ),
and to the right was a wooden container (dòu) filled with deer meat paste (lùní).
One ritual wine vessel (xīzūn)
was placed on a stand (diàn),
with a ladle (sháo) and cup (chā),
to the left of the chamber doors in the hall,
facing north,
filled with wine,
one bottle for each position.
Candles were placed in front of the spirit tablets (shénwèi).
Also, a washing basin (guànjué xǐwèi) was set up slightly east of the south side of the transversal street (héngjiē).
The announcing official's mat (gàoguān rùwèi) was set up
to the south of the east steps of the hall,
facing west.
Other officials were behind him, slightly to the south.
A viewing platform for the sacrificial fire (wàngliáowèi) was also set up to the north outside the West Divine Gate (Xī Shénmén).
Before dawn on the announcing day,
the Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) led the Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiàolìng), the Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù), and the Director of the Palace Quarters (Gōngwéilìng) inside,
where they stood facing north, with the ranking superior to the west, between the steps.
The Ritual Attendant (Fènglǐ) announced,
"Bow twice."
After this,
they ascended from the west steps.
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù) and the Director of the Palace Quarters (Gōngwéilìng) each entered their respective chambers,
brought out the spirit tablets (shénzhǔ), and placed them on the seats,
as per usual practice.
Next, the announcing official (gàoguān) was led in
to his position.
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) moved slightly forward
and announced,
"The officials have reverently prepared;
please proceed with the ceremony."
He then announced,
"Bow twice."
Those in attendance bowed.
After this,
the Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) led the announcing official (gàoguān) to the washing basin (guànxǐwèi),
where he washed his hands.
After this,
he proceeded to stand before the spirit tablet (shénwèi),
tucked his tablet (hù) into his belt,
knelt,
and offered incense three times.
The attending official (zhíshìzhě) handed the silk (bì) to the Ritual Attendant (Fènglǐláng),
who, facing west, handed it to the announcing official (gàoguān).
The announcing official (gàoguān) received the silk,
placed it,
held his tablet (hù),
bowed low (fǔfú),
rose,
retired to his position outside the chamber door,
and bowed twice.
He proceeded to the next position to perform the rites as above.
After this,
he descended and returned to his position.
After a short while,
the announcing official (gàoguān) was led again to the washing basin (juéxǐwèi),
followed by the official who reads the prayer (dúzhùguān) and the official who raises the prayer (jǔzhùguān).
Upon reaching the position,
he stood facing north,
tucked his tablet (hù) into his belt,
washed and wiped the cup (jué).
After this,
he handed it to the attending official (zhíshìzhě).
Holding his tablet (hù), he ascended
to the place of the wine vessel (jiǔzūnsuǒ),
stood facing west,
held the cup (jué).
The official holding the wine vessel (zhízūnzhě) lifted it to pour wine.
The announcing official (gàoguān) handed it to the attending official (zhíshìzhě).
He proceeded to stand before the spirit tablet (shénwèi),
facing north,
tucked his tablet (hù) into his belt,
knelt,
offered wine three times with the cup (jué),
held his tablet (hù),
bowed low (fǔfú),
rose,
retired to his position outside the chamber door,
stood facing north and waited.
The prayer text (zhùwén) was read.
After this,
he bowed twice.
He proceeded to the next position to perform the rites as above.
After this,
he and the official who reads the prayer (dúzhùguān) both returned to their positions.
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) announced,
"Bow twice."
Those in attendance all bowed twice.
Next, the announcing official (gàoguān) and his subordinates were led to the viewing platform for the sacrificial fire (wàngliáowèi).
The attending officials (zhíshìzhě) placed the silk (bìbó) and prayer tablets (zhùbǎn) on the bonfire (liáo).
The Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) said,
"It may be burned."
Halfway through the burning,
the Officer of Rites (Lǐzhíguān) announced,
"The rites are concluded."
The announcing official (gàoguān) and his subordinates retired.
The Director of the Office (Shǔlìng) closed the temple gate
and buried the prayer (zhù) in a pit (kǎn).
In the first month of Zhēnyuán 4 (1156),
an honorary title (zūnhào) was conferred.
Three days prior,
envoys were dispatched to announce to Heaven and Earth (tiāndì).
A mat was set up on the Altar to Heaven (Bàitiāntái) in the Chángwǔ Hall (Chángwǔ Diàn).
The August Emperor of Heaven (Hàotiān Shàngdì) was in the center,
and the Imperial Earth Deity (Huángdìqí) was slightly to the west and behind.
The one-offering rite (yīxiànlǐ) was performed.
On the 13th day of the 1st month of Dàdìng 7 (1167),
an honorary title (zūnhào) was conferred.
Three days prior,
an imperial prince was commanded to preside over the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, Xǔwáng, who was the Grand Administrator of Dàxīng.
An imperial prince was commanded to preside over the sacrifice to the Imperial Ancestral Temple, Yīngwáng, of the Imperial Clan Court.
At the customary place for worshipping Heaven, a seat for Hào Tiān Shàngdì was set up,
facing south in the center.
