The seat for Huáng Dì Qí was slightly to the west of it.
Both used cushions for seating, spirit tablets, and offerings of incense, wine, dried meat, and pickles.
There were three prayer tablets.
The Hanlin Academy composed the sacrificial prayers.
After they were written,
they were presented for the emperor's signature.
After this,
they were handed over to the Ministry of Rites.
A document was transferred to the Xuān Huī Yuàn,
and a Kòng Hè official was dispatched to carry them on a stretcher,
covered with a yellow silk scarf,
to the place of sacrifice, accompanied by the designated official for the announcement.
One day prior,
the officials making the announcement observed a fast for one day at their respective bureaus.
On the day of the announcement, at dawn,
the Xuān Huī Yuàn and the Tàicháng Sì laid out the offerings as per ritual.
One attendant from the Hégmén Shèrén and one academician from the Tàicháng Bóshì led the announcing officials, each in their respective attire,
to take their places in order.
The Lǐ Zhíguān and the attendant stepped slightly forward,
announcing,
"The officials are respectfully ready;
please proceed."
The announcer said,
"Bow,"
and all present bowed twice.
The Lǐ Zhíguān first led the attending officials to their respective positions.
The attendant and academician then led the announcing officials to the positions for hand-washing and cup-washing,
standing facing north,
inserting their tablets into their belts,
washing their hands,
drying their hands,
washing the cups,
and wiping the cups.
Holding their tablets,
they proceeded to the wine vessels,
inserted their tablets,
held the cups,
and the official in charge of the vessels poured the wine.
The announcing officials handed the cups to the officials bearing the sacrificial wine,
held their tablets, and proceeded to the spirit tablets of Hào Tiān Shàngdì and Huáng Dì Qí, bowing twice.
For each deity, three sticks of incense were offered,
and wine was poured kneeling.
After this,
they handed the cups to the officials bearing the cups,
held their tablets,
bowed low,
and rose.
The official presenting the prayer tablets knelt and presented them.
After reading,
they bowed low
and rose.
The announcing officials bowed twice.
The announcement was completed.
The announcing officials and those below were led to descend and return to their positions,
bowing twice.
After this,
they proceeded to the viewing-fire position,
burned the prayer tablets,
and bowed twice.
When half of the tablets were burned,
the announcing officials and those below all withdrew.
Ritual for the Emperor's Respectful Thanksgiving.
In the first month of the seventh year of Dàdìng,
Shìzōng received the honorable title,
and after the rites, he performed the respectful thanksgiving.
Three days prior,
the director of the Tàimiào, leading his subordinates,
swept and cleaned the inside and outside of the temple courtyard and arranged the furnishings.
The Shàngshè set up eleven dining tents
to the west of the temple's southern gate.
The Diànzhōng Jiān, leading the Shàngshè, inspected the main hall (Dàcì Diàn).
A tablet position for the emperor was also set up in front of the ancestral spirit tablets, facing north.
A position for receiving blessings (Yǐn Fú Wèi) was also set up slightly to the southwest of the emperor's tablet position.
Cushions for kneeling and bowing were also set up in front of the spirit seats, corresponding to each room.
The Dàyuèlìng arranged the Dēnggē on the hall,
and the Gōngxuán below the hall.
A position for the imperial crown prince was also set up to the southeast of the eastern steps (Zuòjiē).
Positions for the imperial princes were set up slightly to the east of their southern side.
Positions for imperial clan kings, envoys, and chancellors were set up behind them.
Positions for officiating officials, such as Tàiwèi and Sītú, were set up to the west of the western steps of the hall,
facing east,
with different positions for each rank.
Positions for civil and military officials were also set up to the south of the transverse steps,
facing east and west.
A position for the imperial washing was set up to the east of the eastern steps,
and a position for the Tàiwèi's washing was set up below the western steps, to the south of the transverse steps.
Positions for the Zhāiláng were also set up behind the civil officials of the eastern ranks.
Positions for officials in charge of washing, as well as Fèng Lǐ, Zànzhě, Dà Sīyuè, Xiélǜ Láng, and Dàyuèlìng, were also set up,
each according to the rites of the general seasonal sacrifice (Xiáhxiǎng Zhī Yí).
Wine vessels (Zūn Yí) and sacrificial implements were also set up above and below the hall,
according to the rites of the seasonal sacrifice (Shíxiǎng Zhī Yí).
One day prior,
the Lǐguān and Yùshǐ, leading their subordinates,
inspected the sacrificial animals
and supervised the washing,
as per customary ritual.
On that day, at dawn,
the Lǐguān and Yùshǐ, leading the Tàimiào officials, Tàizhù officials, and Gōngwéi Lìng, brought out the spirit tablets,
as per the seasonal sacrifice ritual.
The officials concerned arranged two thousand yellow imperial guards outside the Yìngtiān Mén.
The Shàngniǎn presented the golden imperial carriage (Jīn Lù) inside the Yìngtiān Mén.
At three quarters past noon,
the Xuān Huī Yuàn requested the emperor to proceed to the hall for fasting and overnight vigil.
All civil and military officials also fasted and stayed overnight at their respective offices.
On the day of thanksgiving, at dawn,
they awaited the various guards to lead their respective units to guard the gates and arrange their formations.
The officials guiding the imperial carriage stood on the left and right below the steps of the hall,
all in court attire.
A Tōngshì Shèrén led the Shìzhōng to the fasting hall,
who bowed low,
knelt and stated,
"Your subject so-and-so reports:
Please prepare for the middle stage of the ceremony."
Then bowed low
and rose.
All requests made by the Shìzhōng
were in accordance with this.
The emperor wore the Tōngtiān Guān and the Jiàngshā Páo.
A short while later,
the Shìzhōng reported,
"Everything outside is ready."
The emperor exited the fasting hall,
immediately took his seat,
and after all officials paid their respects,
the Shìzhōng reported,
"Please ascend the imperial palanquin (Niǎn)."
The emperor ascended the palanquin and departed,
with imperial guards maintaining the customary warnings and clearings.
The officials guiding the imperial carriage led the way.
Upon reaching the Yìngtiān Mén,
the Shìzhōng reported,
"Please descend from the palanquin and ascend the imperial chariot (Lù)."
The emperor ascended the imperial chariot.
The Ménxià Shìláng bowed low,
knelt and reported,
"Please proceed with the imperial chariot."
Then bowed low
and rose.
All requests made by the Ménxià Shìláng
were in accordance with this.
The imperial chariot began to move,
with warnings and clearings as per customary ritual.
Upon reaching outside the Yìngtiān Mén,
the Ménxià Shìláng reported,
"Please halt the imperial chariot for a moment,
and command the attendant officials to mount their horses."
The Shìzhōng stepped forward to receive the command,
then withdrew and announced,
"The imperial decree is permissible."
The Ménxià Shìláng withdrew,
relaying the command,
"Attendant officials mount their horses."
The Tōngshì Shèrén received and relayed the command,
"By imperial decree, attendant officials mount their horses."
The officials guiding the imperial carriage led the way on the left and right.
The Ménxià Shìláng reported,
"Please proceed with the imperial chariot."
As the imperial chariot moved,
the announcement
"Clear the way!" was made,
but no drums or wind instruments were played.
The Diǎnzàn Yí led the imperial crown prince, in ordinary attire on horseback, to the temporary quarters within the temple,
where he changed into a Yuǎnyóu Guān and Zhūmíng Yī,
holding a Guī tablet.
The Tōngshì Shèrén and civil and military officials (all in court attire)
lined up outside the temple gate to welcome him.
When the imperial chariot reached the temple gate,
the Shìzhōng reported in front of the chariot,
"Please descend from the imperial chariot."
The officials guiding the imperial carriage walked a little to the east inside the temple gate.
The Shìzhōng reported,
"Please ascend the imperial palanquin."
The emperor ascended the palanquin,
with umbrellas, fans, and guards as per customary ritual.
Upon reaching the Dàcì,
the Shìzhōng reported,
"Please descend from the palanquin,
and enter the Dàcì."
The emperor entered the Dàcì.
The Tōngshì Shèrén 分引 (Assistant Manager of Diplomatic Affairs) led the civil and military officials through the east and west side gates of the southern shrine into the temple courtyard,
standing facing each other in the east and west.
The Lǐzhíguān (Ceremonial Official) led the Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) and other officiating officials to the cross street, facing north,
where they bowed twice.
After this,
the Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi to the hand-washing position,
inserted his hù (tablet) into his belt,
washed his hands,
wiped his hands,
held his hù,
and proceeded to the ritual goblet washing position.
He stood facing north,
inserted his hù,
washed the zàn (libation ladle),
wiped the zàn,
handed the zàn to the attendant,
held his hù,
ascended the hall via the western steps,
and proceeded to the Sǐzǔ Zūnyí (Ancestral Vessel) location,
standing facing west.
The attendant presented the zàn to the Tàiwèi.
The Tàiwèi inserted his hù,
held the zàn, poured the chàng (aromatic wine),
proceeded to the spirit tablet,
poured the chàng as a libation onto the ground.
After this,
he handed the empty zàn to the attendant,
held his hù,
bowed low,
rose,
exited the hall, faced north,
and bowed twice.
After this.
Next, he proceeded to the Suíshì (adjoining rooms), performing all ceremonies as above.
When the ceremonies were completed,
he descended from the western steps
and returned to his position.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Sītú (Minister of Education) out to the food preparation area,

and led the Jiànzǔ Zhāiláng (Officials Presenting Sacrificial Meat) to present the sacrificial meat, and the Jiàn Biāndòu Fǔguǐguān (Officials Presenting Baskets, Dishes, Square and Round Vessels) to present the biāndòu (baskets and dishes) and fǔguǐ (square and round vessels),
along with the Tàiguānlìng (Director of the Imperial Kitchen).
They entered in order through the main gate.
The Gōngxuán Yuè (Palace Music) began to play,
and continued until they reached the great steps,
where the music stopped.
All the Tàizhù (Grand Prayer Officials) welcomed them at the top of the steps,
each setting up before the spirit seats.
First, a sacrificial ox was presented,
then a sacrificial sheep,
then a sacrificial pig.
After this,
the Lǐzhíguān led the Sītú who had already descended the steps back to his position.
The Diǎnzànyí (Master of Ceremonies) led the Huángtàizǐ (Crown Prince), and the Tōngshì Shèrén led the Qīnwáng (Princes of the Blood),
entering through the east side gate of the southern shrine,
and proceeding to their kneeling mats.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat) and the Jǔcèguān (Officials Presenting Tablets) to ascend from the western steps,
and stand before the Sǐzǔ Shì (Chamber of the First Ancestor),
facing east and west.
The Tōngshì Shèrén led the Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) to the front of the Dàcì (Grand Antechamber),
and announced,
“Please prepare for the central ceremony.”
The Huángdì (Emperor) donned his gǔnmiǎn (ceremonial robe and crown).
A short while later,
the Shìzhōng announced,
“The outer preparations are complete.”
The Shìzhōng proceeded to his original position in the temple courtyard.
As the Huángdì was about to exit the Dàcì,
the Lǐyíshǐ (Master of Ceremonies) and the Tàichángqīng (Grand Master of Ceremonies) guided him.
Whenever the Lǐyíshǐ and the Tàichángqīng guided,
and the Bóshì (Erudites) led the way,
they bowed low,
knelt, and said,
“Your servant [name] guides the Huángdì in performing the rites.”
They bowed low,
and rose.
They led the way to the Dōngshénmén (Eastern Spirit Gate),
where the umbrellas and fans were removed,
and close attendants followed in.
The Diànzhōngjiān (Palace Usher) knelt and presented the Zhènguī (Jade Tablet of State),
and the Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please take the guī.”
The Huángdì took the guī,
and the Gōngxuán Yuè began to play.
The announcement was made,
“Please proceed to the Léixǐ Wèi (Ablution Position).”
Upon reaching the position,
the music stopped.
A Nèishì (Eunuch) knelt and took an yí (ewer),
rose,
and poured water.
Another Nèishì knelt and took a pán (basin),
to catch the water.
If it was cold,
warm water was prepared in advance.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please insert the Zhènguī.”
The Huángdì inserted the Zhènguī,
and washed his hands.
A Nèishì knelt and took a jīn (towel) from a fěi (basket),
rose,
and presented it.
The Huángdì wiped his hands.
After this,
the Fèngjuéguān (Official Presenting Goblets) knelt and presented a jué (goblet).
The Huángdì received the jué.
A Nèishì held the yí and poured water,
and another Nèishì knelt and held the pán to catch the water.
The Huángdì washed the jué.
After this,
a Nèishì knelt and presented a jīn.
The Huángdì wiped the jué.
After this,
the Nèishì placed the pán and yí,
and also placed the jīn in the fěi.
The Fèngjuéguān received the jué.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please take the Zhènguī.”
They led the Huángdì to ascend the hall,
and the attendants to the left and right ascended in proportion to their number.
The Gōngxuán Yuè began to play.
When the Huángdì reached the bottom of the zuòjiē (eastern steps),
the music stopped.
The Huángdì ascended from the zuòjiē.
The Dēnggē Yuè (Ascending Song Music) began to play.
The Lǐyíshǐ led the way.
When the Huángdì reached the bǎnwèi (mat position),
the music stopped,
and the announcement was made,
“Please bow twice.”
The Fènglǐláng (Ceremonial Official) announced,
“The Huángtàizǐ and all officials in their places shall bow twice.”
The announcer conveyed the instruction,
and all bowed twice.
The Lǐyíshǐ led the way.
The Huángdì proceeded to the Sǐzǔ Zūnyí (Ancestral Vessel) location.
The music began to play,
and upon reaching the Zūn (Vessel) location,
the music stopped.
The Fèngjuéguān brought the jué to the Zūn.
The Zhí Zūn Zhě (Vessel Bearer) raised it.
The Shìzhōng knelt and poured the Fànqí (Clear Wine) from the Xīzūn (Sacrificial Vessel in the shape of a rhinoceros).
After this,
the Lǐyíshǐ led the Huángdì to the bǎnwèi,
where he bowed twice.
After this,
the Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please proceed to the kneeling mat before the Sǐzǔ Shénwèi (Spirit Tablet of the First Ancestor).”
The Dēnggē Yuè began to play.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please insert the guī.”
He knelt.
The Fèngjuéguān handed the jué to the Fèngjué Jiǔguān (Official Presenting Sacrificial Wine) to present it.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please take the jué.”
The Huángdì took the jué,
offered wine three times.
After this,
he handed the empty jué to the Fèngjué Jiǔguān.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please take the guī.”
He rose.
The music stopped.
The Fèngjué Jiǔguān handed the jué to the Fèngjuéguān.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
“Please proceed to the Suíshì.”
All ceremonies were performed as above.
The ritual officials first led the Sītú 司徒 to ascend from the western steps,
and stand beside the drinking-of-blessings position.
When the libation and offering were about to be completed,
the blessed meat was presented,
and the blessed wine was poured.
The Tàizhù 太祝 followed the Sītú and stood beside him.
When the libation and offering were completed,
the Shìzhōng 侍中 also stood beside him.
The Lǐyíshǐ 禮儀使 announced,
"Please invite the Emperor to his designated position."
He stood facing north.
The Dengge 登歌 music began.
When he reached the position, the music stopped.
The Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎 knelt and read the imperial edict.
When finished,
the official holding the edict laid it down.
When finished,
the Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please invite the Emperor to bow twice."
When the bows were completed,
the Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please proceed to the drinking-of-blessings position."
The Dengge music began.
Upon reaching the position,
the Tàizhù poured blessed wine into the goblet.
If it was cold, warm wine was prepared in advance,
and presented to the Shìzhōng.
The Shìzhōng received the goblet and stood holding it.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please tuck in the guī 圭 (jade tablet)."
He knelt.
The Shìzhōng, holding the goblet, knelt facing north and presented it.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please take the goblet."
Three libations were offered.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please drink the blessing."
When the drinking of the blessing was completed,
the empty goblet was handed to the Shìzhōng.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please receive the blessed meat."
The Sītú knelt and presented a biān 籩 (bamboo vessel) with millet and rice.
The Emperor received it and handed it to his attendants.
The Sītú again knelt and presented the blessed meat.
The Emperor received it and handed it to his attendants.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please hold the guī."
He rose.
When the two bows were completed,
the music stopped.
The Lǐyíshǐ led the way,
and the Emperor returned to his designated position.
The Dengge music began.
When he reached the position, the music stopped.
The Tàizhùs advanced to remove the biān and dòu 豆 (wooden vessels) respectively.
The Dengge music began.
When the removal was complete,
the music stopped.
The Fènglǐ 奉禮 said,
"Bestow the blessed meat."
The attendant announced,
"The Crown Prince and all officials in attendance below him shall bow twice."
The announcer relayed the command,
and all bowed twice.
The Gōngxuán 宮縣 (orchestra) played.
It stopped after one movement.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please invite the Emperor to bow twice."
The Fènglǐ Láng 奉禮郎 announced,
"The Crown Prince and all officials in attendance below him shall bow twice."
When the bows were completed,
the Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"The ceremony is complete."
He led the Emperor to descend the zuòjiē 阼階 (eastern steps).
The Dengge music began.
When he reached the foot of the steps, the music stopped.
The Gōngxuán played.
He led the Emperor out of the Dōngshénmén 東神門 (East Spirit Gate).
The music stopped.
The parasols, fans, and guards were as usual.
The Lǐyíshǐ announced,
"Please release the guī."
The Diànzhōng Jiān 殿中監 knelt to receive the zhènguī 鎮圭 (jade tablet).
Upon reaching the Dàcì 大次 (Emperor's temporary residence),
the guards turned and escorted him on the return journey,
as they did on the way in.
The Lǐguān Yùshǐ 禮官御史, leading their subordinates,
placed the spirit tablets and stored the imperial edict as usual.
A moment later,
the Tōngshì Shèrén 通事舍人 led the Shìzhōng to announce,
"Please prepare for the intermediate escort."
The Emperor wore the Tōngtiān Guān 通天冠 (Heaven-Connecting Crown) and a jiàngshāpáo 絳紗袍 (crimson gauze robe).
A moment later,
the Shìzhōng announced,
"The outer preparations are complete."
Waiting for the Shàngniǎn 尚輦 to advance the sedan chair,
the Shìzhōng announced,
"Please descend from the seat and ascend the sedan chair."
The Emperor ascended the sedan chair.
The parasols, fans, and guards were as usual.
Upon reaching slightly east of the Nánshénmén 南神門 (South Spirit Gate),
the Shìzhōng announced,
"Please descend from the sedan chair and walk out of the temple gate."
The Emperor walked out of the temple gate.
Upon reaching the imperial carriage (lù 輅),
the Shìzhōng announced,
"Please ascend the lù."
The Emperor ascended the lù.
The Ménxià Shìláng 門下侍郎 announced,
"Please ask the imperial carriage to pause briefly.
Order the attendant officials to mount their horses."
The Shìzhōng advanced to receive the decree,
retreated, and said,
"The decree is approved."
The Ménxià Shìláng retreated
and transmitted the decree, saying,
"Attendant officials mount horses."
The Tōngshì Shèrén relayed the command,
"Order the attendant officials to mount horses."
The imperial carriage returned to the palace.
The drum and wind instruments played vibrantly.
Outside the Yìngtiānmén 應天門,
all officials lined up to welcome and greet him.
The Gōngxuán played the tune "Cǎicí" 采茨.
Entering inside the Yìngtiānmén,
the Shìzhōng announced,
"Please descend from the lù and take the sedan chair."
The Emperor descended from the lù and entered by sedan chair.
The parasols, fans, guards, and warning cries were as usual.
The Emperor entered the palace.
Upon reaching the Zhìzhāidiàn 致齋殿 (Hall of Fasting),
the Shìzhōng announced,
"The restrictions are lifted."
The Tōngshì Shèrén received the order,
"Order all officials to return to their posts,
and all generals and soldiers to return to their stations."
Empress's Ritual of Respectful Gratitude.
After the Empress had received the imperial edict,
on the day before,
she fasted and purified herself in a separate hall.
All inner court ladies who were to accompany her into the temple also fasted and purified themselves for one day.
On that day, two kě 刻 (clepsydra marks) before dawn,
the officials in charge arranged the ceremonial guards to the left and right of the Empress's carriage,
in proper order.
The outer court ladies first entered through the rear gate of the Tàimiào 太廟 (Grand Ancestral Temple).
The inner court ladies, concubines, and those below them all proceeded to the palace courtyard.
After the greetings,
the Xuānhuīshǐ 宣徽使 announced on a tablet,
"Intermediate preparations are complete."
A moment later,
he again announced,
"Outer preparations are complete."
Adorned with her ceremonial headdress and robes,
she rode in a shoulder sedan,
taking a convenient path to where her carriage was.
The court attendant announced,
"Please descend from the sedan and ascend the carriage."
After ascending the carriage,
he announced,
"Please set off."
The carriage exited the Yuándé Dōngpiānmén 元德東偏門 (Yuande East Side Gate).
The inner court ladies, concubines, and those below them all mounted their carriages outside the palace gate,
exited through the Zuǒyèmén 左掖門 (Left Flank Gate),
and followed until outside the Tàimiào gate.
The ceremonial guards stopped outside the gate,
and the carriages turned to face south.
The court attendant announced,
"Please descend from the carriage and ascend the sedan."
The Empress descended from the carriage and ascended the sedan.
She proceeded to the tent outside the Dōngshénmén,
and the curtain was lowered.
The inner court ladies, concubines, and those below them all descended from their carriages
and entered to take their places in the accompanying ranks.
The court attendant led the outer court ladies to the front of the tent.
After the greetings,
they all proceeded to the palace courtyard to take their places in the accompanying ranks.
A short while later,
the Xuānhuīshǐ went to the royal tent,
and announced,
"Perform the court audience ritual."
The curtains were rolled up,
and the Xuānhuīshǐ led the way
to the mat in front of the palace steps, facing west, and stood.
The Xuānhuīshǐ announced,
"Perform two bows,"
and all the inside and outside noblewomen performed two bows.
The Xuānhuīshǐ led the way,
ascended the eastern steps,
and went to the mat in front of the incense table for the spirit tablet of the Shǐzǔ Huángdì.
The Xuānhuīshǐ announced,
"Please offer incense three times,"
and then announced again,
"Perform two bows."
The bows were completed.
The Xuānhuīshǐ led the way,
then proceeded to the ten ancestral chambers from Xiànzǔ downwards,
all in accordance with the ceremony described above.
The Xuānhuīshǐ announced,
"The ritual is complete,"
and guided them back to the royal tent.
The Xuānhuīshǐ announced,
"Please lift the restrictions."
The inside and outside noblewomen returned to their respective tents.
A short while later,
the imperial guard returned to the interior as they had arrived,
and the outside noblewomen withdrew.
An attendant announced,
"Please mount the imperial sedan-chair,"
and they went out to the carriages.
It was announced,
"Please ascend the carriage."
After ascending the carriage,
it was announced,
"Please set off."
The inside noblewomen boarded their carriages.
Upon reaching the eastern side gate of Yuándé,
an attendant announced,
"Please alight from the carriage and mount the sedan-chair."
The Empress then rode in the sedan-chair,
taking a convenient route back inside,
with the inside noblewomen following.
After the enfeoffment ceremony,
all officials submitted memorials to offer congratulations,
and also sent congratulatory letters to the Zhōnggōng.
Ritual for the Huáng Tàizǐ to respectfully offer thanks.
On that day, at dawn,
the officials attending the Dōnggōng each wore their court robes.
The responsible department arranged the ceremonial guard and the golden carriage outside the Zuǒyèmén.
The Huáng Tàizǐ wore a Yuǎnyóuguān and Zhūmíngyī,
and departed in a sedan-chair.
Upon reaching the golden carriage,
he alighted from the sedan-chair and ascended the carriage.
The Zuǒshùzǐ and those below him attended on either side.
The Sānshī and Sānshào rode on horseback, escorting,
and the other officials also rode on horseback, following.
They proceeded eastward,
turning from the western steps of the Tàimiào to the temple,
without sounding gongs or flutes.
Upon reaching outside the western side gate of the temple, he alighted from the carriage and proceeded on foot,
entering the royal tent through the eastern side gate,
where he changed into a Gǔnmiǎn.
Exiting the tent,
holding a guī tablet, he entered through the eastern side gate of the Nánshén,
with palace officials and officials from the Tàichángsì all following.
The Huáng Tàizǐ entered and went to the east of the eastern steps in the palace courtyard,
standing facing west.
The Diǎnyí announced,
"Perform two bows."
After completion,
he ascended from the western steps,
and proceeded to stand facing north in front of the Shǐzǔ's spirit tablet,
performing two bows.
After completion,
he proceeded in order to each chamber to perform the rituals,
all in accordance with the ceremony described above.
After completion,
he descended from the western steps,
and returned to the westward-facing position to wait.
The Diǎnyí declared,
"The ritual is complete."
He exited through the northern side gate of the Dōngshén,
and visited the separate temples according to the ceremony described above.
After completion,
he returned to the royal tent,
and changed back into the Yuǎnyóuguān and Zhūmíngyī.
Exiting the tent,
he only ascended the carriage outside the temple gate.
After passing the temple gate, gongs were sounded as they proceeded.
Upon reaching outside the Zuǒyèmén, he alighted from the carriage,
and entered in a sedan-chair.
The generals and soldiers each returned to their respective posts.
On the following day, he received congratulations from all officials in the Dōnggōng,
following the ritual for receiving congratulations on Yuánzhèng.
Offering of new produce.
In Tiāndé二年,
the officials concerned were ordered to deliberate on the ritual for offering new produce.
It was decided that seasonal items should be used according to traditional rites,
and the Tàichángqīng was to perform the ritual.
In the first month,
sturgeon.
During the Míngchāng era, beef and fish were used;
if unavailable, carp could be substituted.
In the second month,
wild geese.
In the third month,
chives,
with eggs and turnips.
In the fourth month,
ice was offered.
In the fifth month,
bamboo shoots and calamus,
served with cherries.
In the sixth month,
pork,
and hulled wheat.
In the seventh month,
young chickens were tasted with millet,
served with melons.
In the eighth month,
served with foxnuts, water chestnuts, and chestnuts.
In the ninth month,
millet and broomcorn millet were tasted,
served with dates and pears.
In the tenth month,
hemp and rice were tasted,
served with rabbits.
In the eleventh month,
served with roe deer.
In the twelfth month,
served with fish.
This was followed.
In Dàdìng三年,
the officials concerned stated,
"Every year, there are five major sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
If new produce is also offered,
it seems overly frequent.
We propose that during the months of the seasonal sacrifices,
the new produce be attached to the biāndòu and offered,
in accordance with the ancient principle that 'sacrifices should not be frequent'."
The decree was approved.
(Niúyú resembles sturgeon in appearance,
and is a type of sturgeon.)
Meritorious officials enshrined with ancestors.
On the Bǐngyín day of the intercalary tenth month of Míngchāng五年,
Yítóng Sānsī Dàiguó Gōng Huándū, Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū Yěhē, Tèjìn Hégě, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Pénnà, and Yítóng Sānsī Bádá,
were enshrined in the temple courtyard of Shìzǔ.
In the second month of Tiāndé二年,
during the comprehensive sacrifice at the Tàimiào,
the officials concerned proposed the meritorious officials to be enshrined.
An imperial edict specified that Sāgǎi, Cíbúshī, Xiáyěgǎo, Wòlǔ, and Āsīkuí Zhōng, facing east,
be enshrined with Tàizǔ.
And Niángē Zōnghàn, Wòlǐbù Zōngwàng, Shēnmǔ, Lóushì, and Yínzhúkě, facing west,
be enshrined with Tàizōng.
In the tenth month of Dàdìng三年,
during the comprehensive sacrifice,
Xiáyě, Wòlǔ, Sāgǎi, Xíbúshī,
and Āsīkuí were again enshrined with Tàizǔ,
while Zōngwàng, Shēnmǔ, Zōnghàn, Lóushì, and Yínzhúgē were enshrined with Tàizōng.
Thereafter,
the order was frequently changed.
In the eighth year,
the Emperor ordered paintings of meritorious officials to be placed in the Tàizǔ temple.
The officials concerned ranked the ministers who assisted the ancestors and founders,
based on the magnitude of their achievements and the eminence or humility of their official positions, and reported them in order.

Thus, the left side-hall was determined: Kāifǔ Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Sāgǎi, Huángbó Tàishī Yòufù Yuánshuài Sòngwáng Zōngwàng, Kāifǔ Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Wòlǔ, Huángbó Tàishī Liángwáng Zōngbì, Kāifǔ Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Lóushì, Huángshú Zǔ Yuánshuài Zuǒdūjiān Lǔwáng Shēnmǔ, Kāifǔ Suíguó Gōng Ālíhéhǎn, Yítóng Sānsī Yǎnguó Gōng Liú Yànzōng, Yòuchéngxiàng Qíguó Jiǎnyì Gōng Hán Qǐxiān, Tèjìn Zōngrén Xíshī;

the right side-hall: Tàishī Qínwáng Zōnghàn, Huángshú Zǔ Liáowáng Gǎo, Kāifǔ Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Xíbúshī, Kāifǔ Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Wányán Xīyǐn, Tàifù Chǔwáng Zōngxióng, Kāifǔ Qiányànjīng Liúshǒu Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Wányán Yínzhúgē, Kāifǔ Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Wányán Zhōng, Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Wányán Sālǐhē, Tèjìn Zōngrén Wòlǔgǔ, Yòuchéngxiàng Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Héshíliè Zhìníng.

Sāgǎi, Zōnggàn, Zōnghàn, Zōngwàng,

The seals made by the present dynasty.
In the early days of the state, seals from the Liáo dynasty were used.
In the fifth year of Huángtǒng (1145), the golden seals
"Yùqián zhī Bǎo"
(one) and
"Shūzhào zhī Bǎo"
(one) were first cast.
In the eighteenth year of Dàdìng (1178),
beautiful jade was obtained,
and an imperial edict commanded the creation of
"Dàjīn Shòumìng Wànshì zhī Bǎo".
Its dimensions were a diameter of four inches and eight fen, and a thickness of one inch and four fen.
The coiled-dragon knob was four inches and six fen in both height and thickness.
[一九]In the twenty-third year (1183),
the seal
"Xuānmìng zhī Bǎo" was also cast.
Its diameter was four inches and two li,
its thickness one inch and four fen,
the knob's height one inch and nine fen,
and the characters' depth two fen.
An imperial decree ordered the relevant officials to deliberate on its proper use.
They memorialized,
"Among the eight seals currently collected and the 'Yùqián zhī Bǎo' made in the fifth year of Huángtǒng,
the latter should be used for letters of enfeoffment to the Sòng state and for routine memorials.
The 'Shūzhào zhī Bǎo'
should be used for imperial edicts granted to Gāolí and Xiàguó, as well as for publishing edicts.
The 'Dàjīn Shòumìng Wànshì zhī Bǎo' made in the eighteenth year of Dàdìng
should be deliberated upon again by imperial decree.
The golden seals now cast should be used starting with presenting memorials.
Jade seals should be used by officials of the first rank, and by princes, dukes, and imperial consorts.
The golden 'Xuānmìng zhī Bǎo' should be used by officials of the second rank and below."
There was also the
"Lǐxìn zhī Bǎo",
made of bronze,
which was used annually to seal gifts for the Three Kingdoms.
During the Míngchāng era, it was changed to silver.
There were also seals for the Empress Dowager Grand, Empress Dowager, Empress, and Empress Consort Grand,
as well as seals for the Crown Prince and for regents (shǒuguó bǎo),
all made of gold.
In the twenty-fourth year of Dàdìng (1184),
the Crown Prince's seal,
cast in gold with a tortoise knob,
had its inscription determined by the relevant officials as
"Jiānguó" (supervising the state).
The Emperor commanded that
"shǒu" (guarding/regent)
replace
"jiān" (supervising).
It was to be one fen wider and one fen longer than a princely seal.
Miscellaneous rites.
In the eighth month of the third year of Dàdìng (1163),
the relevant officials deliberated:

"For the joint ancestral sacrifice (xiáxiǎng), regarding sacrificial animals and items, according to the 'Kāiyuán Lǐ' of Táng and the 'Kāibǎo Lǐ' of Sòng, each chamber uses one calf, one sheep, and one pig.
The 'Wǔlǐ Xīnyí' adds fifteen fish for each chamber.
The precedents of Tiāndé and Zhēnyuán were the same as Táng and Sòng.
When officials performed the rites, the grand sacrificial offering (tàiláo) was not used.
For the seven altars to meritorious officials, two sheep each were used,
and a total of two hundred and ten bottles of wine.
During Zhènglóng, this was reduced and fixed:
one calf in general,
one sheep and one pig for every two chambers,
and one hundred bottles of wine.
This is a deficiency in ritual.
Now, for the sacrificial animals and wine for the seven altars to meritorious officials, we request to follow the Tiāndé system.
For each chamber in the ancestral temple, we should follow the Sòng system,
adding fish.
However, one calf per chamber might be too lavish."
Shìzōng then commanded that for each sacrifice, one calf in total be used,
with sheep and pigs as before.
Also, for the joint ancestral sacrifice on the fifth day of the ninth month,
fifty catties of venison, thirty-five catties of roe deer meat, and fourteen rabbits were to be used for difficult-to-procure meat pickles.
Since hunting was prohibited during the Zhēnyuán and Zhènglóng periods,
these were all substituted with sheep.
This ritual was considered quite incomplete.
An edict commanded adherence to ancient customs.
In the first month of the tenth year (1170),
an edict instructed the chief ministers:
"According to ancient rites, cattle were slaughtered for sacrifice.
Has this changed in later generations?
Investigate the historical precedents and report."
The relevant officials stated:
"From the Zhōu dynasty onwards,
down to Táng and Sòng,
there was no joint ancestral sacrifice that did not use cattle.
During the Táng Kāiyuán Lǐ, for seasonal sacrifices, each chamber used one grand sacrificial offering.
It was not until the sixth year of Tiānbǎo (747) that the number of cattle was reduced,
with the Imperial Ancestral Temple using one calf for each seasonal sacrifice.
In the Sòng Zhènghé Wǔlǐ Xīnyí, for seasonal sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
when the emperor personally performed the sacrifice, cattle were used;
when officials performed the rites, they were not used.
An edict in the second year of Sòng Kāibǎo (969) stated that
calves were used for Hào Tiān Shàngdì and Huángdìqí;
all other grand sacrifices were substituted with sheep and pigs.
Two sheep and five pigs are sufficient to replace one calf.
Currently, the joint ancestral sacrifice every three years is a personal sacrifice.
Its rites are extremely solemn;
it might be difficult to reduce one calf per chamber."
Thereupon, it was commanded that seasonal sacrifices and sacrifices to the altars of grain and earth be as before.
If the ancestral temple was personally sacrificed to by the emperor, one calf in total was used;
if officials performed the rites, it was not used.
In the tenth month of the twelfth year (1172),
for the joint ancestral sacrifice,
since a proxy official performed the rites,
an edict commanded that three calves in total be used.
In the tenth month of the twenty-second year (1182),
an edict commanded that three calves in total be used for the joint ancestral sacrifice (xiá dì);
if officials performed the rites, deer were used instead.
At the dì sacrifice in the nineteenth year of Dàdìng (1179) for the Zhāodé Queen's temple,
calves were not used.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng (1189),
when Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
the ritual officials stated:
"Since the joint ancestral sacrifice in the tenth month of the twenty-seventh year of Dàdìng (1187),
until the passing of Shìzōng in the first month of this year,
the dì ritual was not performed in the fourth month.
According to the Gōngyáng Zhuàn,
in the second year of Mǐn Gōng, 'a propitious dì sacrifice was performed for Zhuāng Gōng,'
the mention of 'propitious' indicates it was not yet propitious,
meaning not yet three years.
The commentary states: 'This means that dì and xiá sacrifices follow the count from the former ruler,
while court visits and tributary missions follow the count from the current ruler.
After the three-year mourning period is completed,
if it falls on a dì, then dì is performed;
if it falls on a xiá, then xiá is performed.'
According to precedent,
the Xīnhài year should be the 'dàxiáng' (grand sacrifice for mourning),
and the dàn sacrifice should be in the third month.
After a month, it becomes auspicious.
Thus, the first day of the fourth month would be the 'chūjí' (first auspicious day),
which happens to be the time for the dì sacrifice in mid-summer.
It can be a personal sacrifice by the emperor."
An edict commanded adherence.
When the time came,
it was halted due to the death of Xiàoyì Queen.
In the fifth month,
the ritual officials stated:
"It has been three years since Shìzōng's spirit tablet was enshrined (shēngfù),
[二０]yet he has not yet joined the ancestral sacrifices with the ancestors.
If the xiá ritual is performed next winter,
we humbly submit that His Majesty is currently observing a period of heart-mourning (xīnsāng).
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticize the haste of auspicious events during mourning.
Therefore, the winter xiá might not be permissible.
However, the Rites of Zhōu state that when the king is in sorrow and grief, the officials of the Spring Office perform the duties as proxies.
We humbly believe that since the enshrinement of Shìzōng and Xiàoyì Queen,
Your Majesty has not personally visited the temple.
How can we allow officials to perform proxy duties first?
Moreover, in previous dynasties, proxy duties were only for regular sacrifices.
We now request to follow precedent:
after the three-year mourning period is completed,
if it falls on a xiá, then xiá is performed;
if it falls on a dì, then dì is performed.
On the first day of the fourth month of the fourth year of Míngchāng (1193), the heart-mourning should be concluded,
and the dì ritual performed."
The Emperor followed this.
In the twelfth month of the third year of Míngchāng (1192),
the Department of State Affairs memorialized:
"Next year's personal dì sacrifice
will require one calf per chamber.
Qīnhuái Queen is enshrined in the Míngdé temple.
According to the joint ancestral sacrifice in the third year of Dàdìng (1163),
the Míngdé Queen's chamber never used a calf."
An imperial decree commanded that Qīnhuái Queen also use one.
[二一]The Emperor then asked about the number of bows.
The Right Chancellor Wěi answered in detail.
The Emperor said:
"Shìzōng had a long and blessed life,
so the number of bows was reduced,
and he did not stand in position.
Now, we must follow the rites."
In the sixth year of Dàdìng (1166),
the morning libation ritual was formalized.
From the grand seating (dàcì) to the tablet seat (bǎnwèi), for the rite of first seeing the spirits,
two bows were performed.
Again arriving at the tablet seat,
another two bows.
After the libation of fragrant wine (guànchàng) was completed, returning to the tablet seat,
again two bows.
Returning to the small seating (xiǎocì), during the time of offering wine,
after washing hands at the wine-vessel and basin (léixǐ) position,
upon arriving at the tablet seat,
first two bows.
After the wine offering was completed, returning to the tablet seat,
again two bows.
Only the ancestral tablet and prayer scroll of the founding ancestor were placed southwest of the tablet seat.
After reading the scroll, another two bows.
Returning to the small seating,
and then to the blessed wine (yǐnfú) position,
first two bows,
after drinking, two bows.
In total, sixteen bows.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
the Sānzhī Zhèngshì Lǐ Gé was commanded to serve as the Xiūfèng Tàimiào Shǐ.
On an auspicious day in the seventh month, [Two-Two]
The officials, following past precedents, used the ceremony for the emperor's seasonal offerings.
Upon first reaching the tablet positions, there were two bows.
For the chén'guàn (morning libation) and zhuóxiàn (pouring and presenting wine), there were three bows for each position.
For the yǐnfú (drinking of blessed wine), there were five bows.
This totaled seventy-nine bows.
Now, for the initial enshrinement, it would extend to the five chambers of the tiāomiào (ancestral temple beyond the main hall),
making a total of one hundred and nine bows.
During the Míngchāng era, one bow was subtracted from each position after the zhuóxiàn diànjué (presenting the wine goblet),
making it only ninety-two bows.
However, in the sixth year of Dàdìng,
Shìzōng had once ordered the ritual officials to generally reduce it to sixteen bows.
Furthermore, the emperor was supposed to observe sǎnjāi (loose fasting) for four days in a separate hall,
and zhìzhāi (strict fasting) for three days in the Dàqìng Diàn.
As state affairs were currently pressing,
it was suggested to provisionally observe sǎnjāi for two days,
and zhìzhāi for one day.
The Emperor said:
“The number of bows shall follow the Dàdìng precedent,
the rest shall be as proposed.”
The Lǐbù Shàngshū Zhāng Xíngxìn said: [Two-Three]
“Recently, an imperial edict commanded that we follow Shìzōng’s ritual of sixteen bows.
I and the Tàicháng (Grand Master of Ceremonies) have together deliberated on the ritual procedures,
and I have some doubts.
Upon careful examination, the personal sacrifices and ceremonies of the Táng and Sòng dynasties
all included both general bows and bows for each individual position.
In the third year of Dàdìng, when Shìzōng personally performed the fēng'ān (enshrinement) ceremony,
there were also seven general bows,
and five bows for each chamber,
totaling seventy-two bows.
It was not until the dí (imperial ancestral sacrifice) in the sixth year
that an edict was issued for officials to reduce it to sixteen bows.
However, the ceremony of seventy-two bows was still retained;
its intention is thus evident.
Perhaps the initial year's offering ceremony was complete,
hence later it was expediently
re-determined to be general bows.
Now, for Your Majesty's initial miàojiàn fēng'ān (first visit to the temple for enshrinement),
to suddenly adopt this system
means there would be no bows at all for the spirit tablets in each chamber.
This is my first doubt.
In the Dàdìng era, there were twelve chambers;
to provisionally adopt sixteen bows was still acceptable.
Now there are seventeen chambers,
but the number of bows is even fewer than that.
This is my second doubt.
Moreover, the ritual procedures set in the sixth year
only stipulate reading the zhùcè (eulogy tablet) for the chamber of the Shǐzǔ (Progenitor) before the emperor’s tablet position.
Now, sacrifices have zhùcí (eulogies)
which are meant to inform the gods.
Currently, each zhùcè is inscribed with the posthumous titles of emperors and empresses,
and the varying generations of high ancestors and grandfathers.
The emperor's self-appellation also differs.
Yet, only one tablet is read,
the rest being merely ceremonial.
I fear this is not proper according to ritual.
This is my third doubt.
The rituals of the former kings
were adapted to the times,
neither too many nor too few,
but merely appropriate.
Now, the ritual officials of recent years, after weighing ancient and modern practices,
have separately set the ritual of forty-four bows.
Two bows upon first seeing the spirits,
four general bows for the chén'guàn,
two bows after the zhuóxiàn and reading of the zhù (eulogy) for each chamber,
and four bows for the yǐnfú.
This seems to be a balanced approach.”
The Emperor followed this,
and thus the fùxiǎng was set to follow the ceremony of seasonal offerings for twelve chambers.
Also, because the five ancestral tablets of the tiāomiào could not fit in the Shǐzǔ chamber,
they were placed in a single east-west row outside the chamber door,
with the west being the place of honor.
Missing spirit tablets were respectfully crafted inside the temple three days before the enshrinement,
and inscribed before the丑 (chǒu) hour on the day of the offering,
then successively brought up for enshrinement.
On the Jǐwèi day of the tenth month,
princes and all officials, from the Míngjùn Diàn, respectfully escorted the ancestral spirit tablets to the tent area of the Tàimiào.
On the Xīnyǒu day, the ceremony was performed,
using the forty-four-bow ritual,
without court music,
and with sacrifices made sparingly,
using only three calves and nine sheep and pigs for the seventeen chambers.
The Huáng Tàizǐ (Crown Prince) served as the Yàxiàn (Second Presenter),
and the Pú Wáng Shǒuchún as the Zhōngxiàn (Final Presenter).
The Emperor provisionally wore boots and robes,
and on the day of the ceremony wore a gǔnmiǎn (ceremonial robe and crown).
The Huáng Tàizǐ and others wore gōngfú (official robes),
without lúbù (imperial insignia) or yízhàng (ceremonial guards).
After the ceremony, they returned to the palace by horse.

the imperial father was posthumously enfeoffed as Jiǎnsù Huángdì,
with the temple name Ruìzōng,
the imperial mother Púchá Shì as Qīncí Huánghòu,
and the imperial mother Lǐ Shì as Zhēnyì Huánghòu.
On the first day of the eighth month of the second year,
the relevant officials memorialized,
"The posthumous titles of our ancestors are either sixteen characters,
or fourteen characters,
or twelve characters.
Now, Ruìzōng Huángdì should have his honorable posthumous title further augmented,
and the ceremonial book and seal offered before his enshrinement."
The emperor approved.
On the seventeenth day,
Zuǒ Píngzhāng Yuán Yí and others memorialized requesting to augment the honorable posthumous title to Ruìzōng Lìdé Xiǎnrén Qǐshèng Guǎngyùn Wénwǔ Jiǎnsù Huángdì.
The relevant officials memorialized,
"As Ruìzōng Huángdì has not yet been enshrined,
should a divine couch and table not be set up in the Shèngwǔ Diàn of Yǎnqìng Gōng?"
By imperial decree, it was borrowed and set up in the main position in Chóngshèng Gé.
It was also memorialized,
"The emperor himself shall present the ceremonial book and seal,
and the Tàiwèi shall conduct the ceremony."
The emperor approved.
On the twenty-second day of the ninth month,
a report was made to the Tàimiào.
On the twenty-eighth day,
grand music was arranged in Dà'ān Diàn
for rehearsal.
The day before,
the ceremonial book and seal were respectfully welcomed from Yǎnqìng Gōng
and placed in Dà'ān Diàn.
At three *kè* before dawn on the day of presentation,
the relevant officials each commanded their respective departments
to arrange the ceremonial guard.
All officials gathered at the palace gate.
The officiating officials wore ceremonial robes,
and the attending officials wore formal robes.
The emperor rode in his carriage in everyday attire from the palace,
with attendants as per ceremony,
and proceeded to the changing tent behind Dà'ān Diàn.
The Yùshǐ Tái urged the ranks,
and the Tōngshì Shèrén led the Tàiwèi and all officials to their positions.
The Shìzhōng knelt and reported,
"The inner guards are ready."
A short while later,
he again knelt and reported,
"The outer preparations are complete."
The emperor emerged, wearing the Tōngtiān Guān and crimson gauze robe.
The Tàicháng Qīng knelt and reported,
"Your servant, the Tàicháng Qīng, so and so, says,
'Please, Emperor, perform the rite of presenting the ceremonial book and seal.'"
After the report,
he prostrated,
then rose.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ led the way, dividing to left and right,
and the emperor walked to the tent for the ceremonial book and seal.
As he approached the tent,
ascending music played.
Upon reaching the tent, facing north,
the Xuānhuī Shǐ prompted,
"Please, Emperor, bow twice."
The Diǎnyí prompted,
"Officials in position, bow twice."
After bowing,
it was reported,
"Please, Emperor, insert the *guī* tablet."
Three sticks of incense were offered.
After completion,
he held the *guī* tablet.
It was reported,
"Please, Emperor, bow twice."
The Diǎnyí prompted,
"Officials in position, bow twice."
After completion,
they each divided into ranks and stood in the east and west orders.
It was reported,
"Please, Emperor, proceed to the mat position slightly to the east."
The music stopped.
The Zhōngshū Lìng and Zhōngshū Shìláng respectfully escorted the ceremonial book.
The Shìzhōng and Ménxià Shìláng respectfully escorted the seal.
As they proceeded,
ascending music played.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ guided the emperor to descend from the west steps, following the ceremonial book and seal.
The ascending music stopped,
and the palace orchestra music began,
reaching the mat position in the center below Dà'ān Diàn.
The Zhōngshū Lìng and Shìzhōng placed the ceremonial book and seal to the west of the emperor's mat position.
The music stopped.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ reported,
"Please, Emperor, bow twice."
The Diǎnyí prompted,
"All officials in position, bow twice."
After bowing,
the Zhōngshū Lìng inserted his *hù* tablet,
respectfully held the ceremonial book casket,
and the palace orchestra music played.
He went before the emperor's mat position,
prostrated,
knelt,
placed it respectfully,
held his *hù* tablet,
prostrated,
rose,
and retired to stand slightly to the west,
facing east.
The Tàicháng Bóshì led the Tàiwèi to the mat position,
to stand facing north.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ reported,
"Please, Emperor, insert the *guī* tablet,"
knelt and respectfully presented the ceremonial book casket to the Tàiwèi.
The Tàiwèi inserted his *hù* tablet,
knelt and received it,
held his *hù* tablet,
and stood slightly to the east.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ reported,
"Please, hold the *guī* tablet."
He prostrated,
then rose.
The officials carrying the ceremonial book held the casket,
and the Zhōngshū Shìláng respectfully placed the ceremonial book casket on the ceremonial book stand.
The music stopped.
The Shìzhōng inserted his *hù* tablet,
respectfully held the seal casket,
and the palace orchestra music played.
He went before the emperor's mat position,
prostrated,
knelt,
placed it respectfully,
held his *hù* tablet,
prostrated,
rose,
and retired to stand slightly to the west,
facing east.
The Tàicháng Bóshì led the Tàiwèi to the mat position,
to stand facing north.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ reported,
"Emperor, insert the *guī* tablet,"
knelt and respectfully presented the seal casket to the Tàiwèi.
The Tàiwèi inserted his *hù* tablet,
knelt,
received it,
held his *hù* tablet,
and stood slightly to the east.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ reported,
"Please, hold the *guī* tablet."
He prostrated,
then rose.
The officials carrying the seal held the seal casket,
and the Ménxià Shìláng respectfully placed it on the seal stand.
The music stopped.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ reported,
"Emperor, bow twice."
The Diǎnyí prompted,
"Officials in position, bow twice."
The emperor stood facing south,
and the palace orchestra music played.
The Tàicháng Bóshì led the Tàiwèi to respectfully carry out the ceremonial book and seal.
The banner bearer carried the banner and led the way.
The ceremonial book stand was in front,
followed by the seal stand.
The music stopped.
The Zhōngshū and Ménxià Shìláng each led in front of the ceremonial book and seal.
The Tàiwèi was behind them.
Upon reaching outside Dà'ān Mén,
the Tàiwèi, in order, knelt and respectfully placed the ceremonial book and seal into the imperial carriage.
The Zhōngshū Shìláng attended by the side of the carriage.
The relevant department received and guarded it according to regulations.
After the Tàiwèi had respectfully placed the ceremonial book and seal,
he walked out of Tōngtiān Mén.
The leather carriage used its standard imperial retinue,
and the escort was as per ceremony,
but the drums and wind instruments were not played.
After the ceremonial book and seal exited Dà'ān Mén,
the Tàicháng Qīng knelt and reported,
"Your servant, the Tàicháng Qīng, so and so, says,
'The rite is complete.'"
After the report,
he prostrated,
then rose,
and led the emperor to ascend from the east steps.
Ascending music played,
returning to the tent behind Dà'ān Diàn.
The music stopped.
The Shìzhōng knelt and reported,
"The guard is dismissed."
The imperial carriage returned to the inner palace,
with attendants as when it came.
On the first day of the tenth month,
the acting Tàiwèi, Tèjìn Píngzhāng Zhèngshì concurrently Tàizǐ Tàishī, Dìngguó Gōng, your servant Wán Yán Zōngxiàn, led all officials to Yǎnqìng Gōng to perform the rite.
The day before,
a tent for the ceremonial book and seal was set up outside the gate of Shèngwǔ Diàn,
facing west.
That day, at dawn,
officials of the Tàicháng Sì, leading their subordinates,
set up the divine bed-table at the Shèngwǔ Diàn.
The Xuānhuī Yuàn prepared tea, wine, fruits, seasonal delicacies, pastries, incense, flowers, etc.,
all in the same quantities as provided for the death anniversary of Emperor Tàizǔ.
The Dàlè Shǔ set up the Dēnggē music in the southern part of the front verandah of the殿 (hall),
facing north.
When the imperial seals and tablets were escorted to outside the Yǎnqìng Gōng gate,
the Zhōngshū Ménxià Shìlángs, each bearing a seal and a tablet, descended from their carriages,
and each placed them on a bed.
The Tàiwèi arrived outside the gate, descended from his carriage,
and, leading the Zhōngshū Lìng and others,
proceeded to the tent outside the Shèngwǔ Diàn gate,
where they were reverently placed as prescribed.
The ceremonial guards and soldiers then withdrew.
Next, the civil and military officials, each in their respective attire, were led in,
and took their positions in order.
The Dàlè Lìng led the musicians to their positions,
and the Lǐzhí Guān also took his position beforehand.
Those designated for duties all entered the hall courtyard first and stood facing north.
The Lǐzhí Guān intoned
“Prostrate twice,”
and after this was done,
they ascended the hall.
Next, the Tàiwèi was led to his mat-seat at the foot of the eastern steps, where he stood facing west.
The Lǐzhí Guān intoned
“Prostrate,”
and all officials in position prostrated twice.
The Lǐzhí Guān said:
“The proper authorities have reverently prepared everything;
please proceed with the ceremony.”
The Lǐzhí Guān intoned
“Prostrate,”
and all officials in position prostrated twice.
After this was done,
the Tàiwèi was led to the _léixǐ_ to wash his hands.
He ascended the hall,
proceeded to before the divine seat,
inserted his _hù_ into his belt,
knelt,
offered incense three times,
music began,
offered tea and wine.
After this was done,
he held his _hù_,
bowed low,
rose,
and the music stopped.
The Tàiwèi prostrated twice.
After this was done,
he returned to his position and stood for a moment.
Next, the Tàiwèi was led out,
and, leading the Zhōngshū Ménxià Shìlángs and others,
carried the bed with the imperial seals and tablets into the hall through the hall gate.
The Zhōngshū Lìng, Shìzhōng, and others all escorted them.
The Dēnggē music began.
When the bed with the imperial seals and tablets reached the hall courtyard,
it was placed below the western steps,
supported by mats and cushions.
The music stopped.
The Tàiwèi and those below him each took their positions on the mats facing north and stood firm.
The Lǐzhí Guān intoned
“Prostrate,”
and all officials in position prostrated twice.
After this was done,
the Tàiwèi, leading the Zhōngshū Lìng and Shìláng, carried the imperial tablet box up to the hall.
The Dēnggē music began.
Upon reaching the hall,
the imperial tablet box was placed before the food table,
and a mat-seat was also set up.
The music stopped.
Next, the Tàiwèi was led to before the divine seat,
bowed low,
knelt,
and said:
“Your acting Tàiwèi, your servant [name], respectfully states:
I reverently present the added honorary posthumous title tablet
and imperial seal.”
After the pronouncement,
he bowed low,
rose,
and stood slightly to the west.
Next, the Zhōngshū Lìng was led to stand south of the imperial tablet box.
The official holding the tablet raised the tablet,
the Zhōngshū Lìng bowed low,
knelt and read the tablet.
After this was done,
he bowed low,
and rose.
The Zhōngshū Lìng bore the imperial tablet box down from the western steps
and placed it on the bed.
The Dēnggē music began.
Once it was placed,
the music stopped.
Next, the Shìzhōng and Ménxià Shìláng were led to bear the imperial seal casket up to the hall.
Music began.
It was placed before the food table,
and a mat-seat was also set up.
The music stopped.
The official holding the seal raised the imperial seal casket,
the Shìzhōng bowed low,
knelt and read the imperial seal.
After this was done,
he bowed low,
and rose.
The Shìzhōng bore the imperial seal casket down from the western steps
and placed it on the bed.
The Dēnggē music began.
Once it was placed,
the music stopped.
The Tàiwèi went to his mat-seat outside the hall gate,
prostrated twice.
After this was done,
the Tàiwèi and those below him all descended the steps
and took their positions in order.
The Lǐzhí Guān intoned
“Prostrate,”
and all officials in position prostrated twice.
After this was done,
they exited in order.
The Sìguān and Shǔguān, leading the Gǒngwèi Zhí,
carried the bed with the imperial seals and tablets and placed it in the Cèbǎo Diàn.
All then withdrew.
The next day,
the hundred officials offered congratulations as in the usual ceremony.
In the 19th year of Dàdìng,
the posthumous title Xiàochéng Huángdì was conferred.
On the 16th day of the 11th month of the first year,
an imperial edict stated:
“The former sovereign was the eldest grandson of Tàizǔ,
and received the dying command of Tàizōng,
succeeding to the divine artifacts [of rule]
for fifteen years.
He governed by letting go and observing success,
and delegated authority to meritorious relatives.
He abolished the state of Qí to reduce corvée labor and taxes,
and appeased the Sòng people to cease military conflict.
The age reached great harmony,
and customs attained benevolence and longevity.
He unified chariots and writings across north and south,
and standardized patrols from east to west.
Though late in his reign there were excessive punishments,
nearing arbitrariness,
with wrongs inflicted upon his younger brother and empress,
and execution extended to skilled craftsmen,
yet his cruelty did not reach the common people,
and matters were still subject to remonstrance.
Such severe transgressions,
were perhaps not unheard of in antiquity.
The former Prime Minister, Qíguó Wáng Liàng, instead of assisting harmoniously,
committed usurpation and regicide.
He arbitrarily dismissed and deposed [the former sovereign],
and diminished his auspicious title.
Near and far grieved and lamented,
gods and men were filled with indignation.
Heaven repented of the calamity,
and I then arose,
receiving the joyful support of all under Heaven,
and holding great sway within the realm.
In rectifying chaos and restoring order,
the utmost priority is to reform wrongs.
Wishing to treat the deceased as if still living,
I earnestly consider fulfilling the rites.
It is fitting to confer the posthumous title Mǐnzōng Wǔlíng Huángdì.”
In the 18th year,
officials reported:
“The honorary posthumous titles of our dynasty’s ancestors have sometimes been eighteen characters,
sometimes fourteen characters,
sometimes twelve characters,
and sometimes four characters.
Now we propose to additionally confer the honored posthumous title on Mǐnzōng as Hóngjī Zuǎnwǔ Zhuāngjìng Xiàochéng Huángdì,
and also to add to the posthumous title of Empress Dào as Dàopíng Huánghòu.”
They further stated:
“The ceremonial rites for the posthumous honoring of Ruìzōng Huángdì in Dàdìng 3rd year included
the establishment of a yellow banner guard of one thousand men before the Dà'ān Diàn,
and a marching guard of two thousand men outside the Yìngtiān Mén.
The Emperor wore a tōngtiān guān and jiàngshā páo,
descended from the western steps with the imperial seals and tablets,
inserted his _guī_ into his belt,
knelt,
and presented the imperial seals and tablets to the Tàiwèi.
Now we propose to conduct the ceremony at the Dà'ān Diàn,
and in accordance with the historical precedents of Táng and Zhōu,
descend the steps to present the imperial seals and tablets to the Tàiwèi.
Regarding the crown, robes, and ceremonial guards, we propose to follow existing ceremonial examples.”
The Emperor ordered the number of ceremonial guards to be proportionally reduced,
with the rest generally following the previous ceremony.
On the 10th day of the 4th month of the following year,
the imperial seals and tablets were reverently offered,
and he was enshrined in the Tàimiào.
In the 26th year,
an imperial edict was issued to deliberate again on the temple name of Mǐnzōng.
The ritual officials proposed
seven characters: "Xiāng, Wēi, Jìng, Dìng, Huán, Liè, Xī."
By imperial decree, the character
"Xī"
was used.
Thus, on the first day of the fourth month of the following year,
officials were dispatched to make a solemn announcement to the Tàimiào and the Mǐnzōng’s ancestral hall,
changing to the new temple name.
On the Yǐchǒu day of the fourth month of Dàdìng 29,
the posthumous title bestowed upon the deceased emperor was Guāngtiān Xīngyùn Wéndé Wǔgōng Shèngmíng Rénxiào Huángdì,
and his temple name was Shìzōng.
On the Bǐngwǔ day of the fifth month,
a general amnesty was granted
as the ritual for enshrinement in the ancestral temple was completed.
On the Jiǎwǔ day of the fifth month of Dàdìng 29,
the posthumous title bestowed upon the Imperial Father was Tǐdào Hóngrén Yīngwén Ruìdé Guāngxiào Huángdì,
and his temple name was Xiǎnzōng.
On the Dīngmǎo day of the second month of Dà'ān 1,
[one zero] the posthumous title bestowed upon the deceased emperor was Xiàntiān Guāngyùn Rénwén Yìwǔ Shénshèng Yīngxiào Huángdì,
and his temple name was Zhāngzōng.
On the Wùxū day of the first month of Zhèngdà 1,
the posthumous title bestowed upon the deceased emperor was Jìtiān Xīngtǒng Shùdào Qínrén Yīngwǔ Shèngxiào Huángdì,
and his temple name was Xuānzōng.
Collation Notes
Records, Vol. 14, Rites 6: Original Temple,
Court Audience Ceremony, Prostration Ceremony, Separate Temple.
In Tiānhuì 2 of Tàizōng’s reign,
the temple of the Great Sage Emperor was established in the Western Capital.
In Tiānjuàn 2 of Xīzōng’s reign, in the ninth month,
the Qìngyuán Palace in the Supreme Capital was designated as the original temple for Emperor Tàizǔ.
In Huángtǒng 7,
the officials reported:
"The old gate of Qìngyuán Palace was called Jǐnghuī,
and the hall was called Chénjū.
These do not seem to be names suitable for a temple.
It is now appropriate to rename the hall Shìdé."
In the same year,
the Yùróng Hall in the Eastern Capital was completed.
In Dàdìng 2 of Shìzōng’s reign, in the twelfth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Huìníng Prefecture is the place where our dynasty rose.
It is fitting to build a main hall of nine bays at the site of Qìngyuán Palace,
retaining its old name,
and offer sacrifices at the appointed times."
In Tiāndé 4 of Hǎilíng’s reign,
officials stated:
"The Tàimiào has been constructed in Yānjīng,
and an original temple has been re-established.
Before the Three Dynasties, there was no system of original temples.
It was only in the time of Emperor Huì of Hàn that a temple was first established in Cháng'ān, north of the Wèi River,
where seasonal fruits were offered.
Later, temples were also established in Fēng and Pèi,
but no mention is made of sacrificial rites there.
Now, the announcements and sacrifices in both capitals should be limited to those conducted at the original temple built in Yānjīng."
Thereupon,
the palace was named Yǎnqìng,
the hall Shèngwǔ,
and the gate Chóngshèng.
In Dàdìng 2,
the imperial portrait of Ruìzōng was moved to Yǎnqìng Palace.
In the fifth year,
the Tàizǔ Temple in Huìníng Prefecture was completed,
and officials suggested that the imperial portrait should be placed there.
Previously,
Yǎnqìng Palace housed twelve imperial portraits of Tàizǔ: one in ceremonial robes, one standing, one in military attire, one with bow and arrows, two seated, one in headwear and robes,
which were previously placed in Huìníng Prefecture;
two half-length portraits, one in spring attire, and two in headwear and red robes,
which were previously placed in the Yùróng Hall in the Central Capital.
Now all are here.
An imperial edict commanded that one portrait in casual attire
be entrusted to an official for enshrinement, and a day be chosen for the departure.
The day before,
early in the morning,
a report was made to the temple,
using wine and food.
One official was appointed to make the solemn announcement,
serving as the designated envoy,
and presented the inscribed prayer tablet for imperial signature.
On that day, at dawn,
officials arranged a dragon carriage outside and slightly west of the Yǎnqìng Palace gate,
facing east.
The prime ministers and officials, leading the multitude of officials in court attire, proceeded to the front of the palace hall,
stood in formation,
and bowed twice.
The head of the formation ascended the hall,
knelt to offer incense and pour wine,
the music of the imperial music bureau began,
then he retreated slightly,
and bowed twice.
The head of the formation descended the steps and returned to his position,
and all attendant officials bowed twice.
The envoy and deputy, leading the grand invocators, carried out the imperial portrait casket,
while the prime ministers and lower-ranking officials divided to the left and right to lead the procession,
exiting the Yǎnqìng Palace gate.
After the imperial portrait casket was placed on the carriage,
the multitude of officials mounted their horses and followed,
with banners, armored horses, and people in brocade clothes leading the way to the left and right,
and the incense sedan and fans proceeding in front.
Upon reaching the outskirts of the capital gate,
as the imperial portrait carriage paused briefly,
the escorting officials dismounted,
stood in formation in front of the carriage,
and bowed twice.
The envoy and deputy stood at the side, not bowing.
The head of the formation proceeded to the incense sedan,
knelt to offer incense,
prostrated himself,
rose,
returned to the formation,
bowed twice to take leave,
and then retired.
The envoy and deputy then proceeded.
At each stage, they stopped and resided in a hostel or government office.
The road ceremonial guard consisted of
one red silk umbrella,
one dragon carriage,
which was made in the shape of a pavilion with blue cloth,
placed on the carriage,
and drawn by an ox.
Also used were five camels,
fifty flags and drums in total,
ten people carrying the incense sedan,
sixty escorting people,
eight people holding fans,
one hundred soldiers,
and twenty guards,
composed of descendants of imperial clan’s Měng'ān and Móukè.
In the prefectures and counties they passed through,
officials in court attire went out of the city walls with incense and fruit to welcome them,
bowed twice,
the head of the formation offered incense and poured wine,
and bowed twice again.
They escorted the procession to the outskirts,
bowed twice, and then retired.
Upon reaching Huìníng Prefecture,
officials prepared an incense sedan and welcomed them as per the above ceremony,
rode on horseback to the outside of the temple gate, dismounted,
and guided the procession from left and right.
The envoy and deputy, leading four grand invocators,
carried the imperial portrait into the temple,
placed it securely within the curtained chamber on the east wall outside the central gate,
bowed twice,
then retired,
and a day was chosen for the enshrinement.
On that day, at dawn,
the dispatched officials, together with officials from the prefecture and the temple construction officials, all in court attire,
lined up in front of the curtained chamber,
first bowed twice,
knelt to offer incense,
music began,
poured wine,
then bowed twice again.
The grand invocators carried the imperial portrait,
and all officials led the way,
lining up in front of the hall.
The imperial portrait was elevated to the hall for enshrinement,
then they bowed twice,
the head of the formation ascended the hall,
knelt to offer incense,
read the prayer,
poured wine,
music began,
then retreated slightly and bowed twice,
after which,
the head of the formation descended the steps and returned to his position,
and the attendant officials bowed twice,
then retired.
In the second month of the 15th year,
officials reported that the Kàijué Temple in the Eastern Capital housed a true likeness of Emperor Ruìzōng wrapped in a dark robe.
An imperial edict commanded it to be moved to the ancestral temple in this capital for worship,
and the color of the robe to be changed.
In the fourth month of the following year,
an imperial edict commanded that, following the rites for enshrinement of Ruìzōng,
the imperial portrait of Shìzǔ be enshrined in Yǎnqìng Palace.
Prior to this,
officials prepared an incense table, wine and fruit, and imperial music.
On that day, at dawn,
imperial princes and prime ministers, leading the multitude of officials in court attire, welcomed and guided the procession to Yǎnqìng Palace.

The procession included one hundred armored cavalry, two umbrella bearers, twelve fan bearers, eight incense sedan bearers, sixteen colorful sedan bearers, twenty-four attendants, two ritual officials, fifty crossbowmen and fifty crane-controllers each, two chanters, two ritual supervisors,
and thirty officials of the sixth rank and below in court attire, riding horses and leading the procession.
After the enshrinement was completed,
all officials bowed twice,
the ceremony concluded,
they retired and stood outside the palace gate,
to welcome the imperial carriage for a court audience.
In the first month of the sixteenth year,
the responsible officials reported:
“We have respectfully received an imperial edict to deliberate where the imperial portrait of Shìzǔ Huángdì should be placed.
We, your subjects, have carefully considered that Yǎnqìng Gōng is the ancestral temple of the Hàn dynasty,
and whenever the death anniversary of Tàizǔ Huángdì occurs,
all officials pay their respects.
Now, for Shìzǔ Huángdì, a site is to be chosen to construct a hall,
which would suitably convey the solemnity of the veneration.”
This was approved.
An imperial edict was then issued to construct halls for Shìzǔ, Tàizōng, and Ruìzōng to the east and west of Shèngwǔ Diàn.
Afterward, there was a desire to choose another site to build a Tàizōng Diàn at Guīrén Guǎn.
The responsible officials stated:
“Regarding the imperial mausoleums (shānlíng), Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, and Ruìzōng share a single burial ground.
In the Tàimiào, Shìzǔ, Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, and Ruìzōng are also in the same hall but different chambers.
Now, to construct a Tàizōng Diàn at Guīrén Guǎn,
it seems to differ from the system of the imperial mausoleums and the Tàimiào.”
An imperial decree followed the former deliberation,
to construct at Yǎnqìng Gōng seven bays for each hall, five bays for each side chamber (gé), and five bays for each triple gate.
Thus, Shìzǔ Diàn was named Guǎngdé, and its gé Yànchāng;
Tàizōng Diàn was named Pīchéng, and its gé Guāngzhāo;
Ruìzōng Diàn was named Tiānxīng, and its gé Jǐngfú.
On the sixth day of the fifth month of the nineteenth year,
the report was made.
On the seventh day,
the imperial portraits were respectfully enshrined.
There were two ritual officers in charge of affairs for each deity,
each with one incense table, one mat for sacrificial vessels, two kneeling cushions, one washing basin, and a full set of large ladles, baskets, and cloths.
The day before,
the director of the Tàimiào led his subordinates to sweep inside and outside the palace,
and also set up divine seats in the halls,
and set up kneeling positions for imperial princes, chief ministers, and all officials below them in the palace courtyard.
Washing basins were also set up below the eastern steps,
with those holding ewers and baskets positioned behind them.
Furthermore, kneeling cushions facing north were set up before each divine seat,
along with incense tables, incense burners, spoons, incense boxes, incense, wine, flowers, fruits, vessels, and other items,
following previous precedents.
Incense tables, burners, spoons, incense boxes, incense, etc., were also set up in Shèngwǔ Diàn,
and below the hall, one palanquin was set up for each, with sixteen bearers, two umbrella holders, twelve fan bearers, and thirty crossbowmen for escort.
The day before,
a period of purification (zhāi) was observed;
imperial princes remained in their residences,
and all officials in their own homes.
The ritual officers and functionaries practiced the ceremony,
and observed purification at the shrine.
On that day, at dawn,
the ritual officers led the Tàimiào officials to Chóngshèng Gé to respectfully retrieve the imperial portrait of Shìzǔ.
For each casket, two palace eunuchs and one Tàizhù (official in charge of sacrificial prayers) were employed,
with ritual officers and other officials leading the way,
and placed it on the divine seat in Shèngwǔ Diàn.
The duty ritual officer led the imperial princes, chief ministers, and all officials in court attire to stand in ranks in the palace courtyard.
Officials of the seventh rank and below stood outside the palace gate.
The announcer said,
“Bow,”
and all officials present bowed twice.
The duty ritual officer led the head of the ranks to the washing basin,
after washing hands,
ascended the hall,
knelt before the divine seat and offered incense,
after which,
they slightly retreated,
and bowed twice.
The duty ritual officer led the head of the ranks down from the hall to their original position.
The announcer said,
“Bow,”
and all officials present bowed twice.
After this,
the duty ritual officer escorted the imperial portrait of Shìzǔ onto the palanquin,
and the honor guard followed in order,
to Guǎngdé Diàn.
All officials followed behind,
and stood in their designated positions below the courtyard.
The ritual officers led the Tàimiào officials to respectfully take the imperial portrait from inside the palanquin,
and after respectfully enshrining it on the main position in the hall,
all officials stood in ranks below the steps, and officials of the sixth rank and below outside the palace gate.
The announcer said,
“Bow twice,”
and all officials present bowed twice.
The duty ritual officer led the head of the ranks to the washing basin,
after washing hands,
ascended the hall.
The officiating officials followed,
went before the imperial portrait,
knelt and offered incense,
poured wine,
and the music of the Jiàofāng began.
They slightly retreated and bowed twice,
after which,
the music stopped.
The duty ritual officer led the head of the ranks down from the hall to their original position.
The announcer said,
“Bow,”
and all officials present bowed twice.
After this,
the ritual officers led the Tàimiào officials to Chóngshèng Gé.
The Tàizhù and palace eunuchs carried the imperial portrait of Tàizōng.
The ritual officers escorted the imperial portrait of Tàizōng and placed it in Shèngwǔ Diàn.
After the ceremony was completed,
it was then respectfully enshrined in Pīchéng Diàn,
and the ceremony was entirely as described above.
Next, the imperial portrait of Ruìzōng was respectfully enshrined in Tiānxīng Diàn,
and the ceremony was also the same.
After the enshrinement ceremony was completed,
all officials withdrew.
In the intercalary third month of the twenty-first year,
an imperial decree was received to respectfully enshrine Zhāozǔ and Jǐngzǔ above Yànchāng Gé,
Sùzōng, Mùzōng, and Kāngzōng below the gé,
and Míngsù Huángdì below Chóngshèng Gé.
For each position, one yellow silk curtain, two yellow silk gold-thread column coverings, one purple silk kneeling mat, one dragon bed, two footstools, and a full set of robes were provided.
The report was made beforehand.
On the first day of the fourth month, the enshrinement took place,
and on the fifth day, the emperor personally offered sacrifices.
In the fifth month of that year,
the imperial portrait of Ruìzōng Huángdì was moved from Shèng'ān Sì to Yǎnqìng Gōng,
with the imperial crown prince, imperial princes, and chief ministers respectfully receiving and placing it.
Ritual for morning audience.
On the nineteenth day of the fourth month of Dàdìng sixteenth year,
the imperial portrait of Shìzǔ was enshrined,
and the ritual for morning audience was performed.
The day before, the emperor observed purification in the inner palace,
the imperial crown prince in his palace,
imperial princes in their residences,
and all officials in their own homes.
The director of the Tàimiào led his subordinates
to sweep inside and outside Yǎnqìng Gōng,
and set up kneeling positions for imperial princes and all officials in the palace courtyard,
and also set up kneeling cushions for the imperial crown prince before the positions of the imperial princes and officials.
The Xuānhuī Yuàn led its subordinates
to set up a westward-facing imperial tent to the east outside Shèngwǔ Mén,
and the imperial crown prince’s tent near the Língxīng Mén.
On that day,
the responsible officials arranged the guards at Yìngtiān Mén.
After the imperial portraits were enshrined,
the responsible officials set up northward-facing kneeling cushions on the hall and before the divine images,
and placed incense burners, incense tables, and items such as incense and wine vessels.
Before the imperial carriage departed,
the imperial crown prince, in court attire, rode on horseback,
escorted by his palace officials and subordinates,
dismounted west of Yǎnqìng Gōng Mén,
and walked into his tent.
Imperial princes and all officials stood in westward-facing ranks outside Yǎnqìng Gōng Mén.
When the imperial carriage was about to arrive,
the director of ceremonies led the imperial crown prince out of his tent,
to respectfully receive the emperor before the ranks of imperial princes and officials.
Forty officials of the fifth, sixth, and seventh ranks were chosen from among the escorting officials to stand in ranks south of the road outside Yìngtiān Mén and wait.
The Huángdì wore boots and a ceremonial robe, and rode in a palanquin.
Attendant officials, parasols, fans, and guards were arranged as per the usual ceremony.
An imperial edict specified the use of the Dà'ān palanquin and a thousand people for the honor guard.
Exiting the Yìngtiānmén,
the attendant at the palace gate announced loudly,
"The guiding official pays obeisance twice!"
After this,
the attendant at the palace gate conveyed the edict,
"The guiding official mounts his horse!"
They divided to lead the way to the left and right,
dismounting at the west side outside the temple gate.
The imperial carriage arrived at the west side outside the Yǎnqìnggōng gate, and the Huángdì alighted from the palanquin.
The Zǒuyòu Xuānhuīshǐ led the way,
and the Huángdì walked into the imperial tent.
The curtain was lowered.
The attendant at the palace gate first led the Qīnwáng, Zǎizhí, and executive officials of the fourth rank and above,
who entered through the east and west side gates,
