and stood facing each other in east and west rows in the殿庭 (diàntíng).
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huáng Tàizǐ in,
who stood to the west of the kneeling mat,
facing east.
Officials for presenting incense, wine, etc., all ascended the steps,
and stood in sequence on the殿 (diàn), facing east and west.
The Xuānhuīshǐ knelt and reported,
"Requesting the Huángdì to perform the ceremony of reverence."
The curtain was rolled up,
and the Huángdì emerged from the tent.
The Xuānhuīshǐ led the way,
to the kneeling mat on the殿 (diàn),
and stood facing north.
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huáng Tàizǐ to the kneeling mat.
The attendant at the palace gate led the Qīnwáng, Zǎizhí, and executive officials of the fourth rank and above back to their ranks,
all standing facing north.
A space was left in the middle
so as not to obstruct the playing of music.
Officials of the fifth rank and below paid obeisance outside the Shèngwǔmén, and officials of the eighth rank and below paid obeisance outside the palace gate.
The request was made,
(and the Xuānhuīshǐ).
The Huángdì bowed twice,
and the Jiàofáng music began.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice.
The Huángdì was requested to proceed to the kneeling mat before the divine presence,
and stood facing north.
Again, the Huángdì was requested to bow twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice.
The Huángdì was requested to kneel,
offer incense three times,
pour wine three times,
bow down,
and rise.
Again, the Huángdì was requested to bow twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice.
After this,
the Huángdì returned to his position.
Again, the Huángdì was requested to bow twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice.
The Xuānhuīshǐ reported,
"The ceremony is complete."
The above was planned for eight bows;
the Xuānhuīyuàn reported it,
and it followed the old custom of twelve bows.
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huáng Tàizǐ back to stand to the west of the kneeling mat,
facing east.
The attendant at the palace gate led the Qīnwáng, Zǎizhí, and all officials below them,
to stand facing each other from east and west.
First, officials of the fifth rank and below were led out.
The Xuānhuīshǐ led the way,
and the Huángdì returned to the imperial tent.
The curtain was lowered.
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huáng Tàizǐ.
The attendant at the palace gate led the officials in the殿庭 (diàntíng) in groups,
exiting in sequence.
The Xuānhuīshǐ knelt and reported,
"Requesting the Huángdì to return to the palace."
The curtain was rolled up.
He only exited outside the temple gate,
boarded the palanquin, and returned to the palace,
as per the arrival ceremony.
The ceremony of enthronement in the nineteenth year was the same.
Court worship ceremony.
Initially,
on Tàizǔ's death anniversary,
the Huángdì proceeded to the kneeling mat and stood,
bowing twice.
Moving slightly to the east,
facing west,
he proceeded to the incense table,
and bowed twice again.
After offering incense,
he returned to his position,
and bowed twice again.
For presenting food, pouring tea, and bidding farewell to the spirits, he bowed twice and retired.
On the twelfth day of the fifth month of Dàdìng twenty-one,
on Ruìzōng's death anniversary,
the officials concerned revised the ritual.
The day before,
the Xuānhuīyuàn set up the imperial tent to the west outside the Tiānxīngdiàn gate.
On the day, at dawn,
the Huáng Tàizǐ, Qīnwáng, and all officials, wearing formal attire, stood in ranks outside the Yǎnqìnggōng gate
to receive the Huángdì.
The Huángdì rode on horseback to outside the Yǎnqìnggōng gate and dismounted.
Two Xuānhuī led the way,
walking into the palace gate slightly to the east.
The Huángdì rode in a palanquin,
with parasols, fans, and guards as per the usual ceremony,
to the west outside the Tiānxīngdiàn gate.
The Huángdì alighted from the palanquin,
entered the tent,
and the curtain was lowered.
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huáng Tàizǐ, and the attendant at the palace gate led the Qīnwáng, Zǎizhí, and officials of the fourth rank and above to enter through the side gate,
to the殿庭 (diàntíng),
where they stood in fixed ranks to the left and right.
Two Xuānhuīshǐ guided the Huángdì to enter through the main gate of Tiānxīngmén,
ascended the殿 (diàn) from the east steps,
and stood fixed at the kneeling mat.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and officials below him formed ranks.
Officials of the fifth rank and below stood in ranks outside the殿 (diàn) gate.
The Xuānhuīshǐ reported,
"Requesting the Huángdì to bow twice first,"
"Requesting him to proceed to the position of attendant deity."
After the officials concerned had placed the incense table and wine table,
"Requesting him to proceed to the kneeling mat,"
and bow twice again,
offer incense three times, pour wine,
return to his position,
and bow twice.
For the above,
the Huáng Tàizǐ and all below him paid obeisance in accompaniment.
Again, it was reported,
"Requesting him to proceed to the position of attendant deity slightly to the east."
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huáng Tàizǐ to ascend the殿 (diàn) to the kneeling mat,
bowed twice first,
poured wine and bowed twice again,
descended and returned to the kneeling mat.
Next, the attendant at the palace gate led Zhàowáng, the final offering official, to ascend the殿 (diàn) and perform the ritual.
The Xuānhuīshǐ reported,
"Requesting the Huángdì to proceed to the kneeling mat,"
and bowed twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice.
After the ceremony,
all officials stood in ranks as before.
The Huángdì exited outside the殿 (diàn) gate,
entered the tent,
the curtain was lowered,
and he changed clothes.
Next, the Huáng Tàizǐ and officials below him were led out to stand in ranks outside the palace gate.
[一０]The Huángdì rode in a palanquin,
to slightly east of the palace gate, alighted from the palanquin,
walked out of the palace gate,
mounted his horse and returned to the palace.
The guiding and attendant guards were as per the arrival ceremony.
The Huáng Tàizǐ and officials below him
waited for the imperial carriage to depart before retiring.
In Dàdìng five,
an imperial decree was issued:
"On Tàizǔ's death anniversary,
offerings at Yǎnqìnggōng shall only use vegetarian food.
All imperial portraits in various capitals shall be treated likewise.
Furthermore, court worship ceremonies shall be performed on the new moon and full moon."
In six,
the officials concerned reported:
"On Tàizǔ Huángdì's death anniversary,
the imperial carriage personally makes offerings,
and all officials pay obeisance in accompaniment.
Now, if the imperial carriage is on a tour,
the Zǎichén should be the head of the rank,
leading all officials to Yǎnqìnggōng to perform the ritual."
This was approved.
In sixteen,
an imperial decree was issued:
"On Shìzǔ's and Tàizōng's death anniversaries,
offerings shall be made in the same manner."
In the eighth month of eighteen,
on Tàizǔ's death anniversary,
Shìzǔ and Tàizōng were offered sacrifices at the same place.
The officials concerned stated,
"Throughout history, there has been no precedent of sacrificing to multiple ancestors on the death anniversary of one saintly ancestor."
While deliberating,
an edict was issued to send the Tàizǐ,
to perform the ritual for one position,
and also to sacrifice to meritorious officials.
In twenty-six,
due to the difference between internal and external ancestral temples,
it was decided and proposed:
"The Tàimiào shall have five sacrifices annually.
For the mountain mausolea, offerings on the new moon, full moon, death anniversaries, and festival days shall follow previous dynastic precedents.
As for Yǎnqìnggōng, where the imperial carriage has always visited,
when encountering ancestral death anniversaries, officials perform rituals,
and ancestral temples in various capitals perform拜奠 (bàidiàn) on festival days, death anniversaries, new moon, and full moon.
Although there are no precedents to consult,
it is probably appropriate to follow the old customs
to express the utmost reverence."
This was approved.
Other temples.
In the second year of Dàdìng
the responsible authorities proposed that since Mǐnzōng had no heir,
a separate temple should be established.
The authorities suggested that the seasonal sacrifices and offerings
should not be called "zōng" (ancestral)
and that Wǔlíng should be the temple name.
They also proposed:
"When the Táng dynasty established separate temples,
they did not necessarily have to be within the main ancestral temple enclosure.
Now that Wǔlíng Huángdì is not referred to as 'zōng'
and will not participate in the combined sacrifices (xiáxiǎng),
his temple is proposed to be built on the vacant land outside the eastern wall of the Tàimiào."
This was approved.
In the fourteenth year,
the temple was completed.
Since Wǔlíng's empress was posthumously honored as Xiàochéng,
it was also called Xiàochéngmiào.
On the Wùshēn day of the third month of the fifteenth year,
Wǔlíng Huángdì and Dàohòuhòu were enshrined.
The day before,
a notification was made to the eleven chambers of the Tàimiào and the Zhāodé Hòuhòu Miào,
with the remaining rituals following those of Zhāodé's "guòmiào" (passing to the temple).
On the seventeenth day of the fourth month,
the summer sacrifice was offered at the Tàimiào.
At the same time, the ceremony was performed,
and Pànzōngzhèng Yīngwáng Shuǎng was ordered to act as Tàiwèi
and serve as the primary libation officer (chūxiàn guān).
Bīngbù Shàngshū Ràng acted as Sītú,
and Dàlǐ Qīng Tiānxī was appointed to act as Tàicháng Qīng
and serve as the secondary libation officer (yàxiàn).
Dàxīng Shàoyǐn Gāo Jūzhōng acted as Guānglù Qīng
and served as the final libation officer (zhōngxiàn).
From then on,
five sacrifices were performed annually.
In the tenth month of the seventeenth year,
during the xiáxiǎng at the Tàimiào,
"upon reviewing the Táng dynasty rites,
it was found that the seasonal sacrifices at Xiàojìng Huángdì's temple used temple dances, palace musical arrays (gōngxuán), and ascending songs (dēnggē),
while Ràng Huángdì's temple, for the one sacrifice during the dì-xiá month,
only used ascending songs.
The ritual regulations for additions and reductions differed.
Now, the courtyard of Wǔlíng Huángdì's temple differs in layout from the Tàimiào,
making it difficult to accommodate gōngxuán music and dance,
and musical instruments are also lacking.
After consideration, it is feared that it should follow the precedent of Táng Ràng Huángdì's xiáxiǎng,
using dēnggē for the music,
and all sacrificial animals, vessels, and stands for offerings (zūnzǔ) should be the same as for one chamber of the Tàimiào when performing the ritual.
And it was verified that for xiáxiǎng,
when the emperor personally sacrifices, each chamber uses one calf,
and the acting officials performing the ritual collectively use three calves.
Now, with the addition of Wǔlíng Huángdì's separate temple for the ritual,
should we still follow the established agreement of collectively using three calves,
or should the number of cattle be increased?"
The memorial received an imperial decree:
"The Tàimiào and the separate temple shall collectively use three calves,
Wǔlíng Huángdì's temple music shall use dēnggē.
An official shall be sent to present the report.
Both are approved."
In the fourth month of the nineteenth year of Dàdìng,
he was moved to be enshrined in the Tàimiào,
and his old temple was subsequently demolished.
Zhāodé Hòuhòu Miào.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
the responsible authorities cited Táng dynasty precedents,
stating that Zhāodé Hòuhòu should have a separate temple,
and proposed to build it within the northeast corner of the Tàimiào's inner enclosure.
This was approved.
On the seventh day of the tenth month of the third year,
during the Tàimiào's xiáxiǎng,
Ruìzōng Huángdì and Zhāodé Hòuhòu were enshrined.
Their spirit tablets were manufactured and inscribed simultaneously,
then presented to the palace courtyard.
After the audience, they were enshrined to the left of their paternal aunt Qīnrén Hòuhòu.
After the sacrifices and offerings were completed,
the tablets were returned to their original temple.
On the twenty-first day of the twelfth month,
during the winter sacrifice (làxiǎng),
the ritual officials stated:
"According to Táng rites,
offerings in separate temples should follow the ritual for one chamber of the Tàimiào.
We fear that if the temple sacrifice is completed, it will be past dawn.
Please appoint a separate official to act as sacrificer."
The decree was approved.
Later, due to the small size of the hall,
another position was built to the east of the Tàimiào.
In the eighth month of the twelfth year,
the temple was completed.
The main hall had three bays,
with half a bay vacant on both the east and west.
Two bays were used as chambers,
and the reliquary chamber (shìshì) was placed against the western wall of the westernmost bay.
The temple had a convenient gate
connecting it to the Tàimiào.
The old hall was still used as the Cèbǎo Diàn (Hall for Imperial Decrees and Treasures),
and the shìshì was proposed to be demolished.
On the twenty-first day of the sixth month of the thirteenth year,
a report was made to the Tàimiào,
and a sacrificial notification was made to the separate temple.
On the twenty-third day,
the enshrinement took place,
following the previous xiáxiǎng guòmiào ritual.
The authorities stated that a honor guard (lǔbù) should be used,
but since the temples were not far apart,
after deliberation, it was proposed to use two "clearing the way" (qīngdào) attendants,
followed by two round fan holders,
followed by eight duty officers,
followed by twenty-six yáguān (court officials) arranged in thirteen rows,
filled by gōngfèngguān (officials in attendance).
Next was the palanquin (yāoyú),
with sixteen palanquin bearers,
two umbrella bearers,
followed by fourteen round fans in seven rows,
four square fans,
followed by six duty officers in formation,
ten pairs of lantern cages,
and niǎnguān (sedan chair officials) wearing brocade jackets and coiled wraps.
Furthermore, the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) was ordered to lead all officials in performing the ceremony.
The day before,
the officials performing the duties were to purify themselves and fast for one night at the sacrificial site,
and practice the ritual.
The performers were offered food and drink.
The Tàimiào Lìng (Chief of the Tàimiào) led his subordinates in sweeping inside and outside the temple.
The Lǐzhí Guān (Ritual Supervisor) set up the Huáng Tàizǐ's position facing west,
and the duty officials' positions behind the Huáng Tàizǐ,
closer to the south,
facing west,
each standing according to their rank.
The Jiānjì (Supervisor of Sacrifices) stood below the western steps of the hall, facing east.
And the imperial princes (qīnwáng) and all officials were positioned in the temple courtyard,
facing north,
with the superior positions to the west.
A prayer table (zhù'àn) was also set up to the right of the spirit tablet,
and positions for zūnyí (ritual wine vessels) to the left,
each with a spoon, ladle, and stand (diàn).
Sacrificial vessels were also set up,
all resting on mats.
To the left, one biān (basket) was filled with dried deer meat,
and to the left, one dòu (wooden vessel) was filled with venison paste.
Washing basins (guànxǐ) and wine-washing vessels (juéxǐ) were set up slightly to the east of the south side of the cross-street.
The léi (wine vessel) was to the east of the basins,
with a spoon added.
The fěi (basket) was to the west of the basins,
facing south,
filled with towels.
Those holding the léi and fěi were positioned behind them.
The Tàimiào Lìng also set up the spirit tablet inside the chamber, below the northern wall,
facing south, directly opposite the door.

A straight table (zhíjǐ), a ceremonial screen (fǔyǐ), one rush mat (guānxí), one fine straw mat (sāoxí), two ordinary mats (cìxí), one thick purple silk mattress (zǐlíng hòurù), one purple silk mattress cover (zǐlíng méngrù), along with canopies, etc.,
all items were arranged according to the ritual of the old temple.
A wàngliáo (gazing at the pyre) position was also set up to the north outside the western divine gate,
with sacrificial firewood (liáochái) to the north of this position.
A burial pit (yìkǎn) was pre-dug at the pyre site.
The relevant department arranged the ceremonial guard outside the old temple gate.
Two quarters before dawn on the day of enshrinement,
the relevant department placed square fans and lantern cages outside the old temple hall gate,
and set up one palanquin and one umbrella below the hall steps,
facing south.
At dawn,
the Huáng Tàizǐ, in formal attire, rode on horseback,
accompanied by officials and retainers from his palace,
dismounted outside the temple gate,
walked into the temple gate,
to the curtain.
Next, the qīnwáng and all officials, in ordinary attire, were led in through the temple gate,
and stood in the hall courtyard, facing north, with superior positions to the west, in multiple rows.
Next, the Huáng Tàizǐ was led to stand at a position separate from the officials.
The announcer said,
"Bow twice,"
and they all bowed twice.
The Gōngwéi Lìng ascended the hall,
and placed Zhāodé Hòuhòu's spirit tablet on the seat.
The announcer said,
"Bow twice,"
and they all bowed twice.
Next, the Inner Imperial Attendants (Nèi Chángshì) were led to face north and bow down.
Kneeling, they presented a memorial,
saying, "We respectfully request that the spirit tablet of Empress Zhāodé be enthroned in the new temple,
descending from the hall and ascending the sedan chair."
When the memorial was finished,
they bowed down
and rose.
The Inner Attendants (Nèishì) holding the cabinet first respectfully placed the cabinet on the sedan chair,
and then the Director of the Palace Bureau (Gōngwéi Lìng) received the spirit tablet.
The Inner Attendants (Nèishì) led the way,
kneeling and placing it behind the cabinet on the sedan chair,
covering it with a red silk scarf.
The Inner Imperial Attendants (Nèi Chángshì) and those below them split into left and right to lead the way.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) walked from the old temple, leading the procession first.
The Imperial Princes (Qīnwáng) followed him.
All officials (Bǎiguān) followed behind, splitting into left and right.
The ceremonial guard (Yíwèi) escorted them.
They arrived at the foot of the hall of the separate temple, facing north.
The Inner Imperial Attendant (Nèi Chángshì) bowed down in front of the palanquin,
rose,
and knelt to present a memorial,
saying, "We respectfully request that she descend from the sedan chair and ascend to the hall."
The Inner Attendants (Nèishì) advanced, holding the cabinet.
The Director of the Palace Bureau (Gōngwéi Lìng) received the spirit tablet and carried it up to the hall,
placing it on the seat.
The Director of Rites (Lǐ Zhíguān) led the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ), the Imperial Princes (Qīnwáng), and all officials (Bǎiguān) into the temple courtyard,
facing north, ranked from west to east, standing in double rows.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) stood at the end of the mat.
The Director of Rites (Lǐ Zhíguān) announced,
"Bow twice,"
and all bowed twice.
He then announced,
"Let the officiating officials each take their positions."
The Director of Rites (Lǐ Zhíguān) led the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) to his position facing west and stood firm.
The Director of Rites (Lǐ Zhíguān) advanced slightly and announced,
"The responsible officers have respectfully prepared;
please proceed with the rites."
He then led the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) to the washing station,
facing north,
inserting his ceremonial tablet (hù) into his belt,
washing his hands,
drying his hands,
and holding his ceremonial tablet (hù).
He proceeded to the wine cup washing station,
standing facing north,
inserting his ceremonial tablet (hù),
washing the wine cup,
and wiping the wine cup to hand it to the attendant.
Holding his ceremonial tablet (hù),
he ascended
to the wine jar,
standing facing west.
The attendant handed the wine cup to the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
who inserted his ceremonial tablet (hù)
and held the wine cup.
The attendant lifted the jar to pour the wine.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) handed the wine cup to the attendant,
then went before the spirit tablet, facing north,
inserted his ceremonial tablet (hù),
and knelt.
The attendant handed the wine cup to the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
who held the cup and poured wine three times in offering,
then returned the cup to the stand (diàn),
held his ceremonial tablet (hù),
bowed down,
rose,
and stood for a moment.
Next, the Grand Invoker (Tàizhù) and the official holding the prayer text (Jǔ Zhùguān) were led to the prayer reading position, facing northeast.
The official holding the prayer text (Jǔ Zhùguān) knelt and held up the prayer tablet.
The Grand Invoker (Tàizhù) knelt and read the prayer.
When finished,
he placed the prayer on the table,
bowed down,
and rose.
All the officials holding the prayer text (Jǔ Zhùguān) stepped back to stand facing north.
The announcer said,
"Bow twice,"
and the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) bowed twice,
then descended the steps and returned to his position.
The officials holding the prayer text (Jǔ Zhùguān) and reading the prayer followed,
returning to their original positions.
The Director of Rites (Lǐ Zhíguān) said,
"Bow twice,"
and all those present bowed twice.
The Director of the Palace Bureau (Gōngwéi Lìng) placed the spirit tablet in the chamber.
The announcer said,
"Bow twice,"
and all bowed twice.
The rites concluded,
and they retired.
The Director of the Office (Shǔ Lìng) closed the temple gate,
buried the prayer text in a pit,
and all ritual objects were returned to their respective departments.
In the eleventh year,
on the same day as the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tài Miào).
The Dēnggē music was used,
and the three offerings (Sānxiàn Lǐ) were performed.
The responsible officers (Yǒusī) officiated.
In the twenty-sixth year,
an imperial edict commanded the construction of a separate memorial temple (Yǐng Miào) for Empress Zhāodé within the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tài Miào).
The responsible officers (Yǒusī) reported:
"It is fitting to construct a hall of three bays,
with a single building of three gates facing south.
The surrounding wall should be made of bricks.
The outer wall should have one Língxīng gate,
and the spirit chamber and west rooms should each have three bays.
However, the rites do not have a precedent for constructing a separate memorial temple (Yǐng Miào) within the ancestral temple (Miào Zhōng).
Currently, west of the Empress's temple, there is vacant land,
thirty-four paces wide
and fifty-four paces long,
which can be used for construction."
The imperial decree approved this.
A main gate was also newly built facing due south,
and the gate was named Kūnyí.
The old convenient gate was retained,
to be used for the Dìxiá and fùxiǎng sacrifices.
Every year, for the five offerings (Wǔ Xiǎng) and the memorial temple (Yǐng Miào) rituals, entry and exit were through the main south gate.
Outside the temple, twenty-three rooms were built for the fasting corridor (Zhāiláng Fáng).
Temple of Crown Prince Xuānxiào.
In the seventh month of the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng,
the responsible officers (Yǒusī) memorialized:
"According to Tang dynasty regulations,
a temple should be established for a deceased Crown Prince (Tàizǐ),
with officials appointed to offer sacrifices.
It is proposed to construct a hall of three bays east of the Imperial Armaments Storehouse (Fǎwù Kù).
The south wall and outer wall should each have a single building with three gates.
The east and west walls should each have a single building with one gate,
and the gates should have nine halberds.
Fasting rooms (Zhāifáng) and spirit chambers (Shén)
are appropriate for the site."
Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued that since the spirit tablet of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) was to be enshrined,
a separate memorial hall (Yǐng Diàn) should be built.
The responsible officers (Yǒusī) determined the proposed design:
a memorial hall (Yǐng Diàn) of three bays should be built slightly west and in the middle of the existing temple,
separated by a brick wall.
It should have a single building of three gates facing south,
with a surrounding wall of bricks,
without corner openings or east and west gates.
The outer wall should have one main triple gate facing due south,
and two buildings each with three bays for the spirit chamber (Shén) and fasting rooms (Zhāishì).
the temple was completed.
On the eleventh day, the spirit tablet was enshrined.
On the fourteenth day, the portrait was moved.
The spirit tablet was made of chestnut wood,
following the Tang system where feudal lords used one foot long tablets,
with the posthumous title carved on the back.
Officials dispatched by the Secretariat-Chancellery (Shěng Bù) set up a tent facing north in the southwest corner of the temple
to oversee the manufacture,
which was completed the day before the ceremony.
On the evening of that day,
the official bearing the spirit tablet carried it in a box,
covered with a scarf,
and brought it to the tent where the spirit tablet was to be inscribed.
The next day, five quarters before the hour of丑 (chǒu),
the official inscribing the spirit tablet, together with the director of ceremonies (Diǎnyí) and the ritual official (Lǐguān), proceeded to the front of the tent.
The official inscribing the spirit tablet went to the lěixǐ station,
washed and dried his hands.
The official bearing the spirit tablet first offered it a fragrant bath,
and wiped it with a silk towel.
The official inscribing the spirit tablet took his position on the mat,
and inscribed the posthumous title on the back, saying,
"Spirit Tablet of Crown Prince Xuānxiào."
It was written in ink,
using a shiny lacquered mold.
When finished,
it was handed to the official bearing the spirit tablet,
who received it in a box,
covered it with a plum-red silk scarf,
and placed it on a plain silk scarf.
He proceeded to the seat and placed it in the cabinet.
Then the curtains were lowered,
and the attendants stood guard as prescribed.
After the director of ceremonies (Diǎnyí) bowed down,
knelt and requested,
the palanquin, parasol, and fans were prepared and brought to the spirit tablet.
The escort and attendants were fewer than for the Empress Zhāodé temple ceremony.
Regarding the sacrificial rites,
the responsible officers (Yǒusī) reported:
"They should follow the four seasonal sacrifices and offerings (Sìshí Jìxiǎng) of the Ancestral Temple (Zǔ Miào).
The first offering should be made by the imperial grandsons (Huángsūn) and imperial clan (Huángzú), and the second offering by the imperial clan (Huángzú) or officials of the fifth rank and below.
The Dēnggē music should be used, but now it is reduced to twenty-five performers.
For inviting the spirit, Wúshè Gōng should be used,
and for ascending, descending, and removing the offerings, the Jiázhōng song should be sung.
One sheep and one pig should be offered.
There should be eight biān and dòu vessels each,
two fǔ and guǐ vessels each,
and one dēng and xíng vessel each.
The rest of the sacrificial food should also be proportionally reduced."
On the first day of the eleventh month of the twenty-sixth year,
a memorial was presented, stating:
"For the temple of the spirits' tablets (Shénzhǔ Miào),
livestock, pens, and musical instruments are provided by the government.
For the temple of the statues (Yǐng Miào),
the imperial grandsons shall offer sacrifices."
Textual Notes
Records, Volume 15, Rites 7, Shèjì, Wind, Rain, Thunder Master, Five Sacred Mountains, Four Great Rivers
In the intercalary twelfth month of the first year of Zhēnyuán,
the officials concerned memorialized to establish the Altar of Shèjì in Shàngjīng.
In the seventh month of the seventh year of Dàdìng,
another memorial was presented to establish an altar in Zhōngdū.
The altar of Shè (Shèwéi Zhì) was constructed such that
its outer perimeter was a wall,
with one spirit gate opening to the south,
this gate having three bays.
Inside, there was another wall forming a perimeter,
with one spirit gate opening in each of the east, west, south, and north directions,
each gate having three bays,
and each displaying twenty-four halberds.
The four corners were adorned with interlocking ornamental screens (fú sī),
and there were no roofs.
A slightly south-facing altar platform was situated in the center,
making three sides wide and open,
with one level and four flights of steps.
The five colors of earth were used to decorate their respective directions,
and the center was covered with yellow earth,
five zhàng wide
and five chǐ high.
The spirit tablet (zhǔ) was made of white stone,
two chǐ wide at the bottom,
tapering at the top,
shaped like a bell,
with half of it buried.
South of the altar,
chestnut trees were planted to mark it.
Near the west was the Jì altar (Jì Tán),
following the same regulations as the Shè altar but without a stone tablet.
The four outer gates (wěi mén) each had five bays,
the two side-chambers (shú) had three gates,
and the gates displayed twelve halberds.
The outer enclosure (wěi) had corner towers,
the faces of which were decorated according to their respective directional colors.
The food canopy (zhuàn màn) had four pillars,
located west of the northern outer gate,
facing north.
The spirit (shén) was outside the western outer gate,
facing south.
The official residence (xiè) was within the southern enclosure wall,
facing east-west.
There was a Wàngjì Hall (Wàngjì Táng) with three bays,
located north of it.
During rain, prostrations and worship were performed in this hall.
North and south of the hall were two-bay rooms,
which served as temporary quarters for the three presenters and the Sìtú during their fast.
Below the hall, facing north and south, were twenty bays of fasting chambers (zhāishè).
The outer gate had only one bay
and was not adorned with owl-tail ornaments (chīwěi).
Sacrifices were offered on the Wù day of the second month of spring and autumn,
with "Dēnggē" music performed,
and officials dispatched to conduct the ceremonies.
One Tàiwèi,
one Sìtú—
these were appointed by memorial.
For the secondary offering, one Tàicháng Qīng;
for the final offering, one Guānglù Qīng—
these were appointed by the province.
One Tàicháng Qīng,
one Guānglù Qīng,
one Jiāoshè Lìng,
one official from the Xuéshì Yuàn
were requested to have the sacrificial tablets (zhùbǎn) personally inscribed by the emperor.
One Dàlè Lìng,
two Tàiguān Lìng,
two Jiānjì Yùshǐ,
two Tàicháng Bóshì,
one Lǐnxī Lìng,
one Fènglǐ Láng,
two Xiélǜ Láng,
two Sīzūnléi,
one Fèngjué Jiǔguān,
seven Tàizhù,
four Zhùshǐ,
two Guànxǐ Guān,
two Juéxǐ Guān,
four Zhí jīn fěi Guān,
forty-eight Zhāiláng,
one Zànzhě,
ten Lǐzhí Guān—
these were appointed by the respective departments.
Twelve guards,
each dressed in the color of their direction,
with their uniforms provided by the government.
Four grave-diggers (jǔ yì),
dressed in black,
selected from the military,
with their clothing provided by themselves.
Three days before, at dawn,
the officials conducting the ceremony received their oath and admonition at the Shàngshū Shěng and Yùshǐ Tái.
The Tàicháng Sì led all officials to their positions,
and the Lǐzhí Guān announced
"Bow!"
They bowed to each other.
After this,
the Tàiwèi swore, saying:
"On the Wù day of the [specific] month and day,
sacrifices are offered at the Tàishè.
Each of you shall perform your duties.
Those who are disrespectful in this matter
shall be subject to the standing national penalties."
After reading,
they bowed to each other.
After this,
they withdrew.
All participating officials observed a loose fast for two days and a strict fast for one day.
Those who failed to fast but were otherwise engaged in the duties were nevertheless to perform them,
and they were still to practice the rites at the Shè Palace.
The commanders of the various guards (Zhū Wèi Lìng) were to lead their subordinates,
each to guard the gates of the Shè Palace with their directional regalia and attire.
All musicians (Dàlè Gōngrén) were to observe a strict fast for one night.
Three days before,
the Chénshè Jú arranged the positions for the sacrificial officials (gōng qīng and those below) inside the fasting chambers.
And four food canopies were set up outside the western spirit gate of the Shè Palace,
south of the gate,
facing west.
Two days before,
the Jiāoshè Lìng led his subordinates
to sweep the upper and lower parts of the altar.
The Dàlè Lìng set up the music on the altar.
The Jiāoshè Lìng dug two burial pits (yì kǎn) in the Rén position,
square and deep enough to contain the items,
with steps opening to the south.
He also set up a viewing platform for the burial (wàng yì wèi) north of the pits,
facing south.
The day before,
the Fènglǐláng (奉禮郎) led the Lǐzhíguān (禮直官)
to set up mats for the sacrificial officials, from the Gōngqīng (公卿) downwards, inside the west divine gate, south of the path.
The Zhíshìguān (執事官) were north of the path.
Each rank had a different position,
all in double lines,
facing east,
with the highest ranking to the south.
Two positions were set up for the Yùshǐ (御史) below the altar:
one northeast of the Tàishè (太社),
facing west,
and one northwest of the Tàijì (太稷),
facing east.
The Bóshì (博士) were each to their north.
A position was set up for the Fènglǐláng (奉禮郎) on the Jì (稷) altar, northwest,
with one Zànzhě (贊者) to its north,
facing east.
Two positions were set up for the Xiélǜláng (協律郎) on the altar, in the northeast corner,
both facing west.
A position was set up for the Dàyuèlìng (大樂令) between the two altars,
facing south.
Mats for the Xiànguān (獻官) were set up in front of the divine seats on each altar.
A position for inspecting the sacrificial animals (shěngshēngwèi 省牲位) was set up outside the west divine gate.
A board for the sacrificial animals (shēngbǎng 牲榜) was set up at the gate.
Two dark-colored sacrificial animals were placed in front,
and two more dark-colored sacrificial animals slightly behind.
(All three types of animals used were dark-colored.)
The highest ranking were to the north.
A position was set up for the Lǐnxīlìng (廩犧令) northeast of the animals,
facing south.
Positions were set up for the various Tàizhù (太祝) west of the animals,
each behind an animal.
The Zhùshǐ (祝史) accompanied them from behind,
all facing east.
A position was set up for the Tàichángqīng (太常卿) for inspecting the animals, in front, close to the south,
facing north.
Another position for a Yùshǐ (御史) was set up east of the Tàichángqīng (太常卿),
facing north.
The Tàichángqīng (太常卿), leading his subordinates,
set up the positions for the wine vessels.
Two Tàizūn (太罇), two Zhùzūn (著罇), two Xīzūn (犧罇), and two Shānlèi (山罍) were on the altar, in the north corner,
facing south.
Two Xiàngzūn (象罇), two Húzūn (壺罇), and two Shānlèi (山罍) were below the altar, west of the north steps,
facing south.
Two Xiàngzūn (象罇), two Zhùzūn (著罇), and two Shānlèi (山罍) for Hòutǔshì (后土氏) were west of the Tàishè (太社) wine vessels,
all with the highest ranking to the southeast.
Wine vessels for Tàijì (太稷) and Hòujì (后稷) were set up above and below their altars,
following the rites for Tàishè (太社) and Hòutǔ (后土).
Two washing positions were set up northwest of the Shè (社) altar,
facing south.
The Léi (罍) was east of the washbasin,
the Fěi (篚) was west of the washbasin,
facing north.
The Sīzūnléifěi (司罇罍篚) officials
each took their positions behind them.
The Fěi (篚) for jade and silk (yùbó 玉帛) was set up on the altar, at the location of the Zūndiàn (罇坫) stands.
Four settings were prepared,
each with ten Biān (籩), ten Dòu (豆), two Fǔ (簠), two Guǐ (簋), three Xíng (鉶), one Pán (槃), three Zǔ (俎), and four Diàn (坫).
One Biān (籩), one Dòu (豆), one Fǔ (簠), one Guǐ (簋), and three Zǔ (俎) were each placed inside the food canopy.
The Guānglùqīng (光祿卿), leading his subordinates,
entered to fill them.
The contents of the Biān (籩) were
dried fish, dried jujubes, shaped salt, deer jerky, hazel nuts, dried lotus root, peaches, water chestnuts, gorgon fruit, and chestnuts,
arranged in order.
The contents of the Dòu (豆) were
celery pickles, bamboo shoot pickles, mallow pickles, turnip pickles, leek pickles, fish paste, rabbit paste, pork slices, deer jerky paste, and fermented fish paste, arranged in order.
The Xíng (鉶) were filled with soup,
with added slippery herbs.
The Fǔ (簠) were filled with rice and millet,
the Guǐ (簋) with glutinous millet and foxtail millet.
Millet was placed before rice,
and foxtail millet before glutinous millet.
The Tàiguānlìng (太官令) entered to fill the Zūn (罇) and Léi (罍) with wine.
Each one Zūn (罇) was filled with plain water (xuánjiǔ 玄酒).
Five *kè* (刻) before dawn on the day of the sacrifice,
the Jiāoshèlìng (郊社令) ascended to set up the divine seats for Tàishè (太社) and Tàijì (太稷),
each on the altar close to the south,
facing north.
The divine seat for Hòutǔshì (后土氏) was set up to the left of the Tàishè (太社) divine seat,
and the divine seat for Hòujìshì (后稷氏) to the left of the Tàijì (太稷) divine seat,
both facing east.
All mats were made of sedge (guān 莞),
with added padded mattresses matching the color of the ceremonial silks.
The divine tablets were each at the head of their seats.
The day before,
the subordinates of the various Wèi (衞) prohibited pedestrians.
The Jiāoshèlìng (郊社令) and his subordinates
entered with the Zūndiàn (罇坫), Léi (罍), washbasins, and Fěi (篚) and placed them in position.
The Sīzūnléi (司罇罍), Fènglǐláng (奉禮郎), and Zhíshì (執事) ascended from the west steps of the Tàishè (太社) altar to wait.
The inspection of sacrificial utensils and the supervision of washing and rinsing
were all as per the Jīao Miào (郊廟) rites.
Ten *kè* (刻) before dawn on the day of the sacrifice,
the Tàiguānlìng (太官令) led the cooks (zǎirén 宰人) to butcher the sacrificial animals with the Luándāo (鸞刀).
The Zhùshǐ (祝史) took hair and blood in a Dòu (豆),
placing each at the food preparation area.
Blood was taken in a Pán (盤) and placed in front of the divine seats.
Then the animals were cooked.
Three *kè* (刻) before dawn,
all sacrificial officials donned their respective attire.
The Jiāoshèlìng (郊社令) and Tàiguānlìng (太官令) entered to fill the jade, silk, Zūn (罇), and Léi (罍).
The Tàiguānlìng (太官令) led the food presenters to fill the various Biān (籩), Dòu (豆), Fǔ (簠), and Guǐ (簋).
One *kè* (刻) before dawn,
the Fènglǐláng (奉禮郎) and Zànzhě (贊者) entered first to take their positions.
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) led the Guānglùqīng (光祿卿), Yùshǐ (御史), Bóshì (博士), various Tàizhù (太祝), Zhùshǐ (祝史), and Sīzūnléifěi (司罇罍篚) officials in through the west gate.
North of the Tàishè (太社) altar,
they stood in double lines, facing south, with the highest ranking to the east.
The Fènglǐláng (奉禮郎) said,
"Bow twice!"
The Zànzhě (贊者) relayed the command,
and all from the Yùshǐ (御史) downwards bowed twice.
Upon completion,
the Sīzūnléifěi (司罇罍篚) officials all took their positions.
The Zhùshǐ (祝史) carrying the plate of blood and the Tàizhù (太祝) ascended the altar via the west steps.
Each stood at the location of the Zūn (罇).
The Zhùshǐ (祝史) waited to bury the blood,
and the Dàzhù (大祝) waited to take the jade and silk.
The Dàyuèlìng (大樂令) led the musicians (gōngrén 工人) in.
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) led each sacrificial official in,
to take their positions and stand.
The Fènglǐláng (奉禮郎) said,
"All officials bow twice!"
The Zànzhě (贊者) said,
"All present bow twice!"
Those who had bowed earlier did not bow again.
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) advanced to the left of the Tàiwèi (太尉) and said,
"The officials have respectfully prepared;
please commence the ceremony."
He then retreated to his position.
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) led the Guānglùqīng (光祿卿) to the place for burying blood.
He then led the Zhùshǐ (祝史) carrying the plate of blood down from the west steps,
to the burial position.
The Guānglùqīng (光祿卿) buried the blood.
Upon completion,
he returned to his position.
The Zhùshǐ (祝史) returned the plate to the food canopy,
to wait to present the Dòu (豆) with hair and blood.
The Fènglǐláng (奉禮郎) said,
"All officials bow twice!"
All present bowed twice.
The various Tàizhù (太祝) took the jade and silk from the Fěi (篚),
each standing at the Zūn (尊) location.
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) led the Tàiwèi (太尉) to the washing position.
The Xiélǜláng (協律郎) knelt,
bowed low,
raised his banner,
and the music of Tàicùgōng Zhèngníng (太簇宮正寧) began.
Later washings were the same.
Upon reaching the washing position, he stood facing south,
and the music stopped.
After inserting his tablet, washing his hands, and wiping his hands,
he proceeded to the Tàishè (太社) altar.
The music of Yìngzhōnggōng Jiāníng (應鍾宮嘉寧) began.
Later ascensions to the altar were the same.
He ascended from the north steps,
the music stopped,
and he stood facing south.
The Tàizhù (太祝) handed the jade and silk to the Tàiwèi (太尉), facing west.
The Tàiwèi (太尉) received the jade and silk.
The jade for honoring the spirits was placed before the divine seat.
The jade for burial was placed on the silk.
Jade was not used for the accompanying deities.
The jade used consisted of two *guī* (圭) with a base,
contained in a box.
The burial jade was made of jade stone.
The silk used was black *zēng* (繒),
eighteen *chǐ* (尺) long.
The music of Tàicùgōng Jiāníng (太簇宮嘉寧) began.
The same applied to Tàijì (太稷).
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) led the Tàiwèi (太尉) forward,
knelt facing south, and placed the offering before the Tàishè (太社) seat,
bowed low,
and rose.
He led the Tàiwèi (太尉) to retreat slightly,
and at the mat position, he bowed twice facing south.
The Tàizhù (太祝) handed the silk to the Tàiwèi (太尉).
The Tàiwèi (太尉) received the silk,
knelt facing west, and placed the offering before the Hòutǔ (后土) divine seat,
bowed low,
and rose.
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) led the Tàiwèi (太尉) to retreat slightly,
bowed twice facing west.
Upon completion,
the music stopped.
The Lǐzhíguān (禮直官) led the Tàiwèi (太尉) down from the northern steps,
proceeded to the Tàijì (太稷) altar,
washed, ascended, and offered jade and silk according to the rites for Tàishè (太社) and Hòutǔ (后土).
The Zhùshǐ (祝史) brought in hair and blood,
each ascending by their respective steps.
The dou (豆) for hair and blood were placed separately in another dou.
All the Tàizhù (太祝) received them on the altar
and jointly advanced to present them before the divine seats.
The Zhùshǐ withdrew and stood by the zūn (罇).
After the Tàiwèi had ascended and offered the jade and silk,
the Tàiguānlìng (太官令) went out to lead the servers of offerings,
who presented the offerings outside the west gate.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Sītú (司徒) out to the place of offerings.
The Sītú presented the zǔ (俎) for Tàishè.
After all the Tàizhù had presented the hair and blood,
the Lǐzhíguān and Tàiguānlìng led the offerings for Tàishè and Tàijì in through the main gate,
and the offerings for the secondary seats in through the left side gate.
As the offerings first entered the gate,
music began, playing the Tàicùgōng Zhèngníng (太簇宮正寧) melody.
When the offerings reached the steps,
the music ceased.
The Zhùshǐ jointly advanced to remove the dou of hair and blood,
descending from the west steps to exit.
The offerings for Tàishè and Tàijì ascended from the northern steps,
and the offerings for the secondary seats ascended from the west steps.
All the Tàizhù greeted and guided them on the altar,
and after they were all arranged before the divine seats,
the Lǐzhíguān led the Sītú, who had already descended from the west steps,
music began,
returned to their positions,
and the music ceased.
All the Tàizhù returned to the zūn.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi to the léixǐ (罍洗) position,
music began,
upon reaching the position,
the music ceased.
After washing hands and rinsing the jiao (爵),
the Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi to the Tàishè altar,
ascended from the northern steps,
music began,
upon reaching the Tàishè jiǔzūn (酒罇) position,
the music ceased.
The attendant holding the zūn lifted it,
the attendant in charge handed a jiao to the Tàiwèi,
the Tàiwèi held the jiao,
the Tàiguānlìng poured the wine,
upon completion,
music began, playing the Tàicùgōng Fùníng (太簇宮阜寧) melody.
The same applied to Tàijì.
The Tàiwèi handed the jiao to the attendant in charge.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi before the divine seat of Tàishè,
the attendant in charge handed a jiao to the Tàiwèi,
who knelt facing south to offer the jiao,
upon completion,
handed the jiao to the attendant in charge,
bowed deeply,
and rose.
The Tàiwèi retreated slightly,
and the music ceased.
The Dúzhùguān (讀祝官) and Pěngzhùguān (捧祝官) advanced to the right before the divine seat,
knelt facing west to read the prayer,
upon reading it,
the Dúzhùguān bowed once,
and each returned to the zūn.
After the Tàiwèi bowed,
he proceeded to the jiǔzūn for the secondary seat.
The attendant in charge lifted it,
the attendant in charge handed a jiao to the Tàiwèi,
the Tàiwèi held the jiao,
the Tàiguānlìng poured the wine,
upon completion,
music began, playing the Tàicùgōng Zhāoníng (太簇宮昭寧) melody.
The Tàiwèi handed the jiao to the attendant in charge.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi forward before the divine seat of Hòutǔ,
the attendant in charge handed a jiao to the Tàiwèi,
who knelt facing west to offer the jiao,
upon completion,
handed the jiao to the attendant in charge,
bowed deeply,
and rose.
The Tàiwèi retreated slightly,
and the music ceased.
The reading of the prayer was as in the above rite.
The Tàiwèi bowed twice,
upon completion,
the Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi down from the northern steps,
music began,
upon reaching the léixǐ position,
the music ceased.
After washing hands and rinsing the jiao,
the Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi to the Tàijì altar,
ascended from the northern steps,
and everything was as in the rites for Tàishè and Hòutǔ,
with the same melodies.
Upon completion,
the Lǐzhíguān led the Tàiwèi back to his original position.
For the second and final libations,
the washing, ascending, and offering were all according to the rites for the Tàiwèi.
The Lǐzhíguān led the final libationer down to resume his position,
and the music ceased.
All the Tàizhù advanced to remove the dou,
music began, playing the Yìngzhōnggōng Yúníng (應鍾宮娛寧) melody,
they returned to the zūn,
and the music ceased.
For those removing items, one biān (籩) and one dou were taken,
slightly moved from their original places.
The Fènglǐ (奉禮) said,
"Bestow the sacrificial meat."
The Zànzhě (贊者) said,
"All officials bow twice,"
and those present all bowed twice.
The Lǐzhíguān advanced to the right of the Tàiwèi,
inviting him to the wàngyì (望瘞) position,
the Yùshǐ (御史) and Bóshì (博士) followed,
standing facing south.
Before all the officials were about to bow,
the Tàizhù, holding a fěi (篚), advanced before the divine seat to take the jade and silk.
The Zhāiláng (齋郎) carried the sacrificial body on a zǔ, along with millet rice and jiao wine,
(the "body" referred to the left thigh of the sacrificial animal.)
Each descended from their respective steps on the altar,
placed the jade, silk, and offerings in the pit,
upon completion,
the Fènglǐ said,
"It may be buried,"
two people each from the east and west of the pit placed half a pit of earth,
upon completion,
the Lǐzhíguān advanced to the left of the Tàiwèi and said,
"The rite is concluded,"
then led the Tàiwèi out,
and the sacrificial officials and those below followed in sequence to exit.
The Lǐzhíguān led the Yùshǐ, Bóshì, and those below to return to their officiant positions,
and stood still.
The Fènglǐ said,
"Bow twice,"
the Yùshǐ and those below all bowed twice,
upon completion,
exited.
The artisans exited in sequence.
The prayer tablet was burned in the Zhāifāng (齋坊).
The Guānglùqīng (光祿卿) presented the bestowed meat,
the Yùshǐ went to his position to inspect it,
the Guānglùqīng bowed twice towards the imperial palace,
then withdrew.
For sacrifices and offerings in the prefectures and commanderies,
the old rites of the Táng (唐) and Sòng (宋) dynasties were followed.
Wind, Rain, and Thunder Masters.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng (明昌),
the Lǐguān (禮官) stated:
"Among the great affairs of the state,
none is more important than sacrifice.
Kings serve the spirits,
praying for blessings and protection,
all for the sake of the people.
Our state, apart from the five great sacrifices of dì (禘) and xiá (祫) at the ancestral temple,
has only Shèjì (社稷), Yuèzhèn (嶽鎮), and Hǎidú (海瀆) established as regular sacrifices.
However, the rites for Heaven and Earth, Sun and Moon, and the Wind, Rain, and Thunder Masters are still incomplete.
It is fitting to issue an edict to the relevant authorities to deliberate and establish the ceremonial procedures and report them."
The Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) reported:
"For Heaven and Earth, Sun and Moon,
either the Emperor personally sacrifices or orders relevant authorities to act on his behalf.
As for the Wind, Rain, and Thunder Masters, they are classified as medium sacrifices,
and it is appropriate to order relevant authorities to act on his behalf.
Furthermore, these are also worshipped by prefectures and counties,
so it is appropriate to implement them first."
The edict was approved.
An altar was then built southeast outside the Jǐngfēngmén (景豐門),
in the xùn (巽) direction (southeast) relative to the palace gate.
Annually, on the Chou (丑) day after the Beginning of Spring,
sacrifices were offered to the Fēngshī (風師).
The sacrificial animals, silk, and cooked offerings
followed the rites for medium sacrifices.
Another altar was built southwest outside the Duānlǐmén (端禮門),
in the kūn (坤) direction (southwest) relative to the palace gate.
On the Shēn (申) day after the Beginning of Summer, sacrifices were offered to the Yǔshī (雨師).
The rites were as for medium sacrifices,
with one sheep and one pig each.
On that day,
sacrifices were offered to the Léishī (雷師) at a position below the altar.
The rites were the same as for minor sacrifices,
with one libation,
one sheep,
and no pig.
The prayer stated,
"The Son of Heaven respectfully dispatches his servant [name]"
and so on.
The Five Sacred Mountains (Yuè), Four Marchmounts (Zhèn), Four Seas (Hǎi), and Four Rivers (Dú).
In the fourth year of Dàdìng,
the officials of rites said:
"The Yuè, Zhèn, Hǎidú [gods]
should be sacrificed to on the days of迎氣 (yíngqì) during the Five Suburbs rituals."

An imperial edict commanded that, in accordance with the ceremonial codes, sacrifices be offered at their respective temples on the four beginning-of-season days and on the Earth Sovereign day (tǔwáng rì).
For those in other regions, distant sacrifices were to be performed.
On Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring),

sacrifices were made to Dōngyuè (Eastern Marchmount) in Tàinán Zhōu, Dōngzhèn (Eastern鎮) in Yìdū Fǔ, Dōnghǎi (Eastern Sea) in Láizhōu, and Dōngdú Dàhuái (Eastern Waterway, the Huai River) in Tángzhōu.
On Lìxià (Beginning of Summer),
distant sacrifices were made to Nányuè Héngshān (Southern Marchmount Mount Heng) and Nánzhèn Kuàijīshān (Southern鎮 Mount Kuaiji) in Hénán Fǔ;
to Nánhǎi (Southern Sea) and Nándú Dàjiāng (Southern Waterway, the Yangtze River) in Láizhōu.
On the Earth Sovereign day in the third month of summer (Jìxià tǔwáng rì),
sacrifices were made to Zhōngyuè (Central Marchmount) in Hénán Fǔ and Zhōngzhèn Huòshān (Central鎮 Mount Huo) in Píngyáng Fǔ.
On Lìqiū (Beginning of Autumn),
sacrifices were made to Xīyuè Huàshān (Western Marchmount Mount Hua) in Huázhōu, Xīzhèn Wúshān (Western鎮 Mount Wu) in Lǒngzhōu;
distant sacrifices were made to Xīhǎi (Western Sea) and Xīdú (Western Waterway) in Hézhōng Fǔ.
On Lìdōng (Beginning of Winter),
sacrifices were made to Běiyuèshān (Northern Marchmount Mountain) in Dìngzhōu, Běizhèn Yīwūlǘshān (Northern鎮 Mount Yi-wu-lü) in Guǎngníng Fǔ;
distant sacrifices were made to Běihǎi (Northern Sea) and Běidú Dàjì (Northern Waterway, the Ji River) in Mèngzhōu.
The titles of nobility and enfeoffments remained as in the Táng and Sòng dynasties.
During the Míngchāng (明昌) period,
following the request of the Yíshān (沂山) Daoist Yáng Dàoquán,
Yíshān was enfeoffed as Dōng'ān Wáng (東安王),
Wúshān as Chéngdé Wáng (成德王),
Huòshān as Yìnglíng Wáng (應靈王),
Kuàijīshān as Yǒngxīng Wáng (永興王),
Yīwūlǘshān as Guǎngníng Wáng (廣寧王),
Huái (淮) as Chángyuán Wáng (長源王),
Jiāng (江) as Huìyuán Wáng (會源王),
Hé (河) as Xiǎnsheng Língyuán Wáng (顯聖靈源王),
and Jì (濟) as Qīngyuán Wáng (清源王).
Each year, an envoy was dispatched with an imperial seal, an inscribed prayer tablet (zhùbǎn), a coffer (lián) of incense (xiāng),
traveling by post-horse (chéng rì) to the location,
to direct the senior and junior officials of the prefecture and county in performing the rituals.
The ritual employed three offerings (sānxiàn).

There was one prayer reader (dúzhù guān), two prayer bearers (pěngzhù guān), two hand-washing officials (guànxǐ guān), two cup-washing officials (juéxǐ guān), one cup bearer (fèngjué guān), one supervisor of zūn and yí vessels (sīzūnyí), and four ritual directors (lǐzhí guān),
filled by clerks from the prefecture/state (zhōu fǔ sī lì).
Three days prior,
the officials responsible for performing the ritual and the attendants were to observe two days of dispersed fasting (sànzhāi).
They would continue their duties as before,
lodging in the principal hall (zhèngqǐn),
following the usual procedure.
Two days prior,
the appropriate authorities (yǒusī) would set up stations for the performing officials and attendants outside the temple gate.
Those in charge of the temple would sweep clean the interior and exterior of the temple.
One day prior,
the appropriate authorities would lead the sacrificial animals to the shrine (císuǒ).
The sacrificing officials (xiǎngguān) and those below them, in ordinary attire, would inspect the food offerings
and check if the sacrificial animals were plump and abundant.
On the day of sacrifice, five *ke* (quarters of an hour) before the Chǒu hour (1-3 AM),
the attendants would set up the prayer tablet (zhùbǎn) to the right of the deity's position,
placing it on a stand (diàn),
and also place blood bowls (xuèdòu) at the food offering station.
Next, the sacrificial vessels were arranged,
all placed on mats,
and filled by those in charge of the food offerings.
To the left, ten *biān* (baskets) in three rows,
with the rightmost as the uppermost,
filled with dried dates, dried jujubes, shaped salt, dried fish, dried venison, hazelnuts, dried peaches, water caltrops, fox nuts, and chestnuts.
To the right, ten *dòu* (bowls) in three rows,
with the leftmost as the uppermost,
filled with pickled celery, pickled bamboo shoots, pickled chives, pickled mallow, pickled turnip, fish paste, rabbit paste, pounded pork, deer jerky, and thick minced meat paste.
To the left, two *fǔ* (rectangular vessels),
filled with millet and rice.
To the right, two *guǐ* (round vessels),
filled with panicled millet and glutinous millet.
Two *zǔ* (sacrificial stands),
filled with parts of the sacrificial animal.
Next, two *xīzūn* (wine vessels decorated with ox patterns) and two *xiàngzūn* (wine vessels decorated with elephant patterns) were set up,
in the southeast corner of the hall,
facing north, with the western one higher.
The *xīzūn* were in front,
filled with fine wine.
From the *xīzūn*,
the initial offering official (chūxiàn guān) poured wine.
From the *xiàngzūn*,
the secondary and final offering officials poured wine.
Additionally, one *tàizūn* and one *shānzūn* were set up,
in front of the deity's position,
set up but not poured from.
The appropriate authorities set up candles in front of the deity's position.
Two washing basins (*xǐ*) were placed
below the eastern steps,
directly to the north of the eastern eaves,
with a *léi* (wine vessel) to the east of the washing basin,
with a ladle added.
A *fěi* (basket for towels) was to the west of the washing basin,
spread open to the south,
filled with towels.
Those holding the *léi* and *fěi* stood behind them.
Additionally, bowing positions (yīwèi) were set up outside the temple gate,
with the initial offering official to the west,
facing east;
the secondary, final offering officials, and the prayer reader to the east,
facing south,
with the northern one higher.
A burial pit (yìkǎn) was opened in the *rén* (壬) direction within the inner courtyard of the temple.
On the day of sacrifice, five *ke* before the Chǒu hour,
the attendants would each take their places.
Those in charge of the food offerings would lead their subordinates
to complete filling the offering vessels.
All sacrificing officials would wear their respective robes,
and their movements, along with those of the attendants, would be guided by the announcers (zànzhě).
After inspecting the arrangements,
they would retreat to their positions.
The initial offering official and those below him were led to the bowing position outside the south gate of the temple,
stood still,
and the ritual announcer (zànlǐzhě) announced,
"Bow."
Next, the prayer reader was led to ascend the hall and take his position.
Next, the initial offering official was led to the hand-washing position, stood facing north,
inserted his *hù* (tablet) into his belt, washed his hands, dried his hands,
held his *hù*,
went to the cup-washing position, stood facing north,
inserted his *hù*,
washed the cup,
handed the cup to the attendant,
held his *hù*,
ascended the hall,
and went to the pouring vessel station, standing facing west.
The attendant handed the cup to the initial offering official.
The initial offering official inserted his *hù* and held the cup,
the person holding the *zūn* vessel raised it,
and the attendant poured the wine.
The initial offering official handed the cup to the attendant,
held his *hù*,
went to the deity's position, stood facing north,
inserted his *hù*,
knelt,
and the attendant handed the cup to the initial offering official.
The initial offering official held the cup and offered wine three times,
after placing the cup down,
held his *hù*,
bowed low,
rose,
and stood briefly.
Next, the prayer reader was led to the deity's position, stood facing east.
Inserted his *hù*,
knelt,
read the prayer,
after which,
held his *hù*,
rose,
and returned to his position.
The initial offering official bowed twice,
and the ritual announcer led the initial offering official to return to his position.
Next, the secondary offering official was led to pour and offer,
all following the ritual of the initial offering official.
Next, the final offering official,
all following the ritual of the secondary offering official.
The announcer led the initial offering official to the deity's position, standing facing north,
the attendant poured clear wine into a cup,
brought it to the right of the initial offering official,
the initial offering official knelt,
offered wine,
tasted wine,
and placed the cup down.
The attendant brought forward a *zǔ* (meat stand),
removed the second joint of the front leg of the sacrificial meat from before the deity's seat,
placed it together on one *zǔ*,
and handed it to the initial offering official.
The initial offering official handed it to the attendant.
The initial offering official took the cup,
then drank,
emptied the cup,
and the attendant came forward to receive the cup,
returning it to the stand.
The initial offering official rose,
bowed twice,
and the announcer led the initial offering official to return to his position.
The announcer said:
"Bow twice."
(Those who have already drunk the blessed wine and received the sacrificial meat do not bow.)
The secondary offering official and those below him all bowed twice.
After bowing,
the initial offering official and those below were led to the viewing and burial position (wàngyì wèi),
placed the food offerings into the pit,
with two people from each of the eastern and western side rooms.
The announcer said,
"It can be buried,"
and earth was filled into half the pit.
Then he said,
"The ritual is complete,"
and the initial offering official and those below him were led out.
The prayer reader and those holding the *zūn*, *léi*, and *fěi* all returned to their positions and stood still.
The announcer said,
"Bow twice,"
and after bowing twice,
they then exited.
The prayer tablet was burned at the fasting place.
Collation Notes
Volume 16, Rites 8: Xuānshèng Miào, Wǔchéng Wáng Miào, former emperors and kings, various gods and miscellaneous sacrifices, prayers for expiation, bowing to Heaven, national bowing ceremony
Xuānshèng Miào.
In the second month, on the day Wùzǐ, of the first year of Huángtǒng,
Xīzōng proceeded to the temple of Wénxuānwáng to offer sacrifices.
He bowed twice facing north,
and turned to his Confucian ministers, saying:
"One must not fail to strive to do good.
Although Kǒngzǐ had no official position,
his Way is to be revered,
enabling all generations to look up to him like this."
In the fourteenth year of Dàdìng,
the Guózǐjiān stated:
"In the spring and autumn, on the first Dīng day of the middle month,
the Xīdiàn ceremony is performed for Wénxuānwáng.
Sixty strings of cash from the supervisor's official funds are used,
merely to prepare tea, food, and other items,
arranged on large and small trays.
Music from the Liúshǒusī is used,
with musicians serving as ritual officers.
Officers from the Cāngcháng and other departments are gathered to assist in the ceremony.
This does not conform to ancient rites.
We humbly observe that the nation has long enjoyed peace,
and its institutions and cultural artifacts ought to be splendidly complete,
to illuminate ten thousand generations.
Furthermore, the capital is the foremost place of goodness,
looked up to by all four directions.
We propose that the ritual vessels for the Xīdiàn,
and the sequence of performing the rites,
should be deliberated and fixed.
Moreover, Yǎnguógōng received the sacred teachings firsthand,
and Zōuguógōng vigorously upheld the sacred teachings.
They should be placed to the left and right of the statue of Xuānsheng.
Currently, Mèngzǐ is in the back hall in informal attire,
and there is still an empty position next to the statue of Xuānsheng.
It is ritually appropriate to move the statue of Mèngzǐ to the right of Xuānsheng,
facing Yánzǐ,
to recast his crown and robes,
and to decorate him in ceremonial attire,
completely following the old system."
The ritual officials consulted and adapted the Kāiyuán Lǐ of the Táng dynasty,
and proposed the scale of the Xīdiàn ceremony: For Wénxuānwáng, Yǎnguógōng, and Zōuguógōng, each position would have ten biān and dòu, one xīzūn, one xiàngzūn, two fǔ and guǐ, two zǔ, and one zhùbǎn,
all set on tables.
For the seventy-two sages and twenty-one former Confucians,
each position would have one biān, one dòu, and one jué.
Each of the two side halls would have two xiàngzūn.
In total, one hundred and twenty-three biān and dòu,
six fǔ and guǐ,
six zǔ,
three xīzūn,
seven xiàngzūn,
and ninety-four jué would be used.
All zūn would have pedestals.
Two léi,
two xǐ,
two fěi and sháo each,
and six wǔ would be used.
For the principal and accompanying worshipers, mats for zūn, léi, zǔ, and dòu would be provided,
approximately thirty pieces in total.
Zūn mats would be made of reeds,
and zǔ and dòu mats of rush.
The sacrificial animals would be three sheep and three pigs each,
and twenty bottles of wine.
The ceremony would involve three libations,
performed by the Jìjiǔ, Sīyè, and Bóshì.
There would be two Fēndiàn officials,
one Dúzhù official,
one Tàiguānlìng,
two Pěngzhù officials,
one Léixǐ official,
one Juéxǐ official,
two Jīnfěi officials,
and eleven Lǐzhí officials.
Students would accompany in Confucian attire.
Music would use dēnggē,
with one Dàlèlíng,
filled by an officer from the department,
and thirty-nine musicians.
For welcoming the spirits,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Láiníng zhī qū" would be played three times,
with lyrics:
"The capital grandly transforms,
the temple hall made anew.
The spirits arrive and manifest,
their majesty and solemnity fully displayed.
Solemn and dignified are the hanging banners,
lofty and sacred the True One.
From this, literature begins,
observed by all regions."
For the first offering's ritual washing,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Jìngníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"How great is the Uncrowned King,
his conduct utterly pure.
For two thousand years,
this culture has not fallen.
A propitious day and hour are chosen,
and worship is performed.
Washing hands in the courtyard,
the solemn sacrifice is complete."
For ascending the steps,
the melody "Nánlǚgōng Sùníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"How majestic is the Sacred Master,
his Way complete, his virtue profound.
He refined and elucidated the Five Constants,
leaving endless teachings.
We elevate the Confucian academy,
pursuing his enduring legacy.
Solemn worship is offered with reverence,
ascending and descending with grace."
For offering the silks,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Héníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"Heaven gave birth to the sage,
more virtuous than Yáo or Shùn.
The more one looks up, the higher he is,
ground but not worn thin.
The new temple is completed,
its palace walls many rén high.
Envoys offer sacrifices,
this culture revives."
For descending the steps,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Ānníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"Endowed with spirit from Níqiū,
leaving fragrance at Quèlǐ.
Since the birth of humankind,
who equals the Master?
The new shrine stands towering,
observed by all four directions.
The libation announces completion,
respectfully following the rites."
For Yǎnguógōng's libation,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Jìníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"Among the disciples of the Sacred Master,
Yán was foremost.
He was almost perfect,
thus deserving of shared offerings.
With huángguī and gǔnyī,
his solemn image is grand.
Placed in the spirit shrine,
adding glory to our party."
For Zōuguógōng's libation,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Tàiníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"When Zhōu declined,
the royal order fell.
Then a true Confucian was born,
with grand talent to save the era.
His words became scriptures,
pure in benevolence and righteousness.
Vigorously upholding the sacred work,
he will endure for ten thousand generations."
For the second and final offerings,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Xiánníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"Oh, how brilliant is the sacred power,
establishing the ultimate with Heaven.
There are those who inherit its flow,
the humane and imperial virtues.
Not only did he establish words,
teaching and guiding the kingdom.
Resplendent is our civilization,
with countless ritual sacrifices."
For sending off the spirits,
the melody "Gūxǐgōng Láiníng zhī qū" would be played,
with lyrics:
"Auspiciously pure are the offerings,
abundantly good and timely.
Upright words and beautiful speech,
the spirits have responded.
This offering is fitting and appropriate,
the spirits return with blessings.
Since this worship began,
peace has reached its zenith."
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
on the Dīng day of spring,
Zhāngzōng personally officiated the sacrifice,
with imperial princes acting as the second and final officiants,
imperial family members assisting,
and civil and military officials helping with the offerings.
The emperor personally composed the encomium.
Those previously enfeoffed as gōng were raised to guógōng,
those as hóu to guóhóu,
and those from Chéngbó downwards were all enfeoffed as hóu.
Xuānzōng moved to Biàn,
where a temple was built inside the Huìcháomén gate.
Annual sacrifices followed the established rites,
with one sheep and one pig each for Xuānsheng, Yán, and Mèng.
Other aspects were similar to minor sacrifices,
using a total of eight sheep,
and no pigs.
The Xīdiàn ceremonies in other prefectures all followed the Táng rites.
Temple of Wǔchéngwáng.
In the 6th year of Tàihé
an imperial edict ordered the construction of a temple for Zhāoliè Wǔchéng Wáng within the right side of the palace courtyard,
inside the Lìzé Gate.
Its regulations strictly followed the old Tang dynasty system.
The ritual consisted of three offerings,
officials below the fourth rank participated,
the ceremony was equivalent to a medium sacrifice,
and it was held on the *shàngwù* day of the second month.
In the 7th year,
Wányán Kuāng and others stated:
"The founding meritorious officials of our dynasty
should be enshrined as co-worshippers according to ritual."
Thereupon,
Qín Wáng Zōnghán was made to accompany Zǐfáng in co-worship with Wǔchéng Wáng,
while GuǎnMù and those below him were demoted.
Furthermore, Chǔ Wáng Zōngxióng, Zōngwàng, Zōngbì and others were promoted to sit beside Wǔchéng Wáng,
while Hán Xìn and those below him were demoted to stand in the side corridors.
Wáng Měng, Mùróng Kè and over twenty other people were also removed,
and Golden officials such as Liáo Wáng Xiáyě were added.
For the sacrifice,
Wǔchéng Wáng, Zōnghán, and Zǐfáng each received one sheep and one pig.
The remaining (co-worshippers) jointly received eight sheep,
with no pigs.
When Xuānzōng relocated to Biàn,
a temple was built according to the regulations on the right side of the palace courtyard inside the Huìcháo Gate,
and the spring and autumn *shàngwù* sacrifices remained as before.
For various emperors of previous dynasties,
a sacrifice was made once every three years.
During the middle month of spring, Fúxī was sacrificed in Chénzhōu,
Shénnóng in Bózhōu,
Xuānyuán in Fángzhōu,
Shàohào in Yǎnzhōu,
Zhuānxū in Kāizhōu,
Gāoxīn in Guīdé Fǔ,
Táotáng in Píngyáng Fǔ,
Yú Shùn, Xià Yǔ, and Chéng Tāng in Hézhōng Fǔ,
and Zhōu Wén Wáng and Wǔ Wáng in Jīngzhào Fǔ.
In the 3rd year of Tàihé,
the Shàngshū Shěng reported:
"The Tàicháng Sì states: 'Regarding the sacrificial tablets for Dì Kù, Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Hàn Zǔ in the Kāiyuán rites, please request the imperial signature.
In the Kāibǎo rites, please request the imperial signature for Xī, Xuān, Zhuānxū, Dì Kù, Táotáng, Nǚwā, Chéng Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ.
From Hàn Gāozǔ onwards, twenty-seven emperors do not require the imperial signature.'
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Yì, Zuǒ Chéng Kuāng, and Tàicháng Bóshì Wēndíhǎn Tiānxīng stated: 'The gods of the various sacred mountains each have their own domain,
and are relied upon by the state.
It is indeed appropriate to request the imperial signature.
As for ancient emperors,
who are distant and obscure,
their inclusion in the medium sacrifices is already generous,
and an imperial signature is not necessary.'
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Jíkāng and Xuàn believed that the Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ were all rulers who established teachings for the world,
and that during the Tang and Song dynasties, all their sacrifices received the imperial signature.
Now, to demote the sacrificial tablets by not signing them
might be considered incomplete in terms of ritual.
It would be better to simply follow the precedent of external sacrifices to the gods of the land and grain and the offerings to Wénxuān Wáng,
not dispatching imperial tablets,
but instead allowing the Xuéshì Yuàn to draft the sacrificial texts,
and distribute them to various places as a permanent regulation."
An imperial decree ordered that the sacrificial tablets be dispatched as scheduled,
but without requesting the imperial signature.
Chángbái Shān.
In the 12th year of Dàdìng,
officials stated:
"Chángbái Shān is in the land where our kingdom arose.
It is proper to show it respect and veneration,
and to discuss bestowing a noble title and
building a temple."
In the 12th month,
the Lǐbù, Tàicháng, and Xuéshì Yuàn reported an imperial decree to enfeoff it as Xīngguó Língyìng Wáng,
and to build a temple in the northern part of the mountain.
In the 3rd month of the 15th year,
the imperial edict and ceremonial objects were finalized and reported:
a nine-streamer crown,
nine-emblem robes,
a jade tablet (*guī*),
a jade scroll and its box,
incense and silk offerings,
the imperial edict scroll and prayer text.
An envoy and a deputy, each one official,
were dispatched to Huìníng Fǔ.
The officiating officials observed two days of relaxed fasting and
one day of strict fasting.
The responsible authorities arranged the temple as prescribed.
Outside the temple gate, the jade scroll, the emperor's ceremonial robe, and a tent were set up.
The *yázhàng* (yak-tail banner), flags, drums, and accompanying items were treated with the ceremony of the first rank.
The ritual involved three offerings,
like the sacrifices to the Five Sacred Mountains and River Deities.
The text of the imperial edict stated:
"The Emperor speaks: Since the separation of the two primary forces (heaven and earth),
the divine beauty of mountains and peaks has gathered in their respective regions.
When a state is about to flourish,
Heaven truly brings it about.
To respond to divine blessings,
sacrifices must be offered.
Thus, where the kingly enterprise originated,
there was Qíyáng.
The ranking of mountains and rivers is recorded
in the Yu Canon.
This Chángbái,
which carries our Jīn virtue,
we look up to its height;
it is truly the guardian of our old homeland.
The Húntóng River flows radiantly,
its source originating from here.
Orderly and profound,
it possesses the dao of assistance.
The successive sages prospered and flourished,
up to Tàizǔ,
whose divine martial presence was victorious
and invincible throughout the world,
and who established himself as the divine lord.
I, a humble person,
have inherited this sacred lineage.
Within the Four Seas,
there is no famous mountain or great river that is not duly ranked.
How much more so, this place upon which the royal enterprise depends,
looking to its foothills,
can its rites be diminished?
Its vestments and noble title, if not above those of dukes and marquises,
would be insufficient to honor it.
Therefore, I now dispatch a certain official,
carrying the ceremonial staff and bearing all necessary items,
to enfeoff the spirit of this mountain as Xīngguó Língyìng Wáng.
I further command the responsible authorities to offer sacrifices annually.
Alas!
May the enjoyment of temple offerings
last for ten thousand myriad years.
The auspiciousness of Jīn
is boundless like the mountain.
Is this not magnificent!"
From then on,
incense was annually offered,
and the responsible authorities were ordered to choose a day in the middle months of spring and autumn for the sacrifice.
In the 10th month of the 4th year of Míngchāng,
with imperial robes, jade tablets, and ceremonial objects prepared,
the emperor ascended the Dà'ān Diàn,
using eight hundred people with yellow banners and staff-bearers,
and five hundred people in ceremonial procession,
to re-enfeoff it as Kāitiān Hóngshèng Dì.
Dàfáng Shān.
In the 21st year of Dàdìng,
an imperial edict enfeoffed the god of Dàfáng Shān, the imperial mausoleum site, as Bǎolíng Gōng,
with an eight-streamer crown, seven-emblem robes, a jade tablet (*guī*), a scroll, incense, and silk offerings.
An envoy and a deputy, holding the ceremonial staff, performed the rites,
all following the ceremony for enfeoffing Chángbái Shān.
The text of the imperial edict stated:
"The Emperor speaks: In ancient times, when states were established and capitals founded,
there were always famous mountains and great rivers to serve as strategic strongholds.
Our nation has now established its capital in Yān,
and looking west to the suburban territories,
the majestic Dàfáng stands tall,
exquisitely prominent and robust,
the source of clouds and rain,
looked up to by all people,
where the ancestral mausoleums are located.
Reflecting on the ancient order of sacred mountains and guardians,
all recorded in the sacrificial canons,
how could this Dàfáng
have its rites omitted?
Its noble title and vestments shall be ranked above those of marquises and earls,
which should be sufficient to honor it.
Therefore, I now dispatch a certain official,
bearing all necessary items, to enfeoff the god as Bǎolíng Gōng.
I reiterate the command to the responsible authorities
to offer sacrifices annually.
Within its enfeoffed domain,
it is forbidden to gather firewood, hunt, or fish.
This is hereby enacted as law."
Thereafter,
after the envoy completed the rites at the imperial mausoleums,
the imperial mausoleum official performed a single offering ritual.
Húntóng Jiāng.
In the 25th year of Dàdìng,
officials stated:
"In the past, when Tàizǔ conquered Liáo,
he rode his horse directly across the river.
The river god assisted him,
and its divine efficacy was clearly manifested.
It is appropriate to repair its shrine
and bestow an additional noble title."
Thus, the god was enfeoffed as Xīngguó Yìngshèng Gōng,
and sacrifices were offered according to the Chángbái Shān ceremony,
while the enfeoffment ritual followed the precedent of Bǎolíng Gōng.
Its investiture document said:
"In the past, our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Wǔyuán,
received the clear mandate of Heaven.
He swept away the desolation and disorder of the declining Liáo dynasty,
and led his army forth,
reaching the Great River.
The vast, mighty current
was crossed without boats.
Even Mù Mǎn crossing the river with turtles forming a bridge,
and Guāngwǔ crossing the Hé river when the water froze,
seem insignificant when viewed from today.
In the year of Zhíxú (the jǐ-hài year),
in the fourth month of early summer,
I traveled to the old homeland,
standing by the river with a long sigh.
I looked up to the achievements of the Founding Ancestor in establishing the foundation,
and admired the efficacy of the River Spirit.
Upon reaching the Upper Capital,
I discussed the ceremony for its veneration and exaltation.
For in ancient times, the Five Peaks were regarded as equal to the Sān Gōng,
and the Four Rivers as equal to the Zhūhóu.
Since the Táng dynasty,
they have enjoyed the esteemed title of emperor or king.
This is not merely an embellishment of later generations,
but also a natural consequence of honoring virtue and rewarding merit.
Moreover, this river originates from Chángbái,
flows through the Imperial Capital,
and indeed supports the imperial destiny.
If we do not grant it the title of Duke of the Highest Rank (shànggōng),
then we cannot express our gratitude for its divine blessings.
Now I dispatch an official (mǒu guān mǒu),
holding the staff of authority and carrying the ritual objects, to invest the spirit as Xìngguó Yìngshèng Gōng.
I further command the relevant authorities
to offer sacrifices annually.
Alas!
To make the temple majestic,
and to 正封爵 (rectify the feudal title),
the rites are indeed complete.
May the spirit extend its lasting efficacy and virtue,
to assist our nation for a myriad of years.
And may the spirit enjoy temple sacrifices eternally.
How splendid is this not!"
Jiāyīn Hóu.
In Dàdìng 25th year,
an imperial edict enfeoffed the forest spirit of Shàngjīng Hùguó as Hùguó Jiāyīn Hóu.
He was granted a mace-cap with seven tassels,
robes adorned with five patterns,
and a guī tablet identical to the xìngguī.
An envoy was dispatched to the temple
to offer sacrifices with the Sānxiàn ceremony.
Its prayer read:
"That vast, flourishing forest,
truly majestic in the heavenly city,
stretching a hundred *lǐ* far and wide,
is presided over by the spirit.
The temple is solemn,
and the marquis's title is enjoyed.
Accept now these pure offerings,
and protect its luxuriant growth."
Thereafter,
on the seventh day of each month,
an official from the Shàngjīng headquarters was to perform incense offerings,
which became a standing order.
Lúgōu Hé Shén.
In Dàdìng 19th year,
officials reported:
"The Lúgōu River's waters are overflowing and eroding farmlands.
We request an official enfeoffment and title for the spirit."
The ritual officials found it difficult
as it was not recorded in the sacrificial canon.
Soon after,
it was specially enfeoffed as Ānpíng Hóu,
and a temple was built.
In the 27th year,
by imperial decree,
the county magistrate was to offer sacrifices in spring and autumn each year,
as per regulations.
Zhāoyìng Shùnjì Shènghòu.
In Dàdìng 17th year,
the Dūshuǐ Jiān reported:
"The temple of the Yellow River Spirit and Sacred Empress at Yángwǔ Shàngsǎo
