should follow the precedent of the Táng dynasty's mid-spring sacrifice to the Five Dragons' Temple."
In the first month of spring, Dàdìng 27th year,
the Shàngshū Shěng reported:
"The Sacred Empress temple in Héyīn County, Zhèngzhōu,
in previous generations, when the river caused trouble, prayers were repeatedly answered,
and additional titles and temple plaques were granted.
Now, after prayers,
the river flows peacefully.
We request further commendation and conferment."
The Emperor granted their request,
specially bestowing the title Zhāoyìng Shùnjì Shènghòu,
and the temple was named Língdé Shànlì zhī Miào.
Each year, the county magistrate was commissioned to offer sacrifices in spring and autumn,
as per regulations.
Zhèn'ān Gōng.
Formerly named Wàngguó Yá,
Tàizǔ once sojourned here during his campaign against Liáo.
In the fifth month of Dàdìng 8th year,
it was renamed Jìngníng Shān,
and a temple was later built.
In the eighth month of Míngchāng 6th year,
with a mace-cap and robes, and a jade investiture tablet,
the mountain spirit was enfeoffed as Zhèn'ān Gōng.
The investiture document read:
"The Emperor speaks thus: Ancient renowned mountains
are all included in the sacrificial canon.
In the era of Xuānhuáng,
seven thousand spirits were venerated.
In the time of the Yú clan,
ranked sacrifices were performed every five years.
This is because only what benefits the state
is necessarily rewarded for its merit.
As for later kings,
they reiterated this with splendid investiture documents,
and even beyond the Five Sacred Mountains,
titles of nobility were sometimes added.
Thus, Tàibái has the epithet 'Divine Responder,'
and Zhōngnán has the appellation 'Extensive Benevolence.'
Rites arise from righteousness,
and affairs align with the times.
What is transmitted in records
still serves as a model today.
I cultivate harmony in Huáxià,
ensuring all ranks perform their duties without fail.
I look upon this Jìngníng,
standing majestically in the northern wilderness,
its stored benevolence and emanating energy
subtly assisting Kūn Yuán (earth's primal force),
guiding winds and bringing forth clouds,
harmonizing with Qián Zào (heaven's creation).
It is a beacon of the region,
gazed upon by all beings.
Southward, it directly faces the imperial capital;
northward, it serves as a barrier for the frontier.
Extending broadly and richly,
it is where treasures emerge.
Firm and lofty,
the imperial palace is established here.
In the past, the Liáo dynasty often relied on it for its wealth.
Until Dàdìng, it was renamed.
Великий Zōng (Emperor Tàizǔ),
his merits shone among the enlightened sages.
And my late exalted father,
his virtue benefited the people.
Therefore, during seasonal times,
I traveled and visited,
and without resorting to military force,
distant peoples were pacified.
Rain and sunshine were always regular,
and all species flourished abundantly.
This is an endless blessing from the Supreme Lord,
and also a sign of an effective spiritual presence.
Now, aligning with public sentiment,
I reiterate the former practice.
Considering this place where the late Emperor sojourned,
and inheriting the peace and stability of generations,
I receive and continue the lingering blessings,
and manifest divine aid.
Thus, I grant a title befitting its virtue,
and further promulgate the ceremony by official notification.
The appearance of the realm is refreshed,
and the ceremonial displays are fully presented.
Now I dispatch envoy (mǒu), and vice-envoy (mǒu),
holding the staff of authority and carrying ritual objects,
to invest the spirit as Zhèn'ān Gōng,
and further command that sacrifices be offered annually.
Alas!
The grand ceremony shines brightly,
and its efficacy is felt and communicated.
May it, for eternal years,
assist our flourishing destiny.
Will not the spirit, upon receiving this office,
be truly magnificent!"
Ruìshèng Gōng.
This is Máda Gé Shān,
where Zhāngzōng was born.
Shìzōng loved this mountain for its extended terrain and clear air,
so he ordered Zhāngzōng to name it.
Later, it was renamed Hútǔbái Shān,
and a temple was built.
In the eighth month of Míngchāng 4th year,
with a mace-cap and robes, and a jade investiture tablet,
the mountain spirit was enfeoffed as Ruìshèng Gōng.
A temple was built,
and the Fǔzhōu authorities were commanded
to select a day in the second month of spring and autumn
to regularly offer sacrifices.
Its ceremonial text said:
“The emperor speaks thus: The rise of a state
is ordained by destiny.
The primordial transformation of Heaven and Earth
only then aligns with this [mandate].
The mountains, rivers, and all deities
all receive their appointments.
Pure essence offers auspicious signs,
and sagely wisdom continues to emerge.
Great responses are manifested in rare omens,
ushering in a glorious era through subtle assistance.
The rites of trustworthiness and reliability are compiled and followed,
and the writings on expected ranks are all observed.
Praise to this famed mountain,
establishing this auspicious place,
extending downwards to the divisions of Qían,
and directly facing upwards to the splendor of the枢 (Pleiades).
It commands the ford of Xīmù,
and connects to the energy of the Central Plains.
Dispelling miasma and harmful influences,
it nurtures great harmony.
Thinking of the glorious deeds that shine down,
and the virtuous legacy that seems ever-present,
ascending to the heights to clear the summer heat,
it truly embodies longevity and benevolence.
The imperial residence is tranquil and serene,
and abundant grace permeates all.
I respectfully follow the ancestral footsteps,
and in accordance with the times, undertake a tour.
Moved by the beautiful name, I am filled with thoughts,
and wearing the sagely counsel, I receive blessings.
Thinking of the initial extent of this grand land,
it is also due to the spiritual efficacy of the protective guardians.
However, the sacrificial rites are without order,
and the deities have no dwelling.
This is not how one fully expresses gratitude for merit and veneration of virtue,
nor does it fulfill the desire to recall beginnings and rejoice in origins.
Therefore, I bestow a name,
and build a new temple.
I engrave my sincere words on a permanent stele,
and select an auspicious day using the primal tortoise shell,
displaying the ceremonial colors to distinguish majesty,
and cleansing the ritual utensils for the offering.
Propagating great achievements,
and performing numerous ceremonies.
Now I dispatch envoys, So-and-so and Deputy So-and-so,
bearing credentials and ceremonial objects,
to enfeoff the deity as Ruìshèng Gōng,
and further command the relevant officials to offer sacrifices at the prescribed times each year.
Alas!
May it be intelligent,
and accept this sincere intention.
May the good fortune be everlasting,
and may all be peaceful.”
The Temple of Zhēnjiàn Jùnwáng.
In the first month of Míngchāng Wǔ Nián,
those who presented memorials said,
“Yèlǔ and Gǔshén, these two virtuous men, created the Nǚzhēn script.
We request that each be enfeoffed with a prestigious title
and have a temple established for them.
Let Nǚzhēn and Hàn scholars, along with the descendants of Kǒngzǐ, bow to them.”
The officials in charge said that Yèlǔ was difficult to sacrifice to,
and as for Gǔshén, the Zhēnjiàn Wáng of Jīnyuán Jùn, he had already been honored in the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
so it would also be difficult to establish a special temple for him.
An imperial edict ordered
that the matter be deliberated again.
The ritual officials said,
“There is no precedent in previous dynasties for those who created scripts to be admitted into Kǒngzǐ’s temple.
If a shrine were placed behind or to the sides of the temple,
and scholars were allowed to bow there,
there would be no harm.”
The Shàngshū Shěng said,
“If this were done,
it might not align with the state’s intention to greatly honor meritorious officials.”
An edict was then issued, ordering that following the precedent of Cāngjié’s temple in Zhōuzhì,
the government should establish a temple in Nàlǐhún Zhuāng in Shàngjīng.
A local official and the local Qianhu were entrusted to offer sacrifices in spring and autumn,
and all necessary items would be provided as appropriate.
Prayers for Protection.
In the fifth month of Dàdìng Sì Nián,
there was no rain.
Lǐbù Shàngshū Wáng Jìng was ordered to pray for rain at Běiyuè,
with the senior and junior officials of Dìngzhōu serving as the secondary and final presenters of offerings.
An auspicious day was also chosen at the northern suburb of the capital,
for distant sacrifices to the Yuèzhèn and Hǎidú.
The officials in charge carried out the ceremony,
using wine, dried meat, and mincemeat as offerings.
Seven days later, there was still no rain,
so prayers were offered to Tàishè and Tàijì.
Seven more days passed with no rain, so prayers were offered to the Zōngmiào.
Still no rain,
so the prayers to the Yuèzhèn and Hǎidú were repeated as in the initial ceremony.
The divine seats were arranged,
the wine vessels and libation cups were filled,
as per the usual ritual.
For the wine vessels and libation cups, gourds were used;
sweet gourds with their stems removed were selected to serve as the zūn.
Only the prayer tablets for the Five Sacred Mountains, Zōngmiào, and Shèjì were personally inscribed by the Emperor;
the rest were not.
Ten days later, still no rain,
so the market was moved,
slaughtering was prohibited,
umbrellas and fans were forbidden,
and a clay dragon was made for prayer.
When sufficient rain fell, a thanksgiving sacrifice was offered,
and the dragon was sent into the water.
In the sixth month of the summer of Shíqī Nián,
the capital region had long experienced rain.
Following the rain prayer ritual,
various Buddhist and Daoist temples were ordered to open their altars for prayers.
Bowing to Heaven.
The Jīn, following the old custom of the Liáo, performed the ritual of bowing to Heaven on the Dúwǔ, Zhōngyuán, and Chóngjiǔ days.
On Dúwǔ, it was held at the jujuán (ball game field);
on Zhōngyuán, in the inner palace;
and on Chóngjiǔ, outside the capital city.
The ritual involved
hollowing out wood to make a tray,
shaped like a boat,
red in color,
painted with clouds and cranes.
A stand, five or six *chǐ* high, was made,
the tray placed upon it,
and food offered within it.
Family members gathered and bowed to it.
If it was the Supreme Emperor, a platform was built at Chángwǔ Diàn for the bowing to Heaven.
On the morning of Dúwǔ,
after all arrangements were complete,
all officials lined up south of the Lè Tíng on the ball field.
The emperor, wearing boots and robes, rode in a carriage,
led by the Xuānhuī Shǐ,
entered through the south gate of the ball field,
arrived at the bowing to Heaven platform,
descended from the carriage, and went to the mat.
The imperial prince and all officials below him all proceeded to the mat.
The Xuānhuī
announced “bow,”
and the emperor bowed twice.
Incense was offered,
and he bowed twice again.
After the food was arranged and cups thrown,
he bowed twice again.
He drank the blessed wine;
after kneeling and drinking,
he bowed twice again.
All officials bowed in attendance,
and the imperial prince and those below were led out first,
all following the same previous guidance.
The emperor returned to his tent in the carriage,
changed clothes,
and then performed the games of shooting willow and polo,
which were also Liáo customs,
and which the Jīn still favored.
Whenever the bowing to Heaven ritual on Dúwǔ was complete,
willow branches were inserted in two rows on the ball field.
Those who were to shoot were arranged by rank,
each marking their branch with a cloth.
The branches were about several *cùn* from the ground,
their bark peeled to expose the white wood.
First, one person galloped forward as a guide,
then others galloped with featherless, blunt-tipped arrows to shoot.
One who not only cut the willow but also caught it with their hand while galloping away
was deemed superior.
One who cut it but could not catch it and ride away
was second best.
One who cut the green part,
or hit it but could not cut it,
or failed to hit it,
was deemed a loser.
For each shot,
drums were beaten to boost morale.
Afterwards, polo was played.
Everyone rode their accustomed horses,
holding polo sticks.
The sticks were several *chǐ* long,
with ends shaped like a crescent moon.
The crowd was divided into two teams,
who competed to strike a single ball.
First, a double goalpost was erected at the south of the ball field,
with a board placed,
and a hole opened below it as a gate,
with a net added to form a bag.
Whoever could snatch the ball and strike it into the net bag was the winner.
Alternatively, it was said:
“Two gates were erected opposite each other at both ends,
and teams struck at each other,
each winning by getting the ball out of the gate.”
The ball was small, like a fist,
made of light, tough wood, hollow inside, and painted red.
All these activities were to practice agility.
Afterwards, a banquet was granted,
a custom observed annually.
The bowing rituals of this nation.
The Jīn Dynasty's bowing ritual was as follows:
First, one would clasp hands in sleeves, slightly bow the body,
then step back a little,
kneel on the left knee,
and swing the elbows left and right,
as if dancing.
In all, when kneeling,
one would swing the sleeves,
lowering them to brush the knees,
and raising them up to the left and right shoulders,
a total of four times.
After four such kneelings,
one would then press a hand on the right knee,
kneeling on the left knee alone to complete the ritual.
In the national language, "shaking hands and bowing" was called
"sāsù".
In the fifth month of the fifth year of Chéng'ān
(1200 CE), the Emperor issued an edict to the officials concerned, saying:
"Regarding the number of bows by Nǚzhí and Hàn people, let an appropriate mean be deliberated upon
for their mutual observance."
The ritual officials reported, saying:
"The *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhou) lists nine bows,
the first of which is *qǐshǒu*,
which is the most solemn among bows,
and is the ritual for a subject to bow to his sovereign.
We request that from now on,
when in court attire, the Hàn bow be used;
but when in casual clothes, each follow their native custom of bowing."
The Director of Affairs, Chén Sōng, said:
"The bowing ritual of our dynasty
has a long history,
and it is a bow for casual clothes.
It can be decreed that when in court attire, one performs the court bow;
when in casual clothes, one follows the bow of our dynasty."
The Chancellor, Zhāng Wàngōng, held that each bowing ritual was convenient according to what one was accustomed to,
and there was no need to change it.
The Minister of Works, Wán Yán Xiāng, said:
"Now, everyone's collars and hairstyles follow the system of our dynasty,
so it is appropriate to follow the bowing ritual of our dynasty.
What Sōng says is correct."
The Emperor then commanded that for court attire, the court bow be used,
and for all people in casual clothes, the bow of our dynasty be used.

Volume 17, Rituals 9: Rituals for the Emperor's Accession, Rituals for Receiving a Venerable Title, Rituals for Presenting Longevity Wishes, Rituals for Court Audience and Regular Court, Rituals for Issuing General Pardons, Rituals for Subjects Bowing to Imperial Edicts
Rituals for the Emperor's Accession.
In the spring, the first month, on the *rénshēn* day, the first day of the month, of the first year of Shōuguó
(1115 CE), officials and common people, elders from all circuits, all gathered
to deliberate on creating new rituals
to enthrone the Emperor.
Ālíhé Mǎn and Zōnghàn then presented nine farming tools,
offering prayers with the intention of opening up land and nourishing the people.
Then, nine teams of fine horses,
nine horses per team,
each of a different color,
along with armor, helmets, bows, arrows, spears, and swords, were presented to the Emperor.
The national name was Dà Jīn,
and the reign era was established as Shōuguó.
On the sixth day of the ninth month of the first year of Tiānhuì
(1123 CE), the imperial younger brother Ānbǎn Bó Jíliè ascended the imperial throne.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
offerings were made to Heaven and Earth.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
a great amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
Rituals for Receiving a Venerable Title.
On the second day of the first month of the first year of Huángtǒng
(1141 CE), Grand Preceptor Zōnggàn led all officials in submitting a memorial,
requesting that a venerable title of Emperor be conferred upon the sovereign.
After three requests,
an imperial edict granted permission.
On the seventh day,
Shì, the Grand Administrator of Shàngjīng, was dispatched to announce to Heaven, Earth, and the altars of grain and soil;
Zōngqiáng, the Magistrate of Xījīn, announced to the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the tenth day,
the Emperor, wearing *gǔnmiǎn* robes, presided in the Yuánhé Hall.
Zōnggàn led all officials in respectfully performing the investiture ceremony.
The text of the investiture read, "We, your subjects, respectfully offer this jade tablet and jade seal,

and confer the venerable title of 'Chóngtiān Tǐdào Qīnmíng Wénwǔ Shèngdé Huángdì' (Sacred and Virtuous Emperor who Venerates Heaven, Embodies the Way, is Respectful, Enlightened, Civil, and Martial)."
On that day,
the Emperor changed into a *tōngtiānguān* (Heaven-reaching crown)
and hosted a banquet for officials of the second rank and above, and envoys from Gāolí and Xiàguó.
On the twelfth day,
thanks were respectfully offered at the ancestral temple,
then the Emperor returned to preside at Xuānhé Gate,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
In the seventh year of Dàdìng
(1167 CE), the venerable title of Emperor was respectfully conferred.
Three days prior,
envoys were dispatched to report to Heaven, Earth, the imperial ancestral temple, and the altars of grain and soil.
Two days prior,
all departments ceased submitting memorials on punishments.
All civil and military officials practiced the rituals in the courtyard of the Dà'ān Hall.
The Ministry of War led its subordinates
in setting up the yellow imperial guard at the inner and outer gates of the Dà'ān Hall.
The Xuānhuī Institute led the Yíluán Division
in setting up the altar for receiving the imperial tablet and seal in the middle of the Dà'ān Hall the day before,
and also set up the imperial couch on the altar,
and also set up the curtained enclosure for the imperial tablet and seal outside the gate of the Dà'ān Hall,
and also set up the Crown Prince's tent in the east corridor of the hall,
and also set up the assembly of officials outside the Dà'ān Gate.
The Director of Grand Music and the Associate Director of Harmony set up the palace bells and chimes in the hall courtyard the day before,
and also set up the music stands for the ascending chorus in the hall,
and erected dance markers below the hall.
On that day, the Officer of Imperial Seals waited for the civil and military officials to enter,
placed the eight imperial seals on either side of the imperial throne,
and after the imperial tablet and seal were presented,
again carried the seals back to the appropriate department.
At dawn on that day,

the Grand Commandant who presented the imperial tablet, the Minister of Education who presented the imperial seal, the Grand Chancellor who read the imperial tablet, and the Grand Secretary who read the imperial seal, along with other officials in sequence who were to perform duties,
all gathered at the Ministry of Personnel,
awaiting the procession of the imperial tablet and seal,
which they would then ride horses to escort.
When the imperial tablet and seal arrived at the Yìngtiān Gate,
they dismounted and entered through the main gate on foot,
and upon reaching outside the Dà'ān Hall gate,
placed the imperial tablet and seal in the curtained enclosure.
The crossbowmen and others carrying the imperial tablet and seal stands stood divided on the left and right.
All civil and military officials, in court attire, entered their designated places.
The acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and the Director of Grand Music led the musicians to take their positions,
and the Associate Directors of Harmony each took their positions for raising the banners.
The officials carrying the imperial tablet and seal stands entered first through the west side gate,
placed the stands on the cushioned seats in the east and west sections of the hall,
and after placing them,
each retreated to behind the imperial tablet and seal positions on the west steps.

The officials holding the imperial tablet, the officials holding the imperial seal, the officials carrying the imperial tablet casket, and the officials carrying the imperial seal box entered first through the west side gate,
and stood facing east at the west of the imperial tablet and seal cushioned seats below the west steps of the hall,
awaiting the report from the Palace Gate officials.
The Attendant-Secretary led the acting Grand Secretary to present the tablet announcing
"Middle Readiness" (zhōngyán).
Upon completion,
the ritual masters and prompters each took their positions.
The Palace Gate officials led the civil and military officials to enter, dividing to the left and right,
and stand facing each other on the east and west sides of the brick path below the hall steps.
The Officer of Imperial Seals carried the eight imperial seals, entering through the west side gate,
ascended and placed them facing each other in the east and west sections of the hall,
then divided to stand on the left and right behind the seals.
The Attendant-Secretary led the acting Grand Secretary to present the tablet announcing
"Outer Readiness" (wàibàn).
The fans were closed,
and the Emperor, wearing *gǔnmiǎn* robes, emerged,
with the curved and straight imperial canopies, and the imperial guard clearing the way as per usual ritual.
Whips cracked in the hall,
and upon completion,
whips also cracked below the hall.
At the initial call for fans,
the Associate Directors of Harmony knelt,
prostrated,
rose,
and raised the banners.
The artisans beat the drum and struck the *zhù*,
playing the music of Qiánníng.
The Emperor emerged from the east chamber,
took his seat,
the Deputy Commissioners of Rituals and Ceremonies added incense,
the smoke from the censers rose,
the fans opened,
and the curtains rolled up.
The Associate Directors of Harmony lowered their banners,
struck the *yǔ*,
and the music ceased.
The Academicians of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and the Attendant-Secretaries, from the imperial tablet and seal curtained enclosure, divided to lead the imperial tablet;
the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices led the way,
the Vice Minister of Personnel escorted the imperial tablet and proceeded,

the Grand Commandant who presented the imperial tablet, the Grand Chancellor who read the imperial tablet, and the officials who lifted the imperial tablet followed in sequence behind the imperial tablet.
Next, two Academicians of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and two Attendant-Secretaries divided to lead the imperial seal;
the Vice Minister of Rites escorted the imperial seal and proceeded,

the Minister of Education who presented the imperial seal, the Grand Secretary who read the imperial seal, and the officials who lifted the imperial seal followed in sequence behind the imperial seal.
They entered through the main gate,
and the palace bells and chimes played the music of 'Guīměi Yánggōng' (Praising Beauty and Proclaiming Merit).
The Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices led the way in front of the imperial tablet stand,
and at the south of the incense table on the first terrace,
placed the imperial tablet and seal for a short while on the cushioned seats.
The Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and the officials who lifted the imperial tablet and seal retreated slightly to the west of the imperial tablet and seal,
and stood facing east.
The relevant Academicians and Attendant-Secretaries stood behind them,
and the crossbowmen carrying the imperial tablet and seal stands, and the umbrella officials, etc., were further behind them,
all facing east.
The Grand Commandant, Minister of Education, Grand Chancellor, and Grand Secretary all stood behind the imperial tablet,
facing north in sequence.
The Vice Minister of Personnel and the Vice Minister of Rites stood next, behind them.
Once they were in position,
the music ceased.
The gate attendants (Gé-mén Shè-rén 閤門舍人) separately led the officials from the east and west ranks to form a single line.
They turned north and stood,
leaving a small passage in the middle of the ranks.
Once they were standing firm,

four officials, comprising the Erudites of the Grand Court (Tài-cháng Bó-shì 太常博士) and the Attendants for Transmission (Tōng-shì Shè-rén 通事舍人), separately led the Grand Commandant (Tài-wèi 太尉), the Minister of Education (Sī-tú 司徒), the Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōng-shū-lìng 中書令), the Palace Attendant (Shì-zhōng 侍中), and the Assistant Ministers of Personnel and Rites (Lì-bù Lǐ-bù Shì-láng 吏部禮部侍郎) back to their respective ranks in order.
After this was completed,
the Erudites and Attendants withdrew to await.
When they were first led in,
music playing the "Ode to Praising Beauty and Proclaiming Merit" (Guī-měi Yáng-gōng zhī qǔ 歸美揚功之曲) was performed.
When they reached their positions and stood firm,
the music stopped.
The Master of Ceremonies (Diǎn-yí 典儀) said,

The prompters conveyed the order,
and all officials present, from the Grand Commandant down, danced and bowed

After the head of the rank stepped forward and performed the ritual greetings,
the prompter again called,

This followed the usual ceremony for court assemblies.

Four officials, comprising the Erudites of the Grand Court and the Attendants for Transmission, again led the Grand Commandant, the Minister of Education, the Director of the Central Secretariat, the Palace Attendant, and the Assistant Ministers of Personnel and Rites forward again to a spot slightly south of where the imperial edict (cè 冊) and imperial seal (bǎo 寶) were located,

The crossbowmen (nǔ-shǒu 弩手) carrying the imperial edict and seal beds (cè-bǎo-chuáng 冊寶牀) and the umbrella officials (sǎn-zi-guān 傘子官) all advanced,
raising the imperial edict and seal beds.
Two officials, comprising an Erudite of the Grand Court and an Attendant for Transmission, separately led the imperial edict.
The Minister of the Grand Court (Tài-cháng-qīng 太常卿) led the way,
the Assistant Minister of Personnel (Lì-bù Shì-láng 吏部侍郎) escorted the imperial edict as it proceeded,

and the Grand Commandant who presented the imperial edict (Fèng-cè Tài-wèi 奉冊太尉), the Director of the Central Secretariat who read the imperial edict (Dú-cè Zhōng-shū-lìng 讀冊中書令), and the officials who held the imperial edict (Jǔ-cè-guān 舉冊官) followed in order behind the imperial edict.
As the imperial edict began to move,
music playing the "Solemn Serenity" (Sù-níng zhī qǔ 肅寧之曲) was performed.
Next, another two officials, comprising an Attendant for Transmission and an Erudite of the Grand Court, separately led the imperial seal.
The Assistant Minister of Rites (Lǐ-bù Shì-láng 禮部侍郎) escorted the imperial seal as it proceeded,

and the Minister of Education who presented the imperial seal (Fèng-bǎo Sī-tú 奉寶司徒), the Palace Attendant who read the imperial seal (Dú-bǎo Shì-zhōng 讀寶侍中), and the officials who held the imperial seal (Jǔ-bǎo-guān 舉寶官) followed in order behind the imperial seal,
proceeding to the foot of the western steps.
When they reached the mat position for the imperial edict and seal, they paused briefly.

the imperial seal to the south.)

The crossbowmen carrying the imperial edict and seal beds and the umbrella officials withdrew to a spot slightly west behind them,
standing facing east.
The officials holding the imperial edict (Pěng-cè-guān 捧冊官) and the officials carrying the imperial edict (Yú-cè-guān 舁冊官) both advanced,

An Erudite of the Grand Court and an Attendant for Transmission separately led the imperial edict.
The Minister of the Grand Court turned his body and led the imperial edict, ascending first.

The Grand Commandant who presented the imperial edict, the Director of the Central Secretariat who read the imperial edict, the officials who held the imperial edict, and the officials holding the imperial edict followed in order behind the imperial edict as it ascended.
As the imperial edict began to move,
music playing the "Solemn Serenity" was performed.
Upon reaching the main hall,
the Erudites and Attendants stood to the left and right by the front pillars to await.
The Director of the Central Secretariat who read the imperial edict stood slightly west of the front pillar outside the railing to await.
The officials who held the imperial edict and the officials holding the imperial edict stood behind him.
The Grand Commandant who presented the imperial edict followed in ascent.

he inserted his ceremonial tablet (hù 笏),

the officials who held the imperial edict entered next,

After reading,

After this was completed,
the Minister of the Grand Court descended to return to the front of the imperial seal bed, and the officials carrying the imperial edict all advanced,
and together with the officials holding the imperial edict, took the imperial edict casket and raised it,
placing it on the table at the mat position in the eastern chamber of the hall,
facing west.
The officials holding and raising the imperial edict, etc., descended from the eastern steps,
returning to their original ranks.
The officials carrying the imperial edict also withdrew.
An Erudite of the Grand Court led the Grand Commandant who presented the imperial edict, descending from the western steps,
and he stood firm facing east to await.

Next, the officials holding the imperial seal (Pěng-bǎo-guān 捧寶官) and the officials carrying the imperial seal (Yú-bǎo-guān 舁寶官), after the Director of the Central Secretariat who read the imperial edict had finished reading and exited,
both advanced,
taking the imperial seal casket (bǎo-lù 寶盝) and raising it.
An Erudite of the Grand Court and an Attendant for Transmission separately led the imperial seal.
The Minister of the Grand Court turned his body and led the imperial seal,
ascending first.

The Minister of Education who presented the imperial seal, the Palace Attendant who read the imperial seal, the officials who held the imperial seal, and the officials holding the imperial seal followed in order behind the imperial seal as it ascended.
As the imperial seal began to move,
music playing the "Solemn Serenity" was performed.
Upon reaching the main hall,
the Erudites and Attendants both withdrew and did not ascend,

The Palace Attendant who read the imperial seal stood slightly west between the front pillars outside the railing to await.
The officials who held the imperial seal and the officials holding the imperial seal stood behind him.
The Minister of Education who presented the imperial seal followed in ascent.
Upon reaching the mat position,
he inserted his ceremonial tablet,
knelt forward slightly and placed it.

he held his tablet,

The Minister of Education withdrew to the west of the front pillars,
standing to await.
The Minister of the Grand Court withdrew slightly,

The officials carrying the imperial seal stood behind him,
all facing east.
The officials holding the imperial seal entered first,
the officials who held the imperial seal entered next,
and the Palace Attendant who read the imperial seal entered after them.
All four officials holding the imperial seal inserted their ceremonial tablets and knelt with both knees, holding it.
The two officials who held the imperial seal also inserted their ceremonial tablets, kneeling on one knee on either side and holding it up.

knelt and announced,

he bowed low,

After this was completed,
the officials carrying the imperial seal advanced,
and together with the officials holding and raising the imperial seal, took the imperial seal casket and raised it,
placing it on the table at the mat position in the western chamber of the hall,
facing east.
The officials holding and raising the imperial seal, etc., and the Minister of the Grand Court all descended from the western steps,
and the Assistant Minister of Personnel also returned to his original rank.
The officials carrying the imperial seal also withdrew.
An Erudite of the Grand Court led the Minister of Education who presented the imperial seal, followed by the Grand Commandant who presented the imperial edict,
who stood firm facing east.
The Bóshì (Academicians) and Shèrén (Secretaries) led Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) and Sītú (Minister of Education) forward.

The Bóshì and Shèrén then slightly withdrew.
The Diǎnyí (Master of Ceremonies) announced,
"Bow!"
The zànzhě (proclaimers) relayed the command.
All officials present bowed twice.
When finished,
two Bóshì and Shèrén led the Tàiwèi to ascend the eastern steps.
The ceremonial orchestra played the "Chúnchéng Xiǎngshàng" (Pure Sincerity for the Emperor) melody.

they paused.
Two Géménshǐ (Palace Gate Officials) led the Tàiwèi forward to the front.
He stood still,
and the music stopped.
The Géménshǐ bowed, signaling the Tàiwèi to bow and kneel in congratulation.
The Géménshǐ below the dais bowed, and the hundred officials bowed their bodies.
The Tàiwèi stated,

and presented the congratulatory address.
He prostrated himself,
rose,
and withdrew to the top of the steps.
The Bóshì and Shèrén then separated to lead the Tàiwèi down the eastern steps.

The music stopped.
The Bóshì and Shèrén slightly withdrew.
The Diǎnyí announced,

the Tōngshì Shèrén (Attending Secretaries) led the acting Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) to ascend from the eastern steps.

The Diǎnyí announced,

The Tàiwèi, Sītú, and all officials present bowed twice,

the Tōngshì Shèrén led the Shìzhōng back to his position.
The Diǎnyí announced,

All officials present, both on and below the dais, bowed twice and performed the ceremonial dance.

When finished,

The Gémén Shèrén (Palace Gate Secretaries) separated to lead the officials who were to face north.

He knelt to report,

He prostrated himself,
rose,

The screens were closed,
and the curtains lowered.
The Xiélǜláng (Official for Musical Harmony) prostrated himself,
rose,

the musicians beat the drums and chǔ,

He descended from his seat,

and had a meal.
The imperial guards cleared the way as usual.
The screens opened,
and the music stopped.
The officials bearing the imperial registers led the men carrying the register stands.
The officials bearing the imperial seals led the men carrying the seal stands.
All ascended to the hall to retrieve the boxes and caskets.

they placed them in front of the stands.
The Yǐnjìn Sīguān (Officials of the Protocol Bureau) led the way.

They proceeded to the upper eastern palace gate to present them.
The Tōngshì Shèrén then separated to lead the civil and military officials, etc., out in order.
They returned to their tents,
were given food,
and awaited the imperial toast.

the responsible officials prepared the imperial bed and the seats for the banqueting officials,

The acting Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) and the Dàyuèlìng (Director of the Grand Music Bureau) led the musicians in.

awaiting the report from the Shèrén.

standing facing east and west.
The Tōngshì Shèrén first led the acting Shìzhōng to report on a tablet,

After a short while,
he again reported, "Wàibàn" (Outer Preparations).
The screens closed,
and whips were cracked.
The Xiélǜláng knelt,
prostrated himself,
rose,
the musicians beat the drums and chǔ,
and the ceremonial orchestra played the "Gānníng" melody.
He donned the Tōngtiān Guān (Celestial Crown) and the jiàng shāpáo (dark red gauze robe),
took his seat,
and the curtains were rolled up.
The Nèishì (Eunuch Attendant) announced,
"Screens open!"
Whips were cracked throughout the hall,
the yù was struck,
and the music stopped.
The Yíshǐ Fù (Assistant Masters of Ceremonies) and others added incense,
and the smoke from the censers rose.
The Tōngshì Shèrén led the heads of the ranks and those below to form their ranks.

Upon reaching the north-facing positions,
they stood still in double rows,
leaving a small path in the middle of the ranks.
The Tōngshì Shèrén led the acting Shìzhōng to ascend the eastern steps,
standing briefly on the dais.
The Gémén Shèrén led the Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites) out of his rank to the front.

and knelt to report,
stating,
"I, your servant, the Lǐbù Shàngshū [name],
request Your Majesty grant permission for the officials to present their longevity toast."

rose,
and bowed his body.
The Tōngshì Shèrén led the acting Shìzhōng to withdraw slightly.
The Shèrén announced,

When finished,
he announced,

and he returned to his original rank.
The Nèishì Jú (Bureau of Eunuch Attendants) brought in the imperial bed.
Next, the Liángyùn Lìng (Director of Fine Wines) sprinkled wine at the south of the horizontal steps below the dais.
When finished,
the Diǎnyí announced,
"Bow!"
The zànzhě relayed the command.
All officials present bowed twice.
Following the bows, they shouted
"Wànsuì!" three times.
When finished,
they stood upright.
The Tài Cháng Bó Shì and Tōng Shì Shè Rén separately lead the acting Shàng Gōng to ascend from the eastern steps.
As he first ascends,
the Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
On the main hall,
the Shè Rén retreat slightly,
the two Gě Hé Shǐ bow and invite the Shàng Gōng to advance.
Upon reaching the kneeling mat for offering wine,
the music stops.
The Xuān Huī Shǐ presents a goblet to the Shàng Gōng.
The Shàng Gōng inserts his ceremonial tablet into his belt,
receives the goblet,
and goes to the front of the couch to kneel and offer it.
After receiving the goblet,
the Shàng Gōng holds the tray and hands it to the Xuān Huī Shǐ.
After this,
the two Gě Hé Shǐ bow and invite the Shàng Gōng into the railing enclosure,
and the announcer calls

He kneels.
Below the hall,
the Gě Mén bows to all the officials, who all bend their bodies.
The Tōng Shì Shè Rén invites the acting Shì Zhōng to advance,
to the space between the front pillars,
where he personally receives the imperial command.
He then withdraws to the steps, facing west, and declares

The Diǎn Yí says
"Bow!"
The announcers transmit the command,
and the Shàng Gōng and all the officials in their positions bow twice.
Following the bows, they thrice exclaim
"Long live the Emperor!"
After this,
he bends his body and announces:
"Having received your longevity wine,
we celebrate together with you, both inside and outside."
After the Gě Mén Shè Rén announces the imperial message,
the Shàng Gōng and all the officials perform a "dance-bow" five times.
After this,
the Gě Mén Shè Rén leads the officials to take their places in separate ranks, on the eastern and western sides, facing north.
The Bó Shì Shè Rén again leads the Shàng Gōng to ascend from the eastern steps.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
Upon reaching the kneeling mat for offering wine,
the music stops.
The Shàng Gōng inserts his ceremonial tablet into his belt,
the Xuān Huī Shǐ presents the tray to the Shàng Gōng.
The Shàng Gōng goes to the kneeling mat within the railing enclosure,
kneels, and lifts the wine.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Jǐng Mìng Wàn Nián.
After drinking,
the music stops.
After the Shàng Gōng advances and receives the empty goblet,
he returns to the kneeling mat.
He hands the goblet to the Xuān Huī Shǐ.
After this,
the two Gě Hé Shǐ bow and invite the Shàng Gōng to withdraw.
The Nèi Shì Jú brings out the imperial couch.
The Bó Shì Shè Rén both advance and separately lead him,
descending from the eastern steps.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
The Gě Mén Shè Rén separately leads the eastern and western ranks,
who follow the Shàng Gōng and all return to their north-facing positions.
When they are standing still,
the music stops.
The Diǎn Yí says
"Bow!"
The announcers transmit the command,
and the officials in their positions all bow twice.
They thrice exclaim
"Long live the Emperor!"
After this,
they stand upright.
On the main hall,
the Tōng Shì Shè Rén invites the acting Shì Zhōng to advance,
to the space between the front pillars,
where he personally receives the imperial command.
He then withdraws to the steps, facing west.
The Gě Mén official bows first,
and all the officials bend their bodies.
The Shì Zhōng declares
"There is an imperial decree!"
The Diǎn Yí says
"Bow!"
The announcers transmit the command,
and the officials in their positions all bow twice.
After this,
he bends his body and announces
"Invite the kings and dukes and others to ascend the hall."
The Diǎn Yí says
"Bow!"
The announcers transmit the command,
and the officials in their positions all bow twice.
After this,
they insert their ceremonial tablets into their belts,
perform a dance-bow,
and bow twice again.
After this,
the Tài Cháng Bó Shì and Tōng Shì Shè Rén lead the kings and dukes and below, and all the officials attending the banquet,
to ascend the hall in left and right divisions.
Officials not attending the banquet depart in left and right rolled ranks.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
All the officials stand behind their seats on the hall.
The music stops.
The Nèi Shì Jú brings the imperial couch into the hall.
According to the usual banquet protocol,
the first goblet of wine is again offered.
The Dēng Gē plays the melody of Shèng Dé Zhāo Míng.
After drinking,
the music stops.
The attendants serve wine to all the officials.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
The civilian dance enters.
The goblets make one round.
The music stops.
The Shàng Shí Jú presents food.
The attendants arrange food for all the officials.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the dance of Bǎo Dà Dìng Gōng.
It is performed three times,
then stops,
and exits.
The second goblet of wine is again offered.
The Dēng Gē plays the melody of Tiān Zàn Yáo Líng.
After drinking,
the music stops.
The attendants serve wine to all the officials.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
The military dance enters.
The goblets make one round.
The music stops.
The Shàng Shí Jú presents food.
The attendants arrange food for all the officials.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the dance of Wàn Guó Lái Tóng.
It is performed three times,
then stops,
and exits.
The third goblet of wine is again offered.
The Dēng Gē plays the melody of Qìng Yún.
After drinking,
the music stops.
The attendants serve wine to all the officials.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
The goblets make one round.
The music stops.
The Shàng Shí Jú presents food.
The attendants arrange food for all the officials.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
After eating,
the music stops.
The Gě Mén officials separately invite the officials attending the banquet to rise,
and stand behind their seats.
The Tōng Shì Shè Rén leads the acting Shì Zhōng to the front of the couch.
He bows low,
rises,
kneels, and reports
"Your servant, the Shì Zhōng [name], reports,
the ceremony is complete."
He bows low,
and rises.
The Gě Mén Shè Rén separately leads all the officials to descend the eastern and western steps.
The Nèi Shì Jú brings out the imperial couch.
The Gōng Xuàn plays the melody of Sù Níng.
Upon reaching the north-facing positions and standing still,
the music stops.
The Diǎn Yí says
"Bow!"
The announcers transmit the command,
and the officials in their positions all bow twice.
After this,
they insert their ceremonial tablets into their belts,
perform a dance-bow,
and bow twice again.
After this,
they again take their places in separate ranks, on the eastern and western sides.
The fans are closed,
the curtains are lowered.
Whips are cracked above and below the hall.
The Xié Lǜ Láng bows low,
kneels,
raises the banner,
and rises.
The musicians strike the drum and chǔ,
and play the melody of Gān Níng.
The emperor descends from the throne,
enters from the eastern chamber,
and returns to the rear palace.
The imperial guards attend as they did upon his arrival.
The Nèi Shì announces
"Open the fans!"
The yú is struck,
and the music stops.
The Tōng Shì Shè Rén leads the acting Shì Zhōng to report from a tablet,
"The alert is lifted."
The relevant officials receive the command to dismiss the guards,
and all the officials in their positions bow twice and exit in order.
New Year's Day and Emperor's Birthday Longevity Offering Ceremony.
The emperor ascended the throne.
When the鞭 (biān) cracked and the time was announced,
the junior officials of the palace performed their obeisances,
then each returned to their standing position.
The Imperial Attendant led the Crown Prince, along with the ministers, officials, envoys, and guests, to enter in formation.
When they reached the Dānchí,
they bowed five times with ritual dance,
then stood upright.
The Attendant of the Palace Gate presented the memorials from the various circuits,
whereupon the Crown Prince and all below him bowed twice.
The Crown Prince was led to ascend to his mat seat on the dais.
He inserted his hu (hù) into his belt,
held a cup and tray,
and offered wine.
The emperor received it and placed it on the table.
The Crown Prince returned to his mat seat,
passed the tray to the attendant,
and took out his hu (hù).
The two Attendants of the Palace Gate bowed together and entered the railing enclosure,
then knelt and delivered their address, saying:
"On this Yuánzhēng (Yuánzhēng), auspiciousness begins,
and all things are renewed.
We respectfully wish Your Majesty, the Emperor, everlasting joy like Heaven."
If it was a Sòngjié (Sòngjié), they would say:
"On this auspicious day of Wànchūn (Wànchūn),
we respectfully present this cup of longevity.
We humbly wish Your Majesty, the Emperor, ten thousand, ten thousand, ten thousand times ten thousand years."
After the prayer was finished,
they bowed,
rose,
and returned to their mat seats.
The ministers and officials below the dais all bowed twice.
The Xuānkuīshǐ (Xuānkuīshǐ) announced,
"An imperial decree!"
All those present bowed twice,
and the imperial reply was proclaimed:
"Receiving your wishes for longevity on this new beginning,
we share this joy with you, both inside and outside the court."
On a Sòngjié (Sòngjié), it would be said:
"Receiving your wine of longevity,
we share this joy with you, both inside and outside the court."
When the address was finished,
they bowed five times with ritual dance,
and stood upright.
The Crown Prince inserted his hu (hù),
and held the tray.
The ministers and officials divided into ranks,
and the Jiàofāng (Jiàofāng) played music.
When the emperor raised his wine,
all the ministers and officials standing on and below the dais bowed twice.
The Crown Prince received the empty cup,
retired to his mat seat,
passed the tray and cup to the attendant,
and took out his hu (hù).
He descended the dais to the left,
the music stopped,
the ranks reassembled,
and the attending ministers and officials all bowed twice.
The banquet officials were then led in separate groups to ascend the dais.
Next, the retinue of the Sòng (Sòng) state was led to the Dānchí (Dānchí).
They bowed twice,
and without leaving their ranks, presented
"May Your Majesty enjoy ten thousand blessings,"
then bowed twice again.
It was announced,
"By imperial decree, food and drink are bestowed."
They bowed twice again,
each awaiting instructions,
stood upright,
and were led to stand in the left corridor.
Next, the retinues of Gāolí (Gāolí) and Xià (Xià) were led in,
and after performing the same ceremony as above,
were led in separate groups to stand in the left and right corridors.
The imperial fruit table was brought in,
and wine was offered.
When the emperor drank,
all the officials seated at the banquet and those standing by bowed twice.
The wine-offering official returned the cup to their place,
the seated banquet officials bowed twice,
and resumed their seats.
Wine was served,
an imperial message was conveyed,
and they drank standing.
When finished,
they bowed twice,
and sat down.
Next, the retinue bowed twice,
and sat down.
After three cups,
an address was delivered,
and the ministers, envoys, and retinue were invited to stand.
After the oral verse was recited,
all the seated banquet officials and those standing by bowed twice,
and sat down.
Next, the retinue bowed twice,
and sat down.
Food was brought in.
After seven cups,
as the music was about to end,
the retinue was invited to stand,
and after bowing twice,
they were led out.
During the music,
the ministers and envoys were invited to rise,
bow twice,
and descend the dais.
The fruit table was removed.
Upon reaching the Dānchí (Dānchí),
they reformed their ranks to express gratitude for the banquet,
bowed five times with ritual dance,
each awaiting instructions,
and were then led out in separate groups.
In the first month of Dàdìng (Dàdìng) year 6,
the emperor held court in the Dà'āndiàn (Dà'āndiàn)
to receive congratulations from the Crown Prince and all officials below him, as well as foreign envoys.
A banquet was bestowed,
and there was a fixed quota for civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above who were permitted to sit,
which became a regular institution.
In year 17,
an imperial decree stipulated that imperial relatives above the tǎnbō (tǎnbō) mourning grade,
even if they held no official titles, ranks, or fiefs,
should have a designated seating order if they attended the banquet.
The ritual officials stated:
"According to Táng (Táng) regulations,
close imperial relatives are ranked equivalent to third grade officials,
relatives in dàgōng (dàgōng) mourning and venerable relatives in xiǎogōng (xiǎogōng) mourning are ranked equivalent to fourth grade officials,
relatives in xiǎogōng (xiǎogōng) mourning and venerable relatives in sīmá (sīmá) mourning are ranked equivalent to fifth grade officials,
and those above sīmá (sīmá) and tǎnbō (tǎnbō) mourning are ranked equivalent to sixth grade officials."
The emperor ordered this system to be used for seating arrangements.
Court attendance and routine court ceremonies.
In the fifth month of Tiānjuàn (Tiānjuàn) year 2,
the ceremonies for routine court and the first and fifteenth days of the month were thoroughly reviewed.
Following the regulations of previous dynasties,
the first day, the sixth day, the eleventh day, the fifteenth day, the twenty-first day, and the twenty-sixth day of the month were designated as the six court attendance days.
Later, a new system was established,
designating the first and fifteenth days of the month for court attendance,
and the remaining days for routine court.
On all court attendance days (first and fifteenth),
officials would arrive at the curtained waiting area by the máo (máo) hour.
The emperor would hold court at the chén (chén) hour.
The imperial archers and umbrella bearers stood directly outside the palace gate,
arranged in two rows facing each other.
After the time announcer entered the hall and finished announcing the time,
the emperor ascended the dais and sat down.
The whip cracked.
The Gémén (Gémén) announced that the ranks were assembled.
The palace eunuchs holding ceremonial objects descended the palace steps on both sides,
and stood facing south.
The palace guards, from the Dūdǐanjiǎn (Dūdǐanjiǎn) down to the left and right imperial guards,
and the attending officials, from the Xuānkuī Gémén (Xuānkuī Gémén), first bowed twice.
The head of the rank slightly departed from his position,
and presented
"May Your Majesty enjoy ten thousand blessings,"
then bowed twice.
The spear bearers and umbrella bearers were already arrayed facing east and west outside the palace gate.
When
"May Your Majesty enjoy ten thousand blessings"
was presented,
they immediately took their positions, faced north, and performed the mountain-like cheer and greeting.
After the obeisance was completed,
they immediately stood facing each other.
The imperial umbrella bearer stood directly above the left rank of eunuchs.
The Dūdǐanjiǎn (Dūdǐanjiǎn) and those below him ascended the dais.
The Fùdǐanjiǎn (Fùdǐanjiǎn) stood slightly to the south,
facing east and west.
The left and right guards stood below the dais,
facing east and west.
The Gémén (Gémén) then led the rank of imperial princes.
The names of the head of the rank and those below him were announced, and they bowed twice.
When finished,
the head of the rank slightly departed from his position,
and presented
"May Your Majesty enjoy ten thousand blessings,"
then returned to his position and bowed twice.
After this,
they retired first.
Next, the Gémén (Gémén) led the heads of the civil and military official ranks and all officials required to attend court,
as well as officials of the sixth rank and above from the various prefectures and transportation commissions.
They all entered from the left,
and upon reaching the east of the Dānchí (Dānchí),
they bowed facing west.
After the Gémén (Gémén) made the general announcement,
they were led again to the Dānchí (Dānchí).
The Gémén (Gémén) announced the names of the head of the rank and those below him for their obeisance.
They bowed five times with ritual dance,
then bowed twice again.
When finished,
the leading provincial chief ministers and grand councilors ascended the dais to present their reports.
The Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ) stood opposite each other slightly in front and to the north of the left and right generals.
The Xiū Qǐjū (Xiū Qǐjū) stood opposite each other, facing east and west, below the secondary steps within the palace railing.
The rest retired,
exiting to the right.
Initially,
the Emperor took his seat,
placing the precious casket at the southeast corner of the palace steps.
Later, a custom was established:
after the Imperial Preceptors had completed their greetings,
the imperial desk would be brought in from the east,
and once it was set,
the palace attendants carrying the desk would divide, half going east and half west,
and stand guard at the palace corners.
The Duty Officer for the Treasures, holding the treasures, would kneel before the railing in the hall and report,
"All sealed."
One official from the Fúbǎo Láng and one from the Dāngjiān Yìnláng Zhōng,
along with the Lìshǐ designated to oversee the stamping, would apply the seal.
When finished,
the officer in charge of the treasures would seal and present them to the Chief Treasurer.
After the petitions were concluded, the seal would be presented.
Once that was done,
the palace attendants would remove the desk.
During a regular court session,
when the imperial princes retired from their ranks,
officials holding substantive posts of the seventh rank and above
would be led to enter the Dānchí, divided into left and right ranks,
and bow twice.
The head of the rank would step forward slightly, complete their greetings,
return to their position,
and bow twice again.
The Zǎizhí would ascend the hall,
while the other officials would retire in their respective ranks.
In the fifth month of Dàdìng 2 (1162 AD),
the Emperor commanded the Tái Chén to establish the rites for court attendance.
Officials of the fifth rank and above, when going to court, wore court robes;
when entering their bureaus to manage affairs, they would change into black robes.
From then on, for court attendance,
excluding those in the ranks before the palace hall,
on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
all officials with substantive posts of the seventh rank and above would attend.
On other court days,
officials with substantive posts of the fifth rank and above were permitted to attend,
while those of the sixth rank and below remained in their respective bureaus to manage affairs.
Officials such as the Yuánwàiláng of the Zuǒ Yòu Sī, Shìyùshǐ, and those of the Jìzhù Yuàn,
even if not of the fifth rank,
also attended court.
When receiving an imperial edict,
all officials with substantive posts and those without substantive posts of the seventh rank and above
attended.
During court attendance,
clerks, Lìyìshǐ, Tōngshì, and Jiǎnfǎ would wait in their respective bureaus.
After the officials retired from court,
they would proceed to their bureaus to sign documents,
and were not permitted to sign them within the palace.
Officials of the seventh rank and below who were outside the regular bureaucracy
were also not permitted to enter the palace on court days.
However, if a Dūshì of the Zuǒ Yòu Sī needed to present a memorial,
they were permitted to enter the palace.
Officials with substantive posts of the seventh rank and above,
if they encountered envoys or guests for a morning farewell audience,
would attend as on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month.
All would attend.
On New Year's Day, the Emperor's birthday (Shèngjié), when receiving an imperial edict, escorting or welcoming the imperial carriage on a hunt, or going to the ancestral temple to offer sacrifices,
all officials with substantive posts and those without substantive posts of the seventh rank and above
would attend.
All imperial princes and members of the imperial clan who had been appointed officials and were sixteen years of age or older
would attend greetings with their respective ranks.
In Dàdìng 5 (1165 AD),
the Right Jiànyì Dàfū, Yílài Zǐjìng, stated,
"The Měng'ān Móukè should not be excluded from entering for audience with the Zhōuzhèn officials in their ranks;
this goes against the spirit of integrating military and civilian affairs."
The Emperor approved his words
and instructed the Xuānhuī Yuàn to allow them to enter for audience with their ranks.
If the head of a rank, when scheduled for court attendance,
was absent due to a reason,
the next in line would take their place as the head of the rank.

All officials of the fifth rank and above, along with Shìyùshǐ, Lángzhōng of various departments of the Shàngshū, Tàicháng Chéng, Hànlín Xiūzhuàn Jìjūzhù, Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ, Bǔquē, and Shíyí who were summoned,
or who were on leave for more than a month, or who were dismissed from office or dispatched on missions, etc.,
would all enter for audience with their ranks to express gratitude or farewell.
Other officials would meet outside the palace gate.
Those in the gratitude rank would perform seven bows with a dance,
those in the farewell rank would perform four bows,
and those meeting at the gate to express gratitude or farewell would perform two bows.
Amnesty Proclamation Ceremony.
On the eleventh day of the first month of Dàdìng 7 (1167 AD),
after the Imperial Title Conferment Ceremony was completed,
on the fourteenth day,
an amnesty was proclaimed at the Yìngtiān Mén.
The regulations for Dàdìng 11 (1171 AD) were the same.
Before the appointed day,
the Xuānhuī Yuàn Shǐ, leading his subordinates,
would set up arrangements inside and outside the Yìngtiān Mén.
An imperial seat would be placed atop the Yìngtiān Mén,
and a changing tent for the Emperor would be set up slightly to the east outside the Dà'ān Diàn gate,
facing south.
The Gémén Shǐ would place a table for holding the imperial edict box to the left of the imperial seat.
The Shàofǔ Jiān would set up a chicken pole to the left below the gate tower.
On top of the pole, a large tray would be placed,
and in the tray, a golden chicken.
The chicken's beak would hold a crimson banner,
on which were written in gold characters
"Dàshè Tiānxià" (Great Amnesty Under Heaven),
four characters,
rolled up and held in its beak.
Four large iron rings would be fixed near the edges on the four sides of the tray,
and four large vermilion ropes would be suspended near the edges on the four sides of the tray's bottom,
for four acrobats to climb.
Additionally, a wooden crane immortal for holding the imperial edict would be set up,
threaded with a red rope,
and pulled by a windlass,
placed on the railing before the Emperor.
A painted platform for supporting the crane would also be set up in the center below the gate tower,
held aloft by four crossbowmen.
The Dàyuè Shǔ would set up palace chimes below the gate tower,
and a drum slightly to the north of the left of the palace chimes,
facing east.
The Bīngbù would erect the yellow imperial guard (huánghuī zhàng) outside the gate.
The Xíngbù, Yùshǐ Tái, and Dàxīng Fǔ would assemble prisoners outside the left guard.
The Yùshǐ Tái and Gémén Sī would arrange the positions for civil and military officials below the gate tower,
facing east and west.
The Diǎnyí would be positioned slightly to the east below the gate,
facing west.
The Xuānhuī Yuàn would set up a desk for receiving the imperial edict in front of the painted platform.
The Crown Prince's kneeling mat for standing attendance would be placed slightly to the east below the gate,
facing west.
The Crown Prince's kneeling mat for offering congratulations would be placed in front of the officials' ranks.
The Xiélǜ Láng would be positioned slightly to the east in the front portico above the gate tower,
facing west.
The Shàngshū Shěng would delegate the relevant department to set up the position for proclaiming the imperial edict slightly to the east and north of the officials' ranks,
facing west.
The Sītiān Tái would place the Jīchàng Shēng (herald) above the east tower gate.
The Shàngyī Jú would prepare the Emperor's everyday attire,
the same as for daily court attendance.
The Shàngniǎn would set up the imperial sedan chair in front of the changing tent.
After the personal gratitude ceremony was completed,
the Emperor would ride the golden imperial carriage into the Yìngtiān Mén.
Upon reaching the front of the tent,
the Shìzhōng would prostrate themselves,
kneel, and report,
"Please dismount the carriage and enter the tent."
They would prostrate themselves
and rise.
The Emperor would dismount the carriage and enter the tent,
and the curtain would be lowered.
After a short while,
the Shìzhōng would report,
"Zhōngyán (Central Preparations)."
After another short while,
when the Diǎnzànyí had led the Crown Prince to his standing position below the gate,
and the Tōngshì Shèrén had led the multitude of officials to divide into ranks and stand facing each other below the gate,
the Shìzhōng would report,
"Wàibàn (Outer Preparations)."
The Emperor, dressed in his regular court attire,
would have the Shàngniǎn advance the imperial sedan chair.
The Shìzhōng would report,
"Please ascend the sedan chair."
Umbrellas, fans, and guards would be arranged as usual.
He would ascend the Yìngtiān Mén via the ramp of the Zuǒ Xiánglóng Mén,
and upon reaching the east of the imperial seat,
the Shìzhōng would report,
"Please dismount the sedan chair and ascend the seat."
The palace chimes and music would begin.
The relevant department would retrieve the fans
(fifty fans).
As the fans closed,
the Emperor would approach the balustrade and take the imperial seat.
Below the gate tower, whips would be cracked.
The curtain would roll up and the fans would open.
Those holding the imperial umbrella would unfurl it in front of the balustrade to block the sun,
and the music would stop.
The Dōngshàng Gémén Shǐ would place the imperial edict in a box.
Two Gémén Shèrén would follow,
awaiting the pulling of the rope to lower the wooden crane immortal.
The Tōngshì Shèrén would lead the civil and military officials to combine ranks and stand facing north.
The palace chimes and music would begin.
Whenever ranks divided or combined, music would play,
and it would stop once they stood still.
The Diǎnyí would say,
"Bow twice."
All officials present would bow twice.
When finished,
they would divide into ranks and stand facing each other.
The Shìzhōng would proceed to the imperial seat to receive instructions,
then withdraw,
step slightly forward facing south,
and proclaim:
"By imperial decree, erect the golden chicken."
The Tōngshì Shèrén, slightly forward and facing east below the gate,
would proclaim:
"By imperial decree, erect the golden chicken."
Then retire and return to their position.
When the golden rooster was first set up,
the Grand Music Bureau struck the drums.
The drumming ceased when the pole was erected.
Four pole-balancing performers
climbed the pole by rope, vying with each other,
to retrieve the crimson banner held by the rooster.
After displaying it,
they shouted
"Wànsuì" (Long Live) three times.
The Tōngshì Shèrén led the civil and military officials to form ranks, standing facing north.
An immortal on a crane on the upper floor held an imperial decree,
descended along a rope to a decorated platform.
A Gě Héshǐ received and placed it on a table.
Four Gémén Shèrén lifted the table,
and two more held the imperial decree.
The Gě Héshǐ led them to the front of the ranks,
faced west, and announced
"Yǒu Zhì" (There is a decree).
The Diǎnyí said
"Bài" (Bow).
All officials present bowed twice.
After this,
the imperial decree was handed to the chief official of the Shàngshū Shěng.
He advanced slightly, inserted his tablet into his belt,
knelt to receive it.
After this,
he handed it to the Yòusī Guān.
The Yòusī Guān inserted his tablet into his belt,
knelt to receive it.
After this,
the chief official removed his tablet,
prostrated himself,
rose,
and returned to his position.
The Yòusī Guān held the imperial decree and proceeded to the proclamation position.
The Dūshì held it with him.
The Yòusī Guān read aloud
until
"xián shè chú zhī" (all are pardoned and exempted).
The appropriate officials and jailers led the criminals to the south of the ranks,
facing north,
and humbly announced
"tuō jiā" (unfetter).
After this,
they shouted
"Wànsuì" (Long Live) three times,
and the criminals were dismissed.
After the Yòusī Guān finished proclaiming the decree,
he faced west,
and handed the imperial decree to an official of the Xíngbù.
After kneeling to receive it,
he placed the imperial decree on top of his tablet,
withdrew and handed it to his subordinate,
and returned to his original rank.
The Diǎnyí said
"Bài" (Bow).
All officials present bowed twice,
performed a ritual dance,
and bowed twice again.
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huángtàizǐ to a mat in front of the ranks, where he stood still.
The Diǎnyí said
"Bài" (Bow).
The Huángtàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice.
The Diǎnzànyí led the Huángtàizǐ slightly forward,
he prostrated himself,
knelt to deliver his address,
prostrated himself,
rose.
The Diǎnyí said
"Zàibài" (Bow twice).
The Huángtàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice,
inserted their tablets into their belts,
performed a ritual dance,
and bowed twice again.
The Shìzhōng received the imperial instruction in front of the imperial seat,
then withdrew to the balcony and proclaimed
"Yǒu Zhì" (There is a decree).
The Diǎnyí said
"Zàibài" (Bow twice).
The Huángtàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice.
The Shìzhōng proclaimed the imperial reply.
After proclaiming, he returned to his attendant position.
The Diǎnyí said
"Zàibài" (Bow twice).
The Huángtàizǐ and all officials below him bowed twice,
inserted their tablets into their belts,
performed a ritual dance,
and bowed twice again.
After this,
the Diǎnzànyí led the Huángtàizǐ to a mat in front of the gate.
The Tōngshì Shèrén led the officials to divide into ranks and stand facing each other.
The Shìzhōng went before the imperial seat,
prostrated himself,
knelt and reported
"Lǐ Bì" (The ceremony is complete).
He prostrated himself,
rose,
and returned to his position.
The appropriate officials requested the fans.
The palace orchestra began to play.
The fans closed,
the curtains descended.
The Huángdì descended from his seat.
The music stopped.
Whips cracked below the tower.
The Huángdì returned to the inner palace by imperial carriage.
Umbrellas, fans, and guards were arranged as usual.
The Shìzhōng reported
"Jiěyán" (End of vigil).
The Tōngshì Shèrén received the imperial order.
All ministers returned to their respective posts.
All generals and soldiers returned to their original places.
Ritual for ministers to receive an imperial pardon decree.
On the day of the pardon's proclamation,
an incense table was set up outside the Àoyì Mén,
and an incense carriage was placed in front of the table.
Also, a small table was set up on the east side.
From the Huángtàizǐ and prime ministers downward, they arranged themselves in ranks.
A Gémén Guān took the pardon decree from a box, brought it out the gate, and placed it on the table.
A Gémén Guān stood east of the table,
faced south, and announced
"Yǒu Chì" (There is an imperial edict).
He prompted the Huángtàizǐ, prime ministers, and all officials to bow twice.
The Huángtàizǐ advanced slightly, offered incense.
After this, he returned to his position.
All bowed twice.
A Gémén Guān took the pardon decree and handed it to the Shàngshū Shěng Dūshì.
The Dūshì knelt to receive it.
Two Lìshǐ of the Shàngshū Shěng held it together.
They jointly ascended to the small table and read it aloud.
All officials present knelt to listen.
After reading,
the pardon decree was placed on the table.
The Dūshì returned to his position.
The Huángtàizǐ, prime ministers, and all officials below bowed twice,
inserted their tablets into their belts,
performed a ritual dance,
held their tablets,
prostrated themselves,
rose,
and bowed twice.
The Gǒngwèi Zhí and those below shouted
"Wànsuì" (Long Live) three times.
After this,
they withdrew.
For the promulgation of other documents,
the ceremony also followed this standard,
except that
"Wànsuì" (Long Live) was not shouted.
In the outer commanderies,
the Shàngshū Shěng dispatched an official to deliver the pardon decree to the capital prefectures and military garrisons (Jiézèn).
First, a messenger was sent to report.
The chief official immediately led his subordinates and clerks,
prepared flags, music, decorated carriages, and incense carriages,
and proceeded five *lǐ* outside the city to welcome it.
Upon seeing the official delivering the pardon decree,
they immediately dismounted by the roadside.
The dispatched official also dismounted,
took the pardon decree and placed it in the decorated carriage.
The chief official went before the incense carriage to offer incense.
After this,
the dispatched official mounted his horse,
positioned behind the incense carriage.
The chief official and those below all mounted their horses and followed.
Gongs and drums were sounded, music played to lead them to the public office.
They entered through the main gate.
The dispatched official dismounted.
Attendants had already set up a table and prostration mats facing the imperial palace in the courtyard.
The incense carriage was placed in front of the table.
Also, a prostration mat for the dispatched official was set up beside the table.
And a small table was set up to the southeast of the table.
The dispatched official took the pardon decree and placed it on the table.
The decorated carriage withdrew.
The dispatched official announced
"Yǒu Chì" (There is an imperial edict).
The chief official and those below all bowed twice.
The chief official advanced slightly to offer incense.
After this,
he withdrew and returned to his position,
and bowed twice again.
The dispatched official took the pardon decree and handed it to the Dūmù.
The Dūmù knelt to receive it.
And two Kǒumù Guān.
The three of them jointly held the pardon decree,
and read it aloud from a high table.
〔一０〕All officials present knelt to listen.
After reading,
the Dūmù and others returned to their positions.
The chief official and those below bowed twice,
performed a ritual dance,
prostrated themselves,
rose,
and bowed twice.
The Gōnglì and those below shouted
"Wànsuì" (Long Live) three times.
The ceremony was complete.
The next day,
the chief official led his subordinates,
with music, to escort the official to outside the city wall.
