During the reign of Xīzōng,
the Xià envoy entered for an audience.
This was changed to a "Grand Daily Audience."
It was formally established that the Sòng envoys would be ranked in the third-grade class,
while Gāolí and Xià envoys would be in the fifth-grade class.
In the sixth month of Huángtǒng second year (1142),
it was settled that when a minister-envoy had an audience and took leave,
the officials' attire and number of bows would follow the usual morning audience procedure.
The class ranking of the envoys from the three countries remained as before.
After the court session in front of the palace and the minor audience for officials were completed,
the chief ministers would ascend the palace hall,
and when the rest of the officials had taken their positions in their respective ranks,
then the ceremonies for entry to audience and taking leave from court would be performed.
For all audiences, the Sòng envoy would go first,
and after the ceremony, the Xià envoy would enter,
and after that ceremony, the Gāolí envoy would enter.
For taking leave from court, the Xià envoy would go first,
and after the ceremony, the Gāolí envoy would enter,
and after that ceremony, the Sòng envoy would enter.
The gifts for the Xià and Gāolí envoys taking leave from court
would be bestowed by dispatching an envoy to them at the Huìtóng Guǎn.
Only the gifts for the Sòng envoy were presented in the court.
Previously, Gāolí envoys always offered private gifts upon arrival at the palace.
In Dàdìng fifth year (1165),
the Emperor considered that Sòng and Xià envoys did not have this custom,
and it was improper for a smaller country alone to have it.
Therefore,
he ordered it to be abolished.
In the sixth year (1166),
an imperial edict stated that foreign envoys should enter and exit through the Zuǒyèmén for their first audience and when taking leave from court,
and through the east side gate of Yìngtiānmén for court congratulations and banquets.
In the third month of Dàdìng twenty-ninth year (1189),
Zhāngzōng, being in a period of mourning (liàng'àn),
exempted the Sòng envoy from taking leave from court.
The Tàicháng Sì (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) stated:
"If written messages are not personally presented and verbal communications are not transmitted,
there might be omissions or errors later."
Consequently, the Sòng envoy was ordered to first take leave at the spiritual canopy (língwò),
and then proceed to the Rénzhèng Diàn to take leave from court
and present the letter.
At that time, the Right Chancellor Xiāng stated:
"I humbly observe that Xīzōng's birthday was on the seventh day of the seventh month.
Due to avoiding Jǐngxūan's death anniversary, it was moved
to the following day.
Then, the seventeenth day of the first month was again used to receive congratulations from foreign countries.
If the current imperial birthday is held as scheduled,
and foreign envoys are allowed to cross the border,
I fear they might be delayed by heavy rain and floods.
Even if they manage to reach the capital,
they might encounter cloudy and rainy weather, making it difficult to perform the ceremonies.
I request that the eleventh day of the first month or the fifteenth day of the third month be set as the imperial birthday,
and that the Sòng people's border-crossing date be fixed accordingly."
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Zhāng Rǔlín, Cānzhī Zhèngshì Liú Wěi, and others stated:
"An emperor should demonstrate trustworthiness.
To change the date hastily due to rain and road blockages
might lead to a loss of trust.
Moreover, the Sòng Emperor's birthday is also in the fifth month.
At that time, they were all in Huìníng,
and the superior state dispatched envoys to bestow birthday wishes.
Crossing rivers for ten thousand li,
they still did not avoid heavy rains and floods,
arriving as scheduled.
Now, we have long maintained good relations with Sòng;
we should not show insincerity due to minor obstacles.
If they cross the border,
making more planned stops will prevent delays.
Even if they are delayed by rain and water and enter for an audience beyond the scheduled date,
it is still better than using another day."
Yùshǐ Dàfū Tángkuò Gòng, Zhōngchéng Lǐ Yàn,
Xíngbù Shàngshū and Yòujiànyì Dàfū Wányán Shǒuzhēn
and others also all said it was not permissible.
Initially, the Emperor followed their advice,
but later he ultimately adopted Xiāng's proposal,
ordering the relevant authorities to notify
the Sòng envoys clearly of the actual imperial birthday,
and that the date was specially changed to show favor and consideration for travelers.
In the first month of Chéng'ān third year (1198),
the Emperor issued an edict to the relevant authorities, saying:
"I recently heard that during the Sòng state's flower banquets,
no food was served in the hall,
but rather it was prepared in the corridor when the guests rested.
Currently, serving food at our flower banquets is quite restrictive.
Would it be permissible to follow their example?
Also, previously when envoys arrived and departed,
there used to be a wine ceremony in the hall,
but this has now been moved to the guesthouse banquet."
The authorities reported:
"The custom of informal banquets is old.
In their country,
one round of wine and one serving of food must occur together to complete the ceremony.
However, according to our dynasty's custom,
food is only served after the wine ceremony is concluded.
As for the flower banquet day,
when the Sòng envoy arrives at the guest reception tent, there is a wine ceremony,
but when our envoy arrives at their tent, there is food but no wine.
Each follows its own long-standing custom,
and there is no need for them to be the same.
In ancient times, banquets featured food to show kindness and benevolence.
If we change it abruptly now,
I fear distant people may have doubts,
and it would lose the court's intention to show favor and hospitality to its ministers and foreign visitors."
So, it was ordered to remain as before.
In the tenth month of Zhèngdà first year (1224),
the Xià state dispatched envoys to mend relations.
In the ninth month of the second year (1225),
the peace agreement with the Xià state was finalized,
whereby Xià would treat Jīn as an elder brother,
each using its own country's reign title.
Regulations for the envoy's audience and taking leave were established.
The Xià people, since the Tiānhuì period, had made peace
and been vassals of Jīn for over eighty years,
without any military conflicts.
However, at the beginning of Zhēnyòu,
there was minor encroachment,
leading to ten years of conflict,
which exhausted both countries.
By this point,
peace was finally made as brotherly states.
In the tenth month,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Àodūn Liángbì, Dàlǐ Qīng Péimǎn Qīnfǔ, and Shìyùshǐ Wūgǔsūn Hóngyì were dispatched as envoys to report the peace.
In the tenth month of the third year (1226),
the Xià people announced a death, and Zhōngdàfū Wányán Lǚxìn was dispatched as an envoy for condolences and sacrifice.
The Xià people, due to ongoing military affairs,
ceased mutual diplomatic missions.
In the fourth year (1227),
Wáng Lìzhī was dispatched to visit,
but before his return, Xià fell.
Newly established regulations for Xià envoys.
The Xià state's chief envoy, deputy envoy, and one councilor were
called "envoys."
There were three general managers (dūguǎn).
Five were "upper-grade retainers," five "middle-grade retainers,"
and twenty-four "lower-grade retainers";
these were called "three grades of retainers."
Upon receiving the report at the xíngshěng,
a welcoming envoy and a messenger for letters and memorials would be dispatched to meet them at the border.
Upon entering the border,
the itinerary and lodging details at post stations would first be provided.
Upon first arriving at the Jīngzhào xíngshěng,
a banquet would be given the next day.
The same applied upon reaching the Hénán xíngshěng;
this was called the "arrival banquet."
When approaching the capital,
one palace attendant would be dispatched with three silver boxes wrapped in oiled silk,
containing twenty-six kinds of medicinal soups and drinks,
to meet them at Wèishì Xiàn in the nearby border region and present them.
Upon reaching the Ēnhuá Guǎn (formerly called Yànbīn Guǎn,
renamed in Chéng'ān third year),
they would change clothes,
and enter through the Yízhào Mén.
Two officers, a guesthouse companion envoy and a deputy envoy, four scribes for letters and memorials,
and thirty "leading officials" would be pre-dispatched
to await them.
When the arriving envoy's three grades of retainers reached the Huìtóng Guǎn,
this was called "gathering in the hall."
First, the name and title of the guesthouse companion envoy would be given to them,
and the envoy would also present his title.
Then, the chief envoy, deputy envoy, general managers, and upper and middle-grade retainers would in turn meet the guesthouse companion envoy.
The ceremony for the initial meeting with the welcoming envoy was also the same.
Next, the letters written by the guesthouse companion were presented to the envoys.
The "leading officials" of the guesthouse companion and the lower-grade retainers would mutually meet each other.
After this,
the guesthouse companion and welcoming envoy,
and the chief and deputy envoys,
each in their official attire, would simultaneously exit their tents.
They would stand facing each other outside the balustrade of the upper hall,
with the guesthouse companion to the north,
standing opposite.
First, the welcoming envoy would bow,
then the arriving deputy envoy and the guesthouse companion would exchange their credentials,
bow,
each would display them,
and bow again.
Each would take their seat,
and be asked to put away their tablets and sit.
First, a soup was served,
then three cups of wine,
and fruits and delicacies were placed.
After the tea,
they would hold their tablets,
move forward and rise together.
Outside the balustrade, the guesthouse companion would be to the south,
standing opposite.
First, the guesthouse companion would bow,
then display the welcoming envoy's farewell statement,
bow in farewell,
each would display them,
and bow again,
then they would bow to each other and separate.
On this day,
the Emperor dispatched an envoy to express solace and inquire.
When the celestial envoy arrived at the residence,
the reception and sequence were in accordance with the initial meeting ceremony for the guest envoy.
The guǎnbàn, the celestial envoy, and the deputy foreign envoy each wore formal attire,
and proceeded together to their positions,
standing opposite each other.
The deputy foreign envoy was requested to ascend the ceremonial mat and stand facing the imperial palace in obeisance.
Next, the celestial envoy was requested to ascend the ceremonial mat and stand slightly forward.
The deputy foreign envoy bowed,
and the celestial envoy announced,
"By imperial decree."
Thereupon, they bowed twice and genuflected.
After the celestial envoy finished verbally conveying the decree,
they returned to their position.
The foreign envoy bowed twice,
performed a dance (wǔdǎo),
bowed thrice,
and returned to their standing position.
The foreign envoy and the celestial envoy each presented their credentials,
and greeted each other with a bow.
Next, the guǎnbàn bowed.
The foreign envoy had someone convey a message,
inviting the guǎnbàn, the celestial envoy, and the foreign envoy to proceed together to the upper hall.
Each went to their chair and stood,
exchanging a general bow.
They respectfully put away their hu (tablets) and sat.
Soup, wine, dishes, and tea were all served as before.
When finished,
they held their hu,
approached forward,
all requested to rise,
and went to the ceremonial mat,
standing opposite each other as before.
The deputy foreign envoy was requested to ascend to the mat position,
and present a memorial to thank for the solace and inquiry.
They bowed twice,
the deputy envoy stood straight,
and the envoy knelt to offer the memorial.
The celestial envoy approached, tucked in his hu, and received it,
then withdrew his hu and returned to his position.
The foreign envoy then bowed,
retreated,
and returned to standing opposite.
The foreign envoy had someone convey a message to the guǎnbàn,
to send local products to the celestial envoy as customary.
When finished,
the celestial envoy presented his farewell credentials,
they separated with a bow.
Next, the guǎnbàn bowed,
and each was requested to go to their respective positions.
Thereafter,
messages were conveyed every morning and evening,
and the qiānlǒngguān (escort officials) made obeisances as per ceremony.
On the day after arriving at the residence,
an envoy was sent to bestow wine and fruit.
After the celestial envoy's initial reception,
the obeisances, announcements, and all other rituals were the same as for the solace and inquiry ceremony.
The envoy and deputy envoy knelt on one knee,
the wine and fruit passed by their side,
and they bowed and performed the wǔdǎo as per ceremony.
After the soup, wine, and tea in the upper hall were finished,
they proceeded to the ceremonial mat position,
knelt to present a memorial thanking for the bestowed wine and fruit.
The gifts of local products to the celestial envoy were all in accordance with the禮 (lǐ) for the solace and inquiry envoy,
and the soldiers escorting the wine and fruit also received gifts of local products.
Then, the Deputy Minister of the Gémén was ordered to come to the residence to practice the ceremony.
The initial reception and subsequent proceedings were all in accordance with the guǎnbàn's meeting ceremony.
After the soup and tea,
the guǎnbàn and the Gémén Deputy conveyed a message to the envoy and deputy envoy,
stating that they would be granted an audience tomorrow,
and it was customary to practice the ceremony.
The foreign envoy and deputy envoy replied with a message,
and the practice ceremony was completed.
After the second cup (of wine),
a cup of wine was offered directly to the person undergoing the practice ceremony for acceptance.
First, a bow was exchanged,
the wine was drunk,
then two bows were made, and they retreated.
After the three cups and fruit tea were finished,
they held their hu, approached forward, and all rose together.
Outside the railing, south was considered the superior position,
and they stood opposite each other.
As they were to have an audience the next day,
they merely exchanged bows without presenting farewell credentials,
and then took their respective positions.
Then, the roster for the audience was given to the Gémén to take away,
to be delivered to the Lǐjìn Sī.
The foreign envoy and deputy envoy sent local products in writing to the Yǐnjìnshǐ,
as well as to the military personnel responsible for delivering the tribute items,
and the Gémén Deputy and the person undergoing the practice ceremony each received gifts of local products.
On the third day,
they had an audience.
On that day, at dawn,
the dūguǎn and the three ranks of attendants were all dressed,
and the guǎnbàn and the foreign envoy and deputy envoy each wore formal attire.
All were requested to proceed to the horse platform.
The guǎnbàn's qiānlǒngguān shouted,
"Line up the horses!"
The foreign envoy's qiānlǒngguān shouted,
"Lead the horses!"
Each mounted their horse and had their canopy unfurled.
The dūguǎn, on horseback, presented a letter in front of the envoy.
Upon reaching outside the middle gate,
the outside was considered superior,
and they stood opposite each other.
First, the foreign envoy's qiānlǒngguān made two obeisances,
then the guǎnbàn's qiānlǒngguān did likewise,
they all bowed,
each conveyed a message,
bowed again,
and were requested to proceed.
Five hundred paces outside the Left Yèméng,
the guǎnbàn and the envoy and deputy envoy exchanged left and right positions to proceed.
After bowing,
a hundred paces from the gate, they dismounted from under their umbrellas,
took out their hu,
and proceeded opposite each other.
All subsequent audiences for congratulations and banquets followed this same ceremony.
The foreign envoy's attendants carrying items were not allowed to enter the gate;
the qiānlǒngguān temporarily collected them.
Two officials from the Kèxǐng conveyed messages.
The guǎnbàn and the foreign envoy each had someone reply with a message.
Upon reaching the Kèxǐng screen,
the guǎnbàn's written memorial stood above.
They all bowed,
then entered behind the screen.
First, the guǎnbàn's written memorial was conveyed,
then the foreign envoy's written memorial was conveyed.
They stood outside the railing as before,
first bowed,
were offered a cup of wine directly,
bowed again,
and retreated.
The guǎnbàn and the foreign envoy were led into the Kèxǐng screen.
The inside was considered superior,
and after standing opposite and bowing,
they were requested to take their respective positions.
First, the guǎnbàn bowed,
then presented the Kèxǐng's daily greetings,
bowed,
each conveyed a message,
bowed again,
and exchanged a general bow.
They were requested to proceed to their positions and stand,
bowed again,
and were requested to put away their hu and sit.
First, soup was served,
then three cups of wine,
each with fruits and dishes.
After the second cup of wine was finished,
the Kèxǐng conveyed a message to the foreign envoy,
inviting the dūguǎn and the upper and middle ranks to offer wine.
After the reply message was conveyed,
the dūguǎn and the upper and middle ranks were led to stand in formation below the steps in front of the screen.
First, they bowed,
drank wine,
bowed again,
and were led to retreat.
After the third cup of wine was finished and the tea concluded,
they held their hu,
approached forward and all rose together,
standing in front of the screen.
After exchanging a general bow,
each returned to their respective screen position.
After the minor court audience in the palace hall concludes,
the Chief Councillors (zǎi zhí) ascend the hall.
The other ministers retreat in their respective ranks.
The Palace Usher (gé shǐ) announces the arrival of the envoy, presenting the placard (bǎng zi).
Then, the escorts (guǎn bàn) are first invited to enter their ranks.
When the Palace Gate (gé mén) ushers them in,
the Guest Department (kè xǐng) and the chief and deputy envoys (lái shǐ fù) are invited to stand opposite each other in front of the curtain (mù).
The outer position is superior.
The envoy presents the letter.
After bowing, they walk abreast
to outside the Three Gates (sān mén).
The usher bows, and the Palace Usher's deputy bows.
The envoy presents the letter.
The deputy steps forward with the ceremonial tablet (hù) and follows.
To the left, on the exposed platform outside the eaves pillars of the hall,
the envoy presents the letter kneeling on one knee.
(According to old ritual, the letter was presented within the vermilion steps (dān chí).)
The Palace Usher (gé shǐ) receives the letter.
The envoy and deputy then bow
and stand.
The Palace Usher enters to the right within the railings (lán zi),
and reports,
"The seal is intact."
After reading aloud,
(formerly, it was never read aloud)
the usher leads the envoy and deputy into the hall within the railings.
The usher bows, and the envoy and deputy bow again with a deep bow.
The usher leads them a little forward to kneel and report:
"Your younger brother, the Emperor (Dà Xià Huángdì) of Dà Xià, sends greetings to Your elder brother, the Emperor (Dà Jīn Huángdì) of Dà Jīn.
May your sacred person enjoy ten thousand blessings."
They bow again,
rise,
and return to their positions.
The Emperor then sends an inquiry to the Emperor of Xià.
The envoy and deputy bow deeply to receive the imperial command.
After this,
the usher leads the envoy a little forward to kneel and report:
"Your younger brother, the Emperor (Dà Xià Huángdì) of Dà Xià, enjoys ten thousand blessings in his sacred person."
They bow,
return to their positions,
and stand.
They retreat together,
descend the steps to the left,
and stand facing north at the vermilion steps.
The gifts are brought in from the right and out from the left.
When all are presented,
the usher bows to the envoy and deputy, who then turn to join the ranks.
They are led again to the vermilion steps,
where they perform the ceremonial dance (wǔ dǎo),
bow five times,
and report
"May your sacred person enjoy ten thousand blessings" without leaving their ranks.
After this,
they bow again.
The usher leads the envoy and deputy forward,
where they kneel on both knees.
The Emperor dispatches someone to offer a message of comfort and inquiry.
They return to their positions,
express gratitude,
perform the ceremonial dance,
and bow five times.
The usher bows again, leading the envoy and deputy out of their ranks,
where they express thanks for seeing the Emperor's countenance.
They return to their positions,
perform the ceremonial dance,
and bow five times.
The usher bows again to the Palace Usher's deputy,
and leads the envoy out of his ranks,
where he expresses thanks for being sent from afar, for the reception and escort, and for the gifts of medicinal soup and other items.
They return to their positions,
perform the ceremonial dance,
and bow five times.
A shout of
"All attend!" is heard.
The usher leads them out to the right,
to the bottom of the steps of the Three Gates,
where they bow farewell to the Palace Usher's deputy.
They walk with the Guest Department to in front of the curtain, where they bow to each other,
and each returns to their quarters (mù cì).
The usher leads the Chief Attendant (dū guǎn) and the senior and middle-ranking sections (shàng zhōng jié) in from the left.
They stand at the vermilion steps.
The junior section (xià jié) stands outside the gate at the bottom of the steps.
They all bow deeply and announce their names.
First, they bow twice
and report
"May your sacred person enjoy ten thousand blessings" without leaving their ranks.
They bow again.
The junior section bows deeply and utters a greeting (shēng nuò).
The first bow is accompanied by a shout of
"Long live!"
The second bow is accompanied by a shout of
"Long live!"
As they rise, they shout
"Long, long live!"
A shout of
"All attend!" is heard.
They stand upright.
The usher leads them out to the right.
Then, clothes are bestowed upon the envoy.
The bowing and dancing are all according to the ritual for bestowing wine and fruit.
After this,
the envoy and the imperial messenger (tiān shǐ) stand opposite each other.
Next, the Chief Attendant and the people of the three sections are invited to stand facing the palace.
The imperial messenger stands slightly forward.
The Chief Attendant and his retinue bow deeply.
The imperial messenger transmits the imperial decree.
They bow in thanks, following the envoy's ritual.
After bowing,
they express gratitude and bow again.
The junior section bows deeply and utters a greeting,
as in the initial audience ritual.
Then, they are led in again
to be bestowed with wine and food.
The Palace Gate and Guest Department procedures are all as in the initial audience ritual.
At the vermilion steps,
they express thanks for the bestowed clothing and items,
bow again,
perform the ceremonial dance,
bow three times,
and bow deeply.
The announcer (zàn) calls out
"By imperial decree, wine and food are bestowed."
They perform the ceremonial dance,
and bow five times.
A shout of
"All attend!" is heard.
The usher leads them out to the right,
as per the previous ritual,
and they return to their quarters.
Then, they are invited to depart.
The escort and the envoy and deputy stand opposite each other in front of the curtain and bow.
Each communicates something,
then bows again,
and they are invited to proceed.
Upon reaching the original dismounting place (yuán xià mǎ suǒ),
they exchange left and right positions again and proceed.
After bowing,
they each put away their ceremonial tablets,
mount their horses, and go to the guesthouse (guǎn).
Again, they exchange left and right positions upon entering the gate.
The inner position is superior.
They stand opposite each other.
First, the arriving envoy leads his official (lǒng guān).
Next, the escort leads his official.
Each utters a greeting.
They bow twice and then bow,
after which,
they are invited to take their respective seats.
Then, the escorting envoy (yā bàn shǐ) hosts a banquet at the guesthouse.
The escort was led to the residence.
After the credentials were exchanged and returned,
the resident-host and the envoy put on their court robes
and stood facing each other at the kneeling mat.
The escort stood slightly in front.
First, the escort and resident-host were invited onto the kneeling mat,
bowed towards the imperial palace,
thanked for the seat,
bowed again,
performed the ceremonial dance,
bowed thrice,
and rose.
First, the escort was invited to stand on the side steps,
then the envoy and his deputy were led onto the kneeling mat,
bowed towards the imperial palace, and also thanked for the seat.
The ceremony proceeded as before.
Then, they walked with the resident-host to the main hall.
The escort stood on the side steps
and exchanged credentials with the envoy and his deputy.
The envoy and his deputy first sent someone to report to the superior.
The escort returned to convey the message
and bowed again.
The escort was invited in first
to stand at the chair in front of the table.
The resident-host and the envoy and his deputy bowed to each other,
each took their positions,
performed a general bow,
and were invited to hold their tablets upright and sit.
When the hot beverage was served,
the chief attendants and their retinue lined up on the bowing mat.
When the hot beverage cups were brought out,
they bowed and rose.
The escort and others moved away from their seats and stood.
The chief attendants and their retinue bowed deeply,
and the lower-ranking attendants made a respectful salutation,
as in an audience ceremony.
They shouted
"Wànsuì!" (Long live the Emperor!).
When finished,
it was called out,
"The escort and the envoy and his deputy shall all take their seats!"
The three chief attendants and the upper and middle sections of the retinue were led to the hall, dividing left and right.
Entering from the south,
north was considered superior.
The lower section stood in the west corridor.
After the escort and others finished their first cup
and the music ended,
they sat.
At the end of the third cup,
the meal was finished.
At the end of the fourth cup,
the wine was finished.
The escort conveyed to the envoy
to personally offer a cup of wine to the chief attendants and the upper and middle sections.
The envoy replied to the superior.
The chief attendants and the upper and middle sections lined up below the side steps.
First, they bowed,
drank,
conveyed the imperial command to offer wine,
bowed again,
and withdrew.
At the end of the fifth cup,
the wine was finished.
Tea was served.
The chief attendants and their retinue lined up on the bowing mat.
After the tea was finished,
the escort and others were bowed to and rose,
standing away from their seats.
The chief attendants and their retinue bowed deeply,
and it was called out,
"Xiè'ēn!" (Thanks for the grace!).
They bowed.
The lower-ranking attendants made a respectful salutation as in the previous ceremony,
and took their positions.
The escort and others were invited to descend to the hall together
and stand facing each other at the bowing mat.
First, the envoy and his deputy were invited to the kneeling mat,
thanked for the grace,
bowed again,
performed the ceremonial dance,
bowed thrice,
and returned to their positions.
Then, the escort and resident-host were invited to the kneeling mat,
thanked as in the previous ceremony,
and returned to their positions.
On the fourth day,
the banquet-supervising official and the banquet-bestowing official were ordered to hold a banquet at the residence.
First, the banquet-bestowing imperial envoy exchanged credentials as in the previous ceremony.
Each wore court robes.
The resident-host, the imperial envoy, and the foreign envoy were invited to stand facing each other at the kneeling mat.
First, the envoy and his deputy were invited to the kneeling mat
and stood facing the imperial palace.
Next, the banquet-bestowing imperial envoy was invited to the kneeling mat, slightly in front.
The envoy and his deputy bowed deeply.
The imperial envoy conveyed the proclamation.
The envoy and his deputy bowed in thanks,
all as in the previous ceremony.
The envoy and his deputy and the imperial envoy exchanged credentials,
inquired about each other's well-being,
and bowed.
Next, the resident-host bowed.
The envoy and his deputy had someone convey to the resident-host
to offer tea and wine to the banquet-bestowing imperial envoy as per custom.
The resident-host temporarily retired behind the curtain.
The envoy and his deputy and the imperial envoy, as host and guest, walked to the main hall.
Inside the west chamber, each went to their chair, bowed,
put away their tablets, and sat.
First, a hot beverage,
then three cups of wine,
fruits, and dishes were served.
After the tea,
they held their tablets,
approached and were invited to rise.
The banquet-bestowing imperial envoy quietly withdrew.
The banquet-supervising envoy was invited to stand at the kneeling mat.
Next, the resident-host was invited to the kneeling mat.
They bowed twice towards the imperial palace,
stood upright,
inserted their tablets into their belts,
performed three deep bows and ceremonial dances,
knelt on their left knee and kowtowed thrice,
brought out their tablets and bowed,
rose,
bowed again, and returned to their positions,
standing facing each other.
The banquet-supervising envoy was invited to the hall.
Next, the envoy and his deputy were invited to the kneeling mat,
thanked for the seat,
bowed again,
performed the ceremonial dance,
bowed thrice,
and were invited to ascend the hall by different steps.
Outside the railing,
the inside was superior.
They stood facing each other.
First, the resident-host bowed.
Next, they exchanged the banquet-supervising envoy's credentials,
met each other,
and bowed.
Each conveyed messages,
and bowed again.
They performed a general bow,
were invited to take their seats,
and went to their chairs to stand.
They performed a general bow,
and were invited to hold their tablets upright and sit,
as the imperial banquet did not permit the use of footstools.
When the hot beverage was served,
the chief attendants and the three sections of the retinue lined up on the bowing mat.
When the hot beverage cups were brought out,
the banquet-supervising envoy moved away from his seat and stood bowing.
The chief attendants and their retinue bowed deeply,
and the lower-ranking attendants made a respectful salutation,
shouting
"Wànsuì!" (Long live the Emperor!),
as in an audience ceremony.
It was called out,
"Everyone take your seats!"
The banquet-supervising envoy and others were invited to sit.
The Dūguǎn, and the Shàng-Zhōngjié are led to the main hall, dividing left and right.
They enter from the north,
with the south as the superior position,
and stand.
The Xiàjié enter from the south at the west corridor,
with the north as the superior position,
and stand.
After the first round of drinks for the Yāyàn and others is complete,
and the music ceases,
they sit.
At the fifth round of drinks, food is served.
The sixth and seventh rounds are accompanied by variety plays.
After the eighth round,
the drinking concludes.
The Yāyàn instructs the emissaries and deputies
to, according to custom, invite the Dūguǎn and Shàng-Zhōngjié to drink in person.
The emissaries report this upstairs.
Again, they lead the Dūguǎn and Shàng-Zhōngjié to stand in rows on the steps outside the railing.
First, they bow,
drink wine,
then bow again,
and withdraw.
After the ninth round of drinks,
and the drinking concludes,
the Jiàofāng withdraws.
Then, the Tiānshǐ who are granted the banquet are invited to the front of the curtained enclosure.
After the tea is brought in,
the Dūguǎn and the three Jié, with their retinues, stand in rows at the bowing mat.
When the teacups are brought out,
they bow and rise.
The Yāyànguān and others leave their seats and stand.
They bow.
The Dūguǎn and their retinues bow profoundly,
and exclaim,
"Xiè'ēn!"
They prostrate themselves.
The Xiàjié utter a sound of assent,
and shout,
"Wànsuì!"
As in the ceremony of audience,
they then bow profoundly,
〔一０〕and exclaim,
"Gè Zhīhòu!"
All the Yāyàn and other officials are invited to come out together,
descend the steps into the hall,
and walk opposite the Tiānshǐ to the front of the bowing mat and stand.
The emissaries and deputies are invited to their positions to face the palace and express thanks for the imperial grace,
bowing twice again,
performing the dance,
then bowing three times.
When finished,
they stand in their positions.
The Yāyàn and Guǎnbàn are invited to proceed together to the mat to give thanks for the imperial grace.
The visiting emissaries then present a memorial of thanks for the imperial banquet.
First, they bow twice again,
and stand erect.
The emissaries kneel and hold the memorial.
The Tiānshǐ step forward, insert their hu into their belts, and receive the memorial,
then remove their hu and return to their positions.
The emissaries go to the mat to bow,
then withdraw and return to their positions,
and stand.
The emissaries and deputies report this upstairs.
According to custom, they write and send local products to the Tiānshǐ.
After receiving them,
the Tiānshǐ immediately return gifts in kind.
Then, the Tiānshǐ's formal letter of farewell is presented.
They bow twice again,
then the Guǎnbàn bow.
A general bow is exchanged.
They are invited to their respective places.
On this day,
the visiting emissaries bestow gifts upon the officials supervising the banquet, the Jiàofāng personnel, and others.
On the fifth day,
they offer congratulations.
They stand opposite each other at the curtained enclosure of the Kèshěng,
all according to the ceremony for an audience.
Upon retrieving their hu and sitting,
first soup is served,
then three rounds of wine.
When finished,
the Kèshěng conveys to the visiting emissaries
a message saying:
"Please invite the Dūguǎn and Shàng-Zhōngjié to drink in person."
After the message is conveyed back,
the Dūguǎn and Shàng-Zhōngjié are led to stand in rows on the steps in front of the curtained enclosure.
First, they bow,
drink wine,
then bow again,
and are led away.
After the three rounds of wine are finished,
and the tea concluded,
they retrieve their hu and step forward.
All are invited to exit the curtained enclosure,
with the outside as the superior position.
They stand opposite each other,
exchange a general bow,
take their respective positions,
and each return to their own curtained enclosure.
When the Gémen calls and invites them,
the Kèshěng and the emissaries and deputies are invited to the front of the curtained enclosure,
with the outside as the superior position.
They stand opposite each other and bow.
They walk opposite each other to the steps outside the gate,
and bow to the deputy who leads and bows to the Gé.
The emissaries and deputies are led in from the left,
join the ranks of the officials,
and stand facing north on the Dānchí.
Together with the officials, they first bow twice,
stand erect,
insert their hu into their belts,
bow profoundly,
perform the dance three times,
kneel on their left knee and kowtow three times,
take out their hu and prostrate themselves,
rise,
bow twice again,
and stand erect.
After the presentation of wine and the address are completed,
they bow twice again.
The Xuānhuīshǐ proclaims,
"Yǒu Zhì!"
They bow twice again.
After the imperial decree is read out,
they first bow twice,
perform the dance,
stand erect,
and divide into ranks.
When the emperor raises his cup,
they bow twice again.
The assembled ranks bow twice again,
ascend the hall.
The Xià emissaries and deputies stand at the northern end of the second row to the right of the imperial seat.
Next, the dùguǎn and shàngzhōngjié enter from the left,
standing before the Dānchí.
Those of the xiàjié arrange themselves on the steps outside the gate,
all bowing in unison.
After announcing their names,
they first perform a double kowtow,
then bow,
and without leaving their ranks, they intone,
"Shènggōng wànfú" (May the Holy Personage enjoy myriad blessings).
A command is shouted:
"Bài!" (Kowtow!)
They perform another double kowtow.
Those of the xiàjié call out "Nò!" (Yes!) and shout,
"Wànsuì!" (Long live the Emperor!).
The ceremony is as before.
A command is shouted:
"Gè zhīhòu!" (All stand by!).
When this is done,
they stand upright,
and bow again.
A command is shouted:
"Cì jiǔshí!" (Grant wine and food!).
They call out "Nò!", perform a double kowtow, and shout,
"Wànsuì!" (Long live the Emperor!).
The ceremony is as before.
They are led to stand in the left corridor.
After the bed is brought in,
wine is presented.
When the Huángdì drinks wine,
all who are standing by, above and below, perform a double kowtow.
When the official presenting wine reaches their position,
all seated officials perform a double kowtow,
and then all sit.
Immediately, the minister-envoys are offered wine,
a general announcement is made,
they drink standing,
perform a double kowtow,
and then resume their seats.
The next person and attendants perform the ceremony of bowing, calling out "Nò!", and performing a double kowtow and shouting
"Wànsuì!"
as before.
All sit.
Upon the third cup,
an announcement is made, and they drink standing.
When finished,
they perform a double kowtow,
and resume their seats.
The next person and attendants follow as before.
When finished,
they sit.
After the dedicatory speech,
when the drums and flutes are heard,
the minister-envoys are invited to stand.
When the oral declaration ceases,
the minister-envoys perform a double kowtow,
and sit.
The next person and attendants follow the previous ceremony,
and resume their seats.
Next, upon the fifth cup,
as the music approaches its end,
the attendants stand,
perform the previous ceremony again,
and when finished,
they are led out first.
The minister-envoys rise and perform a double kowtow,
retreat to the Dānchí,
form a line,
express thanks for the banquet,
perform a double kowtow,
dance,
perform three kowtows,
and a command is shouted:
"Gè zhīhòu!" (All stand by!).
They are led out,
and upon reaching the steps of the sān mén,
they bow in farewell to the gémén fùshǐ.
They proceed with the kès省
to stand opposite the curtained quarters.
First, they bow,
each conveying their message,
then bow again,
and are asked to take their designated places,
proceeding to the curtained quarters.
A short while later,
the guǎnbàn and the shǐfù are asked to come out of the curtained quarters.
The outer [person] is superior.
They stand opposite each other,
first bowing,
each conveying their message,
then bowing again,
and are led to proceed.
Upon reaching the original dismounting place,
they are asked to switch positions, left and right.
They stand opposite each other and bow,
then put away their tablets and mount their horses.
Upon reaching the guǎn,
they call out "Nò!" and bow to each other, taking their designated places.
This is the same as the return of courtesies during their initial audience.
On the sixth day,
food is distributed,
along with wine and fruit as gifts.
The tiānshǐ arrives at the guǎn.
This is the same as the gifting of wine and fruit on the second day.
On this day,
the distribution of food, wine, fruit, and military provisions is disbursed,
along with the standard provisions for officials and attendants in the guǎn assigned to relevant bureaus.

All the jiāngjūn of the outer gate, the jiānchú zhícháng, the guǎndūjiān, the jiānjiǔshíguān, the chéngyìngbān zhīhòu, the multitude of cooks, the guǎnzǐ, the xúnhùjūn, and the qiānlǒngguān of the guǎnbànsuǒ,
all receive a share.
On the seventh day,
the qǔyàn ceremony
is as before.
On the eighth day,
is the ceremony of bái cí (taking leave).
After the xiǎoqǐjū is finished,
the géshǐ first presents the list of the envoy's departure.
The envoy is led in from the left,
passing through the ranks in a detour,
and performs a double kowtow at the Dānchí.
Without leaving the ranks, they intone,
"Shènggōng wànfú" (May the Holy Personage enjoy myriad blessings),
and perform another double kowtow.
The yífù bows.
The envoy leaves the ranks and expresses words of farewell to the palace (liànquè zhìcí),
returns to their position,
performs a double kowtow,
and a command is shouted:
"Gè hǎoqù!" (May you all go well!).
They are led out to the right.
Next, the zǎizhí are led down from the hall.
The ceremony is complete.
On the ninth day,
they gather in the hall,
are escorted to the Ēnhuáguǎn,
change clothes, and depart.
Whenever an envoy is about to reach the border,
upon receiving the report, a jiēbànshǐ is dispatched.
Upon arrival, a guǎnbànshǐ is dispatched.
Upon departure, a sòngbànshǐ is dispatched.
All have a fù.
All are accompanied by a shūbiǎo.
All officials who oversee banquets or return banquets from the xíngshěng
are designated by the xíngshěng,
and are temporarily granted the titles of high-ranking civil or military officials,
to bring glory to their transition.
The tiānshǐ granted banquets for arrival and departure
are all sent as gémén zhīhòu.
Imperial edicts and oral declarations are all reported to the dūshěng for instructions,
and are drafted by the Hànlín Yuàn.
When the Xià envoy arrives,
they may be permitted to trade in the market for two days.
When an envoy arrives,
the dispatched personnel include one guǎnbànshǐ and one fù each,
one jiānchá, one fèngzhí, and one shěnglìshǐ each,
four shūbiǎo,
one zǒnglǐngtíkòngguān, one jiǔshíguān, one jiānchú, and one chēngròuguān each,
thirty qiānlǒngguān,
one shàngshíjú zhícháng, one zhīshū, one dùguǎn, one jiēshǒu, one tāngyào zhícháng, and one chángxíng each,
five cooks,
one fèngyǐn zhícháng and two chángxíng,
two fèngzhēn,
one yíluán zhícháng and ten chángxíng,
two officials guarding the inner and outer gates,
thirty xúnfángjūn outside the guǎn,
sixty-two jiǎjūn guarding the guǎn,
sixty záyìjūn,
ten jún who pass through positions and do not speak Hànyǔ.
All záyì wear black clothing.
Eighty guòshísīlì,
forty jiēshìchúzi,
one fāngmài and one zákēyī each,
one yīshòu,
twenty-four saddled horses,
later reduced to eight,
and one yāmǎguān.
Also dispatched is one shuōyí chéngshòulǐ zhíguān.
All artifacts and miscellaneous items displayed and arranged in the guǎn
are inspected jointly by an official dispatched by the Hùbù and the dōngshàngzhí gé.
All bridges and roads to be traversed are ordered to be repaired by the Gōngbù in advance.
As for the clothing gifts,
the shǐfù each receive three sets,
the attendants each receive two sets.
The shǐfù receive one hundred forty bolts of silk.
Formerly, two mink furs were also granted.
If not available, the envoy was compensated with three ingots of silver,
and the fù with sixty bolts of silk.
This was later abolished.
Only for raw food was it replaced with thirty-nine bolts of fine silk, sixty-two bolts of ordinary silk, and four bolts of cloth.
Three golden belts,
three gold-plated silver waist belts,
three gold-painted silver decorated saddles and bridles,
one gold-painted silver fully covered book box, and one gold-decorated gold-painted silver nailed black oil imperial edict box, as well as one wrap for the book and edict box respectively.
Upon morning departure,
the attendants are granted two hundred thirty-five liǎng of silver
and two hundred thirty-five bolts of silk.
The number of items granted to the Sòng and Gāolì envoys
cannot be verified.
Jiàokān Jì (Collation Notes)
Zhì No. 20 Yuè Shàng Yǎyuè, Sǎnlè, Gǔchuīyuè, Běncháo Yuèqǔ, Jiāosì Yuègē.
The tradition states:
"When a ruler's achievements are complete, music is created;
when governance is settled, rites are instituted."
How could the two Dì and three Wáng have neglected this cultural embellishment?
Indeed, for those who possess the world,
who would unify standards, rectify customs, harmonize humans and spirits, and bring accord between superiors and inferiors,
how could they do so without rites and music?
When the Jīn first acquired Sòng,
they began to have music of metal and stone instruments.
However, it was not yet perfect.
By the time of Dàdìng and Míngchāng,
it was refined daily and mended monthly,
becoming splendidly complete.
Those belonging to the Tàicháng Sī
were the two dances of the court orchestra and palace orchestra used for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temple offerings, grand banquets, and grand court assemblies.
Those belonging to the Jiàofāng
included ráo gē and gǔ chuī,
music for the emperor's imperial procession and vanguard.
There was Sǎnlè.
There was Bóhǎi Yuè.
There were the old tunes of the native land;
Shìzōng once captured their essence to create elegant tunes.
The historians recorded one of them,
while the vulgar ones were not included.
As for elegant music (Yǎyuè),
it was used for grand sacrifices, medium sacrifices, when the Son of Heaven received imperial seals, ascended the tower to grant pardons, and received congratulations from foreign envoys.
Initially,
Tàizōng captured Biàn,
and obtained the Sòng's ceremonial instruments, bells, chime stones, and chime stands.
He carried them back.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
Xīzōng was given an honorific title,
and the Sòng music began to be used.
Officials found that the characters
"Shèng"
engraved on the bells and chime stones violated Tàizōng's taboo name,
so they were all sealed with yellow paper.
In the fourteenth year of Dàdìng,
the Tàicháng Sī first proposed:
"Music from successive dynasties each has its own name.
The Sòng musical instruments currently used for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, and altars of soil and grain violate the temple's taboo names,
so they should all be scraped clean
and new names created for them."
Therefore,
the Lǐbù, Xuéshì Yuàn, and Tàicháng Sì were ordered to compose names.
They then took the meaning of grand music harmonizing with Heaven and Earth
and named it
"Tàihé."
The two dances, Wénwǔ and Wǔwǔ.
During the Huángtǒng era,
the civil dance was named Rénfēng Dàojià zhī Wǔ,
and the military dance was named Gōngchéng Zhìdìng zhī Wǔ.
The Zhēnyuán regulations later changed the civil dance to Bǎodà Dìnggōng zhī Wǔ,
and the military dance to Wànguó Láitóng zhī Wǔ.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng, there was also Sìhǎi Huìtóng zhī Wǔ,
and thus the system of that generation was finally complete.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
an edict ordered the use of Táng and Sòng precedents
to establish a bureau
for discussing rites and music.
Officials stated:
"Since the Zhōu and Hàn dynasties, only the general principles of elegant music have survived.
From Wèi and Jìn onwards, new pitch standards were created,
but there was no definitive conclusion.
It was not until the Bǎodìng era of the Later Zhōu
that an ancient jade dou was found in the ground,
and a pitch ruler was made based on it.
Later, Niú Hóng considered it unsuitable,
and only the iron ruler of Sū Chuò was used,
which was also used by the Suí.
When Táng arose,
it adopted Suí music without change.
During the chaos of Huáng Cháo,
the court orchestra was scattered and lost.
Tàicháng Bóshì Yīn Yíngsūn cast bó zhōng and biān zhōng according to Zhōu methods,
and recluse Xiāo Chéngxùn and others calibrated stone chimes (shí qìng).
They were combined and performed.
In the Xiǎndé era of Zhōu, millet was used to determine pitch,
and commentators said it was five pitches higher than Táng music.
In the early Sòng, Wáng Pǔ's music was also used.
At that time, Hé Xiàn, believing the pitch of Zhōu Xiǎndé's system to be mournful,
recreated twelve pipes based on the Xījīng bronze wàng niè and stone ruler,
taking a sound one pitch lower than Wáng Pǔ.
In the early Jǐngyòu era,
Lǐ Zhào used millet to accumulate rulers to form pitches.
As its sound was still high,
he further used the Tàifǔ cloth and silk ruler,
thus making it three pitches lower than the Tàicháng music.
In the Huángyòu era,
Ruǎn Yì and Hú Yuàn recreated it, lowering it by only one pitch.
Some said its sound was muffled and disharmonious,
so Wáng Pǔ's music was used again.
During the Yuánfēng era,
Yáng Jié combined Lǐ Zhào's bells and chime stones, adding four qīng shēng,
making it two pitches lower than Wáng Pǔ's music,
and called it new music.
During the Yuányòu era,
Fàn Zhèn also created new pitches,
one pitch lower than Lǐ Zhào's music,
but it was not adopted.
During the Chóngníng era,
Wèi Hànjīn, knowing Fàn Zhèn's old music was high
and having no way to lower it,
used the joints of the contemporary ruler's fingers as a ruler.
The bells and chime stones he created are the music used today.
However, because Wáng Pǔ's system produced high sounds,
it was repeatedly ordered to be revised.
Lǐ Zhào used the Tàifǔ ruler to create pitches,
but people accustomed to the old sounds considered it too heavy.
Later, when Fàn Zhèn and others discussed music,
they reverted to using the Tàifǔ ruler used by Lǐ Zhào,
which was the iron ruler used by Zhōu and Suí,
and which Niú Hóng and others considered to be close to antiquity and appropriate.
Now, taking the existing music,
and calibrating its measurements with the Kāiyuán coins from the early Táng, it is also the same.
Thus, the finger-ruler used by Hànjīn is probably the same as the rulers used by Zhōu, Suí, and Táng.
Hànjīn adopted the theories of Lǐ Zhào and Fàn Zhèn
but was ashamed to admit it.
Therefore, he used the joints of the contemporary ruler's fingers as a ruler,
so that no one dared to lightly dispute it.
Although his ruler involved a specious argument,
its system was in fact the same as the ancient one,
and the clear and turbid, high and low pitches were all appropriate,
not something created by personal whim outside of established methods.
Indeed, although the bells and chime stones of today were made in the Chóngníng era,
they are also the music of Zhōu, Suí, and Táng.
Reviewing the musical pitches currently in use,
the tones are harmonious and peaceful,
without the fault of being too high or too low,
and can be used for a long time.
Only the chén zhōng and chén qìng have frequently been missing since ancient times.
It is appropriate to cast fifteen additional chén zhōng
and twenty-one chén qìng,
making a total of twenty-four sets each, including the old ones."
The Emperor said:
"I have observed the Sòng people discussing music,
believing that pitch is primarily based on human voice,
and should not be rigidly tied to the instruments.
The essential thing is harmony of sound."
Therefore,
the Lǐbù was ordered to issue a warrant to Nánjīng
to obtain old Sòng artisans
and recast twelve chén zhōng.
Moreover, since the old bells Gūxǐ and Yízé were both five pitches too high,
and Wúshè two pitches too high,
separate ones were cast to supplement them,
and then they harmonized.
Additionally, twelve chén qìng were carved,
but half of them were somewhat inferior,
so only the harmonious ones were selected and used.
Initially,
during the Zhènglóng era, Hǎilíng built the imperial ancestral temple (Tàimiào) in Biàn.
During the Zhēnyòu southern migration,
Xuānzōng repaired it
to house the spirit tablets of the various emperors.
Its location
was the site of the former Sòng Jǐnglíng Gōng.
When excavated,
thirteen sets of biān zhōng
and eight sets of biān qìng were found,
all engraved with
"Dàshèng"
characters.
At that time, the court faced many difficulties,
and ritual implements were scattered and lost,
so they could not be fully supplied after all.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng,
the Tàicháng discussed:
“According to the old system in the Táng Huìyào,
twenty sets of gōngxuàn were used for the Northern and Southern Suburbs.
The Six Dynasties of Zhōu, Hàn, Wèi, Jìn, Sòng, Qí, as well as the ceremonies of Táng Kaiyuán and Sòng Kāibǎo,
all used the same number.
The Sòng Huìyào uses thirty-six sets,
and the Wǔlǐ Xīnyí uses forty-eight sets.
This number is large,
and seems too extravagant.
Now, it is proposed that according to the Tàicháng Yīngé Lǐ,
the Son of Heaven’s gōngxuàn music should have thirty-six jù.
The ancestral temples and palace halls are the same,
while the altars in the suburbs use twenty jù.
It is appropriate to use twenty sets of gōngxuàn,
and one jù each of biānzhōng and biānqìng for dēnggē.
Furthermore, according to the Zhōu Lǐ Dàsīyuè,
‘For all music,
huánzhōng is the gōng,
huángzhōng is the jué,
tàicù is the zhǐ,
and gūxǐ is the yǔ.
The léigǔ, léitáo, gúzhú pipes, yúnhé qín and sè,
and yúnmén dance,
are performed on the circular mound on the winter solstice.
If the music changes six times,
then all heavenly deities will descend,
and can be ritualized.’
‘Six changes’
means six completions (chéng).
Táng and Sòng followed this.
Huánzhōng
is jiázhōng,
used as gōng to correspond to Fáng and Xīn above,
symbolizing the Mingtang of the Heavenly Emperor.
The gōng sound is played three times,
and jué, zhǐ, yǔ are each played once,
matching the odd numbers of yáng,
desiring the deities to listen.
All music begins at yáng,
and ends at shàoyīn.
From mǎo to shēn, huánzhōng has six numbers,
thus with six changes the music stops,
and then all heavenly deities descend,
and can be ritualized.
Regarding the names of musical pieces,
Táng used ‘Hé,’
Sòng used ‘Ān,’
and this dynasty designated musical pieces with ‘Níng’
as the name.
Currently, there are only musical pieces for the Tàimiào xiáxiǎng,
but the musical pieces for the suburban sacrifices are not yet complete.
In the ninth year of Huángtǒng, when worshiping Heaven, the music of Qiánníng was used.
Now, for the descent of deities at the Yuánqiū, it can certainly be used.
Now, for the Tàimiào xiáxiǎng,
when the emperor ascends, descends, walks, or stops, the music of Chāngníng is played.
When receiving the sacrificial offerings, the music of Fēngníng is played.
When presenting libations and during the dancers’ entrances and exits, the music of Sùníng is played.
When partaking of the blessed meat, the music of Fúníng is played.
The Sòng Kāibǎo Lǐ can also be adopted.
As for the names of the suburban sacrifice pieces,
for the emperor’s entry into the middle enclosure, presenting jade and silk, receiving the sacrificial offerings, presenting libations, and the dancers’ entrances and exits,
they should all be named with the character ‘Níng’.”
Thus, the Xuéshì Yuàn was ordered to compile them.
When the emperor enters the middle enclosure, the music of Chāngníng is played.
For the descent and departure of deities, the music of Qiánníng is played.
For Hào Tiān Shàngdì, the music of Hóngníng is played.
For Huángdì Qí, the music of Kūnníng is played.
For the secondary deities, the music of Yǒngníng is played.
For partaking of the blessed meat, the music of Fúníng is played.
For ascending, descending, gazing at the burning pyre, and entering/exiting the main and secondary stations,
all are the same as entering the middle enclosure.
The rest are recorded in the ritual instructions and musical scores.
The Tàicháng was also ordered to discuss the proper sequence of the civil (wén) and military (wǔ) dances.
The Tàicháng discussed:
“According to the Táng and Sòng suburban and ancestral temple rituals,
the civil dance always precedes the military dance.
Our dynasty’s self-conducted dì and xiá sacrifices also follow this.
Only Wéi Wànshí of Táng suggested, based on the tradition passed down by former Confucians,
that if the empire was gained through abdication and yielding, then the civil dance should be performed first;
if gained through conquest, then the military dance should be performed first.
Although this was followed at the time,
it was soon changed back.
The Kaiyuán Lǐ established the civil dance first, then the military dance.
The Fāngqiū follows the ritual of the Yuánqiū,
and for the Shèjì, dēnggē is used.”
Ancestral Temple:
When the emperor enters the gate,
the gōngxuàn plays in wúshègōng.
When ascending the hall,
the dēnggē plays in jiázhōng.
All play the music of Chāngníng.
For welcoming and escorting deities, the music of Láiníng is played,
nine times.
In the second year of Tiāndé,
after the morning libation (guàn),
upon returning to the small station,
the music for welcoming deities was just played.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng,
for the court sacrifices (cháoxiǎng),
music was played according to the Kaiyuán and Kāibǎo rituals.
Upon reaching the tablet position,
huángzhōnggōng three times, dàlǚjué two times, tàicùzhǐ two times, and yìngzhōngyǔ two times were played.
The lyrics were all the same.
When advancing the sacrificial offerings, the music of Fēngníng is played.
For presenting libations,
the gōngxuàn plays the music of Wúshè Dàyuán.
The music for various chambers:
Dédì is Dàxī,
Āndì is Dà’ān,
Xiànzǔ is Dàzhāo,
Zhaozǔ is Dàchéng,
Jǐngzǔ is Dàchāng,
Zǔ is Dàwǔ,
Sùzōng is Dàmíng,
Mùzōng is Dàzhāng,
Kāngzōng is Dàkāng,
Tàizǔ is Dàdìng,
Tàizōng is Dàhuì,
Xīzōng is Dàtóng,
Ruìzōng is Dàhé,
Empress Zhaodé’s temple is Yíkūn,
Shìzōng is Dàjūn,
Xiǎnzōng is Dàníng,
Zhāngzōng is Dàlóng,
Xuānzōng is Dàqìng.
When the emperor returns to the tablet position and for the second and final libations,
the music of Wúshègōng Sùníng is always played.
For partaking of the blessed meat,
the dēnggē plays the music of Jiázhōnggōng Fúníng.
When clearing the sacrificial vessels,
the music of Fēngníng is played,
all using Wúshègōng.
In the twelfth year of Dàdìng, it was decreed
that during the xiá and dì sacrifices, the office in charge should perform the rites.
For the initial libation and washing,
the music of Wúshègōng Sùníng is played.
When ascending the steps,
the dēnggē plays the music of Jiázhōnggōng Jiāníng.
The rest are the same as when the emperor personally performs the sacrifice.
The music used for the separate temples of Empress Zhaodé and Prince Xuānxiào
are all recorded in the ritual instructions and musical scores.
According to the old system,
the Tàimiào and the temple of the imperial ancestors (Huángkǎo Miào) each had thirty-nine musicians.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng,
when Xiǎnzōng was interred in the ancestral temple,
the officials in charge believed
that “in the Sòng dynasty, the Tàimiào and separate temples
each had forty-eight musicians in the main hall.
Now, there are eighteen fewer musicians.
It is proposed that all the old musicians from the Huángkǎo Miào should be assigned to the main halls of both temples,
to match the ninety-six musicians of previous eras.”
The Shàngshū Shěng debated
that “ancient musicians had no fixed number,”
and thus proposed that the Tàimiào and separate temples should collectively have one hundred musicians as the fixed number.
In the sixth year of Míngchāng,
gōngxuàn were newly established,
with one hundred and fifty-six musicians.
In the third year of Chéng’ān,
an imperial edict stated:
“It is improper to use the Jiàofáng to perform ancient music for ancestral temple sacrifices.
From now on, recruit talented and beautiful commoners,
provide them with stipends,
and train them for use.”
In the first year of Tàihé,
gōngxuàn musicians were ordered to receive a monthly stipend of two guàn of money and rice.
When a regular musician position was vacant,
it would be filled after examination.
In the fourth year,
the Shàngshū Shěng reported:
“A total of two hundred and fifty-six gōngxuàn musicians are needed,
but only one hundred were previously established.
When they were occasionally used, they were trained by the Jiàofáng affiliated with the ministry.
Since the Míngchāng period,
the Bóhǎi Jiàofáng also practiced,
and an additional ninety-two people were established.
However, gōngxuàn music is only used for grand ceremonies.
If the number is insufficient again,
it is sufficient to simply send the Hàn Rén Jiàofáng and the Dàxīng Fǔ musicians to practice in advance
to be ready for use.”
Thus, an edict was issued to abolish the newly established positions.
Xuānzōng 宣宗 moved south,
and enshrined the spirit tablets of the various emperors in the Tàimiào 太廟 in Biànjīng 汴京.
The ritual officials stated:
"After the enshrinement and offering rituals are complete,
the imperial carriage returns to the palace.
Outside the Chéngtiānmén 承天門,
all officials will respectfully welcome it,
and the gōngxiàn 宮縣 music will play 'Cǎicí 采茨'."
As the instruments' frames were not yet ready,
only the Jiàofáng 教坊 music was used.
When Āizōng 哀宗 moved to Cài 蔡,
on the dīngsì 丁巳 day of the seventh month of Tiānxīng 天興 second year (1233),
the imperial portraits of Tàizǔ 太祖, Tàizōng 太宗, and empresses arrived from Biànjīng 汴京,
and were respectfully placed in the Qiányuánsì 乾元寺.
The Assistant Director of the Left Bureau of Imperial Affairs, Wēndūn Qīshíwǔ 溫敦七十五, suggested that music should be used.
The Emperor said:
"Music must come from the Tàicháng 太常 (Grand Heraldry Office).
What can be done?"
Qīshíwǔ 七十五 replied:
"There is popular music in the market;
it can be borrowed for temporary use."
Wáng È 2 王鶚, acting concurrently as Yuánwàiláng 員外郎 of the Left and Right Bureaus, memorialized:
"How can common music
be performed before the Son of Heaven?"
So it was stopped.

When the Emperor received the imperial patent and seal (cèbǎo 冊寶).
The day before,

When the Emperor proclaimed an amnesty from the imperial tower.
The day before,
the Grand Music Bureau (Dàyuèshǔ 大樂署) set up the gōngxiàn 宮縣 instruments below the tower,
and also set up one drum to the left of the gōngxiàn 宮縣.
