when the golden rooster was first set up,
the Dàyuèshǔ 大樂署 beat the drum;
when it was completely set up,
the drum stopped.
The Shìzhōng 侍中 announced
"Wàibàn 外辦",
the Dàyuèlìng 大樂令 struck the huángzhōng 黃鐘 bell,
the five bells to the right all responded,
the music of Chāngníng 昌寧 began,
and the Emperor then came out.
After the proclamation was read,
all officials bowed and danced,
when the ritual was complete,
the Dàyuèlìng 大樂令 struck the ruíbīn 蕤賓 bell,
the five bells to the left all responded,
the music of Chāngníng 昌寧 began,
the Emperor descended from his seat,
and the music stopped.
Whenever the Emperor entered or exited, ascended or descended, and when ranks were separated or joined,
music always began,
and only stopped when he was seated or stood still.
For the conferment of imperial patents upon empresses, crown princes, and imperial grandsons,
receiving congratulations from foreign envoys,
and banqueting foreign envoys,
gōngxiàn 宮縣 music was always used.
For informal music (sànlè 散樂),
on New Year's Day and the Emperor's birthday when congratulations were offered,
and at banquets for foreign envoys,
the Jiàofáng 教坊 performed.
The names of their instruments and tunes are not preserved.
In Huángtǒng 皇統 second year (1142), the prime minister memorialized:
"From ancient times, there has been no precedent for entertainers to attend court audiences.
All Jiàofáng 教坊 personnel should only await summons,
and not attend the routine court audiences with the hundreds of officials."
This was approved.
On the jiǎyín 甲寅 day of the eleventh month of Míngchāng 明昌 second year (1191) of Zhāngzōng 章宗,
entertainers were forbidden from dramatizing past emperors or shouting "wànsuì 萬歲" (long live the emperor),
as this was deemed a serious offense not in accordance with proper conduct.
In the early Tàihé 泰和 period (1201-1208), the officials again memorialized that the number of Tàicháng 太常 (Grand Heraldry Office) artisans was too few,
and therefore the Jiàofáng 教坊 personnel from Bóhǎi 渤海 and Hànrén 漢人, as well as musicians from Dàxīngfǔ 大興府, should concurrently practice to be ready for use.
Drum and wind music (gǔchuīlè 鼓吹樂)
was mounted music.
The Emperor's drum and wind music (gǔchuī 鼓吹) and transverse wind music (héngchuī 橫吹) each had front and rear sections,
and each section was further divided into two parts.
The Jīn 金 initially used artifacts from the former Liáo 遼 dynasty,
but later mixed them with Sòng 宋 ceremonial items.
When Hǎilíng 海陵 moved to Yān 燕 and for the imperial procession (lǔbù 鹵簿) in Dàdìng 大定 eleventh year (1171),
the gǔchuī 鼓吹 was divided into four parts,
while for other imperial travels, only two sections were used.

Front Section One: Two gǔchuīlìng 鼓吹令; twelve gānggǔ 掆鼓; twelve jīnmíng 金鉦; one hundred twenty dàgǔ 大鼓; one hundred twenty chángmíng 長鳴; twelve náogǔ 鐃鼓; twenty-four singers; twenty-four gǒngchén guǎn 拱辰管; twenty-four xiāo 簫; twenty-four jiā 笳; one hundred twenty dàhéngchuī 大橫吹.

Front Section Two: Two jiégǔ 節鼓; twenty-four dí 笛; twenty-four xiāo 簫; twenty-four bìlì 篳篥; twenty-four jiā 笳; twenty-four táopíbìlì 桃皮篳篥; twelve gānggǔ 掆鼓; twelve jīnmíng 金鉦; one hundred twenty xiǎogǔ 小鼓; one hundred twenty zhōngmíng 中鳴; twelve yǔbàogǔ 羽葆鼓; twenty-four singers; twenty-four gǒngchén guǎn 拱辰管; twenty-four xiāo 簫.

Rear Section One: Two gǔchuīcéng 鼓吹丞; three gānggǔ 掆鼓; three jīnmíng 金鉦; twelve yǔbàogǔ 羽葆鼓; twenty-four singers; twenty-four gǒngchén guǎn 拱辰管; twenty-four xiāo 簫; twenty-four jiā 笳; two jiégǔ 節鼓; twelve náogǔ 鐃鼓; sixteen singers; twenty-four xiāo 簫; twenty-four jiā 笳; one hundred twenty xiǎohéngchuī 小橫吹.
Rear Section Two: Twenty-four dí 笛; twenty-four xiāo 簫; twenty-four bìlì 篳篥; twenty-four jiā 笳; twenty-four táopíbìlì 桃皮篳篥.
Musical compositions of this dynasty.
In the ninth year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng, on the *gēngshēn* day of the eleventh month,
it was the Crown Prince's birthday.
The Emperor held a banquet at the Eastern Palace,
and ordered new music to be performed.
He said to his ministers:
"I composed this tune,
and named it 'Monarch and Ministers' Joy' (Jūnchénlè).
Today, the world is at peace,
and I share this with you, my lords.
Is this not joyful?"
The lyrics and melody were not transmitted.
In the thirteenth year, on the *yǐhài* day of the fourth month,
the Emperor was at the Ruìsī Diàn,
and ordered singers to sing Nǚzhí (Jurchen) lyrics.
He looked at the Crown Prince and said:
"I have never for a moment forgotten
the deeds of the former court.
Therefore, I often listen to these lyrics,
also wishing to let you all know the pure and simple customs of the Nǚzhí.
As for the writing and language, if one does not understand them,
this is forgetting one's roots."
In the twenty-fifth year, in the fourth month,
he visited Shàngjīng.
He hosted a banquet for the imperial clan at the Huángwǔ Diàn,
and while drinking and merrymaking,
the Emperor instructed them, saying:
"Today, I very much wish to become drunk.
Such joy is not easily obtained.
In the past, Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn passed through his hometown,
drank merrily with the elders,
played the *zhú*, and sang,
ordering his children to harmonize.
He rose from commoner status,
and was still like this;
how much more so for our ancestors, who have possessed this land for generations!
Today, the world is unified,
and I travel here.
Why not drink joyfully?"
At that time, the women of the imperial clan rose and danced.
After presenting wine,
the ministers and old retainers rose and danced.
The Emperor said:
"I have been in my hometown for several months now,
and my return date is approaching.
Yet, not a single person has sung the native tune.
You all, come forward,
and I will sing for you."
Thereupon, he ordered all imperial clan members seated below the hall to come up to the hall,
and listen face to face as the Emperor sang.
The song spoke of the difficulties of the ancestors in establishing the empire,
and the intention of their successors.
After the Emperor sang,
when he reached the lines expressing deep yearning for the ancestors' voices and visages as if seen,
he was so overcome with sorrow and emotion that he could no longer make a sound.
After the song,
tears flowed in several streams.
The Right Chancellor Yuánzhōng and the ministers and imperial relatives held up goblets to offer a toast for longevity,
all shouting "Long live the Emperor!"
Thereupon, the old men in turn sang the native tune,
as if at a private gathering,
joyful and harmonious.
The Emperor then continued to adjust the melody of the song,
remaining seated for an entire watch,
and only stopped when the revelry reached its peak.
Its lyrics were: "Oh, our Ancestor,
holy and martial was Yuán!
Born to receive the bright mandate,
his merit shines to the heavens.
Rescuing those drowning and those burning,
he deeply rooted and firmly grounded.
He was able to establish our future,
transmitting
blessings for ten thousand generations.
Alas, Hǎilíng,
lustful, deluded, and full of crimes,
reversed the heavenly dao,
and poisoned the land.
From the earliest foundation,
down to the succession,
the accumulated
enterprise
was on the verge of ruin and collapse.
The aspirations of those who looked up to me converged,
without prior consultation, they agreed.
The imperial ancestral temple was of utmost importance,
and the hearts of the people were difficult to resist.
I endeavored to live up to the joyful acclamation,
and thus I continued the lineage.
Twenty-
four years,
I toiled cautiously with myriad affairs.
Millions of common people
cherished peace and security.
The nation was at leisure,
expansive and without incident.
I then turned my gaze to the former capital,
where the Emperor's residence arose.
Now, as I come to visit,
a sense of poignant reflection fills me.
The landscape and atmosphere have diminished,
hardly as they were in former times.
Both the district and the village
are no longer as they first were.
Though not as they first were,
I myself find joy
here.
Though not as in former times,
I view them without distinction.
I gaze and yearn with emotion,
at the old abode of my ancestors.
Their voices and visages, one after another,
are as if vividly seen.
Childhood play and filial longing,
every
spot is distinct.
Walks taken in adulthood,
are as if suddenly back to old times.
Companionship in former years,
is vaguely like yesterday,
joyful sincerity, long separated,
like morning and evening.
Alas, long
separated,
how can I not be joyful?"
Suburban Sacrifice Ritual Songs.
As the Emperor enters the central sacred enclosure,
the imperial orchestra performs the Chāngníng tune in Huángzhōng Gōng. (All steps and movements are the same.)
In ceremonial robes, majestic and solemn,
he approaches the central sacred enclosure.
He looks upon the circular altar,
upon the august Emperor of Heaven.
The smoke sacrifice is initiated,
its fragrance is virtue.
Reaching all the deities,
they clearly receive their duties.
Descent of the Deities,
the imperial orchestra performs the Qiánníng tune, and the Rénfēng Dàojiā dance.
Yuánzhōng serves as *gōng*,
Huángzhōng as *jiǎo*,
Tàicù as *zhēng*,
Gūxǐ as *yǔ*.
Yuánzhōng
is played three times,
Huángzhōng, Tàicù, and Gūxǐ each once,
the lyrics are all the same: "The rise of our Jīn,
was blessed by August Heaven.
Through the grace of the spirits,
we appear here at the suburban sacrifice.
With jade for the ritual,
with animals for the offering.
They shall receive its brilliance,
come to bestow peace, come to feast."
The Emperor performs ablutions,
the imperial orchestra performs the Chāngníng tune in Huángzhōng Gōng: "By Heaven, serve Heaven,
honor the ancestors, prepare the ritual.
Thus, the responsible officials are ordered,
to present the ritual vessels at the proper time.
From one pour to another,
then ascend the altar steps.
Pious before the rite,
the spirits are pleased and benevolent."
The Emperor ascends the altar,
the ritual chorus sings the Chāngníng tune in Dàlǚ Gōng: "Looking to the south of the capital,
majestic are its foundations.
How grand is the August King,
who attends to the rite at this time.
Utmost sincerity connects with the spirits,
able to offer pure sacrifices.
For ten thousand years,
May August Heaven take him as son."
To August Heaven, the Supreme Emperor,
placing jade and silk,
the ritual chorus sings the Hóngníng tune in Dàlǚ Gōng: "Majestic is the monarch,
solemn and reverent.
Jade pendants clanking,
he ascends the circular altar.
His virtuous deeds reach up,
a fragrance not of millet.
The High and Bright descend to observe,
all spirits receive their duties."
To August Earth, the Earth Goddess,
the Kūnníng tune: "Solemnly respect the bright deities,
personally perform the offering of tribute.
What is the tribute?
Yellow jade *cóng* and silk.
The accompanying spirits,
all arranged in their proper places.
Only the August One can receive,
truly gathering auspicious affairs."
To the co-sacrificed Tàizǔ Huángdì,
the Yǒngníng tune: "Initiating the bright smoke sacrifice,
to August Heaven and Empress Earth.
Our August Ancestor Wǔyuán,
is herein made the spirit lord.
His merit shines, firmly established,
sung with Dàlǚ.
Bring peace to our achievements,
may there be ordered blessings."
The Sītú welcomes the sacrificial vessels.
The palace orchestra plays the "Fēngníng" (豐寧) melody in Huángzhōng Gōng (黃鐘宮). Solemn and majestic,
the Son of Heaven personally offers sacrifice.
His multitude of ministers assist him,
none without reverence.
The sacrificial vessels are all arrayed,
the offerings are truly excellent.
The fragrant aroma begins to rise,
the enlightened spirits joyfully feast.
To Hào Tiān Shàngdì (昊天上帝),
presenting the libation,
intoning the "Jiāníng" (嘉寧) melody in Dàlǚ Gōng (大呂宮). In the suburban sacrifice, reverence is displayed,
to manifest service to the supreme spirits.
The great sacrificial vessel is on the mat,
with fragrant wine therein.
We present this libation,
may the spirits be intoxicated.
May blessings and prosperity come appropriately,
in response to the enlightened sacrifice.
To Huáng Dìqí (皇地祇),
the "Tàiníng" (泰寧) melody. In majestic robes,
approaching the great altar.
Oh, how splendid is the divine palace,
burying silk and interring blood.
Here we raise the gourd goblet,
pouring and presenting purity.
May the terrestrial realm be ever peaceful,
supporting our imperial enterprise.
To the consort of Tàizǔ Huángdì (太祖皇帝),
the "Yànníng" (燕寧) melody. How excellent is the great empress,
who initiated and developed the grand foundation.
Her achievements align with Heaven,
complementing Heaven in promotion.
Presenting this pure and excellent offering,
with utmost solemnity in ceremony.
May she come in peace and feast,
and bestow blessings and prosperity.
The civil dance retires,
the military dance advances,
the palace orchestra plays the "Xiánníng" (咸寧) melody in Huángzhōng Gōng (黃鐘宮). Offering sacrifice at the suburban altar,
the Cloud Gate dance transforms.
Advancing with vermilion shields,
ceasing to wave pheasant feathers.
Oh, how brilliant is the sagely civil [rule],
again resembling the sacred military [might].
Boundless are the achievements,
the Son of Heaven receives blessings.
Second libation at the final offering,
the palace orchestra plays the "Xiánníng" (咸寧) melody in Huángzhōng Gōng (黃鐘宮), and the "Gōngchéng Zhìdìng" (功成治定) dance. Sweeping the ground of the southern suburb,
the heavenly spirits await.
Oh, how august is the sovereign,
who is able to offer sacrifice and worship.
Communicating with the spirits,
with black wine in earthenware vessels.
The sincere heart is pure and simple,
not valuing the taste of food.
The Huángdì partakes of blessings,
intoning the "Fúníng" (福寧) melody in Dàlǚ Gōng (大呂宮). That by which Heaven is received,
nothing surpasses simplicity.
May Heaven bless him,
with utmost refinement and unity.
The great sacrificial vessel is raised,
fragrant offerings presenting virtue.
Bestow upon us boundless favor,
our descendants a thousand million.
Withdrawing the sacrificial vessels,
intoning the "Fēngníng" (豐寧) melody in Dàlǚ Gōng (大呂宮). The great ritual is arrayed,
the vessels are truly grand.
Solemn in their demeanor,
oh, how splendid are the many officials.
The imperial spirits descend and observe,
the fragrance of virtue is heard.
The enlightened sacrifice is thus completed,
trustworthy blessings are boundless.
Sending off the spirits,
the palace orchestra plays the "Qiánníng" (乾寧) melody in Huánzhōng Gōng (圜鐘宮). Glorious is Shàngdì,
overseeing the sacrifice.
He has truly come to accept,
shining brightly in response to his ancestors and consorts.
The round altar is completed in four stages,
the spirits are at peace in their places.
Singing praises to send them off,
Heaven and man rejoice.
Music for the Fangqiū (方丘).
Welcoming the spirits,
the "Zhènníng" (鎮寧) melody.
Línzhōng Gōng (林鐘宮) plays twice,
Tàicù Jiǎo (太蔟角) plays twice,
Gūxǐ Zhēng (姑洗徵) plays twice,
Nánlǚ Yǔ (南呂羽) plays twice,
with the same lyrics: How ultimate is the Kun (坤) principle,
giving life to all beings.
Appropriately bestowing equally,
flowing modestly and transforming the full.
The ritual is performed at the Tàizhé (泰折),
the sacrifice is of utmost sincerity.
The august spirits gaze down,
forever securing the universe.
First offering, washing hands,
the "Sùníng" (肅寧) melody in Tàicù Gōng (太蔟宮). Among the five classics of ritual,
none precedes the sacrificial rites.
At this moment, earnestness is expressed,
at this time, hands are washed.
The offerings are pure and clean,
the deportment is orderly.
Granting pure great blessings,
coming to accept with kindness and gentleness.
First offering, ascending the altar,
the "Sùníng" (肅寧) melody in Yìngzhōng Gōng (應鐘宮). Boundless is the virtue,
how ultimate is the Kun (坤) primeval.
Deep and hidden, firm and overcoming,
giving rise to abundant life.
The ceremony of the Fāngqiū (方丘),
is only reverence, without embellishment.
May the spirits come and reflect,
at this time accepting the bountiful offerings.
First offering, presenting jade and silk,
the "Yìníng" (億寧) melody in Tàicù Gōng (太蔟宮). The ritual proceeds at the Fāngzé (方澤),
all cultural objects are prepared.
To the imperial terrestrial spirits,
manifested and invited to descend.
Presenting and burying jade and silk,
pure sincerity manifested within.
May the divine protectors accept this,
ascending and descending with blessings.
The Sītú presents the sacrificial vessels,
the "Fēngníng" (豐寧) melody in Tàicù Gōng (太蔟宮). The four tiers of ceremonial ranks,
the altar at the Fāngzé (方澤).
Manifesting service to the imperial spirits,
approaching the yin and expanding.
Purity is spread at the altar,
very splendid and grand.
May the spirits bless it,
as if it were near, as if it were proper.
Proper position for libation,
the "Pǔníng" (溥寧) melody in Tàicù Gōng (太蔟宮). Vast and expansive is Kun's (坤) virtue,
nothing is not borne.
Gentle, compliant, beneficial, and firm,
containing immense and glorious greatness.
The bamboo and wooden vessels are arrayed,
the bells and chimes are present.
May the four seas be forever peaceful,
blessings and prosperity bestowed.
Consort's position for libation,
(This refers to Tàizōng (太宗)).
The lyrics are missing.
Second libation, final offering, ascending the altar,
the "Xiánníng" (咸寧) melody in Tàicù Gōng (太蔟宮). How eminent is that splendid altar,
where jade is presented at the Fāngzé (方澤).
All officials are reverent and solemn,
the eight sounds purely played.
The sacrificial matter is greatly manifest,
the gentle spirits are moved and respond.
Withdrawing the sacrificial vessels,
the "Fēngníng" (豐寧) melody in Yìngzhōng Gōng (應鐘宮). The Fāngqiū (方丘) is prepared,
auspicious and pure, as is proper.
The bamboo and wooden vessels are quiet and beautiful,
presented by the officials.
Fragrant and sweet aroma,
coming to accept and oversee.
The suburban ceremony is about to conclude,
the songs are withdrawn.
Sending off the spirits,
the "Zhènníng" (鎮寧) melody in Línzhōng Gōng (林鐘宮). By means of the terrestrial Fāngqiū (方丘),
many ceremonies are orderly.
The music completes eight changes,
the spirits are moved and reflect.
The remaining offerings and withdrawn vessels,
divine blessings clearly bestowed.
For millions of years,
forever protecting the grand foundation.
Proceeding to the Wàngliáo (望燎) position,
the "Sùníng" (肅寧) melody in Tàicù Gōng (太蔟宮).
The lyrics are the same as ascending the altar.
Collation Notes
Monograph Twenty-one, Music, Part 2: Ancestral Temple Music, Palace Court Music, Military Band Music, Cǎicí Qǔ (采茨曲).
For the Dì (禘) and Xiá (祫) sacrifices personally offered,
as the Huángdì enters,
the palace orchestra plays the "Chāngníng" (昌寧) melody in Wúshè Gōng (無射宮): (The steps for entering and exiting are the same.)
At this time of peace and prosperity,
ritual and ceremony originate.
The imperial bells chime as he arrives,
solemnly entering the court.
All officials and ministers,
respectfully welcome and receive.
Reverently treating ancestors,
the divine abodes are at peace.
The Huángdì ascends the hall,
intoning the "Chāngníng" (昌寧) melody in Jiázhōng Gōng (夾鐘宮): (Ascending the steps and returning to the standing position are both accompanied by the same intonation.)
The sheng and yong are arranged,
the wine vessels are at the door.
Ascending and descending with grace,
following rules and regulations.
Reverently honoring the enlightened spirits,
performing the supreme ceremonies in unison.
May he forever preserve them,
receiving Heaven's blessings.
The Emperor washes his hands,
to the tune Wúshè Gōng Chāngníng from Gōngxiàn: Of the merits of water,
It is pure, refined, and subtle.
Washing goblets and setting down wine vessels,
Its virtue shines brightly.
How grand and solemn,
The majesty of the ancestral temple.
It is fitting that it inspires and moves the spirits,
Bringing together blessings and fortune.
The Emperor descends the steps,
to the tune Wúshè Gōng Chāngníng from Gōngxiàn: Oh, the imperial spirit palace,
Reflecting the clear brightness of heaven.
Here come the reverent and solemn,
Assisted by dukes and ministers.
Ritual and ceremony are perfectly observed,
Gentlemen find peace therein.
How timely, how benevolent,
Bringing peace to our aspirations.
Welcoming the spirits,
to the tune Lái Níng from Gōngxiàn.
Huángzhōng Gōng played three times,
Dàlǚ Jué played two times,
Dàcù Zhǐ played two times,
Yìngzhōng Yǔ played two times.
The lyrics are the same: The eight sounds harmonize perfectly,
All rites are fully performed.
Our bright virtue is pure,
Our utmost sincerity is eternally yearned for.
When the spirits descend,
On cloud palanquins and wind chariots.
They come to stay, they come to preside,
Residing peacefully for a thousand generations.
The Sìtú presents the sacrificial meat,
to the tune Wúshè Gōng Fēngníng from Gōngxiàn: These are the sacrificial animals,
Purely and brightly offered in sacrifice.
We present them, we offer them,
Auspiciously and reverently presented.
Plump, robust, and fat,
Fitting for the spirits' taste.
May they enjoy this for a thousand autumns,
Forever bringing peace to the black-haired commoners.
The first ancestor offers the libation,
to the tune Wúshè Gōng Dàyuán from Gōngxiàn: The wine is clear,
The dishes are fragrant.
Fragrant and sweet filial sacrifice,
In the courtyard of the temple.
Offered to the imperial ancestors,
May they come to feast and find peace.
Their achievements are manifest, their virtues are clear,
The ancestors hear this.
To Dédì,
to the tune Dàxī: All lands rejoice and support,
A grand enterprise founded.
From a jade source flows abundance,
A myriad of gourds [descendants] shine brightly again.
Thus we elevate the solemn sacrifice,
Following established regulations.
With sacrificial vessels arranged,
Further perfecting the imperial ceremony.
To Āndì,
to the tune Dà'ān: Planning to establish the state,
Its virtue thrives.
The imperial ceremony is truly solemn,
Bringing forth auspicious blessings.
Bright sincerity moves the spirits,
Amassed virtue radiates light.
Respectfully solemnizing the pure temple,
With the ringing of bells and stones.
To Xiànzǔ,
to the tune Dàzhāo: The sage established the state,
In the very beginning.
Gathering the people and transforming customs,
Settling their abodes.
Guiding with virtue and pure frugality,
With aspirations for a distant plan.
How timely is this splendid sacrifice,
With sincere trust.
To Zhāozǔ,
to the tune Dàchéng: Heaven opened the jade source,
Bequeathing blessings and establishing the foundation.
Following righteousness is courage,
Exercising virtue is might.
Displaying military prowess and expanding territory,
His achievements are grand and mighty.
Forever prospering the imperial throne,
Distributing blessings to the black-haired commoners.
To Jǐngzǔ,
to the tune Dàchāng: Greatly manifest are the grand achievements,
The foundation and lineage flourish greatly.
The sage's destined time arrived,
The nation's domain expanded.
Solemn and majestic is the ancestral shrine,
Clearly invoking auspicious blessings.
How splendid and elaborate are the ceremonies,
Shining brighter for a hundred million years.
To Shìzǔ,
to the tune Dàwǔ: How mighty are the martial achievements,
Heaven observes their brilliance.
His might shakes and overawes,
His virtue brings peace and tranquility.
No divine strategy was overlooked,
Thus the grand plan prospered.
His great-grandson performs the filial sacrifice,
To manifest his accomplishments.
To Sùzōng,
to the tune Dàmíng: Oh, the divine man,
With martial achievements and literary wisdom.
Assisting Shìzǔ,
He pacified and swept away.
His prestige shook far and near,
His transformation reached even insects and fish.
His light endures eternally,
The trust of the accomplished Emperor.
To Mùzōng,
to the tune Dàzhāng: How grand was the cultured ancestor,
Reverent, sacred, profound.
Compassionate, loving, loyal, and trustworthy,
Clearly recorded in the annals and texts.
May he accept this bright sacrifice,
Bringing countless blessings.
It is truly glorious,
May his blessings flow for ten thousand years.
To Kāngzōng,
to the tune Dàkāng: How discerning, how attentive,
How brilliant are his divine achievements.
A model for generations of enterprise,
Manifesting clearly to the high heavens.
The filial grandson, maintaining prosperity,
Presents fragrant offerings abundantly.
Grant us blessings and fortune,
May the imperial transformation grow ever stronger.
To Tàizǔ,
to the tune Dàdìng: His achievements surpassed those of Yīn and Zhōu,
His virtue matched that of Táng and Yú.
Heaven and man responded in harmony,
Unifying the world.
Opening auspiciousness and bestowing abundance,
Laying the foundation for an eternal plan.
The enlightened Son of Heaven,
Reverently inherits the statutes and plans.
To Tàizōng,
to the tune Dàhuì: How majestic his great virtue,
Governing with non-action from behind the screen.
His reign succeeded with divine achievements,

Treatise 22: Imperial Guard, Part 1: Imperial Guard for Ordinary Court Audiences – Inner and Outer Standing Guards – Imperial Guard for Routine Movements – Traveling Imperial Guard (Lawful Carriage) – Yellow Banner Guard
The golden system [of imperial guard],
is the emperor's imperial guard.
One is the standing guard (*lìzhàng*),
the second is the traveling guard (*xíngzhàng*).
Its guardsmen [are called]:
bodyguards (*hùwèi*),
imperial guards (*qīnjūn*),
crossbowmen (*nǔshǒu*),
crane-controllers (*kònghè*),
umbrella bearers (*sǎnzi*),
and long-line guards (*chángxíng*).
The standing guard includes the Inner Palace Guard and Outer Palace Guard.
These are used for grand ceremonies and grand court assemblies.
For ordinary court audiences on the first and fifteenth of the month,
only a hundred crossbowmen stand on the two steps.
The traveling guard includes the Lawful Carriage (*fǎjià*), the Grand Carriage (*dàjià*), and the Yellow Banner Guard (*huánghuīzhàng*).
These are used for imperial travels, suburban sacrifices, and ancestral temple offerings.
For non-grand ceremonies or distant outings,
there are the routine imperial guard (*chángxíng yíwèi*) and palace escorts (*gōngzhōng dǎocóng*).
Broadly, it imitated the Sòng system,
with complexities, additions, and deletions in its application.
The permanent guards (*sùwèi*) are mentioned in the Military Treatise.
Initially,
according to national regulations,
on the days of ordinary court audiences on the first and fifteenth of the month,
guardsmen were arranged in ranks below the palace hall,
and armored soldiers were placed below the curtains.
In Zhènglóng 1st year (1156 CE), Hǎilíng removed the armored soldiers,
leaving only a hundred brocade-clad crossbowmen,
who stood on the two steps.
Their ceremony was as follows:
The Dū Fù Diǎnjiǎn
wore official attire with a side belt.
(For ordinary court audiences, they wore purple robes.)

and the Sùzhí Jiāngjūn
wore purple robes,
with golden sashes,
each holding a *gǔgōng* adorned with jade, crystal, and gold.

with gilt sashes,
and *gǔgōng*,
carrying weapons.
A hundred Gongyù Nǔshǒu and Sǎnzi
all wore *jīnhuā jiāojiǎo fútóu* (golden flower cross-legged headwear),
with gilt bronze buckles supporting flowered sashes,
and *gǔgōng*.
Twenty Nèishì holding ceremonial objects in the left and right ranks
wore purple robes,
with gilt sashes.
On days of court attendance,
the crossbowmen and umbrella bearers stood directly outside the palace gate,
arranged in two rows facing opposite directions.
After the timekeeper finished reporting the time,
the emperor ascended the throne and sat down.

The crossbowmen and umbrella bearers, outside the palace gate, faced north and shouted "long live" (*shānhū*) and bowed (*shēngnuò*).
Afterward,
they stood facing each other east and west outside the palace gate.
The Dū Diǎnjiǎn and the next three officials ascended the hall.
The Dū Diǎnjiǎn was in the east, closer to the south,
the Zǔo Fù was slightly further south,
and the Yòu Fù was in the west,

The Zǔoyòu Wèijiāngjūn stood below the hall, facing each other east and west.
After the ministerial officials completed their greetings in their ranks,

After the Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ completed their greetings in their ranks,

The Xiū Qǐjūzhù stood facing each other east and west on the palace steps, outside the palace railings, at the subordinate steps,
awaiting.
After the memorials were presented,
the emperor returned to his private chambers,
and the imperial guards then withdrew.
Whenever there was a grand ceremony or a grand court assembly,
there were inner and outer standing guards.
In the first month of Huángtǒng 1st year (1141 CE) of Xīzōng,

Moreover, since Tiāndé and Zhēnyuán

Moving guard of honor.
When the Son of Heaven was not performing sacrifices, banquets, inspections, or long journeys,
the regular ceremonial guard was used.
Two hundred crossbowmen and five Jūnshǐ.
Two hundred Kònghè and four Shǒulǐng.
All wore red ground with hidden roots peony brocade robes, gold phoenix flower cross-legged fútóu, and gilt-silver belts.
The Kònghè sometimes wore black caps and green robes.
Each held a gilt-silver garlic-clove bone-handled ruyi.
The Chángxíng had four hundred people,
wearing quanjiao fútóu, red brocade sìpà áo [four-cornered robes], and gilt belts.
Two in purple robes led the way,
holding no objects.
The rest held seventy-eight liè sī gǔ rúyì, eighty-eight guā [melon-shaped clubs], thirty-four dēng [staves],
positioned in front of the Kònghè.
Eighty Jīnwú Zhàng, sixty Jīnhuā Dàjiàn, all with red tassels, and fifty-eight Yíhuángfǔ,
positioned behind the Kònghè.
For regular court audiences, imperial banquets, suburban sacrifices, and imperial visits,
whenever the imperial palanquin entered or exited, it was attended by close personal attendants.

When the Emperor emerged from his private chambers, they stood divided outside the palace gate,
guiding him to the main hall.
When the Emperor ascended the throne, they descended the steps to await him,
and only dispersed the guard after he re-entered his chambers.

when Xīzōng made an imperial visit to Yān,
the Fǎjià was first fully deployed,
using a total of fourteen thousand and fifty-six soldiers,
excluding acting officials.
When Hǎilíng moved the capital to Yān,
ten thousand three hundred and forty-eight people were used for the Huánghuī Zhàng.
In Tiāndé second year
four thousand people were used for the Huánghuī.
Upon Shìzōng's enthronement,
all imperial travels, sacrifices, and banquets used three thousand people,
though sometimes the number was not met.
Before Dàdìng eleventh year
for sacrifices at the southern suburb and ancestral temple banquets, and upon arrival at the suburban altar,
seven thousand people were used for the Dàjià.

Zhì 23, Protocol and Guard, Imperial Grand Procession; Empress Dowager and Empress Procession; Crown Prince Procession; Princes' Retinue and Concubines' Escort; Hundred Officials' Procession
Imperial Grand Procession.
In Shìzōng's Dàdìng 3rd year (1163),
for the jiáhxiǎng sacrifice,
the huánghuī guard of 3,000 people was used,
divided into four sections.
The first section
had no xiànlìng or fǔmù,
but used the first three divisions of the huánghuī,
followed by the front drum and wind instrument ensemble,
then the Jīnwú Yámén flags,
then the carriage head,
then the Yǐnjià Lóngchí contingent,
then the Tiānwáng, Shí'èrchen, and other flags.
The second section
had the fourth and fifth divisions of the huánghuī,
then the Jūnwáng Wànsuì Rìyuè flags,
then the imperial horses,
with an increase of 16 Kòngmǎ Sīyǔ and Xiámǎ Sīyǔ each,
then the Rìyuè Hébì, Wǔxīng Liánzhū, and other flags,
then the Eight Treasures,
with an increase of 18 black-staff bearers who transmitted orders in front of the incense table,
then the Qībǎo niǎn.
The third section
had the first and second divisions of the rear huánghuī,
then the Yùlù,
then the Kǎoláo contingent,
then the Dǎojià Ménzhàng officials.
The fourth section
had the third, fourth, and fifth divisions of the rear huánghuī,
then the Jīnlù,
then the Yámén flags,
then the rear drum and wind instrument ensemble.
In Dàdìng 6th year (1166), ninth month,
upon returning to the capital from Xījīng,
the huánghuī guard of 2,542 people was used,
(including acting officials.
)762 horses,
divided into four sections.
The first section:
54 acting officials,
302 bearers,
170 musicians.
The second section:
32 acting officials,
376 bearers.
The third section:
44 acting officials within the guard,
42 Dǎojià officials,
100 Ménzhàng officials,
eight blue horses for the Yùlù,
140 carriage drivers,
500 Hùjià Kǎoláo contingent,
242 bearers.
The fourth section:
50 acting officials,
eight red horses for the Jīnlù,
94 carriage drivers,
22 Kònghès,
84 musicians,
290 bearers.
That year,
when the Emperor returned from Xījīng,
the authorities prepared the imperial guard.
The Crown Prince rode in a zhuìlù.
The Emperor suspected this to be improper,
and questioned the ritual officials,
but none knew the answer.
The Emperor was angry
and demoted them all.
The following year,
when the Crown Prince was to be formally invested,
the prime minister proposed that the imperial guard be prepared to make an announcement at the ancestral temple.
The Emperor said:
"Previously, when I received the venerable title and offered thanks,
I was merely told to follow the precedent of Sòng Zhēnzōng,
wearing court attire and riding a horse.
This was very light in terms of ritual.
Why should the Crown Prince now use a full ceremonial preparation?"
Chancellor Liángbì apologized.
The Emperor slowly said:
"This is merely the inertia of civil officials,
not paying attention."
Before this,
all imperial processions involved conscripting civilians to bear the guard.
After this, an edict ordered that soldiers replace them.
In Dàdìng 11th year (1171),
when there was to be an event at the Southern Suburb and an imperial sacrifice at the Tàimiào,
Right Chancellor Shí Jū presented the ritual.
The Emperor said:
"In the previous dynasty, Hàn people sacrificed to Heaven,
only focusing on the neatness and solemnity of the imperial guard.
This was self-indulgence,
not reverence for Heaven.
I believe that sacrificing to Heaven lies in sincerity,
not in the grandeur of the imperial guard.
Halve its use."
Thereupon,
the huánghuī guard was increased and decreased to form the Imperial Grand Procession,
totaling 7,000 people,
(including acting officials.

In the 6th month of the 5th year of Míngchāng, during the reign of Zhāngzōng,
the Shàngshūshěng memorialized:
"In the 6th year of Dàdìng,
Emperor Shìzōng returned to the capital from Xījīng,
adopting the Sòng dynasty's ceremony for returning to the capital after inspecting the provinces.
He used 2,000 Huánghuī guards, and the Jīnyù Lù, Kǎolǎo Duì armored cavalry of 500 men, and 42 imperial escorting officials.
Thereafter, these were not used again.
Now that the imperial carriage is proceeding to Jǐngmíng Gōng,
on the day of return to the capital, it is appropriate to use them accordingly."
The Emperor approved.
In the 1st year of Chéng'ān,
the ministers of the Department of State Affairs memorialized:
"For the Nánjiāo Dàlǐ,
the Dàjià Lǔbù should use 21,218 people and 8,198 horses.
When Emperor Shìzōng personally performed the suburban sacrifice,
the guard used 7,000 people.
Now, it is proposed to add 300 armored soldiers beyond the Dàdìng regulations,
and 248 Kǎolǎo Duì and whip-bearers,
totaling 7,548 people,
still divided into eight sections."
This was approved.
In the 6th year of Tàihé,
the Emperor wished to personally conduct the joint ancestral sacrifice,
and ordered the relevant authorities to calculate the expenses.
The Shàngshūshěng memorialized:
"It should use 3,500 guards,
over 10,000 strings of cash,
and 865 horses.
According to old practice,
all horses were borrowed from the people,
and the Qīnjūn and Bānzhī all provided their own (equipment/necessities) for service.
Now that military campaigns are underway,
official horses are kept for emergencies
and cannot be borrowed,
and the people also should not be further burdened.
It is appropriate to order the relevant authorities to take charge of these matters."
The Emperor ordered it to be re-discussed.
In the 4th month of the 8th year,
when the Dì sacrifice was offered at the Tàimiào,
following the precedent of the first year,
3,000 Huánghuī guards
and 500 Túnmén Zhàng were used.

In this year
the Zhòngzhái and other five chariots were changed to use round and square palanquins (lùniǎn),
as well as moving screens (xíngzhàng), sitting screens (zuòzhàng), brocade six-columned screens (jǐn liùzhù), and palace women's carriages (gōngrén chē).
Their regulations and numbers are all seen in the Treatise on Carriages and Attire (Yúfú Zhì).
In the second year of Tiāndé
when Hǎilíng established an Empress,
the Empress rode in a dragon-decorated shoulder sedan (lóngshì jiānyú).
The officials set up two portable screens (bùzhàng) at the western steps of the palace hall,
arranged ten fans on each side,
and one parasol.
This was the guiding ceremony for the palace hall.
Furthermore, sixty attendants (dǎocóng) were arranged for the Imperial Dowager (Huángtàihòu),
not including the parasol bearers.
All wore red brocade jackets (hóngjǐn ǎo) with intertwined four-disk eagle and round flower patterns, gold-flower headdresses (jīnhuā fútóu), and gilded silver belts.
For the Yǒngshòu and Yǒngníng Palaces, each had thirty leading attendants (dǎojià),
and two parasol bearers each.
This was also a regular customary ceremony.
Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ) Procession (lǔbù).
Used when receiving the imperial seal and tablets (cèbǎo) and offering thanks at the ancestral temple,
and for all grand ceremonies and major court assemblies.
The officials proposed using the Táng and Sòng ceremonial rites,
but an imperial edict limited it to one thousand people.

two xiǎojǐ.
Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Detachments — fourteen men each.
(Same as the First Section from the líntóugān downwards.)
Rear First Detachment — forty-seven men: one Yámén banner,
three men,
three Jiānmén Xiàowèi,
one Guǒyì Dūwèi,
one Zhǔshuài,
three jiàngyǐnfān,
nine men,
one Hèjī banner,
five men,
four lances,
three crossbows,
four lances,
three bows and arrows,
four lances,
three bows and arrows,
two zhūdāodùn,
two xiǎojǐ.
(All mounted.)
Rear Second Detachment — twenty-nine men: one Guǒyì Dūwèi,
one Gāngzǐ banner,
five men,
five lances,
three crossbows,
five lances,
three bows and arrows,
three lances,
four bows and arrows.
(All mounted.)
Rear Third Detachment — twenty-nine men: one Guǒyì Dūwèi,
one Huánglù banner,
five men,
five lances,
three crossbows,
five lances,
three bows and arrows,
three lances,
four bows and arrows.
(All mounted.)
Right Column — two hundred and four men,
arranged identically.
Crown Prince's regular ceremonial guard:
sixty-two attendants,
two umbrella bearers,
all wearing méihóng embroidered silk double-coiled phoenix jackets, jīn huā fútóu, and gilded silver belts.
All accompanying items such as gōngluó, spittoons, water pitchers, etc., are adorned with silver and gold.
Umbrellas are made of méihóng silk, with sitting qílín on gilded pagodas.
Chairs have gilded silver rings, double-playing qílín chair backs,
and red velvet tassels.
For banquets in the palace hall, embroidered silk with gold interwoven and coiled phoenixes are used,
and table skirts are embroidered silk with single-horned gold-interwoven coiled beasts.
When the Eastern Palace conducts affairs,
chairs are lacquered red,
with gilded silver animal-head fittings, red velvet tassels, and bright gold round flower chair backs,
while table covers are plain silk,
all in méihóng color,
including the coverlets and footrests.
Princes' retinues:
Ten introducers,
wearing black shirts, coiled headwraps, belts, and mounted on horseback.
Fifty qiānlǒngguān:
Leaders wear purple silk jackets and plain fútóu,
carrying silver-wrapped ivory staffs.
Umbrella bearers wear purple silk round embroidered lotus jackets, 〔一五〕and fútóu with interwoven gold flowers and crossed legs.
The rest wear purple silk embroidered lotus jackets with four corners, and yellow silk yìlán on both sides,
all with gilded silver belts,
and matching fútóu.
Four inviters/announcers.
Umbrellas are blue on the outside and purple on the inside,
with gilded silver pagodas.
Chairs have silver-wrapped rings and backs.
Water pitchers, gōngluó, and spittoons are all made of silver.
Commandery Princes' qiānlǒngguān — thirty men,
twenty if not leaving the palace.
Dukes of State's qiānlǒngguān — twenty men,
fourteen if not leaving the palace.
Commandery Princes' introducers — six men,
Dukes of State's — four men,
with each reduced by half if not leaving the palace.
Retinues and ceremonial items for others conform to the regulations for officials of the first rank.
The imperial consorts and concubines were attended by forty people,
wearing pútóu, purple embroidered banana-leaf-patterned robes, and gilt sashes.
The consorts each used sixteen partial fans, square fans, and round fans.
The concubines each used fourteen,
all held by palace attendants,
who wore cloud-patterned gauze caps, purple sìcháo robes, sashes, and green boots.
Each had one large umbrella,
and two umbrella bearers,
who wore their usual brocade jackets and pútóu.
The grand eldest princesses were attended by twelve people,
and the imperial sisters and imperial daughters by ten people,
all wearing purple silk gauze jackets embroidered with sunflower patterns on the chest and back, coiled hair, pútóu, and large silver pendants and waistbands,
each with two ivory staffs.
As for the other imperial clan women,
their allowances were differentiated based on their closeness to the imperial family.
Regarding umbrella regulations:
The three consorts of the crown prince all used umbrellas with green silk exteriors and purple linings, and golden finials.
Princes, princesses, and princely consorts used umbrellas with gilded silver finials; commandery princesses, county princesses, and fūrén used umbrellas with silver finials,
all with green exteriors and purple linings.
The mothers and wives of all officials used umbrellas according to their husbands’ or sons’ meritorious titles and ranks.
Official retinues:
For officials of the Senior First Rank: the three Imperial Tutors (sānshī), the three Grand Counselors (sāngōng), and the Director of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshūlìng),
each had ten attendants in red robes (zhūyī zhíshěng).
(The sāngōng were called zhífǔ.)
Sixty marshals (qiānlǒngguān) each,
all wearing purple robes and caps, and silver side-sashes.
They carried two pairs of rattan rods, three pairs of bone whips (gǔshào), and three pairs of ivory staffs.
Six horse attendants (cùmǎ),
and two umbrella bearers.
Folding chairs, water pots, gongs (luó), basins (yúzi), spittoons (tuòwǎn), and other items were carried in sequence,
by attendants wearing black robes and caps, and gilt bronze sashes.
(Thereafter, all attendants carrying items wore the same.)
Four heralds (yāohè).
Umbrellas used green silk exteriors, purple linings, and silver finials.

For officials of the Junior First Rank: the Left and Right Chancellors (shàngshū zuǒyòucéngxiàng), the Grand Counselors (píngzhāng zhèngshì), the Grand Marshal (dūyuánshuài), and the Commissioner of Military Affairs (shūmìshǐ),
the zhíshěng were the same.
(The Commissioner of Military Affairs was called zhíyuàn,
staffed by yībānzhī people.)
Fifty marshals,
and four heralds.
For the Judge of the Imperial Clan Court (pàndàzōngzhèng),
ten ushers (yǐnjiē) and forty marshals.
For the Governor of Dàxīng (dàxīngyǐn),
two pairs in front,
the rest were the same.
All folding chairs for the above ranks used silver-wrapped frames and purple silk cords.

For officials of the Senior Second Rank: the three Imperial Tutors of the Eastern Palace (dōnggōng sānshī), the Left and Right Vice Marshals (zuǒyòu fùyuánshuài), and the Left and Right Ministers of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū zuǒyòucéng),
eight zhíshěng,
forty marshals,
three heralds,
umbrellas used vermilion finials.
For officials of the Junior Second Rank: the Vice Grand Counselors (cānzhī zhèngshì), the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (shūmì fùshǐ), and the Censor-in-Chief (yùshǐdàfū),
the zhíshěng were the same.
(The Censorate (yùshǐtái) was called tōngyǐn,
staffed by bāishǐ bānzhī people.)
Thirty-six marshals,
the number of heralds was the same.

For officials of the Senior Third Rank: the three Junior Tutors of the Eastern Palace (dōnggōng sānshào), the Left and Right Supervising Marshals (yuánshuài zuǒyòu jiānjūn), the Commander of the Palace Guard (diànqián dūdiǎnjiǎn), the Ministers of the Six Ministries (liùbù shàngshū), the Grand Co-ordinators of the Capitals (zhūjīng liúshǒu), the Commissioner of the Bureau of Meritorious Awards (xuānhuī), the Commissioner of Agricultural Promotion (quànnóngshǐ), the Chancellor of the Hànlín Academy (hànlín xuéshì chéngzhǐ), and other officials of the same rank,
each had six ushers,
and twenty marshals.
All folding chairs for the above ranks used straight-backed silver-inlaid frames and blue silk cords.

For the Regional Transport Commissioners (zhūjīng dǔnnyùnshǐ), Pacification Commissioners (zhāotǎoshǐ), Judicial Commissioners (zhūlù tíxíngshǐ), Governors of Prefectures (zhūfǔyǐn) concurrently serving as Grand Commanders of Provincial Armies (běnlù bīngmǎ dūzǒngguǎn) and Co-ordinators (liúshǒu),
fifty marshals.
For officials on external assignments:
Commanders of Armies (tǒngjūnshǐ), Transport Commissioners (dōuyùn), Pacification Commissioners (zhāotǎoshǐ), Vice Commissioners (fùshǐ),
Governors of Prefectures (zhūfǔyǐn) concurrently serving as Grand Commanders (zǒngguǎn),
forty-five marshals,
seventy public servants (gōngshǐ).

For officials of the Junior Third Rank: the Left and Right Assistant Commanders of Marshals (yuánshuài zuǒyòu dūjiān), the Vice Commissioner of Agricultural Promotion (quànnóng fùshǐ), the Vice Commander of the Palace Guard (diànqián fùdūdiǎnjiǎn), and the Vice Censor-in-Chief (yùshǐzhōngchéng), and other officials of the same rank,
each had six ushers,
and eighteen marshals.
Among these, the Vice Censor-in-Chief was provided with crimson robes for his attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
Transport Commissioners (yùnshǐ), Military Governors (jiédùshǐ),
forty marshals.
For all military garrisons (zhūjiézhèn) and tribal military governors (zhūbùzú jiédù) of the same rank,
seventy public servants for senior garrisons, sixty-five for medium garrisons, and sixty for junior garrisons.
For the attendants and attire of the above external officials,

except for those Pacification Commissioners, Grand Commanders, tribal military governors, and Pasture Commissioners who have never had military provisions or manpower, who retained their old arrangements,

the manpower for Co-ordinators, Commanders of Armies, Grand Commanders, Transport Commissioners, Pacification Commissioners, Governors of Prefectures, Regional Transport Commissioners, and Military Governors also remained the same.
Although the number was large,
it must not exceed forty people,
all wearing purple robes and silver sashes,
with silver-wrapped folding chairs, silver water pots, gongs, basins, spittoons, and ivory staffs.
Among them, two pairs of silver-wrapped bone whips and two pairs of large swords,
and heralds.
Only the Transport Commissioners did not have bone whips or large swords.

For officials of the Senior Fourth Rank: the Left and Right Supervising Secretaries (zuǒyòu jiànyìdàfū), the Libationer of the Directorate of Education (guózǐ jìjiǔ), the Vice Ministers of the Six Ministries (liùbù shìláng), and other officials of the same rank,
each had eight ushers,
and twelve regular attendants (běnpò).
For officials on external assignments:
Co-ordinators, Assistant Commanders (tǒngjūn dūjiān), and Vice Judicial Commissioners (tíxíng fùshǐ),
each had thirty marshals.

For officials of the Junior Fourth Rank: the Left and Right Generals of the Palace Guard (diànqián zuǒyòu wèijiāngjūn), the Commanders of Mèng'ān and Qiānhù (zhūmēng'ān qiānhù), the Palace Guards of Princely Establishments (qīnwángfǔwèi), the Vice Regional Transport Commissioners of the Capitals (zhūjīng tóngzhī zhuǎnyùn), and other officials of the same rank,
each had four ushers,
and twelve regular attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
thirty-five marshals,
sixty public servants for senior defense commands (shàngfángyù), fifty-five for medium defense commands (zhōngfángyù), and fifty for junior defense commands (xiàfángyù).

For officials of the Senior Fifth Rank: the Directors of the Left and Right Departments of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū zuǒyòusī lángzhōng), the Academician Readers-in-waiting (hànlín dàizhì), the Assistant Ministers of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (tàicháng shǎoqīng), and other officials of the same rank,
each had eight regular attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
thirty marshals,
fifty public servants for senior prefectures (shàngzhōu), forty-five for medium prefectures (zhōngzhōu), and forty for junior prefectures (xiàzhōu).

For all defense commanders (fángyù), prefects (cìshǐ), military governors (zhījūn), as well as the attendants of the Grand Commanderies of Capital Prefectures (jīngfǔ tǒngjūnsī) and subordinate officials of military garrisons (jiézhèn zuò'èr guānrén),
all wore purple robes and horn sashes,
with straight-backed silver folding chairs, gongs, basins, spittoons, and ivory staffs.
Umbrellas used green exteriors, emerald linings, and green finials.
Defense commanders, prefects, and military governors still used silver-wrapped bone whips and one pair of large swords,
and had heralds.
Only the Vice Commanders of Route Armies (suílù fùtǒngjūn) did not have heralds.
For officials of the Junior Fifth Rank: the Directors of the Six Ministries (liùbù lángzhōng), Supervising Censors (shìyùshǐ), Assistant Ministers of the Court of Judicial Review (dàlǐ shǎoqīng)
and other officials of the same rank,
each had seven regular attendants.
Supervising Censors were provided with crimson robes for their attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
ten regular attendants.
All officials of the above ranks were permitted to use canopies.
For officials of the Senior Sixth Rank: the Assistant Directors of the Left and Right Departments of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū zuǒyòusī yuánwài), and other officials of the same rank,

For officials on external assignments:
nine regular attendants.
For officials of the Junior Sixth Rank: the Assistant Directors of the Six Ministries (shàngshū liùbù yuánwài), and other officials of the same rank,
each had five regular attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
nine regular attendants.
For officials of the Senior Seventh Rank: the Palace Supervising Censors (diànzhōng shìyùshǐ), and other officials of the same rank,
each had four regular attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
seven regular attendants.
For County Magistrates (xiànlìng),
ten public servants.
For Military Commanders (dūjūn),
six public servants.
For officials of the Junior Seventh Rank: the Literary Compilers of the Hànlín Academy (yīngfèng hànlín wénzì), and other officials of the same rank,
each had four regular attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
six regular attendants.
For County Magistrates,
ten public servants.
For officials of the Senior Eighth Rank: the Reviewing Officials of the Court of Judicial Review (dàlǐ píngshì), and other officials of the same rank,
each had two regular attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
six regular attendants.
For officials of the Junior Eighth Rank: the Sacrificial Officers of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (tàicháng tàizhù), and other officials of the same rank,
each had two regular attendants.
For officials on external assignments:
five regular attendants.
For officials of the Senior Ninth Rank: the Supervisors of Imperial Medicine (yùyào dūjiān), and other officials of the same rank,

For officials on external assignments:
three regular attendants.
For officials of the Junior Ninth Rank: the Attendants in the Palace (suídiànwèi chéngyìng), Assistant Supervisors (tóngjiān), and other officials of the same rank,
each had one regular attendant.
For officials on external assignments:
one regular attendant.

For the Scribes and Interpreters of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshūshěng) and Bureau of Military Affairs (shūmìyuàn) (lìyìshǐ tōngshì), the Interpreters of the Six Ministries (liùbù) and Censorate (yùshǐtái) and Military Commander’s Office (tǒngjūnsī) (tōngshì), the Clerks of the Proclamation Office (gàoyuàn lìshǐ), the Scribes of the Imperial Historiography Institute (guóshǐyuàn shūxiě), and other such posts,
each was provided with one regular attendant.
For all officials of the above ranks,
the number of attendants and items should not exceed the prescribed limit.
For external officials,
the attendants’ clothing and items
were procured using public funds from their locality or money from fines and confiscations.
For all civil and military officials, from Qīnwáng downwards,
the number and grades of their attendants [jiàncóng] vary.
However, the Zhūyī Zhíshěng are excluded from this.
Among the lower ranks,
the first are called Yǐnjiē,
(also called Yǐncóng).
These are appointed for inner court officials of the fourth rank and above.
The second are called Qiānlǒngguān,
appointed for inner and outer court officials of the principal fifth rank and above.
The third are called Běnpò,
appointed for inner and outer court officials of the principal fourth rank and below.
The fourth are called Gōngshǐ,
appointed for outer court officials of the principal third rank and below.
The fifth are called Cóngjǐ Rénlì,
appointed for outer court officials such as the Jīngdū Liúshǒu, Dàxīng Fǔyǐn, and other officials of the principal third rank and below.
The Běnpò perform duties similar to the Qiānlǒngguān.
The Gōngshǐ attend to public affairs,
while the Cóngjǐ perform private duties.
All five categories are filled by Shèliáng Jūn.
These soldiers are not selected based on their physical strength for combat,
but are specially recruited from commoners aged seventeen to thirty who are tall and strong. They are then registered [shōucì]
and provided with rations,
hence the name Shèliáng.
Their leaders are given titles such as Jiāngjié, Chéngjú, and Shíjiàng,
and all are subordinate to the Suílù Dū Bīngmǎ Zǒngguǎnfǔ.
The reason the Jīn treated their officials with courtesy and ensured they had sufficient attendants [rènshǐ]
must have been a legacy of earlier dynasties.
For outer court officials' Cóngjǐ Rénlì:
Zhū Jīng Liúshǒu and Dàxīng Fǔyǐn,
fifty persons.
Tǒngjūn, Dū Zhuǎnyùn, Zhāotǎo, Ànchásǐ,
and Zhūlù Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn,
forty-five persons.
Zhuǎnyùn and Jiédùshǐ,
forty persons.
Tíkòng, Zhū Qúnmù, and Fángyùshǐ,
thirty-five persons.
Outer court Qīnwáng Fù, Tóngzhī Liúshǒu, Fù Tǒngjūn, Ànchá Fùshǐ, and Zhū Zhōu Cìshǐ Zhī Jūnjì,
thirty persons.
Tóngzhī Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Shì, Fù Zhāotǎo, Fù Liúshǒu, Tóngzhī Fǔyǐn Jiān Zǒngguǎn, Tíjǔ Cáoyùnsī, and Zhū Wǔpǐn Yánshǐ,
twenty-five persons.
Dū Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ, Ànchásī Qiānshì, Shǎoyǐn, Fù Zǒngguǎn, and Tóngzhī Zhuǎnyùn Jiédùshǐ Shì,
twenty persons.
Jīngdū Bīngmǎ Dū Zhīhuīshǐ,
eighteen persons.
Zhuǎnyùn Jiédù Fùshǐ,
seventeen persons.
Bīngmǎ Dū Qiánxiá,
fifteen persons.
Qīnwáng Fǔwèi, Zhū Jīng Liúshǒu Zǒng Pànguān, and Tóngzhī Fángyùshǐ Shì,
thirteen persons.
Jǐngxúnshǐ, Bīngmǎ Fù Dū Zhīhuī, and Tóng Tíjǔ Cáoyùnsī,
principal sixth rank,
Yán Fùshǐ,
subordinate sixth rank,
Jiǔqǔ Yánshuì Shǐ, and Tóngzhī Zhōujūn Shì,
ten persons.
Tǒngjūn Dū Zhuǎnyùnsī Jīngfǔ Zǒngguǎn Sǎnfǔ Děng Pànguān, and Jīng Tuīguān,
nine persons.
Qīnwáng Fǔ Sīmǎ, Zhāotǎo Pànguān,
Chìjù Xiànlìng, Tíjǔ Shàngjīng Huángchéng Bīngmǎ Qiánxiá,
principal seventh rank,
Jiǔqǔ Yánshuì Fùshǐ, Dū Zhuǎnyùn Pànguān, Fǔ Tuīguān, and Jiédù Guānchá Pànguān,
eight persons.
Jīngxiàn Cìjù Xiànlìng, Dū Xúnjiǎnshǐ, Zhèngjiàng, and Fǔjūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ,
seven persons.
Sīshǔ Lìng, Qīnwáng Fǔ Wénxué, 〔一九〕Zhāotǎosī Kānshìguān, Zhū Xiànlìng, Jǐngxún Fùshǐ, and Zhī Chéngbǎo Zhài Zhèn,
subordinate seventh rank,
Yán Pàn, Tóng Tíjǔ Shàngjīng Huángchéng, Jiézhèn Jūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ, Dū Xúnhé, Tóng Qīpǐn Jiǔshǐ, and Fángyù Pànguān,
six persons.
Shìlìng, Lùshì, Chìjù Xiànchéng, Fù Dū Xúnjiǎnshǐ, Fùjiàng, Dū Xúnjiǎn, and Zhōujūn Pànguān,
five persons.
Tǒngjūnsī Zhīshì, Qīnwáng Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn, and Sīshǔ Chéng,
principal eighth rank,
Jiǔshǐ Fù, Jīngxiàn Cìjù Xiànchéng, and Zhū Sīshǐ,
four persons.
Dàxīngfǔ Zhāotǎo, Ànchásī Zhīshì, Jīngfǔ Yùnsī Jiézhènsī Yù, Guǎngōu Héqiáo Guāndù Jīcháguān,
subordinate eighth rank,
Yán Pànguān, Zāoyùnsī Gōudàngguān, Jǐngxún Pànguān, Zhū Xiànchéng, Shìchéng, Sīhòu, Zhǔbù, Lùshìsī Pànguān, Xiànwèi, Fù Dū Xúnjiǎn, Zhū Xúnjiǎn, and Xúnhéguān,
principal ninth rank,
Jiǔshǐ, and Zhū Sī Fùshǐ,
three persons.
Yánchǎng Guǎngōu, Fángcì Yǐxià Sīyù, Bùduì Jiàng, Tóng Guǎngōu Héqiáo, Fù Jīchá, Sīhòu Pànguān, Jiàoshòu, Tǒngjūn Ànchásī Zhīfǎ, Jūnjiá, Zhū Sī Dūjiān, and Jiézhèn Yǐshàng Zhīfǎ,
two persons.
Yánchǎng Tóng Guǎngōu, Fángcì Yǐxià Zhīfǎ, Zhū Sī Tóngjiān, Tǒngjūn Ànchásī Shūshǐ, and Tǒngjūnsī Yìshū Tōngshì,
one person.
The Pōsù Gōngshǐ and Cóngjǐ Rénlì
are recruited from Hàn Chinese commoners in the vicinity of Dōngjīng and Chéngzhōu who volunteer for service,
(meaning those not under the jurisdiction of a Měng'ān Móukè).
For the Hélǎn, Xùpǐn, Húlígǎi, and Púyǔ Lù, able-bodied men are rotated among the upper and middle households under each Měng'ān Móukè's jurisdiction
and paid money and rations according to the Shèliáng Jūn regulations,
with a rotation once a year.
The Bùluóhuǒ and Tǔlúhúndázhíhé are treated similarly.
As for the various resignations [cí] and officials of the Qúnmù,
if a Měng'ān Móukè needs to assign people from their jurisdiction to serve as attendants [rénlì],
they are rotated among the upper and middle households.
If any civil or military official holds concurrent posts, and is entitled to more attendants [réncóng],
they are given the larger number;
otherwise, the number is determined by rank and type.
For the Yǐnjiē and Yǐncóng of Qīnwáng,
they are assigned by the Dū Bīngmǎ Sī.
For princesses attending court, they are assigned from the Gōngzhǔ Suícháo Cóngshǒubù Běnpò.
For those in other regions, they are assigned by the local Zhōufǔ.
The Yǐncóng of royal princes' households and the Qiānlǒngguān and Yǐnjiē of the prime minister's office [Xiàngfǔ]
are rotated annually.
All others serve for ten months before being replaced,
and are all filled by Shèliáng Jūn.
Officials of the sixth rank and below who attend court, as well as those serving in various bureaus,
may, if they wish, pay for their own attendants [cóngjǐ shūyōng];
their names must be submitted to the department,
and the local government offices are not allowed to employ them within that year.
For officials who assume office or leave office for proper reasons,
half of their attendants [rénlì] for escort and reception are provided from among their personal attendants [cóngjǐ rén].
Those who take on attendants must obtain printed vouchers from the local government offices for assignment and acquisition.
Those returning attendants must present a voucher from their original place of assignment to be returned.
If no verification is available, payment is temporarily withheld,
pending an inquiry to confirm there are no absconding or missing attendants.
Only then is payment released.
For retired officials of the third rank or higher,
half of their Cóngjǐ Rénlì are provided at their desired location;
they are not allowed to pay for them themselves [shūyōng].
If an official passes away, those who need to be returned are given half the previous number.
However, if an official retires before the age of sixty or is dismissed,
no attendants are provided.
Collation Notes
Zhi 24, Yu Fu Shang, Emperor's Carriages, Empress's and Consorts' Carriages, Crown Prince's Carriage System, and Carriages and Saddle Ornaments for Princes and Below.
In ancient times, the system of carriages and palanquins [chēyú]
each had specific names and markings,
for sacrifices, enfeoffments,
farming, and military campaigns,
to distinguish ranks and clarify status.
Over successive dynasties, there were mutual adjustments,
sometimes innovations according to the times,
sometimes adhering to old forms to create embellishment,
with novelty and ingenuity increasing daily,
and extravagance becoming ever more rampant.
Furthermore, later generations became accustomed to riding horses,
so the use of carriages became quite rare.
Only for ceremonial processions [fǎjià dǎoyǐn] during suburban sacrifices and temple offerings [jiāomiào sìxiǎng]
were they maintained as a contemporary custom that dared not be abolished.
However, as for the intentions of the ancient kings in governing the world and establishing laws,
they are
vast and distant.
The Jīn initially adopted the ceremonial items of the Liáo;
later, having conquered the Sòng,
they then established a system of carriages and palanquins [chēluò].
When Xīzōng visited Yān,
he first used the ceremonial procession.
By the time of Shìzōng,
the regulations for their manufacture were finally settled,
clearly adhering to ancient principles.
By examining the ceremonial texts [lǐwén]
and corroborating with national histories,
the system of that dynasty is thus revealed.
In Dàdìng 11th year,
when preparations were being made for the Southern Suburbs ceremony,
the Tàichángsì was ordered to examine the Sòng's Southern Suburbs rites.

The processional guard [lǔbù] was to use one each of the Yùluò, Jīnluò, Xiàngluò, Gēluò, Mùluò, Gēnggēn Chē, Míngyuǎn Chē, Zhǐnán Chē, Jìlǐ Gǔchē, Chóngdé Chē, Píxuān Chē, Jìnxián Chē, Huángyuè Chē, Báilù Chē, Luánqí Chē, Bàowěi Chē, Yáochē, and Yángchē,
five Gēchē,
and twelve Shǔchē.
Excluding the existing carriages and palanquins,
the missing items were one each of the Xiàng, Mù, and Gēluò,
Gēnggēn, Míngyuǎn, Píxuān, Jìnxián, Báilù, Yángchē,
and Dàniǎn,
three Gēchē,
and four Shǔchē.
According to the Wǔlǐ Xīnyí,
the Yùluò is blue,
the Jīnluò is scarlet,
the Xiàngluò is silver-brown,
the Gēluò is yellow,
and the Mùluò is black.
Some components match the color of the carriage,
while others require a different color.
For example, the Yùluò uses blue silk embroidered cloud-dragon straps,
blue gauze embroidered auspicious floral straps,
blue painted wheels and shafts,
and blue yak tails.
These match the color of the carriage.
However, the Xiàng, Mù, and Gēluò should use scarlet, silver-brown, yellow, and black respectively.
As for the parts directly used by the emperor,
unlike other items that are merely for aesthetic appeal,
the footrest [tǎchuáng], backrest [yǐbèi], and pathway mats [tàdào zhī rù] are all made of red brocade.
The seat mat [zuòrù], as well as the 'walking horse' mat [xíngmǎ rù], and three hanging soft curtains [tòubì ruǎnlián],
use silver-brown, yellow, and blue gauze brocade in three colors.
Also, the Dàniǎn,
which Táo Gǔ of the Sòng creatively designed,
was later, during the Xiángfú era, reduced in weight by over seven hundred jīn because it was too heavy.
This shows that even at that time, there was no fixed standard;
each was crafted according to discretion and intent.
As for their system,
the Jīn Yùluò was missing.
Those visible were the Xiàngluò, Gēluò, Mùluò,
Gēnggēn, Píxuān, Jìnxián, Míngyuǎn, Báilù, Yángchē,
Gēchē,
and Dàniǎn,
making a total of eleven.
The Xiànglù (Elephant Chariot)
has a yellow body,
with gilded copper fittings
and ivory decorations at the extremities.
The wheel covers are of silver-brown fabric.
A large red banner is erected.
The rest is identical to the Yùlù (Jade Chariot).
The Gélù (Leather Chariot)
has a yellow body,
covered with leather,
with gilded copper fittings.
The wheel covers are yellow.
A large white banner is erected.
The rest is identical to the Yùlù.
The Mùlù (Wooden Chariot)
has a black body,
lacquered.
The wheel covers are black.
A large banner (Dàhuī) is erected.
The rest is identical to the Yùlù.
The Gēnggēn Chē (Ploughshare Chariot)
has a green body,
with a triple canopy.
Its design is like the Yùlù but without jade ornamentation.
The Píxuān Chē (Leather Canopy Chariot)
has a red body,
with lacquered pillars above,
piercing five superimposed wheels,
painted with tiger stripes,
and a single shaft.
The Jìnxián Chē (Chariot for Advancing the Worthy)
has a red body,
like the Géchē (Leather Chariot).
Its crimson wheel covers, netting bands, and door curtains are all embroidered with phoenixes.
Above are set a vermilion lacquered bed and an incense table,
with purple silk brocade covers.
It has a single shaft.
The Míngyuǎn Chē (Bright and Distant Chariot)
is designed like a house,
with a pointed roof,
double eaves,
and a balustrade.
On top of the roof is a golden dragon,
with bells hanging from its four corners.
The upper level has curtains hanging on all four sides,
and the lower level is surrounded by carved panels.
It has three shafts.
The Báilù Chē (White Egret Chariot)
has a red body,
with carved panels all around.
Above are lacquered pillars,
the tips of which are carved into egrets,
holding goose feather tubes in their mouths.
There are red ribbons.
The pillars pierce five superimposed wheels.
The wheel covers, black roof, crimson skirt, and crimson netting bands
are all embroidered with flying egrets.
It has a single shaft.
The Yángchē (Goat Chariot)
has a red body,
with turtle patterns oil-painted on its two sides,
and golden phoenix wings.
The canopy cover and knotting bands are all embroidered with auspicious goats.
It has two shafts.
The Dàniǎn (Grand Palanquin)
has a red body,
is square,
oil-painted,
with gilded silver leaf dragon and phoenix fittings.
Above it, on all four sides, are flying dragons, cloud patterns (yúnxiāo), fire pearls,
square mirrors, silver thread net bags,
pearls and kingfisher feathers forming cloud dragons,
and inlaid mother-of-pearl sunset patterns (xiázǐ).
Dragon heads at the four corners hold incense sachets.
The top wheel is adorned with radiating leaves,
with a silver lotus flower and seated dragon in the center.
There are red silk brocade tassels (hónglínghuá)
and green ivory pressing plates.
Inside are set round mirrors, incense sachets,
silver-decorated balustrade platforms,
and purple silk cord nets (zǐsī tāowǎng) with fittings (kuòtà).
A yellow mat is placed in the center,
on which are set the imperial seat, a curved armrest (qūjǐ),
an incense burner, and brocade knotting ribbons.
The armrest covers, wheel covers, and netting bands are all crimson embroidered with cloud dragons and auspicious flower patterns (bǎoxiànghuā),
pressed with gold threads.
There are four long poles,
decorated with gilded silver dragon heads.
Painted ladders, supporting forks, and movable barriers (xíngmǎ).
The Qībǎo Niǎn (Seven Treasures Palanquin)
is designed like the Dàniǎn,
decorated with jade skirt netting,
seven treasures,
and its pendants (dīzi) use real pearls.
Sòng Qīnzōng made it for the Supreme Emperor (Shànghuáng),
and Hǎilíng (Wányán Liàng) took it from Biàn (Kāifēng) and used it.
There are six chariots for the empress.
One is called the Chóngzhái Chē (Double Pheasant Chariot).
It has a green body,
with gold ornamentation, gilded copper carved flower and leaf segment fittings,
twenty-four radiating leaves,
one brightly gilded standing phoenix,
one purple silk gold-embroidered vibrant auspicious pattern canopy,
one green silk and one green oiled canopy cover,
two red silk net bands and two purple silk brightly gilded vibrant cloud-dragon netting bands,
two side panels with brightly gilded five-colored interspersed pheasant feathers,
three gilded bronze shafts with phoenix heads,
eight standing luan birds on the cross-shafts,
one set of incense burner and incense box,
knotting bands of Yínnán brocade,
one vermilion lacquered stool and one footrest,
one set of handrails shaped like fish,
red silk brightly gilded cover and mat,
one red silk lining mat,
four green silk walking mats,
one green silk brightly gilded vibrant cloud-phoenix curtain,
two red silk brightly gilded-edged red bamboo blinds,
two gilded copper leaf segment movable barriers,
one vermilion lacquered gilded silver leaf fitting-adorned folding ladder,
two green silk folding ladder inspection mats,
ten stepping mats,
two large hemp ropes wrapped in green silk,
and one oiled covering cloth.
The second is called the Yànzhái Chē (Reclining Pheasant Chariot).
It has a red body,
one Dàoxiān brocade canopy,
one purple silk and one purple oiled canopy cover,
two red silk net bands and two Yínnán brocade netting bands.
The rest is identical to the Chóngzhái Chē,
only the walking mats,
curtains, inspection mats (luó), and wrapped ropes, etc., use red.
The third is called the Zhái Chē (Pheasant Chariot).
It has a yellow body,
with gold-adorned bronze leaf segment fittings,
an Yínnán brocade canopy,
a yellow silk oiled canopy cover,
three bronze shafts with phoenix heads,
but no standing luan birds on the cross-shafts.
The rest is identical to the Yànzhái Chē,
but the color of the silk (luósè) used is yellow.
The fourth is called the Ānchē (Comfort Chariot).
It has a red body,
a Dàoxiān brocade canopy,
purple silk and oiled canopy covers,
red silk net bands,
Tiānxiàlè brocade netting bands,
three bronze shafts with phoenix heads,
but no standing luan birds on the cross-shafts, nor incense burner or incense box.
The rest is identical to the Zhái Chē,
but all colors used are red.
The fifth is called the Sìwàng Chē (Four-Gazing Chariot).
It has a vermilion body,
an Yínnán brocade canopy,
green silk and oiled canopy covers,
two chí-dragon heads at the shaft ends.
The rest is identical to the Ānchē.
The sixth is called the Jīngēn Chē (Golden Root Chariot).
It has a vermilion body,
purple silk and purple oiled canopy covers,
two red silk net bands,
and two Dàoxiān brocade netting bands.
The footrest covers and mats use red silk damask (hónglíng).
The inspection mats and stepping mats all use silk damask.
The rest is identical to the Ānchē.
After the six chariots were completed,

they were re-designed into six types: Yuánlù (Round Chariot), Chóngyán (Double Eaves Chariot), Fānglù (Square Chariot), Wǔhuá (Five Splendors Chariot), Tíngtóu (Pavilion-Top Chariot), and Píngtóu (Flat-Top Chariot).
Also, one Jiǔlóng Chē (Nine-Dragon Chariot) was added,
two zhàng high, one zhàng one chǐ wide, and two zhàng six chǐ long.
Four Wǔfèng Chē (Five-Phoenix Chariots),
each one zhàng eight chǐ high,
and of the same length and width.
One Yuánlù Chē, one Fānglù Chē, and one Chóngyán Chē,
each one zhàng seven chǐ high,
one zhàng eight chǐ long,
and eight chǐ wide.
All are drawn by four horses,
with fifty chariot attendants each,
all wearing flat caps (píngjīn zé), vibrant green, crimson, and yellow three-colored auspicious flower pattern shirts, silver-brown waistbands, and wide-legged trousers.
One Píngtóu Niǎn (Flat-Top Palanquin), one Wǔhuá Niǎn (Five Splendors Palanquin), and one Tíngtóu Niǎn (Pavilion-Top Palanquin),
each one zhàng nine chǐ high,
one zhàng five cùn wide,
and three zhàng long.
Ninety-six palanquin bearers for each, working in two shifts,
all wearing vibrant crimson auspicious flower pattern shirts.
The rest is as previously specified.
Thirty-five escort personnel,
wearing long-footed head wraps (chángjiǎo fútóu), purple silk narrow shirts, and fastened with gold-copper belts.
The horses' elaborate bridles (fányīng), straw covers (liángtì), bells, whisks, and tail wraps all match the color of the chariot,
with gold-copper masks,
pheasant tail feathers inserted,
vermilion reins,
and vermilion main harness (zǒng).
The dragon chariots collectively use one red silk umbrella.
Two umbrella bearers wear brocade hats and head wraps in their own attire.
Also, the regulations for fans, screens, and similar items were scrutinized and established.
The fan with a handle on the side (piān shàn) was like an immortal's feather fan.
The traveling screen (xíng zhàng) had six panels,
each eight *chǐ* long and six *chǐ* high.
It was covered with red silk gauze (hóng luó) and lined with crimson damask (zhū luó),
and painted with clouds and phoenixes.
A dragon-head pole held a knotted sash.
Each screen required four palace women (gōng rén) to carry it.
The sitting screen (zuò zhàng) had three panels,
each seven *chǐ* long and five *chǐ* high,
painted with clouds and phoenixes,
covered with red silk gauze (hóng luó) and lined with crimson damask (zhū luó).
The rest was the same as the traveling screen.
The brocade screen (jǐn zhàng) had six pillars and eight panels,
each two *chǐ* wide and three *chǐ* high,
covered with brocade.
Eight inner court attendants (nèi gǐ shǐ) held it.
The carriages for palace women (gōng rén chē) were made like carriages for attendants (shǔ chē).
Eight chariot drivers (jià shì) were employed,
wearing flat headscarves (píng jīn zé), scarlet shirts (fēi shān), wide-mouthed trousers (dà kǒu kù), and shoes and socks (xié wà).
Thirty palace women (gōng rén) served,
wearing cloud-patterned gauze hats (yún jiǎo shā mào), purple shirts (zǐ shān) with sashes (shù dài), and green boots (lǜ xuē).
In the third month of Míngchāng (明昌) first year (1190),
it was stipulated that the carriages and palanquins (chē niǎn) of imperial concubines (fēi pín) should have gilded phoenix heads and yellow knots.
Those for imperial consorts (yù qī) and imperial wives (shì fù) should have partially gilded phoenix heads and plum-red knots (méi hóng jié zǐ).
Regulations for the Crown Prince's (Huáng Tàizǐ) carriage.
In the twelfth month of Dàdìng (大定) sixth year (1166),
a memorial was submitted regarding the traditional regulations for the Crown Prince's (Huáng Tàizǐ) golden chariot (jīn lù),
as well as the ceremonial use of the Emperor's (shàng) golden chariot (jīn lù).
By imperial decree, these were thoroughly reviewed and established.
The shafts (zhōu), flags (qí), flag finials (qí shǒu), and all parts that would normally use dragons were instead decorated with *lín* (kylin).
Dust screens (zhàng chén) and similar items were removed.
For the Emperor's (shàng) golden chariot (jīn lù), the number and color of named parts,
following the nine-section standard for the highest dignitaries (shàng gōng),
were reduced by one-quarter.
For the Emperor's (shàng) chariot (lù),
the golden dragon in front of the armrest (shì) was changed to a recumbent deer (fú lù).
The sitting dragon on the armrest (shì) was changed to a phoenix.
The twelve pennants (qí) were reduced to nine.
The six red-maned horses (chì liú) were reduced to four.
The yellow silk gauze (huáng luó) used for the curtains and cushions was changed to plum-red (méi hóng).
The rest was constructed in full detail.
Its design was
a red body,
with all extremities decorated in gold.
It had a double crossbar (zhòng jiào).
The carriage box (xiāng) was painted with patterns of birds and beasts from the Yú (虞) era.
It had a yellow canopy (huáng wū).
The armrest (shì) was made into a red recumbent deer (chì fú lù).
It had dragon shafts (lóng zhōu).
One golden phoenix
was placed in front of the armrest (shì).
[一０]Dust screens (zhàng chén) were installed.
It had a crimson canopy (zhū gài) with a yellow lining (huáng luó).
The wheels were painted with crimson patterns (zhū yá).
On the left, a nine-pennant banner (jiǔ liú) was erected.
On the right, a *qī jí* (闟戟) was carried.
The flag finial (qí shǒu) held a golden dragon head,
with ribbons (shòu) and tasselled streamers (líng ruí).
Eight bells (bā luán) were on the crossbar (héng).
Two bells (líng) were on the armrest (shì).
It was drawn by four red-maned horses (chì liú),
with golden saddle plates (jīn pàn) and square bridle ornaments (fāng yì).
They had inserted pheasant tails (zhái wěi),
carved forehead ornaments (lóu xī) and saddle flaps (pán),
and nine-layered tassels (yīng jiǔ jiù).
The Emperor's (Huángdì) chariot (lù) was seventeen *chǐ* high from top to ground.
[一一]Now, reduced by one-quarter, it was thirteen *chǐ* and two *cùn*.
The reduction in length and width was also the same.
Regulations for carriages of princes (wáng gōng) and below.
For the first rank (yī pǐn),
the shafts used silver *chī* (螭) heads.
The poles of the sunshade (liáng péng gān zi) and the moon-shaped boards (yuè bǎn) were also permitted to be decorated with silver.
For the third rank (sān pǐn) and above,
*chī* (螭) heads were not allowed to be adorned with silver.
The poles of the sunshade (liáng péng gān zi) and the moon-shaped boards (yuè bǎn) were still permitted to be decorated with silver.
For the fifth rank (wǔ pǐn) and above,
the shafts used lion heads.
For the sixth rank (liù pǐn) and below,
[一二]the shafts used cloud heads.
Commoners' (shù rén) sitting carriages (zuò chē) had flat tops,
and were only painted with a single color of black lacquer.
For princes (qīn wáng), saddles (ān) were gilded and silver-wrapped,
and further engraved with open flowers.
The mudguards (zhàng ní) used purple silk gauze (zǐ luó),
decorated with brocade.
The reins (pèi) were adorned with gilding and silver,
and fastened with silk knots.

For imperial family members (huáng jiā) of *xiǎo gōng* (小功) mourning grade and above, for the Grand Empress Dowager (Tài Huáng Tàihòu) and Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) of *dà gōng* (大功) mourning grade and above, for close relatives of the Empress (Huánghòu) and above,
and for first-rank officials (yī pǐn guān), and officials whose rank reached third-rank (sān pǐn) and above,
mudguards (zhàng ní) were permitted to use gold flowers.
If granted by imperial favor or used within the imperial polo field (yù qiú chǎng),
they were not subject to these prohibitions.
According to old regulations,
princes (qīn wáng) and chief ministers (zǎi zhí) serving outside the capital,
as well as the Magistrate of Dàxīng (Dàxīng Yǐn),
all wore small hats (xiǎo mào), sashes (shù dài), silver saddles (yín ān), and silk whips (sī biān).
During the Dàdìng (大定) reign,
Shìzōng (世宗) considered that the capital magistrate (jīng yǐn) was also an outside official of the third rank,
yet indistinguishable from princes (qīn wáng).
Therefore, he decreed that they were not allowed to wear silver saddles (yín ān) or silk whips (sī biān),
but should only follow the example of outside officials of the third rank,
wearing *fútou* (襆頭), belts (dài), and plain black robes (zhǎn zào) when attending to duties.
In the second year of Chéng'ān (承安) (1197),
it was decreed that the bronze-decorated saddles and reins (tóng zhuāng ān pèi) of guards (hù wèi) could not be lent to others.
Commoners' (shù rén) horse saddles (mǎ ān) were permitted to use black lacquer,
decorated with bone, horn, and iron.
They were not allowed to use jade accessories (yù jiào jù) or gold, silver, rhinoceros horn, or ivory to decorate saddles (ān) and reins (pèi).

In the chapter on carriages and attire: The Emperor's (Tiānzǐ) ceremonial robe and crown (gǔn miǎn), court attire (shì cháo zhī fú), Empress's (Huánghòu) crown and attire (guān fú), Crown Prince's (Huáng Tàizǐ) crown and attire (guān fú), attire for imperial relatives (zōng shì) and maternal relatives (wài qī) and first-rank noblewomen (yī pǐn mìng fù), officials' court attire (chén xià cháo fú), sacrificial attire (jì fú), and public attire (gōng fú).
In ancient times, the sages (shèng rén) established the black and yellow, embroidered and embellished robes,
to symbolize the virtues of heaven and earth,
and to distinguish the etiquette of noble and humble.
The Xià (夏) and Shāng (商) dynasties made additions and subtractions,
until the Zhōu (周) dynasty, when they were perfected.
Nothing further could be added.
Since Qín (秦) abolished ritual law,
the systems of the former kings were largely lost and did not survive.
In the early Hàn (漢), they still wore dark robes for grand sacrifices,
and although successive dynasties gradually restored ancient practices,
they were ultimately not pure.
