The Jīn (金) dynasty's Emperor's (Huángdì) attire of *tōngtiān* (通天) crown, crimson gauze robe (jiàng shā páo), ceremonial robe and crown (gǔn miǎn), and *bī xì* (偪舄) shoes,
were remnants of previous dynasties' systems.
His officials had formal attire with sable and cicada ornaments (diāo chán fǎ fú),
which was known as court attire (cháo fú).
During Zhāngzōng's (章宗) reign,
the officials of rites (lǐ guān) requested to consult the Hàn (漢) and Táng (唐) dynasties
to create new sacrificial attire (jì fú):
green upper garment (qīng yī) and crimson lower garment (zhū shang),
removing the sable and cicada ornaments and vertical pens (shù bǐ),
to distinguish it from court attire (cháo fú).
However, for public court (gōng cháo), there were also three grades of attire: purple (zǐ), scarlet (fēi), and green (lǜ),
along with items like narrow purple robes (zhǎi zǐ) and plain black robes (zhǎn zào),
all recorded in this chapter.
In the third year of Tiānjuàn (天眷) (1139),
the responsible officials (yǒu sī), as the imperial carriage was about to travel to Yānjīng (燕京),
needed the *tōngtiān* (通天) crown and crimson gauze robe (jiàng shā páo).
Based on the missing items,
they were manufactured according to the specifications.
Ritual attire (lǐ fú) included:

robe (páo), skirt (shang), square-collar curved lapel (fāng xīn qū lǐng), inner garment (zhōng dān), knee-cover (bì xī), leather belt (gé dài), great belt (dà dài), jade-ornamented sword (yù jù jiàn), sash (shòu), pendant (pèi), shoes (xì), and socks (wà).
For imperial carriage attire (chéng yú fú):
The great sash (dà shòu) had six colors:
black, yellow, red, white, pale blue, green.
The small sash (xiǎo shòu) had three colors,
the same as the great sash,
interspersed with three jade rings (yù huán).
The great sash (dà shòu) had five hundred strings of pearls (shǒu),
the small sash (xiǎo shòu) half of that.
Two white jade pendants (bái yù shuāng pèi), a leather belt (gé dài), and a jade hook buckle (yù gōu pān).
Crown (miǎn) regulations:
The top board (tiān bǎn) was one *chǐ* six *cùn* long,
eight *cùn* wide.
The front was eight *cùn* five *fēn* high.
The back was nine *cùn* five *fēn* high.
The body circumference (shēn wéi) was one *chǐ* eight *cùn* three *fēn*,
including the ear-plugs (nà yán).
All used blue silk gauze (qīng luó) as the outer fabric,
and red silk gauze (hóng luó) as the lining (luó).
Around the circumference, it used golden trim (jīn léng).
Under the top board (tiān bǎn) were four pillars,
with pearl net knots (zhēn zhū wǎng jié zi) on four sides,
and floral and plain tassels (huā sù zhuì zi).
In total, there were twenty-four pearl strings (zhū liú) front and back.
Each string (liú) was one *chǐ* two *cùn* long.
One sky-river belt (tiān hé dài) woven with blue and green threads,
one *zhàng* two *chǐ* long,
two *cùn* wide,
with three sections of pearl, gold, and green strings (zhēn zhū jīn bì liú) at each end,
and jade teardrop-shaped section flowers (yù dī zi jié huā).
Two red thread woven belts (hóng xiàn zǔ dài),
with pearl, gold, and kingfisher feather strings (zhēn zhū jīn cuì liú),
and jade teardrop-shaped section flowers (yù dī zi jié huā) above,
and two small golden bells (jīn duó zi) below.
One plum-red thread sash (méi hóng xiàn kuǎn màn dài).
Two cotton balls (tǒu kuàng),
suspended with pearls.
Above them were two golden [*è*] (ㄜˋ) ornaments.
Two hairpins (zān kē), two sash brooches (kuǎn màn, zǔ dài diàn kē).
Among them, four sash brooches (zǔ dài diàn kē) were carved from jade to represent cloud patterns (yù lòu chén niǎn zào).
One jade hairpin (yù zān),
the top of which was two *cùn* square.
The shaft was one *chǐ* two *cùn* long.
The hairpin top (zān dǐng) was carved with cloud dragons (yún lóng).
The *gǔn*,
made of lined dark blue silk gauze,
painted with five colors interwoven with gold,
has on the front one sun, one moon, four ascending dragons, and twelve mountains.
On the upper and lower lapels are six pairs each of *huáchóng* and fire,
and six pairs each of tigers and *wèi* (long-tailed monkeys).
On the back are one star, four ascending dragons, and twelve mountains,
twelve pairs each of *huáchóng* and fire,
and six pairs each of tigers and *wèi*.
There is one *zhōngdān*,
made of unlined white silk gauze,
with a silk gauze collar, cuffs (*biāo*), and trim (*chèn*).
There is one skirt (*cháng*),
with a band, cuffs (*biāo*), and trim (*chèn*),
made of lined red silk gauze with eight panels,
embroidered with thirty-two *zǎo*, sixteen *fěn*, sixteen *mǐ*, thirty-two *fǔ*, and thirty-two *fú*.
There is one knee-cover (*bìxī*),
with a band, cuffs (*biāo*), and trim (*chèn*),
all made of lined red silk gauze,
embroidered with two ascending dragons.
There is one set of sashes (*shòu*):
The large sash (*dàshòu*) is woven with six colors—red, yellow, black, white, green, and azure—
and backed with red silk gauze. The small sash (*xiǎoshòu*) has three colors,
same as the large sash.
The sash-heads (*shòutóu*) are yellow silk gauze with gold leaf,
interspersed with three jade rings,
all carved with clouds and dragons.
The large sash has five hundred *shǒu* (loops/folds),
and the small sash has half of that.
There is one crimson and white great belt (*dàdài*),
with a yellow silk gauze belt-head (*dàitóu*) with gold leaf,
and twenty-four shell inlay patterns (*diànkē*).
There is one red silk gauze *lèbó*,
and one dark blue silk gauze *mòdài*.
There are two jade pendants (*yùpèi*),
each with one upper, middle, and lower white jade *huáng* (arc-shaped pendant),
and two half-moon pendants.
All are carved with clouds and dragons.
Each has two jade *dīzi* (droplets),
all strung with real pearls.
Gold combs (*bìgōu*), beast-faces (*shòumiàn*), water leaves (*shuǐyè*), rings (*huán*), and studs (*dìng*).
There is one summer belt (*liángdài*),
wrapped in red silk gauze,
with gold thread,
adorned with seven jade geese on top,
one *èwěi* (goose tail) bundle each,
with golden dragons gripping the mouth,
supported by tortoise shell plates to nail the feet.
The slippers (*xī*)
have thick soles,
red silk gauze uppers,
white damask backing,
*rúyì*-shaped toes,
edges lined with yellow silk gauze with gold leaf,
and jade *bírén* (nose-gems) decorated with pearls.
The socks (*wà*) are made of crimson silk gauze with cotton padding.
For grand sacrifices, conferral of honorific titles, and acceptance of imperial seals and credentials (*cèbǎo*),
the *gǔnmiǎn* (ceremonial robe and crown) is worn.
For imperial tours, fasting and purification outside the palace, or presiding in the main hall,
the *tōngtiānguān* (celestial communication crown) and *jiàngshābǎo* (crimson gauze robe) are worn.
The *zhènguī* (state-guarding ceremonial tablet)
is a large *guī* (jade tablet).
On the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month of the ninth year of *Huángtǒng*,
the Ministry of Rites submitted a drawing of the *zhènguī* style to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàichángsì*).
The Grand Ritual Envoy presented it based on the Three Ritual Classics illustrations,
and it was adopted.
In the eleventh year of *Dàdìng*,
the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, following the Rites,
stated:
"The large *guī* (*dàguī*) is three *chǐ* long,
with a *zhōngkuíshǒu* (bellflower-shaped head) on the upper part of the handle (*shū*),
and is worn by the Son of Heaven."
Since the Western Wèi, Suí, and Táng dynasties,
the *dàguī* was one *chǐ* and two *cùn* long,
the same as the *zhènguī*.
The *zhènguī* was meant to pacify the empire,
adorned with symbols of the four guardian mountains.
Now its *guī* conforms to the ancient system,
but there is no *dàguī*.
The imperial treasury now possesses an old Sòng dynasty white jade *guī*,
which is round,
without the upper tapering (*shà*) or *zhōngkuíshǒu*.
Since the Western Wèi dynasty,
all jade tablets (*yùhù*) made were one *chǐ* and two *cùn* long,
square and unbroken.
Although this was not the method of the ancient kings,
it was because jade was difficult to obtain in later generations,
so it was adapted to circumstances.
It is proposed that the one stored in the imperial treasury be used
for ceremonies.
Attire for imperial audience.
Initially,
after Emperor Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he began to wear ochre yellow.
Thereafter, during audiences with officials, he wore an imperial robe and belt.
When Emperor Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
due to the mourning for Emperor Shìzōng,
the authorities requested he wear pure auspicious attire.
He did not comply,
and instead wore a light yellow robe and a rhinoceros horn belt.
For ordinary audiences, he wore a small cap, a red *lán* (robe with deep lapels), and either a *piāndài* (loose belt) or a *shùdài* (tight belt).
Empress's crown and robes.
The *huāzhūguān* (flower-cluster crown)
uses one *shèngzi* (frame),
with a dark blue silk gauze outer layer, a dark blue silk lining, and a red silk gauze backing with gold.
It features nine dragons and four phoenixes.
In front, a large dragon holds one ear-of-grain sphere (*suìqiú*).
There are twelve flower clusters each in the front and back,
along with *xīqú* (mandarin ducks), peacocks, cloud cranes, Queen Mother of the West immortals,
floating and inserted petals, etc.
At the back, there is a *nàyán* (ear-cover), with a golden cicada and two gilded *bóbìn* (sidepieces).
All the above are crafted with kingfisher feathers (*pūcuì*), powdered decoration (*dīfěn*), gold thread (*lǚjīn*), and pearls.
Below, there is a golden band (*jīnquānkǒu*),
adorned with seven-treasure shell inlay patterns (*qībāodiànkē*).
At the back, there are two golden shell inlay patterns,
and one red silk gauze *kuǎnmàndài* (pleated sash) with gold leaf is threaded through.
The *huīyī* (phoenix robe)
is woven from deep dark blue silk gauze into the shape of pheasants (*huīzhái*),
with a plain body,
and twelve grades.
The collar, cuffs (*biāo*), and trim (*chèn*) are all woven with red silk gauze cloud-dragons.
The *zhōngdān* (inner garment) is made of plain dark blue gauze.
The collar is woven with twelve *fǔ* (axe-head) shapes.
The cuffs (*biāo*), sleeves, and trim (*chèn*) are woven with cloud-dragons,
all made of woven red *gǔ* (fine silk).
The skirt (*cháng*)
has eight panels,
woven from deep dark blue silk gauze with six grades of *zhái* (pheasant) patterns.
The cuffs (*biāo*) and trim (*chèn*) are woven with red silk gauze cloud-dragons,
and it has a gleaming gold waist-band.
The knee-cover (*bìxī*)
is woven from deep dark blue silk gauze with three grades of *zhái* patterns.
The collar edge
is woven with purple-black silk gauze cloud-dragons.
There is one gleaming gold-banded grand sash (*dàshòu*),
five *chǐ* long
and one *chǐ* wide,
woven with six colors: yellow, red, white, black, azure, and green.
The small sash (*xiǎoshòu*) has three colors, same as the grand sash,
interspersed with seven-treasure shell inlay patterns,
adorned with three jade rings,
carved with clouds and dragons.
The large and small sash-heads (*shòutóu*) are woven with twisted gold thread,
backed with red silk gauze flowers.
The great belt (*dàdài*)
is dark blue silk gauze with crimson backing (*tuōyè*),
edged on the outside.
The upper part is crimson brocade,
the lower part is green brocade.
The knots are made with dark blue cords (*qīngzǔ*).
The belt-head (*dàitóu*) is woven with twisted gold thread.
There are two sets of jade pendants (*yùpèi*),
each set having one upper, middle, and lower *huáng* (arc-shaped pendant),
and two half-moon drop pendants,
all carved from jade.
There is one each of an etched gold and chiseled beast-face (*shòumiàn*) and comb-hook (*bìgōu*) pendant,
and the *shuǐyèzi* (water leaf pendants) are strung with real pearls.
The dark blue leather belt (*qīngyī gédài*)
is made by wrapping with etched gold dark blue silk gauze,
adorned with chiselled gold water-ground dragons,
goose-eye *èwěi* (goose tails),
and eight items in total including dragon-mouth fastenings,
supported by tortoise shell and gold-nailed feet.
There are two *mòdài* (sashes),
one red silk gauze and one dark blue silk gauze,
both made with gleaming gold,
each one *zhàng* and five *cùn* long.
The slippers (*xī*)
are made of dark blue silk gauze,
with white damask backing,
*rúyì*-shaped toes,
adorned with gleaming gold and yellow silk gauze as above,
with jade *bírén* (nose-gems) decorated with pearls,
and attached with ties.
The socks (*wà*)
are dark blue silk gauze with backing,
and attached with ties.
The rhinoceros horn crown (*xīguān*)
features a reduced pattern of cut-out flowers,
made with etched gold decoration,
with one jade hairpin (*yùzān*) on top,
and one tortoise shell plate (*dàimàobǎn*) below.
The Crown Prince’s cap and robes.
The miǎn (冕) had nine strings of white pearls,
a red silk cord for the yīng (纓),
blue floss filling the ěr (耳),
and a rhinoceros horn hairpin as the dǎo (導).
The gǔn (袞) robe
was blue on top and vermillion on the bottom.
Five auspicious patterns were on the upper garment:
mountains (山), dragons (龍), pheasants (華蟲), fire (火), and sacrificial vessels (宗彝).
Four patterns were on the lower garment:
algae (藻), millet (粉米), axes (黼), and fu (黻) patterns.
A white gauze zhōngdān (中單),
with blue cuffs, collar, and hem.
A leather belt
with gilt-silver hooks and loops.
The bìxī (蔽膝)
matched the color of the skirt
and had the patterns of fire (火) and mountains (山).
A pair of yúzú (瑜玉) jade pendants,
a grand sash woven with four colors,
interspersed with three jade rings.
White socks and
vermillion clogs.
The clogs were adorned with gilt-silver buckles.
This was worn when visiting temples.
The yuǎnyóu guān (遠遊冠)
had eighteen beams,
gilt-silver flowers,
decorations of Mount Bóshān (博山) with cicadas attached,
a red silk cord for the yīng (纓),
and a rhinoceros horn hairpin as the dǎo (導).
The zhūmíng fú (朱明服)
had a red skirt,
a white gauze zhōngdān (中單),
a square-fronted, curved collar,
a crimson gauze bìxī (蔽膝),
white socks, and black clogs.
The rest was the same as the gǔnmiǎn (袞冕).
This was worn during the enfeoffment ceremony.
The huánguī (桓圭)
was nine cùn (寸) long, three cùn (寸) wide, and half a cùn (寸) thick,
made of white jade,
resembling the central pillar of a house (屋之桓楹),
with two ridges.
When the Prince attended court, for daily greetings, or at banquets,
he wore court robes:
a purple robe, a jade belt, and a double-fish pouch.
When he handled official business or met his teachers, junior officials, or guests,
he wore a small cap, a black robe, and a jade sash.
Imperial relatives and maternal relatives, as well as first-rank noblewomen,
were permitted to use bright gold in their clothing.
Even if close relatives lived separately, and daughters had married out, they were treated the same.
Furthermore, mothers and wives of officials of the fifth rank and above
were allowed to wear xiápèi (霞帔).
However, only for headwear, xiápèi (霞帔), collars, sleeves, and waistbands
was the use of bright gold, caged gold, or inlaid gold permitted.
For their clothing, only bright silver, imitation gold, and gold thread embroidery were allowed.
This also applied to officials of the proper administrative bureaus who were on duty,
even if they had not yet been assigned to a specific post but were still part of the bureau system;
their grandmothers, mothers, wives, daughters-in-law, wives of brothers in the same household, and unmarried daughters, granddaughters, and sisters were all included.
Furthermore, the private use of pure yellow curtains and furnishings was forbidden.
If they had previously been granted lúanyú (鸞輿) chariots and official attire,
or sun-moon-cloud shoulder ornaments, yellow robes with dragon patterns, or saddles with five sheath holes, these must all be changed.
Court robes for officials.
All civil and military officials wore these
when accompanying the imperial carriage or performing grand ceremonies.
For the Zheng yīpǐn (正一品) rank: diāochán lóngjīn (貂蟬籠巾),
a seven-beamed éhuā guān (額花冠),
a sable standing brush (貂鼠立筆),
a silver standing brush (銀立筆),
a rhinoceros horn hairpin as the dǎo (導),
a sword,
one crimson silk large-sleeved robe, one crimson silk skirt, one crimson silk bìxī (蔽膝),
a crimson and white silk grand sash,
one tiānxiàlè yùnjǐn yùhuánshòu (天下樂暈錦玉環綬),
one white silk fāngxīn qǔlǐng (方心曲領), one white gauze zhōngdān (中單), one silver-brown lēibó (勒帛),
two jade-pearl pendants,
a gilt-silver leather belt,
black leather shoes,
and white silk socks.
For the Zheng èrpǐn (正二品) rank: a seven-beamed cap,
a silver standing brush,
a rhinoceros horn hairpin as the dǎo (導),
no sword,
a crimson silk large-sleeved robe,
a variegated-flower yùnjǐn yùhuánshòu (暈錦玉環綬),
the rest being the same.
For the Zheng sìpǐn (正四品) rank: [一九] a five-beamed cap,
a silver standing brush,
a rhinoceros horn hairpin,
a white lion brocade silver-ringed sash,
a pearl pendant,
a silver leather belt.
The Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) wore a xièzhì guān (獬豸冠) and a green lotus sash,
the rest being the same.
For the Zheng wǔpǐn (正五品) rank: a four-beamed cap,
a cluster-of-four-gold-eagle brocade copper-ringed sash,
a silver-pearl pendant,
the rest being the same.
For the Zheng liùpǐn (正六品) to Zheng qīpǐn (正七品) ranks: a three-beamed cap,
a yellow lion brocade copper-ringed sash,
a copper-pearl pendant,
[二０] a copper sash,
the rest being the same.
For the jiáxiǎng (祫享) ceremony in Dàdìng (大定) twenty-second year,
the acting officials and those leading the imperial carriage of the second rank wore seven-beamed caps.
Officials of the third and fourth ranks wore six-beamed caps,
and their robes had gold flowers.
Officials of the fifth rank wore five-beamed caps.
Officials of the sixth rank wore four-beamed caps.
Officials of the seventh rank wore three-beamed caps.
The Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史) wore a xièzhì guān (獬豸冠) and a green sash.
[二一] Officials of the eighth and ninth ranks wore two-beamed caps,
the rest of the regulations being the same.
Sacrificial robes.
In Huángtǒng (皇統) seventh year,
the Tàicháng Sì (太常寺) reported:
"After the Tàimiào (太廟) is completed,
and the spirit tablets are enshrined,
when the jiáxiǎng (祫享) ceremony is performed,
all officials who conduct, assist, or accompany the ritual
should, according to classical tradition, wear gǔnmiǎn (袞冕) with nine patterns depicting descending dragons,
with specific distinctions according to rank.
The Tōngdiǎn (通典) states that during the Yú (虞), Xià (夏), and Yīn (殷) dynasties, there were twelve patterns:
the sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, and pheasants were painted on the upper garment,
and sacrificial vessels, algae, fire, millet, axes, and fu (黻) patterns were embroidered on the lower garment.
The Zhōu (周) dynasty moved the three celestial bodies to the banner,
placed the dragon on the mountain,
and placed fire on the sacrificial vessels,
creating robes with nine patterns:
dragons, mountains, pheasants, fire, and sacrificial vessels painted on the upper garment,
[二二] and algae, millet, axes, and fu (黻) patterns embroidered on the lower garment.
'The duke's attire, from the gǔnmiǎn (袞冕) downwards, was like the king's attire;
the marquises' and earls' attire, from the bìmiǎn (鷩冕) downwards, was like the duke's attire.'
Also, in the Later Wèi (魏) dynasty, the emperor wore gǔnmiǎn (袞冕),
and all those participating in the sacrifice wore court robes.
The Kāiyuán Lǐ (開元禮) states that first-rank officials wore nine patterns.
The Wǔlǐ Xīnyí (五禮新儀) states that Zheng yīpǐn (正一品) officials wore a nine-stringed miǎn (冕), a rhinoceros horn hairpin, and blue robes painted with descending dragons.
Now, officials from Biànjīng (汴京) familiar with old rites say
that since Xuānhé (宣和) second year,
first-rank sacrificial robes have had a seven-stringed miǎn (冕) and large sleeves without dragons.
Although the Táng (唐) dynasty used nine-patterned robes,
at that time, Sūn Màodào (孫茂道), the director of ceremonies, said,
'Although the patterns for various officials differ,
robes adorned with dragons are called gǔn (袞) robes, leading to confusion between senior and junior ranks.
It is advisable for the Three Dukes to wear bìmiǎn (鷩冕) with eight patterns.'
We, your humble servants, believe that the dress codes of successive dynasties have differed.
If we follow the Later Wèi, only court robes would be worn.
If we use Sòng (宋) attire, there would be seven patterns.
If we adhere to the Táng (唐) nine patterns,
then there is the argument of confusing senior and junior ranks due to dragon-adorned gǔn (袞) robes."
The Shàngshū Shěng (尚書省) then proposed following the precedent of the Later Wèi dynasty,
using only the court robes worn during the grand enfeoffment ceremony in Yānjīng (燕京) for sacrifices.
In Dàdìng (大定) third year, eighth month,
an edict was issued to follow the Huángtǒng (皇統) system:
acting officials wore court robes,
and sǎnxūn (散官) officials wore formal robes.
The Crown Prince, as the second offerer,
wore gǔnmiǎn (袞冕).
In the fourteenth year,
following the Táng (唐) system,
if it rained or snowed during a sacrifice, common robes were worn,
which are today's formal robes.
In Tàihé (泰和) first year, eighth month,
ritual officials stated:
"Sacrificial robes are for connecting with deities,
and court robes are for serving the sovereign.
Although successive dynasties have made different additions and subtractions,
there has never been a lack of distinction.
Thus, the gǔnmiǎn (袞冕) with twelve strings of pearls,
dark upper garment and crimson lower garment with twelve patterns,
are the sacrificial robes of the Son of Heaven.
The tōngtiān guān (通天冠), crimson gauze robe, and red silk skirt
are the court robes of the Son of Heaven.
Subordinate officials wear blue upper garments and vermillion lower garments for sacrifices,
and vermillion upper garments and vermillion lower garments for court.
In our dynasty, only the Son of Heaven has the two types of attire: gǔnmiǎn (袞冕) and tōngtiān guān (通天冠).
Currently, officials only have court robes,
and sacrificial robes are still lacking.
For every sacrificial event, they merely use court robes,
which is truly inappropriate according to ritual tradition.
We request to follow the precedents of the Hàn (漢) and Táng (唐) dynasties,
with sacrificial robes having miǎnliú (冕旒) and painted patterns.
However, although the number of patterns on the sovereign's and officials' miǎn (冕) robes differ, both are adorned with dragons and called gǔn (袞) robes.
[二三] And Sūn Màodào (孫茂道) of the Táng (唐) dynasty already raised the issue of confusing senior and junior ranks.
Moreover, the ceremonial robes of the Three Dukes having dragons
might imply usurpation,
which the ritual officials at the beginning of the dynasty also debated against.
We implore consideration of both ancient and modern practices,
to reform the sacrificial robes.
The cap would be like the court cap,
but simply remove the sable cicada and standing brush.
The robes would consist of a blue upper garment, vermillion lower garment, white socks, and vermillion shoes.
Those not performing acting duties would use court robes.
This might achieve some distinction."
The Emperor said:
"Indeed, court and sacrificial robes
should be distinguished."
Court Attire.
The *Dàdìng* 官制 (official system)
stipulated that civil officials of the fifth rank and above wore purple robes.

The three grand tutors (*sān shī*), three grand dukes (*sān gōng*), imperial princes (*qīn wáng*), and prime ministers (*zǎi xiàng*) of the first rank wore *dà dú kē huā luó* (great single-flower patterned gauze),
with the diameter of the flowers not exceeding five *cùn*.
Executive officials wore *xiǎo dú kē huā luó* (small single-flower patterned gauze),
with the diameter of the flowers not exceeding three *cùn*.
Second and third rank officials wore *sǎn dā huā luó* (scattered flower patterned gauze),
〔二四〕meaning without branches or leaves,
with the diameter of the flowers not exceeding one and a half *cùn*.
Fourth and fifth rank officials wore *xiǎo zá huā luó* (small mixed flower patterned gauze),
meaning the flower heads were fine and small,
with the diameter of the flowers not exceeding one *cùn*.
Sixth and seventh rank officials wore *fēi zhī ma luó* (scarlet sesame-patterned gauze).
Eighth and ninth rank officials wore *lǜ wú wén luó* (green unpatterned gauze).
All military officials wore purple.
For all *sàn guān* (supernumerary officials) and *zhí shì* (officials with specific duties), their attire followed the highest of their concurrent ranks.
Higher ranks could also wear the attire of lower ranks,
but lower ranks could not usurp the attire of higher ranks.
The *zhǎi zǐ* (narrow purple robe) also conformed to this color scheme,
each according to the official product standard.
Those serving in various bureaus wore unpatterned plain gauze.
A decree in the fifteenth year stated:
"Robes without a hemmed border are not ancient."
Consequently, all civil officials' court robes were ordered to have a hemmed border.
Belt system:
The crown prince (*huáng tàizǐ*) wore a jade belt,
and carried a double-fish jade pouch.
Imperial princes (*qīn wáng*) wore jade belts,
and carried jade fish.
First rank officials wore jade belts,
and carried gold fish.
Second rank officials wore *hú tóu qiú wén jīn dài* (gold belts with mace-head ball patterns),
and carried gold fish.
Third and fourth rank officials wore *lì zhī* (lychee) or *yù xiān huā* (imperial immortal flower) gold belts,
and all carried gold fish.
Fifth rank officials:
those wearing purple wore red black rhinoceros horn belts,
and carried gold fish;
those wearing scarlet wore red black rhinoceros horn belts,
and carried silver fish;
those wearing green wore black black rhinoceros horn belts.
Military officials:
first and second rank wore the same belts,
third and fourth rank wore gold belts,
fifth, sixth, and seventh rank wore red black rhinoceros horn belts,
none of them carrying fish.
Eighth rank and below all wore black black rhinoceros horn belts.
Officials of the *Sī Tiān* (Bureau of Astronomy), *Tài Yī* (Imperial Academy of Medicine), *Nèi Shì* (Directorate of Palace Attendants), and *Jiàofāng* (Music Bureau)
wore attire similar to civil and military officials,
but without carrying fish.
Officials of the fifth rank and below serving in the palace courts
were not allowed gold belts unless entering the inner palace.
Furthermore, those wearing *zhǎn zǐ* (formal purple robes) in the palace courts
were permitted to wear red,
without carrying fish.
Officials of the second rank and above
were permitted to also wear *tōng xī dài* (transparent rhinoceros horn belts).
Third rank officials, when handling affairs or meeting guests,
were permitted to also wear *huā xī dài* (patterned rhinoceros horn belts).
A *Dàdìng* second year decree stipulated
that all officials, when attending court or going to a provincial office,
must wear a wrapped belt.
Officials of the fifth rank and above,
when attending court, wore court attire;
when going to a provincial office, wore *zhǎn zào* (formal black robes).
If rain or snow stained their clothes, they could wear whatever was convenient.
For all court audiences,
the *zhǔ bǎo* (Master of Seals) and *zhǔ fú* (Master of Tallies) wore *zhǎn zǐ* (formal purple robes)
and *yù xiān huā* or *tài píng huā jīn shù dài* (gold sash belts with imperial immortal flower or great peace flower patterns).
Close attendants (*jìn shì gěi shǐ*), those providing imperial brushes and inkstones, *zhí cháng* (officials in charge), and *fú bǎo lì* (tally and seal officials) wore purple jackets,
with gilt sashes.
When on rotation duty,
close attendants (*jìn shì gěi shǐ*) wore their regular attire,
and for regular attire, they wore *zhǎn zǐ*.
〔二五〕The *Gé Mén Liù Shàng* (Six Superior Offices of the Palace Gate),
when attending court and standing by, wore attire appropriate to their rank.
If on duty in the palace, they wore *zhǎi zǐ* (narrow purple robes) and gold belts.

Officials of the *Xuéshì Yuàn* (Hanlin Academy), *Xiū Qǐjū Zhù* (Compilers of the Diaries of Activity and Repose), *Bǔ Quē* (Corrector of Omissions), *Shí Yí* (Remonstrant), *Mìshū Chéng* (Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat), *Mìshū Láng* (Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat),
when attending court and standing by, wore attire and colored belts appropriate to their rank.
When on duty, they wore *zhǎi zǐ* and gold belts.

The *Dōnggōng Zuǒyòu Wèi Shuài* (Commanders of the Left and Right Guards of the Eastern Palace), *Pú Zhèng* (Chief Steward), *Fù Pú Zhèng* (Deputy Chief Steward), *Diǎn Yí* (Ceremonial Officer), *Zàn Yí* (Assistant Ceremonial Officer), and *Nèi Zhí Láng Chéng* (Attendants in the Inner Palace)
were also permitted to wear such attire when on duty.
The *Tàizǐ Tàishī* (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince) wore *zhǎn zǐ* when entering and exiting the palace,
and *zhǎn zào* when at the Eastern Palace.
The *Sān Shǎo* (Three Junior Grandees) wore *zhǎn zǐ*.
Section on Carriages and Clothes: General Regulations on Clothing
The attire of a *jūnzǐ* (gentleman)
should be commensurate with their virtue.
Thus, those whose virtue is complete will have complete embellishment.
In ancient times, kings, dukes, and commoners all had specific, fixed regulations
which they dared not overstep.
This is because the extravagance or frugality of customs,
and the uniformity of laws,
were necessarily observed here.
The *Shī* (Odes) says:
"Those men of the capital,
their fox furs are gleaming yellow.
Their countenance unchanged,
their words are regulated."
Its third stanza says:
"Those men of the capital,
with jasper plugs in their ears.
Those noble women,
are called *Yǐn Jí*."
This speaks of the prosperity of the capital cities
and the excellence of their people.
During the *Míngchāng* period,
Zhāngzōng said to his prime ministers:
"Current customs are extravagant and ostentatious.
Nothing is better than to regulate them with systems and institutions,
so that the noble and humble have their proper distinctions.
Order the *Lǐbù* (Ministry of Rites) to compile precedents and report them."
Another day, he said to the *Cānzhī Zhèngshì* (Participating in Affairs of State) Zhāng Wàngōng:
"How are the customs in *Shāndōng*?"
Wàngōng replied that they were extravagant.
The *Zuǒ Chéng* (Left Assistant) Shǒu Zhēn then spoke of clothing regulations.
The emperor said:
"As you say,
I am just worried about losing popular support."
Shǒu Zhēn said:
"Only merchants might be displeased."
Wàngōng said:
"I beg for a period of grace,
within three years they will certainly conform to the regulations."
Thereupon,
the emperor, finding the *Lǐbù*'s proposal too complex,
implemented what the *Shàngshū Shěng* (Department of State Affairs) had proposed.
Alas,
for a ruler to speak of customs,
he certainly knows what he should prioritize!
The four common garments of the Jīn people were: belt,
headscarf,
round-collared robe,
and black leather boots.
Their belt was called a *tǔhú*.
The system for the headscarf:
it was made of black gauze or fine silk,
tied at the top with a square crown,
and folded to hang down behind.
Below the crown, at each of the two corners, a square piece of gauze about two *cùn* in diameter was attached.
Below each square piece, a ribbon six or seven *cùn* long was attached.
Above the forehead,
it sometimes formed a gathered fold.
For the noble and prominent, the square crown
was adorned with pearls along the cruciform seam.
A larger pearl was always threaded through the center,
called a *dǐng zhū* (crown pearl).
Pearls were strung on each side of the belt, forming knotted ribbons
half the length of the belt,
which hung down.
The one bestowed upon *Dàxīng Guó* by Hǎilíng is an example of this.
The color of their clothes was mostly white.
Third rank officials wore black.
They had narrow sleeves,
round collars,
sewn armpits,
and were gathered at the bottom,
without being divided for trousers.
Their chests, shoulders, and sleeves
were sometimes adorned with gold embroidery.
Their spring hunting attire often featured falcons catching geese
and various floral decorations.
Their autumn hunting attire was patterned with bears, deer, and forests.
Their length reached to mid-calf,
for convenience while riding.
For *tǔhú* belts,
jade was superior,
gold was secondary,
and rhinoceros horn, ivory, bone, and horn were next.
The *kuà* (ornamental plaques) were arranged around the belt,
smaller ones interspersed at the front,
larger ones placed at the back.
There were double tail-like plaques on the left and right,
inserted into square loops.
Their carvings often resembled spring water and autumn mountain decorations.
A plaque was worn on the left,
a knife on the right.
Precious knives were made of *bīn* (a type of steel).
Handles were preferably made of *jī shé mù* (chicken-tongue wood),
half yellow and half black.
Those with black double spurs were considered superior,
or with three or five features.
The scabbard was decorated with *jiàng bàn huà* (soybean-petal birch),
the mouth decorated with sharkskin,
or powdered gold and brass mixed with lacquer,
applied to the sharkskin gaps and smoothed.
*Jiàng bàn huà* refers to
birch bark with mottled patterns of deep purple like soybean petals in soy sauce.
It was produced in their country,
hence it was highly valued.
Initially,
Nǚzhēn people were not allowed to change to Hàn surnames or adopt Southern-style attire.
Violators were punished with eighty strokes of the cane,
and this was made a permanent regulation.
Women wore *chānqún*,
mostly in black or purple.
They were embroidered with full branches of flowers
and had six pleats around the body.
The jacket was called a *tuánshān*,
made of black, purple, or dark blue fabrics.
It had a straight collar,
a left lapel,
and pleated armpits.
The sides also had double pleats.
The front swept the ground,
and the back trailed more than a *chǐ* (foot).
Belts were red and yellow,
with two ends hanging down in front to the hem.
Elderly women covered their hair buns with black gauze, like a turban,
adorning it with scattered jade hairpins
called *yù xiāoyáo*.
These were all Qìdān (遼) clothes,
which the Jīn (金) also adopted.
Engaged women wore *chuòzi*,
made in the same style as women's regular clothing,
in red, silver-brown, or bright gold.
They had an open front and a colorful collar.
The front swept the ground,
and the back trailed more than five *cùn* (inches).
In the sixth year of Míngchāng (明昌), it was decreed that
civil and military officials of the sixth rank and above, those in attendance, and those with inherited ranks
were permitted to use ivory collars,
purple circular tablet black silk sashes,
and black boots.
Higher ranks could use the attire of lower ranks.
Registered scholars were only allowed to wear white shirts with white collars,
with back straps and purple circular silk sashes,
and dry black boots.
Others were allowed to use plain purple collars,
but no decorative edging.
Mixed-color circular tablet silk sashes were not allowed to be purple.
Boots could be yellow, black-oiled, black-waxed, etc.
Women could wear whatever was convenient.
In the fourth year of Tàihé (泰和),
it was observed that since princely and official ranks already differentiated collar edging,
and there was also a prohibition on black boots,
it seemed overly restrictive.
Thus, princes were allowed to use silver-brown collars with purple edging,
and all officials were allowed purple collars with white edging.
Other regulations followed the Míngchāng (明昌) decrees.
Regulations on book bags.
In the sixteenth year of Dàdìng (大定),
Shìzōng (世宗) observed that there was no distinction between the attire of clerks and commoners,
leading to clerks secretly entering common households to accept bribes and manipulate lawsuits,
which officials were unable to detect.
Therefore, the system of wearing book bags was established.
Chiefs of the Secretariat (省), Bureau of Military Affairs (樞密院), and official interpreters (譯史) used purple ramie silk.
Officials of the Censorate (臺), Six Ministries (六部), Court of the Imperial Clan (宗正), Military Command (統軍司), and Surveillance Department (檢察司) used black leather.
Officials of the Nine Courts (寺), Five Directorates (監), various bureaus (局) in attendance at court,
and all prefectures and counties used yellow leather.
Each bag was seven *cùn* long, two *cùn* wide, and half a *cùn* thick.
They were all hung from the belt.
After official duties, they were hung on casual clothes.
Violators would be admonished by the relevant authorities.
In the thirteenth year of Dàdìng (大定),
the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (太常寺) proposed that scholars, Buddhist monks and nuns, and Taoist priestesses with religious titles, as well as minor officials of the eighth rank and above,
be permitted to wear flowered gauze, damask, silk gauze, and silk floss.
Those in official attendance who had entered service and held ranks below the eighth rank,
or who had not yet received official appointments but were qualified,
were permitted to wear flowered gauze, damask, silk gauze, ramie silk, and silk floss.
Their family members were subject to the same rules.
Women were permitted to use pearls for headwear.
The chief *kǒngmù* (孔目) was treated the same as minor officials of the eighth rank.
[二六]Clerks of the imperial capital, prefectures, and counties were treated the same as commoners.
Commoners were only permitted to wear coarse silk, pongee, fine silk, cotton cloth, wool, plain gauze without patterns, and silk floss.
For headscarves, waistbands, and neckerchiefs, they were allowed to use sesame gauze, and sashes woven from floss.

They were not allowed to use gold, jade, rhinoceros horn, ivory, or various precious stones, agate, or glass for utensils, or for decorating knife handles and scabbards, or for silver-mounted beds and couches.
For women's headwear,
pearls, kingfisher feather ornaments, and similar items were not permitted.
Kingfisher feathers were only allowed for decorating floral crowns and hair ornaments.
All other uses were prohibited.
Soldiers were permitted to wear plain pressed gauze, coarse silk, fine silk, cotton cloth, and wool.
Slaves were only permitted to wear coarse silk, fine silk, cotton cloth, and wool.
When entertainers (倡優) were performing for welcomes or official banquets,
they were permitted to temporarily wear painted clothing.
Their private clothing was the same as that of commoners.
Collation Notes
Treatise Twenty-Five: Military (兵), Military System (兵制), Imperial Army (禁軍), Method of Supporting Troops (養兵之法).
When the Jīn (金) rose,
they employed troops like gods,
winning battles and conquering territories,
unrivaled in their time.
In less than ten years, they established a great empire.
Tracing the speed of their success,
their customs were inherently fierce and strong.
Many people were resolute and courageous.
Brothers, sons, and kinsmen were all capable generals.
Tribal units and mutual defense groups were all elite soldiers.
Moreover, the land was small and not very productive;
in peacetime, hard farming provided food and clothing;
in wartime, hard fighting could secure captives and spoils.
They toiled their bodies, enduring heat and cold.
Conscription and deployment were like one family.
Therefore, the generals were brave and united in purpose,
and the soldiers were elite and cohesive in strength.
Once they rose up,
they transformed from weak to strong,
controlling the many with the few—
this was their method.
When they achieved their ambitions in the Central Plains,
they realized their own clan members and people were few.
Thus, they ceded land and bestowed high titles to Hàn (漢) people,
making them serve and guard for them.
Mèng'ān (猛安) and Móukè (謀克) units were interspersed in Hàn (漢) territory,
allowing intermarriage with Qìdān (契丹) and Hàn (漢) people to consolidate ties.
When the national power gradually flourished,
they reclaimed land and abolished titles,
dismissing the Hàn (漢) people and Bóhǎi (渤海) people in Liáodōng (遼東) who had inherited Mèng'ān (猛安) and Móukè (謀克) positions,
gradually returning military authority to their inner clan.
However, the Bureau of Military Affairs (樞府) conscripted and recruited soldiers, also adopting Hàn (漢) systems.
In the campaign against Sòng (宋), Hàn (漢) armies and various tribal groups were used and commanded by Jīn (金) people.
It was not that they did not know the winning strategy lay in generals united in purpose and soldiers cohesive in strength,
but simply that with the territory so vast,
how could they entrust everything to their close kin?
Gradually reaching their peak,
they then worried about the large numbers of their own clan members and people,
accumulating suspicion,
and ultimately destroying themselves.
This led to their strong foundations being eroded,
their pure customs becoming diluted,
generals and commanders becoming estranged,
and soldiers becoming arrogant and lazy.
By the time of their downfall,
the "Loyal and Filial" (忠孝)
armies caused internal strife,
and various mercenary groups brought disaster from outside.
The previously mentioned unity of purpose and cohesion of strength
could no longer be relied upon.
Was this not self-destruction of their family law?
Or is it that this method can be used for a newly founded state,
but not for maintaining a long-lasting empire?
The Jīn (金) gained their country through military power,
and in compiling the Jīn Shǐ (金史) by imperial decree,
the rise and fall, gains and losses of their military system
are particularly highlighted here.
Military systems, horse administration,
and methods of supporting troops recorded in old histories are detailed in this chapter.
In the early years of the Jīn (金),
the people of various tribes had no other corvée duties.
All able-bodied men were soldiers.
In peacetime, they were allowed to farm, fish, hunt, and practice strenuous activities.
When there was an alert, an order was issued within the tribe,
and envoys were sent to various *bóxīn* (孛菫) to conscript soldiers.
All provisions for infantry and cavalry were prepared there.
Their tribal chiefs were called *bóxīn* (孛菫).
When leading troops, they were called Mèng'ān (猛安) or Móukè (謀克),
named according to the number of people under them.
A Mèng'ān (猛安) was a commander of a thousand,
and a Móukè (謀克) was a commander of a hundred.
The deputy of a Móukè (謀克) was called Púlǐyǎn (蒲里衍).
The deputy of soldiers was called Ālǐxǐ (阿里喜).
The number of tribal soldiers initially had no fixed system.
In the second year after Tàizǔ (太祖) ascended the throne,
after defeating Yēlǜ Xièshí (耶律謝十) with two thousand five hundred men,
he first decreed that three hundred households form a Móukè (謀克),
and ten Móukè (謀克) form a Mèng'ān (猛安).
Subsequently, various tribes surrendered,
and the names Mèng'ān (猛安) and Móukè (謀克) were generally used to appoint their chiefs and organize their people.
In the Battle of Chūhé (出河), their army first reached ten thousand,
and the Liáo (遼) could no longer resist.
When the people of Láiliú (來流), Yāshuǐ (鴨水), Tiělí (鐵驪), and Biēgǔ (鱉古) all pledged allegiance,
and Dōngjīng (東京) was pacified,
Shānxī (山西) was subsequently secured.
Internally, they took in surrendered Liáo (遼) and Hàn (漢) soldiers,
and externally, they levied brave men from various tribes.
They once used the Liáo (遼) man Èlǐyě (訛里野) to form one Móukè (謀克) from one hundred thirty northern households.
The Hàn (漢) man Wáng Liù'ér (王六兒) formed one Móukè (謀克) from sixty-five Hàn (漢) households from various prefectures.
Wáng Bólóng (王伯龍) and Gāo Cóngyòu (高從祐), among others, each led their respective units as one Mèng'ān (猛安).
By the second year of Tiānhuì (天會),
after Píngzhōu (平州) was pacified,
Zōngwàng (宗望) feared that mixed customs would inconvenience the populace.
Thus, this system was abolished.
For surrendered people from various tribes, only chief officials were appointed,
and below them, Hàn (漢) official titles were followed.
In the fourth year,
in the campaign against Sòng (宋),
militias from the eight circuits of Yānshān (燕山), Yúnzhōng (雲中), Zhōngjīng (中京), Shàngjīng (上京), Dōngjīng (東京), Liáodōng (遼東), Píngzhōu (平州), and Liáoxī (遼西), and Chángchūn (長春) were mobilized.
They were subordinate to various *wànhù* (萬戶),
and among these *wànhù* (萬戶), some specifically commanded Hàn (漢) armies.
In the fifth year of Huángtǒng (皇統) of Xīzōng (熙宗),
the system of inherited Mèng'ān (猛安) and Móukè (謀克) for Liáodōng (遼東) Hàn (漢) and Bóhǎi (渤海) people was again abolished,
gradually shifting military authority to their own people.
Mèng'ān (猛安) and Móukè (謀克) were then divided into three grades: upper, middle, and lower.
Imperial clansmen were upper,
and others followed in rank.
During the second year of Tiāndé in the reign of Hǎilíng Shùrén,
the jiézhèn of Zhōngjīng, Dōngjīng, Línhuáng, Xiánpíng, and Tàizhōu circuits, as well as the méng’ān móukè, were merged.
The designations of upper, middle, and lower were abolished,
and they were simply called
“Zhū Méng’ān Móukè” (All Méng’ān Móukè).
Following the old system, conscription occurred every other year
to replenish the numbers of the elderly, infirm, and deceased.
When the capital was moved in Zhēnyuán,
the méng’ān of Tàizǔ, Liáo Wáng Zōnggàn, and Qín Wáng Zōnghàn from Shàngjīng Circuit were relocated.
They were combined into Hézā Méng’ān,
along with the méng’ān of Yòu Jiànyì Wūlǐbǔ,
and the clans of Tàishī Xù and Zōngzhèng Zōngmǐn,
and settled in Zhōngdū.
The three state dukes, Wòlún, Héshàng, and Húlà,
Tàibǎo Áng,
Zhànshì Wūlǐyě,
Fǔguó Bólǔgǔ,
Dìngyuǎn Xǔliè,
and the méng’ān of the late Gǎoguó Gōng Bódiēbā, were settled in Shāndōng.
The clan of Ālǔ was settled in Běijīng.
The tribes of Àndá were settled in Héjiān.
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
Shàngshū of the Ministry of War Xiāo Gōng and others were ordered,
along with the old army, to be distributed among the various Zǒngguǎnfǔ and Jiédùshǐ.
They were granted land and oxen to cultivate and subsist,
thereby defending the capital and the nation.
In the sixth year,
during the southern expedition,
three Dūtǒngzhìfǔ and the Zuǒyòu Lǐngjūn Dà Dūdū were established,
commanding thirty-two armies,

named Shéncè, Shénwēi, Shénjié, Shénruì, Shényì, Shényì, Shényǒng, Shénguǒ, Shénlüè, Shénfēng, Wǔshèng, Wǔdìng, Wǔwēi, Wǔ’ān, Wǔjié, Wǔpíng, Wǔchéng, Wǔyì, Wǔruì, Wǔyáng, Wǔyì, Wǔzhèn, Wēidìng, Wēixìn, Wēishèng, Wēijié, Wēiliè, Wēiyì, Wēizhèn, Wēilüè, Wēiguǒ, and Wēiyǒng.
Each army was staffed with one Dūzǒngguǎn, one Fùzǒngguǎn, and one Xúnchásǐ and assistant.
However, the Qìdān along the border feared their wives and children would be plundered by neighboring bandits
and could not be fully mobilized,
so they all rebelled.
Meanwhile, the armored soldiers of Dàmíng returned to welcome and enthrone Shìzōng in Dōngjīng.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
after Wōwò was pacified,
the scattered Qìdān were attached to various méng’ān móukè.
By the third year,
an imperial edict was issued regarding the conscripted soldiers from Hébĕi, Shāndōng, and other circuits:
if both father and elder brother were already serving as armored soldiers,
and a son or younger brother was also an Ālǐxǐ,
fearing that the family would have no able-bodied men left
and agricultural planting would be delayed,
one able-bodied man should be exempted.
A Dīng (indentured servant) should be used to fill the role of Ālǐxǐ.
If there was no Dīng, then within that méng’ān móukè, a wealthy and strong household with a Dīng would be chosen for conscription.
In the thirteenth year,
the Han armies garrisoned on the northeastern border were relocated to the interior.
In the tenth month of the fifteenth year,
Lángzhōng of the Ministry of Personnel Púchá Wùhǔ and ten others were dispatched to travel throughout the land,
to redefine the méng’ān móukè households.
Each móukè household was not to exceed three hundred,
and seven to ten móukè would constitute one méng’ān.
In the seventeenth year,
considering that the remaining Qìdān partisans of the Xīnán and Xīběi Zhāotǎosī had a naturally cruel and defiant temperament,
and fearing they might cause trouble again,
or that in the future there might be border conflicts,
and they would not serve our purpose,
an order was given to relocate them to the Wūgǔlǐshíluǐ Department and the lands of Shàngjīng.
The emperor said to his chancellors:
“The people stationed as border guards in the north,
who endure cold and heat traversing a thousand li annually,
are extremely toilsome.
Even if they have one or two horses or cattle,
once they go, there is no hope of return.
Moreover, their farming season is disrupted, preventing cultivation.
Therefore, I have often ordered you to deliberate
on how to relieve them of this service
and allow them to settle peacefully in their fields.
I wonder what your deliberation has yielded?”
Zuǒchéngxiàng Liángbì replied:
“The northern lands
are unsuitable for cultivation
and cannot sustain long-term garrisons;
hence the need for rotation.”
The emperor said:
“I handle ten thousand affairs daily;
how can I attend to everything?
Since you are prime ministers,
you treat this urgent matter as a trivial one
and offer no suggestions,
which greatly troubles me.
Formerly, Cāncài Zōng repeatedly told me
that if poor households were permanently settled on the border,
and made to cultivate the land,
with the government providing grain,
then the poor would be relieved,
and wealthy households would be spared the burden of rotation,
allowing them to diligently pursue farming.
Such a Zōng could be said to be devoted to the country.
I have often thought about this;
it is advisable to allocate the two Zhāotǎosī circuits, as well as the Wūgǔlǐshíluǐ tribes, Línhuángfǔ, and Tàizhōucircuits, for rotational garrison duties.
Report the detailed numbers,
and I will personally review them.”
In the eighteenth year,
the tribes and cíbù were combined for rotational border guard duty.
In the twentieth year,
since the establishment of méng’ān móukè by the ancestors upon pacifying the realm
had persisted for a long time,
there were disparities in household population and geographical distance.
Furthermore, after Zhènglóng, grants were excessive,
and during Dàdìng, there were also many meritorious individuals whose contributions had not been rewarded.
Therefore, a new regulation was enacted and proclaimed throughout the empire.
Newly appointed officials were ordered to take up their posts.
Within the móukè population, those with official ranks below the sixth grade and those serving in various bureaus
were all to be relocated.
For clan members from the third degree of kinship upwards who wished to accompany them,
a méng’ān could not exceed ten households,
and a móukè could not exceed six households.
An edict allowed border garrison soldiers aged fifty-five or older
to have their sons, or brothers and nephews living with them, take their place.
Those who used slaves as substitutes would be punished.
In the third month of the twenty-first year,
an imperial edict dispatched Dàxīng Yǐn Wányán Dígǔsù to relocate two méng’ān in Héběi Dōnglù.
The emperor said:
“When I first ordered this relocation,
I wanted them to be intermingled with Nǚzhēn households.
After a long period of settlement, they would intermarry naturally
and develop no ill will.
This is a long-term benefit.
Now, the Mǎhé Méng’ān has been settled by intermingling,
which greatly accords with my wishes.
However, the Yáoluòhé Méng’ān has not done so.
Another envoy, Shàngshū of the Ministry of War Zhāng Nàyě, should be dispatched to inspect their land and ensure they reside intermingled.”
In the twenty-second year,
as the military agricultural households in Shāndōng were bordering the frontier,
an order was given to gather them in one place
to enable cooperative sericulture.
Yòuchéngxiàng Wūgǔlún Yuánzhōng said:
“The people of that region consider the land they obtain as their home.
Even if brothers do not live together,
the poor are numerous.”
Cāncài Niángē Wòtèlà said:
“In the old days, even if brothers separated, they still gathered to cultivate.
This is no longer the case.
They should be ordered to adhere to this.”
Furthermore, as the old registers of méng’ān móukè were unclear,
when conscripting soldiers, assigning various duties, and distributing relief,
the numbers were not truly adjusted.
An order was given to enumerate their population
and register them accurately.
In the twenty-third year,
Shàngshū of the Ministry of Punishments Yílā Zào was dispatched to relocate eight móukè from Shāndōng Dōnglù to Héjiān.
For the abandoned lands, the households of Zhàndá Móukè under Tèhēihé Méng’ān in Shāndōng Dōnglù,
and the Xīpǔ Móukè and Shímǔwēnshān Móukè under Yílǐmǐn Wòlúhún Méng’ān, totaling nine villages, were moved to the former lands of Liúsēng and Ānhé Móukè.
The lands of those who had not yet relocated were all barren and bordered by bandits.
Envoys were sent to inquire who wished to relocate,
to identify suitable dwelling places,
and to submit maps.
The emperor once considered the Sùpín and Húlǐgǎi people to be brave and useful,
and Hǎilíng had tried to relocate them but failed.
In the twenty-fourth year, as the lands of Shàngjīngshuài and Húlàwēn were vast and fertile,
Shàngshū of the Ministry of Punishments Wūlǐyě was dispatched to draw money from the treasury to provide travel funds and livestock,
relocating one Sùpín Méng’ān and two Húlǐgǎi Méng’ān (twenty-four móukè) to settle there.
This was likely to increase the troops in Shàngjīng,
which could serve as a reserve in times of urgency.
At this time,
many of the old settlements in Héběi and Shāndōng were frequently relocated and reorganized.
Public land was surveyed and made into property for them.
Each household was given oxen for cultivation.
Armored soldiers were amassed as a defense.
Their authority was greatly enhanced.
Princes were granted the title of Méng’ān,
or newly established ones were specially given names.
Their extravagance was curtailed,
their drinking prohibited,
their horsemanship and archery practiced,
and their rations stored.
Their preparedness was extremely rigorous.
At this time, there were 170 imperial clan households,
202 méng’ān,
1,878 móukè,
and 615,624 households.
The Dìelàbù (which in Chéng’ān three was changed to Tǔlúhún Zháshíhé Jiédùshǐ)
and Tánggǔbù (which in Chéng’ān three was changed to Bùlúhuǒ Zháshíhé Jiédùshǐ)
were the tribal cíbù armies of the Northeastern Circuit.
These two departments comprised five cíbù,
with 5,585 households.
Other tribes like Zǔlǔbù, Wūlúgǔbù, Shíluǐbù, Ménggǔbù, Jìlǔbù, and Bótběnbù were similarly numbered.
The ten cíbù armies of the Northwestern and Southwestern Circuits were:
Sūmóudiǎn Cí, Yēlādū Cí, Gǔdiǎn Cí, Tánggǔ Cí, Xiámǎ Cí, Mùdiǎn Cí, Ménggǔ Cí, Miē Cí, Húdū Cí – nine in total.
Those of other circuits were Hélǎn, Púyǔ, Pósù, Xùpín, Húlǐgǎi, and Yílǎn.
Yílǎn was later abolished.
All were on the outskirts of Shàngjīng.
Some had Zǒngguǎnfǔ established,
others Jiédùshǐ.
During the Míngchāng period of Zhāngzōng,
wishing for people to be skilled in both civil and military arts,
he ordered méng’ān móukè to recommend jìnshì candidates.
They were tested in policy essays and archery
to determine their academic and military ranks.
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Someone presented a diagram of the Eight Formations.
What is its actual nature?
I once reviewed the *Wǔjīng* compiled by Sòng Bái,
which comprehensively records methods of offense and defense,
but many of them are difficult to implement."
Right Chancellor Qīngchén replied:
"Fixed methods in military treatises
are difficult to adapt to changing circumstances.
Our dynasty, when conducting military campaigns, only uses the orthodox (zhèng) and unorthodox (qí) armies.
When facing an enemy, we adapt to changes,
using the orthodox as unorthodox
and the unorthodox as orthodox,
hence we are always victorious."
The Emperor said:
"From ancient times, military operations have never gone beyond the two methods of orthodox and unorthodox.
Moreover, studying ancient military strategies is like learning to play chess.
If one has not internalized them,
attempting to use old formations to engage the enemy
is shortsighted.
If the enemy's response differs from the old formations,
then it will certainly be unsustainable.
However, although the methods described in the *Wǔjīng* are difficult to follow,
knowing them is still better than not knowing them."
During the Tàihé period,
military examinations were also instituted;
their regulations are detailed in the *Xuǎnjǔ Zhì*.
The so-called Bóhǎi Army
was the army of the eight *mèng'ān* from Bóhǎi.
The so-called Xī Army
was the army of the nine *mèng'ān* of the Xī people, Yáoliǎn Zhāogǔyá.
The Xī Army was initially moved to Shānxī,
and later relocated in parts to Hédōng.
The Hàn Army's Zhōngdū Yǒnggù Army
was established during the Dàdìng period.
The so-called Zhènfáng Army
was selected from various armies to serve rotational garrison duty on the frontier.
On the northwest frontier, there were also distinctions between Fēnfān Túnshù Army, Yǒngtún Army, and Qū Army.
The Qū Army was composed of Líao people's former slaves and servants,
who were exempted from servitude at the beginning of the dynasty and stationed in Tàizhōu.
The Biānpù Army consisted of those from Hénán and Shǎnxī who guarded the border.
The Hédōng Sān Yúhòu Shùndé Army and the various circuit Xiàojié Armies established by Zhāngzōng,
(thirty men were stationed in the capital prefectures and military garrisons,
twenty men in commanderies and inspectorates.)
were in charge of the same duties as archers.
The Shèliáng Army recruited from various circuits
was registered every five years, and strong men aged between thirty and seventeen
were all tattooed on their faces,
so they could also perform miscellaneous duties.
The Jīngshī Fángchéng Army (Capital City Defense Army)
was renamed Wǔwèi Army in the third month of the seventeenth year of Shìzōng's Dàdìng reign,
and was responsible for patrolling and apprehending criminals in the capital.
The Láochéng Army
was composed of those who had committed theft,
assigned to duties of defense and construction.
The Tǔbīng
were responsible for policing and arrest.
As for the Hàn Army,
when there was an emergency, soldiers were conscripted from the populace;
once the matter was resolved, they were sometimes discharged.
Initially,
during the Tiānhuì period,
when Guō Yàoshī surrendered,
there was a "Chángshèng Army"
whose members were all from the vicinity of the Liáo River.
Because their homeland returned to Jīn,
they were all sorrowful and yearned to return home,
so Zōngwàng ordered them to be dismissed and sent back.
[一０]During the Zhènglóng period,
the Hàn Armies of various circuits were also disbanded,
but those that remained still bore the names of Wēiyǒng, Wēiliè, Wēijié, Shùndé, and
"Hán Cháng's Army."
There were thirty-eight prefectures where troops were stationed on the border:

Fèngxiáng, Yán'ān, Dèng, Gǒng, Xī, Sì, Yǐng, Cài, Lǒng, Qín, Hé, Hǎi, Shòu, Táng, Shāng, Táo, Lán, Huì, Jīshí, Zhènjūn, Bǎo'ān, Suídé, Bǎodé, Huán, Jiā, Ào, [一一]Níngbiān, Dōngshèng, Jìng, Qìng, Lái yuǎn, Huán, Chāng, Gélǎn, Pó Sù, Pú Yǔ, Xùpǐn, Húlǐgǎi.
Eleven prefectures were stationed in key regions:
Nánjīng, Dōngjīng, Yìdū, Jīngzhào, Tàiyuán, Líntáo, Línhuáng, Fēng, Tài, Fǔ, Gài.
When Xuānzōng later moved south,
the disaffected troops dispersed,
and military strength further weakened.
Consequently, all the old and young members of the *mèng'ān* households were moved across the river,
and temporary *zǒngguǎnfǔ* were established to govern them.
With weapons lacking
and rations insufficient,
the people's wealth was drained without meeting the need.
Thus, the method of "appropriating grain" was implemented,
where one person going to war
meant the entire family awaited sustenance.
It was also said that there was no way to strengthen the soldiers' morale,
so their families were all ordered to move into the capital.
Within a few years, they had no food,
so they were allowed to leave,
and the state also collapsed.
However, when they first moved south,
all thirty thousand veteran soldiers from Héshuò were divided and assigned to the Hénán Xíngshūmì and *shuàifǔ*.
Often, the strong were concealed,
and the weak were forced to fight,
making it impossible to achieve victory.
Later, they even made twenty-five men a *móukè*
and four *móukè* a *mèng'ān*.
For each *móukè*, five men were assigned to the flag-drum, supply, and fire-stoker duties,
leaving only eighteen men to fight.
This was insufficient to form a proper unit,
but merely served to preserve the name.
Therefore, Liú Qí of Hùnyuán considered Jīn's military system most flawed.
Whenever there was a campaign or border conflict,
an order for conscription would be issued,
causing unrest far and wide.
If all adult males in a family were strong,
they might all be taken without exception,
their cries of lament stirring the neighbors,
and grievances filling the roads.
To send these to battle
and expect them to defeat the enemy
was difficult.
Initially,
during the Zhēnyòu period,
an order for conscription was issued.
At that time, those serving as *jiāndāng* (supervisors) were going to the Ministry of Personnel for selection in the spring.
The chancellors ordered them to be taken as *jiānguānjūn* (supervising military officers).
[一二]All of them, enraged and wailing, appealed collectively to the Imperial Censorate and the Secretariat-Chancellery,
even crashing into the chancellor's retinue to make their complaints.
Chancellor Púsàn Qījīn was furious
and ordered his attendants to take bows and arrows and shoot them away.
Afterward,
the Emperor, knowing they were unusable,
ordered their exemption.
At the end of Yuánguāng,
when preparing for the Tóngguān and Yellow River defense,
troops were again conscripted.
The various envoys traveled through counties and cities,
and apart from those already holding official positions,
all civil and military officials, regardless of rank, were drafted into the army.
Upon reaching Xǔzhōu,
former Imperial Censor Liú Yuánguī, nearly sixty years old,
was also selected as a *qiānhù*.
Upon reaching Chénzhōu,
Qí's father, Cóngyì, formerly an Investigating Censor, was also made a *qiānhù*;
the rest cannot all be enumerated.
Once military units were established,
they were inevitably subjected to military law.
Public opinion was chaotic,
and later this was also abolished.
In the second year of Āizōng's Zhèngdà reign,
it was proposed to select elite troops from various circuits
and place them directly under the Privy Council.
First, six Chief Commanders (*Zǒnglǐng*) were appointed,
who were to inspect the various circuits and then combine the troops.
Each Chief Commander's office commanded tens of thousands of men.
Once the military strength expanded,
the title of Chief Commander was changed to Commandant (*Dūwèi*),
whose rank was among the fourth rank officials in court,
named Jiànwēi, Hǔwēi, Pòlǔ, Zhènwēi, Yīngyáng, Hǔbēn, Zhènwǔ, Zhéchōng, Dàngkòu, Tiǎnkòu.
[一三]These positions had to be filled by those who had previously held command authority;
even the *shuàifǔ* and *xíngyuàn* dared not impose their authority due to their high status.
In the first year of Tiānxīng,
there were fifteen Commandants.
[一四]Six men were first promoted:
Jiànwēi Àotún Wòlǐbǔ in the capital,
Zhéchōng Jiágǔ Zé in Xǔzhōu,
(originally named Fán.)
Zhènwǔ Wēnsà Xīn in Chénzhōu,
(originally named Lǐ.)
Dàngkòu Púchá Dájíbǔ in Càizhōu,
Shēn Yù'ānpíng Wányán Xiéliè,
Sōngrǔ Zhènwǔ Tángkuò Hánsēng.
Subsequently, Húwēi Gésíliè Qí'ér of Jīnchāngfǔ was ennobled,
Guīdé Guǒyì Wányán Zhū'ér of Xuánquán,
and Tiǎnkòu Wányán Āpāi of Nánjīng.
There were three Xuánquán Tóngguān Commandants: Hǔbēn Wányán Chén'ér, Yīngyáng Nèizú Dàlóushì, and Quánjié.
Furthermore, loyalists (*Guīzhèngrén*) from various Héshuò circuits were again recruited,
regardless of whether they had horses or could speak the language,
all were sent to the Privy Council,
their monthly pay was tripled compared to other armies,
and they were given government horses.
Over a thousand people were recruited,
feasted annually,
and named the Zhōngxiào Army (Loyal and Filial Army).
Shímò Yānshānnú and Púchá Dìngzhù commanded them.
In addition, those captured from various circuits after Zhèngdà and those seized in battle
were all released to their homelands,
and received rewards similar to the Zhōngxiào Army,
so that captives from Héshuò would know about it.
Thus, this army eventually reached seven thousand by Tiānxīng,
and generals above the *qiānhù* rank were not included.
As the number of loyalists was too great,
they were separately organized into another army under the Zhōngxiào register,
receiving half the pay of the Zhōngxiào Army.
Those who could not shoot were trained for one or two months,
and then tested for recruitment into the Zhōngxiào Army.
This was called the Hélǐhé Army.
Furthermore, the Imperial Guard cavalry,
whose selection in the past was not rigorous,
were required to undergo further inspection and testing.
Five thousand men whose martial skills were equal to those of the Zhōngxiào Army were selected,
and the rest were discharged to become infantry.
When advancing on a campaign,
the Zhōngxiào were at the front,
followed by the cavalry.
Since the Zhèngdà era, the cavalry was reorganized;
their formations, saddles, bridles, armor, and weapons were all renewed.
The old generals and ministers claimed that during the nation's heyday, there were indeed many horses,
however, regarding the elite nature of the soldiers and the sturdiness and order of their weaponry,
compared to today, there are discrepancies.
The period of restoration is indeed promising.
One day, they were arrayed at the drill ground inside Cáomén:
seven thousand Zhōngxiàojūn,
five thousand cavalry,
ten thousand Jiànwēi Dūwèijūn stationed in the capital,
three thousand Imperial Guard troops commanded by the nine inner clans,
and four thousand commanded by Āpái.
All were selected when Āizōng controlled the Shūmìyuàn.
The drill ground, approximately thirty qǐng, still could not contain them,
and the remaining thirteen or fourteen Dūwèi armies were not included in this count.
In addition,
volunteer armies were recruited and named Zhōngyì.
They were mostly vagrants from Yān and Zhào.
Although they were used for immediate purposes,
they were ultimately uncontrollable.
Later, it was this group that unauthorizedly killed Táng Qìng, the northern envoy, thus hastening the demise of Jīn.
The system of the Imperial Army
originally stemmed from the Hézhá Móukè.
Hézhá
means "Imperial Guard,"
because they were led by close relatives,
hence the name.
When the capital was moved in the Zhēnyuán era,
the armies of Tàizǔ, Liáo Wáng Zōnggàn, and Qín Wáng Zōnghàn were reorganized into Hézhá Měngān,
〔一五〕and called Shìwèi Qīnjūn (Palace Guard).
Thus, the Shìwèi Qīnjūn Sī was established to command them.
Previously, talented and brave individuals from various armies were regularly selected to form the Hùjiàjūn (Escort Army).
Hǎilíng also renamed the Lóngxiángjūn of Shàngjīng as Shényǒngjūn.
In the second year of Zhènglóng, when planning to campaign south,
these were dismissed and returned,
and made subject to general conscription.
Then, from the four Měngān of the Shìwèi Qīnjūn (formerly, there were only three Měngān: Tàizǔ, Liáo Wáng, and Qín Wáng;
now called four Měngān—
it is unclear why;
could it be two Měngān of Tàizǔ?),
within,
1,600 men under the age of thirty were selected.
Cavalry were called Lóngxiáng,
and infantry were called Hǔbù,
to serve as palace guards.
In the fifth year,
the Qīnjūn Sī was abolished,
and its responsibilities were transferred to Dàxīng Fǔ.
The Zuǒyòu Xiāoqí (Left and Right Elite Cavalry) were established,
these were the so-called Cóngjiàjūn (Retinue Army).
A Dū Fù Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief and Deputy Commander) was appointed under the Diǎnjiǎn Sī,
and a Bùjūn Dū Fù Zhǐhuīshǐ (Infantry Commander-in-Chief and Deputy Commander) under the Xuānhuī Yuàn.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
the Imperial Guard consisted of 4,000 men.
In the twenty-second year,
they were reduced to 3,500.
A garrison army was also established in Shàngjīng.
In that year,
the Shàngshū Shěng memorialized that since a Huángchéng Tíjué Guān (Imperial City Supervising Official) had been established in Shàngjīng,
an army should also be established for its defense.
The Emperor said:
"Four hundred and fifty men may be established,
with 120 horses,
divided into three shifts for rotation.
When I arrive in Shàngjīng at a later time,
it will immediately become two shifts for patrol and guard,
with a half-year rotation limit.
Each person will be given fifty coins and one and a half shēng of rice daily.
Horses will be provided with fodder and grain.
Měngān and Móukè officials should be those around forty years old, and soldiers should all be over thirty years old to fill these positions."
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān of Zhāngzōng,
they were increased to five thousand,
and later increased to six thousand.
There was also the Wēijiéjūn.
During Chéng'ān, one thousand crossbowmen were added.
For the system of selecting crossbowmen,
first, a measuring staff,
six chǐ long,
was used; standing upright, it was called the Děngzhàng.
One's height had to be equal to the staff,
they must be able to cock a crossbow with a draw weight of three shí,
and be proficient in stringing, unstringing, cocking, and drawing the bow,
and hit the target with all six arrows,
with two arrows hitting the bullseye.
Furthermore, for the selection of the Imperial Guard,
individuals five chǐ five cùn tall who were skilled in horsemanship and archery were chosen.
Měngān and Móukè would submit their names to the Bīngbù,
and the Diǎnjiǎn Sī and Xuānhuī Yuàn would test and appoint them.
Additionally, two hundred Hùwèi (Guards) were established;
these were close attendants who carried weapons.
Selected from the descendants of fifth to seventh-rank officials, as well as imperial clan members, Imperial Guard, and personnel from various bureaus,
those who were five chǐ six cùn tall
were selected, tested, and appointed.
Two hundred Kònghè (Crane Control) personnel were also established,
all for readiness during imperial comings and goings.
Titles for the administration of the Dàjiàngfǔ (Grand General's Headquarters).
In the twelfth month of the first year of Shōuguó,
the Xiánzhōu Jūnshuài Sī was first established
to manage the Liáo territory
and suppress Gāo Yǒngchāng.
The Nánlù Dūtǒng Sī (Southern Route Commander's Office) was established,
also to suppress Zhāng Jué.
In the fifth year of Tiānfǔ, when attacking the Liáo ruler,
the title Nèi-wài Zhūjūn Dūtǒng (Commander-in-Chief of All Armies, Internal and External) first appeared.
At that time, since the Xī had not yet been pacified,
the Xī Lù Dūtǒng Sī (Xī Route Commander's Office) was also established.
Later, it was changed to the Liùbù Lù Dūtǒng Sī (Six Departments Route Commander's Office).
The nine camps of Yáoliǎn were made into nine Měngān and subordinated to it.
A total of six such establishments were made, including Shàngjīng and Tàizhōu.
Each office commanded fifty to sixty thousand men.
The Bóhǎijūn were also formed into eight Měngān.
Above the Měngān, a Jūnshuài (Military Commander) was placed.
Above the Jūnshuài, a Wànhù (Myriad-Family Commander) was placed.
Above the Wànhù, a Dūtǒng (Commander-in-Chief) was placed.
However, at times, the Jūnshuài was also referred to as Měngān,
and the Měngān were referred to as Qīnguǎn Měngān (Personally Administered Měngān).
After Yānshān was captured,
following the Liáo system, a Shūmìyuàn was established in Guǎngníng Fǔ
to command the Hàn troops.
In the first year of Tiānhuì of Tàizōng,

the Xīnán Dūtǒng Fǔ (Southwest Commander's Office), established during the attack on the Liáo ruler, was changed to the Xīnán and Xīběi Liǎnglù Dūtǒng Fǔ (Southwest and Northwest Two Routes Commander's Offices).
In the third year,
due to the campaign against Sòng, it was further changed to the Yuánshuài Fǔ (Marshal's Office),
with a Yuánshuài (Marshal) and Left and Right Deputies,
and Left and Right Jiānjūn (Supervising Generals),
and Left and Right Dūjiān (Chief Supervisors).
Under the Jīn system,
the Dū Yuánshuài (Grand Marshal) must be held by an Ānbǎnbòjíliè,
who would remain in defense and not go out.
In the sixth year,
an imperial edict ordered the two Marshals to return and guard their respective regions.
Each route established a Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn Fǔ (Military Affairs Commander-in-Chief Office).
Prefectures and towns established Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioners).
Border prefectures established Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioners).
For the Shèliángjūn (Archers Receiving Rations) and Láochéngjūn (Fortress Garrison Army) recruited by prefectures,
every five hundred men formed one Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī (Commandery).
With a Shǐ (Commander) appointed,
and divided into four Dū (divisions).
Each Dū had Left and Right Shíjiàng (Squad Leaders) and Chéngjú Yāguān (Bureau Custodian Officials).
If the number of troops was in excess or insufficient,
they were combined with nearby units.
If they could not be combined, three hundred or two hundred men would also have a Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander).
If one hundred men, only a Jūnshǐ (Military Agent) would be appointed.
Over a hundred men would form a Dū (division).
Less than a hundred men would only have one Shíjiàng and one Chéngjú Guǎnyāguān (Bureau Custodian Official) each.
In the tenth year,
the Nánjīng Lù Dūtǒng Sī was changed to the Dōngnán Lù Dūtǒng Sī,
governing Dōngjīng to guard against Gāolì.
Later, a Tǒngjūn Sī (Military Command Office) was established in Dàmíng Fǔ.
In the eighth month of the second year of Tiāndé of Hǎilíng,
the Zhūjīng Bīngmǎ Dū Bùshǔ Sī (Military Affairs Chief Deployment Offices of Various Capitals) were changed to Běnlù Dū Zǒngguǎn Fǔ (Route Commander-in-Chief Offices).
In the ninth month,
the Dàmíng Tǒngjūn Sī was abolished,
and Tǒngjūn Sī were established in the three routes of Shānxī, Hénán, and Shǎnxī.
With Dūjiān and Jiānjūn from the Yuánshuài Fǔ serving as Shǐ (Commissioners),
to separately command the armies of the realm.
The Wūgǔdíliè Lù Tǒngjūn Sī was changed to the Zhāotǎo Sī (Pacification Office).
And the Pósu Lù Tǒngjūn Sī was changed to the Zǒngguǎn Fǔ (Commander-in-Chief Office).
In the third year,
the Yuánshuài Fǔ was changed to the Shūmìyuàn,
and the office of Wànhù (Myriad-Family Commander) was abolished.
An imperial edict stated:
"When Tàizǔ founded the dynasty,
he adapted to circumstances.
Those capable of leading the multitude were granted the title of Wànhù,
followed by Qiānhù (Thousand-Family Commander) and Móukè.
At that time, official rewards were not yet fixed,
and cities and fortresses had not yet been subjugated.
Establishing this office and allowing it to be hereditary
was a temporary expedient,
not a long-term benefit.
Now, their descendants successively [一六] monopolize authority.
Their households number no less than tens of thousands.
They are no different from Liúshǒu (Resident Commanders) and Zǒngguǎn (Commander-in-Chiefs),
and their hereditary power surpasses them.
This office may be abolished.
If there were previously no Qiānhù positions,
we will continue to consider adding them.
In the early days of the dynasty, imperial surnames were granted.
If they are descendants, they are all ordered to revert to their old surnames."
Late in the Zhènglóng period,
the Shǎnxī Tǒngjūn Sī (Shaanxi Military Commanderate) was again elevated to a Dūtǒng Fǔ (Commander-in-Chief's Bureau).
In the fifth year of Dàdìng,
the bureau was again abolished,
and downgraded to a Tǒngjūn Sī.
Soon after, two Zhāotǎo Sī (Pacification Commissionerates) were established,
making a total of three with the previous one,
to guard the frontier.
The one for the northeast route
was initially established in the Wūgǔ Díliè (Wugu Dilie) tribe,
and later moved to Tàizhōu.
During the Tàihé period,
as it was still three hundred *lǐ* from the border,
Zōnghào then ordered a branch office to be set up at Jīnshān.
The one for the northwest route was established in Yìngzhōu,
and the one for the southwest route in Huánzhōu.
〔一七〕Important officials skilled in military affairs were made envoys.
Castles and moats were established,
and garrison duty was made a permanent system.
Whenever the Shūmìyuàn (Privy Council) deployed troops, it would be renamed Yuánshuàifǔ (Marshal's Bureau);
when the troops were withdrawn, it would revert to the council.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu of Xuānzōng,
five thousand garrison troops from Dàizhōu were levied,
and following Xū Dǐng's advice,
they were kept in Dài to screen Píngyáng.
In the second year of Xīngdìng,
two thousand crossbowmen were selected and recruited from Hénán and Shǎnxī to form one army,
and granted the title "Wēiyǒng" (Mighty and Brave).
When the capital moved south,
nine dukes were enfeoffed in Héběi,
and using their troops, they were given discretion to handle affairs as they saw fit.
Along the Yellow River, various cities established Xíng Shūmìyuàn Yuánshuàifǔ (Branch Privy Council Marshal Bureaus);
the larger ones had
the title of "Biànyí" (Expedient),
and
the smaller ones had
the name of "Cóngyí" (Adaptable).
During the Yuánguāng period,
at that time, righteous armies were recruited, with thirty men forming a Mókè (Moke),
five Mókè forming a Qiānhù (Chiliarchy),
four Qiānhù forming a Wànhù (Myriarchy),
four Wànhù forming a Fùtǒng (Deputy Commander),
and two Fùtǒng forming a Dūtǒng (Commander).
This was a return to the names from the early days of the state.
However, an additional Zǒnglǐng Tíkòng (Overall Supervisor and Controller) was set up externally,
so at that time, all marshals were referred to as Zǒnglǐng.
In the early Jīn dynasty, Qúnmù (Herding Agencies) were established following the Liáo dynasty's system of "Mò" (Mo).
"Mò" refers to a place free of mosquitoes and gnats, with excellent water and grass.
During the Tiāndé period,
five Qúnmù Suǒ (Herding Stations) were established: Díhé Wò’è, Wòlǐbǎo (Bǎo also written as Běn), Púsùwò, Yàn'ēn, and Wùzhě.
All retained their old Liáo names,
and each was staffed with officials to manage them.
Furthermore, from among people of various backgrounds,
those with wealthy families and many able-bodied men, children of officials, Púliǎn troops of Mèng'ān Mókè, surplus able-bodied men from clerical families, and slaves were selected
to manage the herding,
and were called Qúnzǐ (Herders).
They were tasked with herding horses, camels, cattle, and sheep,
and rewards and punishments for breeding, increase, decline, and loss were established for them.
Later, their number was gradually increased to nine.
Five of them were lost during the Qìdān rebellion;
of the four remaining stations, there were only over a thousand horses, over two hundred eighty cattle, eight hundred sixty sheep, and ninety camels.
Shìzōng established seven stations,
named Tèmǎn, Tèmǎn (located in Fǔzhōu),
Wòdǔzhǐ, Púsùwàn (Púsùwàn was originally part of Wòdǔzhǐ,
and was established by partitioning its land in the seventh year of Dàdìng.
In the third year of Chéng'ān, it was renamed Bǎndǐ Yīnwūlǔgǔ),
Ōulǐběn (In the third year of Chéng'ān, it was renamed Wūxiān Wūlǔgǔ.
Wūlǔgǔ means prolific reproduction),
Hélǔwàn, and Yélúwàn
(located at the borders of Wǔpíng Xiàn, Línhuáng, and Tàizhōu).
In the third month of the twentieth year of Dàdìng,
regulations for Qúnmù officials, Xiángwěn Tuō’è, 〔一八〕Zhībǎ, and Qúnmù personnel regarding rewards and punishments for increase, decrease, loss, and damage were revised.
In the twenty-first year,
an imperial decree ordered all stations
to assign three-year-old horses to Nǚzhēn people for herding.
Cattle could either be lent to commoners for plowing,
or commoners could be ordered to raise sheep,
or they could be used to relieve poor households.
At that time, envoys were sent to inspect the actual numbers;
if there was a deficiency, the official would be flogged,
and the herder ordered to compensate.
Those who concealed the actual numbers would be reported by the Jiānchá (Censorate).
In the twenty-eighth year,
