after a long period of breeding,
the number of horses reached 470,000,
cattle 130,000,
and camels 4,000.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
geldings were distributed,
and people in Zhōngdū, Xījīng, and the eastern and western Héběi routes were ordered to raise them based on their material capacity.
People in other routes who raised horses,
if a horse died, would be given a replacement from those raised in the aforementioned four routes.
If they wished to use them, they were all to be sent to the government.
This was the Jīn's horse policy.
However, whenever there was a major campaign,
horses would invariably be requisitioned from the common people,
and surplus cavalry from officials would be taken
to supply the warriors.
In the first year of Xīngdìng of Xuānzōng,
regulations were established for commoners recovering lost horses from defeated armies,
and for sending horses to the government for compensation:
"For a top-grade horse, fifty *liǎng* of silver;
middle and lower grades decreasing by ten *liǎng* respectively.
For those unwilling to accept compensation,
two top-grade horses compensate for one official position,
to be employed in miscellaneous ranks;
three middle-grade horses,
or four lower-grade horses,
likewise.
Report within ten days of the order;
concealing or killing after the deadline
will both result in hanging."
Officials were also dispatched to requisition horses from market-goers,
and reward regulations were established to encourage this:
one thousand *guàn* of paper currency for five hundred horses or more,
one official position for one thousand horses or more,
two official positions for two thousand horses or more.
Methods for supporting the army.
In the first month of the third year of Tiānjuàn of Xīzōng,
an edict ordered annual provisions of silk and satin to garrison soldiers in Liáodōng, varying according to rank.
In the fourth year of Zhènglóng,
the Hénán and Shǎnxī Tǒngjūn Sī, along with the Yúhòu Sī and Shùndé Jūn (Shunde Army), were ordered
to increase rations for both officials and soldiers.
In the sixth year,
intending to campaign south,
ten thousand bolts of silk were exchanged in the capital for ten thousand padded jackets and knee protectors,
to be distributed to the army.
In the third year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng,
during the southern campaign,
soldiers' annual expenses could reach ten million *guàn*,
while the government only had two million *guàn*.
The remainder had to be taken from official and common households;
this was the origin of the army's need for money.
At that time, those who spoke on affairs
suggested that in the routes of Shāndōng, Hénán, and Shǎnxī, following the old practices of Sòng and Qí,
county clerks and bowmen levied money from the common people based on their material capacity,
named "Miǎnyì" (Exemption from Corvée),
and requested that this money be used to support the army.
By this time,
the department presented the detailed figures,
and an imperial edict abolished the "bowmen's money,"
while the "clerks' money" remained as before.
In the sixth month of the fourth year,
a memorial was submitted,
stating that the Yuánshuàifǔ requested military funds.
The Emperor said:
"The Marshal's Bureau spends without limit,
and habitually levies from the common people,
which is greatly against my will.
Instruct the accountants to determine the unspent amount of military expenditures,
and if there is a real shortage in the various routes' Zhuǎnyùn Sī (Transport Agencies) present funds,
then report it separately."
In the fourth month of the tenth year,
Déshùn Zhōu was ordered to construct barracks to house the garrison troops.
In the seventh month of the seventeenth year,
thirty thousand sheepskins were annually bestowed upon the garrison troops of the northwest route.
In the third year of Chéng'ān,
due to the enormous cost of military supplies,
a request was made to levy taxes uniformly based on the material capacity of the whole empire.
It was proposed to levy military funds according to the precedent of the Huánghé Fū Qián (Yellow River Laborer Money):
levy military funds,
based on the material capacity in the new registers of each route,
four *guàn* of money for every *guàn* (of assessed value).
Xījīng, Běijīng, and Liáodōng routes were to levy two *guàn* of money for every *guàn*.
Línhuáng and Quánzhōu were exempt from the levy.
Payments were due in three installments over a year.
Fearing the period was too long,
it was then decided to implement a system of three installments within half a year.
Regulations for rewarding retired **qiānhù**, **móukè**, **púlián**, regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**), and **ālíxǐ** from **Hénán**, **Shǎnxī**, and **Shāndōng**:
Old regular soldiers who served as **qiānhù** for ten years or more are awarded fifty taels of silver and thirty bolts of silk.
If they served less than ten years,
they are to be treated like **móukè** who served ten years or more.
**Móukè** who served ten years or more are awarded forty taels of silver and twenty-five bolts of silk.
If they served less than ten years, they are awarded thirty taels of silver and twenty bolts of silk.
**Púlián** who served ten years or more are awarded thirty taels of silver and twenty bolts of silk.
If they served less than ten years, they are awarded twenty taels of silver and fifteen bolts of silk.
For regular cavalry and infantry soldiers (**mǎbù zhèngjūn**), **ālíxǐ**, etc., regardless of years of service,
retired regular soldiers are awarded fifteen taels of silver and ten bolts of silk.
**Ālíxǐ**, flag-bearers and drummers (**qígǔ**), flutists (**chuīdí**), and mess hall cooks (**běnsī huǒtóurén**) are similarly awarded eight taels of silver and five bolts of silk.
For the three **Yúhòu** **qiānhù**:
Those who served ten years or more are awarded forty taels of silver and twenty-five bolts of silk.
If they served less than ten years, they are awarded thirty taels of silver and twenty bolts of silk.
**Móukè** who served twenty years or more are awarded fifty taels of silver and thirty bolts of silk.
Those who served ten years or more are awarded thirty taels of silver and twenty bolts of silk.
If they served less than ten years, they are awarded ten taels of silver and fifteen bolts of silk.
**Púlián** who served ten years or more are awarded twenty taels of silver and fifteen bolts of silk.
If they served less than ten years, they are awarded fifteen taels of silver and ten bolts of silk.
For regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) and **ālíxǐ**, regardless of years of service,
retired regular soldiers are awarded ten taels of silver and seven bolts of silk.
**Ālíxǐ**, flag-bearers and drummers (**qígǔ**), flutists (**chuīdí**), and mess hall cooks (**běnsī huǒtóurén**) are similarly awarded five taels of silver
and four bolts of silk.
For **wànhù**, **qiānhù**, **móukè**, etc., in the northern region:
Regulations for awards upon completing military merits or retirement due to old age:
(Promotions are handled in accordance with the regulations of the Ministry of Personnel.)
A regular **qiānhù** commanding a **wànhù**,
if they served for fifteen years,
is promoted two ranks to **cóng wǔpǐn**.
If they served less than fifteen years and retire due to old age,
they are promoted one rank to **zhèng liùpǐn**.
If less than ten years,
they are promoted one rank and awarded sixty taels of silver and silk.
A regular **móukè** commanding a **wànhù**,
if they served for fifteen years, is promoted two ranks to **zhèng liùpǐn**.
If they served less than fifteen years and retire due to old age,
they are promoted one rank to **zhèng qīpǐn**.
If less than ten years, they are promoted one rank and awarded fifty taels of silver and silk.
A regular **qiānhù** commanding a **qiānhù**,
if they served for twenty years,
is promoted one rank to **zhèng liùpǐn**.
If they served less than twenty years and retire due to old age,
they are promoted one rank to **zhèng qīpǐn**.
If less than ten years, they are promoted one rank and awarded forty taels of silver and silk.
For regular **móukè** commanding those below **qiānhù**,
follow the precedents of **Hénán** and **Shǎnxī**.
For garrison soldiers (**zhènfáng jūn**):
Annual archery trials are held.
If anyone's shooting is outstanding,
the highest rank is awarded four taels of silver.
Those who are exceptionally distinguished receive ten taels of silver and a horse-trough.
For those drafted as Imperial Guard soldiers (**wǔwèijūn**)
and move to the capital with their families,
each person is given six rations daily,
and four horses are given fodder.
Various recruited soldiers are given regular monthly provisions.
Border post soldiers (**biānpùjūn**) receive fifty strings of cash and ten bolts of silk.
Upper and middle-grade military artisans (**jūnjiàng**) receive fifty strings of cash and five bolts of silk.
Lower-grade military artisans receive forty strings of cash and four bolts of silk.
Yellow River dike soldiers (**huánghé sàobīng**) receive thirty strings of cash and five bolts of silk.
Ration-collecting soldiers (**shèliángjūn**), dike soldiers (**sàobīng**), and boatmen (**shuǐshǒu**) in irrigation channels and other locations
receive twenty strings of cash and two bolts of silk.
Local soldiers (**tǔbīng**) receive ten strings of cash and one bolt of silk.
For commanders (**zhǐhuīshǐ**) of ration-collecting soldiers and dike soldiers of the Yellow and Qin Rivers:
seven strings of cash and grain, and six bolts of silk.
For military officers (**jūnshǐ**): six strings of cash and grain, and silk as above.
For squad leaders (**shíjiàng**): two strings of cash and three *shí* of grain.
Spring clothing money: five strings of cash. Autumn clothing money: ten strings of cash.
For subordinate officers (**chéngjú yāguān**): one string and five hundred cash, and two *shí* of grain.
Spring clothing money: five strings of cash. Autumn clothing money: seven strings of cash.
For prison wardens (**láochéng**) and local soldiers (**tǔbīng**): eight hundred cash and two *shí* of grain.
Spring clothing money: four strings of cash. Autumn clothing money: six strings of cash.
Border post soldiers (**biānpùjūn**) receive provisions the same as ration-collecting soldiers (**shèliángjūn**).
For garrison armored soldiers (**zhènfáng jiǎjūn**) and cavalry (**mǎjūn**) of the **Tǒngjūnsī** in **Hénán**, **Shǎnxī**, and **Shāndōng** Circuits:
**Mèng'ān** receive eight strings of cash, five *shí* and two *dǒu* of rice, eight bolts of silk, and fodder for six horses.
**Móukè** receive six strings of cash, two *shí* and eight *dǒu* of rice, six bolts of silk, and fodder for five horses.
**Púlián** receive four strings of cash, one *shí* and seven *dǒu* of rice, five bolts of silk, and fodder for four horses.
Regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) receive two strings of cash, one *shí* and five *dǒu* of rice, four bolts of silk, fifteen taels of cotton, and fodder for two horses.
**Ālíxǐ** receive one string and five hundred cash, seven *dǒu* of rice, three bolts of silk, and ten taels of cotton.
For infantry (**bùjūn**):
**Mèng'ān** receive fodder for two horses, **móukè** for one horse.
Each horse is given one bundle of fodder and five *shēng* of grain.
This ceases in mid-spring when there is green grass for horses to graze,
except for the seventy-two horses per **mèng'ān** on duty,
which are provided for all four seasons.
It was also stipulated that **Hénán**, **Shāndōng**, and **Hédōng** receive provisions for five months of the year,
and **Shǎnxī** for six months.
Horse replacement money for garrison soldiers (**zhènfángjūn**):
Regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) in **Hénán** Circuit receive five hundred cash.
**Ālíxǐ** and people of various colors (**suísè rén**) receive three hundred cash.
Regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) in **Shǎnxī** and **Shāndōng** Circuits receive three hundred cash.
**Ālíxǐ** and people of various colors (**suísè rén**) receive two hundred cash.
For various garrisoned field-cultivating soldiers (**túntián bèi chā**) and border-stationed soldiers for pursuit and killing (**yuánbiān zhùzhá zhuōsā jūn**):
**Mèng'ān** receive a monthly allowance of six strings of cash, one *shí* and eight *dǒu* of rice, and fodder for five horses.
**Móukè** receive four strings of cash, one *shí* and two *dǒu* of rice, and fodder for three horses.
**Púlián** receive two strings of cash, six *dǒu* of rice, and fodder for two horses.
Regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) receive one string and five hundred cash, four *dǒu* of rice, and fodder for one horse.
**Ālíxǐ** and people of various colors (**suísè rén**) receive one string of cash, four *dǒu* of rice, and fodder for one horse.
For commanders (**zhǐhuīshǐ**) of **Déshùn** Army: six strings of cash, two *shí* and eight *dǒu* of rice, six bolts of silk, and fodder for three horses.
For military officers (**jūnshǐ**) and squad leaders (**shíjiàng**): four strings of cash, one *shí* and seven *dǒu* of rice, and five bolts of silk,
and feed for two horses.
For long-serving soldiers (**chángxíng**): two strings of cash, one *shí* and five *dǒu* of rice, four bolts of silk, and fifteen taels of cotton,

For **Xī** Army **móukè**: one string and five hundred cash, one *shí* and five *dǒu* of rice, and one bolt each of raw silk and silk in spring and autumn,
and feed for three horses.
For **Púlián**: one string of cash, two *shí* and seven *dǒu* of rice, and raw silk and silk as above,

For long-serving soldiers (**chángxíng**): one string of cash, one *shí* and eight *dǒu* of rice, and raw silk and silk as above,

For permanently garrisoned soldiers (**yǒngtún zhùjūn**) in northern areas like **Línhuáng**:
**Qiānhù** receive eight strings of cash, five *shí* and two *dǒu* of rice, eight bolts of silk, and feed for six horses.
Infantry receive feed for two horses and five *qǐng* of land.
**Móukè** receive six strings of cash, two *shí* and eight *dǒu* of rice, six bolts of silk, feed for five horses, and four *qǐng* of land.
**Púlián** receive four strings of cash, one *shí* and seven *dǒu* of rice, five bolts of silk, feed for four horses, and three *qǐng* of land.
Regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) receive two strings of cash, one *shí*, four *dǒu*, and five *shēng* of rice, four bolts of silk, fifteen taels of cotton, feed for two horses, and two *qǐng* of land.
**Ālíxǐ** receive one string and five hundred cash, seven *dǒu* of rice, three bolts of silk, ten taels of cotton, and one *qǐng* of land.
**Qígǔsī** personnel receive the same as **ālíxǐ**.
Replacement soldiers (**jiāotìjūn**) receive two strings of cash and four *dǒu* of rice.
**Ālíxǐ** receive one string and five hundred cash and four *dǒu* of rice.
For Han soldiers (**hànjūn**) serving at the front:
**Qiānhù** receive a monthly allowance of three strings of cash, four *shí* of grain, eight bolts of silk, and feed for four horses.
**Móukè** receive two strings and five hundred cash, one *shí* of grain, six bolts of silk, and feed for two horses.
Regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) receive two strings of cash, nine *dǒu* and five *shēng* of rice, and four bolts of silk.
For permanently garrisoned soldiers (**yǒngtún zhùjūn**) appointed in **Shàngjīng** Circuit:
**Qiānhù** receive a monthly allowance of fifteen strings of cash and grain, ten bolts of silk, twenty taels of cotton, and feed for three horses.
**Móukè** receive six strings of cash, two *shí* and eight *dǒu* of rice, six bolts of silk, and feed for two horses.
Regular soldiers (**zhèngjūn**) receive a monthly allowance of two strings and five hundred cash, one *shí* and two *dǒu* of rice, four bolts of silk, fifteen taels of cotton, and feed for one horse.
**Ālíxǐ** and people of various colors (**suísè rén**) receive two strings of cash, one *shí* and two *dǒu* of rice, four bolts of silk, and fifteen taels of cotton.
For all permanently stationed soldiers (**yǒng zhùjūn**) in the northern region:
A monthly allowance of four hundred cash for horse replacement.
People of various colors (**suísè rén**) receive three hundred cash.
In the third year of **Zhēnyòu** (1215),
appointed military officials and officers commanding troops at the front
were found to be making false claims for rations,
and presuming to hold offices and positions
that had no actual incumbents.
Furthermore, those already holding positions or receiving remote appointments,
who already had stipends,
were also drawing rations with those who had no duties.
Therefore, at the time, there was discussion of reducing the number of officials and the amount of provisions,
to be fully restored when campaigning.
And in the second year of **Xīngdìng** (1218),
**Zhāng Xíngxìn**, the Military Commissioner (**jiédùshǐ**) of **Zhānghuà** Army, said:
"When a family member is drafted for service,
the entire family is provided for.
This is to gladden the hearts of the soldiers
and make them exert their full strength for the country.
As for families without soldiers,
and furthermore without adult males,
why are their wives and daughters still receiving provisions?"
In the fifth year (1221),
**Shímò Wòlǔ**, an official of the three **Xíngsī** South of the Capital, said:
"In the three circuits south, east, and west of the capital, the current garrisoned military households number forty thousand, including old and young,
consuming over 1.4 million *shí* of grain annually.
All of them subsist on the people's taxes,
which is a very poor plan."
His words are recorded in the Land System.
For various field-cultivating soldiers (**túntián jūnrén**):
If they are assigned to escort duties,
they receive one hundred fifty cash daily.
For guards of **Xiàonínggōng** personnel,
each receives monthly five *dǒu* of rice, one cartload of firewood, one bolt of coarse cloth for spring and autumn clothing, two bolts of autumn silk, and fifteen taels of cotton.
For various **Huángyuànzǐ** who reach old age,
from the original requested money and grain, one third
is given as one string of cash and grain for their upkeep in old age.
Collation Notes
Treatise 26: Punishments
In ancient times, the former kings created punishments based on people's knowledge of fear,
and created laws based on people's knowledge of shame.
Fear and shame
are the innate knowledge of the five natures,
and the great restraints of the seven emotions.
Therefore,
punishments are for governing what has already occurred,
laws are for prohibiting what has not yet occurred.
Fear is for dealing with common people,
shame is for treating gentlemen.
When gentlemen know shame,
and common people know fear,
the world will be at peace.
Therefore, the former kings nurtured their awe and utilized it,
for fear can teach love.
They carefully enacted their laws,
for shame can establish integrity.
Love gives rise to benevolence,
integrity gives rise to righteousness.
When benevolence and righteousness flourish,
will not penal laws come close to being abolished?
In the early [Jīn] period,
the legal system was simple and easy.
There was no distinction between light and heavy offenses, or between noble and humble individuals.
Punishment and ransom ran concurrently.
This could be applied to a newly established state,
but it was not a regulation for long-term governance.
Since the [Tiānhuì] era,
it gradually followed the deliberation of officials.
The [Huángtǒng] edicts were promulgated,
incorporating ancient laws.
Thereafter,
during the [Zhènglóng] period, additional imperial edicts were issued.
During the [Dàdìng] period, there were expedient regulations and
revisions of existing statutes.
During the [Míngchāng] era,
both legal principles and imperial decrees were revised,
and the system gradually became comprehensive.
Subsequently, the [Tàihé Lǜyì] (Legal Principles of [Tàihé]) was completed,
which should have left no regrets.
However, as the nation's vitality fluctuated between relaxation and tension,
and customs varied between pure and corrupt,
and the world's morality rose and fell,
a discerning person, observing the penal laws of an era,
often had foreknowledge of its future.
The [Jīn] law converted penal servitude to flogging,
cumulative up to two hundred strokes.
Local authorities, in establishing their authority,
would even attach blades to the staffs,
making it more cruel than physical mutilation.
In later years,
the sovereign and his ministers were fond of the old practices of using baskets and cages (metaphor for entrapment),
thereby considering those who twisted the law with elaborate texts as capable officials,
and those who handled affairs with cruelty as talented individuals.
For true offenders of bribery and corruption in all government departments,
this might be justifiable,
but it was also applied to minor transgressions.
Officials of the Censorate,
if they failed to expose wrongdoing, were also punished.
At the end of their term,
their performance was ranked based on the number of punishments they handed down.
The original intent of this legislation
was to treat both close relatives and distant ones, as well as high and low statuses, equally,
making everyone subject to the restraints of laws and regulations,
so that all would equally obey the public authority.
This was likely the intention of the [Qín] people to strengthen the emperor's authority.
Therefore, it showed little grace to the imperial clan
and little deference to ministers and scholars.
Throughout the [Jīn] dynasty,
many endured humiliation to achieve fame and success,
and even renowned scholars of the time were not exempt.
As for those who avoided humiliation by withdrawing far away,
they were rarely heard of.
Little did they know that if a superior person acts without shame and violates righteousness,
then common people will act without fear and violate the law.
Therefore, commentators, when discussing the principles of teaching affection and establishing integrity,
often sighed deeply.
Nevertheless,
during [Shìzōng]'s reign,
when legal officials presented judgments,
they sometimes departed from legal texts to cite classics,
or deliberated on principles to formulate laws.
Among rulers of recent antiquity who presided over judgments,
few spoke in a way so close to the Dao (truth/reason)
as he did.
[Zhāngzōng] and [Xuānzōng] also frequently dealt with civil affairs personally.
When they made decisions from the imperial throne,
though the balance between leniency and strictness might occasionally be excessive,
their numerous instances of compassion and forgiveness
still reflected the ancestral style.
What remains in historical records,
which can serve as a guide and mirror,
are found in both the "Basic Annals" and the "Treatise on Punishments," which show varying levels of detail.
According to the old customs of the [Jīn] state,
minor offenses were punished with flogging using a willow staff.
Those who committed murder or robbery
were killed by striking their heads,
and their household property was confiscated.
Four-tenths of it went to the government,
and six-tenths compensated the victim's family.
Their family members were also made slaves.
If their relatives wished to redeem them with horses, cattle, or other miscellaneous items, it was permitted.
Even serious offenses were sometimes allowed to be ransomed.
However, to distinguish them from commoners,
their noses or ears were cut off.
Their prisons were pits dug several zhang deep and wide.
Although [Tàizōng] inherited [Tàizǔ]'s instruction not to change the old customs,
he also gradually adopted the laws of [Liáo] and [Sòng].
In the seventh year of [Tiānhuì],
an edict decreed that for all thefts:
mere possession of stolen goods incurred three years of penal servitude;
theft of ten strings of cash or more incurred five years;
tattooing and assignment to the lower army;
theft of thirty strings of cash or more incurred lifelong penal servitude,
with the additional punishment of tattooing on the face if the value of the stolen goods reached the maximum;
theft of fifty strings of cash or more incurred death.
Compensation was collected according to the old system.
In the tenth month of the first year of [Tiānjuàn] during [Xīzōng]'s reign,
princes and those below them were prohibited from wearing swords into the palace.
The law of palace guard and prohibition
truly began from this point.
In the third year,
after regaining the [Hénán] territory,
an edict was issued to its people,
stipulating that the criminal laws applied would all follow the legal texts,
and the cruel and poisonous instruments of torture used by prison guards were abolished,
in favor of leniency.
By the [Huángtǒng] period,
an edict instructed all ministers
to compile a book of laws, combining the dynasty's old system
with elements adopted from the [Suí] and [Táng] systems,
and incorporating laws from [Liáo] and [Sòng].
This was categorized and compiled into a book
named [Huángtǒng Zhì],
and promulgated both internally and externally.
At that time, the regulation was that
flogging up to a hundred strokes
would be divided between the buttocks and back.
However, when [Hǎilíng Shùrén] deemed the back too close to the heart and abdomen,
he prohibited it.
Even if a master flogged a slave,
it would be considered a violation of the regulation.
Many old regulations were also changed,
and by the [Zhènglóng] period,
these were compiled into the [Xùjiàng Zhìshū] (Continued Imperial Edicts),
which circulated alongside the [Huángtǒng Zhì].
However, these two rulers applied laws arbitrarily,
and there were differences from these systems.
When [Shìzōng] ascended the throne,
due to the chaos of the [Zhènglóng] period,
robbers were rampant, and warfare had not ceased.
Many imperial decrees at that time were issued according to immediate circumstances,
and these were compiled as [Jūnqián Quányí Tiáolǐ] (Expedient Regulations for Military Matters).
In the fourth year of [Dàdìng],
the [Shàngshū Shěng] (Department of State Affairs) reported that
Li Shí, a male commoner from [Dàxīng], and Yáng Xiāngē, a woman,
were both subject to execution for seditious speech.
The Emperor said:
"These ignorant people do not understand the laws,
and the officials have never clearly instructed or warned them.
How can such extreme punishment be immediately imposed?"
He reduced their sentence from death.
In the fifth year,
he ordered officials to revise and refine the regulations again,
to be used in conjunction with the previous edicts.
In the seventh year,
there was a robbery at the [Zuǒcángkù] (Left Treasury), where the commander [Guō Liángchén] was killed, and gold and pearls were stolen.
The thieves could not be found.
The [Diǎnjiǎnsī] (Inspection Department) was ordered to investigate.
Eight suspicious individuals were apprehended and interrogated.
Three were tortured to death,
and five confessed under duress.
The Emperor suspected foul play
and ordered [Yílà Dào], the concurrent administrator of [Dàxīng Fǔ], to conduct a mixed investigation.
Later, [Āsībā], a centurion of the imperial guards, was found selling gold in the market.
The matter came to light,
and he was executed.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor said:
"Under the lash and torture,
what cannot be extracted?
Why do interrogators not seek the truth with genuine effort?"
He granted two hundred strings of cash to the families of those who died,
and fifty strings of cash to those who did not die.
Consequently, centurions and fifty-man leaders of the guards were prohibited from carrying swords into the palace unless on duty.
In that year,
twenty death row inmates were executed.
In the eighth year,
it was enacted that officials who violated gambling laws,
if the illegal gains were less than fifty strings of cash, would be flogged,
but allowed to redeem themselves.
Repeat offenders would be flogged.
He also said,
"Flogging is for punishing commoners.
Since one is an official, one should prioritize integrity and shame.
If one lacks integrity and shame,
one should therefore be punished with the punishment of commoners."
In the ninth year,
following a report on legal cases by the [Yùshǐ Tái] (Censorate),
the Emperor said:
"Recently, I have heard that legal officials sometimes insist on their own views,
or observe the intentions of the chief ministers.
From now on, for regulations without specific provisions, the legal texts shall be the standard."
He also ordered that flogging up to a hundred strokes be divided between the buttocks and back,
as per the old law.
After some time,
the Emperor said to his ministers:
"I worried that if criminals did not have their flogging divided,
it might become too severe,
so I ordered the return to the old method.
Now I hear that some common people do not wish for it.
Therefore, order its abolition."
In the tenth year,
the Shàngshū Shěng奏 (Memorialized):
“Zhāng Jǐn of Hézhōng Fǔ declared that he avenged his father’s murder.
According to the law, he ought to die.”
The emperor said:
“He avenged his father’s murder,
and moreover, he declared it himself.
He is a valiant man.
Let his sentence be reduced from death.”
In the eleventh year,
an imperial edict instructed the officials, saying:
“All judicial offices and prison cells must be situated near the prisons.
Matters concerning imprisonment must always be personally supervised.
The prison guards must be chosen from experienced and trustworthy individuals to take turns on duty.”
In the twelfth year,
the Shàngshū Shěng said:
“Púchá Tái Bǔ, the magistrate of Nèiqiū, used money from the treasury to erect a monument to virtuous governance.
Moreover, there remained over two hundred strings of cash.
His crime warrants dismissal.
Now, encountering an amnesty,
he should also be exempted from recovering the embezzled funds.”
The emperor, considering it an act of greed and deceit,
rejected the proposal,
and moreover said:
“As for the embezzled funds,
if they are pardoned by amnesty,
what fault is there for those who gave them?
From now on, all such funds should be pursued and returned to their rightful owners;
only those that should have entered the government coffers are exempted from recovery.”
The Shàngshū Shěng memorialized that
there were tomb robbers.
The emperor said:
“Even the tombs of meritorious officials have been desecrated.
This is likely because there is no reward for reporting and apprehending them,
hence people have no fear.
From now on, those who report and prove the crime will be given appropriate rewards.”
Because Shímò Āmòlà, the former Yin of Xiánpíng, died in prison for corruption,
the emperor said of him:
“Not having his corpse displayed in the marketplace is already a great fortune.
For the poor to turn to robbery,
it is perhaps out of necessity.
For an official of the third rank to die for corruption,
it is truly foolish.
All his sons should be dismissed from office.”
Previously,
an edict had stipulated that henceforth, if descendants of dismissed officials were in office, their cases should all be reported for decision.
In the thirteenth year,
an imperial edict stated that between the Beginning of Spring and the Beginning of Autumn,
as well as during major sacrifices,
on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
during the waxing and waning crescent moons,
on the twenty-four solar terms,
when rain has not yet cleared,
when night has not yet given way to dawn,
on holidays and days when slaughtering is prohibited,
no death sentences shall be executed;
only for serious robbery (qiángdào) is it not necessary to wait until after autumn.
In the fifteenth year,
an imperial edict instructed the officials, saying:
“朕 considers human life to be of utmost importance,
yet the current law prescribes death for those who steal goods worth fifty strings of cash.
From now on, let the threshold for the death penalty be eighty strings of cash.”
In the seventeenth year,
a memorialist requested the establishment of a Tíxíng司 (Judicial Review Office)
to investigate judicial errors across all circuits.
The Shàngshū Shěng deliberated,
opining that in the long run, it might lead to abuses.
The emperor then ordered that those who had grievances and appealed from thousands of miles away from the capital
should have their cases compiled to await examination by selected officials.
At that time, Liáng Sù, the Yin of Jǐnán, said
that those sentenced to penal servitude should be exempted from flogging.
The court believed that the current laws were already lighter than those of ancient times,
and feared that this would encourage wickedness,
so they did not comply.
The emperor once issued an edict to the prime ministers, saying:
“The court dispatches审录官 (judicial review officials) twice a year,
originally to redress the grievances of the people,
yet many of those dispatched do not fulfill their duties wholeheartedly,
merely completing the formalities.
The judicial review officials
are not only to investigate serious crimes;
they must also review all litigation documents,
verify right and wrong,
release prisoners who should not be held,
and report the crimes of officials,
severely punishing those who fail in their oversight,
without allowing redemption.”
Furthermore, a Jiānchá Yùshǐ (Censor) who was inspecting officials in the Northeast Circuit
received a complaint petition,
which was deemed an dereliction of duty,
and he was flogged fifty strokes.
He also said to the prime ministers:
“I have recently heard that the Dàlǐ Sì (Supreme Court) takes several months to decide cases,
even those without doubt.
Why is this?”
Cānzhī Zhèngshì (Assistant Administrator) Yílà Dào replied:
“According to the law,
the maximum time to decide a death sentence is seven days,
for penal servitude five days,
and for flogging three days.”
The emperor said:
“The law has time limits,
yet they are violated.
This is negligence.”
After court was dismissed,
an imperial rescript was sent to the Shàngshū Shěng, saying:
“For all cases, whether serious or minor, decided by the judicial court, there are fixed time limits.
Judicial officials should decide all cases definitively;
how can they dare to violate this?
It is merely that your views are not uniform,
leading to repeated submissions and resubmissions.
Even the memorial of the agreed-upon decision often takes more than ten days,
resulting in many delays.
From now on, this must not happen again.”
He also said:
“Gāo Zhēn, the former Yin of Guǎngníng, governed with excessive severity;
even for minor offenses,
some were flogged to death.
Even if a crime warrants death, and the circumstances might allow for leniency,
it should still be considered,
let alone minor offenses.
How can human life be treated lightly?”
The emperor considered that the imperial decrees issued during the Zhènglóng reign were often based on personal whim,
and were excessively harsh and scrutinizing.
When used alongside the decrees of the Huángtǒng reign,
right and wrong became confused,
and it was unclear which to follow,
allowing corrupt officials to manipulate matters.
Therefore, a bureau was established,
and Dàlǐ Qīng (Minister of the Supreme Court) Yílà Zào was appointed to lead internal and external legal experts in jointly revising them.
Thus, the decrees of Huángtǒng and Zhènglóng, along with the provisional regulations issued before the Dàdìng campaign and subsequent continuous regulations,
were weighed for their severity,
removing redundancies and correcting errors.
Where decrees were deficient, the legal statutes were used to supplement them.
Where both decrees and statutes were deficient, or where there was doubt and no decision could be reached,
an imperial edict was sought for a definitive ruling.
Within the provisional regulations issued before the campaign, those that could be permanently implemented were also established as permanent laws,
while others not yet applicable were stored as a separate compilation.
Incorporating the recently established law reducing penal servitude and flogging by half,
a total of one thousand one hundred and ninety articles were revised and finalized,
divided into twelve volumes,
named Dàdìng Chóngxiū Zhìtiáo (Revised Regulations of Dàdìng),
and promulgated by imperial edict.
In the twentieth year,
the emperor saw people trampling crops,
and said to the prime minister:
“From now on, anyone who tramples people’s fields shall be flogged sixty strokes,
and anyone who steals grain shall be flogged eighty strokes,
and in both cases, they must compensate the value.”
In the twenty-first year,
the Shàngshū Shěng memorialized that Mǎ Jùn, a commoner from Gǒngzhōu, had a wife, Ānjiě, who committed adultery with Guǎn Zhuó.
Jùn killed them with an axe.
His crime warrants death.
The emperor said:
“He may be pardoned one degree from death,
to warn those who corrupt public morals.”
In the twenty-second year,
the emperor said to the prime ministers:
“All documents sent from the Shàngshū Shěng to the Dàlǐ Sì
can be immediately reported to me once a decision is made.
Take the case of Wūgǔlùn Gōngshuō,
which I recently reviewed.
It was first sent to the judicial court for judgment according to law,
then resubmitted to the Sīzhí (judicial official) for detailed review,
and then sent to the entire court for joint deliberation,
repeated three times,
creating unwarranted emotional interpretations and preventing a final decision.
I believe that national affairs should not be delayed.
Although I underwent moxibustion six hundred times yesterday,
I never missed a day of court,
wishing to show you my diligence in governance.
From now on, only one submission to the court is allowed;
the entire court must review it in detail,
and if there are any emotional interpretations, they must be reported immediately,
without causing delay.”
In the twenty-third year,
the Shàngshū Shěng memorialized that
Fàn Dé, a commoner from Yìdū, aged seventy-six,
was beaten to death by Liú Yòu.
By law, Yòu ought to die.
Since Yòu’s parents were both over seventy years old
and had no attendants at home,
a request for leniency was made to the emperor.
The emperor said:
“Fàn Dé was of similar age to Yòu’s parents;
Yòu should have treated him as his own parents.
To beat him to death,
it is difficult to consider a reduced sentence.
Let the judgment be according to the law.”
The Shàngshūshěng impeached officials of the Zhāotǎosī and Tūlǐqǐ for extorting wealth from their respective departments,
and the emperor [shàng] said:
“Distant people should only be treated with compassion.
If they do not neglect to pay tribute,
and yet one uses soldiers to intimidate them,
forcibly seizing their property,
how is that different from brigandage?
Moreover, if incidents arise from this,
how can it not be punished?”
He further said:
“The regulations [zhìtiáo] that I implement
are all those proposed by my subordinates.
There are many affairs in the world,
and human effort is limited;
how can one attend to every single one?
Only by reporting specific incidents
does one realize where there are impediments,
and then corrections are made immediately.
Now there are imperial decrees [shèngzhǐ], regulations [tiáolǐ],
and then there are also detailed regulations [zhìtiáo];
this allows corrupt officials to manipulate the severity [of punishments].”
Zhào Wúshì, a commoner from Dàxīngfǔ, spoke wildly while intoxicated.
His father, Qiān, reported him to the authorities.
By law, he was to die.
The emperor [shàng] said:
“For a father not to pity his son but to report him for arrest,
such righteousness is
something very difficult for people to achieve.
He may be specially pardoned one degree from death.”
Yì, Assistant Administrator of the Wǔqìshǔ, and Gǔ●, Director, were convicted of accepting property from Cǎobànzi.
Yì received eighty strokes of the杖 [zhàng],
Gǔ● twenty strokes of the笞 [chī].
Liáng Xiāng and others, Cèchá Yùshǐ, were punished with a month's salary deduction for failing to supervise.
The emperor [shàng] said:
“The Cèchá are
the eyes and ears of the sovereign.
If matters originate from me,
what is the purpose of the Cèchá?”
The emperor [shàng], when the Fǎsì judged cases,
translated Nǚzhí characters into Hànzì.
When the Fǎhuì again each expressed their personal views [qíngjiàn],
making arbitrary interpretations [chuānzáo] and
only causing delay,
he issued an edict to abolish personal views.
In the second month of the twenty-fifth year,
the emperor [shàng], considering that it was inconvenient for women prisoners
to perform labor service,
and that lashing [zhàng] without distinction
was no different from execution,
commanded that those exempted from death but sentenced to labor service
should receive two hundred strokes of the杖 [zhàng] and be exempted from labor service,
with the strokes divided between the buttocks and back.
At that time, when a member of the empress's family committed a crime,
the Shàngshūshěng invoked
the “Bāyì”
in its memorial.
The emperor [shàng] said:
“Law [fǎ] is
a tool for the public world to maintain fairness.
If relatives commit crimes and receive reduced sentences,
it encourages them to rely on this and act arbitrarily.
In ancient times, Emperor Wén of Hàn executed Bó Zhāo,
which is worth emulating.
Twenty years ago,
Wūlíndá Chāowù, the Jìzhōujiédùshǐ and a member of the empress’s family, once committed a capital offense;
I never pardoned him.
If I pardon him now,
it will open a door for future generations to manipulate severity and leniency.”
The prime minister [zǎichén] said:
“The reason for the ancient system of ‘deliberating on kinship’ [yìqīn] was
to honor the Son of Heaven [tiānzǐ]
and distinguish him from commoners.”
The emperor [shàng] said:
“The imperial maternal relatives [wàijiā] are naturally different from the imperial clan [zōngshì].
The power of the imperial relatives [wàiqī] in the Hàn dynasty was too great,
even leading to the overthrow of the state;
that is why I do not allow princes [zhūwáng] and princesses [gōngzhǔ] to hold power.
Indeed, for those who have rendered meritorious service to the state,
‘deliberating on merit’ [yìxūn] is acceptable.
As for ‘deliberating on sagacity’ [yìxián],
if one is already called sagacious,
would one commit a crime?
If, perchance, one is implicated by association,
then a reduction or petition is indeed appropriate.”
In the twenty-sixth year,

it was thus decreed in a memorial that close relatives of the crown prince's consort [tàizǐfēi] of the Dàgōng degree and above, those who had no mourning relationship with the imperial family, and those who were sagacious but committed private offenses,
should all not be included in the “deliberations” [yì].
The emperor [shàng] said to the prime minister [zǎichén]:
“There are laws that are logical and those that are not;
revise and finalize them.”
Táo Jūn, a Cèchá Yùshǐ, brought courtesans to tour the Běiyuàn,
singing and drinking among the pond islands.
This was dangerously close to the palace court.
Shí Jiè, the Tíkòngguān, heard of it and exposed it.
Jūn asked his friend Yán Shù to plead with Jiè for leniency.
Later, the matter came to light.
The Fǎsī memorialized that
he should be sentenced to two and a half years of penal servitude.
An edict stated that as Jūn was an official of the “eyes and ears,”
and courtesans entered the forbidden garden,
without distinction of rank,
he received sixty strokes of the杖 [zhàng].
Jiè and Shù were also implicated.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the emperor [shàng], finding the regulations [zhìtiáo] constrained by old laws [jiùlǜ],
with some difficult-to-understand terms,
ordered them to be revised and clarified [shānxiū míngbái],
so that everyone could understand them.
It was formerly forbidden for commoners to collect imperial edicts [zhìshū],
for fear of encouraging false accusations and litigation.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng of Zhāngzōng,
a memorialist requested that commoners be allowed to keep them.
Zhāng Rǔlín, Píngzhāng, said:
“In ancient times, Zǐchǎn cast the penal code [xíngshū],
and Shū Xiàng criticized him for it,
presumably because he did not want commoners to pre-emptively gauge the severity [of punishments].
Now, to promulgate an unalterable code [bùkānzhīdiǎn],
making it clear to the people,
is like the Jiāng [River] and Hé [River], easy to avoid but difficult to violate,
sufficient to aid governance.
It is better not to forbid it.”
As the majority of opinions were against it,
an edict was issued to temporarily maintain the old prohibition.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
the emperor [shàng] asked the prime minister [zǎichén]:
“Why do we not exclusively use the text of the statutes [lǜwén] now?”
Zhāng Rǔlín, Píngzhāng Zhèngshì, said:
“In previous dynasties, statutes [lǜ] and ordinances [lìng] had their distinct divisions.
Those who violated an ordinance [lìng]
were judged by the statutes [lǜ].
Now, the state’s regulations [zhì] and statutes [lǜ] are confused;
they should certainly be separated.”
Therefore, the Xiángdìngsuǒ was established,
and it was ordered to examine and finalize the statutes [lǜ] and ordinances [lìng].
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
a law was enacted regarding the acceptance of bribes in military camps:
one guàn or less,
two years penal servitude;
above that, three years penal servitude;
ten guàn, death penalty.
Běijīngnú, a Fúbǎodiǎnshū, stole a gold plaque from the Fúbǎojú.
He was executed [fúzhū]
and his family registration was removed.
Ànhǔ and Āhǔ, for negligence in detection,
each received seventy strokes of the杖 [zhàng].
In the second year of Tàihé,
the Yùshǐtái memorialized:
“Shǐ Sù, a Cèchá Yùshǐ, states that
according to the Dàdìng regulations [tiáolǐ]: prior to the fourth day of the eleventh month of the twentieth year,
if a slave married a free woman as his wife,
it was confirmed as an accomplished marriage;
if the husband died,
she was to be constrained and released at the discretion of her master.
If she was divorced and sold, her original master was to redeem her,
and she was to reunite with her husband as before.
If a free woman left her husband for a free man, she was allowed to be redeemed and exchanged;
if children were born to her and her husband before redemption and exchange, they were all considered free.
However, the new Tàihé regulations [gé] also stipulate that after the husband’s death and the mourning period, she is considered a free person [liángrén],
and if divorced and sold, or released by her husband to be free,
she is also considered free.
If she has not yet left and remarries a slave,
or if children are born from illicit intercourse, they are all permitted to be free.
Such discrepancies
are all due to the arbitrary additions and deletions by the officials compiling the regulations,
leading to widespread lawsuits and disputes,
thus involving injustice.”
An imperial edict instructed the relevant department to rectify this.
Initially,
an edict commanded that all regulations [tiáo gé] included within the imperial decrees [zhìwén]
should be divided into separate volumes.
Then, another edict commanded that cases where imperial decrees [zhì] and statutes [lǜwén] differed in severity,
and cases not covered by the statutes [lǜ],
should each be collated and reported.
For example, prohibitions on slaughtering and similar matters
should be recorded in the ordinances [lìng].
Be cautious and do not neglect this;
once the statutes [lǜ] and ordinances [lìng] are finalized,
they cannot be changed again.
In the seventh month of the third year of Míngchāng,
Sūn Duó, the Yòusī Lángzhōng, first submitted the Mínglìpiān collated by the Xiángdìngsuǒ.
Subsequently, all other chapters were completed,
and an order was again issued to Wáng Jì, the Zhǎnyùnshǐ of the Zhōngdū Lù, and Dǒng Shīzhōng, the Dàlǐ Qīng, and others to re-collate them.
In the seventh month of the fourth year,
the emperor [shàng], finding that the cangues and lashing boards [jiāzhàng] in various circuits often did not comply with regulations,
Shǒuzhēn, Píngzhāng Zhèngshì, said:
“The dimensions of cangues and lashing boards are regulated.
The Tíxíng officials inspect them every two months;
they would certainly not dare to violate the law.”
In the first month of the fifth year,
an order was again issued to review and compile the ordinances (zhì) and laws (lǜ),
and they were immediately submitted to the Detailed Review Office (Xiángdìng Suǒ).
At that time, the detailed review officials stated:
"If the revised ordinances (zhìwén) are adopted as the standard,
then the articles will be increased or decreased,
and the severity of crimes
will differ from the laws (lǜ).
Once finalized, if they are promulgated together with the old ones,
this will confuse people and make it easy for them to commit illegal acts.
We propose that,
using the current articles of the ordinances (zhì),
and taking into account contemporary circumstances,
they should be revised according to the text of the laws (lǜ).
We should selectively adopt suitable provisions from previous penal codes
to supplement omissions and deficiencies,
and use the commentaries from the Xíngtǒng (刑統) to explain them,
establishing them as permanent statutes,
named Míngchāng Lǜyì (明昌律義).
Matters concerning salt and iron monopolies (quèhuò), frontier affairs (biānbù), and expediency (quányí) should be separately compiled
into Imperial Edicts (chìtiáo)."
The Prime Ministers (zǎichén) said:
"The previously stipulated ordinances (lìngwén) are still incomplete.
They should be promulgated after they are all thoroughly finalized.
As for those who are examined on laws (lǜkē),
they should only study the old laws (lǜ)."

Consequently, Ní Pánggǔ Jiàn (尼厖古鑑), the Prefect of Dàxīng Fǔ (大興府), Dǒng Shīzhōng (董師中), the Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), Àotún Zhōngxiào (奧屯忠孝), the Hanlin Academician (Hànlín Dàizhì) (whose infant name was Yágē (牙哥)),

Zhāng Sì (張嗣), the Director of the Astronomical Bureau (Tíidiǎn Sītiān Tái), Wányán Sālà (完顏撒剌), the Hanlin Compiler (Hànlín Xiūzhuàn), Lǐ Tíngyì (李庭yì), the Assistant Minister of Punishments (Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng), and Má Ānshàng (麻安上), the Minister of Justice (Dàlǐ Chéng), were appointed as the reviewing and finalizing officials.

Yán Gōngzhēn (閻公貞), the Minister of Justice (Dàlǐ Qīng), Lǐ Jìngyì (李敬義), the Vice Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng), and Jiǎ Xuàn (賈鉉), the Director of Public Works (Gōngbù Lángzhōng), were appointed as the re-reviewing officials,
to revise the new laws (lǜ).
At that time, when cases were reported to the throne and judges (fǎguān) offered their personal opinions (qíngjiàn),
the Emperor said:
"Some say that judges (fǎguān) should not offer personal opinions (qíngjiàn),
hence there is endless debate.
I believe that personal opinions (qíngjiàn) do not fall outside the law (fǎ),
but merely serve to reconcile with the law (fǎ)."
Píngzhāng Shǒuzhēn (平章守貞) said:
"This practice was abolished in Dàdìng (大定) twenty-three years.
However, there are articles in the laws (lǜ) allowing for requests (qǐqǐng),
which indicates that personal opinions (qíngjiàn) were also permitted in ancient times."
The Emperor said:
"Statutes (kētiáo) are limited,
but human emotions are endless,
so how can personal opinions (qíngjiàn) be dispensed with?"
In the fifth year of Míngchāng (明昌),
the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) memorialized:
"According to the ordinances (zhì), in the law (lǜ) regarding fixed-term penal servitude (túnián) within the general provisions (mínglì),
there is no mention of flogging (juézhàng), therefore it should not be used.
Because previously it was said that exile (liúxíng) was not suitable for the present time,
and all those who served four years or more in place of exile (dàiliúyì) were flogged,
it would be difficult not to flog those sentenced to three years or less of penal servitude.
Although women are treated more lightly than men,
they should also receive a proportional reduction."
Thus, those sentenced to two years or less of penal servitude received sixty strokes of the rod (zhàng),
those to two years or more received seventy strokes,
and women who committed crimes received fifty strokes,
which was recorded in the Imperial Edicts (chìtiáo).
In the third year of Chéng'ān (承安),
an imperial edict (chì) was issued to the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng), stating that
from now on, matters under special imperial decrees (tèzhǐ),
if they conform to the format of laws and ordinances (lǜlìng chéngshì),
may then be sent to the departments.
As for other newly implemented matters,
officials of the departments should simply be summoned to the Department of State Affairs (Shěng) to discuss them.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) requested a further review and finalization of the ordinances (lìngwén).
The Emperor then issued an edict (chì) to the Prime Ministers (zǎichén), saying:
"For matters that are clear and straightforward, simply memorialize them.
For voluminous documents, it is difficult to read them all.
Report only those cases where the three interrogations (sāntuī) raise doubts."
In the fifth month,
the Emperor, finding the laws (fǎ) unfair,
noted that the commonly used flogging (zhàng) standards
were often not implementable.
So, he set the dimensions,
cast copper into standard flogging rods (zhàngshì),
and promulgated them throughout the empire.
He also said:
"If the light and heavy flogging (chīzhàng) is considered too lenient,
and there are circumstances that are difficult to pardon,
the investigative flogging (xùnzhàng) can be re-discussed."
In the fifth month of the fifth year,
Mǎ Fù (馬復), Assistant Minister of Punishments (Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng), reported:
"Local officials who are still harsh do not follow the copper flogging rod standards,
and arbitrarily use large rods,
often causing deaths."
An imperial edict (zhào) ordered the Surveillance Commissioners (Ànchásī) to impeach and dismiss them.
Previously, it had been ordered that for all death row prisoners and those dismissed from office due to crimes,
if the appointed official was more than two hundred lǐ away,
and for those involved in penal servitude (tú) or lesser crimes, if there were more than twenty people,
the official should conduct the review on the spot.
Wányán Gāng (完顏綱), Assistant Minister of Punishments (Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng), said:
"Since this regulation was enacted,
for places as close as Shàngjīng (上京), travel back and forth involves no less than three to two thousand lǐ.
For Běijīng Liúshǒusī (北京留守司), it often takes several months,
leading to further delays,
which is inconvenient."
An imperial edict (zhào) ordered a return to the old system,
where the appointed official would pursue and interrogate them.
In the twelfth month,
Yáng Tíngxiù (楊庭秀), Hanlin Compiler (Hànlín Xiūzhuàn), reported:
"Prefects and magistrates (zhōuxiàn guān) often assume authority and power,
acting on their whims and emotions.
When hearing lawsuits,
they rarely exercise due diligence.
They merely let interpreters (yìrén) transmit messages back and forth,
the severity of crimes
being determined by their words.
Bribery is openly practiced,
and some innocent people cannot get justice even after twenty or thirty years."
The Emperor then ordered the establishment of clear regulations,
and violators were to be impeached by the Surveillance Commissioners (Ànchásī).
He also told the Prime Ministers (zǎichén):
"The system of allowing principal and deputy officials to delegate the investigation of prisoners to secretarial staff and clerks (mùzhí jí sīlì tuīwèn yùqiú),
and ordering this to be reported to the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) for hearing and memorializing,
should be reinstated."
He also ordered the compilation of past and present regulations,
to be recorded in books,
for future reference and examination.
In the first month of the first year of Tàihé (泰和),
the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) memorialized that
the current copper flogging rod standard was too light and slender,
and criminals were not deterred.
Consequently, the relevant authorities (yǒusī) were ordered to use larger rods according to the severity of the offense,
but also prohibited from exceeding five fen (五分) in thickness.
In the twelfth month,
the revised laws (lǜ) were completed,
totaling twelve chapters: one on general provisions (mínglì),
two on palace and imperial guards (wèijìn),
three on official duties (zhízhì),
four on household and marriage (hùhūn),
five on stables and granaries (jiùkù),
six on arbitrary mobilization (shànxīng),
seven on robbery and theft (zéidào),
eight on combat and litigation (dòusòng),
nine on fraud and deceit (zhàwèi),
ten on miscellaneous laws (zálǜ),
eleven on pursuit of fugitives (bǔwáng),
and twelve on judicial decisions (duànyù).
These were effectively the Táng (唐) laws (lǜ),
but all redemption fees (shú tóng) were doubled,
penal servitude (tú) was increased to four and five years in seven instances,
forty-seven articles deemed unsuitable for the time were removed,
one hundred forty-nine articles concerning contemporary regulations were added,
and two hundred eighty-two articles were slightly modified;
the remaining one hundred twenty-six articles remained unchanged;
six articles were further divided into two parts, or into four parts;
making a total of five hundred sixty-three articles,
in thirty volumes,
with annotations to clarify matters,
and commentaries to resolve doubts,
named Tàihé Lǜyì (泰和律義).
Beneath the Ordinances on Official Ranks (Guānpǐn Lìng) and Ordinances on Official Duties (Zhíyuán Lìng),
there were forty-eight articles on Ordinances on Sacrifices (Cí Lìng),
sixty-six articles on Ordinances on Households (Hù Lìng),
eleven articles on Ordinances on Education (Xué Lìng),
eighty-three articles on Ordinances on Selection and Appointment (Xuǎnjú Lìng),
nine articles on Ordinances on Enfeoffment and Titles (Fēngjué Lìng),
ten articles on Ordinances on Posthumous Enfeoffment and Grants (Fēngzèng Lìng),
ten articles on Ordinances on Palace Guards (Gōngwèi Lìng),
twenty-five articles on Ordinances on Military Defense (Jūnfáng Lìng),
twenty-three articles on Ordinances on Ceremonial Regulations (Yízhì Lìng),
ten articles on Ordinances on Clothing (Yīfú Lìng),
fifty-eight articles on Ordinances on Official Forms (Gōngshì Lìng),
seventeen articles on Ordinances on Salaries (Lù Lìng),
seven articles on Ordinances on Granaries and Treasuries (Cāngkù Lìng),
twelve articles on Ordinances on Stables and Pastures (Jiùmù Lìng),
seventeen articles on Ordinances on Fields (Tián Lìng),
twenty-three articles on Ordinances on Taxes and Corvée (Fùyì Lìng),
thirteen articles on Ordinances on Passes and Markets (Guānshì Lìng),
twenty articles on Ordinances on Pursuit of Fugitives (Bǔwáng Lìng),
twenty-five articles on Ordinances on Rewards (Shǎng Lìng),
five articles on Ordinances on Medicine and Illness (Yīzhí Lìng),
fourteen articles on Ordinances on Leave (Jiǎníng Lìng),
one hundred six articles on Ordinances on Prison Officials (Yùguān Lìng),
forty-nine articles on Miscellaneous Ordinances (Zá Lìng),
ten articles on Ordinances on Buddhism and Daoism (Shìdào Lìng),
thirteen articles on Ordinances on Construction and Repair (Yíngshàn Lìng),
eleven articles on Ordinances on River Defenses (Héfáng Lìng),
eleven articles on Ordinances on Mourning Attire (Fúzì Lìng),
supplemented by regulations based on years and months,
known as Lǜlìng (律令) in twenty volumes.
Additionally, there were ninety-five articles of New Fixed Imperial Edicts (Xīndìng Chì),
eighty-five articles on Salt and Iron Monopolies (Quèhuò),
thirty-nine articles on Frontier Departments (Fānbù),
known as Xīndìng Chìtiáo (新定勅條) in three volumes,
and Formats for the Six Departments (Liùbù Géshì) in thirty volumes.
Sīkōng Xiāng (司空襄) submitted them,
and an imperial edict (zhào) ordered their promulgation in the fifth month of the following year.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu (貞祐),
the Emperor told the Prime Ministers (zǎichén),
that from now on, if a surveillance official (jiāncáiguān) commits a crime,
and the matter concerns national military interests,
they shall all be punished by flogging (chījué).
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu (1216),
an edict stated:
"Any Censor (Jiānchá) who fails to impeach [wrongdoing],
shall be judged according to the original law.
Foreign envoys entering the country and secretly communicating their country's affairs;
Palace Guards (Sùwèi), close attendants (Jìnshìguān), and entertainers (Chéngyìngrén) frequently visiting the homes of imperial princes (Qīnwáng), princesses (Gōngzhǔ), and Grand Councilors (Zǎizhí);
officials (Yǒusī) who conduct dishonest inspections of disaster-stricken areas lacking food, leading to loss of life;
those who transport military provisions but carry private goods;
those who supervise examinations for candidates (Jǔrén) but are not strict in preventing irregularities—
their punishments shall all be decided.
Those in the capital who commit such offenses twice,
Grand Censors (Táiguān) shall have their punishment reduced by one degree compared to ordinary Censors (Jiānchá),
subject to commutation by payment;
others shall merely be censured.
For those specifically appointed (Zhuānchāi), the matter shall be deliberated and decided upon the completion of their term.
If, during their term, they were convicted due to a failure in oversight,
even if they are deemed competent according to regulations,
they shall only be considered ordinary;
and those considered ordinary shall be subject to demotion and punishment."
In the eighth month of the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
the Emperor (Shàng) said to his Grand Councilors (Zǎichén):
"The law has the 'Eight Deliberations' (Bāyì).
Now, some people say that those subject to deliberation should immediately have their punishment reduced by a degree.
What do you think?"
The Grand Councilors (Zǎichén) replied:
"For any deliberation, one must first list the charges and the reasons for deliberation in a petition.
Only after deliberation and decision can it be submitted for imperial judgment."
The Emperor (Shàng) approved this,
saying:
"If one were to reduce punishments without regard to their severity,
then all noble relatives would rely on this to oppress the people.
How could the people endure it?"
Collation Notes
Treatise 27: Food and Money (1) – Population, General Inspection, and Re-enumeration
A state having food and money
is like a person having food and drink.
A person cannot live without food and drink;
a state cannot be established without food and money.
However, Suìrén and Páoxī could devise the way of food and drink to teach people,
but they could not make people free from diseases related to food and drink.
The Three Kings (Sānwáng) could devise policies on food and money to bequeath to later generations,
but they could not make later generations free from the problems of food and money.
Only those who are good at nurturing life seem not to desire eating,
yet their food and drink are naturally not lacking.
Thus, they can appropriately manage hunger and satiety,
leading to fewer illnesses and a long life.
Those who are good at enriching the state initially do not engage in trade and accumulation of wealth,
yet their food and money are naturally not lacking.
Thus, they can control the balance between abundance and scarcity,
leading to fewer problems and long-term stability.
As for the Jīn dynasty's food and money policies,
their legislation was comprehensive,
and their collection from the people was cautious.
When Tàizǔ first established the dynasty,
he reduced the taxes of the Liáo dynasty;
his vision was far-reaching.
During the reigns of Xīzōng and Hǎilíng,
the general atmosphere became more open each day,
and they also pursued distant strategies.
Rulers and ministers studied and sought systems for financial management,
earnestly regarding this as their top priority.
Even with the sagacity of Shìzōng,
his ambition for accumulation was never forgotten for a single day.
During Zhāngzōng's reign, literary culture flourished,
and border expenses also expanded.
Discussions on food and money could not but be urgent.
When Xuānzōng moved south,
the national territory shrank daily.
"Polluting ponds and frequently casting nets" (a metaphor for exhausting resources without restraint),
such situations were common.
Examining since its establishment,
the so-called laws of food and money
were predominantly the three: land rent (zūshuì), copper coinage (tóngqián), and paper currency (jiāochāo).
The methods for these three changed repeatedly and were repeatedly exhausted.
Official land was called "rent" (zū);
private land was called "tax" (shuì).
In addition to rent and tax, they calculated the number of fields, gardens, houses, carriages, horses, cattle, sheep, and cultivated plants,
as well as the amount of stored wealth,
and levied money called "asset tax" (wùlì).
The collection of asset tax
from dukes, ministers, and grandees (Gōngqīng Dàfū) at the top,
down to common people (Mínshù) at the bottom,
none were casually exempted.
Close ministers who went on missions to foreign countries,
upon return, would certainly have their asset tax increased,
because they had received gifts.
Households of the Méng'ān Móukè system also had a so-called "Ox-Head Tax" (Niútóushuì).
Grand Councilors (Zǎichén) had to pay this tax.
When its increase or decrease was deliberated in the court,
it can be imagined how much the prefectures and counties extorted from the common people.

Therefore, besides the asset tax, there were also taxes like "relay horses" (Pūmǎ), "military supplies" (Jūnxū), "corvée commutation" (Shūyōng), "clerical fees" (Sīlì), "river laborers" (Héfū), "mulberry bark and waste paper" (Sāngpí Gùzhǐ), etc.
The names of these items were trivial and detailed,
and cannot be fully enumerated.
As for household types, there were several categories:

tax-and-corvée households (Kèyìhù), non-tax-and-corvée households (Bùkèyìhù), principal households (Běnhù), miscellaneous households (Záhù), regular households (Zhènghù), supervision households (Jiānhù), official households (Guānhù), slave households (Núbìhù), and "two-tax households" (Èrshuìhù).
Officials (Yǒusī) initially registered households every three years.
Later, this changed to a "general inspection" (Tōngjiǎn),
and then to a "re-enumeration" (Tuīpái).
For households belonging to prefectures and counties,
and those belonging to Méng'ān Móukè,
their payments and contributions varied greatly.
When the law was first implemented,
they were only afraid it wasn't thorough enough.
Those who spoke on affairs said it oppressed the people,
so it was immediately ordered to be abolished.
Not long after its abolition,
financial officers reported a shortage of funds,
so it was immediately reinstated.
Its abolition was intended to benefit the people,
but the people saw no benefit.
Its implementation was intended to suffice for expenditures,
but funds did not become more abundant.
At that time, words of admonition from rulers and ministers regarding frugality were incessant.
They once calculated their national expenditures,
and the amount was indeed vast,
seemingly sufficient for many years.
However, if a prefecture or county experienced a slight famine,
it would suddenly become insufficient.
Ultimately, no one could ascertain the reason.
As for the problems with copper coinage (tóngqián) and paper currency (jiāochāo),
they were even more severe.
Initially, they used old coins from the Liáo and Sòng dynasties.
Even those cast by Liú Yù,
after Yù was deposed,
were also used concurrently.
From Zhènglóng onwards,
they began to deliberate on minting their own coins.
The prohibition on private copper use became very strict among the populace.
As copper was insufficient for use,
kiln smelting gradually developed.
All copper-producing veins of land
had officials dispatched to investigate them within the territory, leaving none unchecked,
and even beyond the borders.
For copper utensils essential for people's daily use,
all were manufactured by the government and sold.
Afterwards, the government could not handle the excessive burden,
and the people could not bear the hardship.
So, it was permitted for people to smelt copper and manufacture utensils,
with the government setting prices for sale.
This was a change in the copper policy.
As for the changes in the monetary system,
the minting was not extensive,
and the collection and distribution lacked proper methods,
leading to stagnation.
Initially, fearing that the official treasuries would accumulate too much,
and that money would not reach the people,
laws were established for widespread distribution.
Later, fearing that the people would hoard money,
a limit on retention was set,
and the path of denunciation was opened.
Offenders were punished with severe penalties,
but ultimately, it could not be stopped.
With scarcity of money in the zhōus and xiàns,
people minted their own,
and these private coins were extremely debased.
Then, five hundred official coins were exchanged for one thousand private coins,
a policy that only worsened the situation.
When large coins were later reminted,
their standard was increased,
and despite countless efforts to circulate them,
ultimately no effect was achieved.
Supplemented by iron coins,
iron proved unusable.
Temporarily using jiāochāo (paper currency),
the value of coins was high and paper currency low,
the disparity was vast,
commodity prices soared,
and paper currency became unacceptable.
Temporarily using silver currency,
the abuses of silver also multiplied.
With no strategy to remedy this,
copper coins were abolished,
and only jiāochāo and silver currency were used.
However, the abuses of these two were even worse than those of coins.
For officials, it was profitable to use large denominations of jiāochāo,
but as large jiāochāo were issued excessively,
the people increasingly regarded them as worthless.
For private individuals, it was profitable to obtain small denominations of jiāochāo,
but as small jiāochāo flowed in excessively,
it brought no benefit to the state.
Thereupon,
officials were prohibited from using large jiāochāo.
Later, fearing that the people would use silver and not paper currency,
the people were then compelled to pay taxes to officials in jiāochāo,
to demonstrate its mandatory use.
Initially, twenty-string to one-hundred-string denominations were created,
later, two-hundred-string to one-thousand-string denominations were created.
The discrepancies in value between earlier and later issues were illogical,
further confusing the people.
When there was no other recourse,
limitations were imposed by year,
limitations by region,
and public and private transactions were limited by a fraction.
From this, the people's suspicion deepened daily.
During this period,
jiāochāo was changed to bǎojuàn,
and bǎojuàn was soon replaced by tōngbǎo,
which was standardized against silver and used concurrently.
Tōngbǎo was soon replaced by bǎoquán,
and bǎoquán was soon followed by printed silk notes,
named zhēnhuò.
Zhēnhuò was soon replaced by bǎohuì.
There was never a fixed system,
and the Jīn dynasty's fate ended.
Observing from ancient times, the accumulation of wealth and dispersion of the people
leading to the downfall of a state,
like Lùtái and Jùqiáo,
are not worth discussing.
The state's demise and financial exhaustion
happened frequently,
but the depletion of state resources
has never been as severe as in the late Jīn dynasty.
The Jīn government,
though often having the intention to care for the people,
could not cease its harsh tax decrees,
gaining only the reputation of accumulating wealth,
but failing to achieve the reality of a rich nation.
When it was on the verge of collapse,
confiscating grain, cornering the market on grain,
and all policies of exploitation were implemented without exception.
Taxes were increased several times over,
several years' worth of revenue was preemptively borrowed,
or, to obtain paper currency, next year's corvée duties were preemptively sold.
Gāo Qí (高琪) as chancellor,
even proposed a salt monopoly.
For those who advanced and donated to obtain irregular official positions,
they would sell empty official edicts,
or even grant them a substantive fifth-grade position.
For Buddhist and Daoist monks who donated grain,
it started with ordination certificates,
and ended with honorary titles, leadership roles, and head abbots of monasteries and temples being sold according to their wealth.
Even more, those in mourning were sold positions to seek office,
supervised households were sold liberation to become commoners,
and successful candidates in the imperial examinations were sold advanced degrees.
Even more, for the loyalty shown by rebel ministers and notorious bandits,
lacking gold and silk for rewards and encouragement,
they were often given princely titles to solidify their allegiance.
If high titles were insufficient,
they were bestowed with the imperial surname.
Names and realities were confused,
moral principles and laws were corrupted,
all were disregarded.
If the state desired not to be chaotic,
how could that be possible?
When Sòng (宋) cut off annual tributes and refused peace,
coveting the wealth stored in Huáinán (淮南),
and planning to seize it by force,
this led to the loss of all forces from the central military command in the southern campaign.
The emergence of É Kě (訛可) and Shí Quán (時全)
initially aimed at obtaining grain,
but later proved utterly useless.
The three armies were destroyed,
our forces pressed upon the border,
both military and financial resources were exhausted,
and there was nothing to defend against them.
Therefore, those who recorded the food and monetary systems of Jīn
cannot but close their books and sigh with emotion.
The classic says:
"To make laws in a time of frugality,
its abuses will still be greed.
To make laws in a time of greed,
what will its abuses be like?"
The Jīn rose from the East Sea,
their customs were pure and honest,
they could have reverted to ancient ways.
When they first entered the Central Plain,
where their military might reached,
many people fled,
much land lay fallow.
The remaining populace was fearful,
what could they not obtain?
If at that time,
even if they could not restore the systems of well-field and irrigation ditches,
if they had used Táng's (唐) permanent and allocated land systems to regulate people's property,
and emulated its rent, corvée, and tribute laws to sufficiently meet state needs,
how could it be that within a hundred years, their plans and schemes were so numerous and chaotic,
ending with their state?
The problem lay in their eagerness for short-term gain,
following long-corrupted laws.
By their middle period,
they disdained Liáo's (遼) frugality,
and adopted Sòng's elaborate bureaucratic practices;
they punished Sòng's leniency,
and added Liáo's harsh governance.
This was abandoning the strengths of both states,
and concurrently using their weaknesses.
Excessive elaboration inevitably leads to squandering wealth,
and excessive harshness inevitably leads to harming the people.
Throughout the Jīn era,
the state's resources were easily exhausted,
and the people's hearts were easily alienated.
Was this not precisely why?
If laws are not carefully made at the beginning,
and reforms are made to remedy their abuses,
it only makes things worse.
Other laws concerning salt policy, wine yeast, ever-normal granaries, grain purchase, tea tax, merchant levies, and border markets,
were mostly proposed by former Sòng officials.
Their ebb and flow were unstable,
and changes were constant.
How were they different from currency?
Items such as land systems, water conservancy, and field division,
were either hastily implemented and then abandoned,
or repeatedly tried without effect,
or thoroughly discussed but never implemented,
all are recorded in this chapter,
to serve as a record of that dynasty's institutions.
Household Registration.
According to Jīn regulations,
males and females aged two and below were called huáng,
those below fifteen were xiǎo,
sixteen were zhōng,
seventeen were dīng,
sixty were lǎo.
Women without husbands were guǎqīqiè,
and those with severe disabilities were not counted as dīng.
The household head was designated as the eldest.
Households with assets were designated as kèyìhù (tax and corvée households),
those without were bùkèyìhù (non-tax and corvée households).
The people were ordered to form bào with five families.
In the sixth year of Tài​hé,
the Emperor, finding that the previously established bào​wǔ laws
were being neglected and unenforced by the officials,
ordered the formation of bào.
Those who harbored spies, criminals, or bandits would be subject to collective punishment.
The chief ministers said that previously five families formed a bào,
and they feared that it would be too easy for people to frame each other and difficult to detect,
so it was ordered to follow the Táng system:
five families would form a lín, and five lín would form a bào,
to facilitate mutual inspection.
In the gōng of Jīngfǔ and zhōu​xiàn, fāng​zhèng were appointed.
In villages and communities, according to the number of households, lǐ​zhèng were appointed for xiāng.
Their duties included checking household registers,
urging and supervising taxes and labor services,
and encouraging agriculture and sericulture.
In villages and communities with over three hundred households, four zhǔ​shǒu were appointed;
with over two hundred households, three people;
with over fifty households, two people;
and below that, one person,
to assist the lǐ​zhèng in prohibiting and detecting wrongdoing.
Zhuàng​dīng were appointed
to assist the zhǔ​shǒu in patrolling and guarding against bandits.
In the villages and stockades of the Měng'ān Móukè units,
for over fifty households, one zhài​shǐ was appointed,
whose duties were the same as the zhǔ​shǒu.
In temples and monasteries, gāng​shǒu were appointed.
All fāng​zhèng and lǐ​zhèng
were to be recruited from three-tenths of their households,
with wealthy citizens equally contributing money to hire
strong, capable individuals with guarantors.
No person could serve for more than one hundred guàn,
and no service could exceed one year.
(In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng,
Zhāngzōng once wished to abolish fāng and lǐ​zhèng.
However, the zhǔ​shǒu were too far away,
and going to the city for service
interfered with farming, which was inconvenient.
Therefore, it was decided that capable and trustworthy individuals would be replaced every two years.)
All household registers
were to be compiled every three years.
Starting from the first month of the year,
zhōu​xiàn officials, with the lǐ​zhèng and zhǔ​shǒu,
and Měng'ān Móukè officials, with the zhài​shǐ,
would visit each registered household to demand a detailed report,
specifying the age and names of males, females, old, and young.
Those born were added,
and those who died were removed.
On the twentieth day of the first month, the actual numbers were reported to the xiàn.
On the twentieth day of the second month, they were reported to the zhōu,
and within ten days they were to reach the superior office.
Regardless of distance, all were to arrive at the bù and be presented to the shěng by the twentieth day of the fourth month.
Neither Hàn people nor Bóhǎi people were allowed to be Měng'ān Móukè households.
Slaves of Měng'ān Móukè who were emancipated to become commoners
were only attached to their original unit as regular households.
All commoners confiscated by the government
were attached to the Gōngjí Jiān as jiān​hù.
Slaves confiscated by the government
were attached to the Tàifǔ Jiān as guān​hù.
During the second year of Dāngshōu​guó,
laws and regulations were not yet settled,
and warfare had not ceased.
Many poor people relied on the powerful for temporary safety,
and many concealed themselves as slaves.
Tàizǔ issued an edict saying:
"Recently, due to bad harvests and famine,
many people have attached themselves to powerful families,
and have consequently fallen into slavery.
Others, having committed crimes,
could not pay compensation,
and became slaves in exchange for their bodies.
Or, by private agreement with a time limit,
