one person was used to redeem another;
if the deadline passed, they became slaves.
All are now permitted to redeem one person as a commoner with two people.
Those originally agreed to be redeemed with one person should follow that convenience."
In the fifth year of Tiānfǔ,
since the territory had been expanded,
but many of the old units had barren land,
it was planned to move their people to Tàizhōu.
Hence, the Imperial Brother Yù and his clan nephew Zōngxióng were dispatched to inspect the land.
Yù and others sent back samples of the soil,
saying it was suitable for cultivation.
Thereupon, over ten thousand households were selected from various Měng'ān Móukè,
and Zōngrén Póluóhuǒ was ordered to lead them
to garrison and cultivate in Tàizhōu.
Póluóhuǒ previously resided by the Āzhùxǔ River,
(also written Ānchǔhǔ.)
and was now moved there.
Those residing in Níngjiāng Zhōu,
the four Móukè, Shídé, Cháduān, Ālǐtúhuān, and Xītádǎn, were sent,
taking their families, dependents, and farming tools,
to move to Tàizhōu.
Póluóhuǒ was also granted fifty plowing oxen.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ,
after the various zhōu of Shānxī were pacified,
Shàngjīng was designated as the interior.
Therefore, its people were moved to populate it.
Yēlǜ Fódǐng was also ordered to escort the surrendered people with troops to Húnhé Lù,
with Imperial Brother Áng supervising them.
They were ordered to settle as conveniently as possible.
In the seventh year,
because the various tribes of Shānxī were close to the two northwestern borders,
and the Liáo ruler had not yet been captured,
fearing that they might secretly conspire and entice,
Imperial Brother Áng and Bóu​jǐn Shāohè and others were again ordered to escort them with four thousand troops,
and place them east of the ridge.
Only the people of Xī​jīng remained settled as before,
and Áng was also ordered to guard Shàngjīng Lù.
Soon after,
the Emperor heard that Áng had already passed Shàngjīng,
and the surrendered people were again suffering from his disturbances, with many rebelling and fleeing.
So Bóu​jǐn Chūlǐdǐ was ordered to go and admonish him.
By the time he arrived,
the various tribes had already rebelled and left.
Měng'ān Xiángwěn was also ordered to return to Dōngjīng with the surrendered people under his command
and was instructed to constantly pacify them.
They were also lent one year's provisions,
and their relatives who had been captured were all ordered to gather and live together.
In the seventh year, when Yānjīng Lù was taken,
in the second month,
all the powerful families, artisans, and skilled people of the six zhōu were moved to the interior.
In the first year of Tàizōng Tiānhuì,
because the people previously moved from Rùn, Xí, and other four zhōu to the territory of Shěnzhōu
were struggling and unable to sustain themselves,
an edict said:
"Recently, I have heard that people are lacking food to the point of selling their children.
It is permitted to redeem them with laborers of equal strength."
An edict was also issued to Bóu​jǐn Āshílái, saying:
"The former emperor, for people of the same surname who had previously sold or pledged themselves,
ordered officials to redeem them.
Now I hear that there are still some who have not been restored.
All of them should be reviewed and redeemed."
It was also ordered to use official grain to redeem over six hundred people
from the newly relocated Níngjiāng Zhōu households in Shàngjīng Lù who were poor and had sold themselves.
In the second year,
for people who had sold themselves into slavery,
an edict allowed them to be exchanged with laborers of equal strength.
In the third year,
internal and external officials and members of the imperial clan were prohibited from privately conscripting common people.
Powerful families were not allowed to buy poor people as slaves.
Those who coerced purchases would compensate fifteen people for one.
Those who fraudulently purchased would compensate two people for one.
The punishment for all crimes was one hundred strokes of the staff.
In the seventh year,
an edict stated that since the start of the war,
commoners who had been captured and enslaved
were permitted to be redeemed by their parents, wives, and children.
In the fourth year of Xīzōng Huángtǒng, an edict stated that in Shǎnxī, Pú, Xiè, Rǔ, Cài, and other zhōu, due to famine,
people who had fallen into destitution and were pledged or hired as servants
would be redeemed by the government with silk as commoners:
three rolls for an adult male,
and two rolls for a woman or child.
In the second year of Shìzōng Dàdìng,
an edict exempted the "two-tax households" and made them commoners.
Initially,
the Liáo people were excessively devoted to Buddhism,
and often bestowed commoners upon various temples.
Half of their tax was paid to the government,
and half to the temples;
hence they were called "two-tax households."
After the fall of Liáo,
many monks concealed their true status
and suppressed them as low-status.
When someone provided evidence and reported it,
officials from various departments reported it.
The Emperor had long known about this matter,
and therefore specifically exempted them.
In the fifth month of the seventeenth year,
a memorial reported
that "over 1,600 households in Xiánpíng Fǔ Lù
declared themselves to be Nǚzhēn people from Chángbái Shān Xīngxiǎn and Chánchūn Hé.
During the Liáo dynasty, they were conscripted as hunting households,
moved to this place,
called the Yídiǎn Bù,
and subsequently registered under the Qìdān.
When our dynasty's righteous army rose,
they were among the first to surrender to the army,
remaining in their original unit.
Now they request rectification."
An edict approved this.
In the twentieth year,
due to Nǚzhēn households in Shàngjīng Lù
evading property tax
by selling their slaves,
which led to a shortage of farm laborers,
and consequently poverty,
an edict established regulations to prohibit this.
The Emperor also said to the chief ministers:
"For Měng'ān Móukè households,
if brothers and relatives each settle in their allotted land
and intermingle with Hàn people,
every forty or fifty households should form a bào​jù.
During farming season, they should assist each other.
This is also a way to encourage mutual aid."
In the sixth month of the twenty-first year,
the people living by Yínshān were moved to Línhuáng.
It was also decreed that for households evading service who had fled with their whole families to other places,
the original household and the officials of the county where they resided would be held equally guilty,
establishing this as a fixed regulation.
In the twenty-third year,
a regulation was established that,
if a Nǚzhí slave, male or female, proved capable,
and the master permitted their marriage,
it was necessary to inquire of the close relatives and village elders and obtain a document,
only then allowing them to marry a commoner.
In the eighth month of that year,
a report was submitted on the number of households, cultivated land, and farming implements of the Méng'ān and Móukè.
There were two hundred and two Méng'ān,
one thousand eight hundred and seventy-eight Móukè,
six hundred and fifteen thousand six hundred and twenty-four households,
six million one hundred and fifty-eight thousand six hundred and thirty-six people,
(of whom four million eight hundred and twelve thousand six hundred and sixty-nine were free commoners,
and one million three hundred and forty-five thousand nine hundred and sixty-seven were slaves).
Cultivated land amounted to one million six hundred and ninety thousand three hundred and eighty qǐng and a fraction,
and there were three hundred and eighty-four thousand seven hundred and seventy-one cattle-drawn implements.
For the Zōngshì Jiāngjūn Sī in the capital,
there were one hundred and seventy households,
twenty-eight thousand seven hundred and ninety people,
(of whom nine hundred and eighty-two were free commoners,
and twenty-seven thousand eight hundred and eight were slaves).
Cultivated land amounted to three thousand six hundred and eighty-three qǐng and seventy-five mù,
and there were three hundred and four cattle-drawn implements.
For the five cí of the Diélà and Tánggǔ two tribes,
there were five thousand five hundred and eighty-five households,
one hundred and thirty-seven thousand five hundred and forty-four people,
(of whom one hundred and nineteen thousand four hundred and sixty-three were free commoners,
and eighteen thousand eighty-one were slaves).
Cultivated land amounted to sixteen thousand twenty-four qǐng and seventeen mù,
and there were five thousand sixty-six cattle-drawn implements.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the prime ministers were ordered to prohibit a single son of those with official salaries, as well as farmers evading taxes and services,
from becoming monks or Daoists.
In the early Dàdìng period,
there were barely over three million households in the realm;
by the twenty-seventh year, there were six million seven hundred and eighty-nine thousand four hundred and forty-nine households in the realm,
and forty-four million seven hundred and five thousand eighty-six people.
In the eleventh month of the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng under Zhāngzōng,
one who submitted a memorial stated,
requesting that "households paying two taxes" be released to become commoners.
The provincial officials wished to use official documents as a basis,
but Cānzhī Zhèngshì Yílài Lǚ said,
"It is difficult to ascertain the authenticity of evidence.
Henceforth, all children born to Qìdān slaves shall be commoners.
Existing ones may not be pawned or sold.
If this is done, then after thirty years all slaves will be commoners,
and the people will not suffer."
The emperor deemed Lǚ's words inappropriate
and ordered further discussion.
The provincial memorial stated that if not strictly delimited, lawsuits would be endless.
Thus, Wūgǔsūn Zhònghé, Zhìzhōng of Dàxīng Fǔ, and Fàn Jí, Shìyùshǐ, were dispatched to separately investigate the "two tax households" in Běijīng Lù and Zhōngdū Lù.
For those without verifiable evidence,
those declared by their masters or discovered through general inspections,
half of their tax was paid to the government and half to the master.
Those with verifiable evidence were all released to become commoners.
In the first month of the first year of Míngchāng,
one who submitted a memorial stated:
"From ancient times, agriculture and sericulture have been the foundation.
Now, in addition to merchants, there are Buddhists, Daoists, and other itinerant idlers,
causing a hundredfold increase in wasteful expenditure.
Harvests are poor,
and starving vagrants are everywhere.
This is due to the many 'secondary occupations' harming agriculture."
The emperor then issued an order
prohibiting self-ordination as monks or Daoists.
That year,
a report stated there were six million nine hundred and thirty-nine thousand households in the realm,
forty-five million four hundred and forty-seven thousand nine hundred people,
but only just over fifty-two million two hundred and sixty-one thousand shí of grain.
After deducting two years of expenses for government officials and soldiers,
and calculating based on the remaining population,
each person would consume five dòu per month,
which would suffice for forty-four days of food.
The emperor said:
"There are not many reserves;
this is because there are few diligent farmers.
Gather all officials
to discuss ways to make the people prioritize the fundamental and increase reserves,
and report back."
In the sixth month,
a report stated that the "two tax households" exempted in Běijīng and other lùs
amounted to over one thousand seven hundred households,
and over thirteen thousand nine hundred people.
Henceforth, whether they were commoners or forced laborers
was to follow what had already been decided.
In the second month of the sixth year of Míngchāng,
the emperor said to his prime ministers:
"When speaking of Nǚzhí jinshi,
there is no need to refer to 'Nǚzhí characters.'
You have mistakenly avoided Nǚzhí and Qìdān terms,
which is wrong.
Now, if we distinguish households,
Nǚzhí refer to their 'original household,'
Hàn households and Qìdān,
the rest are called 'miscellaneous households.'"
In the twelfth month of the sixth year of Míngchāng,
a report stated there were seven million two hundred and twenty-three thousand four hundred Nǚzhí, Qìdān, and Hàn households in the realm,
forty-eight million four hundred and ninety thousand four hundred people,
and two million six hundred and four thousand seven hundred and forty-two guàn in property tax.
In the sixth month of the seventh year of Tàihé,
an imperial decree stated:
Among households of moderate wealth,
many abscond when there are services to perform.
Commanders then order subordinate households to replace them.
When the task is complete, they resume their original occupation,
which greatly harms those who do not abscond.
The prime ministers were ordered to deliberate in detail.
The prime ministers reported that the old regulations were too lenient.
Thus, it was ordered that those households who absconded entirely from taxes and services would be sentenced to two years of penal servitude,
and informants would be rewarded fifty thousand qián.
Those who had already absconded would be exempt from punishment if they surrendered within one hundred days.
If they were genuinely destitute,
the Yùshǐ Tái internally
and the Ànchá Sī externally
would investigate
and grant exemption.
In the twelfth month,
a report stated there were seven million six hundred and eighty-four thousand four hundred and thirty-eight households in the realm,
and forty-five million eight hundred and sixteen thousand seventy-nine people.
(Households increased by one million six hundred and twenty-three thousand seven hundred and fifteen compared to the twenty-seventh year of Dàdìng,
and population increased by eight million eight hundred and twenty-seven thousand sixty-five.)
This marked the zenith of the Jīn household registers.
By the time of Wèi Shàowáng,
military campaigns were ceaseless.
Xuānzōng ascended the throne and moved south.
Of those who died or were displaced,
many places became empty.
The population dwindled daily,
military expenses grew more urgent daily,
and levies became heavy.
All depended on Hénán.
The people could not endure their plight,
and consequently abandoned their homes and fields,
fleeing one after another.
Although several imperial edicts were issued to recruit them back to their occupations,
exempting them from that year's rent,
yet because the state's finances were exhausted,
the rent of those who had fled was all made to be paid by those who remained.
For this reason, many dared not return.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Xīngdìng,
Xuānzōng wished to offer rewards to recruit people to capture fugitive households,
but then feared unrest.
So he ordered that, in accordance with the previously issued edict,
debts and arrears were already pardoned.
They were to be recruited for another month,
and only those who defied the order and did not come back would then be captured and punished,
and their abandoned land granted to others.
In the fourth year,
the provincial officials reported
that in Hénán, due to annual famine and unceasing taxes and services,
the lost households were to be recruited by officials.
Those who had not returned to their occupations by the third month of the following year
would be judged according to the law.
At that time, the area along the river was the frontier,
and beacon fires repeatedly signaled alarms.
Therefore, Wēndíhán Dá, the Jíqìng Jūn Jiédùshǐ, stated
that Bózhōu previously had sixty thousand households.
Since the move south, they could not bear the levies
and had fled one after another.
Of those remaining, there was not even one-tenth.
The small town of Dàngshān
had no residents in its fields.
General Assessment and Re-evaluation.
The general assessment,
is the system described in the "Rites of Zhōu" (周禮), where the Grand Minister of Works (大司徒) conducts a major census every three years,
recording the population, livestock, and carriages in each district,
and determining the levies based on these assets.
In the Jīn (金) dynasty, after the initial land registration at the founding of the state,
by the fourth year of Dàdìng (大定) [1164 CE],
following the wars and turmoil of Zhènglóng (正隆),
the wealth of the common people had changed,
and the burdens of taxes and labor services were unevenly distributed.
Shìzōng (世宗) issued an edict saying:
"Since the founding of the state,
the officials have regularly conducted general assessments,
and it has now been forty years.
During the Zhènglóng (正隆) era,
military service and labor levies were initiated simultaneously and without limit.
The wealthy are now poor and unable to sustain themselves,
while those not on the registers are now prosperous households yet still manage to escape levies.
Therefore, I am sending trustworthy officials, such as Zhāng Hóngxìn (張弘信), the Military Commissioner (節度使) of Tàiníng (泰寧) Commandery, and twelve others,
to conduct general assessments of the resources of the empire by different routes and re-determine them,
to rectify the former abuses
and ensure that all the common people (元元) have no complaints of inequality,
thus fulfilling my intentions.
All regulations and arrangements
are to be drawn up by the Department of State Affairs (尚書省) and implemented uniformly."
He further commanded:
"Regarding the properties of households under supervision (監戶),
apart from those officially granted,
all other taxable fields and residences acquired by the common people
shall be included in the general assessment."
At that time,
many envoys often sought credit by being harsh and extracting more resources.
Hóngxìn (弘信) was particularly cruel and violent in assessing the prefectures and counties of Shāndōng (山東).
Wányán Yǒngyuán (完顏永元), the Defense Commissioner (防禦使) of Dìzhōu (棣州), confronted him, saying:
"The court appointed envoys to equalize the levies
because of the uneven distributions after Zhènglóng (正隆).
Yet now you are brutal,
arbitrarily increasing the value of people's property by several times.
If anyone comes to appeal,
they are beaten until their flesh and blood are exposed,
and in severe cases, they die under the rod.
What kind of principle is this?"
Hóngxìn (弘信) could not answer.
Therefore, Dìzhōu (棣zhou) was the only place that remained relatively fair.
In the fifth year [1165 CE],
the officials reported that the general assessments in various circuits were uneven.
An edict was issued to re-determine them based on the size of households and the degree of their wealth and poverty,
to achieve a suitable balance.
Subsequently,
a tax law for land and other properties determined by general assessment was also established.
In the ninth month of the fifteenth year [1175 CE],
the Emperor stated that for the empire's resources,
more than ten years had passed since the general assessment,
and the rich and poor had changed their fortunes.
The burdens of taxes and levies were uneven.
He dispatched Liáng Sù (梁肅), the Administrator (尹) of Jìnán (濟南), and twenty-five others
to re-evaluate by different routes.
In the fourth month of the twentieth year [1180 CE],
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Among the households of the 'mynggan' (猛安) and 'jauke' (謀克) system,
the distribution of levies between rich and poor is uneven.
They are all assessed within the 'jauke' (謀克) system.
The ignorant only follow the words of the clerks,
resulting in inconsistent burdens.
Since the rebellion of Wōwò (窩斡),
the rich and poor have reversed positions.
Now we should register their dependent households (夾戶),
and assess their family assets.
Then, if there is military service, it can be distributed fairly."
An edict was issued to gather all officials for deliberation.
The Right Chancellor (右丞相) Kèníng (克寧), the Co-Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (平章政事) Ānlǐ (安禮), and the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (樞密副使) Zōngyǐn (宗尹) said:
"Apart from the 'mynggan' (猛安) and 'jauke' (謀克) servants who perform duties,
the Jurchens (女直人) have no other corvée.
It would be more convenient now not to assess the number of slaves, livestock, and land,
but only to verify and levy based on property."
The Left Chancellor (左丞相) Shǒudào (守道) and others said:
"Only verifying property,
divided into four grades based on quantity,
and registering it for levies,
should ensure fairness."
The Left Chancellor (左丞) Tōng (通), the Right Chancellor (右丞) Dào (道), and the Grand Inspector (都點檢) Xiāng (襄) said:
"If we assess the number of slaves,
the wealth and poverty will become clear.
In times of urgency, a levy based on this will differ from a uniform levy.
We request that during the slack farming season,
the numbers of land and farming implements be registered,
and each report what they have found."
The Emperor said:
"How can a 'jauke' (謀克) not know the wealth or poverty of a household within his 'jauke'?
An 'mynggan' (猛安) oversees eight 'jauke' (謀克)s,
and a uniform levy is imposed.
For example, within one 'jauke' (謀克),
there are those with two or three hundred slaves,
and those with only one or two slaves.
If the levies are the same,
how can there be fairness?
During the Zhènglóng (正隆) wars,
I had tens of thousands of slaves
and thousands of livestock,
yet not a single person or horse was levied from me.
How could that be called fair?
I never act unilaterally in matters of state;
I consult with you, my ministers.
In previous years, when the Khitan (契丹) households were dispersed,
Ānlǐ (安禮) strongly warned of disturbance,
but I decided to proceed,
and it indeed brought stability.
Although Ānlǐ (安禮) is loyal,
he does not always foresee the best long-term strategy.
Let us follow the view of Left Chancellor Tōng (通) and others,
and conduct the registration and re-evaluation."
In the twelfth month
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Among the 'mynggan' (猛安) and 'jauke' (謀克)s, many are newly strong and formerly weak,
and the levies are uneven.
Let the re-evaluation begin with the Zhōngdū (中都) circuit."
By the eighth month of the twenty-second year [1182 CE],
an edict was finally issued to gather elders,
assess wealth and poverty,
verify the numbers of land, farming implements, and slaves,
and divide them into three grades: upper, middle, and lower.
Wányán Wūlǐyěxiān (完顏烏里也先), the Co-Administrator (同知) of the Great Capital Prefecture (大興府事), was to assess the Zhōngdū (中都) circuit.
Subsequently, Fourteen officials, including Àndài (按帶), a Bureau Secretary (主事) of the Ministry of Revenue (戶部), were dispatched
to jointly re-evaluate different circuits with local officials.
In the ninth month,
an edict stated:
"Do not allow the wealthy to conceal their livestock,
or poor households to fear raising horses.
During the time of Hǎilíng (海陵),
livestock were confiscated without any grading.
The wealthy escaped,
while the poor had all theirs taken by the government,
which was extremely unfair.
Now, we shall thoroughly verify the rich and poor and create registers.
In times of urgency, we will take from them according to the registers,
thus avoiding the abuses of inequality."
Zhāng Rǔbì (張汝弼) and Liáng Sù (梁肅) submitted a memorial:
"Once the general assessment for the common households of the empire is established,
if there are changes in property,
taxes should naturally be paid according to the current ownership.
As for movable assets,
they inevitably increase or decrease.
The poor remain poor,
and the rich remain rich.
It seems unnecessary to re-evaluate repeatedly."
The Emperor said:
"Many of the chief ministers and administrators' families have recently become wealthy,
which is why they are unwilling."
Sù (肅) replied:
"As for me,
I am capable of re-evaluating the resources of Zhōngdū (中都).
Because I once served as an envoy to the south,
I first increased my own property tax (物力錢) to over sixty strings of cash (貫),
and among other envoys, none paid more than me.
However, the common people are ignorant;
laws lead to trickery,
and frequent changes easily cause alarm.
During the Táng (唐), Sòng (宋), and Liáo (遼) dynasties,
there were cases where no general assessment was conducted for twenty or thirty years.
Frequent annual re-evaluations
seem difficult."
In the twenty-sixth year [1186 CE],
Lǐ Yàn (李晏) and others were again dispatched to re-evaluate by different routes.
In the twenty-seventh year [1187 CE],
when the number of resources determined by Yàn (晏) and others was reported,
the Emperor said:
"I originally set the empire's property tax at over three million five thousand strings of cash.
Apart from three million strings of cash,
I ordered a reduction of over fifty thousand strings.
Now the reduction is less than the stipulated amount,
and an additional twenty thousand strings of cash are being collected.
This means it is actually twenty thousand strings of cash,
yet it is called 'additional collection.'
Why is that?"
The reply was:
"This refers to those who previously escaped assessment and are now newly registered,
and those whose land was previously uncultivated due to lack of labor,
but is now being cultivated."
The Emperor said:
"The old numbers from the general assessment
only consider the increase or decrease in business operations
and the quantity of houses and land,
and then adjust them.
If one person sells land and another buys it,
these are all within the old numbers.
As for business operations,
if one is strong, another is weak;
the strong are increased, and the weak are decreased—that is all.
Moreover, the number of resources is a method for determining levies;
its overall magnitude is not about being more or less.
I fear that what should truly be borne by wealthy households with thriving businesses
is instead being distributed to the poor."
In the sixth month of the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng of Zhāngzōng's reign,
an order was issued to the deputy of the Guóxìnshǐ
to be exempt from increasing material resources (wùlì).
It was also ordered that if farmers had accumulated grain,
they should not be used for material resources.
In prefectures where cash was scarce,
the payment of money was permitted to be converted into grain or silk.
In the ninth month,
due to the overflowing of the Hé in Cáozhōu,
Mǎ Bǎilù and others were dispatched to investigate and assess the poor and needy in the prefectures and counties affected by floods and drowning.
In the fourth month of the first year of Míngchāng,
Lù Bódá, a Lángzhōng of the Xíngbù, and others stated,
"People's land has already been taxed,
and then material resources are uniformly assessed.
Compared to the corvée levied from 'floating wealth' (fú cái),
this constitutes a double imposition."
Accordingly, the material resources on private land were carefully deliberated and assessed,
reducing them by two-tenths.
The Shàngshū Hùbù reported,
"The roads of Zhōngdū and others were affected by water.
An imperial edict commissioned officials to investigate and assess,
resulting in a reduction of over five thousand six hundred strings of cash compared to the previous assessment."
In the eighth month of the third year of Míngchāng,
an imperial decree was issued to the Shàngshūshěng,
"When the people enjoy abundant harvests, they do not bother to accumulate and store.
Once a famine strikes, they immediately suffer from hunger.
What method can make the people value grain and accumulate more?"
The prime ministers replied,
"In the twenty-ninth year,
an imperial edict already exempted farmers who could accumulate grain from material resource levies.
In the early years of Míngchāng,
it was ordered that the material resources of the people, when assessed in conjunction with land,
should also be reduced by two-tenths.
This is indeed the method."
In the first year of Chéng'ān,
the Shàngshūshěng reported
that the assessment was due in the ninth month of that year,
but could not be carried out due to certain circumstances.
An imperial edict stated that as winter was already deep,
it was feared that completing the matter might interfere with farm work,
so it was temporarily suspended.
In the tenth month of winter in the second year,
an imperial edict commanded a discussion on a general inspection (tōngjiǎn).
The prime ministers reported,
"Since the general inspection in the twenty-seventh year of Dàdìng,
ten years have passed.
Many old households have become poor and weak.
If the re-assessment is delayed,
it may lead to their displacement and wandering."
Therefore, a system was established:
for properties already sold or mortgaged,
the assessment would follow the property itself;
households that had split and lived separately were permitted to register separately;
households that had died out or were impoverished and weak were granted reductions or exemptions;
newly prosperous households would be carefully reviewed and increased,
but only according to actual circumstances,
without necessarily meeting the original quota.
Regions along the border that had suffered from raids
were entirely exempt from assessment.
Consequently,
Jiǎ Zhígāng, the Shàngshū of the Lìbù,
and Gāo Rǔlì, the Shìláng of the Lìbù, were ordered to first assess the two Jǐngxúnyuàn in the capital,
to serve as a model for all other roads.
One official was assigned to each road,
and one official from the Tíxíngsī was appointed as their deputy.
In the ninth month of the third year,
it was reported that the assessed material resource tax for the thirteen roads amounted to 2,586,702 strings and 490 cash,
whereas the old quota was 3,022,718 strings and 922 cash.
Due to poverty, 638,111 strings were exempted.
Excluding the Shàngjīng, Běijīng, and Xījīng roads where there were no new increases from prosperous households,
the other roads collectively received an additional 202,095 strings.
In the intercalary twelfth month of the second year of Tàihé,
the Emperor noted that during the assessment (tuīpái),
after inquiring about people's 'floating wealth' and material resources,
there was also an inspection and comparison.
The tight deadline and complex tasks
made it difficult to ascertain the truth.
He therefore issued an edict to the Shàngshūshěng
to establish a method for assessing and collecting people's material resources as needed.
It was ordered that from now on, those who sold or mortgaged property would have their assessment follow the property;
a separate register (biāobù) would be kept,
and at the time of assessment, only 'floating wealth' and material resources would be considered for increase or decrease.
In the twelfth month of the fourth year of Tàihé,
the Emperor noted that for officials serving in distant places, there were instances where their family's material resources should have been exempted but were not.
Therefore, it was stipulated that real estate transactions should be assessed as they occurred.
If there was no 'floating wealth' for operations
and exemptions were due,
the family itself was to report it,
and people from the surrounding neighborhoods and villages would be gathered to publicly announce it.
Once verified,
it would be exempted.
If no one reported after the register was created,
within one month, the official's document would be used for public announcement,
and the fixed entry would be appended to the register.
In the fifth year,
due to Xījīng and Běijīng being border regions constantly afflicted by warfare and famine,
envoys were dispatched to conduct assessments.
The old quota of over 353,000 strings set in the twenty-sixth year of Dàdìng
was reduced to over 287,000 strings.
In the sixth month of the fifth year,
Lǐ Gé, who was serving as Qīannánjīng Ànchásīshì, stated:
"A recent regulation
instructs households to report their material resources for assessment and to keep a marked register.
During a general assessment,
only new prosperous households are added,
and old weak ones are removed,
thus ensuring accuracy.
However, the authorities are now implementing it carelessly,
fearing that at the time of a general assessment, it will be chaotic and merged,
making detailed examination difficult.
A deadline should be set,
and penalties established to enforce it."
Accordingly, it was ordered that from the first day of the eleventh month of that year,
households were to report to have their assessments marked and appended to the register,
to be completed by the first day of the second month of the following year.
Those who failed to report by the deadline would be punished.
Furthermore, all tax offices were ordered
to report all taxed properties
every half-month to their superiors.
Those who violated this would be punished for negligence and treating matters lightly.
It was also decreed that since material resources followed the property,
during a general assessment, only 'floating wealth' should be determined.
In the ninth month of the eighth year,
Jiǎ Shǒuqīan, the Shàngshū of the Lìbù, Púchá Zhāngjiānú, the Zhī Jǐnánfǔ Shì, Wányán Bǎijiā, the Cìshǐ of Jǔzhōu, Sòng Yuánjí, the Zhuǎnyùnshǐ of Nánjīng Lù, and thirteen other officials
were divided among the roads, each accompanied by an official from the local Ànchásī,
to conduct assessments across the various roads.
The Emperor summoned them to the Xiānggé
and personally instructed them, saying:
"I have selected you all to conduct assessments across the roads.
Besides collecting assessments, for newly prosperous or impoverished households,
even though public announcements are made,
those who are impoverished should not be completely written off.
For example, if a household's original material resources were 300 strings,
and now 250 strings are exempted, this might still not be appropriate.
New prosperous households should not be added to their full extent;
their capacity should be measured and preserved.
For instance, if a household could be increased by 300 strings,
only add 200 strings.
You should all do your utmost.
The interests involved in a single assessment will last for ten years.
If you fail in your duty,
the punishment will not be light."
Jiaokanjì
Zhi Volume 28: Food and Money 2: Land System, Rent and Tax, Cattle Tax
Land System.
Land was measured with the Yíngzào Chǐ (construction foot);
five Chǐ made one Bù;
one Bù wide and two hundred forty Bù long made one Mǔ;
one hundred Mǔ made one Qǐng.
People's land ownership was subject to their convenience;
selling or mortgaging to others was not prohibited,
provided that rent was paid according to the land.
For mulberries and jujubes,
households were encouraged to plant many;
those with few were required to plant on three-tenths of their land.
Měng'ān Móukè households with few were required to plant on one-tenth of their land,
removing dead plants and replanting new ones,
to ensure no deficiency.
For all official land,
Měng'ān Móukè and poor people who requested to rent it were granted one hundred Mǔ per able-bodied man in wide-open areas,
and ten Mǔ in narrow areas;
middle-aged men received half.
Those who requested to rent barren land
had their rent set at half the lowest fifth grade,
with collection starting in the eighth year.
Those who had already cultivated land
were taxed at half the seventh grade,
with collection starting in the seventh year.
Those who voluntarily cultivated neighboring land by stealth
paid two-thirds of the official rent.
Those who cultivated land reclaimed from the Yellow River floods
paid rent in the following year.
In the fifth month of the ninth year of Tiānhuì of Tàizōng's reign,
envoys were first dispatched to various roads to promote agriculture.
In the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì of Xīzōng's reign,
the patrol lands between Láiliú and Hùntóng were abolished
and given to the people for cultivation and pasturage.
In the second month of the first year of Zhènglóng of Hǎilíng's reign,
Hégělì Lóushì, the Shàngshū of the Xíngbù, and ten others
were dispatched to travel through Dàxīngfǔ, Shāndōng, and Zhēndìngfǔ
to seize official or idle pasture lands,
as well as lands occupied by officials or commoners, or those belonging to absconded households,
lands cultivated by garrison soldiers beyond what was recorded in the Palace Registry or what was originally owned by officials in other roads,
and lands belonging to monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female Daoist priests in Dàxīngfǔ and Píngzhōu Lù.
This was intended to be granted to the relocated Měng'ān Móukè households,
and also to allow people to apply for cultivation,
so that the government could collect rent.
In the twelfth month of the fifth year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng's reign,
the Emperor noted that Měng'ān households in the Jīngjī (capital region) did not cultivate their own land
and instead cut down mulberry and jujube trees for firewood to sell.
He ordered Wányán Ràng, the Shàoyǐn of Dàxīng, to inspect.
In the fourth month of the tenth year,
the encroachment on cultivated hunting grounds was forbidden.
In the eleventh year,
he said to his attendant officials:
"Last year,
when I was cooling off west of Mount Shānxī,
the roadsides were all cultivated with grain,
leaving almost no grazing land.
I once issued an order
that the people should only cultivate outside a five-lǐ radius.
Now I hear that the people have left for other places because of this,
which is very pitiable.
Let them cultivate as before,
so they do not lose their livelihoods.
All matters that harm the people are problematic when unknown;
if I know, I will certainly not do them.
From now on, if there are similar matters,
you, my ministers, must immediately report them and not conceal them."
In the thirteenth year,
he decreed to the relevant authorities:
"Every year, officials are sent to encourage the agricultural work of the Měng'ān and Móukè,
but I fear this causes annoyance.
From now on, only the officials in charge of each jurisdiction shall supervise and encourage;
those who are negligent or slow shall be impeached and reported."
In the sixth month of the seventeenth year,
Zhào Díjiǎn, a man from Xíngzhōu, submitted a statement saying:
"Official lands not registered along the roads, and river shoals,
are all occupied by powerful families,
while the poor have barren land and heavy taxes.
I request that officials be sent to seize the registers of those who have falsely leased land,
establish rents and levies,
and further reduce the tax numbers for households,
so that the burdens may be fair and balanced."
The edict was sent to the relevant authorities,
and it was about to be implemented but then stopped.
Again, because the official lands granted to the Měng'ān and Móukè near the capital were mostly barren,
and wealthy commoners had been leasing official land for many years,
often falsely claiming it as their own property,
an order was issued to seize their registers.
He also said to the provincial ministers:
"If not for the common people, who would cultivate official land?
However, the Nǚzhí households moved here from their homeland three or four thousand lǐ away,
and all received barren land.
If good land is not seized and redistributed to them,
they will surely become impoverished over time.
Let officials be sent to investigate this."
He also said to Cānzhī Zhèngshì Zhāng Rǔbì:
"I previously sent an inquiry about Nǚzhí land,
and everyone said it was good land.
But when I went hunting,
I asked them,
and they said that since they moved here,
they could not cultivate,
but cut reeds for mats
or cut fodder to sustain themselves.
You, my ministers, should discuss this."
The provincial ministers reported,
"The reason many people conceal and illegally cultivate official land
is because the punishment for it is light."
Thereupon, new regulations were drafted,
setting a deadline for people to declare themselves,
and after the deadline, those who reported others would be rewarded.
Tóngzhī Zhōngdū Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Zhāng Jiǔsī was sent to seize the registers.
In the second month of the nineteenth year,
the Emperor went on a spring hunt.
Seeing that many mulberry trees of the common people were damaged by livestock,
he decreed that for imperial princes, princesses, and powerful families,
if their livestock damaged the people's mulberry trees,
the local county officials were permitted to immediately impose punishment.
In the twelfth month, he said to the grand councilors:
"The lands allocated during the defunct Liáo dynasty
to our dynasty's Yuánshuàifǔ
have already been registered.
Some people may falsely claim unowned land by pointing it out,
and those who lease or newly open wasteland as their own property can be seized.
However, if the land has been sown for many years,
abruptly taking it away
might cause the people to lose their livelihoods."
Thereupon, he ordered the land-registration official Zhāng Jiǔsī to be cautioned.
He further said to the grand councilors:
"I hear that the land-registration efforts are extremely inappropriate.
For example, estates of the empress or imperial prince's bureaus
are merely designated as official land based on their names,
and the proofs held by the common people
are completely disregarded.
Moreover, those who neighbor and falsely occupy official land
are sometimes fortunately spared.
It is my desire
to enable military households to subsist somewhat
and for the people not to lose their livelihoods."
In the fourth month of the twentieth year,
because the road for the imperial procession was narrow,
causing inconvenience for the retinue,
he decreed to the Hùbù that official lands near the roadside relay stations
should not be leased to the common people for cultivation.
He also decreed that the late Grand Tutor Ālǐxiān had been allocated one hundred and forty qǐng of land in the Shāndōng Lù,
and in the early Dàdìng period, another hundred qǐng of land were granted in the Zhōngdū Lù;
he ordered the land in Shāndōng to be confiscated as official property.
In the fifth month,
he instructed the relevant authorities:
"Between Báishímén and Yěhúlǐng,
many of the lakes and ponds are cultivated by the people,
but official and private livestock have no place to graze when passing through.
Officials should be dispatched to register the original wasteland and the number of falsely leased properties."
In the first month of the twenty-first year,
the Emperor said to the grand councilors:
"The people of the Měng'ān and Móukè households in Shāndōng, Dàmíng, and other circuits
are often arrogant and undisciplined,
not personally engaging in farming,
and not allowing their families to work the land,
instead letting Hàn people cultivate for rent.
Wealthy families wear fine silk and brocade,
and indulge in drinking, eating, and banquets,
while the poor eagerly emulate them.
To hope that every household will have enough and every person will be self-sufficient
is difficult.
Recently, the sale of slaves has been forbidden,
and the rituals for auspicious and inauspicious events have been regulated.
Further, officials should be appointed to inspect the actual number of households,
allocate land according to the number of mouths,
and ensure they cultivate it themselves.
Only those truly lacking in labor
will be allowed to lease land from others.
Furthermore, drinking during the farming season is forbidden."
He also said:
"The six Měng'ān of the Xī people
have already moved to Xiánpíng, Línhuáng, and Tàizhōu.
Their land is fertile,
and they are diligent in farming,
each content in their homes.
Have the Nǚzhí people who moved to Xī territory
harvested their beans and grains?"
Zuǒchéng Shǒudào replied:
"I hear they all cultivate themselves,
and their annual needs are sufficient."
The Emperor said:
"That land is fertile and beautiful,
different from other places.
Only the common people near the capital whose crops are damaged by water should be given relief."
In the third month,
those who presented memorials stated
that powerful families often occupied and seized land.
The Emperor said:
"Former Cānzhèng Nàhé Chūnnián occupied eight hundred qǐng of land,
and I also hear that much land in Shānxī is occupied by powerful figures,
with some families having one mouth occupying up to thirty qǐng,
causing small commoners to have no land to cultivate,
and moving to the poor lands of Yīnshān.
How can they survive?
Order that all those who occupy ten qǐng or more of official land be registered and the land confiscated as official property,
to be equally distributed to the poor."
The provincial ministers then reported,
"Chūnnián's son, Měng'ān Cānmóu Hé, and the grandson of the late Grand Tutor Nòuwǎnwēndūn Sīzhōng, Chángshòu, and others,
their relatives numbering over seventy families,
occupied over three thousand qǐng of land."
The Emperor said:
"By autumn,
apart from Niútóu land,
each will still be granted ten qǐng,
and the rest will all be confiscated as official property.
What was seized by the Shānhòu Zhāotǎosī
should also be treated similarly."
He also said to the grand councilors:
"The commoners' land seized in Shāndōng Lù
has already been distributed to Nǚzhí military-farming households.
There is also idle official land that was registered;
return it to the commoners according to the original numbers,
and exempt them from rent and taxes."
In the sixth month,
the Emperor said to the provincial ministers:
"Recently, in Dàxīngfǔ and the prefectures of Píng, Luò, Jì, Tōng, Shùn, etc.,
the areas affected by floods
are exempted from this year's rent and taxes.
For those not affected by floods, temporarily suspend the summer tax,
and collect it when there is a bumper harvest."
At that time, Zhōngdū experienced severe flooding,
while Bīn and Dì prefectures and the area north of the mountains had bumper harvests.
He ordered the roads south of Huáilái to be repaired
to facilitate grain transport.
He also ordered the capital to sell grain at reduced prices.
He further said:
"Recently, envoys were sent to inspect the autumn crops,
and I heard that Měng'ān and Móukè people only care about drinking,
often renting out their land
and pre-borrowing two or three years of rent and levies.
Some sow but do not weed,
allowing the land to become desolate.
From now on, everyone must accurately assess the labor capacity of each household,
how many qǐng and mǔ can be cultivated,
and they must cultivate and weed it themselves.
Only those whose labor is truly insufficient will be allowed to rent.
If lazy farmers drink,
the encouraging-agriculture Móukè, the Měng'ān and Móukè of their jurisdiction, and the Dūguǎn
shall each be punished according to the severity of the offense.
Those with a large harvest shall also be promoted and rewarded according to their grade."
In the seventh month,
the Emperor said to his ministers:
"Previously, households of the imperial clan were moved to Héjiān,
and land was allocated to settle them.
However, their old land was not reclaimed.
How can it be that they occupy both places?
From now on, they should only be granted one place.
The land in Shāndōng taken from the people has already been distributed to Nǚzhí屯tián households,
and there is still surplus land.
This should be returned to the people, and their rent for this year should be waived."
In the eighth month,
the Shàngshūshěng reported the number of land plots in Shāndōng that had been reclaimed.
The Emperor said to Liáng Sù:
"I once asked you about this,
but you did not speak.
Although this is called people's land,
it all lacks clear evidence.
What is wrong with incorporating it as official land?"
He further said:
"The Yellow River has already shifted its old course,
and the waters of Liángshānluò have receded.
The land is very vast,
and emissaries have already been dispatched to settle garrison farms.
The people used to cultivate it freely,
but now the officials have registered the land,
and the people fear being levied for rent,
so many have fled.
If we levy their rent
and punish them for illicit tenancy without immediately reporting it,
it would be appropriate.
However, if we take it abruptly,
it might cause them to lose their livelihood.
Their levies can be waived,
their crimes pardoned,
and other official land granted to them instead."
The Yùshǐtái reported:
"In Dàmíng and Jìzhōu, due to the reclamation of official land in Liángshānluò,
some people's land was also reclaimed."
The Emperor again summoned his ministers and said:
"Even if it has previously undergone inspection and paid taxes,
if there is no clear evidence,
it should be re-inspected.
If there is public evidence,
even if it has been given to the person concerned,
it still needs to be thoroughly investigated."
In the tenth month,
he again discussed the matter of illicitly occupied fields with Zhāng Zhòngyú.
In the 22nd year,
because households attached to the Dūméng'ān did not cultivate their own land,
but leased it all to the people,
with some families of a hundred mouths having not a single sprout in their fields,
the Emperor said:
"What good is the劝nóngguān if he does not persuade and instruct?
Order them to be punished."
The ministers reported:
"Those who do not cultivate their own land but readily give it to others
should be charged with violating regulations."
The Emperor said:
"That is too severe.
How would ignorant people know?"
He then followed the recommendation of Wáng Xiū, the Shàoyǐn of Dàxīng,
that those who did not cultivate be given sixty strokes of the rod,
the Mókè forty strokes,
and the tenant commoners be acquitted.
He also ordered the return and resettlement of the displaced people from Liángshānluò,
with officials providing them with land.
At that time, if people had title deeds and pointed to graves as proof,
they were also detained by officials.
First, Xī Huì, the Cìshǐ of Ēnzhōu, was entrusted to recruit them,
then Zhāng Guójī, the Cìshǐ of Ānsùzhōu, was sent to verify and allocate land to them.
If it had already been allocated to a Méng'ān,
then they would be compensated with official land.
The Emperor said:
"Zhāng Jiǔsī, the Gōngbù Shàngshū, is stubbornly unreasonable.
When he was sent to reclaim official land,
any place names that dated back to the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
such as Chángchéng and Yànzǐchéng,
were all considered official land.
The common people have considered this land their private property for who knows how many hundreds of years.
What he has done shows
extreme unreasonableness."
In the eighth month,
because the four princely estates, including Zhào Wáng Yǒngzhōng, illicitly occupied official land,
their respective Fǔzhǎngshǐ and Fǔyuàn,
and the officials of the six counties Āncì, Xīnchéng, Wǎnpíng, Chāngpíng, Yǒngqīng, and Huáiróu,
were all punished with fines of varying degrees.
In the ninth month,
Yīlà Zào, the Xíngbù Shàngshū, was dispatched to select eight Mókè commoners from within the Méng'ān of Shāndōng Lù,
and move them to the former residences of the Chóu'àn and Qīnggǒu'ér Méng'ān in Héběi Dōng Lù.
Those without oxen were to be provided by officials.
Those of the imperial clan in Héjiān who had not yet moved were ordered to all move to Píngzhōu.
Those without means were to be provided with travel expenses by officials,
and those with infertile land were to have it exchanged for good land.
It had previously been ordered that official land be registered in years of abundant harvest.
By this year,
the provincial ministers again presented this as a memorial.
The Emperor said:
"This was originally for the poverty of the newly relocated four Méng'ān,
who needed official land to be reclaimed and given to them.
If the stipulations proposed by Zhāng Zhòngyú and others are too harsh,
and only land that commoners initially had no right to,
and which had not paid taxes since pacification,
and was presumptuously taken as private property,
is reclaimed,
then
I fear the people will suffer.
It is acceptable to offer compensation.
First, let the households of the Méng'ān and Mókè
be settled appropriately,
and based on their able-bodied men and cattle,
determine the actual amount of land they are entitled to,
and grant it to them.
If it is insufficient,
then supplement it with the more than twenty thousand qǐng of land previously reclaimed.
If it is still insufficient,
then it will be discussed further."
At that time, Luòwù and Pósà and others disputed over sixty thousand qǐng of land in Yìzhōu.
Since neither party had proof,
it was confiscated by the state.
In the 27th year,
many influential households everywhere requested to occupy official land,
then transferred it to others for cultivation and tenancy,
to profit from rents.
It was ordered that officials seize and register the existing amount
and give it to the poor and landless,
with each able-bodied man receiving fifty Mǔ,
so that none would lose their livelihood.
Only if there was still surplus land not fully tenanted were influential families allowed to lease it based on their able-bodied men.
In the fifth month of the 29th year of Dàdìng under Zhāngzōng,
it was proposed to set another deadline
for poor people to apply to lease official land.
Since the deadline had now passed,
and the number was deemed sufficient,
if those who occupied land had a surplus,
allowing accusations and denunciations
might lead to more malpractice.
Moreover, imperial edicts had already abolished
subsequent accusations of undeclared or illicitly transferred land.
Therefore, those who report beyond the deadline should be rejected,
and only the original tenants should be kept.
Furthermore, as Píngyáng Lù was densely populated and had limited land,
all official land should be fully registered
and allocated to the poor based on their able-bodied men.
The Emperor said:
"Those who report excessive tenancy of official land beyond the deadline
should be rejected,
which is correct.
However, if there is no owner or if they are unwilling to lease,
then others may apply to lease.
As for Píngyáng Lù, the land should be limited according to the number of able-bodied men.
For example, if a family with three able-bodied men owns only thirty Mǔ,
then they may retain an additional one qǐng and twenty Mǔ of the official land they lease,
and the remainder should be registered and given to the poor."
In the seventh month,
an imperial edict was issued to the Shàngshūshěng, stating:
“The areas of Táng, Dèng, Yǐng, Cài, Sù, and Sì
are fertile lands, both by water and land.
If their grades are verified,
and annual rents are set accordingly,
with an extended deadline for collection,
then people can be recruited to tenant them,
which would benefit both public and private interests.
Currently, much of the borderland in Hénán is illicitly occupied by powerful families.
If people migrate to those areas,
they should be recruited to cultivate the land.
This would not only provide for the poor
but also increase official rents.
Those who are granted land and farming tools as able-bodied men
shall be exempted from rent and taxes.”
In the eighth month,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
“Hédōng has narrow land,
and even a slight famine leads to continuous flight.
We humbly suggest that Hénán has vast land but is sparsely populated.
If we allow the recruitment of migrants from other circuits,
and grant them idle land,
the number of starving people in Hédōng will decrease,
and Hénán will no longer have vacant land.”
The Emperor approved the request.
On the day Wùyín of the ninth month,
it was further reported:
“According to existing regulations,
those who request to tenant idle government land are exempted from rent and levies for five years.
Now, we request exemption for eight years,
which might encourage more reclamation.”
Both requests were approved.
In the eleventh month,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
“For people who, verified as able-bodied, tenant barren idle government land in Hénán:
if they wish to cultivate it as government land, they are exempted from rent for eight years;
if they wish to make it their own property, they are exempted from tax for three years.
In neither case is trading, pawning, or selling permitted.
If powerful families or government officials have illicitly tenanted land,
they are given two months to confess,
in which case they will be pardoned and granted the land in full.
Their tax will be determined by assessing neighboring land,
with a one-third reduction.
After the deadline, anyone may report such cases and be granted the land.”
The edict was approved.
In the second month of Míngchāng first year [1190 CE],
an imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities, stating:
“For people's land near water
that has been planted but then submerged by water,
they may be granted nearby government land in exchange.”
In the third month,
an imperial order stated:
“The land received by soldiers
shall only be cultivated by themselves.
Only those lacking sufficient labor may allow others to tenant it.
They shall only pay rent based on the local produce.
Those who wish to pay in money may do so according to their preference.
Those unwilling to tenant shall not be forced.”
In the sixth month,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
“A recent regulation, noting that Měng'ān Móukè households do not diligently plant mulberries and fruit trees,
has already stipulated that one *mǔ* must be planted for every ten *mǔ*.
Now, we request that all judicial commissioners of various circuits and their subordinate prefectures and counties be instructed again
to persuade the households.
If anyone fails to plant, or if their planting falls short of three-tenths,
they shall be penalized according to the severity of their negligence.”
The imperial edict approved it.
In the eighth month,
an imperial order stated:
“For idle government land in various places,
those that have already been tenanted by the common people shall remain as they are.
Those not yet tenanted shall be handed over to the Túntián Měng'ān Móukè.”
In the sixth month of the third year [1192 CE],
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
“The judicial commissioners of the Nánjīng and Shǎnxī circuits stated that
the old pasturage has long not been allocated,
leading to lawsuits between military and civilian households.
Officers were recently dispatched to various circuits to settle these matters.
Whenever civilian households have verified private property,
as well as houses, wells, tombs, and gardens,
which have already been rectified and granted,
and if there is also government land within them,
it has also been exchanged for an equivalent area.
The pasturage in the two circuits:
Nánjīng circuit has over 63,520 *qǐng*,
and Shǎnxī circuit has over 35,680 *qǐng*.”
In the fifth year [1194 CE],
an imperial edict was issued to the Shàngshūshěng:
“The Jurchen and Han Chinese people in circuits like Liáodōng
may all be ordered to engage in sericulture according to their capability.”
In the second month,
a person submitted a proposal to establish a system of merit and demerit for chief officials based on agricultural promotion.
Consequently, regulations were established:
“Those who can promote agricultural fields
shall be awarded ten *liǎng* of silver and ten *pǐ* of silk annually for a Móukè,
and twice that for a Měng'ān.
County officials shall be promoted by five ranks within their grade.
Those who are diligent for three years shall have their Měng'ān Móukè promoted one rank,
and county officials promoted one grade.
If fields are barren by one-tenth, they shall receive thirty strokes of the cane.
If the proportion increases, it leads to one year of penal servitude.
If they are barren for three consecutive years,
the Měng'ān Móukè shall be demoted one rank,
and county officials shall be demoted according to the promotion system.”
This became a permanent regulation.
In the second month of the sixth year [1195 CE],
an imperial edict abolished the land survey in Shǎnxī.
Furthermore, the Shǎnxī judicial commissioner stated:
“The households and people in this circuit operate watermills and oil presses.
The area they occupy on private land is taxed,
and on government land, rent is collected.
If they also have to pay water conservancy fees in silver,
this constitutes a double burden.
We request its abolition.”
The provincial officials reported:
“The water conservancy fees in silver are used to support the circuit's expenses
and cannot be abolished yet.
It is appropriate to exempt them from tax and rent
based on the actual occupied land area.”
It was ordered that other circuits follow this as a model.
In Chéng'ān second year [1197 CE],
Shàngguān Yú, a director in the Ministry of Revenue, was dispatched to Xījīng and along the border
to encourage military and civilian households to cultivate land.
Lǐ Jìngyì, another director in the Ministry of Revenue, was also dispatched to circuits like Línhuáng to plan agricultural affairs.
An old regulation stipulated
that land granted to soldiers could not be rented out to others,
and violators would have their crops confiscated by the landowner.
In the ninth month of Tàihé fourth year [1204 CE], new regulations were established:
For the allocated land within ten *lǐ*, the amount to be self-cultivated
was forty *mǔ* per able-bodied man,
with subsequently added able-bodied men receiving the same.
The remainder could be rented out conveniently or jointly cultivated by mutual agreement.
Violators would have their money and property returned to the original owner.
The Emperor heard that during the land survey in the six circuits,
many military households in the *túntián* system had falsely increased their registered population
to request government land,
and also encompassed civilian land.
As a result, some civilians had to pay taxes in vain and suffered losses of resources.
Many of those who responded to the imperial edict to express their views discussed this issue.
In the second month of the fifth year [1205 CE],
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
“If officials are dispatched again
to investigate based on old records,
when will the disputes cease?”
Consequently, it was ordered that for those who had paid taxes in vain, and whose payments had already been remitted to the government,
the amount would be continuously deducted from their taxes annually.
In Tàihé seventh year [1207 CE],
people were recruited to cultivate land in Qīnghé and other areas,
and its rent was distributed as food for geese and ducks in various spring water locations.
In the eighth month of the eighth year [1208 CE],
Gāo Rǔlì, the Minister of Revenue, stated:
“According to old regulations,
households requesting to tenant barren land
had their rent set at half the rate of the lowest fifth grade in each circuit,
and were exempted from payment for eight years.
If they made it their own property,
they were taxed at half the rate of the seventh grade,
and also exempted from payment for three years.
Those who confessed to illicitly occupying neighboring land
had their rent set at two-thirds of the standard.
Those who requested to tenant land from the receding Yellow River banks
paid rent from the second year.
Previously, common people did not plan for the long term,
and when it was time to pay rent, many cleverly avoided it,
or requested to withdraw.
This was because the initial exemption period was too long,
and there was no one to guarantee or acknowledge their tenancy at the beginning.
Now, those who request tenancy shall be exempted for three years.
Those who make it their own property shall be exempted for one year.
Those who confess to illicit occupation and those who request land from receding banks
shall all pay rent in the current year,
with local leaders acting as guarantors and certifiers,
to establish a lasting system.”
In the seventh month of the third year of Zhēnyòu of Xuānzōng,
since the military households of Héběi had been relocated to Hénán,
the discussion was about how to settle them.
The chief ministers said:
"We should designate official land and pastureland to be distributed to them.
For land already leased by commoners, we should wait until after the autumn harvest,
and continue to provide one shèng of rice daily,
offsetting it with paper money."
Shímò Shìjī, Grand Master of Ceremonies, said:
"Reclaiming barren land and pastureland is laborious.
If we seize land already cultivated by commoners, they will lose their livelihoods.
Moreover, military households generally lack oxen.
It would be better to order military households to send some people back to their original professions,
and return in spring,
as a strategy for solid defense."
The emperor ultimately followed the chief ministers' proposal,
and was about to survey the land.
Shìyùshǐ Liú Yuánguī submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that the court has a proposal to survey land,
and all who hear it are shocked and dismayed.
Previously, Héběi and Shāndōng undertook this measure,
and the people's graves and wells were all taken by the military,
leading to grievances and disputes that have not ceased to this day.
If this is implemented again,
it will greatly lose the hearts of the people.
Barren land cannot be cultivated;
there is only the name of having land,
but no actual benefit.
Even if fertile land is obtained,
they cannot cultivate it themselves,
and would have to lease it back to the commoners.
The gains would be minimal,
and it would cause widespread suffering."
The emperor had a great realization
and abolished the plan.
In the eighth month,
as there was no definite conclusion regarding the land survey,
the north encroached upon Hénán.
Consequently, all military households from various circuits were mobilized to come south,
to collectively plan for defense and preservation,
but they did not know how to secure military provisions.
The general consensus was that officials could be dispatched to gather elders and inquire,
whether increasing taxes,
or giving military land,
which of the two was more convenient.
Cānzhèng Gāo Rǔlì said:
"Official and private lands in Hénán are roughly half and half.
Also, many households entirely lease official land.
If it is suddenly taken away,
how will they live?
Common people are easily moved and hard to pacify.
At one point, to avoid taxes, they might speak of abandoning their fields.
But if given to others, would they not regret it?
Regret would lead to resentment.
As during the land allocation in Shāndōng,
fertile land all went to wealthy families,
while barren land was given to poor households.
This brought no benefit to the military,
but harmed the people.
We should only double the official rent
to supply military provisions,
and then proportionally distribute official barren land and pastureland
for them to cultivate themselves.
Then the people will not lose their livelihoods,
and the officials will not oppress the people."
This was followed.
In the tenth month of the third year,
Gāo Rǔlì said:
"Nearly a million military households from Héběi have relocated to Hénán.
Each person is given one shèng of rice daily,
which annually costs three million six hundred thousand dàn of grain.
Even if half is paid in cash,
it still requires three million dàn of grain.
The rented land in Hénán totals two hundred forty thousand qǐng,
with an annual rent of only one million five hundred sixty thousand.
I request that beyond regular expenses, double the amount be levied to supply them."
So, five people, including Yòusījiàn Féng Kāi, were ordered to divide and go to various prefectures,
and directly assign thirty mǔ of cultivable official barren land and pastureland
to each person.
In the eleventh month,
it was again discussed to survey barren land and pastureland for horses to be given to the military.
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Gāo Rǔlì was ordered to oversee it.
Rǔlì returned and reported:
"The current number of qǐng and mǔ is much less compared to the old records.
Moreover, much of it is barren and infertile, unfit for cultivation.
If only cultivable land is distributed to them, each person will receive very little.
Also, for remote areas, they would have to relocate to occupy it.
They cannot cultivate it themselves
and would surely give it to others,
and then rent would have to be collected from hundreds of lǐ away.
Moreover, even existing farmland cannot be fully cultivated now;
how can there be any surplus effort to cultivate barren land overgrown with thickets and tangled roots?
The military cannot rely on this for food;
this is certain.
Now, when I inquire with the military households,
they all say: 'Receiving half rations is still enough to sustain ourselves.
If we are given land but cannot cultivate it,
and our rations are also stopped,
what will we rely on?'
I know that when the land was initially registered,
its actual state was never inspected,
which is why the numbers do not match,
and the locations are incorrect.
If we were to re-examine the prefectures and counties,
they would surely each falsely comply with the imperial directive,
summoning and investigating endlessly to fulfill the command.
If the numbers are insufficient,
they will falsely designate private land to make up the difference,
which will cause widespread unrest.
Currently, the people's taxes and corvée are three times the usual.
They are constantly busy with transport and supply,
with no time to spare,
and if this measure is imposed again,
how can they endure it?
Furthermore, military households are temporarily relocated,
and there is a time for their return.
Why cause such suffering to the people with this?
Even if it harms the people but benefits the military, it should not be done,
let alone when there is no benefit whatsoever.
I only ask Your Majesty to consider this carefully."
So, an imperial edict was issued to abolish the land distribution,
and only half rations and half cash payment were given.
In the fourth year,
officials were again dispatched to survey the pastureland for horses in Hénán.
After the numbers were registered,
the emperor ordered the ministries and the Censorate to discuss how to distribute it to the military.
The chief ministers said:
"Currently, there are over four hundred forty-eight thousand military households to be supplied with grain.
It is calculated that each person would receive a little over six mǔ,
but those who come later are not included.
However, how can those living hundreds of lǐ away come for the sake of six mǔ?
Moreover, the monthly rations cannot be suddenly stopped.
We humbly believe that military households who wish to lease land should be given it according to their number of mouths.
For those in remote areas who do not wish to,
it should be in accordance with the recent regulation,
which allows military and common people to cultivate official barren land.
Let military and common people occupy and plant it."
The Censorate officials said:
"Pastureland for horses is scarce,
and it has long been barren and difficult to cultivate.
Military households also lack farming tools.
However, if it is not given to them,
then besides their own rations,
they will have no other source of food,
which is not a strategy to preserve strength and await the enemy.
If it is given, their rations cannot be immediately reduced either.
If we can wait for a few years,
until some order is established,
official provisions can gradually be reduced.
Now, taking from those with ability
and giving to those without ability
may make cultivation impossible.
We request that county officials encourage and lead common households
to lend oxen to break the barren land,
and then distribute it next spring.
County officials who can lead common households to assist in cultivation without causing unrest
should be appropriately rewarded,
so that they may be encouraged."
The chief ministers again said:
"If that were the case,
county officials, coveting rewards,
would surely coerce and distribute,
leading to public disturbance.
Currently, common households raise oxen according to the size of their land.
Moreover, in recent years, as soon as farm work is completed, they must exert all efforts for transport and supply, fearing they might not be quick enough.
How could they have time to cultivate others' fields?
Only our previous proposal is convenient."
An imperial edict ordered a re-discussion.
It was then proposed that commoners who could reclaim pastureland for horses and official barren land into cultivated fields
would be given half as permanent property,
and the other half to military households.
The memorial was approved.
In the fourth year,
the ministries reported:
"Since ancient times, when engaged in warfare,
both cultivation and fighting were carried out,
thus ensuring sufficiency of both soldiers and food.
Now, the various commanders have divided their troops, numbering no less than a million,
and once they join the ranks, they all rely on the government.
As for their wives and children, they stay at home, sitting idly and waiting to be fed,
not knowing that military farming is a long-term strategy.
We wish for a clear imperial edict
to order the various commanderies to have their troops cultivate the land,
which is also a strategy of resting and awaiting the weary."
The imperial edict complied with this.
In the first month of Xīngdìng (興定) 3rd year (1219),
Hóu Zhì (侯摯), the Right Chancellor of the Department of State Affairs and concurrently supervisor of the Three Agencies, said:
"Based on the total cultivated land of military and civilian households in Hénán (河南), which amounts to over 1,970,000 qǐng,
the currently cultivated area is over 960,000 qǐng.
Superior land can yield one shí and two dòu,
medium land one shí,
and inferior land eight dòu.
If one-eleventh is collected,
the annual yield will be 9,600,000 shí.
This would be ample to cover annual expenditures,
and also ensure fairness between rich and poor,
and that all, great and small, find their proper place.
I tried implementing this in Dōngpíng (東平) for two or three years,
and the people were not exhausted while military supplies were sufficient."
An imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to deliberate on its implementation.
In the tenth month of the 4th year (1220),
Yílà Bùyán (移剌不言) said:
"Military households have been moved to Hénán (河南),
but after several years, land has not yet been allocated to them.
Furthermore, with frequent migrations,
they cannot settle down,
hence many are impoverished.
I request that all official lands in various garrisons be surveyed
and each person be granted thirty亩 (mǔ).
They should also not be moved to other garrisons.
If this is done, military households can find their place,
and official grain expenses can gradually decrease."
The chief ministers reported:
"Previously, there were also proposals for land grants,
but the Privy Council considered it something to be implemented when affairs were less urgent.
Now Hénán (河南) has suffered from floods,
and many people have become displaced.
The amount of wheat sown is less than 50,000 qǐng,
which is probably more than half less than in previous years.
The annual income is likely insufficient.
If land is allocated as permanent property,
and their household grain allowance is ceased once they have a harvest,
it would also be a way to save expenses."
The emperor assented.
Furthermore, due to the floods in Hénán (河南),
more than half of the households were in arrears,
and the fields were desolate.
Fearing that tax revenue would be low and national expenditure would be insufficient,
an order was issued for the water-affected fields in Táng (唐), Dèng (鄧), Yù (裕), Cài (蔡), Xī (息), Shòu (壽), Yǐng (潁), Bó (亳) and Guīdé Fǔ (歸德府)
that were already dry to be sown with seeds,
and those not yet drained to be planted with rice.
Households resuming their livelihood would be exempt from their original rent and all corvée duties.
Those who could substitute for others in farming would receive the same treatment.
Officials who imposed arbitrary levies would be punished for violating regulations.
Those lacking oxen and food would have rich households lend to them.
In the first month of the 5th year (1221),
Shímò Wòlǔ (石抹斡魯), Administrator of the Three Agencies for Jīngnán (京南), said:
"In the three routes of Jīngnán (京南), Dōng (東), and Xī (西),
there are 400,000 garrisoned soldiers, old and young.
The annual grain expenditure is over 1,400,000 shí,
all of which is consumed from civilian rent.
This is a very poor plan.
It would be advisable to survey the old cultivated lands of households in arrears.
The Jīngnán (京南) route alone has over 398,500 qǐng of old reclaimed land,
of which over 99,000 qǐng are official lands cultivated by the people.
Now, more than half of the hungry people are displaced.
The situation in the Dōng (東), Xī (西), and Nán (南) routes is similar.
Although the court encourages them to resume their livelihoods,
the people fear that after resuming, their livelihood will not be stable while levies will follow,
so they often hide and do not come out.
If thirty mǔ are distributed to each military household,
allowing them to cultivate it themselves,
or to invite others to farm it,
then after a few years, their accumulated wealth will gradually become abundant,
and official grain allowances can be abolished."
The provincial ministers were ordered to deliberate on this,
but it could not be implemented.
Rent and Taxes.
Under the Jīn (金) system,
official land paid rent (zū),
while private land paid tax (shuì).
The system of rent is not transmitted.
Generally, land was divided into nine grades, and differentiated accordingly.
For the summer tax, three hé per mǔ was collected.
For the autumn tax, five shēng per mǔ was collected.
Additionally, one bundle of straw was submitted,
each bundle weighing fifteen jīn.
The summer tax period was from the sixth month to the eighth month,
and the autumn tax period was from the tenth month to the twelfth month,
divided into three deadlines: early, middle, and late.
For prefectures beyond three hundred lǐ,
the deadline was extended by one month.
For garrison households cultivating official land,
the relevant authorities would instruct the méng'ān谋克 (mouke) to supervise them.
In Tàihé (泰和) 5th year (1205),
Zhāngzōng (章宗) instructed his chief ministers, saying:
"In the tenth month, the people have not yet finished harvesting.
Is it appropriate to immediately order them to pay taxes?"
The beginning of the autumn tax deadline was changed to the eleventh month.
In Zhōngdū (中都), Xījīng (西京), Běijīng (北京), Shàngjīng (上京), Liáodōng (遼東), Línhuáng (臨潢), and Shǎnxī (陝西), where the climate was cold
and crops matured late, the beginning of the summer tax deadline was set as the seventh month.
For all transport of grain and wheat,
for distances beyond three hundred lǐ,
five shēng per shí was reduced,
and for every additional three hundred lǐ, another five shēng was progressively reduced.
For millet converted to straw, for every hundred chēng,
within one hundred lǐ, three chēng was reduced;
within two hundred lǐ, five chēng was reduced;
less than three hundred lǐ, eight chēng was reduced;
and for three hundred lǐ and for those submitting actual grass,
ten chēng was reduced respectively.
Based on the people's cultivated fields, gardens, residences, vehicles, livestock, capital for planting,
and the amount of stored cash,
different amounts of money were levied,
which was called 'wealth tax' (wùlìqián).
When corvée duties were imposed,
the household registers were consulted,
and the wealthy were targeted first.
If resources were equal, the household's category (A or B) was determined by the number of able-bodied men.
If there was an extraordinary levy,
it was assessed based on wealth,
distributed evenly from the largest to the smallest households.
If some cases could not be divided or extracted,
they were typically assisted by the next household in line.
Regarding the people's wealth,
their residences were not included.
However, outside of the residences of méng'ān (猛安) and mouke (謀克) households, prison households, and official households,
privately acquired civilian land and houses
were included in the count.
Cemetery land and school land
were exempt from both rent, tax, and wealth tax.
For people who petitioned for exemption due to floods or droughts,
