in Hénán (河南), Shāndōng (山東), Hédōng (河東), Dàmíng (大名), Jīngzhào (京兆), Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), and the affiliated prefectures within Zhāngdé (彰德) Department,
the deadline for summer fields was the fourth month,
and for autumn fields, the seventh month.
For other routes, summer fields were by the fifth month,
and autumn fields by the eighth month.
For paddy fields, the general deadline was the eighth month.
If there was an intercalary month, the deadline was extended by half a month.
Petitions submitted after the deadline were not processed.
For extraordinary disasters, there was no deadline.
Those with losses of eight-tenths or more were fully exempt.
Those with losses of seven-tenths were exempt for the amount lost.
Those with losses of six-tenths were fully taxed.
If mulberry trees were damaged and silkworms could not be raised,
the tax on silk, floss, and silk fabric was exempted.
The amount of rainfall and snow, and the harvest yield of crops in all routes,
were reported monthly to the Board of Revenue via express couriers.
All households of officials ranked in the nine grades
were exempt from miscellaneous corvée,
and for what they should pay based on their wealth,
they only paid hired labor money.

Those who had made contributions to obtain official positions but had not yet reached the status of hereditary privilege for descendants, and all those with a formal entry into officialdom (referring to clerks, interpreters, etc.),

those holding substantive official posts with concurrent honorary titles, those in miscellaneous ranks of the five grades and below, and those in regular ranks who had accepted concurrent honorary titles but had not yet taken up substantive posts,
their descendants and cohabiting brothers,
down to those who had passed the final imperial examinations and registered students, including medical students,
were all exempt from personal corvée.
For families with three generations living together, if their household was already honored, they were exempt from corvée duties and levies,
and after three years, exempt from miscellaneous corvée.
In Tiānhuì (天會) 1st year (1123) of Tàizōng (太宗),
an imperial edict instructed the relevant authorities to lighten corvée and taxes,
and encourage agriculture.
In the 10th year (1132),
seeing that the corvée and tax burden among the literati and common people of Liáo (遼) differed,
an imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities
to equalize them all.
In the twelfth month of Tiānjuàn (天眷) 5th year (1138)
In Huángtǒng (皇統) 3rd year (1143),
the people's outstanding taxes were remitted.
In the fifth month of Dàdìng (大定) 2nd year (1162) of Shìzōng (世宗),
he told his chief ministers:
"For all corvée duties,
they should be equally distributed among strong households,
and not unfairly imposed on poor households."
Someone suggested that due to insufficient expenditure,
they should request advance collection of rent and taxes from the Héběi (河北) East and West routes and Zhōngdū (中都).
The emperor said that although national expenditure was insufficient,
the people's strength was even more difficult,
and thus did not approve it.
In the 3rd year (1163),
due to a poor harvest,
an edict was issued to exempt rent and taxes for two years.
Another edict said:
"I have previously allowed the Marshal's Office to act as it deemed appropriate.
Now I hear that in Hénán (河南), Shǎnxī (陝西), Shāndōng (山東), east of Běijīng (北京), and the northern border prefectures,
there have been many levies and requisitions.
However, the provincial department also levies taxes and corvée in the same way as other prefectures,
which constitutes a double burden.
Therefore, based on what the Marshal's Office has already collected,
these should be remitted and removed."
In the 5th year (1165),
the relevant authorities were ordered
to remit taxes in all areas affected by locusts, drought, or floods.
In the 6th year (1166),
due to floods in Héběi (河北) and Shāndōng (山東),
their rent was exempted.
In the tenth month of the eighth year,
Gāo Chāngfú (高昌福), the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Zhāngdé Prefecture (彰德軍), submitted a memorial stating that the taxes and rents were too heavy.
The Emperor (Shàng 上) instructed Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士) Zhāng Jǐngrén (張景仁), saying:
“The current tax law is much lighter than in recent times,
yet it is considered heavy.
Why is this?”
Jǐngrén (景仁) replied:
“Current taxes are indeed light.
If not for taxes, where would the nation's expenses come from?”
In the second month of the second year,
the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) reported
that the granaries throughout the realm held over 27.9 million shí (石) of grain.
The Emperor (Shàng 上) said:
“I have heard that a nation without nine years of reserves is not truly a nation.
It is for this reason that I have surveyed all the land under heaven to equalize the levies,
collecting nine million shí (石) annually.
Of this, seven million shí (石) are for regular expenses.
Another two million shí (石) are for exemptions due to floods and droughts, and for relief loans.
Only a mere one million shí (石) remain.
I accumulate stores widely
to prepare for famine.
The common people consider the taxes heavy,
and petty officials, to gain popular acclaim,
also often criticize them.
They do not consider the nation's preparations for emergencies.”
In the first month of the twelfth year,
due to floods and droughts, last year's rents and taxes were remitted in Zhōngdū (中都), Xījing (西京), Nánjing (南京), Héběi (河北), Hédōng (河東), Shāndōng (山東), and Shǎnxī (陝西).
In the thirteenth year,
the Emperor (Shàng 上) said to his chief ministers (zǎichén 宰臣):
“Regarding the levies on the common people,
the amount remitted has already exceeded half.
Fearing that the common people may not be fully aware,
and that officials may exploit this for wrongdoing,
still collecting the old amounts,
let it be proclaimed by public notice in all localities.”
In the tenth month,
an imperial edict stated that if local and county officials (zhōuxiàn guān 州縣官) did not diligently press for the collection of rents and taxes,
leading to arrears,
their salaries could be withheld
until the full amount was collected,
and then disbursed.
In the first month of the sixteenth year,
an imperial edict remitted the rents and taxes for those circuits affected by floods and droughts the previous year.
In the seventeenth year,
the Emperor (Shàng 上) asked his chief ministers (zǎichén 宰臣):
“The old tribute and taxes from Liáodōng (遼東) were over 60,000 shí (石).
After a full inspection, it became nearly 200,000.
How were needs met when it was 60,000,
and how much has been accumulated after it became 200,000?”
The Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部) investigated and reported
that previously, expenses could be met due to the small number of officials.
Now, the number of officials, soldiers, and the elderly is large,
thus expenses are greater.
The Emperor (Shàng 上) said:
“We must investigate the truth
and not allow wasteful spending.”
In the third month of the seventeenth year,

an imperial edict remitted last year's rents and taxes for ten circuits, including Héběi (河北), Shāndōng (山東), Shǎnxī (陝西), Hédōng (河東), Xījing (西京), and Liáodōng (遼東), which were affected by drought and locusts.
In the first month of the eighteenth year,
the rents and taxes for circuits such as Zhōngdū (中都), Héběi (河北), Hédōng (河東), Shāndōng (山東), Hénán (河南), and Shǎnxī (陝西), which suffered disasters the year before last, were remitted.
In the autumn of the nineteenth year,
in Zhōngdū (中都), Xījing (西京), Héběi (河北), Shāndōng (山東), Hédōng (河東), and Shǎnxī (陝西), over 137,700 qǐng (頃) of agricultural land were damaged by floods and droughts,
and an imperial edict remitted their rents.
In the third month of the twentieth year,
due to disasters in Zhōngdū (中都), Xījing (西京), Héběi (河北), Shāndōng (山東), Hédōng (河東), and Shǎnxī (陝西) the previous year,
an imperial edict remitted their rents and taxes.
Based on the advice of Cáo Wàngzhī (曹望之), Minister (Shàngshū 尚書) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部),
an imperial edict reduced the taxes of Fūyán (鄜延) and Hédōng Nánlù (河東南路) by over 520,000 shí (石),
and increased the taxes of Héběi Xīlù (河北西路) by 88,000 shí (石).
Another imperial edict stipulated that for all grain taxes from areas not vital for border defense,
except for the designated storage amount,
people were allowed to commute payments as convenient.
In the ninth month of the twenty-first year,
due to floods in Zhōngdū (中都),
rents were remitted.
Previously, people living near official roads who provided oxen and laborers for transport
were compensated by collecting money from households elsewhere that had not been conscripted for service.
In the twenty-third year,
Wáng Zhòngguī (王仲規) from Zōngzhōu (宗州) complained, requesting the return of the money collected for the conscripted oxen and laborers.
The provincial officials (shěngchén 省臣) reported this.
The Emperor (Shàng 上) said:
“Since they have already served,
to again collect money from them,
though this was done before,
I fear the allocated money might not reach the original households.
This is inconvenient for both.
It would be better to simply count the service rendered
and remit rents, taxes, and courier post money (pūmǎqián 鋪馬錢).
Calculate the actual number and report it.
If a fixed price for hiring is also needed, it must be decided.”
The responsible authorities reported the figures,
estimating an annual payment of over 64,000 guàn (貫),
equivalent to over 86,000 shí (石) of grain.
The Emperor (Shàng 上) further decreed
that from now on, households conscripting oxen and laborers
should be selected from those residing within thirty lǐ (里) of the road.
In the twenty-sixth year,
for military and civilian lands affected by floods and droughts,
210,000 qǐng (頃) were exempted from taxes, totaling over 490,000 shí (石).
In the sixth month of the twenty-seventh year,
rents and taxes for military and civilian households in Zhōngdū (中都), Héběi (河北), and other circuits that had suffered from river breaches and floods were remitted.
In the eleventh month,
an imperial edict stated that for farmland inundated by overflowing river water,
a one-year exemption from corvée taxes (chāshuì 差稅) would be granted.
Huái (懷), Wèi (衞), Méng (孟), and Zhèng (鄭) — the four prefectures that engaged in labor to block the river —
were also exempted from this year's corvée taxes (chāshuì 差稅).
In Dàdìng (大定) twenty-ninth year of Zhāngzōng (章宗),
one-tenth of the people's rents were pardoned.
For Hédōng Nánběilù (河東南北路), the reduction was proportionate.
The Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) reported
that much of the land in these two circuits consisted of steep slopes,
and barren land was often cultivated only once every two years.
If reductions were not made according to land grade,
it would be unfair.
Therefore, an imperial edict specifically granted an additional one-tenth reduction beyond the pardoned amount,
a further one-tenth reduction for medium-grade land,
and a two-tenths reduction for low-grade land.
According to the old system,
summer and autumn taxes were paid in three items: wheat, millet, and fodder.
Since the required items varied by locality,
the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部) again ordered that various necessary items could be used for payment in commutation.
A petitioner to the throne stated that this was impractical.
The Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部) argued that if this were done, items needed in various circuits would have to be purchased,
which would further trouble the people.
Thus, the Tàifǔjiān (太府監) was ordered
to handle the commuted payments for items designated for the imperial palace and its needs.
For firewood and straw used in the maintenance of the Yellow River, the value was increased by two qián (錢) for commuted payment.
For materials like wood and stone used along the Yellow River banks, which were not native products,
the local authorities were ordered to procure them,
and other commuted payments were abolished.
In the fourth month of Míngchāng (明昌) first year,
a petitioner to the throne requested
a reduction in the people's rents and taxes,
fearing that stored grain might spoil over time.
The provincial officials (shěngchén 省臣) reported:
“We have deliberated.
In Dàdìng (大定) eighteenth year, Cáo Wàngzhī (曹望之), Minister (Shàngshū 尚書) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部), reported
that taxes in Hédōng (河東) and Fūyán (鄜延) circuits were quite heavy,
and thus over 520,000 shí (石) were reduced.
Last year, one-tenth was pardoned,
and barren land in Hédōng (河東) was further reduced.
Now, with annual income barely exceeding expenditure,
should there be a flood or drought,
we would both remit revenue
and issue grain for relief.
Without reserves, this is impossible.
If we reduce taxes again,
how will we cope?
If spoilage is a concern,
order all circuits to sun-dry the grain in time
to prevent deterioration.
Violators will be punished according to the law.”
The edict was approved.
In the eleventh month,
the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) reported:
“For abandoned official land in Hénán (河南),
people are permitted to apply for tenancy based on their household size.
Those who wish to remain official tenants are exempted from rent for eight years.
Those who wish to claim ownership are exempted from taxes for three years.”
An imperial edict approved this.
In the second month of Míngchāng (明昌) second year,
an imperial edict stated that from now on, if people reported damage from floods or droughts,
an official should immediately be appointed to investigate the facts,
report to the relevant prefecture,
and notify the Tíxíngsī (提刑司).
Only after the joint inspection by the relevant authorities was completed
could the land be plowed anew.
In the sixth month of the third year,
the authorities reported damage in Hézhōu (河州),
and that some starving people still had not paid their rents.
An imperial edict remitted these.
In the ninth month,
due to disasters in three circuits of Shāndōng (山東) and Héběi (河北),
the provisional rents (quángé zhī zū 權閣之租) and loaned grain
were ordered to be collected only when there was a year of abundance.
When the Emperor (Shàng 上) went to Qiūshān (秋山),
half of the summer and autumn rents and taxes for households passing through the imperial hunting ground were remitted for the current year.
In the tenth month of winter of the fourth year,
when the Emperor (Shàng 上) traveled,
he issued an edict to the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省), saying:
“In counties like Hǎirún (海壖) and Shíchéng (石城),
the land is barren and the people are poor,
planting only millet and sorghum.
When paying taxes to the officials,
they must exchange it for grain.
Either allow them to pay only what they produce,
or reduce their taxes according to the Hédōng Lù (河東路) model.
A final decision shall be made and reported upon my return to the capital.”
In the fifth year,
an imperial edict remitted the autumn rents for people affected by river breaches.
In the fourth month of the fourth year of Tài'hé,
due to prolonged drought, an imperial edict was issued, taking the blame,
and remitting this year's summer tax for the drought-affected prefectures and counties.
In the ninth month,
a petitioner stated that for the absconding households in Héjiān and Cāngzhōu,
their property tax amounted to several thousand guàn,
but their corvée assignments
were entirely levied by officials on the existing households,
which the people could no longer bear.
An edict ordered the Ànchásī
to exempt land and property taxes related to their livelihoods,
and for the time being, to suspend the collection of taxes on their floating assets.
In the first month of the fifth year,
an edict instructed officials
that for those places visited by the emperor three times or more since the third year of Tài'hé,
the households that had been levied would be specifically exempted from half a year's rent and tax.
In the fifth month of the eighth year,
〔一五〕as the Sòng dynasty planned for peace,
an edict was issued to the empire,
exempting Hénán, Shāndōng, and Shǎnxī's six circuits from this year's summer tax,
and Hédōng, Héběi, Dàmíng, and five other circuits from half of it.
In the eighth month,
an edict stated that farmers in all circuits who applied to lease wasteland
would be exempted from rent and tax for three years,
and those who cultivated it for their own business would be exempted for one year.
However, those who falsely claimed to lease, or applied to lease land reclaimed from the Yellow River,
were not included in the exemption.
In the tenth month of the third year of Zhēnyòu of Xuānzōng,
Censor Tián Jīxiù stated:
"Currently, all military and state needs
are being entirely levied from Hénán.
Officials disregard the people's strength,
collecting and requisitioning too urgently,
hastening the deadlines,
and inflicting severe beatings.
The people have already exhausted all they possess and it is still not enough,
leading them to flee and seek help in other regions.
Their strength is depleted, their wealth exhausted,
and they scatter and perish one after another.
It cannot be stopped by prohibition.
I beg that from now on, all levies and collections must be announced in advance,
and those that are not urgent should all be stopped,
so that the people's strength may be restored, and those who have absconded may return."
The emperor ordered it to be implemented.
In the twelfth month,
an edict exempted absconding households from rent and tax.
In the third month of the fourth year,
absconding households in Shǎnxī were exempted from rent.
In the fifth month,
Púshàn Ānzhēn, acting governor of Shāndōng province, stated:
"Sìzhōu has been afflicted by disaster,
with corpses lining the roads,
and people eating only grass roots and tree bark.
Yet tens of thousands of garrisoned soldiers in Pīzhōu
are supported by urgent levies and heavy corvée,
all from three counties.
Officials are cruel and tyrannical,
arbitrarily seizing private stores
to meet all demands.
The people have all fled,
and further, idle officials are dispatched to compel and supervise the collection.
All of them abuse their authority for personal gain;
only one-tenth actually reaches the government,
while merely causing the state to bear the name of heavy exaction.
I beg that trusted ministers be ordered to rectify this abuse to bring peace to the common people."
The emperor assented.
In the second month of the first year of Xīngdìng,
arrears of 160,000 shí of grain from Zhōngjīng, Sōng, Rǔ, and other places were remitted.
In the fourth year,
Censor-in-chief Wányán Bójiā memorialized that
Bózhōu had suffered severe floods,
and rent amounting to 300,000 shí should be remitted,
but the officials of the Sān Sī did not report truthfully,
only remitting 100,000 shí.
An edict ordered the Sān Sī officials to be punished for their false report.
In the seventh month,
due to severe floods in Hénán,
an edict was issued to remit rent and encourage planting,
and further, Cānzhī Zhèngshì Lǐ Fùhēng was appointed Xuānwèishǐ,
with Censor-in-chief Wányán Bójiā as his deputy.
〔一七〕In the tenth month,
due to prolonged rain,
an order was given to extend the deadline for people to pay taxes.
In the eleventh month,
the emperor said:
"I hear that many common people have fled,
and all outstanding taxes are being forcibly allocated to existing households.
How can people endure this?
Since military provisions are sufficient,
they should all be remitted.
Now, the additional military expenditure is too high;
how can those who have fled be willing to return to their occupations?"
He then ordered the circuit inspecting officials to verify and remit them,
and those who had already paid on behalf of others would be granted special favors,
or exempted from other corvée.
Furthermore, the tax on mulberry bark and used paper money would be reduced by one-fourth.
In the third year,
it was ordered that absconding households who returned to their occupations would only pay their original rent,
〔一八〕and all other corvée and duties would be remitted.
Those capable of cultivating on behalf of others would be exempted like returning households.
Officials who broke their promise and arbitrarily levied taxes
would be punished for violating regulations.
In the twelfth month of the fourth year,
Zhènnánjūn Jiédùshǐ Wēndíhǎn Sījìng submitted a memorial, stating:
"Currently, there are generally three methods for people to pay taxes.
Upper households deliver to distant granaries,
middle households to less distant ones,
and lower households to the nearest.
However, even the nearest is no less than a hundred lǐ,
and the distant ones several hundred lǐ.
The cost of transport doubles the amount paid,
and there is the penalty for delays due to rain and snow,
and the risk of injury or death from bandits.
It would be better to only pay in their own commanderies,
and order officials to inspect the grain stored in granaries,
matching the number of garrisoned troops,
to allow them to be fed from it.
If there is any shortfall,
then increase the levy on the people.
If the people calculate that the levy is less than the cost of transport,
they will happily comply."
In the tenth month of the fifth year,
the emperor instructed his prime ministers, saying:
"Recently, I wished for the people to plant more wheat,
so I ordered local officials to lend out wheat seeds.
Now I hear that they are not actually lending them out,
but are creating false records,
and instead collecting the amount to compensate for insufficient rent.
Dispatch envoys to investigate and punish this."
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
the emperor heard that previously, due to the urgency of tax collection,
people would harvest their crops before they were ripe
to meet deadlines.
Now that the wheat was about to ripen,
he instructed the prefectures and counties
that anyone who violated this would be punished for undermining military provisions.
In the ninth month,
an interim regulation was established concerning the crime of officials with land not paying rent.
Jīngnán Sīnóngqīng Lǐ Qī stated:
"According to Qímín Yàoshù,
wheat planted late produces small and infertile grains,
so it must be sown in the eighth month.
Currently, the southern circuit must deliver over 1.4 million shí of autumn tax
and over 4.5 million bundles of straw,
all with an eighth-month deadline.
If they deliver to distant granaries or through muddy areas,
the round trip takes no less than twenty days,
preventing the people from taking advantage of the season,
which will hinder next year's food supply.
I beg that the deadline for collection be extended,
so that they can first devote their efforts to the two wheat crops."
The court did not comply.
In the second year of Yuánguāng,
the prime ministers reported:
"Last year in the first month, the capital's available grain was only over 600,000 shí.
Now it is triple that,
and national expenditures are quite sufficient,
yet taxes are continuously levied from the people,
which may cause poor people to have nothing to pay and thus flee."
Thus, an imperial decree was widely circulated to stop these levies.
Niútóu Tax.
This was the cattle equipment tax,
the tax paid by Nǚzhí households under the Měng'ān Móukè system.
According to this system, every three plow cattle constituted one 'set' (jù).
Households of twenty-five people were allocated four qǐng and four mǔ of land and some extra,
annually paying approximately no more than one shí of millet.
Officials and commoners could not occupy more than forty sets of land.
In the third year of Tiānhuì,
Tàizōng, seeing a good harvest,
and that the government had no reserves to prepare for famine,
issued an edict ordering one shí of millet to be levied per plow,
and each Móukè was to establish a separate granary to store it.
In the fourth year,
〔一九〕an edict was issued to the inner circuits,
levying five dǒu of millet for every set of cattle,
which became a fixed regulation.
In the first year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng,
an edict ordered that Móukè who had not been relocated
were to pay the cattle equipment tax in millet,
and Móukè were appointed to supervise their granaries,
being held responsible for any loss.
In the twelfth year,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
"The people of Tánggǔbu originally had their taxes fixed in the same way as Měng'ān Móukè.
Later, it was changed to be like prefectures and counties,
with taxes levied based on acreage,
which they considered quite heavy."
So it was ordered to revert to the old system.
In the twentieth year,
for those granted hereditary Móukè status for their achievements,
and permitted to bring relatives with them,
land was to be granted.
Those with nine sets of cattle or less would receive the full allocation.
For those with ten sets or more, up to forty sets,
six sets of land would be allocated from the estates of wealthy officials.
In the twenty-first year,
Shìzōng said to his prime ministers:
“Previously, the annual revenue could sustain us for three years.
I now hear that this year, Shānxī has had a bountiful harvest,
with a yield sufficient for three years.
In this region, the annual harvest cannot even last half a year,
and moreover, the ox-head tax on grain
only requires each ox to contribute three dòu,
and there are also many arrears.
All this is due to mutual concealment and evasion.
It should be ordered that they genuinely pay in full.”
In the twenty-third year,
the officials concerned submitted a memorial regarding this matter.
Shìzōng said to the Left Chancellor, Wán yán Xiāng:
“Your household used to have only seven units;
now it is set at forty units.
When I first ordered you all to discuss this,
you were all unwilling,
probably each looking out for their private interests.
Thereafter, the limit for commoners was set at twenty-five mouths,
counting one ox-unit.”
In the seventh month,
the Shàngshūshěng again submitted a memorial regarding this matter.
The Emperor worried that the registers, being old, might no longer reflect the true distinctions between rich and poor,
and that the Měng'ān and Móukè were all young,
inexperienced in current affairs.
Should a military campaign suddenly arise,
collecting taxes according to the registers would inevitably lead to inequalities.
Therefore, he ordered a thorough investigation and assessment,
reviewing the number of households, population, and livestock,
and submitting these to the twenty-two circuits of Shàngjīng.
In the eighth month,
the Shàngshūshěng reported
the results of the investigation, setting the numbers of Měng'ān and Móukè households, population, fields, and ox-units.
There were 202 Měng'ān,
1,878 Móukè,
615,624 households,
(of which 4,812,669 were free people,
and 1,345,967 were slaves and servants,)
1,690,380-odd qǐng of land,
and 384,771 ox-units.
For the Zōngshì Jiāngjūnsī in the capital,
there were 170 households,
28,790 people,
(of which 982 were free people,
and 27,808 were slaves and servants,)
3,683 qǐng and 75-odd mù of land,
and 304 ox-units.
For the five sections of the Diélà and Tánggǔ tribes,
there were 5,585 households,
137,544 people,
(of which 119,463 were free people,
and 18,081 were slaves and servants,)
46,024 qǐng and 17 mù of land,
and 5,066 ox-units.
Later, in the twenty-sixth year,
the Shàngshūshěng proposed to collect the ox-head grain tax in arrears all at once.
The Emperor said:
“If five years of arrears
are collected all at once,
how can the people bear it?
Order the people to pay annually,
and those affected by disaster shall be exempted.
For those granted loans, collection shall await a year of good harvest.”
Collation Notes
Treatise Twenty-nine, Food and Money Three, Currency
Currency.
In the early Jīn dynasty, the old coins of Liáo and Sòng were used.
Towards the end of Tiānhuì,
even Liú Yù’s
“Fùchāng Yuánbǎo”
and
“Fùchāng Chóngbǎo”
were used.
After the relocation of the capital in Zhēnyuán second year by Hǎilíng Shùrén,
the Minister of the Board of Revenue, Cài Sōngnián, revived the paper currency system,
and subsequently produced Jiāochāo,
which were used alongside coins.
In Zhènglóng second year,
after more than forty years,
the minting of coins was first discussed.
In the tenth month of winter,
the export of copper beyond the borders was initially prohibited,
with rewards offered for informing on violations.
Private copper and brass vessels were confiscated;
those in Shǎnxī and Nánjīng were to be sent to Jīngzhào,
while all others were to be sent to Zhōngdū.
In the second month of the third year,
two mints were established in Zhōngdū,
the eastern one named Bǎoyuán,
and the western one Bǎofēng.
One mint was established in Jīngzhào,
named Lìyòng.
The three mints cast coins.
The inscription read
“Zhènglóng Tōngbǎo,”
their weight was like the small coins of Sòng,
but their rim, hole, and characters were more refined and sharp,
and they circulated interchangeably with old coins.
In the first year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng,
acting on the advice of the Minister of the Board of Civil Office, Zhāng Zhōngyàn,
it was ordered that the Shǎnxī Circuit could also use the old iron coins of Sòng.
In the fourth year,
they gradually ceased to circulate.
An imperial edict was issued to the Hùbù of Shǎnxī and the two circuits’ Tongjiǎn officials
to investigate the matter thoroughly.
They all said,
“Although the coins used by the common people
are nominally interchangeable with iron coins,
they are not actually treated as standard currency,
causing inconvenience to both public and private sectors.”
So, it was abolished.
In the eighth year,
when there were people who violated the copper prohibition,
the Emperor said:
“Melting coins to make copper
has long been prohibited,
yet there are still people privately casting mirrors.
What else could it be but melting coins?”
Thus, it was also prohibited.
In the tenth year,
the Emperor instructed the officials of the Board of Revenue, saying:
“If official money accumulates without being distributed,
then private money will be scarce,
and trade will inevitably be difficult.
It is advisable to order the purchase of gold, silver, and other goods.
As for the goods subject to state monopolies in various circuits,
they should also be ordered to be paid for by bartering goods at a fair price.”
In the tenth month,
the Emperor reproached the officials of the Board of Revenue, saying:
“Previously, because official money was abundant,
fearing that it would not circulate among the people,
I ordered various places to trade for gold, silver, and silk fabrics
to promote circulation.
Now I learn that some have used forced allocation to harm the common people.
I previously allowed government offices to accept lightweight and common goods as payment to benefit the people;
these were all measures I contemplated before implementing.
If these still come from me,
what use are you?
Also, there are often relief efforts in various places,
but often there is no grain nearby,
and it must be fetched from other places.
The round trip is long,
making it even more difficult for people.
Why not establish granaries everywhere,
buy more grain in years of good harvest for relief,
so that should emergencies arise,
would it not also be easy to manage?
Instead, you merely fill the treasuries with money.
What will it be used for?
The world is vast;
how can I know everything individually?
For all these matters,
why have you allowed them to reach this state?
Moreover, the Board of Revenue is different from other boards;
it should devise appropriate plans.
If you merely adhere to old practices
and fulfill your duties,
then anyone could be an official of the Board of Revenue.”
In the second month of the eleventh year,
private casting of bronze mirrors was prohibited,
and all existing bronze vessels were to be surrendered to the government,
which would pay half their value.
Only images of gods and Buddhas, bells, chimes, cymbals, vajras, waist belts, and fish pouches,
etc., were to be retained.
In the first month of the twelfth year,
due to a shortage of copper,
the Shàngshūshěng was ordered to send envoys to various circuits to arrange for copper loans.
Those who could pinpoint mining sites and yield actual results
would be rewarded.
The Emperor discussed the art of minting with his prime ministers.
The prime ministers said:
“Some say that wherever there are gold and silver mines,
they can be exploited to cast coins.
Your subjects humbly believe that the labor costs would be several times greater than the output,
and thus it might not be feasible.”
The Emperor said:
“Gold and silver are
benefits from mountains and lakes, and should be given to the people.
Only coins should not be privately minted.
Currently, the national finances are abundant and flourishing.
If they circulate widely, how is that different from being in the official coffers?
Although the cost may be high,
as long as it remains among the people,
new coins will increase daily.
Send capable officials to manage this.”
Left Chancellor Shí Jū advanced and said:
“Your subject has heard that the wealth of the Son of Heaven is stored among the people.
Currency, like a spring,
is precisely meant for circulation.”
The Emperor again asked Jū:
“Did common people also mint their own coins in ancient times?”
Jū replied:
“If common people minted their own coins,
then petty individuals would seek profit,
and the coins would become increasingly debased.
This is why it was prohibited in antiquity.”
In the thirteenth year,
orders were issued to states and prefectures not involved in quartering troops
to use money to exchange for gold and silk,
and transport them to the capital,
to facilitate the circulation of currency
and benefit the people's livelihood.
In the eleventh month of the fifteenth year,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Some say that minting coins is useless,
and the gain does not compensate for the cost.
I do not think so.
The realm is like one family;
how can there be a distinction between public and private?
The public expenditure becomes the private gain;
as long as new currency increases daily,
both public and private interests will benefit."
In the third month of the sixteenth year,
envoys were dispatched along various routes to investigate copper mine veins.
In the eighteenth year,
a minting bureau was established in Dàizhōu to cast coins.
Lǐ Tiānjí, Jìedùshǐ of Zhènwǔjūn, and Gāo Jìsūn, Zǐ Zhǐbǎodéjūnshì, were ordered to supervise it.
However, the coins cast were mottled, rough, and unusable.
An edict ordered the demotion of Tiānjí and Jìsūn by two ranks,
their dismissal from office,
and Jìsūn was further punished with eighty strokes of the rod.
Zhāng Dàjié, Lángzhōng of the Gōngbù, and Má Guī, Yuánwàiláng of the Lìbù, were then appointed to supervise the minting.
The inscription on these coins read
"Dàdìng Tōngbǎo,"
and the character style and quality were superior to the Zhènglóng period's design.
It was rumored that a small amount of silver was used in the coin's material.
In the nineteenth year,
minting began, reaching over sixteen thousand strings of coins.
In the twentieth year,
an edict ordered five thousand strings to be presented first,
and then for them to be used alongside old coins.
Initially,
before the new coins were circulated,
Sòng Dàguān coins were used as equivalents of five.
In the second month,
the Emperor heard that in the Xiūnèisuǒ in Shàngjīng,
citizens' goods were not paid for immediately,
and short money was used.
He reprimanded his chief ministers, saying:
"Such minor matters,
how can I know them all?
Why do you not investigate them?"
At that time, the common people considered eighty coins to be a string,
calling it "short money,"
while the government used full strings,
calling it "long money."
Wòlǔbǔ, a man from Dàmíng, submitted a memorial,
suggesting that both official and private use of money should consider eighty coins as a string,
which then became the established rule.
In the eleventh month of the twentieth year,
the Dàizhōu minting bureau was named Fùtōng.
One Supervisor was appointed,
of 正五品 rank,
concurrently held by the Jìedùshǐ of the prefecture.
One Deputy Supervisor was appointed,
of 正六品 rank,
concurrently held by the Tóngzhī of the prefecture.
One Aide was appointed,
of 正七品 rank,
concurrently held by the Pànguān of the Observation Commission.
Two officers for managing affairs were appointed,
of 從八品 rank.
Silver plaques were issued,
and the Deputy Supervisor and Aide were ordered to travel by post station to manage affairs.
In the tenth month of the twenty-second year,
Niángē Wòtèlá, Cānzhī Zhèngshì, was appointed to oversee the Dàizhōu Fùtōng Minting Bureau.
In the twenty-third year,
the Emperor noted that the Fùtōng Minting Bureau had been operating for many years,
yet the amount of coins had not increased.
This was because the senior and junior officials and staff of Dàizhōu concurrently managed it,
and it was overshadowed by prefectural affairs,
preventing them from dedicating their full attention to its management.
Therefore, the Deputy Supervisor and Mint Aide were made full-time positions,
while the Jìedùshǐ oversaw the supervisory affairs.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Emperor said:
"Everyone, both inside and outside the capital, says money is scarce.
I have calculated that
five million strings of accumulated money in the capital is not much.
Although there is some in the outer regions, it is ultimately useless.
Official money from all routes, except for places quartering troops, can be entirely transported to the capital."
Tàiwèi Céngxiàng Kèníng said:
"It is indeed difficult for the common people to obtain money.
If it all returns to the capital,
it will be even harder for the people to get it.
It would be better to bring half of it to the capital,
and convert the other half into easily portable valuables,
then both the capital and the provinces would benefit."
In the eleventh month,
the Emperor instructed his chief ministers:
"The state has long prohibited copper,
yet I still hear that people privately make waistbands and mirrors,
claiming them to be old items,
and openly selling them.
These should be strictly prohibited."
In the second month of the twenty-seventh year,
Qǔyáng Xiàn established a separate minting bureau,
named Lìtōng.
A Deputy Supervisor and a Mint Aide were appointed,
and given post horses to travel and manage copper affairs.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Currently, the amount of visible money in the outer regions is very large,
I hear there are over sixty million strings,
all stored in remote places.
Since it does not circulate,
it is useless to both public and private interests,
as if it didn't exist.
Currently, Zhōngdū's annual expenditure is three million strings,
and disbursements are insufficient.
If it were brought to the capital,
the cost of transportation would be minimal.
Even if the cost were high,
it would only be disbursed among the people."
In the twelfth month of the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng of Zhāngzōng,
Liú Wán and others from Yànmén and Wǔtái complained,
saying: "Since the establishment of minting bureaus,
even though the transportation of copper ore from mining areas is said to be official,
if the transportation fees are insufficient, the people are made to collectively compensate.
We beg that it be equally allocated and distributed by the prefecture, its sub-prefectures, and counties."
Thereupon, Dīng Yòngjí, Céng of the Zhēnguānshǔ, was ordered to investigate its advantages and disadvantages.
He returned and reported
that "the people are levied with labor and resources to assist in the transportation of copper ore,
which they do not wish.
The transportation fees are already low,
and there is also the malpractice of exploitation.
When inspecting mine veins and artisans,
they falsely point to people's houses and temples, claiming they should be mined,
and thus extort bribes.
Moreover, they follow the smelters and artisans,
who are daily required to produce four liǎng of refined copper.
Many fail to meet this quota,
and resort to melting copper artifacts and old coins
to make up the amount for officials.
Currently, the Fùtōng and Lìtōng minting bureaus
annually cast over one hundred and forty thousand strings of coins,
but the annual expenditure reaches over eight hundred thousand strings.
It harms the people and incurs great expense,
with no clear benefit."
The chief ministers reported this,
and consequently, the two minting bureaus in Dàizhōu and Qǔyáng were abolished.
Initially,
during the Zhēnyuán period, after the paper currency system was implemented,
a bureau for printing and issuing paper currency and a bureau for exchange notes were established.
Each had one Commissioner, Deputy, and Judge,
and two Chief Supervisors.
The Deputy of the exchange note bureau was specifically responsible for endorsing, stamping, and matching contracts.
Notes of one, two, three, five, and ten strings were called "large notes,"
and those of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, five hundred, and seven hundred were called "small notes."
They circulated alongside coins,
with a limit of seven years.
Old notes were surrendered for new ones,
following Sòng Zhāng Yǒng's system of Sichuan Jiāozǐ, but extending the period.
This was also a provisional measure due to the scarcity of copper.
At the time, there were those who wished to abolish it.
Now that these two minting bureaus were abolished,
the relevant authorities stated:
"Jiāozī (exchange notes) were previously the same as actual money,
and merchants found it convenient for long-distance travel,
often buying notes with coins.
This benefits both public and private interests;
how can it be abolished?
It is only because there is a fixed renewal period
that cannot avoid causing doubt.
We request to abolish the seven-year renewal method,
allowing people to use them permanently.
If, after many years, the characters are worn away,
they should be allowed to surrender old notes for new ones at local official treasuries,
or be permitted to withdraw money instead."
Consequently, the seven-year renewal limit was abolished.
Exchange notes were only exchanged when the characters became faded.
This practice began from this point,
but there were no effective methods for collection,
and more was issued than collected,
causing the people to gradually devalue it.
Thereafter, the method was repeatedly changed,
but it could not be rectified,
and its shortcomings also began here.
The system of *Jiāochāo* (paper currency)
had a border,
decorated with patterns.
Across the top, the value in *guàn* was written.
On the left, it said,
"*Mǒu* character type"
and on the right, it said,
"*Mǒu* character serial number."
Outside the type and number,
a seal script read,
"Those who counterfeit *Jiāochāo* shall be beheaded.
Those who report and apprehend them shall be rewarded three hundred *guàn* in cash."
Below the type, number, and horizontal border, it said,
"*Zhōngdū Jiāochāo* Treasury,
by order of the Ministry of Revenue of the Department of State Affairs,
pursuant to the directive of the *Dūtáng*,
reviewed and inspected by the Ministry of Revenue,
with the signature of the clerk."
It also stated:
"By imperial decree, *Jiāochāo* are printed for each circuit,
and can be exchanged for cash at treasuries in *mǒu* places.
They are also permitted to be exchanged for cash at treasuries in *mǒu* other places,
circulating between officials and private citizens just like actual cash."
The currency was not limited by year for circulation.
If the characters became faded or
the paper currency was worn,
it was permitted to exchange old notes for new ones at the relevant treasury offices.
If one drew cash from the treasury,
or exchanged for new *chāo*,
a certain number of *wén* for labor and ink fees would be deducted per *guàn*.
The treasury official (*Kùqiā*), collecting officer (*Cuánsī*), treasury deputy (*Kùfù*), deputy envoy (*Fùshǐ*), and envoy (*Shǐ*) each affixed their signatures,
with the date.
The officials of the Treasury for Printing *Chāoyǐn* (*Chāoyǐn Kù Kùzǐ*), treasury offices (*Kùsī*), and deputy envoys (*Fùshǐ*) each affixed their signatures,
up to the officials of the Ministry of Revenue of the Department of State Affairs also affixing their signatures.
The seals for places issuing cash were combined,
while other seals followed customary practice.
Initially,
during the *Dàdìng* period, a system was established:
for copper and brass vessels that the common people were permitted to keep,
if declared and sold to the government,
two hundred *wén* in cash would be given per *jīn*.
For concealed prohibited items,
those who first surrendered them would receive one hundred *wén* per *jīn* in cash;
for non-vessel copper goods, one hundred fifty *wén*;
amounts less than a *jīn* were remunerated proportionally.
For the price of copper vessels made and sold by the capital official bureau and outside circuits,
the assistant officials of the Transport Commission were ordered to inspect them.
Mirrors were three hundred fourteen *wén* per *jīn*.
Gilded imperial fairy flower waistbands were seventeen *guàn* six hundred seventy-one *wén*.
Five-son lychee waistbands were seventeen *guàn* nine hundred seventy-one *wén*.
Carved filigree waistbands were eight *guàn* five hundred sixty *wén*.
Fish pouches were two *guàn* three hundred nine *wén*.
Cymbals, bells, and chimes were one *guàn* nine hundred two *wén* per *jīn*.
Bells and pestles with copper bases were two *guàn* seven hundred sixty-nine *wén*.
Those made of brass were three *guàn* six hundred forty-six *wén*.
In the tenth month of the second year of *Míngchāng*,
an imperial edict reduced the price for selling mirrors,
to prevent private casting and melting of coins.
Previously, laborers and artisans had been sent beyond the northern boundary of the *Tiānshān* mountains to mine copper.
In the third year of *Míngchāng*,
Censor Li Bǐng said:
"Recently, I heard officials report
that the amount of copper in official hands could last ten years.
If we continue to send laborers and artisans across the border for distant mining every year,
not only will it be costly,
but it might also stir up border disputes.
When the reserves are about to be exhausted,
mining and refining should only be conducted within the border."
The emperor approved his words,
and thereafter, crossing the border was not permitted.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict was issued to the Department of State Affairs, stating:
"The *Jiāochāo* circulating among the people
should have its quantity limited,
so that it does not exceed the actual cash."
In the fourth year,
the emperor instructed his chief ministers, saying:
"There are useless official goods everywhere.
Plans can be made for them,
such as iron coins."
Someone suggested that if iron coins were damaged,
the responsible office should compensate with copper coins.
The Privy Councilor Xū Chíguó disagreed.
The emperor said:
"If they are compensated, they will still be damaged;
if not compensated, they will be completely damaged.
If they are indeed useless,
why not make a different plan?"
Chíguó said:
"For example, *Jiāngnán* uses copper coins,
while *Jiāngběi* and *Huáinán* use iron coins,
primarily to prevent copper coins from crossing the border.
In *Shǎnxī*, markets also use silver, cloth, ginger, and hemp.
If there are old iron coins,
they should temporarily be collected and stored,
to be prepared for emergencies."
Consequently, the relevant office was ordered to register iron coins and other useless items,
and store them in the treasury.
In the eighth month,
the Judicial Commissioner's Office reported:
"The *Jiāochāo* issued in *Shǎnxī* exceeds the actual cash,
making it difficult for the people to circulate it."
The chief ministers reported this,
and it was then ordered that all taxes and various other fees in that circuit
be paid in *Jiāochāo*.
For the salaries of officials and soldiers,
it was permitted to pay half in cash, silk, or silver, and half in *chāo*.
If the amount of cash or silver was small,
then the entire amount would be given in *Jiāochāo*.
In the third month of the fifth year,
the chief ministers reported:
"The reason cash is difficult to obtain among the people
is because wealthy official families hoard a lot of it.
During the *Yuánhé* period of the Táng dynasty,
it was once stipulated that wealthy families possessing more than five thousand *guàn* in cash would be executed;
princes and dukes would suffer severe demotion and confiscation,
with one-fifth awarded to the informant."
The emperor ordered them to consider and establish a system,
stipulating that official and private households, according to their rank and material wealth, should have a limit on actual cash.
None should exceed twenty thousand *guàn*.
*Měng'ān Móukè* were differentiated by their cattle and implements,
and should not exceed ten thousand *guàn*.
Any excess
was to be exchanged for other goods and stored.
Those who could report others for retaining cash beyond the allowed amount,
their slaves would be granted freedom,
and their hired laborers released,
with one-tenth of the confiscated cash as a reward,
and the rest confiscated.
An imperial decree also instructed the relevant office
that anyone returning from a mission to *Gāolì*
should be ordered to purchase all copper vessels they obtained.
In the tenth month of the second year of *Chéng'ān*,
the chief ministers reported:
"According to the old *Jiāochāo* law,
anyone exchanging old notes for new ones
was charged fifteen *wén* of labor and ink fees per *guàn*.
By the twenty-third year of *Dàdìng*,
this was not limited by *guàn*,
and eight *wén* were collected per note.
This was neither beneficial to the government
nor conducive to the *chāo* system.
It is advisable to revert to the old system.
If *chāo* were used to buy salt certificates,
each *guàn* could be valued as one *guàn* fifty *wén*,
thus allowing for more sales."
The emperor said:
"For labor and ink fees,
twelve *wén* per *guàn* may be collected.
For those buying salt certificates,
each *guàn* may be valued as one *guàn* one hundred *wén*."
At that time, the amount of *Jiāochāo* issued was excessive,
making it difficult for the people to circulate notes of a full *guàn*.
An edict was issued to provide small notes for the two capitals in the northwest and *Liáodōng* Circuit as appropriate,
and also to permit exchange for cash at official treasuries,
circulating equally with other circuits.
In the twelfth month,
the Department of State Affairs deliberated,
stating that the salaries given to officials and soldiers and the needs of border garrisons at that time
were all a combination of silver and *chāo*.
The old rule was that each silver ingot of fifty *liǎng*
was worth one hundred *guàn*.
Among the people, there were those who cut and chipped the ingots,
and their value also fluctuated.
Thus, new silver currency was cast, named
"*Chéng'ān Bǎohuò*."
It came in five denominations from one *liǎng* to ten *liǎng*.
Each *liǎng* was worth two *guàn* in cash.
It was used by both officials and private citizens like actual cash.
Regulations were also established for penalties and rewards for melting, casting, and accepting or delaying it.
In the first month of the third year of *Chéng'ān*,
the Department of State Affairs reported,
"If actual cash is permitted to cross the border at various customs checkpoints,
even if not melted down,
it is no different from being melted down."
Therefore, a regulation was established:
giving cash to foreign envoys or trading with them
was punishable by five years of penal servitude;
three *jīn* or more carried the death penalty.
Brokers and middlemen were subject to the same punishment.
The reward for the informant
was five hundred *guàn* in cash, advanced by the government.
Those apprehended, as well as those who escorted, hosted, pre-arranged, guided, or wrote memorials for them, were punished in descending order of culpability,
and were ordered to make equal restitution.
At this time, the jiāochāo (paper currency) was somewhat stagnant.
An imperial order was issued that in xī-jīng, běi-jīng, Línhuǎng, Liáodōng, and other circuits, all transactions of one guàn or more must use silver notes or precious goods;
money (coins) was not permitted.
For transactions below one guàn, the people were allowed to decide at their convenience.
As the law limiting the use of money (coins) had just been implemented,
many people did not comply.
The Emperor said:
"The regulations have been established.
They are not to be taken lightly.
Let the Yùshǐ Tái and Tíxíng Sī investigate this."
In the ninth month,
because the jiāochāo was stagnant among the people,
all jiāochāo below one guàn was exchanged for coins for use.
Consequently, the previously set limit was further reduced,
and a new regulation was established for the amount of money (coins) that officials and common people could retain.
Three-tenths was set as the rate.
Princes, princesses, and officials of rank were allowed to keep one-tenth.
All others were allowed half of that.
Any surplus amount was to be exchanged for other goods within fifty days.
Violators would be punished for defying imperial decrees.
Informers would be rewarded with money.
In each of the two Xíngbù (departments), Offices of Exchange were established,
to exchange cotton, silk, and other fabrics for silver notes.
It was also permitted to deposit silver notes at these offices.
To obtain salt certificates from the Quèhuò (monopoly offices),
jiāochāo could be paid in Shāndōng, Héběi, Hédōng, and other circuits,
making it convenient to exchange for money (coins).
Various official appointments and honorary titles, three hundred blank imperial edicts, and one thousand ordination certificates were issued,
to be designated by the two Xíngbù.
There was a four-month deadline for their submission and exchange.
Additionally, one hundred new small notes were created,
and all were permitted to be exchanged for money at official treasuries.
For one guàn and two guàn denominations, only small notes were to be disbursed.
For three guàn denominations, one liǎng of silver and one guàn of small notes were to be disbursed.
For five guàn and ten guàn denominations, four-tenths would be disbursed in small notes and six-tenths in silver.
Those who desired precious goods were permitted to receive them.
Those who obstructed or arbitrarily reduced prices would be punished.
In the third month of the fourth year,
due to the stagnation of silver notes,
the system of conveniently exchanging silver notes for cotton, silk, and salt certificates in all Shāndōng circuits was temporarily suspended.
All taxes and fees in the Yuànwù (court departments) and various offices,
except for Jīngshī, Hénán, and Shǎnxī where silver notes were accepted at convenience,
were permitted to collect silver notes and coins in equal halves.
Furthermore, one-fourth of the jiāochāo could be paid in its respective circuit.
The jiāochāo collected in each circuit,
except for those belonging to that circuit which would no longer be disbursed,
were to be circulated and reused.
For salt certificates sold by the Quèhuò,
precious goods and jiāochāo were to be collected in equal halves.
Each liǎng of silver was to be valued at only two guàn of jiāochāo.
The Shěng (Secretariat) allowed people to continue depositing jiāochāo at the treasuries.
The amounts collected by the various Cáosī (transport offices) in each circuit,
excluding those in excess of the quota,
were to be treated similarly.
The official money disbursed
was also a combination of silver and jiāochāo.
If silver had already been fractionalized, the jiāochāo treasury would no longer disburse it.
If the amount of precious goods was small,
it could be gradually increased by minting.
Once silver notes circulated freely, prices would naturally stabilize.
Even with prohibitive laws, what purpose would they serve?
Thus, the penalties for obstructing silver notes were abolished.
In the fourth year,
based on the report of the Hùbù (Ministry of Revenue),
it was ordered that official money in the capital and salt certificates from the Quèhuò offices
should all accept precious goods.
Nearby salt offices were also permitted to accept supplementary money payments.
When precious goods had a destination among the people,
they would naturally circulate,
and not be melted down.
Previously,
four treasuries were established to print small notes to serve as a substitute for principal notes,
allowing people to easily bring small notes to the treasuries to exchange for money,
which was no different from directly disbursing cash.
Now, there was no longer a need to print them.
Once they were all exchanged,
the four treasuries could be abolished.
Only large notes would be used to verify the amount of money for exchanging cash.
At that time, many private mints
"Chéng'ān Bǎohuò" (precious goods of Chéng'ān)
were mixed with copper and tin,
gradually becoming uncirculable,
and shops in Jīngshī closed.
In the twelfth month of the fifth year,
the zǎichén (chief ministers) reported:
"Previously, due to military provisions and deployments,
a large amount of jiāochāo was disbursed.
Subsequently, precious goods were minted,
used concurrently with money (coins),
to serve as a substitute for the principal notes.
This was a temporary measure,
not a long-term policy."
Consequently, "Chéng'ān Bǎohuò"
was abolished.
In the sixth month of the first year of Tàihé,
Lú Gòu, the Cìshǐ of Tōngzhōu, stated:
"The jiāochāo has indeed circulated among the people,
but only the price of silver has not stabilized.
The official rate is set at 100,000 for each ingot,
but in the markets, it is only worth 80,000.
This is because more is leaving than entering.
If all taxes were to be paid equally in three parts of money (coins), silver, and jiāochāo,
perhaps this defect could be rectified."
The proposal was sent to the Shěng (Secretariat) for deliberation.
The zǎichén said:
"Since the military campaigns began,
we have relied entirely on jiāochāo for assistance.
Due to excessive issuance, it has become stagnant.
Recently, the Yuànwù (court departments) were ordered to collect seven-tenths in jiāochāo,
and it has gradually started circulating.
If it is paid equally with silver,
then as one increases and the other decreases,
one side will inevitably dominate,
which would hinder the jiāochāo system.
If we truly wish for the price of silver to stabilize,
it is advisable to allow half of all payments, such as 'Pūmǎ'
and 'Jūnxū'
money,
to be paid in silver.
Those without silver may pay as they please."
Previously,
the Sānhé Tóng Jiāochāo (Tri-Union Unified Paper Currency) was once in circulation.
By the second year of Tàihé,
it was only circulating among the people,
and the government did not collect it.
The court, fearing it would harm the people,
then ordered all taxes to include one-tenth of it.
Although it was limited to its respective circuit,
it was also permitted to be accepted without circuit restrictions.
The Hùbù, which had been collecting Pūmǎ money for several years,
was also allowed to collect half of it.
In the intercalary twelfth month,
concerning the matter of jiāochāo,
the Emperor summoned Hùbù Shàngshū Sūn Duó and Shìláng Zhāng Fùhēng
to discuss it in the inner palace.
Zhāng Fùhēng argued that the Sānhé Tóng Jiāochāo was workable,
while Sūn Duó requested its abolition.
Eventually, Zhāng Fùhēng's argument was refuted.
From then on,
the state became impoverished and the people became poor.
There were insufficient funds for expenses,
and the jiāochāo was exclusively used to deceive the common people.
Moreover, the laws were not constant,
and the achievements of Shìzōng declined.
By the third year of Tàihé,
the abuses became even more severe.
The Emperor then said to the zǎichén:
"During the Dàdìng era,
money was abundant.
Now there is little money among the people,
and it is not in the hands of the officials.
Why is this?
Gather and question all officials;
surely someone will know."
In the seventh month of the fourth year,
the law limiting the use of money (coins) was abolished,
following the request of Hùbù Shàngshū Shàngguān Yú.
In the fourth year,
wishing to increase the minting of coins,
the Emperor ordered all officials to discuss methods to obtain sufficient copper.
Zhōngchéng Méng Zhù said:
"The melting of coins for copper and its illicit use for export do not stop.
Officials and neighbors should be punished for this."
Tàifǔ Jiān Liáng Yuán and others said:
"Minting coins is very costly;
typically, ten coins are spent to produce one coin.
Those who understand say that even with high costs, it still adds one coin.
We request to mine copper and collect copperware for minting."
The zǎichén said:
"Coinage cannot be rushed.
The smelting of copper should be left to the people,
and the government will purchase it.
Temples and monasteries with fewer than ten people
are not allowed to keep ritual vessels.
Private brassware must be sent to the government within two months for compensation.
Those who conceal it will be punished according to private law.
If someone reports it after the deadline,
the official who knew but did not rectify it will be punished.
For temples and monasteries, child novices who report will be rewarded.
Once there is abundant copper,
a separate report will be submitted."
In the eighth month,
the law for convenient money exchange was established,
allowing people to make payments in Jīngshī,
and to withdraw corresponding amounts in Shāndōng, Héběi, Dàmíng, Hédōng, and other circuits.
Later, large coins worth ten (of ordinary coins) were minted,
with the seal script inscription
"Tàihé Zhòngbǎo" (Precious Treasure of Tàihé),
circulating concurrently with jiāochāo.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor wished to abolish the printing and ink fees for jiāochāo.
Considering the constant cost of printing, it was then ordered that only six wén (cash) be collected per guàn.
In the fourth month of the sixth year,
the jiāochāo in Shǎnxī was not circulating well.
With one hundred thousand strings of ready money as the capital for banknotes,
they were exchanged for notes.
Furthermore, one hundred thousand strings of small notes were added for use.
In the eleventh month of the sixth year,
permission was again granted for various circuits to circulate small notes.
The Zhōngdū Lù was to do so in Zhōngdū and Bǎozhōu.
The Nánjīng Lù was to do so in Nánjīng, Guīdé, and Hénánfǔ.
The Shāndōng Dōng Lù was to do so in Yìdū and Jìnánfǔ.
The Shāndōng Xī Lù was to do so in Dōngpíng and Dàmíngfǔ.
The Héběi Dōng Lù was to do so in Héjiānfǔ and Jìzhōu.
The Héběi Xī Lù was to do so in Zhēndìng and Zhāngdéfǔ.
The Hédōng Nán Lù was to do so in Píngyáng.
The Hédōng Běi Lù was to do so in Tàiyuán and Fénzhōu.
Liáodōng was to do so in Shàngjīng and Xiánpíng.
Xījīng was to do so in Xījīng and Fǔzhōu.
Běijīng was to do so at the official treasury in Línhuángfǔ to exchange for money.
The Hùbù was ordered to print five denominations of small notes,
to be attached to and used with ready money in various circuits.
In the first month of the seventh year,
an imperial edict forbade officials from spending large notes.
For those held by the common people, they were ordered to go to the treasury,
where the quantity would determine the number of small notes and ready money exchanged.
Of court business and commercial taxes, as well as various named monies,
one-third had to be paid in large notes.
Only Liáodōng was allowed to use whatever was convenient.
At that time, the people often complained
and sighed due to the frequent changes in currency,
gathering in the markets to speak.
The Emperor, aware of this,
issued an edict to the Yùshǐ Tái, saying:
"From now on, should anyone dare to gather in the urban markets to discuss the difficulty of the banknote system,
they are permitted to be reported,
and the informant will be rewarded with three hundred strings of money."
In the fifth month,
following the proposal of Gāo Rǔlì, the Hùbù Shàngshū,
the
"Regulations for the Banknote System" were established.
Additional large and small notes were printed.
As the banknote treasury was in urgent need,
one additional Fùshǐ was appointed.
Rǔlì then discussed currency with Sūn Duó, the Zhuǎnyùnshǐ of Zhōngdū Lù.
The Emperor ordered Mèng Zhù, the Zhōngchéng, Qiáo Yǔ, the Lǐbù Shìláng, Liú Áng, the Guózǐ Sīyè, and ten others to deliberate.
More than a month passed without a decision.
In the seventh month,
the Emperor summoned them for a deliberation in the Tàihé Diàn,
and also instructed Rǔlì, saying:
"Henceforth, do not say that there are too many notes
and hastily exchange them without adding a premium.
Adding a premium to money
is acceptable."
The next day,
an imperial edict stated:
"For transactions and pledges among the common people,
any amount above one string must use jiāochāo;
money is not to be used.
For those requiring a contract,
one-third must be in other goods.
West of Liùpánshān and east of the Liáo River, one-fifth shall use notes.
Túntián households in the eastern borderlands shall use notes for one-sixth.
For those not requiring a contract,
only in Liáodōng may money and notes be used as convenient.
Offenders shall be sentenced to two years of penal servitude;
informers shall be rewarded differentially.
Supervising officials who offend shall be flogged and dismissed.
County officials who effectively implement the circulation shall be promoted;
otherwise, they shall be demoted and punished.
Those who gather a crowd to obstruct the law shall be treated as having violated imperial regulations.
For the printing fee, only two coins shall be collected per sheet.
Merchants carrying ready money shall not exceed ten strings.
The relevant authorities shall register and identify banknote verifiers to prevent counterfeiting.
For officials and common households retaining ready money,
the quantity shall be reduced compared to the old system.
If one previously had a large amount of ready money,
they are permitted to send it to the officials to exchange for notes,
but amounts over ten strings are not allowed to leave the capital."
It was also decreed
that the Ānchásī would be deemed competent if the banknote system circulated smoothly.
However, Xiébùchū, the Héběi Ānchásǐ, for a voucher issued by the Xún'àn worth one string of banknotes,
found it difficult to spend,
and ordered to take ready money.
A Censor impeached him for obstructing and undermining the banknote system.
The Emperor said:
"An official responsible for inspection and impeachment is the first to violate the law;
the circumstances are unforgivable."
He was flogged seventy times
and demoted one rank and dismissed.
Gāo Rǔlì, the Hùbù Shàngshū, said:
"The banknote system must be implemented.
Prefectures, subprefectures, counties, and towns should each register banknote verifiers,
issue them with official seals,
and allow them to verify for the people.
Two coins shall be given according to the string,
though the usual rate may be higher, it shall stop at six coins.
Each time a court official is dispatched on an mission,
they shall investigate the flow and stagnation and report it.
Old Sòng huìzǐ among the people
shall also be allowed to be used like ready money,
but amounts over ten strings are not permitted to be carried.
Salt monopoly allows the use of silver and silk,
while other market exchanges and salaries
shall all use jiāochāo.
Odd amounts shall be made up with small notes.
If silver and silk are due but insufficient, they shall also be paid in notes."
The Emperor sent a close attendant to convey an edict to the Shàngshū Shěng:
"Now that the Ānchásī's effectiveness is judged by the smooth circulation of banknotes,
and incompetence otherwise,
furthermore, in the official evaluations given to officials of prefectures, subprefectures, and counties,
the number of offenses shall be clearly written.
Even if a Censor commends a capable official who has violated the banknote law,
they shall not be approved for promotion."
In the tenth month,
Yáng Xù said:
"The material and numbers of the jiāochāo are unclear,
and the dates are deliberately obscured.
Although people are ordered to go to the treasury to exchange for new ones,
there are no designated treasury offices in outer circuits.
There is nowhere to exchange them,
and distant people must travel directly to the capital."
The Emperor asked Rǔlì about this,
who replied:
"Within the treasuries of various prefectures,
there are banknote verifiers.
Even if a note is worn but not counterfeit,
it can be accepted.
In distant cities and towns from the capital,
where combined exchange offices have been set up,
travelers can all exchange them.
Further concerning places without combined offices,
where exchange is difficult,
official treasuries are ordered to accept but not disburse any faded notes they receive,
and to print the names of officials on the back of the notes.
After half a year, they shall go to the capital to exchange for new notes.
In this way,
faded notes will have a place to go and will not be stagnant."
In the eleventh month,
the Emperor instructed the officials of the Hùbù:
"Although the banknote system is now implemented,
you should also carefully observe.
Should there be any slight stagnation,
you must report it immediately.
Do not think it has been implemented and hesitate to make changes."
Rǔlì replied:
"Currently, many of the exchange offices are located within government offices,
making it quite difficult for common people to enter and exit.
Although merchants facilitate exchanges,
they suffer from insufficient note capital.
Recently, the Zhuǎnyùn Sī of Héběi Xī Lù reported
that a wealthy citizen declared
fourteen thousand strings of ready money
beyond what they were allowed to retain.
It is presumed there may be similar cases in other circuits.
We believe that prefectures and counties should assign officials and treasury clerks
to set up exchange offices in key locations within the marketplaces.
The declared money shall serve as note capital.
For prefectures with over one hundred thousand households,
thirty thousand strings shall be allocated,
with amounts scaled down accordingly.
No individual exchanging notes shall exceed two strings.
The collected printing fees shall be used to pay the treasury clerks.
Furthermore, the second-ranked officials of prefectures and one official from the Zhuǎnyùn Sī shall be ordered to supervise."
The Emperor approved this,
and thus ordered the relocation of treasuries to marketplace hubs,
allowing people to exchange notes for money.
In this month,
an imperial edict stated that those who caught counterfeiters of jiāochāo
would all be rewarded with jiāochāo.
At this time, there was again a discussion to reform the banknote system.
The Emperor followed Gāo Rǔlì's advice,
ordering that large notes held by officials were no longer to be disbursed.
People with five-string or ten-string denominations were allowed to go to the treasury to exchange for small notes.
Those who wanted money would receive one string for five strings of notes,
and two strings for ten strings of notes.
Only Liáodōng was allowed to use whatever was convenient.
In Hénán, Shǎnxī, Shāndōng, and other circuits where notes circulated,
for all court taxes and various other named monies,
the rate was set at three parts:
one part to be paid in ten-string denominations,
two parts in five-string denominations,
and the remainder to be collected in ready money.
In the first month of the eighth year,
due to the stagnation of notes in the capital,
regulations for rewards and punishments for the relevant authorities were established.
At that time, the new system stipulated that
Ānchásī and prefecture/county officials
would generally be promoted or demoted based on the smooth or stagnant circulation of notes.
Therefore, Censors were ordered to have the same rewards and punishments as external Ānchásī.
Officials of the Dàxīngfǔ Jǐngxún Yuàn were to be treated the same as officials of external circuit prefectures/counties.
In this month,
large notes were recalled and destroyed,
and small notes were circulated.
In the eighth month,
following the words of Yáng Yúnyì, Surveillance Commissioner of Liáodōng,
—(10)— since merchants and travelers gathered in the two circuits of Xiánpíng and Dōngjīng,
it was decided to follow the precedent of Dū Nán,
whereby all transactions above one string were to use jiāochāo [paper currency],
and cash was not permitted.
In the tenth month,
Sūn Duó again said,
"The common people have too much paper currency;
it is precisely the right time to collect it.
For all various taxes such as court fees and other levies,
paper currency should be accepted entirely.
For autumn and summer taxes, besides payment in kind,
paper currency should also be accepted,
regardless of the string limit.
If farmers know this, they will gradually value paper currency more,
and it can circulate.
Recently, prefectures and counties have been coercing markets to buy paper currency,
which only increases disturbance.
The establishment of paper currency bureaus in various places should be abolished,
and people should only be allowed to go to the provincial treasury for exchange.
Currently, small denominations of paper currency are restricted to specific circuits,
which is also very inconvenient;
they should be made generally usable."
The emperor commanded that this be immediately implemented.
In the twelfth month,
—(11)— the Chancellor reported:
"According to the old system,
the salaries of officials and soldiers, both internal and external, were all paid in paper currency.
For those who absolutely needed cash to make up the amount,
it could be calculated at a rate of one-tenth:
soldiers were given three parts,
and officials and attendants two parts,
not exceeding ten strings.
All large denomination paper currency previously collected,
upon reaching general circulation, should be recounted and remade,
and ultimately it must be exquisitely crafted to ensure its longevity.
For old, worn-out paper currency held by the common people,
we request permission for them to exchange it for new currency at local treasuries.
If officials or influential families cheaply buy jiāochāo [paper currency],
and then exchange it for cash at court offices to engage in speculation,
they shall be prosecuted for violating regulations.
Furthermore, officials should be dispatched to patrol various circuits.
Although exceeding the cash limit was previously allowed to be reported by slaves,
there are instances where local authorities secretly order their masters to conceal it and not genuinely report it.
The Surveillance Commissioner should investigate such cases.
If the old deadline has passed,
it should be extended by another fifty days,
allowing for another exchange of paper currency and commercial certificates [yǐn].
and various goods."
After this regulation was implemented,
Zhāngzōng soon collapsed,
and Wèi Shàowáng succeeded him.
During the Battle of Hézhī in Dà'ān the third year,
—(12)— as many as eighty-four carts were used as military rewards.
The army was defeated, and the nation was ravaged.
There was no time to remedy the弊端 (problems),
and the value of jiāochāo [paper currency] became so light that it was almost useless for transactions.
By the second month of Zhēnyòu the second year during Xuānzōng's reign,
wishing to increase its value,
they again issued jiāochāo [paper currency] in denominations of twenty to one hundred strings,
and also created denominations of two hundred to one thousand strings.
However, since Tàihé,
whenever jiāochāo [paper currency] was changed,
although it was initially valued,
within a few years it would become light and cease to circulate.
By this time, the more it was changed, the more stagnant it became.
After the southward relocation,
the nation was impoverished, the people were distressed,
and military campaigns were incessant,
with limitless expenditure.
Its lightness became even more severe.
In the fourth month of the third year,
Xū Dǐng, Pacification Commissioner of Hédōng, reported:
"The current high prices are due to the stagnation of paper currency,
where there is output but no input.
Although court taxes have increased several-fold,
all payments are in large denominations of ten strings,
what good is this?
Currently, there are many ten-string denominations among the common people,
which have no use,
so transactions mostly use actual cash,
and each string of paper currency is only worth one coin,
not even covering the cost of printing.
My humble opinion is that
actual cash should be temporarily prohibited,
and the Accountancy Bureau should, under the pretext of military provisions,
assess the people's capabilities and levy taxes.
Then currency will circulate,
and commodity prices will stabilize."
From then on,
cash was not used.
Wealthy families were internally constrained by limits on hoarding cash,
and externally harmed by the repeated changes in jiāochāo [paper currency],
all leading to destitution and ruin,
which was called
"sitting transformation" (a euphemism for bankruptcy).
Merchants often transported goods by boat to trade in Jiānghuái,
and much cash flowed into Sòng.
The Sòng people rejoiced at this,
while the Jīn people did not prohibit it.
Those who knew better lamented that they could neither value the useless paper [currency],
nor cherish the treasure that had circulated since ancient times.
In the fifth month,
Wūlíndá Yǔ, Acting Military Commissioner of Xī'ān, said:
"There are many troops in Guānshǎn,
and provisions are insufficient.
The jiāochāo [paper currency] relied upon is obtained from the capital,
which only adds to the burden and expense.
I request that printing blocks be sent down for convenient local production."
He also said:
"Huáizhōu used to have millions of iron coins,
—(13)— which are now useless.
I wish to string them together to make armor [jiǎ],
to be given to soldiers."
At that time,
officials discussed penalties for minor offenses,
mostly allowing redemption with iron.
However, the penalties were unfair,
so it was decreed that redemption with copper and the assessment of stolen goods should all be based on the silver price.
In the sixth month,
an imperial edict discussed the benefits and convenience of jiāochāo [paper currency].
In the seventh month,
the name of jiāochāo [paper currency] was changed to
"Zhēnyòu Bǎoquàn" (Zhēnyòu Precious Certificate),
and crimes of obstruction were also established.
In the ninth month,
the Censorate reported:
"Since many calamities,
we have entirely relied on jiāochāo [paper currency] to assist military provisions.
However, what comes in is less than what goes out,
so its value gradually decreases,
and eventually there is no way to stop it.
This is an inevitable principle.
Recently, 'Zhēnyòu Bǎoquàn' was used
to remedy this problem,
but there is also concern that if it becomes too numerous, the people will devalue it,
and it will be no different from the old paper currency.
Thus, it was ordered that all market transactions among the common people must follow current prices,
with strict penalties and rewards established,
aiming for its definite implementation.
This has caused merchants and travelers to cease activity,
and goods from all directions dare not enter.
With a million people in the capital,
daily expenses are immeasurable;
how can commodity prices not rise daily?
Moreover, current prices are set twice a month,
but market prices among the common people vary from morning to evening.
Now officials are forcing it,
and markets are all closed.
Furthermore, there is a discussion about searching for hidden goods,
and insisting that they be sold according to the set prices.
If so, goods in the capital will be exhausted in a matter of days,
and the common people will be severely distressed.
We, your ministers, believe that
only official purchases and assessments of stolen goods, etc., can use current prices;
the rest should follow convenience."
The decree was approved.
In the twelfth month,
