the emperor heard that many nearby prefectures and counties were purchasing grain from the capital,
causing grain prices to soar.
He ordered the Department of State Affairs to convene the Ministry of Revenue, the Institute for Discussions, Kaīfēng Fǔ, and the Transport Commissioner,
to discuss ways to control this.
The Ministry of Revenue and the Institute for Discussions suggested
that those leaving the city with five dòu [a unit of measure] or more could have half of their grain intercepted.
The Transport Commissioner suggested that all grain leaving the city should be prohibited.
The emperor followed the suggestion of Kaīfēng Fǔ,
which stated:
"When the Precious Certificates were first introduced,
the people valued them greatly.
However, because too many were issued in Héběi and Shǎnxī circuits,
people began to devalue them.
Merchants eagerly brought them into the capital
to purchase gold and silver,
which caused silver prices to soar,
and grain prices followed suit.
If the Precious Certificates had different regulations for each circuit,
then they could not be brought back into Hénán,
and gold and silver in Hénán would be cheap, and grain prices would naturally be low.
If the capital city were simply closed off and grain not allowed to leave,
then the outside would also guard their own grain,
and would not bring it into the capital,
and grain prices would become even more expensive.
It would be appropriate to instruct the common people in the prefectures and counties
not to arbitrarily raise prices,
and the government should set prices,
making sure to follow convenience."
In the first month of the fourth year,
Jiānchá Yùshǐ Tián Quǎnxìu stated:
"The state's expenditures all rely on treasure certificates.
After only a few months of circulation,
they are again stagnant.
This is not due to lax regulations or careless execution.
For currency to circulate,
there must be a proper balance of its value and a skillful management of its issuance and collection.
The current problem lies in too much issuance and too little collection.
If we can adjust and reduce expenditures as appropriate,
and increase what is collected,
perhaps it might work."
He then presented five articles.
First, reduce redundant officials;
second, reduce the wine tax administration;
third, economize on soldiers' pay;
fourth, abolish sinecure officials;
fifth, wine tax and official appointments by grain contribution should all use treasure certificates.
An imperial edict stated that the wine tax should follow the old system of Dàdìng,
but the rest were not adopted.
Soon after, the rewards for capturing counterfeiters of treasure certificates were re-established.
In the third month,
Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì Zhào Bǐngwén stated:
"Recently, the treasure certificates have been stagnant.
This is likely because the court was about to deliberate on reforms,
but then it was falsely rumored that they would be discontinued.
Consequently, they were suppressed [in use],
gradually leading to their disuse.
This means authority has fallen into the hands of the common people.
Since the relocation to Biàn,
the 'exchange bureaus' have been abolished.
Your ignorant minister believes they should be reinstated.
Let officials familiar with market conditions manage them,
giving them silver, paper currency, grain, wheat, silk, and other goods,
and balancing their fluctuating values in transactions.
Furthermore, select good supervising officials to manage them.
If there are no faults for half a year,
and the certificate system circulates smoothly,
then allow them to be appointed to any convenient post."
The emperor decreed to deliberate on implementing it.
In the fourth month,
Hédōng Xíngshěng's Xū Dǐng stated:
"Exchange notes are valuable for their circulation.
Currently, what is produced by the various circuits is insufficient for what is issued.
If we do not collect them skillfully,
there will inevitably be deficiencies.
It is advisable to levy [revenue] according to the people's capacity,
to supplement military expenditures.
Hézhōng Xuānfǔ Sī also stated that because too many treasure certificates had been issued,
the people did not value them,
requesting to assess the people's wealth and poverty and then levy them.
Although it is for Shǎnxī,
if levied uniformly,
〔一四〕all that is available there would daily flow to Hédōng.
How is that different from not levying at all?
Furthermore, since Héběi treasure certificates were not allowed to circulate in Hénán,
they became even more stagnant."
The Zǎichén said:
"Yesterday, due to the Héběi treasure certificates,
merchants and peddlers continuously crossed south,
leading to soaring prices.
Thus, it was expedient to restrict them by circuit.
Now, since Xū Dǐng's (Dǐng's) circuit has heavy expenditures,
and he wishes to levy money for military provisions,
his request should be granted.
As for whether Shǎnxī can be levied or not,
an imperial edict should instruct the Xíngshěng to deliberate and decide before implementation."
In the fifth month,
the emperor observed that official funds from Héběi prefectures had been scattered [and lost],
with much of it among the common people.
He ordered the Shàngshū Shěng to plan for its recovery.
In the eighth month,
Píngzhāng Gāo Qí (高琪) submitted a memorial:
"Since the military campaign began,
expenditures have been immeasurable,
relying solely on treasure certificates.
However, income does not cover expenses,
which is why their value has gradually depreciated.
Now, a thousand-cash certificate is worth only a few cash.
They are printed and spent as soon as they are made.
The cost of labor and materials increases daily.
If there is nothing to remedy this,
the problems will only worsen.
It is advisable to issue new certificates,
treating them as parent and child with the old certificates and circulating both concurrently.
This would save on labor and materials
and prevent a shortage of funds."
However, Pú Wáng Shǒuchún (濮王守純) and others were hesitant to make changes,
and they memorialized:
"From ancient times, military expenses have always been taken from the people.
Previously, the imperial court, deeming small banknotes too light,
temporarily replaced them with treasure certificates
and then prohibited the use of coins.
The common people, with their limited foresight,
believed that paper currency was easily damaged
unlike coins, which last longer.
Thus, they treasured any coins they obtained,
while quickly spending certificates,
fearing they might tear or become obsolete.
Now, the imperial court knows how to spend but not how to collect,
which is why coins become more valuable daily and certificates lighter.
Therefore, the lightness of certificates is not due to the people devaluing them;
it is the state that has caused this.
It would be better to assess the expenditures and then levy them from the people again.
With a circulating inflow and outflow,
they would then know it is an essential commodity
and would cherish it.
Now, merely worrying about depreciation and immediately wanting to issue new ones
will not only cause decrees to be ineffective,
but we also fear that the new certificates will become as light as the old ones."
Afterwards,
Lǒngzhōu (隴州) Defense Commissioner Wán Yán Yù (完顏𧜛) and Shǎnxī (陝西) Provincial Clerk Huì Jí (惠吉) successively spoke about the drawbacks of the certificate system.
Yù (𧜛) requested a temporary halt to printing,
allowing existing certificates to circulate.
If circulation stagnated, they should be collected based on the number of households and individuals and the value of their property.
Jí (吉) said:
"Certificates are meant to remedy a temporary problem;
they cannot circulate and be comparable to actual cash.
If one insists on their circulation,
it merely means collecting more and spending less.
However, collecting too much harms the people,
and spending too little leads to insufficient funds.
Neither is acceptable.
For the present situation,
it is best to issue new certificates
under the name 'Zhēnyòu Tōngbǎo' (貞祐通寶).
They should be in ten denominations, from one hundred to three thousand,
and various transport offices should be permitted to print them,
but still not exceeding five thousand strings [of cash].
Using them alongside the old certificates
should be permissible."
An imperial decree ordered all officials to discuss the matter.
Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎) Àotún Āhǔ (奧屯阿虎), Lǐbù Shìláng (禮部侍郎) Yáng Yúnyì (楊雲翼), Lángzhōng (郎中) Lán Zhī (蘭芝), and Xíngbù Shìláng (刑部侍郎) Féng È (馮鶚) all advocated for issuing new certificates.
Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎) Gāo Kuí (高夔), Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) Zhāng Shīlǔ (張師魯), and Bīngbù Shìláng (兵部侍郎) Tú Dān Ōulǐbái (徒單歐里白) all requested levies.
Only Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書) Xiāo Gòng (蕭貢) believed it should remain as before,
while Gōngbù Shàngshū (工部尚書) Lǐ Yuánfǔ (李元輔) believed both could be implemented concurrently.
Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (太子少保) Zhāng Xíngxìn (張行信) also stated that new certificates should not be issued,
but merely strictly enforcing penalties for non-compliance
would suffice.
Shìyùshǐ (侍御史) Zhào Bóchéng (趙伯成) said:
"The method of issuing new certificates
covertly deprives the people of their profits;
its harm is worse than levying.
As for the method of levying,
it is unacceptable if levied only from farmers.
But if levied from city markets and merchant households,
this is also a way to strengthen the root and suppress the branch."
Xíngbù Zhǔshì (刑部主事) Wáng Shòuníng (王壽寧) said:
"Not so.
Today, those who value coins and devalue certificates are all farmers.
Therefore, any levy must first be taken from the common people."
Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (轉運使) Wáng Kuò (王擴) said:
"When discussing matters, one must investigate their root.
This year, over forty thousand shí of rations have been disbursed to soldiers' families.
If these people could settle down [and cultivate the land],
and the people's burden were eased slightly,
then levying would not be difficult to implement."
Quèhuò Sī (榷貨司) Yáng Zhēn (楊貞) also wanted to cut unnecessary expenses
and dismiss idle and redundant officials.
Some requested the casting of large coins worth a hundred [small ones]
and the creation of small banknotes to save costs.
Some said that the county officials should be chosen carefully.
Only Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Wēndíhǎn Sījìng (溫迪罕思敬) submitted a memorial, stating:
"The state's laws
are all well-equipped,
but the officials concerned are simply unable to uphold them.
If only this minister were given discretionary power,
all officials below the fourth rank in the outer circuits would be permitted to be flogged;
those of the third rank and above would be reported to the emperor.
Furthermore, two censors would be dispatched by post to travel back and forth.
The law need not be changed,
nor need the people be levied.
With a single command,
everyone, high and low, can be made to obey the law.
If not,
I request to be subjected to heavy punishment."
The emperor showed this to the prime ministers, saying:
"He promises so much;
should we try entrusting him?"
The prime ministers had no immediate answer,
but Censor Chén Guī (陳規) and Wán Yán Sùlán (完顏素蘭) argued vehemently,
believing
that "even sages and wise men find some matters difficult to implement.
What is Sījìng (思敬) doing,
but merely harming people?"
The emperor, seeing the myriad opinions,
remained undecided for over a month,
and was annoyed.
He then decreed that things should remain as before,
and postponed the period for levies and collections.
Not long after,
Huì Jí's (惠吉) suggestion was indeed adopted,
and
"Zhēnyòu Tōngbǎo" (貞祐通寶) were issued.
In the second month of the first year of Xīngdìng (興定)
(1217 CE), it was decreed that they should circulate.
Each string [of the new currency] was equivalent to one thousand strings [of the old].
The penalties for counterfeiting or obstructing their use were increased, as were the rewards for their capture.
In the fifth month,
because the banknote system had changed repeatedly,
depreciating as soon as new notes were issued,
the mulberry bark and old paper used for making paper were all taken from the people.
By this time, they became extremely difficult to obtain.
Consequently, it was ordered to calculate their value,
but only treasure certificates and Tōngbǎo were collected.
This was named
"Mulberry Bark and Old Paper Money,"
said to exempt the people from the labor of transportation
and save on the costs of labor and materials.
Gāo Rǔlì (高汝礪) said:
"The levies and dispatches in Hénán (河南) are onerous.
The collected rents and taxes are three times the previous amount,
barely enough to supply the needs.
Such is their heavy burden.
Yet this year, in the fifth month, the provincial department, finding the annual income of Tōngbǎo insufficient for use,
collected seventy million strings of mulberry bark and old paper notes from the populace to supplement it.
This is also too excessive.
And recently, because Tōngbǎo circulated somewhat sluggishly,
this amount was again increased by two times.
Two-thirds of Hénán (河南) households are farmers.
This year's rents and taxes have not yet been fully collected,
and they are again ordered to produce this.
If the people do not sell their grain to pay the required rent,
they will sell the millet they eat.
What else could they obtain?
What is urgently needed and difficult to obtain now are fodder and provisions,
which come from the people and are limited.
What can be delayed and is easy to make are banknotes,
which come from the state and can be changed.
How can the state coerce the people to provide what it itself can control?
Previously, when large banknotes stagnated, they were replaced by small banknotes.
When small banknotes became problematic, they were changed to treasure certificates.
When treasure certificates did not circulate, they were replaced by Tōngbǎo.
The power to change the system is with us,
so why trouble the people?
The people have already exhausted their strength to support the army, yet it is not enough.
They are also levied further based on households, taxes, goods, and productive industries.
If they are stripped like this,
and they cannot provide,
then they will only flee.
When the people flee and fields lie waste,
the soldiers will not have food.
This means both military provisions and the banknote system will be ruined.
This minister does not disregard the banknote system,
nor does he deliberately oppose the provincial department.
But the harm of stagnant banknotes and high prices is light,
while the harm of people fleeing and the army starving is severe."
At the time, his advice was not taken.
In the tenth month of the third year,
the provincial ministers reported:
“Previously, because goods were expensive and money was cheap,
those who committed embezzlement and were judged by the amount of money embezzled would be punished too severely.
Therefore, silver was used as the standard,
with each liǎng of silver being equivalent to two guàn of cash.
Those who embezzled Tongbǎo were directly judged by the amount of Tongbǎo.
For example, due to military expenditures and levies,
if one received Tongbǎo amounting to thirty guàn,
they would have already incurred the death penalty.
However, if converted to the value of gold and silver,
it would only amount to a little over four hundred qián,
which would then warrant a caning.
The disparity in severity is thus extremely great.”
Consequently, an order was issued to judge crimes based on the silver price at the time of the offense.
In the third month of the fourth year,
Li Fùhēng, Associate Administrator of the Affairs of the Secretariat, stated:
“According to recent regulations,
those who embezzle Tongbǎo are all to have their crime determined by converting the value of the goods to silver,
with each liǎng being equivalent to two guàn of cash.
However, for those whose crimes would typically be redeemed with copper,
they only pay the現錢 (xiànqián) of Tongbǎo.
It is requested that they also be ordered to pay silver as above,
which would be sufficient to deter evil
and also benefit the government.”
The emperor ordered the provincial ministers to deliberate,
and it was then decided that those who committed public errors or mistakes would only be required to pay the現錢 (xiànqián) of Tongbǎo,
while those who committed embezzlement or corruption deliberately would pay silver.
In the twelfth month,
Wēndíhán Sījìng, Military Commissioner of Zhènnán Jūn, submitted a memorial stating:
“Cash, as currency,
values circulation and must not be obstructed.
If it accumulates in the government coffers without being disbursed, it harms the people.
If it is disbursed among the people without being collected, it leads to a shortage of funds for use.
It must be balanced in quantity, lightness, and heaviness against goods before it can be effective.
During the Dàdìng era,
there was much cash among the people and little paper currency,
hence cash was valuable and circulated easily.
Since the military campaign began,
there has been very little in government hands,
and not much among the people either.
Military provisions and logistics are entirely dependent on paper currency,
with tens of thousands being issued daily,
to the point where it fills the markets and shops.
How can it not become light in value?
It would be better to relax the restrictions on cash,
allowing the people to mine copper and mint coins themselves.
The government would regulate the molds,
and if coins are thin, poor quality, or not up to standard, the people would be forbidden from using them.
Then cash will surely increase daily,
and less paper currency can be issued.
With less issued, it will become valuable and circulate easily.
Today, the issuance is increasing,
and the people increasingly devalue it.
Officials wish to increase its value but cannot find the right method,
even going so far as to calculate officials' salaries and examine the people's assets to collect it,
yet ultimately failing to increase its value.
They do not even realize the disadvantage of having too little cash.
I suggest that the people be allowed to mint coins,
and those who are to pay paper currency should also be permitted to pay silver.
The people can then mint coins with silver in several denominations,
inscribed with 'Xīngdìng Yuánbǎo,'
with a fixed value to be used for military rewards.
This is also a method to remedy the弊 (bì).”
The imperial court did not adopt it.
In the intercalary twelfth month of the fifth year,
the prime ministers reported:
“Previously, when the Bǎo Quàn became flawed,
'Zhēnyòu Tōngbǎo' was created
to remedy it.
Five years have passed since then,
and its flaws are now like those at the end of the Bǎo Quàn era.
Initially,
four guàn of Tōngbǎo were equivalent to one liǎng of silver;
now it is over eight hundred guàn.
It is advisable to create 'Xīngdìng Bǎo Quán' again,
with subsidiary and parent coins balancing each other,
circulating concurrently with Tōngbǎo.
Each guàn of Xīngdìng Bǎo Quán would be worth four hundred guàn of Tōngbǎo,
and two guàn of Xīngdìng Bǎo Quán would be worth one liǎng of silver.
Treasuries should be set up everywhere,
allowing people to exchange Tōngbǎo for it.
Officials who can ensure its circulation among the people
will be promoted one rank and one grade.
Those who, due to indulgence, cause stagnation
will be demoted and punished accordingly.
Officials of zhōu and fǔ will have their rewards and punishments determined by their subordinate sī and xiàn.
Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) and circuit inspection officials (Zhūlù Xíngbù Guān) are ordered to supervise this,
and laws for obstruction of justice and failure to report will be established.
If a censor fails to report, they will be demoted and punished;
if an inspection official fails, they will be demoted and fined.
Those who gather crowds to foolishly discuss difficult implementation will be sentenced to two years of penal servitude,
and informers will be rewarded with three hundred guàn of cash.”
In the second month of the first year of Yuánguāng,
an imperial edict was first issued to implement this.
In the fifth month of the second year,
a new issue was created, each guàn being equivalent to fifty Tōngbǎo.
Also, 'Yuánguāng Zhēnhuò' was printed on damask,
to circulate alongside silver notes and other notes.
Not long after its implementation,
the price of silver rose daily,
and Bǎo Quán became cheaper day by day.
The people only valued things in silver.
By the second year of Yuánguāng,
Bǎo Quán was almost unused,
so a law was established:
one liǎng of silver should not exceed three hundred guàn of Bǎo Quán.
For any item valued at three liǎng of silver or less, silver was not allowed to be used.
For items valued above that, a three-part ratio was to be followed:
one part in silver,
two parts in Bǎo Quán, Zhēnhuò, and Chóngbǎo.
In the capital (Jīngshī) and the zhōu and jùn, Píngzhǔn Wù were established
to exchange Bǎo Quán and silver.
Those who privately exchanged or violated the law and reported it would receive varying punishments and rewards.
After this order was issued,
markets and shops closed during the day,
and merchants ceased traveling.
The imperial court was troubled by this,
so it abolished the law regarding the use of silver in market exchanges and private exchanges of silver and Bǎo Quán.
However, while there was a name for limited use from above,
there was no actual compliance from below.
Although the authorities knew this,
none could enforce it.
During the Zhèngdà era of Yìzōng,
the people only used silver for market transactions.
In the tenth month of the second year of Tiānxīng, 'Tiānxīng Bǎo Huì'
was printed in Càizhōu,
in four denominations from one qián to four qián,
circulating alongside現銀 (xiànyín).
Within a few months, the dynasty perished.
Collation Notes
Monograph 30, Food and Money 4: Salt, Alcohol, Vinegar, Tea, Various Commercial Taxes, Gold and Silver Taxes
Salt.
Under the Jīn system,
there were ten categories of state-monopolized goods:
alcohol, distiller's yeast, tea, vinegar, incense, alum, cinnabar, tin, iron,
with salt being the foremost.
In the early Zhēnyuán era,
Cài Sōngnián, as Minister of Revenue,
first revived the Chāo Yǐn (paper currency and salt certificate) method,
establishing officials and treasuries to produce Chāo and Yǐn.
Chāo
matched the tallies of the Salt Administration (Yánsī Bù).
Yǐn
matched the numbers for endorsement and payment by sī and xiàn.
It was reformed every seven years.
Initially,
the former territories of Liáo and Jīn, being coastal, produced much salt.
The Shàngjīng and Dōngběi Two Circuits consumed salt from Zhàozhōu.
The Sùpín Circuit consumed sea salt.
North of Línhuáng, there was a large salt lake.
The Wūgúlǐ Shíléi tribe had salt ponds.
All these were sufficient to feed the people within the borders,
and taxes were regularly collected from them.
Upon gaining the central plains,
the number of salt fields doubled,
thus officials were set up and laws were formulated with greater detail.
However, increases and decreases were inconsistent,
and abolition and establishment were without a fixed pattern;
it merely remedied current弊 (bì) as needed.
In Yìdū and Bīnzhōu, two salt administrations were formerly established.
In the fourth month of the thirteenth year of Dàdìng,
they were merged into the Shāndōng Salt Administration.
In the twenty-first year, the various offices in Cāngzhōu and Shāndōng saw increased profits
and illicitly sold salt,
and the imperial court worried that prolonged practice might undermine the law.
Consequently, they were merged into the Hǎifēng Salt Commissioner's Office.
In the eleventh month,
various salt fields in Liáodōng and other circuits were also merged,
forming two salt administrations.
In the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng,
the Gǒuluò was reformed into the Xījīng Salt Administration.
Thereafter, only seven salt administrations were maintained: Shāndōng, Cāng, Bǎochí, Jǔ, Jiě, Běijīng, and Xījīng.
For Shāndōng, Cāng, and Bǎochí, three hundred jīn constituted a bag,
and twenty-five bags constituted a large set (dàtào).
Chāo, Yǐn, and official documents (gōngjù) all had to be complete before sale was permitted.
A small set (xiǎotào) consisted of ten bags,
or five, or one.
Each set required one chāo,
and the yǐn matched the number of bags.
For loose salt in Bǎochí, its jīn weight was calculated,
either three-sixths or one-sixth,
and small chāo yǐn were issued for it
to facilitate its sale.
For Jiě salt, two hundred and fifty jīn constituted one mat (xí),
and five mats constituted a set (tào).
The chāo and yǐn were sold jointly with the Shǎnxī Transport Commissioner's Office.
Those who transported grain to the Shǎnxī military camps
were permitted to exchange official documents (gōngdié) for chāo yǐn.
At Xījīng and other saltworks, salt was measured by stone.
A "large set" was five shí,
a "small set" was three shí.
In Běijīng, a large set was four shí,
and a small set was one shí.
In Liáodōng, a large set was ten shí.
All sets required one chāo (paper currency)
and one yǐn (salt certificate) per shí.
Loose salt, accumulated to ten shí,
also required one chāo for ten yǐn.
The areas for salt distribution
were determined by local suitability.
There were nine saltworks in Shāndōng and Cāngzhōu,
distributing to the circuits and prefectures of Shāndōng, Héběi, Dàmíng, Hénán, Nánjīng, Guīdé,
and the departments of Xǔ, Bó, Chén, Cài, Yǐng, Sù, Sì, Cáo, Suī, Jūn, Dān, Shòu.
There were twelve saltworks in Jǔ.
The Tāoluò saltworks supplied Jǔzhōu.
The Línghóng saltworks supplied Gànyú Xiàn.
The Dúmù saltworks supplied the Hǎizhōu Sìhòusī, Qúshān, and Dōnghǎi Xiàn.
The Bǎnpǔ saltworks supplied Liánshuǐ and Shùyáng Xiàn.
The Xìnyáng saltworks supplied Mìzhōu.
These five saltworks, along with the Dàyánchǎng, also distributed to the six departments of Yí, Pī, Xú, Sù, Sì, Téng.
The Xīyóu saltworks supplied the Láizhōu Lùshìsī and Zhāoyuǎn Xiàn.
The Héngcūn saltworks supplied Jímò and Láiyáng Xiàn.
For these two saltworks, chāo and yǐn, as well as "half-bag small chāo and yǐn",
were allowed to be sold by the local departments and counties.
The five saltworks in Nínghǎizhōu all sold loose salt,
without requiring yǐn certificates.
The Huángxiàn saltworks supplied Huáng Xiàn.
The Jùfēng saltworks supplied the Dēngzhōu Sìhòusī and Pénglái Xiàn.
The Fúshān saltworks supplied Fúshān Xiàn.
These three saltworks also supplied the neighboring Xiáxiá Xiàn.
The Nínghǎizhōu saltworks supplied the Sìhòusī and Mùpíng Xiàn.
The Wéndēng saltworks supplied Wéndēng Xiàn.
Bǎochí salt was distributed to the Zhōngdū Lù.
The Píngzhōu Fùshǐ established an office in Mǎchéng Xiàn to store funds.
Jiě salt was distributed to the Hédōng Nánběi Lù, Shǎnxī Dōng, and Nánjīng Hénán Fǔ, and the departments of Shǎn, Zhèng, Táng, Dèng, Sōng, Rǔ.
Xījīng and Liáodōng salt were each distributed within their own areas.
Běijīng Zōng and Jǐn's "end salt"
was distributed to their own circuit and the areas of Línhuáng Fǔ, Zhàozhōu, and Táizhōu,
and those bordering them were also included.
In the second month of the third year of Shìzōng's Dàdìng reign (1163),
regulations were established for military personnel privately boiling salt and stealing government salt.
Méng'ān and Móukè were ordered to patrol and apprehend.
In the eleventh month of the third year,
an imperial edict granted silver tablets to the Yìdū, Bīn, and Cāng Yánshǐsī.
In the first month of the eleventh year (1171),
based on the words of Sòng Yǔ, the Xījīng Yánpàn,
the Gǒuluò saltworks were reorganized into a sixth-grade salt commissioner's office.
Yǔ was appointed commissioner,
and Bái Zhòngtōng, the magistrate of Shùnshèng Xiàn, was appointed deputy.
The revenue for that year was set as the fixed quota.
In the fourth month,
due to famine among the people of Wūgǔlǐ Shíléi,
their salt pond tax was abolished.
In the tenth month of the twelfth year (1172),
an imperial edict granted edible salt to both poor and wealthy families' slaves and servants under the jurisdiction of the Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎosī Méng'ān.
The prime ministers stated that for those far from the salt ponds,
the amount received did not cover the travel expenses.
It was then ordered to give money based on the number of mouths,
with wealthy families' slaves and servants limited to twenty mouths.
In the second month of the thirteenth year (1173),
the monopoly on Yǒng salt was merged into the Bǎochí Shǐsī,
and the Píng and Luán salt taxes were abolished.
Cāngzhōu had previously abandoned the Hǎifù saltworks.
In the third month,
Lǐ Gé, a man from the prefecture, requested its re-establishment.
An imperial edict ordered an envoy to inspect it.
The relevant authorities stated that if this saltworks flourished, it would harm the Cāng salt revenue,
and while the salt-eating households remained the same,
the salt supply would increase annually,
leading inevitably to excessive accumulation and inability to sell.
Thus, the proposal was shelved.
In the third month,
a salt tax official was established at the Dàyánluò.
The tax on the salt ponds of the Wūgǔlǐ Shíléi tribe was again remitted.
In the eighth month of the twenty-first year (1181),
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Liáng Sù stated:
"Bǎochí and neighboring counties are experiencing food shortages.
The salt price could be reduced and the grain price increased,
exchanging grain for salt."
The Emperor ordered the prime ministers to discuss,
and they all said:
"Salt is not a widely consumed item.
If the price is reduced to exchange for grain,
it might remain unsold for a long time,
leading to a loss in revenue.
This year, over 700,000 shí of grain have arrived in Tōngzhōu,
and recently over 1,000,000 shí of grain from Ēn, Xiàn, and other six departments have followed.
This is sufficient to relieve the distress,
so there is no need for exchange."
The plan was thus abandoned.
In the twelfth month,
the Píngzhōu "stake and apportion" salt tax was abolished.
In the seventh month of the twenty-third year (1183),
Lǐ Zī, a commoner from Bóxīng Xiàn, collected sun-dried salt.
The Dàlǐsì stipulated penalties for private salt and scraping salty earth, both exceeding two methods.
The prime ministers believed it was not comparable to private salt,
but Zhāng Zhòngyù alone said:
"The crime of private salt is severe,
yet offenders are still numerous. It cannot be condoned."
The Emperor said:
"Scraping is not boiling.
How can it be equated with private salt?"
Zhòngyù replied:
"If so, the people of Bóhǎi will freely scrape and consume it,
which will infringe upon government revenue."
He argued persistently,
so the Emperor then punished Zī for scraping as a crime,
ruling that future offenders would be treated under the private salt law.
In the eleventh month,
Zhāng Bāngjī stated:
"For Bǎochí salt revenue,
if 150 jīn of regular tax are collected per shí,
there is a concern for loss due to wind drying."
It was then ordered to add 22.5 jīn of "loss salt" per shí,
and to advance loans one year in advance to pay for it,
to benefit the salt-boiling households.
In the seventh month of the twenty-fourth year (1184),
the Emperor, while in Shàngjīng,
said to Chancellor Wūgǔlún Yuánzhōng and others:
"Púchá Tōng, the prefect of Huìníng, says
that the Méng'ān and Móukè households in his area are in great difficulty.
Formerly, east of Sùpín, people consumed sea salt.
Púyǔ, Húlǐgǎi, and other circuits consumed Zhàozhōu salt.
The initial quota was 10,000 guàn;
now it has increased to 27,000.
If salt certificates are abolished
and the number of salt-boiling households increased,
it might be easier to obtain."
Yuánzhōng replied:
"An envoy has already been dispatched to plan for the area east of Xiánpíng Fǔ."
The Emperor said:
"There is no need to wait for this;
it should be done quickly."
Tōng also said
"the Shàngjīng wine office could be abolished,
allowing people to brew their own and pay taxes."
The Emperor said:
"Previously, in Luánzhōu and other places, people were also allowed to boil salt,
but it was later abolished due to inconvenience.
How can people now be allowed to sell their own?"
In the tenth month of the twenty-fifth year (1185),
the Emperor returned from Shàngjīng
and said to the prime ministers:
"I have heard that in Liáodōng,
any household consuming salt
without a certificate
is immediately punished for private dealing.
How can common people who slowly buy and consume salt obtain a certificate?
It should be stopped, allowing them to make arrangements freely,
or consulting the people
and following their wishes."
Therefore, the Běijīng and Liáodōng Yánshǐsī were abolished.
In the twenty-eighth year (1188),
the Shàngshūshěng discussed salt matters.
The Emperor said:
"Although the Yánshǐsī handles government revenue,
it has long troubled the people.
When salt officials go on patrol,
the patrolmen often privately carry government salt,
demanding bribes, wine, and food wherever they go.
If slightly displeased, they use the salt they carry to falsely accuse people of private salt dealing.
If the salt commissioner's office seeks to increase its surplus,
even knowing the accusation is false, they still impose additional penalties.
It is advisable to establish separate patrol officials,
not associated with the salt commissioner's office,
so as to reform these abuses."
In the fifth month,
the patrol commissioners were established:
two each for Shāndōng, Cāng, and Bǎochí;
one each for Jiě and Xījīng.
For Shāndōng, they were stationed in Wéizhōu and Zhāoyuǎn Xiàn.
For Cāng, in Shēnzhōu and Níngjīn Xiàn.
For Bǎochí, in Yìzhōu and Yǒngjì Xiàn.
For Jiě, in Chéngchéng Xiàn.
For Xījīng, in Dōudá Guǎn.
Their rank was from the sixth grade.
They were directly subordinate to the Provincial Department,
each given a silver tablet.
Archers from the Yánshǐsī were recruited to serve as patrolmen,
and it was prohibited to search private homes.
If the amount of edible salt was less than one dòu, no investigation or punishment was allowed.
Only those stealing, peddling privately, or privately boiling were to be apprehended.
Those within 300 lǐ were under the jurisdiction of the Zhuǎnyùnsī.
Those outside were to be punished by the local Prefectural Tídiǎn.
Stealing taxed salt was treated similarly.
In the tenth month of the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng of Emperor Zhāngzōng,
the Emperor attended court at Lóngqìng Gōng
and decreed to the relevant officials:
“Recently, during a hunt,
I learned that many common people are being punished for violating salt prohibitions.
How can the people endure this?
I wish to instruct that, following the precedent of Píng, Luán, and Tàiyuán's uniform handling,
the people be allowed to boil salt themselves.
Let all officials deliberate on this.”
In the twelfth month,
Dèng Yǎn, Minister of the Board of Revenue, and others stated:
“If the people are made to pay taxes based on the number of mouths to feed,
after they have already paid the dry-processing money,
they will still have to buy salt elsewhere to eat.
This would heavily burden the people's finances,
and only increase the profits of those who boil and sell salt.
Furthermore, the current price of salt
was set during a time when currency was easily obtained.
Today's situation is different from then.
Moreover, with long years of peace,
the population has flourished,
and the annual salt tax ought to have a surplus increase,
yet it has not.
Why is this?
It is because the official valuation is high,
and poor people benefit from the cheapness of private salt,
leading to a deficit in official revenue.
Recently, the price of Bǎochí, Shāndōng, and Cāng salt has been reduced to thirty-eight *wén* per *jīn*.
We beg to reduce it by another eight *wén*.
Annually, the reduction would be no more than one hundred and twenty thousand *guàn*.
Once the official price is low,
sales will surely increase,
and there will naturally be a surplus.
The amount reduced will not be entirely lost.
Furthermore, the imperial treasury now holds gold and silver equivalent to over one hundred million *guàn*.
Even if the salt tax is insufficient,
it is enough to cover over a hundred years of expenditure.
If we measure income against expenditure,
there will certainly be no fear of insufficiency.
We beg that the dry-processing salt tax in Píng and Luán also have its price reduced.
Circuit salt patrol archers should not arbitrarily conduct patrols themselves,
to reform the abuses of false accusations.”
Lǐ Yàn, Minister of the Board of Rites, and others said:
“The so-called ‘dry-processing’
is neither a good name nor
a good method.
If one must eliminate the abuses of private boiling and illicit trading,
nothing is better than reducing the price to twenty-five *wén* per *jīn*,
so that public and private prices are the same.
Then private salt will cease by itself.
Moreover, salt patrol soldiers and officials often use private salt to falsely accuse people.
They should be instructed to coordinate with the subordinate prefectures and counties,
only then are they permitted to conduct patrols.
Violators shall be punished by the Ànchá Sī.”

Guō Bāngjié, Minister of the Board of Punishments, and others stated that Píng and Luán, which are near the sea, and Tàiyuán, which has brine lands, could continue the dry-processing system as before,
while the rest would follow Yǎn's proposal.
Yīlà Zhòngfāng, Censor-in-chief, stated that those who privately boil and illicitly trade salt
are all aware of the prohibition yet violate it.
Competent officials should be selected to serve as salt patrol commissioners,
but they should not be allowed to enter homes to search.
Wáng Xiāo, Associate Administrator of Dàxīng Fǔ, requested a reduction to twenty *wén* per *jīn*
and the abolition of salt patrol officials.
Túdān Yì, Left Remonstrance Grand Master, considered dry-processing convenient.
The Chancellors reported:
“The official cost per *jīn* is ten *wén*.
If reduced to twenty-five *wén*,
it seems appropriate.
Salt patrol archers can be reduced by one-third.
When salt officials go on patrol, they must coordinate with their subordinates to go together.
Those who fail to obtain findings without accompanying officials shall not be punished.
This can be implemented starting from the first day of the fifth month of next year.”
The Emperor then ordered that Bǎochí, Shāndōng, and Cāng salt be reduced to thirty *wén* per *jīn*.
Banknotes already issued but not yet redeemed would be topped up according to the new price,
and the rest of the requests were granted.
In the twelfth month,
the salt patrol commissioners of Xījíng and Xiè salt were abolished.
At that time, an edict had already abolished the dry-processing salt money.

In the twelfth month, based on the proposals of Yīlà Jiǔshèngnú, Dàlǐ Sīzhí, and Sòng Yǐ, Guǎngníng Tuīguān, regarding the advantages and disadvantages of the salt administrations in Běijīng and Liáodōng,
the Salt Commissionerates of Běijīng and Liáodōng were re-established.
Běijīng Lù was set with an annual quota of over one hundred thousand *guàn*,
and Liáodōng Lù with one hundred and thirty thousand *guàn*.
The salt patrol commissioners of Xījíng and Xiè Zhōu were abolished.
In the seventh month of the first year of Míngchāng,
petitioners reported that the dry-processing salt money in Hédōng Běilù, at one hundred thousand *guàn* annually, was too heavy.
Because of this, many people fled,
and they begged for a delay in its collection and enforcement.
The Emperor ordered that an envoy be dispatched to investigate during the agricultural off-season.
In the twelfth month,
regulations were established to prohibit prefectures and counties from arbitrarily levying salt taxes.
In the fifth month of the second year,
ministers of the Secretariat-Chancellery stated that the Shāndōng salt tax was insufficient
because salt administration officials on patrol did not dare to arrest arbitrarily,
and always had to coordinate with their subordinates to go together,
which made people unafraid.
Thus, an edict was issued:
From now on, if there are illicit traders,
salt administration officials are allowed to arrest them immediately.
If people privately boil or conceal salt,
then they must coordinate with their subordinates to conduct searches.
Patrol officers and archers are not allowed to arbitrarily enter homes
unless they have coordinated with the salt administration.
In the sixth month of the third year,
Sūn Jíkāng and others, together with salt administration officials, deliberated:
“If military or civilian personnel violate the private salt laws,
within three hundred *lǐ*, the salt administration shall determine the punishment;
for those further away, they shall be handed over to the Tídiǎn Suǒ.
Rewards for capture shall all be levied from the illicit manufacturers and traders.
For *méng'ān móukè* personnel who boil, trade, or steal salt,
their supervising official shall deliberate on redemption.
Upon the third offense, they shall be caned.
If they can make a capture, they shall be exempt from punishment.
Furthermore, as Yǒnghé Zhèn in Bīnzhōu Bóhǎi Xiàn is far from the *zhōu* capital,
we fear the concealment of stolen goods and private salt.
It can be changed to Yǒngfēng Zhèn, and patrol inspectors should be established at both Yǒngfēng Zhèn and Cáozishān Cūn.
The Judgement Officials of Shāndōng, Bǎochí, and Cāng Salt Administrations beg to be promoted to rank seven,
and be appointed from among *jìnshì*.”
The Emperor ordered a re-deliberation on the caning of *méng'ān móukè* personnel,
and all other points were approved.
The Shàngshū Shěng reported:
“The salt from the nine fields of Bīn and Yì in Shāndōng is distributed in six circuits including Shāndōng.
The five fields of Tāoluo and others are only distributed in the six *zhōu* of Yí, Pī, Xú, Sù, Téng, and Sì.
Each has a fixed quota.
Compared to the nine fields,
the large quotas are different.
If they are made to compare increases and decreases with the nine fields,
the officials of the five fields might rely on the large quotas of the others,
and thus might not exert effort,
leading to further corruption.”
Thus, it was decided that the five fields would conduct their own comparisons.
The old method was to compare with the Salt Commissioner and Vice-Commissioner,
and so it was only now changed.
In the first month of the fifth year,
Zuǒ Bì and others, officials of the eight small salt fields,
submitted an application to retire due to their inability to meet the quota.
An envoy was then dispatched to inspect the thirteen fields and re-determine the quotas.
Except for the five fields including Tāoluo, which had *guǎngòu* established
and could immediately resume operations,
for the eight fields reported by Bì,
following the system of Dàdìng twenty-sixth year,
they would manage their own quotas
and be permanently compared and adjusted according to the new regulations.
Lǐ Jìngyì, Lángzhōng of the Board of Revenue, and others stated:
“The newly determined quotas for the eight small fields have been reduced by half.
If all follow the new quotas,
but the old quotas have already been collected by the government,
we fear that the large amount of money reduced
will lead to fraud,
and the collected money will not be fully and truthfully recorded and submitted to the government.”
Therefore, following the regulations of the Jiǔshuì Yuàn Wù established in the first year of Míngchāng,
it was ordered that collection begin immediately.
In the eleventh month,
as per the old system, *méng'ān móukè* personnel who committed offenses related to private salt, alcohol, or yeast
were judged by the Zhuǎnyùn Sī.
It was then re-decided that all military and civilian personnel who committed private salt offenses
would fall under the jurisdiction of the salt administration,
while private alcohol and yeast offenses would fall under the Zhuǎnyùn Sī.
Those from over three hundred *lǐ* away would be handed over to the Tídiǎn Suǒ.
If a criminal was arrested and the subordinate official did not dispatch them, they would be sentenced to two years of penal servitude.
In the twelfth month,
the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) deliberated that the old regulations for Shāndōng and Cāngzhōu stipulated forty-one *wén* per *jīn* (catty) of salt,
and Bǎochí forty-three *wén* per *jīn*.
Since the amnesty and special decree of Dàdìng (大定) twenty-ninth year,
this was reduced to thirty *wén*,
resulting in a reduction of over 1,854,000 *guàn*.
Later, due to insufficient national expenditure,
it was then decreed that three *wén* should be added back, making it thirty-three *wén* per *jīn*.
By the twelfth month of Chéng'ān (承安) third year,
the Shàngshū Shěng reported:
"The profit from salt is immense.
Today, the population of the empire has greatly increased,
and those who consume salt are twice as many as before.
Those who rely on it for military provisions and for income are also numerous.
Moreover, it is an indispensable item for daily life.
How could its consumption vary much due to its price fluctuations?
If we do not seize the opportunity to profit from it,
we fear it will be lost in vain."
Thus, the price for the three salt administrations of Shāndōng, Bǎochí, and Cāngzhōu was set again at forty-two *wén* per *jīn*.
For Jiězhōu, the old regulation was five *guàn* per mat,
which was increased to six *guàn* four hundred *wén*.
For Liáodōng and Běijīng, the old regulation was nine hundred *wén* per *shí* (dan),
which was increased to one *guàn* five hundred *wén*.
For Xījíng (Western Capital), boiled salt, previously two *guàn* per *shí*,
was increased to two *guàn* eight hundred *wén*.
Raw salt, previously one *guàn* five hundred *wén*,
was increased to two *guàn*.
After increasing its price,
the quantity to be sold was also increased.
The old annual revenue from the seven salt administrations was 6,226,636 *guàn* 566 *wén*.
By this time, it had increased to 10,774,512 *guàn* 137 *wén* 2 *fēn*.
Shāndōng's old annual revenue was 2,547,336 *guàn*,
which increased to 4,334,184 *guàn* 400 *wén*.
Cāngzhōu's old annual revenue was 1,531,200 *guàn*,
which increased to 2,766,636 *guàn*.
Bǎochí's old revenue was 887,558 *guàn* 600 *wén*,
which increased to 1,348,839 *guàn*.
Jiězhōu's old revenue was 814,657 *guàn* 500 *wén*,
which increased to 1,321,520 *guàn* 256 *wén*.
Liáodōng's old revenue was 131,572 *guàn* 870 *wén*,
which increased to 376,970 *guàn* 256 *wén*.
Běijīng's old revenue was 213,892 *guàn* 500 *wén*,
which increased to 346,151 *guàn* 617 *wén* 2 *fēn*.
Xījíng's old revenue was 100,419 *guàn* 696 *wén*,
which increased to 280,264 *guàn* 608 *wén*.
In the fourth month,
the Prime Minister reported,
"According to the law,
if a *mèng'ān móukè* (commander of a chiliarchy and a centuriarchy) reports private salt but fails to apprehend, he is to be beaten with a staff.
If his subordinates commit the offense and he fails to investigate,
the punishment is determined by the quantity involved.
Now, there are those who personally commit such offenses,
along with those who commit private brewing of alcohol and yeast, or slaughter cattle.
These are all from hereditary powerful and noble families,
and it is imperative that these activities not be prohibited."
Thus, regulations were established for penal servitude and the number of staff blows,
and redemption was not allowed.
Those not subject to penal servitude were to receive fifty staff blows.
In the eighth month,
the three salt administrations of Shāndōng, Bǎochí, and Cāngzhōu were ordered
to send envoys each spring and autumn to supervise the Investigation Commissioners and the prefectural and county officials in inspecting private salt.
In the ninth month of Tàihé (泰和) first year,
the provincial officials reported that the salt bags for the two administrations of Cāngzhōu and Bīnzhōu
required buying 1,200,000 mats annually,
all sourced from the common people.
A new Cāngzhōu salt field was established in Běijìng (北靖海) County, Qīngzhōu.
This was originally a hunting ground,
marshy and full of reeds.
It was advisable to lift the prohibition
and allow the people to harvest and weave them seasonally.
In the eleventh month,
Gāo Rǔlì (高汝礪), the Commissioner of Transport for Shǎnxī Circuit, stated:
"According to the old system,
those who apprehended and reported private salt, alcohol, and yeast
were awarded prize money based on the weight,
all collected from the offenders.
However, if supervisory officials seized them, the revenue went to the regular taxes,
and patrol officials received no reward.
Patrol soldiers received half the reward of ordinary people,
and tax-exempt archers received half of that.
This means the crime is the same but the rewards differ.
I request that the unrewarded amount for the patrol officials of the administrations and counties,
and the reduced amount for the patrol archers,
all be collected as official revenue,
so that rewards and punishments are equitable."
An imperial edict approved this.
In the second month of the third year,
the Jiězhōu salt administration envoy was ordered to govern the principal prefecture,
and his deputy to govern Ānyì (安邑).
In the eleventh month,
it was stipulated that *jìnshì* (recipients of the highest degree in the imperial examinations) could be appointed to salt administration official positions,
with appointments based on their examination ranking and seniority in entering officialdom.
In the sixth month of the fourth year,
it was decreed that the revenue quotas for the seven salt administrations would be fixed for seven years.
The price per *jīn* was increased to forty-four *wén*.
At this time, Zhāng Wěi (張煒), the Prefect of Huánzhōu, requested to exchange salt for rice.
The provincial officials were ordered to discuss this.
In the sixth month,
an imperial edict stated that since the new quotas were increased for the Shāndōng and Cāngzhōu salt administrations,
the annual accumulated deficit
was due to officials failing to plan properly,
and the *guāngōu* (supervisors), inspectors, and other involved parties conspiring in corrupt practices,
leading to this situation.
Competent individuals were to be selected to replace the envoys and deputies of the two administrations.

For *guāngōu*, honest and capable individuals were to be chosen from *jìnshì*, departmental clerks, interpreters, scribes, historical interpreters, legal experts, child scholars, and those from various bureaus.
Their former officials were dismissed.
In the tenth month,
for those in the northwest circuit who violated the prohibition on *huāxián* (flowered salt),
it was proposed to equate their crime with that of salt prohibition.
The Prime Minister stated that if compared to private salt,
there were differences.
An imperial edict then established the regulation:
those who collected it would receive eighty staff blows;
for every ten *jīn*, the punishment would increase by one degree,
with the maximum penalty being one year of penal servitude.
The rewards would be the same as for private alum cases.
In the sixth month of the fifth year,
due to revenue shortfalls in the Shāndōng and Cāngzhōu salt administrations,
Shí Xuàn (石鉉), an Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, was dispatched to inspect them.
Upon his return, he suggested that it would be more convenient for the two administrations to divide their responsibilities.

An imperial edict assigned Zhōu Áng (周昂) to supervise the eastern and western circuits of Héběi, Dàmíng Fǔ, Ēnzhōu, Nánjīng, Suīzhōu, Chénzhōu, Càizhōu, Xǔzhōu, and Yǐngzhōu, all subordinate to the Cāngzhōu salt administration.
The eastern and western circuits of Shāndōng, Kāizhōu, Púzhōu, Guīdé Fǔ, Cáozhōu, Shānzhōu, Bózhōu, Shòuzhōu, and Sìzhōu were assigned to the Shāndōng salt administration.
Each was to assess quotas based on household population.
In the tenth month,
Zhāng Déhuī (張德huī), the Acting Investigation Commissioner for the Héběi Eastern and Western Dàmíng Circuits, stated that
people near the coast could easily obtain private salt,
leading to numerous offenders.
He suggested distributing salt based on household population.
The Shàngshū Shěng instructed the Shāndōng Investigation Commissioners to discuss its feasibility.
They stated,
"In Láizhōu, Mìzhōu, and other prefectures, harvests have been poor for consecutive years.
Although the revenue collected from selling salt based on household population is meager,
people consider it a heavy burden,
which might lead to displacement.
Moreover, those who secretly boil salt are all unregistered people;
how could distributing salt for purchase prevent them from doing so?"
Thus, new regulations were established,
ordering both the Shāndōng and Cāngzhōu salt administrations to dispatch special envoys to patrol their respective territories.
In the third month of the sixth year,
Yòu Chéngxiàng (Right Grand Counselor) Zōng Hào (宗浩) and Cānzhī Zhèngshì (参知政事, Vice Grand Counselor) Jiǎ Xuàn (賈鉉) stated:
"The national expenditure relies solely on salt revenue.
Currently, Shāndōng has a deficit of over 500,000 *guàn*,
owing to the formation of gangs by private boilers and illegal sellers.
The salt administrations cannot apprehend them,
nor do the Military Command and Investigation Commissioners prohibit them.
If we only consider the number of private salt offenders,
and merely reduce salaries and demote officials,
they will suppress reports and not submit them,
making it even harder to control.
It is advisable to establish regulations
based on the actual increases or deficits incurred by each official during their tenure,
and have the salt administrations report this to the provincial and departmental authorities
as a basis for promotion or demotion."
An imperial edict was then issued to all Military Command and Pacification Commissionerates,
and officials of imperial prefectures and military districts:
if there were offenders in their jurisdiction,
twice would result in a deduction of half a month's salary;
five times in a year would result in a recommendation for dismissal.
Patrol officials, upon committing an offense, would be immediately punished.
The Investigation Commissioners and Imperial Censors were ordered to supervise this.
In the fourth month,
following the suggestion of Jiágǔ Púnǎi (夾谷蒲乃), the Prefect of Zhuōzhōu,
the salt money paid by the people of Láizhōu was allowed to be paid in silk, cotton, silver, or paper currency.
In the ninth month of the seventh year,

regulations were established for the promotion and demotion of the Xī Běijīng (Western Beijing) and Liáodōng salt administration judicial officers and all field *guāngōu*, based on increases or deficits.
For all civil officials and clerks, personnel from various bureaus, and those whose qualifications were verified for appointment,
if the increase was less than one *fēn*, they would be promoted to the top of their current rank.
A deficit of one *fēn* would result in a demotion of one qualification.
Two *fēn* would result in a demotion of two qualifications and a transfer to a lower office.
Four *fēn* would result in a demotion of two qualifications and a transfer to two lower offices.
A deficit would be regarded as a demotion according to these standards.
For those appointed after verifying their previous service,
an increase of less than one *fēn* would result in promotion to the top of their current rank.
A deficit of one *fēn* would result in a demotion of one qualification.
Two *fēn* would result in a demotion of one qualification and a transfer to a lower rank.
Four *fēn* would result in a demotion of two qualifications and a transfer to two lower ranks.
A deficit would also be regarded as a demotion according to these standards.
In the twelfth month,
the Shàngshū Shěng, based on the words of Lú Fùyì (盧附翼),
established regulations for salt-producing households illegally selling tax-owed salt.
If there was any surplus beyond the required salt tax,
it had to be fully reported to the officials.
If retained, it would be considered one degree less than theft.
If they scraped earth to boil and eat,
or gathered yellow spike grass to burn for ash and leach for brine,
or made alcohol from fermented porridge,
they would receive eighty staff blows.
In the seventh month of the eighth year,
Sòng Kèjùn (宋克俊) stated:
"Since the salt *guāngōu* were changed to *jìnshì* and other examination degree holders,
the supervisory officials have lost the opportunity to be exceptionally promoted to the rank of county magistrate.
Consequently, they have become negligent, leading to revenue deficits.
I request that the old system be reinstated for convenience."
The relevant department stated that when the changes were made in Tàihé fourth year,
people who had arrived at the department at that time were selected to fill the positions.
Thus, it was proposed that those who arrived at the department in autumn be appointed as replacements.
In the seventh month of the eighth year,
an imperial edict ordered that all salt monopoly markets along the Huái River
allow officials and commoners to trade salt for goods.
In the tenth month of the second year of Zhēnyòu of Xuānzōng's reign,
the Ministry of Revenue reported that
the counties of Yángwǔ, Yánjīn, Yuánwǔ, Xíngzé, and Héyīn abounded in brine,
and private salt boiling by the populace could not be prohibited.
Consequently, an imperial edict established markets,
appointing one official (pànguān) and one director (guǎngōu) each,
subordinate to the Ministry of Revenue.
Soon after,
the Censorate memorialized that
these counties had all been seized by powerful individuals,
and commercial trade was stagnant.
Therefore, an imperial edict ordered censors to travel to these areas to reiterate prohibitions and restrictions.
In the twelfth month of the third year,
Wūgǔlùn Qìngshòu, acting Vice-Pacification Commissioner of the Eastern Hédōng Southern Circuit, stated:
“The people of Jiàng and Jiě mostly engage in selling salt,
passing through the Dàyáng Pass to trade for grain from Shǎn and Guó.
Upon their return across the river,
the government requisitions eight parts of it,
leaving them with little after travel expenses.
Moreover, the Hénán Provincial Administration again transports salt itself to trade for grain in Shǎn,
thereby completely depriving the people of their profits.
In recent years, Hédōng has suffered from drought and locusts,
and with the added requisitioning,
prices have skyrocketed,
and the people are migrating,
which is truly deplorable.
I beg that the requisitioning be abolished
to alleviate their distress.”
In the seventh month of the fourth year,
Qìngshòu again stated:
“Hézhōng lacks grain,
and not only is it unable to be relieved,
but it is also subjected to requisitioning, depriving it further.
Indeed, salt is a government commodity.
Officials transport it by land to the river,
then by boat to Jīngzhào and Fèngxiáng,
to trade with merchants,
a difficult and arduous task.
Yet the Shǎnxī Provincial Administration requisitions two dòu for every shí of salt,
meaning government property is being self-requisitioned.
The exchange of salt for goods
was originally intended to aid Hézhōng,
but Shǎnxī forcibly seizes it again.
What is this if not a deprivation?
I beg that both sides allow the people to act at their convenience,
then both public and private interests will be served.”
The emperor acceded.
In the sixth month of the second year of Xīngdìng,
acting Yán'ān Ministry of Six Boards Yuanwailáng Lú Jìn submitted a proposal:
“The areas near the river at Sìwǔchéng, Yìhé, and Kèróngzhài in Suídé produce much salt.
I request the establishment of one salt field director (guǎngōu)
to annually yield over 130,000 jīn,
which can contribute 20,000 guàn in cash to support the army.”
In the third year,
an imperial edict adopted his proposal,
establishing officials to sell salt for border use.
In the fourth year,
Lǐ Fùhēng stated
that 17,000 shí of millet and wheat, formerly exchanged for Jiě salt from the western bank of Hézhōng, should be used for Guāndōng.
Soon after, it was ordered that Jiě salt should not be transported to Shǎnxī,
because there was an alert in the north,
and river prohibitions were urgent.
In the second year of Yuánguāng, the imperial relative Ékě stated
that the common people transporting Jiě salt could assist military provisions,
so an imperial edict ordered the repair of stone walls to secure it.
Wine.
The Jin dynasty's wine monopoly followed the old systems of the Liáo and Sòng dynasties.
In the third year of Tiānhuì, officials were first ordered to manage the monopoly for a full year.
In the third year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng's reign,
an imperial edict ordered that members of the imperial clan who privately brewed wine
be prosecuted by the Transport Commission.
In the third year,
the Secretariat reported that many wine households in Zhōngdū had absconded,
thus causing a greater deficit in tax revenue.
The emperor said:
“This is due to officials not strictly prohibiting private brewing.”
He ordered the establishment of a hundred soldiers,
subordinate to the Military Affairs Commission,
who, together with the Wine Commissioner and his deputy, would patrol;
even powerful families were permitted to be searched.
If bondservants violated the prohibition,
their masters would be beaten with one hundred strokes.
He also ordered the Assistant Administrator of Dàxīng to recruit back the wine households.
In the eighth year,
it was further stipulated that for the Wine Commissioner's office with a revenue target of 50,000 guàn or more,
and for salt fields with less than 50,000 guàn,
civil and military officials would be appointed according to old regulations;
all others would be filled by capable officials with right-side positions who had been repeatedly appointed without deficit.
In the ninth year,
an official of Dàxīng County, fearing that his salary would be withheld due to the revenue deficit of the Guǎngyángzhen office,
distributed wine to the common people
to collect their taxes.
The Grand Court of Justice requested that, since the money was not for personal gain,
it be treated as a redeemable offense.
[一０]The emperor said:
“Although it is not private embezzlement,
the poor people have also been harmed by it.
If it is merely redeemed,
how can future offenses be deterred?”
He specifically ordered his dismissal.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Secretariat reported that since the establishment of fixed quotas for salt, iron, wine, and yeast,
there had been varying increases.
The emperor said:
“When I was in Shàngjīng previously,
the wine tasted poor.
I wish to collect taxes as the麴院 (yeast bureau) in Zhōngdū does,
so that the people may have good wine.
My daily provisions have also been reduced;
once, a princess arrived,
and there were no extra provisions to offer her.
How difficult would it be for me to use fifty sheep daily?
But I fear that all expenses would come from the people,
and I cannot bear to do it.
Supervisory officials only know how to benefit themselves,
not knowing where the benefit comes from.
If those who expand and increase revenue are rewarded and promoted,
and those who incur deficits are punished and demoted,
and the quotas for both increases and deficits are revised
to ensure the original amount is not lost.
For those of the Hèngbān (irregular officials) who only incur deficits,
they should be demoted and punished uniformly with other officials in similar situations,
so that there may be encouragement and deterrence.
For instance, if the reward is for achieving 20,000 guàn,
but only 17,000 or 18,000 is obtained,
and it is difficult to give two rewards,
then only 10,000 guàn will be submitted,
and the remaining money will be taken for personal use.
From now on, the current appointees should not take the remaining reward money;
instead, it should be combined with the increased money from subsequent appointments for calculation as a reward,
so that the money can go to the government.
And for supervisory officials’ salaries,
if they are not given in advance,
how can integrity be expected?
From now on, for those who meet the deadline,
this method shall be used.”
They also requested the abolition of the “lánrén” (market guards).
In the twenty-seventh year,
it was debated that all yamun offices in the realm
should, following the Zhōngdū example,
change to collecting yeast tax
and allow commoners to sell wine.
The Ministry of Revenue dispatched officials to inquire in seven places: Liáodōng Láiyuǎnjūn,
Xīnxī and Yúchéng in Nánjīng Circuit,
the Xī Jīng Wine Commissioner's office, Báidēng County, the Diélà Tribe, and Tiānchéng County in Xī Jīng Circuit.
[一一]Besides the regular taxes,
they wished to undertake the responsibility of collecting and selling wine themselves.
The emperor said:
“From ancient times, supervisory officials often embezzled public funds.
If the common people are allowed to manage it,
this malpractice may be reformed.
Let it be tried.”
In the first month of the first year of Míngchāng,
new quotas were set,
and it was ordered that collection begin immediately.
The Zhōngdū麴使司 (Yeast Commissioner's Office),
during the Dàdìng period,
annually earned 361,500 guàn in cash;
in the first year of Chéng'ān, it earned 405,133 guàn.
The Xī Jīng Wine Commissioner's Office,
during the Dàdìng period,
annually earned 53,467 guàn and 588 wén in cash;
in the first year of Chéng'ān, it earned 107,893 guàn in cash.
In the seventh month,
it was decided that for the Zhōngdū麴使司, the period from the twenty-first year of Dàdìng to the sixth year of Míngchāng would be the benchmark,
and the average annual amount across this period would be taken as the quota.
In the fourth month of the fifth year,
the Secretariat reported:
“Previously, 'lánrén' (market guards) were stationed at various wine tax offices,
recruited from the 'shèliángjūn' (archers) who had served in imperial entourages.
They were abolished in the twenty-sixth year of Dàdìng,
and the soldiers who were supposed to serve in imperial entourages
were each given additional pay in cash and grain as compensation for their labor.
Now, it is proposed to use the original 'lánqián' (market guard fees)
to replace these additional payments,
ordering each yamun office to verify the amount collected,
take three percent of it,
and submit it along with the regular taxes,
without further inclusion in the comparison.
This is estimated to yield over 300,000 cash annually
to aid national expenditure.”
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Tàihé,
the Secretariat reported:
“For the Zhōngdū麴使司, revenue has increased for eight consecutive years since the quota was set.
It is appropriate to follow the old method,
calculating the total revenue over these eight years,
averaging it to an annual figure,
and then including one-tenth of the tax revenue from all newly added items,
to form the total quota.
For future quotas,
the system shall be fixed every five years.”
It was also ordered that all local wine offices
should collect an additional three-tenths above their original quota as “zāojiaòqián” (fermentation fees).
In the sixth year,
the Court of Policy stipulated varying quotas for the sale of wine.
If sales exceeded the quota, or if excess amounts were transported,
they were to be punished.
In the twelfth month of Zhēnyòu (貞祐) third year of Xuānzōng (宣宗),
Censor Tián Kuíxiù (田䄄秀) stated:
“In the Dàdìng (大定) period,
where wine taxes annually reached 100,000 strings of cash,
an office of commissioners was initially established.
Later, it was also established for 20,000 strings of cash.
Now, the Hénán (河南) commissioner's office has over fifty members,
idly consuming monthly stipends.
It should revert to the Dàdìng (大定) system.”
In Yuánguāng (元光) first year,
the Qūshǐsī (麴使司) (Fermented Grains Office) was re-established.
Vinegar Tax.
From the beginning of Dàdìng (大定),
due to insufficient national funds,
officials were appointed to monopolize it
to aid in expenditures.
By the twenty-third year,
as the treasury was full,
it was abolished.
In Míngchāng (明昌) fifth year of Zhāngzōng (章宗),
because the income of the relevant authorities was insufficient for their expenditures,
those who spoke on affairs requested the monopolization of vinegar profits.
Thus, officials were ordered to be established to monopolize it.
The tax quota
was to be determined by the appointed officials.
It was later abolished.
In the third month of Chéng'ān (承安) third year,
the provincial ministers, citing vast national expenditures,
reinstated the vinegar monopoly.
For amounts over 500 strings of cash, a Dūjiān (都監) (Supervisor) was established;
for amounts over 1,000 strings of cash, one Tóngjiān (同監) (Assistant Supervisor) was established.
Tea.
Beyond the annual tribute from the Sòng (宋) people,
all trade was conducted at the state-controlled markets on the Sòng (宋) border.
In Dàdìng (大定) sixteenth year of Shìzōng (世宗),
due to widespread private trafficking,
the regulations for punishments and rewards concerning fragrant tea were revised.
In the eighth month of Chéng'ān (承安) third year of Zhāngzōng (章宗),
it was deemed to consume national resources and benefit the enemy,
so officials were ordered to be established to control it.
Liú Chéng (劉成), a Chéngdéláng (承德郎) clerk of the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省), was sent to Hénán (河南) to inspect government-made tea.
As he did not personally taste its flavor,
but merely gathered popular opinion, calling it "wēnsāng" (溫桑),
which was in fact not tea,
he reported this upon his return.
The Emperor deemed it irrelevant,
punished him with seventy strokes of the rod,
and dismissed him.
In the third month of the fourth year,
one workshop was established in Zī (淄), Mì (密), Nínghǎi (寧海), and Càizhōu (蔡州) respectively,
to produce new tea.
Following the Southern custom, each jīn (斤) was packed in a bag,
priced at 600 wén (文).
As merchants were slow to transport it,

the Zhuǎnyùnsī (轉運司) (Transport Commissioner's Offices) of the four circuits of Shāndōng (山東) and Héběi (河北) were ordered to distribute the bags according to the household populations of their respective circuits,
and deliver them to the various prefectural and county offices for sale.
Those who bought permits
paid in cash or in kind,
whichever was convenient.
In the fifth month,
as households in Shāndōng (山東) were producing and selling private tea,
encroaching on state monopolies,
a regulation was enacted, similar to that for privately boiled alum,
punishing offenders with two years of penal servitude.
In Tàihé (泰和) fourth year,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
“I have tasted the new tea;
though its flavor is not excellent,
is it not edible?
I recently ordered a close attendant to investigate,
and found that all four circuits of Shāndōng (山東) and Héběi (河北) were allocating it to the people.
If it is said to coerce the people,
they should be punished.
It is unknown whether this measure was carried out by the Transport Commissioner's Office or the county officials.
The relevant Ànchásī (按察司) (Surveillance Commissioners) should also be held accountable.
Investigate the facts and report.
From now on, the price per bag shall be reduced by 300 wén (文).
If unsold by the fourth month of next year,
even if it spoils, it will not matter.”
In the spring of the fifth year,
the tea production workshops were abolished.
In the third month,
the Emperor instructed the provincial ministers:
“Although tea is no longer produced now,
do not cut down the trees.
The land should be freely used by the people for farming and gathering firewood.”
In the sixth year,
when tea trees in Hénán (河南) withered,
they were ordered to be replanted.
In the eleventh month,
the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) reported:
“Tea
is a superfluous item of food and drink,
not an essential one.
In recent years, both high and low have competed to drink it,
especially farmers,
and tea houses in the market are numerous.
Merchants often exchange silk for tea,
annually spending no less than one million,
thus exchanging useful goods for useless ones.
If not prohibited,
it is feared that the expenditure of wealth will be even greater.”
Thus, it was ordered that only officials of the seventh rank and above
were allowed to consume tea in their households,
and it was forbidden to sell or gift it.
For those who should not possess it,
punishments and rewards were set according to weight.
In the seventh year,
the regulations for tea consumption were revised.
In the seventh month of the eighth year,
those who spoke on affairs argued that tea was merely grass sprouts from Sòng (宋) territory,
and it was unacceptable to exchange China's useful goods like silk floss, brocade, and silk for it.
It was not permissible.
The state's salt merchandise came from brine,
and could be endlessly produced annually;
it could be used to exchange for tea.
The provincial ministers considered that the scope of exchange would be limited,
so they memorialized to allow the exchange of miscellaneous goods as well.
In the third month of Yuánguāng (元光) second year of Xuānzōng (宣zōng),
the provincial ministers, citing the dwindling national resources and depleted treasury,
memorialized:
“Gold, silver, coins, and grain
are things that the world cannot do without for a single day.
Tea originally comes from Sòng (宋) territory,
and is not an urgent necessity for food and drink.
Yet, since ancient times, merchants have exchanged gold and silk for it,
which is a mere waste.
During the Tàihé (泰和) period,
it was once prohibited.
Later, due to the Sòng (宋) people seeking peace,
it was abolished.
Since the outbreak of war,
it has been resumed.
However, the number of offenders has not decreased,
and border residents, eyeing profit,
cross the border to trade privately,
fearing that military intelligence might be leaked,
or bandits might enter the country.
Currently, Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西) have over fifty prefectures.
Each prefecture consumes about twenty bags of tea daily,
each bag worth two liǎng (兩) of silver.
This means an unnecessary annual expenditure of over 300,000 liǎng (兩) of silver from the people.
[一二]How can we use our useful goods to aid the enemy?”
Thus, it was decreed that imperial princes, princesses, and incumbent officials of the fifth rank and above,
who had traditionally stored tea, could keep it,
but were forbidden to sell or gift it.
All others were prohibited.
Offenders were sentenced to five years of penal servitude,
and informants were rewarded with 10,000 strings of cash from Bǎoqúan (寶泉).
Various commercial taxes.
In the fifth month of Zhēnyuán (貞元) first year of Hǎilíng (海陵),
vacant land in the capital was granted to officials of all ranks attending court and to the imperial guard.
In the seventh month,
various amounts of money were levied from each.
In Dàdìng (大定) second year,
the Court of Policy established regulations for deficits and rewards for achievements.
In the eighth month,
transit taxes on all routes were abolished,
only allowing inspections.
In the third year,
the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) reported that
the Shāndōng (山東) Xīlù (西路) Zhuǎnyùnsī (轉運司) stated that
many workshops, markets, rivers, and ferries had outstanding arrears.
An imperial edict, in accordance with the supervisory system,
granted exemptions and reductions
based on the age of the arrears.
Also, based on the statement of Liú Xíngyì (劉行義), a clerk of the Shàngshū Gōngbù (尚書工部),
a system for taxing rented houses within city walls was established.
In the fifth year,
because officials had previously been dismissed from the Héluò (河濼) region,
the people were again invited to bid for purchase.
After the establishment of the two administrative areas,
officials were re-established as before.
In the first month of the twentieth year,
commercial tax laws were established:
one percent was levied on gold and silver,
and three percent on all other goods.
In Dàdìng (大定) twenty-ninth year of Zhāngzōng (章宗),
the Hùbù (戶部) (Ministry of Revenue) stated that fishing rights in all rivers and lakes had been granted to the people for shared benefit,
and the seven places where officials were established could be abolished.
The relevant authorities were entrusted to prevent powerful families from monopolizing these benefits.
In the first year of Míngchāng, in the first month,
an imperial edict was issued to the Shàngshū Shěng,
to set the tax quota for the yuànwù (government-run production and sales offices) and commercial taxes.
The 1,616 yuànwù of the various lù (circuits) shǐsī (fiscal commissioners)
were reduced by over 941,000 guàn compared to the old quota.
Consequently, the fāngcháng (government workshops and marketplaces) were abolished,
and rent tax was exempted.
In the tenth month,
the Shàngshū Shěng reported:
"Now, for the yuànwù of the shǐsī throughout the realm,
since the tax quotas have been reduced,
and there is a system for officials in charge of supervision to be promoted or penalized based on gains and losses,
the system of rewards and punishments given by the Tídiǎn (Inspector) should be abolished.
Instead, the Tíxíng Sī (Judicial Commissioner) should be entrusted
to investigate any Tídiǎn officials who infringe upon the fāngcháng and yuànwù,
and they shall be punished according to regulations."
The imperial edict approved it.
In the third year,
an edict reduced the rent and land lease fees for government properties in Nánjīng.
In the second year,
the Tíxíng Sī was instructed
to forbid powerful families from monopolizing the profits from mountains and lakes.
Additionally, the Sīzhú Jiān (Bamboo Office) harvested 500,000 poles of broken bamboo annually,
delivering them twice a year (spring and autumn) to the Dōushǔi Jiān (Canal and River Conservancy Office)
for river defense.
The remaining scraps, such as edge cuttings and bamboo shoots, were sold for 3,000 guàn,
and reeds for 2,000 guàn,
which constituted the quota.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
petitioners requested the restoration of the old fāngcháng system.
The Emperor did not allow it,
but only permitted an increase in the number of yuànwù.
An edict instructed the Shàngshū Shěng to deliberate and establish regulations.
Consequently, it was proposed that in Liáodōng and Běijīng, people would still be allowed to operate them as before,
while in the eleven lù, including Zhōngdū, officials would be dispatched to inspect them,
and an additional twenty-three yuànwù would be established.
This would take effect from the first day of the ninth month of the current year.
The decree was approved.
During the Dàdìng reign,
the Zhōngdū Shuìshǐ Sī (Tax Commissioner's Office of Zhōngdū) earned over 164,440 guàn annually.
In the first year of Chéng'ān,
it earned 214,579 guàn annually.
In the fifth month of the sixth year of Tàihé,
a decree stated that if the yuànwù quotas were not met,
the Yùnsī (Transportation Commissioner) should dispatch officials to supervise and collect the taxes.
Gold and Silver Tax.
In the third year of Dàdìng,
a decree permitted common people to mine gold and silver.
One-twentieth of the proceeds was taken as tax.
In the fourth year of Tàihé,
petitioners noted that for gold and silver, one-hundredth was taken,
and for other goods, three-hundredths.
Now, commodity prices were higher than before,
and excluding gold and silver, the quota could not fully cover everything.
Therefore, an additional one percent could be added to all other gold and silver.
The imperial edict approved it.
In the third month of the seventh year,
Gāo Rǔlì, the Shàngshū of the Hùbù (Minister of Revenue), stated:
"According to the old system,
small traders paid four percent in tax on various goods they traded,
but gold and silver, being valuable and fine items,
mostly came from wealthy households,
and yet only three percent was collected.
This is illogical,
and I request that they also be taxed at the same rate."
The provincial officials deliberated and thought that this might lead to more concealment,
so they decided to stick to the old system.
Collation Notes
