Zhì (Treatises) Vol. 31, Shíhuò (Food and Money) 5: Quècháng (Border Markets), Héshí (Purchase of Grain for Storage), Chángpíng Cāng (Ever-Normal Granaries), Shuǐtián (Irrigated Fields), Qūtián (Raised-Bed Fields), Rùsù (Grain Payments), Yù Dùdié (Sale of Monastic Certificates).
Quècháng are places
where trade with enemy states is conducted.
Officials are appointed for all these markets,
strict prohibitions are enforced,
and large buildings are provided to facilitate trade between the two countries.
The annual profits greatly aid in public expenditure.
In the fifth month of the second year of Huángtǒng during the Xīzōng reign,
the request of the Sòng people was granted,
and they were consequently established on both sides of the border.
In the ninth month,
it was ordered that they be established in Shòuzhōu, Dèngzhōu, Fèngxiáng Fǔ, and other places.
In the first month of the fourth year of Zhènglóng during the Hǎilíng reign,
those established in Fèngxiáng Fǔ, Táng, Dèng, Yǐng, Cài, Gǒng, Táo zhōu, and Jiāoxī Xiàn were abolished,
and they were exclusively established in Sìzhōu.
Soon after, as the Sòng were attacked,
these were also abolished.
In the eighth month of the fifth year,
it was ordered that the quècháng be moved to Nánjīng.
In the early days of the dynasty, they were sometimes established between Yānzichéng and Běiyángchéng within the Xīběi Zhāotǎo Sī (Northwest Pacification Commissioner's Office),
to facilitate the exchange of northern livestock.
In the third year of Dàdìng during the Shìzōng reign,
horses were traded at the quècháng with the Xià kingdom.
In the fourth year,
based on a report from the Shàngshū Shěng,
the markets in Sì, Shòu, Cài, Táng, Dèng, Yǐng, Mì, Fèngxiáng, Qín, Gǒng, and Táo were re-established.
In the seventh year,
it was forbidden for the Qínzhōu market to sell rice, flour, dried mutton and pork, and items that could be used as military weapons to outside territories.
In the second month of the seventeenth year,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"The Sòng people are prone to stirring up trouble and breaking alliances,
and perhaps communicating with Dàshí.
I fear that innocent lives might be unjustly harmed,
so we must be prepared.
Only one quècháng along the border in Shǎnxī should be retained,
and all others should be abolished.
The relevant authorities should be ordered to strictly investigate spies."
Before this,
to prevent spies,
the three quècháng on the western border in Lánzhōu, Bǎo'ān, and Suídé were abolished.
In the first month of the twenty-first year,
Lǐ Rénxiào, the King of the Xià kingdom, submitted a memorial requesting their re-establishment.
As Bǎo'ān and Lánzhōu produced nothing
and yielded little tax,
it was suggested that only Suídé, being an important location,
could have its cross-border market re-established.
The provincial officials were ordered to discuss it.
The chief ministers argued that since Shǎnxī bordered Xī Xià,
and border residents privately crossed the border to steal,
the existence of quècháng
allowed infiltrators to come and go.
They proposed that Dōngshèng could be maintained as before,
but those in Shǎnxī should all be abolished.
The Emperor said:
"Dōngshèng and Shǎnxī are separated by roads,
making trade impossible.
Order the establishment of a market in Huánzhōu."
Soon after, a market was re-established in Suídé Zhōu.
In the twelfth month,
the Shòuzhōu quècháng was forbidden from receiving fēnlì.
Fēnlì refers to
the money merchants presented to market officials upon their audience.
In the seventh month of the second year of Míngchāng during the Zhāngzōng reign,
the Shàngshū Shěng, noting that the Sìzhōu quècháng had not been strictly managed before,
reported and resolved to follow the Dàdìng fifth-year decree.
Officials were to enlarge and renovate the buildings,
double the number of barriers and prohibitions,
and entrust the market officials and Tíkòng (Supervising Officer) with the collection of taxes,
with the Tíxíng Sī conducting inspections.
Only Dōngshèng, Jìng,
Qìngzhōu, and Lái Yuǎnjūn remained as before,
while all others were to be repaired and completed.
The Sìzhōu market,
during the Dàdìng reign,
earned 53,467 guàn annually.
In the first year of Chéng'ān,
it increased to 107,893 guàn and 653 wén.
Required miscellaneous goods from

the Sìzhōu market annually supplied: 1,000 kuà of new tea, 500 catties of lychees, 500 catties of longans, 6,000 catties of kumquats, 500 catties of olives, 300 dried bananas, 1,000 catties of sappanwood, 7,000 warm oranges, 8,000 tangerines, 300 catties of sugar, 600 catties of ginger, 90 chēng of gardenia,
while rhinoceros horn, ivory, cinnabar, and similar items were not included.
The Sòng also annually received 43,000 guàn in tax.
The Qínzhōu Xīzǐchéng market,
during the Dàdìng reign,
earned 33,656 guàn annually.
In the first year of Chéng'ān,
it earned 122,099 guàn annually.
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
they were re-established in Bǎo'ān and Lánzhōu.
In the ninth month of the third year,
the Xíng Shūmì Yuàn (Itinerant Bureau of Military Affairs) reported that
Xié Chū and others requested the opening of quècháng,
proposing to set them up in Xiálǐní.
Trade was permitted from the eleventh month of this year.
Soon after, a regulation was established that
anyone at a quècháng who took cash into outside territories and traded with foreigners
would be sentenced to five years of penal servitude,
and those with three catties or more would be executed.
All markets on the Sòng border
were abolished due to the attack on Sòng.
In the eighth month of the eighth year of Tàihé,
due to peace with Sòng,
the Sòng people requested their re-establishment as before.
They were consequently re-established in Táng, Dèng, Shòu, Sì, Xīzhōu, and the areas of Qín and Fèng.
In the first year of Zhēnyòu during the Xuānzōng reign,
the Qínzhōu quècháng was burned down by the Sòng people.
In the second year,
Wūgǔlún Yǎnyán, the Xiǎnxī Ānfǔ Fùshǐ (Deputy Pacification Commissioner of Shǎnxī), re-opened it,
and the annual earnings were in the tens of thousands.
In the seventh month of the third year [of Zhēnyòu],
a proposal was deliberated to permit mutual trade at market barriers using silver,
and to levy taxes based on the counted amount.
The Emperor said:
“If this is done,
it will cause public silver to flow into the outside world.”
Píngzhāng Jìnzhōng and Quán Cānzhīzhèngshì Déshēng said:
“For rewards and expenditures, nothing is better than silver and silk,
but the imperial treasury is insufficient to supply them.
Although mutual trade is prohibited,
those who trade privately do so freely.
If taxes are levied on it,
then taxes will not be collected from the people, and the expenditures can be met.”
Píngzhāng Gāoqí said:
“Petty people dare to violate the law,
but the law is not enforced;
how much more so if it is permitted?
Now, the military campaigns have not ceased,
and all silver-producing areas are in the outside world.
If it is not prohibited, both public and private coffers will be emptied in a matter of days.”
The Emperor said:
“It should be carefully considered.”
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
Jíxián Zīyìguān Lǚjiàn said:
“I once supervised the market barrier at Xīzhōu,
and each market yielded several thousand bolts of cloth
and several hundred liǎng of silver.
After the military campaigns began, all of this was lost.”
Taxes on gold and silver.
In the fifth year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng,
people were permitted to bid for and purchase the silver mines in Bǎoshān Xiàn.
In the ninth year,
the Yùshǐtái memorialized that the Hénán Fǔ acquired gold and silver through “harmonious purchase” (hé mǎi),
coercing the common people
and lowering the price.
The Emperor said:
“Initially,
I wished for currency to circulate,
and therefore issued the order.
How can it, in turn, harm the people?”
Thereupon, it was abolished.
In the twelfth year,
an edict declared that gold and silver mines
should be freely exploited by the people,
without collecting taxes.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Shàngshūshěng memorialized
to permit people to mine silver during agricultural slack seasons,
and to submit official taxes.
In the second year of Míngchāng,
there were over 1,200 silver ingots
and over 552,000 gold ingots in the empire.
In the third year,
based on a report from the Tíxíngsī,
silver mines in various locations were sealed,
and people were prohibited from mining and smelting.
In the fifth year,
based on a memorial from the Yùshǐtái,
which requested to allow people to mine and smelt gold, silver, and copper in various places,
the Emperor ordered the Shàngshūshěng to deliberate on it.
The Zǎichén deliberated, stating:
“The nation has enjoyed a long period of peace,
and the population has increased.
Although it has been prohibited,
poor people, seeking a livelihood,
gather crowds and smelt privately.
There is the name of a prohibition,
but no actual cessation,
thus the officials gain no profit and the people frequently violate the law.
If people are allowed to bid for and purchase them,
then the strong among the poor can become laborers and craftsmen,
while the old and young perform miscellaneous tasks,
each getting their fair share,
and the bidding families also have surplus profit.
If this is done,
it can be long-lasting.
Compared to official labor hiring contract workers,
which involves countless expenses,
there is a significant difference.”
Thereupon, a system was established:
in areas with mines,
the móukè and xiànlìng were entrusted to register the number
and recruit people to bid for and purchase.
Powerful officials, civil servants, archers, and lǐxū were all prohibited from participating.
Following the example of old markets,
one high-ranking official from a zhōufǔ was ordered to oversee it,
and the Tíxíngsī was to investigate and enforce the prohibitions.
The Emperor said:
“This is ultimately not a long-term strategy.”
Cānzhīzhèngshì Xūchíguó said:
“For now, let us allow this;
later, when it becomes profitable, then officials can be established.
It is like a wine shop:
first, a workshop is set up,
and then the government monopolizes it.”
The Emperor also agreed,
and so followed it.
There were 113 silver caves in Fénshān and Xīyínshān.
Hé Dì (Government Grain Purchase).
In the tenth month of the second year of Huángtǒng of Xīzōng,
in Yān, Xī, Dōngjīng,
Hédōng,
Héběi,
Shāndōng,
and Biànjīng circuits, the autumn harvest was good.
Officials were ordered to purchase grain at increased prices.
In the second year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng,
because granaries had been long depleted after Zhènglóng,
Tàizǐ Shàoshī Wányán Shǒudào and others were dispatched
to the eastern and western circuits of Shāndōng to purchase military provisions.
Except for the annual food consumption of households,
all was to be submitted to the government,
and its value was to be paid.
In the third year,
he said to the Zǎichén:
“The nation’s expenditures are immense.
Previously, when Shāndōng was ordered to purchase grain,
only over 450,000 shí were obtained,
which is insufficient for preparation.
Since ancient times, there have been floods and droughts,
and those who suffered no harm
did so because of abundant reserves.
Military garrisons in Shāndōng must urgently prepare two years’ worth of reserves.
If floods or droughts occur, these will be used for relief.
Other prefectures with standing armies
also need to purchase grain to suffice.
The expenses of the capital are very great,
and for the required reserves,
the Hùbù should be commanded to make urgent plans.”
In the fifth year,
he reproached the Zǎichén, saying:
“I consider accumulating reserves to be the foundation of the nation.
Granaries should be repaired to expand grain purchases.
Now I hear that in the outer circuits, official documents are merely formalities.
You all are not paying attention,
which greatly fails to meet the intent of your appointment.”
In the eighth month of the sixth year,
an edict was issued to officials
that after the autumn harvest,
grain should be widely purchased in all circuits
to prepare for floods and droughts.
In the first month of the ninth year,
he instructed the Zǎichén, saying:
“I observe that the Sòng people are boastful and insincere,
and I fear they cannot long adhere to their oaths and agreements.
Command the military commanders to be diligent in preparing border defenses
to guard against unforeseen events.
Last year, Hénán had a bountiful harvest;
local authorities should be ordered to widely purchase grain
to fill the granaries.
Edicts to zhōu and xiàn for grain purchase
must not coerce the common people.”
In the twelfth month of the twelfth year,
an edict ordered grain purchases in the capital to fill the granaries
and also to facilitate the circulation of currency.
Another edict ordered that all prefectures with good autumn harvests
should widely purchase grain to prepare for floods and droughts.
In the fifth month of the sixteenth year,
he instructed Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Gēshíliè Liángbì, saying:
“The western frontier has historically lacked reserves.
Order local authorities to purchase grain
to prepare for emergencies.”
In the spring of the seventeenth year,
the Shàngshūshěng memorialized:
“Previously, we received an edict to provide relief to the starving people in Dōngjīng and other circuits,
but the amount of grain in the three circuits is insufficient.”
The Emperor said:
“I once instructed you all
to widely purchase grain in years of plenty to prepare for famine.
You all claimed that the granaries of the empire were overflowing,
but now, when relief is needed,
you say it is insufficient.
Since ancient times, emperors have all regarded accumulating reserves as a long-term national strategy.
Did I accumulate grain just for my own sole use?
If it is insufficient now,
it can be obtained from neighboring circuits.
From now on, prepare more;
this should be the norm.”
In the fourth month,
the Shàngshūshěng memorialized:
“The twelve méng'ān in the three circuits of Dōngjīng who were especially short of food
have already received relief.
There are still those who have not received relief.”
An edict was issued to send officials to Fùzhōu and Gésūguǎn Circuit
to inspect wealthy families,
and if they had surplus reserves, to purchase them at increased prices.
Local residents were ordered to go there to receive grain.
In the fourth month of the eighteenth year,
it was ordered that all méng'ān under the jurisdiction of Táizhōu, the Xīběilù Zhāotǎosī’s Xī méng'ān,
and places like Qìngyún Xiàn in Xiánpíng Fǔ and Méngsōng Hé, when experiencing abundant harvests,
should widely purchase grain.
In the seventh month of Míngchāng (明昌) fourth year of Zhāngzōng (章宗),
an imperial edict was issued to the officials of the Hùbù (戶部),
saying, "I hear that rice and grain are very cheap in Tōngzhōu (通州).
What if the government purchases them at a fair price?"
Thereupon,
the authorities memorialized, "
Last year, the crops in Zhōngdū (中都) circuit were poor.
The reason their prices are slightly lower now
is that merchants have continued to transport and sell them.
If officials are immediately dispatched to compete in purchasing,
we are deeply concerned that market prices will soar,
and the poor will suffer even more.
We request that we wait until the autumn harvest,
and then procure according to the regulations of the Chángpíngcāng (常平倉)."
The emperor approved it.
In the fifth month of Míngchāng (明昌) fifth year,
the emperor said:
"I hear that rice prices are soaring.
Now, the grain transported by the government is more than sufficient.
It can be sold at a reduced price.
Let this be clearly announced to the people,
so they do not need to privately purchase at high prices."
In the seventh month of Míngchāng (明昌) sixth year,
an imperial command was given to the prime minister, saying:
"An imperial edict ordered that in areas within the imperial domain experiencing famine, grain should be sold at a reduced price.
But how can the poor, who have no money, obtain food?
Let discussion be held on relief measures."
The provincial ministers believed that
for counties and prefectures suffering from food shortages,
if it was for one year, relief loans should be given;
if it was for two years, then relief aid should be provided.
If the people truly had no assets,
even if relief loans were appropriate,
they requested direct relief.
The emperor then ordered that in areas intermittently affected by famine,
those who could afford to buy grain with money should be sold grain at a reduced price,
while the destitute and helpless should receive direct relief.
In the tenth month of Zhēnyòu (貞祐) third year of Xuānzōng (宣宗),
Gāo Rǔlì (高汝礪) was ordered to purchase grain in the various commanderies of Hénán (河南),
and the people were ordered to transport it to the capital.
Furthermore, the granaries in the capital were ordered to purchase the surplus grain transported by the people.
The Supervising Censor Huáng Guónú (黃摑奴) reported:
"The grain purchased by Rǔlì (汝礪) is sufficient for a year's supply.
The people have already toiled
by transporting it, in addition to their rents and taxes.
They should only be allowed to keep the surplus as capital for their return journey.
Is it acceptable to forcibly take it again?
Moreover, the grain procurement has been ongoing for days,
yet only slightly over two hundred shí (石) have been obtained.
How does this help?"
The emperor ordered it to be stopped.
In the twelfth month,
many nearby commanderies and counties purchased grain from the capital,
causing grain prices to soar.
Consequently, its export from the capital was prohibited.
In the fourth year,
Hóu Zhì (侯摯) of the Hébĕi (河北) Xíngshěng (行省) said:
"People in Hébĕi (河北) are resorting to cannibalism.
In Guān (觀) and Cāng (滄) prefectures, a dòu (斗) of rice costs over ten liǎng (兩) of silver.
I respectfully observe that along the various river crossings, merchants are permitted to transport grain across the river northward.
However, the government procures eight-tenths of every shí (石),
leaving merchants without profit;
who would be willing to do it?
Furthermore, the people of Hébĕi (河北) are all Your Majesty's beloved subjects.
Having already suffered from warfare,
to then sit by and watch them die,
I fear that those who exploit warfare will find an excuse to rise up.
I wish for the government procurement to cease,
and for the people to be allowed to transport and sell freely, which would be more convenient."
The emperor approved it.
An additional decree stipulated that any soldier, commoner, or traveler who did not sell their grain at the official procurement points,
but privately transported it across the river,
would receive one hundred strokes of the rod.
For those along the river who were military personnel or influential families caught violating this,
their imprisonment, number of strokes, and definite judgment would be severe,
and their property would be confiscated by the government.
The emperor, noting the abundance of money in Hébĕi (河北) prefectures,
much of which had dispersed among the people,
ordered the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) to devise a plan.
The provincial ministers memorialized:
"We have already ordered the liquor and salt monopolies in Shāndōng (山東) and Hébĕi (河北), as well as the salt administrations in Bīn (濱) and Cāng (滄) prefectures,
to collect a portion of it.
Now, with food shortages in Hébĕi (河北)
and many people transporting grain northward,
it is appropriate to temporarily enact a law to intercept and procure it.
We propose at the south bank of the various ferry crossings,
to select officials skilled in finance and trade,
first to exchange gold, silver, silk, and other goods for the grain of merchants,
then to transfer it to the north bank,
to recoup the procurement capital through trade,
and also collect cash.
This will not only prevent illicit practices
but also bring money into the capital."
The emperor approved it.
Furthermore, a memorializer stated:
"In recent years, food shortages have been frequent.
Although this is due to the complexity of mobilization and collection,
it is also because of the wealthy families who have encroached upon resources.
During harvest, they buy a lot when prices are low,
and when people are in distress, they lend to them,
privately setting up contracts and pledges,
claiming no interest but in reality charging several times the amount.
Starving people are only afraid of not getting it,
and no one dares to dispute it.
Thus, as soon as the harvest is complete,
and before official rents are paid,
their granaries are already empty.
This makes the rich richer
and the poor poorer.
The laws of the state stipulate
that for borrowing property, the monthly interest should not exceed three fen (分),
and the total interest should stop when it reaches double the principal.
But now, sometimes the interest triples in less than a month.
I wish for a clear imperial command to the authorities
to enforce the old laws,
and during times of abundant harvest, to purchase at increased prices through mutual agreement.
This would benefit the public
and not harm private interests."
The emperor ordered the prime minister to implement it.
That year,
Wūgǔlún Qìngshòu (烏古論慶壽), acting Vice-Commissioner of Pacification for Hédōng (河東) Southern Circuit, discussed the matter of forced procurement.
(See Yánzhì (鹽志) part two.)
In Xīngdìng (興定) first year,
the emperor heard that many common people abandoned their livelihoods due to the excessive burden of harmonious procurement,
and ordered the prime minister to pay attention to this.
In the eighth month,
Yáng Zhēn (楊貞), a Lángzhōng (郎中) of the Hùbù (戶部), was appointed acting Shàngshū (尚書) of the Six Ministries for Shǎnxī (陝西) Xíngliùbù (行六部),
to oversee the collection and distribution for the military horses in Tóng (潼) and Shǎn (陝).
He memorialized to reduce by half the grain procured from merchants for Hénán (河南),
to alleviate the burden on the people.
This was approved.
In the sixth month,
a reward system for harmonious procurement was established.
Chángpíngcāng (常平倉).
In Dàdìng (大定) fourteenth year of Shìzōng (世宗),
a system was once established,
and an edict ordered its implementation both inside and outside the capital.
However, the law was soon abolished.
In the eighth month of Míngchāng (明昌) first year of Zhāngzōng (章宗),
a censor requested its re-establishment,
and the emperor commanded the provincial ministers to deliberate in detail and report.
The provincial ministers said:
"According to the old Dàdìng (大定) system,
in abundant years, market prices were increased by two-tenths for procurement,
and in lean years, market prices were reduced by one-tenth for sale.
In normal years, it remained unchanged.
The reason for increasing prices during abundance for procurement
was to prevent low prices from harming farmers.
The reason for reducing prices during scarcity for sale
was to prevent high prices from harming the people.
Prices were increased and decreased to stabilize grain prices,
hence it was called Chángpíng (常平),
not meaning that all the people under heaven should solely depend on it for their livelihood.
Today, the population is very large.
If one were to calculate and store a year's surplus for each mouth,
not only would the quantity be too large and difficult to manage,
but there would also be concern about untimely distribution leading to spoilage.
Moreover, the abuses of forced allocation by officials
are certainly not a long-term solution.
If, for each county and prefecture, based on household registration, a monthly allowance of three dòu (斗) per person is taken as the standard,
and only three months' worth is stored per person,
this would already amount to tens of millions,
and would be sufficient to stabilize prices and relieve famine.
If it is ordered that in all places,
beyond three years' worth of food for government soldiers,
those who can sustain themselves for three months are exempt from procurement,
and those who cannot are to procure in abundant years,
this might be sustainable long-term.
However, the beginning of legislation depends on its strict implementation.
Therefore, let the Tíxíngsī (提刑司) and the various circuit Jìsī (計司) jointly administer it.
County and prefecture officials who obstruct it shall be impeached,
and those who successfully implement it shall be promoted.
As for areas in Zhōngdū (中都) circuit where annual crops are poor,
the grain shall be sold at one-third less than the market price,
according to the Chángpíng (常平) method."
The emperor approved it.
In the eighth month of the third year,
an imperial edict
commanded: "The Ever-Normal Granaries shall buy generously when grain is abundant and sell sparingly when it is scarce.
The officials in charge shall be diligently rewarded or punished for their performance.
This shall be promulgated throughout all the circuits.
If there is any dereliction in its implementation,
the Tíxíngsī (Circuit Fiscal Intendance Office) shall investigate and report it."
He also said to the宰臣 (Chancellor):
"The Ever-Normal Granaries in various places
often exist in name only.
Moreover, how could people from distant counties be willing to travel a long distance
directly to the prefectural or sub-prefectural seat to buy and sell grain?
Granaries should be established in each county,
and prefectural and county officials should be ordered to concurrently oversee and manage them."
A system was then established:
If a county was within sixty *lǐ* of a prefecture, it would use the prefectural granary;
if it was beyond sixty *lǐ*, a special granary would be established.
Previously, it was intended to store three months' supply of grain for each household.
Fearing that a large quantity might result in spoilage,
this was changed to: for households numbering 20,000 or more, 30,000 *shí* should be prepared;
for 10,000 or more, 20,000 *shí*;
for less than 10,000 but 5,000 or more, 15,000 *shí*;
and for less than 5,000 households, 5,000 *shí*.
Counties in Hénán and Shǎnxī with garrisoned troops and stored grain
were exempt from these numbers.
Existing granaries in prefectures and counties were to be maintained,
otherwise new ones were to be constructed.
When prefectural and county officials were replaced,
the purchased millet, if unspoiled,
was to be handed over within one month, and a receipt issued.
If there was no co-manager,
the handover would still proceed as above.
If the deadline was missed,
the prefectural government and the Tíxíngsī were to dispatch officials to urge, supervise, and finalize the handover.
If a locality experienced an abundant harvest,
but the amount purchased and stored was less than one-tenth,
the officials in question would be demoted in rank.
The Tíxíngsī would investigate,
report directly to the Shàngshūshěng (Department of State Affairs),
and a decision on promotion or demotion would be made on that day.
In the ninth month,
an imperial edict ordered that the sites for the Ever-Normal Granaries
should be supervised by prefectural officials,
with county officials concurrently overseeing the matters.
The amount of grain purchased would be used to assess promotions and demotions,
making this a permanent regulation.
He also instructed the Shàngshūshěng:
"The counties in the Shàngjīng Circuit do not yet have Ever-Normal Granaries.
If they can also be established,
determine the appropriate amount of millet to be prepared and report it."
In the tenth month of the fourth year,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
"Currently, in the Shàngjīng, Púyǔ, Sùpín, Hélǎn, Húlígǎi, and other circuits,
the households of *máng'ān* and *móukè* total over 176,000.
Annually, over 205,000 *shí* of tax millet are collected,
and over 66,000 *shí* are disbursed.
The total existing stock is over 2,476,000 *shí*.
We believe that this region collects more than it disburses,
which is sufficient for relief in times of disaster.
It seems unnecessary to establish them."
So, it was stopped.
In the ninth month of the fifth year,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
"Ever-Normal Granaries were first established in the third year of Míngchāng,
and their permanent regulations were set.
There are a total of 519 Ever-Normal Granaries nationwide,
with an estimated 37,863,000 *shí* of millet,
enough to feed the official troops for five years;
over 8,100,000 *shí* of rice,
enough for four years' use.
The total current cash is over 33,430,000 *guàn*,
which is barely enough for more than two years.
Since the current cash is low,
and although the past few years have been relatively abundant, the price of rice is still high,
if we were to buy in advance again,
the price might soar,
which would not benefit the people."
An edict was then issued to temporarily halt the state's purchasing and storage for Ever-Normal Granaries both inside and outside the capital,
to be resumed when there was a surplus of official funds.
Irrigated Fields.
In the intercalary tenth month of the fifth year of Míngchāng,
a memorialist suggested that counties and prefectures with rivers could dig canals
to divert water for irrigation.
An edict was sent to the prefectures and counties.
Subsequently, although all eight Tíxíngsī circuits had rivers, they all reported that irrigation was not feasible,
except for the Zhōngdū Circuit, which reported that Ānsù and Dìngxīng counties could divert river water to irrigate over 4,000 *mǔ* of land.
An edict ordered this to be carried out.
In the tenth month of the sixth year,
〔一二〕a regulation was established:
County officials who, during their tenure, could establish water conservancy projects that benefited one hundred *qǐng* or more of land,
would be promoted to the first rank of their class.
For *móukè* who managed garrison farms (*túntián*) and could newly increase them by thirty *qǐng* or more,
they would be rewarded with twenty *liǎng* of silver and bolts of silk.
Their rent and taxes would only follow those of dry land.
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
an imperial edict commanded the release of water from the eastern sluice of the Báiliántán pond for the common people to irrigate their fields.
In the third year,
it was again ordered not to destroy the gates of the Gāoliánghé River,
allowing the people to use them for irrigation.
In the seventh month of the eighth year of Tàihé,
an imperial edict instructed the Ànchásī (Surveillance Commissions) of all circuits to plan for irrigated fields.
A departmental official stated:
"The benefit of irrigated fields is immense.
Along rivers, canals can be dug,
and like in Píngyáng, wells can be dug for planting, all of which can be irrigated.
In recent years, in Pī and Yí, near the river, beans and wheat have been sown.
If there is no water, wells are dug for irrigation,
totaling over 600 *qǐng*,
yielding several times more than dry land.
Judging by this,
there is no other region where this cannot be done."
Therefore, the Zhuǎnyùnsī (Transport Commission) was ordered to conduct an investigation and assessment.
If the Ànchásī of various circuits, while encouraging agriculture,
could inquire into whether digging canals or wells would be more convenient,
they should submit a detailed plan,
awaiting implementation.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
the memorialist Chéng Yuān stated:
"In the ponds and lakes of Dàngshān counties,
when water arrives, they are turned into rice paddies;
when the water recedes, wheat is planted,
yielding double that of dry land.
It is advisable to recruit people to cultivate them as tenants,
with the government taking one-third,
which could yield 100,000 *shí* annually."
The edict approved this.
In the fifth month of the fifth year of Xīngdìng,
Lǐ Guóruì, the magistrate of Nányáng, initiated the development of over 400 *qǐng* of irrigated fields.
An edict promoted him two ranks
and ordered his achievement to be recorded and promulgated throughout all circuits.
In the eleventh month,
the establishment of irrigated fields was discussed.
The Shàngshūshěng reported:
"Hàn's Zhào Xìnchén irrigated 30,000 *qǐng* in Nányáng.
Wèi's Jiǎ Kuí dammed the Rǔ River to create the Xīnpō reservoir,
making it navigable for over 200 *lǐ*,
which people called Jiǎhóu Qú.
Dèng Ài repaired the Huáiyáng and Bǎichǐ canals,
connecting the Huái and Yǐng rivers, and greatly improved the reservoirs south of the Yǐng,
digging canals over 300 *lǐ* long,
irrigating 20,000 *qǐng* of land.
Today, many counties in Hénán have land that was historically developed for irrigated fields,
with harvests several times greater than dry land."
An imperial edict ordered officials from the Hùbù (Ministry of Revenue) to tour the prefectures and counties,
and if there were suitable areas for development, to encourage people to undertake the work.
Their rent would only follow that of dry land,
without any additional levies,
and officials' rewards would be used to incentivize them.
In Shǎnxī, in addition to the officials managing the Sānbái Qú canal,
similar examples should be followed.
In the first month of the first year of Yuánguāng,
Yáng Dàyǒu, a Langzhong of the Hùbù, and others were dispatched to the Jīngdōng, Jīngxī, and Jīngnán circuits to develop irrigated fields.
The method of plot-field cultivation
is found in Jī Kāng's *Yǎngshēng Lùn*.
Since then, throughout successive dynasties, there has been no method universally adopted, like Zhào Guò's "one *mǔ*, three furrows" method.
In the third month of the third year of Míngchāng of Emperor Zhāngzōng,
the Grand Councilors once discussed this method before the emperor.
The emperor said:
“What you, gentlemen, have said is excellent,
but I fear the farmers do not understand this method.
If it is feasible,
it should be widely publicized.”
In the fourth month of summer of the fourth year,
the emperor and the Grand Councilors again discussed the method.
After some time,
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Xū Chíguó said:
“Comparing today to the Dàdìng era,
the population is much larger,
and expenses are also higher.
If the plot-planting method is implemented,
there will be many benefits.”
The emperor said:
“This method has existed since ancient times.
If it were truly feasible,
then why has it not been implemented?”
Chíguó replied:
“The reason it has not been implemented
is probably that the people have not seen its benefits.
Now it has been ordered to be test-planted in the land south of the city,
and officials have been assigned to supervise it.
If the people see the benefit of the harvest,
they will naturally adopt it without coercion.”
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Jiágǔ Héng believed,
“If it had benefits,
it would have been implemented in ancient times.
Moreover, it requires much effort for little planting,
and I fear it might neglect the cultivation of traditional fields.”
The emperor said:
“Let's try implementing it for now.”
In the sixth month,
the emperor asked Cānzhī Zhèngshì Xū Chíguó:
“How are the plot-planting affairs?”
He replied:
“At the turn of the sixth and seventh months,
it will be observable.”
“Are the crops in Hédōng and Dàizhōu good this year?”
He replied:
“Compared to normal years, the harvest is quite good.”
On that day,
he ordered two close attendants to gallop on relays to inspect the crops in Jīngjī.
In the first month of the fifth year,
an imperial edict was issued to instruct farmers to plot-plant.
Before this,
Gāo Yì of Wǔzhì, a person who submitted proposals, presented the plot-planting method,
and requested to assess the number of able-bodied men and the amount of land,
to determine the quantity to be planted.
The emperor ordered the Department of State Affairs to deliberate and finalize the plan.
Then an imperial edict was issued, ordering that for farmland of one hundred *mǔ* or more,
such as land near rivers where water is easily obtained,
over thirty *mǔ* must be plot-planted.
Those who plant more are permitted.
For land without water, it would be left to the convenience of the people.
Furthermore, each Qiānhù, Móukè, and county official was entrusted to encourage and guide according to the law.
In the fourth month of the first year of Chéng'ān,
the plot-planting method was first implemented.
Men aged fifteen or older and under sixty who owned land were to plant one *mǔ*;
those with many able-bodied men were limited to five *mǔ*.
In the second month of the second year,
Jiǔ Lù Tíxíng Mǎ Bǎilù reported:
“The imperial instruction is that farmers with one *qǐng* of land should plot-plant one *mǔ*.
Five *mǔ* is the limit.
Your subject believes that land fertility varies,
and requests that the number of *mǔ* not be limited.”
The imperial decree approved.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Tàihé,
the Department of State Affairs reported:
“Recently, we received an imperial decree to discuss plot-field cultivation.
Your subjects believe this method was originally intended to benefit the people.
Perhaps it should only be used when there is a drought,
as hasty implementation might not be beneficial.
Moreover, the fertility of land varies in different regions.
If all land were suitable for plot-planting,
farmers, seeing its advantages, would naturally strive to implement it.
Otherwise,
even strict supervision and coercion
would be in vain.”
An imperial edict was then issued, ordering local officials and the Surveillance Commission to persuade and instruct as appropriate,
but it ultimately could not be implemented.
Grain Contribution, Selling Monastic Certificates.
In the third month of the third year of Huángtǒng of Emperor Xīzōng,
Shǎnxī experienced drought and famine.
An imperial decree allowed wealthy commoners to contribute grain in exchange for official positions.
In the first year of Dàdìng of Emperor Shìzōng,
〔一三〕due to military campaigns and poor harvests,
an order was issued allowing commoners to make contributions in exchange for official positions.
Moreover, those who could relieve famine victims were recruited,
and the number of people they helped determined their qualification for official positions.
In the fifth year,
the emperor said to the Grand Councilors:
“Previously, as border affairs were unsettled,
and financial resources were scarce,
outside of the Dōng Jīng and Nán Jīng,
people were ordered to make contributions to obtain official positions,
and monastic certificates for monks, Daoist priests, nuns, and Daoist priestesses were sold,
as well as purple and brown robes for monastic titles,
and temple and monastery quotas.
Now that the border regions are pacified,
all these practices should be abolished.
Qìngshòu Sì and Tiāncháng Guàn are to be given monastic certificates annually,
each certificate to be converted into 200,000 cash and granted to them.”
In the second year of Míngchāng,
an imperial edict allowed people in food-scarce areas of Shāndōng and Héběi to contribute grain for varying official positions.
for varying official positions.
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
monastic certificates, monastic titles, and temple/monastery quotas were sold again,
and people were again allowed to contribute grain for official positions.
In the third year,
Xī Jīng experienced famine.
An imperial decree ordered the sale of monastic certificates to relieve it.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu of Emperor Xuānzōng,
following the request of Zhīdàxīngfǔ Shì Xū Dǐng,
a temporary system for selling pardons and privileges was established.
This included promotion to higher office, allowing those in mourning to take examinations to seek office, allowing registered households to redeem from servitude, and similar cases.
〔一四〕The amount of grain and fodder to be contributed for each was specified.
In the third year,
an edict stipulated that, regardless of whether they were officials or commoners,
those who could persuade and lead others to contribute goods to the government,
for 150 *shí* of rice, would be promoted one rank,
and appointed to regular positions.
For 700 *shí*, two ranks,
and appointed to various departments.
For 1,000 *shí*, three ranks,
and appointed as Vice-Administrators or Secretaries.
If the amount exceeded this, they would request the imperial court to discuss rewards.
Investigative and county officials who could persuade 2,000 *shí* would be promoted one rank,
3,000 *shí*, two ranks,
to aid military provisions.
Furthermore, it was decreed
that investigative and county officials who could persuade the contribution of 5,000 *shí* or more of grain would have one assessment score reduced;
10,000 *shí* or more, would be promoted one official rank and have two assessment grades reduced;
20,000 *shí* or more, would be promoted one official rank and advanced one grade;
all to be registered for vacant positions.
In the fourth year,
Xū Dǐng of the Hédōng Xíngshěng said:
“Hédōng has many soldiers but few commoners,
the granaries are empty, and the year is one of famine.
I have observed that although the Lùzhōu Yuánshuàifǔ has established a system for selling nobility and privileges,
the regulations are too few,
and do not fully utilize the art of persuasion and inducement.
I now propose that for all those who purchase regular official appointments,
according to regulations, only one *yìn* privilege is granted.
If they are willing to contribute more, they may be granted an additional *yìn* privilege.
Monks and Daoist priests who already have monastic titles
should be allowed to purchase official positions in their respective departments.
Officials who are willing to contribute grain, or who do not wish to receive salaries and ration tickets,
should be promoted according to the amount.
Those who have failed three examinations and are fifty years or older,
and those who have failed four examinations and are forty-five years or older,
should all be permitted to contribute grain
to obtain minor official positions or servitor roles.
Orderly clerks and scribes,
though not yet holding regular ranks,
should also be allowed to make contributions for promotion to official positions.
As for ranked officials who should be assigned to various departments,
they may be allowed to offer goods to be provisionally appointed as Vice-Administrators or Secretaries.
Vice-Administrators or Secretaries appointed as county magistrates
will be exempted from one corvée duty.
Military officials who can provide their own fodder and provisions
should be promoted according to the usual rules for civil officials.”
In the fourth year,
〔一五〕the monk Guǎnghuì of Yàozhōu said:
“Military provisions are insufficient.
All monastic officials of prefectures and military garrisons or higher
are requested to contribute 100 *shí* of grain.
Defensive-Inspectorate County Vice-Superintendents, Precentors, etc.,
should contribute 70 *shí* to be appointed,
and after thirty months, they will be replaced.
All Chief Monks should contribute 10 *shí*,
and be replaced after one year.
Those who wish to re-purchase are permitted.”
The imperial decree granted it.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
Niángē Zhēn, Acting Marshal of Lùzhōu, said:
“Recently, a memorial was submitted to establish a system.
For all officials who received general amnesty last year,
according to their rank and grade, they are allowed to contribute grain,
and the Marshal's Office is to fill in blank imperial edicts to grant them appointments.
Thus, people will be spared the trouble of lodging appeals,
and the government will have reserves.
In recent years, general amnesties have been repeatedly granted.
Many who held nominal military positions have not had time to be officially appointed.
If only promotions for newly granted amnesties are allowed,
then it will become an oversight.
I request that their accumulated grain contributions, both past and present, be calculated for promotions.”
The imperial decree granted it.
Collation Notes
Treatise 32: Elections 1

Metropolitan Graduate Examinations, Law Examinations, Child Prodigy Examinations, Imperial Edict Examinations, Military Examinations, Examinations for Officials of the Hanlin Academy, Directorate of Astronomy, and Imperial Medical Bureau.
Since the methods of recommending individuals from villages and selecting individuals from communities in the Three Dynasties were abolished,
from Qín and Hàn onwards, each dynasty adapted to its own circumstances
to utilize the talents of its time.
If it sufficed for their needs, then that was enough.
Thus, the inconsistency of laws and systems has a long history.
During the Hàn dynasty,
although there were various categories like xiánliáng fāngzhèng to recruit scholars,
officials were selected through recommendation.
Through this, they could reach the rank of gōngqīng.
Sons and younger brothers of gōngqīng entered to serve as imperial guards (sùwèi),
and by being favored,
they attained prominent positions.
From Wèi and Jìn downwards, there were successive changes and adaptations.
By the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the jìnshì system flourished.
At that time, if a gentleman-scholar's advancement
did not follow this path, he felt discontent.
This was due to the preferences of the rulers of the time,
and thus the inclination of people's hearts followed suit.
The Liáo dynasty arose at the end of the Táng dynasty
and largely adopted the Táng jìnshì method for selecting people.
However, among those who served in its state,
when examining the origins of their advancement,
jìnshì accounted for only two or three tenths.
The Jīn dynasty succeeded the Liáo,
and in all matters, it wished to surpass the Liáo era.
Therefore, the jìnshì examination categories incorporated and modified the methods of both Táng and Sòng.
Passing the examinations and entering officialdom
was regarded with particular importance compared to previous dynasties,
and the regulations were also stringent.
As for using policy essays (cè lùn) for jìnshì to select their own people,
and employing the Nǚzhí script for the examination papers,
this was likely to capitalize on their strengths to make use of them,
and also to promote their national script,
making people proficient in it and preventing its disuse.
Throughout the Jīn dynasty,
the number of talented individuals obtained through the examination system was considerable.
All palace guards (gōnghùwèi), as well as interpretative scribes (yìshǐ), administrative scribes (lìshǐ), and interpreters (tōngshì) in the central agencies (shěng tái bù),
were listed in the regular official ranks for advancement.
This was something absent since the Táng and Sòng dynasties.
Was it not an adaptation to the times,
based on the Hàn methods?
The administration of Jīn was a mix of pure and impure elements;
commentators often made distinctions in this regard.
When Xuānzōng moved south,
the bureaucratic style became increasingly prevalent,
and harshness became a common practice.
Perhaps it was a time of many troubles,
and being eager for results,
it was unavoidable.
From that time onwards,
the paths to official advancement widened,
and the custom of seeking undue fortune grew rampant.
Military merits
were mixed with positions of county magistrates (lìnglù).
Hereditary appointments (ményìn yòuzhí)
successively occupied prominent court positions.
The imperial examination system for selecting scholars also became overly broad,
and thus the Jīn administration declined.
Examining its initial establishment of principles and rules,
the regulations for promotion and transfer, and the methods of evaluation,
were orderly and well-structured.
For over a hundred years, there was no lack of talent.
Was this not its effectiveness?
By imperial decree, the Jīn Shǐ is being compiled,
and its section on selection (xuǎnjǔ)
allows for a detailed discussion.
The systems for astronomical observation (sītiān), imperial physicians (tàiyī), and palace attendants (nèishì) existed in all dynasties,
and are appended here.
The selling of ranks (yùjué) and the granting of special entry (jìnnà) were the worst abuses of the late Jīn,
which were due to insufficient financial resources.
They are specifically recorded in the Shíhuò Zhì.
The Jīn dynasty's establishment of examination subjects all followed the systems of Liáo and Sòng.
There were categories for prose and poetry (cí fù), classics and meaning (jīng yì), policy questions (cè shì), law (lǜ kē), and child scholars of the classics (jīng tóng).
In the third year of Tiāndé of Hǎilíng Wáng,
the policy questions (cè shì) category was abolished.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng of Shìzōng,
the Nǚzhí jìnshì examination category was established.
Initially, it only tested policy questions (cè),
but later, essays (lùn) were added,
which was known as the cè lùn jìnshì.
In the early Míngchāng era,
the zhìjǔ hóngcí (special examination for broad literary talent) category was also established
to recruit extraordinary individuals.
Thus, there were seven categories for selecting scholars in Jīn.
Those who passed the examinations in cí fù, jīng yì, and cè lùn
were called jìnshì.
Those who passed the lǜ kē and jīng tóng examinations
were called jǔrén.
The place for educating scholars was called the Guózǐjiān,
first established in the third year of Tiāndé.
Later, the system was standardized:
one hundred students for cí fù and jīng yì,
and one hundred junior students (xiǎoxuéshēng).

Princes of the imperial clan (zōngshì) and close relatives of empresses (wàiqī huánghòu) of the dàgōng mourning degree and above, as well as sons and grandsons over fifteen years old of various meritorious officials (gōngchén) and officials of the third rank and above, were admitted to the academy.
Those under fifteen entered the junior school.
The Tàixué was first established in the sixth year of Dàdìng.
Initially, it educated one hundred and sixty scholars.
Later, it was set at one hundred and fifty sons and grandsons of officials of the fifth rank and above,
and two hundred and fifty individuals who had been recommended by prefectures or had completed previous examinations,
totaling four hundred people.
Prefectural schools (fǔxué) were also established in the sixteenth year of Dàdìng,
totaling seventeen locations with one thousand students.

Initially, they admitted those who had participated in the court examinations (tíngshì), members of the imperial clan (zōngshì), royal relatives (huángjiā) of the tǎnbmiǎn mourning degree and above, and those who had passed the jǔrén examination.
Later, county schools (zhōuxué) were added.
Then, sons and grandsons of officials of the fifth rank and above,
and those whose brothers or fathers had served as sixth-rank officials in the imperial court,
and sons and grandsons of other officials
who had been recommended by prefectures,
were admitted by competitive examination for one-third of the available places along with local jǔrén.
Descendants of the temple households (miàozhái zǐsūn) at Quèlǐ, aged thirteen and above, were admitted without limit to their number.
However, those recommended by prefectures or who had completed previous examinations, and were exempt from testing, could not exceed twenty people.
For all students admitted by competitive examination,
the Board of Rites (Lǐbù) oversaw the Tàixué,
while school officials (xuéguān) who were supervisors of education (tíjiǔ xuéxiào) oversaw the prefectural and county schools.
Those who had been recommended by prefectures or had completed previous jǔrén examinations
were all exempt from testing.
For the classics,
the Yì was studied with the commentaries of Wáng Bì and Hán Kāngbó,
the Shū with the commentary of Kǒng Ānguó,
the Shī with the commentary of Máo Cháng and the glosses of Zhèng Xuán,
the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn of the Chūnqiū with the commentary of Dù Yù,
the Lǐ Jì with the sub-commentary of Kǒng Yǐngdá,
the Zhōu Lǐ with the commentary of Zhèng Xuán and the sub-commentary of Jiǎ Gōngyàn,
the Lúnyǔ with the collected commentaries of Hé Yàn and the sub-commentary of Xíng Bǐng,
the Mèngzǐ with the commentary of Zhào Qí and the sub-commentary of Sūn Shì,
the Xiàojīng with the commentary of Táng Xuánzōng,
the Shǐ Jì with the commentary of Péi Yīn,
the Qián Hàn Shū with the commentary of Yán Shīgǔ,
the Hòu Hàn Shū with the commentary of Lǐ Xián,
the Sānguó Zhì with the commentary of Péi Sōngzhī,

as well as Táng Tàizōng's Jìn Shū, Shěn Yuè's Sòng Shū, Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Shū, Yáo Sīlián's Liáng Shū and Chén Shū, Wèi Shōu's Hòu Wèi Shū, Lǐ Bǎiyào's Běi Qí Shū, Línghú Défēn's Zhōu Shū, Wèi Zhēng's Suí Shū, the Xīn Táng Shū and Jiù Táng Shū, and the Xīn Wǔdài Shǐ and Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ.
The Lǎozǐ was studied with the commentary and sub-commentary of Táng Xuánzōng,
the Xúnzǐ with the commentary of Yáng Jìng,
and the Yángzǐ with the commentaries of Lǐ Guǐ, Sòng Xián, Liǔ Zōngyuán, and Wú Mì.
All these were printed by the Guózǐjiān
and distributed to the various schools.
For student lessons,
every three days one policy essay (cè lùn) was written,
and every three days one fu and one poem were written.
A private examination was held every three months.
At the beginning of the quarter, the fu was tested first,
and after a day's interval, the cè lùn was tested.
The top five selected candidates were reported to the Board.
There were holidays on ten-day rests and festivals.
Sick leave was granted for illness.
Leave for visiting relatives or long-distance travel was granted.
Those who violated school rules were punished.
Those who did not follow instructions were expelled.
Those who applied for admission within one hundred days of experiencing mourning
were not allowed to participate in the confucian sacrifice (shìdiàn lǐ).
If a Guózǐjiān student could not qualify for tribute (chōnggòng) within three years,
and wished to serve in various bureaus,
the school officials would test them.
If they could roughly understand one major and one minor classic, they were allowed.
In the 29th year of Dàdìng of Emperor Zhāngzōng,
a petitioner requested the establishment of schools,
the implementation of the Sānshè Fǎ (Three-College System),
the recommendation of candidates to the Chūnguān (Ministry of Rites) from the xiāng (districts) based on the Bāxíng (Eight Virtues),
and the institution of the Zhìjǔ Hóngcí (Special Examination for Grand Eloquence).
The matter was referred to the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) for discussion by all officials.
Hùbù Shàngshū (Minister of Revenue) Dèng Yǎn and others stated:
"The Sānshè Fǎ originated in the Xīníng period of the Sòng dynasty,
when Wáng Ānshí abolished poetry and prose examinations,
focusing exclusively on classical studies.
Students entering the Tàixué (Imperial Academy) would first be assigned to the Wàishè (Outer College),
with no fixed quota.
From the Outer College, they could be promoted to the Nèishè (Inner College),
limited to 200 people.
From the Inner College, they could be promoted to the Shàngshè (Upper College),
limited to 100 people.
Each would specialize in one classic,
and there would be monthly examinations.
Some would be specially exempted from the provincial examination,
or recommended for official appointments.
Although this system was implemented,
it suffered from widespread abuses of favoritism and sycophancy.
Thus, Sū Shì said, '
Once the Sānshè was established,
bribery became rampant.'
Therefore, it was abolished during the Yuányòu period.
Although it was later reinstated,
it was completely abolished in the 3rd year of Xuānhé.
We believe that laws should be enduring.
Entrusting the Sānshè Fǎ to the selection and examination by academic officials
opens the door to opportunism,
and therefore cannot serve as a suitable law.
Emperor Wén of Táng fostered up to 8,000 scholars,
and the fallen Sòng dynasty had 5,000 in its two academies.
Currently, officials are selected through three categories: policy essays, poetic prose, and classical exegesis.
However, the Tàixué accommodates only 160 students,
and some prefectural academies outside the capital have only up to ten people,
totaling barely a thousand across the empire.
If we now establish schools in every zhōu (prefecture),
exclusively appoint professors,
conduct monthly examinations,
and reward the academic officials whose schools produce many successful candidates in each examination,
and if monthly tests determine three grades, which are recorded,
those who frequently achieve the highest grade within a year are given preferential treatment,
and those who are disobedient or commit misconduct are dismissed,
perhaps this would be a way to acquire talent.
Furthermore, the Zhōulǐ (Rites of Zhou) system of selecting from xiāng and lì can never be revived.
The establishment of examination categories should adapt to their respective times.
The Bāxíng (Eight Virtues) are derived from the six virtues of the Zhōulǐ – xiào (filial piety), yǒu (brotherly love), mù (harmoniousness), yīn (kinship), rèn (responsibility), and xù (compassion) –
to which zhōng (loyalty) and hé (harmony) were added by the fallen Sòng dynasty to make eight.
Of all human conduct, none is greater than xiàolián (filial piety and integrity).
There is already a system for recommending xiàolián, and for county officials to recommend talented and virtuous people.
Under the current system,
those who commit the Ten Abominations, such as adultery and robbery,
are not allowed to sit for the examinations.
This also reflects the spirit of the 'Six Virtues and Six Conducts.'
As for the Zhìjǔ Hóngcí,
it is for the Son of Heaven to await extraordinary individuals.
If this examination category is established,
it should not be limited to Jìnshì (Metropolitan Graduates),
but also allow selected persons to take the test.
Those who pass are promoted to high government positions,
which will encourage people to strive. "
The Emperor agreed with their proposal.
Consequently, based on the household populations of the zhōu and fǔ (prefectures),
the number of scholars supported was increased.
In addition to the existing Dàdìng regulations for 17 prefectural academies in the capital supporting 1,000 people,
60 schools were established in jiézhèn (military commands) and fángyù zhōu (defense prefectures),
increasing the number of scholars by 1,000.
Each was staffed with one professor,
selected from those who had passed the fifth stage of the examination or Jìnshì aged 50 or above.
There were 24 fǔxué (prefectural academies),
with 905 students.
(Dàxīng, Kāifēng, Píngyáng, Zhēndìng, and Dōngpíng Prefectures each had 60 students;
Tàiyuán and Yìdū Prefectures each had 50 students;
Dàdìng, Héjiān, Jǐnán, Dàmíng, and Jīngzhào Prefectures each had 40 students;
Liáoyáng and Zhāngdé Prefectures
each had 30 students;
Hézhōng, Qìngyáng, Líntáo, and Hénán Prefectures each had 25 students;
Fèngxiáng, Píngliáng, Yán'ān, Xiánpíng, Guǎngníng, and Xīngzhōng Prefectures each had 20 students.)
There were 39 jiézhènxué (military command schools),
totaling 615 students.
(Jiàng, Dìng, Wèi, Huái, and Cāng Zhōu each had 30 students;
Lái, Mì, Lù, Fén, Jì, Xíng, and Yǎn Zhōu each had 25 students;
Dài, Tóng, and Bīn Zhōu each had 20 students;
Fèngshèng Zhōu had 15 students;
the remaining 23 jiézhèn each had 10 students.)
There were 21 fángyù zhōuxué (defense prefecture schools),
totaling 235 students.
(Bó, Dé, Míng, Dì, and Bó each had 15 students;
the remaining 16 zhōu each had 10 students.)
In total, there were 1,800 students.
Nǚzhí (Jurchen) Schools.
Starting in the 4th year of Dàdìng,
classical texts were translated into the large and small Nǚzhí scripts and promulgated.
Later, talented children from good families within the méng'ān and móukè were selected as students,
totaling 3,000 across all lù (circuits).
In the 9th year,
100 of the most outstanding and intelligent were brought to the Jīngshī (capital),
and taught by Biānxiū Guān (Compiling Official) Wēndíhǎn Dìdá.
In the 13th year,
officials were selected based on policy essays and poetry,
and the Nǚzhí Guózǐxué (Jurchen Imperial Academy) was first established.
Nǚzhí fǔxué (Jurchen prefectural schools) were established in various lù,
with newly appointed Jìnshì serving as professors.
The Guózǐxué had 100 students for policy essays and 100 for elementary studies.
There were 22 fǔzhōuxué (prefectural and subprefectural schools),

established in Zhōngdū, Shàngjīng, Húlígǎi, Xùpín, Hélǎn, Púyǔ, Póxù, Xiánpíng, Tàizhōu, Línhuáng, Běijīng, Jìzhōu, Kāizhōu, Fēngzhōu, Xījīng, Dōngjīng, Gàizhōu, Lóngzhōu, Dōngpíng, Yìdū, Hénán, and Shǎnxī.
The system for recruiting Guózǐxué students and fǔxué students
was the same as for students of poetic prose and classical exegesis.
Furthermore, it was stipulated that
two students were to be recruited from each móukè.
If, within every 20 households of the zōngshì (imperial clan), there were no willing students,
then children from wealthy families, aged between 13 and 20, were to be enrolled.
For all examinations,
one policy essay was to be written every three days,
and quarterly private tests were to follow the system for Hàn (Chinese) students.
In the 29th year of Dàdìng,
an imperial edict commanded that all capital prefectural, jiézhèn, and zhōu schools
should have their affairs supervised by Nǚzhí and Hàn Jìnshì holding the positions of zhǎng and èr guān (first and second officials),
and their official titles recorded.
(The Nǚzhí schools in Hénán and Shǎnxī
were abolished in the 2nd year of Chéng'ān;
the rest remained as before.)
All Jìnshì and candidates,
from the xiāng (district) to the fǔ (prefecture),
from the fǔ to the shěng (province),
and finally to the diàntíng (palace),
if they passed all four examinations,
would be appointed to official positions.
If they were rejected five times at the diàntíng test,
they would be granted a degree,
known as ēn lì (special grace).
There were also those granted a degree by special imperial decree,
known as tè ēn (extraordinary grace).
For ēn lì candidates, only the quality of their essays determined their rank,
and they were not to be rejected.
All Jìnshì of poetic prose
were tested on one fu (rhapsody), one poem, and one policy essay.
Jìnshì of classical exegesis
were tested on one exegesis of their specialized classic and one policy essay.
The establishment of these examinations
began in the 11th month of the 1st year of Tiānhuì of Emperor Tàizōng.
At that time, due to the urgent need for Hàn scholars to pacify and assimilate newly surrendered populations,
there was initially no fixed number
or regular schedule.
Thus, they were conducted twice in the 2nd and 8th months of the 2nd year.
In the 5th year,
as Héběi and Hédōng had recently surrendered and there was a shortage of officials,
and because the systems of Liáo and Sòng differed,
an edict decreed that officials should be selected from the north and south based on their customary studies,
known as Nánběi Xuǎn (Southern and Northern Selection).
In the 5th month of the 1st year of Tiānjuàn of Emperor Xīzōng,
an edict decreed that both Nánběi Xuǎn should select officials through the two categories of classical exegesis and poetic prose.
In the 2nd year of Tiāndé of Hǎilíng Shùrén (the Commoner of Hǎilíng),
the system of diàntíng test was first added,
and the examination schedule was revised.
In the 3rd year,
the Nánběi Xuǎn were merged into one,
the two categories of classical exegesis and policy essays were abolished,
and officials were selected solely by poetic prose.
In the 1st year of Zhēnyuán,
the regulations and procedures for the gòngjǔ (tribute examinations) were standardized.
In the 1st year of Zhènglóng,
it was ordered that questions be drawn from the main texts of the Five Classics and Three Histories,
and it was first stipulated that examinations would be held once every three years.
In the 4th year of Dàdìng,
an imperial edict instructed the zǎichén (chief ministers) that,
if a Jìnshì's literary skills were excellent, they should be recruited,
without limiting the number of people.
In the 18th year,
the Emperor said to the zǎichén,
"Some literati happen to be selected as top candidates
and are immediately appointed to positions in the Hàn Yuàn (Hanlin Academy)
without questioning their conduct.
For example, Zhào Chéngyuán,
I heard he lacked scholarly virtue,
and it was indeed exposed.
From now on, before appointing the top candidate on the榜首 (list),
first investigate their conduct in their hometown.
If they are worthy, then appoint them to Yìngfèng (positions of attendance);
otherwise, they should follow the regular appointment process."
In the 19th year [of Dàdìng],
he said to his chief ministers (zǎichén):
“From ancient times, the topics for the imperial examinations' poetic essays (fù)
have all been those that scholars were accustomed to practicing.
Previously, I personally selected a topic
that was unexpected by people.
Therefore, many famous scholars were selected,
while mediocre talents did not succeed.
This shows that if the topic is difficult, even famous Confucians can excel,
but if the topic is easy, mediocre individuals can easily gain success by chance.”
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Tángguō Ānlǐ respectfully stated:
“What your subject said the other day,
that scholars do not pay attention to policy essays (cèlùn),
is precisely because of this.
It is fitting that all examination venues conduct thorough evaluations,
selecting those who excel in both literary style and reasoning.”
The Emperor (shàng) said:
“And they should also answer policy essays on current affairs,
to observe their arguments.
Their talent will naturally be evident.
You and others should deliberate on this.”
In the 20th year,
he said to his chief ministers:
“I once instructed that there should be no limit to the number of jinshì,
but then I was told that there were no qualified essays beyond those selected.
Hence, few were chosen.
Is this not caused by difficult topics?
If indeed there were many qualified [candidates],
and the responsible officials arbitrarily dismissed them,
that would be utterly unreasonable.”
He further said:
“In ancient times, those who were exemplary in the local recommendations (xiāngjǔ)
were granted official positions.
Now, upon their term's completion (kǎomǎn),
those whose actual conduct in their hometowns is outstanding should be promoted.”
He also said:
“Previously, policy essays were not selected,
but now they are.
However, from now on, the prefecture (fǔ) and metropolitan (huì) examinations need not test policy essays.
After a policy essay has already been selected,
then they will be tested with imperial policy essays (zhìcè),
examined by officials of the Hànlín Zhí Xuéshì Yuàn.”
In the 22nd year,
he said to his chief ministers:
“The leading jinshì of the Hàn dynasty
were customarily appointed as Attendants (Yìngfèng).
If their conduct did not match their reputation,
or if they were not proficient in the style of imperial edicts (zhìgào),
they were given an outside posting.”
In the 23rd year,
he said to his chief ministers:
“During the Huángtǒng era, [talented] jinshì in the Hàn dynasty
were rarely seen again.
Now, Attendants are appointed as zhuàngyuán,
which is merely following the standard.
The imperial edict texts,
each laid out according to the specific duty,
all have a fixed style,
hence they are easy.
However, when it comes to drafting amnesty edicts,
few are capable.”
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Niángē Wòtèlà replied:
“Old-timers, even after passing the imperial examinations, continued to study without ceasing.
Nowadays, once people pass, they abandon their studies.
That is why.”
During a break from attending to government affairs (tīngzhèng), the Emperor
summoned Cānzhī Zhèngshì Zhāng Rǔlín and Hànlín Zhí Xuéshì Lǐ Yàn to read the policy essays submitted by the newly successful jinshì.
When they reached [the question]:
“What is the method for filling vacant county magistrate (xiànlìng) positions?”
The Emperor said:
“I have pondered this day and night,
but do not know the solution.”
Yàn replied:
“Your subject has long reflected on this.
The founding dynasty established the examination system (shèkē),
initially dividing it into northern and southern selections.
The northern selection would promote 150 jinshì for poetic essays (cífu)
and 50 for classical exegesis (jīngyì).
The southern selection would take 150 people,
totaling 350 people.
In subsequent examinations,
the northern selection took 70 jinshì for poetic essays
and 30 for classical exegesis.
The southern selection took 150 people,
totaling 250 people.
As many entered officialdom,
there were no vacant positions.
Later, the northern and southern selections were combined,
and only the poetic essay category was set up.
No more than sixty or seventy people were chosen.
As fewer entered officialdom,
county magistrate positions became vacant.”
The Emperor said:
“From now on, those whose literary style and reasoning are commendable should be selected,
without limiting them by number.”
In the 28th year,
the classical exegesis (jīngyì) category was reinstated.
In the first month of the first year of Zhāngzōng Míngchāng,
those who spoke about current affairs said:
“The four examinations for candidates (jǔrén) make the xiāngshì seem like a mere formality,
and it should certainly be abolished.
For the prefecture (fǔ) and metropolitan (huì) examinations, we request that one out of every ten be selected,
and topics can be drawn from the Five Classics (qúnjīng),
with notes indicating their original source.”
The Emperor approved their words,
and decreed the abolition of the xiāngshì.
For the fǔshì, one out of five was to be selected.
Furthermore, he ordered the responsible officials to deliberate on adding examination bureaus in outer circuits
and on the system for drawing topics from the Five Classics.
The responsible officials reported:
“The number of those selected in the huìshì
was formerly limited to 500 people.
Compared to the imperial edict of Shìzōng that those who met the standard should be selected,
we request that this system be followed.
The fǔshì used to be held in six locations.
Among these, some were distant,
so we propose adding three special locations:
for Shàngjīng and Xiánpíng Fǔ Lù, examinations will be held in Liáoyáng;
for Hédōng Nánběi Lù, in Píngyáng;
and for Shāndōng Dōng Lù, in Yìdū.
Topics will be drawn from the Six Classics, Seventeen Histories, Xiàojīng, Lúnyǔ, Mèngzǐ, as well as Xúnzǐ, Yángzǐ, and Lǎozǐ.
It is decreed that their original sources be annotated below the topics.”
He also instructed the responsible officials:
“Regarding the historical allusions (gùshì) used by candidates in their examination papers (chéngwén),
fearing that the examiners might sometimes fail to recall them immediately
and thus mistakenly overlook talented individuals,
they may annotate the source themselves.
Errors in annotation characters
will not count towards the number of corrections.”
In Míngchāng 2nd year,
an imperial edict stated that officials (guān) whose rank reached the fifth grade
could directly proceed to the imperial examination (yùshì).
In the 4th year,
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Shǒu Zhēn said:
“The ways for the state to appoint officials (guānrén)
rely mostly on Jurchen (Nǚzhí) and Han (Hànrén) jinshì.
The various departments and bureaus that handle routine tasks
previously had no official career background.
They have only been in use since the Dàdìng era,
and to this day, few are capable.
Recently, the number of jinshì released from the examination has been somewhat high.
This measure should be further increased.
If the huìshì is limited to only 500 people,
then even if we wish to select more in the imperial palace examination (tíngshì),
it would not be possible.”
The Emperor then decreed to the responsible officials
that there should be no limit to the number in the huìshì;
if the essay met the standard, it should be selected.
In the 6th year,
those who spoke about current affairs said:
“Scholars generally rely on the officials to fully annotate the original sources for them,
and thus do not exert themselves in reading.
We request reducing the system of annotating original sources for histories and philosophers.
Furthermore, many selected essays in classical exegesis are superficial.
We request selecting academic officials
and people from this specific field to serve as examiners.”
The provincial ministers (shěngchén) said that if the original sources were not provided,
eminent scholars might occasionally make errors of forgetting.
They suggested that only the intent of the topic needed to be known.
It was then ordered to select former classical exegesis jinshì who were widely recommended and exceptionally talented and discerning to serve as academic officials.
When examiners were assigned,
their proficiency in the classics they specialized in would be verified and considered.
For poetic essay jinshì,
the topic annotation of the original source
should not exceed fifty characters.
For classical exegesis jinshì,
in the second round of the imperial examination,
a policy essay would be added to the regular essay.
In Chéng’ān 4th year,
the Emperor instructed his chief ministers:
“To have two zhuàngyuán in one examination round
is not right.
In the subsequent palace examination (tíngshì),
let those in poetic essays and classical exegesis all be tested on policy essays concerning current affairs,
and only one zhuàngyuán shall be selected.
Although there are other categories like classics and law,
they shall only be treated as other categories.”
“When Wáng Ānshí became prime minister in the Sòng dynasty,
〔一０〕he wrote new classics,
and only then began selecting people based on classical exegesis.
Furthermore, poetic essays and classical exegesis are the primary subjects that people are accustomed to studying,
while policy essays are something they study in addition.
Now, to abandon the primary and choose the supplementary
I fear does not accord with Your Majesty’s intention for public selection.”
Therefore, it was decided that on the same day of the imperial examination, each would be tested on their primary subject.
Poetic essays would remain as before,
divided into categories.
The first place would be the zhuàngyuán.
The top classical exegesis candidate would be second,
with the same grace and status as the second-place poetic essay candidate.
The rest would be divided into two lower grades,
both below the poetic essay candidates.
In the 5th year,
an imperial edict ordered that each examiner for poetic essays
should write one model examination paper (chéngwén)
to serve as a standard for candidates,
and after the examination, it should be submitted to the province for storage.
At that time, the chancellor memorialized:
"Before Dàdìng twenty-fifth year (1185),
graduates in cí fù (rhymed prose and poetry) were no more than five hundred.
In the twenty-eighth year (1188), the number was not limited,
and five hundred and eighty-six people were selected.
Formerly, we followed the sacred instruction that if they met the qualifications, they should be selected.
Therefore, in Chéng'ān second year (1197), nine hundred and twenty-five people were selected.
Moreover, there is now an imperial grace policy for those who have entered the final round four times.
If too many people are selected in the provincial examinations,
it will lead to an overflow."
So, the numbers for cè lùn (policy essays), cí fù, and jīng yì (exegesis of the classics) were set.
Although there could be more, they should not exceed six hundred people.
If there were fewer, the vacancies would be left open.
At that time, Tàicháng Chéng Guō Rénjié, in an audience, stated
that candidates specializing in cí fù
should not be allowed to also take the jīng yì examination under a different name,
and that students entering the imperial academy should be rigorously tested and selected
to prevent unqualified appointments.
The Emperor instructed the chancellor, saying:
"It has recently been memorialized and decided
that in the final round, cí fù and jīng yì will be tested on the same day.
If candidates are further prohibited from taking both in the prefectural and provincial examinations,
I fear that fewer will attempt jīng yì,
rendering this subject a mere empty setup.
As for the abuse of taking examinations under different names,
that should certainly be prohibited.
Regarding the supplementary testing of students entering the imperial academy,
there are already old regulations.
I fear they are being implemented carelessly,
so strict prevention is necessary."
Zhāng Xíngjiǎn, in an audience, stated:
"The original intention of drafting model essays
was to provide a standard for examinations.
However, currently, the examiners for the provincial examinations and the readers of examination papers for the imperial examinations all hold prominent positions.
After gaining their degrees, they have been away from writing for a long time
and no longer practice regularly.
If their spontaneously drafted essays for the current examinations
are even slightly imperfect,
it will merely invite criticism."
An imperial edict ordered it to be abolished.
In Tàihé first year (1201),
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Túshān Yì, concerned about the弊 of contemporary essays,
said:
"Students do not thoroughly study the classics and histories,
but only pursue minor studies,
leading to superficial conduct and aspirations.
It should be ordered that on the day of the policy essay examination for jìnshì,
in addition to policy essays on current affairs,
difficult points from the classics should also be included in the questions,
so as to elicit the subtle meanings of the sages and the changes of ancient and modern affairs."
An imperial edict made this a permanent system.
Previously, an imperial decree had forbidden musicians from becoming jìnshì,
but allowed those who had been slaves and were freed to become commoners.
The Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) memorialized:
"Traditionally, 'artisans and musicians'
referred to those in the category of assigned servitude and families of actors and entertainers.
However, currently, the artisans of the Shàofǔ Jiān (Directorate of Imperial Manufactories) and the musicians of the Tàicháng Dàyuè Shǔ (Grand Music Bureau of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices)
are all commoners,
yet they are not allowed to take the examinations.
In previous dynasties, it was stipulated that if any candidate, their father, or grandfather had ever been freed from servitude to become a commoner,
even if they held official positions, they could not hold 'pure' offices or govern the populace.
Now, conversely, they are allowed to take examinations,
which truly tarnishes the integrity of public opinion."
An imperial edict then established a fixed regulation:
freed commoners were not allowed to sit for any imperial examinations,
but their descendants were permitted to.
The Emperor also stated that
virtues and talents were not fully encompassed by the jìnshì examination,
and that the system of recommendation should be generally implemented.
The provincial officials memorialized:
"In the Zhōu Lǐ (Rites of Zhou),
'the Grand Minister of Education teaches the myriad people with the three local matters and recommends them for office.'
The 'myriad people' referred to
farmers, artisans, merchants, and traders, all of them.
In previous dynasties, the establishment of the virtuous was not restricted,
such as the builder of walls or the old man who sharpened knives,
countless examples of those whose brilliance illuminates the historical records.
Currently, for recluses and hermits in the wilderness who possess both talent and conduct,
commandants (móukè) and district magistrates (sīxiàn) are to recommend them,
and the Ànchá Sī (Surveillance Commission) will report fully,
so they may be honored and employed.
There is already a decree to this effect."
The Emperor ordered the decree to be re-proclaimed to emphasize it.
In Xuānzōng Zhēnyòu second year (1214),
the Yùshǐ Tái (Censorate) reported
that for the provincial examinations next year, due to obstructed roads in Zhōngdū, Liáodōng, Xī Běijīng and other circuits,
examinations should be held in Zhōngdū and Nánjīng only.
〔一一〕
In the third year (1215),
the Emperor instructed the chancellor, saying:
"The examination system established at the beginning of our dynasty
has always been known for its strictness.
