I now hear that during the provincial examinations, there is disorderly seating and clamor.
How can abuses be prevented?"
He ordered the punishment of the examining officials and censors.
In Xīngdìng second year (1218),
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Bǎhúlǔ said:
"Although the state selects people through several channels,
the selection of jìnshì is the most esteemed.
We do not seek to complete a set number,
but only to obtain the worthy.
Currently, in the provincial examinations,
for cè lùn jìnshì, less than one in two are selected;
for cí fù and jīng yì, one in two are selected.
Although there was a previous sacred instruction
that the Dàdìng system should be followed,
and those who pass should be taken regardless of number,
however, during the Dàdìng period, there were sometimes up to three thousand candidates,
but no more than five hundred were selected.
In the Tàihé period,
for cè lùn jìnshì, one in three were selected;
for cí fù and jīng yì, one in four were selected.
Earlier, at the beginning of Zhēnyòu,
an edict abolished the prefectural examinations,
and nearly nine thousand people sat for the provincial examinations,
yet just over eight hundred were selected,
which was only one-tenth.
At that time, although there was an instruction to follow the Dàdìng system,
when did they ever select one in two?
Now, the examiners are so indiscriminate;
this is not the way to seek the worthy.
It is advisable, before the provincial examinations,
to request the number to be selected,
so that the grace may originate from the top."
The Emperor ordered civil officials to convene for deliberation,
and eventually followed the Tàihé precedent.
He also said to the chancellor:
"Traditionally, jìnshì in the palace examination
were dismissed from the palace after dusk.
I fear that those whose thoughts come slower cannot fully display their talent.
Let them wait until evening."
He specially granted jīng yì jìnshì Wáng Biāo and thirteen others the degree.
The Emperor examined their model essays,
admiring their literary embellishment,
and sighed with praise for a long time.
He then wondered why scholars were decreasing,
and said to the supervising official, Zuǒchéng Gāo Rǔlì:
"The stipends for nurturing scholars and their academic provisions,
should be provided in kind when the harvest is slightly abundant.
Otherwise, this examination subject will be abandoned."
In the fifth year (1217),
for the provincial examination in jīng yì jìnshì,
the examiners selected more than ten additional people beyond the usual quota.
The Emperor ordered that they be granted degrees as a special act of grace.
He also ordered that candidates from Héběi who had passed the prefectural examinations but were hindered by military conflict
be exempted from future prefectural examinations.
The policy-essay *Jìnshì* (策論進士)
was the examination for Jurchen people.
It began in Dàdìng (大定) fourth year (1164),
when Emperor Shìzōng (世宗) ordered the distribution of Jurchen large and small script translations of Buddhist scriptures.
For every *móu'ān* (謀克), two people were selected to study them.
Soon, desiring to establish Jurchen script schools,
many sons from good families within the *mèng'ān* (猛安) and *móu'ān* (謀克) were chosen as students,
amounting to three thousand across all circuits.
In the ninth year (1169),
one hundred exceptional individuals were selected
and recommended to the capital,
where they were provided with stipends.
Wēndíhǎn Dìdá (溫迪罕締達) was ordered to teach them ancient books,
poetry, and policy essays.
Later, they were re-examined,
and over thirty individuals, including Túshān Yì (徒單鎰), passed.
In the eleventh year (1171),
the system for policy-essay selection was first deliberated.
By the thirteenth year (1173), it was finalized that each session would have one policy essay question,
to be completed in over five hundred characters.
The local and prefectural examinations were waived,
and candidates proceeded directly to the metropolitan and palace examinations.
An imperial edict also commanded the establishment of the Jurchen National Academy (女直國子學) in the capital
and Jurchen prefectural schools (女直府學) in the circuits.
Newly appointed *jìnshì* (進士) were to serve as professors
to teach the sons and younger brothers of scholars and commoners who wished to learn.
Once the system had been in place for a long time and the number of students grew,
it would follow the triennial examination system for Han *jìnshì*.
Then, Túshān Yì (徒單鎰) and others were tested at the Mǐnzhōng Temple (憫忠寺).
Their policy essay question was:
“Worthy individuals are born into the world,
and the world relies on worthy individuals.
The world has never failed to produce worthy individuals,
and worthy individuals have never failed to assist the world.
Indeed, it is not that the world lacks worthy individuals;
it is only a question of whether they are employed or not.
Consider Yī Yǐn (伊尹) assisting Chéng Tāng (成湯),
Fù Yuè (傅說) aiding Gāo Zōng (高宗),
and Lǚ Wàng (呂望) meeting Wén Wáng (文王).
They all rose from among farmers, builders, fishermen, and hunters,
yet their achievements were outstanding,
unreachable by later generations.
This is because the rulers of Yīn (殷) and Zhōu (周) were able to employ these men
and fully utilize their talents.
Our dynasty pacified the realm through divine military might,
and His Majesty stabilizes the four seas with civil virtue.
Both civil and military talents are employed;
even small virtues are certainly heeded,
and minor shortcomings are not discarded.
Indeed, the way of recruiting talent has been exhausted.
Yet, there is still concern that worthy and capable individuals may be overlooked in obscurity.
Now, if we wish to gather all the worthy individuals in the realm and employ them,
and further enable each worthy person to fully utilize their abilities,
by what means can this be achieved?”
Mǐnzhōng Temple (憫忠寺) formerly had twin pagodas.
On the night the *jìnshì* (進士) entered the courtyard,
a sound like music was heard from the East Pagoda,
then it entered the palace.
The examining official, Imperial Censor Wányán Púniè (完顏蒲涅), and others said:
“The path of literature has just opened, and such a phenomenon occurs.
This is an auspicious sign of obtaining worthy individuals.”
Twenty-seven individuals, including Túshān Yì (徒單鎰), were selected.
In the sixteenth year (1176),
it was ordered that royal relatives two generations removed or closer, and sons of chancellors,
should proceed directly to the palace examination.
Royal relatives who had to wear mourning attire for the emperor or closer, and sons of high-ranking officials,
should proceed directly to the metropolitan examination.
By the twentieth year (1180),
with Túshān Yì (徒單鎰) and others serving as professors inside and outside the court,
the study greatly flourished.
Thus, a system was finalized:
henceforth, candidates would be tested in three sessions with policy essays and poetry.
Policy essays would use Jurchen large script,
and poetry would use Jurchen small script.
The schedule for these examinations would follow the precedent of the Han *jìnshì* (進士).
Ministerial officials memorialized,
“Han *jìnshì* (進士) take the local examination on the twentieth day of the third month next year,
the prefectural examination on the twentieth day of the eighth month,
the metropolitan examination on the twentieth day of the first month of the following year,
and the palace examination on the twelfth day of the third month.”

An imperial edict ordered that the prefectural examination would be held on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month next year in four locations: Zhōngdū (中都), Shàngjīng (上京), Xiánpíng Fǔ (咸平府), and Dōngpíng Fǔ (東平府) circuits.
The rest would follow previous regulations.
The Emperor said:
“The Khitan script is ancient.
Observing the poems composed in it,
their meaning and principles are profound and subtle.
Why was a Khitan *jìnshì* (進士) examination system not established at that time?
Although a Jurchen script examination system is now established,
I fear that the Jurchen script, being of recent creation,
may not have meanings and principles as profound as Han characters.
I worry this will be criticized by later generations.”
Chancellor Shǒudào (守道) replied:
“Han characters may not have been so capable at first either;
they were gradually refined and improved by worthy sages throughout successive dynasties.
Your Majesty, with your sagely and discerning nature,
has commanded the translation of scriptures to teach the realm.
If this is practiced for a long time, it can also become like the literature of the Han people.”
The Emperor said:
“Let it follow the precedent of Han *jìnshì* (進士).
Translate the examination papers
and allow Han officials to review them.”
In the third month of the twenty-second year (1182),
the policy essays for Jurchen *jìnshì* (進士) were examined.
By *Guǐchǒu* (癸丑) in the fourth month,
the Emperor addressed his chief ministers, saying:
“The Jurchen *jìnshì* (進士) examination has been held for a long time;
why have the results not yet been finalized?”
Cānzhī Zhèngshì (參知政事) Wòtèlà (斡特剌) replied:
“Because they have been sent for translation and review.”
The Emperor ordered it to be expedited.
In the twenty-third year (1183),
the Emperor said:
“The Jurchen *jìnshì* (進士) examination system has not been established for long.
If they are allowed to accumulate practice and become proficient,
then their abilities will naturally become evident.”
In the twenty-eighth year (1188),
he instructed his chief ministers, saying:
“Jurchen *jìnshì* (進士) are only tested on policy essays.
After this has been practiced for a long time,
people can prepare for it in advance.
Would it now be acceptable to test them on classical commentaries?”
The chief ministers replied:
“Among the Five Classics, the *Shū* (書), *Yì* (易), and *Chūnqiū* (春秋) have already been translated.
Once the *Shī* (詩) and *Lǐ* (禮) are translated,
they can be tested.”
The Emperor said:
“The principles and meanings of the great classics are profound.
One cannot master them without spending years.
For now, it is appropriate to provisionally test them with argumentative topics from the classics,
and later gradually test them on classical commentaries.”
In the twenty-ninth year (1189) of Dàdìng (大定) under Emperor Zhāngzōng (章宗),
an edict permitted all people to take the policy-essay *jìnshì* (進士) examination.
In the seventh month, a ministerial memorial proposed
that if poetry, policy essays, and argumentative essays were all examined on a single day,
candidates might be unable to perform adequately.
Poetry and policy essays should be on one day,
and argumentative essays on another day.
Passing the poetry and policy essays would qualify candidates for selection,
and the argumentative essay would determine their rank.
The Emperor said:
“The argumentative essay is newly added.
By the third examination, a comprehensive decision regarding retention or removal should be made.”
In Míngchāng (明昌) first year (1190),
it was proposed that *mèng'ān* (猛安) and *móu'ān* (謀克) who wished to take the *jìnshì* (進士) examination should follow the rules for others,
and not be allowed to proceed directly to the palace examination.
The Emperor said:
“This only permits Jurchen *jìnshì* (進士) not to take the Han *jìnshì* (進士) examination.”
It was also decreed
that other officials holding the fifth rank of scattered office
should proceed directly to the metropolitan examination,
and officials whose posts and ranks both reached the fifth rank
should proceed directly to the palace examination.
In Chéng'ān (承安) second year (1197),
an imperial edict limited the number of able-bodied men (*dīng* 丁) studying for the policy-essay *jìnshì* (進士) examination.
Thus, a system was finalized:
internal and external officials, personnel in various bureaus, imperial guardsmen, Jurchen from *mèng'ān* (猛安) and *móu'ān* (謀克), and people of various other statuses,
if a household had only one *dīng* (丁), they were not allowed to take the examination.
If there were two *dīng* (丁), one person was allowed.
For four *dīng* (丁), two people.
For six *dīng* (丁) or more, only three people were allowed.
Those who had completed three examination cycles
were exempt from this *dīng* (丁) verification limit.
In the third year (1198),
a system was finalized:
Jurchen people under forty-five years of age,
taking the *jìnshì* (進士) examination,
were to undergo an archery test ten days before the prefectural examination.
This test would be administered by a deputy official skilled in archery.
The regulation was:
a target would be set up sixty paces away.
Fifteen paces from the archer, two poles would be erected opposite each other,
twenty paces apart.
Two *zhàng* (丈) (approx. 6.6 meters) above the ground,
a rope would be stretched horizontally between them.
The strength of the bow was not restricted,
and hitting the target or not was not counted.
Skillful and convenient drawing of the bow and swift and accurate release of arrows were considered proficiency.
Hitting two arrows out of ten,
passing below the rope and reaching the target, constituted passing.
For other circuits, the Tíxíng Sī (提刑司) would be responsible.
In the capital, the Jiānchá (監察) would conduct investigations.
Those who were to proceed directly to the metropolitan or palace examinations
would be tested by deputy officials of Dàxīng Fǔ (大興府).
Those who had completed three examination cycles were exempt.
In the fourth year,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Jiǎ Xuàn said:
"For *cèlùn jìnshì* who are tested in archery,
if those who have failed two times or those under sixteen who are not yet adults,
are disqualified due to archery,
it would mean losing talented individuals.
I request that they be tested after passing the examination (*jí dì*);
those who pass should be given separate appointments,
or promoted,
and those who fail should be demoted."
The court officials said:
"According to the old system, those who failed three times were exempted from the test.
To exempt those who failed two times now
is not permissible.
If those not yet adults are exempted from the test,
there will surely be those who falsely conceal their age.
If they are indeed young,
it's not too late to let them practice slowly.
As for testing and promoting or demoting after passing the examination (*jí dì*),
there are already established regulations."
An imperial edict ordered adherence to the old system.
In the *Tàihé* Regulations,
there was also a system where contemporary policy questions (*shíwù cè*) were combined with historical precedents,
and difficult classical principles were posed as questions.
After Xuānzōng moved south,
in the first year of Xīngdìng,
it was decreed that in Zhōngdū, Xījīng, and other circuits,
*cèlùn jìnshì* and *wǔ jǔrén* would temporarily take their prefectural examinations at four locations: Nánjīng, Dōngpíng, Pó Sù, and Shàngjīng.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor granted *jìnshì* status to Wòlèyèdé and twenty-seven others.
The Emperor reviewed the examination papers,
and, surprised by the small number,
asked his chief ministers.
They replied:
"In the Dàdìng period, schools were established everywhere.
Each *móukè* provided three or two *shēngyuán*,
who were supported with money and grain.
By the middle of the *Tàihé* period,
each person was typically granted sixty *mǔ* of land.
Since the provisions were generous,
there were many students.
Now, although the prefectural school still exists in the capital,
the monthly stipend is only fifty strings of *tōngbǎo* coins.
If schools are established and students supported in all *zǒngguǎnfǔ* of the circuits and in places with military households,
it might increase the numbers.
The capital's prefectural school already accommodates sixty students;
we request to add forty more.
In Zhōngjīng, Bózhōu, and Jīngzhàofǔ, educational officials should be placed within the *zǒngfǔ*,
and those within the *móukè* who are not listed in military registers should be designated as students,
each granted forty *mǔ* of land.
We also request the same for Hàn students in the capital,
while other prefectures should maintain the old system."
The Emperor agreed.
Regarding the number of successful candidates in the metropolitan examination (*huìshì*):
In the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng,
the number of *cífù jìnshì* was not to exceed five hundred.
In the twenty-eighth year,
because there was no limit on the number,
it reached five hundred and eighty-six people.
Zhāngzōng decreed that all who qualified should be selected,
so in the second year of Chéng'ān, it reached nine hundred and twenty-five people.
At that time, as those who had failed four times were again included,
the number was considered excessive,
so an order was issued that no more than six hundred should be selected.
In the second year of Tàihé,
the Emperor ordered the establishment of selection quotas for the various *huìshì* subjects.
Sīkōng Xiāng said:
"Many take the *cífù* and *jīngyì* examinations,
so one in five should be selected.
*Cèlùn* candidates are extremely few,
so one in four can be selected.
The special 'grace list' (*ēnbǎng*) was originally for those who had grown old in the examination halls.
Receiving grace after four failures is too generous;
limiting by age would hinder exceptional talents.
One should receive grace after five failures."
Píngzhāng Túdān Yì and others said:
"From the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng to the early Míngchāng period,
roughly one in three or four was selected."
Píngzhāng Zhāng Rǔlín also said:
"One in five is selected;
among a hundred candidates for the prefectural examination, only five are selected."
Thus, a regulation was established:
for *cèlùn*, one in three was selected;
for *cífù* and *jīngyì*, one in five was selected.
Those who had failed five times and were forty-five years or older, or those who had failed four times and were fifty years or older, would receive grace.
Regarding examination officials:
During the Dàdìng period,
there were six prefectural examination sites.
Each appointed three *cífù* examiners,
and two *cèlùn* examiners.
In the early Míngchāng period,
this was increased to nine sites.
Each circuit appointed nine officials,
and Dàxīngfǔ appointed eleven officials.
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
Tàiyuán was again added, making it ten sites.
The relevant authorities requested to reduce the number,
so it was decreed that for *cèlùn jìnshì* and Nǚzhí *jīngtóng*, if there were over a thousand candidates, four officials would be appointed;
if over five hundred, three officials;
and if under five hundred, two officials.
In each case, one official of higher rank served as the chief examiner,
and the others as associate examiners.
For *cífù jìnshì* and *lǜkē jǔrén* combined, if there were over three thousand candidates, five officials were appointed;
if two thousand, four officials;
and if under two thousand, three officials.
For *jīngyì jìnshì* and *jīngtóng jǔrén*, if there were a thousand candidates, four officials;
if over five hundred, three officials;
if over a hundred, two officials;
and if under a hundred, the *cífù* examiners would also serve.
Later, another regulation was established:
for *cèlùn* examiners,
Shàngjīng, Xiánpíng, and Dōngpíng each had three;
Běijīng, Xījīng, and Yìdū each had two.
For the *lǜkē* examination,
one supervising official
and two legal examiners
were attached to the *cífù* examination bureau.
〔一二〕For *jīngtóng*,
one examiner
was attached to the *jīngyì* examination bureau,
similar to the *huìshì*.
As for the sealing officials (*mífēng guān*), copying officials (*ténglù guān*), and search officials for prohibited materials (*jiǎnsōu huáixiá guān*),
and other tasks like maintaining the examination halls,
and supervising gate officials,
all followed the *huìshì* regulations.
In the twentieth year of Dàdìng,
the Emperor noted that in previous years, officials from distant places were often appointed as examiners,
which was inconvenient,
so he ordered the appointment of those nearby.
For the *huìshì*:
The Chief Examiner (*zhīgòngjǔ guān*) and Associate Chief Examiner (*tóngzhīgòngjǔ guān*),
for *cífù* were formerly ten officials,
reduced to seven in the fifth year of Chéng'ān.
For *jīngyì*, there were six officials,
reduced to four in the fifth year of Chéng'ān.
There were also two reviewing officials (*quándú guān*).
In the third year of Tàihé,
the Emperor, because the sealing officials (*mífēng guān*) had leaked information to the *jǔrén*,
issued an edict that from now on, the Nǚzhí bureau would use Hàn officials from the 'right selection' for sealing,
and the Hàn bureau would use Nǚzhí officials for sealing.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu of Xuānzōng,
because a *fù* topic in the *huìshì* had been previously used,
and some who violated the rules were still selected,
and furthermore, examiners frequently selected their relatives,
the Emperor was angered by the unfairness,
and ordered a thorough investigation and punishment.
For the imperial examination (*yùshì*):
the paper-reading officials (*dújuǎn guān*),
for *cèlùn* and *cífù jìnshì* each had seven officials,
for *jīngyì* had five officials,
and other functional officials each had two.
For the special *zhìjǔ hóngcí* examination, there were three officials in total.
In the seventh year of Tàihé,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Zhāng Xíngjiǎn said:
"According to old practice,
paper-reading officials did not recuse themselves for relatives.
When there were relatives,
some might not dare to decide their pass or fail,
or might vigorously protect them,
leading to suspicion from their colleagues.
If paper-reading officials who have relatives among the *jìnshì* are not used,
then the paper-reading process can be discussed impartially."
The Emperor then ordered that at the time of appointment, many candidates should be proposed,
and those with relatives should be excluded.
For the prefectural examination of *cèlùn jìnshì*:
In the twentieth year of Dàdìng, it was set at four locations: Zhōngdū,
〔一三〕Shàngjīng, Xiánpíng, and Dōngpíng.
By the first year of Míngchāng,
Běijīng, Xījīng, and Yìdū were added, making seven locations, also examining Nǚzhí *jīngtóng*.
All from Shàngjīng, Hélǎn, Sùpín, Húlígǎi, Púyǔ, Dōngběi Zhāotǎosī and other circuits,
would take the prefectural examination at Huìníngfǔ.
Those from Xiánpíng, Lóngzhōu, Pó Sù, Dōngjīng, Gàizhōu, and Yìzhōu,
would take the prefectural examination at Xiánpíngfǔ.
Those from Zhōngdū and Héběi Dōngxīlù,
would take the prefectural examination at Dàxīngfǔ.
Those from Xījīng and the two *zhāotǎosī* of Xīnán and Xīběi,
would take the prefectural examination at Dàtóngfǔ.
Those from Běijīng, Línhuáng, Zōngzhōu, Xīngzhōu, and Quánzhōu,
would take the prefectural examination at Dàdìngfǔ.
Those from Shāndōng Xīlù, Dàmíng, and Nánjīng,
would take the prefectural examination at Dōngpíngfǔ.
Those from Shāndōng Dōnglù would take the examination at Yìdū.
For the prefectural examinations of *cífù jìnshì*, *jīngyì jìnshì*, *lǜkē*, and *jīngtóng*:
During the Dàdìng period,
there were six locations: Dàxīng, Dàdìng, Dàtóng, Kāifēng, Dōngpíng, and Jīngzhào.
In the early Míngchāng period,
Liáoyáng, Píngyáng, and Yìdū were added, making nine locations.
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān, Tàiyuán was again added, making ten.
Those from Zhōngdū and Héběi would be examined at Dàxīngfǔ.
Those from Shàngjīng, Dōngjīng, Xiánpíngfǔ, and other circuits would be examined at Liáoyángfǔ.
The rest would be examined within their respective jurisdictions.
The date for the provincial examination (*xiāngshì*)
was the twentieth day of the third month.
For the prefectural examinations (Fǔshì)
—if they are policy-and-discourse *jìnshì* (cèlùn jìnshì), they take the policy examination (shì cè) on the twentieth day of the eighth month.
After an interval of three days, they take the poetry examination (shì shī).
If they are rhymed-prose-and-poetry *jìnshì* (cí fù jìnshì), they take the rhymed prose and poetry examination (shì fù jí shī) on the twenty-fifth day.
After another interval of three days, they take the policy-and-discourse examination (shì cèlùn).

If they are Classics-and-righteousness *jìnshì* (jīngyì jìnshì), after an interval of three days following the rhymed prose and poetry examination, they take the Classics-and-righteousness examination (shì jīngyì).
After another three days, they take the policy examination (shì cè).
Next are the Law (Lǜ) section candidates,
and next are the Classic Prodigies (Jīngtóng).
Each session is held with an interval of three days between examinations.
For the metropolitan examinations (Huìshì)
—the policy-and-discourse *jìnshì* take the policy examination on the twentieth day of the first month.
All subsequent examinations follow an interval of three days,
as before.
For the imperial examination (Yùshì)
—the policy-and-discourse *jìnshì* take the policy examination on the twentieth day of the third month.
On the twenty-third day, they take the poetry and discourse examination (shì shīlùn).
On the twenty-fifth day, the rhymed-prose-and-poetry *jìnshì* take the rhymed prose, poetry, and discourse examination (shì fù shīlùn).
The Classics-and-righteousness *jìnshì* also take the Classics-and-righteousness examination on this same day.
On the twenty-seventh day, they take the policy-and-discourse examination (shì cèlùn).
If an examination day encounters rain or snow,
it is postponed until a clear day.
After the roll call (chàngmíng) for the imperial examination,
for the policy examination, a report is submitted (bǐnzòu).
For the grand rhetoric (hóngcí) examination, it is scheduled for two days.
According to the old system (jiù zhì),
the examination for Jurchen *jìnshì* (Nǚzhí jìnshì) was held after the re-examination for Han *jìnshì* (Hàn jìnshì).
In Dàdìng twenty-ninth year (1189), with the re-establishment of the Classics-and-righteousness section (jīngyì kē),
this system was revised.
Regarding the system of invigilation (jiānjiǎn zhī zhì),
in Dàxīng Fǔ, soldiers from the Imperial Guard (Wǔwèi Jūn) are dispatched.
In other prefectures, personnel are selected from nearby *méng'ān*.
In Píngyáng Fǔ, soldiers from the Shùndé Jūn are dispatched.
For all prefectural and metropolitan examinations (Fǔ Huìshì),
one person is dispatched for every four successful candidates (*jǔrén*),
and an official (guān) is further assigned to supervise.
For the imperial policy *jìnshì* examination, archers (nǔshǒu) and attendants from the bureau (suí jú chéngyìng rén) are dispatched.
For Han *jìnshì*, personal guards (qīnjūn) are dispatched,
one person for each.
All those used must be illiterate,
with ten bodyguards (hùwèi),
and one commander of a hundred personal guards (qīnjūn bǎirén zhǎng) and one commander of fifty personal guards (wǔshírén zhǎng) to patrol and guard.
In Tàihé first year (1201),
the provincial ministers (shěng chén) submitted a memorial (zòu):
"Although the search and inspection (sōujiǎn) should be strict,
to the extent of untying hair and baring clothes (jiě fà tǎn yī),
and searching ears and nose,
is excessive.
How can this be the proper treatment of scholars?
Therefore, in Dàdìng twenty-ninth year (1189), it was already ordered, following old precedents (qián gùshì),
that they be allowed to bathe,
and officials provide clothes for them to change into.
This can both prevent irregularities and avoid impropriety."
The emperor (Shàng) assented to this suggestion
and ordered it to be implemented.
Regarding special dispensations (Ēnlì):
In Míngchāng first year (1190),
it was decreed
that the provincial first (shěng yuán) could proceed directly to the imperial examination (Yùshì).
Those who did not pass were allowed to be appended to the end of the list (pāng mò).
The provincial top scholar (*jièyuán*) was only exempted from the prefectural examination (Fǔshì).
Those who took the examination four times (sì jǔ) were granted the same special dispensation as those who took it five times (wǔ jǔ).
Regarding the examination papers (wénjuàn), only those that violated imperial names or taboo names of ancestors (yùmíng miàohuì) or were incoherent were disqualified.
All others were ranked according to the quality of their writing.
Also, three topics were examined in one day.
Those taking the examination for the fifth time (wǔ jǔ zhě) only took the rhymed prose and poetry examination (fù shī).
Jurchen *jìnshì* (Nǚzhí jìnshì) also followed this rule.
In Chéng'ān fifth year (1200),
an imperial edict (chì) was issued stating that *jìnshì* who had taken the examination four times were eligible for special grace (gāi ēn).
The rhymed prose and poetry and Classics-and-righteousness (cí fù jīngyì) should be counted as separate examination sessions for their respective sections (gè kē wéi chǎngshù),
and not be combined.
Furthermore, for those on the grace list (ēnbǎng rén) who should be awarded official positions,
the supervising examiners (jiānshì guān) should record their numbers during the examination and report them to the throne,
and those granted special grace (tè ēn zhě) should be appointed.
In Tàihé third year (1203), considering that the Classics-and-righteousness metropolitan first (jīngyì huìyuán) was different from the policy-and-discourse and rhymed-prose-and-poetry *jìnshì*,
if they were disqualified in the imperial examination (Yùshì), appending them to the end of the list
would be too preferential.
If they received the same grace,
it would again be different from those who had taken the examination four times.
Thus, a new system was established:
following the precedent of *jièyuán* who had previously passed the prefectural examination being exempted from it,
if they failed the metropolitan examination (Huìshì),
they could proceed directly to the imperial examination for their second attempt (zài jǔ zhífù yùshì).
Law section *jìnshì* (Lǜ kē jìnshì) were also called "various sections" (zhūkē).
For them, topics were drawn from the statutes and ordinances (lǜlìng).
At the prefectural examination, there were fifteen topics,
and one person was selected for every five.
In Dàdìng twenty-second year (1182), it was decreed
that for the metropolitan examination, there would be fifteen topics per session.
Across three sessions, a total of more than thirty-six articles (tiáo) with excellent writing, appropriate judgments, and precise word usage
were considered successful candidates.
The number of successful candidates was determined at the time
and initially not fixed.
This system first appeared in the first year of Zhènglóng (1156) of Hǎilíng Shùrén.
By Dàdìng twenty-ninth year (1189) of Zhāngzōng,
the relevant authorities (yǒusī) stated:
"Law section candidates (Lǜkē) only know how to read the laws
but do not know the source of moral transformation (jiàohuà zhī yuán).
They should be made to study the *Lúnyǔ* and *Mèngzǐ* to cultivate their demeanor (qìdù)."
Consequently, it was ordered that from the next examination onward,
an essay on a minor point of righteousness (xiǎoyì yī dào) from the *Lúnyǔ* and *Mèngzǐ* would be examined.
For the prefectural and metropolitan examinations (Fǔ Huìshì), a separate day would be set aside for this examination.
The Classics-and-righteousness examiners (jīngyì shìguān) were ordered to set the topics,
and these would be considered together with the main subject for assessment.
Regarding the system for Classic Prodigies (Jīngtóng zhī zhì):
all sons of scholars or commoners (shìshù zǐ) under the age of thirteen
who could recite two major classics and three minor classics,
and also recite the *Lúnyǔ*, various masters (zhūzǐ), and more than five thousand characters (zì),
would be considered for selection if they answered thirteen or more of the fifteen topics correctly in the prefectural examination.
For the metropolitan examination, there were fifteen topics per session,
and those who answered forty-one or more correctly across three sessions
were selected.
The most valued trait was being young and having recited many texts.
If their age was the same,
those who had recited more major classics were considered the best.
Initially,
in Tiānhuì eighth year (1130),
Tàizōng, upon learning that the child Liú Tiānjì from Dōngpíng,
at seven years old, could recite the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Yì*, *Lǐ*, *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn*, as well as the *Lúnyǔ* and *Mèngzǐ*,
ordered that he be educated and nurtured.
However, there was no system for selection at that time.
In the second year of Xīzōng's (1138) enthronement,
an edict (zhào) was issued to open up the tribute selection (gòngjǔ).
Only then were Classic Prodigies fully included,
and up to one hundred and twenty-two were selected.
During the Tiāndé era (1149-1153),
this system was abolished.
In Dàdìng twenty-ninth year (1189) of Zhāngzōng,
the emperor said to his chief ministers (zǎichén):
"Surely there are Classic Prodigies.
Discuss re-establishing this system."
In Míngchāng first year (1190),
Yìdū Fǔ reported:
"The child Liú Zhù'ér, aged eleven,
is capable in poetry and rhymed prose,
can recite the six major and minor classics,
writes in a quite skillful running and cursive script,
and possesses filial piety from an early age.
We request that he be granted entry into officialdom (cì chūshēn) following the precedent of the Sòng child Lǐ Shú,
and further bestow an imperial edict of grace upon him."
The emperor summoned him to the inner palace (nèidiàn),
tested him with the "Phoenixes Coming to Court" (Fènghuáng láiyí) rhymed prose and the "Fish in Algae" (Yú zài zǎo) poem,
and also had him compose a poem on drought.
The emperor praised him,
granted him entry into officialdom (běnkē chūshēn),
provided him with money, grain, and an official residence,
and ordered him to study at the Imperial Academy (Tàixué).
In the third year of Míngchāng,
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Wányán Shǒuzhēn said:
“The examination for scripture students is not an ancient practice.
In the Táng dynasty, various circuits recommended candidates,
sometimes selecting five to ten people.
In recent times, Sòng Rénzōng deemed it useless
and abolished it.
In our dynasty, during the Huángtǒng era, up to fifty people were selected,
and this became customary.
During the Tiāndé era, it was again abolished.
The sagely sovereign has reinstated it,
selecting hundreds of people.
I fear that if this continues to accumulate over time,
it will be impossible to manage the selection and appointment process.
I request an imperial decree to reduce the number of selections.”
The Emperor said:
“What if all those who recite meet the standard?”
Shǒuzhēn replied:
“If we carefully select those who are youngest and recite without error,
then the number of people will not be excessive.”
He then asked Cānzhī Zhèngshì Xū Chígúo,
who replied:
“Whether the recitation is clear or not is easy to see;
how could there be any abuse?”
The Emperor said:
“Limit it to thirty or forty people.
If a hundred people all pass,
we can still re-examine and select the best among them.”
Chígúo said:
“This examination is essentially a method to cultivate education.
When one learns the text in youth
and thoroughly understands its meaning in adulthood,
and then applies it in governance,
talented individuals will emerge.
If those who are selected
further cultivate their studies for the Jìnshì examination,
then all they have learned can be put to good use.
I suggest that they not be allowed to immediately enter officialdom,
but must first study for the Jìnshì examination,
and only then can they be appointed to office.
If they can pass the Jìnshì examination,
they should be treated the same as Jìnshì in appointments.
If they pass the prefectural recommendation or the metropolitan examination,
depending on the number of attempts,
their rank should be elevated.
If after several attempts they still cannot be recommended,
they should return to their original status.
This way, we can encourage and motivate people and thus acquire talent.”
An edict was issued for deliberation and implementation.

The special examinations included categories such as Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng (Virtuous and Upright), Néng Zhíyán Jíjiàn (Able to Speak Frankly and Offer Strong Admonitions), Bóxué Hóngcái (Broadly Learned and Greatly Talented), and Dá Yú Cóngzhèng (Proficient in Governance).
The examinations had no fixed schedule;
whenever the Emperor wished to hold them,
it would be announced to the empire.
Officials, civil and military, inside and outside the capital, of the sixth rank and below, who had no public or private transgressions, were allowed
to be recommended by officials of the fifth rank and above, inside and outside the capital, to their respective superiors,
and then an imperial edict would order their examination.
As for scholars living in reclusion,
if their virtue and conduct were admired by their local communities,
they would be recommended by the prefectures and circuits.
For all examinations,
candidates first submitted thirty essays and policy papers on their chosen field to the Xuéshìyuàn.
Those whose literary style and reasoning were excellent
would then be assigned officials to set questions from the various classics, philosophers, and histories.
On one day, three essays would be tested.
If these were satisfactory,
then one policy paper would be tested in a court examination,
not constrained by ordinary rules,
selecting those who were thoroughly versed in all matters,
and promoting them to superior ranks.
For the Hóngcí (Grand Literary Talent) examination, imperial edicts, proclamations, memorials,表 (biaos), manifestos, and檄書 (xishu)
all used the four-six literary style.
Admonitions, rescripts, eulogies, maxims, inscriptions, prefaces, and records
either followed ancient and modern styles
or blended with the four-six style.
After each examination, Jìnshì recipients and officials of the sixth rank and below, who had no public or private offenses,
were recommended by external officials.
The examining officials would set questions and conduct the tests.
Four questions were tested in total,
and candidates were divided into two grades for promotion.
Both of these examinations were initiated in the first year of Zhāngzōng's Míngchāng era.
The military examination (Wǔjǔ)
was established during the Huángtǒng era.
Its regulations are found in the Tàihé Code,
with three grades: upper, middle, and lower.
Candidates had to be able to draw a bow of one shí strength,
using bamboo arrows weighing seven qián,
and shoot at a standing target at 150 paces.
Out of ten arrows,
one hit was required for the prefectural examination,
two hits for the provincial examination,
and three hits for the final examination.
They also had to perform long-range archery, hitting a target at 220 paces,
with one hit out of three arrows.
Furthermore, within 150 paces,
every fifty paces, two prone deer targets, five cùn high and eight cùn long, were set up.
Candidates had to ride and shoot with a seven dǒu bow and two large chisel-headed iron arrows.
For the prefectural examination, four passes were allowed;
for the provincial examination, three passes;
and for the final examination, two passes,
with two hits required in each.
Additionally, within 150 paces,
every thirty paces, four wooden dummies, three chǐ high, wearing five-cùn square boards, were placed alternately left and right.
Candidates had to ride and pierce them with a spear.
For the prefectural examination, three passes were allowed;
for the provincial examination, two passes;
and for the final examination, three passes,
[一四] each requiring one board to be knocked off on both the left and right.
Also, in accordance with the Yìn (Protection) system, one article of law was questioned,
and ten articles from Sūn Wú's works (Sunzi's Art of War) were questioned.
Those who could explain five were deemed upper grade.
For all final examinations,
if there was even one failure,
all candidates were disqualified.
If the target archery bow was eight dǒu,
long-range archery 210 paces,
deer archery bow six dǒu,
and four out of ten Sūn Wú articles were understood,
it was considered middle grade.
If the target archery bow was seven dǒu,
long-range archery 205 paces,
deer archery bow five dǒu,
and three out of ten Sūn Wú articles were understood,
it was considered lower grade.
Understanding law and piercing boards
were to be the same as before.
Those who knew nothing of the books,
even if they qualified for upper grade, would be treated as middle;
middle would be treated as lower.
For all examinations that resulted in middle or lower grade, those who wished to retry were permitted.
The old system stipulated that
if one failed to achieve the upper grade in the examination,
one was not allowed to reattempt for the middle or lower grades.
In the first year of Tàihé,
regulations were established
that no longer distinguished between old grades,
but simply allowed candidates to choose their desired grade.
If they passed the examination, they would be ranked by the three grades.
In the second year,
the department submitted a memorial stating
that the military examination procedures should be concurrent with the Jìnshì examination.
This year, the prefectural examination in August
was intended to have examination centers set up along the routes,
with officials dispatched at the appointed time.
However, fearing that as a new establishment the number of candidates was unknown,
it was temporarily ordered that candidates attend examinations at their respective locations.
In the third year of Xuānzōng's Zhēnyòu era,
those who passed were granted imperial edicts and official robes, similar to the Jìnshì.
At that time, those who entered the military examinations from various places,
unless they were already holding official positions or had been serving at the front,
were ordered by the commanderies and counties to be sent to the capital,
to form a separate army,
in preparation for emergencies.
Those who had been recommended but not yet appointed to office
were also given responsibilities according to their talents.
In the second year of Yuánguāng,
the Commander-in-Chief of Dōngjīng, Gēshíliè Yáwútǎ, said:
“Those who enter officialdom through the military examination
are all appointed as patrol officers and military commanders.
Although these individuals are skilled in horsemanship and archery,
they have not experienced battle formations
and are ignorant of military matters.
If they suddenly face an enemy,
they might cause defeat.
I request that they all be gathered and sent to the front lines as senior officers,
and promoted when they achieve merit.”
The prime ministers memorialized:
“The state has established this examination on par with the Jìnshì examination,
and to send them all to the military
is not the way to encourage and advance talented individuals.”
So, those who were observing mourning, awaiting appointment, or had resigned from office were assigned to this.
Examination for Xuéshìyuàn officials.
In the twenty-eighth year of Dàdìng,
an imperial edict established an examination to select scholars for the Xuéshìyuàn.
The Ministry of Rites informed the Táicháng Temple,
which, following Táng dynasty regulations,
stated that those first entering the Xuéshìyuàn were to be tested.
Now, for those who had already become Jìnshì and entered officialdom,
they could be recommended by court officials of the sixth rank or external officials of the fifth rank.
Three essays, such as imperial edicts and proclamations, would be tested,
and those with excellent literary style and reasoning would be appointed as aides (Yìngfèng).
Thus, the selection for the Hànyuàn became refined.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
as there were few people in the Xuéshìyuàn capable of writing,
the Shàngshūshěng was ordered to seek out talented writers and provisionally test them.
As for the students of the Sītiāntái (Astronomy Bureau),
there were twenty-six Nǚzhēn and fifty Hàn Chinese.
Officials and commoners aged fifteen to thirty were allowed to test for recruitment.
Also, once every three years,
scholars from reclusion were selected and tested for recruitment.
The examination system for this involved
using the Xuānmíng Calendar to test calendrical calculations,
as well as matching marriages and burials using marriage books and new geography books,
and also the methods of Yìgū fǎ (Yi divination), Liùrén kè (Six Ren divination), and the arts of Sānmìng and Wǔxīng (Three Fates and Five Stars).
For the ten branches of medical science,
thirty students from Dàxīngfǔ,
twenty from other Jīngfǔ,
sixteen from Sǎnfǔ Jiézhèn,
and ten from Fángyùzhōu,
were tested monthly on difficult questions.
Their performance, excellent or poor, determined their commendation or punishment.
Once every three years, all the Imperial Physicians (Tàiyī) were tested.
Even if they were not students,
they were allowed to take the test for appointment.
Collated Notes
Treatise 33, Elections 2, Civil and Military Selection
According to the Jīn system,
both civil and military selections were administered by the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
From the ninth rank (cóng jiǔpǐn) to the seventh rank (cóng qīpǐn) of official posts,
the ministry made the recommendations.
For the seventh rank (zhèng qīpǐn) and above,
they were presented to the Secretariat (Shěng) for imperial appointment.
All successful candidates (jìnshì) were appointed as civil unranked officials (wénsànguān),
referred to as wénzīguān.
All others were military unranked officials (wǔsànguān),
referred to as yòuzhí,
or yòuxuǎn.
Among wénzī officials, jìnshì were superior;
among yòuzhí, those with military achievements were superior.
All followed a system of seniority (xúnzī),
with fixed rules for promotion and demotion that could not be transgressed.
For all appointments (quánzhù),
the official seeking appointment had to submit a detailed application (jiěyóu),
from which the key points of their reported performance, achievements, and qualifications were extracted as the "selection header" (quántóu),
to determine their suitability.
Those who had committed public or private crimes, embezzlement, or bribery (zāngzhī),
were deemed to have "violated the selection criteria" (fàn xuǎngé),
and even if an imperial pardon (ēn) was issued, they were not allowed to participate.
Under the old system,
those who were demoted by one rank up to four ranks (zhuī yī guān yǐ zhì zhuī sì guān),
were all dismissed from office for a full year (zhōunián),
and then reinstated.
In the second year of Chéng'ān (1197),
a new system was established:
for every rank demoted, they were delayed by one year (diàn yī nián).
All those dismissed from office who were covered by an amnesty (huì shè dāng zhě),
and those who were to be removed due to demotion and delay (jiàng diàn dāng chú zhě),
had their crimes fully reported for review (jù zuì yǐ wén),
before they could be reinstated.
Officials promoted to the sixth rank (liùpǐn) due to increased tax revenue (zēngkè)
were demoted upon completion of their term.
If officials promoted through integrity (liánshēng) differed in their performance when reappointed and re-examined,
they were also demoted upon completion of their term.
Apart from jìnshì, jǔrén, those with meritorious service (láoxiào), those entering service through imperial favor (yīnxí), and those benefiting from special grace (ēnlì),
there were still many other paths to officialdom,
and the times of their establishment varied.
For instance, those who entered officialdom through "Pái Yìn" (badge and seal), "Hùwèi" (imperial guards), and "Lìshǐ" (clerks)
were established during the Huángtǒng era.
Judicial reviewers (jiǎnfǎ), judicial administrators (zhīfǎ), and scribes of the Imperial Historiography Institute (Guóshǐyuàn shūxiě)
were established by Hǎilíng Shùrén.

As for princes' generals (zōngshì jiāngjūn), attendants in various palace bureaus (gōngzhōng zhū jú chéngyìng rén), prime ministerial scribes (zǎixiàng shūbiǎo), crown prince's guards (tàizǐ hùwèi), imperial consort's guards (fēi hùwèi), princely mansion attendants (wángfǔ zhīhòu lángjūn), eunuchs (nèishì), and sons of prime ministers, as well as interpreters (yìshǐ), translators (tōngshì), secretariat attendants (shěng zhīhòu lángjūn), and various positions in the imperial elite cavalry (qīnjūn xiāoqí zhū gé),
these were established during the time of Shìzōng,
and the Grand Court Reviewers (Tàicháng Jiǎntǎo) and Eunuch Sinecurists (Nèishì Jìlù Guān) established by Zhāngzōng,
all served as gateways to official careers.
For official ranks, thirty months constituted one evaluation (kǎo).
For officials holding substantive posts (zhíshìguān), thirty months constituted a full term (mǎn) for each appointment.
For commanders of multiple herds (qúnmùshǐ) and tax collection officials (guǎn kègūan), three full years constituted a full term.

For defense commissioners (fángyùshǐ), forty months; for officials of the third rank (sānpǐn) and above, fifty months; and for transport commissioners (zhuǎnyùn), sixty months constituted a full term.
Officials in the Bureau of Astronomy (Sītiān), Imperial Medical Bureau (Tàiyī), and Eunuch Bureau (Nèishì) all stopped at the fourth rank (sìpǐn).
Officials serving in external posts by seniority (xúnzī guān) were called "regularly adjusted" (chángdiào).
Those selected as court officials were called "attending court" (suícháo).
Attending court officials were promoted one grade in their substantive post (zhíshì yī děng) at each evaluation.
Those promoted through integrity and scrutiny (liánchá) were called "integrity promotions" (liánshēng).
Those appointed to border prefectures and counties in the northeast and subsequently promoted were called "border promotions" (biānshēng).
All directors, supervisors, and appointees to various bureaus (yuànwù jiāndāng chāishǐ) were equivalent to the ninth rank (cóng jiǔpǐn).

All ranked officials (pǐnguān) serving as Directors (Dūshì), Clerks (Diǎnshì), Administrators (Zhǔshì), Managers (Zhīshì), and clerks (lìshǐ) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng), Investigators (Fùshí), Archivists (Jiàgé Sī Guǎngōu), directors and deputy directors of various provincial and bureau offices (zhíshěng zhí yuàn jú zhǎngfù), Judicial reviewers (jiǎnfǎ), judicial administrators (zhīfǎ), bureau directors and supervisors (yuànwù jiāndāng chāishǐ), as well as various clerks (zhū lìshǐ), interpreters (yìshǐ), scribes (zhǎngshū), historians (shūshǐ), clerks (shūlì), translators (yìshū), interpreters (yìrén), communicators (tōngshì), and those with official backgrounds serving in various bureau divisions (zhū jú fēn chéngyìng yǒu chūshēn zhě) were all considered "unranked officials" (liúwài zhí).
All these positions
were either appointed by the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng),
or assigned by their respective departments (běn sī pàn bǔ).
Their official positions, whether regular (zhèngbān) or miscellaneous (zábān),
all had specific names and duties.
Once appointed, they had to follow the fixed rules of promotion and demotion.
Although there might have been slight gains or losses at different times,
the established system could not be altered.
Regarding the system of hereditary privilege (ményīn),
during the Tiānjuàn era,
officials from the first to eighth rank (yīpǐn zhì bāpǐn) had no limit on the number of people they could recommend for yin.
In the second year of Zhēnyuán (1154),
the yin law was established:
officials from the first to seventh rank (yīpǐn zhì qīpǐn) were limited in number,
and the system of yin for eighth-rank officials was abolished.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Dàdìng (1164) of Shìzōng,
an edict stated:
"For imperial relatives who are above the 'tǎnmǐan' (first mourning grade) status,
those seeking yin should be tested according to the regulations.
Those who pass the selection should not be assigned to rotate duties (dāng bào shǐ)."
In the tenth month of the fifth year (1165),
a decree stated:
"For officials of the fallen Sòng dynasty whose descendants are eligible for yin,
they shall be treated the same as officials of the fallen Liáo dynasty in terms of yin."
It also said:
"People from the Imperial Music Bureau (jiàofāng),
if they hold ranked official positions (liúnèi zhí),
they shall be treated the same as civil and military officials in terms of yin.
For others with meritorious service,
only rewards and gifts should be given.
During the Zhènglóng era, it was common to appoint people from the jiàofāng to govern cities and oversee the populace (diǎn chéng mù mín),
which I strongly disapprove of."
Furthermore, regulations for punishment and reward regarding fraudulent yin (màoyīn) and officials who accepted yin (qǔyīn guān) were revised.
In the fifth month of the seventh year (1167),
it was ordered that officials of the Bureau of Astronomy (Sītiāntái) of the fourth rank and above, who were reassigned to civil or military ranks (gǎishòu wénwǔzī zhě),
were all allowed to grant yin according to the Imperial Physician (Tàiyī) precedent.
The system stipulated that
regular officials (zhèngbān) could grant yin to regular officials,
and miscellaneous officials (zábān) to miscellaneous officials.
In the first year of Míngchāng (1190),
those who submitted memorials requested an additional yin for sixth-rank officials.
The Ministry of Personnel stated:
"During the Tiānjuàn era,
eighth-rank officials could grant yin,
with no limit on the number of people.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
seventh-rank officials could grant yin,
but the number was limited.
At that time,
civil officials began from Jiāngshì,
and military officials from Jìnyì.
Up to the seventh-rank Rúlín and Zhōngxiǎn,
each had seven grades,
and were allowed to grant yin to one person.
Up to the sixth-rank Chéngzhí and Zhāoxìn,
which totaled nine grades,
they were allowed to grant yin to two people.
From the fourteenth year of Dàdìng (1174),
civil and military officials each increased by two grades from the lowest rank.
The seventh-rank was regarded as nine grades compared to the old system,
and still allowed one yin.
Up to the fifth-rank, there were seventeen grades in total,
and then they were allowed two yin.
From the fifth-rank to the third-rank, there was no gap (jiānyuè),
only the sixth-rank did not use yin.
We request to follow the old regulations:
officials of the fifth-rank and above grant one additional yin,
sixth-rank officials grant yin to two children, grandchildren, siblings, or nephews,
and the seventh-rank remains as per the old regulations."
At that time, it was also considered that although the old regulations allowed for granting yin to brothers and nephews even if one had a son (jǐzǐ xǔyīn dìxiōng zhí),
which was to promote filial piety and brotherly love,
the new regulations prohibited it.
Thus, the allowance for transferring yin (ràngyīn) was permitted.
Under the old system,
officials of the Bureau of Astronomy (Sītiān), Imperial Medical Bureau (Tàiyī), Eunuch Bureau (Nèishì), and long-serving personnel (chángxíng), even if they reached the fourth rank (sìpǐn),
were not allowed to grant yin unless by special grace they were reassigned to civil or military official ranks (tèēn huànshòu wénwǔguānzī zhě),
because their current positions were for attendance and service (jiànchōng chéngyìng),
making it difficult to categorize them into regular ranks (nánshǐ xìbān).
In the second year of Tàihé (1202),
a new system was established:
for those who retired at sixty years or older, or those suffering from illness or who had died,
even if they reached the highest position in their category (zhǐguān),
it was proposed to categorize them into regular ranks.
Except for those who continued to practice their original profession, they were allowed to grant yin to one person.
If they had only one son, that son did not need to practice the profession to receive yin immediately.
For all types of civil and military officials of the first rank (yīpǐn),
they could grant yin to six persons among their descendants (from sons to great-grandsons) and brothers and nephews.
If through hereditary privilege (yīn ményīn), then five persons.
For the second rank (èrpǐn), five persons among their descendants (from sons to great-grandsons) and brothers and nephews.
If through hereditary privilege, then four persons.
For the third rank (sānpǐn), four persons among their sons, brothers, and nephews.
If through hereditary privilege, then three persons.
For the fourth (sìpǐn) and fifth ranks (wǔpǐn), three persons.
If through hereditary privilege, then two persons.
For the sixth rank (liùpǐn), two persons.
For the seventh rank (qīpǐn), one person among their sons and brothers.
If through hereditary privilege, then for the sixth and seventh ranks, one person among their sons and brothers.
According to the old regulations,
hereditary privilege was limited to one person for the seventh rank,
and an additional person for all others.
According to the Míngchāng regulations,
from the fifth rank upwards, one additional person was added for all.
For officials who gained office through contributions (jìnnà guān),
the old regulations allowed regular officials (zhèngbān) of the third rank to grant yin to four persons,
and miscellaneous officials (zábān) to three persons.
For regular military officials (zhèngbān wǔlüè), one son or brother.
For miscellaneous military officials (zábān míngwēi), one person.
For Huáiyuǎn and above, two persons.
For Zhèngguó and above, three persons.

Officials of the Bureau of Astronomy (Sītiān) and Imperial Medical Bureau (Tàiyī) who were promoted to the fourth rank and imperial edict converted to civil or military officials (zhàohuàn wénwǔguān zhě),
could grant yin to one person.
All the ranks that a *Jìnshì* passed through,
and the offices to which they were appointed.
In *Zhēnyuán* first year (1153),
the Southern Selection system was established.
Initially, they were appointed as *Jūnpàn*, *Chéng*, or *Bù*.
(From rank eight.)
Next, they were appointed as *Fángpàn* or *Lùshì*.
(Rank eight.)
Third, they were appointed as *Xiàlìng*.
(From rank seven.)
Fourth, *Zhōnglìng*, *Tuīguān*, or *Jiécá Pàn*.
(Rank seven.)
Fifth and sixth, all *Shànglìng*.
(From rank six.)
For the Northern Selection,
initially *Jūnpàn*, *Bù*, or *Wèi*.
Second, *Xiàlìng*.
Third, *Zhōnglìng*.
Fourth, *Shànglìng*.
Thereafter, all *Shànglìng*.
They were also appointed as *Jiécá Pàn* or *Tuīguān*.
According to the regulations of *Zhènglóng* first year (1156),
those in the Upper Class were initially appointed as *Shàngbù Jūnpàn*, *Chéng*, *Bù*, or *Wèi*.
Those in the Middle Class were initially appointed as *Zhōngbù Jūnpàn*, *Chéng*, *Bù*, or *Wèi*.
Those in the Lower Class were initially appointed as *Xiàbù Jūnpàn*, *Chéng*, *Bù*, or *Wèi*.
For the second appointment, all were *Zhōngbù Jūnpàn*, *Chéng*, *Bù*, or *Wèi*.
For the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh appointments, all were *Xiànlìng*,
and then reported to the *Shěng*.
In *Dàdìng* second year (1162),
an imperial edict stated that civil officials should not be appointed as *Xiànwèi*.
According to the regulations of the eighth year (1168),
after serving five terms as *Lìng*, they were to be reported to the *Shěng*.
In the thirteenth year (1173),
it was decreed that the second appointment could be provisionally made as *Xiàlìng*.
According to the old system,
the *Zhuàngyuán* was granted the title of *Chéngdéláng*.
Based on the official system of the fourteenth year (1174),
both civil and military officials were to have two additional ranks added from below.
The *Zhuàngyuán* was then granted the title of *Chéngwùláng*.
Those previously granted *Rúlínláng*
were changed to *Chéngshìláng*.
Those in the second class and below, who were previously granted *Cóngshìláng*,
were changed to *Jiāngshìláng*.
In the fifteenth year (1175),
it was ordered that the *Zhuàngyuán* be appointed as *Yìngfèng*.
After two evaluations, they were granted a rank six position according to custom.
In the eighteenth year (1178),
it was ordered that if the *Zhuàngyuán* did not live up to their reputation, they would be appointed to an external post.
In the nineteenth year (1179),
it was ordered that their conduct, good or bad, be investigated by their native place.
In the twenty-first year (1181),
it was again ordered that the third appointment be as *Xiànlìng*.
In the twenty-second year (1182),
it was ordered that after *Jìnshì* received their official robes,
they should be re-tested with one policy question on current affairs,
which was called the "policy examination" (*Cèshì*).
Those whose talent and insight were deemed commendable had their names recorded.
Their governance was to be observed after they had served their terms.
If their words and actions matched, they would be promoted and employed.
In the ninth month of that year,
it was again decreed that henceforth, *Jídǐ* recipients
who excelled in the policy examination would be promoted immediately upon their first appointment.
According to the regulations of the twenty-third year (1183),
for *Jìnshì*:
Upper Class:
first, *Lùshì* or *Fángpàn*;
second, *Xiàlìng*;
third, *Zhōnglìng*.
Middle Class:
first, *Zhōngbù*;
second, *Shàngbù*;
third, *Xiàlìng*.
Lower Class:
first, *Xiàbù*;
second, *Zhōngbù*;
third, *Xiàlìng*.
For those who passed the policy examination:
Upper Class:
first, *Lùshì* or *Fángpàn*;
second, *Zhōnglìng*;
third, *Shànglìng*.
Middle Class:
first, *Shàngbù*;
second, *Xiàlìng*;
third, *Zhōnglìng*.
Lower Class:
first, *Zhōngbù*;
second, *Lùshì* or *Fángpàn*;
third, *Zhōnglìng*.
It was also decreed that henceforth the *Zhuàngyuán* would be appointed as *Yìngfèng*.
If, after one year, their writings were not exceptional, they would be appointed to an external post.
According to the regulations of the twenty-sixth year (1186),
one term of service was reduced for those who were successively eligible for *Lìng*.
According to the regulations of the twenty-sixth year (1186),
those whose ranks were lowered thrice or twice would have one lowering exempted.
Civil officials in external posts with a *yòuzhí* (right office) would have their last post reduced.
After one term as *Shànglìng* and a total of five terms, they would be reported to the *Shěng*.
Thus, the regulations were finalized:
Upper Class:
first, *Lùshì* or *Fángpàn*;
second, *Zhōnglìng*;
third, fourth, and fifth, *Shànglìng*.
Middle Class:
first, *Zhōngbù*;
second, *Xiàlìng*;
third, *Zhōnglìng*;
fourth and fifth, *Shànglìng*.
For *Jìnshì* who passed the policy examination:
first, *Lùshì* or *Fángpàn*;
second, third, fourth, and fifth, *Shànglìng*.
Next category:
first, *Shàngbù*;
second, *Zhōnglìng*;
third, fourth, and fifth, *Shànglìng*.
Next category:
first, *Zhōngbù*;
second, *Xiàlìng*;
third, *Zhōnglìng*;
fourth and fifth, *Shànglìng*.
Lower Class:
first, *Xiàbù*;
second, *Xiàlìng*;
third, *Zhōnglìng*;
fourth and fifth, *Shànglìng*.
In the twenty-seventh year (1187),
it was decreed that *Jìnshì* whose rank reached *Zhōngdàfū* should be reported to the *Shěng*.
In *Míngchāng* second year (1191),
the system of investigating the *Zhuàngyuán*'s conduct was abolished.
According to the regulations of the seventh year (1196),
all *Xiànlìng* and *Shǒujué* (acting officials) were to be appointed according to the old regulations.
According to the *Tàihé* regulations,
all *Jìnshì* who passed the examination and were to be granted qualifications and appointments must complete all required terms before being reported to the *Shěng*.
Even if they had not completed all terms,
if their rank had already reached *Zhōngdàfū*, they were also to be reported to the *Shěng*.
Furthermore, for *Cífù* (rhyme-prose) and *Jīngyì* (classical interpretation) *Jìnshì* who passed the examination,
and were selected in the policy examination,
they must complete all required terms before being reported to the *Shěng*.
Moreover, for each appointment, they would be promoted to the head of their respective selection pool.
In *Zhēnyòu* third year (1215),
the *Zhuàngyuán* was granted *Fèngzhídàfū*.
The Upper Class was granted *Rúlínláng*.
The Middle Class and below were granted *Zhēngshìláng*.
*Jīngyì Jìnshì*.
In *Huángtǒng* eighth year (1148),
appointments were made in *Yānjīng*.
In the sixth year (of *Zhènglóng*, 1161),
the top candidate for *Cífù* and *Jīngyì* were both to be appointed as *Xiànlìng*.
The second candidate was to be appointed as *Chápàn*,
but as there were no vacancies, they were provisionally appointed as *Jūnpàn*.
The second and third classes were provisionally appointed as *Jūnpàn*, *Chéng*, or *Bù* according to their place of residence.
According to the old system,
those who passed the Five Classics examination and had not yet served ten years were assigned to internal duties (within the passes).
Those who had served ten years were assigned to external duties (outside the passes).
After forty years, they were appointed as *Xiàlìng*.
In *Zhènglóng* third year (1158),
no assignments were given.
After thirty years, they would be appointed as *Xiànlìng*.
In *Dàdìng* twenty-eighth year (1188), this branch of examination was re-established,
with each examination specializing in one classic.
*Nǚzhí Jìnshì*.
In *Dàdìng* thirteenth year (1173),
all were appointed as *Jiàoshòu*.
In the twenty-second year (1182),
the second and third candidates of the Upper Class were initially appointed as *Shàngbù*.
The Middle Class were appointed as *Zhōngbù*.
The Lower Class were appointed as *Xiàbù*.
In *Dàdìng* twenty-fifth year (1185),
the top candidate of the Upper Class was promoted four ranks.
The rest were each promoted two ranks.
The second and third classes were appointed as *Suílù Jiàoshòu*.
Thirty months constituted one term.
The second term was appointed to rank nine.
The third and fourth terms were appointed as *Lùshì* or *Jūnfáng Pàn*.
The fifth term was *Xiàlìng*.
Soon after, it was again ordered that the fourth term be appointed as *Xiànlìng*.
In the twenty-sixth year (1186),
one term of service was reduced for appointment as *Xiànlìng*.
In the twenty-eighth year (1188),
an essay (*lùn*) examination was added.
Thereafter, all followed the Han regulations.
*Hóngcí* (erudite scholars):
the highest class was promoted two ranks.
The next class was promoted one rank.
They were appointed by imperial decree at the time.
*Ēnbǎng* (Benevolent Roster):
In *Zhāngzōng* *Dàdìng* twenty-ninth year (1189),
it was decreed that henceforth, any *Jìnshì* who had sat for the imperial examination five times
would be allowed to take one more examination without being dismissed.
Their ranking would be determined solely by the quality of their writing.
This was called *Ēnbǎng*.
Nǚzhí people were promoted to *Jiāngshì*.
Han people were promoted to *Dēngshì*.
The initial appointment was *Jiàoshòu*.
After serving thirty months, they were appointed according to the standard regulations from rank nine.
In Míngchāng元年 (1190),
an imperial edict stipulated that those who passed the imperial examination
after four attempts would be granted the same special privilege as those passing after five attempts,
allowing them to proceed directly to the imperial examination.
In Míngchāng五年 (1194),
an imperial edict decreed that child prodigies who passed the final examination three times
would be treated the same as *Jìnshì* on the honor roll for promotions and transfers.
Those who passed the final examination twice
were completely exempted from assigned duties.
In their sixth appointment, they would be made county magistrates (*xiànlìng*),
and their promotions would follow standard regulations.
If one passed the final examination only once,
upon first entering officialdom, they would receive one appointment and one assignment.
For the rest, they would follow their original lineage,
still required to take the examination three times,
before entering officialdom.
Forty people were selected in each examination.
Those who received special privilege appointments or *yìn* (hereditary privilege) equivalent to *Jìnshì*
referred to special favors such as appointments upon retirement from grand ceremonies, posthumous memorials, or death in battle,
appointments through hereditary succession,
and those who married princesses or women of the imperial clan.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng二年 (1157),
the first appointment was *xiàbù*,
the second *zhōngbù*,
the third *shàngbù*,
the fourth *xiàlìng*,
the fifth *zhōnglìng*,
the sixth and seventh *shànglìng*,
after which a report was presented to the secretariat (*shěng*).
Those specially granted the title of *Tóng Jìnshì*
referred to individuals who contributed grain, returned from missions abroad, or died in royal service, and similar cases.
All these were treated as miscellaneous officials,
and their *yìn* appointments were also as miscellaneous officials.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng元年 (1156),
the first appointment was *xiàbù*,
the second *zhōngbù*,
the third *xiànchéng*,
the fourth *jūnpàn*,
the fifth and sixth *fángpàn*,
the seventh and eighth *xiàlìng*,
the ninth *zhōnglìng*,
the tenth *shànglìng*.
Later, it was revised again: the first appointment was to a lower-grade *jūnpàn*, *chéng*, *bù*, or *wèi*;
the next was to a middle-grade *jūnpàn*, *chéng*, *bù*, or *wèi*;
the third was to an upper-grade *jūnpàn*, *chéng*, *bù*, or *wèi*;
the fourth *xiàlìng*,
the fifth *zhōnglìng*,
the sixth *shànglìng*.
For the law and classical examinations.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng元年 (1156),
the first appointment was *Jiāngshìláng*,
all serving as *sīhòu*.
After ten years or more, one would receive one appointment and one assignment;
if less than ten years, the first appointment would be *zhǔbù*,
the second *sīhòu*,
the third *zhǔbù*,
the fourth *zhǔbù*,
the fifth *jǐngpàn*,
the sixth *shìchéng*,
the seventh *zhūxiànchéng*,
the eighth *cìchìchéng*,
the ninth *chìxiànchéng*,
the tenth *xiàxiànlìng*,
the eleventh *zhōngxiànlìng*,
the fifth *shàngxiànlìng* (referring to the fifth appointment as *xiànlìng* or the fifth stage after becoming *xiànlìng*),
and then reported to the secretariat (*shěng*).
According to the three-year system,
those who passed the law examination or had served seven years were assigned duties within the passes (*guānnèi*);
those who had served more than seven years were assigned duties outside the passes (*guānwài*).
Those who passed the classical examinations but had not yet served ten years were assigned duties within the passes;
those who had served ten years were assigned duties outside the passes.
Those from the law examination were appointed *xiàlìng* after forty years.
Child prodigies who passed the examinations would have their service period extended by ten years compared to others
before their months and days were calculated.
In Dàdìng十四年 (1174),
with the addition of new official ranks from the lower levels,
a system was established:
those who passed the law examination were appointed *Jiāngshì Zuǒláng*.
In the sixteenth year (1176), by special imperial decree,
considering that forty years for appointment as *xiàlìng* was too long,
those who had served thirty-two years without committing corruption were appointed *xiàlìng*.
In the seventeenth year (1177),
an imperial edict exempted all those from various examinations who reached the rank of *xiàlìng* from duties.
In the twentieth year (1180),
the secretariat proposed that
those without corruption and deemed blameless by inspectors would have their term reduced to twenty-nine years for appointment as *xiàlìng*.
The same applied to child prodigies.
In the twenty-sixth year (1186),
the secretariat proposed that
those who were next in line to become county magistrates (*xiànlìng*) would have one qualification reduced for selection and appointment.
An imperial edict stipulated that for people of various examinations, when the cumulative months and days of their successive appointments reached forty-two months,
it would be counted as one appointment and one assignment.
Another imperial edict stated that
the old regulation of presenting a report to the secretariat after six appointments as county magistrate
was reduced to five appointments.
In the twenty-eighth year (1188),
the term for *chìxiànchéng* was reduced by one appointment.
In Míngchāng五年 (1194),
a system was established that those who had served for twenty-six years or more,
if eligible for promotion based on integrity, would be appointed *xiànlìng*.
In the sixth year (1195),
after two terms as *zhūxiànchéng* and *chìxiànchéng*, the official regulation was reduced;
within ten years, they would be proposed for assignment;
after ten years, they would receive one appointment and one assignment.
If one served for eight terms or reached thirty-two years and was appointed *xiàlìng*,
they would be exempted from assignments but required to serve through all ranks before reporting to the secretariat.
The ranks served were:
first and second *xiàbù*,
third and fourth *zhōngbù*,
fifth, sixth, and seventh *shàngbù*.
Those who violated selection regulations would serve two more terms as *shàngbù*.
Eighth and ninth would be appointed *xiàlìng*,
tenth *zhōnglìng*,
eleventh and twelfth *shànglìng*.
For military examinations,
according to the regulations of Tàihé三年 (1203),
the first place in the upper category was promoted to *Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi*;
the second and third places were promoted to *Zhōngyì Xiàowèi*.
Those in the middle category were promoted to *Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi*,
and enrolled into the imperial guard (*qīnjūn*).
Regardless of whether they had *yìn* privilege,
their appointment would be hundred months sooner than the old regulations.
Those in the lower category were promoted to *Dūnwǔ Xiàowèi*,
also enrolled into the imperial guard,
and their appointment would be fifty months sooner.
According to the regulations of Chéng'ān元年 (1196),
the positions held by the first-place winner were:
first, *Dūxún* or *Fùjiàng*;
second, *xiàlìng*;
third, *zhōnglìng*;
fourth and fifth, *shànglìng*.
For the second and third place winners:
first, *Xúnwèi* or *Bùjiàng*;
second, *shàngbù*;
third, *xiàlìng*;
fourth, *zhōnglìng*;
fifth and sixth, *shànglìng*.
For other candidates:
first, *Fùxún* or *Jūnhé*;
second, *zhōngbù*;
third, *xiàlìng*;
fourth, *zhōnglìng*;
fifth and sixth, *shànglìng*.
There were six types of military merits:
first, engaging in battle in open fields,
leading the charge,
and routing enemy forces.
Second, attacking and capturing resistant prefectures, counties, or mountain strongholds,
and seizing enemy watchtowers.
Third, contending for ships or bridges,
and being the first to cross dangerous terrain.
Fourth, venturing far to capture enemy informants.
Fifth, successfully reporting critical information from a distant place
during dangerous and difficult situations.
Sixth, successfully executing a strategy,
and distinguishing oneself beyond others.
According to the regulations of Huángtǒng八年 (1148),
for those holding an official title of *Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi* (rank 7a) or higher:
the first appointment was *zhǔbù* or *zhūsī fùshǐ*
(rank 9a);
the second *zhǔbù* or *zhūsī shǐ*
(rank 8a);
the third *xiàlìng*
(rank 7b);
the fourth *zhōnglìng*
(rank 7a);
the fifth *shànglìng*,
or a general appointment as *Zhèn Jūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ* (rank 7a) or *zhèngjiàng*.
For those whose official title did not reach *Zhāoxìn* or who had no title:
from the first to third appointments, they were generally appointed *chéng* or *bù*;
the fourth *xiàlìng*;
the fifth *zhōnglìng*;
the sixth *shànglìng* or *zhīchéngzhài*
(rank 7b).
In Dàdìng二十九年 (1189) of Zhāngzōng's reign,
after those promoted to *Zhènguó* received imperial approval for their promotions and removals,
the established official regulations were:
for Jurchens holding *Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi* or higher,
the first was *xiàbù*,
the second *xiàlìng*,
the third *zhōnglìng*,
the fourth and fifth *shànglìng*.
For Jurchens whose first appointment reached *Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi*, and others whose appointment already reached *Zhāoxìn* or higher,
the first was *xiàbù*,
the second *zhōngbù*,
the third *xiàlìng*,
the fourth *zhōnglìng*,
the fifth and sixth *shànglìng*.
For those who reached *Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn* or higher,
the first was *xiàlìng*,
the second *zhōnglìng*,
the third and fourth *shànglìng*.
As for rewarding meritorious service,
(this refers to old *qiānhù* and *móukè*.)
In the fifth year of Dàdìng (1165),
regulations were established for the Hénán and Shǎnxī Commanderies-in-Chief.
A *qiānhù* with forty or more years of service was to be considered for an office of nominal rank seven (従七品).
A *qiānhù* with thirty years of service, or a *móukè* with forty or more years of service, was to be granted an office of nominal rank eight (従八品).
A *qiānhù* with twenty or more years of service, or a *móukè* with thirty or more years of service, was to be granted an office of nominal rank nine (従九品).
A *móukè* with twenty or more years of service was to be given a regular post or a special assignment.
Those with ten or more years of service were to be rewarded with silver and silk.
All calculations of service were to be based on the cumulative months and days served as *qiānhù*, *móukè*, or *púliǎn*.
In the twentieth year of Dàdìng (1180),
it was decreed that those who had previously served as *jūnguǎn yāqiānhù*, *móukè*, or *púliǎn* for twenty or more years and were sixty-five years old upon retirement,
if found to be robust, would be given assignments or placed in regular posts;
otherwise, they would be granted promotions or rewards in proportion to their service.
Later, the official regulations were further amended.
If one received a single promotion to *Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn* (宣武將軍) or higher,
and was eligible for an office of nominal rank seven,
the first order would grant a lower rank position,
the second a middle rank position,
and the third and fourth, a higher rank position.
If one did not attain *Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn*,
those initially appointed to rank eight were made *lùshì* (錄事).
The second appointment was *chìjùchéng* (赤劇丞).
The third was a lower rank position,
the fourth a middle rank position,
and the fifth and sixth, a higher rank position.
For those initially appointed to rank nine,
the first appointment was *xiàbù* (下簿).
The second was *zhōngbù* (中簿).
The third was *shàngbù* (上簿).
The fourth was a lower rank position,
the fifth a middle rank position,
and the sixth and seventh, a higher rank position.
According to the regulations of the ninth year of Dàdìng (1169),
three *yúhòu Shùndé Jūn qiānhù* (虞候順德軍千戶) with forty or more years of service were granted nominal rank eight.
A *qiānhù* with thirty years of service, or a *móukè* with forty or more years of service, was granted nominal rank nine.
A *qiānhù* with twenty or more years of service, or a *móukè* with thirty or more years of service, was granted a regular post.
Those below these categories were rewarded with silver and silk.
In the fourteenth year of Dàdìng (1174),
it was decreed that when provincial military officers were assigned outside their regular posts,
according to the new system, two higher ranks would be added from the bottom.
Those previously promoted to *Zhōngwǔ Xiàowèi* (忠武校尉) would now be promoted to *Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi* (忠勇校尉).
When the *Zhōngdū Yǒnggù Jūn Zhǐhuīshǐ* (中都永固軍指揮使) and the provincial *sǎobīng zhǐhuīshǐ* (埽兵指揮使) were assigned outside their regular posts,
those previously promoted to *Dūnwǔ Xiàowèi* (敦武校尉) would now be promoted to *Jìnyì Xiàowèi* (進義校尉).
For the Wǔwèi Army,
regulations were set in the seventeenth year of Dàdìng (1177).
Their *méng'ān* (猛安) was called *dūjiāng* (都將),
their *móukè* was called *zhōngwèi* (中尉),
and their *púliǎn* was called *duìzhèng* (隊正).
A *dūjiāng* was promoted one rank every thirty months,
reaching *Zhāoxìn* (昭信) with an office of rank nine.
A *duìzhèng* was promoted to *zhōngwèi*,
and a *zhōngwèi* to *dūjiāng*.
There were four avenues for selecting *shěnglìshǐ* (省令史):
civilian appointments,
Jurchen *jìnshì*,
officials in the right department,
and sons of grand councilors.
The system for their entry into service varied.
For civilian appointees,
