previously only officials of the Left Department were allowed to recommend them.
However, in the eighth year of Huángtǒng (1148) during Xīzōng's reign,
a provincial minister observed that
if the old practice of recommendation was strictly followed,
over time, it would lead to a lack of distinction between the good and the bad, and many would rely on luck.
Therefore, a new system was proposed and established:
from the second year of Tiānjuàn (1139), those whose names appeared on the *jìdì* (及第) examination roster
were to be selected in sequence by roster order, up to fifty years of age or older, with official ranks from *Chéngzhí Láng* (承直郎) (nominal rank six
) to *Fèngdé Dàfū* (奉德大夫) (nominal rank five
), and who had no public or private transgressions.
For each vacant position, two candidates would be selected for trial.
If found suitable, they would be appointed.
If all were suitable, their names would be registered, and they would return to their original posts to await appointment.
For officials who had reached *Chéngzhí Láng* or above,
one evaluation would result in appointment to an office of actual rank seven (正七品) or above, but nominal rank six (従六品) or below.
Two evaluations would result in appointment to an office of nominal rank six or above, but nominal rank five (従五品) or below.
For *Fèngzhí Dàfū* (奉直大夫) (nominal rank six
) or above,
one evaluation would result in appointment to an office of nominal rank six or above, but nominal rank five or below.
Two evaluations would result in appointment to an office of nominal rank five or above, but actual rank five (正五品) or below.
This applied similarly to *jiéyùn* (節運).
In the first year of Zhènglóng (1156),
this system was abolished,
and selection was limited to scribes and clerks within the Privy Council (Mìyuàn), Censorate (Tái), and Six Ministries (Liù Bù).
In the first year of Dàdìng (1161),
Shìzōng believed that the clerks were corrupt,
and entrusting them with provincial affairs meant they lacked a broad perspective,
causing excessive disturbance.
By the second year (1162),
the system of employing clerks was abolished, and the system of selecting *jìnshì* from Huángtǒng was reinstated.
For those who were *Chéngzhí Láng* or above,
one evaluation would result in an actual rank seven position,
appointed as *yùnpàn* (運判),
*jiéchápàn* (節察判), or *jūncì tóngzhī* (軍刺同知).
Two evaluations would result in a nominal rank six position,
appointed as *jīngyùnpàn* (京運判), *zǒngfǔpàn* (總府判), or *fángyù tóngzhī* (防禦同知).
For *Fèngzhí Dàfū* or above,
one evaluation would result in a nominal rank six position,
appointed as before.
Two evaluations would result in a nominal rank five position,
appointed as *jiéyùn fù* (節運副) or *jīngzǒngguǎnfǔ liúshǒusī pànguān* (京總管府留守司判官).
In the seventh year (1167),
officials with *sǎnjiē* (散階) up to rank five were also to be selected for this duty,
but those unwilling were excused.
In the eleventh year (1171),
as many *jìnshì* officials had reached *Chéngzhí* (承直),
selection was based solely on the roster order, regardless of official rank.
In the twenty-seventh year (1187),
due to many vacant official posts in the provinces,
some argued that the restriction of rank and evaluation made promotion difficult.
Therefore, it was decreed that official rank would not be considered.
Anyone with one evaluation was granted rank six.
The next appointment would be a demotion to actual rank seven.
The third appointment would be rank six.
The fourth appointment would be promoted to nominal rank five.
Those with two evaluations were granted nominal rank five.
The next appointment would be a demotion to rank six.
The third and fourth appointments would both be nominal rank five.
The fifth appointment would be promoted to actual rank five.
In the second year of Chéng'ān (1197),

for those in charge of learning and dismissal (*xíxué zhīchú* 習學知除), those in charge of criminal cases (*xíngfáng zhī'àn* 刑房知案), and border pass scribes during wartime (*bīngxīng shí biānguān lìshǐ* 兵興時邊關令史),
they would be appointed to positions at court after thirty months.
In the eighth year of Tàihé (1208), those who had been *xíxué zhīchú* for fifteen months or more
were selected as regular *zhīchú* (知除),
and their qualifications would be assessed after one evaluation.
In the third year of Dà'ān (1211),
because following the roster order resulted in uneven service durations for individuals,
the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù) and other departments were to rank them by their cumulative years and months of service,
and appoint them as *zhīchú*.
After completing their evaluation, they would be appointed to court positions.
In the fifth year of Zhēnyòu (1217),
even *jìnshì* who had not yet held office were allowed to be appointed.
Those with one evaluation were appointed as magistrates of superior counties (*shàngxiàn lìng* 上縣令).
Upon their second appointment as *shàngxiàn lìng*, they would be promoted to actual rank seven.
If they had already served one term as *chéngbù* (丞簿),
the old system would appoint them to rank six,
but this was changed to actual rank seven.
After one term, they would be demoted to nominal rank seven.
Upon their second appointment, they would be promoted from actual rank seven to rank six.
If they had served two terms as *chéngbù*,
one evaluation would previously result in rank six,
but this was changed to actual rank seven.
After one term, they would be exempted from demotion.
After another exemption from demotion, as actual rank seven for one term,
they would then be promoted to rank six.
Those who had served one term as *lìng* (令)
would, according to the old regulations, be rank six.
Upon their second appointment, they would be demoted to rank seven,
then promoted back to nominal rank five.
In the second year of Xīngdìng (1218),
it was decreed that those in their initial term who had not completed it, or those who had not yet held office,
upon completing their evaluation, would be promoted two ranks to nominal rank seven.
Those in their initial term who had not completed it, after two terms; and those who had not yet held office, after four terms, would be promoted back to actual rank seven.
Both who served two terms as actual rank seven would be exempted from demotion.
Those selected not by roster order were promoted and dismissed along with court officials.
They would be allowed to be appointed again when their turn on the roster arrived.
In the fifth year of Xīngdìng (1221),
it was decreed that *jìnshì* scribes and *yòuzhí* (右職) scribes would be subject to the same regulations.
Those who, upon completing their evaluation, were not yet eligible for nominal rank seven, would be granted actual rank seven.
After one term, they would be demoted to nominal rank seven.
Scribes selected for various prefectures who did not complete three evaluations before being assigned outside their regular posts would be appointed to nominal rank seven.
After one term, they would be demoted to rank eight.
If one was eligible for nominal rank seven after one term, they would be appointed to rank six.
After one term, they would be demoted to actual rank seven.
If one was eligible for actual rank seven after one term, they would be exempted from demotion.
For Jurchen *jìnshì* scribes,
according to the regulations of the twenty-seventh year (1187),
one evaluation would result in actual rank seven.
Two evaluations would result in actual rank six.
In the twenty-eighth year (1188),
it was decreed that officials transferred from the Privy Council (Shūmìyuàn) and other departments to the provincial government (shěng)
must all be *jìnshì*.
In the first year of Míngchāng (1190),
it was decreed that those with three evaluations would be appointed to the same positions as Han Chinese with two evaluations.
In the third year of Míngchāng (1192),
Khitan scribes were abolished.
Five Jurchen scribes were added to the vacant positions.
In the fifth year (1194),
considering that the hardships endured by Jurchen *jìnshì* scribes were the same as those of Han *jìnshì* scribes,
and their qualifications should not be differentiated,
it was decided that Jurchen *jìnshì* with one evaluation would be granted nominal rank six,
and with two evaluations, nominal rank five.
Sāi Zhí zǐdì Shěng Lìngshǐ (Secretaries of the Secretariat from the sons and younger brothers of the Grand Councillors)
In Dàdìng twelfth year
an edict was issued that all those
who inherited positions should present themselves to the Secretariat for an audience.
Except for those appointed by special imperial grace,
all were to be received into the inner official ranks.

They were to be assigned to the Guóshǐ Yuàn (Bureau of National History) as scribes, to the Tàicháng Shǔ (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) for review, to the Mìshū Jiān (Imperial Library) for collation, and
Every thirty months they would be promoted one rank,
and after one hundred and fifty months they would be appointed to an official post.
If they had completed one evaluation or more,
to the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) to await assignments.
in which case they would be appointed to an official post after one hundred and twenty months.
Their accumulated months and days would not be discounted.
If they were successful candidates in the final imperial examinations,
they would be directly allowed to take an examination for appointment by the Shàngshū Shěng.
In the seventeenth year,
a regulation was established
that sons of officials holding third-rank functional posts
could take an examination to be appointed as Lìngshǐ (secretaries) in the Shūmì Yuàn (Bureau of Military Affairs).
Thereupon, the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel) was ordered to establish a regulation that
sons of Grand Councillors and princes of the imperial clan in the Secretariat,
if they wished to take the examination for Lìngyìshǐ (secretaries and interpreters),
could take it once a year.
Apart from those appointed after passing the Lìngyìshǐ examination,
princes of the imperial clan in mourning for five months or less (sīmá tǎnmǐan) could be admitted to the Shūmì Yuàn.
In Dàdìng twenty-eighth year,
an edict was issued that the second-degree collateral relatives of the imperial clan and sons of Grand Chancellors
would be appointed to posts equivalent to sixth rank,
while third-degree collateral relatives of the imperial clan and sons of executive officials
would be appointed to posts of regular seventh rank.
All these appointments would occur after one hundred and fifty months.
However, if they were existing officials already transferred to the Secretariat,
they would only be appointed to regular seventh rank after two evaluations.
In the twenty-ninth year,
fourth-degree collateral relatives were also permitted to take the examination for appointment.

Chapter Thirty-four: Elections Three: Right-Ranked Officials and Miscellaneous Selections
Right-ranked officials.
Shěng Lìngshǐ, Yìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters of the Secretariat).
According to the regulations of Huángtǒng eighth year,
after the first evaluation, they would be promoted one rank.
Apart from Jurchens who followed their own law,
other people who advanced in righteousness
would be promoted two ranks every thirty months,
and appointed to official posts after one hundred and twenty months,
excluding officials of regular sixth rank and below, and regular seventh rank and above.
In Zhènglóng second year,
this was changed to one promotion every fifty months.
After the first evaluation,
Jurchens would be promoted to Dūn Wǔ Xiàowèi (Valiant Military Commandant),
and others to Bǎo Yì Xiàowèi (Protector of Righteousness Commandant).
After one hundred and fifty months, they would be appointed to an official post,
which was a regular post of junior seventh rank.
If they were transferred to the Secretariat from the Shūmì Yuàn, Tái (Censorate), or Liùbù (Six Ministries),
their previous accumulated evaluation months would be counted towards their appointment to an official post.
In Dàdìng second year,
it was again stipulated that they would be promoted one rank every thirty months,
and also appointed to an official post after one hundred and twenty months,
with regular or junior seventh rank.
For those transferred to the Secretariat from the Yuàn (Bureau), Tái (Censorate), Liùbù (Six Ministries), or other Fǔ (Prefectures) or Sī (Departments) who had not yet completed an evaluation,
every three months would be counted as two months.
After one evaluation, they would receive junior seventh rank;
after two evaluations, regular seventh rank;
and after three evaluations, sixth rank.
In the third year,
regulations were established:
for those appointed to official posts after seventy-five months,
the first assignment was to senior Lìng (magistrate),
the second to middle Lìng,
the third to junior Lìng,
the fourth and fifth to Lùshì (Registrar),
the sixth to junior Lìng,
the seventh to middle Lìng,
the eighth to senior Lìng.
For those appointed to official posts after one hundred and fifty months,
the first assignment was to Cì Tóng, Yùnpàn, Tuīguān (Assistant Prefect, Judicial Commissioner, Judicial Officer), etc.
The second and third were to middle Lìng,
the fourth to senior Lìng,
then they would return and report to the Secretariat.
In Dàdìng twenty-seventh year,
an edict stipulated that those with one evaluation or who failed to complete an evaluation
would be appointed to junior seventh rank,
and had to serve three terms as Xiànlìng (County Magistrate).
In their fifth term, they would be promoted to regular seventh rank.
Those with two evaluations or more would be appointed to regular seventh rank,
and in their second term, they would be demoted and appointed as Xiànlìng.
In their third and fourth terms, they would all be regular seventh rank,
and in their fifth term, they would be promoted to sixth rank.
Those with three evaluations or more would be appointed to sixth rank,
and in their second term, they would be demoted to regular seventh rank.
In their third and fourth terms, they would be sixth rank,
and in their fifth term, they would be promoted to junior fifth rank.
Shěng Nǚzhí Yìshǐ (Jurchen Interpreters of the Secretariat).
In Dàdìng twenty-eighth year,
an edict stipulated that from the current junior seventh and junior eighth rank officials,
those aged sixty and above would be selected and appointed.
In Míngchāng third year,
Jurchen and Khitan interpreters currently serving who were proficient in Jurchen and Khitan scripts were to be selected.
If there were none, then former Shěng Qìdān Yìshǐ (Khitan Interpreters of the Secretariat) who had already been appointed to official posts, and Jurchen scribes of the Guóshǐ Yuàn,
who were currently serving as seventh, eighth, or ninth rank officials, would be appointed.
Shěng Tōngshì (Translators of the Secretariat).
According to the regulations of Dàdìng twentieth year,
they would be promoted one rank every thirty months,
and appointed to an official post after one hundred and twenty months.
After one or two evaluations, they would be eighth rank;
after three evaluations, junior seventh rank.
The rest, like Bù Lìngyìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters of the Ministries), would be exempt from assignments.
Yùshǐ Tái Lìngshǐ, Yìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters of the Censorate).
According to the promotion and evaluation system of Huángtǒng eighth year,
they would be appointed to official posts after one hundred and twenty months.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng second year,
they would be appointed to official posts after one hundred and fifty months,
all as ninth rank,
as regular posts.
In Dàdìng second year,
they would be appointed to official posts after one hundred and twenty months,
all promoted one rank every thirty months.
For their appointments,
after one or two evaluations, they would all be ninth rank;
after three evaluations, eighth rank.
In Míngchāng third year,
all current serving clerks were dismissed,

and replaced by sons and younger brothers of third-rank functional officials who passed the examination, and successful candidates of the final imperial examinations who passed the Censorate's examination.
If there were not enough,
they would be selected from current serving officials of the Shūmì Yuàn and Liùbù, and sons and brothers of Khitan officials.
In Chéng'ān third year,
an imperial decree stated that for every appointment, the public must be consulted.
Although it was a public selection,
it was feared that over time abuses would gradually arise.
Moreover, being above scribes,
and appointed directly without examination,
this path for those from the Censorate seemed overly preferential.
Thus, it was ordered that, apart from vacancies for Zhǐ (Attendants) and Lìngyìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters) within the Censorate's ranks,
they would be selected according to rank from those who passed the Shūmì Yuàn Lìngyìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters of the Bureau of Military Affairs) examination.
If there were not enough,
they would be transferred from the Zhǐ and Lìngyìshǐ in the ranks of the various ministries.
If vacancies for successful candidates of the final imperial examinations were needed,
then successful candidates from three previous final imperial examinations
would take the examination along with other candidates for scribes after each imperial examination,
and be appointed according to their rank on the list.
There were thirteen Jurchens,
of whom six were Zhǐ within the ranks,
and seven were successful candidates of the final imperial examinations.
There were fifteen Han Chinese,
of whom seven were Zhǐ within the ranks,
and eight were successful candidates of the final imperial examinations.
There were four interpreters,
of whom two were Zhǐ within the ranks,
and two were successful candidates of the final imperial examinations.
Shūmì Yuàn Lìngshǐ, Yìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters of the Bureau of Military Affairs).
Lìngshǐ (Secretaries).
In Zhènglóng second year,
an edict stipulated that promotion and evaluation were the same as the Secretariat,
and appointment to official posts would be regular or junior eighth rank for regular posts.
In Dàdìng twenty-first year,
it was stipulated that Yuánshuài Fǔ Lìngyìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters of the Marshal's Office) would be promoted one rank every thirty months,
and appointed to official posts after one hundred and twenty months.
After one or two evaluations, they would be appointed to eighth rank;
after three evaluations, to junior seventh rank.
In the fourteenth year,
it was ordered that Zhǐ, and those who inherited positions from third-rank functional officials, and Zhǐ of fourth and fifth rank, and clerks, would take a general examination.
Those who passed would be appointed.
In the sixteenth year,
it was stipulated for those with one or two evaluations:
the first assignment was to Lùshì, Jūnpàn, Fángpàn (Registrar, Military Commissioner, Defense Commissioner);
the second to senior Bù (Assistant);
the third to middle Bù;
the fourth the same as the first;
the fifth and sixth to junior Lìng;
the seventh and eighth to middle Lìng;
the ninth and tenth to senior Lìng.
(In the twenty-sixth year,
those with two evaluations were exempted from one term as junior Lìng.)
For those with three evaluations or more:
the first assignment was to senior Lìng;
the second to middle Lìng;
the third to junior Lìng;
the fourth to Lùshì, Jūnfángpàn (Registrar, Military and Defense Commissioner).
(In the twenty-sixth year,
this appointment was exempted.)
The fifth to junior Lìng.
(In the twenty-sixth year,
this appointment was also exempted.)
The sixth and seventh to middle Lìng;
the eighth to senior Lìng.
In the seventeenth year,
an edict stipulated that princes of the imperial clan in mourning for five months or less (sīmá tǎnmǐan) and above could take the examination for appointment.
It was also regulated
that sons and younger brothers of third-rank functional officials would be four persons,
and clerks two persons.
Mùqīn Fǔ, Zōngzhèng Fǔ,
Tǒngjūn Sī Lìngyìshǐ (Secretaries and Interpreters of the Bureau of Family Affairs, Court of Imperial Clan Affairs, and Commander-in-Chief's Office)
had promotions, evaluations, and appointments
the same as the Tái and Bù (Censorate and Ministries).
Clerks and interpreters of departments,
according to the regulations of Huángtǒng 8th year,
for the first examination, a promotion of one grade every thirty months;
for Jurchens, these regulations apply;
for other people, it is based on meritorious advancement.
For the second and third examinations, a promotion of one grade each;
for the fourth examination, a promotion of two grades.
After 120 months, they are appointed to official positions of the 8th rank and below.
In Zhènglóng 2nd year,
the promotion examination was the same as for clerks of the Right Offices of the Secretariat,
appointed to official positions of the 9th rank.
In Dàdìng 21st year,
clerks of the Zōngzhèngfǔ, the Six Ministries, the Censorial Bureau, and the General Military Command,
interpreters of the barbarian departments,
and interpreters of the Yuánshuàifǔ,
were all promoted one grade every thirty months.
After 120 months, they were appointed to positions within the ranks.
One or two examinations qualified for the 9th rank,
three examinations and above qualified for appointment to the 8th rank.
In the 14th year,
descendants of officials from the 3rd to 7th ranks, who had inherited official status, were subjected to a single mixed test for appointment.
Soon, this was deemed inappropriate,
and it was ordered that descendants of 4th and 5th rank officials, as well as clerks who passed the test,
should be appointed according to the old regulations.
Those of the 6th rank and below were not included.
In the 15th year,
it was ordered to exempt them from service.
According to the regulations of the 16th year,
for those with one or two examinations,
the first appointment was to the upper register,
the second appointment to the middle register,
the third to the lower register,
the fourth to the upper register,
the fifth to record-keeper or military defense judge,
the sixth and seventh to lower clerk,
the eighth and ninth to middle clerk,
the tenth to upper clerk.
For those with three examinations and above,
the first appointment was to record-keeper or military defense judge,
the second to the upper register,
the third to the middle register,
the fourth as before,
the fifth to lower clerk,
(later this appointment was exempted.)
the sixth and seventh to lower clerk,
the eighth to middle clerk,
the ninth to upper clerk.
Clerks of the Ànchásī [Surveillance Commissioner’s Office]
were selected and appointed from among candidates who had passed the final imperial examinations.
Their promotions and appointments to official positions were the same as for the Bureau of the Secretariat.
Regarding the system for all internal and external clerks,
since Zhènglóng 2nd year,
the salaries of zhìshì and kǒumù were fixed as their official origins.
All dūmù were appointed directly by the court.
At the beginning of Hǎilíng's reign,
with the exception of clerks in the Shàngshūshěng, the Shūmìyuàn, and the Yùshǐtái,
all were designated as miscellaneous ranks.
He then summoned all clerks to the Chāngmíng Diàn,
and instructed them, saying:
"You all should not be discouraged by the slight lowering of your rank.
If there are truly talented individuals among you,
they will be promoted without regard to precedence."
It was also stipulated that clerks of the Shǎofǔjiān [Court of Imperial Manufactories]
should be appointed from among the old clerks of the Nèishěngsī [Inner Secretariat] and those who passed tests in the outer circuits.
In Dàdìng 2nd year,
Cáo Wàngzhī, a Lángzhōng of the Hùbù, stated,
"There are too many xūlì everywhere,
I request that they be reduced by half."
An imperial edict stated that the number of xūlì should remain as before,
but that the use of tiēshū was strictly forbidden.
It was also ordered that when a county clerk position became vacant,
those whose conduct was virtuous and who were highly regarded by their local community should be nominated and appointed.
In the 3rd year,
due to clerks in the outer circuits not being promoted or transferred for a long time,
they often colluded with powerful local magnates to commit malpractices.
It was ordered that they and kǒumù officials should be transferred every thirty months,
moving to other places.
In the 7th year,
an imperial edict stated that the total number of months spent by clerks, interpreters, and translators serving in miscellaneous ranks in the court should
not be counted if they had already reached a department position.
It was also decreed that
if a clerk was dismissed for embezzlement,
even if an amnesty was granted,
and there was no special imperial decree,
they were not allowed to be reinstated.
It was also ordered that
the number of xūlì in the capital prefectures, subprefectures, counties, and zhuǎnyùnsī [transportation offices]
should be increased or decreased
according to the size of their population and tax revenue.
In the 12th year,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Regarding clerks in the outer circuits,
merely judging by their ranking might not ensure the selection of suitable individuals.
If among them there are those who are honest, cautious, and proficient in clerical duties,
their superior should be entrusted with recommending them.
Those who fail the test
should be assigned to the lower-ranking bureaus in the court to assist in duties,
awaiting a re-test.
Knowing that they cannot avoid the test,
they will surely strive their best to seek advancement."
In Zhāngzōng's Dàdìng 29th year,
a memorialist stated:
"It is not appropriate for clerks from various prefectures and subprefectures to be appointed as court clerks after passing a test.
I request that descendants of officials of the 5th rank and above be appointed after passing a test.
This is because many descendants of officials are honest and diligent,
hence they are suitable for appointment."
The Shàngshūshěng stated:
"The system of appointing clerks by examination
has been in practice for a long time.
If only those with inherited official status are accepted,
we fear they may not be proficient in official documents,
which could lead to errors.
The old regulations only allowed descendants of 5th-rank officials to take the test.
Currently, those taking the test in the Secretariat and ministries are still few,
because the established regulations are not lenient enough."
Thus, new regulations were established:
A scattered official of the 5th rank who holds a 7th-rank position,
or a scattered official not yet of the 5th rank who holds a 5th-rank functional position,
and whose brothers, sons, or grandsons have already inherited official status, are all permitted to take the test.
However, clerks appointed by examination within the Six Ministries should follow the old rules.
In Tàihé 4th year,
Zhāng Xíngxìn, who was concurrently in charge of the Héyáng Ànchásī, stated:
"Since the transfer system was abolished,
the power of clerks has grown,
allowing them to arbitrarily extort,
and the people dare not speak out.
Now there are no court-appointed dūmù,
only the principal clerks are ordered to concurrently manage the six categories of documents,
and they share bribes with their peers.
Clerks can only be appointed to official positions after thirty years of service,
and they constantly exploit people in their local areas,
which is inconvenient."
Thus, new regulations were established:
transfers every thirty months were reinstated,
and after a full term, they were appointed to official positions,
to prevent the abuse of control over prefectures and subprefectures.
In the 8th year,
based on the words of Yáng Yúnyì, who was concurrently in charge of the Dōngjīng Ànchásī,
both writers and scribes should not be from their local circuits.
Instead, scribes from other circuits who were specially recommended to the department were allowed to take a similar test,
and those selected were appointed.
Regarding officials of the Right Rank,
according to the Tiāndé system,
those below Zhōngwǔ were given assignments,
while those of Zhāoxìn and above were given one assignment for every two appointments.
In Dàdìng 12th year,
an imperial edict stated that those of Zhènguó rank and above were to be appointed directly by the Secretariat.
In the 13th year,
it was decreed that Míngwēi should be registered as a lower clerk,
Xuānwēi as a middle clerk,
Guǎngwēi as an upper clerk,
Xìnwǔ Quán as a lower clerk,
and Xuānwǔ and Xiǎnwǔ were exempt from assignments,
provisionally registered as chancellor's clerks.
It was also decreed that for Xuānwǔ and Xiǎnwǔ,
those with merits were assigned to the upper register,
and those without faults to the middle register.
In the 26th year,
it was decreed that only when promoted to Xuānwǔ or Xiǎnwǔ could one be appointed to an official position.
Also, as per the old system, after five terms of general service, a report was to be presented to the Secretariat,
but an imperial edict reduced it to four terms.
In Míngchāng 3rd year,
due to appointments in various offices,
vacancies were open for nearly thirty months,
obstructing selection and transfer.
Henceforth, the old system of one assignment for every two appointments should be followed again.
When the number of personnel and vacancies match,
the old system will be restored.
In the first year of Tàihé
, due to vacancies for county magistrates [xiànlìng],
the nearest wait was fourteen months,
and the furthest was up to sixteen months.
This was because according to the existing regulations [gé],
officials up to Míngwēi were all appointed as county magistrates [xiànlìng].
Some committed selection offenses [xuǎnfàn] or caused loss to Yǒng people [kuīyǒngrén];
if such individuals held the Míngwēi rank, they were also appointed,
which made no distinction.
Therefore, it was ordered that Qūyǒng [kuīyǒng] offenders and those who committed selection offenses [xuǎnfàn gé],
if Jǐnüzhí [nǚzhí] people, would be promoted to Guǎngwēi,
and if Hàn people, to Xuānwǔ,
before being appointed as county magistrates [xiànlìng].
Furthermore, for those holding vacancies as assistant county magistrates [bùchéng],
the nearest wait was nineteen months, the furthest twenty-one months.
According to the existing regulations [gé], officials up to Xuānwǔ, Xiǎnwǔ, and Xìnwǔ were to be appointed as assistant county magistrates [chéngbù].
Therefore, it was ordered that only those who had committed Qūyǒng [kuīyǒng] offenses,
would reach Míngwēi before being appointed as assistant county magistrates [chéngbù].
Regarding the regulations [gé] for clerks [lì],
all officials in the right-hand positions [yòuzhí], both principal and miscellaneous ranks [zhèngzábān],
(meaning those without qualifications [zīlì],
but equal within their ranks)
were to be appointed based on their official qualifications [guānzī].
Those holding Zhōngwǔ and below were assigned to inspect and supervise duties [jiāndāng chāishǐ].
Zhāoxìn and above were nominated for appointments [chúsòu] in various departments [zhūsī],
with two appointments for every one assignment.
Xuānwǔ and above were assigned to the middle register [zhōngbù],
(those with merit compensation [gōngchóurén] to the upper register [shàngbù]).
Míngwēi were appointed as junior magistrates [xiàlìng],
Xuānwēi as middle magistrates [zhōnglìng],
Guǎngwēi as senior magistrates [shànglìng].
After completing four terms as county magistrate [xiànlìng],
or if holding Dìngyuǎn and having already served three terms as county magistrate [xiànlìng],
all were to be reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
However, if they had committed Qūyǒng [kuīyǒng] offenses or selection offenses [xuǎnfàn gé],

(those who had committed public offenses leading to demotion, private offenses leading to dismissal, corruption, received negative appraisals from investigating officials [liánfǎng bùhǎo], or were deemed unfit to govern people by inspection [tǐchá bùkān línmín],
were considered to have committed selection offenses [xuǎnfàn gé]),
Jǐnüzhí [nǚzhí] people would be promoted to Wǔyì,
and Hàn people and people of various other groups [zhūsèrén] to Wǔlüè,
all to be nominated for appointments [chúsòu] in various departments [zhūsī],
with two appointments for every one assignment.
If they reached Míngwēi before being appointed as assistant county magistrates [chéngbù],
Jǐnüzhí [nǚzhí] people would be promoted to Guǎngwēi,
and Hàn people and people of various other groups [zhūsèrén] to Xuānwēi,
all to serve two terms as junior magistrates [xiàlìng],
and one term as middle magistrate [zhōnglìng],
then reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
In the third year of Zhēnyòu,
it was decreed that those promoted to Xuānwǔ
would all be nominated for appointments [chúsòu] in various departments [zhūsī],
also with two appointments for every one assignment.
For those who had not committed selection offenses [xuǎnfàn gé],
if they reached Huáiyuǎn, they would be appointed as assistant county magistrates [chéngbù].
Upon reaching Ānyuǎn, they would serve one term as junior magistrate [xiàlìng] and one term as senior magistrate [shànglìng],
and then be reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
In the fourth year,
it was again decreed that officials reaching Huáiyuǎn would be appointed as junior magistrates [xiàlìng],
Dìngyuǎn as middle magistrates [zhōnglìng],
Ānyuǎn as senior magistrates [shànglìng],
and after four terms, be reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
Inspectors of Law [Jiǎnfǎ], and Administrators of Law [Zhīfǎ].
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
the number of personnel for the Six Ministries [Liùbù] and the method for selection were established.
First evaluation [chūkǎo] and second evaluation [liǎngkǎo] both led to appointment as司候 [sīhòu].
Third evaluation [sānkǎo] led to appointment as upper register [shàngbù].
In the fifth year,
regulations were established:
those within ten years of service, after first evaluation [chūkǎo], were appointed as junior register [xiàbù];
after second evaluation [liǎngkǎo], as middle register [zhōngbù];
after third evaluation [sānkǎo], as警判 [jǐngpàn].
Those beyond ten years of service, after first evaluation [chūkǎo], were appointed as second term司候 [sīhòu];
after second evaluation [liǎngkǎo], as upper register [shàngbù];
after third evaluation [sānkǎo], as market supervisor [shìchéng].
In the second year of Dàdìng,
it was decreed that those who had completed three evaluations [sānkǎo],
regardless of whether they were within or beyond ten years of service,
would all be given the rank of eighth-grade record keeper [lùshǐ] or market administrator [shìlìng],
to be nominated according to their respective categories [ménhù] for appointment.
For appointments [chúsòu],
old appointment letters [zháfù] were given,
but in the third year of Dàdìng, it was first ordered that imperial edicts [chì] be issued,
to be handled by those specializing in legal provisions [lǜkērén].
In the seventh year,
regulations were established:
appointments were made by verifying the rank on the selection roster [bǎngcì gōuqǔ],
following the system for selecting Secretariat clerks [shěnglìshǐ].
In the twenty-sixth year,
it was ordered that third evaluation [sānkǎo] led to appointment as record keeper [lùshǐ],
and thereafter, two appointments for every one assignment.
Jǐnüzhí [Nǚzhí] Administrators of Law [Zhīfǎ] and Inspectors of Law [Jiǎnfǎ].
Regulations [gé] of the third year of Dàdìng:
Translators [yìshǐ] were assigned from the Taibu [Táibù] command [tǒngjūnsī],
nominated from those who had served as county assistants [xiànzuǒ] or market administrators [shìlìng] and had been assigned duties [chāishǐrén].
Upon completion of their evaluation term [kǎomǎn], they were promoted one grade higher than their original status,
and imperial edicts [chì] were issued according to the precedents for local administrators [zhīshìlì].
Each term was thirty months.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
registrars [shūshǐ] and translators [yìshǐ] were nominated from the Secretariat [shěngyuàn], Taibu [Táibù] command [tǒngjūnsī],
under fifty years old, without faults or offenses, and of cautious conduct [shènxíngzhǐ].
They were tested for one month,
and the capable ones were appointed.
Those who were retained again were promoted one grade.
After one evaluation [yīkǎo], they became initial senior magistrates [chūshànglìng].
After two or three, middle magistrates [zhōnglìng].
After four, senior magistrates [shànglìng].
After two evaluations [liǎngkǎo], they were promoted two grades,
and then reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
Two Reviewers [Jiǎntǎo] of the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices [Tàichángsì].
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
promotion occurred every fifty months.
Jǐnüzhí [nǚzhí] people were promoted to Dūnwǔ,
other people to Jìn Yì,
and after one hundred fifty months, they were assigned to an official post [chūzhí],
belonging to the miscellaneous ranks [zábān].
In the second year of Dàdìng,
it was decreed that promotion occurred every thirty months,
and after one hundred twenty months, they were assigned to an official post [chūzhí],
belonging to the ninth principal rank [zhèngbān jiǔpǐn].
Secretariat Waiting Gentlemen [Shěngzhīhòulángjūn].
In the third year of Dàdìng,

it was decreed that those whose relatives of Tǎnmǐan [tǎnmǐan] rank and above wished to serve, and who had passed the examination but found no vacancies, and sons of first-rank officials [yīpǐnguān zǐ],
after being presented for audience,
would only serve as waiting gentlemen [zhīhòu] within their ranks.
Promotions occurred every thirty months.
The first appointment was to principal or junior seventh-rank.
The next appointment was reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
Those within the inner waiting group [nèizhīzàibān],
their first and second appointments were to principal or junior eighth-rank,
third and fourth to junior seventh-rank,
and thereafter reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
Those within the rank waiting group [bānzhīzàibān],
first to ninth-rank,
second and third to principal or junior eighth-rank,
[一０]fourth and fifth to junior seventh-rank,
and thereafter reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
For the three grades above,
sixty months constituted a full term [mǎn],
each leading to a promotion.
In the eighth year,
regulations were established:
they would first serve sixty months to test their talent.
Those who were not capable would be promoted one rank and then dismissed.
Those who were capable would serve another sixty months.
Promotion occurred every thirty months,
one hundred twenty months constituted a full term [mǎn].
Those who knew Jǐnüzhí [nǚzhí] script were required.
In the sixteenth year,
regulations were established:
they were tested with imperial edicts [zhìwén],
and those who could explain the meaning of the edict were deemed excellent.
In the eighteenth year,
it was decreed that sons of first-rank officials [yīpǐnguān zǐ],
first appointed as Military Governors [dōujūn],
second as record keepers [lùshǐ] or military defense judges [jūnfángpàn],
third as Military Governors [dōujūn],
fourth as junior magistrates [xiàlìng],
fifth and sixth as senior magistrates [shànglìng],
[一一]then reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
Inner waiting group [nèizhī]:
first as record keepers [lùshǐ] or military defense judges [jūnfángpàn],
second as upper register [shàngbù],
third the same as the first,
fourth as record keepers [lùshǐ],
fifth as Military Governors [dōujūn],
sixth as junior magistrates [xiàlìng],
seventh as middle magistrates [zhōnglìng],
eighth as senior magistrates [shànglìng],
then reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
Rank waiting group [bānzhī]:
first as upper register [shàngbù],
second as middle register [zhōngbù],
third the same as the first,
fourth as record keepers [lùshǐ] or military defense judges [jūnfángpàn],
fifth as record keepers [lùshǐ],
sixth as Military Governors [dōujūn],
seventh as junior magistrates [xiàlìng],
eighth as middle magistrates [zhōnglìng],
ninth as senior magistrates [shànglìng],
then reported to the Secretariat [shěng].
Scribes [shūxiě] of the Institute of National History [Guóshǐyuàn].
In the first year of Zhènglóng,
regulations were established:
Jǐnüzhí [nǚzhí] scribes [shūxiě]
were tested by translating Khitan script into Jǐnüzhí [nǚzhí] script,
with a minimum of three hundred characters.
Khitan scribes [shūxiě],
proficient in both large and small Khitan scripts,
were to translate Historical Records in Chinese characters into Khitan script, with a minimum of three hundred characters,
and one poem,
either five-character or seven-character with four rhymes,
with the topic given in Khitan script.
Hàn people were tested with one essay [lùn yīdào].
Promotions [qiānkǎo] and official assignments [chūzhí] were the same as for Reviewers [Jiǎntǎo] of the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices [Tàicháng].
Zōngshì Jiāngjūn.
Sixty months constituted a term.
Initially, they served as Cìtóng.
Secondly, as Dūjūn.
Thirdly, as Cìtóng.
Fourthly, they followed the sixth rank.
Fùjiāngjūn were filled by seventh-rank officers.
In Míngchāng year 1 (1190),
ninety months constituted a full term.
In Zhōngdū and Shàngjīng, initially they followed the seventh rank.
Secondly, as Lùshì and Jūnfáng Pàn.
Thirdly, they returned to their original department.
In other circuits,
initially as Lùshì and Jūnfáng Pàn.
Secondly, as Shàngbù.
Thirdly, they returned to their original department.
In Chéng'ān year 2 (1197), the position of Sīshǔlìng was changed to Suícháo.
Nèishì Yùzhí.
There were sixty-four Nèizhí.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng year 2 (1157),
Chángxíngrén were promoted one rank every fifty months.
Nǚzhírén were promoted to Dūnwǔ.
Others were promoted to Jìnyì,
with no prior qualification required.
According to the regulations of Dàdìng year 2 (1162),
the same as above.
In Dàdìng year 6 (1166),
the regulations for recruiting Nèishì were revised.
Those who could recite one major sūtra, could recite one book from the Lúnyǔ or Mèngzǐ, and were also skilled in writing letters,
were given a monthly stipend of eight guàn of grain.
Those who were somewhat literate and could write were given seven guàn of grain.
Those who were illiterate were given six guàn of grain.
In Tàihé year 2 (1202),
because the practice of involving external officials led to deficiencies in preventing minor issues,
the system of Jìlùguān titles was created
to assign them specific responsibilities.
This was sufficient to reward their efforts
without the abuses of encroaching on official duties.
Regarding all the palace bureaus,
in Dàdìng year 1 (1161),
Shìzōng stated that the stipends and salaries of the personnel serving in the various bureaus
were overly generous.
During the Zhènglóng era, there were no prior qualifications,
which was overly harsh.
Furthermore, their official ranks were not determined by the amount of work,
so he ordered a revision.
In Dàdìng year 6 (1166),
he instructed the relevant authorities, saying:
"Among the personnel serving in the various palace bureaus,
some have completed their years of service and are due for transfer,
but they often suffer from delays
and ultimately receive no appointment.
Furthermore, many of those who are appointed
do not understand texts and are not competent,
which is inconvenient for both public and private matters.
Henceforth, those who wish to leave the bureau are permitted to do so.
Those who wish to remain shall have their rank increased,
and continue to serve as before.
As for the leaders of ten,
even if they are old and wish to remain, their rank shall also be increased,
and they shall serve as Chángxíng.
The rest shall be released according to regulations."
In year 7 (1167),
an imperial edict was issued to the Chief Minister, saying:
"Nǚzhírén have always been recruited into the various bureaus without being appointed as Zhīhòu.
From now on, except for Tàiyī, Sītiān, and Nèishì,
all other bureaus shall recruit them as Gōudàng."
Hùwèi.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng year 2 (1157),
they were promoted one rank every thirty months.
Upon initial assessment,
Nǚzhí were promoted to Dūnwǔ,
while others were promoted to Bǎoyì.
After one hundred and fifty months, they were appointed to official positions,
receiving appointments equivalent to fifth-rank subordinates and above sixth-rank subordinates.
According to the regulations of Dàdìng year 2 (1162),
this was changed to an initial promotion to Zhōngyǒng,
and appointment to official positions after one hundred and twenty months.
According to the official system of Dàdìng year 14 (1174),
two additional grades were added from the bottom.
Thus, Nǚzhí were initially promoted to Xiūwǔ,
and others to Dūnwǔ.
In year 18 (1178),
it was stipulated that those initially appointed to the fifth rank would next be appointed to the sixth rank,
and for their third appointment, they would again be appointed to the fifth rank subordinate.
Those initially appointed to the sixth rank would not be demoted.
They would only be granted the fifth rank subordinate for their fourth appointment.
Those who were retained for additional terms were each promoted one rank.
According to the qualification regulations of Míngchāng year 1 (1190),
the initial appointment did not count towards seniority.
For those not retained,
the first appointment was sixth rank subordinate,
the second and third were the same as above,
and the fourth appointment was promoted to fifth rank subordinate.
For those retained,
the first appointment was fifth rank subordinate,
the second and third were the same as above,
and the fourth was fifth rank proper.
For those retained for a second time,
the first appointment was fifth rank proper,
the second was the same as above,
the third was Shǎoyǐn,
and the fourth was Cìshǐ.
In Míngchāng year 4 (1193),
this was demoted to appointments of the sixth and seventh ranks.
According to the Zhēnyòu system (1213-1217),
the first assessment was eighth rank.
Two assessments resulted in appointment as Xiànlìng.
Three assessments resulted in seventh rank proper.
Four assessments resulted in sixth rank.
In year 5 (1217),
it was stipulated that those with one assessment were appointed as Shànglìng.
Those with two assessments, after one term as seventh rank proper, were demoted to seventh rank subordinate;
after two terms as seventh rank proper, they were promoted to sixth rank.
Those with three assessments, after one term as seventh rank proper, returned;
after two terms as seventh rank proper, they were promoted to sixth rank.
Those with four assessments,
after three terms as sixth rank, were promoted to fifth rank subordinate.
Fúbǎoláng.
Twelve individuals.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng year 2 (1157),
all were the same as Hùwèi.
Upon appointment to official positions, they were granted positions equivalent to seventh rank subordinate.
According to the regulations of Dàdìng year 2 (1162),
all were the same as Hùwèi.
In year 14 (1174),
they were first recruited.
〔一二〕Others were promoted to Jìnyì.
In year 21 (1181),
the outstanding were appointed to the sixth rank,
while ordinary individuals were only appointed to the seventh rank.
Fèngyù.
Sixteen individuals.
Filled by Nèifùmǎ.
Formerly known as Rùqǐndiàn Xiǎodǐ.
In Dàdìng year 12 (1172),
the name was changed to the current one.
According to the regulations of Zhènglóng year 2 (1157),
the same as Fúbǎoláng.
In Dàdìng year 2 (1162),
upon appointment to official positions, they were seventh rank subordinate.
Fèngzhí.
Thirty individuals.
Formerly known as Bùrùqǐndiàn Xiǎodǐ,

start at the eighth rank.
After two promotions, they reach 'upper-grade record keeper' (shàngbù);
after three, 'middle-grade record keeper' (zhōngbù);
after four, the eighth rank (again);
after five, 'lower-grade magistrate' (xiàlìng);
after six, 'middle-grade magistrate' (zhōnglìng);
after eight, 'upper-grade magistrate' (shànglìng);
〔一六〕and then they report to the capital.
The clerks of the Crown Prince's palace
are promoted one rank every fifty months.

Those without hereditary privilege are assigned to various duties.

the Dàdìng twenty-first year regulations

Proofreading Notes
Record of Offices 35: Selection 4: Bureau Selection, Provincial Selection, Inspection, Recommendation, Meritorious Rewards and Deficiencies.
Regarding the system of selection and appointment by the Ministry of Personnel,
starting from Tàizōng's Tiānhuì twelfth year,
when ancient laws were first adopted to establish official posts,
up to Tiānjuàn the first year,
when the new official system was promulgated.
By Tiāndé the fourth year,
candidates from both Hénán and Héběi were first required to go to the Central Capital,
where the Ministry of Personnel established separate bureaus for selection and appointment.
Furthermore, the Minister of Personnel, Xiāo Zé,
was ordered to establish unified regulations for official appointments in Hénán and Héběi.
This involved the selection and appointment of those from various departments, as well as grand generals,
who were to be assessed and appointed annually according to established practice.
Other aspiring officials were to be proposed for appointment in four seasonal batches,
which became the established system.
In Zhēnyuán the second year,
it was ordered that when proposing appointments,
according to the old regulations,
the specific number of aspiring officials (who were to be interviewed in person)
(meaning they were personally interviewed)
should not be from their native district.
If they were frail, sick, or elderly, they should not be appointed to demanding or difficult positions.
In Shìzōng's Dàdìng the first year,
an imperial decree stated that appointments below the eighth rank
did not require reporting to the emperor.
It was also decreed that
aspiring officials should not enter powerful households.
Violators would have one rank demoted or removed.
Those who made gifts and those who received them
were to be reported to the throne.
In the second year,
an edict stated that seasonal candidates,
if without fault or if they had performed meritorious service,
were to be assessed and appointed according to regulations.
Those who were honest and capable, or those who were corrupt and abusive,
were to have their ranks raised or lowered proportionally,
and this was to be reported to the province.
In the seventh year,
an order was issued to the relevant officials,
that from now on, at the end of each quarter, when scholars seeking office arrive at the department,
the department should investigate them.
Those whose administrative achievements are outstanding, as well as those who are corrupt,
should be reported to the province for verification and submission.
They should be promoted or punished accordingly.
Elderly individuals should not be appointed as xiànlìng.
The emperor also said to his prime ministers,
"The capabilities of officials in the imperial court
can generally be known.
However, for officials outside the capital, from zhuǎnyùnsī mùguān down to xiànlìng,
only their seniority is verified.
Even if there are diligent, loyal, honest, and upright individuals among them,
they have no path for advancement.
This means such a person will never hope to achieve the third rank in their lifetime.
How can this be the way to promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy?
From now on, after three evaluations, their capabilities shall be assessed,
and this shall be the rule for determining promotions and demotions."
He further said,
"The current method of employing people is very flawed.
Those who do not seek fame and advancement,
even if they have served for a long time,
remain in minor positions,
with some not moving beyond the seventh rank for thirty or forty years.
Meanwhile, newcomers befriend court nobles,
achieving prominence and distinction.
How can this demonstrate a way to encourage and motivate?
You, my lords, must be meticulous in employing people
to rectify this abuse."
At that time, Cháng Déhuī, the Fángyùshǐ of Qīngzhōu, submitted a memorial, stating:
"The regulations of the Lìbù
only consider years of service.
Consequently, even those with talent
are constrained by the law and cannot be promoted,
leading to many talented individuals being stuck in lower positions.
Moreover, the positions of cìshǐ and xiànlìng, which involve direct interaction with the people,
often do not get the right person.
I request that greater investigation be made,
and then public and honest inquiries be conducted,
so that people may have a sense of fear.
Furthermore, even for the position of wine tax commissioner, capable individuals are selected.
How much more so should officials who convey and propagate imperial decrees
not be carefully chosen?
From now on, it is fitting that capable officials who are suitable for the role of wine commissioner be appointed to positions that involve direct interaction with the people."
This was approved.
In the tenth year,
the emperor said to his prime ministers,
"For minor officials below the level of shǒulìng,
their capabilities cannot be fully known.
Recently, I have heard that when the common people request that an official be retained,
such requests are almost always rejected.
Whenever a minor official pleases the people,
their superiors often dislike them,
and those who can serve their superiors well
are bound not to please the people.
From now on, if the people wish an official to remain,
they are permitted to go directly to the department
and report it to the province.
An envoy shall be dispatched to verify the facts.
If their achievements are indeed good, they may be exceptionally promoted,
such as an chéngbù being promoted to xiànlìng,
to serve as an encouragement."
In the twenty-sixth year,
due to official vacancies,
an imperial edict stated,
"Among those who, according to current regulations, are to be demoted in rank,
those scheduled for three or two demotions shall have one demotion waived.
Those scheduled for one demotion shall not be demoted.
Lìngshǐ and yìshǐ in the province, if they meet the qualifications for xiànlìng,
shall be exempted from one term as lùshì and one term as a xiàxiànlìng.
Lìngshǐ in the Mìyuàn who have undergone three evaluations or more
shall be granted the same exemption as above.
Lìngshǐ and yìshǐ in the Tái, Bù, Zōngzhèngfǔ, and Tǒngjūnsī,
who are required to serve a certain number of terms as xiànlìng,
shall be exempted from one term as xiàlìng.
For various categories of wénzī zhū kē in outer-circuit yòuzhí positions,
who are required to serve as xiànlìng, one term shall also be waived.
For those who have served as jiǎnfǎ and zhīfǎ,
and after three evaluations obtained the position of lùshì,
from now on, for every two appointments, one assignment shall be granted."
In Míngchāng’s third year,
the emperor said,
"According to the old system,
scholars seeking office who arrived at the department each quarter,
if literate, were tested with essays and judgments;
if illiterate, they were asked three difficult questions,
and their words and actions were investigated to ensure they corresponded.
Henceforth, all individuals coming to the department each quarter shall be tested according to these regulations."
The prime ministers and executive officials memorialized, saying,
"Since their investigation has confirmed that they match what was recommended,
and they have passed the essay and judgment tests,
if they are not given promotions and appointments in proportion,
there will be no way to show encouragement."
Thus, a system was established:
If they were court officials or outer-circuit officials of the sixth rank or above, they would be appointed according to their seniorities.
Outer-circuit officials of the regular seventh rank would be nominated for promotion to xiànlìng of the first class.
Those whose term expired and were due for demotion would be exempted from demotion.
Officials of the subsidiary seventh rank and below would have two terms reduced from their respective qualification categories for nomination.
Thereafter, if investigations confirmed their suitability, they would be appointed to the elevated position.
If investigations found them unsuitable, they would be appointed to their original rank.
If current xiànlìng were promoted to zhōngshànglìng, or were in charge of money and grain, or left due to parental mourning,
their appointment would await the arrival of their official clearance documents at the department.
Individuals in various bureaus would also await their future assignment dates for nomination according to the above.
For méng'ān móukè, it was proposed to follow the precedent of those recommended by Tíxíngsī for promotion,
but during implementation, one qualification was often reduced depending on their origin.
In Míngchāng’s seventh year,
an imperial edict reinstated the old system.
In Tàihé’s first year,
the emperor noted that the xiànlìng vacancies were such that nearby ones took fourteen months to fill, and distant ones sixteen months.
He also noted that the vacancies for xiànlìng and chéngbù did not match.
He issued an edict to the provincial officials, saying,
"According to the current regulations for selecting officials,
scattered officials up to míngwēi are appointed as xiànlìng,
and xuānwǔ are appointed as chéngbù.
Even those who have violated selection rules or incurred permanent losses are appointed.
This makes no distinction."
Thus, a new system was established:
Those who had violated selection rules or incurred permanent losses,
if guǎngwēi, would be appointed as lìng;
if míngwēi, would be appointed as chéngbù.
In Dà'ān’s first year of Wèishàowáng,
due to a shortage of xiànlìng,
those initially appointed as shàng, zhōng, or xià lìng,
could be re-appointed as chéngbù for one term while awaiting vacancies.
Once vacancies matched, the old system would be restored.
In Zhēnyòu’s second year of Xuānzōng,
due to relocation and displacement,
many official positions were vacant.
The Xuānfǔsī of various Héshuò circuits were temporarily authorized to nominate officials of the seventh rank and below.
Soon, it was discovered that the Lìbù was unaware of these appointments,
and the numerous quarterly vacancies led to duplication.
Consequently, it was proposed to abolish this authorization.
At that time, Lǐ Yīng said,
"Since the war began,
a hundred tasks have become cumbersome.
Governance depends on employing the right people.
Although there were old methods of 'four excellences' and 'seventeen merits,'
promotions are rarely heard of,
making them almost useless.
During the Dàdìng era,
Imperial Censors and Judicial Reviewers were dispatched to various circuits
to investigate and nominate,
which was considered effective in securing talent.
This proven method can be followed,
which might encourage people to exert themselves."
An imperial decree approved this.
In the third year,
Àotún Āhǔ, a Lángzhōng of the Hùbù, stated,
"All types of official transfers should be uniform with those of the Nǚzhí,
but the relevant authorities do not comply,
arbitrarily making distinctions,
which leads to mutual suspicion between superiors and subordinates."
An imperial edict prohibited this violation of regulations.
Initially,
when Xuānzōng moved south,
he ordered the Lìbù to hold selections in Nánjīng during autumn and winter, and in Zhōngdū during spring and summer.
However, those seeking appointments were reluctant to travel north,
and mostly came south,
so the selections were combined and held in Nánjīng.
In the third month,
an order was given to dismiss those unsuitable for office.
Officials of the fifth rank and above were to publicly recommend individuals.
Among those who arrived at the department this quarter,
those with talent and ability were to be prioritized for replacement according to urgency.
In Xīngdìng’s first year,
an imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to deliberate on reducing redundant officials.
Another edict stipulated that,
from now on, for each quarterly selection by the Lìbù,
one Nǚzhí and one Hàn supervisor from the Imperial Censorate should be dispatched to oversee.

Furthermore, all officials previously demoted, dismissed, or terminated for crimes, as well as those who left before completing their assigned duties and were subsequently re-appointed by local official agencies, were to be completely dismissed.
A new system was also established:
Temporarily, following the precedent of heavily burdened counties, all were to be made regular seventh-rank officials.

Court officials of the seventh rank and outer-circuit officials of the sixth rank and above were to recommend one regular seventh-rank official or below annually, who was under sixty years old, free of public or private offenses, and capable of holding office.
Additionally, they were to concurrently hold the position of Tányā in the Mìshùyuàn,
to maintain military discipline.
They were to concurrently hold the position of Tányā in the Mìshùyuàn
to maintain military discipline.
Superiors were not permitted to arbitrarily assign, occupy, insult, or punish them.
After half a year in office,
the Xún'ànguān was to investigate and report their findings for official record.
After another half a year, a re-investigation would take place,
and on the day of their full evaluation, they would be categorized and promoted.
If all six matters were fulfilled, they would be classified as superior,
and promoted one rank.
If four matters were fulfilled, they would be classified as medium,
and two terms of seniority would be reduced.
If classified as inferior, one term of seniority would be reduced.
Those found unsatisfactory would be dismissed.
Regarding the system of provincial selection,
since the eighth year of Huángtǒng in Xīzōng's reign, as the capital was remote,
it was first ordered to proceed to Yānjīng for proposed appointments,
which became a regular practice annually.
When the capital was moved during Zhēnyuán,
this system was first abolished.
As for the regular promotion system:
officials of regular seventh rank would be promoted to sixth rank after two terms;
sixth rank officials would be promoted to auxiliary fifth rank after three terms;
auxiliary fifth rank officials would be promoted to regular fifth rank after two terms;
and regular fifth rank officials would be promoted to cìshǐ after three terms.
All internal and external officials were assessed every thirty months;
court officials served a term of thirty months,
after which they were promoted one grade.
Unless specifically appointed by imperial decree,
the Shàngshū would select external officials,
and order the Zuǒsī to issue a document for their requisition.
In the third year of Chéng'ān,
it was first ordered to establish a register for requisitions.
In the fifteenth year of Dàdìng,
it was decreed that officials of the second rank, as well as zǎizhí and shūmìshǐ, would not have fixed terms;
every thirty months, their service would be recorded on a yellow slip,
and if not yet thirty months, it would be appended to the register of unfulfilled terms.
Internal and external officials of the third rank served a term of fifty months.
In the third year of Tàihé,
it was decreed that all civil officials of the Right Bureau (yòuzhíguān) eligible for promotion to a third-rank official position,
if fifth rank or above, must have served fifty months;
if sixth rank or below, or those from mén'yìn or miscellaneous streams who reached fourth rank or above and whose honorary titles (sǎnguān) qualified for third rank,
all must have served sixty months
before being allowed to apply for promotion.
In the seventh year,
apart from Ànchásǐ and their deputies who continued to be assessed every thirty months,
internal and external officials of the fourth rank were assessed every forty months,
and promoted to third rank after a total of eighty months.
In the eighth year of Tàihé,
an imperial edict stated that officials from mén'yìn who reached fourth rank were very few;
henceforth, those who reached the position of cìshǐ and whose honorary titles qualified for third rank,
were permitted to apply for promotion to third rank.
This was the system of provincial selection and qualification assessment.
In the first year of Dàdìng in Shìzōng's reign,
the emperor said to the zǎichén:
"When I formerly served in external posts,
I could not fully know the merits or demerits of individuals.
Every time an official was appointed, I worried that they might not be competent.
Indeed, recommending the virtuous is the duty of a minister.
You, my lords, should each do your utmost,
lest you become a laughingstock to the world."
He further said:
"When proposing appointments, you should select people for the office,
not merely appoint relatives and old acquaintances,
so that no office remains vacant."
He also said:
"For the posts of shǒulìng, capable and talented individuals should be chosen.
Recently I heard that the frontier regions, which are damaged and broken, often employ the elderly or those demoted for crimes;
this further harms the border populace.
If those with high qualifications should not serve in remote border areas,
then those of lesser but capable talent can be promoted and appointed;
they should not be demoted again.
This way, the borderlands might be fully restored."
The system of frontier promotion
indeed began here.
In the third year,
an edict stated that guāndānguān promoted to third-rank honorary titles who were still serving as xiànlìng,
would be exempted by the province.
In the fourth year,
an imperial decree stated that for court officials of the sixth rank in busy and critical departments where vacancies occurred,
the province was not allowed to propose appointments;
instead, the vacancies and candidates should be reported to the throne.
In the sixth year,
it was decreed that when an official reached the third rank,
the court would assess their merits and years of service,
and grant special favor for promotion.
In the seventh year,
it was decreed that when internal and external officials of the third rank were considered for appointment,
any months or days beyond their completed assessment terms
for which they had not been promoted or added,
or had been transferred,
should be fully recorded in the appointment list and reported.
It was also decreed that
external officials of fourth rank and above, as well as fifth rank officials eligible for promotion,
should all have their vacancies and candidates reported to the throne.
For officials of sixth rank and below,
the Shàngshū Shěng was ordered to propose and then report for approval.
The emperor also said to the zǎichén:
"The proposed appointments for external officials
are often unsuitable.
If a zhōuxiàn official is good, governance prospers;
otherwise, it collapses.
You should discern talented individuals,
and employ both the superior and the inferior,
so that they mutually encourage each other,
and perhaps achieve good governance."
He further said:
"Previously, dùnshèrén were usually made jiéfù.
Now, a tóngqiān Yínshù from the Xuānhuī Yuàn can be specially admitted as dùnshè,
and then appointed as tóngzhī of Cāngzhōu.
What merit does this have?
It is merely that the person is capable of being employed,
hence the appointment as tóngqiān.
Moreover, if those who completed their terms as hùwèi, fúbǎo, or dùnshè are given six-rank or five-rank positions,
and are appointed equally with those like Yuán Kǔxīn who are specially admitted as dùnshè,
then this is inappropriate."
In the tenth year,
he said to the zǎichén:
"Any official,
if not serving in a court position,
cannot deviate from the regular promotion system.
If you rely solely on your personal knowledge for appointments, there might be stagnation.
It is also permissible to verify their entry into officialdom by their names or assessment grades.
If they are not competent,
they should be dismissed from external posts."
In the eleventh year,
the emperor said to the zǎichén:
"Many court officials calculate their service,
thinking that after one assessment term they should get a certain position, and after two terms another certain position,
and thus merely engage in perfunctory service.
When dispatched,
they often delay or disobey.
Recently, Lǐ Bǎo, a Dàlǐ Sīzhí, was appointed Jǐngxúnshǐ,
and in his letter of thanks, he said, 'Your servant has served two terms in the capital,'
implying that he believed he should have received a fifth-rank position but was given a sixth-rank one.
I considered this person capable of handling affairs;
he was once appointed Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
and later Dàlǐ Sīzhí.
He never expressed any personal opinions or insights on any matter.
Therefore, I appointed him as a zhǎngguān,
wishing to observe his governance,
hence this appointment.
From now on, for those appointed to external or internal posts,
if their governance is found to be just and diligent, they shall be promoted;
if they merely seek ease and simplicity,
they should be dismissed from their current rank without waiting for their term to end.
Without clearly defined rewards and punishments,
how can we encourage and motivate them?"
In the twelfth year,
the emperor said to the zǎichén:
"I once reviewed the conduct of all officials in the Shàngshū Shěng,
and found very few suitable for appointments as cìshǐ or zhījūn.
Recently, only the tóngzhī of Shēnzhōu resigned, saying he was not accustomed to the work, which was acceptable,
so he was appointed.
Currently, those holding fifth-rank positions are all individuals who, after two terms, should be demoted according to regulations,
hence they are unsuitable.
Among the hùwèi, there are some who have completed their terms;
if they are released to official posts, I worry that they are too young and unfamiliar with governmental affairs,
and also, it is difficult to find such talented individuals in the palace guard today.
If they are ordered to remain in service,
and their qualifications accumulate,
would it be acceptable to allow them to reach regular fifth rank?"
They all said:
"Good."
In the sixteenth year,
an imperial decree to the zǎichén stated that when selecting and proposing appointments,
external candidates seeking office must be invited,
and brought to the Shàngshū Shěng hall to be assessed for their abilities and assigned positions.
In the twenty-first year,
he said to the zǎichén:
"During Hǎilíng's time, granting original official positions was too excessive;
now it is too restrictive."
He ordered minor honorary officials to report it.
In the twenty-fourth year,
since the old qualification assessment was too stagnant,
it was ordered to reduce each term by one,
and to assess individuals' talent, diligence, qualifications, and age as needed,
and report them in sequence.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng in Zhāngzōng's reign,
a system was established
whereby all officials from regular seventh rank upwards would be promoted after two terms.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng,
because the previous system prohibited officials already holding third-rank honorary titles from applying for promotion,
the responsible departments consequently did not propose them,
leading to no means of promotion.
The emperor, fearing stagnation,
then established a system:
those already holding third-rank honorary titles who had actually served fifty months,
upon verification by the responsible departments,
would be promoted one rank from the previous grade,
and their term would be recalculated starting from after this promotion.
In the fifth year,
the zǎichén were ordered, when proposing appointments,
to summon the candidates for selection and speak with them,
to observe their character.
In the sixth year,
it was ordered that key positions for court officials of the fifth rank,
and external officials of the third rank,
should all have their candidates and vacancies presented to the throne,
awaiting imperial appointment.
In the seventh year,
an imperial decree stated that court appointments must reach thirty months;
if there was an urgent vacancy,
the vacancy and candidate should be reported to the throne.
Soon after, it was further ordered
that there was no need to wait until the assessment term was completed;
their total service should simply be calculated.
In Chéng'ān fourth year (1200),
an imperial edict was issued to the Grand Councilors, saying:
“Regarding all appointments and promotions,
I fear they may not always be appropriate.
Currently, there is no Ménxià Shěng (Chancellery),
and although there are Jǐshìzhōng (Remonstrance Officials), there is no Fēngbó Sī (Bureau of Scrutiny and Rejection).
If one were to be established,
it could meticulously scrutinize proposals before they are officially accepted, ensuring their suitability,
and then appointments could be made. This would be acceptable.”
Thereupon, the Shěngguān Yuàn (Court of Scrutiny for Officials) was established.
All matters sent to it for meticulous scrutiny
were to be reported to the emperor or submitted to the province within five days.
In Chéng'ān fifth year (1201),
due to a shortage of sixth-rank and associate fifth-rank officials,
an imperial edict stipulated that officials must have served three terms as a regular seventh-rank official before being promoted to sixth-rank.
In Tàihé first year (1201),
an imperial decree was issued to the Grand Councilors, saying:
“When encountering an urgent vacancy,
rather than using someone whose qualifications are not yet sufficient,
why not simply reinstate old officials who had been observing mourning leave?”
It was commanded that officials, both internal and external, whose total service
entitled them to a higher rank but who were short by fifteen months,
should remain in their current positions to complete the required time,
and then be promoted or transferred.
Any surplus months or days thereafter would be accumulated.
If a vacancy arose and there was no suitable person,
then a person with the closest qualifications would be proposed to the emperor.
In the second year (1202),
it was decreed that those short by five months or less should be filled in their current post,
while those short by six to fourteen months should be filled in their current post or by a separate appointment.
After this system was implemented,
by the sixth year (1206),
fearing that a uniform, progressive promotion might lead to excessive numbers,
it was commanded that candidates be recommended based on their abilities.
In Dà'ān first year (1209) of Emperor Wèishàowáng,
it was stipulated that among civil officials who had risen through the ranks from their original positions,
those who had reached the first-rank official position and were eligible for promotion to a first-rank honorary title
were only allowed to apply for promotion after serving for fifty actual months.
Second-rank and third-rank officials who were eligible to apply for progressive promotion within their current rank
also needed to serve fifty months,
and could not exceed their current rank.
For fourth-rank and lower officials who were to be promoted to third-rank,
they also needed to serve fifty months,
and were only permitted to apply for one third-rank increment.
Sixth-rank and lower officials applied for promotion after sixty months,
but once they reached third-rank, they were no longer permitted to apply for further promotion.
Those who violated the selection regulations were all disallowed.
If one had already reached a third-rank or higher official position,
sixty months were also acceptable.
For all promotions to third-rank honorary titles, as well as retirement and irregular promotions to third-rank,
the details of their conduct were to be reported to the emperor.
For fourth-rank, promotion could be applied for after sixty months,
but this did not apply to miscellaneous ranks.
In Xīngdìng first year (1216) of Emperor Xuānzōng,
Túdān Wánsēng said:
“Since the outbreak of war,
numerous imperial favors have been bestowed,
and those who have advanced in rank due to meritorious service have been particularly numerous in recent years.
Low-ranking and subordinate honorary officials sometimes reach the highest ranks,
and nothing makes the titles and dignities lighter than this.
From now on, unless one is an imperial prince or a first-rank official,
other individuals, even if their honorary rank reaches first-rank, should not be permitted to be enfeoffed as dukes.
If someone has already been enfeoffed,
although their ceremonial guard will not be stripped,
their ceremonial regulations should be downgraded to those of a second-rank official.”
This was followed.
For the selection of Censor-Inspectors,
the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) would present a list of talented individuals by name,
awaiting imperial appointment.
Upon completion of their term,
the Yùshǐ Tái (Censorate) would report on their competence,
and based on the public affairs they inspected, would record them in their official clearance document,
which was sent to the Shàngshū Shěng.
If the matters they inspected were all free of errors and defects, and they were deemed competent,
then they would receive promotion.
For average performers, an imperial edict would be sought at the time of review.
Those deemed incompetent would be demoted or removed,
and those whose term had not yet expired were not permitted to be reassigned.
Before Dàdìng twenty-seventh year (1187),
it was once stipulated that those aged sixty or above should serve as such.
Later,
the Censorate officials stated that many elderly individuals neglected their duties,
so an imperial edict commanded the Shàngshū Shěng to select honest and capable individuals under sixty from among the sixth- and seventh-rank officials for consideration.
In the twenty-ninth year (1189),
it was decreed that Censorate officials could nominate and appoint their own staff.
In Míngchāng third year (1192),
it was again commanded that the Shàngshū Shěng propose appointments,
listing three or five names for each vacancy,
and an imperial edict would make the appointment.
In Chéng'ān third year (1198),
an imperial edict stipulated that the clearance documents for censors must pass through the relevant department before being presented to the province.
In Tàihé fourth year (1204),
a system was established to determine the excellence of officials based on the number and magnitude of the affairs they inspected, as recorded in their clearance documents.
In the eighth year (1208),
a regulation was established
that those who failed to rectify issues were to be punished for negligence.
In Zhēnyòu second year (1214),
a regulation was established that inspecting five major or ten minor affairs constituted competence;
fewer than these numbers and no pressing duties constituted an average performance;
and two false reports within the inspected matters constituted incompetence.
In the fourth year (1216),
it was commanded that Censorate officials could nominate and appoint,
submitting names to the province
to determine their suitability.
The system of inspection and investigation
first appeared during the reign of Hǎilíng.
Thus, in Zhènglóng second year (1157), sixth month, there was a decree to reinstate officials who had been dismissed due to integrity issues and reassign them to posts.
In Dàdìng third year (1163),
it was decreed that the first-class officials deemed honest and capable by inspection would be promoted one rank and one grade,
while the next class would be assigned based on approximate assessment.
The first-class officials found corrupt and abusive would be demoted by two grades for three years,
the next class for two years,
and the next for one year,
all demoted by one grade.
An imperial edict ordered inspection of Máng'ān and Móukè officials.
The first-class honest and capable would be promoted two ranks,
the next class one rank.
The first-class corrupt and abusive would be flogged a hundred times,
dismissed,
and their brothers selected to replace them.
