The second class would be flogged eighty times,
the third class seventy times,
and all would be ordered to resume their posts.
Púliǎn officials, if found guilty, would be dismissed
and never again appointed to a post.
In the eighth year (1168),
the provincial officials reported on the officials inspected by the Censor-in-Chief Yílā Dào.
The Emperor said:
“Many officials are greedy and abusive,
leading to their downfall and dismissal.
Others simply drift along, passing their days.
If those currently inspected are truly commendable and deserving of praise,
yet if they are immediately promoted or transferred,
I fear it would not satisfy the people's desire to retain them.
Instead, they may receive an additional rank,
and be promoted or transferred once their term expires.”
In the first month of the tenth year (1170),
the Emperor said to the Grand Councilors:
“Currently, many official positions in the prefectures and counties across the realm are vacant.
I wish to employ people without regard to their service records,
but how can I universally know their abilities?
I had considered sending envoys to conduct inspections,
but I worry about disturbing the people and not discovering the truth.
If I were to implement the system of personal recommendation and appointment,
I also fear that in the long run it would lead to abuses.
It would be better to select people to conduct secret investigations and open inspections.
If their findings are consistent,
then promotions and demotions can be made.
What do you think?”
The Grand Councilors replied:
“It should be as Your Majesty instructs.”
In the eleventh year (1171),
when reports on good and bad officials were presented,
the Emperor said:
“For those with serious offenses, send officials to deal with them directly.
For minor infractions, it is probably because they cannot control their wives and children.
They should be admonished and released.
For all honest and capable officials,
those of fourth rank and below shall be entrusted to officials for verification;
if confirmed, they shall be promoted.
Those of third rank and above shall be reported,
and I will personally decide their fate.”
At that time, there were those who suggested
“entrusting one of the Grand Councilors to conduct inspections every three years.”
The Emperor believed that
if high-ranking ministers went out, the prefectures and counties would be disturbed,
and who would then dare to carry out their duties?
The current system of secret investigation and open inquiry,
he believed, struck the right balance.
He also said to the Grand Councilors:
“I wished to know the good and bad qualities of officials throughout the realm,
so I sent out investigators frequently,
and many were promoted or demoted.
This should serve as an encouragement.
However, if investigative officials are always in place,
I fear that if the wrong people are appointed to such roles, it could lead to abuses,
which is why I have temporarily suspended it.”
They all said:
“If this office is not established,
how can we know the good and bad qualities of officials?”
The Left Chancellor, Liángbì, said:
“From now on, we, your humble servants, will personally investigate with utmost diligence.”
The Emperor said:
“You should be more thorough,
and not allow names and reality to become confused.”
In the twelfth year,
regarding the purity and strength of Tóngzhī Chéngyángjūn Shān Héshàng and others,
the emperor said:
"These individuals,
whether secretly investigated or openly observed, all have distinguished political reputations.
Indeed, rewards and punishments must be trustworthy,
then the good will be encouraged and the wicked will be deterred.
If this principle is long maintained, it is possible to acquire talented people.
Let their political achievements be ranked and they be honored and rewarded."
In the third month,
an edict stated that if corrupt officials who had already been investigated for integrity
were allowed to remain in office, they would certainly harm the people again.
Therefore, special envoys should be dispatched to all circuits,
and they should be dismissed immediately.
In the twenty-eighth year of Dàdìng,
it was decreed that officials such as Gémén Zhīhòu, Bǐyàn Chéngfèng, Fèngzhí, Fēi Hùwèi, Dōnggōng Rùdiàn Xiǎodǐ, Zōngshì Lángjūn, Wángfǔ Lángjūn, and Shěnglángjūn
should first be selected and tested for their abilities before being appointed,
without the need for integrity investigations (tǐchá).
Officials such as Nèicáng Běnbǎ, Bùrùdiàn Xiǎodǐ, and Yǔrùdiàn Xiǎodǐ, as well as Zhībǎ Shūhuà,
also did not require integrity investigations.
In the third year of Míngchāng,
it was decreed that for those investigated whose integrity was praised,
but whose political achievements were ordinary,
an imperial order would prevent their demotion.
Regarding Shí Zhòngyuān and four others,
although they were incorruptible and liked by the common people,
there were also comments that their actions sought to pander to popular sentiment.
Thus, they were different from truly fair, incorruptible, and capable individuals,
so an imperial order decreed their demotion.
In general, those with ordinary administrative records
would have one month's salary deducted from the official who originally recommended them.
In the fourth year,
the emperor said:
"When a person is recommended,
sometimes the initial investigation differs
from a subsequent investigation after being re-recommended by others, or
sometimes the initial investigation is consistent,
but a later investigation differs.
How should such cases be handled?
Discuss a method that can be permanently implemented without obstruction and report it."
The provincial ministers (shěng chén) reported:
"If the recommendation and the integrity investigation are inconsistent,
the official can be removed from duties within the jurisdiction of the Tíxíngsī that is not affiliated with the recommender,
and another integrity investigation should be ordered.
If it is consistent, they will be employed according to the regulations.
If inconsistent, they will revert to their original qualifications."
At that time, there was a suggestion
"that officials responsible for recommending people
should be limited by number each year,
and their qualifications for appointment reduced."
On that day,
the provincial ministers collectively reported
that this might lead to the long-term abuses of persistent appeals and seeking undue favors.
Therefore, they proposed
"if the recommended official's integrity investigation matches the recommendation,
they shall be promoted as appropriate.
If they do not live up to the recommendation, the original recommending official shall be demoted or punished proportionally.
If one seeks recommendation through self-solicitation,
or through influential connections, or by having others intercede and recommend them,
each shall be stripped of one official rank.
Those who accepted bribes shall be punished for perverting justice,
and the integrity investigating officials shall also be subject to the same penalties.
There shall be no limit to the number of recommendations made each year.
Failure to recommend shall not be punished,
but if the recommended person does not live up to expectations, there shall be demotion or punishment.
This way, people will not dare to make indiscriminate recommendations,
and truly capable individuals can be obtained."
The emperor said:
"This can be implemented as regulations
for one or two years,
and then we shall consider other methods."
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
since the Ànchásī no longer concurrently handled investigations and interviews,
the system of "píngdǎo biélù chúshòu" (appointment through separate paths for fair and unjust cases) was abolished.
In the first year of Tàihé,
a system was established:
beyond the vacancies of the first rank,
when vacancies of the second rank were filled,
those eligible for appointment as xiànlìng (county magistrates) would be promoted to shànglìng (upper magistrate);
those with one less term would be given zhōnglìng (middle magistrate);
those with two less terms would be given xiàlìng (lower magistrate);
those with three or more less terms would be given lùshì jūnfángpàn (recorder and military defense judge),
and their qualification reduced by one,
and then appointed as xiànlìng.
Those with five or more less terms would be appointed as chéngbù (assistant and registrar).
Upon completing terms of the third rank,
those eligible for appointment as xiànlìng would be promoted to zhōnglìng;
those with one less term would be given xiàlìng;
those with two or more less terms would be given lùshì fángpàn,
their qualification also reduced by one,
and then appointed as xiànlìng.
Those with four or more less terms would all be appointed as chéngbù.
Those who had already served as xiànlìng,
upon completion of their official tenure, would be given shànglìng,
and still, according to their respective ranks and qualifications, have two terms generally reduced before being presented to the province (shěng).
Those who had already served as seventh-grade and sixth-grade officials would have one qualification reduced for appointment.
Those recommended and appointed as xiànlìng,
if their public reputation was consistent with the recommendation,
would be promoted without waiting for term completion based on their qualifications and evaluations.
Those currently serving at court (suízhāo) would be promoted upon completion of their evaluations.
After promotion, if future re-evaluations found them to be fair, incorruptible, and capable, they would not be demoted.
After Xuānzōng moved south,
he often used censors (yùshǐ) for inspections.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
considering that county officials might not be capable,
and that one visit from a supervisory censor (jiānchá yùshǐ) could not fully ascertain the situation,
it was decreed that supervisory censors be dispatched twice a year for inspections.
Additionally, other officials would be selected to conduct visits and investigations,
in order to implement policies of promotion and demotion.
In the first year of Zhèngdà during Āizōng's reign,
the Sīnóngsī was established.
From the minister (qīng) downwards, officials would take turns inspecting the good and bad conduct of local administrations,
and promote or demote based on this.
Recommendations.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
an edict ordered six-grade officials and above serving at court and five-grade officials and above in outer circuits
to each recommend one incorruptible and capable official.
In the third year,
a system was established:
if the investigation found the recommended person to be as described,
their commendation and appointment would be discussed.
If their reputation was汚(wū) (tainted) or excessive,
the recommending official would be proportionally demoted or punished.
In the ninth year,
the emperor said:
"I wish to obtain loyal and incorruptible ministers
to govern together with me. Therefore, I once ordered officials of the fifth rank and above to each recommend those they knew.
Several years have passed since then.
With the vastness of the empire,
how could there be no such people?
It is because those in high positions know them but do not recommend them."
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Wèi Zǐpíng reported:
"Officials who are supposed to recommend people
should be required to recommend one person for each term of office,
and their commendation or reward should be based on whether the recommendation is appropriate."
The emperor said:
"If one recommends one person per term,
it might be difficult to find suitable talent,
and could lead to indiscriminate recommendations.
Furthermore, if the recommended person commits even a small offense, the recommender is punished,
which makes people more fearful and reluctant to recommend.
In Sòng, if a recommended official committed a crime,
even the highest officials (zǎizhí) who made the recommendation could not escape demotion or dismissal.
However, if they had a reputation for ability,
they would be promoted and rewarded.
Moreover, people naturally desire advancement at first,
thus they are often incorruptible and cautious.
Once appointed,
they might lose their integrity.
Since the zǎizhí themselves hold the power of demotion and promotion,
how can they be punished because of their recommendations?"
Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Gēshíliè Liángbì said:
"The previous order has already been issued,
commanding recommendations."
In the tenth year,
the emperor said:
"Regarding the method of recommending people,
if we stipulate how many people a third-grade official should recommend,
this will cause lower-ranking officials to flatter their superiors.
Only by inquiring about previous administrations upon completion of terms
can suitable people be obtained."
In the eleventh year,
the emperor said to his chief ministers (zǎichén):
"Yesterday, I reviewed the notices,
and there are many vacancies for officials of the fifth rank and below,
yet it is difficult to find suitable people.
As for officials of the third rank and above,
I know them myself.
But for officials of the fifth rank and below,
I cannot know them all.
You, my ministers, have never said a word to recommend anyone.
How can I manage the affairs of the state by myself?
I have often thought about this,
wishing to devise a plan for long-term stability
and benefit the common people,
but without good assistants,
whatever I do will only be ordinary matters."
In the nineteenth year,
at that time, the imperial court would promote officials who were praised and highly regarded by the people.
Later,
the emperor found that people from various circuits who came to the capital to recommend or request appointments
often lacked true integrity and capability,
and many were merely used by others to seek fame.
Therefore, such requests were not to be entertained.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng during Zhāngzōng's reign,
the emperor tasked Fèngyù Gérǔ with conveying to the Shàngshūshěng (Department of State Affairs) to devise and propose a system for ten matters concerning selection and appointment.
The first was:
"According to old regulations,
even Jìnshì and those with military merits, who were highest-ranking,
were initially appointed as chéngbù.
Only after their fifth term as xiànlìng would they be promoted to regular seventh grade,
and after two terms as regular seventh grade,
they would..."
His rank rose from the sixth-rank to the sixth-rank.
After three terms in the sixth-rank, he rose to the collateral fifth-rank.
After two terms in the collateral fifth-rank, he rose to the principal fifth-rank.
After three terms in the principal fifth-rank, he then rose to Cìshǐ.
It took over forty years
to finally reach the position of Cìshǐ.
The qualifications for other positions are also evident.
Constrained by the rigidity of qualifications,
it came to this.
He ordered the Tíxíngsī to search for
usable talents,
reduce the requirements for qualifications and appoint them,
so that capable individuals would not become old and infirm. "
The ministers of the province then proposed,
that those who required three terms for promotion be reduced to two terms.
Within
these qualifications,
when there were many vacancies in various ranks,
then from among those who had not yet completed their second term,
individuals of talent and diligence who could be promoted exceptionally,
as well as those identified by the Tíxíngsī
in the outer circuits,
should be promoted.
The second point stated:
"According to the old regulations,
those who served diligently at court and were promoted or demoted based on their qualifications
were demoted again upon completion of their term when they returned.
For example, a principal seventh-rank official, upon returning from a completed term, was demoted to the collateral
seventh-rank;
a collateral fifth-rank official, upon returning, was demoted to the sixth-rank, and so on.
Now, if the person truly possesses talent and ability,
they may be exempted from demotion."
The Shàngshū Lìbù then proposed,
that for those who complete their assessment
at court now,
and are transferred to official positions of the fifth-rank and below in outer circuits,
as well as those who are truly capable upon completion of their assessed tenure in secondary positions,
within fifteen months
to twenty months before the completion of their current official tenure,
they should be investigated and recommended to the province.
The third point stated:
"For honest and capable officials found by the Tíxíng in the various circuits,
they should be directly assigned to suitable positions
and transferred accordingly."
The fourth point stated:
"For a long time, prime ministers have not been allowed to meet with officials seeking promotion.
How then can the quality of talent in the empire be known?
They should be allowed to meet
to
seek out talented individuals."
The Shàngshū Xíngbù commented,
"According to the regulations,
officials seeking promotion were not allowed to visit high-ranking officials at their private residences.
Violators would be stripped of one rank, demoted, and reported for dismissal.
If
there were requests or gifts,
it should be reported to the emperor,
and the Yùshǐ would be entrusted with investigation."
The Emperor then ordered this regulation abolished.
The fifth point stated:
"In the past,
even if a minister knew that a friend or relative was capable,
they would avoid suspicion and not recommend them.
In ancient times, recommending the virtuous did not avoid relatives
or enemies.
For example, Qí Xī recommended his enemy,
Rénjié recommended his son,
and Cuī Yòufǔ appointed eight hundred officials, all of whom were relatives or old acquaintances.
Therefore, officials of the fifth-rank and above
should each recommend several individuals
they know.
Violators will be punished for concealing talent."
The Lìbù deliberated:
Officials of the fifth-rank and above, both inside and outside the court,
shall recommend one honest and capable official each year.
Outer-circuit officials of the fifth-rank
and court officials of the sixth-rank who wish to recommend are permitted.
If the person recommended is not as stated,
the recommender shall be demoted or penalized according to the circumstances.
It is now proposed that those who know of virtuous individuals but do not recommend them
should also be demoted or penalized
according to the circumstances.
The sixth point stated:
"In previous dynasties, after an official arrived at their post,
they would immediately recommend someone capable of replacing them.
It is now ordered that officials of the fifth-rank and above,
from now on, recommend their own replacements to ensure smooth
handover."
The Lìbù consulted the Táng Huìyào:
In the imperial edict of the first year of Jiànzhōng,
besides regular civil and military court officials,
Jiédù, Guānchá, Fángyù, Jūnshǐ, Cìshǐ, Chì
lìng, Jīlìng, and all clean officials of the seventh-rank and above, as well as Dàlǐ Sīzhí Píngshì,
within three days of receiving their appointments,
were to submit a memorial at the Sìfāngguǎn,
recommending one person to
replace themselves.
Outer-circuit officials were to send their reports by swift post.
The memorials would be forwarded to the Zhōngshūménxià,
and whenever there was a vacancy, the most frequently recommended individuals would be appointed.
It is now proposed that officials of the fifth-rank and above,
both inside and outside the court, upon arriving at their posts,
must recommend one capable and virtuous official they know to replace themselves.
The Tàifù, Céngxiàng, and Píngzhāng said,
"Talented individuals have been rare since ancient times.
If we order them to recommend their
own replacements,
we fear it will lead to abuses and fail to secure truly capable individuals."
The Cānzhèng said,
"Recommending a replacement does not mean immediately replacing the person.
It merely means listing their names,
and appointing those who are most frequently recommended
according to the circumstances.
This is perhaps the lingering intention of Shùn's officials yielding to each other,
and Zhōu officials recommending the virtuous."
The Emperor agreed with the Cānzhèng's statement, as it was consistent with the Lìbù's.
He followed it.
The seventh point stated:
"Chief officials at court and in outer circuits,
within one term, are sufficiently aware of the capabilities of their subordinates.
They should be ordered to recommend several individuals during each term."
The Lìbù proposed,
that chief officials of the fifth-rank and above, both inside and outside the court,
must recommend one capable official from among their subordinates.
Those who recommend more than this number are permitted.
The eighth point stated:
"Talent exists in all walks of life.
Among those who oversee various materials and hermits in the wilderness,
there are indeed talented individuals.
They should be recommended and employed."
The Lìbù proposed,
that from among those overseeing various materials,
outer-circuit officials of the fifth-rank and court officials of the sixth-rank and above
should recommend honest and capable individuals,
stating their specific strengths.
A written report should be transferred and submitted
to the province.
An official will be dispatched to investigate and verify the facts,
and they will be appointed according to their abilities.
For hermits in the wilderness,
a general order should be sent to all prefectures and counties,
and the Tíxíngsī should investigate and report to the province.
Individuals of various backgrounds
and talents
should be recommended by officials of the fifth-rank and above, both inside and outside the court.
The ninth point stated:
"Among the imperial guards assigned to official posts,
there are some who are particularly skilled in martial arts and exceptionally brave.
Officials inside and outside the court should recommend them, and the Tíxíngsī should investigate them.
If their qualifications
are high,
they can be appointed as border Cìshǐ, Tóngzhī, or Xiànlìng."
The Lìbù proposed,
that if they adhere to the standard qualifications,
it might impede talented individuals.
If they are truly found through recommendation and investigation,
they should be appointed
by reducing one level of standard qualification.
The Shàngshūshěng proposed,
to promote and appoint them according to the imperial decree.
The tenth point stated:
"For talented individuals recommended by officials inside and outside the court,
they should be tested according to the recommendation.
The Tíxíngsī will be entrusted with investigating the truthfulness of the claims.
If they are indeed competent,
they will be further
promoted.
If they are merely mediocre,
they will be assigned to regular duties.
In ancient times, those who promoted the virtuous received high rewards,
and those who promoted the unworthy were punished.
Clear rules for rewards and punishments should be established,
so that people
dare not act out of private interest."
The ministers of the province deliberated,
that if each section required individuals to be recommended,
then one person would recommend no fewer than five or seven individuals.
[一四] Since ancient times, knowing people has been difficult,
and talented individuals are also hard to find.
If the number limit is too high, people will avoid responsibility and act perfunctorily,
which would not fulfill the sacred ruler's desire for talent.
It is proposed that for each of the aforementioned items,
an individual from each background
who can recommend one person
will fulfill the annual recommendation quota.
This way, there will be no abuses,
and truly capable individuals will be secured.
For the number of tribute individuals each year,
the Shàngshūshěng will review and confirm.
Then, they will be registered in a ledger.
If there is a vacancy, a proposal will be submitted according to their abilities.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
an imperial edict stated that among the common people, those with virtue and talent
should be recommended by prefectures and counties,
and be specially granted the same status as those recommended in four or five selections.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
a regulation was enacted that if the recommended individuals were mediocre and showed no outstanding qualities,
the recommending official would be punished according to the rules.
In the first year of Xuānzōng's Xīngdìng reign (1212),
an order was issued that officials of the seventh rank and above in the court, and those of the sixth rank and above in outlying regions,
should recommend one official of the seventh rank and below who was under sixty, had not committed embezzlement, and was capable of serving.
In the third year (1214),
regulations for the selection and recommendation of xiànlìng (county magistrates) were established.
If the recommended official was competent,
the original recommender's seniority would be reduced by one grade.
If they were average,
their promotion or demotion would be assessed accordingly.
If they were incompetent,
their salary would be docked for one month.
If they committed an offense leading to dismissal,
the recommender would be dismissed from their current office.
If the official was dismissed for a private crime, punished by caning, or committed embezzlement or bribery,
the recommender would be demoted or dismissed accordingly.
If the bribery or embezzlement was severe enough to warrant penal servitude or dismissal from office,
the recommender's service record would not be considered for one term.
For those of the third rank and above who recommended xiànlìng,
if the recommended official was competent, their promotion or demotion would be assessed accordingly;
if incompetent, their salary would be docked for one month.
If the recommended official committed an offense leading to dismissal,
the recommender's salary would be docked for two months.
If the bribery or embezzlement was severe enough to warrant penal servitude or dismissal from office,
the recommender's salary would be docked for three months.
If a case was concluded
but later pardoned by an imperial amnesty,
the recommender would also be pardoned.
In the fifth year (1216),
a regulation was enacted stating that if a recommended xiànlìng was assessed as average,
the original recommender could not recommend again,
but others were permitted to recommend.
Furthermore, according to old regulations,
after a recommended xiànlìng completed their term,
their promotion or demotion was judged based on six criteria:
fewer than three criteria met resulted in a reduction of one grade of seniority,
fewer than four criteria resulted in a reduction of two grades of seniority,
and if all six criteria were met, they would be promoted by one rank.
Subsequently, Censor Zhāng Shēngqīng said:
"Those who passed the imperial examination with a middle or lower grade, and supervisors reaching the rank of Míngwēi (indicating eligibility for xiànchéng or zhǔbù positions),
if they met fewer than three criteria, would have one grade of seniority deducted and be appointed to a lower-grade magistracy.
If they met fewer than four criteria, they would be appointed to a middle-grade magistracy.
Magistrates are all of the seventh rank,
but this would effectively make them eighth rank.
Since the severity of punishments contradicts the ranks,
it is appropriate to revise this."
Thus, new regulations were established:
henceforth, meeting fewer than four criteria would be as previously stipulated,
but for those who met all six criteria,
graduates of the imperial examination with middle or lower grades, and supervisors who were eligible for xiànchéng or zhǔbù positions,
three grades of seniority would be deducted,
and they would be appointed to a higher-grade magistracy.
The same applied to those of other backgrounds.
If they served for more than twenty months,
even if their term was not yet complete,
if they left office for a valid reason,
and their performance regarding the six criteria had already been reviewed and inspected,
their promotion would be assessed as if they had completed their term.
In the fifth year (1216),
because recommenders either showed favoritism to relatives, yielded to requests, or made erroneous judgments, leading to arbitrary recommendations,
over ninety individuals were dismissed for incompetence within a few years.
Consequently, the system of selecting and recommending xiànlìng was abolished.
By the first year of Āizōng's Zhèngdà reign (1224),
a law was enacted
ordering the Censorate and the Sīnóngsī (Ministry of Agriculture) officials
to first investigate officials of the seventh rank and above in the court and those of the sixth rank and above in outlying regions,
identifying those who were clear, cautious, and upright and could serve as recommenders.
Then, official dispatches would be sent, asking them to recommend those they knew.
Their performance would still be assessed by the six criteria,
and the recommenders would be promoted or demoted accordingly.
Thus, recommenders exerted their full effort,
and the recommended officials also exerted their full effort.
Although the country was then facing imminent collapse,
the xiànlìng were said to be well-chosen,
which demonstrates that the method of drafting the law had its merits.
Regulations for "compensating for deficits and eternal accounts."
For all officials responsible for supervising yàuwù (affairs of a yānméng),
they would be promoted one rank every thirty months.
A full year was calculated as a complete cycle,
and only months and days without deficits were counted.
In the fourth year of Dàdìng (1164),
regulations were established:
within one term, a deficit of one fēn or more would result in the demotion of five people;
two fēn or more, ten people;
three fēn or more, fifteen people.
If there was an increase, promotions would be made accordingly.
Any remaining fractional increases or decreases
would be carried over to the next term.
In the twenty-first year (1181),
because the old system of holding supervisory officials responsible for losses,
and those without integrity,
believed that once a judgment was made, they could immediately be reassigned,
and were not deterred by punishment,
it was proposed that henceforth,
if the "eternal accounts" showed a deficit of one "reward" or more,
in addition to being removed from office for one year according to regulations,
even if the deficit in "eternal accounts" was less than one "reward,"
they would also be removed from office for one year.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng during Zhāngzōng's reign (1189),
the annual promotion system was abolished,
and new regulations were established:
if the "eternal accounts" showed an increase of one "reward" compared to the target, they would be promoted one rank;
two "rewards," two ranks.
If there was a deficit, the demotion would be similar,
up to a maximum of two ranks.
Also abolished was the system where junior supervisors of the administrative offices were assessed for increases and deficits along with their superiors,
as well as the system of carrying over fractional increases or decreases to the next term.
[一五]
In the first year of Tàihé (1201),
regulations were enacted for those who violated selection rules or incurred "eternal account" deficits:
Right-rank Han officials up to Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn (senior fifth rank) and Jurchen officials up to Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn (principal fifth rank)
could be appointed as xiànlìng.
Also, according to official regulations,
those who had violated selection rules or incurred "eternal account" deficits,
Jurchen officials up to Wǔyì (junior sixth rank) and Han and other ethnic officials up to Wǔlüè (junior sixth rank),
were all appointed to various ministries,
with one appointment for every two positions.
Only upon reaching Míngwēi could they be appointed as xiànchéng or zhǔbù.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu (1215),
regulations were enacted that those who had incurred "eternal account" deficits or violated selection rules,
upon promotion to Xuānwǔ,
would be appointed to various ministries.
Upon reaching Huáiyuǎn (junior fourth rank),
they could be appointed as xiànchéng or zhǔbù.
Upon reaching Ānyuǎn (senior fourth rank),
they would be appointed as lower-grade xiànlìng.
In the first year of Zhèngdà (1224),
regulations were enacted that those who had violated selection rules or incurred "eternal account" deficits,
upon reaching Guǎngwēi, would be appointed to various ministries,
with one appointment for every two positions.
Upon reaching Ānyuǎn, they would be appointed as xiànchéng or zhǔbù.
After three terms,
upon reaching Zhènguó (junior third rank),
they could be appointed as lower-grade xiànlìng.
Officials of the Qúnmù (Imperial Horse and Livestock Administration) served for three full years.
The livestock they managed was assessed based on a ratio of ten:
an increase of two camels,
two horses,
or two cattle
[一六]or four sheep.
If out of one hundred large horses, fifteen died,
and if they were able to recover deficits from previous officials
at a rate of three parts,
meaning full recovery or recovery of two and a half parts or more,
they would be classified as "superior,"
and promoted one rank.
An increase of one camel,
two horses or cattle,
or three sheep,
with twenty-five large horses dying out of one hundred,
and recovery of two parts or more of previous officials' deficits,
would be classified as "middle,"
and promotions or demotions would be assessed accordingly.
No increase in camels,
an increase of one horse or cattle,
or two sheep,
with thirty large horses dying out of one hundred,
and recovery of one part or more of deficits,
would be classified as "lower,"
and appointments would be made according to their current rank.
For other livestock, the original numbers would be followed.
If forty large horses died out of one hundred,
and less than one part of deficits was recovered,
they would be demoted one rank.
These were the regulations enacted in the fourth year of Míngchāng (1193).
In the fifth year (1194),
regulations were enacted that if horses, cattle, or sheep fell short of the original numbers by one-tenth,
or if forty gelded horses died out of one hundred,
and less than one part of deficits was recovered,
they would be demoted one rank
and fined forty (blows).
If camels, horses, cattle, or sheep fell short of the original numbers by one part, or forty horses died out of one hundred,
and deficits could not be recovered,
they would be caned eighty blows
and demoted as before.
Collation Notes

Chapter 36, Officials (1): Three Masters, Three Dukes, Department of State Affairs, Six Ministries, Grand Marshal's Office, Bureau of Military Affairs, Grand Imperial Clan Court, Censorate, Pacification Commission, Agricultural Promotion Commission, Ministry of Agriculture, Three Judicial Offices, National History Institute, Hanlin Academy, Court of Judicial Review, Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
The Jīn dynasty began building its officialdom with Jǐngzǔ,
unifying various tribes to specialize in military campaigns,
standing distinctly as a separate nation.
Their high officials
were all called bójíliè,
which is why Tàizǔ succeeded to the throne as Dū Bójíliè,
and Tàizōng served as Ānbǎn Bójíliè in charge of defense.
Ānbǎn
was a title of honor and grandeur.
Next was Guólùn Hūlǔ Bójíliè,
Guólùn indicating nobility, and Hūlǔ meaning something like commander-in-chief.
There was also Guólùn Bójíliè,
sometimes positioned on the left and right, who were what we call Guóxiàng (Grand Chancellors).
Above the other bójíliè,
there were the titles Guólùn, Yǐshì, Hūlǔ, Yílái, Āmǎi, Āshè, [unreadable character], and Dié,
which served as the sequence for promoting and bestowing honors upon imperial clan members and meritorious officials.
Their tribal chiefs were called Bóyùn,
and those who commanded several tribes were called Hūlǔ.
All these
were abolished when Xīzōng established the official system.
Thereafter, the only officials responsible for pacifying the border people were called tūlǐ.
Below the Wūlúgǔ were the Sǎowěntuōlú.
Below the Xiángwěn were the Mēhū and Xíníkūn.
These were stipulated in the official system and were not abolished,
all inheriting the names of Liáo officials.
As for the system of Hàn officials,
since the Píngzhōu people were unwilling to serve as Méng'ān Móukè officials,
they began to establish chief administrators and lower ranks.
In the seventh year of Tiānfǔ, Yǐ Zǔqǐgōng served in the Shūmìyuàn in Guǎngníng,
still following the old system of the Liáo Southern Chancellery.
In the fourth year of Tiānhuì,
the Shàngshūshěng was established,
thus instituting the Three Departments system.
It was not until Xīzōng promulgated the new official system and the regulations for official changes,
and appointed external and internal officials,
that the system of meritorious titles, enfeoffments, and official ranks was finally established,
and only then was its system finalized.
However, in general, it largely followed the old systems of Liáo and Sòng.
In the first year of Zhènglóng, Hǎilíng Shùrén abolished the Zhōngshūshěng and Ménxiàshěng,
retaining only the Shàngshūshěng.
Below the department, the various offices were categorized as
yuàn, tái, fǔ, sī, sì, jiān, jú, shǔ, and suǒ,
each overseeing its subordinates to perform its duties.
Positions had fixed responsibilities,
and staff had constant numbers.
The discipline was clear,
and all affairs were managed,
which is why it was maintained throughout the Jīn dynasty and dared not be changed.
In the twenty-eighth year of Dàdìng,
there were 19,700 officials in service,
over a thousand applied for selection seasonally,
and three thousand were appointed to supervise annually.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng, a memorial stated that
in a full year,
670 officials died or left due to incidents,
510 new officials entered service,
and there were 11,499 incumbent officials,
including 4,705 Nǚzhí officials
and 6,794 Hàn officials.
By the seventh year of Tàihé,
there were over 47,000 officials in service,
1,700 were nominated and appointed seasonally by the Board,
and over 9,290 supervising officials arrived at the Board,
which was three times the number during Shìzōng's time.
As for Xuānzōng's Zhāoxiánsuǒ and Jīnglüè Sī,
and Yìzōng's Yìzhèngyuàn,
although they were policies during times of crisis, they must also be listed in their sequence
to record the events of that time.
Three Grand Masters
Grand Preceptor (tàishī), Grand Mentor (tàifù), Grand Guardian (tàibǎo), each one official,
all of the principal first rank,
served as models
and exemplars for all under heaven.
Three Dukes
Grand Commandant (tàiwèi), Minister of Education (sītú), Minister of Works (sīkōng), each one official,
all of the principal first rank,
deliberated on the Way to govern the state,
and harmonized the yin and yang.
Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng)
Director of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshūlìng), one official,
principal first rank,
generally oversaw the regulations,
and served as a model for the chief minister.
Left Chancellor (zuǒchéngxiàng) and Right Chancellor (yòuchéngxiàng), each one official,
auxiliary first rank,
Co-administrators of Governmental Affairs (píngzhāng zhèngshì), two officials,
auxiliary first rank,
served as prime ministers,
assisting the Son of Heaven,
and co-administering all affairs.
Left Vice-Director (zuǒchéng) and Right Vice-Director (yòuchéng), each one official,
principal second rank,
Participators in Political Affairs (cānzhī zhèngshì), two officials,
auxiliary second rank,
served as executive officials,
as deputies to the prime ministers,
assisting in departmental affairs.
Left Bureau (Zuǒsī)
Director (lángzhōng), one official,
principal fifth rank.
(In the early days of the dynasty, Left and Right Bureau Attendants (zuǒ yòu sī shìláng) were established.
In the third year of Tiānjuàn, they first changed to the current name.
Previously, for all court audiences,
executive officials personally presented memorials.
In the second year of Tiāndé, an edict assigned this to the Left and Right Bureau officials,
making it a fixed system.)
Assistant Director (yuánwàiláng), one official,
principal sixth rank,
managed memorial presentations for the bureau,
generally supervised the receipt and transfer of matters for the Boards of Civil Office, Revenue, and Rites,
and concurrently served as officials for compiling the Diary of Activity and Repose,
avoiding describing matters related to their own involvement.
At the first court audience of each month,
those whose terms were completed that month were first gathered to form a roster,
called the Què
běn,
along with the Xingzhǐbù, Tiēhuángbù, and official regulations, which were jointly presented.
After imperial review, they were received and stored.
Whenever appointments were made,
for any positions that the Shàngshūshěng
dared not nominate,
two or three candidates were listed in one Què to await imperial appointment.
Administrator (dūshì), two officials,
principal seventh rank.
(In the second year of Zhēnyuán,
officials of the Left and Right Bureaus were selected from three categories:
those who started their careers in the imperial palace,
jinshì degree holders, and clerks.
In the third year,
Censor-in-Chiefs (jiānchá yùshǐ) were instructed to sequentially report on suitable candidates,
and no longer make nominations.)
They managed the receipt and transfer of matters for the bureau,
inspected and checked for errors, reviewed provincial and agency documents,
and concurrently oversaw overnight duty within the province,
and inspected shelved archives, etc.
The responsibilities of the Right Bureau were the same.
Right Bureau (Yòusī)
Director (lángzhōng), one official,
principal fifth rank,
Assistant Director (yuánwàiláng), one official,
principal sixth rank,
managed memorial presentations for the bureau,
generally supervised the receipt and transfer of matters for the Boards of War, Punishments, and Works,
and concurrently served as officials for compiling notes,
avoiding describing matters related to their own involvement.
Administrator (dūshì), two officials,
principal seventh rank.
Shàngshūshěng Zhīhòulángjūn Guǎnggòuguān,
auxiliary seventh rank,
managed the Zhīhòulángjūn,
diligently supervising their comings and goings and their assignments.
(Before the second year of Chéng'ān,
Zǒumǎlángjūn were nominated.
Tàihé regulations stipulated
that Left and Right Nǚzhí Dūshì concurrently held the post.
During the Zhèngdà period,
trusted retainers were used instead.)
Shelved Archives (Jiàgékù) (Established in the sixth month of the twenty-first year of Dàdìng,
and continued to be overseen by the Dūshì.)
Director (guǎnggòu),
(formerly two officials,
reduced by one in Zhèngdà.)
principal eighth rank,
Deputy Director (tóngguǎnggòu),
(formerly two officials,
reduced by one in Zhèngdà.)
auxiliary eighth rank,
generally supervised the collection and transfer of documents by the Dàchéngguān of the Left and Right Bureaus,
and oversaw the distribution and receipt of paper and brushes by the Xiǎodūjiān,
with other guǎnggòu having similar duties.
(Nǚzhí clerks (lìshǐ) in the Department: thirty-five persons,
twenty in the Left,
fifteen in the Right.
In the twenty-fourth year of Dàdìng, there were thirty:
ten jinshì,
ten sons of chief ministers and imperial clansmen,
ten clerks from the Mìyuàntáibùtǒngjūnsī.
Hàn clerks: thirty-five persons,
twenty-
one in the Left, fourteen in the Right.
Departmental translators (yìshǐ): fourteen persons,
seven in the Left and seven in the Right.
Nǚzhí translators were the same.
Interpreters (tōngshì): eight persons,
four in the Left and four in the Right.
Gāolí, Xiàguó, and Huíhé translators: four persons,
two in the Left and two in the Right.
Interpreters for various tribes: six persons.
Yēlā: twenty persons.
Zǒumǎlángjūn: fifty persons.)
Department for Supervision of Annual Gifts (Tídiǎnsùicísuǒ)
The Directors and Assistant Directors of the Left and Right Bureaus concurrently held this post,
managing the supervision of the receipt and disbursement of money and silk for annual gifts.
Departmental Mess and Public Service Wine Repository (Tángshí Gōngshǐ Jiǔkù)
Administrator (shǐ), one official,
auxiliary eighth rank,
managed the receipt and distribution of annual gift funds,
and generally oversaw repository affairs.
Deputy (fù), one official,
principal ninth rank,
managed deputy administrator affairs.
Departmental Protocol Office (Zhíshěngjú)
Director (júzhǎng),
auxiliary eighth rank,
managed the etiquette of the main hall and the ceremonies for officials' visits and thanks.
Deputy Director (fùjúzhǎng),
principal ninth rank,
managed deputy director affairs.
Administrator of the Department of State Affairs' Musicians (Guǎnggòu Shàngshūshěng Yuègōng),
auxiliary ninth rank.
The system of the Xíngtái.
In Xīzōng's Tiānhuì fifteenth year (1137),
Liú Yù was deposed,
and the Xíngtái Shàngshū Shěng was established in Biàn.
In Tiānjuàn first year (1138),
the land of Hénán was given to the Sòng,
and so the Yānjīng Shūmì was changed to the Xíngtái Shàngshū Shěng.
In Tiānjuàn third year (1140),
it was again moved and established in Biànjīng.
In Huángtǒng second year (1142),
it was decreed that the ranks of Xíngtái officials were all one grade lower than those of the Zhōngtái.
The Six Ministries,
in the early days of the dynasty, had their documents jointly signed with the Zuǒ and Yòu Sī.
It was only in Tiānjuàn third year (1140) that they began to administer separately.
The Lìbù
had one Shàngshū,
of zhèng sān pǐn rank.
One Shìláng,
of zhèng sì pǐn rank.
Two Lángzhōng,
of cóng wǔ pǐn rank.
(In Tiāndé second year (1150),
this was increased to four members,
later reduced.)
Yuánwàiláng,
of cóng liù pǐn rank.
(In Tiāndé second year (1150),
this was increased to four members,
later reduced.)
They were in charge of the administration of civil and military appointments, honors, enfeoffments, performance reviews, and the issuance of imperial edicts.
Based on talent, conduct, effort, and effectiveness,
they evaluated the worthiness or unworthiness of officials;
based on conduct, documents, and the tiēhuáng record,
they determined the crucial matters of official vacancies.
Officials of zhèng qī pǐn and above
were reported by name to the ministry
for imperial appointment.
For officials of cóng qī pǐn and below,
at the end of each quarter, appointments were proposed according to their qualifications.
For those of bā pǐn and above, a memorial was submitted to the emperor,
but not for those below.
From the Shìláng downwards,
all served as deputies to the Shàngshū.
The Lángzhōng managed civil and military appointments, promotions for those outside the regular ranks, assignments for officials, registers of conduct, and decrees for enfeoffments.
One member managed grades of merit, rewards, hereditary succession, promotions through privilege, retirement, performance reviews, and posthumous titles.
The Yuánwàiláng divided and managed the various departmental affairs and participated in discussions,
their responsibilities being the same as those of the Lángzhōng.
For civil officials, there were nine ranks,
comprising forty-two grades in total:
Cóng yī pǐn upper was called Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
middle Yítóng Sānsī,
next middle Tèjìn,
lower Chóngjìn.
Zhèng èr pǐn upper was called Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
lower Yínqīng Rónglù Dàfū.
Cóng èr pǐn upper was called Guānglù Dàfū,
lower Rónglù Dàfū.
Zhèng sān pǐn upper was called Zīdé Dàfū,
middle Zīzhèng Dàfū,
lower Zīshàn Dàfū.
Cóng sān pǐn upper was called Zhèngfèng Dàfū,
middle Tōngfèng Dàfū,
lower Zhōngfèng Dàfū.
Zhèng sì pǐn upper was called Zhèngyì Dàfū,
middle Tōngyì Dàfū,
lower Jiāyì Dàfū.
Cóng sì pǐn upper was called Dàzhōng Dàfū,
middle Zhōngdàfū,
lower Shàozhōng Dàfū.
Zhèng wǔ pǐn upper was called Zhōngyì Dàfū,
middle Zhōngxiàn Dàfū,
lower Zhōngshùn Dàfū.
Cóng wǔ pǐn upper was called Cháoqǐng Dàfū,
middle Cháosàn Dàfū,
lower Cháoliè Dàfū.
(Formerly called Fèngdé Dàfū,
changed in Tiāndé second year (1150).)
Zhèng liù pǐn upper was called Fèngzhèng Dàfū,
lower Fèngyì Dàfū.
Cóng liù pǐn upper was called Fèngzhí Dàfū,
lower Fèngxùn Dàfū.
Zhèng qī pǐn upper was called Chéngdé Láng,
lower Chéngzhí Láng.
Cóng qī pǐn upper was called Chéngwù Láng,
lower Rúlín Láng.
Zhèng bā pǐn upper was called Wénlín Láng,
lower Chéngshì Láng.
Cóng bā pǐn upper was called Zhēngshì Láng,
lower Cóngshì Láng.
Zhèng jiǔ pǐn upper was called Dēngshì Láng,
lower Jiāngshì Láng.
Cóng jiǔ pǐn upper was called Dēngshì Zuǒláng,
lower Jiāngshì Zuǒláng.
(These two grades
were newly added in Dàdìng fourteenth year (1174).)
For military scattered ranks,
all who reached cóng èr pǐn and above up to cóng yī pǐn
used civil ranks.
From zhèng sān pǐn downwards,
the grades were the same as civil ranks:
Zhèng sān pǐn upper was called Lónghǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn,
middle Jīnwǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn,
lower Piàojíwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn.
Cóng sān pǐn upper was called Fèngguó Shàng Jiāngjūn,
middle Fǔguó Shàng Jiāngjūn,
lower Zhènguó Shàng Jiāngjūn.
Zhèng sì pǐn upper was called Zhāowǔ Dà Jiāngjūn,
middle Zhāoyì Dà Jiāngjūn,
lower Zhāoyǒng Dà Jiāngjūn.
Cóng sì pǐn upper was called Ānyuǎn Dà Jiāngjūn,
middle Dìngyuǎn Dà Jiāngjūn,
lower Huáiyuǎn Dà Jiāngjūn.
Zhèng wǔ pǐn upper was called Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn,
middle Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn,
lower Míngwēi Jiāngjūn.
Cóng wǔ pǐn upper was called Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn,
middle Xiǎnwǔ Jiāngjūn,
lower Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn.
Zhèng liù pǐn upper was called Wǔjié Jiāngjūn,
lower Wǔdé Jiāngjūn.
Cóng liù pǐn upper was called Wǔyì Jiāngjūn,
lower Wǔlüè Jiāngjūn.
Zhèng qī pǐn upper was called Chéngxìn Xiàowèi,
lower Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi.
Cóng qī pǐn upper was called Zhōngwǔ Xiàowèi,
lower Zhōngxiǎn Xiàowèi.
Zhèng bā pǐn upper was called Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi,
lower Zhōngyì Xiàowèi.
Cóng bā pǐn upper was called Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi,
lower Dūnwǔ Xiàowèi.
Zhèng jiǔ pǐn upper was called Bǎoyì Xiàowèi,
lower Jìnyì Xiàowèi.
Cóng jiǔ pǐn upper was called Bǎoyì Fùwèi,
lower Jìnyì Fùwèi.
(These two grades
were newly added in Dàdìng fourteenth year (1174).)
Enfeoffed titles:
Zhèng/Cóng yī pǐn was called Jùnwáng,
or Guógōng.
Zhèng/Cóng èr pǐn was called Jùngōng.
Zhèng/Cóng sān pǐn was called Jùnhóu.
Zhèng/Cóng sì pǐn was called Jùnbó.
(Formerly called Xiànbó,
changed in Chéng'ān second year (1197).)
Zhèng wǔ pǐn was called Xiànzǐ,
Cóng wǔ pǐn was called Xiànnán.
Grades of merit (xūn):
Zhèng èr pǐn was called Shàng Zhùguó,
Cóng èr pǐn was called Zhùguó.
Zhèng sān pǐn was called Shàng Hùjūn,
Cóng sān pǐn was called Hùjūn.
Zhèng sì pǐn was called Shàng Qīngchē Dūwèi,
Cóng sì pǐn was called Qīngchē Dūwèi.
Zhèng wǔ pǐn was called Shàng Qí Dūwèi,
Cóng wǔ pǐn was called Qí Dūwèi.
Zhèng liù pǐn was called Xiāoqí Wèi,
Cóng liù pǐn was called Fēiqí Wèi.
Zhèng qī pǐn was called Yúnqí Wèi,
Cóng qī pǐn was called Wǔqí Wèi.
Stipends from enfeoffed land (shíyì):
For an enfeoffed king (fēngwáng), ten thousand households,
with a real stipend from one thousand households.
For a Jùnwáng, five thousand households,
with a real stipend from five hundred households.
For a Guógōng, three thousand households,
with a real stipend from three hundred households.
For a Jùngōng, two thousand households,
with a real stipend from two hundred households.
For a Jùnhóu, one thousand households,
with a real stipend from one hundred households.
For a Jùnbó, seven hundred households;
for a Xiànzǐ, five hundred households;
for a Xiànnán, three hundred households;
all without real stipends.
Since the regulations established in Tiānjuàn,
all stipends from enfeoffed land
were included in the official title alongside scattered ranks.
Officials of the Sītiān and Hànlín,
under the old system, from cóng qī pǐn downwards, only had five grades.
However, by the regulations established in Tiānjuàn,
the Sītiān, from cóng sì pǐn downwards,
established fifteen grades:
Cóng sì pǐn upper was called Qīnxiàng Dàfū,
middle Zhèngyí Dàfū,
lower Qīnshòu Dàfū.
Zhèng wǔ pǐn upper was called Língxiàn Dàfū,
middle Míngshí Dàfū,
lower Bānsà Dàfū.
Cóng wǔ pǐn upper was called Yúnjì Dàfū,
middle Xiéjì Dàfū,
lower Bǎozhāng Dàfū.
Those of Zhèng Liùpǐn Shàng (正六品上) were called Jìhé Dàfū (紀和大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīxuán Dàfū (司玄大夫).
Those of Cóng Liùpǐn Shàng (從六品上) were called Tànzé Láng (探賾郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Shòushí Láng (授時郎).
Those of Zhèng Qīpǐn Shàng (正七品上) were called Jiùwēi Láng (究微郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Língtái Láng (靈臺郎).
Those of Cóng Qīpǐn Shàng (從七品上) were called Míngwěi Láng (明緯郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Hòuyí Láng (候儀郎).
Those of Zhèng Bāpǐn Shàng (正八品上) were called Tuīcè Láng (推策郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīzhèng Láng (司正郎).
Those of Cóng Bāpǐn Shàng (從八品上) were called Xiàojǐng Láng (校景郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Píngzhì Láng (平秩郎).
Those of Zhèng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (正九品上) were called Zhèngjì Láng (正紀郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Qièhú Láng (挈壺郎).
Those of Cóng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (從九品上) were called Sīlì Láng (司曆郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīchén Láng (司辰郎).
For the Grand Physicians (Tàiyīguān),
in the old system, they started from Cóng Liùpǐn (從六品) and went down to seven ranks.
Under the Tiānjuàn (天眷) system,
they started from Cóng Sìpǐn (從四品) and went down,
establishing fifteen ranks:
those of Cóng Sìpǐn Shàng (從四品上) were called Bǎoyí Dàfū (保宜大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Bǎokāng Dàfū (保康大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Bǎopíng Dàfū (保平大夫).
Those of Zhèng Wǔpǐn Shàng (正五品上) were called Bǎoyí Dàfū (保頤大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Bǎo'ān Dàfū (保安大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Bǎohé Dàfū (保和大夫).
Those of Cóng Wǔpǐn Shàng (從五品上) were called Bǎoshàn Dàfū (保善大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Bǎojiā Dàfū (保嘉大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Bǎoshùn Dàfū (保順大夫).
Those of Zhèng Liùpǐn Shàng (正六品上) were called Bǎohé Dàfū (保合大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Bǎochōng Dàfū (保沖大夫).
Those of Cóng Liùpǐn Shàng (從六品上) were called Bǎoyù Láng (保愈郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Bǎoquán Láng (保全郎).
Those of Zhèng Qīpǐn Shàng (正七品上) were called Chéngzhèng Láng (成正郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Chéng'ān Láng (成安郎).
Those of Cóng Qīpǐn Shàng (從七品上) were called Chéngshùn Láng (成順郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Chénghé Láng (成和郎).
Those of Zhèng Bāpǐn Shàng (正八品上) were called Chéngyù Láng (成愈郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Chéngquán Láng (成全郎).
Those of Cóng Bāpǐn Shàng (從八品上) were called Yīquán Láng (醫全郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Yīzhèng Láng (醫正郎).
Those of Zhèng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (正九品上) were called Yīxiào Láng (醫效郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Yīhòu Láng (醫候郎).
Those of Cóng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (從九品上) were called Yīquán Láng (醫痊郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Yīyù Láng (醫愈郎).
For the Palace Attendants (Nèishì),
the Tiāndé (天德) era first established
ranks from Cóng Sìpǐn (從四品) downwards,
with fifteen ranks:
those of Cóng Sìpǐn Shàng (從四品上) were called Zhōngsàn Dàfū (中散大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Zhōngyǐn Dàfū (中尹大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Zhōngshì Dàfū (中侍大夫).
Those of Zhèng Wǔpǐn Shàng (正五品上) were called Zhōngliè Dàfū (中列大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Zhōngyù Dàfū (中御大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Zhōngyí Dàfū (中儀大夫).
Those of Cóng Wǔpǐn Shàng (從五品上) were called Zhōngcháng Dàfū (中常大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Zhōngyì Dàfū (中益大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Zhōngwèi Dàfū (中衞大夫).
Those of Zhèng Liùpǐn Shàng (正六品上) were called Zhōngliáng Dàfū (中良大夫),
(in the Tiāndé (天德) era, it was Zhōngliàng (中亮));
those of Xià (下) were called Zhōngjuān Dàfū (中涓大夫).
Those of Cóng Liùpǐn Shàng (從六品上) were called Tōngjìn Láng (通禁郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Tōngshì Láng (通侍郎).
Those of Zhèng Qīpǐn Shàng (正七品上) were called Tōngyè Láng (通掖郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Tōngyù Láng (通御郎).
Those of Cóng Qīpǐn Shàng (從七品上) were called Jìnjí Láng (禁直郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Shìzhí Láng (侍直郎).
Those of Zhèng Bāpǐn Shàng (正八品上) were called Yèzhí Láng (掖直郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Nèizhí Láng (內直郎).
Those of Cóng Bāpǐn Shàng (從八品上) were called Sīzàn Láng (司贊郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīyè Láng (司謁郎).
Those of Zhèng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (正九品上) were called Sīhūn Láng (司閽郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīpú Láng (司僕郎).
Those of Cóng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (從九品上) were called Sīfèng Láng (司奉郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīyǐn Láng (司引郎).
For the Bureau of Music (Jiàofāng),
they previously used military scattered officials (Wǔsǎnkūan).
In Dàdìng (大定) twenty-ninth year, this was deemed inappropriate,
so twenty-five ranks were newly established.
In Míngchāng (明昌) third year,
starting from Cóng Sìpǐn (從四品) downwards,
they were again established as fifteen ranks:
those of Cóng Sìpǐn Shàng (從四品上) were called Yúnsháo Dàfū (雲韶大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Xiānsháo Dàfū (仙韶大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Chéngsháo Dàfū (成韶大夫).
Those of Zhèng Wǔpǐn Shàng (正五品上) were called Zhāngdé Dàfū (章德大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Chángníng Dàfū (長寧大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Déhé Dàfū (德和大夫).
Those of Cóng Wǔpǐn Shàng (從五品上) were called Jǐngyún Dàfū (景雲大夫);
those of Zhōng (中) were called Yúnhé Dàfū (雲和大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Xiélǜ Dàfū (協律大夫).
Those of Zhèng Liùpǐn Shàng (正六品上) were called Qìngxǐ Dàfū (慶喜大夫);
those of Xià (下) were called Jiāchéng Dàfū (嘉成大夫).
Those of Cóng Liùpǐn Shàng (從六品上) were called Sùhé Láng (肅和郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Chúnhé Láng (純和郎).
Those of Zhèng Qīpǐn Shàng (正七品上) were called Shūhé Láng (舒和郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Diàoyīn Láng (調音郎).
Those of Cóng Qīpǐn Shàng (從七品上) were called Bǐyīn Láng (比音郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīlè Láng (司樂郎).
Those of Zhèng Bāpǐn Shàng (正八品上) were called Diǎnlè Láng (典樂郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Xiélè Láng (協樂郎).
Those of Cóng Bāpǐn Shàng (從八品上) were called Zhǎnglè Láng (掌樂郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Hélè Láng (和樂郎).
Those of Zhèng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (正九品上) were called Sīyīn Láng (司音郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Sīlǜ Láng (司律郎).
Those of Cóng Jiǔpǐn Shàng (從九品上) were called Héshēng Láng (和聲郎);
those of Xià (下) were called Héjié Láng (和節郎).
Regarding the administrative achievements of all internal and external officials,
their accumulated merits and evaluations (zīkǎo) from their previous posts,
the term of their replacement,
and the reasons for their departure or retention,
all were fully detailed in the report upon completion of their term (jiěyóu).
The Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) determined their ability based on this.
Furthermore, the essentials of the jiěyóu
were extracted and read during the selection and recommendation (quānnǐ) process,
which was called the "selection head" (quāntóu).
Also, the quāntóu of all previous appointments were compiled
and recorded in the "conduct ledger" (xíngzhǐbù).
The xíngzhǐbù
classified by surname,
and recorded each person's accumulated merits, evaluations, achievements, and faults from their daily experiences.
Another ledger was created,
listing the official names of all hundred bureaus.
Whenever there was a change of personnel,
the date of replacement,
and the reasons for their departure or retention, were written on small yellow silk,
and the essentials of their selection and recommendation were formulated therein.
For all county magistrates (xiànlìng),
those exempted by the province (shěngchú) and those exempted by the department (bùchú) were all recorded and separately detailed.
In Tàihé (泰和) fourth year,
the evaluation and assessment (kǎokè) methods were established,
following the Tang (Táng) regulations,
creating the system of "Four Virtues" (Sìshàn) and "Seventeen Merits" (Shíqīzuì).
The first of the Sìshàn was "renowned for virtue and integrity" (déyì yǒuwén);
the second was "clear and manifest in integrity and caution" (qīngshèn míngzhù);
the third was "praiseworthy for fairness and impartiality" (gōngpíng kěchēng);
the fourth was "diligent and unwavering, never slacking" (qínkè fěixiè).
The first of the Shíqīzuì was "promoting the flourishing of rites and music,
and purifying the administration of the department,"
considered the best in "governance and education" (zhèngjiào zhī zuì).
The second was "fair and equitable in taxation and corvée,
and expanding cultivated fields,"
considered the best in "governing the people" (mùmín zhī zuì).
The third was "decisive and unhesitant,
and granting or withholding justly,"
considered the best in "judging affairs" (pànshì zhī zuì).
The fourth was "restraining officials and soldiers,
preventing proliferation of crime and theft,"
considered the best in "strictness and clarity" (yánmíng zhī zuì).
The fifth was "clear in records and accounts,
and fair and appropriate in evaluation,"
considered the best in "inspection and audit" (jiǎnjiào zhī zuì).

The above all referred to county magistrates (xiànlìng), assistant magistrates (chéngbù), patrol commanders and their deputies (jǐngxúnshǐfù), record-keepers (lùshì), judicial officials (sīhòu), and judicial assessors (pànguān).
The sixth was "detailed and appropriate in judgment,
and just in consultation and deliberation,"
considered the best in "secretarial duties" (mùzhí zhī zuì).
The seventh was "eliminating bandits and thieves,
and ensuring peace for the people,"
considered the best in "patrol and arrest" (xúnbǔ zhī zuì).
The eighth was "clear in receipts and disbursements,
with no loss of goods,"
considered the best in "warehouses" (cāngkù zhī zuì).
The ninth was "effective in instruction and guidance,
with students completing their studies,"
considered the best in "educational officials" (xuégūan zhī zuì).
The tenth was "effective in inspection,
with travelers unhindered,"
considered the best in "passes and ferries" (guānjīn zhī zuì).
The eleventh was "solid in dikes and defenses,
with no worries about protection,"
considered the best in "river defenses" (héfáng zhī zuì).
The twelfth was "clear and quick in receipts and disbursements,
with no excessive or erroneous figures,"
considered the best in "supervision" (jiāndū zhī zuì).
The thirteenth was "careful in observing prisoners,
with no complaints about leniency or severity,"
considered the best in "prison officials" (yùguān zhī zuì).
The fourteenth was "accurate in commodity prices,
preventing fraud and misconduct,"
considered the best in "market superintendents" (shìsī zhī zuì),
referring to market directors (shìlìng).
The fifteenth was "complete and solemn in military equipment,
and effective in defense,"
considered the best in "border defense" (biānfáng zhī zuì),
referring to chief and deputy commanders of units and garrison officials.
The sixteenth was "grasping the truth in legal cases,
and judging fairly,"
considered the best in "judicial officials" (fǎguān zhī zuì).
The seventeenth was "fair and equitable in labor assignments,
and stopping banditry,"
considered the best in "military officials" (jūzhí zhī zuì),
referring to commanders of all armies (dūjūn) and military supervisors (jūnhá).
For county magistrates (xiànlìng) and below,
those with three "most excellent" (zuì) ratings or more, and four "good" (shàn) ratings or three "good" ratings are considered "superior" (shàng),
and are promoted one grade.
Those with three "most excellent" ratings or more, and two "good" ratings are considered "medium" (zhōng),
and have two years of seniority (zīlì) reduced.
Those with three "most excellent" ratings or more, and one "good" rating are considered "inferior" (xià),
and have one year of seniority reduced.
For judicial commissioners (jiédù pànguān), defense commissioners (fángyù pànguān), military commissioners (jūn pàn), and below,
those with one "most excellent" rating and four "good" ratings or three "good" ratings are considered "superior" (shàng),
and have one year of seniority reduced.
Those with one "most excellent" rating and two "good" ratings are considered "medium" (zhōng),
and are promoted to "top of the list" (bǎngshǒu).
Those with one "most excellent" rating and one "good" rating are considered "inferior" (xià),
and are promoted to "top of their own grade" (běn děng shǒu).
Furthermore, based on the regulations established in Míngchāng (明昌) 4th year (1193),
the system of "incorruptible and capable officials" (liánnéng guān) was established, where both military and civilian officials were designated as "incorruptible and capable" (liánnéng),
and incorporated into this system to determine their selection and promotion.
In Xūanzōng (宣宗) Xīngdìng (興定) 1st year (1217),
the method of appointing county magistrates (xiànlìng) was implemented,
assessing them based on six criteria:
first, "fields opened" (tiányě pì);
second, "households increased" (hùkǒu zēng);
third, "taxes and levies fair" (fùyì píng);
fourth, "bandits ceased" (dàozéi xī);
fifth, "military and civilians harmonious" (jūnmín hé);
sixth, "litigation simplified" (císòng jiǎn).
Those who met all six criteria were considered "superior grade" (shàngděng),
and were promoted one rank.
Those who met four criteria were considered "medium grade" (zhōngděng),
and had two years of seniority (zīlì) reduced.
The next category was "inferior grade" (xiàděng),
and had one year of seniority reduced.
Otherwise, they were deemed "unqualified" (bù chènzhí),
dismissed and demoted.
Those considered "ordinary" (píngcháng) remained in their original grade (běn gé).
For all enfeoffments of kings (wáng):
There were twenty "great states" (dàguó) titles,
named: Yán (燕), (formerly Liáo (遼);
in Míngchāng (明昌) 2nd year (1191), names like Hàn (漢), Liáo (遼), Táng (唐), Sòng (宋), Liáng (梁), Qín (秦), Yīn (殷), and Chǔ (楚)
were all deemed titles of those who had once ruled the empire
and were unsuitable for enfeoffing ministers;
thus, they were all changed.) Shào (邵), (formerly Liáng (梁).)
Biàn (汴), (formerly Sòng (宋).)
Hào (鎬), (formerly Qín (秦).)
Bìng (幷), (formerly Jìn (晉).)
Yì (益), (formerly Hàn (漢).)
Péng (彭), (formerly Qí (齊).)
Zhào (趙), Yuè (越), Qiáo (譙), (formerly Yīn (殷).)
Yǐng (郢), (formerly Chǔ (楚).)
Lǔ (魯), Jì (冀), Yù (豫), Jiàng (絳), (formerly Táng (唐).)
Yǎn (兗), È (鄂), (formerly Wú (吳).)
Kuí (夔), (formerly Shǔ (蜀).)
Wǎn (宛), (formerly Chén (陳).)
Cáo (曹).
There were thirty "secondary states" (cìguó) titles,
named: Jīng (涇), (formerly Suí (隋).)
Zhèng (鄭), Wèi (衞), Hán (韓), Lù (潞), Bīn (豳), Shěn (瀋), Qí (岐), Dài (代), Zé (澤), Xú (徐), Téng (滕), Xuē (薛), Jì (紀), Shēng (昇), (formerly Yuán (原).)
Xíng (邢), Yì (翼), Fēng (豐), Bì (畢), Dèng (鄧), Yùn (鄆), Huò (霍), Cài (蔡), Yíng (瀛), (according to the Jīn Gé (金格),
Gě (葛) should be here.)
Yí (沂), Jīng (荊), Róng (榮), Yīng (英), Shòu (壽), Wēn (溫).
There were thirty "small states" (xiǎoguó) titles: Pú (濮), Suí (遂), (formerly Jì (濟).)
Dào (道), Dìng (定), Jǐng (景), (later changed to Zōu (鄒).)
Shēn (申), Chóng (崇), Sù (宿), Xī (息),
Jǔ (莒), Yè (鄴), Gào (郜), Shū (舒), Zī (淄), Chéng (郕), Lái (萊), (formerly Zōng (宗),
changed due to taboo.)
Yún (鄖), Tán (郯), Shí (嵵), Xiàng (向), Guǎn (管), (formerly Xún (郇),
changed in Xīngdìng (興定) 1st year (1217).)
Mì (密), Zuò (胙), Rèn (任), Dài (戴),
Gǒng (鞏), Jiǎng (蔣), (Shìmín Xūzhī (士民須知) states
it was formerly Gě (葛).)
Xiāo (蕭), Shēn (莘), Ruì (芮).

There were ten "commandery titles" (jùnhào) for enfeoffing kings: Jīnyuán (金源), Guǎngpíng (廣平), Píngyuán (平原), Nányáng (南陽), Chángshān (常山), Tàiyuán (太原), Píngyáng (平陽), Dōngpíng (東平), Āndìng (安定), Yán'ān (延安).

There were thirty "county titles" (xiànhào) for enfeoffing princesses: Lè'ān (樂安), Qīngpíng (清平), Pénglái (蓬萊), Róng'ān (榮安), Qīxiá (棲霞), Shòuguāng (壽光), Língxiān (靈仙), Shòuyáng (壽陽), Zhōngxiù (鍾秀), Huìhé (惠和), Yǒngníng (永寧), Qìngyún (慶雲), Jìnglè (靜樂), Fúshān (福山), Lóngpíng (隆平), Dépíng (德平), Wén'ān (文安), Fúchāng (福昌), Shùn'ān (順安), Lèshòu (樂壽), Jìng'ān (靜安), Língshòu (靈壽), Dàníng (大寧), Wénxǐ (聞喜), Xiùróng (秀容), Yífāng (宜芳), Zhēnníng (真寧), Jiáxiáng (嘉祥), Jīnxiāng (金鄉), Huáyuan (華原).
For surnames with "white" (bái) designation,

Wányán (完顏), Wēndíhǎn (溫迪罕), Jiágǔ (夾谷), Mǎn (滿), Púsàn (僕散), Zhúhǔ (术虎), Yílàdá (移剌荅), Wòlè (斡勒), Wòzhǔn (斡準), Bǎ (把), Ābùhǎn (阿不罕), Zhuōlǔ (卓魯), Huítè (回特), Hēihǎn (黑罕), Huìlán (會蘭), Shěngǔ (沈谷), Sàipúlǐ (塞蒲里), Wúgǔsūn (吾古孫), Shídūn (石敦), Zhuótuó (卓陀), Āsīzhǔn (阿厮準), Pǐdúsī (匹獨思), Pānshúgǔ (潘术古), Ānshílà (諳石剌), Shígǔkǔ (石古苦), Zhuìhǎn (綴罕), Guāngjílà (光吉剌) were all enfeoffed to Jīnyuán (金源) Commandery;

Péimǎn (裴滿), Túdān (徒單), Wēndūn (溫敦), Wùlíndá (兀林荅), Ādiǎn (阿典), Gēshíliè (紇石烈), Nàlán (納闌), BóshúLǔ (孛术魯), Ālègēn (阿勒根), Nàhé (納合), Shízhǎn (石盞), Púxiān (蒲鮮), Gǔlíjiǎ (古里甲), Ādié (阿迭), Nièmōluán (聶摸欒), Mòniǎn (抹撚), Nàtǎn (納坦), Wùsārě (兀撒惹), Āxiān (阿鮮), Bǎgǔ (把古), Wēngǔsūn (溫古孫), Nǒuwǎn (耨盌), Sāgéliè (撒合烈), Wúsāi (吾塞), Hésùjiā (和速嘉), Néngyǎn (能偃), Ālǐbān (阿里班), Wùlǐtǎn (兀里坦), Nièsàn (聶散), Púsùliè (蒲速烈) were all enfeoffed to Guǎngpíng (廣平) Commandery;
Wúgǔlún (吾古論), Wùyán (兀顏), Nǚxīliè (女奚烈), Dújí (獨吉), Huángguā (黃摑), Yánzhǎn (顏盞), Púgǔlǐ (蒲古里), Bìlán (必蘭), Wòléi (斡雷), Dúdǐng (獨鼎), Nímángkū (尼厖窟), (kū (窟) is also written gǔ (古).)

Tuòtè (拓特), Gésàn (盍散), Sātáyá (撒荅牙), Āsù (阿速), Sāchǎn (撒剗), Zhǔntǔgǔ (準土谷), Nàmóulǔ (納謀魯), Yèsùbù (業速布), Ānxùliè (安煦烈), Àishēn (愛申), Nákě (拿可), Guìyìkūn (貴益昆), Wēnsā (溫撒), Suōhǎn (梭罕), Huòyù (霍域) were all enfeoffed to Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery.
For surnames with "black" (hēi) designation,
Tángkuò (唐括), (in old texts written Tónggǔ (同古).)

Púchá (蒲察), Shújiǎ (术甲), Ménggǔ (蒙古), Púsù (蒲速), Niángē (粘割), Àodún (奧屯), XiéMǎo (斜卯), Zhǔngé (準葛), Ānmán (諳蠻), Dúhǔ (獨虎), Shúlǔ (术魯), Móniǎn (磨輦), Yìniǎn (益輦), Tiēnǎn (帖暖), Sūbóniǎn (蘇孛輦) were all enfeoffed to Péngchéng (彭城) Commandery.
For the mother or wife of a Prince (qīnwáng),
the one enfeoffed with a single-character princedom was formerly enfeoffed as a Princess Consort (wángfēi),
holding the rank of Zheng Cóng Yīpǐn (正從一品);
secondary wives were enfeoffed as Princess Matrons (wángfūrén).
In Chéng'ān (承安) 2nd year (1197),
an imperial edict stipulated that Princess Consorts (wángfēi) were only to be enfeoffed as Princess Matrons (wángfūrén);
secondary wives were enfeoffed as Rúrén (孺人).
The mother or wife of a Commandery Prince (jùnwáng) was enfeoffed as Commandery Princess Matron (jùnwáng fūrén);
the mother or wife of a State Duke (guógōng) was enfeoffed as State Duke Matron (guógōng fūrén);
the mother or wife of a Commandery Duke (jùngōng) was enfeoffed as Commandery Duke Matron (jùngōng fūrén);
the mother or wife of a Commandery Marquis (jùnhóu) was enfeoffed as Commandery Lady (jùnjūn),
(in Chéng'ān (承安) 2nd year (1197), this was changed to Commandery Marquis Matron (jùnhóu fūrén).)

The mother or wife of a civil official from the 4th rank, Lesser Grand Master of Court Discussion (shǎo zhōng dàfū) and above, or a military official from the 4th rank, General Who Cherishes Distant Lands (huáiyuǎn dàjiàngjūn) and above, was enfeoffed as County Lady (xiànjūn),
(in Chéng'ān (承安) 2nd year (1197), this was Commandery Lady (jùnjūn).)

The mother or wife of a civil official from the 5th rank, Grand Master for Court Service (cháoliè dàfū) and above, or a military official from the 5th rank, General Who Proclaims Martiality (xuānwǔ jiàngjūn) and above, was enfeoffed as Township Lady (xiāngjūn).
(In Chéng'ān (承安) 2nd year (1197), this was County Lady (xiànjūn).)
In Huángtǒng (皇統) 5th year (1145),
because ancient officials were called
"pastor" (mù)
or
"chief" (zhǎng),
each having a general designation,
while current common officials did not have categorized names,
which was inconvenient for official correspondence.
Thus, the capital prefect (jīngfǔyǐnmù), resident general (liúshǒu), prefect (zhīzhōu), county magistrate (xiànlìng), commander (xiángwěn), and superintendent of pasturages (qúnmù) were designated as
"chief officials" (zhǎngguān);
assistant prefect (tóngzhī), associate (qiānyuàn), vice envoy (fùshǐ), junior prefect (shǎoyǐn), assistant prefect (tōngpàn), and county assistant (chéng) were designated
"deputy officials" (zuǒ'èrguān);
judicial commissioner (pànguān), investigating commissioner (tuīguān), record-keeper (zhǎngshūjì), chief clerk (zhǔbù), and county commandant (xiànwèi) were designated
"secretarial staff" (mùzhíguān);
those in the military inspectorate (bīngmǎ sī) and other military offices were designated
"military officials" (jūnzhíguān);

police chief (jǐngxún), market master (shìlìng), record keeper (lùshì), judicial assistant (sīhòu), various adjutants (zhū cānjūn), law administrator (zhīlǜ), case investigator (kānshì), and judicial reviewer (kānpàn) were designated
"duty officials" (líwùguān);
those in charge of granaries, treasuries, and various offices were designated
"supervisory officials" (jiāndāngguān),
(supervisory officials emerged from major regulations.)
Officials from the chief clerk (zhīshì) and clerk (kǒngmù) downwards who handled documents were designated
"clerks" (lì).
For all appointments,
from the Grand Councilor (shàngshūlìng), Left and Right Chancellors (zuǒyòu chéngxiàng) downwards,
if their official ranks (pǐn) differed [from the nominal rank of the office],
the character
"Acting" (shǒu)
was appended.
For Left and Right Chancellors (zuǒyòu chéng), the characters
"Acting Provisional" (xíngshǒu)
were appended.

For Censorate officials (táiguān), censors (yùshǐ), departmental officials (bùguān), capital prefects (jīngyǐn), junior prefects (shǎoyǐn), magistrates (shǒulìng), assistants (chéng), clerks (bù), commandants (wèi), record keepers (lùshì), various court gentlemen (zhū qīng) down to harmonizer of music (xiéliǜ), judicial review officers (píngshì), remonstrance officials (jiànguān), National Academy (guózǐjiān) scholars (xuégūan), various directorates (zhū jiān) down to assistant director (chéngláng), talisman attendant (fúbǎoláng), Eastern Palace (dōnggōng) grand tutor (zhànshì), metropolitan commandant (shuàifǔ), deputy minister (púzhèngfù), principal and assistant (lìngchéng), and princely establishment officials (wángfǔguān),
if their nominal rank (sàn guān) was higher than their actual office rank (zhíshì), the character
"Provisional" (xíng)
was appended;
if their actual office rank (zhíshì) was one rank higher than their nominal rank (sàn guān), the character
"Acting" (shǒu)
was appended; if two ranks higher, the character
"Probationary" (shì)
was appended.
If the ranks were the same, no character was appended.

For Myng'an (měng'ān), Muhke (móukè), Hanlin Academicians-in-waiting (hànlín dàizhì), compilers (xiūzhuàn), judicial commissioners (pàn), investigating commissioners (tuī), case investigators (kānshìguān), registrar (dūshì), executive officer (diǎnshì), chief clerk (zhīshì), palace attendant (nèichéngfèng), usher (yābān), interpreter-attendant (tōngshì shèrén), presenter of memorials (tōngjìn), compilers (biānxiū), manager (gōudàng), station master (dùnshè), service official (bùyì), district official (xiāngguān), receiver of grants (shòugěi guǎngòu), river inspector (xúnhéguān), director and deputy of provincial departments (zhíshěng zhíyuàn zhǎngfù), various law inspectors (zhū jiǎnfǎ), law administrators (zhīfǎ), chief justice (sīzhèng), professors (jiàoshòu), prison wardens (sīyù), judicial assistants (sīhòu), Eastern Palace (dōnggōng) tutor (yùdé), literary aide (zànshàn), seal keeper (zhǎngbǎo), master of ceremonies (diǎnyí) and below,
as well as princely establishment literary officials (wángfǔ wénxué) and record-keeping adjutants (jìshì cānjūn),
the character
"Concurrent" (chōng)
was appended.

For the Bureau of Military Affairs (shūmì), Bureau of Palace Affairs (xuānhuī), Office of Agricultural Promotion (quànnóng), various military commanders-in-chief (zhū jūn dūzhǐhuī), military governors (tǒngjūn), transport commissioners (zhuǎnyùnshǐ), pacification commissioners (zhāotǎo), judicial inspectors (tíxíng), regional commanders (jiédù), superintendents of pasturages (qúnmù), defense commissioners (fángyù), Guest Reception Bureau (kèshěng), Ushering Bureau (yǐnjìn), Four Directions Hostel (sìfāngguǎn), Palace Gate Bureau (gémén), Imperial Medical Bureau (tàiyī), Music Bureau (jiàofāng), Falconry Bureau (yīngfāng), police chief (jǐngxún), inspection commissioner (xúnjiǎn), and deputy officials of various departments, bureaus, granaries, and treasuries,
the characters
"Concurrent" (chōng)
and
"Manager of (such-and-such) Affairs" (zhī mǒushì)
were appended.
Officials bearing the characters
"Manager" (zhī),
"Judicial Commissioner" (pàn),
or
"Assistant" (qiānshū)
did not bear the characters
"Provisional" (xíng),
"Acting" (shǒu),
or
"Probationary" (shì).
For the characters appended above,
if the ranks were the same, they were omitted.

From the Three Grand Preceptors (sānshī), Three Dukes (sāngōng), Grand Councilor (píngzhāng zhèngshì), Marshal (yuánshuài) downwards, to supervising minister (jiānjūn), Eastern Palace (dōnggōng) Three Grand Preceptors (sānshī), Three Junior Preceptors (sānshǎo), inspector (diǎnjiǎn) down to commandant (zhènsù), attendant (chéngzhǐ), academician (xuèshì), royal tutor (wángfù), deputy commander (fùtǒng), pacification commissioner (zhāotǎo), and those not previously listed,
none bore the characters
"Provisional" (xíng),
"Acting" (shǒu),
"Probationary" (shì),
"Manager" (zhī),
or
"Concurrent" (chōng).
Four Zhǔshì (Director of the Bureau)
of rank cóng qī pǐn (Seventh Rank, Junior Grade),
are in charge of managing appointments and dismissals, and reviewing and checking official documents.
They are separately responsible for matters of enfeoffment, merits, and personnel reviews.
However, for election matters, all of them countersign.
They also manage the receipt and dispatch of affairs, inspecting, verifying, and reviewing the documents of the yámen (government office).
They concurrently oversee the overnight duty of this ministry and inspect the archives.
The Zhǔshì of other ministries,
from the receipt and dispatch of affairs downwards,
have the same responsibilities.
(In the fourth year of Huángtǒng
, Han literati began to be employed as Zhǔshì in the Six Ministries.
In the third year of Dàdìng
, Jinshì (Metropolitan Graduates) were employed;
without a special imperial decree, clerks could not be nominated,
such as when prime ministers recommend talented individuals,
which was not part of the normal practice.
In the fifth year of Chéng'ān
, one Nǚzhí Zhǔshì was added.
Sixty-nine Lìshǐ (Clerks),
including twenty-nine Nǚzhí.
Five Yìshǐ (Translators),
two Tōngshì (Interpreters),
whose duties are the same as Lìshǐ.
In the eighth year of Tàihé
, ten Lìshǐ were added.)
The Jiàgékù (Archival Repository) (established in the sixth month of the twenty-first year of Dàdìng

and concurrently inspects the records of the Lìbù.

one is in charge of household registers, material resources, marriages, successions, fields and residences, property, salt and iron, wine yeast, incense and tea, alum and tin, cinnabar and powder, mining, customs barriers, and market exchanges, etc.

One is in charge of expenditures, national finance, salaries, imperial grants, money and silk, treasures, tributes and taxes, treasuries, granaries, reserves, weights and measures, laws and regulations, granting official lands, collecting official goods, and also auditing and accounting, etc.

Five Zhǔshì
of rank cóng qī pǐn,
two for the Nǚzhí Department,
jointly managing household registrations, expenditures, treasury, and other matters.
Three for the Han Chinese Department,
jointly managing various departmental affairs with the Yuánwàiláng.

, eight were established in the fourth year of Zhēnyòu
