They are in charge of all matters related to rites and music, sacrifices, banquets, schools, imperial examinations, ceremonies, regulations, tallies and seals, memorials and petitions, maps and books, imperial appointments, auspicious omens, astronomy, water clocks, national mourning days, imperial taboos, medicine and divination, Buddhism and Taoism, foreign envoys, tributes from various states, and matters of rewards and arrangements.
(For all examinations of Buddhist monks, nuns, Taoist priests, and Taoist priestesses,
held once every three years,
limited to eighty candidates.
Two staff officials from the capital prefecture or assistant officials from border defense commands are dispatched,
along with two Buddhist officials, one Taoist official, one clerk, one attendant for each, two servants, one gatekeeper, and three miscellaneous laborers.

Novice monks must be able to read five sutras in total, including Fǎhuá (Lotus), Xīndìguān (Contemplation of the Mind-Ground), Jīnguāngmíng (Golden Light), Bàōnen (Requiting Kindness), and Huáyán (Flower Garland),
totaling eight fascicles.
The Huáyán Jīng is divided into four fascicles.
From each fascicle, two scrolls are taken,
and four questions are given per scroll.
The limit for reading is one hundred characters.
Novice nuns are examined on half a sutra,
similar to novice monks.

Taoist priests and Taoist priestesses read Dàodé (Dao De Jing), Jiùkǔ (Sutra of Rescuing from Suffering), Yùjīngshān (Jade Capital Mountain), Xiāozāi (Sutra of Eliminating Disasters), Língbǎodùrén (Sutra of Lingbao for Saving People), and other sutras.
They are considered to have passed if they can recite the sentences and explain the meaning according to the pronunciation.
Those who pass the selection are given certificates by the examining officials,
and their names are reported to the authorities.
Any Buddhist monk or nun official who supervises eighty people, or Taoist priest or priestess who supervises thirty people, is allowed to grant ordination to one person.
If someone dies, the supervising altar official is to report the ordination certificate to the ministry for destruction.)
Two Zhǔshì
of rank cóng qī pǐn.
(Fifteen Lìshǐ,
including five Nǚzhí.
Two Yìshǐ,
one Tōngshì.)
Zuǒ Sān Bù Jiǎnfǎ Sī (Left Three Ministries' Legal Review Department)
Two Sīzhèng (Department Head)
of rank zhèng bā pǐn,

, the Right Department additionally established Jiǎn (Inspector), Zhīfǎ (Director of Law), and Zhǎngfǎ (Head of Law),

Twenty-two Jiǎnfǎ
of rank cóng bā pǐn,
in charge of inspecting and adjudicating legal documents requested by various departments.
The duties of the Right Three Ministries' Legal Review are the same.
(Originally appointed by official warrant,
in the third year of Dàdìng they were ordered to be granted imperial decrees.)
Bīngbù
One Shàngshū
of rank zhèng sān pǐn.

of rank zhèng sì pǐn.

of rank cóng liù pǐn.

It manages military registers, weaponry, city walls, garrisons, pastures, postal stations, carriages, ceremonial guards, topographical records of commanderies and counties, dangerous terrain, barriers, and affairs concerning the native populations of distant regions who have assimilated.
(For those who are granted horses,
from Grade 1 and above,
they are attended by eight people,
given ten horses,
and receive 3 strings and 14 cash for fodder.
From Grade 2 and above,
they are attended by five people,
given seven horses,
and receive 2 strings and 98 cash for fodder.
From Grade 3 and above,
they are attended by three people,
given five horses,
and receive 1 string and 511 cash.
From Grade 5 and above,
they are attended by two people,
given four horses,
and receive 968 cash.
From Grade 7 and above,
they are attended by one person,
given three horses,
and receive 617 cash.
From Grade 9 and above,
they are attended by one person,
given two horses,
and receive 464 cash.
If there are no attendants,
78 cash are deducted.
Those without official rank dispatched by imperial command
are treated as being of Grade 5.
For those with official rank dispatched by the province,
each person receives 451 cash,
and if they have attendants, an additional 68 cash is given.
Those who deliver horses receive 157 cash per person.
Imperial edicts travel 500 *lǐ* per day.
This is the system recorded in the *TiānXīng* 近鑑.
In the sixth year of *Tàihé*, postal stations were established.
Under this system,
there was one station every ten *lǐ* along military roads,
with four people stationed at each,
including one station chief [pùtóu]
and three station soldiers [pùbīng].
They were selected from the soldiers responsible for collecting provisions within the military jurisdiction,
wearing waist bells and traveling 300 *lǐ* per day.
All documents from the Grand Marshal's Office [Yuánshuàifǔ] and the Six Ministries [Liùbù],
bearing imperial dispatch [chìdì] or provincial dispatch [shěngdì] tallies,
entered the stations for onward transmission.
Two Secretaries [Zhǔshì],
of Grade 7.
(In the fifth year of *Zhēnyòu*, the *Chéngfāsī* was also managed by a *guǎngòu* and *Hàn* Chinese *zhǔshì*.
Twenty-seven Clerks [Lìshǐ],

One Minister [Shàngshū],

In charge of construction and building methods, various artisans, garrison farms, prohibitions in mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes, river dikes, and roads and bridges.

In the sixth year of *Zhènglóng*, *Hǎilíng* campaigned south,
establishing the Three Route Supreme Commander's Offices [Sāndào Dūtǒngzhìfǔ] and Left and Right Grand Military Governors [Zuǒyòu Lǐngjūn Dàdūdū],
commanding thirty-two overall commanders [zǒngguǎn],

with titles such as *Shéncè*, *Shénwēi*, *Shénjié*, *Shénruì*, *Shényì*, *Shényì*, *Shényǒng*, *Shénguǒ*, *Shénlüè*, *Shénfēng*, *Wǔshèng*, *Wǔdìng*, *Wǔwēi*, *Wǔān*, *Wǔjié*, *Wǔpíng*, *Wǔchéng*, *Wǔyì*, *Wǔruì*, *Wǔyáng*, *Wǔyì*, *Wǔzhèn*, *Wēidìng*, *Wēixìn*, *Wēishèng*, *Wēijié*, *Wēiliè*, *Wēiyì*, *Wēizhèn*, *Wēilüè*, *Wēiguǒ*, and *Wēiyǒng*.
In the sixth year of *Tàihé*, during the campaign against the *Sòng*,
the temporary rank of Supreme General for Pacifying the South and Comforting the Army [Píngnán Fǔjūn Shàngjiāngjūn] was established,

of Auxiliary Grade 6,
totaling nine ranks:

namely Supreme General for Pacifying the South and Comforting the Army, Grand General for Pacifying the South and Leading the Army, General for Pacifying the South and Rushing Dragon, General for Pacifying the South and Tiger Might, General for Pacifying the South and Sweeping Rivers, Middle Commandant for Annihilating Invaders, Commandant for Annihilating Invaders, Commandant for Annihilating Invaders and Breaking the Charge, and Grand Commandant for Annihilating Invaders with Resolute Action.
These ranks were abolished when the army returned.
(Eighty Clerks [Lìshǐ] and Translating Clerks [Yìshǐ] were appointed,

later *Liú Yánzōng*.
At first, it was similar to the system of the *Liáo* Southern Bureau,
but later it was not.)
In the sixth year of *Tàihé*, it was once changed to the Grand Marshal's Office [Yuánshuàifǔ].

Grand Imperial Clan Court (Dà Zōngzhèng Fǔ).
In the 6th year of Tàihé, to avoid the taboo name of Ruìzōng,
it was renamed Grand Court for Harmonizing Relatives (Dà Mùqīn Fǔ).
One Chief of the Grand Imperial Clan Court (Pàn Dà Zōngzhèng Shì),
of rank *cóng yīpǐn*,
filled by a close relative from the imperial clan,
in charge of strengthening harmony and uniting clan members to respectfully follow imperial decrees.
In the 6th year of Tàihé, this was renamed Chief of the Grand Court for Harmonizing Relatives (Pàn Dà Mùqīn Shì).
〔一一〕
One Co-Chief of the Grand Imperial Clan Court (Tóngpàn Dà Zōngzhèng Shì),
of rank *cóng èrpǐn*.
In the 6th year of Tàihé, this was renamed Co-Chief of the Grand Court for Harmonizing Relatives (Tóngpàn Dà Mùqīn Shì).
One Signatory to the Grand Imperial Clan Court (Tóngqiān Dà Zōngzhèng Shì),
of rank *zhèng sānpǐn*,
filled by a member of the imperial clan.
(Established in the 1st year of Dàdìng.)
In the 6th year of Tàihé, this was renamed Signatory to the Grand Court for Harmonizing Relatives (Tóngqiān Dà Mùqīn Shì).
Two Grand Imperial Clan Court Assistant Ministers (Dà Zōngzhèng Chéng),
of rank *cóng sìpǐn*.
One was selected from capable members of the imperial clan,
the other was not limited by closeness of kinship.
They were to divide their duties as senior and junior officials in Shàngjīng and also oversee the six departments belonging to Línhuáng and eastward.
In the 6th year of Tàihé, this was renamed Grand Court for Harmonizing Relatives Assistant Minister (Dà Mùqīn Chéng).
One Administrator (Zhīshì),
of rank *cóng qīpǐn*.
Legal Inspector (Jiǎnfǎ),
of rank *cóng bāpǐn*.
Various Generals of the Imperial Clan (Zhū Zōngshì Jiāngjūn),
of rank *zhèng qīpǐn*.
There were such positions in both Shàngjīng and Dōngwēntè.
〔一二〕During Shìzōng's reign, they were first ordered to be promoted in office,
and their households numbered 120 in total.
〔一三〕In the 2nd year of Míngchāng, they were renamed Supervisors of the Clan (Sīshǔ),
and a Director (Lìng) and Assistant Minister (Chéng) were established.
In the 2nd year of Chéng'ān, the Director was made equivalent to a Director of the Imperial Court (Suícháo Sīlìng),
of rank *zhèng qīpǐn*,
and the Assistant Minister of rank *zhèng bāpǐn*.
These were established in Zhōngdū, Shàngjīng, Zhālǐguā, Hégǔ Xīnán, Méijiānzhài, Púyǔ, Línhuáng, Tàizhōu, Jīnshān, and other places,
subordinate to the Grand Imperial Clan Court.
Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái).
The Court of Appeals (Dēngwén Jiànyuàn) was subordinate to it.
(See *Shìmín Xūzhī*.
Not recorded in *Zǒnggé* or *Tàihé Lìng*.)
Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Dàfū),
of rank *cóng èrpǐn*.
(Formerly *zhèng sānpǐn*,
promoted in the 12th year of Dàdìng.)
In charge of scrutinizing court rituals, impeaching corrupt officials, and investigating and trying official public affairs.
Whenever internal and external judicial judgments were improper,
those who complained were referred to the Censorate for resolution.
Censor-General (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
of rank *cóng sānpǐn*,
deputy to the Censor-in-Chief.

〔一四〕In charge of submitting memorials and adjudicating Censorate affairs.
Two Rectifying Censors (Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ),
of rank *cóng liùpǐn*,
in charge of the same duties as the Investigating Censors.
Two Palace Censors (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ),
of rank *zhèng qīpǐn*.
Whenever there were court audiences, they stood below the imperial steps,
specifically impeaching the conduct and demeanor of those in audience.
They presented memorials detailing all matters of leave requested by officials.
Twelve Supervising Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ),
of rank *zhèng qīpǐn*,
in charge of scrutinizing internal and external misconduct, auditing accounts of various departments, supervising sacrificial rites, and overseeing diplomatic missions.

eight in the 2nd year of Dàdìng,

Officials from the Minister (Qīng) downwards would take turns on inspection tours,
investigating the integrity of officials and promoting or demoting them accordingly.
Wherever the envoys passed,
corrupt officials would hold their breath.
Within ten years, civil administration was greatly improved,
truly relying on their efforts.

〔一四〕
Cáo Jìdū (曹濟都) was a Patrol Officer of the River.
Below him were four scattered River Patrol Officers, one each for Dìngtáo (定陶), Jǐběi (濟北), Hánshān (寒山), and Jīnshān (金山).
(There were twenty-five dikes in total,
with 12,000 dike soldiers.)
The Material Yard Officers for all dikes
were in charge of receiving and distributing materials for their respective yards.
The Divided-Governance Supervising Material Yard Officers were the same.
However, the Material Yard Officers for the Upper and Lower Chóngfú (崇福) Dikes jointly managed income and expenditure with the local officials.
The Nanjing Yánjīndù (南京延津渡) Bridge Officer
also served as an Inspector.
One Administrator
and one Co-Administrator
were in charge of bridge boats, ferry crossings, inspections of river crossings and ferries, and the receipt and distribution of various materials for the bridge, and other related matters.
The inspection duties were subordinate to the Liúshǒusī (留守司).
Other pontoon bridge officers were similar.
The above were subordinate to the Dūshuǐjiān (都水監).
In the fourth month of Huángtǒng (皇統) 3 (1143),
the Huáizhōu (懷州) Yellow and Qìn Rivers Embankment Grand Administrator Office was established.

In Zhèngdà (正大) 2 (1225),
the Eastern External Supervisorate was established at Guīdé (歸德),
〔一五〕and the Western one at Héyīn (河陰).

Director (*Lìng*, 令) —
auxiliary sixth rank.

(Formerly, an Aide was also established.
In the third year of *Dàdìng* (大定),
the relevant authorities stated that
the annual income from the *Huìmín* interest money was not enough to pay the salaries of officials.
The Emperor said: "This was originally established to help the people.
If officials are not human [i.e., not diligent],
they will be negligent in supervising medicines.
Why should the expenditure be counted?
The number of officials may simply be reduced."

Deputy Commissioner (*Fùshǐ*, 副使) —
auxiliary sixth rank.

Commissioner (*Shǐ*, 使) —
auxiliary sixth rank.
Deputy Commissioner (*Fùshǐ*, 副使) —
auxiliary seventh rank.
Responsible for imperial chariots, ceremonial guards, carriages, robes, and other matters.

principal eighth rank.

Administrator (*Guǎngōu*, 管勾) —
auxiliary seventh rank.
Co-Administrator (*Tóngguǎngōu*, 同管勾) —
auxiliary eighth rank.
Responsible for receiving and sending documents from ministries and outer routes.
These belong to the *Shàngshū Bīngbù* (尚書兵部).

then renamed to its current name).
Director (*Tíju*, 提舉) —
auxiliary sixth rank.
Co-Director (*Tóngtíju*, 同提舉) —
auxiliary seventh rank.
Responsible for guarding the palace city and palace halls.
(Originally fifteen guards).
*Qìngníng Gōng Tíju Sī* (慶寧宮提舉司)
Director (*Tíju*, 提舉) —
principal seventh rank.
Concurrently *Lóngmén Xiàn Lìng* (龍門縣令).
Co-Director (*Tóngtíju*, 同提舉) —
principal eighth rank.
Concurrently *Yíluán Jiān* (儀鸞監).

*Xiūnéi Sī* (修內司) (Established in the seventh year of *Dàdìng*).
Commissioner (*Shǐ*, 使) —
auxiliary fifth rank.
Deputy Commissioner (*Fùshǐ*, 副使) —
auxiliary sixth rank.
Responsible for construction projects within the palace.
(One thousand sixty-five military artisans,
two thousand military laborers,
and the chief official of the *Shǎofǔ Jiān* (少府監) was ordered to oversee them).
Two *Zhízhǎng* (直長) officials —
principal eighth rank.

principal eighth rank.

Director (*Tíju*, 提舉) —
auxiliary sixth rank.
Co-Director (*Tóngtíju*, 同提舉) —
auxiliary seventh rank.
Responsible for repairing and completing temples and altars, city walls and gate keys, public offices of all departments, official residences, and planting trees and other construction work.
Two officials each for the Left and Right Wings (*Zuǒyòu Xiāngguān*, 左右廂官) —
principal eighth rank.
Responsible for supervising laborers.
Two *Shòugěi Guān* (受給官) officials —
principal eighth rank.
Responsible for dispensing and receiving various items, and pottery work.

Ànchá Sī (Investigating Censorate) - originally Tíxíng Sī (Judicial Intendancy).
In Chéng'ān三年 (1198), the Tíxíng Sī of Shàngjīng, Dōngjīng, etc., were merged into one Tíxíng Shǐ,
concurrently acting as Xuānfǔ Shǐ (Pacification Commissioner) for agricultural encouragement and investigation,
which became the official title.
The Fùshǐ and Pànguān were named concurrent Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ and Pànguān.
Later, Xuānfǔ was changed to Ānfǔ (Pacification Commissioner),
each setting up one Ānfǔ Pànguān and one Tíxíng,
totaling four.
Ānfǔ Sī,
responsible for pacifying the people, observing frontier defenses and military affairs, and reviewing serious criminal cases.
The Ānfǔ Pànguān's
title did not include
"quànnóng cǎifǎng shì" (agricultural encouragement and investigation),
allowing them to specialize in managing qiānhù and móukè.

one was dispatched to Xiánpíng and one to
Shàngjīng for sub-offices.

the provincial council debated that the power of the Zhuǎnyùn Sī (Transport Commissioner) was weak,
and prefectures and counties did not fear it,
unable to plan for money and grain.
Thus, an imperial edict was issued for the Dūzhuǎnyùn (Grand Transport Commissioner) in Zhōngdū
to exclusively manage money and grain as before.

Zhōngdū Liúquán Wù. In Dàdìng thirteenth year,
the emperor said to his chief ministers:
"I hear that among the people, interest on pledges and pawns can be as high as five or seven fen,
or interest is treated as principal,
which causes hardship for the common people.
If the government were to establish treasury bureaus,
taking one-tenth as interest,
to assist with the expenses of officials' salaries,
it seems it would benefit the people.
You gentlemen should
discuss this and report back."
The relevant department then proposed to establish pledge and pawn bureaus in places like Zhōngdū, Nánjīng, Dōngpíng, and Zhēndìng,
named Liúquán,
each establishing one Shǐ and one Fù.
For all pledged items,
the Shǐ and Fù personally evaluate the value,
allowing a pledge of seven-tenths,
with a monthly interest of one fen;
if less than one month, it is calculated by day.
After two
full years,
if not redeemed again after an additional month,
it is then permitted to be taken off the shelf and sold.
When issuing a ticket,
the name of the person pledging the item,
the name and type of the item,
the grade and weight of gold and silver,
and the date, month, year, and amount in guàn of the pledge,
and the date of taking it off the shelf, etc., are written.
If lost,
on the day of redemption, the relevant officials are compelled
to verify the original pawned item.
the principal
and accumulated interest.
In addition to compensating the government,
the kùzǐ (treasury attendant) is further instructed
to value and compensate the pawned items according to their appraised value on the day of pawning.
Even if the items are old,
they shall be compensated
at the new price.
Furthermore, one assistant official or staff member from the Yùnsī (Transport Bureau) who is literate shall be assigned as a Tíkòng (Controller).
If there are any violations, they shall be investigated and punished.
Monthly reports shall be submitted
to the superior
office.

Fú System.
Initially,
before Mùzōng,
each tribal chief carved their own signal plates,
which were used to relay messages via post stations,
inquiring about affairs and disturbing the people.
Tàizǔ proposed that
if not by Mùzōng's order,
those who privately made plates and tokens would be subject to severe punishment.
From then on,
orders became unified.
In the ninth month of Shōuguó second year,
gold plates were first made;
later, silver plates and wooden plates were also made.
Gold plates were given to Wànhù,
silver plates to Méng'ān,
and wooden plates were worn by Móukè and Púliǎn.
Therefore, in the early days of the state, blank official appointments were given to military commanders
as rewards for merit.
Dìpái,
which were the signal plates of the early state,
were replaced by new gold and silver plates in the third month of Huángtǒng fifth year.
Their designs are all no longer transmitted.
In Dàdìng twenty-ninth year,
green oil with red characters was made,
used by the Shàngshūshěng for official documents.
Vermillion lacquer with gold characters
was used for imperial decrees.
Both were managed by the Zuǒyòusī.
When there was a need to transmit documents,
the plates were sent to various departments,
entrusted to postal stations for relay,
traveling two hundred and fifty lǐ per day.
If a Tái Department separately received an imperial decree,
it would also be issued with the above-mentioned system.
The system of tiger tallies:
It was established in the first year of Chéng'ān,
based on the words of the officials of rites.
The Hàn dynasty used bronze tiger tallies for the governors and chancellors of commanderies and states,
while the Táng dynasty used bronze fish tallies.
These were used for raising armies, changing chief officials, and similar matters.
By this time,
after deliberating on the precedents of the Hàn and Táng dynasties,
the tallies were made in the shape of a tiger,
with five left halves and one right half.
The left halves were kept before the emperor,
managed by trusted imperial attendants.
The right half was entrusted to the chief officials of the Suílù Tǒngjūn Sī (Route Commandery Command) and Zhāotǎo Sī (Pacification Command);
if the chief official was absent, the deputy official managed it.
If more than three hundred soldiers were to be mobilized, or if soldiers were to be conscripted, or if the chief or deputy officials of the local bureau were to be summoned or replaced,
a request was made to the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) for the first left tally.
The Jìnsì Jú (Bureau of Attendants) would seal it in a bag and hand it to the person making the request.
The Shàngshū (Chancellor) would record the imperial decree,
and seal it together with the tally in a box,
using the seal of the Shàngshū Shěng.
A special envoy with a plaque would then swiftly deliver it to its destination.
The official in charge of the tally would inspect the seal,
and match it with the right tally.
Only then would the order be carried out.
If there was any discrepancy,
they dared not implement it.
The official in charge would then reseal the left tally in a bag,
using their official seal on top.
They would then prepare a report on the troop mobilization and seal it with the tally using the seal of their own bureau.
On the same day, it would be returned to the envoy,
who would deliver it to the Shàngshū Shěng for submission.
The seal would then be changed,
and it would be given to the person in charge within the palace.
If there were further matters,
the left tallies would be issued in sequence,
repeating the cycle.
Each was also provided with a ledger to record the dates of issuance and receipt.
If there was an urgent situation involving bandits or robbers that did not allow for prior presentation,
even if it involved more than three hundred people,
the officials in charge of the troops were permitted to issue the tally.
They were to immediately report it to the emperor,
and the imperial edict would be implemented without delay.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu,
it was revised that the Pīmì Yuàn (Bureau of Military Affairs) would use deer tallies,
the Xuānfǔ Sī (Pacification Commissioner's Office) would use fish tallies,
and the Tǒngjūn Sī (Commandery Command) would use tiger tallies.
When issuing silver plaques,
if they were sent by the Shěng to a department or the Diǎnjiǎn Sī (Inspection Bureau),
the Zuǒyòu Sī (Left and Right Bureaus) would seal them in a box,
and verify the seal upon exchange.
If they were issued elsewhere,
they were all to be sealed, labeled, and signed,
and stored in a box.
Seal System.
Seal of the Crown Prince.
In the twenty-second year of Dàdìng,
Shìzōng traveled to Shàngjīng,
and had the
"Shǒuguó zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Guarding the State)
cast and bestowed upon the crown prince.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Shìzōng fell ill,
and the imperial grandson acted as regent.
The
"Shèzhèng zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Acting as Regent)
was cast. In the twelfth month of the thirtieth year of Zhēnyòu,
as the crown prince Shǒuxù was controlling the Pīmì Yuàn,
an imperial edict ordered the casting of the
"Fǔjūn zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Pacifying the Army) in gold,
following the system of Shìzōng's time,
to be used when presenting memorials and reports.
Seals of All Officials.
In the sixth year of Tiānhuì,
an edict was first issued to distribute seals to all bureaus.
Any previously carried seals, regardless of whether they were old or new,
were all to be handed over to the authorities.
Those who dared to conceal them would be subject to national laws.
By the first year of Zhènglóng,
due to the inconsistency in the names, ranks, and sizes of the old and new seals of internal and external officials,
with some using old Liáo and Sòng seals or Khitan characters,
a new system was consequently established,
and the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) was ordered to recast them.
The Sān Shī (Three Mentors), Sān Gōng (Three Dukes), Qinwáng (Princes of the First Rank), and Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs) all had gold seals,
two inches square,
weighing eighty liǎng,
with a camel knob.
The seals of Yīzìwáng (Princes with a single-character title) were
one inch and seven and a half fēn square,
gold-plated silver,
weighing forty liǎng,
with three gold-plated characters.
The seals of Zhūjùnwáng (Princes of Commanderies) were
one inch and six and a half fēn square,
gold-plated silver,
weighing thirty-five liǎng,
with three gold-plated characters.
Guógōng (Dukes of the State) had no seals.
First-rank seals were
one inch and six and a half fēn square,
gold-plated silver,
weighing thirty-five liǎng,
with three gold-plated characters.
Second-rank seals were
one inch and six fēn square,
gold-plated copper,
weighing twenty-six liǎng.
The Dōnggōng Sān Shī (Three Mentors of the Eastern Palace) and Zǎizhí (Chancellors) used seals similar to those of Jùnwáng.
Third-rank seals were
one inch and five and a half fēn square,
copper,
weighing twenty-four liǎng.
Fourth-rank seals were
one inch and five fēn square,
copper,
weighing twenty liǎng.
Fifth-rank seals were
one inch and four fēn square,
copper,
weighing twenty liǎng.
Sixth-rank seals were
one inch and three fēn square,
copper,
weighing sixteen liǎng.
Seventh-rank seals were
one inch and two fēn square,
copper,
weighing sixteen liǎng.
Eighth-rank seals were
one inch and one and a half fēn square,
copper,
weighing fourteen liǎng.
Ninth-rank seals were
one inch and one fēn square,
copper,
weighing fourteen liǎng.
All Zhūjì (Vermilion Seals) were
one inch square,
copper,
weighing fourteen liǎng.
In the second year of Tiāndé, the Xíng Shàngshū Shěng (Acting Department of State Affairs) found its seal too small,
and was therefore ordered to have it recast, one grade smaller than the Shàngshū Shěng seal.
In the second month of the twenty-fourth year of Dàdìng,
seals were cast for the Xíng Shàngshū Shěng, Yùshǐ Tái (Censorate), and the three bureaus of Zuǒyòu,
to accompany the emperor on his visit to Shàngjīng.
In the eighth month of the first year of Tàihé,
Gāo Yǒulín, the Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner) of Ānguó Jūn, reported:
"My prefecture holds three seals:
one is
'Ānguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ zhī Yìn' (Seal of the Military Commissioner of Ānguó Commandery),
one is 'Xíngzhōu Guānchásǐ Yìn' (Seal of the Surveillance Commissioner of Xíng Prefecture),
used for cases of officials, households, and rites;
and one is 'Xíngzhōu zhī Yìn' (Seal of Xíng Prefecture),
used for cases of military, criminal, and public works.
As the names and actual uses are not correct,
I request recasting."
The Zǎichén (Chancellors) thereupon advised:
"Matters handled exclusively by the Jiédùshǐ should naturally use the Jiédùshǐ seal.
The Guānchásǐ should do likewise.
For military and civil lawsuits under the Tiédiǎn of the six ministries,
the seal of the local prefecture should be used.
This shall be established as a permanent regulation."
The emperor agreed.
In the intercalary fourth month of the eighth year of Tàihé,
an imperial edict ordered the Diànqián Dūdiǎnjiǎn Sī (Bureau of the Grand Inspector of the Palace Front) to cast seals according to the example of the Zǒngguǎnfǔ (Grand Administration Office),
using the five characters
"jīn" (metal),
"mù" (wood),
"shuǐ" (water),
"huǒ" (fire),
"tǔ" (earth)
as designations.
These were to be issued when the bureau dispatched personnel.
Iron Plaques.
Made of iron,
shaped like a curved tile.
Characters were carved and borders drawn,
then filled with gold.
The outside was fitted with the imperial seal,
half was kept in the inner treasury,
to reward extraordinary merit.

In Tiāndé second year,

and Qīnwáng who received their emoluments and also managed other affairs:
previously, salaries were given for all;
now, it should follow the highest one,
and salaries for concurrent positions should not be given repeatedly.
By Dàdìng twenty-sixth year,
an imperial edict stated: "If one official holds multiple positions,
and a concurrent position incurs a crime, they cannot be exempted,
but should they be without emoluments?"
Thus, based on the complexity of duties, a fractional system was established
to provide salaries for concurrent positions.

According to the old system,
for the commercial taxes of supervising and overseeing bureaus, departments, and court offices,
those who showed an increase were rewarded,
while those who showed a deficit had their salaries docked.
In the ninth year of Dàdìng,
the emperor believed that officials without salaries could not maintain integrity,
so he stopped using the increase or decrease in numbers as a measure of performance (殿最, diànzuì).
He then abolished the system of docking salaries and giving rewards,
but the rewards for supervising officials remained as before.
In the twentieth year,
an imperial edict stated that for salt and wine commissioners and others with revenues exceeding 100,000 guàn,
if there was a deficit of five lí,
one fēn of their salary would be docked.
The memorial proposed a reward scale for officials of the Tídiǎn Yuànwù (提點院務) in various places.
For Tídiǎn Guān (提點官) and above in the provincial administration, and for court offices directly managed by the Yùnsī (運司),
if they could achieve an increase, six fēn (60%) of the ten fēn (100%) increase would go to the government,
two fēn (20%) would be given to the Tídiǎn officials, and two fēn (20%) would be given to the supervising officials as a reward.
If there was a deficit, salaries would be docked according to this same rule.
If they met the target, the full amount would be given.
In the twenty-second year of Dàdìng,
it was stipulated that half of the monthly salary would be advanced first.
If there was no deficit, the full amount would be paid.
If there was a deficit of one fēn, that one fēn would be docked,
and supplemented when the balance was paid.
The various commissioner offices, court offices, and market towns along the routes
often suffered from tax deficits.
The emperor said:
"If there are indeed places where the amount can be reduced,
we should appropriately cut it down.
This benefits both the public and private sectors."
In the twenty-third year,
for officials of the provincial Tíkòng (提控) and those stationed in Yùnsī (運司) areas,
a deficit of one fēn in tax revenue resulted in a docking of one fēn in salary,
which was considered too severe a punishment.
It was also ordered that half of the monthly salary be advanced first,
and the other half be docked or supplemented based on the deficit.
Public lands were not subject to this docking limit.
In the fourth month of the twenty-sixth year,
a system was established for supervising officials of court offices to compensate for deficits.

In the twelfth month of the first year of Zhēnyòu of Xuānzōng's reign,
due to insufficient grain reserves,
an imperial edict stipulated that the salaries of court officials and attendants
be paid according to the number of mouths,
and the rest converted at market price.
The emperor's decree to his provincial ministers said:
"I hear that for the imperial guards' salary,
each *shí* of grain is converted into six *dòu* of wheat.
How much can be saved by this,
while losing the hearts of the people?
Henceforth, give the original type of payment."
In the eighth month of the second year,
monthly salaries for clerks in the capital, prefectures, and counties, and the Zhuǎnyùnsī began to be issued with differentiation.
According to the old system, only clerks and *kǒumù* officials received salaries;
others only received food money.
Therefore, a new regulation was established.
In the third year,
an imperial edict reduced the annual allowances for various positions within the palace, with differentiation.
Censor Tián Jiǒngxiù stated:
"The state's financial adjustments
have only been implemented for a few months,
and already they are stagnating.
The problem lies in too much expenditure and too little revenue.
If we can trim expenditures and
increase revenue as needed,
it might last long."
He then listed five matters:
"First, court officials, translators and scribes, various bureau clerks, and various bureau attendants
are too numerous and should be merged and reduced.
Garrisoned troops everywhere are all assigned 'temporary governing officials' (*jìzhì guān*),
who are a waste of salaries.
It would be better to let the responsible authorities manage them concurrently.
Furthermore, along the river, every pavilion and barrier station has local militia,
but these are all untrained commoners
and cannot be used.
It would be better to replace them with regular troops
to save on expenses."
In the fourth month,
due to insufficient funds, officials of the sixth rank and below and attendants were dismissed from their personal obligation to pay for hired labor.
Half of the military laborers employed by the Xiūnèisī were reduced.
In areas with active military operations,
the number of *zhōu*, *fǔ*, and *sī* clerks was halved;
*sī* and *xiàn* clerks were reduced by one-third.
For the rest, except for Kāifēngfǔ and Nánjīng Zhuǎnyùnsī,
they were generally reduced by one-third.
Officials with salaries who did not leave the capital
were dismissed from receiving vouchers;
those who left received half.
In the first month of the second year of Xīngdìng
, an imperial edict
stated: "If county and sub-prefecture officials in Shǎnzhōu and other places collect insufficient taxes
, how can withholding their salaries encourage integrity?
From now on, salaries shall no longer be withheld."
Zhāng Huàjūn military commissioner Zhāng Xíngxìn said:
"Envoys sent to convey imperial decrees
were given a fixed number of gifts based on their rank, from fifth rank upwards.
Later, this practice was abolished.
Now, military officers and those above present gifts to the envoys,
and even those of the sixth rank and below are not exempt from this custom,
but many are unable to afford it.
They then levy contributions from their subordinates to give to the envoys,
sometimes even incurring punishment.
County magistrates are recommended
and their salaries specially increased,
but though this law has been in effect for some time,
there are still some west of the pass who have not taken office.
Is it that too few are recommended to fill the positions?
It would be appropriate to broaden the selection process
to fill these vacancies.
Moreover, assistant magistrates (chéngbù) are also directly involved with the people,
yet their salaries alone are not increased.
How can we prevent them from engaging in exploitation?"

Imperial Clan Table
In ancient times, the Grand Scribe (Tàishǐ) was responsible for the generations of the state
, distinguishing their surnames
and separating their generations (zhāomù),
a practice of great antiquity.
When the Jīn people first rose, there were twelve Wányán tribes.
Subsequently, all of them adopted their tribal name as their surname.
Historians recorded some
as "Zōngshì" (Imperial Clan)
, and some as Wányán.
Those called Wányán also fall into two categories:
some are Wányán of the same surname
, probably distant relatives,
such as Shítǔmén and Dígǔnǎi;
others are Wányán of a different surname
, probably tribal members,
such as Huāndū.
Before Dàdìng, they were called
"Zōngshì".
After Míngchāng, to avoid the taboo name of Ruìzōng, they were called
"Nèizú" (Inner Clan).
In reality, they were one and the same.
Recording names but not surnames
was the established custom.
Xuānzōng decreed that all imperial clan members (Zōngshì) should be called Wányán,
and no longer distinguished them.
Between Dàdìng and Tàihé,
all relatives down to the "tǎnmǐan" degree of mourning
had their names on the official roster
for bestowing official positions.
For those of "dàgōng" mourning degree and above,
court was suspended upon their death.
The principle of honoring relatives was thus observed.
After Zhēnyòu,
genealogies were lost and scattered;
only general outlines remained
, making it impossible to record all details.
Now, we have gathered those that can be ordered and compiled them into this chapter.
Those without ascertainable connections above or descendants below
cannot all be included.
The imperial clan members (Zōngshì) who can be genealogically recorded number eleven clans in total.
Although they are said to be descended from a certain emperor,
their exact generational sequence cannot be traced,
so they are not listed under individual emperors.
This is to ensure accuracy.

Table 2: Diplomatic Missions (Part 1)
How can the affairs of the world ever be constant?
The Jīn people constantly engaged in warfare
to control various tribes and secure their borders,
seeking to achieve their ambitions against the Liáo.
How could this be accomplished in a single day?
By the time Tàizǔ twice achieved victory
and had already ascended the imperial throne,
the Liáo then summoned him to surrender.
This was like a dragon ascending or a tiger transforming—
who could stop it?
Subsequently, envoys went back and forth eight or nine times,
but ultimately failed to establish a settlement.
Why?
Those who conquer an empire do not concern themselves with minor details.
Once their plan is set,
they will not cease their attack for humble words or generous gifts.
The Liáo people miscalculated;
the Sòng people also miscalculated.
The "Treaty from Across the Sea" (Hǎishàng zhī Shū) stated:
"After conquering Liáo,
the Hān territories that fell to the Qìdān during the Five Dynasties period are willingly ceded to the lower state."
What a grave miscalculation this was!
To obtain something through a hundred battles and bloodshed,
then to easily give it away for humble words and generous tributes—
is that human nature?
The Sòng made three miscalculations:
withdrawing from the three passes (Sān Guān), thus failing to secure the Yānshān Pass;
the treaty under the walls of Biànjīng, exhausting public and private treasuries for pledges;
establishing Liáng and Chǔ without fighting vigorously, leading to the Jiangzǎo (Southern Sòng) declaring vassalage.
Did the Jīn people love the Sòng people so much as to make peace?
Once the strategy was flawed
and their standing was compromised,
even if Gāozōng had established his court at Guīdé
and could not recover Héběi,
he could have secured Hénán and Shāndōng.
Otherwise,
he would still not have lost his status as Jìn Yuándì
, and who could have destroyed him?
The Jīn could not control all under heaven
, yet the Sòng people honored them with a respectful title.
Who forced this upon them?
The Jīn people emerged from Gāolí.
Initially, they communicated as enemies
, then became vassals.
The Xià state initially declared vassalage
, and in its later years, became brothers (with Jīn),
with its own ruler proclaiming himself emperor.
The Sòng, in the early Jīn period, sometimes addressed them with the courtesy of a vassal, using
"Biǎo" (memorial),
and eventually exchanged communications with the courtesy of a nephew, using
"Shū" (letter).
Thus, by knowing the years of their friendly relations and occasional military conflicts,
their rise and fall can broadly be observed.
Envoys sometimes wrote their original rank
, or used an honorary appointment.
The two countries each followed their old historical records,
and there was no need to force them to be consistent.

Biographies of Empresses and Consorts (Part 1)

Beginning with Shǐzǔ's Míngyì Empress, Dédé's Sī Empress, Āndì's Jié Empress, Xiànzǔ's Gōngjìng Empress, Zhāozǔ's Wēishùn Empress, Jǐngzǔ's Zhāosù Empress, Shìzǔ's Yìjiǎn Empress, Sùzōng's Jìngxūan Empress, Mùzōng's Zhēnhuì Empress, Kāngzōng's Jìngxī Empress, Tàizǔ's Shèngmù Empress, Tàizǔ's Guāngyì Empress, Tàizǔ's Qīnxiàn Empress, Tàizǔ's Xuānxiàn Empress, Tàizǔ's Chóng Xiāoshì, Tàizōng's Qīnrén Empress, Xīzōng's Dàopíng Empress, Hǎilíng's birth mother Túdānshì, Hǎilíng's mother Dàshì, Hǎilíng's empress Túdānshì (with Hǎilíng's favored concubines appended).
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven married an empress,
three states would send accompanying women
, all including sisters and nieces,
totaling twelve women.
A feudal lord would marry nine women in one go.
This was to rectify the positions of principal wife and concubines,
to broaden the succession,
to quell jealousy,
to prevent immorality,
and to avert calamity and disorder.
If the empress died,
the accompanying women (yìng) would become the successor wife
, each according to her.
If there were no three yìng,
then a sister or niece would succeed as wife
, also each according to her.
The successor wife managed the inner household affairs
but dared not assume the formal title.
According to the Rites,
a temple should not have two consorts worshipped side-by-side,
as they cannot be equally honored.
The practice of two consorts being worshipped side-by-side began with Rǔ Chéngfēng.
The state of Sòng had three yìng;
Qí's Guǎnshì (Guǎn Zhòng) had "three homes" (sān guī).
The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) criticized all of these.
According to the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ), the Inner Steward (Nèi Zǎi)
was followed by subordinates such as the Inner Junior Officials (Nèi Xiǎochén), Gatekeepers (Hūnrén), and Eunuchs (Sìrén);

then by the Nine Concubines (Jiǔpín), Court Ladies (Shìfù), Female Attendants (Nǚyù), Female Shamans (Nǚzhù), Female Scribes (Nǚshǐ), Directors of Women's Work (Diǎnfùgōng), Directors of Silk (Diǎnsī), Directors of Hemp (Diǎnxǐ), and Inner Chamberlains of Dress (Nèi Sīfú).
The "Meaning of Marriage" (Hūnyì) states
: "The Empress establishes six palaces, three empresses' companions (sān fūrén), nine concubines (jiǔpín), twenty-seven court ladies (shìfù), and eighty-one imperial concubines (yùqī)."
This does not align with the Spring and Autumn Annals or the Rites of Zhōu.
Later generations perpetuated this view,
and the number of women in the imperial harem eventually reached several thousand.
During the Jīn dynasty,
empresses were not chosen from commoner families.
The families of nephews and uncles held a similar significance to the Zhōu's Jī and Qí's Jiāng clans.
In the early days of the state, all imperial consorts had no designated ranks.
Xīzōng first established the titles of Guìfēi, Xiánfēi, and Défēi.
Hǎilíng indulged in lust,
and the imperial harem gradually expanded,
with twelve ranks: Yuánfēi, Shūfēi, Huìfēi, Guìfēi, Xiánfēi, Chénfēi, Lìfēi, Shúfēi, Défēi, Zhāofēi, Wēnfēi, and Ròufēi.
The imperial harem was small and simple after Dàdìng,
but became fully elaborate after Míngchāng.
The system of inner officials:
All Fēi ranks were considered equivalent to the principal first rank,
comparable to the Sān Fūrén.
Zhāoyí, Zhāoróng, Zhāoyuán, Xiūyí, Xiūróng, Xiūyuán, Chōngyí, Chōngróng, and Chōngyuán were considered equivalent to the principal second rank,
comparable to the Jiǔpín.
Nine Jiéyú were considered equivalent to the principal third rank,
nine Měirén were considered equivalent to the principal fourth rank,
and nine Cáirén were considered equivalent to the principal fifth rank,
comparable to the Twenty-Seven Shìfù.
Twenty-seven Bǎolín were considered equivalent to the principal sixth rank,
twenty-seven Yùnǚ were considered equivalent to the principal seventh rank,
and twenty-seven Cǎinǚ were considered equivalent to the principal eighth rank,
comparable to the Eighty-One Yùqī.
Furthermore, there were the Shànggōng, Shàngyí, Shàngfú, Shàngshí, Shàngqǐn, and Shànggōng,
all of whom were inner officials.
Tàizǔ's嫡 Hòu Shèngmù gave birth to Jǐngxuān.
Guāngyì gave birth to Zōnggàn.
[Shèngmù and Guāngyì] had the merit of settling the succession.
Qīnxuàn had the merit of protection and aid.
Therefore, from Xīzōng's time, Shèngmù, Guāngyì, and Qīnxuàn were all enshrined.
Xuānxìan gave birth to Ruìzōng.
In Dàdìng, she was enshrined.
Thus, Tàizǔ's temple enshrined four empresses.
Ruìzōng, Shìzōng, Xiǎnzōng, and Xuānzōng each enshrined two empresses.
Only Tàizōng, Jǐngxuān, Xīzōng, and Zhāngzōng's temples enshrined one empress.
Zhēn, Cí, Guāngxiàn, and Zhāoshèng, although of common surnames,
were all elevated due to their sons.
Xuānzōng conferred the Wēndūn family name,
and then granted surnames,
which was a great change from antiquity.
Therefore, from the beginning until the fall of the state,
their lineages are listed,
and their clan and native place are recorded,
which can be examined and used as a reference.
Those who had no involvement in state affairs
are omitted.
The founding ancestor's empress, Míngyì Hòuhòu,
was a Wányán tribeswoman.
She married the founding ancestor when she was over sixty years old.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Dédì's empress, Sī Hòuhòu,
was from an unknown tribe.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Āndì's empress, Jié Hòuhòu,
was from an unknown tribe.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Xiànzǔ's empress, Gōngjìng Hòuhòu,
was from an unknown tribe.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Zhāozǔ's empress, Wēishùn Hòuhòu, of the Túdān clan,
whose given name was Wūgǔlùndūgē,
was from the Túdān tribe in Dírǔxiāng of Huólàhúoshuǐ.
Her father was Bátàndūlúhǎi.
The empress was resolute and firm by nature,
so no one dared to take her as a wife.
When Xiànzǔ was about to find a wife for Zhāozǔ,
he said:
"This son is extraordinarily brave and decisive;
a weak and gentle woman cannot be his match."
So, he found her for Zhāozǔ.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Jǐngzǔ's empress, Zhāosù Hòuhòu,
of the Tángkuò clan,
whose given name was Duōbǎozhēn, was from the Tángkuò tribe in Yācūn by Shuàishuǐ.
Her father, Shípīdésāgǔzhǐ,
was a shaman.
The empress had good judgment and demeanor.
When at her parents' home, she enjoyed entertaining guests.
When her parents were out,
she would often prepare wine and food to entertain neighbors
and even travelers.
Jǐngzǔ ate excessively,
and people at the time called him
"Huólúo,"
the explanation of which is in Jǐngzǔ Jì.
Zhāozǔ said:
"A frugal woman would be stingy with wine and food,
and cannot be his match."
Wūgǔnǎi heard of the empress's character and demeanor,
and thus married her.
When the Liáo envoy Tónggàn came to attack the Púniè tribe of the Five Nations,
Jǐngzǔ sent the empress and Héxūn as hostages to Bá Yǐmén,
and then, with Tónggàn, raided and captured it.
The Liáo lord then made Jǐngzǔ a Jìdùshǐ.
Although the empress enjoyed guests,
she herself did not drink alcohol.
When Jǐngzǔ drank with guests,
the empress would listen intently.
The next day,
she would enumerate the actions of each person,
missing none of their key points.
If there was someone drunk and boisterous,
she would sing to calm their anger and disputes.
If there were those in the army who had been flogged,
she would often console them with wine and food.
When Jǐngzǔ traveled through his territory,
she would always accompany him,
and she would help resolve all political matters and lawsuits.
After Jǐngzǔ's death,
whenever Shìzǔ and his brothers undertook military campaigns,
they would first report to the empress before acting,
and she would give admonitions and encouragement regarding victories and defeats.
During agricultural months,
she personally supervised plowing, weeding, and harvesting.
For distant places, she rode a horse;
for nearby places, she used a walking stick.
She encouraged those who were diligent in their work
and admonished those who were late to start and early to rest.
When the empress went to Yìtúncūn,
Shìzǔ and Sùzōng both followed.
Huánpó and Sàndá happened to arrive together.
At this time, there was already a rift between them.
Under the influence of alcohol,
their words became aggressive and they could not be reconciled.
They then drew their blades against each other.
The empress stood up,
held both their hands,
and said to Huánpó and Sàndá:
"You are all old comrades from my husband's time.
How can you suddenly forget my husband's kindness and quarrel with these young sons?"
She then composed a song,
and Huánpó and Sàndá's anger subsided.
Afterwards, Huánpó's brothers raised troops and attacked.
At that time,
Sùzōng had already suffered two defeats.
Shìzǔ had already repelled Wūchūn's troops
and fought Huánpó at Běiàidiàn.
The tribesman Shīshùkuān fled back,
arriving bare-chested,
and reported to the empress:
"The army is defeated!"
The empress was in distress,
but then Kāngzōng arrived with news of victory,
and the empress was pleased.
Afterwards, Huánpó and Sàndá both surrendered.
The empress was not jealous,
and was unconcerned with women's crafts.
She was able to unite and harmonize the clan,
and at that time, she was considered to possess the magnanimity of a man.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Shìzǔ's empress, Yìjiǎn Hòuhòu,
was of the Nálǎn clan.
She died in the Guǐyǒu year, the first year of Dà'ān.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Sùzōng's empress, Jìngxuān Hòuhòu,
was of the Púchá clan.
When Tàizǔ was about to raise an army,
he went to report to the empress.
The empress said:
"You are the head of the state.
Act when you see it is feasible.
I am old now;
do not bring me worry,
and you certainly will not reach that point."
Tàizǔ offered a cup of wine for her longevity,
then led the empress out the gate,
poured wine as a libation, and prayed to heaven.
The empress ordered Tàizǔ to sit properly
and issue commands to his generals.
From then on, every time Tàizǔ returned from an expedition,
he would lead his generals to visit her,
presenting what they had captured.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Mùzōng's empress, Zhēnhuì Hòuhòu,
was of the Wūgǔlùn clan.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Kāngzōng's empress, Jìngxī Hòuhòu,
was of the Tángkuò clan.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Tàizǔ's empress, Shèngmù Hòuhòu,
was of the Tángkuò clan.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Her father, Liúsù, was granted the title Tàiwèi and Róngguógōng.
Her grandfather, Diéhúběn, was granted Sītú and Yīngguógōng.
Her great-grandfather, Héxìnǎi, was granted Sīkōng and Wēnguógōng.
Tàizǔ's empress, Guāngyì Hòuhòu,
was of the Péimǎn clan.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānhuì, she was posthumously granted a title.
Tàizǔ's empress, Qīnxuàn Hòuhòu,
was of the Gēshíliè clan.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānhuì,
she was honored as Tàihuáng Tàihòu,
with her palace named Qìngyuán.
On Jǐsì day, the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year,
Xīzōng paid respects at Qìngyuán Gōng,
and then ascended to Qiányuán Diàn
to receive congratulations from the officials.
In the same month, on Dīngchǒu day,
she passed away at Qìngyuán Gōng.
On Guǐmǎo day of the second month,
she was enshrined and buried at Ruìlíng.
Tàizǔ's empress, Xuānxìan Hòuhòu,
of the Púsàn clan,
was Ruìzōng's mother.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānhuì,
she was posthumously granted the title Défēi.
In the first year of Dàdìng, she was posthumously granted a title.
Consort Chóng
was from the Xiāo
clan. During Xīzōng's
reign, she was enfeoffed as Guìfēi. In the first month of Tiāndé
second year, she was enfeoffed as Yuánfēi.
That same month,
she was honored as Tàifēi.
Hǎilíng's
mother, the Dà
clan, served the Xiāo
clan with great diligence. When Hǎilíng
usurped the throne, he honored the Dà
clan as Empress Dowager,
residing in the Yǒngníng
Palace. Whenever there were banquets,
Tàifēi
sat in the seat of honor,
while the Dà
clan performed the rites of a daughter-in-law.
Hǎilíng
was increasingly discontented. After
killing Zōngyì
and others, he falsely
accused Tàifēi
of hidden wickedness,
and killed her,
along with her son, Rènwáng Wēihē.
In Dàdìng
nineteenth year, an edict
ordered her reburial.
Dàzōngzhèngchéng Zōng'ān
supervised the funeral arrangements,
and an envoy was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
The Emperor wished to restore
Tàifēi's
former title,
and referred the matter to the ritual officials for discussion.
“In previous dynasties, those called Tàifēi
were all made noble by their sons.
In ancient times, when entering the ancestral temple, the title 'Hòu'
was tied to the husband,
and in court, the title 'Tài'
was tied to the son.
This differs from the present case of Consort Xiāo,
so it may not be appropriate to use 'Tài';
she should merely be posthumously enfeoffed with a consort title.”
The edict followed
this, and so she was enfeoffed
as Consort Chóng.
Empress Qīnrén
of Tàizōng
was from the Tángkuò
clan. When Xīzōng
ascended the throne,
she and Empress Qīnxìan
of Tàizǔ
were both honored as Grand Empress Dowagers,
and her palace was named Míngdé
Palace. Her father, Ālúshù,
was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi
and Sòngguógōng;
her grandfather, Shípī,
was posthumously granted the title of Sītú
and Yīngguógōng;
her great-grandfather, Ālúsuǒ,
was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng
and Wēnguógōng.
On the jǐsì
day of the first month of the fourteenth
year, the Emperor paid respects
to the two Empresses Dowager,
and then held court in the Qiányuán
Hall to receive congratulations.
Thereafter, this became an annual
custom. In Huángtǒng
first year, the Emperor
returned to the capital
from Yānjīng,
and paid a visit to the Míngdé
Palace. The next
year, the Emperor
went to the Tiānkāi
Hall. When the imperial
son was born, an envoy
was sent to report
to the Empress Dowager.
When the Empress Dowager
arrived at Tiānkāi
Hall, the Emperor
and Empress personally
greeted her. In the third
year, she passed away
in Míngdé
Palace. She was given the posthumous
title Empress Qīnrén,
and was interred at Gōnglíng.
Empress Dàopíng
of Xīzōng
was from the Péimǎn
clan. When Xīzōng
ascended the throne,
she was enfeoffed as Guìfēi.
In Tiānjuàn
first year, she was
established as Empress.
Her father, Hūdábài,
was Tàiwèi. Her great-grandfather,
Xiéyě,
was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng;
her grandfather, Gǔshā,
was Sītú. In Huángtǒng
first year, Xīzōng
received an honorific title,
and she was invested
as Empress Címíng Gōngxiào Shùndé.
In the second
year, Crown Prince
Jì'ān
was born. That
year, Xīzōng
was twenty-four
years old, and overjoyed,
he issued a general amnesty,
and made offerings to Heaven,
Earth, and the ancestral temples.
After one full
month, he was invested
as Crown Prince,
but he died before
reaching one year of age.
During Xīzōng's
reign, Zōnghàn,
Zōnggàn,
and Zōngbì
successively held power,
while the Emperor sat
silently at court.
Although the state faced many
challenges in his early
years, the strategies
devised by the ancestral
temple secured victories;
the state of Qí
was abolished,
the Sòng
people requested
vassalage, officials were
honest, governance was
simple, and the populace
enjoyed their livelihoods.
After Zōngbì's
death, many old
officials also passed
away. The Empress
interfered in state
affairs without any
restraint, and court
officials often used
her influence to
gain the position
of chancellor. After
Jì'ān's
death, no successor
was established for
several years, and the
Empress significantly
constrained Xīzōng.
Xīzōng
was inwardly discontent,
and due to his
despair, he indulged
in alcohol, became
furious, and personally
killed people with
a blade. On Left
Chancellor Liàng's
birthday, the Emperor
sent Dàxīngguó
with a portrait of Sīmǎ Guāng,
a jade túhú,
and a horse as gifts.
The Empress
also attached birthday
gifts. When Xīzōng
heard of this,
he was enraged,
and consequently flogged
Xīngguó
In the fourth year of Tiāndé,
Hǎilíng moved the capital to Zhōngdū,
leaving only Túshàn in Shàngjīng.
Túshàn was constantly worried and fearful.
Whenever an imperial envoy arrived,
she would change her clothes to await their command.
Dàshì, in Zhōngdū, often thought of Empress Dowager Túshàn,
and said to Hǎilíng:
“The Yǒngshòu Gōng treated my mother and son very kindly;
be sure not to forget it.”
On the fourteenth day of the twelfth month,
it was Túshàn Shì’s birthday.
Hǎilíng sent the Secretary of the Imperial Library, Nàhé Chūnnián, to Shàngjīng to offer birthday felicitations to the Empress Dowager.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán,
Dàshì fell gravely ill,
regretting that she could not see her even once.
Before her death,
she said to Hǎilíng:
“Because of me,
you did not allow the Yǒngshòu Gōng to come with us to Zhōngdū.
When I die,
you must welcome her here,
and serve the Yǒngshòu Gōng as you would serve me.”
In the third year,
the Right Chancellor Púshàn Shīgōng and the Grand Patriarchal Administrator Hú Bálǔ went to Shàngjīng to relocate the imperial tombs.
Hǎilíng consequently ordered Empress Dowager Yǒngshòu Gōng to come along.
Subsequently, he dispatched the Administrator of Governmental Affairs, Xiāo Yù, to Guǎngníng to perform sacrifices for the ancestral coffins.
Hǎilíng said to Xiāo Yù:
“Yīwūlǘ Shān has many beautiful sights.
After the sacrificial rites are completed,
you may suggest that the Empress Dowager tour the scenic spots.”
When they reached Shāliú Hé,
Hǎilíng welcomed and paid respects to the imperial coffins,
and then paid his respects to the Empress Dowager.
Hǎilíng ordered his attendants to bind two bundles of canes and bring them with him.
He knelt before the Empress Dowager,
and apologized, saying:
“Liàng is unfilial,
having long neglected to attend to your comfort.
I wish for the Empress Dowager to severely flog me.
Otherwise,
I will not feel at peace.”
The Empress Dowager personally helped him up,
and scolded those who had bound the canes, telling them to leave.
The Empress Dowager said:
“Today, if a commoner has a son who can establish a family,
and owns a hundred gold coins' worth of property,
he would still cherish him and not bear to flog him.
I have a son such as this,
how could I bear to flog him?”
In the tenth month,
the Empress Dowager arrived in Zhōngdū.
Hǎilíng led the hundred officials in a welcoming ceremony in the suburbs,
and she resided in Shòukāng Gōng.
On that day,
Hǎilíng, the imperial concubines, and the chancellors and below, offered wine for her longevity,
and dispersed after much merriment.
Hǎilíng attended the Empress Dowager in the palace,
showing utmost respect and deference externally.
Whenever the Empress Dowager sat or rose,
he would personally support her arm.
He often followed her palanquin on foot,
and sometimes personally carried items she used.
Those who saw this considered him extremely filial,
and the Empress Dowager also believed it to be sincere.
When he planned to attack Sòng,
the Empress Dowager advised against it.
Hǎilíng became increasingly displeased in his heart.
Every time he returned from visiting the Empress Dowager,
he would be furious,
and people did not know why.
When he arrived at Biànjīng,
the Empress Dowager resided in Níngdé Gōng.
The Empress Dowager sent her maid Gāo Fúniáng to inquire about Hǎilíng’s well-being.
Hǎilíng favored her,
and then used her to monitor the Empress Dowager’s activities.
Whatever the Empress Dowager did or stopped,
no matter how big or small,
Fúniáng’s husband Tèmògē instructed Fúniáng to embellish her words when reporting to Hǎilíng.
When the Commissioner of Military Affairs, Púshàn Shīgōng, was dispatched to conquer Qìdān Sābā,
he took leave to visit the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager spoke with Shīgōng for a long time.
The general gist was:
“Our state has resided in Shàngjīng for generations.
It then moved to Zhōngdū,
and now from Zhōngdū to Biànjīng.
Now, troops are being raised to cross the Jiāng and Huái rivers to attack Sòng,
exhausting the Central Plains.
I have repeatedly advised against it,
but was not listened to.
The Qìdān matter is again like this,
what is to be done?”
Fúniáng reported this to Hǎilíng.
Hǎilíng interpreted it to mean that the Empress Dowager considered Chōng as her son,
and since Chōng’s four sons were all established,
he feared that with Shīgōng leading troops outside,
the Empress Dowager might have other plans.

So, he summoned the Imperial Inspector Dà Huáizhōng, Hanlin Academy Compiler Wòlún, Supervisor of the Imperial Robes Bureau Hǔ Tèmò, and Chief of the Imperial Armory Xíshī, to kill the Empress Dowager in Níngdé Gōng.
He ordered the imperial guards Gāo Fú, Cí Lè, and Púsùwò, with forty soldiers, to follow.
He also warned them, saying:
“When you see the Empress Dowager,
just say there is an imperial edict,
order the Empress Dowager to kneel to receive it,
then strike and kill her immediately.
Do not let her suffer.
The Empress Dowager’s foster sister Āntè
is garrulous and will surely speak falsely,
she must be made to die quickly.”
He also named several of the Empress Dowager’s attendants,
ordering all of them to be killed.
The Empress Dowager was playing backgammon.
Dà Huáizhōng and the others arrived
and ordered the Empress Dowager to kneel to receive the edict.
The Empress Dowager was startled,
and just as she was kneeling,
Hǔ Tèmò struck her from behind.
She fell and rose again twice.
Gāo Fú and the others strangled her to death,
at the age of fifty-three.
They also killed Āntè, as well as the County Mistresses Báishàn, Ālǔwǎ, and Chāchá;
the wet nurse Nánsā;
the maids Āsī and Wòlǐbǎo;
the Níngdé Gōng guard Wēndíhǎn Chálà;
the Chiefs Wáng Jiānú and Sābā;
and the page Hūsā, among others.
Hǎilíng ordered the Empress Dowager to be cremated in the palace,
and her ashes thrown into the water.
He also killed Chōng’s sons Tánnú, Ālǐbái, and Yuánnú.
Yēbǔér escaped and hid,
returning to Shìzōng.
He recalled Shīgōng from the army
and killed him.
He also killed Āsī’s descendants, Sābā’s two sons, and Hūsā’s two sons.
He enfeoffed Gāo Fúniáng as Yún Guó Fūrén,
and appointed Tèmògē as the Prefect of Zézhōu.
Hǎilíng promised Fúniáng to make her a concubine upon his return from the southern campaign,
and bestowed two thousand taels of silver.
He issued an imperial order warning Tèmògē:
“Do not drink excessively and beat Fúniáng.
If you beat Fúniáng, I will surely kill you.”
During the Dàdìng era,
Túshàn Shì was posthumously given the title Empress Āi.
Tèmògē and Fúniáng were brought in chains from Zézhōu to Zhōngdū and executed.
Afterwards, Hǎilíng was demoted to a commoner.
Zōnggàn’s imperial title was removed,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Liáo Wáng.
Túshàn Shì was demoted and enfeoffed as Liáo Wáng Fēi.
Hǎilíng’s mother was Dàshì.
In the first month of the second year of Tiāndé,
she and Túshàn Shì were both honored as Empress Dowager.
Dàshì resided in Yǒngníng Gōng.
Her great-grandfather Jiānsì was posthumously granted the title Sīkōng.
Her grandfather Chénbǎo was posthumously granted Sītú.
Her father Hàotiān was posthumously granted Tàiyù and Guó Gōng.
Her elder brother Xīngguó’nú was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Wèi Guó Gōng.
In the eleventh month,
Hàotiān was advanced to the rank of Wáng.
On the sixteenth day of the first month of the third year,
it was Hǎilíng’s birthday.
He hosted a banquet for the imperial clan and hundred officials in Wǔdé Diàn.
Dàshì was extremely joyful,
and drank until completely drunk.
The next day,
Hǎilíng sent an imperial envoy to report, saying:
“The Empress Dowager is advanced in years.
Normally, she drinks no more than a few cups of wine,
but yesterday she was seen drinking until thoroughly intoxicated.
As her son is the Son of Heaven,
it is certainly a cause for joy.
However, if Your Sacred Body is unwell,
then Your son’s heart will not be at peace.
Where then is the joy?
The greatest joy is in the heart,
not in wine.”
When the capital moved to Zhōngdū,
the Yǒngshòu Gōng remained alone in Shàngjīng.
Dàshì often brought this up.
In the fourth month of the first year of Zhēnyuán,
Dàshì fell ill.
An imperial edict ordered 100,000 strings of cash to be used to seek remedies.
When her illness became grave,
she left a dying wish to Hǎilíng,
that he should treat the Yǒngshòu Gōng well.
On the day Wùyín,
she passed away.
An imperial edict was issued to the Department of State Affairs:
“All officials attending court shall resume their duties on the first day of the fifth month.
In Zhōngdū,
from the nineteenth day of the fourth month,
music is forbidden for one month.
In other regions,
from the day the imperial edict arrives,
officials shall not attend to affairs for three days,
music is forbidden for one month, and bells shall be rung for seven days and nights.”
Guìfēi Dìnggē,
had the clan name Tángkuò.
She was beautiful.
She was the wife of Wū Dài, the Military Governor of Chóngyì.
Hǎilíng had previously had an illicit affair with her,
which her maid Guìgē knew about.
When Wū Dài was at his post,
whenever there was a New Year's Day assembly or a birthday,
he would send his household servants Gélǔ and Géwēn to the imperial court to offer congratulations.
Dìnggē also sent Guìgē to inquire about Hǎilíng's well-being and the daily life of the two empress dowagers.
Hǎilíng then had Guìgē relay a message to Dìnggē, saying:
"Since ancient times, even emperors have had two empresses.
Can you kill your husband to follow me?"
When Guìgē returned,
she fully conveyed Hǎilíng's words to Dìnggē.
Dìnggē said:
"When I was young, I was ugly,
and that affair was already disgraceful.
Now my children are grown up,
how can I do this?"
When Hǎilíng heard this,
he sent a message to Dìnggē:
"If you do not bear to kill your husband,
I will exterminate your entire clan."
Dìnggē was greatly frightened,
and used her son Wūdá'bǔ as an excuse,
saying:
"He often attends to his father,
so there is no convenient opportunity."
Hǎilíng immediately summoned Wūdá'bǔ to serve as a Palace Guard of the Seals.
Dìnggē said:
"The matter cannot be stopped now."
Taking advantage of Wū Dài's drunkenness,
she ordered Gélǔ and Géwēn to strangle Wū Dài.
This was in the seventh month of the fourth year of Tiāndé
When Hǎilíng heard of Wū Dài's death,
he feigned sorrow.
After Wū Dài was buried,
he immediately brought Dìnggē into the palace as a lady.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán
she was enfeoffed as Guìfēi.
She was greatly loved and favored,
and promised to be made empress.
She often rode in the same carriage with him to tour Yáochí,
while other consorts followed on foot.
As Hǎilíng increasingly indulged in other favorites,
Dìnggē rarely saw him.
One day, she was alone on an upper floor,
when Hǎilíng and another consort passed below in the same carriage.
Dìnggē saw them,
cried out, demanding to leave,
and cursed Hǎilíng.
Hǎilíng feigned not hearing and left.
Since her husband's time,
Dìnggē had an affair with a household servant named Yán Qǐ'ér,
and often gave him clothes.
When she became Guìfēi,
Qǐ'ér, as an old servant of the imperial consort's household,
was assigned to serve in her original post.
Dìnggē, resenting Hǎilíng's neglect,
wanted to resume her affair with Qǐ'ér.
There were three Buddhist nuns who frequented the palace,
and Dìnggē had the nuns ask Qǐ'ér for the clothes she had given him to entice him.
Qǐ'ér understood her intention,
and smiled, saying:
"Has the consort forgotten me now that she is rich and honored?"
Dìnggē wanted to bring Qǐ'ér into the palace by stratagem,
fearing that the gatekeepers would search him.
So she ordered her maid to put her undergarments in a large trunk,
and sent someone to carry it into the palace.
The gatekeepers searched it,
and seeing that the trunk contained only undergarments,
they were already regretting and afraid.
Dìnggē sent someone to reprimand the gatekeepers, saying:
"I am
the Emperor's consort.
These are my personal clothes.
Why do you deliberately look at them?
What is this?
I will report this."
The gatekeepers said in terror:
"This is a capital offense.
Please forgive us; we will not dare to do it again."
Dìnggē then had someone put Qǐ'ér in a trunk and carry him into the palace,
and the gatekeepers indeed dared not search it again.
Qǐ'ér stayed in the palace for more than ten days,
dressed in women's clothes,
mixed among the palace maids,
and was sent out at dusk.
Guìgē reported this to Hǎilíng.
Dìnggē was strangled to death,
and Qǐ'ér and the three nuns were all executed.
Guìgē was enfeoffed as the Lady of Shēnguó.
Initially,
after Hǎilíng had Dìnggē kill her husband Wū Dài,
he sent his junior attendant Yàoshīnú to convey his imperial order to Dìnggē,
informing her of his intention to take her into the palace.
Yàoshīnú knew that Dìnggē had an affair with Yán Qǐ'ér,
and Dìnggē bribed Yàoshīnú with eighteen servants and maids to keep silent about her private affair with Qǐ'ér.
When Dìnggē's plot failed,
Yàoshīnú was flogged one hundred and fifty times.
Earlier,
Yàoshīnú had stolen a jade belt and deserved death,
but Hǎilíng pardoned him
and sent him away.
When the capital was moved to Zhōngdū,
he was recalled to be a junior attendant again.
After Yàoshīnú was flogged for concealing Dìnggē's affair,
he later had an affair with the Lady of Língshòuxiàn, along with Bìshūjiān Wén.
Wén was flogged two hundred times and dismissed from office,
and Yàoshīnú was to be beheaded.
Hǎilíng wanted to flog him instead,
and said to his close ministers:
"Yàoshīnú has rendered meritorious service to me;
if he is flogged again, he will die."
Chancellor Lǐ Dǔ and others insisted that Yàoshīnú could not be pardoned according to the law,
so he was executed.
Hǎilíng made Gélǔ and Géwēn imperial guards.
Géwēn was promoted to the magistrate of Cháng'ānxiàn,
and Gélǔ was promoted to the magistrate of Xiāngchéngxiàn.
In the early years of Dàdìng [1161-1189],
they were both dismissed from office.
Lìfēi Shígē
was Dìnggē's younger sister,
and the wife of Bìshūjiān Wén.
Hǎilíng had an affair with her,
and wanted to bring her into the palace.
So he sent Wén's stepmother Àndūguā to manage Wén's household.
Hǎilíng said to Àndūguā:
"You must send out your wife,
otherwise I will take other measures."
Àndūguā told Wén this,
and Wén found it difficult.
Àndūguā said:
"The Emperor said he would take other measures,
meaning he wants to kill you.
How can you risk your life for one wife?"
Having no choice, Wén
and Shígē embraced and wept, then parted ways.
At this time,
Hǎilíng had moved the capital to Zhōngjīng.
He sent Shígē to Zhōngdū,
and took her in.
Hǎilíng summoned Wén to the private hall,
and had Shígē tell vulgar jokes to Wén for entertainment.
When Dìnggē died,
Shígē was sent out of the palace.
Within a few days, she was recalled,
and enfeoffed as Xiūróng.
In the third year of Zhēnyuán
she was promoted to Zhāoyí.
In the first year of Zhènglóng
she was promoted to Ròufēi.
In the second year
she was promoted to Lìfēi.
Ròufēi Mílè,
had the clan name Yēlǜ.
In the second year of Tiāndé
Hǎilíng sent the Minister of Rites Xiāo Gǒng to fetch her from Biàn.
Passing through Yānjīng,
Gǒng's father Zhònggōng was the Yānjīng Grand Administrator.
Seeing that Mílè's physique did not appear to be that of a virgin,
he sighed, saying:
"The Emperor will surely suspect and kill Gǒng."
Upon entering the palace,
she was indeed not a virgin,
and was sent out of the palace the next day.
Hǎilíng suspected Xiāo Gǒng,
and ultimately caused his death.
Mílè was out of the palace for several months,
then recalled,
and enfeoffed as Chōngyuàn.
Her mother, Zhāng, was enfeoffed as the Lady of Shēnguó,
and her paternal aunt, Xiāo, Lady of Lánlíng Jùnjūn, was enfeoffed as the Lady of Gǒngguó.
Xiāo Gǒng's wife, Zétèlán,
was Mílè's elder sister.
After Hǎilíng took Wén's wife Shígē,
he then married Zétèlán to Wén.
Later, he cunningly used Mílè's recall as a pretext
to summon Zétèlán into the palace,
and had an affair with her.
After that,
Mílè was promoted to Ròufēi.
Zhāofēi Ālǎn
was the wife of Hǎilíng's uncle, the King of Cáoguó, Zōngmǐn.
Hǎilíng killed Zōngmǐn and brought Ālǎn into the palace.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán
she was enfeoffed as Zhāofēi.
Ministers reported
that "Zōngmǐn was a close and revered relative,
this is improper."
So she was ordered to leave the palace.
Xiūyí Gāo-shì,
was the wife of Bǐngdé's younger brother, Círǐ.
Hǎilíng killed many imperial relatives,
but released their women.
The wives of Zōngběn's son Shālílì, Zōnggù's son Húlílì, Húshīlái's wife, and Círǐ's wife,
Hǎilíng wanted to bring them into the palace,
and implicitly suggested that the prime ministers formally request it.
The envoy Dāndān Zhēn implicitly suggested to Xiāo Yù,
“My lineage is not yet extensive.
Among these women of the partisans, some are my close relatives, both paternal and maternal.
How about bringing them into the palace?”
Yù said,
“Recently, many imperial relatives were killed,
and there are widespread and diverse opinions.
How can you do this again?”
Hǎilíng said,
“I knew Yù would not agree.”
Then he ordered Zhēn to implicitly suggest to Yù using his own discretion,
insisting that Yù and others should make the request.
Zhēn said to Yù,
“The Emperor's intention is already set.
If you insist on stopping him,
he will become ill.”
Yù said,
“If he absolutely won't give up,
then let the Emperor choose.”
Zhēn said,
“He absolutely wants you and others to propose it.”
Yù had no choice,
so he submitted a formal memorial,
and they were subsequently taken into the palace.
Before long,
Gāo-shì was enfeoffed as Xiūyí,
her father Gāo Yēlǔwǎ was promoted to Fǔguó Shàngjiāngjūn,
and her mother Wányán-shì was enfeoffed as Mìguó Fūrén.
Gāo-shì complained to Hǎilíng about family matters.
Hǎilíng, ever since the time of Xīzōng,
had seen Empress Dào interfering in politics,
and abhorred it in his heart.
Therefore, from the moment he ascended the throne,
he did not allow his mother or empress to participate in government affairs.
Consequently,
he sent Gāo-shì back to her parents' home.
He issued an edict to the Shàngshū Shěng,
stating that if any empress or concubine made a request to the prime minister,
their messenger should be apprehended and the matter reported.
Zhāoyuán Chábā,
her surname was Yēlǜ-shì.
She had been promised in marriage to Xiāo Tánggǔdài, a Xī man.
Hǎilíng took her,
and enfeoffed her as Zhāoyuán.
Tánggǔdài was a guard.
Chábā instructed her maid Xíniǎn to give him several soft gold quail purses.
The matter was discovered.
At that time,
Tánggǔdài was on leave at Héjiān驛 (驛 stands for Yì).
He was summoned for questioning.
Tánggǔdài told the truth,
and Hǎilíng spared him.
Hǎilíng ascended the Bǎochāng Ménlóu,
and paraded Chábā before all the empresses and concubines.
He personally struck her with a blade,
and she fell from the gate and died.
He also executed her maid Xíniǎn.
Shòuníng Xiànzhǔ Shígǔ,
was the daughter of Sòng Wáng Zōngwàng.
Jìnglè Xiànzhǔ Púlà and Xíniǎn,
were the daughters of Liáng Wáng Zōngbì.
Shīgū'ér,
was the daughter of Zōngjùn.
All were his paternal cousins.
Húntóng Jùnjūn Shālǐgǔzhēn and her younger sister Yúdū,
were the daughters of Tàifù Zōngběn,
his second paternal cousins.
Chéngguó Fūrén Zhòngjié,
was the granddaughter of Zōngpán,
the daughter of his second paternal cousin.
And his mother Dà-shì's maternal cousin Zhāng Dìng'ān's wife Nàláhū, and Lìfēi's younger sister Púlǔhúzhī,
all had husbands,
only Shígǔ was widowed.
Hǎilíng had no shame or compunctions,
and sent Gāo Shīgū, Nèigē, Āgǔ, and others to convey messages,
and had private relations with all of them.
All the imperial consorts, princesses, and imperial kinswomen with whom he had private relations,
were assigned to various concubines,
and entered and exited through their quarters.
Nàláhū entered and exited through Yuánfēi's quarters,
Púlǔhúzhī entered and exited through Lìfēi's quarters,
Shālǐgǔzhēn and Yúdū entered and exited through Guìfēi's quarters,
Shígǔ and Zhòngjié entered and exited through Zhāofēi's quarters,
Púlà and Shīgū'ér entered and exited through Shúfēi's quarters.
Hǎilíng ordered Nèigē to summon Shígǔ.
He first placed a qín and a ruǎn in a small chamber in the warm quarters,
and then summoned her.
Shígǔ's beauty had already faded,
and he often mocked her decline and laughed at it.
Only Xíniǎn and Shālǐgǔzhēn were most favored,
and relying on their power, they flogged their husbands.
Hǎilíng made Xíniǎn's husband Shāo Hēyā guard and stand vigil,
and Shālǐgǔzhēn's husband Sāsù serve as a close attendant and stand vigil.
He said to Sāsù,
“Your wife is young.
When it is your turn to stand vigil,
she should not be allowed to stay at home;
she must always stay in the concubine's quarters.”
Whenever he summoned her,
he would personally wait in the corridor.
If he stood for a long time,
he would sit on Gāo Shīgū's lap.
Gāo Shīgū said,
“Why is the Son of Heaven so toilsome?”
Hǎilíng said,
“I always consider being the Son of Heaven easy to achieve.
But such assignations are hard to come by,
and thus precious.”
Whenever he was in the bedchamber, he would spread carpets everywhere,
and chase people naked for amusement.
Shālǐgǔzhēn engaged in lewd conduct outside.
Hǎilíng was greatly enraged when he heard of it,
and said to Shālǐgǔzhēn,
“You love noble officials,
but is there anyone as noble as the Son of Heaven?
You love talented people,
but is there anyone with both civil and military talents like me?
You love entertainment,
but is there anyone more abundant and impressive than me?”
His anger was so great
that his throat choked and he could not speak.
After a short while,
he comforted her, saying,
“Don't think that because I heard about it,
you should be ashamed.
During banquets,
you should move freely and naturally,
and not let others guess your thoughts,
lest you incur ridicule.”
Later, he often summoned her again.
Yúdū,
was the wife of Páiyìn Sōnggǔlá.
Hǎilíng once said,
“Although Yúdū's appearance is not outstanding,
her skin is pure white and lovely.”
Púlà was promoted to Shòukāng Gōngzhǔ,
Shígǔ was promoted to Zhāoníng Gōngzhǔ,
Shālǐgǔzhēn was promoted to Shòuyáng Xiànzhǔ,
and Zhòngjié was promoted to Pénglái Xiànzhǔ.
Zhòngjié was born to Zhāofēi Púchá-shì.
Púchá was angry that Zhòngjié had illicit relations with Hǎilíng,
and slapped her cheek.
Hǎilíng was angry at Púchá-shì,
and eventually killed her.
All palace women who had husbands outside
were allowed to enter and exit in shifts.
Hǎilíng, wishing to act on his impulses and have relations with them,
sent all their husbands to Shàngjīng,
and forbade the women from leaving the palace.
He always kept the Jiàofāng (Office of Music) on rotation in the Forbidden City.
Whenever he had relations with women,
he would always have music played,
remove their screens and curtains,
or have people speak lewd words in front of them.
Once, he tried to have relations with an unmarried girl but could not succeed,
so he had Yuánfēi assist him with her hands.
Sometimes, when concubines were seated in rows,
he would wantonly engage in debauchery,
and make them all watch.
Sometimes, he would order people to imitate their postures for amusement.
Whenever there were imperial consorts present,
Hǎilíng would personally throw an object on the ground,
and make his close attendants look around for it.
Those who looked elsewhere were killed.
He warned the male attendants in the palace
that anyone who raised their head towards the concubines would have their eyes gouged out.
They were not allowed to walk alone when entering or exiting.
When relieving themselves,
four people had to go together,
and the officials in charge would supervise them with knives.
Those who did not follow the designated path were beheaded.
After sunset,
anyone walking on the steps below the ground level would be killed.
Informers would be rewarded two million coins.
If a man and woman accidentally bumped into each other in haste,
the first to speak out would be rewarded with a third-rank official position.
The one who spoke later would be killed,
and those who spoke simultaneously would all be spared.
The maid Pìlán had a husband outside.
Hǎilíng enfeoffed her as a Xiànjūn,
and wanted to have relations with her.
Disliking that she was pregnant,
he made her drink musk water,
and personally massaged and pulled her abdomen,
trying to induce an abortion.
Pìlán pleaded,
wishing to preserve her life.
