If she could be spared by giving birth,
she would not raise the child.
Hǎilíng disregarded her pleas,
and ultimately aborted her fetus.
Púchá Āhǔdié Nǚ Chāchá was
born to Hǎilíng's elder sister, Princess Qìngyí.
She married Bǐngdé's younger brother, Tèlǐ.
When Bǐngdé was executed,
Chāchá was to be implicated.
The Empress Dowager had Wútóng intercede with Hǎilíng,
and thus she was spared.
Hǎilíng reported to the Empress Dowager his desire to take Chāchá as a concubine.
The Empress Dowager said:
"When this child was first born,
the former emperor personally held her and brought her to my house to be raised,
until she became an adult.
Although you are her maternal uncle,
you are still like a father to her.
This is unacceptable."
Later,
she married Yīlàbǔ, son of the imperial clansman Āndáihǎi.
Hǎilíng repeatedly sent people to hint to Yīlàbǔ to divorce her,
and then he took her.
Chāchá had an illicit affair with Wányán Shǒuchéng (whose
original name was Èlǐlái).
When the affair was discovered,
Hǎilíng killed Shǒuchéng.
The Empress Dowager pleaded for Chāchá,
so she was released.
Chāchá's household slave accused Chāchá of speaking treasonous words.
Hǎilíng personally interrogated her,
and reproached Chāchá, saying:
"Are you cursing me because Shǒuchéng died?"
Thereupon, he killed her.
The wife of the co-administrator of the Imperial Clan Court, Āhǔlǐ, Púsùwǎn,
who was the younger sister of the primary consort,
came to visit the primary consort.
Hǎilíng coerced and defiled her.
From then on, Púsùwǎn never entered the palace again.
When Shìzōng was the Administrator of Jǐnán,
Hǎilíng summoned his wife, Lady Wūlíndá.
Lady Wūlíndá said to Shìzōng:
"If I do not go,
the emperor will surely kill you, my lord.
I must exert myself for your sake;
I will not burden you."
Lady Wūlíndá traveled to Liángxiāng and committed suicide.
For this reason, Shìzōng, during his twenty-nine years on the throne,
never again established an empress.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Part 2: Empresses (continued) Empress Qīncí of Ruìzōng; Empress Zhēnyì of Ruìzōng; Empress Zhāodé of Shìzōng; Primary Consort Zhāng of Shìzōng; Primary Consort Lǐ of Shìzōng; Empress Xiàoyì of Xiǎnzōng; Empress Zhāoshèng of Xiǎnzōng; Empress Qīnhuái of Zhāngzōng; Primary Consort Lǐ of Zhāngzōng; Empress Túdān of Wèishàowáng; Empress Wáng of Xuānzōng; Empress Mínghuì of Xuānzōng; Empress Túdān of Āizōng.
Empress Qīncí of Ruìzōng,
of the Púchá clan.
She was Ruìzōng's primary consort.
The Empress's mother
was Tàizǔ's younger sister.
When Ruìzōng was Left Deputy Grand Marshal,
he died in the 13th year of Tiānhuì (1135).
He was posthumously enfeoffed as King Lù,
and the Empress was enfeoffed as Princess Lù.
In the 6th year of Huángtǒng (1146),
she was promoted to Princess Jìguó.
During the Tiāndé era,
the state title was advanced.
According to the Zhènglóng regulations,
princely titles were limited to one character.
Ruìzōng was enfeoffed as King Xǔ,
and she as Princess Xǔ.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Ruìzōng was elevated and enshrined in the imperial ancestral temple,
and she was posthumously honored as Empress Qīncí.
The Empress's great-grandfather, Sàibǔ, was posthumously granted Sīkōng and Duke of Hánguó;
her grandfather, Púlá, Sītú and Duke of Zhèngguó;
her father, Ànbǔ, Tàiwèi and Duke of Cáoguó.
In the 2nd year of Dàdìng (1162),
she was interred with Ruìzōng in Jǐnglíng.
Shìzōng once said:
"Today's Nǚzhēn [people]
are not like those of previous generations.
Even among close relatives,
one cannot know the details.
The Empress Dowager's mother,
who was Tàizǔ's sister,
people also do not know."
He said to Zōng:
"She is also the younger sister of your father, King Tán.
Do you know this?"
Zōng replied:
"Your servant does not know."
The emperor said:
"If you don't even know your father's sister,
what about more distant relatives?"
In the 19th year (1179),
the Empress's clan member, the勸農使 (Quan-Nong-Shi, "Agricultural Commissioner") Shāluówō, requested to retire.
The prime ministers, noting that Shāluówō had never served outside the capital,
requested to appoint him to an external official post
to balance his service.
The emperor said:
"Shāluówō is not proficient in governance;
he cannot be entrusted with administering the people.
Although he is related to the Empress Dowager,
it is acceptable for him to be wealthy and honored."
He did not approve.
Empress Zhēnyì,
of the Lǐ clan,
was Shìzōng's mother,
a native of Liáoyáng.
Her father, Chúwōzhī,
served the Liáo dynasty,
rising to the office of Guìzhōu Observer.
During the Tiānfǔ era,
elegant and virtuous women from scholarly families in Dōngjīng were selected to go to Shàngjīng.
The Empress entered Ruìzōng's residence.
In the 7th year (1119),
Shìzōng was born.
In the 13th year of Tiānhuì (1135),
Ruìzōng died.
Shìzōng was then ten years old (by traditional East Asian reckoning).
Her clothes, food, and utensils were all exquisitely clean.
She maintained harmony among her relatives,
and generously helped the poor and needy.
She was highly respected among the imperial clan.
The Empress was intelligent and astute,
firm and resolute,
with a dignified appearance,
and she never spoke carelessly.
According to old customs,
when women became widows,
their relatives would continue to support them.
The Empress, however, shaved her head and became a bhikṣuṇī,
taking the name Grand Master Tōnghuì Yuánmíng.
She was granted purple robes
and returned to Liáoyáng,
where she built the Qīng'ān Chán Temple,
and lived in a separate nunnery.
In the 3rd year of Zhēnyuán (1155),
Shìzōng became the Dōngjīng Commissioner.
In the 5th month of the 6th year of Zhènglóng (1161),
the Empress died.
Shìzōng was so deeply grieved that he exceeded the customary rites
and resigned from office due to mourning.
Not long after,
he was reinstated as Commissioner.
In the 10th month of that year,
the Empress's younger brother Lǐ Shí formulated a plan,
and Shìzōng ascended the throne in Dōngjīng.
He posthumously honored her with the title Empress Zhēnyì,
and her burial ground was named Xiàoníng Palace.
In the 2nd year of Dàdìng (1162),
Ruìzōng was reburied in Jǐnglíng.
Initially,
the Empress had built a pagoda in Liáoyáng,
which became Chuíqìng Temple.
Before her death, she told Shìzōng:
"The sentiment for one's homeland
is common to all people.
I have already established a pagoda here according to Buddhist practice;
there is no need for a joint burial.
When I die,
do not forget these words."
Shìzōng deeply remembered her last wishes,
and therefore immediately built the Shényù Hall at Qīng'ān Temple in Dōngjīng,
ordering the relevant authorities to enlarge the old pagoda,
and constructing Fèngcí Hall in front of the pagoda.
He commanded Wáng Jìng, Minister of Rites, to compose an inscription for the pagoda, reflecting her wishes.
The Empress's great-grandfather, Cānjūn, was posthumously granted Sīkōng and Duke of Lùguó;
her grandfather, Bō, Sītú and Duke of Wèiguó;
her father, Chúwōzhī, Tàiwèi and Duke of Suíguó.
In the 4th year (1164),
the Empress's younger sister was enfeoffed as Lady Xíngguó,
and bestowed with a thousand taels of silver, twenty bolts of brocade, and five hundred bolts of silk.
In the 9th year (1169),
Shényù Hall was renamed Bàodé Hall.
He ordered Zhāng Jǐngrén, an academician of the Hànlín Academy, to compose an inscription for Qīng'ān Temple.
The text did not meet his approval,
so he ordered the Left Chancellor Shí Jū to revise it together.
In the 13th year (1173),
Shényù Hall was built at Chuíqìng Temple in Dōngjīng.
The temple grounds were cramped,
so he ordered the purchase of neighboring private land,
generously compensating the owners.
Those unwilling to sell were to exchange their land for government land.
In the 24th year (1184),
Shìzōng visited Dōngjīng,
and toured Qīng'ān and Chuíqìng Temples.
Empress Zhāodé of Shìzōng.
Lady Wūlíndá's ancestors
originally lived by the Hǎiluóyī River.
For generations they served as chiefs of the Wūlíndá tribe.
They led their tribe to submit and settle in Shàngjīng,
establishing marriage ties with the imperial family.
Her great-grandfather, Shèngguǎn,
served as envoy to Gāolí multiple times during Kāngzōng's reign.
Her father, Shítǔhēi,
was unrivaled in horsemanship and archery.
He followed Tàizǔ in conquering Liáo,
and led a Xíngjūn Méng'ān (military commander).
Even amidst military campaigns,
he did not delight in killing.
For his merits,
he was granted a hereditary Móukè (unit commander) and served as Dōngjīng Commissioner.
The Empress was intelligent, filial, and compassionate.
Her demeanor was upright and solemn.
While in her parents' home,
all her relatives respected her.
After marrying Shìzōng,
she served her parents-in-law with filial piety and reverence.
She managed the household well,
demonstrating excellent wifely virtue.
When Ruìzōng attacked Sòng,
he obtained a white jade belt,
which was a garment for emperors to wear and use.
After Ruìzōng's death,
Shìzōng treasured it.
The Empress said to Shìzōng:
"This is not something suitable for a princely residence;
it should be offered to the Son of Heaven."
Shìzōng agreed,
and presented it to Xīzōng.
Thereupon, Dàohòu was greatly pleased.
In his later years, Xīzōng was quite addicted to alcohol,
but he held no ill will towards Shìzōng.
Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
and deeply feared the imperial clan.
Wūdài slandered Bǐngdé, claiming he harbored intentions for Gěwáng.
Bǐngdé was executed.
The Empress advised Shìzōng to present many rare and precious items to appease Hǎilíng,
such as the old Liáo bone-carved rhinoceros horn belt-knife and Tǔhú good jade tea sets,
all of which were extraordinary treasures.
Hǎilíng, seeing Shìzōng's respectful obedience and fear of him,
gradually eased his jealous and resentful feelings.
The Empress was not jealous.
She selected concubines for Shìzōng
to broaden his lineage.
Even after Xiǎnzōng was born, her heart remained unchanged.
The Empress once fell ill.
Shìzōng personally attended to her medicine,
not leaving her for several days.
The Empress said:
"Your Majesty shows too much care for your concubine.
Those who understand will know it is for my illness,
but those who do not will surely suspect special favoritism and jealousy."
She also said:
"The great duty of a wife is to bring order to the household.
I only fear my virtue is shallow,
and I cannot assist in managing the inner court.
How can I act like a concubine whose sole desire
is to benefit herself?"
When Shìzōng was in Jǐnán,
Hǎilíng summoned the Empress to Zhōngdū.
The Empress thought that if she died in Jǐnán,
Hǎilíng would certainly kill Shìzōng.
Only by obeying the edict,
leaving Jǐnán to die,
could Shìzōng be spared.
She said to Shìzōng:
"I must do my best;
I cannot implicate Your Majesty."
She summoned Zhāng Jǐn, a minister-servant of the princely mansion, and instructed him, saying:
"You
are the King's trusted confidant.
Pray for me at the Eastern Peak.
I will not fail the King;
may Heaven and Earth bear witness to my heart."
She summoned her household members and told them:
"From my youth as a wife until today,
I have never seen the King do anything against the Way.
Now, many members of the imperial clan are suspected,
all because of disloyal servants
who hate their masters
and frame them.
You are all old retainers from the late King's time.
You should remember old favors,
and do not scheme wildly.
If anyone violates these words,
after my death, I will observe your actions from the underworld."
All of them wept.
After the Empress left Jǐnán,
her attendants knew she would certainly not be willing to see Hǎilíng
and would take her own life.
They guarded her very strictly.
When they reached Liángxiāng,
seventy *lǐ* from Zhōngdū,
the attendants relaxed their guard slightly,
and the Empress found an opportunity to commit suicide.
Hǎilíng still suspected that Shìzōng had instructed her to do so.
Shìzōng was transferred from Jǐnán to be the Grand Administrator of Xījīng.
Passing through Liángxiāng,
he ordered Princess Lǔguó to bury the Empress at Tǔlúyuán in Wǎnpíng County.
In Dàdìng 2nd year (1162),
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Zhāodé Huánghòu,
and a separate temple was established for her.
Her three ancestral generations were granted posthumous titles:
Her great-grandfather, Shèngguǎn, was titled Sīkōng and Duke of Xúguó;
her great-grandmother, Wányán Shì, was titled Lady of Xúguó;
her grandfather, Shùsīhēi, was titled Sītú and Duke of Dàiguó;
her grandmother, Wányán Shì, was titled Lady of Dàiguó;
her father, Shítǔhēi, was titled Tàiwèi and Duke of Shěnguó;
and her mother, Wányán Shì, was titled Lady of Shěnguó.
An imperial edict commanded the relevant officials to rebury her,
and ordered the Crown Prince to offer a libation.
Her elder brother, Huī's son, Tiānxī, was appointed Tàiwèi.
The position of Shítǔhēi was later granted as a hereditary *Méng'ān*.
The Emperor said to Tiānxī:
"When I was four or five years old, I was engaged to the Empress.
Your ancestor, the Tàiwèi, placed me on his lap and said, 'Of my seven sons-in-law,
this son-in-law is the youngest.
He will surely bring great honor to our family later.'
Now the scheduled burial approaches,
and those words of long ago have been proven true."
In Dàdìng 6th year (1166),
Wūlíndá Chāowù, the Deputy Commissioner of the Líshènjūn military district, was caught receiving bribes from deserting soldiers,
and was sentenced to death.
The officials memorialized, stating:
"Chāowù
is a close relative of the Empress (via her great-grandparents);
his case should be deliberated."
An edict ordered him to be judged according to the law.
In the 7th month of Dàdìng 8th year (1168),
Zhāngzōng was born.
Shìzōng was extremely delighted.
He said to Xiǎnzōng:
"Having obtained an heir for the state,
my joy knows no bounds.
This is due to the Empress's hidden virtue bestowed upon you."
In the 10th month of Dàdìng 10th year (1170),
when preparing for the reburial of Tàiwèi Shítǔhēi,
the officials presented ceremonial procedures,
citing the precedents of the Táng dynasty's burial of Tàiwèi Lǐ Liángqì and Sītú Mǎ Suì,
where all officials, in plain clothes, escorted the coffin five *lǐ* outside the capital gate.
The Emperor said:
"Previously, when reburying the Empress Dowager's parents,
this precedent was not used.
Simply rebury him according to our dynasty's rites;
only relatives should escort the coffin."
An edict ordered the Crown Prince to offer a libation.
In Dàdìng 11th year (1171),
on the Crown Prince's birthday,
Shìzōng held a banquet in the Eastern Palace.
During the feast,
he ordered Princess Yùguó to dance.
The Emperor shed tears and said:
"This girl's mother, the Empress,
possessed ultimate wifely virtue.
The reason I have not appointed a Central Palace (Empress)
is because I believe the Empress's virtue has no equal today."
In the 4th month of Dàdìng 12th year (1172),
a separate temple for the Empress was established in the northeast corner of the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
In the 5th month of that year,
the imperial carriage visited Tǔlúyuán to offer a libation.
In Dàdìng 19th year (1179),
a new burial site was chosen at Dàfángshān.
On the *jiǎyín* day of the 11th month,
the Empress's coffin arrived in the near suburbs,
and all officials came to greet it.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Yángcūn to offer sacrifices.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Emperor ascended his carriage to escort it,
weeping bitterly.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
it was ceremonially interred at Pánnínggōng.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
she was buried in Kūnhòulíng,
with various imperial consorts interred alongside her.
In Dàdìng 29th year (1189),
she was reinterred in Xīnglíng.
During Zhāngzōng's reign,
the officials memorialized that the posthumous title of Tàizǔ contained
the character "Zhāodé,"
and therefore proposed to change her posthumous title to Míngdé Huánghòu.
The Primary Consort, Zhāng Shì,
had a father named Xuánzhēng.
Her mother, Gāo Shì,
was a distant relative of Shìzōng's mother, Zhēnyì Huánghòu.
Shìzōng took her as a secondary consort.
She gave birth to Zhàowáng Yǒngzhōng,
and Zhāng Shì then passed away.
In Dàdìng 2nd year (1162),
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Chénfēi.
In the 10th month of that year,
she was posthumously advanced to Huìfēi.
In Dàdìng 19th year (1179),
she was posthumously advanced to Yuánfēi.
In Dàdìng twenty-fifth year,
the Crown Prince passed away.
Yǒngzhōng was the eldest among the princes,
but Shìzōng and Túshàn Kèníng deliberated and decided to establish Zhāngzōng as the Imperial Grandson.
Shìzōng once said:
"Kèníng is related to Yǒngzhōng,
yet he proposed establishing the Imperial Grandson;
he is truly a minister for the state and its altars."
The Left Assistant Minister of the Department of State Affairs, Rǔbì,
was Xuánzhēng's son,
and Yǒngzhōng's maternal uncle.
Rǔbì's wife, Gāotuódá, repeatedly frightened Yǒngzhōng with perverse words,
drew a portrait of the Consort Yuán,
and worshipped it morning and evening,
hoping to gain blessings
and engaging in heterodox practices.
In Míngchāng fifth year,
Gāotuódá was executed,
and the matter implicated Rǔbì and Yǒngzhōng.
Because Rǔbì's involvement was discovered after his death,
he was spared the posthumous removal of his official title and rank.
However, Zhāngzōng harbored suspicions about Yǒngzhōng,
which remained unresolved for years.
Censors Jiǎ Shǒujíān and Lù Duó submitted memorials hoping to alleviate the Emperor's suspicions,
but Zhāngzōng became even more displeased.
The Chancellor, Wányán Shǒuzhēn, delayed making a decision on the matter,
enraging Zhāngzōng,
who dismissed him to oversee Jìnán prefecture.
All the censors were exiled,
and Yǒngzhōng was granted death.
Among the disasters caused by imperial relatives in the Jīn dynasty,
only the Zhāng clan is mentioned.
Consort Yuán, Lǐ Shì,
was the daughter of Lǐ Shí, Prince of Nányáng Commandery.
She bore Yǔndǎo, Prince of Zhèng, Yǔnjì, Prince Wèisháo, and Yǔndé, Prince of Lù.
The mother of Yǔnchéng, Prince of Yù, Zhaoyí Liáng Shì, died early.
The Emperor ordered Yǔnchéng to be adopted by the Consort.
In Dàdìng first year,
she was enfeoffed as Consort Xián.
In the second year,
she was promoted to Consort Guì.
In the seventh year,
she was promoted to Consort Yuán.
After Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he remembered Empress Zhāodé with affection,
and did not appoint another empress.
He once said:
"The reason I have not appointed another empress
is that the present imperial harem has no one as virtuous as the late empress."
Consort Yuán was one rank below the empress,
and above all other consorts.
Lǐ Shí had the merit of establishing the succession,
so Shìzōng richly rewarded him but also strictly controlled him.
He favored him with the position of Minister of the Department of State Affairs,
but held the Left and Right Chancellors and those below them responsible for actual governance.
Although the Consort was noble,
she was not allowed to participate in government,
and the palace was peaceful.
In the second month of Dàdìng twenty-first year,
the Emperor went on the spring hunt,
stopping at Chángchūn Palace.
On the day of Wùzǐ,
the Consort died of illness.
An imperial edict ordered Yǔnchéng, Yǔndǎo, Yǔnjì, and Yǔndé to all wear mourning clothes and observe the mourning period.
On the day of Jǐchǒu,
the Crown Prince and accompanying officials
offered condolences at Fāngmíng Hall.
On the day of Xīnmǎo,
the resident officials, Chancellor Tángkuò Ānlǐ, Prince of Cáo Yǔngōng, and others submitted memorials of condolence.
The Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Jiǔsī supervised the funeral arrangements.
The Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Manufactories, Zuǒ Guāngqìng, and the Vice Prefect of Dàxīng, Wáng Xiāo, managed the imperial carriages and ceremonial guards.
The Director of the Imperial Household arranged a separate funeral parlor,
and the coffin was returned to the capital.
On the day of Yǐwèi,
entering through Chóngzhì Gate,
all officials greeted it in the suburbs,
and relatives set up offerings along the road.
The coffin was placed in a separate chamber in the western part of Xīngdé Palace.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
the Emperor arrived at the capital
and went to Xīngdé Palace to offer condolences.
Before the burial,
he offered condolences three times.
An imperial edict ordered Chancellor Wūgǔlùn Yuánzhōng to supervise the burial.
On the day of Guǐwèi,
the coffin was [⿳艹⿰坴丸土]菆,
and the Emperor suspended court.
The Crown Prince, imperial princes, imperial relatives, and all officials attended the funeral.
On the day of Jiǎshēn,
she was buried at Hǎiwángzhuāng.
On the day of Bǐngxū,
the Emperor went to Hǎiwángzhuang to offer a meal.
In the ninth month of the twenty-eighth year,
she was interred together with Consort Xián Shímò Shì, Consort Dé Túshàn Shì, and Consort Ròu Dà Shì at Kūnhòulíng.
When the Prince Wèisháo ascended the throne,
she was posthumously granted the title of Empress Guāngxiàn,
and her younger brother, Xiànkě, was given the special rank of Tèjìn.
In the ninth month of Zhēnyòu third year,
the title of Empress was revoked.
Empress Xiàoyì of Xiǎnzōng,
Túshàn Shì.
Her ancestors were from Tèlǐpìlà.
Her great-grandfather, Chāo,
followed Tàizǔ in conquering Liáo and had merits,
so he was ordered to establish his tribe as a méng'ān,
which was hereditary.
Her grandfather, Póluóhuǒ,
had many military achievements,
and his official promotions reached Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
He was posthumously granted Sītú and Duke of Qí State.
Her father, Zhēn, married Princess Liángguó, the daughter of Liáo Prince Zōnggàn,
and was granted Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
He was posthumously granted Tàishī and Prince of Guǎngpíng Commandery.
The Empress was born in Liáoyáng in Huángtǒng seventh year.
Her mother dreamt that a deity gave her a precious pearl,
whose radiance filled the room.
After waking, she gave birth,
and a red light illuminated the courtyard.
The Empress was dignified and spoke little.
Her parents often put her in charge of household affairs,
and she managed everything, large and small,
better than any of her brothers.
When Shìzōng first ascended the throne,
Zhēn was Censor-in-Chief,
and hurried to see him from Nánjīng.
Shìzōng joyfully said to him:
"Although you were a trusted minister of the deposed ruler,
you never assisted him in tyranny.
Moreover, your family tradition is commendable;
let your daughter be a consort to my son."
When Xiǎnzōng became the Crown Prince,
in the ninth month of Dàdìng fourth year,
the Emperor personally welcomed the bride with full ceremonies at Zhēn's residence.
Shìzōng attended the banquet,
and they parted in high spirits.
In the eleventh month of that year,
on Xiǎnzōng's birthday,
she was first enfeoffed as the Crown Prince's Consort.
In the seventh month of the eighth year,
the Emperor sent the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Yílà Shéndúwò, with a prized horse, a precious sword, and imperial meals to the Crown Prince and Consort,
and further instructed them:
"The Consort is now due to give birth;
may she have a safe delivery and bear a son.
After the happy event,
this sword should be kept by your side."
Soon after, the imperial grandson was born,
who became Zhāngzōng.
At that time, the Emperor was visiting Jīnliánchuān,
stopping at Bīngjǐng.
The next day,
the Emperor personally went to visit and look at him,
and the banquet was very joyous.
He also bestowed imperial robes, a waist sword, and other items,
saying to Xiǎnzōng:
"Thanks to the accumulated blessings of our ancestors,
and especially the profound hidden virtue of the Empress,
we have this today.
This is a great fortune for the state and its altars."
He further said to Lǐ Shí and Gēshíliè Zhìníng:
"Although I have many sons,
the Empress only has the Crown Prince.
Now we are fortunate to have an嫡 grandson.
Observing his extraordinary bone structure,
and that he was born on Mádágé Mountain,
where the mountain range is extensive and the qi is clear,
I am very pleased."
He then used the mountain's name as Zhāngzōng's childhood name.
The Empress was always humble and cautious.
She often feared her family's esteemed status and favor,
and would weep before her parents, saying:
"A prominent family is
what ancient people warned against;
I hope you will take good care of yourselves."
Later,
her family indeed suffered ruin due to the Hǎilíng incident.
Such was her foresight.
Shìzōng once said to the imperial princes' consorts and princesses:
"The Crown Prince's Consort's demeanor is appropriate,
and her attire is suitable.
You all should emulate her."
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he honored her as the Empress Dowager,
and renamed her residence Rénshòu Palace to Lóngqìng Palace.

An imperial edict instructed the relevant authorities to annually provide one thousand liǎng of gold, five thousand liǎng of silver, five hundred bolts of precious silk, two thousand bolts of plain silk, twenty thousand liǎng of cotton, five hundred bolts of cloth, and fifty thousand strings of coins.
Other necessities
were to be provided by the imperial treasury,
without restriction of quantity.
In the previous month, there were five or six imperial audiences,
and afterward, she became even more reverent and frugal.
When she met the Grand Elder Princesses (Dà Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ),
her manners were as usual.
She was generous and harmonious with her nine clans (jiǔzú),
and her kindness and discipline were always appropriate.
She particularly disliked hearing people's faults,
and sycophantic words found no entry.
She was forgiving and accommodating,
never showing signs of joy or anger.
However, she was fair in governing her subordinates;
even her closest relatives received no favoritism.
She once admonished her nieces, saying:
"Because of me, the Emperor (Huángdì)
has extended his grace to my maternal family.
You should show utmost loyalty in return.
Do not consider a small good deed to be useless and thus not do it,
nor a small evil to be harmless and thus not abandon it.
Do not rely on my prestige
to wantonly commit transgressions
and violate the standing laws of the state."
One day,
her younger sister, the Lady of Bìngguó (Bìngguó Fūrén),
and her sister-in-law, the Lady of Jīngguó (Jīngguó Fūrén), were attending her side.
She then instructed them, saying:
"Your families' burdens are traditionally heavy,
and not particularly affluent.
You should economize your finances
and not rely on me as someone to depend on.
I receive sustenance from all under Heaven;
how could I accumulate private savings?
Moreover, finances
are the finances of all under Heaven.
I ultimately cannot take much to enrich your private households."
When a family member presented a jade basin,
she refused it,
and said:
"Valuing rare objects and exhausting resources
is not what I desire.
Moreover, my grants and gifts are limited.
Now, if you offer this,
how will you support yourselves?
You would only waste your money,
and I have no use for it.
Do not do this again."
In the first year of Míngchāng (Míngchāng yuánnián),
the officials of rites proposed to present the imperial scroll and seal (cèbǎo) in the fifth month,
but the Empress (Hòu) refused.
The Emperor (Shàng) repeatedly pleaded with her,
but the Empress (Hòu) said:
"Now, the mourning period for Shìzōng is not yet over.
To hastily wear brocade and embroidery, and adorn myself with pearls and jade,
how can this be appropriate according to rites?
This should be done after the mourning period concludes."
The Emperor (Shàng) then instructed the relevant officials (yǒusī), saying:
"The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) is very firm in her resolve;
it should await next year."
In the first month of the second year of Míngchāng (Míngchāng èrnián),
she passed away at Lóngqìng Gōng,
aged forty-five.
Her posthumous title was Xiàoyì (Xiàoyì),
and she was interred with Shìzōng in Yùlíng.
The Empress (Hòu) loved poetry and books,
especially those of Lǎo (Lǎo) and Zhuāng (Zhuāng).
Her learning was pure, serene, and noble;
even in haste, she adhered to propriety.
She treated the imperial concubines (pín yù) with gentleness,
and for those who bore children and then died,
she regarded their children as her own,
nurturing them with continuous maternal instruction.
When the Emperor (Shàng) paid his respects and inquired about her well-being,
if she saw anything inappropriate,
she would surely admonish him sternly.
Empress Zhāoshèng (Zhāoshèng Huánghòu),
née Liú (Liú Shì),
was from Liáoyáng.
On the night of the jǐhài day in the ninth month of the second year of Tiānjuàn (Tiānjuàn èrnián),
her family seemed to see a woman in yellow entering her mother's chamber.
Shortly thereafter,
the Empress (Hòu) was born.
She was intelligent and clever by nature;
any character she saw, she never forgot.
She first read the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng),
completing the scroll within ten days.
She especially loved Buddhist scriptures.
When Shìzōng was the Administrator of Dōngjīng (Dōngjīng Liúshǒu),
he saw her during a polo game and was impressed by her.
He sent her to meet Empress Zhēnyì (Zhēnyì Huánghòu) at the palace,
and her demeanor was elegant and composed,
without any unruly appearance.
In the first year of Dàdìng (Dàdìng yuánnián),
she was selected into the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) at the age of twenty-three.
On the thirteenth day of the third month of the third year of Dàdìng (Dàdìng sānián),
Xuānzōng was born.
On that day,
there was heavy rain and thunder.
The Empress (Hòu), startled, fell ill
and soon passed away.
In the fifth year of Chéng'ān (Chéng'ān wǔnián),
she was posthumously granted the title Zhaóhuá (Zhāohuá) of Yùlíng.
Upon Xuānzōng's enthronement,
he posthumously honored her as Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
raised her tablet to be enshrined in Xiǎnzōng's (Xiǎnzōng) ancestral temple,
and posthumously titled her Empress Zhāoshèng (Zhāoshèng Huánghòu).
Empress Qīnhuái (Qīnhuái Huánghòu) of Zhāngzōng (Zhāngzōng),
née Púchá (Púchá Shì),
was from Hésùhé (Hésùhé) River in Shàngjīng Lù.
Her great-grandfather Tàishén (Tàishén)
had merits in the early days of the state,
and was successively promoted to Guānglù Dàfū,
and posthumously granted Sīkōng (Sīkōng) and Duke of Yìngguó (Yìngguó Gōng).
Her grandfather Āhúdié (Āhúdié)
held the official post of Tèjìn,
and was posthumously granted Sītú (Sītú) and Duke of Qiáoguó (Qiáoguó Gōng).
Her father Dǐngshòu (Dǐngshòu) married Princess Zhèngguó (Zhèngguó Gōngzhǔ) of Xīzōng (Xīzōng),
was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi, Měng'ān (Měng'ān) of Húndéhúnshān (Húndéhúnshān) in Zhōngdū Lù,
and inherited the position of Móukè (Móukè) of Hésùmùdān (Hésùmùdān).
He successively rose to the rank of Shàng Jiāngjūn of Jīnwú Wèi,
and was posthumously granted Tàiwèi (Tàiwèi) and Duke of Yuèguó (Yuèguó Gōng).
When the Empress (Hòu) was first born,
a red light covered her body,
and did not dissipate for a while.
She was raised by her maternal aunt, Princess Jìguó (Jìguó Gōngzhǔ).
When she grew up,
she was as filial and respectful as if serving her birth mother.
In the twenty-third year of Dàdìng (Dàdìng èrshísānnián),
when Zhāngzōng was Prince of Jīnyuán (Jīnyuán Jùnwáng),
the nàcǎi (nàcǎi) betrothal ceremony was performed.
Shìzōng dispatched the Director of the Palace Attendants Bureau, Túshān Huáizhōng (Túshān Huáizhōng),
to bestow one hundred liǎng of gold, one thousand liǎng of silver, six horses, and thirty rolls of rich silk.
During the acceptance of the decree,
auspicious clouds (qìngyún) appeared near the sun,
which observers found extraordinary.
In the eleventh month of that year,
with full rites, the Prince personally welcomed her.
An imperial edict summoned imperial princes, prime ministers (zǎizhí), officials of the third rank and above, and noblewomen to attend the ceremony.
She was enfeoffed as Lady of Jīnyuán Commandery (Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Fūrén),
later promoted to Consort (Fēi),
and then passed away.
The Empress (Hòu) was by nature virtuous and intelligent,
with a refined and solemn demeanor.
She understood reading and writing.
When the Emperor (Dì) ascended the throne,
he posthumously conferred titles upon her,
and further issued an edict announcing it to both the court and the common people.
Her spirit tablet was enshrined in Kūnníng Gōng,
and sacrifices were offered seasonally.
In the early Dà'ān (Dà'ān) period,
she was interred with Zhāngzōng in Dàolíng.
Primary Consort (Yuán Fēi) Lǐ Shī'ér (Lǐ Shī'ér)
came from a family that had committed a crime,
and she was confiscated into the Palace Registry Bureau.
Her father Xiāng (Xiāng)
and mother Wáng Xì'ér (Wáng Xì'ér)
were both of humble status.
At the end of Dàdìng (Dàdìng mò),
she entered the palace as a woman from a registered household.
At that time, the palace instructor Zhāng Jiàn (Zhāng Jiàn) taught in the palace.
Shī'ér and all the palace women studied under her.
According to custom,
the palace instructor was separated from the inside by a screen of green gauze.
The palace instructor resided outside the screen,
and the palace women resided inside the screen,
not being able to see each other face to face.
If anyone did not recognize a character or asked for its meaning,
they would point to the character through the gauze from inside the screen and ask.
The palace instructor would verbally teach them from outside the screen.
Among all the women, only Shī'ér found it easy to comprehend.
Jiàn (Jiàn) did not know who she was,
but only recognized her clear and bright voice.
Zhāngzōng once asked Jiàn (Jiàn),
"Among the palace women instructed by you, who is most teachable?"
Jiàn (Jiàn) replied:
"Among them, the one with the clear and bright voice is the most teachable."
Zhāngzōng, based on Jiàn's (Jiàn) words, sought her out and obtained her.
The eunuch Liáng Dào (Liáng Dào) praised Shī'ér's (Shī'ér) talent and beauty,
and advised Zhāngzōng to take her in.
Zhāngzōng was fond of literature.
The Consort (Fēi) was intelligent and clever,
capable of writing characters,
and understanding literary meanings.
She was especially skilled at observing expressions
and conforming to intentions,
thus she was greatly loved and favored.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng (Míngchāng sìnián),
she was enfeoffed as Zhāoróng (Zhāoróng).
The following year,
she was promoted to Shúfēi (Shúfēi).
Her father Xiāng (Xiāng) was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū, Shàng Zhùguó, and Duke of Lǒngxī Commandery (Lǒngxī Jùngōng).
Her grandfather and great-grandfather were also posthumously granted titles.
Xiōng Xǐ’ér 兄喜兒 had previously been a bandit.
He and his younger brother Tiěgē 鐵哥 were both promoted to prominent and close positions,
their power swaying the court.
Their prestige stirred the four directions,
and those who sought profit and advancement eagerly flocked to their doors.
Lǐ Bǐng 李炳 of Nánjīng 南京 and Lǐ Zhù 李著 of Zhōngshān 中山, who shared their genealogy,
gained extraordinary prominence and beauty.
Xū Chíguó 胥持國 attached himself to them and thereby became a chancellor.
Clinging to wealth and secure in their positions,
high and low were in disarray.
Though their treachery and corruption were known,
no one dared to strike them down.
Even if they were struck down,
no one could remove them.
Gēshíliè Zhízhōng 紇石烈執中 was greedy, obstinate, and unlawful.
Zhāngzōng 章宗 knew of his arrogance,
but repeatedly dismissed him and then reinstated him,
ultimately causing chaos in the realm.
Since the passing of Empress Qīnhuái 欽懷,
the position of empress had been vacant for a long time.
Zhāngzōng 章宗 intended to make Lady Lǐ 李 his empress.
However, according to the established customs of the national dynasty,
the heads of the Túdān 徒單, Tángkuò 唐括, Púchá 蒲察, Nálǎn 拏懶, Púsàn 僕散, Gēshíliè 紇石烈, Wūlíndá 烏林荅, and Wūgǔlùn 烏古論 tribes
had for generations intermarried,
taking empresses and marrying princesses.
Lady Lǐ 李, however, was of very humble origin.
At this point,
Zhāngzōng 章宗 indeed wished to establish her as empress,
but the great ministers firmly resisted.
The Censorate spoke against it.
The Emperor, having no choice,
elevated her to the rank of Yuánfēi 元妃 (First Consort).
Her power and position were so magnificent
that they equaled those of an empress.
One day,
Zhāngzōng 章宗 hosted a banquet in the palace,
and actors wearing caps performed before him.
Someone asked:
"What auspicious omens are there in the capital?"
The actor replied:
"Have you not heard that a phoenix has appeared?"
The person said:
"I know of it,
but I have not heard the details."
The actor said:
"Its flight has four directions,
and its omens are also different.
If it flies upwards, then wind and rain will be timely.
If it flies downwards, then the five grains will be abundant.
If it flies outwards, then the four kingdoms will come to court.
If it flies inwards, then officials will be promoted and salaries increased."
The Emperor laughed and dismissed them.
Empress Qīnhuái 欽懷 and the consorts and concubines had previously given birth to sons,
but they either died young at two or three years old or after only a few months.
In the fifth year of Chéng'ān 承安 (1200),
the Emperor, as no heir had yet been established,
offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the Imperial Tombs.
Zhāng Rǔyóu 張汝猷, the Director of the Lesser Treasury, took the opportunity of a direct audience
to memorialize:
"Since no imperial heir has been established,
I beg Your Sacred Majesty, after personally performing the sacrificial rites,
to dispatch trusted officials to the various sacred mountains and temples to pray."
An edict ordered Sīkōng Xiāng 司空襄 to go to Bózhōu 亳州 to pray at the Tàiqīng Gōng 太清宮.
Afterwards, this was halted,
and Yuányán Kuāng 完顏匡, a Departmental Assistant in the Ministry of Punishments, was sent instead.
On the Dīngyǒu 丁酉 day of the eighth month of the second year of Tàihé 泰和 (1202),
Yuánfēi 元妃 gave birth to the Imperial Prince Tèlín 忒鄰.
All the officials submitted memorials of congratulation.
A banquet was held for officials of the fifth rank and above in the Shénlóng Diàn 神龍殿,
and for those of the sixth rank and below in the east corridors.
An edict ordered Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Túdān Yì 平章政事徒單鎰 to offer thanks at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
Yòuchéng Yuányán Kuāng 右丞完顏匡 to offer thanks at the Imperial Tombs,
and an envoy to Bózhōu 亳州 to offer thanks at the Tàiqīng Gōng 太清宮.
After a full month had passed,
an edict granted him a name
and enfeoffed him as Gé Wáng 葛王.
Gé Wáng 葛王 was the first title granted to Shìzōng 世宗,
and after the Dàdìng 大定 period, it was no longer used to enfeoff subjects.
Therefore, the third rank of princely titles did not include Gé 葛.
The Department of State Affairs memorialized
to request that the title Gé 葛 be appended below Yíng Wáng 瀛王.
The Emperor assented to this.
On the Guǐyǒu 癸酉 day of the twelfth month,
Tèlín 忒鄰 completed three full months of age.
An imperial decree released
3,000 Buddhist and Daoist ordination certificates,
and a Daoist ritual was held at the Xuánzhēn Guān 玄真觀
to pray for Tèlín’s 忒鄰 good fortune.
On the Dīngchǒu 丁丑 day,
the Emperor presided over the Qìnghé Diàn 慶和殿
for the bathing of the Imperial Prince.
An edict ordered all officials to present wine and offer congratulations using the New Year's Day ceremonies,
and those of the fifth rank and above to present gifts.
He died at the age of two.
The elder brother, Xǐ’ér 喜兒,
successively served as Xuānhuī Shǐ 宣徽使 and Ānguó Jūn Jiédù Shǐ 安國軍節度使.
The younger brother, Tiěgē 鐵哥,
successively served as Jìnshì Jú Shǐ 近侍局使 and Shǎofǔ Jiān 少府監.
By the eighth year (1208),
the Imperial Attendants Jiǎ Shì 賈氏 and Fàn Shì 范氏 were both pregnant.
Before they reached the month of delivery,
Zhāngzōng 章宗 had already contracted a cough illness
and was quite ill.
At this time, Wèi Wáng Yǒngjì 衞王永濟 came to court from Wǔdìng Jūn 武定軍.
Among his paternal relatives and elder brothers, Zhāngzōng 章宗 loved Wèi Wáng 衞王 the most,
and wished to make him his successor.
The details are in the biography of Wèi Shàowáng 衞紹王.
When Wèi Wáng 衞王 came to take his leave,
on that day,
Zhāngzōng 章宗, despite his illness, played polo with him,
and said to Wèi Wáng 衞王:
"Does uncle not wish to be the host,
and thus wants to leave so soon?"
Yuánfēi 元妃 was beside him and said to the Emperor:
"This is not something to be spoken of lightly."
On the Yǐmǎo 乙卯 day of the eleventh month,
Zhāngzōng 章宗's illness became critical.
Wèi Wáng 衞王 had not yet departed.
Yuánfēi 元妃 and the eunuch Lǐ Xīnxǐ 李新喜 discussed establishing Wèi Wáng 衞王,
and sent the palace attendant Pān Shǒu 潘守 to summon him.
Pān Shǒu 潘守 was quite learned
and understood the gravity of the situation.
He said to Yuánfēi 元妃:
"This is a major affair,
and should be discussed with the great ministers."
Thereupon, Pān Shǒu 潘守 was sent to summon Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Yuányán Kuāng 平章政事完顏匡.
Yuányán Kuāng 完顏匡
had been an Imperial Reader to Xiǎnzōng 顯宗,
was the most senior of the old ministers,
and had military accomplishments.
Therefore, he alone was summoned.
When Yuányán Kuāng 完顏匡 arrived,
they decided together
to establish Wèi Wáng 衞王.
On the Bǐngchén 丙辰 day,
Zhāngzōng 章宗 died.
His dying edict appointed his imperial uncle Wèi Wáng 衞王 to the imperial throne.
The edict stated:
"Among Our imperial women,
there are two who are currently pregnant.
If one of them bears a son,
he should be established as the heir apparent.
If both are sons,
the one deemed most suitable shall be established."
Wèi Shàowáng 衞紹王 ascended the throne.
In the second month of the first year of Dà'ān 大安 (1209),
an edict stated:
"Emperor Zhāngzōng 章宗 entrusted the great vessel of the realm to my humble self.
His dying instruction stated that there were two women in the Yè Tíng 掖庭 (side palace) who were pregnant,
and if a son was born, he should be established as the heir apparent.
This was clearly and repeatedly conveyed, as bright as the sun in the sky.
Although I am unworthy,
I have truly received this trust.
Desiring to fully live up to his dying wishes,
I have meticulously given my full attention to this,
selecting quiet residences for them to live in,
and dispatching imperial relatives to watch over them.
Princess Zhèngguó 鄭國, the mother of Empress Qīnhuái 欽懷, and Lady Xiāoguó 蕭國, the wet nurse,
have been with them day and night without separation.
Yesterday, I heard of a setback in their wellbeing,
which has caused me deep worry and restlessness.
Therefore, I ordered the great ministers to specially oversee their care.
Now, Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Púsàn Duān 平章政事僕散端 and Zuǒchéng Sūn Jíkāng 左丞孫即康 have memorialized,
stating that Imperial Attendant Jiǎ Shì 賈氏 was due to give birth in the eleventh month,
but three months have now passed,
and her future is unknowable.
As for Fàn Shì 范氏, her expected delivery was in the first month.
However, the Deputy Imperial Physician and master of ritual, Yán Yán 儀師顏, stated
that he diagnosed Fàn Shì's 范氏 pregnancy as having been damaged since the eleventh month of last year.
Despite continuous treatment until now,
although her pulse is stable,
the form of the fetus has been lost.
Moreover, Fàn Shì 范氏 herself has expressed a wish to shave her head and become a nun before the divine presence.
I deeply recall the late Emperor's grave entrustment of this major affair,
and I never expected to hear such news,
which fills me with profound sorrow.
Now that Fàn Shì's 范氏 pregnancy is already damaged,
while Jiǎ Shì's 賈氏 still offers some hope,
I report this to the late Emperor,
hoping he will bestow spiritual blessings
and secretly grant protection,
so that an imperial heir may be born soon.
I still fear that the common people may not fully understand the reasons,
so I shall not hide it but make it widely known,
so that all may be clear about my intentions."
In the fourth month,
an imperial edict stated:
“Recently, there have been accusations against the primary consort, Lǐ Shì,
of secretly plotting ingratitude.
From the first month of Tàihé’s seventh year,
when Zhāngzōng was temporarily unwell,
Lǐ Shì and Lǐ Xīnxǐ secretly conspired,
because a successor had not yet been established.
They intended to have a palace woman feign pregnancy
and secretly obtain another child to pretend to be the imperial heir.
Thus, on the tenth day of the intercalary month of the previous year,
when the Palace Attendant Jiǎ Shì was suffering from vomiting
and had a mass in her abdomen,
Lǐ Shì, together with her mother Wáng Pàn'ér and Lǐ Xīnxǐ, plotted
to have Jiǎ Shì falsely claim to be pregnant.
When the time of delivery approached,
a child would be obtained from the Lǐ family and brought in.
If the timing was not right, they would plan to obtain another
to serve as the imperial heir.
When Zhāngzōng passed away,
the plot could not be carried out.
During the late Emperor’s lingering illness,
he ordered Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Wányán Kuāngdū to oversee all domestic and foreign affairs.
There was a clear imperial edict stating,
‘I have two palace women who are pregnant.’
He further ordered the Píngzhāng to be summoned,
and those on his left and right all heard these words.
Lǐ Shì and Xīnxǐ then dared not follow the imperial edict,
wishing to summon Xǐ'ér and Tiěgē.
When this was not successful,
they secretly summoned Típiǎn Jìnshì Jú Wūgǔlún Qìngshòu to conspire,
and upon evaluating the various princes,
their deliberation remained unsettled.
Knowing that the Vice Envoy of the Jìnshì Jú, Túshà Zhāngsēng, had sent someone to summon the Píngzhāng,
who had already arrived outside Xuānhuá Mén,
they then initiated an inquiry.
When the Píngzhāng entered the palace,
he fully adhered to the late Emperor’s dying wishes
to settle this great matter.
When the late Emperor was critically ill,
he repeatedly summoned Lǐ Shì,
but Lǐ Shì did not arrive.
And when clothes were requested,
Lǐ Shì also did not come immediately upon being summoned,
but instead privately consulted with her mother.
Whenever the late Emperor had favored a consort in the past,
Lǐ Shì, out of jealousy,
ordered the female shaman Lǐ Dìngnú to make paper and wooden figures and mandarin duck talismans to perform sorcery,
thereby cutting off the imperial succession.
Her disloyal acts
are too numerous to fully recount.
The matter having been exposed,
ministers were sent to investigate,
and they all confessed.
The Chancellor was ordered to review it,
and it was confirmed.
The authorities deliberated
that by law, extreme punishment was due.
Considering her long service to the late Emperor,
they wished to spare her death.
However, the dukes, marquises, and all officials
insisted firmly.
Now, Lǐ Shì is granted self-execution.
Wáng Pàn'ér and Lǐ Xīnxǐ shall each suffer the statutory punishment.
Lǐ Shì’s elder brother, Ānguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ Xǐ'ér, and younger brother, Shàofǔ Jiān Tiěgē, shall be treated according to the law,
their titles revoked and they be registered as commoners,
and exiled to a distant place.
All those implicated shall be dealt with according to the laws and statutes.
Palace Attendant Jiǎ Shì is also granted self-execution.”
It is said that three days after Zhāngzōng’s death, Fàn Shì’s pregnancy was reported to have suffered harm.
When Zhāngzōng was lingering in illness,
there was also no imperial edict for Wányán Kuāngdū to oversee domestic and foreign affairs.
Some say that Wányán Kuāng sought to monopolize the credit for establishing the successor,
and thus fabricated this.
Thereafter, the world no longer referred to her as the primary consort,
but only called her Lǐ Shī'ér.
When Húshāhǔ assassinated Wèi Wáng
and enthroned Xuānzōng,
he requested Wèi Wáng be demoted,
downgraded to Hǎihǎi Jùnhóu.
His edict stated:
“At the beginning of Dà'ān,
a proclamation was issued to the world,
stating that Lǐ Shì, together with her mother Wáng Pàn'ér and Lǐ Xīnxǐ, conspired
to have Jiǎ Shì falsely claim pregnancy,
and each suffered their due punishment.
I, however, believe that Emperor Zhāngzōng, with his sagely virtue and intelligence,
would not tolerate such deception.
Recently, during a council meeting,
Wǔwèi Jūn Fùshǐ and concurrently Típiǎn Jìnshì Jú Wányán Dá, and Huò Wáng Fù Dà Zhèngdé, both stated that there was an injustice in Jiǎ Shì’s case.
At that time,
Dá was an official in the Jìnshì Jú,
and Zhèngdé was protecting Jiǎ Shì,
which is how they knew.
I personally inquired for evidence,
and the matter was ambiguous and baseless.
Those who were punished and demoted at that time may all be released and returned home.”
Consequently, Lǐ Shì’s family all obtained their return.
Wèi Shàowáng’s empress, Túshà Shì,
was established as empress in the first year of Dà'ān.
In the first year of Zhìníng,
during Húshāhǔ’s rebellion,
she and Wèi Wáng were both moved to Wèi’s residence.
When the Emperor was assassinated
and Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
Wèi Wáng was demoted to Dōnghǎi Jùnhóu,
and Túshà Shì was stripped of her empress title.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
the capital was moved to Biàn.
An edict ordered that all family members of Wèi Shàowáng and Hàolì Wáng be relocated to Zhèngzhōu,
and further imprisoned,
not allowed to go in or out.
Men and women were forbidden to marry for nineteen years.
In the first year of Tiānxīng,
an edict released them from imprisonment.
At this time,
Hénán could no longer be defended,
and the whereabouts of their descendants are unknown.
Xuānzōng’s empress, Wáng Shì,
a native of Zhōngdū,
was the younger sister of Mínghuì Empress.
When her father was humble, he once dreamed that two jade combs transformed into the moon.
Afterward, the two empresses were born,
and when he died,
lingzhi grew on his coffin.
Initially,
Xuānzōng was enfeoffed as Yì Wáng.
Zhāngzōng decreed that princes seek commoner daughters
to broaden the succession.
At this time,
the Empress and Páng Shì entered the prince’s residence together.
Upon seeing the Empress’s elder sister had beauty,
he also took her in.
In the ninth month of the first year of Zhēnyòu,
the Empress was enfeoffed as Yuánfēi,
her sister as Shúfēi,
and Páng Shì as Zhēnfēi.
Shúfēi gave birth to Āizōng,
Zhēnfēi gave birth to Shǒuchún,
the Empress had no sons,
and adopted Āizōng as her own son.
In the seventh month of the second year of Zhēnyòu,
she was granted the surname Wēndūn Shì
and established as empress.
Her great-grandfather Déshòu was posthumously enfeoffed as Sīkōng and Jìguó Gōng,
her great-grandmother Liú Shì as Jìguó Fūrén,
her grandfather Pú as Sītú and Yìguó Gōng,
her grandmother Yáng Shì as Yìguó Fūrén,
her father Yànchāng as Tàiwèi and Biànguó Gōng,
and her mother Mǎ Shì as Biànguó Fūrén.
In the third year,
Zhuāngxiàn Tàizǐ died,
and Āizōng became the Crown Prince.
When Xuānzōng died,
Āizōng ascended the throne.
In the first year of Zhèngdà,
the Empress was honored as Huáng Tàihòu,
and her palace was named Rénshèng.
Her father was advanced to Nányáng Jùnwáng.
Some say: When Xuānzōng was a prince,
the mother of Zhuāngxiàn Tàizǐ was the principal consort.
Upon his ascension,
she was honored as empress.
In the ninth month of the first year of Zhēnyòu,
an edict stated:
“A certain Yuánfēi has long served in the princely residence
and has already been granted a title under a state name;
she may be established as empress.”
Her name is apparently unknowable.
Others also say: After the Wáng Shì sisters entered the palace,
her favor declined,
and she soon became a nun.
Wáng Shì was then established as empress;
this was all the scheme of the Empress’s elder sister, Mínghuì.
Initially,
on the day the Wáng Shì sisters were enfeoffed,
a great wind and gloomy haze obscured the sky,
and yellow qi filled heaven and earth.
Afterward,
the Empress dreamed of tens of thousands of beggars following her,
and she was deeply troubled by this.
The diviner said:
“The empress
is the mother of the world.
If the common people are poor,
to whom shall they appeal?”
The Empress then ordered the authorities
to set up porridge and cooling medicines in the capital.
In the years Rénchén and Guǐsì,
Hénán suffered from famine.
The great Yuán army besieged Biàn,
further exacerbated by a great plague.
Of the people in Biàn city,
over a million died,
all of which the Empress witnessed with her own eyes.
As Jīngzōng (景宗) mourned,
he was about to perform the dì (禘) sacrifice and feast at the Tàimiào (太廟).
Before the appointed date,
the officials reported that the ceremonial robes were ready.
The Emperor invited the two Empresses Dowager, Rénshèng (仁聖) and Císhèng (慈聖), to the inner palace
and tried on the robes for them to see.
Both Empresses Dowager were greatly pleased.
The Emperor changed into his casual clothes
and offered a toast to the longevity of the two Empresses Dowager.
Empress Dowager Rénshèng (仁聖) admonished the Emperor, saying:
"It was extremely difficult for our ancestors to first acquire this realm.
When will the four quarters be at peace,
the people be content,
and the Son of Heaven wear these ceremonial robes
to perform the dì (禘) sacrifice and feast at the ancestral temple in Zhōngdū (中都)?"
The Emperor said:
"My grandmother (ā pó, 阿婆) has this intention,
and I have never forgotten it either."
Empress Dowager Císhèng (慈聖) also said:
"With this in mind,
the realization of this should come in due course."
Thereupon, they poured wine and toasted the Emperor's longevity,
and then dispersed joyfully.
In the winter of the first year of Tiānxīng (天興)
Āizōng (哀宗) relocated to Guīdé (歸德).
In the first month of the second year,
he dispatched the close attendants Túshàn Sìxǐ (徒單四喜) and Zhújiǎ Dáshībù (术甲荅失不) to escort the two Empresses Dowager.
The Empress Dowager was at the Rén'ān Diàn (仁安殿),
and distributed gold ingots and seven-jeweled gold basins
to the accompanying Zhōngxiào Jūn (忠孝軍).
That night,
the two Empresses Dowager and Consort Róu (柔妃) Pēimǎn (裴滿) and others rode horses out of the palace.
When they reached Chénliú (陳留),
fires broke out on both sides of the city.
Suspecting enemy soldiers,
they dared not advance.
The Empress Dowager immediately ordered a return to the palace.
The next day,
they entered Jīng (京) and rested at Sìxǐ's (四喜) house.
A short while later,
a palanquin came to escort them back into the palace.
Just as they were planning to depart again,
the capital city was breached.
The Empress Dowager and the other consorts were moved north,
and their ultimate fate is unknown.
Only Bǎofú (寶符) Lǐ (李) followed them to Xuāndé Zhōu (宣德州)
and resided in the Móhē Yuàn (摩訶院).
Upon entering the monastery, Lǐ (李)
slept only in the Buddha hall,
making banners and pennants.
When it was time to travel north with the Empress Dowager and consorts,
just before departure,
she hanged herself in front of the Buddha statue,
and personally wrote on the door paper:
"Bǎofú Yùshì (寶符御侍) died here."
Xuānzōng (宣宗) Mínghuì (明惠) Empress,
was the elder sister of Empress Wáng (王).
She gave birth to Āizōng (哀宗).
When Xuānzōng (宣宗) ascended the throne,
she was enfeoffed as Shúfēi (淑妃).
When her younger sister was made Empress,
she was promoted to Yuánfēi (元妃).
When Āizōng (哀宗) ascended the throne,
an edict honored her as Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后),
and her palace was named Císhèng (慈聖).
The Empress Dowager was dignified and strict,
and quite knowledgeable about ancient and modern affairs.
When Āizōng (哀宗) had already been made Crown Prince,
she still sternly reprimanded him for his faults.
Only upon his ascension to the throne
was he spared physical punishment.
One day,
when dining in the palace,
there were three jade bowls and plates on the table:
one was for the Empress Dowager, and two were for the Emperor and the Empress.
Jīngwáng (荊王)'s mother, Zhēnfēi (真妃) Páng (龐), was served food in agate ware.
The Empress Dowager was angered by this,
summoned the person in charge and reproached them, saying:
"Who allowed you to arbitrarily create distinctions?
Is Jīngwáng (荊王)'s mother inferior to my son's wife?
If this were not a minor matter of food and drink,
I would have already ordered the officials to beat you to death."
After this,
Zhēnfēi (真妃) received even greater reverence in the palace.
Someone accused Jīngwáng (荊王) of plotting rebellion;
he was imprisoned,
and a verdict had already been reached.
The Emperor spoke to the Empress Dowager about it.
The Empress Dowager said:
"You have only one elder brother;
how can you wish to harm him with slander?
Zhāngzōng (章宗) killed his elder and younger brothers,
did not live long,
and his imperial line was cut off.
Why do you wish to emulate him?
Quickly pardon him and release him,
and have him come to see me.
If he does not arrive within a short while,
I will not see you either."
The Emperor rose,
and the Empress Dowager stood waiting.
When the Prince arrived,
she tearfully comforted him.
Āizōng (哀宗) greatly favored a palace woman
and wished to make her Empress.
The Empress Dowager disliked her humble origins
and firmly ordered her expulsion.
The Emperor, having no choice,
ordered her to be released from the palace,
telling the messenger:
"Go out through the Dōnghuá Mén (東華門);
no matter who it is,
give her to the first person you meet."
Thereupon, they met a silk merchant,
and she was given to him as a wife.
Diǎnjiǎn Sāhéliǎn (點檢撒合輦) taught the Emperor to play polo.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict to caution him, saying:
"As a subject,
you should always assist your lord with integrity.
How can you teach him games?
If I hear of this again,
I will surely have you severely beaten."
In recent years, with minor victories,
the national power had somewhat revived.
Literati presented essays and eulogies speaking of a "restoration of sagely virtue."
The Empress Dowager heard this and was displeased, saying:
"The Emperor is young and spirited.
Without fear, arrogance and idleness will arise.
Now, after merely one victory,
how can it be considered a 'restoration'?
Yet these sycophants flatter him so."
On the day Bǐngshēn (丙申) in the ninth month of the eighth year of Zhèngdà (正大),
the Empress Dowager passed away.
Her dying wish was that the garden mausoleum's design
should strictly adhere to frugality.
On the day Jǐwèi (己未) in the twelfth month,
she was buried west of Xiàn Tàizǐ (獻太子)'s tomb, five lǐ (里) outside the Yíngshuò Mén (迎朔門) in Biànchéng (汴城).
She was posthumously honored as Empress Mínghuì (明惠).
Āizōng (哀宗)'s Empress,
Túshàn (徒單) clan.
When Xuānzōng (宣宗) and the Empress Dowager were ill,
the Empress once cut her own flesh to offer them.
Xuānzōng (宣宗) heard of this and praised her.
In the fourth year of Xīngdìng (興定),
the Empress's father, Zhènnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ (鎮南軍節度使) Wánsēng (頑僧), committed a crime.
Xuānzōng (宣宗), on account of the Empress's pure filial piety,
pardoned him leniently
and allowed him to retire from office.
In the first year of Zhèngdà (正大),
an edict established her as Empress.
When Āizōng (哀宗) relocated to Guīdé (歸德),
he sent the Empress's younger brother Sìxǐ (四喜) and others to Biàn (汴) to escort her.
They reached Chénliú (陳留) at night
but dared not proceed,
and returned to Biàn (汴).
Soon after,
the city was breached, and she was moved north,
her ultimate fate unknown.
Eulogy says: The Rites of Zhōu
describe "nine Pín,
who oversaw the regulations for women's learning,
namely, women's virtue, women's speech, women's appearance, and women's work."
Bān Zhāo discussed them saying:
"Women's virtue
need not be exceptionally brilliant or talented.
Women's speech
need not be eloquent or quick-witted.
Women's appearance
need not be exquisitely beautiful.
Women's work
need not surpass others in skill.
To be pure, tranquil, chaste, and serene,
to observe propriety and orderliness,
to conduct oneself with standards,
and to act and rest according to rules—
this is what is called women's virtue.
To choose one's words carefully and speak articulately,
not to utter offensive language,
to speak at the right time,
and not to bore others—
this is what is called women's speech.
To wash away dirt and grime,
to keep clothing fresh and clean,
to bathe at appropriate times,
and to keep the body free from filth and disgrace—
this is what is called women's appearance.
To diligently focus on spinning and weaving,
not to indulge in idle laughter,
and to prepare clean and orderly food and drink
to serve guests—
this is what is called women's work."
In later generations, women's learning was neglected,
and they competed by beautiful looks,
vied with clever words,
flaunted their abilities to seek favor,
and ingratiated themselves to secure imperial affection.
Thus, the empress of Dào-Píng (悼平) seized control of the imperial lineage,
thereby bringing about her own downfall;
the empress of Hǎi-líng (海陵) bewitched the many favorites,
almost leading to the ruin of her state.
Lǐ (李) clan of Dào-líng (道陵) monopolized favor and corrupted the government,
ultimately causing the collapse of their clan.
Alas,
how can one not be warned!
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter Three. Below are the sons of the founder, and their descendants: Wòlǔ (斡魯), Bèilǔ (輩魯), Xièkùdé (謝庫德) (grandson Bádá (拔達)), Xièyíbǎo (謝夷保) (son Pénnà (盆納)), Xièlǐhū (謝里忽), Wūgǔchūbàhēi (烏古出跋黑), Chóngchéng (崇成) (original name Púhuī (僕灰)), Hégūsūn (劾孫) (son Pújiānú (蒲家奴)), Mápō (麻頗) (son Màndūběn
), Màndūhēwòdài (謾都訶斡帶), Wòsài (斡賽) (son Zōngyǒng (宗永)), Wòzhě (斡者) (grandson Zhāng (璋)), Áng (昂) (original name Wúdūbǔ (吾都補), son Zhèngjiā (鄭家)).
The founder's Míngyì Empress (明懿皇后) gave birth to Emperor Dé (德帝) Wūlǔ (烏魯),
whose youngest son was Wòlǔ (斡魯),
and daughter was Zhùsībā (注思版);
all were auspicious names.
As sons were born when she was past sixty,
which was unusual,
they were all given auspicious names.
Emperor Dé's (德帝) Sī Empress (思皇后) gave birth to Emperor Ān (安帝),
whose youngest son was Bèilǔ (輩魯).
Bèilǔ and Xiànzǔ (獻祖) both moved to Hǎigū River (海姑水),
where they built houses.
Bèilǔ's grandson was Húshuài (胡率).
Húshuài's son, Hézhě (劾者),
had the same name as the Duke of Hán (韓國公), Hézhě (劾者), the eldest son of Jǐngzǔ (景祖).
The Duke of Hán died earlier;
he is the one referred to as Sùzōng (肅宗) marrying Hézhě's (劾者) wife, the Gǔgǔ (加古) clan member.
In the fourth year of Mùzōng (穆宗), they attacked Āshū (阿疎).
Āshū fled to Liáo (遼).
Liáo sent an envoy to stop the attack on the Āshū army.
Mùzōng (穆宗) feigned acceptance of the Liáo emperor's restrictions,
returned to his country first,
and left Hézhě (劾者) to guard Āshū city.
After three years,
they finally broke through it.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì (天會), he was posthumously granted the title of Tèjìn (特進).
Emperor Ān's (安帝) Jié Empress (節皇后) gave birth to Xiànzǔ (獻祖),
then Xìndé (信德),
then Xièkùdé (謝庫德),
then Xièyíbǎo (謝夷保),
and then Xièlǐhū (謝里忽).
Xièkùdé's (謝庫德) grandson Bádá (拔達),
and Xièyíbǎo's (謝夷保) son Pénnà (盆納),
both assisted Shìzǔ (世祖) with merit.
Pénnà (盆納) was brave, resolute, and skilled in archery;
at that time, there was another person with the same name
who once harbored disloyal intentions,
and was called
"Evil Pénnà (惡盆納)."
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì (天會),
Bádá (拔達) was posthumously granted the title of Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
and Pénnà (盆納) was posthumously granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
During Shìzǔ's (世祖) time,
Huāndū (歡都), Yěhē (冶訶), and Hézhě (劾者), Bádá (拔達), Pénnà (盆納)—these five individuals—
were never far from his side,
as close as hands and feet,
and were the most prominent among the founding heroes.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng (明昌), they were all honored with sacrifices in Shìzǔ's (世祖) ancestral temple.
Zhǔndé (准德) and Shùlǐbǎo (束里保)
were both from the Gǔgǔ (加古) tribe.
Shēnnǎiyīn (申乃因) and Chǒuā (醜阿) were both from the Mǎn (滿) tribe.
Fùzhě Niánmòhǎn (富者粘沒罕) was from the Wányán (完顏) tribe.
Ākùdé (阿庫德) and Báidá (白達) were both Bójǐn (勃菫) from the Wányán (完顏) tribe of Yǎdálán (雅達瀾) water.
These seven individuals
were able to unite their hearts and exert their utmost strength to assist and support
during times of separation.
Dájì (達紀) and Húsū (胡蘇) were both Bójǐn (勃菫) from the Shùjiǎ (术甲) tribe.
Shèngkūn (勝昆) and Zhǔbǎo (主保) were both from the Shùhǔ (术虎) tribe.
Ākùdé (阿庫德)
was from the Wēndíhén (溫迪痕) tribe.
These five individuals
were the next in importance.
In the early years of Shìzǔ (世祖),
Báhēi (跋黑) caused rebellion,
and Wūchūn (烏春) was very powerful.
Shìzǔ sent someone to summon Ākùdé (阿庫德) and Báidá (白達).
Ākùdé (阿庫德) said:
"I know nothing else,
but I will share life and death with the Grand Tutor."
The Grand Tutor (太師)
refers to Shìzǔ (世祖).
Báidá (白達) was overjoyed and said:
"My heart is exactly like this.
If Wūchūn's (烏春) troops come,
we should fortify our defenses and hold out,
and not engage them in battle."
Dájì (達紀) and Húsū (胡蘇) resided by Píbǐguō (琵里郭) water;
Wūchūn's (烏春) troops passed through their territory,
but they did not rebel,
and ultimately resisted and did not comply.
Shèngkūn (勝昆) resided in Húbùgān Village (胡不干村).
His elder brother, Zǐbùnǎi Bójǐn (滓不乃勃菫),
housed Wūchūn (烏春) in his home
while Wūchūn (烏春) surrounded Shèngkūn (勝昆) with soldiers.
When Wūchūn (烏春) left,
Shìzǔ (世祖) killed Zǐbùnǎi (滓不乃).
Shèngkūn (勝昆) pleaded that his family not be killed or enslaved,
and Shìzǔ (世祖) granted his request.
Shìzǔ (世祖) defeated Huánhē (桓●) and Sàndá (散達),
and Zhǔbǎo (主保) died there.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì (天會),
Zhǔndé (准德), Shēnnǎiyīn (申乃因), Ākùdé (阿庫德), and Báidá (白達) were all posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫).

Shùlǐbǎo (束里保), Chǒuā (醜阿), Fùzhě Niánmòhǎn (富者粘沒罕), Dájì (達紀), Húsū (胡蘇), Shèngkūn (勝昆), Zhǔbǎo (主保), Wēndíhén (溫迪痕), and Ākùdé (阿庫德) were all posthumously granted the title of Yínqīngguānglù Dàfū (銀青光祿大夫),
all posthumously granted in the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì (天會).
Additionally, Húlún Jiāgǔ Bù Shèngkūn Bójǐn (胡論加古部勝昆勃菫) and Chánchūn Shuǐ Wūyán Bù Fùzhě Guōhē (蟬春水烏延部富者郭●)
feared Wūchūn's (烏春) strength
and requested Shìzǔ's (世祖) troops to pass through their territory
to strengthen their position.
Shìzǔ (世祖) sent Xiéliè (斜列) and Yuèpán (躍盤) to lead a separate army through.
Guōhē (郭●) instructed Xiéliè (斜列) to capture twenty-two individuals who were previously in Wūchūn's (烏春) army.
Wūchūn (烏春) became aware of this,
killed two individuals,
and captured twenty.
Guōhē (郭●) also added local people to Xiéliè's (斜列) army.
Mùzōng (穆宗) later praised this achievement, unable to forget it,
and married Xiéliè's (斜列) daughter Shǒuníng (守寧) to Guōhē's (郭●) son Húlǐhǎn (胡里罕).
Wòbù Bójǐn (斡不勃菫) of the Péimǎn (裴滿) tribe from Póduōtǔ (婆多吐) water attached himself to Shìzǔ (世祖),
but Huánhē (桓●) burned his settlement.
When Wòbù (斡不) died,
Shìzǔ (世祖) generously cared for his family.
These events are recorded together
to illustrate the difficulties of establishing the state.
Xièlǐhū (謝里忽):
When Zhāozǔ (昭祖) was about to establish laws and regulations,
his paternal uncles and the people of the state were displeased.
They seized Zhāozǔ (昭祖)
and were about to kill him.
Xièlǐhū (謝里忽) rushed there,
drew his bow and notched an arrow,
and shot into the crowd.
The crowd dispersed,
and Zhāozǔ (昭祖) was spared.
According to local custom,
if someone was killed,
a shaman or sorcerer would be employed to curse the killer.
Then, a blade would be tied to the end of a staff,
and with the crowd, they would go to the killer's house,
singing and cursing, saying:
"Take your ox with one horn pointing to heaven and one horn pointing to earth,
your nameless horse
that is bright-faced when approached and white-tailed when turned away from,
and has left and right wings when viewed from the side."
The sound was mournful and poignant,
like the music of Hāolǐ (蒿里) (a dirge).
Afterwards, they would draw lines on the ground with the blade,
and forcibly take livestock, property, and return.
Once a family was subjected to such a curse,
their household fortunes would invariably decline.
When people from the Wū-Sà-Zhā 部 killed people from the Wán-Yán 部,
Zhāo-Zǔ went to the Wū-Sà-Zhā 部 and managed them according to the national custom.
He gained a great deal,
which he distributed among his paternal uncles and brothers, but not to Xiè-Lǐ-Hū.
Xiè-Lǐ-Hū said:
"It was my strength that saved you from death the other day,
and my strategy that led you to go and manage the Wū-Sà-Zhā 部.
Why am I not included in the distribution? "
Zhāo-Zǔ then woke up early,
and personally brought some fine gold and a liè-xiē to present to him.
At that time, Xiè-Lǐ-Hū had not yet risen,
and, wrapped in his sleeping robe, he asked:
"Who are you? "
Zhāo-Zǔ said:
"Shí-Lǔ first selected this treasure,
and then distributed it to others;
I dare to privately present it."
Xiè-Lǐ-Hū had spoken publicly,
and initially felt uneasy,
but now he was greatly pleased.
A liè-xiē
is a waist ornament.
Xiàn-Zǔ Gōng-Jìng Huáng-Hòu gave birth to Zhāo-Zǔ,
followed by Pǔ-Dū,
then Ā-Bǎo-Hán,
then Dí-Kù,
then Dí-Gǔ-Nǎi,
then Sā-Lǐ-Nián,
and then Sā-Gě-Zhōu.
Zhāo-Zǔ Wēi-Shùn Huáng-Hòu gave birth to Jǐng-Zǔ,
followed by Wū-Gǔ-Chū.
His secondary consort, Dá-Hú-Mò,
a person from the Wū-Sà-Zhā 部,
gave birth to Bá-Hēi, Pú-Lǐ-Hēi, and Wò-Lǐ-Ān.
Another secondary consort, a Gāo-Lì person,
gave birth to Hú-Shī-Dá.
Regarding Wū-Gǔ-Chū:
Initially,
Zhāo-Zǔ had no son for a long time.
There was a shaman who could speak divine words,
and whose predictions were very accurate,
so he went to pray there.
After a long while, the shaman said:
"The soul of a male child has arrived.
This child will have great blessings and virtue;
his descendants will be prosperous.
You may bow and receive him.
If he is born,
name him Wū-Gǔ-Nǎi."
This was Jǐng-Zǔ.
After another long while, he said:
"The soul of a female child has arrived;
you may name her Wǔ-Bù-Rěn."
After yet another long while, he said:
"The omen of a female child appears again;
you may name her Wò-Dū-Bá."
After some more time,
he said again:
"The omen of a male child appears again,
however, his nature is not gentle;
when he grows up, he will be cruel,
without the grace of familial affection,
and will certainly act unjustly.
He should not be received."
Zhāo-Zǔ was at that time concerned that he had no successor,
so he said:
"Even if he is not good,
I still wish to receive him."
The shaman said:
"He should be named Wū-Gǔ-Chū."
Later, two sons and two daughters were born,
and their order of birth was exactly as the shaman had foretold,
so they were named according to the names given by the shaman.
When Jǐng-Zǔ first ascended,
Wū-Gǔ-Chū was a drunkard
and repeatedly disrespected Wēi-Shùn Huáng-Hòu.
The Empress said:
"The shaman's words have proven true;
a rebellious person ultimately cannot be kept."
So, she conspired with Jǐng-Zǔ and killed him.
The people of the tribe were angered and said:
"This son's nature is such;
according to our national custom, he should inherit his parents' estate.
How could you kill him?"
They wanted to kill Jǐng-Zǔ.
The Empress then hid Jǐng-Zǔ,
and came out to address the crowd, saying:
"For a son to disrespect his mother,
and to act in such a way,
what use is he?
I sacrificed my affection and killed him;
Wū-Gǔ-Nǎi knew nothing of it.
Would you rather kill me?"
The crowd then dispersed.
Wū-Gǔ-Chū's son, Xí-Bù-Shī,
has his own biography.
Bá-Hēi and his two full brothers,
from a young age, often fought over food and drink.
Zhāo-Zǔ saw this and disliked it,
saying:
"I married this concubine and she bore such children;
they will certainly become a problem for my descendants later."
When Shì-Zǔ first ascended,
Bá-Hēi indeed harbored different ambitions.
He enticed Huán-Mó, Sàn-Dá, Wū-Chūn, and Wō-Móu-Hǎn to sow discord among the tribal members,
making them disloyal to Shì-Zǔ.
Shì-Zǔ was troubled by this,
and therefore paid special attention to him,
making him a Bó-Jǐn but not allowing him to command troops.
Bá-Hēi secretly conspired with Huán-Mó and Wū-Chūn,
and everyone in the country knew about it.
A children's rhyme went:
"Those who wish to live side with Bá-Hēi;
those who wish to die side with Hé-Lǐ-Bō and Pō-Là-Shū."
Shì-Zǔ also used strategy to ascertain the allegiance of his brothers and tribal people.
Wū-Chūn and Huán-Mó successively launched attacks with their armies.
Shì-Zǔ had to defend against the strong enemy outside,
while fearing Bá-Hēi's rebellion within.
As he was about to depart,
he heard that Bá-Hēi had choked on meat and died
while eating at his beloved concubine's father's house.
Both pleased and saddened,
he went to receive the body and wept over it.
Chóng-Chéng,
originally named Pú-Huī,
was a staff member of the Tái-Zhōu Sī-Shǔ-Sī and
a great-great-grandson of Zhāo-Zǔ.
In the eighteenth year of Dà-Dìng, he was recruited as an attendant,
then transferred to the Eastern Palace as a minor attendant,
and then became a guard.
In the twenty-fifth year,
when Zhāng-Zōng was the Prince of Yuán,
he served as a gentleman-in-waiting in his mansion.
The following year,
when the Emperor became the Imperial Grandson,
he again served as a guard.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed as the judicial officer of Hé-Jiān Prefecture.
He left office due to mourning.
He was reinstated as the General of the Imperial Guard,
and successively promoted to Military Commissioner of the Wǔ-Wèi Army.
He died in the third year of Tài-Hé,
and was generously posthumously awarded.
Chóng-Chéng was meticulous and disciplined;
he served in the imperial guard for over twenty years
without ever making a mistake,
which is why he served so long in close proximity to the emperor.
Jǐng-Zǔ Zhāo-Sù Huáng-Hòu gave birth to Hán-Guó-Gōng Hé-Zhě,
followed by Shì-Zǔ,
then Yí-Guó-Gōng Hé-Sūn,
then Sù-Zōng,
and then Mù-Zōng.
His secondary consort Zhù-Sī-Huī,
a Qì-Dān person,
gave birth to Dài-Guó-Gōng Hé-Zhēn-Bǎo.
Another secondary consort, Wēn-Dí-Hén Shì,
named Dí-Běn,
gave birth to Yú-Guó-Gōng Má-Pó, Suí-Guó-Gōng Ā-Lí-Hé-Mèn, and Zhèng-Guó-Gōng Màn-Dū-Hē.
Hé-Zhě and Ā-Lí-Hé-Mèn have separate biographies.
Hé-Sūn:
In the fourteenth year of Tiān-Huì, when the imperial clan was greatly enfeoffed,
Hé-Sūn was posthumously granted a princely title.
According to the Zhèng-Lóng regulations, he was demoted and enfeoffed as Zhèng-Guó-Gōng.
His son, Pú-Jiā-Nú, also named Yù,
once followed Tài-Zǔ in attacking Liú-Kě and Wù-Tǎ.
Tài-Zǔ sent Pú-Jiā-Nú to entice Zhà-Dū,
and Zhà-Dū immediately surrendered.
In the eighth year of Kāng-Zōng,
Ā-Lǐ-Bǎo of the Hē-Shí-Liè 部, a Jurchen registered under the Liáo dynasty, resisted with troops
and harbored fugitives,
causing many border residents to flee and join him.
Pú-Jiā-Nú, with a detachment, traveled by night and rested by day,
reaching Shí-Lè Shuǐ,
where he launched a surprise attack,
captured all their families, and returned.
From then on, no border residents fled again.
Later, he and Zōng-Xióng inspected the land of Tái-Zhōu,
and Tài-Zǔ subsequently moved ten thousand households to settle and farm there.
In the fifth year of Tiānfǔ,
Pújiānú was appointed Bólìliè,
and then Commander-in-Chief.
He was sent to attack the Liáo Emperor,
but could not proceed due to heavy rains.
Afterward,
Hūlǔ Bólìliè Gǎo, the Commander-in-Chief of all forces, internal and external, was to take Zhōngjīng,
and Pújiānú and others were his deputies.
The Liáo Emperor fled west,
and Commander-in-Chief Gǎo sent Pújiānú with a thousand soldiers to assist Tàlǎn in attacking the Liáo Commander-in-Chief Mǎgē.
Pújiānú could not reach Tàlǎn,
so Pújiānú, together with Sàilǐ and Xiáyě, received the surrender of the populace from Jūyán in the northwest.
However, the surrendered people gradually fled and dispersed again,
and the Píshì 部 also rebelled.
So he led troops to attack them.
Upon reaching Tiělǚchuān,
they encountered eight thousand enemies.
They fought fiercely,
but their army was defeated.
Chálà came with troops to reinforce them,
and pursued the enemy soldiers to Huángshuǐ,
capturing a great number of livestock.
In this battle,
Àodùn Àndǎhǎi suffered eleven wounds,
but ultimately defeated the enemy and returned.
They encamped west of Wàngguóyá.
Sàilǐ also brought troops to meet Tàizǔ,
pursuing the Liáo Emperor from Cǎoluò.
Pújiānú and Zōngwàng were the vanguards,
and they were warned:
“If they dig deep trenches and build high ramparts,
do not engage them in battle.
Instead, scout and patrol,
do not let them escape,
and await the main army.
If they are unprepared,
you may attack.”
Next, at Húlízhěnchuān,
Wúshí and Mǎ Héshang reached Xiǎoyúlù.
That night, they secretly entered the Liáo lord's camp,
captured Xīnluónú and returned,
thereby learning the Liáo Emperor's whereabouts.
Pújiānú and others marched day and night,
overtaking him at Shílián Duó.
Our army had four thousand men,
but only a thousand arrived,
and the Liáo army surrounded them.
Yúdǔ pointed to the Liáo Emperor's banner and canopy,
and cavalry charged towards it.
The Liáo Emperor fled,
and his army collapsed,
with many killed.
Zōnghàn was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Northwest and Southwest routes,
with Pújiānú and Wòlǔ as his deputies.
The Wūhǔ 部 rebelled,
and Pújiānú suppressed them.
During the Tiānhuì era,
he became Sīkōng [Minister of Works]
and was enfeoffed as a King.
In the second year of Tiānjuàn,
when Zōngpán and others were executed,
Pújiānú was implicated,
and an imperial edict stripped him of his Sīkōng title.
That year,
he died.
In the early Tiāndé era,
he was given posthumous honors and worshipped in the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ.
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Yùguó Gōng by established custom.
Mápō was
enfeoffed as a King in the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì.
In Zhènglóng, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Yúguó Gōng by established custom.
His eldest son, Màndōuběn,
was filial, friendly, respectful, and cautious,
resourceful and skilled in battle.
At the age of fifteen,
he joined the army
and participated in the attack on Wōlúhuān.
When the Liáo Nǚzhēn Húshīdá and others revolted,
Màndōuběn offered himself as a hostage
and returned with Húshīdá,
but on the way, he used a stratagem to kill his guards and escaped.
He attacked Níngjiāngzhōu,
captured Huánglóngfǔ,
defeated Gāo Yǒngchāng,
and took Chūn and Tàizhōu.
He distinguished himself in all these actions,
received many rewards,
and was appointed Móukè.
He suppressed the unsubdued prefectures and commanderies in Lǐngdōng.
Passing through Tǔhé Dōngshān,
he defeated three thousand bandits.
When the Xī and Qìdān attacked west of Tǔhé,
he joined Měng'ān Ménggē and Májí to strike them.
In the midst of battle, Màndōuběn
spearheaded the charge and fought bravely,
defeating their army of ninety thousand.
More than ten thousand Xī troops took refuge in Ālíndiān,
but he defeated them again,
and brought the neighboring residents to surrender.
Again, with five hundred cavalry, he defeated a thousand Liáo soldiers,
capturing their general alive and returning.
Together with Shémǔ, he attacked Xīngzhōngfǔ.
He was struck by a stray arrow and died at
the age of thirty-seven.
During the Tiānjuàn era,
he was posthumously granted the title Jīn Zǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and given the posthumous name Yīngyì.
Màndōuhē
repeatedly participated in campaigns.
In the second year of Tiānhuì, he became Āshě Bólìliè,
participating in state affairs.
He died the following year.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì,
when the imperial clan was widely enfeoffed,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as a King.
In Zhènglóng, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Zhèngguó Gōng by established custom.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
he was given the posthumous name Dìngjì.
Mántú
inherited his father Mápō's Měng'ān position.
When Mántú died,
his son Sǎohé inherited.
When Sǎohé died,
his son Sǎhélián inherited.
When Sǎhélián died,
his son Wéiróng inherited.
Wéiróng's original name was Mòliè,
his courtesy name Zǐzhù.
He had conjoined ribs and great strength,
and enjoyed helping those in need.
In the early Zhìníng era,
he distinguished himself guarding Yángwénguān,
and was concurrently appointed Dūtǒng,
responsible for guarding grain transport.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he wore a gold plaque and escorted the families of the imperial guard to relocate to Biàn,
remotely appointed Tongzhi of Qízhōu's military and civil affairs,
and served as Tíkòng.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu,
he defeated the Red Scarf bandits at Dàmògū.
Wéiróng entered through the north gate,
and the other armies followed.
They captured Liú Èrzǔ alive,
and he was recognized as having the greatest merit.
He was promoted to Deputy Military Commissioner of Tàinán Jūn,
