then transferred to Wèi Wángfǔ Wèi, Dūshuǐ Shàojiān, and Zhìzhōng of Dōngpíng Fǔ.
He was implicated in accidentally wounding Hégǔliè Yáwútǎ, the Tongzhi Fǔshì, with a blade.
He was to be demoted and have his seniority reduced,
but was still allowed to serve in the army to prove his worth.
He suppressed the Flowery Hat bandits between Cáo and Jì.
The Xíngshěng Ménggǔ Gāng reported his achievements,
and he was reinstated to his former position.
He was promoted to Commissioner of Pízhōu,
and then died.
His son Cóngjié inherited the Měng'ān,
and accumulated merits, being remotely appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhènnán Jūn.
Shìzǔ Yìjiǎn Huánghòu gave birth to Kāngzōng,
next Tàizǔ,
next Wèi Wáng Wòdài,
next Tàizōng,
next Liáo Wáng Xiáyě.
His second consort, of the Shìtúdān clan, gave birth to Wèi Wáng Wòsài,
next Lǔ Wáng Wòzhě.
His third consort, of the Púsàn clan, gave birth to Hàn Wáng Wūgùnǎi.
His fourth consort, of the Shùhǔ clan, gave birth to Lǔ Wáng Shémǔ.
His fifth consort, of the Shùhǔ clan, gave birth to Yí Wáng Chálà.
His sixth consort, of the Wūgǔlún clan, gave birth to Yùn Wáng Áng.
Wòdài,
when he was over twenty years old,
Sǎgǎi attacked Liúkě.
Wòdài, along with Xíbùshī, Ālíhégǎnmàn, and others, all served as junior generals.
The generals debated whether to attack,
and Wòdài advocated directly attacking the city.
When Tàizǔ was about to reach the army,
Wòdài went to meet him,
and said to Tàizǔ:
“The city of Liúkě is about to fall,
do not be swayed by other opinions.”
Tàizǔ agreed.
Upon reaching the army,
the collective decision was made.
Wòdài quickly began to prepare siege equipment.
That night, they advanced and attacked the city,
breaching it at dawn.
When the bandits from Èrniènánghǔlù and Èrchúnchūlù raided,
Wòdài completely pacified them.
Sòng general Wú Lín went out of Sànguān,
occupying the area west of Bǎojī.
A decree ordered Zhāng to proceed to the army of Field Marshal Dōujiān Túdān Héxǐ to serve as an envoy.
Thereupon,
the Sòng people occupied Yuánzhōu.
Níngzhōu Cìshǐ Yánzhǎn Méndū attacked them with four thousand soldiers,
but could not overcome them.
Sòng general Yáo Liángfǔ arrived at Yuánzhōu with one hundred thousand soldiers.
Quán Fùtǒng Wányán Xíníliè came with a thousand cavalry to reinforce Méndū's troops,
but Yáo Liángfǔ had many soldiers,
and all the generals dared not engage in battle.
When Zhāng arrived at the army,
he gathered the garrison troops from Píngliáng, Jīngzhōu, Pānyuán, Chángwǔ, and other places,
totaling twenty thousand men.
Zhāng ordered Yājūn Měng'ān Shímò Xǔlǐ'ābǔ to encamp with two thousand soldiers north of the city,
and Xíníliè to encamp with three thousand soldiers at Màizǐyuán, ten *lǐ* northwest of the city,
both occupying high ground to form their arrays.
Zhāng arrayed his main forces west of the city.
Yáo Liángfǔ emerged from the Northern Ridge,
first dispatching ten thousand men to attack Xǔlǐ'ābǔ,
while he himself arrayed his ninety thousand troops below Màizǐyuán,
defending with swords, shields, and *xíngmǎ* (mobile fences).
Cavalry were arrayed on the outside,
with infantry in the middle.
Dare-to-die soldiers, chained by their feet, stood between the *xíngmǎ*,
holding large swords as a defense,
divided into eight formations.
Separately, two thousand cavalry attacked Zhāng's army.
As Zhāng was about to go out to meet the enemy,
Xíníliè came to report, saying:
"All of Sòng's heavy forces are at Màizǐyuán."
Zhāng dispatched Wànhù Tèlǐshīwūyě with Yājūn Měng'ān Xīqìngxǐ and Zhàosā's two thousand soldiers to reinforce Xǔlǐ'ābǔ,
and sent Sāwūchū and Cuī Yǐn with two thousand soldiers to assist Xíníliè.
Xǔlǐ'ābǔ engaged the Sòng forces,
and after a long time,
defeated them.
The Sòng troops at Màizǐyuán were the most resilient.
Xíníliè, along with Yílābǔ, Àotún Sāwūchū, Cuī Yǐn, and Púgēn Sāqūchū, with five thousand soldiers, laid an ambush along the ditch,
while the remaining soldiers dismounted and fought on foot,
striking their front-line cavalry,
and routing them.
Thereupon,
they charged with long spears against those in front of the *xíngmǎ*,
and shot with strong bows at those behind the *xíngmǎ*.
Liángfǔ's forces were slightly repulsed.
Xíníliè, seizing the advantage, waved his troops forward,
removed their *xíngmǎ*,
and broke seven of their formations.
Liángfǔ reorganized his troops and came out again.
Xíníliè retreated slightly,
but Zhāng had already defeated the Sòng troops below the city
and joined Xíníliè.
He ordered Púgēn to attack Liángfǔ with his ambushing troops.
Xíníliè also reorganized his troops and fought,
bravely attacking them,
thoroughly defeating Liángfǔ's army,
beheading over ten thousand men.
The number of those who fell into ditches and died was countless.
All those chained by their feet in the *xíngmǎ* were killed.
They captured over twenty thousand sets of armor,
and weapons in a similar quantity.
Liángfǔ himself suffered two wounds and escaped.
They then besieged Yuánzhōu,
tunneling into its west wall.
The wall collapsed,
and the Sòng forces fled during the night.
Zhāng and others entered Yuánzhōu.
The Sòng garrison troops west of Bǎojī,
hearing of this, all fled from Sànguān.
Jīngzhàoyǐn Wūyán Púlíhēi and Dānzhōu Cìshǐ Chìzhǎn Húsùlǔ Gǎi had already departed Déshùnzhōu,
and Sòng's Wú Lín reoccupied it.
Dōujiān Héxǐ appointed Zhāng as Quán Dūlǒng,
and he, with Xíníliè, led twenty thousand soldiers to relieve Déshùn.
Zhāng led the cavalry forward,
and fought with Lín's twenty thousand cavalry below Suìshāshān at Zhāngyìbǎo,
defeating them,
and pursuing them for over forty *lǐ*.
Lín's army encountered a defile and could not advance,
and several dozens of heads were cut off.
Zhāng arrived at Déshùn.
Lín occupied a strategic position north of the city as his camp.
Zhāng also set up his camp facing Lín's,
about three *lǐ* away.
The two armies met east of the city,
engaging in battle five times in all.
Lín's army was defeated and fled.
Zhāng pursued them to below the city.
Lín's forces had already occupied the northern hillock of the city,
coordinating with their troops on the city walls,
shooting at Zhāng's army with crossbows from both sides.
Zhāng's army feigned retreat,
and the troops from the city came out to pursue.
Zhāng turned his banners and engaged them,
thoroughly defeating them.
Héxǐ sent Tǒngjūn Dōujiān Níhé with seven thousand soldiers to join them.
They fought Lín's army again
and defeated them.
Lín sent troops to occupy Dōngshānbǎo,
intending to build a stockade.
Zhāng, Xíníliè, and Níhé discussed, saying:
"If the enemy occupies Dōngshānbǎo,
this city also cannot be taken.
It is advisable to attack them quickly."
Thereupon, Zhāng first occupied the crucial ground.
Xíníliè pressed towards Dōngshānbǎo with his troops.
Lín's troops relied on the moat to resist.
They engaged in close combat,
and Lín's troops retreated and fled.
Xíníliè pursued and attacked them.
Lín's camp troops north of the city, about six thousand strong,
ascended the northern hillock to fight.
Zhāng's Hàn army retreated slightly,
with two hundred wounded.
Lín then burned Zhāng's siege equipment.
Zhāng led Yílābǔ's Měng'ān troops to cross the northern hillock and drive them back.
Lín's troops shot at Zhāng's army across a small trench.
Yílābǔ retreated slightly.
Xíníliè saw fire erupting on the northern plain,
so he stopped attacking Dōngshānbǎo,
and immediately rushed to join them with his generals and soldiers,
leading skilled archers to ascend first,
and with Liú Ān's three hundred Hàn soldiers, he defeated them.
Lín's troops all fled to difficult terrain.
Lín occupied the dangerous terrain with thirty thousand troops, forming three formations,
all surrounded by swords, shields, and *xíngmǎ*.
Zhāng sent Wànhù Shímò Diélè to attack them from behind via another route.
Tèlǐshīwūyě and Yílābǔ, with two thousand men, confronted them from the front,
shooting with strong bows.
Lín's army was utterly defeated,
and many fell into ditches and ravines.
Zhāng's army crossed the ravine in pursuit,
beheading several thousand before returning.
Although Lín's army was defeated,
he still relied on his large numbers.
Dōujiān Héxǐ sent Wǔwēi Jūn Fùzǒngguǎn Jiágǔ Cházhá to inquire about strategy.
All the generals said:
"Wú Lín relies on difficult terrain
and is not good at open-field combat.
If we retreat to Píngliáng,
he will surely abandon the difficult terrain and come to the flat ground,
then we can plan."
Zhāng said:
"Not so.
He relies on his large numbers,
not just on difficult terrain.
As an ancient person said,
'It is better to abandon a thousand troops
than to abandon an inch of land.'
Therefore, retreating troops is not as good as reinforcing troops.
If we retreat to Píngliáng,
his army will penetrate deep into our territory,
fortify their defenses to resist us,
then what can we do?"
Cházhá returned and reported,
and Héxǐ then personally led forty thousand men to go there.
At dawn, Wú Lín, under dark and foggy conditions, divided his forces into four routes to attack,
fighting east of the city,
separating and rejoining several times.
Hàn army Qiānhù Lǐ Zhǎn led his subordinate troops to charge first and fight bravely,
and Lín's army formation wavered.
Zhāng, seizing the advantage, followed up and attacked,
and Lín's army was again defeated.
They pursued them to Běigāng.
Lín fled to dangerous terrain,
and Zhāng attacked fiercely,
killing and plundering almost all of them.
Lín divided half his army to guard Qínzhōu.
Héxǐ stationed his army east of Shuǐluòchéng,
distributing troops from Liùpánshān to Shíshāntóu to guard it,
cutting off their supply route.
Lín then withdrew.
Sòng Jīnglüèshǐ Jīnggāo led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry westward from Déshùn.
Zhāng, with eight thousand soldiers, and Xíníliè, with five thousand soldiers, pursued them.
Xíníliè's troops then got ahead of them,
returned from Chìzuǐ,
encountered their vanguard,
and defeated them below Gāochìyá.
They then fought their main army,
from afternoon until dusk,
before stopping.
Jīnggāo attacked their camp by night,
retreating eighty *lǐ*.
The next day,
Xíníliè pursued them.
Zhāng's troops arrived at Shàngbājié.
Sòng troops occupied dangerous terrain to form their array.
Zhāng dismounted to fight on foot.
The terrain was too dangerous for them to engage closely,
and they resisted each other until dawn.
Sòng troops moved,
and Zhāng took advantage of it,
pursuing them to Gāgǔchéng.
Xíníliè's troops also arrived,
and Sòng troops fled during the night.
Zhāng then withdrew his army.
Xíníliè pursued to Fúqiángchéng, but could not catch them, and returned.
The Emperor ordered Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Dáwán to inspect the merits of the various armies.
Dáwán had a long-standing grudge against Zhāng,
and therefore diminished his achievements.
An imperial edict decreed that Zhāng and his officers' rewards would be half of those of other armies.
Zhāng was concurrently the Dūtǒng of the Shǎnxī Lù
and was promoted one rank in office.
When the Yuánshuài Fǔ submitted reports of merits,
Zhāng's were the greatest.
An imperial edict ordered Dáwán to be stripped of two official ranks,
flogged with eighty strokes,
and dismissed from office.
The Emperor then rewarded Zhāng and his officers as he had the other armies,
appointing Zhāng as the Zhāotǎo Shǐ of the Xīběi Lù.
He was summoned to be Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān,
concurrently Jiédù Shǐ of Ānhuà Jūn,
and bestowed with a bow, arrows, clothing, a belt, and a saber.
He was later appointed Yìdū Yǐn,
retaining his position as Zuǒ Dūjiān.
The Sòng people abandoned Hǎizhōu and fled,
burning almost all of the official and civilian dwellings.
When Zhāng arrived at Hǎizhōu,
he obtained over thirty-six thousand dàn of abandoned grain,
settled its people,
and restored its garrison.
In the fifth year,
the Sòng people sought peace,
and the Dūtǒng of the three routes were abolished.
The Shǎnxī Lù Tǒngjūn Sī was re-established,
with Zhāng as Tǒngjūn Shǐ.
The Emperor said:
"Jiānjūn Héxǐ is old;
therefore I grant you this position.
When the border is peaceful,
I shall summon you."
He was concurrently appointed Jīngzhào Yǐn in his original post.
He was summoned to be Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Zhāng memorialized:
"I observe that among the civil and military officials, some form factions.
Currently, in the Bureau, apart from your servant, there are no Nǚzhí people.
I request that without limiting by qualifications or seniority,
talents be assessed and recommended."
The Emperor said:
"Who are these factions?
Investigate and punish them immediately.
I have been selecting Nǚzhí people,
but have not found suitable candidates.
How could I be limited by qualifications or seniority?
It is only about their talent."
After a while,
Zhāng memorialized:
"Tàizǔ Wǔyuán Huángdì received the bright mandate from Heaven,
and Tàizōng Huángdì swiftly settled the Sòng land.
Since ancient times, when emperors rise,
they must claim to have received the mandate.
A 'Dà Jīn Shòumìng Zhī Bǎo' (Great Seal of the Mandate of Dà Jīn) should be cast
to clearly show it to ten thousand generations."
The Emperor said:
"Your words truly accord with my intentions."
So he sent an envoy to Xià Guó to purchase jade.
In the eighteenth year,
the Shòumìng Bǎo was completed.
He presented a memorial to Heaven, Earth, the ancestral temple, and the altars of grain and soil.
The Emperor presided in the main hall.
In the thirteenth year,
he was appointed Dàxīng Yǐn,
and served as an envoy to Sòng for the New Year's Day celebration.
Zhāng received the command to be an envoy to Sòng.
After he had set out,
the Emperor sent someone to ride quickly and instruct Zhāng, saying:
"If the Sòng people do not follow the old rites,
be careful not to deliver the letter.
If they do not allow you to enter for an audience,
then take the letter back.
If they force you to take it,
also do not attend the banquet,
and absolutely do not accept their return letter or gifts."
Zhāng arrived in Lín'ān.
The Sòng people requested that the crown prince receive the letter,
but Zhāng did not agree.
The Sòng people went to his residence and forcibly took the letter.
Zhāng gave it to them,
and also attended the banquet,
accepting many gifts.
The authorities reported this,
and the Emperor was enraged,
wishing to inflict the most severe punishment.
Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Liángbì memorialized:
"As a general, Zhāng
greatly defeated the Sòng army,
and the Sòng people have long held enmity towards him.
It is unknown if they might use this to trap him to his death.
If Zhāng were to be killed now,
perhaps it would be falling into their scheme."
The Emperor considered this correct,
and so flogged Zhāng with one hundred and fifty strokes,
and removed him from the official roster.
The Vice-Envoy, Kèshěng Shǐ Gāo Yì, was flogged with one hundred strokes,
and the gifts he had received were confiscated.
Over a year later,
the Emperor, remembering Zhāng's merits in campaigns,
appointed him Jǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
then promoted him to Wǔdìngjūn Jiédù Shǐ,
then appointed him Mùkè of Púdǐ Shān Názhēlú Hé in Shāndōng Xī Lù,
and then Línláo Yǐn.
In the nineteenth year,
he passed away.
Yùnwáng Áng,
whose original name was Wúdūbǔ,
was Tàizǔ's youngest son.
He often followed Tàizǔ in campaigns.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ,
Áng and Shāohē, with four thousand soldiers, supervised the surrendered people of various tribes,
settling them east of the ridge,
and also stationing troops to guard Línhuáng Fǔ.
Áng was unable to manage them,
and the surrendered people suffered under him,
with many rebelling and fleeing.
The Emperor heard of this
and sent Chūlǐdǐ to warn and admonish Áng.
Having already passed Shàngjīng,
all the tribes had rebelled and left,
except for the Zhāngmǐn Gōng and Xiǎoshìwéi tribes, which reached the interior.
An imperial edict was sent to Ānbǎn Bójíliè Wúqǐmǎi, saying:
"Previously, Áng was sent to relocate various tribes,
which led to much resentment and rebellion.
Shāohē stationed troops but did not attack them,
allowing the surrendered people to return to the Liáo ruler,
disobeying orders and losing the populace.
He should be severely punished.
If there is any doubt,
then imprison him
and await a definite decision after the army returns."
At this time,
Tàizōng was in charge of the defense,
assisted by Cíbùshī.
Cíbùshī persuaded Tàizōng that due to the national celebration, the punishment could be lightened.
Thereupon, Áng was flogged with seventy strokes
and confined to Tàizhōu,
while Shāohē was executed.
In the sixth year of Tiānhuì,
he temporarily served as Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān.
In the fifteenth year,
he became Xījīng Liúshǒu.
In the third year of Tiānjuan,
he became Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
he was enfeoffed as Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng.
In the second year,
an imperial edict ordered Áng to include
the characters "Huáng Shú Zǔ" (Imperial Great-Uncle)
in his title,
and he was enfeoffed as Yùnwáng.
That year,
he passed away.
His sons were Zhèngjiā and Hèshòu.
Hèshòu rose through official ranks to Yělǔwǎ Qúnmù Shǐ,
and died during the chaos of Qìdān Sābā;
his story is in the Records of Loyalty and Righteousness.
Zhèngjiā,
in the early Huángtǒng period,
was appointed Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn as a member of the imperial clan,
and then Cízhōu Cìshǐ.
During the Tiāndé period,
he was Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū,
and successively promoted to Huìníng Yǐn and Ānhuà Jūn Jiédù Shǐ,
then Yìdū Yǐn.
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
he was Zhèdōng Dào Fù Tǒngzhì,
and with Gōngbù Shàngshū Sū Bǎohéng, he led a naval fleet from the sea route towards Lín'ān.
Upon reaching Sōnglín Dǎo, they were blocked by wind
and anchored between the islands.
The next morning,
the boatmen saw enemy vessels in the distance
and requested preparations.
Zhèngjiā asked:
"How far is it from here?"
The boatmen replied:
"According to waterway measurements,
it's about three hundred lǐ.
The wind is swift,
so they will arrive soon."
Zhèngjiā did not understand sea routes or navigation,
and did not believe them.
A moment later,
the enemy indeed arrived.
Seeing our army unprepared,
they immediately threw fire bombs.
Zhèngjiā looked around and saw fires erupting on the surrounding boats.
Realizing he could not escape,
he jumped into the water and died,
at the age of forty-one.
Jiàokān Jì

Lièzhuàn Dìsì Shǐzǔ Yǐxià Zhūzǐ Xù (original name Wūyě, son Zōngxiù) Wēikě Zōngshì Húshímén Hézhù (son Bùhuī) Guābǎo Zhōng (original name Chǒuhàn) Qí (original name Sǎohé) Shùlǔ Húshígǎi Zōngxián (original name Ālǔ) Tàlán Biàn (original name Wúmǔ) Qián (original name Ālǐlà) Yì (original name Sānbǎo) Āxǐ
Wán yán Xù,
whose courtesy name was Miǎndào,
originally named Wūyě,
was the fifth son of Mùzōng.
He was fond of learning,
and the people of the country called him Xiùcái.
At sixteen,
he followed Tàizǔ in attacking Níngjiāng Zhōu,
and followed Zōngwàng in raiding the Liáo ruler at Shíniǎnduó.
When Tàizōng succeeded to the throne,
he summoned Wán yán Xù back from the army
to consult with him on political affairs.
When Zōnghàn and Zōngwàng pacified Biànzhōu,
they received the surrender of the Sòng emperor.
Tàizōng sent Wán yán Xù to the army to console them.
Zōnghàn and others asked what he desired.
He said:
"Only good books."
He returned with several cartloads.
The Nǚzhēn originally had no written language.
When they conquered Liáo,
they captured Qìdān and Hàn people,
and only then did they become proficient in Qìdān and Hàn characters.
Thereupon, all the imperial sons studied them.
Zōngxióng was able to master both the large and small Qìdān scripts in two months,
while Wányán Xīyǐn then imitated the Qìdān characters to create the Nǚzhēn script.
Since the Nǚzhēn had no written language,
they also never had records,
so the deeds of their ancestors were not recorded.
Zōnghàn enjoyed interviewing elderly Nǚzhēn people,
and obtained many anecdotes of their ancestors.
When Tàizōng first ascended the throne,
he reinstated the jinshi examination,
and people like Hán Fǎng were all in the imperial court,
and literary scholars were gradually promoted and employed.
In the sixth year of Tiānhuì,
an imperial edict sought out anecdotes of the ancestors
to be prepared for the national history,
and Wán yán Xù and Yēlǜ Díyuè were appointed to manage this.
Wán yán Xù and others collected oral traditions and old stories,
from the founding ancestor to the ten emperors below him,
compiling them into three volumes.
For all tribes,
they were first referred to as "such and such a tribe,"
then as "such and such a place on such and such a river,"
and also as "such and such a village in such and such a district,"
to distinguish them.
Regarding interactions with the Qìdān and expeditions against various tribes,
all their stratagems and cunning schemes
were concealed in no way.
Some events were detailed, some brief,
but all were factual.
Since Tàizǔ negotiated peace with Gāolí,
all Nǚzhēn who had entered Gāolí were demanded back,
and for over ten years,
the demands never ceased.
Wán yán Xù submitted a memorial remonstrating:
"Your servant has heard that no virtue is greater than enjoying Heaven's will,
and no benevolence comes before showing kindness to those below.
The households being demanded
are all descendants of former rebels, fugitives, and traitors:
Wūchǔn, Émóhàn, Āhǎi, and Āhéshù.
In previous generations, though the four borders were pacified and cherished,
they were not yet subservient.
Since the late sovereign opened communication with Gāolí,
they heard we would become great,
and therefore said they were originally of the same stock,
and gradually submitted.
Since Gāolí did not grant permission (for their return),
border conflicts arose,
leading to military engagements.
It took a long time to establish peace,
about thirty years.
Those who were strong then are all dead now,
their descendants are settled in local customs,
their marriages are firmly established.
If the demands for their return continue,
they certainly dare not delay,
but their flesh and blood will be separated,
which truly is not the wish of the people.
Human resentment is most pitiable,
yet to insist on claiming them as one's own
is merely a blindness on both our parts,
not the greatness of treating all equally.
The state has abundant people and resources,
and its territory spans ten thousand li;
I do not know what benefit will truly be gained from acquiring these people.
If they are not returned now,
it would be no difficulty for us to take them by force with strong soldiers and stout troops.
However, war is a dangerous weapon,
and battle a perilous undertaking,
only to be used as a last resort.
Gāolí calls itself a vassal,
its tribute is not lacking;
the country is already a subordinate,
and its people are not outsiders.
A sage acts righteously,
not blaming minor faults;
where justice lies,
one should not wait a whole day.
Your servant foolishly believes
it is fitting to extend the benevolence of kindness to those below,
and magnify the virtue of enjoying Heaven's will,
allowing the exemption from these demands.
Then they will not consider them their own, but as if we had gained them by ourselves."
It was followed.
In the fifteenth year,
he became Shū Zuǒ Chéng, with the added title of Zhèndōng Jūnjiédùshǐ and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
He participated in quelling Zōngpán's rebellion,
received many rewards,
and was given the added title of Yítóng Sānsī,
with the characters
"Huángshú Zǔ"
prefixed to his title.
Wán yán Xù all strenuously declined to accept.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
he drafted the imperial decree for Xīzōng's honorific title.
The emperor summoned Wán yán Xù to drink in the private palace,
and bestowed upon him a jade belt.
The Veritable Records of the Ancestors he had compiled was completed,
comprising three volumes.
When it was presented,
the emperor burned incense and received it standing,
bestowing varying rewards.

An imperial decree ordered that Zuǒ Chéng Wán yán Xù and Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Yì, in addition to their official salaries, be separately given the stipend and attendants of a second-rank imperial prince.
The old system stipulated that
imperial brothers and sons who were imperial princes received second-rank stipends,
and imperial clan members enfeoffed as single-character kings received third-rank stipends.
Wán yán Xù and others being separately given imperial prince stipends
were all exceptional cases.
When the emperor feasted his ministers at the Wǔyún Lóu,
Wán yán Xù offered wine and expressed gratitude.
The emperor rose to his feet.
The chief minister stepped forward and said:
"It is not proper etiquette for Your Majesty to repeatedly rise for your subordinates."
The emperor said:
"What harm is there in me humbling myself to treat my subordinates?"
On that day,
the emperor and his ministers enjoyed themselves to the fullest.
Soon after, he was made concurrent Jiānxiū Guóshǐ,
and promoted to Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
On the death anniversary of Guāngyì Huánghòu,
Xīzōng was about to go hunting;
Wán yán Xù remonstrated and he stopped.
Xīzōng hunted on an island,
and within three days,
personally shot and captured five tigers.
Wán yán Xù presented the "Dōngshòu Shèhǔ Fù,"
and the emperor was pleased,
bestowing upon him a saber, a jade belt, and a fine horse.
He was able to compose poems and prose in Qìdān characters.
Whenever there was something worth commenting on during outings and banquets,
he would compose a poem to express his thoughts.
At that time, the emperor daily indulged in heavy drinking with his close ministers,
sometimes continuing into the night,
and no one could remonstrate with him.
Wán yán Xù submitted a memorial,
and only then did the emperor stop drinking.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng,
concurrently Shìzhōng and Jiānxiū as before.
In the eighth year,
he presented the twenty volumes of the Tàizǔ Shílù,
and was rewarded with eighty liǎng of gold,
one hundred liǎng of silver,
fifty bolts of heavy brocade,
one hundred bolts of silk,
and one rhinoceros-horn belt and one jade-hook belt each.
He was sent out to lead the Xíngtái Shàngshūshěng affairs,
then recalled and appointed Tàibǎo,
leading the three provinces and the Xíngtái as before,
and enfeoffed as Lǔguó Wáng.
Wán yán Xù was upright and spoke little.
Hǎilíng was then in power,
and many court officials attached themselves to him.
One day,
when the grand ministers were holding a meeting,
Hǎilíng arrived late.
Wán yán Xù sternly reproached him face to face, saying:
"I am over fifty years old,
yet I still dare not be late.
You are young and vigorous,
how dare you act like this?"
Hǎilíng knelt and apologized.
In the ninth year,
he was promoted to Tàishī,
and further enfeoffed as Hànguó Wáng.
When Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
he bestowed favors upon the grand ministers to win popular support,
enfeoffed Wán yán Xù as Qínhànguó Wáng,
and he continued to lead the three provinces and serve as Jiānxiū.
Húshígǎi
was a scion of the imperial clan.
He followed Tàizǔ in attacking Níngjiāng,
defeating the Liáo army at Dálǔgǔchéng,
and routing the Liáo ruler's personal guards,
all with distinction.
When the Liáo army came to reinforce Jìzhōu,
Húshígǎi and his elder brother Shígǔnǎi led troops to meet and attack them,
defeating them.
Returning to attack Jìzhōu,
he was struck by a stray arrow,
but fought with even greater vigor,
and captured the city.
The army praised his bravery.
He followed in attacking Chūnzhōu and Tàizhōu,
subduing them,
and also pacifying the various tribes within the territory.
Those who did not surrender were all attacked and captured.
When the Liáo ruler fled west,
Húshígǎi pursued him to Zhōngjīng,
capturing his palace women and eight hundred carts of supplies.
There was one Sīnígǔ
who rebelled again with his own tribe and left.
Húshígǎi pursued him with five hundred soldiers,
capturing his kinsmen and tribesmen and bringing them back.
Dézhōu rebelled again,
and Húshígǎi captured its city with five thousand soldiers.
He followed Lóushì in defeating twenty thousand enemy soldiers south of Guīhuà,
and also brought Guīhuà to surrender.
He followed in taking Jūyōngguān,
along with the subordinate counties of Yān and its mountain valleys' various garrisons.
After the Yíshī tribe had surrendered,
they rebelled again and left.
Húshígǎi led troops in pursuit,
defeated them in battle,
and captured a great many.
As for those from the various tribes of Zézhōu who had fled,
he pursued and recovered them all.
He also defeated rebels at Línhuáng,
executing their chieftains and pacifying their people.
In Tiānjuàn 2 (1139),
he was promoted to Jiédùshǐ of Yǒngdìngjūn,
then changed to Wǔdìngjūn,
and transferred to serve as Liúshǒu of Biànjīng.
In Tiāndé 3 (1151),
he was granted a hereditary Měng'ān.
He died
at the age of sixty-eight.
Zōngxián,
whose original name was Ālǔ.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Liáo,
he followed in attacking Níngjiāngzhōu and Línhuángfǔ.
When Tàizōng was regent,
he was chosen to attend at his side,
and was much trusted and favored.
When Línhuáng rebelled again,
he followed Zōngwàng to recapture it.
He served as Nèikù Dū Tídiǎn,
then was twice promoted to Jiédùshǐ of Guīdéjūn.
His administration was lenient and simple,
and the territory was greatly well-governed.
When his term was complete,
hundreds of thousands of scholars and common people together went to the imperial court to request his retention.
When he was transferred to Wǔdìngjūn,
the common people, supporting the old and young, escorted him for dozens of *lǐ*,
weeping as he departed.
He was then transferred to Yǒngdìngjūn.
When Bǐngdé, an official of the Liánfǎng, inspected officials,
the scholars and common people held basins of water and mirrors,
bowed before him and said:
"The Prefect is as incorruptible, clear-sighted, and upright as this;
the people truly rely on him."
Bǐngdé said:
"I hear that the county officials are uniformly incorruptible and capable,
what do you all think?"
The crowd replied:
"Their diligence, integrity, and frugality all take the Prefect as their model."
Thereupon he said to Zōngxián:
"People say you govern well,
and should be ranked among the best;
you are indeed a worthy Prefect."
Because of this, he was promoted two ranks.
In early Tiāndé,
he was granted a hereditary Móukè,
and summoned by express messenger.
The elders of Xióngzhōu together hung blue ropes and bright mirrors in the official residence,
and old and young crowded the gate;
it was three days before he could depart.
He was enfeoffed as Dìngguó Gōng,
then again appointed Jiédùshǐ of Zhōngshùnjūn,
and bestowed with a jade belt.
The Commander of Bandit Suppression brought several people to the prefectural office.
Zōngxián asked:
"Are the crimes clear?"
He replied:
"The case is complete."
Zōngxián reviewed the dossier,
and said to his subordinates:
"I observe that these people must be innocent."
Not many days later,
the true criminals were indeed apprehended,
and people admired his discernment.
He was transferred to Hélǎnlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn,
then served successively as Guǎngníng Yǐn,
and was enfeoffed as Guǎngpíngjùn Wáng.
He was transferred to Chóngyìjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and concurrently oversaw imperial clan affairs in Běijīng.
In Zhènglóng, his princely title was stripped according to regulation,
he was promoted to Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū,
and transferred to Línghǎijūn.
In early Dàdìng,
an envoy was sent to summon him.
Zōngxián led the various members of the imperial clan to meet at Liáoyáng,
was appointed Tóng Qiān Dà Zōngzhèngshì,
enfeoffed as Jǐngguó Gōng,
and retired.
He was again appointed Pósùlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn,
then retired again,
and died.
Tèjìn Tàlán
was a scion of the imperial clan.
At the age of sixteen,
he served Tàizǔ,
never leaving his side.
In the Battle of Chūhédiàn,
Tàizǔ wished to fight in person.
Tàlán reined in his horse and stopped him, saying:
"Why does our lord slight the enemy?
I request to exert my strength."
He immediately brandished his spear and advanced,
personally killing seven men.
Soon after, his spear broke,
and nine cavalrymen dragged him down.
Tàizǔ admired him and said:
"If one could truly obtain dozens of such men,
even ten thousand would not be able to withstand them."
When they fought at Dálǔgǔchéng,
one thousand Liáo soldiers arrayed outside the camp.
Tàizǔ sent Tàlán to attack them.
Tàlán charged into the enemy formation,
greatly defeating their multitude.
He attacked Línhuángfǔ, Chūnzhōu, Tàizhōu, and the two capitals Zhōngjīng and Xījīng,
all with distinction.
In Tiānfǔ 6 (1122),
he was granted a Móukè.
In Tiānhuì 4 (1126),
he followed in campaigning against Sòng,
and was repeatedly rewarded for his achievements.
The following year,
he again raised troops and reached Biàn.
Zōngwàng heard that the Sòng people had gathered supporting armies from various routes at Suīyáng,
and sent Tàlán and Ālíguā with two thousand soldiers to resist them.
They defeated their vanguard of thirty thousand soldiers at Shíxiàn,
and further broke three encampments,
capturing Hú Zhírú, Dūzǒngguǎn of Sòng Jīngdōnglù, Suí Shīyuán, Dūtǒngzhì of Nánlù, and their three generals, along with Zhírú's two sons.
Thereupon they took Gǒngzhōu,
and brought Nínglíng to surrender.
They again defeated twenty thousand at Suīyáng,
and advanced to take Bózhōu.
Hearing that one hundred thousand Sòng soldiers were about to arrive,
Zōngwàng augmented his force with four thousand soldiers,
and together they attacked,
greatly defeating them.
Two thousand of their soldiers
stood in formation,
and could not be moved by cavalry charges.
He then commanded his army to dismount and attack them,
annihilating them all,
capturing their general Shí Tián and returning.
The Marshal's headquarters commended his achievements,
and bestowed generous rewards.
Ruìzōng stationed troops in Xīzhōu,
and dispatched various generals to seize territory.
Tàlán, with five hundred soldiers, entered the sixteen strongholds of Liùpánshān,
subduing over eighty officials,
four thousand households,
and capturing two thousand horses.
During the Huángtǒng reign,
he was successively promoted to Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
In early Tiāndé,
he was promoted to Tèjìn,
and granted a hereditary Měng'ān.
He died
at the age of sixty-five.
Hǎilíng moved the various imperial tombs to Dàfángshān.
Since Tàlán had once served Tàizǔ,
he was ordered to make a stone statue,
and place it before Ruìlíng.
Biàn,
originally named Wúmǔ,
was a staff member of the Sīshǔ Sī in Shàngjīng.
In Dàdìng year 2 (1162),
he was recruited as a bodyguard.
After accumulating merits, he was awarded the vice-commissioner of the Jiédù of Zhānghuà Commandery,
then entered the court as the Jiānchéng of Dūshuǐ Jiān.
He was successively promoted to Tíxíngshǐ for the Zhōngdū and Xījīng Circuits,
and then transferred to govern Guīdé Prefecture and serve as Jiédùshǐ of Hépíng Commandery.
Wáng Rǔjiā memorialized that Biàn had rendered service in river management while previously at the Dūshuǐ Jiān,
and so he was appointed Liúshǒu of Běijīng.
Not long after,
he was reassigned to govern Dàxīng Prefecture.
At that time, there were rumors
that Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Jiágǔ Héng had acted unlawfully in the army.
An imperial edict ordered the Xíngbù to investigate.
The matter was sent to Dàxīng Prefecture,
where Biàn immediately ordered his apprehension.
The Emperor deemed this a breach of protocol,
and he was punished with forty strokes of the cane.
After a long time,
he requested to retire,
but this was not permitted.
He was appointed Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Before this,
Zuǒ Sījiàn Chìzhǎn Gāomén had memorialized,
“The position of Yùshǐ Dàfū has been vacant for a long time,
and the imperial discipline is not vigorous.
It is appropriate to select an upright and incorruptible person to rectify all affairs.”
The Emperor then used Biàn.
Previously, Sūn Duó and Jiǎ Xuàn were both Shàngshū.
When Xuàn was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
and Duó was given a second appointment,
he recited a poem by Táng Zhāng Zài to his congratulatory guests,
expressing a sense of frustration.
Biàn impeached him for this,
and Duó was demoted.
Later, he reiterated his previous request,
and was then allowed to retire as Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn,
and passed away.
Gài,
originally named Ālǐlà,
was attached to the Sīshǔ Sī in Shàngjīng.
In Dàdìng year 10 (1170),
being a close relative of the imperial family,
he was recruited as a bodyguard for the Eastern Palace.
He was promoted to Shírén Zhǎng,
appointed Yùyuàn Tōngjìn,
and accompanied Shìzōng on his visit to Shàngjīng.
When the Crown Prince Shǒuguó died,
Shìzōng considered Gài intimate and trustworthy,
and specially ordered him and Téngwáng Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ Gài to ride post-haste to guard the funeral procession.
At that time, Zhāngzōng was Jīnyuán Jùnwáng,
and also remained in Zhōngdū.
Shìzōng ordered Gài and others to protect him,
instructing them:
“The Prince has suffered this family misfortune; his lamentations should be restrained by ritual, and his food and drink should be watched with particular care.”
When Shìzōng returned to the capital,
Gài was promoted to Fúbǎoláng,
and appointed Lìbù Lángzhōng.
Upon Zhāngzōng’s ascension,
he was implicated with Yùshǐ Dàfū Tángkuò Gòng for holding a birthday celebration
that violated the night curfew,
and was stripped of one rank
and dismissed.
In Míngchāng year 1 (1190),
he was reinstated as Tóngzhī Dìzhōu Fángyùshǐ Shì.
He submitted a memorial criticizing the Zǎizhí.
The Emperor, seeing that a minor official dared to satirize and slander the prime ministers,
ordered eighty strokes of the cane,
stripped him of one rank,
dismissed him,
and returned him to his original Měng'ān.
The following year,
he was demoted and appointed Tóngzhī Xuāndézhōu Shì.
He was recalled and appointed Wǔwèi Jūn Fùdūzhǐhuīshǐ,
and after four promotions, became Zhī Dàxīng Fǔshì,
then transferred to Zuǒyòu Xuānhuīshǐ.
In Chéng'ān year 2 (1197),
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
then sent out as Jiédùshǐ of Tàidìng Commandery,
transferred to govern Jìnán Prefecture,
and died.
Yì,
originally named Sānbǎo,
was attached to the Sīshǔ Sī of Méijiānsàiwú.
In Dàdìng year 7 (1167),
being a close relative, he was appointed Shírén Zhǎng of the Eastern Palace guard,
then transferred to become Shàng[⿳竹罒戊] Júshǐ.
Upon Zhāngzōng’s ascension,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Fùjiāngjūn,
and successively promoted to Yòufù Dūdiǎnjiǎn,
concurrently Tídiǎn Shàng[⿳竹罒戊] Júshǐ.
An imperial edict stated:
“You do not possess extraordinary talent;
you have merely been promoted due to long service.
You must be diligent in your duties,
and not commit any further transgressions,
lest I hear of them.”
Not long after,
he was flogged thirty times
for the leanness of the imperial horses.
In Chéng'ān year 2 (1197),
he was reassigned to Zuǒfù Dūdiǎnjiǎn,
with his concurrent duties as before.
Soon after, he was appointed Tóngqiān Dàmùqīn Fǔshì,
and died.
Yì was greedy and vulgar,
and repeatedly failed due to corruption.
However, the Emperor valued his ability to manage the hunting grounds,
and thus promoted him and entrusted him.
Āxǐ,
a member of the imperial clan,
was fond of learning.
He inherited his father’s Měng'ān of Qiābǎishān in Běijīng Circuit.
He judged lawsuits clearly and decisively,
and people trusted and loved him.
He was recognized for his integrity and ability,
and appointed Fùshǐ of Zhāngguó Commandery,
then reassigned as Liúshǒu Pànguān of Shàngjīng.
The Tíxíng Sī memorialized on the governance of Zhāngguó Commandery,
and he was promoted to Tóngzhī Sùpín Lù Jiédù Shì,
then reassigned to Guīdé Commandery,
and successively served as Cìshǐ of Hǎi and Pī Prefectures,
in both cases concurrently commanding all military forces.
When Sòng commander Liú Wénqiān attacked Sùqiān with his troops,
Āxǐ met and repelled them,
defeating them.
He further defeated Qī Chūn and Xià Xīngguó’s naval forces of over ten thousand men,
beheading Xià Xīngguó on the battlefield.
He was promoted to Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn,
again rewarded with silver and silk,
and served as vanguard for Yuánshuài Zuǒjiānjūn Gēshíliè Zhízhōng.
He crossed the Huái River,
and captured the two counties of Bǎoyìng and Tiāncháng.
After the army returned,
he was promoted to Tóngzhī Guīdé Fǔshì,
and reassigned as Sīzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He mourned his mother,
then was reinstated.
In Dà'ān year 2 (1210),
he was reassigned as Huázhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and promoted to Zhènnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In Zhēnyòu year 2 (1214),
he was reassigned to govern Dàmíng Prefecture,
and served as Mǎjūn Dū Tíkòng.
He successively served as Jiédùshǐ for Hénghǎi and Ānhuà Commanderies,
and served as Xuānchāi Shāndōng Lù Zuǒyì Dū Tíkòng.
Soon after, he governed Jìnán Prefecture,
was transferred to Qìnnán Commandery Jiédùshǐ,
promoted to Hénán Tǒngjūnshǐ,
concurrently Chāngwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and died.
A eulogy states: Among the imperial clan of Jīn,
from the Progenitor (Shǐzǔ) to Kāngzōng, there were eight generations.
Xiànzǔ moved to Hǎigūshuǐ Nàgēlǐ Village,
then moved again to Ānchūhǔshuǐ.
Shìzǔ referred to the Hǎigū brothers,
likely indicating their residence.
The twelve tribes of Wányán
all took their tribal name as their surname.
Xuānzōng issued an edict that all imperial clan members should record their surname and given name.
However, there were also tribal people who took their tribal name as their surname,
who were not of the same surname as the imperial clan,
making it impossible to distinguish them.
Collations:
Biographies 5: Shí Xiǎn, Huán Gài (younger brother Sàndá), Wū Chūn (Wēndūn Púlà appended), Lā Pēi (younger brother Má Chǎn), Dùn'ēnliúkě, Ā Shū, Xīwáng Huílíbǎo.
Shí Xiǎn
was a member of the Wūlíndá tribe from Háilǎnshuǐ.
When Zhāozǔ used rules to govern the various tribes,
Shí Xiǎn was unruly and uncontrollable.
When Zhāozǔ died at Bīlàjì Village,
his tribesmen were returning with his coffin.
Upon reaching Háilǎnshuǐ,
Shí Xiǎn and Wányán Wōhūwōchū intercepted them on the road,
attacked and seized the coffin,
proclaiming:
“You all esteemed Shílǔ as capable and elevated him,
and now I have gotten him!”
Zhāozǔ’s followers reported this to Púmǎ Tàiwān.
They, along with Wányán Ménggěbātǔ from Mǎjǐlǐng Hébǎocūn, raised an army, pursued them,
fought,
and recovered the coffin.
The multitude acclaimed Jǐngzǔ as the chief of all tribes,
and Báishān,
Yēhuǐ, Tǒngmén, Yēlǎn, Tǔgǔlún, and the Five Kingdoms all submitted.
When the Liao envoy Hélǔ Línyá came to demand the surrendered people,
Shí Xiǎn refused all and did not obey the command.
Jǐngzǔ attacked him,
but could not conquer him.
Jǐngzǔ assessed that he could not be taken by force,
so he resorted to a stratagem.
He then reported to Liao that Shí Xiǎn had blocked the eastern sea route.
The Liao Emperor sent someone to rebuke him, saying:
"How dare you block the eagle route?
If you truly have no other intentions,
send your chieftain here."
Shí Xiǎn sent his eldest son Pózhūkān to court,
saying:
"I dare not defy the command of the great nation."
The Liao people generously rewarded and sent him back,
telling Pózhūkān:
"Your father truly has no other intentions;
he should personally come to court."
Shí Xiǎn believed this,
and the next year came to an audience during the spring hunt.
Pózhūkān accompanied him.
The Liao ruler said to Shí Xiǎn:
"The crime lies solely with you,
not with your son."
He then ordered Pózhūkān to return,
and exiled Shí Xiǎn to the borderlands.
Jǐngzǔ thus used a scheme to remove Shí Xiǎn, intending to pacify his son and his people.
Pózhūkān harbored resentment but had not yet acted.
Then, Huólàhúnshuǐ Hèshíliè's bù Lápēi and Máchǎn raised an army.
Pózhūkān went to join them.
When they were defeated at Mùléngshuǐ,
Máchǎn fled first.
Pózhūkān and Lápēi were captured,
along with their partisans,
and all were presented to the Liao ruler.
After a long time,
Shìzǔ again sent someone to say:
"If Pózhūkān does not return,
his people will know their guilt is severe,
and will thus be fearful,
unwilling to submit."
The Liao ruler considered it so,
and then sent Pózhūkān and all the criminals previously presented back to them.
Huánhuó and Sàndá, brothers,
were the sons of Guóxiàng Yǎdá.
They resided in Yìtúncūn of the Wányán tribe.
Yǎdá was called Guóxiàng;
his origin is unknown.
Jǐngzǔ once sought a Guóxiàng from Yǎdá with silks and horses,
and Yǎdá granted it.
Jǐngzǔ obtained it,
and bestowed it upon Sùzōng.
Later, Sāgǎi also held this office.
Huánhuó and his brothers once served Jǐngzǔ.
At the beginning of Shìzǔ's reign,
his uncle Bàhēi harbored strange ambitions,
secretly enticing Huánhuó, wishing to rebel with him.
Zháosù Huánghòu went to Yìtúncūn,
with Shìzǔ and Sùzōng accompanying her.
They met Huánhuó and Sàndá, both intoxicated,
arguing fiercely.
They then began to strike each other,
drawing blades against one another.
Zháosù Huánghòu personally intervened to stop them,
and they ceased.
From then on, the plot grew more serious.
At this time, Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn also allied with Bàhēi,
cunningly using Wūbùtún's sale of armor as a pretext for war.
Shìzǔ had no choice but to make peace with them.
After several years,
Wūchūn led his forces across the Huólùn and Láiliú rivers.
Shìzǔ personally went to resist them.
Huánhuó and Sàndá then raised an army.
Sùzōng led a detached force to resist Huánhuó and Sàndá.
Shìzǔ feared their forces might combine,
and cautioned him, saying:
"If peace is possible, then make peace;
otherwise, fight."
When they reached the Wòlǔgànchūshuǐ,
their battle formation was ready.
Sùzōng sent Péndébójǐn to negotiate peace.
Huánhuó, however, relied on Wūchūn being in the north,
and had no intention of peace.
Péndé reported to Sùzōng:
"The enemy wants to fight."
Someone else said:
"The battleground is too close to the villages.
Even if we win, we cannot completely defeat the enemy.
It is better to retreat and lure them to open ground."
Sùzōng was misled by this,
and ordered the army to withdraw slightly,
failing to maintain formation.
Huánhuó and Sàndá took advantage of this,
and Sùzōng was defeated.
Huánhuó, seizing victory,
plundered extensively.
In this campaign,
Wūchūn, due to prolonged rain, could not advance,
and so disbanded his troops.
When Shìzǔ heard of Sùzōng's defeat,
he personally led his army,
passing through the Shèhěn and Tiēgē rivers to seize the homes of Huánhuó and Sàndá.
Huánhuó and Sàndá were unaware.
Shìzǔ burned their residences,
killed and plundered about a hundred people, and then returned.
Before reaching the army,
Sùzōng's army was again defeated.
When Shìzǔ arrived,
he reprimanded Sùzōng for his defeat,
and sent Huāndū and Yěhē with seven *móukè* from their own tribe to assist him.
He also sent someone to negotiate peace again.
Huánhuó and Sàndá demanded Yínggē's great red horse and Cíbùshī's purple-roan horse.
Shìzǔ refused,
and then allied with Bùshùlǔ bù Búhuī, Púchá bù Sāgǔchū, and the armies of the various tribes north of the Pǐgǔdūnshuǐ on both sides of the Hùntóngjiāng.
They gathered a large force into a formation,
beat drums to boost morale, and charged.
Huánhuó, relying on his numerous troops,
was confident of victory.
He issued an order, saying:
"Today the gate of heaven is open!
Bring all your carts with you.
You may take all of Wūgǔnāi's and his wife's treasures, goods, and property as you please.
Anyone who disobeys shall be captured and taken away."
At this time, Pōduōtǔshuǐ Péimǎnbù Wòbùbójǐn joined Shìzǔ.
Huánhuó and others set fire to their settlements.
Wòbù survived.
Shìzǔ generously comforted his family.
After subduing Huánhuó,
he returned their former land to them.
Huánhuó's army came again.
Púchá bù Shāzhǐbójǐn and Húbǔdábójǐn sent Āxǐ by a secret path to report,
and also asked:
"The bandits are approaching;
how should we deal with them?"
Shìzǔ again commanded:
"Things have come to this;
there's no time for deliberation.
Follow them with your forces;
you can save yourselves.
Just distinguish yourselves with banners!"
Whenever enemy forces arrived,
he would send Āxǐ to come secretly through the forest,
ordering him to travel back and forth on the main road with Bìchá,
which was the old secret forest path.
When Huánhuó reached Běi'àidiàn,
Shìzǔ was about to send out troops,
but heard that Bàhēi had died while eating in Mǎncūn.
So he marched along the Ānshùhǔshuǐ,
also intending to annex the forces of Hǎigùshùlièsùbójǐn before battle.
Scouts reported:
"The enemy has arrived!"
Shìzǔ ordered Cíbùshī to organize the army and advance quickly,
making him wait at Tuōhuògǎiyuán.
At this time,
Huánhuó had a large army,
while Shìzǔ's army was small;
the numbers were uneven.
By the time Shìzǔ reached the army,
the morale of the soldiers was very low.
Shìzǔ knew this in his heart but dared not speak,
only ordering them to disarm and rest for a while,
wash their faces with water,
and drink rice water.
After a moment,
the soldiers' morale slightly recovered.
At this time,
Sùzōng had gone to Liao to seek aid,
and was not with the army.
Before the battle,
Shìzǔ dismissed everyone and spoke privately with Mùzōng,
saying that if the army was defeated, he would go with Sùzōng to beg for an army to avenge them.
He also ordered Mùzōng not to participate in the battle,
but to observe the outcome from horseback,
and first plan their retreat or advance.
Then he rolled up his sleeves, put on his bow, and fastened his arrows.
He used the lower part of a coarse robe to protect his chest and back.
He waved the banner three times,
beat the drum thrice,
then cast aside the banner and gripped his sword,
personally leading the vanguard,
fighting with all his might.
Huánhuó's infantry advanced with shields and spears.
Shìzǔ's forces attacked them with long spears,
and the infantry was utterly defeated.
Cíbùshī vigorously attacked them from behind,
and Huánhuó's cavalry was also defeated.
Shìzǔ, seizing the victory, pursued the routed enemy,
making the Duōtuìshuǐ run red with blood.
Shìzǔ ordered his army to stop pursuing,
and captured all the abandoned carts, armor, horses, cattle, and military provisions.
He then announced the victory to heaven and earth,
and distributed the spoils to his generals and soldiers,
each according to their merits.
Not long after,
Huánkuī and Sàndá both came to surrender with their subordinates.
Bǔhuī still held Sā'ālà village,
and would not come out when summoned.
Sāgǔchū occupied Ālúgànchū village.
Shìzǔ sent someone to negotiate peace with him.
Sāgǔchū spoke rudely as a joke,
and replied:
"I originally wanted peace,
but the valiant warrior Bādémén would not agree to peace.
He wept and said to me: 'If we truly make peace,
then beautiful clothes and fat sheep will no longer be obtainable.'
Therefore, I dared not obey the command."
He then let his soldiers plunder and capture nearby villages and estates.
Someone shot him from the roadside,
hitting his mouth and killing him.
A subordinate of Bǔhuī was named Shílǔ.
Shílǔ's mother married Dálǔhàn Bójǐn of the Mǎnbù tribe and became his concubine.
Dálǔhàn and his cousin Mǒsāiyǐn Bójǐn both served Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ wanted to sow discord between Shílǔ and Bǔhuī,
and said to Dálǔhàn:
"Your service to me
is not as steadfast as Mǒsāiyǐn's."
This was to imply that Shílǔ's mother and son were
one here and one there,
thereby shaking Shílǔ.
When Shílǔ heard this,
he killed Bǔhuī and surrendered.
Shílǔ had an affair with Bǔhuī's concubine,
and constantly feared punishment.
When he heard Shìzǔ's words,
he was confused by them
and sent someone to tell Dálǔhàn:
"I am going to kill Bǔhuī and come.
Wait for me by the river."
He waited until Bǔhuī was sound asleep,
then stabbed a blade into his chest and killed him.
The pursuers were urgent.
He hid in the water with only his nose exposed in broad daylight.
By night,
he reached the river
and swam across.
Dálǔhàn had sent someone to wait for him,
and thus he was able to escape.
After a long time,
he got drunk
and had a fierce quarrel with Dálǔhàn.
Dálǔhàn killed him.
Wūchūn,
a man from the Ābásīshuǐ Wēndū tribe,
made his living as an ironworker.
Due to a lean year,
he came with his staff and carrying pole and his tribesmen to surrender.
Jǐngzǔ settled him,
and he supported himself by his original craft.
Later, knowing his courage, decisiveness, and skill in judgment,
Jǐngzǔ appointed him as chief of his tribe,
and also sent his clansman Péndé to escort him back to his former tribe.
Péndé
was Wūchūn's nephew.
When Shìzǔ first succeeded as Jìdùshǐ,
his uncle Báhēi secretly harbored covetous designs,
and subtly enticed Huánkuī, Sàndá brothers, Wūchūn, Wōmóuhǎn, and others.
Wūchūn believed Báhēi was causing trouble from within,
and so
he was somewhat disloyal to Shìzǔ,
and cruelly exploited his tribesmen.
His tribesmen complained to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ sent someone to rebuke him, saying:
"My father trusted you
and made you chief.
Now people report that you truly
kill innocent people,
and administer justice unfairly.
From now on, you must not do so again."
Wūchūn replied:
"I am an old man of your father's generation.
How many days have you been chief?
What concern is it of yours?"
Shìzǔ was inwardly afraid of Báhēi
and feared that his factions would cause trouble,
so he tried to pacify him with kind words,
and wished to win his favor through marriage.
He sent someone to arrange a marriage, but
Wūchūn was unwilling
and laughed, saying:
"How can the children of dogs and pigs live together
and bear offspring?
How can Húlǐgǎi and Nǚzhí be relatives?"
Wūchūn wanted to raise troops,
but Shìzǔ treated him as before,
giving him no pretext.
Wūbùtún from the Jiāgǔ tribe,
also an ironworker,
came to sell ninety suits of armor.
When Wūchūn heard this,
he sent someone to rebuke him, saying:
"The armor
is my armor.
South of the Láiliú river and north of the Pǐgǔdūn river
are all my lands.
Why did you take my armor without permission?
Return it to me immediately."
Shìzǔ replied:
"He came to sell the armor,
and I bought it at a fair price."
Wūchūn said:
"If you are unwilling to give me the armor and make peace,
then send your uncle's sons Xiégé and Sīlè."
Xiégé was Báhēi's son.
Shìzǔ judged that his intention was not truly to negotiate peace,
but rather to take action,
and did not want to send them.
The multitude strongly urged:
"If you don't send them, there will surely be war."
Having no choice,
he sent them.
He said to Sīlè:
"Xiégé is unharmed.
But he will seize you.
Feign illness halfway and do not go."
After they set off,
Sīlè said:
"My illness has recurred;
I will stop and not go."
Xiégé said:
"I cannot go alone either."
Their companions forced them to continue.
Upon meeting Wūchūn,
Wūchūn treated Xiégé with great courtesy,
but indeed seized Sīlè
and said:
"If I get the armor, you live;
otherwise, I kill you."
Shìzǔ gave him the armor,
and Sīlè was able to return.
From then on, Wūchūn became even more fearless.
Several years later,
Wūchūn raised troops to fight,
traveling over Xiécùn Ridge,
crossing the Huólùn and Láiliú rivers,
and stopping at Zhúhǔ tribe's Ālǐ'ǎi village, at Zǎibùnǎi Bójǐn's house.
It was then October.
Heavy rain fell continuously day and night,
and ice covered the ground.
Wūchūn could not advance,
so he withdrew.
Thereupon Huánkuī and Sàndá also raised troops.
Shìzǔ personally resisted Wūchūn,
and sent Sùzōng to resist Huánkuī.
Subsequently, Wūchūn returned due to the rain,
and his uncle Báhēi also died.
Therefore, Shìzǔ was able to concentrate his forces against Huánkuī and Sàndá,
and defeated them in one battle.
Bēinǎi from the Wòlè tribe,
who had previously served Jǐngzǔ,
now harbored other ambitions.
He moved to Nánbìkěntè village,
then falsely accused Huāndū of arson,
intending to eliminate him this way.
The details are in the biography of Huāndū.
Shìzǔ captured Bēinǎi
and released him from his crime.
Bēinǎi ultimately felt uneasy,
moved to Tǔkū village,
and allied with Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn.
Wūchūn raised troops and crossed the ridge.
Shìzǔ stationed his army at Wūpì village to await him.
They advanced to Sūsùhǎidiàn.
Both armies formed ranks,
ready to battle.
Shìzǔ did not personally engage in combat,
but ordered Sùzōng to fight with the left army,
assisted by Xiéliè and Cíbùshī.
This was due to an unusual dream.
Sùzōng bound bundles of straw and set them on fire.
A strong wind rose from behind,
making the fire fierce.
It was August;
the wild grass was still green,
but the fire completely burned it,
and smoke and flames filled the sky.
Wūchūn's army was downwind.
Sùzōng attacked them from upwind.
Wūchūn was greatly defeated.
Bēinǎi was captured again,
offered to the Liáo dynasty,
and Sūsùhǎidiàn was fortified and occupied.
Hēshíliè Làpēi and Má Chǎn fought with Shìzǔ at Yěquèshuǐ.
Shìzǔ was hit by four arrows,
and his army was defeated.
Làpēi sent his old henchmen, Tūhǎn and others, across Qīnglǐng,
to see Wūchūn,
bribing various tribes to establish connections with him.
Làpēi and Má Chǎn sought help from Wūchūn,
and Wūchūn provided them with one hundred and seventeen soldiers from Gūlǐdiàn.
Shìzǔ captured Làpēi and presented him to Liáozhǔ,
and also reported Wūchūn's act of providing soldiers,
charging him with not maintaining the eagle road.
Liáozhǔ sent someone to Wūchūn to inquire about the situation,
Wūchūn was afraid,
and thus made a false statement, saying:
"I never assisted Làpēi.
North of Délínshí,
the people of Gūlǐdiàn,
are not within my jurisdiction."
After Làpēi's defeat,
Shìzǔ captured all one hundred and seventeen Gūlǐdiàn soldiers who had assisted Wūchūn,
and sent their commanders, Wòshàn and Wòtuō, to recruit their people,
then dispatched Xiépō Bójǐn to pacify them.
Xiépō was unable to manage and regulate these people,
and Púchá Bù's Gùshí and Báshí, etc., lured over three hundred people into the city,
trapping them all.
When Shìzǔ returned after building the eagle road,
Xiéliè came to report.
Shìzǔ made Huāndū the Dūtǒng,
and defeated Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn at Xiédūi,
and Gùshí and Báshí were all captured.
Shìzǔ personally led troops across Wūjǐlǐng,
to Wōmóuhǎicūn,
where Húlùn Jiāgǔ Bù's Shèngkūn Bójǐn resided.
Wūyán Bù's wealthy Guōhé requested to divide a force to attack Wūchūn from his own territory,
as his territory was close to Wūchūn's,
and he wanted to protect himself.
So, Xiéliè and Yuèpán were sent with a detached force to guide them to Wūchūn's residence,
while Shìzǔ personally led the main army to rendezvous with Huāndū.
Upon reaching Ābùsāishuǐ,
all the tribes east of the ridge gathered,
and Shítǔmén also brought his tribal soldiers.
At this time,
Wūchūn had already died.
Wōmóuhǎn, hearing that Shìzǔ was coming to attack,
appealed to the Liáo people,
begging for a peaceful resolution.
An envoy had already arrived at his home,
when Shìzǔ's army arrived.
Wōmóuhǎn requested a delay in the advance of the army,
and returned all the fugitives he had previously accepted.
Shìzǔ sent Wūlíndá Gùdéhēi Bójǐn to receive the sent-back fugitives.
Wōmóuhǎn, with three hundred cavalry, attacked while they were off guard,
but Shìzǔ defeated him.
The Liáo envoy was displeased with his lack of trustworthiness,
and no longer acted as a mediator for peace,
but advanced his army and besieged him.
Tàizǔ, wearing short armor, inspected the siege,
issuing orders to all the armies.
Wōmóuhǎn sent Tàiyù to secretly exit the city and attack him.
Tàiyù rode his horse, wielding a spear,
and was about to reach Tàizǔ,
when Huólàhú struck and broke his spear,
and Tàizǔ was thus spared.
Xiéliè arrived at Xiécùnshuǐ,
and following Guōhé's plan,
captured twenty-two people who were previously in Wūchūn's army.
Wūchūn's army realized this,
killed two people,
but the remaining twenty people were all captured,
and were supplemented by local soldiers coming to assist.
Wōmóuhǎn knew he was no match,
and so he fled.
They then captured his city,
and distributed all the wealth and property among the army,
based on their merits,
and all the tribes were pacified.
Mùzōng often praised Guōhé's achievements,
and later married Xiéliè's daughter Shǒuníng to his son Húlíhǎn.
Wūchūn's descendants became the Wēndūn clan,
and his distant grandson was named Púlà.
Wēndūn Púlà first lived at Ābùxīnhé in Chángbáishān,
then moved to Yílǐmǐnhé in Lóngzhōu.
Púlà initially followed Xīyǐn in campaigns,
acting as a Méng'ān Móukè.
When he encountered robbers who suddenly appeared,
he fought fiercely and defeated them,
personally killing over twenty people.
For this, he was promoted to Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi.
At the beginning of Tiāndé,
he was appointed Hùwèi,
then promoted to Sùzhí Jiāngjūn.
When he competed in long-distance archery with other guards,
none could surpass him.
Hǎilíng awarded him an jade saddle and bridle.
He went to Hélǎnlù to select suitable candidates for guards,
and his report upon return pleased the emperor,
so he was promoted to Yēlúwǎnjūn Mùshǐ,
and then changed to Liáozhōu Cìshǐ.
During the Zhènglóng campaign against Sòng,
he was summoned as the Wǔyìjūn Fù Dūzǒngguǎn,
leading two thousand soldiers.
South of Rǔzhōu,
he encountered over twenty thousand Sòng soldiers,
intercepted and defeated them,
personally killing over ten officers and soldiers.
At this time,
many common people in Sōng and Rǔ zhōu had fled.
Púlà gathered them,
and enabled them to return to their occupations.
He was changed to Mòzhōu Cìshǐ,
then summoned as Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuàifǔ Shuài,
and again promoted to Lǒngzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
serving successively as Zhènxi, Húlígǎi, and Xiǎndéjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He retired,
and died.
Làpēi and Má Chǎn, brothers,
were from Hēshíliè Bù in Hélínhé Xiāng, Huólàhúnshuǐ.
There were seven brothers,
who were well-known,
and people respected them.
When Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn created trouble,
the Làpēi brothers took advantage of this opportunity to unite the people of Táowēnshuǐ,
gradually becoming uncontrollable.
Among their fellow villagers, some sought refuge,
moving to the Wild Jurchens in Bìhǎncūn.
Làpēi was enraged,
and intended to attack them.
He then allied with Wūgǔlùn Bù's Sāolà Bójǐn, wealthy Tàlǎn, Húshímǎn Bójǐn, Hǎiluó Bójǐn, and Wòzhuóhuǒ Bójǐn.
Hǎiluó and Wòzhuóhuǒ secretly sent someone to inform the Wild Jurchens,
who were prepared,
and Làpēi and others were defeated and returned.
Làpēi then again attacked the Wild Jurchens from the south road,
defeated them,
and captured many.
Hǎiluó, Wòzhuóhuǒ, and Húshímǎn feared Làpēi,
and sought aid from Shìzǔ.
Xiéliè, with light troops, intercepted and attacked Làpēi and others at Túnmùtǔcūn,
defeated them,
and recovered all the captives.
Làpēi and Má Chǎn drove their captured horses to Láiliúshuǐ.
Shìzǔ reached Húntóngjiāng,
and divided his army with Mùzōng.
Shìzǔ himself marched rapidly from Dùgǔlǔjīn, doubling his pace,
many horses were exhausted,
and were left by the roadside.
With fifty or sixty cavalry,
he encountered Làpēi at Yěquèshuǐ.
It was already dusk,
Làpēi's army was numerous,
Shìzǔ's army was few.
Huāndū fought fiercely,
charging in and out several times,
his horse was wounded,
and over ten men died.
Shìzǔ broke through the enemy lines and fought bravely,
suffering four wounds,
and was unable to continue fighting.
Mùzōng crossed the river from Āntǔhúnjīn,
and encountered the enemy at Púlúmǎishuǐ.
The enemy asked who they were,
and they replied:
"Huāndū."
The questioner shot Mùzōng,
and the arrow struck his quiver.
In this year,
Làpēi and Má Chǎn sent their followers, the old bandit Tūhǎn and Wūxǐ, to plunder four hundred horses from Hùlúbùluò,
and seven hundred odd horses belonging to the wealthy Niánhǎn, totalling over seven hundred horses.
They crossed east of Qīnglǐng,
and allied with Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn.
Shìzǔ personally led an expedition against them,
Làpēi and others feigned surrender,
and the army returned.
Làpēi again sought help from Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn.
Wōmóuhǎn provided him with one hundred and seventeen soldiers from Gūlǐdiàn.
Làpēi occupied Mùléngshuǐ,
fortifying dangerous terrain.
Shíxiǎnzi Pózhūkān also went to join him.
Shìzǔ led troops to besiege them,
defeated their army,
Má Chǎn fled,
and then captured Làpēi and Pózhūkān,
presenting them both to Liáo.
All their soldiers were captured,
and their commanders Wòshàn and Wòtuō were sent to recruit and pacify their people,
and Xiépō was sent to settle them.
Furthermore, Ālíhéwàn was sent to investigate the sentiments of the people in Mùléngshuǐ,
and to recruit soldiers to join Xiépō,
as recorded in the Biography of Wūchūn.
After Shìzǔ died,
Sùzōng inherited the Jiedushi title.
Máchǎn occupied Zhíwūkǎishuǐ,
repaired and fortified his encampments,
harbored fugitives,
and blocked all passage.
Relying on the people of Táowēnshuǐ for assistance,
when summoned, he refused to obey.
Kāngzōng was then sent to attack him.
That year,
a great flood occurred in Báishān Húntóngjiāng;
the water rose to the level of the banks.
Kāngzōng traveled by boat from Ālíngāng to Shuàishuǐ,
then abandoned the boat and proceeded along Shuàishuǐ.
He sent Tàizǔ to take Máchǎn's family from the eastern route,
capturing all of them.
Kāngzōng pressed the siege against Máchǎn.
Tàizǔ arrived to join the army,
whereupon Máchǎn, having fled beforehand,
and his men broke through the encirclement under cover of night and escaped.
Tàizǔ said,
"Máchǎn's household is completely gone.
Where will he go?"
He pursued them.
Máchǎn, unaware that Tàizǔ was eagerly seeking him,
came with three horsemen to scout the army.
One of them fell from his horse.
Tàizǔ recognized him and
asked about the situation.
The man said,
"I came with Máchǎn to scout the army;
the two who fled,
Máchǎn is among them."
Máchǎn and his companion then split up and fled.
Tàizǔ ordered Hégǔlǔ to pursue the one fleeing east
and personally pursued the one fleeing west.
Upon reaching Zhíwūkǎishuǐ,
Máchǎn was lost from sight.
Tàizǔ pursued him urgently,
found discarded armor on the road,
and followed the tracks.
He reached a large marsh,
which was muddy.
Máchǎn abandoned his horse and entered the reeds.
Tàizǔ also abandoned his horse and caught up with him,
challenging him to battle.
The Ūgǔlùn warrior Huólàhú arrived on horseback
and asked,
"Who is this person?"
Tàizǔ did not initially recognize Máchǎn,
but feigned an answer, saying,
"It's Máchǎn."
Huólàhú said,
"Have we finally caught up with this man?"
He then dismounted, drew his spear, and advanced to fight.
Máchǎn repeatedly shot Huólàhú,
and Huólàhú was struck by two arrows,
unable to fight further.
After a moment,
the army arrived
and surrounded him.
Huándū shot Máchǎn in the head,
and he was captured.
No one recognized him,
so Huólàhú stepped forward, supported his head, and examined him,
seeing his gapped teeth.
He said,
"It truly is Máchǎn."
Máchǎn opened his eyes and said,
"Gentlemen, your affairs are settled."
They then killed him.
Tàizǔ presented Máchǎn's head to Liáo.
Dùnēn was
a man of the Ālǐmín Tèshíshuǐ Hégēlìe tribe.
His grandfather was named Hégǔlǔ;
his father was Nàgēnniè.
They were hereditary Bójǐn of their tribe.
The Wòzhǔn tribesmen Yělà Bójǐn and Hǎigě'ān Bójǐn brutalized their kinsman Wòdáhǎn Bójǐn and his younger brothers Wūlǐhēi and Wūtúmén.
They plundered their homes and also plundered the home of Āhuólǐ Bójǐn,
encroaching upon the territory of Nàgēnniè's tribe.
Mùzōng sent Nàgēnniè with his tribal troops to deal with Yělà and others.
Reaching Sūbīnshuǐ,
he immediately recruited people as soldiers; if the leader refused, he would plunder their people.
He then attacked Díkùdé of the Wūgǔlùn tribe
and entered Mǐlǐmíshíhǎn City.
When Wòsài and Yěhē came to inquire about the situation,
they stopped at Nàmùhàn Village west of Sūbīnshuǐ.
Nàgēnniè stopped at Wūmài Village east of Sūbīnshuǐ.
Although Nàgēnniè submitted, he refused to pay compensation.
This was the tenth month of the Jiǎxū year.
In the eighth month of the following year,
Nàgēnniè fled.
Wòsài pursued and killed him,
capturing his mother, wife, and children and returning with them.
He then allowed Dùnēn to reclaim his position.
Liúkě was
a man of the Wūgǔlùn tribe from the confluence of Tǒngmén and Húnchǔn Rivers,
the son of Húshāhún Bójǐn.
Zhàdū was
the son of Ānchūn from Húnchǔnshuǐ.
They secretly incited the people of the Àochún and Wūtǎ tribes to rebel.
Díkùdé and Dùnēn both rebelled and joined Liúkě and Zhàdū.
The two factions proclaimed,
"The faction of the Túshàn tribe consists of fourteen tribes as one,
the faction of the Wūgǔlùn tribe consists of fourteen tribes as one,
and the faction of the Púchá tribe consists of seven tribes as one,
totaling thirty-five tribes.
The Wányán tribe has only twelve.
With thirty-five tribes fighting twelve tribes,
it is three men fighting one.
Victory is certain."
The tribes that Shìzǔ had brought to submission also became disloyal.
At this time,
only Xiélè Bójǐn of the Wūyán tribe,
along with Ālǐbǎo Bójǐn and Sāgězhōu Bójǐn of the Wēndíhén tribe from Tǒngménshuǐ,
all sent messengers to report the difficulty.
Xiélè was
the son of Dájìbǎo.
He first sent his elder brother Bǎogǔlà,
and then came to submit with his armor.
Ālǐbǎo and others said,
"We will certainly not join the rebellion,
but merely beg for troops as reinforcements."
Mùzōng sent Sāgǎi to attack Liúkě,
and Màndūhē to attack Díkùdé.
Later, Tàizǔ arrived at Sāgǎi's army with seventy armed men,
and on the way, he gave forty of them to Màndūhē.
Shítǔmén's army joined Màndūhē below Mǐlǐmíshíhǎn City.
Dùnēn, intending to aid Liúkě,
heard that Màndūhē's troops were few,
and believing them unprepared,
unaware of Shítǔmén's arrival,
decided to attack Màndūhē first.
Màndūhē and Shítǔmén met and attacked him,
thoroughly defeating Dùnēn.
Mǐlǐmíshíhǎn City then surrendered,
and Dùnēn and Díkùdé were captured.
All were released without execution.
Tàizǔ reached Sāgǎi's army,
and the next day attacked and captured Liúkě's city.
All the chieftains in the city were executed,
and their families and property were seized before returning.
Wūtǎ City also dismantled its defenses and surrendered.
Liúkě was already in Liáo,
and Wūtǎ had already escaped,
so neither was captured.
Zhàdū also surrendered to Pújiānú;
Tàizǔ released him.
Thereupon,
all the tribes resumed their peaceful lives as before.
After a long time,
Liúkě and Wūtǎ both came to surrender.
Āshū was
a man of the Xīngxiǎnshuǐ Hégēlìe tribe.
His father, Āhǎi Bójǐn, served Jǐngzǔ and Shìzǔ.
When Shìzǔ returned after defeating Wūchūn,
Āhǎi led his officials, soldiers, and people to greet him at Shuāngyí Dàluò,
presenting five dou of gold.
Shìzǔ explained to him, saying,
"Wūchūn was originally humble and lowly.
My father nurtured him and made him a tribal chief,
yet he forgot this great kindness
and bore enmity towards me,
thus creating great chaos and
bringing about his own destruction.
From now on, I and you, the people of the thirty tribes,
can live in peace and rest.
My fated time is also coming to an end.
When I die,
you all must remember me
and exert yourselves to assist my sons and brothers.
If a single thought of rebellion arises,
then destruction will befall you just like Wūchūn."
Āhǎi and the multitude knelt and wept, saying,
"If Tàishī should meet with misfortune,
upon whom will the multitude rely to live?
Please do not speak such words."
Not long after,
Shìzǔ died,
and Āhǎi also died.
Āshū succeeded him.
From his father's time, Āshū often came for various matters.
Zhāosù Huánghòu loved him dearly.
Each time he visited,
she would keep him for more than a month before sending him back.
After Āshū became Bójǐn,
he once contended with Zhàdū Bójǐn of the Túshàn tribe for seniority.
Sùzōng arbitrated the matter
and declared Āshū the senior.
Mùzōng succeeded to the *jiédù* position.
Hearing that Āshū had rebellious intentions,
he summoned Āshū and bestowed upon him saddles and horses,
deeply soothing and instructing him,
secretly observing his true intentions.
Āshū returned,
and his plotting intensified.
He then openly declared his intentions.
Mùzōng summoned him again,
but Āshū did not come.
Instead, he raised an army with Máodǔlù Bóyín and others from the same tribe.
Mùzōng personally led troops out from Mǎjǐlǐng to attack him,
while Sāgǎi went from Húlùnlǐng to plunder,
securing the Chánchūn and Xīngxiǎn routes,
and capturing Dùn'ēn City.
Mùzōng plundered Āchákuàishuǐ,
recruited more troops,
and arrived at Āshū City.
That day, between *chén* and *sì* hours (7-11 AM),
a sudden torrential rain fell,
darkening the sky.
Thunder and lightning struck Āshū's residence.
Soon after, there was a great light,
sounding like thunder,
which fell into Āshū City.
Those who understood considered this a sign of destruction and downfall.
When Āshū heard of Mùzōng's arrival,
he and his younger brother Dígùbǎo went to appeal to Liáo.
The Liáo envoys came to stop the attack.
Mùzōng had no choice
but to leave Hégě Zhě Bóyín to guard Āshū City and returned.
In the early Jīn dynasty, there were also two Hégě Zhě.
One was Sāgǎi's father,
posthumously granted the title of Hánguó Gōng.
The other was the one who guarded Āshū City,
later posthumously granted the title of Tèjìn, it is said.
Hégě Zhě had guarded Āshū City with troops for two years.
Āshū, in Liáo, dared not return,
so Máodǔlù surrendered.
Liáo envoys came again on behalf of Āshū.
When Mùzōng heard this,
he sent Wūlíndá Shílǔ to assist the army,
and also instructed Hégě Zhě to change their clothes and banners to the same color as those in Āshū City,
so that the Liáo envoys could not distinguish them.
When the Liáo envoys arrived,
he sent Púchá Tribe's Húlǔ Bóyín and Miàoxùn Bóyín with them to Hégě Zhě's army.
The army had already changed their clothes and banners,
making them indistinguishable from those in Āshū City.
The Liáo envoys indeed could not tell the difference.
Hégě Zhě cunningly said:
"We are fighting among ourselves.
What business is it of yours?
Who recognizes your Grand Preceptor?"
Then they stabbed and killed the horses ridden by Húlǔ and Miàoxùn.
The Liáo envoys were startled and terrified and fled,
and subsequently, the city was taken.
Dígùbǎo had returned earlier,
and was killed.
Āshū heard that Mùzōng had used a stratagem to repel the Liáo envoys,
captured his city,
and killed Dígùbǎo.
He appealed to Liáo again.
Liáo sent the Xī *jiédù* envoy Yǐliè to inquire about the situation,
and also ordered Mùzōng to fully compensate Āshū.
Mùzōng again sent people from Zhǔwēi and Tútáshuǐ to pretend to block the Yīnglù (Falcon Route),
and had the Biēgùdé Tribe's *jiédù* envoy tell Liáo
that without him, the Yīnglù could not be pacified.
The Liáo people did not investigate,
and believed him.
Mùzōng hunted at Túwēnshuǐ
and said to the Liáo people:
"I have pacified the Yīnglù."
The Liáo people considered this an achievement
and sent an envoy to reward him.
Mùzōng gave all the items to the people of Zhǔwēi and Tútá and no longer compensated Āshū.
The Liáo people also no longer inquired.
Āshū, in Liáo, had nowhere to go.
Two years later,
he sent his follower Dájì to the border of the Raw Nǚzhēn territories.
The people of Hélǎndiàn feared Mùzōng,
seized him and sent him away.
Āshū thus died in Liáo.
When Tàizǔ later attacked Liáo,
he enumerated Liáo's crimes to Heaven and Earth,
and always mentioned Āshū's defection to Liáo and the Liáo people's refusal to speak on his behalf
in all his correspondence with Liáo.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ (1122),
Shēmǔ and Lóushì raided and pacified the prefectures of Tiāndé, Yúnnèi, Níngbiān, and Dōngshèng,
and captured Āshū.
The soldiers asked him:
"Who are you?"
He replied:
"I am the devil who destroyed Liáo."
A commentary says: The rise of Jīn
had its origins.
Shìzǔ captured Lápēi and Pózhūkān.
He presented them to Liáo as a merit,
but then also said:
"If they are not sent back,
their tribesmen will be suspicious and afraid,
and it will lead to rebellion."
The Liáo people did not investigate
and returned all the criminals previously presented.
Jǐngzǔ stopped Hélǔ Línyá and Zhǐtónggàn.
Mùzōng stopped the Liáo envoys at Āshū City,
consistently misleading them with the Yīnglù,
but the Liáo people did not realize it.
Jǐngzǔ had a yellow horse,
which he rode as he wished.
After Jǐngzǔ's death,
Liáo nobles eagerly desired it.
Shìzǔ did not give it to them,
saying:
"The difficulties are not yet over;
the horse cannot be given to others."
He then cut off both its ears,
calling it a "bald-eared horse."
The Liáo nobles then did not take it.
When pacifying the various tribes, they borrowed from Liáo to enhance their own importance.
When they presented and then requested (the criminals) back, they used it as a trade to enhance their own importance.
They never gave a good battle horse to the Liáo people,
and the Liáo people never realized it.
Perhaps the rise and fall (of dynasties) are predetermined,
or perhaps Heaven stripped them of their spirit.
The Xī,
rose concurrently with the Qìdān.
During the Yuánwèi period, they were called Kùmò Xī.
Throughout Yǔwén Zhōu, Suí, and Táng,
they were all known for strong armies.
Later, the Qìdān defeated and drove away the Xī.
The Xī fled west to Lěngxíng.
Those who remained submitted to the Qìdān
and were called the Eastern and Western Xī.
Later, when Liáo Tàizǔ proclaimed himself emperor,
all the tribes submitted.
Tiělè was
the name of an ancient tribal group.
The Xī occupied their land,
calling it Tiělè Zhōu,
also written as Tiělí Zhōu.
The Xī had five royal clans
who intermarried with the Liáo people for generations,
and were thus affiliated with the Shùlǜ clan.
Details are in the Liáo Shǐ,
and are not recorded here.
The Xī had thirteen tribes, twenty-eight settlements, one hundred and eleven camps, and three hundred and sixty-two clans.
In the *jiǎwǔ* year (1114),
Tàizǔ defeated Yēlǜ Xièshí.
All the generals won consecutive battles.
Xī Tiělí King Huílíbǎo surrendered with his tribe.
Soon after, he fled back to Liáo.
When the Liáo ruler sent an envoy to request peace,
Tàizǔ said:
"Return to me the rebel Āshū, and the surrendered persons Huílíbǎo and Dílǐ, etc.
Other matters can be discussed later."
After a long time,
the Liáo ruler arrived at Yuānyāng Luò.
Dūtǒng Gǎo attacked him,
and he fled to Tiāndé.
Huílíbǎo and Liáo ministers enthroned Prince Qínjìn, Yēlǜ Niēlǐ, in Yānjīng.
Niēlǐ died,
and Consort Xiāo temporarily managed state affairs.
Tàizǔ entered Jūyōng Guān,
and Consort Xiāo fled from Gǔběi Kǒu.
Huílíbǎo arrived at Lúlóng Lǐng,
and then stayed there, not proceeding further.
He gathered Xī officials and commoners in Yuèlǐ Tribe,
usurped the title of emperor,
changed the reign title to Tiānfù,
appointed new officials,
and registered able-bodied Bóhǎi, Xī, and Hàn men for the army.
Tàizǔ issued an edict to Huílíbǎo, saying:
"I hear that you have coerced and enticed officials and commoners,
usurping the imperial title.
The Liáo ruler is now in the wilderness;
his great fortune will not return.
Your ancestors submitted to Liáo.
Now you come to submit,
how is it different from before?
You have a grudge with Yúdǔ,
hence your reluctance to come.
Even if Yúdǔ harbors resentment,
would I follow his lead?
If you can surrender quickly,
all your crimes will be forgiven,
and you will still be allowed to rule the six tribes,
commanding all the Xī people in the mountains,
and your officials and property will be returned.
If you remain stubborn,
I will send troops to punish you,
and you will certainly not be spared."
Huílíbǎo did not listen.
In the fifth month of the seventh year of Tiānfǔ (1123),
Huílíbǎo raided the Yān region to the south,
was defeated between Jǐng and Jì,
and his troops scattered.
Yēlǜ Àogǔzhé and his nephew Bājīn, household slave Báidǐgē, and others killed him.
His wife Āgǔ, hearing of it,
committed suicide by cutting her throat.
Formerly,
the Sùgǔbù people occupied Hégāishān.
The Xīlù Military Commissioner, Tàlǎn, summoned them, but they did not submit.
He went to attack them.
The Tiěníbù people fortified dangerous terrain and resisted,
killing almost all of them.
By this time,
all thirteen mountain strongholds occupied by the Sùgǔ, Chuòlǐ, and Tiění three tribes were pacified.
The Dálǔgǔbù Jiedushi, Yǐliè, who had previously surrendered, rebelled again.
Xī Mǎhéshang attacked Dálǔgǔ and other tribes, including the Wǔyuànsī.
All the tribes surrendered,
so Yǐliè was captured
and given a hundred strokes with a rod.
