His father and other family members who had been captured earlier were all returned to him.
Initially,
Tàizǔ defeated the Liáo army at Dálǔgǔchéng.
Nine hundred Xī camps came to surrender.
By this time,
Huílìbǎo had died,
and the Xī people successively became tributaries,
each also having their own Měng'ān Móukè to lead them.
A eulogy says: The Kùmòxī and Qìdān arose at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
flourished between the Suí and Táng dynasties,
were both strong neighboring states,
and united as ruler and subject.
Over eight hundred years,
they remained interconnected from beginning to end.
There were five Xī groups.
During the Dàdìng era,
the distinguished clans and prominent surnames included Yáolǐ Shì, Bódé Shì, Àolǐ Shì, Méizhī Shì, and Chuǎ Shì.
Collation Notes
Biography 6 Huāndū (son Móuyǎn) Yěhē (sons Ālúbǔ Gǔhé Égǔnǎi Púchá)
Huāndū was
a Wányánbù person.
His ancestor, Shílǔ,
was of the same time, same tribe, and same name as Zhāozǔ.
They got along well
and swore:
"In life, we shall dwell by the same river;
in death, we shall be buried in the same valley."
The local people called Zhāozǔ "Yǒng Shílǔ" (Brave Shílǔ),
and Shílǔ "Xián Shílǔ" (Worthy Shílǔ).
Initially,
the Wūsàzhābù
had a beautiful woman named Bàdíhuǐ.
People from Shúshùishuǐ, east of Qīnglǐng and Húntóngjiāng, plundered and took her away,
and she bore two daughters.
The elder was named Dáhuí,
the younger Zǐsài.
Zhāozǔ and Shílǔ plotted to retrieve them.
They went together to the west of the ridge,
lit fires on arrow tips and shot them.
The Shúshùishuǐ people were startled by this
and all fled to dangerous terrain.
After a long time,
seeing no one again,
they returned to their dwellings.
Zhāozǔ and Shílǔ arrived with their troops,
attacked and seized their property,
and captured the two women to bring them back.
Zhāozǔ took one of them,
and Xián Shílǔ took the other,
both as concubines.
At this time,
the various tribes were unwilling to follow regulations.
Zhāozǔ displayed his military might at Qīnglǐng and Báishān,
entering the lands of Sūbīn and Yēlǎn.
Xián Shílǔ assisted him.
Later, they parted ways.
By the time of Jǐngzǔ,
Shílǔ's son, HéSūn, brought his entire tribe to submit,
settling south of Húkǎishān at the source of Ānchūhǔshuǐ.
Húkǎishān
is what is called the land of Hélíng.
Huāndū was
Hésūn's son.
At the beginning of Shìzǔ's reign,
he inherited the title of Jiedushi.
However, Báhēi, considering his senior lineage,
harbored different intentions
and could not be controlled.
The various tribes refused to accept restrictions
and successively caused trouble.
Huāndū joined in deliberations
and went out to confront battles,
never leaving his side.
Bēinǎi, a person of the Wòlèbù,
had lived with his brothers north of Ānchūhǔshuǐ since Jǐngzǔ's time.
When Wūchūn caused trouble,
Bēinǎi intended to join Wūchūn,
secretly enticing the residents of Wòlúgànchūshuǐ to ally with him,
wishing to first eliminate Huāndū.
It happened that Bēinǎi's house caught fire.
He secretly instructed his servant Bùgēshù
to falsely claim that Huāndū and Hútǔ were the two who started the fire.
He sent Zhùdū to tell Shìzǔ:
"Bùgēshù came to report, 'The fire the other day
was set by Huāndū and others.'
If you do not abandon old friendships,
then seize those who started the fire and bring them."
Shìzǔ was suspicious.
Shílú Wòlè Bójǐn said:
"Bēinǎi is a brother.
How can he, for the sake of one or two people,
create enmity with a brother?
He brought it upon himself,
and whom will he blame?
It is better to give in to him."
Huāndū, in armor and holding a halberd, rose and said:
"He is a rebellious person.
If he were to demand the Grand Preceptor's brothers,
would you also give them to him?
Now he demands us.
We absolutely cannot go.
If we must fight,
we will do our utmost to die."
Mùzōng said:
"Brave Huāndū!
In my opinion,
this is exactly how it is."
He gifted Huāndū a horse,
saying:
"Ride this into battle."
Everyone praised this.
Shìzǔ then went to see Bēinǎi,
and spoke to him across Biēlāshuǐ, saying:
"Since Bùgēshù reported that Huāndū and others set the fire,
we will carefully adhere to the agreement.
You should first send Bùgēshù here."
When Bùgēshù arrived,
Shìzǔ killed him in front of his horse,
making Bēinǎi witness it.
Afterwards, it was heard
that the one who set the fire was Bēinǎi's household member, Āchūhúshān.
Bēinǎi wanted to create this conflict,
and thus falsely accused Huāndū.
Lāpēi and MáChǎn met Shìzǔ at Yěquèshuǐ.
It was already dusk,
and Shìzǔ had only fifty or sixty cavalry with him.
Huāndū charged into the enemy formation and fought fiercely,
entering and exiting several times,
only stopping when Shìzǔ was wounded.
Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn occupied Huólàhúnshuǐ.
Shìzǔ had already accepted their surrender,
so he withdrew his troops.
At this, Sāolà Bójǐn and the wealthy Tàlǎn did not assist the army,
and Sāolà and Tàlǎn had previously allied with Lāpēi and MáChǎn.
Shìzǔ intended to take advantage of the army's return to destroy them,
and rode forward rapidly.
Tàlǎn was
the younger brother of Zhēnhuì Empress.
Huāndū dismounted, grasped the reins, and admonished:
"Do you not remember your beloved younger brother Púyángwēn and your sister-in-law?"
Shìzǔ was moved by his words
and stopped.
Púyángwēn,
in Chinese, means 'youngest brother'.
Among Shìzǔ's younger brothers, Mùzōng was the youngest,
hence the term.
Mùzōng appreciated Huāndū's words,
and later married Tàlǎn's daughter, Gēluóshěn, to his son, Gǔshén.
Tàizǔ pursued MáChǎn.
Huāndū shot him in the head,
and thus captured him.
The Liáo people appointed Mùzōng, Tàizǔ, Cíbúshī, and Huāndū all as Xiángwěn.
Wòshàn and Wòtuō came to submit with soldiers from Gūlǐdiàn,
and Xiépō Bójǐn was sent to pacify them.
From Púchábù, Gùshí and Báshí, etc.,
lured their people into the city,
entrapping over three hundred people.
Huāndū was made Dūtǒng (Commander),
and went to investigate the situation of Xiépō's lost army,
disbanding all the troops led by Xiépō, thoroughly defeating Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn at Xiédūi,
and capturing Gùshí and Báshí.
Initially,
Yēhuǐshuǐ Nàhē-bù Sābā's younger brother, named Āzhù'ā,
contended with someone for a tribal official position.
He did not receive justice,
and came to pledge allegiance to Mùzōng.
Āzhù'ā's nephews were named Sānbīn and Sādá.
Cíbùshī broke the city of Wūchūn Wōmóuhǎn,
capturing Sānbīn and Sādá,
and also capturing their mother,
taking her as his secondary wife,
and raising her two sons.
Sādá warned Āzhù'ā that he would surely cause trouble,
but Āzhù'ā did not believe him and killed him.
As Sādá faced execution, he sighed and said:
"Later, you will surely know."
At this point,
Āzhù'ā indeed caused trouble.
Because Mùzōng had gone out hunting in the morning,
Āzhù'ā gathered seven or eight men, armed them, and entered the residence,
seizing and occupying the bedroom gate,
and abducting Empress Zhēnhuì and her household.
Huāndū entered and saw Āzhù'ā, saying:
"What are you plotting?
How can the empress and her family be sufficient hostages?
You are only causing them alarm and fear.
You certainly know me;
why not take me as a hostage instead?"
He repeated this several times,
and Āzhù'ā agreed,
so Empress Zhēnhuì was released,
and Huāndū was held hostage.
Sāgǎi and Cíbùshī sent someone to report the emergency at the hunting ground.
Mùzōng was also alarmed,
and stopped hunting.
On the way, he met the messenger,
arriving at noon.
Āzhù'ā said to Mùzōng:
"You must arrange for the Xi-àn Nǚzhí renowned officials to cooperate,
and send my brothers and relatives through the Xiánzhōu road into the Liáo state.
Do not begrudge me gold, horses, and treasures.
Huāndū must also accompany me to the Liáo border,
and then return."
He then demanded Mùzōng to make an oath,
and Mùzōng agreed to all of it.
Thereupon, Huāndū, Ālǔtàiwān, Ālǔbùtàiwān, and seven others were seized,
their clothes tied together,
and they journeyed with Āzhù'ā.
Upon reaching the Liáo border,
Huāndū was released.
Huāndū arrived at Jìzhōu,
which was in fact Huánglóng Fǔ,
and sent someone on an urgent dispatch to intercept Āzhù'ā's party,
allowing only his close relatives to leave.
He then killed Sānbīn and his mother,
reported everything to Liáo,
and requested Āzhù'ā's return.
The Liáo people exiled him to Gédǒng City.
Later,
Āzhù'ā yearned for his homeland,
fled back,
and took refuge with the Xi-àn Nǚzhí.
He then caused disorder in the household of their official.
He was captured,
but did not submit,
and was then killed.
At the beginning of Mùzōng's ascension to the throne,
the sons of his uncles, Xíliè and Xiébó, and his elder brothers expressed dissenting opinions,
saying:
"The positions of ruler and minister
are all decided by those fellows.
What is to be done?"
Huāndū said:
"If you all quarrel,
then I certainly will not remain silent."
When the crowd heard this, they immediately quieted down,
and from then on, no one expressed dissenting opinions again.
Huāndū served four rulers,
for forty years,
entering and leaving the court. During campaigns, he would be the first to fight when encountering an enemy,
and his counsel was often used in major court deliberations.
Shìzǔ once said:
"With Huāndū,
what task cannot be accomplished?"
During Sùzōng's time,
he was given more responsibility than any other close official.
When Mùzōng succeeded to the throne,
all matters concerning Liáo were entrusted solely to him.
Kāngzōng, regarding him as an old retainer of his father and uncles,
especially showed him respect,
and he provided much assistance.
In the second month of the eleventh year of Kāngzōng's reign, the guǐsì year
he fell ill,
and sought refuge from his illness at Mǐlǐměi River,
where he passed away
at the age of sixty-three.
When his coffin was returned,
Kāngzōng personally met it on the road,
escorted it to his home,
and personally supervised the funeral arrangements.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì
he was posthumously granted the titles of Yítóng Sānsī and Dàiguógōng.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng
he was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn.
His sons were Gǔshén and Móuyǎn.
Gǔshén has a separate biography.
Móuyǎn,
during the difficulty with Āzhù'ā,
accompanied Huāndū to serve as a hostage.
Later, he and Zōngjùn both served Tàizǔ.
Zōngjùn sat above Móuyǎn,
and the Emperor was angry,
ordering him to sit below Móuyǎn.
Bóyǐn Lǎobólùn, Báhé Rúxiá, and Básù three men contended for the position of Qiānhù.
The Emperor said:
"Can you all serve the state as diligently as Huāndū and his son?"
Thereupon, he appointed Móuyǎn as Qiānhù,
and the three men were all subordinate to him.
Such was the favor shown to him.
He died in the twelfth month of the fifth year of Tiānfǔ
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì
Yěhē's lineage was from Jǐngzǔ.
He resided in the Wányán tribe of Shényǐn River
and was the bóyǐn of his tribe.
Together with Bǎlǐ Bóyǐn of the same tribe,
Húdūhuà Bóyǐn and Sīdū Bóyǐn of the Púchá tribe of Wòmǐn River,
Āntuán Bóyǐn of the Wányán tribe of Tàishéntèbǎo River,
Huólǐgài Bóyǐn of the Wēndíhén tribe of Tǒngmén River,
they all came to pledge allegiance.
From then on,
the state of Jīn grew stronger.
Sùzōng had already suffered two defeats in repelling Huán●.
Shìzǔ ordered Huāndū and Yěhē
to assist him with the Móukè troops of their respective tribes.
Yěhē and Huāndū were always by Shìzǔ's side.
When at court, they participated in deliberations;
when in the field, they oversaw the battle lines,
never absent from the scene.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì
he was posthumously granted Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng
he was posthumously granted Tèjìn,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngjì.
Along with Dàiguógōng Huāndū, Tèjìn Hégě, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Pénnà, and Yítóng Sānsī Bádá,
he was enshrined in Shìzǔ's ancestral temple.
Yěhē's sons were Ālǔbǔ, Gǔ●, Égǔnǎi, and Sàndá.
Sàndá's son was Púchá.
Ālǔbǔ was
Yěhē's son.
He was tall and robust, with much wisdom and strategy,
and brave in battle.
Before reaching adulthood, he joined the army,
conquering Xiánzhōu and Dōngjīng.
When the Liáo people came to take Hǎizhōu,
he followed Bóyǐn Máji to reinforce it.
On the way, they encountered a strong enemy,
fought fiercely,
and beheaded a thousand.
He followed Wòlǔgǔ to attack Háozhōu and Yìzhōu,
defeating seven hundred enemies with just over ten cavalry,
and then advanced to attack the Liáo ruler.
Ālǔbǔ patrolled the northern territory,
receiving the surrender of twenty-four camps
and several thousand households.
At that time, Xījīng had already been conquered,
but Shémǔ was attacking Yìzhōu and had not yet captured it.
He retreated to a camp about ten li north of the city.
At night, he sent Ālǔbǔ leading four hundred soldiers to scout the enemy.
Indeed, three thousand enemy soldiers came out of the city to attack.
Ālǔbǔ met them on the road,
beheaded over a hundred,
and captured sixty horses.
Later, three thousand Liáo soldiers emerged from the border of Mǎyì.
He attacked them with a thousand soldiers,
and cut down their general in battle.
At the beginning of Tiānhuì,
Sòngwáng Zōngwàng was campaigning against Zhāng Jué in Píngzhōu.
Hearing that over ten thousand soldiers from Yìzhōu were coming to reinforce,
he sent Ālǔbǔ and Ālǐdài to intercept them,
beheading and capturing several thousand before returning.
He then again followed his elder brother Yúhuá,
leading three thousand soldiers to attack Gānzhōu.
Yúhuá fell ill and died on the way,
so Ālǔbǔ took command of his troops.
Upon reaching Gānzhōu,
he secured the surrender of its army and thirty camps,
captured forty seals,
and, with Púkuǐ, conquered Yìzhōu.
Zōngwàng 伐 Sòng,

奮戰,

Ālǔbǔ 適當其中,

從 Zōngbì 襲 Kāngwáng,
既渡 Huái,
Ālǔbǔ 以兵四千留 Hézhōu,

Lúzhōu 叛,

明日復破敵二萬於 Shènxiàn,
斬首五百.
Zhāng Yǒnghé 步騎數萬來戰,
Ālǔbǔ 兵止二千,
敵圍之,
Ālǔbǔ 潰圍力戰,
竟敗之,
追殺四十里,
獲馬三百而還.
再攻 Lúzhōu,
與 Dígǔbù 敗敵萬衆於 Tuògāo,
至 Lúzhōu,
騎兵五百出戰,
敗之,
斬其二校.
師遇.
Zōngbì 趨 Shǎnxī,
道聞 Dàmíng 復叛,
遣 Ālǔbǔ 經略之,
獨與譯者至城下,
招之,
Dàmíng 果降.
翌日,
下令民間兵器,
悉上送官,
於是吏民按堵如故.
為 Dàmíng Kāidé Lù Dūtǒng.
Qíguó 建,
Ālǔbǔ 屯兵於 Biànchéng 外.
Tiānhuì shíwǔ nián,
詔廢 Qíguó,
已執 Liú Lín,
Ālǔbǔ 先入 Biànjīng 備變.
明年,
除 Guīdé Yǐn.
割 Hénán 地與 Sòng,

Zōngbì 復 Hénán,
Ālǔbǔ 先濟河,
撫定諸郡,

Sòng 兵來取 Hénán 地,
Zōngbì 召 Ālǔbǔ,
與 Xǔzhōu Hán Cháng, Yǐngzhōu Dàdàn, Chénzhōu Chìzhǎn Huī,

Ālǔbǔ 以敵在近,
獨不赴.
而 Sòng 將 Yuè Fēi, Liú Guāngshì 等,

旁郡皆響應.
其兵犯 Guīdé 者,
Ālǔbǔ 連擊敗之,
復取 Bó, Sù 等州,
Hénán 平,
Ālǔbǔ 功最.
Huángtǒng wǔ nián,
為 Xíngtái Cānzhī Zhèngshì,

PóSù Lù Tǒngjūn,

其在 Biàn 時,
嘗取官舍材木,

至是事覺,
法當

Hǎilíng 嘗在軍中,
惡 Ālǔbǔ,
詔曰:

更有過於此者.
況官至一品,
足以酬之.
國家立法,
貴賤一也,
豈以親貴而有異也."
遂論死.
年五十五.
Ālǔbǔ 以將家子從征伐,
屢立功,
歷官有惠愛,
得民心.
及死,
人皆惜之.
Dàdìng sān nián,
贈 Yítóng Sānsī,
詔以其子為 Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn,
襲 Měng'ān 及親管 Móukè,
賜銀五百兩, 重綵二十端, 絹三百匹.
Gǔdàn,
Yěhē zi,
善騎射,
有材幹.
從討 Huánhé, Sàndá, Wūchūn, Wōmóuhǎn, Liú Kězhī 之叛,
皆有功.
從 Tàizǔ 伐 Liáo,
Gǔdàn 從軍戰 Níngjiāngzhōu Chūhédiàn,
破 Liáozhǔ 親軍,
皆以力戰受賞,
襲其父謀克.
領 Qínwáng Zōnghàn 千戶,
攻下 Zhōng, Xī liǎng jīng.
Zōnghàn 伐 Sòng,
圍 Tàiyuán 未下,
Zōnghàn 還 Xījīng,
Gǔdàn 以右翼軍佐 Yínshùkě 守 Tàiyuán.
是時 Fénzhōu, Tuánbǎi, Yúcì, Lán, Xiàn, Lù 皆有兵來援,
Gǔdàn 凡四戰,
皆破之.
大軍圍 Biàn,
Gǔdàn 引萬戶軍,

Xiàn, Lù 等州復叛,

幷收撫 Bǎodé, Huǒshān 而還.
Hǎilíng crossed the Huái River,
and dispatched envoys to eliminate the imperial clan.
Shuǎng was worried and fearful, not knowing what to do.
Coincidentally, Shìzōng ascended the throne in Dōngjīng.
Zhāng of the imperial clan recommended Shuǎng's younger brother Āsuǒ to act as the Supervisor of Zhōngdū,
and sent someone to report to Shuǎng.
Shuǎng abandoned his wife and children and came to join him,
along with his younger brother Kěxǐ, the Governor of Xīnzhōu,
both arriving in Zhōngdū.
They went east to welcome the imperial carriage,
and met Shìzōng at Liángyúwù.
Shìzōng was greatly pleased,
and immediately appointed him Grand Commander of the Palace Front Horse and Foot Army.
He was enfeoffed as King Wēn,
and later made Secretary-General.
When his mother passed away,
he was soon recalled to office,
promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and advanced to King Shòu.
Shortly thereafter,
Shìzōng's fifth daughter, Princess Shǔguó, was married to Tángguō Dǐng.
At the banquet in Shénlóng Diàn,
Shìzōng said to Shuǎng:
"When We and you, Our brother,
were in the Zhènglóng era,
We constantly feared for Our lives day and night.
How could We have imagined that today, thanks to the blessings of you and your brothers,
We could enjoy peace and happiness?"
Shuǎng wept,
and bowed his head in thanks.
Not long after,
he was appointed Grand Supervisor of the Imperial Clan Affairs,
with his post as Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince remaining as before.
When Shuǎng fell ill,
an edict was issued appointing his son, Sīliè, who held the Fúbǎo Zhǐhòu position, as Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhōngshùn Commandery.
When Shuǎng came to express his gratitude,
the Emperor said:
"Because of your illness, We have promoted your son,
hoping that you will recover due to this joy.
Sīliè is young,
and not yet familiar with government affairs.
You should instruct him in proper conduct,
so that if he performs well,
he will receive further promotions."
Shuǎng's illness improved slightly.
When he was about to accompany the Emperor to Liángxíng,
he was granted ten million coins,
advanced to King Yīng,
and transferred to Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince.
He also inherited the Měng'ān position in perpetuity,
was advanced to King Róng,
and then made Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince.
When Xiǎnzōng's eldest daughter, Princess Yèguó, was married to Wūgǔlún Yì,
a banquet was held in Qìnghé Diàn.
Shuǎng sat facing west,
catching the evening sun,
and his face turned red as if he were drunk.
The Emperor asked:
"Are you drunk, My lord?"
He replied:
"Not yet,
Your servant's face is catching the sunlight;
it is not red from wine."
The Emperor was pleased,
and turned to his ministers, saying:
"This brother of Mine, when he speaks,
it is always the truth;
he has been like this since childhood."
He then said to Xiǎnzōng and his brothers:
"You should take him as an example."
As Shuǎng's expenses were lacking,
he was specially granted ten thousand strings of cash.
In the twenty-third year,
Shuǎng's illness lingered without recovery.
An imperial decree was issued to the officials, saying:
"When King Róng completes a hundred days of illness,
he shall be given a princely stipend."
When he eventually passed away,
the Emperor grieved deeply,
suspended court,
sent officials to offer sacrifices,
and bestowed a thousand taels of silver, forty rolls of embroidered silk, and four hundred bolts of plain silk.
He was interred in the imperial mausoleum,
with princes and officials attending the funeral.
On another day,
the Emperor said to his ministers:
"I regret that I was unable to personally attend King Róng's funeral."
Such was the depth of his fraternal affection.
Kěxǐ,
as a son of the imperial clan,
had successively held the office of Military Commissioner of the Tángguō tribe,
and was demoted to Governor of Xīnzhōu.
When Hǎilíng sent envoys to kill him,
Kěxǐ heard that Shìzōng had ascended the throne,
immediately abandoned his prefecture and came to submit,
meeting with his elder brother Ālín, the Governor of Guīhuàzhōu, in Zhōngdū.
At this time,
his younger brother Āsuǒ was acting as Supervisor of Zhōngdū.
Kěxǐ said to Ālín:
"Āsuǒ is foolish and slow-witted,
I fear he cannot manage the administration.
I wish to stay for a while to assist him."
Ālín then departed.
Kěxǐ remained in Zhōngdū.
When he heard that Shìzōng had departed Dōngjīng,
he went to welcome and meet him at Máji Pù.
He was appointed Minister of War,
and, wearing the golden plaque,
led troops to Nánjīng.
Upon reaching Zhōngdū,
he heard that Nánjīng had already been secured,
and so he stopped.
Kěxǐ possessed exceptional martial prowess,
but was violent and fond of disorder.
Considering himself a grandson of Tàizǔ,
he harbored somewhat ambitious designs.
When Shìzōng first arrived in Zhōngdū,
things were chaotic and numerous,
and the accompanying armies had not yet been rewarded,
leading to some complaints.
Zhāowǔ Grand General Wòlún,
at the end of Zhènglóng,
had been commanded to wear a golden plaque,
take four hundred soldiers from Hénán,
and oversee Wányán Gòuyīng's army at Guīhuà,
then proceed to Zhāngdé.
It happened that Dújí Héshang arrived with the amnesty decree of Dàdìng.
Héshang sent someone to summon him,
but Wòlún refused to listen,
and led his troops to meet him.
Héshang also arrayed his Púliǎn soldiers,
awaiting him.
All of Wòlún's soldiers refused to fight,
and so he requested to surrender.
Héshang invited him into Xiāngzhōu,
collected his armor and weapons,
and offered wine to entertain him.
Wòlún feigned an abdominal illness,
and refused to drink.
By nightfall,
lamps had been lit.
He repeatedly went out,
secretly plotting with his confidants
to seize Héshang.
When he began to prepare bows and arrows,
Héshang perceived it,
but feigned ignorance,
and ordered his attendants to stay close and watch him.
Wòlún was unable to act.
When the Emperor arrived near the suburbs of Zhōngdū,
Wòlún went to pay his respects,
and the Emperor also consoled him.
Wòlún was secretly dissatisfied,
having no intention of surrendering initially.
And then there was Wòlǐwō, the Clerk of the Hénán Commander-in-Chief's Office,
a cunning and dangerous man,
fond of plotting.
When Wòlún took soldiers from Mǎn'é Lǐyě, the Hénán Commander-in-Chief,
Wòlǐwō came with him,
and both felt uneasy.
Lǐ Wéizhōng, Co-Administrator of Yán'ān,
had been involved in the assassination of Xīzōng,
and engineered the killing of Prince Hán Hēng.
Shìzōng had alienated him.
Zhāng, Co-Administrator of Zhōngdū,
had initially taken on his own duties,
and was then formally appointed to them.
Wányán Bùhuī was a Deputy Commander,
but was dismissed from office due to a crime,
and resided in the capital.
Thereupon, Kěxǐ, Wòlún, Lǐ Wéizhōng, Wòlǐwō, Zhāng, and Bùhuī plotted,
intending to incite rebellion among the resentful accompanying soldiers.
Wòlún said:
"The Overseer of the Army Měng'ān Wòkūlà
will certainly not defy me."
Wéizhōng said:
"Wéizhōng was once Commander-in-Chief of the Shényì Army.
I still have two silver plaques,
which can be used to falsely issue awards to soldiers from the imperial treasury.
The Wanhu Gāo Sōng is an old acquaintance of mine,
and will surely listen to me."
The group said:
"If we can gain control of this army,
the uprising will be easy."
Wòlún went to persuade Wòkūlà,
and Wòkūlà followed him.
Wéizhōng went to persuade Gāo Sōng,
but Gāo Sōng refused to listen.
His account is in the biography of Sōng.
In the first month of the second year of Dàdìng, on the day of Jiǎxū,
the Emperor visited the imperial tombs.
Kěxǐ feigned illness midway and returned home.
On the night of Yǐhài,
he summoned Wòlún, Wéizhōng, Wòlǐwù, Zhāng, and Bùhuī to his house for a meeting.
Wòkūlà arrived with troops.
Zhāng said,
"If we do not get the army of Gāosōng now,
the affair cannot be accomplished."
Kěxǐ, Zhāng, and Bùhuī then captured Wòlún, Wéizhōng, Wòlǐwù, and Wòkūlà,
and went to the authorities to surrender themselves.
After they were imprisoned by imperial decree,
Kěxǐ initially refused to confess his original plan.
Only after being confronted face-to-face with Wòlún
did he fully confess.
The Emperor, remembering that his brothers were young
and that only a few grandchildren of Tàizǔ remained,
felt a pang of sorrow.
He decreed that the crime be limited to Kěxǐ alone,
and that his brothers, sons, and grandsons should not be implicated.
Consequently, Wòlún, Wéizhōng, Wòlǐwù, Wòkūlà, and others were executed.
The Móukè officers and soldiers under Wòkūlà were all pardoned.
Zhāng was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Zhānghuà Commandery,
and Bùhuī was appointed Fángyùshǐ of Jùn Prefecture.
On the day of Xīnsì,
an imperial edict was issued to the whole empire.
On that day,
the Wànhù who escorted the Emperor were granted one hundred liǎng of silver,
Měng'ān fifty liǎng,
Móukè ten bolts of silk,
armored soldiers five bolts of silk and six guàn of cash,
and those below Ālǐxǐ were granted varying amounts.
Āsuǒ
was the youngest son of Zōngqiáng.
He was tall and strong.
In the second year of Tiāndé,
as a member of the imperial clan,
he was appointed Fèngguó Shàngjiāngjūn.
He was successively promoted to Jīnwúwèi Shàngjiāngjūn,
residing in Zhōngdū.
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
Púchá Shālízǐ, a Zuǒwèijiāngjūn, was appointed Tóngzhī Zhōngdū Liúshǒushì
and wore a gold tablet,
guarding the keys and seals.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne in Dōngjīng,
Āsuǒ and Zhāng, leading the city-guarding military officers such as Wūlíndá Shíjiānú,
entered the Liúshǒufǔ,
and killed Shālízǐ and Fǔpàn Mòniǎn Sālǐhè.
The crowd appointed Āsuǒ to act as Liúshǒushì,
and Zhāng appointed himself Tóngzhī Liúshǒushì.
They immediately dispatched Móukè Shíjiānú, Wūlíndá Yuàn, Púchá Púchá, and Lǐ Tiānjí's son Pán, who was Shàoyǐn of Dàxīng,
to present a memorial to Dōngjīng.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi Commandery
and was gifted a famous hawk.
An imperial edict stated:
"You are still young;
you should be self-restrained and cautious,
and dedicate your attention to governmental affairs."
He was transferred to Wǔdìng Commandery,
and resigned from office due to mourning for his mother.
He was reinstated as Jìedùshǐ of Xīngpíng Commandery
and was granted official robes and a horse.
He was promoted to Guǎngníng Yǐn.
For embezzlement of over fourteen thousand guàn,
an edict decreed he be beaten with eighty strokes of the rod,
demoted by two ranks,
and relieved of his duties.
He was granted an audience in the Chángwǔ Diàn.
The Emperor said,
"I believed you had talent and ability,
and so entrusted you with governing the people.
Now, by law, you deserve death,
but because of our kinship,
I have leniently pardoned you.
You must reflect and be fearful from now on,
and not let ill reports reach my ears again."
He was transferred to Píngliáng and Jìnán Yǐn.
He died in office
at the age of thirty-seven.
The Emperor ordered the authorities to offer sacrifices
and bestowed a funeral gift of one thousand liǎng of silver, forty bolts of rich colored silk, and four hundred bolts of plain silk.
Zōngmǐn's
original name was Ālǔbǔ.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn,
he was enfeoffed as Xíng Wáng.
In the third year of Huángtǒng,
he served as Dōngjīng Liúshǒu,
was appointed Zuǒ Fùyuánshuài,
and concurrently Administrator of Huìníng.
He was further promoted to Dūyuánshuài
and concurrently Pàn Dàzōngzhèngshì.
He was again promoted to Tàibǎo,
in charge of the three ministries,
and concurrently Zuǒ Fùyuánshuài,
in charge of the Xíngtái Shàngshūshěng,
and enfeoffed as Cáoguó Wáng.
Hǎilíng plotted regicide and usurpation,
and fearing Zōngmǐn's seniority and bravery,
wished to frame him to eliminate him.
At that time, Xīzōng frequently killed high-ranking officials.
Zōngmǐn worried about this
and said to Hǎilíng,
"The Emperor enjoys cruelty and killing,
but the affairs of the state are grave; what should be done?"
When Zōngmǐn spoke,
there happened to be no one else around.
Hǎilíng intended to use this as a pretext to frame him,
but realizing he had no witness, he could not act,
and so stopped.
When Xīzōng was murdered,
he sent Gě Wáng to summon Zōngmǐn.
Gě Wáng
was Shìzōng's initial enfeoffment.
Zōngmǐn heard Hǎilíng's summons
and was suspicious and afraid, not daring to go.
Gě Wáng said,
"Uncle, if you do not go now,
how will you face him tomorrow?"
Zōngmǐn entered the palace.
Hǎilíng wanted to kill him
but was still hesitant,
so he asked his attendants.
Wūdài said,
"He is the son of Tàizǔ.
If you do not kill him,
the populace will surely have differing opinions.
It is better to eliminate him."
Then he sent Púsàn Hūtǔ to kill him.
Hūtǔ struck Zōngmǐn with a blade.
Zōngmǐn ran left and right to avoid the blows.
His skin, hair, blood, and flesh
were scattered everywhere.
Gě Wáng saw Zōngmǐn being killed
and asked the crowd,
"What crime did the King commit to die?"
Wūdài said,
"The great affair sanctioned by Heaven
has already been accomplished;
this is but a louse or flea,
what is there to say about it?"
In the third year of Tiāndé,
Hǎilíng posthumously enfeoffed Zōngmǐn as Tàishī
and advanced his noble rank.
His consort, Púchá Shì,
had her noble title advanced.
His son Sāhéliǎn was enfeoffed as Shūguógōng,
given the name Bāo,
and later advanced to King;
Ālǐhǎn was enfeoffed as Mìguógōng.
In the sixth year of Zhènglóng,
the Qìdān Sābā rebelled.
Hǎilíng sent envoys to kill various imperial clan members,
and Ālǐhǎn was subsequently killed.
During the Dàdìng era,
an edict restored their official positions and noble ranks.
Zuò Wáng Yuán
was the son of Jǐngxuan Huángdì Zōngjùn.
His original name was Chángshèng,
and he served as Běijīng Liúshǒu.
His younger brother Chálà was Jìedùshǐ of Ānwǔ Commandery.
On the day of Wùwǔ in the fourth month of the seventh year of Huángtǒng,
Púchá Āhǔtè's son, who was Zuǒfù Diǎnjiǎn, married a princess,
presented gifts,
and was granted a banquet in the Biàndiàn.
Xīzōng, being drunk,
poured wine and offered it to Yuán.
Yuán could not drink.
The Emperor grew angry,
brandished a sword and pressured him.
Yuán fled.
He ordered Zuǒchéng Zōngxiàn to summon Yuán.
Zōngxiàn and Yuán both left,
and the Emperor became even more furious.
At this time, Hùbù Shàngshū Zōnglǐ was at his side.
He made him kneel
and personally killed him.
Hǎilíng and Tángkuò Biàn plotted to depose and enthrone.
Hǎilíng said,
"If we undertake this great affair,
who should be established as ruler?"
Hǎilíng's intention was that he, being the grandson of Tàizǔ's eldest son,
should be established.
However, Biàn and Bǐngdé's initial intention was not Hǎilíng.
Chángshèng was Xīzōng's younger brother.
Biàn replied,
"Is there not Zuò Wáng Chángshèng?"
Hǎilíng then asked about the next in line.
Biàn said,
"Dèng Wáng's son, Āléng."
Hǎilíng said,
"Āléng's lineage is too distant."
From this, Hǎilíng concluded that Zuò Wáng had popular support,
and if he were not removed, Hǎilíng would not be able to ascend the throne.
Therefore, he was secretly jealous of Chángshèng and Āléng.
At that time,
Āléng was serving as Fèngguó Shàngjiāngjūn.
Sūn Jìn (孫進), a soldier from Hénán (河南), proclaimed himself
"Imperial Brother Inspecting Great King" (皇弟按察大王).
Xīzōng (熙宗) suspected that
the words "Imperial Brother" (皇弟)
might refer to Chángshèng (常勝).
He dispatched Tèsī (特思) to interrogate him.
There was no evidence.
Tèsī (特思) had previously suspected Hǎilíng (海陵) and Tángkuò Biàn (唐括辯) of frequently conferring in secret,
and reported this to Empress Dàohòu (悼后).
Hǎilíng (海陵) knew that Xīzōng (熙宗) was suspicious of Chángshèng (常勝),
and could therefore eliminate him.
He said to Xīzōng (熙宗):
"Sūn Jìn's (孫進) rebellion has a root cause.
He did not call himself by another's name,
but rather called himself 'Imperial Brother Great King'.
Your Majesty's brothers are only Chángshèng (常勝) and Zhālà (查剌).
Tèsī's (特思) interrogation was not truthful,
and so he released him."
Xīzōng (熙宗) believed this to be true,
and sent Tángkuò Biàn (唐括辯) and Xiāo Yì (蕭肄) to question Tèsī (特思).
Tèsī (特思) falsely confessed,
thus implicating Chángshèng (常勝).
Thereupon,
Chángshèng (常勝) and his brother Zhālà (查剌) were killed,
and Tèsī (特思) was also killed.
Hǎilíng (海陵) took advantage of this to also ostracize Āléng (阿楞) and have him killed.
Āléng's (阿楞) brother, Tàléng (撻楞),
Xīzōng (熙宗) originally had no intention of killing,
but Hǎilíng (海陵) said:
"Since his elder brother has already been executed,
how can his younger brother alone be allowed to live?"
And so he was also killed.
Xīzōng (熙宗) considered Hǎilíng (海陵) loyal,
and trusted him even more,
unaware of his deception.
When Hǎilíng (海陵) usurped the throne,
he posthumously granted official titles and ranks to Chángshèng (常勝), Zhālà (查剌), and Āléng (阿楞),
and personally attended their burial places to offer sacrifices.
In the sixth month, on the *dīngsì* (丁巳) day, of the thirteenth year of Dàdìng (大定)
Shìzōng (世宗) summoned the crown prince and various princes,
to dine at Qīnghuī Diàn (清輝殿),
and said:
"Some say Hǎilíng (海陵) was very capable;
how is this so?
Hǎilíng (海陵) was cunning and deceitful,
brutally killing people,
emptying two-thirds of the empire.
Among Tàizǔ's (太祖) grandsons,
only Yuán (元), the Prince of Zuò (胙王), was truly virtuous by nature."
Yuán's (元) son, Yù (育),
originally named Hézhù (合住),
in the twenty-seventh year of Dàdìng (大定)
was promoted from deputy supervisor of Nánjīng (南京) to Assistant Grand Minister of the Imperial Clan Court (Dà Zōngzhèng Chéng 大宗正丞),
concurrently serving as Deputy Commissioner for Promoting Agriculture (Quánnóng Fùshǐ 勸農副使).
The emperor asked his prime ministers:
"What kind of person is Hézhù (合住)?"
The Grand Councilor (Píngzhāng Zhèngshì 平章政事) Xiāng (襄) and Counselor-in-chief (Cānzhèng 參政) Zōnghào (宗浩) replied:
"He is incorruptible, honest, and capable in governance."
The emperor said:
"His father was also like that."
He further said:
"Púyáng (蒲陽) Prince of Zuò (胙王) Wēn Yuán (溫元),
outwardly appeared foolish and slow-witted,
but when faced with matters, he was exceptionally discerning and agile.
Among my brothers,
I am especially close and intimate with Yuán (元)."
The eulogy says:
"Tàizǔ (太祖) personally donned armor,
to establish the state,
leaving no strategy untried,
and his sons' courage, strategies, talents, and insights
were sufficient to fulfill their father's ambitions.
The succession passed to Tàizōng (太宗),
and his grandsons enjoyed the fruits of their accomplishments."
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 8 Sākǎigǎi (撒改) Zōngxiàn (宗憲) (original name Ālán 阿懶) Xíbùshī (習不失) Zōnghēng (宗亨) (original name Tàbùyě 撻不也)
Zōngxián (宗賢) (original name Sàilǐ 賽里) Shítǔmén (石土門) Zhōng (忠) (original name Dígǔnǎi 迪古乃) Xíshì (習室) Sījìng (思敬) (original name Sākǎigǎi 撒改)
Sākǎigǎi (撒改) was
a grandson of Jǐngzǔ (景祖),
the eldest son of Hégě (劾者), Duke of Hánguó (韓國公),
and a nephew of Shìzǔ (世祖).
Hégě (劾者) was the eldest among his siblings.
When Jǐngzǔ (景祖) was planning to unify the various tribes,
he admired Shìzǔ's (世祖) courage, bravery, and talent.
When his sons grew up,
according to tribal custom, they should have resided in separate palaces,
but he ordered Hégě (劾者) and Shìzǔ (世祖) to live in the same residence.
Hégě (劾者) specialized in managing household affairs,
while Shìzǔ (世祖) handled external matters.
Shìzǔ (世祖) inherited the position of Jìdùshǐ (節度使),
bypassing Hégě (劾者)'s grandson, and passed it to Sùzōng (肅宗) and Mùzōng (穆宗);
all this was Jǐngzǔ's (景祖) will.
When Mùzōng (穆宗) first succeeded to the throne,
mindful that Hégě (劾者), the eldest brother, had not been able to ascend,
he appointed Sākǎigǎi (撒改) as Guóxiàng (國相, Chancellor).
Mùzōng (穆宗) followed in the footsteps of his father and elder brothers,
eliminating those who were rebellious and disobedient to him.
He sent Sākǎigǎi (撒改) to take the Mǎjìlǐng (馬紀嶺) route to attack Āshū (阿疎).
Mùzōng (穆宗) personally led his army,
planning to meet at the foot of Āshū (阿疎) city.
Sākǎigǎi (撒改), while on his way, reached the Ābùsài (阿不塞) river.
Xiélè Bójǐn (斜勒勃菫) of the Wūyán (烏延) tribe came to visit,
and said to Sākǎigǎi (撒改):
"I hear that the Guóxiàng (國相) is going to meet the Grand Tutor (Tàishī 太師) at the foot of Āshū (阿疎) city.
This is a deep penetration strategy that is sure to succeed.
It would be better to first pacify the roads of Chánchǔn (潺蠢) and Xīngxiǎn (星顯),
cut off their allies,
and seize their people,
then it will not be too late to combine forces."
Sākǎigǎi (撒改) followed his advice,
attacked Dùněn (鈍恩) city,
and requested reinforcements.
Mùzōng (穆宗) granted them,
and Sākǎigǎi (撒改) then captured Dùněn (鈍恩) city,
and came to meet Mùzōng (穆宗) at the foot of Āshū (阿疎) city.
Dùněn (鈍恩) was in the south,
and Āshū (阿疎) was in the north.
Mùzōng (穆宗) initially sent Sākǎigǎi (撒改) to take a different route,
to then jointly attack Āshū (阿疎).
Hearing that he had adopted Xiélè's (斜勒) plan
and first captured Dùněn (鈍恩) city,
which did not align with the original discussion,
Mùzōng (穆宗) was somewhat displeased.
However, when an envoy from the Liáo (遼) arrived to stop the attack on Āshū (阿疎),
then the prior capture of Dùněn (鈍恩) city was deeply regarded as a meritorious achievement.
He was then appointed Guóxiàng (國相) and Dūtǒng (都統) to lead armies against Liúkě (留可), Zhàdū (詐都), Wùtǎ (塢塔), etc.
Āshū (阿疎) fled into Liáo (遼) territory,
and never dared to return.
Liúkě (留可), Zhàdū (詐都), Wùtǎ (塢塔), and Dùněn (鈍恩) all surrendered.
After Kāngzōng (康宗) passed away,
Tàizǔ (太祖) proclaimed himself Dū Bójílè (都勃極烈),
and divided the rule of the various tribes with Sākǎigǎi (撒改).
Tàizǔ (太祖) governed the area north of Pǐtuō Shuǐ (匹脫水),
and Sākǎigǎi (撒改) governed the people along Láiliú Shuǐ (來流水).
The following year, *jiǎwǔ* (甲午)
the order for the succession of Jìdùshǐ (節度使) arrived.
The Liáo (遼) ruler was decadent, indulging in hunting,
and governance was neglected.
Tàizǔ (太祖) knew that Liáo (遼) could be conquered,
and thus raised an army.
In the ninth month,
he fought the Liáo (遼) people at the border,
capturing Xiè Shí (謝十).
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent a message of victory to Sākǎigǎi (撒改),
bestowing upon him Xiè Shí's (謝十) captured horse.
Sākǎigǎi (撒改) and his officers and soldiers all cheered, saying:
"The righteous army has just reached the Liáo (遼) border,
won one battle,
and the destruction of Liáo (遼) must begin from this point!"
He sent his son Zōnghàn (宗翰) and Wányán Xīyǐn (完顏希尹) to congratulate him on the victory,
and then urged him to ascend the throne.
Tàizǔ (太祖) did not immediately agree.
In the tenth month,
the army captured Níngjiāng Zhōu (寧江州),
and defeated the Liáo (遼) army of 100,000 at Yāzǐ Hé (鴨子河).
The army returned.
In the twelfth month,
Tàizōng (太宗) along with Sākǎigǎi (撒改) and Cíbùshī (辭不失) led various generals to again urge him to ascend.
On the first day of the first month of the first year of Shōuguó (收國)
Tàizǔ (太祖) ascended the throne,
and Sākǎigǎi (撒改) continued to serve as Guóxiàng (國相) as before.
The plan to attack Liáo (遼) was decided by Dígǔnǎi (迪古廼),
but Sākǎigǎi (撒改) was the one who initiated and approved the grand strategy.
Sākǎigǎi (撒改) considered himself a close relative of the imperial clan,
and also from the senior branch,
succeeding Sùzōng (肅宗) as Guóxiàng (國相).
He was both noble and important,
hence he personally took on the grand strategy,
approving it in this manner.
No one else could precede him in this.
After Tài-zǔ ascended the throne,
when the multitude of officials presented memorials,
Sā-gǎi and others knelt forward.
The Emperor rose,
and tearfully stopped them, saying:
"Today's success
is all due to the efforts of you gentlemen assisting me.
Although I occupy a high position,
it is not easy to change old customs."
Sā-gǎi and others were moved and grateful,
and bowed again in thanks.
Whenever officials gathered for banquets,
Tài-zǔ often attended.
When the host bowed,
the Emperor would also return the bow.
After Tiān-fǔ,
the proper rites between ruler and subject were finally established.
In the seventh month,
Tài-zōng was made Ān-bǎn Bó-jí-liè,
Sā-gǎi was made Guó-lùn Bó-jí-liè,
Cí-bù-shī was made Ā-mǎi Bó-jí-liè,
and Gǎo was made Guó-lùn Bó-jí-liè.
Bó-jí-liè
was a prestigious official title among the Nǚ-zhí.
Since Tài-zǔ formally took his title,
it had been half a year,
but no enfeoffments or appointments had yet been heard of.
Tài-zōng was a younger brother, honored above all others.
Gǎo was the youngest of his mother's brothers.
Sā-gǎi and Cí-bù-shī, as members of the imperial clan,
were enfeoffed and appointed together.
In the ninth month,
he was additionally made Guó-lùn Hú-lǔ Bó-jí-liè.
In the fifth year of Tiān-fǔ,
he passed away.
Tài-zǔ went to mourn,
riding a white horse,
gashing his forehead and weeping bitterly.
When it came to the burial,
he again personally attended,
and bestowed his personal horse as a funeral gift.
Sā-gǎi's character was
sincere, honest, and very sagacious.
He was adept at employing people.
His private life was pure and frugal,
and he loved farming.
From the time he first became Prime Minister,
he was able to pacify various tribes.
Litigation and judicial cases were handled with insight into the facts.
At that time, there was a saying:
"Without seeing the Prime Minister,
how can affairs be decided?"
When troops were raised to attack Liáo,
Sā-gǎi always relied on imperial kinsmen for important internal and external matters,
not considering many battles as his achievement.
In the fifteenth year of Tiān-huì,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as King of Yān-guó.
During Zhèng-lóng, he was demoted and enfeoffed as Duke of Chén-guó.
In the third year of Dà-dìng,
he was posthumously granted the title of Prince of Jīn-yuán-jùn,
and accorded sacrificial honors in Tài-zǔ's ancestral temple,
with the posthumous name Zhōng-yì.
In the fifteenth year,
an imperial edict ordered his portrait to be hung in Yǎn-qìng-gōng.
His sons were Zōng-hàn and Zōng-xiàn.
Zōng-hàn has a separate biography.
Zōng-xiàn's original name was Ā-lǎn.
When the Nǚ-zhí script was promulgated,
at the age of sixteen,
he was selected to enter the imperial academy.
When Tài-zōng visited the academy,
Zōng-xiàn and the other students all paid their respects.
Zōng-xiàn's deportment was gentle and elegant.
Tài-zōng summoned him forward
and ordered him to recite what he had learned.
His voice was clear and bright,
and he was skilled in answering questions.
A attending minister reported:
"This is the younger brother of the Left Vice Marshal, Zōng-hàn."
The Emperor sighed in admiration for a long time.
He was also fluent in Qì-dān and Chinese characters.
Before coming of age,
he followed Zōng-hàn to attack Sòng.
When Biàn-jīng was broken,
everyone rushed to the official treasuries to seize wealth,
but Zōng-xiàn alone loaded up books and returned.
When the court discussed systems, rites, and music,
they often continued the old Liáo practices.
Zōng-xiàn said:
"Now that we possess Liáo and Sòng,
we should draw broadly from ancient precedents
and adapt to the times to establish new institutions,
forming the laws of a new dynasty.
Why should we merely adopt the Liáo people's systems?"
Xī-yǐn said:
"Your idea is very much in agreement with mine."
From then on, he was highly regarded.
Tà-lǎn and Zōng-jùn advocated giving the Qí territory to Sòng.
Zōng-xiàn argued against them in court and defeated their proposal.
At the time, his words were not adopted,
but later, Zōng-bì retook the lands of Hé-nán and Shǎn-xī,
just as Zōng-xiàn had advised.
For his achievement in apprehending Zōng-pán and Zōng-jùn,
he was granted the title of Zhāo-wǔ Dà-jiāng-jūn.
He compiled the national history
and successively held the office of Shàng-shū Zuǒ-chéng.
Xī-zōng leisurely said to him:
"Previously, the lands of Hé-nán and Shǎn-xī were given to the Sòng people.
You thought they should not be given.
Now they have been retaken.
This is still following your advice.
Your foresight is deep and far-reaching.
From now on,
speak your mind fully, without concealment."
Zōng-xiàn bowed in thanks
and subsequently served as Acting Mén-xià Shì-láng.
Initially,
Xī-zōng, based on suspicion, killed Left Chancellor Xī-yǐn.
After a long time,
he realized Xī-yǐn was innocent
and deeply regretted it.
He said to Zōng-xiàn:
"Xī-yǐn rendered great service to the state,
but died innocently.
I intend to employ his grandson.
What do you think?"
Zōng-xiàn replied:
"Your Majesty's profound remembrance of Xī-yǐn
and employment of his grandson
is most fortunate.
However, if the innocence of the deceased is not first clarified,
how can the living be employed?"
The Emperor said:
"Your words are right."
That very day, Xī-yǐn's official titles were restored,
and his grandson Shǒu-dào was employed as Yìng-fèng Hàn-lín Wén-zì.
In the fifth year of Huáng-tǒng,
when a general amnesty was to be issued,
it was debated that the special grace should only extend to Nǚ-zhí people.
Zōng-xiàn memorialized:
"Are they not all subjects of the King?
How can there be discrimination in receiving good fortune?"
Therefore, the text was revised
to ensure everyone benefited equally.
He was transferred to become Píng-zhāng Zhèng-shì of the Traveling Chancellery.
At the beginning of Tiān-dé,
he became Resident Minister of Zhōng-jīng and Jíe-dù-shǐ of Ān-wǔ-jūn.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Hé-nèi-jùn.
He was transferred to be Governor of Tài-yuán,
and advanced to be enfeoffed as Prince of Jù-lù-jùn.
During Zhèng-lóng, by rule, his princely title was stripped.
He was twice promoted to be Jíe-dù-shǐ of Zhèn-wǔ and Wǔ-dìng-jūn.
When Shì-zōng ascended the throne,
he dispatched an envoy to summon him,
with an imperial edict stating:
"If my uncle can come,
you should arrive quickly.
If you are obstructed by Hē-shí-liè Zhì-níng or Bái Yàn-jìng,
you need not worry."
When Zōng-xiàn heard that Shì-zōng had ascended the throne,
he had already abandoned his post and returned.
He met the envoy in Zhōng-dū,
then met the Emperor at Xiǎo-liáo-kǒu,
and was appointed Resident Minister of Zhōng-dū,
and immediately dispatched to his post.
An edict ordered him to discuss military affairs with Marshal Wán-yán Gòu-yīng.
The next year,
he was transferred to be Resident Minister of Xī-jīng.
In the eighth month,
he was transferred to Nán-jīng.
When Pú-sàn Zhōng-yì traveled from the Traveling Chancellery to the imperial capital for court,
Zōng-xiàn temporarily managed the affairs of the Traveling Chancellery's Department of State Affairs.
He was summoned to be Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
The Emperor said to Zōng-xiàn:
"You are an old veteran,
and have experienced much.
The Crown Prince is still young,
so please instruct and guide him carefully."
Soon after, he was appointed Píng-zhāng Zhèng-shì,
with the title of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince remaining as before.

An edict granted one copy of the "Veritable Records of Tài-zǔ" to Zōng-xiàn, Píng-zhāng Zhèng-shì Wán-yán Yuán-yí, Left Chancellor Hē-shí-liè Liáng-bì, and Judge of the Secretariat Wēn-wáng Shuǎng, respectively.
Yílā Gāoshānnú was formerly the Prefect of Níngzhōu.
He was dismissed for corruption.
Shìzōng, seeing that among the descendants of meritorious officials, there were no prominent figures in their clans,
appointed him as Secretary of the Secretariat.
At that time,
he was still in mourning for his mother.
The officials reported this matter.
Zōngxiàn said:
"Gāoshānnú is arrogant, cruel, and corrupt;
he should not be kept close to the emperor."
Shìzōng said:
"I appointed him because of his father's and grandfather's merits.
Since he is such a person,
how can he be allowed to tarnish the office?"
He revoked the imperial decree.
Then he turned to the Right Chancellor, Sū Bǎohéng, and the Policy Councillor, Shí Jū, and said:
"This was an error on my part,
which must be corrected.
You, my ministers, should do your best to assist me."
Officials reported that
the Měng'ān Móukè throughout the circuits,
relying on their hereditary status, often harassed the people.
They requested that they be treated like regular officials,
with evaluations every thirty months.
An imperial edict was sent to the Department of State Affairs for discussion.
Zōngxiàn then submitted his deliberation, saying:
"In the past, Emperor Tàizǔ pacified the realm
and swore to enfeoff meritorious officials with hereditary Měng'ān Móukè positions.
If these are now changed to transferable appointments,
it would not accord with Tàizǔ's oath.
Your servant believes that for all Měng'ān Móukè,
their good and bad conduct should be clearly investigated.
The worthy should be promoted, and the unworthy dismissed.
If there is someone unfit for office,
a worthy person should be chosen from among his younger brothers or nephews to replace him."
The emperor followed his advice.
He was promoted to Right Chancellor.
In the sixth year of Dàdìng (1166),
he passed away
at the age of fifty-nine.
The emperor suspended court,
mourning and regretting for a long time.
He ordered all officials to offer condolences,
and bestowed 1,500 liǎng of silver, 50 bolts of heavy silk, and 500 bolts of plain silk.
Xíbùshī was originally written Cíbùshī,
later fixed as Xíbùshī.
He was a grandson of Zhāozǔ
and the second son of Wūgǔchū.
Initially,
Zhāozǔ had no heir for a long time.
He and Empress Wēishùn Túdān prayed to a shaman,
and subsequently Jǐngzǔ and Wūgǔchū were born.
Wūgǔchū grew up to be a heavy drinker
and repeatedly defied his mother.
After Zhāozǔ's death,
Túdān and Jǐngzǔ plotted and killed him.
The tribal people were enraged
and wanted to harm Jǐngzǔ.
Túdān took responsibility for the act herself,
and thus Jǐngzǔ was spared.
Xíbùshī was agile and quick,
skilled at shooting with both hands.
When Shìzǔ inherited the Jiedushi title,
Sùzōng was resisting Huánchí and Sàndá.
They fought at the Ōlǔgànchū River,
and had already suffered two defeats.
When Shìzǔ arrived at the army,
the officers and soldiers looked pale.
Shìzǔ sent Xíbùshī to form the vanguard at Tuōhuògǎi Plains,
while he himself went into hand-to-hand combat,
defeating their infantry.
Xíbùshī charged fiercely from behind the formation,
defeating their cavalry.
His horse was struck by nine arrows
and could no longer gallop,
so he dismounted and continued on foot.
During the battle,
his maternal cousin, Wūgémíng, a skilled archer,
was among the enemy cavalry.
As he was about to shoot,
Xíbùshī looked intently and recognized him,
shouting:
"You young fellow!
Is this something you alone are responsible for?
Why are you pushing to the front like this?"
He struck the horse's head with the end of his bow and left.
In this battle,
Xíbùshī's contributions were substantial.
After Huánchí and Sàndá were defeated,
Xíbùshī's horse, which had been abandoned in the formation, also returned on its own.
Shìzǔ once suspected that Shùjiǎ Bólǐdù might collude with Wūchūn and others to rebel.
He sent Xíbùshī alone on horseback to observe.
Bólǐdù and Hūlǔ hosted him in a wine tower.
Xíbùshī overheard their whispered private conversation
which seemed to indicate they intended to seize him.
He leapt from the tower,
slipped out beyond the fence,
abandoned his horse, and returned.
Such was his bravery and agility.
Bēinǎi then conspired with Wūchūn to raise an army.
Shìzǔ met Wūchūn at Sūsù Hǎidiàn.
Sùzōng advanced to battle,
with Xiéliè and Xíbùshī assisting him.
They bound bundles of kindling and set them on fire,
the smoke and flames obscuring the sky.
They utterly defeated Wūchūn
and captured Bēinǎi, bringing him back.
When Tàizǔ captured Máchǎn
and offered the severed heads to the Liáo,
the Liáo people rewarded their merits.
Mùzōng, Tàizǔ, Huándū, and Xíbùshī all became Xiángwěn.
Later, he, along with Ālǐhé Hǎnmàn and Wòdài, assisted Sāgǎi in attacking Liúkě City
and captured it.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Liáo,
he was made to lead a thousand men,
attending on his left and right.
In the Battle of Chūhédiàn,
only Xíbùshī's strategy accorded with Tàizǔ's,
and they ultimately defeated an army of one hundred thousand,
blunting their military edge.
He then, along with Tàizōng, Sāgǎi, and others, urged Tàizǔ to ascend the throne.
In the seventh month of the first year of Shōuguó (1115),
he, along with Tàizōng, Sāgǎi, and Gǎo, all became Bójíliè,
and Xíbùshī became Āmǎi Bójíliè.
In the seventh year of Tiānfǔ (1123),
Tàizōng and Xíbùshī remained to guard the capital.
Prince Yùn Āng violated discipline and lost troops,
a crime punishable by death according to the law.
At that time,
the Liáo people surrendered Yānjīng,
and the Sòng people promised annual tribute.
In the third month,
Shìzōng was born.
Xíbùshī said to Tàizōng:
"Between brothers and kin,
one should cover justice with benevolence,
rather bending the law to preserve them.
Now the state has experienced repeated great celebrations.
We can reduce Āng's punishment so that he does not die.
If the sovereign blames us,
use me as the one who persuaded you."
Tàizōng agreed
and then flogged Āng as punishment, reporting this to the emperor.
Whenever Tàizǔ campaigned against Liáo,
he always ordered Xíbùshī and Tàizōng to stay and guard.
Although he had no regional accomplishments,
he was entrusted and relied upon, comparable to Sāgǎi.
In the seventh month of that year,
he passed away.
It happened that Tàizǔ fell ill on his way back to the capital.
Tàizōng went to welcome and visit him,
fearing that Tàizǔ would be emotionally agitated and his illness would worsen,
so he dared not announce Xíbùshī's death.
Tàizǔ repeatedly asked:
"Where is Āmǎi Bójíliè?"
Tàizōng falsely replied:
"He will arrive immediately."
In the second year of Zhènglóng (1157),
he was posthumously granted Kǎifǔ Yítóng Sānsī
and enfeoffed as Duke of Cáoguó.
In the third year of Dàdìng (1163),
he was further enfeoffed as Prince of Jīnyuánjùn,
honored with a place in Tàizǔ's ancestral temple,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngyì.
His son was Gǔshāhǔ.
He rendered service in the early days of the state.
During the Tiānhuì period,
he served as Resident Overseer of Zhēndìng.
His son was Tàbùyě.
Zōnghéng's original name was Tàbùyě.
He was loyal and discreet by nature.
In the early Tiānjuàn period (1138),
as a member of the imperial clan,
he served as a guard.
For his meritorious service in capturing Zōngpán and Zōngjùn,
he was promoted to Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi,
then transferred to Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi and Shàngjú Zhícháng.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Deputy Envoy of the same bureau.
When his father died, he observed mourning.
At that time, officials of the Clan Court
were selected based on talent.
Zōnghéng was among those selected,
so he was reinstated
as Shūwēntè Imperial Clan General.
He was transferred to Shàoyǐn of Huìníngfǔ,
served successively as Prefect of Dēngzhōu,
then Prefect of Xiànzhōu,
then Commander of the Tèyǔ Mùqún, and Co-Administrator of the Transport Commissioner of Běijīng Circuit,
and then Jiedushi of Dìngguó Army of Zézhōu.
When the commoner Hǎilíng campaigned south,
he led the Wǔyáng Army as Dūtǒngguǎn in his original capacity,
Shìzōng 世宗 ascended the throne.
He sent a handwritten edict to Zōnghēng 宗亨.
Zōnghēng 宗亨 received the edict
and immediately went to court.
In Dàdìng 大定 two years (1162),
he was appointed Right Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (yòu xuānhuīshǐ 右宣徽使).
Not long after,
he was made Overall Commander of the troops and horses of Běijīng 北京 Circuit
to suppress the Khitan rebels.
The Right Deputy Marshal Púshàn Zhōngyì 僕散忠義 encountered Wōwò 窩斡 at Huādào 花道.
Zōnghēng 宗亨, along with the Left Wing Myriad-Household Púchá Shìjié 蒲察世傑 and others,
fought them with a seven-móukè 謀克 army,
but were defeated.
When Wōwò 窩斡 was defeated,
his partisans Kuòlǐ 括里 and Zhābā 扎八 led their followers south.
Zōnghēng 宗亨 caught up with them.
Zhābā 扎八 feigned surrender,
and Zōnghēng 宗Hēng believed him.
Zhābā 扎八 cunningly said:
"Kuòlǐ 括里 has fled.
I wish to go and intercept him."
Zōnghēng 宗亨 let him go.
He greatly indulged his soldiers
in taking the bags, possessions, people, and livestock abandoned by the enemy,
much of which they kept for themselves.
Kuòlǐ 括里 and Zhābā 扎八 escaped into Sòng 宋 territory.
Because of this,
Zōnghēng 宗亨 was demoted to Administrator of Níngzhōu 寧州.
Zōngxián 宗賢's original name was Sàilǐ 賽里.
He was the grandson of Xíbùshī 習不失.
He followed Overall Commander Gǎo 杲 to take Zhōngjīng 中京,
and attacked the Líao 遼 emperor at Yuānyāng Luò 鴛鴦濼.
Zōnghàn 宗翰 sent Tàlǎn 撻懶 to attack Yēlǜ Mǎgē 耶律馬哥.
The Overall Commander sent Pújiānú 蒲家奴 and Sàilǐ 賽里 and others
with troops to assist him.
Pújiānú 蒲家奴 sent Sàilǐ 賽里, Xiéyě 斜野, Péimǎn Hútá 裴滿胡撻, Dálǔgǔsīliè 達魯古厮列, Yēlǜ Wúshí 耶律吳十 and others, each leading troops, to go in different directions to recruit and persuade.
They captured the family and baggage of the Líao 遼 Resident Administrator Díyuè 迪越,
and also secured the surrender of the Director of Pasturage Mùlúwǎ 木盧瓦.
They obtained many horses
and had them herded where there was water and grass.
Sàilǐ 賽里 and others hurried to Yèdié 業迭,
and then advanced deep with a detached force.
The enemy intercepted and attacked them,
and Sāhé 撒合 was killed in battle.
Pújiānú 蒲家奴 reached the west of Wàngguó Yá 旺國崖.
Sàilǐ 賽里's troops joined him.
He successively held positions up to Left Deputy Palace Inspector (zuǒfù diǎnjiǎn 左副點檢).
In Tiānjuàn 天眷 two years (1139),
when Zōngjùn 宗雋 was being apprehended,
Sàilǐ 賽里 was implicated for having dined at his house,
and his official title and rank were revoked.
Not long after,
he was reinstated.
In Huángtǒng 皇統 four years (1144),
he was granted an hereditary móukè 謀克,
then transferred to Overall Palace Inspector (dū diǎnjiǎn 都點檢),
and enfeoffed as Duke of Bīn 豳國公.
He was appointed Minister of the Right (píngzhāng zhèngshì 平章政事).
He was promoted to Right Chancellor (yòuchéngxiàng 右丞相)
and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat (zhōngshūlìng 中書令).
He was promoted to Grand Tutor (tàibǎo 太保) and Left Chancellor (zuǒchéngxiàng 左丞相),
and concurrently supervised the compilation of the National History.
He was dismissed and made Left Deputy Marshal.
Soon after,
he was again made Grand Tutor and Left Chancellor,
with his position as Left Deputy Marshal remaining.
He was promoted to Grand Preceptor (tàishī 太師),
in charge of the affairs of the Three Departments (sānshěng 三省),
concurrently Overall Marshal (dūyuánshuài 都元帥),
and supervised the compilation of the National History.
He was dispatched as Resident Administrator of Nánjīng 南京,
in charge of the affairs of the Traveling Department of State Affairs (xíngtái shàngshūshěng 行臺尚書省).
He was again made Left Deputy Marshal
and concurrently Resident Administrator of Xījīng 西京.
He was again made Grand Tutor
and in charge of the affairs of the Three Departments.
He was again made Left Chancellor
and concurrently Overall Marshal.
Sàilǐ 賽里, starting from a bodyguard position,
in less than ten years held the positions of both general and chancellor.
He was always grateful
and wished to exert himself to repay the court.
Although he was related to the Lamented Empress on her mother's side,
and the empress held great power,
and some high officials advanced their careers by relying on her,
Sàilǐ 賽里 never attached himself to her.
When Crown Prince Jì'ān 濟安 died,
and King of Wèi Wèi Wáng Dàojì 道濟 died,
Xīzōng 熙宗 had no heir.
Sàilǐ 賽里 advised Xīzōng 熙宗 to select concubines from the palace to broaden the succession,
without any reservations concerning the empress.
The empress resented him for this.
While he and Hǎilíng 海陵 were both in the chancellorship,
Sàilǐ 賽里 never showed the slightest willingness to compromise.
Though Hǎilíng 海陵 was dominant, he was inwardly wary of Sàilǐ 賽里.
Outwardly, he treated Sàilǐ 賽里 with respect due to his seniority, but inwardly, he was always jealous of him.
Hǎilíng 海陵 knew that the Lamented Empress resented Sàilǐ 賽里,
so he conspired with the empress to jointly force him out.
Sàilǐ 賽里 did not change because of this.
When King of Zuò Zuò Wáng Chángshèng 常勝 died,
Xīzōng 熙宗 took his wife into the palace.
Soon after,
he killed the Lamented Empress and several concubines,
intending to make Chángshèng 常勝's wife empress,
but it was not carried out.
When Hǎilíng 海陵 assassinated Xīzōng 熙宗,
he deceptively claimed that Xīzōng 熙宗 was going to discuss establishing an empress
and summoned the princes and high officials.
Sàilǐ 賽里 heard the summons
and believed it to be true.
As he was about to enter the palace,
he said to someone:
"The emperor surely wants to make Chángshèng 常勝's wife empress.
I must strenuously argue against it."
When he was arrested,
he still thought that Xīzōng 熙宗 was going to establish Chángshèng 常shèng's wife,
and had been killed first.
He said:
"Who can speak for me?
My death is not to be regretted,
but I only worry that the emperor has no help at his side."
Then he was murdered.
Shítǔmén 石土門,
whose name is also written as Shéntúmén 神徒門 in Chinese characters,
was a Wányán 完顏 tribesman from the Yēlǎn 耶懶 road.
His family had been its tribal chief for generations.
His father, Zhílǐhǎi 直离海,
was the fourth-generation descendant of Bǎohuólǐ 保活里, the younger brother of the founder (shǐzǔ 始祖).
Although they were of the same clan,
they had not communicated for a long time.
During Jǐngzǔ 景祖's time,
Zhílǐhǎi 直离海 sent his tribesman Miǎosūn 邈孫 to come,
requesting to resume communication within the clan.
Jǐngzǔ 景祖 kept Miǎosūn 邈孫 for over a year,
generously providing him with food and drink,
and treated him kindly.
When he returned,
Jǐngzǔ 景祖 presented him with several baskets of silk as a gift
to secure their goodwill.
After a long time,
Yēlǎn 耶懶 suffered a famine.
Jǐngzǔ 景祖 gave them horses and cattle
as a subsidy for grain purchases,
and sent Shìzǔ 世祖 to deliver them.
It happened that Shìzǔ 世祖 fell ill,
and Shítǔmén 石土門 stayed by his side day and night.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 recovered from his illness and prepared to return,
they shook hands in farewell,
promising not to forget each other in the future.
Shítǔmén 石土門 was physically imposing,
brave and skilled in battle,
honest, filial, and brotherly,
with a strong memory and quick wit,
and decisive in action.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 succeeded to the throne,
their friendship deepened.
Neighboring tribes were displeased
and consequently joined forces to attack them.
Shítǔmén 石土門 sent his younger brother Āsīmàn 阿斯懣 to lead two hundred men south to resist the enemy.
The enemy, with a thousand soldiers,
had already moved to their east and occupied a high mound.
Shítǔmén 石土門 led five hundred men to meet and attack them.
The enemy general, Wòlǐběn 斡里本,
was a brave warrior.
He came out to challenge,
and Shítǔmén 石土門 shot his horse.
Wòlǐběn 斡里本 shot back,
hitting Shítǔmén 石土門 in the abdomen.
Shítǔmén 石土門 pulled out the arrow
and fought with even greater vigor.
Āsīmàn 阿斯懣 and seven brave warriors fought on foot,
killing Wòlǐběn 斡里本.
The troops of the various tribes then fled.
Shítǔmén 石土門 then persuaded the various tribes
to submit to Shìzǔ 世祖.
Shìzǔ 世祖 commended him.
Later, in campaigns against Wūchūn 烏春, Wōmóuhǎn 窩謀罕, Dùn'ēn 鈍恩, Díkùdé 狄庫德, and others,
he participated in battles with his contingent
and performed meritorious service.
His younger brother, Āsīmǎn 弟阿斯懣, soon died.
After the mourning period ended,
a grand assembly of his clan was held.
Tàizǔ 太祖 led his officials and subordinates to it,
and used the occasion to consult them on the plan to attack Liáo 遼.
During the ancestral sacrifice,
a flying crow came from the east and flew west.
Tàizǔ 太祖 shot it,
and the arrow pierced its left wing, causing it to fall.
Shítǔmén 石土門 carried it to the front and offered congratulations, saying:
"Crows and ravens are greatly disliked by people.
Now that one has been shot and captured,
this is an auspicious omen."
He then presented a golden plaque.
Later, he joined the army with his tribal soldiers to attack Gāolì 高麗.
When Liáo 遼 was attacked,
his contributions were particularly numerous.
When the royal army captured Xīīng 西京,
he was bestowed with a golden plaque.
His son Chánchǔn 蟬蠢 accompanied him.
The Emperor said to him:
"My consort's younger sister, Báosàn 白散, is in Liáo 遼.
Once she is captured,
I shall make her your wife."
This was eventually carried out as he said.
When the Emperor campaigned in the west,
all the generals followed him.
Shítǔmén 石土門 then led three hundred skilled archers to guard the capital.
At that time, Tàizōng 太宗 was in charge of the defense.
Delighted by their arrival,
he personally went out to welcome and honor them.
Later, upon hearing that Huánglóngfǔ 黃龍府 had rebelled,
he joined Ruìzōng 睿宗 in suppressing it.
Ruìzōng 睿宗 bestowed upon him five hundred slaves.
When the army returned,
he was generously rewarded.
He died at this time,
at the age of sixty-one.
In the second year of Zhènglóng 正隆 (1157),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王.
His sons were Xíshī 習失 and Sījìng 思敬.
Wányán Zhōng 完顏忠, whose original name was Dígǔnǎi 迪古乃,
with the courtesy name Āsīkuí 阿思魁,
was Shítǔmén's 石土門 younger brother.
Tàizǔ 太祖 greatly valued him.
He was about to raise an army to attack Liáo 遼,
but had not yet made a decision.
He wished to discuss the matter with Dígǔnǎi 迪古乃.
Thus, Zōnghán 宗翰, Zōnggàn 宗幹, and Wányán Xīyǐn 完顏希尹 all accompanied him.
After several days,
when there was a moment of leisure,
Tàizǔ 太祖 leaned on Dígǔnǎi's 迪古乃 shoulder and said:
"My coming here is not for nothing.
I have a plan to discuss with you,
and I want you to make the decision for me.
Liáo 遼 is called a great nation,
but in reality, it is empty.
Its lord is arrogant and its soldiers are cowardly;
they lack courage in battle.
It can be conquered.
I wish to raise an army,
uphold righteousness, and march west.
〔一五〕 What do you think, my lord?"
Dígǔnǎi 迪古乃 replied:
"With your Excellency's martial prowess,
〔一六〕 the soldiers are willing to serve.
The Liáo 遼 emperor is obsessed with hunting,
and his decrees are inconsistent.
It will be easy to deal with them."
Tàizǔ 太祖 agreed.
The following year,
Tàizǔ 太祖 attacked Liáo 遼,
and sent Póluohuǒ 婆盧火 to summon troops.
Dígǔnǎi 迪古乃 brought his troops to join the army.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Shōuguó 收國 (1115),
the Emperor engaged the Liáo 遼 main army.
When he reached Yáolà 爻剌,
Dígǔnǎi 迪古乃 and Yínzhúgē 銀术哥 defended Dálǔgǔlù 達魯古路.
In the second year (1116),
he met Wòlǔ 斡魯 and Púchá 蒲察 at Wòlǔgǔ 斡魯古,
attacked Gāo Yǒngchāng 高永昌,
defeated his army,
and Dōngjīng 東京 surrendered.
He then, with Wòlǔgǔ 斡魯古 and others, resisted Yēlǜ Niēlǐ 耶律捏里,
defeated him at Jílísān 蒺藜山,
captured Xiǎnzhōu 顯州,
and Qián 乾 and Huì 惠 and other prefectures surrendered.
In the second year of Tiānfǔ 天輔 (1118),
he and Lóushì 婁室 both came to have an audience.
The Emperor said:
"The Liáo 遼 lord is currently in Zhōngjīng 中京, yet you dared to come here (without permission).
Each of you will receive thirty blows with a staff."

Tàizǔ 太祖 stationed his troops at Cǎoluò 草濼.
Dígǔnǎi 迪古乃 captured Fèngshèngzhōu 奉聖州,

Xíshī 習室 spearheaded the charge and fought bravely,
and was appointed Měng'ān 猛安.
Later, he followed Xiáyě 斜也 in conquering Zhōngjīng 中京,
raided the Liáo 遼 lord at Yuānyāng Luò 鴛鴦濼,
generally pacified Shān Yán 山□ ,
〔一九〕 defeated Xià's 夏 general Lǐ Liángfǔ's 李良輔 army,
and with Lóushì 婁室, captured the Liáo 遼 emperor in Yúdǔ Gǔ 余睹谷.
When Zōnghán 宗翰 attacked Sòng 宋,
he and Yínzhúkě 銀术可 besieged and defended Tàiyuán 太原.
The following year,
he attacked Xiāngyuán 襄垣,
captured Lùchéng 潞城,
received the surrender of Xīīng 西京,
and reached Biàn 汴.
The Yuánshuàifǔ 元帥府, considering that Huái 懷 and Mèng 孟 were blocked to the north by Tàiháng 太行 and bordered by the Yellow River to the south,
controlling strategic passes,
sent Xíshī 習室 to lead twelve Měng'ān 猛安 armies to garrison and pacify them.
Thus,
he annihilated bandits and thieves,
gathered back the displaced,
and the
four borders became secure.
In the fifth year of Tiānhuì 天會 (1127),
he passed away.
During Xīzōng's 熙宗 time,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tèjìn 特進.
During the Dàdìng 大定 era,
he was given the posthumous name Wēimǐn 威敏.
Shìzōng 世宗, reflecting on the arduous task of Tàizǔ 太祖 and Tàizōng 太宗 in founding the dynasty,
sought out the most outstanding ministers and their achievements from that time,

and had their portraits painted in Yǎnqìng Gōng 衍慶宮: the Prince of Liáo 遼, Xiáyě 斜也; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Sāgǎi 撒改; the Prince of Liáo 遼, Zōnggàn 宗幹; the Prince of Qín 秦王, Zōnghán 宗翰; the Prince of Sòng 宋王, Zōngwàng 宗望; the Prince of Liáng 梁王, Zōngbì 宗弼; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Xībùshī 習不失; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Wòlǔ 斡魯; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Xīyǐn 希尹; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Lóushì 婁室; the Prince of Chǔ 楚王, Zōngxióng 宗雄; the Prince of Lǔ 魯王, Dúmǔ 闍母; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Yínzhúkě 銀术可; the Duke of Suí Guó 隋國公, Ālíhé Mǎn 阿离合懣; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Wányán Zhōng 完顏忠; the Duke of Yù Guó 豫國公, Pújiānú 蒲家奴; the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Sālǐhē 撒离喝; the Duke of Yǎn Guó 兗國公, Liú Yànzōng 劉彥宗; the Tèjìn 特進, Wòlǔgǔ 斡魯古; the Duke of Qí Guó 齊國公, Hán Qǐxiān 韓企先,
totaling twenty-one individuals including Xíshī 習室.
Initially,
Hǎilíng 海陵 abolished the Wànhù 萬戶 of all circuits,
and established the Sūbīn Lù Jiédùshǐ 蘇濱路節度使.
During Shìzōng's 世宗 time,
a close official memorialized to request changing Sūbīn 蘇濱 to Yēlǎn Jiédùshǐ 耶懶節度使,
so as not to forget the old merits.
The Emperor said:
"The two rivers, Sūbīn 蘇濱 and Yēlǎn 耶懶, are a thousand *lǐ* apart.
The Jiédùshǐ 節度使 governs Sūbīn 蘇濱,
so there is no need to change it.
For the descendants of Shítǔmén 石土門 who personally managed the Měng'ān 猛安 and inherited the enfeoffment,
it can be changed to Yēlǎn Měng'ān 耶懶猛安,
to show that their origins are not forgotten."
Sījìng 思敬, originally named Sāgǎi 撒改,
was from Yālǎnhé 押懶河,
the son of the Prince of Jīnyuán Jùn 金源郡王, Shéntǔmǎn 神土懣,
and the younger brother of Xíshī 習失.
〔二０〕 His original name was Sīgōng 思恭,
changed to avoid the taboo name of Xiǎnzōng 顯宗.
He had a majestic physique,
a beautiful beard,
and was pure, upright, and capable.
At the age of eleven,
he followed his father to meet Tàizǔ 太祖.
Tàizǔ 太祖 was in Nàlíndiàn 納鄰淀,
hunting.
He was then summoned to join the hunt,
and shot a yellow goat, capturing it.
Tàizǔ 太祖 bestowed upon him a horse from his retinue.
When Zōnghán 宗翰 attacked Sòng 宋 from Tàiyuán 太原,
he followed his elder brother Xíshī 習室 in attacking Tàiyuán 太原.
When Zōnghán 宗翰 captured Hénán 河南,
Sījìng 思敬 followed Wányán Huónǚ 完顏活女 across the Yellow River,
captured Luòyáng 洛陽, and besieged Biàn 汴, all with merit.
When the army returned,
he was placed under the command of the Prince of Liáo 遼, Zōnggàn 宗幹.
When Tàizōng 太宗 visited the hot springs of Dōngjīng 東京,
Sījìng 思敬 temporarily served as a guard,
leading a hundred guard soldiers to accompany him.
He commanded a Móukè 謀克.
He performed meritorious service in the campaign against Shùhǔlín 术虎麟,
and was subsequently made a permanent guard.
In the second year of Tiānjuan 天眷 (1139),
for his功 in capturing Zōngpán 宗磐 and Zōngjùn 宗雋,
he was promoted to Xiǎnwǔ Jiāngjūn 顯武將軍.
Xīzōng was fishing in the Húntóngjiāng River,
when the net rope broke.
Cáoguó Wáng Zōngmǐn, emboldened by drink,
whipped his horse and entered the river,
personally pulling the main rope of the net,
and submerged into the water.
Xīzōng called for his attendants to save him,
but in their haste, none responded.
Sījìng leaped into the water,
and pulled Zōngmǐn out.
Xīzōng praised him profusely
and rewarded him handsomely.
He was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
inherited the post of Yāǎn Lùwànhù,
and was granted a hereditary Mǒukè.
In the seventh year,
he was summoned for an audience
and bestowed with an inherited robe, a horse, and ten thousand strings of cash.
When he returned,
an envoy was again dispatched to bestow him with a bow and sword.
That year,
he entered the court as Gōngbù Shàngshū,
and was then transferred to Diànqián Dūdiǎnjiǎn.
Before long,
he became Lìbù Shàngshū.
In the early Tiāndé period,
he served as an envoy to Sòng, tasked with conveying a message.
The Sòng people, following old customs,
requested to view the tide of the Qiántángjiāng River.
Sījìng declined to view it,
saying:
“My country has a vast sea to the east,
and rivers larger than the Qiántáng.”
He ultimately did not go.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
then dismissed to become Zhēndìng Yǐn.
For his integrity,
he was enfeoffed as Hénèi Jùnwáng,
then transferred and enfeoffed as Jùlù.
When his mother passed away,
he was reinstated to his original post,
and transferred to Yìdū Yǐn.
In Zhènglóng year two,
he was customarily stripped of his princely title
and made Qìngyáng Yǐn.
In Dàdìng year two,
he was appointed Xīnán Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
enfeoffed as Jìguó Gōng,
and concurrently Tiāndé Jūnjiédùshǐ.
Soon after, he became Běilù Dūzhǒngtǒng,
wearing two plaques, one gold and one silver.
The Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ, Tángkuò Bóɡǔdǐ, was his deputy.
He led two thousand soldiers from his route,
met with Bóɡǔdǐ,
surveyed important strategic terrain,
and sometimes stationed troops at Gǒuluò,
watching for the movements of Qìdān bandits.
He set up defenses,
and sent out distant scouts.
When bandits arrived, they would engage in battle,
without regard for day or night.
An imperial edict to Bóɡǔdǐ stated:
“Your troops are few,
and Sījìng has not yet arrived.
You must not engage in battle first.”
Púsǎn Zhōngyì defeated Wōwò at Xiànquán.
An imperial edict commanded Sījìng to select three thousand new horses
to prepare for pursuit and attack.
Wōwò entered the Xī region.
Sījìng served as Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān,
leading his former troops into the Xī region at Zhānggēzhái,
where they joined the main army to suppress them.
They defeated the pseudo-Jiédù Tèmòyě,
capturing over two hundred people.
The rebellious general Xiǎohézhù and his confederate Shéndúwò,
captured Wōwò, his mother Xúniǎn, his wife, children, younger brothers, nephews, and other family members, along with his gold and silver plaques and seals, and presented them to Sījìng in surrender.
Sījìng presented the captives to the capital,
and was bestowed with one hundred taels of gold, one thousand taels of silver, forty bolts of heavy brocade, a jade belt, a horse, and a famous hawk.
He was appointed Yòufù Yuánshuài,
to manage the southern frontier,
stationed in Shāndōng.
He was dismissed and appointed Běijīng Liúshǒu.
He was again appointed Yòufù Yuánshuài,
still managing Shāndōng.
〔二一〕
Initially,
the Měngān Mǒukè were settled as military farmers in Shāndōng,
each following the land they had received,
Shìzōng did not want the Měngān Mǒukè to be mixed with common households;
he wanted them to live together in concentrated settlements.
He dispatched Hùbù Lángzhōng Wányán Ràng to the Yuánshuàifǔ to discuss this.
Sījìng and Shāndōng Lùzǒngguǎn Túdān Kèníng deliberated, saying:
“The grand army is currently advancing to attack Sòng.
It would be advisable to temporarily settle their families in prefectures and counties,
and leave a measured number of troops for defense.
Once the border situation stabilizes,
scattered across prefectures and counties.
which would be convenient for both the military and the populace.”
This was reported back,
and the emperor followed it.
Thereafter, the Měngān Mǒukè were made to form their own concentrated settlements,
and their fields that were interspersed with commoners' fields like dog's teeth
were mutually exchanged.
In the fourth month of the third year,
he was summoned back to the capital,
to be Běijīng Liúshǒu,
and was bestowed with a gold saddle and bridle.
In the seventh year,
he was summoned to be Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
Previously,
Měngān Mǒukè were merged and consolidated,
and those who had received Měng or Kè ranks without merit during the Hǎilíng period
were all dismissed.
〔二二〕Many lost their positions.
Sījìng requested that they be employed according to their talents,
and the emperor followed his request.
Sījìng had previously served as Zhēndìng Yǐn,
and his son had taken a woman from the local populace as a concubine.
At this time,
her brother requested a separation.
The concubine, fearing Sījìng's position as a minister,
dared not leave.
An edict commanded her return to her family.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Shūmìshǐ,
and submitted a memorial discussing five matters: Firstly,
Jurchen people could be selected and tested based on literary ability, following the Hàn people.
Secondly,
Khitan people could be divided and assigned to Jurchen Měngān.
Thirdly,
Salt Lake officials could be dismissed.
Fourthly,
the position of vice-centurion who served concurrently with Měngān could also be dismissed.
Fifthly,
officials of the princely households should be appointed based on their literary qualifications,
and taught the Jurchen language and script.
The emperor adopted all of them.
Thereafter, Jurchen people who passed the imperial examinations,
such as Jiágǔ Héng, Nípánggǔ Jiàn, Túdān Yì, and Wányán Kuāng,
all attained premiership through this,
which was indeed initiated by Sījìng.
After a long time,
the emperor said to Sījìng:
“I wish to compile the Veritable Records of Xīzōng.
You once served as an attendant,
and must be able to recall his deeds.”
He replied:
“During Xīzōng’s time,
talented people were found both within and outside the court.
The wind and rain were timely,
the harvests were abundant,
bandits ceased,
and the people were at peace.
This is the general outline.
Why bother with other details?”
The emperor was greatly pleased.
Shìzōng was fond of establishing achievements,
hence this subtle admonition.
In Dàdìng year thirteen,
he passed away.
The emperor suspended court,
personally attended the funeral,
and wept grievously,
saying:
“He was an old minister.”
The funeral gifts were increased,
and all funeral rites were officially provided.
His grandson, Wúkǎnshùtè,
in Dàdìng year twenty-four,
was appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn,
and awarded the Sùbīn Lù Bǎolín Shān Měngān.
A eulogy states: Hégé ceded the throne to the founder of the dynasty,
thereby establishing the imperial enterprise.
Sākǎi governed the country,
stabilized the state,
and honored and enthroned Tàizǔ.
His profound strategies and far-reaching plans
made him a great minister of his generation.
How worthy he was!
Xíbùshī covered the transgressions of his predecessors,
achieving merit across five generations.
The Yì Jīng says,
“If one has a son, the deceased father has no blame.”
Does this not refer to him?
The progenitor lived in a different tribe from his youngest brother,
yet their descendants all became powerful clans.
The strategy for capturing Liáo
was finally settled by Dígǔnǎi.
Was this not due to a hidden assistance from the Heavenly Dao?
Collated Notes
Biography Nine: Wòlǔ, Wòlǔgǔ Bójǐn, Póluóhuǒ, Wúzāhū, Shēmǔ Zōng (original name Déshòu)
Wòlǔ
was the third son of Hánguó Gōng Hèzhě.
At the beginning of Kāngzōng's reign,
the Bójǐn Wòhuò of the Hánguó tribe of Sūbīnshuǐ, and the Wòzhǔn and Zhídé tribes harbored rebellious intentions.
Wòdài governed them,
with Wòsài and Wòlǔ as his assistants.
They then attacked Wòhuò,
captured his city, and returned.
Gāolí built nine cities in Gélǎndiàn.
When Wòsài's mother fell ill,
Wòlǔ commanded his troops for several months in his stead.
Wòlǔ also built nine cities opposite Gāolí to resist them.
When they went out, they fought;
when they came in, they defended.
Wòsài used him,
and ultimately defeated Gāolí.
In the fourth month of the second year of Shōuguó,
an imperial edict ordered Wòlǔ to command all armies,
and together with Shēmǔ, Púchá, Dígǔnǎi, and the Dūtǒng Wòlǔgǔ of the Xiánzhōu Road,
to attack Gāo Yǒngchāng.
The edict said:
"Yǒngchāng enticed and coerced border guards,
and secretly occupied a region.
We should simply exploit his weakness and take it.
This is not a far-reaching plan;
his downfall can be awaited instantly.
The Bóhǎi people of Dōngjīng have long been grateful for our virtue;
they are easy to win over.
If they do not comply,
then we shall deliberate on a punitive expedition,
without unnecessary slaughter."
Gāo Yǒngchāng, a Bóhǎi man,
was a deputy general under Liáo,
and with three thousand soldiers,
was stationed at Dōngjīng Bāchándnkǒu.
Yǒngchāng saw that the Liáo government was deteriorating daily,
and that Tàizǔ's uprising
could not be resisted by the Liáo people,
so he coveted extraordinary power.
At this time,
there was animosity between the Hàn people and the Bóhǎi people in Dōngjīng,
and many Bóhǎi people were killed.
Yǒngchāng then enticed all the Bóhǎi people,
and together with his border guards, entered and occupied Dōngjīng.
Within a mere ten days,
people far and near responded,
amassing eight thousand soldiers.
He then presumptuously proclaimed himself emperor,
and changed the era name to Lóngjī.
The Liáo people attacked him,
but were unable to defeat him for a long time.
Yǒngchāng sent Tàbùyě and Sháohé
with valuables to seek aid from Tàizǔ,
and also said:
"We wish to combine forces to take Liáo."
Tàizǔ sent Húshābǔ to instruct him, saying:
"It is certainly permissible to combine forces to take Liáo.
But Dōngjīng is nearby,
and you presumptuously occupy it
and assume a grand title. How can this be?
If you can submit,
