you shall be granted a princely title.
Moreover, send the Nǚzhēn Hútūgǔ, who is registered under Liáo, here."
Gāo Yǒngchāng sent Tàbùyě to come with Húshābǔ and Hútūgǔ,
but Yǒngchāng's memorial was disrespectful,
and he also requested the return of the captured Bóhǎi people.
Tàizǔ detained Hútūgǔ and did not send him back,
and sent Dàyàoshīnúnú with Tàbùyě to go and persuade him.
Wòlǔ was just approaching Dōngjīng
when six thousand Liáo troops came to attack Zhàosànchéng.
The Bójǐn Wūlùnshízhǔn of Ātúhǎn fought them in the land of Yìtuì,
and greatly defeated them.
In the fifth month,
Wòlǔ encountered the Liáo army at Shěnzhōu,
defeated them,
and advanced to attack Shěnzhōu,
taking it.
When Yǒngchāng heard that Shěnzhōu had been taken,
he was greatly terrified.
He sent his household slave Duólà with one gold seal and fifty silver plaques,
wishing to relinquish his title
and declare himself a vassal.
Wòlǔ sent Húshābǔ and Sābā to report this.
It happened that the Bóhǎi Gāo Zhēn surrendered,
saying that Yǒngchāng was not truly surrendering,
but merely trying to delay the army.
Wòlǔ advanced his troops,
and Yǒngchāng then killed Húshābǔ and others,
and led his forces to resist.
They met at Wòlǐhuóshuǐ.
After our army had crossed,
Yǒngchāng's army retreated without a fight.
We pursued them to the foot of Dōngjīng city.
The next day,
Yǒngchāng led all his forces to battle,
and was again greatly defeated.
He then fled with five thousand cavalry to Chángsōngdǎo.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ conquered Níngjiāngzhōu,
all the captured Bóhǎi people from Dōngjīng were released.
They often fled midway.
The generals requested to kill them,
but Tàizǔ said:
"Since we have defeated the enemy and taken the city,
why kill many?
In the past, the late Grand Preceptor once defeated an enemy,
captured over a hundred people,
and released them;
they all fled.
Later,
they often brought their tribesmen to surrender.
Now these people flee,
but they will prove useful in the future."
At this point,
the Dōngjīng people, Ēnshèngnú, Xiāngē, and others,
captured Yǒngchāng's wife and children and surrendered the city.
These were the Dōngjīng Bóhǎi people who had been released at Níngjiāngzhōu.
The late Grand Preceptor
refers to Shìzǔ.
Not long after,
Tàbùyě captured Yǒngchāng and Duólà and presented them.
They were all executed.
At this,
the Nǚzhēn registered under Liáo in the southern road, and all the prefectures and counties of Dōngjīng, surrendered.
Wòlǔ was appointed Nánlù Dūtǒng and Diébójíliè,
and Wūchǔn was left to manage affairs in Dōngjīng.
An edict was issued to abolish Liáo laws,
reduce taxes,
and establish Měng'ān and Móukè in accordance with the system of the present dynasty.
In the ninth month,
Wòlǔ paid his respects to the emperor at Pólǔmǎishuǐ.
The emperor consoled and rewarded him.
On the day of Xīnhài,
the emperor visited Wòlǔ's residence,
held a banquet,
attended by all officials,
and bestowed gifts according to rank.
Zhúwēishuǐ Bù Shílǐgǔdá
killed Chóuwò and Púhūdédé.
Wòlǔ divided the troops of Húlàgǔ and Wūchǔn to suppress them.
Chóuwò was a member of the imperial clan,
tall and skilled in battle.
At fifteen,
he joined the army
and was often given important assignments.
With five hundred soldiers,
he defeated the Shìwéi
and captured their people.
He also persuaded the Zhúwēishuǐ tribe to surrender,
and was made a Móukè for his merits.
Púhūdédé first served Sāgǎi,
followed him in attacking Xiāo Hǎilǐ,
and accepted the surrender of the Zhúwēishuǐ tribe,
leading a Qiānhù of the marching army.
He participated in the capture of Huánglóngfǔ
and the battle of Dálúgǔchéng,
both with distinction.
When Níngjiāngzhōu was captured,
the Bóhǎi Yǐsāibǔ rebelled and fled,
and Púhūdédé pursued and recaptured him.
At this time,
he and Chóuwò were victims together.
When Wòlǔ reached Shílǐhànhé,
Shílǐgǔdá fled.
He was pursued and overtaken at Hétàlálashān.
The four chief culprits were executed,
and the remaining people were pacified.
The edict said:
"You have pacified the rebellion
without tiring the army and people.
I commend you greatly.
Chóuwò and others died for state affairs.
I heard their bodies were abandoned in the river.
Once the ice thaws,
they must be sought and buried.
Their people can be organized into one Móukè for every three hundred households,
led by those chosen and respected by the populace,
and their sons and younger brothers shall be sent as hostages."
Wòlǔ then returned.
During the Tiānjuàn era,
Chóuwò was posthumously granted the title Fèngguó Shàngjiāngjūn,
and Púhūdédé was posthumously granted Zhāoyì Dàjiāngjūn.
Wòlǔ, following the Military Commissioner, attacked the Liáo Emperor.
The Liáo Emperor fled west.
Xījīng had already surrendered but then rebelled again.
The enemy occupied the pagoda west of the city,
shooting down at those attacking the city.
Wòlǔ and Gǔbālǔ attacked the pagoda
and seized it.
Then, with elite troops, they used the pagoda to shoot down into the city,
thus breaking Xījīng.
The King of Xià Guó sent Lǐ Liángfǔ with thirty thousand soldiers to rescue Liáo.
They arrived at the border of Tiāndé.
Lóushì and Wòlǔ combined their forces and defeated them,
pursuing them to Yěgǔ
and killing several thousand people.
The Xià people crossed the stream.
The water suddenly rose,
and the drowned were countless.
The Liáo Emperor was between Yīnshān and Qīngzhǒng.
Wòlǔ was the Military Commissioner of the Xīnán Lù
and went to attack him.
He sent Bólàshú and Sāhémèn with two hundred soldiers
to attack Hēlízì, the provisional head of the Liáo Six Bureaus, at Báishuǐ Luò
and captured him.
The Liáo Emperor left his baggage at Qīngzhǒng,
led ten thousand soldiers,
and went to Yìngzhōu.
He dispatched Zhàolǐ and Bèidá, each leading troops, to intercept them.
Zōngwàng unexpectedly arrived at the Liáo Emperor's camp,
capturing all of his wives, children, and clan members,
and obtaining his imperial seal.
Wòlǔ sent an envoy to report the victory, saying:
"By Your Majesty's divine might,
we have repeatedly defeated the enemy's soldiers.
The Liáo Emperor has nowhere to return,
and will certainly surrender.
We have already strictly warned neighboring regions
not to admit Sòng people.
We should jointly supply military provisions.
Order Yínshùkě to go to Dàizhōu to receive them."
An edict stated:
"Inform all meritorious officers and soldiers.
When We arrive there,
rewards will be progressively bestowed.
Do not remove the Liáo Emperor's relatives from their carriages and tents.
Treat them kindly.
The Liáo Emperor, all alone and driven from his country,
bears sorrow and shame.
We fear he might lose his life.
Although his evil deeds were self-inflicted,
he once held a great position.
We deeply cannot bear it.
If he is willing to come upon invitation,
his clan members shall be handed over to him.
We have already sent Yáng Pú to levy provisions from Sòng.
Yínshùkě does not need to go anymore.
The Liáo Zhào Wáng, Xíníliè, and other officials,
shall all be pardoned
and comforted."
Tàizǔ returned to the capital.
Zōnghàn became the Military Commissioner of both the Xīběi and Xīnán Circuits.
Wòlǔ and Pújiānú served as his deputies.
Zōnghàn had an audience at the capital.
An edict stated:
"Regarding what the Xià people said,
that Sòng is invading the newly ceded territory,
decide on it according to expediency."
Wòlǔ reported:
"The Xià people have not fully returned the registers of households, property, and treasury.
Moreover, they claim the Sòng people are encroaching on the granted territory and request reinforcements.
The Sòng border officials intend to seize the territory granted to the Xià people.
They probably have ulterior motives."
An edict stated:
"The Xià people repeatedly request reinforcements.
Perhaps they do not wish to return our household registers,
hindering our pursuit of the Liáo Emperor.
The Sòng people dare to speak of seizing territory from Xià for themselves.
They indeed have ulterior motives.
You should carefully guard your defenses,
demand all household registers within Xià,
inform both countries,
and handle the matter judiciously."
Wòlǔ again requested not to cede Shānxī to Sòng.
Otherwise, the Liáo Emperor would be able to communicate with Guō Yàoshī of Sòng.
Another edict stated:
"Zōnghàn requested that the Shānxī territory not be given to Sòng.
You also brought this up.
Border affairs must be handled carefully and not neglected."
When Zōnghàn and others attacked Sòng,
Wòlǔ acted as the Military Commissioner for both the Xīnán and Xīběi Circuits.
In the fifth year of Tiānhuì,
he passed away.
In the fifth year of Huángtǒng,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Zhèng.
In the second year of Tiāndé,
he was enshrined in the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ.
His son was Sābā,
Grand Master of Silver-Green Light.
His son was Sàilǐ.
Wòlǔgǔ Bójǐn,
was a member of the imperial clan.
When Tàizǔ attacked Liáo,
he sent Wòlǔgǔ and Ālǔ to pacify the Liáo-affiliated Nǚzhí of Wòhū and Jísài Circuits.
They fought against Tābùyě, the Liáo military governor,
and defeated him.
They beheaded Tābùyě.
Ālǔtáihǎn and fourteen other Tàiwān from Kùniǎnlǐng all surrendered.
The Wòhū and Jísài Circuits also surrendered.
They fought against Shílóu, the Liáo Military Commissioner, west of Xiánzhōu,
and defeated him.
They beheaded Shílóu on the battlefield,
and, with Lóushì, captured Xiánzhōu.
Mǎnhūtǔ surrendered with his department to Wòlǔgǔ.
Seven thousand households from neighboring tribes also came to submit.
Then, they fought against Hēbǔ, a Liáo general,
and defeated his army of several tens of thousands.
Tàizǔ praised him
and made him the military commander of Xiánzhōu.
When Wòlǔ attacked Gāo Yǒngchāng at Dōngjīng,
Wòlǔgǔ assisted him with the Xiánzhōu army.
Yēlǜ Niēlǐ, the Liáo Prince of Qínjìn, came to attack.
Dígǔnǎi, Lóushì, Pólúhuǒ, and others led twenty thousand men,
and, combining with Wòlǔgǔ's Xiánzhōu forces, went to attack him.
Hútúgǔ had previously rebelled and defected to Liáo.
He resided in Dōngjīng.
When Gāo Yǒngchāng occupied Dōngjīng,
Tàizǔ demanded his return.
When Wòlǔgǔ attacked Yǒngchāng,
he provisionally appointed Hútúgǔ as a Chiliarch.
Sǎndūlǔ and Èlǔbǔ were both without merit,
but were also provisionally appointed to office.
He also, by expediency, dismissed the provisional Móukè, Húbálǔ, Huánggē, Dájíbǎo, and others from their posts.
None of whom were guilty of any crime.
Tàizǔ heard of this
and fully reinstated Húbálǔ and the others as Móukè.
Hútúgǔ and the others were all dismissed.
Tàizǔ heard that Wòlǔgǔ's army often lacked horses,
while many official horses were hidden in private homes.
So he conducted an inspection.
Yēlǜ Niēlǐ and Fódǐng sent Wòlǔgǔ a letter,
requesting peace.
Wòlǔgǔ submitted Niēlǐ's letter along with his reply,
and further requested:
"If there are further letters,
how should I respond?"
An edict stated:
"If they come again to request peace,
you should say that Āshū and others rebelled and fled,
and because they were sought but not found, it led to military engagement.
Our envoy Sàilà was also not sent back.
If Sàilà is returned
and Āshū and others are handed over,
then discussion of peace can be reported to Us.
However, fear that the peace talks are not genuine.
Do not neglect your defenses."
Yēlǜ Niēlǐ's army was at Jílíshān.
Wòlǔgǔ, with ten thousand soldiers,
garrisoned Dōngjīng.
Tàizǔ sent Dígǔnǎi and Lóushì with another ten thousand soldiers to reinforce him.
An edict stated:
"The Liáo Emperor has lost the Way
and recklessly embarks on campaigns.
You, officers and soldiers,
should understand Our intention.
Those who resist orders shall be suppressed.
Those who submit shall be pacified.
Do not be greedy for plunder.
Do not engage in wanton slaughter.
The edict granted to Niēlǐ
can be delivered."
The edict to Niēlǐ stated:
"If you truly wish for peace,
you should depose the benighted ruler
and choose a worthy person to enthrone,
to conform to Our intention of punitive expeditions and compassion.
Only then can peace terms be discussed.
Otherwise,
We shall entirely annex your country.
Consider this carefully."
Niēlǐ replied to Wòlǔgǔ,
saying:
"If the defector Hénbó is returned,
then Āshū and others will be handed over."
The emperor said:
"Hénbó and the others surrendered after military engagement,
while Āshū fled due to his crimes in peacetime.
The circumstances are entirely different."
He again issued an edict to Niēlǐ,
ordering him to send Āshū to Xiǎnzhōu on the thirteenth day of this month,
and for each side to send high officials to discuss border affairs.
Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) and others attacked Xiǎnzhōu (顯州).
Wánýán Wòlún (完顏斡論), who was in charge of Dōngjīng (東京) affairs, came to join them with troops.
He immediately led three thousand soldiers to cross the Liáoshuǐ (遼水) first,
gaining over a thousand surrendered households.
They then advanced on Xiǎnzhōu (顯州).
Guō Yàoshī (郭藥師) came to raid them,
but Wòlún (斡論) repelled him.
Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) and others then fought Nīelǐ (捏里) and others at Jílímíngshān (蒺藜山),
soundly defeating the Liáo (遼) army.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Ālǐzhēnpō (阿里真陂),
capturing Fódǐng's (佛頂) family.
They then besieged Xiǎnzhōu (顯州),
attacking its southwestern side.
Soldier Shéndǔ (神篤) scaled the wall and entered first,
burning its Buddhist temple.
The smoke and flames choked the people,
and those defending the battlements could not stand.
All the armies took advantage of this,
and thus Xiǎnzhōu (顯州) was captured.
Thereupon,
the prefectures of Qián (乾), Yì (懿), Háo (豪), Huī (徽), Chéng (成), Chuān (川), Huì (惠), and others all surrendered.
Qiánzhōu (乾州) later became Lǘyáng Xiàn (閭陽縣).
Many Liáo (遼) imperial tombs were located here,
and a prohibition was issued against violating them.
The people from Chéngzhōu (成州) and Chuānzhōu (川州) were resettled in Tóngzhōu (同州) and Yínzhōu (銀州).
Nīelǐ (捏里) again sent a letter requesting peace.
Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古), acting on a previous imperial edict,
used Āshū (阿疎) as the basis for his reply
and responded to him.
He garrisoned his troops in Xiǎnzhōu (顯州) to await orders.
Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) and others were granted ten horses.
An imperial edict stated:
"You have crushed great enemies
and captured many cities.
We greatly commend you.
The Liáo (遼) ruler has not yet been captured,
and people's hearts are easily swayed.
Do not rely on victory and neglect your defenses."
Zhāng Chóng (張崇), the Liáo (遼) Military Governor of Shuāngzhōu (雙州), surrendered.
Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古), exercising his discretion, ordered his restoration to office,
and further stipulated that it be hereditary.
Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) had been in Xiánzhōu (咸州) for a long time,
achieving many merits,
but also indulging in many excesses.
Hélibǎo (劾里保) and Shuānggǔ (雙古) reported Wòlǔgǔ's (斡魯古) unlawful acts: not pursuing the Liáo (遼) emperor when he was in Zhōngjīng (中京) and could have been pursued,
falsifying reports about the abundant grain and fodder in Xiánzhōu (咸州),
and appropriating much of the captured people, wealth, and livestock from the attack on Xiǎnzhōu (顯州).
Nīelǐ (捏里) and Bólàshù (孛剌束) also reported that Bójǐn Mēnggé (孛菫瞢葛), Májí (麻吉), Wōlún (窩論), Chìrùn (赤閏), Ālàběn (阿剌本), Yǐlà (乙剌), and others had appropriated many people, wealth, and livestock.
Therefore, Shégē (闍哥) was appointed to replace him as the commander-in-chief of Xiánzhōu Lù (咸州路).
Shégē (闍哥) was also a son of the imperial clan.
He then replaced Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) in governing Xiánzhōu (咸州).
Initially,
Dígǔnǎi (迪古乃) and Lóushì (婁室) had reported that
among the newly surrendered people from the attack on Xiǎnzhōu (顯州),
the wealthy could be moved to Xiánzhōu Lù (咸州路),
while the poor should be moved to the interior.
Thereupon,
an imperial edict ordered Shégē (闍哥) to select those capable of managing affairs and appoint them as Móukè (謀克).
Those powerful local magnates who sincerely surrendered were to be nominated as Mèng'ān (猛安),
and their names recorded and reported.
The hungry and poor people
were to be relieved by the government,
and Shé Mǔ (闍母) was made his deputy commander.
After a long time,
over eight hundred households from Liáo Tōngzhōu (遼通州), Qízhōu (祺州), Shuāngzhōu (雙州), and Liáozhōu (遼州)
came to the Xiánzhōu Dūtǒng (咸州都統) to surrender.
The Emperor said:
"The Liáo (遼) people's taxes and levies are excessive,
and the people cannot endure their fate.
They have gathered to seek survival,
and they must not be disappointed.
Divide them among various departments
and settle them in good locations."
Tàizǔ (太祖) summoned Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) and questioned him personally.
Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) admitted his guilt.
Shégē (闍哥) interrogated Wōlún (窩論) and others.
An edict demoted Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) to Móukè (謀克),
and imprisoned Wōlún (窩論) and others.
In Tiānfǔ (天輔) 6th year (1122),
he died of illness on the way while campaigning against bandits at Niúxīnshān (牛心山).
During the Tiānjuàn (天眷) reign (1138-1141),
he was posthumously granted the title of Tèjìn (特進).
In Tiāndé (天德) 2nd year (1150),
he was granted the honor of being enshrined in Tàizǔ's (太祖) ancestral temple.
In Dàdìng (大定) 15th year (1175),
he was given the posthumous name Zhuāngyì (莊翼).
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火)
was a fifth-generation grandson of Ān Dì (安帝).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) attacked Liáo (遼),
he sent Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) to summon Dígǔnǎi's (迪古乃) troops.
He missed the deadline
and was flogged.
Later, with Húnhú (渾黜), he led four thousand men
to assist Lóushì (婁室) and Yínzhúgē (銀術哥) in attacking Huánglóng Fǔ (黃龍府).
Cílèhǎn (辭勒罕) and Zhébódé (轍孛得), brothers,
were from the Zhílí (直●里) tribe.
They often raided Yēlán Lù (耶懶路).
Mùzōng (穆宗) sent Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) to subdue them.
Upon reaching Ālíménhé (阿里門河),
Cílèhǎn (辭勒罕) feigned surrender,
then seized three hundred horses and cattle and left,
and again plundered twenty-five camps of the Wūlè (兀勒) tribe.
Tàizǔ (太祖) again sent Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) to subdue them.
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) crossed the Sūgǔnhé (蘇袞河),
recruiting and pacifying nearby tribes.
He then conscripted able-bodied men into an army.
Upon reaching Tèténgwúshuǐ (特滕吳水),
Zhébódé (轍孛得) feigned surrender,
then rebelled again.
He was captured and killed.
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) reached Tèlín Chéng (特鄰城)
and besieged it.
Cílèhǎn (辭勒罕) fled.
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) broke into the city
and captured his wife and children.
Cílèhǎn (辭勒罕) then surrendered,
saying:
"All my horses, cattle, and wealth are gone.
How shall I live?"
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) gave him ten horses.
The Zhílí (直●里) tribe produced good horses.
Tàizǔ (太祖) ordered Hégúliè Āxíhǎn (紇石烈阿習罕) to manage their livestock.
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) and his son Pósù (婆速)
both became Móukè (謀克).
In Tiānfǔ (天輔) 5th year (1121),
over ten thousand households were selected from the Mèng'ān (猛安) of various circuits
to settle and farm in Tàizhōu (泰州).
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) was made Dūtǒng (都統),
and granted fifty oxen for farming.
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) previously resided by the Ànchūhǔshuǐ (按出虎水),
and from then on, he moved his residence to Tàizhōu (泰州).
He also sent Shídé (拾得), Cháduān (查端), Ālǐtúhuān (阿里徒歡), Xītáhǎn (奚撻罕), and others to move there as well.
Only his clan nephew Sālāhē (撒剌喝), who had been adopted by Shìzǔ (世祖),
was uniquely allowed not to move.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) captured Yānjīng (燕京),
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) was the right wing.
His troops exited Jūyōngguān (居庸關),
greatly defeating the Liáo (遼) army,
and thus captured Jūyōng (居庸).
Xiāo Fēi (蕭妃) fled.
Dūjiān Gāo Liù (都監高六) and others came to offer their submission and beg for surrender.
Xígǔnǎi (習古乃) pursued Xiāo Fēi (蕭妃) to Gǔběikǒu (古北口),
but Xiāo Fēi (蕭妃) had already passed three days prior,
so he could not catch her and returned.
The Emperor ordered Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) and Húshílái (胡實賚) to lead light cavalry to pursue her.
Xiāo Fēi (蕭妃) had already gone far away.
They captured her attendant officials Tǒngjūn Chálà (統軍察剌) and Xuānhuī Chálà (宣徽查剌),
along with their families,
and two silver plaques and eleven seals.
When Diélà (迭剌) rebelled,
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) and Shígǔnǎi (石古乃) suppressed them.
Those officials who led their followers to surrender
were immediately allowed to command their original departments.
Tàizōng (太宗) gave them blank declarations and silver plaques.
At the same time, there was another Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火).
When Lóushì (婁室) pacified Shǎnxī (陝西),
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) and Shéngguǒ (繩果) supervised the battle.
Later, he served as the Magistrate of Píngyáng (平陽),
and Commissioner of Pacification for the Southwest Circuit,
finally ending his career as the Magistrate of Qìngyáng (慶陽).
Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) of Tàizhōu (泰州) repeatedly distinguished himself in border defense.
Tàizōng (太宗) granted him a set of robes
and also granted his son Pōushū (剖叔).
In the 8th year (1130),
he was given armor and helmets to bestow upon the Móukè (謀克) of his department.
In Tiānhuì (天會) 13th year (1135),
he was promoted to Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì (同中書門下平章事).
In Tiānjuàn (天眷) 1st year (1138),
while stationed at Wūgǔ Díliè Dì (烏骨迪烈地),
he passed away.
He was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司)
and given the posthumous name Gāngyì (剛毅).
His son, Pōushū (剖叔),
inherited the Mèng'ān (猛安) title.
In Tiānjuàn (天眷) 2nd year (1139),
he became the Deputy Dūtǒng (都統) of Tàizhōu (泰州).
His son, Wòdài (斡帶),
was a Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn (廣威將軍).
Pósù (婆速)
held the official title of Tèjìn (特進).
His son was Wúzāhū (吾扎忽).
Wúzhāhū
was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
At the age of twenty,
he was appointed Dūguǎn of the Běnbān Zhīhóu Lángjūn.
He achieved merit in campaigns
and was granted the title Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi.
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
he provisionally commanded the forces of Tàizhōu.
During the pacification of Shǎnxī,
when he reached Jīngzhōu,
he dealt a major blow to the Sòng army at Mǎxī Zhèn.
He was swiftly promoted to Níngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn
and inherited the title of Měng'ān.
He then served under Zōngbì with his own contingent,
acting as Quyền Dūtǒng.
At the end of Zhènglóng,
he followed Hǎilíng in the campaign against Sòng.
When the Qìdān rebelled,
he, along with Yíshì Mǎn, the Jiédùshǐ of Déchāng, jointly suppressed the Qìdān.
He was granted discretionary powers to act as he saw fit.
In the early Dàdìng period,
he was appointed Xiánpíng Yǐn
and stationed his troops in Tàizhōu.
Soon after, he was transferred to Línhuáng Yǐn
and concurrently served as Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān.
He, along with Púsǎn Húntǎn, the Guǎngníng Yǐn, followed Yuánshuài Yòu Dūjiān Shéntǔ Mǎn to relieve the siege of Línhuáng.
The Qìdān led their forces eastward,
and Wúzhāhū pursued them, catching up at Wālì Shān.
The Yāyī Měng'ān, Qìdān Hūláshú, assisted the enemy with his troops,
attacking the imperial army.
The imperial army suffered a defeat.
Wūlǐyǎ, the Jiédùshǐ of Tàizhōu, came to their rescue.
Before reaching Línhuáng, he encountered the enemy.
Wūlǐyǎ was defeated,
barely escaping with a few cavalrymen.
The enemy attacked Tàizhōu,
their morale greatly boosted.
The city was terrified,
and the officers and soldiers dared not sally forth.
The enemy scaled the city walls from all sides.
Yāyī Měng'ān Wūgǔsūn Ālǐbǔ led several soldiers, armed with battleaxes, along the walls,
engaging the enemy fiercely.
They cut down a great many,
and the enemy then retreated.
Tàizhōu was thus preserved.
Wúzhāhū then ordered the Móukè Púlúhún to relocate the populace to nearby towns and strategic strongholds,
awaiting the main army.
The following year,
he gathered thirteen thousand armored soldiers in Jìzhōu,
joined Yuánshuài Móuyǎn,
and defeated Wōwò at Chángluò.
He fought at Méngwù Hé
and at Xiànquán,
achieving merits in both.
He was appointed Húlǐgǎi Jiédùshǐ
and then died.
Wúzhāhū was intelligent and astute,
possessed talent and wisdom,
and was skilled in military strategy.
He often caught the enemy by surprise,
thus he could defeat the many with the few,
and everywhere he went, he was victorious.
He was known as
"Hú Jūn"
(Falcon General).
Shé Mǔ
was the eleventh son of Shìzǔ,
and the paternal half-brother of Tàizǔ.
When Gāo Yǒngchāng occupied Dōngjīng,
Wòlǔ went to attack him,
with Shé Mǔ and others serving as his aides.
After conquering Shěnzhōu, Shé Mǔ intercepted and virtually annihilated those who fled the city.
When they faced Yǒngchāng across the Wòlǐhuó Shuǐ,
the troops encountered a marsh and dared not advance.
Shé Mǔ led his contingent to cross first,
and then all the other armies crossed.
When the army reached the foot of Dōngjīng city,
people from inside the city came out to fight.
Shé Mǔ defeated them at Shǒushān,
annihilating their forces
and capturing five hundred horses.
When Wòlǔ Gǔ was removed from Xiánzhōu due to an offense,
Shé Mǔ replaced him.
Thus, Shé Mǔ became the Fùtǒng of Xiánzhōu Lù.
The Liao’s peace negotiations dragged on without success.
Tàizǔ advanced his troops
and issued an edict to the Xiánzhōu Lù Dūtǒng Sī,
ordering Xiégé to leave one thousand soldiers to guard the area,
while Shé Mǔ was to rendezvous with the remaining troops at Húnhé.
Tàizǔ attacked Shàngjīng,
which was Línhuáng Fǔ in reality,
but it refused to surrender.
The Liao people relied on their stored provisions to hold out.
The emperor personally supervised the battle,
and Shé Mǔ led his troops in the first assault,
capturing the outer city.
The Liúshǒu Tābùyě then led his forces out to surrender.
When Dūtǒng Gǎo’s army arrived at Zhōngjīng,
Shé Mǔ advanced from the west of the city along the Tǔhé.
Three thousand soldiers still remained in the city,
but they could not hold it.
It was subsequently captured.
When Zōnghàn and others attacked Xījīng,
Shé Mǔ and Lóushì, among others, built wooden shelters on the east side of the city to ward off arrows and stones.
On the northern corner, they filled the moat with straw.
More than ten thousand soldiers sallied forth from the city,
intending to burn the shelters.
Wēndíhǎn Púxiá led his troops to fight fiercely.
When the standard-bearer was wounded,
Púxiá personally took the flag
and fought with valor, repelling them.
They also constructed four-wheeled leather chariots,
which were taller than the battlements.
Shé Mǔ and his subordinates rode these chariots in the first assault.
The other armies followed,
and Xījīng was thus captured.
They fought five thousand Liao infantry and cavalry in the vicinity of Shuòzhōu,
beheading three hundred.
They then defeated three hundred Liao cavalry at Héyīn.
Five thousand Liao troops were encamped south of Mǎyì Xiàn.
They attacked and defeated them again,
demolishing their camps
and seizing all their chariots, horses, and equipment.
Thirty thousand Liao troops
formed camps west of Xījīng.
Shé Mǔ attacked them with three thousand.
Shé Mǔ ordered all his soldiers to dismount,
forming a battle line between the ditches and trenches,
saying:
"To attack ten with one,
one must not avoid the path of death;
otherwise, they cannot be made to fight."
He told his troops:
"If you do not defeat the enemy,
you cannot seek to live."
At this, everyone fought to the death,
and the Liao army was defeated.
They pursued them to their camp and then stopped.
The next day,
they again defeated more than seven hundred of their soldiers.
Yízhōu, of Xīngzhōng Fǔ, rebelled again.
Shé Mǔ suppressed them
and also issued an edict to pacify them.
The edict to Shé Mǔ said:
"The lands of Liao are all mine.
Even if they rebel again,
they are ultimately my people.
Allow them to cultivate their fields,
and do not invade or plunder them."
Bójǐn Méngguā, Xiébó, Wútà and others captured Qìdān Jiǔjīn,
and Xīngzhōng was pacified.
Shé Mǔ served as Nánlù Dūtǒng
to suppress Huílíbǎo.
The edict said:
"Huílíbǎo, with his disorderly crowd,
occupies dangerous strongholds.
His forces will inevitably collapse on their own.
If he does not raid,
there is no need to attack him."
Yēlǜ Àogǔzhé and others killed Huílíbǎo between Jǐng and Jì,
and his forces subsequently disintegrated.
Zhāng Jué rebelled, occupying Píngzhōu,
and entered Sòng territory.
Shé Mǔ went from Jǐnzhōu to suppress him.
Jué intended to use his troops to force the migration of the people of Qiān, Lái, Rùn, and Xí four prefectures.
When Shé Mǔ reached Rùnzhōu,
he attacked and routed Zhāng Jué’s army.
He pursued them northward to Yúguān,
sending a captive with a letter to entice them.
He again defeated Jué's troops northeast of Yíngzhōu,
intending to press on to capture Nánjīng while victorious.
It was then hot and rainy.
He retreated to encamp by the sea,
seeking water and grass to rest.
He sent Púhuī and Méngguā, two Měng'āns, to station at Rùnzhōu,
to control the unconquered prefectures and counties,
preventing them from communicating with Jué.
In the ninth month,
Shé Mǔ defeated Jué’s general Wáng Xiàogǔ at Xīn'ān
and routed Jué’s army at Lóufēng Kǒu.
He again fought Jué at Tù'ěr Shān,
where Shé Mǔ suffered a major defeat.
Tàizōng sent Zōngwàng to inquire about the state of Shé Mǔ’s defeated army.
Zōngwàng then used Shé Mǔ’s army to suppress Jué.
After Zōngwàng defeated Zhāng Jué,
Tàizōng pardoned Shé Mǔ
and summoned Zōngwàng to the capital.
Shémǔ連破偽都統 Zhāng Dūngù,
遂克 Nánjīng,
執 Dūngù 殺之.
上遣使迎勞之,
詔曰:
「聞下 Nánjīng,
撫定兵民,
甚善.
諸軍之賞,
卿差等以給之. 」
又詔曰:
「Nánjīng 疆埸如舊,
屯兵以鎮之.
命有司運米五萬石于 Guǎngníng,
給 Nánjīng、Rùnzhōu 戍卒. 」
遂下 Yízhōu,
拔 Chāyá Shān,
殺其節度使 Hán Qìngmín,
得糧五千石.
詔以南路歲饑,
許田獵.
其後 Sòng Tóng Guàn、Guō Yàoshī 治兵,
Shémǔ 輒因降人知之,
即具奏,
語在 Sòng Shì 中.
而 Zōnghàn、Zōngwàng 皆請伐 Sòng,
於是 Shémǔ 副 Zōngwàng 伐 Sòng,
Zōngwàng 以 Shémǔ 屬尊,
先皇帝任使有功,
請以為都統,
己監戰事.
於是 Shémǔ 為都統,
Sǎohē 副之,
敗 Guō Yàoshī 兵于 Báihé,
遂降 Yānshān,
以先鋒渡河圍 Biàn,
Sòng 人請盟.
將士分屯于 Ānsù、Xióng、Bà、Guǎng、Xìn 之境,
Zōngwàng 還 Shānxī,
Shémǔ 與 Liú Yánzōng 留 Yānjīng,
節制諸軍.
八月,
復伐 Sòng,
大軍克 Biànzhōu,
諸軍屯于城上.
城中諸軍潰而西出者十三萬人,
Shémǔ、Tálǎn 分擊,
大敗之.
師還,
Shémǔ 為元帥左都監,
攻 Héjiān,
下之,
大破敵兵萬餘於 Mòzhōu.
Zōngfǔ 為右副元 帥,
徇地 Zī、Qīng.
Shémǔ 與 Zōngbì 分兵破山谷諸屯.
Sòng Lǐ Chéng 兵圍 Zīzhōu,
Wūlíndá Tài 欲破之.
Shémǔ 克 Wéizhōu.
Dígǔbǔ、Shùlièsù 連破 Zhào Zǐfǎng 等兵,
至于 Héshàng.
Wūlíndá Tài 欲破敵于 Língchéngzhèn.
及議伐 Kāngwáng,
Shémǔ 欲先定 Héběi,
然後進討,
Tàizōng 乃酌取羣議之中,
使 Lóushì 取 Shǎnxī,
Zōnghàn、Zōngfǔ 南伐.
Tiānhuì 七年,
薨,
年四十.
Xīzōng 時,
追封 Wú Guówáng.
Tiāndé 二年,
配享 Tàizǔ Miàotíng.
Zhènglóng,
改封 Tánwáng.
Dàdìng 二年,
徙封 Lǔwáng,
諡 Zhuāngxiāng.
子 Zōng.
Zōng,
本名 Déshòu,
Shémǔ 第四子也.
奇偉有大志,
喜談兵.
Tiāndé 二年,
充護衞,
授 Wǔyì Jiāngjūn.
明年,
授世襲謀克,
擢御院通進,
遷 Hànlín Dàizhì,
兼修 Qǐjūzhù,
轉 Guózǐ Sīyè,
兼 Zuǒ Bǔquē.
Zhènglóng 初,
轉 Fúbǎoláng,
在宮職凡五年,
皆帶劍押領宿衞.
遷 Dàzōngzhèng Chéng,
以母憂去官.
以本官起復,
未幾,
遷 Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
改 Zuǒ Xiāoqí Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
明年,
Hǎilíng 幸 Nánjīng,
Zōng 至 Biàn.
Qìdān Sābā 反,
Zōng 為 Xiánpíng Yǐn,
兼本路兵馬都總管,
以甲仗四千付之,
許以便宜.
Zōng 出 Sōngtíng Guān,
取牛遞于 Guǎngníng.
聞 Shìzōng 即位,
將歸之.
Guǎngníng Yǐn Àndáhǎi 弟 Yānjīng 勸 Zōng,
乃還 Xīngzhōng.
Bái Yànjìng、Gēshíliè Zhìníng 使 Zōng 奉表降.
Zōng 見 Shìzōng 於 Liángyúwù,
授 Níngchāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
明年二月,
Qìdān 攻 Níngchāng,
Zōng 止有女直、渤海騎兵三十、漢兵百二十人,
自將擊之.
遇 賊千餘騎,
漢兵皆散走,
Zōng 與女直、渤海三十騎盡銳力戰,
身被二創,
所乘馬中箭而仆,
遂為所執.
居百餘日,
會賊中有 Línhuáng 民 Yílà Ātǎ 等,
盜馬授之,
得脫歸.
Zōng had been captured by the rebels for a long time,
and had fully learned their strengths and weaknesses.
He met with Grand Marshal Wán Yán Móuyǎn and Minister of Political Affairs Wán Yán Yuányí,
and said to them:
"The rebel forces are a disorganized rabble,
without discipline.
Defeating them is easy."
Thereupon, the Marshal's Residence wished to bestow military office upon him.
Zōng saw that Móuyǎn was greedy for plunder,
and missed opportunities.
Desiring to return to report to the emperor,
he refused to accept office,
saying:
"I have a secret matter
that must be reported to His Majesty in person."
That night,
he absconded.
Arriving at Guǎngníng,
he fraudulently took an post-horse,
and galloped to the capital.
However, the Marshal's Residence had already reported the matter in advance.
The emperor dispatched a palace envoy to question him, saying:
"As a Jìedù,
you failed to assess the numerical strength of your forces,
were defeated in battle and captured.
Fortunately, you escaped and returned,
yet you refused the order from the Marshal's Residence,
and presumptuously traveled by post-horse to the capital.
I will temporarily suspend your punishment.
You must quickly return to the army
and join forces to defeat the rebels."
Zōng replied in a memorial:
"Your subject is not one who shirks difficulties.
The matter required a face-to-face report,
so I had no choice but to come."
He was then summoned in,
and consequently reported in detail the rebels' strengths and weaknesses,
as well as the various armies' advances and retreats that did not align with the opportune moment.
The emperor ordered the high ministers to deliberate,
and they all considered his words to be true.
At this time,
an imperial edict had already appointed Púsàn Zhōngyì to replace Móuyǎn as Grand Marshal to advance and attack.
Thereupon, Zōng was appointed Minister of War,
and in his concurrent capacity, led the Right Wing Commander-in-Chief.
He commanded Zōng Níng, Wūyán Chálà, and Wūlíndá Lásā, each with one thousand soldiers,
totaling thirty thousand,
to assist Zhōngyì's army.
Upon reaching Huādào,
they encountered the rebels.
In the battle,
the Left Wing Commander-in-Chief, Zōng Hēng, was first defeated and fled.
[一０] Zhōngyì also retreated.
Zōng commanded his own unit to intercept and strike the rebels.
He waved his three hundred personal guards
to dismount and fight on foot,
preventing the rebels from succeeding.
The main army regrouped and arrived again,
combining their forces to attack.
The rebels were then defeated and fled.
Meanwhile, Grand Marshal and Right Supervising Army Gēshíliè Zhìníng led his army to arrive.
He pursued and caught Wōwò at Xiànquán,
thoroughly defeating them.
Zōng then joined Zhìníng and Túdān Kèníng
in pursuit to Qīdùhé,
where they inflicted another major defeat.
Grand Marshal Zhōngyì subsequently kept Zōng to follow him.
After the rebels were pacified,
he entered the court as Right Supervisor of the Privy Council.
Song troops occupied Hǎizhōu,
intending to penetrate deeper.
An imperial edict appointed Zōng as Grand Marshal and Right Supervising Army,
to go and defend against them.
Zōng was stationed in Shāndōng,
dividing his troops to garrison strategic points,
preventing the enemy from advancing west.
Soon after, he received an imperial edict
to consult on military affairs with Left Deputy Grand Marshal Gēshíliè Zhìníng.
In the fourth year,
Zōng came to court,
and memorialized, saying:
"The hot months are approaching,
and stationing troops on the border will make provisioning quite difficult.
I request that we await the cool autumn before advancing."
The emperor followed his request.
Upon his return to the army,
he was given a well-thought-out plan,
and bestowed with imperial robes, bows, and arrows.
In the ninth month,
they crossed the Huái River.
Zōng departed from Táng and Dèng,
and upon reaching Xiāngyáng,
won every battle.
The following year,
the Song people requested peace.
The army returned,
and he was appointed Commander of the Hénán Circuit.
The Yellow River burst its banks at Lǐgùdù,
with a branch flowing between Cáo and Shàn.
An imperial edict dispatched Liang Sù of the Directorate of Waterways to inspect the breach.
Zōng stated:
"The riverbed is silted up and cannot hold water,
hence the problem of breaches and overflows.
Now, to restore the river to its old course
would be difficult to accomplish quickly.
Even if it could be fortunately blocked,
it would inevitably burst its banks in Shāndōng in the future,
which would be worse than Cáo and Shàn.
Forcing a great levy on several prefectures along the river
would stir up public sentiment.
I fear the Song people might take advantage of the opportunity to incite and entice,
creating border trouble."
Liang Sù also requested to allow the two rivers to flow separately,
to reduce the force of the water.
Consequently, the blocking was halted.
In the tenth year,
he was summoned to the capital,
and appointed Administrator of Political Affairs.
The emperor said:
"Your memorial on the advantages and disadvantages of the Yellow River
greatly accords with my wishes.
I consider the corvée levies on the common people,
and the corruption of officials,
who collect taxes like sparks flying,
with expenses five times over.
Supplies piled up for years
rot and become unusable.
Such matters,
with countless flaws,
how can the common people endure them?
You participate in governing the court.
Choose what is beneficial and act,
to fulfill my expectations."
When discussing the southern border with the emperor,
Zōng said:
"The southerners send spies here
and often obtain our military information.
When we send spies,
they often fail to obtain accurate intelligence.
This is probably because of their generous rewards."
The emperor said:
"They use generous profits to finance spies,
merely wasting their wealth.
What can they accomplish?"
In the eleventh year,
he received an imperial edict to inspect the border.
[一一] In the sixth month,
he arrived at the army.
As they were about to battle,
he fell ill.
An imperial edict appointed Right Chancellor Gēshíliè Zhìníng to replace him,
and Zōng returned.
In the seventh month,
his illness worsened.
He left a memorial addressing the gains and losses of court governance,
and the advantages and disadvantages of border defense,
enduring his illness,
and had his son present it to the emperor.
He passed away
at the age of forty-six.
The emperor saw his last memorial,
and was immensely grieved.
He suspended court sessions,
and dispatched Privy Council Supervisor Jìng Sìhuī to offer sacrifices,
bestowing a thousand taels of silver, forty bolts of colored silk, and four hundred bolts of plain silk.
The emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Zōng diligently served the nation;
no one else could match him."
Initially,
Zōng had once requested to recruit poor people to guard the border and cultivate land,
providing them with grain.
Thus, the poor would not suffer from difficulties in eating,
while wealthy families would be free from the labor of alternating service,
and could focus on agriculture.
The emperor approved his words,
but it was not implemented.
In the seventeenth year,
the emperor said to his chancellors:
“The soldiers guarding the border
endure cold and heat year-round,
traveling back and forth for their shifts.
When they go to guard the border with horses and cattle,
they often all die.
Moreover, their farming season is taken away,
and their livelihoods are ruined.
I deeply pity them.
I wish to enable the common people to live peacefully in their villages,
and for the border defenses to be strong and secure.
What methods do you, my lords, have to achieve this?”
Left Chancellor Liángbì said:
“The border regions are unsuitable for cultivation,
and cannot be guarded for long,
which is why there are shifts.”
The emperor said:
“Do you, my lords, consider this urgent matter a trivial one?
Last year,
Councillor Zōng once spoke to me about this matter.
Someone like Zōng
can be said to have devoted his heart to the state.
Now, regarding the two circuits' Pacification Commissionerates, the Wūgǔlǐ Shílěi tribes, and the circuits of Línhuáng and Tàizhōu,
set up fortifications,
detail the plans, and report them to me.
I will personally review them.”
The emperor, recalling Zōngxù,
heard that his descendants' household expenses were insufficient,
and issued an edict granting them three thousand strings of cash.
In Míngchāng fifth year,
he was honored by being enshrined in Shìzōng's ancestral temple.
Collation Notes
Biography 10 Lóushì, Huónǚ, Móuyǎn, Zhòng (original name Shígǔnǎi), Hǎilǐ, Yínshúkě Gòuyīng (original name Tàilán), Májí (son Wòcè), Bálísu, Xígǔnǎi
Lóushì,
courtesy name Wòlǐyǎn,
was a member of the Wányán tribe.
At twenty-one,
he succeeded his father Báidá as chief of the seven Shuǐ tribes.
When Tàizǔ conquered Níngjiāngzhōu,
he sent Lóushì to persuade the Jurchens registered under the Liáo dynasty to surrender.
Thus, Yídùn Yìhǎi Lù Tàiwān Zhàosā and others surrendered.
He defeated the Liáo troops at Pólàgǎnshān.
Again, he defeated the Liáo troops,
capturing two generals.
Subsequently, both the Yìgǎi and Nàmòlán circuits surrendered.
He advanced his troops to Xiánzhōu,
and captured it.
Various tribes successively came to surrender,
and he captured the households of the northern Jurchens registered under Liáo.
Liáo Commander Yēlǜ Élǐwǔ came to guard the border with over two hundred thousand troops.
Tàizǔ hurried to Dálǔgǔchéng,
stopping west of Níngjiāngzhōu,
and summoned Lóushì.
Lóushì met the emperor in the army.
The emperor saw that Lóushì's horses were mostly exhausted,
and gave him three hundred,
assigning him to the Right Wing Commander Zōnghàn's army.
With Yínshúkě, he led troops to charge into the enemy's center,
breaking through the formation nine times,
each time fighting fiercely to get out.
Again, he guarded the border with Yínshúkě.
When the Jiǔbǎi Xīyíng and other tribes surrendered,
he then attacked Huánglóngfǔ with Yínshúkě.
The emperor sent Wányán Húnchù, Póluóhuǒ, and Shígǔnǎi with four thousand soldiers to assist him,
and defeated over ten thousand Liáo soldiers at Báimǎpò.
Zōngxióng and others captured Jīnshānxiàn,
and sent Lóushì to lead two thousand soldiers
to recruit the scattered people along the mountains.
Yēlǜ Niēlǐ's army was stationed at Jílízīshān,
Wòlǔgǔ, Lóushì and others defeated them,
and then took Xiǎnzhōu.
When Tàizǔ took Huánglóngfǔ,
Lóushì requested:
“Huánglóng is a major city,
and also remote.
If there is any trouble,
neighboring prefectures will stir up and rise.
Please allow me to garrison it with my division.”
Tàizǔ agreed,
and also merged the various circuits' Mòkè,
appointing Lóushì as Wànhù,
to guard Huánglóngfǔ.
He was promoted to Dūtǒng,
and followed Gǎo in taking Zhōngjīng.
With Xīyǐn and others, he ambushed and drove away Díliù, Héshàng, Yǎlǐsī, etc.,
defeated the Xī King Xiámò,
and received the surrender of Xī部的西節度 Élǐlà.
The Liáo emperor fled westward from Yuānyāngpò,
and Lóushì and others pursued him to Báishuǐpò,
capturing treasures from his inner treasury.
Lóushì then, with Shémǔ, attacked and captured Xījīng.
Again, with Shémǔ, he went to Tiāndé, Yúnnèi, Níngbiān, and Dōngshèng.
Their officials and people all surrendered,
and Āshū was captured.
The Xià people sent aid to Liáo,
their troops arriving at Tiāndé.
Lóushì sent Tūniǎn and Bǔ** with two hundred cavalry as scouts.
The Xià people defeated them,
almost annihilating them.
Ātǔhǎn then went with two hundred cavalry,
but encountered an ambush,
and only Ātǔhǎn escaped back.
At that time, it had been raining for a long time,
and the generals wanted to rest.
Lóushì said:
“They have defeated our cavalry twice.
If we do not go back,
they will think us timid,
and immediately come to attack us.”
So he selected a thousand cavalry,
and went with Xíshī and Bálísu.
Wòlǔ was impressed by his words,
and followed him.
Lóushì departed Língyělǐng at dawn,
leaving Bálísu with two hundred soldiers to hold the strategic pass.
They captured a prisoner and questioned him,
learning that their commander was Lǐ Liángfǔ.
Approaching Yěgǔ,
they climbed a high point to observe.
The Xià people, relying on their numbers, were not in formation,
and were crossing the river to form ranks.
He then sent someone to report to Wòlǔ.
Lóushì divided his army into two,
alternately charging in and retreating out,
fighting back and forth for thirty *lǐ*.
After crossing Yíshuǐ,
Wòlǔ's army also arrived,
and they jointly attacked and defeated them.
Liáo Commander Dàshí attacked Fèngshèngzhōu,
encamping twenty-five *lǐ* east of Lóngmén.
Lóushì, Zhàolǐ, Mǎ Héshàng and others took them with their troops,
capturing Dàshí alive,
whereupon his troops surrendered.
Liáo Bìlǐlà, who was guarding Fèngshèngzhōu,
abandoned the city and fled.
Later, with Zōngwàng, he pursued the Liáo emperor.
Lóushì and Púchá, with twenty cavalry, awaited the enemy,
and defeated their three thousand troops at Sānshān.
When a thousand men were about to advance to Fèngshèngzhōu,
Púchá again defeated them,
captured their commander, and returned.
The Xià people stationed troops at Kědūnguǎn.
Zōnghàn sent Lóushì to garrison Shuòzhōu,
and build a city twenty *lǐ* southwest of Bàdéshān.
He then defeated twenty thousand Xiānpíng Xiànbīng soldiers west of Shuòzhōu,
capturing their commander Zhào Gōngzhí.
Afterward, he again ambushed the Liáo emperor at Yúdūgǔ,
and captured him.
He was granted an iron certificate,
meaning that only for capital offenses would he be flogged;
other offenses would not be questioned.
Yínshúkě (銀术可) besieged Tài-yuán (太原).
The Sòng (宋) commissioner Liú Zhēn (劉臻) came to rescue Tài-yuán (太原),
leading an army of 100,000 out of Shòu-yáng (壽陽).
Lóushì (婁室) defeated them.
Subsequently, he defeated several thousand Sòng (宋) soldiers at Yú-cì (榆次).
Sòng (宋) General Zhāng Hào's (張灝) army came out of Fén-zhōu (汾州).
Bálí-sù (拔离速) attacked and drove them away.
Hào (灝) re-established his camp at Wén-shuǐ (文水).
Lóushì (婁室), Tūgě-sù (突葛速), and Bálí-sù (拔离速) fought with them,
and Hào (灝) was greatly defeated.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) pacified Tài-yuán (太原).
Lóushì (婁室) took Fén-zhōu (汾州) and Shí-zhōu (石州),
as well as their subordinate counties Wēn-quán (溫泉), Fāng-shān (方山), and Lí-shí (離石).
Púchá (蒲察) captured Shòu-yáng (壽陽),
and took Píng-dìng-jūn (平定軍) and Lè-píng (樂平).
He then persuaded Liáo-zhōu (遼州) and the counties of Yú-shè (榆社), Liáo-shān (遼山), and Hé-shùn (和順) to surrender.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) hastened to Biàn-zhōu (汴州),
ordering Lóushì (婁室) and others to proceed first to Hé-nán (河南) via the Píng-yáng (平陽) road.
He said:
"If you reach Zé-zhōu (澤州),
and meet Sàilǐ (賽里), Pólú-huǒ (婆盧火), and Xíshī (習失),
you should advance together."
Xíshī's (習失) vanguard, three móukè (謀克),
defeated 3,000 Sòng (宋) soldiers at Xiāng-yuán (襄垣).
They encountered an ambush of 2,000 soldiers
and defeated them again.
Sālàdá (撒剌荅) broke through Tiān-jǐng-guān (天井關),
and again defeated infantry south of the Kǒngzǐ-miào (孔子廟).
He then captured Hé-yáng (河陽).
When Lóushì's (婁室) army arrived,
they crossed the river
and advanced towards Xī-jīng (西京).
The city's troops came out to resist,
but Xíshī (習失) counter-attacked and defeated them.
Xī-jīng (西京) surrendered.
Lóushì (婁室) took Yǎn-shī (偃師).
Yǒng-ān-jūn (永安軍) and Gǒng-xiàn (鞏縣) surrendered.
Sālàdá (撒剌荅) defeated Sòng (宋) soldiers at Sì-shuǐ (汜水).
At this point,
Xíng-yáng (滎陽), Xíng-zé (滎澤), Zhèng-zhōu (鄭州), and Zhōng-móu (中牟) all surrendered one after another.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) had already joined forces with Zōngwàng (宗望) at Biàn (汴),
and sent Lóushì (婁室) to lead his army towards Shǎn-jīn (陝津),
to attack the remaining unconquered counties of Hé-dōng (河東).
Ālítǔhǎn (阿离土罕) defeated the enemy on the river.
Sā'àn (撒按) defeated the enemy beneath Shǎn-chéng (陝城).
Gǔshāhǔ (鶻沙虎) received the surrender of 300 wall defenders from Guó-zhōu (虢州),
and then captured Shǎn-fǔ (陝府).
Xígu-nǎi (習古乃) and Sānggǔn (桑袞) defeated scattered Shǎn (陝) soldiers northwest of Píng-lù (平陸).
Huónǚ (活女) separately defeated the enemy at Píng-lù (平陸).
Lóushì (婁室) defeated an army of 20,000 from Pú (蒲) and Jiě (解),
completely annihilating them.
Ān-yì (安邑) and Jiě-zhōu (解州) both surrendered,
and he then captured Hé-zhōng-fǔ (河中府),
receiving the surrender of Jiàng (絳), Cí (慈), Xí (隰), and Shí (石) and other prefectures.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) went to Luò-yáng (洛陽),
sending Lóushì (婁室) to take Shǎn-xī (陝西).
He defeated the Sòng (宋) general Fàn Zhì-xū's (范致虛) army,
captured Tóng (同) and Huá (華) prefectures,
and took Jīng-zhào-fǔ (京兆府),
capturing the Sòng (宋) commissioner Fù Liàng (傅亮).
He then captured Fèng-xiáng (鳳翔).
Ālín (阿隣) and others defeated a large Sòng (宋) army at Hé-zhōng (河中).
Wòlǔ (斡魯) defeated the Sòng (宋) army of Liú Guāng-liè (劉光烈) at Féng-yì (馮翊).
É'tèlà (訛特剌) and Sānggǔn (桑袞) defeated the enemy at Wèi-shuǐ (渭水),
and then took Xià-guī (下邽).
Zōnghàn (宗翰) joined Zōngfǔ (宗輔) to attack King Kāng (康王),
ordering Lóushì (婁室) and Púchá (蒲察) to focus solely on Shǎn-xī (陝西),
with Pólú-huǒ (婆盧火) and Shéngguǒ (繩果) supervising the battles.
Shéngguǒ (繩果) and others encountered the enemy at Pú-chéng (蒲城) and Tóng-zhōu (同州),
defeating them both.
Lóushì (婁室) and Púchá (蒲察) captured Dān-zhōu (丹州),
defeated Lín-zhēn (臨真),
and advanced to capture Yán-ān-fǔ (延安府).
They then received the surrender of Suī-dé-jūn (綏德軍) and sixteen other walled camps like Jìng-biān (靜邊) and Huái-yuǎn (懷遠),
and again defeated Qīng-jiàn-chéng (青澗城).
The Sòng (宋) pacification commissioner Zhé Kě-qiú (折可求) surrendered Lín (麟), Fǔ (府), and Fēng (豐) three prefectures,
as well as nine fortresses and walled camps,
to Lóushì (婁室).
All nine camps under Jìn-níng (晉寧) surrendered,
but Jìn-níng-jūn (晉寧軍) had not fallen for a long time.
Lóushì (婁室) wanted to leave it,
but Sàilǐ (賽里) disagreed,
saying:
"This borders Xià (夏),
and will inevitably lead to other changes."
There were no wells in the city,
and they daily drew water from the river for drinking.
So a channel was dug to the east,
draining its water,
and the city was thus distressed.
Lǐ Wèi (李位) and Shí Yǐ (石乙) opened the city gate and surrendered.
The various generals led their troops into the city.
The defending general Xú Huī-yán (徐徽言) held the inner city,
fighting for three days.
When his forces scattered,
Huī-yán (徽言) fled,
but was captured.
He was ordered to bow,
but refused.
Threatened with weapons,
he remained unmoved.
He was tied up in the camp.
Those who had surrendered earlier were sent to persuade him,
but Huī-yán (徽言) cursed loudly.
He and Commissioner Sūn Áng (孫昂) both refused to submit,
so they were both killed.
Then Dìng-ān-bǎo (定安堡), Wèi-píng-zhài (渭平寨), and Fū (鄜) and Fāng (坊) two prefectures surrendered.
At this point,
Lóushì (婁室) and Pólú-huǒ (婆盧火) guarded Yán-ān (延安),
Zhé Kě-qiú (折可求) garrisoned Suī-dé (綏德),
and Púchá (蒲察) returned to guard Pú-zhōu (蒲州).
Yán-ān (延安), Fū (鄜), and Fāng-zhōu (坊州) were all ruined and devastated.
Few people remained.
Lóushì (婁室) established official offices to pacify them.
A separate general, Wòlún (斡論), captured Jiàn-chāng-jūn (建昌軍).
Jīng-zhào-fǔ (京兆府) rebelled,
and Lóushì (婁室) again attacked and pacified it.
He then went with Ālúbǔ (阿盧補) and Móulǐyě (謀里也) to Sān-yuán (三原).
Égē-jīn (訛哥金) and Āgǔ-yù (阿骨欲) attacked the Chún-huà (淳化) army,
defeating them.
Lóushì (婁室) attacked Gān-zhōu (乾州).
A covered siege approach had already been built
and siege engines arranged,
when the prefecture surrendered.
He then advanced and captured Bīn-zhōu (邠州),
and encamped at Jīng-zhào (京兆).
The cities and towns of Shǎn-xī (陝西) that had already surrendered and been pacified
frequently rebelled again.
Therefore, Ruì-zōng (睿宗) was appointed Right Deputy Field Marshal,
to command the Shǎn-xī (陝西) expedition.
At this time, Lóushì (婁室) was already ill.
Ruì-zōng (睿宗) fought Zhāng Jùn (張浚) at Fù-píng (富平).
Zōngbì's (宗弼) left flank had already retreated,
but Lóushì (婁室) fought bravely on the right flank,
and the army's morale was restored.
Zhāng Jùn's (張浚) army was then defeated.
Ruì-zōng (睿宗) said:
"Fighting fiercely despite illness,
in service of the king,
thus defeating a formidable enemy –
even ancient famous generals could not have done more."
He gave him the rhinoceros horn, jade, gold, and silver vessels he used,
as well as armor and helmets,
and seven horses.
In the eighth year of Tiān-huì (天會)
he died.
In the thirteenth year,
he was posthumously granted the title of Jié-dù-shǐ (節度使) of Tài-níng-jūn (泰寧軍),
concurrently Shì-zhōng (侍中),
and additionally Tàizǐ-tàishī (太子太師).
In the first year of Huáng-tǒng (皇統),
he was posthumously granted Kāifǔ-yítóng-sānsī (開府儀同三司),
and posthumously enfeoffed as Xīn-wáng (莘王).
According to the Zhèng-lóng (正隆) precedent, he was re-granted Jīnyuán-jùn-wáng (金源郡王),
and enshrined in the ancestral temple of Tài-zōng (太宗),
with the posthumous title Zhuàngyì (壯義).
His sons were Huónǚ (活女), Móuyǎn (謀衍), and Shígu-nǎi (石古乃).
Huónǚ (活女),
at the age of seventeen, participated in the attack on Níng-jiāng-zhōu (寧江州).
He fought bravely and was severely wounded,
being carried out of the battle line.
Tài-zǔ (太祖) looked down from a height and saw him,
asked about him,
and knowing he was Lóushì's (婁室) son,
personally comforted him and bestowed medicine,
sighing:
"This child will surely become a famous general in the future."
During the attack on Jì-zhōu (濟州),
he defeated 8,000 enemy soldiers.
When he encountered the enemy at Xìn-zhōu (信州),
Yílà-běn (移剌本) was trapped in the formation,
but Huónǚ (活女) fought bravely to rescue him,
and the enemy then fled north.
He defeated Yēlǜ Fó-dǐng (耶律佛頂) and other forces at Shěn-zhōu (瀋州).
When Zōnghàn (宗翰) attacked Xī (奚) King Xiá-mò (霞末) with his army,
Huónǚ (活女) with 300 soldiers
defeated 2,000 enemy soldiers.
He followed in the attack on the Yǐ-shì (乙室) tribe,
defeated them,
and destroyed their two camps.
When the Diélà (迭剌) tribe rebelled,
he led two móukè (謀克) to charge in,
and greatly defeated them.
Huó Nǚ (活女) often followed Lóu Shì (婁室) in besieging Tài Yuán (太原).
The Sòng (宋) general Zhǒng Shīzhōng (种師中) came to his aid with an army of one hundred thousand,
but Huó Nǚ (活女) defeated him.
The great army reached the river,
but there were no boats,
so they could not cross.
Lóu Shì (婁室) sent Huó Nǚ (活女) to scout up and down the river.
Huó Nǚ (活女) led three hundred soldiers,
starting from Mèng Jīn (孟津) downstream,
and determined a passable crossing.
He then led his army across,
and the great army all followed him.
The Sòng (宋) general Guō Jīng (郭京) led tens of thousands of soldiers out,
advancing towards Lóu Shì's (婁室) camp.
Huó Nǚ (活女) furiously attacked from the flank,
the enemy fell into disarray,
and was subsequently routed.
When the army returned,
they defeated the enemy at Píng Lù Dù (平陸渡),
and acquired their boats to cross.
They also used their troops to defeat the enemy at Zhāng Diàn Yuán (張店原).
At that time, Tún Liú (屯留), Tài Píng (太平), and Yì Chéng (翼城) all had formidable enemies,
and all were defeated.
He also divided his troops to take Shǎn Xī (陝西).
Pú Zhōu (蒲州) surrendered,
and Huó Nǚ (活女) was left to garrison it.
When Fèng Xiáng (鳳翔) was attacked,
Huó Nǚ (活女) was the first to ascend the walls.
When Ruì Zōng (睿宗) pacified Shǎn Xī (陝西),
Huó Nǚ (活女) was made a Dū Tǒng (都統),
and then attacked Jīng Zhōu (涇州),
defeating its forces.
Wáng Kāishān (王開山) blocked their return route with troops,
challenging them to battle.
They engaged twice,
and he was defeated twice,
whereupon Jīng Zhào (京兆) and the various counties of Fèng Xiáng (鳳翔) surrendered.
When Lóu Shì (婁室) died,
Huó Nǚ (活女) inherited the Hé Zhā Měng'ān (合扎猛安) position
and succeeded him as the Wàn Hù (萬戶) of the Huáng Lóng Fǔ Lù (黃龍府路).
In Tiān Juàn (天眷) 3,
he became Yuán Shuài Yòu Dū Jiān (元帥右都監),
and was promoted to Zuǒ Jiān Jūn (左監軍).
When the Yuán Shuài Fǔ (元帥府) was abolished,
he was made Ān Huà Jūn Jié Dù Shǐ (安化軍節度使).
He successively held the post of Jīng Zhào Yǐn (京兆尹),
was enfeoffed as Gǔang Píng Jùn Wáng (廣平郡王).
Following the precedent of Zhèng Lóng (正隆),
he was re-enfeoffed as Dài Guó Gōng (代國公),
and then promoted to Suí Guó Gōng (隋國公).
His posthumous title was Zhēn Jì (貞濟),
and he died at the age of sixty-one.
Móu Yǎn (謀衍)
possessed extraordinary strength and courage,
and was skilled at fighting with a long spear.
During the Tiān Juàn (天眷) period,
he served as Pái Yìn Zhī Hòu (牌印祗候),
was granted the title Xiǎn Wǔ Jiāng Jūn (顯武將軍),
and promoted to Fú Bǎo Láng (符寶郎).
In Huáng Tǒng (皇統) 4,
his elder brother Huó Nǚ (活女) inherited the Wàn Hù (萬戶) of Jì Zhōu Lù (濟州路),
and ceded his personal Guǎn Ào Jí Měng'ān (親管奧吉猛安) to Móu Yǎn (謀衍).
The imperial court approved this,
and he provisionally held the position of Jì Zhōu Lù Wàn Hù (濟州路萬戶).
In the 8th year,
he became Yuán Shuài Yòu Dū Jiān (元帥右都監).
In Tiān Dé (天德) 3,
he became Shùn Tiān Jūn Jié Dù Shǐ (順天軍節度使),
and successively held the posts of Hé Jiān (河間) and Lín Huáng Yǐn (臨潢尹).
A few months later, he was transferred to Pú Sù Lù Bīng Mǎ Dū Zǒng Guǎn (婆速路兵馬都總管).
When Sā Bā (撒八) rebelled,
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) went to suppress him.
At this time, Shì Zōng (世宗) was the Dōng Jīng Liú Shǒu (東京留守).
He was returning from personally leading an expedition to suppress Kuò Lǐ (括里),
and met Móu Yǎn (謀衍) in Cháng Ān Xiàn (常安縣),
entrusting all his armored soldiers to him.
When Shì Zōng (世宗) returned to Dōng Jīng (東京),
Wán Yán Fú Shòu (完顏福壽) and Gāo Zhōngjiàn (高忠建) led their southern expeditionary forces,
defecting back to Dōng Jīng (東京).
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) also led his army to join them,
and immediately sought an audience, treating Shì Zōng (世宗) with the rites of a subject.
Subsequently, Gāo Cúnfú (高存福) and Lǐ Yànlóng (李彥隆) were executed.
Móu Yǎn (謀衍), Fú Shòu (福壽), Zhōngjiàn (忠建), and other generals, officials, and common people urged him to ascend the throne.
Shì Zōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
and appointed Móu Yǎn (謀衍) as Yòu Fù Yuán Shuài (右副元帥).
Dū Tǒng (都統) Bái Yànjìng (白彥敬)
and Fù Tǒng (副統) Hé Shíliè Zhìníng (紇石烈志寧) were in Běi Jīng (北京),
refusing to accept the imperial decree.
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) attacked them,
encountering their forces on the border of Jiàn Zhōu (建州).
They all refused to fight,
and Yànjìng (彥敬) and Zhìníng (志寧) subsequently surrendered.
In the first month of the second year,
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) led various armies to suppress Wō Wò (窩斡),
mustering troops in Jì Zhōu (濟州).
With thirteen thousand armored soldiers,
they passed Tái Zhōu (泰州),
and arrived at Shù Hǔ Yá (术虎崖).
Thereupon, they abandoned their baggage,
carrying only a few days' provisions,
and pursued on light cavalry.
At this time, Wō Wò (窩斡) had recently been defeated at Tái Zhōu (泰州),
and was about to flee to Jì Zhōu (濟州).
Móu Yǎn's (謀衍) army reached the south of Cháng Luò (長濼),
captured enemy spies,
and learned that the enemy was planning to intercept supply convoys via a different route.
So he divided his forces to meet them.
An enemy officer who had resigned came to surrender.
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) adopted his strategy,
and immediately rushed at night to intercept the enemy's baggage train.
Suddenly, a great wind blew,
preventing them from lighting torches,
and the road was dark, making it impossible to discern each other.
By dawn, they had only traveled over thirty *lǐ*.
As they neared the enemy camp,
the generals and soldiers rested briefly.
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) led several tens of skilled archers on horseback
to reconnoiter.
However, Dū Tǒng (都統) Zhìníng (志寧) and Kèníng (克寧) and others
had already defeated over twenty thousand enemy troops at Cháng Luò (長濼),
killing many during the pursuit.
The enemy then fled west.
Zhìníng's (志寧) army first caught up with them at Mú Hé (霿●河),
and fiercely attacked and defeated them.
But Móu Yǎn (謀衍) was greedy for plunder,
and did not pursue further,
allowing the enemy to escape.
They then entered the territory of Yì Zhōu (懿州),
capturing the counties of Líng Shān (靈山), Tóng Chāng (同昌), Huì Hé (惠和), etc.,
attempting to take Běi Jīng (北京),
and attacking Sān Hán Xiàn (三韓縣) to the west.
Only Kèníng's (克寧) army continued the pursuit.
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) feigned that his horses were weak
and returned to Yì Zhōu (懿州).
Upon hearing this,
the emperor issued an edict severely reprimanding Móu Yǎn (謀衍),
appointing Pú Sàn Zhōngyì (僕散忠義) as Yòu Fù Yuán Shuài (右副元帥) to replace him,
and Hé Shíliè Zhìníng (紇石烈志寧) as Yòu Jiān Jūn (右監軍) to replace Wán Yán Fú Shòu (完顏福壽).
Meanwhile, Móu Yǎn's (謀衍) son Xié Gē (斜哥) was violent and unruly in the army,
so an imperial edict ordered him to return to his native place.
When Móu Yǎn (謀衍) arrived at the capital,
he was appointed Tóng Pàn Dà Zōng Zhèng Shì (同判大宗正事).
Shì Zōng (世宗) reprimanded him, saying:
"I appointed you as a general,
but you did not pursue the rebels;
your crime should be punished.
Because your father Lóu Shì (婁室) had great merits,
I specifically spare you from death.
Although you are not of the imperial clan,
you are granted this position,
so you should strive hard."
Not long after,
a soldier from Sù Pín Lù (速頻路) named Shù Lǐgǔ (术里古)
accused Xié Gē (斜哥) of sending a letter to Móu Yǎn (謀衍) to conspire rebellion.
The authorities submitted the letter along with the accusation.
Shì Zōng (世宗) discerning the falsehood,
ordered the accuser to be interrogated.
Shù Lǐgǔ (术里古) confessed,
and was subsequently executed.
Móu Yǎn (謀衍) was summoned, and the emperor said to him:
"Someone accused your son of plotting rebellion.
I knew that you would never do such a thing.
Now the accuser has indeed confessed his crime,
so you should understand my intention."
Initially,
when Wō Wò (窩斡) was rampant,
the emperor ordered Wēn Díhǎn Ālúdài (溫迪罕阿魯帶) to guard Gǔ Běi Kǒu (古北口).
When Wō Wò (窩斡) was defeated at Xiàn Quán (陷泉),
he entered the Xī (奚) territory
and led various Xī (奚) tribes to attack Gǔ Běi Kǒu (古北口).
Ālúdài (阿魯帶), because it was his wife's birthday,
rashly left the army by sixty *lǐ*.
When the rebels heard of this,
they came to raid,
killing and wounding many soldiers.
Ālúdài (阿魯帶) was stripped of his rank.
An imperial edict ordered Móu Yǎn (謀衍),
Pú Chá Wūlǐyǎ (蒲察烏里雅), and Pú Chá Tōng (蒲察通) to take three thousand soldiers
and join the previously stationed troops
to attack them.
They captured the rebel leader Měng'ān Hé Zhù (猛安合住).
Not long after,
Wō Wò's (窩斡) rebellion was quelled,
and they returned.
In the 7th year,
he was sent out as Běi Jīng Liú Shǒu (北京留守).
The emperor held court in the side hall,
bestowed food,
and imperial robes, belts, and a sword,
saying to him:
"Because you are an elder statesman,
I wish to distribute the arduous and leisurely duties,
hence I grant you this position;
you should strive hard."
He was then transferred to Dōng Jīng Liú Shǒu (東京留守)
and enfeoffed as Róng Guó Gōng (榮國公).
In Dà Dìng (大定) 11,
he died,
at the age of sixty-four.
Móuyǎn's nature was loyal and honest.
He was skilled at polo and hunting.
At the time, the general consensus was that although his strategies and intelligence were not equal to his father's,
his bravery was very much like his.
Zhòng,
originally named Shígǔnǎi.
His physique was imposing,
and he understood Jurchen, Khitan, and Chinese characters.
His elder brother, Wòlǔ, was a tǒngjūn (commander-in-chief).
Wòlǔ loved Zhòng's talent
and wanted him to become familiar with official affairs.
Whenever he handled matters,
Zhòng was always by his side.
When Wòlǔ encountered issues, he would ask Zhòng about them.
Zhòng's responses were like an echo.
Wòlǔ sighed and said,
"This child will surely become an outstanding official."
In the early years of Huángtǒng,
he was made a hùwèi (imperial guard)
and granted the hereditary title of móukè.
In Tiāndé元年 (1149),
he temporarily managed his elder brother Huónǚ's post as Jìzhōu wànhù (Myriad Household of Jìzhōu).
His administration of the territory was well-regarded.
He was appointed Bīnzhōu cìshǐ (Prefect of Bīnzhōu),
but left office due to mourning for his mother.
He was recalled to serve as zhījīshí jūnfàn (administrator of military affairs in Jīshí)
and then transferred to tóngzhī Hénán Yǐn (Vice Administrator of Hénán).
In Zhènglóng 六年 (1161),
he participated in the campaign against Sòng
as the fùdūzǒngguǎn (Deputy Commander-in-Chief) of the Shényǒng Army.
After returning north with the main army,
he was appointed tóngzhī Dàxīng Yǐn (Vice Administrator of Dàxīng).
He commanded two thousand soldiers,
reinforcing the garrison in Zūnhuà
to guard against the Khitans.
He was promoted to Xīnánlù zhāotǎoshǐ (Pacification Commissioner of the Southwest Route),
concurrently serving as Tiāndéjūn jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Tiāndé Prefecture).
His governance emphasized loyalty and trustworthiness,
and his judicial decisions were fair.
The barbarian tribes did not dare to raid the border.
He was summoned to serve as zuǒfùdūdiǎnjiǎn (Left Vice Commander of the Palace Guards).
His palace guard duties were strict and meticulous.
Everything he did followed a set rule,
and later successors observed his methods,
unable to change them.
Shìzōng often said to his attendants,
"When Shígǔnǎi is on duty,
My sleep is more peaceful."
Five years later,
the Sòng people requested peace,
agreeing to be a nephew state
and not to claim vassalage.
Zhòng was sent as the bào wèn shǐ (envoy for reciprocation).
Zhòng requested instructions on the protocol for meeting the Sòng ruler.
Shìzōng said,
"If the Sòng ruler personally rises to receive the letter,
then present it to him."
Upon arrival in Sòng,
everything was performed according to the prescribed ritual.
During the Zhènglóng campaign,
the Sòng people had captured Wányán Shǒunéng, the cìshǐ of Shāngzhōu, and taken him back.
By this time,
Zhòng retrieved Shǒunéng and returned with him.
The emperor praised him.
He was promoted to dūdiǎnjiǎn (Commander of the Palace Guards),
concurrently serving as shìwèiqīnjūn dūzhīhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards).
He was then transferred to Hénánlù tǒngjūnshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of Hénán Route).
The emperor said,
"You, my lord, served close to me,
with caution and prudence.
Hénán controls the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and is a crucial area for the country.
You must exert yourself even more."
He was bestowed with a horse, a golden belt, and a jade túhú (tugh or hawk ornament).
Later, due to an offense,
he was relieved of his post.
After a long time,
he was reinstated as Xīběilù zhāotǎoshǐ (Pacification Commissioner of the Northwest Route).
He was then made Běijīng liúshǒu (Resident Commissioner of Běijīng),
where he died.
Hǎilǐ,
a nephew of Lóushì.
His physique was robust and impressive,
and he was skilled at using the spear.
When Lóushì was Huánglóngfǔ wànhù (Myriad Household of Huánglóng Prefecture),
Hǎilǐ accompanied him in his relocation to Shújí'émǔ.
He followed Lóushì in pursuing the Liáo ruler to Adūn Shān in Shuòzhōu.
The Liáo ruler escaped with several dozen horsemen.
Lóushì dispatched Hǎilǐ and Zhúté
to meet the Liáo ruler
and persuade him to surrender.
The Liáo ruler, already desperate and exhausted,
waited to the east of Adūn Shān.
The Sòng people, fearing the completion of the plank road,
came to resist with troops.
He defeated their forces
and was awarded one hundred fifty liǎng of silver and ten slaves.
In Tiānjuàn 元年 (1138),
he was promoted to Sùzhí jiāngjūn (General of the Imperial Guard).
During the rebellions of Dìngzōng Pán and Zōngjùn,
he was again promoted to Guǎngwēi jiāngjūn (General of Broad Might)
and appointed Dūshuǐ shǐzhě (Commissioner of Waterways).
He was transferred to Xīběilù zhāotǎo dūjiān (Assistant Pacification Commissioner of the Northwest Route),
then successively served as Fùzhōu, Luánzhōu cìshǐ (Prefects of Fùzhōu and Luánzhōu), Yélúwǎn qúnmùshǐ (Supervisor of Herds in Yélúwǎn),
Diélàbùzú jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Diélà Tribe),
tóngzhī Dàxīng Yǐn (Vice Administrator of Dàxīng), concurrently Zhōngdūlù bīngmǎdūzǒngguǎn (Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Zhōngdū Route),
and then Wǔníngjūn jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Wǔníng Prefecture)
and Guǎngníng Yǐn (Administrator of Guǎngníng).
He died
at the age of sixty-two.
Yínzhúkě,
a member of the imperial clan.
When Tàizǔ succeeded to the throne,
he sent Pújiānú to Liáo to retrieve Āshū.
The matter remained unresolved for a long time.
Then he sent Xígǔnǎi and Yínzhúkě to go next.
At that time,
the Liáo ruler neglected governance,
and the administration disintegrated.
Yínzhúkě and others returned,
reporting in detail to Tàizǔ about the Liáo government and public sentiment,
and also stating that Liáo could be attacked.
Tàizǔ resolved to attack Liáo,
which indeed stemmed from Yínzhúkě and the others' report.
Tàizǔ fought against Yēlǜ Élíwán at Dálǔgǔ Chéng.
The Liáo army numbered over two hundred thousand.
Yínzhúkě and Lóushì led their troops to charge into the center of the enemy formation.
They broke through the lines nine times,
fighting their way in and out each time,
and thoroughly defeated the Liáo army.
Yínzhúkě was made a móukè.
He then garrisoned the border with Lóushì.
Again with Lóushì, Húnhuó, Pólúhuǒ, Shígǔnǎi, and others, he attacked Huánglóng Fǔ,
defeating over ten thousand Liáo soldiers at Báimǎ Luò.
Tàizǔ resisted the Liáo forces,
and Yínzhúkě defended Dálǔgǔ Chéng.
In Shōuguó 二年 (1122),
two thousand households of móukè, relocated from Yātǎ and Ālǎn, were assigned.
Yínzhúkě was made their móukè
and stationed at Níngjiāng Zhōu.
The Liáo grand envoy Xíníliè was sent back,
having agreed to arrive by mid-July.
However, by the end of September, Xíníliè had not come.
The emperor ordered the various armies to cross the river and station themselves.
Thirteen Liáo Yèlá and Mádá,
with eight soldiers, set fire to Húnhé
to cut off fodder and pasture.
Yínzhúkě captured them,
and thus learned that the Liáo border official Yǐxuē had instructed them.
Tàizǔ ordered their release.
He followed the dūtǒng Gǎokè in attacking Zhōngjīng.
Yínzhúkě, with Xígǔnǎi, Púchá, and Húbālǔ, led three thousand soldiers
to attack Xī King Xiámò seventy lǐ west of Jīng.
Xiámò abandoned his troops and fled.
The Liáo ruler fled west to Tiāndé.
Yínzhúkě used his troops to cut off his retreat,
and the Liáo ruler was subsequently captured.
Later, he followed Zōnghàn in attacking Sòng
and besieged Tàiyuán.
Zōnghàn advanced to Zézhōu.
When Zōnghàn returned to Xījīng,
Tàiyuán had not yet fallen.
Yínzhúkě was ordered to leave troops to besiege it.
Zhāotǎo dūjiān (Assistant Pacification Commissioner) Mǎwǔ defeated the Sòng forces at Wénshuǐ.
Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner) Gěng Shǒuzhōng and others defeated the Sòng forces of Huáng Dí at Xīdū Gǔ.
The number killed was immeasurable.
Sòng armies led by Fán Kuí, Shī Shēn, Gāo Fēng, and others came to relieve Tàiyuán,
occupying nearby areas.
Yínzhúkě, with Xíshī, Bēilǔ, and Wánsù, decisively defeated them.
Suǒlǐyǐshì defeated Sòng forces at Tàigǔ.
Sòng forces occupied Tàigǔ and Qíxiàn.
Āgǔlǎn and Bálísuù recaptured them.
Zhǒng Shīzhōng emerged from Jǐngxíng,
occupied Yúcì,
and came to relieve Tàiyuán.
Yínzhúkě dispatched Wòlún to attack him,
defeating his army.
Huónǚ killed Shīzhōng at Shāxióng Lǐng.
He then advanced to attack the Sòng zhìzhìshǐ (Commissioner) Yáo Gǔ's army in Lóngzhōu Gǔ,
and utterly routed them.
Sālǐtǔ defeated Sòng forces at Huímǎ Kǒu.
Guō Qǐzhōng annihilated Sòng forces at Wǔtái.
When Zōnghàn pacified Tàiyuán
and joined forces with Zōngwàng at Biàn,
Yínzhúkě and others attacked Biàn Chéng
and conquered it.
When the army returned,
Yínzhúkě received the surrender of Kělán, Nínghuà, and other prefectures.
He attacked Lánzhōu and captured it,
and obtained the surrender of Huǒshān Jūn.
He was granted an iron certificate along with Xīyǐn.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) rushed to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Sàilǐ (賽里) took Rǔzhōu (汝州).
Yínshùkě (銀术可) took Dèngzhōu (鄧州),
killing its general Lǐ Cāo (李操) and others.
Sàmóulǔ (薩謀魯) entered Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Bálísù (拔离速) entered Jūnzhōu (均州).
Mǎ Wǔ (馬五) took Fángzhōu (房州),
capturing the Transport Commissioner Liú Jí (劉吉) and the Dèngzhōu (鄧州) Vice Prefect Wáng Bīn (王彬).
Bálísù (拔离速) broke through Táng (唐), Cài (蔡), and Chén (陳) three prefectures,
and captured Yǐngchāng (潁昌) Prefecture.
Shāgǔzhì (沙古質) separately captured the old Yǐngchāng (潁昌).
Zōnghàn (宗翰) would gather to attack King Kāng (康王).
Yínshùkě (銀术可) guarded Tàiyuán (太原).
In Tiānhuì (天會) 10th year,
he served as the Defense Commissioner of Yānjīng (燕京).
In Tiānhuì (天會) 13th year,
he retired from office,
was promoted to Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of the Bǎodà (保大) Army,
Píngzhāngshì (平章事) of the Zhōngshūménxià (中書門下),
then moved to Zhōngshūlìng (中書令),
and enfeoffed as King Shǔ (蜀王).
In Tiānjuàn (天眷) 3rd year,
he passed away,
at the age of sixty-eight.
Following the Zhènglóng (正隆) precedent, he was posthumously granted the title of Jīnyuán (金源) Prince,
and enshrined in the temple of Tàizōng (太宗).
In Dàdìng (大定) 15th year,
he was posthumously given the epithet Wǔxiāng (武襄),
and re-enshrined in the temple of Tàizǔ (太祖).
His son was Gòuyīng (彀英).
Gòuyīng's (彀英)
original name was Tàlǎn (撻懶).
As a child, he was alert, intelligent, ambitious, and brave.
When he was first called upon,
Tàizǔ (太祖) saw him and was struck by his uniqueness.
At the age of sixteen,
his father Yínshùkě (銀术可) gave him armor
and made him follow in the campaign against Liáo (遼).
He often served as the vanguard
and was awarded the hereditary title of Móukè (謀克).
When Zōnghàn (宗翰) returned from Tàiyuán (太原) to Xījīng (西京),
Yínshùkě (銀术可) besieged him.
Gòuyīng (彀英) was in the ranks
and repeatedly achieved meritorious service.
Tens of thousands of Sòng (宋) soldiers came to rescue Tàiyuán (太原),
reaching Nánguān (南關).
Yínshùkě (銀术可), together with his younger brother Bálísù (拔离速) and Wányán Lóushì (完顏婁室) and others, attacked them.
In a narrow alley,
a soldier swung a knife at Bálísù (拔离速).
Gòuyīng (彀英) used his knife to cut off his wrist.
Another soldier then stabbed him with a spear from the side.
Gòuyīng (彀英) broke the spear
and pursued and killed the soldier.
After capturing Tàiyuán (太原)
and subduing the prefectures of Hédōng (河東),
he attacked Biànjīng (汴京),
all with meritorious service.
With the Commander Mǎ Wǔ (馬五), he campaigned in the region of Hànshàng (漢上).
Upon reaching Shàngcài (上蔡),
as vanguard, he defeated Kǒngjiā (孔家) Army.
When Ruìzōng (睿宗) attacked Kāizhōu (開州),
Gòuyīng (彀英) was the first to scale the walls.
A stray arrow struck his mouth.
Ruìzōng (睿宗) personally attended to him.
Before his wound had healed,
he was compelled to rise
and attack Dàmíng (大名) Prefecture.
In the ranking of merits,
Zōngbì (宗弼) was first,
Gòuyīng (彀英) second.
When attacking Dōngpíng (東平),
Gòuyīng (彀英) was foremost.
When Bálísù (拔离速) attacked Sòng (宋) King Kāng (康王) in Yángzhōu (揚州),
Gòuyīng (彀英) was the vanguard.
When Bálísù (拔离速) pursued Sòng (宋) Empress Mèng (孟后) in Jiāngnán (江南),
Gòuyīng (彀英) advanced towards Tánzhōu (潭州).
With a large Sòng (宋) army in Chángwǔ (常武),
Gòuyīng (彀英) used elite troops to approach its city,
defeating over a thousand men.
The next day,
troops from the city came out to fight.
Gòuyīng (彀英) with five hundred cavalry defeated them,
capturing two hundred horses.
He then attacked Chángwǔ (常武).
Bálísù (拔离速) arrayed all the armies in a grand formation,
remaining at the rear.
Gòuyīng (彀英) with five hundred cavalry formed a smaller formation,
advancing to the front.
He immediately ordered his troops to charge the Sòng (宋) army.
The Sòng (宋) army fell into disarray
and was utterly defeated.
Bálísù (拔离速) observed his maneuverings
and praised him.
Later, many counties and prefectures in Hédōng (河東) rebelled.
Gòuyīng (彀英) as vanguard attacked Jiàngzhōu (絳州)
and captured it.
He then attacked Qìnzhōu (沁州) again.
A flying cannonball struck his right flank,
and he was carried back to camp.
All the armies attacked Qìnzhōu (沁州)
but could not capture it for three days.
The other general Gǔgé (骨●) compelled Gòuyīng (彀英) to rise and direct the soldiers,
and they then captured it.
He was appointed acting Commander of Hédōng (河東) Circuit
and followed the Left Army Inspector Yílà Yúdǔ (移剌余睹) to pacify the various tribes in the northwest.
Gòuyīng (彀英) led three thousand five hundred cavalry,
pacified nine of their tribes,
captured three thousand captives,
and one hundred fifty thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
As vanguard, he defeated the Sòng (宋) Wúshān (吳山) Army.
In two battles, he won twice,
then repelled the Sòng (宋) army in the pass.
The dead were innumerable,
and the Sòng (宋) army fled.
Zōngbì (宗弼) again took Héshàngyuán (和尚原).
Gòuyīng (彀英) with his own unit defeated fifty thousand Sòng (宋) soldiers
and then seized Xīnchākǒu (新叉口).
Zōngbì (宗弼) left troops to guard it.
That night,
there was heavy snow,
and the roads were all icy.
The Sòng (宋) army's strength at Héshàngyuán (和尚原) was too great to take directly.
Zōngbì (宗弼) used Gòuyīng's (彀英) strategy
to enter through the nearby high mountains, thickets, and dense foliage,
catching them by surprise,
and thus took Héshàngyuán (和尚原).
Gòuyīng (彀英) requested to quickly enter Dàsàn (大散) Pass,
with his own unit forming the rear guard
to guard against ambushes.
When Zōngbì (宗弼) reached Xiānrén (仙人) Pass,
Gòuyīng (彀英) attacked first.
Zōngbì (宗弼) stopped him,
but Gòuyīng (彀英) did not stop.
Zōngbì (宗弼) struck his helmet with the back of his saber
to make him retreat.
Gòuyīng (彀英) said:
"The enemy's morale is already low.
If we do not seize this opportunity to take it,
we will surely regret it later."
And so it proved.
Zōngbì (宗弼) sighed, saying:
"Let bygones be bygones."
Then he withdrew the army.
Gòuyīng (彀英) guarded the rear,
fighting and retreating,
and thus reached Qínzhōng (秦中).
When the Qí (齊) state was first abolished,
the Marshal and Right Army Inspector Sālǐhē (撒离喝) rode swiftly to pacify the various commanderies.
Upon reaching Tóngzhōu (同州),
the former Qí (齊) Surveillance Commissioner Lǐ Shìfǔ (李世輔) came out to welcome him,
pretending to fall from his horse and claim a broken arm,
and was carried back.
When Sālǐhē (撒离喝) entered the city,
Shìfǔ (世輔) cunningly sent the Vice Prefect to present armor,
with ten brave men
wearing armor going up to the main hall.
Shìfǔ (世輔) himself emerged from behind a screen
and seized Sālǐhē (撒离喝).
Gòuyīng (彀英) was just outside looking for a horse.
The event occurred so suddenly
that he could not enter.
The city gates were already closed,
all guarded by soldiers.
Upon reaching the East Gate,
Hédáyǎ (合荅雅) led over thirty cavalry
and met Gòuyīng (彀英).
They then cut down the gatekeepers and exited.
Meanwhile, Shìfǔ (世輔) led his men out from the West Gate.
Gòuyīng (彀英) and Hédáyǎ (合荅雅) attacked them,
advancing and retreating to hold Shìfǔ (世輔)
and prevent him from moving quickly.
Shìfǔ (世輔), fearing that reinforcements would arrive,
then compelled Sālǐhē (撒离喝) to make an alliance with him,
not to pursue him.
Sālǐhē (撒离喝) was left by the roadside.
Gòuyīng (彀英) recognized his voice
and returned with his cavalry.
He was appointed Grand General of Ānyuǎn (安遠),
acting Prefect of Tàiyuán (太原).
The four borders were all well-governed.
He concurrently served as the overall commander of the Hédōng (河東) Southern and Northern Army and Horse Divisions.
The court offered Hénán and Shǎnxī to Sòng,
but later reclaimed them.
The army arrived at Yàozhōu.
Every morning, the Sòng people would emerge from the city,
unfurl their flags, and inspect their troops,
returning at dusk.
The path was narrow,
so cavalry could not exert their full power.
Gòu Yīng requested five hundred soldiers.
At dusk, he first sent fifty men to rush to the mountaintop,
instructing them:
"Tomorrow, when you see the enemy emerge,
raise a banner and point it in the direction they are heading."
He then concealed the remaining soldiers in the mountain valley.
The next day,
the people in the city came out for inspection as before.
A banner was raised on the mountaintop,
and the hidden troops attacked.
The Sòng soldiers raced to flee back into the city.
Gòu Yīng waved his army to scale the city walls,
removed the Sòng banners,
and erected the Jīn army's flags.
The Sòng soldiers who were lagging behind saw this and dared not enter,
so they surrendered.
The people in the city also surrendered.
Sòng's Wú Jiè held significant forces and occupied Jīngzhōu.
〔一０〕 Most of the area west of Jīngyuán responded to him.
Grand Marshal Sālíhē wanted to retreat to defend Jīngzhào,
awaiting the Hénán and Hédōng armies.
Gòu Yīng said:
"If I retreat,
Wú Jiè will certainly take Fèngxiáng, Jīngzhào, Tóng, and Huá,
and occupy Tóngguān.
Our kind will be lost."
Sālíhē asked:
"What plan should we adopt?"
Gòu Yīng replied:
"The situation is perilous;
it is better to fight quickly.
Our army will array on the southern plain of Jīng,
and the Sòng army will certainly come from Xīyuán.
Gòu Yīng and Xiébǔchū, each with five hundred chosen cavalry, will crush their two wings,
and the Grand Marshal will strike them in the middle.
This way, we can succeed."
Supervising Military Affairs Officer Bálísu said:
"These two will take their flanks;
Bálísu is willing to take the center.
The Grand Marshal will occupy the high ground,
displaying many banners as a feint.
This way, we can succeed."
Sālíhē followed this advice.
Wú Jiè's army indeed came from Xīyuán.
Gòu Yīng and Xiébǔchū attacked their flanks.
From dawn until noon,
Wú Jiè's left and right armies slightly retreated.
Bálísu charged and attacked them in the front,
ultimately defeating Wú Jiè's army.
Corpses lay piled up,
filling the great ravines.
From then on, the people of Shǔ lost heart,
daring not venture out again,
and Guān and Shǎn were thus pacified.
