He successively served as Acting Vice Minister of Personnel and Vice Minister of Works in the mobile chancellery.
He accompanied Zōngbì on a border inspection,
was promoted to Minister of Punishment,
and then transferred to Grand Marshal's Left Chief Supervisor.
In Tiāndé second year (1150),
he was promoted to Right Supervising Military Affairs Officer.
When the Grand Marshal's office was abolished,
he was reassigned as the Commander-in-Chief of the Shānxī Circuit,
leading the recruiting forces of both the Southwest and Northwest Circuits.
Due to his lack of merit,
he was demoted to Commissioner of Línhǎi Commandery,
and successively served as Prefect of Píngyáng and Tàiyuán.
At the end of Zhènglóng (1161),
he became the Resident Commissioner of Zhōngdū,
concurrently serving as Commander-in-Chief of the Northwest Front.
To suppress the Qìdān Sābā,
he stationed his army in Guīhuàzhōu.
Shìzōng ascended the throne in Liáoyáng,
sending Gòu Yīng's nephew Ālǔwǎ with an imperial edict to Guīhuà,
appointing Gòu Yīng as Left Vice Grand Marshal.
He also dispatched an envoy to summon Shǎnxī Commander Túshàn Héxǐ,
to proclaim the edict of the Dàdìng era change and an amnesty in the Southwest and Northwest Recruiting Offices,
and in various prefectures and garrisons of Hédōng, Héběi, and Shāndōng Circuits,
and to mobilize the *mèng'ān* troops to garrison the capital region.
When Ālǔwǎ met Gòu Yīng,
Gòu Yīng was hesitant and undecided.
However, all the officers and soldiers wished to return to Shìzōng,
so Gòu Yīng had no choice
but to accept the edict.
He issued a Grand Marshal's order to the various circuits,
urgently requesting twenty thousand mud troughs for horses.
When the various circuits heard of this,
they thought a large army was about to arrive.
Only then did he send people to proclaim the amnesty,
and all places complied.
In the eleventh month of the first year of Dàdìng (1161),
Gòu Yīng arrived in Zhōngdū with his army.
The concurrent Resident Commissioner Zhāng requested a meeting at the residence to discuss affairs.
Gòu Yīng suspected Zhāng of having a plot,
so he feigned agreement.
He arrayed his ceremonial guard as if he were about to go,
but then led his cavalry out through Shīrénmén
and stationed his troops in Tōngzhōu.
He met Shìzōng in Sānhé.
An edict ordered Gòu Yīng to expediently plan and arrange border affairs for Hénán, Shǎnxī, and Shāndōng.
In the first month of the second year (1162),
he arrived in Nánjīng,
and subsequently recovered Rǔ, Yǐng, Sōng, and other prefectures and counties.
He was granted a hereditary *mèng'ān*.
Upon entering the court, he was appointed Minister of Political Affairs,
then dismissed and made Resident Commissioner of Dōngjīng.
Before he could depart,
he was reassigned as Prefect of Jǐnán.
Initially,
Gòu Yīng, being an old general and relying on his merits,
was quite corrupt in Nánjīng
and did not care for the military or the people.
When an imperial envoy was sent to question him about border affairs,
Gòu Yīng did not answer,
telling the envoy:
"What do you know?
I will report on it when I arrive at the palace."
However, when he was summoned,
he did not utter a single word about border affairs.
In his position as minister, he often acted unilaterally,
proceeding with whatever he desired on his own initiative.
When he was made Resident Commissioner,
he immediately became indignant and refused to receive guests,
even close officials were not granted an audience.
The Emperor was angry,
and thus reassigned him to Jǐnán.
The Emperor rebuked him, saying:
"I remember that your father rendered great service to the state,
and you, an old general, also have merits.
Therefore, I have reassigned you to this post;
you should understand this.
If you do not change your ways,
not only will you not retain your official position,
but you will also be unable to preserve your own life."
Gòu Yīng prostrated himself and thanked him.
After a long time,
he was reassigned as Prefect of Píngyáng,
and then retired.
He was recalled to serve as Resident Commissioner of Xījīng,
but left office due to mourning for his mother.
Soon after, he was reinstated to his original post.
Later, he served again in Dōngjīng,
and successively in Shàngjīng.
An imperial edict stated:
"Shàngjīng is where our dynasty began;
its customs are daily becoming more cunning and shallow.
The imperial clan resides there in large numbers,
making it known as difficult to govern.
You are an elder statesman,
whom all listen to and obey.
You must rectify the customs,
restrain the imperial clan,
and uphold the greater principles."
In the fifteenth year (1175),
he retired.
After a long time,
the historians presented the Veritable Records of Tàizōng and Ruìzōng.
The Emperor said:
"Among the old people who personally witnessed those events,
only Gòu Yīng remains."
An edict ordered Compiler Wēndíhǎn Dìdá to go to Běijīng to his home and question him,
and many revisions were made.
In the nineteenth year (1179),
he died
at the age of seventy-four.
In total, he was rewarded for his merits eleven times,
receiving two hundred fifty *liǎng* of gold,
six thousand five hundred *liǎng* of silver,
eight hundred *pǐ* of silk,
two thousand *liǎng* of cotton,
three hundred fourteen horses,
six thousand five hundred cattle and sheep,
and one hundred thirty slaves.
Máqí
was Yínzhútā's younger brother.
At fifteen,
he was enlisted in the army,
followed in defeating the Gāolí (Goryeo) army,
took Níngjiāng Zhōu,
pacified the Xì Liáo Nǚzhēn,
and captured Huánglóng Fǔ.
In all these, he personally led the charge and fought with all his might,
and for his achievements, he was made a móukè,
and later led a mèng'ān.
He defeated more than a thousand Xī soldiers.
From Wòlǔgǔ, he attacked and took Xián, Xìn, and Shěn Zhōu, as well as the various cities of Dōngjīng;
Máqí had merits in all these.
When Dūtǒng Gǎo took Zhōngjīng,
he, along with Shāohé and Húshídá, submitted to the Chǔlǐdí tribe separately,
and stationed troops in Gāozhōu.
He sent troops to aid Méngguābójǐn,
greatly defeating the enemy,
and then again defeated five thousand Ēnzhōu soldiers.
He suppressed and pacified the Liáo people gathered in the mountains and valleys of Zhōngjīng,
receiving the surrender of over three thousand people.
During a battle on the border of Gāozhōu,
he was struck in the eye by a hidden arrow,
and thus died.
Máqí fought over thirty battles, large and small,
and was victorious wherever he went.
During the Huángtǒng reign,
he was posthumously granted the title Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū,
with the posthumous name Yìmǐn.
His son was Wòcè.
Wòcè,
at seventeen,
was enlisted in the army,
and followed Bálísu to attack the Liáo general Mǎwǔ,
defeating him.
Upon Máqí's death,
he inherited his position.
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
he reached the river.
The Sòng army was stationed outside the river,
sending two boats to scout our forces.
Wòcè was then sent to lead several brave warriors,
taking one boat to meet them,
and returned with all of them captured.
He participated in the raid on Kāngwáng between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Wòcè was involved in all of it.
When the army returned,
they were stationed in Dōngpíng.
Upon the abolition of Qí,
troops were stationed north of the river,
recruiting and receiving the surrender of nearby camps,
acquiring many livestock, equipment, and weapons.
The army commander commended him,
rewarding him with armored horses.
Following the attack on Shǎnxī,
he served as the Right Wing Dūtǒng,
and had merits in attacking cities and defeating enemies.
He was instrumental in all of this.
Upon the army's return,
he was formally appointed móukè.
He was promoted to Huázhōu Fángyùshǐ.
At a time when Guānzhōng suffered a famine,
and bandits were rampant,
Wòcè recruited soldiers to suppress and pacify them,
bringing peace to his department.
The local people submitted petitions requesting his retention,
but it was not granted.
Not long after,
he was appointed Díliè Bùzú Jiédùshǐ,
and later changed to Diézhà Bù.
Due to his integrity, he was appointed Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě.
Upon completing his term,
he concurrently served as Tóngzhī Yānjīng Liúshǒu Shì,
and then as Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
Sābā had completed his term several months earlier,
but continued to receive his salary,
not immediately vacating the post.
Wòcè exposed his actions.
When Sābā rebelled,
Wòcè was killed.
Bálísu
was Yínzhútā's brother.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ,
Zōnghàn was in Běi'ān Zhōu,
about to meet Xiáyě at Xīwáng Líng,
when Liáo forces suddenly arrived at Gǔběi Kǒu.
He sent Pólúhuǒ and Húnhù each to lead two hundred soldiers
to attack them.
Húnhù requested reinforcements.
Zōnghàn wanted to go himself,
but Xīyǐn and Lóushì said:
"This is easy to deal with,
please let us defeat them for you with a thousand men."
Húnhù advanced with thirty cavalrymen,
and upon reaching Gǔběi Kǒu,
encountered their scouts.
He pursued them into the mountain valley.
The Liáo people, with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry, pressed forward to battle,
losing five cavalrymen.
Húnhù retreated and held the pass.
When Xīyǐn and Lóushì arrived,
Bálísu, Émóuhǎn, and Húshíhǎi bravely charged and attacked,
greatly defeating them,
slaughtering a great many,
and capturing all their armor, helmets, and baggage.
Xīyǐn, along with Sālǐgǔdú and Péimǎn Tūniǎn, defeated their ambush,
killing over a thousand men
and capturing over a hundred horses.
Lóushì resisted the Xī people emerging from Língyě Líng,
leaving Bálísu with two hundred soldiers
to hold the strategic pass.
Yínzhútā besieged Tàiyuán.
The nearby counties had already surrendered,
but Sòng forces coming to relieve Tàiyuán reoccupied Tàigǔ and Qíxiàn.
Bálísu and Āgǔlǎn retook them.
The Sòng army of Yáo Gǔ was in Lóngzhōu Gǔ;
Bálísu defeated them.
Zhāng Hào's troops came out of Fénzhōu;
he also attacked and routed them.
In the fourth year of Tiānhuì,
Tàiyuán was captured.
Bálísu was appointed Guǎngōu Tàiyuán Fǔ Lù Bīngmǎ Shì,
and again with Lóushì, defeated Sòng forces at Wénshuǐ,
then followed Zōnghàn to besiege Biàn.
With Yínzhútā, he swept through Xiāng and Dèng,
entered Jūnzhōu,
and then attacked Táng, Cài, and Chén three zhōu,
all of which he broke,
capturing Yǐngchāng Fǔ.
Then, with Tàiyù and Mǎwǔ, he ambushed Sòng Kāngwáng at Yángzhōu.
Kāngwáng crossed the Jiāng and entered Jiànkāng.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was promoted to Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān.
When Zōngbì re-pacified Hénán,
and Sālǐhē campaigned in Shǎnxī,
reaching Jīngzhōu,
Bálísu greatly defeated the Sòng army at Wèizhōu.
Wèizhōu and Déshùn Jūn both surrendered,
and Shǎnxī was pacified.
He was promoted to Yuánshuài Zuǒ Jiānjūn,
and given the additional title Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiàngjūn.
He died
with the posthumous name Mǐndìng.
Xígǔnǎi
is also written as Shígǔnǎi.
〔一一〕He once went with Yínzhútā to the Liáo kingdom to retrieve Āshū.
Upon his return, he reported on the state of the Liáo people, indicating they could be taken.
Tàizǔ then decided to attack Liáo.
When Pólúhuǒ captured Jūyōng Guān,
Empress Xiāo fled from Gǔběi Kǒu.
Tàizǔ sent Xígǔnǎi to pursue her,
but he did not catch her.
Later, he became the Jūnshuài of Línghuáng Fǔ,
suppressing and pacifying the Diézhà.
When their various officials led their people to surrender,
they requested to be allowed to continue leading their respective tribes.
Tàizōng granted them blank xuāntóu and silver plaques,
allowing them to confer titles as they saw fit.
He captured Liáo Xǔwáng Shāluó and Fùmǎ Dūwèi Xiāo Yǐxīn.
Liáo Liángwáng Yǎlǐ had established himself at Hélǐ Shuǐ.
〔一二〕It was not known where he actually was until now.
It was then that his location became known.
Consequently,
the surrendered Liáo people were relocated to Tàizhōu.
As it was still summer and unsuitable for relocation,
Xígǔnǎi requested that they be temporarily settled west of the ridge.
When Xígǔnǎi built a new city at Qìdān Zhōutè Chéng,
an imperial edict established Huìpíng Zhōu there.
Díliè and Huàshā of the Wūhǔlǐ tribe led their kin to surrender.
The imperial court appointed Tàpúyě as Jiédùshǐ of their tribe,
and Wūhǔ as Dūjiān.
Xígǔnǎi returned Tàpúyě's and others' proclamations,
and at his discretion, added a scattered official rank to Tàpúyě,
filling in a blank gaòshēn to confer it,
and also recorded 893 former officials who had surrendered and rendered meritorious service.
The imperial court approved.
Thus,
Díliè was promoted to Fángyùshǐ,
and became Jiédùshǐ of his tribe.
Huàshā was promoted to Zhū Sīshǐ,
and became Jiédù Fùshǐ,
managing the affairs of the Dílièdǐ tribe.
Tàlídá was promoted to Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiàngjūn,
Jiédù Fùshǐ,
managing the affairs of the Tūjú tribe.
Āxǐ was promoted to Guāncháshǐ,
and became Jiédùshǐ of his tribe.
The others received various promotions and appointments.
Land from Pánggě Chéng was allocated to the Wūhǔlǐ and Dílièdǐ two tribes, as well as the Qìdān people.
Uncultivated land was allowed to be occupied by force.
After a long time,
he was put in charge of the affairs of the fire and smoke of Xiánzhōu.
In the 6th year of Tiānhuì (1128),
〔13〕 Wányán Shènsī's division and the remaining households not yet assigned to a *mèng'ān móukè* [system],
were ordered to be thoroughly reviewed and registered by Xíɡǔnǎi.
In the 10th year of Tiānhuì (1132),
the Jūnshuài Department of Nánjīng Lù was renamed the Dūfǔ Department of Dōngnán Lù.
Xíɡǔnǎi was made Dūtǒng,
and his headquarters were moved to Dōngjīng
to garrison Gāolí.
The eulogy says: When Jīn opened up its territory,
Wòlǔ and Wòlǔɡǔ had the earliest and most prominent achievements in specific areas.
Pólúhuǒ and Lóushì were enfeoffed the earliest.
The border defenses of Tàizhōu
and the strategic vital point of Huánglóng
also carried heavy responsibilities.
The arduous labors of Zhāmǔ in the Southern Route
and Lóushì's operations in Shǎnxī,
and Yínshùkě's siege and defense of Tàiyuán,
were all extremely difficult.
The illness of Wòlǔɡǔ
and the defeat of Zhāmǔ,
and the urgency of their condemnation and punishment,
struck fear into all the generals.
That they were able to ultimately control the strong and powerful with their weakness
is indeed a testament to their effectiveness.
Yínshùkě and Xíɡǔnǎi observed other nations and knew they could be attacked.
The ancient saying goes,
"A state has eight observations,"
which is excellent indeed!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 11: Ālíhéhǎn

Yàn (original name Wòlùn) Zōnɡyǐn (original name Ālíhǎn) Zōnɡníng (original name Ātǔɡǔ) Zōnɡdào (original name Bāshí) Zōnɡxióng (original name Móuliánɡhǔ) Ālín Àndáhǎi Xīyǐn (original name Gǔshén) Shǒuzhēn (original name Zuǒyǎn) Shǒunénɡ (original name Húlà)
Ālíhéhǎn
was the eighth son of Jǐnɡzǔ.
He was agile, swift, and skilled in battle.
At the age of eighteen,
Làpéi and Máshǎn raised an army and occupied the Mùléngshuǐ.
Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn assisted them with soldiers from Gūlǐdiàn.
Shìzǔ captured Làpéi,
but the people of Mùléngshuǐ were still rebellious
and restless.
So Ālíhéhǎn was sent to pacify and inspect them,
and he joined forces with Xiépō to attack Wōmóuhǎn.
Wūchūn had already died,
and Wōmóuhǎn abandoned the city and fled.
Later, he followed Sāgǎi in suppressing Liúkě,
and Ālíhéhǎn contributed greatly.
Tàizǔ captured Xiāo Hǎilǐ,
and sent Ālíhéhǎn to present the severed heads to Liáo.
When Tàizǔ planned to attack Liáo,
Ālíhéhǎn actually supported it.
And when the army was raised,
Ālíhéhǎn repeatedly fought with merit in the ranks.
When Tàizōnɡ and others urged him to ascend the throne,
Tàizǔ had not yet agreed.
Ālíhéhǎn, Yù, Zōnɡhàn, and others said:
"Now that great achievements have been gathered,
if we do not establish a dynastic title in due time,
there will be no way to secure the hearts of the people."
Tàizǔ said:
"I shall consider it."
In the 1st year of Shōuguó (1115),
Tàizǔ ascended the throne.
Ālíhéhǎn and Zōnɡhàn presented nine farming tools,
and prayed:
"May Your Majesty never forget the hardships of farming."
Tàizǔ respectfully accepted them.
Soon after,
he became the Guólùn Yìshì Bójíliè.
He was intelligent, astute, and eloquent.
Anything he heard or saw once,
he would never forget for his entire life.
In the beginning, when there was no writing,
he could silently recall all the ancestral lineages, family members, and events,
and together with Xiégé, he compiled the imperial genealogy.
If he met someone he had never seen before,
upon hearing their father's and grandfather's names,
he could immediately state their tribe, lineage, and origins.
Or if old events from many years ago
were incidentally mentioned due to something else,
and others might have forgotten,
he would always clarify and explain them one by one,
and resolve any doubts for those who questioned.
Shìzǔ once praised his strong memory,
which was unparalleled by others.
In the 3rd year of Tiānfǔ (1119),
he fell ill.
Zōnɡhàn visited him daily to inquire about his health,
and learned all about the old customs and laws of the ancestors.
When he was seriously ill,
the Emperor personally visited his home to inquire about his sickness
and asked him about state affairs.
He replied:
"Horses are used for military purposes,
and now that the four directions are not yet pacified,
our national custom is to bury good horses with the dead,
which should be prohibited."
He then presented the warhorse he had ridden all his life.
When he presented the horse to Tàizōnɡ,
he had his son Púlǐ act as an intermediary to present the memorial.
If there was a mistake in the speech,
he would immediately smile at it,
and Zōnɡhàn, from the side, would revise it.
After the memorial was presented,
he passed away
at the age of forty-nine.
When the Emperor heard that Ālíhéhǎn had presented a memorial before his death,
he said:
"To not be confused at the point of death,
and to think of state affairs,
he is truly a worthy minister!"
He wept bitterly for him.
At the funeral,
the Emperor personally attended.
During Xīzōnɡ's reign,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as the King of Suí.
During the Tiāndé era,
he was posthumously granted Kǎifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Duke of Suí.
During the Dàdìnɡ era,
he was honored with sacrificial offerings at the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ,
and given the posthumous title Gāngxiàn.
His sons were Sàiyě and Wòlùn.
Sàiyě's son was Zōnɡyǐn.
Yàn, whose original name was Wòlùn,
was the grandson of Jǐnɡzǔ
and the second son of Ālíhéhǎn.
He was intelligent, astute, and full of strategies,
and understood Qìdān script.
In the early Tiānhuì era,
Wǔdǐgǎi rebelled.
Tàizōnɡ visited Běijīng,
and seeing that Yàn had good strategies,
he summoned him for questioning.
His answers pleased the emperor,
so he was ordered to supervise the imperial guard and other armies to suppress the rebellion.
When he arrived at the Húntónɡ Jiāng,
he instructed his generals and soldiers, saying:
"Now the rebels are relying on the mountains and valleys;
the terrain is rugged and perilous,
and the forests are dense.
Our cavalry cannot form ranks,
and we cannot defeat them in a matter of months or years."
So he prepared boats and moored them by the river,
ordered the various armies to occupy high mountains,
connected wood to form fences,
and displayed many banners
to show a long-term strategy,
publicly stating that they would wait for the main army to fully assemble before attacking.
Then, he secretly sent a naval force down the river,
directly striking their camp,
and utterly defeated them.
The rebels entrenched in the perilous terrain collapsed without a fight.
Within a month,
the entire region was pacified.
When the army returned,
he was appointed Upper General of the Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi,
became the Administrator of Guǎnɡníng,
and then entered the court as Shàngshū of both the Ministry of Personnel and the Ministry of Rites.
In the 1st year of Huánɡtǒnɡ (1141),
he served as the Běijīng Liúshǒu,
then was changed to Administrator of Xiánpínɡ,
and moved to Dōngjīng.
In the early Tiāndé era,
he was enfeoffed as King of Gě,
entered the court and was appointed Tónɡpàn Dàzōnɡzhènɡ Shì,
then promoted to King of Sònɡ,
and granted a hereditary *mèng'ān*.
When Hǎilínɡ moved the capital,
Yàn remained as Liúshǒu in Shànɡjīng,
and was granted one gold plaque and two silver plaques.
He was successively enfeoffed as King of Yù and King of Xǔ,
and then changed to King of Yuè.
In the early Zhēnyuán era,
he was promoted to King of Qí.
At that time, hunting was prohibited in the near suburbs,
but Yàn was specially granted 300 men to accompany him on hunts.
He served in Shànɡjīng for five years in total.
In the 2nd year of Zhènɡlónɡ (1157),
his royal title was abolished as per regulations,
and he was changed to Xīyīng Liúshǒu.
Not long after,
he became the Administrator of Línhuánɡ,
then retired,
and returned to reside in Huìníng.
When Hǎilínɡ launched the southern expedition,
Shìzōnɡ served as the Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
Generals and soldiers all returned from Huáinán to defect,
and Yàn's son Nìlǐnǎi also led his troops from the front to defect to Shìzōnɡ.
Bái Yànjìnɡ and others in Běijīng heard that Nìlǐnǎi and others had fled back,
and ordered Gāo Guóshènɡ, the Tónɡzhī of Huìníng, to detain Yàn's family.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
he sent an envoy to summon Yàn,
and then again sent Yàn's elder brother's son, Gúlǔbǔ, to rush on horseback to urge him.
Yàn then led several members of the imperial clan to meet the Emperor,
and was immediately appointed Zuǒ Chénɡxiànɡ,
enfeoffed as Prince of Guǎnɡpínɡ Commandery,
and entertained and honored for an entire day.
Not long after,
he concurrently held the position of Dū Yuánshuài.
In the first month of the second year of Dàdìng,
the Emperor went to the imperial mausoleums.
After the rituals,
the Emperor was about to hunt.
The relevant officials had already made preparations early.
Yàn remonstrated, saying:
"Border affairs are not yet settled;
hunting and pleasure trips are inappropriate."
The Emperor graciously accepted this.
He then said to Yàn and others:
"Ancient emperors received remonstrances with an open mind;
I have always admired this.
You all should speak frankly without concealment."
He was promoted to Tàiwèi.
He subsequently retired from office
and returned to his hometown.
In that year,
he passed away.
An imperial edict ordered officials to offer sacrifices,
and he was generously bestowed with silver and silk.
Zōngyǐn,
whose original name was Ālǐhǎn.
As a son of the imperial clan, he was appointed to the imperial guard,
then became a páiyìn zhīhòu,
and was granted the hereditary position of móukè,
serving as the Right Guard General.
He successively held positions as Military Commissioner of Shùntiān, Guīdé, Zhānghuà, Tánggǔ Tribe, and Hénghǎi Army.
During the southern campaign of Zhènglóng,
he served as the supreme commander of the Shénlüè Army,
leading the vanguard across the Huái River,
and capturing Yángzhōu and Guāzhōudù.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was transferred to be the Vice Commander of the Hénán Circuit,
stationing troops in the border region of Xǔzhōu.
At this time,
the Sòng captured Rǔzhōu,
killing the Cìshǐ Wūgǔsūn Mápō and two thousand Hàn soldiers.
Zōngyǐn dispatched ten-thousand-household commanders Bóshùlǔ Dìngfāng, Wányán Āhēlǎn, Jiágǔ Qīngchén, Wūgǔlún Sānhé, and Qúchú Ézhī to lead four thousand cavalry to attack it,
and thus recaptured Rǔzhōu.
He was appointed as the Prefect of Dàmíng,
while retaining his vice-commander position as before.
After a while,
he became the Commander-in-Chief of the Hénán Circuit,
then promoted to Deputy Left Supervisor of the Marshal's office,
and appointed as Nanjing Resident Guard.
The Emperor said:
"You are young and strong,
but your mind and strength are often sluggish.
When you previously served as Inspector and Capital Prefect,
you worked diligently and tirelessly,
but your handling of affairs was often confused and mistaken.
Strive to improve your professional duties,
to match My expectations."
He was bestowed with a tōngxī belt and a horse.
In the eighth year,
the Shāndōng Circuit Military Command was established,
and Zōngyǐn was appointed its commissioner.
He was promoted to Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
In recognition of his father's merits,
he was granted the hereditary position of púyǔlù túnhé méng'ān,
along with direct command of a móukè.
He was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
while retaining his position as Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
The Emperor asked his chief ministers:
"Although Zōngyǐn's talent does not particularly surpass others,
his character is pure and honest,
and he is an old official of the state.
Formerly, when he was a high official,
you had not yet entered officialdom.
What do you think if I appoint him as Píngzhāng Zhèngshì?"
All the chief ministers replied:
"Zōngyǐn as chancellor
would greatly conform to public expectation."
On that very day, he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
ennobled as Duke of Dài,
and concurrently Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince.
At this time, the common people suffered from the stagnation of currency.
The Emperor asked Zōngyǐn,
who replied:
"Money is a limited commodity;
what is accumulated above obstructs what is below,
hence the stagnation.
During Hǎilíng's military campaign,
various levies were imposed, such as
vegetable garden tax, housing tax, and horse-raising money.
In the early Dàdìng period,
military affairs had not yet ceased,
and provisions were insufficient,
so these were retained without change.
Now that the empire is peaceful,
the imperial treasury is full,
and all these should be abolished."
The Emperor said:
"You care for the common people;
what more do I have to worry about?
Tàiwèi Shǒudào is old;
who else but you?"
Thereupon,
the horse-raising money and other taxes were finally abolished.
Another day,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Zōngyǐn manages his household with strictness and meticulousness;
others cannot compare."
He then looked at Zōngyǐn and said:
"State affairs should also be managed in this way."
After a while,
the northern regions suffered from famine that year,
and military provisions were insufficient.
The court deliberated on transporting grain for relief.
Some said that although the harvest was poor,
the old stores were abundant,
and the autumn harvest was approaching,
so there was no need to labor further with transport.
Zōngyǐn said:
"The state's normal accumulation of grain
is precisely to prepare for lean years.
If we wait for the autumn harvest,
many will be exhausted.
If people are emaciated,
what about border defense?"
The Emperor adopted his suggestion.
Zōngyǐn requested that his son, Yínshùkě, inherit his méng'ān.
Coincidentally, Tàiwèi Shǒudào also requested that his son, Shénguǒnú, inherit his móukè.
For all inheritors who did not know the Nǚzhēn script,
they were ordered to learn it.
Shìzōng said:
"Among these two sons,
I know that one has learned Hàn characters,
but has not learned Nǚzhēn characters.
From now on, if one has learned one of the Nǚzhēn, Qìdān, or Hàn characters,
they will be permitted to inherit."
This was then enacted into law.
Zōngyǐn fell ill
and could not attend court.
The Emperor asked his chief ministers:
"Why does Zōngyǐn not attend court?"
Tàiwèi Shǒudào replied that he was ill.
The Emperor said:
"Chancellor Zhìníng once said,
'If I am ordered to go on a campaign,
I dare not refuse.
But as for the office of chancellor,
I truly dare not assume it.'
Does Zōngyǐn perhaps have this same intention?"
In the twenty-fourth year,
Shìzōng was about to visit Shàngjīng.
The Emperor said:
"Línhuáng and Wūgǔlí Shíléi have had poor harvests for years.
I wish to travel by the southern route,
passing through Dōngjīng in the third month to pay respects at the Empress Dowager's tomb,
and reaching Shàngjīng in the fifth month.
In spring, birds and beasts breed,
and agricultural work is beginning;
there is no need for hunting expeditions to conduct affairs.
What do you all think?"
Zōngyǐn replied:
"The southern route has had good harvests,
and fodder and grain are cheap.
It should be as Your Majesty commanded."
Thus, they proceeded by the southern route.
When Shìzōng arrived at Shàngjīng,
he heard that the concurrently serving Commissioner of the Imperial Clan, Zōngníng, was unable to properly manage the imperial clan members in Shàngjīng,
and that sons of the imperial clan often did not pursue productive livelihoods.
The Emperor said to Zōngyǐn:
"You investigate this matter
and punish them appropriately."
Zōngyǐn reported:
"Sons who accompany officials in service,
after their fathers' deaths, do not return to their native lands,
and this is why many are fond of idleness."
The Emperor ordered them to be recalled.
He feasted the imperial clan in Huángwǔ Hall,
and they played polo for entertainment.
The Emperor said:
"Granting rewards to the imperial clan
is a small favor,
and it's also impossible to promote everyone uniformly.
I wish to assign them to various bureaus for appointment.
Among them, who are capable?"
Zōngyǐn replied:
"Ānchūhǔ, son of Fèngguó Wòzhǔn, and Ālú, great-grandson of Yùguó Gōng Yù, can be put to use."
The Emperor said:
"Determine what positions they can hold,
and investigate others to report to Me."
An imperial edict appointed Ānchūhǔ and Ālú as Fèngyù.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he requested to retire.
Shìzōng said:
“This old man is not managing affairs well,
his request may be granted.”
The ministers reported:
“An old official should remain by Your Majesty’s side.”
The Emperor said:
“The prime minister supervises all affairs of the realm,
it is not a place for the elderly.
If one is not competent for the position,
I too would feel ashamed.
If a worthy man is in court,
it benefits the common people,
and all four quarters look up to him,
I too share in his glory and beauty.”
The ministers had no reply.
Zōngyǐn entered to express his gratitude.
The Emperor said:
“You have served long as an external official,
and no faults have been reported,
but I regret having employed you somewhat late,
and now your energy seems to have declined.
The affairs of the province are extremely bothersome,
if I were to reluctantly retain you,
then the four quarters would consider me biased,
and you yourself would not be at ease.”
A short while later,
the Emperor asked Zōngyǐn’s son:
“Your father has retired,
where will he reside?”
His son said:
“With many family members gathered,
he cannot remain in the capital.”
The Emperor sent an envoy to ask Zōngyǐn:
“I wish to keep you,
and occasionally tour with you,
your son’s words are thus,
what is your definite plan now?”
Zōngyǐn said:
“How could your servant not wish to remain here,
but in my remaining years of leisure,
to still be beneath the imperial carriage,
I fear it would trouble the Sacred Master’s heart.
Since you, in pity, do not bear to discard this old servant,
and I can occasionally gaze upon Your Majesty’s face,
how dare your servant go elsewhere.
There are no old acquaintances remaining in my hometown,
even if I were to go there,
with whom shall I associate?”
Thereupon, he was granted a mansion of the highest quality in one district,
and he accompanied the Emperor in all banquets, gatherings, and hunts.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he passed away.
Zōngníng’s original name was Ātǔgǔ,
he was descended from Jǐngzǔ,
and was the grandson of Grand Commandant Ālíhéhǎn.
He was diligent and honest by nature,
and possessed great ambition.
He began his career as the Commander of the Southern Expedition for Hǎilíng,
fought at Guāzhōu Dù,
and his merits were the greatest.
He successively served as the Prefect of Qízhōu.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he became the Commander of the Troops for Huìníng Fǔ Lù,
and was promoted to Commissioner of the Guīdé Army.
At that time, there was a drought and locusts,
Zōngníng supervised the people to catch them,
and for every dòu of dead locusts caught,
a dòu of grain was given,
and in a few days the locusts were eradicated.
He was transferred to govern Níngchāng Jūn,
then appointed to oversee the affairs of Línhuáng Fǔ,
and then moved to Tiāndé Jūn.
Shìzōng once said to his ministers:
“Although Zōngníng’s wisdom and foresight are shallow,
he is loved by all people wherever he goes.”
He was then appointed as the Commander of the Right Wing of the Expeditionary Army,
and served as the envoy to congratulate the Sòng on the New Year.
He was successively promoted to Minister of War,
and granted the hereditary Míngān Lièlǐmò of Héduán for Lóngzhōu Lù.
He went out to oversee the affairs of Dàmíng Fǔ,
was moved to govern Lìshè Jūn,
and soon after, concurrently served as Deputy Administrator of Dàmùqīn Fǔ.
Zōngníng was often ill,
Shìzōng wished to place him in a cool region,
and assigned him to govern Xiánpíng,
and issued an edict making his son Fúbǎoláng ● the Prefect of Hánzhōu,
to facilitate his care.
Not long after,
he entered the court and was appointed concurrently as Deputy Administrator of Dàmùqīn Fǔ,
and then appointed to the Privy Council.
In the second year of Míngchāng,
he passed away.
Zōngníng lived a simple and frugal life at home like a commoner,
but was intelligent and discerning in handling affairs.
When he governed Línhuáng,
a neighboring country was on alert,
Zōngníng heard they lacked provisions,
and immediately released grain from the granaries,
ordering them to exchange it for cattle,
when the enemy knew they had obtained grain,
they immediately retreated.
The border people, after the Wōwò rebellion,
suffered from a lack of cattle,
Zōngníng again ordered the people to exchange grain for cattle,
and thereafter the people obtained cattle and the granaries had double the grain as before,
such was his planning.
Zōngdào’s original name was Bāshí,
he was a member of the Sìshǔ Sì in Shàngjīng,
descended from Jǐngzǔ,
and was the youngest son of Grand Commandant ÉLùn.
He was knowledgeable in the Zhōu Yì and Mèngzǐ,
and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
In the fifth year of Dàdìng,
he was appointed Gate Attendant,
and successively promoted to Supervisor of the Imperial Attendants Bureau.
Right Chancellor Wūgǔlùn Yuánzhōng, Left Guard General Púsàn Kuí, and others once gathered for a banquet,
and had a private discussion,
Zōngdào immediately secretly reported it.
Shìzōng commended him,
appointed him Right Guard General,
and sent him out as Deputy Commander of the Southwest Route.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed concurrently as Administrator of Píngyáng Fǔ.
Yílà Zhòngfāng, Deputy Commander of the Shǎnxī Route and Left Executive of the Privy Council, recommended him as his successor,
and he was appointed Commander of the Northwest Route.
According to custom,
the various tribes presented over eight hundred horses as tribute,
Zōngdào declined to accept them,
the various tribes were pleased and submitted,
and the border regions were peacefully governed.
The Judicial Investigation Bureau, observing his integrity,
summoned him to be the Right Deputy Commander of the Palace Guard.
Soon after, he was appointed Commander of the Shǎnxī Route,
and due to his stability and calm, he won the hearts of the military and the people,
and was specially promoted three ranks,
concurrently overseeing the affairs of Jīngzhào Fǔ.
At that time, there was a drought in Xià,
he ordered the Prefect of Cháng’ān to draw water from Tàibái Qiū,
and personally welcomed it from the distant suburbs,
and it rained upon reaching the city.
That year saw a great harvest,
people believed it was due to his sincere intention,
and engraved a stone to commemorate it.
In the second year of Chéng’ān,
he served as the envoy to congratulate the Sòng on the New Year,
and was soon after appointed Commander of the Hénán Route.
A man named Zhāng Wěi from Sìzhōu captured a Sòng man, Wáng Wàn,
who revealed information about their territory,
Zōngdào suspected he was wrongly accused,
and investigated to find the truth.
Wàn was
a merchant from Chǔzhōu,
Wěi owed Wàn over five thousand strings of goods,
and had not repaid him for three years,
Wàn sought repayment,
and was falsely accused by Wěi.
Thereupon, Wěi was punished and Wàn was returned,
people at the time admired his fairness.
Later, he requested to retire,
the imperial court, knowing it was not his true intention,
appointed him to govern Hézhōng Fǔ,
where he implemented benevolent policies,
and the people erected his statue in a lofty pavilion,
and offered sacrifices to it in due season.
He was transferred to govern Líntáo,
but resigned due to illness.
In the fourth year of Tàihé,
he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Senior General of the Dragon and Tiger Guard.
Zōngxióng's original name was Móuliánghǔ,
Kāngzōng's eldest son.
When he was first born,
Shìzǔ saw him and was struck by his unusual appearance,
saying,
"This child has extraordinary bearing and character;
he will surely become a vessel of the state in the future."
He then unclasped his scabbard and dagger,
and had it always placed beside the child,
saying,
"When he comes of age, let him wear it."
At nine, he could shoot a fleeing rabbit.
At eleven,
he shot a running deer.
Shìzǔ sat him on his knee and said,
"This child is already like this when young;
in the future, he will surpass his peers."
He bestowed upon him a silver wine vessel.
When he grew up,
he had a remarkably imposing appearance,
was skilled in debate,
and possessed great strategies and wisdom.
He was filial, respectful, humble, and cautious,
and people loved and respected him.
After Kāngzōng died,
the Liáo envoy Āxībǎo came,
riding his horse to the steps of the spirit-draped bier,
and selected horses among the funeral gifts.
Tàizǔ was enraged
and wanted to kill Āxībǎo,
but Zōngxióng remonstrated,
and Tàizǔ then stopped.
When Tàizǔ was about to raise an army,
Zōngxióng said,
"The Liáo ruler is arrogant and extravagant,
and his people are ignorant of military matters;
they can be captured.
They could not capture a single Xiāo Hǎilǐ,
yet our troops captured him."
Tàizǔ approved of his words.
When attacking Níngjiāngzhōu,
the Bóhǎi troops were very fierce.
Zōngxióng, with his division, defeated the Bóhǎi troops,
and for his merit, he was granted the hereditary title of Qiānhù Mǒukè.
When Tàizǔ defeated the Liáo troops at Chūhédìan,
Zōngxióng spearheaded the assault and fought bravely,
gaining many merits.
In the battle of Dálǔgǔchéng,
Zōngxióng commanded the right army,
personally leading his soldiers into battle.
When the Liáo troops facing the right army had already retreated,
the emperor ordered Zōngxióng to assist the left army in attacking the Liáo troops.
Zōngxióng went around behind the Liáo troops and attacked them,
and the Liáo troops were utterly routed.
He pursued the fleeing enemy, capitalizing on the victory.
As night fell,
they surrounded them.
At dawn,
the Liáo troops broke through the encirclement and escaped.
They were pursued and killed until Yǐlǘ Báishí before returning.
The emperor patted his back and said,
"With this son,
what task can I not accomplish?"
He bestowed upon him his imperial robes.
When the Liáo emperor arrived at the gate with seven hundred thousand men,
all the generals said,
"The Liáo army is very strong;
it is not advisable to engage quickly."
Zōngxióng said,
"Not so.
Though the Liáo troops are numerous,
they are all led by mediocre generals,
and their soldiers are fearful;
they are not to be feared.
If we fight, we can crush them in the palm of our hand."
The emperor said,
"Excellent."
They pursued and caught up with the Liáo emperor at Hùbùdágāng.
Zōngxióng led his troops straight forward,
engaging in close combat.
Zōngxióng ordered the front line to hold spears and strike the Liáo cavalry's horses' heads,
while those behind shot at them,
utterly defeating the Liáo troops.
The emperor praised Zōngxióng's merit,
holding his hand and commending him.
He bestowed upon him his imperial armor and helmet, his imperial warhorse, precious goods, and slaves.
When Xiéyě attacked Chūnzhōu,
Zōngxióng, along with Zōnggàn and Lóushì, captured Jīnshānxiàn.
As they approached Báiyīnglín,
they captured seven scouts,
and released one of them to return.
When the county people heard that the main army had arrived,
they dispersed,
and Jīnshānxiàn was then taken.
He joined Xiéyě in taking Tàizhōu.
Tàizǔ personally led the capture of Línhuángfǔ,
sending Zōngxióng to set out first.
They encountered five thousand Liáo troops;
Zōngxióng fought them,
and the main army also arrived,
utterly defeating them.
When the defending commander Tàbùyě surrendered,
the emperor gave his daughter to Zōngxióng,
rewarding his merit in setting out first and defeating the Liáo relief force.
Later, he inspected the land of Tàizhōu with Pújiānú.
Zōngxióng brought a sample of the soil and reported,
"The soil is like this;
it can be cultivated."
The emperor followed his advice.
From then on, over ten thousand families were moved to Tàizhōu to establish military agricultural colonies,
because Zōngxióng and others had said the land was suitable for cultivation.
After Xījīng surrendered, it rebelled again.
At that time, provisions were almost exhausted,
and there was discussion about abandoning the siege.
Zōngxióng said,
"Xījīng
is a major metropolis.
If we abandon it and leave,
those who have surrendered will lose heart,
and the remaining factions of Liáo and the Xià people will be able to spy on us."
He then offered heavy rewards to motivate the soldiers.
Soon after,
there was a fire at night,
as large as a bushel,
that fell into the city.
Zōngxióng said,
"This is an omen that the city will be breached."
When Xījīng was captured,
Zōngxióng was given one hundred taels of gold,
ten sets of clothing, slaves, and other items.
He joined Zōnghán and others in attacking Gěng Shǒuzhōng's seven thousand troops forty lǐ east of Xījīng,
utterly defeating them.
He welcomed Tàizǔ at Yuānyāngluò,
and followed him to Guīhuàzhōu.
He became gravely ill,
and Zōnggàn asked what he wished to say.
Zōngxióng said,
"The great enterprise of the state is accomplished,
the Emperor may live for ten thousand years,
and the four directions are pacified.
I have no regrets even if I die."
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ,
he passed away,
aged forty.
Tàizǔ came to inquire about his illness,
but did not see him in time,
and wept bitterly.
He said to his ministers,
"This son's strategies surpassed others,
and he was brave and decisive in battle.
Few could compare to him."
His funeral gifts were increased.
An imperial decree ordered the Házhá Qiānhù Fùmǎ Shíjiānú to escort his coffin back,
to be buried in Guīhuàzhōu,
and a Buddhist temple was built at the place of his death.
Zōngxióng loved learning and was fond of books.
Once, while hunting with the emperor,
he was accidentally struck by a stray arrow,
but his expression did not change,
fearing that the emperor would find out and punish the archer.
After pulling out the arrow,
he feigned illness and returned home,
lying in bed for two months.
During this time, he studied the large and small scripts of Qìdān,
mastering them completely.
Whenever the Jīn state was initially established,
in enacting laws and setting regulations,
he always consulted and planned with Zōnggàn.
And when negotiating peace with Liáo,
for documents and imperial edicts in Qìdān and Chinese characters,
Zōngxióng, along with Zōnghán and Xīyǐn, managed the affair.
He was also strong and nimble,
able to draw a powerful bow and shoot far,
almost three hundred paces.
Once, he rode a horse and shot at three roe deer,
hitting two of them.
When he drew his bow again,
his horse stumbled.
He leaped off,
held the bowstring as before,
and then drew it fully and shot, capturing the deer.
Once, as Zōngxióng was chasing a rabbit,
Tàlǎn also shot at it from behind.
Having already loosed his arrow,
Tàlǎn shouted,
"The arrow is coming!"
Zōngxióng looked back,
caught the arrow with his hand,
then shot the rabbit,
hitting it.
His agility was like this.
During the Tiānjuàn
period, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Tàishī and Qíguó Wáng.
In Tiāndé 2nd year,
he was additionally granted the title Qín Hàn Guó Wáng.
In Zhènglóng 2nd year,
this was changed to Tàifù and Jīnyuán Jùn Wáng.
In Dàdìng 2nd year,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Chǔ Wáng,
with the posthumous name Wēimǐn,
and enshrined in Tàizǔ's ancestral temple.
In the 15th year,
an imperial edict commanded his portrait be hung in Yǎnqìng Gōng.
His sons were Púlǔhǔ, Àndáihǎi, and Ālín.
His grandsons were Chángchūn, Húlǐlà, Húlà, Gǔlǔ, Cházhá, Pàbā, and Échū.
Originally,
Zōnggàn had taken Zōngxióng's wife,
which Hǎilíng resented.
When he usurped the throne,
he sent the palace guard general Cháo Xiá and the seal-bearer Lǘ Shān to Héjiān,
where they imprisoned Zōngxióng's wife in the government office.
The next day,
she, her daughter-in-law, Chángchūn's brothers, and Cházhá's son—seven people in total—were all killed and burned,
and their bones cast into the Háoshuǐ.
In Dàdìng 17th year,
an imperial edict ordered the relevant officials to collect and bury them.
Originally,
Púlǔhǔ inherited the post of Méng'ān.
When Púlǔhǔ died,
he was posthumously granted Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū.
His son Huánduān inherited the post,
and rose to the rank of Jīnwúwèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
When Huánduān died,
his son Niǎopín died before he could inherit.
Zhāngzōng commanded Zōngxióng's grandson Púdài to inherit the post.
Púdài,
at the end of the Dàdìng period,
had successively served as Tóngqiān Dàmùqīnfǔ Shì.
Upon Zhāngzōng's ascension to the throne,
the Nine Circuits Judicial Commissioners' Office was first established,
and Púdài was appointed Běijīng Línhuáng Tíxíngshǐ.
The imperial edict stated:
"When I first ascended the throne,
I worried about the myriad common people.
I constantly reflected that justice in prisons was not yet achieved,
and agriculture and sericulture were not yet encouraged.
Officials sometimes did not follow laws and regulations,
thus undermining My governance.
Although the imperial court sent envoys to investigate,
it was difficult to cover everything thoroughly.
Only the officials for judicial administration, agricultural promotion, and investigation
have existed since ancient times.
Now, these positions are specially established for the Nine Circuits.
You must exert your utmost effort
and proceed with your duties diligently."
Since Xīzōng's time,
envoys had been sent to investigate the merits and demerits of official administration.
Upon Shìzōng's ascension,
envoys were dispatched every few years to assess and dismiss officials.
Therefore, during the Dàdìng period,
officials in all prefectures and counties adhered to the law,
the common people prospered,
and it was known as a period of minor peace.
Someone once said that the investigating envoys
often judged officials based on personal likes and dislikes,
and asked the Chancellor.
The Chancellor replied:
"We ministers will again investigate for Your Majesty."
For this reason, Shìzōng had often wanted to establish the Judicial Commissioners' Office but had not succeeded.
Zhāngzōng, recalling the former dynasty's practices,
thus implemented it at the beginning of his reign.
When the Nine Circuits Judicial Commissioners had their farewell audience in Qìnghé Diàn,
the Emperor said:
"In establishing official systems,
leniency and severity must be appropriately balanced.
All matters involving both military and civilian affairs
should be resolved justly and fairly.
Restrain your family and subordinates,
and do not let them obstruct or disturb county affairs.
Now, prison wardens are subordinate to the Judicial Commissioners' Office;
I only hope that there will be no unjust cases in prisons."
After they withdrew,
he again sent a close minister to instruct them, saying:
"You are all exceptionally selected for your talent and virtue,
entrusted with special responsibilities.
If you perform your duties with dedication,
there will be commendations and rewards.
Otherwise, there will be punishments."
The following year,
Púdài then inherited the Méng'ān, it is said.
Ālín
was intelligent, astute, and eloquent.
He was proficient in both Jurchen and Khitan scripts, as well as Chinese characters.
As a child, he once entered the palace,
and Xīzōng saw him and was impressed,
saying:
"This child will surely serve the state with distinction in the future."
At eighteen,
he was appointed Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn
and served as Shùntiān Jūn Jiédu Shǐ.
In Tiāndé 2nd year,
because of his integrity,
he was promoted to Yìdū Yǐn concurrently Shāndōng Dōng Lù Bīngmǎ Dōuzǒngguǎn,
and successively served as Jiédu Shǐ for the Tàiníng, Dìnghǎi, Zhènxī, and Ānguó armies.
When Hǎilíng campaigned south,
he appointed Ālín as the Dōuzǒngguǎn of the Shényǒng and Wǔpíng armies,
crossing the Huái River via the Shòuzhōu route,
and combined forces with the agricultural commissioner Yílà Yuán Yí, leading thirty thousand soldiers as the vanguard.
In the tenth month of that year,
they reached Lúzhōu
and battled Sòng general Wáng Quán's army of over one hundred thousand at Zhè Gāo Zhèn Wèizǐ Qiáo,
defeating them.
Upon reaching the south of Hézhōu,
they again engaged Wáng Quán's army of over eighty thousand in a decisive battle,
and again defeated them,
pursuing and killing them to the river's edge,
beheading several thousand.
The Emperor ascended the throne in Liáoyáng.
Hǎilíng died,
and the main army returned north.
As they were about to cross the Huái River, there were very few boats,
and the soldiers competed for boats, unable to cross quickly.
Ālín captured some locals
who knew of a passable spot,
marked it with willow branches,
and ordered his own unit to wade across.
After reaching the north bank,
the other armies, still fighting to cross, were indeed ambushed by the Sòng people.
When he later had an audience,
the Emperor heard of Ālín's meritorious service at the Huái River,
and also that he returned with his entire army.
He was promoted to Bīngbù Shàngshū,
and supervised the planning and provisioning of the armies campaigning against Wōwò,
receiving one gold plaque and four silver plaques.
When Wōwò was defeated,
he returned to Yìzhōu,
where he died of illness.
When his coffin arrived in the capital,
the Emperor ordered a memorial service at Yǒng'ān Sì,
and all officials attended the mourning.
He was granted five hundred taels of silver, thirty bolts of brocade, and one hundred rolls of silk.
Àndáihǎi,
also named Ālǔwǎn,
was Zōngxióng's second son.
He was dignified and composed by nature,
not speaking lightly,
and possessed his father's demeanor.
At fifteen,
Tàizǔ bestowed upon him a first-grade umbrella.
At over twenty,
he played polo on the imperial field, divided into teams,
and won three consecutive rounds.
The imperial clan and old veterans were all impressed.
When the winning gifts were presented,
Àndáihǎi was the leader of the group,
and Tàizōng joyfully said:
"Today's victory
is due to the strength of this grandson."
He was especially richly rewarded.
In Tiānjuàn 2nd year,
he inherited his father's Méng'ān.
He was appointed Dàzōngzhèng Céng,
ceded the Méng'ān to his elder brother's son Huànduān,
was additionally made Wǔdìng Jūn Jiédu Shǐ,
and attended court.
He was changed to Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūzhīhuī Shǐ,
enfeoffed as Jīnyuán Jùn Wáng,
promoted to Tán Wáng,
transferred to Tóngpàn Dàzōngzhèng Shì,
and separately granted a hereditary Méng'ān.
When Hǎilíng was about to move the capital to Zhōngdū,
Àndáihǎi remonstrated, saying:
"To abandon the ancestral land where the dynasty arose and move elsewhere
is unrighteous."
Hǎilíng was displeased
and kept him in Shàngjīng.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Yùn Wáng,
then changed to Wèi Wáng,
and appointed Jìnán Yǐn.
Àndáihǎi could not endure the low, damp climate
and often reported sick.
When Hǎilíng heard of this,
he changed him to Xījīng Liúshǒu.
According to the Zhènglóng regulations, his princely title was revoked, and he was appointed Guǎngníng Yǐn.
Shìzōng ascended the throne in Dōngjīng.
An edict of amnesty reached Guǎngníng.
His younger brother Yānjīng tried to persuade Āndáhǎi to refuse it.
Āndáhǎi accepted it.
At that time, Hǎilíng sent an envoy to the city walls.
Āndáhǎi ascended the city wall and told the envoy:
"This prefecture is close to Liáoyáng,
and it is impossible to resist.
I am merely complying for now;
it is not of my own volition."
Yānjīng also ascended the watchtower and spoke with the envoy,
pointing and criticizing rudely.
When all the commanderies arrived in Dōngjīng,
Āndáhǎi and his brother also went to pay their respects.
The officials deliberated,
saying, "They accepted the edict of amnesty,
yet they spoke differently afterwards,
holding two ends of a rope."
They requested that both be executed.
The Emperor said:
"Zhènglóng ruthlessly purged the imperial clan;
I cannot follow his example.
Āndáhǎi was merely misled by his brother."
Therefore, Āndáhǎi was released,
and Yānjīng was executed.
Within a few days,
he was again appointed acting Grand Supervisor of the Imperial Clan.
He was promoted again to Grand Mentor to the Crown Prince,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Lánlíng Commandery.
He was then appointed Director of Agricultural Affairs.
During Hǎilíng's time,
he moved from Shàngjīng to Héjiān.
The land was barren.
An imperial edict allowed Āndáhǎi's clan of twenty-five families
to relocate to a nearby place at their convenience.
So they moved to Píngzhōu.
An edict granted three hundred qǐng of official land in Píngzhōu,
and three hundred rooms,
and one hundred qǐng of official land in Zōngzhōu.
He was promoted to Prince of Jīnyuán Commandery
and retired.
In Dàdìng eighth year,
he was summoned for an audience.
The Emperor said:
"How many elders of the imperial clan like you
are there?"
He was granted ten thousand strings of cash,
and one mansion.
He was retained in the capital
to participate in imperial tours, hunts, and banquets.
In the fourteenth year,
he passed away
at the age of sixty-seven.
On his deathbed,
he warned his sons:
"You should not become violent and arrogant just because you were born into wealth and nobility.
You should be humble and reserved.
Hǎilíng, out of suspicion, annihilated the imperial clan.
I escaped death because of my pure conscientiousness.
You should only do good every day,
and not disgrace our family."
Wányán Xīyǐn's original name was Gǔshén.
He was the son of Huāndū.
Since Tàizǔ raised his army,
he was always in the ranks,
sometimes following Tàizǔ, sometimes Sāgǎi,
or campaigning with various generals,
and thus had accomplishments.
The Jīn people initially had no writing system.
As the state grew stronger
and fostered good relations with neighboring countries,
they began to use Qìdān characters.
Tàizǔ ordered Xīyǐn to create a writing system for their own country
and establish its regulations.
Xīyǐn then imitated the Hàn Chinese regular script,
based on the Qìdān character system,
and combined it with their native language,
to create the Nǚzhēn script.
In the eighth month of Tiānfǔ third year,
the character book was completed.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and ordered its promulgation.
Xīyǐn was granted one horse and one set of clothing.
Later, Xīzōng also created Nǚzhēn characters,
and both Xīyǐn's and Xīzōng's characters were used concurrently.
The characters created by Xīyǐn were called the Nǚzhēn Great Script,
and those created by Xīzōng were called the Small Script.
The Liáo people Dīliù, Héshàng, and Yǎlǐsī abandoned Zhōngjīng and fled.
Xīyǐn, along with Dígǔnǎi, Lóushì, and Yúdǔ, pursued them.
Dīliù and others, hearing of Xīyǐn's army,
fled again.
They then subjugated the nearby people and returned.
The Xī person Luòhǔ surrendered.
Xīyǐn sent Luòhǔ to persuade his father, the Western Military Commissioner Érǐlà.
Érǐlà surrendered with his entire tribe.
Zōnghàn was stationed in Běi'ān.
He sent Xīyǐn to manage the nearby territories,
and Xīyǐn captured the Liáo guard Yēlǜ Xíníliè,
who revealed that the Liáo ruler was hunting at Yuānyāng Luò.
Zōnghàn then requested to advance his troops.
Zōnghàn planned to meet the Grand Marshal Gǎo at Xīwáng Lǐng.
Liáo troops were stationed at Gǔbèikǒu.
He sent Póluóhuǒ with two hundred soldiers to attack them,
and Húntù also led two hundred men as reinforcements.
Húntù, hearing that the Liáo troops were numerous,
requested more soldiers.
Zōnghàn wanted to go himself,
but Xīyǐn and Lóushì said:
"These are minor bandits.
Please allow us to defeat them for you with a thousand soldiers."
When Húntù arrived at Gǔbèikǒu,
he encountered Liáo skirmishers
and pursued them into the valley.
Over ten thousand Liáo infantry and cavalry pressed into battle,
and several men died.
Húntù held the pass.
Xīyǐn and the others arrived,
and severely defeated the Liáo forces,
slaughtering a great many,
and capturing all their armor, helmets, and baggage.
They again defeated their ambush,
killing over a thousand men
and capturing over a hundred horses.
They then proceeded with Zōnghàn to Xīwáng Lǐng,
planning to meet at Yángchéng Luò.
Zōnghàn ambushed the Liáo Emperor at Wǔyuàn Sī.
Xīyǐn served as the vanguard,
leading only eight cavalrymen,
and fought the Liáo ruler,
defeating him three times in one day.
The next day,
Xīyǐn captured the surrenderer Mázhé,
who reported that the Liáo ruler was in the desert,
abandoning his baggage,
and was about to flee to Xījīng.
They almost caught the Liáo ruler south of Báishuǐ Luò.
The Liáo ruler escaped with light cavalry.
They seized all the treasures from his inner treasury
and then proceeded to Xījīng.
Xījīng surrendered,
and Púchá was appointed to guard it.
Xīyǐn reached the Yǐshì Tribe
but missed the Liáo ruler and returned.
When Zōnghàn returned to the court,
Xīyǐn temporarily commanded both the Southwest and Northwest Circuits.
At this time,
the Xià people had already accepted the alliance,
the Liáo ruler had been captured,
Yēlǜ Dàshí had declared himself emperor,
and the Xià kingdom sent a letter to Lóushì, blaming the generals for abandoning the alliance,
as their troops had entered Xià territory
and looted extensively.
Xīyǐn submitted this letter,
and also reported:
"I hear that Xià envoys are arranging with Dàshí to take the various commanderies of Shānxī.
In my opinion,
the Xià alliance cannot be trusted."
The Emperor said:
"The matters with Xià should be handled appropriately.
Whether the army entering their territory is trustworthy or not, I do not know.
The conspiracy with Dàshí
cannot be overlooked;
prepare strictly for it."
When the great expedition against the Sòng was launched,
Xīyǐn served as the Right Supervisor-General of the Marshal's office.
In the second expedition against the Sòng,
he captured the two emperors and returned.
When the army returned,
Xīyǐn was granted an iron certificate,
exempting him from crimes not usually pardoned by general amnesties,
while other matters were dismissed without investigation.
When Zōnghàn attacked King Kāng,
Xīyǐn pursued him to Yángzhōu,
but King Kāng fled.
Later, he and Zōnghàn both attended court in the capital,
and requested that Xīzōng be established as the heir apparent.
Tàizōng then appointed Xīzōng as Ānbānbójíliè.
Xīzōng 繼位,
Xīyǐn was Grand Councilor of the Left and concurrently Attendant Counselor,
and was granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When Xīyǐn was chancellor,
for all major policies, he personally took the blame first.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn,
he requested to retire,
but it was not permitted.
He was dismissed to become the Administrator of Xīngzhōng.
In the second year,
he was again made Grand Councilor of the Left and concurrently Attendant Counselor,
and shortly after, was enfeoffed as King Chén.
He and Zōnggàn together executed Zōngpán and Zōngjùn.
In the third year,
an imperial edict was bestowed upon Xīyǐn, saying:
“The chief ministers have secretly reported
that treacherous conduct has already begun to sprout,
with a heart disloyal to the sovereign,
and words uttered that are impious.
During private gatherings, clandestine discussions take place,
questioning to whom the imperial regalia truly belongs.
This has been heard for a long time,
and now it has led to its exposure and downfall.”
Thereupon, he was granted death,

and concurrently the Right Grand Councilor Xiāo Qìng and Xīyǐn's sons, Bádá, who was Administrator for the Compilation of National History, and Màn dài, who was Director of Imperial Regalia, were also killed.
At this time,
Xīzōng had no imperial sons,
so those who were jealous of Xīyǐn used these words to slander him.
In the third year of Huángtǒng,
the emperor knew that Xīyǐn had truly no ulterior motives,
and that his death was not for his crime.
Xīyǐn was posthumously granted Yítóng Sānsī and Duke of Xíng,
and reburied.
Xiāo Qìng was granted Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as King Yù.
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
he was demoted by precedent to Prince of Jīnyuán Commandery.
In the fifteenth year of Dàdìng,
he was given the posthumous name Zhēnxìan.
His grandsons were Shǒudào, Shǒuzhēn, and Shǒunéng.
Shǒudào has his own biography.
Shǒuzhēn's original name was Zuǒyè.
In the second year of Zhēnyuán,
he inherited his grandfather Gǔshén's hereditary company commander (móukè) position.
When Dàdìng changed its reign title,
he was appointed to serve as Director of Imperial Regalia Attendant,
granted Tongjìn,
appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhāngdé Commandery,
transferred to be Resident Administrator of Běijīng,
and then moved to Shàngjīng.
He was punished for settling Qìdān households and marrying a wife within the Ministry of Revenue,
receiving a hundred strokes with the rod
and being stripped of his name.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was reinstated as Commander of Imperial Guards of Xījīng.
Shìzōng admired his uprightness,
appointed him Commander of Imperial Guards of the Left of Zhōngdū,
promoted him to Prefect of Dàxīng Prefecture,
then advanced him to Vice Prefect,
and changed his position to Vice Resident Administrator of Xījīng.
The Censorate reported Shǒuzhēn's excellent administrative performance.
Shìzōng then said to his attendant ministers:
“Shǒuzhēn is the son of a meritorious minister,
and moreover, he possesses talent and ability,
completely surpassing his elder brother Shǒudào.
He can be put to use in the future.”
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Minister of Punishments,
and concurrently Right Remonstrance Official.
Shǒuzhēn, along with Zhāng Wěi, who was Compiler of the Diaries of Activity and Repose, memorialized:
“During the Táng dynasty, when officials from the Central Secretariat and Chancellery entered the imperial chambers,
the remonstrance officials would follow them,
desiring them to participate in hearing about government affairs
so that they could offer their insights.
Furthermore, the Clerks of the Diaries of Activity and Repose and the Recorders of the Diaries of Activity and Repose,
whenever the emperor held court,
stood to his left and right.
If there was an imperial decree, they would descend the steps and listen respectfully,
then withdraw and record it
to compile the Diaries of Activity and Repose.
Because attendant officials were always present at court,
they were expected to stand in attendance.
From ancient times, when officials from the Left Bureau ascended to the palace,
remonstrance officials and compilers of the Diaries of Activity and Repose did not avoid them.
It was only when attendant officials were appointed or dismissed, or when expedient matters were discussed,
that they were instructed to avoid them.
Recently, all of us ministers have been uniformly ordered to withdraw,
and even when memorials and documents were presented in the imperial chambers,
we ministers were not allowed to stand in attendance.
Thus, for all imperial instructions and matters of government discussed,
we ministers have no way of knowing,
what can be recorded?
What can be expounded?
This does not seem to align with the original purpose for establishing these offices.
If government affairs are leaked,
there is a specific crime for lack of secrecy.”
The emperor accepted this.
Soon after, he was dispatched as an envoy to congratulate the Sòng emperor on his birthday.
Upon his return, he was appointed Assistant Administrator of Affairs.
At that time, the emperor had just taken charge of governance
and was quite keen on good governance.
He once asked about Emperor Xūan of Hàn's method of "comprehensive examination of names and realities,"
and what the actual implementation of it was like.
Shǒuzhēn recited
“the pivotal mechanisms were thorough and precise,
and the regulations were detailed and complete”
in reply.
The emperor asked:
“When did its implementation truly begin?”
Shǒuzhēn replied:
“It lies in Your Majesty's diligent effort without weariness.”
After a long time,
he was promoted to Grand Councilor of the Left,
and granted the hereditary company commander (móukè) position in Shàngjīng.
In the summer of the third year of Míngchāng,
there was a drought.
The Son of Heaven issued an edict acknowledging his own faults.
Shǒuzhēn, in apprehension,
memorialized requesting to resign from his post.
The imperial edict stated:
“Heaven has withheld timely rain,
causing successive years of disaster,
which is to warn and frighten me for my shortcomings.
I am now planning with a few assisting ministers to rectify my oversights.
You should consider how to assist me in reforming governance,
to respond to the heavenly warnings,
eliminate calamities and summon harmony,
thereby bringing peace to the common people.
You understand state affairs and
are someone I deeply trust.
Yet you attribute faults to yourself and seek to leave.
What about your thought to assist me?”
Shǒuzhēn earnestly resigned,
and was then sent out to govern Dōngpíng Prefecture.
The Assistant Administrator of Affairs, Jiágǔ Héng, was ordered to admonish him, saying:
“You are a descendant of a meritorious minister,
and have early ascended to a high office.
Your talent, capability, and achievements
I have long known.
Therefore, at the beginning of my reign,
I promoted you to a government position.
For several years now,
you have provided much assistance.
Since you have served in demanding positions for a long time,
it is appropriate to provide you with a period of ease and comfort.
Moreover, internal and external positions
should also be rotated.
I now specially bestow this appointment upon you.
Dōngpíng has long been known as a formidable principality,
and in recent years, it has suffered from famine.
It truly depends on your planning.
You should go and pacify it for me.”
He was also granted gold, silk, and a horse
to honor his departure.
Another day,
the emperor asked his chancellors:
“How is Shǒuzhēn governing Dōngpíng?”
They replied:
“He doesn't have to exert much effort.”
The emperor said:
“With his talent,
governing an entire circuit is indeed more than sufficient.”
The Right Grand Councilor Liú Wěi said:
“At present, there is no talent superior to Shǒuzhēn.
To keep him outside [the capital]
is truly a pity.”
The emperor remained silent.
Soon after, he was reassigned as Resident Administrator of Xījīng.
Censor Púlàdū impeached Shǒuzhēn, alleging that he had taken bribes during a past feast given to the northern tribes.
The report was not acted upon.
Right Remonstrance Official Lù Duó submitted a memorial defending him.
In the fourth year,
he was summoned and appointed Grand Academician,
and enfeoffed as Duke Xiāo.
The emperor, in his private chambers,
summoned Shǒuzhēn and said:
“I have specially appointed you
because you were recommended by the Grand Preceptor.
However, your actions recently have often been excessive,
and the people in your department are not carefully selected enough.
Furthermore, you are not in harmony with the Grand Councilor,
which is why I sent you out to an external post.
I remember that since our Illustrious Ancestor and Grand Progenitor established our dynasty,
your ancestor assisted in establishing the mandate,
accumulating meritorious services.
Therefore, I have now summoned and employed you.
You should strive to exert your utmost.
When discussing matters with the Grand Councilor, you should be harmonious,
follow the old regulations,
and not lightly implement reforms.”
Then, he bestowed a jade belt,
and also gave him Púlàdū's impeachment report,
saying:
“I believe you would not do such a thing,
so I am showing this to you.”
Under the old system,
the Censorate had eight censors.
Four Hànren (漢人) were all Jìnshì (進士),
while the four Nǚzhí (女直) were civil officials with senior posts participating in selection and appointment.
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) said:
"Censors hold an important and reputable position,
their caliber is naturally different,
and all should uniformly be selected purely from Jìnshì (進士)."
One day, during a court audience,
the Emperor asked about the transfer of clerks.
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) replied:
"Currently, the power of clerks is great, and deep-seated abuses have accumulated;
transfers would be beneficial."
The Emperor once lamented that among scholars, none were comparable to Dǎng Huáiyīng (党懷英).
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) reported that among the Jìnshì (進士), Zhào Fěng (趙渢) and Wáng Tíngyún (王庭筠) were highly acclaimed at the time.
The Emperor said:
"It is difficult to find those who stand out from the crowd."
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) replied:
"Talents appearing once in a generation
have always been rare since ancient times.
However, if the state cultivates them for a long time,
then talented individuals will naturally emerge."
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) then said:
"Regarding the state's examination system,
it is primarily through the Nǚzhí (女直) and Hànren (漢人) Jìnshì (進士) that many talented people are obtained.
This examination should be further expanded.
In the past, those who served in various offices and bureaus had no official background;
only after the Dàdìng (大定) era were they permitted to serve.
The examination for classics students (jīngtóng zhī kē, 經童之科)
was not always established in antiquity.
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, various circuits recommended candidates,
sometimes selecting five to ten people.
In recent times, it was deemed ineffective
and was abolished.
In our dynasty, during the Huángtǒng (皇統) era,
up to fifty people were selected,
making it a regular selection.
During the Tiāndé (天德) era,
it was soon suspended.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
this examination was reinstated.
The court's generosity
allowed for hundreds of selections,
but I truly fear that over time, it will become impossible to manage the appointments.
It should be slightly reduced
to purify the ranks."
He also spoke of ways to economize and save expenses,
and all were graciously accepted.
Previously,
Zhèng Wáng Yǔndǎo (鄭王允蹈) and others had been executed.
The Emperor then distributed their family property among the various princes.
Lǐ Jìngyì (李敬義), a Langzhōng (郎中) of the Ministry of Revenue, said he feared this might cause trouble.
The Emperor also appointed Dǒng Shòu (董壽) as Dūguǎngōu (都管勾) of the Palace Registry (gōngjíjiān, 宮籍監),
and both matters were referred to the Shàngshū Shěng (尚書省) for deliberation.
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) reported:
"Your Majesty wishes to divide the family property of Yǔndǎo (允蹈) and others among the imperial relatives.
The imperial decree has already been issued,
and I fear it cannot be changed.
Now that the bows and arrows of the princes have been reduced,
and the Fǔwèi (府尉) manages their ingress and egress,
I believe bestowing it causes no harm.
As for Dǒng Shòu (董壽), he is a criminal.
It is already fortunate that he was specially pardoned by imperial grace;
it is already a blessing;
he should not be further awarded with titles and rewards."
The Emperor approved what Shǒuzhēn (守貞) said.
Since the beginning of the Míngchāng (明昌) era,
there had been repeated alarms on the northern frontier.
Some requested to dispatch troops to attack them.
The Emperor said:
"We are now negotiating with the south to block the river;
would it be appropriate to again use troops in the north?"
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) said:
"They have repeatedly raided our borders.
If we punish them now,
they will not return again in the future;
this will be evident next year."
The Emperor then discussed methods of defense.
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) said:
"There are only the precedents from before the Huángtǒng (皇統) era;
besides these, there are no other methods."
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) was well-read,
understood the laws,
and was thoroughly familiar with the country's historical precedents.
At that time, the Jīn (金) dynasty had been established for seventy years.
Its rites, music, laws, and administration were based on old systems from Liáo (遼) and Sòng (宋),
being mixed and inconsistent.
When Zhāngzōng (章宗) ascended the throne,
he then reformed and revised them,
making them the laws of that era.
Many of their ceremonies and regulations
were edited and finalized by Shǒuzhēn (守貞).
Therefore, the Míngchāng (明昌) reign
was known as clean and enlightened.
He also liked to promote good people
and assist those who came after.
Many upright officials in the court
came from his tutelage.
Earlier,
the Emperor, out of suspicion and jealousy, had executed Zhèng Wáng Yǔndǎo (鄭王允蹈).
Later, the case of Zhāng Rǔbì (張汝弼)'s wife, Gāo Tuówò (高陀斡), arose,
and the Emperor's suspicion seemed to fall again on Hào Wáng Yǔnzhōng (鎬王允中).
At that time, Jiǎ Shǒuqīan (賈守謙), the Right Jìan Yì Dàfū (右諫議大夫), submitted a memorial discussing current affairs,
hoping to alleviate the Emperor's suspicions.
Lù Duó (路鐸), the Right Shíyí (右拾遺), followed suit,
speaking with even greater directness.
The Emperor was displeased.
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) held the case,
and it remained undecided for a long time.
The Emperor suspected a faction was at play,
and so he sent Shǒuzhēn (守貞) out to govern Jìnán Fǔ (濟南府),
ordering him to depart immediately.
Those who had previously recommended Shǒuzhēn (守貞), such as Dǒng Shīzhōng (董師中) and Lù Duó (路鐸), were all reassigned to outside posts.
The Emperor told his chief ministers:
"Shǒuzhēn (守貞) indeed possesses talent and ability,
but as for his scholarship,
compared to a true Confucian, he is not quite there.
However, he seeks too much power and fame.
With his talent, if he could maintain an impartial heart and uphold righteousness,
how could the court dispense with him?
This current order
is issued after careful consideration."
Shortly after, it was alleged that during his time in government, he had secretly spoken about palace affairs with close attendants
and falsely claimed they were reported to the Emperor.
The Emperor ordered the authorities to interrogate him.
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) confessed voluntarily,
was stripped of one rank,
and relieved of his duties.
An imperial envoy was dispatched with an edict to admonish him, saying:
"Conspiracy and deception against the ruler
have always been subject to standard penalties since ancient times.
Forming cliques and cultivating connections
are great prohibitions for a minister.
Who would have thought that I, as your ruler,
would witness you fall into such guilt?
You originated from a house of merit
and gradually rose to a high office.
When I first inherited the throne,
I eagerly wished to employ you.
Before a year had passed,
you were promoted to a chief minister.
I always hoped for your advice
to jointly achieve great peace.
Indeed, I sought your strengths
without examining your past character.
Your promotion was not without boldness,
and your appointment was not without absolute trust.
Yet, you did not think of repaying my grace,
but instead arbitrarily established your own power,
communicated with close attendants,
secretly inquired about my daily life,
spied on my intentions,
and plotted your future course.
Because your fear of losing position was severe,
your crime of deceiving the ruler became manifest.
You fabricated baseless accusations
and claimed to have offered advice when you never had.
Your righteousness was certainly not about attributing merit to others;
your intention was solely to manipulate the ruler.
Such elaborate deceit,
how could it be fitting for a minister?
Further reviewing the impeachments,
even more private motives are revealed:
seeking the support of relatives and acquaintances and deploying them in the palace,
and allowing criminals and disgraced individuals to enter your fold.
Furthermore, for all official appointments,
you appropriated the benevolence for yourself,
claiming they were all involved in corruption
and should not be appointed to internal or external positions.
Judged by public opinion,
this is certainly intolerable;
measured by your own conscience,
how can you be without shame?
We will temporarily apply a lighter penalty,
thereby showing a mild punishment."
Furthermore, because of Shǒuzhēn (守貞)'s injustice,
an edict was proclaimed to all officials in the Shàngshū Shěng (尚書省).
In the first year of Chéng'ān (承安) (1196),
he was demoted to Hèzhōng Fángyùshǐ (河中防禦使).
Five years later (1200),
he was reassigned as Bùluóhuǒzháshíhé Jiédùshǐ (部羅火扎石合節度使).
When he passed through the capital,
the Emperor issued a handwritten edict to admonish him
and ordered him to proceed to his post.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Zhī Dūfǔ Shì (知都府事).
At that time, there was warfare on the southern frontier.
The Emperor, considering Shāndōng (山東) a crucial region,
needed a high official to pacify it,
so he transferred Shǒuzhēn (守貞) to govern Jìnán Fǔ (濟南府),
where he eventually died.
Upon hearing this,
the Emperor mourned him.
He ordered the relevant authorities to perform sacrifices
and to provide funeral gifts according to the usual regulations for a Gù Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Púchá Tōnglì (故平章政事蒲察通例).
His posthumous name was Sù (肅).
WánYán Shǒuzhēn was steadfast and upright, bright and discerning.
Whenever the court discussed matters or the Emperor had questions,
he would respond by citing classics.
The Emperor once broadly discussed talent with him,
and Shǒuzhēn then traced their character and conduct,
praising and criticizing without the slightest concealment.
Therefore, he was resented by people like Xū Chígúo,
and was ultimately dismissed due to his straightforwardness.
Later, Zhào Bǐngwén entered the Hànlín Academy from an external post
and immediately submitted a memorial, saying:
“I wish Your Majesty would advance gentlemen and retire petty individuals.”
The Emperor asked who he meant by gentlemen and petty individuals.
Bǐngwén replied:
“The gentleman is the former Chancellor Wányán Shǒuzhēn;
the petty individual is the current Cānzhī Zhèngshì Xū Chígúo.”
Such was his high regard throughout the realm.
Wányán Shǒunéng, whose original name was Húlà,
rose through official ranks to become the Cìshǐ of Shāngzhōu.
At the end of the Zhènglóng reign,
the Sòng people captured Shāngzhōu,
and Shǒunéng was taken captive.
In the fifth year of Dàdìng,
the Sòng people requested peace,
and the sworn document stated:
“All prisoners of war
shall be fully returned.”
Wányán Zhòngwéi, serving as the Envoys for Replying to National Messages,
sought Shǒunéng and Wányán Ànchén, the Magistrate of Xīnxī County, from the Sòng,
and they subsequently returned together.
When Shǒunéng and others arrived in the capital,
they had an audience,
and an edict granted them their former official salaries.
In the nineteenth year of Dàdìng,
he became the Zhāotǎoshǐ of the Northwest Circuit.
At this time,
an edict ordered the relocation of Wōwò's remaining followers to Línhuáng and Tàizhōu.
Yālàmínliè had once followed Wōwò;
his younger brother Zhádí was also to be relocated,
but he falsely claimed his brother had died,
bribed Shǒunéng with a horse,
and firmly concealed him, not sending him away.
When he accepted a bribe to appoint Sàiyě Fānbù as an interpreter,
the matter came to light.
At this time,
Xī Shā'ābǔ, the Deputy Jiédùshǐ of the Wūgǔlǐ Shílěi tribe, had beaten a blameless Zhènbiān Méng'ān to death with a staff.
The Shàngshūshěng jointly reported their cases.
The Emperor said:
“Shǒunéng was exceptionally promoted from Cìshǐ to this position,
yet dares to indulge in corruption.
