Previously, many officials of the Zhāotǎosī presented fine horses, camels, falcons, and other items,
which was merely a pretext for extortion.
From now on, all such practices are abolished.”
He then reprimanded Shǒunéng's elder brother, Shǒudào, saying:
“Shǒunéng leaped from Cìshǐ to Zhāotǎo;
among external officials,
there is no position more esteemed.
The former Zhāotǎo Zhédiǎn was executed for corruption;
how could Shǒunéng not know this,
yet dare to act in such a way?
What was his intention?
He is your own brother;
why did you not admonish him beforehand?”
The Emperor said to the Chancellors:
“The Censorate is solely responsible for impeachment and correction.
When Āsīmàn, the Jiédùshǐ of Zōngzhōu, first took office,
he harassed the common people on his journey,
and all his actions after arriving at his post violated laws and regulations.
Wányán Shǒunéng, as Zhāotǎoshǐ,
was notoriously corrupt.
Yet, none of these high-ranking and influential officials were ever impeached.
When Púsàn Nàyě, the Deputy Qúnmùshǐ of Wòdǔzhī, took two polo sticks from tribesmen,
he was immediately impeached.
From now on,
Censors (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) will only be promoted after their duties are diligently performed.
Those who fail to perform their duties
will receive severe punishment if the transgression is major,
or minor reprimand if minor,
and will still not be allowed to leave their posts.”
The Shàngshūshěng reported
that neither of Shǒunéng's two acts of bribery amounted to fifty strings of cash,
and he was sentenced.
Xī Shā'ābǔ was dismissed from his current office
and also relieved of his hereditary Mùkè title.
The Emperor said:
“This is an error in the old system.
For officials who commit offenses warranting expulsion,
both their current office and hereditary title shall be revoked;
for those not warranting expulsion, they shall not be revoked.”
This was then formalized into law.
A special edict ordered Shǒunéng to be flogged two hundred times
and expelled from office.
The eulogy states:
The excellent praise of Ālíhéwàn,
Zōngxióng's strong memory,
Xīyǐn's quick learning,
and the added merit of military campaigns—
how could they not be magnificent!
Collation Notes:
Biographies, Volume Twelve:
Zōnghàn (original name Zhānhǎn; son Xiégē); Zōngwàng (original name Wòlíbù; sons Qí, Jīng, Wén).
Zōnghàn's original name was Zhānmòhē,
which was corrupted in Chinese to Zhānhǎn.
He was the eldest son of the Chancellor, Sākǎi.
At seventeen,
the army admired his bravery.
When discussing the campaign against the Liáo,
Zōnghàn's views aligned with Tàizǔ's.
Tàizǔ defeated the Liáo army at the border,
capturing Yēlǜ Xièshí.
Sākǎi sent Zōnghàn and Wányán Xīyǐn to congratulate the victory
and immediately declared Tàizǔ Emperor to celebrate.
When Tàizōng and other imperial clansmen and ministers all urged him to ascend the throne,
Tàizǔ still humbly declined.
Zōnghàn, with Ālíhéwàn, Pújiānú, and others, stepped forward and said:
“If we do not establish the imperial title in a timely manner,
there will be no way to secure the hearts of the people.”
Tàizǔ then made up his mind.
Yēlǜ Élǐwān, the Liáo Grand Coordinator, garrisoned over two hundred thousand troops at the border.
Tàizǔ attacked them preemptively,
with Zōnghàn leading the right army,
and thoroughly defeated the Liáo people at Dálǔgǔchéng.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of Tiānfǔ,
Zōnghàn memorialized, saying:
“The Liáo ruler has lost his virtue;
those at court and abroad are disaffected.
Our dynasty raised an army,
and the great enterprise is already established,
but if the root cause is not eliminated,
it will surely become a future problem.
Now, seizing this opportunity,
we can launch a surprise attack and capture it.
Heaven's timing and human affairs
must not be missed.”
Tàizǔ agreed,
and immediately ordered all circuits to prepare militarily.
On Wùxū day of the fifth month,
there was an archery contest and a banquet for the ministers.
The Emperor looked at Zōnghàn and said:
“Now that we are discussing a western campaign,
your previous plans and discussions have largely aligned with My will.
Among the imperial clan,
although there are those older than you,
if we are to strategize as Marshal,
no one can replace you.
You should prepare the troops
and await the time for the expedition.”
The Emperor personally poured wine and gave it to him to drink,
and also ordered him to drain the cup,
and took off his imperial robe to dress him.
The ministers said it was the height of summer,
so he stopped.
Shortly thereafter,
he was made Yílàibójíliè,
and deputized Pújiānú to attack the Liáo Emperor in the west,
but it was not carried out.
In the eleventh month,
Zōnghàn again requested, saying:
“The various armies have been stationed for a long time;
the men are eager to exert themselves,
and the horses are strong and healthy.
It is fitting to seize this opportunity to advance and capture Zhōngjīng.”
The ministers said it was still winter,
but Tàizǔ did not listen
and ultimately adopted Zōnghàn's strategy.
Thereupon,
Hūlǔ Bójíliè Gǎo commanded all internal and external armies,
with Pújiānú, Zōnghàn, Zōnggàn, and Zōngpán as his deputies.
Zōngjùn led the Hézhá Méng'ān.
All received golden plaques,
and Yúdǔ served as a guide,
capturing Zhōngjīng (which was actually Běijīng).
After capturing Zhōngjīng,
Zōnghàn led a detachment to Běi'ānzhōu,
joined forces with Lóushì and Túshàn Chuòlǐ,
and utterly defeated Xīwáng Xiámò,
whereupon Běi'ān surrendered.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) stationed troops at Běi'ān (北安),
and sent Xīyǐn (希尹) to manage the nearby territories.
They captured the Liáo (遼) imperial guard Yēlǜ Xíníliè (耶律習泥烈),
and then learned that the Liáo (遼) ruler was hunting at Yuānyāngluò (鴛鴦濼),
and had killed his son, Jìn Wáng (晉王) Àolǔwò (敖魯斡).
The populace became increasingly disloyal,
and the armies of both the northwest and southwest routes were weak
and unusable.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) sent Nòuwǎnwēndū (耨盌溫都) and Yílàbǎobǎo (移剌保報) to report to Dūtǒng (都統) Gǎo (杲), saying:
“The Liáo (遼) ruler, though pressed hard in Shānxī (山西),
still engages in hunting,
cares not for the crisis of his impending doom,
and has even killed his own son.
His subjects are disappointed.
Regarding the strategy for attack and capture,
please kindly instruct us swiftly.
If there is a different opinion,
this area should be pacified with a detached force.”
Gǎo (杲) sent Bēndǔ (奔睹) and Yílàbǎo (移剌保) to report back, saying:
“Previously, we received an imperial edict
not to advance directly to Shānxī (山西),
but to deliberate carefully and slowly.”
At that time,
Zōnghàn (宗翰) sent someone to report to Gǎo (杲),
and immediately assembled his forces, awaiting the campaign date.
When Bēndǔ (奔睹) arrived,
and Zōnghàn (宗翰) learned that Gǎo (杲) had no intention of advancing,
Zōnghàn (宗翰) feared that waiting for Gǎo's (杲) agreement might cause them to lose the opportunity,
so he immediately decided to advance his troops.
He sent Yílàbǎo (移剌保) back again to report to the Dūtǒng (都統), saying:
“Although the initial order did not allow us to take Shānxī (山西) immediately,
it also permitted us to act according to expediency.
The Liáo (遼) people are ripe for capture;
the situation is already evident.
If we lose this opportunity,
it will be difficult to plan later.
Now that we have advanced,
where should we rendezvous with the main army?
Please kindly inform us.”
Zōnggàn (宗幹) advised Gǎo (杲) to follow Zōnghàn's (宗翰) plan,
and Gǎo (杲)'s mind was then made up.
They agreed to meet at Xīwánglǐng (奚王嶺).
Zōnghàn (宗翰) arrived at Xīwánglǐng (奚王嶺)
and met with Dūtǒng (都統) Gǎo (杲).
Gǎo's (杲) army departed from Qīnglǐng (青嶺),
and Zōnghàn's (宗翰) army departed from Piáolǐng (瓢嶺),
planning to meet at Yángchéngluò (羊城濼).
Zōnghàn (宗翰) led six thousand elite troops to raid the Liáo (遼) ruler.
Upon hearing that the Liáo (遼) ruler was coming from Wǔyuànsī (五院司) to resist,
Zōnghàn (宗翰) doubled his march,
arriving in one night,
and the Liáo (遼) ruler fled.
Then he sent Xīyǐn (希尹) and others to pursue him.
Xījīng (西京) rebelled again.
Gěng Shǒuzhōng (耿守忠) came with five thousand troops to relieve it.
When they reached forty *lǐ* east of the city,
Púchá Wūliè (蒲察烏烈) and Gǔ... (谷●) attacked them first,
beheading over a thousand.
Zōnghàn (宗翰), Zōngxióng (宗雄), Zōnggàn (宗幹), and Zōngjùn (宗峻) arrived subsequently.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) led his immediate command to charge through their center,
and ordered the rest of his troops to dismount and shoot from the flanks.
Shǒuzhōng (守忠) was defeated and fled,
and his troops were annihilated.
Zōnghàn's (宗翰) brother, Zhābǎodí (扎保迪), died in battle.
During the Tiānjuàn (天眷) reign,
Zhābǎodí (扎保迪) was posthumously granted the title of Tèjìn (特進).
After Zōnghàn (宗翰) had pacified the prefectures, counties, and tribes of the western route,
he visited the emperor at the imperial encampment
and then followed the emperor to capture Yānjīng (燕京).
After Yānjīng (燕京) was pacified, Zōnghàn (宗翰), Xīyǐn (希尹), Tàlǎn (撻懶), and Yēlǜ Yúdǔ (耶律余睹) were each rewarded with gold vessels of varying grades.
After Tàizǔ (太祖) had given Yānjīng (燕京) to the Sòng (宋) people,
he returned with his army and encamped at Yuānyāngluò (鴛鴦濼).
Feeling unwell,
he was about to return to the capital.
He appointed Zōnghàn (宗翰) as Dūtǒng (都統),
with Zè Bójíliè Yù (昃勃極烈昱) and Diébójíliè Wòlǔ (迭勃極烈斡魯) as his deputies,
and stationed them at Yúnzhōng (雲中).
When Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
he issued an edict to Zōnghàn (宗翰), saying:
“You are entrusted with an entire region.
Those who should be promoted in rank and title
may be appointed at your discretion.”
He then provided him with one hundred blank imperial decrees.
When the Sòng (宋) envoys came to request the cession of various cities,
Zōnghàn (宗翰) responded by ceding Wǔzhōu (武州) and Shuòzhōu (朔州).
Zōnghàn (宗翰) pleaded:
“The Sòng (宋) people do not return our fugitives and rebels,
and they obstruct the routes of passage through Yānshān (燕山).
Later, they are bound to break the alliance.
Please do not cede the commanderies and counties of Shānxī (山西).”
Tàizōng (太宗) said:
“The former emperor once promised them,
so we must give them.”
When the generals captured Yēlǜ Mǎgē (耶律馬哥),
Zōnghàn (宗翰) sent him back to the capital.
An edict ordered seven hundred horses to be given to Zōnghàn's (宗翰) army,
and one thousand *dàn* of grain seeds and seven thousand *dàn* of rice to be distributed to the newly surrendered people.
The edict stated:
“For the newly surrendered people,
when the farming season arrives,
measure out land for them to settle.”
Zōnghàn (宗翰) requested to divide the elite troops of Zōngwàng (宗望), Tàlǎn (撻懶), and Shígǔnǎi (石古乃) to attack various tribes.
The edict stated:
“Zōngwàng's (宗望) army cannot be divided.
An additional five thousand elite soldiers will be given to you.”
Zōnghàn (宗翰) paid respects at Tàizǔ (太祖)'s mausoleum,
and upon entering to see the emperor,
he reported:
“During the time of the former emperor,
Han officials and military commanders in Shānxī (山西) and Nánjīng (南京) were all permitted to appoint and dismiss officials by imperial decree.
Now, Nánjīng (南京) follows the old system,
but Shānxī (山西) is exclusively appointed by imperial command.”
The edict stated:
“Act in accordance with the imperial edicts issued by the former emperor in Yānjīng (燕京).
You and others may promote and appoint them based on their diligence.”
Zōnghàn (宗翰) further reported:
“At the beginning of the former emperor's campaign against Liáo (遼),
he planned to cooperate with Sòng (宋) for a pincer attack,
hence he promised the Yān (燕) territory.
After the Sòng (宋) people made the alliance,
they asked for additional tribute to acquire the various garrisons of Shānxī (山西),
but the former emperor declined the additional tribute.
The alliance treaty states: ‘No harboring of fugitives
or inciting trouble among border residents.’
Now, several Sòng (宋) routes are recruiting fugitives and rebels,
and lavishly rewarding them.
We have repeatedly submitted lists of the names of the rebels
and demanded them from Tóng Guàn (童貫),
and he has often set a date
and made promises with oaths,
but nothing has been returned.
The alliance is not even a year old,
and it is already like this.
How can we hope for it to be upheld for ten thousand generations?
Furthermore, the western border is not yet pacified.
If we cede the various commanderies of Shānxī (山西),
then our various armies will lose their garrisons.
If there are military operations,
they might not be sustainable.
I request that this matter be set aside for now and not ceded.”
The emperor granted all his requests.
The emperor praised Zōnghàn (宗翰) for defeating Liáo (遼)
and for compelling the Xià (夏) Kingdom to submit a memorial acknowledging vassalage.
Deeply commending his achievements,
he gave ten horses,
allowing Zōnghàn (宗翰) to choose two for himself,
and the rest were bestowed upon the various commanders.
When Wòlǔ (斡魯) reported that Sòng (宋) had not sent the annual tribute of households and population,
and was about to break the alliance,
necessitating preparations.
Tàizōng (太宗) ordered Zōnghàn (宗翰) to obtain household registers from all routes and demand compensation based on them.
And Zhēmǔ (闍母) again reported evidence of Sòng (宋) breaking the alliance,
whereupon Zōnghàn (宗翰) and Zōngwàng (宗望) both requested to attack Sòng (宋).
Thus,
Ānbān Bójíliè Gǎo (諳班勃極烈杲) was appointed Dū Yuánshuài (都元帥)
and resided in the capital,
while Zōnghàn (宗翰) was made Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài (左副元帥)
and attacked Sòng (宋) from the Tàiyuán (太原) route.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) set off from Héyīn (河陰),
then captured Shuòzhōu (朔州),
conquered Dàizhōu (代州),
and besieged Tàiyuánfǔ (太原府).
Four tens of thousands of Sòng (宋) Hédōng (河東) and Shǎnxī (陝西) troops came to relieve Tàiyuán (太原),
but were defeated north of the Fánhé (汾河),
with over ten thousand killed.
Zōngwàng (宗望) advanced to Biàn (汴) from Héběi (河北),
and there was no news from him for a long time.
So, Zōnghàn (宗翰) left Yínshùkě (銀术可) and others to besiege Tàiyuán (太原),
and led his army south.
In the fourth year of Tiānhuì (天會), he brought down and pacified various counties and Wēishèngjūn (威勝軍),
and took Lóngdé fǔ (隆德府), which was Lùzhōu (潞州).
When the army reached Zézhōu (澤州),
a Sòng (宋) envoy arrived in the army,
and only then did he learn about the agreement to cede three garrisons and make peace.
Lù Yǔndí (路允迪) came with the Sòng (宋) imperial edict to cede Tàiyuán (太原),
but the people of Tàiyuán (太原) did not accept the edict.
Zōnghàn (宗翰) took Wénshuǐ (文水) and Méngxiàn (盂縣),
and again left Yínshùkě (銀术可) to besiege Tàiyuán (太原).
Zōnghàn (宗翰) then returned to Shānxī (山西).
The Sòng Shàodì lured Xiāo Zhònggōng to send a letter to Yú Dǔ,
using the restoration of the Liáo dynasty to move him.
Xiāo Zhònggōng presented the letter,
and an imperial edict commanded a renewed attack on Sòng.
In the eighth month,
Zōng Hǎn departed from Xījīng.
On the bingyín day of the ninth month,
Zōng Hǎn captured Tàiyuán,
and seized Sòng Military Commissioner Zhāng Xiàochún and others.
Húshāhǔ took Píngyáo,
and accepted the surrender of the counties of Língshí, Jièxiū, and Xiàoyì.
On the jiǎzǐ day of the eleventh month,
Zōng Hǎn proceeded from Tàiyuán to Biàn,
accepted the surrender of Wēishèngjūn,
captured Lóngdé Fǔ,
and then took Zézhōu.
Sālálá and others had already broken through Tiānjǐng Guān,
advanced to press Héyáng,
defeated ten thousand Sòng soldiers,
and accepted the city's surrender.
Zōng Hǎn attacked Huáizhōu,
and captured it.
On the dīnghài day,
he crossed the Yellow River.
In the intercalary month,
Zōng Hǎn reached Biàn,
and joined forces with Zōng Wàng.
Sòng proposed to use the river as a boundary,
and again requested to mend relations.
Peace was not achieved.
On the bǐngchén day,
Yínshùkě and others captured Biànzhōu.
On the xīnyǒu day,
the Sòng Shàodì proceeded to the military camp,
and stayed at Qīngchéng.
On the guǐhài day of the twelfth month,
the Shàodì presented a memorial of surrender.
An imperial edict to the Yuánshuài Fǔ stated:
"For generals, commanders, officers, and soldiers who have rendered meritorious service,
rank their merits from high to low and grant them promotions and rewards.
For those who perished in battle,
and died for royal affairs,
generously provide for their families,
and bestow official titles and honors with utmost generosity."
An envoy was sent to the army to reward Zōng Hǎn and Zōng Wàng,
shaking their hands to congratulate them.
In the fourth month of the fifth year,

the two Sòng emperors and their clan of over four hundred and seventy people, along with guīzhāng, precious seals, gǔnmiǎn, chariots, sacrificial vessels, grand music, the spiritual platform, and books,
returned north with the grand army.
In the seventh month,
Zōng Hǎn was granted an iron certificate,
meaning that except for rebellion,
all other matters would not be questioned;
he was given very generous rewards.
Zōng Hǎn memorialized that for the prefectures, garrisons, and counties of Héběi and Hédōng, capable former officials should be chosen to govern them,
to pacify the new populace.
The emperor dispatched Yēlǜ Huī and others to accompany Zōng Hǎn.
An imperial edict ordered the Huánglóng Fǔlù, Nánlù, and Dōngjīnglù to each select individuals like Yēlǜ Huī from their respective jurisdictions and dispatch them.
Zōng Hǎn then proceeded towards Luòyáng.
Sòng Dǒng Zhí arrived at Zhèngzhōu with troops,
and the people of Zhèngzhōu rebelled again.
Zōng Hǎn ordered his generals to attack Dǒng Zhí's army,
and recaptured Zhèngzhōu.
He then relocated the people of Luòyáng, Xiāngyáng, Yǐngchāng, Rǔ, Zhèng, Jūn, Fáng, Táng, Dèng, Chén, and Cài to Héběi,
and sent Lóushì to pacify the prefectures and commanderies of Shǎnxī.
At this time, there were still many bandits in Hédōng,
so Zōng Hǎn left some generals and soldiers,
stationed them along the river,
and returned his army to Shānxī.
Hūndégōng sent a letter
"requesting the establishment of a Zhào ruler,
who would perform duties and offer tribute;
the people's hearts would surely rejoice,
and it would be beneficial for ten thousand generations."
Zōng Hǎn received the letter but did not reply.
King Kāng sent Wáng Shīzhèng to present a memorial,
secretly enticing Qìdān and Hàn people with a letter.
The letter was seized and presented.
Tàizōng issued an edict to attack King Kāng.
The generals in Héběi wanted to withdraw the troops from Shǎnxī
and concentrate their forces for a southern campaign.
The generals in Hédōng disagreed,
saying:
"Shǎnxī borders Xī Xià,
the matter is grave and extensive,
the troops cannot be withdrawn."
Zōng Hǎn said:
"Initially, we agreed with Xià to jointly attack Sòng,
but the Xià people did not respond.
And Yēlǜ Dàshí is in the northwest,
communicating with Xī Xià.
If I abandon Shǎnxī and join forces in Héběi,
they will certainly think I am in urgent difficulty.
Héběi is not to be worried about,
we should first deal with Shǎnxī,
subdue the five circuits,
weaken Xī Xià,
and then take Sòng."
Zōng Hǎn indeed had intentions regarding the Xià people.
The discussion lasted long without a decision,
so a memorial was presented to the emperor,
who said:
"We must pursue King Kāng Gòu to the extent of his flight.
After Sòng is pacified,
we should establish a vassal like Zhāng Bāngchāng.
The land to the west of Shǎn [Shǎnxī]
also cannot be left untaken."
Thereupon, Lóushì and Púchá led the army,
Shéngguǒ and Pólúhuǒ supervised the battle,
and pacified Shǎnxī.
Yínshùkě guarded Tàiyuán,
and Yēlǜ Yúdǔ remained in Xījīng.
Zōng Hǎn joined the eastern army at Líyáng Jīn,
and then met Ruìzōng at Pú.
The army advanced to Dōngpíng,
where Sòng Prefect Quán Bāngyàn abandoned his home and fled by night,
and the city surrendered,
and the army was stationed fifty lǐ southeast of Dōngpíng.
Xúzhōu was recaptured.
Previously,
the Sòng people had transported all the gold and currency from Jiāng and Huái to the official treasury in Xúzhōu,
all of which was obtained [by the Jīn] and
distributed to the various armies.
Xíqìng Fǔ surrendered.
Sòng Prefect of Jìnán Fǔ, Liú Yù, surrendered the city to Tálǎn.
Then Bálí Sù, Wūlíndá Tàiyù, and Mǎwǔ were dispatched to attack King Kāng at Yángzhōu.
Before reaching within one hundred and fifty lǐ,
Mǎwǔ with five hundred cavalry first galloped to the foot of Yángzhōu city.
King Kāng, hearing of the approaching army,
had already crossed the river the night before.
Thereupon,
King Kāng sent a letter requesting the preservation of the Zhào clan's altars of soil and grain (dynasty).
Previously,
King Kāng had sent a letter to the Yuánshuài Fǔ,
stating,
"Gòu, the Emperor of Great Sòng, respectfully sends a letter to the tent of the Grand Marshal of Great Jīn,"
but now he omitted the grand title,
calling himself
"Zhào Gòu, King Kāng of Sòng, respectfully sends a letter to His Excellency the Marshal."
Both his letters of the fourth and seventh months were like this.
The Yuánshuài Fǔ replied to his letter,
enticing him to surrender.
Thereupon,
Tálǎn, Zōngbì, Bálí Sù, Mǎwǔ, and others divided their forces for the southern campaign.
Zōngbì's army crossed the river to take Jiànkāng,
and entered Hángzhōu.
King Kāng entered the sea,
and Ālǐ, Púlúhún, and others sailed three hundred lǐ from Míngzhōu,
pursuing him but failing to catch him.
Zōngbì then returned.
Later, Zōng Hǎn wanted to use Xú Wéncè's strategy to attack Jiāngnán,
but Ruìzōng and Zōngbì disagreed,
so it was stopped.
The account is in the biography of Liú Yù.
Guīdé rebelled,
and Commander-in-Chief Dàcí Lǐ pacified it.
Initially,
Tàizōng appointed Xiáyě as Ānbān Bójíliè,
but in the eighth year of Tiānhuì,
Xiáyě died,
leaving this position vacant for a long time.
However, Xīzōng was the son of Zōng Jùn,
and the legitimate grandson of Tàizǔ, but Zōng Gàn and others did not mention him to Tàizōng,
and Tàizōng also had no intention of establishing Xīzōng.
Zōng Hǎn attended the imperial court in Jīngshī,
and said to Zōng Gàn:
"The position of heir apparent has been vacant for quite some time.
Hélá is the legitimate grandson of the former emperor,
and should be established.
If he is not settled early,
I fear the position will be given to the wrong person.
Zōng Hǎn has never forgotten this day or night."
He then, together with Zōng Gàn and Xī Yǐn, made a decision,
and spoke to Tàizōng,
requesting it repeatedly.
Tàizōng, considering Zōng Hǎn and the others to be great ministers,
and that their righteousness could not be gainsaid,
then agreed,
and so established Xīzōng as Ānbān Bójíliè.
Thereupon,
Zōng Hǎn became Guólùn Yòu Bójíliè,
also serving as Dū Yuánshuài.
Upon Xīzōng's ascension,
Zōng Hǎn was appointed Tàibǎo and Shàngshū Lìng,
presiding over the affairs of the three ministries,
and enfeoffed as King of Jìnguó.
He requested to retire,
but an imperial edict did not permit it.
He died in the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì,
at the age of fifty-eight.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as King of Zhōu and Sòngguó.
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
he was enfeoffed as Jīnyuán Jùnwáng as per custom.
During the Dàdìng era,
he was re-granted the title of King Qín,
with the posthumous name Huánzhōng,
and his spirit tablet was placed in the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ.
Sūn Bǐngdé, Xiégē.
Bǐngdé has a separate biography.
Xiégē,
cumulatively served as the Assistant Military Commissioner (Tóngzhī Jiédùshǐshì) of Hésūguǎn.
At the beginning of the Dàdìng reign,
he was appointed Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng)
and concurrently Grand Commander (Dūtǒng).
He and Deputy Commander Wányán Bùhuī departed from Dōngjīng first for Zhōngdū,
where they arbitrarily appointed officials
and privately used public funds.
When Shìzōng arrived at Zhōngdū,
the matter came to light.
Xiégē was to be executed,
and Bùhuī was to be dismissed.
An imperial edict granted leniency:
Xiégē was dismissed,
Bùhuī had two ranks reduced
and was relieved of his post.
In the second year,
he was reappointed as Assistant of the Imperial Clan Court (Dàzōngzhèngchéng),
and then appointed Administrator of Qízhōu (Qízhōu Cìshǐ).
He was implicated in corruption and perversion of justice,
for which he was to be executed.
An imperial edict ordered him to be flogged one hundred and fifty times
and dismissed.
The Left Imperial Guard General (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn) Jiágǔ Zhālà was sent to convey to Xiégē, saying:
"What face do you have to return to your hometown and meet your relatives?
You are now exiled to Fūzhōu,
with your family accompanying you.
After your death,
your family may do as they please."
After a long time,
he was reappointed Assistant Administrator of Xīngzhōng (Tóngzhī Xīngzhōng Yǐn),
then promoted to Military Commissioner of the Tángkuò Tribe (Tángkuò Bùzú Jiédùshǐ),
and successively served in Kāiyuǎn and Shùnyì Armies.
Previously, Xiégē had received bribes in Yúnnèi.
The Censorate impeached him.
The Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Xiégē has now committed offenses three times.
His character is truly vile to this extent."
He ordered a capable official to investigate him.
When the case was concluded,
by law he was to be executed.
The Emperor said:
"Xiégē's grandfather, Prince Qín Zōnghán, rendered great service.
Therefore, he is specially exempted from death,
flogged one hundred and fifty times,
and dismissed."
After a long time,
he was again reappointed Deputy Commissioner for Encouraging Agriculture (Quànnóng Fùshǐ).
The eulogy states: Zōnghán was capable of planning for the country internally
and devising strategies against the enemy externally.
His decisive policies led to victories,
embodying the spirit of ancient famous generals.
After the victory at Línhuáng,
all the generals harbored thoughts of laxity,
but he incessantly requested to attack.
Traversing a thousand li to raid the Liao Emperor,
all the generals harbored fears and hesitations,
but he incessantly requested a date.
Observing his desire to establish control over Jiāng-Huái
and focus solely on Shǎnfú,
at that time, no one could understand his intentions.
As soon as the fighting ceased,
he gathered his robes and returned to court,
thereby establishing Xīzōng's position.
The sincerity of his actions,
who could conceal it?
Zōngwàng's original name was Wòlǔbǔ,
also written Wòlíbù,
and he was Tàizǔ's second son.
Whenever he accompanied Tàizǔ on campaigns,
he was always by his side.
Commander Gǎo had already captured Zhōngjīng,
and Zōnghán was in Běi'ānzhōu.
He captured Xí Níliè, a Liao guard,
and learned that the Liao Emperor was at Yuānyāng Luò.
Zōnghán requested to raid him.
Gǎo exited Qīnglǐng.
Over three hundred Liao soldiers plundered the property of surrendered families.
Zōngwàng said:
"If we capture these people alive,
we can ascertain the true whereabouts of the Liao Emperor."
So he and Zōngbì led a hundred cavalry to advance.
Most of the cavalry were exhausted,
and only he and Mǎ Héshàng pursued Yuè Lú, Bògǔ, Yělǐsī, and others.
Leaving one cavalryman to rush to the rear army,
he immediately charged and defeated them,
capturing five people alive.
Thus, it was confirmed beyond doubt that the Liao Emperor was still at Yuānyāng Luò and had not departed.
Thereupon, they advanced their troops.
Zōnghán marched double-speed,
pursuing the Liao Emperor to Wǔyuàn Sī,
but did not catch him.
Lóushì and others pursued him to Báishuǐ Luò,
and the Liao Emperor fled to Yīnshān.
The Liao Prince of Qín-Jìn, Niēlǐ, proclaimed himself emperor in Yānjīng.
The newly surrendered prefectures and departments,
whose people were not firmly loyal,
Gǎo sent Zōngwàng to request Tàizǔ to personally lead the army.
When Zōngwàng arrived in the capital,
all officials came to congratulate him.
The Emperor said:
"Zōngwàng, with over ten cavalry, traversed several thousand li through war-torn areas.
This is commendable."
The Emperor hosted a banquet for his ministers,
which was very joyous.
Zōngwàng reported:
"Now Yúnzhōng has just been pacified,
and there are still tens of thousands of Liao soldiers on various routes.
The Liao Emperor is still between Yīnshān and Tiāndé,
while Niēlǐ has proclaimed himself emperor in Yānjīng.
The hearts of the newly surrendered people
are not yet firm.
Therefore, the generals hope Your Majesty will come to the army."
The Emperor said:
"An army sent on a distant campaign,
if given pre-determined plans,
may not fully adapt to changing circumstances.
I shall set out on the first day of the sixth month."
When he reached the southwest of Dàluò,
Gǎo sent Xīyǐn to memorialize, requesting to relocate the various tribes of the Southwest Pacification Command (Xīnán Zhāotǎosī) to the interior.
The Emperor looked at his ministers and said:
"Through which route should these tribes be relocated?"
Zōngwàng replied:
"Zhōngjīng is devastated and impoverished;
fodder and provisions are insufficient.
It would be appropriate to go via Shàngjīng.
However, if the newly surrendered people
are suddenly disturbed,
those who have not yet surrendered will certainly become suspicious and fearful.
This would exhaust the army and harm the people,
leading to great losses."
Shàngjīng refers to Línhuáng Fǔ.
The Emperor then tabled the discussion
and ordered the military commanders to assess what was appropriate and act accordingly.
The Emperor heard that the Liao Emperor was at Dàyú Luò,
and personally led ten thousand elite soldiers to raid him.
Pújiānú and Zōngwàng led four thousand soldiers as the vanguard,
marching day and night.
Many horses were exhausted.
They overtook the Liao Emperor at Shíliǎn Yì,
but only a thousand soldiers had arrived.
The remaining Liao army numbered twenty-five thousand.
As they were setting up camp,
Pújiānú discussed with the generals.
Yúdǔ said:
"Our army has not yet gathered,
and the men and horses are extremely weary.
We cannot fight yet."
Zōngwàng said:
"If we overtake the Liao Emperor now but do not fight immediately,
and he flees at sunset,
then it will be too late."
So they fought.
With short weapons engaged,
the Liao army surrounded them in several layers,
and all the soldiers fought to the death.
The Liao Emperor thought that Zōngwàng's small army would surely be defeated,
so he and his consorts descended from a high mound to the flat ground to watch the battle.
Yúdǔ showed the generals and said:
"That is the Liao Emperor's banner and canopy.
If we concentrate and press upon it,
we can achieve our goal."
The cavalry galloped towards it.
The Liao Emperor saw them and was greatly alarmed.
He immediately fled,
and the Liao army consequently collapsed.
Zōngwàng and others returned.
The Emperor said:
"The Liao Emperor is not far.
Pursue him immediately."
Zōngwàng, with over a thousand cavalry, pursued him,
and Pújiānú followed as reinforcements.
Tàizǔ had already pacified Yānjīng.
Wòlǔ was appointed Dudǒng,
and Zōngwàng was his deputy.
They attacked the Liáo lord between Yīnshān and Qīngzhǒng.
Zōngwàng, Lóushì, and Yínzhúkě, with three thousand troops, assaulted him from different routes.
When they reached Qīngzhǒng,
they encountered muddy terrain,
and the troops could not advance.
Zōngwàng, with Dānghǎi and four horsemen, tied Liáo Dudǒng Línyá Dàshí with a rope,
making him their guide,
and went directly to the Liáo lord's camp.
At that time, the Liáo lord had gone to Yìngzhōu.
His consorts and all his daughters, seeing the enemy soldiers suddenly arrive, were terrified and wanted to flee.
He ordered his cavalry to seize them.
After a short while,
the rearguard arrived.
The Liáo Tàishū Húlúwǎ Fēi,
Guówáng Niēlǐ Cìfēi,
Liáo Hàn Fūrén,
along with their sons Qínwáng and Xǔwáng,
and daughters Gǔyù, Yúliyǎn, Wòliyǎn, Dà'àoyě, Cì'àoyě,
Zhàowáng Fēi Wòliyǎn,
Zhāotǎo Díliù,
Xiángwěn Liùjīn,
Jíedùshǐ Bódié, and Chìgǒuer all surrendered.
They captured over ten thousand carts.
Only Liángwáng Yǎlǐ and his eldest daughter escaped amidst the military chaos.
Lóushì and Yínzhúkě captured his personal sedan and tents.
They advanced to Sǎolǐmén,
and wrote a letter to summon the Liáo lord.
The Liáo lord came from Jīnchéng.
Knowing that all his relatives had been captured,
he led more than five thousand soldiers to fight a decisive battle.
Zōngwàng, with a thousand soldiers, defeated him.
The Liáo lord, a hundred paces away,
fled.
They captured his son Zhàowáng Xíníliè and the imperial seal.
They pursued for over twenty *lǐ*,
and seized all his accompanying horses.
Meanwhile, Zhàolǐ, Tèmò,
Húbālǔ, and Bèidá separately captured fourteen thousand pastured horses and eight thousand carts.
When the imperial seal was presented at the temporary imperial residence,
Tàizǔ said:
"This is the achievement of the officials."
He then placed the seal in his bosom,
faced east, and respectfully thanked Heaven and Earth.
Then he greatly recorded the merits of all the commanders
and bestowed rewards.
The Liáo lord then sent Móulúwǎ, carrying a gold seal with a rabbit knob, to request surrender.
Zōngwàng accepted it.
Looking at its inscription,
it was
"Seal of the Yuánshuài King of Yān State."
Zōngwàng
again sent a letter to summon him,
explaining the matter of Shíjìn's northern relocation.
He then sent envoys to instruct the Xià State,
showing goodwill,
in order to thwart and cause doubt in their intention to aid the Liáo.
Zōngwàng hastened to Tiāndé,
where Liáo Yēlǜ Shènsī surrendered.
Then, the scouts Wú Shíhuí,
all reported that the Xià State had welcomed and protected the Liáo lord across the Great River.
Zōngwàng then issued a proclamation to the Xià State, saying:
"If you truly wish to align with us,
you should, as previously instructed,
capture and hand over the Liáo lord.
If you still hesitate or are disloyal,
you may have regrets later."
When Liáo Qínwáng and others were presented as captives to Tàizǔ,
Tàizǔ praised Zōngwàng's accomplishments
and bestowed upon him Liáo Shǔguó Gōngzhǔ Yúliyǎn.
Shé Mǔ fought with Zhāng Jué
and suffered a great defeat at Tù'ěrshān.
The Emperor sent Zōngwàng to inquire about the situation,
and subsequently ordered Shé Mǔ's army to attack Zhāng Jué,
receiving the surrender of coastal prefectures and counties.
They then fought Jué east of Nánjīng city.
Jué was defeated
and fled at night to Sòng;
the story is in Jué's biography.
The people in the city captured Jué's father and his two sons and brought them to surrender.
Zōngwàng killed them.
He then issued an imperial edict to persuade Zhāng Dūngù and others in the city to surrender.
He sent an envoy with Dūngù into the city to collect weapons.
The city dwellers killed the envoy,
appointed Dūngù as Dudǒng,
looted the armories and treasuries,
plundered the residents,
and held the city in defiance.
Tàizōng rewarded those who had contributed to defeating Zhāng Jué, and the meritorious generals and soldiers were all rewarded differentially.
Initially,
Zhāng Jué fled to Sòng and entered Yānjīng.
Zōngwàng blamed the Sòng people for harboring a rebel,
and also demanded military provisions.
For a long time, there was no response.
Zōngwàng wanted to send a letter to urge them,
and requested a thousand blank imperial decrees,
additional credential plaques,
to appease the newly surrendered people.
An imperial edict stated:
"Newly appointed senior officials shall retain their former positions.
It has already been ordered for various routes to transport military provisions;
do not demand them from Sòng.
Ten silver plaques and fifty blank imperial decrees are granted.
As for the people from the four prefectures of Qiān, Rùn, Lái, and Xí
who were relocated to Shěnzhōu,
they shall resume their former occupations after the farming season."
Then, an edict ordered Xiánzhōu to transport grain to Zōngwàng's army.
Zhāng Dūngù, with eight thousand soldiers, divided into four detachments, sallied out to fight
and suffered a great defeat.
Zōngwàng repeatedly tried to persuade them,
but Dūngù and others said:
"We have repeatedly resisted in battle;
we dare not surrender immediately."
Zōngwàng promised that they could bow from afar towards the imperial palace.
Dūngù then opened one of the gates.
Zōngwàng had Shé Mǔ report the matter,
and an imperial edict was issued pardoning the officials and common people of Nánjīng;
all crimes, great and small, were forgiven,
and their official positions remained as before.
A separate imperial order instructed the relevant authorities to lighten corvée and taxes, encourage agriculture,
and all matters concerning the borders
were to be decided by Zōngwàng.
It also said:
"Discuss the demand for Zhāng Jué and the absconded households from Sòng.
It is heard that recent years have seen poor harvests;
if taxes are levied as before,
the people may suffer from scarcity.
Estimate their grain needs and levy accordingly.
Soldiers who wish to return to civilian life
shall be allowed to resume their rural occupations.
All matters, great and small, should be reported to the military commander;
they should not be reported directly to the imperial court."
An edict to Zōngwàng said:
"Select meritorious and virtuous individuals and those with popular support to be the Grand Administrator of Nánjīng,
and for all vacant positions,
report their names and official ranks."
At this time,
many people from the four prefectures of Qiān, Rùn, Lái, and Xí were sheltering in mountain strongholds.
Zōngwàng requested to select capable officials to recruit and appease them.
The Emperor agreed.
The Emperor summoned Zōngwàng to the imperial court,
but Shé Mǔ captured Nánjīng.
His soldiers seized the false Dudǒng Zhāng Dūngù and killed him,
and Nánjīng was pacified.
Zōngwàng then proceeded to the capital.
At this point,
Zōnghàn requested that no land in Shānxī be ceded to Sòng,
and Wòlǔ also spoke on this matter.
Shé Mǔ argued that there was evidence of Sòng violating the alliance,
and that preparations must be made.
When Zōngwàng returned to the army,
the Emperor said:

"I will levy an annual tribute from Sòng of two hundred thousand *liǎng* of silver and three hundred thousand bolts of silk to be distributed among your army, the Six Ministries, and all armies in Dōngjīng."
When Zōngwàng arrived at the army,
three thousand Sòng soldiers came by sea,
destroyed nine stockades,
killed the county garrison commander and Jíedùshǐ Dùlúwò at Mǎchéng,
and took his silver plaques, weapons, and horses before leaving.
Zōngwàng demanded the return of the households,
but the Sòng people did not send them,
and it was also heard that Tóng Guàn and Guō Yàoshī were training armies in Yānshān.
Zōngwàng memorialized, requesting to attack Sòng, saying:
"If we do not strike first,
it may become a future problem."
Zōnghàn also made the same argument.
Therefore, the strategy to attack Sòng
was actually initiated by Zōngwàng.
Zōngwàng was appointed Dudǒng of Nánjīng Circuit,
with Shé Mǔ as his deputy,
and they attacked Sòng from Yānshān Circuit.
Zōngwàng memorialized, saying:
"Shé Mǔ is my uncle.
I request that Shé Mǔ be made Dudǒng,
and I will supervise the battles."
The Emperor agreed.
He appointed Zōngwàng to supervise the battles of Shé Mǔ's and Liú Yánzōng's two armies.
Zōngwàng arrived at Sānhé,
and defeated Guō Yàoshī's forty-five thousand troops at Báihé.
Pú Xiàn defeated three thousand Sòng soldiers at Gǔběikǒu,
and Guō Yàoshī surrendered.
He then took Yānshān Fǔ,
seizing all its military supplies:
ten thousand horses, fifty thousand sets of armor and helmets, seventy thousand soldiers,
and all prefectures and counties were pacified.
Sòng Zhōngshān garrison commanders Wáng Yàn and Liú Bì led two thousand soldiers to surrender.
Púchá and Shéngguǒ, with three hundred cavalry, encountered thirty thousand men from Zhōngshān in a narrow pass,
fought valiantly,
and died.
Shúliè Sù and Huólǐgǎi's armies arrived subsequently,
killing over twenty thousand people.
Zōngwàng defeated five thousand Sòng Zhēndìng soldiers,
then captured Xìndé Fǔ,
and proceeded to Hándān.
Sòng Lǐ Yè requested to restore former friendly relations.
Zōngwàng kept him in the army and did not send him back.
Since Guō Yàoshī's surrender,
awareness of Sòng's actual strength and weakness increased.
Zōngwàng requested that he be appointed Left-behind Commissioner of Yānjīng.
And when Dǒng Cái surrendered,
awareness of Sòng's geography increased.
Zōngwàng requested that he be assigned military affairs.
Tàizōng bestowed upon them both the surname Wányán,
and gave them each a golden plaque.
In the first month of the fourth year, on the day Jǐsì,
all the armies crossed the river
and took Huázhōu.
Wú Xiàomín was sent into Biàn,
with an imperial decree to inquire about the sheltering of Zhāng Jué from Píngzhōu,
ordering the arrest and delivery of Tóng Guàn, Tán Zhěn, and Zhān Dù,
taking the Yellow River as the border,
and offering hostages and tribute.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
all the armies besieged Biàn.
Sòng Shàodì requested to become a fraternal state,
offering hostages, ceding territory,
and increasing annual tribute in exchange for peace.
Consequently, the three garrisons of Tàiyuán, Zhōngshān, and Héjiān were ceded.
The document used the ritual of a fraternal relationship,
with King Kāng Gòu and Grand Preceptor Zhāng Bāngchāng as hostages.
Shěn Huì arrived at the army camp with the sworn agreement and maps of the three garrisons.
The annual tribute and ceded territory were entirely in accordance with the agreed-upon terms,
as recorded in the Sòng Shì.
On the first day of the second month, Dīngyǒu,
peace was made with Sòng,
and the army retreated to Mèngyáng.
That night,
Yáo Píngzhòng's army of four hundred thousand came to attack.
The scouts detected them,
and various generals were dispatched to meet and attack them,
thoroughly defeating Píngzhòng's army.
Then they advanced again to attack Biànchéng,
inquiring about the circumstances of the raising of the army.
Shàodì was greatly frightened,
and sent Yǔwén Xūzhōng to clarify, saying:
"We initially knew nothing of this matter,
and moreover will punish the person responsible."
Zōngwàng ceased the attack,
exchanging Prince Sù Shū as hostage,
and sending King Kāng Gòu back.
When the army returned,
two garrisons in Héběi had not surrendered,
so the army was divided to subdue them.
Zōngwàng disbanded the Chángshèngjūn,
returned their fields and property to the Yān people,
and ordered the generals and soldiers to garrison in the territories of Ānsù, Xióng, Bà, and Guǎngxìn.
Zōngwàng returned to Shānxī.
Shortly thereafter,
he was made Right Vice Grand Marshal,
and meritorious generals and soldiers received varying promotions and rewards.
After a while,
Sòng Shàodì used a letter to lure Yú Dǔ.
Xiāo Zhònggōng presented the letter,
and an imperial edict commanded another campaign against Sòng.
In the eighth month,
Zōngwàng convened the generals
and departed from Bǎozhōu.
Yēlǜ Duó defeated an enemy force of thirty thousand at Xióngzhōu,
killing over ten thousand men.
Nàyě defeated seven thousand Sòng troops at Zhōngshān.
Gāo Liù and Dǒng Cái defeated three thousand Sòng troops at Guǎngxìn.
Sòng's Zhǒng Shīmǐn's army of forty thousand men was stationed at Jǐngxíng,
and Zōngwàng utterly defeated them,
then took Tiānwēijūn.
Returning eastward,
they then captured Zhēndìng,
killed the prefect Lǐ Miǎo,
obtained thirty thousand households,
and received the surrender of five counties.
Then from Zhēndìng they rushed to Biàn.
In the eleventh month, on the day Wùchén,
Zōngwàng reached the river,
and Wèixiàn surrendered.
All the armies crossed the river,
leaving various generals to spread out into the territory of Dàmíng.
Línhéxiàn surrendered,
and Dàmíngxiàn,
Déqīngjūn, and Kāidéfǔ
were all captured.
Ālǐguā, with three thousand cavalry, advanced first to Biàn,
defeating six thousand Sòng troops on the way.
They took Zuòchéng,
reached the walls of Biànchéng,
routed a thousand Sòng soldiers,
and captured several generals.
Zōngwàng arrived at Biàn,
and dispatched various generals to intercept Sòng's relief forces.
Bēndǔ, Nàyě, Sàilá, and Táishí repeatedly defeated Sòng's relief forces.
On the first day of the intercalary month, Rénchén,
ten thousand Sòng troops sallied forth from Biànchéng to fight.
Zōngwàng selected five thousand elite brave men,
and had Dānghǎi, Hūlǔ, and Chúgǔshī defeat them.
On the day Guǐsì,
Zōnghàn's army from Tàiyuán joined forces at Biàn.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Biànzhōu was captured.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Sòng Shàodì went before the army.
In the twelfth month, on the day Guǐhài,
the Sòng Emperor submitted a memorial of surrender.
The Emperor sent Xù to the army to reward and console Zōnghàn and Zōngwàng,
having him grasp their hands to comfort them.
In the fourth month of the fifth year,
with the two Sòng emperors and over four hundred seventy of their clan members,
as well as precious jade tablets, imperial seals, ceremonial robes, imperial carriages, sacrificial vessels, grand music, the Spirit Platform, and books,
the grand army returned north.
Zōngwàng then divided the generals to garrison Héběi.
Dǒng Cái brought Guǎngxìnjūn and neighboring counties and towns to surrender.
Zōngwàng then proceeded west to Liángxíng.
An imperial edict to Zōngwàng said:
"Now that the north of the river
has been divided,
considering that its people, upon seeing their cities and towns damaged,
might obstruct orders and hold firm,
you should spread word to recruit and pacify them.
If they stubbornly refuse to yield,
they will naturally be subdued by force.
If any of the armies dare to profit from taking captives and looting,
or wantonly destroy and devastate,
they shall be punished."
That month,
Zōngwàng died.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was enfeoffed as King of Wèi.
In the third year of Huángtǒng,
he was advanced to King of Xǔguó,
and later transferred to King of Jìnguó.
In the second year of Tiāndé,
he was posthumously granted the title Grand Preceptor,
additionally enfeoffed as King of Liáoyànguó,
and accorded sacrificial honors in Tàizōng's ancestral temple.
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
he was demoted in enfeoffment according to regulations.
In the third year of Dàdìng,
he was re-enfeoffed as King of Sòng,
with the posthumous title Huánsù.
His sons were Qí, Jīng, and Wén.
Initially,
when the Liáo Emperor fled to Yīnshān,
Liáo's military commissioner Héshàng, along with Línyá Mǎgē and Nán Shènsī, were all captured.
The Grand Commander Gǎo ordered Ālín to escort Délǐdǐ,
Héshàng, Yǎlǐsī, and others to the capital.
Délǐdǐ escaped en route,
and Tàizǔ executed Ālín.
Héshàng's younger brother Dàowēn was the governor of Xīngzhōng.
Tàizǔ sent Màndūběn with a thousand soldiers to go with Héshàng to recruit him.
Héshàng tried to flee,
but failed.
When he reached the walls of Xīngzhōng,
he tied a letter to an arrow and shot it into the city,
instructing Dàowēn not to surrender.
The matter was exposed,
and Màndūběn rebuked him, saying:
"Why are you so treacherous?"
He replied:
"Reporting loyalty to the state,
how can there be treachery?
Even death would bring no regret."
So he was killed.
Later, Zōngwàng's army encountered Liáo's Grand Commander Bódé and others,
with Dàowēn among them.
They spoke to each other across the water.
Zōngwàng, acting on imperial authority, tried to recruit them.
Bódé merely assented,
showing no intention of surrendering.
Zōngwàng said to Dàowēn:
"Your brother Héshàng was captured in battle
and was never punished.
Later he was executed for rebellion.
How can you not feel sorrow?"
Dàowēn replied:
"My brother was humiliated by being captured,
but glorified by dying for his country."
Zōngwàng looked at Mǎ Héshàng and said:
"Can you capture this person for me?"
He replied:
"Yes."
So he led his unit across the water and defeated their forces,
heading directly for Dàowēn,
shooting and wounding his arm,
capturing and killing him.
Qí (齊) was originally named Shòusù (受速).
He was tall and had a handsome beard.
In the 3rd year of Tiānjuàn (天眷) (1130),
as a child of the imperial clan, he was appointed Zhèn Guó Shàng Jiāngjūn (鎮國上將軍).
In the 1st year of Huángtǒng (皇統) (1141),
he was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫).
In the 6th year of Zhènglóng (正隆) (1161),
he was promoted to Yínqīng Rónglù Dàfū (銀青榮祿大夫).
At the beginning of Dàdìng (大定) (1161),
he was promoted to Tèjìn (特進),
and given the additional title of Ānwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ (安武軍節度使).
He remained in the capital, attending court.
Because Qí (齊) was a close relative,
he was favored and treated with kindness by the emperor,
but he was lazy, stagnant, and lacked talent.
In the 3rd year of Dàdìng (大定) (1163),
he was relieved of his Jiédùshǐ (節度使) post
and given a 3rd-rank salary for attending court.
He successively held the office of Tèjìn (特進).
He died.
His younger brothers Jīng (京) and Wén (文) were both executed for treason.
〔一０〕Shìzōng (世宗) gave all their family property to Qí's (齊) son Yǎozhù (齩住).
He issued an edict to Qí's (齊) wife, saying:
"You all would normally be implicated,
some even facing execution or banishment.
However, I remember Sòngwáng (宋王),
and therefore I will overlook this and not investigate.
Furthermore, I will bestow their family property upon your son.
You should understand my intentions."
In the 15th year (1175),
the emperor summoned Yīngwáng Shuǎng (英王爽) and said:
"From among the princesses and other women, you should choose a spouse for Yǎozhù (齩住).
The ceremonial gifts and mandates should be provided by the relevant authorities."
Soon after, he inherited his uncle Jīng's (京) Shāndōng Xīlù Túmǔjiānměng'ān (山東西路徒毋堅猛安) position.
Jīng (京) was originally named Hūlǔ (忽魯).
As a child of the imperial clan, he was successively promoted to Tèjìn (特進).
In the 2nd year of Tiāndé (天德) (1150),
he was appointed Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ (翰林學士承旨),
concurrently serving as Xiūguóshǐ (修國史),
and given the additional title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
He was promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū (工部尚書),
then transferred to Lǐbù (禮部) and Bīngbù (兵部).
He served as Pàn Dàzōngzhèng Shì (判大宗正事),
was enfeoffed as Cáowáng (曹王),
and appointed Héjiān Yǐn (河間尹).
In the 2nd year of Zhènglóng (正隆) (1157),
he was enfeoffed as Shěnguó Gōng (瀋國公) according to custom,
and made Běijīng Liúshǒu (北京留守).
He resigned due to mourning.
He was reinstated as Yìdū Yǐn (益都尹).
In the 6th year (1161),
he was punished for violating regulations
by drinking with Túdān Zhēn (徒單貞) on Lìchūn (立春) day
and demoted to Luánzhōu Cìshǐ (灤州刺史).
Not long after,
he was reassigned as Jiàngyáng Jūn Jiédùshǐ (絳陽軍節度使).
Hǎilíng (海陵) sent the imperial guard Hūlǔ (忽魯) to Jiàngzhōu (絳州) to kill him.
Jīng (京) escaped by a secret path into Fénzhōu (汾州) territory.
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
Jīng (京) came to see him at Táohuā Wù (桃花塢).
He was reinstated as Pàn Dàzōngzhèng Shì (判大宗正事)
and enfeoffed as Shòuwáng (壽王).
On the first day of the 1st month (Wùchén 戊辰) of the 2nd year (1162),
there was a solar eclipse.
Drums were beaten and ceremonial money was used.
The emperor did not hold court,
reduced his meals, and stopped playing music.
He ordered Jīng (京) to perform the rites in his stead.
Shìzōng (世宗) was determined to correct Hǎilíng's (海陵) distrust and alienation of the imperial clan,
so he bestowed special honors upon Jīng (京) and his brothers,
treating them as if they were born of the same parents.
He said to Jīng (京) and others:
"Whenever I see celestial anomalies,
I reflect on the shortcomings of my governance,
and I blame myself day and night without rest.
All matters must be carefully considered before action is taken,
yet I still fear that my individual insights may not be entirely perfect.
Therefore, I often gather my officials for discussion,
hoping to avoid mistakes."
At this time,
the war against Sòng (宋) had not yet ended,
expenditures were insufficient, and officials were not receiving full salaries.
Jīng's (京) family consisted of several hundred people,
and their financial resources were meager.
Upon hearing this, the emperor
bestowed upon him 150 liǎng (兩) of gold, 100 bolts of brocade, and 500 bolts of silk.
He was reassigned as Xījīng Liúshǒu (西京留守)
and given a sabre and a horse.
When Jīng (京) arrived in Xījīng (西京),
his wife once summoned the fortune-teller Sūn Bāngróng (孫邦榮) to divine Jīng's (京) fortune.
Bāngróng (邦榮) said that the Liúshǒu (留守) official would reach the rank of Tàishī (太師)
and be enfeoffed as a king.
Jīng (京) asked:
"Is there nothing beyond this?"
Bāngróng (邦榮) replied:
"It stops here."
Jīng (京) said:
"If it stops here,
what is the point of this official position?"
Bāngróng (邦榮) perceived his intention
and fabricated a prophecy,
composing a poem
which included the phrase
"Hūlǔ (鶻魯) will be."
He presented it to Jīng (京).
Jīng (京) asked:
"Will the future truly be like this?"
He then accepted the poem
and had him divine again.
Bāngróng (邦榮) claimed that the hexagram he obtained
indicated a sign of sole authority.
Jīng (京) again had Bāngróng (邦榮) divine Shìzōng's (世宗) birth year and month.
A family servant, Sūn Xiǎogē (孫小哥), fabricated rumors to mislead Jīng (京)
as instructed by Bāngróng (邦榮),
and Jīng (京) believed him.
Jīng's (京) wife, Gōngshòu (公壽), knew all about the matter.
In the 3rd month of the 5th year of Dàdìng (大定) (1165),
Sūn Bāngróng (孫邦榮) reported the conspiracy.
The emperor ordered Xíngbù Shìláng (刑部侍郎) Gāo Déjī (高德基) and Hùbù Yuánwàiláng (戶部員外郎) Wányán Wùgǔchū (完顏兀古出) to investigate.
Jīng (京) and the others all confessed.
Once the investigation was complete,
they returned to report.
The emperor said:
"Hǎilíng (海陵) was lawless.
If Guāngyīng (光英) were still alive,
I would protect him,
let alone Jīng (京) and the others."
Therefore,
Jīng (京) and his wife were specially spared execution,
given 100 strokes of the staff,
stripped of their titles,
and settled in Lóufán Xiàn (樓煩縣), Lánzhōu (嵐州).
They were allowed 100 slaves to accompany them,
and the government provided them with good land.
〔一一〕Wùgǔchū (兀古出) and Liú Chú (劉珫) were sent to deliver the imperial edict to Jīng (京),
which read:
"You and I are both grandsons of Tàizǔ (太祖).
Hǎilíng (海陵) lost his way
and decimated the imperial lineage.
I regret that there are so few brothers left,
and I am especially fond of you.
You know this yourself,
so why did you harbor such intentions?
I remember our kinship
and cannot bear to apply the full force of the law.
If you still do not reflect on your wrongs,
even if I do not punish you,
how can Heaven and Earth tolerate you?"
In the 4th month of the 10th year (1170),
an edict was issued in Lóufán Xiàn (樓煩縣)
to build a residence for Jīng (京)
and provide him with a monthly salary equivalent to that of a Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
In the 12th year (1172),
his elder brother Wén (文), the Dézhōu Fángyùshǐ (德州防禦使), plotted rebellion.
The emperor asked Huáng Tàizǐ (皇太子), Zhàowáng Yǔnzhōng (趙王允中), and his prime ministers:
"Jīng (京) plotted rebellion,
and I specially spared him from death.
Now he would be implicated again. What should be done?"
Some prime ministers said that since Jīng (京) had plotted treason,
if he was not eliminated now,
he might become a future menace.
The emperor said:
"The great vessel of the empire belongs to the virtuous.
Hǎilíng (海陵) lost his way,
and I obtained it.
I only need to focus on cultivating virtue;
what else is there to worry about?"
The Crown Prince said:
"It is truly as Your Majesty has instructed."
An envoy was then sent to deliver an edict to Jīng (京),
which read:
"Your elder brother Wén (文),
who was formerly enfeoffed as a Duke of the State,
did not perform his duties.
I promoted him to the rank of prince
and entrusted him with a great feudatory.
Previously in Dàmíng (大名),
he committed a crime involving embezzlement
and was only stripped of his rank and demoted.
He did not appreciate the grace and favor,
but instead harbored resentment
and plotted treason,
bringing guilt upon his brothers.
I remember Sòngwáng (宋王)
and therefore exempt all of you from implication.
Wén's (文) family property, which should have been confiscated,
is all given to your brother's son Yǎozhù (齩住).
You should understand this intention."
In the eleventh month of the twentieth year,
the Emperor inquired of his chief ministers, saying:
"Jīng’s crime began with his wife,
who presumptuously divined good and ill fortune.
There are not many surviving grandsons of Tàizǔ.
I wish to summon and keep them by my side,
not assigning them official duties,
but merely providing for them.
What do you all think of this?"
They all replied,
"To place them in such close proximity
is, in our opinion, inappropriate."
The Emperor said,
"If I cultivate virtue,
why must I harbor suspicion and jealousy beforehand?"
After a long while,
the Emperor again wished to summon Jīng.
The chief ministers said,
"Jīng's
crime is unforgivable.
To have pardoned him was already the greatest good fortune,
how can he be restored?"
The Emperor remained silent for a long time,
then desisted.
Wén's original name was Húlà.
During the Huángtǒng reign,
he was granted a hereditary mòkè,
promoted to Fèngguó Shàngjiāngjūn,
and resided in Zhōngjīng.
When Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
Wén was granted twenty thousand guàn of cash.
At that time,
Zuǒ Yuān was the Zhōngjīng Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
There was a "knocking immortal" practitioner of unsavory arts in the market.
Wén and Yuān both associated with him.
When Hǎilíng returned to Zhōngjīng,
he heard about this,
summoned the "knocking immortal" for questioning,
and fully investigated the matter.
Afterward, he had him executed in the market,
and reprimanded Wén and Yuān.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán,
Wén was appointed Mìshū.
He was implicated in an affair with Língshòu Xiànzhǔ Ālǐhǔ,
received two hundred strokes of the rod,
and was stripped of his name.
Soon after, he was again appointed Mìshūjiān
and ennobled as a Prince.
According to the Zhènglóng precedents, he was ennobled as Yún Guógōng,
but resigned his office due to mourning.
He was reinstated as Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ, Tóngpàn Dàzōngzhèngshì, and Chāngwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he was transferred to Wǔdìngjūn,
remained in the capital,
and served at court.
In the third year,
he was given a sash and court robe frequently worn by the Emperor, along with a saber, and sent off.
The Emperor said to Wén,
"I have no brothers.
Seeing you go to an outer prefecture,
I feel a pang of sorrow.
You are rather unrestrained;
you should exercise greater self-control."
He was appointed Guǎngníng Yǐn,
then summoned to be Pàndàzōngzhèngshì,
and ennobled as Yīng Wáng.
At this time,
his younger brother Jīng was disgraced.
The Emperor said to Wén,
"I did not treat Jīng poorly,
yet he harbored malicious intentions
and plotted rebellion.
Unable to bear punishing him as a kinsman,
I opted for a lighter sentence.
You too are arrogant and unrestrained.
The Sòng Wáng rendered service to the state.
Wǔlíng ennobled the grandsons of Tàizǔ as princes,
but you alone were not ennobled.
When I ascended the throne,
I ennobled you and your brothers as princes.
From now on, repent your faults and regret your transgressions,
and serve me with a pure heart.
Do not worry that I will not know it."
He was appointed Zhēndìng Yǐn
and granted clothing and a belt.
He was then transferred to Dàmíng Yǐn
and re-ennobled as Jīng Wáng.
When Wén arrived in Dàmíng,
he extensively acquired good horses from mèng'ān and mòkè,
sometimes exchanging them for inferior horses,
and purchased people's goods without paying their full value.
He habitually commandeered over forty archers for private service
and fraudulently submitted one hundred and sixty thousand bundles of tax fodder.
When public funds were lacking,
he took over nineteen thousand guàn of cash from the people.
For this, he was stripped of his princely title
and demoted to Dézhōu Fángyùshǐ.
His subordinates were all dismissed for failing to correct him.
Censor Dǒng Shīzhōng, who had been appointed Shàngshūshěng Dūshì, was demoted to Qìnnánjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ for failing to investigate Wén’s affairs.
He had been appointed Shàngshūshěng Dūshì,
and was demoted to Qìnnánjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
An imperial edict stated:
"From now on, if a superior official acts unlawfully,
and his subordinates fail to correct him
or report him to the Emperor,
they shall all be severely punished."
After Wén lost his position,
he was constantly disgruntled,
complaining daily with his household slaves Shímò Hézhù and Hūlǐzhě.
Hézhù, sensing his mood,
then mentioned that mèng'ān Āgǔ and Hézhù and mòkè Pōlǐ of Nánjīng Lù,
and Yínshùkě, were good friends with the Grand Prince (Wén),
and if he indeed wished to undertake a major endeavor,
they would all be willing to follow.
Wén believed him.
He then summoned the diviner Kāng Hóng to predict good and ill fortune,
and secretly informed Hóng of his plan.
Hóng said the coming year would be very auspicious.
Wén heavily rewarded Hóng
and sent his household servant Gānggē and others to Nánjīng with letters and silks for Āgǔ and the others.
[一二] Gānggē asked Hézhù how he knew that Āgǔ and the others would certainly follow.
Hézhù replied,
"Āgǔ and the others are good friends with the Grand Prince;
that's why I surmise they will certainly follow."
When Gānggē arrived in Nánjīng,
he met Āgǔ and the others,
but did not mention the original matter.
Upon his return,
he deceived Wén, saying,
"Āgǔ has sided with the Grand Prince."
Wén then manufactured weapons
and had his household slave Wòdí draw battle plans.
His household slave Zhòngxǐ went to Héběi Dōnglù to report the rebellion.
The prefecture dispatched Zǒngguǎn Pànguān Bótè to rush to Dézhōu to arrest Wén.
When Bótè arrived in Dézhōu,
it was already late.
It happened that Wén was out hunting.
Bótè summoned Fángyù Pànguān Chóuyyuè to consult on arresting him at the hunting grounds.
Chóuyyuè said,
"Wén has many guards,
and it is already night.
Tomorrow is Wén's birthday;
he can be arrested at the celebratory gathering."
Bótè then stopped.
That night,
Wén, knowing that the prefectural envoy had arrived,
realized his plot had been discovered,
and fled with Hézhù, Hūlǐzhě, and others.
The Héjiān Fǔ envoy reported Wén's affair.
An imperial edict commanded Yòusī Lángzhōng Gēshíliè Zhédié and Hànlín Xiūzhuàn Ābùhǎn Érěyě to go to Dézhōu to interrogate.
When the Emperor heard Wén had fled,
he said to his chief ministers,
"Hǎilíng nearly annihilated the imperial clan.
I, mindful that few grandsons of Tàizǔ survive,
have shown them special leniency,
yet Wén did not appreciate his good fortune
and still harbored rebellious plans.
How utterly insane and perverse!"
The Emperor feared that if Wén was not captured for a long time,
many people would be implicated.
He urged local authorities to arrest him.
An edict offered a promotion of five ranks
and a reward of three thousand guàn of cash to anyone who captured Wén.
Wén's plot was discovered in the ninth month of the twelfth year of Dàdìng.
He remained a fugitive for four months,
until he was captured in the twelfth month
and executed.
Kāng Hóng was sentenced to death,
and the others were all punished according to the law.
An edict pardoned his wife Shùshílǎn.
Bótè and Chóuyyuè were punished for not immediately apprehending him,
which allowed Wén to escape.
Bótè received two hundred strokes of the rod
and was dismissed,
while Chóuyyuè received one hundred strokes
and was demoted by two ranks.
An edict stated:
"Dézhōu Fángyùshǐ Wén, Běijīng Cáoguì, and Fūzhōu Lǐfāng were all led to great calamity
by diviners' groundless talk of fate and fortune.
Many diviners merely seek illicit gain,
and freely spread strange doctrines.
From now on, members of the imperial clan and imperial princesses registered in the imperial genealogy, and officials of the third rank,
except for divination regarding marriages, construction, and burials,
are forbidden from calculating and predicting destinies.
Violators shall be sentenced to two years of penal servitude;
serious offenses shall be punished more severely."
The Emperor granted Wén's family property to his late elder brother Tèjìn Qí's son Yǎozhù,
and also granted him the confiscated family property of Xījīng Liúshǒu Jīng.
A赞曰 (Zànyuē) says: Wán-yán Zōngwàng (完顏宗望) set out from Píngzhōu (平州),
won a victory at Báihé (白河),
swept southward,
moved like the wind and struck like lightning,
with no obstacles for his troops.
In two more months, the Bìanjīng (汴京) siege was underway.
Is this what is meant by "the enemy cannot contend with him"?
He then took Xìndé (信德),
left troops to guard it,
making it a rear strongpoint.
How could this be taken lightly?
Guǎnzǐ (管子) said:
"He goes straight into impossible terrain,
attacks the stronghold of the confident,
emerging and entering alone,
and no one can stop him."
Could this be referring to Wán-yán Zōngwàng?
校勘記 (Jiàokānjì)

Biographies, Chapter 13: Lú Yànlún (盧彥倫) (Zǐjī (子璣), Hēngsì (亨嗣), his grandson); Máo Zǐlián (毛子廉); Lǐ Sānxī (李三錫); Kǒng Jìngzōng (孔敬宗); Lǐ Shīkuí (李師夔); Shěn Zhāng (沈璋); Zuǒ Qǐgōng (左企弓); Yú Zhòngwén (虞仲文) (Cáo Yǒngyì (曹勇義), Kāng Gōngbì (康公弼) attached); Zuǒ Bì (左泌) (Yuān (淵), his younger brother; Guāngqìng (光慶), his nephew).
Lú Yànlún
was from Línhuáng (臨潢).
In the early Tiānqìng (天慶) era of the Liáo (遼) dynasty,
Xiāo Zhēnyī (蕭貞一), the Lǐushǒu (留守) of Shàngjīng (上京),
appointed him as an official,
and he was praised for his ability.
At that time,
the Línhuáng (臨潢) region was plagued by bandits,
and the troops in the city had no unified command.
The prefecture, recognizing Yànlún's talent,
recommended him to the court,
and he was immediately appointed Diànzhí (殿直) and Gōudàng Bīngmǎ Gōngshì (勾當兵馬公事).
When the Liáo (遼) army was defeated at Chūhédìan (出河店)
and returned to Línhuáng (臨潢),
they dispersed among the civilian homes
and ordered to be fed.
The soldiers indulged in wanton harassment
and left no stone unturned,
causing great distress to the common people.
Yēlǜ Chìgǒu'ér (耶律赤狗兒), the Lǐushǒu (留守), was unable to restrain them.
So he summoned the military and civilians and explained to them, saying:
"Qìdān (契丹) and Hàn (漢) people have long been one family.
Now, with an alarm on the border
and insufficient national resources,
it has caused soldiers to linger among the elders.
Even if there is harassment, you should tolerate it."
No one dared to speak.
Only Yànlún said:
"Since the war began,
the people's financial resources have been exhausted.
Now, they are again made to support soldiers.
Given the many challenges facing the country,
we naturally dare not refuse.
However, these men act with arrogant brutality,
which people cannot endure.
Furthermore, both Fān (番) and Hàn (漢) people are the emperor's children.
To take from one and give to another,
what does that mean?"
When Línhuáng (臨潢) was first taken,
there was a Xīn Étuōlà (辛訛特剌) in the army
who was formerly a postal official in Línhuáng (臨潢)
and was on good terms with Yànlún.
He was sent to persuade Yànlún,
but Yànlún killed him.
The Liáo (遼) appointed Yànlún as Tuánliànshǐ (團練使) and Gōudàng Lǐushǒusī Gōngshì (勾當留守司公事).
In the fourth year of Tiānfǔ (天輔),
Yànlún followed Lǐushǒu Tàbùyě (撻不野) in surrendering.
He was appointed Xiàzhōu Guāncháshǐ (夏州觀察使)
and temporarily put in charge of the Lǐushǒu (留守) affairs of Shàngjīng (上京).
When the army returned,
Tàbùyě (撻不野) rebelled with the city.
Yànlún then led his subordinates to pursue Tàbùyě (撻不野),
killed all the Qìdān (契丹) in the city,
and sent an envoy to report.
Soon after,
the Liáo (遼) general Yēlǜ Mǎgē (耶律馬哥) took Línhuáng (臨潢) with troops.
Yànlún resisted for seven months.
When reinforcements arrived,
the enemy lifted the siege and departed.
He then went to the capital.
In the second year of Tiānhuì (天會),
he was appointed Zhī Xīnchéng Shì (知新城事).
As the city was newly built,
Yànlún was in charge of planning,
and civilian residences and public buildings were all orderly.
He was redesignated Jìngjiāngjūn Jiédù Lǐuhòu (靜江軍節度留後)
and Zhī Xiánzhōu Yānhuǒ Shì (知咸州煙火事).
Not long after,
he was promoted to Jìngjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ (靜江軍節度使).
In the early Tiānjuàn (天眷) era,
he served as Shǎofùjiān (少府監) concurrently Dūshuǐshǐzhě (都水使者),
and was appointed Tídian Jīngchéng Dànèi Suǒ (提點京城大內所).
He was redesignated Lìshèjūn Jiédùshǐ (利涉軍節度使).
Less than a month later,
he returned
to serve again as Tídian Dànèi Suǒ (提點大內所).
Yànlún was clever and resourceful
and was able to ingratiate himself with the mournful empress,
thus he was considerably favored and employed.
Over a year later,
he was promoted to Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ (侍衞親軍馬步軍都指揮使)
and served as the New Year's envoy to the Sòng (宋) state.
He was redesignated Lǐbù Shàngshū (禮部尚書),
given the additional title of Tèjìn (特進),
and enfeoffed as Xúanguó Gōng (郇國公).
In the second year of Tiāndé (天德),
he was sent out as Dàmíng Yǐn (大名尹).
The following year,
an imperial edict ordered Yànlún to oversee the construction of palaces in Yānjīng (燕京).
He died of illness,
aged sixty-nine.
His son was Zǐjī (子璣).
Zǐjī's courtesy name was Zhèngfǔ (正甫).
Through蔭 (yìn) privilege, he was appointed Gémén Zhīhòu (閤門祗候),
and successively promoted to Kèshěngshǐ (客省使),
concurrently Dōngshàng Géménshǐ (東上閤門使).
He was redesignated Tídian Tàiyī (提點太醫), Jiàofāng (教坊), Sītiān (司天).
He served as Deputy Envoy for the Sòng (宋) Emperor's birthday in the fifteenth year of Dàdìng (大定).
He was promoted to Tóngzhī Xuānhuīyuàn Shì (同知宣徽院事).
He resigned to observe mourning for his mother,
then was reinstated as Tàifǔjiān (太府監).
He was redesignated Kāiyuǎnjūn Jiédùshǐ (開遠軍節度使)
and entered the court as Yòuxuānhuīshǐ (右宣徽使).
When Zhāngzōng (章宗) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Zuǒxuānhuīshǐ (左宣徽使)
and then retired.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng (明昌),
he was reinstated as Zuǒxuānhuīshǐ (左宣徽使),
redesignated Dìngwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ (定武軍節度使),
and again served as Zuǒxuānhuīshǐ (左宣徽使).
At this time,
Zǐjī was already seventy years old,
and an imperial edict permitted him to sit in the corridor during court audiences.
He retired again.
In the early Tàihé (泰和) era,
an imperial edict invited Zǐjī to the Tiānshòujié (天壽節) banquet.
In the second year,
the primary consort Lǐ (李) gave birth to an imperial prince.
After three months,
Zhāngzōng (章宗), seeing Zǐjī as old but strong and healthy,
ordered his staff to be given as a gift for the baby's first bath ceremony.
When Zhāngzōng (章宗) visited Yùquánshān (玉泉山),
he decreed that Zǐjī and the retired prime ministers should dine together,
allowing them to use their staffs and be assisted.
Later, at the Tiānshòujié (天壽節),
the emperor ordered Zǐjī to play shuò (槊) with the high officials,
and Zǐjī won.
He accompanied the emperor to Qiūshān (秋山)
and was bestowed a famous horse.
The emperor said:
"I am rewarding your straightforwardness."
Such was the favor he received.
He died in the sixth year of Tàihé (泰和),
aged eighty.
His son was Hēngsì (亨嗣).
Hēngsì's courtesy name was Jìzǔ (繼祖).
Through 蔭 (yìn) privilege, he was appointed Gémén Zhīhòu (閤門祗候)
and Nèi Gòngfèng (內供奉).
He was transferred to Tóngjiān Píngliángfǔ Cùwù (同監平涼府醋務),
then redesignated Tóngjiān Tiānshān Yánchǎng (同監天山鹽場).
He resigned to observe mourning for his mother.
After the mourning period,
he supervised the wine tax in Láizhōu (萊州),
and was successively transferred to supervise wine affairs in Fēngzhōu (豐州), Rènqiū (任丘), Jíxiàn (汲縣), and Dōngpíng (東平).
His performance was excellent,
and he was promoted to Báidēng Xiànlìng (白登縣令).
In the fourth year of Míngchāng (明昌),
he served in Lìubù (六部) to arrange military provisions at the front.
He entered the court as Diǎngěi Zhícháng (典給直長),
then was redesignated Xījīng Hùjí Pànguān (西京戶籍判官).
He successively served as Xījīng (西京) and Zhōngdū (中都) Tàicāngshǐ (太倉使),
Zhōngdū Hùjí Pànguān (中都戶籍判官),
and Shàngyùnshǔ Chéng (尚醞署丞).
He resigned to observe mourning for his father.
In the early Dà'ān (大安) era,
he was reinstated as Diǎngěishǔ Chéng (典給署丞) concurrently Tàizǐ Jiālìng (太子家令).
In the first year of Chóngqìng (崇慶),
he was promoted to Tóngzhī Shùntiānjūn Jiédùshǐ Shì (同知順天軍節度使事).
At this time,
with the outbreak of war,
conscriptions and levies were frequent and urgent.
Hēngsì's (亨嗣) efficiency was exceptional,
and he was promoted to Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn (定遠大將軍)
and entered the court as Hùbù Yuánwàiláng (戶部員外郎).
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (貞祐),
he was promoted to Jǔzhōu Cìshǐ (莒州刺史).
In the third year,
the Shāndōng Xuānfǔsī (山東宣撫司) campaigned against Yáng Ān'ér (楊安兒).
Hēngsì served in the Lìubù (六部).
When the troops withdrew,
he returned to the prefecture.
He died in the second year of Xīngdìng (興定),
aged sixty-one.
Hēngsì and his younger brother Hēngyì
fully embodied the Way of fraternal love.
Hēngsì initially obtained an official position through his grandfather's patronage.
In the 16th year of Dàdìng (1176 CE),
his father Jī was appointed Tongzhī Xuānhuīyuànshì (同知宣徽院事, Associate Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs),
and was entitled to patronize a son.
Hēngsì yielded this opportunity to his younger brother Hēngyì.
Hēngyì died early,
leaving a son named Shēn.
As Shēn was young,
Hēngsì gave him all of his former properties, including fields, houses, servants, livestock, and wealth.
Máo Zǐlián, whose original name was Bāshí,
was a native of Línhuáng Chángtài.
He was brave, strong, and skilled in archery.
At the end of the Liáo dynasty, when bandits rose everywhere,
brave warriors were recruited.
Zǐlián answered the call.
The Liáo emperor summoned him for an audience,
bestowed upon him armor and weapons,
and had him lead a hundred men
to assist the local officials and soldiers in suppressing the bandits.
For his achievements, he was appointed Dōngtóu Gōngfèngguān (東頭供奉官, Eastern Head Attendant Official)
and given a fine horse.
In the 4th year of Tiānfǔ (1120 CE),
the court dispatched Mòkè Xīnwòtèlā and Yílà Kūxié to persuade Línhuáng to surrender.
Zǐlián led 2,600 households to join them.
He was ordered to lead his own troops,
wear a silver plaque,
and recruit the military and civilians who had not yet surrendered.
Lú Yànlún was enraged by Zǐlián's early surrender,
killed Zǐlián's wife and two sons,
and sent 2,000 cavalrymen to lie in wait for Zǐlián.
Zǐlián and Kūxié were passing through a dangerous defile
when the cavalry surrounded them.
Two horsemen broke out and charged directly at Zǐlián.
Zǐlián drew his bow and killed one of them.
The other thrust his spear, almost hitting Zǐlián's armpit.
Zǐlián dodged the spear
and engaged in hand-to-hand combat,
capturing him alive.
It was Sūn Yánshòu, a strong general under Yànlún.
The rest of the enemy scattered.
In the 3rd year of Tiānhuì (1125 CE),
he was appointed Fùliúshǒu (副留守, Vice Grand Guardian) of Shàngjīng.
After a long time,
he was also put in charge of salt and iron affairs.
During the Tiānjùn (1138-1140 CE) era,
he was appointed Dūjiān (都監, Director) of the Qūyuàn (麴院, Wine Yeast Bureau) in Yānjīng.
Liáo Wáng Zōnggàn asked the prime ministers,
"Zǐlián has rendered meritorious service,
why has he been demoted?"
The prime ministers replied citing precedents.
Zōnggàn said,
"Why is Lú Yànlún not appointed to this position?
Zǐlián's merits are ten times those of Yànlún.
He was in Línhuáng for over ten years,
and officials and common people feared and loved him as if it were only one day.
Who can match this?"
At this time, Lú Yànlún had already been appointed Jiédùshǐ (節度使, Military Commissioner) from the position of Shàofǔjiān (少府監, Director of the Imperial Manufactories),
so Zōnggàn used him for comparison.
He was appointed Níngchāngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Hǎilíng assassinated Xīzōng,
Zǐlián heard of it
and sighed,
"Does he not remember the king's contribution to establishing the policies of the state?"
He then retired.
In the 2nd year of Dàdìng (1162 CE),
he died.
Lǐ Sānxī, courtesy name Huáibāng,
was a native of Jǐnzhōu Ānchāng.
He obtained an official position through wealth.
At the end of the Liáo dynasty,
bandits attacked Jǐnzhōu.
The people of the prefecture recommended Sānxī to take charge of military affairs.
He set up defenses and adapted to changes,
and the city was saved thanks to him.
For his merits, he was appointed Zuǒ Chéngzhì (左承制, Left Commissioner).
When the Liáo emperor fled to Tiāndé,
Liú Yànzōng appointed Sānxī to lead troops to guard Báiyúnshān.
When the Jīn army reached Láizhōu,
Sānxī surrendered with his troops.
He temporarily served as Fùshǐ (副使, Vice Commissioner) of Línhǎijūn Jiédù,
participated in the military affairs of the Yuánshuàifǔ (元帥府, Marshal's Office),
and was later appointed Zhī Yánzhōu (知嚴州, Administrator of Yánzhōu).
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
Sānxī led the Xíngjūn Měng'ān (行軍猛安, Marching Měng'ān)
and defeated Guō Yàoshī's army at Báihé.
He was promoted to Ānzhōu Fángyùshǐ (安州防禦使, Defense Commissioner of Ānzhōu).
When Biànjīng was captured a second time,
Sānxī followed Shé Mǔ to escort the two Sòng emperors northward.
He again became Zhī Yánzhōu,
and was later appointed Guīdéjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
When an edict abolished the state of Qí,
thirty officials were selected to accompany it,
and Sānxī was among those chosen.
He returned to become Qìngzhōu Cìshǐ (慶州刺史, Prefect of Qìngzhōu),
and was thrice promoted to Wǔshèngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was ranked first in an evaluation of integrity,
promoted three ranks,
appointed Ānguójūn Jiédùshǐ,
and then Hébèixīlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (河北西路轉運使, Transport Commissioner for the Western Hebei Circuit),
before retiring.
Sānxī was strong and discerning in governance,
and wherever he served, his administration was praised.
Shìzōng had long known of his reputation.
At the beginning of Dàdìng (1161 CE),
he was appointed Běijīnglù Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ (北京路都轉運使, Chief Transport Commissioner for the Beijing Circuit).
The imperial order was issued,
but Sānxī had already died.
Kǒng Jìngzōng, courtesy name Zhòngxiān,
was originally from Dōngyuán.
At the end of the Shíjìn dynasty,
his family moved to Liáoyáng.
At the end of the Liáo dynasty,
Jìngzōng was a staff official under Liú Hóng of Níngchāng.
When the Wòlǔgǔ (斡魯古) army arrived at the border,
Jìngzōng advised Liú Hóng to surrender.
Thereupon, Jìngzōng served as a local guide,
and after taking Xiǎnzhōu,
he was appointed Shùn'ānlìng (順安令, Magistrate of Shùn'ān) for his achievements.
In the 2nd year of Tiānfǔ (1118 CE),
an imperial edict ordered Jìngzōng and Liú Hóng to lead the people of Yìzhōu to relocate to the interior.
He was granted a hereditary Měng'ān (猛安) title
and appointed Zhī Ānzhōu Shì (知安州事, Administrator of Ānzhōu).
He led 1,000 soldiers to follow Zōngwàng in attacking Sòng.
When Biànjīng was pacified,
Zōngwàng ordered Jìngzōng to guard Biàn.
He once galloped by express relay from Biàn to Hébèi.
Returning to the river,
he found it was dusk and there were no boats.
Jìngzōng spurred his horse into the turbulent current
and successfully reached the south bank.
He was promoted to Jìngjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and successively served as Cìshǐ (刺史, Prefect) of the four prefectures of Shí, Chén, Xìn, and Cí.
His rank was Guānglùdàfū (光祿大夫, Grand Master of Guanglu).
Hǎilíng asked Zhāng Hào,
"Do you know Kǒng Jìngzōng?
Why is his rank high but his position low?"
Hào replied,
"In the early days of the dynasty,
Jìngzōng advised Liú Hóng to surrender Yìzhōu.
Later, he accumulated merit through military service.
The responsible officials were unaware,
so he was generally treated as an ordinary appointee."
The next day,
he was appointed Níngchāngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was transferred to Guīdéjūn,
then retired.
In the 2nd year of Dàdìng (1162 CE),
he died.
Lǐ Shīkuí, courtesy name Xiánzuǒ,
was from Fèngshèng Yǒngxīng.
In his youth, he was unconventional
and had great ambitions.
He entered officialdom through patronage
and became the Qújiān (麴監, Wine Yeast Supervisor) of his home prefecture.
In the 6th year of Tiānfǔ (1122 CE),
Tàizǔ attacked the Liáo emperor at Yuānyāngluò.
The prefect abandoned the city and fled,
and the populace, without leadership,
knocked on Shīkuí's door, asking him to take charge of the prefecture.
Shīkuí agreed,
then gathered soldiers and organized his army.
When Dígǔnǎi's army arrived at Fèngshèngzhōu,
Shīkuí and his old friend Shěn Zhāng secretly plotted to surrender,
saying,
"The fate of an entire city hangs on this action."
Zhāng replied,
"Your words are correct.
What if the military and civilians do not agree?"
Shīkuí immediately led a dozen or so trusted followers out of the city at dawn
and met Yúdǔ.
He made an agreement with him, saying,
"We have now submitted.
