We hope that no troops will enter the city and that there will be no capturing or plundering within the borders."
Yúdǔ agreed.
An edict appointed Shīkuí as Jiédù (節度, Military Commissioner)
and Zhāng as his assistant.
Shīkuí was given two excellent horses
and empowered to recruit those who had not yet submitted,
with permission to act expediently.
The following year,
he was promoted to Zuǒjiānménwèi Dàjiāngjūn (左監門衞大將軍, Grand General of the Left Gate Guard).
The formidable bandit Zhāng Shèng (張勝) with ten thousand men besieged the city.
Shī Kuí (師夔) judged that his forces were no match for the enemy,
so he feigned peace with them.
Daily he sent provisions and supplies.
Zhāng Shèng (張勝) trusted him.
Shī Kuí (師夔), taking advantage of their unpreparedness,
sent men to assassinate Zhāng Shèng (張勝)
and killed him.
He paraded Zhāng Shèng's (張勝) head and said:
"You all are good citizens,
compelled to join these bandits.
Now the principal culprit has been executed.
You may abandon your weapons and return to your homes."
The bandit multitude was greatly astonished
and all dispersed.
Other bandits, Jiāo Wàngtiān (焦望天) and Yǐn Zhìmù (尹智穆), led several thousand troops to raid.
Shī Kuí (師夔) led his forces to confront them,
setting up an ambush on their return path,
and sent someone to sow discord among them.
Zhìmù (智穆) indeed became suspicious,
and Wàngtiān (望天) led his forces away first.
Zhìmù (智穆), isolated,
also turned back,
encountered the ambush, and was defeated.
He was captured and executed.
After this, the bandits dared not enter the territory again.
For his merits, he was promoted to Provisional Administrator (Liúhòu) of the Jìngjiāng (靜江) Army Commissioner (Jiédù) office.
He was successively promoted to Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Wǔpíng (武平) Army,
then transferred to Transport Commissioner (Zhuǎnyùnshǐ) of the Dōngjīng (東京) Circuit,
and then moved to Transport Commissioner (Zhuǎnyùnshǐ) of the Shǎnxī Dōnglù (陝西東路) Circuit.
He retired due to illness
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Rèn (任國公).
He died
at the age of eighty-five.
Shěn Zhāng (沈璋), courtesy name Zǐdá (之達),
was a native of Yǒngxīng (永興), Fèngshèng (奉聖) Prefecture.
He studied for the Jinshì (進士) examination.
When Dígǔnǎi's (迪古乃) army arrived at Shànggǔ (上谷),
Shěn Zhāng (沈璋) conspired with Lǐ Shīkuí (李師夔)
to open the city gates and surrender.
The next day,
they selected someone suitable to be the defender.
The multitude all recommended Shěn Zhāng (沈璋).
Shěn Zhāng (沈璋) firmly advocated for Lǐ Shīkuí (李師夔).
Thereupon, Lǐ Shīkuí (師夔) was appointed Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Wǔdìng (武定) Army,
and Shěn Zhāng (璋) was made his deputy.
He was appointed Assistant Minister (Shàqīng) of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng),
then promoted to Minister (Qīng) of the Court of Diplomatic Reception (Hónglú).
He mourned his mother.
He was reinstated as Deputy Transport Commissioner (Dūzhuǎnyùnfùshǐ) of the Shānxī (山西) Circuit
and granted the additional title of Minister (Qīng) of the Court of the Imperial Regalia (Wèiwèi).
He accompanied the campaign against Sòng (宋).
When Biànjīng (汴京) was pacified,
everyone scrambled for wealth and goods,
but Shěn Zhāng (璋) alone took nothing,
only carrying several thousand volumes of books back with him.
Bandits from Tàiháng (太行) captured Lùzhōu (潞州),
killing its defender Yáo Fán (姚璠).
The imperial army pacified them.
Shěn Zhāng (璋) was ordered to provisionally oversee the prefecture's affairs.
Upon arrival, Shěn Zhāng (璋)
recalled the absconders,
relieved and cared for the impoverished and starving,
and collected and buried the unburied corpses.
Before long,
the people were largely settled and at peace.
Initially,
when the bandit faction occupied the city,
seven hundred soldiers from Lù (潞) were implicated and subject to collective punishment.
The Marshal's office (Shuàifǔ) dispatched a document ordering Shěn Zhāng (璋) to execute them all.
Shěn Zhāng (璋) refused to comply.
The Marshal's office (Shuàifǔ) heard of this
and was greatly enraged.
They summoned Shěn Zhāng (璋) and reprimanded him,
even intending to kill him.
Those around were terrified,
but Shěn Zhāng's (璋) countenance remained unmoved.
He calmly replied:
"Recalling the fugitives and comforting the survivors is
my duty.
These people initially had no rebellious intentions;
they were coerced by the bandits
and had no choice,
which is why I recalled them and they returned.
If I were to kill them now,
it would be killing those who surrendered.
If it benefits the multitude,
what regret would I have in dying?"
A moment later,
the anger subsided.
The Marshal (Shuài) then summoned the Lù (潞) soldiers and said:
"I initially ordered your execution,
but now your prefect (Jūnjūn) has saved you."
They all shed tears of gratitude and departed.
The imperial court heard of this and praised him,
appointing him Grand Master of Remonstrance (Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū)
and Administrator (Zhī) of Lùzhōu (潞州) affairs.
The common people erected a shrine for him.
He was transferred to administer Xīnzhōu (忻州),
then appointed Concurrent Administrator (Tóngzhī) of Tàiyuán (太原) Municipality,
and given the additional title of Assistant Minister (Shìláng) of the Board of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
At that time, Zhāng Jué (張覺) from Jièxiū (介休) gathered a band of outlaws in the mountains and valleys,
plundering towns and counties.
When summoned, he refused to surrender,
saying:
"Previously, there were those who surrendered
and all were killed.
Now they use kind words to entice me,
which is just to kill me.
Only if I hear a word from Assistant Minister (Shìláng) Shěn Gōng (沈公)
will I have no doubts."
Thereupon,
Shěn Zhāng (璋) was ordered to go and summon him,
and Zhāng Jué (覺) surrendered that very day.

He was transferred to Assistant Minister (Shìláng) of the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù Shàngshū), Deputy Left-Behind Administrator (Fùliúshǒu) of Xījīng (西京), and Concurrent Administrator (Tóngzhī) of Píngyáng (平陽) Municipality.
He was promoted to Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Lìshè (利涉) Army
and became Transport Commissioner (Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ) of the Dōngjīng (東京) Circuit,
then transferred to Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhènxī (鎮西) Army.
In the first year of Tiāndé (天德) (1149),
he retired due to illness.
He died
at the age of sixty.
His son, Yízhōng (宜中),
in the third year of Tiāndé (天德) (1151),
was granted a Jinshì (進士) degree by Yáng Jiànzhōng (楊建中).
The encomium says: In times of crisis,
when two armies contend,
the commander of a sole city
holds the nation's fate in the balance.
Lǐ Shīkuí (李師夔), though not acting on an imperial decree,
was recommended by the multitude,
and moreover saved the lives of his people.
There is still much to be said for him.
As for Lú Yànlún's (盧彥倫) surrender,
although it is said the city fell,
his initial resolve was not firm.
How can Máo Zǐlián (毛子廉) be blamed?
As for Zǐlián (子廉) not serving Hǎilíng (海陵),
and Shěn Zhāng (沈璋) bringing Zhāng Jué (張覺) to surrender with a single word,
one good deed is enough to be praised,
how could it be overlooked?
Zuǒ Qǐgōng (左企弓), courtesy name Jūncái (君材).
His eighth-generation ancestor, Hào (皓),
was the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Dìzhōu (棣州) during the Later Táng (後唐).
He was stationed in Yān (燕) as an Army Administrator (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
When the Liáo (遼) took Yān (燕),
they ordered him to guard Jì (薊),
and he consequently made his home there.
Qǐgōng (企弓) studied
and mastered the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋).
He passed the Jinshì (進士) examination
and was twice promoted to Surveillance Judge (Guānchá Pànguān) of Láizhōu (來州).
When Xiāo Yīngbì (蕭英弼) rebelled against the Crown Prince Zhāohuái (昭懷太子),
and all his accomplices were thoroughly investigated,
many were implicated.
Qǐgōng (企弓) distinguished and clarified their injustices,
and many were acquitted.
From Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ) in charge of miscellaneous affairs,
he was sent out as Deputy Left-Behind Administrator (Fùliúshǒu) of Zhōngjīng (中京),
overseeing criminal cases in Liáoyáng (遼陽).
There was a case that was inherently minor but had been made serious.
A memorial had already been submitted awaiting a response,
but Qǐgōng (企弓) released the accused and reported it.
He was successively promoted to Administrator (Zhī) of the Three Departments of Finance (Sānsīshǐ) affairs.
Towards the end of Tiānqìng (天慶) (c. 1120),
he was appointed Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Guǎnglín (廣陵) Army,
concurrently Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì) and Administrator (Zhī) of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn Shì).
When the Jīn (金) army had already captured Shàngjīng (上京),
the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs (Běi Shūmìyuàn) feared offending the emperor's will
and did not report it in a timely manner.
According to Liáo (遼) precedent,
military and governmental affairs were all decided by the Northern Bureau of Military Affairs (Běi Shūmìyuàn)
before being reported to the emperor.
Qǐgōng (企弓) reported it.
The Liáo (遼) ruler said:
"Are military affairs perhaps not within your responsibilities?"
He replied:
"Given the state of the nation,
how dare I follow precedent as a means of self-preservation?"
Thereupon, he presented a strategy for defense.
He was appointed Assistant Minister (Shìláng) of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū) and Grand Councilor (Píngzhāngshì),
and concurrently Supervisor of the Compilation of National History (Jiānxiū Guóshǐ).
At that time, the Liáo (遼) ruler, hearing that the Jīn (金) had already conquered Zhōngjīng (中京),
intended to move west to avoid them.
Qǐgōng (企弓) remonstrated, but was not heeded.
Liáo zhǔ, fleeing from Yuānyāng Luò, sought refuge in Yīnshān.
Qínjìn Guówáng Yēlǜ Niēlǐ declared himself emperor in Yān,
deposing Liáo zhǔ as Xiāngyīn Wáng,
and changed the era name to Déxīng.
Qǐgōng served as Sītú,
and was enfeoffed as Yān Guógōng.
Yú Zhòngwén became Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
concurrently serving as Xījīng Liúshǒu, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, and Nèiwài Zhūjūn Dūtǒng.
Cáo Yǒngyì was Zhōngshū Shìláng Píngzhāngshì, Shūmìshǐ, and Yān Guógōng.
Kāng Gōngbì was Cānzhī Zhèngshì, Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì,
and was bestowed the title
“Zhōngliè Yìshèng Gōngchén.”
Défēi governed as regent,
and Qǐgōng was promoted to Shìzhōng.
Sòng troops attacked Yān,
suddenly reaching the city,
but were later defeated and fled.
Some suspected internal collusion
and wished to root it out,
but Qǐgōng argued against it,
and so they stopped.
Tàizǔ arrived at Jūyōng Guān,
and Xiāo Fēi fled from Gǔběikǒu.
Dūjiān Gāo Liù and others offered their submission to Tàizǔ,
who proceeded directly to the city walls.
Gāo Liù and others opened the gates to receive him.
Tàizǔ entered the city and accepted the surrender;
Qǐgōng and others were still unaware.
Tàizǔ stationed his imperial retinue south of Yānjīng city,
and Qǐgōng and others presented a memorial of surrender.
Tàizǔ allowed them to resume their former positions,
and they all received golden plaques.
Qǐgōng served as Tàifù and Zhōngshū Lìng;
Zhòngwén as Shūmìshǐ, Shìzhōng, and Qín Guógōng;
Yǒngyì retained his old office as Sīkōng;
Gōngbì was Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, Shūmì Fùshǐ Quán Zhīyuàn Shì, and Qiān Zhōngshū Shěng,
and was enfeoffed as Chén Guógōng.
Liáo retired prime minister Zhāng Lín submitted a memorial of surrender,
and an imperial edict stated:
“All of Lín’s fields, houses, and wealth in Yānjīng shall be returned to him.”
Lín was old
and unable to attend an audience,
so only his sons and younger brothers were ordered to come.
After Tàizǔ pacified Yān,
he followed the initial agreement
to cede it to the Sòng people.
Qǐgōng presented a poem,
which roughly stated:
“May Your Majesty not heed the counsel to abandon Yān;
an inch of mountains and rivers is an inch of gold.”
Tàizǔ did not listen.
At this time,
the Shūmìyuàn was established in Guǎngníng Fǔ.
When Qǐgōng and others were about to depart for Guǎngníng,
Zhāng Jué in Píngzhōu harbored ulterior motives.
Tàizǔ wished to send them with an escort of troops.
Qǐgōng and others declined the troops, saying:
“If so,
this would hasten the rebellion.”
When they passed Píngzhōu and
rested under a chestnut forest,
Zhāng Jué sent men to kill them.
Qǐgōng was seventy-three years old,
and was posthumously named Gōngliè.
In Tiānhuì seventh year,
he was posthumously granted Tàishī,
and an envoy was dispatched to offer condolences.
In Zhènglóng second year,
he was re-granted Tèjìn and Jì Guógōng.
Yú Zhòngwén, courtesy name Zhìfū,
was a native of Wǔzhōu Níngyuǎn.
At seven, he could compose poetry;
at ten, he could write prose;
he wrote a thousand characters daily,
and studied diligently.
He passed the Jinshì examination,
and successively served in prefectures and counties,
earning a reputation for honesty and competence.
He was recommended as Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng,
and his policy proposals received excellent marks.
He was promoted to Qǐjū Láng and Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn,
and thrice transferred to Tàicháng Shǎoqīng.
When a prime minister was demoted,
Zhòngwén alone went to see him off.
Some pointed to this as partisanship,
so Zhòngwén requested to retire to care for his parents.
After a long time,
he was summoned to resume his former post.
The prime minister recommended him as foremost in literary conduct,
and he was made Quán Zhīzhìgào,
then appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén.
After helping to pacify Báixī,
he was appointed Shūmì Zhíxuēshì,
Quán Hànlín Xuéshì,
and then Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì.
At fifty-five,
he died,
posthumously named Wénzhèng.
In Tiānhuì seventh year,
he was posthumously granted concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng.
In Zhènglóng second year,
he was re-granted Tèjìn and Pú Guógōng.
Cáo Yǒngyì
was a native of Guǎngníng.
He passed the Jinshì examination
and was appointed Chángchūn Lìng.
The Shūfǔ appointed him Lìshǐ.
He presented a memorial on current affairs,
and was successively promoted through the Guǎngé,
then transferred to Shūmì Fùdū Chéngzhǐ,
Quán Yānjīng Sānsī Shǐ,
and promoted to Gěishìzhōng.
He was summoned to be Shūmì Fùshǐ,
and promoted to Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
He was on good terms with Dàgōng Dǐng, Yú Zhòngwén, and Gōng Yì.
When he and Yú Zhòngwén were both in the Shūmì,
petty officials ostracized them.
He was again sent out to be Sānsī Shǐ,
and promoted to Xuānzhèngdiàn Dàxuéshì.
He died,
posthumously named Wénzhuāng.
In Tiānhuì seventh year,
he was posthumously granted Tàibǎo.
In Zhènglóng second year,
he was re-granted Tèjìn and Dìng Guógōng.
Kāng Gōngbì, courtesy name Bódí,
had ancestors from Yìngzhōu.
His great-grandfather, Yìn,
was granted a sworn contract for military achievements during the Liáo Bǎoníng era,
and settled in Wǎnpíng, Yān.
Gōngbì loved learning,
and at twenty-three passed the Jinshì examination,
appointed Zhùzuò Láng and Wǔzhōu Jūnshì Pàn Guān.
He was appointed Lìshǐ in the Shūfǔ,
but sought an external appointment,
and was sent out as Níngyuǎn Lìng.
When frost damaged crops in the county,
the Cáosī pressed urgently for taxes,
and imprisoned people.
Gōngbì submitted a memorial,
and the imperial court then released them,
and consequently exempted the county from rent and taxes;
the county people built a shrine for him while he was alive.
He supervised the Píngzhōu Qiánbókù,
and allocated corvée grain to Chuānzhōu.
The great bandit Hóu Gài captured Chuānzhōu,
and ordered his men to escort Gōngbì out of the territory,
saying:
“He is a good official.”
He was made Quán Gānzhōu Jiédùshǐ.
He died,
posthumously named Zhōngsù.
In Tiānhuì seventh year,
he was posthumously granted Shìzhōng.
In Zhènglóng second year,
he was re-granted Tèjìn and Dào Guógōng.
Qǐgōng had sons Bì, Yíng, and Yuān.
Bì, courtesy name Chángyuán,
was Qǐgōng’s eldest son.
He served in Liáo,
reaching the office of Dìzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Tàizǔ pacified Yān,
Bì followed Qǐgōng to the court.
Later, they moved east to Píngzhōu,
where Qǐgōng was harmed by Zhāng Jué,
and Bì returned to Yān.
At this time,
as Yān was ceded to Sòng,
the Xuānfǔ Sī sent him to Biàn,
but Bì, knowing his enemy from Píngzhōu was there,
took a secret route to flee back.
The imperial court praised him
and promoted him to Xī Shànggéménshǐ.
He followed Sòng Wáng Zōngwàng in the southern campaign,
and was meritorious in defeating Zhēndìng,
then became Zhī Qízhōu,
and successively served as Cìshǐ of Zé, Xí, and other prefectures.
In early Zhēnyuán,
he became Jùnzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
then transferred to Shǎnxī Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and was enfeoffed as Dài Guógōng.
Bì was placid and calm by nature,
and fond of reading Zhuāng and Lǎo.
At sixty-one,
he requested to retire.
His friends and relatives thought it was too early,
but Bì sighed and said:
“I held military command at thirty,
and have served for another thirty years,
achieving renown and being able to withdraw my body,
which is fitting.”
People of his time held him in high esteem.
He died at seventy-four.
Yuān was successively promoted to Vice Prefect of Yānjīng and Superintendent of Transport for the Zhōngjīng Circuit.
He successively served as Superintendent of Transport for Héběi Dōnglù and Zhōngdū Circuit.
Yuān was greedy and mean-spirited.
In his three terms handling grain transport affairs,
he always sought to profit personally from money and grain.
He stayed in Zhōngdū for eight years,
not seeking promotion.
He colluded and exchanged bribes with Lǐ Tōng and Xǔ Lín,
fraudulently reporting the delivery of various goods to the Transport Office,
thereby acquiring illicit gains.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Yuān sent his son Yíqìng to Tōnjīng to present a memorial.
Yíqìng was specially bestowed the title of Jìnshì (third class) on the Zhōngjié roster
and appointed Cóngshìláng.
When Yíqìng returned to Zhōngdū,
Shìzōng issued an imperial edict to Yuān, saying:
"All palace decorations and arrangements shall follow the old system;
do not add anything.
Do not employ a single laborer
to disturb the common people.
Simply be vigilant about entries and exits in the forbidden palace."
In Dàdìng second year (1162),
he was transferred to be Jìnnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Shìzōng, who already knew his character,
warned him, saying:
"You are the son of a chancellor,
practiced in court affairs.
Formerly, as a Transport Commissioner,
I found you very contemptible.
Do not oppress or exploit the common people.
If you dare to do so again,
do not expect to be employed again."
Not long after Yuān arrived in Huáizhōu,
he was impeached for having previously misappropriated official timber while serving as Zhōngdū Zhuǎnyùn.
He was dismissed from office.
His son was Guāngqìng.
Guāngqìng, courtesy name Jūnxī,
was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
profound and spoke little.
Yuān once told his close associates:
"This son will carry on our family line."
By virtue of protection (yīn),
he was appointed Gémén Zhīhòu,
and then promoted to Xīshàng Gémén Fùshǐ.
After observing mourning for his father,
he was reinstated as Dōngshàng Gémén Fùshǐ,
then successively promoted to Xīshàng Gémén Shǐ and Dōngshàng Gémén Shǐ,
also serving as Tàimiào Shǔlìng.
Guāngqìng loved antiquity,
read books and understood great principles,
enjoyed writing poetry,
excelled at seal and clerical scripts,
and was particularly skilled in large characters.
When Shìzōng performed the suburban sacrifice,
received the esteemed title,
and received the imperial seal,
all were engraved by Guāngqìng.
All palace and temple inscriptions written by Guāngqìng
were praised by people for their excellent technique.
He oversaw the construction work at Yuánmiào, Kūnhòulíng, and Shòu'āngōng,
without being harsh or severe,
ensuring that labor and rest were balanced.
He held several positions simultaneously,
was diligent, cautious, and thorough,
and never boasted about himself.
Shìzōng alone observed his qualities.
Originally,
Yùshǐ Dàfū Zhāng requested the creation of the Great Jīn Imperial Seal.
The officials presented the text of the Qín seal,
but the Emperor ordered
"Dàjīn Shòumìng Wànshì zhī Bǎo"
(Great Jīn Imperial Seal of Ten Thousand Generations) as the inscription.
It was four inches and eight fen in diameter,
one inch and four fen thick,
with a coiled dragon knob,
and both its height and thickness were four inches and six and a half fen.
Lǐbù Shàngshū Zhāng Jǐngrén and Shàofù Jiān Zhāng Jǐnyán oversaw the construction,
and Guāngqìng was ordered to engrave it.
He was promoted to Tóngzhī Xuānhuī Yuànshì,
then changed to Shàofù Jiān.
After observing mourning for his mother,
he was reinstated as Yòu Xuānhuī Shǐ.
When Shìzōng visited Shàngjīng,
Guāngqìng went to Shàngjīng to manage the ceremonial guard system,
and people at the time considered his arrangements appropriate.
In the twenty-fifth year (1185),
he passed away
at the age of fifty-one.
The Emperor sent an envoy to offer sacrifices,
bestowing three hundred liǎng of silver, ten bolts of heavy brocade, and one hundred rolls of silk.
In ordinary times, he loved to speak good words
and collected good medicines,
earning the nickname
"Shànshàn Dàorén" (Taoist of Goodness).
In his later years, he believed in Buddhist teachings,
wrote his own true encomium,
and his words were all free-spirited.
The encomium says: Zuǒ Qǐgōng, Yú Zhòngwén, Cáo Yǒngyì, Kāng Gōngbì, these four men,
were all talented and discerning scholars.
In their service to the Liáo ruler, they offered several proposals and recommendations.
However, when they received titles through usurpation and assumed positions,
pledged allegiance to two rulers,
and perished among rebellious factions,
all three aspects were lost to them.
Alas!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 14: Sons of Tàizōng: Zōngpán (original name Púlǔhǔ),

Zōnggù (original name Húlǔ), Zōngběn (original name Ālǔ; Xiāo Yù is attached), Gǎo (original name Xiéyě), Zōngyì (original name Bóji), Zōnggàn (original name Wòběn), Chōng (original name Shéntǔmǎn; sons Tánnú etc.), Yǒngyuán (original name Yuánnú), Yǎn (original name Wútóng), Xiāng (original name Yǒngqìng), Gǔn (original name Pújiǎ).
Tàizōng had fourteen sons: Púlǔhǔ, Húlǔ, Húlǔbǔ, Ālǔdài, Ālǔbǔ, Húshāhǔ, Ālín, Ālǔ, Hǔlǎn, Húlijia, Shéntǔmén, Húbóbù, Wòliè, Hǔshā.
Zōngpán's original name was Púlǔhǔ.
In Tiānfǔ fifth year (1121),
Commander-in-Chief Gǎo captured Zhōngjīng, and Zōngpán, along with Wòlǔ, Zōnghàn, and Zōnggàn, all served as his deputies.
In Tiānhuì tenth year (1132),
he became Guólún Hūlǔ Bójíliè.
When Xīzōng ascended the throne,
he became Shàngshū Lìng
and was enfeoffed as Sòng Guówáng.
Not long after,
he was appointed Tàishī
and, along with Zōnggàn and Zōnghàn, jointly managed the affairs of the Three Departments.
Xīzōng treated the imperial clan with great courtesy.
After Zōnghàn's death,
Zōngpán became increasingly overbearing.
He once had a dispute with Zōnggàn before the Emperor,
and immediately submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
Wūyě memorialized, saying:
"Your Majesty is in your prime,
but your great ministers are not in harmony.
I fear this is not a blessing for the state."
Xīzōng then reconciled them.
Zōngpán became even more arrogant and reckless.
Later, he held a knife towards Zōnggàn in front of Xīzōng,
but Dūdiǎnjiǎn Xiāo Zhònggōng stopped him.
Afterwards, Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài Tàlán and Dōnjīng Liúshǒu Zōngjùn came to court.
Zōngpán secretly colluded with them,
and Zōngjùn subsequently became Yòu Chéngxiàng
and gained influence.
Tàlán was of senior rank
and had many accomplishments.
He had previously recommended Líu Yù
to be established as Qí Dì.
At this point, he proposed giving Hénán and Shǎnxī to Sòng,
and making Sòng declare itself a vassal.
Xīzōng ordered his ministers to deliberate,
and the imperial clan and high ministers stated that it was unacceptable.
Zōngpán and Zōngjùn supported it,
and ultimately it was given to Sòng.
Later, Zōngpán, Zōngjùn, and Tàlán conspired to rebel.
Zōnggàn and Xīyǐn exposed their plot,
and Xīzōng issued an edict to execute them.
Those who attended their banquets
were all demoted, stripped of their ranks, or reprimanded to varying degrees.
His brothers, Húlǔbǔ and nine others, were pardoned,
and Tàlán was also pardoned
and sent out as Xíngtái Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
On the Empress's birthday,
the prime ministers, imperial princes' consorts, and imperial ladies came to offer congratulations.
Xīzōng ordered the music to be stopped,
saying:
"Zōngpán and others are close relatives,
yet they conspired treason.
I cannot feel joyful."
He presented a golden box and two silver tripods to Míngdé Gōng Tàihúang Tàihòu,
and also bestowed a golden box and silver tripods upon Zōnggàn and Xīyǐn.
Zōnggù's original name was Húlǔ.
In Tiānhuì fifteenth year (1137), he became Yānjīng Liúshǒu
and was enfeoffed as Bīnwáng.
Zōngyǎ's original name was Húlǔbǔ
and he was enfeoffed as Dàiwáng.
Zōngwěi's original name was Ālǔbǔ
and he was enfeoffed as Yúwáng.
Zōngyīng's original name was Húshāhǔ
and he was enfeoffed as Téngwáng.
Zōngyì's original name was Ālín
and he was enfeoffed as Xuēwáng.
Zōngběn's original name was Ālǔ
and he was enfeoffed as Yuánwáng.
Hǔlǎn was enfeoffed as Yìwáng.
Zōngměi's original name was Húlijia
and he was enfeoffed as Fēngwáng.
Shéntǔmén was enfeoffed as Yùnwáng.
Húbóbù was enfeoffed as Huòwáng.
Wòliè was enfeoffed as Càiwáng.
Zōngzhé's original name was Hǔshā
and he was enfeoffed as Bìwáng.
All were enfeoffed in Tiānjuàn first year (1138).
Zōngshùn's original name was Ālǔdài.
He died in Tiānhuì second year (1124).
In Huángtǒng fifth year (1145), he was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and later enfeoffed as Xúwáng.
Zōngpán 既誅,
Xīzōng 使 Zōnggù 子 Jīng 往 Yānjīng 慰諭 Zōnggù.
既而 Yì Wáng Gǔlǎn 復與行臺左丞相 Tàlǎn 謀反伏誅.
詔曰:
「Yānjīng 留守 Bīnwáng Zōnggù 等或謂當絕屬籍,
朕所不忍.
Zōnggù 等但不得稱皇叔,
其母妻封號從而降者,
審依舊典. 」
Huángtǒng 二年,
復封 Zōngyǎ 為 Dàiwáng.
Zōnggù 為判大宗正,
六年,
為 Tàibǎo、右丞相兼中書令.
是歲,
薨.
Hǎilíng 在 Xīzōng 時,
見 Tàizōng 諸子勢強,
而 Zōngpán 尤跋扈,
與 Gǔlǎn 相繼皆以逆誅,
心忌之.
Xīzōng 厚於宗室,
禮遇不衰.
Hǎilíng 嘗與 Bǐngdé、Tángkuò Biàn 私議,
主上不宜寵遇 Tàizōng 諸子太甚.
及篡立,
謁奠太廟.
Hán Wáng Hēng 素號材武,
使攝右衞將軍,
密諭之曰:
「爾勿以此職為輕,
朕疑 Tàizōng 諸子太強,
得卿衞左右,
可無慮耳. 」
遂與祕書監 Xiāo Yù 謀去 Zōngběn 兄弟.
Tàizōng 子孫於是焉盡,
語在 Zōngběn 傳中.
Zōngběn 本名 Ālǔ.
Huángtǒng 九年,
為右丞相兼中書令,
進 Tàibǎo,
領三省事.
Hǎilíng 篡立,
進 Tàifù,
領三省事.
初,
Zōnggàn 謀誅 Zōngpán,
故 Hǎilíng 心忌 Tàizōng 諸子.
Xīzōng 時,
Hǎilíng 私議 Zōngběn 等勢強,
主上不宜優寵太甚.
及篡立,
猜忌益深,
遂與祕書監 Xiāo Yù 謀殺 Tàizōng 諸子.
誣以 Bǐngdé 出領行臺,
與 Zōngběn 別,
因會飲,
約內外相應.
使尚書省令史 Xiāo Yù 告 Zōngběn 親謂 Yù 言:
「以汝於我故舊,
必無它意,
可布腹心事.
領省臨行,
言彼在外諭說軍民,
無以外患為慮.
若 Tàifù 為內應,
何事不成. 」
又云:
「長子 Suǒlǐhǔ 當大貴,
因是不令見主上. 」
Zōngběn 又言:
「左丞相於我及我妃處,
稱主上近日見之輒不喜,
故心常恐懼,
若 Tàifù 一日得大位,
此心方安. 」
Tángkuò Biàn 謂 Zōngběn 言:
「內侍 Zhāng Yàn 善相,
相 Tàifù 有天子分. 」
Zōngběn 答曰:
「Zōngběn 有兄 Dōngjīng 留守在,
Zōngběn 何能為是. 」
時 Zōngměi 言
「Tàifù 正是 Tàizōng 主家子,
秪 Tàifù 便合為 Běijīng 留守」 ．
Biàn 臨行與 Zōngběn 言
「事不可遲」 ．
Zōngběn 與 Yù 言
「大計只於日近圍場內予決」 ．
Zōngběn 因以馬一匹、袍一領與 Yù,
充表識物．
Yù 恐圍場日近,
身縻於外,
不能親奏,
遂以告祕書監 Xiāo Yù．
Yù 具以聞．
Xiāo Yù 出入 Zōngběn 家,
親信如家人．
Hǎilíng 既與 Xiāo Yù 謀殺 Zōngběn、Bǐngdé,
詔天下,
恐天下以 Zōngběn、Bǐngdé 輩皆懿親大臣,
本無反狀,
Yù 搆成其事,
而 Xiāo Yù 與 Zōngběn 厚,
人所共知,
使 Yù 上變,
庶可示信．
於是使人召 Zōngběn 等擊鞠,
Hǎilíng 先登樓,
命左衞將軍 Túdiān Tèsī 及 Xiāo Yù 妹壻近侍局副使 Yēlǜ Pìlílà Xiǎodǐ 密伺 Zōngběn 及判大宗正事 Zōngměi,
至,
即殺之．
Zōngměi 本名 Húlíjiǎ,
臨死神色不變．
Zōngběn 已死,
Xiāo Yù 使人召 Xiāo Yù．
是日,
Yù 送客出城,
醉酒,
露髮披衣,
以車載至 Yù 弟點檢 Xiāo Zuò 家．
逮日暮,
Yù 酒醒,
見軍士圍守之,
意為人所累得罪,
故至此．
以頭觸屋壁,
號咷曰:
「臣未嘗犯罪,
老母年七十,
願哀憐之． 」
Yù 附耳告之曰:
「主上以 Zōngběn 諸人不可留,
已誅之矣,
欲加以反罪,
令汝主告其事．
今書汝告款已具,
上即問汝,
汝但言 Zōngběn 輩反如狀,
勿復異詞,
恐禍及汝家也． 」
Yù 乃以巾服與 Yù,
引見 Hǎilíng．
Hǎilíng 問 Yù．
Yù 言 Zōngběn 反,
具如 Yù 所教．
Hǎilíng 遣使殺 Dōngjīng 留守 Zōngyì、Běijīng 留守 Biàn．
及遷 Yìdū 尹 Bì Wáng Zōngzhé、Píngyáng 尹 Bǐng、左宣徽使 Jīng 等,
家屬分置別所,
止聽各以奴婢五人自隨．
既而使人要之於路,
幷其子男無少長皆殺之．
而 Zhōngjīng 留守 Zōngyǎ 喜事佛,
世稱
「善大王」 ,
Hǎilíng 知其無能,
將存之以奉 Tàizōng．
後召至闕,
不數日,
竟殺之．
Tàizōng 子孫死者七十餘人,
Tàizōng 後遂絕．
Biàn 本名 Kěxǐ．
Bǐng 本名 Húlígǎi．
Jīng,
Zōnggù 子,
本名 Húshílái．
Xiāo Yù 既如 Xiāo Yù 教對 Hǎilíng,
Hǎilíng 遂以 Zōngběn、Bǐngdé 等罪詔天下,
以 Yù 上變實之．
Yēlǜ Niēlǐ sent a letter to Gǎo requesting peace.
Gǎo replied,
reprimanding him for not first reporting to the superior state
and presumptuously assuming a grand title.
He stated that if Niēlǐ could surrender,
he would be appointed as the Defense Commissioner of Yānjīng.
Niēlǐ sent another letter,
which roughly stated:
"When I ascended the throne yesterday,
it was at a time when diplomatic ties between the two countries were severed and our armies were clashing.
The Xī King and all the civil and military officials unanimously supported and enthroned me;
how could there be leisure to ask for a mandate?
Now that all the armies have gathered,
if you intend to attack,
we will not stand by idly and await death.
In the past, our ancestors
never harmed the people of Dàjīn.
You bestowed upon them titles,
and they grew stronger day by day.
Now you forget this kindness
and wish to exterminate my ancestral sacrifices.
What justice is there in that?
If we receive your benevolent consideration,
then our gratitude for your grace
will be boundless."
Gǎo replied:
"Your Excellency was formerly a Marshal,
commanding all armies.
Your responsibility was not light,
yet you achieved not an inch of merit.
To hold a single city
and resist the national army,
is this not difficult?
As for those you employ,
since they could not die for the country before,
who among them would be willing to serve Your Excellency now?
And to say that if the lord is disgraced, his subjects die,
and to wish to rely on this for success,
your plan is indeed flawed.
The headquarters, in accordance with the imperial edict,
will grant office to those who surrender
and suppress those who resist.
If you remain obstinate and refuse to comply,
we will not stop until you are utterly annihilated."
Niēlǐ then dispatched an envoy to request an audience with Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ bestowed an edict upon Niēlǐ, saying:
"You,
a close relative of Liáo,
holding the position of general and minister,
were unable to share the country's fate.
Instead, you seized an isolated city
and presumptuously assumed a grand title.
If you do not surrender and submit,
you will later regret it."
In the sixth month,
the Emperor departed the capital
and issued an edict to the Metropolitan Commanders, saying:
"You desired that I personally lead the campaign,
and I have set out on the first day of this month.
Where is the Liáo lord now?
What strategy can be used to capture him?
Report it in detail."
Gǎo sent Mǎ Héshàng to welcome Tàizǔ at Tálǔ Hé.
Wòlǔ and Lóushì defeated the Xià general Lǐ Liángfǔ.
[一０]Gǎo sent Wányán Xīyǐn and others to report the victory
and also requested to relocate the various tribes of the Southwestern Pacification Commission to the interior.
Xīyǐn and others met the Emperor southwest of Dàluò,
and the Emperor praised and rewarded them.
When the Emperor arrived at Yuānyāng Luò,
Gǎo came to pay respects.
The Emperor pursued the Liáo lord to Huílízhěn Chuān,
then marched south to attack Yānjīng,
stopping at Fèngshèng Zhōu.
An edict was issued, stating:
"From now on, all petitions and lawsuits shall be forwarded to Metropolitan Commander Gǎo for resolution.
If there is a major doubt,
report it to the throne immediately."
Tàizǔ pacified Yānjīng
and returned to Yuānyāng Luò.
He appointed Zōnghàn as Metropolitan Commander,
and Gǎo followed the Emperor back to the capital.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
Gǎo became Ānbān Bójíliè,
governing state affairs together with Zōnggàn.
In Tiānhuì third year (1125), they campaigned against Sòng,
with Gǎo leading as Grand Marshal,
remaining in the capital.
Zōnghàn and Zōngwàng advanced their armies along separate routes.
In the fourth year (1126),
they again campaigned against Sòng
and captured two Sòng emperors, returning with them.
In Tiānhuì eighth year (1130),
he passed away.
In Huángtǒng third year (1143),
he was posthumously enfeoffed as King of Liáoyuè.
In Tiāndé second year (1150),
he was ritually enshrined in Tàizǔ's ancestral temple.
In Zhènglóng, he was regularly enfeoffed as King of Liáo.
In Dàdìng fifteenth year (1175),
he was given the posthumous title Zhìliè.
His son was Bójí.
Zōngyì, originally named Bójí,
was the ninth son of Xiéyě.
During the Tiāndé era,
he served as Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
Hǎilíng had already killed Tàizōng's descendants,
and he was particularly wary of the growing strength of Xiéyě's sons,
wishing to eliminate all imperial relatives, meritorious officials, and old ministers.
At this time,
the Left Deputy Marshal Sālǐhē was in Biànjīng and had a rift with Tàbùyě.
Tàbùyě's daughter was Hǎilíng's concubine,
so Hǎilíng secretly instructed Tàbùyě to plot against Sālǐhē.
Thereupon, Yáoshè, a clerk in the Metropolitan Marshal's office, eager to ingratiate himself,
forged a family letter from Sālǐhē to his son Zōng'ān.
Zōng'ān accidentally left it outside the palace,
where Yáoshè picked it up
and reported it as evidence of treason.
The letter was written in small Khitan characters,
and its seal had already been broken.
Inside was a blank sheet of paper
with faint, white characters,
appearing as if it had been soaked in water,
making the strokes legible.
It bore Sālǐhē's signature and a certain prince's seal.
The letter read:
"Āhún,
are you well and happy?
When will you arrive at the palace gate?
When you came on horseback previously,
we discussed my instructing you, Āhún Píngzhāng, and Mólǐyě Āhún, to observe the situation and resume communications,
and to devise plans in times of urgency.
I know you have already explained this in detail.
What Mólǐyě Āhún said is correct;
if we only kill Tàbùyě, then there will be no worries on the southern road."
The details are found in the biography of Sālǐhē.
Nǚzhēn refers to a son as
"Āhún."
The former
"Āhún"
refers to Sālǐhē's son,
whose son was Zōng'ān.
The latter
"Āhún Píngzhāng"
refers to Zōngyì.
Zōngyì was originally an imperial clan member,
still retaining the old appellation.
Because of this, Zōngyì and Mólǐyě were killed,
along with Zōng'ān, Tàizǔ's consort Xiāo shì, Prince Rèn Wēihē, and Wèi King Wòdài's grandson Huólǐjiǎ.
Yáoshè's forged letter did not mention Huólǐjiǎ,
but Hǎilíng, seeing him as forthright and skilled at embellishment,
disliked him.
Ministers pleaded for their innocence,
but Hǎilíng said:
"Just kill them;
say no more."
Over a hundred descendants of Xiéyě were killed,
and over twenty descendants of Mólǐyě.
Mólǐyě was
a grandson of Jǐngzǔ,
the second son of Màndūhē.
Xiéyě had a young son, Āhǔlǐ,
whose wife was Tàbùyě's daughter,
and Hǎilíng's consort Dà shì's elder sister.
When Āhǔlǐ was to be killed,
the envoy could not bear to see his face,
so he covered him with a quilt and strangled him.
The pressure was on his chin,
and he did not die for a long time.
When the quilt was removed, he was strangled again.
Hǎilíng sent an envoy to pardon his death,
and thus he was spared.
Later, he was enfeoffed as a king
and granted a hereditary chiliarch position.
In the early Dàdìng era,
Zōngyì's official titles and ranks were posthumously restored
and he was granted the title Tèjìn.
His younger brothers Púmǎ, Bólùnchū, Ālǔ, and Wēihē were all posthumously granted the title Lónghǔ Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn.
Zōnggàn's original name was Wòběn,
the eldest illegitimate son of Tàizǔ.
When Tàizǔ attacked Liáo,
the Liáo people came to resist,
meeting them at the border.
Zōnggàn was sent to lead the troops ahead to fill the trenches,
and all the soldiers crossed.
The Bóhǎi army charged forward,
and the seven mòkè of the left wing faltered slightly,
thus striking the central army.
Gǎozhé went out to battle,
and Tàizǔ said:
"One must not be careless when encountering a formidable enemy."
He ordered Zōnggàn to stop Gǎo.
Zōnggàn rode out in front of Gǎo,
reining in the horse of the scout Zhejié,
and only then did Gǎo return.
In the battle of Dálǔgǔ City,
Zōnggàn used the central army as a feint.
After Tàizǔ captured Huánglóng Fǔ,
he immediately wanted to take Chūnzhōu.
The Liáo ruler heard that Huánglóng was undefended,
was greatly alarmed,
and personally led his army,
conscripting young members of the imperial clan and powerful families, brave warriors from all four directions, and those skilled in military strategy,
all to be enlisted in the army.
Zōnggàn advised Tàizǔ not to attack Chūnzhōu,
but to let the soldiers rest.
Tàizǔ thought this was sound,
and so he withdrew his army.
Zōnggàn obtained a surrendered man
who said that Chūnzhōu and Tàizhōu had no defenses
and could be taken.
Thereupon, Xiéyě took Chūnzhōu and Tàizhōu,
and Zōngxióng, Zōnggàn, and others captured Jīnshān Xiàn.
Zōngxióng then assigned three thousand soldiers to Zōnggàn,
to gather the various tribes that had not yet surrendered.
Zōnggàn selected talented local people
and issued an imperial edict to persuade them.
Consequently, the four tribes of Nǚgù and Píshì, as well as the Bóhǎi people, all surrendered.
Tàizǔ conquered Línhuáng Fǔ
and reached Wòhēi Hé.
Zōnggàn admonished him, saying:
"The distance is great and the weather is hot;
the soldiers are weary and the horses are exhausted.
If we penetrate deep into enemy territory,
our provisions will not be sustained,
and I fear future difficulties."
The emperor followed his advice,
and so the army was withdrawn.
He followed Dūtǒng Gǎo to capture Zhōngjīng.
Zōnghàn sent a letter to Gǎo from Běi'ān Zhōu.
At this time,
Xīyǐn captured a Liáo man,
learning that the Liáo ruler was at Yuānyang Luò,
and could be attacked by surprise.
Gǎo could not decide.
Zōnghàn sent another envoy.
Zōnggàn said to Gǎo:
"Yílái Bójíliè has a keen insight into the situation;
he has sent another envoy to request this,
he certainly would not act lightly.
Moreover, he has already dispatched troops,
and cannot stop now;
please follow his plan."
He said it repeatedly,
and Gǎo then reported to Zōnghàn to meet at Xīwáng Lǐng.
If Zōnggàn had not been there at that time,
Gǎo would never have had the intention to advance.
After the armies met at Yángchéng Luò,
Gǎo sent Zōnggàn and Zōnghàn with six thousand elite soldiers to raid Liáo, reaching Wǔyuàn Sì.
The Liáo ruler had already fled,
and they fought with the Liáo general Gěng Shǒuzhōng forty li east of Xījīng City.
Shǒuzhōng was defeated and fled.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
Zōnggàn was made Guólùn Bójíliè,
assisting in governance with Xiéyě.
In Tiānhuì 3rd year,
the Liáo ruler was captured at Yúdǔ Gǔ, west of Yìngzhōu.
The discussion of rites and institutions began,
official titles were rectified,
court attire was standardized,
schools were established,
elections were set up,
and the calendar was corrected to clarify the seasons –
all were initiated by Zōnggàn.
In the 4th year,
the official system was implemented,
proclaimed throughout the realm.
In the 10th year,
Xīzōng became Ānbān Bójíliè,
and Zōnggàn became Guólùn Zuǒ Bójíliè.
When Xīzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Tàifù,
and with Zōnghàn and others, jointly managed the affairs of the Three Departments.
In Tiānjuàn 2nd year,
he was promoted to Tàishī,
enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáng and Sòng,
and was exempt from bowing at court,
allowed to walk with a staff onto the main hall,
and the staff was bestowed upon him.
Zōnggàn had a foot ailment,
and an edict allowed him to sit when presenting matters.
Not long after,
he supervised the compilation of the national history.
In Huángtǒng 1st year,
Zōnggàn was granted a palanquin to enter the hall,
and in imperial edicts, his name was not used directly.
The emperor visited Yānjīng,
and Zōnggàn accompanied him.
When Zōnggàn fell ill,
the emperor personally visited to inquire.
Returning from Yānjīng,
upon reaching Yěhú Lǐng,
Zōnggàn's illness became critical and he could not proceed.
The emperor personally visited to inquire,
and when speaking of military and national affairs,
the emperor wept ceaselessly.
The next day,
the emperor and empress together went to see him,
and the empress personally fed Zōnggàn,
returning at dusk.
Consequently, they pardoned criminals
and performed rituals to ward off Zōnggàn's illness.
After several days,
he passed away.
The emperor mourned him deeply,
suspending court for seven days.
The practice of suspending court for the death of a high minister
began with Zōnggàn.
The emperor offered sacrifices,
on that day, Gēngxū,
the Grand Astrologer reported that crying was inappropriate during Xū and Hài hours.
The emperor did not listen, saying:
"When I was an infant,
the Grand Tutor provided the care and instruction of a guardian,
how could I not cry?"
He wept bitterly.
The emperor's birthday celebrations were canceled.
The emperor returned to Shàngjīng,
and visited his residence to oversee the funeral arrangements.
When the funeral procession reached Shàngjīng,
the emperor personally mourned him.
At the burial,
he personally oversaw it.
Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
posthumously naming him Xiàngǔ Hóngdào Wénzhāo Wǔliè Zhāngxiào Ruìmíng Huángdì,
with the temple name Dézōng,
and converting his former residence into Xīngshèng Gōng.
In Dàdìng 2nd year,
the temple name was removed,
and the posthumous name was changed to Míngsù Huángdì.
After Hǎilíng was deposed as a commoner,
in the 22nd year,
Crown Prince Yǔnkōng submitted a memorial,
which read in brief:
"Recalling Xīzōng's legitimate imperial lineage,
Hǎilíng, being without moral principles,
murdered the emperor and enthroned himself.
To uphold the proper order of generations,
his title of Yángwáng was abolished,
and he was relegated to the rank of commoner.
Buried in an open, desolate place,
without a tomb mound or tree,
this has already established great righteousness and demonstrated utmost impartiality.
Hǎilíng posthumously honored his parents,
inappropriately enshrining them in the imperial temple.
Now that Hǎilíng has been deposed as a commoner,
Míngsù still presumptuously holds the title of emperor,
and is counted among the ancestral tablets in the imperial temple.
Hǎilíng's great treachery,
which has been rectified in name and punished in crime,
should also implicate Míngsù.
At that time, Míngsù had already passed away
and was not involved in the rebellion.
Your subject believes that Míngsù's imperial title should be abolished,
and he should revert to his former noble rank.
Or, following the precedent of Tàizǔ's meritorious princes,
he should be granted an official title and enfeoffment,
and a clear edict should be issued throughout the realm
to make the great principle known."
When the memorial was submitted,
Shìzōng greatly approved and accepted it,
and sent it down to the Shàngshū Shěng for deliberation.
Thereupon, the imperial title of Míngsù was posthumously abolished,
and he was enfeoffed as Huángbó, Tàishī, Prince of Liáo,
with the posthumous name Zhōngliè.
His wife, children, and grandchildren all suffered demotion.
In Míngchāng 4th year,
he was accorded joint sacrifice at Tàizǔ's ancestral temple.
His sons were Chōng, Liàng, Yǎn, Xiāng, and Gǔn.
Liàng
was the commoner Hǎilíng.
Chōng's original name was Shéntǔmǎn.
His mother was Lady Lǐ,
but the Túdān氏 adopted him as her son.
In the early Xiīzōng period,
he was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū.
During the Tiānjuàn reign,
he served as the Liúshǒu of Biànjīng.
During the Huángtǒng reign,
he was enfeoffed as the Zīguó Gōng,
served as Lìbù Shàngshū,
was further enfeoffed as the Dài Wáng,
and then transferred to be Tóngpàn Dàzōngzhèng Shì.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
he passed away.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Zhèng Wáng.
In the twenty-second year of Dàdìng,
he was posthumously demoted to Yítóng Sānsī and Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
His sons were Tánnú, Yuánnú, Yēbǔ'ér, and Ālǐbái.
Tánnú
served as the Guīdéjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Ālǐbái was
a Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn, and Hélǔhūtǔ Méng'ān Hūlín Hé Mòkè.
Hǎilíng assassinated the Túdān氏.
Because Chōng had once been adopted by the Túdān氏,
Hǎilíng consequently also killed Tánnú and Ālǐbái.
Yuánnú and Yēbǔ'ér fled to Shìzōng.
Tánnú was posthumously granted Rónglù Dàfū,
and Ālǐbái Fǔguó Shàngjiāngjūn.
An imperial edict ordered the relevant officials to rebury them.
During the Shìzōng period,
Yuánnú served as Zōngzhèng Chéng;
Yēbǔ'ér served as Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn,
and later as Tóngzhī Jìnán Yǐn Shì.
Yǒngyuán, courtesy name Dūnli,
was originally named Yuánnú.
He was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
reciting a thousand characters daily.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
he took an examination for imperial kinsmen to compose poetry,
and Yǒngyuán passed.
He was skilled in the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū,
understanding its profound meaning.
In the early Tiāndé period,
he was appointed Báinǚshān hereditary Mòkè.
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
and had already crossed the Huái River,
many soldiers deserted and returned home, and the Qìdān rebelled.
Because of this, his suspicion towards the imperial clan grew even stronger.
He had already killed Yǒngyuán's brothers Tánnú and Ālǐbái,
When Shìzōng ascended the throne in Liáoyáng,
he and Yēbǔ'ér both came to submit,
and the emperor comforted and treated them very kindly.
He was appointed Zōngzhèng Chéng,
then changed to Fúbǎoláng,
and served as the Cìshǐ of Luánzhōu.
He was granted hereditary Méng'ān,
and asked to give the Mòkè position to Yēbǔ'ér,
which was permitted by imperial edict.
He was transferred to Dìzhōu Fángyùshǐ and Tàiníngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Zhāng Hóngxìn, while conducting a general inspection of Shāndōng,
solely valued the amount of private wealth he obtained as his achievement,
and his supervision was harsh and urgent.
Yǒngyuán directly admonished Hóngxìn, saying:
"The court established the general inspection law
because the levying of taxes and labor was uneven.
Now, wherever the envoy goes,
he cruelly and arbitrarily seizes the fields and properties of farmers,
whipping common people, some even to death.
Merchants in markets have profits and losses in their trade,
and the income from fields and houses varies;
the descendants of former officials shut themselves in their homes,
yet are forced to endure the same labor as merchants.
Is this the original intention of the law?"
Hóngxìn had no reply.
Consequently, Dìzhōu's taxes were allowed to be self-declared based on actual circumstances.
He was transferred to Zhènwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the sixth year of Dàdìng,
he observed mourning for his mother,
then was recalled to office as Chóngyìjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and later moved to Shùnyìjūn.
The western border of Shuòzhōu was rife with bandits,
and corrupt officials and powerful families plagued lawsuits,
Yǒngyuán rooted out these old villains,
and the common people felt secure.
He was dismissed from office for selling horses to couriers for profit,
and Juànzhōu Fángyùshǐ Wòlùn was dismissed for allowing livestock to trample people's fields.
Both were relieved of their duties.
Soon after,
Yǒngyuán was reinstated as Bǎodàjūn Jiédùshǐ,
successively holding positions in Zhāoyì, Jiàngyáng, and Zhènwǔjūn,
then transferred to Jìnán Yǐn and Běijīng Fùliúshǒu.
Níngguó's maid Chǒudǐ had an affair with Huàhú from Xiánpíng.
Chǒudǐ deceitfully obtained a blank paper with a seal impression from where her mistress kept the seals and gave it to Huàhú,
who then wrote down Yǒngyuán's and Níngguó's birth dates and times,
falsely accusing Yǒngyuán and Níngguó of conspiracy to rebel.
An imperial edict ordered the relevant officials to investigate.
It was found that Chǒudǐ desired to become a free person,
and had Huàhú do this.
The emperor said:
"Huàhú and Chǒudǐ had an affair,
fabricated malicious words,
and falsely accused a member of the imperial clan.
Huàhú shall be executed by beheading,
and Chǒudǐ put to death."
He was then appointed Xìngzhōng Yǐn,
and served as Zhāngdéjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He died in office
at the age of fifty-one.
When his coffin passed through Zhōngdū,
an envoy was dispatched to offer sacrifices,
and he was granted three hundred taels of silver, ten bolts of colorful silk, and one hundred rolls of plain silk.
Yǒngyuán successively governed major prefectures,
and had a deep understanding of the people's welfare.
Wherever he served, he was praised for his governance;
his administrative achievements in Xiāng, Dì, and Shùnyì were particularly notable,
and the people there all erected shrines for him.
Yǎn's original name was Wútóng.
In the seventh year of Huángtǒng,
he was Zuǒfù Diǎnjiǎn,
then transferred to Dūdiǎnjiǎn.
In the ninth year,
he served as Huìníng Mù,
then changed to Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ.
When Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
Yǎn returned from his mission to Sòng,
and was appointed Sītú concurrently Dūyuánshuài,
overseeing the affairs of the Three Departments,
and further promoted to Tàiwèi.
After Empress Xiāo, Tàizǔ's consort, was killed,
all her property was given to Yǎn.
The Dūyuánshuàifǔ was abolished,
and the Shūmìyuàn was established;
Yǎn became Shūmìshǐ,
with Tàiwèi and overseeing the Three Departments as before.
On the last day of the twelfth month of the fourth year of Tiāndé,
he passed away.
The next day,
the New Year's Day of the first year of Zhēnyuán,
Hǎilíng suspended court for Yǎn,
and did not receive felicitations.
Envoys from Sòng, Xià, Gāolí, and Huíhú who came to congratulate on New Year's Day,
were ordered by the relevant officials to receive their tributes.
He was posthumously advanced to the peerage of Yǎn Wáng.
In the twenty-second year of Dàdìng,
he was posthumously demoted to Tèjìn.
Yǎn's wife, Lady Wūyán,
was killed by Hǎilíng in the sixth year of Zhènglóng
for having an affair with a slave.
Her younger brother, Xíníliè, the Nánjīng Bīngmǎ Fùdū Zhīhuīshǐ, had a private affair with the wife of his clan cousin Wūmóulǔ.
Wūmóulǔ's slave plotted to seize Xíníliè,
whereupon Xíníliè killed the slave.
When Hǎilíng heard of this,
he then killed Xíníliè.
Yǎn's son, Āhé,
served as Fúbǎo Zhīhòu during the Dàdìng period,
and soon after was transferred to Tóngzhī Dìngwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
The emperor said:
"Your annual service is not yet complete,
but I grant you this promotion out of consideration for your grandfather and father.
Do not be wicked,
and you should learn with all your heart."
Xiāng's original name was Yǒngqìng,
and he was Hǎilíng's younger brother by the same mother.
He served as Fǔguó Shàngjiāngjūn.
He died,
and in the second year of Tiāndé,
was posthumously enfeoffed as Wèi Wáng,
and again granted Sītú.
In the twenty-second year of Dàdìng,
he was posthumously demoted to Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
His son Heshàng was enfeoffed as Yìngguó Gōng,
and given the name Lèshàn.
Xǔ Lín, the Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ's son Zhīzhāng, quarreled with Heshàng.
Heshàng's mother, the imperial consort, ordered her household slaves to seize and humiliate Zhīzhāng,
and sent someone to drag Lín to her residence to beat and curse him.
The next day,
Lín complained to the court.
An imperial edict ordered Xiāo Yù, the Dàxīng Yǐn; Liáng Bì, the Zuǒ Chéng; Zhāng Zhōngfǔ, the acting Yùshǐ Dàfū; and Wáng Quán, the Zuǒsī Yuánwàiláng, to conduct a joint investigation.
The consort was given one hundred strokes with a staff,
the ringleader among her household slaves was executed,
and the others received varying numbers of staff strokes.
Lín had once knelt before the consort,
which was a loss of the dignity of a high official,
and some of his complaints were exaggerated,
so he received twenty strokes with a bamboo stick.
During the Dàdìng reign,
the household slave Xiǎosēng said wildly one month that there were strange omens when Heshàng was deeply asleep.
Xiāngfēi and Sēngkù truly believed it.
They summoned the diviner Lǐ Duān to consult him.
Duān said he would become an emperor.
Zhāng Yǒuzhí of the Bureau of Astronomy also said he would achieve great nobility.
The household slave Lǐ Tiānshòu reported the matter.
Sēngkù and Heshàng were interrogated by officials, and their confessions were obtained.
They were all executed.
The emperor said:
"I have often grieved that Hǎilíng extinguished the imperial clan.
Now, what Heshàng has done is like this.
If I were to pardon his crime,
then those who engage in monstrous delusions and mislead the ignorant populace
would take it as real,
and it cannot but be eradicated.
As for this person,
I have no choice but to act thus."
He grieved for a long time.
Gǔn's original name was Pújiǎ,
also written Pújiā.
He was unruly and fierce.
Hǎilíng disliked his character.
Initially, he was Fǔguó Shàngjiāngjūn.
At the beginning of the Tiāndé reign,
he was given the special appointment of Tèjìn,
enfeoffed as a king,
and served as Lìbù Shàngshū,
concurrently managing the affairs of the Dàzōngzhèng.
He was impeached for discussing the records of the daily life in the Forbidden City.
Bīngbù Shìláng Xiāo Gōng first questioned him,
and the guard Zhāng Jiǔ spoke of it in full detail.
Hǎilíng personally interrogated him.
Gōng was stripped of his official position and dismissed.
Zhāng Jiǔ did not answer truthfully,
and was especially put to death.
Gǔn, along with Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ Zōng Xiù, the guard Má Jí, and the attendant Wáng Zhīzhāng, all received varying degrees of flogging.
From then on, Hǎilíng became even more wary of him.
Not long after,
he was appointed Méng'ān.
When they moved to Zhōngdū,
Pújiā was made Xījīng Liúshǒu along the way.
Wányán Mólúwǎ, commander of the Xījīng troops, had an old acquaintance with Pújiā.
They were both in Xījīng,
so they began to interact.
Pújiā once gave him a jade belt as a gift.
Pújiā praised Mólúwǎ's bravery, saying he was no less than Yùchí Jìngdé.
Yuánfú Nǔ, a Compiler, had a wife who was related to Pújiā.
Yuánfú Nǔ once cautioned Pújiā, saying:
"Your Royal Highness's fame is too prominent;
you should be a little more modest and reserved."
Pújiā knew in his heart that Hǎilíng was wary of him,
and he once summoned a diviner to inquire about fortunes.
The household slave Hēlǐ knew Hǎilíng suspected Pújiā,
so he reported him,
saying that he was plotting rebellion with Mólúwǎ and others,
and had often summoned a diviner to inquire about the Mandate of Heaven.
Yùshǐ Dàfū Gāo Zhēn and Xíngbù Shìláng Yēlǜ Shèn Xūlǚ went to Xījīng to investigate him,
but found no evidence.
Hǎilíng was enraged and
sent envoys to arrest Pújiā and others and bring them to Zhōngdū.
He did not interrogate them further,
and executed them in the marketplace.
Mólúwǎ, Yuánfú Nǔ, and the diviner were all executed by slow slicing.
A eulogy says: The Jīn dynasty deliberated on rites and institutions,
graded official ranks and stipends,
rectified criminal laws,
managed the calendar and clarified seasons,
performed the duties of the Son of Heaven,
and established the codes of an era.
Gǎo and Zōnggàn contributed greatly to these initial efforts.
Gǎo's son, Zōngyì, was killed by Hǎilíng.
After Zōnggàn, unfortunately, there was Hǎilíng,
thus their descendants' prosperity was scarce,
and they could not escape disgrace and humiliation.
From Qín and Hàn onwards,
how few indeed were the venerable ministers and aristocratic families who shared the nation's glory!
How few indeed were such!
A gentleman, contemplating this,
can observe the changes of the world.
Collation Notes
Biography 15: Zōngbì (original name Wùzhú) Hēng (original name Bódiē) Zhāng Bāngchāng Liú Yù Tàlǎn
Zōngbì's
original name was Wòchuò,
also written Wùzhú,
also written Wòchū,
or Huàng Wòchū.
He was Tàizǔ's fourth son.
Xīyǐn captured Xí Níliè, a Liao guard,
and learned that the Liao emperor was hunting at Yuānyāng Luò.
Dūtǒng Gǎo exited Qīnglǐng.
Zōngwàng and Zōngbì led a hundred cavalry with Mǎ Heshàng to pursue Yuèlú, Bógǔ, Yělǐsī, and others,
and charged and defeated them.
Zōngbì ran out of arrows,
so he seized a spear from a Liao soldier
and single-handedly killed eight people,
and captured five alive.
He then ascertained that the Liao emperor was indeed hunting at Yuānyāng Luò
and had not yet left,
so he could be ambushed and captured.
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
Zōngbì joined the army,
captured Tāngyīn County,
and accepted the surrender of three thousand of its soldiers.
Upon reaching the Yùhé River,
the Sòng people had already burned the bridge,
making it impossible to cross.
Hélǔsuǒ crossed with seventy cavalry,
killing five hundred Sòng soldiers who had burned the bridge.
Zōngwàng sent Wú Xiàomín to enter Biàn first to persuade the Sòng people.
Zōngbì advanced with three thousand cavalry towards Biànchéng.
The Sòng former emperor fled,
and a hundred cavalry were selected to pursue him,
but they did not catch him.
They captured three thousand horses and returned.
After Zōngwàng died,
Zōngfǔ became Yòufù Yuánshuài,
and took control of Zī and Qīng regions.
Zōngbì defeated Sòng's Zhèng Zōngmèng's tens of thousands of troops,
and then captured Qīngzhōu.
He again defeated the rebel general Zhào Chéng at Línqú,
and heavily defeated Huáng Qióng's army,
and then captured Línqú.
When Zōngfǔ's army returned,
they encountered thirty thousand enemy troops on the river.
Zōngbì attacked and defeated them,
killing over ten thousand people.
An imperial edict ordered an attack on Sòng's Kāng Wáng.
Zōngfǔ set out from Héběi,
and Zōngbì attacked Kāidé Fǔ.
When supplies ran low,
he turned to attack Púzhōu.
His vanguard, Wūlíndá Tài, intended to defeat Wáng Shàn's two hundred thousand troops,
and then captured Púzhōu,
accepting the surrender of five nearby counties.
Attacking Kāidé Fǔ,
Zōngbì's army was the first to scale the walls,
and fought fiercely to break it.
Attacking Dàmíng Fǔ,
Zōngbì's army again was the first to scale the walls,
and broke its city.
Héběi was pacified.
The Sòng ruler fled from Yángzhōu to Jiāngnán.
Zōngbì and others divided their forces to attack him.
Advancing troops to Guīdé,
those within the city who emerged from the west and north gates
were again defeated by Dānghǎi.
Then, the moat was filled and a road was built,
cannons were arrayed on the moat,
and they prepared to attack.
The people in the city were afraid
and then surrendered.
First, Ālǐ and Púlúhún were sent to Shòuchūn,
and Zōngbì's army followed.
Sòng's Ānfǔshǐ Mǎ Shìyuán led his officials and subordinates out to surrender.
They advanced and captured Lúzhōu,
and then again captured Wáng Shàn's army in Cháoxiàn.
Dānghǎi and others defeated Lí Qióng's more than ten thousand troops at Hézhōu,
and then crossed the Yangtze River from Hézhōu.
When they were about twenty lí west of Jiāngníng,
Sòng's Dù Chōng led sixty thousand infantry and cavalry to resist and fight.
Húlúbǔ, Dānghǎi, Díhǔ, and Dàgē jointly attacked and defeated them.
Sòng's Chén Bāngguāng surrendered Jiāngníng Fǔ.
Cháng'ān Nú and Wòlǐyě were left to guard Jiāngníng.
Ālúbǔ and Wòlǐyě were dispatched to lead separate forces to conquer territory,
capturing Tàipíng Zhōu, Háozhōu, and counties like Jùróng and Lìyáng.
They ascended the river westward,
repeatedly defeating Zhāng Yǒng's and other forces,
and Dù Chōng then surrendered.
Zōngbì (宗弼) himself, starting from Jiāngníng (江寧), took the Guǎngdé (廣德) military route,
pursuing and attacking the Sòng (宋) ruler in Yuèzhōu (越州).
Arriving at Húzhōu (湖州),
he took it.
He first sent Ālǐ (阿里) and Púlúhún (蒲盧渾) to Hángzhōu (杭州),
where they prepared boats on the Qiántáng (錢塘) River.
When Zōngbì (宗弼) arrived at Hángzhōu (杭州),
the officials, guards, and prominent families had all fled,
so he attacked Hángzhōu (杭州)
and took it.
The Sòng (宋) ruler, hearing that Hángzhōu (杭州) could not be held,
fled from Yuè (越) to Míngzhōu (明州).
Zōngbì (宗弼) remained in Hángzhōu (杭州),
sending Ālǐ (阿里) and Púlúhún (蒲盧渾) with four thousand elite troops to attack it.
Élǔbǔ (訛魯補) and Zhúlièsù (朮列速) surrendered Yuèzhōu (越州).
Dà (大) ● (the character is missing) greatly defeated the Sòng (宋) army of Zhōu Wāng (周汪).
Ālǐ (阿里) and Púlúhún (蒲魯渾) defeated three thousand Sòng (宋) soldiers,
then crossed the Cáozé (曹澤) River.
Twenty-five *lǐ* (里) from Míngzhōu (明州),
they severely defeated the Sòng (宋) army,
pursuing them to the base of their city wall.
Troops emerged from the city,
and the battle went unfavorably,
so the Sòng (宋) ruler fled into the sea.
Zōngbì (宗弼) divided his troops,
and they jointly attacked Míngzhōu (明州),
capturing it.
Ālǐ (阿里) and Púlúhún (蒲盧渾) sailed across the sea to Chāngguó (昌國) County,
capturing Zhào Bó'è (趙伯諤), the Sòng (宋) prefect of Míngzhōu (明州).
Bó'è (伯諤) said,
"The Sòng (宋) ruler has fled to Wēnzhōu (溫州),
and will proceed from Wēnzhōu (溫州) to Fúzhōu (福州)."
They then sailed in pursuit for over three hundred *lǐ* (里),
but did not catch up.
Ālǐ (阿里) and Púlúhún (蒲盧渾) then returned.
Zōngbì (宗弼) returned from Hángzhōu (杭州)
and then took Xiùzhōu (秀州).
Chìzhǎn Huī (赤盞暉) defeated the Sòng (宋) army at Píngjiāng (平江)
and then took Píngjiāng (平江).
Ālǐ (阿里) led his troops to Zhenjiāng (鎮江) first.
The Sòng (宋) general Hán Shìzhōng (韓世忠) blocked the river mouth with his fleet.
Zōngbì's (宗弼) boats were small,
and over two hundred Qìdān (契丹) and Hàn (漢) soldiers drowned,
so he sailed upstream westward from Zhènjiāng (鎮江).
Shìzhōng (世忠) attacked him,
and Zōngbì (宗弼) seized ten of Shìzhōng's (世忠) large boats.
Thereupon, Zōngbì (宗弼) followed the south bank,
and Shìzhōng (世忠) followed the north bank,
fighting and advancing.
Shìzhōng's (世忠) *méngchóng* (艨艟) and large ships outnumbered Zōngbì's (宗弼) army several times over,
extending several *lǐ* (里) ahead of and behind Zōngbì's (宗弼) army.
The sound of his watchman's clappers
lasted from night until dawn.
Shìzhōng (世忠) came to challenge them with light boats,
engaging several times a day.
When they were about to reach Huángtiāndàng (黃天蕩),
Zōngbì (宗弼) then utilized the old course of the Lǎoguànhé (老鸛河) to open a thirty-*lǐ* (里) channel to the Qínhuái (秦淮) River.
This was completed in one day and one night,
allowing Zōngbì (宗弼) to reach Jiāngníng (江寧).
Tàlǎn (撻懶) sent Yílàgǔ (移剌古) from Tiāncháng (天長) to Jiāngníng (江寧) to reinforce Zōngbì (宗弼).
Wūlíndá Tàiyù (烏林荅泰欲) also came with troops to join them,
repeatedly defeating the Sòng (宋) army.
Zōngbì (宗弼) departed from Jiāngníng (江寧),
intending to cross the river northward.
Zōngbì's (宗弼) army crossed from the east,
Yílàgǔ (移剌古) crossed from the west,
and they fought Shìzhōng (世忠) at the river crossing.
Shìzhōng (世忠) divided his fleet to cut off the river flow both upstream and downstream,
intending to encircle and attack them from both sides.
All of Shìzhōng's (世忠) boats had five *lián* (緉) (layers of sail) hoisted.
Zōngbì (宗弼) selected skilled archers,
who, in light boats,
shot rockets at the five *lián* (緉) on Shìzhōng's (世忠) boats.
The *lián* (緉), catching fire from the rockets,
all burned by themselves.
Smoke and flames filled the river,
and Shìzhōng (世忠) was unable to command his forces.
They pursued him seventy *lǐ* (里) north,
annihilating his naval forces.
Shìzhōng (世忠) barely managed to escape.
Zōngbì (宗弼) crossed the river and returned north,
then followed Zōngfǔ (宗輔) to pacify Shǎnxī (陝西).
They fought Zhāng Jùn (張浚) at Fùpíng (富平).
Zōngbì (宗弼) was trapped in a heavy encirclement.
Hán Cháng (韓常) was struck in the eye by a stray arrow.
Angrily, he pulled out the arrow.
Blood dripped profusely.
He stopped the wound with earth,
leaped onto his horse, shouted fiercely, and fought,
thus breaking the encirclement
and emerging with Zōngbì (宗弼).
After defeating Zhāng Jùn's (張浚) army at Fùpíng (富平),
he then joined Ālúbǔ (阿盧補) to induce the surrender of the Xīhé (熙河) and Jīngyuán (涇原) two circuits.
When attacking Wú Jiè (吳玠) at Héshàngyuán (和尚原),
they encountered perilous terrain and could not advance,
so they withdrew their troops.
The ambushed troops rose up,
fighting and retreating.
After traveling thirty *lǐ* (里),
they were about to reach flat ground,
but the Sòng (宋) army had arrayed themselves at the exit.
Zōngbì (宗弼) suffered a major defeat,
and many of his officers and soldiers were killed in battle.
The following year,
they again attacked Héshàngyuán (和尚原)
and captured it.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì (天會) (1137),
he was made Right Vice Grand Marshal
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Shěn (瀋).
In the first year of Tiānjuàn (天眷) (1138),
Tàlǎn (撻懶) and Zōngpán (宗磐) proposed ceding the territory of Hénán (河南) to Sòng (宋).
An imperial edict was issued, sending Zhāng Tōnggǔ (張通古) and others as envoys to Jiāngnán (江南).
The following year (1139),
the Sòng (宋) ruler sent Hàn Xiàozhòu (韓肖冑), a scholar of the Duānmíng (端明) Hall, with a memorial of thanks.
He also sent Wáng Lún (王倫) and others to request the return of his father's remains and his mother, Wéi (韋) née, and brothers.
Zōngbì (宗弼) entered the court from the military camp
and was promoted to Grand Marshal.
Zōngbì (宗弼) perceived that Tàlǎn (撻懶) was colluding with and bribing the Sòng (宋) people.
Thus, regarding Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西) with Sòng (宋),
he memorialized to request the execution of Tàlǎn (撻懶)
and the restoration of the former territories.
At this time,
Zōngpán (宗磐) had already been executed.
Tàlǎn (撻懶) was at the traveling court,
and was again plotting rebellion with Gǔlǎn (鶻懶).
Coincidentally, a traveling court was established in Yānjīng (燕京).
An edict appointed Zōngbì (宗弼) as Grand Tutor,
concurrently leading the Traveling Department of State Affairs,
and retaining his position as Grand Marshal.
He was to proceed to Yānjīng (燕京) to execute Tàlǎn (撻懶).
Tàlǎn (撻懶) fled south from Yānjīng (燕京),
intending to defect to Sòng (宋).
He was pursued to Qízhōu (祁州)
and killed.
An edict stated,
"Matters of military affairs in all prefectures and commanderies
shall be decided by the Grand Marshal's Residence.
Civil lawsuits and financial matters
shall be handled by the Traveling Department of State Affairs."
Zōngbì (宗弼) concurrently managed all these affairs
and then deliberated on a southern expedition.
Grand Preceptor Zōnggàn (宗幹) and others all said:
"Gòu (構) received the grace of being rebuilt,
yet he does not think of repaying this kindness.
Instead, he presumptuously becomes arrogant,
and his demands are insatiable.
If we do not take it now,
we fear it will be difficult to achieve later."
The emperor said:
"They will think that I cannot completely possess the land of Hénán (河南).
Moreover, the Grand Marshal has long been in charge of the frontier,
thoroughly understanding the advantages and disadvantages.
It is appropriate to immediately raise an army to attack them."
Thereupon, the Marshal's Residence was ordered to recover the territory of Hénán (河南),
and an edict was issued throughout the realm.
Zōngbì (宗弼) advanced from Líyáng (黎陽) to Biàn (汴).
Right Supervising General Sālìhē (撒离喝) departed from Hézhōng (河中) towards Shǎnxī (陝西).
The Sòng (宋) generals Yuè Fēi (岳飛) and Hán Shìzhōng (韓世忠) separately occupied important prefectures and commanderies in Hénán (河南),
and further sent troops across the Yellow River eastward,
stationed in the borders of Lán (嵐), Shí (石), and Bǎodé (保德),
to mutually constrain (the Jīn).
Zōngbì (宗弼) sent Kǒng Yànzhōu (孔彥舟) to take Biàn (汴) and Zhèng (鄭) prefectures.
Wáng Bólóng (王伯龍) took Chénzhōu (陳州).
Lǐ Chéng (李成) took Luòyáng (洛陽).
He personally led his forces to take Bózhōu (亳州) and Shùnchāng (順昌) Prefecture.
Sōng (嵩), Rǔ (汝), and other prefectures subsequently all fell.
As it was summer,
Zōngbì (宗弼) returned his army to Biàn (汴).
Yuè Fēi (岳飛) and other armies all retreated.
Hénán (河南) was pacified.
This was the third year of Tiānjuàn (天眷) (1140).
The emperor sent an envoy to comfort Zōngbì (宗弼) and his generals and soldiers below him.
All three thousand meritorious soldiers
were promoted to Loyal and Brave Colonel.
Lán (嵐), Shí (石), and Bǎodé (保德) were all attacked and captured.
Zōngbì (宗弼) entered the court.
At this time,
the emperor was touring Yānjīng (燕京),
and Zōngbì (宗弼) met him at the imperial traveling residence.
After staying for twenty days,
Zōngbì (宗弼) returned to his army.
The emperor rose, poured wine, and gave it to him to drink,
bestowing upon him armor, helmets, bows, arrows, and two horses.
Zōngbì (宗弼) had already departed for four days
when he was recalled.
On the day he arrived,
Xī Yǐn (希尹) was executed.
Five days later,
Zōngbì (宗弼) returned to his army
and advanced to attack Huáinán (淮南),
capturing Lúzhōu (廬州).
The emperor traveled to Yānjīng.
Wán​yán Zōngbì held court in Yānjīng
and requested to take Jiāngnán.
The emperor acceded to this.
An imperial edict commanded Grand Marshal Wán​yán Zōngbì to return with his army and enter the court with the prime ministers to report on affairs.
Soon after, he was made Left Chancellor of the Department of State Affairs and concurrently Attendant Counselor,
while his titles of Grand Tutor, Grand Marshal, and Head of the Branch Secretariat remained as before.
An imperial edict placed the Yānjīng Circuit under the Department of State Affairs,
and Xījīng and the various tribes north of the mountains under the Grand Marshal’s Office.
He then returned with his army
and subsequently attacked Jiāngnán.
After crossing the Huái River,
he sent a letter of reproach to the Sòng people.
The Sòng people replied with a letter begging for leniency.
Wán​yán Zōngbì ordered the Sòng ruler to send trusted envoys to convey their proposals.
The Sòng ruler requested,
"First withdraw the troops,
then permit our humble state to present a memorial at your palace gate."
Wán​yán Zōngbì, finding it expedient, agreed to use the Huái River as the border.
The emperor dispatched Guard General Sāgǎi to his army to comfort him.
In the second month of the second year of Huángtǒng,
Wán​yán Zōngbì held court in the capital
and concurrently supervised the compilation of the National History.
The Sòng ruler sent Grand Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, Hé Zhù, and others to present a sworn memorial.
The memorial stated:
"Your servant Gòu respectfully states,
now that the border is to be drawn,
it shall be along the middle of the Huái River.
To the west, Tángzhōu and Dèngzhōu shall be ceded to the superior state.
From Dèngzhōu, forty lí to the west and forty lí to the south shall form the boundary,
belonging to Dèngzhōu.
Beyond those forty lí to the west and southwest, all shall belong to Guānghuàjūn,
as the border prefectures and cities of our humble state.
Having received your benevolent grace,
we are permitted to serve as a tributary state,
and our descendants for generations
shall diligently observe the duties of a vassal.
Annually, on the emperor's birthday and New Year's Day,
envoys shall be sent to offer ceaseless congratulations.
A yearly tribute of 250,000 liǎng of silver and 250,000 bolts of silk
shall commence from the year Rénxū.
Each spring, agents shall be sent to transport and deliver them to Sìzhōu.
Should this alliance be violated,
the bright spirits shall strike down
our mandate and destroy our clan,
overturning our state.
Now that your servant has presented this sworn memorial,
we humbly hope that the superior state will soon issue a sworn edict,
so that our humble state may forever have a basis to rely upon."
Wán​yán Zōngbì was promoted to Grand Preceptor.
Thereupon, he dispatched Left Commissioner of Xuanhui, Liú Kuò, as an envoy to Sòng,
to invest Kāngwáng as the Sòng emperor with a ceremonial cap, robe, jade tablet, jade pendants, and jade document.
The text of the document read:
"The Emperor says: Oh! You, Kāngwáng Zhào Gòu of Sòng!
Unfortunate it was,
that Heaven brought calamity upon your state.
Repeatedly violating the solemn alliance,
you brought about your own downfall,
causing you to dwell beyond the Jiāngbiǎo region.
For this, our armies have toiled
for eighteen years now.
I am deeply grieved by this;
what sin have these people committed?
Now Heaven repents of its misfortune,
inspiring your heart.
Memorials have come frequently,
expressing a desire to be counted among the tributary states.
Now, I dispatch Grand Master of Guanglu, Left Commissioner of Xuanhui, Liú Kuò, and others, bearing the imperial credentials, to invest you as Emperor.
Your state shall be named Sòng,
and you shall serve as a vassal for generations,
forever a bulwark.
Alas, be reverent!
Humbly listen to my command."
An edict was also proclaimed throughout the realm.
Wán​yán Zōngbì was bestowed with a thousand people, a thousand cattle, a hundred camels, and ten thousand sheep,
and annually from the Sòng state's tribute, he was to receive two thousand liǎng of silver and two thousand bolts of silk.
Wán​yán Zōngbì submitted a memorial requesting to retire,
but it was not granted.
He was replied to with a gracious edict
and presented with a golden tablet.
In the seventh year of Huángtǒng,
he was made Grand Tutor,
presiding over the affairs of the Three Departments.
His titles of Grand Marshal and Head of the Branch Secretariat remained as before.
In the eighth year of Huángtǒng,
he passed away.
In the fifteenth year of Dàdìng,
he was given the posthumous title Zhōngliè.
In the eighteenth year,
he was honored with sacrificial rites in the temple court of Tàizōng.
His son was Bódié.
Hēng's original name was Bódié.
During Xīzōng's time,
he was enfeoffed as Ruìwáng,
made a Mèng'ān,
and awarded the title Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
In the early Tiāndé period,
he was promoted to Tèjìn.
Hǎilíng was wary of Tàizōng's sons.
When he was about to visit the Tàimiào,
he made Hēng a Right Guard General,
as recorded in the biography of Tàizōng's princes.
Hǎilíng bestowed a fine bow upon him.
Hēng was by nature forthright,
extraordinarily talented and brave,
and prone to pride.
He declined, saying:
"The bestowed bow
is weak and unusable."
Hǎilíng then became wary of him
and sent him out as the Administrator of Zhēndìng,
saying to Hēng:
"Tàizōng's sons are still powerful,
many of them residing in Héshuò and Shāndōng.
Zhēndìng occupies a crucial strategic position.
Should there be any unrest,
I would rely on you to hold the weight of responsibility."
In reality, he was wary of Hēng.
He successively served as Resident Administrator of Zhōngjīng and Dōngjīng.
His household servant, Liáng Zūn, accused Hēng of conspiring with the guard, Fú Gōngbì, to rebel.
An investigation found no evidence,
and Liáng Zūn was executed.
Hǎilíng grew even more suspicious of him.
He was reassigned as Administrator of Guǎngníng,
and Lǐ Lǎosēng was again sent to observe Hēng's activities
and instructed to fabricate charges against him.
When Hēng was first appointed to Guǎngníng,
various princesses and imperial kinswomen went to congratulate his mother, Túdān Shì.
The eldest daughter of Tàizǔ, Wùlǔ, said:
"Although Bódié has been slightly demoted,
do not take it amiss.
The state regards a capital prefecture as one (i.e., of equal importance).
Moreover, Bódié is still in his prime;
why worry about not attaining high honors?"
At this time,
Wùlǔ was married to Túdān Xiéyě.
Xiéyě's concubine, Hūtá, was favored by Empress Túdān.
Hūtá went to the empress
and reported
that "Wùlǔ's words hinted at resentment and discontent,
and she also made direct accusations,
and further said that Bódié would achieve great honor."
Hǎilíng ordered Xiāo Yù to interrogate her.
Those on the left and right dared not speak up during the verification.
Consequently, Wùlǔ was killed, and Xiéyě was flogged,
and his office was removed.
This was because Wùlǔ harbored resentment and discontent,
and Xiéyě had not reported it first.
Hūtá was then enfeoffed as Lady of Xīn Commandery.
In the ninth month of the *wùshēn* day of the eighth year of Tiānhuì,
a ceremony was prepared to install
Yù as Emperor of Dàqí,
with his capital at Dàmíng,
still designated as Běijīng.
Officials from the Chancellor downwards were appointed,
and an amnesty was declared throughout the territory.
He then returned from Dàmíng to reside in Dōngpíng,
designating Dōngpíng as Dōngjīng,
Biànzhōu as Biànjīng,
and degrading Sòng's Nánjīng to Guīdé Fǔ.
Huáiníng, Yǒngchāng, Shùnchāng, and Xīngrén Fǔ were all demoted to zhōu.
Zhāng Xiàochún and others were made chancellors.
His younger brother, Yì, was made Běijīng Liúshǒu.
His mother, Lady Zhái, was made Empress Dowager.
His concubine, Lady Qián, was made Empress.
Lady Qián
was a court lady from Xuānhé.
The *xīnhài* year was designated as Fùchāng Yuánnián.
His son, Lín, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéngxiàng and Grand Commander of all armies and horses.
The Sòng people feared him,
treating him with the courtesies due to a rival state,
and state documents referred to him as the Emperor of Dàqí.
The families of Yù's chancellors, Zhāng Xiàochún, Zhèng Yìnián, and Lǐ Yè, were all in Sòng territory,
and the Sòng people took special care to comfort them.
In Fùchāng Èrnián,
Yù moved his capital to Biàn.
When Ruìzōng pacified Shǎnxī,
Tàizōng bestowed that land upon Yù,
following the previous enfeoffment received by Zhāng Bāngchāng.
The Marshal's Office envoy Xiāo Qìng went to Biàn
to discuss the invasion of Sòng with Yù.
Yù replied:
"The Sòng ruler's military commander, Hán Shìzhōng, is stationed at Rùnzhōu,
and Liú Guāngshì is stationed at Jiāngníng.
If we now raise a large army
and intend to cross the Jiāng at Cǎishí,
Liú Guāngshì will resist at Jiāngníng.
If we march out from Sùzhōu to Yángzhōu,
then Shìzhōng will surely gather seagoing vessels to intercept us at Guāzhōu Dù.
If we send light troops directly to Cǎishí,
they will be unprepared,
and we will surely cross the Jiāng directly.
Guāngshì's seagoing vessels are also at Rùnzhōu,
and Hán Shìzhōng will certainly seize them first.
The two generals will inevitably fall out over this.
Using this to pressure the Sòng ruler
should be feasible."
Not long after,
Xú Wén, a宣贊舍人 of the Sòng ruler's Imperial Court, defected with sixty large and small boats and over seven hundred soldiers.
Upon reaching Mìzhōu territory,
he led his officers to Biàn.
Yù wrote to the Marshal's Office, saying:
"Xú Wén and his party
have been at sea for a long time
and know all the advantages and disadvantages of Jiāngnán.
Wén said: The Sòng ruler is in Hángzhōu,
and outside the Hòucháo Gate, within the Qiántáng Jiāng, there are two hundred boats.
When the Sòng ruler first fled to sea,
he boarded a boat there.
After crossing the Qiántáng Jiāng, there is another river that enters Yuèzhōu,
leading towards Míngzhōu's Dìnghǎi Kǒu, stretching forward to Chāngguó Xiàn.
That county is in the sea,
a place where the Sòng people gather boats and store provisions.
Now, our large army can first proceed to Chāngguó Xiàn
to attack and seize the boats and provisions,
then return to the foot of Míngzhōu city,
seize the Sòng ruler's imperial boats,
and head directly to the mouth of the Qiántáng Jiāng.
Now, if we embark from Mìzhōu,
and the wind is favorable,
we can reach Chāngguó Xiàn in five days and nights.
If the wind is a bit slow,
it may take ten days or half a month."
Originally,
Zōngbì returned north from Jiāngnán,
and Zōnghàn was about to go to court
to discuss the invasion of Sòng again.
Zōnghàn firmly insisted that it was feasible to invade.
Zōngbì said:
"Jiāngnán is low-lying and damp.
Our soldiers and horses are now exhausted,
and our provisions are not ample.
I fear we will not succeed."
Zōnghàn said:
"The supervising censor only seeks temporary ease."
When Yù sent his report,
Ruìzōng also refused to use Yù's plan,
and sent Tàlǎn to lead an army to Guāzhōu and then return.
In Tiānhuì Shísìnián,
an imperial edict stated,
"When Qíguó and our dynasty's military and civilians sue each other,
and it involves official documents,
the year should only use Tiānhuì."
In Tiānhuì Shíwǔnián,
an edict abolished Qíguó
and demoted Yù to Prince of Shǔ.
Yù had claimed the grand title for eight years.
Thereupon,
the Xíngtái Shàngshūshěng was established in Biàn,
and Yù's harmful policies were abolished,
much to the delight of the people.
Zhāng Xiàochún, the former chancellor of Qí, was made acting Xíngtái Zuǒchéngxiàng,
and Yù's family was moved to Línhuáng Fǔ.
In Huángtǒng Yuánnián,
Yù was granted ten thousand strings of cash, fifty *qǐng* of land, and fifty cattle.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Prince of Cáo.
In the sixth year,
he died.
His son was Lín.
Lín, courtesy name Yuánruì,
was Yù's son.
During Sòng's Xuānhé period,
he was appointed Jiāngshìláng due to his father's influence,
and successively promoted to Chéngwùláng.
In Tiānhuì Qīnián,
Yù surrendered Jǐnán,
and Lín consequently joined the army,
campaigning against the water bandit Wáng Jiāng,
whom he defeated and forced to surrender.
Yù was in charge of Dōngpíng,
and appointed Lín as Prefect of Jǐnán Fǔ.
When Qíguó was established,
Jǐnán was made Xīngpíng Jūn,
and Lín was appointed Jiédùshǐ, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Duke of Liáng,
concurrently Grand Commander of all armies and horses,
and Prefect of Jǐnán Fǔ.
The following year,
he became Qí's Shàngshū Zuǒchéngxiàng.
