The year after that,
he moved to Biàn with Yù,
ceased to be Prefect of Jǐnán,
retained his former Kāifǔ title,
and was allowed to appoint advisors.
Yù requested that Lín be established as Crown Prince,
but the court refused,
saying:
"If he renders meritorious service in our campaign against Sòng, then he shall be established."
Thereupon,
Lín led armies in southern campaigns for several consecutive years,
but all returned without success.
When the court discussed abolishing Qí,
they reported the date of the southern campaign,
ordering Yù to first dispatch troops to station along the Huái River.
Tàlǎn abolished Yù's army,
stopping at Diāomǎ Hé.
Lín, with several hundred cavalry, went out to meet him.
Tàlǎn instructed Lín's retinue
to stop on the south bank,
and summoned Lín alone to cross the river,
whereupon he seized Lín.
After Yù was deposed,
Lín was moved to Línhuáng.
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed Běijīng Lù Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and successively served as Zhōngjīng, Yānjīng Lù Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ, Cānzhī Zhèngshì, and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
then again as Xīngpíng Jūn Jiédùshǐ, Shàngjīng Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Hánguó.
He died
at the age of sixty-four.
During the Zhènglóng period,
officials above the second rank were demoted from their enfeoffments,
and he was posthumously granted Tèjìn, Duke of Xīguó.
Chāng's original name was Tàlǎn,
son of Mùzōng.
Zōnghàn attacked the Liáo ruler at Yuānyāng Luò.
Liáo Dūtǒng Mǎgē fled to Tǎodǐ,
and Tàlǎn collected his herds.
Zōnghàn ordered Tàlǎn to pursue and attack him,
but he failed to catch him,
instead capturing Liáo Shūmìshǐ Délǐdǐ and his sons Mógē and Nàyě and returning.
Tàizǔ personally led an attack on the Liáo ruler at Dàyú Luò,
leaving his baggage train at Cǎo Luò,
and ordered Tàlǎn and Yámǎo to guard it.
Xī Lù Bīngguān Húnchù was unable to pacify his troops,
so Tàlǎn was appointed Xī Liù Lù Jūnshuài to garrison them.
Xígǔnǎi and Pólúhuǒ escorted the Chángshèng Jūn and prominent families and artisans from Yānjīng through Sōngtíng Guān into the interior.
The Emperor warned them, saying:
"If you encounter dangerous obstacles,
then divide your troops to proceed."
Xígǔnǎi and Pólúhuǒ then joined Tàlǎn.
After a long time,
he was ordered to attack and impeach the Xī people of the Shānsùgǔ (山速古) tribe.
The Xī people occupied strategic positions and fought,
killing almost all of them.
The thirteen caves of Sùgǔ (速古), Chuòlǐ (啜里), and Tiěnī (鐵尼) were all pacified.
An imperial edict stated:
"Considering the treacherous and difficult terrain of the Xī (奚) route,
and the difficulty of strategy,
I commanded you to undertake this task,
and you have indeed fulfilled the trust placed in you.
I am truly filled with admiration.
Now, the Huílíbǎo (回离保) tribe has come to submit,
and the remaining masses have scattered and fled,
unable to achieve anything.
I previously ordered Xígǔnǎi (習古廼) and Pólúhuǒ (婆盧火) to escort the surrendered people.
If they encounter dangerous obstacles,
they are to divide their forces to proceed,
and the remaining troops are all to join you.
I have issued twenty imperial edicts
to summon and persuade those who have not yet surrendered.
You should carefully consider the matter
and handle it appropriately."
Thereafter, he pacified the Xī (奚) tribes and demarcated the southern border,
and submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of officials to garrison them.
The Emperor said:
"Follow the precedent of Dōngjīng Bóhǎi (東京渤海) in establishing chiliarchies (qiānhù, 千戶) and company commanders (móukè, 謀克)."
The tribe of Yáolián Zhāogǔyá (遙輦昭古牙), a maternal relative of the Liáo (遼) imperial family, was in Jiànzhōu (建州).
Xiéyě (斜野) attacked and drove them away,
capturing their wives, children, and families of officials and prominent individuals.
Tàlǎn (撻懶) then attacked them again,
capturing their company commanders Hélǔzào (曷魯燥) and Báishāgē (白撒葛),
and killing them.
Over a thousand civilian households surrendered,
and then Jīnyuán (金源) county surrendered.
An imperial edict ordered an additional reward of ten silver plaques.
He also received the surrender of two other Yáolián (遙輦) tribes,
again defeated the Xīngzhōng (興中) forces,
received the surrender of Jiànzhōu (建州) officials and subordinates,
and acquired twenty mountain strongholds
and five hundred eighty villages and fortresses.
Āhū (阿忽) again defeated Zhāogǔyá (昭古牙),
receiving the surrender of even more of his officials and people.
Zhāogǔyá's (昭古牙) power was curtailed, and he also surrendered.
Xīngzhōng (興中) and Jiànzhōu (建州) were both pacified.
An imperial edict ranked the achievements and rewards of the generals and soldiers,
and pacified the new population.
Tàlǎn (撻懶) requested that the nine Yáolián (遙輦) encampments be made into nine *mèng'ān* (猛安).
The Emperor, considering Duólín (奪鄰) to have rendered meritorious service,
appointed him to command four *mèng'ān*,
while Zhāogǔyá (昭古牙) remained a *mèng'ān* directly under imperial control.
For the commander of the five *mèng'ān*,
Tàlǎn (撻懶) was ordered to select and appoint someone.
Tàlǎn (撻懶) and Liú Yànzōng (劉彥宗) recommended Xiāo Gōngyì (蕭公翊) as the Administrator (Yǐn, 尹) of Xīngzhōng (興中),
and that the various prefectures and commanderies be governed by Qìdān (契丹) and Hàn (漢) officials,
which the Emperor all approved.
When Zōnghàn (宗翰) and Zōngwàng (宗望) attacked Sòng (宋),
Tàlǎn (撻懶) served as the commander-in-chief of the six route armies.
After Zōngwàng (宗望) had accepted the Sòng (宋) alliance,
and his army returned,
Tàlǎn (撻懶) then returned to Zhōngjīng (中京).
In the eighth month of Tiānhuì (天會) four (1126),
he again attacked Sòng (宋).
In the intercalary month,
Zōnghàn's (宗翰) and Zōngwàng's (宗望) armies both arrived at Biànzhōu (汴州).
Tàlǎn (撻懶) and Ālǐguā (阿里刮) defeated twenty thousand Sòng (宋) troops at Shí (嵵),
overthrowing their three camps.

They captured Hú Zhírú (胡直孺), the Commander-in-Chief (dū zǒngguǎn, 都總管) of the Jīngdōng (京東) route, along with his two sons, and Suí Shīyuán (隋師元), the Commander (dūtǒngzhì, 都統制) of the Southern Route, along with his three generals.
[一０]They then captured Gǒngzhōu (拱州),
received the surrender of Nínglíng (寧陵),
defeated Suīyáng (睢陽),
and took Bózhōu (亳州).
When Sòng (宋) troops came to retake Suīyáng (睢陽),
they again attacked and repelled them,
capturing their general Shí Tián (石瑱).
After the two Sòng (宋) emperors had surrendered,
the grand army returned north.
Tàlǎn (撻懶) served as the Left Supervisor of the Army (zuǒ jiānjūn, 左監軍) for the Marshal,
campaigning through Shāndōng (山東) province
and taking Mìzhōu (密州).
Díhǔ (迪虎) took Shànzhōu (單州).
Tàlǎn (撻懶) took Jùlù (鉅鹿).
Ālǐguā (阿里刮) took Zōngchéng (宗城).
Dígǔbù (迪古不) took Qīngpíng (清平) and Línqīng (臨清).
Méngguā (蒙刮) took Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Ālǐguā (阿里刮) campaigned and took Jùn (濬), Huá (滑), Ēn (恩), and Gāotáng (高唐),
and dispatched various generals to seize Cí (磁) and Xìndé (信德),
all of which surrendered.
Liú Yù (劉豫) surrendered Jìnán (濟南) Prefecture.
An imperial edict appointed Yù (豫) as Pacification Commissioner (ānfǔshǐ, 安撫使),
governing Dōngpíng (東平).
Tàlǎn (撻懶), as Left Supervisor of the Army, pacified and administered it,
making major decisions independently.
Later, he became the Right Vice Marshal (yòu fù yuánshuài, 右副元帥).
In Tiānhuì (天會) fifteen (1137), he became Left Vice Marshal (zuǒ fù yuánshuài, 左副元帥)
and was enfeoffed as King of Lǔ (魯國王).
Initially,
after the Sòng (宋) people executed Zhāng Bāngchāng (張邦昌),
Emperor Tàizōng (太宗) ordered his generals to again seek someone like Bāngchāng (邦chāng) to establish.
Some recommended Zhé Kěqiú (折可求),
but Tàlǎn (撻懶) strongly recommended Liú Yù (劉豫).
Yù (豫) was enthroned as emperor,
adopting the reign title Dà Qí (大齊).
Yù (豫) was emperor for several years,
without gaining an inch of merit.
Consequently, Yù (豫) was deposed and made King of Shǔ (蜀王).
Tàlǎn (撻懶) and the Right Vice Marshal Zōngbì (宗弼) were both in Hénán (河南).
The Sòng (宋) envoy Wáng Lún (王倫) sought the lands of Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西) from Tàlǎn (撻懶).
The following year,
Tàlǎn (撻懶) paid court in the capital
and advocated the proposal to cede the former territory of Qí (齊) to Sòng (宋).
Emperor Xīzōng (熙宗) ordered his ministers to deliberate.
It happened that Zōngjùn (宗雋), the Grand Marshal (liúshǒu, 留守) of Dōngjīng (東京), came to court,
and he and Tàlǎn (撻懶) combined forces.
Zōnggàn (宗幹) and others argued against it but could not prevail.
Zōngjùn (宗雋) said:
"If we give this land to Sòng (宋),
Sòng (宋) will surely be grateful to us."
Zōngxiàn (宗憲) refuted him, saying:
"We have captured the fathers and elder brothers of Sòng (宋) people;
their resentment is not of one day.
If we further provide them with territory,
this is aiding an enemy.
What gratitude will there be?
It should not be given."
Tàlǎn's (撻懶) younger brother Xù (勗) also considered it impermissible.
After they retired,
Tàlǎn (撻懶) reproached Xù (勗), saying:
"Others still follow me,
yet you express a different opinion?"
Xù (勗) replied:
"If it benefits the state,
how can I harbor private thoughts?"
At this time,
Zōngpán (宗磐), the eldest son of Emperor Tàizōng (太宗), was Chancellor (zǎixiàng, 宰相),
his position superior to Zōnggàn (宗幹).
Tàlǎn (撻懶) and Zōngjùn (宗雋) allied with him,
and ultimately pushed through the proposal to cede Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西) to Sòng (宋).
Zhāng Tōnggǔ (張通古) was made envoy to convey the imperial edict to Jiāngnán (江南).
After a long time,
Zōngpán (宗磐) became increasingly overbearing,
and Zōngjùn (宗雋) also became Chancellor.
Tàlǎn (撻懶) held military power,
and there were signs of rebellion.
Zōngpán (宗磐) and Zōngjùn (宗雋) were both executed.
An imperial edict declared that Tàlǎn (撻懶) was of senior rank
and had rendered great service,
and therefore he was pardoned without prosecution,
and sent out as Left Grand Councilor (zuǒ chéngxiàng, 左丞相) of the Mobile Secretariat (xíngtái shàngshū, 行臺尚書),
with a personal imperial edict of consolation and dispatch.
When Tàlǎn (撻懶) arrived in Yānjīng (燕京),
he became even more arrogant, unbridled, and lawless.
He again plotted rebellion with Prince Yì (Yì Wáng, 翼王) Gǔlǎn (鶻懶).
Meanwhile, the court gradually became aware that he had initially colluded with Sòng (宋) and advocated the ceding of Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西) territories.
Zōngbì (宗弼) requested to retake Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西).
At that time, there was someone who reported Tàlǎn's (撻懶) treason.
Emperor Xīzōng (熙宗) then issued an edict to execute him.
Tàlǎn (撻懶) fled south from Yānjīng (燕京),
was pursued and killed in Qízhōu (祁州).
Prince Yì (Yì Wáng, 翼王) and the imperial clansmen Huólíhútǔ (活离胡土), and Tàlǎn's (撻懶) two sons Wòdài (斡帶) and Wūdábǔ (烏達補) were also killed,
but his partisans were pardoned.
Zōngbì (宗弼) became Grand Marshal (dū yuánshuài, 都元帥)
and again pacified Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西).
When he attacked Sòng (宋) and crossed the Huái (淮) River,
King Kāng (Kāng Wáng, 康王) of Sòng (宋) pleaded for peace.
Consequently, he declared himself a vassal,
and the Huái (淮) was demarcated as the border.
Then the troops were withdrawn.
A eulogy says: The positions of ruler and minister
are like the established division between cap and shoes,
not to be changed for a moment.
During the extreme chaos of the Five Dynasties,
the principles of morality were ruined.
Emperor Tàizōng (太宗) of Liáo (遼),
disrespecting the divine mandate,
inverted cap and shoes,
supported and established Shí Jìn (石晉),
exchanging a minister for a ruler.
This was a major upheaval since the beginning of the universe.
The Jīn (金) people imitated this,
and the affairs of Zhāng Bāngchāng (張邦chāng) and Liú Yù (劉豫) arose.
Although Bāngchāng's (邦chāng) actions were not from his true heart,
he resigned with his life.
Who would say this was impermissible?
Yù (豫) seized the opportunity to gain advantage.
The Jīn (金) people wanted to rely on him for achievements.
How could such a principle exist?
Tàlǎn (撻懶) initially recommended Liú Yù (劉豫),
and later returned Shǎnxī (陝西) and Hénán (河南) to Sòng (宋),
viewing them as merely incidental.
He initially had no firm resolve in handling this.
His accumulated frivolity and impulsiveness
ultimately led him into a rebellious plot.
When his plot failed and he fled south,
it merely served to confirm his collusion with Sòng (宋).
Alas!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 16: Liú Yànzōng (劉彥宗), Liú È (劉萼), Liú Kuò (劉筈), Liú Zhònghuì (劉仲誨), Liú Kuǐ (劉頍), Shí Lì'ài (時立愛), Hán Qǐxiān (韓企先) (son Duó (鐸)).
Six years later,
he was appointed Acting Grand Councilor of the Right,
concurrently managing the affairs of the Commissioner of the Left Bureau of Military Affairs,
and remained in the capital, Jīngshī.
Someone requested to rectify the excessive and mixed officials in Hénán,
and Kuò said:
“After the fall of Qí and campaigning south of the Yangtze River,
seeking immediate results,
the people employed were not necessarily all according to regulations.
Thus, there were those who became high officials without passing examinations,
and those who wielded military power without being tested in archery and horsemanship.
Now, the pacification is not long past;
it is better to win the hearts of the people for now.
How can we make such confusing changes?”
So, he maintained the old system.
In the seventh year,
the commander’s headquarters discussed building three forts in Guǎntáo,
thinking that in case of alarm, the Northern Army could enter and reside there.
Kuò said:
“Now the whole country is one family;
who are North and South?
Should there be any trouble,
could the soldiers entering the city
alone bring peace?
We should strengthen military preparedness to detect treachery,
and not show any distinction between ourselves.”
Afterward,
Kuò’s suggestion was followed.
Initially,
three prefectures beyond the Yellow River were granted to the Xià people.
Someone said that several thousand Qín people in Xià
all wished to return.
The generals requested to take them,
but Kuò said:
“Three small prefectures are not significant enough
to risk losing the great trust of the court.
Moreover, there are twice as many Qín people in Shǔ as there are here;
why abandon them and take only these?”
His suggestion was then followed.
The border commander of Shǎnxī requested to complete the defensive walls along the border to guard against Southern invaders,
but Kuò said:
“We benefit from cavalry, not from defending cities.
If we build walls now,
it will burden the people and create resentment.
Furthermore, the alliance is already settled;
how can we act rashly?”
So, it was dismissed.
In the eighth month of the ninth year,
he was appointed Minister of Works. In the ninth month,
he was appointed Administrator of Governmental Affairs,
enfeoffed as Duke of Wú,
and remained Acting Grand Councilor of the Right as before.
In the first year of Tiāndé,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Téng.
In the second year,
he was appointed Grand Councilor of the Right and Director of the Central Secretariat,
and further enfeoffed as Prince of Zhèng.
Not long after,
due to illness, he requested to be relieved of government duties.
He was appointed Defense Commissioner of Yānjīng,
and further enfeoffed as Prince of Cáo.
After a few months,
he requested to retire.
From the time Kuò served as Commissioner of Military Affairs,
by being able to please Empress Dào,
he attained the position of Chancellor.
When Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
he somewhat disdained Kuò.
When Kuò sought to retire,
the imperial edict generally stated:
“He was not obscure in handling affairs,
nor was he obsequious in serving his sovereign.
Permission to return home is not yet granted,
but for now, release from duty is allowed.”
Kuò thereupon died of shame and fear
at the age of fifty-eight.
His son was Zhònghuǐ.
Zhònghuǐ’s courtesy name was Zǐzhōng.
At the beginning of Huángtǒng,
as the son of a Chancellor, he was granted the position of Valiant and Loyal Colonel.
In the ninth year,
he was awarded the Jinshi degree,
and appointed Drafter of the Hanlin Academy.
Hǎilíng was severe and violent,
and his officials often responded improperly.
Hǎilíng once questioned court officials about current policies,
and Zhònghuǐ calmly presented his views,
without showing fear.
Hǎilíng praised him.
At the beginning of Zhēnyuán,
he observed mourning for his father,
then was reinstated as Compiler of the Hanlin Academy.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was promoted to Attendant Scholar,
and soon concurrently served as Diarist of the Emperor’s Activities and Left Remonstrance Official.
In the third year,
an imperial edict ordered Zhònghuǐ and Púchá Púsùyuè, Supernumerary Assistant Director of the Left Department, to investigate the prefectures and counties they passed through.
Upon their return, Zhònghuǐ and others submitted their report.
An imperial edict promoted Lǐ Fāng, Magistrate of Yùtián County, one rank;
Wáng Zōngyǒng, Judge of Shùn Prefecture and acting official of Mìyún County, was promoted to County Lieutenant of Mìyún County;
Zhāng Lín, Supervisor of Guards of Shùn Prefecture, and Shímò Wūzhě, County Lieutenant of Mìyún County, were both dismissed.
He observed mourning for his mother,
then was reinstated as Right Instructor to the Crown Prince,
promoted to Academician-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy, and then appointed Defense Commissioner of Dì Prefecture.
Dì County arrested dozens of bandits
and brought them to the prefecture, hoping for a reward for their full capture.
Zhònghuǐ suspected there was injustice
and delayed their case.
A colleague said:
“There are many bandits in the county;
please apply the law to them
to punish the rest.”
Zhònghuǐ then chose the elderly and young among them and released them first.
Not long after,
the true bandits were apprehended.
He entered court as Vice Minister of Rites and concurrently Left Instructor,
then promoted to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince and concurrently Left Grand Master of Remonstrance.
The Emperor said:
“The officials of the Eastern Palace
must especially be selected from upright individuals.
Those whose conduct is not proper or who are unsuited for their positions
should have their names reported.”
He also said:
“When lecturing or discussing in the Eastern Palace,
you should instruct them on filial piety, frugality, virtue, and rectifying oneself.”
A while later,
the Eastern Palace requested to increase the number of herdsmen and household items.
The Emperor said to Zhònghuǐ:
“The Crown Prince was born into wealth and nobility;
I always teach him modesty and frugality.
I have never presumptuously added to my own imperial wardrobe and provisions.
You should convey this sentiment to him.”
He was reassigned as Censor-in-chief.
In the fourteenth year,
he served as the New Year's Envoy to the Sòng State.
The Sòng ruler wished to change the ceremony of personally rising to receive the letter,
and sent his reception official Wáng Biàn to discuss it,
who argued forcefully with subtle distinctions,
insisting on compliance.
Zhònghuǐ said:
“As an envoy acting on orders,
I have traveled far to cultivate good relations,
and certainly wish to complete the ceremony.
However, what is stipulated in the treaty
is not something an envoy dares to change.
You, gentlemen, are the trusted officials of the Sòng State;
do not seek temporary advantage
and lose the favor of a great nation.”
After going back and forth repeatedly,
the old ceremony was finally used,
and the Sòng ruler personally rose to receive the letter, completing the ceremony, and Zhònghuǐ returned.
He again served as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
then promoted to Minister of Personnel,
and transferred to Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince and concurrently Censor-in-chief.
He was implicated for failing to impeach matters concerning the Grand Princess
and, along with Palace Censor Lǐ Yú, was each demoted one rank.
Zhònghuǐ served as an official of the Eastern Palace for about fifteen years in total,
offering many admonitions and warnings.
Xiǎnzōng particularly treated him with礼 respect.
In the nineteenth year of Dàdìng,
he died.
Zhònghuǐ was upright and strict in court,
with a solemn and grave demeanor.
Shìzōng once said:
“When I see Liú Zhònghuǐ, he always seems about to offer a sharp remonstrance.”
His reputation for being firm and severe was thus.
Kuí, courtesy name Yuánjǔ.
As a descendant of a high official, he served as Attendant at the Imperial Gate,
was transferred to Magistrate of Shēnxīàn County,
then summoned to be Chief of the Imperial Attendants,
promoted to Deputy Commissioner of the Western Imperial Gate and concurrently Director of the Imperial Parks,
and successively promoted to Commissioner of the Western and Eastern Imperial Gates.
In the second year of Tàihé,
the Sòng Xūyí Army reported that next year's New Year's Day envoys would be Lǔ Bó and Yáng Mínghuī.
However, upon crossing the border,
the deputy envoy was Wáng Chǔjiǔ.
Upon entering to audience,
Lǔ Bó did not kneel on both knees in the hall.
An imperial edict ordered Kuí to question him in the palace about why the previously reported envoy Yáng Mínghuī was changed to Wáng Chǔjiǔ without notification,
and why he did not kneel on both knees.
Lǔ Bó replied
that he knelt on both knees during the obeisance,
but a foot ailment made it appear as if he only knelt on one.
Previously,
there was an old Táng dynasty stele in the Southern Park,
which read:
“Burial of Grand Censor Liú Pēng in the tenth year of Zhēnyuán.”
The Emperor saw it and said:
“It is not appropriate to have a tomb in the imperial park.”
Kuí’s family was originally descended from Pēng,
so an imperial edict granted Kuí three hundred strings of cash to rebury it.
He was thrice transferred to the position of Right Xuānwēishǐ.
In Zhēnyòu (貞祐) second year (1214),
he was transferred to Left Xuānwēishǐ.
The following year,
he retired,
and was promoted one rank.
The Emperor said:
"You are an old retainer.
Now the imperial court has many troubles,
how can it be fitting for you to leave your post?
Since Our Crown Prince passed away,
Our thoughts have been incomplete.
When things calm down a little,
We will place you in a high-ranking position in an upper commandery."
A short while later,
he was recalled to serve as Zhī Kāifēngfǔ.
In the first month, on the first day of the fourth year (1216),
he temporarily served as Left Xuānwēishǐ.
He again requested to retire due to old age,
but before half a year passed, he was recalled again to serve as Yùshǐzhōngchéng.
An edict commanded him to pacify Hénánlù
and capture bandits.
He was dismissed from his post
for sitting and drinking with the Bǎojìngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was recalled to serve as Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
and then promoted to Tàizǐ Shàoshī.
The Zhānshìyuàn wished to widen the outer wall of the Eastern Palace.
Kuǐ (頍) pleaded with the Crown Prince, saying:
"At a time of war and famine,
why undertake such a project?"
Thus, it was stopped.
Soon after, he died.
Shí Lì'ài (時立愛), courtesy name Chāngshòu,
was a native of Xīnchéng (新城), Zhuōzhōu (涿州).
His father, Chéngqiān (承謙),
was wealthy and influential in the local community.
In years of famine, he opened his granaries to relieve the poor,
and those who borrowed from him were given a discount on their bonds.
In Liáo Tàikāng (遼太康) ninth year (1083),
he passed the Jìnshì examination
and was appointed as a staff official in Tàizhōu (泰州).
After observing mourning for his father,
and when the period of mourning ended,
he was appointed as Tóngzhī Chūnzhōushì (同知春州事).
Before a year passed,
he was transferred to be Magistrate of Yúnnèixiàn (雲內縣),
then again appointed as Magistrate of Wéndé (文德).
The Shūmìyuàn selected him as Fù Dūchéngzhǐ (副都承旨) of the Lìfáng (吏房),
and he was then promoted to Dūchéngzhǐ.
He was successively promoted to Yùshǐzhōngchéng,
being firm and upright and daring to speak out,
which offended the powerful and noble.
He was appointed as Fù Liúshǒu (副留守) of Yānjīng.
After observing mourning for his mother,
he was reinstated to his old post,
and then transferred to Liáoxīngjūn Jiédùshǐ (遼興軍節度使) concurrently Hànjūn Dūtǒng (漢軍都統).
After Tàizǔ had pacified Yānjīng,
he sought out Hán Xún (韓詢) from Píngzhōu (平州) and dispatched him with an edict to persuade Píngzhōu to submit.
At this time,
Xīwáng Huílíbǎo (奚王回离保) was in Lúlónglǐng (盧龍嶺).
Lì'ài (立愛) did not dare to immediately go for an audience,
but first sent someone to deliver a message, saying:
"The people are foolish and stubborn,
and did not immediately submit.
We pray for Your Majesty's generous grace,
to soothe their unsettled hearts."
The edict said:
"We personally inspected the Western lands,
and have completely pacified all of Yān (燕).
Wherever Our commands reached,
cities and towns all submitted.
Therefore, We commend your loyalty,
and specifically show Our generous grace.
All officials, great and small, currently there, may retain their old posts,
and all prisoners and those assigned to penal servitude shall be released and pardoned."
At this point,
the Liáo Emperor was still in Tiāndé (天德),
and although Píngzhōu had surrendered,
the people's loyalty was not yet firm.
Xīwáng Huílíbǎo's (奚王回离保) army was gathered and fortified,
and Jìzhōu (薊州) which had surrendered, rebelled again.
Rumors circulated among the people, saying
that "the cities taken by the Jīn (金) people,
are initially treated with kindness and pacified,
but later plundered and captured."
Although Shí Lì'ài (時立愛) tried to explain and persuade at the time, people were unwilling to believe it.
So he submitted a memorial,
"begging for a clear imperial edict to be issued,
and officials dispatched to various commanderies and prefectures
to proclaim virtue and righteousness.
Later, when troops approach Sòng (宋),
those who submit will be pacified,
and those who resist will be suppressed.
Then the world will be pacified without tiring the troops."
The Emperor read the memorial and praised him,
and replied with an edict:
"You first led your officials and people to surrender and pledge allegiance,
and then enumerated the advantages and disadvantages.
All are in line with Our intentions.
We commend and do not forget this.
The tribes in Shānxī (山西) were relocated to the east of the ridge
for fear of secret connections,
because the Liáo ruler had not yet been captured.
The people of Xījing (西京) have no other aspirations,
and all remain settled as before.
There may be some greedy and fierce generals and soldiers
who violate discipline
and plunder surrendered people.
We have already instructed all tribes and military commanders
to restrain their soldiers;
if even a hair is violated,
they shall certainly be punished without pardon.
Now We dispatch Wòluó Ālǐ (斡羅阿里) and others to serve as your deputies,
to pacify these people.
You should inform your subordinates
so they understand Our intentions."
Afterwards,
Píngzhōu was made Nánjing (南京),
and Zhāng Jué (張覺) was appointed Liúshǒu (留守).
Shí Lì'ài (時立愛) then left Píngzhōu.
Then Zhāng Jué (張覺) capitalized on the eastward migration of the Yānjīng people,
and his followers became resentful.
Juéd (覺) then rebelled and defected to Sòng.
After Lì'ài (立愛) left Píngzhōu and returned to his hometown,
Tàizǔ ceded Yān (燕) and Jì (薊) to Sòng,
and Xīnchéng (新城) became part of Sòng.
Sòng repeatedly issued edicts to Lì'ài,
but Lì'ài, seeing the Sòng government deteriorating daily,
refused to serve,
and warned his clan not to seek official positions.
When Zōngwàng (宗望) recaptured Yānshān,
Lì'ài went to the headquarters to pay his respects.
He was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (同中書門下平章事),
and several of his sons and nephews were appointed.
Lì'ài followed Zōngwàng's army for several years,
and contributed many plans.
He was enfeoffed as Chénguógōng (陳國公).
He submitted a memorial to resign from state affairs,
but it was not granted.
In the ninth year (1131),
he became Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhī Shūmìyuànshì (知樞密院事).
After a long time,
he was promoted to Zhōngshūlìng (中書令).
In Tiānhuì (天會) fifteenth year (1137),
he retired,
and was granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) and Zhèngguógōng (鄭國公).
He died at home
at the age of eighty-two.
There were varying amounts of money, cloth, and silk bestowed as funeral gifts.
An edict commanded Zhào Qìng (趙慶), Tóng Qiānshū Yānjīng Shūmìyuànshì (同簽書燕京樞密院事), to oversee the funeral arrangements,
and all funeral expenses were provided by the state.
Hán Qǐxiān (韓企先)
was a native of Yānjīng.
His ninth-generation ancestor, Zhīgǔ (知古),
served Liáo as Zhōngshūlìng,
and relocated to Liǔchéng (柳城).
His family was prominent for generations.
During the Qiántǒng (乾統) era (1101-1110),
Qǐxiān (企先) passed the Jìnshì examination,
but remained stagnant.
After Dūtǒng Gǎo (都統杲) pacified Zhōngjīng (中京),
he was promoted to Shūmì Fù Dūchéngzhǐ (樞密副都承旨),
and gradually transferred to Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (轉運使).
When Zōnghàn (宗翰) served as Dūtǒng (都統) to manage Shānxī,
he was appointed Xījing Liúshǒu (西京留守) by memorial.
In Tiānhuì (天會) sixth year (1128),
Liú Yànzōng (劉彥宗) died,
and Qǐxiān (企先) replaced him,
as Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (同中書門下平章事) and Zhī Shūmìyuànshì (知樞密院事).
In the seventh year (1129),
he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) concurrently Shìzhōng,
and enfeoffed as Chǔguógōng (楚國公).
Initially,
when Tàizǔ pacified Yānjīng,
he first used Han officials as prime ministers, such as Shǎng Zuǒ Qǐgōng (賞左企弓) and others,
and established the Zhōngshūshěng (中書省) and Shūmìyuàn (樞密院) in Guǎngníngfǔ (廣寧府).
However, the prime ministers in the imperial court themselves used Jurchen official titles.
In the early years of Tàizōng (太宗),
no changes were made.
When Zhāng Dūngù (張敦固) was executed,
the Zhōngshū (中書) and Shūmì (樞密) were moved to Píngzhōu.
When Cài Jìng (蔡靖) surrendered with Yānshān,
they were moved to Yānjīng.
All matters concerning the selection, appointment, dispatch, taxes, and levies in the Han territories were conducted by imperial decree.
Therefore, from the time of Shí Lì'ài (時立愛), Liú Yànzōng (劉彥宗), and Qǐxiān (企先),
their duties as prime ministers were largely like this.
Xiéyě (斜也) and Zōnggàn (宗幹), while in power,
persuaded Tàizōng to change the old Jurchen system
and adopt the Han official system.
In Tiānhuì (天會) fourth year (1126),
the official system was finally established,
and the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) and other various offices, prefectures, and courts below it were set up.
In his twelfth year,
Hán Qǐxiān was appointed Grand Councilor of the Right in the Department of State Affairs,
and summoned to Shàngjīng.
Upon audience,
Tàizōng was greatly surprised and said:
“I once dreamed of this man in the past,
and now I truly see him.”
Thereupon,
he began to discuss ritual and institutional systems,
making adjustments to the old regulations.
Qǐxiān was widely learned in the classics and histories,
and understood the precedents of previous dynasties.
Whether adopting or reforming,
he always found a balanced solution.
As a chancellor, Qǐxiān
always sought to select the right people for offices,
making it his responsibility to nurture and encourage promising younger talents.
He promoted worthy scholars,
and distinguished capable individuals;
for a time, the court and various ministries were filled with gentlemen.
He diligently remedied omissions,
and, with discreet planning and forthright remonstrance,
always consulted the Emperor.
Zōnghán and Zōnggàn greatly respected him,
and he was known to the world as a worthy chancellor.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Pú.
In the sixth year,
he passed away
at the age of sixty-five.
In the second year of Zhènglóng,
he was demoted by precedent to be enfeoffed as Duke of Qíguó.
In the eighth year of Dàdìng,
he was honored with a place in Tàizōng’s ancestral temple.
In the tenth year,
Sīkōng Lǐ Déqù’s grandson Yǐnqìng sought to inherit his grandfather’s position as méng’ān.
Shìzōng said:
“Déqù had no merit;
his méng’ān position shall remain vacant for now.
Among the Hán (Chinese) chancellors, only Hán Qǐxiān was most worthy;
others do not compare.”
In the eleventh year,
when planning to commission portraits of meritorious officials in Yǎnqìng Gōng,
the Emperor said:
“Chancellor Qǐxiān,
many of the institutional systems of this dynasty came from his hand.
As for deciding major policies,
and deliberating with high ministers,
he did not let outsiders know,
which is why no one could recognize his merit.
No Hán (Chinese) chancellor before or after him could equal him.
Including him among the portraits of meritorious officials
is also sufficient to encourage future generations.”
In the fifteenth year,
he was given the posthumous title Jiǎnyì.
Hán Duó, courtesy name Zhènwén,
was Qǐxiān’s second son.
At the end of Huángtǒng,
as the son of a high minister, he was granted the title Wǔyì Jiāngjūn.
Xīzōng, hearing of his classical scholarship,
bestowed upon him the rank of Jìnshì,
and appointed him Xuānhuī Pànguān.
He was successively promoted to Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng.
Hǎilíng sent an imperial envoy to instruct him, saying:
“A Lángguān
is a high selection.
You are the son of a meritorious and worthy man;
if you conduct yourself well and govern your office,
you can perpetuate your family’s legacy,
hence I appoint you to this.
If you can serve the public day and night,
you will be promoted without exception,
even to the rank of chancellor.”
Duó was inspired and stimulated.
Whenever there were doubtful cases in prisons,
he would base his deliberations on the classics.
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
he was reassigned as Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he was promoted to Lángzhōng of that same ministry.
He successively held the office of Hézhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He requested to care for his parents,
and was relieved of his post.
He was summoned to be Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū,
and then promoted to Zhōngdū Lù Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
Soon after,
the Emperor said to his chancellors:
“Hán Duó is old
and cannot handle strenuous tasks,
and his mother is also old;
he can be given a convenient prefecture.”
Thus,
he was reassigned as Shùntiān Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He died.
The encomium says: When Tàizǔ entered Yān,
he first adopted the official systems of the southern and northern faces of Liáo.
Thus, Liú Yànzōng and Shí Lì'ài devised the arrangements,
which were not seen at the imperial court.
During leisure from military campaigns,
they managed civil administration,
organized civilian affairs,
encouraged agriculture, and stockpiled grain.
Internally, they supplied the capital;
externally, they provided provisions for transport.
This was their achievement.
Hán Qǐxiān served as chancellor in two reigns,
for almost twenty years.
He achieved success and established his legacy,
and Shìzōng praised his worthiness.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume XVII: Lí Qióng, Lǐ Chéng, Kǒng Yànzhōu, Xú Wén, Shī Yíshēng, Zhāng Zhōngfú, Zhāng Zhōngyàn, Yǔwén Xūzhōng, Wáng Lún
Lí Qióng, courtesy name Guóbǎo,
was a native of Línzhāng, Xiāngzhōu.
He was a supplementary student of the prefecture.
During the Xuānhé era of Sòng,
when bandits rose,
Qióng then learned to fence, stab, and draw a strong bow.
He was tested in archery and horsemanship,
and assigned to Zōng Zé’s army,
stationed in Cízhōu.
Not long after, he returned home,
gathered seven hundred righteous volunteers,
and rejoined Zé.
Zé appointed Qióng as the commander of the seven hundred men.
After Zé’s death,
he was transferred to guard Huázhōu.
At that time, Zōngwàng was attacking Sòng,
and was about to cross the river.
The garrison revolted,
killed their commander Zhào Shìyàn, and nominated Qióng as their leader.
Qióng then enticed the crowd,
proclaimed loyalty to the emperor,
and gathered troops as he marched.
By the time he crossed the Huái River,
he had over ten thousand men.
Kāng Wáng appointed him as Chǔzhōu Ānfǔshǐ and Huáinán Dōnglù Bīngmǎ Qínxiá,
and he was successively promoted to Wǔtài Jūn Chéngxuānshǐ.
Not long after,
he led his more than ten thousand infantry and cavalry to defect to Qí,
and was granted the title Jìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and made Administrator of Gǒngzhōu.
When the state of Qí was abolished,
he was made Bózhōu Fángyùshǐ.
For his integrity,
he was promoted to Piàojì Shàngjiāngjūn.
When Zōngbì recovered Hénán,
he appointed Qióng as Shāndōng Lù Nǔshǒu Qiānhù,
and Administrator of Bózhōushì.
Upon mourning his mother,
he resigned from office.
When Zōngbì again campaigned south of the Jiāngnán,
he summoned Qióng, knowing his familiarity with the difficult and easy terrain of the southern mountains and rivers,
to the army to strategize.
He calmly spoke to his colleagues, saying:
“Qióng once followed the grand army in the southern campaign.
Each time I saw Marshal Guówáng personally supervise the battle on the front lines,
with arrows and stones falling like rain,
the King removed his helmet,
commanded the three armies,
and his spirit remained calm and composed.
His use of troops to achieve victory
was entirely consistent with Sūn Wǔ (Sun Zi and Wu Qi),
and he can be called a generational hero.
As for personally facing the sharp edges of weapons,
advancing without avoiding danger,
when officers and soldiers see this,
who would dare to spare their lives?
It is fitting that he is irresistible in every direction,
expanding his territory by a thousand lǐ daily.
As for the various commanders in Jiāngnán,
their abilities do not even reach those of ordinary men.
Whenever they must dispatch troops,
they always remain hundreds of lǐ away,
calling this ‘maintaining gravitas.’
Or, when they summon troops
and replace generals and officers,
they merely send a single messenger with empty documents to announce it,
calling this ‘issuing orders.’
They entrust defeating the enemy and deciding victory to their subordinates,
which causes the wise to become disheartened and the foolish to lose their armies.
If they are fortunate enough to achieve a small victory,
they quickly send reports,
exaggerating the number of captives to claim credit for themselves,
thereby incurring resentment from their generals and soldiers.
Even if they do personally attend,
they always flee first.
Moreover, their national governance is disorganized:
if there is even slight merit,
generous rewards are immediately given;
if there is a grave crime,
it is left unpunished.
It is already a blessing from Heaven that they have not immediately perished;
how can they ever revive?”
The assembled considered this a sound argument.
Marshal
refers to Zōngbì.
When Zōngbì questioned Qióng about the success or failure of invading Jiāngnán,
asking who would dare to resist them.
Qióng said:
“The armies in Jiāngnán are timid and weak,
all remnants of defeated forces.
Moreover, they have no good commanders.
How can they resist us?
I have heard that Qín Huì is in power and holds sway in the court.
Qín Huì,
an old scholar,
is what is called a high official who brings about the ruin of his country.
He is overly cautious,
only fearing overthrow.
When our great army approaches them,
their ruler and ministers will surely be disheartened and terrified,
having no time even to lament.
Indeed, a bird wounded by a bow can be brought down by an empty string.”
Soon after,
Jiāngnán indeed declared itself a vassal state,
and Zōngbì was pleased that Qióng’s words proved prescient.
Earlier,
not long after Qióng left Bó,
Sòng troops captured it but did not hold it,
abandoning it again.
They then assigned Sòng Chāo, a local, to defend it.
When the great army arrived,
Chāo again entrusted the affairs of the prefecture to his commander Wèi Jīng and fled.
The marshal’s office sent someone to summon Jīng,
but Jīng did not surrender.
When the city fell,
the common people were terrified, awaiting their fate.
Qióng requested the Marshal, saying:
“Those who did not surrender the city were
the villains who incited it.
What crime have the people committed?
I wish to comfort and reassure them.”
The Marshal, knowing Qióng had previously defended Bó,
therefore stopped the execution of Jīng and released the people of the prefecture,
and again ordered Qióng to defend Bó.
For six years,
the people of Bó were grateful to him.
He was promoted to Military Commissioner of Wǔníng.
In the eighth year,
he became Military Commissioner of Tàiníng.
In the ninth year,
he was promoted to Governor of Guīdé.
In the first year of Zhēnyuán,
he was awarded the Grand Master of Golden and Purple Light,
and died in office
at the age of fifty.
Lǐ Chéng, courtesy name Bóyǒu,
was a native of Guīxìn, Xióngzhōu.
He was exceptionally brave and strong,
able to draw a three-hundred-catties bow.
In the early years of Sòng Xuānhé,
when he was tested as an archer,
he displayed extraordinary strength in drawing a strong bow.
He successively held the post of Mobilization Commissioner for Huáinán.
Chéng then gathered a crowd and became a bandit,
plundering Jiāngnán.
Sòng sent troops to defeat him,
and Chéng then defected to Qí.
He was successively appointed Prefect of Kāidé Prefecture,
and followed the great army in attacking Sòng.
When Qí was abolished,
he was again appointed Military Commissioner of Ānwǔ.
Among the surrendered generals, Chéng was the bravest and most fierce,
his commands were very strict,
and none of the multitude dared to violate them.
In battle, he personally led the charge ahead of the generals.
He would not eat before his soldiers had eaten,
and personally attended to those who were ill.
He did not carry rain gear,
and remained composed even when soaked.
Someone accused Chéng of rebellion,
but Zōngbì realized it was a false accusation,
and let Chéng handle it himself.
Chéng flogged the accuser but released him,
such was his magnanimity.
Because of this,
his soldiers were happy to serve him,
and wherever he went, he achieved victories.
When Zōngbì again took Hénán,
Lǐ Xìng of Sòng held Hénán Prefecture.
Chéng led his army into Mèngjīn.
Xìng led his troops to approach the city,
beating drums and shouting, requesting battle,
but Chéng did not respond.
As the sun began to set,
Xìng’s soldiers were tired and hungry.
Chéng opened the gate and attacked swiftly,
routing them completely.
Xìng fled to Hànnán,
and Chéng then took Luòyáng, Sōng, Rǔ, and other places.
After Hénán was pacified,
Zōngbì memorialized to appoint Chéng as Governor of Hénán,
and overall commander of the troops in that circuit.
He once took surplus grain from the officials to cover public expenses,
and was demoted two ranks
and relieved of his duties.
During the Zhènglóng era,
he was reappointed Governor of Zhēndìng,
and enfeoffed as a prince of a commandery,
then according to regulation, enfeoffed as Duke of Jì.
He died
at the age of sixty-nine.
Kǒng Yànzhōu, courtesy name Jùjì,
was a native of Línglǜ, Xiāngzhōu.
He was dissolute,
did not engage in productive work,
and fled to Biàn to avoid punishment.
He registered himself in the army.
Imprisoned for a crime,
he persuaded the guard to untie him,
and escaped by scaling the city wall at night.
Later, he committed murder
and became a fugitive bandit.
In the early years of Sòng Jìngkāng,
he answered the call to enlist,
and successively held the post of Army Commander for the Eastern and Western Circuits of the Capital.
Hearing that the great army was about to arrive in Shāndōng,
he then led his subordinates,
slaughtered residents,
burned dwellings,
plundered valuables,
and crossed the Yellow River southwards.
The Sòng people again offered him an appointment,
making him Mobilization Commissioner along the Jiāng River.
Yànzhōu was tyrannical and overbearing,
disregarding regulations.
The Sòng people were about to arrest him with troops,
so Yànzhōu fled to Qí.
He followed Liú Lín in attacking Sòng,
and served as General Commander of the Expeditionary Army,
later redesignated as Left Grand Commander of the Expeditionary Camp.
When the Qí state was abolished,
he successively served as Prefect of Zīzhōu.
He followed Zōngbì in taking Hénán,
captured Zhèngzhōu,
seized its defender Liú Zhèng,
and defeated Mèng Bāngjié at Dēngfēng.
He was appointed Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu.
He pacified the bandits at Chēyuánlǐng in the Tàiháng Mountains.
He followed the expedition to Jiāngnán,
crossed the Huái River and defeated Sūn Huī’s army of over ten thousand men,
and took Ānfēng and Huòqiū.
When attacking Háozhōu,
Yànzhōu was made the vanguard.
He sailed downriver and approached the city,
captured Shào Qīng, the commander of its navy,
and then captured Háozhōu.
After the army returned,
he successively held the posts of Minister of Public Works and Minister of War,
Governor of Hénán,
and was enfeoffed as Prince of Guǎngpíng Commandery.
During the Zhènglóng era, he was demoted by regulation to Grand Master of Golden and Purple Light,
and appointed Left-overstaying Administrator of Xī Jīng.
Yànzhōu was dissolute with women,
and behaved like a beast.
His concubine gave birth to a beautiful daughter.
Yànzhōu cruelly tormented her mother,
forcing her to declare that the child was not his own,
and then took the daughter as his concubine.
When his officials owed public funds,
he had private relations with their wives in exchange for cancelling the debts.
However, when Háozhōu was captured,
all captured individuals by other armies were executed.
Yànzhōu issued an order not to kill indiscriminately,
and several thousand people were spared.
People praised him for this.
Nevertheless, from youth to old age, he was always in the ranks,
skilled in military affairs,
and knew their strengths and weaknesses.
Hǎilíng wanted to make him a general and aide for the southern expedition.
In the fifth year of Zhènglóng,
he was appointed Left-overstaying Administrator of Nán Jīng.
Yànzhōu fell ill,
and some court officials spread rumors that Yànzhōu had died,
but Yànzhōu was still alive.
Hǎilíng had all those who falsely spread rumors of Yànzhōu's death flogged,
to encourage him.
Not long after, he eventually died in Biàn
at the age of fifty-five.
His dying memorial stated,
“When attacking Sòng, one should first take Huáinán.”
Thus it was.
Xú Wén 字 Yànwǔ,
a native of Yè Xiàn, Láizhōu,
relocated to Jiāoshuǐ.
In his youth, he made a living as a salt merchant,
traveling to and from several coastal prefectures.
He was brave and spirited,
and his peers all feared him.
In the late Sòng dynasty, bandits arose,
and he recruited warriors,
becoming the Left Tenth General of Bǎnqiáo, Mìzhōu.
His strength was extraordinary;
he wielded a huge blade weighing fifty jīn,
and was irresistible wherever he went.
People called him
"Xú Dàdāo."
Later, he served under Wáng Lóngtú,
and in a battle with the Xià people,
he captured an enemy general alive,
and was appointed Jìnwǔ Xiàowèi.
Returning east,
he defeated the bandit gangs of Yáng Jìn and others,
and was promoted to Chéngxìn Láng.
When Sòng Kāng Wáng crossed the river,
he summoned Wén as a Zhǔnbèi Jiàng of the Shūmìyuàn,
and captured Miáo Fù and Hán Shìjī.
For his accomplishments, he was promoted to Húaidōng, Zhèxī, Yánhǎi Shuǐjūn Dūtǒngzhì.
The other generals were jealous of his talent and bravery.
At this time,
Lǐ Chéng and Kǒng Yànzhōu had both defected to Qí,
and the Sòng people also suspected Wén of having intentions to return north.
The great general Yán Gāo had a grudge against Wén,
and thus slandered him.
A Sòng envoy, Dūtǒngzhì Zhū Shīmǐn, came to attack Wén,
so Wén led several tens of warships and sailed to defect to Qí.
Qí appointed Wén Hǎi, Mì Èrzhōu Cānghǎi Dū Zhāozhuō Shǐ concurrently Shuǐjūn Tǒngzhì,
then promoted him to Hǎidào Fù Dūtǒng concurrently Hǎidào Zǒngguǎn,
and bestowed upon him a golden belt.
Wén offered a strategy to Liú Yù,
intending to attack Lín'ān by sea,
but Yù did not adopt it.
When the state of Qí was abolished,
the Yuánshuàifǔ, acting on imperial authority, appointed Wén Nánjīng Bùjūn Dū Yúhòu,
and acting Mǎbùjūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ.
In Tiānjuàn元年,
he defeated the Tàiháng bandit Liáng Xiǎogē,
and concurrently held his original post as Shuǐjūn Tǒngzhì.
The imperial court ceded Hénán to Sòng,
and appointed Wén Shāndōng Lù Bīngmǎ Qiánxiá.
Zōngbì recaptured Hénán,
and Wén defeated Sòng general Lǐ Bǎo at Púyáng and Mèng Bāngjié at Dēngfēng.
Sòng general Jiǎng Zhījūn occupied Héyáng.
Wén arrived at its city gate at dawn,
and sent a subordinate general to attack the northeast of the city,
while he personally led his elite troops in a stealthy attack on the south gate.
The city's forces concentrated to rescue the northeast,
whereupon Wén cut through the gate and entered the city from the south gate.
The Sòng army collapsed and fled,
and he pursued and defeated them.
He defeated Guō Qīng and Guō Yuǎn in Rǔzhōu.
Zhèngzhōu rebelled,
and he recaptured it,
driving away Sòng general Qī Fāng.
After Hénán was pacified,
Zōngbì rewarded his officers and soldiers,
awarding Wén silver, silk, saddles, and horses.
He was made Xíngjūn Wànhù,
and followed Zōngbì to capture Lú, Háo and other prefectures,
and was exceptionally promoted to Wǔyì Jiāngjūn.
He became Zhī Jìzhōu,
serving for seven years,
then transferred to Zhī Tàian Jūn.
When Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
he recognized Wén's past achievements,
and Wén was successively promoted to Zhōngdū Bīngmǎ Dū Zhīhuīshǐ,
bestowed a golden belt,
and appointed Jùnzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
Not long after,
Hǎilíng planned to attack Sòng,
and Wén was reassigned to Xíngdū Shuǐjiān,
supervising the construction of warships in Tōngzhōu.
Xú Yuán and Zhāng Wàng of Dōnghǎi Xiàn rebelled.
Fáng Zhēn and three others from the county fled to Hǎizhōu,
and also fled to the Zǒngguǎnfǔ,
reporting the rebellion.
Both the prefecture and the administration sent envoys to follow Zhēn and others to Dōnghǎi to observe the bandit situation,
but all were harmed by the bandits.
The prefecture and administration combined their forces to attack them,
but failed to subdue them for several months.
Hǎilíng was about to attack Sòng,
and disliked hearing about this matter.
He decreed Wén, along with Bùjūn Zhīhuīshǐ Zhāng Hóngxìn, Tóngzhī Dàxīng Yǐn Lǐ Wéizhōng, and Sùzhí Jiāngjūn Xiāo Āwā, to lead nine hundred warships by sea to suppress them,
saying to Wén and the others:
"My intention is not about a single locality;
I will use this to test the navy."
When Wén and the others arrived at Dōnghǎi,
they fought with the bandits,
defeated them,
beheaded over five thousand,
captured Xú Yuán and Zhāng Wàng,
and the remaining forces surrendered.
In this campaign,
Zhāng Hóngxìn, upon reaching Láizhōu,
claimed illness and stayed there,
spending his days drinking with courtesans and musicians.
Hǎilíng heard of this.
When the army returned,
Hóngxìn was flogged two hundred times.
Wén was promoted to Dìnghǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Fáng Zhēn and the other three received varying official rewards.
Those who died fighting the bandits were all posthumously granted three ranks,
and their families were given one hundred liǎng of silver and one hundred rolls of silk.
In Dàdìng二年,
he went to the palace to personally declare his old age and failing eyesight,
earnestly requesting to retire.
This was granted.
By imperial grace, he was promoted to Lónghǔ Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn,
and died at home.
Shī Yíshēng, 字 Míngwàng,
was a native of Shàowǔ.
He was widely read and had a strong memory.
Before reaching manhood,
he entered the Tàixué through the xiānggòng examination.
In Sòng Zhènghé四年,
he was promoted to the upper class,
tested for official academic positions,
and appointed Yǐngzhōu Jiàoshòu.
When the imperial army entered Biàn,
Yíshēng fled to Jiāngnán.
Later, due to a crime, he fled north to Qí,
and submitted a letter outlining strategies for capturing Sòng.
Qí appointed him Dà Zǒngguǎnfǔ Yìshìguān.
He fell out of favor with Liú Lín,
and was demoted to Zhāngxìn Jūn Jiédù Pànguān.
When the state of Qí was abolished,
he was promoted to Tàicháng Bóshì,
then transferred to Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
then to Shàngshū Lìbù Yuánwàiláng,
and became Běnbù Lángzhōng.
Soon after, he was reassigned to the Lǐbù,
and sent out as Xízhōu Cìshǐ.
In Tiāndé二年,
based on the recommendation of Cānzhī Zhèngshì Zhāng Hào that Yíshēng could serve as a consultant,
Hǎilíng summoned him as Hànlín Zhíxuégshì,
and he drafted the epitaph for the Grand Tutor Liáng Wáng Zōngbì's tomb,
advancing two official ranks.
In Zhènglóng元年,
he was sent out as Zhī Shēnzhōu,
then summoned back as Shàngshū Lǐbù Shìláng,
and promoted to Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì.
In the winter of the fourth year,
he became the New Year's Day envoy to the Sòng state.
Yíshēng, feeling ashamed to face the Sòng people due to his past crime and flight north,
strongly declined,
but was not permitted.
Sòng ordered Zhāng Táo to host him at Dūtíng,
and Zhāng Táo, seizing an opportunity,
hinted at the desire to return to one's roots.
Yíshēng, seeing that his attendant was not nearby,
spoke cryptically:
"Today the north wind is very strong."
He then picked up a brush from the table and tapped it, saying:
"Brush come,
brush come."
At this, Sòng first became alert.
His deputy envoy, Yēlǜ Pìlílà, reported it upon his return,
and Yíshēng was executed for this.
Originally,
when Yíshēng was struggling in the examinations,
he met a monk skilled in physiognomy,
who told him:
"Your face has the bone of authority;
you can be a duke or a minister.
But looking at the hair on your body,
it all grows upwards,
and covers your wrists;
there must be something to match this before you can become noble."
Yíshēng heard his words
and was greatly pleased.
He eventually joined Fàn Rǔwéi in Jiàn and Jiàn.
Later,
Rǔwéi was defeated,
and Yíshēng disguised himself as a servant in the home of Wú Wēng in Yōngtài for three years.
Wēng found him unusual,
and one day, dismissing others, questioned him about his name.
Yíshēng said:
"I served diligently as a servant;
why does the master also have doubts?"
Wēng insisted on questioning him,
so Yíshēng asked for his reason.
Wēng said:
"The other day, when I entertained guests,
you served all the dishes,
but you alone scorned your peers,
and sighed when removing the utensils.
This is how I knew you were not a true servant."
Yíshēng then told him the truth.
Wēng gave him gold,
and he crossed the Huái river by night to return.
In an examination, he obtained the highest score, "獲熊三十六賦,"
and thereafter, it truly was as the monk had said.
The following year,
he was appointed Nanjing Liúshǒu.
At that time, there was warfare in Huái-Chǔ,
and the local people and garrison soldiers lived mixed together.
Lawsuits were numerous and complicated,
and the officials in charge were all indecisive.
Zhāng Zhōngyàn caught garrison soldiers who were committing robberies,
and had them all judged according to the law.
The Shuàifǔ was angry at his arbitrary decisions
and impeached him,
but the imperial court ignored the matter.
Upon completion of his term,
he was transferred to Zhēndìng Yǐn, concurrently serving as Héběi Xīlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
Not long after,
he retired,
and returned west to Jīngzhào.
The next year,
he was reappointed as Líntáo Yǐn, concurrently serving as Xīqín Lù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
When Liú Hǎi of Gǒngzhōu instigated a rebellion,
and was subsequently defeated,
several thousand people who had joined the rebellion were registered.
Zhāng Zhōngyàn only had the ringleaders executed.
The Xīqiāng tribes of Chuīzhé, Mìzàng, Lǒngbū, and Pángbài relied on the treacherous terrain and remained unsubdued.
The Shìyùshǐ Shā Chúnzhī was sent to consult Zhāng Zhōngyàn on strategies.
Zhāng Zhōngyàn said:
“These Qiāng alternately submit and rebel.
If I do not go myself,
it will surely be impossible.”
He immediately went to Jīshí Dá Nánsì.
Four chieftains came,
and he negotiated their surrender with them.
The matter was thus settled,
and he rewarded them and sent them away.
When he returned and reported,
the emperor was greatly pleased,
and sent Zhāng Rǔyù by express post to commend him,
granting him a qiúwén gold belt,
and by grace of the suburban sacrifices, elevated him to Yítóng Sānsī.
He died in office from illness
at the age of seventy-five.
The common people wailed in sorrow and closed their markets,
erecting statues to worship him.
A eulogy states: From ancient times, brave generals and warriors,
the untalented among them,
upon facing changes in the world,
rushed to surrender for fear of being too late.
This is their normal state,
and a gentleman would not blame them for it.
Lì Qióng and Xú Wén are examples of this.
Shī Yíshēng was a treacherous and fickle man,
Lǐ Chéng a robber and a wastrel,
Kǒng Yànzhōu openly lusted after women,
cutting himself off from humanity;
what blame can there be for such people?
Although Zhāng Zhōngfú and Zhāng Zhōngyàn had small commendable virtues,
yet as sons of Sòng ministers,
whose father died in battle against the Jīn,
whether Jīn or Qí,
both were enemies with whom they could not coexist under the same heaven.
If Jīn gave territory to Qí, they would willingly serve Qí.
If Jīn returned territory to Sòng, they would endure shame and serve Sòng.
If Jīn seized their territory, they would again stand shoulder to shoulder and serve Jīn.
It was like rushing to a marketplace,
wherever profit lay.
At such a time,
how could they still know what was called constant principles?
Alas!
Yǔwén Xūzhōng, courtesy name Shūtōng,
was a native of Shǔ.
Initially serving Sòng,
he successively held the office of Zīzhèngdiàn Dàxuéshì.
In the fourth year of Tiānhuì,
after the Sòng Shàodì had already concluded an alliance,
Zōngwàng led his army back to Mèngyáng.
The Sòng general Yáo Píngzhòng launched a night raid,
and the next day again advanced and besieged Biàn.
The Shàodì sent Yǔwén Xūzhōng to Zōngwàng’s army
to explain that the attacking troops acted on their own initiative,
and to request the peace negotiations to resume as before,
and also to ascertain the well-being of Kāngwáng.
Shortly thereafter,
the Censorate blamed Yǔwén Xūzhōng for the peace negotiations,
and he was dismissed to Qīngzhōu,
then further demoted to a sacrificial post.
In the first year of Jiànyán,
he was demoted to Sháozhōu.
In the second year,
Kāngwáng sought someone who could serve as an envoy.
Yǔwén Xūzhōng responded to the imperial summons from his demotion,
was reinstated as Zīzhèngdiàn Dàxuéshì,
and became Qǐqǐngshǐ.
At this time,
when an army was raised to attack Sòng,
Wáng Lún and Zhū Biàn had already been detained and not allowed to return.
Yǔwén Xūzhōng was also detained;
this was in the sixth year of Tiānhuì.
The imperial court was then discussing ritual systems,
and rather appreciated Yǔwén Xūzhōng’s talent and skill,
granting him official titles and ranks.
Yǔwén Xūzhōng accepted them immediately,
and, along with Hán Fǎng and others, was in charge of drafting imperial edicts.
The next year,
Hóng Hào arrived in Shàngjīng and found Yǔwén Xūzhōng very contemptible.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānhuì,
Xīzōng ascended the throne.
Zōnghàn, as Tàibǎo and head of the three departments,
was enfeoffed as Jìn Guówáng,
and requested retirement.
The imperial reply did not permit it;
the text was written by Yǔwén Xūzhōng.
During the Tiānjuàn reign,
he successively held the offices of Hànlín Xuéshì Zhī Zhìgào, concurrently Tàicháng Qīng,
and was enfeoffed as Hénèi Jùn Kāiguó Gōng.
He wrote the monument for Tàizǔ’s illustrious virtue and divine merits,
and was promoted to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
the Sòng people requested peace.
Their oath stated:
“Henceforth, for those who have migrated south,
if they officially state their desire to return,
they shall no longer be forbidden.
For the superior state and our humble domain,
we also ask that this agreement be applied equally.”
Thereupon,
an edict was issued to the Shàngshū Shěng to send a dispatch to the Sòng state,
requesting the families of Zhāng Zhōngfú, Zhāng Zhōngyàn, Zhèng Yìnián, Dù Chōng, Zhāng Xiàochún, Yǔwén Xūzhōng, and Wáng Jìn;
and sending Lǐ Zhèngmín and Bì Liángshǐ back to Sòng.
Only Méng Yǔ’s departure or stay was left to his own will.
At that time, Yǔwén Xūzhōng’s son Shīyuàn served in Sòng,
reaching the position of Zhuǎnyùn Pànguān,
and his family came north.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Chéngzhǐ,
and given the additional title of Tèjìn.
He was transferred to Lǐbù Shàngshū,
while retaining his Chéngzhǐ position.
Yǔwén Xūzhōng relied on his talent and was unrestrained,
fond of mockery and slander.
Whenever he saw a Nǚzhí person, he would disdainfully refer to them as "barbarians,"
causing resentment among the nobles and high officials, who often found it hard to bear.
Yǔwén Xūzhōng once composed inscriptions for palace halls,
which were originally all auspicious and beautiful names.
However, those who disliked Yǔwén Xūzhōng picked apart his words, alleging they slandered the imperial court,
thus fabricating his crime.
In the second month of the sixth year,
Du Tiānfóliú, a slave of Tángguō Chóuwò, accused Yǔwén Xūzhōng of rebellion.
An edict commanded the relevant authorities to investigate,
but found no evidence.
So they fabricated evidence by identifying books and maps in Yǔwén Xūzhōng’s house as tools for rebellion.
Yǔwén Xūzhōng said:
“Death is my fate.
As for books and maps,
every Sòng scholar-official’s family coming south has them.
Gāo Shìtán has even more books and maps than my family.
Is he also a rebel?”
The authorities, following the implicit imperial will, also killed Gāo Shìtán,
which is still considered an injustice today.
Gāo Shìtán, courtesy name Jìmò,
was a descendant of Gāo Qióng.
At the end of Xuānhé,
he served as Xīnzhōu Hùcáo Cānjūn.
Upon entering the court,
he rose to the office of Hànlín Zhí Xuéshì.
Yǔwén Xūzhōng and Gāo Shìtán both had literary collections circulating in the world.
Wáng Lún, courtesy name Zhèngdào,
was the great-great-grandson of Wáng Miǎn, brother of the former Sòng chancellor Wáng Dàn.
He was a dissolute and roguish character,
and even at over forty years old, still associated with ruffians in Biàn.
In the fifth year of Tiānhuì,
the Sòng appointed Wáng Lún as acting Xíngbù Shìláng,
and, with Gémén Shèrén Zhū Biàn, served as Tōngwènshǐ.
At this time,
an attack on Sòng was being planned,
and all Sòng envoys such as Wáng Lún, Yǔwén Xūzhōng, Wèi Xíngkě, Gù Zòng, Zhāng Shào, etc.,
were detained and not allowed to return.
After several years,
Wáng Lún, long in distress,
proposed peace negotiations and sought to return.
The Yuánshuàifǔ sent someone to him and said:
“This is not the true sentiment of Jiāngnán;
you are merely saying this yourself.”
Wáng Lún said:
“My mission had instructions;
otherwise, why would I have come?
Only the Yuánshuài should examine this.”
In the tenth year of Tiānhuì,
Liú Yù's consecutive military campaigns all ended in failure.
Tàlǎn, serving as the Marshal's Left Supervisor-General and Administrator of the Southern Border,
secretly pursued peace negotiations,
and thus dispatched Lún to return.
Before this,
Sòng had already sent envoys to beg for peace,
but the imperial court had not yet granted it.
Lún met King Kāng and spoke of the peace negotiations.
King Kāng was greatly pleased,
promoted Lún in office,
and also appointed his sons and younger brothers to official positions.
Sòng was then engaged in warfare with Qí,
and peace was not yet possible.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānhuì,
King Kāng heard that the Prince of Tiānshuǐ Commandery had already passed away,
and sent Lún, acting as a scholar of the Zhíxuèshì academy, to request his coffin.
He had Lún ask Tàlǎn:
"The land of Hénán,
since the superior country does not keep it for itself,
rather than enfeoffing Liú Yù with it,
why not return it to the Zhào clan?"
That year,
Liú Yù had been enfeoffed for eight years,
but could not establish his state independently.
He still frequently deployed garrisons.
The imperial court, weary of his incompetence,
thus deposed Liú Yù.
Tàlǎn, as the Left Vice-Marshal, guarded Biànjīng,
and it was then that Lún arrived.
Tàlǎn was
Tàizǔ's cousin
and an ancestral generation to Xīzōng.
Tàizōng's eldest son Zōngpán, as Grand Preceptor, led the affairs of the Three Departments,
his position being above Zōnggàn.
Zōnghàn had passed away a long time ago,
and Zōnggàn could not single-handedly contend with Zōngpán.
The following year,
the first year of Tiānjuàn,
Tàlǎn and Zōngjùn, the Prefect of Dōngjīng, both entered the imperial court.
Xīzōng appointed Zōngjùn as Left Chancellor.
Zōngjùn was
Tàizǔ's son.
Tàlǎn, Zōngpán, and Zōngjùn were all overbearing and greedy for profit,
secretly harboring different ambitions.
They thus agreed to give the land of Qí to Sòng,
and even Zōnggàn and others below him could not dispute it successfully.
They sent Servitor Zhāng Tōnggǔ as an envoy to convey the imperial edict to Jiāngnán,
and dispatched Lún to return first.
The following year,
Sòng appointed Lún as a scholar of the Duānmíngdiàn Academy
and Vice-Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
He was given one thousand liǎng of gold vessels and ten thousand liǎng of silver vessels,
and again came to request the coffin of the Prince of Tiānshuǐ Commandery,
as well as his mother Wéi Shì, brothers, and other relatives.
Lán Gōngzuǒ, the Military Commissioner of Bǎoxìn Commandery, served as his deputy.
That year,
Zōngpán, Zōngjùn, and Tàlǎn were all handed over to officials for plotting rebellion.
Xīzōng executed Zōngpán and Zōngjùn.
Because Tàlǎn was of a senior generation,
he was pardoned from death
and made Left Chancellor of the Xíngtái Shàngshūshěng,
his military authority was stripped.
Right Vice-Marshal Zōngbì reported:
"Tàlǎn and Zōngpán secretly communicated with the Sòng people,
and thus gave the lands of Hénán and Shǎnxī to the Sòng people."
At this time, Tàlǎn again plotted rebellion.
He was arrested and killed in Qízhōu.
When Lún arrived at Shàngjīng,
the authorities carefully read King Kāng's memorial.
It did not state the year.
Upon reviewing the tribute document,
it referred to "gifts" instead of "tribute."
The emperor had the chancellor interrogate Lún, saying:
"You only know of the Marshal;
do you not know of the superior country?"
He was then detained and not sent back,
and his deputy, Lán Gōngzuǒ, was sent home.
In the fifth month of the third year,
Zōngbì recaptured the lands of Hénán and Shǎnxī
and then attacked Jiāngnán,
having already crossed the Huái River.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
the Sòng people requested peace.
In the second month of the second year,
Hé Zhù, a scholar of the Duānmíngdiàn Academy, and Cáo Xūn, the Surveillance Commissioner of Róngzhōu, presented the oath memorial.
In the third month,
Left Vice-Inspector Sàilǐ and Liú Táo, the Commissioner of Western Shāndōng Circuit, were dispatched to escort the coffin of the Prince of Tiānshuǐ Commandery
and Emperor Sòng's mother, Wéi Shì, back to Jiāngnán.
In the fifth month,
Lǐ Zhèngmín and Bì Liángshǐ returned south.
In the seventh month,
Zhū Biàn, Zhāng Shào, and Hóng Hào returned south.
In the fourth year,
Lún was appointed Commissioner of Píngzhōu Circuit.
Lún had already received the order but again declined,
whereupon the emperor said:
"This is a duplicitous person."
He was then executed in Shàngjīng,
aged sixty-one.
A eulogy states: Confucius said,
"One who acts with a sense of shame,
and when sent as an envoy to the four quarters does not disgrace his sovereign's commission,
may be called a scholar."
Yǔwén Xūzhōng arrived at Shàngjīng in the morning
and received official titles that evening.
Wáng Lún was a pampered son,
a street thug.
How could such
a person who "acts with a sense of shame"
be
entrusted as an envoy?
Although the deaths of these two men were unjust,
they largely brought it upon themselves.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 18. Xīzōng's two sons (Jì'ān, Dàojì). Xié Mǎo Ālǐ, Tūhé Sù, Wūyán Púlúhún, Chìzhǎn Huī, Dàxiè (original name Tābùyě), Pán (original name Púsùyuè), Ālí Bǔ (son Fāng).
Xīzōng's sons:
The Empress Dàopíng gave birth to Crown Prince Jì'ān;
the Worthy Consort gave birth to Wèi Wáng Dàojì.
Jì'ān
was born on the day Wùzǐ in the second month of the second year of Huángtǒng, in the Tiānkāidiàn Palace.
The emperor, at twenty-four years old, finally had a royal son;
he was overjoyed,
and dispatched envoys to swiftly report to the Grand Empress Dowager in Míngdé Palace.
Five days later, he was named,
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
On the day Jiǎyín in the third month,
an announcement was made to Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral temples.
On the day Dīngsì,
his topknot was cut,
and this was reported to Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral temples.
On the day Wùwǔ,
he was invested as Crown Prince.
The empress's father, Grand Commandant Hútǎ, was enfeoffed as a king,
and bestowed with five hundred people, horses and cattle, fifty camels, and five thousand sheep.
All officials at court were promoted one rank,
and all received gifts.
On the day Jǐwèi,
an imperial edict was issued to the realm.
In the twelfth month,
Jì'ān's illness became severe.
The emperor and empress visited a Buddhist temple to burn incense,
weeping and praying earnestly,
and granted a limited amnesty to prisoners within five hundred lǐ.
That night,
he passed away.
His posthumous title was Yīngdào Crown Prince,
and he was buried beside Xīnglíng.
The emperor escorted him to Wūzhǐhēishuǐ and then returned.
He commanded artisans to sculpt his image in Chǔqìng Temple,
and the emperor and empress visited the temple to place it.
Hǎilíng destroyed the palaces in Shàngjīng,
and the temple was also destroyed in the process.
Dàojì,
in the third year of Huángtǒng,
was appointed Prefect of Zhōngjīng.
Scholar Ālǎn was made Chief Inspector,
and Zhāng Xuánsù was made Co-Inspector,
to assist and guide him.
Soon after, he was enfeoffed as Wèi Wáng,
and his mother was enfeoffed as Worthy Consort.
Initially, he lived outside,
but from then on, he was raised in the palace.
Not long after,
Xīzōng, in anger, had him killed.
A eulogy states: In the early days of the dynasty, institutions were not yet established.
Tàizōng and Xīzōng both ascended the throne from the position of Ānbānbólìliè.
Ānbānbólìliè,
in Chinese, means "the most honored official."
Xīzōng's establishment of Jì'ān as Crown Prince
was the beginning of regularizing titles and positions
and establishing institutions.
Xié Mǎo Ālǐ.
His father, Húntǎn,
joined us during Mùzōng's reign,
and achieved numerous military merits.
Ālǐ, at seventeen, followed his paternal uncle, Húmágǔ, to suppress Zhàdū,
and captured Zhàdū's younger brother, Shālǐzhī.
Gāolí (Goryeo) built nine cities in Gélǎn Diàn.
Húntǎn attacked them,
encountering the enemy at Mùlǐmén Diàn.
After a long and fierce battle,
Ālǐ brandished a spear and rode to stab their general in the midst of the formation,
and the enemy subsequently collapsed.
Húntǎn and Shí Shìhuān joined forces at Túmén Shuǐ.
Ālǐ was the first to defeat the enemy troops,
taking two of their cities.
When Gāolí invaded,
our troops garrisoned strategic points,
preventing their advance,
so they withdrew.
Ālǐ pursued and caught up with them at Gélǎn Shuǐ.
The Gāolí people scrambled to flee across the ice.
Ālǐ took advantage of this,
killing and plundering almost all of them.
He then joined forces with Shí Shìhuān.
On the way, they encountered five myriad enemy troops
and routed them.
Again, he and Shí Shìhuān met seven myriad enemies.
Ālǐ was the first to ascend [the battlements/charge],
and fiercely attacked, utterly defeating them.
Shí Shìhuān said:
"Within a single day,
you have thrice defeated powerful enemies.
How could your achievements be forgotten!"
Thereupon, he rewarded him generously.
Wòsài and Wūdǔběn were attacking Tuójí Chéng.
Ālǐ breached the city wall to create a gate.
By then, dusk had fallen,
and they could not enter.
He guarded it with troops,
and the next morning, they captured the city.
Wūdǔběn bestowed upon him armor and a warhorse.
Following the attack, they captured Níngjiāng Zhōu,
and he was appointed Měng'ān.
He also followed in attacking Xìn Zhōu and Bīn Zhōu,
capturing both.
When people from Liáo came to attack Bó Jǐn Hūshā Lí Chéng,
Ālǐ led over a hundred cavalry to relieve it.
The Liáo army numbered several myriad.
Ālǐ had few troops,
so he ordered his soldiers to tear their clothes into many banners.
When they emerged from the mountain valleys,
the Liáo army, seeing them from afar,
fled.
Sū and Fù Zhōu rebelled,
with their forces reaching ten myriad.
The neighboring Nǚzhí people all took refuge with Tàiwèi Húshā,
building a stronghold for defense.
The enemy besieged them in several layers.
The defenders' provisions and fodder were exhausted.
Cattle and horses began eating each other's manes and tails.
People exchanged children to eat.
At night,
two men were lowered out [of the city]
to report the emergency to Ālǐ.
Ālǐ rushed there.
They attacked from both inside and outside,
defeating their forces at Pìlí Mìhǎn Shuǐ,
slaughtering almost all of them.
The water ceased to flow because of it.
At Púlígǔ Húshíjí Shuǐ and Mǎhán Dǎo, in over ten battles,
they defeated several hundred thousand troops.
Qìdān and Xī people gathered a thousand boats,
intending to enter the sea.
Ālǐ intercepted them with twenty-seven boats.
He was struck by a stray arrow,
lay in the boat,
and only revived in the middle of the night.
The enemy ships had already entered Wángjiā Dǎo.
That very night, he took the sea route and pursued them.
The enemy fled to treacherous terrain to resist.
Ālǐ used cavalry to intercept and attack.
He was struck by stray arrows again,
but fought bravely without retreating,
ultimately defeating them,
capturing all their boats.
Thereupon,
Sū and Fù Zhōu, and Pó Sù Lù were all pacified.
He attacked Xiǎn Zhōu,
captured Língshān Xiàn,
took Liángyú Wù,
and defeated Yúdǔ's forces.
His achievements were all the most outstanding.
Later, he and Sǎndǔlǔ garrisoned Gāo Zhōu.
Qìdān Zhāogǔyá and Jiǔjīn combined with several myriad troops from Xīngzhōng to attack Húlí Tè Zhài.
Ālǐ led eight Mòkè (companies) of troops to relieve it.
Húlí Tè had gone ahead,
and was defeated below the city.
Ālǐ pointed to over twenty scarlet-robed figures in front of the formation and said:
"These must be the bandit chiefs!"
He waved his troops forward to fiercely attack,
killing all of them.
The remaining forces utterly collapsed.
Troops from Láizhōu and Xízhōu besieged Húlí Tè Chéng.
Hearing that Ālǐ was coming to relieve it,
they immediately lifted the siege and departed.
Jīnmǔ was suppressing Zhāng Jué.
When troops emerged from the Lóufēng Kǒu mountain valley,
Ālǐ, Sǎndǔlǔ,
and Hūlúbǔ, three Měng'ān, defeated them.
Zōngwàng replaced Jīnmǔ in suppressing Zhāng Jué.
Ālǐ again defeated the Píngzhōu troops.
When attacking Sòng,
Ālǐ separately attacked the Sòng forces
and defeated them.
In the battle of Mèngyáng,
Ālǐ held the bridge crossing and fought fiercely.
The following year,
in the second expedition against Sòng,
they reached Bǎozhōu and Zhōngshān,
repeatedly defeating them.
They advanced to besiege Zhēndìng.
Ālǐ, along with Lóushì and Huòlú, took advantage of the wind to set fires,
burning their watchtowers and turrets.
All the armies then ascended,
capturing the city.
When the army reached the river,
Niángē Húsā attacked and drove away the Sòng people,
securing the river ford.
Several thousand troops then crossed the river.
The various generals divided and entered Dàmíng's territory.
Ālǐ defeated four hundred enemy soldiers, annihilating them all,
and then besieged Biàn.
That night, troops from Biàn sallied out to burn the siege equipment.
Ālǐ and Mòkè Chángsūn Yáng'ā repelled them,
and their forces were utterly routed.
They returned to attack Zhàozhōu
and secured its surrender.
In the sixth year of Tiānhuì (1128),
when attacking the Sòng emperor,
they captured Yánggǔ and Xīnxian,
defeated eighty thousand Hǎizhōu troops,
and Hǎizhōu surrendered.
They destroyed over ten thousand bandit ships at Liángshān Pō.
They persuaded the bandits of Téngyáng, Dōngpíng, and Tàishān to surrender.
When bandits attacked Fànxiàn,
they were driven away,
and seven hundred boats were captured.
Zōngbì captured Suīyáng.
He, along with Wūyán Púlúhún, first went with two thousand men to persuade Shòuchūn to surrender,
and prepared boats on the Huái Shuǐ.
At that time, Kāngmín had gathered four hundred merchant ships near Shòuchūn.
Shùlièsù, with four hundred cavalry, defeated Kāngmín,
beheading several thousand.
Along with Dānghǎi and Dàlā, they defeated ten myriad bandits south of the Huái River.
By the time they reached the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
they had repeatedly defeated Sòng forces,
capturing two hundred boats.
When Zōngbì reached Jiāngníng,
Ālǐ and Púlúhún separately secured the surrender of Guǎngdé Jūn,
and advanced first towards Hángzhōu.
About ten *lǐ* from Hángzhōu,
they encountered two thousand Sòng ambush troops,
who captured thirty of our vanguard armored soldiers.
Ālǐ ordered all his troops to dismount and fight hand-to-hand.
The ambush troops were defeated,
and all were forced into the water and died.
When Zōngbì reached Yúháng,
the Sòng emperor had fled to Míngzhōu.
Ālǐ and Púlúhún, with four thousand elite cavalry, raided him,
defeated the Dōngguān forces,
crossed the Cáoe Jiāng,
and defeated Sòng forces at Gāoqiáo Zhèn.
Upon reaching Míngzhōu,
they suffered considerable setbacks.
The Sòng emperor had already entered the sea,
so they retreated to Yúyáo.
Zōngbì sent Dānghǎi to cross the river with his army,
and subsequently captured Míngzhōu,
seizing the Sòng prefect Zhào Bó'è.
They advanced to Chāngguó Xiàn.
The Sòng emperor fled from Chāngguó to Wēnzhōu.
They pursued by sea for over three hundred *lǐ*,
but did not catch him.
Thereupon, they destroyed Míngzhōu,
and returned north with Zōngbì.
Ruìzōng (睿宗) campaigned in Shǎnxī (陝西),
stationed at Jīngzhōu (涇州).
Ālǐ (阿里) first captured Wèizhōu (渭州).
Ruìzōng (睿宗) then proceeded to Xīhé (熙河).
Ālǐ (阿里), Xiéhē (斜喝), and Hán Cháng (韓常), three *mĕng'ān* (猛安), formed the vanguard.
In the twelfth year,
he supervised water transport with Gāo Biāo (高彪).
When the Sòng (宋) obstructed the Bózhōu (亳州) river route with their naval forces,
he defeated them,
pursuing and slaying them for over sixty *lǐ* (里),
capturing their general Xiāo Tōng (蕭通).
He broke the water stockade of the bandits at Liánshuǐ (漣水),
obtaining all their large ships,
and then captured the Liánshuǐ (漣水) military command,
recruiting and pacifying its people.
During the Tiānjuàn (天眷) era,
bandits occupied Shízhōu (石州),
and Ālǐ (阿里) campaigned against them.
Niángē Húsā (粘割胡撒) and his unit were the first to ascend,
and they subsequently captured the city,
pacifying Shízhōu (石州).
Zōngbì (宗弼) again attacked Sòng (宋),
Ālǐ (阿里) was already old,
so he supervised the construction of warships.
When Sòng (宋) declared itself a vassal,
an imperial edict bestowed ten million cash upon Ālǐ (阿里).
From the time he first tied up his hair and joined the army,
he fought dozens of battles, large and small,
and was particularly skilled with boats and ships.
In campaigns on the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers,
he never failed to participate.
People of the time called him the "Water Star."
He served as the Military Commissioner of the Diélǐ (迭里) Department,
and successively held the posts of Military Governor of Shùnyì (順義) and Tàiníng (泰寧) commands,
and Governor of Guīdé (歸德) and Jìnán (濟南) prefectures.
In the early Tiāndé (天德) era,
he retired from office,
was promoted to Special Grand Master,
and enfeoffed as a Prince.
According to the Zhènglóng (正隆) regulations, he was enfeoffed as Duke of Hánguó (韓國).
He was summoned to the imperial court
and ordered to build warships.
He died of illness
at the age of seventy-eight,
and was posthumously named Zhìmǐn (智敏).
Ālǐ (阿里) was loyal and upright by nature,
and possessed great strategies.
He and his brothers were fond of each other.
His family was originally wealthy,
and he gave his own *mĕng'ān* (猛安) and all his property to his younger brother Àibálǐ (愛拔里).
Àibálǐ (愛拔里) refused to accept,
and fled for over a year,
but Ālǐ (阿里) eventually gave it to him.
Tūhésù (突合速) was a son of the imperial clan,
from Náhǎnsāi (拏罕塞).
Initially, he served under the *wànhù* (萬戶) Shíjiānú (石家奴).
He once led a detachment to break the mountain bandits in Yúnzhōng (雲中).
When Zōngwàng (宗望) attacked Píngzhōu (平州),
he sent Tūhésù (突合速) to suppress the bandits in Yìngzhōu (應州).
