He pacified them,
comforted and settled the people, and returned.
When they later attacked Sòng (宋),
he was in Zōnghàn’s (宗翰) army.
With eight *móukè* (謀克), he broke through the garrison of tens of thousands at Shílǐngguān (石嶺關),
slaughtering almost all of them.
When the army reached Tàiyuán (太原),
Qíxiàn (祁縣) surrendered but then rebelled,
so Tūhésù (突合速) attacked and captured it.
He then advanced to take Wénshuǐxiàn (文水縣).
Afterwards, he followed the various commanders to establish garrisons in the territory of Fénzhōu (汾州).
The Sòng (宋) military commanders of Hédōng (河東), Hǎo Zhònglián (郝仲連) and Zhāng Sīzhèng (張思正),
and the Shǎnxī (陝西) military commander Zhāng Guānsuǒ (張關索) and his commander Mǎ Zhōng (馬忠),
combined their forces of tens of thousands to provide aid.
He defeated them all.
When Zōnghàn (宗翰) marched south to Lù (潞) and returned,
Tàiyuán (太原) had not yet been taken,
so Wányán Yínzhúkě (完顏銀术可) was left to take overall command of the various armies
and manage that region.
At this point,
a large Sòng (宋) relief force arrived.
Tūhésù (突合速), Mǎ Wǔ (馬五), and Wòlǔ (沃魯) defeated four thousand Sòng (宋) soldiers at Wénshuǐ (文水).
Hearing that the Sòng (宋) general Huáng Dí (黃迪) and others had thirty thousand soldiers barricaded on the western mountain of the county,
he again joined forces with Gěng Shǒuzhōng (耿守忠) with nine thousand men to attack them,
killing over eighty thousand people,
and capturing a great number of horses and supplies.
Sòng (宋) Commissioner Yáo Gǔ (姚古) led his troops to Lóngzhōugǔ (隆州谷).
Tūhésù (突合速) and Bálí sù (拔离速) defended against them with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry.
Zhǒng Shīzhōng (种師中) with ten thousand troops occupied Yúcì (榆次).
Yínzhúkě (銀术可) then summoned Tūhésù (突合速),
made him divide his troops in half and return,
and joined forces with Huónǚ (活女) and others with eight thousand men to defeat them,
beheading Shīzhōng (師中) at Shāxiónglǐng (殺熊嶺).
The Sòng (宋) general Zhāng Hào (張灝) encamped with ten thousand soldiers in the vicinity of Wénshuǐ (文水).
He again joined Bálí sù (拔离速) to defeat them.
Lùzhōu (潞州) rebelled again,
with Sòng (宋) troops numbering one hundred and seventy thousand.
Gǔlā (骨●), Tūhésù (突合速), and Bálí sù (拔离速) were all besieged.
Tūhésù (突合速) commanded his soldiers
to dismount and fight fiercely,
and they successfully broke out of the encirclement.
When they launched the second campaign against Sòng (宋),
Zōnghàn (宗翰) ordered Lóushì (婁室) to lead the army and quickly advance to Biàn (汴).
When Lóushì (婁室) reached Zézhōu (澤州),
Tūhésù (突合速) and Wòlǔ (沃魯) with five hundred cavalry served as the vanguard,
going to recruit Héyáng (河陽).
They first occupied the ford on the Yellow River.
The Sòng (宋) army of over ten thousand men formed a battle array with their backs to the water.
They advanced and defeated them,
pushing them all into the water,
and then captured Héyáng (河陽).
When Biànjīng (汴京) was pacified,
the various generals headed west to Shǎnjīn (陝津),
subduing and stabilizing the prefectures and counties of Hédōng (河東).
Tūhésù (突合速) captured Xiànzhōu (憲州),
encountered its relief forces,
defeated them,
and captured their general alive.
Bóhǎi Jǐn (孛菫), Nóngguī (濃瑰), Shùlǔ (术魯) and others attacked Bǎodé (保德),
but had not taken it.
Tūhésù (突合速) advanced with his troops to assist in the attack.
Ladders and siege towers advanced together,
and they successfully captured the city.
Bóhǎi Jǐn (孛菫) Wūgǔ (烏谷) attacked Shízhōu (石州),
but was repeatedly defeated,
losing three of his generals,
and several hundred soldiers perished.
Tūhésù (突合速) said to Wūgǔ (烏谷):
"The enemy are all infantry;
we cannot fight with cavalry."
Wūgǔ (烏谷) replied:
"I heard that the bandits use demonic arts;
they draw horses to bind their feet,
making them run as fast as galloping horses.
How can infantry combat catch up to them?"
Tūhésù (突合速) laughed and said:
"How can such a thing be?"
He then ordered all his troops to dismount and fight,
and they completely annihilated them.
In the sixth year,
Zōngfǔ (宗輔) stationed his army at Dèngzhōu (鄧州).
Tūhésù (突合速), Mǎ Wǔ (馬五), and Bálí sù (拔离速) went west to capture Jūn (均) and Fáng (房),
and subsequently took those cities.
They attacked Táng (唐), Cài (蔡), Chén (陳) prefectures, and Yǐngchāngfǔ (潁昌府),
all of which they captured.
In the early Tiānjuàn (天眷) era,
he was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhāngdé (彰德) Command.
In the third year,
he became the Marshal's Left Supervisor of the Army.
In the eighth year of Huángtǒng (皇統),
he was transferred to be Governor of Jìnán (濟南).
During the Tiāndé (天德) era,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Dìngguó (定國),
and granted the hereditary position of *qiānhù* (千戶).
He died
at the age of seventy-two.
In the second year of Zhènglóng (正隆),
he was posthumously granted the title Duke of Yìngguó (應國).
Initially,
Tūhésù (突合速) received his enfeoffment through his secondary wife,
and her sons were therefore able to inherit his *mĕng'ān* (猛安).
When they divided the property and lived separately,
the secondary wife's sons took twelve hundred slaves,
while the principal wife's sons received eight hundred slaves.
After a long time,
the principal wife's sons contended for the inheritance.
The dispute remained unresolved for years,
and their family assets were almost exhausted.
Of the principal wife's sons' slaves, two hundred remained,
while only fifty or sixty of the secondary wife's sons' slaves remained.
When Shìzōng (世宗) heard that Tūhésù’s (突合速) sons were impoverished,
he asked his close officials.
They fully explained the reason for the inheritance dispute.
Shìzōng (世宗) said:
"How could the secondary wife's sons be allowed to receive the enfeoffment?"
Therefore, the eldest son of the principal wife inherited.
Wūyán Púlúhún (烏延蒲盧渾) was from Wūgǔdíhūnshān (烏古敵昏山) in Hélǎnlù (曷懶路).
His father, Bógǔlá (孛古剌),
was a Superior General of the Dragon and Tiger Guard.
Púlúhún (蒲盧渾) possessed extraordinary physical strength
and could draw a bow and shoot an arrow two hundred and seventy paces.
He and his elder brother Gǔshāhǔ (鶻沙虎) both served in Jīamǔ’s (闍母) army due to their bravery and robustness,
residing under his tent.
They fought bravely and earned merit in the attack on Huánglóngfǔ (黃龍府).
When Jīamǔ (闍母) was defeated at Tùěrshān (兔耳山),
Zhāng Jué (張覺) reorganized his army and returned.
The other generals dared not fight.
Púlúhún (蒲盧渾) ascended a mountain to observe them,
then deceived the generals, saying:
"The enemy army is small;
an immediate attack can break them.
If they enter the city,
they cannot be controlled again."
So they engaged in battle
and defeated them.
Guō Yàoshī and Cài Jìng surrendered Yānjīng.
Púlúhún led ninety horsemen to first scout the movements of the city residents.
Then he led a thousand Hàn soldiers,
subordinate to Wányán Méngshì, to attack Zhēndìng.
They advanced to attack Zànhuáng,
capturing it,
and seized over ten thousand people, animals, armor, and weapons.
When Biànchéng was breached,
it was already dusk.
The Sòng forces still fought fiercely;
a spear pierced Púlúhún’s hand,
but he fought even harder,
and consequently defeated the Sòng army.
He was awarded fifty liǎng of gold.
Ruìzōng, acting as the Right Vice Grand Marshal,
had already secured Guān and Shǎn,
and discussed taking the various prefectures beyond Jiàn.
Subsequently, Heshàngyuán was captured.
The Grand Marshal’s Office, by imperial decree, appointed Púlúhún as the Grand Military Governor of the Western Hébĕi Circuit.
When the Sòng emperor was in Yángzhōu,
Púlúhún and Méngshì led ten thousand cavalry to assault him.
The Sòng emperor had already crossed the Jiāng,
but they defeated his remaining forces.
Later, he and Xiá Mǎo Ālǐ followed Zōngbì from Huáixī, crossed the Jiāng, and took Jiāngníng.
Zōngbì entered Hángzhōu,
and the Sòng emperor fled to Míngzhōu,
then again to Wēnzhōu.
He was pursued by sea for over three hundred lǐ.
They razed Míngzhōu and returned.
The account is in the biography of Ālǐ.
In the second year of Tiānjuàn (1139),
he was granted the title of Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn,
and appointed as the Commander of Ānguó Army,
but resigned due to illness.
In the sixth year of Huángtǒng (1146),
he was appointed hereditary Mǒukè,
and recalled to serve as Yán’ān Yǐn.
He was given a suit of imperial robes,
and soon retired.
When Hǎilíng moved the capital to Zhōngdū,
he was recalled to serve as Guīdé Yǐn.
The appointment was conferred at his home,
and he was granted a silver tablet, a suit of robes, and a jade túhú,
and dispatched to his post by post-horse.
Púlúhún remained for several tens of days,
having already missed his deadline for reporting.
He was again allowed to retire.
He was summoned to the capital,
and upon reaching Jìzhōu,
he met Hǎilíng at a hunting ground.
The next day,
he joined the hunt
and captured a fox.
Hǎilíng said:
"You are old,
yet still able to gallop and strike beasts,
so vigorous and agile."
He was given imperial robes
and enfeoffed as Bīnguó Gōng.
He was appointed Junior Preceptor of the Crown Prince,
promoted to Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince,
reassigned as Zhēndìng Yǐn,
and then entered to oversee the affairs of the Grand Imperial Clan Court.
Shortly thereafter, during the campaign against Sòng,
he served as Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Right Leading Army with his original rank.
The army reached Xīcǎishí.
Hǎilíng wanted to cross the Jiāng,
but Púlúhún said:
"The Sòng army's ships are tall and large,
while our ships are low and small.
I fear we cannot cross immediately."
Hǎilíng angrily said:
"Did you, in the past, follow Liáng Wáng to pursue Zhào Gòu on a sea island,
also with large boats?
Now you are hindering our military affairs.
Even if we cannot cross the Jiāng immediately,
it will only be a small loss.
You are already seventy years old;
even if you cherish your life,
is there any reason not to die?
Tomorrow, you and Bēndǔ shall cross first."
However, he was later stopped again.
Instead, another general was sent to cross the Jiāng first.
Their small boats were unsuitable for battle,
and they suffered a defeat.
Two Mĕng'ān and over two hundred soldiers were all lost.
Hǎilíng was assassinated,
and the army returned.
In the second year of Dàdìng (1162),
he went to Zhōngdū for an audience,
and was appointed Tōkyō Liúshǒu.
Shìzōng summoned him and asked his age.
He replied:
"Your servant is seventy-three this year."
The Emperor said:
"You are an experienced general,
long skilled in military affairs.
Though old,
your spirit has not waned."
He was then ordered to report to his post,
overseeing affairs once every ten days or month.
He was granted a suit of robes,
promoted in rank to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and still enfeoffed as Bīnguó Gōng.
That year,
he died.
In the eighteenth year (1178),
his grandson Zhāhǔ was promoted to Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn,
inherited the hereditary Mĕng'ān of Wūgǔdí Hūnshān,
and personally managed a Mǒukè.
Chìzhǎn Huī, courtesy name Zhòngmíng,
whose ancestors were formerly attached to Liáo,
resided in Zhānghuángbǎo,
and thus often used Zhāng as his surname.
Later, his family moved to Láizhōu.
Huī had a heroic and imposing physique,
and was magnanimous with strategic vision.
As a youth, he studied in the local schools.
In the late Liáo period, for his achievements in defeating bandits,
he was appointed Deputy Envoy of the Reception Office,
commanding the garrison troops of the four prefectures of Lái, Xí, Qiān, and Rùn.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ (1122), he surrendered.
He was still ordered to lead his troops,
following Shēmǔ to pacify the prefectures of Xìngzhōngfǔ Yì, Jǐn, and others.
When Zhāng Jué was defeated,
he contributed significantly to all these efforts.
He provided fifteen thousand shí of grain to assist the army,
and was appointed Míngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Zōngwàng first attacked Sòng,
during the Battle of Mèngyáng,
the enemy's central army directly advanced on Zōngwàng's camp.
Huī and the other generals defeated them,
pursuing and killing them to the city walls.
After the army returned,
he repeatedly distinguished himself in battle.
The following year,
during the second campaign against Sòng,
Bǎozhōu and Zhēndìng were captured,
and Huī participated in all of them.
They advanced to besiege Biàn.
One night, the Sòng forces sent out twenty thousand troops to burn our siege engines.
Huī, with the troops of two Mǒukè, attacked and routed them.
Whenever troops from the city came out to resist,
wherever Huī confronted them,
he was victorious.
After conquering Sòng and returning,
he followed in the attack on Héjiān.
The enemy general Lǐ Chéng came with troops from Xióng and Mò to provide aid.
Huī and his unit met and attacked them.
His horse was wounded and he fell,
but Huī immediately rose and fought on foot,
ultimately defeating Chéng's forces.
On that day,
he fought seven battles and won all of them.
Many enemies were forced to their deaths in the moat.
Huī's arms were also struck by several stray arrows.
The bandit general Liú Xiānsheng, with twenty thousand troops, launched a night attack on the camp.
Huī fought fiercely until dawn,
when the bandits finally fled in defeat,
all drowning in the water.
Huī then pressed the city walls and fought fiercely.
This continued for months.
The various armies launched a combined assault from all four sides,
and finally captured it.
He was granted the additional title of Guìzhōu Guǎnnèi Guānchásǐ,
and then remained to pacify Héjiān.
At that time, the residents had all been plundered by the soldiers,
and few elderly or young survived.
Huī issued an order that soldiers could ransom them back.
Soon after,
everyone settled back as before.
He followed Ruìzōng to manage affairs in Shāndōng.
After capturing Qīngzhōu,
he again followed Shēmǔ to attack Wéizhōu.
Huī led his sub-officers to be the first to ascend.
Inside the city, accumulated straw and fodder, fueled by the wind, set fire to and launched stones from siege machines.
Huī led his officers and soldiers, charging and descending through the danger,
and fought fiercely to defeat them.
When the army returned,
he again used thirty cavalry to defeat the enemy at Fànqiáo.
The Grand Marshal's Office, by imperial decree, granted him the additional title of Jìngjiāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
As they advanced to attack,
a catapult shot from the city
nearly hit Huī,
brushing against and tearing his armored skirt.
Huī attacked with even greater fervor,
and eventually captured the city.
He then followed in the attack on Sìzhōu,
capturing it.
Returning to garrison Wènyáng,
he defeated a large bandit force at Liángshān Luò,
capturing over a thousand boats.
Moving his army to attack Jìzhōu,
after defeating the enemy forces,
he then pressed the city walls and persuaded them with arguments of good and ill fortune.
The entire city then surrendered.
Huī strictly disciplined his soldiers,
allowing no slightest transgression.
From then on, prefectures like Cáo and Shàn all heard of his reputation and submitted.
Zōngbì 宗弼 attacked Jiāngnán 江南.
He crossed the Huái 淮 River.
The Sòng 宋 general Shíkāngmín 時康民 led 170,000 troops to resist.
Tàipíng 太平 led his own command to strike,
defeating them.
Again, with 2,000 cavalry, he and Dānghǎi 當海 defeated 100,000 bandits from Huáinán 淮南,
killing over 10,000 men.
Wáng Shàn 王善 came to surrender.
When about to cross the Jiāng 江 River,
Tàipíng's 太平's army crossed first.
While the boats were still far from the bank,
the Sòng 宋 soldiers were arrayed at the river mouth.
Tàipíng 太平 saw that the water was fordable,
so he waved his troops to abandon their boats and swiftly rushed the bank to attack them.
The Sòng 宋 troops fled,
and the main army followed, crossing the river.
Soon after, they encountered Dù Chōng's 杜充's 60,000 troops west of Jiāngníng 江寧.
Tàipíng 太平 and Gǔlúbǔ 鶻盧補 attacked and routed them.
The army returned,
and Tàipíng 太平 was left as the Military Commissioner (Dūtǒng 都統) of Yángzhōu 揚州,
tasked with governing the area between the Huái 淮 River, the sea, and Gāoyóu 高郵.
He was again appointed Prefect (Yǐn 尹) of Héjiān 河間,
simultaneously commanding the troops and horses of the eastern circuit of Héběi 河北.
In the eleventh year,
he had an audience.
Tàizōng 太宗 granted him a seat,
consoled and praised him for a long time,
and specially promoted him to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo 太子太保).
He was given one suit of clothes, two horses, and saddles, bridles, and armor.
His title was changed to Right Grand Marshall's Supervisor (Yuánshuài Yòu Dūjiān 元帥右都監).
After the state of Qí 齊 was abolished,
Tàipíng 太平 guarded Biànjīng 汴京.
Xīzōng 熙宗, considering Tàipíng's 太平's long service,
bestowed an imperial decree to honor and distinguish him.
In the third year of Tiānjuàn 天眷,
the Han and Bohai Qīanhù Móukè 千戶謀克 were abolished.
As Tàipíng 太平 was an old minister,
he alone was ordered to retain his hereditary Qīanhù 千戶 status.
That year,
he was appointed Right Military Supervisor (Yuánshuài Yòu Jiānjūn 元帥右監軍).
Zōngbì 宗弼 again attacked Sòng 宋.
The Sòng 宋 people declared themselves vassals and sued for peace,
so the army returned.
Tàipíng 太平 alone remained in Biàn 汴,
acting as the Grand Marshall's office.
In the third year of Huángtǒng 皇統,
he was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司.
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Left Military Supervisor (Zuǒ Jiānjūn 左監軍).
In the second year of Tiāndé 天德,
he was changed to Right Deputy Grand Marshall (Yòu Fù Yuánshuài 右副元帥),
concurrently acting as Left Censor-in-chief (Zuǒ Chéng 左丞) of the Mobile Chancellery (Xíngtái 行臺).
He was promoted to Manager of Affairs of the Mobile Chancellery (Píngzhāng Xíngtái Shěngshì 平章行臺省事),
then advanced to Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng 右丞相) of the Mobile Chancellery,
retaining his position as Right Deputy Grand Marshall.
Hǎilíng 海陵 suspected the Left Deputy Grand Marshall Sālìhē 撒离喝,
so he appointed Tàipíng 太平 as Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng 左丞相) of the Mobile Chancellery,
and made Tàipíng 太平 observe him.
An edict ordered that Sālìhē 撒离喝 was not to be involved in military matters.
Sālìhē 撒离喝 did not know Hǎilíng's 海陵's true intention,
and often contended with Tàipíng 太平 over military affairs without success,
thus creating a rift between them.
Hǎilíng 海陵 eventually killed Sālìhē 撒离喝,
summoned Tàipíng 太平 to court,
appointed him Right Chancellor (Shàngshū Yòu Chéngxiàng 尚書右丞相),
and enfeoffed him as Prince (Jùnwáng 郡王) of Shénlù 神麓.
In the fourth year,
he requested retirement,
and became the Grand Guardian of the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng Liúshǒu 東京留守).
In the third year of Zhēnyuán 貞元,
he was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅),
overseeing the affairs of the Three Departments (Sānsěng 三省),
and was successively enfeoffed as Prince (Wáng 王) of Hàn Hàn.
In the twelfth month,
he fell ill.
Hǎilíng 海陵 personally visited his residence to inquire about him.
That year,
he passed away,
at the age of sixty-eight.
Hǎilíng 海陵 personally mourned him,
and issued an edict to suspend official business for three days,
and prohibit music for three days.
The three-day banquet for the envoys of the three nations
was held without music from the Imperial Music Bureau (Jiàofāng 敎坊).
He ordered the Left Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ 左宣徽使) Jìng Sìhuī 敬嗣暉 to announce this.
He was posthumously honored as Grand Preceptor (Tàishī 太師) and Prince (Wáng 王) of Jìn 晉,
with the posthumous title Jiézhōng 傑忠.
An envoy was sent to escort his coffin back for burial.
During Zhènglóng 正隆, his princely title was revoked,
and he was posthumously granted Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅) and Duke (Guógōng 國公) of Liáng 梁.
His son was Pán 磐.
Pán 磐's original name was Púsùyuè 蒲速越.
As the son of a high minister, he rose through official ranks to become the Prefect (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Dēngzhōu 登州,
and inherited the rank of Měng'ān 猛安.
In the third year of Dàdìng 大定,
he was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Sōngzhōu 嵩州,
and rendered meritorious service by accompanying Púsàn Zhōngyì 僕散忠義 in attacking Sòng 宋.
In the fifth year,
he was summoned to be the Supervisor of Imperial Charms (Fúbǎoláng 符寶郎),
and promoted to Commander of the Imperial Guard (Gǒngwèi Zhídūzhīhuīshǐ 拱衞直都指揮使).
Initially,
Pán 磐, for his meritorious service in attacking Sòng 宋,
was promoted one rank.
Pán 磐 felt this was too little,
and somewhat expressed it in words.
The emperor heard of it,
ordered officials to investigate,
and he was given one hundred and fifty strokes of the rod.
His position was changed to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍).
An imperial edict sought good bows,
and Pán 磐 took many for himself.
Also, when guards came on duty,
he would replace them according to his own will.
The guard Lóushì 婁室 reported this matter,
and an edict ordered the Palace Investigation Bureau (Diǎnjiǎn Sī 點檢司) to interrogate him.
Pán 磐 had a sister who was a Noble Lady (Bǎolín 寶林) in the palace.
Pán 磐 entrusted the inner attendant Sēng'ér Yuánsīzhōng 僧兒員思忠 to speak to the Noble Lady, saying,
"I am innocent,
but the interrogators are pressuring me
to falsely confess."
The Noble Lady appealed to the emperor.
The emperor was angered,
gave Sēng'ér 僧兒 one hundred strokes,
and demoted Pán 磐 to Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ 防禦使) of Lǒngzhōu 隴州.
The emperor warned him, saying:
"You were in a close and secret position,
yet you stubbornly acted on your own.
Because of your father's merits,
I cannot bear to abandon you.
For now, I order you to be assigned to an outer post.
You should reflect and strive."
He was changed to Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ 防禦使) of Bózhōu 亳州,
then promoted to Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Wǔníngjūn 武寧軍.
He was later stripped of his name for an offense.
He was reinstated as Prefect (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Hánzhōu 韓州,
changed to Prefect (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Qízhōu 祁州,
and again, for an offense,
had four official ranks stripped
and was dismissed from his post.
After a long time,
the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng 尚書省) memorialized,
"Dàpán 大磐 is of suitable age,"
The emperor said:
"This violent and headstrong person
has repeatedly violated penal statutes,
and cannot be reused.
Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅) Dàpíng 大太平 had no other direct heir,
so his hereditary Měng'ān Móukè 猛安謀克
cannot be changed."
Ālíbǔ 阿离補 was a son of the imperial clan,
descended from Jǐngzǔ 景祖.
He repeatedly participated in campaigns,
and rendered meritorious service in both the destruction of Liáo 遼 and the capture of Sòng 宋.
In the ninth year of Tiānhuì 天會,
Ruìzōng 睿宗 governed Shǎnxī 陝西.
Ālíbǔ 阿离補 was the Commander of the Left Wing (Zuǒyì Dūtǒng 左翼都統),
and with the Commander of the Right Wing (Yòuyì Dūtǒng 右翼都統) Zōngbì 宗弼,
pacified and settled the military prefectures of Gǒng 鞏, Táo 洮, Hé 河, Xīníng 西寧, Lán 蘭, Kuò 廓, etc.,
and the walled strongholds of Láibīn 來賓, Dìngyuǎn 定遠, Hézhèng 和政, Gānyù 甘峪, Níngtáo 寧洮, Ānlǒng 安隴, etc.,
as well as over forty garrisons, fortresses, and encampments of both indigenous and Han peoples.
The number of Han officials, soldiers, civilians, and indigenous tribal chiefs was immense.
Thus, the two circuits of Jīngyuán 涇原 and Xīhé 熙河 were all pacified.
An edict ordered that the remaining households of his elder brother Měng'ān Shālízhi 沙离質's direct command Móukè 謀克
be given to Ālíbǔ 阿离補 as a hereditary Móukè 謀克.
In the twelfth year of Tiānhuì 天會,
he became Right Grand Marshall's Supervisor (Yuánshuài Yòu Dūjiān 元帥右都監).
In the fifteenth year,
he was promoted to Left Military Supervisor (Zuǒ Jiānjūn 左監軍).
In the third year of Tiānjuàn 天眷,
he accompanied Zōngbì 宗弼 in recapturing Hénán 河南,
and was promoted to Left Deputy Grand Marshall (Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài 左副元帥).
In the third year of Huángtǒng 皇統,
he was enfeoffed as Duke (Guógōng 國公) of Tán 譚.
In the sixth year,
he became Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng 左丞相) of the Mobile Chancellery,
retaining his position as Grand Marshall.
That year,
he passed away.
During the Dàdìng ēn,
greatly honoring meritorious officials,
their portraits were hung in the Yǎnqìnggōng.
Huāndū died during Kāngzōng's time,
and did not get to participate in the rapid campaigns in Liáo and Sòng territories.
Nevertheless, among officials of different surnames, none surpassed him.
Therefore, the meritorious officials ranked in the Yǎnqìnggōng were: Dàiguógōng Huāndū,
Jīnyuánjùnwáng Shítǔmén,
Xúguógōng Húnhū,
Zhèngguógōng Màndūhē,
Púguógōng Shígǔnǎi,
Jìguógōng Púchá,
Hánguógōng Xié mǎo Ālí,
Yuánshuài Zuǒjiānjūn Bálí sù,
Lǔguógōng Púchá Shíjiānú,
Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū Méngshì,
Suíguógōng Huónǚ,
Tèjìn Tūgésù,
Qíguógōng Póluóhuǒ,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Wūyán Púlúhún,
Yítóng Sānsī Ālǔbǔ,
Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn Wūlíndá Tàiyù,
Tàishī Lǐng Sānsheng Shì Xù,
Tàifù Dàhē,
Dàxīng Yǐn Chìzhǎnhuī,
Jīnwúwèi Shàngjiāngjūn Yēlǜ Mǎwǔ,
Piàojíwèi Shàngjiāngjūn Háncháng bìng Ālí bǔ xián zhùxūn yān.
His sons were Yán and Fāng.
Yán has a separate biography.
Fāng, as a member of the imperial clan, rose through various official positions to Jīngzhào Shàoyǐn,
then transferred to Shǎnxīlù Tǒngjūn Dūjiān.
Fāng focused solely on acquiring wealth
and did not care for the military.
An imperial edict admonished him, saying:
"You are an old member of the imperial clan,
yet you are unrestrained and break the law,
only seeking profit.
I greatly detest this.
From now on,
should you do this again,
you will certainly be punished without pardon."
In the third year of Dàdìng (1163),
he was transferred to Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān,
then to Yuánshuài Zuǒjiānjūn,
and then made Shùntiānjūn Jiédùshǐ.
The Emperor said:
"You originally had no merit,
yet you have held prominent official positions.
You cannot get along with your colleagues and friends,
often falling out with them.
In Jīngzhào, your greed and meanness were widely known,
which is utterly disgraceful.
I believe that since you have passed middle age,
you will be able to reform.
Be careful not to do so again."
He was appointed Xīnánlù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
The court appointed Bīngbù Lángzhōng Gāotōng as Zhāotǎo Dūjiān
to assist him.
An edict to Tōng stated:
"When you arrive in Tiāndé,
do not blindly comply with your superior's wishes.
Review the soldiers along the border;
do not use weak or frail individuals,
and do not let servants replace soldiers in service.
The old custom of the Nǚzhí
was that during gatherings for food and drink,
they would enjoy riding and archery.
Now, however, they play board games (yì and shuānglù).
These should all be strictly prohibited,
and they should be made to practice riding and archery.
However, follow the convenience of their living arrangements
and do not gather them in a way that would disturb them."
After some time,
Fāng was impeached for forcibly buying two horses from a local resident,
had one rank stripped,
was dismissed from his position,
and demoted to Yàozhōu Cìshǐ.
Tōng was also removed from office due to corruption.
Fāng was later transferred to Hénghǎijūn Jiédùshǐ,
and then entered the court as Tóngqiān Dàzōngzhèngshì,
and Qiānshū Shūmìyuàn Shì.
Originally,
Ālǔbǔ was to be granted the position of Mókè,
but died before being enfeoffed.
Wūdài received it.
When Wūdài died,
Wútābǔ inherited it.
When Wútābǔ died,
Wūyěābǔ was to inherit it.
At this time,
Hǎilíng had already been demoted to a commoner.
Shìzōng believed that Wūdài was among Xīzōng's rebellious faction,
and his descendants should not be granted enfeoffment.
The enfeoffment was suspended for a long time.
However, Ālíbǔ's merits also could not be completely disregarded,
so a special edict allowed Fāng to inherit it.
The eulogy states: Xié mǎo Ālí, Tūgésù, Wūyán Púlúhún, Chìzhǎnhuī, Dàhē, and Ālíbǔ—these six individuals
were all considered "bear and tiger warriors" and loyal, unwavering ministers since the founding of the state.
Their accomplishments are worthy of record.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 19 Húmóupá, Dígūdié, Ātúhǎn, Jiágǔ Xiènú, Ālègēn Mòdūlú Huángguó Dígǔběn, Púchá Húzhǎn, Jiágǔ Wúlǐbǔ, Wáng Bólóng, Gāo Biāowēndíhǎn Púlǐtè, Bódétlíbǔ
Yēlǜ Huáiyì, Xiāo Wángjiānú Tiánhào, Zhào Yàn
Húmóupá was
a native of the Xiémǎo tribe of Jìjíshuǐ.
He was loyal, upright, generous, and benevolent by nature,
valued integrity and righteousness,
and was brave in battle.
His father, Āgǔtǔ,
was posthumously granted the title of Jīnwúwèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
During Mùzōng's reign,
Húmóupá submitted to the court,
first sending his son Níngjí through a secret path to present his submission.
Subsequently, Huólǐtuǎn was dispatched to join Húmóupá's army to attack and subdue various tribes.
He then led his troops,
along with his younger brothers Húmágǔ and Húntán, and his nephew Ālí, to capture various cities.
He followed Sāgǎi in defeating Wùtǎchéng,
and Mùzōng rewarded him repeatedly.
He defeated the Gāolí garrison.
He joined Shíshìhuān in suppressing various tribes.
When Púchá tribe's Yālǐbójiǎn and his brothers Húbā and Shuāngkuò wished to rebel and return to Liáo,
Húmóupá captured them
and sent them to Kāngzōng,
who bestowed lavish gifts upon him.
He achieved merit in defeating Gāolí's Hélǎndiàn and capturing Lǔchéng.
He died in the sixth year of Tiānfǔ (1122),
at the age of seventy-two.
During the Tiānjuàn era,
he was posthumously granted Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
Dígūdié was
a native of the Wēndíhǎn tribe.
His grandfather, Zāgǔnǎi,
and father, Āhúdié,
were hereditary chiefs of Húlùnshuǐ.
At over twenty years old, Dígūdié inherited his father's Mókè position,
attacked Níngjiāngzhōu,
defeated the Liáo reinforcements,
and captured armor, horses, and treasure.
He attacked and broke the Xī camp,
and when returning to Hánzhōu,
encountered two thousand enemies
and drove them away.
When Wòlǔgǔ fought the Liáo people at Xiánzhōu,
and the army was already retreating,
Dígūdié fought valiantly with his own troops.
The various armies rallied again
and utterly defeated them.
In the battle of Hùbùdágāng,
Yǐlǐbǔbójiǎn was trapped among the enemy,
and Dígūdié rescued him.
He attacked Huánglóngfǔ,
suffered several wounds,
and was awarded the rank of Měng'ān.
In the seventh year of Tiānfǔ (1123),
he followed the Emperor to Shānxī,
and died of illness,
at the age of forty-seven.
During the Tiānjuàn era,
he was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū.
Ātúhǎn was
a native of the Wēndíhǎn tribe.
At seventeen, he followed Sāgǎi and Wòdài in suppressing various tribes,
always leading the charge and fighting bravely.
When Gāolí built nine cities in Hélǎndiàn,
Wòsāi defended against them,
and Ātúhǎn was the vanguard.
Gāolí had troops stationed on an island.
Ātúhǎn led thirty men to cross by night,
burned their camps, stockades, and warships,
and utterly defeated them,
thereby capturing Jíchéng.
Subsequently, all eight cities fell,
and he made the greatest contribution.
When Liáo troops exited the east gate of Níngjiāngzhōu,
Ātúhǎn counter-attacked
and annihilated them all.
For this merit, he was granted the position of Mókè.
He followed in the attack on Huánglóngfǔ,
fought bravely,
suffered dozens of wounds,
and eventually ascended its walls.
Later, he and Wúlùn Shízhǔn reinforced Zhàosànchéng.
Ātúhǎn requested to take advantage of the enemy's unpreparedness to launch a swift attack.
They crossed Yìtuìshuǐ by night,
and the next morning
utterly defeated the enemy.
Wòlǔ reported his achievement,
and he was bestowed with silk and horses.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Tiānfǔ, he fell ill.
He was granted a fine horse.
An imperial edict stated:
“If you recover, ride it.”
He died at the age of sixty-five.
The Emperor lamented and grieved for him,
and sent an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices,
presenting the horse as a gift.
Ātúhǎn was filial and brotherly,
generous with his favors,
agile and skilled in hunting with arrows.
From horn wrestling to polo,
he mastered all these skills.
Jiágǔ Xiènú was
from Nàlǔhuǐ Hé in Lóngzhōu.
At the beginning of the dynasty,
his ancestor, Āhǎi, led his tribe to submit,
offering tools, armor, and weapons.
His father, Bùlāsù,
succeeded as Bójǐn of his tribe,
and followed Tàizǔ in his campaign against the Liáo.
He was granted the hereditary rank of Měng'ān,
personally oversaw Móukè,
and served as Dūtǒng of Gēlǎnlù.
Xiènú was
his eldest son.
He was tall with a bushy beard,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and conversant in both the large and small scripts of Nǚzhí and Qìdān, as well as Hàn characters.
After coming of age,
he followed his father to meet Tàizǔ,
who ordered him to wear a golden plaque
and take overall command of the Left Wing Guards.
Before Xījīng was captured,
Xiènú captured some captives from inside the city,
and thus learned that people had been secretly sent out of the city to seek help from outside.
The Dūtǒng Fǔ was able to prepare for this,
repelling the relief forces,
and Xījīng was subsequently taken.
Returning from Yānjīng,
he passed Pàntúní'ēnnà'ā,
and encountered the enemy in a pass.
Xiènú personally led his men,
shooting and killing two enemy vanguards.
The enemy scattered and fled.
Zǒngguǎn Púlǔhǔ presented him with armor and a horse.
Later, he took over his father's Měng'ān
and followed in the attack on Héshàng Yuán.
Exiting Xiānrén Guān,
the Sòng troops occupied a strategic position.
Měng'ān Chú'ézhī launched an assault but failed.
Xiènú selected fifty men from his command to fight,
and conquered the position.
When confronting Wú Jiè,
Wūlǐyǎ’s formation was disorganized.
Wú Jiè capitalized on this,
but Xiènú led his troops to counterattack,
and decisively defeated the enemy.
Considering his accumulated merits,
he inherited his father’s Měng'ān Móukè.
When Zōngbì recaptured Hénán and Shǎnxī,
the Sòng people attempted to send secret troops to raid the camps of Shírùn and others.
Xiènú, from Dàyǔ Zhèn in Wèinán, ambushed their hidden forces,
shooting their army commander.
The Sòng troops were defeated and fled,
and many banners, weapons, and armor were captured.
The Shuàifǔ rewarded him generously.
He was appointed as Huázhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He entered the court as Gōngbù Shìláng,
then was promoted to the Shàngshū of the same department.
He was later reassigned as Píngliáng Yǐn and Zhāoyìjūn Jiédùshǐ.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he passed away.
Ālègēn Méidōulǔ was
from Nàlín Hé in Shàngjīng,
later relocating to Méihēi Hé in Xiánpíng Lù.
He was imposing, with a beautiful beard and mustache,
brave, resolute, and skilled in archery.
At the beginning of the dynasty, during the campaign against Liáo,
Méidōulǔ was in the army,
leading Móukè and Měng'ān.
Whenever he encountered the enemy,
he would charge back and forth,
and no one dared to stand in his way,
hence all his battles were victorious.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
in recognition of his merits, he was promoted to Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn.
The following year,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Tōngyuǎnjūn Jiédùshǐ,
then reassigned as Yílàdū Cíxiángwěn.
He was granted the hereditary Móukè of Níngdǎhún Hé in his local region.
He served as Huázhōu Cìshǐ,
then reassigned as Zhàozhōu Fángyùshǐ and Púyǔ Lù Jiédùshǐ,
and promoted to Piàojì Shàngjiāngjūn.
He accumulated official positions to Jīnwúwèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
That year,
due to old age, he retired from office,
and passed away.
He was seventy-three years old.
Huángguó Dígǔběn
was from Xīngxiǎn Shuǐ, where his family had resided for generations.
He participated in the capture of Níngjiāng,
the taking of Xiánzhōu,
and the pacification of Dōngjīng Lù and various mountain strongholds and stockades,
all with distinction.
He followed Májí in defeating seven thousand Liáo troops led by General Héshàng Jiéshǐ at Shàngjīng,
and then defeated Nàyě’s army of twenty thousand.
Later, he again followed Májí and encountered the enemy at Ālín Diàn.
Májí was wounded
and unable to fight.
Dígǔběn led his troops to defeat them,
slaughtering almost all of them.
He participated in the attack on Huíhúchéng,
defeating their army of ninety thousand,
and defeated Mùjiàng Zhísā’s troops behind the mountains,
capturing many.
He defeated Zhāogǔyá’s army of three thousand,
and returned with their families.
When attacking Zhāng Jué in Píngzhōu,
Wúchūn was besieged on Xīshān.
Dígǔběn led troops to rescue him,
lifting the siege,
and captured five thousand hú of grain,
recruiting many surrendered households.
He participated in the pacification of Xīngzhōng,
calming and settling its people.
During the Tiānhuì period,
the grand army attacked Sòng.
Dígǔběn participated in taking Jùn, Kāidé, and Dàmíng,
as well as Jìnán, Gāotáng, Dì, and Mì prefectures.
During the Huángtǒng period,
due to his merits, he inherited the Móukè,
and moved to garrison as a Qiānhù in the Shouguāng Xiàn area.
In the sixth year,
he was granted the hereditary Qiānhù and Dìzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He died.
Púchá Húzhan was
from Ànchū Hǔshuǐ.
At eighteen, he joined the army.
When his father Tèsī died,
he inherited the Móukè.
During the Tiānfǔ period,
Xià sent thirty thousand troops out of Tiāndé Lù.
Húzhan followed Lóushì to meet them in battle.
With three hundred men,
he defeated two thousand enemy soldiers.
In the third year of Tiānhuì,
the grand army attacked Tàiyuán.
More than ten thousand troops sallied from the city to fight.
Húzhan led his Qiānhù army to attack them.
He again defeated over thirty thousand enemy troops in the Yúcì area.
In the sixth year,
he followed Lóushì to attack Jīngzhào.
His troops repeatedly engaged Sòng forces,
always being among the first to assault and achieving merit.
In the seventh year,
when taking Bīnzhōu,
they encountered over two hundred thousand Sòng troops.
Our army's right wing momentarily faltered.
At that time, Húzhan was the Qiānhù of the left wing.
He charged and broke through the enemy formation,
and the enemy was then defeated and fled.
He again achieved merit in defeating Zhāng Jùn at Fùpíng.
In the thirteenth year,
he attacked Guān Shīgǔ
at Líntáo, with over thirty thousand troops.
He participated in the attack on Jīngzhōu,
and in the capture of Déshùn, Qín, Gǒng, Líntáo, Hé, and Lán prefectures.
He defeated Wú Lín’s army,
and Húzhan played a crucial role in all these.
He was appointed Déshùnzhōu Cìshǐ,
then reassigned as Lǒngzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and Fèngxiáng Yǐn.
He died
at the age of fifty-five.
Jiágǔ Wūlǐbǔ was
from Àntǔhún Hé,
and later moved to Tiāndé.
His father, Wùtún,
had merits in suppressing Wūchūn and Wōmóuhǎn.
Wūlǐbǔ was subordinate to Lóushì.
He attacked the Liáo-affiliated Nǚzhí,
and induced Tàiwānzhào Sān and others to surrender.
He followed Lóushì to rescue Wòlǔgǔ at Xiánzhōu,
defeating Liáo troops at Yālǔhǔ Chéng.
When the Liáo army encamped on the Liáo River,
Wūlǐbǔ’s five Móukè armies attacked them by night.
The Liáo army panicked and scattered,
almost all of them killed or captured.
Wòlǔ伐 Gāo Yǒngchāng,
Wūlǐbǔ, with a few horsemen, fiercely attacked on the Liáoshuǐ River.
Then, with forty horsemen, he ambushed a strategic ford.
When they encountered the enemy's scouts,
they attacked them,
capturing prisoners.
Through this, they learned all of Yǒngchāng's strengths and weaknesses.
Tàizǔ praised him
and rewarded him with eight slaves.
Yǒngchāng's army was stationed at [●]ér,
having first occupied the strategic ford,
so the army could not cross.
Wūlǐbǔ and Sābā shot and killed two of their vanguards,
and Yǒngchāng's forces slightly recoiled.
The main army then crossed the Liáoshuǐ River.
When attacking Guǎngníng,
the military commander selected brave warriors to be the first to ascend.
Wūlǐbǔ and Chìzhǎn Hūmòhún each led their respective units,
storming into their formation.
The main army followed,
and thus Guǎngníng was captured.
When Tàizǔ attacked Línhuáng,
Wūlǐbǔ suffered a severe wound to his face,
but he fought fiercely as if nothing had happened.
He was rewarded with two palace women from Liáo.
When Liáo King Gǎo had already taken Zhōngjīng,
Wūlǐbǔ, with forty horsemen, scouted the enemy.
He captured a key Liáo official,
and thus learned the whereabouts of the Liáo ruler.
Later, he followed Dūtǒng Wòlǔ to pacify Yúnzhōng,
and followed Zōnghàn to garrison Yìngzhōu.
When the Liáo army was in the vicinity,
Wūlǐbǔ led his unit to defeat them.
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
the Sòng Pacification Commissioner, Cài Jìng, surrendered to Wūlǐbǔ.
When Lóushì attacked Shǎnxī,
various commanderies frequently rebelled again.
Wūlǐbǔ attacked and defeated them.
He defeated Zhāng Jùn's army at Fùpíng,
with Wūlǐbǔ being the first to ascend.
Ruìzōng rewarded him with golden vessels and famous horses.
He then, as a vanguard, attacked Lánzhōu,
taking the city.
He was promoted to Zhāowǔ Dàjiāngjūn
and granted a hereditary Měng'ān.
He successively held the office of Bótè Běnbùzú Jiédùshǐ.
Due to old age, he retired,
and was enfeoffed as Ruìguó Gōng.
Wūlǐbǔ possessed much wisdom and strategy,
and his physical strength surpassed that of others.
Even in extreme old age,
his bravery and vigor did not diminish.
In the early Dàdìng era,
fierce bandits gathered,
emerging from Tèbǐ Guān.
Wūlǐbǔ led the young men of his village to counterattack them,
and the bandit gang then scattered.
When the matter was reported,
he received very generous rewards.
He died in the 26th year of Dàdìng,
at the age of 105.
Wáng Bólóng was
a native of Shuāngchéng, Shěnzhōu.
At the end of the Liáo dynasty,
he gathered a band of robbers.
In the second year of Tiānfǔ,
he led 20,000 men and their baggage train to surrender.
He was granted a hereditary Měng'ān
and appointed Zhī Yínzhōu,
concurrently Zhī Shuāngzhōu.
In the fourth year,
when Tàizǔ attacked Línhuáng,
Bólóng and Hán Qìnghé led troops to escort grain provisions.
The 1,500 porters were all armored.
Qìnghé had already led troops ahead,
while Bólóng followed behind with the provisions.
They encountered over 5,000 Liáo soldiers ambushing them on the road.
Bólóng led the porters to defeat them,
capturing 500 horses.
In the sixth year,
he participated in the attack and capture of Zhōngjīng,
and also captured various mountain strongholds within the territory,
serving as Jìngjiāng Jūn Jiédù Liúhòu.
In the first year of Tiānhuì,
he was formally appointed Jiédùshǐ.
He followed Zōngwàng to suppress Zhāng Jué at Píngzhōu.
Bólóng was the first to charge,
personally killing hundreds of men.
He was promoted to Yòujíngwú Wèi Jiāngjūn.
In the Battle of Báihé,
Bólóng commanded the left wing.
He waved his banner, and his troops swiftly charged and trampled the enemy.
The Sòng army fell into disarray,
and our forces, seizing the advantage, fought fiercely and defeated them.
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
Bólóng served as the vanguard.
Approaching Bǎozhōu,
he encountered 50,000 enemy troops
and defeated them,
receiving the surrender of over 100,000 military and civilian personnel from Xīnlè.
When the main army besieged Biàn,
Sòng Tàiwèi Hé Mǔ led tens of thousands of troops out of Sānzǎo Mén.
Bólóng, with his own unit, intercepted and attacked them,
achieving many kills and captures.
Upon the capture of Biàn,
Bólóng rendered meritorious service in constructing siege equipment.
He then defeated Kǒng Yànzhōu and Lì Qióng's force of 30,000 at Míngzhōu.
he served as Tóngzhī Bǎozhōu Bīngmǎ Ānfǔ Sīshì,
leading several thousand troops to attack Běipíng,
and captured it.
He then recaptured Bǎozhōu and Héjiān.
When Ruìzōng campaigned in Shāndōng,
Bólóng followed in the attack on Qīngzhōu.
Before it fell,
the city's troops launched a night raid on Bólóng's camp.
Bólóng, without time to don his armor,
stood alone, clad in his clothes, brandishing his blade to defend the camp gate.
The enemy could not enter,
and he fiercely fought, killing several dozens of men.
Soon after,
all the soldiers were armored and emerged,
inflicting countless casualties on the Sòng army,
and also capturing one of their generals,
whom they executed.
Upon the capture of Qīngzhōu,
when merits were tallied,
Bólóng ranked first.
In the sixth year,
he returned to attack Mòzhōu,
receiving its surrender.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Shàobǎo and Mòzhōu Ānfǔshǐ.
He defeated Lǐ Gùzhài's force of over 100,000 at Púzhōu.
Púchéng held out,
with the city's defenders melting iron and pouring it onto our army.
It could not be overcome by assault.
Bólóng wore heavy armor,
crowned his head with a large cauldron,
and, brandishing a spear, was the first to ascend.
He killed over twenty defenders on the ramparts,
and the main army followed,
thus conquering it.
He then attacked Xúzhōu,
and Bólóng was again the first to ascend.
He was appointed Xú, Sù, Pī Sānlù Jūnmǎ Dūtǒng.
He defeated Gāo Tuōshān's force of over 150,000 at Qīnghé.
driving him away.
He met with the main army at Sùqiān,
pursuing Shìzhōng to Yángzhōu.
He returned to attack Sìzhōu.
The Sìzhōu garrison commander surrendered the city.
He garrisoned Zīyáng,
defeating Chén Hóng's bandit force of over 400,000.
He defeated Huáng Jiǎn at Dānzhōu.
He then attacked Guīdé.
The military commander sent Bólóng to set up siege equipment.
Bólóng, with over twenty horsemen, went to survey the terrain.
Suddenly, over a thousand enemy troops emerged from the city,
intending to capture Bólóng alive.
Bólóng spurred his horse and charged them.
The enemy troops fell into disarray,
with nearly 200 falling into the moat and dying.
He defeated Wáng Shàn's force at Cháoxiàn,
and captured Lúzhōu and Hézhōu.
Bólóng's contributions were numerous.
When the army crossed Cǎishí,
they defeated the forces of Yuè Fēi, Liú Lì, Lù Shàng, and others,
Returning through Zhēn and Yáng,
they encountered the armies of Lì Qióng and Hán Shìzhōng on the way,
and again fought and defeated them.
He was again appointed Mòzhōu Ānfǔ,
then transferred to Zhī Zézhōu.
Bandits in the Tàiháng Mountains often gathered,
but Bólóng pacified them all.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn,
he became Yānjīng Mǎjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
He followed the Yuánshuàifǔ to retake Hénán,
and temporarily served as Wǔdìng Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
concurrently Dūtǒng of this route.
When Sòng troops occupied Xǔzhōu,
Bólóng attacked and drove them away,
recalling and restoring its people.
In the autumn of that year,
Zhāng Guì, a gang leader from Tài'ān, coerced good citizens
and occupied strategic locations to cause rebellion.
Bólóng suppressed and pacified them.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
he followed Zōngbì in the southern campaign with his部,
attacked and captured Háozhōu, and returned.
In the third year,
he was made Jìedùshǐ of Wǔdìngjūn,
then changed to Yán'ān Yǐn,
and Jìedùshǐ of Níngchāngjūn.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
he was changed to Hézhōng Yǐn,
then moved to Yìdū Yǐn,
and enfeoffed as Guǎngpíngjùnwáng.
He died
at the age of sixty-five.
During the Zhènglóng period,
he was posthumously granted Tèjìn and Dìngguógōng.
Gāo Biāo,
whose original name was Zhàohéshī,
was from Bóhǎi in Chénzhōu.
His grandfather, Ānguó,
was the Jìedùshǐ of the three towns of Liáoxīng, Chén, and Kāi.
His father, Liùgē,
was a Zuǒ Chéngzhì,
reaching the rank of Cìshǐ.
When Biāo was first born,
his father, following the words of an augur,
believed the time of his birth was unfavorable to him,
and wanted not to raise him.
His mother protected him.
After several years,
his father eventually drove him away,
and Biāo hid with his maternal relatives.
When the Liao people mobilized troops in Dōngjīng,
Liùgē was already old
and supposed to join the army.
He sadly said to his close acquaintances:
"If my son were here,
he could command troops."
His acquaintances told him the truth in detail,
and Biāo then took his father's place in the army.
They fought at Chūhédiàn,
and the Liao army was defeated and fled.
Biāo fought alone with great effort,
and the army commander saw him and said:
"This is a brave warrior!"
He ordered him to be captured alive.
When Wòlǔ attacked Dōngjīng,
Liùgē led his fellow villagers to surrender,
and was made Qiānhù of Yúhézhōu.
After a long time, he requested to retire due to old age,
and Biāo took over command of his men.
Dūtǒng Gǎo attacked Zhōngjīng,
and Biāo, leading his móukè,
followed Wòlǔ to defeat the Liao generals Hélǔzào and Hán Qìngmín in the border region of Gāo and Huì.
Afterwards, the army encamped at Wǔ'ān.
Hélǔzào came to raid with twenty thousand elite soldiers.
Biāo followed Wòlǔ to engage in battle,
dismounting with his unit to be the first to charge,
and vigorously attacked and defeated them.
The Xī people, relying on treacherous terrain, defied orders,
forming strongholds everywhere.
Biāo repeatedly achieved merits in battle.
When Zōngwàng attacked Píngzhōu,
Biāo campaigned in the northwest region,
defeated the enemy,
and induced the surrender of the Shíjiāshān fortress.
He again followed Zōngwàng to campaign against Sòng,
becoming a Měng'ān.
When the army reached Zhēndìng,
Biāo led seventy soldiers
to build a covered path up to the city.
The city's defenders sallied out at night to burn the siege equipment.
Biāo attacked and drove them away.
The main army besieged Biàn,
and Biāo, with fifty cavalry, garrisoned at the southeast water gate.
The Sòng people again sallied out with heavy forces to fight,
and Biāo defeated them all.
When the army returned,
they were garrisoned in Héshuò,
and again defeated the enemy at Bàzhōu,
capturing their deputy general Zhù Áng.
Héjiān sallied out with twenty thousand troops at night to raid our encampment.
Biāo led the troops of three móukè to attack and defeat them.
In the fifth year of Tiānhuì,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Jìngjiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Shòuzhōu.
The following year,
he campaigned against Sòng,
following the Commander's Residence to patrol the lands of Shāndōng,
attacking cities and defeating enemies,
and was frequently heavily rewarded.
In the seventh year,
the army arrived at Suī.
Biāo, with his unit, attracted and recruited people from Jīngxī.
When they reached Zhàichéng Xiàn,
[一三] its officials and people surrendered.
Biāo alone entered the city with fifty-plus cavalry.
Subsequently, over three thousand people in the city rebelled again.
Biāo led his men to fight fiercely and defeat them,
then pacified the people and returned.
He followed Liángwáng Zōngbì to attack Kāngwáng,
reaching Hángzhōu.
When the army returned,
Sòng general Hán Shìzhōng blocked the river north of the Jiāng with several hundred warships.
Zōngbì led his forces west,
and when they were about to reach Huángtiāndàng,
over thirty enemy boats approached the south bank.
One of the first to arrive carried over two hundred soldiers.
Biāo, judging it was almost within reach,
used a hook to pull it,
and led several brave warriors
to leap onto the enemy boat.
They killed many,
and the rest were forced to their deaths in the water.
The following year,
he followed in the attack on Shǎnxī.
When the army reached Níngzhōu,
Biāo and his clansman Áng led three thousand troops to take Kuòzhōu.
Upon their arrival,
a surrenderer said,
"The defenders in the northeast corner of the city are planning to act as an inside informant."
Biāo immediately ascended that night with two household servants.
The guards on either side became aware of them.
Biāo and his followers fought desperately,
and the various armies followed,
then captured the city.
He followed in the attack on Héshàngyuán and Xiānrén Guān.
He accompanied Ālǐ to supervise the transport of grain and warships to Bózhōu.
The Sòng people blocked the river with fifty boats,
but Biāo attacked and defeated them,
capturing their general Xiāo Tōng.
He attacked the water stronghold of the Liánshuǐ bandits,
and advanced to take Liánshuǐjūn.
Its officials and people had already fled,
but he managed to persuade them all to surrender.
Biāo was exceptionally brave and strong,
able to travel three hundred lǐ in a day.
Wearing heavy armor,
he traversed dangerous terrain as if flying.
When facing the enemy,
he was always at the forefront of his soldiers,
never looking back.
In dozens of battles, large and small,
he often used a small force to attack a large one,
and always achieved victory.
After the Qí State was abolished,
he provisionally served as the Dūtǒng of all forces in the various routes east of Téngyángjūn.
He pacified Xú, Sù, Cáo, Dān,
Téngyáng and its subordinate cities, and they all became orderly as before.
He was made Jìedùshǐ of Wǔníngjūn,
but was rather corrupt,
and was once charged with embezzlement.
Hǎilíng, on account of his past merits,
flogged and released him.
He was changed to Yízhōu Fángyùshǐ,
[一四] successively serving as Jìedùshǐ of Ānhuà, Ānguó, and Wǔshèngjūn,
then promoted to Xíngtái Bīngbù Shàngshū,
then changed to Jīngzhàoyǐn,
and enfeoffed as Gàoguógōng.
He left office due to mourning,
but was reinstated as Jìedùshǐ of Wǔdìngjūn,
and Guīdé Yǐn.
In the Zhènglóng period, he was regularly granted Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū.
After a long time, he retired,
but was again appointed Pīmì Fùshǐ and Shūguógōng,
and granted the name Biāo.
He died at the age of sixty-seven,
and was posthumously given the epithet Huánzhuàng.
Biāo was ingenious and clever,
skilled in music,
and treated everyone, noble or humble,
with a warm countenance.
Wēndíhǎn Púllǐtè
was from the Yílí Mǐnhélèchūzhài of Lóngzhōu.
[一五] He was burly and had a beautiful beard,
possessed strategic acumen,
and was known for his wisdom and bravery.
When Dūtǒng Gǎo captured Zhōngjīng,
Púllǐtè provisionally served as Měng'ān,
leading five thousand troops.
They encountered over ten thousand Qìdān bandits,
and fought and defeated them.
He went out through Gǔngǔlǐ Dào,
defeating over eight thousand enemies.
Upon reaching Lāmén Huá Dào,
he again used an ambush to defeat ten thousand enemies.
When Tàizǔ settled Yān,
Púllǐtè went from Rúzhōu to Jūyōng Guān,
capturing their key personnel.
Shortly after,
over three thousand bandits again invaded Lāmén Huá Dào.
Púllǐtè organized his troops and was the first to charge.
The bandits recognized his banner,
and fled at the sight of it.
He then vigorously attacked them,
and personally captured the bandit leader.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
he followed Liángwáng Zōngbì to attack Sòng,
and was stationed in Tángzhōu.
When a large enemy force suddenly arrived,
PúLǐtè attacked them.
The Dàmíng army, numbering 14,000, was reported as 200,000.
PúLǐtè led his personal *méng'ān*,
and personally led his soldiers,
charging.
The enemy retreated slightly,
so he spread out his left and right wings and attacked them simultaneously.
The enemy forces scattered and fled.
He then encountered another army of 20,000 coming as reinforcements,
and again, with 3,000 soldiers, routed them.
At that time, local bandits in Pīzhōu gathered,
numbering nearly 200,000.
PúLǐtè, with 3,000 soldiers,
divided them into several teams and attacked them rapidly.
The bandits collapsed and fled.
When the Nánjīng Circuit encountered an enemy army of 20,000,
PúLǐtè, with 3,000 soldiers, defeated them.
On that day,
when soldiers came out from the city,
he again defeated them.
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
he was promoted to Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn
and concurrently served as Tóngzhī Fèngxiáng Yǐn.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Jīngzhàoyǐn,
then transferred to Níngzhōu Cìshǐ,
then appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Dūjiān,
and promoted to Yǒngdìngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Hǎilíng campaigned south,
he was appointed Wǔwèijūn Dūtǒngguǎn.
In the third year of Dàdìng,
he was appointed Kāiyuǎnjūn Jiédùshǐ,
then appointed Tàiníngjūn.
He died.
In the nineteenth year,
due to his achievements, his son Wùdài was appointed Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn, and his *běnméng'ān* Xīchūhén inherited the position of *móukè*.
BóDétèlíbǔ
was a member of the Qìdān royal clan,
and a Tongjin of the Liáo Imperial Academy.
In the early Tiānhuì period,
he and his father Tàbùyě submitted to the dynasty,
and he was appointed hereditary *móukè*.
Later, he retired from the position of Jīngzhàoyǐn.
Tèlíbǔ persuaded the unconquered soldiers and civilians of Sōngshān and other prefectures to surrender,
and also persuaded those within Píngzhōu and Jìzhōu to surrender,
and supervised them in farming.
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
Tèlíbǔ served as a Jūnmǎ Méng'ān,
and stayed with the various generals
to plan the capture of Bǎo, Suì, and Ān prefectures.
When attacking Ānsùjūn,
more than 100,000 soldiers from Héjiān, Xióng, Bǎo, and other places came to rescue.
Tèlíbǔ led his division to fight first,
with the main army following,
and thoroughly defeated their army,
thus capturing Ānsù.
Tèlíbǔ acted as Tōngpànshì.
The surrendered general Hú Yù secretly gathered a crowd and plotted rebellion.
Tèlíbǔ led his troops to capture Yù and more than fifty of his followers.
Ānsùjūn was changed to a prefecture,
and he was appointed concurrently as Tóngzhīzhōushì.
He was then appointed to Cízhōu,
where he captured the bandits of Tàiháng.
The Yuánshuàifǔ assigned the garrisoned troops of Cí and Xiāng prefectures to him,
and he captured Wáng Huì, Sūn XiǎoShí, Miáo Qīng, and others,
and the banditry was thus pacified.
He was promoted to Bīnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and rated excellent in integrity.
He left office due to mourning for his mother,
was reinstated to his original post,
and then appointed Zhuōzhōu Cìshǐ.
He entered the court as Gōngbù Lángzhōng,
and followed Zhāng Hào in constructing palaces in Dōngjīng.
When the affair of Tián Jué's faction arose,
the imperial court was almost emptied.
Tèlíbǔ acted as administrator of the Six Ministries,
and was promoted to Dàlǐ Qīng,
then went out to serve as Tóngzhī Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
he again served as Dàlǐ Qīng,
and Tóngzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu.
He observed mourning for his father,
and was reinstated as Míngzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
When rebellions arose in Zhènglóng,
the prefectures and counties had no soldiers
and could not defend themselves.
Míng originally had a river flowing below the city wall.
Tèlíbǔ then diverted water into the moat to fortify it,
and the bandits could not approach,
so the prefecture relied on it for safety.
He was promoted to Chóngyìjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Not long after,
he requested retirement due to old age and returned to his hometown,
where he died.
Tèlíbǔ was filial and cautious as a person.
In his administration, he was simple and tranquil, not accumulating wealth,
often saying:
"My salary is enough to maintain integrity.
What need is there for accumulation
beyond clothing and food?"
Whenever he was transferred to an official post,
his luggage consisted of only one carriage and a few servants.
Yēlǜ Huáiyì, originally named Bódié,
was a member of the Liáo imperial clan.
At the age of twenty-four,
he was repeatedly promoted to Tóngzhī Diǎnjiǎn Sīshì for his military achievements.
When Zōnghàn had already captured Xījīng,
the Liáo ruler planned to flee to Xià.
Huáiyì advised against it,
but was not heeded,
so he secretly took the Liáo ruler's horse and surrendered.
When Tàizǔ returned his army from Yān,
he left Zōnghàn and Wòlǔ to manage the western region.
Huáiyì led his *móukè* to join the army.
In the early Tiānhuì period,
the Shuàifǔ, seeing that the newly surrendered tribes varied greatly in size and distance,
ordered Huáiyì to reorganize them,
and appointed him Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Shǐ by imperial decree.
He then selected strategic locations among the various tribes,
built cities,
and facilitated commerce.
After the wars, many people in the tribes were in dire need.
From then on, their clothing and food increased year by year,
and their livestock prospered.
He followed Zōnghàn to attack Sòng,
captured Mǎyì,
defeated Yànmén,
stationed troops,
and advanced to attack Tàiyuán.
With his division, he separately captured Xúgōuzhèn in Qīngyuán county,
then encamped with the various generals in the border region of Fénzhōu.
At that time, soldiers from Hédōng and Shǎnxī Circuits came to relieve Tàiyuán.
Liú Guāngshì and Zhé Kěqiú built stockades in the western mountains of Wénshuǐ.
Huáiyì captured a captive,
and learned all the strategic positions where the Sòng troops were stationed,
so he divided his forces and attacked and defeated them.
The following year,
he again attacked Sòng,
following Lóushì to capture Fénzhōu and its dependent counties,
then passed through Píngyáng,
emerged from Zé and Lù to advance towards Héyáng,
and all places surrendered wherever he went.
When the main army besieged Biàn,
Huáiyì was stationed west of the capital.
After Biàn city fell,
he intercepted and killed
all Sòng soldiers who fled.
He participated in attacking Zhèng and Dèng prefectures and suppressing rebels in Zhèngzhōu,
captured Púzhōu and Léizé County,
and participated in defeating Dàmíng, Dōngpíng Fǔ, Xú, Yǎn, and other prefectures.
He achieved merit in all these actions.
In the seventh year,
he returned to his garrison.
In the tenth year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè,
and appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Shǐ.
Huáiyì was in the western frontier for several decades,
governing with kindness.
When he left,
the old and young blocked his path, clinging to him,
and he could not depart for several days.
In the early Tiānjuàn period,
he served as Tàiyuányǐn,
and had a reputation for capable governance.
He was then appointed Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu.
He followed Zōngbì across Wūnàshuǐ,
and returned to Zhōngjīng.
He requested retirement due to old age,
but was refused.
He was then appointed Dàmíng Yǐn,
but was ordered not to report to his post,
only to be provided with his salary and servants.
Each year he accompanied the emperor during the spring hunt,
and was otherwise free to do as he pleased.
The following year,
he again requested retirement and was granted it,
receiving half his salary and servants.
When Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Qīshuǐ Jùnwáng,
then promoted to Xīnwáng.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Xiāowáng.
In Zhènglóng, he was regularly enfeoffed as Jǐngguó Gōng.
His son Shénduō was Xīběilù Zhāotǎo Dūjiān,
an official who served and attended to him.
When Shénduō accompanied Hǎilíng in the southern campaign,
Huáiyì died in Yúnzhōng,
at the age of eighty-two.
Xiāo Wáng Jiānú
was a Xīrén.
He lived by the Kùdǎnghé.
He was a robust and strong man.
Before reaching manhood, he served the Liáo,
as a Shuàifǔ Shuài for the Crown Prince.
In the seventh year of Tiānfǔ,
Dūtǒng Gǎo settled the Xī territory.
Wáng Jiānú led his villagers to surrender,
and was appointed a Qiānhù to command them.
After Xīwáng Huílíbǎo died,
his kinsman Jīnchén Āgǔzhě still held Sāgěshān.
Wáng Jiānú and Tūniǎn went to attack them,
captured Jīnchén Āgǔzhě alive,
and received the surrender of his remaining forces.
At that time, Píngzhōu and Luánzhōu were plagued by bandits.
Wáng Jiānú, with his detachment, repeatedly defeated the bandit forces,
beheading, capturing, and taking prisoners.
He was frequently rewarded.
When Zōngwàng attacked the Sòng,
and defeated Guō Yàoshī at Báihé,
Wáng Jiānú also contributed to the success.
Upon reaching the river,
Sòng soldiers blocked the ford.
He joined the generals in defeating them.
They then besieged Biàn,
and broke through its East Gate defenses.
The following year,
they again attacked the Sòng.
Zōngwàng's army reached Zhōngshān,
where Sòng forces sallied out from various gates to engage in battle,
and burned our siege equipment.
Qízhōu
and Héjiān each sent troops to reinforce,
but they were all defeated.
The army returned,
garrisoning the Héquò region.
In Bīnzhōu, the bandit Gě Jìn gathered tens of thousands of men at Línzī.
Bólì Zhàolǐ (照里) led two thousand cavalry to attack them.
Wáng Jiānú led his Móukè as the vanguard,
and fought fiercely, decisively defeating their forces.
The following year,
they attacked Cāngzhōu.
Sòng forces resisted,
but he again followed Zhàolǐ to defeat and drive them away.
Sòng general Xú Wén moored a hundred ships at a sea island.
(Wáng Jiānú) immediately attacked with eighteen merchant ships,
beheading seven hundred,
and capturing twenty ships.
In the eighth year of Tiānhuì,
he was appointed Jìngjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and granted a hereditary Qiānhù.
He followed Liángwáng Zōngbì on campaigns,
as a Wànhù.
Upon his return, he became Wǔyuànbù Jiédùshǐ.
In the second year of Tiāndé,
he was transferred to Wūgǔdíliè Zhāotǎo Dūjiān,
and died.
Tián Hào, courtesy name Mòzhī,
was from Xìngzhōng.
He passed the Jinshì examination in the eighth year of Tiānqìng of the Liáo dynasty,
and successively held the post of Jīnbù Yuánwàiláng,
and Acting Guīdé Jiédùshǐ.
When Tàizǔ pacified Yān,
Hào presented the maps and registers of four prefectures to the court,
and was promoted to Dūguān Lángzhōng,
acting Jiédùshǐ.
He was promoted four times to Zhī Zhēndìngfǔshì.
He persuaded over five thousand bandits, including Qí Bó and Yóu Guì, to surrender.
Later,
Guì rebelled again and fled.
Hào sent Qí Bó to feign rebellion and join Guì,
then ordered him to seize an opportunity to kill Guì,
and receive the surrender of his followers,
thus pacifying all the bandit strongholds.
He was promoted three times to Xíngtái Zuǒchéng and Zhāngdéjūn Jiédùshǐ.
At this time,
new labor services were imposed.
Hào exempted half of the registered households and reported it,
so the corvée taxes in his prefecture were uniquely light compared to other prefectures.
He was transferred to Tóngzhī Héběidōnglù Dūzǒngguǎn,
then changed to Tóngqiān Yānjīng Liúshǒusīshì.
The people blocked him, preventing his departure,
so he changed his clothes and left at night.
He was transferred to Hédōngnánlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
then soon changed to Jiàngyángjūn Jiédùshǐ.
After three years,
he requested to resign due to illness,
and directly returned his seal and went home.
His repeated requests were not granted, and he was transferred to garrison Zhènwǔjūn.
He entered the court as Xíngbù Shàngshū,
but after three months requested retirement due to old age,
and died at home.
Zhào Yí, courtesy name Dé gù,
was from Liáoyáng.
His father-in-law gained favor with the Liáo ruler as an entertainer.
Yí was appointed Gémén Zhīhòu,
and was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài.
Later, he resided in Luánzhōu.
When Zōngwàng attacked Zhāng Jué,
Yí climbed over the city wall and surrendered.
He was appointed Luòyuàn Fùshǐ,
and Qiānhù of Luánzhōu.
He was promoted to Luòyuànshǐ,
and Jiǎnjiào Gōngbù Shàngshū.
He followed on the campaign against the Sòng,
reaching Biàn,
and was promoted to Dìzhōu Cìshǐ and Shìwèi Bùjūn Dūyúhòu.
When the Sòng were attacked again,
he contributed to the attack on Zhēndìng,
and was transferred to Shāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Jiǎnjiào Shàngshū Yòupúshè.
In the fifth year,
he was Tóngzhī Xìndéfǔlù Tǒngyājūnbīng,
concurrently serving as Yánbiān Ānfǔsīshì.
The following year,
he was Acting Zhī Jìzhōushì.
In the eighth year,
he participated in the pacification of Hénán,
and was appointed Lǒngzhōu Tuánliànshǐ.
In the tenth year,
he was transferred to Zhī Shízhōu.
Yí had long been in military service,
and was not skilled at governing the people.
He was impeached for slander,
and demoted to oversee the production of Tiánshuǐ salt in Píngzhōu.
When the Qí state was abolished,
Hénán was entirely guarded by veteran generals.
Yí was appointed Sùzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
commanding the troops of that circuit.
Yí valued righteousness
and welcomed scholars.
He once went to Biàn on business.
A son of an old friend owed a million guan to the government.
Yí gave him a pouch of gold.
The son spent it all for personal use.
Yí again paid the debt for him.
A short while later,
someone accused Xu Shuài of illegal conduct.
The imperial court ordered Yí to investigate and prosecute.
Yí went to great lengths to protect him,
and was consequently dismissed,
residing in Yān.
Hǎilíng went out to take charge of the Xíngtáishěng.
When he arrived in Yān,
Yí went to see him,
and then appealed his case.
When Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
Yí was appointed Bǎodàjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the early Zhēnyuán period,
he was transferred to Nèishěngshǐ.
Not long after,
he became Zhōngdōulù Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ.
The following year,
he was again transferred to Shùnyì and Xīngpíng,
then entered the court as Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
garrisoning Qìnnán,
and died of illness at the age of sixty-six.
More than ten years later,
Yí's descendants and Sìtú Zhāng Tōnggǔ's descendants were all depraved and dissolute,
squandering their wealth
and selling their land and homes.
Shìzōng heard of this,
and issued an edict saying:
"From now on, for officials and commoners whose ancestors have passed away,
their descendants are not allowed to divide their family residences.
Only the legitimate youngest son shall manage it,
to prevent its sale."
This was then codified into law.
Jiàokān Jì

Lièzhuàn No. 20: Guō Yàoshī (son Ānguó), Yélǜ Túshān, Wūyán Húlígǎi, Wūyán Wúlǐbǔ, Xiāo Gōng, Wányán Xíbùzhǔ, Gěshíliè Húlà, Yélǜ Shù, Guō Qǐzhōng, Wūsūn Éluàn, Yánzhǎn Méndū, Púsǎn Húntǎn, Zhèng Jiànchōng, Wūgǔlún Sānhé, Yílà Wēn, Xiāo Zhònggōng (son Gǒng), Xiāo Zhòngxuān, Gāo Sōng, Hǎilíng's sons Guāngyīng, Shěnsī Ābǔ, Guǎngyáng.
Guō Yàoshī
was a Bóhǎi native from Tiězhōu.
The Liáo state recruited men from Liáodōng to be soldiers,
to avenge grievances against the Nǚzhēn,
calling them
"Yuànjūn".
Yàoshī was their leader.
Wòlúgǔ attacked Xiǎnzhōu,
and defeated Yàoshī beneath the city walls.
The Liáo emperor fled to protect Tiāndé.
Yélǜ Niēlǐ declared himself emperor,
changed
the "Yuànjūn"
to
"Chángshèngjūn",
and promoted Yàoshī to Zhūwèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
After Niēlǐ died,
his wife Empress Xiāo acted as regent.
Yàoshī surrendered Zhuōzhōu and Yìzhōu to the Sòng.
Yàoshī, with six thousand Sòng soldiers, suddenly arrived at Yānjīng.
Zhēn Wǔchén, with five thousand men, captured the Yíngchūn Mén,
and both entered the city.
Empress Xiāo ordered the city gates to be closed and engaged the Sòng soldiers in street fighting.
Yàoshī was utterly defeated,
lost his horse, and fled on foot,
escaping by climbing over the city wall.
The Sòng still generously rewarded him.
Tài-Zǔ割Yānshān六州與Sòng人，
Sòng使 Yào-Shī 副Wáng Ānzhōng 守Yānshān．
及Ānzhōng不能庇Zhāng Jué 而殺之，
函其首以與Zōngwàng，
Yào-Shī 深尤Sòng人，
而無自固之志矣．
Zōngwàng 軍至Sānhé，
Yào-Shī 等拒戰于Bái-Hé．
兵敗，
Yào-Shī 乃降．
Zōngwàng 遂取Yānshān．
Tài-Zōng 以Yào-Shī 為Yānjīng 留守，
給以金牌，
賜姓Wányán氏．
從Zōngwàng 伐Sòng，
凡Sòng事虛實，
Yào-Shī 盡知之．
Zōngwàng 能以懸軍深入，
駐兵Biànchéng 下，
約質納幣，
割地全勝以歸者，
Yào-Shī 能測Sòng人之情，
中其肯綮故也．
及兩鎮不受約束，
命諸將討之，
Yào-Shī 破Shùn’ān-jūn 營，
殺三千餘人．
Hǎilíng 即位，
詔賜諸姓者皆復本姓，
故Yào-Shī 子Ānguó 仍姓Guō氏．
Guō Ānguó，
Yào-Shī 子也．
累遷Fèngguó Shàngjiàngjūn、Nánjīng Fùliúshǒu．
Zhēnyuán 三年，
Nánjīng 大內火，
Hǎilíng 使Yòusī Lángzhōng Liáng Qiú、Tóngzhī Ānwǔ-jūn Jiédù-shì Wáng Quán 按問失火狀．
Liúshǒu Féng Chángníng、Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Zuǒ Yíng 各杖一百，
除名．
Ānguó 及Liúshǒu Pàn Guān Dà Liángshùn 各杖八十，
削三官．
火起處勾當官Nánjīng Bīngmǎ Dū Zhīhuīshǐ Wú Jùn 杖一百五十，
除名．
失火位押宿兵吏十三人並斬．
諭之曰：
「朕非以宮闕壯麗也．
自即位 以來，
欲巡省Hénán，
汝等不知防慎，
致外方姦細，
燒延殆盡．
本欲處爾等死罪，
特以舊人寬貸之．
押宿人兵法當處死，
疑此輩容隱姦細，
故皆斬也． 」
Ānguó 性輕躁，
本無方略．
Hǎilíng 將伐Sòng，
以Ānguó 將家子，
擢拜Bīngbù Shàngshū，
改Xíngbù Shàngshū．
軍興，
領Wǔjié-jūn Dū Zǒngguǎn，
與Wǔshèng、Wǔpíng-jūn 為前鋒．
Hǎilíng 授諸將方略，
Ānguó 前奏曰：
「Zhào Gòu 聞王師至，
其勢必逃竄．
臣等不以遠近，
追之獲而後已，
但置之何地？ 」
Hǎilíng 大喜曰：
「卿言是也．
得Gòu 即置之寺觀，
嚴兵守之． 」
及聞Shìzōng 即位，
Hǎilíng 謀北還，
更置Zhèxī-dào Bīngmǎ Dūtǒngzhì-fǔ，
以Wányán Yuání 為Dūtǒngzhì，
Ānguó 副之．
及Hǎilíng 遇弒，
衆惡Ānguó 所為，
與Lǐ Tōng 輩皆殺之．
贊曰：Guō Yào-Shī 者，
Liáo之餘孽，
Sòng之厲階，
Jīn之功臣也．
以一臣之身而為三國之禍福，
如是其不侔也．
Wèi Gōngshǔ Cuó 勸其君殺Wèi Yāng，
豈無所見歟．
Yēlǜ Túshān 系出Yáoliǎn-shì，
在Liáo世為顯族．
Túshān 仕至Jīnwèi Dàjiàngjūn、Yáolǐ Xiāngwēn．
Liáo-Dì 奔Tiāndé，
Túshān 以所部降，
Zōnghàn 承制授Shàngshū，
為Xīběi-lù Zhāotǎoshǐ．
Zōnghàn 伐Sòng，
Túshān 率本部為先鋒．
至Fénzhōu，
遇Sòng將Zhéjiā-jūn，
請濟師倂力破之．
從攻Tàiyuán、Lóngdé-fǔ，
從入Biàn，
克Luòyáng．
及從Lóushì 平Shǎnyòu．
Tiānhuì 七年，
授Tàizǐ Shàobǎo．
十年，
遷Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè．
致仕，
卒，
年九十一．
Zhènglóng 例贈Tèjìn、Gàoguó-gōng．
Wūyán Húlígǎi，
Gélǎn-lù Xīngxiǎn-shuǐ 人也．
後授Àiyěkū Móukè，
因家焉．
從Shémǔ 圍Píngzhōu，
有功．
及伐Sòng，
圍Biàn，
五móukè 與Sòng兵萬人遇于城南，
Húlígǎi 先馳擊敗之，
Yuánshuàifǔ 遂賞良馬一匹．
Tiānhuì 五年，
攻Zōngchéng-xiàn，
敵棄城走Ēnzhōu，
Húlígǎi 追殺千餘人，
獲車四百兩．
Shuàifǔ 賞牛三十頭、馬一匹．
七年，
討Tàishān羣盜，
平之，
毀其營柵．
Yǎnzhōu羣寇三千餘保據山險，
Húlígǎi 復破之．
賞牛二十二頭、馬四匹．
八年，
攻Lúzhōu，
至Zhégāo-zhèn，
Húlígǎi 領甲士三十為前鋒，
執Sòng所遣持書與Liú Sìxiāng Qí者七人．
復以先鋒軍攻Hézhōu，
比至Hánshān-xiàn 五里，
獲甲士二人，
乃知Sòng三將將兵且至，
Húlígǎi 伏其軍，
遂獲Yáo Guānchá．
Shuàifǔ 賞馬二匹．
九年，
定Shǎnyòu，
Húlígǎi 以所部遇敵千人，
敗之，
生擒甲士一人，
盡得敵之虛實．
又從Púlǔhún 徇地Xī Qín，
敗敵兵二千於Qínzhōu，
賞馬一匹．
Sòng人屯Xiāngyáng-fǔ，
Jiānjūn Ànbǔ 遣Húlígǎi 領四máng’ān 往攻之．
Sòng兵三千已渡江，
方營壁壘，
乘其未就，
突戰破之．
Liáng-Wáng Zōngbì 復Hénán，
將攻Chénzhōu，
遣Húlígǎi 以甲士三十捕偵候人．
至Càizhōu 西，
遇兵八十餘，
戰敗之，
獲Nándùn-xiàn-lìng．
及攻Chénzhōu，
夜將 四更，
忽聞敵開門潰走，
Húlígǎi 亟領二móukè-jūn 追及之，
而Máng’ān Tūgěsù 亦領軍繼至，
大敗之．
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
he was transferred to be Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Líntáo Shàoyǐn,
concurrently Xīqínlù Bīngmǎ Fùdūzǒngguǎn.
In the ninth year,
he was reassigned as Tóngzhī Jīngzhàoyǐn,
concurrently Běnlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
In Tiāndé,
he was reassigned as Tóngzhī Píngyángyǐn,
concurrently Hédōngnánlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
In the third year of Zhēnyuán,
he was reassigned as Tóngzhī Gélǎnlù Zǒngguǎn.
In the fourth year of Dàdìng,
he was appointed Húlígǎi Jiédùshǐ.
In the seventh year,
he was reassigned as Guīdéjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the tenth year,
he was transferred to garrison Xiǎndé.
He died in office
at the age of sixty-nine.
In the nineteenth year,
an imperial edict appointed his son, Wǔshíliù, Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn,
and granted him hereditary status as Bōtūhuǒhé Móukè of his native route.
Wūyán Wūlǐbǔ,
was a native of Chánlǐng in Gélǎnlù.
He relocated to Dàmínglù.
During the Tiānhuì period,
he followed his father, Dájíbǔ, serving under the command of the Yuánshuài Yòujiānjūn.
Tàlán went to the imperial court for a matter,
taking Dájíbǔ with him.
Wūlǐbǔ led his father's móukè
and followed the main army in attacking Cāngzhōu.
As they were leveling the moats and ramparts,
soldiers from within the city came out to resist.
Wūlǐbǔ repelled them with his own troops.
When the imperial army took Qīngzhōu,
he fought bravely and rendered meritorious service,
capturing a hundred horses, which he presented.
A great number of enemy partisans surrendered or were captured.
Díjíbǔ, the garrison commander of Qīngzhōu, having many troops in Láizhōu,
requested aid from the Marshal's residence.
Wūlǐbǔ led twelve móukè troops to rescue them.
He then secured the surrender of four enemy camps
and captured one camp,
obtaining four thousand households.
He also defeated fifty thousand enemy troops at Ēnzhōu,
breaching their camp,
securing the surrender of fifty thousand households,
and capturing over ten thousand cattle.
Approaching Línqīng Xiàn,
he encountered three thousand enemy soldiers
and defeated them again,
capturing a great number of prisoners,
and taking the enemy leader alive, whom he presented.
The Marshal's residence commended his achievements,
rewarding him with a hundred slaves and thirty cattle.
At that time, Díjíbǔ was defeated in the vicinity of Ēnzhōu.
Wūlǐbǔ again led four thousand soldiers to rescue him,
defeating over ten thousand enemies.
When a hundred thousand Sòng troops were between Shānfù,
the Zǒngguǎn, a member of the imperial clan Yīlà Wūxuǎn, selected ten thousand infantry and four thousand cavalry to suppress them.
Wūlǐbǔ led his personally commanded móukè to accompany them.
He was the first to charge upon encountering the enemy
and fought valiantly, achieving merit.
When the main army campaigned in Mìzhōu,
Wūlǐbǔ led two thousand soldiers as the vanguard.
He encountered ten thousand enemies at Gāomì,
and subsequently defeated their forces,
pursuing them to the city walls,
slaughtering almost all of them,
and capturing over three thousand horses and cattle.
Wūlǐbǔ and Bó Tài defeated over one hundred thousand of the rebel Wáng Yì's army south of the prefecture.
That night,
several thousand enemy soldiers attacked the camp.
Wūlǐbǔ counterattacked them and drove them away.
Later, he followed the main army in attacking Chǔ, Yáng, Tōng, Tàiděng Zhōu.
In the second year of Tiānjuàn,
he inherited his father's hereditary Méng'ān,
and was appointed Níngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn.
In the seventh year of Huángtǒng,
he was additionally granted personally commanded móukè.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Guīdéyǐn.
In the early Zhènglóng period,
he served as Tánggǔbùzú Jiédùshǐ.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he served as Bǎodàjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In that same year, he was reassigned to garrison Tōngyuǎn.
At this time,
over one hundred thousand Sòng troops entered Hé and Lǒng,
occupying strategic strongholds
and attacking prefectures and cities.
The Yuánshuài Zuǒdūjiān, Héxǐ, requested additional troops.
An imperial edict granted seven thousand additional troops,
and dispatched Wūlǐbǔ along with Zhānghuàjūn Jiédùshǐ, a member of the imperial clan Zhāng, and five others,
to be available for assignment.
He was promoted to Lónghǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
He died in the army.
Xiāo Gōng, courtesy name Jìngzhī,
was a descendant of Xièlíxī Wáng.
His father, Yì,
returned to the court during the Tiānfǔ period,
followed in attacking Xīngzhōng,
and was subsequently appointed Xīngzhōngyǐn.
When the army returned,
Gōng was made a hostage.
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
Yì was supposed to lead the troops of Jiàn, Xīng, Chéng, Chuān, and Yì five prefectures as Wànhù.
The military commander, recognizing Gōng's talent and bravery,
had him take his father's place,
at which time he was twenty-three years old.
Upon reaching Zhōngshān,
Sòng troops came out to fight,
and Gōng was the first to lead his unit in defeating them.
He was with the army
as it passed through Shāndōng,
crossed the Huái River,
and launched a surprise attack on Kāng Wáng.
When the army returned,
the Marshal's residence, acting on imperial authority, appointed him Dézhōu Fángyùshǐ.
All the Xī people garrisoned between Bīn and Dì
were placed under his command.
He was reassigned as Dìzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
During the Huángtǒng period,
he was reassigned as Tóngzhī Hénghǎijūn Jiédùshǐ.
He left office for his father's mourning,
but was reinstated as Tàiyuán Shàoyǐn.
Due to his integrity,
he was promoted to Tóngzhī Zhōngjīng Liúshǒushì.
He was successively promoted to Bīngbù Shìláng,
and granted hereditary móukè status.
He was subjected to flogging
and stripped of one official rank
for inquiring about the emperor's daily life in the forbidden palace.
In the second year of Zhēnyuán,
he served as Tóngzhī Dàxīngyǐn.
After more than a year,
he was promoted to Bīngbù Shàngshū,
and served as an envoy for the Sòng Kingdom's birthday celebration.
He resigned from office due to his mother's mourning,
but was reinstated as Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
In the fourth year of Zhènglóng,
he was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū,
and again served as Bīngbù Shàngshū.
In that year,
while planning the border with the Xià Kingdom,
he lost the golden tablet he wore
when passing through Líntóng on his return.
Upon reaching Tàiyuán,
he fell ill from anxiety and grief.
At that time, the matter had already been reported to the court by express messenger.
Hǎilíng then ordered a replacement to be issued,
and sent an envoy to convey to Gōng:
"You lost the imperial tablet;
this is indeed carelessness.
I am waiting for you,
intending to entrust you with a mission,
and yet you claim illness?
You must have worn the imperial tablet on the day you departed,
and upon your return, with nothing to offer as an excuse,
you wished me to know in advance."
When the envoy arrived,
Gōng was already critically ill.
He kowtowed to receive the imperial command,
and died shortly thereafter.
Hǎilíng had just dispatched an envoy with his son, Hùwèi Jiǔgē, to rush to see him.
He had instructed the prefectural officials to guard him well.
By the time they reached Bǎozhōu,
the news of his death had already arrived.
Hǎilíng was deeply saddened and regretful.
He ordered Jiǔgē to escort the coffin back,
and memorial services were held in all the prefectures and circuits they passed through.
When the coffin arrived in the capital,
he ordered all officials to offer sacrifices.
He personally attended the memorial service,
bestowing generous funeral gifts
and also a horse.
He said to Jiǔgē:
"Your father carried out his imperial mission,
and died en route,
which is deeply regrettable.
I have ridden this horse for ten years.
Now I bestow it upon your father.
You may constantly lead it to the front of the coffin.
After the burial,
you may ride it."
Húntǎn held seventeen official posts,
but never served as a deputy.
His nature was deep, steady, and discerning.
Although he never studied,
he was insightful in listening and judgment.
Wherever he served, he was said to have a reputation for good governance.
Zhèng Jiànchōng, courtesy name Zhòngshí,
was originally from Jīngzhào,
but settled in Fūzhōu.
He served the Sòng dynasty,
