and successively held the post of Zhī Yán'ān Fǔshì.
In Tiānhuì seventh year, he surrendered,
and was still appointed Zhī Yán'ān Fǔ,
with three thousand soldiers stationed under him.
The Sòng general Liú Guāngliè attacked Jiànchōng with eighty thousand troops,
and they were stalemated for over forty days.
As the attack intensified,
Jiànchōng sent someone to gather the Xiéhē army,
and they launched a pincer attack, defeating the Sòng forces,
capturing their deputy general, Hè Guì.
He was promoted to Jiézhì Sī Tǒngzhì Jūnmǎ.
Then he was transferred to Jīngzhàofǔ Lù Bīngmǎ Dūjiān.
He defeated Sòng general Qǔ Duān at Péngyuán.
When Gāo Chāngzōng occupied Yán'ān
and held it for Sòng,
Jiànchōng attacked him
and completely recovered the cities and towns.
He was again appointed Zhī Yán'ān Jūnfǔshì.
When Qí Guó was established,
he was successively promoted to Bózhōu Tuánliànshǐ,
and Zhī Níngzhōu.
When Qí Guó was abolished,
the imperial court ceded the territory to Sòng.
He then became Sòng's Huánqìng Lù Jīnglüè Ānfǔ Fùshǐ,
and continued to be Zhī Níngzhōu.
When Tiānjùn reconquered Shǎnxī,
he was reappointed Jīnglüè Ānfǔshǐ
and Zhī Qìngyáng.
After participating in the capture of Gāngǔ Chéng,
he was transferred to Píngliáng Yǐn.
At that time, palaces were being built in Nánjīng,
and a large amount of timber from Hédōng and Shǎnxī was requisitioned.
It was floated down the river.
Passing through the treacherous Tǐzhù,
many raft workers drowned.
The officials in charge dared not report this,
but instead falsely accused them of desertion,
and imprisoned their families.
Jiànchōng reported the matter,
requesting permission to go to Tǐzhù to untie the rafts,
letting them float down freely.
He arranged for skilled swimmers to retrieve the timber downstream,
and those who had been imprisoned were released.
During the Zhènglóng military campaign,
tendons and horns were requisitioned to make weapons.
The common people often slaughtered their cattle for these,
or even pulled out their horns alive,
causing some cattle to weep.
Jiànchōng reported this matter to the court.
Jiànchōng was of a violent and aggressive nature.
He always kept more than ten rabid dogs.
When a servant was guilty and had been flogged,
he would then incite the dogs to bite him,
until nothing but bones were left.
Although he was humble and treated lesser officials with respect,
he would not yield to anyone above him.
If official documents from the provincial departments did not conform to regulations,
he would immediately place them under his seat,
or even tear them up.
Because of this, those in power resented him.
The military clerk Lǐ Huàn embezzled public funds.
Believing he could not escape punishment,
he falsely accused Jiànchōng of hoarding armor with rebellious intent.
He was interrogated twice more,
but no evidence was found.
Just as the report was about to be submitted,
the acting official, who had a long-standing grudge against Jiànchōng,
feared he would be released.
He sent a clerk with documents to deceive Jiànchōng, saying:
"The imperial court has issued an order,
what should we do?"
Jiànchōng replied:
"Do as you please."
That night,
he died in prison.
His eldest son, Suò, also died there.
Wūgǔlún Sānhé,
a native of Àiyěwūhé in Gēlǎnlù,
later moved to Zhēndìng.
When Ruìzōng was Yòu Fù Yuánshuài,
he heard of Sānhé's bravery and strategy,
and selected him to serve as a Zhāyě.
and was appointed Qūyuàn Dūjiān.
Not long after,
he joined the campaign against Sòng.
He encountered Sòng troops in Yǐngzhōu,
Later, he followed Zōngbì on campaigns,
In Huángtǒng first year,
he was appointed Líng Hànjūn Qiānhù,
and the commander's office assigned an additional four thousand troops to him.
He was appointed Tóngzhī Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐshì,
and then twice promoted to Tàizǐ Shàozhānshì.
In Dàdìng sixth year,
he was transferred to Míngzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
The Emperor said:
"You served Ruìzōng in the past,
accumulating much hardship.
When you served Us,
assisting the Crown Prince,
you exerted great effort.
Now you govern an important prefecture,
this is to reward your efforts."
He was promoted to Yǒngdìngjūn Jiéduzhīshǐ,
and successively served as Línhuáng, Fèngxiáng Yǐn,
Shǎnxī Lù Tǒngjūnshǐ,
and Dōngpíng Yǐn.
He controlled the prefectures and counties,
practicing personal frugality,
and prioritizing leniency and simplicity in governance.
The border regions were peaceful for a long time,
and the people enjoyed security.
He was summoned to serve as Qiānshū Shūmìyuànshì.
He died.
In the eighteenth year,
Shìzōng posthumously recognized Sānhé's past merits,
and appointed his son, Dàxīng, as the hereditary Méng'ān of Àiyěwūhé and Móukè of Ālǐmén Hé in Hébĕi Xīlù,
with the rank of Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn.
Yílà Wēn, originally named Āsà,
was a Liáo Héngzhàng person,
skilled in Khitan small script.
When Ruìzōng was Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài and campaigned against Sòng,
Wēn followed Dàdà across the river,
and was appointed Jiāngníngfǔ Dū Xúnjiǎn.
When Jiāngníng and Tàipíng were first captured,
Sòng sent spies to incite the populace,
with tens of thousands responding.
Wēn captured the spies,
and thereafter they dared not secretly instigate trouble.
Zōngbì commended him,
bestowing upon him a thousand liǎng of silver, a hundred pieces of fine silk, and two hundred bolts of plain silk.
Whenever Zōngbì went on a campaign,
Wēn was always with him.
He was appointed Tóngzhī Hébĕi Xīlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐshì.
It happened that Zōngbì was inspecting the border,
and Wēn accompanied the army,
not going to his official post.
When Zōngbì returned to court,
Xīzōng hosted a banquet for his officials.
Zōngbì wished to make a request,
but was already drunk and spoke out of turn.
Wēn helped him out of the palace.
The next day,
Xīzōng said to Zōngbì:
"Āsà serves his uncle very diligently,
he should not leave your side."
Because of this, Zōngbì trusted him even more.
He once said to his son-in-law, Hégélì Shìníng:
"You should emulate Āsà's character;
you can almost compare to the ancients."
Not long after,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Zhōngjīng Lù Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐshì,
and successively promoted to Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū concurrent Xiū Qǐjūzhù.
During the Zhènglóng campaign against Sòng,
he was appointed Jìzhōu Lù Xíngjūn Wànhù in his original capacity,
and followed to Yángzhōu.
When the army returned,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Xuānhuīyuànshì.
When Shìzōng's imperial meal was not to his taste,
he summoned Wēn to taste it.
Wēn reported:
"The flavor is not bad,
but rather, as the border affairs in the north and south have not ceased,
Your Majesty's thoughts are elsewhere."
The Emperor's mind was then put at ease.
At this time,
Shìzōng had been on the throne for a long time,
was familiar with the affairs of the realm,
and desired to find worthy talents to help him achieve good governance.
However, his high officials were indecisive and temporized,
recommending no one.
One day,
Shìzōng summoned his chief ministers and said:
"You, sirs, hold the positions of assistants and chancellors,
yet you have never recommended anyone. Why is this?
Moreover, you are old,
is there truly no one who can replace yourselves?
It is only when I have said that a certain person is usable
that you then speak of it.
Since you yourselves have nothing to say,
must you wait for me to know someone before they are promoted and employed?
How many more such people will there be?"
He then looked at Rǔlín and said:
"Take the Right Chancellor for instance,
he too was known through the recommendation of the Right Grand Chancellor."
Rǔlín replied:
"If we, your humble servants, knew of anyone,
how would we dare not recommend them?
But there is no one."
The Emperor said:
"During the Spring and Autumn period, the various states were divided,
their territories small,
yet all claimed to have worthy men.
Now, with the realm so vast,
how can there be no talent?
It is simply that you, sirs, do not recommend them.
Now I exert myself,
hoping to achieve good governance.
But in the future, with whom will my descendants govern?"
Rǔlín and the others all showed looks of shame.
In the 28th year,
he was promoted to Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
concurrently supervising the compilation of the National History,
and enfeoffed as Ruìguó Gōng.
When Shìzōng was unwell,
he, along with Tàiwèi Túdān Kèníng and Yòuchéngxiàng Xiāng, received the imperial dying charge.
Upon Zhāngzōng's ascension,
he was granted the title Yínqīng Rónglù Dàfū,
and advanced to the enfeoffment of Shēn.
Previously,
Yòuchéngxiàng Xiāng had said:
"Xīzōng's birthday festival was on the seventh day of the seventh month,
which coincided with Jǐngxuān's death anniversary,
so it was changed to the first month for receiving felicitations from foreign countries.
Now, the Tiānshòu Festival is in July,
when there are excessive rains,
making it difficult for foreign envoys to travel to the capital
and hindering their journey.
I request that it be moved to another month for convenience."
Rǔlín said:
"The way of an emperor is to show credibility to the world.
In the past, the birthday of the Sòng ruler Gòu
also fell in the fifth month.
At that time,
when the capital was in Huìníng,
and the superior state sent envoys to bestow gifts,
no mention was made of rain or floods obstructing them.
Now that our good relations with Sòng Gòu have lasted for a long time,
to suddenly use summer rain as an excuse
would show a lack of sincerity.
Should the rainfall exceed the norm,
and they arrive late at the capital,
it is still better than changing to another day."
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Liú Wěi, Yùshǐ Dàfū Tángkuò Gòng, Zhōngchéng Lǐ Yàn, Xíngbù Shàngshū concurrently Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū Wányán Shǒuzhēn,
Xiū Qǐjūzhù Wányán Wūzhě, and Tóngzhī Dēngwén Jiǎnyuànshì Sūn Duó also all stated its unsuitability.
The Emperor initially followed this,
but later still adopted Xiāng's suggestion.
At that time, the Emperor was in the mourning period,
and he first went hunting,
prompting the Censorate to submit multiple memorials arguing it was improper during deep mourning.
Later, he went winter hunting,
and Rǔlín remonstrated against it.
The imperial edict replied:
"If you can be like this in every matter,
what worries would I have?
However, times change and circumstances differ,
making it difficult to follow ancient precedents.
If you can deliberate appropriately,
that would be fitting."
One day,
the Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"The way people are employed now
is too rigid regarding qualifications.
How can we obtain talented people this way?"
Rǔlín replied:
"Not being rigid about qualifications
is for awaiting extraordinary talents."
The Emperor said:
"Cuī Yòufǔ, as a chancellor,
recommended eight hundred people in less than a year.
Were all of them extraordinary talents?"
At that time, an official reported that people were privately collecting imperial decrees and edicts,
fearing this might incite lawsuits,
and requested that it be prohibited.
Rǔlín said:
"The laws of a sovereign
are like the Jiāng and Hé rivers;
one wishes them to be easy to avoid and difficult to violate.
The laws and regulations of our dynasty
are open and clear.
Now they have been established as immutable codes,
and everyone in the realm hears and recites them.
If private individuals are allowed to collect them,
then everyone will clearly understand and not dare to do wrong,
which is also a means of assisting in governance.
It is better not to prohibit it."
The imperial edict agreed.
In the third month of Míngchāng first year,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
which was not granted.
In the twelfth month,
he died.
At that time, the Emperor was hunting in Ráoyáng.
Upon hearing the news,
an imperial edict instructed all officials to attend the funeral,
and the mourning gifts were increased.
He was posthumously named Wénxiāng.
Rǔlín was intelligent and well-versed in affairs.
Whenever he made a suggestion, he would always try to guess the Emperor's subtle intentions,
and he allied himself with many people to make his points,
thus his words did not offend yet appeared loyal.
Initially,
when Zhāngzōng had just ascended the throne,
officials reported that renovating the palace halls and all their furnishings
would require one thousand two hundred embroiderers daily
and two years to complete.
The Emperor, considering the great expense,
intended to halt the construction.
Rǔlín said:
"These are not for the Emperor's personal use;
they are not excessively extravagant.
In the future, when foreign envoys gather for audience,
magnificent palace buildings
are also a matter of national prestige."
Thereafter, luxurious spending gradually expanded,
perhaps because Rǔlín had initiated it.
Zhāng Xuánsù, courtesy name Zǐzhēn,
shared a great-grandfather with Hào.
His grandfather was Yòu,
his father Kuāng,
who served the Liáo dynasty as a Jiédùshǐ.
Xuánsù initially obtained office through hereditary privilege.
Gāo Yǒngchāng occupied Liáoyáng,
and Xuánsù was among his followers.
When Ōulǔ's army arrived,
he opened the gates and surrendered,
and was specially appointed as a hereditary Tóngzhōu Méng'ān.
During the Tiānhuì period,
he successively served as Xīshàng Géménshǐ, Kèxǐngshǐ, and Dōnggōng Jìsī.
In Tiānjuàn first year,
he was appointed Zhī Zhuōzhōu with the title Jìngjiāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was deemed most upright in his assessments
and promoted one rank.
The imperial prince, Wèi Wáng Dàojì, held the nominal title of Zhōngjīng,
and Xuánsù was appointed Tóng Tídiǎn of the Wèi Wáng's residence.
Soon after, he was reappointed Zhèn Xī Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
then transferred to Dōngjīng Lù Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and then to Xīngpíng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the late Zhènglóng years,
banditry erupted throughout the realm.
Xuánsù mobilized common laborers to reinforce and expand the city walls.
His colleagues advised him to stop,
but he did not listen.
Not long after,
bandits plundered neighboring prefectures,
all of which were unprepared,
but Xīngpíng alone remained secure.
Upon Shìzōng's accession,
Xuánsù came to see him in Dōngjīng.
While in Dōngjīng, Xuánsù
had sought to please Hǎilíng's intentions,
by stating that Shìzōng had once taken official grain
and by fabricating several other matters about him.
When he came to see him this time,
Shìzōng asked him nothing about any of it.
Xuánsù and Lǐ Shí strongly argued that the Emperor should proceed to Yānjīng early,
and the Emperor deeply agreed.
He was promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū,
then sent out to govern Dìngwǔ,
and subsequently retired.
He died at the age of eighty-four.
[He] died.
Xuánsù was generous and resolute,
and people feared and respected him.
He would often write characters on a piece of paper to treat malaria,
and it would always cure it,
which people found extraordinary.
Rǔbì, courtesy name Zhòngzuǒ,
had a father Xuánzhēng,
who was the Jǐedùshǐ of Zhāngxìn Commandery,
and an elder brother of Xuánsù.
Rǔbì initially received an official post through his father's荫 (yīn, influence).
In the second year of Zhènglóng (1157),
he passed the Jìnshì examination,
and was appointed as the Zhǔbù of Lèjiāo County, Shěn Prefecture.
Xuánzhēng's wife, Lady Gāo, was related to Shìzōng's mother, Empress Zhēnyì.
Shìzōng took Xuánzhēng's daughter as his secondary consort,
who became Yuánfēi.
She, Lady Zhāng, gave birth to Zhào Wáng Yǔnzhōng.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne in Liáoyáng,
Rǔbì and his uncle Xuánsù both went to pledge allegiance to him,
and he was promoted to Yìngfèng Hàlín Wénzì.
Shìzōng was at the Cuìluán Pavilion,
and summoned Zuǒsī Lángzhōng Gāo Kàn and Rǔbì, asking:
"Regarding recent appointments,
what is the public opinion?
You should report truthfully,
without the slightest concealment.
If anyone is unsuitable, they should be replaced."
Both Kàn and Rǔbì had no reply.
Since the Huángtǒng era,
the inner treasury's expenses had been excessive,
and officials had taken advantage of their positions to commit fraud,
resulting in many losses.
Rǔbì, along with Gōngjí Zhícháng Gāo Gōngmù and Rùdiàn Xiǎodǐ Wáng Tiān'ér, audited and verified the items,
categorizing them into registers,
and created four treasuries to store them.
Thereupon,
the Inner Treasury Commissioner Wáng Kědào and others were each given one hundred strokes,
while Rǔbì and the others were each promoted one rank.
After a short while,
he concurrently served as Xiū Qǐjūzhù,
and was transferred to Yòusī Yuánwàiláng.
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
He was reinstated as Lìbù Lángzhōng,
and progressively promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
then appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
An imperial edict commanded the relocation of Nǚzhēn Měng'ān Móukè to Zhōngdū,
granting them official land in the nearby suburbs,
which was all barren and poor.
The fertile fields had long been leased by powerful commoners,
who then claimed them as their own.
When the Emperor went hunting,
the Měng'ān Móukè people came forward to complain that the land they were given was unsuitable for cultivation.
An edict ordered that official lands long leased by commoners be seized and given to them.
Consequently, Rǔbì was ordered to deliberate on the matter.
He requested
"to establish stipulations and deadlines,
allowing the common people to report themselves.
After the deadline,
people would be allowed to report,
and those whose reports were verified would receive rewards."
The Emperor approved his memorial.
He also dispatched Tóngzhī Zhōngdū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Zhāng Jiǔsī to seize and register the lands.
The Emperor asked:
"Gāolì and Xià both claim vassalage.
When envoys arrive in Gāolì,
they exchange courtesies with the King as equals.
The King of Xià stands to receive them,
and the envoys bow;
why is this?"
Zuǒchéng Xiāng replied:
"The former Liáo and Xià were related as uncle and nephew,
and the King of Xià, because of the princess,
received the envoys' bows.
Our dynasty, when agreeing to peace with Xià,
adopted the old Liáo rites;
that is why it is so."
Rǔbì said:
"The sworn agreement states to fully follow the old ceremonies of the Liáo kingdom;
this has been practiced for forty years now,
and cannot be changed."
The Emperor said:
"Your words are correct."
The Emperor heard that many minor officials appointed by the Shàngshūshěng were incompetent,
so he summoned Rǔbì to the Xiānggé and told him:
"The other Prime Ministers are old,
you and the others should exert yourselves."
Rǔbì replied:
"My abilities are meager, insufficient to meet Your Majesty's expectations."
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
At that time,
the Hùbù was selling grain from official granaries,
and Rǔbì requested that the Nuǎntāngyuàn be allowed to purchase it.
The Emperor reproached him, saying:
"Do you wish to accumulate hidden virtues?
Why be so petty?"
Zuǒchéngxiàng Túdān Kèníng was relieved of his political duties
and became Púmìshǐ.
On that same day,
Rǔbì also presented a memorial requesting to retire.
The Emperor sent someone to stop him, saying:
"You are not yet old,
it is not yet time to retire."
He was promoted to Zuǒchéng,
and was appointed on the same day as his clan cousin Cānzhī Zhèngshì Rǔlín,
which their clan regarded as an honor.
There was a person who requested to retire before the age of sixty,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Rǔbì said:
"Your Majesty once permitted retirement at sixty."
The Emperor rebuked him, saying:
"I indeed permitted those who reached sixty to retire,
but not those who had not yet reached sixty.
Moreover, if I say sixty for retirement,
it is to be followed,
otherwise you should speak up.
You and others do not speak up;
it is always like this."
After a long time,
for unauthorized increase of provisions for the imperial grandsons,
he, along with Prime Minister Shǒudào, Yòuchéng Niángē Wòtèlā, and Cānzhèng Zhāng Rǔlín, were each demoted one rank.
The Emperor said:
"According to the law, you should be dismissed from office,
but this is merely a minor reprimand."
When Rǔbì was on sick leave,
the Emperor told the Prime Ministers:
"Rǔbì has long held executive power,
is well-versed in regulations,
and is quite capable of evaluating talent,
but his intentions are not upright."
He was then dismissed and made Guǎngníng Yǐn,
and given a tōngxī belt.
As Prime Minister, Rǔbì
was unable to remonstrate directly.
What the Emperor wished to do,
he would follow and guide him in;
what the Emperor did not wish to do,
he would subtly hint at to gauge his intention.
When the Emperor blamed him,
he would use gentle words to admit fault,
never opposing him.
And the Emperor also knew this.
Moreover, he was greedy for bribes,
using schemes to acquire famous gardens, mansions, rare treasures, and curiosities from various families,
which scholars held in low esteem.
In the twenty-seventh year (1187),
he passed away.
Rǔbì and Yǒngzhōng were related as uncle and nephew through marriage,
and secretly formed a faction.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
Rǔbì's wife, Lady Gāo, often used sinister words to frighten Yǒngzhōng into coveting improper ambitions,
painted a portrait of Yǒngzhōng's mother to worship and pray to,
and had soothsayers calculate Yǒngzhōng's future.
The authorities investigated and prosecuted the matter,
and Lady Gāo was executed.
The matter involved Rǔbì,
but the Emperor, knowing that the incident came to light after Rǔbì's death,
spared him from posthumous degradation.
Yélǜ Ānlǐ, originally named Nàhé,
was descended from the Yáoniǎn clan.
He was orphaned young,
and was known for his filial piety towards his mother.
In the late Liáo Dynasty,
he travelled through difficult terrain to avoid disaster,
never for a day neglecting to care for his mother's warmth and coolness.
Upon joining the court,
those in power valued his conduct and righteousness,
making him the secretary (Wénzì) in the Marshal's office,
and bestowing upon him the title of Zuǒbān Diànzhí.
In the early Tiānjuàn era (1138),
he followed the Marshal to Shānxī.
When his mother died,
he was unable to return home for her burial,
so the Marshal pitied him
and gave him a generous funeral endowment.
Ānlǐ, enduring the great heat,
pulled the coffin for over a thousand lǐ,
grieving so much that he became emaciated,
causing passersby to sigh in admiration.
After the mourning period,
he rose from Xíngtái Lì, Lǐbù Zhǔshì to Gōngbù Shìláng,
and then changed to Zuǒsī Lángzhōng.
The next year,
Shìzōng was enthroned in Liáodōng.
Four years later,
an imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Zīzhèng Dàfū,
and restored his fields and residence.
Upon Zhāngzōng's ascension,
an imperial edict sought out his son, Gōng Shǐ, a Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi and liquor supervisor of Píngdìng Zhōu,
and promoted him to Dūjiān of the Shàngyào Jú.
In the early years of Tàihé,
an imperial edict set about determining posthumous titles for meritorious officials.
Lǐ Bǐngjūn, a clerk in the Shàngshū Shěng, submitted a memorial, saying:
"There are matters that should be treated slowly but are treated urgently,
or lightly but are treated gravely.
The teaching of names (míngjiào) is such a matter.
I humbly observe that the late Zīzhèng Dàfū, Qí Zǎi, was executed for his loyal words,
and those who admired righteousness
grieved in their hearts.
Shìzōng, upon his ascension,
granted him a posthumous office,
and Your Majesty has recorded and employed his son,
which is a great kindness.
Though King Wǔ sealed the tomb of Bǐgān,
and Confucius praised the benevolence of Yí and Qí,
how is this different?
Yet the officials, adhering strictly to the text,
deem him ineligible for a posthumous title because his office was not of the third rank.
I privately doubt this.
If only those whose office reached the third rank could request a posthumous title,
then at that time, those holding high office and enjoying generous stipends
were not few.
All of them, fearing punishment, were timid and servile,
not daring to utter a single word,
or propose a single plan,
for the sake of the state.
This ultimately leads to those who establish their name and die for their principles
coming from the ranks of doctors and diviners,
which is somewhat shameful.
I believe that extraordinary people
should be treated with extraordinary rites.
I beg that an imperial edict order the relevant officials to specially grant a posthumous title to commemorate his loyalty;
this would also be one way to uphold the teaching of names."
The imperial decree stated:
"Granted."
It was sent down to the Tàicháng,
and he was posthumously titled Zhōngyì.
The eulogy states: Alas,
Hǎilíng as a ruler,
wielded cunning and controlled his subordinates without compassion.
A gentleman serving at court,
must act with propriety,
only then can he avoid shame.
Zhāng Tōnggǔ and Yēlǜ Ānlǐ, whose positions were not as high as Zhāng Hào's,
in their conduct from beginning to end,
were far more virtuous.
Hào did nothing he wouldn't do,
participated in every campaign,
served as prime minister for the longest time,
was generously employed,
but poorly treated.
Did he perhaps bring this upon himself?
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
Hào and Ānlǐ were both high ministers.
One (Hào) used subtle words,
the other (Ānlǐ) offered secret remonstrances;
this was better than not remonstrating at all.
Qí Zǎi, a mere physician,
alone was able to remonstrate most strongly,
and his later predictions all came true.
Hǎilíng's murder of him
was sufficient to establish his name for a hundred generations.
Nàhé Chūnnián invited good men to serve,
possessing the demeanor of a gentleman.
His death occurred just before the Sòng troops were raised,
but observing his eagerness to accumulate wealth,
he was perhaps not a man who forgot himself for the country.
Qí Zǎi is indeed extraordinary and unsurpassed!
