Biographies, Chapter 22 Gǎo (originally Sālīhē
) Nòuwǎnwēndūn Sīzhōng (son Yǐdié) Wēndūn Wùdài Bēndǔ Gāo Zhēn Bái Yànjìng Zhāng Jǐngrén
Gǎo's original name was Sālīhē.
He was a sixth-generation descendant of Āndì,
a member of the Pólúhuǒ clan of Tàizhōu,
and the son of Húlǔbǔshān.
He was heroic and resourceful,
and Tàizǔ loved him,
always keeping him in the army.
When Pólúhuǒ became the Dūtǒng of Tàizhōu,
all of his relatives moved with him to Tàizhōu.
Sālīhē was once an adopted son of Shìzǔ,
and alone was exempt from the move,
remaining in Ānchūhǔshuǐ.
Zōnghàn and Zōngwàng had already twice captured Biàn,
and taken the two Sòng emperors north.
Zōngwàng dispatched various generals to pacify Héběi.
Zuǒdūjiān Shémǔ attacked and captured Héjiān.
Lǐ Chéng of Xióngzhōu abandoned the city and fled.
Sālīhē intercepted and attacked him,
decisively defeating him.
Xióngzhōu then surrendered.
Ruìzōng campaigned in Shāndōng,
leaving Sālīhē on the river.
Within the territory of Zhēndìng, there were bandits
who called themselves Yuánshuài Qínwáng.
Sālīhē attacked and defeated their forces,
captured and executed their leader.
Following the pacification of Shǎnxī,
Sālīhē surveyed the territory west of Wèi,
receiving the surrender of Déshùn Jūn.
He then received the surrender of Zhènrong Jūn in the Jīngyuán Lù,
advanced to pacify Xīhé,
received the surrender of Gānquán and three other forts,
and then took Bǎochuān Chéng.
The next year,
together with Bēndǔ, he pacified Héwài,
receiving the surrender of Níngtáo and Ānlóng, two stockades,
and also the surrender of Xiàhé and Yuèzhōu.
Upon reaching Xīníng,
he received the complete surrender of its Dūhù officials and subordinates.
Thereupon, the tribal chiefs of Mùbō and others all came to surrender.
He attacked Qìngyáng,
defeated those who resisted,
and then received the city's surrender.
Mù Wěi came to surrender with Huánzhōu,
bringing thirteen cities and stockades,
and ten thousand infantry and cavalry.
At this time,
Zōngbì's army was defeated at Héshàngyuán,
and the emperor praised Sālīhē while cautioning and encouraging Zōngbì.
After Ruìzōng had pacified Shǎnxī,
he left troops garrisoned at strategic points,
and made Sālīhē their commander-in-chief.
Not long after,
he requested to recover the thirteen prefectures outside Jiàn.
He encountered Sòng general Wáng Yàn's army of seven thousand men at Shāhuìluò,
defeated them,
and then captured Jīnzhōu.
He repeatedly defeated Wú Jiè's various armies at Ráofēng Guān,
then took Zhēnfú Xiàn,
and took Yángzhōu entering Xīngyuán Fǔ.
He defeated Wú Jiè's troops at Gùzhèn,
capturing two of their generals.
Sàgězhù and others defeated Sòng troops,
taking all the stockades and Xiānrén Guān.
In the fourteenth year of Tiānhuì,
he was appointed Yuánshuài Yòujiānjūn.
In the third year of Tiānjuàn,
Zōngbì recaptured Hénán.
Sālīhē advanced from Hézhōng into Shǎnxī.
Upon arriving at Fèngxiáng,
he attacked and routed the Sòng army.
At this time,
there were many Sòng troops west of Jīngzhào.
The generals, due to the summer rain,
wanted to encamp.
Moreover, they heard that ninety thousand Sòng troops were gathering at Jīngzhōu,
and the Dū Yuánshuài had sent Hénán infantry to join the army.
Sālīhē left the other generals to garrison Huánqìng,
and alone, with light cavalry, took Jīngzhōu.
In June,
he defeated the Sòng army at Jīngzhōu.
The Sòng army fled to Wèizhōu.
Bálí Sù pursued them,
and decisively defeated them.
Soon after,
he was appointed Yòufù Yuánshuài.
In the third year of Huángtǒng,
he was enfeoffed as Yìngguó Gōng,
and received generous rewards.
When Xīzōng went hunting,
he was given two fully equipped horses,
and ordered to shoot within the hunting ground.
He was additionally granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When he was about to return to the army,
the prime minister was ordered to hold a farewell banquet for him.
In the sixth month of the third year of Tiānfǔ,
the Grand Tutor Xíníliè (習泥烈), the Great Envoy of Liáo, arrived with the imperial patent and seal at one stage from Shàngjīng.
He first took a duplicate copy of the imperial patent to review it.
The text did not refer to the ruler as "brother",
did not refer to Dàjīn (大金),
but instead called it the "Eastern Huái (懷) Kingdom."
Tàizǔ (太祖) refused to accept it.
He ordered Zōnghán (宗翰), Zōngxióng (宗雄), Zōnggàn (宗幹), and Xīyǐn (希尹) to discuss and finalize the meaning and intent of the imperial patent's text.
Yáng Pǔ (楊朴) polished the language.
Hú Shídá (胡十荅), Āsā (阿撒), and Gāo Qìngyì (高慶裔) translated the Qìdān (契丹) characters.
He sent Zànmóu (贊謀) to accompany Xíníliè.
When Zànmóu arrived in Liáo,
he saw that the Liáo people had rewritten the imperial patent,
and it still did not entirely conform to the intentions of his own country.
He wished to see the Liáo ruler to state his case personally,
but the gatekeepers stopped him.
Zànmóu ignored them
and entered directly.
The gatekeepers struggled with him
and broke his credential tablet.
The Liáo people, in fear,
hastily sent Zànmóu back.
Tàizǔ again sent Zànmóu to Liáo.
The Liáo people sent envoys thirteen times in total,
but the peace negotiations ultimately could not be concluded.
Tàizǔ personally led his army,
and consequently conquered Línhuáng (臨潢).
Later, when attacking Sòng,
Sīzhōng (思忠) followed Zōnghán's army.
Liú Yù (劉豫) was enfeoffed as the Qí (齊) Emperor,
and Sīzhōng was appointed as the Transmission Envoy,
then soon after granted the title of Móukè (謀克).
He followed Zōngbì (宗弼) in conquering Héshangyuán (和尚原).
Upon his return, he served as the Co-Administrator of Xījīng (西京) Garrison Affairs.
In the early Tiānjuàn (天眷) era,
he was transferred to be the Prefect of Púzhōu (蒲州).
The officials and subordinates of the Grand Marshal's Residence in Shǎnxī (陝西)
often oppressed the poor as slaves.
When a thousand artisans were ordered to come east,
upon reaching the river,
Sīzhōng detained them and reported the matter.
An imperial edict ordered them all to return.
He served as the Assistant Minister of the Left in the Traveling Secretariat.
At that time,
Zànmóu was the Consultant for Political Affairs in the Traveling Secretariat.
Sīzhōng was insatiably corrupt,
and Zànmóu disdained him.
The two thus became hostile.
Hǎilíng (海陵) killed the Left Chancellor Bǐngdé (秉德) at the Traveling Secretariat.
Zànmóu's wife
was Bǐngdé's wet nurse.
Sīzhōng used this to frame Zànmóu
and had him killed.
That year,
Sīzhōng entered the court as the Right Chancellor.
Soon after, he was promoted to Joint Administrator of Governmental Affairs
and enfeoffed as Duke of Gàoguó (郜國).
He was further promoted to Left Chancellor and concurrently Grand Astrologer,
enfeoffed as Duke of Yíguó (沂國).
In the third year of Tiāndé (天德),
he retired due to old age.
In the tenth month of the second year of Zhēngyuán (貞元),
Hǎilíng led officials of the third rank and above to Sīzhōng's residence,
and ordered him to appear according to family rituals.
He said to Sīzhōng:
"Your vigor is strong and robust.
You are familiar with the old affairs of the previous court.
No one but you can know them.
You should rise for me
and together govern the state."
Sīzhōng replied:
"Your Majesty's command,
how dare your subject not respectfully obey?
But I regret my old age and illness, and my mistakes,
with nothing to repay my responsibilities."
Hǎilíng then ordered Sīzhōng to ride a horse and follow him into the palace,
appointed him Grand Tutor,
and Head of the Three Departments,
enfeoffed as Prince of Qíguó (齊國).
He was soon appointed Grand Preceptor and concurrently Commissioner for Encouraging Agriculture.
Later, the Secretariat and Chancellery were abolished,
and the position of Head of the Three Departments was not re-established.
The Grand Preceptor was appointed,
ranking above the Chancellor.
Sīzhōng became the Grand Preceptor.
Eight 'scattered attendants' were specially appointed
to be allowed to follow him to the palace,
report on memorials, and be granted seats.
Hǎilíng wished to establish the system of enfeoffments and noble ranks,
and hinted to Sīzhōng to make a proposal.
All enfeoffed princes were demoted,
and those of different surnames were either enfeoffed as dukes or given first or second-rank official titles.
Only Sīzhōng was enfeoffed as Prince of Guǎngpíng (廣平) Commandery
and given a jade belt.
Sīzhōng said that officials should not enfeoff their wives,
and Hǎilíng agreed.
Only Sīzhōng's secondary wife was enfeoffed as a Commandery Lady.
Sīzhōng also considered himself an old minister of Tàizǔ
and was quite self-reliant.
Although Hǎilíng would reject advice and refuse to listen,
Sīzhōng spoke his mind without reservation.
When Hǎilíng was about to attack Sòng,
he asked his ministers,
but they all dared not reply.
Sīzhōng said:
"It is not advisable."
Hǎilíng was displeased
and said to Sīzhōng:
"Do not discuss whether it is advisable or not,
just say when it can be conquered."
Sīzhōng said:
"Give it ten years."
Hǎilíng said:
"Why so long?
A month will suffice."
Sīzhōng said:
"Tàizǔ's campaign against Liáo
still took several years.
Now the people are distressed and resentful,
and the army's cause is without justification.
The area between Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) is hot and humid,
unsuitable for prolonged residence,
and cannot be conquered within months or even years."
Hǎilíng was enraged
and looked around him,
as if wishing to draw weapons.
Sīzhōng, without fear,
replied again:
"This old subject has served four reigns,
and risen to the position of Grand Chancellor.
If I can be of any benefit to the state,
what regret would death hold?"
After a while,
Hǎilíng said:
"Since ancient times, emperors unified all under heaven,
and only then could they be considered legitimate rulers.
You old fool certainly do not know this.
Your son Yǐdié (乙迭) studies books,
you can go and ask him."
Sīzhōng said:
"Your subject saw Tàizǔ conquer the realm in the past,
was there any scholarly text at that time?
Your subject is nearly seventy,
and has experienced much.
That young brat,
how is he fit to be asked?"
Since Hǎilíng did not heed Sīzhōng's words,
he transported weapons and armor from all directions to Zhōngdū (中都).
Sīzhōng said:
"If the prefectures and commanderies have no troops,
how will they defend against bandits?"
Hǎilíng registered all able-bodied men as soldiers.
Sīzhōng said:
"The Qìdān tribes beyond the mountains may not all be suitable for conscription."
Hǎilíng listened to none of this.
Afterwards,
bandits arose in the prefectures and commanderies,
and the prefects and magistrates could not control them.
The Qìdān Sābā (撒八) and Wōwò (窩斡) indeed rebelled,
and it took a year to suppress them.
At that time,
Hǎilíng was attacking Sòng.
Qí Zǎi (祁宰) remonstrated and died,
Zhāng Hào (張浩) made a proposal and was flogged,
Sīzhōng was alienated,
and Kǒng Yànzhōu (孔彥舟) planned to first take Liǎnghuái (兩淮),
with no one else able to match him.
In the sixth year of Zhènglóng (正隆),
Sīzhōng passed away,
aged seventy-three.
Hǎilíng deeply mourned and cherished him,
personally attended his funeral,
increased the funeral endowments,
bestowed a golden-dragon-headed carriage,
and sent an envoy to supervise
and provide travel expenses.
In the twelfth year of Dàdìng (大定),
an edict restored Wūlíndá Zànmóu's (烏林荅贊謀) official titles and ranks,
and posthumously honored him as Grand Master of the Imperial Court.
The Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Zànmóu was loyal, honest, resolute, and firm,
even ancient people could not surpass him.
Because he had a grudge with Sīzhōng,
Sīzhōng persuaded Hǎilíng to kill him.
Now Sīzhōng's descendants are all unworthy,
which is also a hidden retribution."
Originally,
after Sīzhōng had framed and killed Zànmóu,
he then took Zànmóu's wife, Lady Cái (曹氏),
and seized all of his family's property.
When Zhāngzōng (章宗) ascended the throne,
Zànmóu's daughter, Wǔshíjiǔ (五十九), requested a reburial.
An edict granted burial land in Huáizhōu (懷州),
and also ordered the return of the family property Sīzhōng had originally seized.
Qiān’s original name was Yǐdié.
He successively held the posts of Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Shìzōng said to him:
“Officials in the ministries and departments accept solicitations,
some using their families to transmit messages.
Official punishments are not strict,
and the士fēng is in such a state of decline.
You should rectify this.”
Earlier,
when Shìzōng arrived in Zhōngdū,
he released many palace women to return home.
There were several individuals, such as Chēngxīn, on the list for release,
but the department concerned failed to check properly,
and they were unable to leave the palace.
Chēngxīn was often resentful.
On the night of Guǐsì in the intercalary second month of Dàdìng 2nd year (1162),
she then set fire in the sixteen positions,
which spread and burned the Tàihé and Shénlóng Halls.
The Emperor ordered his close ministers to trace the source of the fire.
Six palace women, including Yuán Liùniáng, from the sixteen positions, reported
that Chēngxīn and others were indeed responsible.
Chēngxīn and others were executed.
Yuán Liùniáng and the other five women were rewarded
and released from the palace to become commoners.
Qiān felt that with the palace halls burned,
there would soon be a resumption of construction work,
which would burden the people and waste resources.
So he submitted a memorial requesting a temporary postponement of the repairs.
The Emperor sent Zhāng Rǔbì to issue an imperial edict to Qiān, saying:
“I reflect that during the Zhènglóng period, there were years of forced labor,
and the common people’s wounds have not yet healed.
Border affairs have not ceased,
so how could there suddenly be construction?
You should understand this.”
After a long time,
he inherited his father Sīzhōng’s post as Jìzhōu Měng'ān and Lìshèjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
Wūlíndá Chāowù pursued runaway soldiers
into the Měng'ān district.
Qiān, fearing their disturbance,
collected money from the common people to buy silver and bribe Chāowù.
When the matter was discovered,
Chāowù was punished,
and Qiān was stripped of his Měng'ān post.
He encountered an amnesty
and requested (reinstatement).
The Emperor said:
“Yǐdié did not personally take bribes;
let him be restored to his former position.”
Nòuwǎn Wēndūn Wùdài
was the nephew of Grand Preceptor Sīzhōng.
During the Tiānhuì period,
he served as a female Jurchen character student (nǚzhí zì xuéshēng),
was knowledgeable and well-versed,
read historical texts,
and was skilled in poetry.
He was selected as a Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
appointed Yòusī Dūshì,
transferred to Xíngtái Yòusī Lángzhōng,
and then became Zuǒsī Yuánwàiláng.
He successively held the post of Tóngzhī Dàxīng Yǐn.
The banditry in the capital ceased,
and no affairs were delayed.
He was again promoted to Xíngbù Shàngshū,
then reassigned as Dìnghǎijūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū,
and then reassigned to Lìbù.
During the Zhènglóng campaign against Sòng,
he served as Wǔdìngjūn Dū Zǒngguǎn.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he sent an envoy to summon him,
appointed him Xiánpíng Yǐn,
and made him Běibiān Xíngjūn Dūtǒng.
He was reassigned as Huìníng Yǐn,
with his Dūtǒng position remaining as before.
At this time,
Wōwò had just been suppressed,
and people’s hearts were not yet at peace.
Wùdài governed with leniency and simplicity,
made extensive defensive preparations,
and maintained careful scouting.
The border commanderies were thus pacified.
He was reassigned as Běijīng Liúshǒu.
He was commended for his integrity and scrutiny,
with the remark, “Wùdài has a reputation for ability wherever he serves,
and no private faults.”
Because of this, he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Shìzōng instructed him, saying:
“If those above you
act inappropriately,
and their advice is not followed,
you should report what you see.
If there are capable talents in lower positions,
you should recommend them.”
After a long time, he fell ill.
The Emperor ordered Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ Jìng Sìhuī to visit him
and sent doctors for treatment.
He died
at the age of forty-seven.
The Emperor heard of his death and mourned him,
bestowing a thousand liǎng of silver, forty lengths of heavy silk, and four hundred bolts of fine silk,
and ordered the relevant officials to offer sacrifices.
After a long time,
the Emperor said to his attendants:
“The late Cānzhī Zhèngshì Wùdài, Xíngbù Shàngshū Yànzhōng, Cāngzhōu Jiédùshǐ Wùbùhē, Shìláng Díwò, and Lángzhōng Gǔmǒ were all loyal and upright individuals.
Among the later generations, few can match them.
I delight in finding loyal and upright people.
Are there any like Wùdài and his peers?
You gentlemen should recommend them to me.”
Such was the extent of his remembrance.
Áng’s original name was Bēndǔ,
grandson of Jǐngzǔ’s younger brother Bóhēi,
and son of Xiéwò.
As a child, he served Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ ordered several people to wrestle in pairs.
At that time, Áng was fifteen years old.
Tàizǔ looked at him and said:
“Can you do this?”
He replied:
“If commanded,
how dare I not strive?”
He then consecutively threw six men.
Tàizǔ joyfully said:
“You are
my kin, my younger brother.
From now on, do not leave my side.”
After a few days,
he was given a gold plaque,
which he was ordered to wear while serving.
At seventeen,
Tàizǔ campaigned against Liáo
and said to him:
“You may now don armor and join the army.”
Áng then wore the bestowed gold plaque and joined the army.
When Tàizǔ pacified Yān,
he honored his achievements
and bestowed upon him the finest mansion.
In Tiānfǔ 6th year (1122),
Zōnghàn was stationed at Běi'ānzhōu.
Hearing that the Liáo ruler Yánxǐ was at Yuānyāng Luò,
he sent Nòuwǎn Wēndūn Sīzhōng to request from the Guólùn Bójíliè Gǎo
permission to pursue him with his army.
Gǎo could not decide,
so he sent Áng and Sīzhōng to Zōnghàn to discuss the matter,
and the plan was then settled.
In Tiānhuì 2nd year (1124),
Nánjīng rebelled.
The military commander Shémǔ sent Áng and Liú Yànzōng to divide their forces and suppress it.
When Zōngwàng campaigned against Sòng,
he was authorized to be Hénán Zhūlù Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng,
known as
“Jīnpái Lángjūn” (Lord of the Golden Plaque).
When Bìanzhōu was attacked,
Zōngbì and Áng, with three thousand soldiers, formed the vanguard.
By dusk,
Áng first arrived at its north gate with a thousand men.
At that time, an envoy from the army was sent into the city,
but the Sòng people did not admit him.
Áng explained the situation to them,
and thus gained entry.
When Zōngwàng arrived at Biàn,
he ordered Shémǔ, Tàlǎn, and others to encamp at the northeast corner of the city.
Fearing that the Sòng ruler might flee,
he sent Áng and others to lead light cavalry to patrol around the city.
Áng, leading only eight mókè,
encountered ten thousand enemy soldiers.
He engaged them in battle
and defeated them,
with more than half of their infantry drowning in the Biàn River.
In the 7th year (1129),
the main army crossed the river,
defeating the Sòng army by the river.
The commander's headquarters sent Áng and others with troops to pursue the Sòng ruler.
The Sòng ruler entered Kuàijī,
as if preparing for a staunch defense,
with several thousand soldiers arrayed in formation among the bamboo and reeds east of the outer wall.
The generals wanted to attack them.
Áng said:
“This is a deception.
It would be better to immediately attack the city,
otherwise he will escape through another gate.”
The generals hesitated and could not decide,
and indeed the Sòng ruler escaped through another gate in a single boat into the sea,
so they failed to capture him and returned.
Zōngfǔ pacified Shǎnxī.
Zōngbì managed Xīqín.
He dispatched Áng and Sālǐhē to lead eight thousand troops to attack and seize the prefectures and counties of Héxī.
Áng and the others then took the two stockades, Níngtáo and Ānlǒng.
They advanced to Hézhōu,
where its Tongpàn led the gentry and commoners to welcome their surrender.
They attacked Lèzhōu,
and its Dūhù and the Anfǔshǐ of Hézhōu, Guō Níng, surrendered together.
They then advanced and took three more stockades,
arriving at Xīníngzhōu.
The Dūhù Xǔ Jūjiǎn surrendered the city,
and Zhào Qiánxiá, the grandson of a Túfān chieftain, led five leaders of his Mùbō部 to surrender.
Áng separately led four thousand troops to Jīshí Jūn,
where he received the surrender of its garrison and the officials of its five subordinate stockades.
He pursued twelve Túfān Qiánxiá and others to Kuòzhōu,
but they refused to surrender when summoned,
so he attacked and captured them.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn (1138),
he was appointed Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn
and made Dōngpíng Yǐn.
In the summer of the following year,
the Sòng general Yuè Fēi, with an army of one hundred thousand,
claiming a million,
came to attack Dōngpíng.
Dōngpíng had five thousand troops;
Áng hastily led them out to resist.
At that time, mulberry and zhe trees were luxuriant.
Áng had many banners displayed in the woods
as a feint,
while he himself arrayed his elite troops in front.
Yuè Fēi dared not advance,
and after several days of standoff, he retreated.
Áng ordered his troops to pursue and attack him.
When they reached Qīngkǒu,
Yuè Fēi’s forces boarded boats and went upstream.
At that time, the continuous rain did not stop day or night.
Áng then camped by the water.
Towards midnight,
he suddenly urged his troops to move north.
The generals remonstrated, saying:
“The soldiers have traveled far through mud and mire,
hungry and exhausted without having eaten.
We fear it will be difficult to proceed immediately.”
Áng angrily did not respond,
but beat the drums to urge them on,
issuing an order:
“Those who dare to fall behind after the drumbeat ceases will be beheaded.”
He then abandoned the camp and left,
stopping after nearly twenty lǐ.
That night,
Sòng forces came to raid the camp,
found nothing, and left.
The generals came to congratulate him
and asked the reason.
Áng said:
“Those who go downstream
are fleeing.
Those who go upstream
are luring me to pursue them.
Now, with heavy rain and mud,
their boat travel is safe,
but our land travel is arduous.
Our soldiers are hungry and exhausted,
and our bows and arrows are damaged and weak.
Our army is located downstream from them,
which is a disadvantageous position.
They are certain to attack us.”
Everyone praised his wisdom.
Yuè Fēi besieged Pīzhōu very tightly with one hundred thousand troops.
The city had only over a thousand soldiers,
and the defending general, in fear,
sent someone to ask for help.
Áng said:
“Tell the defending general for me
that I once visited Xiàpī.
In the southwest corner of the city, there is a trench over a zhàng deep.
He should quickly fill it in.”
The defending general followed his instruction
and filled it.
Yuè Fēi indeed dug a tunnel from this spot to enter,
but realizing there were preparations,
he stopped.
Áng raised an army to provide support,
and Yuè Fēi then retreated.
After seven years in Dōngpíng,
he was transferred to Yìdū Yǐn,
promoted to Dōngběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
then transferred to Chóngyìjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and promoted to Huìníng Mù.
In early Tiāndé (1149),
he was transferred to Ānwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ,
promoted to Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān,
then to Zuǒjiānjūn,
and appointed to the hereditary position of Yílǐmǐn Wòlǔhún Hé Shìxí Měng'ān for Shàngjīnglù.
Hǎilíng said:
“You have rendered great service.
One Měng'ān is not enough to reward you.”
He added four Mókè.
Áng accepted the Qīnguǎn Mókè,
and ceded the other three Mókè to his clan brothers.
He was appointed Pīmì Fùshǐ,
then transferred to Tàizǐ Shàobǎo,
and promoted to Pīmìshǐ and Shàngshū Zuǒchéngxiàng.
Áng was angry at his clan brother’s wife,
removed her clothes, and flogged her back.
When Hǎilíng heard of this,
he flogged Áng fifty times.
After a long time,
he was appointed Tàiwèi
and enfeoffed as Shěn Guógōng.
He was promoted to Tàibǎo,
became Pàn Dàzōngzhèng Shì,
and was enfeoffed as Chǔ Guógōng.
He was successively re-enfeoffed as Jǔ, Wèi, and Qí Guógōng,
concurrently holding the post of Pīmìshǐ,
with Tàibǎo remaining as before.
When Hǎilíng launched his southern campaign,
he divided the armies of various circuits into thirty-two Zǒngguǎn,
subordinate to the Zuǒ and Yòu Lǐngjūn Dàdūdū Fǔ.
He then appointed Áng as Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Dàdūdū.
Hǎilíng built a platform by the river
and summoned Áng and the Yòu Lǐngjūn Fùdàdūdū Púlúhún, telling them:
“The boats are ready.
We can cross now.”
Púlúhún said:
“The boats are too small to cross.”
Hǎilíng was angry
and ordered Áng and Púlúhún to cross first tomorrow.
Áng was afraid
and wanted to flee.
By dusk,
Hǎilíng sent someone to stop him, saying:
“What I said before was just a moment of anger.”
Later, when they arrived at Yángzhōu,
a military mutiny occurred,
and Hǎilíng died.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne in Liáoyáng,
Áng sent someone to kill Crown Prince Guāngyīng in Nánjīng,
and dispatched his son, the Qǐndiàn Xiǎodǐ Zōnghào, and his son-in-law, the Páiyìn Zhīhòu Huíhǎi, and others to present a memorial congratulating the new emperor on his ascension.
As the main army returned north,
Áng feared that the Sòng people would pursue them,
so he immediately wrote a letter to the Sòng to cease hostilities.
In the second year (1162),
he had an audience with Shìzōng,
who expressed deep comfort and commendation.
He was promoted and enfeoffed as Hàn Guógōng,
appointed Dūyuánshuài,
with Tàibǎo remaining as before.
A Yuánshuài Fǔ was established in Shāndōng
to manage border affairs.
Not long after,
he was ordered to escort the coffin of Emperor Ruìzōng to the imperial tomb,
with Áng appointed as the Chìzàngshǐ.
After the task was completed,
he returned to Shāndōng.
In the third year (1163),
he was summoned to the capital
and died of illness,
at the age of sixty-four.
The emperor suspended court for him,
personally attended the funeral,
and bestowed one thousand liǎng of silver, fifty bolts of heavy brocade, and five hundred bolts of silk.
In the first month, on the day of Xīnyǒu, of the second year of Míngchāng,
Empress Xiàoyì passed away.
Wú Wáng Yǒngchéng, who was the acting governor of Zhēndìng Prefecture, and Suí Wáng Yǒngshēng, who was the acting military commissioner of Dìngwǔ Circuit, were late in arriving to mourn.
Each was fined one month's salary,
and their chief clerks were flogged fifty strokes with a rod.
Yǒngzhōng happened to have a cold illness
and could not attend.
The Emperor was angry,
and suspected that the princes had a disrespectful attitude.
He sent an envoy to rebuke Yǒngzhōng, saying:
"The period of public mourning is almost over,
so there is no need for you to come."
In the second month, on the day of Bǐngxū,
the Dàn (final) sacrifice was performed.
Yǒngzhōng then arrived
and attended the mourning.
On the day of Xīnmǎo,
he was finally able to perform the Shāofàn (burning of cooked rice) ritual.
On the day of Rénchén,
Yǒngzhōng and the other princes took their leave from the court.
They were given gifts of remaining items.
Although the ceremonial courtesies were still extended,
suspicion and jealousy began from this point.
In the fourth month,
he was promoted to Prince of Bìng.
In the third year,
he was appointed acting governor of Píngyáng Prefecture
and promoted to Prince of Hào.
Initially, tutors for the princes (wángfù) and prefectural adjutants (fǔwèi) were established,
nominally as officials,
but in reality, they were to oversee and restrict them.
The prefectural adjutants eagerly sought to curry favor
and became excessively harsh and restrictive.
Yǒngzhōng, considering himself the eldest son of Shìzōng,
and moreover being old,
found every action constrained.
His feelings became unbearable,
and he was exceedingly depressed.
He then submitted a memorial requesting to live in retirement.
An imperial edict denied it.
In the fourth year,
Zhèng Wáng Yǒngdǎo was executed for conspiracy to rebel.
One additional Sīmǎ (controller) was appointed for each prince,
to monitor their household's comings and goings.
Ball games, hunting, and banquets all had restrictions,
and the comings and goings of family members were all prohibited.
Bǎlǐhǎi, the judicial commissioner of Hédōng Circuit, was punished with one hundred strokes with a rod
and dismissed from office
for privately visiting Yǒngzhōng.
Péimǎn Kěsūn, formerly a deputy envoy of the Imperial Attendants Bureau, had once accepted a request from Yǒngzhōng
to secure an official post for Shígǔnǎi.
Kěsūn, who had already been transferred to be co-administrator of the Western Capital Garrison,
was still dismissed because of this.
The former Assistant Minister of the Right, Zhāng Rǔbì,
was Yǒngzhōng's maternal uncle.
Rǔbì's wife, Gāotuówò, had from the Dàdìng era painted a portrait of Yǒngzhōng's mother,
which she honored with great reverence.
She practiced heterodox arts to pray for Yǒngzhōng's blessings,
hoping for things beyond her station.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
Gāotuówò was executed for curses and prayers.
The Emperor suspected Yǒngzhōng was involved in the matter,
but had no means to uncover it.
It happened that the Tutors and Adjutants of Hào Wáng reported that Yǒngzhōng's fourth son, Ālíhé Mǎn, due to the strict prohibitions,
had uttered inappropriate words.
An imperial edict commanded Dútā, co-administrator of the Great Royal Affairs Bureau, and Sūn Jíkāng, Censor-in-Chief, to interrogate him.
They also found that the poems and songs composed by his second son, Shéntú Mén, contained disrespectful words.
The household slave, Dégē, reported that Yǒngzhōng had once said to his concubine, Ruìxuě:
"If I obtain the world,
my son will be a great prince,
and you will be empress."
An imperial edict sent officials to re-examine the case, and their findings were similar.
Officials were sent a second time: Zhāng Wěi, Minister of Rites, and Wūgǔlún Qìngyì, Vice Minister of War, to review it.
The Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Hào Wáng's offense is only verbal,
different from Yǒngdǎo's crime."
Mǎ Qí, Grand Councilor, said:
"Although Yǒngzhōng's and Yǒngdǎo's crimes differ in specifics,
a subject having no ambition to usurp is
the same principle."
The Emperor said:
"Why did the Grand Councilor suddenly say this?"
Qīngchén, Left Chancellor, said:
"He has long harbored unrealistic ambitions."
An imperial edict ordered Yǒngzhōng's crimes to be announced to all officials for discussion.
Officials of the fifth rank and below submitted their memorials,
while those of the fourth rank and above were to enter the private audience hall to deliberate.
All said:
"We request judgment according to the law."
Only Lú Lìyòng, Supervisor of the Palace Household, pleaded for his life to be spared.
An imperial edict ordered Yǒngzhōng to be put to death,
and Shéntú Mén, Ālíhé Mǎn, and others were all executed in the marketplace.
An imperial command instructed the relevant authorities to bury Yǒngzhōng with the rites of a Duke of the State.
Píngyáng Prefecture supervised the burial,
and the government provided the funeral implements.
His wife and children were settled in Wēizhōu.
In the seventh year of Tàihé,
an imperial edict restored Yǒngzhōng's princely title
and granted him the posthumous name Lì.
An imperial command instructed Shígǔnǎi to choose a site in Wēizhōu
and rebury him with proper rites,
performing sacrifices seasonally.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
an imperial edict ordered Yǒngzhōng's wife, son Shígǔnǎi, and others to be resettled in Zhèngzhōu.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu,
Liú Quán, a man from Tàikāng County, who had once been a bandit,
fled into Wèizhēn territory.
He falsely claimed to be the "Beloved Prince" (àiwáng).
The so-called "Beloved Prince"
referred to Shígǔnǎi.
Shígǔnǎi had in fact never been enfeoffed as a prince;
common people mistakenly called him this.
Liú Quán, desiring to cause rebellion,
then made this false claim to deceive the masses.
He enticed a woman of the Wáng family to be his wife,
and also said that her son was currently gathering troops in Hébĕi.
Lǐ Níng, a man from Dōngpíng, lived on Sōngshān
and practiced sorcery.
Shí Wēn, a man from the same county as Quán, claimed that Níng could discuss important matters.
So he had Fàn Yuán write a false summons to him.
When Níng arrived,
he was acclaimed as the National Preceptor,
and they discussed usurpation.
The matter was discovered,
and Quán, Wēn, and Níng were all executed.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
Tóngguān fell.
Yǒngzhōng's descendants were moved to Nánjīng.
In the second year of Xīngdìng,
Sūn Xuéjiū, a scholar from Qiáo County, Bózhōu, privately spread seditious rumors, saying:
"The Beloved Prince will eventually rise up.
He is now hiding among the common people,
calling himself Liú Èr."
The common people of Wèizhēn, such as Wáng Shēn, all believed it to be true.
A certain Liú Èr appeared and assumed the identity.
He sent people like Ōu Róng to assemble a rebellious party,
purchase weapons,
and prominently display banners,
planning to usurp the throne.
The matter was discovered,
and fifty-two people were executed,
while over sixty were implicated.
Yǒngzhōng's descendants were imprisoned
from Míngchāng until the end of Zhèngdà,
nearly forty years.
In the early Tiānxīng era,
an imperial edict lifted the imprisonment.
Not long after,
Nánjīng also reportedly fell.
Zhèng Wáng Yǒngdǎo's original name was Yínshúkě,
and initially, he was called Shígǒuer.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Téng.
Before a month passed, he was promoted to Prince of Xú.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he became the Administrator of Dàxīng.
Upon Zhāngzōng's ascension to the throne,
he was appointed acting military commissioner of Zhāngdé Circuit
and promoted to Prince of Wèi.
In the second year of Míngchāng,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Zhèng.
In the third year,
he was reassigned to act as military commissioner of Dìngwǔ Circuit.
Initially,
Cuī Wēn, Guō Jiàn, Mǎ Tàichū, and Yǒngdǎo’s household slave, Bì Qìngshòu, privately discussed prophecies of disaster and good fortune.
Bì Qìngshòu then told Yǒngdǎo:
“Guō Jiàn is quite skilled at physiognomy.”
Yǒngdǎo then summoned Guō Jiàn to read his own face and those of his wife and children.
Jiàn said to Yǒngdǎo:
“Your Majesty’s appearance is extraordinary;
your consort and two sons are all destined for great nobility.”
He further added:
“Your Majesty,
as the eldest son of the primary consort,
you are not comparable to other princes.”
Yǒngdǎo summoned Cuī Wēn and Mǎ Tàichū to discuss prophecies and celestial phenomena.
Cuī Wēn said:
“There will be military disaster in the Chǒu year.
Those born in the year of the rabbit will gather troops and gain position in the spring of the following year.”
Guō Jiàn said:
“Yesterday, I saw red qi invading the Purple Star,
and a white rainbow piercing the moon,
all indicating military conflict and usurpation between the Chǒu and Yín years.”
Yǒngdǎo deeply believed their words,
and secretly allied with the inner attendant Zhèng Yǔ’ér to monitor the emperor’s daily life,
making Cuī Wēn his chief strategist,
while Guō Jiàn and Mǎ Tàichū traveled about to persuade others.
The Commander of Henán, Pú Sǎn Kuí, was married to Yǒngdǎo’s sister, Princess Hánguó.
Yǒngdǎo plotted to acquire the Henán army for assistance,
and conferred with his sister, Princess Zéguó Chánglè.
He sent the Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant, Púlàdǔ, to deliver a letter to Kuí,
and first proposed a marriage
to gauge his intentions.
Kuí refused the marriage,
and the envoy dared not speak of treasonous matters again.
Yǒngdǎo’s household slave Dǒng Shòu remonstrated with Yǒngdǎo,
but he did not listen.
Dǒng Shòu spoke of this to his fellow slave Qiānjiānú,
who then reported the treason.
At this time,
Yǒngdǎo was in the capital.

An imperial edict ordered the Minister of Political Affairs, Wányán Shǒuzhēn; the Assistant Administrator, Xū Chíguó; the Minister of Revenue, Yáng Bótōng; and the Administrator of Dàxīng Prefecture, Nímánggǔ Jiàn, to interrogate the matter.
Many were implicated,
and a decision could not be reached for a long time.
The emperor grew angry
and summoned Shǒuzhēn and others to inquire about the situation.
The Right Chancellor, Jiágǔ Qīngchén, reported:
“It is crucial to conclude this matter swiftly
to calm the people’s hearts.”
Thereupon,
Yǒngdǎo, his consort Biàn Yù,
their two sons Ànchūn and Āxīn,
and Princess Chánglè were all granted permission to commit suicide.
Púlàdǔ, Cuī Wēn, Guō Jiàn, Mǎ Tàichū, and others were all executed.
Although Pú Sǎn Kuí was not questioned,
he was still dismissed from his post.
Dǒng Shòu was spared death
and relegated to the penal servitude register.
Qiānjiānú was rewarded with two thousand strings of cash
and specially promoted to Administrator of the Five Officials Miscellaneous Ranks.
From then on, the restrictions and prohibitions on princes became stricter.
In the seventh year of Tàihé,
an edict restored Yǒngdǎo’s princely title,
provided full rites for his reburial,
and bestowed the posthumous title Lì.
Ànchén, son of Prince Wèi Yǒngjì, was made Yǒngdǎo’s successor
to maintain his sacrifices.
Prince Yuè Yǒnggōng, originally named Sònggé,
also known as Guǎngsūn, was born in the second year of Zhēnyuán.
He was silent, spoke little, and rarely smiled;
he was exceptionally brave and strong,
read books and histories,
and was fond of calligraphy and famous paintings.
In the fourth year of Dàdìng,
he was enfeoffed as Prince Zhèng.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Prince Suí.
In the eleventh year,
he was promoted to Prince Cáo.
In the fifteenth year,
he was appointed Minister of Punishments.
The emperor said:
“Attendant Censor Zhāng Rǔlín
is your maternal uncle by seniority;
you can learn governance from him.”
In the seventeenth year,
he was granted the hereditary military command (méng’ān) of Huóhuotu.
In the eighteenth year,
he was made Administrator of Dàxīng.
When Emperor Shìzōng visited Jīnliánchuān,
he first departed from the Central Capital.
Two guards (cāngtóu) from the imperial army let their horses graze on commoners’ fields.
An edict was issued to Yǒnggōng:
“Each cāngtóu is to be given one hundred strokes of the rod.
The two centurions (dànyā bǎihù) who failed to supervise them
are to be dismissed.”
Later, when the emperor was at Wàngjīngdiàn,
Yǒnggōng memorialized:
“The imperial army soldiers are served by only one cāngtóu and two dànyā,
and this has been the case for a long time.
I humbly risk death to defy the edict,
suggesting that the cāngtóu be lightly punished,
and the dànyā be allowed to await judgment.
They can be made to compensate for the value of the fields.
I beg Your Majesty’s compassion and consideration.”
The emperor agreed to all of it.
An old woman and a man and woman were resting by the roadside.
The woman eloped with her lover.
Someone told the old woman:
“I just saw a young woman leave by a small path near the water.”
The old woman reported it to the local constable (wǔzhǎng) to track her.
A man had privately slaughtered an ox,
holding a bloody knife in his hand.
Seeing the wǔzhǎng,
he thought he was being arrested
and immediately fled.
The old woman and the wǔzhǎng suspected he had killed the woman,
arrested him, and sent him to the county.
Unable to bear the torture,
he falsely confessed.
When asked where the body was,
he falsely replied:
“I threw it into the water.”
They searched the water
and indeed found a body,
already half-decomposed.
The county officials believed the man had truly killed the woman
and immediately prepared the case for appeal.
Yǒnggōng doubted this, saying:
“How many days has the woman been dead
for the body to be half-decomposed so quickly?”
Soon after,
the old woman found her daughter with her lover.
Yǒnggōng said:
“This man was coincidentally imprisoned for murder;
his torture is sufficient punishment for the crime of slaughtering an ox.”
Then he released him.
The Huáng clan of Wǔqīng and the Wáng clan of Wàngyún were powerful, cunning, and lawless.
Yǒnggōng exposed their crimes,
and the capital region became orderly.
In the twenty-third year,
he was appointed Acting Governor of the Eastern Capital.
That month,
he was reassigned as Administrator of Héjiān.
A month later,
he was reassigned as Governor of the Northern Capital.
Not long after,
the emperor said to his chancellors:
“I hear that Yǒnggōng’s governance in the Northern Capital is not good.
Although he is my son,
if it is exposed,
can the law be discarded?
I have already warned and instructed Yǒnggōng.
You all should instruct his chief secretary
to rectify him.”
He was in the Northern Capital for a total of seven months,
then reassigned as Governor of the Eastern Capital.
When Emperor Shìzōng visited the Supreme Capital,
passing through the Eastern Capital,
Yǒnggōng accompanied him.
The next year,
when the emperor returned to Tiānpíng Mountain’s Hǎoshuǐ Stream,
the Crown Prince passed away.
An edict ordered Yǒnggōng to oversee the funeral arrangements,
and soon after, he was appointed Grand Censor.
Emperor Zhāngzōng enfeoffed him as Prince Yuán
and granted him the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Prince Zhào Yǒngzhōng and Yǒnggōng, as brothers, were both granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
The next year,
he was appointed Acting Grand宗正 (Dàzōngzhèng).
A monk from Yìng Prefecture, who had a past connection with Yǒnggōng,
was going to appeal a case to Yílà Húlà, the Military Commissioner of Zhāngguó Commandery,
and sought a letter from Yǒnggōng to Húlà as a favor.
Húlà received the letter
and reported it.
The emperor said to his chancellors:
“Yǒnggōng wrote a letter to Húlà on behalf of someone’s case.
Although this is a minor matter,
it must be punished.
If small transgressions are not dealt with,
they lead to great calamities.
Any offense must be punished
to encourage reform;
this is also a form of education.”
They all said:
“Your Majesty’s enforcement of the law is impartial;
how can your ministers not be respectful and fearful?”
Thereupon, Yǒnggōng was dismissed from his post.
Not long after,
he was reinstated as Acting Grand宗正 (Dàzōngzhèng).
Yùwáng Yǒngchéng, personal name Hèyě,
also known as Lóushì.
His mother was Zhaoyí Liáng shì.
Yǒngchéng had an extraordinary demeanor,
was learned,
and skilled at writing.
Shìzōng especially loved and respected him.
In Dàdìng seventh year (1167),
he was first enfeoffed as Shěnwáng.
Wáng Yànqián, a doctor of the Imperial Academy, was appointed his prefectural Literary Scholar.
Yǒngchéng took him as his teacher.
In the eleventh year (1171),
he was promoted to Bīnwáng.
In the fifteenth year (1175),
he moved to an outer residence.
In the sixteenth year (1176),
he was appointed Acting Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat.
The following year (1177),
he was granted the hereditary Bǎlǔgǔ Mèng'ān of Shāndōng Dōnglù,
and appointed Acting Governor of the Dàmùqīn Prefecture.
Shortly after, he was transferred to Hútǔ'ǎigēmán Mèng'ān of Zhōngdū Lù.
In the twentieth year (1180),
he was appointed Hanlin Academician Compiler.
In the twenty-third year (1183),
he was appointed Acting Jìedùshǐ of Dìngwǔ Jūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to Acting Governor of Guǎngníng Fǔ.
In the twenty-fifth year (1185),
Shìzōng visited Shàngjīng.
He ordered Yǒngchéng to stay behind in Zhōngdū,
appointed him Acting President of the Ministry of Personnel,
promoted him to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and made him Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was reinstated,
promoted to Wúwáng,
and appointed Acting Governor of Zhēndìng Fǔ.
In Míngchāng first year (1190),
he was transferred to Péngmǎbìlà Mèng'ān of Shāndōng Xīlù.
The following year (1191),
he was promoted to Yǎnwáng.
Due to leading military and civilian personnel on a hunt,
he was dismissed from his post
and submitted a memorial to apologize.
The Emperor bestowed a handwritten imperial edict, saying:
"You are truly my closest kin,
and have long demonstrated loyalty and purity.
You served my late father in the Crown Prince's palace,
showing utmost brotherly love.
Upon my succession to the throne as a young ruler,
your loyal and devoted heart became even clearer.
During difficult times,
you provided much assistance.
My heart is aware of this,
and no words can fully express it.
Therefore, I reinstated you from your period of mourning,
and entrusted you with the responsibility of safeguarding the state.
Since governing a vassal state,
years have passed.
In the small state of Zhào,
you knew your talents were difficult to fully employ.
In the remote prefecture of Zhènfǔ,
your abilities were certainly underutilized.
I was just contemplating summoning you by express dispatch to court,
how could I have expected you to suddenly fall afoul of state law?
It happened that during a seasonal hunt,
you somewhat disturbed the populace.
The law does not allow leniency,
and the Censorate reported it.
I tolerated it for months,
unwilling to act immediately.
Although I wished to follow my private affection,
I could not go against public opinion.
Therefore, I relieved you of your previous post,
though your hereditary enfeoffment remains.
Alas,
the laws established by our ancestors
cannot be privately contravened by any single person;
yet, the closest of kin
cannot be alienated by a thousand miles.
By this minor admonition for your retirement,
I wish to fulfill my enduring great favor.
The classics say, 'Not arrogant when in high position,
high yet not imperiled.'
Thus, knowing restraint and prudence is the foundation of self-cultivation,
while arrogance is the source of moral decay.
I constantly strive to remind myself of this,
and now use it to caution you.
In the past, Dōngpíng (Jì) loved goodness
and achieved an immortal reputation;
Liáng Xiào was extravagant and debauched,
and eventually met with regret born of anxiety and suspicion.
The actions of predecessors
can serve as a mirror.
You possess both civil and military talents,
and many skills.
If you follow the Dao,
what can you not accomplish?
If your virtue and achievements improve daily,
there is no need to worry about being reinstated late.
I am not skilled in literary composition,
and hastily wrote this document,
directly expressing my thoughts,
hoping that the words do not obscure the meaning."
Before long,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Qìnnán Jūn.
In the third year (1192),
he was appointed Acting Governor of Xiánpíng Fǔ.
Before he could depart,
he was transferred to Acting Governor of Tàiyuán Fǔ.
On Yǒngchéng's birthday,
the Emperor personally composed a poem to bestow upon him,
which contained
the lines: "Good reputation naturally shines in the jade records,
loyalty needs not be revealed by golden boxes."
This was considered a great honor at the time.
In the seventh year (1196),
he was appointed Acting Governor of Píngyáng Fǔ.
When Chéng'ān changed its reign title (1196),
he was promoted to Yùwáng due to the general amnesty.
In the winter of the following year (1197),
he presented eighty horses
to aid in defense preparations.
The Emperor issued an edict praising and encouraging him, saying:
"You have long enjoyed a distinguished reputation,
and are a prominent relative.
You are knowledgeable about ancient and modern times,
and dedicated to loyalty and righteousness.
While sharing the burdens in the outer provinces,
you came to present fine horses to the imperial stables,
wishing to assist border defense
and enhance military preparedness.
Your wholehearted devotion to the state
is evident through this act.
We recall your earnest diligence
and deeply commend it."
In the fifth year (1200),
he was reappointed.
Shortly after, he was summoned back,
but was unable to have an audience due to illness.
The Emperor personally visited his residence to check on him.
In Tàihé fourth year (1204),
he passed away.
Upon hearing the news,
the Emperor was deeply grieved.
He bestowed a generous funeral grant,
and his posthumous name was Zhōngxiàn.
Yǒngchéng loved reading from a young age,
and his studies became even more refined in his later years.
Whenever he had free time, he would invite literati to discuss and exchange ideas with him,
treating them with courtesy,
never showing any arrogance.
He styled himself
"Lèshàn Jūshì" (Layman Who Delights in Goodness),
and his collected works circulated in the world.
Kuíwang Yǔnshēng,
whose name was changed to Yǒngshēng,
with the original name Xiébùchū,
also known as Hèshòu.
In Dàdìng 11th year (1171),
he was enfeoffed as Xúwáng,
and later promoted to Yúwáng.
In the 26th year (1186),
he was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
The following year (1187),
he served as Pàn Lìbù Shàngshū [Acting Minister of Personnel]
and was appointed Shāndōng Xīlù Ànbìchū Hǔbìlà Měng'ān.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he bestowed favors upon the imperial clan
and transferred Yǔnshēng to the title of Suíwáng,
appointing him Dìngwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In Míngchāng 2nd year (1191),
his title was changed to Cáowáng.
After a long time,
his title was changed to Wǎnwáng.
When Wèishàowáng ascended the throne,
his title was moved to its current one.
In Zhēnyòu 1st year (1213), 9th month,
Xuānzōng, considering Yǔnshēng's advanced age
and his habitual frailty and illness,
decreed that he be allowed to use a staff in the palace.
Soon after, he passed away.
After the funeral preparations,
a memorial feast was held,
and the Emperor personally attended the libation.
The eulogy states: Shìzōng completely preserved the imperial clan,
leaving nothing undone.
Although this corrected the mistakes of Hǎilíng,
it was also due to his naturally benevolent and generous disposition.
His sons Yǒngzhōng and Yǒngdǎo both died at the hands of Zhāngzōng;
the reasons for this are perhaps unchallengeable.
Zhāngzōng had no heir,
so this retribution was not without effect.
Collation Notes
Hàowáng Yǒngzhōng – Note that
"Hào"
appears as
"Gào" in the preceding text.
Also, all the sons of Shìzōng were named with the character
"Yǔn".
Later, Zhāngzōng, to avoid the taboo of his father Yǔngōng's name,
changed
"Yǔn"
to
"Yǒng".
See the supplementary collation notes in Volume 19 of this book.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Sūn Jíkāng interrogated –
"Wèn" (interrogate)
was originally written as
"Mén" (gate),
corrected according to the quote in Yǒnglè Dàdiǎn, juan 6766.
In the 17th year, granted Huóhuótǔ hereditary měng'ān – Note that in Volume 6, Shìzōng Jì, of this book, it states Dàdìng 11th year, 12th month:
"Zhàowáng Yǒngzhōng and Cáowáng Yǒnggōng were both granted měng'ān."
Sons Fú Sūn Shòusūn Niánmògé –
"Mò"
was originally written as
"Yì",
corrected according to the Palace edition.
In the 2nd year, promoted to Bīnwáng –
"Èr" (two)
was originally written as
"Sān" (three).
Note that in Volume 9, Zhāngzōng Jì, of this book, in Míngchāng 2nd year, 4th month:
"Jiǎwǔ, Yǒngdé was renamed Bīnwáng."
Corrected accordingly.
Appointed Shāndōng Xīlù Ànbìchū Hǔbìlà Měng'ān – Note that in Volume 89, Yílà Zàozhuàn, of this book, it states:
"In Dàdìng 19th year, eight měng'ān, including Ànchūhǔ, were relocated from Hénán to the borders of Dàmíng and Dōngpíng."
It is written as
"Ànchūhǔ",
without the character
"Bì".
It is suspected that the character
"Bì"
here is a superfluous character copied from the following character
"Bìlà".
Biographies Chapter 24: Lǐ Shí (Zǐxiànkě) Wányán Fúshòu Dújí Yì Wūyán Púlíhēi Wūyán Púxiánnú Wūyán Chálà Lǐ Shīxióng Nímánggǔ Chāowù Bójílǔ Dìngfāng Jiágǔ Húlà Púchá Wòlùn Jiágǔ Chálà
Lǐ Shí, courtesy name Zǐjiān,
a native of Liáoyáng,
and the younger brother of Empress Zhēnyì.
His ancestors served the Liáo dynasty,
holding the position of prime minister.
His great-great-grandfather Xiānshòu
once rescued the maternal uncle of the Liáo emperor from danger.
The Liáo emperor bestowed upon Xiānshòu a thousand qǐng of land in Liáoyáng and Tāngchí,
with other properties commensurate with this,
and he was often referred to as Lǐ Jiù (Uncle Li).
His father, Chúwōzhǐ,
was Guìzhōu Guānchásǐ.
When Gāo Yǒngchāng occupied Dōngjīng,
Chúwōzhǐ led his troops to attack him,
but was defeated and died.
Shí was honest and reserved in speech,
but his intelligence and insight surpassed ordinary people.
In Tiānhuì 2nd year (1124),
he was granted a hereditary móukè
and served as Xíngjūn Měng'ān.
Ruìzōng, as Yòufù Yuánshuài,
brought him into the army
and assigned him to Zōngbì.
In the 8th year (1130),
he was appointed Lǐbīn Fùshǐ,
and then transferred to Luòyuàn Fùshǐ.
In Tiānjuàn 1st year (1138),
a Xíngtáishěng was established in Biàn,
and Shí was appointed Biànjīng Dōu Xúnjiǎnshǐ.
He successively served as Dàmíng Shàoyǐn, Biànjīng Mǎjūn Fù Dōuzhǐhuīshǐ,
and was promoted to Jǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Hǎilíng was constructing palaces in Yānjīng,
Shí supervised the work at Huángchéng Duānmén.
When Hǎilíng moved the capital to Yānjīng,
Shí attended an audience as per custom.
Hǎilíng pointed at Shí and said:
"Is this not the maternal uncle of Géwáng?"
Géwáng
referred to Shìzōng.
Not long after,
he was appointed Xìngzhōng Shàoyǐn.
Shí knew that Hǎilíng was wary of the imperial clan,
and felt somewhat uneasy about his earlier remark.
Upon completing his term,
he feigned illness and returned to his hometown.
When Shìzōng was garrisoned in Dōngjīng
to defend against the Qìdān Kuòlǐ,
Shí remained in Dōngjīng to patrol the city.
Hǎilíng sent Fù Liúshǒu Gāo Cúnfú to secretly observe Shìzōng's movements.
Jūn Lǐ Púsùyuè learned of Cúnfú's plot
and informed Shìzōng.
Shí then advised Shìzōng to first eliminate Cúnfú,
and then launch his campaign.
Shìzōng followed his advice.
In Dàdìng 1st year (1161), for his merit in determining the imperial succession, he was made Hùbù Shàngshū.
Shortly after,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Āsuǒ killed Tóngzhī Zhōngdū Liúshǒu Púchá Shālízǐ
and sent an envoy to present a memorial to Dōngjīng.
Many officials, however, urged Shìzōng to proceed to Shàngjīng.
Shí reported, saying:
"Zhènglóng is far away in Jiāng and Huái,
with bandits rising everywhere.
The myriad people are looking eastward.
It is fitting at this time to directly proceed to Zhōngdū,
to command the empire from its heart,
which is an enterprise for ten thousand generations.
May Your Majesty not be swayed by the confusion of the masses."
The Emperor's resolve was thus made,
and he departed that very day.
Shìzōng took Shí's daughter into the imperial harem,
and she gave birth to Zhèngwáng Yǒngdǎo and Wèishàowáng Yǒngjì.
She was Yuánfēi Lǐshì.
In the 3rd year (1163),
Hùbù Shàngshū Liáng Qiú submitted a memorial, stating:
"Before Dàdìng, the certificates for salaries and grain for officials, soldiers, and commoners were a mix of genuine and counterfeit.
I request that all be suspended."
Shí bought and replaced the old certificates,
and disbursed grain from the granaries.
The granary officials dared not disobey
and gave him new grain.
The Emperor heard of this matter
and questioned Liáng Qiú.
Liáng Qiú did not respond truthfully.
The Emperor ordered Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Zhái Yǒnggù to interrogate him.
Liáng Qiú was demoted four ranks
and sent to govern Huǒshānjūn.
Shí was dismissed as Yùshǐ Dàfū.
After some time,
he was enfeoffed as Dàoguó Gōng.
Wūyán Chálà
was the son of Púxiá Nǔ, Grand Master of Silver-Green Light-Giving.
He possessed the strength of several men,
and was courageous and unrivaled.
In the sixth year of Zhènglóng (1161), when the expedition against Sòng was launched,
all the *méng'ān* and *móukè* troops were deployed,
leaving the prefectures and counties unprepared.
Qìdān Kuòlǐ captured Hánzhōu
and besieged Xìnzhōu,
causing alarm far and wide.
Chálà's route passed through Xiánpíng,
so he immediately led his own troops back to Xìnzhōu
and defeated them in battle.
Later,
the rebels regrouped and attacked again, surrounding the city,
and even scaled its walls.
Chálà dropped huge logs on them,
killing many rebels,
whereupon Kuòlǐ withdrew.
Chálà held two large iron maces in his left and right hands,
each weighing several tens of *jīn*,
and people called him
"Iron Mace Wànhù."
He pursued Kuòlǐ about eight *lǐ* east of Hánzhōu.
The rebels were arraying their formation on a flat plain.
Chálà personally led his elite soldiers,
wielding his iron maces left and right to strike them,
and none failed to fall dead.
The rebels could not maintain their formation,
so they changed horses and urged their troops to attack again.
The rebel forces were utterly routed,
and fled.
The people of Dōngjīng, Xiánpíng, and Lóngzhōu were then able to live peacefully again.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Chálà had an audience with him.
He was appointed Imperial Guard,
became Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Valiant Cavalry,
and concurrently held the title of Wànhù.
He attacked Wō'wò
and fought at Huādào.
Before the main army had assembled,
Chálà was in the left wing,
leading six hundred cavalry to fight the rebels,
killing over three thousand of them.
Zōnghēng and Púchá Shìjié's seven *móukè* troops fought unfavorably.
Shìjié fled to Chálà's army,
and the rebels surrounded and attacked them.
Chálà resisted in a circular formation and fought.
When Zōng's army came to reinforce,
the rebels then retreated.
Passing west over Niǎolǐng,
they caught up with the rebels at Xiànquán.
The rebels first attacked the right wing.
Chálà met and repelled them,
and the rebels retreated.
Wō'wò recruited someone to assassinate him.
The fake Imperial Guard Ābùshā, who was tall and strong,
brandished a large saber and chopped at Chálà from behind.
Chálà looked back,
and struck Ābùshā with the back of his mace,
breaking his right arm.
Together with Hélíliè Zhìníng's army, they launched a combined attack,
and the rebels were utterly defeated.
After Wō'wò was pacified,
he was appointed General of the Palace Guard,
and was given three hundred *liǎng* of silver and twenty bolts of fine colored silk.
When his father died,
he was reinstated to his original post,
succeeded his father as *méng'ān*,
and was appointed Defense Commissioner of Càizhōu.
He was transferred to Sùzhōu,
then promoted to Military Governor of Chāngwǔ Command,
and moved his garrison to Bīnzhōu.
He was appointed envoy to Sòng to offer New Year's greetings.
He shot an arrow at a willow tree on the Huái River,
and the arrow buried its fletching deep into the tree.
The Sòng people had long heard of his reputation
and were greatly astonished.
He was transferred to Fengxiáng Yǐn,
entered court as Right Deputy Inspector,
and then went out as Xīngzhōng Yǐn,
then transferred to General Administrator of Pósu Sùlù.
Gāolí feared his prestige
and all who came to Pósu Sùlù on business
would kneel upon seeing him from a distance.
In the twenty-fifth year (1185),
he became Military Governor of Xīngpíng Command
and died in office.
Chálà was upright and quiet,
and usually very amiable.
But when facing battle, he fought with courage,
and all who saw him were terrified and retreated.
Even when surrounded by tens of thousands of enemies,
he could enter and exit as if there were no one there.
Lǐ Shīxióng, courtesy name Bówēi,
was a native of Yànmén.
He possessed talent and strength,
enjoyed discussing military tactics,
and admired the heroes of antiquity,
hence his name Shīxióng.
During the Xuānhé era of Sòng, he passed the imperial examination in archery and horsemanship,
and successively held offices as Lieutenant of Dàmíng and Qīngpíng.
When the royal army reached Dàmíng,
Shīxióng surrendered with the prefectural officials
and temporarily held the post of Inspector of Military Affairs for that circuit.
When the Qí state was established,
he was made Vanguard Commander-in-Chief of the Grand Administration and Prefect of Zīzhōu.
When Qí was abolished,
he became Director of Imperial Horse Herds in Biànjīng,
and successively held posts as Prefect of Nínghǎi Command and Administrator of Cáozhōu.
In the second year of Huángtǒng (1142),
he became Military Governor of Wǔshèng Command.
At the end of Zhènglóng,
he was Defense Commissioner of Hézhōu.
When the Sòng general Wú Lín's army attacked Qín and Lǒng,
Shīxióng happened to be arrested and brought to Líntáo for an incident.
When the Sòng army reached the city walls,
the local people defended the city,
but planned to surrender.
Shīxióng stopped them.
As the Sòng general Quán Yí was whipping his horse and ascending a pontoon bridge,
Shīxióng shot him,
and he fell into the river below the bridge.
Quán Yí was then captured,
and the Sòng army retreated.
Later, he followed Marshal Left Supervisor of the Army Túdān Héxǐ in attacking Hézhōu with troops,
and distinguished himself.
Soon after,
he returned to Biàn due to illness
and died.
Ní'pánggǔ Chāowù
was a native of Hésùguǎn.
He was initially a Grand Officer,
and was appointed Interpreter for the Marshal's Residence.
When the Sòng general Hán Shìzhōng led tens of thousands of troops to besiege Pīzhōu,
Chāowù led a few hundred light cavalry and several scouts along a side road to rescue it,
defeating six thousand enemy soldiers.
The next day,
the Sòng army again besieged Xiàpī,
and Chāowù defeated them again.
The Sòng people attacked Jìzhōu,
capturing almost all the warships.
At this time,
Chāowù went to Sùzhōu,
divided Púlǔhǔ's army,
and returning to the Great River,
encountered the enemy.
He fought valiantly and defeated them,
recovering all the warships.
When the royal army recovered Hénán,
a detached Sòng general attacked Bó Dǒngbùhuī's camp by night from Húlíng,
and all the soldiers were lost.
Chāowù fought together with the Grand Administrator of Dōngpíng
and repelled them.
The Marshal's Residence rewarded him with silver and silk.
Chāowù was brave
and skilled at discerning the enemy's strengths and weaknesses,
which led to his repeated victories.
The Marshal's Residence, acting on imperial authority, promoted him to Loyal and Manifest Cavalry Commander,
made him Administrator of the Barbarian Tribes of Túlǐ,
and bestowed upon him ten thousand *guàn* of cash, three hundred bolts of silk, one set of clothing, and two horses.
When he was about to take up his post,
Héjiān Yǐn Dà Bái reported to the Marshal
requesting that Chāowù be kept to handle border affairs,
which was granted.
He was again bestowed ten thousand *guàn* of cash, two hundred fifty *liǎng* of silver, three hundred bolts of fine colored silk, and three horses.
His merits were recorded,
and he was appointed Junior Prefect of Qìngyáng.
When Hǎilíng was about to attack Sòng,
the Qìdān rebelled.
He was summoned and instructed:
"You have been in the border regions for a long time
and have repeatedly achieved military success.
Yesterday, We dispatched Privy Council Vice Director Púsàn Hūtǔ, Resident Overseer Shímò Huáizhōng, and others to suppress the Qìdān,
but their campaign was long and fruitless,
and they have already been punished by law.
Now We order you, along with Commander-in-Chief Bái Yànjìng and Deputy Commander Hélíliè Zhìníng, to advance and suppress them."
Thereupon, he was given four armored horses.
Chāowù and Yànjìng reached Běijīng
but could not advance further.
At this time, Shìzōng ascended the throne in Liáoyáng.
Chāowù went to pay his respects,
was promoted to Grand General Stabilizing the State,
and, with Commander-in-Chief Wúzhá Hū and Deputy Commander Húntǎn, suppressed Wō'wò.
Chāowù reached Wālì,
and encountered Wō'wò.
The left wing briefly retreated.
Chāowù, brandishing his spear, charged into their formation,
personally killing over twenty men,
and the rebels then retreated.
Marshal Púsàn Zhōngyì pursued them from Huādào,
and Chāowù, as vanguard, caught up with them at Xiànquán,
and utterly defeated them.
After the affair was settled,
he was promoted to Pacification Commissioner of the Northwest Circuit,
and then transferred to the Northeast Circuit.
At that time, Zōngshì Zhāng (宗室璋) and others, who were Jǐedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhānghuà Jūn (彰化軍), were resisting the Song general Wú Lín (吳璘) at Déshùn Zhōu (德順州).
Marshal Zuǒ Dūjiān (左都監) Túshàn Héxǐ (徒單合喜) sent Chálà (查剌) to discuss a strategy to defeat the enemy with the various generals.
Zhāng (璋) and others deliberated, saying:
"Although our troops have won repeatedly,
the enemy troops do not retreat,
which indicates that our army is small.
The Dūjiān (都監) must personally come;
only then can we defeat the enemy."
Thereupon, Héxǐ (合喜) led forty thousand troops to arrive,
and subsequently took Déshùn Zhōu (德順州).
He entered and became Diànqián Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (殿前右衞將軍),
inherited his father's Méng’ān (猛安),
was changed to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍),
and promoted to Yòu Fù Diǎnjiǎn (右副點檢).
When he fell ill,
Chancellor Liángbì (良弼) visited him,
and said to his close associates:
"This man is a pillar of the state.
When others are ill,
I have never gone to visit them."
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Northeast Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ (東北路招討使) concurrently Déchāng Jūn Jǐedùshǐ (德昌軍節度使),
and was also granted a golden belt.
Upon arriving at his post,
he governed diligently and effectively,
and the borders became secure.
His judgments in legal cases were fair,
and nothing was lost on the roads.
He was promoted to Línhuáng Yǐn (臨潢尹) concurrently Běnlù Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn (本路兵馬都總管),
and the indigenous tribes were awed and submitted.
He was changed to Northwest Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ (西北路招討使).
The Emperor sent an envoy to proclaim, saying:
"Now that the various tribes have just submitted,
I order you to pacify and settle them,
and your reputation for good governance must reach my ears."
He died in Dàdìng (大定) twelfth year.
Chálà (查剌) was loyal and honest by nature,
inwardly intelligent and sharp-witted.
Whenever he discussed important matters,
he surpassed his peers.
Grand Tutor Xù (勗) once said:
"Chálà (查剌) knows without learning;
compared to the ancients,
such people are rare."
A eulogy states: The victory at Xiánquán (陷泉) was
like dazzling thunder and lightning.
The conquest of Fúlí (符離)
made our power resplendent.
Lǒng (隴) and Dǐ (抵) were like a shower of arrows,
Thus, the achievements of the various generals are listed here.

Also, in the following text
"Jiágǔ Chálà" (夾谷查剌),
"谷" (gǔ)
was also originally
Now standardized together.
"石抹突剌" (Shímò Tūlà),
in Volume 6 of this book, the Annals of Shìzōng (世宗紀), under the second month of Dàdìng (大定) second year, on the day of Bǐngchén (丙辰), it is written as
"石抹術突剌" (Shímò Shùtūlà).
"●螥" (shībāng)
was originally
"螥●" (bāngshī).
According to the Wénxuǎn (文選), Zhāng Héng's (張衡) Xījīng Fù (西京賦) says,
"流鏑●螥" (liú dí shībāng, flowing arrows like a shower),
it has now been changed accordingly.
Biographies, Volume 25: Gēshíliè Zhìníng (紇石烈志寧), Púsǎn Zhōngyì (僕散忠義), Túshàn Héxǐ (徒單合喜)
Gēshíliè Zhìníng's (紇石烈志寧) original name was Sāhélián (撒曷輦),
a native of Shàngjīng Hútǎ’ān (上京胡塔安).
From the time of his fifth-generation ancestor, Grand Tutor Hánchì (韓赤),
his family had been in a maternal uncle-nephew relationship with the state for generations.
His father, Sābā (撒八),
was granted the name Huáizhōng (懷忠) during the Hǎilíng (海陵) period,
and served as the hereditary Mòkè (謀克) of Yánhé (顏河) in Tàizhōu Lù (泰州路),
then promoted to Méng’ān (猛安),
and once served as Dōngpíng Yǐn (東平尹) and Kāiyuǎn Jūn Jǐedùshǐ (開遠軍節度使).
Zhìníng (志寧) was resolute and had great strategic ability.
He married the daughter of Liáng Wáng Zōngbì (梁王宗弼), Yǒng’ān Xiànzhǔ (永安縣主).
Zōngbì (宗弼) loved him the most among all his sons-in-law.
During the Huángtǒng (皇統) era,
he served as Hùwèi (護衞).
Hǎilíng (海陵) appointed him Yòu Xuānhuīshǐ (右宣徽使),
then sent him out as Fényáng Jūn Jǐedùshǐ (汾陽軍節度使),
then brought him back as Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書),
changed to Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ (左宣徽使) and Dū Diǎnjiǎn (都點檢),
promoted to Shūmì Fùshǐ (樞密副使),
and Kāifēng Yǐn (開封尹).
The Qìdān Sāba (契丹撒八) rebelled.

The Púshàn Hútǔ (僕散忽土), Commissioner of Military Affairs; Xiāo Zé (蕭賾), Resident Administrator of Běijīng (北京); and Xiāo Huáizhōng (蕭懷忠), Resident Administrator of Xī Jīng (西京), all failed in their campaigns to suppress the rebellion,
and were consequently executed.
Thereupon,
Zhìníng (志寧) was appointed Vice Commander of the Northern Front,
and, with Commander-in-Chief Bái Yànjìng (白彥敬),
led the armies of the three circuits of Běijīng (北京), Línhuáng (臨潢), and Tàizhōu (泰州) to quell it.
When Zhìníng (志寧) reached Běijīng (北京),
Hǎilíng (海陵)'s campaign against the Sòng (宋) had already crossed the Huái (淮) River.
Yànjìng (彥敬) and Zhìníng (志寧) heard that Shìzōng (世宗) harbored different intentions,
so they secretly conspired with Wányán Púsùlài (完顏蒲速賚), Magistrate of Huìníng (會寧), and Dújí Yì (獨吉義), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Lìshè Jūn (利涉軍),
intending to attack him.
But Shìzōng (世宗) had already ascended the throne
and sent Shímò Yídíe (石抹移迭) and Yílà Hébǔ (移剌曷補) to summon them.
Yànjìng (彥敬) and Zhìníng (志寧) killed their nine envoys.
Shìzōng (世宗) sent Wányán Móuyǎn (完顏謀衍) to attack them.
Their troops refused to fight,
so they surrendered along with Yànjìng (彥敬).
Shìzōng (世宗) asked,
"Zhèng lóng (正隆) was tyrannical,
the people's hopes were dashed.
I, as the grandson of Tàizǔ (太祖), ascended the great throne.
You killed my envoys,
and yet you could not die for Zhèng lóng (正隆).
Fearing that you would be conspired against,
you then came to surrender.
If I kill you now,
what excuse will you have?"
Yànjìng (彥敬) had no reply,
but Zhìníng (志寧) stepped forward and reported,
"Your subjects received great favor from Zhèng lóng (正隆),
which is why we did not surrender.
Our crime deserves ten thousand deaths."
The Emperor said,
"Your initial intentions can be considered loyal to your duties.
From now on, serve me,
and you should strive for loyalty and integrity."
Shìzōng (世宗) sent Zhābā (扎八) to summon Wōwò (窩斡).
Zhābā (扎八) then persuaded him,
and he consequently declared himself Emperor.
Shìzōng (世宗) sent Wányán Móuyǎn (完顏謀衍), Vice Marshal of the Right, to attack him.
Zhìníng (志寧), as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Línhǎi (臨海),
commanded the Right Wing Army.
Wōwò (窩斡) was defeated at Chángluò (長濼)
and fled west.
Zhìníng (志寧) overtook him at the Mùyán Hé (霿●河).
The bandits had already crossed,
formed an array along the bank,
and destroyed the bridge and banks to create an obstruction.
Zhìníng (志寧) and the bandits were separated by the river.
He created a feint,
and with Myriarch Jiágǔ Qīngchén (夾谷清臣) and Túshā Hǎiluó (徒單海羅), forded the river downstream.
Having crossed,
there was a branch channel ahead with steep banks,
and it was muddy within.
So they bound willows to fill and cover it,
and all the soldiers crossed.
After marching several *lǐ* (里),
they reached level ground.
As the officers and soldiers were eating,
the bandits suddenly arrived.
The bandits occupied the southern ridge
and charged down Zhìníng (志寧)'s formation three times.
The formation held firm.
They fought fiercely,
and a stray arrow struck his left arm,
but he continued to fight as if nothing happened.
The bandits, taking advantage of the wind, set fires,
and charged and attacked with the momentum of the smoke.
Zhìníng (志寧)'s infantry arrived subsequently,
and they fought back and forth for over ten engagements.
The fire grew fiercer,
and the wind and smoke were overwhelming and unstoppable.
Coincidentally, rain began to fall,
and the wind and smoke subsided.
They then fiercely attacked
and thoroughly routed them.
Thereupon,
Marshal Móuyǎn (謀衍) and Right Supervising Inspector Fúshòu (福壽) did not press the attack against the bandits,
and for a long time achieved no success.
Púshàn Zhōngyì (僕散忠義), Right Chancellor, requested to personally lead an expedition against the bandits.
As Zhìníng (志寧) had achieved success in attacking the bandits,
the Emperor appointed Zhōngyì (忠義) to replace Móuyǎn (謀衍),
and Zhìníng (志寧) to replace Fúshòu (福壽).
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Dìngguó (定國公),
and Púchá Tōng (蒲察通) was sent to the army to announce the decree.
The bandits raided the borders of Yìzhōu (懿州),
captured the three counties of Língshān (靈山), Tóngchāng (同昌), and Huìhé (惠和),
and cast their eyes on Běijīng (北京).
Coincidentally, the Tǔ Hé (土河) River swelled,
and the bandits could not cross,
so they headed west towards Sānhán Xiàn (三韓縣).
Zhìníng (志寧) was pursuing them.
Marshal Zhōngyì (忠義) encountered the bandits at Huādào (花道),
and his army suffered a minor setback.
The bandits saw Zhìníng (志寧) following close behind them
and dared not press their advantage,
so they fled west.
At this time,
the grand army's horses were thin and weak,
and unfit for pursuit.
The generals wanted to halt the army and not pursue.
Zhìníng (志寧) captured a bandit scout
and learned that the bandits had separated their elite forces from their old, young, and baggage train,
planning to rendezvous beyond the mountains.
He realized that their baggage train could be attacked.
Zhōngyì (忠義) agreed.
So they crossed Yímǎ Lǐng (移馬嶺)
and advanced to Xiànquán (陷泉) west of Niǎolǐng (裊嶺).
The bandits saw the left wing occupying the southern ridge and forming an array
and dared not engage.
The right wing Myriarch Wūyán Chálà (烏延查剌) attacked the bandits, causing them to retreat slightly.
Zhìníng (志寧), with Jiágǔ Qīngchén (夾谷清臣) and others, attacked them.
The bandit forces were utterly defeated
and fled across the water.
Wōwò (窩斡)'s mother Xúliǎn (徐輦) moved her entire camp west from Luòguō Gāng (落括岡).
Zhìníng (志寧) pursued and overtook them,
seizing all their baggage,
capturing over fifty thousand people,
and countless livestock.
Six false Jìedùshǐ (節度使)
and their tribes all surrendered.
Wōwò (窩斡) fled into the Xī (奚) territory.
Upon reaching Qīdù Hé (七渡河),
Zhìníng (志寧) defeated him again.
The bandits crossed Húníng (渾嶺)
and entered the Xī (奚) territory.
Zhìníng (志寧) captured the bandit general Shāohézù (稍合住),
released him without execution,
promised him official rewards,
and sent him back,
with the agreement that he would prove his loyalty by capturing Wōwò (窩斡).
After Shāohézù (稍合住) left,
he saw Wōwò (窩斡),
secretly did not mention being captured,
but instead instigated the Xī (奚) people against Wōwò (窩斡), saying,
"At Xiànquán (陷泉), we suffered a defeat,
and the Xī (奚) people have wavering loyalty.
One must be vigilant."
At that time,
Wōwò (窩斡) had been repeatedly defeated,
and his subordinates each had their own intentions.
Shāohézù (稍合住), along with the bandit leader Shéndúwò (神獨斡), seized Wōwò (窩斡)
and surrendered him to Right Overseer-in-Chief Wányán Sījìng (完顏思敬).
Zhìníng (志寧), with Myriarchs Qīngchén (清臣), Zōngníng (宗寧), Sùgē (速哥), and others,
pursued the remaining rebels to Yànzǐ Chéng (燕子城),
obtaining all their good horses.
They then reached the land of Mòbálǐdá (抹拔里達)
and captured all of them.
After the rebellious faction was pacified,
he entered court as Left Vice Marshal
and was bestowed with a jade belt.
Managing affairs with the Sòng,
stationing troops at Suīyáng,
Dū Yuánshuài Zhōngyì resided in Nánjīng,
controlling all the armies.
Sòng general Huáng Guānchá occupied Càizhōu,
and Yáng Sī occupied Yǐngchāng.
Zhìníng sent Wányán Wángxiáng to retake Càizhōu,
and Huáng Guānchá fled.
Wányán Xiāng attacked Yǐngzhōu,
captured it,
and apprehended Yáng Sī.
Then a dispatch was sent to Sòng Shūmìshǐ Zhāng Jùn,
instructing him to follow the old protocols since the Huángtǒng era.
Jùn replied in a letter, saying:
“I respectfully send an envoy to your command to discuss this.”
At this time,
the Sòng acquired Wōwò's partisans Kuòlǐ and Zhābā,
and using their counsel, attacked Língbì and Hóngxiàn.
Dūtǒng Xī Tàbùyě rebelled and defected to the Sòng,
thereby seizing Sùzhōu.
Kuòlǐ and others strategized, saying:
“Northerners rely on their cavalry and archery
to achieve victories and capture territories.
Now, it has been raining for a long time this summer,
the glue [on the bows] has dissolved,
and bows cannot be used.”
Therefore, Lǐ Shìfǔ came with them to attack Sùzhōu.
Guīdé Yǐn Shùjiǎsā Sù, Sùzhōu Fángyùshǐ Wūlíndá Làsā, Wànhù Wēndíhǎn Sùkě, and Péimǎn Lóushì
did not abide by their orders,
and were unwilling to hold fast to their defenses and await the main army.
Instead, they recklessly went out to engage in battle,
which resulted in the defeat of their army
and the fall of the city.
Làsā had previously sent people to trade in Sòng territory,
communicating with Lǐ Shìfǔ,
and receiving bribes from him.
After a long time,
the matter was discovered,
and he was executed.
Móukè Sàiyī was dismissed
for failing to report the matter.
Tàbùyě's mother, Wòlǐlán,
was implicated and slated for execution.
The emperor said:
“Tàbùyě betrayed his country and abandoned his mother;
what good would killing her do?
I pity her old age,”
and thus pardoned her from death.
An imperial edict commanded Sàsù, Làsā, Sùkě, and Lóushì to each be caned with varying numbers of strokes,
and Sàsù and Làsā were moreover dismissed from their posts.
Shìfǔ, thinking he had succeeded,
daily held grand banquets with Kuòlǐ and Zhābā.
Zhìníng, with ten thousand elite troops,
departed from Suīyáng
and advanced towards Sùzhōu.
A palace envoy arrived to supervise the army.
Zhìníng submitted a report, saying:
“This campaign does not trouble Your Majesty’s thoughts;
I am only concerned that Shìfǔ might escape.”
When Shìfǔ heard that Zhìníng’s army comprised only ten thousand men,
he greatly underestimated them,
saying:
“We can have ten men capture one.”
Kuòlǐ and others asked those who had seen the supreme general's banners,
and knowing it was Zhìníng,
they said to Shìfǔ:
“This is Sāhélǐn’s inspector-general;
even if his army is only ten thousand men,
you must not underestimate him.”
On the twentieth day of the fifth month of Dàdìng 3rd year,
when Zhìníng was about to reach Sùzhōu,
he ordered all the accompanying troops to display their banners,
stationing them west of the city as a feint.
Three Méng'ān units were stationed south of the city.
Zhìníng himself, with the main army,
was stationed southeast of the city,
blocking their return path.
Shìfǔ saw the vast array of banners and flags of the troops west of the city,
and indeed believed the main army was there.
He considered the smaller force to the southeast negligible
and attacked it first.
With tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
all carrying shields,
they formed a battle line with their backs to the city,
and defended the outer perimeter with chevaux-de-frise.
He sent a separate general with three thousand troops
out from the east gate,
intending to attack Zhìníng’s army from behind their lines.
However, Wànhù Púchá defeated them.
The right-wing Wànhù Jiágǔ Qīngchén advanced as the vanguard,
tore down the chevaux-de-frise,
and engaged in close-quarters combat.
Shìfǔ's army was thrown into disorder,
and the generals pressed the advantage,
pursuing and killing them to the city walls.
That night,
Shìfǔ interrogated all the defeated generals
and was about to execute them.
One of his Tǒngzhì, Jí, fearing for his life, defected,
thereby revealing all the strengths and weaknesses within the city.
The next day,
Shìfǔ deployed all his troops for battle,
with the cavalry in front.
Zhìníng sent Jiágǔ Qīngchén to confront them.
Shìfǔ’s separate general led a contingent of five to six thousand cavalry,
and when they met Qīngchén,
Qīngchén pursued and attacked them closely,
preventing the Sòng general from turning his banner.
Zhìníng waved his armies to fight with full strength,
and Shìfǔ suffered another great defeat.
Those who fled trampled upon each other,
dead bodies piled up,
and they struggled to enter the city gate.
The gate became jammed,
people obstructed each other,
and they then climbed over the city walls.
Our army shot at them from beyond the moat,
and many fell and died in the ditch.
Fifteen thousand cavalry and
over thirty thousand infantry were killed.
Shìfǔ escaped under cover of night.
The next day,
Jiágǔ Qīngchén and Zhāng Shīzhōng pursued and caught up with Shìfǔ,
beheading over four thousand people,
and countless others drowned themselves in the water.
Thirty thousand suits of armor were captured,
and other weapons were numerous.
The emperor sent Yílà Dào to the army to bestow upon Zhìníng an imperial gold-threaded robe, a jade túhú, and a steel ceremonial sword.
All meritorious generals and soldiers,
Méng'ān and Móukè, were rewarded and promoted as in Shǎnxī.
Púlián was promoted three ranks in office, given three bolts of brocade, and six bolts of silk.
Flag bearers, drummers, trumpeters, and clerks were each granted ten strings of cash.
