The imperial edict to Zhìníng stated:
“Though you are young,
in the previous campaign against the Qìdān, your battle merits were the greatest.
Now you have again defeated a formidable enemy;
I greatly commend you.”
The Sòng people debated peace but could not decide.
Dū Yuánshuài Púsàn Zhōngyì moved his army to Tàihé,
and Zhìníng moved his army to Línhuàn.
They then crossed the Huái River.
Túdān Kèníng captured Xūyí, Háo, Lú, Hé, and Chú prefectures.
The Sòng people were terrified
and thus decided to request peace.
Envoys went back and forth six or seven times,
and the agreement was finally settled.
The Sòng would forever be a nephew-state,
agreeing to an annual tribute of two hundred thousand liǎng of silver and bolts of silk.
Wèi Shí presented the oath document upon audience,
and good relations were re-established.
Zhìníng returned his army to Suīyáng.
The emperor bestowed upon him an imperial robe, a jade-handled sword, and a 'through-rhinoceros' imperial belt.
An imperial edict stated:
“As for the soldiers who died at Língbì,
Hóngxiàn, and Sùzhōu,
I truly pity them.
They should be buried in their hometowns,
with officials arranging their transportation,
and each person receiving thirty strings of cash as a funeral allowance.”
Fèngxiáng Yǐn Bójúlǔ Dìngfāng and below, including Méng'ān and Móukè,
were to have official sacrifices performed for them.
Dìngfāng received five hundred liǎng of silver and twenty bolts of brocade as a funeral allowance;
Méng'ān received three hundred strings of cash;
Móukè received two hundred strings of cash;
Púlǐyǎn received one hundred strings of cash;
acting Méng'ān received two hundred strings of cash;
acting Móukè received one hundred fifty strings of cash;
and acting Púlǐyǎn received seventy strings of cash.
In the third month of the fifth year,
Púsàn Zhōngyì went to the imperial capital,
Héshíliè Zhìníng was stationed in Nánjīng.
In the fifth month,
Zhìníng was summoned to the imperial capital,
and appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
with his title as Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài remaining as before.
Zhìníng returned to his army,
and was bestowed with a jade belt.
The Emperor said:
"You, my dear, in your prime, are able to achieve such merits.
I greatly admire this.
Although the Southern territories are settled,
it has been but a short time.
You must go there to plan and regulate it."
In the second month of the sixth year,
Zhìníng returned to the imperial capital,
and was appointed Shūmìshǐ.
On the eighth day of the eleventh month of the seventh year,
it was the Crown Prince's birthday.
A banquet was held for all the officials in the Eastern Palace.
Zhìníng offered a cup to toast the Emperor.
The Emperor was pleased,
and turning to the Crown Prince, said:
"The world is at peace,
and my son and I can enjoy ourselves today,
all thanks to this man's efforts."
He ordered the Crown Prince to take a large jade ladle from before him to pour wine,
and the Emperor personally offered it to Zhìníng.
He then bestowed upon him the jade ladle and five hundred taels of gold.
His fourteenth daughter was married to Zhìníng's son, Zhūshénnú.
In the tenth month of the eighth year,
tribute was offered,
and a banquet for all officials was held in the Qìnghé Diàn.
The imperial daughter came to pay her respects with the rites of a daughter-in-law.
Zhìníng and his wife sat to receive her.
They drank merrily all day,
and only dispersed late into the night.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Yòu Chéngxiàng.
In the eleventh year,
Dàizōng went on a northern expedition.
Upon his return,
envoys were sent to welcome and comfort him,
bestowing upon him a bow and arrows, and a jade hǔgǔ.
When he entered to have an audience,
the Emperor comforted and praised him for a long time.
On that day,
he was enfeoffed as Guǎngpíng Jùnwáng,
and envoys were again sent to his residence to comfort him.
On the Crown Prince's birthday,
a banquet for all officials was held in the Eastern Palace.
A jade belt was bestowed upon Zhìníng.
The Emperor said:
"This is the one worn by Liángwáng Zōngbì,
therefore I bestow it upon you."
During the suburban sacrifice, a general amnesty was granted.
Those who had followed in the expedition and served as guards
all received gifts,
and he was promoted to be enfeoffed as Jīnyuán Jùnwáng.
In the twelfth year,
Zhìníng fell ill.
Court eunuchs came to inquire after him,
three or four groups daily.
When his illness became critical,
he was bestowed thirty pills of golden elixir.
An imperial edict stated:
"This elixir has never been given to anyone else."
When the envoy arrived,
Zhìníng could no longer speak,
but only bowed his head.
In that year,
he passed away.
The Emperor ceased court sessions,
and attended his funeral,
entering with weeping,
his grief moving those around him.
When he was about to be buried,
the Emperor offered sacrifices,
and upon seeing the armor displayed before the coffin,
he wept bitterly again.
One thousand five hundred taels of silver, fifty bolts of fine silk, and five hundred bolts of plain silk were bestowed as funeral gifts.
The funeral arrangements and ancestral hall
were all provided by the government.
His posthumous title was Wǔdìng.
In the fifteenth year,
his portrait was placed in the Yǎnqìng Gōng.
Zhìníng's wife, the Princess of Yǒng'ān County, was extremely jealous.
She once killed a pregnant concubine.
After Zhìníng's death,
Zhūshénnú and his brothers all died from illness.
Shìzōng greatly lamented this,
and sent an envoy to instruct the Princess of Yǒng'ān County, saying:
"The Chancellor has three great merits.
Among the old officials of the previous dynasty,
only Qín and Sòng Wáng had greater achievements;
others cannot compare.
Now, you should raise his illegitimate son,
and treat him as your own son."
In the twenty-second year,
the Emperor asked his ministers:
"Who is superior, Púsàn Zhōngyì or Héshíliè Zhìníng?"
Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng Xiāng reported:
"Zhōngyì's military tactics are precise and refined,
this is his strength."
The Emperor said:
"Not so.
Zhìníng, when facing the enemy,
personally led his soldiers,
his bravery and courage have not been seen in anyone like him since Grand Tutor Liángwáng."
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
he was enshrined and worshipped in Shìzōng's ancestral temple.
Púsàn Zhōngyì, originally named Wūzhě,
was from Bálúgǔ Hé in Shàngjīng.
He was the nephew of Xuānxìan Huánghòu
and the elder brother of Yuánfēi.
His great-grandfather was Wòlǔbǔ.
His great-granduncle was Bāndǔ.
His grandfather was Húlán.
His father was Bèilǔ.
At the beginning of the state, he inherited the title of Móukè,
and served as Bōgǔ Lù Tǒngjūnshǐ,
retiring from office.
Zhōngyì was tall and imposing,
with a long beard.
He enjoyed discussing military affairs
and possessed great strategies.
At sixteen,
he led his clan's Móukè troops
and followed Zōngfǔ to pacify Shǎnxī.
During the battle, he shot and killed a Song general.
The Song army then collapsed,
and he became famous for this.
The marshal's office recorded his merit
and appointed him as Móukè by imperial decree.
When Zōngbì recaptured Hénán,
he recommended Zhōngyì for the position of Měng'ān.
He was the first to ascend when attacking Jìzhōu.
When attacking Dàmíng Fǔ, he fought fiercely with his own troops,
defeating an army of over one hundred thousand,
and was rewarded with slaves, horses, cattle, gold, silver, and fine silks.
He followed Zōngbì across the Huái River to attack Shòu, Lú, and other prefectures.
Zōngbì praised him, saying:
"This young man's bravery and strategy surpass others,
he is the material of a great general."
He was rewarded with five horses, one hundred and fifty cattle,
and five hundred sheep.
He led the imperial guard Wànhù,
was promoted to Níngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn,
and inherited his father's hereditary Móukè title.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng,
he was appointed Bózhōu Fángyùshǐ.
In his leisure time, he studied the Nǚzhēn script
and ancient arithmetic.
Within a month, he had mastered them completely.
In the commandery, he did not engage in hunting or leisurely outings,
but focused on his official duties.
The commandery universally praised his governance.
One night, it was dark and gloomy.
The prisoners plotted to revolt in the prison.
In the sudden chaos,
the officers and generals were all panicked and at a loss.
Zhōngyì remained calm,
and simply ordered the watchman to beat the drum and blow the horn.
The prisoners thought dawn was approaching,
and dared not come out,
voluntarily returning to their shackles.
When he was evaluated,
the people of the commandery went to the palace gate, wishing for him to remain.
An imperial edict granted their request.
In the eighth year,
he was transferred to Tóngzhī Zhēndìng Yǐn,
concurrently serving as Héběi Xī Lù Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn.
He was promoted to Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
and then entered court as Bīngbù Shàngshū.
Púsàn Hútǔ had conspired with Hǎilíng to usurp the throne.
He relied on his power to be arrogant and disrespectful to his peers.
Zhōngyì, during a banquet, publicly humiliated him.
Hǎilíng was displeased
and sent him out as Zhènwǔjūn JiéDùshǐ.
The bandit Lǐ Tiěqiāng from Huǒshān attacked during the summer heat.
Zhōngyì, in light clothing and with a single horseman, rode out to meet him,
shooting and killing several men.
The bandits then retreated.
He was transferred to Líntáo Yǐn,
concurrently serving as Xīqín Lù Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn.
Hǎilíng summoned him to the imperial capital and said to him:
"The Táohé area is adjacent to Tǔbō and Mùbō.
In the past, they plundered and harmed the good people,
and the prefectures and counties could not control them.
You are an experienced general,
therefore I entrust this to you."
He was bestowed with a tassel robe, jade fittings, and a saber.
After two evaluations,
he was transferred to Píngyáng Yǐn,
and then again to Jìnán Yǐn.
In his current official capacity, he was appointed Hànnán Lù Xíngyíng Fù Tǒngzhì
to attack Song,
and captured Tōnghuà Jūn.
When Shìzōng was enthroned,
Hǎilíng died in Yángzhōu,
and the troops were withdrawn to the capital.
He was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
When Yílā Wōwò usurped the title,
the war dragged on indecisively.
The Right Vice Marshal Wányán Móuyǎn had already defeated him at Měnghū River,
but then gathered his troops,
greedy for plunder,
and did not pursue the enemy.
Instead, he allowed his son Xiégē to behave atrociously in the army,
so the soldiers were not motivated to fight.
The rebels acquired good land with water and grass,
while the imperial army followed in their wake,
lacking water and grass,
and their horses grew weaker.
The rebels advanced into Shānxī,
and for a long time no success was achieved.
Zhōngyì requested, saying:
"The Qìdān brigands,
not eliminated in time,
have caused Your Majesty much worry.
Your servant hears that when the sovereign is troubled, the minister is shamed.
I wish to exert my utmost to eliminate them."
Shìzōng was greatly pleased.
He immediately recalled Móuyǎn
and ordered Xiégē to return to his hometown.
Zhōngyì was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
concurrently Right Vice Marshal,
ennobled as Róngguó Gōng,
and bestowed with an imperial sable coat, Bīntiě Tǔgǔ bows and arrows, a great saber, fully caparisoned horses, Ānshān iron armor, and a gold plaque.
The imperial edict stated:
"If any officer or soldier in the army commits an offense,
apart from those directly responsible, all others shall be dealt with by military law.
Those with merit shall be promoted and rewarded according to regulations."
The edict to all officers and soldiers stated:
"The army has been stationed on the border for a long time,
wasting resources
and preventing the people from resting.
Now, Right丞Zhōngyì has been appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì and Right Vice Marshal.
You should unite your efforts
and not be negligent or slow."
When Zhōngyì reached the army,
the rebels had captured Lǐngshān, Tóngchāng, Huìhé, and other counties,
and were arrayed for battle, moving westward.
Zhōngyì pursued them
and overtook them at Huādào.
Zōnghēng was the left wing,
and Zōng was the right wing,
arrayed against the rebels across the river.
The rebels crossed the river
and first attacked the left wing,
which was partially defeated.
The right wing came to its rescue,
and the rebels withdrew.
Wōwò then took his elite troops with him,
and with his weak troops protecting his mother, wife, and baggage train, he fled westward by a different route,
planning to rendezvous in the mountains.
The pursuit caught up with them again at Niǎolǐng, which fell to the west of Quán.
They met the rebels,
and at that time, a dense fog filled the four directions,
making it impossible to see anything even a short distance away.
Zhōngyì prayed, saying:
"The mad bandits are rampant,
slaughtering the innocent.
Heaven does not aid evil;
it should clear up."
After the offering,
the dense fog suddenly cleared.
When they fought,
Zhōngyì positioned his left on the southern hill,
forming a crescent array,
extending his right northward,
and thoroughly defeated them.
He captured his brother Niǎo,
captured 300,000 people,
and seized over 100,000 various livestock,
and countless chariots, tents, gold, and treasures.
All were distributed among the various armies.
The rebels fled toward Xī territory,
and a general was dispatched to pursue them.
At Qīdùhé,
they were again defeated.
After crossing Húnlǐng,
they again advanced to attack them.
Seeing their approach, the rebels collapsed and fled,
escaping into Xī territory,
with surrenderers continuously appearing on the road.
The edict to Zhōngyì stated:
"Your talent and ability have long been evident,
and you have indeed greatly defeated the rebel forces.
I commend this greatly.
Now I send someone to console you,
as if I went myself.
I bestow upon you imperial robes, a bone-decorated rhinoceros-horn-handled saber, a through-rhinoceros-horn belt, etc.
Also, take the captives and spoils
and distribute them evenly among the soldiers."
After Wōwò was defeated,
he entered Xī territory.
Gāo Zhōngjiàn defeated the Xī at Kǎolǎo Mountain,
and Yílā Dào captured the households of Mǒbái and other Xī.
The Mǒbái Xī then surrendered,
and Wōwò's power further weakened.
Gēsīliè Zhìníng captured the rebel general Shāohézù,
released him,
and made him promise to capture Wōwò to redeem himself,
also promising him an official reward.
Shāohézù and his confederates
captured Wōwò and brought him to Wányán Sījìng to surrender.
The Qìdān were pacified.
Zhōngyì went to the capital,
was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéngxiàng,
and his title was changed to Yíguó Gōng,
and he was bestowed with a jade belt.
Since Hǎilíng was assassinated,
the large army returned north,
while Wōwò's forces grew audacious.
Generals were ordered to go on expeditions.
When Wōwò was defeated,
his followers Kuòlǐ and Zhābā fled into Sòng territory.
The Sòng people adopted their strategies,
invading and plundering the borderlands,
and capturing Sì, Shòu, Táng, and Hǎizhōu.
Thereupon,
the Sòng sovereign abdicated in favor of a member of the imperial clan,
who became Sòng Xiàozōng.
Although he occasionally sent envoys,
he wished to use the rites of an equal state.
Shìzōng entrusted Gēsīliè Zhìníng with the strategy concerning Sòng affairs,
and issued an imperial edict appointing Zhōngyì as Chéngxiàng to command all military affairs,
stationing him in Nánjīng to oversee all generals.
This was the second year of Dàdìng.
As Zhōngyì was about to depart,
he took his leave before the emperor.
The emperor instructed him, saying:
"If they return the encroached territory
and their tribute and rites are as before,
then the troops can be withdrawn."
Upon arriving in Nánjīng,
he inspected the soldiers,
stationed them in strategic locations,
and warned all generals to maintain strict readiness.
He sent the Left Vice Marshal Zhìníng to deliver a letter to Sòng Pímìshǐ Zhāng Jùn,
which roughly stated:
"You must return the inner territory of our dynasty that you have encroached upon,
and each side shall observe the boundaries demarcated from ancient times.
All matters shall be conducted according to the old treaties since Huángtǒng.
The Marshal's headquarters shall also lift its state of alert.
If you insist on resisting,
please gather your troops for an encounter."
Sòng Xuānfǔshǐ Zhāng Jùn replied to Zhìníng, saying:
"Boundaries of territories sometimes shift,
and in warfare, there are sometimes victories and sometimes defeats.
How can there be permanence?
Let us not discuss this.
I respectfully send officials
to come under your banner to discuss it."
At this time,
Sì, Shòu, and Dèngzhōu had already been recovered.
It was requested to demolish their walls
and relocate their inhabitants to Sù, Bó, and Càizhōu.
The emperor said:
"These three prefectures are originally our land.
Once gained, that is enough."
Zhōngyì ordered the officers and soldiers to choose good land with water and grass to rest
and graze their horses,
awaiting the next year to take Huáinán.
Initially,
Shìzōng had ordered all generals to advance via the three routes of Sì, Shòu, and Táng-Dèng.
When the Sòng people heard this,
they immediately burned and laid waste to the fields from Fāngchéng and Yèxiàn,
leaving no fodder for grazing.
Zhōngyì ordered the troops of the Táng-Dèng route to graze their animals between Xǔ and Rǔ.
In the third year,
Wán yán Zhōngyì entered to report on affairs,
and was consequently made Chancellor concurrently Grand Marshal.
Not long after,
he returned to the army.
Zhōngyì and the Sòng [dynasty] had been in a standoff for a long time.
Fearing that a prolonged summer rain [season]
would easily reduce the strength of their bows,
and that Sòng might take the opportunity to attack,
he preemptively selected ten thousand strong bows from a separate armory.
When he later went from Biàn [liáng] to the capital to discuss affairs,
and arrived at Jùnzhōu,
the Sòng general Lǐ Shìfǔ indeed seized Língbì and Hóngxiàn by surprise,
and then captured Sùzhōu.
Zhōngyì sent someone back to Biàn [liáng]
to issue the stored strong bows to Zhìníng's army.
They fought against the Sòng people,
and consequently achieved a great victory,
ultimately recovering Sùzhōu.
When Zhōngyì returned,
he sent a letter of reproof to Sòng.
Hóng Zūn, Co-Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs, and Lú Zhòngxián, a deliberation official, of Sòng,
dispatched two envoys carrying a letter and a personal note for Zhìníng,
to return the encroached territories of Hǎi, Sì, Táng, and Dèng Zhōu,
and proposed to establish a relationship as uncle and nephew states.
The reply letter set a date for the envoys to enter the border in the eleventh month.
Sòng again sent someone to say
that the gifts were not yet ready,
and requested to wait until the twelfth month to conclude the peace.
Zhōngyì swiftly reported this matter to the emperor,
requesting a fixed format for the letter,
and further stated that if the Sòng letter conformed to the format,
then they would be allowed to enter the border;
if it did not,
they would have to be sent back to their own country
to report to their lord again.
Such back-and-forth
would take seventy or eighty days,
which might delay the army's advance.
Shìzōng issued an edict to him, saying:
"If the Sòng people return the territory,
and the annual tribute is as before,
they may be exempt from submitting a memorial and declaring themselves as subjects,
and will be allowed to be a nephew state for generations."
Zhōngyì then sent letters to the Sòng people,
seven in total,
but the Sòng people found other pretexts and did not comply.
Zhōngyì moved a large army to press the Huái [River] border,
and sent Zhìníng to lead a detached force across the Huái [River],
capturing Xūyí, Háo, Lú, Hé, Chú, and other zhōu.
The Sòng people were afraid.
However, Shìzōng's intention was that the world was weary of war,
and he wished to let the people rest.
He issued an edict to Zhōngyì to act as he deemed appropriate.
In the first month of the fourth year,
Zhōngyì sent the Right Superintendent of the Army, Zōng, to report to the throne,
saying that as the hot month was approaching,
he requested to wait until the cool autumn to advance.
An edict was issued granting his request.
The Sòng envoy Hú Fǎng arrived with a letter from Right Executive of the Secretariat, Tāng Sītui.
Sòng referred to itself as a nephew state,
but refused to add the character 'shì' (世, generations).
Zhōngyì detained Fǎng in the army,
replied to their letter,
and sent an envoy to report it.
The edict said:
"What crime has the envoy committed?
Send Hú Fǎng back to his country.
Border affairs should be managed expediently."
In the eighth month,
an edict was issued to Zhōngyì, saying:
"Previously, you requested to wait until the cool autumn to advance.
It is now the eighth month,
how much longer will you wait?"
Earlier,
Zhōngyì had requested an increase in gold and silver plaques.
The Emperor said:
"Grand Preceptor, Prince of Liáng, held several positions,
but was never increased."
Now, one gold plaque and twenty silver plaques were added for the Grand Marshal;
one gold plaque and ten silver plaques for each of the Left and Right Vice Marshals;
one gold plaque and six silver plaques for each of the Left and Right Superintendents;
one gold plaque and four silver plaques for each of the Left and Right Chief Commanders;
and two silver plaques for each of the three routes' Commanderies-in-Chief.
Then, regulations were established for rewarding officials and common people from the southern border who defected.
The Marshal's office captured the Sòng spy Fú Zhōng.
Fú Zhōng had previously been to Zhōngdū.
Officials of Dàxīng Fǔ interrogated him,
but Fú Zhōng produced documents,
and also knew Zhāng Déhēng, the Defense Judge of Sìzhōu,
and was thus exempted.
He generously thanked Déhēng,
and Déhēng accepted it.
Fú Zhōng confessed fully.
This matter was then reported to the court.
Consequently,
Wáng Quán, the Deputy Prefect of Dàxīng, was dismissed from his post,
and Déhēng was stripped of his official title.
The peace negotiations began with Zhāng Jùn,
and later involved Hóng Zūn and Tāng Sītui.
When Túshān Kèníng defeated the Sòng's Wèi Shèng at Shíbālǐ Zhuāng,
and captured Chǔzhōu,
Shìzōng issued an edict to advance the army.

At this point, Zhōu Kuí, Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs, and Wáng Zhīwàng, Co-Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs, of Sòng, fully complied with the terms in their letters,
and the peace agreement was finally settled.
Sòng dispatched Wèi Shí, acting Minister of Rites,
and Kāng Xù, Circuit Intendant of Chóngxìn Army,
to serve as Envoys for Communication and National Credentials.
They obtained the format of the Sòng Emperor's national letter,
and also a duplicate of the national letter.
Sòng was to be a nephew state for generations,
and the annual tribute was set at two hundred thousand liǎng (taels) and pǐ (bolts) of silver and silk.
The national letter was still to be signed with a name and a repeated bow,
and not to include
the character "dà" (大, great).
In the first month of Dàdìng fifth year,
Wèi Shí and Kāng Xù had an audience.
Their letter stated:
"Your Nephew, the Sòng Emperor,
respectfully bows twice and submits this letter to Your Uncle, the Great Jīn Sage, Benevolent, and Filial Emperor, at the steps of the palace."
When Wèi Shí returned,
the reply letter
referred to "Uncle, the Great Jīn Emperor"
without using a personal name,
and did not write
"respectfully bows twice,"
but only said
"submitting this letter to Your Nephew, the Sòng Emperor,"
without using an honorific title,
or referring to "at the steps of the palace."
Peace and good relations having been established,
the troops were disbanded,
and an edict was issued to the whole realm.
Wán yán Zhòng, Left Vice Commander of the Palace Guard, was appointed Envoy for Replying to Inquiries and National Credentials,
and Yáng Bóxióng, Attendant to the Crown Prince, was his deputy.
Zhōngyì reported that there were 173,300 government troops.
He proposed to retain 116,200 cavalry and infantry for garrison duty.
The Emperor said:
"Now that Sòng has been permitted to make peace,
and yet so many troops are still garrisoned,
in addition to the old army,
select 12,000 cavalry — Àlǐxǐ are considered good [for this] —
a total of 15,000 infantry from the Yúhóu司 army,
and 10,000 drafted troops.
With the old army, a total of 60,000 will be retained.
Among those with many strong and rich able-bodied men, some will be selected and retained.
For the poor and needy, Àlǐxǐ officials will provide.
For the rich, their slaves will be used.
The retained cavalry and infantry will be selected from the armies of Héběi Dōngxī, Dàmíng Fǔ, Sùpín, Húlígǎi, Huìníng, Xiánpíng Fǔ, Jìzhōu, Dōngjīng, Hésùguǎn, and other routes.
The Southwestern and Northwestern Pacification Commands, Lín huáng Fǔ, Tàizhōu, Běijīng, Pó sù, Hélǎn, and Shāndōng Dōngxī routes
shall all be dismissed and sent back."
An edict was issued to Pèi mǎn Zǐníng, Envoy of the Bureau of Attendants, to wear a gold plaque,
and Wěidǐ, Guardsman, and Fúbǎo Zhíhòu Měnhuíhǎi to wear silver plaques,
to inform the generals and commanders of all routes
that the 200,000 liǎng of silver and pǐ of silk received from Sòng as annual tribute
should be entirely distributed as rewards to the currently retained and dismissed troops.
Those who had crossed the border
would each receive two bolts of silk and two liǎng of silver.
Those who had not crossed the border would each receive two liǎng of silver and one bolt of silk.
Àlǐxǐ would receive one bolt of silk.
Mòkè would receive double that of the soldiers,
and Mèng'ān double that of Mòkè.
Elderly Mèng'ān and Mòkè who had commanded troops and had meritorious service
would be duly appointed or promoted.
Another edict stated:
"Those routes that are entirely disbanded
shall be dispatched first."
A jade belt was bestowed upon Zhōngyì.
In the third month,
an edict said:
"If the main army has already been dismissed and sent back,
Chancellor Zhōngyì should return first.
Left Vice Marshal Zhìníng and Right Superintendent Zōng shall remain stationed in Nánjīng.
Other officials, unless urgently needed, shall be ordered to return to their posts."
Zhōngyì朝京師 (Jīngshī),
the Emperor comforted him, saying:
"The Sòng (Sòng) state has requested peace,
to cease military action and allow the people to rest—
these are all your efforts."
He was appointed Left Chancellor (Zuǒchéngxiàng),
and concurrently Grand Marshal (Dū Yuánshuài).
In the early Dàdìng (Dàdìng) period,
many matters were handled by temporary regulations.
An imperial edict ordered the relevant officials to revise and finalize them.
The Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"For all matters that have been reported to me,
I always review them a second time.
You all should not feel anxious.
How could I
not trust my great ministers?
But military and state affairs
cannot be taken lightly,
for fear there might be a mistake."
Zhōngyì replied:
"How would we dare to secretly presume about Your Majesty?
It is simply that our wisdom and strength are insufficient.
Your Majesty's careful attention to the myriad affairs of state
is a blessing to the empire."
In the first month of the sixth year of Dàdìng (Dàdìng),
Zhōngyì fell ill.
The Emperor sent imperial physicians to examine him,
bestowed upon him imperial medicines,
and imperial envoys came to comfort and inquire,
continuously arriving on the road.
In the second month,
he passed away.
The Emperor personally attended and wept bitterly for him,
suspended court sessions for the funeral rites,
and bestowed 1,500 taels of silver, 50 bolts of heavy silk, and 500 bolts of plain silk.
When Shìzōng (Shìzōng) was about to visit Xī Jīng (Xī Jīng),
he again personally offered libations.
He ordered Cānzhī Zhèngshì (Cānzhī Zhèngshì) Tángkuò Ānlǐ (Tángkuò Ānlǐ) to oversee the funeral arrangements,
ensuring that all funeral rites and sacrifices were carried out with exceptional generosity,
provided by the government.
Dàzōngzhèng (Dàzōngzhèng) Assistant Jìng Chōng (Jìng Chōng) was appointed Imperial Sacrifice Envoy (Chìjìshǐ),
and Zhōngdū (Zhōngdū) Transport Vice Administrator Wáng Zhèn (Wáng Zhèn) was appointed Imperial Burial Envoy (Chìzàngshǐ).
All officials attended the funeral procession,
with the full regalia of a first-rank official,
and the flags and drums of a great general were displayed,
escorting the coffin to the burial ground.
His posthumous title was Wǔzhuāng (Wǔzhuāng).
Zhōngyì's (Zhōngyì) every action was guided by ritual and righteousness,
he was humble in his dealings with subordinates,
respected scholars,
and was extremely gentle and agreeable with people,
always frank and upright.
He was skilled at commanding his officers and soldiers,
and could inspire them to fight to the death.
When he became a chief minister,
he spoke his mind without reservation.
From the Hàn (Hàn) and Táng (Táng) dynasties onward,
maternal relatives often achieved wealth and rank through imperial favor,
but many did not maintain it to the end.
None had concurrently held the posts of general and chief minister,
with their achievements and reputation remaining consistent from beginning to end, like Zhōngyì (Zhōngyì).
In the eleventh year,
an edict stated:
"Regarding the clan members of the late Left Chancellor Zhōngyì (Zhōngyì),
and the relatives of Empress Zhāodé (Zhāodé),
those with usable talents
are to be investigated and reported by Left Deputy Inspector Wūgǔlún Yuánzhōng (Wūgǔlún Yuánzhōng)."
In the twenty-first year,
the Emperor, remembering Zhōngyì's (Zhōngyì) contributions,
ordered an inscription for his tombstone.
In the first year of Tàihé (Tàihé),
his portrait was placed in Yǎnqìng (Yǎnqìng) Palace,
and he was honored in the ancestral temple of Shìzōng (Shìzōng).
His son was Kuí (Kuí).
There is a separate biography for him.
Túshān Héxǐ (Túshān Héxǐ)
was from Sùsū (Sùsū) Water in Shàng Jīng (Shàng Jīng).
His father, Pú Yě (Pú Yě),
held the hereditary post of Měng'ān (Měng'ān).
Héxǐ (Héxǐ) was tall and robust,
with exceptional physical strength.
What he heard or saw once,
he never forgot for the rest of his life.
During the Tiānfǔ (Tiānfǔ) period,
he followed Jīnyuán (Jīnyuán) Prince Lóushì (Lóushì) as his Zhāyě (Zhāyě),
and was greatly favored by him.
In the sixth year of Tiānhuì (Tiānhuì),
for his merits, he became a Móukè (Móukè),
and soon after took command of Lóushì's (Lóushì) personal Měng'ān (Měng'ān).
The Marshal's office, hearing of his talent,
ordered him to provisionally command the Left Wing Army.
In the second year of Huángtǒng (Huángtǒng),
he became the Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Lǒngzhōu (Lǒngzhōu).
With fifteen soldiers, he defeated two hundred Sòng (Sòng) soldiers at Gāolíng (Gāolíng);
with five hundred soldiers, he defeated two thousand Sòng (Sòng) soldiers at Qínzhōu (Qínzhōu);
with eight hundred soldiers, he defeated three thousand five hundred Sòng (Sòng) soldiers at Fèngxiáng (Fèngxiáng).
With two Móukè (Móukè) companies, he defended Ráofēng (Ráofēng) Pass.
Two thousand Sòng (Sòng) soldiers came to seize the pass,
but he vigorously attacked and defeated them,
allowing all the armies to pass through the dangerous terrain.
He was promoted to Administrator (Yǐn) of Píngliáng (Píngliáng),
and then moved to Líntáo (Líntáo) and Yán'ān (Yán'ān) as Administrator.
At this time,
west of Guān (Guān) and Shǎn (Shǎn),
military conflict had just ceased,
and many people were displaced.
Héxǐ (Héxǐ) maintained order with tranquility,
and many people returned to their homes.
In the second year of Tiāndé (Tiāndé),
he became Left Grand Supervisor (Zuǒ Dūjiān) of the Marshal's Office,
and Commander (Tǒngjūnshǐ) of Shǎnxī (Shǎnxī).
In the second year of Zhēnyuán (Zhēnyuán),
he concurrently held his existing official post and was appointed Administrator of Hézhōng (Hézhōng).
In the sixth year of Zhènglóng (Zhènglóng),
he became Commander-in-Chief (Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng) of the Western Shǔ (Shǔ) Circuit.
When Shìzōng (Shìzōng) ascended the throne,
he personally issued an imperial edict to Héxǐ (Héxǐ), saying:
"The King of Qí (Qí) lost the Way,
killed his mother and empress,
brutally oppressed his brothers,
and poisoned the common people.
I, remembering the hardship of Tàizǔ's (Tàizǔ) founding the dynasty,
reluctantly accepted the great position.
Your sons and younger brothers have all returned from the army;
as an old minister of the state,
how could you not know the ways of Heaven and human affairs?
Your army is not numerous,
and it is not advisable to advance deep.
You should lead your army and garrison on the border.
The region west of Shǎn (Shǎn) is a crucial area,
and no one but you can plan for it.
After the military affairs are settled,
I will summon you.
You should exert yourself."
In the second year of Dàdìng (Dàdìng),
he was again appointed Commander (Tǒngjūnshǐ) of the Shǎnxī (Shǎnxī) Circuit.
Not long after,
he was changed to Right Grand Supervisor (Yòu Dūjiān) of the Marshal's Office.
He presented a memorial outlining a strategy for attacking Sòng (Sòng),
and an imperial edict granted him permission to act expediently.
He was transferred to Left Grand Supervisor (Zuǒ Dūjiān).
He defeated Sòng (Sòng) forces at Huázhōu (Huázhōu).
At this time,
Sòng (Sòng) general Wú Lín (Wú Lín) invaded Gǔzhèn (Gǔzhèn),
separately occupying Sǎnguān (Sǎnguān), Héshàngyuán (Héshàngyuán), Shénchākǒu (Shénchākǒu), Yùnǚtán (Yùnǚtán), Dàchónglǐng (Dàchónglǐng), Shíbìzhài (Shíbìzhài), and Bǎojī (Bǎojī) County.
With over one hundred thousand soldiers,
he captured Hézhōu (Hézhōu) and Zhènrónɡ (Zhènrónɡ) military garrison.
Héxǐ (Héxǐ) requested reinforcements,
and an imperial edict dispatched ten thousand troops from Hénán (Hénán) to him.
Héxǐ (Héxǐ) sent Dānzhōu (Dānzhōu) Prefect Chìzhǎn Húsùlǔ Gǎi (Chìzhǎn Húsùlǔ Gǎi) with four thousand soldiers to defend Déshùn (Déshùn),
and Wú Lín (Wú Lín) besieged it with two hundred thousand men.
Commander (Tǒngjūn) Grand Supervisor Shímò Diélè (Shímò Diélè) led ten thousand soldiers,
defeated Sòng (Sòng) forces at Hézhōu (Hézhōu),
and on his return passed Déshùn (Déshùn).
He stationed his troops at Píngliáng (Píngliáng),
and requested more troops from Héxǐ (Héxǐ)
to relieve the siege of Déshùn (Déshùn).
Héxǐ (Héxǐ) dispatched Wàn Hù (Wàn Hù) Wányán Xíníliè (Wányán Xíníliè) and Dà Liángshùn (Dà Liángshùn),
and Níngzhōu (Níngzhōu) Prefect Yánzhǎn Méndōu (Yánzhǎn Méndōu), each leading their respective units,
totaling twenty thousand men,
under the overall command of Shùnyì (Shùnyì) Army Military Commissioner Wūyán Púlíhēi (Wūyán Púlíhēi),
to rendezvous with Diélè (Diélè).
Wú Lín (Wú Lín), hearing of this,
sent a subordinate general with five thousand soldiers to meet them.
The vanguard, Tèlǐshī Wūyě (Tèlǐshī Wūyě) and Xī (Xī) King Héshàng (Héshàng), defeated them,
pursuing them to a small stream south of Déshùn (Déshùn) city.
Lín (Lín) personally led the main army and emerged from behind a hill.
Wūyě (Wūyě) and others swiftly attacked them.
Diélè (Diélè) and Púlíhēi (Púlíhēi) arrived subsequently,
and they fought with combined forces.
As night fell,
the two armies could no longer distinguish each other,
and thus disengaged.
Shortly after,
Lín (Lín) sent a report saying:
"The Sòng (Sòng) Emperor has sent an envoy,
and the two states are negotiating peace.
Please each withdraw your troops."
Lín (Lín) then fled.
Púlíhēi (Púlíhēi) also withdrew his army.
From the time the Sòng (Sòng) army besieged the city
until then, it had been over forty days before the siege was lifted.
Initially,
Déshùn 德順 was under siege.
The supervising army Měng'ān 猛安 Wēndūn Púlǐhǎi 温敦蒲里海 led his troops from the front,
fighting with all his might and never suffering the slightest setback.
When relief forces arrived
and the siege was lifted,
Púlǐhǎi's 蒲里海功 was most significant.
Soon after,
Wú Lín 吴璘 again came to invade the prefectures and commanderies of Shǎnxī 陝西,
with over 100,000 troops.
An imperial edict ordered 7,000 soldiers to reinforce Héxǐ's 合喜 troops,
totaling 20,000 men.
Qìngyáng Yǐn 慶陽尹 Wūyán Púxiánnú 烏延蒲轄奴 and Yán'ān Yǐn 延安尹 Gāo Jǐngshān 高景山 were to command them separately.

Zhāng 璋, the Jìedùshǐ 節度使 of Zhānghuà Jūn 彰化軍; Wūyán Wúlǐbǔ 烏延吾里補, the Jìedùshǐ 節度使 of Tōngyuǎn Jūn 通遠軍; Yílà Gāoshānnú 移刺高山奴, the Cìshǐ 刺史 of Níngzhōu 寧州; Zōngshì Níhé 宗室泥河, the Shàoyǐn 少尹 of Jīngzhào 京兆; and Wányán Móuliánghǔ 完顏謀良虎, the Cìshǐ 刺史 of Ēnzhōu 恩州,
were all prepared for military deployment.
The Sòng 宋 people, driving 50,000 civilians from Shāng 商, Guó 虢, Huàshān 華山, and Nánshān 南山,
came to besiege Huázhōu 華州.
The supervising army Wànhù 萬戶 Péimǎn Ruólà 裴滿挼剌 wanted to hold out behind strong fortifications,
but Měng'ān 猛安 Yílà Shālǐlà 移剌沙里剌 said:
"Although the Sòng 宋 army is numerous,
half of them are civilians
unaccustomed to battle.
It is better to attack them."
Thereupon, Ruólà 挼剌, with 1,000 cavalry, defeated the Sòng 宋 vanguard,
pursued them to their main army,
and also defeated them,
beheading over 5,000.
Afterward,
Zhāng 璋 defeated Sòng Sòng Yáo Liángfǔ's 姚良輔 army at Yuánzhōu 原州.
The Sòng 宋 garrison forces from Bǎojī 寶雞 westward
to Dàchónglǐng 大蟲嶺
all fled from Sànguān 散關.
Soon after,
Wú Lín 吴璘 heard that Chìzhǎn Húsùlǔgǎi's 赤盞胡速魯改
and Wūyán Púlǐhēi's 烏延蒲里黑軍 armies had left Déshùn 德順.
He led an army reportedly of 200,000,
again occupied Déshùn 德順,
and captured Gǒngzhōu 鞏州 and Líntáo Fǔ 臨洮府.
Líntáo Shàoyǐn 臨洮少尹 Hégǔliè Sāojià 紇石烈騷洽 died in this,
and an imperial edict posthumously promoted him one rank
and bestowed 500 strings of cash.
Héxǐ 合喜 appointed Zhāng 璋 as acting Dūtǒng 都統,
and Xíníliè 習尼列 as acting Fùtǒng 副統,
leading 20,000 troops to attack them.
In successive battles,
although the Sòng 宋 army was defeated,
Lín 璘, relying on his numerous forces,
refused to withdraw.
He divided half of his troops
to guard Qínzhōu 秦州.
Héxǐ 合喜 then personally marched
and stationed at Shuǐluò Chéng 水洛城.
From Liùpán Shān 六盤山 in the east
to Shíshān Tóu 石山頭 in the west,
he divided his forces to guard the area,
between Déshùn 德順 and Qínzhōu 秦州,
cutting off their supply routes.
Lín 璘 then withdrew.
Dūtǒng 都統 Zhāng 璋 and Fùtǒng 副統 Xíníliè 習尼列 ambushed the Sòng Jīnglüèshǐ 宋經略使 Jīng Gāo 荊臯
from Shàngbājié 上八節 to Gāngǔ Chéng 甘谷城,
killing several thousand people.
Xíníliè 習尼列 captured Sòng Jiāng 宋將 Zhū Yǒng 朱永 and twelve other officers.
Sòng Zhāng Ānfǔ 宋張安撫, who was guarding Déshùn 德順,
also abandoned the city and fled.
Húsùlǔgǎi 胡速魯改 ambushed them,
killing more than half,
and capturing over ten officers,
thus recovering Déshùn Zhōu 德順州.
Those Sòng 宋 forces guarding Qínzhōu 秦州
also retreated on their own.
Gāo Jǐngshān 高景山 pacified Shāng 商 and Guó 虢,
and Zōngshì Níhé 宗室泥河 took Huánzhōu 環州.
Thus,
Líntáo 臨洮, Gǒng 鞏, Qín 秦, Hé 河, Lǒng 隴, Lán 蘭, Huì 會, Yuán 原, Táo 洮, Jīshí 積石, Zhènjóng 鎮戎, Déshùn 德順, Shāng 商, Guó 虢, Huán 環, and Huá 華—sixteen prefectures and administrative seats in total—
were all recovered,
and Shǎnxī 陝西 was pacified.
An imperial edict commended and encouraged them,
bestowing jade belts.
The imperial edict for the generals and soldiers of Shǎnxī 陝西 stated:
For Měng'ān 猛安,
those with rank Zhaoyì 昭毅 and below were promoted two ranks,
and Zhaowǔ 昭武 and above were promoted one rank.
For Móukè 謀克,
those with rank six and below were promoted two ranks,
and five and above were promoted one rank.
For supervising army Měng'ān 猛安,
those with rank Zhaowǔ 昭武 and above were promoted one rank;
those with Zhaoyì 昭毅 and below, Wǔyì 武義 and above, were promoted two ranks;
those with Zhaoxìn 昭信 and below,
Nǚzhì 女直 people were appointed Xuānwǔ 宣武,
and others were appointed Fèngxìn 奉信.
[一０]Those without official positions,
Nǚzhì 女直 people were granted Dūnxìn 敦信,
[一一]and others were granted Zhōngwǔ 忠武.
For supervising army Móukè 謀克,
those with rank Wǔgōng 武功 and below, [一二]Zhōngxiǎn 忠顯 and above, were promoted two ranks;
those with Zhōngyǒng 忠勇 and below,
Nǚzhì 女直 people were appointed Zhaoxìn 昭信,
and others were appointed Zhōngxiǎn 忠顯.
Those without official positions,
Nǚzhì 女直 people were granted Zhōngxiǎn 忠顯,
and others were granted Zhōngyì 忠翊.
For regular soldiers,
those with official positions were promoted one rank,
and those without official positions were granted two ranks.
Měng'ān 猛安 were rewarded fifty liǎng 兩 of silver, five duān 端 of heavy silk, and ten pǐ 匹 of ordinary silk;
acting and full officials received the same.
Regular soldiers were given thirty strings of cash,
and Ālǐxǐ 阿里喜 ten strings.
For officers, soldiers, and permanent staff killed in battle,
official titles were posthumously granted and money bestowed with distinctions.
In the fifth year,
the Shǎnxī Lù Tǒngjūnshǐ 陝西路統軍使 was established,
also serving as Jīngzhào Yǐn 京兆尹.
The Yuánshuàifǔ 元帥府 was moved to Hézhōng Fǔ 河中府.
When Tǒngjūnshǐ 統軍使 Zhāng 璋 took leave to pay respects at court,
the emperor said:
"Héxǐ 合喜 is old.
I entrust the military affairs of Shǎnxī 陝西 to you, Minister.
For all matters of defense and their advantages and disadvantages,
you may consult Héxǐ 合喜."
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to be Púmì Fùshǐ 樞密副使,
then changed to Dōngjīng Líushǒu 東京留守.
He was bestowed clothes, a belt, and a saber.
The imperial edict said:
"You, Minister, are old.
This position offers ease and relaxation.
You should exert yourself."
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to be Píngzhāng Zhèngshì 平章政事.
He presented several achievements of Ruìzōng 睿宗 in recovering Shǎnxī 陝西.
The emperor happily accepted them
and stored them in the imperial archive.
He was enfeoffed as Dìngguó Gōng 定國公.
In the eleventh year,
he passed away.
[一三]The emperor was playing polo,
and upon hearing the news, immediately stopped.
The relevant authorities offered sacrifices,
and he was buried with full ceremonial rites.
One thousand two hundred and fifty liǎng 兩 of silver and heavy silk fabrics were bestowed for his funeral.
In the twenty-first year,
the emperor, remembering his contributions,
promoted his grandson Sānhé 三合 to Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn 武功將軍,
and granted him hereditary succession to his original Měng'ān Hélǎnrúokūshēn Móukè 猛安曷懶若窟申謀克.
In the first year of Tàihé 泰和,
he was enshrined in the ancestral temple of Shìzōng 世宗.
The eulogy states: At the beginning of Dàdìng 大定,
wars raged along the Jiāng 疆 and Huái 淮 rivers,
and troubles arose from the Qìdān 契丹.
Móuyǎn 謀衍, relying on his achievements,
and Wōwò 窩斡 fiercely ravaging,
there was a fear that they would not be restrained.
Shìzōng 世宗 made a sole decision
to recall Móuyǎn 謀衍,
and Púsǎn Zhōngyì 僕散忠義 was entrusted with responsibility.
Therefore, it is said,
"The army is commanded by its general;
if the general is virtuous, the soldiers are brave."
Is this not what it refers to?
Hégǔliè Zhìníng 紇石烈志寧 once said:
"If I receive an edict to go on a campaign,
I would not dare to refuse.
But to be a prime minister, I truly cannot."
To know the difficulty of being a prime minister
is truly what is called virtuous.
The armies of Qín 秦 and Lǒng 隴
were truly in precarious danger.
Túdān Héxǐ 徒單合喜's assessment of the enemy and his adaptation to changes was so astute;
this was indeed difficult!
Collation Notes:
Hégǔliè Liángbì 紇石烈良弼; Wányán Shǒudào 完顏守道 (original name Xíníliè 習尼列);
Shí Jū 石琚; Tángkuò Ānlǐ 唐括安禮;
Yílà Dào 移剌道 (original name Zhào Sān 趙三, son Guāngzǔ 光祖)
Héshíliè Liángbì,
originally named Lóushì,
was a native of Huípàchuān.
His great-grandfather was Hūlǎn.
His grandfather was Tèbùlǔ.
His father, Tàiyǔ,
inherited the post of Púliǎn,
and moved to Xuānníng.
During the Tiānhuì era,
students of Nǚzhí characters were selected from various circuits and sent to the capital.
Liángbì and Nàhé Chūnnián were both young boys,
and both were chosen.
At this time,
Xīyǐn was the prime minister.
He was on a trip to an outer prefecture for some matter.
Liángbì met him on the way.
Upon seeing him,
he sighed, saying:
"We, who study the prime minister's characters,
have traveled a thousand *lǐ* to the capital.
It is only proper that we meet him."
So he entered the relay station and sought an audience,
bowing beneath the hall.
Xīyǐn asked:
"What child is this?"
Liángbì introduced himself, saying:
"I am one whom the officials recommended to study the prime minister's characters."
Xīyǐn was greatly pleased,
and asked about his studies.
Liángbì responded without a trace of fear.
Xīyǐn said:
"This child will surely become a great instrument for the nation in the future."
He kept him for several days.
At fourteen,
he became a professor in Běijīng.
He usually had two hundred students.
People at the time had a saying about him:
"First there was Gǔshén,
then there was Lóushì."
Those who studied under him
later all became famous.
At seventeen,
he was appointed Clerk in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng Lìshǐ).
He would grasp the hidden depths of documents
as soon as his eyes passed over them.
Even for lengthy dispatches,
he would dictate them and they would be completed immediately,
with both their words and reasoning perfect.
At the time, he was considered the best among those who studied Xīyǐn's methods.
He was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Zhǔshì).
At the beginning of the Tiāndé era,
he was successively promoted to Director of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Lángzhōng),
then changed to Director of the Right Bureau (Yòusī Lángzhōng),
and temporarily served as Assistant Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat (Bìshū Shàojiān) to be the annual envoy to the Sòng emperor.
At this time,
Nàhé Chūnnián was a Participator in Political Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
He recommended Liángbì as being superior in talent to himself.
For this reason, Liángbì was made Minister of Punishments (Xíngbù Shàngshū),
and given his present name.
When his father died,
he was reinstated to his original post.
Hǎilíng once said:
"Left Chancellor Zhāng Hào is experienced in affairs,
but somewhat insincere.
Minister of Punishments Lóushì's conduct and words are upright,
without any flattery."
He then said to Chūnnián:
"You can truly be said to have recommended a capable person.
Most people often envy those superior to themselves,
but you recommended one superior to yourself,
which is far more virtuous than others."
He was reassigned as Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards' Cavalry and Infantry (Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ).
Liángbì's voice was clear and bright.
When Hǎilíng issued edicts to his ministers,
he would always have Liángbì transmit the imperial decree.
Those who heard it were invariably moved,
and for this reason, he was often summoned for questioning.
Less than a year later,
he was appointed Participator in Political Affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
then promoted to Right Chancellor (Shàngshū Yòuchéng),
granted a sword to wear into the palace,
and then transferred to Left Chancellor (Zuǒchéng).
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
Liángbì advised against it, but was not heeded.
He was made Grand Commander of the Right Vanguard Army (Yòulǐngjūn Dàdūdū).
When Hǎilíng was in Huáinán,
he decreed that Liángbì and Supervising General Túdān Zhēn should pacify Shàngjīng and Liáoyòu.
Soon after,
many troops deserted and returned north,
and Shìzōng was enthroned in Liáoyáng.
Liángbì then returned to Biànjīng.
After Hǎilíng's death,
Shìzōng immediately made Liángbì the Garrison Commander of Nánjīng and concurrently the Mayor of Kāifēng (Kāifēng Yǐn),
then concurrently Commander-in-Chief of Hénán (Hénán Dūtǒng),
and summoned him to be appointed Right Chancellor (Shàngshū Yòuchéng).
Shìzōng said to Liángbì:
"You once advised against Zhènglóng's attack on Sòng,
but your words were not used,
leading to his downfall.
Those who clung to their positions and sought temporary peace at that time,
I have all dismissed.
Now I reuse you.
Regarding all matters of the state,
you should speak exhaustively,
without any further apprehension."
Liángbì kowtowed in thanks.
After Wōwò was defeated at Xiànquán
and entered Xī territory,
Liángbì was decreed to wear a gold tablet and four silver tablets,
and went to Běijīng to pacify the Xī and Qìdān.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Left Chancellor (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng).
He submitted a memorial, stating,
"Regarding those who have not been recorded for their merits and rewarded since the time of our ancestors,
I have examined and found thirty-two individuals.
They should be ranked and rewarded."
An edict stated:
"For those who already hold officials of the fifth rank or above,
report to me.
For those of the sixth rank or below, and those without official posts,
the Department of State Affairs shall determine their promotions and appointments."
From then on, all meritorious services were rewarded.
He was further appointed Chancellor (Píngzhāng Zhèngshì)
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Zōng State (Zōngguó Gōng).
Initially,
the *méng'ān móukè* of the two Shandong circuits were intermingled with the common people.
Liángbì was decreed to suitably rearrange them,
so they would live separately from the common people.
Where their lands were intertwined with the common people's fields,
all were exchanged for government land.
From then on, there were no more disputes.
In the eleventh month of the sixth year,
on the Crown Prince's birthday,
the emperor hosted a banquet in the Eastern Palace.
Liángbì and Zhìníng were both given wine.
The emperor said:
"The borders are peaceful,
and the internal and external affairs are tranquil.
This is the strength of the generals and ministers."
Liángbì replied:
"We are untalented,
filling the positions of chancellors.
How dare we not exert ourselves like dogs and horses?"
The emperor was pleased.
He was further appointed Right Chancellor (Yòuchéngxiàng)
and Supervisor of the National History Compilation (Jiānxiū Guóshǐ).
Shìzōng said to Liángbì:
"During Hǎilíng's time,
the records and annotations were incomplete.
The good and evil of a monarch
serve as encouragement and warning for ten thousand generations.
If records and annotations are missing,
what will later generations observe?
Let the historians widely seek and record them."
He also said:
"Regarding collateral imperial relatives of the fifth degree or above who are waiting in the department,
if they possess usable talent,
report their names to me.
Those who are mediocre and unfit for office
should also be reported and dismissed."
Left Chancellor Wányán Shǒudào reported:
"Among the two *méng'ān* near the capital,
fathers, sons, and brothers often live separately,
and the land they receive is insufficient to support them,
making them increasingly impoverished."
The emperor asked the chancellors about this.
Liángbì replied:
"If you definitely want fathers and brothers to live together,
it is advisable to exchange their allotted land with the local people.
Although it may cause temporary disruption,
it will be very convenient in the long run."
Right Chancellor Shí Jū said:
"It is better for the common people to each enjoy their own livelihood,
rather than changing the old ways."
The emperor ultimately followed Liángbì's suggestion.
When the Veritable Records of Tàizōng (Tàizōng Shílù) were completed,
Liángbì was granted a golden belt and twenty bolts of rich silk.
Zhāng Jǐngrén, Cáo Wàngzhī, Liú Zhòngyuān, and others who also compiled the National History were given varying rewards.
Shìzōng, when discussing with his attendants who among ancient and modern officials were worthy and unworthy,
then said to the prime minister:
"During the Huángtǒng and Zhènglóng eras, many officials were killed,
often dying for no crime.
I entrust you, my lords, with the great affairs of state;
do not deviate from the Way to bring disaster upon yourselves,
and do not merely acquiesce, thereby misleading me.
Only by being loyal and filial,
by rectifying, saving, assisting, and benefiting,
can we hope to achieve great peace."
Liángbì replied:
"We, your servants, have received excessive kindness.
Though we are shallow and humble,
how dare we not exert our utmost?
Your Majesty's edicts are earnest and profound;
we, your servants, are immeasurably fortunate."
Liángbì requested that horses be purchased at the border markets
without restriction by gender.
"Currently, official horses are very few.
Should there be an alarm on the border,
to then mobilize from the people,
would it not be too late?"
The emperor assented.
In the eighth year,
the imperial guards were selected.
Shìzōng heard that many of them were not skilled in archery,
so he issued an edict to make them practice shooting.
A short while later,
he asked Liángbì and Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Sījìng:
"Have the Nǚzhēn people not yet begun practicing archery?"
Liángbì replied:
"It has already been implemented."
Tóngzhī Qīngzhōu Fángyùshì Cháng Déhuī submitted a memorial, stating:
"The regulations of the Lìbù [Ministry of Personnel]
only consider years of service.
Even those with talent are constrained to lower positions.
Thus, most Cìshǐ and Xiànlìng [governors and county magistrates] are not the right people.
I beg that you secretly investigate,
and then conduct integrity inquiries.
Currently, even for the position of Jiǔshuìshǐ [Wine Tax Commissioner], able officials are selected.
How can a Xiànlìng not be chosen for talent?
I beg that able officials who are currently serving as Jiǔshuìshǐ [Wine Tax Commissioners]
be appointed to positions that directly involve the people."
The emperor approved his words
and said to the prime minister:
"I reflect that many common officials are not the right people;
I wake up in the middle of the night,
or cannot sleep until dawn.
You, my lords, must pay attention to selection,
and I will also secretly conduct observations."
Liángbì replied:
"For Nǚzhēn and Qìdān people,
they must have studied Hàn characters [the Chinese script]
before they can be considered.
Currently, the majority tend to form factions,
either praising one another
or slandering others,
which makes it difficult."
The emperor said:
"That is why I secretly order observations."
The emperor said to Liángbì:
"The grain tax collected from Niútóushuì Měng'ān Móukè [Mongol-Manchu military units]
is originally to prepare for lean years;
it should be used to provide relief in places suffering from floods, droughts, or food shortages."
He was promoted to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng [Left Chancellor]
and continued to supervise the compilation of the national history as before.
Having served as prime minister for a long time, Liángbì
was well-versed in court affairs.
To the emperor's inquiries, he would respond with utmost sincerity,
maintaining his composure,
and his proposals on governance often met the emperor's approval.
He left office due to his mother's mourning
and was later reinstated to his former position.
At that time,
Lǐ Rénxiào, the King of Xià, requested to divide half of his kingdom
to enfeoff his minister Rèn Déjìng.
The emperor consulted his ministers,
and many ministers said that this was an external matter,
and it would be acceptable to grant it.
The emperor said:
"This is not Rénxiào's true intention;
it cannot be granted."
Liángbì's opinion aligned with the emperor's.
Subsequently,
the state of Xià indeed executed Rèn Déjìng
and sent a memorial expressing gratitude.
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Zōng requested the construction of moats and trenches along the border.
Liángbì said:
"If an enemy state truly comes to invade,
how can these possibly defend against them?"
The emperor said:
"Your words are correct."
Wáng Xiàn, the King of Gāolì, submitted a memorial abdicating the throne to his younger brother Hào.
The emperor suspected this
and asked the prime minister, Liángbì.
Liángbì deduced that the abdication was not Wáng Xiàn's true intention.
Later, Zhào Wèichǒng requested to defect with forty prefectures,
and his memorial indeed stated that Wáng Hào had murdered his elder brother Xiàn,
just as Liángbì had deduced.
The details are in the Biography of Gāolì.
Shìzōng dismissed the Cǎifǎngguān [Investigation Officials]
and said to his prime minister:
"How can I know the good and bad qualities of officials?"
Liángbì replied:
"We, your servants, shall investigate them for Your Majesty."
Upon the presentation of the Ruìzōng Shílù [Veritable Records of Emperor Ruìzōng],
he was bestowed a tōngxī belt and twenty bolts of rich brocade.
That year,
there was a ceremony at the Southern Suburb,
and Liángbì served as Dàlǐshǐ [Grand Master of Ceremonies].
Since the founding of the state,
this rite had never been performed.
The historical precedents of various dynasties also differed greatly.
Liángbì discussed and deliberated on the additions and deletions,
making each suitable,
and people admired his capability.
The emperor discussed with Liángbì and Shǒudào that Měng'ān Móukè officials were often young,
not accustomed to instruction,
and lacked proper respect for elders.
In former times,
the elders in the villages would guide them.
Now, if there are elders in the villages who can provide guidance,
some consider it not their responsibility and do not intervene,
or people do not listen because it is not their official duty.
"We can establish Xiānglǎo [Village Elders] according to the Hàn system,
selecting those who are honest, upright, and fit to be role models,
to instruct them."
Liángbì reported:
"Your Majesty's foresight extends to this;
it is the blessing of the myriad commoners."
On another day,
the emperor asked:
"I have observed in previous histories
that there were those in lower positions who kept the welfare of the state in their hearts,
speaking frankly for the people.
Why is it that such people are absent now?"
Liángbì replied:
"How can there be no such people now?
It is because by acting with integrity,
they are instead slandered and criticized,
and disaster befalls them,
which is why they do not do so."
In the fourteenth year of Dàdìng,
the year being Jiǎwǔ,
Zhāng, the Yǐn of Dàxīng, was sent as an envoy to felicitate the Sòng court on New Year's Day.
The Sòng people seized his credentials at the guesthouse.
An imperial edict ordered Liáng Sù to inquire thoroughly into the matter.
Opinions were divided.
It was said that whenever the year was a Wǔ year, there would inevitably be military action.
The Emperor asked Liángbì about this.
He replied,
"Emperor Tàizǔ attacked Liáo in a Jiǎwǔ year,
and Emperor Tàizōng conquered Sòng in a Bǐngwǔ year.
Now, the Sòng people have seized our credentials,
and it happens to be a Wǔ year,
hence this saying.
It is not necessarily so."
Soon after,
when Liáng Sù arrived in Sòng,
the Sòng ruler stood up to receive and present the credentials,
following the old ceremony.
After Liáng Sù returned,
the Sòng ruler sent Zhāng Zǐyán, Shàngshū of the Gōngbù, and Liú Duó, Zhī Gémén Shì, to come and make a request.
Their letter stated:
"Thinking of my humble self,
I have long inherited the great succession.
Having received the grace of the superior nation's illumination,
the alliance has been renewed and continued for ten years.
The diligence of mutual visits between the two courts has been cultivated,
and goodwill has been maintained without a single day's neglect.
However, regarding the reception of the diplomatic letter,
the ceremony of receiving guests should be updated.
We have repeatedly expressed this earnestly,
and instructed envoys to request it again.
We humbly pray for your favor and consideration,
and that you graciously grant our request."
The Emperor discussed this with his ministers.
Liángbì reported,
"The Sòng state has been exempted from calling itself 'subject' to 'nephew,'
and from presenting 'memorials' to 'letters.'
The favors granted are already many.
Now they again ask to be exempted from personally receiving credentials.
This is insatiable,
and must not be granted."
Wányán Shǒudào, Píngzhāng Zhèngshì, and Yílà Dào, Cānzhī Zhèngshì, agreed with Liángbì's opinion.
Shí Jū, Zuǒchéng, and Tángkuò Ānlǐ, Yòuchéng, believed that not granting the request
would inevitably lead to military conflict.
The Emperor said to Jū and others,
"What you all say
is incorrect.
If they were to request something greater than this,
would you wish to grant it then?"
So, he followed Liángbì's advice
and replied to their letter,
roughly stating:
"Without following the established norm,
you again request a new ceremony for presenting letters.
Claiming to have inherited the great succession,
you appear even more self-important.
How can such conduct
still achieve your desires?
Moreover, the rites are already established,
and cannot be changed."
The ceremony for receiving and presenting credentials
was ultimately not altered.
The Emperor asked his chief ministers,
"I have frequently sought internal and external officials to recommend talented individuals,
but have not heard of any recommendations.
Why is this?"
Cānzhèng Wèi Zǐpíng requested
that those who should make recommendations must recommend one person per post,
and based on their suitability,
awards or punishments would be given.
The Emperor said,
"Under the Sòng system of recommendation,
if the recommended person commits a private offense,
the recommender, even if a prime minister,
is also punished with demotion.
Few people have such integrity;
tempted by profit,
they may lose their principles.
Chief ministers bear great responsibilities;
how can their promotion or demotion be based on such matters?"
Liángbì said,
"The previous edict ordered court officials of the sixth rank and above,
and external officials of the fifth rank and above,
to each recommend those they know.
Why not reiterate the previous edict?"
This was followed.
The Emperor said,
"I wish to know the good and bad deeds of officials.
If I simply send officials to investigate,
I fear they might not be suitable for the task.
In that case,
how can I know the good and bad deeds of officials?"
Liángbì replied,
"Your ministers will investigate for Your Majesty."
The Emperor said,
"Yes,
but do not let reputation and reality become confused."
The Emperor wanted to relocate the rebellious faction of Wōwò,
dispersing them to Liáodōng.
Liángbì reported,
"These people have already been pardoned; relocating them will cause resentment."
The Emperor said,
"This is a matter of immediate pros and cons;
I am thinking of future generations of my descendants."
Liángbì said,
"This is beyond what your ministers can achieve."
Thereupon,
those who had participated in the rebellion
were relocated to the Wūgǔlǐshílěi tribe.
The Emperor asked his chief ministers,
"Yáo experienced a nine-year flood,
and Tāng experienced a seven-year drought,
yet the people did not suffer from hunger.
Now, after one or two years of poor harvest,
the people lack food.
Why is this?"
Liángbì replied,
"In ancient times, the land was vast and the people simple,
they highly valued frugality,
and moreover, they focused solely on agriculture.
Therefore, their stores were abundant,
and there was no threat of famine.
Now, the land is small and the population large,
and many abandon agriculture for commerce,
so few cultivate the land,
but many consume.
Therefore, as soon as a lean year occurs, the people suffer."
The Emperor deeply approved of this,
and thereupon ordered the relevant authorities to punish those who were extravagant, idle, and neglected their livelihoods.
In the seventeenth year,
he resigned from his prime minister position due to illness,
but it was not permitted.
After his leave of absence reached one hundred days,
an imperial edict granted further leave,
and imperial physicians were sent to examine him,
and eunuchs frequently sent to inquire about his health.
As Liángbì had been on leave for a long time,
many matters in the department were delayed.
The Emperor asked the prime minister and Cānzhèngs about this.
Zhāng Rǔbì replied,
"There are none."
The Emperor said,
"How can you say there are none?
From now on, any doubtful matters that cannot be decided for a long time
must be fully reported."
In the eighteenth year,
Biǎo requested to retire and return to his hometown.
The emperor sent an envoy to comfort and instruct him, saying:
"Recently, you have been on leave due to illness,
and We are deeply concerned.
Now We hear you plan to go to Xījīng to recuperate.
The climate there
is not suitable for the elderly or sick.
In the capital, you are weary of official duties.
If you were to reside in a good commandery near the capital,
once your illness improves a little,
please let Us know quickly."
Liángbì memorialized, saying:
"Your subject has encountered a sagely and enlightened ruler,
and has been undeservedly entrusted with a great responsibility.
Day and night, I have been anxious and fearful,
to the point of becoming ill.
Recently, I have been favored by imperial grace,
with several envoys sent to inquire after me,
and given medicine.
That your subject has barely survived until now
is all due to Your Majesty's benevolence.
How would your subject dare to hope that arriving in my hometown
would immediately cure my illness?
Your subject has been away from home for many years,
and most of my relatives and acquaintances have already passed away.
Only this old subject remains.
The longing for my native land
truly cannot be forgotten.
Your subject humbly reflects that among all human subjects who have received the favor of a ruler,
none has surpassed your subject.
Though your subject were to be ground to dust and shattered to pieces, there would be no way to repay this.
If I could just return to my ancestral home
and see my old relatives and friends,
then I would die without regret."
The emperor asked the chancellor, saying:
"Chancellor Liángbì insists on returning to his hometown.
We intend to grant his son, Fúbǎo Hégé Dā, a hereditary position as mèng'ān,
and let him accompany his father.
What do you think?"
Right Chancellor Wányán Shǒudào said:
"It would be better to bestow the mèng'ān upon Liángbì,
and let his son temporarily manage its affairs."
The emperor agreed.
Thereupon, Húlún Sònggé was appointed mèng'ān,
and the chancellor's salary and attendants were provided.
Liángbì then retired and returned home.
The emperor said to the chancellors:
"It is not that you are not dedicated,
but simply that your talent and ability do not equal Liángbì's.
That is why We regret his departure."
Afterwards,
when the Shàngshū Shěng presented nominations for appointments,
the emperor said:
"Chancellor Liángbì, when proposing appointments,
never arbitrarily granted positions to those undeserving,
and his recommendations often resulted in finding suitable people.
Niángē Wòtèlá, Yílà Zào, and Péimǎn Yúqìng
were all recommended by him.
As for private solicitations,
there was absolutely none."
Once he asked Liángbì,
"Why is the sun red every morning and evening?"
Liángbì replied:
"When its color is red in the morning, it corresponds to the East,
which Gāolí embodies.
When its color is red in the evening, it corresponds to the West,
which Xiàguó embodies.
May Your Majesty cultivate virtue to respond to Heaven,
then calamities and anomalies will naturally cease."
Soon after,
the disturbance of Rèn Déjìng occurred in Xiàguó,
and the trouble of Zhào Wèichǒng in Gāolí.
All his words were verified.
That year,
he passed away,
aged sixty.
The emperor mourned and regretted his loss,
sending Tàifǔ Jiān Yílà Zào and Tóngzhī Xījīng Liúshǒu Wáng Zuǒ as imperial envoys for the funeral rites and offerings,
granting extra white silver and colored silk,
and making all funeral expenses officially provided.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Jīnyuán Jùnwáng,
and Hànlín Dàizhì Yílà Lǚ was ordered to carve an inscription for his tombstone,
with the posthumous title Chéngmǐn.
Liángbì was intelligent, sharp-witted, loyal, and upright,
skilled at making decisions.
His discourse and discernment were extraordinary.
Although he rose from humble origins
to the position of chancellor,
morning and evening he was diligent and devoted to the nation,
his strategies were profound and far-reaching,
and he was always eager to recommend talented individuals
as if he couldn't do enough.
At home, he was clean and frugal,
providing relief to impoverished relatives and friends.
His respect for others grew with time.
He held office for nearly twenty years,
achieving the accomplishments of a peaceful and prosperous era,
and was hailed as a virtuous chancellor.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
he was enshrined in Shìzōng's ancestral temple.
Shǒudào's
original name was Xíníliè.
Due to his grandfather Gǔ Shén's merit,
he was promoted to Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì.
In the ninth year of Huángtǒng,
he served as Tóngzhī Lúlóng Jūnjié Dùshǐ Shì,
and successively as Cìshǐ of the four prefectures Xiàn, Qí, Bīn, and Jì.
When Shìzōng visited Zhōngdū,
passing through Jì,
the elders blocked the road, requesting his reappointment.
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Yílà Yuányí recommended him as his own successor.
Thereupon, he was promoted to Zhāoyì Dàjiāngjūn
and appointed Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū.
The imperial relative Yàn was appointed Zuǒ Chéngxiàng due to imperial favor and long-standing acquaintance.
Shǒudào remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
the empire is largely settled,
but border alarms have not ceased.
This is a time for great endeavors,
and I fear Yàn is not of the right caliber.
If you must show him affection,
it would be better to grant him a generous salary
and exempt him from duties."
Consequently, Yàn was appointed Tàiwèi
and retired.
Shìzōng wished to reward the soldiers and officers who had served in his entourage,
acknowledging their efforts,
but the imperial treasury was depleted.
It was proposed to borrow funds from the people to reward them.
Shǒudào said:
"The people, having suffered cruel governance,
are just now rejoicing in a new lease on life.
Now, imperial benevolence has not yet reached them,
but levies are suddenly imposed.
What will become of the hopes of the masses?
It is better to use what is in the palace
than to take from the people."
His advice was followed.
When the Qìdān rebelled,
some of the mèng'ān and móukè in Liáodōng who were in their territory
sided with the rebels.
The court deliberated relocating them inland.
Shǒudào strongly argued against it.
Right Vice Marshal Móuyǎn led troops to quell the rebels
but did not attack immediately.
Shǒudào vehemently spoke to the court,
and an imperial edict was issued, sending Púsǎn Zhōngyì and Gēshíliè Zhìníng to replace him,
and the East was pacified.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
sixteen locations in the palace caught fire.
While reconstruction was underway,
summer had already begun,
greatly burdening the people.
Shǒudào remonstrated, and the work was halted.
Soon after,
he was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
concurrently serving as Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū,
and dispatched by imperial post to plan military provisions for the two circuits of Shāndōng
and to relieve the famine among the people.
Shǒudào registered the households of prominent families,
limiting their annual reserves,
and made them surrender all their surplus to the government,
then returned the value to them.
Thus, both military and civilian needs were met.
He was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì, concurrently Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
Shǒudào earnestly declined,
and Shìzōng instructed him, saying:
"Your ancestor's meritorious service was to the imperial house,
and We also know your loyalty and diligence.
That is why We promote you.
Do not decline too much."
At that time, many remnants of the Qìdān party had not yet submitted,
and the people of Běijīng, Línhuáng, and Tàizhōu were uneasy.
Shǒudào was ordered to wear a golden tally and go to pacify them,
and was given a thousand horses from the imperial herds
for military use.
Shǒudào successfully attracted Qìdān Gǔdié Nièhé and others to submit,
and the people found peace.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng,
concurrently Tàizǐ Shàoshī.
Once, when accompanying a hunt in the near suburbs,
a tiger injured a hunter.
The emperor wished to shoot it himself,
but Shǒudào blocked his horse and remonstrated strongly, and the emperor stopped.
Soon after, he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
In the fourteenth year,
an envoy from the Sòng people requested to personally receive a letter.
Zuǒ Chéng Shí Jū and others debated whether to grant the request.
The emperor was undecided,
but Shǒudào and others deemed it unacceptable.
The emperor ultimately followed their advice,
details of which are in the biography of Gēshíliè Liángbì.
Afterwards,
he was promoted to Yòu Chéngxiàng,
concurrently supervising the compilation of national history,
then again promoted to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng,
and granted a hereditary móukè position.
In the twentieth year,
the Veritable Records of Xīzōng were completed.
The Emperor then said to him:
"Your ancestor, Gǔshén,
had some inappropriate actions,
yet they were not concealed,
which shows your upright brushwork."
Soon after, he requested to retire for a worthy successor,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
He was promoted to Grand Preceptor (Tàiwèi) and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng),
then reassigned as Left Chancellor (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéngxiàng).
The Emperor admonished him, saying:
"The position of Chancellor cannot remain vacant.
It requires an experienced elder,
which is why I have again placed you in it.
You should understand this."
Not long after,
he again begged to retire,
to which the Emperor said:
"Because you are a descendant of a meritorious minister from the previous reign,
I specially entrusted you with the heavy responsibility of a San Gōng (Three Ducal Ministers).
Since taking charge of government,
you have diligently and loyally served,
and I greatly commend this.
Now you seek to retire due to age,
which is certainly in keeping with the conduct of a Chancellor.
However, there is no one yet to replace you,
which makes it difficult to grant your request.
Strive on!"
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was demoted one rank
for unauthorized disbursement of provisions to the princes and imperial grandsons of the Eastern Palace.
Soon after, he was reappointed to concurrently hold the title of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī).
His son, Guī, was specially allowed to inherit the Móukè position
and serve as a Fúbǎo Zhǐhòu (Guard of the Imperial Seals).
When Zhāngzōng was Prince Yuán,
an edict commanded him to practice polo (qíjú).
Shǒudào (the Chancellor) remonstrated, saying:
"This is not permissible during the period of mourning."
The Emperor said:
"This is merely for practicing military preparedness.
If he were to do it on his own, it would be unacceptable.
But if it's done at my command,
what harm is there?
However, it should not be done frequently."
In the twenty-sixth year,
he earnestly requested to retire,
and an imperial edict graciously granted it.
A special banquet was held for him in the Qìngchūn Diàn,
where the Emperor personally offered him a cup of wine
and bestowed upon him generous gifts.
His son, Guī, accompanied him on his departure,
and his second son, Zhāng, was also granted the Jinshì degree.
He died in the fourth year of Míngchāng,
at the age of seventy-four.
Upon hearing of his death, the Emperor was deeply saddened,
and dispatched his younger brother, the Diǎnjiǎn Sī Pànguān Púdài, to offer sacrifices,
along with one thousand liǎng of silver, fifty bolts of fine silk, and five hundred bolts of plain silk.
The Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng) proposed the posthumous title of Jiǎnnxiàn,
but the Emperor changed it to Jiǎnjìng,
presumably valuing his ability to maintain integrity from beginning to end.
Shí Jū,
courtesy name Zǐměi,
was from Dìngzhōu.
He was profound and fond of learning.
His father, Gāo,
served as a county official,
managing affairs with integrity and honesty,
and was known as a worthy elder.
He followed Prince Lǔ, Cháimǔ, in attacking Qīngzhōu.
The people of the prefecture held firm and did not surrender.
Cháimǔ was angered,
and upon the city's fall,
ordered Gāo to count the number of prefectural residents,
intending to allow the various armies to plunder and seize them.
Gāo delayed the matter.
Cháimǔ reproached him,
to which Gāo replied:
"Your Royal Highness is to pacify and stabilize the prefectures and counties for the imperial court.
You should ensure the common people live peacefully,
without being troubled or harmed.
If you take cities and towns but massacre their people,
then those not yet subdued will surely defend to the death to resist us.
As for my delay,
how dare I evade punishment?"
Cháimǔ was moved and enlightened,
and then issued an order, saying:
"Anyone who dares to harm the people of the prefecture
shall be judged by military law."
He pointed to his seat and said to Gāo:
"Your descendants will surely occupy this seat."
Gāo subsequently defended Dìngzhōu.
Wáng Bā, a man from Tángxiàn, conspired to rebel,
writing the names of his county's people in a register,
numbering several thousand.
His partisans brought the register to the prefecture to expose them.
Gāo presided over the investigation.
It was winter at the time,
and Gāo carried the register into the main hall.
He feigned a stumble and fall,
dropping the register into the brazier fire,
burning it completely.
Their names could no longer be recovered,
and only the ringleaders were punished,
while all others were released.
Jū Shēng, at seven years old,
could recite a book after reading it once.
When he grew older, he was widely versed in the classics and histories,
and was skilled in literary composition.
In Tiānjuàn second year (1139),
he passed the Jìnshì examination first,
and was twice appointed county magistrate of Hóngzhèng and Xíngtái.
The prefect of Xíngtái was greedy and violent towards the subordinate counties,
extorting wealth from the people
to satisfy his desires.
Jū alone gave nothing.
Soon after, the prefect was disgraced due to corruption,
and other magistrates and assistants were all implicated.
Jū was spared because of his integrity,
and was reassigned as magistrate of Xiùróng.
He was again promoted to the position of Zhǔshì in the Ministry of Rites, operating as Hànhuáng,
then summoned to be Zuǒsī Dūshì,
and successively promoted to Lìbù Lángzhōng.
In Zhēnyuán third year (1155),
he resigned from office due to his father's mourning.
Soon after, he was recalled to his original post as Shìláng of the same ministry.
Shìzōng had long heard of his reputation.
In Dàdìng second year (1162),
he was promoted to Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū,
while retaining his position as Shìláng.
He was ordered to meticulously determine institutions and regulations.
Jū submitted a memorial with six points,
generally speaking of rectifying the disciplinary rules,
clarifying rewards and punishments,
drawing close the loyal and upright,
keeping away the wicked and sycophantic,
reducing non-urgent tasks,
and abolishing unnamed levies.
The Emperor praised and accepted them.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
From Yuánwàiláng to Shàngshū, Jū
never left the Ministry of Personnel,
for nearly ten years.
Having long presided over appointments,
he could, for all the various rules of official appointments and transfers of the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
and the comprehensive systems of official selection of the North and South,
count them off on his fingers in their proper sequence.
At the time, he was known for his thoroughness and clarity.
After a while,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Jū repeatedly declined,
but the Emperor said:
"There is nothing that your talent and reputation cannot handle.
Why do you decline?"
Right Chancellor Sū Bǎohéng was overseeing sixteen construction projects.
A decree ordered them to jointly manage the matter,
granting twenty-four silver tallies,
permitting them to plan as they saw fit.
The Emperor said to Jū:
"I do not wish for this project to trouble the people.
All laborers and craftsmen shall be paid wages.
Do not allow corrupt officials to use their connections for illicit gain,
thereby inciting popular resentment.
You all must exert yourselves
to meet my expectations."
Túdān Héxǐ pacified Shǎnxī.
Jū requested a partial amnesty for Qín and Lǒng,
to bring peace to the common people,
and the Emperor granted it.
He observed mourning for his mother,
but was soon recalled to office,
and promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
There was a disaster at the Tiāncháng Temple.
