A decree ordered the relevant authorities to repair it.
The authorities demolished private residences to expand it,
spending three hundred thousand guàn of money.
Yùzhōu collected wild mushrooms,
employing several hundred thousand people.
Jū reported this to the Emperor,
who said:
"From now on, anything referred to as 'for imperial use'
must first be reported and approved."
Jū and Mèng Hào replied:
"Such a sagely instruction
is a blessing for the common people."
At that time,
there was a discussion about prohibiting the netting and hunting of wild animals like foxes and rabbits.
The cumulative count of their catches
could even lead to penal servitude.
Jū memorialized, saying:
"To punish the hunting of birds and beasts with penal servitude
is probably not His Majesty's intention.
It would be acceptable to punish them with flogging and then release them."
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
After a long time,
he was promoted to Zuǒchéng,
and concurrently Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàoshī).
The Emperor asked his prime ministers:
"In ancient times, there were those in lower positions who could worry for the country and its people, speaking frankly without reservation.
Why are there none today?"
Jū replied:
"How could there be none?
It's just that they have not yet been able to convey their thoughts to the top."
The Emperor said:
"It is fitting that we wholeheartedly seek them out and promote them."
Shìzōng was about to perform the suburban sacrifice (jiāosì),
and there was a discussion about who should be enshrined as co-sacrificant.
Jū said:
"The co-sacrificant
is one who assists the spirit and acts as its host.
Those who come from outside will not settle without a host.
Therefore, one's ancestors are put forth to be co-sacrificants with Heaven,
to grant them equal veneration.
The Xiàojīng says: 'Sacrifice to Hòujì in the suburbs as co-sacrificant with Heaven.'
The Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn all co-sacrificed with one emperor.
Táng Gāozōng first honored Gāozǔ and Tàizōng as co-sacrificants.
In the early Chuígǒng era (685-689),
Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Gāozōng were all co-sacrificants.
In Xuánzōng's Kāiyuán eleventh year (723),
the ritual of multiple co-sacrificants was abolished,
and Gāozǔ alone was co-sacrificant.
During Sòng Tàizōng's time,
Xuānzǔ and Tàizǔ were co-sacrificants.
During Zhēnzōng's time, Tàizǔ and Tàizōng were co-sacrificants.
During Rénzōng's time,
the relevant authorities requested that three emperors be co-sacrificants,
and so the founding ancestor, Tàizōng, and Zhēnzōng were all co-sacrificants.
Later, the Bureau of Rites deliberated that for Heaven and Earth and the spirits, there should not be two masters (or more),
and Tàizǔ should be the co-sacrificant.
Thus, the Táng and Sòng changed the ancient practice to have three emperors co-sacrificate with Heaven,
but eventually reverted to the ancient practice of one ancestor co-sacrificant.
In future personal suburban sacrifices, we should follow the ancient rites
and co-sacrificate with one ancestor."
The Emperor said:
"The Táng and Sòng are not worthy of being models.
We should only venerate Emperor Tàizǔ as co-sacrificant."
Jū once requested that the Crown Prince be instructed in governance.
Someone slandered him, saying:
"Jū seeks favor with the Eastern Palace."
Shìzōng perceived that he had no ulterior motives,
and told him of this remark.
Jū replied:
"I was originally an orphan.
By Your Majesty's promotion,
I hold a position among the executive officials,
and also bear the responsibility of a tutor.
Your humble servant foolishly believes that the Crown Prince is the foundation of the realm,
and should be made aware of the affairs of the people.
Hence I spoke of it."
He then begged to be relieved of the Shàoshī position.
In the second month of the tenth year (1170),
when sacrificing to the altars of earth and grain (shè),
the relevant authorities memorialized requesting the Emperor to personally sign the sacrificial tablet.
The Emperor asked Jū:
"Should I sign it?"
Jū replied:
"There is a precedent for it."
The Emperor said:
"For sacrificial ceremonies and rituals,
you all must be careful,
so as not to invite criticism from later generations.
When Xīzōng posthumously honored Tàizǔ,
Yǔwén Xūzhōng decided on the ritual,
using ordinary court attire for the ceremony.
Although I was a child then,
I still felt it was wrong."
Jū replied:
"Sacrifices
are important matters.
We would not act without precedent."
The Emperor said to Jū:
"Jurchen people often directly occupy important positions,
unaware of the hardships of the common folk.
You once served as an assistant (Chéngbù).
What affairs of the people are you not aware of?
Fully explain all advantages and disadvantages."
The Emperor discussed minting coins with his prime ministers.
Some argued that the cost of minting was several times over
and wished to exploit gold and silver mines instead.
The Emperor said:
"The profits from mountains and marshes can be shared with the people,
but currency should not be privately minted.
If wealth circulates throughout the four directions,
how is that different from being under official control?"
Jū advanced and said:
"Your humble servant has heard that the wealth of the Son of Heaven is stored throughout the realm,
just like a spring, wishing for its free flow."
The Emperor asked Jū:
"In ancient times, did the common people also mint money?"
He replied:
"If the common people were allowed to mint their own money,
then petty individuals would seek high profits,
and the coins would become increasingly thin and poor in quality.
This is why it was prohibited in ancient times."
At that time, among the common people, there were often fabricated seditious rumors,
forming factions and plotting rebellion.
When the matter was discovered, they were executed.
The Emperor asked his chief ministers,
"Why is there still so much disloyalty in the south?"
Jū replied,
"Unscrupulous individuals in the south
falsely claim to be Buddhist or Daoist,
using sorcery and illusion to mislead people.
The ignorant common folk,
unaware, then commit crimes."
The Emperor said,
"Monk Zhìjiū is an example of this.
Such people are not to be pitied,
but when soldiers pursue and capture them,
they profit by taking people's wealth
and harm innocent citizens.
It would be better to gradually stop this."
Zhìjiū,
a monk from Dàmíng Fǔ,
and his fellow temple monk Yuàn Zhìyì told Zhìjiū
that the *Lotus Sūtra* records that in the Five Turbid Eons, the Buddha would appear in Wèi territory,
and the *Heart Sūtra* has the phrase "ultimate Nirvāṇa of dreams."
Yuàn Zhìyì said, "Your dharma name, Zhìjiū,
precisely corresponds to the scripture.
Our late master, Heshang Zàngpíng, knew you had this good fortune
and even wrote a eulogy and entrusted it to you."
Zhìjiū believed his words
and consequently plotted rebellion.
He traveled through the prefectures and commanderies of Dàmíng and Dōngpíng,
falsely claiming to be collecting alms
to entice ignorant people,
and secretly gathered wicked confederates.
They planned to first seize Yǎnzhōu on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the eleventh year,
and gather their followers at Yìshān,
using
the three characters "Yì Tiānshí" (Comply with Heaven's Time)
as their slogan,
then divide and take Dōngpíng and other prefectures.
On the appointed night,
he sent his rebel associates Hú Zhì'ài and others
to raid nearby military camps
and plunder weapons and armor.
The soldiers defeated them.
At the same time, Fù Jiǎn and Liú Xuān also revolted in Yánggǔ and Dōngpíng.
All were executed,
and over four hundred and fifty people were implicated.
Some imperial clan members were not competent in their official duties,
and Shìzōng wanted to grant them honorary official titles,
giving them a suitable allowance
to support them.
He asked his chief ministers,
"How does this compare to previous dynasties?"
Jū replied,
"Yáo cared for his nine paternal kindred,
and the Zhōu house was internally harmonious with its nine paternal kindred;
these were all great achievements of emperors and kings."
Many of Jū's complaisant responses were of this kind.
In the thirteenth year,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
In the sixteenth year,
he submitted another memorial requesting retirement.
Both were disallowed.
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Tángkuò Ānlǐ displeased the Emperor,
and was sent out as Military Commissioner of the Hénghǎi Army.
For several years, he was not recalled.
Jū, in the side palace,
casually said,
"Tángkuò Ānlǐ is loyal and upright,
and has been an external official for a long time."
Shìzōng deeply approved of this,
and consequently recalled him from his post as Nanjing Retainer to be Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
Jū once recommended Shì Shàoxiān as a Yuánwàiláng of the Right Ministry.
Shàoxiān suddenly died of a stroke,
which the Emperor greatly regretted.
He said to Jū,
"This was someone you recommended,"
sighing with emotion repeatedly.
In the seventeenth year,
he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì
and enfeoffed as Xīnguó Gōng.
The following year,
he was appointed Yòuchéngxiàng.
The Compiler of the Diaries of Activity and Repose, Yílà Jié, submitted a letter stating,
"When discussions are held in the court without others present,
the historians are not allowed to hear,
and thus have no way to record them."
The Emperor asked the chief ministers about this.
Jū and Yòuchéng Tángkuò Ānlǐ replied,
"In ancient times, historians
would record every word and action of the Son of Heaven
to warn and admonish the ruler,
hoping they would have reverence.
When King Chéng of Zhōu cut a tung tree leaf to make a gui tablet
and jokingly enfeoffed Shú Yú,
Shǐ Yì said, 'The Son of Heaven cannot speak in jest;
if he speaks, the historian records it.'
From this, we know that the ruler's words and actions
can all be recorded by historians,
and cannot be avoided."
The Emperor said,
"I have read *Zhēnguān Zhèngyào*,
and when Emperor Tàizōng of Táng discussed matters with his ministers,
how the discussion began
and how it eventually concluded,
this was precisely because the court historians were present to record it.
If there is fear of leaking confidential matters,
then trustworthy and discreet individuals should be chosen to handle it."
From this time onward, when court discussions were held without others present,
the diarists no longer avoided recording them.
Due to old age and illness, he firmly resigned,
but the Emperor said,
"I know you are old,
but please try to stay for me.
Wait one or two years,
and I will consider it."
The Emperor said to his chief ministers,
"As the Son of Heaven,
I have never dared to act arbitrarily or make decisions alone.
For every matter, I ask all of you.
If it is feasible, then I proceed;
if not, then I stop."
Jū and Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Tángkuò Ānlǐ memorialized,
"To be eager to ask is to be ample;
to be self-willed is to be petty.
That Your Majesty practices this
is a great fortune for the empire."
One year later,
he again memorialized to retire,
and this time it was permitted.
An imperial edict appointed one of his grandsons as Gémén Zhīhòu.
He immediately ordered his carriage and returned to his hometown.
After a long time,
Shìzōng said to his chief ministers,
"Knowing people is the most difficult task.
Recently, many selected for the 'left' posts have been unsuitable.
Only when Shí Jū was chancellor
did he often recommend capable people for their offices.
Zuǒchéng Yílà Dào and Cānzhèng Zhāngē Wòtèlā recommended people for the 'right' posts,
and they were quite successful.
I often feel inadequate because I cannot recognize all talented individuals.
This is the chancellor's duty;
although my close attendants often speak,
I dare not lightly trust them."
He also said,
"Recently, there have been many vacancies for prefects and county magistrates.
Capable and efficient individuals should be chosen and appointed,
and it matters little if their rank is not yet high enough."
He further said,
"Only Shí Jū was most discerning of people."
When Tángkuò Dǐng was Military Commissioner of the Dìngwǔ Army,
the Emperor said to Dǐng,
"I haven't seen Shí Jū for a long time.
How is his vigor compared to before?
When you arrive at your post, go visit him."
Xiǎnzōng also thought of him,
and on Jū's birthday,
sent him a poem to express his feelings.
In the twenty-second year,
he died of illness at home,
aged seventy-two.
His posthumous name was Wénxiàn.
In the first year of Tàihé,
his portrait was placed in Yǎnqìng Gōng,
and he was granted the honor of sacrifice at Shìzōng's ancestral temple.
Tángkuò Ānlǐ,
original name Wòlǔgǔ,
courtesy name Zǐjìng.
He was fond of learning,
well-versed in classics and history,
skilled in literary composition,
and understood the broad principles of governance.
During the Zhēnyuán period,
he successively held the post of Military Commissioner of the Línhǎi Army,
then entered the court as Hànlín Shìdú Xuéshì,
and was later transferred to be Defense Commissioner of Jùnzhōu and Military Commissioner of the Zhānghuà Army.
In the early Dàdìng period,
he was promoted to Yìdū Yǐn,
then recalled to be Dàxīng Yǐn.
The Emperor said,
"There are many false rumors in the capital.
Corrupt officials in the metropolitan prefecture are a plague to the people.
Although you are young,
you have governing talent.
Remove these long-standing abuses;
do not perpetuate them."
He was assessed as first-class in the integrity examination
and advanced in rank to Rónglù Dàfū.
In the fifth month of the seventh year,
the prisons of Dàxīng Fǔ were empty.
An imperial edict bestowed a feast to reward the officials.
For all prefectures and commanderies where prisons were empty,
money was granted for the feast expenses.
Dàxīng Fǔ received three hundred strings of cash for its feast,
with others receiving different amounts.
After a long time,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
then dismissed to be the Jiédùshǐ of Hēnghǎi Jūn.
He successively served as Hélián Yǐn and Nánjīng Liúshǒu.
He left office due to mourning,
and was later reinstated as Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
An imperial edict stated:
“Among the Nánlù Nǚzhí households, there are many poor ones.
Hàn households who rent and cultivate land
gain little,
and their expenses are not met.
They are not skilled in riding and archery,
and are not fit for military service.
All able-bodied men shall be enrolled in the military register,
and be given money and rice monthly,
to be settled along the border of Shāndōng Lù.
Discuss this and report it.”
After ten days,
the Emperor asked:
“How do the prime ministers suggest dealing with the poor Mèng'ān households in Shāndōng?”
He replied:
“Not yet.”
Then he asked Ānlǐ:
“What is your opinion?”
He replied:
“The Mèng'ān people and the Hàn households
are now all one family.
Some plow, some sow;
all are people of the state.
If they are drafted into the army immediately,
I fear it will hinder farm work.”
The Emperor rebuked Ānlǐ, saying:
“I thought you had knowledge.
You always imitate the Hàn people in everything. If there is no conflict, they may engage in farming;
judging by the Sòng people's intentions, this will lead to conflict.
If the state is in trouble,
how can there be time for farming?
You are skilled in Hàn characters,
and read the Shī and Shū.
Put these aside for now and discuss the laws of this dynasty.
Previously, all prime ministers were appointed Nǚzhí;
you alone are Hàn.
Is this right or wrong?
The 'one family' you speak of refers to all of one kind.
Nǚzhí and Hàn people
are in fact two.
When I ascended the throne in Dōngjīng,
the Qìdān and Hàn people did not come;
only the Nǚzhí people came with me.
Can this be called one kind?”
He further said:
“Day and night I ponder
how to prevent the achievements of Emperor Tàizǔ from falling,
to pass them down for ten thousand generations,
and to ensure the Nǚzhí people's resources are not depleted.
All of you should understand this.”
Thereupon, regarding several matters beneficial to the poor Mèng'ān,
an imperial edict instructed Zuǒsī Lángzhōng Niángē Wòtèlā to write them down,
and all officials gathered to discuss them in the Shàngshū Shěng.
In the seventeenth year,
an imperial edict dispatched Jiānchá Yùshǐ Wányán Dígǔsù to patrol the border,
accompanied by four Qìdān Yālā.
Ruólā, Zhāodé, Yǎlǔ, and Wòliè'ā
fled from the border and returned to Dàshí.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor
issued an edict, saying:
“Dàshí is to the northwest of Xià Guó.
When Wōwò caused unrest,
the Qìdān and others responded.
I pardoned their crimes,
allowed them to resume their former occupations,
and sent envoys to pacify them.
Yet their rebellious hearts have not ceased.
If Dàshí sends agents to entice them,
it will surely cause border troubles.
Send envoys to resettle them,
allowing them to live mixed with the Nǚzhí people,
with men marrying and women being betrothed,
gradually changing their customs.
This is a long-term strategy.”
Thereupon, he dispatched Tóng Qiān Shūmì Yuànshì Gēshíliè Àoyě, Lìbù Lángzhōng Péimǎn Yúqìng, and Hànlín Xiūzhuàn Yílà Jié,
to resettle Qìdān people from the northwest road who had participated in Wōwò's rebellion, placing them in Shàngjīng, Jì, Lì, and other circuits.
He appointed Bīngbù Lángzhōng Yílà Zǐyuán as the Zhāotǎo Dūjiān of the northwest road,
and issued an edict to Zǐyuán, saying:
“You should explain to the Qìdān people being resettled in Shàngjīng and Jìzhōu,
that the land there is fertile and rich,
suitable for procreation.
Marrying among the Nǚzhí people
is also a plan for your long-term peace.
You and Àoyě shall jointly urge their departure and relocation.
Furthermore, dispatch one Mèng'ān officer with troops to escort them eastward.
Do not allow them to pass near the imperial herds along the route.
Should there be any rebellion,
immediately suppress it.
Once they cross the pass,
you shall return to your post.”
After the Emperor had dispatched Àoyě, Zǐyuán, and others,
he said to the prime ministers:
“During Hǎilíng's time,
the Qìdān people were especially trusted,
but ultimately rebelled.
Qúnmùshǐ Hèshòu, Fùmǎ Dūwèi Sài Yī, Zhāowǔ Dàjiāngjūn Shùlǔgǔ, and Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn Púdōu were all killed.
Sài Yī and others were descendants of meritorious officials;
while in office, they never had grievances with the Qìdān.
Their wild ambitions
are also evident.”
Ānlǐ replied:
“The sagely ruler broadly loves all under Heaven,
nurturing all nations.
There should be no distinctions.”
The Emperor said:
“I do not make distinctions;
rather, I reward the good and punish the evil,
this is how to govern.
Should there be border conflicts at another time,
would the Qìdān truly be of one heart with us?”
Another day,
the Emperor again said:
“Recommendation
is the duty of high ministers.
Even external officials of the fifth rank can recommend people;
why do prime ministers not recommend anyone?”
Ānlǐ replied:
“Confucius said talent is hard to find.
Wise and noble individuals
are not numerous in the world.
If Your Majesty truly desires to obtain talented people,
you should broaden the paths for selecting scholars,
and distinguish and utilize their abilities.
Only then will you gain talented people.”
The Emperor said:
“The regulations for appointments and dismissals are illogical.
Those who serve are all descendants of prominent families,
whom I know.
There are specified dates for their entry into service based on their qualifications.
The imperial guards are not recruited based on family background;
those without official hereditary privilege cannot gain official positions unless they reach Wǔyì.
However, Nǚzhí people have accelerated promotion qualifications,
so their appointments often precede those who serve.
The world is one family;
why do only Nǚzhí have accelerated promotion rules?”
Ānlǐ replied:
“This rule was established by the ancestors,
and it may be difficult to change it arbitrarily.”
He was promoted to Zuǒchéng,
appointed on the same day as Yòuchéng Púchá Tōng.
The Emperor said to them:
“I am now fifty-five years old.
If I pass sixty,
I will surely grow weary of state affairs.
While I am still hale and strong,
all Nǚzhí Mèng'ān Mòkè should review and implement governance,
and revise laws and decrees.
Few within the imperial clan live as long as I have;
I am quite familiar with the old customs of the Nǚzhí,
but how can my descendants know them,
let alone state affairs?
All of you should understand this intention.”
The Emperor further said:
“Many cases in the Dàlǐ Sì are delayed;
why do the prime ministers not supervise them?”
Ānlǐ replied:
“It is an old rule to set deadlines for difficult and doubtful documents.”
The Emperor said:
“Is the old rule right or wrong?
Are we not investigating the matters now,
and just setting deadlines arbitrarily?”
Cānzhèng Yílà Dào said:
“When I was in Dàlǐ Sì,
there were never any delayed cases.”
The Emperor said:
“You had no delayed cases in Dàlǐ Sì;
as a prime minister, why can you not inspect and manage them?”
Dào had nothing to say and withdrew.
The Emperor asked the prime ministers:
“Do the officials of the Yùshǐ Tái
also associate with relatives and friends?”
They all replied:
“They associate very little.”
The Emperor said:
“Tái officials must completely cut off personal connections.
Jiànguān and Jìzhùguān, who are privy to discussions,
also should not associate with others.”
Ānlǐ replied:
“Among relatives and friends,
it may be impossible to cut off all connections.”
The Emperor said:
“Given their official responsibilities,
why should they care about others' opinions?”
He was promoted and appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
enfeoffed as Ruìguó Gōng,
and granted a hereditary Móukè.
The Emperor instructed Ānlǐ,
"The historical records of previous dynasties are detailed and complete,
but the Veritable Records of Our ancestors are too brief."
He replied,
"The histories of previous dynasties are all compiled books,
with Imperial Annals and Biographies.
When history is compiled in the future,
there will also be Imperial Annals and Biographies,
and the details will naturally be seen in the biographies."
Ānlǐ once discussed the examination system,
saying to the Emperor,
"Your servant observes that recently scholars do not pay attention to policy essays.
If now, in the examinations for poetry, rhapsodies, and policy essays,
those who excel in both literary style and reasoning are chosen,
and their capacity and insight are judged by current affairs policy essays,
then worthy individuals may be obtained."
The Emperor said,
"You and the others discuss it."
The Emperor said to his chancellors,
"Rewarding meritorious service must not be delayed,
for delayed rewards offer no encouragement for good deeds."
Ānlǐ replied,
"What the ancients called 'rewards not exceeding the season'
refers precisely to this."
In the 21st year,
he was appointed Yòuchéngxiàng,
and further enfeoffed as Shēnguó Gōng.
He firmly declined, saying,
"Your servant occupies the position of chancellor,
but is of no benefit to the state.
Day and night I worry and fear,
only afraid of incurring offense,
failing Your Majesty above,
and the common people below.
Your servant truly dares not accept the chancellorship;
may Your Majesty choose someone more virtuous than your servant to employ."
The Emperor said,
"We know that you are upright,
no different from Zuǒchéngxiàng Xíxiǎn.
Furthermore, in practicing governance,
no one surpasses you.
Do not decline further."
Ānlǐ bowed his head and thanked him.
That year,
he passed away.
In the first year of Tàihé,
he was enshrined and offered sacrifices in Shìzōng's ancestral temple.
Yílà Dào,
whose original name was Zhào Sān,
was originally from the Yǐshì Tribe.
He first moved to Xiánpíng.
He was generous and tolerant,
had great ambition,
and was renowned for filial piety.
He was fluent in Nǚzhēn, Qìdān, and Chinese characters.
In the early Huángtǒng period,
he was appointed Clerk of the Board of Punishments,
then transferred to Clerk of the Department of State Affairs,
and again promoted to Assistant Judge of the Grand Court of Justice.
He observed mourning for his mother,
was recalled to office,
and promoted to Assistant Director of the Board of Revenue.
In the third year of Zhènglóng,
he was moved to the three *máng'ān* of Línhuáng, Xiánpíng Road, and Bìshāhé,
to garrison Wòlúsù.
When he returned and reported,
Hǎilíng said to his attendants,
"Dào has an extraordinary physiognomy;
one day he will certainly rise to the rank of grand councilor."
The next year,
he was promoted to Director of this board.
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
he served as Chief Clerk of the Military Governor's Office.
When Hǎilíng died,
the army returned without
any discipline.
The soldiers plundered Huáinán,
causing suffering to the common people.
Over two hundred men and women
voluntarily offered themselves as Dào's slaves.
Dào accepted them,
and when they reached the Huái River,
he waited for all the armies to cross.
Then he sent them all back.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was reappointed Director of the Board of Revenue
and, with Liáng Qiú, pacified Shāndōng,
recruiting and reassuring bandits.
If people had fled from bandits or corvée,
they were all ordered to return to their occupations,
and regardless of the severity of their crimes, all were pardoned.
Soldiers were not permitted to take advantage of this to plunder.
When Púshàn Zhōngyì attacked Wōwò,
Dào served as a staff advisor in the marshal's headquarters.
When the rebels were pacified,
the Marshal's Office distributed captured people as slaves to officials.
Dào released them all.
Upon returning to the capital,
he had an audience.
After he withdrew,
Shìzōng watched him go
and said,
"This man has administrative talent
and can be put to great use."
He was promoted to Academian of the Hanlin Academy,
concurrently serving as Compiler of the Diaries of Activity and Repose.
After a short while,
Shìzōng said,
"Dào is incorruptible and capable;
the refined position of the Hanlin Academy
is insufficient to fully utilize his talent."
As the transport in Zhōngdū was busy and complex,
he was then reassigned as Joint Administrator of Transport for Zhōngdū Road.
An imperial edict ordered Dào to convey imperial decrees for the promotion and demotion of officials based on their good or bad conduct, to Hébĕi, Shāndōng, and other roads for inspection.
The Emperor said,
"When you participated in the campaign against the Qìdān,
you did not covet plunder;
your ambition is commendable.
Therefore, We appoint you as envoy.
May you exert yourself."
That year,
among those promoted for integrity were
Cízhōu Inspector Wányán Púsùliè, who became Vice Defender-in-chief of Běijīng;
Wéizhōu Inspector Púchá Púchá, who became Defense Commissioner of Bózhōu;
and Wēizhōu Inspector Wányán Wùdábo, who became Inspector of Cízhōu.
Among those demoted due to poor administration were
Dēngzhōu Inspector Dà Pán, who became Inspector of Sōngzhōu;
Joint Administrator of Nánjīng Garrison Gāo Déjī, who became Joint Administrator of Běijīng Transport;
Wèizhōu Defense Commissioner Wányán Ālín, who became Defense Commissioner of Chénzhōu;
Zhēndìng Magistrate Túdān Bágǎi, who became Military Commissioner of Xīngpíng Commandery;
and Ānguó Military Commissioner Tángkuò Chóngguó, who became Military Commissioner of Zhānghuà Commandery.
He was also to proclaim their merits, faults, good deeds, and misdeeds,
and not accept gifts.
He was promoted to Grand Judge.
In the fifth year,
the Sòng people requested peace,
and the troops were withdrawn.
Dào went to Shāndōng
to inspect military equipment
and provide relief to the wives and children of the garrison soldiers.
He was again appointed Joint Administrator of Dàxīng Commandery.
Wányán Āsībō, a centurion of the Imperial Guard, entered the palace with a saber on a day he was not on duty,
and that night he entered the Left Treasury,
killed Treasury Supervisor Guō Liángchén,
and stole gold and pearls.
The Inspectorate seized eight suspects,
flogged three to death,
and the other five falsely confessed,
but the stolen goods could not be recovered.
The Emperor suspected foul play
and ordered Dào to investigate.
Dào prolonged the case,
and later Āsībō's sale of the gold was discovered,
and he was executed.
The Emperor said,
"Under torture,
what cannot be extracted?
Why did the Inspectorate not seek the truth with compassion?"
Money was bestowed upon the families of those flogged to death,
two hundred strings of cash each to provide for them,
and fifty strings of cash each to those who did not die.
An imperial edict stated that from now on, centurions and fifty-man captains of the Imperial Guard
were not permitted to enter the palace with a saber unless on duty.
He was promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū.
The Emperor said:
"When I first ascended the throne,
you were an Assistant Director in the Hùbù,
and I heard you were assiduous in doing good.
I promoted you to Lángzhōng,
and you indeed proved worthy of praise.
When you served as the Deputy Jīngyǐn,
you were also able to govern well.
The Hùbù manages the national finances,
so you must exert yourself."
Dào kowtowed and thanked him.
He was appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
and bestowed a golden belt.
According to custom,
when a Zhāotǎoshǐ arrived at his post,
all the tribes would present camels and horses,
sometimes several hundred.
Dào declined all of them,
and within a few months, all resumed performing their duties.
He left office due to his father's death,
and was recalled to serve as Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Originally,
when there were lawsuits among the tribes,
the Zhāotǎosī would customarily send clerks to investigate and interrogate,
who often engaged in corrupt practices for personal gain.
Dào requested the special establishment of an official post.
The Emperor praised and accepted it,
and the establishment of the Kānshìguān in the Zhāotǎosī began from this point.
The Emperor said to the Grand Councilors:
"I recently heard that the Dàlǐsì, when judging cases,
always takes ten days to a month.
Why is this?"
Dào reported:
"According to the law,
the sentencing of a death row prisoner should not exceed seven days,
penal servitude five days,
and caning three days."
The Emperor said:
"The law has prescribed limits,
but they are always violated.
This is the responsibility of the officials.
Strictly warn and constrain them to eliminate this malpractice."
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
He requested retirement.
The Emperor said:
"You are filial at home,
loyal to me,
and proficient in laws, decrees, and state affairs.
Although you are over sixty,
your mental and physical strength has not yet diminished,
so you may not retire yet."
He was then appointed Nánjīng Liúshǒu,
and bestowed a rhinoceros horn belt.
The Emperor said:
"Wūgǔlùn Sīliè, the Hénán Tǒngjūn, is a bit simple-minded.
All border affairs must be discussed with you.
You should explain my intentions to Sīliè."
He entered court and was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
Dào's younger brother, Yòuābǔ, the Magistrate of Líntóng, committed a capital crime.
Dào awaited punishment at home.
On the Crown Prince's birthday,
a banquet was held at Qìnghé Hall.
The Emperor asked why Dào was not present.
The Cānzhī Zhèngshì, Zhāngē Wòtèlá, reported:
"His younger brother committed a capital crime,
and according to regulations, it is inappropriate for him to enter the palace."
The Emperor said:
"What harm is there in that?"
He immediately issued an edict for Dào to resume his duties.
At this time,
many county magistrate posts were vacant.
The Emperor asked the Grand Councilors about this.
Dào reported:
"Supernumerary officials of Xuānwǔ rank and above could be temporarily appointed to fill them."
The Emperor said:
"Those former officials who served in oversight positions of the 8th rank and below,
Assistant Recorders and Administrators with a reputation for being clean and capable,
and County Lieutenants who achieved an excellent grade,
should all be granted county magistracies.
Supernumerary officials up to the 5th rank,
who have no reputation for corruption or dereliction of duty,
may also be granted these posts.
Once there is no longer a shortage of county magistrates,
then revert to the old regulations."
In the 23rd year,
he was dismissed (from his central post) and appointed Xiánpíng Yǐn,
and enfeoffed as Shēnguógōng.
The Emperor said:
"Several years ago, you once requested retirement,
but I did not permit it.
You are old now.
Xiánpíng is your hometown.
It is a cool place with few affairs,
suitable for an old man."
He was bestowed a rhinoceros horn belt.
The next day,
he again sent his close attendant, Cáo Yuān, to convey an imperial decree, saying:
"Since the Wōwò rebellion, Xiánpíng
its people's livelihoods have not yet returned to normal.
I am allowing you to return to your hometown
in order to pacify and settle the entire region."
In the 24th year,
he passed away.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he mourned and regretted for a long time.
That year, he visited Shàngjīng.
When passing by Xiánpíng,
he sent an envoy to offer sacrifices,
and the funeral gifts were exceptionally generous.
He decreed that Dào's portrait be stored in the imperial archives,
and promoted his son Bāgǒu to Gémén Zhīhòu.
Guāngzǔ, courtesy name Zhònglǐ,
his childhood name was Bāgǒu.
By hereditary privilege, he was appointed Gémén Zhīhòu,
then transferred to Píngjìn Lìng, Chief River Inspector of Wèizhōu, and Nèi Chéngfèng Yābān.
He was successively promoted to Dōngshàng Géménshǐ,
concurrently serving as Diǎnkèshǔ Lìng.
During the Dà'ān era,
he was appointed Shàofǔ Shàojiān.
He went into mourning for his mother,
and was recalled to serve as Yíluánjú Shǐ,
concurrently managing the affairs of the Xuānhuīyuàn Shǐ,
Mìshūjiān, and Yòu Xuānhuīshǐ.
In the 11th month of the 2nd year of Xīngdìng,
an edict was issued to gather all officials to deliberate on how to achieve long-term benefits.
Guāngzǔ and two others proposed:
"Recruit local people and grant them regional powers and responsibilities,
so that people are self-motivated,
and each can protect their own region."
From this, discussions about establishing ducal feudal systems arose.
The full discussion is in the
"Jiǔgōng"
biography.
In the 3rd year,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ.
In the 5th year,
he died.
An appreciation says: Liángbì, Shǒudào, Jū, Ānlǐ, and Dào,
were all unknown during the Zhènglóng era,
but when they participated in governing the court,
assisted enlightened sovereigns,
their advice was followed, and their words were heeded.
Their beneficence descended upon the people.
Was it not because they met their opportune time?
Official positions were complete,
superiors and subordinates were at peace with each other.
The ruler enjoyed a good reputation,
and ministers enjoyed their emoluments to the end.
It can be called truly flourishing.
Hǎilíng was able to recognize that Yílà Dào possessed the talent for grand statesmanship,
but was unable to employ him.
Therefore, his administrative achievements only became manifest during the Dàdìng era.
The prominence or obscurity of talented individuals
depends on the decline or prosperity of the prevailing conditions.
This has always been so.
During the Jīn dynasty, at private imperial banquets,
only imperial princes, princesses, and imperial sons-in-law were allowed to participate.
One day, Shìzōng specially summoned Jū to enter.
The princes and others below them whispered to each other,
probably despising him in their hearts.
Shìzōng became aware of this,
and immediately spoke to them, saying:
"The fact that my father, son, family, and relatives can live peacefully and without incident,
and enjoy today's happiness,
is due to this man's efforts."
He then enumerated several tens of recent events,
prominent and known to all at the time, to enlighten them.
All bowed down and apologized.
With such mutual understanding between ruler and minister,
who would not exhaust their loyalty?
At the end of the Dàdìng era,
Shìzōng was about to make his principal consort empress.
He asked Jū about this.
Jū dismissed the attendants and said:
"The establishment of the principal consort (as empress)
originally has no differing opinion.
But what about the Crown Prince?"
Shìzōng was startled and said:
"What do you mean?"
Jū said:
"The principal consort has her own sons.
If the principal consort is established (as empress),
the Crown Prince will be endangered."
Shìzōng realized and stopped (the plan).
Moreover, a ruler's family affairs
are what ministers find difficult to speak about.
Xǔ Jìngzōng, with a single word, almost destroyed the Táng dynasty's rule.
Jū's reply,
his planning for the Jīn dynasty reached the ultimate degree.
Collator's Notes
Biographies No. 27: Sū Bǎohéng, Zhái Yǒnggù, Wèi Zǐpíng, Mèng Hào (with Tián Jué appended), Liáng Sù, Yílà Zào, Yílà Zǐjìng.
Sū Bǎohéng, courtesy name Zōngyǐn,
was a native of Tiānchéng, Yúnzhōng.
His father, Jīng,
was a Liaó jìnshì,
and served as the Liúshǒu of Xījīng.
When Zōnghàn's army reached Xījīng,
Jīng surrendered.
After a long time,
Jīng fell gravely ill,
and entrusted Bǎohéng to Zōnghàn.
After Jīng's death,
Zōnghàn recommended him to the court.
He was granted the qualification of jìnshì出身,
appointed as the Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and transferred to be the Jūnshì Pànguān of Jiězhōu.
The Zuǒ Jiānjūn, Sālīhē, was stationed in Shǎnxī,
and invited Bǎohéng to his staff,
to deliberate on military affairs.
He was successively promoted to Tóngzhī Xīngzhōng Yǐn.
During the Tiāndé era,
when Zhōngdū was being repaired,
Zhāng Hào recommended Bǎohéng to oversee the construction work.
He was then appointed Dàxīng Shàoyǐn,
overseeing the construction work of various mausoleums.
He was again promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū.
When Hǎilíng mobilized troops to attack Sòng,
he, along with Xú Wén and others, built ships in Tōngzhōu.
Hǎilíng hunted in the nearby suburbs,
and thus went to Tōngzhōu to inspect the work.
When the war broke out,
Bǎohéng was appointed as the Shuǐjūn Dūtǒngzhì of Zhèdōng Dào,
and led a fleet by sea,
heading directly for Lín'ān.
When Sòng troops came to attack,
they were defeated at sea,
and the Fùtǒngzhì, Zhèng Jiā, died in the battle.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was summoned to Zhōngdū.
At this time,
bandits in Shāndōng gathered,
and Khitans attacked and plundered Línhuáng and other prefectures,
causing distress to the common people.
An imperial edict ordered Bǎohéng to pacify Shāndōng,
and the former Tàizǐ Shàobǎo, Gāo Sīlián, to pacify Línhuáng.
Granary grain was distributed to relieve them,
those without clothes were given silk and fabric,
if official grain was deficient,
it was purchased and supplied,
and the names of those without wives were submitted.
Upon his return, he was appointed Xíngbù Shàngshū.
He, along with Gōngbù Shàngshū Zōngyǒng and Bīngbù Shìláng Wányán Yúlíyě,
went to Hénán, Shāndōng, and Shǎnxī to inquire about military colonists.
Those who had defeated great enemies or made achievements in sieges and field battles,
were to have their names submitted.
Or those who, with few, defeated many,
or who, equally matched with the enemy, were able to be the first to climb and defeat the enemy,
the Zhèngjūn and Huànjiǎ Ālǐxǐ were to be promoted one rank.
Méng'ān Móukè were to submit their records of merit to the Shàngshūshěng.
Those who had followed Hǎilíng's army to the Huái River and defeated the enemy were also to be granted promotions and rewards.
When Púsàn Zhōngyì attacked Sòng,
Bǎohéng managed the Hùbù in Guānzhōng,
and also served as an inspector,
being allowed discretion.
He dismissed over ten unlawful local officials.
The Bīn Prefect Fù Shènwēi offended powerful figures,
and was slandered, imprisoned, and near death.
Bǎohéng strongly interceded for him, and he was spared.
Bǎohéng was appointed Tàicháng Qīng,
and then promoted to Lǐbù Shàngshū.
In the third year,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
The Sòng people requested peace,
and an imperial edict ordered Bǎohéng to Nánjīng,
to discuss and implement the matters with Púsàn Zhōngyì.
He carried it out.
Upon his return to court,
he was promoted to Yòuchéng.
In the fourth year,
the Sòng people requested peace,
and the army returned.
Bǎohéng attended court in the capital.
Initially,
the palace maid Chènxīn set fire to sixteen locations,
which spread and burned various halls.
The Emperor, considering that troops were being used and national resources were insufficient,
did not rebuild them.
After the Sòng peace,
an imperial edict ordered Bǎohéng to supervise the construction work,
and sent the Shàofǔ Jiān, Zhāng Zhòngyù, to retrieve the blueprints of the Nánjīng palace buildings.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he said to Bǎohéng:
"Recall Zhòngyù.
The common people will say that I am imitating Zhènglóng's extravagance and ostentation."
In the winter of the sixth year,
he fell ill,
and requested to retire,
but it was not permitted.
Jìng Sìhuī was sent to convey the imperial edict, saying:
"You were promoted to a high administrative position due to your loyalty and uprightness.
Your hair and teeth have not yet deteriorated,
yet you suddenly seek to retire due to a minor illness.
Take good care of your health,
and await your recovery to resume your duties."
Not long after,
he passed away,
at the age of fifty-five.
Shìzōng was about to go hawk hunting in the nearby suburbs,
but upon hearing the news, he returned.
He suspended court sessions for him,
provided funeral expenses and gifts,
and ordered the relevant officials to offer sacrifices.
Zhái Yǒnggù, courtesy name Zhòngjiān,
was a native of Liángxiāng, Zhōngdū.
Tàizǔ and Sòng agreed to attack Liaó,
and upon success, Yān was to be returned to Sòng.
The Sòng people selected scholars based on classics and policy essays.
Yǒnggù ranked first,
and was appointed Yícáo Cānjūn of Kāidé Fǔ.
When Jīn conquered Sòng,
Yǒnggù returned north.
He passed the Cífù examination in the sixth year of Tiānhuì,
and was appointed Huái'ān Chéng,
then promoted to Wàngyún Lìng,
and then appointed Shūmìyuàn Lìshǐ.
He was invited to serve as a Yuàn in the mansion of the Zuǒ Fùyuánshuài, Zōnghàn.
Yǒnggù's family was poor,
and he sought an external appointment.
Zōnghàn admired his ability,
and did not permit it,
instead giving him three thousand strings of cash to assist him,
and recommended him to the court.
He temporarily served as Zuǒsī Lángzhōng.
He was appointed Dìngwǔjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ,
successively served as Tóngzhī Qīngzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and then entered the court as Gōngbù Yuánwàiláng.
He resigned due to mourning for his mother,
but was reinstated as Lǐbù Lángzhōng,
and then promoted to Hànlín Zhíxuěshì.
When Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
the Sòng envoy for the New Year's congratulations arrived in Guǎngníng.
Hǎilíng sent an envoy to inform the Sòng envoy about the abdication and enthronement,
and then sent him back.
He appointed Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ Wányán Sīgōng as the envoy to report and inform the Sòng,
with Yǒnggù as his deputy,
and also ordered Yǒnggù to observe the Sòng people's movements.
Upon the envoy's return,
he was appointed Lǐbù Shìláng.
After a long time,
he was assigned to oversee the construction work of the Yānjīng palaces.
Yǒnggù requested to paint the "Wúyì Tú" on the hall walls,
but it was not accepted.
Soon after, he was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng,
and examined the jìnshì candidates of the second year of Zhēnyuán.
He set the examination topic as "Zūn Zǔ Pèi Tiān Fù".
Hǎilíng thought that he was trying to guess his intentions,
and summoned Yǒnggù, asking:
"The examination topic does not suit my intentions.
When my ancestors were in power, did they bow when sacrificing to Heaven?"
He replied:
"They bowed."
Hǎilíng said:
"How can one bow to them when they are alive,
but then, after death, have them share the same status and offerings as Heaven?"
He replied:
"It has been done in ancient times,
recorded in the rites and ceremonies."
Hǎilíng said:
"If Jié and Zhòu had done it,
do you also want me to do it?"
Thereupon, Yǒnggù and Zhāng Jǐngrén were each flogged twenty times.
And the jìnshì, Zhāng Rǔlín, in the eighth rhyme of his fu, wrote:
"Currently,
the suburban sacrifice is about to be performed."
Hǎilíng questioned him, saying:
"How do you know I am performing the suburban sacrifice?"
He was also flogged thirty times.
Shortly after,
Yǒnggù was promoted to Lǐbù Shàngshū,
and was granted a gold belt with a "hútoú qiúwén" pattern.
He was then appointed Yǒngdìngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the 29th year,
Zhāngzōng issued an edict to the Shàngshū Shěng, saying:
"Former Língbù Shìláng Tián Jué and others were all upright gentlemen,
but petty individuals framed them with charges of factionalism,
and they consequently incurred guilt.
Shìzōng employed Mèng Hào as Yòuchéng,
and all those who were alive at the time have already been reinstated;
however, those who have passed away have not yet been posthumously restored.
Discuss this and let it be known."
Zhāng Rǔlín memorialized, saying:
"Jué wielded power arbitrarily and formed factions,
and the previous court had already justly determined their crimes,
which everyone acknowledged as appropriate.
Now, to posthumously grant official titles and ranks
might not serve as a deterrent or encouragement."
Rǔlín was a high official in the previous court,
and had participated in the appointment of a regent.
When the emperor first ascended the throne,
he was unwilling to readily oppose Rǔlín's wishes,
so he said to him:
"Since you believe it is not permissible,
let us temporarily set it aside."
This was probably because Zhāng Hào was good friends with Cài Sōngnián,
which is why Rǔlín still sought to denounce him.
After Rǔlín's death,
Zhāngzōng again issued an edict to the Shàngshū Shěng, saying:
"Indeed, since the affair of Tián Jué's faction,
officials have taken it as a warning,
focusing only on expediency,
which has become ingrained as a custom.
The late emperor knew that Jué and others were innocent,
and appointed and employed those who were still alive,
some of whom were promoted to Zǎizhí;
others became Jiédù, Fángyù, or Cìshǐ.
However, those who died have not yet been posthumously restored,
and their descendants are still among the common populace. I deeply pity them.
It is right to commend the worthy and manifest goodness,
regardless of whether they are alive or deceased.
It is appropriate to extend the late emperor's intention to praise and record the loyal and upright,
and grant both grace and compassion
to encourage virtuous customs.
Regarding Tián Jué and his associates, apart from those already reinstated,
those who died without having been appointed
shall all have their former official titles and ranks restored.
For their descendants who held official positions at the time
but were dismissed because their fathers or grandfathers were implicated in the faction,
their positions shall also be posthumously restored.
For descendants of those who should have their titles and ranks posthumously restored but did not qualify for hereditary privilege,
they shall all also be granted appropriate special favors."
Liáng Sù, courtesy name Mèngróng,
was a native of Fèngshèng Zhōu.
From a young age, he was diligent in his studies,
often reading until dawn on summer nights,
and his mother, Gě shì, would often extinguish the candle to stop him.
In Tiānjuàn the 2nd year,
he was selected as a Jìnshì,
and appointed as Píngyáo Xiàn Zhǔbù, then promoted to Wàngdū and Jiàng Xiànlìng.
Due to his integrity,
he was appointed as Shàngshū Shěng Lìshǐ.
He was appointed as Dìnghǎi Jūnjiédù Fùshǐ,
then transferred to Zhōngdū Jǐngxúnshǐ,
and promoted to Shāndōng Xīlù Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ.
When constructing the Biàn Gōng,
Sù was responsible for supervising the labor.
He briefly served as Dàmíng Shàoyǐn.
At the end of Zhènglóng,
bandits arose in the region,
seizing several thousand common people who were unable to defend themselves and implicating them as rebels.
All were imprisoned in Dàmíng.
Upon arriving at his post, Sù
investigated and ascertained the facts of the cases,
and eighteen or nineteen out of every twenty were released.
In Dàdìng the 2nd year,
Zhào Zhí of Wǎnpíng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Recently,
during the Zhènglóng reign, eunuchs were employed.
Shǎofǔ Shàojiān兼Shànglínshǔlìng Hú Shǒuzhōng, taking advantage of his cunning and good fortune,
sought to seize benefits from the people.
Former Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Wányán Shǒudào and former Zhōngdū Jǐngxúnshǐ Liáng Sù
are diligent, cautious, and incorruptible.
I wish for them to be promoted."
Thereupon, Shǒuzhōng was stripped of his Shàojiān title,
Shǒudào was summoned from Bīnzhōu Cìshǐ to be Jiànyì Dàfū,
and Sù, then Zhōngdū Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ, was transferred to Dàxīng Shàoyǐn.
Sù submitted a memorial, stating:
"Currently, expenditures are insufficient,
and not merely due to the costly border troops.
The Lìbù, through regular appointments, assigns old and senior officials to be staff members of the Cáosī,
who are mostly unfit for the job.
I propose that all those with military merits, Jìnshì and other academic degrees, and hereditary privilege,
who understand the advantages and disadvantages of finance and grain, and can make the nation's resources abundant without harming the people,
be permitted to submit memorials to express themselves.
From these, those who are suitable should be selected
and entrusted with official duties.
Every five years, the Lìbù should be commissioned to comprehensively audit for floods, droughts, and garrisons,
and their promotions or demotions should be based on increases or decreases in resources.
Since Emperor Wǔ of Hàn used Sāng Hóngyáng to first establish the monopoly on salt and iron,
two or three tenths of the people's annual grain and wheat have been consumed by wine.
It is advisable to prohibit the sale of wine yeast throughout the empire.
From the capital to the prefectures and commanderies' official establishments,
the sale and transport out of the city should remain forbidden.
As for counties, towns, and villages,
sales should be temporarily suspended."
The proposal was not adopted.
In the 3rd year,
he was demoted for failing to eradicate locusts on schedule
to Chuānzhōu Cìshǐ,
had one official rank removed,
and was dismissed from office.
The emperor, in the Biàndiàn,
summoned Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū Xī Xū, Hànlín Dàizhì Liú Zhònghuǐ,
and Mìshū Shàojiān Yílā Zǐjìng,
to inquire about historical and contemporary affairs.
After a while,
Xū calmly requested:
"Liáng Sù's talent is regrettable;
his dismissal is too harsh."
The emperor said:
"Your words are correct."
Thereupon, he was appointed Héběi Dōnglù Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ.
At this time,
it was after the Wōwò Rebellion.
As military provisions were insufficient,
Sù was ordered to arrange for military provisions along the border.
He issued dispatches to the salt fields of Zhàozhōu, Běijīng, and Guǎngníng,
allowing the people to exchange rice for salt,
which benefited both the military and the populace.
In the 4th year,
he comprehensively audited the household registrations and material wealth of the Dōngpíng and Dàmíng circuits,
and his assessment was praised as fair and balanced.
Other envoys, wherever they went, considered increasing and augmenting [records] as their achievement,
causing the common people to complain of hardship.
The court then ordered all circuits to use the Dōngpíng and Dàmíng comprehensive audit as a standard,
and thus a standard was finally established.
In the 7th year,
he left office due to his father's mourning.
He was reinstated as Dūshuǐ Jiān.
The river burst its banks at Lǐgù,
and Sù was ordered to inspect it.
He returned and reported:
"Six-tenths of the river water flowed into the breach,
and four-tenths remained in the old course.
If we now dam the breach
and restore it to its old course entirely,
and it breaches again to the south, then Nánjīng will be in trouble;
if it breaches again to the north, then Shāndōng and Héběi will both be in trouble.
It is better to build a dike south of Lǐgù,
allowing the two rivers to flow separately,
to reduce the force of the water."
The emperor adopted his suggestion.
He was transferred to Dàlǐ Qīng.
The Shàngniǎnjú's supervisor, Shímò Ālǐgē,
and the nail-maker Chén Wài'ér,
jointly stole silver nails and leaves used for making chariots from the palace.
Sù held that Ālǐgē, as the supervisor,
should be the primary culprit.
Other court officials argued that Chén Wài'ér was the primary culprit,
deserving death.
The emperor said:
"When guilt is in doubt, lean towards leniency.
Both shall be spared death,
exiled for five years,
and stripped of their names."
At that time,
Dōngjīng had long been poorly governed.
The emperor personally selected Sù to serve as Tóngzhī Dōngjīng Liúshǒushì.
He was promoted to Zhōngdū Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ,
then transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
He submitted a memorial discussing the Táijiàn,
the main point of which was:
"Officials of the Tái, from Dàfū to Jiānchá,
and officials of the Jiàn, from Dàfū to Shíyí,
Your Majesty should personally select them,
and not entrust them to the Zǎixiàng,
lest private favors be established
and avenues for remonstrance be blocked."
The emperor praised and accepted it.
He further requested that enslaved persons should not wear silk gauze.
The emperor said:
"Recently, enslaved persons were already prohibited from wearing bright gold patterns;
this can be gradually implemented."
Sù recommended Gāo Xù, the Tóng'ān Zhǔbù,
who was then appointed Píngyáng Jiǔshǐ.
Sù memorialized, saying:
"An enlightened ruler employs people
according to their abilities.
Xù is a scholar,
excellent at governing the people;
to make him sit in a shop
and manage wine monopolies
is not what he is capable of.
Your humble servant believes that the salt and iron commissioners of various circuits should still be appointed according to the old system, including both civil and military officials,
and the vice commissioners for wine tax should be chosen from among the three highest-ranked in the 'right selection' category."
The emperor said:
"Good."
He was transferred to Xíngbù Shàngshū.
The Sòng zhǔ 宋主 repeatedly requested exemption from the ceremony of personally receiving the national letter,
but Shìzōng 世宗 did not comply.
When Yǐn Zhāng 尹璋, the Prefect of Dàxīng 大興, served as the New Year's Day envoy in the fourteenth year,
the Sòng zhǔ 宋主 sent someone to his residence to seize his letter,
and bribed him heavily.
When Zhāng 張 returned,
he was flogged one hundred and fifty times
and dismissed from his post.
Sù 肅 was appointed as the investigator and envoy to the Sòng 宋 state.
His letter generally stated:
“What is recorded in the covenant document
is limited to the addition of the character 'huáng' 皇 to 'dì' 帝,
exemption from presenting memorials, declaring oneself a vassal, stating one's name, and performing two prostrations,
a reduction in the annual tribute,
and the use of the old ceremony
for personally receiving the national letter.
This ritual was established
ten years ago.
Now we learn that when the New Year's state envoy arrived there,
he was not granted an audience according to ritual,
but instead was forced to yield the letter in his residence.
Is this how a nephew state's etiquette should be?
We send you to inquire into the details;
you should report back truthfully.”
When Sù 肅 arrived in Sòng 宋,
the Sòng zhǔ 宋主 complied with everything as agreed,
and personally received the national letter.
When Sù 肅 returned,
a letter of thanks was attached.
Its general contents were:
“Your nephew, the Sòng Huángdì 宋皇帝, respectfully bows twice
and sends this letter to the uncle, the Dà Jīn Yìngtiān Xìngzuò Qīnwén Guǎngwǔ Réndé Shèxiào Huángdì 大金應天興祚欽文廣武仁德聖孝皇帝, at his palace.
Although the alliance has been followed for ten years,
without a single deviation from the agreement,
considering only the ritual forms,
it is appropriate to strike a balance.
Moreover, having received the gift of a sealed letter,
yet still adhering to the ceremony of personal reception,
and having been pressed by public sentiment,
we have repeatedly made sincere requests.
Because of the arrival of the New Year's envoy,
we then deliberated and agreed to act expediently.
We dare to trouble the returning envoy
to first convey our humble and earnest sentiments.
For the rest, the special envoy Sù 肅 will personally present our requests.”
When Sù 肅 returned to Sìzhōu 泗州,
he first sent Mǎnpúmǎ 滿蒲馬, the Commander of the Grand Steward of Zhào Wángfǔ 趙王府, to report to the emperor.
Shìzōng 世宗 was greatly pleased
and wanted to appoint Sù 肅 as a chief minister.
However, the Left Chancellor, Liáng Bì 良弼, said:
“Liáng Sù 梁肅 can be a chancellor,
but if he is made one immediately upon his return from Sòng 宋,
the Sòng 宋 people will look down upon us from then on.”
The emperor then stopped the plan.
After a long time,
he became the Prefect of Jìnán 濟南.
He submitted a memorial stating:
“Punishments vary in severity across generations.
Since Hàn Wén Hàn Wén abolished corporal punishment,
those whose crimes warranted penal servitude wore shackles and performed labor,
and were released when their term expired.
If a family had no extra adult males,
flogging was substituted for penal servitude.
Now, adopting the laws from the late Liáo 遼 dynasty,
one year of penal servitude is equated to one hundred strokes of the staff,
which means one crime receives two punishments.
The severity of punishment
is extreme in this regard.
Now that peace has lasted a long time,
moderate regulations should be applied.
But officials still use severe laws,
which truly pains your servant.
From now on, those sentenced to penal servitude
should only perform labor
and not be subjected to flogging.”
There was no response.
Not long after,
he retired.
He was recalled to serve as the Military Commissioner of Zhāngdé Jūn 彰德軍,
then summoned and appointed as Cānzhī Zhèngshì 參知政事.
The emperor said to his attendant ministers:
“Liáng Sù 梁肅's governance stands out,
leading him to a great responsibility.
Honest officials can thus be encouraged.”
Sù 肅 memorialized:
“The Yǔlín 羽林 of Hàn 漢 were all proficient in the Xiàojīng 孝經.
Today's imperial guards
are equivalent to the Hàn's Hàn's Yǔlín 羽林.
I request that one copy of the Xiàojīng 孝經 be bestowed upon every hundred households,
so that they may be taught to read it,
thus understanding the principles of subjects and sons.
When they take up official posts,
they will understand governance.”
The emperor said:
“Excellent.
Of human conduct,
nothing is greater
than filial piety,
which is also learned through teaching.”
An edict ordered that it be bestowed upon the guards and escorts.
He further memorialized:
“Currently, a 'dòu' 斗 of rice costs three hundred,
and people are already suffering from hunger,
because money is hard to come by.
It is estimated that the annual national income is over twenty million strings of cash,
with a surplus of over ten million for annual expenses.
The sums owed by official bureaus and factories, and by the common people,
total several millions in reductions.
Official bureaus and factories could pay in grain and silk,
and these could be used to pay officials and soldiers,
allowing money to circulate among the people,
making it somewhat easier to obtain.”
The emperor said:
“Allowing the outstanding debts of official bureaus
to be paid in kind
is acceptable.”
Sù 肅 submitted a memorial discussing eight matters for generating wealth and easing expenditure.
First,
abolish the general affairs officers in various departments.
Second,
dismiss the tasters at the wine tax offices.
Third,
the main lineage of the Tiānshuǐ Jùn Wáng 天水郡王 no longer exists,
and the remaining are distant relatives,
so their welfare provisions can be abolished.
Fourth,
reduce the Khitan officials in various departments.
Fifth,
abolish the salt monopoly
to benefit the people.
Sixth,
appropriately reduce salt prices,
so that private salt does not circulate,
and the people do not violate the law.
Seventh,
allow various regional wine taxes to be paid in other goods.
Eighth,
this year's harvest is abundant;
I request extensive purchase of grain and wheat
to ensure money circulates.
The emperor said:
“The welfare provision for the Zhào 赵 clan
is a benevolent policy of the state
and cannot be abolished.
As for the other seven matters,
the chancellors should deliberate in detail and report.”
The emperor further said:
“I have been on the throne for over twenty years,
and learning from Hǎilíng's 海陵 mistakes,
I have often made reforms.
Yet, there are still inevitable errors and improprieties.
You, my ministers, should wholeheartedly report them.”
Sù 肅 argued:
“When regular officials are seconded,
and acting officials commit public offenses,
or when regular officials return to their posts,
they are all considered to have left office without being punished.
Often, such individuals are careless
and neglect their duties.
I request that ten county magistrates be retained to be seconded,
and regular officials not be seconded.”
The emperor said:
“From now on, if acting officials commit public offenses,
even if regular officials have returned but have not yet replaced them in their original posts,
they should not be treated as having left office.”
Sù 肅 said:
“As Your Majesty commands.”
Sù 肅 and the chancellors reported on matters.
After they finished,
Sù 肅 knelt and said:
“Hunting in the four seasons,
though an ancient ritual,
sages also regarded it as a caution.
Your Majesty is advanced in years,
and it is severely cold.
Galloping through mountains and forests –
the imperial palace for rest
is also sufficient to refresh the spirit.
I wish Your Majesty would take care of yourself for the sake of the ancestral altars and the state;
this would be a blessing for the world.”
The emperor said:
“My sons are still young and strong,
and I want them to practice martial arts,
so I occasionally go.”
Dèng Bǐngjūn, the Assistant Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ-jūn, presented four matters in a memorial.
One stated that there were many vacant official posts outside [the capital],
and that those who were nominated and appointed based on seniority were not the right people.
The emperor asked Prime Minister Zhāng Rǔbì about this.
[He] replied,
"Acting according to qualifications has been in practice for a long time;
it is better to keep it as it is."
Sù said,
"Not so.
For example, the defunct Liáo is certainly not worth mentioning,
but their method of employing people was that if an official served for forty years without incident,
they would be granted the title of Military Commissioner.
How could it be limited to seniority?"
The emperor said,
"One who has served forty years is already old and infirm.
Observe their administrative achievements;
promote those who are good.
Later, examine their governance again;
if still good, promote them again.
This way, suitable people can be obtained,
and no tasks will be neglected."
Sù said,
"Indeed, as per Your Sacred Instruction."
Sù discussed the persistent banditry,
and requested that weapons not be prohibited.
The emperor said,
"If weapons are everywhere,
what are the benefits and harms?"
Sù said,
"Other circuits are one thing,
but allowing farmers in the Central Capital circuit to possess them
seems harmless."
The emperor said,
"I shall ponder this."
Whenever envoys were sent to Sòng,
the Sòng people presented gifts:
the chief envoy received two hundred liǎng of gold
and two thousand liǎng of silver;
the deputy envoy received half of that,
and the silks and sundry items were commensurate.
When assessing wealth and resources,
Sù, considering himself a high official,
having previously been an envoy to Sòng,
and having received many gifts,
ought to set an example for the common people.
So he voluntarily increased his declared assets by over sixty guàn,
which many commentators praised.
In the twenty-third year,
Sù requested retirement.
The emperor said to his prime ministers,
"Liáng Sù speaks all he knows without reservation;
he is an upright man.
As for you, if you know and do not speak,
I truly despise it.
However,
Sù is old,
so his request should be granted."
He was thus allowed to retire a second time.
An imperial edict appointed his son Rǔyì as Assistant Keeper of the Imperial Gate.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he passed away.
His posthumous name was Zhèngxiàn.
Yīlà Zào, originally named Yídíliè,
was a man from the Yúlǚ tribe of Qìdān.
Proficient in Qìdān and Chinese characters,
he was appointed by the Secretariat-Chancellery as a Qìdān clerk,
acting as Provisional Zhīchú,
and was promoted to Registrar of the Right Department.
During the Zhènglóng Southern Campaign,
he concurrently served as Registrar for both the Qìdān and Chinese character departments.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was appointed Vice Administrator of Zhēndìng,
and then entered service as a Censor.
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
He was reinstated as a Supernumerary Official of the Right Department,
and progressively rose to the rank of Defense Commissioner of Chénzhōu.
When Left Chancellor Gēsīliè Liángbì retired,
the emperor asked, "Who can replace you, my lord?"
[He] replied,
"Yīlà Zào, the Defense Commissioner of Chénzhōu,
is honest, capable, loyal, and upright;
I am not his equal."
He was then summoned to be the Director of the Imperial Treasury.
He was transferred to be a Vice Minister of Justice.
In the nineteenth year,
the eight méng'ān units, including Ànchūhǔ,
were relocated from Hénán to the borders of Dàmíng and Dōngpíng.
He returned to serve as Grand Judge,
and was tasked by imperial edict to preside over the revision of the penal code.
Originally,
during the Huángtǒng era, after consulting the laws and ordinances of Suí, Táng, Liáo, and Sòng,
the Huángtǒng Penal Code was established.
Hǎilíng's tyrannical laws
were arbitrarily altered,
sometimes with different penalties for the same crime,
sometimes with disproportionate severity,
sometimes with redundant articles,
or with superfluous wording,
causing officials to be unsure of which to follow,
and leading to corrupt legal practices.
Zào compiled the old Huángtǒng statutes and Hǎilíng's subsequent decrees,
thoroughly categorizing and proofreading them,
streamlining obstacles
and condensing redundancies.
Cases where precedents applied but were not explicitly stated in articles
were supplemented with precedents.
Specific omissions were added using existing laws.
For all legal provisions that were incomplete or ambiguous and could not be resolved,
imperial directives were sought for clarification.
All special imperial dispositions,
and provisional regulations that could be made permanent,
were incorporated as perpetual statutes.
The remaining parts that could not yet be eliminated
were compiled into a separate section.
In total, there were one thousand one hundred ninety articles,
divided into twelve volumes.
Upon presenting the book,
an imperial edict ordered its promulgation,
and silver and silk were bestowed in varying amounts.
Soon after,
eight mòukè units of the relocated Shāndōng méng'ān were moved to the eastern circuit of Héběi,
settling them in the former lands of the Chóuwò and Qīnggǒur méng'ān units.
An edict ordered that those without plowing oxen be supplied with oxen.
He served as Acting Censor-in-Chief.
After several months,
he was appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief,
concurrently serving as Co-Compiler of the National History,
then promoted to Minister of Justice,
and then transferred to Minister of Personnel.
Shortly thereafter, he was transferred to Prefect of Dàxīng.
When the imperial chariot visited Shàngjīng,
Xiǎnzōng remained to govern the country.
He sent a messenger to inform him,
saying,
"Since the imperial chariot's eastern tour,
the administration by the Metropolitan Prefect has been excellent.
I am about to embark on a spring hunt,
and you should be even more diligent in your duties."
Upon his return, he bestowed the captured geese and ducks upon him.
When he was ill and on leave,
an imperial physician was dispatched to diagnose and treat him.
He was reinstated as Minister of Justice.
When the emperor returned from Shàngjīng,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Xī Jīng,
then transferred to Prefect of Líntáo,
where he passed away.
Yīlà Zǐjìng, courtesy name Tóngwén,
originally named Wūgǔfǔlǔ,
was a man from the Five Divisions of Liáo.
His great-grandfather, Bàgē,
was a Concurrent Grand Councilor.
His father, Bálǔ,
was an official serving in the provisional appointment.
When the Commander Gǎokè occupied the Central Capital,
and the Liáo emperor fled west,
Bálǔ was left to oversee the baggage train.
Subsequently, the baggage train was plundered,
so Bálǔ shaved his head
and fled to the mountains.
Zǐjìng was studious and loved learning.
During the Huángtǒng era,
the Grand Master Yīlà Gù was compiling the History of Liáo,
and appointed him as a clerk.
When the History of Liáo was completed,
he was appointed Assistant Administrator of Liáozhōu.
The old prefectural office had its own appropriated land,
yielding several hundred guàn annually.
The prefectural officials collected this revenue each year,
and the landowners considered it customary,
never questioning it.
Zǐjìng said,
"Since there is already public land,
why take from the people's land?"
and ultimately did not collect it.
Upon completion of his term,
the people of the prefecture requested his retention at the Traveling Chancellery,
but it was not granted.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
he entered service as a Hanlin Compiler,
and was promoted to Department Director of the Board of Rites.
The state of Qí was abolished,
and a provisional provincial government (Xíngtái Shěng) was established in Zōuzhōu.
Over ten distinguished scholars were selected to fill official positions.
Zhào Yuán was among those selected,
and was appointed Xíng Bīngbù Lángzhōng.
The Xíngtái moved to Dàmíng,
and then again to Qízhōu.
When Wánfán Zōngbì recaptured Hénán,
Zhào Yuán always took charge of Hùbù affairs,
managing the collection of taxes and provisions for the army.
In Tiānjuàn 3rd year (1130),
he became Xíngtái Yòusī Yuánwàiláng.
There was a prisoner who had committed murder and deserved death.
The Xíngtái wanted to pardon him,
but Zhào Yuán disagreed.
He repeatedly argued several times,
and his resolve could not be shaken.
So he looked up to heaven and sighed, saying:
"If a murderer can be pardoned,
then what crime did the deceased commit?
Why would one seek one's own fortune by disrupting the laws of the realm?"
The Xíngtái ultimately could not sway him.
He was reassigned as Zuǒsī Yuánwàiláng,
and took charge of Lìbù affairs.
He served in the Xíngtái for a total of ten years.
His administration of affairs was clear and quick-witted,
and Wánfán Zōngbì knew him deeply.
Whenever the Xíngtái had matters to report to the Prime Minister's office,
Wánfán Zōngbì would invariably ask,
"Has this passed through Zhào Yuán yet?"
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
He served as Tóng Qiān Biànjīng Liúshǒu Shì,
then was reassigned as Tóngzhī Dàmíng Yǐn.
For his integrity, he was promoted to Héběi Xīlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and successively held positions as Jiédùshǐ of Zhāngdé and Wǔshèng armies, etc.
He retired due to old age,
and passed away at home.
Yílā Dàoběn's original name was Àn.
An imperial clan member, Yílā Gǔ, was Shāndōng Dōnglù Bīngmǎ Dōuzǒngguǎn,
and invited him to manage the military government's records.
He frequently traveled to the Marshal's Residence to discuss border affairs.
The Right Deputy Marshal Wánfán Zōngbì admired his talent,
and summoned him to be a Marshal's Residence Orderly (Yuánshuàifǔ Lìshǐ).
He was appointed Shàngshū Shěng Lìshǐ,
and specially promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
He was again promoted to Dàlǐ Chéng,
and concurrently served as Gōngbù Yuánwàiláng.
When Hǎilíng (Dì) launched his southern campaign,
he was sent to oversee the transport of fodder and grain.
Bandits arose everywhere,
and the roads were blocked.
With great difficulty, he only reached Huáinán.
He had an audience with the emperor,
and when asked,
he thoroughly reported the situation of bandits in all directions.
Hǎilíng (Dì) disliked hearing his words,
and had him flogged seventy times.
He was then sent to supervise the crossing of warships across the Jiāng (Yangtze River).
Coincidentally, Hǎilíng (Dì) died,
and the army returned.
In Dàdìng 2nd year (1162),
he was appointed Gōngbù Lángzhōng.
He was ordered to pacify various Xī tribes.
At this time,
Xú Liè and others from the Mǒbái Měng'ān wanted to surrender,
but were constrained by Měng'ān Hézhù,
and dared not surrender immediately.
Dào dispatched troops to ambush Hézhù's son, wife, grandchildren, male and female nephews,
as well as Mǒukè Liúzhù,
and Púliǎn Báisà's wife and children.
On that day,
Wō'wò happened to send Báisà to mobilize the Mǒbái Měng'ān army.
Báisà, hearing that his family had been captured,
then came to surrender.
He was reassigned as Lǐbù Lángzhōng.
He followed the expedition against Wō'wò,
wearing a golden plaque,
and with Yīngfèng Hànlín Wénzì É'lǐyě, he persuaded the rebellious Xī to surrender.
He was sent on a mission to Hénán,
to encourage farming and sericulture,
and secretly investigate the successes and failures of official administration.
He was successively promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng and Tóng Xiū Guóshǐ.
He investigated the merits and demerits of officials,
and returned to report.
The Emperor said:
"Corrupt officials are dismissed due to their crimes,
while others merely muddle through year after year.
If the honest and capable are immediately promoted,
it will not satisfy the people's desire to retain them.
They may be promoted in rank now,
and after their term, they will be promoted to higher positions."
Thus,
honest and capable officials, such as Jǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Yēlǜ Bǔ, were advanced one grade.
Shānzhōu Cìshǐ Shímǒ Jìnjiānú, Tàiníngjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ Yǐn Shēngqīng, Nínglíng Xiànlìng Jiān Bāngyàn, and Jùnzhōu Sīhòu Zhāng Kuāngfú were each advanced two grades.
Corrupt officials, such as Tóngzhī Jùnzhōu Fángyùshǐ Shì Púsùyuè and Zhēndìng Xiànlìng Tèmóu Gě, were spared death,
flogged one hundred and fifty times,
and stripped of their official titles.
Tóngzhī Suīzhōu Shì Wūgǔsūn Ālǐbǔ was flogged one hundred times,
demoted four grades,
and was not to be employed again without an imperial decree.
After this,
Dào was reassigned as Tóngzhī Dàxīng Yǐnshì.
An imperial edict stated:
"In the capital, scholars and commoners converge,
and many commit crimes.
Their offenses are self-evident;
do not be constrained by written words,
but judge them impartially.
I have often instructed the executive officials;
I will certainly not reprimand you for minor flaws.
Strive to live up to my intentions."
He was promoted to Xíngbù Shàngshū.
Shàngjú Shǐ Zōngkuí and Fùshǐ Shímǒ Qīnggǒu privately used official fodder,
and the matter came to light.
The Shàngjú was subordinate to the Diǎnjiǎn Sī,
so the Xíngbù should have handled the inquiry itself.
Diǎnjiǎn Wūlíndá Tiānxī instructed the Xíngbù to lighten their punishment.
The Xíngbù then handed it over to Dàxīng Fǔ for investigation.
Consequently, Dào, Tiānxī, and Lángzhōng Dīng Wěirén were all dismissed from their posts.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Dàlǐ Qīng,
concurrently signing documents in the Púmìyuàn.
He was again promoted to Xījīng Liúshǒu,
and died.
Gāo Déjī, courtesy name Yuánlǚ,
was a Bóhǎi person from Liáoyáng.
In Huángtǒng 2nd year (1142),
he passed the Jinshì examination.
In the 6th year (1146),
he became Shàngshū Shěng Lìshǐ.
When Hǎilíng (Dì) was Prime Minister,
he was opinionated and self-willed,
and no one dared to cross him.
Gāo Déjī often debated thoroughly with him.
When Hǎilíng (Dì) usurped the throne,
he ordered Zuǒsī Lángzhōng Jiǎ Chāngzuò to convey an imperial decree, saying:
"You are upright, straightforward, and decisive.
I now entrust you with the duties of Nánjīng Xíngshěng Gōudāng."
Before he could depart,
Hǎilíng (Dì) decided to make Yānjīng his capital.
He ordered Gāo Déjī to provisionally serve as Yānjīng Xíngtái Shěng Dūshì.
He was reassigned as acting Yòusī Yuánwàiláng,
then appointed Hùbù Yuánwàiláng,
reassigned as Zhōngdū Lù Dū Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ,
and promoted to Hùbù Lángzhōng.
In Zhènglóng 3rd year (1158),
an imperial edict ordered Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Zhāng Hào and Cānzhī Zhèngshì Jìng Sìhuī to supervise the construction of palaces in Nánjīng.
The following year,
Gāo Déjī, along with Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Lǐ Chóu and Xíngbù Shìláng Xiāo Zhōngyī, were all appointed as supervisors of construction (Yíngzào Tídiǎn).
Hǎilíng (Dì) sent a palace envoy to Gāo Déjī and others, saying:
"Do you wish to travel by post-horse
or by your own horse?
You can collect the silver plaques from the Nánjīng Shàngshū Shěng."
Lǐ Chóu requested that the silver plaques be issued first.
Hǎilíng (Dì) then sent another palace envoy to Lǐ Chóu, saying:
"Whether the plaque is given or not
is up to my decision.
How dare you speak so freely?
Is it because among the three of you,
your rank is uniquely high?"
Then he had him flogged thirty times,
and sent him to travel by his own horse.
Gāo Déjī and Xiāo Zhōngyī traveled by post-horse.
He was transferred to Tóngzhī Kāifēng Yǐn.
In Dàdìng three years (1163 CE),
because his administration of the corruption investigation was not good,
he was demoted to Assistant Commissioner of the Běijīng Circuit Transport Office.
In the autumn of that year,
the Túhé River overflowed,
and water entered the capital city.
Dégī immediately ordered the opening of the Chánglè Gate,
diverting the water into the imperial moat
to reduce its force,
and the water was unable to cause harm.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of the Board of Punishments.
In seven years (1167 CE),
he was transferred to Commissioner of the Zhōngdū Circuit Transport Office.
In nine years (1169 CE),
he was transferred to Minister of the Board of Punishments.
There was a criminal who deserved death,
and the Chancellor wished to reduce the sentence,
but Dégī said:
“The law has no two doors;
an unjust release is as bad as an unjust conviction.”
He did not comply.
When it was reported to the Emperor,
the Emperor said:
“The Board of Punishments’ opinion
is correct.”
He then summoned the various Ministers and instructed them, saying:
“Since I ascended the throne,
among those who have debated right and wrong with the Chancellor over government affairs,
Dégī is the only one.
From now on, if a department’s three proposals to the Secretariat do not agree,
report them fully.”
He served as envoy for the Sòng Emperor’s birthday.
Upon his return,
the Sòng people’s gifts, in addition to three thousand kuà of beeswax tea,
were not personally sealed.
Dégī said:
“A nephew presenting to an uncle
without a seal
is an item without a name.”
He rejected it.
In eleven years (1171 CE),
he was transferred to Minister of the Board of Revenue.
Dégī submitted a memorial,
requesting exemption from military supply and house tax money,
and reduction of agricultural taxes and salt and wine duties,
but received no reply.
The salaries of court officials, paid in grain, were commuted to cash,
and they were given an increased market price,
resulting in an overpayment of nearly four hundred thousand guàn of official money.
The Emperor sent someone to instruct him, saying:
“As Minister,
you have sought to please the Chancellors, executives, and close officials,
and wantonly disbursed official funds.
Your official rank
comes entirely from me;
how can you act like this?”
Thereupon, he was sentenced to eighty strokes of the cane.

Wáng Zuǒ, a Director in the Board of Revenue; Lú Yànchōng, an Associate Director; Liú Xīn, Assistant Commissioner of the Zhōngdū Transport Office; Shímò Chángshòu, Deputy Commissioner; Hán Zhèn, Fiscal Judge; Lǐ Kèqín, Left Inspector-General; Lǐ Bǎo, Right Inspector-General; and Judges Qiáng Ruìchāng, Yáo Zōngshì, and Nípánggǔ Dájíbù,
all received varying numbers of strokes.
An imperial edict declared that from the Dàdìng eleventh year, eleventh month, after the suburban sacrifice amnesty,
the Secretariat, the Censorate, the Board of Revenue, the Transport Offices, and the Inspection Bureaus had overpaid salaries in commuted grain money,
