and all such overpayments were to be recovered.
Dégī was demoted to Administrator of Lánzhōu,
Wáng Zuǒ to Judicial Assistant of Dàxīng Prefecture,
Lú Yànchōng to Register Judge of Héběi Xīlù,
Liú Xīn to Inspector-General of Dōngjīng,
Shímò Chángshòu to Judicial Assistant of Dōngjīng Retainer,
Hán Zhèn to Register Judge of Hédōng Nánlù,
Lǐ Kèqín to Magistrate of Tōngyuǎn County,
Lǐ Bǎo to Magistrate of Qīngshuǐ County,
and Qiáng Ruìchāng, Yáo Zōngshì, and Nípánggǔ Dájíbù were all appointed Judicial Officers.
In Dàdìng twelve years (1172 CE),
Dégī passed away
at the age of fifty-four.
His son was Xī.
Mǎ Fèng, courtesy name Liángbì,
was a native of Huòyīn in Dàxīng Prefecture.
In the early days of the state, when Yān was ceded to Sòng,
Fèng traveled to Biànliáng to study,
and passed the Imperial Examination in Xuānhé six years (1124 CE).
When Zōnghàn conquered Biànjīng,
Fèng returned to the court,
again passed the Imperial Examination,
and was appointed Assistant Magistrate of Guǎnglíng in Yùzhōu,
then promoted to Magistrate of Guīxìn in Xióngzhōu.
There was a river in the territory called Bāchǐkǒu,
which every autumn would overflow and harm the people’s fields.
Fèng surveyed the terrain,
dredged and diverted the water,
and the problem ceased.
He was summoned to serve as a Clerk in the Secretariat,
and then appointed Administrator of Xiànzhōu.
In the early Tiāndé period (1149-1153 CE),
he was transferred to Níngzhōu.
A person accused others of plotting rebellion,
implicating dozens, even hundreds of people.
Fèng investigated and found no evidence,
then interrogated the accuser,
who fully confessed to the false accusation.
The crowd cheered and wept with gratitude.
He was again promoted to Deputy Retainer of Nánjīng,
then entered the court as Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
At this time,
Gāo Zhēn was Censor-in-Chief,
highly esteemed and respected,
and showed no deference in administering justice.
The powerful and influential feared his authority,
so they appointed Fèng and Zhāng Zhōngfǔ as Deputy Censors,
hoping to damage him.
Fèng and Zhōngfǔ were both learned officials skilled in law,
and could not concede even a hair's breadth to Zhēn.
Zhēn feared they would harm him,
so he appealed to Hǎilíng,
who, regarding Zhēn as an old minister of Tàizǔ,
always comforted him.
Fèng was transferred to Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
and after more than a year, was dispatched as Military Commissioner of Shùntiān Army.
In Dàdìng two years (1162 CE),
he again became Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
was promoted to Minister of the Board of Punishments,
then transferred to Military Commissioner of Zhōngshùn Army,
and retired.
He died.
Wányán Wùbūhē was
a native of Hǎigūzhài in Huìníng Prefecture.
At thirteen,
he was selected to be a female Jurchen script student.
He was appointed as a Jurchen clerk in Shàngjīng,
then again studied small script and was proficient in Qìdān script.
He served as a Clerk in the Secretariat.
In the early Tiāndé period (1149-1153 CE),
he was appointed Principal of the Board of Personnel.
He investigated the case of the false inheritance of a Mǒukè position in the Yāllǎn Circuit,
and people praised his ability,
so he was promoted to Right Remonstrance Official.
Hǎilíng said to him:
“I first heard your name,
and tested you as Principal of the Board of Personnel.
Now, evaluating your actual performance,
it far surpasses what I heard.”
He was successively promoted to Director of the Right Bureau.
He followed Hǎilíng in the campaign against Sòng,
and upon reaching Huáinán,
heard that Shìzōng had ascended the throne in Liáoyáng.
Wùbūhē entered and reported the matter,
and Hǎilíng pondered for a long time,
saying:
“Did you all just hear of this?
I already know,
and have sent people.
This is a major matter; do not leak it outside.”
In Dàdìng two years (1162 CE),
his term of office was complete and he was due for replacement,
but Shìzōng, appreciating his skillful reporting,
issued a special edict for his re-appointment,
telling the Chancellors:
“Wùbūhē is public-spirited and loyal.
If there are such people in the future,
you all should recommend them.”
Such was the Emperor’s recognition of him.
After Wō'è's rebellion was pacified,
an edict abolished the Qìdān Mèng'ān Móukè units.
Their original registered households,
and those who surrendered after joining Wō'è in rebellion,
were all placed under Jurchen Mèng'ān Móukè units.
Wùbūhē was sent to redistribute them to areas with fewer Mèng'ān Móukè households.
Those Mèng'ān Móukè units that had not yet been abolished and were eligible for succession
were still permitted to succeed.
The poor among them were relieved,
and Qìdān horses were still purchased,
but horses belonging to elderly officials were not subject to purchase.
Soon after,
Shìzōng believed it was incorrect to place all Qìdān, both those who had never rebelled and those who had surrendered, under Jurchen Mèng'ān units.
It was inappropriate;
those who had never joined the rebellion could remain as before.
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Wányán Yuán'yí proposed that
the abandoned Qìdān lands could be settled by Jurchen people mixed with Qìdān who had not rebelled.
The Emperor asked Right Censor Sū Bǎohéng and Policy Councilor Shí Jū about this,
but neither could answer.
The Emperor rebuked them, saying:
“You always thoroughly discuss matters before presenting them,
and answer when asked.
How can you not know this?”
Bǎohéng and Jū bowed their heads and apologized.
The Emperor said:
“The Qìdān should be assigned [to their own Mèng'ān units],
and their original Mèng'ān taxes should be used to support them.
As for the abandoned lands, nearby Jurchen people and other households
who wish to reside there are permitted.
The Mèng'ān Móukè officials
should be selected from Qìdān officials who were not involved in the rebellion.”
He was transferred to Assistant Governor of Dàxīng,
and then promoted to Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi Army.
Upon first arriving at the post,
he was able to ascertain the truth in judging prisoners,
and people believed no one was wronged.
In five years (1165 CE),
he died in office.
Yīlà Wòlǐjīn,
also named Bājīn,
hailed from the Five Prefecture Bureaus of the Liáo dynasty,
and understood Qìdān characters.
In Tiānhuì 3 (1125), when the Sòng dynasty was campaigned against,
he was assigned to the army.
Whenever there was a battle, he was always the first to charge,
and repeatedly captured scouts.
The authorities reported his achievements,
and he was appointed as a clerk in the Secretariat Department.
In the 15th year (1137),
troops from various tribes were conscripted from beyond the mountains.
They were to meet with the Right Chancellor Xiāo Qìng.
At that time, several thousand imperial soldiers had fled south.
Wòlǐjīn led his troops to intercept and attack them,
seizing all their baggage and valuables.
He sent everything to the authorities and left,
not taking even a single hair.
For his efforts, he was promoted to Xiūwǔ Jiàowèi.
When Zōngbì recovered Hénán,
Wòlǐjīn supervised the various provincial commanders in the campaign.
After the matter was settled, he was promoted to Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn for his efforts.
At that time, the Six Ministries had not yet been separated,
so he was appointed as the director for the Ministries of War and Punishments.
Soon after,
he was promoted to Dūshì of the Right Bureau.
In Huángtǒng 2 (1142),
he was appointed Dàlǐ Zhèng,
and successively served as Co-Administrator of Zhāodé Commandery's Military Governor affairs.
For his integrity, he was promoted to Méngzhōu Defending Commissioner.
During the Zhènglóng period (1156-1161),
he was transferred to Co-Administrator of Běijīng Left-behind Agency affairs.
At that time, the Měng'ān Qìdān of Yóugǔhé Lánzishān and other places plotted rebellion.
Troops were being dispatched to suppress them.
Wòlǐjīn was specially sent to command troops south.
Upon reaching Sōngshān County, he was captured by the rebel leader Jiāng Gē,
who wanted to make him their chief convenor
and bind him by agreement.
Wòlǐjīn angrily said:
"I have received profound grace from the state.
How can I rebel with you?
I would rather be killed;
an agreement is impossible to obtain."
The rebels knew he could not be swayed,
so they humiliated him,
making him walk barefoot in plain clothes, chasing horses,
and even intending to harm him.
Wòlǐjīn persuaded his captor's servant,
and thus managed to escape and return.
In the ninth month of the 6th year (1161),
he was reassigned as Běijīng Circuit Transport Commissioner.
In the early Dàdìng period (1161-1189),
he became Bózhōu Defending Commissioner,
then was twice promoted to Lìshè Military Governor.
Previously,
some farmers, fleeing rebels, sought refuge in the city.
One of them entrusted thirty thousand cash to a neighbor.
After the rebels were pacified, he asked for it back,
but the neighbor denied it and refused to return it.
He sued in the county court,
but the county official dismissed the case due to lack of a contract or evidence.
So he sued in the prefecture.
Wòlǐjīn feigned anger and had the farmer chained and imprisoned,
then arrested his neighbor,
put him in cangue,
and interrogated him, saying:
"Your neighbor Yǐ was arrested for robbery and murder,
and he implicated you as an accomplice."
The neighbor was greatly frightened
and began to confess the truth about the fraudulent money.
Wòlǐjīn then ordered him to return the hidden money and released him.
The people of the commandery were astonished and submitted.
He was reassigned as Tōngyuǎn Military Governor,
and died there.
Ālèpú Yànzhōng, originally named Wāhéshān,
was from Hésùguǎn.
He loved learning
and was proficient in administrative affairs.
In Tiānhuì 14 (1136),
he was selected to serve as the registrar for the Ministry of War in the Secretariat Department,
then promoted to clerk in the Secretariat Department,
and appointed Dūshì of the Right Bureau.
In the 7th year (1149),
he was reassigned as Dàlǐ Chéng,
became Vice Prefect of Huìníng,
then advanced to Co-Administrator of Huìníng Prefecture,
and entered government as Lángzhōng of the Ministries of Personnel and Rites in the Secretariat Department.
In Zhēnyuán 2 (1154),
he was promoted to Vice Minister of these ministries.
Whenever Hǎilíng Shùrén had doubts,
he often had Yànzhōng decide them,
and Yànzhōng would answer according to the law.
If occasionally his answer was not satisfactory,
Yànzhōng would be summoned and reprimanded.
Yànzhōng would insist on his original opinion,
never yielding.
His colleagues were all afraid,
but Yànzhōng firmly held his ground.
Hǎilíng admired his fortitude.
The following year (1155),
he was appointed Imperial Censor-in-Chief,
and successively served as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue in the Secretariat Department and Deputy Commander of the Imperial Guard.
When Hǎilíng campaigned south,
he was appointed Běijīng Circuit Transport Commissioner.
In Dàdìng 2 (1162),
he was reassigned as Dàmíng Prefect,
concurrently serving as the Chief Military Commander of that circuit.
In the 4th year (1164),
he entered government as Minister of Punishments.
An imperial edict ordered planning for the difficult-to-feed households in the northern border region.
Where Táizhōu and Línhuáng bordered each other,
it was deemed appropriate to establish seventy forts and garrisons,
stationing thirteen thousand troops.
The supply of fodder and provisions was to be planned locally.
Before he could report back to court,
he died of illness
at the age of fifty-three.
Yànzhōng was filial and friendly by nature.
Once, when he went on a mission to Sòng,
he distributed all the gold and silk he received
among his brothers, relatives, and friends.
He was posthumously granted Rónglù Dàfū,
and the authorities were ordered to offer sacrifices,
and silver and silk were also bestowed upon his family.
Zhāng Jiǔsī, courtesy name Quánxíng,
was from Jǐnzhōu.
In the early Huángtǒng period (1141-1149),
he was appointed Jurchen interpreter for the Provisional Secretariat Department,
then appointed Co-Administrator of Yìzhōu affairs,
and thrice promoted to Bózhōu Defending Commissioner and Guīdé Prefect.
Liú Zhòngyán received the annual tribute from the Sòng state at Sìzhōu,
and Jiǔsī was his deputy.
In previous years, those who received the annual tribute
would always criticize the Sòng envoys for the poor quality of the goods,
and the Sòng envoys would routinely offer private gifts of silver and silk, each worth several hundred thousand,
but Jiǔsī alone refused to accept them.
Zhòngyán followed his example,
and from then on, private gifts ceased.
From Dàlǐ Píngshì,
he was twice promoted to Dàlǐ Shàopǐng.
The Magistrate of Qīngchí, Shuāng Shēn, submitted a memorial stating:
"My father Qián,
in the early Tiānjùan period (1138-1140),
was Administrator of Yǒng'ān Commandery.
He encountered the rebel leader Mèng Bāngjié,
who captured and coerced him.
He refused to comply
and was subsequently killed.
I request a proper official rank through his posthumous merit."
The Grand Court of Judicial Review deliberated
and concluded that Qián's son should only be ranked as a miscellaneous official.
Jiǔsī said:
"Qián bravely disregarded his own safety
and died upholding his integrity.
His son should be granted a proper official rank through posthumous merit
to encourage loyalty and filial piety."
Shìzōng followed Jiǔsī's deliberation.
He was reassigned as Lángzhōng of the Ministry of Works,
then Vice Prefect of Dàxīng,
then Co-Administrator of the Central Capital Transport Commissioner's affairs,
then transferred to Vice Minister of Punishments,
and then reassigned to the Ministry of Works.
Jiǔsī was known for his integrity and frugality,
but he was eager for advancement
and focused solely on achievements and profit.
He acted on his own will and emotions, without concern for the common people.
An imperial edict ordered the survey of official lands.
For all places with questionable names,
such as the Empress's Inn, the Crown Prince's Estate, Yànlè City, etc.,
regardless of whether they had title deeds for private land,
everything was registered as official land.
There were also cases where people occupying land adjacent to official land managed to escape scrutiny by chance.
When Shìzōng heard about this,
he summoned and admonished him, saying:
"Lands allocated during the Liáo dynasty,
and private farmlands seized by the Grand Marshal's office in the early days of our state and rented out,
which have in recent years been fraudulently claimed as private property –
these types of lands should be registered and seized.
As for other private lands,
if they are suddenly taken, the common people will lose their livelihoods.
This is certainly not my intention."
He was transferred to Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
Jiǔsī stated that Měng'ān farmers engaged in military farming were forced to compensate for stolen goods,
and if their families were poor, they often sold the garrison land they cultivated.
For those poor families unable to make compensation,
he proposed that the creditor should simply be allowed to lease out the land,
collecting the rental income,
and when the estimated value of the income matched the compensation owed,
the land should be returned to them.
Líntáo Prefect Wányán Ràng also discussed poor military farmers selling land for compensation
and requested to follow Jiǔsī's deliberation.
An imperial edict approved it.
He was promoted to Shàngshū of the Ministry of Works.
As he grew older, he became increasingly self-willed.
The Emperor said to the Left Vice Minister, Zhāng Rǔbì:
"Jiǔsī is old and confused,
and quite stubborn and self-willed.
I wish to assign him to an external post,
what do you think?"
At that time,
Jiǔsī's son, Ruòzhuō, was a Secretarial Clerk in the Department of State Affairs.
He unauthorizedly filled out imperial edicts.
When the matter came to light,
he fled.
Rǔbì then reported the incident to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"How could Jiǔsī not know Ruòzhuō's whereabouts?
He may be removed from his office.
Capture Ruòzhuō,
and I will grant him office the day he is apprehended."
Jiǔsī was terrified upon hearing the command,
and subsequently fell ill
and died.
Gāo Kàn, courtesy name Mùzhòng,
was a Bóhǎi person from Liáoyáng.
He was sharp and loved learning.
From a young age, he was skilled at composing prose.
His fellow students, wishing to test his talent,
jokingly challenged him to compose ten pieces in one day.
Kàn held his brush with ease and contentment;
before dusk, all ten compositions were finished,
polished and admirable.
At the age of twenty-six, he passed the Jìnshì examination.
He requested leave to care for his mother.
More than two years later, he was appointed Assistant Magistrate of Huòyīn.
He was summoned to be a Secretarial Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
then appointed Grand Administrator of the Right Bureau.
He resigned from office due to his mother's mourning.
He was reinstated as a Supernumerary Official of the Ministry of Personnel,
acting as a Supernumerary Official of the Left Bureau.
Wáng Yànqián, Cháng Dàróng, and Lǐ Qìngzhī were all selected for the Ministry of Personnel.
The Ministry of Personnel proposed that Yànqián and Dàróng both ranked first in the Jìnshì examination,
thus their ranking should be above Qìngzhī.
Yànqián was a Defense Judge of Míngzhōu,
Dàróng was a Jiedushi Judge of Línhǎijūn,
and Qìngzhī was an Observation Judge of Shěnzhōu.
Jiǎ Chāngzuò, the Director of the Left Bureau, harbored a private bias
and wanted to assign Qìngzhī to Míngzhōu.
He deceptively said:
"Although Míng is a good prefecture,
the staff officer for defense is subordinate to the military governor."
So, he re-proposed Yànqián for Línhǎijūn,
Dàróng for Shěnzhōu,
and Qìngzhī for Míngzhōu.
When Qìngzhī first sought selection,
Chāngzuò had made Qìngzhī an examiner for the metropolitan examination.
Meanwhile, Qìngzhī's younger brother, Qìngyún, was a Secretarial Clerk in the Department of State Affairs
and frequently associated with powerful and influential figures.
Hǎilíng secretly disliked this.
He once said to the Left and Right Bureaus,
"Chāngzuò must be in collusion with Qìngzhī."
Dà Fèngguó Chén was
a person from Liáoyáng,
a relative of Empress Dowager Yǒngníng.
He had previously been the Commissioner of the Eastern Capital Police Department.
He was dismissed due to corruption.
He wished to seek an audience through the Empress Dowager,
but Hǎilíng did not permit it.
Kàn had an old acquaintance with Fèngguó Chén from their hometown
and proposed him as Magistrate of Guìdé County.
Hǎilíng was furious.
Consequently, Chāngzuò, Kàn, and Fèng Zhòng, the Vice Minister of Personnel, among others,
were all caned with varying degrees of severity.
Qìngyún was given one hundred and fifty strokes of the cane
and dismissed.
Not long after,
Zhòng, Chāngzuò, and Qìngyún all died.
Kàn was demoted to Chief Clerk of Qīngshuǐ County.
Yáng Bāngjī, a Supernumerary Official of the Ministry of War acting as a Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Personnel, was demoted to Chief Clerk of Yíjūn County.
Sòng Tóng, a Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Personnel, was demoted to Chief Clerk of Huòyīn County.
Yáng Bójié, the appointer in the Department of State Affairs,
was demoted to Chief Clerk of Lǘyáng County.
After two years,
he became a Judicial Investigator of the Court of Judicial Review,
then promoted to Supernumerary Official of the Ministry of Revenue,
co-administrator of the Metropolitan Transport Commissioner,
Minor Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
At the beginning of the Dàdìng era,
he was transferred to Director of the Left Bureau.
Shìzōng diligently sought remonstrance,
but his officials all complied with his will,
offering no corrections.
The Emperor said:
"When I first ascended the throne,
I was unfamiliar with many administrative matters.
I truly relied on my generals, prime ministers, and great ministers to assist me with one heart.
Even common people submit memorials offering advice,
which can sometimes be helpful.
As for hearing and judging lawsuits,
and managing documents and appointments,
who cannot do that?
Even the sages like Táng and Yú
said, 'Consult the multitude,
set aside one's own views and follow others.'
Zhènglóng relied solely on his own judgment
and did not consult his ministers,
which led to defeat and chaos.
You, gentlemen, should understand my intention."
He ordered Kàn to transmit an edict to all bureaus and departments, saying:
"Should any memorial or advice
be obstructed by officials,
they are permitted to submit a memorial directly to the throne."
He was promoted to Shàngshū of the Ministry of Personnel.
Whenever candidates arrived for the quarterly selection,
the Ministry of Personnel used the pretext of reviewing old records,
calling it "examining the rolls,"
and some would be delayed until the next quarter without being able to leave.
Kàn, having served in the Ministry of Personnel three times, knew its弊 (malpractices).
After more than a year, the selection process was rectified,
and the candidates found it convenient.
In the fifth year,
he was sent as an envoy to congratulate the Sòng state on the Emperor's birthday.
He fell ill en route and resigned from his post.
In the seventh year of Dàdìng,
he died.
Yáng Bāngjī, courtesy name Démào,
was a Huáyīn person.
His father, Táo,
served as Assistant Magistrate of Yìzhōu at the end of the Sòng dynasty.
When Zōngwàng attacked Sòng,
Cài Jìng surrendered Yānshān,
and Yìzhōu immediately pledged allegiance.
Táo was killed.
Bāngjī, then just over ten years old,
hid in a monastic dwelling
and escaped death.
When he grew up,
he loved learning.
In the second year of Tiānjuàn,
he passed the Jìnshì examination.
He was appointed Military Judge of Luánzhōu,
then promoted to Magistrate of Jiāochéng, Tàiyuán.
Túshān Gōng, the Administrator of Tàiyuán, was corrupt and unlawful.
Under the pretext of casting gold Buddhas,
he ordered the subordinate counties to supply gold.
Bāngjī alone refused to comply.
Túshān Gōng was enraged.
He summoned Bāngjī to the prefectural office
and was about to strike Bāngjī's face with an iron staff.
Bāngjī did not flinch.
Bǐngdé, when inspecting officials for integrity,
dismissed both the Administrator and all nine county magistrates.
Bāngjī was ranked first in Hédōng for his integrity,
and was summoned to be a Chief Clerk in the Ministry of Rites.
He acted as a personnel selector for the Ministry of Personnel while serving as a Supernumerary Official of the Ministry of War.
He was implicated in the appointments of Lǐ Qìngzhī and Dà Fèngguó Chén,
and like Gāo Kàn and others, was demoted.
Bāngjī was demoted to Chief Clerk of Yíjūn, Fāngzhōu.
He was transferred to Magistrate of Gāomì.
At the beginning of the Dàdìng era,
the Department of State Affairs proposed Bāngjī as Director of the Ministry of Justice.
Shìzōng said:
"To promote a county official directly to Director,
how is that?"
Grand Preceptor Zhāng Hào replied:
"Bāngjī was formerly a Supernumerary Official of the Ministry of War,
and moreover, his talent is useful."
The Emperor assented.
He was appointed Minor Minister of the Court of Imperial Manufactories,
administrator of the Office of Imperial Petitions,
then Minor Minister of the Secretariat,
promoted to Academician of the Hanlin Academy,
then again promoted to Minister of the Secretariat concurrent with Left Remonstrance Grand Master,
and was responsible for compiling the Imperial Diary.
Zhāng Zǐyǎn, the Metropolitan Police Commissioner, was Bāngjī's relative by marriage.
Zǐyǎn encountered the Imperial Crown Prince's guard on the road.
He reined in his horse at the market gate but did not close his umbrella.
The guards reprimanded him.
Zǐyǎn whipped the guard who had reprimanded him.
The Censorate impeached Zǐyǎn.
Bāngjī met with Censorate officials to plead for Zǐyǎn,
and upon entering to see Xiǎnzōng,
he sought to absolve Zǐyǎn of his crime.
An imperial edict demoted Zǐyǎn two ranks.
Bāngjī was demoted one rank for his involvement,
and sent out as Co-Administrator of the Western Capital Garrison.
He was transferred to Transport Commissioner of Shāndōng East Circuit,
then Jiedushi of Yǒngdìngjūn,
and retired.
In the twenty-first year of Dàdìng,
he died.
Bāngjī was skilled at writing
and excelled at painting landscapes and figures.
He was particularly renowned in his time for his painting.
Dīng Wěirén
from Wǎnpíng, Dàxīng Fǔ.
His great-grandfather was Shì.
His grandfather was Wéishòu.
His father, Jūn,
was appointed to various prefectures and counties as an official.
Wherever he went, he had a reputation for good governance.
Later, he retired
and kept his doors shut, refusing to go out.
When there were disputes or lawsuits among the villagers,
they would not go to the authorities but would seek Jūn for arbitration.
Wěirén was placid and had few desires.
Apart from studying,
he had no other hobbies.
During the late Liáo dynasty, when he was fleeing from danger,
even when traveling through difficult roads, he never let go of his books.
In the second year of Huángtǒng (1142),
he passed the *jìnshì* examination
and was appointed Assistant Magistrate of Wǔqīng County.
After the county had experienced warfare,
there were no schools.
Wěirén summoned the talented young men of the town and taught them.
The common people gladly followed him.
He was transferred to become Military Commissioner of Cí Zhōu.
At that time,
an imperial edict ordered officials to inspect and assess other officials.
Wěirén, known for his integrity, was appointed acting prefect.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Héchuān.
The previous magistrate was weak and ineffective.
Petty individuals overstepped the law and violated prohibitions without fear.
Wěirén re-emphasized the laws and prohibitions,
and everyone became quiet and restrained,
some even fleeing to other counties to avoid him.
There was a very strong and unruly person named Dǒng Yòu.
He was awed and submitted to Wěirén.
He cut off his finger with a knife,
swearing never to violate the law again in his lifetime.
All taxes and levies were agreed upon with the common people beforehand,
and they were settled earlier than in other districts.
He successively served as Judicial Reviewer of Běijīng,
then was twice promoted to Investigating Censor of the Grand Court of Justice (*Dàlǐ Sīzhí*).
Due to mourning, he left office,
but was soon reinstated.
In the third year of Dàdìng (1163),
he was appointed Vice Military Commissioner of Dìngwǔ Prefecture.
As the Military Commissioner and Associate Administrator were both vacant,
Wěirén managed the administration with no outstanding lawsuits.
He was transferred to Censor of the Grand Court of Justice (*Dàlǐ Chéng*),
then to Assistant Director of the Board of Civil Office (*Lìbù Yuánwàiláng*),
and then to Director of the Board of Revenue (*Hùbù Lángzhōng*).
At this point,
Jiǎ Shàochōng was Director of the Board of Punishments (*Xíngbù Lángzhōng*).
The emperor said to the Left Chancellor, Géshíliè Liángbì:
"Shàochōng is gentle and lenient in character,
and not suited for the position of the Board of Punishments.
Discuss replacing him."
Thus, Wěirén was made Director of the Board of Punishments.
He was impeached for officials of the Imperial Storehouse privately using government fodder,
which violated regulations, and was sent to Dàxīng Fǔ for interrogation.
He was dismissed from office.
He was reassigned as Governor of Qí Zhōu.
Qí Zhōu was a branch prefecture of Dìngwǔ.
When the gentry and common people heard of Wěirén's appointment,
they flocked to welcome him at the border,
forming an unbroken line.
He was then appointed Associate Administrator of Xījīng Supervising Residence.
He immediately promoted schools,
to clarify the method of cultivating scholars.
He was promoted to Transport Commissioner of Shǎnxī Xīlù.
〔一０〕In the twenty-first year of Dàdìng (1181),
he died in office.
The encomium says: When officials rose,
was it at the end of Qín?
When officials were selected and tested,
was it during the Liáo and Jīn eras?
Its character
"from one,
from history"
— does it mean to uphold the law without wavering?
Upholding the law without wavering—
that is a true official.
The cunning manipulate documents to distort the law,
the narrow-minded cling to one principle and are inflexible.
These are all ways in which the path of an official goes astray.
Gāo Kàn, Gāo Déjī, Zhāng Jiǔsī and their like
all went astray by distorting the law.
Collated Notes

Biographies Vol. 29: Wányán Sāgǎi, Páng Dí, Wēndíhǎn Yíshìměn, Shéntǔměn, Yīlà Chéng, Shímò Biàn, Yáng Zhòngwǔ, Púchá Shìjié (original name Āsà), Xiāo Huáizhōng, Yīlà Àndá, Bóshùlǔ Ālúhàn, Zhào Xīngxiáng, Shímò Róng, Jìng Sìhuī.
Wányán Sāgǎi,
was from Nàlúhún Hé in Shàngjīng.
His ancestors lived along the Wūlěngkū Hé.
He was tall and strong,
skilled in using a spear.
When the imperial army campaigned south,
Ruìzōng was Right Vice Marshal.
He placed Sāgǎi under his command,
bestowed upon him a golden tablet,
and made him supervise military affairs.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn (1138),
he was appointed Bodyguard and Protector of his own clan.
Later, he followed the army to Tàizhōu Lù.
The army commander appointed Sāgǎi as Myriad Household,
leading the Yínshúkě and other *méng'ān* units.
Stationed on the northern border,
he achieved several military merits.
In the first month of the second year of Tiāndé (1150),
the commoner of Hǎilíng sent an envoy to the Xià kingdom,
to inform them of his accession to the throne,
and also to ascertain their intentions.
Upon his return,
he reported favorably to the emperor,
and was made Director of the Board of War (*Shàngshū Bīngbù Lángzhōng*).
He was transferred to Associate Administrator of Huìníng Yǐn,
then promoted to Military Commissioner of the Diélà Tribe,
then transferred to Administrator of the Ōulǐběn Herds,
and then Commander-in-Chief of Gélǎnlù.
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
he was appointed Defense Commissioner of Wèizhōu,
and Commander-in-Chief of Wǔzhèn Army.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he sent an envoy to summon Sāgǎi.
Upon his arrival,
he was appointed Military Commissioner of Chāngwǔ Army.
Later, he became Vice Commander-in-Chief of Shāndōng Lù Marshal,
then transferred to Military Commissioner of Ānhuà Army,
still concurrently serving as Vice Commander-in-Chief.
In the fourth year (1164),
he was transferred to garrison Ānwǔ,
still concurrently serving as Vice Commander.
He led over 80,000 troops from Shāndōng, Dàmíng, and Dōngpíng routes across the Huái River,
to join the main army in attacking Sòng.
When they reached Chǔzhōu,
Sòng sent an envoy to offer annual tribute.
He returned to Pīzhōu
and died.
Páng Dí
from Yán'ān.
In his youth, he was unrestrained
and enjoyed reading military texts,
practiced horsemanship and archery,
and studied the arts of divination and astronomy,
but none of these were put to use.
He joined the army,
serving as the Third Vice General of Jīngyuán Lù.
He distinguished himself by defeating bandits,
and was appointed Protector of Righteousness (*Bǎoyìláng*).
Once, with over a hundred cavalrymen, he was traveling through valleys
when they encountered several thousand Xià soldiers.
Everyone was terrified and pleaded to retreat.
Dí, however, spurred his horse and charged into their formation.
The enemies scattered,
and though he sustained severe wounds,
his demeanor remained calm.
He returned with his army intact.
From then on, he became famous,
and was promoted to General,
and provisionally appointed Military Supervisor of Jīngyuán Lù.
When the Qí state was established,
Zhāng Zhōngfú, the Pacification Commissioner of Jīngyuán Lù, recommended Dí to provisionally take charge of Huáidé Army,
concurrently serving as Border Pacification Commissioner.
The Xià people amassed an army of 50,000 and approached Huáidé City.
Dí opened the city gates and awaited them.
The Xià people dared not enter.
Then, with several thousand cavalry, he launched a sally from various gates,
and utterly defeated them,
beheading 500 enemies
and capturing many military supplies, sheep, and horses.
He again defeated Guān Shīgǔ's troops,
and was promoted to Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Before reaching his post,
he was transferred to Governor of Zhènrong Army and Border Pacification Commissioner.
Later, he was provisionally appointed Vice Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry of Huáinán Dōnglù,
managing Yí, Mì, and Huáiyáng,
and concurrently provisionally holding the post of Governor of Yízhōu.
When his father died,
he left office,
but was soon reinstated as Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Huánqìng Lù,
provisionally holding the post of Governor of Bīnzhōu.
When the Qí state was abolished,
he was reassigned as Defense Commissioner of Huázhōu.
After a short while,
there was a military mutiny,
and he was captured and taken into the mountains.
Soon after, the bandits regretted, saying:
"You have always governed well,
how can we plunder and insult you?"
So they released him,
and he resumed governing the prefecture.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn,
he was appointed Grand Military Commissioner of the Yǒngxīngjūn Circuit and concurrently Prefect of Jīngzhàofǔ.
He was then transferred to be the Governor of Líntáo,
and concurrently Grand Military Commissioner of the Xīqín Circuit.
There was a great famine in Shǎnyòu,
and refugees gathered from all directions.
Dī dug canals to irrigate the fields,
and the migrants benefited from the food supply,
while the residents utilized their labor.
Each found their place,
and the people of the commandery erected a stele to commemorate his administrative achievements.
When the official system was implemented,
the Ministry of Personnel specially appointed him as Grand General Dìngyuǎn, holding the rank of Wǔgōng Dàfū and serving as Commander of the 博 Zhōu Militia.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Prefect of Qìngyáng.
Having served for three assessments without change,
he was renowned for his excellent governance,
and an imperial edict praised him,
which the people of the west considered an honor.
In the first year of Zhènglóng,
he was promoted to Prefect of Fèngxiáng,
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
but was not permitted.
When Hǎilíng led a southern expedition,
taxes and levies were vexatious and urgent,
and officials took advantage of the situation to commit malpractices.
The rich used bribes to escape,
while the poor went bankrupt and became even more distressed.
Dī summoned all the people to discuss adjustments to the levies,
and without coercion, the labor was distributed fairly,
and public sentiment was greatly pleased.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to be the Military Commissioner of Fényángjūn.
In the early Dàdìng period,
he was again made Governor of Líntáo,
then promoted to Grand Transport Commissioner of the Nánjīng Circuit.
For his frugality in managing affairs and saving expenses,
and for his peaceful and stable governance,
Hénán praised him.
He was transferred to be the Military Commissioner of Jiàngyángjūn.
He died in office
at the age of seventy.
Dī was by nature purely filial.
When his father fell ill,
medicine was ineffective.
Dī looked up to heaven, wept, and prayed,
then cut a piece of flesh from his thigh to make soup,
and from then on, his father recovered.
When his brothers divided the family property,
Dī gave everything to them,
taking nothing for himself.
Regarding official positions and peerage by imperial favor,
he gave precedence to his nephews.
When his illness was critical,
he bathed and put on court robes before passing away.
Wēndíhǎn Yíshìmèn,
Sùpíntún Mènhuānchūn Rén,
was transferred to the upper capital Hūlúnshīlǎn.
His elder brother Shùliǎn
had rendered meritorious service in the early days of the state,
and was granted a hereditary Móukè.
Yíshìmèn was by nature loyal, upright, strong, and resolute,
skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and possessed extraordinary physical strength.
In the early Huángtǒng period,
he inherited his elder brother's Móukè.
Through accumulated military achievements,
he became the Prefect of Táozhōu.
He said to people:
"The Móukè
is my brother's position.
My brother's son Wòlǔgǔ is now grown up."
He then yielded the Móukè back to his brother's son.
Zōngbì heard of this and praised him, saying:
"To be able to yield a hereditary position
can be said to be difficult."
He was appointed Prefect of Guìdézhōu,
then changed to Yídiǎn Cíxiángwěn,
and promoted to Military Commissioner of the Wūgǔlǐ Tribe,
later changed to Déchāngjūn.
In the fourth year of Zhènglóng,
a large army was conscripted for a southern expedition.
Měng'ān Dìngyuǎn Ābǔ of Tàizhōu rebelled with his subordinate troops and returned.
Yíshìmèn, with seven Móukè, captured Dìngyuǎn Ābǔ,
and forced his troops to join the main army.
The Qìdān rebelled,
defeating six Měng'ān of Huìníng at Dìmǔlǐng,
and garrisoned at the borders of Xìn and Hán Circuits.
Yíshìmèn led several thousand men and killed over ten thousand rebels at Yīgǎihé,
and for his meritorious service, was promoted to Governor of Línhuáng.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he issued a handwritten edict saying:
"The generals and soldiers from various routes in the southern campaign, and your nephews Ānyuǎn, Wòlǔgǔ, and Xié Pǔ and his brothers,
fully armored and armed, all came to support me,
and I reluctantly assumed the great position.
You are an elder statesman of generations of merit,
and as the border affairs are not yet settled,
Línhuáng is a critical post,
so you should temporarily remain in your old office.
I hear that the Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Bái Yànjìng, and the Nanjing Left-over Guard, Gēshíliè Zhìníng, are coming to suppress the Qìdān.
I have already sent someone to recruit them.
Their families are all in Nanjing,
and I fear they might flee
or plot a rebellion.
If they arrive, so be it,
but if they do not,
you should capture and present them by stratagem.
I have twice sent people to persuade and recruit the Military Inspector-in-Chief Lǎo Héshàng,
but the envoys do not know his whereabouts
and have not returned for a long time.
Moreover, Lǎo Héshàng does not know that I have already ascended the throne.
You can send someone to convey my intentions to him.
If he surrenders,
all will be restored to their former state.
For border affairs,
you must set up intelligence networks."
At this time,
Wōwò had already rebelled,
leading tens of thousands of troops to attack Línhuáng.
As the armies from various routes had not yet arrived,
Wōwò's power grew.
Yíshìmèn led six hundred soldiers from within the city to intercept and attack Wōwò.
After several engagements,
he annihilated many,
but the horse he rode was struck by a stray arrow and fell,
and he was captured by the rebels.
The rebels forced Yíshìmèn to call out to the people in the city, saying:
"Your life and death are in this instant.
If you can persuade the city to surrender,
your official positions and peerage will remain as before;
otherwise, we will kill you."
Yíshìmèn angrily cursed the rebels, saying:
"I receive the state's titles and emoluments,
how could I follow you rebels?"
The rebels took him to the foot of the city walls,
coercing him to call out to those inside.
His wife, children, officials, and generals all ascended the city walls to look down.
Yíshìmèn shouted in a stern voice:
"I regret that my army was too small to annihilate the rebels.
Everyone must die one day!
You must not surrender to the rebels!
If you open the gates and let the rebels in,
all the common people in the city will be slaughtered and plundered.
Do not ruin the state's affairs because of me;
the rebels can do nothing!"
Enraged, the rebels killed him.
The people in the city were all moved to gratitude by this,
and the Judicial Administrator Má Guī further repaired and strengthened the city walls,
while the Right Supervising General Shéntǔmèn and the Upper General Fǔguó Āsīmèn defended the city firmly.
The rebels failed to breach the defenses
and then led their forces eastward.
Shéntǔmèn was originally from the imperial clan,
the son of Húsùlǔ Gǎi, who was posthumously granted Silver-green Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
At the age of fifteen,
he served Tàizōng as Left Palace Attendant.
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
he was appointed Imperial Guard,
then Chief of the Ordnance Bureau,
and successively served as Defense Commissioner of Zhàozhōu.
In the early Dàdìng period,
he was appointed Right Assistant Military Commissioner of the Marshal's Office.
He and Wúzhāhū, Prefect of Xiánpíng, led the Tàizhōu troops and fifteen hundred troops from the Gélǎnlù Circuit,
to rendezvous with Yíshìmèn, Governor of Línhuáng, to suppress the Qìdān.
The Qìdān attacked Línhuáng,
and Yíshìmèn died.
They could not breach the city,
so they led their forces eastward.
Shéntǔmèn submitted a memorial requesting reinforcements.
On the jiǎchén day of the twelfth month,
Shìzōng arrived at Hǎibīn County,
received the memorial,
and said:
"The armies of Shéntǔmèn and Wúzhāhū are not small;
they can launch protracted attacks."
At this time, the Right Vice Marshal Móuyǎn arrived with a large army.
Shéntǔmèn was changed to Military Commissioner of the Gésùguǎn Circuit,
subordinated to the right wing.
He and Gēshíliè Zhìníng defeated the rebels at Chángluò,
and fought at Mògéhé,
both with merit.
He was changed to Grand Military Commissioner of the Pōsuō Circuit,
and then died.
Yīlà Chéng's original name was Luòwù.
His ancestors were Khitan people of the Liáo dynasty's Hétent tribe.
He was brave and resourceful,
and understood both Khitan and Chinese characters.
During the Tiānhuì era,
he served under Tàlǎ as a traveling *móu'ān* (commander of a thousand households).
When fighting the Sòng people between Chǔ and Sì,
Chéng, with his unit, was the first to ascend,
greatly defeating the Sòng army.
His merits surpassed all other generals.
Liú Lín convened a meeting at Tiāncháng to discuss advance and retreat.
Chéng, along with Jiāgǔ Cháhénǐ, served as Tàlǎ's vanguard.
They captured Sòng captives to serve as guides,
and thus reached Tiāncháng.
Ruìzōng praised him.
Later, he followed Zōngbì in leading troops to abolish the Qí state.
When Sòng was attacked again,
Háo Zhōu was besieged.
In every battle, he was always the first to ascend,
destroying and breaking through many defenses.
When Zōngbì retook Hénán,
Chéng and Xiāo Huáizhōng, among eight *móu'ān*, were the first to cross.
After Hénán was pacified,
he was rewarded for his merits, granted the title of Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and appointed as the Cìshǐ of Wēizhōu.
Due to his integrity,
he was promoted to Tóngzhī Yán'ān Yǐn,
and then again to Zhāoyìjūn Jiédùshǐ.
During the Zhènglóng Southern Expedition,
he served as the Dū Zǒngguǎn of the Wǔyì Army.
When Sābā rebelled,
Hǎilíng executed famous Khitan generals for their involvement.
Chéng, with his own army, guarded Cí,
and immediately sent his wife and children back to Biàn.
Hǎilíng did not suspect him because of this.
People at the time highly regarded his foresight.
He was appointed Dū Zǒngguǎn of the Shénwǔ Army,
and, with Bèi Zhú Lǔ Dìngfāng, served as the vanguard of the Zhèdōng Route,
ordered to advance troops from Huái'yīn.
He led his unit to escort grain to Yángzhōu.
Enemy forces attacked at night.
Chéng arrayed his troops and fought valiantly,
slaying a great number.
When Hǎilíng Shùrén died,
the army returned,
and he was again stationed at Zhāoyì.
In Dàdìng 2nd year,
he was rated excellent for his integrity,
and appointed Hézhōng Yǐn.
Again, he was appointed Líntáo Yǐn,
and persuaded the leader of the Qiáojiā and other tribes, Jiéshíjiǎo, to surrender.
He was promoted to Nánjīng Liúshǒu,
summoned and appointed Pīmì Fùshǐ,
and enfeoffed as Rèn Guógōng.
He was then appointed Běijīng Liúshǒu.
He died.
Upon hearing the news of his death,
the Emperor expressed sorrow and regret,
and granted his son Shùnsī Ābù the title of Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn,
inheriting the *móu'ān* position of Chábulǔ in the Xiánpíng Lù Chāochìlín.
As for Jiéshíjiǎo,
after the Western Fān declined,
his descendants were called Jǐnzhān,
and Jǐnzhān's son was Bāzhān.
Jiǎo first submitted to Sòng,
was granted the surname Zhào,
and renamed Shùnzhōng.
Shùnzhōng's son was Yǒngjí,
and Yǒngjí's son was Shìchāng.
Both received Sòng official positions,
serving as Zuǒwǔ Dàfū,
remotely leading the Láizhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and inheriting the leadership of the Bǎyáng tribe.
When the court pacified Shǎnxī,
Shìchāng was appointed Zhōngyì Xiàowèi.
Later, Jīngzāng, the leader of the Guǐlú tribe, killed Shìchāng.
The court sent troops to capture Jīngzāng,
executed him in the Líntáo market,
and appointed Shìchāng's son, Tiěgē, as the Dūguǎn of the Bǎyáng tribe.
In Dàdìng 4th year,
the Sòng people conquered Táozhōu.
Tiěgē's younger brother Jiéshíjiǎo and his mother fled into the Qiáojiā tribe to avoid them.

Bōbū, the leader of the Qiáojiā tribe, along with the elders Dàsēng and others of the neighboring Mùbō Lǒngbū, Pángbài, and Bǐnglí tribes, totaling four tribes, established Jiéshíjiǎo as the chief of the Mùbō Four Tribes,
and he was styled
"Wángzǐ" (Prince).
His territory bordered Táozhōu and Jīshí Jūn to the north.
To the south was the Lǒngbū tribe,
bordered by a great mountain range to the south, extending over 800 *lǐ* and impassable to humans.
To the southeast, it bordered the Qiāng of Diézhōu.
To the west was the Bǐnglí tribe,
bordering the Lúgān Qiāng to the west.
To the north was the Pángbài tribe,
bordering the Rónglǔ tribe of Xīxià.
The land was high and cold,
without silk, hemp, or the five grains;
it only produced qīnkē (highland barley),
which was eaten with wild vegetables and butter and cheese.
Its territory encompassed 8,000 *lǐ* (circumference),
comprising over 40,000 households.
Their dwellings followed water and grass for pasturing livestock,
and their migrations were not constant.
Jiéshíjiǎo remembered that the court had avenged his father
and wished to abandon the four tribes and return to the court,
but the four tribes did not permit it.
When Chéng arrived at Líntáo,
he sent someone to invite Jiéshíjiǎo,
who then led the four tribes to submit,
offering 100 horses,
and further requested to pay annual horse tribute.
An imperial edict stated:
"These distant people admire righteousness;
We greatly commend them.
Let capable officials be sent to pacify their populace,
and bestow generous rewards."
Initially,
during the Tiānhuì period,
an edict granted the old Jīshí territory to the Xià people,
who called it Qí'ān Chéng.
There were four Zhuānglàng tribes:
one called Chuīzhémén,
second called Mìzàngmén,
third called Lǒngbūmén,
and fourth called Pángbàimén.
Although they belonged to the Xià state,
their loyalty was inconsistent.
In Dàdìng 6th year,
the Xià people defeated and annihilated the Chuīzhé and Mìzàng gates.
The Lǒngbū and Pángbài gates, bordering the Qiáojiā tribe,
then submitted to Jiéshíjiǎo.
The Xià state sent envoys to report that the Zhuānglàng tribe had disobeyed orders and rebelled,
and that they intended to raise an army to eliminate them.
The court, unaware that the Lǒngbū and Pángbài gates had previously belonged to the Xià state,
replied that they would investigate the historical allegiance of that territory,
and that the Xià should not unilaterally dispatch troops.
Jiéshíjiǎo's mother resided among the Zhuānglàng tribe.
In Dàdìng 9th year,
Jiéshíjiǎo went to visit his mother.
The Xià people, learning of this,
dispatched troops to surround Jiéshíjiǎo,
inviting him to surrender.
Jiéshíjiǎo refused,
and led his unit to fight fiercely,
breaking through the encirclement.
The Xià people chopped off his arm,
and captured his mother.
Many of his soldiers also perished.
Jiéshíjiǎo soon died as well,
leaving a dying wish to request the court
to re-establish a leader for the Qiáojiā tribe.
Shǎnxī reported:
"We have heard that Lǐ Rénxiào, the king of the Xià state, and his minister Rèn Déjìng have divided their country,
and dispatched 40,000 troops and 30,000 laborers
to build Qí'ān Chéng,
and killed Jiéshíjiǎo, the leader of the Qiáojiā and other tribes.
We have repeatedly captured Sòng spies
who say that Sòng intends to ally with the Xià state to invade the border."
An imperial edict sent Dàlǐ Qīng Lǐ Chāngtú and Zuǒsī Yuánwàiláng Niángē Wòtèlā to investigate,
and also to stop the Xià people from building Qí'ān Chéng and from dealing with the Qiáojiā and other tribes by establishing a separate leader.
The Xià state replied:
"Qí'ān was originally the old Jīshí city,
which had long been abandoned.
Our border officials requested to establish garrison troops to pacify the Zhuānglàng tribe.
This is for defense against bandits,
and nothing else.
Jiéshíjiǎo entered our territory with troops,
and thus he was killed.
We did not know he was the leader of the Qiáojiā tribe."
Lǐ Chāngtú and others investigated and found that
the place where Jiéshíjiǎo was killed was originally within Xià territory,
and the construction of Qí'ān Chéng had been completed.
They all returned,
finding no evidence of Sòng-Xià communication.
Thus, they increased garrison troops at the critical strategic points near Xī and Qín, bordering Sòng and Xià.
When they asked the people of the Qiáojiā and other tribes,
they wished for Jiéshíjiǎo's nephew, Zhào Shīgǔ, to be their leader.
Thereupon, an edict appointed Zhào Shīgǔ as the Dūqiánxiá of the Mùbō Qiáojiā, Bǐnglí, Lǒngbū, and Pángbài Four Tribes,
and added the title Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn.
Shímò Biàn's original name was Ālúgǔliè.
His fifth-generation ancestor, Wáng Wǔ,
was a Liáo Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
His father, Wǔjīn, was a Qúnmùshǐ.
He followed Ruìzōng to Qiūshān.
Biàn, then thirteen years old,
was already skilled in archery,
and successively hunted two deer.
Ruìzōng was astonished by him,
and bestowed upon him a good horse and a golden *tǔhú* (hunting device/ornament).
At that time, conscriptions and levies never ceased,
the people could not endure the hardship,
and transgressors of the law were numerous.
Xíngzhōu had long been without a chief official,
and the prisoners in its jails numbered over four hundred.
When Shìjié arrived at his post, after little more than a month,
he had almost completely resolved and dispatched all cases.
He was appointed as the Shùzhí Jiāngjūn.
On a mission to Húlǐgǎi Lù,
upon his return he reported:
"The Qìdān tribes have mostly all rebelled,
and the common people are alarmed and uneasy.
Now the entire nation is invading the south.
If the rebels take advantage of this emptiness to occupy the fundamental heartland of the Eastern territory,
even if we gain Jiāng and Huái,
it will be of no benefit.
It would be best to first pacify the Qìdān;
the southern invasion will not be too late."
Hǎilíng was displeased and said:
"The imperial edict has already been issued.
Now, with thirty thousand troops and selected generals stationed north of Zhōngdū,
that is sufficient to suppress them."
Shìjié further said:
"If the great clans of the Eastern territory join the rebels,
I fear that thirty thousand men may not be easy to contend with."
Hǎilíng did not listen.
When he departed from Biànjīng,
he was appointed Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and concurrently served as the Fù Zǒngguǎn of the Wǔjié Army.
When the main army crossed the Huái River,
Shìjié led three thousand troops to escort provisions eastward,
defeating several thousand Sòng soldiers
and capturing many of their warships.
Upon reaching the border of Hézhōu,
he attacked five thousand Sòng soldiers and routed them.
The next day,
he sent his son Wùdié to lead two hundred and eighty cavalry as a supporting force,
while he himself led eight hundred cavalry to fight in the vanguard.
He consecutively shot over sixty men, all of whom fell at the sound of the bowstring.
The Sòng army then broke and fled.
Hǎilíng wanted to observe a naval battle,
and ordered Shìjié to lead a hundred men of the navy to try it.
The Sòng people had many large boats,
while Shìjié's boats were small.
He then advanced rapidly,
achieved victory in midstream, and returned.
In the early Dàdìng period,
Shìjié again took Shǎnxī Zhōu,
defeated Sòng soldiers at Shíháo Zhèn,
and again defeated three thousand Sòng reinforcements,
then besieged Shǎnxī Zhōu.
Two thousand Sòng soldiers came from Tóngguān.
Shìjié engaged them with two hundred and forty soldiers,
shooting and killing over ten men.
The Sòng soldiers were defeated and fled.
He again defeated them at Tǔháo Shān,
capturing one general alive.
He then led three hundred soldiers to Dǒumén Chéng,
where he encountered over ten thousand Sòng soldiers.
Three Sòng generals came forward with spears to stab Shìjié.
Shìjié used his saber to cut their spears,
and the Sòng soldiers then retreated.
He again used four Mòkè units to defeat Sòng soldiers at Tǔhuá,
and again besieged Shǎnxī Zhōu.
Shìjié often donned armor, wore his saber,
and carried a hundred arrows at his waist,
holding a spear and leaping onto his horse,
moving back and forth among the troops.
The enemy saw him and were astonished.
They said:
"He is truly a divine general!"
He personally led over two hundred chosen soldiers to dig tunnels and enter,
and the city was captured.
He again broke a Sòng army of thirty thousand men,
and recovered Guózhōu.
Not long after,
he was appointed Wèizhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and then transferred to Hénán Lù Tǒngjūn Dūjiān.
He was summoned to the court,
where the emperor comforted and praised him for a long time.
He was appointed Xīběi Lù Fùtǒng,
and bestowed with a horse, bow and arrows, and a saber.
He followed Púsàn Zhōngyì to suppress the Qìdān.
After the rebels were pacified,
he was appointed Huázhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and with Túdān Héxǐ, managed Lǒngyòu.
Héxǐ recovered Déshùn,
and upon reaching Dōngshān Bǎo,
Sòng soldiers blocked the firewood path.
Shìjié attacked and routed them,
pursuing them to the city walls.
About twenty thousand soldiers came out from the city.
He defeated them,
inflicting many casualties.
The Sòng Jīnglüèshǐ, Jīng Gāo, abandoned Déshùn and fled.
Shìjié and Zuǒ Dūjiān Zhāng pursued and broke their army.
He was appointed Bózhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and after four promotions, became Tōngyuǎn Jūnjié Dùshǐ.
The Sòng people often entered Gǒngzhōu territory to sell rice and flour.
The officials apprehended them.
Shìjié signed the document labeling them as "people who submitted,"
and released them.
The interpreter, Cài Sōngshòu, falsely accused the prefectural governor of plotting rebellion,
and he was executed.
In the eighteenth year,
he was reappointed Hóngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He left office due to mourning his mother.
He was successively promoted to Bózhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and then died.
Shìjié was poor in his youth,
but he was generous with his wealth and valued integrity.
Whenever he faced a battle,
once the enemy forces were defeated,
he would certainly warn his soldiers not to indulge in killing and looting.
In daily life, he would not speak unless it concerned loyalty or filial piety.
He befriended the virtuous and delighted in goodness,
and thus gained much praise from his contemporaries.
Xiāo Huáizhōng's original name was Hǎohú,
and he was a Xī person.
He served as Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
When Xiāo Yù and others plotted to establish a successor to the Liáo dynasty,
they sent Xiāo Zhāozhé to Xīběi Lù to connect with Huáizhōng,
and also to secure the support of Jǐedùshǐ Yēlǜ Lǎng.
Huáizhōng and Lǎng had a rift,
so he seized Zhāozhé and also seized Lǎng,
and sent an envoy to report the change.
After Yù and others were executed,
Huáizhōng became Pūmì Fùshǐ,
and was granted his current name.
He again served as Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
Xījīng Liúshǒu,
and was enfeoffed as a king.
He was then transferred to Nánjīng Liúshǒu.
When the Qìdān Sābā rebelled,
Huáizhōng was again made Xījīng Liúshǒu and Xīnánmiàn Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng,
and was sent with Pūmìshǐ Púsàn Sīgōng, Běijīng Liúshǒu Xiāo Zé, Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn Xiāo Tūlà, and the head of ten guards, Wòlúbǎo, to suppress him.
Xiāo Tūlà achieved nothing in battle,
and the main army failed to catch Sābā.
However, Hǎilíng believed that Huáizhōng and Xiāo Yù were both Qìdān people,
originally co-conspirators,
and only after a year did he seize Zhāozhé and report the change.
Furthermore, Sābā was also of the Qìdān tribe,
and he feared their alliance.
Because Sīgōng spoke secretly with the Empress Dowager,
and Tūlà had no achievements,
and Huáizhōng, Zé, and Sīgōng allowed the rebel to escape,
he first killed Sīgōng
and exterminated his clan.
He then sent an envoy to the army to kill Zé and Huáizhōng,
and their clans were also exterminated.
Wòlúbǎo
and Tūlà were initially considered the main culprits,
but were only executed.
In the third year of Dàdìng,
Zé, Huáizhōng, Tūlà, and Wòlúbǎo's official ranks and titles were posthumously restored.
Yí's younger brother, Ānzhōu Cìshǐ Zé, requested to inherit Zé's Mòkè position.
The emperor did not permit the Mòkè, but gave Zé's family property to him.
Yílà Àndá
was a Liáo Héngzhàng person.
His father, Liúwò,
and Yēlǜ Yúdǔ both surrendered.
After Xījīng fell,
they rebelled again,
and Liúwò was killed.
Àndá, as the son of a person who died for the cause,
was appointed Zuǒ Fèngchén.
In the early Xīzōng period,
he served as a personal guard,
then was appointed Ānzhōu Cìshǐ,
and successively rose to Tōnjīng Fùliúshǒu.
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Wányán Shǒudào managed the northern regions,
and acted as Xiánpíng Lù Túnjūn Dūtǒng.
He was appointed Bīngbù Shìláng,
and relocated the old forts and garrisons of the Xīběi and Xīnán regions that were too close to the interior to the extreme borders.
These were to connect with the border forts of Tàizhōu and Línhuáng.
He was appointed Wǔdìng Jūnjié Dùshǐ,
and for his achievements in attracting border tribes, was promoted to Dōngběi Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
then transferred to Línhuáng Yǐn,
and then died.
Àndá was unparalleled in horsemanship and archery,
and was good at judging horses.
Once, when discussing skilled archers,
Shìzōng said:
"Can anyone be as good as you?"
When inspecting horses in the market,
if he saw a good horse,
even if it was emaciated,
he would always buy it at a good price.
On another day, it would indeed be a good horse.
Bèi Shùlǔ Ālǔhǎn,
a native of Pálígé Mountain, Lóngzhōu.
At the age of eight,
he was selected to learn Khitan script,
and then selected again to learn Jurchen script.
When he grew up,
he became a lìshǐ in the Wànhù office of Huánglóng Fǔlù.
In the second year of Zhēnyuán,
three hundred xiūlì from outer circuits were tested for appointment to court positions.
Ālǔhǎn placed first,
and was appointed lìshǐ of the Zōngzhèng Fǔ.
He was successively promoted to lìshǐ of the Shàngshū Shěng.
Púsàn Zhōngyì, when campaigning against Wōwò,
recruited him into his staff,
where he managed frontier documents,
and was greatly trusted.
After Wōwò was pacified,
Ālǔhǎn gathered scattered and lost people,
and tens of thousands resumed their occupations.
He then followed Zhōngyì in campaigning against Sòng,
frequently entering to make reports,
discussing what was feasible and what was not.
The Emperor said to his prime minister:
“What Ālǔhǎn says,
if it is feasible, then implement it.”
When the Sòng people requested peace,
Zhōngyì sent Ālǔhǎn.
After the peace agreement was settled,
Ālǔhǎn entered to report,
and was granted one hundred taels of silver and ten bolts of rich brocade.
Zhōngyì recommended that Ālǔhǎn had talent and ability,
and could be appointed Dūshì of the Shàngshū Shěng.
An imperial edict appointed him Dàlǐ Sīzhí.
Not long after,
he was granted the position of Dūshì of the Shàngshū Shěng,
and then appointed Tóngzhī Shùntiān Jūn Jiédù Shì.
When Gēshíliè Zhìníng made his northern inspection,
Ālǔhǎn temporarily held the post of Zuǒyòu Sī Lángzhōng.
Upon his return to court,
he was appointed Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng,
and then promoted again to Shìyùshǐ.
The Emperor asked Gēshíliè Liángbì:
“What kind of person is Ālǔhǎn?”
He replied:
“He has ability and talent,
his heart is loyal and upright,
and his words are not flattering.”
A few days later,
he was promoted to Quànnóng Fùshǐ,
concurrently Tóngxiū Guóshǐ,
with his Shìyùshǐ post remaining.
He was then changed to Yòusī Lángzhōng.
He memorialized to request that the Hénán garrison troops encamped within the city walls be moved to outside ten lǐ,
and this was granted.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shìláng,
and then appointed Shāndōng Tǒngjūn Dūjiān,
and moved the eight Měngān to Hénán.
He was promoted to Wǔshèng Jūn Jiédù Shǐ.
[一一]He entered the court as Lìbù Shàngshū,
and was then changed to Xīnán Lù Zhāotǎo Shǐ.
The authorities pressed the Měngān households in his circuit to repay official grain loans.
Ālǔhǎn petitioned to await a year of good harvest,
which was granted.
There were soldiers who traded armor plates for various goods
at the Tiāndé border market and outside the border annually mined copper.
Some also privately carried military iron to trade with them;
all of this was completely prohibited.
Frontier soldiers were not allowed to use relatives, slaves, or hired laborers.
Damaged encampments were to be repaired in a timely manner.
He did not feast with the Měngān and Mǒukè under his command,
hence both soldiers and common people respected and loved him.
The Emperor said to Tàiwèi Shǒudào:
“Ālǔhǎn and Shàngjīng Liúshǒu Wányán Wūlǐyě both rose from being xiūlì.
Ālǔhǎn is a man of greater integrity;
his virtue surpasses the other.”
He was changed to Shǎnxī Lù Tǒngjūn Shǐ concurrently Jīngzhào Yǐn.
There were vacancies in the Shǎnxī military registry.
The old practice was to fill them with sons and brothers,
but most were not capable.
Ālǔhǎn selected and supplemented from among the Ālǐxǐ flag-and-drum bearers.
Soldiers would graze their horses in spring,
but would not collect and feed them through summer,
resulting in many becoming emaciated and dying.
Ālǔhǎn ordered them to be collected and fed in a timely manner,
thus fewer died or were injured.
He also inspected the soldiers' horsemanship and archery in spring and autumn,
to strengthen military preparedness.
For those collecting lacquer in Zhōngnán,
he limited their time period
and checked their comings and goings,
to prevent spies.
The Emperor said to his prime minister:
“Wherever Ālǔhǎn has gone, he has been praised for his governance.
His political achievements in Shǎnxī are particularly notable.
Although he was employed late,
he can still provide several years of service.”
He was summoned to be Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
and ordered to list his actions in Tiāndé and Shǎnxī.
The Emperor praised them.
Due to illness, he requested retirement,
was appointed Běijīng Liúshǒu,
and died.
A eulogy states: The Records say,
“When a jūnzi hears the sound of chimes,
he thinks of ministers who died guarding the frontier.”
The Commentary says,
“In matters of the frontier,
one must carefully guard it and prepare for unforeseen circumstances.”
Therefore, ministers who guard and defend the borders cannot be left unmentioned.
Zhào Xīngxiáng,
a native of Lúlóng, Píngzhōu.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Sīwēn,
was Liáo Yānjīng Liúshǒu,
and was enfeoffed as Tiānshuǐ Jùnwáng.
His father, Jǐn,
was Liáo Jìngjiāng Jūn Jiédù Shǐ.
Xīngxiáng, by virtue of his father's appointment, was Gémén Zhīhòu.
He requested leave to visit his parents in Báixì.
At that time, in the late Liáo period, local bandits occupied the commandery and rebelled.
Xīngxiáng took his mother, younger brothers, and sisters and fled to Yānjīng,
but could not proceed.
So he crossed the sandy desert from Liǔchéng,
traveling by night by the stars.
He barely reached the Liáo army,
but did not know the Liáo ruler's whereabouts,
and so returned to Liǔchéng.
When Lóushì captured the Liáo ruler,
Xīngxiáng then returned to the (Jīn) state,
followed Zōngwàng in campaigning against Sòng,
and became Liùzhái Shǐ.
In early Tiānjuàn,
he was successively promoted to Tóngzhī Xuānhuī Yuànshì.
He resigned from office due to mourning for his mother.
Xīzōng had long heard of Xīngxiáng's filial conduct.
When Yīngdào Tàizǐ was formally invested,
he was reinstated to his original post,
to guard and attend the Crown Prince.
He was transferred to Yòu Xuānhuī Shǐ.
In early Tiāndé,
he was changed to Zuǒ Xuānhuī Shǐ.
Hǎilíng once asked Xīngxiáng,
wishing to appoint his sons and brothers to official positions,
that he should speak up.
Xīngxiáng declined with thanks.
Hǎilíng approved of this,
and granted him a jade belt,
with an imperial edict stating:
“Although your rank has not yet reached the first grade,
you may wear this when attending.”
He became Jìnán Yǐn,
and was granted carriages, horses, gold and silk fabrics, and gold and silver vessels.
He was changed to Jiàngyáng Jūn Jiédù Shǐ,
summoned to be Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo,
enfeoffed as Guǎngpíng Jùnwáng,
and then re-enfeoffed as Jùlù.
In early Zhènglóng,
by general rule, his princely title was revoked.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Shǎofù,
enfeoffed as Shēn Guógōng,
and then reinstated as Dìngwǔ Jūn Jiédù Shǐ.
When Hǎilíng campaigned against Sòng,
Xīngxiáng's two sons accompanied the army.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Hǎilíng was still in Huáinán,
and his two sons had not yet returned.
Xīngxiáng came to see Shìzōng in Píngzhōu.
Shìzōng praised his sincerity and loyalty,
appointed him Mìshū Jiān,
and reinstated him as Zuǒ Xuānhuī Shǐ.
The Emperor said:
“The cooks in the Imperial Kitchen are too numerous,
merely wasting salaries.
When I was in the princely residence,
all household affairs were entrusted to those in charge.
Since my ascension,
I have paid close attention to everything.
Salaries come from the common people;
they cannot be squandered.
The number of cooks should be appropriately reduced.”
A close minister presented a pípa.
Shìzōng rejected it,
saying to Xīngxiáng:
“I am anxious and toiling for the empire;
I have never focused on music or entertainment.
From now on, there shall be no more such presentations.
You should fully convey my intention.”
The authorities reported that border affairs in the north and south were not yet settled,
fearing that finances would be insufficient,
and requested to halt the construction work on the cool pavilion of Shénlóng Diàn.
The Emperor immediately had Xīngxiáng transmit an edict to stop it.
After a long time,
he appointed Xīngxiáng's grandson, Xún, as Gémén Zhīhòu.
Máo Shuò 毛碩, courtesy name Zhòngquán 仲權,
was a native of Gānlíng 甘陵.
At the end of the Sòng 宋 dynasty,
when youths capable in archery and horsemanship were tested,
Shuò 碩 was selected
and appointed to the Prepared Service of the Gaōyángguān Lù Ānfǔ Sī 高陽關路安撫司.
Soon after, he was appointed Hedān Wèi 河間尉,
then promoted to Bīngmǎ Dūjiān 兵馬都監.
When Zōngwàng's 宗望 army arrived,
Shuò 碩 led his unit to surrender.
When the Qí Guó 齊國 was established,
he was promoted from First Deputy General of Huáidōng Lù 淮東路 to Zhī Huázhōu 知滑州.
When Liú Lín 劉麟 attacked Sòng 宋,
he served as the Tǒngzhì Jūnmǎ 統制軍馬 of the Xíngyíng Zhōngjūn 行營中軍.
During the Tiānjuàn 天眷 reign,
he successively served as Bīngmǎ Dūjiān 兵馬都監 for Biànjīng Lù 汴京路 and Shāndōng Xī Lù 山東西路.
In the first year of Huángtǒng 皇統,
he was appointed Qúanzhī Gǒngzhōu 權知拱州.
When the Sòng 宋 general Zhāng Jùn 張俊 occupied Bózhōu 亳州,
and Fáng Rénjié 房人傑, the wine supervisor of Zhéchèng 柘城, rebelled to support Jùn 俊,
Shuò 碩 dispatched troops to suppress him.
Upon arriving at Zhéchèng 柘城,
he personally knocked on the city gate,
and called out to the elders to explain his intentions.
The county people bound Rénjié 人傑 and surrendered.
Shuò 碩 directly entered the county office
and summoned the common people to comfort them.
Everyone was grateful and pleased,
and carved a stone to commemorate the event.
In the fourth year,
he was formally appointed Gǒngzhōu Cìshǐ 拱州刺史.
Marshal Liáng Wáng Zōngbì 梁王宗弼, acting by imperial command, promoted him to Chāo Wǔyì Jiāngjūn 超武義將軍,
and transferred him to Zhī Cáozhōu 知曹州.
A scholar submitted a letter to Shuò 碩,
the language of which involved slander and ridicule.
His subordinates were all unable to tolerate it.
Shuò 碩 invited him to the seat of honor
and thanked him, saying:
“If I could often hear such words,
I would perhaps have fewer faults.”
Thus, the scholars praised him.
He was promoted to Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ 鄭州防禦使,
and soon after transferred to Tōngzhōu 通州.
In the second year of Tiāndé 天德,
he was appointed Shǎnxī Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ 陝西路轉運使.
Shuò 碩 noted that the right side of Shǎnxī 陝西 was remote and barren,
and crops were limited to hemp and millet,
and buckwheat.
Tax revenues were very meager.
Market transactions were only in Sichuan silk and dried ginger,
and commerce was not developed.
Income from wine tax had decreased.
He requested that the circulation of banknotes be permitted according to the precedents of Biànjīng 汴京 and Yānjīng 燕京.
Furthermore, the roads in Gǒng 鞏, Kuài 會, and Déshùn 德順 were often dangerous,
and the weight of salt permits was too heavy.
He requested that one permit be divided into three or four,
for greater convenience.
The court adopted all his proposals.
There was old grain stored in Qínzhōu 秦州 granaries,
and for those common people who needed to relocate,
they were allowed to pay the equivalent value in their original prefecture,
which was convenient for both the government and the people.
He was transferred to Hédōng Nánlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ 河東南路轉運使.
He submitted a memorial saying:
“Recently,
when the commercial wine tax was established,
it did not take into account the richness or scarcity of local products, the size of the population, or the increase or decrease in prices then and now.
Instead, a uniform tax was levied,
causing supervising officials to be arrested,
lose their positions and ruin their families,
or flee as hired laborers.
Some corrupt officials secretly took real money,
and submitted credit vouchers to the government.
Consequently, Hédōng 河東 accumulated a debt of over four million guàn 貫,
which caused suffering to both the government and the people.
I request that from now on, wine officials be prohibited
from offsetting or lending on credit,
and only be allowed to collect real money.
Then both officials and common people will benefit.”
This policy has been in effect ever since.
Upon completing his term,
he was appointed Nánjīng Lù Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ 南京路都轉運使.
In the sixth year of Dàdìng 大定,
he retired,
and passed away at home.
Shuò 碩 was refined and fond of good deeds,
and his character was cautious and disciplined.
Whenever he saw the beneficial actions of ancient people,
he would often write them down and place them by his seat,
as a warning for his conduct in office.
Lǐ Shàngdá 李上達, courtesy name Dádào 達道,
was a native of Jìyīn 濟陰, Cáozhōu 曹州.
During the Sòng 宋 dynasty, he entered officialdom through hereditary privilege,
and successively served as Sīhù Cānjūn 司戶參軍 of Dōngpíng Fǔ 東平府.
When Tàlǎn 撻懶 captured Dōngpíng 東平,
Shàngdá 上達 provided military supplies
and was renowned for his organizational skills.
When the Qí Guó 齊國 was established,
he became Lìbù Yuánwàiláng 吏部員外郎,
and concurrently managed the affairs of Hùbù 戶部.
Liú Yù 劉豫 implemented the "one-tenth law,"
whereby more was collected in good years and less in lean years.
This was indeed an ancient system of taxation.
However, at the time of collection,
people would hoard and conceal their produce,
and the officials would not fully trust them.
Consequently, accusations arose, and lawsuits multiplied,
causing suffering to both the government and the people.
Shàngdá 上達 discussed these abuses,
and Yù 豫 revised the system to five grades.
When the Qí Guó 齊國 was abolished,
and Hénán 河南 was returned to the Sòng 宋 people,
Shàngdá 上達 followed the territory and returned to Sòng 宋.
When Zōngbì 宗弼 recaptured Hénán 河南,
Shàngdá 上達 became Tóngzhī Dàmíng Yǐn 同知大名尹,
and inspected Shǎnxī 陝西 and Hénán 河南.
At that time,
the people of Guān 關, Shǎn 陝, Pú 蒲, Xiè 解, Rǔ 汝, and Cài 蔡 suffered from famine.
Shàngdá 上達 readily took the initiative to open granaries and distribute grain to the populace.
He was successively promoted to Zhī Shāndōng Xī Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ 知山東西路轉運使.
Within two terms of Shàngdá 上達 taking office,
the revenue increased by over 300,000 guàn 貫 compared to before.
The Hùbù 戶部 then promulgated his method to neighboring circuits.
Shàngdá 上達 was skilled in official affairs
and capable of managing complex matters.
Corrupt officials could not deceive him,
and he was praised wherever he went.
He died in office
at the age of sixty-one.
Cáo Wàngzhī 曹望之, courtesy name Jǐngxiāo 景蕭,
his ancestors were from Línhuáng 臨潢,
and in the late Liáo 遼 dynasty, his family moved to Xuāndé 宣德.
During the Tiānhuì 天會 reign,
he was selected as a Nǚzhí Zì Xuéshēng 女直字學生 due to being the son of an excellent commoner.
At the age of fourteen,
he completed his studies
and was appointed Xīwèi Jiàoshòu 西京教授.
He served as a Shūlìshǐ 書令史 in the Yuánshuài Fǔ 元帥府,
was promoted to Zhènglìshǐ 正令史,
then transferred to Xíngtái Shěng Lìshǐ 行臺省令史.
Based on his qualifications as a professor,
he was appointed Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi 修武校尉,
and then Yòusī Dūshì 右司都事.
Lìbù Shìláng Tián Jué 吏部侍郎田瑴 had always disdained Wàngzhī 望之.
Wàngzhī 望之 wished to befriend him but he refused,
and thus collaborated with Cài Sōngnián 蔡松年 and Xǔ Lín 許霖 to frame him in a factional case.
He was transferred to Xíngtái Lìbù Yuánwàiláng 行臺吏部員外郎.
When Hǎilíng 海陵 became chancellor,
he once wrote to Wàngzhī 望之 regarding a private matter,
but Wàngzhī 望之 did not comply.
In the first year of Tiāndé 天德,
he was transferred to Tóngzhī Shízhōu Jūnguān Shì 同知石州軍州事,
but was dismissed due to an incident.
After observing a long period of mourning for his mother,
he was appointed Jiàngyángjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ 絳陽軍節度副使,
and then entered the court as Hùbù Yuánwàiláng 戶部員外郎.
An imperial edict ordered the purchase of ten thousand cattle to be given to Ānchūhǔ Bāměng'ān 按出虎八猛安 who had relocated to Nánjīng 南京;
Wàngzhī 望之 was in charge of their distribution.
When Sābā 撒八 rebelled,
he was tasked with transporting eighty thousand sets of armor from Míngzhōu 洺州 to Yànzǐchéng 燕子城.
He also transported eight hundred thousand hú 斛 of rice from Cáishuǐ 蔡水 into the Huái 淮 River
to supply the armies attacking Sòng 宋,
with a deadline of one day.
Wàngzhī 望之 completed the task on schedule.
He was promoted to Lángzhōng 郎中 of his department,
and specially awarded the Jinshì Jídì 進士及第.
At the beginning of Dàdìng 大定,
when Wōwò 窩斡 was suppressed,
Wàngzhī 望之 was in charge of army provisions.
He managed the supplies with restraint,
saving 300,000 dàn 擔 of grain
and 500,000 dàn 擔 of fodder.
When the Marshal's office reported the victory,
some suggested to immediately halt the transport of supplies,
but Wàngzhī 望之 believed that the chief culprit had not yet been executed,
and preparedness should not be relaxed.
Later, when the main army pursued the rebels,
they indeed relied on these provisions.
For his meritorious service, he was promoted one rank
and concurrently appointed Tóngxiū Guóshǐ 同修國史.
He requested that an official salt monopoly be established at Dàyánluò 大鹽濼,
allowing the people to trade with rice.
He argued that if people gathered to form settlements,
the border defenses could be strengthened,
and the benefits would be endless.
This was approved.
Subsequently, a total of over 200,000 dàn 擔 of rice were stored there.
When the northeastern circuit suffered famine,
countless people were saved by these provisions.
Three years later,
the Emperor said:
“Since the military uprising of Zhèng-Lóng,
agriculture and sericulture have been neglected,
and the Túntián of Méng-Ān and Móu-Kè often do not conform to regulations.”
An imperial edict was issued, sending Hu-Bù Shì-Láng Wèi Zǐ-Píng, Dà-Xīng Shǎo-Yǐn Tóng-Zhī Zhōng-Dū Zhuǎn-Yùn-Shì Lǐ Dí, Lǐ-Bù Shì-Láng Lǐ Yuàn, Lǐ-Bù Láng-Zhōng Yí-Lá Dào,
Hù-Bù Yuán-Wài-Láng Wán-Yán Wù-Gǔ-Chū, Jiān-Chá Yù-Shǐ Jiá-Gǔ Ā-Lǐ-Bǔ, and Wàng-Zhī to various routes to encourage farming,
and to investigate the integrity of officials.
Upon his return, Wàng-Zhī reported,
requesting the reduction of clerks in all routes,
which could be cut by half.
The edict ordered the clerks to remain as they were.
At this point, the use of ‘Tiē-Shū’ was first prohibited.
He was promoted to Běn-Bù Shì-Láng,
in charge of reviewing and repairing the financial expenditures of the imperial palace,
resulting in significant savings.
He was again promoted for his efforts,
and the Emperor summoned him for an encouraging audience.
Wàng-Zhī's household slave Yuán Yī-Yán was involved in matters of sorcery and delusion,
and the Dà-Xīng Fǔ conducted an investigation.
Wàng-Zhī was afraid,
and sent Hù-Bù Lì-Shǐ Liú Gōng-Fǔ to inquire about the matter with Dà-Xīng Shǎo-Yǐn Wáng Quán.
Wáng Quán fully explained the matter to Liú Gōng-Fǔ,
and Liú Gōng-Fǔ relayed it to Wàng-Zhī.
The Yù-Shǐ Tái impeached Liú Gōng-Fǔ for leaking judicial information.
The Emperor said:
“Why are such words of sorcery and delusion
being spread among people?”
Consequently,
Wàng-Zhī was given one hundred strokes of the stick,
Wáng Quán eighty strokes,
and Liú Gōng-Fǔ one hundred fifty strokes and dismissed from office.
Soon after,
the Grand Canal became blocked.
Shì-Zōng went to the outskirts and saw it,
asking the reason.
The officials in charge reported:
“The Hù-Bù was unwilling to plan and manage it,
and so over the years, it has come to this.”
The Emperor reprimanded Wàng-Zhī, saying:
“With water transport, if it is not dredged,
but instead land transport is used,
it burdens the people and wastes resources.
The fault lies with you and others.
Go and manage it.”
The Shàng-Shū Shěng reported that tens of thousands of laborers would be needed.
The Emperor said:
“It is spring plowing season,
and the people should not be burdened.
Use households from the Gōng-Jí-Jiān, and extract followers from the Dōng-Gōng and various princes for the labor.
If that is not enough, then supplement with military laborers from within five hundred *lǐ*.”
When the *Tài-Zōng Shí-Lù* was completed,
Jiān-Xiū Guó-Shǐ Hé-Shí-Liè Liáng-Bì was granted a golden belt and twenty bolts of fine silk.
Tóng-Xiū Guó-Shǐ Zhāng Jǐng-Rén, Liú Zhòng-Yuān, and Wàng-Zhī were all granted silver and silk of varying amounts.
Wàng-Zhī lamented the meager reward,
saying to others:
“Planting flowers and grafting trees leads to titles and appointments,
while diligent laborers are not promoted.”
Before long,
Zhāng Jǐng-Rén was promoted to Hàn-Lín Xué-Shì.
Wàng-Zhī again said:
“Others are readily promoted,
but why not me?”
When Shì-Zōng heard this,
he sent Wàng-Zhī out as Dé-Zhōu Fáng-Yù-Shǐ,
saying to him:
“You are capable, but your heart is not loyal.
When I previously visited Ān-Zhōu for the spring hunt,
people said you lacked the duty of serving your sovereign.
I have instructed my officials
to remonstrate immediately if there is a fault.
You merely outwardly comply,
but criticize when you withdraw.
This is disloyalty and disrespect.
You were promoted from fifth rank to fourth rank.
When the *Tài-Zōng Huáng-Dì Shí-Lù* was completed,
you were generously granted silver and silk.
Instead of thinking of devoting yourself fully,
you only covet official rewards.
Now I send you out.
You should change your heart and cleanse your mind.
Otherwise,
you may not even preserve yourself.”
Upon arriving in Dé-Zhōu, Wàng-Zhī
implemented benevolent policies,
and the people erected a shrine for him while he was still alive.
He was later changed to Tóng-Zhī Xī-Jīng Liú-Shǒu-Shì.
He submitted a memorial discussing matters of expediency: Firstly,
he discussed how in Shān-Dōng and Hé-Běi, Méng-Ān and Móu-Kè were mixed with the common people,
causing many people to lose their livelihoods.
The area between Chén, Cài, Rǔ, and Yǐng was vast but sparsely
populated.
It would be advisable to relocate common people to settle these areas,
and remit their taxes for several years to pacify them.
For commoners who had fled or avoided military service,
their identities should be verified,
and they should be made
to return to their original registered households.
Or they could be registered in nearby counties as guest households,
