or those who remained as tenant farmers
should also have their names registered.
Cases involving both prefectures and counties and Méng-Ān should not be mutually
concealed,
so that the military and civilians might live in harmony,
and banditry would cease.
Secondly,
he discussed how the system of recommendation was empty and without substance.
The prime ministers promoted those they knew,
but not those they did not know.
Officials inside and outside the court often did
not use those recommended,
or accused them of forming factions,
thus they no longer dared to recommend.
It should be ordered that the chief ministers recommend two third-rank officials annually,
and from the Yù-Shǐ Dà-Fū down, officials inside and outside the court
should recommend two officials during their entire tenure.
From this down, the ranks would decrease proportionally.
Those who did not recommend during their entire tenure would be prevented from promotion when their turn came for transfer,
and third-rank officials would have three
months' salary deducted from their next appointment.
For those who were recommended and then transferred to another position,
the Lì-Bù should classify and grade them,
and report quarterly.
If there was a vacancy for a third-rank official, it would be filled from among the fourth-rank officials of the same category.
Fourth-rank and fifth-rank
officials below this would be handled proportionally.
For those to be treated exceptionally,
the chief ministers should report their talents, conduct, and achievements in detail.
The judgment of correct or incorrect recommendations would be punished according to the law.
Upright and incorruptible scholars
who grew old in secretariats without a patron, or who had served seven evaluations without corruption or private wrongdoing,
would be treated equivalently to court officials who had served three evaluations with merit.
The Lì-Bù should annually chart the names of officials in outer
routes,
with each route having a chart,
and prominently mark corrupt individuals below their names,
to instill caution.
When outside officials of fifth rank and above were transferred,
their successors should report
their merits and demerits.
Those aged sixty and above,
who no longer needed to attend periodic selection,
should have their eyesight, hearing, and vigor checked by the authorities.
If they were old and sick and unable to perform their duties,
they should be given half their salary
and retired.
Thirdly,
he discussed how border generals and commanders and officials in border prefectures and counties exploited the military and civilians,
and arbitrarily conscripted forced labor.
It should be ordered that Jiān-Chá Yù-Shǐ be sent annually to inspect.
In border disputes,
the Zhāo-Tǎo-Sī should not arbitrarily send unauthorized personnel to conduct investigations and judgments.
Instead, from among those in the provinces and ministries who had graduated, or from Nǚ-Zhēn and Qì-Dān people, or from among county magistrates, assistant magistrates, and registrars,
select those who are incorruptible and capable.
Based on their customs,
briefly establish regulations,
striving for simplicity.
The number of sheep and horses levied and entered into official registers,
if the border areas encountered famine,
should be used
to provide relief.
Zhāo-Tǎo and Dū-Jiān-Shì-Shì should limit the amount of camels and horses supplied by the border regions.
Nǚ-Zhēn households under the Zhāo-Tǎo-Sī sometimes gathered wild vegetables to supplement their meager
food,
while in the military, according to old regulations, if a horse died, a village would pool money to buy a replacement,
often forcing them to sell wives and children, or plow cattle to acquire it.
I fear that after several years, the border
defenses will be impoverished and depleted.
Providing relief at that time will
cost ten times as much and be of no benefit.
If measures are taken early,
then finances will be saved and border defenses will be strengthened.
Official issue of arrows for the military, when
used up,
are supplemented by purchasing from the market,
which are all rotten and blunt and unusable.
It would be better to issue an annual supply of official arrows
to make up for the deficiency.
For border people lacking food, if rice is issued,
due to the long distances
and heavy burdens,
they often sell it cheaply at granaries and leave.
It would be better to distribute money based on household size,
which would benefit both public and private interests.
For the chief and deputy officials in Shǎn-Xī,
it would be advisable to appoint one local person, like the Méng-Ān and Móu-Kè.
Squad leaders should also include local people,
who should hold their posts for a long time.
Increase the bow and arrow fields,
and restore their taxes and corvée.
Appoint incorruptible officials as Tí-Jǔ,
to supervise the Zǒng-Guǎn.
officials below the prefectural level.
During the slack season for agriculture, they should be reviewed
to strengthen military preparedness.
Thus, even in times of peace, there would be a system of strategic planning.
He also discussed the use of personnel for the six salt fields,
suggesting that the Ministry of Revenue should publicly deliberate and appoint them.
Regarding grain transport by canal,
he first calculated how much grain was currently stored in river granaries,
how much Tongzhōu could accommodate,
and how much the capital consumed annually.
Currently, the annual tax revenue of prefectures and counties near the river was sometimes
sixty or seventy thousand shí.
Common people incurred expenses for contributing funds,
while wealthy households profited from transportation.
He suggested calculating the actual amount to levy taxes accordingly.
Regarding the proliferation of poor quality private currency among the people,
he suggested that 500 units of official currency should exchange for 1,000 units of private currency,
with a one-month period for exchange.
After the deadline, those who held private currency would be punished according to the law for destroying currency.
Regarding the money and goods for corvée labor in prefectures and counties,
the Ministry of Revenue should issue printed blank registers,
requiring all to be recorded therein,
to await scrutiny.
Those who feared or avoided recording would be punished.
He argued that the Ministry of Works' demands for construction
hindered people's livelihoods.
For the military units drawing grain rations across all circuits, he suggested estimating the number of people,
training them in martial arts,
with a three-year period for completion,
to alleviate
the impressment of commoners.
His memorials were submitted
and many were adopted.
He was appointed as an official to manage the affairs of the six ministries in the northern border region,
and then summoned and appointed as Hùbù Shàngshū.
The Emperor admonished him, saying:
"You were previously a Shìláng and were sent out due to disloyalty.
However, you are quite skilled in managing money and grain,
so I entrust you with the important post of Shàngshū.
You should correct your past mistakes
and strive for new achievements."
At that time,
Hùbù Shàngshū Gāo Déjī was demoted for overestimating the value of official salaries paid in grain.
Shìzōng, fearing Wàngzhī would be stingy in disbursements or perhaps punishing Déjī,
after Wàngzhī left,
sent someone to instruct him, saying:
"Do not devalue the grain as Gāo Déjī did;
the key is simply to make a fair assessment."
In the fifteenth year, when the new palace was completed,
Shìzōng visited the new palace
and issued an edict to Wàngzhī, saying:
"Whatever is needed in the new palace
must not be taken from the common people."
There was a case of a good commoner couple who pledged themselves to Wányán Gòuyīng, the Liúshǒu of Dōngjīng,
but were not released when their term ended.
The Shàngshūshěng ordered Dōngjīng to investigate and handle the case.
Wàngzhī stated that since Gòuyīng was the Liúshǒu,
his colleagues would surely show favoritism
and not thoroughly investigate.
The case should be transferred to another prefecture.
Wàngzhī had long been familiar with affairs
and had a reputation for managing money and grain.
He was inherently stubborn and opinionated,
and quite fond of showing off,
hoping to become a chief minister.
Meanwhile, Xíngbù Shàngshū Liáng Sù, upon his return from a detailed inquiry with the Song envoy,
Shìzōng had once considered making him a chief minister,
but had not yet used him.
He also quite conspicuously sought promotion.
Shìzōng said to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Hélíshí Liángbì:
"Cáo Wàngzhī and Liáng Sù are eager to be recognized
and are inclined towards rash advancement."
Subsequently, Liáng Sù was sent out as the Yǐn of Jìnán.
Several years later,
he was recalled and appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Wàngzhī, however, died as Hùbù Shàngshū
at the age of fifty-six.
Shìzōng regretted that he had not been fully utilized,
and bestowed 3,000 guàn of cash,
ordered an imperial envoy to offer sacrifices,
and granted 500 liǎng of silver, twenty bolts of patterned silk, and 200 bolts of plain silk as funeral gifts.
His son Yuān was appointed Fèngyù,
and his son Zé was appointed Bǐyàn Chéngfèng.
Later,
the Shàngniǎnjú recommended a former official over sixty years old who could handle matters,
and Shìzōng said:
"How could I begrudge official positions to such people?
But these people specialize in devising schemes to embezzle official funds for their livelihood,
so they cannot be used."
Therefore, he wanted to change the format for supervising officials
and consulted Hùbù Shàngshū Liú Wěi.
Wěi feared that supervising officials would slander him
and was unwilling to answer truthfully.
Shìzōng then thought of Wàngzhī
and sighed, saying:
"He is not as courageous in action as Wàngzhī was."
Wàngzhī was initially uneducated,
but after he became prominent,
he gradually learned to read
and then painstakingly dedicated himself to scholarship,
producing a collection of thirty volumes of poetry.
Dà Huáizhēn, courtesy name Zǐzhèng,
was a native of Liáoyáng.
In the fifth year of Huángtǒng,
he was appointed Gé Mén Zhīhòu,
and successively promoted three times to Dōng Shàng Gé Mén Shǐ.
After observing mourning for his mother,
he was reinstated as Fúbǎo Láng,
and successively promoted to Yòu Xuānhuī Shǐ.
During Zhènglóng's campaign against Song,
he served as Wǔshèngjūn Dū Zǒngguǎn.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was appointed Míngzhōu Fángyùshǐ concurrently with Yā Jūn Wànhù,
then transferred to Yízhōu,
and again promoted to Zhāngguó and Ānwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
A county尉 caught a thief
and found a banner with
the constellation Kàng depicted on it.
Upon interrogation,
there was evidence of a rebellion plot,
implicating tens of thousands of people.
Huáizhēn, treating it as a case of rebellious commoners,
requested the execution of the eighteen ringleaders,
and released all others.
He once, on a private memorial day, fed several monks,
and among them, one monk was unusual.
Huáizhēn asked:
"Where are you from?"
He replied:
"A native of Shānxī."
He asked again,
"Have you ever stolen or killed anyone?"
He replied:
"No."
Three days later, when interrogating thieves,
this monk was indeed implicated.
Everyone admired his keen observation,
and he was transferred to Xīngzhōng Yǐn.
A wealthy resident of Jǐnzhōu, Xiāo Hèshòu, committed murder on the road
and hid in the home of a Fǔ Shàoyǐn.
Officials could not apprehend him.
Huáizhēn captured him by stratagem
and brought him to justice.
He was transferred to Zhāngdéjūn Jiédùshǐ
and died.
Lú Xiàojiǎn
was a native of Xuāndézhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Tiānjuàn,
was appointed Xìanzhōu Jūnshì Pàn Guān,
then assigned as Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
and successively promoted to Tàiyuán Shàoyǐn.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
there was a military campaign in Shǎnxī,
and the Shàngshūshěng ordered the local tax grain to be sent to Píngliáng for military provisions,
with a very strict and pressing deadline.
Xiàojiǎn promptly substituted it with gold and silk,
galloped to Píngliáng,
used it economically without missing the deadline,
and everyone praised him.
For his integrity, he was promoted two ranks,
and transferred to Tóngzhī Guǎngníng Yǐn.
Guǎngníng suffered a great famine,
and many people were displaced and jobless.
He borrowed grain from monks,
leaving them one year's supply,
and had it sold at a fair price to the poor people,
thereby both relieving the populace
and allowing the monks to profit.
He was successively promoted to Shāndōng Dōnglù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
Xiàojiǎn was always narrow-minded and irritable,
and had a falling out with his colleague Wáng Gōngjǐn.
His son once privately used government funds,
which Xiàojiǎn was unaware of.
Later, he was transferred to Héběi Xīlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and Gōngjǐn then exposed the matter.
Xiàojiǎn, hearing he was to be arrested,
could not fathom the reason.
Upon reaching Zhāngqiū,
he hanged himself and died.
Lú Yōng, courtesy name Zǐxiàn,
was a native of Fēngrùn, Jìzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in Dàdìng 28 (1188)
and was appointed as a Military Judicial Assistant (Jūnshì Pànguān) of Tángzhōu.
He was then re-appointed as the Magistrate of Dìngpíng County.
Yōng repaired an old weir
and channeled the Jīng River water to irrigate fields,
which benefited the people.
He was promoted to Clerk (Lìshǐ) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng),
then appointed as Vice Commissioner of Transportation (Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ) for Nánjīng,
and later transferred to Judicial Assistant of Household Registration (Hùjí Pànguān) for Zhōngdū.
After being assessed as incorruptible,
he was promoted to Principal (Zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù),
and successively served as Administrator (Zhìzhōng) of Fèngxiáng.
In Dà'ān 3 (1211),
soldiers for land reclamation (túntián jūnwèi) in Shǎnxī were conscripted to Zhōngdū.
Yōng was appointed to manage the affairs of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Shì),
in charge of military provisions.
When he reached Lùzhōu,
the reclamation soldiers were sent back.
Yōng was transferred to Inspector of Qiánzhōu,
then entered the court as Director (Lángzhōng) of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
In Zhìníng 1 (1213),
he was transferred to Vice Commissioner of Surveillance (Ànchá Fùshǐ) for Shǎnxī.
When the Xià people invaded the border,
Yōng repaired the city walls of Píngliáng,
accumulated fodder and grain,
and organized local militia for defense.
In the eleventh month,
the Xià people plundered Zhènrónɡ,
captured Jīnɡ and Bīn,
and then besieged Píngliáng.
Yōng ran out of arrows,
so he recruited people to retrieve arrows shot by Xià soldiers onto the city walls to meet urgent needs.
He distributed rewards from the official treasury to those who performed meritorious deeds.
People were willing to die for him,
and Píngliáng was thus preserved.
In Zhēnyòu 2 (1214),
Yōng wrote to Púsàn Duān, the Administrator of the Shǎnxī Provincial Government (Xíngshěng),
generally stating that Qìnɡyánɡ, Píngliáng, and Déshùn were crucial strongholds in Shǎnxī,
and Bīn, west of Cháng'ān, served as a barrier,
which should be heavily garrisoned.
An imperial edict awarded his meritorious service in Píngliáng,
Yōng was promoted four ranks in office
and transferred to Commissioner of Surveillance and Transportation (Ànchá Zhuǎnyùn Shǐ).
In the third year,
an imperial edict instructed the Surveillance Commissioners (Ànchá Sī) of all circuits to study autumn defense.
Yōng presented his practical suggestions, saying:
"From Fūyán to Jīshí,
although there are many ravines and slopes,
there are no long rivers or great mountains to serve as a shield.
Relying on archers to resist invaders,
these people are all strong, fierce, and skilled in combat,
familiar with the local terrain,
and the Xià people fear them.
Previously, they were relocated elsewhere.
The Xià people immediately invaded the border,
which has been a serious problem in recent years.
People are attached to their land;
they farm and fight.
In times of urgency, they will spontaneously exert themselves."
He also said:
"During the autumn defense,
it is advisable to first clear the fields (qīnɡyě)."
He further said:
"Officials in charge of the military should not be replaced temporarily,
as this is taboo for military strategists.
If the general is not the right person,
what good is frequent replacement?"
Soon after,
someone said that Yōng was old and incompetent,
and he was dismissed.
Not long after,
he was transferred to Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Dìnghǎi.
As there was rebellion in Shāndōng,
he was unable to take up the post.
The Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchá Sī) impeached him,
and he was to be stripped of two offices,
but the judicial officer (shěnlǐguān) cleared him.
Yōng requested medical treatment due to illness
and subsequently retired.
In Xīngdìng 3 (1219),
he passed away.
Lǐ Sī, courtesy name Zǐyǒu,
was a native of Ānxǐ, Dìngzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in Tiānjuàn 2 (1139)
and was appointed as a Clerk (Bù) of Liáoshān.
He successively served as Principal (Zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
Upon the death of his mother, he observed mourning,
then resumed his former post,
and was appointed as Concurrent Commissioner of Transportation (Tóngzhī Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Shì) for Hédōng Southern Circuit.
In the early Dàdìng period (1161-1189),
he was transferred to Concurrent Grand Commissioner of Transportation (Tóngzhī Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Shì) for Zhōngdū Circuit.
When Púsàn Zhōngyì was acting as Provincial Administrator (Xíngshěng Shì) in Biànjīnɡ,
he recommended Sī for his staff.
Shìzōnɡ said:
"Lǐ Sī is currently managing the grain transportation affairs of the imperial capital (Jīnɡjī Cáoyùn Shì).
The provincial government (Xíngshěng) can choose someone else."
In the third year (1163),
he temporarily served as Director (Quánzhī) of the Court of Petitions (Dēnɡwén Jiǎnyuàn).
He was again promoted to Vice Minister (Shìlánɡ) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
The Emperor said:
"The Ministry of Revenue
handles the inflow and outflow of finances,
and I find it difficult to find the right person.
You are not an old hand,
and your qualifications are still shallow.
Do not assume that you will be promoted to the third rank simply because your term is full.
If you merely drift along year after year
and do not strive,
I will certainly not spare you."
During court assemblies, Sī often conversed privately with Gāo Déjī, keeping others away.
The Emperor heard of this and was puzzled.
He asked Right Chancellor (Yòuchénɡ) Shí Jū:
"What kind of person is Lǐ Sī, really?"
Jū replied:
"He is merely a capable official."
He was transferred to Concurrent Acting Superintendent of Běijīnɡ (Tóngzhī Běijīnɡ Liúshǒu) and Defense Commissioner (Fánɡyùshǐ) of Yízhōu.
Yízhōu was a border prefecture in the south.
The Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) issued a document requesting the use of idle land from the people
to plant grain for straw,
to be prepared for urgent military needs.
Sī said:
"This would cause farmers to lose their livelihoods."
He fully reported this and stopped it.
The Transportation Commissioner (Zhuǎnyùn Sī) issued a document to the prefecture to transport grain to Qúshān,
mobilizing tens of thousands of emergency laborers.
At that time, there was prolonged rain and muddy roads,
making transportation impossible.
Sī sent an official to Qúshān to investigate the official granary there,
and found that the stored grain could last for half a year.
He immediately reported this matter to the Transportation Commissioner (Yùn Sī)
and requested to extend the deadline,
so as not to distress the people.
Previously,
people were allowed to build stalls and shops (chánshè) in the streets and alleys of prefectures and counties,
and rent was collected from them.
By this time,
the collection of rent was abolished,
and all stalls and shops were demolished.
Other prefectures obeyed the orders
and compelled the people to completely demolish everything,
until the streets and alleys were straight as a string and as clear as arrows, returning to their original state, before stopping.
Sī, however, only instructed the people to remove and repair three to five irregular structures at the front,
and once the lanes and roads were neat, that was sufficient.
The people found this convenient.
He was transferred to Transportation Commissioner (Zhuǎnyùnshǐ) for Shǎnxī Western Circuit,
and then passed away.
A eulogy says: Máo Shuò, Lǐ Shànɡdá, Cáo Wànɡzhī, Lǐ Sī and their like,
were all capable officials of the Jīn Dynasty.
Wànɡzhī was eager to be employed in great capacities,
but a gentleman would not approve of this.
Túdān Kèníng's original name was Xíxiǎn.
His ancestors were from Jīnyuán County,
then moved to Bǐɡǔtǔ,
and later relocated to a Mènɡ'ān in Shāndōng,
thus settling in Láizhōu.
His father, Kuànɡ,
reached the official position of Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Fényánɡ Army.
Kèníng was naturally sincere and robust,
spoke little and rarely laughed.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
possessed courage and strategy,
and was conversant in both Nǚzhēn and Qìdān scripts.
Left Chancellor (Zuǒchénɡxiàng) Xīyǐn
was Kèníng's maternal uncle.
Xīzōnɡ asked Xīyǐn who among his relatives was suitable to be an imperial guard.
Xīyǐn replied:
"Xíxiǎn is capable."
So he was appointed as Bearer of Imperial Tallies (Fúbǎo Zhīhòu).
At that time,
Empress Dào interfered in politics.
Her brother, Péimǎn Hūtǔ, insulted Kèníng,
and Kèníng beat him.
The next day,
Hūtǔ reported this to Empress Dào,
who said:
"Xíxiǎn is upright and frank,
it must be your fault."
Later,
he served as Imperial Guard (Hùwèi),
then transferred to Director of Imperial Tallies (Fúbǎo Láng),
and promoted to Commander of the Imperial Vanguard Cavalry and Infantry (Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ),
then transferred to Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhōnɡshùn Army.
Kèníng married the County Princess of Jiāxiánɡ, the daughter of Zōnɡgàn.
His elder half-brother Pújiǎ was serving as Administrator of the Imperial Clan Court (Pàn Dàzōnɡzhènɡ Shì).
Hǎilín resented him in his heart,
appointed him as Acting Superintendent of Xījīnɡ,
fabricated charges, and executed him.
Consequently, Kèníng was demoted to Administrator of Ténɡyánɡ Army.

He successively served as Defense Commissioner (Fánɡyùshǐ) of Sùzhōu, Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Húlígǎi Circuit, and Grand Commandant of Troops and Horses (Bīngmǎ Dūzǒnɡguǎn) of Hélǎn Circuit.
In the early years of the Dàdìng reign,
an imperial edict commanded Kèníng to lead the soldiers from his circuit to rendezvous at Dōngjīng.
He was promoted to Left Wing Commander-in-Chief.
An imperial edict ordered him, along with Púsǎn Húntǎn, the Administrator of Guǎngníng, Wányán Yányǎ, Associate Administrator of Guǎngníng, and Tángkuò Wūyě, the Defense Commissioner of Zhàozhōu,
to follow the Right Vice-Marshal Wányán Móuyǎn in suppressing the Qìdān Wōwò.
They marched rapidly towards Jìzhōu.
Móuyǎn adopted the strategy of a surrendered Qìdān official who had offered to ambush the enemy's baggage train,
with Kèníng and Gēsīliè Zhìníng forming the rear guard.
They encountered the enemy at Chángluò.
Móuyǎn positioned an ambush on the flank of the left wing.
Over twenty thousand of the enemy pursued our rear,
and more than four hundred cavalry suddenly appeared between the left wing and the ambush,
intending to encircle our formation and attack us from the rear.
Kèníng, with over twenty skilled archers, resisted them.
The troops said:
"The enemy is numerous, and we are few.
It would be better to combine forces with the ambush,
or to rely on the main army,
for complete safety."
Kèníng said:
"No.
If the enemy gets behind our formation,
they will attack us from front and rear,
and we will be defeated.
We cannot wait for the main army."
Thereupon, they fought vigorously,
and the enemy retreated.
The Left Wing Myriarch Xiāng, combining forces with the main army, attacked them,
and the enemy was utterly defeated.
They pursued the fleeing enemy for over ten *lǐ*.
This was on the first day of the fourth month of the second year.
Nine days later,
they again caught up with the enemy at the Mùchè River.
The left wing army engaged the enemy first,
while Kèníng, with two thousand cavalry, pursued and enveloped them for fifteen *lǐ*.
The enemy, pressed against a ravine, could not cross quickly,
and suffered heavy casualties.
The enemy rallied their forces and turned their banners,
but the main army had not yet arrived.
Kèníng ordered his soldiers to dismount and shoot at the enemy,
who then withdrew southward.
At this time,
Wōwò had already fled north twice.
Marshal Móuyǎn, keen on plunder,
stationed his troops at Báiluò.
Shìzōng was surprised by the prolonged delay
and sent an envoy to inquire.
Móuyǎn said:
"The enemy cavalry is strong,
while our cavalry is weak.
This brief halt is for the purpose of resting and recuperating our horses.
Otherwise,
we cannot win without an additional ten thousand cavalry."
Kèníng vehemently stated:
"Our horses are certainly not few,
but the commander is not the right person.
His intention is always to profit from plunder;
when the enemy approaches, he withdraws to avoid them;
when the enemy departs, he slowly follows them.
Thus, the enemy always manages their horses well,
while we always pick up what they have trampled upon.
This is why our horses are weak.
If we can truly appoint a capable commander,
even without increasing our troops,
we can achieve success.
Otherwise,
even if our cavalry is ten times more numerous,
I do not see any benefit."
The court, aware of his advice,
recalled Móuyǎn
and appointed Púsǎn Zhōngyì, Minister of the Right and Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs, to concurrently serve as Right Vice-Marshal.
As the army was about to set out,
the enemy loudly declared their intention to surrender.
Kèníng said:
"The enemy, initially in distress,
has no genuine intention of surrendering.
Their public declaration
is meant to delay our army's departure.
It would be better to attack them while they are unprepared.
If the enemy is defeated,
their surrender will surely be swift.
If they do not surrender,
we should take advantage of their complacency and strike quickly,
settling the matter in one battle."
Zhōngyì agreed with this,
and so he and Kèníng advanced through the central route,
subsequently defeating the enemy forces at Luóbùlǔ.
The enemy fled to Qīduòhé,
where they built barricades relying on the treacherous terrain.
Kèníng observed that the rear of the enemy's barricade was ascendable,
so he secretly led his troops to climb it during the night,
shooting down at them.
The main army attacked from below,
and the enemy scattered,
all fleeing.
After the Qìdān were pacified,
Kèníng was appointed Administrator of Tàiyuán.
Less than a month later,
Wú Lín of Sòng invaded Shǎnxī's right flank.
The Right Inspector-General of the Marshal's Office, Túshān Héxǐ, requested more troops.
Kèníng was dispatched, bearing a golden tablet, to garrison Píngliáng.
An imperial edict to Héxǐ stated:
"I have sent Kèníng to participate in military discussions.
His wisdom and courage are sufficient to contend with ten thousand men,
so there is no need to add more troops."
Upon Kèníng's arrival,
he issued orders to pacify and settle the region.
Before long,
the people had all returned and gathered.
He organized his troops to attack Sòng.
The Right Chancellor Púsǎn Zhōngyì was stationed in Nánjīng to oversee all armies.
The Left Vice-Marshal Gēsīliè Zhìníng managed border affairs.
Kèníng was appointed Administrator of Yìdū,
concurrently serving as Supreme Commander of all military forces in the Shāndōng circuit and Marching Commander-in-Chief.
In the fourth year,
the Marshal's Office intended to send the Left Inspector-General Zhāng with four thousand troops to advance by water.
An imperial edict stated:
"This task should be entrusted to Commander-in-Chief Túshān Xíxiǎn,
with an additional two thousand troops,
and a good general chosen to assist him.
Zhāng can manage Shāndōng affairs."
Thereupon,
Kèníng led his army between Chǔ and Sì,
confronting the Sòng general Wèi Shèng at Shíbālǐkǒu in Chǔzhōu.
Wèi Shèng took old boats, drilled holes in their bottoms,
and inserted large timbers,
planting them in the water in rows.
Separately, he used boats to carry huge stones, threaded with iron chains,
and sank them to the bottom of the water,
to block Shíbālǐkǒu and the river crossing on the Huái River.
He stationed forty thousand infantry on the south bank of the Huái River crossing, between it and the Grand Canal.
Kèníng ordered Xiémǎo Héshàng to select skilled swimmers to dive underwater,
tie large ropes to the planted timbers,
and have hundreds of men on the bank pull the ropes to drag out each timber.
They pulled them all out
and cleared away the sunken boats.
They advanced to the mouth of the Huái River.
Sòng troops came to resist them,
firing arrows and stones from across the water.
Xiémǎo Héshàng used bamboo-woven fences to block the arrows and stones,
and again pulled out the planted timbers and sunken boats,
allowing the army to enter the Huái River.
They contended with the Sòng army for the crossing,
engaging in several battles.
Myriarch Chángshòu advanced first to the shallow bank.
The water was shallow,
so he first led several strong soldiers across the water to climb ashore,
defeating five hundred Sòng soldiers at the ford.
The rest of the troops then crossed.
Over four hundred Sòng soldiers came from Qīnghékǒu.
The Defender-General Púchá Ālíhégěnmǎn defended against them with one hundred infantry.
Kèníng himself, with Zhāyě Yínshùkě and five cavalrymen, advanced six or seven *lǐ* to engage them.
Yínshùkě was the first to charge,
fighting fiercely and defeating them.
The large Sòng army formed ranks and came to resist.
Kèníng waved his banner for his troops to advance and fight.
From dawn to noon,
the Sòng army was defeated,
crossing the Grand Canal to form a new formation.
Thousands of remaining Sòng troops fled into their camp.
Kèníng ordered rocket arrows to be shot at their camp,
burning it completely.
They crossed the river and dismantled the bridge,
meeting with their main army.
They shot at the Sòng troops from across the water,
preventing the Sòng army from forming a proper formation.
Myriarch Chāowù, with sixty cavalry, attacked over a thousand Sòng cavalry,
but was unsuccessful
and retreated slightly.
Kèníng, with Myriarch Sàilá and ninety cavalry, attacked them from the flank,
and the Sòng army was greatly defeated.
They pursued them to Chǔzhōu,
where Wèi Shèng was shot and killed.
They then captured Chǔzhōu and Huáin County.
In this campaign,
Sàilá contributed the most.
At this time,
Sòng repeatedly sent envoys to request peace.
Púsǎn Zhōngyì and Gēsīliè Zhìníng agreed to establish a relationship where the two nations would be perpetually uncle and nephew,
and to return the four prefectures of Hǎi, Sì, Táng, and Dèng.
The Sòng people still procrastinated with their requests,
but after Kèníng captured Chǔzhōu,
the Sòng people became greatly alarmed
and complied with every part of the agreement.
The troops were dismissed.
He was made Dàmíng Yǐn,
then successively Hélián and Dōngpíng Yǐn,
and was summoned to be Dūdiǎnjiǎn.
In the eleventh year,
he followed Chancellor Zhìníng on the northern expedition,
and the army returned.
In the eleventh month, on the Crown Prince’s birthday,
Shìzōng held a banquet in the Eastern Palace,
and bestowed a golden belt upon Kèníng.
The following year,
he was promoted to Shūmì Fùshǐ,
concurrently managing the affairs of Dàxīng Fǔ,
and was appointed Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
with Shūmì Fùshǐ as before.
He was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
and enfeoffed as Mì Guógōng.
Kèníng’s daughter married Shěn Wáng Yǒngchéng as his concubine,
and incurred displeasure.
Kèníng was displeased
and requested to retire,
which was not granted.
He was dismissed and made Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
The following year,
the Emperor intended to reinstate Kèníng as chancellor.
He was made Nánjīng Liúshǒu,
concurrently Hénán Tǒngjūnshǐ.
An envoy was sent to instruct him, saying:
"A Tǒngjūnshǐ has never concurrently held the position of Liúshǒu.
This is my intention.
You may pass through the capital and have an audience."
When Kèníng arrived at the capital,
he was again appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
and granted a hereditary bùzā-tǔhé-méng'ān concurrently qīn-guǎn-móukè.
Shìzōng wanted to personally bestow the imperial edict upon Kèníng,
but the official in charge did not understand the Emperor's intention.
By the time Kèníng had already received the edict,
the Emperor said to Kèníng:
"I wanted to personally bestow this edict upon you,
but it was mistakenly given to you outside."
He also said:
"I want to relocate all your clan members in Shāndōng to nearby areas.
Your clan is numerous,
and the official land is scarce,
so there is not enough to fully provide for them."
Therefore, he selected the closest relatives and relocated them.
In the nineteenth year,
he was appointed Yòuchéngxiàng,
and re-enfeoffed as Tán Guógōng.
Kèníng declined, saying:
"Your subject has no merit,
and does not understand the great affairs of the state.
Taking on such heavy responsibilities, both inside and outside,
I ought to be ashamed.
I beg to return to my hometown
to live out my remaining years."
The Emperor said:
"I consider that among all people, none surpasses you in merit.
You are prudent and possess the deportment of a great minister.
Do not decline further."
When Kèníng left the court,
the Emperor sent Túdān Huáizhōng to instruct him, saying:
"When people are drunk and sober, their actions differ.
Today, with your relatives and friends celebrating,
you may have a drink,
but after today, you should not drink."
Kèníng kowtowed and thanked him, saying:
"That Your Majesty thinks of your subject to this extent
is my good fortune."
When Kèníng was chancellor,
he upheld righteousness and maintained the grand principles,
and as for minor matters of documents and appointments,
he was not meticulous.
Shìzōng once said:
"Xí Xiǎn in the Shūmì (Chamber) never made a mistake."
He said to Kèníng:
"The duty of a chancellor
is primarily to promote the worthy."
Kèníng thanked him, saying:
"Your foolish subject is fortunate enough to hold the position of chancellor and aide,
but I am unable to clearly discern people,
and this is my regret."
In the twenty-first year,
Zuǒchéngxiàng Shǒudào became Shàngshū Lìng,
and Kèníng became Zuǒchéngxiàng,
re-enfeoffed as Dìng Guógōng.
He earnestly requested to retire.
The Emperor said:
"You have established merits and achieved deeds,
thus ascending to the chancellorship.
The court relies on you.
Although your age has come,
you cannot leave yet."
Three days later,
when he and Shǒudào presented matters,
they both knelt and pleaded, saying:
"Your subjects' teeth and hair are both declining.
We beg Your Majesty to grant us our remaining years."
The Emperor said:
"The Senior Chancellor sits and discusses the Way.
One values the person, not just the office.
How can it be frequently changed?"
After a moment,
Kèníng was made Shūmìshǐ,
and it was difficult to find a replacement for him.
Shǒudào was again made Zuǒchéngxiàng,
and the position of Shàngshū Lìng remained vacant for several years,
showing how highly it was regarded.
Not long after,
he was made Sītú concurrently Shūmìshǐ.
In the twenty-second year,
an imperial edict bestowed his current name.
In the twenty-third year,
Kèníng again requested to retire due to old age.
The Emperor said:
"In the past, when you were in government,
you toiled diligently day and night.
Appointing you Shūmìshǐ should already allow for ease and comfort.
I consider that there are few old ministers left.
Should there, by chance, be an alert on the frontier,
for selecting generals and commanders,
assigning strategies,
understanding the treacherous terrain of mountains and rivers,
and military tactics and plans,
who other than you can share this with me?
Please stay for me!"
Kèníng then dared not speak again.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Shìzōng traveled to Shàngjīng,
and the Crown Prince supervised the state.
An edict ordered Zuǒchéngxiàng Shǒudào and Kèníng to both remain in Zhōngdū to assist the Crown Prince.
The Emperor said to Kèníng:
"After I complete my inspection,
should anything happen,
you must personally attend to it,
and not overlook even the minutest details.
Plan for the difficult while it is still easy,
and that will suffice."
In the twenty-fifth year,
Zuǒchéngxiàng Shǒudào was granted a banquet in the northern region,
and an edict ordered Kèníng to act as Zuǒchéngxiàng.
At this time,
Shìzōng returned from Shàngjīng,
stopping at Tiānpíng Shān to escape the summer heat.
The Crown Prince died in the capital.
Various princes, imperial consorts, and princesses entered the palace to mourn and weep.
Many servants followed them in,
making it quite noisy, chaotic, and lacking solemnity.
Kèníng sent them out,
personally guarded the palace gates,
and strictly enforced the regulations for the palace and gate guards as prescribed by law.
Only then did he allow imperial relatives and maternal relatives to enter to pay their respects,
with a limited number of attendants.
He said to the officials of the Eastern Palace:
"The Emperor is on an inspection tour
and has not yet returned to the palace.
The Crown Prince has unfortunately passed away.
Can you now repay the state with your lives?
I, too, dare not cherish my own life."
His words and demeanor were stern,
and those who heard him were awed and respectful.
Zhāngzōng was at that time Jīnyuán Jùnwáng,
and was mourning excessively.
Kèníng admonished him, saying:
"Weeping
is customary.
As Jùnwáng holds the position of heir,
how can he disregard the importance of the imperial ancestral temple and state by observing only customary rites?"
He summoned the Crown Prince's attendant-reader, Wánýán Kuāng, saying:
"You have served the Crown Prince for a long time
and are a close minister.
Jùnwáng is grieving excessively.
You should earnestly remonstrate with him.
Carefully attend to Jùnwáng,
and do not leave his side."
Shìzōng was at Tiānpíng Shān.
When the news of the Crown Prince's death arrived,
he grieved deeply many times.
Hearing that Kèníng had strictly ordered the palace guards
and carefully protected the Imperial Grandson,
he praised his loyalty and integrity, and valued him even more.
In the twelfth month, on the *yǐhài* day,
Shìzōng fell ill.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Kèníng led the chancellors and administrators to inquire about the emperor's health.
The emperor said,
"My illness is critical."
He said to Kèníng:
"Although the Imperial Grandson is still young, not yet having reached the age of twenty,
he was born intelligent and perspicacious.
You and the others must exert yourselves to assist him."
He further said:
"The affairs of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng) should be entirely entrusted to the Imperial Grandson."
Kèníng reported:
"When Your Majesty was in Shàngjīng,
Xuānxìao Tàizǐ supervised the state,
and was permitted to appoint officials of the sixth rank and below. This can now be provisionally implemented."
The emperor said:
"Why not also include those of the fifth rank and below?"
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
an imperial edict commanded the Imperial Grandson to provisionally administer state affairs
and to appoint officials of the fifth rank and below.
An edict further commanded the Imperial Grandson and all the princes and high officials to lodge within the forbidden palace.
Kèníng reported:
"The Imperial Grandson and the various princes should avoid suspicion
and rectify their proper positions.
Their lodging together in the same place
is not entirely proper according to ritual."
An edict then commanded the Imperial Grandson to reside in the East Wing of Qìnghé Diàn.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
an edict appointed Kèníng as Tàiwèi concurrently Shàngshūlìng,
and enfeoffed him as Yán'ān Jùnwáng.
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Xiāng was appointed Yòuchéngxiàng,
and Yòuchéng Zhāng Rǔlín was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
an edict commanded Kèníng, Xiāng, and Rǔlín to lodge in the inner palace.
In the first month of the twenty-ninth year, on the *guǐsì* day,
Shìzōng passed away in Fú'ān Diàn.
On this day,
Kèníng and others proclaimed the imperial testament, establishing the Imperial Grandson as emperor,
who became Zhāngzōng.
He was transferred and enfeoffed as Dōngpíng Jùnwáng.
An edict commanded Kèníng to attend court on the new moon and full moon,
and on the day of his attendance, a seat was to be placed in the palace hall.
Kèníng firmly declined,
and an edict commanded close officials to gently persuade him.
Kèníng, shedding tears, declined, saying:
"Out of compassion for this old minister,
I am fortunate to be excused from regular court attendance;
how could I dare to accept a seat?"
Thereafter,
a seat was always set for Kèníng at every court session,
but Kèníng stood in attendance with even greater respect.
Upon Zhāngzōng's enthronement, an edict stated:
"All officials who were dismissed or demoted shall be re-employed according to their talents."
Zhāng Rǔlín reported that true thieves and those who distorted the law should not be pardoned.
Kèníng said:
"When Your Majesty first ascends the throne, an extraordinary measure is implemented.
Even if corrupt officials mistakenly receive grace and pardon, the harm is minor;
the great trust of the state must not be lost."
Zhāngzōng deeply approved of this.
Before long,
he was promoted to Tàifù,
concurrently Shàngshūlìng,
and was bestowed with an imperial jade belt.
He requested to retire,
but it was not permitted.
An edict ordered the translation of the Biography of Zhūgě Kǒngmíng and bestowed it upon him.
An edict was sent to the Shàngshūshěng, stating:
"Tàifù is advanced in years;
in addition to his ten-day break, he shall have an extra day off every four days.
Important matters should be recorded for him,
but there is no need for him to personally attend to minor affairs."
He was granted five hundred *liǎng* of gold, five thousand *liǎng* of silver, ten million cash, two hundred bolts of heavy patterned silk, and two thousand bolts of plain silk.
The Shàngshūshěng reported that those *mèng'ān* and *móukè* who wished to attempt the *jìnshì* examination should be permitted to do so.
The emperor said:
"Is it permissible for those who are to inherit the *mèng'ān* and *móukè* positions to study at the Imperial Academy (Tàixué)?"
Kèníng said:
"Peace has prevailed for a long time.
The martial talents of the current *mèng'ān* and *móukè* are already inferior to their predecessors.
Should an emergency arise,
whom shall we send to repel it?
Practicing literary arts
and neglecting military preparedness
is not beneficial to the state."
The emperor said:
"Tàifù's words are correct."
When Zhāngzōng first ascended the throne,
he was quite fond of literary composition,
but there were border conflicts,
hence Kèníng spoke about this.
In the second year of Míngchāng,
Kèníng fell ill.
Zhāngzōng went to visit him.
Kèníng bowed his head in thanks, saying:
"Your unworthy servant
was once entrusted by the late emperor.
Upon Your Majesty's enthronement,
I was appointed as prime minister.
Now, old and ill,
I shall precede the dogs and horses into the grave
and will be unable to assist the enlightened sovereign in pacifying the four directions.
Your Majesty, remembering your servant's incompetence and timidity,
personally honored me with your carriage and presence.
I have more than enough sins even in death."
On that day,
he was appointed Tàishī by the bedside,
enfeoffed as Zīwáng,
and given exceptionally generous additional rewards.
In the second month of that year,
he passed away.
His dying memorial,
in its general outline, stated:
"Monarchs often value *jūnzǐ* (men of noble character) but then alienate them,
and disdain *xiǎorén* (petty individuals) but ultimately grow close to them.
May Your Majesty be as careful at the end as at the beginning,
not forget danger in times of peace,
and let your words not touch upon private matters."
An edict commanded the relevant authorities to manage the funeral arrangements
and to inter him in Láizhōu.
His posthumous title was Zhōngliè.
In the fifth year of Míngchāng,
he was honored with a place in Shìzōng's ancestral temple,
and his portrait was placed in Yǎnqìng Gōng.
In the first year of Dà'ān,
he was re-assigned to be honored in Zhāngzōng's ancestral temple.
A eulogy says: Túdān Kèníng can be called a great minister.
His merits were high, but his bearing grew more humble;
his position was prominent, but his heart grew more diligent.
The classics say:
"Do not be arrogant when in a high position,
be lofty but not precarious,
regulate and be cautious in measure,
be full but not overflow,"
which is how one long maintains wealth and nobility.
Therefore, it is said that being loyal and trustworthy without slacking,
not displaying one's achievements,
and remembering not to be complacent when at the height of success
is the highest virtue.
To be diligent and assiduous,
faithfully fulfilling one's duties,
not occupying a position that cannot be fulfilled,
and not undertaking what cannot be accomplished,
and for the sovereign to know this,
is secondary.
To ensure that advice will certainly be followed,
that words will certainly be heard,
and that one's actions will certainly yield results,
is yet another step below.
Collation Notes:
Xiǎnzōng's sons: Cóng, Guī, Cóngyí, Cóngxiàn, Jiè.
Zhāngzōng's sons: Hóngyù, Hóngjìng, Hóngxī, Hóngyǎn, Hónghuī, Tèlín.
Wèishàowáng's son: Cóngkè.
Xuānzōng's three sons: Zhuāngxiàn Tàizǐ, Xuánlíng, Shǒuchún.
Dújí Sīzhōng, Chéngyù, Púsǎn Kuí, Mǒniǎn Shǐgētā, Zōnghào.
Xiǎnzōng's Xiàoyì Huánghòu gave birth to Zhāngzōng;
Zhāoshèng Huánghòu gave birth to Xuānzōng;
Concubine Tián gave birth to Yùnwáng Cóng, Yíngwáng Guī, and Huòwáng Cóngyí;
Concubine Liú gave birth to Yíngwáng Cóngxiàn;
Concubine Wáng gave birth to Wēnwáng Jiè.
Yùnwáng Cóng's original name was Chéngqìng.
His mother was Concubine Tián,
who was later enfeoffed as Yùlíng Chōnghuá.
Cóng had a grand and imposing appearance,
was quick-witted and eloquent,
of a generous and magnanimous nature,
and fond of learning.
Shìzōng selected famous and virtuous *jìnshì* Nàtǎn Móujiā to teach him.
He was proficient in both Jurchen small script and Chinese characters.
When he grew up,
he was light with wealth and fond of giving,
without resentment.
He was good at reciting poetry
and disliked hearing about others' faults.
As for the arts of horsemanship, archery, painting, and sculpture,
he achieved exquisite mastery in all.
In the eighteenth year of Dàdìng,
he was enfeoffed as Dàoguó Gōng.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was further promoted.
Upon Zhāngzōng's enthronement,
he was moved to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sān Sī,
and enfeoffed as Yùnwáng.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
he was granted the hereditary *mèng'ān* of Bāshúlù Huòhuǒluó Hédá,
and remained in the capital.
In the fifth year,
he passed away.
The emperor suspended court,
and personally attended the offering at the funeral parlor.
His posthumous title was Zhuāngjìng,
later changed to Zhuānghuì.
Yíng Wáng Guī (瀛王瓌), whose original name was Huán Dǔ (桓篤),
was the full brother of Yùn Wáng Cóng (鄆王琮).
He was steady and reserved,
cultivated in his private conduct,
skilled in poetry,
and proficient in horsemanship, archery, calligraphy, and the large and small scripts of the Nǚzhēn.
In the twenty-second year of Dàdìng (大定),
he was enfeoffed as Chóng Guó Gōng (崇國公).
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was promoted to Chóng Jìn (崇進).
When Zhāngzōng (章宗) ascended the throne,
he was moved to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司)
and enfeoffed as Yíng Wáng (瀛王).
In the third year of Míngchāng (明昌),
he passed away.
An imperial edict ordered that all necessary expenses for his funeral be provided by the government,
and the Minister of Works, Xū Chígúo (胥持國), was appointed to oversee the funeral arrangements.
Before the burial,
the Emperor personally attended the memorial three times,
weeping in great sorrow.
His posthumous title was Wénjìng (文敬).
Afterward, the Emperor told his assisting ministers,
"The Prince's nature was loyal and filial,
the best person among my brothers.
Therefore, I often kept him by my side.
Wēn Wáng (溫王), though young,
was also excellent.
For both to pass away within two weeks is truly lamentable."
Huò Wáng Cóngyí (霍王從彝), whose original name was Ālián (阿憐),
lost his mother, Lady Tián (田), early.
Concubine Wēn (溫妃) Shímò (石抹) adopted him as her own son.
In the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng,
he was enfeoffed as Sù Guó Gōng (宿國公),
and promoted to Chóng Jìn.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was granted the name Zàn (瓚).
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Yí Wáng (沂王).
In the first year of Míngchāng,
an imperial decree was issued to the relevant authorities, stating:
"The four princely estates of Fēng (豐), Yùn (鄆), Yíng (瀛), and Yí (沂) are each granted seven hundred servants."
In the fourth year,
an edict posthumously enfeoffed the late Lǔ Wáng Shúlián (魯王孰輦) as Zhào Wáng (趙王),
and Cóngyí was made the heir of Zhào Wáng.
In the first year of Chéng'ān (承安),
he became Minister of War
and was re-enfeoffed as Cài (蔡).
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān 祕書監).
In the fifth year of Tàihé (泰和),
he was granted his current name.
In the eighth year,
he was enfeoffed as Huò (霍).
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (貞祐),
he passed away.
Yíng Wáng Cóngxiàn (瀛王從憲), whose original name was Wūlǐbù (吾里不),
had mother Lady Liú (劉),
who was later enfeoffed as Yùlíng Màoyí (裕陵茂儀).
In the twenty-sixth year of Dàdìng,
he was granted the name Qí (琦).
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī
and enfeoffed as Shòu Wáng (壽王).
In the first year of Chéng'ān,
due to the grace of the suburban sacrifices, he was further enfeoffed as Yīng (英).
In the fourth year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Yíng.
In the fifth year of Tàihé,
he was again granted his current name.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Secretary of the Imperial Library.
In the eighth year,
he passed away.
Cóngxiàn was imposing in appearance,
generous in nature,
and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He treated his subordinates with courtesy,
and those who left after completing their terms all received parting gifts.
The Emperor particularly loved and esteemed him.
When news of his illness first arrived,
the Emperor immediately went to inquire,
and granted five million cash.
Upon returning to the palace,
an edict instructed his princely subordinates to report on the fluctuations of his illness,
and further ordered the palace gate officials to report at the first drum of the night,
and again at the fifth watch.
When he passed away,
the Emperor wept in great sorrow,
and twice suspended court to personally attend the memorial.
An imperial decree was issued to Wǎn Wáng Yǒngshēng (宛王永升), who oversaw the Great Directorate of Relatives (Dà Mùqīnfǔ Shì 大睦親府事), saying:
"The Yíng Wáng's family affairs
should be planned by you, uncle.
I hear his two concubines are pregnant;
if they bear sons,
they should be entrusted to you."
Yílà Dūhù (移剌都護), the Right Grand Minister of Proclamations (Yòu Xuānhuī Shǐ 右宣徽使), was tasked with overseeing his mourning and burial.
He was dressed in garments from the inner treasury,
and all other necessities
were also provided by the government.
His posthumous title was Dūn Yì (敦懿).
Wēn Wáng Jiè (溫王玠), whose original name was Móuliánghǔ (謀良虎),
had mother Lady Wáng (王),
who was later enfeoffed as Yùlíng Wǎnyí (裕陵婉儀).
Jiè was intelligent and outstanding from a young age,
gentle in nature,
and fond of learning.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng,
when Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī
and enfeoffed as Wēn Wáng (溫王).
In the third year of Míngchāng,
he passed away
at the age of eleven.
Upon hearing the news,
the Emperor suspended court
and personally attended the memorial and wept for him.
His posthumous title was Dàomǐn (悼敏).
Zhāngzōng's Qīnhuái Empress (欽懷皇后) gave birth to Jiàng Wáng Hóngyù (絳王洪裕).
Zīmíng Fūrén Lín (資明夫人林氏) gave birth to Jīng Wáng Hóngjìng (荊王洪靖).
Other concubines gave birth to Róng Wáng Hóngxī (榮王洪熙), Yīng Wáng Hóngyǎn (英王洪衍), and Shòu Wáng Hónghuī (壽王洪輝).
Yuán Fēi Lǐ (元妃李氏) gave birth to Gé Wáng Tèlín (葛王忒隣).
Hóngyù
was born in the twenty-sixth year of Dàdìng.
At that time, Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) had passed away more than a year earlier,
and Shìzōng (世宗) was deeply moved.
When he heard that his imperial great-grandson was born,
he was extremely pleased.
When he was three months old,
a banquet was held at Qìnghé Diàn (慶和殿),
and the great-grandson was given a golden tripod,
a golden incense burner,
twenty bolts of fine silk,
a rhinoceros horn *gǔdú* (骨覩), a jade mountain ornament from Tǔhú (吐鶻), and a pair of rabbit-head pendants,
and two famous horses.
Zhāngzōng presented a jade twin-camel paperweight, a jade pipa pick, a jade phoenix hook, a rhinoceros horn *gǔdú* set with a佩刀 (pèidāo, belt knife), and a suit of clothes.
Shìzōng drank wine and sang merrily
until late into the night.
On the *bǐngyín* day of the tenth month in the twenty-eighth year,
he passed away.
In the third year of Míngchāng,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Jiàng Wáng (絳王)
and granted a name.
Hóngjìng (洪靖), whose original name was Āhǔlǎn (阿虎懶),
was born in the third year of Míngchāng.
He was intelligent and outstanding from birth,
and much loved by the Emperor.
In the fourth year,
he passed away.
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Jīng Wáng (荊王),
granted a name,
and promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Hóngxī (洪熙), whose original name was Élǔbù (訛魯不),
was born in the third year of Míngchāng
and passed away before completing a month.
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Róng Wáng (榮王),
granted a name,
and promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Hóngyǎn (洪衍), whose original name was Sǎgǎi (撒改),
was born in the fourth year of Míngchāng
and passed away soon after.
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Yīng Wáng (英王),
granted a name,
and promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Hónghuī (洪輝), whose original name was Èlún (訛論),
was born in the fifth month of the second year of Chéng'ān.
When he completed a month,
he was enfeoffed as Shòu Wáng (壽王).
On the *rénwǔ* day of the intercalary sixth month,
he suffered from an acute seizure.
Doctors capable of curing him were offered the rank of Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn (宣武將軍)
and five million cash.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
he recovered from the illness.
Ten thousand copies of the Wúliàngshòu Jīng (無量壽經) were printed in gratitude.
A seven-day universal grand ritual (Pǔtiān Dàjiào 普天大醮) was held at Yǎnqìng Gōng (衍慶宮),
no criminal cases were reported,
and butchering was prohibited.
On the *dīnghài* day of the tenth month,
he passed away,
and was buried with full rites.
Tè lín,
born in the eighth month of the second year of Tàihé.
The Emperor had long been without an imperial heir,
and had offered prayers at the suburban altars, the ancestral temples, Yǎnqìng Gōng, and Bózhōu Tàiqīng Gōng.
Upon this birth, he was exceedingly joyful.
When the child was a month old,
he was to be enfeoffed.
None of the three grades of princely titles pleased the Emperor.
Considering that Shìzōng had reigned for the longest time
and was the most senior in age,
and his initial enfeoffment was as Gě Wáng,
he was thus enfeoffed as Gě Wáng.
On the *guǐyǒu* day of the twelfth month,
marking one hundred days since his birth,
three thousand monastic certificates were issued to monks and Daoists.
A Daoist ritual was held at Xuánzhēn Guān,
and a banquet was given at Qìnghé Diàn.
All officials observed the Tīanshòu Jié ceremonies,
offering wine and congratulations.
Officials of the third rank and above presented gifts.
In the third year of Tàihé,
he passed away.
Wèi Shàowáng had six sons.
In the twenty-sixth year of Dàdìng,
Měng'ān was granted the name Jū,
Ànchū the name Xuān,
and Ànchén the name Zǎo.
In the seventh year of Tàihé,
an edict commanded Ànchén to be adopted as the heir of Zhèng Wáng Yǒngdǎo.
The edict stated:
“I recall the former residence of Zhèng Wáng,
who tragically strayed from the proper path,
and was buried hastily in the wilderness.
Many years have passed,
and I feel a pang of sorrow,
which I cannot suppress.
Thus, I decreed the posthumous restoration of his princely rank
and a proper reburial with full rites.
Now, following classical precedents,
I appoint you as the heir of Zhèng Wáng,
to maintain his ancestral sacrifices.”
In the first year of Dà'ān,
his six sons were enfeoffed as kings.
Cóngkè was Zhà Wáng,
Yǒurèn was Wáng, and Gǒng Wáng;
the others were not recorded.
In that year,
Cóngkè became Left Chancellor.
In the eighth month of the second year,
Cóngkè was established as Crown Prince.
Towards the end of Zhìníng,
Hú Shāhǔ killed Wèi Wáng,
and Cóngkè and his brothers were all deposed and resided in Zhōngdū.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
they were relocated to Zhèngzhōu.
In the fourth year,
they were relocated to Nánjīng.
In the first year of Tīanxīng,
Cuī Lì appointed Cóngkè as Liáng Wáng.
When Biànjīng fell,
he died there.
A eulogy: In Zhāngzōng's later years,
no heir was established,
and so he set his intentions on Wèi Shàowáng.
Wèi Shàowáng's reign was not long.
All his sons were imprisoned for over twenty years.
Hàolì Wáng's sons were imprisoned for over forty years.
His eldest daughter and sons were all unable to marry.
At the beginning of Tīanxīng,
the prohibitions were finally relaxed.
The fate of the Jīn dynasty's descendants thereafter can be imagined.
Zhuāngxìan Tàizǐ's name was Shǒuzhōng,
the eldest son of Xuānzōng.
His mother is not detailed,
the account is in the biography of the empresses.
After Hú Shāhǔ deposed Wèi Wáng,
the Emperor had not yet arrived,
so he immediately welcomed Shǒuzhōng to reside in the Eastern Palace.
On the *jiǎshēn* day of the intercalary ninth month in the first year of Zhēnyòu,
he was established as Crown Prince.
The edict stated:
“I, with my humble person,
have inherited the glorious mandate.
Remembering the legacy of the imperial ancestors,
I toil day and night without rest,
to respectfully serve the spirits of the nine ancestral temples above,
and to fulfill the hopes of the many people below.
Crown Prince Shǒuzhōng possesses a gentle and kind nature,
and holds the position of the eldest legitimate son.
Speaking in terms of seniority,
he is suitable to ascend to the position of heir.
Judging by rites and ceremonies,
he is well-suited to satisfy the sentiments of the masses.
Let him be established as Crown Prince.”
On the *jǐwèi* day of the tenth month,
Ālǔhǎn, Grand General of the Protectorate and Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince, was made Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor sent a message saying:
“In my palace, every expenditure is reduced.
You, too, should be aware of the difficulties of the times,
and make adjustments and economize.”
He further said:
“The times are full of hardship.
Every matter should be subject to reduction.
I have already dismissed over a hundred palace women.
Those who are not needed in the Eastern Palace should also be sent away.
You are a scholar;
you must surely understand this.”
In the fourth month of the second year,
Xuānzōng moved to Biàn,
leaving him to guard Zhōngjīng.
In the seventh month,
he was summoned to Biàn.
In the first month of the third year,
he passed away.
The Emperor personally paid his respects at the funeral bier four times.
In the fourth month,
he was buried five *lǐ* outside Yíngshuò Mén.
His posthumous title was Zhuāngxìan.
In the fifth month,
his son Kēng was established as Imperial Grandson,
being only two years old.
In the twelfth month, he passed away.
In the first month of the fourth year,
he was granted the posthumous title Chōnghuái Tàisūn.
Xuánlíng,
some say he was Zhuāngxìan Tàizǐ’s younger brother by the same mother,
died young
without being enfeoffed.
Others say he was born to Concubine Lì, Lady Shǐ.
Jīng Wáng Shǒuchún, originally named Pándū,
was the second son of Xuānzōng.
His mother was Consort Zhēn, Lady Páng.
In the first year of Zhēnyòu,
he was enfeoffed as Pú Wáng.
In the second year,
he became Grand Inspector of the Palace Guard and Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Bodyguard,
acting as Grand Marshal.
The Emperor instructed the Marshal's residence, saying:
“Pú Wáng is young,
and quite unfamiliar with public affairs.
You all must not, because he is my son, fail to admonish him.
Whenever you see generals and officers,
tell them to treat them with humility and kindness.”
In the third year,
he became Minister of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Grand Councilor.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he was granted the hereditary Měng'ān of Sāntún, Dōngpíng Fǔlù.
In the third year,
due to the knowledge and management of clerk Liáng Huán,
who mistakenly wrote the imperial edict for Transport Vice-Envoy Zhāng Zhènglún,
he requested punishment.
The Emperor said:
“If a clerk commits an offense,
the prime minister should deal with it himself.
Why must it concern me?”
In the third month of that year,
he was advanced to become Yīng Wáng.
At that time, Censor Chéng Zhèn spoke of his unlawful conduct.
Xuānzōng severely reprimanded him,
and flogged several of his *sīmǎ* and great servants who were particularly unruly.
In the ninth month of the fourth year,
Shǒuchún wished to expose the crimes of Chancellor Gāo Qí.
He secretly summoned the case manager Púxiān Shílǔlà, clerk Púchá Húlǔ, and supernumerary official Wáng Ālǐ to conspire,
and instructed them not to leak it.
However, Shílǔlà and Húlǔ immediately reported it to the administrator Púsǎn Núshībù.
Núshībù then reported it to Gāo Qí.
After Gāo Qí was executed,
Shǒuchún impeached the three for leaking secrets.
Núshībù was spared death
and stripped of his name;
Shílǔlà and Húlǔ were each flogged seventy times
and dismissed.
On the *rénzǐ* day of the third month in the second year of Yuánguāng,
the Emperor admonished Shǒuchún, saying:
“Originally, I appointed you as Chancellor,
hoping that you would assist me,
and not become a subject of ridicule.
But you only indulge in drinking and pleasure,
and completely neglect public affairs.
Why is this?
I often hear people speak of my faults.
Even if I examine myself and find none,
I still do not dare to easily dismiss it from my mind.”
He further said:
“The reason I criticize you
is only because of your excessive drinking and neglect of duties.
Do not worry excessively
to the point of having your power removed.
Now, all the other Chancellors are old ministers.
Discuss every matter with them,
so that there will be no public criticism; that will be sufficient.”
In the sixth year of Tàihé [1206 CE],
he participated in the campaign against Sòng.
He was transferred to Deputy Commander of the Shǎnxī Circuit Army.
Soon after, he was made Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎn Commandery and Deputy Commander of the Shǎnxī Forces.
He was stationed with Wányán Lín, the Defense Commissioner of Qínzhōu, at the border of Chéngjì.
Sòng general Wú Xī, with five thousand troops, attacked Qínzhōu through the valleys of Bǎochà and Gūsū.
Chéngyù and Lín, with over a thousand cavalry, repelled them.
They pursued the fleeing enemy for forty *lǐ*.
In six battles,
the Sòng army was utterly defeated,
and over four thousand heads were taken.
An imperial edict to Chéngyù stated:
“In the past, your ancestors, your grandfather and your father,
exerted themselves in military service.
You are still young,
yet skilled in your duty.
Therefore, I command you to go out to the border with Wányán Lín.
Previously, you said that three thousand troops would be sufficient to accomplish the task.
Now, with Shímò Zhòngwēn, Zhúhǔ Gāoqí, and Qīngyíkě joining your army,
the total should be about sixty thousand,
which should also be sufficient to accomplish it.
Zhòngwēn and Gāoqí's route is treacherous,
while your route is very easy.
From Qínzhōu to Xiānrén Pass is only four hundred *lǐ*.
Plan carefully,
to fulfill My intentions.”
An imperial edict to Wányán Lín stated:
“You were formerly on the northern frontier,
known for your bravery and capability.
Recently, due to a transgression,
you were handed over to the authorities for questioning.
Knowing that you recently fought bravely against the Sòng,
I have specially granted you a pardon,
and you are to remain as Deputy Commander.
If you can assist Chéngyù in achieving merit,
how could I be stingy
with official rewards?
I hear you are quite cunning in action.
If you again bring trouble upon yourself,
I will not pardon you.”
Sòng general Wú Xī sent his commanders Féng Xīng, Yáng Xióng, and Lǐ Guī with eight thousand infantry and cavalry into Chìgǔ.
Chéngyù, Lín, and Púchá Bǐngxüàn, the Defense Commissioner of Hézhōu, met and defeated them.
The Sòng infantry held the western hills,
while the cavalry fled to Chìgǔ.
Chéngyù sent his subordinate general Tángkuò Àndáhǎi to lead two hundred cavalry to swiftly attack the Sòng infantry.
Jiǎshì Méngkuò personally charged first, taking them by surprise.
The Sòng infantry were utterly routed,
pursued to Zàojiāo City,
where over two thousand heads were taken.
Méng'ān Bǎtiānnú pursued the Sòng cavalry,
killing over a thousand men,
and beheaded Yáng Xióng and Lǐ Guī on the battlefield.
Féng Xīng barely escaped with his life.
Chéngyù advanced and captured Chéngzhōu.
In the eighth year [1208 CE],
the troops were disbanded.
He was transferred to Military Commissioner of Hénán Dōnglù,
concurrently serving as Prefect of Guīdé Fǔ.
Soon after, he was made Prefect of Línhuáng Fǔ.
He was awarded a golden belt, ten bolts of heavy silk, and one hundred fifty *liǎng* of silver.
At the beginning of Dà'ān [1209 CE],
he was recalled to serve as Censor-in-Chief.
In the third year [1211 CE],
he was appointed Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and was sent with Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Dújílì Sīzhōng to govern a province and guard the border.
During the Battle of Wūshābǎo, no preparations were made,
resulting in a defeat.
The court held only Sīzhōng responsible,
and an edict commanded Chéngyù to take charge of military affairs.
In the eighth month,
the great army of the Dà Yuán arrived at Yěhú Lǐng.
Chéngyù lost morale
and dared not engage in battle,
retreating to Xuānpíng.
Local gentry in the county requested to use their local troops as the vanguard,
with the provincial army as support.
Chéngyù, out of fear and trepidation, dared not employ them.
He only asked about a shortcut from there to Xuāndé.
The local gentry scoffed, saying:
“The streams and ravines are winding,
and we are familiar with them.
The provincial administrator does not know how to utilize the terrain for a decisive battle,
but only schemes to flee.
Now, it is lost.”
That night,
Chéngyù led his troops south.
The Dà Yuán army pursued and attacked them.
The next day,
upon reaching Huìhé Chuān,
Chéngyù's army was utterly routed.
Chéngyù barely escaped with his life,
fleeing into Xuāndé.
Dà Yuán light cavalry entered Jūyōng Guān,
and Zhōngdū was placed under martial law.
Knowledgeable people said that the fall of Jīn was decided by this campaign.
Wèishào Wáng still downplayed his crime,
only stripping him of his name.
In the first year of Chóngqìng [1212 CE],
he was reinstated as Pacification Commissioner of Shǎnxī.
In the first year of Zhìníng [1213 CE],
he was promoted to Right Supervising General of the Grand Marshal's office,
concurrently serving as Grand Commander of the Hánpíng Fǔ Circuit Army,
and fought against Qìdān Liú Kě,
suffering a defeat.
He was reassigned as Acting Co-Administrator of Dàmùqīn Fǔ and Pacification Commissioner of Liáodōng.
At the beginning of Zhēnyòu [1213 CE],
he was reassigned as Military Commissioner of Línhǎi Commandery,
and died.
A eulogy says: Cáo Guì once said:
“The first drumbeat inspires valor,
the second weakens it,
the third exhausts it.”
Indeed, the military relies on morale.
In the Battle of Huìhé Bǎo,
Dújílì Sīzhōng and Chéngyù were so disheartened that they could not recover.
The demise of the Jīn dynasty
was foreshadowed there.
Púsàn Kuí, whose original name was Línxǐ,
was a native of Shàngjīng.
He was the son of the Left Chancellor and Grand Marshal, the Wǔzhuāng Duke of Yíguó, Zhōngyì.
As a youth, due to his aristocratic lineage,
he was selected to serve as a palace attendant.
In the fifteenth year of Dàdìng [1175 CE],
he married Princess Hánguó Dàzhǎng.
He was promoted to Deputy Commissioner of the Directorate of Imperial Regalia [Qìwù Jú],
and specially granted the hereditary *méng'ān* of Hèshā Ā of the Línhuáng Fǔ Circuit.

He successively served as Deputy Commissioner of the Directorate of Imperial Attendants [Jìnsì Jú], Commissioner of the Directorate of Imperial Wardrobe [Shàngyī Jú], Deputy Commander of the Palace Guard,
and General of the Left Palace Guard.
When dismissed from office,
Emperor Shìzōng admonished him, saying:
“Because you are related to Empress Xuānxuàn,
I allowed you to marry the princess and
placed you in the palace guard,
expecting you to exert yourself in loyalty and filial piety.
But recently, you have secretly discussed matters with outsiders.
I cannot fathom what is in your heart.
Therefore, you are dismissed and returned to your hometown.”
Soon after, he was reinstated as Administrator of Luánzhōu,
then transferred to Lǐzhōu,
and then entered the court as Vice Minister of War, Grand Justice, and Minister of Punishments.
When Emperor Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was sent out as Military Commissioner of Tàidìng Commandery,
then reassigned as Prefect of Líntáo Fǔ.
He became known for his administrative achievements.
He was promoted to Military Commissioner of Hénán Lù.
The Shǎnxī Circuit Judicial Commissioner reported Kuí
as “upright and decisive,
with no wrongful detentions in his prisons.
He restrained his family members,
and the common people did not even recognize his face.
The old bandits of Jīshí and Táo prefectures all fled,
and merchants could travel freely.”
Thereupon,
he was promoted one rank,
and an imperial edict further praised and commended him.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng [1193 CE],
Zhèng Wáng Yǒngdǎo plotted rebellion.
When the plot was discovered,
Kuí was implicated for having privately appraised the various princes,
and uniquely praised Yǒngdǎo as gentle by nature,
quiet and not fond of trouble.
He was spared death,
but stripped of his name.
Not long after,
he was restored to a fifth-rank official,
and reinstated as Acting Co-Administrator of Chóngyì Commandery.
For his military merits, he was promoted to Deputy Pacification Commissioner of the Northwest Circuit,
advanced seven ranks,
and awarded one golden *mǎyú* vessel, two hundred *liǎng* of silver, and ten bolts of brocade.
Again for military merit, he was promoted to Pacification Commissioner of the Southwest Circuit and concurrently Military Commissioner of Tiāndé Commandery,
awarded fifty *liǎng* of gold and ten bolts of brocade.
He was again sent out to defend the frontier,
and once fought his way seven hundred *lǐ* beyond the Great Wall,
reaching the territory of Chìhúdǔ before returning.
He received generous imperial commendation,
was promoted one rank,
and his son Ānzhēn was permitted to marry Princess Xíngguó Zhǎnggōngzhǔ.
Furthermore, Kuí was permitted to enter the court to express gratitude,
and after the ceremony,
he returned to his post.
Soon after,
the Sòng commander, Qiū Mó, indeed sent a letter seeking peace.
Pú-sàn Kuí instructed him with the previously mentioned five conditions and sent him away.
The army then advanced again to besiege Hé-zhōu.
The enemy stationed fifteen thousand cavalry in Liù-hé.
Pú-sàn Kuí detected this,
and immediately used his right wing to launch a surprise attack,
beheading eight thousand.
He then encamped at Wǎ-liáng-hé to control the strategic passes of Zhēn and Yáng.
Then he arranged the cavalry in formation,
displayed all the banners,
and along the Jiāng (Yangtze River), both upstream and downstream,
all were Jīn soldiers.
At this, the region south of the Jiāng was struck with terror.
Several tens of thousands of Sòng soldiers from Zhēn-zhōu held Hè-qiáo.
Pú-sàn Kuí again sent Commander Hé-shí-liè Zǐ-rén to attack them.
He divided the army to ford the shallow waters,
secretly appearing behind the enemy.
When the enemy saw this, they were greatly alarmed,
and scattered without a fight.
More than twenty thousand were beheaded,
and their commanders Liú Tíng, Cháng Sī-jìng, Xiāo Cóng-dé, and Mò Zǐ-róng were captured alive,
all of whom were valiant Sòng generals.
Thus, Zhēn-zhōu was captured.
The Sòng again sent Chén Bì to announce peace.
Pú-sàn Kuí believed their plea was insincere,
and merely wished to delay the army,
so he rejected it.
Since the Sòng people had suffered losses,
and failed to secure peace,
they then breached the accumulated waters of Jù-shèng, Chéng-gōng, and Léi-táng-zhǔ to create an obstruction.
They burned all their houses and stored provisions,
and fled across the Jiāng.
Pú-sàn Kuí considered that it was spring and the ground was wet,
making it unsuitable for prolonged stay,
and also wished to allow his soldiers and horses to rest and recuperate.
So he led his army back.
Upon reaching Xià-cài,
he fell ill.
An imperial edict sent the Xuān-huī Envoy Lǐ Rén-huì and his son Níng-shòu to bring imperial physicians for diagnosis and treatment.
Furthermore, a eunuch envoy was dispatched to offer comfort.
In the second month of the seventh year of Tài-hé (1207),
he passed away.
Upon receiving the news of his death,
the Emperor mourned him deeply,
suspended court,
and sent an envoy to receive the coffin and inter it north of the capital city.
All officials gathered to offer condolences.
The imperial carriage personally attended the mourning, weeping.
He was bestowed with one thousand five hundred taels of silver, fifty bolts of heavy silk, and five hundred rolls of plain silk.
All items for his funeral and sacrifices were provided by the state.
His posthumous title was Wǔ-sù.
Pú-sàn Kuí had a firm body and a gentle disposition,
and never conflicted with others.
He governed the people with benevolent policies.
As a general,
his military headquarters were calm and steady,
and rewards and punishments were strictly enforced.
When he first crossed the Huái River,
he immediately ordered the pontoon bridge to be dismantled.
Wherever he went, he provisioned his army from the enemy,
eliminating the toil of logistics.
He never lightly used his soldiers,
and shared their joys and hardships,
so people were happy to serve him.
Therefore, in both southern campaigns and northern expeditions,
he was considered a famous general.
Mò-niǎn Shǐ-gē-dā was
a native of Lín-huáng-lù.
His ancestors were granted hereditary command of a clan militia (Móu-kè) for their merits.
Shǐ-gē-dā inherited the title in his youth
and rendered meritorious service guarding the border.
In the sixth year of Tài-hé (1206),
when war broke out on the southern frontier,
he was appointed Assistant Administrator of Cài-zhōu Defense Affairs.
In the fifth month,
Sòng general Lǐ Shuǎng besieged Shòu-zhōu,
and Tián Jùn-mài captured Qí-xiàn.
The Prime Minister (Píng-zhāng Zhèng-shì) Pú-sàn Kuí said to his generals:
“Fú-lí and Péng-chéng are the shields of Qí and Lǔ.
If Fú-lí cannot be held,
then Péng-chéng is gone.
If Péng-chéng falls, then Qí and Lǔ are in danger.”
He then dispatched Assistant Military Commissioner (Jié-dù Fù-shǐ) of Ān-guó Army, Nā-lán Bāng-liè, and Shǐ-gē-dā with three thousand elite cavalry to garrison Sù-zhōu.
Jùn-mài indeed led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack.
Bāng-liè and Shǐ-gē-dā met them in battle
and severely defeated them.
Bāng-liè was hit by a stray arrow.
Sòng generals Guō Zhuó and Lǐ Rú-yì followed with fifty thousand troops,
then besieged the city,
attacking with great force.
Arrows rained down from inside the city,
preventing the enemy from approaching.
At that time, continuous rain caused flooding,
and the enemy, exposed and fatigued,
was ambushed by two hundred cavalry dispatched by Bāng-liè, who secretly came out from behind them.
The enemy fell into disarray.
Shǐ-gē-dā led the cavalry to trample them,
killing and wounding several thousand people.
The enemy also heard that reinforcements were coming,
and so they fled during the night.
Bāng-liè and Shǐ-gē-dā pursued them.
At dawn, they launched a combined attack,
greatly defeating them,
and capturing Tián Jùn-mài.
In the tenth month,
Pú-sàn Kuí led thirty thousand provincial troops out through Yǐng and Shòu.
Shǐ-gē-dā served as the Deputy Commander of the Central Army of the valiant cavalry.
They captured Ān-fēng-jūn,
and fought at Huò-qiū and Huā-yè,
contributing greatly.
In the twelfth month,
while participating in the attack on Hé-zhōu,
he was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Shǐ-gē-dā was not taller than an average person,
but he was powerfully brave and skilled in combat.
The spear he used was twenty feet long,
and he was known in the army as
“Long Spear Deputy Commander.”
He was also skilled in using hand arrows.
The arrows were less than a grip long,
and he used hundreds at a time,
scattered within his armor.
When encountering the enemy, he would draw an arrow,
wave it with his whip,
or grasp it with his fingers and throw it,
releasing several arrows at once,
all hitting their mark.
The enemy considered him divine.
All his arrows were ingeniously crafted,
and even his sons could not learn his method.
When he guarded Yàn-shān Camp in the north,
the enemy particularly feared him,
daring not to approach.
Upon his death,
all the generals and soldiers greatly lamented him.
Nèi-zú Zōng-hào, courtesy name Shī-mèng,
originally named Lǎo,
was a fourth-generation descendant of Zhāo-zǔ,
and the son of Tài-bǎo and Grand Marshal (Dū Yuán-shuài) Hàn-guó-gōng Áng.
During the Zhēn-yuán era,
he was a minor attendant (Xiǎo-dǐ) in the palace for Hǎi-líng Shù-rén.
When Shì-zōng ascended the throne in Liáo-yáng,
Áng sent Zōng-hào to rush his congratulations.
Shì-zōng was pleased to see him
and ordered him to serve as Fu-bǎo Zhǐ-hòu (Guardian of Imperial Seals and Tallies).
In the winter of the second year of Dà-dìng (1162),
Áng, as Grand Marshal, established his headquarters in Shān-dōng.
Zōng-hào, leading ten thousand households, accompanied him,
and was also appointed Assistant Commander (Pàn-guān) of the Shān-dōng Eastern Circuit Army and Horse Commander-in-Chief.
He observed mourning for his father.
After resuming office,
he inherited the Yīn-mǐn Wò-lǔ-hún Méng-ān title,
and was appointed Assistant Administrator of Hé-nán Prefecture.
He resigned due to his mother's death.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Assistant Administrator of Shǎn-zhōu Defense Affairs.
He was rated first-class for his integrity and competence,
and promoted one rank,
then to Assistant Military Commissioner of Zhāng-huà Army.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Tóng Qiān Shū-mì-yuàn Shì),
and then transferred to be Military Commissioner (Jié-dù Shǐ) of Hé-sū-guǎn.
Shì-zōng said to his chief ministers:
“Zōng-hào has great talent and ability,
few can equal him.”
In the twenty-third year (1183),
he was summoned to be Minister of the Grand Court of Judicial Review (Dà-lǐ Qīng).
After more than a year, he was appointed Military Commander (Tǒng-jūn Shǐ) of Shān-dōng Circuit,
concurrently serving as Administrator of Yì-dū Prefecture.
When he took leave from the Emperor,
Shì-zōng instructed him, saying:
“You are still young.
As you are a close relative
and have a record of good governance,
I bestow this office upon you.
You should understand My intentions.”
Thereupon, he was bestowed a golden belt and sent off.
In the twenty-sixth year (1186),
he was sent as an envoy to present birthday wishes to the Sòng emperor Zhào Dūn.
Upon his return,
