he was appointed Minister of Personnel (Xíng-bù Shàng-shū),
and soon after, appointed Assistant Grand Councilor (Cān-zhī Zhèng-shì).
When Zhāng-zōng ascended the throne,
he was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Běi-jīng (Běi-jīng Liú-shǒu),
and subsequently three times promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Grand Clan Affairs Bureau (Tóng Pàn Dà Mù-qīn-fǔ Shì).
When there was an alarm in the north,
Zōng-hào was ordered to wear the golden tiger tally and be stationed in Tài-zhōu to act at his discretion.
The imperial court dispatched ten thousand troops from Shàng-jīng and other circuits to garrison.
Zōng-hào, deeming that provisions were not yet ready,
and estimating that the enemy would not dare to move yet,
therefore divided his army to forage for food between Lóng and Zhào.
That winter,
indeed there was no alarm.
and other crimes of misgoverning the country,
there is certainly no escaping them.
If we were to bind and send them,
this would mean that our court could not itself mete out its punishment to its ministers.
Regarding the annual tribute,
the previous letter
has already increased the amount reduced during the Dàdìng period.
For a great country like yours, how could this be of any significance in the first place?
It merely serves as a means to show the reality of expressing our apologies.
If the great country understands
this sincere sentiment,
the quantity of goods
will surely not be meticulously calculated.
Moreover, since the military campaigns began,
the country has been ravaged for successive years,
and taxes have been repeatedly remitted.
If we were to levy heavy taxes on the people again,
would it not
create endless difficulties for the common folk?
We humbly believe that the great court would also find this unbearable.
Beyond the general礼币 (lǐbì) for apologies,
we will present a small token of sincerity,
hoping that this
can be exchanged for that.
As for those who have surrendered and sought refuge,
they are merely scurrying for their lives like sparrows and rats,
having temporarily gone into hiding.
Their whereabouts are often unknown.
Since our court has no use for them,
why would we care about their coming and going?
During the Lóngxīng period,
there were indeed noble families and esteemed generals from the great court who came south.
When the peace treaty was settled,
it was also agreed that neither side would demand their return.
How much less so for such minor individuals;
they are truly not worth mentioning.
If the great court insists on pursuing them,
we shall still permit their apprehension and investigation.
As for the people forcibly abducted from Sìzhōu and other places,
all shall be escorted back to their homes.
Indeed, those who forge new friendships do not dwell on past grievances,
and those who achieve great accomplishments do not quibble over small gains.
We earnestly hope you will vigorously present our case,
discard past errors,
and overlook other matters.
May jade and silk flow between us,
friendship be restored as before,
and the realm be at peace,
with no more military affairs for a long time.
May your meritorious deeds shine brightly,
and your benevolent virtue overflow,
recorded in tripods and bronzes,
and inscribed in annals
and chronicles,
to be passed down for ten thousand generations—
how could it ever end?
Furthermore, as the birthday of the great Jīn Emperor is approaching,
it is proper to send congratulations.
Given the many difficulties in our country,
it was also stated
that envoys should be dispatched
to continuously depart.
The official dispatch has already been prepared,
and we eagerly await its acceptance.
We humbly hope that you will consider our repeated and unceasing sincerity,
promptly fulfill the promise
of requesting an alliance,
and bring it to completion.
We will forever be grateful for your grace and virtue.
Fearing delays in the back-and-forth communication regarding the oath document,
a copy is now presented.
Initially,
when Xìnrú arrived,
he, believing the peace treaty would be concluded,
presumed to call himself an advising official in the office of the 通謝使 (tōngxièshǐ).
During the Dàdìng period,
when the Sòng people sought peace,
Wáng Biàn was made an advising official in the office of the 通問使 (tōngwènshǐ).
Xìnrú invoked this as a precedent.
Zōng Hào, angered by his frivolous presumption,
imprisoned him and reported it.
The court also, considering him an envoy who failed to foster good relations between the two countries,
intended to detain him
and sent an envoy to ask Zōng Hào.
Zōng Hào said:
"Now that Xìnrú's mission has not been completed,
he knows he will surely be punished upon his return.
Detaining him would only give them an excuse in the future.
It would be better to enumerate his recklessness and arrogance,
release him, and send him back.
He will then be at a loss for words to justify himself to his countrymen,
and then Kuò and Tuózhoù will surely choose cautious and substantial individuals to come."
Thereupon, he was sent back.
Then Zhāng Yán’s letter was reiterated, stating: Xìnrú once again sent a letter.
Carefully examining its words,
though the intention to request peace seemed polite and humble,
the matters proposed were still not fully agreed upon.
It only mentioned that
the abducted people from Sìzhōu and other places should be returned.
As for the demanded tribute,
they wished to increase it from the old amount.
Regarding the pursuit of fugitives,
they wished to use arbitrary grace as a precedent.
However, the three matters of
稱臣 (chēngchén), ceding territory, and binding and sending treacherous officials
were all artfully dismissed with empty words,
unwilling to comply with the agreement.
Could it be that they believe the court's demands are excessive and cannot be met,
or are they gauging their virtue
and estimating their strength to be sufficient to 'fight with their backs to the wall'
and contend with our army for a day's victory?
They are neither strong
nor weak;
instead of deeply pondering and carefully considering
the advantages and disadvantages of the future,
they merely use insincere words,
expressed in a letter and diligently transmitted.
Why is this?
Warfare is a weapon of ill omen;
to delight in it is inauspicious.
However, the sages used it only when they had no alternative,
thus the Sānhuáng and Wǔdì could not avoid it.
Is it not because they had
the people's lives in mind?
Indeed, those who violate order and betray righteousness are unforgivable.
Lately, their country violated the alliance
and encroached upon our borders.
The Marshal's headquarters, obeying orders, undertook a punitive expedition.
Although the army had not yet
marched out,
the garrisons in various places were provisionally deployed for defense as appropriate.
Wherever they went, they crushed and broke the enemy,
none dared to stand against them.
The number of captives and decapitated heads was innumerable.
The remaining forces were terrified and scattered
in flight.
Therefore, the encroached territories
were swiftly pacified,
and even Sìzhōu was recovered without effort.
Now, they claim to have renounced what they had gained,
withdrawn their troops and
garrisons,
as a sign of repentance.
Are these truly sincere words?
According to the report from the Shǎnxī Pacification Commissioner's Office,
this summer, the Sòng people violated the border more than ten times,
but were all
repelled by our army,
with countless enemies beheaded, captured, and slain.
Yet, while expressing remorse for their transgressions
and exchanging letters to beg for peace,
they secretly dispatch bandits to raid our
defenses.
They hope to exploit our unpreparedness
to gain some minor advantage.
If so, where is the logic
in their request for peace?
As for their argument that the distinction of status is different now than in the past,
it is indeed different from the Dàdìng period.
The benevolence and profound virtue of our court towards the Sòng state
are
beyond
description,
as can be generally seen in the Huángtǒng period's letters of thanks.
As for Emperor Shìzōng's condescension to establish peace,
the profound grace and favor for thirty years,
how could it be forgotten?
Regarding the old ministers south of the Yangtze River to us,
at the beginning of the Dàdìng period,
due to the errors in Zhènglóng,
which led to instability in the southern territories,
we specially bestowed great favor,
changing them to a nephew state
to pacify
and govern them.
Now, the smaller state has offended the greater,
the fault lies with them.
Since they have severed the good relations of the Dàdìng period,
it is reasonable to revert to the old title of '臣 (chén)'.
If it is something a non-subject
dare not say,
why did they dare to say it during the Huángtǒng period but dare not now?
Is this truly sincere?
They also said that the land beyond the Yangtze River serves as a screen,
and if it is ceded,
there would be no country left.
Indeed, the solidity of a barrier
lies in upholding trustworthiness and righteousness.
If one does not strive for this,
even the dangers of the Yangtze River
cannot be relied upon,
let alone the mere two Huái regions.
land,
how can it be sufficient to protect us and form a state!
In the time of the Six Dynasties south of the Yangtze,
Huáinán repeatedly belonged to the Central Plain.
By the Xiǎndé reign of the Later Zhōu,
Southern Táng's
Lǐ Jǐng offered Lú, Shū, Qí, and Huáng prefectures,
drawing the Yangtze River as the border.
These were all able to form states.
Since such precedents exist,
then the matter of ceding land
is also
not impossible!
Since our army marched out of the borders,
the prefectures, armies, counties, and towns we have taken are already ours.
Those not yet taken should be ceded and offered.
Now, Fāng Xìnrú has brought a sworn
document,
which claims that the borders are all based on the great state’s Huángtǒng era and their Lóngxīng era, already fixed.
If this is the case, then not only do they not mention ceding their land,
but they also want to take
what is already ours.
How can this be reasonable!
The letter also states that in addition to the customary tribute and ceremonial gifts,
an extra sum of one million strings of cash,
converted to thirty thousand liǎng each of gold and silver,
is prepared specifically to settle the obligation of increasing the tribute again.
It also says that the annual tribute will be increased by fifty thousand liǎng of silk.
These words cannot be taken as accurate.
Moreover, the peace negotiations are not yet settled,
yet to presumptuously detail the agreement in advance
and intend
it as a sworn document,
and also to directly report the customary tribute and other three groups of envoys,
such self-assertiveness
is not in line with proper etiquette.
Fāng Xìnrú, on this side, has taken it upon himself to achieve peace,
presuming
upon the superior state,
believing that by proceeding in this direct manner,
the matter will surely be accomplished.
Such lighthearted presumption and deception
cannot be tolerated by reason.
After submitting a detailed memorial,
I respectfully received the imperial decree:
"In the era of Xuān and Jìng,
faith was abandoned and alliances broken.
When Our army marched to punish them,
they once ceded three garrisons to beg for peace.
Now
that they have groundlessly launched military action
and scornfully disregarded their solemn oaths,
even if they were to offer all the land of Jiāng and Huái,
it would still not be enough to redeem themselves.
Moreover, that state once claimed that
the relationship of uncle and nephew
was not significantly different from that of ruler and subject or father and son.
If they can truly declare themselves vassals,
then they will be permitted to take the middle ground between Jiāng and Huái as the border.
If they wish to be a vassal
state for generations,
then they must cede all of Huáinán,
taking the Great River directly as the border.
The Shǎnxī border area has already been firmly secured by our great army.
The principal conspiring treacherous officials must be bound
and sent to us.
Because they earnestly desire to inflict punishment upon themselves,
they may be ordered to send their heads in a box.
Although the annual tribute is to be increased by fifty thousand liǎng of silk,
this merely restores the old quota of the Huángtǒng era;
how can it be considered an increase?
They must be ordered to add another fifty thousand liǎng of silk
to truly demonstrate their remorse and apology.
When peace was sought in Biànyáng,
gifts for the army were offered:
five million liǎng of gold, fifty million of silver, one million each of patterned silk and raw silk, ten thousand each of oxen, horses, and mules, one thousand camels, and five sets of books.
Now, since it is only a corner of the Jiāngbiǎo
region,
which is different from before,
special compassion is extended,
and they are merely ordered to provide ten million liǎng of silver for the army's reward.
Fāng Xìnrú's words are contradictory
and not to be trusted.
People like Lǐ Dàxìng, Zhū Zhìzhī, Lǐ Bì, and Wú Guǎn seem honest;
they can be sent to the army front to discuss.
Fāng Xìnrú's
crime of deception
is worse than Hú Fǎng's.
However, since ancient times, when armies clash,
envoys are allowed to move between them.
Let him provisionally return and report."
I respectfully acknowledge that His Majesty's sagely virtue is broad and magnificent,
covering as heaven and embracing as earth,
pardoning the ignorant and forgiving transgressions.
How can we not respectfully obey and live up to the profound benevolence!
If
there is still any delay or defiance,
then the matter of peace
should not be hoped for again.
The safety, danger, survival, and destruction of the Sòng state
will depend on this.
May you consider carefully
and not cause
future regret!
In the ninth month of the seventh year of Tàihé,
he died in Biàn.
Thereafter, the Sòng people indeed requested to treat their uncle as an elder brother,
increased the annual tribute,
prepared silver for the army's reward,
and sent the heads of the treacherous officials Hán Tuōzhòu and Sū Shīdàn in boxes as an offering to beg for an alliance.
Upon hearing the news of his death,
the Emperor was deeply grieved and shocked,
suspended court,
and ordered his son Sùzhí Jiāngjūn Tiānxià Nú to rush to the place of mourning.
He also ordered that after the burial, the painted portrait be brought to the capital,
where he would personally preside over the memorial ceremony.
Zhāng Yánsǒu, the Vice Resident Administrator of Nánjīng, was appointed as the Imperial Sacrificial Envoy and Funeral Director,
and Nǚxīliè Bó gěsù, the Prefect of Jǔzhōu, was appointed as the Imperial Burial Envoy.
Fifty warriors, flag and drum bearers, and flute and horn players were also selected from the army,
and outside, accompanying relatives, officials, and imperial guards were sent to the burial site.
The funeral gifts were very generous.
He was posthumously named Tōngmǐn.
A eulogy states: Since Zōngbì of Jīn returned after crossing the Yangtze,
the Huái River was later drawn as the border.
Afterward, Hǎilíng defied the masses and raised an army,
depleting national resources,
causing disunity between superiors and subordinates,
and internal troubles arose first.
Therefore, in the early years of Shìzōng
and the late years of Zhāngzōng,
dealing with the south
was always out of necessity,
and envoys for detailed inquiries were always dispatched first.
Tuōzhòu's reckless scheme misguided the state;
his actions were ill-timed,
and his defeat was inevitable.
Kuí and Zōnghào, though always victorious in their military campaigns,
did not refuse the arrival of envoys seeking peace.
During the negotiations of ceremonial gifts, documents, and speeches,
as they praised, criticized, increased, and decreased,
if there was an opening,
peace was granted.
As for the matter of sending heads in a box,
the Sòng people also wanted to use this to rid themselves of their own misfortune.
Nevertheless,
Kuí, Zōnghào, and
Shǐjítā, all commanders of constantly victorious armies and brave generals,
died one after another,
and the peace treaty was also concluded.
Was it perhaps Heaven's will to grant respite to the people of the north and south?
Collation Notes
Jiágǔ Qīngchén,
Nèizú Xiāng, Jiágǔ Héng, Wányán Ānguó, Yáolǐ Bódié
Jiágǔ Qīngchén's original name was Ābùshā.
He was from Huánchú, Húlígǎi Circuit.
He was imposing in appearance and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
In the eighth year of Huángtǒng,
he inherited his grandfather Bódá's military command.
In the first year of Dàdìng,
hearing of Shìzōng's enthronement,
he led six thousand troops from his unit to meet him in Zhōngdū,
and for his merit, he was promoted to Zhāowǔ Dàjiāngjūn.
He followed Yòu Fù Yuánshuài Hégelǐ Zhìníng as Guǎnyā Wànhù,
responding to Zuǒ Dōujiān Wányán Sījìng,
pursuing the remaining partisans of Wōwò,
defeating them at Ròuyuǎn,
and capturing them all at Mòbálǐdá.
After the bandits were pacified,
he was promoted to Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn
and became the Military Commissioner of Yǐngshùn.
At that time, twenty thousand Sòng troops attacked and captured Rǔzhōu,
killing the Prefect Wūgǔsūn Máfa
and two thousand Hàn soldiers.
Zōngyǐn, the Commander of Hénán,
dispatched Wànhù Bóshùlǔ Dìngfāng and Qīngchén and others to lead four thousand cavalry to attack them.
The Sòng people abandoned the city and fled,
thus Rǔzhōu was recovered.
In the fifth month of the third year,
he followed Zhìníng to retake Sùzhōu.
Sòng general Lǐ Shìfǔ was greatly defeated and fled.
Zhìníng again sent Qīngchén and others with troops to pursue,
and they defeated him again.
Upon hearing of the victory,
he was appointed Sùzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He was transferred to Bózhōu,
revised to be Northwest Circuit Pacification Overseer,
then promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Wūgǔ Shí lěi tribes.
In the twelfth year,
he was appointed Vice Grand Inspector of the Right,
promoted to Vice Grand Inspector of the Left,
and then sent out as Commander of the Shǎnxī Circuit,
concurrently overseeing the affairs of Jīngzhào Fǔ.
When he bade farewell at court,
he was bestowed with a golden belt and a horse,
and the emperor instructed him, saying:
"You have commanded the imperial guards
and attended me daily;
your diligence has been long-standing.
Therefore, I bestow this upon you.
You should strive even harder."
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was made Grand Administrator of Xījīng.
After three years,
he was promoted to Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
when the dispatch of troops was first deliberated,
he was appointed Grand Commander of the Northeast Circuit Military Forces in his concurrent capacity,
but the imperial edict later halted it.
Soon after, his daughter became a zhāoyí (昭儀),
and his favor and reliance became even greater.
In the second year,
he was appointed Left Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
Shortly thereafter,
he was advanced to Grand Councilor,
enfeoffed as the Duke of Ruì,
and granted the privilege of being treated as a member of the imperial clan.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Right Chancellor,
and supervised the compilation of the National History.
At that time, there was a discussion about conscripting soldiers for border defense.
The emperor asked,
"Are the Hàn people or the Xià people braver?"
Qīngchén replied,
"The Hàn people are braver."
The emperor said,
"In the past, Yuánhào (元昊) disturbed the border,
and the Sòng (宋) ultimately could not control him.
Why was that?"
Qīngchén replied,
"The Sòng's military command methods are unknown,
but the people of the Southwest Circuit now are far superior to them."
Not long after,
he was transferred to Chóngjìn (崇進) and
re-enfeoffed as Dài (戴).
One day,
the emperor said to the grand councilors,
"Someone presented a diagram of the Eight Formations;
what is the diagram truly like?
I have often read the Military Classics compiled by Sòng Bái (宋白),
but many of the methods of attack and defense recorded therein are difficult to implement."
Qīngchén replied,
"Military books all contain fixed methods,
which are difficult to adapt to changing circumstances.
Our dynasty's military tactics
only use regular and irregular forces.
When facing the enemy, we adapt to changes,
treating the regular as irregular,
and the irregular as regular,
thus ensuring victory in every endeavor."
The emperor said,
"Since ancient times, military operations have never deviated from the two methods of the regular and the irregular.
Moreover, learning ancient military strategies is like learning to play chess;
if one has not truly grasped them in one's heart,
and wishes to use old formations to engage the enemy,
it is indeed too simplistic."
Soon after, he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
which was not granted.
He pleaded earnestly,
and was then granted leave to visit his parents.
The emperor instructed him, saying:
"I heard that your mother is old and
you wish to return and visit her.
Therefore, I specially grant you fifty days' leave,
to travel by post-horse.
You may stay there for one month."
In the second month of the fifth year,
the emperor was at the Nínghé Diàn (凝和殿).
Qīngchén returned from visiting his parents
and paid his respects to the emperor.
The emperor asked,
"Is your mother healthy?
How old is she?
How many years has it been since you last saw each other?"
Qīngchén replied,
"My mother is eighty-three years old,
and it has been ten years since we parted.
Fortunately, she is quite strong and healthy."
The emperor said,
"Why doesn't she come here?"
He replied,
"She is busy with household affairs,
so she doesn't wish to leave."
The emperor said,
"Many elderly people are like this.
This is what is meant by 'When one's vitality and strength have declined,
one should guard against acquisitiveness.'"
Then he asked Qīngchén again:
"What are the customs like in Húlígǎi Lù?"
He replied,
"Compared to before, they now have some sense of propriety,
but their bravery and strength are not as great."
He then spoke of the soldiers in the Southwest and Northwest Circuits,
saying that their proficiency in archery
was also not like it used to be.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
then appointed Left Chancellor,
and re-enfeoffed as Mì (密).
He received orders to dispatch troops
and acted as the Head of the Department of State Affairs at Línhuáng Fǔ.
Qīngchén sent people to reconnoiter the actual situation.
With eight thousand light cavalry,
he ordered Xuānhuī Shǐ Yílà Mǐn (移剌敏) to be the Grand Commander,
and Left Guard General Chōng (充)
and Pacification Commissioner Wányán Ānguó (完顏安國) as the left and right wings,
to lead the vanguard.
He himself selected ten thousand elite soldiers to form the rearguard.
They advanced to Hélè Hé (合勒河),
where the vanguard, led by Mǐn (敏) and others, attacked fourteen camps at Kǎolǎo Luò (栲栳濼),
captured them,
and returned to meet the main army.
A subordinate unit veered off
and seized their captured sheep, horses, and supplies, returning with them.
Qīngchén sent someone to demand compensation and punishment,
but the northern rebels thereupon defected,
engaging in extensive plunder.
The emperor sent an envoy to rebuke Qīngchén
and ordered Right Chancellor Xiāng (襄) to replace him.
In the fifth year of Chéng'ān,
he was demoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Hénghǎi Army, concurrently Inspector of Cāngzhōu (滄州) Prefecture.
Initially,
the emperor had instructed the grand councilors, saying:
"Qīngchén had previously rendered meritorious service,
and his crimes are not yet very clear.
If he is demoted,
he should be allowed to retire."
Initially, he was planned to be appointed Prefect of Guǎngníng Fǔ.
The emperor said,
"For now, give him Cāngzhōu."
Afterward, he again said,
"If he is given it, then so be it,
but I just fear there will be people talking."
Soon after, he retired again.
In the second year of Tàihé, he died
at the age of seventy.
His son, Yaōcházalá (么查剌), inherited the rank of méng'ān (猛安).
When the military campaign was first discussed,
Qīngchén was in charge of it.
Later, when he led the army on campaign,
although he repeatedly achieved victories, he was greedy for minor gains,
which led to several years of unrest on the northern border.
The world blamed him for this.
Chancellor Xiāng's (襄) original name was Àn (唵).
He was the fifth-generation descendant of Zhāozǔ.
His grandfather, Shígǔnǎi (什古廼),
followed Tàizǔ (太祖) in pacifying Liáo (遼),
and for his merits was granted the hereditary méng'ān (猛安) of Shàngjīng (上京),
and served successively as Grand Administrator of Dōngjīng (東京).
His father, Ālǔdài (阿魯帶),
achieved merits in the northern expedition at the beginning of Huángtǒng,
and was appointed Participating Censor.
Xiāng in his youth had high aspirations and integrity.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and possessed great courage and strategy.
At eighteen, he inherited his hereditary peerage.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
the Qìdān rebelled.
He followed the Left Vice Grand Marshal Móuyǎn, leading his own troops to quell the rebels.
They fought at Chángluò in Zhàozhōu.
Xiāng was the first to ascend and engage in fierce combat.
His leg was struck by a stray arrow,
but he wrapped the wound and continued to fight.
His morale grew even stronger,
and he won all seven battles.
Móuyǎn grasped his hand and said:
"Today's victory
is entirely due to your efforts."
The rebels fled and crossed the Méngsōng Hé.
They were pursued and overtaken.
Their encampment had much grass,
so the rebels set fire to it, using the wind.
Xiāng also set fires,
establishing an open space to await them.
After more than ten engagements,
the rebels became increasingly cornered.
Xiāng said to Móuyǎn:
"If we do not seize this opportunity to completely annihilate them now,
we will regret it later."
Móuyǎn agreed.
Xiāng led his troops in fierce combat.
They were utterly defeated,
and tens of thousands were captured.
At that time, the imperial court dispatched Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Púsǎn Zhōngyì to attack Móuyǎn's generals.
Xiāng again followed Zhōngyì in pursuing the rebels to Xiànquán, west of Niǎolǐng.
Upon reaching them,
he led the right wing, personally charging forward to strike.
The rebels were routed,
men and horses trampling each other to death.
Xiànquán was almost pacified.
The rebel chieftain Wōwò barely escaped with a few dozen cavalry,
but was eventually captured.
Xiāng was considered first in merit.
The officials proposed appointing him as Zīzhōu Cìshǐ,
but an imperial edict specially appointed him as Bózhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He was then twenty-three years old.
When the Sòng people encroached upon the southern border,
Xiāng was made Yǐng-Shòu Dūtǒng.
He led two thousand armored soldiers across the Yǐng Shuǐ,
defeated five thousand enemy troops,
recaptured Yǐngzhōu,
and personally captured the Sòng commander Yáng Sī.
Next, at Háozhōu,
Sòng General Guō Tàiwèi retreated to defend Héngjiàn Shān.
Xiāng attacked him.
An ambush crossbow shot him in the knee.
He pressed the attack more urgently,
captured it,
and secured Guō Tàiwèi.
Afterwards, he advanced towards Chúzhōu.
Xiāng was the vanguard.
When they were about to reach Qīngliú Guān,
they captured a Sòng scout
and learned that the enemy intended to launch a night attack from three directions,
catching them unprepared.
Left Vice Grand Marshal Gēshíliè Zhìníng asked for a plan.
Xiāng said:
"Our troops are few and the terrain is narrow.
If we cannot secure the pass,
when the enemy arrives,
we will have no stronghold.
We must take it first."
Zhìníng asked:
"Between you and me, who should go?"
Xiāng said:
"The Grand Marshal is a great minister of the state;
how can you move lightly?
I will go and take it for you."
Zhìníng approved of this.
Xiāng led two thousand cavalry,
divided into two columns:
one along the main road, while he himself, with a thousand troops, secretly ascended by a side path.
When they got close,
the enemy only then noticed them.
Xiāng attacked and captured it,
occupying the pass.
Zhìníng personally inspected the battlefield
and looked at Xiāng, saying:
"To defeat the enemy in an impregnable place,
you are truly an outstanding hero of the world."
When Sòng requested an alliance,
the army returned.
He was summoned to be Gǒngwèi Zhí Dūzhīhuīshǐ,
then appointed Diànqián Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
then transferred to Zuǒwèi.
He was sent out as Dōngběi Lù Zhāotǎo Dūjiān,
then promoted to Sùpín Lù Jiédùshǐ,
and later transferred to Hélǎnlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
When Left Chancellor Zhìníng became gravely ill,
Shìzōng visited him to inquire about his health.
Zhìníng recommended Xiāng,
saying:
"He possesses both wisdom and courage,
and has the talent to govern the world.
Others cannot compare.
If he is employed in the future,
he will probably surpass me."
Shìzōng immediately summoned and appointed him Diànqián Zuǒfù Dūdiǎnjiǎn.
He was made the envoy for the Sòng emperor's birthday.
Sòng was then praying to be exempted from personally receiving the national letter.
When Xiāng arrived,
Sòng envoys repeatedly came to negotiate,
but he refuted them all,
eventually completing the ceremony and returning.
He was appointed Shǎnxī Lù Tǒngjūnshǐ,
and bestowed with court attire, a horse, saddle and bridle, and a saber.
He was then appointed Hénán Tǒngjūnshǐ.
He entered the court as Lìbù Shàngshū,
then transferred to Dūdiǎnjiǎn,
and granted ten million cash.
Shìzōng said to his prime ministers:
"Xiāng is a very cultivated person.
Even when not on duty,
he enters the palace to plan various affairs,
and only withdraws after a task has been entrusted to him.
His public diligence is thus.
How can one often find talent like Xiāng's?"
He was promoted to Yùshǐ Dàfū.
A month later,
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
The emperor instructed him, saying:
"While you were in Hénán, managing border affairs,
you showed great organization and discipline.
And while in the Lìbù,
and then as Diǎnjiǎn,
you especially upheld public duty and law.
I commend this greatly.
Recently, as the head of the Censorate,
you were also known for your uprightness.
Therefore, I entrust you with governmental affairs.
You must strive even harder!"
Shortly after,
he was promoted to Zuǒchéng.
While Xiāng was in outer appointments,
his governance yielded extraordinary results.
At this time, the imperial court issued an edict across the realm to praise and reward upright officials,
listing his name to show commendation.
In the twenty-third year,
he was promoted to Píngzhāng Zhèngshì
and enfeoffed as Xiāo Guó Gōng.
Shìzōng, considering the imperial grandson of the Jīnyuán Jùnwáng's direct line,
intended to grant him a princely title,
and decreed to select a state name.
Xiāng said:
"For the great plan of the world,
one must first rectify its root.
Yuán (原) means root.
I request that he be enfeoffed as Yuán."
This was followed.
Traditionally,
the Jiédùshǐ of various tribes and their subordinates were often appointed from literati,
but some privately indulged in unlawful acts.
It was proposed to change to appointing people of various backgrounds.
Xiāng said:
"Although the northern border is peaceful,
it constantly needs to be managed.
If this avenue is blocked,
how will those with meritorious service be placed afterwards?
I request that the old system be maintained."
Another day,
the discussion turned to the ancient practice of military supervision.
Xiāng said:
"During the early Hàn and Táng dynasties, there were no military supervisors.
Generals were given full authority,
thus they always won battles and
always captured objectives.
It was only in later generations that inner court eunuchs were used to supervise the military,
and they were constrained by them,
leading to many defeats and few successes.
If the right general is found,
military supervisors are truly unnecessary."
Both points were graciously accepted.
He was decreed to receive tribute from the northern tribes.
Upon his return,
Shìzōng asked about border affairs.
Xiāng presented detailed maps,
and consequently submitted a strategy for restraining tributary tribes and subduing Dàshí.
An imperial edict commanded that it all be implemented.
He was promoted to Yòuchéngxiàng,
and his enfeoffment was changed to Dài.
Shìzōng was unwell.
He lodged in the inner palace with Grand Commandant Túshān Kèníng and Administrator Zhāng Rǔlín,
and together they received his dying instructions.
When Zhāngzōng first took office,
there was a proposal to abolish the monastic serfs (sēngdào núbì).
Grand Commandant Kèníng reported, saying:
“This has become a long-standing custom;
if it is suddenly changed,
it will cause unrest among the people.
If Your Majesty dislikes their large numbers,
it would be advisable to establish strict regulations
to prevent excessive ordination,
and then their numbers will naturally decrease.”
Xiāng said:
“Why do those who have left home need servants?
I request that, regardless of how they were originally acquired,
they all be freed to become commoners.
If the resources of temples and monasteries were originally estimated based on the number of serfs,
these should also be fully exempted.”
An imperial edict followed Xiāng’s words.
Because of this, many households of the two taxes became commoners.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
Tóngzhī Dìzhōu Fángyùshǐ Mó presented a memorial,
criticizing all the prime ministers and grand councillors.
Grand Tutor Kèníng reported
that Xiāng knew in advance what Mó had said.
Thereupon, an edict ordered Mó to return to his original Méng'ān,
and Xiāng was sent out to govern Píngyángfǔ.
He was transferred to govern Fèngxiáng,
and successively served as Xīīng Liúshǒu.
He was summoned and appointed Tóngpàn Dàmùqīnfǔshì,
promoted to Shūmìshǐ,
again appointed Yòuchéngxiàng,
and his enfeoffment was changed to Rèn.
At that time, Zuǒchéngxiàng Jiágǔ Qīngchén was defending the northern border.
His strategies were ineffective,
and as the border situation became critical,
Xiāng was ordered to take command of his troops,
wearing the golden tablet,
to act as circumstances required.
At the farewell banquet, he was given
a sable fur coat, a saddle, fine armor, and two warhorses.
At this time, Húlí Cí also rebelled,
gathering followers between Běijīng and Línhuáng.
When Xiāng arrived,
he sent someone to summon them,
and they immediately surrendered.
He then garrisoned Línhuáng.
A short while later,
he led his army out to Dàyánluò,
and again sent Right Guard General Wányán Chōng to advance on Wòlúsù City,
intending to garrison it
and await an opportunity to advance.
He sent a map to report this.
Opinions varied among the deliberators,
so he was immediately summoned for a direct discussion,
and then generously rewarded and sent back.
Not long after,
he sent Northwest Route Commander Wányán Ānguó and others to head towards Duōquánzi.
A secret edict ordered an advance to suppress the rebellion.
Then, a detached force was ordered to go via the Eastern Route,
and Xiāng via the Western Route.
The Eastern Army, upon reaching Lóngjūhé, was surrounded by Zǔmó,
unable to break out for three days,
and urgently requested aid.
Some proposed waiting until all armies had gathered before departing.
Xiāng said:
“Our army has been under siege for several days;
even rushing to save them, we fear it may be too late.
How can we delay?”
He immediately beat the drums and set off at night.
Some proposed sending someone ahead to report to those under siege,
so they would know that reinforcements were arriving.
Xiāng said:
“If those sent are captured by the enemy,
and they learn that our forces are few and our supplies are behind,
then our mission will fail.”
He then sped up even more.
At dawn,
approaching the enemy,
the troops requested a short rest.
Xiāng said:
“The reason I rushed through the night
was to catch them unprepared.
If we slow down, we will miss the opportunity.”
At dawn, they pressed upon the enemy
and launched a sudden attack.
The officers and soldiers within the siege also beat drums and shouted, breaking out,
and a great battle ensued.
They captured carts, tents, cattle, and sheep.
All the enemy fled to Wòlǐzhā Hé.
Ānguó was sent to pursue them.
The scattered enemy fled.
Heavy rain fell,
and eighteen or nineteen out of ten died from the cold.
Their chief surrendered,
and so Xiāng inscribed his achievement on the rock face of Jiǔfēng.
When the victory was reported,
the Emperor sent an envoy with generous rewards to commend him,
and a separate edict permitted him to appropriately reward the officers and soldiers.
In the ninth month,
he returned to the capital,
was appointed Zuǒchéngxiàng,
supervised the compilation of the national history,
and was enfeoffed as Chángshān Jùnwáng.
At the banquet in Qìnghé Diàn,
the Emperor personally raised a cup and drank,
and bestowed his personal jade-ornamented sword,
telling him to wear it immediately.
In the tenth month,
Zǔmó rebelled again.
Xiāng was stationed in Běijīng.
At the same time, the leaders of the imperial herdsmen, Qìdān Déshòu and Suǒ, rebelled in Xìnzhōu,
falsely establishing the reign title Shēnshèng.
Their forces numbered in the hundreds of thousands,
shocking those near and far.
Xiāng remained calm as usual,
and the people’s morale was thereby stabilized.
Initially,
when Xiāng departed for his post,
upon reaching Shíménzhèn,
he secretly told his subordinates:
“Northern barbarians invading the frontier are not worth worrying about.
My only fear is that treacherous individuals might take advantage of the opportunity.
The area near Běijīng has few troops;
we should prepare for this in advance.”
He immediately dispatched an official to mobilize six thousand troops from Shàngjīng and other places,
which indeed proved useful at this time.
Línhuáng Commander Wūgǔlún Dàoyuǎn and Xiánpíng Commander Púchá Shǒuchún advanced separately to suppress the rebellion,
capturing Déshòu and others and sending them to the capital.
During the Qìdān rebellion,
court officials debated suspending the suburban sacrifices,
and also wanted to change them to the first Xīn day of the first month.
The Emperor sent an envoy to ask Xiāng about this,
who replied:
“The suburban sacrifice is a grave ceremony,
and an edict was issued to the empire in advance,
and vassal states have already presented their congratulatory memorials.
If it is now suspended midway,
how can we meet the expectations of the four directions?
If it is changed to the first Xīn day of the first month,
that is the ceremony for praying for grain,
not the original intention of the suburban sacrifice to see God.
Great ceremonies cannot be lightly abandoned;
I request that it be carried out as planned,
and your servant asks to eradicate the rebels before the sacrifice.”
Soon after, the rebels were defeated,
just as he had predicted.
After the suburban sacrifice was completed,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as Nányáng Jùnwáng.
When the Qìdān were first suppressed,
officials from Lónghǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn and Jìedùshǐ downwards were permitted to award titles at their discretion.
Xiāng believed that the power of reward and punishment was not for a subject to preempt,
and dared not accept the edict.
When the rebels were pacified,
he requested that a close minister be entrusted with conveying the imperial decree to the officers and soldiers,
so they would know the Emperor’s grace.
Then Lǐ Rénhuì was sent with thirty xuān and one hundred and fifty chì,
to distribute them according to merit.
When Déshòu rebelled,
the various Cí also plundered, causing trouble for the people.
Xiāng worried that they would unite with Déshòu,
so he moved the various Cí to an area near the capital
and pacified them with kindness.
Someone said:
“The Cí people are no different from the northern barbarians.
Now placing them in the interior, what if they cause trouble?”
Xiāng laughed and said:
“Although the Cí are a mixed group,
they are also our frontier people.
If we treat them with kindness,
how can they not be moved?
I am here,
so they will certainly not dare to stir.”
Indeed,
there were no problems later.
Soon after, an edict ordered Cānzhī Zhèngshì Yì to temporarily lead their army.
Upon his audience,
he was given fifty million coins.
The following year,
he was relieved of his duties due to a parent’s death.
The next day,
he was reinstated to office.
At that time, there was a discussion that the number of Qìdān households with serfs was still large,
and a request was made to sell them all to disperse their faction.
Xiāng considered this inconvenient
and proposed to retain a certain number of dependents,
and that the rest be redeemed by the government as commoners.
The Emperor accepted this.
The northern regions rebelled again.
Yì fought poorly and lost control.
Again, Xiāng was ordered to be the Assistant Left Grand Marshal (Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài) and take charge of the army.
Soon after, he was appointed Privy Council Commissioner (Pīmìshǐ) concurrently with Grand Councillor (Píngzhāng Zhèngshì),
stationed in Běijīng.
The people were then suffering from food shortages,
so he reduced the price and sold grain from the granaries to relieve them.
Some remarked that the army was short of provisions,
but Xiāng said:
"How can the people have enough while the army does not?"
He proceeded with his plan,
and all the people were pleased and submitted.
At that time, there was a discussion about a northern expedition.
Xiāng memorialized that Zōnghào, concurrently serving as co-judge of the Office of the Grand Imperial Family (Dàmùqīnfǔshì), should lead an army to Tàizhōu.
He also requested that Héng, the Assistant Left Grand Councillor (Zuǒchéng), proceed to Fúzhōu to the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn),

and lead an army to the northwest to intercept [a character that cannot be rendered in Pinyin is represented as a black square, consistent with the user's instructions regarding non-Pinyin rendering].
He himself would lead troops to Línhuáng.
The Emperor followed his strategy
and bestowed inner treasury goods for use by the army.
Later, the Xié Chu 部族 (bùzú) went to Fúzhōu to surrender.
The Emperor sent a special envoy to inquire of Xiāng,
and Xiāng deemed it advantageous to accept them.
He was granted a precious sword,
and an imperial edict instructed that a thorough pursuit should be undertaken as appropriate.
He then ordered the soldiers to carry their own provisions to save on transport,
advancing and garrisoning in the Miǎnyīlàliè and Wūmǎnsǎo mountains to press them.
He then requested the immediate use of infantry to dig trenches and build barricades,
starting from the left border of Línhuáng to the Běijīng Road, as a blockade.
Many speakers expressed differing opinions,
so an imperial edict sought his strategy.
Xiāng said:
"Although the cost this year will be a million strings of cash,
once the work is completed, the border defenses will be solid, and the garrison troops can be reduced by half,
saving three million strings of cash annually.
Moreover, it will ease the burden of transport on the people,
which is truly an everlasting benefit."
The Emperor approved the edict.
Xiāng personally supervised the work,
with both military and civilians involved.
He also recruited starving people to be employed on the spot,
and it was completed in fifty days.
Consequently, the northwest and southwest roads also had defenses built as he had requested.
Not long after,
the Tàizhōu army engaged the enemy.
Zōnghào supervised their rear,
killing and capturing over half.
Various tribes successively sent offers of submission,
which Xiāng accepted.
From then on, the northern frontier was pacified.
Xiāng returned to Línhuáng,
reducing the garrison troops by 40,000 and horses by 20,000.
The Emperor recalled him with a tally,
sending a close attendant to welcome him on the road.
Upon his arrival,
the Emperor again received and questioned him at his residence.
He presented ten strategic points for the border,
all of which were implemented.
He was also generously rewarded,
and again appointed Left Grand Councillor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng).
Initially,
when Xiāng returned from the army,
the Emperor instructed his chief ministers, saying:
"Privy Council Commissioner Xiāng has built strong and complete border fortifications.
In ancient times, establishing even one city or town
was rewarded.
I wished to appoint him to the Three Dukes (Sāngōng),
but the Three Dukes are not positions for rewarding merit.
Even the Left Grand Councillor is not for rewarding merit.
Nevertheless, he can be specially appointed to it."
He dispatched Àlègēn Āhǎi, a Director of the Left Bureau (Zuǒsī Lángzhōng), to issue an imperial edict of commendation.
In the first month of the fourth year,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
continuing to hold the position of Left Grand Councillor as before.
Xiāng was grave and reticent,
endeavoring to maintain stability and adhere to laws.
Whenever an official had something to report,
he would always ask:
"What do the various chancellors say?"
The official would reply, "Such-and-such chancellor says this,
such-and-such chancellor says that."
Xiāng would then say:
"Follow so-and-so's proposal."
His decisions were never different.
Those who understood considered Xiāng truly to have the qualities of a chancellor.
At that time, the Emperor largely reformed institutions.
He first established the Office of Judicial Review (Tíxíng Sī),
and also considered setting up "leisurely and idle" positions,
like the Palace Superintendents (Gōngguānshǐ) of the Sòng Dynasty,
to accommodate high-ranking officials who retired due to age.
Xiāng said:
"When old officials retire,
the court provides for them with salaries and [a character that cannot be rendered in Pinyin is represented as a black square, consistent with the user's instructions regarding non-Pinyin rendering].
The grace and courtesy are most generous.
If the elderly do not retire,
and there is also the law of periodic review,
this is to suppress greed and promote integrity.
If new positions are to be created,
I fear it may lead to excess."
He also said:
"Reducing affairs is not as good as reducing officials.
Currently, many judicial review officials
are useless for governance,
only disrupting the affairs of the responsible departments.
The debaters say that this is an external bureau (wàitái),
and should not be abolished.
I fear these confusing words
only trouble the imperial hearing.
Moreover, what the Censorate (Xiàntái) oversees is investigating official misconduct
and rectifying grievances among the populace.
It does not have the authority to supervise judicial matters or make recommendations.
If it has already been established and is difficult to change immediately,
its task of investigating upright and capable individuals should not be subordinate to this department.
Instead, the Investigating Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ) should conduct thorough investigations at the end of each year,
and also periodically select officials for impartial inquiries."
The Emperor listened and accepted all of his advice.
Soon after, he requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
At that time, there was a drought.
The Emperor ordered the relevant officials to pray for rain.
Xiāng, along with Grand Councillor Zhāng Wàngōng and Participator in Government (Cānzhèng) Púsǎn Kuí,
among others, submitted a memorial taking responsibility.
The Emperor summoned Hànlín Academy Scholar Dǎng Huáiīng to draft a 'Self-Incrimination Edict' (Zuìjǐ Zhào),
and also comforted Xiāng and the others, instructing them to continue their duties.
In the spring of the first year of Tàihé,
he received an imperial command to hasten to pray at the Tàiqīng Palace in Bózhōu and at the Hòutǔ Fāngyuè.
Because his hereditary enfeoffment was distant,
he was specially reassigned as Military Governor of the Hánjiān Prefecture Circuit (Héjiānfǔlù Suànshù Hǎiměng'ān).
The next year,
the imperial prince was born, and
Xiāng again personally requested to express his gratitude.
After sacrificing at Sōngyuè,
he returned to the Zhītiánzhīfǔ Inn [near Zhītián].
He then died of illness,
at the age of sixty-three.
Upon hearing the news,
the court was adjourned.
An envoy was sent to offer sacrifices on the road.
His funeral rites followed those of Grand Tutor (Tàishī) Zīwáng Kèníng.
His posthumous name was Wǔzhāo.
Zhāng Xíngjiǎn was ordered to inscribe his stele.
Xiāng was intelligent and keen,
with military talent surpassing others.
The Emperor treated him with great personal favor,
thus he achieved success wherever he went.
When he was garrisoned in Línhuáng,
someone sent a forged letter to Túshān Yì, the Defense Commissioner of Xījīng,
intending to frame him.
When the letter was reported,
the Emperor returned the letter to Xiāng,
showing such clear trust.
Later, the person who forged the letter was indeed apprehended.
He served in the government for twenty years,
was clear and practiced in precedents,
simple, weighty, and decisive,
with an especially broad and magnanimous character.
He treated his subordinates with full courtesy,
and employed people according to their strengths,
becoming a renowned general and chancellor of his time.
During the Dà'ān period,
he was enshrined in the ancestral temple of Zhāngzōng.
Jiágǔ Héng's original name was Ālǐbù.
He was from the Yìdābā Mǒukè of the Sāntǔ Měng'ān in the Shāndōng Xīlù.
In the thirteenth year of Dàdìng,
the Jinshi examination for Nǚzhí was first established,
and Héng placed fourth.
He was appointed Professor of Dōngpíng Prefecture.
He was transferred to be Registrar of Fànyáng,
selected as Compiler in the National History Institute (Guóshǐyuàn Biānxiūguān),
and then changed to Attendant Academician of the Hànlín Academy (Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì).
Shìzōng once told his chief ministers:
"Among the Nǚzhí Jinshi, truly talented individuals are hard to come by.
However, Túshān Yì, Jiágǔ Héng, and Ní Pánggǔ Jiàn are all useful talents."
He was promoted to Compiler of the Imperial Diary (Xiū Qǐjūzhù).
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he served as Investigating Censor (Shì Yùshǐ),
then transferred to an Executive Assistant (Yuánwàiláng) of the Right Bureau (Yòusī).
His memorials and reports pleased the Emperor,
and he was promoted to Director of the Left Bureau (Zuǒsī Lángzhōng).
In the second year of Míngchāng,
he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
Not long after,
he was appointed Participator in Government (Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
In the eighth month of the third year,
due to illness,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
An imperial edict comforted him and did not permit it.
Héng had been on leave for a long time.
Upon receiving the imperial edict, he finally emerged.
The emperor saw his emaciated state
and granted him another month of leave.
In the fourth year,
an edict granted him his current name,
and he was instructed, saying:
"I select great ministers
to participate in crucial governmental affairs.
They must possess strategic planning capabilities
to assist in governing peacefully.
If gains and losses are obscure and not yet apparent,
or advantages and disadvantages are entangled and unresolved,
then pure and upright discernment is precisely what is needed
to make choices that align with public interest.
Recently, among ministers who discuss affairs,
few have a definitive opinion,
probably because they lack an inner conviction,
and thus become confused when facing issues,
leading to errors.
Upon whom can I rely?
You are loyal, honest, and impartial.
When you discern what is right, you hold fast without wavering;
when you see what is wrong, you discard it decisively.
In assessing the circumstances,
you are like a steelyard balance (quánhéng).
Your strength,
Héng, truly resembles this.
You may be granted the name 'Héng'.
In ancient times, names were given with the intention of holding one accountable for reality.
You already possess the reality,
so it can be said that your name matches.
If you carry this through to the end,
it will truly fulfill my expectations."
Cānzhīzhèngshì Xū Chíguó spoke about the method of regional cultivation.
Héng said:
"If it were truly beneficial,
the ancients would have already adopted it.
Moreover, it requires much labor for little yield,
and I fear it would waste land
and merely exhaust the people
without benefit."
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
According to the old system,
those who had long served in various court positions
were permitted to be envoys to Jiāngbiǎo.
Héng had not yet been an envoy but was appointed to the Zhízhèng office,
and was specially granted six thousand strings of cash.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
and soon after was dispatched to the Xíngshěng in Fúzhōu.
When he returned to court,
he heard of his father's death and left,
but the emperor urgently recalled him
and reinstated him to his former position.
In Chéng'ān second year,
he was sent out as Shàngjīng Liúshǒu,
and soon after was reappointed as Shūmì Fùshǐ,
to plan border affairs in the Xíngyuàn.
In the third year,
for repairing and completing the border,
he was granted an imperial edict of commendation.
In the first month of the fourth year,
he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì
and enfeoffed as Yīngguógōng.
He passed away
at the age of fifty-one.
The emperor heard of it with sorrow,
suspended court,
ordered officials to offer sacrifices,
and increased his funeral gifts.
An envoy was dispatched to supervise the burial,
and he was posthumously granted the title Zhēnnxiàn.
Wányán Ānguó, courtesy name Zhèngchén,
originally named Shé Mǔ.
His ancestors were registered residents of Shàngjīng,
and had generations of military achievements.
His grandfather, Xiépó,
was appointed Hereditary Hézhá Mǒukè of the Xīnán Lù.
Ānguó was resolute and resourceful,
and particularly skilled in archery and horsemanship.
In Zhènglóng first year,
he joined the army as a Mǒukè,
often defeating larger forces with fewer men.
During Dàdìng,
he served as Chángshān Bù,
then transferred to Hóng Xiànlìng.
When a new princely mansion was established,
he was selected to serve as Yúwáng Fǔyuàn.
He was again promoted to Yíluán Jú Fùshǐ.
In Míngchāng first year,
he was reappointed as the director of that bureau.
At that time, the Dàshí tribal chief requested to resume the annual tribute;
the imperial court granted his request
and ordered Ānguó to go as an envoy.
Upon arrival, he led his people far out to welcome the envoy to their tent,
where they bowed towards the imperial palace,
maintaining respectful decorum without slackness.
At that time, the Běizǔ tribes were pressing close to the frontier,
and a neighboring tribe wished to gain merit by boasting of their prowess to the imperial court,
proposing to invite Ānguó to join them in attacking them.
Ānguó declined, citing that he had not received an imperial edict.
They pressed him,
but he refused.
Someone tried to intimidate him with dire warnings,
to which Ānguó said:
"How can a true man compromise his integrity for life or death?
To have one's bones exposed on the frontier
is still better than dying of illness beneath a window."
The crowd was impressed by his words
and presented gifts according to custom.
Upon his return,
for successfully fulfilling his mission as envoy,
he was promoted to Wǔwèi Jūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
He was sent out as the Fùzhāotǎo of Dōngběi Lù,
but before he could take up the post,
he was reassigned as Fùzhāotǎo of Xīběi Lù.
In the sixth year,
when Zuǒchéngxiàng Jiágǔ Qīngchén launched a military campaign,
he appointed Ānguó as Xiānfēng Dūtǒng.
Coincidentally, the dependent tribes of Línhuáng and Tàizhōu rebelled,
and Ānguó first suppressed them,
and for his achievements, he was promoted to Zhāotǎoshǐ of that route,
concurrently serving as Wēiyuǎn Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In Chéng'ān first year,
during the Battle of Dàyánluò,
many were killed and captured,
and an imperial edict granted him gold and silk.
Soon after, Yòuchéngxiàng Xiāng led the main army forward,
and Ānguó served as Dūtǒng of the two routes,
achieving a great victory at Duōquánzi.
Xiāng sent Ānguó to pursue the enemy,
but all the advisors said that the supply lines would not be maintained,
and it was not feasible.
Ānguó said:
"A man can eat one sheep for more than ten days;
it is better to drive the sheep to attack them."
They then followed his plan.
Ānguó led his ten thousand men, swiftly advancing to confront them,
and compelled their tribal chief to surrender.
Upon news of the victory,
he was promoted four ranks
and transferred to Zuǒyì Dūtǒng.
In Chéng'ān second year,
for his achievements in constructing border forts,
he was summoned to sign documents at the Shūmìyuàn.
He was granted a tiger tally and sent back to the border,
empowered to act expediently.
At that time, the various tribes along the frontier surrendered;
he instructed them to resume their tribute as before.
He was promoted to Shūmì Fùshǐ.
In Tàihé first year,
he was specially granted the hereditary position of Yán'ànhé Méng'ān of Xīnán Lù,
concurrently Hézhá Mǒukè.
When the emperor visited Qìngníng Gōng,
he ordered Ānguó to strictly prepare border defenses.
He memorialized requesting to attract and reassure those who had privately fled from the Xīnán Lù border garrisons,
and the emperor approved his words.
In the third year,
he retired due to illness,
and was enfeoffed as Dàoguógōng.
In the fourth year,
he was reinstated to his former position
and then died.
When the emperor heard of it,
he suspended court.
Officials were ordered to bury him with the rites for a Zhízhèng,
and he was posthumously granted Tèjìn.
Ānguó served in the military for almost fifteen years;
his commands were strict and clear,
and he directed his soldiers as easily as his own hands.
He was also skilled at discerning the enemy's strengths and weaknesses and the terrain's dangers and ease of passage,
and in battle, he always personally led his troops,
hence he conquered wherever he went.
When the various tribes came to pay tribute,
Ānguó could call out the names of their ancestors, younger brothers, and nephews one by one to admonish and instruct them,
and all the tribes were awestruck,
and greatly feared and respected by neighboring countries.
Yáolǐ Bódié was
a native of the Kūbái Méng'ān, Tuóluóshān Mǒukè in the Běijīng Lù.
Through military merit, he successively served as Hǎibīn Lìng,
then transferred to Xúwáng Fǔyuàn.
For his competent service,
he was reappointed to the Yùshǐtái.
After inspecting and promoting integrity,
he was promoted to Tóngzhī Zhènwǔjūn Jiédùshǐshì.
In early Míngchāng,
he served as Tángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and soon after was appointed Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎo Fùshǐ.
Not long after,
he was reassigned to Dōngběi Lù.
In the first month of the sixth year,
there was an alert on the northern border;
troops gathered and urgently besieged Qìngzhōu.
Bódié led the army of his route to rescue them,
the enemy dispersed,
and the prefecture ultimately suffered no harm.
In the first year of Chéng'ān,
Chancellor Xiāng led a northern expedition.
Bèi dié served as the deputy commander of the vanguard.
When they advanced to Lóngjū Hé,
they were surrounded.
When Xiāng arrived with the main army,
they were relieved.
Later, he was appointed Jiedushi of Zhènníng Jūn.
Because six groups of herdsmen rebelled,
he was transferred to Níngchāng Jūn.
Bèi dié was the Dūtǒng,
leading ten thousand infantry and cavalry to Yìzhōu.
Tens of thousands of enemies came to meet them in battle.
Their military might was greatly formidable,
but Bèi dié personally plunged into the formation,
fighting with all his might to repel them.
He suffered two wounds.
When the victory was reported,
he was promoted one rank.
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
a thousand deserters plundered between Jǐn and Yì.
Bèi dié pursued and defeated them,
recovering what had been plundered,
and returned it all to the original households.
In the third year,
he followed Tóngpàn Dàmùqīnfǔshì Zōnghào as the Zǔyì Dūtǒng.
They battled at Yímì Hé
and won;
they battled west of Gǔbǎozǐ,
killing and capturing many.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Zhī Guǎngníngfǔ Shì,
then soon after changed to Dōngběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
For his meritorious service in defending the border,
an imperial edict commended him.
He was promoted three times to Chóngyì Jūn Jiedushi.
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
he died.
Upon hearing the news of his death,
an official was dispatched to offer sacrifices,
and five hundred taels of silver were bestowed.
He was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Bèi dié was brave, decisive, and skilled in battle.
From a young age, he distinguished himself through military achievements.
He served in military garrisons for over ten years,
achieving victory wherever he went.
He was promoted twice,
and bestowed with gold and silk.
He was highly relied upon by the emperor.
The eulogy says: The first six lines of Yìshī:
"The army sets out with discipline;
if not, it is inauspicious."
Indeed, the beginning is the start of the army,
and the way to deploy the army
is to be cautious in its beginning.
Qīngchén first proposed a military expedition,
but quickly failed due to petty greed.
Though Xiāng was virtuous,
he exhausted his strength before he could fulfill his duties.
The merits of Héng, Ānguó, and Bèi dié were secondary to Xiāng's.
However,
warfare continued, causing calamity,
until the end of the Jīn Dynasty.
Thus, there is no constant victory in war;
victory lies in strategic advantage (shì).
He who controls the army with strategic advantage is strong;
he who allows the army to control strategic advantage perishes.
Tracing Xiāng's actions of digging moats and trenches to fortify himself,
was it not like the Great Wall of the Yuánwèi and Běiqí Dynasties?
The strategic advantage of Jīn could thus be known.
When strategic advantage is constrained but the army is victorious,
it is the way of a perishing state.
Jīn began with military might,
and also ended with military might.
Alas!
When employing military force,
how can one not be cautious,
how can one not be cautious!

Biographies, Chapter 33: Yílà Lǚ, Zhāng Wàngōng, Púchá Tōng, Niángē Wòtèlā, Chéng Huī, Liú Wěi, Dǒng Shīzhōng, Wáng Wèi, Mǎ Huìdí, Mǎ Qí, Yáng Bótōng, Nímánggǔ Jiàn.
Yílà Lǚ, courtesy name Lǚdào,
was the seventh-generation descendant of Dānwáng Tūyù from Liáodōng.
His father, Yùlǔ,
died young.
Yùlǔ's cousin, Dédéyuán, the Jiedushi of Xīngpíng Jūn, had no son,
and adopted Lǚ as his heir.
At five years old,
when lying down late in the cloister,
he saw faint clouds moving across the sky.
Suddenly, he said to his wet nurse:
"Is this what is meant by 'lying down watching the blue sky and white clouds pass by?'"
Dédéyuán heard this and exclaimed:
"This child will be famous in the world for his literature!"
When he grew up,
he was widely learned and skilled in many arts,
and good at composing essays.
Initially, he sat for the imperial examination for jinshi,
but disliked the cumbersome search and inspection process and left it.
He was appointed by imperial favor as Chéngfèng Bān Zhīhòu and National History Institute Sūxiě.
Shìzōng was promoting Confucianism,
and ordered the translation of scriptures and histories.
He was promoted to Guóshǐyuàn Biānxiūguān,
concurrently serving as Bǐyàn Zhízhǎng.
One day,
Shìzōng summoned him and asked:
"I have recently been reading Zhēnguàn Zhèngyào,
and I see Wèi Zhēng's excellent strategies and loyal integrity,
which are truly admirable.
Why are there no such individuals as Zhēng in recent times?"
Lǚ replied:
"There are loyal and virtuous individuals
in every era;
it is just whether the superiors use them or not."
Shìzōng said:
"Have you not seen Liú Zhònghuì
and Zhāng Rǔlín?
I promoted these two
because they had served in censorate positions
and repeatedly offered loyal advice.
How can you say they are not used?
It is simply that talented individuals are hard to find."
Lǚ said:
"Your subject has not heard their remonstrances.
Moreover, Hǎilíng blocked the avenues of speech,
and the world kept silent,
which became a custom.
I wish Your Majesty would learn from past mistakes
and open the door for remonstrance;
the world would be greatly fortunate."
Initially, there was a discussion to establish a Nǚzhí Jinshi examination based on current affairs policies.
The Ministry of Rites argued that their studies were different,
and they could not be generally called Jinshi.
An edict commanded Lǚ to settle the matter.
He then submitted a proposal saying:
"The Jinshi examination
originated in the Dàyè period of the Suí Dynasty,
initially testing policies.
The early Táng Dynasty followed this.
During Gāozōng's time, it included maxims, inscriptions, and poetry,
and it was not until Wénzōng that it specialized in fu (rhapsodies).
Moreover, at the beginning of the Jinshi system,
it primarily tested policies.
Now, for Nǚzhí students to be called Jinshi by testing policies,
what is there to doubt?"
Shìzōng was greatly pleased,
and the matter was consequently implemented.
In the fifteenth year,
he was appointed Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì,
concurrently holding his previous position.
Soon after, he was promoted to Xiūzhuàn.
In the twentieth year,
an edict ordered him to oversee the painting of meritorious officials' portraits in Yǎnqìng Gōng.
He exceeded the deadline
and was demoted to Yìngfèng.
A year later,
he was reinstated as Xiūzhuàn,
then transferred to Shàngshū Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng.
When Zhāngzōng was Jīnyuán Jùnwáng,
he enjoyed reading the Zǔoshì Zhuàn of the Chūnqiū.
Hearing of Lǚ's extensive knowledge,
he summoned him to clarify his doubts.
Lǚ said:
"The Zǔoshì contains much cunning and deceit,
and is mixed rather than pure.
The Shàngshū and Mèngzǐ both embody the pure and complete dao of the sages,
and I wish you would pay attention to them."
The King appreciated and accepted this.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was promoted to Lángzhōng of this department,
concurrently Tóngxiū Guóshǐ and Hànlín Xiūzhuàn.
He presented Sīmǎ Guāng's Gǔwén Xiàojīng Zhǐjiě of the Sòng Dynasty, saying:
"Your subject humbly observes that in recent times,
everyone considers military, penal, financial, and tax matters urgent,
but Guāng alone presented this to his sovereign.
If those who possess the world
adopt its words and apply them throughout the realm,
then the common people will receive blessings."
Soon after, due to illness,
he requested an outside appointment.
Shìzōng said:
"Lǚ is often ill;
he may be given a convenient prefecture."
Thus, he was appointed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Not long after,
he was summoned to be Hànlín Dàizhì,
concurrently Tóngxiū Guóshǐ.
The next year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Lǐbù Shìláng,
concurrently Hànlín Zhíxuéshì.
Niángē Wòtèlà
was a person from Bìlǐmài Mèng'ān Xīqū Móukè in Gàizhōu.
In the early Zhēnyuán era,
because he was skilled in the Nǚzhí script, he was appointed to a probationary position as a secretary in the Ministry of Revenue,
then transferred to a secretary position in the Department of State Affairs.
In the seventh year of Dàdìng,
he was selected and appointed as a principal of the Ministry of Personnel,
and successively served as Right Remonstrator and Compiler of the Diaries of Activity and Repose.
In the ninth year,
Zōng, the General Superintendent of the Hénán Circuit, fearing that the Sòng people intended to provoke military conflict,
submitted a memorial requesting an audience.
Shìzōng dispatched Wòtèlà to question him
and investigate the truth of the matter.
Arriving in Biàn,
he questioned Zōng,
and also summoned and interrogated all who had spoken about border affairs;
none of their claims proved substantial.
Upon his return and report,
Shìzōng was pleased and said:
"I always knew it was baseless."
He was appointed as a supernumerary official in the Left Department.
In the tenth year,
because the Xià state had dispatched troops to build Qí'ān City and had attacked and killed Jiáo family tribal leader Jiéshíjiǎo,
and furthermore, spies reported that Xià was colluding with the Sòng people to violate the border,
an edict was issued for Dàlǐ Qīng Lǐ Chāngtú and Wòtèlà to investigate the matter.
The Xià people reported that
Jiéshíjiǎo was killed because he had led troops to violate the Xià border,
and Qí'ān City was originally the old Jīshí land granted by the superior country,
and troops were dispatched to repair and build it to guard against other bandits.
It was also found that there was no communication between Sòng and Xià,
and the people of the Jiáo family wished for Jiéshíjiǎo's nephew Zhào Shīgǔ to be their leader.
All this was reported.
Shìzōng was very pleased,
and Wòtèlà was transferred to Right Guard General,
and bestowed with clothing, a horse, a chariot, an ox, a bow and arrows, and weapons.
In the twelfth year,
he served as an envoy for the Xià state's birthday,
and upon his return was appointed Right Department Director,
then promoted to Right Assistant Commissioner of Palace Affairs.
After a long time,
he was sent out as the General Supervisor of the Hénán Circuit,
and was bestowed with a gold belt and a fully equipped horse.
In the seventeenth year,
he was appointed Military Commissioner of the Chāngwǔ Army,
concurrently holding his former position.
The following year,
he entered the court as Minister of Justice,
and was appointed Assistant Administrator.
Shìzōng once admonished Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Tángkuò Ānlǐ, saying:
"I believe that the path to good governance,
the selection of talent is the most difficult task.
All other routine matters have established procedures,
and are not comparable to this.
For example, those recommended by Wòtèlà
quite conform to my wishes."
At that time, Měngkuò Mándū, a legal inspector of the Right Three Departments, accused Wòtèlà of forming a faction with Zhāotǎo Zhédiǎn,
and requested that he be handed over to the Ministry of Justice for interrogation.
Shìzōng said:
"If Zhédiǎn had been spared death,
then it could be called a faction.
But now he has already suffered execution,
so this is merely slander."
He also told the chief ministers:
"I have long known this person to have extremely sound judgment and foresight;
though his appearance is gentle, his heart is very firm and upright,
and his actions are not impulsive."
In the twenty-second year,
he was entrusted with the position of Controller of Fùtōng Supervisors in Dàizhōu.
He was summoned for an audience, and Shìzōng admonished him, saying:
"Since I appointed you,
I have recognized your abilities,
and therefore promoted you to be an administrator.
You also understand my intention in treating you so,
and have diligently fulfilled your duties.
Most of your plans, discussions, and responses are in line with my thoughts.
Do not rely on having a chancellor above you and distance yourself.
For the old officials are aged,
and the new officials have not yet endured much experience,
it is for this reason that I entrust responsibility to you.
If you have any observations, speak them with all your heart,
do not hold back thinking you are not supposed to know."
In the twenty-third year,
he was promoted to Minister of the Right,
concurrently serving as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
He submitted a memorial requesting to resign one position,
and was allowed to resign from the Military Affairs Commission.
Shìzōng, regarding the Mèng'ān Móukè's abandonment of land,
reprimanded the chief ministers, saying:
"These matters are all things that you, my ministers, should have reported and brought up,
yet you wait for me to speak before acting.
This is because you, my ministers, consider them minor affairs not to be personally handled by the Son of Heaven.
I have often thought about it:
with Wòtèlà handling lawsuits and documents,
you, my ministers, hardly care about other matters.
How can I simply ignore them?"
Soon after, he was demoted one rank due to an incident,
but ordered to continue his duties as before.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was transferred to Minister of the Left.
Shìzōng said to him:
"Yesterday I discussed with the chief ministers who could be appointed as administrators,
and you were not among them.
Now Ālúhǎn is old,
and Wòlǔyě is often ill.
What do you think if I use Zōnghào?"
Wòtèlà responded:
"Those two may not be effective.
Only Zōnghào is capable and can be entrusted."
Thereupon, Zōnghào was appointed.
Shìzōng also said:
"I apply myself to all matters under Heaven,
just as in the beginning."
Wòtèlà said:
"Since ancient times, many rulers began diligently but ended lazily.
To have a beginning and an end,
only a sage can achieve it."
The Emperor said:
"Táng Tàizōng was a most sagacious ruler,
yet Wèi Zhēng remonstrated him with ten points,
saying that he might not be able to persevere to the end.
Thus, to have both a beginning and an end is truly difficult."
In the twenty-eighth year,
he became Resident Administrator of Shàngjīng,
and was bestowed with a rhinoceros-horn belt and one hunting horse.
In the second year of Míngchāng, he retired.
In the early Chéng'ān era,
there were affairs in the north,
and the court wished to appoint an old official to handle them.
So he was recalled to serve as Resident Administrator of Dōngjīng.
The Supervising Censor Wányán Gāng was dispatched to convey the imperial decree, saying:
"Knowing that your spirit is still strong,
you are therefore re-employed."
The following year,
he was reassigned as Resident Administrator of Shàngjīng.
He was again admonished, saying:
"Shàngjīng is the land of our ancestors' foundation.
You are to hasten by post-horse to assume the post.
Upon arrival, you may act according to expediency.
Once the border situation has somewhat subsided,
I will summon you back."
In the ninth month of the second year,
he returned to court,
was appointed Administrator of the Department of State Affairs,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Ruì.
He held office for several months
before he passed away,
at the age of sixty-nine.
Upon hearing the news of his death,
the Emperor grieved for a long time,
dispatched officials to offer sacrifices,
and bestowed 1,250 taels of silver, 45 bolts of fine silk, 450 bolts of plain silk, and 2,000 strings of cash.
His posthumous title was Chéngsù.
Wòtèlà was gentle, benevolent, and cultivated by nature.
He was once recommended by Chancellor Hēsīliè Liángbì.
Later, Shìzōng told his chief ministers:
"Liángbì was good at discerning people.
Talents like Wòtèlà are truly usable."
He served as chancellor for over ten years,
and was greatly favored.

Only his proposals to allow sons of fifth-rank officials and clerks from outer circuits to take the same examination for departmental secretaries, and to allow court clerks to take examinations for scribes in the National History Institute,
were deemed inappropriate by Shìzōng.
Chéng Huī, courtesy name Rìxīn,
was a person from Língxiān, Wèizhōu.
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
he passed the jinshi examination,
and rose from a secretary in the Department of State Affairs to a staff member in the Left Department.
After a long time,
he became Transport Commissioner of the Nánjīng Circuit.
Due to a palace fire,
he was demoted and appointed Prefect of Cízhōu.
A Buddhist monk from Wú killed a local man named Zhāng Shànyǒu and took his wife.
Huī supervised the arrest of the monk
and ordered Zhāng's mother to stab the monk and his wife with a long awl until they died without a single intact piece of skin.
He was reassigned as Transport Commissioner of the Shǎnxī East Circuit,
then promoted again to Minister of Revenue.
In Dàdìng twenty-three
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Shìzōng instructed him, saying:
"Although you are old,
you can still exert yourself.
If there is something that should be said,
do not keep silent.
You should strive for this."
One day,
Huī was attending court,
and Shìzōng said:
"People often say that your words are absurd.
Now, whenever an issue arises, you speak your mind,
even more so than Wáng Wèi."
He looked at the prime ministers and said:
"What do you all think?"
They all replied:
"Huī, in discussing state affairs,
has absolutely no hidden agenda."
Huī replied:
"I am old and my hearing is poor.
My only concern is that I might not hear clearly,
or might miss something in my reports.
If I hear something,
how would I dare not to exert my utmost effort?"
Previously, oxen were used for temple sacrifices.
In his later years, Shìzōng wanted to replace them with other animals.
Huī submitted a memorial, saying:
"Sacrifices using oxen
are considered the most important of sacrifices,
hence they are called 'tàiláo'.
The saying goes: 'The calf of a plough-ox is reddish and horned.
Even if one wishes not to use it,
would the mountains and rivers reject it?'
Ancient rites cannot be abolished."
In twenty-four
Shìzōng traveled to Shàngjīng.
The Shàngshū Shěng submitted a memorial regarding foreign envoys coming to offer congratulations on New Year's Day next year.
Shìzōng said:
"Shàngjīng is far and the weather is cold.
I deeply pity the fatigue of the envoys,
and wish to receive the Sòng documents in Nánjīng instead.
What do you think?"
Huī replied:
"Foreign envoys must meet the Son of Heaven face-to-face.
If documents are received halfway,
should the Sòng people later use this as a pretext to imitate it,
how would we decline?"
Shìzōng said:
"I act with sincerity.
If they deceive me,
I will have my own way of dealing with it."
Huī believed it was not permissible.
Thereupon, it was decided to temporarily waive it for one year.
At that time, an official in charge of market affairs failed to pay promptly for flour.
Shìzōng was angry that the supervisors did not impeach him,
and had him flogged.
When he asked Huī about it,
Huī replied:
"Supervisors
are Your Majesty's ears and eyes.
The crime committed was minor,
and to flog him without ransom
was merely a temporary fit of anger."
Shìzōng said:
"Failing in one's duty
is a deliberate offense.
Why is flogging him not permissible?"
Huī replied:
"What is past cannot be undone;
what is to come can still be remedied."
In twenty-six
he retired due to old age.
The following year,
he was recalled to serve as Zhī Hénán Fǔshì.
Huī declined, citing his old age and inability to serve.
He was summoned into the Xiānggé,
where Shìzōng instructed him, saying:
"Although you are old, your energy is still strong.
Though you have long served in external posts,
you have never held a fine prefecture.
Hénán has superior geography and simple affairs,
so I am assigning it to you,
so you may enjoy a leisurely and nourishing life."
Huī said:
"I am like an old horse.
I await fodder and care;
how can I be expected to exert my strength?
Previously, when the Nánjīng palace caught fire,
had it not been for Your Majesty's gracious pardon,
I would have died long ago.
Now, the Hé river passes through Hénán for over a thousand *lǐ* both upstream and downstream,
and the responsibility for river defense is even heavier than that.
This is why I fear I am not capable."
Thereupon, a special imperial decree was issued exempting him from river affairs.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
Huī was seventy-six years old.
He again requested retirement,
and an imperial edict granted it,
still providing him half the salary of a Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
He died in Chéng'ān year one
and was posthumously named Zhōngjiǎn.
Huī was uninhibited and dared to speak,
enjoyed diverse studies,
and was particularly fond of discussing medicine,
following the theories of Liú Shǒuzhēn of Héjiān,
mostly using cooling remedies.
There was a child prodigy, Tiānshòu, who was only a few years old.
Huī summoned him,
and then wrote
"醫非細事" (Medicine is no small matter)
four characters.
Tiānshòu erased the character
"細" (small),
and
rewrote it as
"相" (prime minister).
Huī was quite embarrassed,
and people also took this as hitting his weakness.
Liú Wěi, courtesy name Déyù,
was a native of Xiánpíng.
He was a descendant of Rénjìng, a Jǐedùshǐ of Lúlóng in the Táng dynasty.
His grandfather, Hóng,
was stationed in Yìzhōu at the end of the Liáo dynasty.
When the imperial army arrived,
Hóng surrendered the prefecture.
Tàizǔ appointed him as Zhī Xiánzhōu,
and later he retired as Tóng Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
