His father, Jūnzhào,
was Tóngzhī Xuānhuī Yuànshì.
Wěi was astute as a child,
and pursued the *jìnshì* examination.
Xīzōng, in consideration of his family's past,
specially granted him the *jí dì* degree.
He was appointed Āncì Chéng.
From Zūnhuà Xiànlìng, he was appointed Shàngshū Shěng Lìshǐ,
and successively held posts as Hùbù Zhǔshì and Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
and was successively promoted to Shàngshū Shěng Dūshì.
The prime ministers proposed Wěi to plan and manage military and civilian land.
Shìzōng, seeing his name, said:
"Is Liú Wěi still stagnating here?"
He was promoted to Hùbù Yuánwàiláng.
At that time, Shìzōng was about to make an eastern tour,
and ordered Wěi, along with Gōngbù Lángzhōng Sòng Zhōng, to go and build the temporary palace,
whereupon he was promoted to Lángzhōng.
He was then transferred to Tóngzhī Xuānhuī Yuànshì,
and served as the Fùshǐ for the Sòng Kingdom envoy.
Wěi's father and elder brother had both served as envoys to Jiāngzuǒ in this capacity,
which was considered an honor at the time.
Upon his return, he was appointed Hùbù Shìláng.
Initially,
Shìzōng valued Wěi's ability and talent,
believing there was no task he could not handle.
When Shìzōng was about to travel to Shàngjīng,
since all necessary provisions for the temporary palace fell under the Tài Fǔ,
he wanted Wěi to lead the matter.
Fearing his rank was slightly too low,
he transferred Hùbù Shìláng Zhāng Dàjié to the Gōngbù,
and assigned the Hùbù to Wěi.
Upon the emperor's return,
he said to the prime ministers:
"Liú Wěi possesses great mental and physical strength;
he is calm in handling affairs.
It's just that his intentions are not entirely upright.
If his intentions were truly upright,
such a talent would be unobtainable."
The following year,
he was promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū.
At that time, the river breached its banks in Wèi,
and the area from Wèi to Qīng and Cāng was all affected.
An imperial edict ordered him, also holding the title of Gōngbù Shàngshū, to go and block it.
Some believed that such a natural disaster was rampant
and could not be resisted by human effort,
and that only relocating the people to avoid its impact was viable.
Wěi said:
"Not so.
Heaven created the Five Elements,
which alternately flourish and decline.
Now, the river has breached because earth cannot overcome water.
Wait until the transition between autumn and winter,
when the water level slightly recedes,
then gradually construct and repair,
and it may be possible to block it."
The following spring,
Wěi observed a fast and prayed to the river.
Construction efforts proceeded simultaneously,
and the river returned to its former course.
He was recalled, his rank was increased,
and he was appointed the Fùshǐ for Sòng condolence and memorial envoy.
Shìzōng became ill,
and Wěi was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
still overseeing the Hùbù.
Later, he served as Shānlíng Shǐ.
Soon after, he submitted a memorial requesting an outside post,
and was dispatched as Zhī Jìnán Fǔshì,
then transferred to govern Hézhōng.
In Míngchāng year two
he was transferred to Zhī Dàmíng Fǔ,
still overseeing river defense affairs.
Three years later,
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
The Emperor once asked if the method of evaluating officials was still feasible today.
Yòuchéngxiàng Jiágǔ Qīngchén said:
"It can be implemented,
but if the regulations are too complicated, the officials will find it difficult to apply them."
Wěi said:
"The method of evaluating officials is fundamentally about comprehensively checking names and realities.
Now the Tíxíng Directorate investigates integrity and competence, as well as corruption and abuse, to administer rewards and punishments.
This is also its intent.
If a separate method were to be discussed and established,
I fear it would become too complicated."
The Emperor asked what the situation was like in the Táng Dynasty.
Wěi replied with
"the four virtues and twenty-seven excellences."
In June of the following year,
he passed away.
On that day,
the Emperor was about to play polo at Línwǔ Diàn.
Upon hearing of Wěi's death, he stopped
and conferred upon him the posthumous title Ānmǐn.
Later, the Emperor said to his ministers:
"Some people, when they are minor officials, may be praised for their talent and ability,
but when they are given great responsibility, it is not so.
Líú Wěi, for example, was indeed very capable,
yet from the reign of Shìzōng until he assisted Us,
he often knew things about affairs but did not speak.
If he were truly foolish, there would be no need to discuss it,
but knowing it and being unwilling to exert his full effort,
how can this be?"
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Wányán Shǒuzhēn said:
"The principle of the Chūnqiū [Annals] is to hold worthy individuals to high standards."
The Emperor said:
"To be a prime minister and desire to accrue favor and avoid blame,
making everyone praise oneself as righteous,
is this truly the way of a worthy person?"
Dǒng Shīzhōng, courtesy name Shàozǔ,
was a native of Míngzhōu.
In his youth, he was quick-witted and eloquent,
fond of learning and had a strong memory.
He passed the imperial examination in the ninth year of Huángtǒng,
and was appointed military judge of Zézhōu.
He was later transferred to be the assistant magistrate of Píngyáo.
There was a notorious bandit in the county named Wáng Yǐ,
who was always fierce and uncontrollable.
Shīzhōng captured him, flogged him to death,
and the entire region became peaceful.
At that time, after the large army had passed,
there were many withered corpses in the wilds.
There were also coffins left in the post station in the county.
He buried them all.
He was promoted to magistrate of Miánshàng,
then appointed clerk in the Shàngshūshěng.
Yòuxiàng Tángkuò Érlǔgǔ especially valued him,
patting his seat and saying:
"Your arguments are brilliant and articulate,
your temperament is open and bright.
One day, you will surely occupy this seat."
After another evaluation,
he was promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
then transferred to Shàngshūshěng Dūshì.
Initially,
when Shīzhōng was a Jiānchá [Yùshǐ],
he failed to investigate Hūlá, the governor-general of Dàmíng, for impropriety.
When Hūlá was executed for his crimes,
Shìzōng angrily said:
"The Jiānchá [Yùshǐ] is dispatched to prefectures and counties,
with the duty of impeachment and rectification.
Hūlá, being a close relative and noble, should have been especially scrutinized,
yet he indulged him and did not report it."
He was demoted by one rank
and appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Qìnnán Commandery.
He was successively promoted to Prefect of Fāngzhōu.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
when the nine Tíxíng Directorates were first established,
Shīzhōng was selected as the Deputy Commissioner for the Shǎnxī Circuit.
He was found guilty of excessive spending of public funds for renovating public offices,
and was sentenced to a ransom.
When the Yùshǐtái reported that he was lenient and well-mannered,
he was summoned to become Dàlǐ Qīng.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Wú Dǐngshū recommended him as his successor,
and the Shàngshūshěng also reported his talent and conduct,
so he was promoted to Zhōngchéng.
At that time, Zōngsù, the Military Commissioner of the Northwest Circuits, upon the recommendation of Píngzhāng Jiágǔ Qīngchén,
was appointed Prefect of Dàxīng Fǔ.
Shīzhōng submitted a memorial stating:
"Zōngsù was recently investigated by the authorities for bribery,
and his case has not yet concluded.
It is not appropriate to transfer him to a new post."
The Emperor accepted his words,
saying:
"I understand.
If merits are not rewarded and
crimes are not punished,
even Táng and Yú would not be able to transform the world."
He ordered Zōngsù to be returned to the authorities for further investigation.
In the fourth year,
the Emperor was about to visit Jǐngmínggōng.
Shī Zhōng, together with Supervising Censor Jiǎ Xuàn and Judicial Supervising Censor Niángē Zūngǔ, remonstrated,
saying:
"Troubling the people and wasting resources
are but minor concerns.
Unexpected dangers arising
are matters of no small import.
The Sage models himself on Heaven and Earth, moving in accordance with nature,
hence all his endeavors are perfectly secure.
Currently, the border regions are restive,
with unrest and instability.
Bìlǐgē Bówǎ is tyrannical, rapacious, and fierce,
which is deeply worrisome.
If Your Majesty asks those around you,
there will surely be sycophants who will say,
'This is a great and majestic nation;
why should we worry about them?'
However, even wasps and scorpions are venomous,
and trouble often arises from what is overlooked.
Now, the capital is magnificent,
and the inner and outer imperial gardens are sufficient to gladden the imperial heart.
The mountains and rivers in the nearby environs are teeming with game,
sufficient for practicing military affairs.
Why must you bring thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of cavalry,
sleep in the grass and under the open sky,
approach the remote frontiers,
trouble scouts from afar,
and risk unforeseen regrets?"
The Emperor did not accept this.
Shī Zhōng and others again submitted a memorial, saying:
"In recent years, floods and droughts have been calamities.
Your Majesty issued clear edicts blaming yourself and seeking advice,
suspending non-urgent projects
and economizing on unnecessary expenses,
which delighted the entire realm.
Now, it is spring, a time for eastern cultivation,
yet officials are being urgently dispatched to construct an imperial traveling palace.
Judging by the circumstances,
this seems non-urgent.
Furthermore, the two capitals, Xī and Běi,
and the various circuits of Línhoáng,
have suffered poor harvests for several years.
In addition, the people are burdened with the tasks of raising horses, conscripting soldiers, and digging trenches,
their financial resources are severely depleted,
migrants have not yet returned,
and rice prices are very high.
If Your Majesty's retinue travels there,
prices will surely increase further.
Tens of thousands of people rely on daily purchases of small measures of grain.
They previously depended on merchants from Běijīng and other circuits for supply.
If, due to high prices or untimely arrival,
the hungry masses should again experience what happened last year,
killing the Grand Marshal's horses, destroying the Grand Minister of the Treasury's melons and fruits, voicing resentment, and rising in rebellion,
the 'Book of Documents' states: 'The sentiments of the people are clearly visible;
it is difficult to secure the loyalty of common folk.'
Moreover, the tribal groups from the northern and southern dependencies, who have defended the frontier for decades,
are now being enticed and coerced by Bìlǐgē Bówǎ,
leading entire clans to depart.
The frontier is unstable to such a worrisome degree.
If Your Majesty disregards this and proceeds,
how can it be the way of a Sage whose every endeavor is perfectly secure?
Recently, Venus was seen in broad daylight,
the capital experienced an earthquake,
and in the north, there was a red light
that only dispersed at dawn.
These celestial signs
are intended to warn the Sacred Mind,
to cultivate virtue and avert calamity.
Moreover, leisurely excursions
were cautioned against by the ancients.
From the distant Zhōu and Qín dynasties
to the more recent Suí, Táng, and Liáo dynasties,
all gave rise to trouble because of this.
How can one not be cautious?
How can one not be wary?"
Left Remonstrance Official Xǔ Ānrén and Right Remonstrance Official Lù Duó also submitted memorials to remonstrate.
On that day,
the Emperor presided over the rear chambers,
summoned Shī Zhōng and others for an audience,
and immediately acceded to their petition.
He then sent an envoy to inform his auxiliary ministers, saying:
"I wished to tour the region beyond the mountains,
for no other reason than to escape the summer heat.
Now, since the Supervising Censors have all stated that there are many places where the people lack food,
I initially did not know this entirely.
Now that I know it,
though the heat is formidable,
how could I bear to indulge my personal comfort and further burden the people?"
Thus, the northern tour was canceled.
Soon after, Shī Zhōng was appointed Envoy to the Sòng court to celebrate the Emperor's birthday.
Upon his return, he distributed the gold and silk he had received among his relatives and old friends.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor again went to Jǐngmínggōng.
Shī Zhōng and the Supervising Censors again submitted fervent remonstrances.
The Emperor was enraged,
and dispatched Lǐ Rényuàn, Director of the Bureau of Imperial Attendants, to the Department of State Affairs
to summon Shī Zhōng and others and inform them:
"What you have said
is not without merit,
but there are also parts that transgress the decorum between ruler and minister.
Now, I order the Grand Councilor to convey my decree;
you should go and listen."
Mǎ Qí, Minister of Revenue, petitioned to appoint a successor for himself,
and was promoted to Minister of Personnel.
Previously,
Wányán Shǒuzhēn had been reassigned as Resident Administrator of Xījīng.
When he came to the capital for an audience,
the Emperor wished to reappoint him.
Inspecting Censor Púlàdū and others impeached him on several counts.
Shī Zhōng defended him against the false accusations
and recommended Shǒuzhēn as an upright and capable man.
Because of this, Shǒuzhēn was again appointed Grand Councilor.
When Shǒuzhēn was later dismissed due to an offense,
the Emperor said:
"Those who recommended Shǒuzhēn should be demoted or dismissed.
As Dǒng Shīzhōng said, if the Censorate and ministries lack such people, governance will fail.
Lù Duó and Lǐ Jìngyì also once recommended him.
They can be demoted to external posts.
However, these three individuals can all be used again later.
For now, let them be sent out
to rectify the fault of erroneous recommendation."
Shī Zhōng was appointed Transport Commissioner for the Western Circuit of Shǎnxī.
After more than a year,
he was summoned to be Censor-in-Chief
and ordered, along with Zhāng Wěi, Minister of Rites, to review submitted memorials and documents.
After more than three months,
he was appointed Participant in Determining State Affairs
and promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Left in the Department of State Affairs.
Another day, when reporting on state affairs,
the Emperor said to his auxiliary ministers:
"Censor Jī Duānxiū said there are petty people by my side.
Who could they be?"
Shī Zhōng replied:
"It must refer to people like Lǐ Xǐ'ér."
The Emperor remained silent.
Shī Zhōng was knowledgeable about ancient and modern affairs,
skillful in presenting memorials,
and experienced and discerning in institutions and laws.
He was precise and astute in handling matters.
He once said:
"A prime minister should not concern himself with trivial matters;
his main duty is to recognize talent,
and uphold discipline and order.
If his mind is righteous and his vision clear,
that is sufficient."
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
he petitioned to retire due to old age.
An imperial edict granted him a residence
to remain in the capital.
As it was the Cold Food Festival,
he requested to visit his family and tend to ancestral graves.
This was granted,
and he was also ordered to compose a poem "Returning Home for Cold Food to Tend Ancestral Graves."
On every festival and court assembly,
he was summoned to attend the imperial banquet.
Such was the Emperor's favor and courtesy towards him.
In the second year of Tàihé,
he passed away
at the age of seventy-four.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor
mourned and lamented deeply,
and turned to his great ministers, saying:
"Upright people are often unyielding and inflexible,
but Shī Zhōng alone was upright yet adaptable."
An imperial edict ordered his funeral and sacrifices to follow the precedent of currently serving prime ministers and grand councilors,
and also granted him posthumous gifts.
His posthumous title was Wéndìng.
Shī Zhōng was skilled in literature,
and his nature was open and understanding.
He was generous with wealth and upheld righteousness.
In his daily life, he was cheerful, easygoing, and sincere,
but when facing matters, he was resolute and firm,
unwavering and incorruptible.
His younger brother, Shī Jiǎn,
initially pursued the jinshi examination.
He wished to use Shī Zhōng's influence for promotion.
Shī Zhōng, however, guaranteed him a position,
secretly arranged for someone to provide him with an official document,
and allowed him to continue his studies.
Shī Jiǎn was moved by his righteous conduct,
studied diligently, and later passed the examination.
While in government,
an attendant conveyed an imperial decree
to appoint Shī Zhōng's son.
Shī Zhōng memorialized, saying:
"Your subject has a nephew who is an orphan and still young.
If he could receive Your Majesty's gracious appointment,
it would be better than for my own son."
The Emperor admired his righteousness
and appointed his nephew as a Palace Attendant for Literary Affairs.
He served as an auxiliary minister with Xū Chíguó,
and they were quite close,
which people at the time somewhat criticized.
Qí's nature was bright and astute,
he was accustomed to clerical matters,
and was especially skilled in managing money and grain.
However, he was stingy and fond of profit,
which was somewhat disliked by his superiors.
Yáng Bótōng
courtesy name Jífǔ, was a man from Hóngzhōu.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in Dàdìng year 3
and rose from a clerk in the Shàngshū Province to Registrar in the Ministry of Personnel, and then Deputy Commissioner of the Shùnyì Army Jìedù.
He left due to mourning.
Mǎ Qí, the Minister of Personnel, recommended Bótōng as honest and capable.
The Shàngshū Province reviewed the matter and found it as reported,
so he was summoned to be Director of Affairs in the Shàngshū Province,
and then appointed Deputy Commissioner of the Dìngwǔ Army Jìedù.
In Míngchāng year 1,
he was promoted to Assistant Minister of the Left Bureau,
then to Minister,
and successively became Minister of Personnel,
and soon after transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
In Chéng'ān year 2,
he was appointed Assistant Administrator of Political Affairs.
Lù Duó, an Investigating Censor, impeached Bótōng, accusing him of
using public office to cultivate private favors by employing his fellow townsman, Lǐ Hào.
Jiǎ Yì, a Minister of the Left Bureau, anticipating the imperial intention,
did not re-examine the details,
but reported it to the Censorate,
intending to initiate impeachment.
However, Grandee Zhāng Wěi immediately prevented it.
The Emperor ordered Jiǎ Xuàn, the Assistant Administrator of Dàxīng Prefecture, to investigate the matter.
Bótōng stayed at home awaiting his punishment.
Xuàn reported:
"Wěi said that impeaching a high minister
requires concrete evidence.
The impeachment is inappropriate;
it merely damages the integrity of the Censorate.
Yì said that all appointments and removals were decided by the public deliberation of the prime ministers
and did not mention Bótōng's private wrongdoing."
An imperial edict reprimanded Duó for speaking carelessly,
and comforted and instructed Bótōng to handle his affairs.
Bótōng submitted two more memorials to resign,
but was not permitted.
In year 4,
he was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Left,
then retired,
and died.
Ní Pánggǔ Jiàn,
whose original name was Wàiliú, was from Lóngzhōu.
He was familiar with both Jurchen small script and Chinese characters.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in Dàdìng year 13,
and was assigned as an instructor in Lóng'ān.
He was transferred to be a Registrar in Jìmò,
then summoned to be an Assistant Instructor in the National Academy,
and promoted to Director of the Imperial Attendants Bureau.
Shìzōng valued his talent,
and said to his chief ministers:
"Among the new *jìnshì*, people like Túshān Yì, Jiágǔ Héng, and Ní Pánggǔ Jiàn
are all usable."
He was transferred to be a Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince.
[一０]After a year,
he was promoted to Academician-in-waiting of the Hànlín Academy,
concurrently serving as Chief Officer of the Right Three Bureaus.
Shìzōng again said to his chief ministers:
"Jiàn once served me closely,
and I know he is upright and capable in administration.
When he became a Palace Attendant to the Eastern Palace,
he protected the Imperial Grandson,
and his conduct in rites and speech still retained the pure and simple old customs of our nation,
which I greatly commend."
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was successively promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue,
concurrently an Academician of the Hànlín Academy.
Soon after, he was transferred to be Assistant Administrator of Dàxīng Prefecture.
Upon the recommendation of high ministers,
he was made Administrator of Dàxīng Prefecture.
In Míngchāng year 5, he was appointed Assistant Administrator of Political Affairs.
He died,
and was posthumously named Wénsù.
The eulogy states: Yílà Lǚ calmly offered advice,
gaining the trust of the sovereign.
His discussions on governance were pure and unadulterated,
taking filial piety as the foundation of government.
Perhaps he inherited the lost learning of the ancients.
In ancient times, Zāng Sūndá offered loyal remonstrance in Lǔ,
and the gentlemen knew that his lineage would prosper.
This is indeed true.
Zhāng Wàngōng upheld integrity and maintained himself,
speaking plainly without embellishment.
His proposal to dig canals and delineate land
clearly explained the benefits and harms,
as if pointing to them in his palm.
He was constrained by various opinions and did not yield,
and so retired and returned home.
This was a natural course of events.
Púchá Tōng's weeping for Hǎilíng,
where the great righteousness between sovereign and minister meant life and death were one,
his ambition was ardent.
Chéng Huī and Wòtèlà were upright and straightforward;
Liú Wěi and Dǒng Shīzhōng were intelligent and agile.
Their talents were all sufficient to make them known,
however, Shīzhōng was criticized for attaching himself to sycophants,
and Liú Wěi was blamed for avoiding responsibility.
Compared to their predecessors, they had much to be ashamed of.
As for Wáng Wèi, Mǎ Huìdí, and their ilk,
they are not worth mentioning.
Collation Notes
Biographies Thirty-four: Huáng Jiǔyuē, Lǐ Yàn, Lǐ Zhònglüè, Lǐ Yù, Wáng Bēn, Xǔ Ānrén, Liáng Xiāng, Lù Bódá.
Huáng Jiǔyuē,
courtesy name Mídà, was from Xūchéng, Dōngpíng.
His great-grandfather Xiàochuò possessed hidden virtue,
and was known as
"Master Qiánshān."
His father, Shèng,
was the Vice Prefect of Jìzhōu.
His mother, Lady Liú,
was the younger sister of Chángyán, the Assistant Administrator of the Right in the Ministry of Personnel.
One night, she dreamed of a mouse holding a bright pearl,
and when she awoke, Jiǔyuē was born.
His birth year truly fell in the *zǐ* branch.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and was assigned as a Registrar in Yùnchéng.
He was successively promoted three times to Judicial Assistant of Cáozhōu.
There was a case where thieves stole people's property,
and the accusers claimed it was robbery with violence.
The Prefect wanted to impose a heavy penalty,
but Jiǔyuē reviewed the facts,
and the prisoners were spared from death.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
concurrently an Editor in the Hànlín Academy,
then rose to Attendant Academician,
and was appointed Prefect of Cízhōu.
Cízhōu bordered mountains
and had always been plagued by many bandits.
When they were caught and confessed,
the judicial reviewing officials sometimes did not arrive in time,
and many prisoners were beaten to death with staves,
or died in prison.
Jiǔyuē compassionately said:
"Even if people commit robbery, should they die outside the law?"
So he requested to interrogate all of them before executing any judgment.
After a long time,
he re-entered the Hànlín Academy as an Academician,
and soon after was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left,
concurrently Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
and served as the deputy envoy for congratulating the Sòng Emperor on his birthday.
When he arrived in Lín'ān,
it happened that the host envoy was ill.
The Sòng people discussed having the deputy envoy act as the principal envoy.
Jiǔyuē said:
"If the deputy envoy also falls ill,
will you then make the Commander or the Master of Ceremonies perform the rites?"
In the end, the chief envoy was made to proceed alone,
while the deputy envoy and the deputy host envoy rode together as before,
and thus the ceremony was completed before they returned.
On their way through Sù and Sì,
he saw people presenting fresh loquats,
with the prefectures and counties conscripting laborers to transport them.
Upon his return, he memorialized to abolish this practice.
At the time, due to the uneven distribution of wealth,
some wished to compel wealthy citizens to lend to the poor.
This was sent down to the relevant authorities for deliberation.
Jiǔyuē said:
"The inequality of things
is their natural state.
The uneven distribution of wealth
is also a constant principle.
If we follow the suggestion of some,
it will only suffice to accumulate resentment,
and is not the way to reduce surplus and supplement insufficiency."
During Zhāngzōng's reign, the Right Chancellor,
approved of his proposal.
Soon after, he submitted a memorial requesting retirement due to old age.
An imperial edict instructed him, saying:
"Your Lordship is loyal and upright in speech,
and has provided many benefits and assistance.
You cannot yet be allowed to leave my side."
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
still concurrently holding the remonstrance post.
At that time, many posts in the prefectures and counties were vacant.
Jǐu Yuē
spoke at length, saying: “How can there be a lack of talent in the world?
It is obstructed by qualifications.
The clear edicts often blame ministers for adhering to regulations and hindering talent.
I beg Your Majesty to make a decision from your imperial heart and implement it vigorously.”
Shìzōng said:
“Is it that the Chancellor does not pay attention to this matter,
and so allows a remonstrance official to speak of it?”
On that very day, several people were appointed as Cìshǐ.
Jǐu Yuē further suggested that princes and officials below them should recommend each other in turn.
Shìzōng said:
“Recommending talent is solely the Chancellor’s duty.
Though other officials may be of high rank,
how can they all possess the discernment to know men?
Currently, the position of Xiànlìng is most lacking.
It is fitting to order Cìshǐ and above to recommend those capable of serving as Xiànlìng.
I will examine their actual abilities and employ them.”
He then said to Jǐu Yuē:
“Recently, all those good officials selected through examination are supervisors of various branches.
Why are there no Jìnshì at all?
Has the method of recommendation already become corrupt
and thus cannot be continued for long?”
Jǐu Yuē replied:
“Are there no honest and capable people among the various branches?
Without the examination system, some would never reach the position of Xiànlìng in their lives.
This method should not be abolished yet.”
The Emperor said:
“Was Sūn Bìfú, whom you recommended, one such person?”
Jǐu Yuē replied:
“When your servant was serving in Cízhōu,
Bìfú was the Wǔ'ān Chéng.
Your servant saw him as honest, upright, and unafraid of anything,
which is why I recommended him.
I did not expect Bìfú, after taking up the post of Jǐngxúnshǐ,
to handle pending cases so slowly.”
The Emperor said:
“Bìfú was not only slow,
but also completely ignorant of affairs.
The reason the guarantor was not punished
was fortunate that Bìfú was not involved in corruption.”
Jǐu Yuē had no reply.
Bìfú had entered officialdom through the Wǔjīng examination,
being a person from the various branches,
which is why the Emperor mentioned him.
The next day, when attending court,
it was customary for
close officials to withdraw when the Chancellor presented matters.
Jǐu Yuē was about to leave,
but Shìzōng stopped him.
From then on, it became customary for remonstrance officials not to withdraw.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,

Jǐu Yuē presented eight matters: the country being rich but the people poor, the fundamental being light and the superficial heavy, too many people being appointed, official power being too great, the high price of government salt, the harm caused to the people by government workshops, and the selection of attendants and district magistrates.
All were graciously accepted.
He again requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
He was appointed as Hénghǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ to allow him ease and leisure.
He retired in the second year of Míngchāng and
died.
Jǐu Yuē was brilliant and eloquent, daring to speak out.
He was affectionate towards his younger brothers by nature.
His writings were elegant and refined,
said to possess the style of his maternal grandfather.
Lǐ Yàn, courtesy name Zhìměi,
was a native of Gāopíng, Zézhōu.
He was naturally sharp and quick-witted,
and magnanimous with a strong sense of spirit.
In the sixth year of Huángtǒng,
he passed the Jīngyì Jìnshì examination.
He was appointed as Yuèyáng Chéng.
He was then transferred to Liáoyángfǔ Tuīguān,
and subsequently served as Zhōngmóu Lìng.
It happened that Hǎilíng was then constructing Biànjīng,
transporting timber on the river.
Yàn was in charge of this.
Yàn, seeing that many had failed before him due to the dangers of the Sānmén section,
quickly reported to the Xíngtái,
scattering the timber into the water
and having laborers retrieve it downstream.
Everyone found this convenient.
He observed mourning for his mother,
and after the period of mourning,
was summoned to serve as Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ.
He resigned this post
and became Wèizhōu Fángyù Pànguān.
Shìzōng had long known his talent and reputation,
and soon summoned him to be Yìngfèng Hàlín Wénzì.
He was specially ordered to go to the imperial chamber to express his gratitude.
The Emperor looked at his attendants and said:
“Lǐ Yàn’s spirit is as it was before,”
and offered him many comforting words.
At that time, the suburban sacrificial rites were being discussed,
and he was appointed acting Tàicháng Bóshì,
and soon after, was formally appointed.
He served as the reader of official documents for Gāolí,
was promoted five times to Mìshū Shǎojiān,
concurrently Shàngshū Lǐbù Lángzhōng,
and was appointed Xījīng Fùliúshǒu.
Shìzōng said to his attendants:
“There are few old hands in the Hàlín Academy,
and the new Jìnshì are generally unlearned.
Few are capable of drafting edicts, pardons, and imperial commissions.
Capable literary scholars serving in outer posts should be selected for this.”
His attendants recommended Yàn.
The Emperor
said:
“Lǐ Yàn is known to me personally.”
Thereupon, he was summoned to be Hàlín Zhíxuégshì,
concurrently Tàicháng Shǎoqīng.
Due to his mother’s old age, he requested to return home to care for her,
and was appointed Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
Before he could take up the post,
his mother died.
He was reinstated as Hàlín Zhíxuégshì.
Shìzōng was in the inner imperial chamber,
and summoned Yàn to read the policy essays submitted by the new Jìnshì.
When he reached
“What method should be used to fill vacant Xiànlìng positions?”,
the Emperor said:
“I have pondered this day and night,
but do not know how to resolve it.”
Yàn replied:
“Your servant has reflected on this for a long time,
but without a means, dared not speak.
Now, fortunately, I am serving as an attendant,
and have received this great question.
I wish to exhaust what I know.”
The Emperor said:
“Then what do you suggest?”
He replied:
“Our dynasty, when establishing the examination system for selecting scholars, initially divided it into Northern and Southern selections.
One hundred people were selected from the North,
and one hundred and fifty from the South,
totaling two hundred and fifty people.
As many people entered officialdom through the Cífù and Jīngyì examinations,
the Xiànlìng positions were never vacant.
Afterwards, the Northern and Southern selections were combined,
and only the Cífù examination was held,
with only sixty or seventy people selected each time.
As fewer people entered officialdom,
the vacancy of Xiànlìng positions is likely due to this.”
The Emperor deemed it correct
and issued an edict that future selections of people should not be limited by number.
Soon after, he was promoted to Lìbù Shìláng,
concurrently holding his former position.
The imperial decree stated:
“You are naturally resolute
and possess a spirited resolve,
therefore I bestow this upon you.
You should exercise greater caution,
and not be reckless.”
Shortly after, he became Zhōngdū Lù Tuīpái Shǐ,
then promoted to Hàlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì,
concurrently Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
It happened that a court official feigned illness and requested leave.
Shìzōng suspected him of deceit,
and said to Yàn:
“You have always been upright and firm.
Now so-and-so is feigning illness,
and because of his close relation to the Chancellor,
are you afraid to impeach him?”
Yàn knelt and replied:
“Although your servant is old,
what I have relied on throughout my life is sincerity and straightforwardness.
When officials request leave due to illness,
the Supervising Censors should investigate.
As a Zhōngchéng,
I should speak out if officials commit illicit acts.
But regarding illness and leave,
this is a small matter about which your servant might not know.
How could I be afraid of the Chancellor?”
After he left,
Shìzōng watched him go,
and said:
“Yàn is old,
but his spirit is not yet diminished.”
One day,
the Yùshǐtái presented a memorial requesting an increase in Supervising Censors.
The Emperor said:
“Investigating internal and external officials
is indeed the duty of Supervising Censors.
However, if you hear or know of something,
you should also impeach it.
Moreover, correcting wrongdoings
is the duty of the Censorate officials.
If you cannot rectify yourselves,
how can you rectify others?”
He looked at Yàn and said:
“Bīnwáng is young and inexperienced.
I entrust the affairs of the Censorate to you.
You must pay careful attention to everything.”
Dàdìng was proclaimed as the new era name in Liáodōng.
Xī奔 hastened to the traveling court,
and an edict restored him to his former position.
The following year,
he was appointed Associate Administrator of Héjiān Prefecture.
He was granted an audience in the xiānggé,
where he was warned, saying:
"I hear that the imperial clan members residing there are very unrestrained;
you must restrain them with the law."
Xī, upon taking office, proclaimed the imperial edict,
and thereafter, no one dared to obstruct governance or harm the people.
He was promoted to Defense Commissioner of Mèngzhōu,
and repeatedly advanced to become Military Commissioner of Jiàngyáng Commandery.
He was then transferred to administer Jǐnán Prefecture.
He requested to retire due to old age,
which was granted.
He died in the fifth year of Míngchāng,
at the age of eighty-three.
Dèng Yǎn, courtesy name Zǐwēi,
was a native of Yímín, Yìzhōu.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
he was selected as a successful candidate in the imperial examination.
During the Dàdìng era,
he served as a Supernumerary Assistant Director of the Left Department and a Director of the Right Department,
and soon transferred to the Left Department,
managing state affairs for several years.
When the relevant office proposed sending an envoy to Sòng,
Shìzōng ordered the selection of one Hán official.
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Liáng Sù presented Wáng Xiāo, Minister of the Board of Revenue, Zhāng Dàjié, Minister of the Board of Works, and Dèng Yǎn, Director of the Left Department.
Shìzōng said:
"Wáng Xiāo and Zhāng Dàjié regrettably lack experience,
and their diligence differs from that of the officials of the Left and Right Departments.
Let Yǎn go."
He once said to the prime ministers:
"People say that Dèng Yǎn's intentions are not upright,
but I see that when Yǎn reports on affairs, his judgment is very clear,
and in the Táifǔ Jiān, his heart is also for the public good."
The prime ministers then reported that Yǎn understood the workings of government and had capability,
so he was promoted to Minister of the Board of Revenue.
The next day,
Shìzōng again said to the prime ministers:
"The Board of Civil Office is in charge of selection and appointment;
it needs a knowledgeable and experienced person.
Yǎn can be placed in the Board of Civil Office."
Consequently, his appointment was changed.
He was successively promoted to Superintendent of Transport for the Central Capital Circuit.
In the early Míngchāng era,
he became Minister of the Board of Revenue.
The Emperor ordered the Secretariat-Chancellery to gather all officials for a discussion
on how to encourage the people to abandon secondary pursuits and focus on fundamental ones to increase savings.
Yǎn said:
"The current customs are marked by extravagant competition.
It would be best to establish a fixed system
so that nobility and commoners, superiors and inferiors, attire, carriages, houses, and utensils each have their proper distinctions.
Restrain excessive wedding and funeral rites,
and abolish the baseless expenses of local community gatherings and pursuits.
If expenditures are regulated, savings will increase daily."
Soon after, he administered Guīdé Prefecture,
retired,
and died.
Originally,
after Yǎn retired, he again sought advancement through connections.
The Emperor asked his attendants,
"Can Dèng Yǎn be reinstated?"
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Wányán Shǒuzhēn replied:
"Yǎn has talent and capability,
but his mind is set on personal gain."
The Emperor said:
"I also know that.
But to whom can Yǎn be compared?"
Shǒuzhēn said:
"In matters of business, he is not inferior to others,
but he often seeks his own convenience.
Yǎn previously requested retirement,
and Your Majesty granted it because he was rather shrewd,
which greatly satisfied public opinion.
If he is now reinstated in the court,
I fear that moral integrity will be corrupted thereby."
The Emperor agreed,
and thus he was not reinstated.
Jù Gòu, courtesy name Zǐchéng,
was a native of Pínggǔ, Jìzhōu.
As a child, he was diligent in his studies,
and at the age of twenty, he passed the imperial examination.
From Assistant Magistrate of Xìndū, he was honorably selected as Magistrate of Shíchéng,
then appointed Clerk of the Secretariat-Chancellery,
and bestowed the title of Vice Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ Commandery.
He was transferred to be Associate Supervisor of the Salt Administration for Production and Distribution.
Because of increased revenue from his administration, he became an Assistant Director of the Imperial Manufactory.
He was twice promoted to Administrator of the Office of Memorials
and concurrently Assistant Supervisor of Waterways.
At that time, Duàn Guī, Director of the Right Department, died.
Shìzōng said:
"This man was very clear and upright and could have been used,
unlike Jù Gòu, who merely went along with everything."
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was appointed Vice Retainer of Nánjīng.
The Emperor said to the prime ministers:
"Jù Gòu is outwardly simple and honest, but inwardly intelligent,
only lacking in firmness and integrity.
The duty of an assistant official is to be able to discern right from wrong with his superior,
and I fear this man cannot do that.
If he is appointed as a chief official,
he will surely have commendable achievements."
Upon Zhāngzōng's accession,
he was promoted to Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi Commandery.
He retired in the fifth year of Chéng'ān,
and died.
Gòu was tolerant, mild, and taciturn by nature;
his governance was known for its tranquility.
He was particularly serene and modest,
so after people became prominent, he no longer associated with them.
If he first sent a letter, he would only reply with seasonal greetings.
During the Dàdìng era,
an edict ordered him and close officials to jointly manage the construction of the Xiāngshān Temporary Palace and Buddhist temples.
One of these close officials privately said to Gòu:
"You are a man of virtue now.
I wish to recommend you to the throne,
and you will soon receive a great appointment."
Gòu declined.
He was listed in the Ministry of Civil Affairs' records for his integrity, caution, and adherence to the law,
and remained blameless throughout his career.
Hè Yángtíng, courtesy name Gōngsǒu,
was a native of Jìyīn, Cáozhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the classical scholarship category in the third year of Tiāndé.
He was appointed Chief Clerk of Fàn County and concurrently County Lieutenant,
and gained a reputation for good governance.
In the thirteenth year of Dàdìng,
from Magistrate of Ānsù, he was appointed Clerk of the Secretariat-Chancellery,
bestowed the title of Vice Military Commissioner of Qìnnán Commandery,
and entered court as Censor.

He successively served as Recorder of the Right Department, Supernumerary Assistant Director of the Board of Revenue, Investigating Censor, and Supernumerary Assistant Director of the Right Department.
Shìzōng admired his resoluteness and courage,
and said to Yángtíng:
"Southerners are straightforward and daring,
while Hán people are insidious by nature
and often avoid difficulties in handling affairs.
In earlier times, southerners were not accustomed to poetic prose,
so few passed the examinations.
In recent years, many people from Hénán and Shāndōng have passed,
perhaps even excelling Hán people in official service."
Soon after, due to his integrity and competence, he was promoted to Director of the Board of Revenue,
advancing two ranks.
A short while later,
he was appointed Director of the Left Department,
then transferred to Assistant Minister of the Board of Punishments and Transport Commissioner of Shāndōng East Circuit.
Upon Zhāngzōng's accession,
nine judicial inspection circuits were initially established.
He was urgently summoned to the capital
and appointed Judicial Inspector of Shāndōng East and West Circuits.
Yángtíng's nature was to abhor evil,
not tolerating the slightest transgression.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
an edict ordered all Judicial Inspectors to have an audience.
The Emperor personally questioned them about the cases they had investigated.
When it came to Yángtíng, he reproached him, saying:
"Why is your administration so troublesome?"
The following year,
he was demoted to Defense Commissioner of Míngzhōu.
At that time, the year was lean and the people were starving.
Yángtíng advised wealthy households to sell their surplus grain.
The hungry were saved,
and the people of Míngzhōu erected a stone monument to praise his virtue.
He was transferred to Transport Commissioner of Shǎnxī West Circuit.
He submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
The Emperor said:
"Yángtíng is capable.
What should be done?"
Right Vice Grand Counselor Liú Wěi spoke of his illness,
and so it was granted.
He died at the age of sixty-seven.
The eulogy says: Péimǎn Hēng was chosen as a court attendant through the imperial examinations.
He was able to expound on the principles of governance of Táng and Yú in both public and private court settings,
and also to denounce the villainy of the favored eunuch Liáng Dào'ér.
Wòlè Zhōng achieved his position through administrative skill
and never associated with powerful figures throughout his career.
Shìzōng established himself in Liáodōng,
and those who returned were like a market crowd,
but Zhāng Dàjié alone upheld righteousness and did not go.
Hán Xī took office in Héjiān,
personally addressing the imperial clan members residing there who were arrogant and unruly,
ensuring they were restrained by law.
While sycophants would surely flatter the emperor to gain power,
Xī, upon taking office, merely proclaimed the warning.
These were all discerning individuals,
unswayed by wealth and status.
Jù Gòu was compliant,
Hè Yángtíng was unyielding.
During the Dàdìng era, there were repeated evaluations of the merits and demerits of northern and southern literati's conduct based on these two.
Was it truly so?
Zhāng Hēng was initially looked down upon for his mediocrity,
but later praised for his discussions and arguments;
was this also the result of his self-discipline and refinement?
Dèng Yǎn was solely focused on his own gain,
described as shrewd by all,
and even after retirement sought reinstatement;
indeed, he could not be changed.
Yán Gōngzhēn, courtesy name Zhèngzhī,
was a native of Wǎnpíng, Dàxīng.
In Dàdìng 7 (1167), he passed the presented scholar examination,
and was appointed Registrar of Cháoyì.
From Magistrate of Pǔrùn, he was appointed Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
and for his integrity,
was promoted to Associate Defender of Bózhōu,
then transferred to Left General Patrol Commissioner of Zhōngdū.
He was known for his administrative achievements,
and was promoted to Associate Military Commissioner of Wǔdìng Prefecture.
In the early years of Míngchāng,
he was summoned to be Grand Judge,
and was successively promoted to Minister of Justice.
In Chéng'ān 1 (1196),
he was promoted to Academician in Waiting of the Hànlín Academy,
still retaining his previous post,
and was ordered to review documents of memorials with Jiǎ Yì of the Court of Petitions.
Gōngzhēn served in the judiciary for several decades,
with meticulous care and thoroughness,
never making a single error.
He was appointed to proofread and correct laws and statutes,
and made many rectifications.
The Jīn people regarded him as the "ancestor of legalists."
Jiāo Xù, courtesy name Míngruì,
was a native of Bǎixiāng, Wòzhōu.
He passed the presented scholar examination,
and was appointed Registrar of Ānxǐ.
He was twice transferred, becoming Magistrate of Dàxīng,
and concurrently held the post of Left General Patrol Commissioner.
When he caned a hundred chiefs of the imperial guard,
the relevant authorities deliberated that his crime merited a caning and dismissal.
Shìzōng said:
"Xù is an official close to the people.
If, because he caned an official, he is to be caned in return,
how can he carry out his duties?
Let him pay a fine to redeem his offense."
He was appointed Magistrate of Liángxiāng.
When Shìzōng visited Chūnshuǐ,
he saw that the Magistrates of Shíchéng and Yùtián were both old and ineffective,
and said to his chief ministers:
"County magistrates are closest to the people;
they must be virtuous and talented.
If it is like this even in the imperial domain,
one can imagine the state of the whole realm."
The Grand Councilor Shí Jū recommended Xù as capable and worthy of employment.
The emperor agreed,
and summoned him to be Right General Patrol Commissioner.
Xù was resolute and self-reliant,
and did not avoid powerful individuals.
Initially,
when a commoner in Xù's jurisdiction appealed a case,
Xù, lacking written proof, remanded the case to the original parties.
He encountered a Censor on the road who complained about the matter,
and whose words were confusing and disorderly.
The Censor immediately arrested and handed him over to Xù.
Xù released him without questioning,
for which he was impeached by the Censor,
demoted two ranks,
caned one hundred eighty times,
and sent out as Judicial Officer of Dàmíng Prefecture.
Soon after, he was appointed Judge in the Right Three Departments,
and replaced Hán Tiānhé as Censor.
At that time, the Censorate stated:
"The Censor is a post for supervision and impeachment.
Tiānhé, having risen through various academic paths,
is difficult to place in this position."
The emperor ordered another recommendation.
Vice-Censor-in-chief Lǐ Yàn recommended Xù as upright and capable,
and so he was appointed,
while Tiānhé was reassigned as Magistrate of Huòlù.
At the beginning of Zhāngzōng's reign,
Grand Tutor Kèníng and Right Chancellor Xiāng requested the emperor to go hunting.
Xù impeached them for this impropriety.
The emperor consoled him,
and cancelled the hunt.
In Míngchāng 1 (1190),
when officials were first appointed to the Court of Petitions,
the chief ministers recommended Judicial Advisor Guō Ānmín, Remonstrance Official Xǔ Ānrén, and Xù as all worthy of promotion.
He was transferred to Imperial Censor,
and after four promotions, became Director of the Directorate of Waterways.
For his meritorious work in river defense, he was promoted one rank,
appointed Transport Commissioner of Xījīng Circuit,
and died.
Xù was quick-witted
and experienced in contemporary governance.
He, along with Wáng Xiāo and Liú Zhòngzhū, were renowned as capable officials.
Liú Zhòngzhū, courtesy name Shīlǔ,
was a native of Wǎnpíng, Dàxīng.
In Dàdìng 3 (1163),
he passed the presented scholar examination.
He successively served as Registrar of Lóngmén and Commissioner of Liquor Taxes in Xiānghé,
then was transferred to Magistrate of Shēnzé.
The county was near the Hūtuó River.
When the autumn harvest was underway,
the river suddenly overflowed.
Zhòngzhū made every effort to protect the embankments,
and there was ultimately no harm.
When robbers committed a crime at night,
the residents were alarmed.
Zhòngzhū led the county police to capture one of them alive,
and the rest of the gang scattered.
By morning, they were all rounded up and apprehended.
Soon after, for his integrity and ability, he was promoted one rank,
and elevated to Judicial Reviewer of the Department of Finance, Héběi West Circuit.
He entered the capital as Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Justice,
and after six promotions, became Supernumerary Director of the Right Department,
and shortly after transferred to the Ministry of Personnel.
Shìzōng said to his chief ministers:
"Among people, some are articulate and eloquent but ordinary and not upright,
while others are awkward in speech but intelligent, perceptive, and sincerely inclined towards rectitude.
For example, Liú Zhòngzhū is well-regarded for his talent and conduct,
yet he is very inarticulate."
Right Chancellor Zhāng Rǔlín said:
"There are many such people,
and I wish Your Majesty would observe them closely."
In Dàdìng 29 (1189),
he was sent out as Prefect of Qízhōu.
He taught using "six virtues,"
and the people were transformed by him.
Upon Zhāngzōng's accession,
he was appointed Vice-Commissioner of Judicial Review for Zhōngdū, Xījīng, and other circuits.
Previously,
more than thirty families, including Tián Jué, had been disgraced and banished for factional crimes.
Zhòngzhū knew they were wronged,
and submitted a memorial vigorously defending them.
The emperor followed his advice,
restoring Jué's official title and rank, and thus lifting the ban on factions.
In Míngchāng 2 (1191),
he was appointed Grand Tutor to the Prince of Bīng, concurrently Associate Administrator of Dàtóng Prefecture,
then shortly after transferred to Píngyáng,
and moved to Defender of Dézhōu.
Transport Commissioner Guō Bāngjié and Military Commissioner Lǐ Yàn both recommended Zhòngzhū as their successor.
He was promoted to Military Commissioner of Dìnghǎi.
During a famine,
Zhòngzhū memorialized requesting to open the granaries.
Before a reply was received,
he proceeded to provide relief loans.
The relevant authorities impeached him,
and his crime was judged redeemable by a fine.
At that time, Zhòngzhū's elder brother, Zhòngyuān, had been punished for a crime and exiled to Shízhōu.
Zhòngzhū submitted a memorial requesting to exchange Lái for Shí.
The court considered it righteous but did not permit it.
After a long time,
due to old age, he requested to retire,
and only after repeated memorials was he permitted.
He died in Tàihé 8 (1208),
aged seventy-five.
Zhòngzhū was upright and straightforward,
decisive in governance,
and especially skilled in administering the people.
Wherever he served, he had meritorious achievements;
indeed, he was a capable official of his time.
Lǐ Wán, courtesy name Quándào,
was a native of Mǎyì, Shuòzhōu.
He began his career as a classics student,
and later passed the presented scholar examination in prose and poetry.
He was appointed Registrar of Chéngchéng,
where he left a legacy of benevolence,
and the people erected a shrine for him.
For his integrity, he was promoted to Magistrate of Dìngxiāng,
then summoned to be Clerk in the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, due to a shortage of upright county magistrates,
Shìzōng selected eight capable officials to inspect the realm,
and Wán was one of them.
In the early years of Míngchāng,
he served as Censor.
Traditionally,
clerks in the Censorate were appointed from those who had served long in the Six Ministries.
Since all the clerks were from similar backgrounds,
none were willing to impeach or investigate.
Wán stated:
"During the Zhènglóng reign, clerks in the Department of State Affairs were drawn from various backgrounds.
In the early Dàdìng reign, upon the Grand Tutor Zhāng Hào's request,
they began to be exclusively selected from presented scholars,
which the whole realm considered appropriate.
Now, I request that the sons and grandsons of third-rank officials, and candidates who have passed the final examination,
be entrusted to the Censors for appointment."
The emperor accepted his suggestion.
He was promoted to Secretary of the Department of State Affairs,
and then sent out as Associate Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi and Administrator of Héjiān Prefecture.
The Judicial Review Department stated,
"Wán is skilled in law,
has the talent to manage difficult cases,
and there are no dissenting voices from the military or the populace."
He was promoted to Prefect of Qìnzhōu,
and further commended by imperial decree.
He was transferred to Associate Administrator of Guǎngníng Prefecture.
Initially,
a commoner named Cuī Yuán from Liáobīn entered the city to drink and did not return.
His body was later found in the water.
The authorities arrested those who had drunk with him and interrogated them,
and they all falsely confessed.
The Judicial Review Department suspected they were wronged,
and assigned the case to Wán.
Wán investigated and discovered the real culprit was a boatman,
thus exonerating those who had drunk with the victim.
He was reassigned as Vice-Commissioner of Judicial Review for Běijīng Línhuáng Circuit.
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
he was transferred to be the Transport Commissioner of Xīlù, Shǎnxī.
Soon after, he was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Nánjīnglù,
and then died.
Wán excelled in administration.
Wherever he went, evildoers disappeared,
and the people all found it convenient.
Mǎ Bǎilù, courtesy name Tiānxī,
was from Sānhé, Tōngzhōu.
His father, Róudé,
passed the *jìnshì* examination at the beginning of Tiānhuì,
and was successively promoted to Compiler in the Hànlín Academy.
He was dismissed from office for being a member of Tián Jué’s faction.
When Emperor Shìzōng ascended the throne, the factional prohibitions were lifted,
and he was recalled to service.
Bǎilù was devoted to learning in his youth,
and was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
He passed the *cífu* *jìnshì* examination in the third year of Dàdìng,
and was appointed Clerk of Wǔqīng.
From being the Magistrate of Lóngshān, he was summoned to fill the post of Secretariat Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
but did not accept it.
He was then changed to be Deputy Commissioner of Market Control and Judicial Assessor of Píngyáng Prefecture,
before entering the court as Erudite of the Directorate of Education.
The court, noting his integrity and administrative achievements during his time as county magistrate,
specially promoted him by one rank,
raising him to Associate Commissioner for Transport of Běijīnglù.
He was entrusted with overseeing criminal justice in the northern and southern circuits,
and wherever he went, there were no unjust cases.
He was summoned to be a Supernumerary Assistant Minister in the Ministry of Revenue in the Department of State Affairs,
and, along with Lǐ Jīng, Associate Commissioner for Transport of Héběi Dōnglù, served as Commissioner for Assessment and Arrangement of Zhōngdū and other circuits.
At the beginning of Míngchāng,
he was promoted to Prefect of Yàozhōu,
where officials and common people both feared and loved him.
The Surveillance Commission reported his merits,
and he was appointed Tutor to Prince Hán and Concurrent Associate Commissioner for Military Affairs of Ānwǔ Commandery.
Soon after, he was reappointed Concurrent Associate Commissioner of Xīngpíng Commandery.
As he was again commended for his integrity by the Surveillance Commission,
he was promoted to Defense Commissioner of Mèngzhōu,
and then again transferred to Surveillance Commissioner of Nánjīnglù.
The Censorate praised him for his uprightness and capability,
and he was transferred to Prefect of Hézhōng Prefecture.
He retired in the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
and died.
His posthumous name was Zhēnzhōng.
Yáng Bóyuán, courtesy name Chángqīng,
was from Wèishì, Kāifēng.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the third year of Dàdìng,
and was appointed Clerk of Yǎnchéng.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Yúcì,
then summoned to be a Grand Judge,
and successively appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Dìnghǎi Commandery.
For his integrity, he was exceptionally promoted to Associate Commissioner for Transport of Héběi Běilù,
and entered the court as a Supernumerary Assistant Minister in the Ministry of Punishments in the Department of State Affairs.
He was dismissed due to mourning,
but was later appointed Prefect of Liáozhōu.
In the first year of Míngchāng,
he was transferred to Zhuōzhōu.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of Public Works,
and then, through four more transfers, became Military Commissioner of Ānwǔ Commandery.
He retired in the third year of Tàihé,
and died.
Bóyuán was often entrusted with important tasks due to his talent and ability.
He served twice as Commissioner for Assessment and Tax Determination,
and repeatedly as Reviewing Official,
earning praise for his fairness.
Whenever there was a doubtful case,
he would be specially dispatched to resolve it,
and his clear judgments often hit the mark.
He was granted the posthumous name Dá.
Liú Jī, courtesy name Zhòngzhāng,
was from Yìdū.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the third year of Tiāndé.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he was an Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
then changed to Left Remonstrance Official,
concurrently serving as Literary Scholar for the princely establishment of Prince Xǔ.
Jī reported on matters of the princely establishment,
and Emperor Shìzōng reprimanded him, saying:
"Your duty is to teach and guide;
why do you involve yourself in reporting on affairs of state!"
He then ordered a close attendant to convey an imperial decree to Yǒngzhōng, saying:
"You have a Chief Clerk;
why do you let a Literary Scholar report on matters?
Do not repeat this in the future."
He was successively appointed Associate Commissioner of the Transport Bureau.
He once submitted a memorial stating:
"The remuneration for canal households is too high,
resulting in a wasteful expenditure of government resources.
It would be advisable to reduce it.
If one-third were cut,
the annual saving for the government would exceed 150,000 strings of cash."
Emperor Shìzōng agreed with his statement.
He was appointed Supernumerary Assistant Minister in the Ministry of Revenue,
and submitted several proposals for expedient measures.
Emperor Shìzōng said to his chief ministers:
"Jī’s suggestion to plant willows along the river dikes could save the annual cost of dike maintenance,
and his comments on the advantages and disadvantages of government funds
are highly commendable.
Previous officials in the Ministry of Revenue often procrastinated,
and those like Jī are hard to come by.
You all should discuss and implement the feasible proposals.
Jī’s previous statement about saving expenses in canal transport
shows his utmost dedication to public service.
Without a generous reward, there would be no encouragement for future officials."
Thus, he was given 3,000 strings of cash.
He was promoted to Prefect of Wéizhōu,
then transferred to Prefect of Jìzhōu.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Associate Commissioner of Běijīng Left-behind Administration.
He was demoted to Prefect of Guǎnzhōu
for bending the law to release slaves who claimed to be free.
Emperor Shìzōng asked his chief ministers:
"What kind of person is Jī?"
Associate Administrator Chéng Huī replied:
"Jī is stubborn and overbearing.
He once relentlessly pursued government funds in Jìnán Prefecture,
leading to forced transactions and harm to common people."
The Emperor said:
"I heard that when Jī was in Běijīng,
whenever slaves claimed to be free, he would release them without regard for the authenticity of their contracts.
If he intended to seek blessings from the unseen,
then why did he not release his own slaves?"
He also said:
"Jī released my household slaves,
intending to seek blessings through this.
If his intentions are like this,
he should not be reappointed."
In the second year of Míngchāng,
he entered the court as Assistant Supervisor of the Directorate of Education.
He requested retirement but was not permitted.
He was transferred to Libationer of the Directorate of Education,
and soon after promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Due to his senility and inability to perform his duties, he was impeached and dismissed by the Censorate.
He died in the second year of Chéng'ān,
aged eighty-two.
His elder brother was Liú Qióng.
Qióng, courtesy name Bóyù,
was originally named Tàipíng.
As the son of a meritorious official, he was appointed Gate Guard.
After his father's death, he requested to observe the full mourning period.
However, when Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
he was not permitted,
and was instead made a palace guard.
Hǎilíng was wary of the imperial clan.
Qióng was dismissed and sent to reside in his hometown
for associating with them.
During the Míngchāng period,
the Shǔqiāng leader Yǐbiāo killed the prefecture official and rebelled.
At this time, Gāng was a Fèngyù.
He received an imperial edict to consult with Cáo Fóliú about the matter,
and then summoned Qīngyíkě to gather troops and defeat Yǐbiāo.
Cáo Fóliú was promoted to Tóngzhī Líntáo Yǐn,
concurrently Táozhōu Cìshǐ.
His son, Pǔxián, became Táozhōu Guǎnnèi Xúnjiǎnshǐ.
Gāng frequently traveled to Táo for various matters.
Fóliú often told Gāng that Qīngyíkě wished to submit to the court,
expressing his genuine sincerity.
Gāng would then report this to the emperor,
but the emperor ultimately did not accept it.
When Gāng was deployed to Shǎnxī,
the emperor secretly ordered him to strategize on Western affairs.
By then,
Cáo Fóliú had died,
and Pǔxián was Huáiqiāng Xúnjiǎnshǐ.
When Gāng arrived in Táo,
he swiftly summoned Pǔxián to temporarily manage the affairs of Tóngzhī Táozhōu.
Pǔxián sent a dispatch arrow into the Qiāng territory.
Qīngyíkě was greatly pleased,
and led all his tribal chiefs,
registering their territory, people,
and went to Gāng to request submission.
Gāng reported the matter.
The emperor appointed Qīngyíkě as Diézhōu Fù Dūzǒngguǎn,
and added the title Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn.
The imperial edict to Qīngyíkě stated:
“You command your people,
and have been a powerful leader for generations.
You have longed for our influence and admired our righteousness,
turning away from deceit and returning to the court.
You wish to show pure sincerity
and offer loyal service.
We recall this with fond admiration,
and shall bestow rich commendations.
We have reviewed the false credentials you submitted.
The court’s governance of various tribes has indeed no such precedent.
Wishing to enable you to pacify your tribes and enhance your prestige,
we have therefore specially granted a new appointment,
bestowing one gold plaque and two silver plaques.
Upon their arrival, you shall respectfully receive them,
accept our new grace,
and forever be a loyal vassal.”
Cáo Pǔxián was officially appointed Tóngzhī Táozhōu affairs.
Gāng was promoted to Gǒngwèi Zhídū Zhīhuīshǐ,
and raised three ranks,
with his Anfǔ and Dū Dà Tíju titles remaining as before.
The matter was assigned to the Shāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wūgǔlùn Yǎnzhōu as领 (líng), Cáo Pǔxián as押领 (yālǐng), and Qīngyíkě as勾当 (gōudàng).
The imperial edict said:
“Wányán Gāng,
when you first set out, you did not know about Qīngyíkě’s matter in the imperial court.
You solely said that he could be won over,
and would certainly be useful.
Soon enough, he indeed came to show loyalty.
Now, you must not, because Qīngyíkě’s military power is great,
humble yourself and lose decorum;
nor must you, because he is a barbarian tribe, despise him.”
In the ninth month,
an imperial edict was issued to console Shǎnxī,
which roughly stated:
“In the three circuits of Jīngzhào, Fèngxiáng, and Líntáo,
those who were coerced by Sòng troops,
turned their backs on the state and followed the pretenders,
or were lost to foreign lands,
if they can return voluntarily,
officials shall resume their duties as before,
the common people shall each be allowed to resume their livelihoods,
and their original abandoned lands shall be returned according to their numbers.
As for those who received Sòng flags, banners, structures, and so on,
or fled due to panic and thus evaded service,
if not yet discovered,
they are permitted to confess to the local officials.
All shall be released and pardoned,
and no further investigation will be conducted.
Those useful for the front lines shall be employed as appropriate.
Those who do not confess within the deadline
will be punished as before.”
Sòng Chéng Sōng dispatched a separate general, Qǔ Chāngshì, to attack Fāngshān Yuán.
He personally led tens of thousands of troops in separate routes to attack Héshàng Yuán, Xīshān Zhài, Lóngmén, and other passes.
On that day,
a dense fog enveloped all sides,
followed by a sudden downpour.
The garrison troops at Héshàng Yuán, Xīshān Zhài, and Lóngmén Guān did not know of the Sòng army’s arrival,
so Sōng seized them.
Púchá Zhēn dispatched the Xíngjūn Fùtǒng Péimǎn Ālǐ and Tóngzhī Lǒngzhōu Shì Wányán Bólùn with a thousand men to lie in ambush below Fāngshān Yuán.
Wànhù Àotún Sāhémén and Měiyuán Xiànlìng Shúhǔ Hétá, with five hundred picked valiant men,
took a hidden path and stealthily ascended,
appearing above the Sòng troops.
Attacking from above,
the Sòng troops were greatly alarmed.
The ambushing troops joined the attack,
and they were defeated.
Zhēn then separately dispatched Shúhǔ Hétá and his general Wányán Chūjūnnu with a thousand men to go through Huáng'ér Gǔ to take Héshàng Yuán.
Tóngzhī Huìzhōu Shì Nǚxīliè Nánjiā and Yājūn Měng'ān Niángē Sāgǎi led a thousand men to go through Dàníng Gǔ to take Xīshān Zhài.
Zhēn himself led seven hundred men through the middle route to take Lóngmén and other passes.
Chéng Sōng had already burned the plank roads.
Zhēn repaired the roads while advancing his troops.
Upon reaching Xiǎoguān,
Sòng general Yáng Tíng held the strategic position and shot arrows,
preventing Zhēn from advancing.
He ordered Xíngjūn Fùtǒng Péimǎn Ālǐ to create a diversion,
and secretly sent Měng'ān Hú Xìn with fifty armored soldiers to bypass to their rear,
and attack them from behind.
The Sòng army was thrown into great disarray,
and Tíng was killed on the battlefield.
The Sòng troops fled to Èrlǐ Guān,
and were again defeated.
Sòng general Péng Tǒnglǐng led the Sòng troops to flee to Lóngmén,
and they were pursued and decisively defeated.
Hétá stealthily ascended the summit of Héshàng Yuán under cover of night.
The Sòng people were astonished, thinking he was a god,
and all scattered and fled.
He defeated two thousand of their troops,
and captured dozens alive.
Nánjiā cut wood to clear a path and ascended Xīshān.
He encountered Sòng troops again,
and scattered them all.
[一三]Thus, they fully recovered the old territories.
Sòng Wú Xī’s generals Fēng Xīng, Yáng Xióng, and Lǐ Guī, with eight thousand infantry and cavalry, entered Chìgǔ,
intending to raid Qínzhōu.
Chéngyù, Wányán Lín, and Hézhōu Fángyùshǐ Púchá Bǐngxuàn met them and attacked,
defeating them.
The Sòng infantry moved towards Xīshān,
and the cavalry fled to Chìgǔ.
Chéngyù divided his troops to pursue the Sòng infantry.
The Sòng infantry held the mountain and fought.
His general Tángkuò Àndáhǎi led two hundred cavalry to charge and attack them.
The armored soldier Ménggē personally rushed into their formation first.
The troops followed,
and the Sòng infantry was utterly routed,
killing several hundred people.
The pursuers reached Zàojiāo Chéng,
beheading two thousand.
Měng'ān Bǎtiānnú pursued the Sòng cavalry,
killing over a thousand.
Fēng Xīng barely escaped with his life.
Yáng Xióng and Lǐ Guī were both killed by the Jīn army.
In the tenth month,
Gāng led ten thousand barbarian and Hàn infantry and cavalry out from Líntán.
Chōng led ten thousand troops from Guānzhōng out from Chéncāng.
Púchá Zhēn led ten thousand troops from Qí and Lǒng out from Chéngjì.
Shímò Zhòngwēn led five thousand infantry and cavalry from Lǒngyòu out from Yánchuān.
Wányán Lín led five thousand of his own troops out from Láiyuǎn.
Initially,
Wú Jiè and Wú Lín were both great Sòng generals.
Brothers, fathers, and sons successively guarded the Western lands,
winning the hearts of the soldiers and people between Liáng and Yì.
Lín’s grandson Xī, who was Tàiwèi, Zhāowǔ Jūnjiédùshǐ, and Chéngdū Tóngchuān Fǔ Kuí Lì Děngzhōu Lù Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ,
mobilized troops to Xīngyuán in Tàihé year six,
with the ambition of eyeing Guān and Lǒng.
He enticed border residents to become bandits,
and sent spies to bribe Fèngxiáng soldier Wēn Chāng with promises of gain,
conspiring with the three Yúhòu armies to act as an internal應.
Chāng went to the prefectural office to report the treachery.
Xī sent his generals out between Qín and Lǒng,
and they confronted Gāng and the other armies.
The emperor heard that Hán Tuōzhòu was jealous of Xī’s prestige,
and that he could be lured through division.
Liáng and Yì were upstream of Sòng,
and could be used to gain control over Sòng.
Therefore, he enfeoffed Xī as King of Shǔ,
cast an imperial seal, and bestowed an imperial edict.
The edict instructed Gāng to manage the situation.
The edict bestowed upon Xī stated: “Ever since Sòng Jí and Huán lost their positions,
they fled to the Jiāngbiǎo,
usurped titles,
and clung to life in Wú and Huì.
At that time, your ancestor, Duke Wǔ’ān Jiè, defended the two Chuān.
Later, King Wǔshùn Lín inherited great achievements.
It is fitting that your family should continually be granted the title of Grand Marshal,
thus securing the Western lands,
and forever serving as a protective buffer,
swearing by mountains and rivers.
Even if your descendants had the arrogance
of Luán Yǎn,
they should still be forgiven for ten generations.
However, those whose might and strategy overshadow their lord are in danger,
and those whose achievements surpass the world are not rewarded.
This has been so since ancient times,
not just today.
Your family has exclusively controlled Shǔhàn
for many years.
As suspicion has already arisen,
you are in a dilemma.
If you are replaced, you will not accept;
if summoned, you will not go.
The relationship
between ruler and minister is already like strangers.
It is like the leaves of a split paulownia, which cannot be rejoined;
or riding a tiger, from which one cannot dismount midway.
This matter has been circulating,
and has been known to Us
for a long time.
Whenever We think of it, We cannot but sigh with sorrow,
yet you remain complacent.
Furthermore, do you consider your achievements in aiding and supporting to be superior to those of Yuè Fēi?
