In the fifth year of Chéng'ān,
the Emperor asked his chancellors:
"Among the Han officials today, who is capable?"
Sīkōng Xiāng recommended Jíkāng.
The Emperor said:
"Is he not frivolous?"
Xiāng replied:
"He can be reappointed as Cenzhōngchéng to observe him."
Thereupon, the Emperor summoned Jíkāng again to be Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
In the third year of Tàihé,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
The following year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
In the sixth year,
Sòng broke the alliance, and there were signs of trouble.
The ministers still regarded it as petty thievery and not worth worrying about.
Jíkāng, along with Zuǒchéng Púsǎn Duān and Cānzhèng Dújí Sīzhōng, believed that military action was necessary,
and the Emperor agreed.
The Emperor asked Jíkāng and Cānzhī Zhèngshì Jiǎ Xuàn:
"For the taboo characters of Tàizōng's temple name that are homophones,
some read the character as 'chéng'
but since it's not a homophone,
it shouldn't have a missing stroke or dot.
Rùizōng's temple name was changed to 'chóng'
yet the lower part retains the complete original character.
Wouldn't it be better to write the 'shì'
(示) radical as 'wèi'
(未) in the style of the Lántíng Tìe?
[一０] For Xiǎnzōng's temple name 'yǔn' (允),
the character 'chōng'
(充) should have a missing stroke or dot.
[一一] However, for 'chōng'
(充) as part of 'tǒng'
(統), it seems it should not be omitted."
Jíkāng memorialized, saying:
"Táng Tàizōng's personal name was Shìmín.
Characters with a radical that infringed upon it, such as 'yè'
(葉) was written as '⽥'
and 'mín'
(泯) was written as 'hóu'
Then he proposed:
"Xīzōng's temple name should follow the 'miàn'
(面) and 'qiě' (且) components.
Rùizōng's temple name's upper character should follow 'wèi'
(未), and the lower character should follow '[⿰耳卑]'.
[一二] Shìzōng's temple name should follow 'xì'
Xiǎnzōng's temple name, for its direct infringing characters,
only the diagonal stroke should be written.
The characters 'yǎn'
(沇) and 'yǔn' (鈗) should each follow 'kǒu'
Characters like 'duì'
(兌) and 'yuè' (悅) should each follow their original form."
[一三] This was adopted,
and from then on, excessive avoidance was no longer practiced.
He was promoted to Zuǒchéng.
When the Sòng people requested peace,
he was promoted one rank.
According to old regulations,
a scribe in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng lìshǐ) who completed their term with excellent performance was given a superior transfer,
but their next appointment would be a demotion.
Cuī Jiànchāng had already received a superior transfer as Deputy Military Commissioner (Jiédù Fùshǐ) of Xīngpíng Prefecture,
but before his demotion, he was appointed Dàlǐ Sīzhí.
An imperial edict ordered that Guō Bāngjié and Lǐ Qī be flogged seventy times and dismissed,
and Zuǒsī Yuánwàiláng Gāo Tíngyù be flogged forty times and removed from office.
Jíkāng awaited punishment,
but there was an imperial edict that he should not be questioned.
When Zhāngzōng died,
Wèishàowáng ascended the throne.
Jíkāng was promoted to Píngzhāng Zhèngshì
and enfeoffed as Chóngguó Gōng.
In the third year of Dà'ān,
he retired.
That year,
he passed away.
An envoy was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Lǐ Gé, courtesy name Jūnměi,
was a native of Héjīn.
His father, Yúqìng,
attended the imperial examination three times,
but was unsuccessful,
and so he gave up.
Gé was brilliant and intelligent;
he would read a book once or twice,
and would always remember it without forgetting.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng.
He was appointed Zhēndìng Zhǔbù.
He was assessed as honest and incorruptible,
and transferred to Hánchéng Lìng.
A Tongzhi Zhōushì accepted bribes from wealthy merchants,
assigning the annual military provisions to the affiliated counties.
Gé alone refused to comply,
and the Tíxíng Sī considered him capable.
He was transferred to Héběi Dōnglù Zhuǎnyùn Dūgōu Pànjuàn and Tàiyuán Tuīguān.
He left office due to his mother's mourning,
was reinstated,
and transferred to Dàxīng Xiànlìng, Zhōngdū Zuǒ Jǐngxún Shǐ, Nánjīng Tíxíng Pànjuàn, Jiānchá Yùshǐ, and Tongzhi Zhāoyìjūn Jiédù Shì.
He left office due to his father's mourning,
was reinstated,
and appointed Qiān Nánjīng Ànchá Shì.
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
when Sòng was being attacked,
the Shàngshū Shěng memorialized:
"When military campaigns are underway,
officials along the routes
who are assigned to temporary posts should be specially noted;
vacancies should be filled by selection;
those too old for their duties should be dismissed;
and each department and county should retain one capable principal officer."
Gé, along with Qiān Shǎnxī Gāo Lín and Qiān Shāndōng Mèng Zǐyuán, were all commanded by edict
to investigate the capabilities of officials in the three routes,
register the retained principal officers,
the number of officers temporarily assigned by the Xíngshěng, Xíngbù, and Yuánshuài Fǔ, as well as vacant positions due to incidents,
and those too old for their duties,
and report to the court.
He was reappointed Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng,
transferred to Guānzhōu Cìshǐ concurrently Tiíjǔ Cáoyùn,
Shǎnxī Xīlù Ànchá Fùshǐ,
and Dàxīng Fǔ Zhìzhōng.
The Zhīfǔ, Túshān Nánpíng, was a favorite of the court and held great power,
influencing both the court and the provinces.
He sent his close associates to entice Gé with promises of promotion,
but Gé rejected them.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was promoted to Hùbù Shìláng.
When Xuānzōng moved to Biàn,
he oversaw the affairs of the Six Departments in Héběi Xīlù,
and was promoted to Zhī Kāifēng Fǔshì,
Hénán Quànnóng Shǐ,
Hùbù and Lìbù Shàngshū,
and Shǎnxī Xíngshěng Cānyì Guān.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Gé memorialized, saying:
"Various departments, acting on their subjective views, cite and apply precedents,
stretching and forcing interpretations to fit,
which in fact opens doors for opportunistic behavior.
I humbly request that all precedents, imperial edicts, and special decrees that are not intended to be permanent regulations
should not be cited,
and all matters should be judged by the established laws."
An edict was issued to follow this.
That year,
the great Yuán army broke through Tóngguān.
Gé, believing that as an executive official he had failed in his defensive strategy,
submitted a memorial asking for punishment.
This was not granted,
but he was dismissed as Jiàngyángjūn Jiédù Shǐ.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
Xū Dǐng moved his garrison from Píngyáng to Shǎnxī.
Gé, as Zhī Píngyáng Fǔshì,
acted as Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
replacing Dǐng as Hédōng Xíngshěng.
At this time, the people were roused to attack Sòng.
Gé submitted a letter, saying:
"The current plan should be to cease military action and rest the people,
preserving our strength to await the enemy.
Although Sòng initiated the conflict,
we should only prepare our own defenses.
If we cannot endure a small grievance and exert ourselves in distant strategies,
I fear that others might take advantage,
and we will not be able to sustain it."
This was not adopted.
After the Tàiyuán military campaign, there was a food shortage.
Gé transferred seventy thousand dàn of grain to relieve them.
In the second year,
the imperial envoy Niángē Suōshī arrived in Hédōng.
At that time, the late-season crops were not yet ripe,
and he issued a document to the Xíngshěng ordering the destruction of crops to clear the land.
Gé memorialized, saying:
"This year, the rain has been timely,
and a good autumn harvest can be expected.
If we order the destruction of crops,
the people will not be able to bear it."
An edict was issued to follow Gé's memorial.
In the tenth month,
Píngyáng was besieged.
The city had fewer than six thousand soldiers,
and after repeated sallies,
more than half were wounded within ten days.
Troops were summoned from Jí, Xí, and Huò prefectures,
but they did not arrive in time.
The deputy general, Lǐ Huáidé, slipped down the city wall and surrendered,
and the enemy troops entered from the southeast of the city.
His attendants urged Gé to mount a horse and break through the siege.
Gé sighed, saying:
"I could not protect this city,
how can I face the Emperor!
You all may leave."
Then he committed suicide.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
In the sixth year of Tàihé
a campaign was launched against Sòng.
Wěi advanced five thousand taels of silver.
An imperial edict stated:
"It is your duty to manage the collection and storage of resources.
This is your proper function.
Do not allow soldiers to discuss state affairs.
I know all about
your shortcomings,
but only by being able to generate profit
can this be your achievement."
He was recalled from the Xīběi Lù
to audit the storehouses of all circuits,
and was appointed Assistant Commissioner of the Sānsī.
The Emperor asked:
"Who can replace you in planning and management?"
Wěi recommended Wáng Qiān, the Registrar-Judge of the Zhōngdū Transit Office.
Qiān arrived in the Xīběi Lù
and fully exposed Wěi's previous misappropriations and losses of money and goods, amounting to tens of millions,
and those implicated faced investigation for years.
In the third year of Dà'ān,
he was reappointed Assistant Commissioner of the Sānsī.
At the time of the defeat at Hé Pù,
the soldiers still grumbled, "Zhāng Xuānchāi has exploited us!"
They wanted to turn their weapons against him and kill him.
He was successively promoted to Vice Minister of the Hùbù.
At the beginning of Zhēnyòu,
he was promoted to Judicial and Transport Commissioner of the Héběi Xī Lù.
In the spring of the second year of Zhēnyòu,
Zhōngdū suffered from a grain shortage,
and he was decreed Acting Associate Commissioner of the Metropolitan Transport Office.
Biān Yuán, with ten thousand soldiers, escorted a shipment of accumulated grain from Tōngzhōu,
but his army was defeated and he died.
Gāo Qí, the Píngzhāng Zhèngshì, recommended Wěi to take Yuán's place in managing the six ministries.
For his efforts, he was promoted one rank
and transferred to Transport Commissioner of the Héběi Dōng Lù.
When Xuānzōng moved to Biàn,
he assisted the Assistant Executive of the Shàngshū Yòuchéng, Xū Dǐng, in arranging the forward route
and repairing the palace in Nánjīng.
Not long after,
he was demoted to Defense Commissioner of Mèngzhōu for an offense.
Three years later,
he was promoted to Military Commissioner of Ānguó Jūn.
He retired from office.
Xuānzōng initially considered Wěi talented,
but after realizing his lack of substance,
he never employed him again.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
he died.
Gāo Hóng,
a Bóhǎi person.
He was appointed to office by privilege
and successively served as County Commandant of Guìdé.
The Tíxíng Sī recommended him for difficult and complex duties,
and he was promoted to Registrar of Fèngshèng Zhōu.
He was assessed as incorruptible,
and promoted to Magistrate of Nèihuáng,
and successively served as Deputy Officer of the Zuǒzàngkù.
Empress Lǐ requested to exchange black silk for red silk,
but Hóng alone refused to exchange it.
The Empress reported him.
Zhāngzōng was greatly pleased
and sent someone to instruct him, saying:
"Your adherence is very good.
For now, grant her the exchange,
but it shall not set a precedent for the future."
He was transferred to the Yíluán Jú and then to Junior Supervisor of the Shàofù,
and then transferred to Supernumerary Secretary of the Hùbù and Prefect of Ānzhōu.
During the Dà'ān era,
Yuèwáng Yǒnggōng served as Administrator of Zhōngshān,
and Hóng, as the King's Tutor, concurrently held the position of Associate Prefect.
He was transferred to Associate Prefect of Hénán Fǔ
and concurrently served as Pacification Commissioner.
He was then moved to Associate Prefect of Dàmíng Fǔ,
concurrently serving as Pacification Commissioner of that circuit.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was promoted to Judicial and Transport Commissioner of the Héběi Xī Lù.
For his achievements in Dàmíng,
he was promoted three ranks
and retired from office.
In the fourth year of Xīngdìng,
he died.
Lǐ Fùhēng, courtesy name Zhòngxiū,
was a native of Héjīn, Róngzhōu.
〔一０〕At eighteen,
he passed the civil service examination.
He again ranked excellent in the Zhōngshū examination,
and was appointed Chief Clerk of Línjìn.
While escorting official horses to the prefecture,
he stayed at an inn.
Some bandits killed a horse.
Fùhēng said:
"Killing it without benefit
must mean there is an enemy."
He had all the merchants and travelers at the inn searched.
A man from the same district had a sheathed dagger in his bag.
Fùhēng said to him:
"If a knife is stained with horse blood,
the blade will turn blue if heated."
The man confessed,
and indeed had an enemy.
Recommended by the Tíxíng, he was promoted to Magistrate of Nánhé.
Bandits cut off the ears of a villager's ox.
Fùhēng summoned everyone in the village,
and had the ox owner lead the ox past each person.
When it reached one man,
the ox suddenly started and jumped.
When questioned,
the man confessed.
Assessed as incorruptible,
he was promoted to Registrar-Judge of Líntáo Fǔ,
then transferred to Registrar-Judge of Shǎnxī Dōng Lù,
and then to Revenue Judge of Hédōng Běi Lù.
〔一一〕
During the Tàihé era,
a campaign was launched against Sòng.
He served as a Staff Officer in the Xuānfǔ Sī,
and was promoted to Deputy Commissioner of Jiěyán,
and successively served as Associate Military Commissioner of Bǎodà and Zhènwǔ.
Upon the death of his mother,
he was recalled to serve as Associate Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ,
and was given the honorary title of Prefect of Xīnzhōu.
During the Zhēnyòu era,
he successively served as Supernumerary Secretary and Director of the Zuǒsī,
and was promoted to Grand Academician of the Hànlín and Acting Commissioner of the Sānsī.
In the third year of Xīngdìng,
he submitted a memorial, stating:
"Recently, an army was raised to attack Sòng.
I fear the Sòng people may exploit this weakness to launch a surprise attack on our southern border.
Therefore, border residents were conscripted as soldiers.
Now that the main army has returned,
I request that they be dismissed and returned to their original professions."
This was adopted.
Fùhēng recommended twenty-nine people, including Chénliú County Magistrate Chéng Zhèn, for their effectiveness in agriculture and sericulture,
and for their fair and uniform taxation.
The imperial court promoted all of them.
In the seventh month of that year,
three branch Sānsī offices were established in Jīngdōng, Jīngxī, and Jīngnán circuits,
to manage agricultural promotion, rent collection, military levies, and salt, iron, and wine monopolies.
Hùbù Shìláng Zhāng Shīlǔ temporarily administered the Eastern Circuit,
governing Guīdé.
Hùbù Shìláng Wányán Májiān went out to temporarily administer the Southern Circuit,
governing Xǔzhōu.
Fùhēng temporarily administered the Western Circuit,
governing Zhōngjīng (Hénán Fǔ).
The Sānsī Commissioner Hóu Zhì oversaw them all.
Fùhēng memorialized:
"People are destroying agricultural tools to supply military weapons.
I humbly believe this is inconvenient.
Rúzhōu's Lǔshān and Bǎofēng,
and Dèngzhōu's Nányáng all produce iron.
〔一二〕Recruiting laborers and establishing foundries
can generate profit
without harming the people."
He also memorialized:
"Yángwǔ has set up official salt sales to assist military expenditures.
I request that the salt from Cāng and Bīn be prohibited from crossing the river,
so that Hénán consumes salt from Yángwǔ and Jiě,
and Héběi consumes salt from Cāng and Bīn.
This will benefit both the north and the south."
An imperial edict instructed the Shàngshū Shěng to implement it.
In the ninth month,
for his efforts in promoting agriculture,
he was promoted to Minister of the Bīngbù.
Two months later,
he was transferred to Minister of the Lìbù
and provisionally served as Assistant Grand Councilor.
In the third month of the fourth year,
he was formally appointed Assistant Grand Councilor,
concurrently compiling the National History.
In the seventh month,
in Hénán, excessive rain damaged the crops.
Fù Hēng was appointed Pacification Commissioner,
with Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Wányán Bójiā as his deputy.
They toured the commanderies and counties.
Any corrupt officials
were to be dismissed, investigated, and prosecuted.

Fù Hēng memorialized, requesting a prohibition on Pacification Commissioner officials from holding drinking gatherings with officials from the zhōu, fǔ, sī, xiàn, xíng zǒngguǎnfǔ, and military officers.
He also memorialized, saying:
“The imperial decree instructs your servant
to remit public levies that can be remitted.
The people feed the post horses;
this service is the most onerous.
Envoys demand a hundred things,
all coming from the families that keep the horses.
Many people abscond;
this is the reason.
It is permissible to re-establish the ‘return horse officials’ as before,
and all provisions for envoys should be supplied by the government.
At the end of the year, accounts can be settled,
〔一三〕 and the tax burden distributed equally among the people.”
He also memorialized:
“There is much uncultivated land in Hénán.
Immigrants from Hédōng and Héběi could be recruited to farm it.
Rent and taxes for disaster-stricken and border-area commanderies and counties should be completely remitted,
and for inland areas, half,
to save the suffering people
and provide for their sustenance.”
An imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to deliberate on its implementation.
Upon his return, he memorialized:
“Although the grain and wheat in Nányáng were damaged,
the soil is suitable for rice.
Now, due to the prolonged rain,
it has become even more luxuriant.
There are altogether over five hundred qǐng of fields,
each畝 can yield five dàn,
totaling over two hundred and fifty thousand dàn.
It is advisable to increase direct rice purchases to supply the armies in Táng and Dèng.
Since the imperial decree states that urgent levies and services should be remitted,
your servant dares not act arbitrarily.
If your majesty deems my words correct,
I beg that it be submitted to the relevant authorities for consideration.”
The emperor approved.
Not long after,
he was ordered to oversee military provisions and fodder.
Fù Hēng memorialized:
“The river crossings are impassable,
and the price of salt in Shǎnxī is soaring.
I request that millet be exchanged for it to supply the soldiers.”
An imperial edict ordered the Hùbù to plan it carefully.
Fù Hēng possessed a talent for accounting
and was renowned as an able official.
At the time, he was highly respected,
and thus rapidly rose to prominence.
Once in power,
he became quite arrogant
and engaged in self-enrichment,
causing his reputation to sharply decline.
In the third month of the fifth year,
Fù Hēng supervised the imperial examination for jinshì.
Fù Hēng supervised the examination.
The jinshì Lú Yuán made errors
and was improperly granted jinshì status.
The examining officials, Lǐbù Shàngshū Zhào Bǐngwén, Hànlín Dàizhì Cuī Xǐ, Guīdé Zhìzhōng Shí Jiǎn, and Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì Chéng Jiāshàn, were to be stripped of three official ranks and demoted,
and Fù Hēng was to be stripped of two official ranks.
Zhào Bǐngwén had previously requested retirement;
Xuānzōng, pitying his old age,
demoted him by two ranks
and allowed him to retire as Lǐbù Shàngshū.
Fù Hēng was dismissed and made Jiéduǒshǐ of Dìngguó Jūn.
〔一四〕In the eleventh month of Yuánguāng first year,
the city fell, and he committed suicide
at the age of forty-six.
He was posthumously granted Zīdé Dàfū and Zhī Hézhōng Fǔ Shì.
The encomium states: Generally, when military campaigns arise, financial resources are insufficient.
Thus, Zhāng Wěi and Lǐ Fùhēng seized the opportunity to profit,
making accumulation their achievement.
During Dà'ān,
soldiers wished to turn their weapons on Wěi and kill him.
Fù Hēng pacified Nányáng
and returned to report that the ripe rice could be purchased.
These two individuals
were what is meant by "officials who accumulate wealth."
Gāo Hóng’s stewardship of resources
is something the junzǐ greatly appreciated.

Chéng Huī, courtesy name Wéimíng,
originally named Fúxīng.
He loved learning and was well-versed in classics and histories.
He inherited his father’s position as Yìdōu Yǐn Zhèngjiātǎ Gēlà Wúmò Mǒkè.
In the fifteenth year of Dàdìng,
he was selected to serve as Fúbǎo Zhǐhòu,
then transferred to Bǐyàn Zhícháng,
then to Jìnsì Jú Zhícháng,
and later transferred to Zhōngdū Yòu Jǐngxún Shǐ.
When Zhāngzōng was the imperial grandson,
he was selected to serve as Shìzhèng.
After Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Jìnsì Jú Shǐ.
The empress Xiàoyì’s brother-in-law, Wúyělán,
had been banished during Shìzōng’s reign for a crime.
One evening,
an imperial edict ordered the palace gate to be opened to summon him.
Chéng Huī did not obey the edict.
The next day, he memorialized:
“Wúyělán offended the late emperor;
he should not be summoned.”
Zhāngzōng said:
“Good.”
Soon after,
he was promoted to Bīngbù Shìláng concurrently with Yòu Bǔquē.
When the nine-circuit Tíxíng Sī were first established,
Chéng Huī served as Tíxíng Fùshǐ for the Dōngjīng Xiánpíng and other circuits,
then was transferred to Tóngzhī Shàngjīng Liúshǒu Shì.
The Yùshǐ Tái memorialized:
“When Chéng Huī was previously Tíxíng,
the powerful and cunning were held in check.”
He was promoted to Línhǎi Jūn Jiéduǒshǐ.
He successively served in Lìshè and Liáohǎi Jūn,
then was promoted to Běijīng Lù Tíxíng Shǐ.
He successively served as Zhī Xiánpíng and Línhuáng Fǔ,
then as Běijīng Liúshǒu.
The Deputy Liúshǒu, Lǐ Dōngyáng, was always highly placed.
Unless it was for public affairs, Chéng Huī
would not exchange a single word with him.
He was transferred to Zhī Dàmíng Fǔ,
then summoned to serve as Xíngbù Shàngshū,
concurrently Zhī Shěn’guān Yuàn.
Yú Lǐhén Dū, Dudū Jiān of the Huìmín Sī, was transferred to Zhīrán Shǔ Zhícháng.
Chéng Huī submitted a dissenting memorial, saying:
“Hén Dū obtained office through patronage
and has no other talents.
Previously, he was a jīchá at Dàyáng Dù.
After only eight months, he was promoted to Dū Dū Jiān of the Huìmín Sī,
which was already excessively generous.
According to regulations, after two such promotions,
he should again be assigned to a supervisory post.
Now, he is exceptionally promoted to an eighth-rank official position in the imperial court.
Furthermore, Hén Dū is the nephew of Píngzhāng Yì,
so this cannot but invite public criticism.”
The emperor followed Chéng Huī’s suggestion
and summoned Túshàn Yì to severely reprimand him.
He was transferred to Zhī Dàxīng Fǔ Shì.
The eunuch Lǐ Xīnxǐ, who was favored and influential,
requested musicians from Dàxīng Fǔ.
Chéng Huī refused to provide them,
and Xīnxǐ was ashamed.
Zhāngzōng heard of this and praised him.
A powerful commoner, in a dispute over irrigation rights for rice fields,
unjustly bribed Lǐ Rénhuì, the empress Yuánfēi’s brother and Zuǒ Xuānwēi Shǐ, with a large sum.
Rénhuì sent someone to ask Chéng Huī to rule in his favor.
Chéng Huī immediately flogged the powerful commoner and dismissed him,
telling the messenger:
“You can report this to the Xuānwēi.”
He was again transferred to Zhī Dàmíng Fǔ Shì.
When heavy rain damaged the crops,
Chéng Huī decided to divert the floodwaters into the moats and canals.
When the campaign against Sòng began,
he was promoted to Shāndōng Lù Tǒngjūn Shǐ.
Bandits arose in Shāndōng,
and Chéng Huī said:
“If bandits are not immediately apprehended,
by the time a report is made, officials may have been promoted or transferred.
I request the authority to execute them summarily.”
The Shàngshū Shěng deliberated:
“Měng'ān should continue to handle ransoms as before,
Mǒkè should report,
while other qiánxiá, dūjūnxún, and wèishì may execute first and then report,
and revert to the old system after order is restored.”
This was approved.
When the military campaign ceased,
the bandit leaders gradually surrendered.
However, they still often hid in the caves and crevices of Mount Tài.
The Ànchá Sī requested that tens of thousands of people be dispatched to clear the forests,
so that the bandits would have nowhere to hide.
Chéng Huī memorialized:
“Mount Tài is the foremost of the Five Sacred Mountains,
hence it is called Dàizōng.
When kings receive the Mandate of Heaven,
they perform the fēngshàn sacrifices to announce their succession.
Although our state does not perform this ritual,
the mountain should not be stripped bare.
The people of Qí are easily agitated.
Driving them into the mountains
will certainly lead to suffering from cold, hunger, and displacement.
This would encourage banditry, not stop it.
There are many mountains in the world;
how can they all be stripped bare?”
The proposal was subsequently dropped.
Jìnzhōng and Gāo Qí had always been at odds.
He suspected Xuānzōng was rather distant from him,
and Gāo Qí created estrangement between them.
His elder brother, Wūlǐyě, was the Supervisor of Wine in Xǔzhōu.
After his term expired,
he sought transfer to Nánjīng.
Jìnzhōng spoke with Wūlǐyě about matters in Zhōngdū,
saying:
"Recently, the Emperor has been rather distant from me.
This is Gāo Qí's doing.
If I were to lead the troops again,
I would certainly not tolerate this.
Who would undertake the task of Húshāhǔ's affair then!"
Wūlǐyě said:
"Indeed."
In the ninth month,
the Shàngshūshěng reported:
"Túshān Wúdiǎn, who was nominally granted the title of Deputy Military Commissioner of Wǔníng Circuit, has accused Jìnzhōng of plotting rebellion."
The Emperor sighed and said:
"What have I done to displease Tǔduō?
When he abandoned Zhōngdū,
he disregarded all the ancestral imperial portraits and the imperial consorts in the Dàolíng mausoleum,
coming only with his concubine.
This itself is a crime."
So he ordered the relevant authorities to interrogate and investigate.
It was found that he had spoken of these matters with his elder brother Wūlǐyě,
and consequently, both he and Wūlǐyě were executed.
Púsàn Duān, whose original name was Qīyīn,
was a man from the Huǒlǔhǔ Bìlà Mèng'ān of Zhōngdū Circuit.
He was filial to his parents and was selected to serve as a guard.

He was appointed Crown Prince's Chief Usher, Chief Clerk of the Téngwáng Mansion, Commander of the Imperial Guard, Prefect of Pīzhōu, Deputy Commissioner of the Imperial Workshop, and General of the Right Guard.
Upon Zhāngzōng's ascension,
he was transferred to the Left Guard.
During Zhāngzōng's reign, at the Lóngqìnggōng palace,
guard Huāgǒu intercepted the imperial carriage and made a statement:
"Duān's paternal uncle Húdú participated in the assassination of Hǎilíng.
Duān should not be among the imperial guards."
An edict ordered Huāgǒu to be flogged sixty times,
and the person who drafted the memorial on his behalf to be flogged fifty times.
After observing mourning for his parent,
he was recalled to office as Deputy Pacification Commissioner for the Northeast Circuit.
He was then reassigned as Deputy Left Inspector,
promoted to Grand Inspector,
and successively served as Military Commissioner for Hénán and Shǎnxī.
He was again recalled to serve as Grand Inspector.
In the fourth year of Chéng'ān,
the Emperor went to Jìzhōu for an autumn hunt.
Duān accidentally shot a deer that had entered the imperial hunting ground,
for which he was flogged
and dismissed from office.
In the third year of Tàihé,
he was reinstated as Censor-in-Chief.
The following year,
he was appointed Left Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
an edict ordered high officials to deliberate on an expedition against Sòng.
All said there was nothing to worry about.
Left Chancellor Zōng Hào and Co-administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs Jiǎ Xuàn also said:
"These are mere dog-thieves and rat-pilferers;
it is not a full-scale military mobilization."
Duān said:
"Petty bandits hide by day and come out by night.
How could they dare to openly array their forces in broad daylight,
assault Língbì, enter Wōkǒu, and attack Shòuchūn?
These Sòng people intend to mislead us through various means.
If we do not make preparations early,
once they launch a major invasion,
we will fall into their trap."
The Emperor deeply agreed with this.
Not long after,
he went into mourning for his mother,
and was recalled to office as Left Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
Púsàn Kuí, a Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs, launched an expedition against Sòng,
dispatching troops from Nánjīng.
An edict ordered Duān to oversee the traveling provincial administration
and manage affairs in his absence.
Púsàn Kuí had already crossed the Huái River
and reached Lúzhōu.
The Sòng envoy Huángfǔ Gǒng presented a letter requesting peace,
and Duān reported the letter to the throne.
The court deliberated that since the troops from various circuits had already advanced,
they suspected Sòng was using a stratagem to delay the army.
An edict ordered Duān to send Gǒng back to Sòng.
In the seventh year,
Púsàn Kuí returned the army due to summer rains,
and Duān returned to court.
Earlier,
a woman named Ālǔbù, married to a soldier of the Wǔwèijūn,
bore two daughters and then became a widow.
She often claimed to speak in dreams to delude the masses,
and her predictions were often accurate,
so some considered her divine.
She then claimed that in her dreams she repeatedly saw a white-haired old man who pointed to her two daughters and said:
"They are both blessed individuals.
If they serve in the imperial inner court,
they will surely bear imperial heirs."
At that time,
Zhāngzōng had been on the throne for a long time,
but no imperial prince had been established.
Duān requested that they be taken into the palace.
Zhāngzōng agreed.
Subsequently, the capital suffered a long drought.
Ālǔbù again claimed:
"I dreamed that the white-haired old man sent me to pray for rain,
and within three days there would surely be abundant rainfall."
After three days, no rain fell.
Zhāngzōng suspected her of being deceitful and boastful,
and sent her to the relevant authorities for interrogation.
Ālǔbù confessed.
An edict reproached Duān, saying:
"What about what you previously memorialized?
How is it now?
Later generations will say that I believed in her outlandish claims.
In reality, it was you who initiated this matter,
causing distress in my heart.
It is difficult to put aside the thought of it.
You should reflect on your past fault
and think of how to make good amends in the future.
Rectify your heart diligently
to match my intentions!"
Duān submitted a memorial to await punishment,
but an edict released him without questioning.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs
and enfeoffed as Duke of Shēn.
In the eighth year,
the Sòng people requested an alliance,
and Duān was promoted one rank.
Zhāngzōng's last will stated:
"There are two palace women who are pregnant.
If they give birth to a son, he shall be established as the heir."
Upon Wèi Shàowáng's ascension,
he ordered Duān and Left Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs Sūn Jíkāng to oversee the pregnant palace women of Zhāngzōng.
On the twentieth day of the eleventh month of the eighth year of Tàihé,
Zhāngzōng died.
On the twenty-second day,
Deputy Imperial Physician Yí Shīyán reported:
"It is diagnosed that Consort Fàn's fetal qi is damaged."
In the fourth month of the following year,
someone accused Primary Consort Lǐ of instructing Cchéngyù Jiǎ to falsely claim pregnancy.
Both the Primary Consort and the Chéngyù were executed.
Duān was promoted to Right Chancellor
and granted a hereditary Móukè.
In the fifth month of the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he served as Acting Nánjīng Prefect,
and together with the Hénán Military Commissioner Chángshòu and the Surveillance and Transport Commissioner Wáng Zhì, memorialized three times to request the move of the capital south.
Xuānzōng's intention was finally decided.
All officials, scholars, and common people deemed it impossible.
Four hundred Imperial Academy students, including Zhào Fǎng, submitted a memorial vigorously arguing the pros and cons.
Xuānzōng comforted and dismissed them,
and then issued an edict to relocate the capital.
The following year,
Zhōngdū fell.
When Xuānzōng arrived in Nánjīng,
he appointed Duān as the Prefect of Kāifēng.
Shortly thereafter,
he became Censor-in-Chief.
Not long after,
he was appointed Left Chancellor of the Department of State Affairs.
In the third year,
he concurrently served as Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Not long after,
he was promoted to concurrently serve as Commissioner of Military Affairs.
A few months later,
as Left Chancellor, he concurrently served as Grand Marshal and Governor of Shǎnxī Province,
provided with thirty imperial guards and three hundred cavalry as an escort.
His second son, Commander of the Imperial Guard Nàtǎn, accompanied him on the expedition.
He was granted an imperial decree that read:
"In times of urgency or need, use this to summon you."
Duān summoned Wányán Gǒugér, who nominally held the title of Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎn Circuit, to return immediately,
and reported his transfer to serve as Prefect of Píngliáng.
When the generals heard this,
all were deeply moved.

He dispatched Nàlán Bànzēng to persuade and recruit the chiefs of the five tribes of Gūlí in Líntáo, Qīngjuér, the chief of Zhāngluó Yèlán Dōng of Jīshízhōu, the chief of the Duóyīng tribe Ālíngjié, and the chief of the Pā'é tribe Wāng Sānláng of Lánzhōu,
all of whom subsequently submitted.
Wāng Sānláng was granted the surname Wányán and later became a famous general in the west.
Four years later,
due to illness, he requested to retire from office,
but it was not permitted.
The emperor sent close attendants with imperial physicians to examine him.
Although Duān was old and infirm,
whenever imperial envoys arrived, he would always go far to greet them,
and would entertain and console them tirelessly.
Thus, slanderous accusations against him failed to take effect.
Xuānzōng heard of this
and issued an edict stating that from then on, a special envoy could have three rounds of wine and then bid farewell at the Yímén gate.
Those passing through for other matters should be seen once and then dismissed.
Initially,
the old garrisons of Tóng and Huá, consisting of over nine thousand troops from Shǎnxī and infantry and cavalry from Hénán,
were all subordinate to Yǒngxī, the Deputy Pacification Commissioner of Shǎnzhōu.
Duān memorialized:
"West of Tóngguān
is all Shǎnxī territory.
I request that these troops be subordinate to the Xíngshěng,
so they can be deployed in times of urgency."
The imperial court followed his advice.
When the army of Dàyuán entered Tóngguān,
Yǒngxī was executed for his offense,
but the blame did not extend to Duān.
In Xīngdìng元年 (1216),
the imperial court appointed Chéngyì, the Zhī Líntáofǔshì, as the Yuánshuài Zuǒdōujiān,
to establish the Yuánshuàifǔ in Fèngxiáng.
Duān memorialized:
"The ten prefectures beyond Lǒng,
situated between Sòng and Xià,
and intermingled with various barbarian tribes,
previously had a Yuánshuàifǔ established in Gǒngzhōu to guard them.
Now Chéngyì is moving the ten thousand troops from beyond Lǒng to Fèngxiáng.
I fear that should an alarm suddenly arise,
reinforcements would not arrive in time.
I humbly request that Chéngyì establish the Yuánshuàifǔ in Gǒngzhōu.
If it is argued that Fèngxiáng is close to the Sòng border,
then there are already many troops garrisoned in that circuit.
It would suffice to merely have the Zǒngguǎn temporarily act as commander,
coordinating with Jīngzhào and Gǒng as head and tail,
to be prepared for any emergency."
His advice was followed.
That year,
he passed away.
Upon hearing the news,
Xuānzōng was greatly saddened,
and suspended court.
He was posthumously granted the title of Yán'ān Jùnwáng
and the posthumous name Zhōngzhèng.
In Zhèngdà三年 (1226),
he was accorded a place in Xuānzōng's ancestral temple.
His son, Nàtǎnchū, served as the Dìngguójūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the eleventh month of Tiānxīng元年 (1232),
Nàtǎnchū's son, Mángyāmén, drank with his elder brother Shílǐmén and bodyguard Yánzhǎn Zōng'ā.
Mángyāmén deceptively went out on a pretext and defected to the northern army.
The Xíngshěng ordered Zhào Nán, a Lángzhōng of the Xíngbù, to investigate his family and those who drank with him.
At that time, officials both high and low sought to curry favor,
insisting on treating them as complicit,
even Mángyāmén's wife was interrogated and tortured.
His mother, Wányán Shì, said:
"Mángyāmén had an affair with his father's concubine.
His father killed this concubine,
and Mángyāmén felt unsafe,
so he rebelled,
only seeking to escape with his life."
After thorough investigation,
there was no evidence of complicity.
The Xíngshěng subtly heard of this,
and summoned the minor official Guō Cónggé to convey the hint,
and Cónggé spoke of it.
Nán, who was eating,
threw his chopsticks and spoon onto the table,
and declared loudly:
"I would rather Zhào Nán be dismissed from office
than wrongfully convict innocent people!"
He then memorialized that they were not complicit,
and also reported the matter of the concubine.
The Emperor said:
"The Chancellor is a meritorious official,
and Nàtǎnchū and his son have both received imperial favor.
I already vouched for their innocence."
He immediately ordered their release.
Nán, courtesy name Cáiměi,
was a Jinshì
from Gāopíng.
Gěng Duānyì, courtesy name Zhōngsì,
was from Bópíng, Bózhōu.
He attained the Jinshì degree in Dàdìng二十八年 (1188).
He was appointed Jūnshì Pànguān of Huázhōu,
then served as Lìng of Shàngluò County,
Pànguān of Ānhuà and Shùnyì Jūn Jiédù,
was appointed Lìngshǐ of the Shàngshūshěng,
and then Deputy Jiédùshǐ of Fényáng Jūn.
He was transferred to the Hùjí Pànguān of the Dū Zhuǎnyùnsī,
then promoted to Tàicháng Bóshì,
then to Tàicháng Chéng concurrently Bìshū Láng,
then again appointed Yuánwàiláng of Zuǒsī,
and successively held the positions of Tàicháng Shàocīng concurrently Lìbù Yuánwàiláng,
jointly compiled the Guóshǐ,
Hùbù Lángzhōng,
Deputy Àncháshǐ of Héběi Dōnglù,
Tóngzhī Dōngpíngfǔshì,
and was appointed Shāndōng Ānfǔshǐ.
Xuānzōng had governed Fényáng Jūn,
and at that time Duānyì was his deputy.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he summoned him,
inquired about current affairs,
and promoted him to Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì concurrently Hùbù Shìláng.
Not long after,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
In Zhēnyòu二年 (1214),
when Zhōngdū was besieged,
the generals and commanders were all unwilling to fight.
Duānyì memorialized:
"Today's calamity
was initiated by Wèiwáng.
Even if the common soldiers cannot be mobilized,
there are no fewer than ten thousand military officers in the city, from Dūtǒng down to Móukè.
If we send these people out for a single sortie,
we might yet succeed."
The proposal was ultimately not implemented.
When Zhōngdū was relieved from siege,
Duānyì requested a move to Nánjīng.
Later, Púsàn Duān submitted three memorials, all advocating the relocation of the capital,
and Xuānzōng's resolve was thus firm.
That year,
he passed away.
Xuānzōng suspended court,
bestowed generous funeral gifts,
and sent an envoy to offer sacrifices and preside over the burial.
Lǐ Yīng, courtesy name Zǐxián,
was originally from Liáoyáng,
then moved to Yìdū.
He passed the Jinshì examination in Míngchāng五年 (1194),
and was appointed Zhǔbù of Chúnhuà, Jūnshì Pànguān of Dēngzhōu, and Lìng of Fēngqiū.
After his father's mourning,
when the mourning period was over,
he was appointed Lìng of Tōngyuǎn.
When barbarian tribes took people's property without payment,
and failed to appear when summoned,
he would arrest them
and judge them according to the law.
He was appointed Lìngshǐ of the Shàngshūshěng.
In Dà'ān三年 (1211),
when officials of the third rank and above were assembled to discuss military affairs,
Yīng submitted a memorial stating:
"For military campaigns, one must employ those who are skilled.
Shùhǔ Gāoqí, Wūgǔsūn Wùtún, Nàlán ●tóu, and Mòniǎn Jìnzhōng were all previously employed by the former emperor,
and can be consulted.
The others are numerous and chaotic,
and might jeopardize the grand strategy."
He also said:
"Recently, cities and walls have been strengthened,
and watchtowers repaired,
the situation is evident.
If Shāndōng and Héběi do not sufficiently extend their support,
then the capital will become an isolated city."
No reply was given.
He was appointed Zhǔshì of the Lìbù.
At the beginning of Zhēnyòu,
he served as acting Dōushì of Zuǒsī,
then was promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
The Right Deputy Marshal, Shùhǔ Gāoqí, appointed him Jīnglìguān,
whereupon he wrote to Gāoqí:
"Jūyōng for Zhōngdū
is like Xiáo and Hán for Qín,
or Jiànmén for Shǔ.
Recently, the Jūyōng troops were withdrawn,
and our strategic position was lost.
Now local strongmen guard it.
The imperial court should send an official to command them.
If this opportunity is missed,
loyal and righteous individuals
will turn to other sides."
He also said:
"The remaining people of Xuāndé and Déxīng should be pacified and comforted,
and encouraged to join the army.
There are existing stores of provisions in those areas,
sufficient for their needs.
Thus, the state would not spend a measure of grain or a foot of silk,
yet would recover the lost passes.
Jūyōng, so close,
is the northern gate of the capital,
and to be unable to defend it,
Yīng truly considers it a disgrace."
Gāoqí memorialized his letter,
and he was immediately appointed Yuánwàiláng of the Shàngshū Gōngbù,
and then appointed Xuānchāi Dūtíkòng,
with Jūyōng and other passes all subordinate to him.
That year, in the tenth month,
the army moved to Lúshì,
and [Wányán] Zhòngyuán was made Jīnglüèshǐ of Shāngzhōu,
acting as the Right Dūjiān of the Yuánshuài.
An imperial edict stated:
"Shāng, Guó, and Tóngguān
are truly interconnected.
You should devise a plan for complete security."
Not long after,
Tóngguān fell.
Zhòngyuán's army hastened to Shāng and Guó,
then again to Sōng and Rǔ,
but failed to arrive in time.
Zhòngyuán submitted a memorial, stating:
"In the sixth month of last year,
your servant once petitioned the court,
requesting the selection of a renowned general to command the various armies,
while your servant would lead the charge,
personally going before the soldiers.
As provisions were insufficient,
it was ultimately not carried out.
Now, if we are to sit in armor awaiting the enemy,
then the army will be weary and finances depleted,
daily moving towards distress and ruin."
The general idea was to attack Xīxià to strengthen military might.
He also said:
"The entire Shǎnxī route is the most crucial area.
Tóngguān, Jìnkēng, and the various strategic passes of Shāngzhōu must all be prepared in advance.
Previously, Zhōngdū,
and Jūyōng were the most vital points,
yet they were bypassed via Xiǎolǐng and Zǐjīng,
our army was attacked from front and rear,
and ultimately could not hold.
Recently, they came out through Jìnkēng,
and Tóngguān was lost.
Elite troops should be selected and stationed to guard these areas."
Afterward, defensive positions were established at Qín and Lán,
and troops were deployed against Xīxià.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he was again made Jīnglüèshǐ of Dānzhōu.
He defeated two thousand Sòng people at Guīshān,
again defeated over a thousand infantry and cavalry at Xūyí,
and defeated the Hóng'ǎo at Báilǐgǎng,
capturing over ten thousand old and young people,
all of whom he released.
When the Sòng people besieged Hǎizhōu,
Zhòngyuán's army was at Gāoqiáo.
He ordered Tíkòng Wányán Ālín to lead cavalry to flank them from the rear and attack from both sides.
The Sòng troops dispersed.
He was bestowed a golden belt
and a gracious imperial edict of commendation.
The Hóng'ǎo bandits captured Cáomǎchéng,
and plundered the area between Xú and Dān.
Tíkòng Gāo Wǎn and others divided their troops to attack them,
capturing two thousand commoners.
In the third year,
Zhòngyuán memorialized:
"The prefectural city is now secure,
twenty thousand shí of grain have been accumulated,
and over ten thousand local volunteers have been assembled,
all of whom are undergoing regular training.
This is sufficient for defense.
I request to lead my unit across the river."
An edict ordered him to garrison Xùzhōu,
and to jointly manage the Yuánshuài Fǔ affairs with Right Dūjiān Hélìshí Liè Dé.
Zhòngyuán had a leg ailment;
after a hundred days,
an edict stated:
"You are to manage urgent affairs and pacify and retain the generals and soldiers.
Lǐ Xīn may be sent to lead the troops."
In the fourth year,
he concurrently held the title of Jiédùshǐ of Bǎojìng Jūn,
and soon after was made Quànnóngshǐ.
In the fifth year,
he was made Zhènnán Jiédùshǐ.
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
he was made Zhī Fèngxiáng Fǔ Shì.
When Fèngxiáng was besieged,
Left Jiānjūn Shízhǎn Héxǐ came with relief troops.
Zhòngyuán yielded command of all military affairs to Héxǐ.
Héxǐ said:
"You have always enjoyed the trust of the masses;
there is no need to yield based on official position."
Zhòngyuán requested to lead the charge personally,
and instructed his generals and soldiers, saying:
"Whoever achieves extraordinary merit
will be promoted exceptionally by imperial decree."
In times of crisis,
he would immediately promote to the fourth rank and below.
Yánzhǎn Xiāwǎn [蝦●] fought with the greatest valor,
and was immediately appointed Jiédùshǐ of Tōngyuǎn Jūn.
After the siege was lifted,
he memorialized requesting punishment for unauthorized appointments.
Xuānzōng commended his achievements
and granted all his requests.
He was promoted to Right Jiānjūn of the Yuánshuài,
appointed Táowěibìlàméng'ān of Hébĕidōng Lù,
bestowed fifty liǎng of gold, fifteen duān of fine silks, and a tōngxī belt,
with a gracious imperial edict of praise and commendation.
During the Zhèngdà period,
he served as Bīngbù Shàngshū
and Wèiwèi to the Empress Dowager,
and then passed away.
As a general, Zhòngyuán
was resolute and resourceful;
after the southward migration, he was widely acclaimed as a renowned general.
Wányán Ālín's original surname was Guō;
he was granted the surname Wányán for his achievements.
During the Dà'ān period,
Lǐ Xióng recruited soldiers,
and Ālín, along with Wányán Zhòngyuán and others, enlisted,
achieving numerous merits.
Upon Xuānzōng's ascension,
he was promoted to Fángyùshǐ of Tōngzhōu.
When Xuānzōng moved to Biàn,
Ālín was reappointed Tóngzhī Héjiān Fǔ Shì concurrently Fángyùshǐ of Qīngzhōu,
leading his troops to garrison Qīng and Cāng,
controlling Shāndōng.
He was promoted to Jiédùshǐ of Hénghǎi Jūn
and bestowed the imperial surname.
Ālín and the Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ of Shāndōng Lù, Yánzhǎn Tiānzé, were not on good terms.
An edict instructed Ālín to cooperate with Tiānzé in state affairs,
without holding partial views
or drawing distinctions between themselves.
Soon after, he was reappointed Jiédùshǐ of Tàidìng Jūn and Xuānfǔshǐ of Shāndōngxī Lù.
At this time,
Zhòngyuán had also accumulated merits,
was Zhī Jìnán Fǔ,
and was bestowed the surname Wányán.
Both he and Ālín were promoted to Cóngyí Zhāofǔshǐ.
An imperial edict commended them
and ordered them to coordinate with the army of Zhuōzhōu Cǐshǐ Cóng Tǎn and others to recover Zhōngdū.
Thus,
the troops under Zhòngyuán and Ālín were excessively numerous.
An edict ordered them to be classified into three ranks:
the upper rank for punitive expeditions,
the middle and lower for garrison duty,
and the weak and cowardly to be dismissed,
with land allotted to support their families.
Ālín's unit,
the "Huánghè Xiù Jūn,"
stationed at Yútái,
was unruly and lawless,
plundering commoners
and robbing merchants,
making roads impassable.
Officials requested their relocation to Téngzhōu.
An edict ordered Ālín to deal with it himself.
Shortly thereafter,
he defeated the Hóng'ǎo bandit Hǎo Dìng at Zhégōu Cūn in Sīshuǐ Xiàn,
captured Hǎo Dìng alive,
and sent him to the capital to be executed.
According to recent regulations,
those granted the imperial surname
who defeated three thousand enemies with a thousand men were allowed to extend the privilege to their relatives of sīmá (mourning) or higher;
those who defeated over two thousand enemies to their relatives of dàgōng (mourning) or higher;
and those who defeated over a thousand enemies only to their immediate family.
After Ālín was granted the surname,
he requested it for his elder brother Shǒu Jí and his paternal cousins.
The prime minister memorialized that Ālín's merit only warranted the grant for his immediate family,
but Xuānzōng issued a special edict granting it.
At this point, Zhòngyuán memorialized:
"When your servant was recently in the army,
I merely rendered a small service,
and immediately received imperial grace,
being granted the imperial surname,
which your servant cannot repay even by sacrificing his life.
My clan brother Xúzhōu Jīchá Fùshǐ Sēng Xǐ,
former Fénzhōu Jiǔ Tóng Jiān Sān Xǐ, former Jiězhōu Yán Guǎngōu Tiān Zhāng, and Shǒuxīngpíng Xiàn Jiān Jiǔ Tiān Fú still bear the surname Guō.
Considering that your servant and Sēng Xǐ and others were once of the same family,
but are now two clans,
and Wányán Ālín shared the same merit as your servant,
and imperial grace was extended to his entire clan,
I request that Sēng Xǐ and the other four persons be treated according to this precedent."
This was not granted.
He was reappointed Jīnglüèshǐ of Huīzhōu.
In the early Zhēnyòu reign,
the Directorate-Generals for Military Affairs of the Eastern and Western Fronts were established.
He was appointed Director-General for Military Affairs of the Western Front.
He memorialized, saying:
“The various passes of Dàhé Lǐng within my jurisdiction are garrisoned with troops
to control strategic border points.
The Acting Grand Marshal's Office has arbitrarily detached twelve thousand of my troops to garrison Zhēndìng,
leaving insufficient numbers for defense.
Recently, another two thousand seven hundred elite soldiers were selected and sent there.
Now, the active troops number less than ten thousand,
and seventeen or eighteen tenths of them are old and weak.
My death is certainly not to be regretted,
but the affairs of the state must not be disregarded.
The newly established Directorate-General of Military Affairs has sent dispatches to Xīyīng, Tàiyuán, and Hédōng to request troops and horses,
but the large numbers all claim not to be under my command.”
An imperial edict ordered the Zhēndìng Grand Marshal's Office to return the two thousand seven hundred elite soldiers.
If there were urgent alarms in Xīyīng, Tàiyuán, or Lánzhōu,
they were to agree to provide assistance.
As the prefectures and commanderies were all unwilling to be subordinate to the Directorate-General for Military Affairs,
the office of Director-General of Military Affairs was abolished.
He entered the government as a Signatory to the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and was then made Left Vice Grand Inspector.
In the fourth year (1216),
he was promoted to Minister of War.
In the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
he retired.
In the fourth year (1220),
he died.
Jiágǔ Shílǐgē
was a *méng'ān* from the Shàngjīng Circuit.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the fifth year of Míngchāng (1194).
He served as a Defense Adjutant in Tàizhōu,
then was appointed Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
and successively served as General Administrator and Adjutant in Línhuáng and Pósu Tàolù.
He was repeatedly promoted to Principal of the Ministry of Justice,
and then appointed Vice Controller of Jìzhōu,
stationing his troops in Dàmíng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Academician of the Hànlín Academy and Attendant,
and made Controller of Sùzhōu.
Together with Wányán Bì, the Pacification Commissioner of Shāndōng, he attacked Dàmògū.
Over a thousand bandits resisted,
but Shílǐgē attacked them with cavalry,
annihilating them completely.
Controller Mòliè entered through the north gate,
and subsequently captured Liú Èrzǔ.
For this achievement, he was promoted to Vice Deputy Commander of the Wǔwèi Army.
He was impeached for having previously plundered commoners for slaves in Sùzhōu,
and was subject to the death penalty.
An imperial edict specifically ordered a punishment of eighty strokes of the cane.
He was then transferred to serve as Defense Commissioner of Míngzhōu and Deputy Commander of the Shāndōng Circuit.
He was impeached for not advancing his troops in time
and for going to Sùqiān to fetch his wife and children.
[一０]He was dismissed from his post.
He was re-appointed as Controller of the Eastern Expeditionary Army.
In the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
he defeated Sòng troops in Sùzhōu.
For this achievement, he was remotely granted the title of Military Commissioner of Ānhuà Commandery,
and then transferred to Dìnghǎi Commandery,
where he died.
Shújǐa Chénjiā
was a *méng'ān* from the Běijīng Circuit.
He inherited his father's *móu kě* position.
During the Tàihé campaign against Sòng,
he served under Wányán Gāng in Shǎnxī.
He successively served as Associate Prefect of Tōngzhōu and Hǎizhōu.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
he was appointed Assistant of the Bureau of Military Provisions.
He gained merit in rescuing Jíníng,
and was promoted to Adjutant of the Hénán Commander, Vice Deputy Commander of the Gǒngwèi Guard, and Administrator of Hénán.
He was remotely granted the title of Prefect of Suízhōu and concurrently Administrator of Yán'ān.
He was then promoted to Associate Prefect,
and later made Associate Prefect of Héjiān Prefecture.
In the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
the Bureau of Military Affairs operated in Shòuzhōu,
and from Shòu and Sì, they crossed the Huái River to attack Sòng.
In the second month of the second year (1218),
he defeated three thousand Sòng troops at Jiànhú Tān,
[一一]beheading three hundred.
An imperial edict ordered them to ravage the Sòng borderlands,
but not to advance too deeply.
Chénjiā stationed his troops at Zhāgāng Cūn in Huòqiū,
and dispatched light cavalry to raid and plunder,
burning down stored provisions.
He captured a Sòng spy, Zhāng Cōng,
who revealed that two thousand Sòng troops were encamped at Gāoliǔ Qiáo,
with many old people and children.
Their encampment had two walled towns,
surrounded by water.
Chénjiā sent Zhāng Cōng with a document to summon them to surrender,
but they refused.
He first ordered the naval forces to cross directly and attack.
The soldier Niú Qīng wielded his spear and stabbed the gate guards,
who all broke ranks and fled.
They then scaled the ramparts,
and the main army followed,
leveling their encampment before returning.
They encountered several thousand Sòng troops at Méijǐng Cūn.
Chénjiā concealed troops in the forest,
and used infantry to lure them out.
When the ambush was sprung,
the Sòng army was routed.
They pursued the fleeing enemy for over ten *lǐ*,
capturing their general Ruǎn Shì'ān and four others,
and seizing numerous weapons.
In the seventh month,
in recognition of his achievements in the southern campaign,
[一二]his rank was raised by one grade,
and he was promoted to Right Grand Commander of the Marshal's Office,
serving as Councillor to the Shǎnxī Branch Secretariat.
In the fourth year (1220),
he concurrently held the position of Military Commissioner of Jīn'ān Commandery.
In the fifth year (1221),
he was made Prefect of Yán'ān,
and then transferred to Left Grand Commander,
stationing his troops in Jīngzhào.
In the first year of Yuánguāng (1222),
he died.
Gēshíliè Huánduān
was a *méng'ān* from Hūlùn Sònggē in the Xīnán Circuit.
He inherited his elder brother Yínzhúkě's *móu kě* position.
During the Tàihé campaign against Sòng,
he served as an Expeditionary Army Commander of Ten Thousand.
He defeated two thousand Sòng troops at Càizhōu,
and was awarded the title of Xuānwǔ General.
Crossing the Huái River from Shòuzhōu,
he defeated fifteen thousand Sòng infantry and cavalry at Yàozǐ Lǐng,
and subsequently captured Ānfēng Commandery.
Upon his army's return,
he was appointed Associate Military Commissioner of Huáiyuǎn Commandery,
and Acting *Mùdiǎn Cíxiángwěn*.
In the third year of Dà'ān (1211),
he was selected by the Xīyīng Branch Secretariat as a Hezha Commander of Ten Thousand.
He was remotely granted the title of Associate Defense Commissioner of Qīngzhōu,
then appointed Vice Military Commissioner of Xīngpíng Commandery,
remotely granted the title of Vice Military Commissioner of Xiǎndé Commandery,
and transferred to Commander-in-Chief of the Liáodōng Circuit Pacification Commission.
[一三]He defeated Yílà Liúgē's fifteen thousand troops at Yùhé Zhài,
seizing several thousand carts
and accepting the surrender of over ten thousand people.
He was awarded the title of Cavalry and Guard Grand General,
and remotely granted the title of Associate Military Commissioner of Shùntiān Commandery.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
he was appointed Provisional Vice Controller,
Associate Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry of Pósu Circuit,
and Acting Prefect.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu (1215),
Púxiān Wànnú captured Xiánpíng, Dōngjīng Shěn, Chéng, and other prefectures,
and many *méng'ān* and *móu kě* also followed him.
In the third month,
Wànnú's nine thousand infantry and cavalry invaded the vicinity of Pósu.
Huánduān dispatched Commander Wēndíhǎn Pàgē Niǎn to attack and repulse them.
In the fourth month,
they again plundered Shàngjīng City.
[一四]He dispatched Commander Wūyán Bōxiá to resist the attack.
Wànnú separately sent five thousand men to attack Wàngyún Yì.
Commander Àotún Mǎhéshàng attacked them.
Commander Jiágǔ Hébò routed several thousand of their troops at Sānchā Lǐ.
In the fifth month,
Commander Wēndíhǎn Fúshòu attacked Wànnú's forces at Dàníng Zhèn,
capturing their stronghold,
and their troops were annihilated.
In the ninth month,
Wànnú's nine thousand troops emerged from Yífēng and Tāngchí.
Huánduān led his troops to battle them,
and Wànnú's forces broke and fled.
Consequently, he recruited the eleven *méng'ān* of Ānjíwò, Dūmáhún, Bīngē, Chūtái, Dá'ài, Yángē, Bùhuī, Huózhuō, Ànchū, Bóde, and Lièlín to rejoin them.
He selected their able-bodied men to replenish the army,
and attacked the cities and towns that had not yet been subjugated.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu (1216),
Huánduān dispatched Wáng Rǔbì to report on affairs by sea.
Xuānzōng commended his achievements.
Huánduān was promoted to Military Commissioner of Liáohǎi Commandery and Associate Prefect,
while his position as Provisional Controller remained unchanged.
Wēndíhǎn Gēbù'ǎi, the hereditary *méng'ān* of Pósu Circuit and Acting Associate Prefect, was promoted to Military Commissioner of Xiǎndé Commandery,
and concurrently Administrator of Pósu Prefecture.
Péimǎn Àndài, the Acting Adjutant and former Compiler of the Diaries of Activity and Repose, was promoted two ranks
and two grades.
Wáng Rǔbì was promoted four ranks
and four grades.
For other officers and soldiers who had distinguished themselves,
an imperial edict ordered the Liáodōng Pacification Commissioner to grant promotions and rewards according to his authority.
In this year,
he was made Prefect of Pīzhōu,
and concurrently served as Commander-in-Chief of the Xúzhōu border region.
The Red Jacket rebels, numbering several tens of thousands, attacked Pīzhōu.
Huán Duān defeated them at Huángshān.
The rebels returned.
Huán Duān pressed upon their camp,
forcing them to flee and secure Běishān.
He pursued and defeated them,
with a great number drowning in the Yíshuǐ River.
Tens of thousands of rebels besieged Yízhōu.
The Co-Administrator of Defense Affairs, Púsàn Sāhé, broke through the siege to seek rescue.
Huán Duān led troops to assist him.
Sāhé returned to Yízhōu,
and, together with Huán Duān, attacked the rebels from both inside and outside,
killing over ten thousand people.
The rebels then departed.
The Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs, Púsàn Ānzhēn, reported their accomplishments,
and then memorialized, saying:
“Huán Duān is naturally loyal and honest,
with deep strategic planning,
and is skilled in military affairs.
Sāhé is brave and resourceful.
Both have won the hearts of the military and the people.
I beg that they be promoted and employed.”
Huán Duān was advanced to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
concurrently serving as Co-Administrator of Wǔníngjūn Military Governorship Affairs,
with his command authority remaining as before.
He was summoned to be the Vice Envoy for Agricultural Promotion,
and appointed as the Grand Commissioner of Command,
stationed in Chénzhōu.
In Xīngdìng First Year (1216),
he crossed the Huái River from Xīnxī to attack the Sòng,
defeated Zhōngdùdiàn,
and reached Dìngchéng.
He used a small force to strike a larger one,
fighting relentlessly.
Before long,
he was appointed as an Envoy and Counselor,
and again crossed the Huái River,
repeatedly defeating Sòng forces,
and capturing their general Shěn Jùn.
He was promoted to Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Wǔwèijūn Army.
The Sòng people held their fortified cities and did not sally forth,
so he divided his troops to attack their mountain strongholds and water forts,
killing and capturing many.
In Xīngdìng Second Year (1217),
he was promoted to Military Governor of Zhènnánjūn,
and provisionally served as Right Grand Commissioner of the Marshal’s Office.
A few months later,
he was reappointed as Commander-in-Chief of the Wǔwèijūn Army,
still provisionally serving as Right Grand Commissioner,
operating the Marshal’s Office from Xīzhōu.
The acting Bureau of Military Affairs in Xúzhōu, Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, was obstinate and self-willed,
so an imperial edict ordered Huán Duān, with his original office, to provisionally serve as a Commissioner of Military Affairs,
to go and replace him.
In the winter of the Fourth Year (1219),
he memorialized, saying:
“I secretly hear that the Sòng people and Lǐ Quán’s generals will combine their forces to attack.
We should prepare defenses in advance.”
The Bureau of Military Affairs approved the memorial.
Huán Duān was summoned to discuss the matter face-to-face with court officials.
Soon after, he fell ill,
and was granted imperial medicine from the Grand Physician.
In the first month of the Fifth Year (1220),
he was summoned to the capital.
Due to his illness, he could not enter for an audience,
but he exerted himself to draft a memorial.
The general gist was that since military campaigns were ongoing in both the north and south,
precautions should be taken against potential dangers,
as well as several strategies for river defense.
Not long after,
he passed away,
at the age of forty-five.
An imperial decree ordered the relevant authorities to provide for his funeral.
Wányán Ālǐbùsūn, courtesy name Yánchéng,
was a man of the Hélǎnlù Tàishēnbìlá Měng'ān.
He passed the imperial examination in Míngchāng Fifth Year (1194),
and was appointed as Military Judicial Officer for Yìzhōu and Xīnzhōu, and Magistrate of Ānfēng County.
He was appointed as a Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
then made Vice Military Governor of Xīngpíngjūn,
and served as an Attendant and Compiler in the Hanlin Academy.
He was promoted to Compiler,
and appointed as the Manager for Hélěliè Zhízhōng, the Left Supervising General of the Marshal’s Office.
When Zhízhōng besieged Chǔzhōu,
he allowed his troops to plunder extensively.
For failing to remonstrate,
Ālǐbùsūn was sentenced to fifty strokes of the cane.
In the early Dà'ān period (1209),
he was reassigned as a Supernumerary Official in the Ministry of Revenue and Prefect of Jūnzhōu.
When Zhízhōng operated the Bureau of Military Affairs in Xījīng,
he was again made a Manager.
He was then reassigned as Prefect of Wēizhōu.
In the early Zhēnyòu period (1213),
he was successively promoted to Libationer of the National Academy,
served as Tutor to the Prince of Yuè and Prince of Pú,
and then reassigned as Co-Administrator of Píngyáng Prefectural Affairs,
concurrently serving as Vice Commissioner of Pacification for that circuit.
He was summoned to be Assistant Minister of War,
and promoted to Hanlin Imperial Lecturer.
He was reassigned as Vice Commissioner of Pacification for the Shǎnxī Circuit,
and promoted to Left Grand Commissioner of the Marshal’s Office.
He was reassigned as Military Governor of Hépíngjūn and Vice Commissioner of Pacification for the Héběi West Circuit.
He was reassigned as Imperial Censor-in-Chief and Vice Commissioner of Pacification for Liáodōng.
After another two months,
he was provisionally made Right Vice Marshal and Censor-in-Chief, and Administrator of the Liáodōng Circuit Branch of the Department of State Affairs.
He was granted imperial robes, a horse, and Ānshān armor.
Púchá Wǔjīn of the Shàngjīng Branch of the Department of State Affairs memorialized his achievements,
and he was granted one hundred taels of gold and one hundred bolts of silk.
In Xīngdìng First Year (1216),
he was officially appointed as Censor-in-Chief,
provisionally serving as Right Vice Marshal,
operating the Department of State Affairs and the Marshal’s Office from Pósuōlù,
and by imperial authorization appointed and dismissed officials from prefectural governors downwards.
This caused discord.
Púxiān Wànnú occupied Liáodōng,
and raided the borders of Pósuō.
Gāolí, fearing his strength,
provided eighty thousand *shí* of grain.
When Púchá Wǔjīn of the Shàngjīng Branch of the Department of State Affairs came to court,
the military situation in Liáodōng became even weaker.
Wǔjīn left Jiāng Shān to guard Zhàozhōu,
and Jiāng Shān also harbored thoughts of changing allegiance.
When the Shàngjīng Pacification Commissioner Púchá Yílàdū was reassigned as a Counselor in the Shǎnxī Branch of the Department of State Affairs,
Bódé Hútǔ then harbored treacherous intentions.
The Pacification Commissioner Hǎinú did not welcome the imperial envoy,
but received the edict while seated.
Ālǐbùsūn shackled and imprisoned him.
A short while later,
Ālǐbùsūn arbitrarily forged an imperial edict for a general amnesty throughout the circuits,
whereupon the populace gradually settled down.
He then requested punishment from the court for this act.
Originally,
Liú Gē occupied Guǎngníng.
Wēndíhǎn Qīnggǒu, the Administrator of Guǎngníng Prefecture, resided in Gàizhōu,
his wife and children remaining in Guǎngníng.
He had sworn brotherhood with Bódé Hútǔ.
Qīnggǒu’s troops were subordinate to Ālǐbùsūn,
but there was internal suspicion and discord.
Púchá Yílàdū had once memorialized that Qīnggǒu should not be subordinate to Ālǐbùsūn.
Xuānzōng then summoned Qīnggǒu.
Qīnggǒu did not accept the edict.
Ālǐbùsūn killed him.
Hútǔ then resented Ālǐbùsūn.
Later, when Hútǔ led troops to attack Gāolí,
he used his soldiers to assassinate Ālǐbùsūn.

Nàtǎn Yù, the provisional Left Grand Commissioner, along with the Supervising General Wēndíhǎn Gēbù'āi, and Guō Shù, the remotely appointed Judicial Officer and Counselor for Military Affairs in Dōngpíng, plotted to execute Hútǔ.
They did not dare to act yet.

It happened that Púchá Wǔjīn, the Shàngjīng Garrison Commander, sent the Deputy Garrison Commander Jiágǔ Àidá and the Supernumerary Officials of the Left and Right Bureaus, Mòniǎn Dúlǔ, to Yù to discuss matters.
Yù revealed the plot to the two men,
who agreed.
They then summoned Hútǔ to the tent and killed him.
After Ālǐbùsūn’s death,
the court first received the memorial regarding the forged amnesty.
An edict ordered the relevant authorities to commend and instruct.
Not long after,
hearing that Ālǐbùsūn had died in the chaos,
an edict posthumously conferred upon him the titles of Píngzhāng Zhèngshì and Ruìguógōng.
Nàhé Yù was truly appointed Left Grand Commissioner,
and Àidá, Dúlǔ, and Guō Shù were promoted in official rank and position to varying degrees.
Ālǐbùsūn was magnanimous and benevolent,
and astute in administrative affairs.
He was capable of managing difficult and important matters.
Those who knew him believed his talents had not been fully utilized.
Wányán Tiěgē was honest and straightforward by nature,
with a majestic appearance,
and a rudimentary understanding of books.
At the age of twenty-four,
he inherited his father’s Hélǎnhédá Měng'ān in Sùpínlù.
He was granted the title of Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn.
He treated his subordinates with kindness and affection.
Upon being evaluated as honest and incorruptible,
he was appointed as Vice Military Governor of Línhǎijūn,
and then reassigned as Dǐlá Cíxiángwěn.
Chancellor Xiāng hànhxíngshěng (巡行省) in Běijīng.
Tiěgē was the vanguard commander of ten thousand households,
and distinguished himself.
When his mother died,
and the period of mourning was over,
he was promoted to Tongzhī Wǔshèngjūn Jiédùshǐ Shì (同知武勝軍節度使事),
and served as the deputy commander to the Right Deputy Marshal Wányán Kuāng,
receiving the title Píngnán Dàngjiāng Jiāngjūn (平南盪江將軍).
He attacked Guānghuàjūn.
Commander Wáng led infantry and cavalry out of the East Gate to engage them.
Tiěgē repelled them,
pulled down the deer-horn fences,
forced open the gates,
and thus captured the city.
Advancing to attack Xiāngyáng,
he served as the vanguard,
captured captives,
and learned of places where the river could be forded.
Secretly, he planted markers to identify them.
When the main army arrived,
Tiěgē guided them across the river.
They won every battle,
and for his merits, he was promoted two ranks.
When Kuāng besieged Dé'ān,
Tiěgē took overall command of the attack,
building a rampart on Fènghuángtái to the south of Dé'ān,
and constructing a covered walkway next to the city wall.
He erected 'goose carts' (siege towers),
and attacked with opposing towers,
routing Commander Zhāng's troops.
As it was summer,
they returned to camp at Dèngzhōu.
When the campaign ended,
he was promoted two ranks,
and transferred to Tongzhī Línhuángfǔ Shì (同知臨潢府事),
then reassigned as Xīnánlù Fù Zhāotǎo (西南路副招討) and Sùzhōu Fángyùshǐ (宿州防禦使).
In Zhēnyòu (貞祐) second year (1214),
Privy Councilor Túdān Dùyīlà (徒單度移剌) appointed Tiěgē as Dūtǒng (都統),
to guard Zhōngdū.
He was promoted to Dōngběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ (東北路招討使),
concurrently Jiàndéchāngjūn Jiédùshǐ (兼德昌軍節度使).
Púxiān Wànnú (蒲鮮萬奴) was in Xiánpíng,
and, fearing Tiěgē's strong army,
he sent a dispatch to requisition two thousand of his cavalry,
and also summoned three thousand troops from Táizhōu and moved their households to Xiánpíng.
Tiěgē perceived his rebellious intentions,
and did not send them.
Marshal Chéngchōng (承充) summoned Tiěgē to Shàngjīng,
and ordered him to attack Púyǔlù (蒲與路).
Upon his return,
Wànnú had replaced Chéngchōng as Marshal.
He accused Tiěgē of not dispatching his troops earlier,
imprisoned him, and had him killed.
He was posthumously granted the title Yǒngyì (勇毅).
Nàlán Húlǔlà,
was a Pàlǔhuān Méng'ān (怕魯歡猛安) person from Dàmínglù.
He was by nature simple and upright,
spoke little and rarely laughed,
was fond of reading,
and widely conversant with ancient and modern times.
In Chéng'ān (承安) second year (1197),
he passed the Imperial Examination as number one,
and was appointed Yìngfèng Hàlín Wénzì (應奉翰林文字).
He was ordered by imperial decree to inventory cattle in Línhuáng, Shàngjīng, and other circuits.
Chancellor Xiāng had fields in Zhàozhōu,
and his household servants concealed cattle and did not report them truthfully.
Húlǔlà immediately shackled and imprisoned them, punished their crimes, and seized all the cattle.
Thereupon, the powerful families were all afraid,
and none dared to conceal anything.
Upon his return,
Xiāng praised his ability.
[一七]He observed his father's mourning with complete propriety,
and the censor praised his integrity and incorruptibility.
When the period of mourning was over,
he was promoted to Xiūzhuàn (修撰).
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事) Púsǎn Duān (僕散端) recommended him for his honesty, ability, and literary talent.
He was promoted to Tongzhī Shùntiānjūn Jiédùshǐ Shì (同知順天軍節度使事),
and followed in the campaign against Sòng.
For his merits, he was awarded Cháoqǐng Dàfū (朝請大夫),
then reassigned as Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng (禮部員外郎) and Cáozhōu Cìshǐ (曹州刺史).
The powerful family of Púsǎn Sǎohé (僕散掃合) had established illegal ferries between Dìngtáo,
where deserters and bandits congregated,
all of whom they enrolled into their private retinue.
Many officials had been unable to question them.
Húlǔlà arrested and interrogated them,
and thoroughly investigated their faction,
making the entire prefecture orderly.
He was reassigned to Wòzhōu.
Then reassigned as Nánjīnglù Ànchá Fùshǐ (南京路按察副使).
In Zhēnyòu (貞祐) second year (1214),
he was reassigned as Sìzhōu Fángyùshǐ (泗州防禦使).
He was summoned to be Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎),
then promoted to Jiàngyángjūn Jiédùshǐ (絳陽軍節度使),
and provisionally Qúanhédōngnánlù Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ (權河東南路宣撫副使).
At that time, military conflicts were rising.
Húlǔlà completed the city walls,
repaired weapons,
and organized the able-bodied men into local militia.
[一八]He extensively consulted with elders,
and invited scholars,
seeking their advice on defense strategies.
He stockpiled salt and rice,
and persuaded wealthy families to contribute grain,
thus preserving the prefecture.
An imperial edict commended him,
he was awarded Zīshàn Dàfū (資善大夫),
and his second son Wúshēn (吾申) was given an official post.
He was reassigned as provisional Jīnglüèshǐ (經略使).
He was summoned,
but could not travel due to illness,
and died in Jiàngzhōu.
The encomium says: Between Tàihé (泰和) and Zhēnyòu (貞祐),
there were only five years,
so former generals and old officials were often still there.
[一九]When Gāo Qí (高琪) gained the emperor's favor,
all the veteran generals were dismissed to the outside.
When Gāo Rǔlì (高汝礪) held office,
all the old ministers became provincial governors.
They were given important responsibilities,
but in reality, they were distanced.
Therefore, beginning with Shímò Zhòngwēn (石抹仲溫),
we see the generals and officers of that time.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 42: Nàtán Móujiā (納坦謀嘉), Zōu Gǔ (鄒谷), Gāo Lín (高霖), Mèng Kuí (孟奎), Wūlín Dá Yǔ (烏林荅與), Guō Yǔ (郭俁), Wēndíhǎn Dá (溫迪罕達), Wáng Kuò (王擴), Yīlà Fúsēng (移剌福僧), Àotún Zhōngxiào (奧屯忠孝), Púchá Sīzhōng (蒲察思忠), Hégé liè Húshīmén (紇石烈胡失門), Wányán Kuì (完顏𧜛), Wòlēhé Dǎ (斡勒合打), Púchá Yīlàdōu (蒲察移剌都).
Nàtán Móujiā,
was a Yátǎlán Méng'ān (牙塔懶猛安) person from Shàngjīnglù.
He first studied essay writing for the imperial examination.
In Dàdìng (大定) twenty-sixth year (1186),
he was selected to enter the Eastern Palace,
to teach Yùnwáng Cóng (鄆王琮) and Yíngwáng Guī (瀛王瓌) to read.
As a successful candidate from the final examination, he was provisionally appointed as a clerk in the Shàngjīng Judicial Intendancy,
and was known for his integrity and ability.
In Chéng'ān (承安) first year (1196),
the Qìdān Tuósuǒ (契丹陀鎖) raided Hánzhōu and Xìnzhōu.
The Judicial Intendancy asked its clerks,
"Who will go to present the report to the emperor?"
Everyone found it difficult,
but Móujiā requested to go.
In the fifth year (1200),
he was specially granted the degree of Tóng Jìnshì Chūshēn (同進士出身),
and assigned as Dōngjīng Jiàoshòu (東京教授), Tāngchí Zhǔbù (湯池主簿), and Tàixué Zhùjiào (太學助教).
When his mother died,
and the period of mourning was over,
he was successively appointed Hàlín Xiūzhuàn (翰林修撰),
concurrently Xiūqǐjūzhù (修起居注) and Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史).
In early Zhēnyòu (貞祐) (1213),
he was promoted to Lìbù Yuánwàiláng (吏部員外郎), Hàlín Dàizhì (翰林待制), and Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
Wányán Kuì recommended Móujiā for his talent and conduct,
stating that he had the ambition to rectify the country,
and could participate in military affairs.
He was appointed as a staff officer in the Marshal's office.
When Zhōngdū was besieged,
and food was running out,
Xū Dǐng (胥鼎) reported,
"For officials and commoners in the capital who can provide for the poor,
their official rank will be promoted according to what they provide,
and all will first be issued a certificate."
Móujiā refused the certificate and left.
When Zhōngdū was in dire straits,
Móujiā said,
"The marshal commands tens of thousands of troops but cannot lead them out of the city for a single battle;
why not tie himself up and surrender?"
Xuānzōng (宣宗) considered moving the capital.
Móujiā said,
"This is not permissible.
Hénán's territory is narrow and its soil thin.
In the future, if Sòng and Xià encroach upon us from both sides,
Héběi will no longer be ours.
We should select princes to be stationed in Liáodōng and Hénán,
but Zhōngdū cannot be abandoned."
This was not heeded.
Shortly after,
he was appointed Tángzhōu Cìshǐ (唐州刺史).
He entered the court as Tàicháng Shàoqīng (太常少卿) concurrently Zuǒ Shíyí (左拾遺),
and was promoted to Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ (鄭州防禦使).
He was reassigned as Zuǒ Yùdé (左諭德),
then transferred to Shào Zhànshì (少詹事),
acting as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
Not long after,
he acted as Tàizǐ Zhànshì (太子詹事).
In Xīngdìng (興定) first year (1217),
Tóngguān was lost.
He was promoted to Hénán Tǒngjūnshǐ (河南統軍使) concurrently Chāngwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ (昌武軍節度使),
acting as Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì (簽樞密院事).
He established his office in Xǔzhōu,
and dismissed over two thousand redundant soldiers.
He submitted a memorial admonishing against attacking Sòng,
but it was not heeded.
After three years,
he was demoted to Defending Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Yǐngzhōu.
Someone reported that the Sòng people were about to attack Yǐngzhōu.
Soon after, Sòng troops indeed arrived,
but Móu Jiā was prepared,
so they withdrew.
The officials reported his merits,
but did not mention the informant.
Móu Jiā requested that the informant be rewarded, and this was granted.
In the fourth year,
he was summoned to be Hanlin Academician-in-waiting (Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì) concurrently with Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng),
and co-compiler of the National History (Guóshǐ).
In the fifth year,
he died.
Zōu Gǔ, courtesy name Yìngzhòng,
was a native of Zhūchéng, Mìzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the thirteenth year of Dàdìng,
and successively served as Literary Retainer (Wénxué) in the Shěn Prince's residence.
The Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng) proposed him as Director of Justice (Sīzhí) of the Grand Court of Justice (Dàlǐ),
but the Emperor said:
"The Director of Justice disputes legal matters and clarifies difficult cases.
Gǔ is not skilled in this."
The Chief Minister (Zǎichén) said:
"Gǔ has administrative talent;
he performed competently in investigations and tax assessments in Shǎnxī and Hénán."
The Emperor then appointed Gǔ as Vice Administrator (Tóngzhī) of Cáo Zhōu's military and civil affairs.
He was summoned to be a Principal Official (Zhǔshì) in the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù),
then transferred to Judicial Review Commissioner (Tíxíng Pànguān) of Běijīng and Línhuáng,
and later entered as Secretary (Chéng) of the Grand Court of Justice.
The Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng) selected officials to escort the Sòng envoy.
The clerk Zhōu Áng prepared a list of several names for approval.
Lǐ Bǐng, a Staff Supervisor (Dūshì) of the Left Bureau (Zuǒsī), saw it while drunk,
and angrily said:
"I can name two people right now;
why do we need so many?"
He ordered his attendants to grab Áng's clothing, intending to flog him.
Just then, an official from the Left Bureau summoned Áng away, and the matter ceased.
He cursed the other clerks as slaves and animals.
The next day, he told the acting clerk Lǐ Bǐngjūn:
"Not only can I flog and curse,
but your promotion, demotion, leaving, or staying
are all within my power!"
The clerks were about to file a complaint,
when an official impeached him.
The case was sent to the Grand Court of Justice for deliberation.
The matter of selecting escort officials required imperial approval (zòuwén).
Bǐng's statement of "naming two people"
should be punished as
"violating regulations" (wéizhì).
Gǔ said:
"'Naming two people' was a momentary utterance;
it should be punished by caning with redemption.
Grabbing Áng's clothing and intending to flog him
should incur thirty strokes."
The Emperor said:
"Lǐ Bǐng is a scholar;
how could he go so far?"
The Chief Minister replied:
"Lǐ Bǐng detests evil,
and others cannot tolerate him."
The Emperor said:
"Bǐng is truly at fault,
but the accusers may not be entirely correct."
So he followed Gǔ's suggestion.
