He successively served as Administrator (Zhìzhōng) of Jǐnán and Zhāngdé Prefectures,
Director (Lángzhōng) in the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù),
Vice Censor-in-chief (Ànchá Fùshǐ) of Hédōng,
and Defending Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Yízhōu.
He successively served as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Dìnghǎi and Tàiníng armies.
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
he retired.
In the early Jiānzhōng period,
he died.
Gāo Lín, courtesy name Zǐyuē,
was a native of Dōngpíng.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng,
and was appointed Registrar (Zhǔbù) of Fúlí.
He was recognized for integrity,
promoted to Magistrate (Lìng) of Sìshuǐ,
and then re-appointed as Judicial Review Commissioner (Jiédù Pànguān) of the Ānguó Army.
Due to his father's mourning (fùyōu), he returned to his hometown
and taught students,
numbering several hundred.
After the mourning period,
he became Judicial Review Commissioner (Jiédù Pànguān) of the Jiàngyáng Army.
Through recommendations,
he was summoned to be a Compiler (Biānxiū Guān) in the National History Institute (Guóshǐyuàn).
He proposed:
"The reason the Yellow River harms the people
is because the river flows with twists and turns,
and when it encounters narrow sections,
it causes rapid flows and breaches.
According to the water conservancy records (shuǐjīng), its blockages should be cleared,
allowing it to flow unhindered.
If we now open the Jīzhuǎ River to reduce its force,
we can avoid the labor of repeatedly constructing dikes (sǎo).
All materials and labor for building dikes
are taken from the people,
which is a great burden at present.
I request that elm and willow trees be widely planted along the riverbanks.
After a few years,
the embankments will be solid,
the materials for dikes will also be readily available,
and the people's labor will gradually decrease."
The imperial court adopted his suggestion.
He was promoted to Hanlin Drafter of Rescripts (Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì) concurrently holding his former position,
then transferred to Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
He observed mourning for his mother (dīngmǔyōu),
and was reinstated as Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Bóshì).
He was transferred to Vice Director of Waterways (Dūshuǐ Jiānchéng),
and concurrently served as Assistant Censor (Ànchá Sīshì) for Shǎnxī Circuit,
to investigate the competence of officials,
and then return to the capital for an audience.
At that time, the southern expedition required frequent and urgent levies,
and the people were slightly delayed.
Officials were all punished for missing military deadlines.
Lín argued that this was unjust,
and all were released.
He was appointed Junior Director of Waterways (Dūshuǐ Shàojiān).
In the early Dà'ān period,
he became Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yàozhōu.
After three years,
he was promoted to Vice Censor-in-chief (Ànchá Fùshǐ) of Héběi Dōng Lù,
then transferred to Tutor to Prince Hán (Hánwáng Fù),
concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Zhí Xuéshì).
In the early Chóngqìng period,
he was transferred to Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng) concurrently Academician.
In the eighth month of the first year of Zhìníng,
Lín, bearing the imperial decree (chúzhì), escorted Emperor Xuānzōng to Xīnchéng.
He was then commanded to go south to escort the imperial concubines.
Upon his return,
he was granted a thousand strings of cash
and promoted three ranks.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Hépíng Army concurrently Director of Waterways (Dūshuǐ Jiān).
Lín requested to fortify Yícūn as Wèizhōu to protect the northern gate,
and the Emperor approved.
He entered the court as Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū),
and concurrently served as Administrator of Dàxīng Fǔ,
then temporarily served as Assistant Administrator (Quán Cānzhī Zhèngshì),
and, with Right Grand Councilor (Yòu Chéngxiàng) Chénghuī, administered the province in Zhōngdū.
Soon after, he was transferred to Garrison Commander of Zhōngdū (Zhōngdū Liúshǒu),
concurrently Commander-in-chief of all military forces of that circuit.
When Chancellor (Píngzhāng Zhèngshì) Mòlián Jìnzhōng abandoned Zhōngdū and fled south,
Lín and his son Yìjié led their followers out at night.
Unable to advance,
Lín said to Yìjié:
"You must seek survival;
I will die here."
Lín died,
and Yìjié survived by hiding among the corpses.
He was posthumously granted Academician Reader-in-waiting (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ),
with an order to erect a stele in his hometown
and offer sacrifices annually.
His descendants were sought out for official appointments,
and he was granted the posthumous title Wénjiǎn.
Mèng Kuí, courtesy name Yuánxiù,
was a native of Liáoyáng.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-first year of Dàdìng,
and was appointed Registrar (Zhǔbù) of Líyáng.
He observed mourning for his mother (dīngmǔyōu),
and after the mourning period (fúquè),
he was appointed Military Judicial Review Commissioner (Jūnshì Pànguān) of Zīzhōu,
and promoted to Magistrate (Lìng) of Jíxiàn.
He was recognized for integrity,
and transferred to Magistrate (Lìng) of Dìngxīng.
He was appointed Clerk (Lìshǐ) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūshěng),
and followed Assistant Administrator (Cānzhī Zhèngshì) Mǎ Qí in damming the breach of the Chányuān River.
He was transferred to Left Patrol Commissioner (Zuǒ Jǐngxúnshǐ) of Zhōngdū.
Chancellor (Píngzhāng Zhèngshì) Wányán Shǒuzhēn courteously received literati who visited his residence,
calling them
"Ten Talents of Lěngyán."
Kuí was one of them.
He was transferred to Financial Review Commissioner (Zhīdù Pànguān) in the General Transport Commission (Dū Zhuǎnyùnsī),
and Judicial Review Commissioner (Tíxíng Pànguān) for Shàngjīng and other circuits.
Héshíliè Húshīmén,
a Mèng'ān from Shàngjīng Lù.
He passed the Jinshì examination in the fifth year of Míngchāng (1194).
He successively served as an official scribe in the Shàngshūshěng,
and was appointed Judge of Expenditure for Zhōngdū Lù,
then transferred to Inspector of Accounts for Héběidōng Lù.
He successively held the positions of Hànlín Zhíxuégshì, Dàlǐqīng, and Yòujiànyì Dàfū.
In the second year of Xīngdìng (1218),
during the campaign against the Sòng,
he served as an adviser to Marshal Zuǒdūjiān Héshíliè Yáwūtǎ.
When Yáwūtǎ reached Chǔzhōu,
he advanced his troops without waiting for the command of the Xíngshěng servant Púsàn Ānzhēnjì.
The Sòng people strengthened their defenses and did not engage.
There was nothing to plunder in the fields,
the soldiers were exhausted,
and many starved to death.
They advanced straight to the river and then retreated.
Ānzhēn impeached him.
Yáwūtǎ was found guilty of not following the imperial edict,
and Húshīmén was found guilty of not correcting him.
By special imperial decree, they were pardoned.
Húshīmén was
reassigned as Tongzhī Zhāngdé Fǔshì.
After five promotions, he became Lìbù Shàngshū.
In the fifth year (1221),
he was appointed Yùshǐ Dàfū.
In the first year of Yuánguāng (1222),
he also held the position of Dàsīnóng.
In the second year (1223),
he passed away.
Xuānzōng suspended court,
and all officials offered sacrifices.
Wányán Juàn, originally named Échū,
was a Mèng'ān from Xīnán Lù.
He passed the Jinshì examination in the twenty-eighth year of Dàdìng (1188).
He was successively transferred to Zhīshì of Tíxíngsī for Hédōngběi Lù,
then reassigned as Tongzhī Liáozhōu Jūnzhōushì.
He was summoned to be a Biānxiūguān in the Guóshǐyuàn,
and promoted to Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì and Nánjīng Lù Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ.
After his father's mourning period,
he was reinstated as Tàifǔ Jiānjìng,
and then reassigned as Lìbù Yuánwàiláng.
In the early Dà'ān period (1209-1212),
he was appointed Zhī Dēngwén Jiǎnyuàn,
and successively promoted to Yòusī Lángzhōng, Hànlín Dàizhì,
and concurrently Shìyùshǐ.
In the early Zhēnyòu period (1213-1217),
he discussed matters concerning Wèi Shàowáng.
His words are recorded in the annals of Wèi Shàowáng.
When Zhōngdū was under urgent siege,
an imperial edict established the Zhāoxiánsuǒ at the Dōnghuámén,
where officials and commoners alike could speak on affairs of state.
Some were granted official positions without proper order,
and thus ordinary people from the villages
often boasted and sought opportunities.
Wáng Shǒuxìn,
originally a village man,
dared to speak grandly,
considering Zhūgě Liàng as ignorant of military tactics.
Juàn recommended him to the court.
An imperial edict appointed him Xíngjūn Dūtǒng.
He recruited idlers from the market to be soldiers,
training them in advancing, retreating, jumping, and throwing,
which largely resembled children's games.
His battle formations bore the four characters
"Gǔjīn Xiāngduì"
("Ancient and Modern Counterparts") on their banners.
He made thirty-six yellow cloth robes, thirty-six black turbans, and thirty-six tin shields,
and sixty-four ox-head bells,
intending to frighten the enemy and make them flee.
Most of these were preposterous.
He then went out of the city with his troops,
killing common people who were gathering firewood and claiming it as merit.
Jiǎ Nàier,
originally a storyteller from the streets,
earned his living by telling humorous stories in colloquial language.
He manufactured a thousand supply carts.
At that time, timber was extremely scarce,
and the cost was enormous.
Onlookers all secretly laughed at him.
Lǐ Dòng, a recluse, had served Lǐ Tiānhuì, the Superintendent of the Imperial Observatory, during the time of Wèi Shàowáng.
He relied on astronomy,
falsely claiming divination,
and associated with influential officials,
both becoming officials of the Imperial Observatory.
Dòng once secretly reported in a memorial that a white qi penetrated the Zǐwēixīng,
indicating military unrest in the capital.
Fortunately, it did not pass through completely,
so it did not result in a disaster.
Later, Gāo Qí killed Húshāhǔ,
and Xuānzōng trusted him even more.
Zuǒjiànyì Dàfū Zhāng Xíngxìn memorialized, saying:
"Madmen and mediocre individuals are being
recklessly promoted
to participate in important state affairs,
which is utterly senseless.
Officials of the Imperial Observatory
observe celestial phenomena
and report based on the classics,
so that the ruler may examine himself and reform his governance,
turning misfortune into fortune.
If there are celestial phenomena,
I request that all officials of the observatory jointly report them.
If their observations differ,
then each should report their findings.
It is not appropriate to listen to one side only."
The Emperor summoned Xíngxìn and Juàn to discuss the matter of Shǒuxìn face-to-face.
〔12〕He further consulted with his close attendants and then with Gāo Qí.
Gāo Qí stated that Shǒuxìn was unusable,
so the Emperor agreed with Xíngxìn's words.
Soon after,
Juàn was promoted to Lǐbù Shìláng,
then reassigned as Dōngjīng Fùliúshǒu and Lǒngzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He was promoted to Ānhuàjūn Jiédùshǐ,
concurrently Shāndōng Lù Tǒngjūn Fùshǐ.
In the fourth month of the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
an edict ordered Juàn, in his current capacity, to temporarily act as Marshal Zuǒdūjiān,
exercising the functions of the Marshal's office,
to reconcile the forces of Miáo Dàorùn and Yílà Tiěgē.
This is recorded in the biography of Dàorùn.
In the twelfth month,
Mìzhōu was captured,
and Juàn was killed by mutinous soldiers.
Wòlèhédá,
was a Mèng'ān from Běndéshān, Gàizhōu.
He entered officialdom by privilege (yīn),
served in the imperial guards,
and was transferred to Shānyīn Wèi.
〔13〕The county was subjected to military attack,
and Hédá led the local gentry and government troops to be the first in battle.
In the early Zhēnyòu period (1213-1217),
he was promoted to county magistrate for his merits.
The county was elevated to Zhōngzhōu,
and Hédá served as its Cìshǐ.
The prefecture had long been ravaged by war,
and farming and sericulture were abandoned.
An imperial edict ordered its people to move south of Tàihé Lǐng.
Hédá was remotely appointed Tongzhī Tàiyuán Fǔshì,
still leading his people.
Soon after, in his current capacity, he was remotely appointed Zhāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ,
and acting Héběidōng Lù Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ,
supervising the transport of grain and provisions to Dàizhōu.
Hédá did not want to go,
and therefore argued with Xuānfǔshǐ Wányán Bójiā.
Hédá, fearing that Bójiā would report him,
first reported Bójiā for insulting him.
The Yùshǐtái investigated the matter.
Before the report could be submitted,
Bójiā and Hédá were both reassigned.
Hédá was reassigned as Wǔníngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Several months later,
he was summoned to be Quànnóngshǐ.
After a long time,
he became Jīn'ānjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
he again became Quànnóngshǐ,
successively served as Zhī Héjiān Fǔ,
acting Marshal Yòudūjiān,
exercising the functions of the Marshal's office,
stationing troops between Cài and Xī.
He temporarily held the position of Tong Qiānshūmìyuànshì,
guarding Héqīng,
and was reassigned as Zhī Guīdé Fǔshì.
Hédá repeatedly defended critical border areas.
He had no other military strategy,
and although he never suffered defeat,
he also achieved no great merit.
In the first year of Yuánguāng (1222),
he died.
Púchá Yílàdū,
was a Mèng'ān from Dōngjīng.
His father, Wúdíe,
retired as Tàizǐ Tàifù.
Yílàdū was brave and strong,
and served as a Shírénzhǎng in the imperial guards.
He was transferred to Tongzhī Qínzhōu Fángyùshǐshì and Wǔwèijūn Qiánxiá,
and left office due to mourning.
He was reinstated as Wǔqìshǔ Lìng.
He joined the army,
and when the army was routed, he was captured.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
he escaped with over ten thousand surrendered soldiers.
He was promoted to Zhìzhōng of Lóng'ān Fǔ,
awarded one hundred taels of silver and six bolts of fine silk,
and remotely appointed Cìshǐ of Xìnzhōu.
For his merits,
he was promoted to Púyǔ Lù Jiédùshǐ, concurrently Tongzhī Shàngjīng Liúshǒushì.
He advanced three ranks,
and was reassigned as Zhī Lóng'ān Fǔshì.
More than a year later,
he was appointed Xuānfǔshǐ for Liáodōng, Shàngjīng, and other routes, concurrently Zuǒfù Yuánshuài.
Two more months passed,
and he was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
Liú Shū 劉樞, courtesy name Jūzhōng 居中,
was a native of Sānhé 三河, Tōngzhōu 通州.
While young, as a son of a good family, he joined the army
and was stationed at Héjiān 河間.
His peers all practiced archery and horsemanship,
but Shū 樞 alone diligently studied the classics and histories.
He passed the Jinshi examination in Tiānjuàn 天眷 second year (1129)
and was appointed Registrar (Zhǔbù 主簿) of Tángshān 唐山.
He was transferred to Magistrate (Lìng 令) of Fēihú 飛狐.
The Prefect (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Wèizhōu 蔚州, relying on his achievements, was corrupt and unprincipled,
and the subordinate counties all suffered from him.
Shū 樞 gave no response to his demands,
so the Prefect trumped up another charge and imprisoned him,
intending to put him to death.
Among the people of the prefecture, there were those who pitied Shū 樞,
helped Shū 樞 escape,
and appealed to the court.
Coincidentally, an Imperial Inspector (Liánchásǐ 廉察使) arrived,
and the prefect, his deputy, and others below were all condemned and dismissed.
Only Shū's 樞 administration record was rated excellent,
and he was promoted successively to Grand Master of Rectitude (Fèngzhí Dàfū 奉直大夫).
Zhāng Hào 張浩 was overseeing the construction of the palace buildings in Yānjīng 燕京,
and Shū 樞 was selected to manage a portion of the construction work.
He was promoted to Senior Secretary (Yuánwàiláng 員外郎) of the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù 刑部) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng 尚書省),
and was responsible for investigating the rebellion of Túshān Ālǐchūhǔ 徒單阿里出虎, Administrator (Yǐn 尹) of Tàiyuán 太原.
[一０]In ten days, the case was concluded.
He was transferred to Director (Lángzhōng 郎中) of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù 工部),
and then promoted to Vice Minister (Shìláng 侍郎) of the same ministry.
At the end of Zhènglóng 正隆 (1161),
he returned from the Yangzi River with the army.
At the beginning of Dàdìng 大定 (1161),

he, along with the Director (Lángzhōng 郎中) of the Left Bureau (Zuǒsī 左司) Wáng Wèi 王蔚, and the Senior Secretary (Yuánwàiláng 員外郎) of the Right Bureau (Yòusī 右司) Wáng Quán 王全, were all sent out to serve in the provinces.
Shū 樞 was appointed Commissioner of Transport (Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Shì 轉運使事) for Nánjīng Lù 南京路.
Initially,
Shìzōng 世宗 wanted to re-employ Shū 樞 and others.
The Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái 御史臺) submitted a memorial:
"Shū 樞 and others, during the Zhènglóng 正隆 era, all advanced through clever means,
undermining the law and corrupting the government.
Many people resented and envied them."
The Emperor, considering Shū 樞 and others to be quite capable,
still employed them,
and admonished them, saying:
"If you can repent and amend your errors,
you will surely be promoted.
Otherwise,
I will dismiss you all."
At this time,
Ālēgēn Yànzhōng 阿勒根彥忠 was the Commissioner of Transport for Nánjīng Nándū 都,
but he was not skilled in official affairs,
so Shū 樞 was employed to assist him.
He was transferred to Commissioner of Transport for Shāndōng Lù 山東路,
and then to Commissioner of Transport for Zhōngdū Lù 中都路.
In Dàdìng 大定 fourth year (1164),
he died in office.
Wáng Xiāo 王翛, courtesy name Xiāorán 翛然,
was a native of Zhuózhōu 涿州.
He passed the Jinshi examination in Huángtǒng 皇統 second year (1142),
and from a Clerk (Lìshǐ 令史) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng 尚書省), he was appointed Associate Administrator (Tóngzhī 同知) of Bàzhōu 霸州.
He was successively promoted to Senior Secretary (Yuánwàiláng 員外郎) of the Ministry of Punishments (Xíngbù 刑部).
He was punished for having solicited a favor for an old friend involved in a crime of adultery,
receiving forty strokes with the stick,
and demoted to Deputy Commander (Jiédù Fùshǐ 節度副使) of Tàidìng Jūn 泰定軍.
After four transfers, he became Administrator (Zhìzhōng 治中) of Dàxīng Fǔ 大興府,
and was appointed Vice Minister (Shìláng 侍郎) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù 戶部).
Shìzōng 世宗 said to his chief ministers:
"Wáng Xiāo 王翛 previously served as a provincial official,
and was known for his uprightness.
Now, I hear he is exclusively dedicated to acquitting criminals as a 'secret virtue,'
and many matters are unfairly treated leniently.
Moreover, he is artfully opportunistic and seeks comfort.
If he were truly upright,
he would forget himself for the sake of the country,
and uphold justice without bias.
Why would he sell out the law to seek good fortune?"
Soon after, he was ordered to provide famine relief to the Meng'an 猛安 households in Mìyún 密雲 and thirty-six other counties.
He falsely claimed over 30,000 *shi* 石 of grain,
and the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng 尚書省) impeached him, leading to the deprivation of one rank of his official position.
He was sent out to be Associate Administrator (Tóngzhī 同知) of Běijīng Liúshǒu Shì 北京留守事.
The Emperor said:
"Many people say Wáng Xiāo 王翛 is a capable official,
but in my opinion,
he is unwilling to exert his full effort in anything,
he is simply an old rogue."
In the twenty-fourth year (1184),
he was transferred to Commissioner of Transport for Liáodōng Lù 遼東路.
After more than a year,
he was appointed Commander (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Xiǎndé Jūn 顯德軍.
Because he had previously, as Commissioner of Transport, humiliated and abused the Granary Administrator (Cāngshǐ 倉使) Wáng Qí 王祺, causing his death,
he was retroactively deprived of two official positions and dismissed from office,
and was ordered to receive seventy strokes with the stick,
and demoted to Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ 防禦使) of Zhèngzhōu 鄭州.
Upon the ascension of Zhāngzōng 章宗,
he was promoted to Associate Administrator (Tóngzhī 同知) of Dàxīng Fǔ 大興府.
The Judicial Review Officials (Shěnlù Guān 審錄官) reported that
Xiāo 翛, during his previous tenure in Xiǎndé 顯德, was clean, incorruptible, and upright,
and military officials restrained themselves,
with no lawsuits.
He was promoted to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書),
concurrently serving as Chief Justice of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Qīng 大理卿).
After returning from his mission to Sòng 宋,
it happened that the reburial of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī 太師) Prince of Guǎngpíng Jùn 廣平郡 Wáng Túshān Zhēn 徒單貞 was taking place.
Zhēn 貞 was
the father of Empress Xiàoyì 孝懿, Zhāngzōng's 章宗 mother.
The Emperor wanted to use the precedents of previous dynasties,
including the ceremonial guards of banded swords (Bānjìan 班劍), drum and wind instruments (Gǔchuī 鼓吹), and feathered canopies (Yǔbǎo 羽葆).
The chief ministers found it difficult,
as Zhēn 貞 had been involved in the assassination of Xīzōng 熙宗 and executed.
Thereupon,
an edict was issued to the officials of rites to deliberate.
Xiāo 翛 said:
"The Jin dynasty buried Chancellor Wáng Dǎo 王導,
and he was provided with feathered canopies (Yǔbǎo 羽葆) for front and rear, drum and wind instruments (Gǔchuī 鼓吹), military guards (Wǔbēn 武賁), and one hundred banded swords (Bānjìan 班劍).
Since the Tang dynasty,
the Imperial Grand Procession (Dàjià Lúbù 大駕鹵簿) had banded swords,
but the processions of princes and dukes and those below did not have banded swords,
and feathered canopies (Yǔbǎo 羽葆) were not appropriate for subjects to use.
Our dynasty's burials of high ministers also do not include them."
The Emperor already knew that Tang dynasty burials of high ministers like Lǐ Jìng 李靖 and others all used banded swords (Bānjìan 班劍) and feathered canopies (Yǔbǎo 羽葆),
and angrily said:
"What is not found in precedents can certainly be followed,
but using them would not be excessive."
One day,
an edict summoned Xiāo 翛 and Grand Master for Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū 諫議大夫) concurrently Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng 禮部侍郎) Zhāng Wěi 張暐 to the palace gate,
and admonished them, saying:
"For matters of the court,
you remonstrating officials and officials of rites should debate and analyze.
Even if a commoner's words are worth adopting,
I still follow them,
how much more so for you, my lords?
From now on, when deliberating on matters,
do not simply comply with the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng 尚書省)."
In Míngchāng 明昌 second year (1191),
he was transferred to Administrator (Zhī Dàxīng Fǔ Shì 知大興府事) of Dàxīng Fǔ 大興府.
At that time,
many monks frequented the gates of noble relatives.
Xiāo 翛 detested this,
so he prohibited monks from leaving their temples after noon.
Once, a monk violated the prohibition,
and the Grand Princess (Dàcháng Gōngzhǔ 大長公主) pleaded for him.
Xiāo 翛 said:
"If I follow the Princess's order,
I will immediately release him."
He then immediately summoned the monk,
gave him one hundred strokes with the stick, causing his death.
The capital became solemn.
Later, he was punished for intentionally releasing a criminal,
and again stripped of his office and dismissed.
The following year,
he was specially appointed Commander (Jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Dìnghǎi Jūn 定海軍.
The imperial edict stated:
"Your nature is too stern,
and you act on impulse,
thus you bring punishment upon yourself.
Considering your advanced age
and your long service in officialdom,
and that you possess some steadfastness,
I specially raise you from your state of guilt and demotion,
and appoint you to your current post.
Furthermore, that area suffers from a lean year and starving people,
with many bandits.
We need an old hand to suppress and pacify them,
so that peace and order may be achieved.
Strive to do your best,
to achieve future results."
Not long after,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
The Emperor said:
"Xiāo 翛 is capable,
and has been of great service."
He did not permit it.
He applied again,
and this time it was granted.
In Tàihé 泰和 seventh year (1207),
he died,
aged seventy-five.
Xiāo's 翛 character was stern and strict,
and he was decisive in handling matters.
Officials and common people feared his authority,
and even powerful magnates dared not offend him.
During the Chéng'ān 承安 era (1196-1200),
when the post of Administrator (Zhī Dàxīng Fǔ Shì 知大興府事) of Dàxīng Fǔ 大興府 was vacant,
an imperial edict was issued to the chief ministers, saying:
"Choose someone of extreme fortitude, like Wáng Xiāo 王翛, and employ him."
Such was the Emperor's understanding of him.
Yáng Bóxióng 楊伯雄, courtesy name Xīyún 希雲,
was a native of Zhēndìng Chéng 真定城.
His eighth-generation ancestor Yànchóu 彥稠,
during the Qīngtài 清泰 period of Later Tang, was the Commander of Troops (Bīngmǎshǐ 兵馬使) of Dìngzhōu 定州.
Later, he followed the Prince of Jin (Jìnzhǔ 晉主) north,
[一一]and thus settled in Línhuáng 臨潢.
His father, Qiūxíng 丘行,
was the Left Commander (Zuǒwèi Shuàilǜ Fǔ Shuài 左衞率府率) of the Crown Prince's Guards.
Yáng Bóxióng 楊伯雄 passed the *jìnshì* 進士 examination in the second year of Huángtǒng 皇統 (1142).
Hǎilíng 海陵 was serving as the Resident-General of the Central Capital.
Qióu 丘 was in his *mùfǔ* 幕府 (private secretariat).
Bóxióng 伯雄 came to pay a visit.
Hǎilíng 海陵 saw him
and deeply admired and valued him.
After some time,
he was transferred to be the Judicial Supervisor of Hánzhōu 韓州.
There were two bandits who falsely claimed to be merchants.
The innkeeper was deceived,
and they came to the prefecture office to file a complaint,
but their real intention was to rob Bóxióng 伯雄.
Bóxióng 伯雄 sensed their deception in his heart,
arrested and interrogated them,
and also apprehended over ten of their accomplices.
The entire prefecture was awestruck and submitted.
He was promoted to Attendant Academician in the Hanlin Academy (Yìngfèng Hàlín Wénzì 應奉翰林文字).
At this time,
Hǎilíng 海陵 was in power.
Considering that he had known Bóxióng 伯雄 for a long time,
he instructed him to come to his residence often.
Bóxióng 伯雄 assented but did not go.
One day,
Hǎilíng 海陵 asked him in surprise.
He replied:
“A *jūnzǐ* 君子 (gentleman) who receives recognition from others should advance with propriety.
To curry favor and rush about
is not my original intention.”
From then on, Hǎilíng 海陵 treated him even more favorably.
After Hǎilíng 海陵 usurped the throne,
a few months later,
he was promoted to Right Remonstrance Official (Yòu Bǔquē 右補闕)
and appointed as Reviser of the Diaries of Activity and Repose (Xiū Qǐjūzhù 修起居注).
Hǎilíng 海陵 was eager to achieve good governance,
and discussions often continued until midnight.
He once asked:
“What is most valued in a ruler’s governance of the world?”
He replied:
“Stillness (jìng 靜).”
Hǎilíng 海陵 remained silent.
The next day,
he said again:
“I am transferring the various *méng'ān* 猛安 (regiments) to frontier garrisons.
Was your answer last night perhaps indicating that this is not stillness?”
He replied:
“Moving troops and dividing them among garrisons,
allowing the north and south to support each other,
is a long-term strategy.
What I meant by ‘stillness’
is simply not disturbing the people.”
Late at night,
he again asked about matters of ghosts and spirits.
Bóxióng 伯雄 stepped forward and said:
“When Emperor Wén 文 of Hàn 漢 summoned Jiǎ Shēng 賈生,
he moved his mat forward in the middle of the night,
not asking about the common people but about ghosts and spirits.
Later generations have criticized this quite a bit.
Your Majesty, though you do not consider your servant foolish and crude,
you are concerned with major national policies.
As for matters of ghosts and spirits, I have not studied them.”
Hǎilíng 海陵 said:
“Just speak your mind,
to relieve the weariness of this long night’s thoughts.”
Bóxióng 伯雄 had no choice
and then said:
“My family has a scroll
that records a person who died and was resurrected.
Someone asked the underworld official how to avoid punishment.
The answer was,
‘You should keep a daily record.
Whatever you do in the daylight,
write it down at night.
That which cannot be written down is that which should not be done.’”
Hǎilíng 海陵 changed his expression because of this.
One summer day,
Hǎilíng 海陵 ascended Ruìyún Lóu 瑞雲樓 (Auspicious Cloud Tower) to enjoy the cool air,
and ordered Bóxióng 伯雄 to compose a poem.
Its final stanza read:
“In June, one does not know the arrival of heat and humidity;
The refreshing coolness will be shared with all under heaven.”
Hǎilíng 海陵 was delighted,
and showed it to his attendants, saying:
“Bóxióng 伯雄’s words do not forget counsel and admonition;
A minister should indeed be like this.”
He was again promoted to Supernumerary Secretary in the Ministry of War (Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng 兵部員外郎).
After observing mourning for his father,
he was reinstated as Hanlin Attendant (Hànlín Dàizhì 翰林待制)
and concurrently Reviser of the Diaries of Activity and Repose.
He was promoted to Academician-in-waiting (Zhí Xuéshì 直學士),
then again promoted to Right Remonstrance Official (Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū 右諫議大夫),
concurrently Editor in the Imperial Library (Zhùzuò Láng 著作郎),
and continued as Reviser of the Diaries of Activity and Repose.
When the imperial prince, Shènsī Ābù 慎思阿不, died young,
Bóxióng 伯雄 was reproached for secretly discussing it with his colleagues who were on duty with him.
The details are in the biography of Hǎilíng’s 海陵 sons.
When Hǎilíng 海陵 deliberated on a campaign against Jiāngnán 江南,
Bóxióng 伯雄 memorialized:
“When Emperor Wǔ 武 of Jìn 晉 pacified Wú 吳, he always appointed generals.
Why bother personally overseeing the military regulations?”
He did not listen.
Thus, Bóxióng 伯雄 was removed from the Diaries of Activity and Repose,
and was no longer summoned for audiences.
In the early Dàdìng 大定 period (1161-1189),
he was appointed Assistant Magistrate of Dàxīng 大興,
then observed mourning for his mother.
When Xiǎnzōng 顯宗 was the Crown Prince,
officials for the Eastern Palace were being selected.
Zhāng Hào 張浩 recommended Bóxióng 伯雄,
who was reinstated as Junior Mentor of the Crown Prince (Shǎo Zhànshì 少詹事).
His nephew Pán 蟠 was Left Advisor to the Crown Prince (Zuǒ Zànshàn 左贊善).
His words were heard, and his remonstrances were followed,
and public opinion at the time honored him.
He compiled a book on the good and bad qualities of ancient crown princes,
titled *Yáoshān Wǎngjiàn* 瑤山往鑒 (Past Mirror of Mount Yao),
and presented it.
He also presented admonitions such as *Yǔliè* 羽獵 (Feather Hunt) and *Bǎochéng* 保成 (Protect Completion),
all of which were graciously accepted.
He was again appointed Left Remonstrance Official (Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū 左諫議大夫) and Academician-in-waiting (Hànlín Zhí Xuéshì 翰lín直學士).
When the position of Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhànshì 太子詹事) became vacant,
the Prime Minister again recommended Bóxióng 伯雄.
The Emperor said:
“Bóxióng 伯雄 cannot leave my side,
but the Eastern Palace also needs guidance.”
Thus, he was appointed Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince concurrently with Remonstrance Official.
In the sixth year (1166),
the Emperor went to the Western Capital,
intending to go to Liángxíng 涼陘 to escape the summer heat.
Bóxióng 伯雄 led a group of remonstrance officials to remonstrate.
The Emperor said:
“I will consider it slowly.”
Bóxióng 伯雄 continued to speak without ceasing,
while all his colleagues retreated.
Only after a long time did he rise.
That year,
when they arrived at Liángxíng 涼陘,
there were indeed security oversights during the patrols.
The Emperor remembered Bóxióng 伯雄’s words,
and upon his return,
promoted him to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū 禮部尚書),
saying to his close ministers:
“Many ministers are capable,
but none can compare to Bóxióng’s 伯雄 loyalty and honesty.”
The Emperor said to Bóxióng 伯雄:
“Lóng Páng 龍逄 and Bǐ Gān 比干 both died due to loyal remonstrance.
If they had met enlightened rulers,
how could this have happened!”
Bóxióng 伯雄 replied:
“Wèi Zhēng 魏徵 wished to be a good minister,
precisely because he met an enlightened ruler.”
Then, looking at the Prime Minister, he said:
“The *Shū* 書 (Book of Documents) says, ‘Do not outwardly comply,
then speak ill behind my back.’
I and you, gentlemen, govern the world together.
If there is anything right or wrong,
you should immediately state it to my face.
You gentlemen have reached the position of prime minister.
Now is precisely the time to practice the Way and make your name.
If you seek ease and convenience for yourselves,
and strive for temporary good fortune,
what will you do for future generations?”
All the ministers cheered, “Long live!”
In the twelfth year (1172),
he was appointed Military Commissioner of Qìnnán Jūn 沁南軍 (Qìnnán Circuit),
then recalled to be Academician Recipient of Edicts (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ 翰林學士承旨).
When Prime Minister Shí Jū 石琚 retired,
the Emperor asked:
“Who can replace you, minister?”
Jū 琚 replied:
“Bóxióng 伯雄 can.”
Public opinion at the time considered Jū’s 琚 recommendation to be excellent.
He was again temporarily appointed Grand Mentor (Quán Zhànshì 權詹事).
Bóxióng 伯雄 spoke without reservation,
and his corrections and assistance were numerous and extensive.
Later, if a palace official was obsequious,
people would invariably mention Mentor Yáng 楊詹事 to shame him.
He was appointed Military Commissioner of Dìngwǔ Jūn 定武軍 (Dìngwǔ Circuit),
and then transferred to be Governor of Píngyáng 馮陽 (Píngyáng Yǐn 平陽尹).
Previously,
Zhāng Hào 張浩 had governed Píngyáng 馮陽
with benevolent policies.
When Bóxióng 伯雄 became governor,
the people praised him,
saying:
“First there was Zhāng 張,
then there was Yáng 楊.”
He was transferred to be Governor of Hézhōng 河中.
He died
at the age of sixty-five.
His posthumous name was Zhuāngxiàn 莊獻.
His younger brothers were Bójíe 伯傑 and Bórén 伯仁,
and his clan cousin was Bóyuān 伯淵.
Xíngjiǎn said:
“According to the Táng system,
when the Púshè and Zǎixiàng had their ‘upper day’ (day of official reception),
all officials would assemble to offer congratulations,
and they (Púshè and Zǎixiàng) would descend the steps to return the bows.
In our dynasty, on the Yuánzhèng festival and birthday of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
the Three Grand Tutors (Sān Shī), Three Dukes (Sān Gōng), and Grand Councilors (Zǎizhí) and below must all assemble to offer congratulations,
and the Crown Prince stands to receive and return the bows twice.
Now, when the Zǎizhí of the Shàngshū Shěng have their ‘upper day,’
officials of the sixth rank and below are separated into a different group to offer salutations with a bow (yī hē),
and the Zǎizhí remain seated to return the bows.
The Lángzhōng of the Zuǒ Yòu Sī, who are fifth-rank officials, offer their salutations in the courtyard,
and they (Zǎizhí) also return them while seated.
I believe that sitting and raising a hand to return a bow
is akin to receiving while seated,
and the Zǎizhí receiving congratulations
is a ritual that is even more solemn than that of the Crown Prince.
I fear this is inappropriate in principle.
‘Distinguishing suspicion and clarifying subtlety’
is a great principle of ritual.
I humbly request that on the ‘upper day’ of the Zǎizhí, officials of the third rank and below be permitted to offer congratulations together in one group,
and the Zǎizhí should stand up
and return the salutations according to the ceremony for seeing a third-rank official.”
The Emperor said:
“Why was this matter not rectified earlier?
If the Dūshěng acted presumptuously,
your argument is correct.”
Xíngjiǎn replied:
“The Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) had indeed deliberated on ancient and modern rites,
and drafted a ceremonial procedure,
but the Provincial Court (Shěngtíng) did not comply,
and presumptuously changed it when submitting the memorial.”
The matter was sent to the Shàngshū Shěng for discussion,
and it was then adopted.
On the ‘upper day’ of the Zǎizhí,
all officials of the third rank and below offered congratulations in a single group,
and they (Zǎizhí) stood up to return the bows;
this practice began from this point.
Xíngjiǎn was summoned for a special audience,
and on that occasion discussed the study of historical precedents.
He requested the establishment of two “Inspector-Reviewer” (Jiǎnyuèguān) posts under the Tàicháng Bóshì (Erudites of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices),
to be filled by those with less experience in ritual studies,
and they would be promoted to Bóshì after accumulating experience.
He also said:
“Although we now have the ‘National Collection of Rites’ (Guócháo Jí Lǐ),
regarding the evolution of food and wealth (shíhuò), official posts (guānzhí), and military and penal laws (bīngxíng),
there is no completed work.
I request the compilation of a ‘Comprehensive Digest’ (Huìyào),
to serve for eternity.”
In the fifth year of Chéng'ān,
he was promoted to Shìjiǎng Xuéshì (Academician of the Imperial Lecture),
and concurrently remained Co-Compiler of History (Tóng Xiū Shǐ) and Tián Si Tiān (Supervisor of the Astronomical Bureau) as before.
In the second year of Tàihé,
he served as Deputy Envoy for the Sòng Emperor’s birthday.
The Emperor summoned Wányán Táng, the envoy for the birthday, and warned him, saying:
“When you cross the border, do not drink alcohol,
and in all matters, listen to Xíngjiǎn.”
He said to Xíngjiǎn:
“The Sòng people are particular about rituals,
and fond of minor details.
If there is anything incorrect,
it must all be rectified.
But existing precedents must not be neglected.”
The Emperor further said:
“I have heard that previous envoys, when crossing the Huái River,
upon reaching midstream,
would dispute the boat for demarcation purposes;
this is very unceremonious.
You must warn the boatmen yourself,
and also tell the Sòng envoy: ‘Our two nations have been in peace and harmony for a long time,
it is inappropriate to dispute trivial matters and harm the greater relationship.’
Instruct him carefully,
so that he fully understands this intention.”
In the fourth year,
an edict stated:
“Whenever a memorial is presented,
Zhāng Xíngjiǎn must always be present by my side.”
In the fifth year,
the assembled officials again requested the bestowal of an honorific title (zūn hào) upon the Emperor.
The Emperor did not permit it,
and ordered Xíngjiǎn to draft a reply.
He then asked Xíngjiǎn about Fàn Zǔyǔ’s discussion of honorific titles in the Táng Jiàn during the Sòng dynasty.
Xíngjiǎn replied:
“Sīmǎ Guāng also once admonished against honorific titles,
but his words were not as profound and comprehensive as Zǔyǔ’s,
who argued that for a subject to bestow a posthumous title on an emperor or father
seemed somewhat grievous.”
The Emperor said:
“You should use Zǔyǔ’s meaning to reply,
and also state that although Tàizǔ had an honorific title,
Tàizōng never accepted one.”
Xíngjiǎn requested not to be bound by rhetorical parallelism,
and to cite Zǔyǔ to subtly convey his meaning.
This was granted.
His prose was profound and elegant,
and greatly captured the essence of speaking on behalf of the Emperor.
He was appointed Shùntiān Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Shùntiān Prefecture).
The Emperor said to Xíngjiǎn:
“You have not yet governed the people.
Now that you are going to Bǎozhōu,
it is difficult to accurately assess the true feelings of the populace.
How should you govern
to do it well?”
He replied:
“I will uphold and enforce laws and decrees,
not daring to deviate or err.
In matters of litigation,
I will investigate with compassion.
I will control government clerks,
and restrain the powerful and cunning,
making tranquility my priority,
hoping to achieve even one in ten thousand.”
The Emperor said:
“After half a year or a year in office,
report on the advantages and disadvantages you have found.”
Upon arriving in Bǎozhōu, Xíngjiǎn
submitted a memorial, saying:
“Recently, government lands were requisitioned and allocated to the military.
Once settled,
if there was a complaint requesting a different allocation,
the complaint would be immediately acted upon,
and this continues to this day.
Though called government land,
it is actually taken from the people to be given away,
depriving some to give to others,
thus merely stirring up disputes.
In the area under my jurisdiction, over three hundred qǐng of land in Shēnzé Xiàn had already been allocated,
but now two-thirds are again reported as inundated or saline.
If all such requests are granted,
when will it ever be settled?
I believe a deadline should be set,
and no further complaints allowed for convenience.”
The matter was sent to the Shàngshū Shěng for discussion,
which then memorialized, requesting:
“If there is truly land inundated by water or collapsed into the river, making it unfit for cultivation,
the local administration (běnlù) and Transport Office (Yùnsī) assistant officials should inspect it.
The Shàngshū Shěng will then instruct the Surveillance Commissioner (Ànchásī) to confirm,
and only then will a re-allocation be made.
If the land is saline, alkaline, or barren,
it should be fixed according to the original allocation.”
An imperial edict stated:
“Approved.”
In the sixth year,
he was summoned to be Lǐbù Shàngshū (Minister of Rites),
concurrently Shìjiǎng and Tóng Xiū Guóshǐ (Co-Compiler of National History).
The Mìshūjiān (Director of the Imperial Library) presented the Tàiyī Xīnlì (New Calendar of Tàiyī),
and an edict ordered Xíngjiǎn to proofread it.
In the seventh year,
the Emperor dispatched the inner envoy Féng Xiántóng with a sealed imperial rescript (yùzhá) to Xíngjiǎn, saying:
“I reflect that the two princes of Hào and Zhèng mistakenly violated the immutable principles of heaven,
and thus brought distress upon themselves.
They were buried in straw in the wilderness,
and many years have passed;
I am deeply saddened by this.
I wish to posthumously restore their former noble ranks
and rebury them with full rites.
You should carefully review the Táng dynasty’s bestowal of posthumous titles on Yǐn and Cháo during the Zhēngguān era,
as well as precedents from previous dynasties,
and report it in a sealed memorial.”
He further said:
“I wish for Shí Gǔnǎi to select a site in Wēizhōu for the tomb construction,
and to perform annual sacrifices.
Additionally, one of the sons of Wèi Wáng is to be established as the heir of Zhèng Wáng,
to diligently perform the sacrifices.
Once this matter is carried out,
an imperial edict must naturally be issued.
Draft the general gist of the edict,
and submit it together in a sealed document.”
Xíngjiǎn then prepared a memorial detailing the precedents of Hàn’s Huáinán Lì Wáng Cháng, Chǔ Wáng Yīng, Táng’s Yǐn Tàizǐ Jiànchéng, Cháo Lì Wáng Yuánjí, and Qiáo Wáng Chóngfú,
and also submitted the draft edict,
which was then implemented.
He was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince) and Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ (Academician-in-waiting of the Hànlín Academy),
remaining Shàngshū and Xiūshǐ as before.
Gāo Rǔlì, courtesy name Yánfū,
was a native of Jīnchéng, Yìngzhōu.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the 19th year of Dàdìng (1179)
and gained a reputation for competence while serving in office.
In the 9th month of the 5th year of Míngchāng (1194),
Emperor Zhāngzōng issued an edict to the chief ministers,
asking them to recommend suitable candidates from within and outside the capital for the position of Cìshǐ (prefect).
The emperor personally reviewed the recommendations, noting merits and demerits,
and generally promoted those who were jointly recommended by two officials.
Consequently,
Rǔlì was appointed Shízhōu Cìshǐ, having previously served as Tongzhi of the Jiàngyáng Military Command.
In the 7th month of the 1st year of Chéng'ān (1196),
he was appointed Zuǒ Sī Lángzhōng.
One day, when he was presenting a memorial in the Zǐchén Palace,
all the attending officials had withdrawn.
The emperor's personal fan for cooling suddenly fell off the table.
Rǔlì, considering it outside his duty, dared not pick it up and present it.
After he finished presenting the memorial,
the emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Gāo Rǔlì did not pick up the fan;
he can be said to understand protocol."
Not long after,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū.
Regarding the levying of taxes for military supplies,
the officials in charge in the prefectures and counties sometimes made poor appointments.
The *zhuīxū* (runners) and *zǒuzú* (minor functionaries) exploited the urgency of the matter,
extorting bribes,
which greatly harmed the people.
He proposed,
"From now on, if anyone commits an offense when troops are mobilized,
I request that they be temporarily dealt with according to the 'Law for Investigating and Seizing Bribes'
to punish them,
so that petty individuals may have something to fear."
In the 6th month of the 2nd year (1197),
a regulation was established:
those who accepted bribes during military levies
would receive two years of penal servitude for amounts under one *guàn*,
three years for amounts over one *guàn*,
and execution for amounts over ten *guàn*.
This followed Rǔlì's suggestion.
At that time, when memorials were presented,
the censorial officials were also ordered to withdraw.
Rǔlì then submitted a memorial, stating:
"The state appoints remonstrating officials to serve as attendants,
intending for them to be fully informed about current affairs to evaluate their successes and failures,
not merely to stand in order in a line.
Therefore, the Táng dynasty system stipulated that
whenever officials from the Zhōngshū and Ménxià Secretariats, or those of the third rank and above, entered the palace,
remonstrating officials must accompany them,
so that they could be privy to political matters
and hopefully offer their insights.
Now, from the Provincial Secretariats downward,
whenever memorials are presented at court, everyone withdraws,
advancing and retreating with the various palace guards.
Discussions in the imperial hall are initially unheard,
and when policies are already implemented,
their full details are not known.
To remonstrate after the fact
is truly difficult.
What then is the purpose of the remonstrating office?
If it is said that the officials are not capable,
then select suitable people.
How can they be assigned the responsibility of remonstrance yet kept so distant?
I request that from now on,
remonstrating officials be allowed to be privy to matters when various departments present memorials,
hoping to somewhat rectify this.
Furthermore, the *xiūzhù* (compiler) officials,
who are responsible for recording words and deeds,
should be treated similarly."
The emperor followed his advice.
He also stated:
"In the tenth month of last year, the method of *tuīpái* (investigation and assessment) was implemented,
but it was soon halted after a period,
which truly shows Your Majesty's deep love for the people.
I have heard that according to the Zhōu system,
the population's size and
the quantity of resources were determined seasonally,
and these figures were submitted to the Xiǎo Sītú
to guide governance and education
and to issue levies and commands.
Every three years, a grand census of the empire was conducted,
and this was established as a fixed law.
Since the general inspection in the 4th year of Dàdìng (1164) and thereafter,
over thirty years have passed.
Although *tuīpái* was conducted twice during this period,
the assessment of excess wealth and resources
relied solely on the temporary statements of common people for increases or decreases.
Officials were only concerned with rapid completion
and did not thoroughly investigate the truth.
Consequently, the powerful and influential colluded and escaped,
while the poor and weak, lacking support, were suppressed and had no recourse.
Moreover, in recent years,
there have been repeated levies in the border regions,
increasing the number of impoverished households.
If we simply follow the usual *tuīpái*,
since the regulations from last year have already been implemented,
and are known to everyone,
I fear that new wealthy families will preemptively bribe cunning individuals
hoping that they will make similar declarations when the time comes.
Or they might falsely claim poverty,
deliberately pledging their property at low prices,
or moving their assets elsewhere,
temporarily halting their operations.
With such countless deceptive practices,
hoping for an equitable distribution of wealth
will be difficult.
To reform these abuses,
nothing is better than a factual general inspection.
Order officials in advance to investigate according to the regulations of the 4th year of Dàdìng,
strictly establish rewards and punishments,
set deadlines,
and enforce prohibitions.
For cases that can be treated more leniently or severely, exercise discretion,
eliminate tedious details and simplify procedures,
warn against harassment and promote calmness,
so that the rich cannot escape by chance,
and the distressed can hope for some relief.
Then, taxes will be easy to manage,
and people will avoid the hardship of unfairness."
The emperor ordered the Shàngshū Shěng to implement it after the border situation stabilized.
In the 10th month of that year,
the emperor instructed the Shàngshū Shěng
to dispatch officials to various circuits to conduct a general inspection of the people's resources.
He ordered Hùbù Shàngshū Jiǎ Zhígāng and Rǔlì to first conduct *tuīpái* in the two Jǐngxún (Patrol and Investigation) offices in the capital,
so that officials dispatched to other circuits could use this as a model.
Soon after, he became Tongzhi of Dàxīng Prefecture.
In the 12th month of the 4th year (1199),
he became the Zhuǎnyùnshǐ of Shǎnxī East Circuit.
In the 7th month of the 1st year of Tàihé (1201),
he was transferred to become the Zhuǎnyùnshǐ of Xījīng Circuit.
In the 1st month of the 2nd year (1202),
he became the Ànchásǐ of Běijīng Línhuáng Prefecture Circuit.
In the 2nd month of the 4th year (1204),
he was promoted to Zhuǎnyùnshǐ of Héběi West Circuit.
In the 11th month,
he was promoted to Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ of Zhōngdū Circuit.
In the 6th month of the 6th year (1206),
he was appointed Hùbù Shàngshū.
At that time, the paper currency system was not functioning smoothly.
Rǔlì submitted memorials on various matters,
making many revisions,
which greatly benefited the people.
Details are in the Shíhuò Zhì (Treatise on Food and Money).
The emperor praised his proposals.
An imperial edict was issued to the Shàngshū Shěng, stating:
"The responsibilities of officials inside and outside the court differ.
Recently, those who responded to the call to speak on affairs numbered more than a thousand,
but they were all unaware of the advantages and disadvantages of each department,
making vague statements
that were not comprehensive.
Recently, only Hùbù Shàngshū Gāo Rǔlì,
in discussing several matters of his department,
addressed the pertinent issues,
and all his proposals have been implemented.
Therefore, instruct all internal and external departments to thoroughly investigate and clearly report their advantages and disadvantages.
If something that could be reported is not immediately submitted,
leading to its implementation by a higher authority,
the offender shall be punished accordingly."
In the 6th month of the 2nd year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
Xuānzōng moved south.
When he reached Hándān,
Rǔlì was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
When he reached Tāngyīn,
the emperor heard that grain prices in Biànjīng were soaring,
and feared they would become even more expensive when his entourage arrived.
He asked the chief ministers how to handle it.
They all requested to order the Liúshǒu Sī (Resident Office) to impose restrictions.
Rǔlì alone said:
"Commodity prices fluctuate,
sometimes differing from morning to night.
However, many buyers and few sellers lead to high prices.
As people from various circuits converge on Hénán,
with so many buyers,
how can prices not be high?
If we prohibit trade,
those with goods will close their doors and not sell,
and merchants will no longer transport goods into the city.
Then buyers will be even more desperate, and prices will rise even higher.
There are easy and difficult aspects to this matter;
one must understand them.
What is scarce and hard to obtain now is grain,
while what is abundant and easy to acquire is paper currency.
We should prioritize the difficult and then the easy.
By employing various methods of encouragement,
we must ensure that grain is exchanged for currency.
Then grain prices
will naturally stabilize."
The emperor followed his advice.
In the fifth month of the third year,
the imperial court debated relocating the households of military families from Héběi to Hénán,
leaving the soldiers to guard the commanderies and counties.
Rǔlì said:
"If this matter is indeed carried out,
it will only benefit powerful and wealthy families;
how can poor households relocate?
Furthermore, to be content with one's native land and reluctant to move
is human nature.
Now, if they are all made to go to Hénán,
and they suddenly leave their fields and gardens,
carrying their old and young,
hurrying on the roads,
wandering and losing their homes,
how can this not be pitiable?
Moreover, when the common people along the way see all the military households relocating,
they will certainly be alarmed and suspicious,
thinking that the state is distinguishing between people.
How can their hearts not be shaken?
Furthermore, the soldiers have already left their families,
yet are ordered to protect others.
Judging by human nature,
their unwillingness to exert themselves fully is certain.
The people are extremely foolish yet divine.
Even if they are told of the intention to protect them,
they will not believe it,
which will only lead to mutual chaos
and no one finding peace.
The benefits and harms involved in this are extremely important.
I beg that the marshallates of all circuits, the Pacification Commissioner's Offices, and the General Administration Offices first thoroughly discuss whether it is feasible.
If there is nothing questionable,
then it can be implemented."
The request was not granted.
After the military households were relocated,
it was planned to survey land and distribute it to them,
but there was no fixed decision.
The Emperor then decreed to the Shàngshūshěng, saying:
"Northern soldiers are about to reach Hénán,
and because of this, all military households from various circuits have been mobilized
to collectively plan for defense and preservation.
Now that they have arrived,
food supplies must be provided,
but there is no way to settle them.
Officials can be dispatched to gather elders and ask them:
whether to increase taxes
or give them land,
which of the two is more convenient."
This was also conveyed to Rǔlì.
After a while, the dispatched officials reported:
"The farmers all say
that in recent years, rent and taxes have already been heavy,
and if they are increased further,
their strength is truly insufficient.
They dare not lease official land again
and wish to give it to the army."
Thereupon, Rǔlì memorialized:
"Relocating military households
is a temporary matter.
Farmers leasing official land
is a long-term plan.
In Hénán, private land and official land
are roughly half and half in number.
Moreover, many families entirely lease official land,
with their ancestral graves and estates and wells all within it.
They are mostly poor people;
if it is taken from them all at once,
how will they sustain themselves?
The common people are easily moved and difficult to settle.
Temporarily avoiding taxes,
they made this statement.
But when it is given to others,
the former owner becomes a guest.
Can they not regret it?
If they regret it, resentment will arise.
As when land was allocated in Shāndōng,
fertile and rich fields all went to powerful families,
while barren and poor land was given to poor households.
This was of no benefit to the army,
but the people suffered,
leading to mutual hatred and animosity,
which has not ceased even now.
Past events are not distant
and serve as a clear warning.
The only solution is to double
the official rent to provide half of the military rations,
and then allocate a certain amount of idle official land and horse pasturage to them
for them to cultivate themselves.
Then the common people will be spared the hardship of losing their livelihoods,
and government offices will not have to do things that harm the people.
Moreover, the land in Hénán is most suitable for wheat.
Now, with sufficient rain,
it is precisely the time for sowing.
I sincerely fear that the people's doubts may cause them to miss the seasonal agricultural window,
so it is advisable to decide early."
The Emperor agreed to his request.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
At that time, the Emperor considered that the military households' land should be allocated
so that they could cultivate it in time.
But Rǔlì again memorialized, saying:
"Much of the idle official land and horse pasturage
is privately cultivated by the people.
Now is precisely the time for planting wheat,
and if they know it will be given to others,
they will certainly abandon it.
Even if military households receive it,
it will already be past the season,
only leading to desolation and waste.
If we wait until the harvest is completed before allocating it,
and then collect the yield
to supplement military provisions,
then both public and private interests will benefit.
I beg that officials not be dispatched until the end of the ninth month."
In the tenth month,
Rǔlì said:
"Now, nearly a million people from Héběi military households have relocated to Hénán.
If each person is given one sheng of rice daily,
it amounts to 3.6 million shi annually.
Even if half is given in cash, it still requires 3 million shi of grain.
Hénán's rented land accounts for 240,000 qǐng,
yielding only a little over 1.56 million shi of grain annually.
I further request that beyond regular expenses, additional taxes be levied to provide for them,
and that idle official land and cultivable horse pasturage be given to them."
The memorial was approved.
Then, the Right Supervising Secretary Péimǎn Púlàdū and others were dispatched to various commanderies to distribute it,
thirty *mǔ* per person,
with Rǔlì overseeing the operation.
Subsequently,
the land survey officials returned,
all saying:
"The number of *qǐng* and *mǔ* is very small,
and the land is barren and uncultivable.
If the cultivable land is equally distributed among them,
each person receives very little.
Moreover, they cannot avoid relocating to remote areas,
which the soldiers all consider inconvenient."
Rǔlì then reported this to the Emperor,
who issued an edict ordering the relevant authorities to stop the distribution,
and instead provide only half of the military rations
with the other half commuted into actual cash.
In the first month of the fourth year,
he was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
but all were rejected with gracious imperial edicts.
At that time, the imperial court discussed sending troops to Héběi
to protect the people while they harvested wheat,
but rumors circulated among the populace that the officials would take all of it.
The Emperor heard this
and asked the Chief Ministers:
"What should be done about it?"
Gāoqí and others memorialized:
"If the Privy Council dispatches troops to occupy strategic points
to suppress local bandits,
and also allows the collection of land from fleeing households,
then both the military and the people will benefit.
Should there be an emergency,
the soldiers will certainly do their best."
Rǔlì said:
"This is a very bad plan.
The people of Héshuò rely solely on this wheat for food.
Now there are already rumors,
and if troops are sent again,
this will only increase their suspicion and fear.
It is better to let them be,
and order the Pacification Commissioner's Office to restrain the lawless
to prevent harassment, which would be sufficient.
As for the land of fleeing households, let the relevant authorities collect it
to supplement military provisions; that would be acceptable."
Thereupon, an edict was issued dispatching Péimǎn Púlàdū, a Yuánwàiláng of the Ministry of Revenue, to survey the amount of land
and inquire whether the people wished for troops to be dispatched.
He returned and reported:
"From Huái and Mèng in the west
to Cáo and Shàn in the east,
the wheat seedlings are sparse and not abundant.
Upon questioning the farmers,
they often organize themselves into militia.
When I announced the court's intention to dispatch troops,
they all expressed gratitude but did not wish for it."
Thus, the plan was abandoned.
Rǔlì, having repeatedly begged to retire from office, was not permitted to do so.
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial, saying:
“To achieve extraordinary accomplishments,
one must rely on extraordinary individuals.
Now that the great army has retreated,
it is precisely the time to repair and fortify the passes and to train the soldiers.
It is essential to have talented and astute strategists to make plans in advance,
to aid in the restoration.
I humbly observe that Shàngshū Zuǒchéng and concurrent Xíng Shūmì Fùshǐ, Xū Dǐng,
possesses a multitude of talents
and excels in many capacities.
I request that he be recalled to the court.”
This was not granted.
At that time, Gāo Qí wished that those who spoke on affairs would conduct an annual review of civilian land to levy rents.
The court was about to agree to this.
Rǔlì said:
“I have heard that governing a great nation is like cooking a small fish,
which is the best analogy for good governance.
Since the Dàdìng comprehensive survey in our dynasty,
material resources have been assessed once every ten years,
solely valuing simplicity and tranquility, and avoiding burdening the people.
Now, those who speak propose to follow the example of Héběi, where fields actually sown are measured annually,
and taxes are levied based on these numbers.
This is tantamount to a constant comprehensive survey,
which would surely alarm people and disturb their peace.
Furthermore, the circumstances in Hénán and Héběi are different.
Héběi has repeatedly suffered plunder,
its households have fled or gone into hiding,
and its fields are desolate.
Taxes and levies cannot be based on the original quotas.
Therefore, this provisional method was adopted,
because military provisions are not greatly increased,
and the land is small and easily surveyed.
Since the imperial carriage toured Hénán,
the populace has gathered,
and all fallow land and land abandoned by fleeing households
have been almost entirely cultivated.
Each household pays rent according to its original registration,
and all taxes levied are in accordance with the quotas of the comprehensive survey.
Even though the number of soldiers and horses has increased,
there has been no shortage or error.
How could it be appropriate to disturb everything indiscriminately?
If there is fear that powerful gentry might conceal land and evade taxes,
then even if the officials conduct a survey, would it be entirely accurate?
It would be better to strictly establish rewards and punishments,
allowing people to confess voluntarily
and permitting others to report infractions.
Offenders would be charged with stealing military provisions,
and the land would be given to the accuser.
This alone would be sufficient to instill fear in people,
and all taxes would flow into the government.
Why must we cause such widespread commotion?
Moreover, there are three great unsuitabilities.
If an annual survey is conducted,
then summer fields would be measured in spring,
autumn fields in summer,
and intercropped fields would also be measured in season.
There would be almost no rest within a year.
The people would grow weary and avoid it,
missing planting seasons.
Or they might only cultivate fertile land and abandon the rest.
In that case, the harvest would remain the same, but the taxes paid would decrease.
This is the first unsuitability.
During the survey,
county officials cannot visit every household.
Village headmen would be able to secretly exchange bribes,
manipulating the figures
and creating false documents,
thereby losing the true record.
This is the second unsuitability.
Civilian land and military land are intricately intertwined like dogs' teeth.
They might secretly collude with soldiers to falsely claim military land,
and the court would only rely on the registers of the relevant officials.
If, at that time, the amount were less than the original quota,
then a shortage and error in resources and provisions would be inevitable.
This is the third unsuitability.
When the court undertakes a matter,
it must be put into effect.
If, once implemented, it is then halted,
how can this be considered a good plan?”
The proposal was subsequently shelved.
In the tenth month of Xīngdìng First Year (1216),
he submitted a memorial, stating:
“Those who speak propose to tentatively negotiate peace with the Sòng people to relieve the border populace.
I strongly believe this is not a good plan.
The Sòng people are often deceitful and untrustworthy.
Even if official documents are exchanged,
border defenses cannot be hastily withdrawn.
Since defenses are not withdrawn,
there is no essential difference between negotiating peace or not.
What if they further expand their demands with empty words,
seeking things beyond established protocols and customs,
and their words involve insolence?
What then should be done?
Some say, ‘During the Dàdìng period, envoys were also sent first.
Why is it impossible now?’
I argue that times are different and circumstances vary,
making it difficult to speak by analogy.
In the past, Hǎilíng's army advanced without a just cause,
and the fault lay with us.
Therefore, when Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he first sent Gāo Zhōngjiàn and others to report and explain to the Sòng ruler,
withdrawing from the territories invaded in Huáidiàn to restore old friendly relations.
They subsequently sent envoys,
whose letters were arrogant and disrespectful,
no longer presenting memorials and acknowledging subservience,
but wishing to return to their old borders and be a brotherly state.
Although their Shūmìyuàn occasionally communicated with our Shuàifǔ,
their incursions never ceased.
Soon after,
Commander-in-Chief Zhēngxī Hégéxǐ defeated Sòng generals Wú Lín and Yáo Liángfǔ at Déshùn and Yuánzhōu.
Right Chancellor Púsàn Zhōngyì and Right Deputy Commander Hégé liè Zhìníng defeated Lǐ Shìfǔ at Sùzhōu,
beheading fifty thousand,
and military might greatly increased.
Shìzōng said to his chancellors: ‘In the past, the Sòng people spoke of sending envoys to request peace,
but taking advantage of our unpreparedness, they attacked Sùzhōu.
Now, having been greatly defeated by our army,
with excessive slaughter,
they dare not resume communications.
I pity the long-suffering people of the north and south, who are exhausted by war.
I originally intended to bring peace to the people.
Why dispute minor issues?
Let the Shuàifǔ send a letter to the Sòng people to discuss peace and good relations.’
The Sòng indeed sent envoys to declare peace.
With such imposing power at that time,
and without border troubles,
they were ultimately exempted from the ritual of presenting memorials and acknowledging subservience.
Now, the Sòng have abandoned their trust and broken their alliance,
invading our borders.
The fault lies with them.
If they request peace,
it would be reasonable.
Why should we initiate this discussion and show weakness ourselves?
I fear it would not only be useless,
but would invite slander and insult.”
In the eleventh month,
Rǔlì said:
“I have heard that a nation is founded on its people,
and the people are rooted in their wealth.
Therefore, a ruler must first love and nurture these foundations.
In the state's levies and requisitions,
Hénán bears a heavy burden,
and the collected taxes and rents are often three times the old rate.
Now, the provincial departments calculate that the annual collection of currency (tōngbǎo) is insufficient to cover expenditures,
and thus demand seventy million strings of mulberry bark and old paper money from the people to make up the deficit.
Recently, as currency became somewhat stagnant,
this was further doubled.
Among Hénán households,
farmers constitute two-thirds.
Now, the collected taxes and rents are still largely insufficient,
and this order is issued again.
If they do not sell grain to pay the required rent,
they will surely reduce their food to meet the demand.
There are matters of difficulty and ease,
and situations of urgency and delay.
What is currently urgent and difficult to obtain is fodder and grain,
which comes from the people's labor,
and its supply is limited.
This can be planned for gradually.
What is easy to manage is the paper currency system,
which is administered by the state,
and its changes are inexhaustible.
Previously, large banknotes became stagnant and were exchanged for small banknotes.
When small banknotes became problematic, they were changed to precious notes (bǎoquàn).
When precious notes did not circulate, they were changed to currency (tōngbǎo).
Adaptations and changes were all made by the superior authorities.
Why bother the people for this?
They are already struggling to fully supply military provisions, which are still insufficient,
and now additional currency (tōngbǎo) is levied.
If they cannot provide it,
they will flee.
If the people flee, agricultural work ceases,
and from where will military provisions be obtained?
Officials do not investigate long-term plans but covet immediate results,
not securing the fundamental source but arguing over minor details.
I sincerely fear that both military provisions and the paper currency system will be hindered.
It is not that I am unconcerned about the paper currency system,
nor that I intentionally oppose the provincial departments.
It is simply that the harm of slightly stagnant paper currency and slightly increased prices is minor,
while the harm of an unsettled populace and insufficient military provisions is severe.
I humbly request Your Majesty to externally consider the circumstances,
and inwardly consider my words,
and specifically order the relevant authorities to reduce or exempt these levies,
so that the hearts of the people will be harmonious and joyful,
and there will be hope for the unmet rent.”
In the second month of the third year,
he was made jiedushi of Ānwǔ Jūn,
and concurrently jianchashi within Jìzhōu.
When he first arrived,
he immediately submitted a memorial outlining four matters.
The first said:
"The bandit faction of Yáng Ān'ér will be captured any morning or evening;
they are truly nothing to worry about.
The urgency of today
lies only in winning the hearts of the people.
Previously, when the imperial army campaigned against the rebels,
they did not distinguish between good and evil,
but indiscriminately exterminated all,
plundering their assets
and seizing their women.
This caused the residents to become fearful and suspicious,
fleeing and gathering in the mountains and forests.
Now, it is appropriate to issue clear edicts to the officials in charge,
strictly restraining them,
and not allowing them to plunder common people.
If this is done, the common people will have no unease in their hearts,
the schemes of treacherous individuals to deceive and coerce will not succeed,
and their power will gradually wane."
The second said:
"Since the outbreak of the military chaos,
many powerful officials in commanderies and counties
have been able to gather righteous volunteers,
crushing local bandits.
Although the court granted them local official positions,
before long, people were dispatched to replace them.
Now, the former officials are those whom the people have long respected,
while the new ones may not all be capable.
In times of urgency, this can
provoke animosity and spoil affairs.
From now on, when there are vacancies in commanderies and counties,
I request that the Shàngshū Shěng select and propose candidates for appointment.
As for the former officials,
those who are convenient and comforting to the people should be promoted and employed.
If their rank and grade are insufficient,
let them temporarily hold the position,
and upon achieving merit, they should be officially appointed.
This way, everyone can fully utilize their talents,
and affairs will be easily established."
The third said:
"Among the military officers, scarcely one or two in ten dare to advance and fight.
If there are such,
they should immediately be tasked with achieving merit,
and should not be assigned to other posts."
The fourth said:
"The military provisions in Shāndōng were all acquired through the sale of official ranks.
And some, holding imperial edicts, sought official positions.
The selection bureau, finding that some grades were not suitable for sale, often rejected them.
Indeed, if what was sold was inappropriate,
it is the fault of the officials in charge;
how can they blame those individuals?
Moreover, Hǎidài is a critical region,
with bandits still unpacified.
The fields yield nothing,
and the granaries have no stores.
If military provisions are suddenly insufficient,
and one wishes to sell official ranks again,
who will believe it?"
The court adopted many of his suggestions.
In the eighth month,
he was summoned to become lìbù shàngshū.
In the ninth month,
he was changed to hùbù shàngshū.
In the twelfth month,
he was transferred to lǐbù shàngshū,
concurrently holding the position of tóng xiū guóshǐ.
In the second month of the fourth year,
he was made tàizǐ shàobǎo,
concurrently with his former posts.
At this time, the Shàngshū Shěng memorialized:
"Wánýán Hǎinú, the vice-envoy for pacification and proclamation in Liáodōng, said:
'The councilor Wáng Kuì once said,
our dynasty inherits from Gāoxīn,
and is a descendant of the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì).
In the past, Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn revered Táo Táng,
and Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng revered Lǎozǐ,
both establishing temples for them.
Our dynasty has existed for a hundred years until now,
yet has not established a temple for the Yellow Emperor.
Is this not a source of shame compared to Hàn and Táng?'"
It also said:
"When our dynasty first arose,
its banners were still red,
clearly indicating the Fire virtue.
The ancestral sacrifices for the ruling virtue
are neglected and not discussed,
which also does not accord with the emphasis on sacrifices in the Rítuál Classics.
This is what your servant heard from Kuì.
I request that the court deliberate on this matter."
An imperial edict questioned the relevant officials.
Xíngxìn memorialized, saying:
"According to the 'Veritable Records of the Founder,' it merely states that he came from Gāolì,
and it has not been heard that he originated from Gāoxīn.
Now, the basis for wishing to establish a temple for the Yellow Emperor,
the Yellow Emperor being the ancestor of Gāoxīn –
even if one were to say we inherit from him,
we should correspond to the Wood virtue.
Yet now it speaks of the Fire virtue;
what does this mean?
Moreover, in the early days of the state, Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) had a teaching:
because the Wánýán tribe mostly esteemed white,
and also took 'gold' for its unchanging nature,
he established 'Great Gold' (Dà Jīn) as the state name,
and never discussed the succession of virtues.
Recently, in Zhāngzōng's reign, the hundred officials were first gathered to discuss it,
and by succeeding the demise of the Sòng, which was of the Fire element,
it was settled as the Earth virtue,
which was announced to the ancestral temple and proclaimed throughout the empire.
Clearly, what Kuì said is utterly preposterous."
The emperor approved this.
In the eighth month,
when the emperor was about to perform the ritual of associating and enjoying sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào),
an edict ordered adherence to the sixteen prostrations (bài) ritual of Shìzōng.
Xíngxìn, along with the ritual officials, participated in determining the ceremonial procedures.
He memorialized, suggesting that the ritual of forty-four prostrations should be followed.
The emperor praised and accepted it;
the account is in the 'Treatise on Rites' (Lǐ Zhì).
After the sacrifice,
Xíngxìn was bestowed with a precious warrant for twenty thousand strings of cash and ten rolls of precious silk.
The emperor admonished him, saying:
"For the bowing ritual at the Grand Ancestral Temple,
I initially intended to follow Shìzōng's practice.
Your memorial
fully described the reading of the祝 (zhù) prayer with each chamber,
which was especially reasonable.
If not for your words,
I would almost have erred.
Therefore, I especially commend and reward you with this.
From now on, you should be even more dedicated in every matter."
In the twelfth month of that year,
Xíngxìn resigned from office
due to the death of his father, Wěi.
In the third month of Xīngdìng First Year,
he was reinstated to his former position,
provisionally serving as cān zhī zhèngshì.
In the sixth month,
he was formally appointed cān zhī zhèngshì.
At that time, Gāo Qí was prime minister,
monopolizing power and exercising authority.
He resented those who did not align with him,
and scholars and officials often suffered humiliation.
Only Xíngxìn repeatedly cited old regulations and strongly opposed his wrongdoings.
Coincidentally, Sòng troops invaded the border,
and the court debated sending an envoy to investigate.
Gāo Qí and others considered it undignified,
but Xíngxìn alone memorialized, saying:
"To consider sending an envoy inappropriate now,
your servant is truly perplexed.
The argument is merely: 'Sending an envoy would be to first show weakness.
If they do not respond,
or respond disrespectfully,
it would further undermine national dignity.'
Your servant alone believes otherwise.
They exploit our weaknesses and openings,
repeatedly engaging in invasions and plunder.
Border officials repel them with troops, and they return again.
If our great nation does not reproach them with words but confronts them with arms,
is this not showing weakness?
As for inquiring without a response,
or responding disrespectfully,
the fault lies entirely with them;
how does it harm us?
In the early days of Dàdìng,
they once violated our order.
Although Shìzōng sent Prime Minister Wūzhě to serve as xíngshěng in Biàn,
he actually ordered Marshal Sāhélián to first question them with diplomatic words,
whereupon they submitted to guilt.
Later, the Sòng ruler seized our national letters,
and the court again wished to deploy troops.
Prime Minister Lóushì alone deemed it unacceptable.
When Lǐang Sù, Shàngshū of the Board of Punishments, went with the imperial mandate,
he soon also yielded.
During Zhāngzōng's time,
their wantonness was most extreme,
yet we still first investigated and questioned before resorting to military action.
Therefore, sending an envoy to investigate is precisely a national precedent;
how is there any loss of dignity?
Moreover, the nation faces many difficulties,
and the garrisoning of troops has been prolonged.
If we do not consider ways to allow them to rest,
what will become of the people's strength?
Your servant, a mere scholar, has no exceptionally profound theories,
but when the matter presents an opportunity,
I dare not refrain from fully expressing my humble opinion.
May Your Majesty discern it."
The emperor again ordered the Shàngshū Shěng to deliberate.
Gāo Qí and others memorialized:
"What Xíngxìn said indeed follows old regulations,
but the situation today is different from the past."
An edict ordered to wait for now.
Afterwards,
Gāo Rǔlì also memorialized that sending an envoy first was inconvenient,
and the proposal was thus dropped.
The account is in the 'Biography of Rǔlì'.
At that time, many Censorate (jiānchá yùshǐ 監察御史) officials were subjected to flogging.
Xíngxìn (行信) then submitted a memorial, saying:
"During the Dàdìng (大定) era,
Censorate officials who committed crimes were mostly allowed to redeem themselves with a fine,
or at most had their salaries withheld.
In serious cases, they were merely demoted to an outer post.
Those who were flogged were all for specific reasons.
At that time, the presiding official Chéng Huī (程輝) had already personally discussed its impropriety,
and there was also an imperial decree
that censors' duty was to impeach.
If they were lenient or followed others,
it did not mean that all cases of oversight were treated the same.
Recently, regardless of the magnitude of the matter or the severity of the circumstances,
all were indiscriminately flogged,
claiming it was a precedent from the Dàdìng (大定) era and a clear instruction from the previous reign.
