This is excessive."
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū shěng 尚書省) to revise the regulations concerning the crimes of Censorate officials.
When the Imperial Historiography Office (shǐguǎn xiūzhāng 史館修章) was compiling the *Veritable Records of Zhāngzōng* (*Zhāngzōng Shílù* 章宗實錄),
the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū shěng 尚書省) memorialized:
"According to old regulations,
whenever history was compiled,
chancellors and presiding officials all participated.
However, there was one Jurchen and one Han Chinese official for each.
During the Chóngqìng (崇慶) era,
Liáng Kuò (梁𤨠), an Associate Administrator of the Department of State Affairs (cānzhī zhèngshì 參知政事), was concurrently appointed,
and then Zhāng Xíngjiǎn (張行簡), an Academician Remonstrant (hànlín chéngzhǐ 翰lín chéngzhǐ), was ordered to work with him.
This was because Xíngjiǎn (行簡) had a family tradition of scholarship,
and had extensive research.
Now, in compiling the *Veritable Records of Zhāngzōng* (*Zhāngzōng Shílù* 章宗實錄),
Ruǐlì (汝礪), the Left Assistant (zuǒ chéng 左丞), has already been appointed concurrently.
It is fitting to order Xíngxìn (行信), an Associate Administrator of the Department of State Affairs (cānzhī zhèngshì 參知政事), to participate in the compilation, following Xíngjiǎn's (行簡) precedent."
The decree was approved.
In the second month of the second year,
he was sent out as the Military Commissioner (jiédu shǐ 節度使) of Zhānghuà Commandery (zhānghuà jūn 彰化軍),
and concurrently the Surveillance Commissioner (guǎnnèi guānchá shǐ 管內觀察使) of Jīng Prefecture (jīng zhōu 涇州).
He was instructed, saying:
"Initially,
I appointed you to participate in state affairs because many court officials praised your talent.
However, during court discussions,
you often failed to adhere to correctness,
arbitrarily proposing differing views,
which is far from the way of a chancellor.
Furthermore, I hear that recently you have shown no interest in actively managing affairs.
Is it because you seek a relaxed position?
Now that you are given this post,
you should understand this."
Previously,
Hézhōu (合周) of the imperial clan avoided the enemy and did not engage,
and moreover falsely claimed to have secretly received an imperial edict.
He was imprisoned and was to be executed.
Many imperial relatives submitted petitions to plead for a lighter sentence.
Gāo Qí (高琪) believed that since ancient times, there had been no one who committed a crime and was exempted from punishment by appeal.
Xíngxìn (行信) alone said:
"There is no distinction between ancient and modern times in this matter.
However, Hézhōu (合周) has always been loyal and filial,
so perhaps he can be pardoned."
Furthermore, because Xíngzhēn (行貞), Xíngxìn's (行信) cousin, was living in Shāndōng (山東)
and had accepted a spurious appointment from the Red Jacket rebels (hóng'ǎo zéi 紅襖賊),
and the Bureau of Military Affairs (shūmì yuàn 樞密院) had obtained a letter from the Sòng (宋) people
implicating Xíngxìn (行信),
he was therefore sent out.
His son Jǔ (莒),
who was then a clerk in the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū shěng lìngshǐ 尚書省令史),
was also ordered to be given a separate appointment.
Previously,
Xíngxìn (行信) had stated:
"According to current law,
when officials are sentenced for crimes,
they are often subjected to flogging.
I humbly observe that during the Dàdìng (大定) era, Emperor Shìzōng (世宗) issued an imperial decree
that officials who deliberately disobeyed imperial edicts should be punished with penal servitude for a certain number of years, flogging for a certain number of strokes, and also flogging.
However, for more than thirty years thereafter,
officials in charge of sentencing never cited this,
as it was not a regulation intended to be a lasting precedent.
I request that it be thoroughly reviewed."
After Xíngxìn (行信) was sent out,
the Emperor referred his memorial to the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū shěng 尚書省).
At this point,
the prime ministers memorialized:
"From now on, for those who violate the directives in the memorialed articles and other regulations,
and are to be punished for violating imperial decrees,
their penal servitude and flogging sentences can be commuted by ransom.
However, for those who specifically violate an imperial edict,
they shall be dealt with according to the Dàdìng (大定) precedent."
The decree was approved.
Not long after Xíngxìn (行信) left,
the Emperor once instructed the prime ministers, saying:
"Since Zhāng Xíngxìn (張行信) was demoted,
you all have become silent.
This is utterly wrong.
You all fully know Xíngxìn's (行信) case.
Is it because of what was said?
From now on, you should all speak your minds fully,
without further fear or reservation."
Upon his arrival in Jīng (涇), Xíngxìn (行信) immediately wrote a letter, saying:
"Horses are the foundation of military strength,
and with military campaigns not yet ceased,
horse administration cannot be neglected.
Since my arrival in Jīng (涇),
I have heard that many wealthy commoners in Shǎnxī (陝西) purchase horses in Hé Prefecture (hé zhōu 河州)
and then transport them inland,
profiting perhaps a hundredfold.

I also saw the provincial horse-purchasing official, Úgǔlùn Huánduān (烏古論桓端), an Assistant Prefect (pàn guān 判官) of Píngliáng Prefecture (píngliáng fǔ 平涼府), purchasing in Táo Prefecture (táo zhōu 洮州).
With a hundred ingots of silver, he nearly obtained a thousand horses,
saying that the Mó Bō (木波) tribes of the Qiāng (羌) barbarians and other barbarian households have extensive livestock.
It seems that previous officials sent there either suppressed their prices
or forcibly seized them,
thus losing their harmony.
Moreover, they often lacked silver,
which is why they could not obtain many horses.
I also hear that the barbarian lands had a poor harvest this autumn,
and they readily exchange silver obtained from selling horses for grain.
At the turn of winter and spring, food will certainly be scarce,
and horse prices will be very low.
I request that the relevant authorities transport silver and grain to Táo (洮) and Hé (河) prefectures,
and select and entrust those who understand barbarian customs and grasp current changes, like Huánduān (桓端), to trade with them.
If ten thousand taels of silver are invested,
a thousand good horses can be acquired.
This opportunity must not be missed;
the court should plan for it urgently."
He further said:
"Recently, when border soldiers achieved merits,
the court dispatched envoys to proclaim and comfort them,
and bestowed upon them official rewards.
All were grateful for the imperial favor
and wished to exert their utmost effort.
This is indeed an effective way to encourage them.
However, the practice of presenting gifts to the envoys, whether horses or gold,
has become customary,
which I do not understand.
During the Dàdìng (大定) era,
a regulation for sending gifts to envoys was once established,
with fixed amounts for officials of the fifth rank and above,
but it was later abolished.
Moreover, the current situation is different from the past.
Officials of the sixth rank and below, and those who only received promotions to sinecure positions,
also cannot avoid presenting gifts.
If they cannot afford it,
they collect from their subordinates to meet the demand,
even leading to some being punished for it.
Those soldiers risked their lives and rendered meritorious service,
only to receive imperial favor,
yet they are troubled by these presentations.
Is this the intention of the court?
I request that the relevant authorities follow the Dàdìng (大dìng) precedent,
considering current affairs,
and clearly establish ranks,
so that what is given and taken has limits,
without harming the overall system,
thus benefiting both superiors and subordinates."
In the fourth month of the second year,
Xū Dǐng requested to retire.
The Emperor dispatched a close attendant to convey a message, saying:
"You are already advanced in years,
which I am not unaware of.
However, affairs of the realm are just beginning to take shape.
You are an old retainer,
so you should endeavor to see them through."
Xū Dǐng believed that Xuānzōng was too involved in minor matters,
which was not the style of an emperor.
So he submitted a memorial, stating:
"The world is vast,
the affairs of government are numerous,
and the complexities of finance and grain are many.
These cannot all be handled by the nine layers of the imperial court.
They must be entrusted to the proper officials.
The Son of Heaven merely grasps the main principles and holds officials accountable for success.
Especially now, with many difficulties,
how can one personally attend to minor details?
May Your Majesty delegate power to trusted ministers,
and merely await the successful outcomes.
Then the time for restoration will not be far off."
The Emperor read his memorial and was displeased.
He said to his chief ministers:
"I only fear negligence,
but Xū Dǐng speaks in such a way, why is this?"
Gāo Qí thereupon memorialized:
"The Sacred Ruler has the imperial ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain at heart,
embodying the principle of Heaven's vigorous movement.
He diligently attends to all governmental affairs,
working day and night without rest.
This is the path to great peace.
Xū Dǐng's words are incorrect."
The Emperor was pleased with this.
In the first month of the third year,
the Emperor said:
"Regarding officials in border prefectures and sub-prefectures, there is already a regulation for reducing the required years and months of service.
As for those who command troops and guard border passes,
who campaign and are exposed to the elements,
enduring all kinds of hardships,
they should uniformly receive reductions and exemptions
to demonstrate encouragement."
This was followed.
In the second month,
the Emperor said:
"According to recent regulations,
individuals who achieve merit or commit crimes at the front lines
cannot be summarily punished or rewarded by the Xíngshěng, Xíngyuàn, or Shuàifǔ.
Indeed, rewards originating from the central court properly convey imperial grace;
this is certainly most appropriate.
However, if main commanders are unable to enforce punishments for specific crimes,
then subordinates will have no fear, and orders cannot be carried out."
The chief ministers found this difficult.
The Emperor asked the officials of the Shūmìyuàn,
who responded in agreement with Xū Dǐng's previous statement.
Thereupon, an edict was issued,
stating that from now on, officials of the fourth rank and below would all be permitted to make such decisions.
At this time, Marshal Nèizú Chéngyì and Yílà Niánhé were attacking Sòng,
and many of the cities they captured were burned and plundered.
Thereupon, Xū Dǐng memorialized, saying:
"Chéngyì and others were ordered to proclaim the nation's power,
which is 'to comfort the people and punish the guilty.'
Now the grand army has already taken Wǔxiū
and will soon reach Xīngyuán.
Xīngyuán is the strategic throat of Hanzhōng and Xīshǔ.
I request that the marshals be instructed
not to burn and plunder the captured cities for now,
but to endeavor to pacify and comfort the people.
If even one commandery is truly tranquil,
and not a single autumn hair is harmed,
then the remaining thirty armies
will submit without attack.
If they resist the royal army,
then it is appropriate to slaughter them."
The Emperor greatly approved of his words,
and accordingly issued an edict to Chéngyì.
Xū Dǐng, due to old age, repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to retire.
The Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Xū Dǐng requests to retire due to old age,
but I observe that his energy has not yet declined.
I have already sent someone to comfort and persuade him.
Xū Dǐng once recommended Bǎhúlǔ,
believing him to be far superior to himself,
and wished him to be his replacement.
Bǎhúlǔ is indeed good,
but when it comes to managing talented individuals
and making decisions on crucial matters,
he falls far short of Xū Dǐng."
Soon after, for his merits in the campaign against Sòng,
he was promoted one rank.
In the eighth month,
the Emperor said:
"I was ordered to concurrently oversee Hédōng.
Recently, the Shuàifǔ of Jìn'ān ordered that within a hundred li, only mulberry, jujube, and fruit trees be left,
and all others be cut down.
Now is the autumn harvest,
and to take such action to hinder the people's work
not only fails to repel the enemy but also harms the people.
This is not a good plan.
Moreover, in case of sudden alarm,
how can all the felled trees be cleared away
so as not to be used by the enemy?
Even if other trees are felled,
are mulberry, jujube, and house timbers not also wood?
This is largely futile.
I have already instructed the Shuàifǔ to stop this,
but the Assistant Grand Commissioner Zuǒ Dūjiān Wányán Lǘshān said that he had received an imperial decree to clear the fields.
I do not understand how this can be."
An edict was issued to allow Xū Dǐng to make plans as he saw fit.
At this time,
the grand army of the Yuán dynasty launched a large-scale invasion into Shǎnxī.
Xū Dǐng had many strategies for assessing the enemy,
but some court officials attempted to obstruct him.
The Emperor instructed the officials of the Shūmìyuàn, saying:
"Xū Dǐng's plans are certainly without error.
From now on, you and others need not instruct him."
Soon after, another message was sent, saying:
"You are the sole authority in your region.
You may plan all matters as you deem appropriate,
so why must you report back to the central court for every single thing,
merely causing delay?"
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to the title of Wēnguó Gōng,
and retired.
An imperial edict stated:
"You have repeatedly requested to retire,
which I initially did not permit,
hoping that once things settled down,
you would once again be of use to me.
Now I grant your request.
You may still reside in the capital,
and should there be important matters, you can be consulted."
In the third month of the fifth year,
the Emperor sent a close attendant to convey a message to Xū Dǐng and Zuǒchéng Jiǎ Yìqiān, saying:
"From last winter until now,
there has been exceptionally little rain and snow.
The people's hearts are uneasy,
and military supplies may be lacking,
causing severe harm.
You are all renowned ministers and old veterans.
How should this situation be handled now?
I wished to summon you to the Shàngshūshěng for a meeting,
but feared disagreement with the current prime ministers,
making it difficult to openly dispute.
Therefore, I order you to be consulted at your residences.
Please present your thoughts fully,
without concealment."
In the fifth month of Yuánguāng first year,
the Emperor issued an imperial decree to his prime ministers, saying:
"Former Píngzhāng Xū Dǐng, Zuǒchéng Jiǎ Yìqiān, Gōngbù Shàngshū Zhālǐjí, and Hànlín Xuéshì Bódié
are all retired veteran ministers
who have extensive experience in national affairs.
They should be invited to the ministry to discuss matters of advantage and disadvantage."
An attendant was then sent to each of the four individuals to convey this intention.
In the sixth month,
Jìnyáng Gōng Guō Wénzhèn memorialized:
"Héshuò has been under attack for years.
Previously, they would always come in autumn and leave in spring,
but now they remain even in the height of summer,
and moreover, they do not delight in slaughtering,
allowing the people to cultivate their fields freely.
This is indeed unfathomable.
The Shūfǔ repeatedly dispatches me to assemble local troops for battle,
but although the ducal residences are nominally enfeoffed,
their power is actually weak and scattered,
and they do not command each other.
They are busy enough trying to protect themselves.
If the imperial court does not immediately send troops as reinforcement,
I fear that the people will think that Héběi has been abandoned,
which is a very poor strategy.
I humbly observe that former Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Xū Dǐng
possesses both military and civil talents,
and his prestige is very high.
When he previously served as Xíngshěng in Hédōng,
people gladly served him.
Although he is now retired,
his vigor has not declined.
I beg that he be entrusted with heavy troops
and made to oversee all the ducal residences,
to fight and defend together.
Then perhaps everyone will respond,
making restoration easy.
May Your Majesty consider this."
At that time, Marshal Púchá Qīqǐn (蒲察七斤) rebelled in Tōngzhōu (通州).
Jiāng Zhì (江摯) was repeatedly sent by spies to instigate him.
Zhì (摯) feared that he would be implicated,
so he submitted a memorial to defend himself.
An imperial edict was issued to reassure him, saying:
"We have known you for a long time,
how could you be incited?
You should focus wholeheartedly on your duties,
and not be discouraged by suspicion and mistrust."
In the eighth month,
he was made acting grand councilor.
Soon after, he was appointed grand councilor,
and established the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) in Héběi (河北).
Earlier,
Zhì (摯) had said:
"The eastern and western routes of Héběi (河北) are strategic locations,
but Hú Lùn (胡論), the commander of Zhēndìng (真定), repeatedly abandons the city and flees south,
causing alarm in the prefectures and counties.
With autumn defenses imminent,
this is highly concerning.
I wish to recruit soldiers and go with my former unit, the Xīshān Zhōngyì Jūn (西山忠義軍), to pacify the region."
The emperor approved this,
hence this appointment.
In the eleventh month,
he had an audience with the emperor.
On the day Rénshēn (壬申),
he was sent to offer sacrifices to the River God in Yícūn (宜村).
In the twelfth month,
he resumed his duties in the Department of State Affairs in Héběi (河北).
In the first month of the fourth year,
he was promoted to Vice-Minister of the Right (Shàngshū Yòuchéng).
He had previously submitted a memorial
suggesting the opening of Qìnshuǐ (沁水) for easier transport of provisions.
By this time,
an edict ordered the relevant officials to open it.
At this time,
Héběi (河北) suffered a great famine.
Zhì (摯) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Currently, Hèshuò (河朔) is experiencing severe famine,
people are resorting to cannibalism,
and in Guān (觀), Cāng (滄) and other prefectures, a *dǒu* of rice costs over ten *liǎng* of silver,
with dead bodies piled up everywhere.
I humbly observe that merchants are permitted to transport grain across the river,
but for every *shí* of grain, the government purchases eight tenths of it.
Those merchants do not have a charitable heart;
their crossing the river is merely for the sake of high profits.
If there is no profit,
who would do it again?
Thus, although there is the name of aiding the people,
there is effectively no grain being transported across.
How is this different from not transporting it at all?
In ancient times during the Spring and Autumn period, various states had their own borders,
yet when Jìn (晉) was famished, Qín (秦) supplied it with grain.
When Qín (秦) was famished,
Jìn (晉) closed its granaries,
which has been ridiculed for a thousand ages.
Moreover, today the whole world is one family,
and the people of Hèshuò (河朔) are all Your Majesty's children.
Having suffered from war,
they are especially to be pitied.
How can Your Majesty bear to sit idly and watch them die without rescue?
The hearts of men are precarious;
I fear that those who incite rebellion
will seize this as an excuse to rise up.
I request that the government grain purchase be stopped,
and that people be freely allowed to transport and sell grain for convenience."
An edict ordered the Department of State Affairs to implement this.
At that time, tens of thousands of Hóng'ǎo Zéi (紅襖賊) entered the borders of Línyí (臨沂) and Fèixiàn (費縣).
The government army defeated them
and captured the fake Grand Commissioner of Military Affairs (Xuānhuī Shǐ), Lǐ Shòufǔ (李壽甫), alive.
When questioned,
he stated that his followers were remnants of Yáng Ān'ér (楊安兒) and Liú Èrzǔ (劉二祖),
and had now regrouped to sixty thousand.
The bandit leader Hǎo Dìng (郝定), a native of Sìshuǐ (泗水), Yǎozhōu (兗州),
had appointed various officials
and usurped the title of Emperor of Dàhàn (大漢).
He had already attacked the prefectures of Tài'ān (泰安), Téng (滕), Yǎn (兗), and Shàn (單),
as well as more than ten counties including Láiwú (萊蕪) and Xīntài (新泰).
He had also breached Pīzhōu (邳州) and Guǎizigu (碙子堌),
acquiring hundreds of boats.
Recently, he had sent people north to conspire and south to connect, all reaching agreements,
and was about to cross the river to cause chaos.
Zhì (摯) reported his words to the emperor,
and further said:
"Currently, the route between Pī (邳) and Téng (滕) is blocked,
so this scheme may indeed be true."
An edict was then issued appointing Zhì (摯) to oversee the Department of State Affairs in Dōngpíng (東平),
concurrently acting as the Grand Commander of Troops for that route,
to entice the bandits;
if they did not comply, he was to lead troops to capture and suppress them.
In the fourth month of Xīngdìng (興定)元年,
local bandits in Jǐnán (濟南), Tài'ān (泰安), Téng (滕), Yǎn (兗) and other prefectures rose simultaneously,
engaging in rampant looting.
Zhì (摯) dispatched Tíkòng (提控) Yáoshòu (遙授), the Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Dìzhōu (棣州), Wányán Tíng (完顏霆), to lead troops to suppress them.
In total, over a thousand heads were cut off,
and the remaining followers of the fake marshal Shí Huāwǔ (石花五) and Xià Quán (夏全), amounting to twenty thousand able-bodied men
and fifty thousand old and young, surrendered.
In the winter of that year,
he was promoted to Zīdé Dàfū (資德大夫)
and concurrently served as the Minister of the Three Judicial Offices (Sānsī Shǐ).
In the second month of the second year,
Zhì (摯) submitted a memorial:
"Shāndōng (山東) and Héběi (河北) have repeatedly suffered from war and unrest;
the remaining populace is lamenting,
truly pitiable.
Recently, the imperial court dispatched officials to various places to pacify and consolidate them,
which is a great benevolence.
However, as I am honored to be among the chief ministers,
I humbly request to continue my journey
to proclaim the nation's virtue and trustworthiness,
so that the exhausted and suffering may find some relief.
This is also a way of repaying [Your Majesty]."
The chief ministers found it difficult,
but not long after,
an edict ordered Zhì (摯) to oversee the Department of State Affairs in Héběi (河北),
concurrently managing the affairs of the Three Judicial Offices and pacifying the region.
After he set out,
he again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Recently, when I passed the south bank of Huánglínggǎng (黃陵崗),
many poor old and young people declared themselves to be farmers from Héběi (河北),
who had moved south to avoid the enemy's disturbances.
They now wish to return to their homeland for spring plowing and planting,
but the river prohibitions obstruct them.
I believe that the river prohibitions were originally intended to guard against those coming from the north.
These people are going from south to north;
how can there be any deceit?
I request that the relevant authorities verify their identities and allow them to cross."
The edict was sent to the Department of State Affairs,
and the chief ministers reported,
"It is appropriate to order the Bureau of Military Affairs (Jīnfǔ) to deliberate on this."
The emperor said:
"The people are starving and dying;
why are you still arranging procedures?
Order them to be released quickly!"
In the fourth month,
the Pacification Deputy Commissioner Huángguó Ālúdá (黃摑阿魯荅) defeated Lǐ Quán (李全) in Mìzhōu (密州).
Initially,
the bandit leader Lǐ Quán (李全) occupied Mìzhōu (密州) and the counties of Jiāoxī (膠西) and Gāomì (高密).
Zhì (摯) commanded troops to suppress him.
At that time, four bandits from Gāomì (高密), including Chén Quán (陳全), secretly reported to the Pacification Deputy Commissioner Huángguó Ālúdá (黃摑阿魯荅)
that they wished to act as an inside force.
Ālúdá (阿魯荅) then dispatched Tíkòng (提控) Zhū Chēn (朱琛) to lead five hundred soldiers to assist them.
At that time, Lǐ Quán (李全) and his subordinate Yú Máng'ér (于忙兒) were both in the city.
Hearing that the government army was approaching from the west,
Lǐ Quán (李全) secretly escaped,
leaving Máng'ér (忙兒) at a loss.
Ālúdá (阿魯荅) rushed to the city walls,
beating drums and shouting to press them.
The eight hundred bandits defending the parapets all came down to surrender.
The remaining four thousand bandits fled,
and the army advanced to intercept and attack them,
beheading over a thousand
and capturing more than a hundred people.
The military supplies seized were numerous,
and the city was thus recovered.
That night,
Chēn (琛) again used Chén Quán's (陳全) plan
and captured Gāomì (高密).
In the sixth month,
the emperor sent an edict to Zhì (摯), saying:
"You have toiled diligently for the royal house,
not shying away from difficulties,
holding a ministerial position while traveling between mountain strongholds and water stockades,
protecting the farmers in harvesting their two crops of wheat.
Your loyalty and dedication are fully known to Us.
Nevertheless,
as a high minister,
during the autumn defense period, you must also choose a safe place to reside,
and not fall into their trap."
Zhì (摯) replied:
"I have received Your Majesty's great grace,
and cannot repay it even with death.
However, I dare not fail to follow the sacred instruction.
I plan to station troops at Língyánsì (靈巖寺) in Chángqīngxiàn (長清縣),
which has over three hundred rooms.
It is also connected to Tiānshèngzhài (天勝寨) in Tài'ān (泰安),
situated between Dōngpíng (東平) and Yìdū (益都).
Should an army come,
it will be sufficient for mutual support."
Fearing that this would divide his troops and provisions,
the emperor then issued an edict to temporarily move the Department of State Affairs to Pīzhōu (邳州).
In the ninth month,
Zhì submitted a memorial, saying:
“East of Dōngpíng, there have been repeated devastations,
especially severe in Pī and Hǎi.
The households in Hǎi number less than a hundred, yet there are five thousand troops stationed there.
Pī has barely eight hundred households,
with troops in the tens of thousands.
In ancient times, when levying soldiers, eight families formed a unit;
one family would provide a soldier, and seven families would support him.
Even then, there were laments of injury to life, neglected livelihoods, and weariness from travel.
Now, the troops are numerous, but the common people are insufficient.
Even if Xiāo Hè and Liú Yàn were to be reborn, they would have no way to apply their skills,
let alone what a humble minister like myself could do.
I humbly observe that between Pī and Hǎi,
there are many poor and unemployed people,
eating wild vegetables daily,
with no one to depend on.
I fear they might gather and form bands, thereby increasing the enemy’s strength.
I request that we recruit and select them as soldiers,
providing them with provisions from the tenth month,
to serve as garrison troops.
They would be discharged in the second month.
Each person would be granted thirty *mǔ* of land,
lent seeds and grain, and their harvest inspected.
A quantity would be collected from them.
By autumn, they would again be enlisted in the military ranks.
Fighting and farming alternately
would benefit both the state and the people.
It is also hoped that captured people would be easier to recruit. ”
An imperial edict ordered it to be carried out.
At this time,
the Privy Council, finding the military provisions in Hǎizhōu insufficient
and transport difficult,
memorialized to request its relocation to the interior.
The emperor asked Zhì,
who memorialized, saying:
“Hǎizhōu is bordered by mountains and obstructed by the sea,
and together with Yí, Jǔ, Pī, and Mì, these are all strategic border areas.
The reason they have become a den for bandits in recent years
is due to the Sòng people's provisions.
If we abandon them and move elsewhere,
then directly up to Dōngpíng, there would be nothing but enemy territory,
their power would greatly increase,
and it would be difficult to plan for the future.
I do not see how that would be acceptable.
Moreover, the court’s reason for wishing to relocate
is merely concern about insufficient grain storage.
I request to exert my full effort in planning and
persuading farmers to seize the season for cultivation.
Furthermore, salt can be exchanged for grain,
or a market can be established in Sùqiān
to facilitate trade.
This can be accomplished without exhausting the people's labor.
Also, select a suitable location in Shùyáng for encampment
and dispatch troops to guard and patrol it.
Even without relocation, there would be no cause for concern. ”
The emperor approved his words
and halted the plan.
In the tenth month,
previously,
Wáng Rǔlín (王汝霖), the Deputy Commander of Pīzhōu, finding the state granaries nearly empty,
incited his troops to mutiny.
Chéng Jiǎn (程戩), the Assistant Transport Commissioner of Shāndōng Dōnglù and concurrently the Commander of Yízhōu, feared that disaster would befall him,
and so conspired with him,
allying with Sòng forces as external support.
When Zhì heard this,
he immediately dispatched troops to arrest them.
After interrogation, they fully confessed.
Rǔlín and Jiǎn, along with their confederates, Superintendent Cuī Róng (崔榮), Deputy Commander Hán Sōng (韓松), and Commander of Ten Thousand Qī Yì (戚誼), were all executed.
This was reported at that time.
In the seventh month of the third year,
the Three Agencies (Sānsī) were established in three routes (east, west, and south) of Biànjīng.
An imperial edict commanded Zhì to oversee their affairs from the center.
In the tenth month,
due to the completion of Bìchéng,
he was promoted one rank.
In the seventh month of the fourth year,
he was promoted to Rónglù Dàfū (榮祿大夫)
and retired.
In the first month of Tiānxīng (天興)元年 (1232),
he was reinstated as Dàsīnóng (大司農).
In the fourth month,
he returned the seal of Dàsīnóng
and retired again.
In the eighth month,
he was reinstated as Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事),
enfeoffed as Xiāo Guógōng (蕭國公),
and put in charge of the affairs of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Shěng) for Jīngdōng Lù.
With three thousand troops escorting him, he boarded a boat at Zhāngjiā Dù.
When they reached Fēngqiū,
the enemy detected them,
and they could not advance.
The generals and soldiers conspired to turn their weapons south and flee,
leaving a few cavalrymen to guard Zhì.
Zhì knew of their plan,
so he dismounted
and sat down to address the generals, saying:
“The enemy surrounds us;
advance or retreat is up to us.
You do not consider holding fast.
I would rather die at your hands
than be trampled by mutinous soldiers
and disgrace the mandate of my sovereign and father. ”
The generals assented and stopped,
allowing the entire force to return.
Those who heard of it admired his courage.
In the eleventh month,
he retired again.
Residing in Biàn,
he had a garden and pavilion by the Cài River,
where he daily feasted and drank with old friends.
When Cuī Lì (崔立) surrendered Biànchéng,
he was killed by the grand army.
Zhì was a person of dignity and authority;
none dared to violate his command of troops.
In court, he spoke out boldly when issues arose,
and also delighted in recommending worthy men.
Figures such as Zhāng Wénjǔ (張文舉), Léi Yuān (雷淵), and Má Jiǔchóu (麻九疇) were all promoted through Zhì's recommendation.
Among the chief councilors after the southward relocation,
he was the most highly regarded.
Bǎ Húlǔ (把胡魯),
his early origins are unknown.
In the fifth month of Zhēnyòu (貞祐)二年 (1214),
when Xuānzōng (宣宗) moved south,
he was promoted from Left Remonstrance Official (Zuǒ Jiàn Yì Dàfū) to Imperial Front Official of Experience (Yùqián Jīnglì Guān).
The emperor personally instructed him, saying:
“On this journey,
I will personally command the military forces.
If there are matters of advantage or disadvantage, you may report them through the Imperial Attendants' Bureau. ”
In the eleventh month of the third year,
he was sent out as Military Governor of Zhānghuà Jūn (彰化軍),
concurrently Inspector of Jīngzhōu (涇州) and its administrative area.
In the fifth month of the fourth year,
he was appointed Prefect of Jīngzhào Fǔ (京兆府),
concurrently General Commander of Troops and Horses for that circuit,
and served as Advisory Official of the Traveling Secretariat (Xíng Shěng Cānyì Guān).
In the third month of Xīngdìng (興定)元年 (1217),
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Shǎnxī Lù (陝西路),
concurrently holding his previous posts.
In the first month of the second year,
he was summoned to be Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
In the third month,
he memorialized, saying:
“When the state selects talent,
the selection of *jìnshì* is of paramount importance.
It does not seek to merely fill numbers,
but to secure worthy individuals.
I observe that in the current palace examination,
the examiners are excessively lenient in their selection of candidates,
which is not the way to seek the worthy.
The malpractice should be reformed,
following the old system of Dàdìng. ”
An imperial edict ordered the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) to gather civil officials for a discussion,
and ultimately, the system of Tàihé (泰和) was followed.
In this month,
he was appointed Vice Grand Councilor (Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
In the sixth month,
an imperial edict commanded him to provisionally act as Left Deputy Marshal (Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài),
working with Grand Councilor Xū Dǐng (胥鼎) to defend against autumn invasions.
In the sixth month of the third year,
an earthquake occurred in Píngliáng (平涼) and other places.
Húlǔ then memorialized, saying:
“Heaven does not speak,
but alerts people through phenomena.
The occurrence of disasters must have its reasons.
I request a clear edict to the relevant authorities
to reverently heed Heaven's warning. ”
The emperor graciously accepted his words,
and sent Right Censor-Remonstrant Guō Zhù (郭著) to investigate the signs
and to pacify and instruct the military and civilians.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
he provisionally served as Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòuchéng) and Left Deputy Marshal,
administering the Department of State Affairs and the Marshal's Office in Jīngzhào.
At that time, Shǎnxī annually transported grain to assist Guāndōng,
and the people's strength was increasingly exhausted.
Húlǔ memorialized, saying:
“If boats were used to enter the Yellow River from the Wèi River,
flowing downstream,
the people’s labor could perhaps be somewhat alleviated. ”
This was adopted.
At the time, it was considered convenient.
In the second year of Yuánguāng,
he was successively promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
In the seventh month of that year,
he presented a memorial discussing two matters of defense.
The first stated:
"Since ancient times, that by which states have been pacified and calamities and rebellions have been quelled
has been nothing more than the four methods of warfare, defense, evasion, and conciliation.
For the present situation,
defense and conciliation are paramount.
What is meant by defense
is to necessarily seek out wise and resourceful individuals,
so that internally they are sufficient to win the hearts of the garrison soldiers,
and externally they are sufficient to blunt the enemy's sharpness.
Not only will the enemy be unable to attack,
but we can also seize their weaknesses and defeat them.
As for what is meant by conciliation,
the rulers of Hàn and Táng certainly used this strategy before;
how could it be unusable today alone?
I beg that Your Majesty order the relevant officials to deliberate thoroughly and implement it."
The second stated:
"Many have recently defected from the enemy and returned.
It is fitting to enrich their provisions and rations,
and treat them generously.
If they truly prove willing to serve us,
then select dozens of resourceful and capable individuals
to secretly go and entice the rest to join us.
When many come,
the enemy will surely become mutually suspicious and disloyal.
Then, we can slowly rise and plan to conquer them,
and the success of restoration will not be far off."
The emperor praised and adopted his proposals.
In the ninth month,
he was impeached for fabricating a supplementary memorial for Prince Yīng, Shǒuchún,
and was sentenced to a caning and stripped of his office.
When Āizōng ascended the throne,
in the first year of Zhèngdà, he was promoted to Tóng Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì.
In the second year,
he was reinstated as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
In the third year,
he became Gōngbù Shàngshū and acting Zuǒ Cāncè.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
In the fifth year,
the investigating censors impeached the close attendants Zhāng Wénshòu, Zhāng Rénshòu, and Lǐ Línzhī.
Ānshí also repeatedly criticized these three.
The emperor was extremely angered,
and issued an edict to Ānshí saying:
"You are clearly taking on the role of a worthy minister,
while I am a muddled ruler;
that is enough."
There were hundreds of such words.
Ānshí, who had suddenly received an important appointment,
swiftly encountered setbacks,
and died from a carbuncle on his brain.
The emperor greatly mourned and regretted his death.
A eulogy states: When Xuānzōng moved south,
Heaven's mandate was gone.
At that time, even with loyal and virtuous assistants, and resourceful and brave generals,
it would still have been difficult to achieve success.
However, Rǔlì and Xíngxìn rescued the state internally,
while Xū Dǐng and Hóu Zhì defended it externally,
ultimately enabling Xuānzōng to avoid national ruin,
and Āizōng to reign for another ten years.
Talent can indeed be so beneficial to a state!
Húlǔ's arguments on raising troops and valuing grain
were excellent.
Ānshí did not fail Chénghuī's trust,
and thus gained recognition and appreciation.
He died by incurring wrath for criticizing close attendants—
how tragic!

Biographies Chapter 47: Wányán Sùlán, Chén Guī, Xǔ Gǔ
Wányán Sùlán, also named Yì,
with courtesy name Bóyáng,
was a successful candidate in the policy examination in the first year of Zhìníng.
In the early years of Zhēnyòu,
he was successively promoted to Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì and acting Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
In the second year,
when Xuānzōng moved to Biàn,
he left the Crown Prince in Yāndū.
Later, he summoned him.
Sùlán thought this was inadvisable.
Píngzhāng Gāo Qí said:
"The sovereign resides here,
so the Crown Prince should follow.
Moreover, can you guarantee that the capital city will remain intact?"
Sùlán replied:
"I dare not guarantee its complete integrity,
but if the Crown Prince is there, both his prestige and power will be significant.
If the border passes are defended, then the capital city can be without worry.
In the past, when Táng Mínghuáng fled to Shǔ,
the Crown Prince was indeed in Língwǔ,
intending to secure the hearts of all under heaven."
His advice was not followed,
and the Crown Prince was indeed summoned to follow.
In the seventh month,
when the imperial carriage arrived in Biàn,
Sùlán submitted a memorial discussing affairs,
which briefly stated:
"In the past, Dōnghǎi, when in power,
trusted sycophants,
alienated and dismissed loyal and upright officials,
leading to the daily advancement of petty individuals
and the daily retreat of noble-minded individuals.
Discipline became chaotic,
and laws and regulations increasingly deteriorated.
Wind broke the city gate bolts,
and fire consumed houses in the market streets.
These were surely heavenly signs to warn and frighten him.
Those who spoke advised him to be close to noble-minded individuals,
keep away from petty individuals, and, fearing, cultivate himself to respond to the heavenly changes.
Dōnghǎi did not comply,
and thus came to ruin and destruction.
One who is skilled at remedying chaos must trace the origins of the chaos.
One who is skilled at reforming弊 must investigate the roots of the弊.
If Your Majesty can truly clarify promotions and demotions to reform Dōnghǎi's policies,
then the effectiveness of peace and order can be expected in due course.
Your Majesty's ascension,
without considering this,
then decided upon a southern migration.
On the day the edict was issued, officials and commoners alike submitted memorials requesting to stay.
On the day of departure, winds and rains were untimely, and bridges repeatedly broke.
The sentiments of the people and the will of Heaven were also evident.
Since this matter has passed,
how can it be reversed?
However, from now on, it is especially important to be cautious.
The overturned cart's tracks should not be followed again by pulling the shaft."
He also said:
"A state cannot be without soldiers for a single day,
and soldiers cannot be without food for a single day.
Your Majesty, for the sake of the state,
has reduced all court expenditures.
However, the relevant officials have appointed many military officers,
disregarding wasteful spending,
which is utterly senseless.
Some say that the multitude of military officers serves to enhance prestige and power.
Your servant humbly believes this is not the case.
If they are not carefully selected but merely numerous,
can they be useful in an emergency when facing the enemy?
Moreover, it was only due to the lack of provisions in Zhōngdū
that the imperial carriage came here.
Having found a somewhat safe place,
they then forget the danger and fail to prepare for it.
If by any chance things become like before,
we do not know where the relevant officials will again ask Your Majesty to go."
At that time, Aizōng was the Crown Prince.
Many of the teachers, guardians, and advisors appointed to the Eastern Palace were not suitable persons.
Thereupon, Sùlán submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your subject has heard that the Crown Prince is the foundation of the empire.
To govern the empire, one must first rectify its foundation.
The essence of rectifying the foundation is nothing else
but selecting individuals to assist and support him.
Indeed, one born in Qí can speak the Qí dialect but not the Chǔ language,
which is due to not having practiced it.
Human nature is also simply a matter of practice.
In ancient times, when Chéngwáng was in swaddling clothes,
Zhōu and Zhào were immediately appointed as his teachers and guardians,
to caution him against a life of ease and indulgence,
and to instruct him in the way of steadfastness.
Ultimately, his achievements illuminated those of Wén and Wǔ,
leaving endless glory for posterity.
Reverently, Your Majesty, in accordance with the will of heaven and men,
has preemptively established the Eastern Palace.
The Crown Prince's benevolence, filial piety, and intelligence come from his natural endowments;
his overall management of crucial affairs is already more than adequate.
If you were to further select worthy individuals like Zhōu and Zhào to assist him,
then the governance of Chéngzhōu would not be comparable."
The Emperor praised this as good.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Zhícháng of the Nèishìjú.
Soon after, he was transferred to Jiànyì Dàifū,
and advanced to Shìyùshǐ.
In the fourth month of Xīngdìng 2nd year (1218),
because Púxiān Wànnú rebelled,
Sùlán was dispatched with Ékě, the Fùshǐ of the Jìnshìjú and a member of the imperial clan, to Liaodōng.
The imperial decree instructed them, saying:
"The matter of Wànnú is still unknown as to its exact nature.
When you arrive there, you should obtain the details.
However, you should stop at Tiěshān.
If you venture further,
then it will be difficult for Us to receive news."
It also said:
"We consider Ékě's temperament rather straightforward and rash,
therefore We specifically command you to accompany him.
For every matter, you must deliberate carefully."
As Sùlán was about to depart,
he addressed the Emperor, saying:
"Your subject recently requested to issue a proclamation to Gāolí to reopen mutual markets.
I heard that the imperial edict was given to the Xíngshěng, Bìlánchū.
If the Xíngshěng is simply ordered to dispatch a messenger to proclaim it,
it will only be received in the neighboring region,
and I fear that there may be some impediments in between,
preventing Your Majesty's grace from reaching Gāolí,
and Gāolí will also have no way of knowing the court's original intention.
Moreover, they have for generations been a tributary state,
never failing in the rites of a subject.
If an envoy is dispatched to clearly convey the gracious edict,
one of the two matters—lending grain or opening markets—will surely be accomplished.
If neither is agreed to,
then the fault lies with them,
and only then can other plans be discussed."
The Emperor approved his words,
and thereupon dispatched Liú Bǐng, a Shūbiǎo of the Diǎnkèshǔ, to accompany them.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Hànlín Dàizhì.
In the first month of Zhèngdà 1st year (1224),
an imperial edict summoned the ministers to discuss the repair and restoration of Hézhōngfǔ.
Sùlán and Chén Guī, among others, memorialized that it was not yet feasible;
their words are found in Guī's biography.
In the same month,
he was transferred to Xíngbù Lángzhōng.
At that time, Bù Chén, a man from Nányáng, plotted rebellion,
and several hundred people were implicated and imprisoned.
Sīzhí Bái Huá said to Sùlán:
"In this case, many have been wrongly implicated.
The new Emperor is currently dedicated to leniency,
and later will surely issue another edict for re-examination.
By the time their innocence is established,
many will have died under torture."
Sùlán ordered Huá and Biān Zé, the Jiǎnfǎ, to differentiate between those who deserved death and those who should be pardoned.
Sùlán reported this to the Emperor,
and only the principal culprits and those designated as false generals and ministers, a few individuals, were punished.
The rest were all released.
In the eighth month,
he was provisionally appointed Hùbù Shìláng.
In the third month of 2nd year (1225),
he was appointed Jīngxī Sīnóngqīng,
and shortly after, changed to Sīnóng Dàqīng,
then transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
In the seventh month of 7th year (1230),
he was provisionally appointed Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān and Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
and acted as Xíngshěng in Jīngzhào.
Not long after,
he was transferred to Jīn'ānjūn Jiédùshǐ,
concurrently serving as Tóng and Huá Ānfǔshǐ.
Subsequently,
he was recalled to the court.
When he reached Shǎn, he was besieged.
After a long time,
he fled to Xíngzài,
but was killed en route.
Sùlán earned a reputation for meticulousness and carefulness in his official duties,
though he was particular and could not handle major affairs;
compared to his peers, he was quite commendable.
From his promotion to Zhícháng of the Jìnshìjú,
his frequent advice was often beneficial.
During his father's mourning,
he abstained from alcohol,
and maintained a vigil by the tomb for three years;
contemporary opinion considered this difficult to achieve.
Chén Guī, courtesy name Zhèngshú,
was a native of Jìshān, Jiàngzhōu.
In Míngchāng 5th year (1194), he passed the civil service examination with a focus on phú.
After the southern relocation, he became a Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
In the eleventh month of Zhēnyòu 3rd year (1215),
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Cānzhèng Hóu Zhì initially gained merit by establishing his authority in Dūxī,
and received an unusual appointment,
whereupon he voluntarily requested to govern Héběi.
Your Majesty hastily appointed him to a high office,
presumably intending to hold him accountable for his service.
Subsequently, he lingered in Xīshān,
unable to advance or retreat.
When summoned back to the capital,
he should have declined the appointment,
but instead he calmly settled in,
even inspecting warehouses
and planning salt and liquor monopolies.
How can this be appropriate for a high minister?
At present, our territory shrinks daily,
generals are lacking,
soldiers are not trained,
and there are too many redundant officials.
Governors and magistrates are corrupt and cruel,
the people are displaced,
bandits are rising,
and disasters are ceaseless.
Therefore, he should have day and night investigated the causes
and reported them to Your Majesty,
yet Zhì has never touched upon these matters.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would especially scrutinize and examine this,
and based on his talent, assign him to appropriate duties,
so as not to incur the censure of the world."
There was no reply.
He also said:
"Jǐngxúnshǐ Féng Xiáng rose through clerical work,
possessing no other talent.
He merely specializes in cruel and harsh supervision.
His promotion based on this, I fear, will foster a climate of tyranny.
I request his demotion to encourage others."
An edict immediately dismissed Xiáng from his post,
and also instructed Guī, saying:
"You understand the duty of a subject,
to dare to speak thus;
We greatly commend you."
In the first month of 4th year (1217),
he memorialized, saying:
"I humbly observe that all crossings along the river prohibit grain from crossing northward,
thus causing food shortages in Héběi
and unrest among the people.
In ancient times, Qín and Jìn were enemies,
yet when one experienced famine, they mutually transported grain.
Now, a wise ruler is on the throne,
treating all with equal benevolence.
How can the people of one family be divided by north and south,
and allowed to suffer starvation without relief?
Moreover, soldiers and civilians are sacrificing their lives to resist the enemy.
If they again lack food,
what enjoyment can they have in life?
Once people's morale wavers,
the harm will not be minor.
Your subject suggests that officials should be appointed at the Dàyáng, Mèngjīn, and other crossings to inspect goods.
For every shí of goods crossing the river, the government should collect no more than half,
then wealthy families would profit from the high interest,
converging there,
and hopefully both public and private needs would be met."
The prime ministers considered the military provisions in Hénán to be of great importance,
so an edict ordered officials at the two crossings to take eight parts,
leaving two for the people.
When spring brought sufficient harvests,
and the main army returned northward,
then Guī's request was followed.
The decree was approved.
In the third month,
he memorialized, saying:
"Your subject, during a巡按 (tour of inspection), reached Xúzhōu.
Last year, the Hóng'ǎo bandits rose in Héběi.
The prefecture dispatched Jiédù Fùshǐ Gēsìliè Hèshòu to lead troops to suppress them,
but he instead greatly plundered the families of good commoners as captives,
which is highly inappropriate.
I humbly request a clear imperial edict to the relevant authorities,
that all those captured by Hèshòu be released and pardoned.
For soldiers in other circuits who have captured their own countrymen as captives,
I also request that the same policy be uniformly implemented,
so that Héshuò will have something to look forward to,
and Your Majesty's grace will be boundless."
The matter was sent down to the Shàngshūshěng,
which ordered the Xúzhōu and Guīdé Xíngyuàn to arrest and release them.
Those who concealed captives were subject to the law against enslaving people.
Furthermore, all persons were permitted to report such incidents,
and rewards would be given according to regulations.
Those who were captured and reported it themselves would also be rewarded.
In the fourth month,
a memorial was presented by
an official stating:
“In the prefectures and counties along the Héběi River,
a fort is established every *yī shè*, and residents are enlisted as soldiers.
For several forts, one Chief Commander [zǒnglǐng guān] is appointed,
under the title of 'Commissioner by Imperial Order [xuānchāi cóngyí].'
These individuals are mostly idle officials.
Leaders of righteous armies and subordinates of *piānpí* generals are especially numerous among the unreliable lot.
They extort and feast, taking their livelihood from the people below,
making it a daily routine.
When the enemy arrives, they hide and do not emerge.
When the enemy leaves, they resume their harassment as before.
These scoundrels are given important authority.
Is it not that the court's decrees and authority are too light?
I propose that all of them should be dismissed,
and the matter entrusted to the Pacification Commissioner's Office [xuānfǔ sī] to make appropriate arrangements.”
The emperor approved.
In the seventh month,
a memorial was presented stating: “Your Majesty, with your sagely and benevolent disposition,
is facing a time of extreme adversity for Heaven and Earth.
You have broadened channels for remonstrance to seek ultimate counsel,
and even those who speak wildly or inaccurately are not
punished.
I, your humble servant, holding an office that serves as eyes and ears,
and being in a position to speak,
if I were to remain silent,
how could I repay such a great kindness?
I respectfully present eight proposals.
I hope they will not be disregarded
due to my humble status.
Even if none are adopted,
I beg to be allowed to return to the mountains and forests, to atone for the sin of holding office without merit.
First: Charge high-ranking officials with personal responsibility for national safety.
Now, the northern troops, rising from the frontier,
have deeply penetrated our territory.
In every battle, large or small, they have been victorious,
leading to
the fall of the Divine Capital [Shéndū] and
the emperor's southward journey [cuìhuá nánshǒu].
The people of the Central Plains are utterly devastated,
and the region north of the Yellow River [Dàhé] is largely infested with bandits.
Every time I think of this,
I am greatly alarmed.
Moreover, prime ministers and high-ranking officials are those upon whom the state [shèjì] and the people's lives [shēnglíng] depend for safety.
How can they not worry on Your Majesty’s behalf?
Every court discussion barely touches upon current
issues.
They are merely trifles,
leading to mutual disagreements,
and none are urgent for saving the times.
Furthermore, a recent edict stipulated that military affairs
are to be exclusively managed by the Bureau of Military Affairs [Shūfǔ].
The Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū Shěng] merely observes
the situation without concern,
generally not inquiring,
believing that the responsibility does not lie with them.
While this strategy of avoiding suspicion and protecting oneself is achieved,
what will the state and the people rely upon?
An ancient saying
goes:
“If in doubt, do not employ;
if employed, do not doubt.”
It also says:
“Deliberate broadly,
but decide alone.”
Since Your Majesty has entrusted prime ministers with their roles,
how can they be allowed
to concern themselves with trivialities but neglect the greater picture?
I humbly wish Your Majesty would make a decisive imperial judgment:
for matters concerning military equipment and routine documents, let the Bureau of Military Affairs [Shūfǔ] act independently.
However,

for major strategies of defense and offense, and secret plans for campaigns, both the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū Shěng] and the Censorate [Yuàn] must jointly deliberate on their feasibility.
This way, high-ranking officials will know their responsibilities,
and the empire can be saved.
Second: Appoint censors and remonstrance officials [táijiàn] to broaden channels of information.
A ruler has officials for governance and officials for deliberation.
Officials for governance are the prime ministers and executive officials,
who harmonize *yīnyáng*,
facilitate the myriad things,
pacify the four barbarians,
and endear themselves to the common people,
assisting the Son of Heaven in governing from the imperial court.
Officials for deliberation are the remonstrance officials [jiànguān] and
imperial censors [yùshǐ],
who help the Son of Heaven distinguish right from wrong and rectify injustices.
How can these two be neglected?
In the past, Emperor Wén of Tang [Táng Wénhuáng] decreed that whenever officials from the Central Secretariat [Zhōngshū Shěng] and Chancellery [Ménxià Shěng] met in the inner court for deliberation,
remonstrance officials [jiànguān] were to accompany them,
and remonstrate whenever a mistake occurred.
Although the current dynasty has established remonstrance officials [jiànguān],
they are merely supernumeraries.
Whenever a memorial is presented, they are ordered to withdraw.
Some hold other posts,
or are assigned duties by the Department of State Affairs [Shěng] or various boards [Bù].
There are those who complete their term without ever seeing the emperor's face or uttering a single word.
Although there are imperial censors [yùshǐ],
they are merely tasked with investigating officials,
reviewing documents, and inspecting storehouses.
Matters concerning significant interests or changes in policies [zhènglìng]
are all considered secret and kept from them.
What if officials for governance
act arbitrarily, wielding power and authority as they please,
or military commanders ruin important matters through personal bias?
How could Your Majesty know?
I humbly wish that scholars
with broad learning,
who are well-versed in worldly affairs, and who are upright and dare to speak, be selected as censors and remonstrance officials [táijiàn].
All matters concerning significant interests should be subject to their prior deliberation.
If anything is deemed inappropriate,
they should be allowed to fully discuss and criticize it.
They should not be allowed to hold concurrent posts or be assigned duties by the Department of State Affairs [Shěng] or various boards [Bù].
If they shrink from speaking out due to fear or partisanship, they should be dismissed.
Third: Promote frugality to respond to Heaven's will.
In the past, Duke Wén of Wèi [Wèi Wéngōng], after the Dírén people destroyed his state,
moved to Chǔqiū.
With only thirty war chariots,
he
personally practiced frugality,
wearing a coarse silk cap [dàbó zhī guān]
and clothes of coarse cloth [dàbù zhī yī].
In his later years, he had three thousand mares and stallions,
thus achieving prosperity.
Emperor Wén of Hàn [Hàn Wéndì], succeeding after the wars between Qín [Qín] and Xiàng [Xiàng Yǔ],
found the four seas impoverished.
The Son of Heaven could not even provide a team of four matching horses.
He therefore demonstrated simplicity,
wearing clothes of dark coarse silk [yìtí]
and leather sandals [géxiè].
Before long, the empire became wealthy
and peaceful,
and the four barbarians all submitted.
Since the outbreak of war in the nation,
prefectures and counties have been devastated.
Those that remain intact are further plagued by local bandits.
Only Hénán is somewhat complete,
yet wherever the imperial entourage [dàjià] resides,
the expenses are immense.
To levy support from the entire empire and burden only one region,
is it not difficult?
Thanks to Your Majesty's benevolence,
and Heaven's favor,
after the locust plague,
last year's autumn crops and this year's summer wheat have provided some sustenance.
To respond to Heaven, one must be sincere.
To practice frugality, Heaven will surely bestow blessings.
I have observed that provisions for the palace [gōngzhōng] and
the Eastern Palace [Dōnggōng] are no different from normal times.
Officials attending court and personnel of various bureaus have also not been subject to any reduction.
As for noble officials, powerful families, and military
officers, none fail to compete in extravagance.
Their clothing, food, carriages, and horses are all ostentatious.
Today in the capital [Jīngshī], the number of those selling bright gold clothing, pearls, jade, rhinoceros horn, and ivory is daily increasing compared to the past.
None of this is the way to exercise self-restraint and avert disaster.
I wish Your Majesty would take Duke Wén of Wèi [Wèi Wéngōng] and Emperor Wén of Hàn [Hàn Wéndì] as examples,
and severely curtail all provisions,
dismiss redundant officials,
reduce
unnecessary expenses,
forbid extravagance,
and prohibit bright gold attire and ornaments.
Then, perhaps, August Heaven will reverse the calamity,
and great peace can be achieved.
Fourth: Select competent administrators [shǒulìng] to win the hearts of the people.
At present, the expenses for officials and soldiers throughout the empire, as well as the labor for transport and construction,
are all supported by Hénán [Hénán] and
Shǎnxī.
Moreover, successive years of locusts and droughts
have caused widespread famine among the people.
If relief is provided, storehouses are empty.
If levies are remitted, funds are insufficient.
To genuinely bring practical benefits to
the people,
only virtuous administrators [xián shǒulìng] can achieve this.
During times of heavy taxes and levies and urgent deadlines,
if arrangements are made skillfully, the people's burden will be lightened and tasks easily completed.
However,
if there is any mismanagement, the suffering can be unbearable.
Moreover, the abuses of county magistrates [xiànlìng] are unprecedented today.
Eight or nine out of ten gain their positions through military merit, supervision, or financial contributions.
The cunning ones exploit the times with greed and license, while the incompetent ones leave power to corrupt clerks.
Although officials have recently been sent to investigate
and punish their malpractices [jiānlàn] and replace their ineffective ones,
the replacements are also
not carefully chosen.
This is what is called 'getting a tiger after getting rid of a wolf.'
I humbly implore Your Majesty to issue a clear edict to the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū Shěng],
to publicly select officials who are honest, impartial, and capable of governing the people,
to fill positions in prefectural [zhōufǔ]
administrations.
Furthermore, purify the selection of county magistrates [xiànlìng],
and require all court officials of the seventh rank and above, and external officials of the sixth rank and above, to each recommend one person suitable to serve as a county magistrate.
If in the future they commit
贓 zāng (embezzled goods) will also lead to co-implication.
If their qualifications are already that of a regular seventh-rank official,
or if they are currently serving as a xiànlìng (county magistrate),
they are permitted to hold a temporary position
until their term is complete and they are promoted.
Furthermore, order the jiāncá (supervisory officials) to
regularly patrol and inspect,
investigating and punishing those who are unlawful or fail in their duties.
Then, real benefits will reach the people, and their loyalty will be secured.
Fifth, extensively consult with all ministers to determine major policies.
Recently, more than a million households of military personnel were relocated from Héběi to Hénán.
Although redundant and excessive elements were removed, those remaining
still number over 420,000.
Annually, over 3.8 million hú (bushels) of grain are expended,
exhausting the entire year's revenue of that region,
yet still unable to support these non-farming, non-fighting
people.
Even without border incidents,
they will eventually be trapped in hardship,
let alone when military affairs are escalating
with no end in sight.
Recently, there has been a desire to distribute them along the river
to allow them to cultivate their own land.
However, these idle
people do not know how to farm.
Group drinking and gambling have become ingrained habits,
which would only trouble the officials with collecting taxes and rents.
To have hundreds of thousands of people idly consume provisions
and stipends –
if delayed, resources will be lacking;
if expedited, the people will be exhausted.
The imperial court is already at a loss as to how to handle this one matter,
so how can it prepare for the enemy?
This is due to a lack of foresight at
the beginning
and a failure to consider the consequences
which led to this error.
If, at the time of the initial relocation, people were allowed to stay or go according to their wishes,
then those who wished to come would be self-sufficient families
who would not
need official stipends.
Those who stayed would surely have places to avoid danger
and would not need to be forcibly dispatched.
This would not have led to the difficulties in planning that exist today.
In ancient times, when a ruler was about to undertake a major endeavor,
they would consult their own heart,
consult with ministers, common people, and diviners.

I humbly request that from now on, whenever there is a major matter, the officials of the shěng yuàn tái jiàn (secretariat, chancellery, censorate, and remonstrance bureaus) and those of the fifth rank and above in attendance at court
be ordered to deliberate together for convenience.
Sixth, value official rewards to encourage merit.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you have repeatedly bestowed extensive grace to share in the great celebrations,
not begrudging official titles to stir people's hearts.
There have even been instances of promotion by ten ranks before completing a single term,
and those serving in minor roles already bearing the titles of piáojì rónglù (General of Agile Cavalry and Glorious Beneficiary).
The extent of redundancy and excess has reached this point.
Furthermore, the door has been opened
for selling titles and making presentations.
In that case, what encouragement is there for those who don armor, grasp weapons, and dedicate their lives on the battlefield?
Official titles are inherently nominal,
merely issued from the mouth of the ruler,
yet
people throughout the land eagerly pursue them
because the imperial court values them.
If merits are not considered,
and one is granted an official position in the morning
and promoted in the evening,
people will also come to slight them
and no longer desire them.
Since what has already happened cannot be blamed,
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will treasure the future,
not allowing public instruments to become common tools
or rewards for merit to be taken advantage of by
chance.
Furthermore, today's honorary official titles often reach the third rank,
making it difficult for the relevant officials to promote and appoint.
It would be appropriate to moderately increase the number of ranks within the eight abolished ranks
and replace them with auspicious names.
This way, officials who hold positions will not be promoted too rapidly,
and the state's power and grace will not be diminished too lightly.
Seventh, select generals and commanders to clarify military law.
A general is the nation's arbiter of destiny,
upon whom the peace and danger of the world rely.
To entrust the lives of tens of thousands of people
to one person,
deciding life and death in a breath—
is this responsibility not heavy?
Since the northern troops entered the country,
in open battle, the entire army perishes;
in city defense, the entire
prefecture is massacred.
Is this always because the soldiers are weak or the defenses are lax?
It is simply because incompetent generals do not know the art of war.
An ancient saying goes:
"When the three luminaries (sun, moon, stars) are not in
their proper orbits,
select scholars to be chancellors.
When the four barbarians invade,
elevate soldiers to be generals."
Today's generals and commanders largely prioritize their background and official rank,
perhaps being sons of prominent families
or those who gained positions through favoritism and connections.
In peacetime, they are arrogant;
when encountering the enemy, they shrink back in fear.
If the generals and commanders themselves are timid,
who among the soldiers
would be willing to advance?
Furthermore, they habitually exploit
and collect tributes,
leading soldiers to disturb good citizens with impunity.
When they lead troops to confront the enemy,
on the march, they travel in
disorganized formations;
when encamped, they force their way into homes and choose dwellings,
oppressing the common people
and indulging their demands.
To then expect them to fear the law and die for the cause,
how could that not be difficult?
Moreover, today,
there are many military officers.

With ten sheep and nine shepherds,

To exert sole authority over a region, is it necessary to have many
(officers)?

In ancient times, good generals always shared hardship with their soldiers.
Today's military

Generals and commanders are overly well-fed,

send them to various regions,

It is essential that fifty men constitute a móukè,

For every ten thousand men, one dūtǒng should be appointed,

Furthermore, order the ministers of the shěng yuàn and officials of the fifth rank and above, both inside and outside the court,

without
restriction of official rank,

Reiterate military law,
conduct regular training and drills,
ensuring that generals and commanders are clear on the principles of orthodox and unorthodox, empty and solid tactics,
and soldiers are proficient in the procedures of standing, sitting, advancing, and retreating.
As for bows,
arrows, armor, and weapons, they must be carried by themselves,
habituating them to hardship.
If any offense is committed,

Then, with the right generals and commanders,
military morale will rise daily,
making it possible to confront
the enemy.
Eighth, train soldiers to boost military prestige.
Emperor Shìzōng of Zhōu once said:
"Troops are valued for their excellence, not their number.
A hundred farmers cannot support one fighting
soldier.
Why then deplete the people's wealth to support these useless troops?
If the brave and cowardly are not distinguished,
how can the multitude be encouraged?"
Consequently, he extensively reviewed the soldiers,
then conquered Huáinán,
What is accumulated,
even in private chambers, is still the property of the state.
Now, officials are searching and seizing surplus grain,
causing merchants who deal in it to no longer dare to enter.
This should be stopped immediately.
Your minister recently read reports,
and found that those who spoke righteous words with all their heart and sincerity were mostly humble and lowly people from the common folk.

ministers among the hundreds of officials

The edict was sent to the Shàngshūshěng,

Soon after, he was promoted to Yuánwàiláng of the Zuǒsī in the Shàngshūshěng,

At that time, Chancellor Gāo Qí established a law:

“Propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame are used to govern gentlemen;

Recently, the imperial court has been eager to achieve good governance,

Now, rank and emolument are used to control the noble.
If the noble cannot avoid disgrace,

The imperial carriage’s residence is not the same as a military campaign,

Is this not excessive?
Your Majesty’s benevolence and clemency

Initially, the emperor wished to implement it,

In the fourth year,
he held the concurrent post of Shìyùshǐ while serving as Yòusījìan.
At that time, a large army crossed Tóngguān and advanced eastward.
An edict was issued to the Shàngshūshěng to gather all officials for deliberation.

The emperor showed it to the Shàngshūshěng,
but Gāo Qí obstructed his proposal,
so it was not implemented.
In that month,
the Zhāoxiánsuǒ was first established,
and Gǔ and others were put in charge of its affairs.

He then instructed his chief ministers, saying:
“The Sòng people have long instigated trouble.

Now that we have been invaded several times,
what should be done?
You and the other officials should deliberate on this.”
Thereupon, the assembly gathered for deliberation in the Dūtáng.
Gǔ said:
“The Sòng people are weak and feeble,
and have always deeply feared us.
Moreover, they know the northern army is strong,
and will rely on us as a shield.
Although they may occasionally act presumptuously,
they surely dare not penetrate deeply.
Their insulting words
are merely the work of marketplace butchers and vendors;
how can they be worth contending with?
We should simply instruct the appropriate officials to issue a diplomatic message [yíwén],
advising them of
the many great benefits our dynasty has repeatedly bestowed,
and the holy ruler’s intention of cherishing all living beings.
If they are sensible,
and resume the former good relations,
then what more do we seek?
However, if they persist in their wickedness and do not repent,
raising an army to punish them will not be too late either.”
At that time, there were more than ten participants in the deliberation.
Although there were minor differences, the general outline was the same.
Afterward, Chancellor Gāo Qí and others reported:
“The consensus of the officials’ deliberation
is to all request strengthening military defenses and awaiting the fatigued enemy at leisure.
This is the best strategy.”
The emperor approved it.
At that time, the imperial court found that the various route commanders [bǎjūnguān] often had disagreements and disobeyed orders,

Gǔ submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your minister believes that the good should be encouraged,
and the wicked should be punished;
this is the great law of the state.
If good and evil are not distinguished,
then superiors and subordinates will deceive each other,
and there will be no way to apply punishment or encouragement.”
The emperor praised and accepted it.
Gǔ, seeing that the imperial court intended to raise an army to attack Sòng,
submitted a memorial to admonish, saying:
“In the early part of Dàdìng era,
the Sòng people invaded Sùzhōu.
Afterwards, they were repeatedly defeated.
Shìzōng assessed that they would not immediately beg for peace,
and thus ordered the Yuánshuàifǔ to send someone to negotiate.
From then on, there was peace for nearly thirty years.
During the Tàihé era,
Hán Tuōzhòu recklessly provoked border conflicts.
Zhāngzōng sent the imperial son-in-law Púsàn Kuí to punish him.
Kuí feared that a protracted war would incur heavy expenses and could not be sustained.
Secretly, he sent a relative of Tuōzhòu, bearing a portrait of his ancestor Qí and family records,
falsely claiming allegiance,
to meet Qiū Chóng.
Through this, good relations were restored,
and the army returned.
Even with the prosperity of Shìzōng and Zhāngzōng,
with full treasuries [fǔkù] and
a rich and prosperous realm,
they still first humbly yielded to achieve success,
reported it to their ancestral temples,
recorded it in historical annals,
as a beautiful tale for ten thousand generations.
How can we not strive for this now?
Now that the great army has somewhat rested,
if the southern border also becomes peaceful,
then great peace is not far off.
Some say that solely relying on military might can force the Sòng people to submit.
This is merely empty talk,
not delving into practical application.
Even if we occasionally achieve a minor victory,
it is not worth celebrating much.
They, seeing our great power,
will surely hold firm and not sally forth.
Our army, in a hurry, will gain nothing,
and must return for provisions.
They will then take the opportunity to attack us,
making us unable to fight when we wish, and unable to retreat when we desire.
Then the time for ceasing hostilities may not be seen.
Moreover, they have surplus accumulations from Jiāngnán,
while we only have the disadvantages of levies and taxes from the Hénán region alone.
This is truly disheartening.
I wish Your Majesty would endure and be tolerant,
and quickly implement this strategy.
If peace is indeed reached,
then the great army, upon hearing of it, will also withdraw their forces,
because we will have no constraints.
Once Hénán has rested,
then we can plan to manage Shuòfāng.
Then Your Majesty will enjoy the blessings of a mid-dynasty revival,
and the world will rely on the fortune of nurturing care.
May Your Majesty disregard immediate gains and consider future troubles.
This would be a great blessing.”
The emperor considered his words correct,
and immediately ordered Gǔ to draft the peace negotiation documents.
After completion, he showed them to the chief ministers,
who said they contained an implied plea,
showing weakness,
so they were not used.
Censor Niángē Suōshī impeached Máoduānqīng, co-administrator of the Bureau of Monopoly Goods, for corruption and unlawful conduct.
Gǔ often simplified the complex legal texts,
which resulted in many omissions.
Suōshī reported this,
and Gǔ was demoted one rank
and dismissed from office.
He was specially exempted from a year's service.
In the first month of the third year,
the Shangshūshěng reported a vacancy among the admonishing officials
and requested Gǔ for the position.
The Emperor said:
"Last night I was just thinking of Gǔ,
and you gentlemen have mentioned him,
which perfectly aligns with my intentions.
Quickly summon him."
He was reinstated as Zuǒbǔquē.
In the eighth month,
he was demoted four ranks
and dismissed from office.
Initially,
the court dispatched Wēndūn Bǎijiānú, director of the Bureau of Imperial Attendants, and Àotún Húsāhé, Vice Minister of Punishments, to relocate the people of Jízhōu to Dān to avoid the edge of war.
The provincial residents were reluctant to move
and blocked the road to protest.
Bǎijiānú explained to them the Emperor's concern that the common people might be harmed
and ordered the summoning of Jìn'ān soldiers to escort the old and young on their journey.
The crowd believed that if soldiers arrived, they would surely be forced to comply.
So they surged into the provincial office,
demanding Bǎijiānú's death.
Húsāhé, fearing calamity,
falsely yielded to the popular sentiment,
