The crowd, carrying him on their shoulders, escorted and cheered him, bowing in thanks before leaving.
Upon his return,
an imperial edict ordered Gǔ and Censor Héshíliè Tiělùn to investigate the matter.
The imperial decree stated:
"Bǎijiānú's death was entirely due to Húsāhé's betrayal.
Investigate the facts and report."
After Àotún Húsāhé was imprisoned,
the Emperor was extremely angry,
eager to ascertain the facts to apply the law correctly.
However, Gǔ and others were quite lenient with him.
Húsāhé hanged himself.
The officials then issued a judgment against Gǔ based on this.
Thus, this punishment occurred.
At the beginning of Āizōng's reign,
Gǔ was summoned to be a Bǔquē,
and soon after was promoted to Zuǒsījìan.
His remonstrances were somewhat less impactful than before.
Not long after,
he retired,
residing in Yīyáng.
The prefect built the Yīchuāntíng for him.
Gǔ had a fondness for wine,
which did not wane with age.
He would often take a boat to visit villages,
staying to drink for ten or more days without returning.
When he ascended the river,
the old and young would vie to pull his boat,
for dozens of *li* without interruption,
such was the affection and admiration he received from his contemporaries.
He died in the seventh year of Zhèngdà,
at the age of seventy-four.
Throughout his life, Gǔ enjoyed writing poetry and calligraphy,
but he was not highly regarded by scholars and officials.
Contemporary opinion only praised his uprightness.
During the Tiānxīng era,
there was a Zuǒsījìan named Chén Kē,
who spoke on every matter without the slightest reservation.
The Emperor once personally commended him.
When Biànjīng was under siege,
he repeatedly submitted memorials concerning gains and losses.
His "Letter Pleading for War" was particularly incisive.
Its summary stated:
"Today's situation
is all due to Your Majesty's indecision and the cowardice of the generals and ministers.
If we continue to procrastinate,
and one day find ourselves helpless,
I fear that monarch and subjects will only be able to weep before each other."
This can be said to have sharply hit the maladies of the time,
but the then-chancellor Chìzhǎn Héxǐ and others thwarted it,
so the strategy was not adopted.
Those who understood the situation lamented this.
Kē's courtesy name was Hézhī,
and he was from Cāngzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the first year of Dà'ān.
A Eulogy says:
Upon his accession, Xuānzōng diligently sought to emulate Shìzōng,
but all his actions were contrary to this.
During Dàdìng, there was peace,
and both north and south enjoyed good governance.
During Zhēnyòu, military campaigns plunged the people into misery.
When Shí Jū was chancellor,
monarch and subjects endeavored to be lenient and generous.
When Gāo Qí held power,
he disliked scholars and favored clerks,
leading to harsh scrutiny from top to bottom.
Wányán Sùlán was the first to attack Qí's misconduct,
stating that Qí would surely disrupt the state's order.
Chén Guī strongly argued that cruel legal clerks
would corrupt customs.
Xǔ Gǔ requested peace with the Sòng,
his words full of loyalty and love.
The statements of these three all sharply addressed the ills of the time,
possessing the spirit of ancient upright officials.
Xuānzōng knew of their uprightness,
yet did not adopt their advice.
To wish to rival Shìzōng in such a manner

Yáng Yúnyì (楊雲翼) was by nature refined and solemn,

When he formed a connection with someone, it was fixed,

Regarding affairs of state,
he spoke whatever he knew.
During the Zhēnyòu (貞祐) period,
the commanders of the army, unable to repel foreign invaders, sought to compensate by attacking the Sòng (宋).

Anyone who spoke against this

Yáng Yúnyì, however, put forward his views, saying:

Therefore, they wish our army to seize the initiative and move first,

Tàihé used the full strength of the empire,

Bǐngwén then said:
“Initially, when I wanted to submit the memorial,
I discussed it privately with Compiler Wáng Tíngyún (王庭筠), Censor Zhōu Áng (周昂), Provincial Clerk Pān Mou (潘●), Zhèng Zàndào (鄭贊道), Gāo Tǎn (高坦), and others.”
Wáng Tíngyún and the others were all imprisoned,
and received varying degrees of punishment.
The officials argued that Bǐngwén's memorial was presumptuous and arrogant,
and according to law, he should be stripped of his title.
However, the emperor did not wish to punish a person for his words,
and thus specially exempted him.
At that time, a saying circulated:
“In ancient times there was Zhū Yún (朱雲),
now there is Bǐngwén.
Zhū Yún clung to the railing,
Bǐngwén clung to people.”
No scholar-official failed to be ashamed of him.
Because of this, he remained idle for a long time.
Later, he was appointed as Joint Prefect of Kělán Jūzhōu (岢嵐軍州),
and then transferred to Assistant Judge of the Běijīng Lù (北京路) Transport Commission.
In the tenth month of winter in Chéng'ān (承安) 5,
it was gloomy for days.
When Prime Minister Zhāng Wàngōng (張萬公) had an audience,
the emperor looked at Wàngōng and said:
“Your statement that ‘the heavens are dark and obscured,
just as a ruler fails to distinguish between upright and wicked people,’
is very reasonable.
As for Zhào Bǐngwén, who was demoted for his words in the past,
I hear that he possesses talent and literary skill, excels at calligraphy,
and is also brave in speech.
I have not abandoned him, nor do I intend not to use him.
As military affairs on the northern frontier are just beginning,
I am merely testing him.”
In Tàihé 2,
he was summoned to be Principal of the Board of Revenue,
and then promoted to Compiler of the Hanlin Academy.
In October,
he was appointed Prefect of Níngbiān Zhōu (寧邊州).
In the third year,
he was transferred to Píngdìng Zhōu (平定州).
The previous administration was harsh in its application of punishment.
Whenever news of an impending amnesty arrived,
they would first beat thieves to death before accepting the amnesty,
but robberies only became more frequent.
Bǐngwén's governance was consistently lenient and simple.
Within ten days to a month, all thieves disappeared.
During a famine,
he used his official salary grain and encouraged wealthy commoners to provide relief,
saving many lives.
In Xīngdìng (興定) fourth year (1220),
because the Sòng (宋) people resisted the envoy on the Huái (淮) River,
troops were dispatched to campaign south.
An imperial edict ordered the Jīngdōng (京東) Commander-in-Chief, Hégǔliè Yáwūtǎ (紇石烈牙吾塔), to attack Xūyí (盱眙).
Yáwūtǎ (牙吾塔) did not obey the command,
but instead led elite cavalry from Chúzhōu (滁州) to raid Xuānhuà (宣化),
and let his troops plunder extensively.
Thus, wherever the troops went, the fields were desolate,
utterly devoid of resources.
The Sòng (宋) people fortified their walls and refused to fight,
so he returned without achieving any success.
The Xíngshěng (行省) impeached Yáwūtǎ (牙吾塔) for deliberately violating discipline.
An imperial edict ordered Bì (璧) to wear a gold tally and investigate him.
Bì (璧) galloped into Yáwūtǎ’s (牙吾塔) army,
seized his gold tally,
and replaced him with another commander to take charge.
When Yáwūtǎ (牙吾塔) was imprisoned,
the soldiers rioted,
claiming their commander was innocent.
Bì (璧) angrily rebuked Yáwūtǎ (牙吾塔), saying:
"Does the commander wish to use his troops to resist the imperial commissioner?
The ceremony for awaiting punishment is surely not like this.
When the envoy returns and reports,
will the imprisonment be completed?"
Yáwūtǎ (牙吾塔) prostrated himself, begging for death.
Bì (璧) said:
"According to military law,
those who act independently in advance or retreat,
thereby losing opportunities and leading to defeat, are to be executed."
He immediately drafted a memorial to that effect.
At the time, public opinion praised his courage.
In the tenth month,
he was transferred to be a Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) of the Lǐbù (禮部),
and concurrently served as Yòusī Jiàn (右司諫) and Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (治書侍御史).
An imperial edict asked about the most urgent matters of the time.
Bì (璧) submitted six proposals,
generally speaking about reducing redundant expenditures,
preparing elite vanguards,
deferring doubtful cases to exercise caution in punishments,
selecting impartial and incorrupt officials to inspect civil servants,
reforming the abuses of exploitation in garrison settlements,
and strictly enforcing regulations against solicitations from powerful officials.
He also listed four self-governance strategies,
namely distinguishing between the worthy and the wicked,
ensuring reliable rewards and punishments,
listening and reviewing to understand the sentiments of the people,
and implementing demotions and reductions to heed heavenly warnings.
An imperial edict stated that due to famine in the east,
bandits had risen everywhere.
Wányán Bójia (完顏伯嘉), the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), was made Xuānwèishǐ (宣慰使),
and Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史) Dàoyuǎn (道遠) was to accompany him.
Dàoyuǎn (道遠) exposed the illicit gains recorded by the Yǒngchéng (永城) magistrate.
Bójia (伯嘉), who had a conflict with the magistrate,
handed the magistrate over to the relevant authorities,
but released the register without investigation.
During a casual conversation, he also promised command positions to his subordinates Kèzhōng (克忠) and others.
Bì (璧) impeached all of them,
and Bójia (伯嘉) was ultimately punished and removed from office.
Initially,
spies reported to the Guīdé (歸德) Xíng Shūmìyuàn (行樞密院) that
rebel forces north of the Yellow River had secretly planned to cross south.
The Xíngyuàn (行院) official Hútǔmén (胡土門) and the Dūshuǐjiānsǐ (都水監使) Máohuāniǎn (毛花輦) dismissed the reports,
and made no preparations.
One day,
hundreds of Hóngnà (紅衲) on rafts crossed south,
ravaged a subordinate county, and left.
Bì (璧) was ordered to investigate.
Bì (璧) concluded that the two generals had feigned illness for personal gain,
relaxed their defenses upon hearing of the bandits,
and neither fought when the bandits came nor pursued them when they left.
According to the law, all deserved execution.
Someone remarked to him:
"These two generals are both favored officials,
and the Dūshuǐjiān (都水監) possesses immense wealth.
If they seek intervention from the imperial court,
they will certainly receive a lighter sentence.
You will only incur the resentment of powerful officials.
What good will that do?"
Bì (璧) sighed, saying:
"Suīyáng (睢陽) is an important outpost,
where the heavy forces of the eastern frontier are stationed.
If even bandits at our gates cannot be resisted,
what hope is there if something greater occurs?"
He then fully reported his proposed judgment.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Xíngbù Lángzhōng (刑部郎中).
There was a drought in Guānzhōng (關中).
An imperial edict ordered Bì (璧) and Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎) Wèixīn (畏忻) to review wrongful imprisonments.
At that time, the Hézhōng (河中) commander Āhǔdài (阿虎帶) and a dozen or so of his subordinates were all sentenced to death for abandoning the city,
and were imprisoned in Tóngzhōu (同州) awaiting confirmation.
The officials of Tóngzhōu (同州), anticipating the imperial will,
asked Bì (璧) how he would handle them.
Bì (璧) said:
"Hézhōng (河中) is a strategically important location today.
The court has proposed it as a place for the emperor's temporary residence.
If this is lost, Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西) will face the danger of losing their protective cover.
They were made to guard it because they were imperial relatives and meritorious nobles.
In times of peace, they exhausted the people's wealth for construction and dredging.
Once there was an alarm, they hastily burned and abandoned it.
If these are not executed,
the three-foot law is useless."
Ultimately, he reported that there was no injustice.
In the winter, tenth month,
he was appointed Guīdé Zhìzhōng (歸德治中).
Not long after,
he was transferred to be Tóngzhī Bǎojìngjūn Jiédùshǐ (同知保靜軍節度使),
and then transferred again to be Tóngzhī Jíqìngjūn Jiédùshǐ (同知集慶軍節度使).
Upon arriving at his post, he immediately submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
was promoted one rank, and retired.
In Zhèngdà (正大) ninth year (1232),
when Hénán (河南) fell,
he returned north,
and died several years later,
at the age of seventy-nine.
Lǐ Xiànfǔ (李獻甫), courtesy name Qīnyòng (欽用),
was a younger cousin of Xiànnéng (獻能).
He was widely knowledgeable in classics and commentaries,
especially proficient in Zuǒshì (左氏) and geography.
He was a man of strong character,
and his insight far surpassed others,
thus people at the time called him full of spirit.
In Xīngdìng (興定) fifth year (1221), he passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination,
served as Xiányáng Bù (咸陽簿),
and was appointed Xíngtái Lìshǐ (行臺令史).
In the early Zhèngdà (正大) period,
an envoy from Xià (夏) came to request peace.
The imperial court sent Hànlín Dàizhì (翰林待制) Féng Yándēng (馮延登) to negotiate.
At that time, Xiànfǔ (獻甫) was a Shūbiǎo Guān (書表官),
and accompanied him.
The Xià (夏) envoy was eloquent,
and Yándēng (延登) could not refute him.
After several days of back-and-forth, no agreement was reached.
When the annual tribute became the topic,
Xiànfǔ (獻甫) could not tolerate it,
and stepped forward from the side, saying:
"The Xià (夏) country has maintained peace with us for a hundred
years. Although the titles of ruler and subject have now been changed to a relationship between brotherly states,
is there any basis for the elder brother to pay tribute?"
The envoy said:
"Let's not discuss brotherhood.
The Sòng (宋) annually paid our country 250,000 bolts of silk as tribute.
The precedents are all there.
Are you alone unaware?
If the Jīn (金) court truly wishes to restore the old friendship,
it must follow this example."
Xiànfǔ (獻甫) flushed with anger and said:
"Does the envoy still dare to speak of this?
The Sòng (宋) baited your house with annual tribute and bestowed surnames upon you,
haughtily considering themselves your father.
No one among the Xià (夏) rulers and subjects realized this.
I truly thought the envoy should have kept it a secret,
yet now you speak of it publicly.
If the envoy can truly uphold this proposal,
and follow the precedent of being granted a surname,
even if our humble state annually donates 500,000,
Xiànfǔ (獻甫) requests to bear the responsibility himself."
The Xià (夏) envoy was speechless,
and the peace negotiations were thus settled.
Later, the imperial court recognized his merit,
and appointed him Jīnglì Guān (經歷官) of the Qìngyáng (慶陽) Commander-in-Chief's residence.
Soon after, he was appointed Cháng'ān Lìng (長安令).
As Jīngzhào (京兆) Xíngtái (行臺) was located there,
the provisions and contributions were very numerous.
Xiànfǔ (獻甫) always managed them with apparent ease,
and the county residents relied on him for peace.
He entered the capital to serve as Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ (尚書省令史).
In Tiānxīng (天興) first year (1232),
he was made Xíng Liùbù Yuánwàiláng (行六部員外郎),
and his defense strategies were constantly relied upon at the time.
For his merits, he was promoted to Zhènnánjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ (鎮南軍節度副使),
concurrently Yòujǐngxúnshǐ (右警巡使).
He died in the disaster of Càizhōu (蔡州),
at the age of forty.
His collected writings, titled Tiānnǐ Jí (天倪集),
remained in Biànjīng (汴京).
After Xiànfǔ (獻甫) died,
his family was also broken up.
His contemporary, Wáng Yuánlǐ (王元禮) of Huáyīn (華陰), acquired them,
and they were passed down to posterity.
Léi Yuān, courtesy name Xīyán,
also courtesy name Jìmò,
was a native of Húnyuán, Yìngzhōu.
His father, Sī,
was a renowned *jìnshì* [scholar-official].
He served as Tongzhī Běijīng Zhuǎnyùnshǐ [Assistant Administrator of the Beijing Transport Commission]
and his commentary on the *Yìjīng* was circulated in the world.
Yuān was born to a concubine,
the youngest of all his siblings.
His elder brothers disdained him,
and after his father's death, he could not live peacefully at home.
So, he entered the Tàixué [Imperial Academy] in a burst of determination.
With worn clothes and tattered shoes,
and no mat on his couch,
he sat bare-legged and unadorned, engrossed in his studies.
He did not greet or see off guests,
and everyone considered him arrogant.
His friend, Shāng Héng, often defended him,
and also provided him with relief.
Later, he associated with Lǐ Zhīchún
and consequently became famous.
In the first year of Zhìníng, he passed the Imperial Examination in rhymed prose and poetry with the highest honors (jiǎkē).
He was appointed Lùshì [Registrar] of Jīngzhōu.
He nearly died due to being implicated in the Gāotíng Yù case.
Later, he was transferred to Dōngpíng.
This was a region where heavy troops of Héshuò were stationed.
The arrogant generals and fierce soldiers relied on foreign enemies for their importance,
and everyone from the Xíngtái [traveling chancellery] downwards sought to appease them.
Yuān moved in and out of the military camps with composure, refusing to be subservient.
Within a few months,
many portraits of Yuān were painted in the alleys and streets.
Even great generals dared not treat him as a newly advanced scholar.
Soon after, he was promoted to Dōng'é Lìng [Magistrate of Dōng'é],
and then transferred to Xúzhōu Guānchá Pànguān [Surveillance Commissioner's Adjutant].
At the end of Xīngdìng,
he was summoned to be Wénxué [Literary Attendant] and Jìshì Cānjūn [Record-keeper and Military Advisor] in the palace of Prince Yīng.
He was then transferred to Yìngfèng Hánlín Wénzì [Calligrapher of the Hànlín Academy by imperial command].
He was appointed Jiānchá Yùshǐ [Censor].
He spoke on five matters that pleased the emperor,
and also impeached without fear of powerful magnates.
When he toured various prefectures and districts, he earned a reputation for authority.
He immediately flogged and executed wicked and lawless powerful families.
When he arrived in Càizhōu,
he flogged and executed five hundred people.
At that time, he was known as
"Léi Bànqiān" [Léi Five Hundred].
Because of this, he was impeached [by others]
and dismissed from office.
After a long time,
through the recommendation of the prime minister Hóu Zhì,
he was appointed Tàixué Bóshì [Erudite of the Imperial Academy] and Nánjīng Zhuǎnyùnsī Hùjí Pànguān [Adjudicator of Household Registration for the Southern Capital Transport Commission].
He was then promoted to Hànlín Xiūzhuàn [Compiler of the Hànlín Academy].
One night, he died suddenly
at the age of forty-eight.
In the *gēngyín* year of Zhèngdà, during the battle of Dàohuí Gǔ,
Yuān had submitted a memorial refuting the court officials' desperate last-ditch strategy,
with profound and incisive arguments,
clearly evident.
However, those in charge of the military frustrated him,
and his plan was ultimately not implemented.
He was a man of imposing physique,
with a thick beard and a wide mouth.
His face was ruddy,
and his eyes were like gazing at the ocean.
When encountering injustice, an expression of abhorrence for evil appeared on his face.
Sometimes he would grind his teeth and curse incessantly.
Though he tried to discipline and correct himself severely,
he could not change this nature.
His essays and poems delighted in novelty and uniqueness.
He was good at making friends.
All powerful and important figures in office, as well as commoner literati, all interacted with him.
When he lived in the capital,
guests flocked to his door and never left his residence.
He had no surplus wealth at home,
yet he entertained guests with great generosity.
When holding office, he liked to establish a name for himself.
Initially, after passing the examination, he temporarily managed the affairs of Suípíng Xiàn.
Young and spirited,
he struck down powerful local gentry
and exposed hidden evildoers.
The entire district was greatly shaken,
and he was called "divinely enlightened."
He once arbitrarily flogged a chief clerk of the prefecture.
When the prefecture issued a summons for him, he did not respond,
and was dismissed.
Thereafter, whenever he held an office, he would cause a sensation,
but this also prevented him from achieving greater success.
Chéng Zhèn, courtesy name Wēiqīng,
was a native of Dōngshèng.
He and his elder brother Dǐng both passed the imperial examination.
Zhèn gained a reputation for competence in his official career.
At the beginning of Xīngdìng,
when an imperial edict commanded all officials to recommend county magistrates,
Zhèn obtained Chénliú.
His administration was the best in Hénán.
He was summoned and appointed Jiānchá Yùshǐ [Censor].
He impeached without any hesitation.
At that time, the imperial prince, Prince Jīng, was the prime minister.
His household servants, relying on his power, encroached upon the common people.
Zhèn impeached them according to the law,
and memorialized, saying:
"Prince Jīng, as Your Majesty's son,
holds a position of great importance in the realm.
He fails to assist his sovereign father above
and overcome difficulties together.
Instead, he exclusively relies on his power,
disregards rites and regulations,
accepts bribes,
and promotes or demotes officials.
He allows his slaves to invade and exploit the common people.
Nominally, it is 'harmonious trade,'
but in reality, it is extortion.
The numerous unlawful acts cannot be fully enumerated.
If Your Majesty cannot rectify your own family,
how can you hope to rectify the realm?
It will be difficult."
Thereupon,
the emperor reprimanded Prince Jīng
and ordered silver from the imperial treasury to compensate for the goods,
and flogged several of the most lawless chief slaves.
Not long after,
he was dismissed from office, having been impeached by a former subordinate.
He died of blood vomiting
a little over a year later.
Zhèn was a man of integrity and talent,
who disregarded his own safety for the sake of the country,
without the slightest personal gain.
When he served as Censor,
the imperial censorship system was greatly invigorated.
Because of this, many petty individuals watched him with hostile eyes,
and he could not remain in court for long.
Scholars lamented his fate.
A eulogy says: Hán Yù, Fény Bì, Lǐ Xiànfǔ, and Léi Yuān were all heroes of the late Jīn dynasty.
During the chaos in Bīn and Jīng,
Yù recruited ten thousand soldiers within ten days.
Facing the brutality of Yáwūtǎ,
Bì restrained him with the imperial laws,
and he ultimately dared not act.
When the Xià people sought annual tribute citing the Sòng precedent,
Xiànfǔ refuted them with the matter of the Sòng granting a surname to Xià,
causing the Xià envoy to fall silent and peace negotiations were settled.
When Yuān was Censor,
the powerful and noble kept their distance,
What could the *guóshì* [national scholars] of antiquity add to this?
Yù was unjustly accused due to suspicion,
Bì and Yuān were excessively zealous in suppressing evil.
Critics mocked them for their harshness.
However, how can a flaw overshadow the jade?
Chéng Zhèn impeached Prince Jīng and brought him to justice,
rivalling Fény and Léi.
Yet, he also died due to obstruction from petty individuals.
It has long been that upright officials are not tolerated in this world.
Alas!
Collations and Notes
Biographies, Chapter 49: Gǔlǐjiǎ Shílún, Nèizú Èkě, Sāhén, Qiáng Shēn, Wūlíndá Hútǔ, Nèizú Sīliè, Hésíliè Yáwūtǎ.
Gǔlǐjiǎ Shílún
was a native of Lóng'ān.
He rose through military examinations.
He was a strong and fierce man, somewhat self-willed.
Wherever he was, he was at odds with others.
Xuānzōng, because of his bravery and skill in battle,
always employed him.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was successively promoted to Fùtíkòng [Deputy Commander] and Tàiyuánfǔ Pànguān [Adjudicator of Tàiyuán Prefecture].
He disagreed with Wányán Púlàdōu, the Cóngyídu Tíkòng [Commander of Cóngyí] and Zhènwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ [Military Commissioner of the Zhènwǔ Army], regarding the strategy of resistance and defense.
Their arrangements were at cross-purposes,
and consequently, the enemy made a massive invasion,
becoming almost irresistible.
Subsequently, both submitted memorials debating and defending their innocence.
The emperor disliked their disharmony,
and issued an edict to divide their troops for separate command.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Tóngzhī Tàiyuánfǔ Shì [Associate Administrator of Tàiyuán Prefecture].
He memorialized requesting to recruit volunteer armies,
establish commanders and officers,
and set up various ranks.
Dūtǒng [Commander-in-chief] was granted a regular seventh-grade position,
Fùtǒng [Deputy Commander] a regular eighth-grade,
Wànhù [Myriad-household Commander] a regular ninth-grade,
Qiānhù [Thousand-household Commander] was given regular appointments,
and Móukè [Hundred-household Commander] was given miscellaneous appointments.
Furthermore, thirty men constituted one Móukè,
five Móukè constituted one Qiānhù,
four Qiānhù constituted one Wànhù,
four Wànhù constituted one Fùtǒng,
two Fùtǒng constituted one Dūtǒng.
Additionally, a Zǒnglǐng Tíkòng [General Commander] was established.
The imperial decree approved this.
Four years later,
he was transferred to be the Vice Pacification Commissioner of Hédōng.
He submitted a memorial stating that Pacification Commissioner Wūgǔlún Lǐ was unwilling to divide his troops to resist the enemy,
and that many of his actions were unlawful.
An imperial edict ordered Lǐ's dismissal from office.
Shí Lún was promoted to Jìngyángjūn Military Commissioner,
and acting Regional Commander.
Soon after, he was appointed Prefect of Yán'ān Fǔ and concurrently Grand Military Commander of Fūyán Lù.
When the Great Yuán army besieged Xīnzhōu,
Shí Lún led troops to reinforce it.
He used his soldiers to escort the people into Tàiyuán,
and a great many soldiers and civilians were protected.
In the seventh month of the first year of Xīngdìng,
he was reassigned to Hépíngjūn Military Commissioner and concurrently Inspector of the area under Wèizhōu's jurisdiction.
An imperial edict admonished him, saying:
“Initially, We thought you were courageous and resolute,
and would exert yourself for the nation,
therefore We relied on you to accomplish things.
Soon after, We heard that you indulged in alcohol and acted unlawfully,
and Wūgǔlún Déshēng, the Prefect of Tàiyuán, also frequently reported this to Us.
However, these were all trivial matters.
But not rescuing Fénzhōu,
how can that be a minor issue?
The officials have deliberated your punishment thus,
you should know all about it,
and exert even greater effort
to cover up your past faults.”
In the eleventh month of that year,
he was transferred to Zhènxījūn Military Commissioner and concurrently Inspector of the area under Lánzhōu's jurisdiction, and acting Marshal.
In the fourth month of the second year,
Shí Lún reported:
“Last year, the northern army broke through Tàiyuán,
and roving soldiers frequently entered the territory of Lánzhōu.
However, the officials, common people, generals, and soldiers exerted all their strength to defend against them,
and were ultimately able to hold out safely.
Previously, the inner prefectures of Hédōng were all garrisoned with elite armor [troops],
and well-stocked with provisions,
appearing even more complete and wealthy than the border cities.
Yet, once the enemy arrived, they successively fell.
Lánzhōu's troops are few and provisions insufficient;
it is only because the superiors and subordinates cooperated,
responding to each other like lips and teeth,
that they achieved peace and stability.
When the large army first entered,
the commanderies and prefectures were in a panic.
If not for this Marshal's office maintaining control,
then Yù, Guǎn, Bǎodé, Kělán, and Nínghuà would all have been lost.
Now the autumn defense is not far off;
I beg the imperial court to grant additional commendations and rewards,
to ensure they exert even greater effort,
and make it easier for them to guard the territory.”
An imperial edict ordered that those who had rendered meritorious service should each be promoted one rank,
and also issued blank imperial edicts for promotion,
ordering the Privy Council to confer them.
In the second month of the third year,
Shí Lún memorialized:
“Previously, after Bìng and Fén had fallen,
and the troops had entered the interior,
I believed they would surely attack Píngyáng.
If Píngyáng could not be held,
they would then reach Lùzhōu,
and their return path would be through Lóngzhōu Gǔ to enter Tàiyuán.
Therefore, I once requested troops to block their return route,
but the imperial court did not agree.
Subsequently, everything happened as I had predicted.
When the enemy first entered Hédōng,
the people of the commanderies and prefectures, both old and young, moved to reside in dangerous mountains.
Later, although Tàiyuán fell,
the masses ultimately did not follow [the enemy].
Their intention was that the enemy would not stay long,
and they also hoped for the return of the government troops.
Now the enemy has resided there for half a year,
sending infantry and cavalry to harass the various fortified settlements,
yet no government troops have arrived.
How can the people resist much longer?
Indeed, Tàiyuán
is the key prefecture of Hédōng;
Píngyáng
is the barrier for Shǎnxī and Hénán.
If the enemy troops stay for a long time,
and all the residents follow them,
garrisoning troops and accumulating provisions to solidify their base,
and then further harass our commanderies and prefectures that are not yet ruined,
then the border cities will all fall in a matter of days.
If the northern route is not held,
then the southern route becomes the border,
even closer to Shǎnxī and Hénán.
I am secretly worried about this,
and therefore once again request troops to plan for combat and defense.
The Privy Council, however, dispatched me,
together with Guō Yùzǔ, the acting Vice Administrator of Tàiyuán, and Lǐ Tiānlù of the義軍 (Yìjūn) and others, totaling over ten thousand men,
and their five thousand shí of provisions,
to join Mònián Húlà, the acting Right Supervisor of the Marshal's office in Fénzhōu, to retake Tàiyuán.
I summoned Yùzǔ,
wishing to give orders to his troops,
but Yùzǔ did not comply.
Soon after, I received a report from Húlà saying: ‘I asked Yùzǔ about the number of troops,
but he only said that Tiānlù and others spoke of them, and he had never personally inspected them.
When I asked about provisions,
he said they were scattered in several places.’
It seems his true intention was to show the imperial court that he had troops and provisions,
hoping to be used and obtain an important position,
and it cannot be considered actual utility.
Nevertheless,
I have already dispatched Commander Shízhǎn Wūlǐxīn and others to lead the troops there.
However, the enemy's strength is quite formidable,
and those going are all newly assembled raw recruits,
completely without elite forces.
I fear they cannot prevail.
I beg that from Hénán and Shǎnxī, a quantity of elite troops be allocated
to augment my strength.
Furthermore, order the prefectures and commanderies of Shǎnxī that are close to Hédōng to provide provisions,
and also order the various armies on the southern route to engage the enemy's south,
to divide their strength.
If this is done,
perhaps Tàiyuán can be retaken.”
An imperial edict ordered the Hénán and Shǎnxī Provincial Administrations to allocate provisions to them.
However, the request for troops was not granted because they were currently attacking Sòng.
In the third month,
Shí Lún again memorialized:
“Recently, the large army broke through Tàiyuán,
and recruited civilians to farm, establishing a basis for prolonged occupation.
I consider Tàiyuán a crucial strategic point,
which must be contested.
I dispatched Commander Shízhǎn Wūlǐxīn to lead government troops and volunteer forces to plan its recapture.
Furthermore, those soldiers who have rendered meritorious service should be promptly rewarded.
Therefore, I proposed that Wūlǐxīn be granted a ninth-rank position,
and sought this from the court.
However, the executives believed that both rewarding merit and punishing crime require central review.
Indeed, Hédōng is very far from the capital.
Reporting back and forth would take dozens of days,
and the government troops are remnants of defeats,
their sharp edge almost completely gone.
The volunteer forces are also unaccustomed to battle formations,
no different from a disorganized rabble.
Even tempting them with rich rewards,
I fear they may not be used effectively,
let alone when those with merit wait long without receiving recognition.
If the masses cannot be utilized, then the enemy cannot be repelled.
If the enemy is not repelled, then Tàiyuán cannot be retaken.
If Tàiyuán cannot be retaken, then the situation in Píngyáng becomes more precarious day by day,
and our territory will shrink daily.
Now the imperial court suppresses and does not permit [my request],
it is nothing more than concern about excessive rewards.
Even if there is the drawback of excessive rewards,
which is more serious, that or the harm of losing Tàiyuán?”
Thereupon, an imperial edict granted his request,
allowing Shí Lún to transfer and appoint officials from the Vice Administrator of Tàiyuán and other prefectures down to the seventh rank,
and from the fourth rank and below for honorary officials.
An encomium states: Since Hú Shāhǔ and Gāo Qí came into power,
the customs completely changed.
The imperial court, correcting policies of leniency and generosity,
favored strict scrutiny.
However, this was not carried out effectively,
instead resulting in indulgence.
The generals and commanders disdained refined scholarly ways,
preferring to be coarse and overbearing.
However, this was not used appropriately,
ultimately leading to arrogance and insubordination.
Yáwūtǎ won battles and captured territories,
his might extended across the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
yet he was arrogant, violent, and lawless,
freely insulting imperial envoys.
How could such a person be controlled?
To abandon Shǎn and return,
and die on the road,
was perhaps his good fortune.
His son followed his example,
and ultimately fell into great disgrace.
Thus, the junzǐ knew that Kāng Xī’s words were not excessive.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 50: Wányán Hédá, Yílà Pú'ā
Wányán Hédá’s personal name was Zhān,
his courtesy name Jǐngshān.
He grew up amidst military affairs,
practiced archery and horsemanship,
and was able to inspire others to fight to the death.
In the early Zhēnyòu period,
he was sent with the imperial guard to escort Princess Qíguó,
serving as a bodyguard.
In the third year,
he was appointed Tuīguān of Línhuáng Fǔ,
and concurrently served as Yuánshuài Yòujiānjūn.
At that time, Línhuáng was evacuated,
and its people, along with those from Quán and Qìng Prefectures, fortified Píngzhōu together.
Hédá was subordinate to its Jīnglüèshǐ, Wūlíndá Qǐzhù.
Qǐzhù, acting on expediency, appointed him Dūtǒng in the army,
and he was successively promoted to Tíkòng,
wearing a golden talisman.
Not long after,
when the generals from Yànnán led troops to recapture the capital city,
and reached Qiān'ān County in Píngzhōu,
the armies of Línhuáng and Quánqìng rebelled,
killed Qǐzhù,
and acclaimed Hédá, bringing him back to Píngzhōu,
promoting him to commander,
to lead Qǐzhù’s army.
Hédá, by stratagem, executed several of the ringleaders.
In the sixth month of that year,
the great general of the Northern army, Hǎndébù, dispatched the Jiānzhàn Tíjūn to the foot of Píngzhōu city,
and sent a local named Huáng Shāng into the city to solicit surrender.
The elders refused to comply.
Hédá led his troops to engage in battle.
Realizing the situation was unfavorable,
he surrendered his army on the battlefield.
Jiānzhàn took Hédá north,
where he remained for half a year,
then ordered him to return and guard Píngzhōu.
Afterward,
he planned to escape and return,
and thus sent the Magistrate of Fèngxiān County, Gěshíliè Bùlǐgē, the Professor of Běijīng, Púchá Húlí'ān, and the Jiǎnfǎ of the Right Three Divisions, Púchá Pú Nǚshè, to cross the sea and report.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year,
Hédá indeed led his部 and the people of the prefecture southwest across the sea back to the country.
An imperial edict promoted him three ranks in office,
and raised him to Zhènnánjūn Jiédùshǐ,
stationed at Yìdū,
to coordinate with Marshal Ménggǔgāng,
serving as Xuānchāi Dūtíkòng.
In the twelfth month,
the great Yuán army swept through Bóxīng, Lè'ān, and Shòuguāng,
extending eastward into Wéizhōu.
Ménggǔgāng dispatched Hédá to lead troops in several battles at Shòuguāng and Línzī.
In the first month of Xīngdìng元年,
he was transferred to Tōngyuǎnjūn Jiédùshǐ, and concurrently Jǐngzhōu Guǎnnèi Guānchásǐ.
In the seventh month,
he was reassigned to Píngxījūn Jiédùshǐ, and concurrently Hézhōu Guǎnnèi Guānchásǐ.
In the first month of the second year,
he became Zhī Yán'ānfǔshì, and concurrently Fūyán Lù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
In the first month of the third year,
an imperial edict ordered an expedition against Sòng,
and Hédá was appointed Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān.
In the third month,
he defeated the Sòng army at Méilín Guān,
capturing the commander Zhāng Shí.
He again defeated the Sòng army at Mǎlíng Bǎo,
capturing a hundred horses.
He also captured Máchéng County,
taking its magistrate Zhāng Tì and staff officer Guō Shǒujì.
In the fourth month,
the Xià people attacked Tōngqín Zhài.
Hédá led his troops out to Ānsài Bǎo,
reaching Lóngzhōu.
Two thousand Xià infantry and cavalry emerged from the city to meet the attack.
He advanced and attacked them,
beheading several tens of heads,
and capturing ten people.
He then attacked Lóngzhōu,
breaching its southwest corner,
and returned when dusk fell.
In the sixth month,
he served as the acting Yuánshuàifǔ in Táng and Dèng.
The emperor sent an edict saying:
"Because of your talent and capability, I entrust this to you.
Do not let the enemy invade.
Just strengthen our defenses."
In the first month of the fourth year,
he was again appointed Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān,
stationed at Yán'ān.
In the tenth month,
the Xià people attacked Suídé Zhōu,
stationing their troops at Zhǔtiān Shān.
Hédá led his troops to attack them.
He separately dispatched the Vanguard Tíkòng Fán Zé and others, each leading their respective divisions in three routes to advance,
all converging at the mountain peak.
Seeing tens of thousands of Xià soldiers arrayed against the mountain,
they immediately unleashed their forces and attacked in divisions.
Zé was the first to ascend,
destroying their left wing.
The other generals then attacked their right,
defeating them.
In the fifth month of the fifth year,
he was appointed Zhī Yán'ānfǔshì,
concurrently holding his previous post.
He stated:
"Because military officers are frequently relocated,
they often do not know the topography of their assigned locations – whether they are circuitous, direct, dangerous, or easy to traverse.
In times of urgency, this could lead to defeat.
From now on, I request that they not be relocated."
He also stated:
"The garrison troops in Hénán and Shǎnxī are all dispersed and stationed in various circuits.
Only the old and young remain in the camps.
I request that experienced elders be selected as commanders for each circuit to pacify and govern them,
and moreover, to urge their sons and younger brothers to practice horsemanship and archery,
so that they may be useful in the future."
All requests were granted.
In the eleventh month,
the Xià people attacked Ānsài Bǎo.
Their army arrived first.
Hédá and the campaigning marshal Nàhé Mǎizhù defended against them.
Hédá strategized, saying:
"Before the northern army arrives,
if we first defeat the Xià people, then the later effort will be easier."
Thereupon, he secretly led his army, carrying provisions, and doubled their pace, advancing rapidly,
launching a night raid on their camp.
The Xià people indeed suffered a great rout,
and were pursued and killed for forty lǐ.
Those who fell into ravines and died were countless.
Upon hearing this, the emperor
bestowed fifty liǎng of gold and ten bolts of heavy silk upon each,
and issued an imperial edict stating:
"You have achieved great merit.
I am truly delighted to hear of it.
With such planning,
they will surely know fear.
Within a few years,
you may all rest."
He also decreed that Hédá’s achievements should be made known to all the commanders in Hénán.
In this month,
he and Marshal Mǎizhù fought again at Yán'ān,
both suffering heavy losses.
In the twelfth month,
for his meritorious service in defending Yán'ān, he was awarded a golden belt, one jade tùhú, and ten bolts of heavy silk.
In the eleventh month,
Dèngzhōu reported
that the northern troops had advanced to Ráofēng Guān,
proceeding east from Jīnzhōu.
Thereupon,
the armies of the two provinces entered Dèngzhōu,
and sent Tíkòng Liú Tiānshān with a dispatch to Xiāngyáng Zhìzhì Sī,
requesting a joint defense against the northern troops,
and also demanding military provisions.
The two provinces had marched in the Guǐmǎo month prior,
leaving Yáng Wòyǎn's army to guard Ménxiāng.
Wòyǎn soon received an imperial decree to take the Luònán Lù, enter Shāngzhōu,
garrison Fēngyáng Chuān to guard Shàngjīn,
and act in concert with Shāngōng Xiān.
Hédá further left Yùwǔ Zhōnglángjiàng Wányán Chénhéshàng fifteen *lǐ* south of Ménxiāng,
before proceeding.
Chénhéshàng also followed and went.
Wòyǎn's army of eight thousand and the Mùguā Píng of Shāngzhōu,
rode three hundred *lǐ* in one day and night to enter Táohuā Bǎo,
learned that the northern troops had gone east from Fēngyáng,
also turned east,
and joined the main army at Zhènpíng.
Shāngōng Xiān's ten thousand men were originally stationed at Húlíng Guān,
and by this time also came to join via Jīngzǐkǒu and Shùnyáng.
On the first day of the twelfth month,
they all arrived below Dèngzhōu,
and encamped at Shùnyáng.
Then Tiānshān was sent into Sòng territory.
Initially,
the Sòng people had addressed our imperial dynasty's rulers as *Jūn Zhī*, *Bó Zhī*, *Shū Zhī*,
and paid annual tributes for nearly a hundred years.
After the Southern Crossing,
Sòng considered us not worth worrying about,
and completely ceased all communication.
Thus, when Xuānzōng campaigned south,
the soldiers and horses suffered immense losses, with barely one in ten surviving.
Although several prefectures on the Huái River were captured,
it merely allowed arrogant generals and fierce soldiers to indulge in slaughter and plunder, and satisfy their private desires.
Moreover, when Xuānhuī Shǐ Àodūn Āhǔ was sent as an envoy to the north,
a high-ranking official in the north pointed to a map and asked him:
"How many troops does your central army have from Shāngzhōu to here?"
Then, pointing to Xīngyuán, he said:
"If I don't go through Shāngzhōu,
I will take the Xīngyuán Lù and enter your territory."
Āhǔ reported this upon his return,
and Xuānzōng was greatly worried.
When Āizōng ascended the throne,
his ministers suggested sending an envoy to report the national mourning,
accompanied by posthumous gifts,
and using the opportunity to negotiate with them,
completely withdraw border defenses,
and jointly guard the strategic pass of Wǔxiū.
Thereupon, the matter was referred to the ministries and court for discussion,
but those in power, suffering from the affliction of being unable to bow after looking up,
all used the excuse that the court sending people first would be detrimental to national dignity.
In the first year,
the Emperor decreed to the southern border commanders
to send someone to Chúzhōu to establish good relations with Sòng.
The Sòng people always used the excuse of having to report to their court,
and so the peace negotiations were not pursued.
However, over ten years,
the imperial court repeatedly ordered border generals not to invade or plunder recklessly,
allowing both sides to somewhat rest.
The Sòng people began to believe this,
and thus had intentions of renewing good relations.
When Tiānshān arrived in Sòng with the dispatch,
the dispatch (*zháfù*) is another name for a command,
the Sòng commander Chén Gāi angrily insulted Tiānshān,
and replied with harsh words.
When the report reached them,
those who knew better all sighed secretly.
On the Wùchén day,
the northern troops crossed the Hàn Jiāng northward.
The generals thought they could attack them while they were halfway across,
but Pú'ā disagreed.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
the troops had all crossed,
and a battle was fought in front of Yǔshān.
The northern troops retreated a little,
and encamped thirty *lǐ* away.
The two chancellors reported a great victory by fast post.
All officials submitted congratulations.
The chancellors hosted a banquet in the provincial office.
Zuǒchéng Lǐ Qī was both joyful and tearful, saying:
"Without today's victory,
how could the calamities for the populace be recounted?"
He truly believed it to be so.
Previously,
when Hénán heard that the northern troops had emerged from Ráofēng,
the common people often entered city walls or sought refuge in strongholds.
When they heard the enemy had retreated,
some even remained calm and inactive.
Within two or three days, light cavalry arrived,
and people had nowhere to escape.
All were misled by the victory reports.
In the ninth year, on the Dīngyǒu day of the first month,
the armies of the two provinces were routed at Sānfēng Shān in Yángzhái.
Initially,
during the battle of Yǔshān,
the two armies confronted each other.
The northern army scattered northward,
and the Jīn army feared they would take advantage of the emptiness to attack the capital.
Thus, they planned to go to its aid.
At that time, the northern troops had sent three thousand cavalry toward the river,
and it had been more than twenty days.
Mìyáng, Nányáng, Fāngchéng, Xiāng, Jiá, and all prefectures up to the capital were breached,
and all accumulated provisions were burned, leaving nothing.
The Jīn army, moving east from Dèngzhōu, had no supplies.
They then moved along the mountains into Yángzhái.
After they set off,
the northern troops immediately attacked them.
As they marched and fought,
the northern troops also suffered many casualties.
A unit of the Héngshān army was charged by three thousand light cavalry.
The army fought desperately,
and the northern cavalry retreated.
While pursuing them,
a dense fog suddenly spread everywhere.
The two provincial commanders ordered the army to regroup.
A short while later,
the fog dispersed, and they advanced.
Before them was a great ravine several *lǐ* long and wide.
If not for this fog, the northern troops and their horses would have filled it.
The next day,
they reached Sānfēng Shān,
and were routed.
This event is recorded in Pú'ā's biography.
Hédá knew that the great cause was lost,
and wanted to dismount and fight,
but Pú'ā was already nowhere to be found.
Hédá fled to Jūnzhōu with several hundred cavalry.
The northern troops dug trenches outside its walls and attacked it.
He tried to escape through the gate but couldn't,
and hid in a cave dwelling.
When the city was breached,
the northern troops discovered and killed him.
At that time, the imperial court did not know of his death,
some said he had fled to Jīngzhào.
An imperial handwritten edict was issued,
recruiting people to search for him.
When Biàn was attacked,
they publicly declared:
"The only things your house relies on
are the Huáng Hé and Hédá.
Now Hédá has been killed by us,
and the Huáng Hé is ours.
Why do you not surrender?"
Hédá was thoroughly familiar with the enemy's situation,
and skilled in formations.
Moreover, he valued righteousness and lightly regarded wealth,
sharing joys and sorrows with his subordinates.
Whatever was captured, he immediately distributed.
When facing the enemy, he would lead the charge without hesitation,
and his troops were also happy to serve him.
His character can thus be known.
Zuǒchéng Zhāng Xíngxìn once recommended him, saying:
"Wányán Hédá is a good general of our time."
Yílà Pú'ā was originally a Qìdān person.
He joined the army young,
and was promoted from *qiānhù* to *dūtǒng* for his merits.
Initially,
when Āizōng was the Crown Prince,
he controlled the Púmì Yuàn,
and Pú'ā was selected as the General Commander of the Imperial Guard,
wearing a golden tally.
In the twelfth month of the winter of Yuánguāng second year, on the Gēngyín day,
when Xuānzōng's illness became critical,
the Crown Prince's elder half-brother, Yīng Wáng Shǒuchún, entered first to attend to the illness.
The Crown Prince knocked on the door from the Eastern Palace to request an audience,
and ordered Pú'ā to don armor and gather troops at Gèn Yuè,
to prepare for any unforeseen circumstances.
When Āizōng ascended the throne,
he once said to his close ministers:
"If not for Pú'ā then,
how could it have come to this?"
Thus, he was remotely appointed as Co-Administrator of Suīzhōu Military and Civil Affairs,
and Acting Court Councillor of the Púmì Yuàn.
From then on, many major military and state affairs were decided by him.
In the twelfth month of Zhèngdà fourth year,
the Héshuò army suddenly entered Shāngzhōu,
destroying Zhūyáng and Lúshì. Pú'ā resisted and fought to the east of Língbǎo,
encountering more than ten light cavalry.
He captured one person,
the rest immediately retreated.
Pú'ā nevertheless reported it as a victory.
He was rewarded with a hereditary *móukè*,
and also given generous gifts.
Everyone knew he was deceiving the Emperor,
but no one dared to speak out.
Lìbù Lángzhōng Yáng Jūrén incurred wrath with his subtle criticism.
In the second month of the sixth year, on the day Bǐngchén,
Pú'ā was appointed acting Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Since the summer of the previous year,
the northern army in Shǎnxī had advanced rapidly to Jīngzhōu,
and was blocking the grain route to Qìngyáng.
Pú'ā memorialized:
"Shǎnxī established two Branch Secretariats
originally to defend Hénán.
Now the northern army has been here for three years.
The Branch Secretariats command two to three hundred thousand troops and horses,
but have never faced the enemy in battle,
nor have they even broken a single arrow [in combat].
What use are these Branch Secretariats?"
The officials of the Bureau also unanimously memorialized that in the future, the military forces of the Bureau of Military Affairs would be needed for these matters.
The Emperor remained silent for a long time.
Thereafter,
Chancellor Sài Bùxíng was dispatched to Guānzhōng to manage the affairs of the Department of State Affairs,
while Pingzhang Zhengshi Hédá was recalled to the court.
Báisā was also summoned to the capital.
Pú'ā led one thousand of Wányán Chénhéshang's Loyal and Filial Army to garrison Bīnzhōu,
and was ordered to observe the northern situation.
In the eighth month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
Pú'ā recaptured Lùzhōu.
On the first day of the tenth month, which was Yǐwèi,
Pú'ā returned eastward.
In the twelfth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
an edict ordered Pú'ā, together with Grand Commander Yáwūtǎ and acting Auxiliary Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs Ékě, to relieve Qìngyáng.
In the first month of the seventh year,
they fought the northern soldiers at Dàchāng Yuán.
〔一０〕The northern army retreated,
and the siege of Qìngyáng was lifted.
An edict ordered Ékě to garrison Bīnzhōu,
while Pú'ā and Yáwūtǎ returned to Jīngzhào.
Soon after,
Pú'ā was appointed acting Provisional Administrator and, together with Hédá, served in the Branch Secretariat at Ménxiāng.
In the first month of the eighth year,
the northern army entered Shǎnxī.
Fèngxiáng fell.
The two Branch Secretariats abandoned Jīngzhào and went east.
Upon reaching Luòyáng Post Station,
they were summoned to discuss the affairs of Hézhōng.
The details are found in the biography of Báihuá.
In the twelfth month,
the northern soldiers crossed the Hàn Jiāng.
The armies of the two provinces entered Dèngzhōu,
and debated where the enemy would emerge from.
They considered whether it would be better to intercept them at Guānghuà by fighting across the river, or to let them cross and then fight them.
Zhāng Huì argued:
"It is better to intercept them across the river.
If we let them cross,
will our vulnerable interior not be routed?"
Pú'ā waved him off, saying:
"You only know about southern affairs;
what do you know about northern affairs?
I previously received an imperial decree at Yùzhōu which said,
'Even if they were in the desert, we should still go and seek them out,'
how much more so now that they are coming on their own?
You must not let them pass as you did at Dàchāng Yuán, Old Wèizhōu, or Shànchē Huí."
Dìngzhù, Gāo, and Fán all agreed with Pú'ā's words.
Hédá then asked Àndémù,
who thought otherwise.
The army considered Àndémù to be a northerner,
who understood the enemy's military situation,
and that his words were reasonable.
However, they could not overturn Pú'ā's decision.
They stayed at Shùnyáng for twenty days.
Scouts from Guānghuà arrived,
reporting
"a thousand cavalry have already crossed north."
That night, the two provinces advanced their army.
By dawn, they reached Yǔshān.
More scouts reported
"all northern cavalry have crossed."
On the day Guǐyǒu,
the northern army approached.
The two provinces positioned their armies on a high mountain,
each occupying favorable terrain.
The infantry advanced to meet them at the foot of the mountain,
while the cavalry encamped behind the mountain.
On the day Jiǎxū,
before sunrise,
the northern soldiers arrived.
The great commander led two small flags to reconnoiter.
After scouting, they did not advance,
but dispersed like wild geese wings,
circling the mountain slope and appearing behind the cavalry,
advancing in three divisions.
Excluding the baggage train, there were two tens of thousands of men.
Hédá ordered all armies,
"Given today's situation, we should not fight.
Let us wait."
Suddenly, the northern cavalry charged forward.
The Jīn soldiers had no choice but to fight.
They engaged in close-quarters combat.
After three exchanges,
the northern cavalry slightly retreated.
The northern soldiers on the west side saw Pú'ā personally lead the armored cavalry to charge them from behind,
three times.
They were strongly repelled by Púchá Dìngzhù and retreated.
The great commander gathered his generals with a flag,
and they deliberated for a long time.
Hédá understood the northern army's intentions.
At that time, Gāo Yīng's army was facing north,
and the northern soldiers attacked their rear, pushing them.
Yīng's army moved.
Hédá almost executed Yīng,
but Yīng again rallied his troops to fight fiercely.
The northern soldiers slightly withdrew to observe the situation.
When Yīng's army stabilized,
they again pressed Fán Zé's army.
Hédá executed a chiliarch.
The army fought desperately,
and repelled them.
The northern soldiers returned to their formation,
facing south towards their original path.
The two provinces deliberated again,
"Although they are said to be thirty thousand strong,
one-third of that is baggage train.
Moreover, they have been stalemated for two or three days without food.
We should press them while they are retreating."
Zhāng Huì championed this view.
Pú'ā said:
"The river route is cut off,
the Yellow River is not frozen.
If they enter our core territory,
where will they go?
Why be so hasty?"
They did not follow his advice.
On the day Yǐhài,
the northern soldiers suddenly disappeared.
Their campfires were silent, with no trace.
The two provinces and the generals deliberated:
"We haven't seen their army for four days,
nor their camp.
There are continuous supplies from Dèngzhōu and travelers on the road,
but no one has seen them either.
Have they crossed south and returned?"
On the day Jǐmǎo,
scouting cavalry finally discovered the northern army in a jujube forest on the opposite bank of Guānghuà.
They cooked food by day
and did not dismount at night.
People were seen moving about in the forest,
but even within fifty or sixty paces, no sound was heard.
Their strategizing was evident.
Initially,
after the battle at Yǔshān, two cavalrymen got lost and entered the camp.
When questioned,
it was learned that the northern army consisted of seven main divisions,
each commanded by a great general.
Then ten men, feigning surrender, arrived,
wearing ragged clothes and riding weak horses, weeping and complaining of hardship.
The two provinces believed them,
gave them fat horses,
offered them wine,
and warm clothes and food, placing them behind the formation.
The ten men then whipped their horses and rode away.
Only then did they realize they were enemy scouts.
On the day Gēngchén,
the two provinces decided to enter Dèngzhōu for supplies.
Between the hours of Chén and Sì, they arrived at the rear of the forest.
The northern soldiers suddenly attacked.
The armies of the two provinces met them in battle.
During the engagement,
the northern soldiers used a hundred cavalry to intercept the baggage train and departed.
The Jīn army almost broke formation.
By night, they entered the city.
Fearing that the soldiers might get lost,
they rang bells to summon them.
Fán Zé garrisoned west of the city,
and Gāo Yīng garrisoned east of the city.
On the first day of the ninth year, which was Rénwǔ,
they displayed their might below Dèngchéng.
The northern soldiers did not engage in battle.
The great general sent someone to request wine.
The two provinces gave him twenty bottles.
On the day Guǐwèi,
the grand army departed Dèngzhōu,
heading towards the capital.
There were twenty thousand cavalry and one hundred and thirty thousand infantry.
The cavalry commanders were Púchá Dìngzhù and Púchá Dájíbǔ,
the senior commander was Àntèmù.
The commanders of the Loyal and Filial Army were Jiágǔ Àidá and the imperial clansman Dálúhuān.
The commander-in-chief was Jiágǔ Yītèlá.
The commissioner for infantry was Línzī Jùnwáng Zhāng Huì.
The annihilating commanders were Wányán Āpái, Gāo Yīng, and Fán Zé.
The central army was Chénhéshang,
and they were to join the armies of Shān Gōng Wǔxiān and Yáng Wòyǎn.
On this day,
they encamped below Wǔlíng Shān,
taking the Yālù route.
The northern soldiers, with three thousand cavalry, followed behind them.
They then set up camp to await Yáng Wǔ.
Yáng Wǔ (楊武) arrived.
He learned that Shēn (申) and Yù (裕) two prefectures had already surrendered.
On the seventh day, at night,
it was discussed that the Northern cavalry would probably attack us again tomorrow.
They only had three thousand cavalry,
and if we showed weakness,
we would be underestimated.
We ought to fight them.
So, fifty cavalry were ambushed on the Dèngzhōu (鄧州) road.
The next day, as the army marched,
the Northern cavalry attacked them as before.
The Jīn (金) army, with ten thousand men, surrounded them and moved eastward.
The ambush was sprung,
and the Northern soldiers retreated south.
That day, it rained,
and they encamped in a bamboo grove.
On Gēngyín (庚寅) day,
they halted at Āngāo (安臯).
On Xīnmǎo (辛卯) day,
they encamped at Yālù (鴉路) and Lǔshān (魯山).
The Héxī (河西) army had already offered Shēn (申) and Yù (裕),
and were escorting old people, children, cattle, and sheep via Yālù (鴉路).
The Jīn (金) army happened to encounter them,
and seized their cattle and sheep to provision the army.
On Guǐsì (癸巳) day,
they sighted Jūnzhōu (鈞州),
and reached the Shāhé (沙河).
Five thousand Northern cavalry were waiting north of the river.
The Jīn (金) army seized the bridge to cross.
The Northern army immediately turned west and retreated.
The Jīn (金) army charged,
but the Northern army did not fight,
and again crossed the Shāhé (沙河) to the south.
The Jīn (金) army wanted to set up camp,
but the Northern army crossed the river again to attack.
The Jīn (金) army could not get food,
nor could they rest.
At dusk,
rain began,
turning to snow by dawn.
The Northern soldiers increased to ten thousand men,
marching and fighting.
Upon reaching Huángyúdiàn (黃榆店),
twenty-five *lǐ* (里) from Jūnzhōu (鈞州),
the rain and snow prevented further advance,
so they camped for three days.
On Bǐngshēn (丙申) day,
a close attendant entered the army to convey an imperial decree,
gathering all commanders to receive instructions.
The imperial decree stated:
"The armies of both provinces are all to proceed to the capital.
I will personally preside over a banquet for the army at the imperial gate,
and exchange imperial horses.
It will not be too late to go out and fight then."
There was also a secret decree that said:
"It has recently come to my knowledge that two or three hundred cavalry leaked through at Zhāngjiāwān (張家灣),
and have already moved to Wèi (衞) and Mèng (孟) prefectures.
Both provinces must always be strictly on guard."
After receiving the decree,
Pú'ā (蒲阿) flung his sleeve and stood up.
Hédá (合達) wanted to discuss again,
but Pú'ā (蒲阿) said:
"This is all there is.
What more is there to discuss?"
He had evidently lost his nerve.
The army immediately set off.
The Northern armies that had crossed from the north all gathered.
They blocked the Jīn (金) army's path with large trees in front and behind.
The Wòyǎn (沃衍) army forced its way through
and succeeded.
Hédá (合達) then suggested that Chén Héshang (陳和尚) first occupy the high ground on the mountain.
Before they could reorganize,
the Jīn (金) army had already reached the bamboo grove,
only a little over ten *lǐ* (里) from Jūnzhōu (鈞州).
The Jīn (金) army then advanced.
The Northern army indeed retreated to the northeast and southwest of Sānfēng (三峯).
Wǔ (武) and Gāo (高) as vanguards occupied their southwest,
and Yáng (楊) and Fán (樊) occupied their northeast.
The Northern soldiers all retreated,
remaining only to the east of Sānfēng (三峯).
Zhāng Huì (張惠) and Àndémù (按得木) stood on the mountain, observing two or three hundred thousand Northern soldiers,
approximately twenty *lǐ* (里) deep.
Àndémù (按得木) consulted with Zhāng Huì (張惠) saying:
"If we don't fight here, what else can we do?"
So, he led over ten thousand cavalry to charge down from above and surround them.
The Northern soldiers retreated.
Soon, heavy snow began,
and white mist obscured the sky,
so people could not see each other.
By then, it had been snowing for three days.
The battlefield had many hemp fields,
often plowed four or five times,
so the mud and mire where men and horses trod reached their shins.
Soldiers, clad in armor, stood stiffly in the snow,
their spears and lances frozen solid like rafters.
Some soldiers had not eaten for up to three days.
The Northern soldiers merged with the Héběi (河北) army,
surrounding them on all sides.
They lit large fires to roast beef and mutton,
and rested in shifts.
Taking advantage of the Jīn (金) army's exhaustion,
they opened the Jūnzhōu (鈞州) road to let them escape,
and then attacked them from the flanks with fresh troops.
The Jīn (金) army then collapsed,
with a sound like a collapsing mountain.
Suddenly, the weather cleared,
and the sunlight shone brightly.
Not a single Jīn (金) soldier escaped.
Wǔ Xiān (武仙) led thirty cavalry into the bamboo grove.
The armies of Yáng (楊), Fán (樊), and Zhāng (張) vied for a path.
The Northern soldiers surrounded them several layers deep,
and together with the remnants of Gāo Yīng's (高英) troops, they fought south of Shìlíncūn (柿林村).
Wòyǎn (沃衍), Zé (澤), and Yīng (英) all died.
[一一]Only Zhāng Huì (張惠), holding a large spear, fought fiercely on foot until his death.
Pú'ā (蒲阿) fled to the capital,
but before he arrived,
he was pursued
and captured.
In the seventh month,
he was shackled and brought to Guānshān (官山).
He was summoned and asked if he would surrender.
After hundreds of exchanges,
he only said:
"I am a high minister of the Jīn (金) state.
I should only die within the borders of the Jīn (金) state."
He was then killed.
The encomium says: Since the Jīn (金) moved south,
the historical records are full of their successful military campaigns.
However, their territory did not expand,
and the casualties were equal.
Gentlemen are suspicious of this.
In a previous campaign against Sòng (宋),
the battle of Tángzhōu (唐州) resulted in the loss of seven hundred troops.
The commanding general, Éluàn (訛論), concealed it,
and reported a victory.
The censor Nàlán (納蘭) impeached him.
Xuānzōng (宣宗) praised the censor,
but did not punish Éluàn (訛論).
This showed that both ruler and ministers collectively sought empty renown.
At the victory of Yǔshān (禹山),
the two provinces were deceitful,
thus leading to the ruin of the state.
Was this not instigated by Xuānzōng's (宣宗) past actions?
As for the defeat at Sānfēngshān (三峯山),
it was beyond recovery.
High and low stared in astonishment,
and nine-tenths of the Jīn (金) state's affairs were already lost.
The Heavenly Dynasty (天朝) took the route through Xiāng (襄) and Hàn (漢),
sending an isolated army deep into enemy territory.
Their strategic brilliance was godlike,
and they also received divine aid,
thus being able to defy military taboos,
and achieve a glorious deed for ten thousand generations.
Even if Hédá (合達) was a good general,
how could he withstand this?
Pú'ā (蒲阿) lacked strategy,
but was uniquely blameless in his death.
That is still commendable.
Collation Notes
Biographies Volume 51: Wányán Sàibù (完顏賽不), Báisā (白撒) (also known as Chéngyì (承裔)), Chìzhǎn Héxǐ (赤盞合喜)
Wányán Sàibù (完顏賽不) was a descendant of Bǎohuólǐ (保活里), the brother of the progenitor.
He had a magnificent physique
and was profound with great strategic vision.
Initially appointed to the imperial guard,
during the reign of Zhāngzōng (章宗),
he was selected to serve as a bodyguard.
In the eighth month of Míngchāng (明昌) first year (1190),
he was promoted from general of the imperial night guard to prefect of Nínghuàzhōu (寧化州).
Not long after,
he was transferred to be deputy commander-in-chief of the Wǔwèi (武衞) army.
In Tàihé (泰和) second year (1202),
he was transferred to be military commissioner of Húlǐgǎi (胡里改) circuit.
In the fourth year (1204),
he was promoted to commander-in-chief of the Wǔwèi (武衞) army,
and soon after became Left Deputy Inspector-General of the Palace Guard.
When Púshàn Kuí (僕散揆) was Pingzhang (平章) and attacked the Sòng (宋),
he was appointed Right Wing Commander (右翼都統).
In the sixth year, sixth month,
the Sòng (宋) general Huángfǔ Bīn (皇甫斌) was dispatched with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry, who advanced from Quèshān (確山) and Bāoxìn (褒信) in separate routes to invade Cài (蔡).
Upon hearing of the defeat of Guō Zhuó (郭倬) and Lǐ Shuǎng (李爽),
they halted at the Zhēnshǔi (溱水) and dared not advance.
Thereupon,
Kuí (揆) sent Sàibù (賽不) and Deputy Commander (副統) Shàng Júshǐ (尚局使) Púxiān Wànnú (蒲鮮萬奴), as well as Shēnzhōu (深州)刺史 Wánýán Dájí (完顏達吉), and others, with seven thousand cavalry to attack them.
At this time, the Zhēnshǔi (溱水) was overflowing.
The Sòng (宋) troops held the bridge to resist.
Sàibù (賽不) and the others planned to secretly lead their troops out by night.
Dájí (達吉) led his cavalry across the water to their right flank,
while Wànnú (萬奴) and the others went to their left.
Sàibù (賽不), after estimating that all his troops had crossed,
then led Deputy Commander (副統) Ālǔdài (阿魯帶) with elite soldiers directly towards the bridge.
The Sòng (宋) troops could not hold them back.
By dawn, they suffered a great rout.
Wànnú (萬奴) used his troops to cut off the Zhēnyáng (真陽) road.
The various armies pursued and attacked them to Chénzé (陳澤),
beheading more than twenty thousand.
They captured over a thousand warhorses and various livestock.
When the troops returned,
Sàibù's (賽不) noble rank was advanced by one degree,
and he was generously rewarded with gold and silk.
In the early Jiānzhōng (貞祐) period,
he was appointed Assistant Administrator (同簽) of the Bureau of Military Affairs (樞密院事).
In the third year,
he was promoted to Prefect of Líntáo Fǔ (臨洮府事),
concurrently serving as Deputy Commander of Shǎnxī Lù (陝西路副統軍).
The emperor summoned him and admonished him, saying:
“When you were in Xījīng (西京), you devoted yourself to the country,
and when you governed Huàzhōu (華州), you also exerted your efforts.
Now you have finally reached the third rank.
I specially promote you to this position
because Wūgǔlún Yǎnzhōu (烏古論兗州), the Deputy Pacification Commissioner of Shǎnxī (陝西安撫副使), did not obey the orders of Pacification Commissioner Dájí (達吉),
which led to many failures.
Now Yǎnzhōu (兗州) has been punished,
and I order you to assist him.
You should strive even harder to devote yourself fully.
If you fail to do so,
I will have to reconsider and act otherwise.”
In the eighth month,
he became Prefect of Fèngxiáng Fǔ (鳳翔府事),
concurrently serving as Grand Marshal of Horse and Foot of this Circuit (本路兵馬都總管).
Soon after, he became Right Overseer (右都監) of the Marshal's Office (元帥).
In the fourth year, fourth month,
he deployed troops and captured the Mùdǒu Guān (木陡關) from Sòng (宋).
In the fifth month,
the Xià (夏) people repaired the Zhéqiáo (折橋) at the border of Láiqiāng Chéng (來羌城),
guarding it with troops.
Sàibù (賽不) sent troops to burn it.
In the eighth month,
the Xià (夏) people invaded Jiéyēzǐ Chuān (結耶觜川).
He dispatched troops to attack and drive them away.
Soon after, he again defeated their forces at Chē'ér Bǎo (車兒堡).
In the first year of Xīngdìng (興定), second month,
he was promoted to Administrator (簽) of the Bureau of Military Affairs (樞密院事).
At this time, the emperor, seeing that the Sòng (宋) annual tribute had not arrived
and that they were again invading and plundering,
ordered Sàibù (賽不) to suppress them.
In the fourth month,
he fought the Sòng (宋) people at Xìnyáng (信陽),
beheading eight thousand,
capturing Commander Zhōu Guāng (周光),
and seizing several thousand horses and five hundred cattle and sheep.
He again encountered Sòng (宋) people at Lǒngshān (隴山) and Qīlǐ Shān (七里山),
fighting six battles in total,
killing and capturing many.
Soon after, he dispatched troops across the Huái (淮) River,
raided Zhōngdù Diàn (中渡店),
captured Guāngshān (光山), Luóshān (羅山), Dìngchéng (定城) and other counties,
and broke through the two passes of Guāngzhōu (光州),
beheading over ten thousand.
He captured horses, cattle, and cloth,
which were distributed among the generals and soldiers.
An imperial edict bestowed upon him one jade rabbit falcon and ten bolts of heavy silk from the imperial treasury.
In the seventh month,
he submitted a memorial, stating:
“The capital is the foundation of the empire.
Its city walls should be extremely high and deep.
Although the outer wall is strong,
it spans over sixty li, and in times of sudden alarm, it is difficult to defend.
I have observed that there is an old foundation of a smaller inner city within the city.
It would be advisable to build and renovate it during the agricultural off-season,
which would be of long-term benefit to the state.
And for all prefectures and sub-prefectures in Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝陝西),
I request that they be repaired as appropriate.”
The emperor agreed.
In the second year, first month,
he defeated the Sòng (宋) people at Tiěshān (鐵山), Shàngshí Diàn (上石店), and Tángxiàn (唐縣).
In the fourth month,
he was promoted to concurrently serve as Pacification Commissioner (招討使) of the Southwest Circuit and other circuits,
Military Commissioner of Xī'ān (西安軍節度使), and Surveillance Commissioner (觀察使) of Shǎnzhōu (陝州).
He received an imperial edict to attack Zǎoyáng (棗陽).
The Sòng (宋) dispatched thirty thousand troops to resist the battle.
He skillfully lured and attacked them.
The Sòng (宋) troops were defeated and fled to the city.
He pressed them against the moats,
killing and drowning over three thousand people.
He then advanced and besieged the city.
One thousand Sòng (宋) cavalry and ten thousand infantry came to reinforce,
but he met and again greatly defeated them.
In the seventh month,
he was transferred to serve as Grand Marshal of Horse and Foot (兵馬都總管) of Shāndōng Xī Lù (山東西路),
concurrently Military Commissioner of Wǔníng Jūn (武寧軍節度使).
In the third year, second month,
he seized the Báishí Guān (白石關) from Sòng (宋),
killing over a thousand of its defenders,
and capturing thousands of armor and weapons.
In the third month,
he defeated the Sòng (宋) troops at Qīkǒu Cāng (七口倉),
and also seized the Xiǎohú Cāng (小鶻倉) from Sòng (宋),
capturing nine thousand piculs of grain and over thirty thousand weapons.
In this month,
he again defeated three thousand Sòng (宋) troops at Shígǔ Yá (石鶻崖).
In the fourth year, third month,
he received an imperial edict to lead troops to Hébĕi (河北) to persuade surrenders.
Huángfǔ Guī (皇甫珪), acting Prefect of Jìn'ān (晉安權府事), and Xí Yǒngjiān (席永堅), Magistrate of Zhèngpíng Xiàn (正平縣令), led over five thousand people to surrender,
obtaining ten thousand piculs of grain.
At this time, in Hébĕi (河北), the loyalist militias, officials, and common people in various places firmly defended their fortresses and stockades,
and many fought bravely to defeat the enemy.
Sàibù (賽不) submitted a memorial, stating:
“Such loyal and sincere individuals are commendable.
If they are not honored and rewarded, it will not inspire people's morale.
I request that the court appropriately grant them official positions and rewards.
If, by any chance, enemy troops return,
they will eagerly strive to serve.”
The emperor reviewed the memorial,
and summoned the officials of the Bureau of Military Affairs, saying:
“I and you all have also discussed this,
but because we did not see the situation there,
we simply allowed the military commanders to plan.
Now, looking at this memorial,
it greatly aligns with my wishes.
Order the relevant authorities to promote and reward them.”
In the fourth month of this year,
he was promoted to Vice Director (副使) of the Bureau of Military Affairs (樞密).
In the fifth year, fifth month,
he received an imperial edict to lead troops to relieve Hédōng (河東).
He won many battles,
and recovered the two cities of Jìn'ān (晉安) and Píngyáng (平陽).
A Censor (監察御史) reported that he failed to restrain his officers and men,
allowing them to plunder,
and requested that he be punished for his crime.
The emperor, considering his achievements,
decreed that he not be questioned.
In the second year of Yuánguāng (元光), fifth month,
he recovered Hézhōng (河中).
In the sixth month,
an imperial edict was issued to the Grand Councilors, saying:
“Vice Director Sàibù (賽不) of the Bureau of Military Affairs (樞密) is originally of the imperial clan;
his ancestors were merely separated by chance.
I value him as an old acquaintance and because he has long labored for the royal house,
I have already ordered the Mùqīn Fǔ (睦親府) to include him in the family registry.
You all should be aware of this.”
In the first year of Zhèngdà (正大), fifth month,
he was appointed Pingzhang (平章) of Political Affairs (政事).
Soon after,
he was transferred to be Right Chancellor (右丞相) of the Department of State Affairs (尚書).
He got along very well with the Assistant Administrator (參知政事) Lǐ Qī (李蹊).
When Qī (蹊) was dismissed for a public offense and appointed Prefect of Jīngluò (京洛),
Sàibù (賽不) repeatedly recommended Qī (蹊), comparing him to Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) of the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Because of this, Qī (蹊) was reinstated as chancellor.
In the third year,
when the Xuānzōng (宣宗) Temple was completed,
and the Dì (禘) sacrifice was to be performed,
there was a discussion about which meritorious officials should be enshrined and sacrificed alongside.
Opinions were divided.
Sàibù (賽不), as the Commissioner for Grand Rites (大禮使),
therefore said,
“Chancellor Fúxīng (福興) died in the service of the state,
and Qī Jīn (七斤) faithfully guarded Hénán (河南) to welcome the imperial carriage.
Their merits qualify them for joint sacrifice.”
The decision was thus made.
In the fourth year,
Yáng Jūrén (楊居仁), a Director of the Ministry of Personnel (吏部郎中), submitted a sealed memorial,
stating that the prime ministers should be carefully selected.
The emperor told his high ministers,
“If the prime minister is not the right person,
the censors and remonstrance officials should speak up. What does a clerk in the Ministry of Personnel have to do with this?”
Yánzhǎn Shìlǔ (顏盞世魯), Left Chancellor (尚書左丞), who always envied Jūrén (居仁),
also considered it presumptuous.
Sàibù (賽不) slowly advanced and said,
“When the empire is well-governed,
even commoners are allowed to offer advice,
not to mention a Director.
Your Majesty possesses the virtue of magnanimity,
which is why those who are not supposed to speak still speak.
If his words are useful, then act upon them;
if not, there is no need to show them to your subordinates.”
The emperor agreed with this.
Jūrén (居仁), courtesy name Xíngzhī (行之),
was a native of Dàxīng (大興).
He became a jinshi (進士) in the third year of Tàihé (泰和).
At the end of Tiānxīng (天興), when the north was crossed,
his entire family threw themselves into the Yellow River and died.
In the fifth year,
the Directorate of the Grand Secretariat was established in Jīngzhào.
He said to Dūshì Shāng Héng,
"Throughout history, prime ministers have always been literati,
because they understand the way of a prime minister.
What does Sàibù know,
to be placed in this position?
I fear that one day, when the historians record this,
they will write: 'At a certain time, a certain person was made prime minister, and the state perished.'"
He immediately urged Héng to draft a memorial requesting retirement.
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Hóu Zhì was straightforward and lacked subtlety,
which the imperial court despised.
In the first year of Tiānxīng, the military situation was urgent.
He was recalled from retirement to serve as Dàsīnóng.
Before long, he retired again.
When the Directorate of the Grand Secretariat in Xúzhōu had no one daring to serve,
Zhì was again appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
During a meeting in the Dūtáng,
Zhì, seeing that the state's power was unsustainable,
discussed several matters,
saying,
"There is simply no further strategy."
Báisā angrily said,
"If the Píngzhāng says this,
what hope does the state have?"
His intention was to put Zhì in an unpredictable situation.
Sàibù looked at Báisā and said,
"Minister Hóu's words are very appropriate."
Báisā then withdrew, seething with anger.
At that time, Dàyuán troops were pressing upon Biàn.
Báisā, anticipating that in the future, peace negotiations or the surrender of a hostage would require a prime minister to act,
strongly urged Sàibù to oversee the provincial affairs.
He was appointed Zuǒchéngxiàng,
but soon retired again.
In the winter of that year,
Āizōng moved to Guīdé.
He was recalled to serve as Yòuchéngxiàng and Shūmìshǐ,
concurrently Zuǒfù Yuánshuài,
and enfeoffed as Shòuguó Gōng,
accompanying the emperor on the journey.
After the collapse of the Héběi army,
he followed to Guīdé,
and again requested retirement.
In the seventh month of the second year,
an imperial edict again ordered him to preside over the Directorate of the Grand Secretariat in Xúzhōu.
Upon arrival,
as the prefecture lacked provisions,
he dispatched Lángzhōng Wáng Wànqìng to gather troops from Xú, Sù, and Língbì to take Yuánzhōu,
ordering Yuánshuài Guō Ēn to command them.
In the ninth month,
Ēn reached the city walls of Yuánzhōu,
but was defeated and returned.
He then ordered Zhuó Yì to attack Fēngxiàn,
and it was captured.
Initially,
Guō Ēn, shamed by his defeat,
feigned illness and did not act.
He then secretly conspired with Héběi rebel generals like Guō Yělǘ to surrender to the nation's security forces.
He seized Yuánshuài Shāng Yǔ and his son, and Yuánshuài Zuǒdūdūjiān Hégéliè Shànzhù,
and killed them all.
He also drove out Dūwèi Wòzhuǎnliúní, Ní páng Gǔhuánduān, Púchá Shìmóu, Yuánshuài Yòudūdūjiān Lǐ Jūrén, and Yuánwàiláng Cháng Zhōng.
From then on,
the city defenders and gate guards were all Héběi rebel forces,
entering and exiting as they pleased.
Sàibù had previously suffered from a carbuncle,
and had long ceased to attend to affairs.
He was severely constrained by the rebel faction,
and could only submit to their commands.
Initially,
when Yuán and Xú were engaged in mutual attacks,
Guō Yělǘ often feigned illness and did not participate.
Sàibù then appointed Yělǘ as Xúzhōu Jiédù Fùshǐ and concurrent Fángchéng Dūzǒnglǐng,
effectively restraining him.
After Yělǘ saw that Xúzhōu was undefended,
he conspired with Yuánzhōu rebel general Má Cóng to act in concert from inside and outside.
On the Jiǎshēn day of the tenth month,
at dawn,
they launched a surprise attack and captured Xúzhōu.
At that time, Cài was already under siege.
