The generals and soldiers of Xúzhōu, with imperial commands cut off,
and facing a large approaching army,
discussed surrendering.
Sàibù refused,
fearing capture.
At this point, he threw himself into the river seeking death,
but floated for over thirty paces without sinking.
Soldiers pulled him out.
Five days later,
he hanged himself in the prefectural residence.
Má Cóng then sent people to surrender the prefecture to Dàyuán.
His son, Ànchūn,
served as a bodyguard during the Zhèngdà era.
He was implicated in an illicit affair with an imperial clan woman,
beaten with one hundred strokes, and imprisoned.
While living in Xǔzhōu,
when the Dàyuán army reached Xǔ,
Ànchūn opened the south gate and surrendered.
He followed in the attack on the capital.
When Prince Cáo was sent as a hostage,
and some court officials and imperial guards followed him out,
Ànchūn vehemently cursed them,
even pointing fingers and denouncing them.
In the winter of that year,
he again escaped from Běizhōng and returned.
An imperial edict ordered him to be brought to the Directorate,
and questioned about the situation.
Ànchūn ascended the steps with the attendants, feigning tears.
The emperor asked the prime minister, saying,
"Ànchūn has come from Běizhōng.
Prime Minister, please inquire about the news from that place."
Sàibù appended a memorial, saying,
"This old minister is unfortunate to have given birth to such a wretch.
Things have come to this point;
I regret not having slain him with my own hands.
How can I bear to speak to him face-to-face?"
In the twelfth month,
the imperial carriage moved eastward.
The two remaining prime ministers were taken to Kāifēng,
captured, and executed in prison.
A eulogy: Sàibù, when facing the enemy lines, possessed military strategy.
When he held the reins of power,
observing his rescue and interpretation of Yáng Jūrén and Hóu Zhì's words,
he showed remarkable foresight.
The affair concerning Ànchūn especially had the character of ancient people.
Later, due to old age and illness, he was controlled by rebel ministers,
leading to the fate of an ordinary man and woman.
This is like a great mansion about to collapse;
it cannot be supported by a single pillar.
Alas!
The imperial kinsman Báisā, courtesy name Chéngyì,
was the elder brother of the last emperor Chénglín,
and a descendant of Shìzǔ's grandchildren.
From a young age, he served as Fèngyù.
During the Zhēnyòu era,
he successively held office as Zhī Líntáofǔ Shì and concurrent Běnlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he became Yuánshuài Zuǒdūdūjiān, overseeing the Yuánshuài Fǔ affairs in Fèngxiáng.
In that year,
an imperial edict ordered the Shǎnxī Xíngshěng to attack Sòng.
Báisā advanced from Gǒngzhōu Yánchuān,
encountered Sòng troops at Zàojiāobǎo,
and defeated them.
He again encountered Sòng troops at Tiānshuǐjūn,
launched a surprise attack,
and the Sòng army was utterly routed.
In the fourth month of the second year,
he again defeated Sòng troops.
Upon reaching Jīgōng Shān,
he then captured Xīhézhōu,
destroying its various passes and garrisons.
He dispatched Hézhá Dūtǒng Wán Yán Xíniè'ābù to lead an army towards Chéngzhōu.
Sòng commander Luó Cāncè and commander Lǐ Dàhēng burned their residences, abandoned the city, and fled.
They left over a thousand men to defend the city.
He commanded his troops to attack,
and thus captured it,
obtaining seventy thousand hú of grain and several tens of millions in cash.
The commander of Héchí Xiàn, Yáng Jiǔdǐng, also burned the county residences and fled to defend Qīngyěyuán.
Commander Gāo Qiān held Hēigǔ Guān very firmly.
He dispatched troops to launch a surprise attack,
Qiān fled,
and twenty thousand hú of grain were obtained,
along with an equivalent amount of weaponry.
He then razed its fortifications and returned.
In the third year,
he broke through Hǔtóu Guān,
and defeated Sòng troops at Qīpánzi and Jīguān Guān.
The officials and common people of Bāochéng Xiàn set fire to the city and fled,
and thus he took their city.
Zhào Xīxī, the Tíxíng and concurrent Zhīfǔshì of Xīngyuán Fǔ, hearing that the army was approaching,
led the officials and common people to flee.
Thus, Báisā then took Xīngyuán,
and stationed his troops there.
He ordered Tíkòng Zhāng Xiùhuá to ride to survey Yángzhōu.
The officials and common people also fled,
and he again took that city.
Soon after, he heard that thirty lǐ south of the river,
two thousand Sòng troops were arrayed on a mountain.
He dispatched Tíkòng Tángguō Yíshībù to attack and drive them off.
The Xíngshěng reported the victory,
and Xuānzōng was greatly pleased,
promoting Báisā one rank.
At that time, the court discussed that Lánzhōu was at the heart of Xīxià,
and had long been occupied by the enemy.
They intended to send Báisā to recover it.
Báisā memorialized, saying,
"Your minister recently entered Sòng territory,
raided Héchí,
subjugated Fèngzhōu,
defeated Xīngyuán,
reached Yángzhōu, and returned.
Having traversed thousands of lǐ of dangerous terrain,
the soldiers and horses are exhausted
and have not had adequate rest.
To wish to undertake such an endeavor again
is a very poor plan.
It would be better to rest the troops and nourish the soldiers in preparation."
This was approved.
Not long after,
Bái Sā became an acting assistant administrator of governmental affairs,
administering the provincial affairs in Píngliáng.
In the fourth year,
he submitted a memorial saying:
“The Fān (Tibetan) tribes in the Sòng territory, such as the mountain prefectures of Shānzhōu, Dàngchāng, Dōngshàngzhá,
formerly offered their allegiance
and were settled between Déshùn and Zhènrong.
Thereafter,
the officials failed to protect and cherish them,
and they subsequently fled.
Recently, it is heard that they again have a desire to return;
however, if they are not invited, they will not come on their own.
If we could gain their multitude,
they could assist our army
and bring peace to that region.

Your servant, considering that Wūgǔlún Chángshòu, who is acting as the Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎn Commandery, and Wēndūn Yǒngchāng, the Deputy Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎn Commandery, both belong to those Fān tribes,
and have long guarded the frontier,
deeply understand their sentiments,
has already ordered people to be sent to invite them.
Those sent and those who come to submit should all be recognized and rewarded.
I request that a reward system be predetermined to await them.”
The emperor approved his words.
That year,
a Xià army of 30,000 invaded Dìngxī Prefecture via Gāofēnglǐng,
encircling the city with palisades.
Bái Sā dispatched Cìshǐ Àishēn Āshīlá with the Field Army Commander Wūgǔlún Chángshòu and Wēndūn Yǒngchāng to engage them in battle,
and utterly defeated them,
beheading over a thousand
and capturing a great number of horses and weapons.
In the fifth month of the fifth year,
Bái Sā stated:
“Recently, I was ordered by imperial decree to send officials to persuade the various Fān tribes to attack Xīxià.
I immediately ordered Nǚxīliè Gǔlǐjiān, the General Administrator of Líntáo Circuit, to discuss and negotiate with the tribal chief of the Qiáojiā Bǐnglíng clan to persuade the other tribes.
Additionally, I separately dispatched Quán Zuǒyòusī Dūshì Zhào Méi to commission Liú Zhēn, who was remotely appointed as the Hégé County尉, to go along and reassure them.
Not long after,
Méi and Zhēn reported that the various tribes in places like Xīgēchéng,
along with the previously surrendered tribes, all wished to contribute over 78,000 soldiers.
Our own Fān tribes wish to contribute 9,000 soldiers.
If imperial troops are further provided as support,
victory over Xià is assured.
I have already ordered Gǔlǐjiān to lead 30,000 troops from Gǒngzhōu.
It would be appropriate to select another courageous and resourceful official to be his deputy.
Since Méi and Zhēn thoroughly understand the situation,
they should be given military positions at the front.
The Fān monk Nàlínxīnbō also rendered meritorious service in recruiting and attracting people.
I request that he be promoted and granted office to reward him.”
The emperor assented to all his requests.
In the second month of the first year of Yuánguāng,
the acting province submitted a memorial stating:
“Recently, I discussed with Marshal Wányán Hédá and Nàhé Mǎizhù from Yán’ān: the prefectures and counties north of the Yellow River have all been ruined and destroyed,
and Shǎnxī and Hénán have also been plundered.
Recently, the two enemies from the northwest attacked Fūyán simultaneously,
and cities and towns fell one after another;
only the isolated fortress of Yán’ān managed to remain intact.
If they return this autumn,
they will certainly advance deeply.
Although Jīngzhào, Fèngxiáng, Qìngyáng, and Píngliáng have all increased their forces,
these are mostly infantry,
and they are widely separated,
making it difficult to provide timely support.
If the various garrisons in Guānzhōng cannot hold,
then Hénán will also not be secure.
Now that the two enemies have departed far,
and the northwest has a brief respite,
it is advisable to seize this opportunity to directly take Shǔ and Hàn.
This is truly a perfectly secure plan for the nation’s foundation.”
An imperial edict was issued for the Privy Council to discuss it.
Before this,
a Xià army of several hundred thousand soldiers divided to invade Gāngǔ, Fūyán, Dàtōng, and other cities.
The emperor summoned Bái Sā and others, instructing them on strategy,
and ordered troops to attack their pontoon bridges,
then to advance to Xīliáng.
He separately dispatched a general to take Dàtōng City,
pass through Xīgē Road,
and plunder the Xià territory.
Bái Sā slowly advanced from Zhènrong,
and Hédá advanced from Huánzhōu,
in response to the three-pronged campaign.
Bái Sā galloped to Líntáo,
and dispatched General Administrator Nǚxīliè Gǔlǐjiān and Jīshízhōu Cìshǐ Túdān Yáwǔ, each acting as a marshal,
to lead troops westward.
They encountered over a thousand Xià soldiers at Tànánsì
and routed them.
The Xià people occupied Dàtōng City;
therefore, they besieged it,
and divided their forces to seize its bridge,
fighting against 7,000 defending soldiers.
They utterly defeated them,
killing almost half,
and countless others drowned in the river.
The remaining soldiers burned their bridge and fled westward.
Then, they returned to attack Dàtōng,
conquered it,
beheading 3,000,
and subsequently rallied the monks and laypeople from various monasteries and clans who had been coerced,
all of whom were settled back in their original places.
As the river bridge had been burned,
and the land beyond the pass was cold with little grass,
the army then returned.
In the twelfth month,
the acting province stated:
“Recently, someone coming from the north
claimed that King Mùhuálǐ had mobilized his entire army westward along the Wèi River,
planning to attack Fèngxiáng.
After Fèngxiáng fell, they would then target Jīngzhào.
If Jīngzhào could not be taken quickly,
they would leave troops to guard it,
and in spring, trample the two harvests of wheat to exhaust us.”
Not long after,
the main army indeed besieged Fèngxiáng,
and the military governor’s mansion sent someone to report the emergency.
Your servant believes that these two garrisons are like lips and teeth:
if Fèngxiáng falls, Jīngzhào will certainly be in peril,
and the whole of Shǎnyòu will be greatly shaken.
However, the wide, flat plains are indeed a place for cavalry to gallop freely,
and it is not advisable to directly confront them there.
I have already dispatched Commander Luó Huán with 2,000 soldiers
to advance along the Nánshān,
seeking an opportunity to attack their stockades
to relieve the siege of the city.
I further request that infantry and cavalry from Hénán be mobilized to guard Tóngguān.”
An imperial edict was issued to the Department of State Affairs and the Privy Council for discussion.
In the winter of the second year,
Emperor Āizōng ascended the throne,
and frontier affairs became even more urgent.
In the eighth month of the fifth year of Zhèngdà,
Bái Sā was recalled to the court,
and appointed Shangshū Yòuchéng.
Not long after,
he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
Bái Sā resided in the western frontier for nearly several decades.
During the period of Sòng and Xià relations,
although he achieved some minor successes,
they were all due to the efforts of his generals.
However, he was originally timid and incompetent,
concerned only with outward appearance.
He was by nature stubborn, greedy, and contemptible.
When he entered the court as prime minister,
his stubbornness was especially pronounced.
He often disliked the food served at official banquets,
and always brought his own meals.
When the state was on the verge of collapse,
he cared not at all.
In the first month of the ninth year,
the various armies suffered a crushing defeat at Sānfēngshān.
The main army joined with the Bái Pō army
and advanced rapidly towards Biàn.
The clerk Yáng Jūrén requested to attack them while they were still far off,
but Bái Sā refused,
and secretly resented him.
He then dispatched Wányán Máijīnchū, Shào Gōngmào, and others, along with 10,000 commoners,
to open a short dike and divert river water
to solidify the imperial city.
Before the work was completed,
the cavalry suddenly arrived.
Máijīnchū and the others were all killed,
with not two or three hundred able-bodied men managing to return.
On the Rénchén day,
Wèizhōu was abandoned,
and defensive equipment was transported into the capital.
Originally,
when the main army had broken Wèizhōu,
Emperor Xuānzōng had moved south,
relocating the prefectural seat to Yícūn Dù,
and building a new city on the north bank of the river,
only a few paces from the river.
Only its northern side was exposed to attack,
and it was reinforced with stone.
Heavy troops were stationed there every year,
and even when the main army arrived repeatedly, they could not approach it.
At this point,
it was abandoned,
and subsequently occupied by the main army.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the towers and battlements of the imperial capital were repaired.
Originally,
Xuānzōng, finding the capital expansive and difficult to defend,
ordered Gāo Qí to build the Wēngchéng.
Public and private resources were exhausted, and it was barely completed.
By this time,
the defense was discussed.
Some court officials said that the Wēngchéng was absolutely indefensible,
and the outer city could absolutely not be abandoned.
"If the great army first takes the outer city,
and supplies are exhausted and relief cut off,
not a single person will be able to escape.
The Wēngchéng might be useful in an unforeseen circumstance."
Thus, the decision was made to defend the outer city.
At that time, the total number of troops in the city was less than 40,000.
The imperial capital was 120 *lǐ* in circumference,
and there were not enough men to defend even a single weak point.
Therefore, it was decided to conscript displaced civilians into the army.
Additionally, military officers in the capital were summoned to the Shàngqīng Gōng.
Those who had distinguished themselves in city defense in the past, such as the imperial clansmen Ànchūhǔ, Dàhé'ér, Liú Bó'gāng, and others, all responded to the summons,
making up for deficiencies and serving on a temporary basis,
numbering over a hundred.
They also gathered the two *dūwèi* from the old garrisons along the river east and west of the capital, as well as the insurgent army from Wèizhōu,
totaling 40,000 men with the addition of the Jiànwēi forces.
An additional 60,000 able-bodied men were added,
and they were distributed among the four city sides.
On each side, a thousand men were specially selected,
named
the "Fēihǔ Jūn,"
to be dedicated to emergency response.
However, even they were not a proper army.
In the third month,
the imperial capital was attacked.
The high ministers divided up the defense of the four sides.
Báisā commanded the southwest,
which suffered the most urgent attacks.
Towers and battlements were repeatedly destroyed as soon as they were nearly built.
An order was issued to obtain bamboo for protective screens.
The responsible officials rushed into the city to search extensively,
but found nothing.
Báisā was enraged and wanted to execute them.
Yuánwàiláng Zhāng Gǔn whispered to the officials:
"If you have plenty of gold, you'll manage.
Why not immediately seek it from the Píngzhāng Fǔ?"
The officials, carrying three hundred *liǎng* of gold, went straight there.
They bribed the family servants,
and indeed obtained it.
Afterwards, the enemy troops retreated.
The court discussed dismissing Báisā.
Báisā felt uneasy,
and said to the clerk Yuán Hàowèn:
"I have blocked the path of the worthy for too long.
To be allowed to retire would be fortunate.
Please draft a memorial requesting my retirement for me."
A short while later,
the emperor had already dispatched an envoy with an imperial edict to his residence,
ordering him to retire.
After his dismissal,
the soldiers resented him for failing to fight and thus endangering the country,
and openly declared their intention to kill him.
Báisā was afraid,
and moved several times in one night.
The emperor secretly provided him with two hundred imperial guards.
The soldiers, having no way to vent their anger,
thereupon joined together to destroy his villa and then left.
His partisan, Yuánshuài Wányán Xiánìan'ābù, leading his own division, was garrisoned in Biàn.
Hearing of this, he went directly to the location,
and executed one person who was passing by the wall to suppress the unrest.
At this time,
Sùbùshòu and other forces were scattered in garrisons in Hénán.
Biànchéng's provisions were almost exhausted,
and repeated calls for reinforcements went unanswered.
In the tenth month of winter,
Báisā was again appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì, Quán Shūmìshǐ, and concurrently Yòufù Yuánshuài.
Thereupon,
the ministers presented to the emperor a plan to leave the capital.
Sàibù was appointed Yòuchéngxiàng, Shūmìshǐ, and concurrently Zuǒfù Yuánshuài.
The imperial clansman Échū was appointed Yòufù Yuánshuài, concurrently Shūmì Fùshǐ, and Quán Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Lǐ Qī was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū, and Quán Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
Túdān Bǎijiā was appointed Yuánshuài Zuǒ Jiānjūn, and acting Zǒngshuàifǔ Shì.
The eastern front commander was Yuánshuài Gāo Xiǎn,
assisted by Guǒyì Dūwèi Niánhé Yǎozhù with five thousand troops.
The southern front commander was Yuánshuài Wányán Zhū'ér,
assisted by Jiànwēi Dūwèi Wányán Wòlúnchū with five thousand troops.
The western front commanders were Yuánshuài Liú Yì and Shàngdǎng Gōng Zhāng Kāi,
assisted by Ānpíng Dūwèi Jì Gāng's five thousand troops.
The northern front commander was Yuánshuài Nèizú Lóushì,
assisted by Zhèwēi Dūwèi Zhāng Rùn's five thousand troops.
Zhōngyì Dūwèi Hèdūxǐ's four thousand troops
were subordinate to Zǒngshuài Bǎijiā.
Dūwèi Nèizú Jiǔzhù, Fùdūwèi Wáng Jiǎn, and Zǒnglǐng Wáng Fúyìn's Shénbì Jūn numbered three thousand five hundred.
Zuǒyì Yuánshuài Nèizú Xiǎolóushì's personal guards numbered one thousand.
Yòuyì Yuánshuài Wányán Ànchūhǔ's personal guards numbered one thousand.
Zǒnglǐng Wányán Chánglè and Fùshuài Wēndūn Chāngsūn's cavalry numbered three hundred.
Jùnwáng Wáng Yìshēn's cavalry numbered one hundred fifty.
Jùnwáng Fàn Chéngjìn and Zǒnglǐng Sū Yuánsūn's Guī Jūn numbered three thousand.
These were subordinate to Zǒngshuài Bǎijiā.
Fēiqí Dūwèi concurrent Hélǐhé Zǒnglǐng Shùhǔ Zhǐlúhuān, Zǒnglǐng Jiágǔ Débó, Cí Jūn Tián Zhòngjiānú and other hundred people, as well as various ministers and their subordinates,
departed the capital.
On the *jiǎchén* day of the twelfth month,
the imperial carriage reached Huánglínggāng.
Báisā had first surrendered two large enemy camps,
and obtained surrendered generals from Héshuò.
The emperor pardoned them,
and bestowed upon them seals and golden tiger tallies.
The ministers discussed having the Héshuò generals lead the vanguard,
marching boldly into Kāizhōu,
taking Dàmíng and Dōngpíng.
"Heroes will surely respond,
and the momentum will be irresistible."
Wēndūn Chāngsūn said:
"The Empress Dowager and the Empress are both in Nánjīng.
If a journey north proves unfavorable,
what will the Sacred Lord do alone?
If we go to Guīdé,
it will be another five or six months before we can return to the capital.
It would be more convenient to first take Wèizhōu,
and then return to the capital."
Báisā reported:
"The Sacred Body is not accustomed to saddles and horses,
and furthermore, we must not let the main enemy army know His Majesty's whereabouts.
We should now stay in Guīdé.
Your servants will lead the surrendered generals to Dōngpíng.
Once the various armies arrive,
we can take it in one fell swoop,
and then strategize for Héshuò,
and also empty the Hénán army."
The emperor agreed.
At that time, the emperor had already sent Guānnú with three hundred cavalry to scout Ōumágāng, and they had not yet returned.
The emperor was about to board a boat,
and bestowed a sword upon Báisā,
giving him discretionary power to proceed with the plan for Dōngpíng.
Guānnú returned and reported that Wèizhōu had provisions that could be seized.
The emperor summoned Báisā to ask him,
and Báisā said:
"The capital itself cannot be defended;
even if we obtain Wèizhōu, what would be the purpose?
In your servant's opinion,
the Dōngpíng plan is more convenient."
The emperor sided with Guānnú's suggestion.
On the first day of the first month of the following year,
they reached Huánglínggāng.
On this day,
the defending minister of Guīdé arrived with over three hundred boats of provisions as tribute.
They then used these boats to cross to the south bank.
Ten thousand men had not yet crossed.
The great Yuán general Huí Gǔnǎi led four thousand cavalry to pursue and attack them.
Hèdūxǐ waved a yellow banner to supervise the battle,
and was hit by sixteen or seventeen arrows.
The troops fought desperately,
and captured over ten soldiers,
and the main enemy army retreated slightly.
The emperor sent a hundred pots of wine to reward them.
A moment later,
a strong north wind arose,
blowing all the boats to the south bank.
The various enemy forces attacked again,
and nearly a thousand men drowned.
Yuánshuài Zhū'ér and Dūwèi Hésīliè Élún died.
Jiànwēi Dūwèi Wányán Élóunchū surrendered to the great Yuán.
The emperor, observing from the north bank, was deeply shaken and terrified.
He led his attendants in offering sacrifices for Zhū'ér and others,
weeping for them.
All were posthumously granted official titles,
and their sons and nephews were appointed to positions.
The two younger brothers of Élóunchū were executed as a public warning.
Thereupon, he ordered Bái Sā to attack Wèizhōu.
The Emperor stationed his troops by the river,
leaving three thousand of his personal guard to attend him,
along with ten thousand infantry under Dūwèi Gāo Xiǎn,
one thousand Zhōngxiào troops under Yuánshuài Guānnú,
and the armies of Jùnwáng Fàn Chéngjìn, Wáng Yìshēn, Shàngdǎnggōng Zhāng Kāi, Yuánshuài Liú Yì, and others, all commanded by Bǎijiā Zǒngzhī.
Each was to carry ten days' provisions,
and be subject to Chéngyì's command.
They departed from Púchéng.
The Emperor had already dispatched Sàibù with cavalry to the north.
Bái Sā, with thirty horsemen, caught up with him,
and said to Sàibù:
"There is an imperial decree
ordering me to command the cavalry."
Sàibù said to the Emperor:
"The plan for the northern expedition has already been decided;
it should not be changed midway."
The Emperor said:
"The Prime Minister should be in harmony with the Grand Councillor."
Wányán Zhòngdé, holding the imperial horse's bridle, earnestly remonstrated, saying:
"Survival or destruction depends on this one action;
Wèizhōu absolutely cannot be attacked."
The Emperor waved him away, saying:
"The Chancellor is unaware."
Bái Sā then attacked Wèizhōu.
When the troops reached the city walls,
the imperial banner and yellow umbrella beckoned, but the city did not surrender.
That night,
three thousand northern cavalry suddenly arrived.
Guānnú, Hésùjiā Wùdìbù, and Ànchūhǔ fought them,
and the northern troops retreated sixty *lǐ*.
However, from their departure from Púchéng, they delayed for eight days before reaching Wèi,
and suddenly had no siege equipment.
They bound spears together to make cloud ladders.
The people of the prefecture knew it could not be taken,
and defended it even more strictly.
After three days of attack, it was not captured.
When they heard that a large force from Hénán had crossed at Zhāngjiā Dù and arrived southwest of Wèi,
they retreated.
The large army pursued them,
and fought at Báigōng Miào,
suffering a defeat.
Bái Sā and others abandoned their troops and fled.
Liú Yì and Zhāng Kāi were both killed by commoners.
The imperial carriage returned to a stop thirty *lǐ* east of Púchéng.
Bái Sā secretly sent someone to report that Liú Yì's army had rebelled and left.
Diǎnjiǎn Mòniǎn Wùdiǎn and Zǒnglǐng Wēndūn Chāngsūn were attending in the traveling tent at the time.
They asked the Emperor to board a boat.
The Emperor said:
"We are at the moment of decisive battle,
why retreat so hastily?"
A short while later,
Bái Sā arrived,
and hurriedly said to the Emperor:
"The army has already collapsed,
and the main enemy force is close by outside the embankment.
Please, Holy Lord, proceed to Guīdé."
The Emperor then boarded the boat.
The imperial guards were all unaware,
and patrols continued as usual.
It was already the fourth watch of the night.
They then fled in disarray into Guīdé.
Bái Sā gathered the scattered troops at the Great Bridge,
obtaining over twenty thousand men,
but he was afraid and dared not enter.
When the Emperor heard this,
he sent the Tídiǎn of the Office of Imperial Attendants, Yílà Niángǔ,
Héshíliè Ālíhé, and two guards with a boat to welcome him.
Upon his arrival,
he was not permitted to enter and be seen, and both he and his son were imprisoned.
The officers and soldiers of the various commanderies, seeing that Bái Sā had retreated without fighting,
became indignant and voiced complaints.
The Emperor then exposed his crimes, saying:
"All you officers and soldiers,
listen clearly to my words.
When I first led the grand army and achieved victory at Huánglíng Gāng,
Bái Sā immediately reported that we should cross the river and take Wèizhōu,
where we could obtain one hundred thousand *shí* of grain,
and ride on the victory to recover Héběi.
I followed his plan,
ordering him to lead all the armies to attack Wèi.
Two hundred *lǐ* from Púchéng, Bái Sā delayed for eight days before arriving,
and also failed to prepare siege equipment,
leading to defeat.
Bái Sā abandoned the army and fled back to Púchéng,
then claimed that all the armies had collapsed,
and that the northern forces were too strong to resist,
causing me to believe him and board the boat,
nearly dying in the water.
If I had known then that the armies had not truly collapsed,
even dying in battle in Héběi would have left a name for posterity.
Now Bái Sā has been imprisoned,
and will no longer be employed.
His property will be confiscated and given to you all.
Exert yourselves fully for the state,
do not emulate this man."
Bái Sā was imprisoned for seven days and starved to death.
His younger brother, Chénglín, and son, Gǒugér, were dispatched to Xúzhōu for resettlement.
At the time, commentators opined that
the campaign against Wèizhōu had originally been Guānnú's idea,
and attributing it to Bái Sā was thus an error.
Initially,
residents along the river, hearing that the imperial army had crossed north,
built walls and barricaded their doors,
and hid in caves.
But when they saw Guānnú's army, whose orders were clear and strict,
and whose treatment of the people was thorough and considerate,
committing not the slightest transgression wherever they passed,
the old, young, women, and children faced them openly,
no longer fearing or avoiding them.
Soon, Bái Sā and his ilk let their troops loose,
plundering, taking captives,
digging up and burning,
leaving nothing untouched.
Cries of lamentation followed one after another,
and corpses filled the fields.
Dūwèi Gāo Lùqiān, Miáo Yòngxiù, and their associates even plundered people to eat them.
Bái Sā, however, had executions and beheadings on his lips.
Wherever he passed, the local officials were brutally oppressive beyond measure;
the cost of a single meal was several tens of gold, which could not be provided.
Both public and private affairs were in turmoil,
and everyone daily awaited the arrival of the main army.
Bái Sā was illiterate,
but overly cunning and devious.
He understood official documents and state affairs as soon as he heard them,
was good at discussion,
and knowledgeable.
When dealing with people, he was warm and genial.
He loved trade and wealth,
and was skilled at manipulating the minds of rulers,
thereby gradually permeating and obtaining positions as generals and prime ministers.
Once rich and noble,
he built a residence in the western part of Biàn,
its scale rivaling that of the imperial palace.
He had hundreds of maids and concubines,
all dressed in gold-embroidered clothes.
His slaves' monthly stipends were equal to those of senior generals,
yet he still considered it insufficient.
The Emperor once sent an imperial envoy to reproach him, saying:
"You are so eager for this;
do you perhaps have no intention of returning north?"
Bái Sā never repented,
and thus brought disaster upon himself.
A eulogy states: Bái Sā was not a general by nature,
his timidity ruined the state.
He merely flattered to gain wealth and high status.
He was stubborn, greedy, and contemptible.
At this time of crisis,
he still plotted to accumulate property for his own ease.
This is like a swallow or sparrow unaware that a grand mansion is about to burn.
Chìzhǎn Héxǐ was
stubborn and self-willed.
The imperial court appointed him because of his talent and ability.
During Xuānzōng's reign,
he was successively promoted to Cìshǐ of Lánzhōu and Tíkòng Jūnmǎ.
In the eleventh month of Zhēnyòu 4 (1216),
four tens of thousands of Xīxià cavalry besieged Dìngxī,
transporting siege equipment,
intending to capture the city.
Héxǐ and Yáng Ànliè and others
led troops to fight fiercely and repel them,
beheading two thousand,
capturing dozens of people,
and seizing over eight hundred horses.
The number of weapons was commensurate.
The rest all fled.
In the first month of Xīngdìng 1 (1217),
for repeatedly defeating the Xīxià,
he was remotely granted the concurrent title of Tóngzhī Líntáo Fǔshì,
in addition to his previous post.
That winter,
the Shǎnxī Xíngshěng, by imperial decree, attacked the Sòng.
Héxǐ temporarily served as the Yuánshuài Fǔ,
stationed at Láiyuǎn Zhài to project power,
and soon achieved victory.
In the fourth month of [Xīngdìng] 2 (1218),
several thousand Sòng soldiers invaded Líntáo.
Héxǐ attacked and repelled them,
killing and capturing many.
In the fourth month of [Xīngdìng] 3 (1219),
he was promoted to Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān,
and served as the Yuánshuài Fǔshì in Gǒngzhōu.
In the fourth year, fourth month,
the Xìa people raided the border.
Héxǐ attacked them.
His army reached Lù'ér Yuán,
where they encountered a thousand Xìa soldiers.
He dispatched Tíkòng Wūgǔlún Shìxiǎn to lead a detachment to defeat them.
〔十四〕Dūtǒng Wáng Dìng also broke their host of one thousand five hundred men at Xīnquánchéng.
In the ninth month,
the Xìa people attacked Gǒngzhōu.
Héxǐ sent troops to strike them.
In one day, there were more than ten battles.
The Xìa people retreated to Nángāng,
and sent thirty thousand elite soldiers to press against the city.
Héxǐ again drove them away,
capturing Xìa generals Liú Dǎ and Jiǎ Yù, among others.
Upon interrogation, it was learned that the Xìa grand generals Nǐsīdīng and Wūmíng had conspired,
believing that Gǒngzhōu was the location of the marshal's headquarters,
and that once Gǒngzhōu fell, Líntáo, Jīshí, Hé, and Táo and other cities would fall without attack.
Therefore, they first targeted Gǒngzhōu,
and also arranged for Sòng Tǒngzhì Chéng Xìn and other generals to lead forty thousand troops to attack.
When Héxǐ heard this,
he ordered his troops to prepare strictly.
Soon after, the troops indeed arrived.
Héxǐ personally led his troops in battle,
repelling them
and killing several thousand people.
The attack intensified.
The officers and soldiers fought to the death,
with casualties numbering in the tens of thousands.
The Xìa people burned their siege equipment
and withdrew their palisades before departing.
Héxǐ had already laid an ambush at strategic points to intercept them,
and then led his forces to pursue them from behind,
beheading many.
In the tenth month,
for his achievements, he was remotely awarded the title of Píngxījūn Jiédùshǐ.
In Yuánguāng first year,
Grand General Ménggǔbùhuā attacked Fèngxiáng.
The imperial court, considering that the chief general Wányán Zhòngyuán's isolated army was insufficient for defense,
ordered Héxǐ to lead troops to reinforce him.
In the second year, second month,
King Mùhuálí, Xiélǐjíbùhuā, and others, along with hundreds of thousands of Xìa infantry and cavalry, besieged Fèngxiáng.
From Fúfēng and Qíshān in the east,
to Bīn and Lǒng in the west,
their camps and palisades stretched for hundreds of *lǐ*.
The attack on the city was extremely urgent.
Héxǐ exerted all his strength,
barely able to defend it.
At this point,
Héxǐ, seeing that Tóngzhī Líntáofǔ Shì Yánzhǎn Xiāwú fought with exceptional bravery,
then, by special authority, promoted him to Tōngyuǎnjūn Jiédùshǐ.
The emperor commended his achievement
and approved it.
In this year,
he was promoted to Qiānshūmìyuàn Shì.
When Āi Zōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Cānzhīzhèngshì and acting Shūmì Fùshǐ.
In Zhèngdà eighth year, eleventh month,
a urgent report from Dèngzhōu stated that the Dà Yuán army had broken through Yáofēngguān
and was moving eastward from Jīnzhōu.
When the report arrived, it was already dusk.
Officials from the province and secretariat entered to report to the emperor.
The emperor said:
"What can be done now that things have come to this?"
The emperor had been on the throne for eight years up to this point.
From his days in the Eastern Palace, he had established thirteen Dūwèi,
〔一五〕each *wèi* having no fewer than ten thousand men,
strong, agile,
and extremely well-trained.
Infantry carrying armor, provisions, and dry rations weighing up to sixty or seventy *dǒu*,
could march two hundred *lǐ* in one day and night.
There were eighteen thousand Zhōngxiàojūn,
all of whom were Uighurs, Hexi people, and people from the central plains who had been captured and then escaped back.
Each man had a horse,
and they were selected based on their skill in archery on horseback.
Besides the Imperial Guards, cavalry, Wǔwèi, and Hùwèi,
there were more than two hundred thousand other troops.
Thus, in previous years, there had been victories at Dàchāngyuán and Dàohuí Gǔ.
With morale boosted,
they then had the resources for a single decisive battle.
At this point,
the court officials jointly reported:
"The Northern army has braved the dangers of ten thousand *lǐ*,
endured for two years,
and only now entered Wǔxiū.
Their exhaustion is extreme.
Our plan is
to station troops in Suī, Zhèng, Chāngwǔ, Guīdé, and various counties in the capital region,
and have grand generals guard Luòyáng, Tóngguān, Huái, Mèng, and other places,
maintaining strict military preparedness.
The capital has accumulated several million *hú* of grain.
Order the prefectures and commanderies of Hénán to strengthen their defenses and clear the fields.
Those common people unable to enter the cities should gather for protection in mountain strongholds.
If the enemy's deep-penetrating army
wishes to attack, they cannot;
if they wish to fight, they cannot.
Their army will be exhausted and their food supplies depleted,
and they will withdraw without needing to be attacked."
The emperor sighed deeply and said:
"Twenty years since the southward relocation,
the people everywhere have broken up their fields and homes, and sold their wives and children to support the soldiers.
Moreover, there are no fewer than two hundred thousand troops.
Now, with the enemy at hand, we cannot meet them in battle,
only preserve ourselves.
Even if the capital survives,
how can it be a nation?
What will the world say of me?"
He further said:
"Survival or destruction is a matter of Heaven's will;
only not failing the people is what matters."
Thereupon, he issued an edict to Hédá, Pú'ā, and others to station troops in Xiāng and Dèng.
In the ninth year, first month,
the armies of the two provinces were routed at Sānfēngshān,
and the Northern army advanced to threaten the capital.
On the *gēngzǐ* day of the third month,
it was proposed that Prince Cáo be sent as a hostage.
The main army went north,
leaving Sùbùtái to attack the city.
Siege equipment was already prepared.
When the request for a hostage was made,
it was then said:
"I am commanded to attack the city.
However, if Prince Cáo comes out, I will retreat;
otherwise, I will not desist."
On the *rén yín* day,
Prince Cáo entered to bid farewell,
〔一六〕and was feasted in the palace.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
the Northern army set up siege equipment,
arranged wooden palisades along the moat,
and filled the moat with firewood and straw,
leveling it for more than ten paces in an instant.
Those commanding the soldiers, due to the peace negotiations, dared not engage in battle,
but merely watched from atop the city walls.
The city was in an uproar.
The Emperor heard of it,
and with six or seven horsemen, rode out of the Duānmén gate to the Zhōujiáo bridge.
At the time, the new rain had made the ground muddy.
When the imperial carriage suddenly appeared,
people were startled and bewildered,
only kneeling by the roadside.
Some also looked and bowed.
The Emperor personally waved them away, saying:
"Do not bow,
lest the mud stain your clothes."
In the confusion,
rice and beans from the market stalls were scattered on the ground.
The Emperor ordered the guards to let everyone return to their homes.
Old and young crowded together, to the point where some accidentally touched the imperial robe.
A short while later,
the Chancellor and his retinue all arrived.
When a hat was offered to him, he refused it,
saying:
"The soldiers are exposed to the elements;
what use do I have for this?"
Wherever he passed, he comforted and encouraged the soldiers,
who all cheered "Long live the Emperor!"
and said, "We would have no regrets dying in battle,"
some even weeping from emotion.
Fifty or sixty soldiers from the southwest gathered as if they had something to say.
The Emperor approached and asked them,
and they knelt and said:
"The great army has filled the moat with straw and earth;
the task is more than half done.
However, the Píngzhāng has ordered us not to fire a single arrow,
fearing it would damage the peace talks.
Could there possibly be a plan?"
The Emperor looked at the eldest among them and said:
"For the sake of the people's lives,
I have complied with every request to submit and offer tribute.
I have only one son,
whom I have raised to adulthood,
and he is now going as a hostage.
You all must endure a little longer.
Wait until Cáo Wáng has departed;
if the great army does not withdraw,
it will not be too late for you to fight to the death."
Again, some bowed and wept, saying:
"The situation is dire!
Holy Master, do not hope for peace talks!"
Thereupon, an imperial decree was issued to fire arrows from the city walls.
Liú Shòu, the chiliarch of the Xīshuǐmén gate, reined in his horse and looked up, saying:
"The Holy Master should not trust traitorous officials.
When the traitorous officials are eliminated,
the great army will withdraw!"
The guards wanted to strike him,
but the Emperor stopped them, saying:
"He is drunk,
do not question him."
On that day,
Cáo Wáng departed to the front of the army, and
the great army attacked with full force.
On the Jiǎchén day,
the Emperor again went out to console the soldiers and officers at the Dōngmén gate.
Yáng Huàn and other Imperial Academy students came forward to report something.
The Emperor asked what they wished to say,
and they replied:
"We are all Imperial Academy students,
and we have been ordered to serve as artillerymen.
This may not be in line with the nation's treatment of scholars for the past hundred years."
He ordered their names to be recorded
and immediately exempted them from the service.
Passing the Nánxūnmén gate,
he encountered wounded individuals,
personally applied medicine,
and poured a cup of wine by hand to bestow upon them.
He also brought out gold and silk from the imperial treasury to reward those who performed meritorious service.
On that day,
the great army drove Hán captives, women, old people, and children to carry firewood and straw to fill the moats and trenches.
Arrows rained down from the city walls,
and in an instant, the moats were leveled.
The Lóngdé Gōng palace produced artillery stones,
using artificial mountains from Sòng Tàihú and Língbì for this purpose.
They varied in size and weight,
and were spherical like lanterns.
Those that did not meet specifications had their workers flogged.
The great army's use of artillery was different;
they broke large millstones or rollers into two or three pieces,
and all were used.
Some clustered bamboo cannons had as many as thirteen barrels,
and other cannons were similar.
At each corner of the city, over a hundred cannons were placed,
fired in turns,
day and night without cease.
Within a few days, the stones were almost level with the city walls.
The watchtowers on the city walls were constructed from large timbers dismantled from the former palace, Fānghuá, and Yùxī.
Even timbers of a man's embrace in girth were shattered upon impact.
Horse dung and wheat straw were spread on them,
and they were reinforced with nets, ropes, felt, and blankets.
Outside the suspended windboards,
cowhide was used as a barrier,
which was deemed impenetrable.
However, the great army attacked it with fire cannons,
which immediately ignited and could not be put out.
According to elders' tradition, when Zhōu Shìzōng built the capital city,
he used earth from Hǔláo,
which was as hard and dense as iron,
and only dented when struck by cannons.
Outside the moat, the great army built a surrounding wall a hundred and fifty lí in circumference.
The wall had defensive bulges and watchtowers,
and the moat was about a zhàng deep,
and equally wide.
Every thirty to forty paces, a post was established,
with about a hundred men guarding it.
Initially,
Bái Sā ordered the construction of a short wall outside the gate,
winding and narrow, allowing only two or three people to pass,
to prevent the great army from seizing the gate.
When attacked,
the generals requested to launch a night raid on the enemy camp,
but the army could not sally forth suddenly.
By the time they came out, they had already been detected by the northern troops.
Later, a thousand suicide warriors were recruited at night
to tunnel through the city, cross the moat,
and burn their artillery platforms.
Red paper lanterns were hung on the city walls as a signal,
agreeing to cross the moat when the lanterns lit up,
but this was also detected by the besiegers.
They also released paper kites
with documents placed on them,
to be cut down when they reached the northern camp,
to entice those who had been captured.
Knowledgeable people said that with yesterday's paper lanterns and today's paper kites,
it would be difficult for the Chancellor to repel the enemy with such flawed tactics.
The Right Chancellor, Shìlǔ, ordered the composition of a "River Water Melody"
for people on the city walls to sing quietly at night.
It seems there was an earlier version of this tune in Héshuò to express feelings of lament.
Such were his mistaken schemes.
Héxǐ had previously boasted about defending Fèngxiáng.
When he was ordered to defend the northwest corner,
the area was under the most urgent attack.
Héxǐ, confronting this,
spoke incoherently
and looked pale.
The soldiers, inspired by the Emperor's frequent visits to comfort them,
were self-motivated
and eagerly offered their lives.
Among their defensive weapons [一七]was a fire cannon named
"Zhèntiānléi" (Thunder-Shaking Heaven).
It consisted of an iron container filled with explosive powder,
which was ignited with fire.
When the cannon fired, it produced a burst of flame
and a sound like thunder,
heard a hundred lí away.
The area it scorched covered more than half an acre,
and the fire spots could penetrate armor and iron.
The great army also used "cowhide tunnels,"
extending directly to the base of the city wall,
where they dug a niche in the wall,
just large enough for a person.
The people on the city walls were powerless against this.
Someone offered a strategy:
to suspend the
"Zhèntiānléi"
with an iron rope,
lower it along the city wall,
and ignite it at the digging point.
People and cowhide would be shattered and scattered without a trace.
There was also the "flying fire spear,"
which contained powder ignited by fire.
It would burn forward for more than ten paces,
and no one dared approach it.
The great army reportedly feared only these two weapons.
The attack ceased in the fourth month.
By then, sixteen days and nights had passed,
and the dead, both inside and outside, numbered in the millions.
The great army, knowing they could not take the city,
then deceitfully spread good news, saying:
"The two nations have already made peace;
why are we still fighting?"
The imperial court also responded accordingly.
The next day,
the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, Yáng Jūrén, was sent out through the Yíqiūmén gate with wine and roasted meat to reward the troops.
Thereupon, the camps gradually moved outwards,
and the army consequently withdrew.
That year,
Qìngshānnú suffered a defeat at Guīshān.
In the autumn of the fifth year,
the city of Guīdé was expanded,
with an estimated several million laborers.
The Chancellor reported and dispatched Huá to oversee the project.
Huá met the xíngyuàn Wēnsà Xīn
and spoke to him about the people's toil
and the court's intention to cherish and nurture them.
He reduced the labor by one-third.
Wēnsà
was Lǐ Xīn, granted a surname.
In the sixth year,
Huá was granted provisional authority as Pàn Guān of the Zhūmìyuàn.
The Emperor summoned Púchá Dìngzhù, the Zǒnglǐng of the Zhōngxiào Army, Wáng Zhòngzé, the Jīnglì, Diāo Bì, the Lángzhōng of the Hùbù, and Huá, and instructed them, saying:
"Lǐ Quán occupies Chǔzhōu
and gazes ambitiously at Shāndōng,
which will certainly become a problem in the long run.
Now that the northern situation has slightly eased,
we should seize this opportunity. Let Dìngzhù temporarily supervise the army,
leading the thousand troops under his command.
Separately dispatch ten thousand infantry from the Dūwèisī.
With Bì and Zhòngzé as advisors,
they are to proceed together to the border of Yí and Hǎi to recruit him.
If he does not comply, then engage him with military force.
What do you gentlemen think of this?"
Huá replied:
"Your subject believes that Lǐ Quán, relying on the power of the great army,
demands provisions and supplies from the Sòng people.
He is merely a cunning bandit.
An old fox digs a burrow and waits for night to emerge;
he is not worth bothering about.
What I fear is the strength of the North.
Now the North is preoccupied,
and has no time to plan for the South.
Once their affairs are settled,
they will certainly come to attack.
It is they who will contend with us for天下 (tiānxià),
what concern is Quán?
If the northern situation is settled,
Quán will be too busy obeying orders.
Should he overstep his bounds
and harbor further ambitions,
would the people of天下 (tiānxià) not know what is right and what is rebellious?
Would they abandon what is right to follow what is rebellious?
The current plan should be
to provision and train our soldiers and horses
to prepare for the North.
If Quán indeed harbors rebellious schemes,
it will also surface on the day the northern court ceases military action.
At that time, we will find him easy to deal with."
The Emperor pondered for a long time and said:
"You gentlemen may withdraw for now.
Let me consider further."
The next day,
Dìngzhù was sent back to garrison Wèishì.
At that time, the main force in Shǎnxī had already withdrawn,
with Tuōhuò Luán remaining in Qìngyáng to harass Héshuò.
There was also news of an attack on Hézhōng.
As the Shuàifǔ in Wèizhōu and the Shāngōngfǔ existed side by side,
it was feared that in the event of an emergency,
their command would not be unified.
It was desired to merge the two fǔ into one,
but there was concern they might not get along.
Huá was ordered to plan this out.
Initially,
Huá, while in the Yuàn, had repeatedly received direct imperial instructions saying:
"As a Yuàn Guān,
you are not tasked with military command.
You are articulate.
Because Héxǐ and Púā are both military men,
if they disagree on a single word,
it immediately leads to friction,
which can seriously harm affairs.
Now I task you with mediating between them.
If there is any discord,
you will be held responsible.
All matters in the Yuàn must be reported to me;
this is your duty.
This assignment to Wèizhōu also stems from the previous intention to mediate."
The national system stipulated that
anyone within the Zhūmìyuàn whom superiors relied upon
was called a Zòushìguān (Reporting Official).
There were three main functions:
first, receiving imperial edicts;
second, presenting memorials;
and third, deliberating on matters with the Shěngyuàn.
All these were managed by a single person.
For "receiving imperial edicts,"
whenever Yuàn Guān presented memorials,
or when the Emperor issued a decree,
only the Zòushìguān would be summoned to receive it,
often up to one or two hundred words.
Sometimes, the imperial edict was directly conveyed,
and if the wording was extensive, it was written down by officials of the Jìnshìjú.
For "presenting memorials,"
it meant matters requiring imperial decision were presented in the殿 (diàn).
Such memorials were often deemed too verbose,
and were required to be concise and clear in meaning.
After presentation, for execution,
a written document was immediately drawn up, called a Jiǎnmù.
When Shěngyuàn officials deliberated on matters in the殿 (diàn), they memorized them silently.
After deliberation and returning to the Yuàn, a Jiǎnmù was also prepared
and submitted for review.
If there were doubts, it was reported again;
otherwise, it was handed to the Yuánshǐ for implementation.
For those attending deliberations at the Shěng,
once a decision was made,
the Zòushìguān stayed with the Zǔoyòusī officials of the Shěng to jointly draft the memorial.
If there was no disagreement after circulating it among the Chancellors,
then the Yòusī presented it to the Emperor.
Beyond these three, there was an even more difficult role,
namely, "being available for consultation."

This involved matters such as military horses, provisions, weapons, the names and numbers of military commanders and their troops, as well as the locations of garrisons, dangerous passes, and distances.
For all affairs of the Shěngyuàn,
if one failed to respond to a single consultation,
they were frequently reprimanded for not being attentive.
This position was exceedingly difficult,
which is why Huá was placed in it.
In the fifth month,
Chancellor Sài Bùxíng was dispatched to Guānzhōng to manage affairs of the Shàngshūshěng.
Púā, leading Wányán Chénhéshàng's thousand Zhōngxiào troops, was stationed in Bīnzhōu,
and ordered to observe the northern situation.
After two such months,
the Emperor said to Bái Huá:
"Can you go to Bīnzhōu and return within six days?"
Huá, estimating he could travel three hundred *lǐ* a day,
replied:
"Yes."
The Emperor secretly instructed Púā to await the beginning of spring
to operate in Qìngyáng.
Huá returned on schedule.
One day, the Emperor looked at Huá and said:
"I observe that whenever you speak of military expeditions,
you always show a difficult expression.
But this particular expedition, you are exceptionally keen,
why is that?"
Huá replied:
"Previously, when deploying troops,
the southern campaign and the campaign against Lǐ Quán obstructed us,
preventing us from fully focusing on the North.
Hence, facing North was deemed difficult.
Today is different from before,
and moreover, the situation has come to this,
so we must make a move.
The main army has already entered the border by over three hundred *lǐ*.
If we allow them to descend into Qínchuān, how can we save it?
Ultimately, we must fight a battle to crush them.
Rather than fighting on the open plains near us,
it is better to fight in the dangerous passes near the border."
The Emperor also agreed.
In the first month of the seventh year,
the siege of Qìngyáng was lifted,
and the main army returned.
Bái Huá submitted a memorial:
"For all current plans,
soldiers and provisions are the most urgent.
Besides the Zhōngxiào Army and the Dūwèisī infantry of the cavalry, which are sufficient for one battle as determined by the Mìyuàn,
the prefectures and subprefectures in Hénán should also conscript garrison troops.
They should be gathered in autumn and dismissed in spring,
following the ancient principle of combining farming with military training.
Each is to guard its own prefectural or subprefectural city.
With the current ninety-seven thousand,
prevent them from becoming resources for the enemy in the future."
In the fifth month,
Huá was formally appointed Pàn Guān of the Zhūmì.
The Emperor sent Qī Jīn, the Fùshǐ of the Jìnshìjú, to convey the imperial decree:
"I appoint you as a Yuàn Guān,
not to command troops on the battlefield,
but merely to establish military regulations, dispatch documents, harmonize generals, investigate wrongdoing.
As for the training of soldiers and the repair of weapons,
these are all your responsibilities.
Therefore, exert all your effort for the state
to fulfill My expectations."
In the eighth year,
the grand army, since last year, entered Shǎnxī,
hovering between Jīngzhào, Tóng, and Huá prefectures,
destroying over sixty stockades and strongholds in the Nánshān mountains.
Afterwards, they attacked Fèngxiáng.
The Jīn army stationed themselves from Wénxiāng to Miǎnchí,
but the two Xíngshěng remained inactive.
The prime ministers and supervising officials all criticized the Píngzhāng Shūmìyuàn for indecisiveness and dawdling.
The gentry and commoners of Jīngzhào debated fiercely and rose up,
leading to the various prime ministers earnestly appealing to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"Hédá and Pú'ā must gauge the opportunity;
they will advance when it is opportune to do so.
If I press them to fight,
it will ultimately be a forced effort,
and I fear it will be useless and even harmful."
Therefore, he dispatched Bái Huá and the Right Sī Lángzhōng Jiágǔ Bālǐmén to convey the words of the prime ministers and all officials to the Píngzhāng Shūmìyuàn,
and also asked them:
"Now, more than half of February has passed,
and there are signs of them wanting to return due to weariness.
Why are the various armies not moving?"
He also decreed that Huá and the others should go back and forth for six days.
When Huá and the others arrived at Tóng,
they conveyed the Emperor's intention to the two Xíngshěng.
Hédá said:
"I do not see an opportunity;
I will move when I see one."
Pú'ā said:
"The enemy army has absolutely no provisions or supplies,
making them unable to fight even if they wished to,
and unable to stay.
They will exhaust themselves."
Hédá told Pú'ā and the various commanders that they should not move,
but to the gentry, he said they could move.
People said that Hédá had recently fallen into disgrace,
and also feared Pú'ā, who was currently in favor with the Emperor,
and dared not oppose him,
yet he also said they should not move.
Huá and the others observed that both prime ministers were fearful of the large Northern army's strength,
so they privately asked Fán Zé, Dìngzhù, and Chén Héshang what they thought.
The three all said:
"Others say the Northern army is exhausted and thus can be attacked;
this statement is incorrect.
How can the location of a large army be lightly estimated?
It is truly not advisable to move."
When Huá and the others returned,
they reported the intentions of the two prime ministers and the various generals.
The Emperor said:
"I knew they were timid and dared not move."
He immediately dispatched Huá again to convey an imperial edict to the two prime ministers, saying:
"Fèngxiáng has been under siege for a long time;
I fear the defenders will not be able to hold on.
The Xíngshěng should lead the army out of the pass and camp in Huáyīn district,
reach Huáyīn the next day,
and Huázhōu the day after.
Slightly engage with the army north of the Wèi River.
It is calculated that the grand army, hearing of this, will surely rush to the scene,
thereby slightly relieving the urgency at Fèngxiáng,
and I will also be able to use it as a stratagem to impede them."
The two prime ministers reported back accepting the decree.
When Huá returned east and reached Zhōngmóu,
the messenger for the two Xíngshěng's memorial had already caught up.
Huá took the copy from the Mìyuàn and read it.
It stated:
"We have received the decree and led the army out of the pass twenty *lǐ* to the Huáyīn border,
engaged with the army north of the Wèi River,
and that evening, we withdrew the army back into the pass."
Huá sighed deeply to the heavens, saying:
"Things have come to this;
there is nothing that can be done."
When Huá arrived in the capital,
the memorial had already arrived,
and he knew his report would be in vain.
Within two or three days, Fèngxiáng fell.
The two Xíngshěng then abandoned Jīngzhào,
and together with Yágǔtǎ, moved the residents to Hénán,
leaving Qìngshānnú to guard it.
In the fifth month of summer,
Yáng Miàozhēn, whose husband Lǐ Quán had died in Sòng territory,
constructed a pontoon bridge north of Chǔzhōu,
and sought aid from the Northern commander Suōlǔhútú to avenge herself.
The imperial court, having learned of this,
thought that if the Northern army could indeed cross the Huái River,
the Huái and Hénán would be but a short distance apart.
They dispatched Hédá and Pú'ā to station troops at Táoyuán border, Áohékǒu, to prepare for it.
The two Xíngshěng then arranged with the Sòng commanders Zhào Fàn and Zhào Kuí for a pincer attack.
The two Zhào also sent envoys to reciprocate,
all under the pretext of negotiating peace,
to create a show of force.
The two prime ministers repeatedly emphasized the scarcity of troops,
but the Xíngshěng and Píngzhāng Shūmìyuàn found it difficult.
Consequently, they memorialized, saying:
"Previously, we were stationed near the pass for half a year.
Having just returned to our old camps,
we have not even had a moment's rest,
and now we are expected to march east in the summer month.
There is truly nothing to be gained;
we would only exhaust ourselves.
Moreover, Táoyuán and Qīngkǒu are marshy, mosquito-infested, and damp places,
unsuitable for pasturing.
Currently is not the time for expeditions;
we absolutely dare not make rash moves.
Furthermore, our only concern
is specifically the pontoon bridge at Chǔzhōu.
Let us first devise a plan for it.
We have already dispatched Tíkòng Wáng Ruì to investigate its feasibility."
Upon receiving the memorial,
the Emperor sent Bái Huá to convey this message to the two prime ministers,
and also to lead Wáng Ruì's mission.
The two prime ministers were displeased.
Pú'ā dispatched the naval Tíkòng Wáng, who was stationed at Hóngxiàn, with twenty-four small boats, ordering Huá to go down the river,
with a deadline to reach the city gate of Bālǐzhuāng,
and said:
"From here, Bālǐzhuāng looks as if it's among the clouds in the heavens.
The Xíngshěng and Píngzhāng Shūmìyuàn merely sit and talk.
Now that a Píngzhāng Shūmìyuàn official has personally come, he can observe whether it is feasible
and report back."
Huá vehemently declined but could not get out of it,
so he boarded the boat.
When he reached the confluence of the Huái and the river,
just as he was directly opposite the city gate of Bālǐzhuāng,
the city defenders, with fifty large *bái yào* boats, ascended the current,
occupying the upstream to cut off Huá's return path.
Huá barely managed to return;
in the dusk and darkness, he found a path and returned first.
He then realized that the two Xíngshěng were angry that the central court had not augmented the army,
believing that Huá and his colleagues were responsible for this,
and thus pushed him into a dangerous situation.
That night, after the second watch,
the second-in-command at Bālǐzhuāng sent someone to surrender, saying:
"Earlier, the commanding general left the city and launched boats
to cut off the Dàjīn's return path.
We discussed it,
and decided that when the commanding general returns, we will close the gate and not let him in.
He has already fled to Chǔzhōu.
We request that troops and horses be sent to receive us."
The two prime ministers immediately dispatched cavalry and launched boats to fulfill the agreement.
The next morning, they entered the city to reassure the people.
They also learned that the main army at Chǔzhōu had already returned north of the river,
and the Sòng general had burned the pontoon bridge.
The two prime ministers attached their memorial to Huá's report.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Initially,
Hédá plotted to seize Sòng's Huáiyīn.
In the fifth month, he crossed the Huái River.
Hú Lùqín, the administrator of Huáiyīn, went to Chǔzhōu to discuss matters with Yáng Miàozhēn.
By the time he returned,
the Tízhèngguān Guō Ēn had already surrendered to Jīn.
Hú was not admitted upon his return,
and wept bitterly as he departed.
Hédá then entered Huáiyīn,
and an imperial edict renamed it Guīzhōu.
Xíngshěng Wūgǔlún Yèlǐgē was appointed to guard it,
and Guō Ēn became the Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān.
Later,
the Sòng people offered fifty thousand *liǎng* of silver and bolts of silk to redeem Xūyí's Guīshān.
The Sòng envoy was kept in the residence.
Guō Ēn plotted to rob them of it.
Someone reported this to the Xūyí Commander's Office,
which immediately sent troops.
Ēn did not manage to carry out his plan.
The next day,
Sòng generals Liú Hǔ and Tāng Xiàoxìn, with thirty boats, burned the pontoon bridge,
and then sent their general Xià Yǒuliàng to attack Xūyí,
but it was not captured.
Sìzhōu Zǒnglǐng Wányán Shǐgēlì, who had the silver and silk in his residence,
then revolted.
The Fángyùshǐ Túdān Tǎlá, hearing of the change,
blocked the path at Fúshāntíng.
He said to them:
"Allow me to bid farewell to the imperial court before I die."
Then he donned his court robes, bowed towards the palace gate,
wept for a long time,
and threw himself into the water beneath the pavilion to his death.
Shǐgē then surrendered the prefecture to Yáng Miàozhēn.
Zǒngshuài Nàhé Mǎizhù also surrendered Xūyí to Sòng.
In the ninth month,
the Shǎnxī Xíngshěng planned for autumn defense.
At that time, the Dàbīng were in Hézhōng.
Ruìzōng had already led troops into the border.
Qìngshānnú reported that provisions were exhausted,
and intended to abandon Jīngzhào and move east.
One day,
Bái Huá reported,
“Scouts have ascertained that Ruìzōng commands forty thousand cavalry,
and there is an additional ten thousand in the field camp.
The deployment is as follows.
As for the current plan, instead of defending against them in Hàn,
which would take half a month for our armies to arrive,
it would be better to proceed directly to Hézhōng.
Presently, those garrisoning along the river can cross in one day.
If we succeed in this,
the Xiang and Hàn armies will certainly hesitate and not advance.
For the north, it would be an opportunistic move;
for the south, it would be a hindrance.
I believe this would be expedient.”
The Emperor asked,
“Did you devise this strategy,
or did you get it from someone else?”
Huá replied,
“This is my humble opinion.”
The Emperor was usually keen on military matters;
upon hearing Huá’s words, he seemed pleased,
yet he ultimately did not act on it.
Not long after,
Hédá submitted a memorial from Shǎnzhoū,
also concerning this matter.
The Emperor was very pleased upon receiving the memorial.
Púʼā was then in Luòyáng,
and was summoned by express messenger.
It seems the Emperor was inclined towards this idea.
When Púʼā arrived,
he did not mention this matter during their discussion,
only stating that the vanguard of the Dàbīng, commanded by Tèmùshòu,
was about to emerge from Lěngshuǐ Gǔkǒu,
and that this army should be resisted first.
The Emperor said,
“I am not asking about this;
I only want to know if Hézhōng can be attacked.”
Púʼā, having no choice,
began to say, “Although Ruìzōng’s cavalry are numerous,
they are all a mixed lot.
The Dàbīng army is small but elite,
consisting entirely of chosen vanguard troops.
If the Jīn army crosses to the north,
the Dàbīng will certainly send their baggage train to garrison north of Píngyáng,
concealing their elite vanguard a hundred *lǐ* away.
They will allow our forces to cross,
and then cut off our retreat and engage us in a decisive battle.
I fear we may not succeed.”
The Emperor said,
“I expected you to say this;
it is as I thought.
There is no need to discuss it further.
Return to Shǎnzhoū for now.”
Púʼā said,
“The matter discussed by Privy Councilor Hédá,
I fear that the local arrangements may not be entirely sufficient.
I beg that he be summoned to discuss whether it is feasible.”
The Emperor said,
“It seems Hédá also has only this to say.
Back and forth delays will
only lead to mistakes.”
Huá memorialized that Hédá must see an opportunity,
and that summoning him to discuss it together would be expedient.
Vice Privy Councilor Chìzhǎn Héxǐ also stated that the words of Púʼā and Bái Huá were correct.
The Emperor then followed their advice.
Hédá was summoned.
The Emperor ordered that he first deliberate and decide with the Privy Council,
and then be granted an audience.
After the discussion,
Huá held up Hédá’s memorial and presented it repeatedly,
yet no one spoke first.
After a while,
Púʼā said,
“What about handling the army at Lěngshuǐ Gǔ first?”
Hédá said,
“That is right.”
Thereupon they entered for an audience.
The Emperor asked how their deliberations went.
Hédá reported,
speaking at great length,
but generally stating that the situation at Hézhōng was different from when he had memorialized earlier,
and that he dared not make a decision on his own.
The discussion was thus shelved.
The two Chancellors returned to Shǎn,
and with their troops, went out to Lěngshuǐ Gǔ,
simply following established procedure.
In the twelfth month,
Hézhōng Fǔ was conquered.
In the ninth year,
the capital city was attacked.
In the fourth month, the enemy forces withdrew.
The reign era was changed to Tiānxìng.
On the sixteenth day of this month,
the Privy Council was merged into the Shàngshūshěng,
with the Chancellors concurrently holding Privy Council posts,
and the principal officials of the Left and Right Bureaus concurrently holding the posts of Recorder.
Only Píngzhāng Báisā, Vice Privy Councilor Héxǐ, Privy Council Administrator Bái Huá, and Acting Privy Council Administrator Wányán Hūlǔlà were dismissed.
Hūlǔlà was eloquent,
and the Emperor favored him.
The court deliberated Hūlǔlà’s offenses,
while the literati, jealous of Huá’s favor with the Emperor,
had previously tried to undermine him with words,
which is why he was dismissed.
According to the Jīn system,
although the Privy Council was in charge of military affairs,
its control rested with the Shàngshūshěng.
Since the outbreak of war,
this system had gradually changed;
in all military matters,
officials of the Shàngshūshěng were not allowed to interfere,
and Privy Council officials made decisions independently,
often leading to defeats.
Many critics believed that the authority of generals and chancellors should not be divided,
and it was only now that they were merged.
On the first day of the twelfth month,
the Emperor sent the director of the Imperial Secretariat, Yèlā Niángǔ, to Bái Huá’s residence,
to inquire about the current state of affairs,
and what course of action should be taken.
Huá submitted a memorial:
“Now cultivation has ceased,
and provisions are running out.
No external relief forces can be relied upon.
The imperial carriage should go out to join the external forces.
Your Imperial Brother, Jīngwáng, can be left to supervise the state,
allowing him to make decisions.
Once the Sacred Lord has departed,
send envoys to report to the Northern Court,
stating that our departure is not to regroup our armies elsewhere,
but merely because the soldiers presumptuously executed Táng Qìng,
thus severing the peace talks.
The capital is now entrusted to Jīngwáng.
We beg for one or two prefectures to live out our old age.
In this way, the Empress Dowager and the imperial clan can be preserved,
just as in the Spring and Autumn period, Jì Jì entered Qí to become a vassal state.
The Sacred Lord will also gain a little respite.”
Thereupon, Huá was appointed as Yòusī Lángzhōng.
Initially,
when the plan for an imperial inspection was decided,
all the generals participated in the discussion.
When they were about to withdraw,
the principal officials Zhāng Gǔn and Niè Tiānjì reported,
“There are still old officials who are proficient in military affairs,
but they are neglected and unused.
Those currently employed are not familiar with military matters;
this is not entirely proper.”
The Emperor asked who these unused officials were.
They all replied, “Privy Council Administrator Bái Huá.”
The Emperor nodded,
hence this appointment was made.
The next day,
he summoned Huá to instruct him, saying:
"The plan for a personal imperial inspection has been decided.
However, the destination is still under debate.
Some say that Guīdé is surrounded by water on all four sides and can be self-protected.
Others say we can follow the Xīshān mountains into Dèng.
Still others say that if we intend to go to Dèng,
Grand General Sùbùshòu is currently in Rǔzhōu.
It would be better to take the road through Chén and Cài to Dèng.
What do you think?"
Huá replied:
"Although Guīdé city is strong,
eventually food will run out,
and we will sit there waiting for death.
We absolutely cannot go there.
If we wish to go to Dèng,
since Sùbùshòu is in Rǔzhōu,
we definitely cannot go.
Given the current situation,
it is what gamblers call 'staking everything on one throw.'
'Staking everything on one throw' means
there is only one battle: a fight with our backs to the city wall.
For the current plan, we should head directly to Rǔzhōu,
and fight a decisive battle there.
If there is Chǔ, there is no Hàn;
if there is Hàn, there is no Chǔ.
A battle at Rǔzhōu is not as good as a battle halfway there,
and a battle halfway there is not as good as a battle outside the city.
Why is this so?
Our army still has its fighting strength,
and the horses still have their bean strength.
If we move further away from the capital,
the army's food will decrease daily,
the horses will eat wild grass,
and things will become even more difficult.
If our army can fight immediately,
our survival will be decided by this one action.
Externally, it can inspire the morale of the three armies;
internally, it can comfort the hearts of the capital's people.
If it is merely a plan to avoid relocation,
people's hearts will be attached to their homes and livelihoods,
and they may not resolutely follow.
Please consider this carefully."
Thereupon, all the chancellors and chief officials were summoned to discuss.
Hésùjiā Wùdìbù, Marshal Zhū'ér, Gāo Xiǎn, and Wáng Yìshēn all supported the Guīdé proposal.
Chancellor Sàibù supported Dèng.
The discussion ended without a decision.
The next day,
an imperial decree was issued: the capital city's food supply was exhausted,
and it was now proposed that His Majesty would personally go out.
The soldiers were gathered at the Dàqìng Diàn
and informed of this intention.
After the announcement,
all the marshals and assistant generals jointly memorialized, saying:
"Your Sacred Majesty must not go out personally.
Only generals should be ordered to go.
The three armies are delighted and willing to die for the state."
The Emperor hesitated,
intending to appoint Guānnú as the commander of the cavalry,
Gāo Xiǎn as the commander of the infantry,
and Liú Yì as his deputy.
This was to adopt public opinion,
and these three also wished to accept the command.
The acting councilor, Nèizú É'chū, loudly cursed, saying:
"You lot, wielding hoes, don't know your place!
How dare you casually undertake such a major state affair?"
Everyone fell silent,
except Guānnú who said:
"If the generals and chancellors could resolve it,
why would it come to us?"
The matter was also dropped.
The next day,
it was rumored among the people that the imperial carriage intended to take the Empress Dowager and the imperial consorts to Guīdé,
leaving the soldiers' families behind.
It was said that with food now exhausted,
everyone in the city would starve to death.
Even if they could reach Guīdé, how many days could the army's provisions last?
The Emperor heard this and
summoned Sàibù, Hézhōu, É'chū, Wūgǔsūn Bǔjí, and Wányán Zhèngfū to discuss.
Others were not included.
After some time, they emerged,
and the chief officials and chancellor said,
"The plan for the imperial inspection decided the other day has been changed by none other than Bái Huá.
Now, we are going to Rǔzhōu to engage the army in battle."
Thereupon, a day was chosen to sacrifice at the Tàimiào and swear in the army,
intending to depart on the twenty-fifth.
On the last day of that month,
the imperial carriage arrived at Huánglínggāng,
and there was again a proposal to go north.
The details are in the biography of Bái Sā.
On the first day of the first month of Tiānxīng Ěr Nían (Year 2),
the Emperor stopped at Huánglínggāng.
Boats were prepared from Guīdé for a northern crossing.
All the chancellors jointly memorialized,
"The capital and the various prefectures of Hénán, upon hearing that Your Majesty is going to Hébĕi,
may cause other disturbances.
An imperial edict should be issued to reassure them."
At this time,
elders, monks, and Daoists in the vicinity offered food,
and those who brought cattle and wine to reward the army came one after another.
The Emperor personally comforted them,
and everyone was moved to tears.
Thereupon, an amnesty was granted to Héshuò,
to recruit soldiers and provisions.
The amnesty document contained more than ten articles,
which were transmitted by various routes.
Two days later,
someone said:
"The Hénán edict issued yesterday might fall into the hands of the enemy army.
What if the secret is leaked?"
The Emperor was angry
and ordered the attendants of the Neocourt Bureau to transmit an imperial decree,
saying that the chief officials Zhāng Gǔn, Bái Huá, and Nèizú É'kě, when issuing the edict, did not consider the future.
All of them should be judged and executed.
At this time,
the Wèizhōu army reached Púchéng in two days,
and the main army slowly followed behind them.
On the fifteenth day,
the prime ministers and marshals jointly discussed before the Emperor.
Langzhōng Wányán Húlǔlà held the brush and wrote:
"Such and such an army will be the vanguard,
such and such an army will be the rear guard,"
and all other matters were stipulated.
After writing,
only the destination was not mentioned.
Huá privately asked Húlǔlà,
who pretended not to know.
That evening,
the Píngzhāng and all the marshals returned to the army camp in Púchéng.
In the middle of the night,
É'kě and Gǔn called Huá in his tent, saying:
"The Emperor has already boarded the boat!
Don't you know?"
Huá then asked why.
É'kě said:
"Yesterday I already knew that the Emperor intended to go to Guīdé first with Left Chancellor Lǐ and Langzhōng Wányán,
ordering all armies to march along the north bank,
and cross the river at Fèngchí.
Tonight,
the Píngzhāng and Hésùjiā, Marshal Guānnú, and others came
saying that the main army had engaged the Jīn army in Púchéng,
and could not withstand the pressure.
So they escorted the Emperor onto a boat,
abandoning all military supplies.
Only the Zhōngxiào Army was allowed to board the ship,
and all horses were left in the camp.
It is estimated that the boat has already traveled several miles."
Huá again asked:
"Why didn't you go with them?"
He replied:
"Yesterday, it was decided that among the chief officials, only Húlǔlà would board the boat;
all others would follow the army.
Therefore, I dared not."
That night,
Commander Bǎijiā led the various armies in boats towards Fèngchí.
When the main army realized this,
the troops collapsed.
The Emperor was in Guīdé.
In March,
Cuī Lì surrendered Biànjīng.
Right Xuānhuī Tídian Jìnsìjú Yílā Zhānggǔ plotted to go to Dèng,
but the Emperor did not approve.
At that time, Zhānggǔ's elder brother Yuàn was the Military Commissioner of Dèngzhōu and concurrently held the post of Xíng Shūmìyuàn Shì.
His son and Zhānggǔ's son both accompanied the imperial carriage as guards.
When the court was about to summon the Dèng troops for reinforcement,
Zhānggǔ conspired with Huá to go to Dèng together,
and also take their two sons with them.
The Emperor discovered this
and ordered Huá to go alone,
while Zhānggǔ was transferred to Xúzhōu.
After Huá arrived in Dèng,
as the matter was long unsettled,
he lingered in the residence,
as if he had no interest in the world.
It happened that Yuàn surrendered Dèng to the Sòng,
and Huá also followed him to Xiāngyáng.
The Sòng appointed him Zhìgàn,
and then changed him to Jūnzhōu Tídū.
Later, Fàn Yòngjí killed the chief official of Jūn and offered the city to the Northern court,
so he returned north through this means.
Scholars and officials disparaged Huá, saying that although he was a venerable scholar and achieved prominence, he failed to uphold righteousness when the country was in peril.
Fàn Yòngjí
originally bore the surname Bóshùlǔ,
and his given name was Jiǔzhù.
When he first submitted to the Sòng,
he met with the military commissioner Zhào Fàn,
intending to use a scheme to move his heart.
Therefore, he changed his name to Fàn Yòngjí.
Zhào was angered by the transgression of his taboo,
and he dismissed him.
Yòngjí, however, responded as before.
It was a long time before Zhào understood,
and finding that his plan aligned with his own,
he promoted him and kept him by his side.
He hardly doubted anything Yòngjí said or did.
He then changed his surname to Huā,
appointed him as grand marshal,
and reassigned him to govern Jūnzhōu.
Not long after,
he submitted an offer of allegiance to the North.
Later, his family accused him of desiring to rebel,
and he was harmed by his colleagues.
A eulogy says: Bái Huá, as a scholar, was adept at official affairs,
and as a classicist, he understood military matters.
The theories and proposals he advanced
frequently hit upon the crucial point of affairs.
However, after the defeat and rout of the army,
and with morale not recovering,
could his words truly be put into practice?
After following Yuán to submit to the Sòng,
his reputation was ruined.
That he could still be listed in the biographies of Jīn officials
is by analogy with the cases of Shǔ's Qiáo Zhōu and others.
Xié Mǎo Àishí, whose courtesy name was Zhèngzhī,
was a jinshi through policy discussions.
During the Zhèngdà era,
he successively held the offices of Hanlin Academician Direct
and concurrently Assistant Director of the Left Bureau.
In the first month of the first year of Tiānxīng,
hearing that the great army was approaching,
he appointed the inspector Jiágǔ Sāhé as commander-in-chief,
to lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to patrol and cross the river.
He ordered the general on duty, the clan leader Chánglè, to act as director of the Imperial Secretariat,
to supervise his army.
They marched to Fēngqiū and then returned.
Upon entering through Liángmén,
