the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs, Géxǐ, met him,
and smilingly said to Sāhé:
"My words are true;
you should act as host for me."
This was an expression of customary gratitude.
The next day,
the main army indeed assembled,
but the court ignored it and did not question it.
〔一０〕Thereupon, Àishí submitted a memorial saying:
"Sāhé commanded thirty thousand troops,
originally intending to strike the main army when it arrived from afar,
before it could catch its breath.
Having left the capital only a few dozen li,
he did not encounter a single horseman,
yet he already became fearful and dared not advance.
If he were to encounter the main army,
would he be willing to obey orders?
I request that these two men be executed to enforce military discipline."
There was no reply.
This was because Géxǐ and his ilk considered the capital's survival to depend on this single army,
and from the outset dared not send it out to battle.
It was merely that external discussions were tumultuous,
so they temporarily sent it out to respond, they said.
The families of the two princes, Wèi Shào and Háo Lì,
were all protected by soldiers,
and officials were appointed to supervise them.
The strictness of the patrolling and guarding surpassed that of prisons.
By this time,
the Wèi Shào residence had been under guard for twenty years,
and the Háo Lì residence for forty years.
〔一一〕During the Zhèngdà era,
courtiers repeatedly spoke of this,
but there was no reply.
Àishí then submitted a memorial saying:
"The two clans are in decline,
no different from commoners.
Even if they wished to do evil,
who would conspire with them?
Marriage is a great human desire for both men and women.
How can they be imprisoned for life,
forever without hope of a spouse?
Even for others, one would not bear it,
let alone for one's own flesh and blood."
Àizōng was moved by his words,
and for the first time permitted them freedom.
Not long after,
there was the disaster of Qīngchéng.
Àishí was indignant that the current prime ministers were not the right people,
and once enumerated them, saying:
"Píngzhāng Bái Sā is indeed powerful and grants favors,
but beyond playing polo, he is utterly incompetent.
Prime Minister Sài Bù cannot distinguish beans from wheat;
even if one calls him lacking in talent,
it should not come to such a person being prime minister.
Councilor and concurrently Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs Chìzhǎn Géxǐ is coarse and violent;
he is only fit to be a cavalryman,
yet he is given the power of both general and prime minister.
Right Chancellor Yánzhǎn Shìlǔ has been in the prime ministerial position for seven or eight years,
achieving nothing and simply filling a role.
In times of trouble,
to rely on such people
makes hoping for a revival difficult indeed."
Thereupon,
Shìlǔ was dismissed from prime minister,
Sài Bù requested retirement,
but Bái Sā and Géxǐ were not troubled.
In the fourth month of that year,
the siege of the capital was lifted,
and the great army retreated.
Afterward,
due to the affair of harming Táng Qìng,
the peace negotiations were completely broken off.
Thereupon,
militia were again conscripted for defensive preparations.
In the eighth month,
grain in the capital was requisitioned.
The Transport Commissioners Wányán Zhūkē, Zhāng Jùnmín, Yìlà Kèzhōng, and others set up a bureau,
under the pretense of "recommendation."
Zhūkē admonished the people, saying:
"You should truly report and declare.
If indeed one day the grain runs out,
and your wives and children are made military provisions,
will you still be able to be stingy?"
Soon after,
the order to requisition grain was abolished,
and it was again obtained through "tributes."
The former Grand Censor Nèizú Hézhōu again hoped for advancement,
and proposed that over a million shí of grain could be requisitioned from the capital.
The court believed him
and appointed him acting Councilor of State,
to manage the matter together with Left Chancellor Lǐ Qī.
First, each household was ordered to truthfully declare their holdings.
Adults were to retain three dòu per shí,
and children half of that.
The numbers were to be written on their doors,
and anyone daring to conceal would be punished according to the sheng and dou measurements.
In the thirty-six wards of the capital,
harsh and severe individuals were selected to take charge.
Nèizú Wányán Jiǔzhù was particularly cruel and brutal.
There was a widow with two dependents
who declared six dòu of beans,
among which were about three shēng of weeds.
Jiǔzhù laughed and said:
"I've got her!"
He seized her and made an example of her to the crowd.
The woman cried and pleaded:
"My husband died in the war,
and my elderly mother-in-law cannot support herself.
Therefore, I mixed weeds and husks to feed myself,
not daring to use them for military provisions.
Moreover, three shēng is but a trifle
among six dòu."
He did not listen,
and she died under the beating.
When the capital heard of this, they trembled with fear,
and threw all their remaining grain into latrines.
Someone reported this to Lǐ Qī,
who frowned and said:
"Report it to the Councilor."
That person then reported it to Hézhōu,
who said:
"People say, 'Do not harm the flower,
and the honey will be made.'
I say, if the flower is not harmed,
how can honey be made?
Furthermore, the capital is in dire straits.
Now, do we wish to preserve the state
or preserve the common people?"
At that time, no one dared to speak.
Àishí then submitted a memorial,
which generally stated:
"Abolish the grain requisition,
and change oppressive rule into benevolent rule,
and transform resentment into harmony."
There was no reply.
At that time, what was requisitioned did not amount to thirty thousand *hú*,
and the capital became even more desolate.
From then on,
the dead lay piled upon each other,
and the rich and poor alike simply waited for death.
The Emperor heard of this,
and ordered the release of rice from the Tàicāng granary to make gruel for the starving.
Àishí heard of this and sighed, saying:
"Rather than feeding them,
it would be better not to have taken it in the first place."
He was accused by the Imperial Attendant Bǎnúnú.
Furthermore, as close attendants interfered in court affairs,
Àishí submitted a memorial, admonishing:
"Currently, the power of the close attendants is too great,
and the prime ministers and great ministers dare not oppose them.
Since ancient times, servants and attendants were merely for supplying and directing,
and although nominally servants,
they must also be chosen from upright individuals.
Now, regardless of their virtue or lack thereof,
only those of noble lineage or civil officials are chosen for this.
Indeed, those with the talent to be mere servants
are made to participate in the great affairs of the state –
what could such people possibly know?"
Once the memorial was submitted,
several close attendants wept and complained to the Emperor, saying:
"Àishí considers us as slaves;
where does that leave Your Majesty?"
The Emperor grew even angrier
and sent him to the appropriate authorities.
Lǐ Dàjié, the Deputy Commissioner of the Close Attendants Bureau, calmly interceded on his behalf,
and he was pardoned,
and sent out as the Resident Administrator of Zhōngjīng.
Afterward, his end is unknown.
Hézhōu, also named Yǒngxī,
during the Zhēnyòu period,
served as the Left Supervising General of the Grand Marshal.
He failed to relieve Zhōngdū,
and Xuānzōng stripped him of his official titles and ranks,
and had him flogged eighty times.
Soon after, he was reappointed.
In the fourth year,
he served as the Grand Censor, acting as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs,
commanding all troops in Shǎnxī.
Hézhōu remained in Miǎnchí for several days,
〔一二〕advancing to Jīngzhào,
but the main army had already arrived,
and Hézhōu ultimately did not deploy his troops,
thus losing Tóngguān.
The authorities deemed that failing to deploy troops when the enemy arrived warranted execution.
Over a hundred imperial relatives submitted a memorial to intercede for him.
The Emperor said:
"Previously, when Hézhōu was to relieve Zhōngdū,
before he arrived, the army collapsed,
causing the ancestral temples and imperial tombs to be lost.
His crime deserved execution,
but I specifically granted him clemency to spare his life.
Soon after, he was restored to an important position,
and now, commanding Shǎnxī,
he commits such an offense.
How can the great laws of the state be privately disregarded?"
He was then again stripped of his title
and dismissed from his post, but spared death.
By this time,
he served as an Associate Administrator of Governmental Affairs.
He was fond of composing poetry and lyrics,
but his language was crude and vulgar,
and people would quote his words to make fun of him.
Because of this, he personally drafted a proclamation for requisitioning grain,
which contained phrases like
"A sparrow without wings cannot fly,
a snake without a head cannot move,"
and so on.
He used
"ér"
instead of
"ér" (as in the particle),
and the clerks, knowing this, dared not change it.
The capital called him
"Sparrow-boy Associate Administrator."
Àizōng employed him but did not realize his shortcomings,
eventually leading to his downfall.
Shímò Shìjì, courtesy name Jǐnglüè,
was diligent in his studies as a youth,
and his writings had a proper style.
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
because his father Yuányì died in service to the king,
he was appointed to a ceremonial position.
In the fifth year,
he passed both the *Cífù* and *Jīngyì* sections of the Imperial Examination for *Jìnshì*.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu,
he was successively promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
participating in the affairs of the Lecture and Deliberation Bureau.
At that time, the imperial court moved military households from Héběi to Hénán,
and the prime ministers deliberated on granting them land.
Shìjì submitted a memorial, saying:
"For barren and idle land, and grazing grounds,
the initial cultivation
requires double the effort,
and cannot yield a harvest in one year.
If we seize the cultivated land of the people to give to them,
then the people will lose their homes,
and this will also sow discord.
Moreover, military households generally lack oxen for farming,
and even if some have them,
their rations cannot be suddenly reduced.
Having come south,
the land and houses they left behind are now owned by others.
If they were to return north suddenly,
how could there not be disputes?
I earnestly believe that military households should be ordered to return to their original occupations in groups,
harvesting their late crops,
and returning in spring to reinforce the defenses."
Coincidentally, Supervising Censor Liú Yuánguī also spoke against the inconvenience of granting land.
The Emperor greatly realized his mistake
and therefore ceased the plan.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Assistant Commissioner of the Jīn'ān Military Governor.
In the second year of Xīngdìng,
he was selected to be the Consultant to the Huázhōu Marshal's Office.
Initially,
Wányán Hédá, the Right Chief Commissioner, established the Marshal's Office in Zhēnzhōu,
and had previously appointed Zhuōlǔ Hú Púnǎisù, former Assistant Administrator of Píngliáng Prefecture, as Consultant.
When the office moved to Huázhōu,
the Shǎnxī Branch Secretariat requested to reuse Púnǎisù,
with Shìjì as his deputy.
The Emperor said:
"Púnǎisù can only flatter others;
he has no other strengths.
He is not like Shìjì, who can be entrusted with affairs.
Huá is a crucial stronghold,
and lightly using such a person
might lead to defeat."
Thus, only Shìjì was appointed.
Soon after, he entered the court as Director of the Left Bureau of the Department of State Affairs.
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
he was stripped of one official rank
and relieved of his duties.
Initially,
when Shìjì was serving in Huázhōu,
someone recommended him as deeply knowledgeable in financial matters.
A re-investigation found him not as skilled as represented,
and this was not recorded in his official conduct register.
Later, the official in charge discovered it,
and Prince Yīng, the Grand Councilor, believed that Shìjì wanted to avoid the burdens of the Metropolitan Bureau,
and had privately instructed the register clerk to hope for a different post.
This was reported to the Emperor and then sent down to the authorities,
which is why he received this reprimand.
After a long time,
he was appointed Minister of Rites,
then transferred to Director of Agriculture,
and later changed to Grand Master of Ceremonies.
During the Zhèngdà period,
he served as Minister of Rites,
concurrently serving as Attendant Lecturer of the Hànlín Academy.
In the winter of the first year of Tiānxīng,
Āizōng was about to cross the river northwards.
Shìjì, along with twenty court officials including Liú Sù and Tián Zhī, sought an audience in Rén’ān Diàn.
The Emperor asked, "What do you gentlemen wish to say?"
Shìjì replied,
"Your Majesty, we have heard that you intend to personally lead the army out.
We sincerely believe this expedition is inconvenient."
The Emperor said,
"If I do not go out,
the army will be divided into two:
one part to defend,
and one part to fight.
If I go out, the army will be united as one."
Shìjì replied,
"If Your Majesty goes out, the army will be divided into three:
one to defend, one to fight, and one central army to escort you.
It would be better not to go out."
The Emperor said,
"You gentlemen do not understand.
If I could entrust military affairs to Wányán Zhòngdé and Héngshān Gōng Wǔ Xiān,
why would I bother to go out?
How could I not know that today's generals
have Guānnú commanding only three hundred cavalry,
and Liú Yì leading only five thousand infantry?
How can I avoid leading the army myself?"
The Emperor then pointed to his imperial couch and said,
"How could I expect to return from this expedition?
My only regret is that I, innocent, am losing the country.
I have never been extravagant,
nor have I ever trusted petty individuals."
Shìjì immediately responded,
"Your Majesty has indeed employed petty individuals."
The Emperor asked,
"Who are these petty individuals?"
Shìjì enumerated them, saying,
"Yílà Niángǔ, Wēndūn Chāngsūn, Wùsārě, and Wányán Chánglè are all petty individuals.
Your Majesty did not know they were petty individuals,
which is why you employed them."
Sù and Shìjì continued to speak for a long time,
and after a considerable period,
the monarch and his subjects wept and parted.
Originally,
Sù and others sought an audience
with the intention of denouncing these four individuals.
At this point,
Shìjì alone spoke of them.
Thereupon, Āizōng took Shìjì with him on the expedition.
From Púchéng to Guīdé.
In June of the following year,
they fled to Càizhōu,
stopping at Jiāngzhài in Xīncài Xiàn.
Shìjì's son, Sōng,
who was then the county magistrate,
bowed to the Emperor before his horse.
After the chaos of war, father and son met for the first time.
The Emperor commended him,
granting Sōng the position of Yìngfèng Hàlín Wénzì,
to facilitate caring for his parents.
When Cài Chéng fell,
both father and son died.
Sōng, whose courtesy name was Qǐlóng,
was a Jīngyì Jìnshì in the second year of Xīngdìng.
The eulogy says: Ài Shíyán spoke of the abuses of imprisoning the families of Wèi and Hào,
the brutality of seizing grain in the capital,
and the tyranny of close attendants interfering in politics.
Shìjì spoke of the inconvenience of distributing land to military households north of the Yellow River,
and the ill-advised plan for the Emperor to personally lead the army across the river.
All were words of medicine and stone (wise counsel).
However, by this time, the Jīn Dynasty
was already critically ill;
what could Cāng Biǎn (a legendary physician) do?
Nevertheless, their loyalty and uprightness
should not be dismissed.
Collation Notes
Biography 53: Wányán Núshēn, Cuī Lì, Niè Tiānjì, Chìzhǎn Wèixīn
Wányán Núshēn, courtesy name Zhèngfǔ,
was the younger brother of Sùlán.
He passed the Cèlùn Jìnshì examination
and served in prestigious positions.
In August of the third year of Zhèngdà,
he was appointed Yìzhèng Yuàn Shuōshūguān
from Hàlín Zhíxuéshì.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shìláng.
Censor Wūgǔlún Shílǔlà impeached the palace attendants Zhāng Wénshòu, Rénshòu, and Lǐ Lín for receiving gifts from enemy commanders.
An imperial decree ordered Núshēn to interrogate them,
and their illicit activities were uncovered.
The Emperor leniently pardoned their crimes,
and they were all dismissed.
The court was pleased with this.
In September,
he was reappointed Shìjiǎng Xuéshì,
and was sent as an envoy to Dà Yuán as Yùshǐ Dàfū.
He reached Lóngjū Hé,
and had an audience with Emperor Tàizōng.
In December,
he returned.
In June of the following year,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
and went again.
In the spring of the eighth year,
he returned.
The court, recognizing his efforts, appointed him Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
In the spring of the first year of Tiānxīng,
the great army encamped at Hǎitān Sì in Zhèngzhōu,
and sent an envoy to summon Āizōng to surrender.
Núshēn was again sent to plead for peace,
but it was not granted,
and the attack on Biàn became more urgent.
Biàn had been besieged for several months,
and its granaries were depleted.
Wǔ Xiān and others were summoned to provide aid but did not arrive.
Āizōng was afraid,
and offered Cáo Wáng Ékě as a hostage,
requesting an end to the attack.
In the tenth month of winter,
Āizōng debated personally leading the defense.
He appointed Núshēn as Cānzhī Zhèngshì and concurrent Pīmì Fùshǐ,
Wányán Xíābù as Pīmì Fùshǐ, concurrent Zhī Kāifēng Fǔ, and acting Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
to jointly command all armies and remain to guard the capital.
He also appointed Hàlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ Wūgǔsūn Bōjí as Tíkòng Zhūwángfǔ,
concurrent Pàn Dàmùqīnfǔ Shì and Dūdiǎnjiǎn Nèizú Hézhōu to manage the imperial palace affairs.
Zuǒ Fùdiǎnjiǎn Wányán Āsā and Yòu Fùdiǎnjiǎn Wēndūn Ālí were his deputies.
Hùbù Shàngshū Wányán Zhūkē was concurrent Sīchéng Sìmiàn Dū Zǒnglǐng.
Yùshǐ Dàfū Péimǎn Āhǔdài was concurrent Zhènfǔ Jūnmín Dū Tányā.
Jiànyì Dàfū Jìnsì Júshǐ Xíngshěng Zuǒyòu Sī Lángzhōng Wūgǔsūn Núshēn was concurrent Zhī Gōngshěng Shì.
He also appointed Bǎsāhé as the Marshal for the eastern section of the outer city,
Shùjiǎ Yǎozhù as the Marshal for the southern section,
Cuī Lì as the Marshal for the western section,
and Bójīlǔ Mǎinú as the Marshal for the northern section.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
the appointments were finalized,
and the capital was entrusted to them.
He also appointed Hùbù Shìláng Diāo Bì as Ānfǔ Fùshǐ,
to oversee the Zhaōfǔ Sī,
planning the transportation of grain and provisions into and out of the capital.
A Jiǎngyì Suǒ was established
to receive written suggestions,
with Dàlǐ Qīng Nàhé Déhuī, Hùbù Shàngshū Zhòng Píng, and Zhōngjīng Fùliúshǒu Àishī, among others, overseeing its affairs.
On Xīnchǒu day in December,
the Emperor departed the capital,
wearing a crimson gauze robe,
riding a horse with his retinue in the usual ceremonial manner.
The officials remaining in the capital and the elders of the city followed him outside the city to bid farewell.
An imperial edict was issued to reassure them,
and he also saluted them with his whip.
Sùbùshòu, hearing that the Emperor had departed,
again gathered his troops to besiege Biàn.
Previously,
the Emperor, finding the Eastern Marshal Lǐ Xīn unruly and uttering resentful words,
dismissed him as Bīngbù Shìláng.
Before departing,
he secretly instructed Núshēn and others to restrain him.
After the Emperor left,
Núshēn and others summoned Xīn.
Xīn was afraid,
plotted to surrender,
abandoned his horse, and escaped by climbing over the city wall.
Núshēn and others sent people to pursue and overtake him,
beheading him at the provincial gate.
The people of Biàn, believing the Emperor had personally led the army,
listened daily for victory reports,
and also, with the two chief ministers holding firm,
hoped for no trouble.
Soon, news arrived that the army had been defeated at Wèizhōu,
and had hurriedly fled to Guīdé.
The people were greatly alarmed, fearing there was no salvation.
At that time, communication inside and outside Biànjīng was cut off.
A sheng of rice cost two taels of silver.
The people's food supplies were exhausted,
and the starved lay everywhere.
Many gentry and women begged in the markets,
some even resorted to eating their own children,
and all types of leather and artifacts were consumed.
Noble residences, market towers, and inns were all dismantled for firewood.
When Guīdé sent envoys to welcome the two palaces,
public sentiment became even more unstable.
Thus, among the populace, there was talk of establishing Jīng Wáng as regent and surrendering the city,
but the two chief ministers were unaware of this.
In the first month, on the day `bǐngyín`, of the second year of Tiānxīng,
the `shěnglìngshǐ` Xǔ Ānguó went to the `Jiǎngyìsuǒ` and said:
"In ancient times, when there was a great dilemma,
counsel was sought from the high officials (`qīngshì`),
and counsel was sought from the common people.
Now the situation is such that
we should gather all the officials, monks, Daoist priests, and commoners,
and ask for plans to preserve the state (`shèjì`) and save the people (`shēnglíng`)."
The `Zuǒsīdūshì` Yuán Hàowèn reported Ānguó's words to Núshēn,
and Núshēn said:
"This argument is excellent.
Discuss it with the `Fùshū`."
The `Fùshū` also agreed with Ānguó's words.
Hàowèn said:
"It has been about twenty days since the emperor's carriage left the capital,
and envoys have also been sent to welcome the two empresses.
The common people are in turmoil,
all saying that the state wishes to abandon the capital.
How will you, `Xiànggōng`, handle this?"
Ābù said:
"The two of us have only one choice: death."
Hàowèn said:
"Death is not difficult.
If we can truly secure the state and save the people,
then death is acceptable.
If not,
and it's merely to satisfy the fifty `hóngnàjūn` with our own bodies,
can that even be called death?"
Ābù spoke softly, saying:
"Today, it's just the two of us;
what cannot be said?"
Hàowèn then said:
"I hear people inside and outside the court saying
that they wish to enthrone two princes as regents,
to preserve the two empresses and the imperial clan."
Ābù said:
"I know it, I know it."
Immediately, he ordered the officials and commoners of the capital to be summoned,
and the next day they all gathered in the `Shěngzhōng`,
where they were informed of the perilous situation and asked what should be done.
Seven elders presented a petition, saying thus and so,
and the two prime ministers ordered Hàowèn to receive their petition.
He reported it to Núshēn,
who looked at him and said:
"This is also for this matter."
He also asked the `Fùshū`,
"How many days have we been deliberating on this matter?"
Ābù counted on his fingers and said:
"Seven days."
Núshēn said:
"The envoy from Guīdé has not yet left;
be careful not to leak it."
Some say that at this time the outer siege was not lifted,
and it was like being in a trap.
The deliberators wished to enthrone Prince Jīng to surrender the city,
which was also in the spirit of Jì Jì entering Qí in the Spring and Autumn period,
especially since Prince Cáo was already among the northern troops.
The crowd resented the two for having no plan,
but only saying,
"Hold out to the death."
Suddenly, they heard that the scholars and commoners of the capital were summoned to discuss affairs.
Núshēn stood with clasped hands, silent,
while only Ābù repeatedly explained and admonished,
"The state has reached this point, and there is nothing that can be done.
Whatever is feasible should be discussed together,"
and he followed it with tears.
The next day, on `wùchén`,
the `Xīmiàn Yuánshuài` Cuī Lì, together with his partisans Bóshùlǔ Chánggē, Hán Duó, Yào Ānguó, and others, instigated a rebellion.
They led two hundred armed soldiers, with swords drawn, into the `Shěngzhōng`,
and pointed their swords at the two prime ministers, saying:
"The capital is in extreme peril and distress.
Why do you two sit by and watch the people starve to death,
indifferent and unconcerned?"
The two prime ministers were greatly alarmed and said:
"If you have something to say,
you should discuss it properly.
Why such haste?"
Lì waved his hand, and his partisans first killed Ābù,
then killed Núshēn and the `Zuǒsī Lángzhōng` Nàhé Déhuī and others.
The rest is in the Biography of Cuī Lì.
Liú Qí said:
"After the Jīn moved south,
those who served as prime ministers (`zǎizhí`) often had no plans for restoration.
When faced with matters, they would habitually speak in low, slow tones, pushing responsibility to each other,
believing this to be the proper conduct for a prime minister.
Whenever there were calamities or strange phenomena in the four directions, or suffering among the people,
before presenting a memorial, they would invariably say to each other:
'I fear the sacred ruler will be distressed.'
When matters reached a critical point, they would often disperse,
saying, 'Let's wait and discuss it again,'
and then it would be the same again.
If anyone suggested reform,
they would immediately suppress it as 'stirring up trouble.'
Thus, those they employed were invariably chosen for being 'smooth and polished,' without sharpness, and easy to control.
Whenever the northern army pressed upon the border,
the ruler and ministers would weep together,
or sigh deeply in the imperial hall, and that was all.
When the army retreated,
they would set up a grand feast,
and drink together in the `Huánggé`.
Through procrastination and muddled compromise,
the state ultimately perished.
They also often placed those who were 'simple and unadorned' in high office.
Xuānzōng once admonished Prime Minister Púsàn Qījīn,
'Where are the court's rules and regulations nowadays?'
Qījīn could not answer.
Upon retreating, he said to the `lángguān`,
'The emperor asked where the rules and regulations are;
when have you ever allowed the rules and regulations to appear before me?'
Therefore, upright gentlemen (`zhèngrén jūnzǐ`) were often not employed,
or even if employed, they did not last long before being dismissed."
Qí's courtesy name was Jīngshú,
and he was from Húnyuán.
A commendation states: While Liú Jīngshú's Guīqiánzhì and Yuán Yùzhī's Rénchénzábian differ slightly,
the events of the chaos at the end of the Jīn dynasty are still worth examining in them.
Àizōng's retreat to the north entrusted an isolated city and weak troops to Núshēn and Ābù;
this can be called difficult indeed.
Nevertheless,
Jìmò had Ānpíngjūn,
and Yùbì had Wéi Xiàokuān;
there must have been a way to handle this.
Cuī Lì was a native of Jiānglíng.
In his youth, he was poor and had no proper conduct.
He once carried cymbals and drums for a temple monk.
During the military turmoil, he followed Shàngdǎnggōng, becoming a `Dūtǒng` and `Tíkòng`.
He gradually accumulated ranks and nominally held the position of `Tàiyuán Zhīfǔ`.
At the beginning of Zhèngdà,
he sought to enter officialdom,
but was rejected by the `Xuǎncáo`.
He always regretted not reaching the third rank.
During the siege, he was granted the title of `Ānpíng Dūwèi`.
In the twelfth month of winter in the first year of Tiānxīng,
the emperor personally led an army
and appointed him `Xīmiàn Yuánshuài`.
His nature was licentious and cruel;
he constantly thought of stirring up trouble to satisfy his desires.
Yào Ānguó was from Guǎnzhōu,
in his early twenties,
and possessed great strength.
He had once served as the `Lánzhōu Zhāofǔshǐ`,
but was imprisoned in Kāifēng for a crime.
After his release,
he was poor and had nothing to eat.
When Lì planned his rebellion,
he secretly befriended him.
Ānguó was a hearty eater,
and Lì fed him fish daily,
so he conspired with him.
First, he placed his family on the west wall of the city,
planning to take them and flee if the plot failed.
Daily, he and `Dūwèi` Yáng Shàn entered the `Shěngzhōng` to observe the situation.
Once the arrangements were made,
he summoned Shàn for an early meal,
and killed him.
In the first month of the second year,
he led two hundred armed soldiers
and crashed through the `Shěngmén` to enter.
The two prime ministers, hearing the commotion, rushed out.
Lì drew his sword and said:
"The capital is in peril and distress;
how do you two intend to handle it?"
The two prime ministers said:
"This matter should be discussed properly."
Lì ignored them,
waved his hand, and his partisans Zhāng Xìnzhī and Bóshùlǔ Chánggē went out of the `Shěng`,
He galloped to the Dōnghuámén,
and on the way encountered the `Diǎnjiǎn` Wēntún Ālí.
Seeing that he was wearing armor,
he killed him.
He then announced to the common people:
"I killed the two prime ministers for their closed-door inaction and lack of planning.
I am now pleading for the lives of you, the people of this city."
Everyone cheered.
On that day,

the `Yùshǐ Dàfū` Péimǎn Āhūtài, the `Jiànyì Dàfū` and `Zuǒyòusī Lángzhōng` Wūgǔsūn Núshēn, the `Zuǒfù Diǎnjiǎn` Wányán Āsàn, the `Fèngyù` Mánggē, the `Jiǎngyì` Púchá Qí, and the `Hùbù Shàngshū` Wányán Zhūkē all died.
Cuī Lì (崔立) then returned to the provincial government office,
gathered the hundred officials, and deliberated on whom to enthrone.
Cuī Lì (崔立) said:
"Wèi Shào Wáng's (衛紹王) crown prince Cóngkè (從恪),
can be enthroned."
So he dispatched his partisan Hán Duó (韓鐸) with the Empress Dowager's (太后) command to summon Cóngkè (從恪).
In a moment, he entered,
and with the Empress Dowager's (太后) decree, Liáng Wáng (梁王) was made regent.
The hundred officials bowed, danced, and shouted "Long live the King!"
whose sister, the princess, is among the northern troops,
and then sent the two chancellors with their tiger tallies to Sùbùtái (速不臺) to surrender.
All appointments and dismissals were made in the name of the regent.
Cuī Lì (崔立) styled himself Grand Tutor (太師), Grand Marshal of Military Affairs (軍馬都元帥), Grand Secretary (尚書令), and Zhèng Wáng (鄭王).
When going out and entering, he rode in an imperial carriage,
called his wife a princess (王妃),
his younger brother Yǐ (倚) Minister of Political Affairs (平章政事),
and Kǎn (侃) Commander of the Palace Guard (殿前都點檢).
His partisan Bóshùlǔ Zhǎnggē (孛术魯長哥) was Censor-in-chief (御史中丞),
Hán Duó (韓鐸) Grand Marshal (都元帥) concurrently in charge of Kāifēng Fǔ (開封府) affairs,
Shī Sù (師肅) Left and Right Bureau Directors (左右司郎中),
Jiǎ Liáng (賈良) Minister of War (兵部郎中) concurrently Recorder of the Right Bureau (右司都事),
and he presided over all affairs of the imperial treasury.
Initially,
Cuī Lì (崔立) relied on Ānguó's (安國) bravery to accomplish his aims,
but now he again grew wary of him.
Hearing that Ānguó (安國) had taken a certain Commandant's (都尉) wife,
he enumerated his transgressions and beheaded him.
On Rénshēn (壬申) day,
Sùbùtái (速不臺) arrived at Qīngchéng (青城).
Cuī Lì (崔立) wore imperial robes
and went to meet him with a ceremonial escort.
The great marshal was pleased
and offered him wine.
Cuī Lì (崔立) treated him as a father.
After returning,
he burned all the towers and turrets of the capital city.
When the fire started,
the great marshal was greatly pleased,
finally believing in his true surrender.
Cuī Lì (崔立) feigned that the army needed the families of the imperial retinue officials,
gathered them in the provincial government office,
and people reviewed them themselves.
Daily, a chaotic number of people, yet it seemed insufficient.
He also prohibited marriage in the city.
There were some who killed several people because of one daughter.
Not long after,
Liáng Wáng (梁王) and the imperial clan and close relatives were all moved and housed in the palace,
guarded by his trusted confidants,
with their entry and exit restricted.
He made Jīng Wáng Fǔ (荊王府) his private residence
and filled it with precious treasures from the imperial treasury.
In the second month, on Yǐyǒu (乙酉) day,
the Son of Heaven's (天子) ceremonial robes and empress's attire were presented.
He also confiscated gold and silver in the city,
searching and digging,
interrogating and torturing cruelly.
All kinds of suffering were inflicted.
Chéngguó Fūrén (郕國夫人) and court eunuch Gāo Yòu (高祐), and the commoner Lǐ Mínwàng (李民望) and his kind
all died under the rod.
Wēntún Wèiwèi's (溫屯衛尉) eight relatives
could not endure the torture and all committed suicide.
Báisā Fūrén (白撒夫人) and Right Chancellor Lǐ Xī's (李蹊) wife and children were all plundered and died.
They abetted each other in their wickedness,
viewing people as enemies,
resolved to take revenge until their objective was met.
Everyone secretly said to each other:
"Within seven or eight days after the city fell,
the Kaifeng Prefectural Office (開封府) recorded that those buried from all gates totaled over one million people.
We regret not having been among them earlier and instead facing this misfortune."
At that time, Cuī Lì (崔立) and his wife entered the palace,
and the two empresses bestowed upon them countless gifts.
Cuī Lì (崔立) then subtly urged the Empress Dowager (太后) to write a letter outlining the timing and human affairs,
and dispatched the imperial wet nurse to recruit Guīdé (歸德).
At that time, those eager for advancement competed, citing the precedent of Liú Qí (劉齊) in hopes of undue favors,
shoulder to shoulder, heel to heel.
In the fourth month, on Rénchén (壬辰) day,
Cuī Lì (崔立) took the two empresses, Liáng Wáng (梁王), Jīng Wáng (荊王), and all imperial relatives to Qīngchéng (青城).
Cuī Lì's (崔立) wife, Wáng Shì (王氏), with guards, escorted the two empresses to Kāiyáng Mén (開陽門).
On that day,
there were thirty-seven imperial carriages.
The Empress Dowager (太后) went first,
followed by the Empress (中宮),
then the imperial concubines.
There were over five hundred men and women of the imperial clan.
Next, people from the three religions, medical practitioners, artisans, and embroiderers were all taken north.
In the fourth month,
the northern troops entered the city.
Cuī Lì (崔立) was outside the city at the time.
The soldiers first entered his home,
took his wives, concubines, precious jewels, and left.
Cuī Lì (崔立) returned and grieved greatly,
but there was nothing he could do.
Lǐ Qí (李琦) was a native of Shānxī (山西),
a commandant.
In Chénzhōu (陳州), he served as a provincial official with Zhāng Gē (粘哥奴) and Shēn (申).
When Chénzhōu (陳zhōu) revolted,
he entered the capital
and allied with Cuī Lì's (崔立) brother-in-law, Zhé Xīyán (折希顏),
and married Jiágǔ Yuán's (夾谷元) wife.
His wife was over twenty,
with a beautiful appearance.
Cuī Lì (崔立) initially detained the families of officials accompanying the emperor,
but his wife, being ill, was carried there and thus
escaped.
After Lǐ Qí (李琦) married her,
some spoke of her beauty,
and Cuī Lì (崔立) wanted to force her.
Whenever Lǐ Qí (李琦) saw Cuī Lì (崔立) wanting to seize someone's wife,
he would dispatch her husband far away.
One day, he dispatched Lǐ Qí (李琦) out of the capital.
Lǐ Qí (李琦) took his wife with him.
This happened two or three times, and
Cuī Lì (崔立) then wanted to kill Lǐ Qí (李琦).
Lǐ Qí (李琦) had also been humiliated by Zhé Xīyán (折希顏) multiple times,
so he initiated the plot to kill Cuī Lì (崔立).
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) was a native of Bǎochí (寶坻),
originally a thousand-householder in the Ānpíng (安平) Commandant's Office.
He was handsome and deeply cunning.
He was always indignant at Cuī Lì's (崔立) wickedness
and wished to righteously kill him.
Lǐ Jiànnú (李賤奴) was a native of Yān (燕).
He had once, for military merit, remotely held the position of Judge of Jīngzhào Fǔ (京兆府).
In the winter of Rénchén (壬辰),
when the imperial carriage went east on a hunt,
he was appointed acting Eastern Marshal (東面元帥) by the commandant.
When Cuī Lì (崔立) first rebelled,
he treated Lǐ Jiànnú (李賤奴) with apparent respect,
as he was formerly his peer.
After several months,
his power was consolidated,
and he then treated Lǐ Jiànnú (李賤奴) like a subordinate.
Lǐ Jiànnú (李賤奴) had long been discontent
and frequently uttered grievances.
By this time, he joined Lǐ Qí (李琦) and others.
In the sixth month of Jiǎwǔ (甲午) in the third year,
it was reported that Sòng (宋) troops were near the border.
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) and others ostensibly conspired with Cuī Lì (崔立) on defense strategies.
The evening of the next day,
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) and others burned the outer Fēngqiū Mén (封丘門) to alarm Cuī Lì (崔立).
That night,
Cuī Lì (崔立) was extremely uneasy,
rising and lying down a hundred times throughout the night.
By dawn,
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) and others personally came to ask Cuī Lì (崔立) to inspect the fire.
Cuī Lì (崔立) went with Yuàn Xiù (苑秀) and Zhé Xīyán (折希顏) on a few horses,
ordering all men in the capital city, aged fifteen to seventy, to gather at Tàimiào Jiē (太廟街) for roll call.
After returning,
as they reached Shūháng Jiē (梳行街),
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) wanted to escort Cuī Lì (崔立) back to Èr Wáng Fǔ (二王府).
Cuī Lì (崔立) declined several times,
but Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) insisted on personally escorting him.
Cuī Lì (崔立) was unsuspicious.
In a sudden move, Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) embraced Cuī Lì (崔立) on horseback.
Cuī Lì (崔立) looked back and said:
"Are you trying to kill me?"
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) said:
"What harm is there in killing you?"
He immediately drew a dagger and stabbed him horizontally,
piercing through and hitting his hand where it held Cuī Lì (崔立).
He stabbed him again,
and Cuī Lì (崔立) fell from his horse and died.
The hidden soldiers rose,
and Marshal Huáng Guā (黃摑三合) killed Yuàn Xiù (苑秀).
Zhé Xīyán (折希顏) arrived later, unaware.
Seeing Cuī Lì (崔立) fall from his horse,
he thought he was fighting with someone
and intended to step forward to separate them.
He was then hacked by soldiers,
wounded, and fled outside Liáng Mén (梁門),
where he was pursued and beheaded.
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) tied Cuī Lì's (崔立) corpse to a horse's tail
and, arriving before the palace, shouted to the crowd:
"Cuī Lì (崔立) committed murder, robbery,
incest, rape, and tyranny,
an act of great treason and wickedness
unparalleled in ancient and modern times!
Should he not be killed?"
Ten thousand voices uniformly replied:
"Even dismembering him into inches would not be enough!"
So they decapitated Cuī Lì (崔立)'s head
and, facing Chéngtiān Mén (承天門), offered sacrifice to Āizōng (哀宗).
Lǐ Bóyuān (李伯淵) and the military and civilians below him all grieved,
some even cut out his heart and ate it raw.
The three corpses were hung on the locust tree in front of the palace gate.
The tree suddenly fell out of the ground.
People said the tree had a spirit and also detested being defiled by him.
Afterwards,
someone reported that Cuī Lì (崔立) had hidden precious treasures in the palace.
His home was then confiscated,
and his wife, Wáng Huā'ér (王花兒), was bestowed upon a soldier under Chancellor Zhènhǎi (鎮海)'s command.
Initially,
during Cuī Lì's change of power,
the former Imperial Guard Púxiān Shílǔ carried five imperial portraits of the ancestors,
and fled to Cài.
Former Imperial Censor-in-chief Púchá Shìdá and Western Front Marshal Bǎsāhé also extricated themselves and their families to return to Cài.
On the *jǐsì* day of the seventh month,
Shìdá was appointed Attendant-Minister of the Ministry of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs,
and temporarily oversaw the Six Ministries of the Department of State Affairs.
Shìdá had previously served as Director of the Left Bureau,
Co-signing Official of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and Official of the Yìzhèng Yuàn,
all of which were to the emperor's liking.
When the emperor went to Guīdé,
he dispatched Shìdá to supervise the transportation of grain from Chén.
When Chén changed sides,
Shìdá was also coerced into joining,
but soon took a detour to Biàn.
By this time, he had gone to the traveling court,
and the emperor, remembering his past service,
appointed him.
Officials of the Left and Right Bureaus then memorialized that Bǎsāhé and Shílǔ should also be appointed.
The emperor said,
"Shìdá was coerced into complying, not willingly.
Nevertheless, I still slightly reduced his rank to show a minor punishment.
Bǎsāhé commanded one front of the army,
〔一五〕and Shílǔ guarded the inner palace.
During Cuī Lì's change of power, they were not heard to fire even a single arrow;
they merely submitted to others.
Though they have now returned,
to spare their lives is sufficient to show grace.
How can they be treated equally with Shìdá?
Bǎsāhé is old;
it is acceptable to appoint his son to a suitable position.
Shílǔ should only be compensated for his effort in carrying the imperial portraits."
Shortly after,
Bǎsāhé was appointed Commandant of the Northern Gate,
and his son became Commander of his original army.
Shílǔ was reinstated as an Imperial Guard.
Shìdá's courtesy name was Zhèngfū.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the third year of Tàihé.
The commentary states: Cuī Lì's submission would have been acceptable if he had sealed the treasuries and registered the populace to await the orders of the Great Court.
However, he took advantage of the situation to usurp power,
engaged in widespread licentiousness and cruelty,
and extorted with brutal arrogance,
always using "supplying the great army" as an excuse,
indulging his own desires,
and accumulating resentment against the state.
His crimes are unforgivable.
Moreover, his ambition was to demand the same treatment as Liú Yù.
How could our Great Court possibly emulate the Jīn people?
The Jīn people captured their lord and made a minister their emperor.
A hundred years later, this directly inspired Cuī Lì's reckless scheme,
leading to the severe disaster of Qīngchéng.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Beware,
beware!
What comes out of you will return to you."
Is this not true?
Niè Tiānjì, courtesy name Yuánjí,
was a native of Wǔtái.
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the first year of Zhìníng,
and was appointed Registrar of Rǔyīn,
then successively served as Judicial Officer of Suīzhōu and Magistrate of Fēngqiū.
At the beginning of Xīngdìng,
he was recruited as a Clerk in the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, minor officials wielded great power,
and scholars often attached themselves to them,
but Tiānjì alone never conceded an inch,
nor could they harm him.
He was soon appointed Principal Official of the Ministry of Personnel
and acting Imperial Censor.
When the Xià envoys congratulated on New Year's Day,
trade took place at the Huìtóng Guǎn.
There were imperial relatives engaged in trade there.
Tiānjì memorialized, saying:
"High officials seeking profit
lose the dignity of the court,
and moreover, incur contempt from foreign lands."
Thus, he displeased the Empress Dowager.
He was sent out as Vice-Administrator of Rǔzhōu Commandery,
but before he could take office,
he was summoned by the post station of the Shǎnxī Traveling Department of State Affairs,
and by special imperial decree, he was remotely appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Jīn'ān Commandery,
and concurrently Do-shi of the Traveling Department of State Affairs.
Not long after,
he entered as a Supernumerary Official of the Right Bureau,
then transferred to Judicial Administrator of Jīngzhào,
and soon after, oversaw the Six Ministries of the Department of State Affairs in Wèizhōu.
When Qìngyáng was under urgent siege,
the court dispatched Generalissimo Yágǔtǎ of Sùzhōu to relieve it,
and Tiānjì was appointed Experiential Officer.
After the siege was lifted,
he followed another commander to guard Bīn.
The commander wished to abandon the prefecture and move east,
but Tiānjì strongly urged him to stop.
He was not heeded,
and the commander was subsequently impeached and arrested for this,
while Tiānjì was demoted to Judicial Administrator of Jīngzhào.
Soon after, someone lodged a complaint about his injustice,
and he was immediately summoned to serve as Signatory Official of Kāifēng,
and within ten days, he was reinstated as Supernumerary Official of the Right Bureau.
He observed mourning for his mother,
but before the mourning period ended,
he was forced to cease mourning and return to his post.
When Emperor Āizōng moved to Guīdé,
Tiānjì remained in Biàn.
During Cuī Lì's change of power,
Tiānjì was severely wounded,
and lay ill for over ten days.
〔一五〕His daughter Shùnyīng sought a doctor for treatment.
Tiānjì sighed, saying:
"I would be fortunate to die.
My children are seeking a doctor;
do they still want me to live?"
He eventually died of depression.
Shùnyīng buried her father,
and the next day, she also hanged herself.
There is a biography.
Tiānjì was calm and reserved,
and did not associate recklessly.
Rising from the countryside,
he was able to conduct himself with noble principles.
His career in the central government seemed as if he were an accustomed official,
and many others considered themselves inferior to him.
Chìzhǎn Wèixīn, courtesy name Dàyòng,
was a native of Shàngjīng.
He was supposed to inherit his father's position as commander of a *móukè*,
but he was unwilling to accept it.
He passed the *cèlùn* examination for the *jìnshì* degree in the fifth year of Míngchāng.
Later, he was selected as Clerk in the Department of State Affairs, Principal Official of the Ministry of Personnel, and Imperial Censor.
He stated,
"When imperial princes and imperial sons-in-law come to the capital to purchase various goods,
it compromises the dignity of the court."
An imperial decree prohibited this.
He was promoted to Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhènnán Commandery and Prefect of Xīzhōu.
When grain was planted in the ball-playing field,
two stalks merged into one ear,
which was presented to the court.
A special imperial decree commended him.
He was transferred to Dānzhōu,
then promoted to Defensive Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu,
and acting Commander of Xǔzhōu.
Chancellor Gāo Rǔlì once recommended his talent as suitable for a chancellor.
In the first month of the second year of Yuánguāng,
he was summoned to be Attendant-Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
Soon after,
he was made acting Associate Administrator of the Department of State Affairs.
In the second month,
he became Minister of Revenue,
with his acting duties remaining as before.
In the third month,
he was appointed Associate Administrator of the Department of State Affairs,
concurrently Compiler of National History.
The emperor issued an edict to his close officials, saying:
"Wèixīn's disposition is pure and honest,
and he can be entrusted with affairs.
Moreover, he is filial by nature.
Now that I appoint him as chancellor,
the state will surely have hope.
You all should emulate him."
In the fifth month of the first year of Zhèngdà,
he was appointed Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
When Emperor Āizōng wished to renovate the palaces,
Wèixīn strongly remonstrated,
even mentioning the phrase "sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall."
The emperor was startled and complied.
Sāhālián, a relative of the imperial family who was Co-Administrator of the Bureau for Imperial Kin, had connections both inside and outside the court,
and had long been close to the emperor.
When Emperor Āizōng was crown prince,
he had the merit of settling the succession,
and thus was quite swayed by his words,
and relied on him increasingly deeply.
The censors frequently spoke against this.
The Empress Dowager once warned and instructed him, saying:
"The emperor's horse polo and music are all taught by you.
If you offend again, I will have you caned."
Emperor Āizōng ultimately could not dismiss him.
Wèixīn remonstrated, saying:
"Sāhālián is the worst of flatterers,
and he is by the emperor's side daily.
This is not a blessing for the state."
The emperor repented and understood,
and sent him out as Resident-General of Zhōngjīng.
The court welcomed this.
In the fifth year,
he retired,
and resided in Biàn.
The day after Cuī Lì's change of power,
he summoned his family, entrusted them with his final affairs,
looked towards Suīyáng and wept bitterly,
then hanged himself with a bowstring,
at the age of sixty-three.
He had one son named Dǒngqī,
who died in the warfare.
His younger brother Bǐngfǔ had the courtesy name Zhèngzhī.
The eulogy states: Niè Tiānjì's character was always pure and cautious.
Chìzhǎn Wèixīn's nature was loyal and honest.
In a time of peace, both would have been capable officials.
Unfortunately, they served in a time of chaos and disunion,
and their wish was to die.
Alas!
Textual Notes
Biographies, Chapter 54: Túshàn Wùdiǎn, Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, Púchá Guānnuánèi Zú Chénglì (also named Qìngshānnú).
Túshàn Wùdiǎn,
his origins are unknown.
He successively held office as the Military Commissioner of Wǔshèng Army,
stationed in Dèngzhōu.
Soon after, he was transferred to be the Central Capital Administrator,
in charge of Jīnchāng Fǔ,
stationed in Luòyáng.
Wùdiǎn fortified both Dèng and Luòyáng,
and recruited a thousand fugitives,
calling them
"Bear and Tiger Army" (Xiónghǔjūn),
whose business was to plunder the southern border.
The Sòng people also retaliated from time to time,
causing unrest among the border populace.
Wùdiǎn's nature was severe and shrewd,
and he held himself in high esteem.
He liked to set up informants,
ordering his close associates to report daily on all trivial matters concerning his generals, officials, subordinates, and even common families,
so as
to ensure he could not be deceived.
During the Zhèngdà era,
he served as Minister of War with the concurrent post of Grand Councilor,
and concurrently managed the provincial administration in Xúzhōu.
Presuming on the emperor's favor,
he showed no leniency in discussions,
and his colleagues all feared him.
In the first month of the first year of Tiānxīng,
the imperial court heard that the grand army had entered Ráofēng,
and moved Wùdiǎn to govern the province of Ménxiāng,
to guard Tóngguān.
Túshàn Bǎijiā was made the overall commander of Guānshǎn,
with discretionary powers.
Bǎijiā rode swiftly into Shǎn,
posting notices to the provincial people saying:
"The southern army has infiltrated,
and it is feared they will pass through Tóngguān.
The position cannot be held.
Counties and towns should move into major cities.
Grain and supplies should be gathered in Shǎnzhōu.
Those near the mountains should enter mountain strongholds to avoid the troops."
At this time, Ālǐhé conveyed an imperial decree summoning Wùdiǎn to provide aid.
Wùdiǎn then, together with the Tóngguān overall commander Nàhé Hérùn, Qínlán overall commander Dōudiǎnjiǎn Wányán Chóngxǐ, Ānpíng Commandant Miáo Xiù,
Dàngkòu Commandant Shùjiǎ Mǒu, Zhènwǔ Commandant Zhāng Yì, and the two commanders of Hǔwēi, Yīngyáng, and Jiāzhōu, Liú and Zhào,
a total of 110,000 soldiers and 5,000 cavalry,
completely abandoned the defenses of the Qínlán passes,
and entered Shǎn from Guó.
Hundreds of thousands of *hú* of military provisions in the areas of Tóng, Huá, and Ménxiāng,
along with over two hundred prepared pass boats,
all flowed downstream to the east.
Suddenly hearing the grand army was near,
they could not load all the provisions,
and all the boats went downstream empty.
They again mobilized all the provincial people
to transport millet from the granaries of Língbǎo and Xiáshí.
When the enemy cavalry arrived,
the slaughter and plunder were beyond count.

They also dispatched Mòlián Sùyě, the Assistant Surveillance Commissioner of Shǎnzhōu and concurrent Assistant Commissioner for Planning and Transport, with eighty boats to transport provisions from Tóngguān and Ménxiāng.
They reached the sandbanks of Běihé Jiázhān in Língbǎo.
The righteous army leaders Zhāng Xìn and Hóu Sān gathered over three hundred brave men,
protected the old and young,
and established a water stockade.
The northern general Hūlǔhǎn Zhī, finding the shallow attack unsuccessful,
surrendered immediately upon the arrival of Sùyě's boats.
The grand army, having obtained these boats, then broke Hóu and Zhāng's forces,
killing almost all of them.
At this time, Nèizú Tànchūn, the Deputy Administrator of Shǎnzhōu, wished to join the provincial army on expedition.
Wùdiǎn gave him a command,
allowing him to recruit citizens within the city as soldiers.
Tànchūn offered generous official rewards,
but for several days, not a single person came.
He then recruited under Wùdiǎn's direct order,
and obtained eight hundred brave men.
Xuānchāi Zhào Sānsān, named Wěi,
also recruited according to Tànchūn's method.
Wěi was known to many,
and in less than two days, he obtained over eight hundred soldiers,
named
"Enemy-Breaking Army" (Pòdí Jūn).
Wùdiǎn was jealous of Wěi for gaining a following
and wanted to trick and trap him.
Wányán Sùlán, who was then the Pacification Commissioner of Tónghuá,
strongly advised against it, and Wùdiǎn stopped.
Soon after, Wěi was provisionally appointed Military Commissioner of Xīngbǎo Army,
and concurrently managed the Marshal's office,
leading three hundred soldiers,
stationed at Jīnjībǎo.
When the grand army knew that Tóngguān had been burned and abandoned,
they advanced rapidly to Shǎn.
Hè Dōuxǐ, without waiting for orders, went out of the city to engage in battle.
His horse stumbled, and he was almost captured.
Wùdiǎn exchanged a horse for him,
and then issued an order that no one should go out again.
The grand army also left.
From then on, all the ferry boats and rafts at Tóngguān were gone,
and Wěi also had no boats to cross.
Initially,
when Wùdiǎn departed from Ménxiāng,
he worshipped Heaven
and rewarded the army,
giving three *liǎng* of silver to each man,
with higher amounts for generals and officers.
The provincial treasury,
military supplies, and weapons
were completely emptied.
He set a date for departure,
but then did not move.
He spent days making silver vessels, army tent signs, and seals,
and also seized the signs of Shǎnzhōu and the Salt Administration.
He also wanted to seize the property of the provincial people to fund the army.
Sùlán advised against it, and he stopped.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the second month,
he finally set off.
A certain Mr. Lǐ advised him, saying:
"Currently, the grand army is all in Hénán,
and Héběi is empty.
Your Excellency can first seize Wèizhōu,
catching them by surprise.
When they know our army is in the north,
they will certainly divide their forces to cross north,
and the capital will gain some respite,
making it easier for Your Excellency to enter and provide aid."
Wùdiǎn was furious,
believing he was leaking military secrets,
and had him executed in the marketplace,
then continued his march.
Each soldier brought their old and young with them.
Within the province, there were also merchants' old and young who had moved from Guānzhōng and Hézhōng,
who also relied on the army's strength to follow along.
Women were all married to soldiers,
and there were also cases of forced marriages and abductions within the army.
On that day,
the army exited through the two eastern gates and the southern gate,
not following the Luòyáng road,
but instead entering the great mountains and ice and snow through a path southwest of the province.
The two commanders of Jiāzhōu, Liú and Zhào, mutinied and left that very day.
The grand army, with several hundred cavalry, pursued them from a distance.
The next day,
Zhāng Yì's army mutinied and went to Zhūyáng,
entering Lùlúguān.
The grand army pursued and forced them to surrender.
The mountain roads were covered in snow.
During the day, the ice melted,
and the mud was knee-deep.
Women following the army abandoned their young children,
and their mournful cries filled the road.
When the army reached Tiělǐng,
the grand army secretly summoned the Luòyáng grand army to pass through the three western counties via Lúshì,
burning official and civilian houses and accumulated supplies wherever they went,
fearing they would be occupied by the Jīn army.
They then returned to hold Tiělǐng,
cutting off the retreat path.
The Jīn soldiers knew they were doomed to die,
and all were determined to fight.
However, they had not eaten for several days,
and after marching about two hundred *lǐ*,
they were exhausted and could not hold on,
and many also scattered and fled.
At this point,
Wányán Chóngxǐ surrendered first,
and the grand army beheaded him before their horses.
Zhèng Tì and Miáo Yīng surrendered.
Yīng refused to comply,
and was killed.
His head was used to induce surrender,
and then the soldiers completely collapsed.
Wùdiǎn and Hérùn fled into the mountains with several tens of cavalry.
The pursuing cavalry captured them,
and killed them all.
Previously,
Wùdiǎn had served as the Military Commissioner of Dèngzhōu.
Huángguó Sānhé, a hereditary *móukè* and then Xuānchāi Dōuzǒnglǐng,
was close to Wùdiǎn.
Therefore, he was determined to enter Dèng.
In this campaign,
among the commandants of Ānpíng, Dàngkòu, Yīngyáng, and Zhènwēi,
and the armies of Xī'ān, Jīnjī, etc.,
only one or two out of a hundred escaped.
In the second month,
Sùlán fled back.
Someone reported to Túshàn Bǎijiā, saying,
"The Xíngshěng is arriving."
Bǎijiā wished to go out and welcome him,
but the elders blocked his horse, pleading sorrowfully:
"If the Xíngshěng comes again,
our prefecture will be shattered.
We beg you not to go out to welcome him."
Bǎijiā enlightened them, saying:
"The other day, Wūdiǎn wanted to [⿱艹疎] this prefecture,
but Sùlán strongly persuaded him to stop.
This Xíngshěng is not Wūdiǎn, but Sùlán."
Only then did the elders allow Bǎijiā to leave the city.
After Shǎnzōu's army departed,
there were daily returns of fugitives.
Bǎijiā embraced and absorbed them all,
acquiring as many as ten thousand people.
Bǎijiā also recruited and collected abandoned armor and weapons.
If two sets were obtained,
one was given to the person,
and the other was purchased by the officials at its true value.
Because of this, the army gradually recovered.
In the fifth month,
the Grand Marshal's Deputy Inspector, Yánzhǎn, led an army to re-establish the Grand Marshal of Shāngzhōu.
A man named Wáng from Huázhōu established Guózhōu,
acting as governor.
In the seventh month,
an imperial decree summoned Bǎijiā to provide aid.
Ābùhǎnnúshílà, who was acting Jìedùshǐ of Xī'ānjūn and in charge of the Grand Marshal's Residence, was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Jīn'ānjūn and Guānshǎn Grand Marshal.
In the ninth month,
Wányán Hūxiéhǔ, the Zhīfǔ and Marshal of Gǒngchāng, entered Shǎnzōu.
An imperial edict appointed him Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
and acting Shàngshūshěng affair.
Lǐ Xiànnéng, the Jīnglì of the Hózhōng Grand Marshal's Residence, was appointed Yuánwàiláng of Zuǒyòusī.
Xiànnéng's courtesy name was Qīnshú.
He passed the Jinshì examination in Zhēnyòu third year.
Mountain strongholds were re-established,
and the army and people were pacified.
On the first day of the tenth month,
an imperial decree summoned Hūxiéhǔ to Nányáng Líushān Temple.
Ābùhǎnnúshílà was appointed acting Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
and Xíngshěng.
At that time, Zhào Wěi was the Marshal of Héxié,
stationed at Jīnjībǎo.
Military affairs were subordinate to Shǎnshěng.
The Xíngshěng provided monthly rations to supply his army.
In the fifth month of the following year,
when the wheat was ripe,
the province issued an order for Wěi to arrange provisions for the soldiers,
temporarily suspending the monthly supply.
In the tenth month,
Wěi's army again ran out of food.
He repeatedly reported to Shǎnshěng,
saying there was no grain to provide.
Wěi privately told his army:
"I have a grudge with Yuanwàiláng Lǐ,
who just sits by and watches our army starve,
offering no care or relief."
Thereupon,
he went personally to Yǒngníng to persuade and explain.
Wěi was quite trusted by the common people,
who often offered grain,
or guided him to uncover hidden stores.
The Tíkòng of the border pass army in the southern county reported Wěi's arrogance and tyranny to the Xíngshěng.
The Xíngshěng dispatched a Tíkòng named Zhào to act as Marshal,
to guard Yuáncūn Fortress in Yǒngníng.
Wěi returned to Jīnjī.
On the winter solstice in the eleventh month,
the main army had already attacked and captured Yuáncūn Fortress.
Wěi attacked Jiězhōu but could not take it.
Thereupon, he secretly dispatched General Wáng Mào and thirty soldiers into Shǎnzōu,
where they hid in a vegetable garden for three or four days.
At night,
Wáng Mào killed the night watchman of the north city,
raised a signal to summon Wěi's army of eight hundred to cross the river,
entered the city to [⿱艹疎] and kill Ābùhǎnnúshílà, Lǐ Xiànnéng, Tíkòng Púxiān Mǒu, and Grand Leader Lái Dào'ān.
Then he falsely accused them, saying:
"Núshílà and others intended to rebel;
your servant executed them."
The imperial court knew they were wronged but no one dared to challenge him.
Wěi was then appointed Marshal Zuǒ Jiānjūn,
concurrently Jìedùshǐ of Xī'ānjūn,
and acting Grand Marshal's Residence affairs.
Food ran out.
Grain was requisitioned.
The grain also ran out.
In the third month of the following year, he surrendered to the main army.
Some said that Wěi's army lacked provisions,
and that he resorted to [⿱艹疎] and plunder to sustain himself.
One day he went to Lǐ Xiànnéng.
Xiànnéng was stingy with him,
saying:
"It is not easy to defeat the enemy expediently."
Because of this, he resented him.
So, taking advantage of Núshílà's feasting without preparation,
he selected twenty-eight elite soldiers.
At night, they scaled the city wall from the back river beach,
and threw broken stones from a cake oven at roof tiles and door panels, mimicking the sound of arrows.
The people of the prefecture suspected a large number of rebel soldiers
and dared not move.
Consequently, the gates were opened to admit the army.
Twenty-one officials and subordinates, including the Xíngshěng, were killed.
Xiànnéng was the most hated,
and thus his death was especially brutal.
During Wěi's rebellion, Zhāng Shēng, courtesy name Jìnzhī, the Lùshì of Jiàngzhōu,
a native of Dàtóng,
who started as a Lìshǐ in Hùgōngbù,
once served as Bù in Yúyáng,
and was promoted to Lùshì of Jiàngzhōu,
told his acquaintances:
"I am but a humble man,
who has received official emoluments from the state.
Today the state faces misfortune,
and I cannot follow the rebels."
After speaking, he threw himself into the water and died.
Hundreds of people on the bank all sighed and lamented him.
When Túshàn Bǎijiā was defeated west of Zhèng,
he rode alone through secret paths for hundreds of *lǐ* to the capital,
and reported to the emperor the defeat of Wūdiǎn and others at Tiělǐng.
Thereupon, the properties of Zhòngxǐ, Hérùn, and Wūdiǎn were confiscated,
and Wūdiǎn was publicly denounced as the chief culprit,
with notices posted on main streets.
Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān,
originally named Shíliù.
In Xīngdìng third year,
he was appointed Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān as Hénán Lùtǒngjūnshǐ,
and acted as Píngliáng Grand Marshal's Residence affairs.
Prior to this,
Xú Dǐng, Xī'ān Xíngshěng, had said:
"Píngliáng controls the western frontier,
and is indeed a vital strategic location.
Dūjiān Nǚxīliè Gǔlǐjiān's talent and discernment are mediocre,
and he is not skilled in military affairs.
Moreover, he obtained his official position by contributing grain,
thus achieving promotion.
Holding heavy troops,
and commanding a region,
how can he command the respect of the masses?
Autumn defense is imminent;
it is advisable to select someone with talent, strategy, established reputation, and skill in leading troops to replace him."
Therefore, the command was given to Nǚlǔhuān.
In the eleventh month,
Nǚlǔhuān reported:
"Zhènróng Chìgōuchuān,
forty *lǐ* east to west,
has no natural defenses.
It is a crucial passage for the Xià people's movements,
and has been repeatedly invaded and raided.
The Jīn army has often been at a disadvantage.
Next spring,
when we fortify Zhènróng,
they will surely send troops to disrupt us.
I request that in the second and third months,
troops from surrounding prefectures be summoned, ostensibly for defense,
and also that Fū and Gǒng each station troops on their borders to show an offensive posture,
thereby restraining them.
Your servant will lead the forces of Píngliáng to enter through Zhènróng,
attacking their vital center.
They will be too busy saving themselves,
how can they reach us?
If this is done, Zhènróng can be fortified,
and they will not dare to invade.
Furthermore, many of the government troops stationed in various places are displaced people from Héběi and Shānxī.
Their families rely on county officials for sustenance,
and always suffer from insufficiency.
The soil of Zhènróng is fertile,
and also flat.
The nearly eight thousand men under your servant's deputy generals
often suffer from constant relocation.
If they are given wasteland to farm and fight,
they can defend a region,
the county officials will save expenses, and food will also be sufficient.
The other border prefectures should also implement the same measures."
The emperor praised and adopted his suggestions.
He was promoted to Jìedùshǐ of Chāngwǔjūn.
In the ninth month of Yuánguāng (元光) second year,
he also said:
"Shāngluò (商洛) is a strategic place,
controlling Qínshǎn (秦陝) to the west,
and bordering Hénán (河南) to the east.
Military affairs are complex and numerous;
it is advisable to select capable and talented individuals to serve as Defensive Commissioner and acting Commander to garrison it.
Furthermore, the officials guarding the various passes in the old days
were all appointed by the Commander's Office.
Many of those appointed were their close relatives,
who acquired property for personal gain,
and engaged solely in exploitation.
When their term expired,
they were again retained.
This is the greatest harm.
It is advisable to let the Privy Council (樞府) elect them
to reform this abuse.
Moreover, the garrison soldiers in the prefectures suffered from difficult provisions and transport;
it is also appropriate for them to establish military colonies (屯田) as above,
to avoid the costs of transportation."
He further said:
"Annually, for autumn defense,
the guards at the various passes number no more than a few tens of people,
while the rest of the troops are all stationed at Bǎo'ān (保安), Shímén (石門), Dàjīng (大荊), and Luònán (洛南) as reinforcements.
The distance between them can be as much as a hundred *lǐ*;
how can they be mobilized in an emergency?
It is advisable to build camps near the passes,
and move the existing soldiers to live there,
to await emergencies.
Furthermore, the ten巡檢 (Xúnjiǎn) established in the southern border,
with a force of a thousand men,
were meant to investigate spies in peacetime.
Since there is already a large army,
they should all be dismissed."
The imperial court generally implemented these suggestions.
In the second month of Zhèngdà (正大) ninth year,
he was appointed acting Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (行樞密院事) to guard Guīdé (歸德).
On the *yǐchǒu* (乙丑) day,
the Great Yuán (大元) general Tèmùshòu (忒木[⿰木受]) led the armies from Zhēndìng (真定), Xìn'ān (信安), Dàmíng (大名), Dōngpíng (東平), and Yìdū (益都) to attack.
On that day,
there was thunder without clouds.
Someone, interpreting this with the 'Divine Martial Secret Stratagem,'
said,
"The city will suffer no harm,"
and people's hearts were somewhat eased.
Just then, Qìngshānnú's (慶山奴) routed troops also arrived,
and the city gained them,
boosting their fighting spirit.
On the *jǐsì* (己巳) day,
the Commander Zhāng Dìng (張定) launched a night raid on the enemy camp,
firing a few cannons before returning.
Dìng (定) was usually fond of discussing military tactics.
Nǚlǔhuān (女魯歡) ordered him to recruit his own army,
making him a Commander (提控).
He achieved victory in a small test,
and subsequently, everyone relied on him as usable.
Initially, there was a shortage of cannons.
They wanted to make them out of mud or bricks,
but the deliberators feared they would be ridiculed by the enemy,
so they did not proceed.
Elders said that in a vegetable garden west of the North Gate, ancient cannons were often found,
claiming they were buried by Táng (唐) dynasty's Zhāng Xún (張巡).
They dug and found more than five thousand,
some bearing engraved characters or the
character "大吉" (dàjí).
The great army attacked the city day and night,
stationing their camp outside the south wall,
where the terrain was slightly elevated.
It was traditionally believed that Yǐn Zǐqí (尹子奇), a general of Ān Lùshān (安祿山), attacked Xún (巡) and Yuǎn (遠) here,
and captured Suīyáng (睢陽).
At that time, the Prefect (經歷) Jì Yǔxí (冀禹錫) and his subordinates Wáng Bì (王璧), Lǐ Qí (李琦), and Fù Yú (傅瑜) defended with utmost effort,
preventing the city from being captured.
While the great army besieged the city,
there was a proposal to breach the water of the Fèngchí (鳳池) Great Bridge to protect the city.
The Director of Waterways (都水官) said that
when the river breached at Áoyóugù (敖游堌) last year,
its water level was measured,
and that place was level with the Lóngxīng (龍興) Pagoda inside the city.
If this breach were made, there would be no city left.
When the great army arrived,
they had no choice but to send the Appeasement Officer (招撫) Chén Guì (陳貴) to breach it.
As soon as he left the gate, he was intercepted by light cavalry,
and not one returned.
On the first day of the third month, *rénwǔ* (壬午),
the attack on the city failed.
Among the great army, someone proposed a plan to breach the river,
and the commanding general adopted it.
After the river was breached,
the water flowed down from the northwest,
reaching the southwest of the city,
and entering the old Suī (濉) waterway.
The city, instead, became fortified by the water.
They sought to kill the person who offered the plan,
but his whereabouts were unknown.
In the fourth month,
Nǚlǔhuān (女魯歡) was made Supreme Commander (總帥),
wearing the golden tiger tally.
The Ministry of Agriculture (司農司) was abolished,
and its official Púchá Shìdá (蒲察世達) was made Jìqìng (集慶) Military Governor (節度使) and acting Vice Minister of Six Ministries (行六部侍郎).
Wēntèhǎn Dàosēng (溫特罕道僧) became the Vice Prefect (同知) of Guīdé (歸德) Prefecture,
and Lǐ Wúdǎng (李無黨) became the Prefectural Judge (府判).
In the fifth month,
the siege of the city slackened somewhat,
and many civilians were moved out of the city to find food.
In the twelfth month,
Emperor Āizōng (哀宗) stopped at Huánglínggāng (黃陵岡),
and sent the Official Servitor (奉職) Shùjiǎ Dāshībù (术甲搭失不) and the acting Imperial Palace Attendant (奉職權奉御) Niánhé Xiéliè (粘合斜烈) to Guīdé (歸德) to requisition grain.
Nǚlǔhuān (女魯歡) sent Vice Minister Shìdá (世達),
Judicial Officer (治中) Wáng Yuánqìng (王元慶) as acting Bureau Director (權郎中),
and Yífēng (儀封) Subordinate Officer (從宜) Wányán Hútǔ (完顏胡土) as acting Grand Marshal (權元帥),
to escort one thousand five hundred *shí* of grain.
On the last day of this month, the boats departed at the second watch.
In the first month of the second year,
they reached twenty *lǐ* east of Púchéng (蒲城).
The provisions for the six armies ran out,
so the boats were detained and not allowed to return.
Furthermore, Zhāng Bù (張布) was ordered to set up a tent,
and the Emperor then used this boat to cross.
When the Emperor came to Guīdé (歸德),
the imperial guard armies often went out of the city to forage for food.
At that time, there was only Mǎ Yòng's (馬用) army of nearly seven hundred men in the city.
Yòng (用),
a native of Shānxī (山西),
was from the same village as Lǐ Xīn (李辛),
and had once served as a military supervisor (彈壓) for Xīn's (辛) army.
In Guīdé (歸德), he was acting Commandant of Cavalry (權果毅都尉).
When the imperial carriage arrived,
he was appointed to a command position.
Besides this army, there were also four hundred and fifty loyal and filial imperial slaves' (官奴忠孝軍) troops.
The routed armies from Héběi (河北) that arrived were all dismissed.
Thus, only these two armies remained in the city.
The Emperor often summoned Yòng (用) for discussions,
but neglected the imperial slaves (官奴).
Therefore, the imperial slaves (官奴) harbored disloyal intentions.
The court knew that the two were not in harmony,
fearing a mutiny.
On the *wùchén* (戊辰) day of the third month,
an imperial decree ordered the Chancellor to host a banquet in the provincial office
to reconcile them.
That night,
Yòng (用) withdrew his defenses,
and the imperial slaves (官奴) took advantage with their troops to cause a disturbance.
The next day,
they attacked Yòng's (用) army.
Yòng (用) was defeated, fled, and was killed.
His men who descended the wall, jumped into the water, and seized boats to escape, were all gone in an instant.
The imperial slaves (官奴) were at Shuāngmén (雙門),
driving the Prefect (知府) Nǚlǔhuān (女魯歡) to them,
saying, "Since the imperial carriage arrived at the prefecture,
you have not provided sufficient tribute,
nor have you given good sauces.
How can you deny your crimes?"
Then they put him on a horse,
ordered soldiers to escort him to his home,
inspected his house for a total of twenty jars of various sauces,
and also took out all his gold artifacts,
before killing him.
Then they led their troops to an audience,
saying,
"Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān (石盞女魯歡) and others rebelled;
your subject has killed them."
The Emperor had no choice but
to pardon their crimes on the spot,
and publicly denounce Nǚlǔhuān's (女魯歡) wickedness.
Later, his nephew Dà'ān (大安) entered Cài (蔡),
and the Emperor was asked to clear his name.
The Emperor restored his office.
The details are in the biography of Wūgǔlún Hào (烏古論鎬).
Hésùjiā Wùdǐ (禾速嘉兀底) replaced Nǚlǔhuān (女魯歡) as Supreme Commander (總帥).
During the mutiny,
the imperial slaves (官奴) had no intention of harming Wùdǐ (兀底).
They sent two soldiers to summon him,
saying that the imperial slaves (官奴) meant well.
Wùdǐ (兀底) was pleased,
and each gave them ten gold stars,
and went to meet the imperial slaves (官奴) together.
The two soldiers then feared that the matter of receiving gold would be exposed,
so they also killed him.
Initially,
retreating armies from Héběi arrived at Guīdé,
where provisions and pay were insufficient.
The imperial court ordered Bóshùlǔ Āhǎi to act as Superintendent-in-chief,
and all imperial and palace guard troops were placed under his command.
They went to Sùzhōu to forage for food,
but some soldiers were unwilling,
muttering complaints along the way.
The imperial court learned of this
and sent someone to inquire about the reason.
Some said they wished to go to the capital or Chénzhōu.
Āhǎi requested to grant their wish,
issuing them vouchers,
and the morale of the troops became somewhat stable.
Afterward, an order was given to find those who had muttered complaints.
Āhǎi apprehended four men,
and executed them in front of the Guózǐjiān.
Consequently, the various armies became agitated.
On the night of Gēngzǐ in the second month,
they robbed nine families, including the prefectural commoner Wǔ Bāngjié and Púchá Yǎozhù.
One army then dispersed.
A few days later,
the mutiny of Guānnú occurred.
Púchá Guānnú,
when young, had once been captured by northern soldiers
and traveled between Hèshuò.
Later, he was imprisoned in Yānchéng for a scandalous affair.
He escaped to Xiàjīn,
killed a Huíhé envoy, and obtained saddles, horses, and goods.
He then made his way back.
Considering his ethnic background, the imperial court
granted him special favor and appointed him Wànhù of the Zhōngxiào Army.
This army received excellent monthly pay.
Guānnú frequently gambled with a group of unruly individuals,
which led to him being impeached by the authorities.
When the matter was reported,
because he had recently come from Hèshuò
and was unaware of the laws and prohibitions,
an imperial edict ordered that he not be questioned.
When Yílà Pú'ā attacked Píngyáng,
Guānnú requested to participate.
He was credited with the greatest achievement,
and promoted to Tíkòng of his army,
wearing a golden talisman.
After the defeat at Sānfēngshān,
he fled to Xiāngyáng,
persuading a Sòng commander to let him prove his worth by capturing Dèngzhōu.
The commander believed him,
even dining and feasting with him.
Soon after,
learning that the attack on Biànchéng had ceased,
he again planned to return north.
He sent Yílà Liúgē into Dèng,
to persuade the Dèng commander Niánhé,
claiming he wanted to hijack the southern army for a return to the north.
Liúgē revealed the true situation to Niánhé.
Guānnú then entered the city with over ten cavalrymen to discuss matters.
Niánhé intended to capture him in the barbican.
Guānnú, realizing his plot was exposed,
immediately galloped back.
He met the commander, obtained five hundred cavalrymen,
and plundered the small border towns of Dèng,
acquiring several hundred cattle and sheep.
The Sòng people were not suspicious.
Guānnú ambushed a Sòng army, acquiring three hundred horses.
He then went to the foot of Dèngzhōu city,
sent a letter to Niánhé to argue the right and wrong,
left the horses at Dèng, and departed.
He then bound Jī Wàng, the Tíkòng of the Zhōngxiào Army,
falsely presented him as the Prefect of Tángzhōu,
and sent him north in shackles.
He obtained supplies from the encampments along the way,
thus gaining entry into Biàn.
Some said that his movements between the northern and southern armies, traveling thousands of *lǐ* without fear,
showed a commendable intelligence and strategy.
The prime minister agreed,
and so made him acting Vice Commander.
Not long after,
he led several hundred troops, riding swiftly into the northern army's hunting party,
and returned with a captured Huíhé alive.
He then patrolled places like Huánglíng and Bāgǔ,
plundering a large amount of cattle, sheep, and provisions.
Soon, he was promoted to regular Commander.
He again led his army to Huánglíng,
nearly capturing a major general from Zhènzhōu.
At this, everyone, both within and outside the court, believed him to be capable,
and he was thus appointed Yuánshuài,
commanding the cavalry.
In the twelfth month of Tiānxīng 1,
he followed Āizōng in his northern crossing.
When they encamped at Huánglínggāng,
Píngzhāng Báisā led the generals in battle,
and Guānnú's contribution was significant.
Upon crossing the Hèshuò,
only Guānnú's army maintained clear and strict orders,
not violating even a hair's breadth.
In the first month of the following year,
the emperor arrived at Guīdé.
The Prefect, Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, knew that the army's provisions were scarce,
feared he could not supply them,
and requested of the emperor
that the retreating armies from Héběi who arrived should forage for food in Xú, Sù, and Chén three prefectures.
The imperial guard troops were also dispatched outside the city to find food.
The emperor reluctantly agreed.
He then summoned and instructed Guānnú, saying:
“Nǚlǔhuān has dispersed all the guard troops;
you must be cautious.”
At this time,
only Guānnú's Zhōngxiào Army of 450 men
and Mǎ Yòng's army of 700 men
remained in the prefecture.
Yòng was originally a Guǒyì Commander.
He was only promoted to Yuánshuài when the emperor arrived at Guīdé,
and the emperor often summoned him to discuss matters,
but did not include Guānnú.
Thus, Guānnú began to harbor ambitions against Yòng.
At this time,
the Grand Yuán general Tèmùshòu was attacking Guīdé.
Guānnú, now holding overall military power,
secretly conspired with Guó Yòng'ān,
wanting to escort the emperor to Hǎizhōu.
And when the Director of the Imperial Household Bureau, Ālègēn Wùyǎ, sent Ānhuí,
he attached a memorial,
stating that at Hǎizhōu they could rely on the heroes of Shāndōng to plan a restoration,
and that boats and ships were already prepared,
which could connect to Liáodōng.
The emperor read the memorial but did not comply.
He had also once requested the emperor to cross north
and plan for a restoration again,
but Nǚlǔhuān thwarted him.
From then on, he harbored disloyal intentions.
Moreover, his army relied on external forces for rampant plunder,
which Guānnú did not prohibit.
Consequently,
Left Prime Minister Lǐ Xī, Right and Left Department Lángzhōng Zhāng Tiāngāng, and Imperial Household Bureau Vice Envoy Lǐ Dàjié all reported to the emperor that Guānnú showed signs of rebellion.
The emperor secretly worried about this,
and ordered the Cavalry Superintendent Hésīliè Ālǐhé and the imperial kinsman Xí Xiǎn to secretly investigate his movements.
When speaking of it to court officials,
he would say:
“I raised Guānnú from humble beginnings to be a grand marshal;
how could he betray me when I have not wronged him?
