You all should not worry excessively.”
Ālǐhé and Xí Xiǎn knew that Guānnú was gradually becoming uncontrollable,
and instead leaked the emperor's intentions.
The emperor also feared that Guānnú and Mǎ Yòng might conspire against each other,
leading to chaos.
He ordered the prime ministers and executive officials to host a banquet to reconcile them.
Yòng withdrew his defenses.
Suddenly, Guānnú seized the opportunity and led his army to attack Yòng.
Yòng's army was defeated and fled.
Guānnú wantonly killed soldiers and civilians,
left fifty soldiers to guard the temporary palace,
and gathered all court officials at the residence of the Superintendent of Rivers, Máohuālián,
guarding them with soldiers.
He drove the Counsellor-to-the-Secretariat, Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, to his home,
forced him to hand over all his gold artifacts,
and then killed him.
He then sent Commander Mǎ Shí, armored and armed with a blade, to abduct Director Bǎ Núshen before the emperor.
The emperor initially grasped a sword,
but seeing Shí,
he threw the sword to the ground and said:
“Tell the Marshal for me,
I only have this person by my side;
let him stay to serve me.”
Shí did not dare to press further,
and retreated hesitantly.
In total, more than three hundred court officials, from Left Prime Minister Lǐ Xī downwards, were killed.
Three thousand soldiers, imperial guards, and common people died.
Lángzhōng Wányán Húlǔlà and Dūshì Jì Yǔxī drowned themselves.
Yǔxī, courtesy name Jīngfǔ,
was from Lóngshān.
He passed the imperial examination in Zhìníng 1 and served in various prefectures and counties with a reputation for ability.
When Guīdé was attacked,
Yǔxī served as a Dūshì of the provisional government,
and the entire prefecture relied heavily on his plans for defense.
Hearing of the mutiny,
some advised him to escape in disguise,
but he refused
and was killed.
That day, at dusk,
Guānnú brought his troops to see the emperor
and said:
“Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān and others rebelled;
your servant has killed them.”
The emperor had no choice
but to pardon his crime
and appointed him Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs and acting Counsellor-to-the-Secretariat.
Initially,
Guān Nú's mother,
when the army in Héběi collapsed,
was captured by the northern soldiers.
By this time,
the Emperor ordered Guān Nú to use his mother as leverage to propose peace.
Therefore, Guān Nú secretly discussed peace with Tèmùshòu,
sending Ālǐhé to convey the message,
intending to coerce the Emperor into surrendering.
Tèmùshòu believed him,
returned his mother,
and thus finalized the peace plan.
Guān Nú then went back and forth daily to discuss matters,
sometimes meeting and drinking in a boat mid-stream.
The envoys he sent, over twenty of them,
were all Nǚzhí and Qìdān people.
The Emperor secretly ordered Guān Nú to give them gold and silver plaques,
and not let them return to their camp.
Through this, he learned the location of the main general at Wángjiāsì,
which allowed Guān Nú to devise a strategy for attacking the camp.
Before this,
a Zhāng-surnamed Dūtǒng of the Zhōngxiào Army,
believing Guān Nú definitely wanted to coerce the Emperor into surrendering to the north,
led 150 men of his army to surround Guān Nú's residence,
and reproached him, saying:
"If you intend to surrender the Emperor,
we, who are unforgivable by the Great Court,
where shall we go?"
Guān Nú was frightened,
and presented his mother as a hostage,
saying:
"If you suspect me of conspiring with the north
because my mother came from the north,
then kill her,
I will not regret it."
Zhāng's anger somewhat subsided,
and he made a good-natured agreement with him, saying:
"If it is truly as Cānzhèng said,
then henceforth do not speak of peace again,
and when northern envoys arrive, they must be killed."
Guān Nú said:
"To kill is acceptable,
not to kill is also acceptable,
and to memorialize and then kill is also acceptable."
Zhāng then withdrew.
Guān Nú immediately gathered his army at Běicǎochǎng,
declaring that he had no rebellious intentions,
and that they should no longer suspect each other.
Thus, he devised the strategy for attacking the camp.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
a sacrifice to Heaven was offered.
The army secretly prepared firearms and combat equipment.
Leading 450 men of the Zhōngxiào Army,
they boarded boats from the south gate,
proceeding east then north.
At night, they killed the patrolling soldiers on the outer embankment,
and reached Wángjiāsì.
The Emperor was at the north gate,
with boats tied, waiting for them,
fearing that if they failed, he would flee to Xúzhōu.
At the fourth watch, battle commenced,
and the Zhōngxiào Army initially retreated slightly.
Advancing again,
Guān Nú used small boats to divide his army into groups of fifty to seventy outside the palisade,
attacking from both front and rear.
They burst in with firearms,
and the northern army could not withstand them,
immediately suffering a major defeat.
Over 3,500 people drowned and died,
and they burned all their palisades before returning.
Guān Nú was then truly appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì and concurrently Zuǒfù Yuánshuài,
and also awarded an imperial horse.
Regarding the firearm design:
sixteen layers of imperial yellow paper were made into a tube,
about two feet long,
filled with willow charcoal,
iron slag, porcelain powder, sulfur, and arsenic,
with a rope tied to the end of the gun.
Each soldier carried a small iron pot containing fire.
When in battle, they would ignite it,
and flames would shoot out a zhang (about 3.3 meters) in front of the gun.
The gunpowder would be exhausted, but the tube would remain undamaged.
This had been used when Biànjīng was attacked,
and was now used again.
After the troops retreated,
Guān Nú entered Bózhōu,
leaving Xí Xiǎn to command his army.
The Emperor was at Zhàobìtáng,
with no one daring to memorialize or respond,
and cried sadly daily, saying:
"Since ancient times, there has been no country that has not perished, no ruler who has not died,
but I only regret that I did not know how to use people,
and thus was imprisoned by this slave."
Thereupon,
the Nèijú Lìng Sòng Qǐnú, together with Fèngyù Wúgǔsūn Àishí, Nàlán Yìdá, and Nǚxīliè Wánchū, secretly plotted to execute Guān Nú.
Some said
Guān Nú secretly ordered Wúyá Jìgòu Guóyòng'ān
to coerce the Emperor into abdicating,
and to recover Shāndōng.
If the plan failed, he would surrender the Emperor to Sòng,
to atone for his repeated treachery.
Guān Nú went to Bózhōu in the Jǐwèi year.
On Xīnyǒu day,
he was summoned back,
but did not come.
Summoned again,
he returned on the Jǐmǎo day of the sixth month.
The Emperor lectured him about the journey to Càizhōu,
and Guān Nú left indignantly,
even clenching his fists and stamping his feet,
his intentions unfathomable.
The Emperor resolved to execute him,
and thus arranged with the Nèishì Sòng Qǐnú,
ordering Péimǎn Chāohé to summon the prime ministers for discussion.
Wánchū lay in ambush between the doors of Zhàobìtáng.
Guān Nú entered to see him.
The Emperor called out "Cānzhèng!",
and Guān Nú immediately responded.
Wánchū stabbed him in the ribs from behind,
and the Emperor also drew his sword and hacked at him.
Guān Nú, wounded, threw himself down the steps and fled.
When the Zhōngxiào Army heard of the trouble, they all donned their armor.
Wánchū requested the Emperor to personally soothe and comfort them.
He called out Lǐ Tàihé's name,
gave him a tiger tally,
and sent him to comfort the troops,
then summoned Fàn Chénsēng, Wáng Shān'ér, Bái Jìn, and Ālǐhé.
Bái Jìn arrived first,
and was killed below the hall.
Ālǐhé realized what was happening mid-journey,
regretted his late departure,
and was shot to death by a volley of arrows.
Qǐnú, Àishí, and Yìdá were all appointed Jiédùshǐ and hereditary Qiānhù.
Wánchū concurrently served as Diànqián Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Fàn Chénsēng and Wáng Shān'ér became Yuánshuài of the Zhōngxiào Army.
Thereupon,
the Emperor was at Shuāngmén,
pardoning the Zhōngxiào Army to calm unrest.
Except for Cuī Lì, who was not pardoned,
all others who were usually not forgiven were pardoned.
Initially,
when Guān Nú relieved the siege of Suīyáng,
the attendants and officials had long suffered from hunger and hardship.
Hearing that Càizhōu had strong city walls, abundant troops, and ample provisions,
they all advised the Emperor to move south.
Only Guān Nú, having previously passed through Càizhōu with Diǎnjiǎn Nèizú Xiěliè,
knew that its defenses were not as good as Suīyáng's,
and strongly argued against it,
thus proclaiming to the multitude:
"Those who dare to speak of moving south shall be executed!"
The multitude considered Guān Nú disloyal,
and subtly advised the Emperor to act early.
When the change occurred,
he was executed by strategem.
Later, Wūgǔlún Púxiān was sent to Càizhōu,
and upon his return, reported that its city walls, troops, and provisions were indeed insufficient to rely upon.
The Emperor was already en route,
and nothing could be done.
When Càizhōu was attacked,
he finally regretted not having heeded Guān Nú's words,
and specially decreed that the Shàngshūshěng provide monthly rations to his mother and wife,
so they would not be left destitute.
Xí Xiǎn, being Guān Nú's partisan,
one day led the Zhōngxiào Army to loot 4,000 liǎng of gold from the imperial treasury.
The Emperor ordered Guīdé Zhìzhōng Wēntèhǎn Dàosēng and Shuàifǔ Jīnglì Bǎnúshen to investigate.
Xí Xiǎn confessed and was imprisoned.
When Guān Nú's rebellion broke out,
Xí Xiǎn escaped,
killed Zǒnglǐng Wányán Chánglè at the palace gate,
killed Dàosēng and Bǎnúshen at their homes,
and then fled to Bó.
When Guān Nú was executed,
an edict ordered Diǎnjiǎn Àlègēn Āshīdá to execute Xí Xiǎn and several leaders of the Zhōngxiào Army in Bózhōu.
Wúyá Shǐyòng'ān had not yet returned;
he was ambushed mid-journey,
his crimes enumerated, and then killed.
Nèizú Qìngshānnú, personal name Chénglì,
courtesy name Xiànfǔ,
was the son of Tǒngjūnshǐ Guǎishān,
and the paternal cousin of Píngzhāng Báishā.
He was of imposing appearance,
but inwardly timid and without substance.
In the early Jiàníng
period, Xuānzōng traveled from Zhāngdé to the capital.
Qìngshānnú met him at Táichéng.
Xuānzōng was pleased
and sent him ahead to Zhōngdū to observe the situation.
After Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
he made Chénglì the Vice Resident Commissioner of Xījīng,
and acting Director of the Jìnshì Jú,
advancing him five ranks,
and granting him five thousand strings of cash.
The imperial edict stated:
"Although you have been granted this position,
for now remain by my side;
only when there is a vacancy should you assume it.
You will still receive the salary of a Vice Resident Commissioner.
This is a special favor from me,
and you should be aware of it."
In the early Zhēnyòu period,
he was promoted to Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Wǔwèi Army,
and concurrently Supervisor of the Jìnshì Jú.
When Húshāhǔ wielded excessive power and usurped authority,
Qìngshānnú once spoke to Xuānzōng about it.
Later, after Húshāhǔ was executed,
Qìngshānnú became even more favored,
and was appointed Right Vice Inspector-General of the Palace Guard.
In the third year,
when the Dàyuán army besieged Zhōngdū,
an edict appointed Qìngshānnú as the Expedient Commander-in-Chief,
to lead the recruited troops to its aid.
Soon after, he became the Right Vice Military Commissioner,
acting in the capacity of the commander's office,
and retaining his previous position.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Prefect of Qìngyáng Fǔ,
and concurrently Grand Commander of all horse and foot soldiers of Qìngyuán Lù.
He presented captured horses and camels,
and an edict replied:
"These were all obtained by the soldiers;
you may give them to them.
What use are they to me?
Do not present them again in the future."
He then ordered this message to be circulated to all military commissioners' offices.
In the first month of the first year of Xīngdìng,
the Dàyuán army and the Xìa people passed through Níngzhōu on their return journey.
Qìngshānnú intercepted and defeated them,
and for his merits, he was promoted to Left Vice Military Commissioner,
and concurrently Military Governor of the Bǎodà Army,
acting in the capacity of the commander's office in Fūzhōu.
In the fifth month of the second year,
the Xìa people, with three thousand infantry and cavalry, invaded from Jiāzhōu.
Qìngshānnú met them with his troops
and fought at Mǎjí Fēng,
killing over a hundred men,
beheading two enemy chiefs,
and capturing dozens alive,
acquiring over thirty horses.
In the fourth month of the third year,
the Xìa people occupied Tōngqín Zhài.
Qìngshānnú dispatched Commander Nàhémǎizhù to attack them.
The Xìa people, with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry, met them in battle.
Mǎizhù defeated them,
and the Xìa people fled via Jiālú Chuān,
beheading a total of eight hundred heads.
Soon after,
they attacked and occupied the fort again.
Qìngshānnú led his troops to battle,
beheading five thousand heads,
and retaking the fort.
An edict bestowed upon Qìngshānnú a gold belt,
and the officers and soldiers were rewarded according to their merits.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
he defeated the Xìa army at Yòuzhōu,
beheading over a thousand men,
and then besieged Shénduī Fǔ.
Qìngshānnú attacked it from four sides.
As the soldiers were scaling the battlements,
reinforcements arrived in great numbers,
and he attacked and drove them away again.
In the fourth year of Zhèngdà,
Lǐ Quán occupied Chǔzhōu.
An edict appointed Qìngshānnú as Military Commissioner,
to jointly command with Marshal Wányán Ékě, to defend Xūyí,
and also ordered them to hold the city and not sally forth to battle.
Soon after,
Lǐ Quán's army arrived at the border of Xūyí.
The two marshals met the enemy and were greatly defeated.
Over ten thousand men died,
and much equipment and provisions were abandoned.
At that time, the army had no provisions,
and transport was interrupted.
The people were exhausted from being pressed into service,
and lamentations filled the roads.
The various chancellors were unwilling to speak plainly.
Pàn Guān Báihuá of the Púmì Yuàn presented a memorial requesting their execution to appease the world,
but it was not granted.
He was demoted to Military Governor of Dìngguó Army,
and then deprived of one official rank for accepting bribes.
In the first month of the eighth year,
Fèngxiáng was broken.
The two traveling departments moved the residents of Jīngzhào to Hénán.
Qìngshānnú was ordered to defend it with the traveling department.
At that time, the Jīngzhào Traveling Department had only eight hundred sick soldiers and two hundred emaciated horses.
Chénglì feared he could not defend it
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to return.
Each memorial
was accompanied by a letter to his elder brother Báishā,
asking him to intercede.
The court did not permit it.
In the tenth month,
Qìngshānnú abandoned Jīngzhào and returned to court,
leaving Gǒu Qí, who was concurrently Administrator of Gānzhōu Military and Civil Affairs and Commander of Bǎoyì Army, to defend it.
When Qìngshānnú reached Wénxiāng,
Aizōng sent the palace attendant Péimǎn Qījīn to give him instructions concerning Huánglíng Gāng,
and did not allow him an audience.
Soon after,
he replaced Túdān Wùdiǎn as the acting head of the traveling department in Xúzhōu.
In the first month of the ninth year,
he led troops from Xúzhōu to aid the capital.
He selected fifteen thousand elite soldiers,
and with Xúzhōu commander Wánpín Wùlùn commanding them,
they were about to march to Guīdé.
Hóu Jìn, Dù Zhèng, Zhāng Xīng, and others, leaders of the Yìshèng Army, led their three thousand men to surrender to the main army.
Qìngshānnú stayed in Suīzhōu for three days, not daring to advance.
Hearing that the main army was approaching,
fearing that the city could not be defended,
he retreated to secure Guīdé.
In the second month,
while on the march at Yángyì Diàn,
they encountered the Xiǎonǎi [⿰木受] army,
and subsequently scattered.
Wùlùn died in battle.
Qìngshānnú's horse stumbled, and he was captured.
Only Marshal Guō Ēn and Commandant Wūlíndá Ādū led over three hundred men and fled to Guīdé.
The main army put Qìngshānnú on a single horse
and forced him to march.
On the way, he saw Marshal Shǐ from Zhēndìng.
Chénglì asked:
"Who are you?"
Marshal Shǐ said:
"I am Shǐ Wànhù of the Five Routes of Zhēndìng."
Chénglì asked:
"Is that Tiānzé?"
He replied:
"Yes."
He said:
"Our country is already ruined and broken;
may you take the lives of the people into consideration."
When he saw Grand Marshal Tèmù [⿰木受],
he was tempted to invite him to attack the capital,
but he did not comply.
He also remained stubborn and unyielding.
His attendants used a knife to hack his foot, breaking it,
but he still did not surrender,
so they killed him.
Commentators believed that although Chénglì had suffered repeated defeats and could not be excused from his military duties,
and thus deserved further blame for his death,
his ability to die for his country
was also worthy of praise.
Initially,
Zhāng Wénshòu, the Prefect of Suīzhōu, hearing that the main army was approaching,
moved residents from neighboring counties into the city
and gathered a large amount of fodder and grain.
However, he had no intention of holding out firmly,
and day and night plotted to escape for his own convenience.
Soon after,
hearing that Chénglì was coming to aid,
he immediately entrusted the affairs of the prefecture to his subordinates,
pretending to go and assist the Xúzhōu troops.
At night, he opened the gate and took his family, fleeing to Guīdé.
Qìngshānnú made him the Bureau Director of the Traveling Department.
He died at Yángyì.
Soon the main army besieged Suīzhōu,
and because it had no commander,
it was severely devastated.
Wùlùn was
the nephew of Chancellor Sàibù.
During the Yuánguāng period, all marshals were usually appointed as commanders,
but Wùlùn alone was not dismissed due to being the chancellor's relative.
The Jīn dynasty guarded against close relatives but employed distant ones,
thus Báishā, Chénglì, Wùlùn and their like were all relied upon as trusted confidants.
The encomium says: Guānníu's conduct was always fickle,
now south, now north,
like a dragon breaking apart.
Aizōng, once relying on him as a trusted confidant,
was ultimately controlled by him.
How was the situation at Zhàobì different from being imprisoned?
His affair is largely similar to, but slightly different from, that of Liángwǔ and Hóujǐng.
Túdān Wùdiǎn and Qìngshānnú were both greedy as generals,
and it was fitting that they suffered repeated defeats.
Nǚlǔhuān did not commit any great wrong,
yet he died at the hands of Guānníu.
Aizōng still denounced his crime.
How unjust!
Collation notes
Biographies, Volume 55: Túshàn Yìdū, Zhāngē Jīngshān (with Liú Jūn appended), Wáng Bīn (with Wáng Jìn and others appended), Guó Yòng'ān, Shí Qīng
Túshàn Yìdū,
his career details are unknown.
He had successively served as the Jīnglǐng of Yán'ān.
In the first month of the ninth year of Zhèngdà,
he served as Xíngshěngshì in Xúzhōu.
At that time, Qìngshānnú withdrew the defenses of the east to provide reinforcements.
Before reaching Suīzhōu,
Hóu Jìn, Dù Zhèng, and Zhāng Xīng, general leaders of the Yìshèng Army of Xú and Pī, led their forces to surrender to the grand army at Yǒngzhōu.
On Xīnchǒu,
the grand army guarded Zhāngpén Dù in Xú.
Yìdū had only been in office for three days.
Fearing that his forces were too few to defend,
he immediately ordered Yílài Chángshòu to lead a thousand armored soldiers to meet the grand army.
Chángshòu's army was undisciplined,
and the grand army enveloped them.
The entire army was annihilated,
and Xú was in grave danger.
Yìdū registered the people of the prefecture and the soldiers from the grain transport rafts, totaling ten thousand men.
On Yǐsì,
the grand army advanced to the city,
burned the South Gate, and then left.
Hóu Jìn, having surrendered to the north,
was immediately appointed Xíngshěng of Jīngdōng.
Jìn then requested a thousand men to come and attack.
Before dawn on Gēngshēn in the second month,
the grand army breached the southern wall and ascended.
The defenders all scattered and fled,
and a great shout arose in the city:
"The grand army has entered the South Gate!"
Yìdū, hearing this, had no time to don his armor.
He led three hundred soldiers of the prefecture office who were on night duty,
proceeded south from Huánglóu,
and fought fiercely to repel the enemy.
After the chaos settled,
promotions and rewards were distributed according to merit.
From then on,
the army's morale slightly revived.
They recaptured Zhāngpén Dù,
took Xiāoxiàn,
defeated Báitǎ,
fought at Tǔshān,
and rescued five thousand captured elderly and children, returning them to Xú.
Soon after,
Hóu Jìn fled and stationed himself at Língbì.
Dù Zhèng and Zhāng Xīng also feared being harmed by the north,
and, in distress, returned on their own.
Yìdū comforted and accepted them.
Xīng remained in Xú,
while Dù Zhèng returned to Pīzhōu.
Yìdū's disposition was benevolent and generous,
and he held to the greater good.
His two sons and two nephews were military generals,
and they often encroached upon the military and civilians.
Wáng Yòu, a man from Qīngzhōu, was the general leader of the raft soldiers,
commanding seventeen hundred men.
Yìdū always relied on him,
and even if he made mistakes, he would not blame him.
Because of this, Yòu also became arrogant and unruly.
Together with Zhāng Zuò from Héjiān, Lǐ Rùn, the magistrate of Xiàyì, Fēng Xiān, the Dūtǒng of Yìshèng, Chéng Jìnzhōng, the nominally appointed Cǐshǐ of Yǒngzhōu, and others,
they took advantage of the military administration's laxity
and the city's emptiness.
On the night of Dīngsì in the sixth month, they set fire to the hay storage and started a rebellion.
At that time, Zhāng Xīng was ill in bed.
Yòu feared the plot would fail,
so he roused Xīng to join him.
Yìdū suspected that all his subordinates had rebelled.
He took his wife and children, rappelled down the city wall, and escaped,
joining Zòngcóngyí Zhòngsēngnú's army and Liú Ānguó's army from the eastern front.
Zhāng Xīng proclaimed Yòu as the Dū Yuánshuài.
Then, fearing Yòu would plot against him,
he executed Yòu,
and also killed Zhāng Zuò.
Consequently, they plundered the city greatly.
On Rénxū,
Guó Yòng'ān, serving as Xíng Shāndōng Lù Shàngshūshěng Shì, led his troops to Xú.
Zhāng Xīng led his armored soldiers to meet him.
Yòng'ān entered with light cavalry,
arrested Xīng and more than ten of his associates,
and executed them in the marketplace.
Then, he appointed Fēng Xiān as Yuánshuài,
concurrently Jiédùshǐ,
to govern Xúzhōu.
Yìdū was in distress with nowhere to go,
so he fled to Sùzhōu.
The Jiédùshǐ Hésīliè Āhǔ, seeing that Yìdū had been driven out by others, did not accept him,
so Yìdū and his generals stationed themselves south of the city.
At that time, some of Sùzhōu's garrison soldiers had deserted and returned.
Āhǔ, thinking they were returning rebels, also did not accept them.
Gāo Lágē, a thousand-commander of the city's garrison,
colluded with the petty official Guō Zhòng'ān,
plotting to coordinate with Xúzhōu generals and soldiers from within to seize Sùzhōu,
and then surrender to Yáng Miàozhēn.
At midnight on Jiǎxū,
they opened the city gate and admitted Wáng Déquán, the general leader of Xúzhōu, and his wife's younger brother, Gāo Yuángē's army.
Liú Ānguó soon also entered the city,
captured Āhǔ and his son, and killed them.
The people of the prefecture requested Yìdū to take charge of the commandery affairs.
Yìdū refused, saying:
"I am an old servant of the state,
and have been a general for a long time.
Due to my unworldly and easygoing nature, I was unable to fully defend,
and thus lost a strategic stronghold.
Now that the great cause is lost,
I barely have time to escape punishment.
How could I change my hairstyle and clothes, seize another's city, and surrender to an external power?"
That very day,
he led his officials and departed.
Upon reaching the east of Gǔshú,
he encountered the grand army
and died unyielding.
After Xúzhōu returned to Hǎizhōu,
Wùlíntǎ Mǒu, the commander of Pīzhōu, also ceded his seal to Dù Zhèng,
and then sent his submission to Yòng'ān.
Soon after,
Wáng Déquán and Liú Ānguó of Sùzhōu also sent their submission to Hǎizhōu.
Only Yìdū did not change his hairstyle and clothes,
even to his death.
Zhāngē Jīngshān,
his origin is unknown.
During the Zhèngdà era,
he successively served as Jiédùshǐ of Bózhōu.
On Jǐchǒu in the first month of the ninth year,
cavalry scouts traveled from Dèng to Bó,
raided Lùyì,
and encamped fifty *lǐ* northwest of Wèizhēn.
Gāo Ángxiāo, the magistrate of Lùyì, knowing that Tàikāng had already surrendered,
immediately rushed to Bó that night.
Passing through Wèizhēn,
he called out to the magistrate Chǔ Héng, inviting him to travel together.
Chǔ Héng, knowing the situation was untenable,
immediately clearly instructed the county people of his intention to evacuate,
and then fled to Bó together.
On Dīngwèi,
both counties surrendered.
On that day,
the army arrived at the city walls of Bózhōu.
The prefecture only had four hundred soldiers from Shànzhōu,
known as
"Zhèn'ān Army."
Tíkòng Yáng Chūn, Xíng Mǒu, and Dūtǒng Dài Xīng had been stationed there for six years.
Jīngshān registered all able-bodied men in the city as soldiers,
and repaired the defenses,
but the grand army did not have time to attack.
In the fourth month,
they moved north with the surrendered people.
The city gates were closed,
and this was not known.
In the fifth month,
they released the displaced people to harvest wheat.
The elderly and children were allowed to leave,
but the able-bodied men were all retained.
The people often refused to stay and fled,
and within a few days,
the city became empty.
Jīngshān sent generals to their respective areas to recruit,
but even the generals did not return.
The "Zhèn'ān"
soldiers were all remnants of the Hóng'ǎo bandits.
They returned only when their strength was exhausted.
They were deceitful and fickle,
and the imperial court always treated them as bandits.
Jīngshān used the displaced people as soldiers,
presumably to guard against them.
When he summoned external troops, they did not arrive,
so he requested assistance from Guīdé,
and obtained over a hundred armored cavalry,
commanded by two general leaders.
Upon their arrival,
the "Zhèn'ān"
soldiers suspected a plot against them.
So, taking advantage of the newly arrived generals and soldiers being unprepared,
that night,
they launched a surprise attack and massacred almost all of them.
Jīngshān fled to Wèizhēn.
Chǔ Héng provided him with a horse and departed.
The prominent and wealthy families in the prefecture were all plundered.
Liú Jiān
initially served in the imperial army, defending Chéngfù.
When Bózhōu was recovered,
he was captured
and imprisoned.
Yáng Chūn, contemplating surrendering to the North,
released him
and appointed him Xuānchāi.
On the Yǐsì day,
General Shí of the imperial army entered the prefecture.
The prefecture was renamed Shùntiānfǔ,
and Yáng Chūn was made Zǒngguǎn,
Dài Xìng as Tóngzhī.
During Liú Shùnzhì's
tenure, a thousand Dǎngxiàng soldiers were stationed there.
All dependent counties submitted,
except for Chéngfù Magistrate Lǐ Yòngyí, who refused to surrender.
His wife and children were in Bó,
and Yáng Chūn held them as leverage,
but Lǐ Yòngyí ultimately did not yield and died.
After Yáng Chūn occupied the prefecture,
he sat with Liú Jiān on a tower
and summoned Deputy Tíkòng Xíng Mǒu.
Xíng was upright and adhered to principles,
and the generals and soldiers greatly feared him.
At that time, he was ill in bed.
Hearing of Yáng Chūn's rebellion,
he wept uncontrollably.
Yáng Chūn sent people to carry him there.
Xíng pointed at Yáng Chūn and cursed him loudly.
Yáng Chūn was ashamed and speechless.
Yáng Chūn wanted to kill the Jīngshān family.
Xíng strongly advised against it
and ordered that they be given travel expenses and sent out of the city.
Xíng soon died of his illness.
In the fourth month of summer in the second year,
Tèmùshòu of the Northern Province attacked Guīdé.
Yáng Chūn sent Dài Xìng with elite troops,
while he alone guarded the city with exhausted and weak soldiers.
Wáng Bīn, a local of the prefecture, then restored order.
Yáng Chūn crossed the river and fled north.
Soon after,
Cuī Qījīn rebelled,
killing Wáng Bīn.
The imperial court had no choice
but to appoint Qījīn as Jiédùshǐ,
and with his troops and weapons, he entered Cài.
In the eighth month,
Liú Shùn attacked Bózhōu,
breaching it.
Qījīn was killed by the Chéngfù Magistrate.
Not long after,
the Shānzhōu army, because the people of the prefecture had killed their family members,
summoned the imperial army to attack.
They could not capture it,
and killed the people of the dependent counties before leaving.
After crossing the river,
knowing that the people of Bó did not suspect them,
they returned to attack.
The prefecture was eventually breached by Yáng Chūn.
In the sixth month of that year,
the Sòng people came to attack.
Yáng Chūn surrendered,
and Liú Jiān fled north.
Liú Jūn, a native of Línglǜ,
was then the Guānchá Pànguān of Bózhōu.
After Yáng Chūn drove out Jīngshān
and made overtures to the imperial army,
he coerced Liú Jūn into surrendering with him.
Liú Jūn pretended to agree,
returned home to fetch and put on his court attire,
and looking at his wife and children, said:
"I started my career with clerical work,
and was greatly favored by the emperor's knowledge,
first joining the ranks of the court,
and then assisting a great frontier command.
To die now is quite enough.
My head is already thus.
Even if I were to have ten more years of life,
how could I face the late emperor underground?"
He then took poison and died.
Wáng Bīn, courtesy name Déqīng,
was a native of Bózhōu.
He passed the civil service examination in the second year of Zhēnyòu.
Outwardly, he appeared broad-minded,
but he had deep strategic plans.
Initially, he was appointed Lánlíng Zhǔbù,
then promoted to Hóngxiàn Magistrate.
Soon after, he entered the central government as Shàngshūshěng Língshǐ,
but was dismissed due to an incident and returned to his hometown.
In the first month of the first year of Tiānxīng,
a military mutiny occurred in Bózhōu.
Jiédùshǐ Niángē Jīngshān fled,
and Yáng Chūn surrendered the prefecture.
Soon after,
he guarded it himself with his weakened troops.
Wáng Bīn, along with former Qiáoxiàn Lieutenant Wáng Jìn, Wèi Jiéhēng, and Lǚ Jūn, rallied the city's military and civilians to recover their prefecture.
Yáng Chūn then fled.
Wèi Jiéhēng was sent to Guīdé to report the news.
Emperor Āizōng praised them,
appointing Wáng Jìn as Jiédùshǐ,
Wáng Bīn as Tóngzhī Jiédùshǐ,
Wèi Jiéhēng as Jiédù Fùshǐ,
and Lǚ Jūn as Guānchá Pànguān.
Yáng Chūn returned with troops to attack,
but after more than a month, he could not capture it.
He then crossed the river and went north.
In the sixth month,
Emperor Āizōng moved to Cài.
Wáng Bīn received him at Gāo'ān, north of the prefecture.
The emperor conversed with him and was greatly pleased,
regretting that he had employed him late.
He was promoted to Xíngbù Shàngshū and hereditary Móukè.
When the emperor first arrived at Bó,
Wáng Bīn and others were just conscripting male commoners to carry iron armor into Cài,
and accounting for the rations of loyal and filial military families.
Therefore, Cānzhī Zhèngshì Zhāng Tiāngāng was left to oversee it,
and meritorious generals and soldiers were transferred.
At that time, Bó's grain reserves were not ample,
and Wáng Bīn and others were often parsimonious,
which caused the soldiers to harbor resentment.
And during the task of transporting armor,
they again were unwilling to proceed.
It happened that Zhāng Tiāngāng and Wáng Bīn and others were on a tower, ranking the merits of those who had performed deeds.
Cuī Fùgē and Wáng Liùshí and others of the Zhenfang Army donned armor, rioted, and ascended the tower.
Zhāng Tiāngāng asked:
"If you intend to kill me,
allow me to gaze towards the palace and bid farewell."
The rebels said:
"This does not concern you, Xiànggōng."
They then dragged Wáng Bīn and Lǚ Jūn to the marketplace.
Lǚ Jūn walked while kneeling,
tears flowing down.
Wáng Bīn, however, was defiant and fearless,
crying out loudly:
"It's nothing more than killing me.
Just kill me,
just kill me!"
They then killed them both.
Jiédù Fùshǐ Wèi Jiéhēng, Jiédù Pànguān Sūn Liáng, and Guānchá Fùshǐ Sūn Jiǔzhù were all killed.
A few days later,
Jiédùshǐ Wáng Jìn was killed.
Wáng Jìn had once responded to Jīngshān's recruitment,
entering Biànjīng through a secret path to present a memorial.
He refused the reward given to him.
He also distributed all his family's possessions to aid the poor,
spurring himself with the thought of death.
Upon arriving in Biàn,
he was promoted to Jiédù Pànguān of his home prefecture for his efforts,
and was given white gold,
which he also refused.
He was highly praised at the time.
There was a Lǐ Xǐzhù,
originally a Xuānchāi under the monks of Sùzhōu.
In the fourth month of the second year of Tiānxīng,
he delivered grain to Guīdé.
As he was about to return,
he heard that Wáng Jìn of Bózhōu had restored order.
An imperial decree appointed Lǐ Xǐzhù as Zhènwǔ Dūwèi,
leading three thousand troops to provide support.
At this time,
Tàichì besieged Bó with a hundred thousand infantry and cavalry.
Lǐ Xǐzhù, deeming his forces unequal,
entered the city alone with three men via a secret path.
Wáng Jìn was then discussing moving to Lín, the Left Army's base.
Lǐ Xǐzhù disagreed.
Wáng Jìn then handed over his troops to Lǐ Xǐzhù.
The imperial army attacked for eight days but could not capture it.
On the Rénzǐ day of the fifth month,
the army retreated.
On the Jǐwèi day,
Guānnú and Ālǐhétí arrived in Bó with a hundred loyal and filial troops.
They discussed with the generals whether to move.
They considered it inadvisable,
suggesting that the baggage train should be left in Cài,
and chosen troops escort them into Shèngduǒ to join the Wǔxiān Army,
then entering Guānzhōng.
The strategic advantages of Guānzhōng could be relied upon,
and there were also Guō Xiāpo's troops in the west that could be relied upon.
On the Jiǎzǐ day of the fifth month,
Guānnú was summoned back to Guīdé.
He did not go.
Summoned again, he left half of his army in Bó before departing.
In the sixth month, on the *rénchén* day,
the imperial carriage traveled by boat to Bó.
Wáng Jìn reported,
"Your servant's original profession was military,
I do not understand the art of governance.
If Lǐ Xǐzhù accompanies Your Majesty to Cài,
then Bó will not be defended.
I beg to remain here to govern this prefecture."
An imperial edict appointed Xǐzhù as the *Jié dù shǐ* of the Jíqìng Army,
with full authority to act as he saw fit,
advancing him to a commanding position.
In the seventh month,
Jìn died.
Xǐzhù had previously gone to Chéngfù to oversee the transport of grain,
and upon hearing of the unrest, he dared not enter Bó,
later defecting to Sòng.
A commentary states: During the chaos of the late Jīn,
soldiers wished to replace their lower-ranking officers,
and lower-ranking officers wished to replace their commanders,
then they would rise en masse and overthrow them,
without any scruples.
Yìdū and Jīngshān were both loyal and upright men,
and Bīn and Jìn were particularly capable and strategic,
yet none of them escaped disaster,
what a pity!
Guó Yòng’ān's earlier name was Ānyòng,
his original name was Yǎo'ér,
a native of Zībó.
He was a remnant of the Red Turban bandits Yáng Ān'ér and Lǐ Quán.
He once submitted to the Great Yuán,
serving as *Dū yuánshuài* and acting *shàngshūshěng shì* for the Shāndōng Circuit.
In the sixth month of Tiānxīng First Year (1232),
Wáng Yòu, *Zǒnglǐng* of the Xúzhōu *sǎobīng*, Fēng Xiān, *Dūtǒng* of the Yìshèng Army, and Zhāng Xīng, *Zǒnglǐng*, among others, rebelled by burning the straw fields at night,
expelling *Yuánshuài* Túndān Yìdū.
Ānyòng led troops into Xúzhōu,
arrested Zhāng Xīng and over ten of his associates and beheaded them,
appointing Fēng Xiān as *Yuánshuài* and *Jiédùshǐ*,
to govern Xúzhōu.
Gāo Lágē, a *Qiānhù* of the Sùzhōu garrison army, and Liú Ānguó, *Zǒngshuài* of the eastern front, conspired with Wáng Déquán, *Zǒngshuài* of Xúzhōu,
killed the Sùzhōu commander Gēshíliè Āhǔ,
and submitted his prefecture to Hǎizhōu.
Wùlíndá Mǒu, *Cóngyí* of Pīzhōu, also yielded the prefecture to Dù Zhèng,
and sent *fā* to Hǎizhōu.
Soon after,
all submitted to Ānyòng.
The northern general Āzhúlǔ heard that Ānyòng occupied Xúzhōu, Sùzhōu, and Pīzhōu,
and was furious, saying:
"These three prefectures should be taken by my attack;
who is Ānyòng,
that he dares to accept their surrender?"
He dispatched Xìn'ān and Zhāng Jìn, among others, to lead troops into Xúzhōu,
intending to seize Ānyòng
and take his army.
Ānyòng was afraid,
and conspired with Déquán to
ambush and kill Zhāng Jìn and Tián Fú, *Yuánshuài* of Hǎizhōu, and several hundred others,
severed ties with Yáng Miàozhēn,
and then returned to Pīzhōu.
Then the generals of Shāndōng and the commanders of Xúzhōu, Sùzhōu, and Pīzhōu met,
slaughtered a horse and swore an oath,
vowing to return allegiance to the Jīn court.
After the alliance,
all the generals dispersed,
and Ānyòng had nowhere to go,
so he, along with Déquán and Ānguó, entrusted themselves to Cóngyí Zhòngsēngnú to communicate with the imperial court.
Zhòngsēngnú sent someone to memorialize:
"Ānyòng has brought several prefectures back to allegiance,
his merit is very great.
Moreover, his military strength is formidable,
and his talent and strategy are commendable.
If the state truly wishes to rely on him,
nothing less than the highest rank and substantial power will suffice to strengthen his loyalty to the state."
There was no reply.
Ānyòng led an army of ten thousand men to attack Hǎizhōu,
but before arriving,
his troops gradually dispersed.
Ānguó then advised Ānyòng to sincerely return to the state,
and Ānyòng also realized that his repeated changes of allegiance were a miscalculation,
and the situation was beyond remedy,
so he resumed the Jīn court's attire.
Miàozhēn was enraged by his betrayal,
and also feared being targeted,
so she slaughtered Ānyòng's entire family and fled to Yìdū.
Ānyòng then selected soldiers and divided his generals,
determined to capture Miàozhēn,
and from then on, there was no peace along the Huái River and the sea.
Not long after,
the imperial court sent Yīn Shìyīng, *Zhícháng* of the *Jìnsì Jú*, and Gāo Tiānyòu, *Dūshì*, with an imperial edict to Pīzhōu,
appointing Ānyòng as *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*, *Píngzhāng Zhèngshì*, concurrent *Dū Yuánshuài*, and acting *shàngshūshěng shì* for the Jīngdōng and Shāndōng Circuits,
specially enfeoffing him as Yǎn Wáng,
bestowing the title
"Heroic and Loyal Minister Who Suppresses Rebellion and Preserves Integrity,"
granted the surname Wányán,
registered him in the imperial clan,
changed his name to Yòng'ān,

bestowed a gold-plated silver seal, a gold knobbed seal, a gold tiger tally, an imperial declaration for a hereditary *qiānhù*, an imperial decree template, a tablet template, an imperial painting, a blank amnesty document for Héshuò and Shāndōng,
with full authority to act as he saw fit,
and also entrusted the Queen of Péng Wáng with the task of recruiting Miàozhēn through Yòng'ān.
When Yòng'ān first heard of the envoy's arrival,
he hesitated and was undecided,
sending *Zǒnglǐng* Yáng Mào to welcome the envoys,
detaining them in the prefectural office,
and asking why they had come.
Shìyīng replied with matters of enfeoffment,
which pleased him somewhat.
The generals, such as Wáng and Dù, all did not wish to publicize this,
and wanted to kill the envoys.
The next day,
Yòng'ān came out to see the envoys,
bowing and saluting as equals,
and after sitting down,
he said to Shìyīng:
"I previously followed the large army to attack Biàn,
and once discussed with Hóu Zhì at the Kāiyáng Gate about an inside-outside pincer attack.
At that time, many in the large army were dying of illness,
and seventeen leaders were all in the capital.
If my plan to send out troops had been followed,
the restoration would have happened long ago.
Yet there was not a single person at court who dared to make a decision.
What good is regret today?"
After saying this, he rose.
Then he selected people to examine all the items bestowed by the imperial court,
and his countenance brightened with joy.
He then privately discussed with the envoys,
wishing not to receive them with court rituals,
but Shìyīng and others disagreed,
so a banquet was set up, and the items were presented and received with due ceremony.
He sent Cháng Jǐn, *Zhǔshì*, and others to accompany the envoys to present a memorial of thanks.

The Emperor again sent Shìyīng and Tiānyòu to bestow an iron certificate, six tiger tallies, one dragon-patterned robe, one jade fish belt, two bows and arrows, imperial declarations for the enfeoffment of his parents and wife,
and ten each of princely declarations, hereditary declarations, great trust tablets, and jade rabbit-falcon belts,
allowing him to bestow them upon his allies who were eligible.
When the envoys arrived at Pīzhōu,
Yòng'ān welcomed and received them with ceremony,
and then began to entertain the idea of offering aid.
When he heard that the Emperor was moving to Càizhōu,
he sent someone with a wax-sealed letter stating six reasons why moving to Cài was not advisable,
the main points being:
"Guīdé is surrounded by water,
making it difficult to attack, while Cài has no such natural defense; this is one.
Although Guīdé is short of provisions,
fish and water chestnuts can be obtained for sustenance, whereas if Cài is besieged,
food supplies will be limited; this is two.
The reason the great army left Guīdé
was not out of fear of us, but to let them out and then pursue them,
abandoning the difficult and attacking the easy; this is three.
Cài is not a hundred *lǐ* from the Sòng territory,
should enemy troops and provisions be supplied by them,
the disaster would be irremediable; this is four.
If Guīdé cannot be held,
one can still leave by waterway to the east, but if Cài cannot be defended,
where will one go? This is five.
It is currently the hot, rainy season,
with a thousand *lǐ* of muddy mire,
and Your Majesty's robust physique
is not suited for riding,
should you encounter the enemy in a rush,
it is not something your humble servants dare to speak of; this is six.
Nevertheless,
if Your Majesty insists on leaving Guīdé,
it would be best to temporarily reside in Shāndōng.
Shāndōng is the richest and most prosperous region under heaven,
and your servant controls a portion of its territory,
connecting Yí and Hǎi to the east,
Xú and Pī to the west,
controlling Xū and Chǔ to the south,
and commanding Zī and Qí to the north.
If the imperial carriage were to briefly halt there,
your servant, relying on your divine prestige,
could stabilize the Héshuò region with but a declaration.
May Your Majesty thoroughly consider this."
The Emperor showed his words to the Grand Councilors.
The Grand Councilors memorialized that Yòng'ān was treacherous
and had no intention of assisting,
and that this proposal must have been advised by Zhāng Jiè, *Cānyì*, and others.
Since the relocation to Cài had already occurred,
the deliberation was dropped.
Initially,
Shìyīng and others passed through Xúzhōu.
Wáng Déquán and Liú Ānguó persuaded them, saying:
"How can the imperial court's gracious decrees be issued arbitrarily by Yòng'ān?
The Jùnwáng Xuān and the two of us are the most deserving ones.
We beg you to keep them here."
Shìyīng then kept two each of Jùnwáng Xuān, Shìxí Xuān, and Yùdài.
From this, a rift developed with Yòng'ān.
Fearing that they would be plotted against,
they all refused to obey his command.
The ten Jùnwáng were
Lǐ Míngdé, Fēng Xiān, Zhāng Yǔ, Zhāng Yǒu, Zhuó Yì, Kāng Cóng, Dù Zhèng, Wú Wāitóu, Wáng Déquán, and Liú Ānguó.
Yòng'ān was determined to take Shāndōng,
repeatedly summoning troops from Xúzhōu and Sùzhōu,
but only using "serving the emperor" as a pretext.
The two commanders did not respond.
Yòng'ān was furious,
ordering Dù Zhèng and others to lead three thousand soldiers,
under the guise of procuring provisions,
to raid Xúzhōu and Sùzhōu.
Upon entering the city,
Déqúan became aware of it
and detained Dù Zhèng and Fēng Xiān, not letting them leave.
Yòng'ān grew even more enraged,
believing that Déqúan and Ānguó must be plotting something.
He then arrested Wú Mǒu, the commander of Táoyuán, and eight or nine others, imprisoning and interrogating them.
The two commanders sent Wēn Tèhǎn Zhāng Gē to report to Yòng'ān that Dù Zhèng and Fēng Xiān intended to raid and seize Xúzhōu,
but he did not listen.
He drove Wú Shuài, Zhāng Gē, and nine others away and executed them all.
Zhāng Gē, about to die, cried out loudly:
"Guó Yǎ'ér!
You have no inch of merit,
yet you received a great enfeoffment and peerage from the state.
How have I wronged you
that you follow Dù Zhèng and others in rebellion,
and moreover kill innocent people?
Though I die today,
I will argue with you in the underworld!"
At that time, the court sent Zāng Guóchāng with a secret edict to summon troops from the east.
Therefore, Yòng'ān, feigning an imperial order, declared that he was coming to aid.
He dispatched a summons appointing Liú Ānguó as vanguard
and personally led three thousand soldiers to station outside Xúzhōu city, summoning Déqúan.
Déqúan remained suspicious of being plotted against
and did not come out.
He imprisoned Fēng Xiān
and killed him,
then sent Dù Zhèng out of the city.
After Ānguó arrived at Sùzhōu,
Yòng'ān again recalled Ānguó.
Ānguó refused to comply
and went to aid with the衆僧奴 (zhòng sēngnú) alone.
When they reached Línhuàn Lóngshān Temple,
Yòng'ān sent someone to ambush and kill him.
He then attacked Xúzhōu,
but failed to take it after more than three months.
He retreated to Liánshuǐ.
Thereupon,
because Shìyīng believed Yòng'ān would never come to aid,
he returned to court.
Upon reaching west of Sùzhōu, he encountered a large army,
and died rather than surrender.
When the matter was reported,
he was posthumously granted the title of Rúzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
Later,
Yòng'ān's army lacked provisions,
and he begged for grain from the Sòng.
The Sòng outwardly agreed,
and he immediately changed to Sòng attire and headdress,
while secretly maintaining close relations with the imperial envoy.
Soon, food became even scarcer,
and many soldiers and civilians deserted.
He then ordered Xiāo Jūn to use severe punishments to prevent desertions,
causing blood to flow in the streets.
Zhālà, the Wànhù of Dōngpíng in Dà Yuán, led troops to Liánshuǐ,
and he surrendered.
After Zhālà crossed the river
and headed for Càizhōu,
Yòng'ān, using a trick, returned to Liánshuǐ
and rebelled again, returning to the Sòng.
He received the titles of Zhèdōng Zǒngguǎn and Zhōngzhōu Tuánliànshǐ,
subordinate to Huáikùn.
In the first month of Jiǎwǔ (1234 AD),
hearing that a large army was besieging Pèi,
Yòng'ān went to relieve it,
but was defeated and fled to Xúzhōu.
At that time, the army moved to attack Xúzhōu.
Yòng'ān threw himself into the water and died.
His body was sought and found,
then his face was tied to a horse's tail
and his body was dismembered and completely consumed by the troops of Tián Fú, his enemy.
Yòng'ān was short and small in stature, without a beard.
He enjoyed associating with frivolous people,
and would play polo daily in the market.
He would look around and preen himself,
lacking the proper bearing of a general.
Jiè, courtesy name Jièfǔ,
was a native of Píngzhōu.
In the first year of Zhèngdà, he ranked first in the Jīngyì Jinshì examination.
At that time, he served as Yòng'ān's Cānyì.
Initially,
Tiānyòu and others left Biàn,
traveling incognito.
They passed through the Northern Army encampments
and only found an office of the Righteous Army Recruitment and Pacification Commissioner in Tōngxǔ Cuīqiáo,
two hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
Upon reaching Chénzhōu,
the Fángyùshǐ Niángé Núshēn had just established the state affairs.
They stayed for two days,
then reached Xiàngchéng.
The Xiànlìng Zhū Zhēn had established the county affairs
and had one thousand two hundred soldiers.
Upon reaching Tàihé County,
the Xiànlìng Wáng Yì had already established the county for five months.
In the eighth month,
they arrived at Sùzhōu.
The衆僧奴 (zhòng sēngnú) received the report
and knew that the imperial court had appointed them as Qúansùzhōu Jiédùshǐ and concurrently Yuánshuài Zuǒdūdjiān.
They prepared a colorful palanquin and honor guard and went out five *lǐ* from the city to welcome them.
At that time, the east had not heard any news from the imperial court for eight months.
Officials and common people, seeing the envoy arrive,
both bowed and wept.
There was a certain Zhāng Xiǎn, a chivalrous and spirited man who understood righteousness.
He immediately said to Tiānyòu:
"The east has not heard any news from the imperial court for several months.
Now that we see the envoy,
all the people are deeply moved.
If we do not comfort them with an imperial edict,
I fear we will lose the hearts of the eastern people.
I wish to falsely claim an imperial decree to make an announcement and pacify them.
What do you think?"
Tiānyòu, being a scholar who adhered to rules,
did not dare to agree.
He merely gathered the prefectural people and comforted them with the prime minister's order,
and the prefectural people wept bitterly again.
The next day,
they went to Xúzhōu.
At that time, Qīng,
a native of Téngyáng,
initially served as a "Red Turban" bandit with his uncle Quán.
After Yáng Ān'ér and Liú Èrzǔ were defeated,
they came to surrender under amnesty
and were assigned to the army.
In the early Xīngdìng period,
Qīng was the Wànhù of the Yìjūn of Jìzhōu.
At this time,
his uncle Quán was the Jīnglìguān of the Xíng Pīmìyuàn.
In the winter of the second year of Xīngdìng,
Quán rode an express post through Dōngpíng.
Qīng came to see him
and informed Quán that he was about to rebel and join the Sòng.
Quán kept it a secret.
Soon after,
Qīng led his troops to join the Sòng.
The Sòng people placed him in Huáinán,
stationed at Guīshān,
with tens of thousands of troops.
In the fourth year of Xīngdìng,
Hélìliè Yáwūtǎ, acting Grand Marshal of Sìzhōu, sent someone to recruit him.
Qīng responded with a letter.
The letter said:
“I, Qīng, was originally a good commoner of Téngyáng,
but encountered times of chaos and separation.
I led my elderly and young to take refuge in the wilderness.
The officials did not understand my heart,
and labeled me a rebel,
leaving me nowhere to escape death,
so I hid in Huáihǎi.
To leave one's relatives and old friends, and abandon one's hometown,
how could this be something a person willingly enjoys?
Although I live precariously and am fed in another country,
the thought of returning to my native land has never left me for a single day.
If the imperial court pardons my crimes,
I beg for the loan of Pīzhōu to settle my elderly and young.
I will then attack and capture Xūyí,
pacify all of Huáinán,
to atone for my past mistakes.”
Yáwūtǎ wrote back, saying:
“You and your group were originally innocent.
If you can truly perform meritorious service for the state,
and bring your entire army to surrender,
then you are our people.
Pīzhōu is our city,
what is wrong with our people living in it?
The Book of Changes says: ‘The gentleman acts when he sees the opportune moment,
not waiting until the end of the day.’
You should act quickly.
To return alive to your parents’ land,
enjoy wealth and honor your whole life,
and leave a good name for future generations,
compared to being restrained in a foreign land,
and labeled as a captive,
which is better?”
Yáwūtǎ reported the matter to the throne.
In the tenth month,
an edict was issued, promoting Qīng to Silver-Green Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Téngyáng,
and keeping him as Grand Marshal and Pacification Commissioner of the local troops.
Qīng secretly submitted a memorial expressing gratitude,
and again requested Pīzhōu.
The Privy Council reported:
“We fear that Qīng’s intention is only to obtain Pīzhōu.
Yáwūtǎ should be instructed
that if Qīng truly surrenders in earnest,
he should be granted it.
If he is judged to be deceitful,
men can be sent into Sòng territory to disseminate the communications back and forth,
and the official titles granted.
This is also a tactic of sowing discord.”
Since Qīng did not get Pīzhōu,
he returned to serve the Sòng.
On the night of the twenty-fifth day of the first month of the fifth year of Xīngdìng,
Qīng raided and broke into the western wall of Sìzhōu,
and Commander Wáng Lù was killed.
At this time,
Shí Quán was acting as Associate Administrator of the Privy Council.
The court did not know that Qīng had attacked and breached the western wall,
only stating that it was by Sòng people.
An edict ordered Quán to supervise the Sìzhōu troops in recapturing the western wall.
When Quán arrived at Sìzhōu,
he captured a Red Turban bandit.
Upon questioning him,
he learned that Qīng was the Sòng Director of Military Affairs for Jīngdōng,
and had attacked and breached the western wall.
Quán was quite pleased,
and then killed the man to silence him.
Yáwūtǎ fought day and night,
recruiting brave men to approach the city with ladders and ramming devices.
Qīng lowered soldiers to resist but could not advance.
Yáwūtǎ sent Commander Wáng Yìngsūn to tunnel into the city at the northeast corner.
Qīng led troops out at night to attack,
and repelled them.
Two days later,
he again led troops out and again repelled them.
The siege became more urgent.
Qīng, with two thousand marine troops combined with the city's forces, attacked Yáwūtǎ’s camp.
Commander Wòlǔyì had prior knowledge,
set up an ambush,
and Qīng's army was greatly defeated.
A thousand men drowned in the Huái River.
From then on, he no longer ventured out.
Wáng Yìngsūn's tunnel was nearing the city's interior.
Qīng dug tunnels and burned firewood, forcing them out.
Qīng directed from atop the city walls.
A stray arrow struck his eye,
and many of his remaining troops were wounded.
The watchtowers and battlements collapsed one after another,
and the city dwellers were terrified,
losing all will to resist.
On the night of the twenty-sixth day of the second month,
Qīng led his forces away,
and the western wall was thus recovered.
In the second month of the first year of Yuánguāng,
Quán, along with Grand Marshal and Left Overseer Èkě,
commanded three armies to attack the Sòng.
An edict stated:
“You bear heavy responsibilities;
do not cause disharmony leading to defeat.
If provisions can be obtained,
but are not obtained due to improper planning,
the fault lies with Èkě.
If they are obtained,
but cannot be transported and utilized by us,
the fault lies with Quán.”
Quán and Èkě advanced from Yǐng and Shòu, crossed the Huái River,
defeated the Sòng forces at Gāotángshì,
attacked Gùshǐ County,
and routed the Sòng general Jiāo Sīzhōng’s troops from Lúzhōu.
Soon after,
they captured a living prisoner who said
that Qīng had been ordered by the Sòng to resist Quán’s forces.
Quán concealed this matter.
In the fifth month,
the army returned.
When they were twenty *lǐ* from the Huái River,
and the various armies were about to cross,
Quán falsely claimed a secret imperial edict
“for all armies to temporarily stay and harvest wheat in Huáinán.”
He then ordered each soldier to harvest three *shí* of wheat for the army’s provisions.
The troops were misled.
Èkě and the other generals and assistants advised against it, but he did not listen.
The army remained for three days.
Èkě said to Quán:
“Now the Huái River is shallow and narrow,
we can cross quickly.
It is currently the hot, rainy season.
If there is a sudden flood,
and the Sòng pursue us,
we will not be able to return intact.”
Quán firmly refused.
Cóngyí Dá'ā, Yíshībù, Xiéliè, and Lǐ Xīn gradually became discontent.
Quán angrily said:
“Èkě is just one marshal!
You all side with him.
That you all have reached your present positions
is all thanks to my efforts.
I am an official of the Privy Council,
there is nothing I cannot do to you.”
The others then dared not speak.
That night,
there was heavy rain.
The next day,
the Huái River surged.
So, a bridge was built to cross the army.
The Sòng army attacked them,
and the army was defeated.
The bridge broke,
and Quán crossed first in a light boat,
while the soldiers were all drowned.
Xuānzōng then issued an edict to execute him,
and sent officials to gather the scattered troops.
The edict said:
“Whenever the grand army crosses the Huái River,
it always achieves merits.
Due to the generals' errors,
troops scattered and perished,
wandering in distress and suffering.
We are deeply saddened by this.
Each should return to their old camps
and strive to prove themselves.”
Another edict said:
“For the descendants of military officers who died in battle,
those aged fifteen or above shall be appointed to positions according to the precedent for children of officials.
Those below fifteen and above ten shall be given salaries according to their rank and assigned to various departments.
Upon reaching adulthood, they shall be given duties by their respective departments.
If there are no children, the official’s salary
shall be given according to regulations.
All posthumous titles, funeral grants, and military families that require support
shall follow the old system.”
Commentary says: Since the final years of Zhāngzōng of the Jīn,
Hán Tuōzhòu of the Sòng stirred up trouble,
recruiting and enticing fugitives from neighboring areas to disrupt the Central Plains.
His efforts ultimately came to nothing.
However, the people in the suburbs of Qīng, Xú, and Huáihǎi were agitated.
In years of famine,
bandits rose everywhere,
vying to be powerful leaders.
They also massacred each other,
harming the innocent.
For over ten years, the chaos never ceased.
Xuānzōng did not consider pacifying the difficulties,
but instead undertook another campaign against the Sòng.
Until the fall of Jīn,
its calamity was even greater.
The records of Guóyòng'ān, Shí Qīng, and others' neglected deeds,
even today, humane gentlemen read them and frown all day long.
The common people at that time
were like fish in a pot;
how could they survive?
War
is a destructive tool.
The Jīn gained the country through war,
and also lost the country through war.
How can one not be cautious?
How can one not be cautious?
Collation Notes
Biographies 56: Miáo Dàorùn, Wáng Fú, Yílà Zhòngjiānú, Wǔ Xiān, Zhāng Fǔ, Jìng Ānmín, Guō Wénzhèn, Hú Tiānzuò, Zhāng Kāi, Yàn Níng
Miáo Dàorùn,
at the beginning of the Zhēnyòu reign,
was a captain of the rebel army in Héběi.
When Xuānzōng relocated to Biàn,
the local people of Héběi often banded together as soldiers,
or became bandit gangs.
Dàorùn was brave and resourceful, daring in battle,
and able to win the hearts of the multitude.
With successive victories,
he pacified cities and towns,
and sent someone to Nánjīng to request official titles and appointments.
The prime minister found it difficult to grant this,
so Xuānzōng summoned Wáng Kuò, the Commissioner of Transportation for Hénán, and asked:
“You are wise and thoughtful;
please decide this matter of Dàorùn for me.
If I were to immediately appoint him a general with his troops,
would he truly exert his full effort for me until the end?”
Kuò replied:
“One who controls all under heaven must consider the whole realm.
Dàorùn has gained the support of the multitude and achieved merit; if you consequently bestow a title upon him,
and allow him to govern his own territory,
managing him with a loose rein,
this is the best policy.
If you do not allow it now,
he will rely on his multitude,
and there is nothing he cannot do.”
Xuānzōng looked at his prime ministers and said:
“Wáng Kuò’s words
truly align with my heart.”
Thus,
Dàorùn was appointed Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn and Deputy Military Commissioner of Shùntiān Jūn.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
he was again promoted for his merits to Huáiyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn and Deputy Administrator of Zhōngshān Fǔ.
After two more months,
he again achieved merit in battle,
and was promoted to Piáoqí Shàngjiāngjūn, Commissioner of Military Affairs for Zhōngdū Lù, and concurrently Administrator of Zhōngshān Fǔ.
Soon after,
he was made Grand Guardian of Zhōngdū and concurrently Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Dàorùn pacified over fifty cities before and after.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
an imperial edict ordered Dàorùn to recover Zhōngdū,
supplementing him with troops from Shāndōng.
Dàorùn reported:
“Last November,
I sent the overall commander Zhāng Zǐmíng to persuade Dújí Qīijīn of Lízhōu to surrender.
Recently,
Yílà Tiěgē, the General Commander of Military Affairs for Héběi Dōnglù, moved his troops to Lízhōu,
attacked and defeated Zǐmíng’s army,
killing several hundred people;
Zǐmíng was also wounded.
I intended to lead troops to punish him,
but considering that Tiěgē had defected and joined us,
I merely prepared for him.
Now, desiring to retake the capital city,
I beg that Tiěgē not be punished,
but be directly ordered to submit to my command,
so that affairs may be accomplished.”
Xuānzōng consulted the prime minister about this,
who reported:
“Dàorùn and Tiěgē are not harmonious,
and cannot be subordinate to each other.”
An edict appointed Wányán Kū as acting Chief Military Commissioner,
to supervise Dàorùn in recovering Zhōngdū,
and to reconcile with Tiěgē’s army.
Earlier,
Dàorùn and Lǐ Chēn, the Military Commissioner of Shùntiān Jūn, were not compatible.
Their soldiers consequently attacked each other.
Chēn sent troops to attack Mǎnchéng and Wánzhōu.
Dàorùn’s army resisted,
killing Chēn’s elder brother Róng and younger brother Míng, among others.
Chēn reported:
“Wūlíndá Wúdiǎn, the Provost of Lùzhōu, following Dàorùn’s instigation,
continually plots aggression.
The Shāndōng Xíngshěng repeatedly admonished Dàorùn to make peace with me,
but he never complied,
and even killed my elder brother Róng and younger brother Míng, among others.
His lawlessness is such
that it will become a future disaster.”
He also presented a memorial:
“I beg that officials in the prefectures and counties of Héběi not be subordinate to each other,
but all be under the command of the Shuàifǔ.
Furthermore, dispatch officials to adjust the military strength of the various circuits,
so that their power is balanced and rival forces cannot annex each other,
then the people will be at peace in their fields.”
Dàorùn reported that Lǐ Chēn rebelled with his multitude,
captured Mǎnchéng,
and attacked Wánzhōu.
Chēn also reported Dàorùn’s rebellion.
The court deliberated, believing that their disharmony
had led to this situation.
An order was issued to the Shāndōng Xíngshěng and Púmìyuàn to admonish Chēn:
“The Xíngshěng is there;
you should all naturally obey its command,
why wait for the Shuàifǔ?
Soldiers originally banded together by righteousness,
and both cultivated and fought.
Now they are gathered in fortified camps,
and thus annex each other.
The people are not at peace,
all because officials are without scruples and cause this.
Strictly enforce discipline,
cultivate crops according to the seasons,
and avoid causing trouble.”
An imperial edict instructed Dàorùn and Yílà Tiěgē to combine their forces to pacify Héběi,
and ordered the troops of various circuits to support each other.
Later,
Dàorùn, Jiǎ Tóng,
and Jiǎ Yǔ attacked each other.
An edict ordered Dàorùn, Jiǎ Tóng, Wáng Fú, Wǔ Xiān, and Jiǎ Yǔ to divide and control the various circuit military commissioner's offices,
while the Zhāngdé Wèihuī Pacification Bureau was subordinate to the Púmìyuàn.
After Jiǎ Yǔ had attacked Dàorùn,
he then feigned a peace agreement.
Dàorùn believed him,
whereupon Jiǎ Yǔ ambushed and assassinated Dàorùn.
The imperial court was unable to investigate.
Dàorùn’s army, wandering aimlessly, without reliance,
its Provost Jìng Ānmín requested temporary subordination to the Lùzhōu Xíng Yuánshuàifǔ,
to be under its command.
This was the second year of Xīngdìng.
The Right Chancellor Hóu Zhì requested that the three prefectures of Bǎo, Lí, and Wán be subordinated to Zhēndìng.
However, Lízhōu had previously been under the command of Yílà Zhòngjiānú.
If it were suddenly transferred to Zhēndìng,
it was feared that conflicts might arise.
Jìng Ānmín and others wished to be subordinate to Lùzhōu,
so the Héběi Xíngshěng was ordered to investigate and handle the matter.
The Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs, Zhāng Róu, reported:
“Jiǎ Yǔ attacked the Yìzhōu stockade,
killed the Prefect Mǎ Xìn and his subordinate officers,
and took their golden tallies before leaving.”
Soon after,
Zhāng Róu attacked Jiǎ Yǔ and killed him.
After Dàorùn’s death,
Jìng Ānmín took over his troops.
It was after this that he was enfeoffed.
Initially,
in Zhēnyòu (貞祐) fourth year (1216),
Yòusījiàn (右司諫) Shù Jiǎzhídūn (術甲直敦) requested the enfeoffment of the Héshuò (河朔) region.
An imperial edict ordered the Shàngshūshěng (尚書省) to deliberate,
but the matter was shelved and not acted upon.
In Xīngdìng (興定) third year (1219),
as Tàiyuán (太原) could not be defended,
and the prefectures and counties of Héběi (河北) could not stand on their own,
an imperial edict ordered all officials to discuss what would be of long-term benefit.
Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ (翰林學士承旨) Túshàn Háo (徒單鎬) and sixteen others stated:
"There are three ways to manage the military:
first, war;
second, peace;
third, defense.
Now, if we wish to wage war, our military strength is insufficient;
if we wish for peace, they (the enemy) will not comply.
Only defense remains.
Since the prefectures and commanderies of Héshuò (河朔) are already ruined,
they cannot all be defended equally.
It is advisable to select those who are willing to relocate and settle them in Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西).
Those unwilling should be allowed to choose their own leaders
and gather in strategically difficult places."
Xíngbù Shìláng (刑部侍郎) Àotún Húsāhé (奧屯胡撒合) and two others said:
"Héběi (河北) serves as a strategic buffer to Hénán (河南), and Pú (蒲) and Jiě (解) are vital to Shǎnxī (陝西) like a collar and throat.
To relocate all their people
It is advisable to order the various commanderies
to select capable and respected individuals who can organize the relocation of the populace,
willingly to Hénán (河南), or Jìn'ān (晉安), Hézhōng (河中), and other difficult passes.
They should be given sufficient provisions,
granted vacant land,
and urged to exert full effort in farming.
Officials for temporary administration should be appointed
to pacify and care for them.
Select the able-bodied among them
and teach them warfare.
Order the defenders of Jìn'ān (晉安) and Hézhōng (河中) to summon troops from Shí (石), Lán (嵐), Fén (汾), and Huò (霍)
to plan for recovery,
which is the greatest convenience."
Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書) Wūlíndá Yǔ (烏林荅與) and twenty others said:
"For the various prefectures of Héshuò (河朔),
regarding the positions of 'governor of the people' and 'commander of troops,'
select local people who have served as officials and possess talent and strategy to appoint to these roles.
In times of emergency, they should retreat to strategic locations;
in times of peace, they should engage in farming."
Xuānhuīshǐ (宣徽使) Yílà Guāngzǔ (移剌光祖) and two others said:
"Assessing the situation in Tàiyuán (太原),
although it has been temporarily lost,
it can soon be recovered.
We should recruit local people who command prestige and public respect,
and grant them significant regional authority.
If they can recover an entire circuit,
they should be appointed as the Zǒngguǎn (總管) of that circuit.
If they can defend prefectures and commanderies,
they should be appointed as their senior assistants.
This will surely enable each to protect their own region
and allow the people to resume their livelihoods."
Típiǎn Shàngshí Jú (提點尚食局) Shímò Mù (石抹穆) proposed recruiting commoners with high ranks,
which was generally similar to Guāngzǔ's (光祖) proposal.
The chief ministers wished to establish ducal administrations (gōngfǔ, 公府),
but Xuānzōng's (宣宗) decision was pending.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Wányán Bójiā (完顏伯嘉) said:
"The Sòng (宋) people used an empty title to attract Lǐ Quán (李全),
and thus gained real territory in Shāndōng (山東).
If one can command the populace and defend the territory,
why begrudge even the Three Dukes (Sāngōng, 三公)?"
Xuānzōng (宣宗) said:
"In the future, when the situation is settled,
won't there be too many ducal administrations?"
Bójiā (伯嘉) said:
"If the situation is settled,
what is wrong with assigning the Three Dukes to frontier garrisons?"
Xuānzōng's (宣宗) mind was then made up.
In the second month of the fourth year (1220),
Wáng Fú (王福), the Cāngzhōu Jīnglüèshǐ (滄州經略使), was enfeoffed as Cānghǎi Gōng (滄海公).
Yílà Zhòngjiānú (移剌衆家奴), the Héjiān Lù Zhāofǔshǐ (河間路招撫使), was enfeoffed as Héjiān Gōng (河間公).
Wǔ Xiān (武仙), the Zhēndìng Jīnglüèshǐ (真定經略使), was enfeoffed as Shān Gōng (山公).
Zhāng Fǔ (張甫), the Zhōngdū Dōnglù Jīnglüèshǐ (中都東路經lüèshǐ), was enfeoffed as Gāoyáng Gōng (高陽公).
Jìng Ānmín (靖安民), the Zhōngdū Xīlù Jīnglüèshǐ (中都西路經lüèshǐ), was enfeoffed as Yìshuǐ Gōng (易水公).
Guō Wénzhèn (郭文振), the Liáozhōu Cóngyí (遼州從宜), was enfeoffed as Jìnyáng Gōng (晉陽公).
Hú Tiānzuò (胡天作), the Píngyáng Zhāofǔshǐ (平陽招撫使), was enfeoffed as Píngyáng Gōng (平陽公).
Wányán Kāi (完顏開), the Zhāoyìjūn Jiédùshǐ (昭義軍節度使), was enfeoffed as Shàngdǎng Gōng (上黨公).
Yàn Níng (燕寧), the Shāndōng Ānfǔ Fùshǐ (山東安撫副使), was enfeoffed as Dōngjǔ Gōng (東莒公).
All nine dukes concurrently held the title of Xuānfǔshǐ (宣撫使),
and their rank was Yínqīng Rónglù Dàfū (銀青榮祿大夫).
They were granted the honorary title of
"Xuānlì Zhōngchén" (宣力忠臣),
and were to command all military forces in their respective circuits,
appoint officials,
collect taxes,
and carry out rewards, punishments, and orders at their discretion.
An imperial edict was also bestowed, stating:
"When the frontier defenses failed
and Héshuò (河朔) lost its peace,
you all took charge of the army
and utterly exhausted your loyalty and strength.
If you can prove your effectiveness,
what more worries would I have?
It is fitting to grant you enfeoffment with territories,
and again bestow upon you the title of 'Loyal Minister.'
Apart from the prefectures and counties already designated for your administration,
if you can recover adjacent prefectures and counties,
they shall also be subject to your governance."
Wáng Fú (王福) was originally
a leader of the Héběi (河北) loyalist army.
Through accumulated military achievements, he was successively promoted to Tóngzhī Hénghǎijūn Jiédùshǐshì (同知橫海軍節度使事) and Cāngzhōu Jīnglüè Fùshǐ (滄州經略副使).
In Xīngdìng (興定) first year (1217),
Fú (福) dispatched Tíkòng (提控) Zhāng Jù (張聚) and Wáng Jìn (王進) to recover Bīn (濱) and Dì (棣) prefectures.
Jù (聚) was made acting Dìzhōu Fángyùshǐ (棣州防禦使),
and Jìn (進) acting Bīnzhōu Cìshǐ (濱州刺史).
After a long time,
Fú (福) and Jù (聚) had a falling out,
and Jù (聚) submitted Dìzhōu (棣州) to Zhāng Lín (張林) of Yìdū (益都).
In the ninth month of Xīngdìng (興定) third year (1219),
Fú (福) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Cāngzhōu (滄州) borders the Cānghǎi (滄海) to the east,
is connected to Zhēndìng (真定) to the west,
and guards against a large army to the north;
it can be called a strategic location.
I beg to select a high-ranking minister to be the Jīnglüèshǐ (經略使),
to act with discretion,
and to pacify and control the military and civilians."
The imperial court considered that Fú (福) had initially led loyalist troops to recover Cāngzhōu (滄州),
gathered remnant civilians,
now had over ten thousand men,
with complete weaponry,
and was a powerful independent force in the region.
He was neighbors with Zhāng Lín (張林) of Yìdū (益都) and Zhāng Jù (張聚) of Dìzhōu (棣州).
Now Lìjīn (利津) was already undefended,
and the road to Liáodōng (遼東) was difficult.
Moreover, his true intention was to become the Jīnglüèshǐ (經lüèshǐ) himself,
and this was merely a pretext.
Therefore, it was decided to grant him the appointment,
so that he could gather the people of Bīn (濱) and Dì (棣),
and establish communication with Liáodōng (遼東).
If he were not permitted now,
the Sòng (宋) people might coerce him with a large army,
or entice him with official titles,
which would lead to future regret.
Xuānzōng (宣宗) agreed,
and so appointed Fú (福) as the Jīnglüèshǐ (經lüèshǐ) of his prefecture,
and further allowed him to select his own Fùshǐ (副使).
At this time, Fú (福) had military achievements,
and was promoted to the nominal appointment of Tóngzhī Dōngpíngfǔshì (同知東平府事), acting Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān (元帥右都監),
with his Jīnglüè (經lüè) and Jiédù (節度) titles remaining as before.
In Xīngdìng (興定) fourth year (1220),
he was enfeoffed as Cānghǎi Gōng (滄海公),
with Qīng (清), Cāng (滄), Guān (觀) prefectures,
Yánshān (鹽山), Wúdì (無棣), Lèlíng (樂陵), Dōngguāng (東光), Níngjīn (寧津), Wúqiáo (吳橋), Jiānglíng (將陵), Fùchéng (阜城), and Tiáoxiàn (蓨縣) under his jurisdiction.
In the fourth month,
the Red Jacket Bandit Lǐ Èr Tàiwèi (李二太尉) raided Lèlíng (樂陵),
and Zhāng Jù (張聚) from Dìzhōu (棣州) came to attack.
Fú (福) repelled them both.
Lǐ Èr (李二) again raided Yánshān (鹽山).
Jīnglüè Fùshǐ (經lüè Fùshǐ) Zhāng Wén (張文) engaged him in battle,
and Lǐ Èr (李二) was utterly defeated.
Two of his統制 (tǒngzhì) were captured,
two thousand heads were severed,
and thirty horses were captured.
In the seventh month,
the Sòng (宋) people and the Red Jacket Bandits entered Héběi (河北).
Fú (福) held the city firmly.
Zhāng Lín (張林) of Yìdū (益都) and Zhāng Jù (張聚) of Dìzhōu (棣zhou) attacked and plundered daily.
Cāngzhōu (滄州) was in a critical state,
and Fú (福) was about to flee south
but was stopped by his men.
He then submitted to Zhāng Lín (張林).
The Dōngpíng Yuánshuàifǔ (東平元帥府) requested to punish Fú (福),
begging for an additional seven thousand Hénán (河南) infantry and five hundred cavalry,
and for Huá (滑), Jùn (濬), and Wèizhōu (衞州) to provide fodder and grain.
They also requested to establish a reward system in advance for those with achievements.
The imperial court considered that the autumn defense was approaching,
Hénán (河南) troops could not be dispatched,
and Dōngpíng's (東平) troops were too few to succeed alone.
It was decided to wait until the spring of the following year,
and have the Dōngpíng Yuánshuàifǔ (東平元帥府) and Gāoyáng Gōng (高陽公) combine forces to attack him.
Thus, the plan was halted.
Yílà Zhòngjiānú (移剌衆家奴),
through accumulated military achievements,
was successively promoted to Héjiān Lù Zhāofǔshǐ (河間路招撫使),
nominally appointed Kāizhōu Cìshǐ (開州刺史),
acting Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān (元帥右都監),
and granted the surname Wányán (完顏).
In Xīngdìng (興定) fourth year (1220),
he was enfeoffed along with Zhāng Fǔ (張甫).
Zhòngjiānú (衆家奴) was enfeoffed as Héjiān Gōng (河間公),
with Xiàn (獻), Lí (蠡), Ān (安), Shēn (深) prefectures, Héjiān (河間), Sùníng (肅寧), Ānpíng (安平), Wǔqiáng (武強), Ráoyáng (饒陽), Liùjiā Zhuāng (六家莊), and Lángshān Zhài (郎山寨) under his jurisdiction.
At the end of the Xīngdìng reign,
the prefectures and counties under his command were all indefensible.
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
he moved his garrison to Xìn'ān,
which was originally within Zhāng Fǔ's territory.
Zhāng Fǔ thereupon memorialized:
"Xìn'ān is originally the northern border of your servant.
Its location is strategically vital.
I beg that it be temporarily designated a prefecture to give it more importance."
An imperial edict changed Xìn'ān to Zhèn'ān Fǔ.
That year,
he combined forces with Fǔ,
and they recaptured Héjiān Fǔ and the three prefectures of Ān, Lí, and Xiàn.
Both he and Zhāng Fǔ were promoted to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
In the second year,
Zhòng Jiānú and Zhāng Fǔ together defended Zhèn'ān,
each holding a sector.
He separately dispatched the Commander-in-Chief Tíkòng
Sūn Rǔjí, Yáng Shòu, and Tíkòng Yuán Dé, Lǐ Chéngfēn to defend the outer walls,
thus securing Zhèn'ān.
Before long,
Zhòng Jiānú memorialized:
"Zhèn'ān is over two hundred *lǐ* from Yínglè Gù Hǎikǒu,
and is truly a vital thoroughfare for travel to and from Liáodōng.
Gāoyáng Gōng Fǔ has seagoing vessels northwest of Zhèn'ān.
People can be recruited to go directly to Liáodōng
to establish communication between the interior and the outside.
If the rewards are not generous, it will not be enough to motivate people.
We propose that those who volunteer be specially promoted to Zhōngxiǎn Xiàowèi,
granted an eighth-rank official position,
and moreover rewarded with five thousand strings of *bǎoquán*.
If their official rank has already reached Zhōngxiǎn or above the eighth rank,
they shall be promoted two ranks and their position elevated one grade.
Upon their return, they shall again be promoted two ranks and their position elevated two grades."
The imperial edict approved this.
Wǔ Xiān,
a native of Wēizhōu.
Some say he was once a Daoist priest,
and people of the time referred to him as such.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
Xiān led local troops to defend the Western Mountains of Wēizhōu.
His followers increased daily.
An imperial edict appointed Xiān acting Wēizhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he defeated Shí Hǎi at Zhēndìng.
Xuānchāi Zhāofǔshǐ Wéi Hóng requested additional official honors and rewards.
He was formally appointed Wēizhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently Zhīzhōng of Zhēndìng Fǔ,
and acting Zhī Zhēndìng Fǔ Shì.
He was promoted to Míngzhōu Fángyùshǐ, concurrently Tóngzhī Zhēndìng Fǔ Shì,
and remotely granted Hépíngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the fourth year of Xīngdìng,
he was promoted to Zhī Zhēndìng Fǔ Shì,
concurrently Jīnglüèshǐ,
remotely overseeing Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu,
and acting Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān.
Before long,
he was enfeoffed as Shāngōng.
Zhōngshān and Zhēndìng Fǔ,
Wò, Jì, Wēi, Zhènníng, and Píngdìng Zhōu,
Bàodú Zhài,
Luánchéng, and Nángōng Xiàn were subordinated to him.
Among the nine prefectures at that time,
Shān was the most prosperous in wealth and military strength.
That year,
he submitted to Dàyuán.
The Vice Grand Astrologer Shǐ Tiānnì administered Zhēndìng.
Xiān's elder brother, Guì, was Ānguójūn Jiédùshǐ.
Shǐ Tiānxiáng attacked him,
and Guì also submitted to Dàyuán.
Xiān and Shǐ Tiānnì both administered Zhēndìng for nearly six years,
accumulating animosity.
Fearing that Tiānnì would plot against him,
he once wanted to flee south.
Xuānzōng heard of this
and ordered the Púmì Yuàn to send a dispatch to summon him.
Xiān was overjoyed upon receiving the dispatch.
In the second year of Zhèngdà,
Xiān treacherously killed Shǐ Tiānnì
and again offered Zhēndìng in surrender.
The Dàyuán general Xiào Nǎishòu attacked Xiān,
and Xiān fled.
After a month,
he re-entered Zhēndìng by night.
Xiào Nǎishòu attacked him again,
and Xiān then fled to Biànjīng.
In the fifth year,
he was summoned for an audience.
Āizōng ordered Púmì Pànguān Bái Huá to guide him through the ceremonies,
and he was again enfeoffed as Shāngōng,
establishing his headquarters in Wèizhōu.
In the seventh year,
Xiān besieged Shàngdǎng.
Soon after, a large army arrived,
and Xiān retreated.
Before long,
Wèizhōu was besieged,
and internal and external communication was cut off.
An imperial edict ordered Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Hédá and Púmì Fùshǐ Pú'ā to rescue it.
Xiān's troops were moved to garrison Húlíng Guān,
blocking the Jīnzhōu road.
In the eleventh month of the eighth year,
Dàyuán troops crossed the Xiāng and Hàn rivers.
Hédá and Pú'ā were stationed at Dèngzhōu.
Xiān joined the Dèngzhōu army from Jīngzǐkǒu.
On the *dīngyǒu* day of the first month of the first year of Tiānxīng,
Hédá and Pú'ā were defeated at Sānfēng Shān.
Xiān fled to Mìxiàn with over forty horsemen,
heading towards Yùzhài.
Dūwèi Wūlíndá Hútǔ did not admit him,
and he was almost captured by the pursuing cavalry.
He then abandoned his horse
and ascended on foot to Qīngliáng Sì on the summit of Sōngshān.
He said to Dēngfēng Lánruòzhài Zhāofǔshǐ Huò Zhuósēngxiù:
"How could I dare to enter Biànjīng?
Should an emergency arise,
they would bind me and present me to the great state!"
He then fled to Liúshān in Nányáng,
