gathered ten thousand routed soldiers,
and garrisoned Liúshān and Wēiyuǎn Zhài.
He established official organs,
amassed provisions,
repaired weapons,
and his military strength somewhat revived.
In the third month,
Biànjīng was besieged.
Āizōng appointed Xiān Cānzhī Zhèngshì, Púmì Fùshǐ, and Hénán Xíngshěng,
and ordered him to combine forces with Dèngzhōu Xíngshěng Sīliè to go to its rescue.
In the eighth month,
he reached east of Mìxiàn
and encountered the Dàyuán general Sùbùtái's army passing through.
Xiān immediately halted his army at Méishān Diàn
and reported to Sīliè:
"Build a camp by the stream and wait for me to arrive, then advance together.
Otherwise, we will be defeated."
Sīliè, eager to reach Biàn,
did not listen.
Upon reaching Jīngshuǐ,
the great army attacked them,
and they were routed without a fight.
Xiān also ordered his army to scatter and flee,
agreeing to rendezvous at Liúshān.
When Xiān arrived at Liúshān,
the number of routed soldiers arriving increased.
Āizōng dismissed Sīliè as Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu
and decreed to Xiān:
"Sīliè does not understand military strategy.
If he had followed your plan to block the stream,
how could there have been a defeat?
All military affairs are entrusted to you.
I await you day and night,
to work together with one heart to plan the next move."
In the eleventh month,
he dispatched Xíngbù Zhǔshì Wūgǔlún Hūlǔ to summon Xiān.
Xiān was reluctant to go,
so he submitted a memorial outlining the advantages and disadvantages,
requesting a delay of three months
before entering to provide aid, even at the cost of his life.
Initially,

when Sīliè arrived at Dèngzhōu, he, by imperial commission, appointed Xuānchāi Zǒnglǐng Huángguā Sānhé to oversee the Xíng Yuánshuài Fǔ affairs in the Wǔyuánshān area, concurrently acting as the Shàngshū of the Six Boards.
When Xiān returned to Liúshān,
he disliked Sānhé's growing power,
so he changed his title to Zhēngxíng Yuánshuài
and had him garrison Bǐyáng.
Sānhé resented Xiān for seizing his authority,
and thus submitted to Dàyuán.
General Sùbùtái appointed Sānhé to defend Yùzhōu.
Sānhé then fraudulently wrote to Xiān, inviting him to take Yùzhōu,
promising that he could achieve his ambitions.
Xiān believed him.
Sānhé then reported to the Dàyuán general,
who sent troops to attack from both sides,
defeating Xiān at Liǔhé.
Xiān fled by leaping to Shèngyuán Zhài.
Initially,
Shěnqiū尉 Cáo Zhèng, acting on imperial orders, summoned troops to Xīshān.
Yùzhōu防禦使 Lǐ Tiānxiáng disobeyed the command.
Zhèng executed him as a warning.
Xiān arrived at Shèngyǔ,
and said to Zhèng:
"Why did you arbitrarily execute my general?"
Zhèng replied:
"Tiānxiáng violated the edict by delaying and not proceeding.
Zhèng exercised discretion and executed him."
Xiān angrily said:
"Today, an imperial envoy comes to raise an army;
tomorrow, an imperial envoy comes to raise an army.
Because of this, our soldiers have almost all died in battle.
From now on, no matter who comes, I will not listen.
For now, let the lads rest in the mountains."
He further said:
"If Tiānxiáng indeed had a crime,
wait for me to come and deal with it.
Who are you to dare to kill him?"
Zhèng said:
"参政 Liǔ Hé suffered a defeat,
and his fate is unknown.
Tiānxiáng violated the edict,
why should he not be killed?"
Xiān was greatly enraged,
and shouted at his attendants to confiscate Zhèng's silver plaque,
ordering 总领 Yáng Quán to shackle and imprison him.
A general amnesty was issued,
but he was still imprisoned.
He was only released after Xiān's defeat,
and along with Yáng Quán, surrendered to Sòng.
At this time,
Āizōng fled to Guīdé,
and dispatched Hàlín Xiūzhuàn Wèi Fán by secret path to summon Xiān.
Upon reaching Yùzhōu,
Fán encountered Xiān's defeat at Liǔhé.
Fán feigned an imperial edict to rally the scattered troops to await Xiān.
Xiān suspected that Fán was plotting against him.
In the first month of the second year,
Xiān reviewed his troops.
His elite vanguard still numbered 100,000.
Fán said:
"The emperor daily looks west, hoping for your arrival,
you should not stay here long."
Xiān was angry,
and nearly killed Fán.
When Fán and Hūlǔlà returned to Guīdé,
Xiān then submitted a memorial requesting Fán's execution.
Āizōng did not assent,
and appointed Fán as Guīdé Yuánshuàifǔ Jīnglìguān.
Fán's courtesy name was Bāngyàn,
and he was from Húnyuán.
He became a *jìnshì* in Zhēnyòu second year, it is said.
Xiān's general Dǒng Yòu had military merits.
An edict granted him a tiger tally,
but Xiān feared his proximity to him,
and for a long time did not allow him to wear it.
Yòu resented this,
and consequently conspired with Guānnú to kill Xiān,
but hesitated and dared not act.
Jìnsìjú Shǐ Wányán Sìhé was resourceful and decisive.
He once levied troops at Dèngzhōu.
Yǔmùshǐ Yílà Dáihé had other intentions.
Sìhé executed him by stratagem.
Yòu's envoy said to Sìhé:
"Xiān will ultimately not enter to provide aid.
Yòu and others are of low rank,
and lack the power to execute him.
Only you can plan for the state."
Sìhé said:
"Having already killed Dáihé,
and now to kill Wǔ Xiān again,
when envoys come another day,
who will believe us?"
He did not agree.
Xiān learned that Yòu had once harbored this plot,
and sent Yòu as an envoy to Héběi,
and later indeed killed him.
In the third month,
Xiān, due to insufficient provisions for the army at Shèngyǔ,
moved his troops to Dèngzhōu,
relying on 总帅 Yílà Yuàn of Dèngzhōu for supplies.
The granaries of Dèngzhōu were also depleted,
so he divided his army among Xīnyě, Shùnyáng, and Xīchuān to forage among the civilian households.
He dispatched Jiǎngyìguān Zhū [ ], Liú Zhuó to Xiāngyáng,
to borrow grain from the Sòng Zhìzhìshǐ Shǐ Sōngzhī.
Zhuó and [ ] held conflicting views,
and feared being detained.
So they confided in Shǐ Sōngzhī, saying:
"Xiān's military power will not recover."
They also said:
"The name is 'borrowing grain,'
but it is truly a desire to submit.
We just await your general's word."
Sōngzhī believed this to be true,
and sent Tián Jùn with a letter to report to Xiān.
In the fourth month,
Xiān dispatched Dàlǐ Shàopíng Zhāng Bózhí to retrieve grain from Xiāngyáng,
encamping his army at Xiǎojiāngkǒu to await him.
Sōngzhī was greatly pleased upon hearing that Zhāng Bózhí had arrived,
thinking that Xiān was submitting.
When he opened the letter, it was merely a thank-you note.
He was furious,
and detained Bózhí, not sending him back.
Xiān entered Dèngzhōu from Shùnyáng.
Yílà Yuàn, fearing pressure,
gave his daughter to Xiān in marriage.
Xiān accepted without suspicion,
and then returned to Shùnyáng.
When Dèngzhōu's grain ran out,
Yuàn ultimately suspected Xiān.
In the fifth month,
Yuàn surrendered the city to Sòng.
Sōngzhī thus knew the true state of Xiān's army even better,
and sent Mèng Gǒng to lead five thousand soldiers to attack Xiān's army at Shùnyáng.
At this time,
Xiān had ordered his soldiers to harvest wheat for the army.
They only realized the attack when it was less than two *lǐ* away.
Xiān led over a hundred men from his personal guard to meet the attack,
and Mèng Gǒng dared not advance.
In a moment,
more soldiers gathered,
numbering five or six hundred,
and thoroughly defeated Gǒng's troops.
Gǒng escaped with a few hundred men,
but dozens of his commandants and leaders were captured alive,
and over a thousand horses were seized.
By this time,
the false claim by [ ] and Zhuó that they would submit to Sōngzhī was revealed.
Xiān executed them both.
Yílà Yuàn's original name was Niánhé,
and his courtesy name was Tíngyù.
He was hereditary Qìdān *mēng'ān*,
and through accumulating merits became Dèngzhōu Biànyí Zǒngshuài.
After arriving at Xiāngyáng,
he was ordered to change his name,
calling himself Guīzhèng Rén Liú Jiè,
and presented himself with the ceremony of a general to the Zhìzhìshǐ.
Yuàn was greatly regretful.
In the third month of the following year,
a carbuncle erupted on his back, and he died.
Although Mèng Gǒng had been defeated and retreated,
Xiān feared that the Sòng troops would return.
In the seventh month,
he moved to the stone caves of Xīchuān.
At this time,
Āizōng was in Càizhōu,
and dispatched his attendant Wùyán to rebuke Xiān for not coming to aid.
The edict stated:
"I have never wronged you in the past.
The nation is in such dire peril,
how can you bear to hoard your troops and rely on yourself,
passively awaiting destruction?"
When the generals and soldiers heard this,
they looked at each other and choked with emotion,
all wishing to go to aid and share life and death with the country.
Xiān feared that the hearts of the multitude would change,
so he killed horses and cattle,
and swore a blood oath with three thousand generals and soldiers,
vowing not to betray the state.
The multitude was then greatly pleased.
Before long,
Xiān again said to the multitude:
"The road to Càizhōu is blocked,
and our troops have little food.
I fear we cannot reach it.
Moreover, Cài cannot be held firmly,
so even if we arrive, it will be useless.
Recently, I sent people to scout Sòng's Jīnzhōu.
The people occupy mountains and have built extremely perilous fortifications,
extending a hundred *lǐ* in width and breadth,
with an estimated three million *shí* of stored grain.
Now I will plan with you all to take it.
It can be taken without much effort.
We will leave the old and weak to guard this stronghold as our base,
and then select the strong and brave to proceed to Cài,
and it will not be too late to welcome the Emperor to the west."
The multitude had not yet responded,
when he immediately ordered them to prepare their luggage.
They took Xīchuān and ascended the river.
The mountain roads were treacherous,
and continuous rain for ten days made the water fierce and swift.
Countless old and young drowned,
food ran out,
and eight or nine tenths of the soldiers died.
Xiān had no plan,
and in the eighth month,
he returned east via Jīngzǐkǒu.
From Nèixiāng, he intended to enter Shèngyǔ Zhài.
Upon reaching Xiáshí and the surrounding Bādié Qiūlín,
he heard that 总领 Yáng Quán had already surrendered to Sòng.
He stayed in Qiūlín for ten days before moving to Dàhé.
In the ninth month,
he arrived at Hēigǔpō,
having lost ground both in advance and retreat.
He then planned to flee north.
Xíngbù Shàngshū Lú Zhī and Shìláng Shí Jiè did not follow.
Zhī, courtesy name Tíngruì,
was a native of Hédōng.
He obtained an official post through the privilege of his ancestors.
He served as Xī'ān Military Commissioner, acting Shàngshū.
Jiè, courtesy name Zǐjiān,
was a native of Hézhōng.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Chóngqìng.
He served as Rǔzhōu Defense Commissioner, acting Shìláng.
The two conferred with each other, saying:
"We have long known that Xiān cares not for the state.
When we remonstrate, he does not listen.
To leave is not yet possible.
Things have come to this point today;
all that is lacking is a death at Càizhōu.
If we cannot reach Càizhōu,
dying on the way is still better than dying at Xiān's hands."
After they departed,
Xiān first became aware [of it],
and pursued Jiè, killing him.
Zhī fled to Nányáng
where he was killed by local bandits.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Càizhōu was captured.
Provisions were almost exhausted,
and the officers and soldiers were greatly resentful,
all dispersing.
Xiān had nowhere to go,
so he crossed the river northward with eighteen men,
and five more were lost.
In the fifth month,
he hastened to Zézhōu,
and was killed by the garrison soldiers of Zé.
Zhāng Fǔ
was bestowed the surname Wányán.
Initially, he submitted to Dàyuán.
Lǐ Quèlǘ, the Cǐshǐ of Zhuōzhōu, recruited him.
In the first month of the first year of Xīngdìng,
Fǔ and Zhāng Jìn both came to surrender.
Měnggǔ Gāng, the Xíngshěng of Dōngpíng, by Imperial authority, appointed Fǔ as Zhōngdū Lù Jīnglüèshǐ,
and Jìn as Jīnglüè Fùshǐ.
In the second year,
Miáo Dàorùn died.
Hóu Zhì, the Xíngshěng of Héběi, by Imperial authority, appointed Lǐ Quèlǘ as acting Zhōngdū Lù Jīnglüèshǐ in Dàorùn's place,
with Fǔ and Zhāng Róu as deputies.
Shortly after,
Miáo Dàorùn's forces requested that Jìng Ānmín replace Dàorùn.
At this time,
Zhāng Róu and Ānmín effectively divided control of Dàorùn's troops.
The court then appointed Quèlǘ as Zhōngdū Dōnglù Jīnglüèshǐ,
with all territories from Xióng and Bà eastward subordinate to him.
Fǔ, Jìn, and Jiǎ Tóng, the Jiédùshǐ of Yǒngdìngjūn, were at odds.
They attacked each other with troops,
seizing Tóng's territory.
They took Tóng's horses and presented them to Jīnglüèshǐ Lǐ Quèlǘ,
who accepted them.
The court was surprised that Quèlǘ could not reconcile the prefectures and counties,
resulting in shifting loyalties.
Quèlǘ was summoned back and given other official posts.
An Imperial edict ordered Měnggǔ Gāng of Dōngpíng to mediate between Fǔ and Jiǎ Tóng.
Gāng dispatched Wáng Yù, Tongzhī of Ānwǔjūn, and Gāo Chángzhù, magistrate of Bóyě, to pacify them.
He then detained Quèlǘ, not sending him away,
and thereupon memorialized, saying:
"Zhāng Fǔ was originally recruited and surrendered by Quèlǘ;
their relationship is deeply harmonious.
Now, it is advisable to first send Yù to discuss with Quèlǘ how to pacify them.
Furthermore, Fǔ and his like are men who do not understand propriety and righteousness.
If Quèlǘ is summoned, they will all become suspicious,
fearing other disturbances might arise.
Therefore, I do not shrink from the crime of acting without authorization."
The Emperor approved Gāng's memorial.
Not long after,
Jiǎ Tóng again used troops to capture Fǔ's villagers,
killing Fǔ's consultant officer Xíng.
Fǔ led troops to attack him.
Jiǎ Tóng was defeated and fled,
then hanged himself.
Fǔ requested seals and credentials to pacify his troops,
and an Imperial edict granted them.
Before long,
Lǐ Quèlǘ submitted to Dàyuán.
Fǔ became Zhōngdū Dōnglù Jīnglüèshǐ, remotely appointed Tongzhī of Zhāngdé Fǔ, and acting Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān.
In the third year,
Zhāng Jìn became Zhōngdū Nánlù Jīnglüèshǐ.
Fǔ memorialized:
"Zhēndìng is under military assault.
I beg that a high-ranking official be sent to defend it with Shān Gōng Wǔ Xiān."
There was no reply.
When Zhēndìng could not be defended,
Fǔ again memorialized:
"Acting Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān Chái Mào is defending the water stockade in Jìzhōu.
He is isolated and without aid.
If additional troops are not provided,
it is beyond my knowledge what will happen."
In the fourth year,
Fǔ was enfeoffed as Gāoyáng Gōng,
with Xióng, Mò, and Bà Prefectures,
and Gāoyáng, Xìn'ān, Wén'ān, Dàchéng,
Bǎodìng, Jìnghǎi, Bǎochí, Wǔqīng, and Āncì Counties subordinate to him.
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
Yílà Zhòngjiānú could not hold Héjiān.
Fǔ resided in Xìn'ān.
That year,
for his merits, he was promoted to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and was first bestowed the surname Wányán.
In the second month of the second year,
Zhāng Jìn was also promoted to Yuánshuài Zuǒjiānjūn
and bestowed the surname Wányán.
Jìng Ānmín
was from Yǒngxīng County, Déxīng Fǔ.
At the beginning of Zhēnyòu,
he served in the volunteer army,
successively holding positions such as Móukè, Qiānhù, Zǒnglǐng, Wànhù, and Dūtǒng,
all under Miáo Dàorùn's command.
For his merits, he was remotely appointed as magistrate of Dìng'ān County,
promoted to Cǐshǐ of Zhuōzhōu,
remotely appointed Shùntiānjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and served as Tíkòng.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he was remotely appointed Ānwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the second year of Xīngdìng,
he was promoted to Zhī Déxīng Fǔ Shì and Zhōngdū Lù Zǒnglǐng Zhāofǔshǐ.
That year,
Miáo Dàorùn died,
and Ānmín took over his forces.
The Xíngshěng, by Imperial authority, appointed Lǐ Quèlǘ, Cǐshǐ of Zhuōzhōu, as acting Zhōngdū Lù Jīnglüèshǐ.
In the third year,
an Imperial edict made Quèlǘ Zhōngdū Dōnglù Jīnglüèshǐ for the area east of Xióng and Bà,
and Ānmín Zhōngdū Xīlù Jīnglüèshǐ for the area west of Yìzhōu.
All Zhāofǔ officials and garrisons of the Xīshān volunteer army were subordinate to him.
In the fourth year,
he was remotely appointed Zhī Déxīng Fǔ Shì,
acting Yuánshuài Zuǒjiānjūn,
and served in the Zhōngdū Xīlù Yuánshuàifǔ.
In the third month,
Ānmín submitted a memorial, saying:
"Miáo Dàorùn pacified over fifty cities in prefectures and counties.
His achievements were immense.
Liú Duó, the Xījīng Lù Jīnglüèshǐ, envied his achievements
and sowed discord between Jiǎ Yǔ, Lǐ Chēn and Dàorùn,
causing them to attack each other,
and ultimately killed Dàorùn through a conspiracy.
Duó ordered his subordinates, Liú Zhìyuán and others, to plunder more than twenty family members of Zhènfǔ Sūn Zīsūn and Zhāofǔ Yáng Déshèng,
imprisoning them in a mountain stockade.
If Duó continues to reside there,
I fear it will lead to disaster."
Liú Duó also dispatched his deputy, Liú Zhāng, to Nánjīng to complain,
and also stated:
"Ānmín invaded Fēihú territory,
arrogantly distributed appointments,
misled the people,
and forcefully compelled Zǒnglǐng Féng Tōng and others to pay silver and grain.
He demanded Wáng Yànhuī, Zǒnglǐng of Fēihú, and the controllers Liú Zhìyuán and Dù Guì,
intending to appoint them as subordinates.
Yànhuī and the others refused him,
whereupon he killed Guì and flogged Zhìyuán,
ultimately driving Yànhuī away."
He also said:
"My position as Jīnglüè is lowly,
which has led to Zòngyí Lǐ Bǎishān and others constantly plotting to harm me.
I beg permission to resign."
The court deliberated.
Liú Duó's original purpose was to recruit fugitives.
Now, he and Ānmín are accusing each other, causing disputes.
When Miáo Dàorùn died,
Ānmín actually took over his forces.
Yànhuī's troops and others were originally subordinate to Dàorùn,
and should obey Ānmín's command.
Therefore, Duó was recalled.
Shortly after,
he was enfeoffed as Yìshuǐ Gōng,
with Zhuō, Yì, Ānsù, and Bǎo Prefectures,
and Jūnshì Chuān, Jìlù, Sānbǎohé, Běijiāng, Fánshān Zhài, Qīngbáikǒu, Cháotiān Zhài, Shuǐgǔ, Huāngǔ, and Dōng'ān Zhài subordinate to him.
In the tenth month,
Ānmín led troops to Fánshān
and recaptured Yánchē Zhài.
Dàyuán troops besieged the mountain stockade where Ānmín resided.
Tíkòng Mǎ Bào and others defending the stockade surrendered with Ānmín's wife and children and the old and weak.
When Ānmín's army heard of this, they were alarmed and chaotic.
The consensus was to surrender to protect their wives and children.
Ānmín and the administrator Hǎo Duān refused to comply,
and were subsequently killed.
An Imperial edict posthumously granted him Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Guō Wénzhèn, courtesy name Zhěngzhī,
was a native of Tàiyuán.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Chéng'ān.
He successively held official posts, reaching Cǐshǐ of Liáozhōu.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
Bìlán Ālǔdài, the Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ, requested that Liáozhōu be elevated to a military governorship.
The court deliberated that the city and population of Liáozhōu were not commensurate with a military governorship,
but Wénzhèn had merit and deserved promotion.
Therefore, he was appointed Xuānchāi Cóngyí Dūtíkòng with his current rank.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
an Imperial edict ordered Wénzhèn to assist Miáo Dàorùn
in recovering Zhōngdū,
but they stopped when Dàorùn and Jiǎ Tóng attacked each other.
Wén Zhèn (文振) governed Liáozhōu (遼州),
deeply gaining the hearts of the people.
In the third year of Xīngdìng (興定) (1219),
he was transferred to the remote appointment of Vice Grand Administrator (Fù liúshǒu 副留守) of Zhōngdū (中都),
concurrently acting as Left Superintendent of the Grand Marshal (Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān 元帥左都監),
overseeing the affairs of the Grand Marshal's Residence (Yuánshuài Fǔ 元帥府) in Hédōng Běilù (河東北路).
His positions as Cìshǐ (刺史) and Cóngyí (從宜) remained as before.
Wén Zhèn (文振) persuaded more than two hundred villages in the eastern mountains of Tàiyuán (太原) to surrender,
relocating the old and young to mountain strongholds,
and gaining seven thousand able-bodied men.
These were stationed in various camps and stockades
to protect the autumn harvest.
Wén Zhèn (文振) memorialized:
"If in autumn the sky is clear and there are no enemy troops,
we can directly seize Tàiyuán (太原),
and Hédōng (河東) can be recovered."
An imperial edict graciously granted his request.
In the tenth month,
acting as Right Superintendent of the Grand Marshal (Yuánshuài Yòu Dūjiān 元帥右都監) and overseeing the affairs of the Grand Marshal's Residence,
he, together with Zhāng Kāi (張開) and the troops from Jiānhé (堅合) and Táizhōu (臺州), recaptured Tàiyuán (太原).
In the fourth year (1220),
an edict elevated Lèpíng (樂平) county to Gāozhōu (臯州),
and Xīzhāngzhài (西張寨) in Shòuyáng (壽陽) county to Jìnzhōu (晉州).
This was done at Wén Zhèn's (文振) request.
Wén Zhèn (文振) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yáng Zǐyún (揚子雲) said,
'If control is exercised correctly, then all the world's schemers and deceivers will be made to serve;
if control is lost, then all the world's schemers and deceivers will become enemies.'
Those who possess the realm must carefully consider how to exercise control.
Since the military campaigns in Héshuò (河朔),
the prefectures and counties have been desolate,
with no officials.
Ruffians and fierce soldiers have taken advantage of the situation, believing they have achieved their ambitions,
usurping titles and positions,
carving up territories and competing with each other, invading and plundering.
Although there are officials appointed by the court, they cannot take up their posts.
How can one possibly enumerate
all their unlawful deeds?
It is requested that the Grand Marshal's Residence (Shuài Fǔ 帥府) be allowed to act on its own discretion, requesting expediency,
arrogantly boasting to aggrandize its power.
Its hidden motives can surely be known.
The imperial court then appeases them,
granting and entrusting them with power,
to the extent that they rival and are equal in strength to the various Grand Marshal's Residences (Shuài Fǔ 帥府),
not being subordinate to each other.
The Shǎnxī Xíngshěng (陝西行省) is nominally in overall control,
but it is far away,
and the roads are blocked,
making it difficult to hear of matters quickly.
Therefore, they are presumptuous and unrestrained, fearing nothing.
Neighboring circuits look on, not daring to interfere.
Since the fall of Píngyáng (平陽) city,
no Xíngshěng (行省) has been established in Hébĕi (河北).
Trusted officials of the imperial court no longer travel back and forth to spread imperial decrees and teachings.
Only messenger-envoys are sent to report.
The relevant authorities ply them with wine and food,
delight them with goods and wealth,
borrowing their prestige to jointly deceive the imperial court.
Once treachery and opportunism prevail,
they become arrogant and unrestrained,
and what kind of unforeseen changes will not occur?
This is why your subject has been heartbroken day and night and worried about this.
It is requested that honest and incorruptible officials be dispatched to all places to investigate,
so that the actual advantages and disadvantages of each locality may be known.
Your subject observes that in Zézhōu (澤州) and Lùzhōu (潞州) and other places, fodder and grain are still abundant,
and the population is still large.
The terrain is mostly rugged.
It is requested that trusted ministers be selected to re-establish a Xíngshěng (行省) there,
with all matters subject to its control.
With superiors and subordinates mutually supporting each other, they can be commanded like arms and fingers.
Then the national power will grow stronger day by day,
and evil will not sprout."
At this time,
Zézhōu (澤州) and Lùzhōu (潞州) had already been assigned to Zhāng Kāi (張開) for planning via imperial edict.
Wén Zhèn's (文振) words could not be fully implemented,
and only Nánjīng Bīngmǎshǐ (南京兵馬使) Shùjiǎsài yě (術甲賽也) was ordered to establish a Grand Marshal's Residence (Shuài Fǔ 帥府) in Huái (懷) and Mèng (孟) only.
That year,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jìnyáng (Jìnyáng Gōng 晉陽公),
and all of Hédōng Běilù (河東北路) was under his jurisdiction.
Wén Zhèn (文振) memorialized:
"Mèngzhōu (孟州) always uses cunning and unruly individuals to act as its prefectural administrators.
The imperial court is hesitant to replace them and simply allows them to lead.
Last year,
Bódéhé (伯德和) acted as Cìshǐ (刺史).
Tíkòng (提控) Bódé'ān (伯德安) murdered him
and seized his position.
The Hédōng Xíngshěng (河東行省) appointed Chén Jǐngfán (陳景璠) to replace Ān (安).
Ān (安), unable to submit internally,
then falsely accused Jǐngfán (景璠) of a capital crime.
Before the imperial court could investigate,
Ān (安) immediately drove him out.
Ashamed to be subject to my control,
he declared to the multitude
that once the roads became somewhat passable, he would submit to the control of Duke Shān (Shān Gōng 山公).
Now Zhēndìng (真定) is already indefensible,
yet Ān (安) still yearns for it endlessly.
When I levy troops from the various prefectures,
Ān (安) invariably uses deceptive words to refuse to send them.
If I were to raise an army,
it would be creating an enemy myself,
which is not beneficial to the state.
Hearing that Ān (安) has a daughter,
I, in violation of regulations, immediately arranged for my grand-nephew Shù (述) to marry her.
Ān (安) then agreed.
I do not wish to be related by marriage to Ān (安),
but for the sake of the public good,
I reluctantly consented.
Since forming this marital tie,
Ān (安) has been somewhat compliant and followed royal commands.
I dared to marry her when it was not appropriate to do so by law,
and I ask for punishment for this crime."
Xuānzōng (宣宗) praised his intention
and sent a close minister to comfort and instruct him.
Wén Zhèn (文振) further memorialized:
"Wǔ Xiān's (武仙) territory is very large.
Although he and the Línzhōu Yuánshuài Fǔ (林州元帥府) are jointly recruiting and pacifying,
it is requested that officials from the local prefectures and counties be selected,
their duties be emphasized,
and they work together to settle the people,
so that the area can return to stability."
Xuānzōng (宣宗) adopted his strategy.
In the fifth year (1221),
Wén Zhèn (文振) memorialized:
"The prefectures under my jurisdiction—Lánzhōu (嵐州), Guǎnbǎo (管保), Àozhōu (隩州), Shízhōu (石州), Nínghuà (寧化), and Báodé (保德)—
have vast and distant territories,
making it impossible for me to fully understand their advantages and disadvantages,
which may jeopardize major military and national plans.
Your subject observes that Jiāzhōu Cìshǐ (葭州刺史) Gǔlǐjiǎ Púchá (古里甲蒲察) possesses extraordinary wisdom and courage,
and is deeply familiar with the situation in Hédōng (河東).
It is requested that he be ordered to oversee the affairs of the Grand Marshal's Residence (Xíng Yuánshuài Fǔ Shì 行元帥府事),
or serve as the Overall Commander of Troops (Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn 兵馬都總管) for this circuit,
sharing governance with me."
An edict instructed Wén Zhèn (文振) to choose a suitable person and place him in a convenient location,
remaining subject to Wén Zhèn's (文振) control.
Shàngdǎng Gōng (上黨公) Zhāng Kāi (張開) enticed Wén Zhèn's (文振) officers and soldiers with rich rewards,
and quite a few deserted to him.
An edict ordered the distribution of millet from Liáozhōu (遼州) and Lùzhōu (潞州) to relieve the famine in Tàiyuán (太原),
but Zhāng Kāi (張開) did not comply.
Wén Zhèn (文振) reported the matter,
and an edict was issued, sending an envoy to comfort and instruct him.
Wén Zhèn (文振) reiterated his previous request
to have Jiāzhōu Cìshǐ (葭州刺史) Gǔlǐjiǎ Púchá (古里甲蒲察) jointly govern the prefectures west of Lánzhōu (嵐州) and Guǎnbǎo (管保).
The imperial decree assented,
further ordering him to determine what was appropriate after the autumn defense.
Wén Zhèn (文振) requested to distribute millet from Shàngdǎng (上黨) to provide for Tàiyuán (太原).
An edict ordered Wén Zhèn (文振) to discuss and decide with Zhāng Kāi (張開).
Shortly thereafter,
an edict placed Shízhōu (石州) under the jurisdiction of the Jìnyáng Gōng Fǔ (晉陽公府).
In the first year of Yuánguāng (元光) (1222),
Línzhōu Xíng Yuánshuài Fǔ (林州行元帥府) Wéiliáng (惟良) incurred blame and was recalled.
Wén Zhèn (文振) memorialized:
"Recently, I heard that Wéiliáng (惟良) was recalled.
Your subject secretly believes this is inappropriate.
Wéiliáng (惟良) served in Línzhōu (林州) for five years,
and his governance was lenient and generous,
greatly winning the hearts of the people.
Now that he has been recalled,
the army and people block the roads, weeping and begging him to stay.
Not long after his departure,
a crowd of 'dagger-point' bandits (biāo jiān zhī zhòng 鏢尖之衆) rebelled
and drove out the Recruiter and Pacifier (Zhāofǔ Shǐ 招撫使) Kāng Táng (康瑭).
It is requested that Wéiliáng (惟良) be sent back to Línzhōu (林州) for convenience."
This was not granted.
Wén Zhèn (文振) submitted a letter:
"It is requested that the former Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事) Xū Dǐng (胥鼎) be sent to govern the Xíngshěng (行省) in Hébĕi (河北).
All public and marshal's residences should be subject to his control.
An imperial edict should inform the people that the intention to not abandon the remnants of the populace has not been forgotten.
Afterwards, combine the elite troops from Hénán (河南) and Shǎnxī (陝西) to recover the territory with combined strength."
This was not reported.
Wén Zhèn (文振) further memorialized:
"The people of Héshuò (河朔) look south with anticipation.
Your subject has repeatedly petitioned the Privy Council (Shūfǔ 樞府),
but they only speak of combining the prefectural troops.
Although the public residences (Gōngfǔ 公府) are called enfeoffments,
their strength is actually weak and scattered,
and they are not subordinate to each other,
and are attacked wherever they are.
If the imperial court does not immediately send troops to recover Hébĕi (河北),
the people will think that it has abandoned Héshuò (河朔),
which is a very poor plan."
Wén Zhèn (文振) largely wished to bring Xū Dǐng (胥鼎) out of retirement to establish a Xíngshěng (行íngshěng),
stabilize Hébĕi (河北),
but the imperial court could not adopt his suggestion.
In the second year (1223),
an edict ordered Wén Zhèn (文振) to reinforce Shǐ Yǒng (史詠) in recovering Hédōng (河東).
That year,
Liáozhōu (遼州) could not be defended,
so its troops were moved to Mèngzhōu (孟州).
His subordinates, such as Hǎo Ān (郝安), were made Wén Zhèn's (文振) deputies
to guard the various mountain strongholds along the range.
Wén Zhèn (文振) resigned from the public residence (Gōngfǔ 公府),
but an edict did not permit it.
Shortly thereafter,
Wén Zhèn's (文振) subordinate, Fénzhōu Zhāofǔ Shǐ (汾州招撫使) Wáng Yù (王遇), and Mèngzhōu Fángyù Shǐ (孟州防禦使) Nàlán Móugǔlǔ (納蘭謀古魯) were at odds.
He was then moved to Wèizhōu (衞州).
However, this also could not be formed into an army.
Until the Zhèngdà (正大) period (1224-1232),
he remained in Wèizhōu (衞州).
Hú Tiānzuò (字 Jǐngshān),
a native of Guǎnzhōu.
Initially, he used local militias to defend his prefecture,
and through accumulated merits, he became a Lesser Grand Master (shǎo zhōng dàfū) and Prefect (cìshǐ) of Guǎnzhōu.
In the second year of Xīngdìng (1218),
he was remotely appointed Joint Administrator (tóngzhī) of Tàiyuán Prefecture (Tàiyuán Fǔ),
with his prefectural post remaining unchanged.
That year,
Píngyáng fell.
He was then reassigned as Joint Administrator of Píngyáng Prefecture (Píngyáng Fǔ).
In the third year (1219),
Píngyáng was recovered.
Tiānzuò said:
"Both Fén and Lù have Marshal Offices (shuàifǔ).
Píngyáng is a major strategic town,
now gradually restored.
The prefectures and counties under its jurisdiction amount to no less than one hundred thousand households,
and those returning to their occupations are ceaseless.
It far surpasses Fén and Lù in importance.
〔一０〕It should be treated on par with them."
At that time,
Jìn'ān and Lánzhōu both had Marshal Offices.
Tiānzuò was then appointed Expedient Pacification Commissioner (biànyí zhāofǔ shǐ) and acting Left Supervisor of the Marshal Office (quán yuánshuài zuǒ dūjiān).
In the fourth year (1220),
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Píngyáng (Píngyáng Gōng),
and Píngyáng and Jìn'ān Prefectures (Píngyáng Fǔ, Jìn'ān Fǔ),
along with Xí and Jí Prefectures (Xí Zhōu, Jí Zhōu), were subordinated to him.
Tiānzuò requested that Yìchéng County (Yìchéng Xiàn) of Jìn'ān Prefecture be made Yìzhōu,
with Yuánqǔ and Jiàng Counties (Yuánqǔ Xiàn, Jiàng Xiàn) subordinated to it.
He also requested the establishment of Píngshuǐ County (Píngshuǐ Xiàn) west of the Fén River (Fén Hé).
The court granted all his requests.
Initially,
Xuān Chéng was subordinate to Chéng Zhuó.
After Zhuó's death,
Chéng led his forces to secure Xízhōu,
and was appointed Joint Administrator of Xízhōu Military and Civil Affairs (tóngzhī Xízhōu jūnzhōu shì) and concurrently Supervisor of Military Horses (jiān tíkòng jūnmǎ).
Chéng enhanced his armaments
and recruited desperadoes,
harboring other ambitions.
At that time,
Xízhōu was engaged in warfare
and could not be controlled.
Tiānzuò requested the establishment of more strategically important prefectures and counties
to divide his power.
Pú County (Pú Xiàn) in Xízhōu's territory was most critical;
it could be elevated to a prefecture.
Wǔchéng Town (Wǔchéng Zhèn) in Xíchuān could be made a county,
and officials should be selected to guard them.
An imperial edict elevated Pú County to Púzhōu,
subordinating Dàníng County (Dàníng Xiàn) to it,
and Wǔchéng Town to Wǔchéng County.
Tiānzuò defended Píngyáng for four years,
achieving numerous merits.
An imperial edict recorded his son, Dìnggē, as a court attendant (fèngzhí).
In the tenth month of the first year of Yuánguāng (1222),
Qīnglóngbǎo was in critical danger.
An imperial edict ordered Gǔlǐjiǎ Shílún to join Zhāng Kāi and Guō Wénzhèn with troops to rescue it.
They reached thirty li east of Tánpíngzhài,
but could not advance.
The Prefectural Administrator (zhīfǔ shì), Shùhǔ Hūshīlái, and the Overall Commander (zǒnglǐng tíkòng), Wáng Hé, each brought their troops to surrender.
They demanded their wives and children at the city gates.
Both soldiers and commoners collapsed,
and Tiānzuò was captured and taken out.
Tiānzuò had already surrendered.
An imperial edict ordered the execution of Hūshīlái's son who was in Nánjīng,
and commanded Tiānzuò's son, Dìnggē, to continue in his previous post.
Tiānzuò had already accepted official titles from Dà Yuán
and wore a tiger tally,
pacifying the people of Huái and Mèng.
Upon hearing this, Dìnggē hanged himself.
He was posthumously granted General of Trustworthy Valor (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Joint Administrator of Suīzhōu Military and Civil Affairs (tóngzhī Suīzhōu jūnzhōu shì).
An imperial edict ordered Zhāng Kāi and Guō Wénzhèn to summon Tiānzuò.
Tiānzuò arrived at Jìyuán and attempted to escape,
having first sent someone to present a memorial to Nánjīng.
The great generals of Dà Yuán, disliking his vacillation,
then executed him.
After Tiānzuò's death,
Xuānzōng appointed Shǐ Yǒng, the Joint Administrator of Píngyáng Prefecture, to provisionally administer the affairs of the Duke of Píngyáng's office (Píngyáng Gōng Fǔ).
Later, he was enfeoffed as Duke of Píngyáng.
When Píngyáng was first broken,
Yǒng's father, Zuò, and mother, Lady Xiāo, hid in a cave.
They were sought out and captured,
and Zuò was made to summon Yǒng.
Zuò then hanged himself,
and Lady Xiāo escaped and returned.
Yǒng's wife, Lady Gěng, also died by her own hand.
Xuānzōng posthumously granted Zuò the title of Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Rónglù Dàfū) and Duke of Jīngzhào Commandery (Jīngzhào Jùn Gōng),
with the posthumous name Chéngzhōng.
Lady Xiāo was enfeoffed as Grand Lady of Jīngzhào Commandery (Jīngzhào Jùn Tàifūrén)
and bestowed the honorific Guīyì.
Lady Gěng was posthumously granted Lady of Jīngzhào Commandery (Jīngzhào Jùn Fūrén),
with the posthumous name Yìliè.
Not long after,
Yǒng requested to move inland,
relocating his army to Xièzhōu and Hézhōng Prefecture (Hézhōng Fǔ).
Zhāng Kāi was granted the surname Wányán.
He was a native of Jǐngzhōu.
Towards the end of Zhìníng,
when troops rose in Héběi,
Kāi rallied local militias for a firm defense.
Through accumulated merits, he was remotely appointed Joint Administrator of Qīngzhōu Defense (tóngzhī Qīngzhōu fángyù shì)
and concurrently Joint Administrator of Guānzhōu Affairs (tóngzhī Guānzhōu shì).
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu (1216),
Kāi led his command to recover Héjiān Prefecture (Héjiān Fǔ) and the two prefectures of Cāng and Xiàn (Cāng, Xiàn Èr Zhōu), comprising thirteen counties.
Kāi had two hundred blank imperial edicts (xuānchì) left by the Pacification Commissioner's Office (Xuānfǔ Sī).
He memorialized requesting permission to provisionally appoint officials,
restoring former officials to the recovered prefectures and counties where he was stationed,
and filling vacancies.
An imperial edict promoted him to Joint Administrator of Guānzhōu Military and Civil Affairs (tóngzhī Guānzhōu jūnzhōu shì).
Kāi recovered Qīngzhōu
and requested to exchange salt for grain.
An imperial edict granted him grain.
He was promoted to Prefect of Guānzhōu and acting Commissioner of Pacification of the Prefecture (quán běnzhōu jīnglüè shǐ).
It was at this point
that he was first granted the surname Wányán.
Kāi memorialized requesting discretionary authority
and discussed how Qímén, Ānyáng, and Líyáng all had dikes blocking the water,
obstructing river transport.
He requested the opening of waterways,
but received no reply.
Guānzhōu ran out of grain.
That autumn,
his army moved to Huīzhōu.
He requested three thousand shí of wheat seeds and three hundred donkeys/mules or two hundred strings of precious currency (bǎoquàn).
The Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) refused.
The Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) memorialized:
"Kāi fought his way here from Guānzhōu,
having long shown meritorious service.
He wishes to have his army cultivate crops to sustain themselves,
but the relevant authorities, calculating small expenses, refuse to grant it.
We request a decisive imperial decision
to grant him wheat seeds.
If there are no oxen,
provide him with precious currency."
The edict was approved.
That year,
Tóngguān fell,
and he was summoned to guard Nánjīng.
In the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
he was remotely appointed Prefect of Zézhōu.
In the second year (1218),
he was remotely appointed Joint Administrator of Zhāngdé Prefecture (Zhāngdé Fǔ) and concurrently Overall Commander.
In the third year (1219),
he was appointed Pacification Commissioner of Lùzhōu.
The Línzhōu Marshal Office relocated the people of Lù to populate Línzhōu,
but later sent them back.
Kāi requested to be subordinated to the Jìn'ān Marshal Office
or to have a Marshal Office established alongside Línzhōu,
each governing independently.
In the tenth month,

Kāi, as acting Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì (quán Zhāoyì Jūn Jiédù Shǐ), remotely appointed Defense Commissioner of Mèngzhōu (Mèngzhōu Fángyù Shǐ), acting Left Supervisor of the Marshal Office, and administering the Marshal Office affairs,
along with Guō Wénzhèn, recovered Tàiyuán.
In the fourth year (1220),
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Shàngdǎng (Shàngdǎng Gōng),
with Zé, Lù, and Qìn Prefectures (Zé, Lù, Qìn Zhōu) subordinated to him.
In the fifth year (1221),
an imperial edict restored Shè County as Chóngzhōu,
following Kāi's request.
In the first year of Yuánguāng (1222),
Gāopíng County and Zézhōu were recovered.
In the second year (1223),
he fought a great battle at Húguān
and gained merits.
Later, Lùzhōu was in critical danger.
Kāi memorialized:
"Enfeoffing ducal offices (gōngfǔ) solidifies the frontier defenses.
Now, Hú Tiānzuò has left Píngyáng,
and Guō Wénzhèn has moved south to Hédōng.
Among the ducal offices, only I and Shǐ Yǒng remain.
I request that Zé and Qìn Prefectures be elevated to military districts (jiézhèn)
to strengthen their defense."
An imperial edict designated Zé as Zhōngchāng Army (Zhōngchāng Jūn)
and Qìn as Yìshèng Army (Yìshèng Jūn).
The multitude at ● Jiānzhài in Línzhōu rebelled,
expelling the Pacification Commissioner Kāng Táng,
and pushing Dù Xiān as Pacification Commissioner.
Kāi requested Lú Zhīruì as his deputy
to lead these people on his behalf.
He further memorialized:
"I hear that Guō Wénzhèn is drawing provisions from Huái and Mèng,
Shǐ Yǒng has moved to Xièzhōu,
and Gāo Lún has relocated to Gébozhài.
They are each defending themselves.
Where can the people turn for support?
I lead an isolated army,
with no internal stores
and no external reinforcements.
I dare not evade the blame for a loss of defense,
but I fear it will only increase the court's worries."
During the Zhèngdà period,
Lùzhōu fell.
Kāi resided in Nánjīng,
his troops dispersed.
Though known as an elder duke,
he was no different from a commoner.
In the early Tiānxīng period,
he was reinstated
and, along with Liú Yì, appointed Western Marshal.
Leading the Ānpíng Commandant Jì Gāng's army of five thousand, they attacked Wèizhōu.
They were defeated at Báigōng Miào.
At this time,
Āizōng fled to Guīdé.
Kāi and Liú Yì plotted to gather the scattered troops and follow him to Wèi,
but it did not succeed.
They then fled west with Chéngyì
and were all killed by common households.
When the Ducal Residence was first established,
Kāi, along with Shān Gōng and Wǔ Xiān, was the strongest.
Later, he stationed his troops at Mǎwǔ Shān
and sent a messenger via a secret path to request twenty thousand *shi* of grain.
Those in power found it difficult
and only provided two thousand *shi*.
When the ducal residence's generals and aides received the report, they dared not inform him.
When Kāi heard,
he prepared a feast and summoned his generals, saying,
"The court has treated me exceptionally well.
Today, I shall get drunk with you all."
When the generals asked why,
he said,
"Recently, I requested grain because it was exhausted,
asking for twenty thousand and receiving two thousand.
This means my lord and ministers do not regard me as they do Wǔ Xiān and his like."
At this time,
Guō Wénzhèn was to Kāi's northwest,
bearing the brunt of the military operations.
The people were poor and the land barren.
Kāi also did not follow orders to distribute grain to Wénzhèn's army.
Wénzhèn was driven to destitution and flight,
making Kāi's position increasingly isolated,
which led to his defeat.
Yān Níng was
initially a Tíkòng of Jǔzhōu,
defending Tiānshèng Zhài.
He, Tián Zhuó of Yìdū, and Ménggǔ Gāng of Dōngpíng formed a mutually supporting alliance.
Although Shāndōng was devastated,
it still relied heavily on these three men.
The Red Jacket bandit Wáng Gōngxǐ occupied Zhùzi Gū,
[一一] and led his forces to raid and seize Yízhōu.
Níng attacked and repelled him,
thus retaking Yízhōu.
The details are in the biography of Tián Zhuó.
Níng repeatedly defeated the Red Jacket bandits,
and persuaded Hú Qī and Hú Bā to surrender,
taking them as trusted confidants.
Many among the bandits, upon hearing this, wished to surrender.
He was successively promoted to the nominal position of Tóngzhī Ānhuà Jūn Jiédù Shǐshì and Shāndōng Ānfǔ Fùshǐ.
In the fourth year of Xīngdìng,
he was enfeoffed as Dōngjǔ Gōng,
and the Yìdū Fǔlù was subordinate to him.
In the fifth year,
he, Ménggǔ Gāng, and Wáng Tíngyù preserved Dōngpíng.
For this accomplishment, he was promoted to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
He returned to Tiānshèng
and died in battle.
Ménggǔ Gāng memorialized:
"Níng exerted ultimate loyalty and filiality.
Although he held the position of a senior duke,
his ancestors had not received any noble titles.
After his death, his elderly and young dependents have no clothing or food.
May an extraordinary grace be granted to encourage men of integrity and righteousness."
An imperial edict posthumously granted his late grandfather Gāo the title of Yínqīng Rónglù Dàfū,
his grandmother Zhāng Shì the title of Fànyáng Jùn Fūrén,
his father Xīqiān the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and his mother Péng Shì, stepmother Xǔ Shì, and wife Huò Shì all the title of Fànyáng Jùn Fūrén.
Fifty-two members of his clan were also provided with stipends.
After Zhāng Lín of Yìdū expelled Tián Zhuó,
and subsequently Níng died,
Ménggǔ Gāng's position became isolated.
He moved his army to Pīzhōu,
and Shāndōng could no longer be defended.
The encomium says: When Miáo Dàorùn died,
his territory was divided in two.
Jìng Ānmín possessed the western half.
The eastern half of the division was later held by Zhāng Fǔ,
but there was no northern border.
Generally, the nine dukes enfeoffed,
as recorded in the Xuānzōng Shílù, are thus.
Other books record Cānghǎi Gōng Zhāng Jìn, Héjiān Gōng Yílà Zhōnggē, Yìshuǐ Gōng Zhāng Jìn, and Jìnyáng Gōng Guō Dòng.
These must have been successively enfeoffed during the Zhèngdà period,
like Shǐ Yǒng succeeding Hú Tiānzuò,
but this cannot be verified.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 57 Niángé Nùshēn (with Liú Tiānqǐ attached), Wányán Lóushì, Wūgǔlún Hào, Zhāng Tiāngāng, Wányán Zhòngdé
Niángé Nùshēn
entered officialdom through his family connections, or, some say, as a *cèlùn* jinshi.
In the early Tiānxīng period,
he was
an Assistant Prefect of Kāifēng Fǔ,
known for his strictness and efficiency.
In the fifth month of that year,
he was promoted to Chénzhōu Fángyù Shǐ.
At the time, there was widespread warfare and looting,
and roads were impassable.
Nùshēn received his mandate and, resolutely, rode alone along a secret path.
Since the start of the war, Chénzhōu's
military and civilian population had all evacuated to other commanderies.
Nùshēn selected officials and administrators for it,
clarified orders,
completed the city walls,
erected dwellings,
filled granaries,
and prepared equipment.
Before long,
he gathered hundreds of thousands of displaced people.
One *hú* of rice cost four *liǎng* of silver,
and the markets were bustling like those in Biàn.
People from the endangered and distressed capital looked towards him and returned in an endless stream,
and he was thus designated the "Eastern-Southern Lifeline."
The following year,
Āizōng fled to Guīdé.
Chénzhōu was renamed Jīnxīng Jūn,
and an envoy was dispatched to commend and instruct,
appointing Nùshēn as Jiédù Shǐ.
Soon after, he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì
and established the Xíng Shàngshū Shěng in Chénzhōu.
Thereupon,
Nùshēn established five Commandants to lead his troops:
Jiànwēi Zhū Fèn, Hǔwēi Púchá Hédá, Zhènwǔ Lǐ Shùn'ér, Zhènwēi Wáng Yì, and Guǒyì Wányán Mǒu.
All those who came from the Zhāofǔ Sī were placed under the command of the Commandant's Office.
At this time,
there was no day without battle,
and the troops garrisoned in the prefecture numbered over one hundred thousand.
Nùshēn consulted with his officials, saying,
"The large army arrives daily,
but our prefecture's grain supplies are limited.
What shall we do?"
So he reduced the soldiers' rations:
what was one *hú* and five *dǒu* per month became one *hú*,
then eight *dǒu*,
then six *dǒu*.
Generals, however, received no rations.
The morale of the people began to sour.
Therefore, Lǐ Shùn'ér and Commandant Cuī had ulterior motives,
and Tíkòng Liú and Tíkòng Wányán Bùrúgē were involved.
Nùshēn knew of their plot
and always kept troops for self-defense.
When he heard that the Dà Yuán army was going to Zhūxiān Zhèn for trade,
Nùshēn dispatched two hundred men from each of the five Commandant armies,
with Lǐ Shùn'ér and Vice-Commandant Cuī Mǒu leading them,
to raid Xiàngchéng Zhài.
He ordered Sun Zhènfǔ to summon Shùn'ér to discuss military matters.
When Sun arrived at his house,
Shùn'ér had already donned his armor.
Sun wanted to see his saber.
Shùn'ér drew it and showed it to him.
Sun's face changed color,
and he immediately ran out the door.
Shùn'ér pursued and killed him,
then mounted his horse
and led two hundred men into the provincial office.
He addressed the soldiers, saying,
"The Xíngshěng has cut military rations.
If you want to eat your fill, follow me;
if not, follow the Xíngshěng."
Thereupon,
the soldiers in the office all remained seated and did not rise.
Nùshēn heard of the mutiny and fled to the rear hall,
but was pursued and killed.
Tíkòng Liú Mǒu harmed him,
removed his tiger tally, and gave it to Shùn'ér,
also killing his sons, nephews, son-in-law, and the local Commandant Wáng.
Shùn'ér ordered all five Commandant armies to arm themselves
and guard the streets.
He declared himself Xíngshěng
and appointed marshals and commandants.
Because Tíkòng Liú's words were not compliant,
he beheaded him in their midst.
The next day,
he sent Kèshíliè Zhèngzhī to convey his submission to Biàn.
Cuī Lì then sent his younger brother Yǐ Jiù to confer on Shùn'ér the title of Huáiyáng Jūn Jiédù Shǐ,
with the Xíngshěng office remaining as before.
Not long after,
Hǔwēi Commandant Púchá Hédá and Marshal Gāo killed all of Shùn'ér's followers
and led the entire city to Cáizhōu.
The Dà Yuán army became aware
and pursued them to Sūnjiālín,
where few of the hundreds of thousands of old and young escaped.
Initially,
Núshen heard of Cuī Lì’s coup
and sent someone to investigate the situation.
Meanwhile, Shùn'ér and Commander Cuī also secretly sent people to conspire with Cuī Lì.
It so happened that they went and returned at the same time as the person sent by Núshen.
Shùn'ér feared that his plot would be exposed,
so he acted even more quickly.
Núshen also knew of the plot,
and thus sent troops to attack Xiàngchéng,
intending to ambush and kill him during his journey.
However, he was preempted.
Liú Tiānqǐ rose from a commoner,
and was initially very ordinary and vulgar.
When Biànjīng was under strict戒严,
he once submitted a memorial to appeal to the emperor and chancellor,
wishing to be temporarily granted an office to prove his worth.
He often spoke of the military strategies of the Warring States period,
and Píngzhāng Báshā and others believed him,
ordering the Jǐngdé Temple to supervise the construction of three thousand leather chariots.
In the first year of Tiānxīng,
he was appointed Dū Zhāofǔshǐ,
wearing a golden tally.
When summoned for an audience,
he requested to go to Chénzhōu to transport grain.
The emperor agreed,
and everyone at the time secretly laughed at his good fortune.
When he arrived at Chén,
his military campaigns were notably strategic,
and he often achieved success in battles.
The people of Chén greatly relied on and respected him.
During Shùn'ér’s coup,
Tiānqǐ remained resolute and refused to comply,
and was consequently killed.
At the same time, a Tángkuò Zhāofǔshǐ also refused to yield and died.
The three Wányán Lóushì,
all members of the imperial clan,
were distinguished by their seniority
due to their shared name at the time.
In the eighth year of Zhèngdà,
Qìngshānnú abandoned Jīngzhào.
It so happened that the Yīngyáng Dūwèi, Dà Lóushì, was transporting military equipment to Báilùyuán,
where he encountered a large army and engaged in battle.
After his weapons were exhausted,
he tied a golden plaque to a sash
and fought fiercely until death.
In the first month of the ninth year,
the grand army reached Xiāngchéng.
Marshal Zhōng Lóushì and Xiǎo Lóushì met them with three thousand cavalry at Rǔfén.
At that time, the grand army, with thirty or forty cavalry, entered Xiāngchéng,
drove out the post horses,
then entered the East Camp,
killing a chiliarch.
The Jīn people only then became aware.
The two Lóushì were drinking with their generals and officers on New Year's Day,
and all were too drunk to command troops.
Consequently, they were defeated
and retreated to Xǔzhōu.
Subsequently, an imperial envoy summoned them to the capital.
In the first month of the second year of Tiānxīng,
the Hésuò army collapsed,
and Emperor Āi fled to Guīdé.
Zhōng Lóushì became the commander-in-chief of the Northern Front,
and Xiǎo Lóushì the Right Wing Marshal.
They gathered the disbanded soldiers and General Jiágǔ Jiǔshí and fled to Càizhōu.
The commander of Cài, Wūgǔlún Kǎolǎo, knowing their arrogance, did not admit them.
So they fled to Xīzhōu,
where the commander of Xī, Shímò Jiǔzhù, received them.
At that time, Báihuá, following imperial orders, sent a tiger tally to Jiǔzhù, appointing him as the acting commander of Xīzhōu.
Jiǔzhù dismissed his close attendants,
liked to make a show of himself,
and had numerous retainers filling the roads.
The three Lóushì envied him.
Each, under the pretext of recruiting loyalist soldiers,
gathered five or six hundred men.
The prefecture provided them with armor and weapons.
After a long time,
mutual suspicion gradually arose.
Jiǔzhù also recruited several hundred peddlers and brokers
to form the "Tiger Cub Army,"
and at night, they would don armor as a precaution.
One day,
Jiǔzhù sent a myriad commander to patrol the city.
The three marshals seized him and drove him away,
making him shout,
"Do not emulate me; I wish to open the west gate and rebel!"
Then they executed him.
They then summoned Jiǔzhù.
Jiǔzhù wished not to go,
but fearing that the people of the prefecture would be implicated,
he went with three hundred soldiers.
The three marshals ordered armored soldiers to guard the streets and alleys.
As Jiǔzhù’s followers passed,
they were seized everywhere.
Jiǔzhù entered alone.
The three marshals asked, "Why do you wish to rebel?"
Jiǔzhù replied,
"How could I rebel?"
The three marshals were enraged,
and for a long time, intended to kill him.
Xiǎo Lóushì’s anger somewhat subsided,
and he advocated for Jiǔzhù, who was thus spared from death
and ordered to be put in chains.
Jiágǔ Jiǔshí was appointed commander,
also acting as governor of Xīzhōu.
Cài Commander Kǎolǎo heard that Jiǔzhù had been falsely accused by the three marshals
and submitted a memorial to clarify the matter.
The three marshals also gathered Jiǔzhù’s faults and reported them to the throne.
The court sided with Kǎolǎo’s clarification
and deemed the three marshals unjust.
In the sixth month,
an amnesty decree arrived at Cài.
Kǎolǎo feared that Jiǔzhù would be executed by the three marshals,
so he dispatched two soldiers to swiftly deliver the imperial edict to Xī.
Jiǔzhù was thus pardoned.
When the emperor was about to proceed to Cài,
he secretly summoned Zhōng Lóushì to lead troops to meet him.
Lóushì hesitated for a long time,
then led the soldiers he had recruited to welcome the emperor.
In the seventh month,
the emperor sent an attendant from the Bureau of Imperial Attendants to Xīzhōu to requisition horses,
and immediately summoned Jiǔzhù.
When Jiǔzhù arrived,
he debated with Zhōng Lóushì before the emperor.
At that time, Zhōng Lóushì had already been appointed Tóng Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì.
The emperor did not wish the dispute to continue,
so he dismissed Jiǔzhù from his command,
appointed him Hùbù Lángzhōng,
and made Wūgǔlún Hūlǔ the governor of Xīzhōu.
At this time, local gentry Liú Tū'ér and Mǎ Ānfǔ returned from the court in Cài.
Due to insufficient military provisions, they rebelled and defected to the Sòng,
and the northern gate of the prefecture was burned down by them.
At this time,
there were few troops in the city,
and daily there were defections.
Moreover, it was discovered that the Sòng people had intentions of spying on Xī.
The commander of Xī was afraid,
and submitted a memorial requesting more troops for defense.
The court appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì Mònián Wùdiǎn to govern the branch secretariat in Xīzhōu.
Zhōng Lóushì, as Tóng Qiān Shūmìyuàn Shì, was made commander-in-chief.
Xiǎo Lóushì, as Fù Diǎnjiǎn, was made marshal.
Wáng Jìn was appointed Tányāshuài,
and Jiágǔ Jiǔshí as Dūwèi.
Two hundred loyal and filial cavalry and five hundred infantry were placed under their command,
and the branch secretariat and council were established in Xī.
Before their departure,
the emperor instructed them, saying:
"The Northern armies always achieve complete victory
because they rely on the strength of their northern horses
and the ingenuity of the Central Plains.
We are indeed hard-pressed to match them.
As for the Sòng people,
what are they worth mentioning?
If I had three thousand armored soldiers,
I would have more than enough strength to traverse the Jiāng and Huái regions.
You gentlemen, strive hard!"
On Rénchén day of the eighth month,
the branch secretariat sent a person to report the victory at Zhōngdùdiàn.
Initially,
Wùdiǎn and others went to Xī.
On the night of their arrival,
they secretly dispatched over a hundred loyal and filial cavalry to raid the Sòng camp at Zhōngdù.
Our army all spoke northern dialects,
and also appeared scattered like them.
The Sòng people, seeing this, were shocked, fled, and scattered,
and many were slain and captured.
They also reported that Marshal Zhāng Rùn had not followed orders
and had lost soldiers,
requesting severe punishment.
Lóushì memorialized that Rùn was innocent.
The emperor sent someone to pardon him,
but by the time the pardon arrived,
he had already died in prison.
It was because Rùn was Lóushì’s confidant,
and the case of Jiǔzhù had all been initiated by Rùn.
Wùdiǎn, having discovered this,
executed him for his breach of discipline.
In the ninth month,
Hūlǔ was dismissed from his post
due to his timid retreat
and inability to govern, which caused many people to rebel and leave.
Jiágǔ Jiǔshí was appointed to act as governor of Xīzhōu.
In the eleventh month,
Song forces, twenty thousand strong, came to attack.
Food in the city ran out,
so grain was requisitioned by agreement,
but later it was seized,
with only one斗 kept for every石.
Gold, silk, clothing, and other items were also seized.
Everyone in the city was miserable.
Two months prior,
Caízhōu had sent ten thousand old and young under military escort to seek food.
Northern troops became aware of this
and pursued them twenty里 outside the city,
with only a dozen or so surviving to Xī.
By this time,
communication with Caí was cut off.
The xíngshěng and various commanders spent their days with singing and drinking,
with music never ceasing.
Down to the soldiers, they forcibly married widows and young girls,
extinguishing human decency,
stopping at nothing.
In the first month of the third year, jiǎwǔ,
ominous news from Caí arrived.
The commanders killed the messengers to silence them,
but the common people also knew much of it.
Initially,
the commanders wanted to surrender to the north,
but they suspected each other
and none dared to make the first move.
Several days later,
when news from Caí spread tumultuously,
the commanders dismissed others and met to discuss,
all saying that it would be more convenient to send an envoy to the south.
At that time, Lǐ Yù was an official under the rank of jīnglìguān, serving as tóngqiān of the Mùqīnfǔ and xìnshǐ for Huán Duānguó.
He was then sent to offer terms to the Sòng.
Thereupon, a funeral was held and sacrifices offered.
Àizōng was posthumously honored as Zhāozōng.
The people of the zhōu honored the xíngshěng as lǐngshěng.
The chéngxiàng, zǒngshuài, and zuǒ píngzhāng all took wives.
On the thirteenth day,
the entire city moved south.
Sòng forces burned the zhōulóulǔ.
The old and young of the zhōu crossed the Huái River and traveled south,
entering Luóshān,
and thence circuitously to Xìnyáng.
Northern troops, seeing the fire,
pursued them,
and none escaped.
They also seized and executed officials from the xíngshěng down, for the Sòng.
The Sòng people ordered the officials to enter the city,
under the pretext of granting rewards.
Six or seven hundred people, from wànhù upwards, were all killed.
In the army, there were also those who fought to the death to save their lives.
The Sòng people informed the various armies,
“The culpable officials, from the xíngshěng down, have been dealt with.
You are to encamp safely in Míhúnzhài.”
They then garrisoned troops there.
Later, when they engaged the northern army,
the southern army retreated,
and one whole army was utterly slaughtered.
Wūgǔlún Hào’s original name was Kǎoláo.
He was from the Northeastern Route Zhāotǎosī.
He started his career in the Hùwèi [guards],
and rose through the ranks to Qìngyáng zǒngguǎn.
At the beginning of Tiānxīng,
he was promoted to biànyí zǒngshuài of Caí, Xī, Chén, Yǐng, and other zhōu.
In the second year,
when Àizōng was in Guīdé,
Púchá Guānnu and Guóyòng'ān wanted to move the emperor to Hǎizhōu,
but it was undecided.
Just then, Hào sent over four hundred hū of rice to Guīdé,
and also requested the emperor to move to Caí.
The emperor’s resolve was thus settled.
First, he dispatched the zhíxuèshì Wūgǔlún Púxiān to Caí
to inform the people of Caí of the impending imperial visit.
In the sixth month,
troops from Caí and Xī were summoned to welcome him.
As Caí was a critical defense point,
and fearing unexpected incidents,
an edict ordered Hào not to go too far to welcome the emperor.
On the day xīnmǎo,
the imperial carriage departed Guīdé.
It had been raining for a long time,
and the court officials accompanying him walked in the mud,
eating green dates for sustenance.
After several days, their legs were completely swollen.
Cāncèng Tiāngāng was also in the same condition.
On the day rénchén,
they arrived at Bó.
The emperor wore a yellow robe, a black hat, and a golden rabbit-hawk belt,
with two green and yellow banners leading the way,
and a yellow umbrella behind him,
accompanied by only two or three hundred people
and fifty or so horses.
As they passed through the city,
monks, Daoists, fathers, and elders knelt by the roadside to bow.
The emperor sent a close attendant to instruct them,
“The state has nurtured you for over a hundred years.
Now, I am without virtue,
causing you hardship.
I have nothing more to say.
You must not forget the virtues of your ancestors.”
They all cried, “Long live the Emperor!”
and tears flowed.
They stayed for one day.
Sixty里 south of Bó,
they sought shelter from the rain in Shuānggōusì.
Mugwort filled the eyes,
with no human trace.
The emperor sighed deeply, saying,
“All the living are gone!”
He wept for this.
On this day,
Xiǎolóushì came from Xī to welcome them,
bringing two hundred horses.
On the day jǐhài,
they entered Caí.
A thousand fathers and elders of Caí bowed in rows along the road.
Seeing the emperor’s sparse imperial guard,
none were not moved to tears.
The emperor also sighed for a long time.
In the seventh month,
Hào was made yùshǐ dàfū,
remaining zǒngshuài as before.
Initially,
when Hào defended Caí,
the gates were strictly controlled.
Men and women collecting firewood had their faces marked with ink.
If anyone left with money,
one and a half tenths were taken to supply the army.
When the emperor arrived in Caí,
some suggested this was inconvenient,
so the ban was immediately lifted.
At this time, with the main army far away,
merchants gathered quite a bit.
The common people cheered, thinking they had seen peace again.
Both public and private accumulated wines were consumed in a single day.
Lú Jìn, a local strongman from Yǎnchéng, killed his magistrate,
declaring himself zhāofǔshǐ,
with Fàn Tiānbǎo, formerly jīnglì of Guān and Shǎn Shuàifǔ, as his deputy.
At this point,
Tiānbǎo came to visit,
bringing three hundred shí of wheat, dried venison and deer meat, tea, honey, and other items.
Thereupon, Jìn was granted a golden plaque,
and Tiānbǎo was promoted.
From then on, those who brought tribute arrived continuously.
Subsequently,
the palace attendant diàntóu Sòng Guī and Hào’s wife were dispatched to select palace women for the rear palace.
Several had already been chosen,
when the yòuchéng Hūxiéhǔ remonstrated, saying,
“The common people are ignorant.
They will say that since Your Majesty's arrival, there has been no talk of long-term recovery,
but instead, you first sought virgins, indicating a long stay.
The people are foolish, but their divine intuition must not be disregarded.”
The emperor said,
“I ordered the selection because my six palaces were scattered
and I had no one by my side.
Now that I have received your advice,
how dare I not respectfully comply?
I will only keep one who understands literature;
all the others shall be sent away.”
At that time,
the attendant officials and close retainers were mostly impoverished,
all relying on Hào to provide for them.
Hào also could not satisfy everyone's desires,
and they slandered him to the emperor day and night,
especially mentioning the shortage of provisions from the Imperial Kitchen as a complaint.
The emperor was angry.
Although he promoted Hào to Dàfū,
his audience with the emperor became particularly distant.
Xiǎolóu Shì, while in Xīzhōu,
had a rift with Shímò Jiǔzhù,
and resented Hào for discerning the right and wrong between him and Jiǔzhù.
When the emperor traveled to Cài,
Lóu Shì met him at Shuānggōu,
and took the opportunity to heavily slander Hào's transgressions.
The emperor somewhat believed him.
Hào, knowing he was being slandered,
was worried, indignant, and depressed,
often feigning illness and taking leave.
It so happened that Dà'ān, the nephew of the former Cānzhī Zhèngshì Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, came,
stating that Nǚlǔhuān had shown no signs of rebellion
and had been killed by Guānnú.
He reported this to the Shàngshūshěng, requesting rectification.
The Shàngshūshěng reported it to the emperor.
The emperor said:
"I once thought Nǚlǔhuān was rebellious,
but found no traces.
If I say he was not rebellious,
when I was exposed to danger,
I sent people to request reinforcements,
but he kept his elite troops to protect himself,
sending only his weak and infirm ones.
Upon reaching Suīyáng,
he lived in luxury,
while I lacked even basic condiments.
As a sovereign,
I should not speak of such trivial matters,
but which of the prefectures and counties within the four seas does not belong to the state?
To merely hold one city,
it is the duty of a subject and son.
Yet he became arrogant and harbored thoughts of pride towards his sovereign.
What is this if not rebellion?
However, I am currently employing capable people to overcome difficulties,
and this is the time to record merits and forget faults.
Let it be rectified."
The assembled officials knew the emperor's thoughts were with Hào,
and repeatedly spoke of him to Yòuchéng Zhòngdé.
Every time Zhòngdé saw the emperor, he would praise Hào's achievements,
suggesting he should participate in important military and political affairs,
and even recommended him to replace himself.
The emperor's anger somewhat subsided.
When Cānzhèng Mǒniǎn Wùdiǎn took charge of Xīzhōu as Xíngshěng,
Hào was then made Yùshǐ Dàfū and provisionally Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
In the ninth month,
the great army besieged Cài.
Hào defended the southern side,
with Zhōngxiào Jūn Yuánshuài Cài Bā'ér as his deputy.
Not long after,
the city fell and he was captured.
Because he failed to persuade Xīzhōu to surrender,
he was killed.
Wūgǔlùn Xiānshēng was
originally a servant from a noble family,
who became a Quánzhēn master.
He feigned madness,
wandering naked with bare feet,
wearing clothes made of hemp.
People also called him
"Má Pèi Xiānshēng."
Xuānzōng once summoned him to the palace
to ask about secret arts.
He then frequently visited the Dàchángzhǔ's residence,
and had many scandalous affairs.
The emperor vaguely heard of this,
and ordered the relevant authorities to arrest him,
but he had already fled.
Towards the end of Zhèngdà,
he followed Hào to serve in Rǔnán.
Everyone knew he was having an affair with Hào's wife,
but Hào was unaware.
Xiānshēng felt uneasy,
and sought to leave.
Hào arranged a dwelling for him on Dàoyǔ,
personally leading monks and Daoists to send him there to live.
As the imperial carriage was approaching Cài,
Xiānshēng wanted to flee but had nowhere to go.
He then claimed he could enable soldiers to sustain themselves on vital energy without consuming grain.
Yòuchéng Zhòngdé knew he was lying,
and then memorialized:
"To emulate Tián Dān's strategy of using a false divine master to repel the enemy,
grant him the title of a Zhēnrén,
and then devise a surprising stratagem.
The northern soldiers, believing in witchcraft, will surely be astonished,
and perhaps this can achieve success."
Cānzhèng Zhāng Tiāngāng considered it impossible,
so it was stopped.
He then requested another audience,
claiming to have a cunning plan to repel the enemy.
Upon being granted an audience,
he made a long bow but did not prostrate himself,
and spoke many boastful words,
wanting to persuade the great commander Pēnzhan as a means of escape for himself.
At that time, Lángzhōng Yílài Kèzhōng and Yuánwàiláng Wáng È both reported the previous
"Má Pèi" affair,
and the emperor, enraged, had him killed.
A eulogy states: Liú Yuèshí of Jìn was skilled at pacification and acceptance,
but poor at command and control,
which led to his defeat.
Niángé Nú's actions regarding Chénzhōu
are quite similar.
The three Lóu Shìs were all members of the Jin imperial clan;
only Dàlóu Shì died appropriately,
while the other two Lóu Shìs were slanderous and malicious individuals.
When Xiāngchéng was in grave danger,
they were too drunk to command the army,
thus escaping death.
The Jin's loss of proper governance and justice reached such a point.
Wūgǔlùn Hào's request to go to Cài,
though not the most profound strategy,
was a humble display of loyalty, yet he was viewed with suspicion due to slander.
The sagacity of Āizōng is thus evident.
Zhāng Tiāngāng, courtesy name Zhèngqīng,
was a native of Yìjīn, Bàzhōu.
In the first year of Zhìníng, he passed the civil service examination with a focus on classical prose and poetry.
He was broad-minded, honest, and upright,
his discussions were pure and correct,
and he never deviated, even in haste.
He successively served as Magistrate of Xiánníng and Líntóng,
then entered the Shàngshūshěng as a Lìshǐ,
and was appointed Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
known for his integrity and frankness.
He was promoted to Hùbù Lángzhōng,
and provisionally Yuánwàiláng of Zuǒyòusī.
When Āizōng moved east,
he was promoted to Zuǒyòusī Lángzhōng,
and escorted the emperor to Guīdé,
where he was reassigned as Lìbù Shìláng.
Knowing that Yuánshuài Guānnú showed signs of rebellion,
he repeatedly reported it to the emperor,
but the emperor did not heed him.
Guānnú indeed rebelled,
and Tiāngāng was then promoted to provisional Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
When he followed the emperor in relocating to Cài,
he stayed in Bózhōu.
When a military mutiny occurred,
Tiāngāng expediently granted official positions to the rebels,
and the prefecture relied on him to restore peace.
Upon reaching Cài,
he was transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
still provisionally Cānzhèng.
Liú Chāngzǔ, a Zhīshì of the Fúgōu Xiàn Zhāofǔsī, submitted a sealed memorial,
proposing a large-scale invasion of the Sòng,
the gist of which was:
"Our army will be at the front,
the starving populace behind;
we will advance south into Jiāng and Huái,
and west into Bā and Shǔ."
This somewhat pleased the emperor.
The emperor ordered Tiāngāng to question him in person about the details,
and upon summoning and speaking with him, found nothing commendable.
However, being reluctant to defy the emperor's command,
and also fearing that it would obstruct avenues of speech,
he memorialized that he should be appointed as an official by the Shàngshūshěng.
Hùwèi Nǚxīliè Wánchū, Jìnshì Jú Zhícháng Niánhé Xiéliè, Fèngyù Chén Qiān, and provisional Jìnshì Jú Zhícháng Nèizú Tàihé—these four individuals,
complained about insufficient provisions,
requesting to go to Chénzhōu for food.
Tiāngāng memorialized to allow them to leave the gate and go wherever they wished.
As soon as they left and reached the banks of the Rǔnán,
they encountered northern soldiers and were all killed.
People at the time were pleased by this.
The sorcerer Wūgǔlùn Xiānshēng claimed he could enable soldiers to subsist on air
without needing provisions.
Right Chancellor Zhòngdé, citing the story of Tián Dān,
wished to employ his art to shock the enemy.
The details are in the biography of Wūgǔlùn Hào.
The Emperor was somewhat inclined to agree,
but Tiāngāng strongly argued against it, deeming it impossible,
so it was stopped.
He further said:
"If not for Zhāng Tiāngāng,
I would almost have been deceived by this villain."
The military official Shímò Hǔ'ér sought an audience with Zhòngdé,
claiming to have an ingenious plan to repel the enemy.
He produced horse masks shaped like fierce lions,
and separately crafted feet and tails from blue hemp cloth.
He then said:
"The northern soldiers rely solely on their horses.
To subdue their men,
we must first subdue their horses.
If our army advances to battle
and then slightly retreats,
they will surely pursue us.
We should take over a hundred trained horses, all in this guise,
and tie large bells to their necks.
Brave warriors will ride them
to charge their cavalry.
Their horses will surely be startled and flee.
Our army will then advance with drums and shouts, following close behind.
This is how Tián Dān defeated Yān."
Tiāngāng said:
"That will not do.
They are numerous and we are few;
this is unreliable.
Even if they are startled away,
how can we ensure they won't return?
I fear it will be a mere waste of labor and materials,
only to invite the enemy's ridicule."
So it was abandoned.
When Cáichéng fell,
it was taken by the Sòng general Mèng Gǒng.
Tiāngāng was confined in a caged cart and shackled to Lín'ān,
and sacrificial rites were performed to the ancestral temple.
Soon after,
Xuē Qióng, the Prefect of Lín'ān, was ordered to question him, saying:
"What face do you have to come here?"
Tiāngāng replied:
"Regarding the rise and fall of nations,
which dynasty has been without it?
How does the fall of our Jīn compare to your two Emperors?"
Qióng angrily shouted:
"Drag him away!"
The next day,
he reported Tiāngāng's words.
The Sòng Emperor summoned and questioned him, saying:
"Tiāngāng, do you truly not fear death?"
He replied:
"A true man worries that his death may not be fitting for the occasion;
what is there to fear?"
He then repeatedly begged for death.
The Sòng Emperor did not grant it.
Earlier,
an official ordered that a confession must write "Luǒ Zhǔ" (Barbarian Lord).
Tiāngāng said:
"If you want to kill me, just kill me;
what's the use of a confession?"
The official could not force him
and allowed him to write as he pleased.
Tiāngāng merely wrote "Gù Zhǔ" (Former Lord).
Those who heard of it pitied him.
Later, his ultimate fate is unknown.
Wányán Zhòngdé, originally named Hūxiéhǔ,
was from Hélǎnlù.
As a youth, he was remarkably intelligent and exceptional,
studying books and practicing policy essays,
possessing both civil and military talents.
He first passed the examination to join the imperial guard,
and though he served as a guard, he never ceased his studies.
In the third year of Tàihé (1203), he passed the imperial examination for jinshi,
and successively served in various prefectures and counties.
During the military campaigns of Zhēnyòu (1213-1217), he was appointed to a military post.
He was once captured by the troops of the Great Yuán,
but within a year, he completely learned their language.
Soon after, he led over ten thousand surrendered men back to allegiance.
Xuānzōng summoned him,
was impressed,
and appointed him Governor of Pízhōu and Concurrent Commissioner of Military Affairs.
He fortified the city walls
and diverted water to encircle it,
making the prefecture defensible.
Upon Àizōng's ascension,
he was remotely appointed Concurrent Prefect of Guīdé Fǔ
and Concurrent Commissioner of the Privy Council,
with his office in Xúzhōu.
Xúzhōu city was bordered on the east, west, and north by the Yellow River, with only the south being flat land.
Zhòngdé piled stones as a foundation
and raised half of the city wall,
further deepening the moat and drawing in water for defense,
on which the people relied for security.
In the fifth year of Zhèngdà (1228),
an imperial edict appointed him to oversee the Marshal's Office south of Guānshǎn,
to defend Xiǎoguān and Shànchēhuí.
At that time, northern troops were attacking the pass.
Zhòngdé was just in the process of replacing the former commander Àotún Ālǐbù over wine,
when the troops suddenly arrived,
and so he drove them eastward.
Ālǐbù had no defense strategy,
and was impeached by the relevant authorities,
deserving death.
Zhòngdé submitted a memorial taking the blame,
stating:
"At the time the northern troops crossed the pass,
the seals of office had already been exchanged.
How can the former commander be blamed?
I request to suffer the execution."
The Emperor admired his righteousness,
only flogged Ālǐbù and spared his life.
In the sixth year (1229),
he was transferred to become Prefect of Gǒngchāng Fǔ
and Concurrent Commissioner of the Grand Commander's Office.
At that time, the various prefectures in Shǎnxī were already devastated.
Zhòngdé gathered scattered and lost people,
acquiring tens of thousands of troops.
He built stockades in the mountains,
established military farms, and accumulated grain,
and many people came to him.
That region alone achieved a measure of peace and prosperity,
and his decrees were clear and strict,
to the point where lost items were not picked up from the road.
In the fourth month of the eighth year (1231),
an imperial edict appointed Zhòngdé to the Gǒngchāng Provincial Administration
and bestowed upon him the tiger tally and silver seal.
In the ninth month of the first year of Tiānxīng (1232),
he was appointed Minister of Works and Grand Councillor,
overseeing the Provincial Secretariat in Shǎnzhōu.
At that time, Wūdiǎn had just been defeated,
and Shǎnzhōu was ruined.
Zhòngdé again established mountain stockades
and pacified the military and civilians.
The Emperor then sent a wax-sealed letter summoning troops from all circuits to reinforce.
The provincial administrations and marshal's offices often hesitated and did not advance,
or collapsed upon encountering enemy troops en route.
Only Zhòngdé led a lone army of a thousand men,
passing through Qín, Lán, Shāng, and Dèng,
foraging for fruits and vegetables for food,
enduring countless dangers to reach Biàn.
On the day he arrived,
the Emperor happened to be moving east.
His wife and children had been in the capital for five years.
Zhòngdé did not enter his home,
but hastened to see the Emperor at Sòngmén,
and asked about the purpose of the eastward journey.
Knowing that the Emperor intended to cross the Yellow River northwards,
he strongly remonstrated, saying:
"The northern troops are in Hénán,
yet Your Majesty intends to move far to Héběi.
If by any chance it fails,
will you be able to return safely?
The nation's survival depends on this one action;
I beg you to consider it carefully.
I have repeatedly sent people to report that
the mountain fastnesses between Qín and Gǒng are deep and secure,
with abundant provisions and supplies.
It would be better to move west,
reside in the secure heights,
order the commanders to fight along separate routes,
then advance to take Xīngyuán,
and manage Bāshǔ.
This is a foolproof plan."
The Emperor had already decided with Bá Sā,
and did not follow his advice.
However, he had always held Zhòngdé in high regard,
and moreover commended him for coming to the rescue.
He promoted him to Right Chancellor of the Secretariat and Concurrent Vice Commissioner of the Privy Council,
with the army encamped at Huánglínggāng.
In the first month of the second year,
the imperial carriage arrived at Guīdé.
Zhòngdé was appointed to serve in the Shàngshū Shěng in Xúzhōu.
Upon his arrival,
he dispatched someone to convey greetings to Guóyòng'ān.
Zhuó Yì and Sūn Bìchōng from Pèixiàn had initially joined Yòng'ān.
Yòng'ān enfeoffed Yì as the Prince of Dōngpíng Prefecture
and Bìchōng as the Duke of Bóyáng.
Pèixiàn was elevated to Yuánzhōu.
Soon after,
Yì and Bìchōng came to pledge allegiance.
Zhòngdé restored them to their former positions,
ordering them to command the various fortresses north of the river
and manage the affairs of the Yuánzhōu Commander’s Office.
Yòng'ān repeatedly sent dispatches to Wáng Déquán to come to their aid,
but he did not respond.
When Zhòngdé arrived in Xúzhōu,
Déquán was greatly alarmed
and sought to proceed to Guīdé.
Zhòngdé kept him there
and sent a message to the emperor saying:
"Xúzhōu is a vital location,
Déquán should not leave his post."
Zhòngdé left the Xúzhōu prefectural office empty and did not reside there,
nor did he have guards for self-protection.
He spent his days reading books.
This made Déquán even more suspicious.
In the second month,
Zhāng Huán, the Commander-in-Chief of Yúshān, rebelled,
killing Marshal Wányán Hútǔ and defecting to the north.
