Zhòngdé repeatedly proposed to suppress him,
but Déquán did not comply.
Zhòngdé then led about ten men from his command,
personally persuaded three hundred militiamen,
and went directly to Yúshān.
By then, Cóngyí Yán Lù had already executed Huán and restored order.
Zhòngdé pacified the soldiers and civilians and returned.
There was a Commander-in-Chief Cáo
who stole an imperial horse and went east.
An imperial edict instructed the Traveling Secretariat to suppress him.
After Zhòngdé killed the bandit,
Déquán wanted to claim credit for himself,
and killed forty-eight of Cáo’s followers.
In the third month,
Āzhúľǔ attacked Xiāoxiàn.
His cavalry patrols reached Xúzhōu,
and all of Déquán’s horses were intercepted.
Zhòngdé was at Sùzhōu at the time.
Because of the loss of horses, Déquán first proposed to rescue Xiāoxiàn,
dispatching Zhāng Yuángē and Miáo Xiùchāng with eight hundred cavalry.
Before they could engage in battle,
Yuángē retreated.
The northern troops ambushed them,
and they were all captured and killed.
Xiāoxiàn was subsequently lost.
In the fourth month,
Zhòngdé feigned transporting grain to Pīzhōu.
The prefectural officials came out to welcome him.
He then seized Déquán and his son and executed them.
Beyond his immediate faction, no one else was implicated.
The entire prefecture rejoiced.
Earlier,
Wányán Hútǔ was remotely appointed Military Commissioner of Xúzhōu,
and went to command Yán Lù's army at Bǎo'ānzhèn, north of Yǒngzhōu.
At that time, Lù had already become a Cóngyí
and had been in Dàngshān for several years,
winning the hearts of the soldiers.
When Hútǔ arrived,
the soldiers were displeased.
On the night of Xīnmǎo in the second month,
he was killed by Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Huán and Cuī Zhèn.
Zhāng Mǐnxiū, a Director in the Ministry of Personnel,
who was Hútǔ's staff officer,
then coerced Yán Lù with the military mutiny to surrender to the north.
Lù feigned compliance,
secretly summoning Chén Lì, the Administrator of Yǒngzhōu, and Guō Shēng, the Deputy Pacification Commissioner,
to gather various volunteer armies to Bǎo'ānzhèn to execute the rebels.
When the army arrived at night,
Lù sent Mǐnxiū to summon Huán and Zhèn to discuss matters.
The two did not suspect anything
and arrived in full armor,
along with their followers, all of whom were killed by Lù.
Xúzhōu was a hundred *lǐ* from Bǎo'ān.
The Traveling Secretariat heard of it and came to suppress the rebellion.
As Lù had already restored order,
he was granted the expedient title of Acting Right Commander-in-Chief,
and was given Hútǔ's tiger tally.
The court then remotely appointed Lù as the Administrator of Guīdé Prefecture and concurrently Acting Commander-in-Chief.
Not long after,
the Grand Yuan general Āzhúľǔ's army arrived at Bǎo'ān,
and Lù fled during the night.
Later, Lù heard of Guānnú's mutiny.
His army was stationed between Xúzhōu and Sùzhōu for nearly a month,
then defected to Liánshuǐ.
Mǐnxiū entered Xúzhōu.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict summoned Zhòngdé to the temporary imperial residence.
At this time, Guānnú had already rebelled,
and the officials feared being deceived,
advising him not to go.
Zhòngdé said:
"How can the command of a ruler and father
be questioned as to its authenticity?
Even if it means death, I must go."
Soon, the envoy arrived,
and it was indeed Guānnú's deception.
In the sixth month,
Guānnú was executed.
An imperial edict ordered Zhòngdé to discuss moving the capital to Cài.
Zhòngdé had always desired to escort the emperor west,
and therefore supported the plan.
Upon arriving at Cài,
he took charge of the Shěng Yuàn.
He personally attended to every matter, big or small.
He selected soldiers, requisitioned horses,
and repaired armor and weapons,
never for a single day abandoning the ambition to move west.
The close attendants, who had long suffered in Suīyáng,
were happy to settle down in Rúyáng,
and all married and engaged in business, unwilling to relocate.
They constantly told the emperor that moving west was inconvenient.
Not long after,
the main army blocked the road,
and the move ultimately did not proceed.
Zhòngdé often sat deep in his dwelling,
closing his eyes and sighing deeply,
regretting that he could not move west.
In this month,
the emperor arrived at Cài.
He ordered the relevant authorities to renovate the Jiànshāntíng and Tóngzhīyámén
as a place for leisure.
Zhòngdé admonished:
"Since ancient times, when a ruler faces calamity
and is displaced to a remote location,
they must endure self-inflicted hardship and reduce their own comforts,
only then can they hope to restore their former possessions.
Moreover, now all the prefectures are ruined,
and only Cài remains intact.
The public offices in Cài are certainly not one ten-thousandth as grand as palaces,
but compared to living in the wilderness or sleeping in the open, they are an improvement.
Furthermore, the emperor's initial relocation has already caused the people to labor in renovation,
and now to undertake another construction project for comfort
will likely cause people's morale to slacken,
which is insufficient for accomplishing great deeds."
The emperor immediately ordered a halt.
In the seventh month,
a reward system for presenting horses was established.
the rewards varied.
From then on,
marshals such as Fàn Zhēn and Jī Rǔzuò from Xīshān each presented horses,
totaling over a thousand,
which were led by Mǒniǎn Ādiǎn.
Envoys were also dispatched to various circuits to conscript soldiers to Cài,
obtaining ten thousand elite troops.
As the weapons and armor were incomplete,
Zhújiǎ Yǎozhù, an Assistant Minister of Works, was ordered to supervise their repair,
which was completed in less than a month.
Military morale somewhat revived.
Those who accompanied the emperor, seeking temporary peace,
then considered Cài defensible.
Yuán Zhì, Marshal of Lǔshān, led over a thousand troops to assist.
At this time, many marshals often hoarded troops for self-preservation.
Zhì alone risked several hundred *lǐ*,
fighting and marching,
losing nearly half his men by the time he reached Cài.
The emperor praised his uniqueness in a memorial,
bestowed upon him a grand token of trust,
and promoted him to Grand Marshal.
Cài Bār and Wáng Shān'ér, commanders of the Zhōngxiào Army in Xīzhōu, also came to assist.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Lǐ Dé (李德), the Director of the Zhōngxiào Army (忠孝軍), rode into the provincial office with over ten men and shouted loudly,
complaining that the monthly rations were insufficient,
almost to the point of cursing.
The郎zhōng Yílā Kèzhōng (移剌克忠) reported this to Wányán Zhòngdé (完顏仲德).
Zhòngdé (仲德) was furious,
bound Dé (德) below the hall,
and flogged him sixty times.
The Emperor then instructed Zhòngdé (仲德), saying:
“This army is effective;
We are about to rely on them.
Why do you not show tolerance,
and punish them so severely?”
Zhòngdé (仲德) replied:
“Times are troubled;
to record merits and overlook faults is the virtue of Your Majesty.
However, for the duty of a general, it is not so.
Minor offenses are dealt with resolutely;
major offenses are punished by death.
Strong soldiers and fierce troops must not be allowed to be without discipline for even a single day.
For the nature of common people, indulgence leads to arrogance,
and arrogance makes them difficult to control.
The disaster of Suīyáng (睢陽) was not solely the fault of Guānnú (官奴);
it was also because the authorities were too lenient.
Now, if we wish to change the former ways,
we should not hesitate to exert our authority.
Rewards must come from the heart;
for punishments, your servant takes responsibility.”
When the soldiers heard this,
until the fall of the state, none dared to offend.
In the ninth month,
Càichéng (蔡城) was put under strict martial law.
The Acting Grand Secretary of the Six Ministries, Púchá Shìdá (蒲察世達), knowing that a large army was approaching,
requested an edict instructing the people to quickly harvest their late-season crops,
and to trample and destroy any that could not be harvested in time,
so as not to supply the enemy.
The request was approved.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
an edict was issued to cut down redundant officials
and dismiss excess troops,
and to fix the monthly salary for officials, civil servants, and soldiers.
From the chief ministers down to the lowliest servants,
each person was to receive six *dǒu* per month.
Initially,
the authorities had decreed a reduction in rations,
and the people greatly resented it.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he wanted to divide the army into three ranks:
the upper army would receive eight *dǒu* per month,
the middle seven *dǒu*,
and the lower six *dǒu*.
The people again complained about the inequality.
When archery contests were instituted,
the upper and middle armies often received more rewards;
those who hit the target repeatedly were sometimes personally given wine.
People were increasingly encouraged by this,
and secretly, there was an increase in rations that people did not notice.
This was Zhòngdé’s (仲德) strategy.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the army was divided to defend the four sides.
On the first day of the tenth month, *rénshēn*,
the great army completed its fortifications and ditches,
and paraded its might beneath the city walls,
with banners covering the sky.
The people in the city were terrified.
Towards evening,
they burned the four gates,
leveled their walls, and retreated.
On the *xīnchǒu* day of the eleventh month,
the great army brought siege engines up to the city walls.
The authorities registered all able-bodied men for defense.
When these were insufficient, they conscripted strong women,
dressed them in men's clothes and caps, and made them transport timber and stones.
Once Cài (蔡) was besieged,
Zhòngdé (仲德) planned and arranged the defenses,
never once returning home.
He comforted and cared for the soldiers,
and all were pleased with him.
For generals and officers who died in battle,
he personally attended their funeral rites and offered condolences,
weeping with utmost sorrow.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
the west wall was breached.
However, the city had previously built fences and deepened moats as preparation,
so even though it was breached, the enemy could not enter.
They only erected fences on the city wall,
with a gap of over a hundred paces between north and south.
Zhòngdé (仲德) selected elite troops from three sides to fight and defend day and night,
and they could not be dislodged.
On the first day of the first month of the third year, *gēngzǐ*,
the great army held a banquet to celebrate New Year's Day,
with drums and wind instruments playing continuously.
Inside the city, there was only hunger, distress, and lamentation.
Since the city had been besieged,
four marshals and three commandants had died in battle,
with countless others from unit commanders downwards.
There were too many to count.
By this time,
all who were close to the Forbidden Palace were called out,
even palace secretaries, seal-bearers, and clerks from the provincial offices and ministries
were all pressed into service.
On the *wùshēn* day,
the great army dug five gates into the west wall,
and entered with organized troops.
They fought fiercely under the supervision of their commanders until evening before retreating,
announcing that they would gather again the next day.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
the great army indeed returned.
Zhòngdé (仲德) led a thousand elite soldiers in street fighting.
From *mǎo* (5-7 AM) until *sì* (9-11 AM),
suddenly, fire broke out in the inner city.
Upon hearing that the Emperor had hanged himself,
he said to his officers and men:
“My sovereign has already fallen;
why should I continue to fight?
I cannot die by the hands of unruly soldiers.
I shall go to the Rǔshuǐ (汝水) river
to follow my sovereign.”
“You all, make good plans for yourselves.”
Having spoken,
he plunged into the water and died.
All the officers and men said:
“If the Grand Councilor can die,
why can't we?”
Thereupon, the Councilors Bóshùlǔ Lóushì (孛术鲁娄室) and Wūlíndá Hútǔ (兀林荅胡土),
the Grand Commander Yuán Zhì (元志),
the Marshals Wáng Shānr (王山兒), Hélìliè Báishòu (紇石烈栢壽), Wūgǔlún Huánduān (烏古論桓端), and over five hundred soldiers
all died with him.
Zhòngdé’s (仲德) appearance was not out of the ordinary.
Throughout his life, his emotions never erupted inappropriately.
When he heard of others' faults,
he often protected and concealed them.
Even when in the army,
he always held a book.
His disciples and former subordinates often taught him about proper roles and duties.
His family was always poor,
he wore worn-out clothes and ate coarse food,
and remained content throughout his life.
He had a refined fondness for guests
and recommending talented individuals.
If a person had any small skill,
he would praise it enthusiastically.
When he commanded military affairs,
rewards and punishments were clear and trustworthy,
and his orders were strict and well-ordered.
Therefore, wherever he went, the military and civilians would serve him.
Even in moments of dire danger and life or death,
not a single officer harbored disloyal thoughts.
After the Southern Crossing,
among the generals, ministers, civil, and military officials,
Zhòngdé (仲德) alone remained loyal and blameless from beginning to end.
He was the only one.
A eulogy says: The fall of Jīn (金)
cannot be said to have been due to a lack of talent.
Were not Wányán Zhòngdé (完顏仲德) and Zhāng Tiāngāng (張天綱) indeed capable of being generals and ministers?
In ancient times, when Zhì Bó (智伯) died without an heir,
his retainer Yù Ràng (豫讓) did not forget the kindness of a 'state scholar' (guóshì) and sought revenge.
Gentlemen say he did what he did for its own sake,
a truly righteous knight.
Jīn (金) has fallen,
yet Zhòngdé (仲德), Tiāngāng (天綱), and other ministers did not change their loyalties.
How could they be ashamed compared to the righteous knights of antiquity?
Collation Notes
Biographies Fifty-Eight: Shìqī (世戚) Shíjiānú (石家奴), Péimǎn Dá (裴滿達), Hútú (忽覩), Túshàn Gōng (徒單恭), Wūgǔlún Púlǔhǔ (烏古論蒲魯虎), Tángkuò Déwēn (唐括德溫), Wūgǔlún Niánmòhé (烏古論粘沒曷).

Púchá Āhǔdié (蒲察阿虎迭), Wūlíndá Huī (烏林荅暉), Púchá Dǐngshòu (蒲察鼎壽), Túshàn Sīzhōng (徒單思忠), Túshàn Yì (徒單繹), Wūlíndá Fù (烏林荅復), Wūgǔlún Yuánzhōng (烏古論元忠) (son Yì [誼]), Tángkuò Gòng (唐括貢), Wūlíndá Lín (烏林荅琳), Túshàn Gōngbì (徒單公弼), Túshàn Míng (徒單銘), Túshàn Sìxǐ (徒單四喜).
Jīn Zhāozǔ (金昭祖) married into the Túshàn (徒單) clan,
and the imperial consorts' families began to appear from this time.
During the reign of Shìzǔ (世祖),
when Wūchūn (烏春) caused trouble,
Shìzǔ (世祖) wanted to seek marriage to win his favor.
Wūchūn (烏春) said:
“How can Nǚzhí (女直) and Húlígǎi (胡里改) intermarry?”
During the reign of Shìzōng (世宗),
Jiágǔ Qīngchén (夾谷清臣)'s clan was granted the same status as the imperial kinsmen.
Qīngchén (清臣) was a Húlígǎi (胡里改) man.
Thus, among the forty-seven tribes, there were those who did not intermarry.
The reason for this cannot be determined.
For a state,
to have marital alliances with certain clans,
and to thereby solidify customs,
ensure unchanging kinship and righteousness, and distinguish between nobility and commoners,
is indeed a good system.
Hence, the Biographies of Imperial Relatives (Shìqī Chuán) was compiled.
Shíjiānú (石家奴) was from the Púchá (蒲察) tribe,
whose family had resided at the Ànchūhǔshuǐ (案出虎水) for generations.
His grandfather Húlǔduǎn (斛魯短)
was the maternal grandson of Shìzǔ (世祖).
During the rebellion of Huán● (桓●) and Sàndá (散達),
the parents and siblings of Empress Zhāosù (昭肅皇后) were all in enemy territory.
Húlǔduǎn (斛魯短) ingeniously brought them back.
Shí Jiānú (石家奴) was raised in Tài Zǔ's (太祖) household from childhood.
When he grew up,
Tài Zǔ (太祖) gave him his daughter in marriage.
At the age of fifteen,
he followed in the attack on Níngjiāng Zhōu (寧江州),
defeated the Líao (遼) ruler's elite troops,
and made contributions in the attack on Línhuáng Fǔ (臨潢府).
He inherited the rank of mòukè (謀克).
Thereafter,
he escorted the coffin of Qí Guówáng Móuliánghǔ (齊國王謀良虎) back to Shàngjīng (上京) from Shānxī (山西).
His route passed through Xīngzhōng (興中).
At that time,
Xīngzhōng (興中) was under attack but not yet captured.
Shí Jiānú (石家奴) placed the coffin at the courier station
and led the méng'ān (猛安) troops under his command to assist the imperial army,
thus breaking the city.
He followed Zōngwàng (宗望) to suppress Zhāng Jué (張覺).
He twice followed Zōnghàn (宗翰) to campaign against Sòng (宋).
When Zōnghàn (宗翰) heard that Zōngwàng's (宗望) army had already besieged Biàn (汴),
he sent Shí Jiānú (石家奴) to discuss matters.
Upon reaching Píngdìng Jūn (平定軍), he encountered tens of thousands of enemy soldiers,
defeated them,
and then met Zōngwàng (宗望).
After returning to report,
Zōnghàn (宗翰), hearing of his battle at Píngdìng (平定),
praised him greatly.
The following year,
he again campaigned against Sòng (宋),
serving under Lóushì (婁室) in Shí Jiānú's (石家奴) army.
Lóushì (婁室) was campaigning in Shǎnxī (陝西) but had not yet secured it.
Shí Jiānú (石家奴) led his troops to reinforce him.
Soon after,
he garrisoned Xījīng (西京) with his own troops.
When Qìdān Dàshí (契丹大石) fled,
with Yúdǔ (余睹) as yuánshuài (元帥)
and Shí Jiānú (石家奴) as his deputy,
they attacked various tribes and returned.
Not long after,
he fell ill
and retired to his hometown.
During the Tiānjuàn (天眷) period,
he was appointed Shìzhōng (侍中) and Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉).
Again, as Dūtǒng (都統), he pacified the Biānjūn (邊軍) tribes.
Xīzōng (熙宗) bestowed him with an imperial letter of commendation.
He was enfeoffed as Lánlíng Jùnwáng (蘭陵郡王).
He was appointed Dōngjīng Líushǒu (東京留守)
but retired due to illness.
He died
at the age of sixty-three,
and was posthumously granted the title of Yúnwáng (鄖王).
During Zhènglóng (正隆), his princely title was revoked,
and he was enfeoffed as Lǔ Guógōng (魯國公).
Péi Mǎndá (裴滿達), originally named Hūtà (忽撻),
was a native of the Póluómù (婆盧木) tribe.
He was honest, straightforward, filial, and friendly.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ (天輔),
he followed Pújiānú (蒲家奴) in pursuing rebellious bandits in Tiělǚ Chuān (鐵呂川),
fighting bravely and achieving merit.
Xīzōng (熙宗) married Hūtà's (忽撻) daughter,
who became Dàopíng Huánghòu (悼平皇后).
In the first year of Tiānjuàn (天眷),
he was granted the hereditary méng'ān (猛安).
The following year,
as the Empress's father, he was appointed Tàiwèi (太尉)
and enfeoffed as Xú Guógōng (徐國公).
In the first year of Huángtǒng (皇統),
he was appointed Huìníng Mù (會寧牧).
After several years,
as Tàiwèi (太尉), he attended court.
In the ninth year,
Empress Dào (悼后) died.
Shortly after,
Hǎilíng (海陵) assassinated Xīzōng (熙宗).
Wishing to win popular acclaim,
he publicized Xīzōng's (熙宗) faults.
Because Empress Dào (悼后) had died unjustly,
Hūtà (忽撻) was enfeoffed as a king.
In the third year of Tiāndé (天德),
he passed away.
His son, Hūxǔ (忽覩),
was the Yānjīng Líushǒu (燕京留守).
He was dismissed due to an offense
and resided in Zhōngdū (中都).
Hǎilíng (海陵) ordered an express envoy to go to him.
At the funeral,
he sent the Mìshūjiān (祕書監) Nàhé Chūnnián (納合椿年) to offer sacrifices
and bestowed five hundred liǎng (兩) of silver as funeral expenses.
Hūxǔ (忽覩) served as acting méng'ān (猛安) in the third year of Tiānjuàn (天眷).
In the first year of Huángtǒng (皇統), he became an xíngjūn méng'ān (行軍猛安).
He successively held the posts of jiéduwèi (節度使) for Hénghǎi (橫海) and Chóngyì Jūn (崇義軍).
As a maternal relative of the Empress, he exploited his influence, engaged in corruption, and acted unlawfully.
While at Hénghǎi (橫海),
he acknowledged a wealthy man as his father.
When the man died,
he performed mourning rites for him and divided his assets.
At Chóngyì (崇義),
he subtly urged temple monks to hold vegetarian feasts and accepted their offerings.
When he was Líushǒu (留守) of Zhōngjīng (中京),
he became even more arrogant and unrestrained,
doing anything to acquire wealth.
He selected sons of wealthy families from various méng'ān (猛安) to be zháyě (扎野),
scheming to obtain their wealth.
They were then called
"Xián Lángjūn" (閑郎君).
The court, considering Hūxǔ (忽覩) and Túshàn Gōng (徒單恭) and others to be excessively corrupt,
ordered Bǐngdé (秉德) to evaluate and dismiss officials throughout the realm.
Hūxǔ (忽覩) was dismissed for corruption.
Hǎilíng (海陵), noting that Hūxǔ (忽覩) allowed his domestic servants to harass the people wherever he served,
then established regulations prohibiting unauthorized personnel from external officials' residences.
In the third year of Tiāndé (天德),
he was again appointed Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ (鄭州防禦使),
and later changed to Ānguójūn Jiéduwèi (安國軍節度使).
He died
at the age of thirty-nine.
Túshàn Gōng (徒單恭) was originally named Xiéyě (斜也).
In the second year of Tiānjuàn (天眷),
he was appointed Fèngguó Shàngjiàngjūn (奉國上將軍).
For reporting the rebellion of Wú Shí (吳十),
he was exceptionally promoted to Lónghǔwèi Shàngjiàngjūn (龍虎衞上將軍).
He served as Hùbù Shìláng (戶部侍郎),
then was appointed Jǐnán Yǐn (濟南尹),
promoted to Huìníng Mù (會寧牧),
and enfeoffed as Tán Guógōng (譚國公).
He was again appointed Tàiyuán Yǐn (太原尹).
Xiéyě (斜也) was avaricious and base.
He had an artisan paint a Buddha image,
claiming he had seen the Buddha,
and that the image was exactly as he had seen it,
and should be cast in gold.
Thus, he levied gold from the subordinate counties,
but never cast the Buddha,
keeping all the gold for himself.
The common people called him
"Jīn Zǒngguǎn" (金總管).
When Bǐngdé (秉德) investigated officials for integrity,
Xiéyě (斜也) was dismissed for corruption.
When Hǎilíng (海陵) usurped the throne,
Hǎilíng's (海陵) Empress was of the Túshàn (徒單) clan,
and she was Xiéyě's (斜也) daughter.
Because of this, he was again appointed Huìníng Mù (會寧牧)
and enfeoffed as a king.
Not long after,
he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事).
When Hǎilíng (海陵) hunted at Húlàhún Shuǐ (胡剌渾水),
Xiéyě (斜也) arranged the hunting ground,
and any who had previously been at odds with him were beaten.
Hǎilíng (海陵) said to his chancellors:
"Xiéyě (斜也) is chancellor;
I do not favor him.
Now I hear that regarding all important military and state matters, whatever Xiéyě (斜也) suggests,
you all reject entirely.
Can it be that among a thousand thoughts, he has not one good idea?"
The other chancellors had no reply.
Wēndū Sīzhōng (溫都思忠) brought up several matters and replied:
"Such and such a matter should have been thus,
but Xiéyě (斜也) always considered it otherwise.
He always raised baseless dissenting opinions
and did not understand what was appropriate.
Your servant served Kāngzōng (康宗)
and never saw a chancellor as autocratic as Xiéyě (斜也) throughout those reigns."
Hǎilíng (海陵) was silent.
Xiéyě (斜也) flogged the clerk Fèng Zhòngyǐn (馮仲尹) in the Dudtáng (都堂).
The Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺) impeached him.
Hǎilíng (海陵) had him flogged twenty times.
Sāhéchū (撒合出), a member of Xiéyě's (斜也) méng'ān (猛安) unit,
reported that Xiéyě (斜也) forcibly extorted property from his unit members.
Hǎilíng (海陵) ordered Shìyùshǐ Bǎolǔ (侍御史保魯) to investigate.
Bǎolǔ (保魯) did not investigate truthfully.
Hǎilíng (海陵) had Bǎolǔ (保魯) flogged,
and appointed Sāhéchū (撒合出) as Fúbǎo Zhǐhòu (符寶祗候),
transferring him to the Házhá Méng'ān (合扎猛安).
Xiéyě 兄 Dìnggē 尚 Tàizǔ 長女 Wūlǔ.
Dìnggē died childless.
His younger brother's son Zhālà was made his successor.
Xiéyě plotted to seize his brother's family property,
and forcibly took Wūlǔ as his wife, but they were incompatible.
Wūlǔ often resented and reviled Xiéyě.
Xiéyě's concubine Hūtá and Wūlǔ did not get along,
so Hūtá slandered Wūlǔ to Hǎilíng's 后 Túdān shì, saying:
"Wūlǔ resents the Emperor for killing her brother Zōngmǐn,
and has spoken with resentment and discontent."
At that time, Hánwáng Hēng was transferred to be the Prefect of Guǎngníng.
The princesses and imperial relatives went to congratulate his mother.
Wūlǔ consoled Hēng's mother with words.
Hūtá also falsely accused Wūlǔ of speaking with resentment and discontent.
Hǎilíng sent Xiāo Yù to interrogate her.
Hūtá was favored by Túdān 后.
Those who could provide corroborating evidence dared not speak.
Consequently, Wūlǔ was killed.
Xiéyě then seized all of Zhālà's family property.
During the Dàdìng period, all this was rectified posthumously.
Hǎilíng, on the grounds that Wūlǔ had spoken with resentment and discontent,
and Xiéyě had not reported it,
caned Xiéyě
and dismissed him from his current office.
Soon after,
he was reinstated as Sītú,
then promoted to Tàibǎo,
and put in charge of the affairs of the Three Departments,
concurrently serving as Quànnóngshǐ.
He was further promoted to Tàishī,
and enfeoffed as Liáng Jìn Guó Wáng.
In the ninth month of the second year of Zhēnyuán,
Xiéyě accompanied Hǎilíng on a hunt in Shùnzhōu.
While hunting,
they heard that Xiéyě had died.
The hunt was immediately called off that day.
Hǎilíng attended his funeral,
personally selected a burial site for him,
and dispatched envoys to oversee the preparations.
At the time of burial,
a wēnlángchē was bestowed.
The Emperor and the Empress led the officials in offering sacrifices to him,
and he was granted the posthumous title Zhōng.
During the Zhènglóng period,
he was re-enfeoffed as Zhào Guó Gōng,
and later promoted to Qí Guó Gōng.
His wife had died before Xiéyě.
Hǎilíng once visited her burial place to offer sacrifices,
and reinstated their son Wūlǐbǔ, who was a Shuàifǔ Shuài, as Jiànyì Dàfū.
During the Dàdìng period,
Hǎilíng was demoted to commoner,
TúDān shì became a commoner's wife,
and Xiéyě was demoted to Tèjìn Gǒng Guó Gōng.
Wūgǔlún Púlǔhǔ.
His father Dānghǎi
had merits at the founding of the dynasty.
Púlǔhǔ was skilled in Khitan large and small scripts.
He married Zhāoníng Gōngzhǔ Shígǔ, daughter of Sòngwáng Zōngwàng.
At the beginning of Xīzōng's reign,
he served as a Hùwèi,
then was appointed Páiyìn,
and often attended at the Emperor's side.
He was transferred to Tōngjìn,
inherited his father's Mòkè position,
and was again promoted to Línhǎijūn Jiédùshǐ,
then transferred to Wèizhōu Fángyùshǐ.
Hǎilíng granted him a meal in the inner palace,
saying to him:
"The climate and customs of Wèizhōu are excellent.
Do not consider Fángyùshǐ a demotion."
He replied:
"I have heard that the official residences in Wèizhōu are not favorable for those who hold the post."
The same day,
he was transferred to Fényángjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and bestowed with clothes, jade ornaments, and a sword.
He entered court service as Tàizǐ Zhànshì,
and died
at the age of forty-one.
Hǎilíng personally attended and wept for him.
The Empress and imperial concubines all offered condolences and sacrifices,
and the funeral gifts were very generous.
The relevant authorities handled the funeral arrangements,
and he was posthumously granted Tèjìn Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
During the Zhènglóng period, he was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū according to precedent.
Tángkuò Déwēn, original name Ālǐ,
was a native of Shàngjīng Shuàihé.
His great-grandfather Shígǔ
followed Tàizǔ in pacifying Lāpéi Máshǎn
and held the Mòkè position.
His grandfather Tuōbó Lǔ
held his father's Mòkè position,
followed Tàizǔ in attacking Liao,
and had merits in battles at Níngjiāng and Tàizhōu.
His father Tàlǎn
married the daughter of Kāngzōng,
and followed Sòngwáng Zōngwàng with an army of twenty thousand to recover Píngzhōu.
About ten li east of the city, they encountered a large enemy force.
They defeated them.
Tàizǔ rewarded him generously,
and appointed him Xíngjūn Měng'ān.
At the beginning of the Huángtǒng period,
he was promoted to Lónghǔwèi Shàngjiàngjūn,
and successively served as Jiédùshǐ of Xīngpíng, Línhǎi, and other armies.
Déwēn was skilled in archery
and married Chǔguó Cháng Gōngzhǔ, daughter of Ruìzōng Huángdì.
In the third year of Tiānjuàn,
he was appointed Xuānwǔ Jiàngjūn.
In the first year of Huángtǒng,
he followed Dū Yuánshuài Zōngbì on a southern expedition.
For his skill in offensive combat, he was promoted to Guǎngwēi Jiàngjūn.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Dìngyuǎn Dàjiàngjūn.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Diànqián Yòu Fù Dū Diǎnjiǎn.
At the beginning of the Tiāndé period,
he was transferred to Diànqián Zuǒ Fù Dū Diǎnjiǎn,
and promoted to Bīngbù Shàngshū.
He was sent out as Dàmíng Yǐn, concurrently Dū Zǒngguǎn of the troops in that circuit,
then transferred to Hénghǎijūn Jiédùshǐ,
and Yán'ān Yǐn, concurrently Dū Zǒngguǎn of the troops in Fūyán circuit.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Dàoguó Gōng,
and served as Diànqián Dū Diǎnjiǎn and Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
due to the merits of his father and grandfather, he was appointed hereditary Mòkè of the Ànchūhǔ Měng'ān.
On the ninth day of the ninth month of the third year,
Shìzōng went hunting according to tradition.
He said to Déwēn:
"The two thousand escorting soldiers,
will their food and fodder not disturb the common people?"
He strictly disciplined them
and distributed ten thousand strings of cash among them.
In the fourth year,
he served as Quànnóngshǐ,
then was sent out as Xījīng Liúshǒu,
bestowed with a rhinoceros horn bow and a jade belt.
He was recalled to serve as Huáng Tàizǐ Tàifù,
and then died.
The Emperor suspended court,
personally attended his funeral and offered sacrifices,
and the funeral gifts were very generous.
In the eighteenth year,
his father Tàlǎn's and Déwēn's cumulative merits were posthumously recorded.
His eldest son Dǐng, Fùmǎ Dūwèi, was granted the hereditary Mòlǐshān Měng'ān in the Northwest Circuit,
and was transferred to be subordinate to Tàizhōu.
Wūgǔlún Zhānmòhé,
a native of Húlàwēntún in Shàngjīng,
later moved to Héjiān.
His grandfather Huànduān
often attended Tàizǔ's side during the campaign against Liao,
and had merits in pursuing Liáo Zhǔ Yánxǐ and repelling Xìarén's reinforcements.
He was appointed hereditary Mòkè.
His father Huāndǔ's
highest office was Guǎngwēi Jiàngjūn.
Zhānmòhé married Jìguó Cháng Gōngzhǔ, daughter of Ruìzōng.
Initially, he served as a Hùwèi.
In the second year of Tiāndé, he inherited the Mòkè position.
When Hǎilíng attacked Song,
he served as Yājūn Měng'ān.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
the army returned.
He was appointed Shìwèi Qīnjūn Bùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
and additionally Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
He successively served as Zuǒ Fù Diǎnjiǎn.
During his guard duty, he was drunk and did not personally inspect the locks,
and was punished with forty strokes of the cane.
He was promoted to Yòu Xuānhuīshǐ and Quànnóngshǐ,
then sent out as Xīngpíngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was transferred to Guǎngníng Yǐn,
and bestowed three thousand strings of cash.
When Zhānmòhé arrived in Guǎngníng,
he indulged in drink and neglected his duties.
The Emperor appointed Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng Zōng'ān as Shàoyǐn,
and issued an edict for Zōng'ān to admonish him.
The Emperor said to Zōng'ān:
"If you can continue the previous good governance,
I will not forget you.
Strive for it."
During the Dàdìng period,
Zhānmòhé died.
Upon hearing this,
the Emperor sent his son, Fùmǎ Dūwèi Gōngshuō, by express post to attend the funeral,
bestowed three thousand strings of cash,
and all offerings along the way were provided by officials.
Púchá Āhúdié,
was initially granted the title of Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He married Díbō, the eldest princess of the Liáoguó, Emperor Hǎilíng's sister,
and became Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
When the Liáoguó princess passed away,
he subsequently married Cuīgē, the eldest princess of Dèngguó.
In the third year of Huángtǒng,
he was appointed Yòu Fù Diǎnjiǎn.
In the fifth year,
he was sent as an envoy to Sòng as the Hèzhèngdàn Shǐ.
He was re-appointed as Zuǒ Fù Diǎnjiǎn,
then Shàngshū of the Lǐbù and Gōngbù,
Yǐn of Guǎngníng, Xiánpíng, and Línhuáng,
Jiedushi of Wǔdìng Jūn,
and was enfeoffed as Gé Wáng.
He died at the age of twenty-eight.
Emperor Hǎilíng personally attended his funeral,
and posthumously granted him the title of Tán Wáng.
In the Zhènglóng period, he was posthumously granted the title of Tèjìn Chǔguó Gōng as per custom.
Wūlíndá Huī's original name was Móuliánghǔ.
He was the elder brother of the Míngdé Huánghòu.
At the beginning of Tiānjuàn,
he served as a Hùwèi.
For his merit in capturing Zōngpán and Zōngjuàn, he was granted the title of Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi,
and promoted to Míngwēi Jiāngjūn.
He followed Zōngbì on the northern expedition,
and was promoted to Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn,
rewarded with gold and silk, and a polo horse.
After a long time,
he was appointed Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
and then Púsùwǎn Qúnmù Shǐ.
He managed the livestock carefully,
did not indulge in banquets,
and the animals reproduced abundantly.
He was promoted,
and transferred to Tèmǎn Qúnmù Shǐ.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned for an audience at the imperial residence.
He was appointed Zhōngdū Bīngmǎ Dūzhīhuī Shǐ.
When Shìzōng arrived in Zhōngdū,
he intended to send an envoy to Sòng,
and appointed Huī as the envoy.
Shìzōng said:
"Huī once privately used five hundred strings of official money."
Then he enumerated his crimes and dismissed him,
sending Gāo Zhōngjiàn instead.
He then said to his prime ministers:
"Regarding rewards and punishments,
I make no allowance whatsoever.
If one is truly just, upright, and efficient in governance,
even if I have not liked them previously, I will certainly promote them.
But if one violates public law,
even if they are my closest relatives, I will not show any leniency."
He was transferred to Dū Diǎnjiǎn and concurrently Shìwèi Qīnjūn Fù Dūzhīhuī Shǐ,
and then died.
An official was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
The crown prince, princes, and all officials attended the funeral.
He was gifted one thousand taels of silver, forty bolts of fine colored silk, and forty bolts of plain silk.
An imperial edict ordered that Huī's third son, Tiānxī, inherit the position of Nàlín Hé Méng'ān Qīguǎn Móukè.
Púchá Dǐngshòu's original name was Héshàng.
He was from Gésù Hé, Shàngjīng.
He was the father of Qīnhuái Huánghòu.
He had a profound and discerning nature,
was proficient in Khitan and Chinese characters,
and was skilled in official affairs.
He married Zhèngguó Gōngzhǔ, Emperor Xīzōng's daughter.
In the third year of Zhēnyuán,
because he was the son of Qìngyí Gōngzhǔ, Emperor Hǎilíng's younger sister, he was granted the title of Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn,
and appointed Shàngyī Júshǐ.
He successively held the office of Qìwù Júshǐ.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was granted the title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
his duties remaining as before.
He successively served as Fúbǎo Láng, Líchōu Cìshǐ, and Jùnzhōu Fángyù Shǐ.
He had benevolent governance,
and the people of both prefectures carved his deeds into stone.
He was promoted to Tàiníng Jūn Jiédù Shǐ,
and successively served in Dōngpíng Fǔ and Hénghǎi Jūn.
He entered the court as Yòu Xuānhuī Shǐ,
and was then transferred to Zuǒ Xuānhuī.
He was appointed Zhōngdū Lù Hūndéhún Shān Méng'ān Gésùmù Dān hereditary Móukè.
He was then appointed Héjiān Yǐn.
His decrees were strictly enforced,
and powerful local magnates disappeared.
There was a member of the imperial clan living in Héjiān
who oppressed the residents.
Dǐngshòu memorialized to relocate his clan to Píngzhōu,
and the prefecture was greatly reformed.
He died in office.
When the Emperor heard of it, he deeply mourned his loss.
When the funeral procession reached Xiāngshān,
the crown prince went to offer sacrifices,
and all officials offered their condolences.
He was gifted silver, colored silk, and plain silk.
In the third year of Míngchāng,
as the Emperor's father-in-law, he was posthumously granted the titles of Tàiwèi and Yuèguó Gōng.
Dǐngshòu was connected to the imperial family through marriage for generations,
his daughter became empress,
and his eldest son, Cíbùshī, successively married Dìngguó, Jǐngguó, and Dàoguó Gōngzhǔ three times.
Such was his favor and status,
yet he never became arrogant due to his wealth and status.
At that time, he was considered the foremost of the imperial in-laws.
Túdān Sīzhōng, courtesy name Liángbì,
was originally named Níngqìng.
His great-grandfather, Sàibǔ,
married the daughter of Jǐngzǔ.
He followed Tàizǔ in the campaign against Liáo,
and died in battle at Húnhé in Línhuáng.
His father, Sàiyī,
married Emperor Xīzōng's younger sister.
At the end of Zhènglóng,
he was Zǐwǎn Qúnmù Shǐ.
When the Khitan bandit Wōwò harassed the northern border,
Sàiyī fought and died there.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he was posthumously granted the title of Jīnwǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
Sīzhōng was intelligent, capable,
and quite knowledgeable in classics and history.
When Shìzōng was still in his latent residence,
he fostered him.
He had a broad and generous nature.
At the age of twelve, he accompanied the Emperor to Jǐnán.
One day,
he was out with some relatives' sons on an outing near the suburbs.
A drunk man, with a bow and arrows at his waist, rode past at a gallop.
The young gentlemen were angry and wanted to whip him.
Sīzhōng said:
"A drunk man is muddled,
what is there to blame?"
So they let him go.
The man rode a few tens of steps,
then suddenly grasped his bow and arrows.
Sīzhōng feared he might harm someone,
so he quickly rode to his side,
snatched his bow,
released it, and returned it to him.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he praised his discernment and magnanimity,
and from then on, often kept him by his side.
He married Tángguó Gōngzhǔ, the second daughter of the Emperor's brother.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
Shìzōng sent Sīzhōng to welcome the Southern Expedition Wànhù Gāo Zhōngjiàn and Wányán Fúshòu at Liáokǒu,
to observe their intentions.
Sīzhōng knew their sincerity,
so he accompanied them to Dōngjīng.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
and went to Zhōngdū,
Sīzhōng followed,
and provided much valuable assistance in military and state affairs.
In the tenth month of the first year of Dàdìng,
he was appointed Diànqián Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the second year,
he was granted the title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and then died.
The Emperor suspended court for him,
personally attended his funeral,
and ordered officials to arrange a proper burial,
with all expenses covered by the government.
In the nineteenth year,
the Emperor recalled Sīzhōng's merit in assisting his ascent,
and posthumously granted him the title of Piàoqíwèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
Furthermore, his son Duó was granted the title of Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn and inherited the position of Zhōngdū Lù Wūdúhún Móukè.
Túdān Yì's original name was Shùbèi.
His ancestors were from Ànchūhú Dá'ā, Shàngjīng.
His grandfather, Sāhé Mèn,
had merits at the beginning of the dynasty,
and was appointed Lóng'ān Fǔ Lù Hézhā Móukè
and Duógǔ Ālín Méng'ān.
Yì had a handsome appearance
and was proficient in several foreign languages.
He married Shěnguó Gōngzhǔ, Emperor Xīzōng's seventh daughter.
He served as Fúbǎo Zhīhòu,
was promoted to Yùyuàn Tōngjìn,
and appointed Fúbǎo Láng.
He successively served as Cìshǐ of Xuāndé, Tài'ān, and Zīzhōu,
and was known for his integrity.
He was transferred to be Tóngzhī Guǎngníng Fǔ Shì,
but due to mourning for his mother, Èguó Gōngzhǔ,
he did not take up the post.
Shìzōng specifically permitted him to inherit his father's enfeoffment during the mourning period.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Jǐnán Fǔ Shì.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was promoted to Dìzhōu Fángyù Shǐ.
His administrative achievements were well-known,
and he was promoted to Línghǎi Jūn Jiédù Shǐ,
and then died.
Yì's family had been noble and favored for generations.
From his great-grandfather Zhào down to Yì, there were four generations who married princesses.
Wūlíndá Fù's original name was Ālǐlá,
a native of Dōngpíng.
He began his career as a Fèngyù.
In Dàdìng 7th year, he married Shìzōng's seventh daughter, Wǎnguó Gōngzhǔ,
and was granted the title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
He was then appointed Yǐnjìn Shǐ and concurrently Fúbǎoláng.
He was sent out as the Cìshǐ of Lízhōu,
and after three promotions, became the Jiédùshǐ of Guīdé Jūn.
In Míngchāng 3rd year,
he was transferred to Zhī Xīngzhōng Fǔshì.
After a long time,
he became the Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn of Hélǎn Lù.
In Chéng'ān 4th year,
he was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Jiàngyáng Jūn,
and then died.
Wūgǔlún Yuánzhōng's original name was Èlǐyě.
His ancestors were from Dúbágǔ, Shàngjīng.
His father, Èlún,
married Tàizǔ's daughter, Bìguó Gōngzhǔ.
Yuánzhōng was exceptionally brilliant in his youth.
When Shìzōng was still in his private residence, he gave his eldest daughter to him in marriage,
who was later enfeoffed as Lǔguó Dàzhǎng Gōngzhǔ.
At the end of Zhènglóng,
he followed Hǎilíng on his southern campaign.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne in Liáoyáng,
at that time Tàibǎo Áng was Hǎilíng's Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Dà Dūdū,
he sent Yuánzhōng to attend court at the temporary imperial residence.
He was subsequently granted the title of Dìngyuǎn Dà Jiāngjūn,
and promoted to Fúbǎoláng.
Shìzōng admonished him, saying:
"When I first ascended the throne,
no one is as close and intimate as you.
You should be vigilant against unforeseen circumstances while attending and guarding me."
In Dàdìng 2nd year,
he was granted the additional title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
appointed Jìnsì Júshǐ,
and promoted to Diànqián Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn.
When accompanying Shìzōng on a hunt,
the emperor wished to shoot a tiger,
but Yuánzhōng advised against it.
He was promoted to Diànqián Yòu Fù Dū Diǎnjiǎn,
and served as the envoy to the Sòng for the New Year's festival.
Upon his return,
he was transferred to Zuǒ Fù Dū Diǎnjiǎn.
He was dismissed from office for his household servants illegally monopolizing the collection of public taxes.
In the 11th year,
he was restored to his former position.
The following year,
he was promoted to Dū Diǎnjiǎn.
In the 15th year,
when the northern frontier made tribute,
Yuánzhōng was ordered to go and receive it.
Upon his return,
an imperial edict stated:
"Whenever you were on duty for me,
I always slept peacefully.
This summer, I am at Jǐngmíng Gōng,
and you have been gone for a long time.
I miss you very much."
Coincidentally, there was a vacancy for the guardian of Dàxīng Fǔ,
so Yuánzhōng was appointed Zhīfǔ Shì.
A monk violated the law,
and the officials apprehended him and imprisoned him.
Imperial aunt Liángguó Dàzhǎng Gōngzhǔ requested his release,
but Yuánzhōng refused.
The princess then reported the matter,
and Shìzōng summoned him and said:
"Your refusal to indulge personal feelings
is highly commendable.
If the capital is governed in this way,
what else do I have to worry about?"
After his term expired,
he was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
His son Yì married Xiǎnzōng's eldest daughter, Xuēguó Gōngzhǔ.
In the 18th year,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Dàfū,
and granted the hereditary Mòkè of Sābā Shān.
Shìzōng asked Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Hégēlì Liángbì who was suitable for the chancellorship.
Liángbì replied with Yuánzhōng,
who was then appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
enfeoffed as Rènguó Gōng,
and promoted to Shàngshū Yòu Chéngxiàng.
When the policy examination for advanced scholars was established,
Yuánzhōng supported it.
When Shìzōng was about to travel to Huìníng,
Yuánzhōng remonstrated against it but was not heeded.
He was sent out as Zhī Zhēndìng Fǔ,
but soon after was recalled by imperial edict to be Yòu Chéngxiàng.
Shìzōng wanted to pave the Shàngjīng city with bricks.
Yuánzhōng said:
"This region suffered from the military campaigns during Zhènglóng,
and the common people are impoverished.
Even after Your Majesty's twenty-plus years of rest and recovery,
it has not yet fully recovered.
Moreover, the soil quality is poor and loose;
paving it with bricks may not last long.
If it is destroyed by wind and rain,
and needs repairs year after year,
the people will become even more distressed."
The imperial carriage remained in the east for a long time without returning.
Yuánzhōng submitted a memorial, saying:
"The imperial carriage has been stationed here for a year.
The granaries are diminishing daily,
market prices are gradually increasing,
and many from the imperial guard and various government offices have fled.
Officials apprehending and punishing them according to the law might harm Your Majesty's benevolence and love."
Shìzōng praised and accepted his advice.
Soon after, he was sent out as Běijīng Liúshǒu.
Shìzōng admonished him, saying:
"You are headstrong and self-willed,
usurping authority and forming close ties with intimates.
Your heart is unfathomable.
Hurry to your post."
Later, Zuǒ Chéng Zhāng Rǔbì reported on affairs.
Shìzōng disliked his flattery,
and said to his attendants:
"You all equivocate and evade on every matter,
unwilling to speak truthfully.
How can you be worthy of high office and generous salaries?
If Wūgǔlún Yuánzhōng were prime minister,
he would be upright and dare to speak,
acting righteously without regard for himself.
He is truly worthy of respect."
Thereupon,
he was reassigned as Zhī Zhēndìng Fǔshì,
then moved to Zhī Héjiān.
In Míngchāng 2nd year,
he was Zhī Guǎngníng Fǔ.
Because the construction of a polo field in Héjiān disturbed the people,
he was pardoned when a general amnesty was issued,
and appointed Shùnyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He requested retirement but it was not granted.
He was specially granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Běijīng Liúshǒu.
He was then moved to Zhī Jìnán Fǔ.
Passing through the imperial capital, he was ordered to attend a banquet,
seated above the Píngzhāng Zhèngshì.
In Chéng'ān 2nd year,
he was moved to guard Nánjīng,
soon after reassigned as Zhī Zhāngdé Fǔ,
and then died.
Upon hearing the news of his death,
the emperor sent Xuānhuī Shǐ Bái Wǎn to conduct the funeral rites,
and bestowed a very generous funeral gift.
Yuánzhōng was always noble,
bold and uninhibited by nature, but deeply jealous inwardly.
Shìzōng had once reprimanded him for this.
Moreover, wherever he went, he could not restrain his servants,
and people often criticized him for this.
His son was Yì.
Yì's original name was Xióngmíng.
In the 8th year of Dàdìng,
he married Hǎilíng's daughter.
At a banquet for the imperial clan and officials of the sixth rank and above,
noblewomen were present.
The Emperor said:
「This girl is also a great-granddaughter of Tàizǔ,
just like Our own daughter.
Her father was deposed and died,
which is not the fault of his daughter. 」
Hǎilíng's daughter died.
In the 21st year of Dàdìng,
he married Xiǎnzōng's daughter, Princess Guǎngpíng.
Yì served successively in the palace guards.
His character was [missing character] and bold, like his father.
In the 26th year,
the Emperor said to Prince Yuán:
「Yuánzhōng should not hope that he can ever be reinstated as chancellor.
Xióngmíng is also not as good as his father.
We have always treated him leniently,
but he utterly fails to appreciate Our grace.
You should know what kind of person he is. 」
He said to Xiāng, the Píngzhāng Zhèngshì:
「Xióngmíng can be appointed to an outside post.
From now on, any palace official who has already been ordered to an outside post,
before they receive their formal court appointment,
must not be allowed to enter the palace. 」
Thereupon,
Yì was appointed as the Associate Administrator of Chéngzhōu Military and Civil Affairs.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
Princess Guǎngpíng was promoted to Elder Princess of Yè State.
Yì was reappointed as the Deputy Military Commissioner of Shùntiān Circuit,
and given the added title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
In the 1st year of Chéng'ān,
he was successively promoted to Director of the Imperial Library, concurrently serving as Vice Minister of Personnel.
He was then transferred to the Ministry of Punishments,
and promoted to Minister of Works.
In the 1st year of Tàihé,
he encountered the mourning period for his father Yuánzhōng.
In the 2nd year,
he was reinstated to his original office after mourning.
In the 3rd year,
he was appointed Administrator of Dōngpíng Prefecture,
and then Administrator of Zhēndìng Prefecture.
In the 6th year,
during the campaign against Sòng,
he was promoted to Left Grand Supervisor of the Grand Marshal.
In the 7th year,
he was transferred to Left Military Supervisor.
In the 8th year,
he was appointed Grand Censor.
During the Dà'ān era,
he was Administrator of Dàmíng Prefecture.
In the early Zhìníng era,
he was executed for conspiracy to rebel.
Tángkuò Gòng's original name was Dágē.
He was the son of Grand Tutor Ālǐ.
He married Shìzōng's fourth daughter, Princess Wú State,
and was granted the title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
serving as Imperial Attendant.
He was specially appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard Corps.
He was promoted five times, reaching Vice Minister of Punishments.
For unauthorized leave of absence, he was demoted one rank,
and sent out as Defense Commissioner of Dézhōu.
He was promoted to Military Commissioner of Shùntiān Circuit,
and then transferred to govern Hénghǎi.
He was recalled to serve as Left Commissioner of Military Affairs,
promoted to Minister of War,
then transferred to the Ministry of Personnel,
and moved to Minister of Rites, concurrently serving as Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
Earlier,
when the post of Minister of the Court of Judicial Review was vacant,
Shìzōng ordered his chancellors to select a suitable candidate.
Left Chancellor Zhāng Rúbì recommended Yáng Zǐyì, Deputy Resident Administrator of the Western Capital, for his detailed understanding of law.
The Emperor said:
「Although Zǐyì understands the law,
his intentions are not upright.
How can he be entrusted to distinguish right from wrong throughout the empire?
The Court of Judicial Review must employ a just and upright person. 」
Right Chancellor Niángē Wòtèlà recommended Gòng as suitable for handling the simple and minor duties while concurrently holding this post.
Consequently, Gòng was appointed to it.
In the 28th year,
he was appointed Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs.
When Zhāngzōng ascended,
he became Grand Censor.
On Gòng's birthday,

Right Grand Chancellor Xiāng, Associate Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs Liú Wěi, Director of a Bureau in the Ministry of Personnel [missing character], and Commander-in-Chief of the Metropolitan Cavalry and Infantry Héxǐ celebrated Gòng's birthday.
Consequently, they violated the night curfew.
Héxǐ dispatched soldiers to escort Xiāng to his residence.
Investigating Censor Túdān Déshèng impeached them for this matter.
The Ministry of Punishments was ordered to arrest [missing character] and others for interrogation.
The Emperor released Xiāng and Wěi because they were high-ranking officials,
while Gòng and the others were dismissed from their posts.
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator of Dàxīng Prefecture,
and reinstated as Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs.
He requested to retire, but it was not granted.
He was promoted to Commissioner of Military Affairs,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Shēn State,
then re-enfeoffed as Duke of Xiāo.
He again submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
The Emperor said:
「You have already made this request before.
Later, We learned you wished for an outside appointment.
What will your current request lead to next? 」
So, a gracious imperial edict granted his request.
Soon after, he was re-appointed Administrator of Zhēndìng Prefecture.
In the 2nd year of Tàihé,
he passed away.
Wūlíndá Lín,
his original name was Liúzhù.
He married Princess Gào State,
and was given the added title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
In the 1st year of Zhēnyòu, he became Military Commissioner of Jìngnán Circuit.
When the Xià people invaded Bīnzhōu,
Lín surrendered.
Coincidentally, Yán'ān Prefecture sent its envoy Zhāng Fúsūn to the Xià kingdom.
The Xià people had Fúsūn meet Lín.
At that time, he had already suffered a stroke.
The Princess had a letter delivered to Fúsūn,
entrusting him to earnestly petition the Imperial Court,
hoping for peace soon so they could return home.
Fúsūn reported all of this.
An imperial edict granted him medicines.
Túdān Gōngbì, his original name was Xíliè,
was a Mang'an from Suànzhǔhǎi, Héběi Eastern Circuit.
His father, Fǔjūnnú,
married Xīzōng's daughter,
was given the added title of Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and ended his career as Military Commissioner of Wǔdìng Circuit.
Gōngbì first served as Imperial Attendant.
In the 27th year of Dàdìng,
he married Shìzōng's daughter, Princess Xī State,
and was given the added titles of General Who Pacifies Distant Regions and Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
He was re-appointed as Director of the Bureau of Utensils.
then transferred to Deputy Administrator, concurrently serving as Director of the Bureau of Personal Attendants.
He entered mourning for his father,
and was reinstated as Deputy Administrator of his original bureau after mourning.
Zhāngzōng shot a tiger on Autumn Mountain.
The tiger, enraged, charged forward.
All the imperial guards fled.
Gōngbì remained motionless.
The tiger then collapsed and died.
An imperial edict reprimanded the imperial guards and commended Gōngbì.
He was appointed Prefect of Bīnzhōu.
then twice promoted to Vice Minister of War,
and successively appointed Administrator of Dàmíng Prefecture.
At this time,
a military campaign against Sòng was launched.
The authorities were urgently collecting overdue taxes and the cattle head tax.
Gōngbì memorialized:
「Soldiers are serving in the army.
The people are also exhausted.
It would be advisable to collect taxes slowly to relieve the people. 」
The Imperial Court followed his advice.
In the early Dà'ān era,
he was appointed Administrator of Dàxīng Prefecture.
In judging a case of robbery in Wǔqīng,
he suspected injustice.
Later, the true culprit was indeed apprehended.
More than a year later, he was appointed Associate Administrator of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
promoted to Right Chancellor,
and then Left Chancellor.
In the early Zhìníng era,
he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Dìng State.
In the early Zhēnyòu era,
he was promoted to Right Grand Chancellor,
and dismissed to serve as Administrator of Zhōngshān Prefecture.
At this time,
the Central Capital was under urgent siege, making travel impossible.
When the siege was lifted,
Xuānzōng said:
「Zhōngshān has just suffered from war.
It would not be as good as Hézhōng. 」
So he was re-appointed Administrator of Hézhōng Prefecture.
He successively held the posts of Acting Military Commissioner of Dìngguó Circuit, Grand Tutor of the Imperial Grandson, and Co-Administrator of the Grand Imperial Kinship Affairs.
He passed away in the 5th year of Xīngdìng.
Xuānzōng suspended court sessions,
offered posthumous gifts,
and granted the posthumous name Kèyuàn.
Túshān Míng (銘), courtesy name Guóběn (國本),
was granted the name Zhòngtài (重泰) by Xiǎnzōng (顯宗).
His grandfather was Zhēn (貞),
who has a separate biography.
His father was Tèjìn (特進), Duke of Jīng (涇國公).
He was by nature serious, silent, and spoke little,
had a rough understanding of the classics and histories,
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
At the end of Dàdìng (大定),
he was appointed Fèngyù (奉御).
When Zhāngzōng (章宗) ascended the throne,
he was specially decreed to inherit the office of Méng'ān (猛安) of Húntèshān (渾特山) in Zhōngdū Lù (中都路).
In the fifth year of Míngchāng (明昌),
he was appointed Zhícháng (直長) of the Shàngyùn Shǔ (尚醞署),
and successively promoted to Shìyí Sīlìng (侍儀司令), Sùzhí Jiāngjūn (宿直將軍), Shàngyī Júshǐ (尚衣局使), and Bīngbù Lángzhōng (兵部郎中).
Together with Dàlǐ Píngshì (大理評事) Sūn Rénjiàn (孫人鑑), he served as Cǎifǎngshǐ (採訪使),
re-examining cases of the Tíxíng Sī (提刑司).
He was transferred to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍),
then to Zuǒwèi (左衞),
and went out to serve as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yǒngdìng Jūn (永定軍),
then transferred to Ànchásǐ (按察使) and Zhuǎnyùnshǐ (轉運使) of Héběi Dōngběi Lù (河東北路).
In the third year of Dà'ān (大安),
he was transferred to Zhī Dàmíng Fǔ (知大名府),
and was promoted to Ānfǔshǐ (安撫使) of Héběi Dōngxī Dàmíng Lù (河北東西大名路).
Dàmíng (大名) suffered from severe famine and distress,
so Míng (銘) requested a large issuance of jiāochāo (交鈔) to relieve the people.
At the beginning of Chóngqìng (崇慶),
he was transferred to Zhī Zhēndìng Fǔ (知真定府),
and again appointed Xuānfǔshǐ (宣撫使) of Héběi Dōngxī Dàmíng Lù (河北東西大名路).
In the ninth month of the first year of Zhìníng (至寧),
he was ordered to welcome Xuānzōng (宣宗) at Zhāngdé Fǔ (彰德府).
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng (尚書右丞),
and then went out to serve as Běijīng Liúshǒu (北京留守),
but could not proceed due to blocked roads.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (貞祐),
he died.
The eulogy says: When the Son of Heaven marries a empress,
and royal princesses marry commoners,
how could this not be a weighty matter?
Since the Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢) dynasties,
there have been no families where nephews and uncles intermarried for generations.
The Way of Guānjū (關雎) was lacking,
and maternal relatives became arrogant and excessive.
Why were the verses "Hé bǐ nóng yǐ" (何彼穠矣) not composed,
and the principles of quiet and graceful royal princesses (王姬肅雝) almost lost?
In ancient times, different surnames held hereditary ducal or marquis ranks and formed marital alliances with the Son of Heaven,
while other surnames were not allowed to participate.
When a daughter became empress,
and one married a royal princess,
one's own status was elevated,
but wealth and abundance were not added,
nor was favor and glory granted.
If the Hàn (漢) and Táng (唐) dynasties had followed this path,
there would have been no disasters of the Lǚ (呂) clan, Wáng (王) clan, or Wǔ (武) clan.
Princesses marrying commoners would each have found their proper place and been content.
The Túshān (徒單), Nálǎn (拏懶), Tángkuò (唐括), Púchá (蒲察), Péimǎn (裴滿), Gēshíliè (紇石烈), Púsǎn (僕散) clans of the Jīn (金) dynasty were all noble families.
The Son of Heaven would certainly marry an empress from these clans,
and princesses would certainly marry into these clans.
This was no different from the Qí (齊) and Jì (紀) states of the Zhōu (周) dynasty.
This was the most appropriate form of marriage ceremony,
superior to those of the Hàn (漢) and Táng (唐) dynasties.
Túshān Sìxǐ (徒單四喜)
was the younger brother of Empress Àizōng (哀宗).
On the night of Xīnyǒu (辛酉) in the first month of the second year of Tiānxīng (天興),
〔一０〕Sìxǐ (四喜) and the palace attendant Mǎ Fúhuì (馬福惠) arrived from Guīdé (歸德).
At that time, the Héshuò (河朔) region had already been lost,
but the capital city was still unaware.
The two had received an imperial decree to welcome the two empresses (liǎnggōng),
so they pretended to report a victory,
carrying small yellow flags as they entered.
Upon arrival, they presented the intention to welcome the two empresses.
On that day,
the two chief ministers were summoned to discuss the matter.
The two chief ministers and Wūgǔsūn Núshēn (烏古孫奴申) advised against it.
Sìxǐ (四喜) said with a change of color:
"I have received an imperial decree to welcome the two empresses;
anyone who dares to speak against it shall be dealt with according to a separate imperial edict."
The two chief ministers no longer dared to speak,
and the decision to proceed was made.

Besides the two empresses specified in the imperial decree, Consort Róu (柔妃) Péimǎn (裴滿) clan, and female attendants Zhāng Xiùruǐ (張秀蘃), Dūxiá (都轄), Chéngyù (承御), Tāngyào (湯藥), Imperial Wet Nurse Gǒngguó Fūrén (鞏國夫人), and more than ten others,
all others were dismissed.

They also took palace treasures: four hundred ingots of horseshoe gold, seven thousand large pearls the size of chestnut yolks, one mountain of raw gold, two pieces of borneol, and the Xìnruì imperial seal.
Moreover, it was permitted to grant half of the items accompanying the two empresses to the Zhōngxiào Jūn (忠孝軍).
On Rènyín (壬寅),
the Empress Dowager held court in Rén'ān Diàn (仁安殿),
〔一一〕distributing gold ingots and seven-treasure gold basins to the Zhōngxiào Jūn (忠孝軍).
That night,
the two empresses rode out.
Upon reaching Chénliú (陳留),
they saw fires rising in two or three places outside the city.
Suspecting the presence of soldiers,
while they hesitated,
Núshēn (奴申), who initially did not wish to go,
immediately carried out the Empress Dowager's order and rode back.
On Guǐmǎo (癸卯),
they entered the capital and stayed at Sìxǐ's (四喜) house.
〔一二〕After a short while,
they returned to the palace.
They discussed going again that night,
but the Empress Dowager was too exhausted from riding to move,
so they stopped.
The next day,
Cuī Lì (崔立) rebelled.
Sìxǐ (四喜), Shùjiǎ Tǎshībù (术甲塔失不), Tǎshībù's (塔失不) father Yǎozhù (咬住), and Sìxǐ's (四喜) wife Wányán (完顏) clan,
with ninety-seven cavalry of the Zhōngxiào Zú (忠孝卒), forced their way out of Cáomén (曹門),
intending to go to Guīdé (歸德).
Unable to exit,
they turned to Chénzhōu Mén (陳州門),
but were also stopped by the gate guards.
The gate commander, Yùzhōu Fángyùshǐ (裕州防禦使) Ābùhǎn Xiéhé (阿不罕斜合), had already fled.
The director Wányán Hézhù (完顏合住) temporarily took charge of the command,
and waved the gate guards to let Tǎshībù (塔失不) and others go,
saying:
"The fault is mine,
not yours."
The next day,
Lì (立) arrived with dozens of cavalry and summoned Hézhù (合住).
Hézhù (合住) knew he would surely die,
so he changed his clothes and cap and went.
Lì's (立)左右 clenched their fists, wanting to kill him.
Lì (立) saw him from afar
and asked:
"Are you the one who let the Zhōngxiào Jūn (忠孝軍) out of the gate?"
Hézhù (合住) said:
"Yes.
It was an imperial command,
I did let them go.
The fault is mine."
Lì (立) suddenly seemed to realize something
and addressed his soldiers:
"I know this official.
He worked with me when we built the Xiǎngchéng (𩹉城) before.
More than ten soldiers under my command stole official timber, a crime punishable by death,
but this official did not interrogate them,
only flogged them a few dozen times.
This family can kill people,
and can save people."
Then he kindly said to Hézhù (合住):
"Since they have already been released,
I will not punish you."
When Sìxǐ (四喜) and others arrived in Guīdé (歸德),
the Emperor asked in surprise about the two empresses.
The two replied that there was a military rebellion in the capital and they were unable to enter the palace.
The Emperor said:
"Did only your father and your wife manage to escape?"
They were thrown into prison,
and both were beheaded in the marketplace.
The eulogy says: Sìxǐ (四喜) was sent to welcome the two empresses,
but encountered Cuī Lì's (崔立) rebellion.
A wise man in this situation,
would have protected the two empresses amidst the soldiers,
awaiting the stabilization of the situation before making further plans.
If by any chance that failed,
he would have died for them;
there was no other recourse.
Sìxǐ (四喜) brought back his private relatives,
and hoped the sovereign would pardon his death.
Was he not foolish?
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 59, Zhōngyì (忠義) 1: Húshābǔ (胡沙補), Tèhǔ (特虎),

Púhūdē (僕忽得), Niángé Hánnú (粘割韓奴), Cáogūi (曹珪), Wēndíhǎn Púdǔ (溫迪罕蒲睹), É'ěrlǐyě (訛里也), Nàlán Chuòchì (納蘭綽赤), Wèi Quán (魏全), Shànyáng (鄯陽), Jiágǔ Shǒuzhōng (夾谷守中), Shímò Yuányì (石抹元毅), Bódéméi Héshàng (伯德梅和尚), Wūgǔsūn Wùtún (烏古孫兀屯), Gāo Shǒuyuē (高守約), Hésùjiā Ānlǐ (和速嘉安禮), Wáng Wéihàn (王維翰), Yílà Gǔyǔniè (移剌古與涅), Sòng Yǐ (宋扆), Wūgǔlún Róngzǔ (烏古論榮祖), Wūgǔlún Zhòngwēn (烏古論仲溫), Jiǔzhù (九住), Lǐ Yǎn (李演), Líu Déjī (劉德基), Wáng Yì (王毅), Wáng Huì (王晦), Qí Yīngyáng (齊鷹揚), Shùjiǎ Fǎxīn (术甲法心), Gāo Xī (高錫).
Luán Gòngzǐ (欒共子) said:
"People are born for three things;
they serve them as one.
Wherever they are, they should dedicate their lives."
Dukes, ministers, and grand masters hold their positions,
receive their stipends.
When the state faces difficulties,
those in court die in their offices;
those guarding prefectures and cities die by their city walls;
those leading armies die in battle formations.
Even commoners and officials from the marketplace and countryside, driven by indignation, die,
all in their proper place.
Therefore, to die in one's proper place
is to desire something more than life itself.
The Jīn (金) dynasty praised officials who died for their integrity,
not only granting posthumous official titles and ranks,
but also employing their descendants.
Since Zhēnyòu (貞祐),
this custom was further enhanced,
with temples erected and steles carved,
and sacrifices offered seasonally.
This can be said to be perfect.
The Holy Yuán (元) Emperor decreed the compilation of the histories of Liáo (遼), Jīn (金), and Sòng (宋).
The imperial historians discussed the editorial principles,
requesting that all loyal servants of previous dynasties be recorded without reservation.
The court followed this.
Alas,
how benevolent was the governance of the Holy Yuán (元) Emperor!
Sīmǎ Qiān (司馬遷) recorded Yù Ràng's (豫讓) words to Zhào Xiāngzǐ (趙襄子), saying:
"A lord should not conceal the merits of others,
and loyal subjects have the righteousness of achieving renown."
How profound these words are!
The governance of the Holy Yuán (元) Emperor serves as a lesson for ten thousand generations.
Herein are compiled the Biographies of the Loyal and Righteous.
Húshābǔ,
a Wányánbù man.
At thirty-five, he joined the army,
and was greatly trusted and employed.
Tàizǔ sent Púguālā to Liáoguó to invite Āshū,
but in reality, to observe their situation.
Púguālā returned and reported that the number of Liáo troops was unknown.
Tàizǔ doubted this,
and sent Húshābǔ instead.
He returned and reported:
"Liáo is currently mobilizing troops,
but they have not yet gathered in large numbers."
When he met the general,
the general made his grandson stand beside him in armor,
and said:
"People say that you are about to rebel,
so we are prepared."
As he traveled on the road,
he encountered Bóhǎi troops.
The Bóhǎi troops laughed and spoke to Húshābǔ, saying:
"We hear that the Nǚzhí want to cause trouble,
is that you?"
He reported everything to Tàizǔ,
and also said:
"Now is the time to undertake a great enterprise, we must not delay.
If we wait for the river to freeze,
the Liáo troops will gather in force and attack.
If we strike early before they gather,
we can achieve our goal."
Tàizǔ deeply agreed with this.
When Níngjiāngzhōu was conquered,
and in the battle at Dálǔgǔchéng,
he distinguished himself,
and was awarded banners, drums, and imperial weapons.
Gāo Yǒngchāng requested peace.
Húshābǔ went to recruit him,
and brought Hútúgǔ back.
Gāo Yǒngchāng falsely surrendered to Wòlǔ.
Wòlǔ sent Húshābǔ and Sābā to report.
It so happened that Gāo Zhēn surrendered,
saying that Yǒngchāng was not genuinely surrendering.
Wòlǔ then advanced his troops.
Yǒngchāng was enraged,
and consequently killed Húshābǔ and Sābā,
dismembering them both.
When Húshābǔ was seized,
his composure was unruffled.
He cursed Yǒngchāng, saying:
"You betray your lord and defy Heaven.
Today you kill me;
tomorrow it will be your turn."
He cursed without cease
until his death.
He was fifty-nine years old.
During the Tiānhuì period,
he and Sābā were both posthumously granted the title of Yáozhèn Jiéduúshǐ.
Tèhǔ,
a Yǎtàlánshuǐ man.
His physique was imposing,
and he was brave in battle.
During the battle of Dálǔgǔchéng,
Huónǚ was trapped by the enemy,
and Tèhǔ rescued him.
When attacking Zhàosànchéng,
three thousand Liáo soldiers came to resist.
Tèhǔ was the first to ascend the walls,
and defeated them.
When attacking Lúgěyíng,
Má Jí fell from his horse.
Tèhǔ single-handedly killed several Liáo soldiers,
and carried him out.
His rewards were exceptionally generous.
When the army returned from Línhuáng,
they reached the Liáohé.
Yúdǔ came to attack.
Lóushì had already withdrawn.
Tèhǔ alone held the rear.
When his horse was exhausted, he fought on foot.
Lóushì came with several cavalrymen to rescue him.
Tèhǔ stopped him, saying:
"I will defend against the enemy with my life.
Do not come, Your Grace;
it would be useless for us both to perish."
He then died in battle.
During the Huángtǒng period,
he was posthumously granted the title of Míngwēi Jiāngjūn.
Púhūdē,
a son of the imperial clan.
Initially, he served Guóxiàng Sāgǎi,
and distinguished himself in the campaign against Xiāo Hǎilǐ.
Together with Chóuwò,
he recruited and pacified the Zhúwēishuǐ tribe.
Chóuwò was made a Móukè,
and Púhūdē commanded a Xíngjūn Qiānhù.
He participated in the conquest of Huánglóngfǔ,
and in the battle at Dálǔgǔchéng,
both with distinction.
When Bóhǎi Yǐsāibǔ of Níngjiāngzhōu rebelled,
Púhūdē pursued and recovered the territory.
In the ninth month of the fifth year of Tiānfǔ (1121),
Chóuwò and Púhūdē went to Bīegǔhé to register military horses.
Shílǐgúdá and seven others from the Zhúwēishuǐ tribe killed Chóuwò and Púhūdē,
and threw their bodies into the river.
They were both forty-three years old.
Tàizǔ mourned and regretted them,
and sent envoys to offer condolences and funeral donations of an elevated rank.
In the first month of the sixth year (1122),
Wòlǔ campaigned against Shílǐgúdá at Shílǐhànhé,
pursuing them to Hétāláshān,
killing four people,
and pacifying the remaining population.
An imperial edict ordered Wòlǔ to search for the bodies of Chóuwò and Púhūdē for burial.
During the Tiānjuàn period,
Chóuwò was posthumously granted the title of Fèngguó Shàngjiāngjūn, and Púhūdē that of Zhāoyì Dàjiāngjūn.
Chóuwò
was also a son of the imperial clan.
At fifteen, he joined the army.
He followed Tàizǔ in campaigning against Liáo.
Leading the Táowēn Lù troops, he recruited and pacified the three Tǎntān, Shílǐhěn, and BáKǔ Sānshuǐ Bīegǔchéngyì,
all of whom surrendered.
He defeated five hundred Shìwéi at Āliánggěchéng,
capturing their people.
He died at this point.
Zhāngé Hánnú,
as a bodyguard, followed Zōngbì on campaigns,
and was awarded armor, bows, arrows, and warhorses.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ entered Jūyōngguān,
Liáo Línyá Yēlǜ Dàshí fled from Gǔběikǒu.
He attacked Fèngshèngzhōu with his troops,
encamping twenty-five *lǐ* east of Lóngmén.
Lóushì went to capture him,
seizing Dàshí and inducing his followers to surrender.
Zōngwàng raided the Liáo lord's baggage train at Qīngzhǒng,
using Dàshí as a guide.
An edict stated:
"Liáo Zhàowáng Xíníliè, Línyá Dàshí, Běiwáng Hēlízhì, Jiéduúshǐ Élílà, Bójǐn Chìgǒuer, Zhāotǎo Díliù, Xiángwěn Liùjīn, Tóngzhī Hǎilǐ, and all other officials and common people,
are hereby absolved of their crimes."
Another edict to Wòlǔ stated:
"Although Línyá Dàshí did not surrender,
he was useful as a guide.
You may clearly instruct him."
This was in the sixth year of Tiānfǔ (1122).
Afterwards, he fled,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
In the second year of Tiānhuì (1124),
Liáo Xiángwěn Tābùyě came to surrender,
saying that Dàshí had proclaimed himself king in the north,
and appointed officials for both the northern and southern regions,
having ten thousand warhorses,
and abundant livestock.
An edict stated:
"When pursuing the Liáo lord,
actions must be taken according to circumstances.
As for campaigning against Dàshí,
we must await further reports."
In the third year (1125),
Dūtǒng Wányán Xīyǐn reported:
"I hear that the Xià people made an agreement with Yēlǜ Dàshí, saying:
'Since Dà Jīn has captured the Liáo lord, all their armies will return home,
so we should combine forces to seize the various tribes in Shānxī.'"
The imperial reply stated:
"The Xià people might be conspiring with Dàshí to cause trouble,
which must be investigated.
Be prepared for it."
In the seventh year (1129),
Tàizhōu Lù Dūtǒng Pólúhuǒ submitted a memorial:
"Dàshí has already gained two northern camps.
I fear it will be difficult to control him later,
and he is close to the imperial pastures.
We should establish garrisons."
The imperial reply stated:
"To dispatch troops because of two camps
would certainly disturb the various tribes.
We should merely be diligent in scouting."
In the eighth year (1130),
Yēlǜ Yúdǔ, Shíjiānú, and Bálísu were sent to pursue and campaign against Dàshí.
Troops were levied from various tribes,
but the tribes did not comply.
Shíjiānú returned after reaching Wùnàshuǐ.
Yúdǔ reported to the Yuánshuàifǔ:
"I hear that Yēlǜ Dàshí is in the territory of Hézhōu.
Fearing he might ally with the Xià people,
an envoy should be sent to demand him."
The Xiàguó replied:
"Our small country does not border Hézhōu,
and we do not know where Dàshí has gone."
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng (1144),
the Huíhú sent an envoy with tribute,
stating that Dàshí's country was adjacent to theirs,
and that Dàshí had already died.
An imperial edict sent Hánnú along with the envoy,
to observe the customs of their country,
promoted him to Wǔyì Jiāngjūn,
and dispatched him as an envoy to Dàshí.
After Hánnú departed,
nothing more was heard from him.
During the Dàdìng reign,
three Uighurs, Yíxílǎn and his companions, arrived at the Xīnán Zhāotǎo Sī (Southwest Pacification Commissioner's Office) to trade.
They said:
“Our native land is the Uighur Zhōukuò tribe.
The name of the city where we reside is Gǔsīéluólǔ.
Our people customarily have no weapons;
we farm as our occupation.
One-tenth of what we harvest is paid to the officials.
The elders pass down stories that,
in earlier times, the Qìdān came, and we could not resist them,
so we became their subjects.
The Qìdān's encampment
was so large that it took a horseman from dawn until noon to circle it.
In recent years, the Qìdān sent their son-in-law, Āběnsī, to lead 50,000 troops north to attack the Yèbùlián and other tribes,
but they failed and returned.
Fighting has continued ever since.”
An imperial edict stated:
“These individuals do not belong to a tribe under the imperial court.
There is no need to send them away.
They can be settled among the existing Uighurs in Hánpíng Fǔ,
so they do not lose their homes.”
That year,
the commander of the Niánbá'ēn, Sālǐyǎyīntèsī, along with the Kānglǐ chieftain Bógǔ and over 30,000 households, sought to pledge allegiance to the interior,
requesting to surrender the plaques and seals previously granted by Dàshí [Yēlǜ Dàshí]
and receive plaques and seals from the imperial court.
An edict commanded the Xīnán Zhāotǎo Sī to send someone to offer comfort and inquire,
and also to observe their intentions.
Tūlǐ Yúdǔ and the interpreter Ālǔdài went to their country and met Sālǐyǎ,
who fully expressed his desire to submit to the imperial court,
requesting the grant of plaques and seals,
and stating that there were no other intentions.
They then said:
“In past years, our great nation once sent Niángē Hánnú from Hé Zhōu as an envoy to Dàshí.
After he entered their territory,
Dàshí happened to be out in the wilderness.
He met Hánnú
and asked Hánnú who dared not dismount.
Hánnú replied: 'I am an envoy from the Celestial Empire.
I come by the Son of Heaven's command to summon you to surrender.
You should dismount and listen to the imperial edict.'
Dàshí said: 'You come alone as an envoy;
do you intend to engage in mere words?'
He had his men drag him down
and forced Hánnú to kneel.
Hánnú cursed, saying: 'Rebel!
The Son of Heaven, unwilling to bring an army against you,
sent me to summon you.
Even if you cannot tie yourself up and beg for forgiveness at the imperial palace,
you should still show utmost respect to the Son of Heaven's envoy.
How dare you instead insult me?'
Dàshí became enraged and killed him.
At this time, Dàshí Línyá had already died,
and his descendants succeeded him,
but the various Western tribes still referred to them as Dàshí.”
Yúdǔ and
Ālǔdài returned and reported,
also reporting the incident involving Hánnú.
Shìzōng praised Hánnú's loyalty and integrity,
posthumously awarding him the title of Zhāoyì Dàjiāngjūn.
He summoned Hánnú's sons, Xiánggǔ, Surveillance Commissioner of Wine for Yǒnghé Xiàn, and Lóushì, Patrol Inspector of Rǔ Zhōu, and instructed them:
“Your father, as an envoy, traveled ten thousand *lǐ*
and did not disgrace the imperial command.
He was able to fulfill his duty unto death.
I deeply mourn him.”
He appointed Xiánggǔ as Zhícháng of the Shàngniǎnjú,
and promoted him to Wǔyì Jiāngjūn,
and Lóushì as Zhícháng of the Wǔqìshǔ.
Cáo Guī
was from Xú Zhōu.
In the fourth year of Dàdìng,
Jiāng Zhì, a man from the same prefecture, rebelled.
Guī's son, Bì, was among the rebel party.
Guī plotted to execute Zhì,
and killed Bì as well.
The Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) deliberated
that he should be appointed to two miscellaneous official ranks.
An imperial edict stated:
“Guī's unwavering loyalty to the state,
sacrificing his kin for the greater good,
is rarely heard of since ancient times.
Though the law is as such,
it is still not sufficient to recompense his achievement.
He shall be promoted by one further rank
and appointed to a regular official position.”
Wēndíhǎn Púdǔ
served as the Qúnmùshǐ (Superintendent of Herds) of Wùzhě.
When the Qìdān Sābā and others rebelled in the northwest region,
all the Qúnmùshǐ responded to them.
Púdǔ, hearing of the rebellion,
selected dozens of brave and capable household servants,
provided them with weapons,
and secretly prepared for it.
The rebels, unable to launch their attack,
deceived the servants, saying:
“The officials are inspecting weapons;
we wish to borrow your weapons for the inspection.”
The servants believed it was true
and lent them the weapons.
The next morning,
the rebels arrived,
and Púdǔ had no means to resist them.
The rebels seized Púdǔ and asked him:
“Will you rebel now or not?”
Púdǔ said:
“My family has for generations received great kindness from the state,
and my sons and nephews all hold official positions.
I cannot rebel with you and bring disgrace upon my clan.”
The rebels, enraged,
dismembered and killed him.
His son and grandson were also killed.
At this time,
Túdān Sàilǐ, Qúnmùshǐ of Díwò, and Chìzhǎn Húshīdá, the deputy superintendent;
Hèshòu, Qúnmùshǐ of Yēlǔwǎ;
Wányán Shùlǐgǔ, Qúnmùshǐ of Ōulǐbù,
and Wányán Cíbùshī, the deputy superintendent;
Chìzhǎn Húshīlái, deputy superintendent of Bǔdíbù;
Jiāgǔ Mǎizhù, Xiángwěn (Pacification Commissioner) of Sùmùdiǎncí;
Wányán Sùmògě, Xiángwěn of Húdǔcí;
Gāo Péngzǔ, Xiángwěn of Xiámùcí, and others were all killed.
Hèshòu
was the son of Wú Néng Wáng (Prince Wú Néng), Āng,
his original name being Wúdūbù.
Lǎo Héshang, a man from the Wǔyuànbù, led his followers to invite Hèshòu to rebel with them.
Hèshòu said:
“I am a descendant of the imperial clan and have received great kindness from the state.
I would rather be killed
than rebel with you traitors.”
Consequently, he and his two sons were all killed.
Élǐyě
was a Qìdān.
He served as Zhícháng of the Shàngjú.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
when Qìdān were being persuaded to surrender,
Wōwò shouted and ordered Élǐyě to kneel before him.
Élǐyě refused,
saying:
“I am an envoy of the imperial court;
how can I compromise my integrity before you?
If you surrender early, you can save your lives.
If the great army arrives,
it will be too late for you to regret it.”
Wōwò angrily said:
“You are originally a Qìdān,
yet you do not follow me.
How dare you utter such words?”
Then he killed him.
The cavalrymen accompanying him, Rùnsūn, Shǐ Dà, and Xímǎ Xiǎodǐ Pōdá, were all killed.
Three years later,
Élǐyě was posthumously granted the title Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and his son Ābùshā was appointed Wàizhàng Xiǎodǐ.
Rùnsūn and Shǐ Dà were both posthumously granted Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi.
Pōdá was posthumously granted Zhōngyì Xiàowèi.
Nàlán Chuòchì
was a Měng'ān from Yīgǎihé in Hánpíng Lù.
The Qìdān Guōlǐ sent someone to invite him to join them,
but Chuòchì refused.
When Guōlǐ's troops were about to arrive,
Chuòchì organized the surrounding villages and strongholds into a military force,
provided them with over a hundred of his own horses,
and taught them methods of combat and stabbing.
Together, they resisted Guōlǐ at the Yīgǎi ferry crossing,
which prevented the rebels from advancing for over a month.
Subsequently, Guōlǐ's army of 40,000 arrived in full force.
Chuòchì fought against them,
but the rebel forces were ten times his number.
He was captured
and dismembered and killed.
An imperial edict granted him a posthumous promotion of two ranks,
and both his sons were able to enter officialdom through hereditary privilege.
Wèi Quán
was from Shòu Zhōu.
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
Lǐ Shuǎng of Sòng besieged Shòu Zhōu.
The刺史 (Prefect), Túdān Xī, registered all the soldiers, civilians, and retainers in the city, totaling over 3,000 people,
and resisted staunchly, adapting to circumstances.
Xī was skilled at managing and controlling,
winning the hearts of the people,
so even women were happy to serve.
The Tongzhī (Associate Administrator), Púliègǔ, died from an arrow wound,
but Xī was even more determined and did not falter.
He recruited men to go and attack Shuǎng's camp.
Quán was among those selected
