and was captured by Shuǎng's soldiers.
Shuǎng said to Quán:
“If you curse the Jīn emperor for me,
I will spare your life.”
Quán went to the city wall,
but instead cursed the Sòng emperor.
Shuǎng then killed him.
He continued cursing until his death.
Pú-Sǎn Kuí dispatched the Henan General Military Governor's Assistant Judge, Qǐ-Zhù, and Mǎi-Gē, with two thousand cavalry to relieve Shòu-Zhōu.
Ten-plus *lǐ* from Shòu-Zhōu, they encountered Shuǎng's troops.
Qǐ-Zhù divided his forces into two wings and attacked Shuǎng's troops from both sides,
utterly defeating them.
They decapitated over ten thousand heads,
pursued the fleeing enemy to the city walls,
captured three of their palisades,
and burned their pontoon bridge.
Xī led his troops out to support them.
Shuǎng's troops were utterly routed,
and many drowned in the Huái River.
Shuǎng and his deputy Tián-Lín barely escaped with their lives;
only four-tenths of the remaining soldiers escaped.

An imperial edict promoted Xī to Defense Commissioner, Qǐ-Zhù to Assistant Administrator of the Chāng-Wǔ Military Commissioner's office, and Mǎi-Gē to Assistant Judge of the Henan Circuit General Military Governor's office.
Pú-Liè-Gǔ was posthumously granted the title of Grand General of Illustrious Valor,
and his son Tú-Lá was given an official position.
Quán was posthumously granted the title of General of Martial Valor and Magistrate of Méng-Chéng County,
his wife was enfeoffed as Xiāng-Jūn,
and she was granted three rooms in an official residence in the prefecture and one million cash.
His son, upon reaching the age of fifteen, was to be enrolled as an eighth-rank official in the Zhèng-Bān Bureau's attendant section,
benefiting from the official position granted as an *yīn* privilege.
Furthermore, Quán's death as a loyal martyr was to be recorded in the Imperial Historiography Office
and engraved on blocks for promulgation throughout the empire.
Shàn-Yáng
was a member of the imperial clan.
He served as a Guardian of the Imperial Seals.
Wán-Yán Shí-Gǔ-Nǎi was a Commander of Ten Guardsmen.
In the eighth month of the first year of Zhì-Níng,
Hé-Shí-Liè Zhí-Zhōng started a rebellion,
entering through the Tōng-Xuán Gate.
On that day,
the uprising was sudden and urgent;
those inside and outside the court knew not what to do.
Shàn-Yáng and Shí-Gǔ-Nǎi went to Tiān-Wáng Temple to summon five hundred Dà-Hàn soldiers to meet the crisis.
They fought Zhí-Zhōng outside the Dōng-Huá Gate.
Zhí-Zhōng loudly proclaimed:
"The Dà-Hàn soldiers have rebelled!
Kill one person and be rewarded with one *dìng* of silver!"
Zhí-Zhōng's forces were numerous,
while the Dà-Hàn soldiers were few.
The two did not prevail and died.
In a moment,
Zhí-Zhōng's soldiers had almost completely annihilated the five hundred men.
After Zhí-Zhōng's death,
an imperial edict stripped him of his official titles and ranks.
The edict stated:
"General of Martial Valor, Commander of Ten Guardsmen Wán-Yán Shí-Gǔ-Nǎi,
and Cultivator of Martial Arts Commandant, Guardian of the Imperial Seals Shàn-Yáng,
were loyal, filial, brave, and resolute,
and perished in service to the state.
Shí-Gǔ-Nǎi is posthumously granted the title of Supreme General who Guards the State and Prefect of Shùn-Zhōu.
Shàn-Yáng is posthumously granted the title of General of Martial Valor and Deputy Military Commissioner of Shùn-Tiān Military Command.
Those *méng-ān* who previously followed and resisted in battle are rewarded five hundred *guàn* of cash, *móu-kè* three hundred *guàn*, and Pú-Liǎn scattered troops two hundred *guàn*.
Each is promoted two ranks.
For those who died in battle,
the posthumous rewards are to be given to their families.
Shí-Gǔ-Nǎi's son is still young,
so he shall be granted an eight-rank official's stipend,
and this will be reported when he reaches fifteen years of age."
Jiá-Gǔ Shǒu-Zhōng,
a native of Xián-Píng,
originally named Ā-Tǔ-Gǔ.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-second year of Dà-Dìng,
and served successively as Chief Clerk of Qīng-Chí and Wén-Xǐ,
was appointed Registrar in the Department of State Affairs,
then served as Department Director in the Ministry of Justice, Censor, and Compiler of the Diary of Activity and Repose.
He was transferred to Supernumerary Assistant Director of the Ministry of Rites, then Judicial Administrator of Dà-Míng,
and successively served as Surveillance Vice Commissioner for Sōng-Zhuó,
Běi-Jīng, and Lín-Táo Circuits.
He resigned due to mourning,
was reinstated as Assistant Administrator of the Hè-Lǎn Circuit Military Affairs General Command,
and was demoted to Prefect of Hán-Zhōu due to an incident.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Assistant Administrator of Píng-Liáng Prefecture.
In the second year of Dà-Ān,
he became Defense Commissioner of Qín-Zhōu,
and was promoted to Military Commissioner of Tōng-Yuǎn Command.
Towards the end of Zhì-Níng,
he was transferred to Zhāng-Huà Command,
but before he could assume office,
tens of thousands of Xī-Xià troops entered Gǒng-Zhōu.
Shǒu-Zhōng defended the city from the walls,
but with few troops, he could not hold out.
The city fell,
and all officials and clerks surrendered,
but Shǒu-Zhōng alone did not yield.
The Xī-Xià people admired him,
and both lured and threatened him, but Shǒu-Zhōng became even more steadfast,
so they transported him westward.
Upon reaching Píng-Liáng,
they demanded that he persuade the people of the prefecture to surrender.
Shǒu-Zhōng feigned agreement,
but upon reaching the city walls, he loudly shouted:
"The enemy's arrows are exhausted and they are about to flee!
Do not surrender!"
The Xī-Xià soldiers immediately killed him.
In the first year of Xīng-Dìng,
Censor Guō-Zhe investigated the matter in Qín-Zhōng
and reported it.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Grand Master of Aiding Goodness and Resident Administrator of Dōng-Jīng,
and his son Wù-Mǔ was to be taken in as an attendant in the Bureau of Stationery.
Shí-Mò Yuán-Yì, originally named Shén-Sī,
was from the Shā-Guǒ-Gē-Xiān *móu-kè* of the Zhuó-Chì-Liè *méng-ān* in the Xián-Píng Prefecture Circuit.
He was appointed Registrar in the Ministry of Personnel through *yīn* privilege.
He was twice transferred to Magistrate of Níng-Jīn in Jǐng-Zhōu.
There was a notorious bandit gang that openly robbed and harmed the people.
Yuán-Yì used strategies to defend against them,
and the bandits dispersed.
He entered the capital to serve as Judicial Administrator in the Grand Court of Justice,
then was appointed Assistant Administrator of Bó-Zhōu Defense Command.
He was commissioned by the secretariat
to investigate criminal cases in the five circuits west of Shǎn,
and found no innocent person wronged.
He was again entrusted to receive the annual tribute from Sòng.
Traditionally, there were private gifts,
but Yuán-Yì received nothing.
In early Míng-Chāng,
he was summoned by express courier to serve as Assistant Judge for Judicial Administration of Dà-Míng and other circuits.
He was promoted to Deputy Military Commissioner of Fén-Yáng Command for his outstanding performance.
At that time, bandit gangs gathered between Shí and Lán prefectures,
openly plundering.
The court ordered Yuán-Yì to capture them.
The bandits, fearing him, fled.
Yuán-Yì pursued them and utterly annihilated them,
bringing peace to the two regions.
He was promoted to Assistant Administrator of the Wǔ-Shèng Military Commissioner's office.
In another prefecture, there was a murderer
who repeatedly refused to confess despite interrogations.
Yuán-Yì questioned him for only a few words, and he confessed completely.
In the northern part of Hé-Dōng Circuit, much of the land was mountainous, barren, and infertile.
During the major land survey, it was classified for high taxation,
and the people had long been impoverished.
The court ordered a re-survey of the land for taxation.
Yuán-Yì equalized the tax using the method of three soil grades,
and the people benefited from it.
He was reassigned as Judicial Administrator of Zhāng-Dé Prefecture,
and soon after, due to border alarms, he was appointed Prefect of Fǔ-Zhōu.
At that time, a border general had lost his defense,
and fodder, grain, horses, and cattle were almost completely burned and plundered.
Yuán-Yì led over thirty officials and soldiers out of the prefecture to plan for military provisions,
and unexpectedly encountered the enemy.
The prefectural deputy and his accompanying officials firmly urged him to return.
Yuán-Yì said:
"Our responsibility is to guard the border.
If we flee upon encountering the enemy, what will become of the common people?
Even if we save ourselves,
what face will we have to see the court?"
He then held his bow and arrows and commanded the troops.
The troops, moved by his loyalty, vied to fight to the death.
Yuán-Yì fought bravely,
his arrows never missing their mark.
The enemy retreated and then reassembled.
Yuán-Yì's spirit grew fiercer.
After a long and fierce battle,
being outnumbered, he was ultimately killed.
He was forty-seven years old at the time.
When the matter was reported,
the emperor was deeply shocked and grieved,
posthumously granting him the title of General of Trustworthy Valor.
His son, Shì-Jì, was summoned to serve as an attendant in the Bureau of Ceremonial Affairs.
Shì-Jì later passed the imperial examination.
On the day his name was announced,
the emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Is this Shén-Sī's son?"
He sighed in admiration for a long time.
Yuán-Yì was by nature profound and sincere,
and his martial bravery surpassed others.
Whenever he read historical accounts of loyal and righteous ancient figures, he never failed to sigh in admiration and longing,
his face visibly moved.
Thus, when facing difficulty, he was able to die for his duty.
Bó-Dé-Méi Hé-Shàng,
was a native of Tài-Zhōu.
He was by nature forthright and honest,
and valued integrity.
In the fifth year of Zhèng-Lóng,
he was taken in as a guard,
and appointed Deputy Commissioner of Herding for the Hè-Lǔ-Wǎn Herds.
Not long after,
he was again summoned to be a Commander of Ten Guardsmen,
then changed to Deputy Commissioner of the Imperial Workshop,
promoted to Commissioner of that bureau,
and transferred to General of the Right Guard, Palace Guard Commissioner.
He supervised the Imperial Workshop for over ten years,
accumulating merit and being specially promoted two ranks,
and appointed Prefect of Fù-Zhōu.
In early Míng-Chāng,
he served as Deputy Commander of the Northwest Circuit Pacification Command,
was reassigned as Defense Commissioner of Qín-Zhōu,
and promoted to Military Commissioner of Wǔ-Shèng Command.
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to govern Chóng-Yì Command.
At that time, there were affairs on the northern border.
Left Chancellor Jiá-Gǔ Qīng-Chén was acting provincial governor in Lín-Huáng,
and commissioned Bó-Dé-Méi as his deputy commander.
When the enemy entered Lín-huáng,
Méi Hé-shàng and the bodyguard Pì-hé-tǔ and others led their troops to intercept and attack them.
The enemy formed up their ranks to await,
Méi Hé-shàng charged directly into their formation,
killing and wounding many.
The enemy, knowing it was an isolated force with no reinforcements,
gathered their troops and surrounded them.
Realizing they could not escape,
they dismounted and shot back-to-back,
killing over a hundred more men.
Even when their arrows were exhausted, they still fought with their bows,
and he was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Pì-hé-tǔ and the others were all lost.
The Emperor was shocked and grieved upon hearing this,
and issued an edict posthumously promoting him to Lóng-hǔ-wèi Shàng-jiàng-jūn,
skipping ten ranks,
and specially granted him 200,000 cash.
He ordered him to be buried with proper rites,
with all expenses provided by the government.
His son Dū-nú was made Jūn-qián Měng-ān,
and Zhōng-nú was ordered to oversee the funeral.
Lǐ Dá-kě, who was provisionally serving as Tóng-zhī Lín-huáng-fǔ-shì, was appointed as the Commissioner for Imperial Sacrifices,
and Shí-mò Hé-shàng, Tóng-zhī Dé-chāng-jūn Jié-dù-shǐ-shì, was appointed as the Commissioner for Imperial Burial.
In the fifth year of Chéng-ān,
the Emperor addressed the Shàng-shū-shěng, saying:
“Méi Hé-shàng died for the royal cause,
and his son Dū-nú has long served in the military and has meritorious service.
Deliberate on how to reward him.”
Thereupon, he was appointed Diǎn-shǔ-chéng.
Wū-gǔ-sūn Wù-tún,
a native of Shàng-jīng-lù.
At the end of Dà-dìng,
he inherited the Měng-ān title.
In the seventh year of Míng-chāng,
he was made Wàn-hù with his original troops,
and having meritorious service in border defense,
he was appointed Guī-dé-jūn Jié-dù-fù-shǐ,
then transferred to Pán-ān-jūn.
He was assessed as honest and capable,
and promoted to Tóng-zhī Sù-pín-lù Jié-dù-shǐ-shì.
He resigned due to mourning,
then was reinstated as Guī-dé-fǔ Zhì-zhōng,
and promoted to Táng-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
In the fourth month of the sixth year of Tài-hé,
Sòng general Huáng-fǔ Bīn led 10,000 infantry and cavalry to invade Táng-zhōu.
Wù-tún had very few troops,
so he dispatched Mì-yáng-wèi Bái-sā-bù and Xún-jiǎn Pú-xián, each with fifty men, to man the walls and defend.
Wù-tún saw that the Sòng troops in the northeast of the city could be broken,
so he ordered Jūn-shì Pàn-guān Sā-hǔ-dài to take a hundred elite soldiers out from the west gate,
circle around behind the Sòng encampment in the northeast, and ambush them.
They killed several hundreds of men,
and the Sòng army fell into great disarray,
retreating at nightfall.
In the fifth month,
Huáng-fǔ Bīn returned with tens of thousands of troops to attack.
The Xíng-shěng dispatched Mì-yáng-fù-xún-jiǎn Nà-hé Jūn-shèng to relieve Táng-zhōu.
Wù-tún led his troops out to join Jūn-shèng’s forces northeast of the city,
setting up an ambush to await them.
Then he divided his cavalry into three groups,
one going out and one coming in to lure the Sòng troops.
The Sòng troops got stuck in the mud,
the ambush was sprung,
splitting the Sòng army in two,
and they were utterly routed.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Hú-yáng,
beheading over 10,000 men
and capturing 300 horses.
Another Sòng general came with 3,000 troops to raid,
they encountered them at Zhú-lín-sì,
and annihilated them.
Nà-hé Jūn-shèng personally killed a Sòng general,
taking his golden belt and seal to present.
An edict promoted Wù-tún to Tóng-zhī Hé-nán-fǔ-shì,
and Jūn-shèng to Liáng-xiàn-lìng,
each advancing two ranks.
Wù-tún was awarded 350 taels of silver and ten bolts of brocade,
and became Yòu-fù-yuán-shuài Wán-yán Kuāng’s Yòu-yì Dū-tǒng.
When Kuāng took Zǎo-yáng,
he sent Wù-tún to attack Shén-mǎ-pō.
The Sòng army, 50,000 strong, was arrayed along the water,
defending the bank with strong crossbows.
Wù-tún divided his troops to seize their three bridges,
and from chén (7-9 AM) to wǔ (11 AM-1 PM) he successively captured thirteen stockades,
thus taking Shén-mǎ-pō.
He followed in the attack on Xiāng,
and upon reaching the Hàn-jiāng,
Wù-tún crossed the swift current directly.
He was further advanced one rank,
and given the title Píng-nán Hǔ-wēi Jiàng-jūn.
When the Sòng requested peace,
he was promoted to Hé-nán Fù-tǒng-jūn.
At the beginning of Dà-ān,
he was promoted to Chāng-wǔ-jūn Jié-dù-shǐ,
retaining his position as Fù-tǒng-jūn.
He was then promoted to Xī-nán-lù Zhāo-tǎo-shǐ.
Wù-tún was harsh in governing his subordinates,
and many soldiers deserted,
for which he was flogged sixty times.
He was appointed Tóng-zhī Shàng-jīng Liú-shǒu-shì.
In the third year of Dà-ān,
he led 20,000 troops to defend Zhōng-dū,
and was promoted to Yuán-shuài Yòu-dū-jiān,
then transferred to Zuǒ-dū-jiān, concurrently Běi-jīng Liú-shǒu.
Having meritorious service,
he was granted a golden spittoon and ten bolts of brocade.
He was promoted to Yuán-shuài Zuǒ-jiān-jūn,
retaining his position as Liú-shǒu.
In the intercalary month of the first year of Zhēn-yòu,
he led troops to defend Zhōng-dū,
and was ordered to deploy 16,000 troops to guard Dìng-xìng.
The army was defeated,
and Wù-tún died in battle.
Gāo Shǒu-yuē, courtesy name Cóng-jiǎn,
a native of Liáo-yáng.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-eighth year of Dà-dìng,
and rose through various offices to Guān-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
When the Dà-yuán army swept through Hé-shuò,
Guō Bāng-xiàn had already surrendered.
He accompanied them to the city walls,
and called out to Shǒu-yuē, saying:
“Cóng-jiǎn, you should consider saving your family.”
Shǒu-yuē ignored him.
When he repeated it a second and third time,
Shǒu-yuē sternly said:
“I do not know you.”
The city was captured, and he was apprehended.
They ordered him to kneel,
but Shǒu-yuē refused to submit,
and so he was killed.
An edict posthumously promoted him to Chóng-yì-jūn Jié-dù-shǐ,
and he was given the posthumous title Zhōng-jìng.
Hé-sù-jiā Ān-lǐ, courtesy name Zǐ-jìng,
originally named Zhuó,
a native of Dà-míng-lù.
He was intelligent and learned,
thoroughly versed in the classics and histories.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-eighth year of Dà-dìng.
At the end of Zhì-níng,
he became Tài-ān-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
At the beginning of Zhēn-yòu,
Shān-dōng was ravaged by war,
and commanderies and counties fled at the mere sight of the enemy.
Someone advised Ān-lǐ to leave,
but Ān-lǐ said:
“If I leave,
who will guard the city?
And will I betray the nation’s grace by avoiding danger?”
So he organized and repaired the defenses,
making preparations for defense.
Soon after,
the Dà-yuán army arrived.
They fought for ten days but could not take it.
They said to him:
“This is but an isolated city,
without grain storage inside,
and without military aid outside.
If you do not surrender, none will be left.”
Ān-lǐ did not listen.
The city was captured, and he was apprehended.
Initially, they did not know who he was,
and someone mistakenly identified him as a wine inspector.
Ān-lǐ said:
“I am the Cì-shǐ;
why should I conceal it?”
They ordered him to kneel,
but Ān-lǐ refused to submit,
so they struck his chest with a spear and killed him.
An edict posthumously promoted him to Tài-dìng-jūn Jié-dù-shǐ,
and he was given the posthumous title Jiān-zhēn.
Wáng Wéi-hàn, courtesy name Zhī-hàn,
a native of Lì-zhōu Lóng-shān.
His father, Tíng,
led the county people to protect the eastern mountain of the county at the end of Liáo,
and later surrendered with his followers.
Wéi-hàn was studious and tireless,
passing the imperial examination in the twenty-eighth year of Dà-dìng.
He was appointed Jūn-shì Pàn-guān of Guì-dé-zhōu,
and after an honest and capable assessment, was promoted to Yǒng-bà-lìng.
A powerful local clan wanted to test Wéi-hàn,
so they fabricated a case and brought a complaint.
Wéi-hàn thoroughly investigated it,
uncovering their deception.
He had them flogged to death,
and vexatious lawsuits declined.
He successively served as Hóng-zhèng and Huò-jiā-lìng.
He assisted Xū-chí-guó in managing river breaches,
and for his efforts,
was promoted one rank.
He was transferred to Běi-jīng Zhuǎn-yùn Hù-jí Pàn-guān,
and appointed Shàng-shū-shěng Lì-shǐ.
He was appointed concurrently as the Commissioner of the Baǒjìng Army,
responsible for auditing household registers.
The entire prefecture praised his fairness.
In a subordinate county, a slave murdered his master,
and then falsely accused the master's younger brother of the murder.
The Ministry of Justice suspected foul play.
Wéihàn meticulously investigated the case,
even conducting a secret investigation to gather evidence.
He obtained the facts,
and the slave confessed.
He was transferred to Deputy Commissioner of Transportation for Zhōngdū,
acting as an Imperial Censor,
and presented memorials in the imperial hall.
Zhāngzōng said:
“An excellent Imperial Censor.”
He was then formally appointed Imperial Censor.
He was transferred to Director of the Left Bureau of Appointments,
then promoted to Director of the Right Bureau of Appointments.
Púsàn Kuí campaigned against Sòng,
and Wéihàn served as Director of the Left and Right Bureaus in the Field Administration.
In the seventh year of Tàihé (1207),
Hénán suffered from drought and locusts.
An imperial edict ordered Wéihàn to investigate the condition of the crops and report.
In the seventh month,
it rained.
Another edict to Wéihàn stated:
“Although the rain is sufficient,
it is too late for autumn planting.
It would be better to plant many vegetables than to leave the land barren.
How can the eggs left by locust nymphs be eradicated?
In areas previously affected by locusts, it would be advisable to plant soybeans and wheat next year.
Inform the
people so they know.”
In the eighth year (1208),
the Sòng people accepted the alliance.
He returned to his post as Director of the Right Bureau of Appointments,
and was promoted one rank.
The Emperor asked:
“Since the Sòng people have requested peace, will they betray the alliance again?”
Wéihàn replied:
“The Sòng emperor is negligent in governance,
the southern troops are frivolous and weak,
and the lands along the Huái River are desolate for a thousand *lǐ* after the wars.
Their officials, chastened by Hán Tuōzhòu and Sū Shīdàn,
no longer dare to take responsibility,
so there is nothing to worry about.
Only the North should concern Your Sacred Majesty.”
After a long time,
he was promoted to Minister of Justice, concurrently Tutor to Prince Lù,
and concurrently Administrator of the Court of Review.
According to new regulations,
musicians of the Jiaòfāng reached the fourth rank,
exchanged for civil and military official qualifications,
and wore golden-purple robes.
Wéihàn memorialized:
“It is not proper for lowly performers
to wear the robes of high officials.
This does not uphold the dignity of the court.”
His suggestion was followed.
In the early period of Dà'ān (1209),
he served as acting Right Remonstrance Official.
When the Three Judicial Offices wanted to tax land and houses,
Wéihàn remonstrated, but was not heeded.
He was transferred to Censor-in-Chief.
Soon after,
he was promoted to Minister of Works, concurrently Minister of Justice,
then transferred to Minister of Punishments,
and appointed Grand Councilor.
In the early period of Zhēnyòu (1213),
he was dismissed and made Commissioner of the Dìnghǎi Army.
At that time,
roads were impassable.
Wéihàn encountered bandits while traveling by boat.
He called out to them:
“You were originally good people;
it is due to chaos that you have come to this.
I do not value possessions;
do not harm my family.”
The bandits were moved by his words and departed.
Upon arriving at his post,
there were no military defenses.
Neighboring prefectures had all fled in fear.
Wéihàn said to the officials and common people:
“An isolated city cannot be defended.
This prefecture is blocked by mountains and surrounded by sea;
there must be a path to safety.
Do not all become fish and meat.”
So he allowed the people to escape.
Wéihàn led officials and people who wished to follow him to flee to the northeastern mountains,
where they built camps and fortifications to defend themselves.
When their strength was exhausted, he was captured but refused to surrender.
His wife, Lady Yaó, also refused to yield,
and died with Wéihàn.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Grand Master of the Middle Counsel,
and upon Lady Yaó the title of Lady of Ruì State,
with the posthumous name Zhēnjié.
Yílā Gǔyǔniè was
Commissioner of the Ānhuà Army.
In the early period of Zhēnyòu (1213),
when the Dà Yuán army took Mìzhōu,
Gǔyǔniè led his troops in a fierce battle.
A stray arrow repeatedly struck his neck.
After it was pulled out, another struck his cheek,
and he died.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu (1215),
an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great General for Pacifying the Distant, and Administrator of Yìdū Prefecture.
Sòng Yǐ was
a native of Wǎnpíng, Zhōngdū.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the fifth year of Zhènglóng (1160).
He successively served as Military Judicial Officer of Chénzhōu and Nínghuàzhōu,
Archivist to the Prince of Caó,
and Assistant Commissioner of Transportation for Shǎnxī West Circuit.
He was appointed Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
and then Deputy Commissioner of the Wǔdìng Army and Right Patrol Commissioner of Zhōngdū.
At that time, Liú Zhāo, the County Magistrate of Gù'ān, was disputing with Peí Yuán, a local resident, over the purchase of adjacent land.
Yǐ favored Zhāo's side,
and pressured Yuán to cease the dispute.
The Censorate impeached him in a memorial,
resulting in the loss of one official rank,
dismissal from office,
and demotion to Judicial Inspector of Guǎngníng Prefecture.
He was transferred to Salt Commissioner of Liaódōng Circuit.
After observing mourning for his father,
he was reinstated as Director in the Ministry of Personnel,
and successively served as Prefect of Jì, Caó, and Jǐng prefectures.
〔一０〕He concurrently administered the Transportation Office of Zhōngdū Circuit,
and was promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Běijīng, Línhuáng, and other circuits.
He was transferred to Commissioner of the Ānguó Army and Transportation Commissioner of Hédōng South Circuit.
The Censorate impeached him for encroaching upon private dwellings in his previous post as Surveillance Commissioner, deeming him incompetent.
He was demoted to Defense Commissioner of Yízhōu,
then transferred to Jùnzhōu,
promoted to Transportation Commissioner of Shāndōng West Circuit,
and transferred to Commissioner of the Dìnghǎi Army.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
he was transferred to Qìnnán Army.
〔一一〕In the first month,
the Dà Yuán army arrived at Huaízhōu.
The city fell, and he died.
Yǐ had a severe and cruel nature;
wherever he went, he was intolerant,
and thus suffered setbacks in his career.
Wūgǔlùn Róngzǔ, originally named Fúxīng,
was from Héjiān.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Míngchāng (1191),
and successively held official posts, being appointed Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
then Assistant Commissioner in the General Transportation Office,
transferred to Collator in the Institute for the Advancement of Literature,
promoted to Judicial Officer in the General Administration of Zhōngdū,
and after an integrity review, appointed Deputy Commissioner of the Zhènwǔ Army and Sīmǎ of Zhāngdé Prefecture.
He was successively promoted to Director in the Ministry of Revenue and Prefect of Nínghǎizhōu.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214), when the city fell,
Róngzǔ fought valiantly
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Commissioner of the Ānwǔ Army
and given the posthumous name Yìyǒng.
Wūgǔlùn Zhòngwēn, originally named Húlà,
was a native of Ànchūn *Méng'ān* in Gàizhōu.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng (1185).
He successively held official posts as Assistant Instructor in the Imperial Academy, Attendant to the Hanlin Academy, and Judicial Inspector for Hédōng Circuit.
He was transferred to Deputy Transportation Commissioner for Héběi East Circuit.
A Censor recommended him for his excellent performance in his previous post as Judicial Inspector.
He was promoted to concurrently Administrator of the Shùntiān Army,
and also served as Surveillance Officer for Shàngjīng, Dōngjīng, and other circuits.
He was transferred to Superintendent of Caoyùn in Zhàozhōu, concurrently Administrator of the Wǔxīng Army, and Prefect of Dōngshèngzhōu.
For incompetence in his previous post in Shàngjīng,
he was demoted to Deputy Commissioner of the Zhènníng Army.
He was transferred to Prefect of Huázhōu, Deputy Surveillance Commissioner for Hédōng South Circuit, and Defense Commissioner of Shòuzhōu.
In the early period of Zhēnyòu (1213),
he was promoted to Commissioner of the Zhènxī Army.
At that time,
Zhōngdū was besieged,
so he went to Tàiyuán.
He sent a letter to the Pacification Commissioner Jiǎ Yìqiān,
agreeing to use local militia to rescue Zhōngdū.
He then rode a post-horse to Píngyáng,
intending to meet Yìqiān in Jiàng,
but could not advance.
He reached Píngyáng and returned.
Zhòngwēn had previously governed Píngyáng,
and the officials and people vied to keep him.
Zhòngwēn said:
“Píngyáng is a major strategic point,
easy to defend.
This would be personally beneficial,
but what about Ānzhōu?”
So he returned to his post.
Soon after,
the Dà Yuán army arrived in great numbers.
The city fell,
and he died, refusing to surrender.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Virtuous Counsel and Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Pō Sù Circuit,
with the posthumous name Zhōngyì.
Sacrifices were offered to him annually.
Jiǔzhù,
a prince of the imperial clan,
served as the Cìshǐ of Wǔzhōu.
Tángkuò Bóguǒsù served as the Jūnshì Pànguān.
In the eleventh month of the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
the soldiers of Dàyuán captured Jiǔzhù’s sons and nephews and brought them to the city walls.
They said to him:
“Shāndōng and Héběi have all surrendered to us now.
We have also captured your family members.
If you do not surrender quickly, we will kill them.”
Jiǔzhù replied:
“I shall repay the state with my death.
How could I care for my family?”
Soon after,
the city fell,
and he died fighting bravely.
Bóguǒsù also refused to yield and died there.
An imperial edict posthumously granted Jiǔzhù the title of Línhǎijūn Jié dùshǐ,
and he was promoted to Piàojíwèi Shàngjiàngjūn.
Bóguǒsù was granted the title of Jiànzhōu Cìshǐ,
and promoted to Zhènguó Shàngjiàngjūn.
Furthermore, an order was given to erect steles
and offer sacrifices at appropriate times each year.
Lǐ Yǎn, courtesy name Jùchuān,
was a native of Rènchéng.
In the sixth year of Tàihé (1206), he placed first in the Jìnshì examination
and was appointed Yìngfèng Hàlínwénzì.
After twice mourning his parents,
he lived in his hometown.
At the beginning of Zhēnyòu (1213),
Rènchéng was attacked by soldiers.
Yǎn, still in mourning attire, became the Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu
and devised a defensive strategy.
He gathered the people of the prefecture to form an army.
They fought for three days,
but the troops were all ordinary townspeople who could not fight
and scattered.
Yǎn was captured.
The general saw his extraordinary cap and clothing,
and also knew his name.
He asked him:
“Are you not Lǐ Yìngfèng?”
Yǎn replied:
“I am.”
He was ordered to kneel but refused.
Attempts to appease him with kind words also failed.
He was offered official positions and emoluments,
but Yǎn said:
“I am a scholar.
How has this court wronged me
that I should desire the official positions and emoluments of others?”
The general grew angry,
struck and broke his shin,
then dragged him out and killed him.
He was then just over thirty years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
and an imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to erect a stele for him.
Liú Déjī
was a native of Dàxīng.
In the first year of Zhēnyòu (1213), he was specially granted the title of Tóng Jìnshì Chūshēn.
Serving as an official in a border town,
the Xīxià soldiers attacked the city.
Déjī sat in the main hall,
with firewood piled beside him.
He said to his family:
“If the city falls, burn me.”
When the city fell,
his family could not bear to set the fire,
so he was captured.
Threatened to kneel and surrender,
Déjī refused to yield.
A former colleague and friend deceived the Xīxià people, saying:
“This man has always suffered from madness,
which is why he dares to act this way.”
Déjī exclaimed:
“As a loyal minister, one should act like this!
How am I mad?”
The Xīxià people admired his righteousness,
so they imprisoned him,
hoping he would change his mind.
Later, they summoned him and questioned him.
Déjī cursed vehemently
and ultimately would not comply,
saying:
“How could I be one who clings to life?”
So they killed him.
He was posthumously granted the title of Cháoliè Dàfū and Tóngzhī Tōngyuǎnjūn Jié dùshǐ Shì.
Wáng Yì
was a native of Dàxīng.
Having passed the Jīngyì Jìnshì examination,
he successively held office as Dōngmíng Lìng.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
Dōngmíng was in dire straits.
Yì led several hundred militiamen who volunteered to fight and defended the city.
When the city fell,
Yì still led his men in resistance.
Overwhelmed, he was captured.
He and four other county residents, including Wáng Bā, were driven outside the city wall.
Two were killed first.
Wáng Bā immediately stepped forward to kneel and surrender.
Yì kicked him down
and shouted sternly:
“A loyal minister does not serve two masters!
Are you going to surrender?”
The captors of Yì struck his shin with a blade.
Yì died unyielding.
He was posthumously granted the title of Cáozhōu Cìshǐ.
Wáng Huì, courtesy name Zǐmíng,
was a native of Gāopíng, Zézhōu.
From a young age, he was spirited and confident,
often admiring Zhāng Yǒng's character.
When his friend’s wife had an affair with someone,
Huì personally killed her with a blade.
In the second year of Míngchāng (1191), he passed the Jìnshì examination
and was appointed Zhǔbù of Chánggé,
earning a reputation for competence.
He was appointed Dūgōu Pànguān of the Liáodōng Lù Zhuǎnyùnsī through an integrity investigation.
The Tíxíngsī recommended his ability,
and he was transferred to Běijīng Zhuǎnyùn Hùjí Pànguān.
He was promoted to Ānyáng Lìng,
and successively appointed Qiān Shǎnxī Xīlù Ànchásī Shì,
then changed to Píngliáng Zhìzhōng.
He was summoned to be Shàofǔ Shàojiān,
and promoted to Hùbù Lángzhōng.
At the beginning of Zhēnyòu (1213),
Zhōngdū was under martial law.
Someone suggested that Huì had the talent of a commander.
He was ordered to recruit and lead soldiers himself,
and he gathered over ten thousand loyal fighters to command.
He led his troops to escort grain from Tōngzhōu into Zhōngdū,
for which he was rewarded.
He was promoted to Huòwáng Fù.
He was ordered to defend Shùnzhōu with his troops.
When Tōngzhōu was in urgent siege,
Huì attacked Niúlán Shān to relieve the siege of Tōngzhōu.
He was generously rewarded
and promoted to Hàlín Shìdú Xuéshì,
and given the additional title of Quànnóng Shǐ.
In the ninth month,
Shùnzhōu was attacked by soldiers.
Huì had a detached force in Cāng and Jǐng,
and he sent someone to break through the siege to summon them.
Everyone was eager to fight,
but the person in charge refused to send them.
Wáng Zhēn,
a former subordinate of Huì,
removed his helmet and came to see him,
bowing and saying:
“The situation is critical!
Why suffer yourself?
If you would only follow me,
you would not lose wealth and honor.”
Huì replied:
“How has the imperial court wronged you?”
Zhēn said:
“Although I may betray the state,
I cannot bear to betray you, my lord.”
Then he wept.
Huì shouted:
“I am sixty years old
and have reached a third-rank position.
Death is my fate.
How could I follow you?”
He was about to shoot him,
but Zhēn covered his face and wept as he left.
Soon after,
the officers and soldiers lowered themselves from the city walls and surrendered.
Huì was captured
but refused to surrender,
and so met his death.
Earlier,
when Huì was captured,
he asked his favorite general, Niú Dǒu:
“Can you die?”
Dǒu replied:
“Since Dǒu has received your recognition,
how can I bear to live alone?”
They were both killed.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Rónglù Dàfū and Shūmì Fùshǐ,
and also ordered the relevant authorities to erect a stele
and offer sacrifices at appropriate times each year.
His son Rǔlín was appointed Bǐyàn Chéngfèng.
Qí Yīngyáng,
military judicial officer of Zīzhōu.
Yáng Mǐnzhōng,
retired as屯Lú Xiàn Wèi.
Zhāng Qīlǘ,
a commoner from Zīzhōu.
In the early Zhēnyòu era,
Dàyuán troops captured Zīzhōu.
Yīngyáng and others recruited soldiers for defense.
When the city fell,
they led their men in street fighting.
Yīngyáng and the other two were severely wounded and captured.
They were urged to surrender.
Yīngyáng, watching for a moment when the guards were careless,
snatched a spear and killed several men.
He, Mǐnzhōng, and Qīlǘ all died unyielding.
〔一二〕An imperial edict posthumously granted Yīngyáng the title of Jiāyì Dàfū and Zīzhōu Cìshǐ,
and a temple was erected in the prefecture
for regular sacrifices.
Mǐnzhōng was posthumously granted the title of Zhāoyǒng Dàjiāngjūn and Tóngzhī Hénghǎijūn Jiédùshǐshì.
Qīlǘ was specially granted the title of Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn and Tóngzhī Zīzhōu Jūnjōushì.
Shújiǎ Fǎxīn,
a Mèng'ān from Jìzhōu.
He rose to the office of Běijīng Fùliúshǒu.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he served as Tíkòng,
defending Mìyún Xiàn together with Wēndíhǎn Yǎocházhá, Tóngzhī Shùnzhōu Jūnjōushì.
Fǎxīn's family was in Jìzhōu.
The Dàyuán troops captured them
and showed them to Fǎxīn, saying:
"If you surrender quickly, we will hand them over to you;
otherwise, we will kill them."
Fǎxīn replied:
"I served this dynasty and received great favor.
If there's a battle, let's fight quickly.
I will never surrender.
How can I consider my family's life or death?"
When the city fell,
he died in battle.
Yǎocházhá was captured
and also died unyielding.
Púchá Císhè, Jiédù Pànguān of Pán'ānjūn, and Wēndíhǎn Shífāngnú, Jīzé Xiànlìng, jointly defended Jìzhōu.
Their forces scattered and fled,
and Císhè and Shífāngnú died.
An imperial edict posthumously granted Fǎxīn the titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Shūmì Fùshǐ,
and enfeoffed him as Sùguógōng.
Yǎocházhá was granted Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn and Shùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Císhè was granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Shífāngnú was granted Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
It was also ordered that steles be erected
and sacrifices be offered regularly.
Gāo Xī, courtesy name Yǒngzhī,
was the son of Déjī.
He entered officialdom through hereditary privilege.
After years of service, he was appointed Zīzhōu Jiǔshǐ,
where his performance was outstanding.
He was promoted to Píngxiāng Lìng.
〔一三〕He was honorably promoted to Liáodōng Lù Zhuǎnyùn Zhīdù Pànguān, [一四]Tàicāng Shǐ, Fǎwù Kùshǐ, concurrently Shànglínshǔ Zhízhǎng, and Tízhǔ Dūchéngsuǒ.
He successively served as Běijīng and Liáodōng Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ, and Tóngzhī Nánjīnglù Zhuǎnyùnshǐshì.
In the early Zhēnyòu era,
he was successively promoted to Héběi Dōnglù Ànchá Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
When the city fell,
he threw himself from the city wall and died.
Collated Notes

Biography Sixty, Loyal and Righteous Two: Wú Sēnggē, Wūgǔlún Déshēng, Zhāng Shùn, Mǎ Xiáng, Bódéwāgē, Àotún Chǒuhéshang Cóngtǎn, Bóshùlǔ Fúshòu, Wú Bāngjié, Nàhé Púlàdū, Nǚxīliè Wòchū Shìmàoxiān, Wēndíhǎn Lǎor, Liáng Chíshèng, Jiǎ Bāngxiàn

Yílà Ālǐhé Wányán Liùjīn, Gēshíliè Hèshòu, Púchá Lóushì, Nǚxīliè Zīlù, Zhào Yìhóu Xiǎoshú, Wáng Zuǒ, Huángguā Jiǔzhù, Wūlíndá Qǐzhù, Tuómǎn Xiéliè Nípánggǔ Púlǔhǔ, Wūyán Wèikě, Wūyán Échūtǔ, Zhāngē Zhēn.
Wú Sēnggē,
a native of the Tánggǔ Yīlàcí Shàngshāyàn tribe in the Xīnánlù.
He was strong and skilled in archery from horseback.
During the Dà'ān era,
people from Shānxī were conscripted into the army.
Sēnggē served as a Mǎjūn Qiānhù
and achieved merit.
In the early Zhēnyòu era,
he was promoted to Wànhù
and provisionally appointed Shùnyìjūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Shuòzhōu fell,
Sēnggē recaptured it,
and was formally appointed Tóngzhī Jiédùshǐshì.
His younger brother, Dīlà, provisionally Tóngzhī Jiédùshǐshì, was formally appointed Jiédù Fùshǐ.
Yàn Cáor, provisionally Jiédù Fùshǐ, was formally appointed Jiédù Pànguān.
Tíkòng Mǎ Shòu'er and others
were promoted with varying ranks.
As the troops suffered from lack of food,
Sēnggē requested a grant of 150,000 hu of grain.
The court, believing that Yìngzhōu had already fallen,
and Shuò being an isolated city,
its position was indefensible,
then moved the 90,000-plus soldiers and civilians of Shuò to be quartered between Lán, Shí, Xí, Jí, Jiàng, and Xiè.
Before they could depart,
Dàyuán troops arrived at Shuòzhōu.
After seven days and nights of fighting,
Sēnggē achieved merit,
and was additionally granted the remote appointment of Tóngzhī Tàiyuánfǔshì, concurrently Tóngzhī Jiédùshǐshì.
Dīlà was appointed Shízhōu Cìshǐ.
Cáor was appointed Tóngzhī Kèlánzhōu Fángyùshǐshì.
In the fourth year,
the people finally began their southward migration.
They fought and marched for dozens of li.
Sēnggē, exhausted and his horse stumbling, died there,
at the age of thirty.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn and Shùnyìjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Wūgǔlún Déshēng, originally named Liùjīn,
was a Mèng'ān from Yìdúlù.
He passed the Jinshì examination in the second year of Míngchāng.
He successively served as Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
managing appointments and dismissals.
He was appointed Lìbù Zhǔshì and Jiàngyángjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
After mourning his father,
he was reinstated as Tàicháng Bóshì and Dōngpíng Zhìzhōng.
In the early Dà'ān era,
he was appointed Zhī Hóngwényuàn.
He was reassigned as Shìyùshǐ,
and impeached Gēshíliè Zhízhōng, Xījīng Liúshǒu, for treachery and evil.
Wèi Shàowáng did not listen,
and he was transferred to Zhàozhōu Fángyùshǐ.
When Xuānzōng moved to Biàn,
he was summoned to the court
and submitted a memorial:
"Tàizhōu is ruined,
and the Mèng'ān and Móukè of the Dōngběilù Zhāotǎosī are all residing in Zhàozhōu.
All levies and assignments are extremely difficult to manage.
I request that Zhàozhōu be elevated to a Jiédùshǐ,
with the Zhāotǎoshǐ concurrently holding the position.
Two Zhāotǎo Fùshǐ should be appointed
to separately govern Tàizhōu and Yíchūn."
The emperor's edict followed this.
He was promoted to Hànlín Shìdú Xuéshì, concurrently Hùbù Shìláng.
Soon after, he provisionally served as Cānzhī Zhèngshì while still Hànlín Shìdú.
He and Mòlián Jìnzhōng, Píngzhāng Zhèngshì, discussed the involvement of the Jìshìjú in politics.
Xuānzōng was angry.
The details are in the biography of Jìnzhōng.
Not long after,
he was dispatched as Jíqìngjūn Jiédùshǐ,
then reassigned as Fényángjūn Jiédùshǐ and Hédōng Běilù Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ,
and again reassigned as Zhī Tàiyuánfǔshì, provisionally Yuánshuài Zuǒjiānjūn.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
Dàyuán troops urgently attacked Tàiyuán,
and the grain supply route was cut off.
Déshēng repeatedly led troops to battle,
and the grain route was reopened.
An imperial edict promoted him one rank.
Déshēng submitted a memorial:
"The Crown Prince is intelligent, benevolent, and filial.
His guardians are already in place,
but it would be even better to select men of esteemed virtue to be by his side day and night.
To hear righteous words and see righteous conduct daily
would be a great blessing for the state and a great joy for the people."
Xuānzōng graciously accepted this.
In the second year,
he was formally appointed Zuǒjiānjūn,
acting as Yuánshuàifǔshì.
Dàyuán troops again besieged Tàiyuán,
surrounding it several times.
They had already breached the outer wall.
Déshēng erected barricades for defense
and used his family's silver, silk, and horses to reward the warriors.
The northern army broke through the northwest corner of the city and entered.
Déshēng blocked them with linked carts.
They were repelled three times and ascended three times.
Arrows and stones rained down like showers,
and the defenders on the ramparts could not stand.
When the city fell,
Déshēng went to the prefectural office
and said to his aunt and wife:
"I have defended this for several years,
but unfortunately, my strength is exhausted."
Then he hanged himself and died.
His aunt and wife both committed suicide.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ.
His son, Wùlǐwěi, was still young,
and an imperial edict ordered that he be supported with the salary of a Fèngyù.
Zhāng Shùn
was a militiaman from Zīzhōu.
When Zīzhōu was besieged,
the Provincial Governor Hóu Zhì dispatched Wáng Tíngyù, the General Commander of Defense, to lead troops to relieve it.
Tíngyù recruited Shùn and thirty others to scout the enemy's strength,
and also to let the city know that reinforcements were arriving.
They stealthily reached the city walls by night,
and Shùn was captured.
He was forced to declare that the provincial army had been defeated,
and that Tíngyù was also dead,
urging them to surrender quickly.
Shùn outwardly agreed,
but then shouted to the city,
"There are not many enemy troops!
General Wáng's army will arrive soon!
Hold fast and do not surrender!"
With weapons pointed at him,
Shùn said,
"To die a loyal and filial ghost
is enough."
Thereupon, he died.
The people of Zīzhōu knew that reinforcements were coming
and held out to the death,
and the city was preserved thanks to this.
Afterwards, he was posthumously granted the title of Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn and Concurrent Administrator of the Affairs of Dìzhōu Defense Command.
An imperial edict commanded officials to provide for his parents
and to seek out his descendants
for preferential appointment.
Mǎ Xiāng
was a native of Yǔchéng.
He passed the imperial examination and became a *jìnshì*,
serving in various official posts with distinction.
In the third year of Zhēnyòu (1215),
he served as the Magistrate of Jìyīn in Cáozhōu.
In the fourth month,
the Dà Yuán army captured Cáozhōu,
and Xiāng was seized.
Soldiers beat and plundered him for gold,
Xiāng said,
"I am a scholar;
where would I get such things?"
They then ordered him to kneel,
Xiāng said,
"My knees cannot bend.
If you want to kill me, then kill me.
To die as a ghost of Dà Jīn
is enough."
Thereupon, he died.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Cháoliè Dàfū and Deputy Military Commissioner of Tàidìng Command,
and a stele was erected in the prefecture,
with annual sacrifices.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Zhēnyòu (1216),
an imperial edict appointed his son, Wéixián, to a position in the Bāguànshí Bureau.
Bódé Wāgē was
a Xi man from the Southwest Circuit of Miēcí.
He was robust, steadfast, and brave.
When the Dà Yuán army conquered the Southwest Circuit,
neighboring prefectures all surrendered,
but Wāgē alone refused to yield.
In the fifth year of Zhēnyòu (1217),
after Dōngshèng Prefecture had been broken,
Wāgē, along with Yáolǐ Yāhú and Yáolǐ Yār, gathered a volunteer army
and, clearing thorns and brambles, re-established the prefectural administration.
The Office of the Acting Grand Marshal of the Hédōngběi Circuit, acting on imperial authority, appointed Wāgē as Wǔyì Jiāngjūn and Deputy Military Commissioner of Níngyuǎn Command,
Yáolǐ Yāhú as Wǔyì Jiāngjūn and Judicial Officer of the Military Commission,
and Yáolǐ Yār as Wǔyì Jiāngjūn and Observation Officer.
Wāgē and others, feeling that the grace did not originate from the imperial court,
harbored considerable resentment
and allowed their troops to plunder.
In the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
an imperial edict remotely appointed Wāgē as the Prefect of Wǔzhōu and Acting Military Commissioner,
Yáolǐ Yāhú as Acting Concurrent Administrator of the Military Commission,
and Yáolǐ Yār as Acting Deputy Military Commissioner,
each advanced two ranks.
In the third year of Xīngdìng (1219),
Wāgē was specially promoted three ranks,
remotely appointed Concurrent Administrator of Jìn'ān Prefecture,
and soon after genuinely appointed Military Commissioner of Dōngshèng Command.
When Dōngshèng was besieged,
food in the city ran out,
and reinforcements were cut off.
Wāgē led his troops to break the siege
and escaped to secure Chángníng Zhai.
An imperial edict granted each an advancement of one rank,
and those who died in battle were posthumously granted three ranks.
In the ninth month,
the stronghold was again besieged,
and Wāgē died there.
Àotún Chǒuhéshang
served as the Grand Administrator of Dáizhōu.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Zhēnyòu (1216),
the Dà Yuán army attacked Dáizhōu.
Héshang engaged in battle, was defeated,
sustained several wounds,
and was captured.
They tried to induce him to surrender,
but he refused to yield
and subsequently died.
Cóng Tǎn
was a prince of the imperial clan.
During the Dà'ān era,
he was appointed as a Gentleman-in-waiting in the Secretariat.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
he personally recruited several thousand volunteer soldiers
and was appointed as the Special Commissioner for Overall Defense.
An imperial edict commanded Cóng Tǎn to oversee the troops of the three commands of Fèngxiān and Fányáng.
He was appointed Concurrent Administrator of Zhuōzhōu,
promoted to Prefect,
bestowed with a golden plaque,
and tasked with administering Hǎizhōu.
After a short while,
he was appointed Special Commissioner for Overall Defense
to pacify the military and populace of Shānxī
and to reinforce Zhōngdū.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"Jiàng and Xiè prefectures can barely hold their cities,
and the villagers have all suffered from warfare.
Coupled with consecutive years of poor harvests,
many people face food shortages,
all relying on salt and cloth to exchange for rice.
Now, crossings like Dàyáng do not permit grain and wheat to cross the river.
I wish for this prohibition to be lifted,
with an official tax of one-thirteenth,
then both public and private needs will be met."
He also said:
"Jiàng, Xiè, and Hézhōng are strategic locations.
If only the Military Commissioner of Bǎochāng Command could, as he deems appropriate, plan for the benefits of the salt ponds
to enrich these two prefectures,
then the people would benefit,
and the army could be strengthened."
He further said:
"South of Zhōngtiáo,
Yuánqǔ, Pínglù, Ruìchéng, and Yúxiāng
are the strategic points of Hédōng
and the gateway to Shǎn and Luò.
Twelve thousand infantry and cavalry from Shǎn Prefecture could be divided into one Defense Commander and four Overall Commanders
to garrison these four counties.
This is a perfectly secure strategy."
He also said:
"Pínglù produces silver and iron.
If salt is exchanged for rice,
and workers are recruited to smelt and forge,
it can expand financial resources, prepare military equipment,
and common people, working for food,
can stop banditry."
He further said:
"The poor people of Héběi cross the river to seek food,
and then return to relieve their hungry families,
suffering extreme hardship.
Cruel and violent officials suppressing and extorting them
is the greatest malpractice."
He also said:
"The deployment in Hénán and Shǎnxī is not yet urgent.
If warhorses and mares are selected for group grazing,
in no more than two or three years, tens of thousands of cavalry can be added,
and the military might will naturally revive."
He further said:
"The printing and issuance of treasure notes in various circuits
have grown excessively over time,
and they are bound to accumulate and become stagnant.
If issuance is confined to Nánjīng,
it can perhaps be sustained long-term."
He also said:
"Although appointments in Héběi are made without regard to normal sequence,
people are generally unwilling to serve
because commodity prices are ten times higher than in Hénán,
salaries are insufficient,
and hunger and cold are imminent.
If half of their salary in grain were actually provided,
it would somewhat suffice to encourage integrity,
and then their efforts could be demanded."
He further said:
"For officials in Héběi,
the imperial court reduces their qualifications and promotes them out of sequence to reward their efforts.
I hear that officials in Hénán view this as a demotion or banishment.
If they truly believe this,
who would not lose morale?"
The memorial was presented
and sent to the Secretariat for deliberation.

Only the permission to open crossings like Dàyáng, the pacification commissioner's office determining salaries for Héběi officials based on the people's capacity, and a prohibition against viewing Héběi as a place of demotion were adopted.
In the fourth year,
when the Bureau of Military Affairs was located in Hénán Prefecture,
he submitted a memorial saying:
"The campaigns have been ongoing for years,
always failing to achieve success,
because the troops are not adequately trained.
Common soldiers are already filling the ranks,
how much more should the imperial family share the joys and sorrows of the nation?
All should join the army,
personally facing arrows and stones as pioneers for the soldiers,
to slightly alleviate the sacred sovereign's worries.
My kinsman Dàogē shares this sentiment
and wishes to serve under my command."
Xuānzōng praised his loyalty
and granted his request.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he was reappointed as the Cìshǐ of Huīzhōu,
acting Jiédùshǐ of Hépíng Jūn and Jīnglüèshǐ of Mèngzhōu.
Previously,
the Yùshǐ Dàfū, acting Shàngshū Yòuchéng, Yǒngxī, was ordered to manage affairs in Shǎnxī.
Xuānzōng said:
“If the enemy forces are strong, then guard Tóngguān diligently,
and do not let them go east.”
After Yǒngxī departed,
he stayed in Miǎnchí for several days,
then stationed his troops in Jīngzhào without moving.
A short while later,
Tóngguān fell,
and the Dàyuán army reached the near suburbs.
Consequently, Yǒngxī was imprisoned,
and his case remained undecided for a long time.
Cóngtǎn then submitted a memorial to save him,
which roughly stated:
“I have heard that the Zhōu dynasty lasted eight hundred years,
and the Hàn enjoyed its rule for over four hundred years,
all because they enfeoffed their relatives,
maintaining a staggered defense.
The isolated Qín and Cáo Wèi dynasties perished quickly;
though the eight kings of Jìn preyed upon each other,
it still lasted longer than Qín and Wèi.
Since ancient times, there has been no instance of close relatives of the same surname not rising and falling with the state.
During the Húshāhǔ rebellion in our dynasty,
no official or general dared to do anything.
Shànyáng and Shígǔ, however, bravely fought,
and died in loyal service.
Yùshǐ Dàfū Yǒngxī was not competent for the task,
yet he was insisted upon,
which is the fault of the imperial court.
The branches and leaves of the state are already few.
I implore Your Majesty to consider this carefully.”
At this,
over four hundred members of the imperial clan submitted memorials criticizing Yǒngxī,
but none were acted upon.
After a long time,
Yǒngxī was given one hundred strokes of the staff
and stripped of his official name.
At this time, troops from all circuits entered cities to defend themselves,
and the common people lost their livelihoods in farming.
Cóngtǎn submitted a memorial saying:
“Maintaining an army is for protecting the people.
Currently, in Héshuò, only the forces of Zhēndìng and Héjiān should remain to defend the cities.
The troops from all other prefectures and subprefectures should be dispersed to encamp outside,
to serve as a defense for the people.
After the harvest is complete, they can then be moved to garrison locations.
This is a long-term strategy.”
This was followed.
He was additionally given the remote appointment of Tóngzhī Dōngpíng Fǔ Shì,
acting Yuánshuài Zuǒ Jiānjūn, and Xing Yuánshuài Fǔ Shì,
and together with Cānzhī Zhèngshì Lǐ Gé, he guarded Píngyáng.
In the tenth month of the second year of Xīngdìng,
Cóngtǎn reported:
“Tàiyuán has already fallen,
and the enemy is approaching Píngyáng.
All counties and prefectures in Hédōng are undefended,
largely due to a small number of stationed troops and the failure of reinforcements to arrive.
The Xing Shěng troops are fewer than six thousand.
Píngyáng is the foundation of Hédōng
and the barrier of Hénán.
I beg that the troops from Huái, Mèng, and Wèizhōu be combined to reinforce Lùzhōu,
and the troops from Zézhōu, Qìnshuǐ, Duānshì, and Gāopíng be mobilized to form camps along the mountains,
to serve as a relief force for Píngyáng.
I only pray for a sacred decision
to save us from this dire situation.”
On the rénzǐ day of that month,
the Dàyuán army reached Píngyáng.
Tíkòng Guō Yòng fought at the moat wall north of the city
and was captured, but he refused to yield and died.
On the guǐchǒu day,
the city fell,
and Cóngtǎn committed suicide.
He was posthumously granted the title of Chāngwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Bóshùlǔ Fúshòu
served as the Zhǔbù of Tángyì.
When the Dàyuán army attacked Tángyì,
Fúshòu fought against them
and died.
He was posthumously granted an official rank of three grades
and five hundred strings of cash in funeral allowance.
Wú Bāngjié
was the Jūnshì Pànguān of Dēngzhōu.
Bāngjié lived in a village in Rìzhào
and was captured by the Dàyuán army.
He was ordered to attack the city.
Bāngjié said:
“I have received grace from my country.
How can I bear to attack the city of my lord?”
He disregarded their offers of wine and food,
so they killed him.
An imperial edict granted him posthumously the titles of Cháoliè Dàfū and Dìnghǎi Jūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
Nàhé Púlàdōu
was a Měng'ān from Dàmíng Lù.
He obtained the Jinshì degree in the second year of Chéng'ān
and was appointed as a Dàmíng Jiàoshòu.
He successively became the Magistrate of Bǐyáng,
was appointed as a Lìshǐ in the Shàngshū Shěng,
and then made Fùshǐ of Zhāngdé Jūn Jiédù.
He resigned due to mourning.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Xī'ān Jūn Jiédùshǐ Shì,
and successively Tóngzhī Líntáo, Píngliáng Fǔ Shì,
and Fángyùshǐ of Hézhōu.
In the third year,
the Xià people besieged Dìngqiāng.
Púlàdōu attacked and drove them away,
and for his merit, he was remotely granted the title of Zhānghuà Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the fourth year,
Hézhōu was elevated to Píngxī Jūn,
and Púlàdōu was directly made its Jiédùshǐ.
He reported:
“In ancient times, when one man joined the army,
seven families supported him.
When an army of one hundred thousand was raised,
seven hundred thousand families could not attend to their affairs.
Now, seven or eight tenths of the people in various circuits are conscripted as soldiers,
while only two or three tenths support them.
How can the people not be distressed?
Indeed, the quality of troops is paramount,
not their number.
Select the brave and resourceful as soldiers,
and let the timid and weak return to their farms.
This is also a way to alleviate the people's burden.”
He also requested appointments for those who redeemed their crimes to increase resources,
and he asked for permission for people to hunt and farm on barren lands in Shǎnxī and to mine,
but this was not approved.
He was reappointed Zhī Píngliáng Fǔ Shì,
and then entered the court as Hùbù Shàngshū.
At this time,
there was a great victory against the Sòng.
Púlàdōu reported:
“The Sòng people have repeatedly been defeated;
their morale must be low.
We can take advantage of this to send envoys to persuade them
to seek the old alliance.
If the Sòng people do not comply,
then we can attack them.
An enemy that is angry and stubborn
is easy to defeat.”
The court did not adopt his advice.
Púlàdōu also said:
“The various armies should dismiss the old and weak,
and carefully select elite soldiers,
so that victory may be achieved.
The archers in Shǎnxī are not accustomed to cavalry archery;
those skilled in riding should be chosen to replace them.
There are many troops stationed in Yán'ān;
ten thousand should be moved to Píngliáng.
There are too many Yuánshuài in Guānzhōng;
except for the important garrison of Jīngzhào,
all others can be dismissed.
North of Gǒngxiàn,
on the south bank of the Yellow River,
and at Jīngōu, Diàojiáo, Hǔláoguān, and the Èlíng of Guózhōu,
all minor paths and remote routes should have troops stationed for defense.”
The edict was sent to the Shàngshū Shěng and the Shūmì Yuàn for discussion,
but it was never implemented.
Soon after,
he was reappointed Yuánshuài Yòu Jiānjūn, concurrently Jiédùshǐ of Zhāoyì Jūn, and Xing Yuánshuài Fǔ Shì.
In the second year of Xīngdìng,
Lùzhōu fell,
and he died fighting bravely.
He was posthumously granted the title of Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Nǚxīliè Wòchū
served as Cìshǐ of Zhēnjiāozhōu.
He was ordered by the Xing Shěng to move the people of the prefecture to Jīnshèngbǎo.
Soon after, a large army arrived,
and Wòchū resisted,
but was struck by a stray arrow,
and lay wounded.
Tíkòng Zhāng, of the Huāmào Army, said:
“The enemy's momentum is irresistible;
we should surrender quickly.”
Wòchū said:
“We eat the salary of the state;
how can we forget the nation's kindness?
Have you not heard of Zhào Fāngzhōu?
He gave gold, silks, and women to the enemy,
but ultimately did not escape.
We should only fight with all our might and die.”
At night,
Tíkòng Zhāng led several men with weapons and entered,
threatening Wòchū to surrender.
Wòchū said:
“Do as you wish,
I will never yield.”
So they killed him
and seized his wife and children to surrender.
Initially,
many people from Zhèngzhōu who were relocated to Jīnshèngbǎo were unable to reach it.
The Military Judge, Wáng Jǐn, gathered the scattered population
and separately garrisoned them at Zhōunānbǎo.
Zhōunānbǎo had not completed the repair of its battlements or prepared for defense.
When the enemy arrived,
Wáng Jǐn resisted for more than ten days,
but an internal collapse occurred.
He was captured and died without yielding.
An imperial edict granted Wòchū and Wáng Jǐn each six ranks in office and a promotion of three grades in position.
At that time, Mào Xiān,
the liquor supervisor of Shāgōu in Rìzhào County,
was residing in Zhūchéng.
The Red Jacket bandits, led by Fāng Guōsān, occupied Mìzhōu.
When they passed through his village,
the residents eagerly went out to welcome them.
The bandit leader proclaimed himself Grand Marshal.
Mào Xiān, enraged, said to the crowd:
"This is just a bandit chief!
What Grand Marshal is there?"
Fāng Guōsān heard this and seized him,
cutting off his wrist.
Mào Xiān cursed loudly.
The bandit, unable to contain his fury,
gouged out his eyes
and hacked him to pieces with multiple blades.
He continued cursing until his death.
An imperial edict granted him the title of Wǔjié Jiāngjūn and concurrent acting prefect of Yízhōu Defense Command.
Wēndíhán Lǎo'ér
served as the concurrent acting commandant of Shàngjīng.
When Púxiān Wànnú attacked Shàngjīng,
his son Tiěgē captured Lǎo'ér alive.
He coerced him to recruit the remaining people,
but Lǎo'ér refused.
Tiěgē, enraged,
hacked him to death.
He was posthumously granted the title of Lónghǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn and Pōshù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
His nephew, Hēisī, was appointed as his successor,
and specially granted four official ranks.
Liáng Chíshèng, courtesy name Jīngfǔ,
originally named Xúnyì,
changed it to avoid the taboo name of Xuānzōng.
He was the son of Xiāng, the Jìedùshǐ of Bǎodà Army.
He possessed great strength and was skilled in archery.
In the sixth year of Tàihé (1206), he passed the Imperial Examination as a Jìnshì,
and later passed the Hóngcí examination.
He successively held office as Tàicháng Bóshì,
and was promoted to Jīnglìguān in the Xiánpíng Circuit Pacification Commission.
At the beginning of Xīngdìng,
the Pacification Commissioner Púxiān Wànnú had rebellious intentions.
He wished to abandon Xiánpíng and move to Hélǎnlù.
Liáng Chíshèng strongly advised against it,
which enraged Wànnú,
who had him flogged eighty times.
Liáng Chíshèng fled to Shàngjīng
and reported to the Traveling Province Administrator Tàipíng.
At this time,
Tàipíng had already colluded with Wànnú.
He verbally praised Liáng Chíshèng's loyalty,
but in his heart, he did not.
He appointed Liáng Chíshèng as Yuánwàiláng of the Zǔoyòusī.
Later,
Tàipíng, acting on Wànnú's orders,
burned down the ancestral temples in Shàngjīng,
seized Grand Marshal Chéngchōng,
and took his army.
Liáng Chíshèng, along with Tíkòng Xiánpíng Zhìzhōng Péimǎn Sàibù and Wànhù Hán Gōngshù, conspired
to kill Tàipíng,
and reinstate Chéngchōng as the Acting Province Administrator
to jointly attack Wànnú.
The plot was exposed,
and all were killed.
An imperial edict granted Liáng Chíshèng the posthumous title of Zhōngshùn Dàfū and Hánzhōu Cìshǐ;
Sàibù was granted Zhèngguó Shàngjiāngjūn and Xiǎndéjūn Jìedùshǐ;
and Gōngshù was granted Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jiǎ Bāngxiàn
was from Chéncūn, Huòyì County, Huòzhōu.
He passed the Imperial Examination as a Jìnshì.
He was straightforward, brave, and resourceful.
When the Great Yuán attacked Hédōng,
Jiǎ Bāngxiàn gathered residents to organize a defense.
Later,
when a large army arrived,
all the residents surrendered.
Jiǎ Bāngxiàn abandoned his family
and, with only his son Yì, sought refuge in Sōngpíngzhài.
At this time,
Liú Zhēn, the acting Prefect, was in the stronghold.
They defended it together
and ultimately succeeded.
Liú Zhēn repeatedly wanted to appoint him,
but Jiǎ Bāngxiàn always declined, citing old age.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of Xīngdìng (1225),
a large army arrived again.
He was ill and unable to escape.
He and Yì were both captured.
They wanted to make him the Zhèn Xī Yuánshuài
and threatened him with a blade.
Jiǎ Bāngxiàn did not yield,
secretly sending Yì back to Sōngpíng,
and then committed suicide by cutting his own throat.
He was posthumously granted the title of Fèngzhí Dàfū and Magistrate of his home county.
Yílà Ālǐhé
was a Khitan.
During the Xīngdìng era,
he was successively promoted to Huòzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first month of the fourth year of Xīngdìng (1225),
the seat of Huòzhōu was moved to Hǎoyìbǎo.
When the Great Yuán army arrived,
Ālǐhé fought valiantly but could not resist them.
His army was defeated, and he was captured.
He was enticed to surrender,
but Ālǐhé said:
"I would rather die than betray."
When ordered to kneel,
he merely stood facing the palace.
Thereupon, he was shot to death by a volley of arrows.
Kǒng Zǔtāng, the Deputy Jìedùshǐ of Bǎochāng Army, was captured at the same time.
When Zǔtāng was also ordered to kneel,
Zǔtāng refused
and also died.
An imperial edict granted Ālǐhé the posthumous title of Lónghǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn and Tàidìngjūn Jìedùshǐ,
and Zǔtāng the title of Zīshàn Dàfū and concurrent acting prefect of Píngyángfǔ.
Zǔtāng
passed the Imperial Examination as a Jìnshì in the third year of Tàihé (1203).
Wányán Liùjīn
was from Hútǔ'àigěmǎnměng'ān in the Zhōngdōu Circuit.
During the Dà'ān era,
he was appointed to office by inheritance
and selected to serve in the Imperial Guard.
He was transferred to Fùpíng Wèi,
promoted to Fāngchéng Lìng,
then appointed Tōngzhōu Jūnshì Pànguān,
and for his merits, promoted to Cìshǐ of his home prefecture.
Shortly thereafter,
the Right Supervising Marshal Púchá Qīqīn captured him and took him away.
Not long after,
he escaped with his family and returned.
He was appointed concurrent acting prefect of Líntáofǔ,
then transferred to Qìngyáng,
and promoted to Bǎodàjūn Jìedùshǐ.
In the fifth year of Xīngdìng (1226),
when Fūzhōu fell,
Liùjīn threw himself off a cliff and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tèjìn and concurrent acting prefect of Yán'ānfǔ.
An imperial edict ordered the Shǎnxī Traveling Province Administration to locate his descendants and report.
Gēshíliè Hèshòu
was from Shānchūnměng'ān in Héběi Xīlù.
He was simple and honest by nature,
with a majestic physique.
He initially served in the Imperial Guard.
In the third year of Tàihé (1203), he passed the martial imperial examination,
and was transferred to Bāoxìn County as Deputy Patrol Inspector.
In the sixth year (1206),
when the Sòng army besieged Càizhōu,
Hèshòu requested permission from the Defense Commissioner
and, with fifty brave warriors, launched a night attack on the Sòng camp,
while the various armies shouted from atop the city walls.
They cut down over three hundred heads.
The Sòng soldiers trampled each other,
resulting in over a thousand deaths.
At dawn,
the Sòng army lifted the siege and departed.
Hèshòu pursued them,
having the rear drag firewood [to create dust].
The Sòng people, seeing the rising dust,
thought a large army was approaching,
and fled.
He pursued them to Chénzhài and then returned.
Subsequently,
the Sòng army again occupied the three counties of Xīncài, Xīnxī, and Bāoxìn.
Hèshòu recaptured all of them,
obtaining three hundred horses.
He was appointed Xíngjūn Wànhù
and followed the main army out to Shòuchūn.
He defeated the Sòng forces at Guōkǒu,
seizing over a thousand horses,
and captured Zhēn and Chú Prefectures, as well as Xūyí Military Command.
Upon the army's return,
he was promoted nine ranks
and transferred to concurrent acting prefect of Xīzhōu and Military Prefect.
He was then appointed concurrent manager of Wànnínggōng.
In the third year of Dà'ān (1211),
he was appointed Southwest Circuit Cavalry Wànhù.
When fifty thousand Xià soldiers besieged Dōngshèng,
Hèshòu came to its rescue,
breaking through the encirclement and entering the city.
The Xià army withdrew.
He was promoted two ranks,
and awarded one hundred liǎng of silver and ten bolts of brocade.
He was promoted to Shàngfāngshǔ Lìng
and appointed Deputy Commander of the Expeditionary Army,
then promoted to Left Wing Commander of the Traveling Province Administration.
He was transferred to Wǔwèijūn Dūtǒng
and appointed Deputy Supervisor of Cavalry.
He was transferred to Qiánxiá
and appointed Deputy Supervisor of the Eastern Sector of the Capital via Imperial Edict.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu
he mourned his father's death,
and was reinstated as Vice Military Commissioner of Wǔníngjūn.
He defeated the Hóng'ǎo bandits at Lánlíng Shíchénggù,
who had taken all civilians as captives.
Cén Guī, Censor, memorialized:
"I request an imperial edict to the relevant authorities,
that all those captured by Hèshòu should be released."
An edict commanded the Xúzhōu and Guīdé administrative circuits to detain and release them.
Soon after, he was remotely appointed Acting Co-Military Commissioner of Wǔníngjūn,
also holding the position of Vice Military Commissioner.
He was punished for going hunting and setting a fire that spread to government hay,
receiving one hundred strokes of the cane,
and was transferred to Acting Co-Military Commissioner of Hépíngjūn.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he was made Grand Controller of the Cavalry,
entered the Sòng territory of Xiāngyáng,
was remotely appointed Acting Co-Military Commissioner of Wǔshèngjūn,
and then remotely appointed Prefect of Suīzhōu.
In the second year,
he attacked Zǎoyáng,
and thrice defeated Sòng troops,
and was then remotely appointed Acting Co-Administrator of Guīdé Fǔ.
In the third year,
he captured the Sòng Shíqúzhài,
and diverted the moat water of Zǎoyáng.
He was promoted to Imperial Commissioner for Military Affairs of Dèngzhōu Lù with discretionary power,
and remotely appointed Defense Commissioner of Rǔzhōu.
In the fourth year,
Sòng Grand Commandant Hù, with 100,000 infantry and cavalry, besieged Dèngzhōu.
Hèshòu divided his troops to resist and defend,
distributing gold and silk from the government treasury to reward his soldiers,
and promised them promotions and titles.
He personally led the remaining forces out to fight daily,
until the Sòng troops burned their camp and left.
Hèshòu was wounded and unable to ride a horse,
so he sent Assistant Pacification Commissioner Shúhǔ Yílàdá to pursue them,
killing dozens of people,
and recovering their captives before returning.
An edict declared that the distributed gold and silk would not be questioned,
and the officers and soldiers would receive special promotions and titles.
Hèshòu was promoted to Gold and Purple Grand Master of Illustrious Happiness,
and remotely appointed Military Commissioner of Wǔshèngjūn.
Soon after, he mourned his mother's death.
He was reinstated to his original post,
appointed acting Left Chief Inspector of the Marshal's Office,
and established the Marshal's Office in Fūzhōu.
In the intercalary twelfth month of the fifth year of Xīngdìng,
Fūzhōu was captured.
Hèshòu and a few horsemen broke out of the city,
but were pursued and overtaken.
Hèshòu defended a dirt mound and fought valiantly until his death.
His posthumous name was Guǒyǒng.
Púchá Lóushì was a native of the Ānchūhǔ Gēlǐhǎn Military-Agricultural Colony in the Northeast Circuit.
He passed the imperial examination in the third year of Tàihé.
He was appointed Chief Registrar of Qìngdū and Mǒupíng,
and promoted to Vice Inspector of the Right Police Bureau of the Central Capital due to his honesty and ability.
He was appointed Clerk in the Department of State Affairs,
managing appointments and dismissals.
In the early Zhēnyòu period,
he was appointed Principal of the Ministry of Personnel and Censor.
He mourned his mother's death,
and after the period of mourning,
he served as Experience Officer of the Branch Secretariat,
then transferred to Judicial Administrator of Jīngzhào,
remotely appointed Prefect of Dìngxīzhōu,
and served as Advisory Officer to the Marshal.
In the second year of Xīngdìng,
he and Marshal Chéngyì attacked and captured Xīhézhōu.
Báisā advanced from Qínzhōu to Zhàn Dào,
and the Sòng people mobilized all their forces to resist.
Lóushì erected banners on high ground,
then galloped his horse back and forth,
raising dust as a diversion.
He secretly dispatched elite cavalry to attack from behind,
and the Sòng army was utterly defeated.
Taking advantage of the victory, they captured Xīngyuán.
He was promoted one rank,
and appointed Prefect of Dānzhōu.
He was again promoted to Co-Administrator of Hézhōng Fǔ,
acting Right Chief Inspector of the Marshal's Office, and Pacification Commissioner of Hédōng Lù.
He recaptured Píngyáng and Jìn'ān.
An imperial edict praised and favored him,
promoting him one rank,
and bestowing upon him two hundred taels of silver and twenty rolls of fine silk.
He was remotely appointed Defense Commissioner of Mèngzhōu,
retaining his acting Chief Inspector post.
Leading troops to rescue Fūzhōu,
he fought his way there,
but died when the city fell.
He was posthumously granted Grand Master for Assisting in Virtue and Military Commissioner of Dìngguójūn,
and given the posthumous name Xiāngyǒng.
An imperial edict commanded the Branch Secretariat to seek his body for burial.
Nǚxīliè Zīlù's original surname was Zhāng,
and he was a native of Xiánpíng Fǔ.
During the Tàihé campaign against Sòng,
he distinguished himself in military service,
and was appointed Magistrate of Yìxiàn,
then promoted to Chief Registrar of Lùxiàn.
In the early Zhēnyòu period,
he was remotely appointed Acting Co-Defense Commissioner of Dézhōu,
then transferred to Qínzhōu.
In the third year,
he was remotely appointed Acting Co-Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎnjūn.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he was transferred to Prefect of Xīníngzhōu,
and granted the present surname.
After a long time,
he was remotely appointed Acting Co-Administrator of Líntáo Fǔ,
also holding the position of Prefect of Dìngxīzhōu.
He followed Acting Right Chief Inspector of the Marshal's Office Wányán Ālín in defeating Sòng troops at Shāozǐ Lǐng.
In the third year,
he attacked and captured Wǔxiū Guān,
with Zīlù performing the most meritorious service.
An edict stated that in addition to the promotions of five official ranks and two functional grades granted to other officers and soldiers,
Zīlù would receive an additional promotion of one official rank and one functional grade,
and be remotely appointed Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎnjūn,
retaining his position as Prefect.
In the fifth year,
he was remotely appointed Military Commissioner of Lǒng'ānjūn,
and soon after transferred to Jīn'ānjūn.
The edict stated:
"The Shǎnxī Branch Secretariat has reported vacancies among military officers.
You have long been in the front lines,
and manage your subordinates with discipline.
Many of your former soldiers are in Jīngzhào.
Now is precisely the autumn defense,
and the passes and rivers are vital strategic points;
you must diligently prepare defenses."
He led troops to rescue Fūzhōu.
In the intercalary twelfth month,
Fūzhōu was captured.
He was captured but refused to surrender,
and subsequently died.
He was posthumously granted Silver and Blue Grand Master of Glorious Happiness and Resident Administrator of Zhōngjīng.
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
those who spoke about current affairs believed Zīlù's posthumous honors were still too meager.
An edict ordered his two sons, Lièshān and Línquán, to be recorded,
promoted one functional grade,
and employed in the Shǎnxī Branch Secretariat army.
Zhào Yì was a native of
Tàiyuán.
He was a scholar.
When the Dà Yuán army entered the territory,
Yì gathered local strongmen,
and took refuge in the mountain gorges,
achieving merit in numerous battles.
Gūo Wénzhèn, Duke of Jìnyáng, appointed him Magistrate of Shòuyáng,
stationing troops at Yúcì Chóngyuánzhài.
He then led his forces to recapture Tàiyuán,
ascending the city wall at night,
slaughtering many,
and acquiring countless horses and weapons.
He escorted over twenty thousand elderly and young out.
He was promoted to Judicial Administrator of Tàiyuán,
then further promoted to Co-Administrator of the Prefecture and concurrently Pacification Commissioner.
In the eighth month of the first year of Yuánguāng,
the Dà Yuán army arrived in great numbers,
and pressed the siege of the city with increasing urgency.
Knowing it could not be held,
he set fire to his own official treasury and armory,
killed his wife and children,
and sank his seals of office into a well,
then committed suicide.
Xuānzōng heard of it and praised him with admiration,
posthumously granting him Silver and Blue Grand Master of Glorious Happiness and Pacification Commissioner of Hédōngběi Lù,
and further instructed the authorities to seek out his descendants for employment.
Hóu Xiǎoshū was a native of
Hédōng Xiàn.
He was a boatman in Héjīn.
In the early Zhēnyòu period,
he was registered and assigned to the Zhènwēijūn,
and appointed to office for his meritorious service.
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
he was promoted to Judge of Hézhōng Fǔ,
and acting Assistant Pacification Commissioner of Hédōngnán Lù.
Xiǎoshū fully protected the farmers by bringing them into the city,
and used his family wealth to reward the warriors.
When the siege of Hézhōng was lifted,
he was promoted to Judicial Administrator,
retaining his Pacification Commissioner post.
The Bureau of Military Affairs memorialized:
"Xiǎoshū's talent is useful,
but his acting position is too low to command authority over the multitude.
We request he be granted imperial credentials."
In the twelfth month,
an edict appointed him acting Right Chief Inspector of the Marshal's Office,
with discretionary powers.
The supervisor Wú Dé told Xiǎo Shū to surrender.
Xiǎo Shū scolded him out and had him executed.
His cousin, Zhāng Xiān, calmly stated that the great army was powerful
and that surrender could save their wives and children.
Xiǎo Shū angrily said to Zhāng Xiān:
"I am a boatman's son,
and I have risen to this position.
What do you mean by surrender?"
He had Zhāng Xiān bound to a pillar and killed him.
He offered food to monks, performed sacrifices, and buried him,
fulfilling the rites due to a relative.
Soon after,
the Privy Council sent the supervisory commissioner É Lùn to discuss military affairs with Xiǎo Shū.
Xiǎo Shū left the city to meet É Lùn.
Shí Tiānyīng took advantage of this to capture Hézhōng Fǔ,
building a pontoon bridge to connect with Shǎnxī.
Xiǎo Shū was stationed at Lè Lǐ Shānzhài.
All the troops assembled,
and in the middle of the night, they dug into the city wall and ascended.
They burned the watchtowers,
and the fire lit up the city.
Shí Tiānyīng was greatly alarmed and did not know what to do.
He abandoned all his baggage, official seals, horses, cattle, and various livestock.
He died at Shuāng Shì Mén.
Xiǎo Shū burned and destroyed the pontoon bridge,
and pacified his troops.
He was promoted to Zhāoyì Dàjiāngjūn,
and remotely appointed Méngzhōu Fángyùshǐ and Tóngzhī Fǔshì,
with his positions as Jiānjūn and Ānfǔ remaining as before.
In the first month of the second year,
the Great Yuán cavalry, numbering one hundred thousand, besieged Hézhōng.
Commander-in-chief É Kě dispatched supervisor Sūn Chāng to lead five thousand troops,
and Privy Council Vice-commissioner Wányán Sàibù dispatched Lǐ Rénzhì to lead three thousand troops,
all to relieve Hézhōng.
Xiǎo Shū set a time for gongs to be struck in the middle of the night,
for internal and external forces to respond to each other.
When the time came,
Xiǎo Shū led his troops out to battle,
but Sūn Chāng and Lǐ Rénzhì dared not move.
Xiǎo Shū gathered his troops and re-entered the city.
The siege became even more urgent.
The crowd debated retreating to the mountain stronghold,
but Xiǎo Shū said:
"Where would we go?"
