He secretly dispatched his administrative officer, Zhāng Sīzǔ, to break through the siege,
and rush to inform Biànjīng.
The next day,
the city fell,
and Xiǎo Shū died;
his body was not found.
Commander-in-chief É Kě appointed Jí Āwài, the judicial officer of Hézhōng Fǔ, to provisionally serve as Yòudūjiān in place of Xiǎo Shū.
The Privy Council reported:
"Xiǎo Shū's achievements were extraordinary.
Some suspect he is still alive.
To immediately replace him with Āwài
would cut off the path for him to return."
By this time,
Xiǎo Shū had already been dead for over forty days,
and the various strongholds in Zhōngtiáo were without leadership.
Thus, an imperial edict appointed Āwài to provisionally take charge.
Xuānzōng, reflecting on Xiǎo Shū's merits,
issued an edict of praise and posthumous honors,
and severely rebuked É Kě for the crime of not relieving Hézhōng.
Wáng Zuǒ, courtesy name Fǔzhī,
was the son of a farming family in Huòzhōu.
He was carefree and did not engage in production,
valued wealth lightly, was fond of giving,
and was skilled in archery and horsemanship.
During the Xīngdìng era,
he gathered several thousand troops
and provisionally managed the affairs of Huòzhōu.
Hú Tiānzuò of Píngyáng, by imperial order, promoted him to Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi and Zhàochéng Chéng,
then transferred him to Huòyì Lìng and Tóngzhī Púzhōu Jūnshì,
and provisionally to Zhāofǔ Fùshǐ and Púzhōu Jīnglüèshǐ.
An imperial edict promoted him to Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and remotely appointed him Bǎochāng Jūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
When the Great Yuán army captured Qīnglóng Bǎo,
Wáng Zuǒ was captured
and appointed garrison commander of Huòzhōu,
subordinate to Marshal Cuī Huán,
with his wife and children held as hostages.
Recruiter Ānfǔshǐ Chéng Tiānyòu had a rift with Cuī Huán.
Wáng Zuǒ conspired with Chéng Tiānyòu to kill Cuī Huán.
Chéng Tiānyòu asked:
"What about your wife and children who are hostages?"
Wáng Zuǒ replied:
"How could I, Wáng Zuǒ, care for my family?"
In the seventh month of the second year of Yuánguāng,
he took advantage of Cuī Huán's hunting trip to kill him,
and led tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians to pledge allegiance.
He was promoted to Lónghǔ Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn, Yuánshuài Yòujiānjūn, and concurrently Zhī Píngyáng Fǔshì.
Wáng Zuǒ and Píngyáng Gōng Shǐ Yǒng had always been at odds,
so he requested to move to Yùnǚ Zhài in Qìnzhōu.
The imperial edict granted this request,
and further ordered him to be subject to the command of Shàngdǎng Gōng Wányán Kāi.
In the seventh month of that year,
while relieving Xiāngyuán,
he was hit by a stray arrow and died.
He was posthumously granted Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn,
and his son was appointed Fúbǎo Diǎnshū.
Huángguā Jiǔzhù,
was from Línhuáng.
During the Dàdìng era, he was appointed Bù Lìshǐ through inherited privilege,
transferred to the Privy Council as Lìshǐ,
and then appointed Ānsùzhōu Jūnshì Pànguān.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng,
he became Dàlǐ Zhífǎ,
then Tóngzhī Jìzhōu Jūnshì,
and again transferred to Lù Wáng Fǔ Sīmǎ.
He successively held positions as Héběi Dōnglù Ànchásǐ and Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and was transferred to Zhī Zhāngdé Fǔshì.
He died in battle.
He was posthumously granted Rónglù Dàfū and Nánjīng Liúshǒu,
and his sons and grandsons were allowed to enter official service.
Wūlíndá Qǐzhù,
was from the Méng'ān of Dàmíng Lù.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-eighth year of Dàdìng.
He successively held positions as Bù Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
and was appointed Shāndōng Tíxíng Pànguān and Yīng Wáng Fǔ Sīmǎ.
The Censorate recommended him for his competent service in Shāndōng,
and he was transferred to Tàiyuán Fǔ Zhìzhōng.
He signed on to the Shǎnxī Ànchásī,
and successively served as Rǔzhōu and Qìnzhōu Cìshǐ,
then Běijīng and Línhuáng Ànchá Fùshǐ,
and was promoted to Púyǔ Lù Jiédùshǐ.
Not long after,
due to an offense, he was stripped of three official ranks,
dismissed from his post,
and demoted to Déchāng Jūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
In the early Chóngqìng era,
he achieved merits in border defense,
was promoted one rank,
awarded one hundred taels of silver and ten bolts of fine silk,
and transferred to Lìzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the early Zhēnyòu era,
he was transferred to Tóngzhī Xiánpíng Fǔshì,
and promoted to Guīdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was transferred to Xīngpíng Jūn,
and concurrently served as Dōngmiàn Jīnglüèshǐ.
Soon after, the Jīnglüè Sī was abolished,
and he was transferred to Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān.
He went to reinforce Zhōngdū and died in battle.
He was posthumously granted Rónglù Dàfū and Cānzhī Zhèngshì,
with half of a Cānzhī Zhèngshì's salary given to his family.
Tuómǎn Xiéliè,
was from the Méng'ān of Xiánpíng Lù.
He inherited his father's Méng'ān position.
During the Míngchāng era,
he was appointed Yā Jūn Wànhù with his tribal troops
and garrisoned the border.
During the Chéng'ān era,
he achieved merits in suppressing the Qìdān,
and was appointed Chénzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He was promoted to Zhī Píngliáng Fǔshì,
transferred to Bǎodà Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and then transferred to Zhī Zhāngdé Fǔshì.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
the Great Yuán army re-captured Zhāngdé,
and Tuómǎn Xiéliè died there.
Nímánggǔ Púlǔhǔ,
was from the Méng'ān of Zhōngdū Lù.
He passed the imperial examination in the fifth year of Míngchāng.
He successively held positions as Bù Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
and followed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Púsàn Kuí to attack Sòng.
After the campaign ended,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Chóngyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ Shì.
He was deemed honest and competent,
and transferred to Dōngpíng Fǔ Zhìzhōng.
He successively served as Huánzhōu and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
then Hànlín Dàizhì,
Kāifēng Fǔ Zhìzhōng,
and Dàlǐ Qīng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhī Hénán Fǔshì,
and concurrently Hénán Lù Fùtǒngjūn.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
he urgently prepared the defenses of Jīngxī,
serving as Shǎnzhōu Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ and concurrently Xī'ān Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In that year,
the Great Yuán army captured Tóngguān,
and all the garrisoned troops scattered.
Púlǔhǔ engaged in resistance,
but his army was defeated and he died there.
Wùyán Wèikě,
a *mèng'ān* from Lóng'ān Lù.
He was appointed to the imperial guards [qīnjūn],
served as a bodyguard [hùwèi],
and was made Assistant Judge [pànguān] of Yìdū General Administration [Zǒngguǎnfǔ] and Deputy Commander [Fù Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ] of the Central Capital Army and Horse [Zhōngdū Bīngmǎ].
He successively held office as Inspector [Cìshǐ] of Huìzhōu.
In the early years of Zhēnyòu,

he served as General of the Left Guard [Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn], Commander of the Arching Guard [Gǒngwèi Zhídū Zhǐhuīshǐ], Deputy Commander of Shāndōng [Shāndōng Fù Tǒngjūn], and Military Commissioner [Jié Dù Shǐ] of Ānhuà Commandery.
Local bandits occupied Jiǔxiān Shān as their stronghold,
but Wèikě, though having a large force, did not attack them,
so the bandits grew stronger.
Měnggǔ Gāng, the Provisional Governor [Xíngshěng] of Dōngpíng, impeached Wèikě for being unfit as a commander,
but the court did not investigate.
He was reassigned to Zhènxī Commandery,
acting as Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs [Jīnglüè Fùshǐ],
and successively served in Jīn'ān and Wǔshèng Commanderies.
〔一０〕In the fourth year of Xīngdìng,
he was transferred to Tàidìng Commandery.
In the fifth month of that year,
Yǎnzhōu was captured,
and he died there.
Wùyán Échūhǔ,
a *mèng'ān* from Lóng'ān Fǔ.
He passed the imperial examination as an advanced scholar [jìnshì] in the 28th year of Dàdìng.
He successively served as Clerk [Lìshǐ] of the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshūshěng],
then as Deputy Military Commissioner [Jié Dù Fùshǐ] of Shùntiān Commandery.

He was summoned to serve as Censor-at-Large [Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ], Supernumerary Secretary [Yuánwàiláng] of the Ministry of Justice [Xíngbù], Inspector [Cìshǐ] of Dānzhōu, Director [Lángzhōng] of the Ministry of Revenue [Hùbù], Deputy Surveillance Commissioner [Ànchá Fùshǐ] of Hénán Běilù, concurrently Administrator [Tóngzhī] of Dàxīng Fǔ, and Defense Commissioner [Fángyùshǐ] of Qínzhōu.
Upon the death of his mother,
he was reinstated as Defense Commissioner of Sìzhōu,
then promoted to Military Commissioner of Wǔníng Commandery,
and then transferred to Hépíng Commandery, concurrently serving as Supervisor of Waterways [Dū Shuǐ Jiān].
He was demoted to Defense Commissioner of Yízhōu
for falsely reporting military achievements while previously serving in Wǔníng,
then promoted to Military Commissioner of Fényáng Commandery, concurrently serving as Commissioner of Military Affairs [Jīnglüèshǐ].
In the ninth month of the second year of Xīngdìng,
the city fell and he died there.
Niángē Zhēn, whose original name was Chāohé,
was from the Xīnán Lù Recruitment Bureau [Zhāotǎosī].
He passed the imperial examination as an advanced scholar [jìnshì] in the 28th year of Dàdìng.
He successively served as Professor [Jiàoshòu] and Registrar [Zhǔbù],
and was appointed to the post of Judicial Inspector [Tíxíng Zhīshì] of Dàmíng, Héběi, through recommendation.
After an evaluation for integrity, he was promoted to Judge of Household Registration for the General Transportation and Revenue Department [Dū Zhuǎnyùn Hùjí Pànguān],
and successively held office as Deputy Military Commissioner [Jié Dù Fùshǐ] of Tàidìng Commandery.
Upon the death of his father,
after the mourning period,
he was appointed to the post of Administrator [Zhìzhōng] of Déxīng and Inspector [Cìshǐ] of Xuāndézhōu.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Zhēnyòu,
Zhēn, as Director [Lángzhōng] of the Ministry of Rites [Lǐbù], acting concurrently as Libationer of the Imperial Academy [Guózǐ Jìjiǔ],

along with Niángē Hédá, Inspector [Cìshǐ] of Ēnzhōu acting concurrently as Deputy Commander [Fù Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ] of the Imperial Guard [Wǔwèi Jūn], and Méizhǐ Qǐnú, Judge [Pànguān] of Héjiān Fǔ acting concurrently as Administrator [Tóngzhī] of Shùntiān Military Commission [Jié Dù Shǐ Shì], and Bódé Zhāngnú, Recorder [Lùshì] of Bǎozhōu acting concurrently as Deputy Military Commissioner [Jié Dù Fùshǐ] of Yǒngdìng Commandery, went to discuss peace.
〔一一〕In the second year,
the peace agreement was concluded,
and he was rewarded with 200 taels of silver, ten bolts of fine silk, and a jade *tùhú*.
He was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue [Hùbù Shìláng],
and successively served as Military Commissioner [Jié Dù Shǐ] of Qìnnán, Hépíng, Zhènnán, Jíqìng, and Fényáng Commanderies.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
he was transferred to Zhāoyì Commandery,
serving as Commissioner of Military Affairs [Jīnglüèshǐ] of Lùzhōu.
In the second year of Xīngdìng,
he entered the court as Minister of Works [Gōngbù Shàngshū].
He attacked the Sòng from Shòuzhōu,
achieving merit in the assault on Zhèngyáng.
He acted as Left Senior Inspector of the Grand Marshal's Office [Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān],
and defended Jìn'ān Fǔ.
In the eleventh month of the third year of Xīngdìng,
the city fell,
and Zhēn, along with over ten officials of the prefecture, all died.
Textual Criticism Notes
Biographies (Lièzhuàn), Volume 61: Loyal and Righteous (Zhōngyì) 3: Túshānháng, Wányán Chénhéshàng, Yáng Wòyǎn.
Wūgǔlún Hēihàntuómǎnhútúmén, Jī Rǔzuò, Àishēn (with Mǎjiānlóng as an attachment), Yǔxiǎn.
Túshānháng, also known as Zhāng Sēng,
was the son of the Imperial Son-in-Law and Grand Councilor [Fùmǎ Shūmìshǐ] [name omitted].
His father was known as the Nine Imperial Son-in-Law.
When Wèi Wáng had affairs in the northern frontier,
he was reassigned as Grand Marshal [Dū Yuánshuài],
and still concurrently held the position of Grand Councilor [Píngzhāng],
but he was extremely unpopular.
Zhāng Sēng was then Vice Minister of Personnel [Lìbù Shìláng],
and strongly urged his father to resign from the marshal's post,
whereupon he was appointed Grand Councilor [Píngzhāng].
In the first year of Zhìníng,
Húshāhǔ committed regicide,
and Háng was demoted to Inspector [Cìshǐ] of Ānzhōu.
Just then, a large northern army arrived at the city walls,
claiming that the capital had already fallen,
and that "you should surrender quickly."
Háng said to his people:
"Although the city defense is strict,
if it should by any chance be breached,
none of you will survive.
My family has been imperial sons-in-law for two generations,
and has received great kindness from the state;
we absolutely cannot surrender.
What plan will you make?"
His people said:
"Since the Grand Administrator [Tàishǒu] will not yield,
how can we bear to surrender?
We are willing to defend to the death."
Háng then brought out all his family's wealth to reward the soldiers and civilians,
and all the soldiers and civilians did their best to prepare for defense.
Five more days later,
the city was in peril.
Háng judged that it could not be held,
and said to his wife and children:
"The situation is dire now;
there is only death."
He then first hanged his wife and children,
and said to his household:
"When I die, dismantle the house and burn it."
Then he hanged himself.
When the city fell,
people still fought fiercely,
saying:
"Since the Grand Administrator is dead,
we cannot surrender alone."
Many died.
Wányán Chénhéshàng, whose given name was Yí,
and courtesy name was Liángzuǒ,
was known by his childhood name throughout his life.
He was from Fēngzhōu.
He was descended from the grandsons of Xiāo Wáng.
His father, Qǐgē,
participated in the southern campaign during Tàihé,
and was awarded the concurrent post of Administrator of Jiēzhōu Military Affairs [Tóngzhī Jiēzhōu Jūnshì] for his merits.
When the Sòng recaptured Jiēzhōu,
Qǐgē died in battle at Jiālíng Jiāng.
During Zhēnyòu,
Chénhéshàng was over twenty years old,
and was captured by northern troops.
The commander greatly favored him,
keeping him in his tent.
At that time, Chénhéshàng's mother remained in Fēngzhōu,
and his cousin Xiéliè, Commander of Ānpíng [Ānpíng Dūwèi], served her very respectfully.
Chénhéshàng stayed in the north for over a year,
then, feigning a visit to his mother, requested to return.
The commander sent a soldier to supervise him to Fēngzhōu.
There, he and Xiéliè ambushed and killed the supervising soldier,
seized a horse, and supported his mother as they fled south.
The large army discovered this,
and a combined cavalry force pursued them,
but they escaped via another route.
Later, they lost their horse,
and his mother was old and unable to walk.
They carried her in a deer-antler cart,
and the brothers pulled it together,
crossing the river to the south.
Xuānzōng marveled at him.
Xiéliè was granted the hereditary official post of Area Commander [Dūtǒng],
and Chénhéshàng was tested and appointed to the Imperial Guards [Hùwèi],
and shortly thereafter promoted to Gentleman of the Imperial Household [Fèngyù].
When Xiéliè took charge of the Marshal's Office of Shòu and Sì [Shòu, Sì Yuánshuàifǔ],
he recommended Chénhéshàng to accompany him.
An edict appointed him to serve as Provisional Controller [Xuānchāi Tíkòng],
wearing a golden tally.
Xiéliè appointed Wáng Wò of Tàiyuán as his Registrar [Jīnglì].
Wò, courtesy name Zhòngzé,
was comparable to Léi Yuān and Lǐ Xiànnéng in literary skill and discourse,
and thus Chénhéshàng considered him a mentor and friend.
Chénhéshàng was naturally intelligent and perceptive,
and was very fond of literature and history.
From the time he was in the imperial guard,
people regarded him as a scholar [xiùcái].
By this time,
Wò taught him the *Xiàojīng*, *Xiǎoxué*, *Lúnyǔ*, and *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn*,
and he generally understood their meanings.
When there was no military activity,
he would write tiny characters like ox hair by the window,
like a struggling scholar,
with utter indifference to worldly pleasures.
In the second year of Zhèngdà,
Xiéliè was relieved of his marshal's post,
and assigned as a general commander,
stationed at Fāngchéng.
Chén Héshàng followed him there,
and was privy to all matters concerning his elder brother's army.
Xiéliè was ill at the time.
Among the troops, a certain Lǐ Tàihé had an altercation with Gě Yíwēng of the Fāngchéng garrison,
and they reported it to Chén Héshàng.
Yíwēng was in the wrong,
so Chén Héshàng measured out a flogging for him.
Yíwēng was by nature fierce and truculent,
and felt ashamed to be beaten for being in the wrong,
so he died of resentment,
leaving instructions to his wife that she must avenge him against Chén Héshàng.
His wife sued Chén Héshàng, alleging that he had used personal animosity to usurp official authority
and thus killed her husband.
She reported it to the Táishěng,
and to the attendants of the court,
piling up firewood south of Lóngjīnqiáo,
vowing that if she did not get justice, she would immolate herself to atone to her husband.
For this reason, Chén Héshàng was imprisoned.
The deliberators suspected Chén Héshàng,
believing that he, being familiar with the court and relying on the importance of his military authority, must have acted oppressively and illegally,
and should be executed.
The memorial was submitted,
but a decision could not be reached for a long time.
Chén Héshàng gathered books in prison and read them,
for a total of eighteen months.
The following year,
Xiéliè recovered from his illness,
and was summoned by imperial edict to lead troops west.
Upon entering the court,
Āizōng was surprised by how thin he had become,
and asked:
"Are you perhaps troubled because the Fāngchéng case is still unresolved?
You may proceed;
I will pardon him now."
However, as the Táijiàn again raised objections,
he dared not grant the pardon.
Not long after,
Xiéliè passed away.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor
finally issued a swift pardon for Chén Héshàng,
saying:
"The officials reported that you killed a man out of personal animosity.
With your elder brother's death,
we have lost a famous general.
Now, for your elder brother's sake,
I am bending the law to pardon you.
The world will surely criticize me for this.
In the future,
if you exert yourself and achieve great deeds,
and the state benefits from your strength,
then people will acknowledge that my pardon was not granted lightly."
Chén Héshàng wept and bowed,
his grief moving those around him,
unable to utter a single word of thanks.
He was then, in plain clothes, appointed Dūtǒng of the Zǐwēi Army,
and a year later transferred to be Tíkòng of the Zhōngxiào Army.
In the fifth year,
Northern troops entered Dàchāngyuán.
Píngzhāng Hédá asked who could serve as the vanguard.
Chén Héshàng stepped forward to answer the call,
having already bathed and changed clothes,
as if preparing for death.
He donned his armor, mounted his horse, and did not look back.
On that day,
with four hundred cavalry, he defeated eight thousand men.
The soldiers of the three armies were eager and spirited to fight,
as this was the first victory of its kind in twenty years since the war began.
His achievement was ranked first.
An imperial edict personally praised and commended him,
appointing him Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn and Píngliángfǔ Pànguān,
with hereditary Mókè status.
His name became famous throughout the land in a single day.
The Zhōngxiào Army consisted entirely of Huíhé, Nǎimǎn, Qiāng, Hún, and those from the Central Plains who had been captured, fled crimes, and then returned.
They were fierce, arrogant, and difficult to control.
Chén Héshàng managed them effectively;
their sitting, rising, advancing, and retreating all conformed to regulations.
Wherever they passed through prefectures and cities, they committed not the slightest offense beyond what was allotted to them,
and the streets were no longer noisy and chaotic.
In every battle, they were the first to ascend and breach enemy lines,
swift as wind and rain.
All other armies relied heavily on them.
In the sixth year,
there was the victory at Wèizhōu.
In the eighth year,
there was the victory at Dàohuí Gǔ.
From being a convict, he was promoted in no more than four or five steps to Yùwǔ Zhōnglángjiāng.
The Deputy Grand Councilor, Yílài Pú'ā, lacked a strategy of prudence.
He once rode two hundred *lǐ* in a single day and night to pursue a minor advantage,
and no one in the army dared to advise against it.
Chén Héshàng privately told his colleagues:
"The Deputy Grand Councilor treats major generalship as a matter of petty raiding.
Today he gets three hundred captives,
tomorrow one or two thousand cattle and sheep,
but the soldiers who die of exhaustion are no longer accounted for.
What the state has accumulated over several years
will surely be completely squandered by this man."
Someone reported this to Pú'ā.
One day,
he hosted a banquet for the generals.
When the wine reached Chén Héshàng,
Pú'ā said:
"You once criticized me,
and said that the state's military power would be utterly ruined by me.
Is this true or not?"
Chén Héshàng finished his drink
and calmly said:
"It is."
Pú'ā saw that he showed no fear,
and casually offered a conciliatory remark, saying:
"If there are faults, discuss them face-to-face;
there will be no further comments."
In the first month of the ninth year,
after the defeat at Sānfēngshān,
he fled to Jūnzhōu.
When the city fell,
and the large army entered,
they immediately engaged in street fighting.
Chén Héshàng sought refuge in a hiding place.
When the killing and looting had somewhat subsided, he emerged,
and declared:
"I am a great general of the Jīn state.
I wish to see your commander to report."
The soldiers, with a few horsemen flanking him,
led him to the front of the commander's tent.
When asked his name,
he replied:
"I am Chén Héshàng, commander of the Zhōngxiào Army.
I was the one who achieved the victory at Dàchāngyuán,
and the victory at Wèizhōu was also by me,
and the victory at Dàohuí Gǔ was also by me.
If I die in chaotic fighting,
people will say I failed the state.
Today, I die clearly,
and surely there will be those in the world who know me."
At that time, they wished him to surrender,
but he was hacked until his shins broke, yet he did not yield.
His mouth was slit open to his ears,
and he spat blood while shouting,
without ceasing until death.
The great general respected him,
and poured mare's milk as a libation,
praying:
"Good man,
when you are reborn,
may I obtain you."
He was forty-one years old at the time.
In the sixth month of that year,
an imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Zhènnánjūn Jiédùshǐ,
and a statue was placed in the Bāozhōng Temple,
with a stone tablet commemorating his loyalty and heroism.
Xiéliè's given name was Dǐng,
and his courtesy name was Guóqì.
He was a hereditary Méng'ān from Bìlǐhǎi.
At twenty,
he became known for his skill in battle.
From Marshal of Shòu and Sì, he was transferred to Ānpíng Dūwèi,
stationed at Shāngzhōu.
His prestige and authority were very significant.
He respected the worthy and treated subordinates with deference,
possessing the demeanor of ancient virtuous generals.
Upon his initial arrival at Shāngzhōu,
one day while searching for hidden enemies,
he found descendants of Ōuyáng Xiū in a large bamboo forest.
After questioning and learning their identity,
he released them and over three thousand of their clan members and villagers.
Yáng Wòyǎn, also named Wòliè,
was granted the surname Wùlíndá.
He was from Jìngbiān Guānzhuāng in Shuòzhōu,
originally belonging to the Tángkuò Dílà tribe.
When young, he once served as a minor official in border屯田.
When the Dàyuán army entered the territory,
the court ordered the Tángkuò tribe to relocate inland.
Wòyǎn stayed and did not move,
leading his tribe and those willing to follow him to take refuge in Cháshí Gōu, South Mountain, Shuòzhōu.
He had several thousand followers
who nominated Wòyǎn as Zhāofǔshǐ,
and called his ravine a "Fǔ."
Thus, remnants from ruined towns and counties gathered daily.
The official army could not control them,
and he also fought against the large army,
winning several small victories.
When food ran short, he resorted to plundering.
The official army pursued him,
but could not defeat him in major battles.
He then moved through the various prefectures of Níng, Ào, Wǔ, Shuò, and Níngbiān,
causing distress to the people.
The imperial court sent envoys to persuade him,
and Wòyǎn immediately returned with his followers.
At that time, Xuānzōng was relocating south,
and was at Qímén.
Hearing of this, he was very pleased,
and appointed him Wǔzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wǔzhōu had repeatedly suffered destruction.
Wòyǎn entered the prefecture, and not long after, a large army attacked.
They fought fiercely for twenty-seven days and nights but could not conquer it.
So, they retreated.
This was in the second month of the second year of Zhēnyòu.
Subsequently,
the imperial court, considering Wǔzhōu ultimately indefensible,
ordered Wòyǎn to move his troops and civilians to Kělánzhōu.
For his merits at Wǔzhōu, he was promoted to Defense Commissioner of that prefecture.
Soon after, Kělán was elevated to a military commissioner's region (Jiézhèn),
and Wòyǎn was made a Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ).
An imperial edict also stated:
“You have been utterly loyal to the state
and have repeatedly rendered meritorious service.
Now you are specially promoted to the third rank;
the imperial favor is indeed generous.
May you further strive in loyalty and diligence,
and live harmoniously with the Pacification Commission (Xuānfǔsī) to bring peace to the military and civilians.”
From the moment Wòyǎn received the edict, he dedicated himself to the state,
saying:
“To die at home instead of dying in service to the king
is not the act of a true man.”
In the third year [of Zhēnyòu],
he was ordered to garrison the three prefectures of Jīng, Bīn, and Lǒng.
Wòyǎn divided his nine thousand troops into ten wings and five commanders (Dūtǒng),
personally leading four-tenths of them.
That winter,
the Xī Xià (Western Xià) with over forty thousand cavalry besieged Dìngxīzhōu.
Marshal Right Supervising Commissioner Wányán Sàibù appointed Wòyǎn to command the military affairs [of the expeditionary force].
He led troops to battle the Xià people,
beheading nearly two thousand,
capturing several tens alive,
and seizing over eight hundred horses.
The amount of weaponry was commensurate.
The rest all fled.
An edict ordered the Shǎnxī Provincial Administration (Shǎnxī Xíngshěng) to assess the merits and bestow rewards.
In the spring of the first year of Xīngdìng,
the Emperor, recognizing Wòyǎn’s accumulated military achievements,
bestowed upon him his present surname.
Not long after,
he was nominally appointed Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎn Commandery and concurrently Inspector within the jurisdiction of Gǒngzhōu.
That winter,
an edict ordered the Shǎnxī Provincial Administration to attack Sòng.

Wòyǎn, along with Marshal Left Supervising Commissioner Nèizú Báisā, Military Commissioner of Tōngyuǎn Commandery Wēndíhǎn Lóushì, Concurrent Administrator of Tōngyuǎn Commandery Affairs Wūgǔlùn Chángshòu, and Deputy Military Commissioner of Píngxī Commandery Hésùjiā Wùdí, led five thousand troops out of Gǒngzhōu’s Yánchuān.
Upon reaching Gùchéng, they encountered three hundred Xià soldiers,
and defeated them.
They then entered Xīhézhōu and reached Qíshānbǎo,
where they met six thousand soldiers in three divisions.
They dispatched troops to attack them separately,
chasing the fleeing enemy for over thirty lǐ,
beheading four hundred,
capturing ten alive, two hundred horses, and countless armored weapons.
Soon after, they recovered Sànguān.
In the first month of the second year,
the victory report arrived.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and issued an edict promoting Wòyǎn one rank
and nominally appointing him Administrator of Líntáofǔ Affairs.
In the third year,
in the victory at Wǔxiūguān,
Wòyǎn’s contribution was significant.
An edict specially promoted him one rank.
In the first month of the first year of Yuánguāng,
he was nominally appointed Grand Guardian of Zhōngjīng.
In the sixth month,
he was promoted to Marshal Right Supervising Commander
and also inherited the hereditary title Nàgǔhúlí'àibìláimóukè.
In the spring of the second year,
several hundred Northern cavalry raiders pillaged Yán'ān and headed south.
Wòyǎn led troops to pursue them,
battling them at Yězhūlǐng,
capturing four, and then returning.
Soon after,
a large army arrived,
stationed at Dé'ānzhài,
and was again defeated and driven away.
Not long after,
when the main army attacking Fèngxiáng returned,
passing through Bǎo'ān,
Wòyǎn dispatched Supervising Commissioner Wányán Chálà to defeat them at Shílóutái,
capturing two hundred horses and several tens of tallies and seals before and after.
An edict ordered the relevant authorities to discuss rewards.
Originally,
upon hearing there were troops at Yězhūlǐng,
Wòyǎn had arranged with Tuómǎn Hútúmén to meet and battle with infantry.
Hútúmén was an experienced general
who often looked down upon Wòyǎn,
and consequently missed the appointed time.
After Wòyǎn returned from battle,
he convened his generals and intended to execute Hútúmén,
but the generals pleaded for him, so he was released.
At this time, the main army's prestige and power grew,
and the Shǎnxī Provincial Administration ordered Wòyǎn to clear the fields (qīngyě).
He did not comply,
saying:
“If I clear the fields,
what will the people eat next year?”
So, he held his position across a large ravine, allowing the people to finish their wheat harvesting.
In the second year of Zhèngdà,
he was promoted to Marshal Left Supervising Commander
and nominally held the position of Grand Guardian of Zhōngjīng.
In the winter of the eighth year,
Grand Councilor Hédá and Political Counsellor Pú'ā moved west from Dèngzhōu.
Wòyǎn met them from Fēngyángchuān at the foot of Wǔdàshān.
He asked how the battle at Yǔshān went.
Hédá replied:
“Although our army was victorious,
the main enemy forces have dispersed and are heading towards the capital.”
Wòyǎn indignantly exclaimed:
“Grand Councilor and Political Counsellor, having received great imperial favor,
wielding military power,
lost the strategic moment,
and could not engage in battle and defense.
Instead, you allowed the enemy to penetrate deep.
What more is there to say?”
After the defeat at Sānfēngshān,
Wòyǎn fled to Jūnzhōu.
His subordinates Báilíunú and Dáiliúshèng, having already surrendered,
requested permission from the great commander [of the enemy]
to enter Jūnzhōu and persuade Wòyǎn.
The great commander held Báilíunú as hostage
and sent Dáiliúshèng into Jūnzhōu to see Wòyǎn,
conveying the great commander's intention:
if he surrendered, he would be granted a high official position.
Wòyǎn spoke kindly and comforted him,
then sent him forward,
drew his sword and struck him,
saying:
“I rose from humble beginnings and received great imperial favor.
Do you wish to defile me with this?”
He then left final instructions for his subordinates,
looked towards Biànjīng, bowed, and wept, saying:
“I have no face to see the imperial court.
There is only death.”
Then he hanged himself.
His subordinates lit a fire and burned the house where he lodged,
and over ten people died with him.
Wòyǎn was fifty-two years old at the time of his death.
Initially,
when the great army broke the Xī Xià
and advanced rapidly,
the thousand-lǐ region of Guānfǔ was in turmoil and unrest.
Even the wise could do nothing.
Wòyǎn and his general Liú Xīnggē led troops back and forth between Bīn and Lǒng,
repeatedly fighting and repeatedly winning.
Therefore, the great enemy army could not suddenly advance eastward.
Xīnggē,
a native of Guó County in Fèngxiáng,
rose from among bandits.
People called him
“Rè Liú” (Hot Liu).
Later, he died in battle at Qīnghuà.
When the great army arrived, they poured wine to mourn him,
and the elders of Xīzhōu spoke of him with tears.
Wūgǔlùn Hēihàn
began his career in the imperial guard.
He once served as a military officer in the Marshal's Residence of Táng and Dèng prefectures.
In the second year of Tiānxīng,
the Prefect of Tángzhōu, Nèizú Xiélǔ, died of illness.
The Grand Commander's Residence of Dèngzhōu appointed Púchá Dūwèi to temporarily administer Tángzhōu affairs.
The Sòng army twice besieged Táng,
and much of Táng’s grain was taken by Dèngzhōu,
resulting in a food shortage.
In the sixth month,
Wànhù Jiágǔ Dìngzhù was sent to Guīdé
to request military provisions,
but there was no reply.
In the seventh month,
Commander Fèng and Zhēn Gǎizhù of the garrison army mutinied,
killing Púchá Dūwèi.
At that time, the imperial court's communication was blocked,
so the Commander's Residence (Shuàifǔ) provisionally appointed Hēihàn as Prefect to act on behalf of the Commander's Residence.
Subsequently,
the garrison army had a plan to surrender to Sòng.
At that time, Commander Niè Dūtǒng of Dàchéngshān in Yùzhōu, with five hundred troops, was in the prefecture,
and he alone did not wish to surrender to Sòng.
He became an enemy of the garrison army.
The garrison could not defeat him,
abandoned their old and young, and fled to Zǎoyáng.
The Sòng people thus learned the strengths and weaknesses of Tángzhōu.
Coincidentally, Dèng commander Yílài Yuán rebelled with his city and surrendered to Sòng,
sending a letter to Hēihàn to recruit him.
Hēihàn killed the messenger without replying.
Sòng King Ānfǔ led troops to attack Táng.
Èsī King Tàiwèi arrived subsequently,
and the attack intensified.
Hēihàn heard that Emperor Āizōng had moved to Cài,
and sent someone to request rescue.
The Emperor ordered Acting Political Counsellor Wùlíndá Hútǔ to lead troops there.
The Sòng people set up an ambush,
allowing half of them to enter the city, then intercepted and attacked them.
Hútǔ was greatly defeated,
returning with only thirty cavalrymen remaining.
Inside the city, provisions were exhausted.
People resorted to cannibalism.
Hēi Hàn killed his beloved concubine and fed her to the soldiers.
The soldiers then contended to kill their wives and children.
The officials gathered to discuss surrender.
Hēi Hàn and Niè Dūtǒng insisted on holding out even more firmly.
Féng Zǒnglǐng then secretly went out of the city to drink with Wáng Ānfǔ.
They agreed that the Sòng army would enter the city the next day.
Féng returned,
but the Sòng army could not enter.
Niè Dūtǒng invited Féng to discuss matters,
and then immediately executed him in the meeting.
His partisans were all killed.
Zǒnglǐng Zhào Chǒunǐ, who had initially conspired with Féng,
felt uneasy.
He opened the west gate and admitted the Sòng army.
Hēi Hàn led the Dàchéngshān army in street battles.
From Chén (7-9 AM) to Wǔ (11 AM-1 PM),
the Sòng army was utterly defeated and retreated,
suffering countless casualties.
The Sòng people shouted to Zhào Chǒunǐ from below the city,
agreeing to join forces to kill the Dàchéngshān army.
The Dàchéng army was defeated.
The Sòng people captured Hēi Hàn,
threatening him to surrender.
Hēi Hàn did not yield
and was killed.
More than ten people escaped,
including Zǒnglǐng Yílài Wàngjūn, Nǚxīliè Jūn, and Chǒunǐ, who fled to Càizhōu.
They all received promotions and rewards,
but later all died in the Jiǎwǔ Disaster.
Tuōmǎn Hútǔmén, courtesy name Zǐxiù,
was a Jinshì (進士) in policy essays.
He successively served as Hànlín Dàizhì.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
he was promoted to Zhī Zhōngshān Fǔ.
In the third year (1215),
he was reassigned to Zhī Líntáo Fǔ and concurrently Běnlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
Rebel leaders Chéng Chénsēng (程陳僧) and others in Lánzhōu enticed the Xià people to invade.
Líntáo was besieged for half a month.
There were only a few thousand soldiers in the city, and provisions were about to run out.
Everyone was alarmed.
Hútǔmén explained daily the principles of loyalty and rebellion, and the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
and all were roused to valor.
He then arrested twenty of their partisans who intended to be internal collaborators,
executed them,
and threw their heads outside the city.
The bandits attacked from all sides.
He then launched a night raid on the bandit encampments.
The Xià soldiers were in great disarray.
The Jīn army took advantage of this
and achieved a great victory.
The Xià people fled.
In the fourth year (1216),
he became Zhī Hézhōng Fǔshì,
and acting Hédōng Nánlù Xuānfǔ Fùshǐ.
In the tenth month,
he was promoted to Yuánshuài Yòujiānjūn, concurrently holding his previous posts.
In the second year of Xīngdìng (1218),
he became Jiàngyáng Jūn Jiédùshǐ and concurrently Guǎnnèi Guānchásǐ of Jiàngzhōu.
In the tenth month,
he was promoted to Yuánshuài Zuǒjiānjūn, Xing Yuánshuàifǔ Shì, and concurrently Zhī Jìn'ān Fǔ and Hédōng Nánlù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
Thereupon,
he repaired city walls,
maintained armor and weapons,
and accumulated fodder and provisions,
in preparation for defense.
The people were displeased.
Xíngshěng Xū Dǐng heard of this,
and sent him a letter saying:
“When the marshal first took charge of Hézhōng,
his benevolence and love were cherished by the people.
When he transferred to Jìn'ān,
those near and far rejoiced and looked up to him.
Last year, when the army invaded,
Píngyáng did not hold,
but the only part of Hédōng that remained intact was Jiàng.
This was because you, Sir, planned victories from your seat,
and your prestige and virtue were well-known.
Thus, without much fanfare, you achieved security.
Recently, it has been rumored
that your governance is too rigid,
and taxes and levies are too heavy.
Dǐng is deeply concerned about this.
The ancients said,
if one is not lenient with subordinates, people will fear calamity;
if one has doubts when employing people, scholars will not exert their utmost.
Moreover, a large army is near,
neighboring areas are already vacant,
and common people are easily swayed,
so this must be considered.
I wish, Sir, that you would treat your subordinates with humility,
bind people with loyalty and filial piety,
clearly administer rewards and punishments,
and equalize taxes and levies.
Upwards, this would share the worries of the sagely emperor who toils day and night;
downwards, this would entrust you with being the Great Wall of Hédōng.”
Hútǔmén received the letter,
fearing that the people would not obey or might even rebel.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
“I, your subject, am but of meager talent,
yet have been presumptuously entrusted with a heavy responsibility.
I was about to repair moats and walls, and accumulate fodder and provisions as a defensive measure.
But the common people are difficult to consult at the outset.
They complain that my administration is rather harsh,
and thus have many grievances,
causing worry to the Xíngshěng.
Since hearing your instruction,
I have found myself at a loss,
repenting internally
and externally applying leniency and comfort,
hoping to somewhat soothe the hearts of the multitude.
However, recently, due to an imperial order, a division of troops crossed the river.
Then there were clamors that the marshal did not augment troops to defend and hold,
but instead aided Hénán,
and would abandon us.
With such public sentiment,
I fear that other changes may suddenly arise.
Previously, Lǐ Gé was in Píngyáng,
and the people were uneasy,
but Lǐ Gé endured and did not speak,
leading to defeat.
I am truly clumsy and mistaken,
unable to subdue people.
I dare to present Dǐng’s letter to the court,
and only ask the court to consider it.”
The court, based on Dǐng’s words,
dispatched Shàngshū of Lìbù, Wányán Lǘshān, to replace him.
Some said
that Hútǔmén intended to leave Jìn'ān by stratagem,
and so he initiated large-scale public works,
and indulged in killings,
deliberately alienating the people's hearts.
Hence, Dǐng mentioned it.
Not long after,
Jìn'ān fell,
and nearly a million people died,
thus losing Hédōng.
In the eighth month of the third year (1224),
he was reassigned to Tàicháng Qīng, acting Qiān Shūmì Yuàn Shì, and Zhī Guīdé Fǔ Shì.
In the second month of the second year of Yuánguāng (1223),
he was demoted one rank for submitting a false memorial.
In the seventh month of the third year of Zhèngdà (1226),
he was reinstated as Líntáo Fǔ Zǒngguǎn.
In the fifth month of the fourth year (1227),
the city was captured, and he was seized.
They tried to entice him to surrender, but he refused.
They ordered him to kneel, but he did not comply.
They hacked at his knees and shins with knives,
but he ultimately did not yield,
and was killed.
In the fifth year (1228),
an imperial edict posthumously appointed him Zhōngjīng Liúshǒu,
erected a statue of him in Bāozhōng Miào,
and granted official positions to his descendants.
His wife, Wūgǔlùn Shì, also died for her integrity,
and has a biography.
Jī Rǔzuò, courtesy name Qīnzhī,
was a Rǔyáng native,
and the grand-nephew of Duānxiū, the Fùshǐ (副使) of Quánzhōu Jiédù (節度).
His father, Mào, passed the departmental clerk examination through hereditary privilege,
and was promoted to Shàngshūshěng Língshǐ.
Rǔzuò studied and understood principles of righteousness.
His nature was unrestrained and he did not concern himself with minor conduct.
He was always praised for his talent and magnanimity.
At the end of Zhèngdà,
he avoided the war in Sōngshān,
protecting several hundred local families.
The multitude treated him as their elder.
Later, he moved to Jiāoyáshān zhài (fortress).
It happened that U_gǔlùn Sìhé (烏古論四和), the Jìnshì Júshǐ (近侍局使), was pacifying Xīshān,
and expediently appointed Rǔzuò as Běishān Zhāofǔshǐ,
wearing a silver tally.
He then moved into Rǔzhōu.
Initially,
after Rǔzhōu was devastated,
in the first month of Tiānxīng (天興) first year (1232),
Zhāng Kǎi (張楷), Co-Administrator of the Xuānhuī (宣徽) Academy, was appointed Defense Commissioner.
He led over a hundred local soldiers from Xiāngxiàn (襄縣) and Jiáxiàn (郟縣) from Biàn (汴) into Qīngyángzhài (青陽𣛀).
At that time, Hūyán Shí (呼延實) was in charge of Qīngyángzhài.
Shí
was from Zhàochéng (趙城).
Originally, he was a subordinate of Yáng Wòyǎn (楊沃衍).
Due to his military achievements, he rose to become a Military Commissioner of Bǎochāngjūn (寶昌軍).
He was living in retirement in the western mountains of Rǔ (汝).
Kǎi (楷) felt that he could not command the populace,
so he entrusted the affairs of the prefecture to Shí,
and then went to Dèngzhōu (鄧州) to join Shān Gōng Wǔ Xiān (山公武仙).
Later, when the Dà Yuán (大元) army arrived,
the city fell.
Thousands of people were killed.
Then, surrender was permitted,
and Zhāng Xuānchāi (張宣差) was put in charge of the prefecture's affairs.
In the third month,
Liǔ Qiānhù (柳千戶), a fleeing officer from Jūnzhōu (鈞州), entered the prefecture.
Zhāng fled,
and Liǔ thus occupied it.
Not long after,
the city was again breached.
When Rǔ Zuò (汝作) arrived,
although the northern army had departed,
it was merely an empty city.
Rǔ Zuò gathered the scattered and displaced,
re-established markets.
The northern army repeatedly tried to persuade him to submit, but he refused.
Several battles were fought with alternating victories and losses.
Soon after,
the northern army attacked again.
Rǔ Zuò personally supervised the soldiers,
resisting them to the death.
After the enemy retreated,
he secretly submitted a memorial through a side route.
Āizōng (哀宗) issued a decree:
"This prefecture has no strong natural defenses to rely upon,
yet you have been able to serve the state with your life.
You are now appointed Co-Administrator of Rǔzhōu and Defense Commissioner,
with discretion to act as you deem fit."
At this time,
this prefecture's south connected to Dèngzhōu,
its west to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and its east to Biànjīng (汴京).
It was where imperial envoys were dispatched from,
supplying and communicating with all three sides,
transmitting intelligence.
However, Hūyán Shí, who was the General Commander in Qīngyáng,
was jealous of Rǔ Zuò's achievements in defending the city,
and they could not get along.
The affairs of the prefecture were often controlled by him.
Shí wanted to relocate the prefectural seat into the mountains,
saying that it would certainly be broken by a large army in the future.
Rǔ Zuò believed that there was still much grain in the granaries,
and fleeing soldiers arrived daily from all directions.
These people had survived a hundred deaths,
and could all be put to use if motivated.
"The imperial court relies on me to defend this prefecture,
yet the General Commander wishes to abandon it?
What kind of heart is that?"
Slanderous schemes were set in motion,
creating an opportunity for mutual plotting.
The Consulting Official, Yáng Péng (楊鵬), explained, saying:
"External difficulties are not yet resolved, yet you are concerned with private grievances."
His words were very earnest and heartfelt.
Shí then returned to the mountains.
Péng then advised Rǔ Zuò to submit a memorial,
pleading to defend this prefecture to the death,
to strengthen the morale of the army and the people.
That winter,
they fought in Xiāng (襄) and Jiá (郟),
obtaining over a hundred horses,
and the morale of the troops was greatly boosted.
Consequently, Rǔ Zuò was appointed General Commander,
and no longer had any dealings with Shí.
In the sixth month of Tiānxīng second year (1233),
Āizōng was in Càizhōu (蔡州),
and sent an envoy to request troops for reinforcement.
The people of the prefecture were harassed by patrols,
farming was completely abandoned,
and grain in the city was almost depleted.
That month,
Zhōngjīng (中京) fell.
The subordinates privately discussed their fear of "the teeth being cold when the lips are gone,"
and conspired to surrender the city.
Fearing Rǔ Zuò,
they dared not speak,
but instead presented the idea of moving the prefectural seat into the mountains.
Rǔ Zuò angrily said:
"My ancestors have enjoyed imperial emolument for a hundred years.
Now the imperial court has entrusted me with the affairs of the prefecture and the position of commander.
I shall live as a citizen of Jīn (金),
and die as a ghost of Jīn.
Do you wish to flee to the mountains?
Is it not to surrender?
Whoever speaks again of relocating, I will surely execute him."
In the eighth month,
Tǎchá (塔察) led a large army to attack Cài (蔡),
passing through Rǔzhōu.
Liáng Gāo (梁臯), a man from the prefecture, instigated a rebellion,
and with the former officials Wēn Zé (溫澤) and Wáng Hé (王和) and seven or eight others, directly entered the prefectural office.
Rǔ Zuò was unprepared,
and was consequently killed by them.
At that time, the imperial envoy Shí Guī (石珪) was investigating the reasons for Luòyáng's fall and the death of Qiáng Shēn (強伸) as a loyal martyr.
Due to blocked roads,
he stayed at the Rǔzhōu post station.
After Liáng Gāo had killed Rǔ Zuò,
he rushed to tell Guī:
"Rǔ Zuò privately hoarded grain,
and did not care for the soldiers and people.
The populace, in their anger, killed him.
Gāo does not covet Rǔ Zuò's official position;
I only ask for the imperial envoy's judgment."
Guī was afraid,
and so appointed Gāo as acting Defense Commissioner of Rǔzhōu and acting Commander-in-Chief.
He then fled to Cài (蔡),
and reported Gāo's killing of Rǔ Zuò.
Āizōng lamented it greatly,
and sent his close attendant Zhāng Tiānxī (張天錫) to posthumously bestow Rǔ Zuò with the title of Military Commissioner of Chāngwǔjūn (昌武軍),
and grant his descendants hereditary leadership of a *móukè* (謀克).
He also issued an imperial edict ordering Hūyán Shí, Commander of Xiànshān (峴山), and Fàn Zhēn (范真), Commander of Dēngfēng (登封), to jointly attack Gāo.
Tiānxī (天錫) avoided Xiànshān, as it was far,
and first made an agreement with Fàn Zhēn.
Zhēn sent one of his subordinates, Lǐ Mǒu (李某),
under the pretense of pacifying the army and people.
Gāo led his soldiers to welcome him at the east gate.
Knowing that the imperial court intended to act against him,
he secretly made preparations.
Lǐ (李) hesitated and dared not strike.
Gāo lodged Tiānxī in Wàngsōnglóu (望崧樓),
and secretly poisoned his food.
Tiānxī subsequently died of poisoning.
Gāo was later killed by the Dà Yuán army.
Yáng Péng, courtesy name Fēiqīng (飛卿),
was skilled in poetry.
Ài Shēn (愛申) was known by his clan and personal name,
or some say his other name was Mánggē (忙哥).
He was originally a garrison soldier from Guóxiàn (虢縣),
and through accumulated merits, he rose to become the General Leader in the army.
Lǐ Wénxiù (李文秀) occupied Qínzhōu (秦州).
Xuānzōng (宣宗) ordered the Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) army to attack him.
The army besieged Qínzhōu city.
At that time, Ài Shēn was in the army,
and had committed a crime punishable by death.
Xuānzōng questioned the commander-in-chief,
and someone who knew his name reported that this man had the talent of a general and was loyal and reliable.
Xuānzōng ordered him to be pardoned immediately,
and appointed him Military Commissioner of Déshùn (德順) and acting Commander-in-Chief.
In the spring of Zhèngdà (正大) fourth year (1227),
a large army came from the west,
intending to make Déshùn its summer encampment.
Déshùn had no troops,
and people were very alarmed.
Ài Shēn knew Mǎ Jiānlóng Shùnqīng (馬肩龍舜卿) from Fèngxiáng to be capable of strategizing,
and sent a letter inviting him.
Jiānlóng received the letter and wished to go.
Hésùjiā Guójiàn (禾速嘉國鑑), the General Administrator of Fèngxiáng, said that since a large army was advancing,
their city could be relied upon,
but Déshùn certainly could not be defended,
and advised him not to go.
Jiānlóng said:
"Ài Shēn has never known me in his life,
yet at first sight, he considered me a bosom friend.
I know Déshùn cannot be defended,
and going means certain death.
However, for the sake of a bosom friend,
I cannot but die for him."
He then entrusted his belongings to his paternal cousin,
clearly saying his last farewells,
and went at great risk.
Upon arrival,
within a few days, they were besieged.
Inside the city, there were only eight or nine thousand militia and local troops.
The great army attacked with the might of the whole world.
Ài Shēn provisionally appointed Shùnqīng as Judge of the Fèngxiáng General Administrator's Office,
and shared all defense responsibilities with him.
They were attacked for 120 days and nights.
When their strength was exhausted, the city fell.
Ài Shēn committed suicide with his sword
at the age of 53.
The army offered rewards for Jiānlóng to be captured alive,
but his fate is unknown.
There were remonstrances from the censors that those who died defending Déshùn should be posthumously honored with official titles
to encourage those inside and outside the court.
An edict was issued to posthumously grant official titles to all,
and they were enshrined in the Temple of Commendable Loyalty (Bāozhōngmiào, 褒忠廟).
Mǎ Jiānlóng 馬肩龍, courtesy name Shùnqīng 舜卿,
was a native of Wǎnpíng 宛平.
His ancestors were a prominent family in Liáo 遼.
One held the position of Zhī Xīngzhōng Fǔ 知興中府,
hence people called them the Mǎ 馬 family of Xīngzhōng 興中.
His grandfather, Mǎ Dàzhōng 馬大中,
passed the imperial examination in the early Jīn 金 dynasty
and served as Jìdù 節度 of the two prefectures of Quán 全 and Jǐn 錦.
His father, Mǎ Chéngyì 馬成誼,
passed the imperial examination in the fifth year of Míngchāng 明昌 (1194),
and served as Pànguān 判官 of the Jīngzhàofǔ Lù Tǒngjūn Sī 京兆府路統軍司.
Mǎ Jiānlóng 馬肩龍 was known for his literary talent (fù 賦) in the Grand Academy (tàixué 太學).
At the beginning of Xuānzōng's 宣宗 reign,
someone falsely accused the imperial clansman Cóngtǎn 從坦 of murder,
and he was about to be sentenced to death.
No one dared to speak of his injustice,
but Mǎ Jiānlóng 馬肩龍 submitted a memorial,
which roughly stated:
"Cóngtǎn 從坦 possesses the talent of a general and commander;
few are his equal.
I, a mere scholar,
am useless in this world.
I wish to die in Cóngtǎn's 從坦's stead,
so he may be kept to lead the emperor's troops."
When the memorial was presented,
an imperial edict asked:
"Are you and Cóngtǎn 從坦 close friends?"
Mǎ Jiānlóng 馬肩龍 replied:
"I know of Cóngtǎn 從坦,
but Cóngtǎn 從坦 has never known me.
Cóngtǎn 從坦 is an innocent man whom no one dares to speak for;
I guarantee his innocence with my life."
Xuānzōng 宣宗 was moved and enlightened,
pardoned Cóngtǎn 從坦,
and appointed Mǎ Jiānlóng 馬肩龍 as Lùshì 錄事 of Dōngpíng 東平,
entrusting him with examinations for the Xíngshěng 行省.
The Chancellor Hóu Zhì 侯摯 found his conversation disagreeable,
so after a few months, he was dismissed and returned home.
When he was about to cross the river,
he had a dispute with a riverbank official.
His satchel was searched, and they found a list of military horses and provisions, as well as several sensitive documents.
They suspected him of being a spy
and imprisoned him in Guīdé 歸德 for investigation.
It happened that Cóngtǎn 從坦 arrived,
and immediately secured his release.
In the third year of Zhèngdà 正大 (1226),
he was a guest in Fèngxiáng 鳳翔.
Marshal Àishēn 愛申 deeply valued him.
At this point,
they died together in the disaster.
Yǔ Xiǎn 禹顯 was
a native of Yànmén 雁門.
In the early Zhēnyòu 貞祐 period,
he served under Gōng Zhāng Kāi 公張開 of Shàngdǎng 上黨.
Through repeated military achievements, he was appointed Jìdùshǐ 節度使 of the Yìshèngjūn 義勝軍 and concurrently Fùshǐ 招撫副使 of Qìnzhōu 沁州.
In the fourth month of the second year of Yuánguāng 元光 (1223),
the great commanders Dá'ěrshòu 達兒[⿰木受] and Ànchá'ér 按察兒 attacked Hédōng 河東.
Zhāng Kāi 張開 dispatched Yǔ Xiǎn 禹顯 to hold Lóngzhūgǔ 龍猪谷,
and they jointly attacked and defeated the enemy,
capturing Marshal Hán Guāngguó 韓光國
and seizing numerous supplies, armor, and weapons.
They pursued the enemy to Qíxiàn 祁縣 before returning,
and all the prefectures and counties they passed through were recaptured.
Yǔ Xiǎn 禹顯, with three hundred soldiers,
defended Xiāngyuán 襄垣
for eight years without promotion.
A great commander once gathered tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry from Héshuò 河朔 to attack him,
but after several attempts, they could not overcome him.
Later,
they fought at Yùnǚzhài 玉女寨,
achieving a great victory.
Zhāng Kāi 張開 reported this to the court,
and Yǔ Xiǎn 禹顯 was granted the temporary position of Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān 元帥右都監.
In the twelfth month of the winter of the sixth year of Zhèngdà 正大 (1229),
there was a mutiny within the army;
the city was broken, and he was captured.
The commander respected his righteousness
and did not wish to harm him.
Initially, he was bound with iron chains.
Later,
he secretly escaped with twenty of his former subordinates.
Hearing that the army of Gōng Zhāng Kāi 公張開 of Shàngdǎng 上黨 had regrouped,
he intended to join them.
A large army pursued them from all four directions.
Yǔ Xiǎn 禹顯 happened to be separated from a soldier carrying a cooking pot,
and he asked for food in a mountain temple.
A monk reported him,
and he was captured but refused to surrender and died,
at the age of forty-one.
Zhāng Bāngxiàn 張邦憲, courtesy name Zhèngshū 正叔, a native of Qínzhōu 秦州,
passed the Jìnshì 進士 examination during the Zhèngdà 正大 period
and served as the magistrate of Yǒnggù 永固.
In the second year of Tiānxīng 天興 (1233),
he sought refuge in Xúzhōu 徐州.
Zhuó Yì 卓翼 led troops to the city,
and Zhāng Bāngxiàn 張邦憲 was captured.
When they were about to drive him north,
Zhāng Bāngxiàn 張邦憲 cursed, saying:
"I am a Jìnshì 進士,
and by the grace of the court, I was made a county magistrate.
How can I rebel with you scoundrels?"
He was then killed.
Liú Quán 劉全
was a commoner from Péngchéng 彭城.
He led several hundred villagers to take refuge from the soldiers in Mògōu 沬溝
and was elected as the leader of the stockade.
When the northern army reached Xú 徐,
they captured all the old and young,
including Liú Quán's 劉全's father.
The northern army held his father hostage to lure Liú Quán 劉全.
Liú Quán 劉全 tied up the messenger and sent him to Xúzhōu 徐州,
then secretly rescued his father and returned.
The commander of Xú 徐, Yìdū 益都, praised his loyalty
and, acting on imperial authority, appointed him Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi 昭信校尉,
remotely leading the county constabulary of Péngchéng 彭城.
Later, he encountered Guó Yòng'ān 國用安,
who, angered by his refusal to join him,
had him killed.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 62: Loyal and Righteous (4) Mǎ Qìngxiáng 馬慶祥, Shāng Héng 商衡, Shú Jiǎtuōlúhuī 術甲脫魯灰, Yáng Dáfu 楊達夫, Féng Yándēng 馮延登, Wūgǔsūn Zhòngduān 烏古孫仲端, Wūgǔsūn Núshēn 烏古孫奴申, Púchá Qí 蒲察琦, Cài Bā'ér 蔡八兒, Wēndūn Chāngsūn 溫敦昌孫, Wányán Jiàngshān 完顏絳山, Bì Zīlún 畢資倫, Guō Xiāgě 郭蝦●
Mǎ Qìngxiáng 馬慶祥, courtesy name Ruìníng 瑞寧,
originally named Xílǐjísī 習禮吉思.
His ancestors moved from the Western Regions to reside in Línqín Dídào 臨洮狄道,
taking Mǎ 馬 as their surname.
Later, their family moved to Jìngzhōu Tiānshān 淨州天山.
During the Tàihé 泰和 period,
he was tested and appointed as Yìshǐ 譯史 in the Shàngshūshěng 尚書省.
In the early Dà'ān 大安 period,
when Prince Wèi 衞 first made contact with Dàyuán 大元,
envoys and deputies were selected.
The emperor said:
"Xílǐjísī 習禮吉思 is intelligent and eloquent, fluent in six languages.
His mission will surely be without disgrace."
Upon his return,
he was appointed Pànguān 判官 of Kāifēngfǔ 開封府.
During the battle of the Inner City, he served as Yìngbànshǐ 應辦使;
the task was completed without disturbance.
Soon after,
the Dàyuán 大元 army advanced from Shǎnyòu 陝右.
The court appointed Wányán Zhòngyuán 完顏仲元 as Marshal of Fèngxiáng 鳳翔,
and Mǎ Qìngxiáng 馬慶祥 was recommended as his deputy.
The emperor said:
"This is my intention,
and he has also contributed to city construction."
He was immediately appointed Pànguān 判官 of Fèngxiángfǔ Lù Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn 鳳翔府路兵馬都總管.
In the eleventh month of the winter of the first year of Yuánguāng 元光 (1222),
upon hearing that the great general Ménggǔbùhuā 萌古不花 was about to attack Fèngxiáng 鳳翔,
the Xíngshěng 行省 issued a dispatch ordering Mǎ Qìngxiáng 馬慶xiáng and Zhìzhōng Xū Qiān 治中胥謙 to clear the countryside along different routes.
Before departing,
he ordered a painter to make a portrait of him
and gave it to his family.
Someone said:
"You are in your prime; why do something so inauspicious?"
Mǎ Qìngxiáng 馬慶xiáng said:
"You do not understand."
The next day, he departed.
He encountered the vanguard at Kuàishuǐ 澮水,
and the battle went unfavorably.
As they continued to advance and fight,
they were about to reach the city
when the main enemy force cut off their retreat.
Realizing he could not escape,
he ordered his cavalry, saying:
"We have received great kindness from the state;
it is our duty to exert our utmost strength and die for it."
All the cavalry responded:
"Yes."
Everyone fought desperately.
After a long time, their arrows were exhausted.
The great army surrounded them in several layers,
intending to force their surrender.
They were pushed forward by the soldiers,
exchanging words back and forth,
but he ultimately refused to yield and died,
at the age of forty-six.
Marshal Guō Zhòngyuán 郭仲元 carried his body back
and buried it east of Pǔmén Sì 普門寺 in Fèngxiáng 鳳翔.
When the matter was reported,
an imperial edict posthumously awarded him the title of Fǔguó Shàngjiàngjūn 輔國上將軍 and Zhōucìshǐ 州刺史,
with the posthumous name Zhōngmǐn 忠愍.
Xū Qiān 胥謙 and his son Xū Sìhēng 胥嗣亨 also died without yielding.
Xū Qiān 胥謙 was posthumously awarded Fǔguó Shàngjiàngjūn 輔國上將軍 and Zhānghuàjūn Jìdùshǐ 彰化軍節度使.
Xū Sìhēng 胥嗣亨 was posthumously awarded Wēiyuǎn Jiàngjūn 威遠將軍 and Fèngxiángfǔ Pànguān 鳳翔府判官.
Púsǎn Húshā 仆散胡沙, Tíkòng 提控 of Jīnshèngbǎo 金勝堡 in Zhēnjiāozhōu 楨州, also died
and was posthumously awarded Yínqīng Rónglù Dàfū 銀青榮祿大夫.
In the second year of Zhèngdà 正大 (1225),
Emperor Āizōng 哀宗 issued an edict to commend those who died faithfully,
such as Mǎ Xílǐjísī 馬習禮吉思, Wáng Qīng 王清, Tián Róng 田榮, Lǐ Guì 李貴, Wáng Bīn 王斌, Féng Wànnú 馮萬奴, Zhāng Déwēi 張德威, Gāo Xíngzhōng 高行中, Chéng Jì 程濟, Jī Jǐ 姬玘, Zhāng Shān 張山, and ten others.
A temple for praising loyalty was erected for them,
and their orphans were also recorded.
The names of two persons were omitted,
and no further information could be found for the others.
Shāng Héng 商衡, courtesy name Píngshū 平叔,
was a native of Cáozhōu 曹州.
In the first year of Zhìníng 至寧 (1213),
he was specially appointed as the foremost candidate,
and was given the position of chief clerk (zhǔbù 主簿) of Luòjiāo 洛郊, Fūzhōu 鄜州.
On account of his honesty and ability, he was transferred to Méixiàn 郿縣,
and soon thereafter appointed as Magistrate (lìng 令) of Wēiróng 威戎.
In the third year of Xīngdìng 興定 (1219),
there was a famine.
The people had no means to buy grain.
Shāng Héng 商衡 reported to the Xíngshěng 行省 (Provincial Administration),
and obtained permission to open granaries for relief loans.
A great many people were saved.
Later, due to an earthquake, the city walls collapsed.
The Xià 夏 people took advantage of the situation to invade.
Shāng Héng 商衡 led the Fānbù 蕃部 (tribal people) and local gentry in defense against the enemy,
and ensured safety.
When his term of office expired,
the people of the county erected a shrine for him while he was still alive.
He was again appointed Magistrate of Yuánwǔ 原武.
Not long after,
he entered the capital to serve as a clerk (lìshǐ 令史) in the Shàngshūshěng 尚書省 (Department of State Affairs),
then transferred to the position of director (zhǔshì 主事) in the Hùbù 戶部 (Ministry of Revenue).
Two months later, he was appointed Censor (jiānchá yùshǐ 監察御史).
Āizōng’s 哀宗 aunt, the Lady of Chéngguó 郕國 fūrén 夫人, frequently entered and exited the imperial palace,
interfering in government affairs.
Her reputation was very bad.
Shāng Héng 商衡 submitted a memorial speaking strongly against her.
From then on, the Lady of Chéngguó 郕國 only dared to enter and be seen when summoned.
The imperial kinsman Qìngshānnú 慶山奴 led troops to guard Xūyí 盱眙,
but was defeated in battle against Lǐ Quán 李全.
The court ignored the matter.
Shāng Héng 商衡 memorialized:
“From ancient times, generals who lost battles were always punished according to the law;
otherwise, there would be no way to account to the world.”
An imperial edict demoted Qìngshānnú 慶山奴 to Regional Commander (jiédùshǐ 節度使) of Dìngguójūn 定國軍.
The daughter of Cáo Wēn 曹溫, the Vice Minister (shìláng 侍郎) of the Ministry of Revenue who was concurrently acting as Minister (shàngshū 尚書), was in the Yèting 掖庭 (imperial concubines' quarters).
Her relatives and old acquaintances interfered with power,
and her family members filled various offices.
Their corruption was blatant.
No court official dared to speak,
but Shāng Héng 商衡 enumerated her crimes.
An imperial edict dismissed Cáo Wēn 曹溫 from the Ministry of Revenue,
and transferred him to the position of Commandant of the Imperial Guards (wèiwèi 衞尉) for the Empress Dowager’s residence.
Shāng Héng 商衡 again memorialized:
“If Cáo Wēn 曹溫 is truly guilty, he should be demoted and expelled.
If he is innocent, then I have spoken falsely.
How can there be a situation where right and wrong are not distinguished, and both options are acceptable?”
Āizōng 哀宗 was moved by this,
and then sent Cáo Wēn 曹溫 out as Defense Commissioner (fángyùshǐ 防禦使) of Rǔzhōu 汝州.
Not long after,
he became an administrator (dūshì 都事) in the Yòusī 右司,
and was transferred to be Concurrent Commissioner (tóngzhī 同知) of Hépíngjūn 河平軍 Regional Command.
Before he could take up the post,
he was transferred to be an experienced official (jīnglì guān 經歷官) in the Pólímìyuàn 樞密院 (Bureau of Military Affairs),
remotely holding the position of Concurrent Commissioner of Chāngwǔjūn 昌武軍 Regional Command.
The Chancellor, Wányán Sàibù 完顏賽不, led the Shǎnxī Xíngshěng 陝西行省,
and memorialized that Shāng Héng 商衡 should be appointed as a supernumerary official (yuánwàiláng 員外郎) in the Zuǒyòusī 左右司.
The Pólímìyuàn 樞密院 memorialized to retain him.
There was an imperial decree:
“The Xíngshěng 行省 is an important region,
and urgently needs capable people.
The Chancellor’s request can be granted.”
The following year,
he was recalled,
but the Xíngshěng 行省 again memorialized to retain him.
In the eighth year of Zhèngdà 正大 (1231),
he returned to the capital due to his mother’s mourning.
In October,
he was reinstated as an experienced official in the Qínlán Zǒngshuàifǔ 秦藍總帥府 (General Command of Qín and Lán).
In the second month of the first year of Tiānxīng 天興 (1232),
Tuódān Wùdiǎn 徒單兀典 and others from the Guānshǎnxíngshěng 關陝行省 were defeated at Tiělǐng 鐵嶺.
Shāng Héng 商衡, not knowing whether the various commanders were alive or dead,
gathered the scattered troops to await their arrival.
He was then captured by enemy soldiers.
They wanted him to surrender,
but he refused to yield.
He was brought to the front of the Dōngyuè 東岳 Temple in Chángshuǐxiàn 長水縣.
They tried to induce him to summon Luòyáng 洛陽.
Shāng Héng 商衡 said:
“Who do I know in Luòyáng 洛陽 that I can summon for you?”
The soldiers knew he could not be persuaded.
They wanted to tear off his headscarf.
Shāng Héng 商衡 glared and shouted:
“Are you trying to coerce me?”
He ultimately refused to surrender,
looked towards the palace and bowed, saying:
“The commander-in-chief was incompetent,
and the army was defeated and lost.
My responsibility for this crime is inescapable.
I shall only repay the country with my death.”
He then drew his dagger and slit his own throat.
He was forty-six years old.
In the early years of Zhèngdà 正大,
Xǔ Gǔ 許古 of Héjiān 河間 went to the palace and presented a memorial,
stating:
“The eight high officials are mostly not of suitable talent.
Among the lesser officials of the departments and ministries, there are those capable of serving as chancellor.
Unless there are major promotions and demotions, there will be no way to achieve a middle revival.”
After the memorial was presented,
an imperial edict summoned Xǔ Gǔ 許古 to the imperial council
and asked who was suitable for chancellor.
Xǔ Gǔ 許古 replied with Shāng Héng 商衡.
Thus, Shāng Héng’s 商衡 talent can be known.
Shùjiǎ Tuōlǔhuī 術甲脫魯灰,
a native of Shàngjīng 上京,
whose family had for generations served as chiefs (bùzhǎng 部長) of the Běijīnglù 北京路.
His ancestors had rendered founding merits,
and were granted the command of Sòng Ādá’ā Měng’ān 宋阿荅阿猛安 in Běijīnglù 北京路.
Tuōlǔhuī 脫魯灰 inherited the title from childhood.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu 貞祐 (1214),
when Xuānzōng 宣宗 moved the capital to Biàn 汴,
he led his tribal troops to Zhōngdū 中都 to escort the emperor.
The emperor was pleased,
and specially appointed him as Commander-in-Chief (dūzǒnglǐng 都總領) of the Imperial Cavalry and Infantry.
When the Sòng 宋 people encroached upon the southern border,
he was ordered, along with Shí Quán 時全, who was concurrently in charge of the Pólímìyuàn 樞密院 (Bureau of Military Affairs), to lead a large army on a southern expedition.
Tuōlǔhuī 脫魯灰 led his troops, repeatedly defeating Sòng 宋 forces and capturing their cities and fortresses.
For his merits, he was remotely appointed Regional Commander of Chāngwǔjūn 昌武軍,
Right Supervising General (yuánshuài yòudūjiān 元帥右都監), and acting official (xíngshì 府事) of the Marshal’s Residence (yuánshuàifǔ 元帥府) for Cài 蔡, Xī 息 and other routes.
Soon after,
some Sòng 宋 people crossed the border with their livestock.
The patrolmen captured them.
By law, they should have been sent in shackles to the imperial court.
Tuōlǔhuī 脫魯灰 said:
“Since the state moved its capital,
its territory has shrunk daily,
and the people’s strength has been depleted.
Fortunately, with peace on the border, people can rest somewhat.
If these people are executed, border hostilities will resume,
leading to continuous warfare and disaster.
It is better to release them,
to end the conflict.”
When Āizōng 哀宗 ascended the throne,

he appointed Tuōlǔhuī 脫魯huī as Regional Commander of Zhènnánjūn 鎮南軍, Inspector (guǎnnèi guānchásǐ 管內觀察使) of Càizhōu 蔡州, and acting Minister (xíng shàngshū 行尚書) of the Ministries of Revenue (hùbù 戶部) and Works (gōngbù 工部).
At that time, the Dàyuán 大元 army entered Shǎnxī 陝西.
He then memorialized:
“The Sòng 宋 people are our enemies.
Recently, they have been preserving themselves out of weakness,
which is not their true intention.
Now Shǎnxī 陝西 is under attack,
and Hénán 河南 has dispatched troops.
Battles have raged continuously for years.
Soldiers die on the battlefield,
the people are exhausted by service,
and the national strength is depleted.
The area around Shòu 壽 and Sì 泗 borders Xū 盱 and Chǔ 楚 to the south,
which is the lair of the Red Turban bandit Lǐ Quán 李全.
If by any chance the Sòng 宋 people get intelligence
and, together with Lǐ Quán 李全, exploit the emptiness to invade,
we will be attacked from both front and rear.
This would not be a wise plan.
Your servant has already ordered his subordinates to patrol the border,
to be prepared for any eventuality.
It is advisable to instruct the commanders of Shòu 壽 and Sì 泗 to carefully maintain scouts,
strictly manage beacon fires,
and always be as if the enemy is at hand.
This is what the art of war calls, ‘Do not rely on the enemy not coming,
but rely on our readiness to meet them.’
This is the way.”
The emperor agreed and acted on it.
In the autumn of the second year of Zhèngdà 正大 (1225),
rumors spread that the Sòng 宋 people were about to invade.
The agricultural official ordered the people to harvest their crops early.
Tuōlǔhuī 脫魯灰 said:
“What the people rely on to support their families and pay taxes to the state
is the autumn harvest.
Now, if there is no harvest in autumn,
how will the state be supported,
and how will the people be provided for?”
So, he dispatched troops to patrol,
allowing the people to wait until their crops were ripe before harvesting.
The Sòng 宋 people ultimately did not invade.
Spies again reported that Grand Commandant (tàiwèi 太尉) Wāng 汪 of Guāngzhōu 光州 would dispatch troops in August to take Zhènyáng 真陽.
Advisors requested to register able-bodied men for preparation.
Tuōlǔhuī 脫魯灰 said:
“Grand Commandant Wāng 汪 is a timid person.
How would he dare to do this?
It must be wicked people spreading rumors of invasion,
wanting our people to abandon their work.
It cannot be believed.”
And so it turned out.
The rebel Jiāo Fēngzǐ 焦風子,
who had repeatedly caused trouble across Hénán 河南,
was granted the position of Commander (tíkòng 提控) by the imperial court,
and ordered to lead three thousand men to garrison Suípíng 遂平.
In the spring of the fourth year (1227),
Jiāo Fēngzǐ 焦風子 plotted to lead his troops into Sòng 宋 territory.
Tuōlǔhuī 脫魯灰 devised a plan,
and ambushed the Pōyángdào 鄱陽道 with several thousand soldiers.
The bandits indeed came out by this route at night.
The ambush was sprung, and they were annihilated.
In the seventh year,
the army of the Dà Yuán attacked Lán'guān.
They retreated upon reaching Bādùcāng.
The entire court celebrated,
believing there was no further danger.
Tuōlǔhuī alone said:
"Tóng'guān is a perilous pass,
and our elite troops are sufficient.
However, the region south of Shāng and Luò borders the Sòng territory,
with layered mountains.
The Sòng people do not know how to defend it,
nor can our state cross into Sòng territory to garrison it.
If the main army were to enter Xīngyuán via Sǎn'guān,
descend into Jīn and Fáng,
then bypass and emerge in Xiāng and Hàn,
and proceed north into Dèngbǐ,
then the great undertaking would be lost.
It would be advisable to reconcile with the Sòng people,
and explain to them the principle of the 'cart and axle' (interdependence),
and 'lips gone, teeth cold' (mutual destruction).
They will surely agree.
Based on their strategic strongholds, we should prepare.
Otherwise, we are doomed to fail."
That autumn,
he was reassigned as Xiǎoguānzǐ Yuánshuài,
stationed at Dàjíkǒu in Shāngzhōu.
In the spring of the ninth year,
following Xíngshěng Cānzhèng Túdān Wúdiǎn, he led the Tóng'guān troops to provide aid.
They encountered snow at Shāngshān,
and the main army ambushed them.
The soldiers, starving and freezing, were unable to fight and routed.
Tuōlǔhuī was captured but refused to submit,
drawing his scabbard knife and committing suicide.
Yáng Dáfū, whose courtesy name was Jìnqīng,
was a native of Sānyuán in Yàozhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the third year of Tàihé.
He was talented and capable,
and his achievements in every post were noteworthy.
He was summoned to serve as a provincial clerk,
drafting memorials.
Because of a mistaken character,
he was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Píngliáng Fǔ.
He once served as the County Clerk of Hùxiàn,
where he simplified all matters,
and the officials and common people rejoiced.
Dáfū also loved the beauty of its mountains and rivers,
and therefore made it his home.
He spent his days amusing himself with poetry and wine,
without any desire for an official career.
Coincidentally, an imperial edict ordered the people to move east into the pass.
Dáfū traveled with the populace,
and upon reaching Sháo,
he sought refuge from the soldiers at Hénglǐng, north of the prefecture.
He was captured by cavalry scouts,
who intended to strip him of his clothes and harm him.
Dáfū stood upright and firm at the horse's head,
showing no fear whatsoever.
When they began to insult him slightly,
he loudly declared:
"I am a subject of the Jīn state.
Since I have been captured by you,
it is nothing more than death.
How can I endure being naked and exposed, defiling the heavens and the sun?"
He was then killed.
The people hidden in the two mountains, who secretly observed this,
all said to each other:
"Such a good official as this,
if we sacrifice to him in the future,
he shall be the god of our Hénglǐng."
Féng Yándēng, whose courtesy name was Zǐjùn,
was a native of Jíxiāng in Jízhōu.
His family had been physicians for generations.
Yándēng was intelligent and perceptive from a young age.
When he grew up, he pursued a career through examinations.
In the second year of Chéng'ān, he passed the imperial examination in lyrical essays.
He was appointed Clerk of Línzhēn and Military Judicial Officer of Déshùn Zhōu.
In the first year of Tàihé,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Níngbiān.
In the seventh month of autumn, the first year of Dà'ān,
frost damaged the crops,
and the people faced hardship in obtaining food.
Yándēng distributed grain for relief loans,
saving many lives.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was appointed Clerk in the Shàngshū Shěng,
and soon after was granted Assistant Magistrate of Hézhōng Fǔ, concurrently serving as Yuánwàiláng in the Left and Right Departments of the Xíng Shàngshū Shěng.
In the fifth year of Xīngdìng,
he entered the court as a Biênxiūguān in the Guóshǐ Yuàn,
and was subsequently appointed Tàicháng Bóshì.
In the second year of Yuánguāng,
he was made Director of the Dēngwéngǔ Yuàn,
concurrently Hànlín Xiūzhuàn.
He was dispatched as an envoy to the Xià state,
and also served as the accompanying envoy for reception and departure.
In the twelfth month of the seventh year of Zhèngdà,
he was promoted to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
He was temporarily appointed Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ,
and served as Guóxìn Shǐ.
In the spring of the eighth year, he presented the state letter and had an audience at the imperial camp in Guóxiàn.
An imperial decree asked:
"Do you know the commander of Fèngxiáng?"
He replied:
"I know him."
Again, it was asked:
"What kind of person is he?"
He said:
"He is diligent in affairs."
Again, it was asked:
"If you can persuade him to surrender, your death will be spared.
Otherwise, you will be killed."
He replied:
"I am an envoy sent to request peace.
How can persuading surrender be an envoy's duty?
Whether I persuade surrender or not, I will die.
Whether I return to court or not, I will die.
It is better to die today."
The next day,
he was asked again:
"Have you thought about it?"
He replied as before.
He was asked repeatedly,
but he held firm to his righteousness without wavering.
The day after that,
an imperial decree was conveyed, saying:
"Your crime deserves death,
but it is ancient custom not to kill envoys.
You love your beard and mustache as much as you love your life."
He was ordered to have his attendants cut them off with a knife.
Yándēng stood tall and unwavering,
and was then imprisoned in Fēngzhōu.
Two years later, he was released and returned.
Empress Ài consoled him for a long time,
and reinstated him as Jìjiǔ.
He successively served as Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Rites and the Ministry of Personnel,
and temporarily as Minister of the Ministry of Punishments.
The following year,
the Dà Yuán army besieged Biànjīng.
In haste, he fled,
but was captured by cavalry.
They intended to take him north.
Yándēng's words were spirited and generous;
he righteously refused to suffer humiliation.
He then leaped into a well by the city wall,
at the age of fifty-eight.
Wūgǔsūn Zhòngduān, whose original name was Bǔjí,
and courtesy name Zǐzhèng.
He passed the imperial examination in policy essays in the second year of Chéng'ān.
During Xuānzōng's reign,
he successively held the position of Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
He, along with Hànlín Dàizhì Ān Yánzhēn, was dispatched as an envoy to request peace from the Dà Yuán,
and met with the Grand Tutor, King Mùhuálí.
At this point, Ān Yánzhēn remained,
while Zhòngduān continued alone.
He passed through Dàxià,
crossed the shifting sands,
and traversed the mountains,
reaching the Western Regions.
He had an audience with Emperor Tàizǔ,
and fulfilled his mission before returning.
He set off in the seventh month of the fourth year of Xīngdìng,
and returned in the twelfth month of the following year.
The imperial court commended him for his arduous service as an envoy,
promoting him by two ranks,
while Yánzhēn was promoted by one rank.
He successively served as Governor of Yùzhōu.
In the first year of Zhèngdà,
he was summoned to be Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and was commanded to pacify Shǎnxī.
Upon his return,
he was temporarily appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
In the twelfth month of the fifth year of Zhèngdà,
Wányán Máqīnchū, Director of Kāifēng Fǔ, and Yáng Jūrén, Lìbù Lángzhōng, were deemed to have failed in their duties as envoys.
The Shàngshū Shěng prepared their case.
An imperial decree released them to be prepared for a second mission.
Zhòngduān stated:
"Máqīnchū and others disgraced the imperial command,
failed in their duty as subjects,
and showed great disrespect.
They should compensate with ceremonial gifts and be executed."
After the memorial was submitted,
Máqīnchū and others were spared death but dismissed from their positions.
During a discussion regarding capitulating to the great army,
and his remonstrance against the Empress Dowager's devotion to Buddhism,
he spoke of 'family ruin and national collapse'.
The Emperor was enraged,
and he was demoted to Military Commissioner of Tóngzhōu.
When Āi Zōng was about to move to Guīdé,
he was summoned to be a hànlín xuéshì chéngzhǐ,
concurrently serving as a tóng qiān dàmùqīnfǔ shì,
and left to guard Biànjīng.
When the Great Yuán army besieged Biàn,
after a long time, food ran out.
The generals were not united.
Zhòngduān himself judged that the situation in Biàn might change unpredictably.
One day, he had a small drink with Péimǎn Sīzhōng, the rúzhōu fángyù, who was of the same age.
They talked about their classmates in the Imperial Academy, taking pleasure in the memories.
He then repeatedly said,
"Dying is an easy matter for a person."
Sīzhōng said,
"Why does my elder brother frequently utter such words?"
Zhòngduān then wrote a poem and showed it to him.
The general idea of the poem was that human life is very much like that of nesting swallows:
some are in magnificent houses with apricot beams,
some are in village dwellings with thatched roofs;
but when the autumn ancestral festival arrives,
all must depart.
Although human life has differences in wealth, nobility, poverty, and lowliness,
ultimately, there is only death.
After finishing writing,
he drank several cups continuously,
then saw Sīzhōng out the door,
saying,
"This will be our final parting."
After Sīzhōng left,
Zhòngduān immediately hanged himself,
and his wife also followed him in death.
The next day,
Cuī Lì rebelled.
Zhòngduān was easygoing, generous, and understood the greater good.
He was diligent in public service and fond of goodness,
uniquely earning the praise of scholars.
He had one son named Àishí,
who once served as a hùwèi and fèngyù.
For his功 in executing government slaves, he was awarded the jiedu and the hereditary position of qiānhù.
Sīzhōng's given name was Zhèngzhī,
originally called Púlàdù.
He was also a jìnshì in Chéng'ān second year.
Wūgǔsūn Núshēn,
courtesy name Dàoyuǎn.
He entered officialdom from being a yishǐ.
He was proud and independent, daring to act with integrity and straightforwardness.
He once served as a jiānchá yùshǐ.
At that time, zhōngchéng Wányán Bǎijiā was known for his harshness.
