Núshēn impeached and removed him for an incident,
which startled the court officials.
Later, he served as zuǒsī lángzhōng and jìnshìjú shǐ,
all with good repute.
When Āi Zōng moved east,
he became a jiànyì dàfū, jìnshìjú shǐ, xíngshěng zuǒyòusī lángzhōng, and concurrently zhī gōngshěng shì,
remaining in Biànjīng to guard it.
The day after Cuī Lì rebelled,
he hanged himself in the yáitái with yùshǐ dàfū Péimǎn Āhǔdài.
On that day,
hùbù shàngshū Wányán Zhūkē also hanged himself.
Āhǔdài's courtesy name was Zhòngníng,
Zhūkē's courtesy name was Zhòngpíng,
both were Nǚzhēn jìnshì.
Those who died without being disgraced at that time were
fèngyù Wányán Mánggē, dàmùqīnfǔ shì Wūgǔsūn Zhòngduān,
dàlǐ Péimǎn Déhuī, yòufù diǎnjiǎn Wányán Āsā, cānzhèng Wányán Núshēn's son Máyīn.
These are the few known individuals,
others have their own biographies.
Púchá Qí, originally named Ālián,
courtesy name Rénqīng,
was from Yángxìn, Dìzhōu.
He was tested and appointed as a xíngbù yuàn.
His elder brother inherited the title of móukè.
When his brother died,
Qí inherited it.
In the sixth year of Zhèngdà,
the Qín-Lán Zǒngshuàifǔ appointed Qí as ānpíng dūwèi xiángē hédiǎn's subordinate dūtǒng and concurrently zhìshì.
That winter,
Xiǎoguān fell,
and the situation was already urgent.
Qí was often by Hédiǎn's side.
Hédiǎn ordered him to avoid arrows and stones,
but Qí refused to leave,
saying,
"Since I have committed to serving the public,
we should share life and death.
Where else could I avoid them?"
When Āi Zōng moved to Guīdé,
a Jiǎngyì Suǒ was established in Biànjīng
to receive proposals and documents.
Its officials included yùshǐ dàfū Nāhé Níng and seventeen others,
all chosen court ministers,
and Qí was among them for his eloquent discussions.
At that time, zuǒsī dūshì Yuán Hàowèn led the jiǎngyì
and concurrently read the proposals and documents,
getting along very well with Qí.
After Cuī Lì rebelled,
an order was given to change headwear.
Qí said to Hàowèn,
"Today's change of headwear
is acceptable for everyone in the capital,
but not for Qí alone.
Qí is but a xíngbù yìshǐ,
inheriting my elder brother's hereditary title.
How can I bear to do this?
Now I entrust my death to you,
but if I am to die, I will die immediately;
even entrusting a word to you is superfluous."
He then wept and bade farewell.
When Qí arrived home,
his mother was taking a daytime nap
and woke up in surprise.
Qí asked his mother what was wrong.
His mother said,
"I just dreamed of three people lurking among the beams,
which startled me awake."
Rénqīng knelt and said,
"The people on the beam
are ghosts.
Your son intends to hang himself from the beam,
Mother, you merely had a premonition in your dream."
His family members cried and pleaded,
"Do you not think of your old mother?"
His mother stopped them, saying,
"Do not dissuade him.
What my son is doing is right."
He then hanged himself,
at the age of over forty.
Qí was quiet and fond of reading,
knowledgeable about ancient and modern affairs.
His mother, of the Wányán clan,
was known for her filial piety and caution.
Cài Bā'ér,
his origin is unknown.
He was agile and brave,
with a pure and trustworthy nature.
He served as the zhōngxiàojūn yuánshuài at that time.
In the second year of Tiānxīng,
he came from Xīzhōu to assist.
General Bēnzǎn sent several hundred cavalry to be stationed east of the city,
ordering someone to shout loudly,
"Those in the city, surrender quickly,
and you will be spared slaughter.
Otherwise, none shall survive."
Thereupon,
the Emperor ascended the city wall and sent Bā'ér to lead over a hundred elite archers to secretly exit through a hidden gate,
cross the Rǔ River,
and shoot at them from both sides.
From then on, the enemy troops no longer pressed against the city,
but built long ramparts for a prolonged siege.
The Emperor ordered the army to be divided to defend the four gates,
with diànqián dūdiǎnjiǎn Wùlíndá Hútǔ guarding the west side,
and Bā'ér as his deputy.
Afterwards,
Āi Zōng judged that Cài City could not be held,
and abdicated to Chénglín.
The officials entered to congratulate him,
and when the ranks were settled,
Bā'ér did not bow.
He said to his confidants,
"Things have come to this;
there is only death.
How can I serve another ruler?"
He then died in battle.
Máo Quán
was from Ēnzhōu.
During the Zhēnyòu era, he was a bandit.
When Xuān Zōng moved south,
he led his followers to surrender to the nation
and was appointed as a yìjūn zhāofǔ.
When Āi Zōng moved to Cài,
he made Quán a dūwèi.
In the siege battles,
Quán contributed greatly.
When the city fell, he hanged himself.
His son had died in battle before him.
Those who died for the cause at that time included Yán Zhōng, Hǎo Yǐ, Wáng Ālǘ, and Fán Qiáo.
Zhōng
was from Huázhōu.
During the reign of Wèi Wáng,
Kāizhōu cìshǐ Sàigē rebelled.
Zhōng rode alone into the city,
captured Sàigē, and brought him out.
From then on, he was gradually promoted.
Yǐ
was from Cízhōu;
he died in battle on the same day.
Āi Zōng posthumously bestowed official titles upon him.
Ā-Lǘ and Fán Qíao were both from Hézhōng.
Initially, they served as ten thousand-households of the artillery army.
When Fèngxiáng fell,
they surrendered to the north [of the Jīn dynasty].
They followed the army to attack Biàn,
serving as artillery officers as before.
They then deceived their superiors, saying:
"Artillery is effective at short range,
but not at long range."
Believing them,
their superiors ordered them to shorten the wooden components by several feet and the ropes by more than ten grips.
As a result, although the machines were still operated,
their shots had no power.
On that very day,
the two men abandoned their families and fled into the city.
At this time,
there were no Nǚzhí people among those who died for the cause.
The eldest princess spoke to Āizōng, saying:
"Lately, many people of various ethnicities have been performing meritorious service and sacrificing their lives.
When there is no trouble, our own people vie for power,
but when there is trouble, others exert themselves fully.
How can they not resent this?"
The emperor remained silent.
The others each have their own biographies.
Wēndūn Chāngsūn was
the nephew of the Empress Dowager and
the son of the Grand Minister of the Guards, Qīshíwǔ.
He was short and stout, but energetic and resolute,
and his nature was generous and kind.
He was successively promoted to various departmental official positions.
When the emperor went to Cài,
he was appointed Assistant Commander of the Imperial Guard in front of the Palace.
During the siege of the city,
he frequently led troops out on secret patrols.
At that time, fish was required for imperial meals,
and the fish from the Rǔ Hé were very delicious.
However, the emperor disliked them
because of the many floating corpses in the river.
To the west of the city was an accumulated body of water called Liàn Jiāng,
where fish were large and plentiful.
To catch them, military guards were necessary.
Chāngsūn often personally led troops there.
They would catch over a thousand catties,
which he distributed to the generals and soldiers.
Later, [the enemy] learned of his sorties.
They set up an ambush on both sides,
waiting to intercept him.
He fought bravely and died.
When Cài City fell,
the former Supervising Censor Nàtán Húshīdá heard of it
and wept bitterly,
then threw himself into the water and died.
Wányán Jiàngshān was
Āizōng's Palace Attendant,
descended from the founding ancestor.
In the tenth month of Tiānxīng ēn 2
Cài City was besieged.
Over ten thousand starving people in the city appealed to the authorities to be allowed to leave.
The authorities found it difficult.
The people cried out loudly in the streets.
Hearing this,
the emperor dispatched close attendants to supervise the four gates,
allowing a thousand people to leave each day from each gate.
Only the elderly, children, weak, and sick were permitted to leave.
Jiàngshān was at the north gate at the time.
Pitying the hungry people,
he allowed more than the allotted number to leave.
He was ordered to be flogged forty times.
However, many of those who left revealed the city's weaknesses,
so the exits were soon stopped.
On the *jǐyǒu* day of the first month of [Tiānxīng] ēn 3
Cài City fell.
Āizōng abdicated in favor of Chénglín,
then hanged himself in Yōulán Xuān.

The acting Grand Commander of the Imperial Guard Nèizú Xiéliè, by falsely issuing an imperial decree, summoned Palace Attendant Shízhǎn Shì, Chief of the Bureau of Imperial Attendants Jiāo Chūnhé, and Palace Head of the Bureau of Inner Palace Servants Sòng Guī to appear before the emperor.
He explained to them the great principle of their proper roles.
The attendant officials Bāliángbì and Ālègēn Wénqīng also died with him.
As Xiéliè was about to die,
he left instructions for Jiàngshān,
telling him to burn Yōulán Xuān.
While the fire was still raging,
the inner city fell,
and the great army stormed in.
All the close attendants and those nearby fled,
but Jiàngshān alone remained and did not leave.
He was seized by soldiers,
who asked:
"Who are you?"
Jiàngshān replied:
"I am the Palace Attendant Jiàngshān."
The soldiers said:
"Everyone else has scattered and fled,
so why are you alone remaining behind?"
He said:
"My lord met his end here.
I am waiting for the fire to die down and the ashes to cool
to collect and bury his bones."
The soldiers laughed, saying:
"Are you insane?
You cannot even save your own life,
how can you bury your lord?"
Jiàngshān said:
"Each person serves their own lord.
My lord ruled the realm for over ten years;
his achievements and enterprises were not completed,
and he died for the nation.
How could I bear to let his remains be exposed like those of ordinary soldiers?
I knew beforehand that you would not spare me.
That is why I stayed.
If I can indeed bury my lord,
even if I am cut into a thousand pieces, I will have no regrets."
The soldiers reported this to their commander.
Bēnnzhǎn said:
"This is an extraordinary man!"
And he granted his request.
Jiàngshān then gathered the remaining embers,
wrapped them in a worn blanket,
and buried them beside the Rǔ Shuǐ.
He bowed twice and cried out loudly,
then prepared to throw himself into the Rǔ Shuǐ to die.
The soldiers rescued him, and he was spared.
His ultimate fate is unknown.
Bì Zīlún was
a man from Jìnshān.
During the southern campaign of Tàihé,
he joined the army as a mercenary.
When the army returned,
he was routinely appointed Vice Commander of the Advancing Righteousness.
In the first year of Chóngqìng
Jìnshān was renamed Zhènzhōu.
Shùhǔ Gāoqí was appointed Defense Commissioner and acting Marshal of that prefecture.
Zīlún was selected as a thousand-household of the city defense army.
In the autumn of Zhìníng ēn 1
the Dà Yuán army arrived at Zhènzhōu.
Gāoqí abandoned the city and fled.
Zīlún reached Chāngpíng,
gathered the civilian militia who had evacuated,
and gained merit through successive battles.
He was promoted to Commander-in-Chief.
His army numbered several thousands.
Along with the army commanders Shěn Sīzhōng and Zǐdū and others, he was subordinate to a single administration,
stationed in Zhèngzhōu and Wèizhōu.
At that time, they were known as
"the Shěn-Bì army."
Through accumulated merit, he rose to be Grand Commander.
Sīzhōng was his Vice Commander.
Púshàn Āhǎi embarked on a southern campaign.
His army was stopped at Méilín Guān and could not pass.
Āhǎi asked his generals who could capture this pass.
Zīlún was the first to step forward and accept the command.
When asked how many soldiers he needed,
he replied:
"Only the troops under Zīlún's command are sufficient;
no other troops are needed."
The next day, at dawn,
he caught the Sòng army by surprise,
led his troops to attack them,
and the entire host collapsed.
Thus, he captured Méilín Guān.
Āhǎi's army was able to proceed south.
He left the Commander Wáng Lù with ten thousand troops to guard the pass.
Within a few days,
the Sòng army recaptured and held the pass.
With Méilín, his return route, occupied by the enemy,
Āhǎi had no strategy.
He again asked:
"Who can recapture Méilín?
He will be rewarded with the rank of commander-in-chief."
Zīlún again stepped forward and accepted the command,
recapturing Méilín with his own troops.
Āhǎi then defeated Qí and Huáng.
When he returned with his army,
Zīlún was ranked first for his meritorious service.
He was appointed titular Military Governor of Chāngwǔ Circuit and Commissioner-General of All Commanders.
Soon after,
the Shūmìyuàn, deeming Zīlún and Sīzhōng to be incompatible,
feared they would spoil matters.
Therefore, they ordered Zīlún to command his original army and garrison Sīzhōu.
In the first month, on the day Wùxū, of the fifth year of Xīngdìng (1221),
during a Tangbǐng banquet and feast held by Commander Tíkòng Wáng Lù among the troops,
Sòng Guīshān's commander Shí Qīng seized the opportunity to attack and capture the western wall of Sīzhōu.
Zīlún, realizing his miscalculation,
leapt from the southern wall, seeking death.
He was captured by the Sòng army
and brought before Shí Qīng.
Qīng persuaded him, saying:
"Bì Xuānchāi,
I know you are a good man,
and you should also adapt to the times and circumstances.
The state of Jīn is already weak.
If you are willing to surrender to me,
Sòng will not let you down.
If you do not comply,
you will die once you see Grand Commander Liú."
Zīlún cursed vehemently, saying:
"Shí Qīng, you rebel, listen to me!
I started from the humblest origins,
making a living by weaving wickerware.
It was only from the Southern Expedition that I obtained an official position,
and now my rank is third grade.
Unhappily, I have lost the nation's city.
I willingly accept death, yet I cannot repay [my country],
how could I seek life by following you, a rebel?"
Qīng knew he had no intention of surrendering
and imprisoned him in Xūyí.
At that time, the Prefect of Línhuái, a certain Lǐ, was also captured.
He later returned
and reported the matter to Yīlà Yánggē, the Inspector of Sīzhōu.
Yánggē, knowing that Zīlún's harsh words to Shí Qīng would surely lead to his death,
reported to the court that Zīlún would die rather than yield his integrity.
At that time, Zīlún's son, Niú'ér, was twelve years old
and resided in Sùzhōu.
He was taken in and made a Shěréntrained in the Empress's residence.
The Sòng people also admired Zīlún's loyalty and unyielding spirit.
Wishing to spare his life,
they bound him with iron ropes
and imprisoned him in an earthen dungeon in Zhènjiāng Fǔ.
They provided him with just enough clothes and food to prevent him from suffering from cold and hunger.
They tried every means to coerce and entice him.
From time to time, he would be brought out and asked:
"Will you surrender?"
Zīlún would either curse or remain silent.
This went on for fourteen years.
When the generals and soldiers of Xūyí surrendered to Sòng,
the Sòng dispatched Commander-in-Chief Nàhé Mǎizhù and others to look north and bow in tears,
calling it a farewell to their former lord.
Zīlún was forced to stand by and watch.
Upon seeing Mǎizhù, Zīlún cursed him, saying:
"Nàhé Mǎizhù,
the state has never failed you.
Why can you not seek death honorably,
but instead act in such a despicable manner?"
Mǎizhù bowed his head, not daring to look up.
When Càizhōu fell
and Āizōng hanged himself,
the Sòng people informed Zīlún.
Zīlún sighed, saying:
"I have nothing left to hope for.
Allow me to offer one sacrifice to my lord, and then I will surrender."
The Sòng people believed him
and slaughtered oxen and sheep to set up a sacrifice on the southern bank of the Zhènjiāng River.
After Zīlún completed the sacrifice,
he prostrated himself on the ground and wept bitterly.
Taking advantage of their inattention, he threw himself into the river and died.
The Sòng people honored his righteousness,
proclaimed it throughout the land,
and even discussed building a shrine for him.
Among the prisoners in Zhènjiāng was a hermit who had personally seen him
and reported the matter to Yuán Hàowèn,
also recounting the fall of Sīzhōu city and Zīlún's capture.
He further said:
"Zīlún was tall,
with a reddish face,
slightly prominent cheekbones,
and a sparse, yellowish beard.
He was inherently straightforward and honest,
and highly valued his promises.
Thus, his steadfastness and integrity were extraordinary."
The Xuānzōng Shílù states that Zīlún was killed by mutinous soldiers,
but this was merely hearsay at the time and not the true account.
Guō Xiākuò,
a native of Huìzhōu.
His family had for generations been Bǎojiǎ archers, and he and his elder brother Lùdà both enlisted due to their skill in archery.
In the early years of Xīngdìng,
Lùdà, for his accomplishments, was promoted to the honorary title of Tóngzhī Píngliáng Fǔshì, concurrent with Huìzhōu Cìshǐ,
advanced one rank,
and granted the surname Yánzhǎn.
When the Xià people attacked Huìzhōu,
Lùdà remotely spotted their commanding general, whose horse and rider were both clad in gold,
moving in and out of the formation.
From about two hundred paces away,
he fired one arrow that struck him in the throat,
killing him.
He then shot another person,
the arrow piercing both hands and pinning them to a tree.
The enemy was greatly alarmed.
When the city fell,
Lùdà and Xiākuò were both captured.
The Xià people admired their skill
and imprisoned them.
Both brothers swore to die rather than submit.
The imperial court, upon hearing of this,
discussed giving them high honors,
but not knowing if they were alive or dead,
they specially promoted Lùdà's son, Bànniú, one rank
and appointed him to the position of Xúnwèi
to commend his loyalty.
Later, the brothers plotted to escape and return to Huìzhōu.
They plucked out their beards.
When their plot was discovered,
Lùdà was ultimately killed by them,
while Xiākuò alone managed to escape and return.
The Emperor, remembering Lùdà's loyalty,
ordered Bànniú to be further promoted one rank
and honorably appointed as Huìzhōu Jūnshì Pàn Guān.
Xiākuò was honorably appointed as Gǒngzhōu Qiánxiá.
At that time, an official requested that Lùdà's younger brother be rewarded and employed.
Consequently, Xiākuò was promoted two ranks
and appointed as Tóngzhī Lánzhōu Jūnzhōushì.
In the winter of the fifth year of Xīngdìng (1221),
the Xià people, numbering over ten thousand, invaded Dìngxī.
Xiākuò defeated them,
beheading seven hundred
and capturing fifty horses.
For this achievement, he was promoted to Tóngzhī Líntáo Fǔshì.
In the second year of Yuánguāng (1223),
the Xià people, with hundreds of thousands of infantry and cavalry, attacked Fèngxiáng very urgently.
Grand Marshal Chìzhǎn Héxǐ put Xiākuò in overall command of military affairs.
While patrolling the city walls,
a man outside the moat sat on a folding stool.
Because an arrow could not reach him,
his demeanor seemed to despise the city defenders.
Héxǐ pointed him out to Xiākuò, saying:
"Can you shoot this man?"
Xiākuò measured the distance
and said:
"Yes."
Xiākuò, when firing arrows,
would usually wait for an unprotected spot under the armpit and shoot, never missing.
He immediately took his bow and arrow and waited for the seated man to raise his elbow.
With one shot, he killed him.
When the enemy retreated,
he was promoted to the honorary title of Jìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Soon after, this was changed to Tōngyuǎn Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and he was appointed Shāndōng Xīlù Wòkě Bìlà Mòkè.
Envoys were also sent to bestow rewards
and announce his achievements throughout the various prefectures.
In the winter of that year,
Xiākuò, together with Gǒngzhōu Marshal Tián Ruì, attacked and captured Huìzhōu.
Xiākuò led five hundred cavalry, all wearing ochre robes,
descending from the south mountain of the prefecture, concealed.
The Xià people, suddenly seeing them, thought they were divine.
Someone on the city wall raised his hand over a hanging wooden board.
Xiākuò shot him,
and both the hand and the board were pierced.
He shot and killed several hundred people in total.
The Xià people were terrified
and then surrendered.
Huìzhōu had been occupied by the Xià people for nearly four years,
and was now recovered.
In the early days of Zhèngdà,
Tián Ruì rebelled, occupying Gǒngzhōu.
An edict ordered the two Xīwǎn Xíngshěngs to combine forces and attack him.
Xiākuò led his troops to be the first to ascend.
Ruì opened the gates and rushed out,
only to be killed by his younger brother Jì.
Over five thousand heads were cut off.

For this achievement, he was promoted to the honorary title of Zhī Fèngxiáng Fǔshì, concurrently Běnlù Bīngmǎ Dū Zǒngguǎn, Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān, and concurrently in charge of Lán, Huì, Táo, and Hé Yuánshuàifǔ affairs.
In the ninth month of the sixth year (1229),
Xiākuò presented two Xīmǎ horses.
The imperial edict said:
"Your martial skill is extraordinary.
These horses are suitable for battle.
How could I, riding them, fully utilize their strength?
Since they have been presented,
they are now esteemed objects.
I will bestow them upon you."
He was also given one golden tripod and one jade rabbit-falcon,
along with various other items for Guō Lúngē and others who were sent.
In the second year of Tiān Xīng,
Āi Zōng moved to Cài Zhōu.
Fearing that the isolated city could not be held,
he intended to move to Gǒng Chāng.
Nián Gé Wán Zhǎn was appointed acting governor of Gǒng Chāng Province.
In the first month of spring in the third year,
Wán Zhǎn heard that Cài had fallen.
Wishing to calm the hearts of the people,
he held the city, awaiting the enthronement of a successor.
So he sent a person, claiming to be an envoy from Cài,
to announce an imperial decree.
The commander of Suí Dé Zhōu, Wāng Shì Xiǎn, also knew of the dire news from Cài,
and furthermore resented Wán Zhǎn's control over him.
He wanted to issue a forged edict
and consequently plotted against Wán Zhǎn with his troops.
However, he feared Xiā Gé's prestige,
so he sent an envoy to ask Xiā Gé to join forces to attack Gǒng Chāng.
When the envoy arrived,
Xiā Gé said to him:
"Lord Nián Gé received an imperial decree to be acting governor;
who dares not obey his commands?
Now the emperor is besieged in Cài,
intending to move to Gǒng Chāng.
At this time of national crisis,
since we cannot die for the cause and rush to the rescue,
nor can we unite the populace to welcome him,
are we then to attack Lord Nián Gé
and first destroy the place where the emperor is to seek refuge?
Where will the emperor go?
If your commander wishes to betray the nation,
he may do so himself;
why involve me?"
Shì Xiǎn then attacked Gǒng Chāng and captured it,
abducted and killed Wán Zhǎn,
and offered his allegiance to the Great Yuán.
He again sent more than twenty envoys to Xiā Gé to explain the consequences (of compliance or defiance),
but Xiā Gé refused to comply.
In the spring of the Jiǎ Wǔ year,
the Jīn kingdom had already fallen,
and there was no one in the western prefectures who did not submit,
but Xiā Gé alone held his isolated city firmly.
In the tenth month of winter in the Bǐng Shēn year,
the great army combined forces to attack him.
Xiā Gé, judging that he could not hold out,
gathered all the gold, silver, copper, and iron in the prefecture,
mixed and cast them into cannons to attack the besiegers.
He slaughtered oxen and horses to feed his soldiers,
and also personally burned down dwellings and stockpiles,
saying:
"Let nothing fall into the hands of the enemy."
He fought bloody battles daily,
but the great army could not capture it quickly.
When the number of soldiers dead and wounded was great,
he ordered firewood to be piled up in the prefectural office,
called together his family members and the wives and daughters of the generals and officers in the city,
shut them in a single room,
and prepared to burn them himself.
Xiā Gé's concubine wished to make a plea,
but he immediately beheaded her as an example.
When the fire was raging,
he led his generals and soldiers to stand before the fire, bows drawn, awaiting.
The city was breached,
and soldiers poured in.
After a long, fierce battle,
some soldiers, having exhausted their bows and arrows,
threw themselves into the fire.
Xiā Gé alone climbed onto a large pile of straw,
shielding himself with a door panel.
He shot two to three hundred arrows, every one hitting its mark.
When his arrows were exhausted,
he threw his bow and sword into the fire and immolated himself.
Not a single person in the city was willing to surrender.
Xiā Gé was forty-five years old when he died.
The local people erected a shrine for him.
Wán Zhǎn's courtesy name was Shì Chāng.
In the third year of Tài Hé, he passed the imperial examination with an essay on policy.
Initially, as acting governor,
he used a wax pellet as an imperial edict,
setting the second year of Tiān Xīng, ninth month, as the date for a large army to gather and meet the emperor at Ráo Fēng Guān,
to unexpectedly capture Xīng Yuán from the Sòng.
However, this plan was not carried out.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 63, Arts and Letters I: Hán Fǎng, Cài Sōng Nián (courtesy name Guī), Wú Jī, Mǎ Dìng Guó, Rèn Xún, Zhào Kě, Guō Cháng Qiàn, Xiāo Yǒng Qí, Hú Lì, Wáng Jìng, Yáng Bó Rén, Zhèng Zǐ Dān, Dǎng Huái Yīng.
In the early Jīn period, there was no writing system.
Since Shì Zǔ, regulations were gradually established.
When Tài Zǔ rose to power, he employed old Láo officials.
Their exchanges through envoys were already eloquent.
When Tài Zōng succeeded,
he implemented the examination system.
And when he campaigned against the Sòng,
he acquired books and maps from Biàn,
and many Sòng scholars defected to him.
Xī Zōng paid his respects to the Former Sage,
facing north with the ritual of a disciple.
During the reigns of Shì Zōng and Zhāng Zōng,
Confucianism underwent a great transformation,
schools flourished daily,
and scholars who entered officialdom through the examinations rose to positions as prime ministers, succeeding one another.
At that time, although Confucian scholars did not have specialized schools of thought with famous masters,
yet the court's decrees,
and the correspondence with neighboring countries,
were splendid and admirable.
The Jīn gained the empire through military force,
no different from the Láo,
but the achievements of their era were able to establish themselves between the Táng and Sòng,
something the Láo era could not match,
by means of culture, not military might.
The Analects say:
"If speech is not refined,
it will not travel far."
How could cultural governance's contribution to one's family and nation
be the result of a single day's effort?
Thus, the biographies of Arts and Letters are compiled.
Hán Fǎng, courtesy name Gōng Měi,
was from Yàn Jīng.
He served the Láo,
and his family was prominent for generations.
Fǎng lost his father at the age of five,
and his weeping could express his full sorrow.
In the second year of Tiān Qìng,
he placed first in the *jìnshì* examination.
He was appointed Right Remonstrance Official,
then transferred to Compiler in the Imperial Academy.
He was successively promoted to Assistant Supervisor of the Imperial Manufactories and Scholar of the Qián Wén Pavilion.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
Director of the Secretariat,
and sent as envoy to the Gāo Lí kingdom.
Although Gāo Lí had previously maintained good relations,
in the fourth year of Tiān Huì,
they submitted a memorial declaring themselves vassals but refused to present a sworn declaration.
Repeated envoys pressed for an agreement,
but none achieved a clear outcome.
When Fǎng again arrived in Gāo Lí,
he repeatedly urged them.
Gāo Lí summoned scholars from across the kingdom who knew ancient and modern affairs,
to deliberate on the wording
and enable appropriate replies.
After nearly ten days,
they finally replied,
saying to Fǎng:
"Our small country served the Láo and Sòng for two hundred years without a sworn declaration,
and never failed in the duties of a vassal.
Now, serving the superior country, we should observe the same rites as when serving Láo and Sòng.
Repeated oaths lead to disorder, which the sages would not condone;
we dare not use a sworn declaration."
Fǎng said:
"If your esteemed country insists on using ancient rites,
Shùn made a tour of inspection every five years,
and the various lords appeared at court four times.
The Zhōu had a system where every six years, the five domains appeared at court once,
and after another six years, the King made a seasonal tour,
and the feudal lords each appeared at court in their respective regions.
Now, the Son of Heaven is conducting a western tour,
so your esteemed country should attend the court assembly."
The Gāo Lí people had no reply,
and then said:
"Let us discuss it further."
Fǎng said:
"A sworn declaration and court assembly,
is decided with one word."
Thereupon, Gāo Lí presented the sworn declaration as agreed,
and Fǎng returned.
Zōng Gàn was greatly pleased and said:
"Without you, who could have accomplished this?"
He then told his attendants:
"From now on, envoys sent abroad should all be carefully selected."
The following year,
he was promoted to Straight Scholar of the Zhāo Wén Pavilion,
concurrently serving as official of the Imperial Palace.
He was again promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance,
and transferred to Hanlin Academician, Lecturer.
He was transferred to Minister of Rites,
then promoted to Hanlin Academician,
concurrently Grand Minister of the Imperial Sacrifices and Compiler of National History,
with his position as Minister (of Rites) remaining unchanged.
Fǎng entered the Ministry of Rites in the twelfth year of Tiān Huì,
serving in that office for seven years in total.
At that time,
the court was discussing rites,
and systems were either continued or reformed.
Therefore, Fǎng remained in the Ministry of Rites concurrently as Grand Minister of the Imperial Sacrifices for a long time.
He was appointed Administrator of Jì Nán,
then appointed as Counselor to the Secretariat.
In the fourth year of Huáng Tǒng,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
which was denied.
In the sixth year,
he again submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
whereupon he was appointed Defender of Biàn Jīng,
and ennobled as Duke of Yùn.
He again requested to revert to his former request,
and retired with the rank of *Yí Tóng Sān Sī*.
In the early Tiān Dé period,
he was promoted to *Kāi Fǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī*.
He passed away.
He was sixty-eight years old.
Fāng's nature was benevolent and厚,
and he treated others with great宽.
A household slave falsely accused Fāng of supplying horses to rebels to help them escape the country.
An investigation found no evidence,
so the authorities returned the slave to Fāng.
Fāng treated him as before,
saying:
"The slave falsely accused his master of a crime
to seek freedom;
what is there to be surprised about?"
People called him a magnanimous gentleman.
Although Fāng was noble,
he never let a book leave his hands,
and he was skilled at writing.
He excelled especially at imperial edicts and decrees,
and his "Monument to Tàizǔ's Sage Virtue and Divine Accomplishments"
was praised by his contemporaries.
After his return from an embassy to Gāolì,
later Gāolì envoys always inquired about Fāng's well-being.
Cài Sōngnián's courtesy name was Bójiān.
His father, Jìng,
was the defender of Yānshān
at the end of Sòng Xuānhé era.
Sōngnián accompanied his father,
managing confidential documents.
When Zōngwàng's army reached Báihé,
Guō Yàoshī was defeated.
Jìng surrendered Yānshān Prefecture,
and the Grand Marshal's Residence appointed Sōngnián as a clerk.
During the Tiānhuì era,
all former officials of Liáo and Sòng were reappointed.
Sōngnián became Prince Zhongyǔn
and was appointed as a judicial officer for Zhēndìng Prefecture.
From then on, he was considered a person of Zhēndìng.
He once accompanied the Grand Marshal's Residence and Qí in attacking Sòng.
At that time,
the bandits in the Xīshān mountains of Zhēndìng had just been suppressed.
More than a thousand families of mountain residents had been implicated with the bandits.
Sōngnián vigorously argued on their behalf,
and they were eventually acquitted.
When the State of Qí was abolished,
the Xíngtái Shàngshūshěng was established in Biàn.
Sōngnián became a Xíngtái Xíngbù Lángzhōng.
Dū Yuánshuài Zōngbì led the Xíngtái affairs
and attacked Sòng.
Sōngnián concurrently managed the affairs of the six ministries in the army.
When Sòng acknowledged suzerainty,
the army returned.
Zōngbì entered the court as Zuǒ Chéngxiàng
and recommended Sōngnián as Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng.
In the seventh year of Huángtǒng,
Xǔ Lín, a clerk in the Shàngshūshěng, reported on the faction of Tián Jué.
Sōngnián had always been at odds with Jué.
At that time, Zōngbì held power.
Jué was strong-willed and liked to critique people.
His faction were all gentlemen,
and Hán Qǐxiān, as prime minister, highly valued them.
However, Sōngnián, Xǔ Lín, and Cáo Wàngzhī wanted to form connections with Jué.
Jué rejected them,
which caused resentment.
Therefore, Sōngnián and Xǔ Lín fabricated charges against Jué and his associates
and persuaded Zōngbì to execute them.
The faction of gentlemen was thus suppressed.
That year,
Sōngnián was promoted to Zuǒ Sī Yuánwàiláng.
Sōngnián had previously been in Zōngbì's residence,
and Hǎilíng, as an imperial clan member, served in Zōngbì's army,
which led to their close friendship.
In the early Tiāndé era,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shìláng,
and soon after, to Hùbù Shàngshū.
Hǎilíng moved the capital to Zhōngdū,
relocating the salt and iron monopoly office to enrich the capital
and reviving the system of paper money and tax certificates.
All these initiatives originated from Sōngnián.
Hǎilíng planned to attack Sòng.
Because Sōngnián's family had served Sòng for generations,
Hǎilíng quickly promoted him to prominent positions to attract the attention of the southerners.
Thus, Sōngnián was appointed as the envoy to Sòng for the New Year's Day celebration.
Upon his return from the mission,
he was changed to Lìbù Shàngshū,
and soon after, was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
That year,
he was advanced from Chóngdé Dàfū to Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū,
promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and shortly thereafter,
became Zuǒ Chéng,
and was enfeoffed as Gàoguó Gōng.
Initially,
Hǎilíng loved the "mountain-call" cheers of the Sòng envoys
and had the Shénwèi Army practice them.
When Sūn Dàofū offered congratulations for the New Year's Day of the third year of Zhènglóng,
he was granted an audience,
but the "mountain-call" cheers were not like those of previous years.
After Dàofū retired,
Hǎilíng said to his chief ministers:
"The Sòng people know that I had the Shénwèi Army practice their cheers.
This must have been leaked by Cài Sōngnián and Hú Lì."
Sōngnián, in fear, replied:
"If your servant harbored such a thought,
his entire clan should be exterminated."
After some time,
he was promoted to Yòuchéngxiàng,
granted the title Yítóng Sānsī,
and enfeoffed as Wèiguó Gōng.
In the fourth year of Zhènglóng, he died
at the age of fifty-three.
Hǎilíng mourned and lamented him,
offered a sacrifice at his residence,
and ordered a eulogy to be written to express his sentiments.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Wúguó Gōng
and given the posthumous name Wénjiǎn.
His son Guī, who was the Sānhé Zhǔbù, was reinstated as Hànlín Xiūzhuàn,
and Zhāng was granted the rank of Jìnshì.
Xiāo Xū, a Hànlín Dàizhì, was dispatched to escort his coffin
back to Zhēndìng for burial.
Officials of the fourth rank and below accompanied the funeral for ten *lǐ* outside the capital,
and all travel expenses were covered by the government.
Sōngnián was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother,
and he enjoyed helping his relatives and associates.
His nature was also extravagant and luxurious,
disregarding his household's financial situation.
His literary style was clear and beautiful,
and he was particularly skilled in *yuèfǔ* (musical poetry).
He was as famous as Wú Jī,
and at the time, their style was called
"Wú-Cài Tǐ."
His collected works circulated in the world.
His son was Guī.
Guī's courtesy name was Zhèngfǔ.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination,
but did not seek an official appointment.
After a long time, he was appointed as the military judicial officer for Chéngzhōu,
and then promoted to Sānhé Zhǔbù.
He observed mourning for his father.
He was reinstated as Hànlín Xiūzhuàn
and concurrently held the position of Tóngzhī Zhìgào.
After eight years in office,
he was transferred to Hùbù Yuánwàiláng
and concurrently Tàicháng Chéng.
Guī was renowned for his extensive knowledge and discernment.
All changes and improvements to the court's institutions
were compiled, thoroughly reviewed, examined, and revised by Guī.
Originally,
the tombs of the two Yān kings were located outside the eastern city wall of Zhōngdū.
When Hǎilíng expanded the perimeter of the capital,
the tombs ended up inside the eastern city.
Previously, there had been grave robbers who disturbed the tombs,
so in the ninth year of Dàdìng, an imperial edict ordered their reburial outside the city.
It was popularly believed that these were the tombs of the Yān King and Prince Dān from the Six States period.
When the burial pits were opened,
the inscription on the eastern coffin read,
"Yān Líng Wáng Jiù" (燕靈王舊).
"Jiù" (舊)
was an ancient character
for "Jiù" (柩),
and they were used interchangeably.
It turned out to be the tomb of Liú Jiàn,
the son of Gāozǔ of the Western Hàn dynasty.
The western tomb
was probably the tomb of Yān Kāng Wáng Liú Jiā.
Guī wrote "Disquisition on the Tombs of the Two Yān Kings," detailing the burial system, names of objects, and inscriptions.
Gāo Yuándǐng, the judicial officer of Ānguó Jūn Jiédù, was implicated in a case of bribery concerning supervision.
He sought assistance from Tián Jūshí, a Tàicháng Bóshì; Wú Chángxíng, a Dàlǐ Sīzhí; Gāo Zhènhēng, a Lìbù Zhǔshì; and Wáng Yuánzhōng, a Dàlǐ Píngshì.
Zhènhēng then approached Lǐ Zhòngróu, an official overseeing interrogations in the Yùshǐtái.
Zhòngróu exposed the matter.

Guī, along with Wáng Xiāo, a Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng; Rèn Xún, a Wǎnpíng Zhǔbù; Yán Shù, a former Wèizhōu Fángyù Pànguān; Gāo Fùhēng, a Chéngshì Láng; Zhái Xún, a Wénlín Láng; Wáng Jǐngxī, a Dūnwǔ Xiàowèi; and Rèn Shīwàng, a Jìnyì Xiàowèi,
were all implicated for
transmitting messages back and forth with Jūshí and others,
or instructing Yuándǐng to escape.
Jūshí, Chángxíng, Zhènhēng, and Yuánzhōng each received eighty strokes of the rod.
Xiāo, Guī, Xún, Shù, Fùhēng, and Zhái Xún each received forty strokes of the bamboo.
Jǐngxī and Shīwàng each received two years of penal servitude.
All sentences were to be carried out, except for those who could redeem themselves by office.
After a long time,
he was appointed as Hàodōngběilù Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ,
then returned as Xiūzhuàn,
promoted to Lǐbù Lángzhōng,
and enfeoffed as Zhēndìng Xiànnán.
Guī had already contracted a stroke,
losing his voice and unable to speak.
He was then appointed Wéizhōu Cìshǐ.
His colleagues had already made their formal thanks,
but Guī alone could not enter for an audience.
Shìzōng admonished Yòuchéng Tángkuò Ānlǐ and Cānzhèng Wáng Wèi, saying:
"You gentlemen, who read histories, have you ever heard of a person unable to speak who could govern?"
He then said to Zhōngchéng Liú Zhònghuì:
"Cài Guī, suffering from a stroke, cannot offer his thanks.
Why have you not impeached him?
People say you form factions to shield each other;
is this true now?"
Guī then retired from office
and passed away soon after.
Guī zhī Wén (珪之文) wrote five chapters on "Supplementing and Correcting the *Shuǐjīng* (水經),"
and combined the records of Sòng, Qí, and Northern Wèi from Shěn Yuē (沈約), Xiāo Zǐxiǎn (蕭子顯), and Wèi Shōu (魏收) to form "Records of the Northern and Southern Dynasties" in thirty chapters,
"Sequel to Collected Inscriptions and Lost Writings with Postscripts" in ten chapters,
"Records of Jìnyáng (晉陽)" in twelve chapters,
and a "Collected Works" in fifty-five chapters.
The "Supplementing and Correcting the *Shuǐjīng*," "Records of Jìnyáng," and "Collected Works" are extant today;
the rest are all lost.
Wú Jī (吳激), courtesy name Yàngāo (彥高),
was a native of Jiànzhōu (建州).
His father, Shì (拭),
was a *jìnshì* of the Sòng (宋) dynasty
and held the official post of Cháofèngláng (朝奉郎) and Zhī Sūzhōu (知蘇州).
Jī
was the son-in-law of Mǐ Fú (米芾).
He was skilled in poetry and prose,
and his calligraphy and painting were elegant and captured Mǐ Fú's brushwork.
He was especially proficient in *yuèfǔ* (樂府) poetry,
creating verses that were clear and graceful,
mournful but not overly sorrowful.
When he went to Jīn (金) with a Sòng (宋) imperial mission,
he was kept there due to his renown and not allowed to return,
and was appointed Hànlín Dàizhì (翰林待制).
In the second year of Huángtǒng (皇統) era,
he was sent out to govern Shēnzhōu (深州).
He died three days after arriving at his post.
An imperial decree granted his son one million *qián* (錢), three hundred *hú* (斛) of grain, and three *qǐng* (頃) of land to support his family.
His "Collected Works of Dōngshān" (東山集) in ten chapters circulated in the world.
"Dōngshān" (東山)
was his self-proclaimed sobriquet.
Mǎ Dìngguó (馬定國), courtesy name Zǐqīng (子卿),
was a native of Chípíng (茌平).
From a young age, his aspirations were extraordinary.
At the end of Xuān (宣) and Zhèng (政) eras,
he wrote a poem on the wall of a wine shop,
and was implicated for satire, thus becoming known.
He also became famous because of this incident.
In the early Fùchāng (阜昌) era,
he traveled to Lìxià (歷下).
He impressed Qí Wáng Yù (齊王豫) with his poetry,
and Yù (豫) was greatly pleased,
appointing him Jiānchá Yùshǐ (監察御史).
He rose to the position of Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士).
Since the Táng (唐) dynasty, there had been no definitive conclusion on the Shígǔ (石鼓, Stone Drums).
Dìngguó (定國) examined them based on their calligraphy and script,
and concluded that they were made during the time of Yǔwén Zhōu (宇文周).
He wrote a treatise of over ten thousand words,
drawing on various records and biographies,
with very clear argumentation.
Scholars compared it to Cài Zhèngfǔ's (蔡正甫) treatise on the Tomb of the King of Yān (燕王墓).
Initially,
he had not found his way in poetry.
He dreamt that his father gave him a white brush the size of an inch,
and from then on, his writing improved greatly.
His collected works circulated in the world.
Rèn Xún (任詢), courtesy name Jūnmó (君謨),
was a native of Jūnshì (軍市) in Yìzhōu (易州).
His father, Guì (貴), was talented and capable,
good at painting,
and enjoyed discussing military affairs.
During the Xuān (宣) and Zhèng (政) eras, he traveled to Jiāng (江) and Zhè (浙).
Xún (詢) was born in Qiánzhōu (虔州).
He was generous and had great integrity.
His calligraphy was considered the best of his time,
and his painting also reached a marvelous level.
Critics said his painting was superior to his calligraphy,
his calligraphy superior to his poetry,
and his poetry superior to his prose.
However, Wáng Tíngyún (王庭筠) alone praised him for his overall talent.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Zhènglóng (正隆).
He successively served as Pànguān (判官) of Yìdū (益都) Dūgōu (都勾) and
Salt Commissioner of Běijīng (北京).
At sixty-four, he retired,
enjoying a leisurely life in his hometown,
with several hundred scrolls of famous calligraphy and paintings in his collection.
He died at the age of seventy.
Zhào Kě (趙可), courtesy name Xiànzhī (獻之),
was a native of Gāopíng (高平).
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of Zhēnyuán (貞元).
He rose to the position of Hànlín Zhí Xuéshì (翰lín直學士).
He was learned, highly talented,
and exceptionally outstanding.
During the Tiāndé (天德) and Zhēnyuán (貞元) eras,
he was well-known in examination circles.
Later, he entered the Hànlín (翰林) Academy,
and many imperial edicts and proclamations of that time came from his hand,
earning him admiration from his peers for his classical elegance.
He was especially skilled in his songs and *yuèfǔ* poetry,
known as "Collected Works of Yùfēng Sànrén" (玉峯散人集).
Guō Chángqiàn (郭長倩), courtesy name Mànqīng (曼卿),
was a native of Wéndēng (文登).
He passed the second class of the *jīngyì* (經義) examination in the *Bǐngyín* (丙寅) year of the Huángtǒng (皇統) era.
He rose to the position of Mìshū Shǎojiān (秘書少監),
concurrently Lǐbù Lángzhōng (禮部郎中),
and compiled the *Qǐjūzhù* (起居注).
He was good friends with Shī Péngwàng (施朋望), Wáng Wújìng (王無競), Liú Yánlǎo (劉嵓老), and Liú Wúdǎng (劉無黨).
His "Biography of Shíjuémíng" (石決明傳) was praised by his contemporaries.
His "Collected Works of Kūnqū" (崑●集) circulated in the world.
Xiāo Yǒngqí (蕭永祺), courtesy name Jǐngchún (景純),
originally named Púliè (蒲烈).
He was studious in his youth
and proficient in both large and small Khitan scripts.
Yēlǜ Gù (耶律固), the Administrator of Guǎngníng (廣寧), was ordered by imperial decree to translate books.
He invited Yǒngqí (永祺) to his residence,
and Yǒngqí (永祺) consequently learned all of his master's craft.
When Gù (固) died,
Yǒngqí (永祺) led his disciples in wearing mourning clothes (*qīcuī sàng*).
Gù (固) had started compiling the *Liáo Shǐ* (遼史, History of Liao) but had not finished it.
Yǒngqí (永祺) continued it,
producing thirty chapters of "Annals" (紀), five chapters of "Treatises" (志), and forty chapters of "Biographies" (傳),
which he presented to the throne.
He was promoted to Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn (宣武將軍) and appointed Tàicháng Chéng (太常丞).
When Hǎilíng (海陵) served as the Commander of the Central Capital,
Yǒngqí (永祺) received special intimacy and courtesy.
In the early Tiāndé (天德) era,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū (左諫議大夫),
then transferred to Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì (翰林侍講學士),
concurrently Shǐ Xuéshì (史學士),
and again transferred to Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士).
The following year,
he was transferred to Chéngzhǐ (承旨).
When Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞) Yēlǜ Ānlǐ (耶律安禮) was sent to govern Nánjīng (南京),
Hǎilíng (海陵) wanted to appoint Yǒngqí (永祺) to replace him.
He summoned him to the inner cabinet
and explained his intention.
Yǒngqí (永祺) declined, saying:
"Your subject's talent and discernment are humble
and insufficient to disgrace the position of a high official."
Hǎilíng (海陵) said:
"Today, the world is at peace,
and I am governing with culture and literature.
You are excellent for this."
Yǒngqí (永祺) firmly declined.
After he left,
someone asked:
"You have met with the emperor's favor.
Why do you give way so much
when you could advance in rank and position
and assist the times with your principles?"
Yǒngqí (永祺) replied:
"The high officials are responsible for the well-being of the world.
Even if I wished to be greedy for honor and favor,
what would become of the common people?"
Hǎilíng (海陵) once selected ten court officials for consultation.
Yǒngqí's (永祺) discussions alone were broad and benevolent,
and he was praised by his contemporaries as a truly virtuous person.
He died at the age of fifty-seven.
Hú Lì (胡礪), courtesy name Yuánhuà (元化),
was a native of Wǔ'ān (武安) in Cízhōu (磁州).
He loved learning in his youth.
During the Tiānhuì (天會) era,
when the great army marched south of the Yellow River,
Lì (礪) was captured by soldiers.
When he reached Yān (燕),
he escaped and hid in Xiāngshān Sì (香山寺),
living among servants and laborers.
Hán Fǎng (韓昉) saw him and was struck by him.
He asked Lì (礪) to compose a poem to express his aspirations.
Lì (礪) picked up a brush and finished it immediately.
His thoughts were clear and elegant.
Fǎng (昉) was very pleased
and took him into his household,
arranging for him to live with his son
and be educated together.
From then on, Lì's (礪) scholarship progressed daily.
Fǎng (昉) once said to others:
"Mr. Hú's (胡) talent advances a thousand *lǐ* (里) a day;
one day he will surely become famous in the world."
Ten years later,
he came first in the *jìnshì* examination
and was appointed Yòu Shíyí (右拾遺),
serving concurrently as Hànlín Xiūzhuàn (翰林修撰).
After a long time,
he was transferred to Dìngzhōu Guānchá Pànguān (定州觀察判官).
The schools in Dìngzhōu (定州) were the best north of the Yellow River,
and the number of scholars residing there often reached hundreds.
Lì (礪) tirelessly supervised their education.
All those he guided became top performers in the examinations,
calling his examination essays
"Yuánhuà (元化) style."
In the early Huángtǒng (皇統) era,
he became Héběi Xīlù Zhuǎnyùn Dūgōu Pànguān (河北西路轉運都勾判官).
Lì (礪) was upright and unyielding by nature.
Gāo Zhēn (高楨), the Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事) of the Xíngtái (行臺), traveled to Biàn (汴).
On his way, he passed through Zhēndìng (真定)
and was entertained at the Caosī (漕司).
Lì (礪) wanted to take his seat,
but Zhēn (楨) rebuked him.
Lì (礪) said:
"When you are in the government, etiquette dictates that you are above all officials.
Today's gathering has its own etiquette for host and guest."
Zhēn (楨) said:
"What will you do if you become a provincial official someday?"
Lì (礪) said:
"When in office, I will act accordingly;
what is there to avoid?"
Zhēn (楨) admired his words
and apologized to him instead.
He was transferred to be the Assistant Military Administrator of Shēnzhōu,
and promoted to Cháofèng Dàfū.
The Prefect of the commandery was tyrannical,
and looked down upon his subordinates.
Lì often used propriety to restrain him,
and the Prefect became ashamed and submissive.
All commandery affairs were then entrusted to Lì.
The zhōu administered five xiàn,
and it was customary to employ over a hundred archers,
with the minimum being sixty or seventy.
Annually, over fifty million coins were levied from the people for their wages.
These men were all shiftless ruffians from the marketplace,
who used the pretext of tracking bandits
to harass the people wherever they went.
Lì recognized this malpractice
and dismissed them all.
Soon after, a rumor spread, saying:
"On a certain day, bandits will rise,
and intend to kill the Assistant Administrator."
Some requested preparations be made,
but Lì said:
"Bandits are only interested in wealth.
I am as poor as this,
what preparations should be made?"
That evening,
he ordered the public office to unbar its gates,
and indeed, nothing happened.
He was again appointed as a Xiūzhuàn in the Hànlín Academy,
then transferred to Lǐbù Lángzhōng.
At that time, he made many decisions regarding ceremonial matters.
When Hǎilíng was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
all officials congratulated him in the ancestral hall,
but Lì alone did not kneel.
Hǎilíng asked him why,
and Lì replied with an edict,
adding:
"To kneel in court attire
is the proper禮 to a ruler or father."
Hǎilíng deeply esteemed him for this.
In the early Tiāndé period,
he was again promoted to Shìjiǎng Xuéshì,
and concurrently compiled the Guóshǐ.
He resigned due to mourning his mother.
He was recalled to serve as the Deputy Envoy for the annual mission to the Sòng state.
Xíngbù Shìláng Bái Yàngōng was the chief envoy.
Hǎilíng said to Lì:
"Yàngōng's rank is below yours,
but because of his past contributions,
I have made you his deputy."
He was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì,
then transferred to Xíngbù Shàngshū.
While accompanying the imperial retinue to Biàn, he fell ill.
Hǎilíng repeatedly sent envoys to inquire about him.
When he died,
Hǎilíng deeply mourned his loss.
He was fifty-five years old.
Wáng Jìng, courtesy name Wúqìng,
was a native of Zhāngdé.
He was intelligent, astute, and fond of learning.
At seventeen, he entered officialdom through hereditary privilege.
During the Xuānhé era of the Sòng,
he passed both examinations at the Tàixué,
and was appointed Zhǔbù of Túnliú.
Upon the establishment of the Guó Cháo (Jin Dynasty),
he was appointed Magistrate of Dàníng,
then served as Salt Official of Bǎoshèng,
and was transferred to be Magistrate of Hénèi.
At that time, there was a famine and bandits arose.
Jìng devised strategies to capture the bandits,
and within a few months, all were apprehended.
During the transition from summer to autumn,
the Qìnshuǐ overflowed.
Annually, people were conscripted to build dikes,
and powerful gentry and corrupt officials exploited this for their own illicit gain.
Jìng thoroughly investigated the facts,
reducing expenses by nearly half.
The xiàn people had a saying for this:
"From Xīshān to the riverbank,
two and a half county officials."
This was because in the previous administration, Hán Xīfǔ and Jìng successively governed the xiàn,
both demonstrating ability and competence.
Zhāng Yuán, the Magistrate of Zhèngpíng in Jiàngzhōu, also had administrative achievements but was somewhat inferior,
hence the saying.
In the first year of Tiānjuàn,
he was transferred to be Magistrate of Gù'ān.
In the early Huángtǒng period,
Cānzhèng Hán Fǎng recommended him,
and he was summoned to provisionally serve as Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì,
concurrently Tàicháng Bóshì.
An imperial edict ordered him to compose the tomb inscription for the Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Wányán Lóushì.
Jìng, using the conduct record, wrote everything truthfully,
and then requested the Guóshǐ be corrected and published,
which people at the time considered a model.
In the second year,
he took the palace examination,
and Jìng's essay ranked first,
thus he was officially appointed.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng.
At that time, Hǎilíng was in power,
and policies originated from him.
He wished to make all officials avoid the taboo name of the ancestral hall.
Jìng stated that subjects did not have public taboos,
and so the matter was stopped.
Xiāo Zhònggōng, as Tàifù, was in charge of the Sānshěng affairs and enfeoffed as a Prince.
He wished to invoke the precedents of Liáo,
where Princes used purple silk parasols.
The matter was referred to the Lǐbù.
Jìng, along with Lángzhōng Zhái Yǒnggù, clearly stated its impropriety,
and the matter was ultimately not carried out.
Hǎilíng therefore esteemed him.
In the early Tiāndé period,
he was transferred to Hànlín Dàizhì,
then promoted to Hànlín Zhí Xuéshì,
transferred to Lǐbù Shìláng,
promoted to Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì,
transferred to Tàicháng Qīng,
concurrently compiled the Guóshǐ,
and then promoted to Lǐbù Shàngshū,
still concurrently compiling the Guóshǐ.
In the spring of Dàdìng second year,
he accompanied Tàifù Zhāng Hào to the capital.
An imperial edict reinstated him as Lǐbù Shàngshū.
That year,
he was ordered to oversee the relocation of Ruìzōng's imperial tomb.
The ceremonial arrangements did not conform to established rites,
and Jìng was demoted by two ranks.
An imperial edict commanded the reconstruction of the Wǔlóng Chē,
and he was concurrently Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ,
and compiled the Guóshǐ.
In the fourth year,
he died in office.
Jìng was erudite and skilled in writing,
excelled at cursive and clerical scripts,
and was particularly good at large characters.
The plaques and inscriptions in the palaces of both capitals were all written by Jìng,
and scholars considered him the foremost in this.
Yáng Bórén, courtesy name Āndào,
was the younger brother of Bóxióng.
He was naturally filial and fraternal,
and could recite a text after reading it once.
He passed the Jìnshì examination in the ninth year of Huángtǒng,
but did not seek an appointment to serve his parents.
In the second year of Tiāndé,
he was appointed Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì.
His original name was Bóyīng,
but to avoid the taboo name of Prince Guāngyīng,
it was changed to his current name.
Hǎilíng once summoned him at night to compose poetry.
The summons was very urgent.
Before the second drum, he presented ten poems.
Hǎilíng was pleased,
and bestowed his robe upon him.
When Hǎilíng shot a crow,
Bórén presented a poem about catching a crow to remonstrate him.
He suffered the death of his father,
but was recalled to office.
He was bestowed a golden belt and an official robe,
and also given silver to support his mother.
He was transferred to Zuǒ Shíyí.
When the Jìnshì Lǚ Zhōnghàn had already placed first in the palace examination,
before the names were announced,
Hǎilíng showed Zhōnghàn's examination paper to Bórén,
and asked about its quality.
Bórén replied:
"It should be in the superior class."
Hǎilíng said:
"This is today's Zhàngyuán."
Bórén, knowing Zhōnghàn's name was first,
then stayed overnight in the remonstrance office,
waiting until the names were announced before leaving.
Hǎilíng commended his careful discretion.
He was transferred to Hànlín Xiūzhuàn.
When Mèng Zōngxiàn ranked first in the local examination,
Bórén read his examination paper and praised him, saying:
"This person will achieve great fame."
That year,
Zōngxiàn was first in the prefectural, provincial, and palace examinations,
and was known as
"Mèng the Quadruple First."
Contemporary opinion considered this a testament to Bórén's discernment in literature.
According to custom,
the Zhàngyuán held the official rank of Cóng Qīpǐn,
with the grade of Chéngwù Láng.
However, Shìzōng, considering Zōngxiàn uniquely exceptional,
granted him Cóng Liùpǐn,
with the grade of Fèngzhí Dàfū.
He was reassigned as Zuòzuò Láng (著作郎).
During his mother's mourning period,
after the period of mourning ended,
he was appointed as the Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhèn xī Jiédù (鎮西節度).
He was brought into the capital as Qǐjū Zhù (起居注) concurrently with Zuǒ Shíyí (左拾遺),
and submitted a memorial discussing six contemporary issues.
He was reassigned as Dàmíng Shàoyǐn (大名少尹).
The powerful gentry in the prefecture were extremely arrogant and unrestrained,
and could not be controlled.
The common people suffered from this.
Bóréng (伯仁) thoroughly investigated and pursued their factions,
and the four borders became peaceful.
He heard a case of capital punishment in Guǎntáo (館陶)
and uncovered the injustice of it.
The people of Guǎntáo (館陶) erected a shrine for him.
The Prefect Jīng Wáng Wén (荊王文) was stripped of his title for bribery,
and demoted to Dèzhōu Fángyùshǐ (德州防禦使).
The Assistant Administrator Péi Mǎnzǐníng (裴滿子寧) and Bóréng (伯仁), as well as the Judicial Officer Xiè Nú (謝奴), were all dismissed for failing to rectify the situation.
Bóréng (伯仁) was demoted to Nánjīng Liúshǒu Pànguān (南京留守判官),
then reassigned as Assistant Administrator of Ānhuà Jūn Jiédùshǐ (安化軍節度使).
Three days after arriving at his post,
he was summoned to be the Crown Prince's Right Yùdé (右諭德) concurrently with Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
He was reassigned as Hànlín Dàizhì (翰林待制),
and again concurrently held the post of Right Yùdé (右諭德).
He was appointed as Bīnzhōu Cìshǐ (濱州刺史).
In the prefecture, there was a custom of slaves escaping,
and people would capture them to claim a reward.
When Bóréng (伯仁) arrived,
he reprimanded the masters and flogged the slaves to death.
After several such incidents,
this malpractice ceased.
He was brought into the capital as Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū (左諫議大夫),
concurrently with Lǐbù Shìláng (禮部侍郎) and Hànlín Zhíxuéshì (翰林直學士).
According to custom,
censors and literary officials on duty in the forbidden palace,
out of compassion for their toil,
were specially exempted from duty.
He was reassigned as Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎),
with his position as Zhíxuéshì (直學士) remaining unchanged.
When Zhèng Zǐdān (鄭子聃) died,
the prime minister recommended Bóréng (伯仁) to replace him.
He was then promoted to Shìjiǎng (侍講),
concurrently with Lǐbù Shìláng (禮部侍郎).
Bóréng (伯仁) had been in the Hànlín Academy for a long time,
and his writing was elegant and refined.
The emperor said:
"After Hán Fǎng (韓昉) and Zhāng Jūn (張鈞),
there was Zhái Yǒnggù (翟永固).
More recently, there were Zhāng Jǐngrén (張景仁) and Zhèng Zǐdān (鄭子聃).
Now there is only Bóréng (伯仁).
I have not seen others who are capable writers.
Lǚ Zhōnghàn (呂忠翰) drafted the imperial edict to demote Hǎilíng Shùrén (海陵庶人),
but after repeatedly revising it, he still could not fully express My intention.
Although the Zhuàngyuán (狀元) excels in prose and poetry above all others,
when it comes to imperial decrees and commands, not all of them are necessarily capable.
All Jinshì (進士) can be appointed to external posts,
and those found to be good writers should be summoned and employed."
Within a few months,
he was concurrently Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū (左諫議大夫),
and soon after, concurrently Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿).
The high officials recommended several people capable of compiling the Qǐjū Zhù (起居注),
and the emperor appointed Bóréng (伯仁) to oversee them.
He accompanied the emperor on a journey to Shàngjīng (上京).
Bóréng (伯仁) suffered from many illnesses.
Upon reaching Línhuáng (臨潢),
the cold climate caused him to fall ill,
and he returned to Zhōngdū (中都).
The following year,
when the emperor returned to Zhōngdū (中都),
he sent an envoy to inquire after him
and bestowed upon him medicinal pills.
That year,
he died.
Zhèng Zǐdān (鄭子聃), courtesy name Jǐngchún (景純),
was a native of Dàdìng Fǔ (大定府).
His father, Hóng (宏),
was the Zhīnyuán Lìng (金源令) during the Liao Dynasty.
He had two sons, Zǐjīng (子京) and Zǐdān (子聃).
Yáng Qiūxíng (楊丘行) once said to others:
"The two sons of Zhīnyuán (金源) are like phoenix feathers.
The younger one is especially brilliant
and will surely achieve fame in later generations."
Zǐdān (子聃) had a reputation for his poetic talent upon reaching adulthood.
In the third year of Tiāndé (天德)
Qiūxíng (丘行) was the Zǐdān Yòuwèi Shuàifǔ Shuài (太子左衞率府率).
The day after the palace examination,
Hǎilíng (海陵) showed Zǐdān's (子聃) examination paper to Qiūxíng (丘行),
who replied:
"He can enter the A or B ranks."
When the papers were unsealed,
he indeed ranked third in the First Class.
He was appointed as Yìchéng Céng (翼城丞),
promoted to Zàn huáng Lìng (贊皇令),
and then summoned to be Shūhuà Zhícháng (書畫直長).
Zǐdān (子聃) was quite proud of his talent and reputation,
and often felt dissatisfied at not being the first in the First Class.
In the second year of Zhènglóng (正隆), after the metropolitan examination was completed,
Hǎilíng (海陵) asked Zǐdān (子聃) about the paper of the first-ranked candidate.
Zǐdān (子聃) disparaged it.
Hǎilíng (海ilíng) asked what he thought of the fu (賦) composition.
He replied:
"It's very easy."
He then boasted,
and further claimed that no one was as good as him.
Hǎilíng (海陵) was displeased,
and so he made Zǐdān (子聃) take a miscellaneous examination for Jinshì (進士) along with Hànlín Xiūzhuàn (翰林修撰) Qí Jiǎn (綦戩),
Yáng Bóréng (楊伯仁), Xuānhuī Pànguān (宣徽判官) Zhāng Rǔlín (張汝霖), and Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì (應奉翰林文字) Lǐ Xīyán (李希顏).
On the guǐwèi (癸未) day of the seventh month,
Hǎilíng (海陵) observed the examination from the porch of Báochāng Mén (寶昌門).
He set
"If one does not value rare objects, the people will be content"
as the fu (賦) topic,
"Loyal ministers are like filial sons"
as the poem topic,
and "Worrying for the country as if hungry and thirsty"
as the essay topic.
The emperor said to the reading official Zhái Yǒnggù (翟永固):
"I have set the fu (賦) topic.
Whether one can speak of it or act upon it,
remains to be seen.
The poem and essay topics
are intended to admonish My subjects."
On the dīnghài (丁亥) day,
he personally reviewed the examination papers in the biàndiàn (便殿).
Seventy-three candidates passed.
Zǐdān (子聃) indeed came first,
and Hǎilíng (海陵) was astonished by him.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted three ranks
and appointed Hànlín Xiūzhuàn (翰林修撰).
He was reassigned as Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
There was a drought in Jīngjī (京畿).
An imperial edict ordered Zǐdān (子聃) to judge prisoners,
and then heavy rain fell.
People compared him to Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿).
He was promoted to Dàizhì (待制),
concurrently with Lìbù Lángzhōng (吏部郎中),
and reassigned as Mìshū Shàojiān (祕書少監).
He was promoted to Hànlín Zhíxuéshì (翰林直學士),
concurrently with Tàizǐ Zuǒ Yùdé (太子左諭德).
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) deeply esteemed him.
Due to illness, he requested an external appointment,
and thus became Yízhōu Fángyùshǐ (沂州防禦使).
The Crown Prince sent him very generous gifts and money,
and ordered him to travel in an enclosed carriage.
He was summoned back
to be Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū (左諫議大夫) concurrently with Zhíxuéshì (直學士).
He was reassigned as Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎) concurrently with Tóngxiū Guóshǐ (同修國史),
his position as Zhíxuéshì (直學士) remaining unchanged.
He was promoted to Shìjiǎng (侍講) concurrently with Xiū Guóshǐ (修國史).
The emperor said:
"To compile the 'Veritable Records of Hǎilíng' (海陵實錄), no one knows the details as well as Zǐdān (子聃)."
This was to specifically entrust him with historical matters.
In the twentieth year,
he died
at the age of fifty-five.
Zǐdān (子聃) was intelligent and upright,
and his writing was likewise.
Throughout his life, he authored over two thousand poems and essays.
Dǎng Huáiīng (黨懷英), courtesy name Shìjié (世傑),
was an eleventh-generation descendant of Dǎng Jìn (黨進), the Grand Commandant of the former Song Dynasty,
and a native of Féngyì (馮翊).
His father, Chúnmù (純睦),
was the Lùshì Cānjūn (錄事參軍) of Tàipíng Jūn (泰安軍).
He died in office,
and his wife and children could not return home,
so they settled there.
He was unsuccessful in the imperial examinations,
and so he abandoned worldly affairs
and roamed freely among the mountains and rivers.
His basket and gourd were often empty,
yet he was content.
In the tenth year of Dàdìng (大定),
he passed the Jinshì (進士) examination.
He was appointed as Jǔzhōu Jūnshì Pànguān (莒州軍事判官),
and successively promoted to Rǔyīn Xiànlìng (汝陰縣令),
Guóshǐyuàn Biānxiū Guān (國史院編修官), Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì (應奉翰lín Wénzì), Hànlín Dàizhì (翰lín Dàizhì), and concurrently Tóngxiū Guóshǐ (同修國史).
Huáiīng (懷英) was skilled at composing prose
and proficient in zhuànzhòu (篆籀) script,
considered the best of his time,
and scholars looked up to him.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàdìng (大定),
he and Hǎo Yǔ (郝俁), the Zhìzhōng (治中) of Fèngxiáng Fǔ (鳳翔府), served as Liáo Shǐ Kānxiū Guān (遼史刊修官).
Yìlá Yì (移剌益) and Zhào Fěng (趙渢), who were Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì (應奉翰lín Wénzì), and seven others served as Biānxiū Guān (編修官).
All stele inscriptions, epitaphs from the Liao period found among the populace, and various collected works,
or those who remembered old Liao events,
were all to be sent to the officials.
At this time,
Zhāngzōng had just ascended the throne.
He was fond of literary writings
and widely sought literary scholars to serve as his attendants.
He said to his chief ministers:
"The Hanlin Academy lacks people, what should be done?"
Zhāng Rǔlín memorialized:
"Hǎo Yǔ is able to compose literature,
and his official career is also good."
〔一一〕The Emperor said:
"Recently, among imperial edicts, Dǎng Huáiyīng's are the best."
Yílā Lǚjìn advanced, saying:
"After jinshì pass the examinations, they only learn administrative matters,
and no longer study.
Recently, they have just begun to know how to learn."
The Emperor said:
"Today's jinshì are very negligent;
they do not even know many events from the Táng History.
I am truly displeased."
The Emperor said to his chief ministers:
"Hǎo Yǔ's poetry is quite good;
in earlier times, Liú Yíng could do this,
Lǐ Yàn was not his equal."
In the first year of Míngchāng,
Huáiyīng was again promoted to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Shìjiǎng Xuéshì.
The next year,
when a discussion arose about digging moats for border defense,
Huáiyīng and sixteen others requested that the project be abandoned.
An imperial edict approved their request.
He was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì.
In the seventh year,
there was an affair at the southern suburb (for sacrifices).
〔一二〕He temporarily held the position of Zhōngshū Shìláng to read the sacrificial prayers.
The Emperor said:
"When reading the scroll, upon reaching my name,
the voice was lowered.
Although this is said to be showing respect to the sovereign,
in the context of the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
the ritual is not appropriate.
It should be read at an even tone."
In the second year of Chéng'ān, he requested to retire due to old age,
and was appointed Tàiníng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
The next year,
he was summoned to be Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ.
In the first year of Tàihé,
three additional officials were appointed for compiling the Liáo Shǐ.
An imperial edict ordered the division of work into compiling records, treatises, and biographies, with revised sections to be copied from books.
Those who had been reappointed were to bring their previous work with them.
After a long time,
he retired.
He died in the third year of Dà'ān,
at the age of seventy-eight,
and was posthumously given the epithet Wénxiàn.
After Huáiyīng retired,
Zhāngzōng issued an edict instructing the Directing Academician Chén Dàrèn to continue and complete the Liáo Shǐ.
Collated Notes

Biography 64, Literature (Part II): Zhào Fěng, Zhōu Áng, Wáng Tíngyún, Liú Áng, Lǐ Jīng, Liú Cóngyì, Lǚ Zhōngfú (with Zhāng Jiàn appended), Lǐ Chúnfǔ, Wáng Yù, Sòng Jiǔjiā, Páng Zhù, Lǐ Xiànnéng, Wáng Ruòxū, Wáng Yuánjié, Má Jiǔchóu, Lǐ Fén, Yuán Démíng (son Hǎowèn).
Zhào Fěng, courtesy name Wénrú,
was a native of Dōngpíng.
He became a jinshì in the twenty-second year of Dàdìng,
and served as Lǐbù Lángzhōng.
He had a tranquil and detached nature,
and achieved some understanding in studying the Dao.
He was particularly skilled in calligraphy,
and styled himself
"Huángshān."
Zhào Bǐngwén said:
"Fěng's regular script combines the styles of Yán and Sū,
and his running and cursive scripts incorporate various masters' styles.
His unrestrained and free quality is also similar to Yáng Níngshì,
placing him between Sū and Huáng in terms of seniority."
Dǎng Huáiyīng's small seal script,
since Lǐ Yángbīng, few have surpassed it.
Contemporaries paired Fěng with him,
calling them
"Dǎng and Zhào."
His Huángshān Jí circulated in the world.
Zhōu Áng, courtesy name Déqīng,
was a native of Zhēndìng.
His father Bólù, courtesy name Tiānxī,
was a Dàdìng jinshì,
and served as Tóngzhī Qìnnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Áng passed the examination at the age of twenty-four.
He was appointed Nánhé Bù,
where he showed extraordinary governance.
He was promoted to Liángxiāng Lìng,
then entered the court as Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
Lù Duó was dismissed for speaking out,
and Áng sent him off with a poem,
which contained slanderous remarks.
He was suspended from official selection.
After a long time,
he was reappointed as Lóngzhōu Dūjūn.
For his achievements on the border, he was recalled to serve as an official in the Three Departments.
When the Dà'ān army was raised,
he temporarily held the position of Liùbù Yuánwàiláng.
His nephew Wáng Ruòxū once studied under Áng.
Áng taught him, saying:
"Literature that is skilled outwardly but clumsy inwardly
can astonish an audience but not satisfy one in solitude;
it can earn verbal praise but not true approval."
He also said:
"Literature takes meaning as its master
and language as its servant.
If the master is strong and the servant is weak, no command will be disobeyed.
Today's people often pride themselves on their servants,
to the point where they become unruly and difficult to control,
and some even make their servants rule over their master.
Even if the language is extremely skillful,
how can it be proper literature?"
Áng was filial and friendly,
valued reputation and integrity.
His scholarship was pure and upright,
and his writing style was lofty and elegant.
All scholars respected him as their teacher.
After serving in the Censorate and ministries,
he was pushed out by others,
and was eventually punished for a poem,
exiled to the eastern sea for over ten years.
When he first entered the Hanlin Academy,
he spoke out even more urgently.
Serving as an assistant in the Three Departments was not to his liking.
He followed the imperial clan member Chéngyù's army.
Chéngyù suffered a defeat
and fled to Shànggǔ.
The troops wanted to return directly,
but Áng alone refused to comply.
When the city fell,
he died in the calamity with his cousin's son SìMíng.
SìMíng, courtesy name Huìzhī.
Wáng Tíngyún, courtesy name Zǐduān,
was a native of Liáodōng.
Before he was one year old,
he could recognize seventeen characters when looking at books.
At seven, he studied poetry;
at eleven, he composed complete poems on given topics.
When he was slightly older,
Wáng Xiāo of Zhuōjùn saw him once
and expected him to become a national talent.
He passed the jinshì examination in the sixteenth year of Dàdìng.
He was appointed Ēnzhōu Jūnshì Pànguān,
and immediately gained a reputation in governance.
A local resident named Zōu Sì plotted a rebellion.
When the matter was discovered,
over a thousand people were arrested,
but Zōu Sì had hidden and could not be found.
The imperial court sent Dàlǐ Sīzhí Wáng Zhòngkē to handle the case.
Tíngyún, using a stratagem, captured Zōu Sì,
distinguished between those mistakenly implicated,
and only twelve individuals were found to be involved in the premeditated plot.
He was again appointed Guǎntáo Zhǔbù.
In the third month of the first year of Míngchāng,
Zhāngzōng issued an imperial instruction to the Hànlín Academy, saying:
"The essays Wáng Tíngyún tested with
have sentences that are too long.
I do not like this,
and I also fear that people from all directions will imitate it."
He also said to Píngzhāng Zhāng Rǔlín:
"Wáng Tíngyún's literary and artistic skills are quite good,
but his wording is not vigorous.
His talent is high,
so it should not be difficult to change."
In the fourth month,
Tíngyún was summoned to take an examination for a court position
and was selected.
The Yùshǐ Tái stated that Tíngyún had committed a corruption offense while in Guǎntáo
and should not be placed in the Guǎngé.
Consequently, he was dismissed.
He then chose to live in Zhāngdé,
bought land in Lónglǜ,
and studied at Huánghuáshān Temple,
thereby adopting its name as his own style.
In the twelfth month of that year,
the Emperor, when discussing academicians,
sighed at the lack of talent.
Cānzhèng Shǒuzhēn said:
"Wáng Tíngyún is such a person."
In the third year,
he was summoned to be Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì.
He was ordered to categorize famous calligraphies and paintings with Mìshū Láng Zhāng Rǔfāng,
and they divided the classified works into five hundred and fifty scrolls.
In the eighth month of the fifth year,
the Emperor looked at his chief ministers and said:
“Wáng Tíngyún (王庭筠), as an Acolyte (應奉),
I wish to entrust him with edicts and imperial pronouncements.
Such a talent is not easily found.
Recently, Dǎng Huáiyīng (黨懷英) composed the encomium for Chángbái Shān (長白山),
but it was not at all skillful.
I hear that many literati are jealous of Tíngyún (庭筠),
and they criticize him based on his conduct, not his writing.
Generally, scholars are often argumentative,
or they form factions.
In ancient times, the scholars of the Eastern Hàn (東漢) Dynasty divided into factions with the eunuchs;
this is certainly not strange.
But why did people like Niú Sēngrú (牛僧孺) and Lǐ Déyù (李德裕) in the Táng (唐) Dynasty,
and Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光) and Wáng Ānshí (王安石) in the Sòng (宋) Dynasty,
all being Confucians,
mutually denounce and undermine each other?”
Thereupon, Tíngyún (庭筠) was promoted to Hanlin Compiler (翰林修撰).
In the first month of the first year of Chéng'ān (承安),
due to the matter of Zhào Bǐngwén (趙秉文)’s memorial,
he was demoted by one rank,
received sixty strokes of the rod,
and was dismissed from office.
The details are in the biography of Bǐngwén (秉文).
In the second year,
he was demoted to Defense Commissioner’s Judge (防禦判官) of Zhèngzhōu (鄭州).
In the fourth year,
he was reinstated as Acolyte of the Hanlin Academy (應奉翰林文字).
In the first year of Tàihé (泰和),
he was again made Hanlin Compiler (翰林修撰).
He accompanied the Emperor on the autumn hunt (秋山),
and composed over thirty imperial poems (應制賦詩),
which the Emperor greatly praised.
The following year,
he died
at the age of forty-seven.
The Emperor, long aware of his poverty,
decreed that the authorities should provide 800,000 cash for his funeral expenses,
and ordered the collection of his lifelong poems and essays to be stored in the Imperial Library (祕閣).
He also bestowed his own imperial poems upon Tíngyún (庭筠)’s family,
with a preface stating:
“Wáng Zūngǔ (王遵古)
was a friend of mine.
His son, Tíngyún (庭筠),
was again chosen for his talent to serve in the Forbidden Forest (禁林) for ten years from beginning to end.
Now that he has passed away,
the Jade Hall (玉堂) and Eastern Pavilion (東觀) will no longer have such a person.”
Tíngyún (庭筠) had a distinguished and magnificent appearance,
was good at witty conversation and laughter.
Outwardly, he seemed reserved and noble,
so people initially dared not approach him.
Once met,
a genial atmosphere radiated from his face,
and he would greet people with such warmth as if he feared not being timely enough.
If there was anything commendable, he would praise it profusely,
and even if he was wronged a hundred times later, he would bear no resentment.
Those who followed him, such as Hán Wēnfǔ (韓溫甫), Lù Yuánhēng (路元亨), Zhāng Jìnqīng (張進卿), and Lǐ Gōngdù (李公度),
and those he recommended, such as Zhào Bǐngwén (趙秉文), Féng Bì (馮璧), and Lǐ Chúnfǔ (李純甫),
were all prominent scholars of their time.
The world acknowledged his ability to discern talent.
His writing expressed what he wanted to say.
In his later years, his poetic meter became profound and rigorous,
and he was particularly skilled in difficult rhymes in his seven-character long poems.
He authored ten volumes of *Cóng Biàn* (藂辨)
and forty volumes of collected works.
His calligraphy followed Mǐ Yuánzhāng (米元章),
and he, along with Zhào Fēng (趙渢) and Zhào Bǐngwén (趙秉文), was known as a master.
Tíngyún (庭筠) was especially skilled in landscape paintings and ink bamboo.
His son, Mànqìng (曼慶),
was also good at poetry and calligraphy,
and served as a Right Section Chief (右司郎中) in the Provincial Secretariat (行省).
He styled himself
“Dànyóu” (澹游).
Liú Áng (劉昂), courtesy name Zhī'áng (之昂),
was a native of Xīngzhōu (興州).
He obtained his *jìnshì* degree in the nineteenth year of Dàdìng (大定).
From his great-great-grandfather downwards, seven generations had passed the imperial examinations.
Áng (昂) was naturally sharp and intelligent.
His rhymed prose (律賦) formed a unique style,
and his poetry adopted the late Táng (唐) style,
excelling especially in *juéjù* (絕句) quatrains.
According to Lǐ Chúnfǔ (李純甫)’s *Gùrén Wài Chuán* (故人外傳),
Áng (昂) entered officialdom early.
At the age of thirty-three, he became a clerk in the Department of State Affairs (尚書省掾),
and was later transferred to Deputy Transport Commissioner (轉運副使) of the Píngliáng (平涼) circuit.
At that time, a fortuneteller said that Áng (昂)'s highest office would be a fifth-rank official,
but Áng (昂) did not believe it.
Soon after, he resigned due to mourning for his mother,
and remained without office for ten years.
He settled in Luòyáng (洛陽),
intending to spend the rest of his life there.
Someone recommended his talent to Zhāngzōng (章宗).
In the early Tàihé (泰和) period,
he was promoted from Assistant Instructor of the Directorate of Education (國子司業) to Left Section Chief (左司郎中).
It happened that Zhǎngshū Dàzhōng (掌書大中) and Jiǎ Xuàn (賈鉉) leaked information about appointments,
and they were impeached by remonstrators.
The legal proceedings implicated Áng (昂).
Zhāngzōng (章宗) was furious.
Prominent figures of the time, such as Shǐ Sù (史肅), Lǐ Zhù (李著), Wáng Yǔ (王宇), and the imperial clan member Cóng Yù (從郁), were all banished.
Xuàn (鉉) was also dismissed from his post soon after.
Áng (昂) was demoted to Defense Commissioner’s Judge (留守判官) of Shàngjīng (上京),
and died en route.
It turned out exactly as the fortuneteller had predicted.
Lǐ Jīng (李經), courtesy name Tiānyīng (天英),
was a native of Jǐnzhōu (錦州).
He composed poetry with extreme diligence,
enjoyed using striking phrases,
and did not imitate his predecessors.
Lǐ Chúnfǔ (李純甫) saw his poetry and said:
“He is truly the Tàibái (太白) of this era.”
From then on, his reputation greatly soared.
He failed the examinations twice
and then left official life.
After the southern migration,
a memorial from his local commander reached the imperial court.
Scholars and officials recognized it, saying:
“This is the writing of Tiānyīng (天英).”
The court deliberated and, based on his military achievements (武功), appointed him as Assistant Prefect (倅) of his prefecture.
His ultimate fate is unknown.
Liú Cóngyì (劉從益), courtesy name Yúnqīng (雲卿),
was a native of Húnyuán (渾源).
His great-great-grandfather, Huī (撝),
obtained his *cífù jìnshì* (詞賦進士) degree in the first year of Tiānhuì (天會).
