Many of his descendants entered officialdom through the imperial examinations.
Cóngyì (從益) passed the *jìnshì* examination in the first year of Dà'ān (大安).
He successively held the post of Censor (監察御史).
He incurred disfavor and was dismissed for arguing right from wrong with those in power.
After a long time,
he was reinstated as Magistrate of Yèxiàn (葉縣).
He reformed education and encouraged good customs,
displaying the demeanor of an upright ancient official.
Since the outbreak of war in Yè (葉),
its households had decreased by one-third.
There were over seventeen thousand *mǔ* of uncultivated land,
yet its annual revenue remained seventy thousand *shí* of grain as before.
Cóngyì (從益) requested from the Grand Minister of Agriculture (大司農)
to reduce this by ten thousand *shí*,
which greatly benefited the people,
and over four thousand returning refugee households came back.
Not long after,
he was summoned to the capital.
The common people went to the Department of State Affairs (尚書省) to beg for him to stay,
but it was not granted.
He entered the capital and was appointed Acolyte of the Hanlin Academy (應奉翰林文字).
A month later, he died of illness
at the age of forty-four.
Upon hearing this, the people of Yè (葉)
stopped their Dūanwǔ (端午) festivities, set up an empty seat, and wept,
and also erected a stone to praise his virtues
to express their sorrow.
Cóngyì (從益) was broadly learned and had a strong memory,
excelling in classical studies.
As a writer, he was skilled in poetry,
especially in five-character verse.
He authored *Péngmén Jí* (蓬門集).
His son, Qí (祁), courtesy name Jīngshú (京叔),
was a student of the Imperial Academy (太學生)
and had a great literary reputation.
During the chaos and decline at the end of the Jīn (金) Dynasty,
he wrote *Guīqián Zhì* (歸潛志) to record events of the Jīn (金) Dynasty,
which was extensively used in the compilation of the *Jīn Shǐ* (金史).
Lǚ Zhōngfú (呂中孚), courtesy name Xìnchén (信臣),
was a native of Nángōng (南宮), Jìzhōu (冀州).
Zhāng Jiàn (張建), courtesy name Jífǔ (吉甫),
was a native of Púchéng (蒲城).
Both were renowned for their poetry.
Zhōngfú (中孚) authored *Qīngzhāng Jí* (清漳集).
Jiàn (建),
in the early Míngchāng (明昌) period,
was appointed Instructor (教官) of Jiàngzhōu (絳州).
He was summoned to be an Imperial Instructor (宮教) and Acolyte of the Hanlin Academy (應奉翰林文字).
Due to old age, he requested to retire.
Zhāngzōng (章宗) cherished his pure and unadorned character
and did not want him to leave.
He was appointed Concurrently in Charge of the Defense Commissioner (同知防禦使) of Huázhōu (華州),
and was also bestowed with a poem as a mark of favor.
He styled himself
“Lánquán” (蘭泉),
and his collected works circulated in the world.
Lǐ Chúnfǔ 李純甫, courtesy name Zhīchún 之純,
was a native of Xiāngyīn 襄陰, Hóngzhōu 弘州.
His grandfather, Ānshàng 安上,
once topped the imperial examinations in Xījīng 西京.
His father, Cǎi 采,
died while serving as Zhìzhōng 治中 of Yìdūfǔ 益都府.
Chúnfǔ 純甫 was exceptionally intelligent in his youth.
He initially studied cí fù 詞賦 (rhapsodies and prose poems),
but after reading the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū 左氏春秋 (Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals),
he greatly loved it
and thus changed to studying jīngyì 經義 (classical exegesis).
He passed the jīngyì 經義 jinshì 進士 examination in Chéng'ān 成安 second year.
His writing style emulated Zhuāng Zhōu 莊周, Liè Yùkòu 列禦寇, the Zuǒ Shì 左氏, and the Zhàn Guó Cè 戰國策 (Strategies of the Warring States),
and many later scholars took him as their model.
He also enjoyed discussing military strategy
and was deeply concerned with governing the world.
When Zhāngzōng 章宗 launched a southern campaign,
Chúnfǔ 純甫 twice submitted memorials outlining the probable outcome,
which the Emperor found remarkable.
He was dispatched to the army,
and later events largely unfolded as he had predicted.
The Prime Ministers admired his writing
and recommended him to the Hànlín Hànlín (Hanlin Academy).
When the Dà Yuán 大元 (Great Yuan) army arose,
he again submitted a memorial discussing current affairs,
but received no response.
When Xuānzōng 宣宗 moved to Biàn 汴,
he re-entered the Hànlín Hànlín.
At that time, Prime Minister Gāo Qí 高琪 wielded arbitrary power,
and Chúnfǔ 純甫 was promoted to Zuǒsī Dūshì 左司都事 (Investigator of the Left Department).
Chúnfǔ 純甫 realized that Gāo Qí 高琪 was destined to fail,
and resigned, citing his mother's old age.
Soon after, Gāo Qí 高琪 was executed,
and Chúnfǔ 純甫 re-entered the Hànlín Hànlín,
successively serving as Zhī Gòngjǔ 知貢舉 (Examiner of the Imperial Examinations).
Towards the end of Zhèngdà 正大,
he was demoted for exceeding the new regulations in selecting candidates
and was sent out as Cúi Fāngzhōu 倅坊州 (Assistant Administrator of Fangzhou).
Before he could take up the post,
he was reassigned as Pànguān 判官 (Judicial Administrator) of Jīngzhàofǔ 京兆府.
He died in Biàn 汴
at the age of forty-seven.
Chúnfǔ 純甫 was intelligent and astute.
In his youth, he was self-assured of his talent,
believing that fame and success were easily attainable.
He composed the "Ǎibǎi Fù 矮柏賦" (Rhapsody on the Short Cypress),
comparing himself to Zhūgě Kǒngmíng 諸葛孔明 and Wáng Jǐnglüè 王景略.
From a minor official position, he submitted a ten-thousand-word memorial,
citing the Sòng 宋 dynasty as evidence,
which was very incisive.
However, those in power suppressed him, deeming him impractical.
In middle age,
realizing that his principles would not be put into practice,
he indulged more in wine and lived unrestrainedly,
with no ambition for official advancement.
Before completing his official assessment,
he soon retired to seclusion.
He spent his days associating with Chan monks and scholars,
engaging in literature and drinking.
He would sing and shout, bare-chested, disregardful of etiquette,
sometimes drinking for months without sobering up.
If anyone invited him to drink,
he would always go, regardless of their status.
He would always get drunk,
but even when heavily intoxicated, he never stopped writing.
In his later years, however, he became fond of Buddhism
and diligently explored its profound meanings.
He categorized his own writings:
those discussing human nature and principles, and relating to the Buddhist and Daoist schools, were called
"Nèi Gǎo 內藁" (Inner Drafts),
while other writings on external matters were called
"Wài Gǎo 外藁" (Outer Drafts).
He also wrote commentaries on the Léngyán Jīng 楞嚴經, Jīngāng Jīng 金剛經, Lǎozǐ 老子, and Zhuāngzǐ 莊子.
Additionally, he wrote Zhōngyōng Jíjiě 中庸集解 (Collected Commentaries on the Doctrine of the Mean) and Míngdào Jíjiě 鳴道集解 (Collected Commentaries on the Clang of the Dao),
which he referred to as
"Zhōngguó Xīnxué 中國心學 (Chinese Philosophy of Mind) and Xīfāng Wénjiào 西方文教 (Western Literary Teachings)".
These amounted to hundreds of thousands of words,
and for this reason, he was criticized by followers of orthodox Confucianism.
Wáng Yù 王欝, courtesy name Fēibó 飛伯,
was a native of Dàxīng 大興.
He had a magnificent appearance,
with eyes like a falcon's.
In his youth, he lived at Diàotái 釣臺,
studying behind closed doors
and avoiding human interaction.
After a long time,
his writing style emulated Liǔ Zōngyuán 柳宗元;
it was expansive, unconventional, and ancient,
often running to several thousand words.
His poetry was outstanding and unrestrained,
imitating Lǐ Bái 李白.
He once wrote "Wángzǐ Xiǎozhuàn 王子小傳" (A Short Biography of Prince Wáng) as an autobiography.
In the first year of Tiānxīng 天興,
when Biànjīng 汴京 was besieged,
he submitted a memorial on current affairs,
but received no response.
In the fourth month,
when the siege somewhat eased,
he bravely broke out,
and was captured by soldiers.
Their general treated him very well,
but Yù 欝 acted without caution or defense,
which made his subordinates wary,
and he was killed.
At the time of his death,
he took out a book from his bosom and said,
"This is my life's work.
It can be passed on to the scholar-officials of Zhōngzhōu 中州, saying:
Wáng Yù 王欝 is dead."
He was in his thirties.
Those who gained renown for their poetry at the same time
were Léi Guǎn 雷琯, Hóu Cè 侯冊, and Wáng Yuáncuì 王元粹.
Sòng Jiǔjiā 宋九嘉, courtesy name Fēiqīng 飛卿,
was a native of Xiàjīn 夏津.
He was upright, straightforward, and bold.
In his youth, he studied at the Imperial Academy
and was known for his ability in composing fù 賦.
Later, he studied with Lǐ Chúnfǔ 李純甫;
his writing possessed an unusual spirit,
and he was considered on par with Léi Yuān 雷淵 and Lǐ Jīng 李經.
He passed the jinshì 進士 examination in Zhìníng 至寧 first year.
He successively served as magistrate of four counties: Lántián 藍田, Gāolíng 高陵, Fúfēng 扶風, and Sānshuǐ 三水,
and was praised for his competence in all of them.
He entered the Hànlín Hànlín as Yìngfèng 應奉 (Attendant for Special Service).
During the Zhèngdà 正大 era,
he left due to illness.
He died during the calamity of the Guǐsì 癸巳 year.
Páng Zhù 龐鑄, courtesy name Cáiqīng 才卿,
was a native of Liáodōng 遼東.
He passed the examination at a young age
and made a name for himself in officialdom.
After the southward relocation,
he served as Hànlín Dàizhì 翰林待制 (Academician in Attendance),
and was promoted to Hùbù Shìláng 戶部侍郎 (Vice Minister of Revenue).
He was demoted for associating with powerful relatives
and was sent out as Cúi Dōngpíng 倅東平 (Assistant Administrator of Dongping).
He was then reassigned as Jīngzhàolù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ 京兆路轉運使 (Transport Commissioner of Jingzhao Circuit),
and died.
He was widely learned and skilled in writing,
and good at poetry.
His expressions were uniquely vigorous and extraordinary,
and many people spread them.
Lǐ Xiànnéng 李獻能, courtesy name Qīnshú 欽叔,
was a native of Hézhōng 河中.
His ancestors included a Jīnwǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn 金吾衞上將軍 (General-in-chief of the Imperial Guard),
and at that time, they were known as
"Lǐ Jīnwǔ Jiā 李金吾家" (The Li Family of the Imperial Guard).
By the time Xiànnéng 獻能 and his brothers were renowned for their literary talents,
his elder cousins Xiànqīng 獻卿 and Xiànchéng 獻誠, and younger cousin Xiànfǔ 獻甫, successively passed the imperial examinations.
Hence, the Lǐ 李 family had
"Sìguìtáng 四桂堂" (Hall of Four Laurels).
Xiànnéng 獻能 studied diligently and read widely;
in writing, he was particularly skilled in sìliù 四六 (parallel prose).
In Zhēnyòu 貞祐 third year,
he was specially granted the cí fù 詞賦 jinshì 進士 degree,
ranked first in the court examination,
and achieved superior grade in the Hóngcí 宏詞 (grand style) examination.
He was appointed Yìngfèng Hànlín Wénzì 應奉翰林文字 (Attendant for Special Service in the Hanlin Academy).
He served in the Hàn Yuàn 翰苑 (Hanlin Academy) for a total of ten years,
then was sent out as Fūzhōu Guānchá Pànguān 鄜州觀察判官 (Judicial Administrator of Fuzhou Prefecture).
Upon recommendation, he was reinstated as Yìngfèng 應奉,
and soon promoted to Xiūzhuàn 修撰 (Compiler).
Towards the end of Zhèngdà 正大,

he was appointed Zhèn Nánjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ Chōng Hézhōng Shuàifǔ Jīnglìguān 鎮南軍節度副使充河中帥府經歷官 (Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhennan Commandery concurrently serving as Judicial Official of Hezhong Commander's Residence).
When the Dà Yuán 大元 army captured Hézhōng 河中,
he fled to Shǎnxī Zhōu 陝州.
The Xíngshěng 行省 (Provincial Administration) provisionally appointed him Zuǒyòusī Lángzhōng 左右司郎中 (Director of the Left and Right Departments).
He was killed during Zhào Sānsān's 趙三三 military mutiny
at the age of forty-three.
Xiànnéng 獻能 was small in stature and dark-complexioned,
with a considerable beard.
He was skilled in discussion;
whenever he expounded on ancient and modern topics, his voice was clear and resonant, pleasant to listen to.
In his poetry, he aimed for the elegance of the Fēng Yǎ 風雅 (Airs and Odes),
and also meticulously crafted musical compositions.
In the Hàn Yuàn 翰苑,
he was known for his quick wit and appropriateness in responding to situations.
Zhào Bǐngwén 趙秉文 and Lǐ Chúnfǔ 李純甫 once said,
"Lǐ Xiànnéng 李獻能 is naturally gifted as a Hanlin scholar of this age."
Therefore, they frequently recommended him
and did not allow him to leave the academy.
His family was originally wealthy,
but lost everything during the Zhēnyòu 貞祐 rebellion.
In the capital, he had no means to support himself.
His mother, who was accustomed to extravagance
and indulged herself greatly,
would inevitably scold him if things were not to her liking.
People considered his situation almost unbearable,
but Xiànnéng 獻能 handled it with composure.
People of his time praised him for his filial piety.
He once told others,
"In my youth, I dreamed that my official rank would reach the fifth grade,
and my lifespan would not reach fifty."
Later, it turned out exactly as he had said.
Jiǔchóu's nature and disposition were wild and unconstrained.
He was aloof and self-indulgent.
When interacting with people,
if a single word didn't align, he would leave directly without looking back.
He felt that he could never get along with the world.
After a short while,
he again pleaded illness and departed.
He lived in Yǎnchéng.
In the first year of Tiānxīng (1232),
the Great Yuán army entered Hénán.
He took his family and fled to Quèshān,
where he was captured by soldiers.
He was driven to Guǎngpíng
and died of illness
at the age of fifty.
Jiǔchóu initially studied the Yìjīng due to its philosophical interpretations.
Later, he liked Shào Yáofū's Huángjí Shū,
and thus studied mathematics.
He also liked the arts of divination and guessing hidden objects (shèfù).
In his later years, he especially enjoyed medicine,
and associated with the famous physician Zhāng Zǐhé,
who fully transmitted his teachings.
Jiǔchóu also embellished the books Zhāng Zǐhé had written.
His writings were precise, unique, and robust,
and his poetry was particularly exquisite.
Later, to avoid slander and jealousy,
he observed a precept not to write.
Since Míngchāng,
five individuals were praised as "divine prodigies."
Cháng Tiānshòu of Tàiyuán could compose poetry at the age of four.
Liú Zī, Liú Wēi, and Zhāng Hànchén later had no reputation.
Only Zhījí was able to establish himself.
Elderly scholars like Zhào Bǐngwén
referred to him as "recluse" without using his given name.
Lǐ Fén, courtesy name Chángyuán,
was a native of Píngjìn, Tàiyuán.
He was high-spirited
and unrestrained.
He had a quick and irritable temper;
when provoked, he would immediately become angry.
Because of this, he was disliked by many.
He enjoyed reading history.
He was skilled in poetry,
which was bold, robust, and structured.
He fled the chaos and entered Guānzhōng.
Jīngzhàoyǐn Zǐróng appreciated his talent
and invited him to his retinue.
He stayed for two years, then left
for Jīngzhōu,
where he called upon Zuǒchéng Zhāng Xíngxìn.
Upon their first meeting, Zhāng Xíngxìn treated him with the courtesy due to an esteemed guest.
During the Yuánguāng era (1222-1224),
he traveled to Dàliáng.
He took the jìnshì examination but failed.
Through a recommendation, he became a copyist in the History Academy.
A copyist
was merely a junior clerk who copied books.
Whenever a compiler received daily records,
and the compilation was finalized,
the draft would be given to the copyist.
The copyist would then transcribe a clean copy and present it to the head of the academy.
Fén, having taken on this role,
was extremely dissatisfied.
At that time, Zhào Bǐngwén was a Grand Academician,
and Léi Yuān and Lǐ Xiànnéng were also in the academy.
During the process of editing and revising,
Fén would sit beside them, straightening his robe and sitting upright,
reading a chapter from Tàishǐgōng (Sīmǎ Qiān) or Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
sometimes several hundred words.
His voice was resonant and clear,
as if no one else was present.
After finishing,
he would look at the seated officials and casually say a word:
"See?"
The officials holding the brushes accumulated resentment,
and Léi and Lǐ especially gnashed their teeth.
They then accused him of insulting his superiors to the authorities.
However, contemporary opinion also included those who considered Léi and Lǐ to be in the wrong.
Soon after, he was dismissed and returned to Guānzhōng.
The following year, he came to the capital,
submitted a memorial discussing current affairs,
but it was not accepted.
He left to stay between Táng and Dèng.
Shān Gōngwǔ Xiān appointed him as a lecturer and debater in the mobile secretariat (xíng shàngshūshěng).
However,
Xiān and the Vice-Chancellor Wányán Sīliè had differing opinions
and were somewhat plotting for their own security.
Fearing Fén's outspokenness,
Xiān wished to eliminate him.
Fén realized this
and fled to Bìyáng.
Xiān ordered Commander Wáng Dé to pursue and capture him.
He was imprisoned in Mǎpíng
and died by refusing food
before the age of forty.
Fén wrote many poems in his lifetime,
but did not collect them himself.
Only two or three tenths of them are transmitted in the world.
Yuán Démíng
was descended from the Tuòbá Wèi,
a native of Xiùróng, Tàiyuán.
From childhood, he loved to read.
He never spoke of vulgar worldly matters.
He was cheerful and without boundaries,
and content with simple clothes and vegetarian food.
His family dared not trouble him with matters of livelihood.
He failed examinations repeatedly,
and roamed among mountains and rivers,
drinking wine and composing poetry to amuse himself.
He died at the age of forty-eight.
He has a collection, Dōngyán Jí, in three volumes.
His son, Hàowèn,
was most famous.
Hàowèn, courtesy name Yùzhī,
could compose poetry at the age of seven.
At fourteen,
he studied with Hǎo Jìnqīng of Língchuān.
He did not pursue examination studies,
but was thoroughly versed in the Classics, commentaries, and various schools of thought.
After six years, his studies were complete.
He descended Mount Tàiháng
and crossed the Yellow River,
composing poems like "Jīshān" and "Qíntái."
Zhào Bǐngwén of the Ministry of Rites saw them
and believed there had been no such works in recent times.
Consequently, his name shook the capital.
In the fifth year of Zhōngxīng Dìng (1216), he passed the examination
and successively served as Magistrate of Nèixiāng.
During the Zhèngdà era (1224-1232),
he was Magistrate of Nányáng.
In the early Tiānxīng era (1232),
he was promoted to Clerk in the Secretariat (shàngshūshěng yuàn).
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed Dūshì of the Zuǒsī,
then transferred to Yuánwàiláng of the Zuǒsī in the Mobile Secretariat.
After the fall of Jīn,
he did not serve.
His writing followed rules
and encompassed various styles.
His poetry was unique and rugged, utterly without carving or embellishment;
it was skillfully intricate but free from excessive splendor.
His five-character verse was lofty, ancient, and deeply melancholic.
His seven-character yuefu did not use ancient titles,
but specifically expressed new ideas.
His ballads were impassioned, embodying the spirit of Yōu and Bìng.
His long and short verses,
praising new tunes,
to express grievances and affections numbered several hundred pieces.
After the war,
the old scholars were all gone.
Hàowèn emerged as a leading master of his generation.
Commemorative tablets and epitaphs from all directions flocked to his door.
His writings include several volumes of essays and poems, one volume of Dùshī Xué, three volumes of Dōngpō Shīyǎ, one volume of Jǐnjī, and ten volumes of Shīwén Zìjǐng.
In his later years, he especially took on the responsibility of writing historical works,
believing that since the Jīn Yuán clan had ruled the empire,
its institutions and laws had nearly reached the level of the Hàn and Táng,
and with the fall of the state, its history should be written,
a task he ought to undertake.
At that time, the Veritable Records of the Jīn Dynasty were in the possession of Myriarchy Zhāng in Shùntiān.
He then spoke to Zhāng,
expressing his wish to compile them.
However, he was later obstructed by Lè Kuí and stopped.
Hàowèn said:
"One generation's accomplishments cannot be allowed to perish without being transmitted."
So he built a pavilion at home
and wrote his works there,
thus naming it
"Wild History."
He gathered the posthumous words and past deeds of Jīn Yuán rulers and officials,
collecting what he heard.
Whenever he gained something, he would record it in tiny characters on small pieces of paper,
reaching over a million words.
What is transmitted today includes the Zhōngzhōu Jí and several volumes of Rénchén Zábiān.
He died at the age of sixty-eight.
The compilation of the Jīn Shǐ largely drew upon his writings.
A赞 says: Hán Fǎng and Wú Jī
were Chu (楚) talents employed by Jìn (晉);
they were also sufficient to represent the literature of their generation.
Cài Guī and Mǎ Dìngguó were comprehensive and erudite;
Hú Lì and Yáng Bórén were sharp and eloquent;
Zhèng Zǐdān and Má Jiǔchóu were outstanding and brilliant;
Wáng Yù and Sòng Jiǔjiā were soaring and unrestrained.
The three Lǐs were extraordinary:
Lǐ Chúnpǔ understood the Way,
Lǐ Fén was strong-willed,
and Lǐ Xiàn was especially praised for his pure filial piety.
Wáng Tíngyún, Dǎng Huáiīng, and Yuán Hàowèn were well-known in different eras.
Wáng Jìng, Liú Cóngyì, and Wáng Ruòxū excelled in governance,
and their literary achievements did not overshadow their strengths.
Cài Sōngnián, among literary figures,
held the highest official rank.
It is said that he spoke of profit to the Jīn (金) emperor,
instigated factional disputes,
and killed Tián Jué.
Did his literary talent fail to cover his shortcomings?
He had admirable conduct towards his stepmother,
and upon his death, his family had no surplus assets.
These are points worth noting.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 65: Filial Piety and Friendship Wēndíhǎn Wòlǔbǔ, Chén Yán, Liú Yú, Mèng Xìng, Wáng Zhèn, Liú Zhèng
Filial piety and friendship are the ultimate human conduct,
and they are inherent in human nature.
A father desires his son to be filial,
a brother desires his younger brother to be friendly.
Is this not human sentiment?
To be filial as a son
and friendly as a younger brother,
is this not human nature?
Yet, when human sentiment demands human nature,
there are cases where the desired outcome is not met.
To exert all one's strength in this
is it not difficult?
Heaven produces the five grains to nourish people;
the five grains have their nature.
To till fields and labor diligently, hoping for a harvest,
is the sentiment of a farmer.
When the five grains ripen,
people are nurtured;
how is this different?
However, even in the eras of Táng (唐) and Yú (虞),
"the common people were hindered by hunger,"
and Yǔ (禹) could not avoid entrusting the matter to Jì (稷).
"The hundred clans were not affectionate, the five relationships were not harmonious,"
and Yǔ (禹) could not avoid entrusting the matter to Xiè (契).
From this, we know that successful completion is not guaranteed,
just as filial piety and friendship are not easily attained.
Therefore,
"a good year"
and
"a great good year"
are written differently in the scriptures of the sages,
and filial piety and friendship are recorded as ultimate conduct in the histories of successive dynasties.
The teachings of encouraging agriculture and promoting filial piety have not ceased in the governance of successive dynasties,
and since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, there have been official categories for filial piety, fraternal love, and diligent farming.
Zhāngzōng once said:
"For people of filial piety and righteousness,
their moral conduct is already complete;
even if they have aspirations for gain, they still do not cease to do good."
This is perhaps a good teaching from an emperor.
In the Jīn (金) era, only six people demonstrated filial piety and friendship to the extent of being recognized and recorded in historical texts.
Hence, the Biographies of Filial Piety and Friendship are compiled.
Wēndíhǎn Wòlǔbǔ was
a *méng'ān* (猛安) from Sònggěxié Sīhún in Xīběi Lù.
At the age of fifteen,
during his father's mourning,
he abstained from alcohol and meat,
and built a hut by the graveside.
When his mother fell ill,
he cut flesh from his thigh to treat her,
and she recovered.
An imperial edict appointed him as an imperial guard.
Chén Yán was
from Jí Xiàn, Wèi Zhōu.
His family had been farmers for generations.
His father, Chén Guāng,
was selected in the martial arts examination during the late Sòng (宋) dynasty,
and was appointed as the magistrate of Shòuyáng,
but did not take office.
When Jīn (金) forces captured Biàn (汴),
Chén Guāng fell ill
within the besieged city.
Chén Yán, after much difficulty, crossed the river
to visit his father,
and then helped the ailing Chén Guāng return north.
Chén Guāng's family servant, Mǒu Liáng, harbored ill intentions,
and falsely accused Chén Guāng of killing someone with a bandit.
Chén Guāng was imprisoned,
and unable to endure the torture,
he falsely confessed.
Chén Yán went to the prefecture to plead to die in his father's place.
The prefect, Xú (徐) Mǒu, pitied him
and dared not make a decision.
Just then, a military commander arrived at the prefecture.
Chén Yán's situation was reported to him,
and the commander said:
"This is truly a filial son!"
So, he released both of them.
In the seventh year of Tiānhuì,
an imperial edict honored his household.
Liú Yú was
from Dì Zhōu.
His family was extremely poor,
and he could not afford a proper funeral for his deceased mother.
So, he pawned his son to cover the funeral expenses.
In the third year of Míngchāng,
an imperial edict bestowed grain and silk upon him
and exempted him from levies for life.
Mèng Xìng lost his father early
and served his mother with filial piety and reverence.
After his mother's death,
he performed the mourning and burial rites completely.
He served his elder brother as if he were his father.
In the third year of Míngchāng,
an imperial edict bestowed ten rolls of silk and twenty *shí* (石) of grain upon him.
Wáng Zhèn was
from Wéndēng Xiàn, Nínghǎi Zhōu.
He was a student of the *jìnshì* (進士) examination.
When his mother suffered from a stroke,
he cut flesh from his thigh and mixed it into her food and drink,
and her illness subsequently healed.
After his mother's death,
he mourned and wept excessively,
causing an opacity in his eyes.
After the mourning period ended,
his eyes healed without treatment,
all believed this to be due to his filial piety.
He was specially granted the title of *tóng jìnshì chūshēn* (同進士出身),
and an imperial edict instructed the Ministry of Personnel to propose an official appointment for him.
Liú Zhèng was
from Míng Zhōu.
He was inherently profoundly filial.
When his elderly mother lost her sight,
Liú Zhèng would frequently lick her eyes with his tongue,
and after more than ten days, his mother could see things again.
When his mother fell ill,
he attended her day and night,
without loosening his clothes.
He cut flesh from his thigh and fed it to her two or three times.
After his mother's death,
he carried earth to build her tomb.
When neighbors wished to assist him,
Liú Zhèng declined.
On the day of the funeral,
birds sang mournfully,
soaring and gathering among the trees on the hill.
He lived in a hut by the tomb for three years.
The Defensive Commissioner reported this,
and he was appointed *tàizǐ zhǎngyǐn chéng* (太子掌飲丞).
Recluses Chǔ Chéngliàng, Wáng Qùfēi, Zhào Zhì, Dù Shíshēng, Hǎo Tiāntǐng, Xuē Jìxiān, Gāo Zhòngzhèn, Zhāng Qián, Wáng Rǔméi, Sòng Kě, Xīn Yuàn, Wáng Yǔkě
Kǒngzǐ praised the recluses Bóyí, Shúqí, Yíyì, Zhū Zhāng, Liǔxià Huì, and Shǎolián.
Their differences and similarities in establishing their minds and conduct
were each given specific praise,
and Liǔxià Huì had even served in government at the time.
As for the likes of Chángjú and Jié Nì,
there was nothing to commend them.
In later generations,
why are the names of all reclusive scholars listed in historical biographies?
What is the reason?
Perhaps in ancient times, officials
intended to implement the Way,
and even those who served in lower positions due to poverty
still had to perform their duties before receiving their emoluments.
In later generations, many sought official positions for gain,
and few were able to abandon the ambition of surpassing others and the lament for old age and humble status.
Therefore, gentlemen particularly praise and describe those scholars who withdraw far and ascend high,
hoping that hearing of their conduct would still be enough to strengthen the weak and enlighten the stubborn.
Hence, the Biographies of Recluses are compiled.
Chǔ Chéngliàng, courtesy name Mào Xiān,
was from Zhēndìng.
When Sòng Sū Shì was demoted from Dìngwǔ and passed through Zhēndìng,
Chǔ Chéngliàng presented his writings to him
and was greatly praised.
In the autumn of the fifth year of Xuānhé,
he took the provincial examination;
among eight hundred examinees,
Chǔ Chéngliàng ranked first.
The following year,
he passed the imperial examination.
He was appointed as *hùcáo* (戶曹) of Yì Zhōu,
but before he could take office,
Jīn (金) forces advanced south.
In the sixth year of Tiānhuì
, Wòlíbù had already broken Zhēndìng
, and conscripted scholars within the territory to take the imperial examination at Ānguó Sì.
Chéngliàng’s name was also on the register
, but he hid and did not come out.
The army, knowing his talent
, strictly ordered him to be brought forward
to answer questions with the other students.
The policy questions
were "The Former Emperor was without the Way, and the Young Emperor was untrustworthy."
The candidates, following the implied directive
, heaped extreme calumny upon them.
Chéngliàng went to the chief examiner, Liú Shìzhōng, and said
, "How can a subject speak of the faults of his sovereign and father?"
He bowed deeply and exited.
Liú was moved by this.
All the others were passed
, totaling seventy-two people
, and it was then called the "Seventy-Two Sages List."
The *zhuàngyuán*, Xǔ Bìshì, became a郎官 (lángguān).
One day, as he exited the Left Wing Gate
, he fell from his horse
, his head striking a stone by the gate, and he died.
None of the others achieved prominence.
Liú highly regarded Chéngliàng’s integrity
and recommended him for the position of magistrate of Mòchéng Xiàn.
He responded indifferently
, then abandoned it.
He died at the age of seventy
, and his disciples privately conferred upon him the posthumous title of
"Xuánzhēn Xiānshēng."
His son, Xízhēn
, passed the imperial examination in the second year of Zhènglóng
, and served with distinction in various prefectures and counties.
Wáng Qùfēi, courtesy name Guǎngdào
, was a native of Píngyīn.
He once sat for the examination
, but being dissatisfied, he withdrew
and directed his wife and children to farm and weave to provide for the annual sacrifices.
He taught at home
, and whenever he had surplus income from teaching, he would share it with others.
His disciple Bān Chǐn was so poor he could not afford daily meals.
When Bān Chǐn's daughter reached marriageable age
, Qùfēi arranged for her dowry and marriage.
A neighbor to the north had a funeral, and it was taboo to exit to the east.
The west and north were both inhabited,
and to the south was Qùfēi's home.
Qùfēi demolished his silkworm shed to allow the funeral procession to exit to the south
, and thus the burial was possible.
He died in the twenty-fourth year of Dàdìng
, at the age of eighty-four.
Zhào Zhì, courtesy name Jǐngdào
, was a descendant of the Liao Chancellor Sīwēn.
Towards the end of Dàdìng
, he failed the imperial examination
and lived in seclusion south of Yānchéng
, teaching as his profession.
During the Míngchāng era
, Zhāngzōng, while on a spring outing, passed by
and, hearing the sound of stringed instruments and chanting,
visited his study.
He saw the poems written on the wall
and recited them for a long time
, admiring their extraordinary aspirations.
He summoned Zhào Zhì to his traveling palace
and offered him an official post.
Zhào Zhì firmly declined, saying
, "Your subject has a peculiar wild and unrestrained nature
, and my ambition lies in vast forests and lush grasses;
golden bridles and jade trappings are not what I desire.
Moreover, with a sagacious and enlightened ruler above
, how can one not tolerate a Cháo or a Yóu as an unofficial subject?"
The emperor admired him even more
, granted him a thousand *mǔ* of land
, and exempted him from taxes for life.
He died in the second year of Tàihé
, at the age of eighty-five.
Dù Shíshēng, courtesy name Jìnzhī
, was a native of Xìn'ān, Bàzhōu.
He was widely learned and understood astronomy
, but was unwilling to pursue an official career.
During the Chéng'ān and Tàihé eras
, the prime minister repeatedly recommended Shíshēng as capable of great service.
Shíshēng said to his close friends
, "I see a crimson aura like blood directly to the north
, extending across the sky from east to west.
The world will suffer great chaos
, and after the chaos, north and south will unite as one.
Waxing and waning, filling and emptying
, an endless cycle;
observing the past and examining the future
, who can defy it?"
At this time
, customs were extravagant
, and the societal order was utterly ruined
, and Shìzōng's legacy consequently declined.
Shíshēng then crossed the river south
and lived in seclusion in the Sōng and Luò mountains
, attracting many students.
It was largely
"Yīluò zhī Xué"
that Shíshēng began to teach to people.
During the Zhèngdà era
, when the Dà Yuán army attacked Tóngguān
, the defense was very strong
, and everyone congratulated each other.
Shíshēng said
, "The main forces are all between Qín and Gǒng.
If they obtain passage through Sòng
, emerge from Xiāng and Hàn, and enter Wǎn and Yè
, their cavalry will ride swiftly like wind and rain
. With no high mountains or great rivers to obstruct them
, it will be a landslide."
Shortly after
, the Dà Yuán army indeed crossed through Ráo Fēng Pass, traversed Xiāngyáng, and emerged from Nányáng.
The Jīn forces were defeated at Sānfēng Shān
, Biànjīng could not be defended
, all just as Shíshēng had predicted.
He died at the end of Zhèngdà.
Hǎo Tiāntǐng, courtesy name Jìnqīng
, was a native of Língchuān, Zézhōu.
He suffered early debility and frequent illnesses
, and was tired of the imperial examinations
, so he no longer participated.
Yuán Hàowèn of Tàiyuán once studied the *jìnshì* curriculum under him.
Tiāntǐng said
, "People today consider quick success in composition as achievement
. They dismember and stitch together the Six Classics and the Hundred Schools
, sometimes not even understanding the chapters, verses, or punctuation.
If they are fortunate enough to succeed
, they cannot avoid becoming ordinary people."
He also said
, "To study not for literary arts
, and to become an official not for profit
, only a truly wise person can do this."
He also said
, "Most officials today are ruined by greed
, all because they cannot endure hunger and cold and maintain their integrity.
A man who cannot endure hunger and cold
can accomplish nothing.
If you seek it according to my words
, the imperial examination is already within it."
Someone asked
, "Is it not contrary to use this kind of learning to pursue the imperial examination?"
Tiāntǐng replied
, "I just want him not to become a mere examination candidate."
During the Zhēnyòu era
, he lived in Hénán
, traveling between Qí and Wèi.
He was a man of strong principles
, deeply self-confident
, preferring to be down-and-out and impoverished
rather than ever visiting the homes of the wealthy and powerful.
At the age of fifty
, he died in Wǔyáng.
Xuē Jìxiān, courtesy name Mànqīng.
After the southward crossing
, he lived in seclusion in the mountains west of Luò
, teaching children to read.
He was filial to his mother
, and humble and gracious in his interactions with others
, and his residence was transformed by his influence.
His son, Chúnxiào, courtesy name Fāngshú
, possessed his father's character.
There was someone who forged Mànqīng's letter to Fāngshú to obtain goods.
Mànqīng was already old but his appearance was like that of a younger man.
The visitor did not realize he was Mànqīng and thought he was Fāngshú
, and presented the letter to him. Mànqīng gave him the goods as requested.
The Censor Shí Jiè, while on circuit, passed by Mànqīng
, but Mànqīng did not meet him.
Someone asked, "Why do you have no local sentiment?"
Mànqīng replied
, "You haven't thought about it.
Not all current government policies are necessarily good.
If the Censor impeaches someone
, it will be said that I initiated it.
Those who share evil will protect each other
, and in the future, my neighbors and I will surely suffer disaster."
His cautiousness was all of this kind.
During the chaos of Rénchén
, he died of illness in Yíyáng.
Gāo Zhòngzhèn, courtesy name Zhèngzhī,
was a native of Liáodōng.
His elder brother commanded the troops of Kāifēng Prefecture,
and Zhòngzhèn resided with him.
Later, he entrusted his family property to his brother,
and took his wife and children to Mount Sōng.
He widely read all sorts of books,
and was especially profound in the learning of the Yì Jīng and the Huángjí Jīngshì.
Content in his poverty, he found joy,
and did not enter cities.
Even the common folk in the mountains and fields knew to respect him.
He often walked in mountain valleys with his disciples Zhāng Qián and Wáng Rǔméi;
people looked upon them as if they were soaring immortals.
Some said that Zhòngzhèn had once met an extraordinary person who taught him the art of nurturing life.
He often sat in meditation all day,
his bones and joints making creaking sounds.
What he spoke of were all matters beyond this world,
and if anyone questioned him, he would often no longer speak.
Zhāng Qián, courtesy name Zhòngshēng,
was a native of Wǔqīng.
From a young age, he had lofty ambitions and integrity,
and admired Jīng Kē and Niè Zhèng.
At the age of thirty, he finally changed his ways and began to study.
People of his time held his conduct in high esteem,
and called him:
"Zhāng the Ancient One."
Later, he sojourned on Mount Sōng
and studied the Yì Jīng under Zhòngzhèn.
At fifty years old,
he first married a woman from the Sūn clan of Lǔshān.
She also possessed virtuous conduct;
the couple respected each other as guests,
carrying firewood, gleaning grain,
singing as they walked, contented and self-sufficient,
unaware of their poverty.
There was a neighbor who planted melons for Qián;
when they ripened, he offered them to Qián.
Qián would not accept,
but eventually divided and ate them.
Once, while walking on a path, he picked up an axe.
The couple pondered for a long time
before taking it home to find its owner and return it.
In the village, there were brothers dividing their property.
The younger brother said:
"Our family is like this;
are you not afraid that Mr. Zhāng will know?"
So they reverted to their original state.
During the Tiānxīng era,
Qián took his family to evade the war in Shàoshì.
He then died after seven days without food,
and Mrs. Sūn also threw herself into a sheer gorge and died.
Wáng Rǔméi, courtesy name Dàyòng,
was a native of Dàmíng.
Initially, he became an accountant for Yīyáng through legal studies.
When his term of office was complete,
he then retired and did not serve.
He had a fondness for books
and always acted with propriety.
To students who came to him for legal studies,
he also taught classical studies.
All the students respected his teachings
and dared not act improperly.
His colleagues often pitied his poverty
and sometimes gave him aid,
but he always declined to accept.
Later, his end was unknown.
Sòng Kě, courtesy name Yǔzhī,
was a native of Wǔzhì.
His aunt had married into a prominent clan.
During the Zhēnyòu wars,
both her husband and son died in the calamity.
The aunt gave fifty plaques of white gold to Kě,
which Kě accepted without refusing.
Later, the aunt found a distant relative of her clan and adopted him as her heir.
She took him to visit her maternal family.
Kě then prepared a feast for his neighbors,
and said to his aunt:
"Aunt, you previously gave me gold.
I accepted it because the Shì clan had no son.
Now they have a son;
this gold belongs to the Shì clan,
it is not yours.
By what right should I take it?"
He then called his wife and children to carry the gold back to her.
The villagers consequently held him in high regard.
Not long after,
Northern troops were stationed in Shānyáng.
Among the army, there were those who had heard of Kě's reputation.
They inquired and found his whereabouts,
detained his son,
and sent someone to summon Kě, saying:
"Those who follow me will share in fortune and misfortune;
otherwise,
your son will die."
His relatives and old friends all urged him to go,
but Kě politely refused to comply,
saying:
"Whether I have a son or not,
and whether my son lives or dies,
all is decreed by fate.
How can I, for the sake of one son,
destroy what I have upheld all my life?"
Later, he indeed had no sons.
Xīn Yuàn, courtesy name Jìngzhī,
was a native of Fúchāng.
At twenty-five, he first learned to read.
He took Bái's Fèngjiàn Jí to test himself,
and in one day, he could recite it from memory.
He then gathered books and read them in his enclosed dwelling.
When he read the Yī Xùn and the Hé Guǎng from the Shī Jīng, he seemed to have gained some profound understanding.
He wished to stop but could not,
and so he applied himself with even greater effort.
From then on, he widely read books and histories,
and his writing had structure.
His poetry was refined and strict, with a unique personal flair.
He was wild and unrestrained by nature, not bothering with formality.
When noblemen invited guests,
he would appear among them in hemp clothes and straw sandals, with bare shins, completely at ease,
engaging in spirited conversation and hearty drinking,
as if no one else were present.
He once said to Wáng Yù:
"Kings, lords, generals, and ministers
are what the world universally craves.
Sages, if they obtain them through the proper way, do not avoid them.
But to obtain them not through the proper way,
or to hold such a position but be unable to act according to one's will,
is like wanting to bathe one's body and then lying in a latrine.
This is difficult to explain to others;
you should cherish this thought."
Such was his ambition and taste.
Later, he became a guest of Gāo Tíngyù, the Administrator of Hénán Prefecture.
When Tíngyù was falsely accused by Wēndíhǎn Fúxīng, the Prefect of Hénán,
Yuàn was also interrogated and tortured,
barely escaping.
From then on, his life became even more difficult.
Yuàn possessed a naturally lofty spirit
and could not conform to worldly ways or stoop low.
Pressed by hunger, cold, and displacement,
this often appeared in his poetry.
He had several thousand poems,
which he usually kept in a bamboo satchel.
Towards the end of the Zhèngdà era,
he died in Luòxià.
One of his poems says:
"Huáng and Qǐ briefly came as friends to Hàn;
Cháo and Yóu were never ultimately subjects of Táng."
Truly the words of a hermit.
Wáng Yǔkě, courtesy name Nányún,
was a native of Jízhōu in Hédōng.
His father was originally a military officer,
and Yǔkě had also once been enrolled.
Around the age of thirty,
after a serious illness, he suddenly went mad.
After a long time, he was able to hold a brush and compose poetry and prose,
and speak of vague, otherworldly matters.
After the Southern Crossing,
he resided between Shàngcài, Suípíng, and Yǎnchéng.
When he met literati, he called himself
"General Dàchéng";
before Buddhas, he called himself
"Dìmó Lóngshí";
among Taoists, he called himself
"Zōu Tiānxuánjùn";
among the noble and distinguished, he called himself
"Master of Wēijǐntáng."
He was a man of imposing physique,
with a strange and ancient appearance.
He wore a dark kudzu headscarf,
with two dangling straps behind his neck like ox ears,
and a gold-embroidered ring between his crown and forehead.
His cheeks were dyed blue to form "jade dimples."
His clothes were long but could not cover his shins.
He was uninhibited and fond of wine.
Whenever he entered a city,
the townspeople vied to give him food and drink.
At night, he slept in an earthen room.
In summer months, he was unconcerned even if there was a corpse nearby or maggots crawling about.
When people gave him paper,
he would write hundreds of words,
either poetry or prose,
scattered and fragmented,
without punctuation or proper beginning and end.
Much of it consisted of phrases from the Six Classics and ancient, rare characters from phonologists.
His calligraphy was sharp and vigorous,
and he sometimes avoided characters that were taboo in the Sòng dynasty.
If asked about historical events,
his replies were like echoes,
and all the books he cited were unknown to the world.
During his conversations, if there was a slight hint of order,
he would then disrupt it with fantastical and bizarre words.
Má Jiǔchóu and Zhāng Jué were his closest companions.
They said that of his poetry, taking one hundred percent as the rate,
only two or three percent were comprehensible.
During the *Rénchén* military unrest,
he was captured by a commander from Shùntiān.
Knowing his name,
they secretly planned to take him north,
and housed him in the Ruìyún Guàn of the prefecture.
When Yǔ Kě was about to meet the commander the next day, he said,
"I cannot reside in your Ruìyún Guàn."
He died a few days later.
Later, he was seen again on the Huái River.
A eulogy states: In the Jīn dynasty, recluses were not often seen.
Now, among those recorded in the archives,
we find twelve individuals.
Among them, three were exceptionally outstanding.
Chǔ Chéngliàng, a Sòng man,
sat for the *jìnshì* examination.
The presiding official issued a policy question regarding the faults of Sòng Huī and Qīn.
Chéngliàng bowed deeply and departed.
While the Jīn people highly valued scholarship and official careers,
Dù Shíshēng resided in the mountains
and was the first to
teach the "Yīluò school of thought"
to later generations.
Sòng Kě was unwilling to serve as an official.
When people seized his son as a hostage,
he preferred to abandon him rather than comply,
and thus ended up without a son.
Though his conduct might have been excessive,
how could he not be superior to those who killed their wives to seek a grand generalship?
Officials and scholars see good clearly and have firm intentions,
which enables them to do what others find difficult, just like these examples.
Collation Notes

Model Officials: Lú Kèzhōng, Niú Déchāng, Fàn Chéngjí, Wáng Zhèng, Zhāng Yì, Lǐ Zhān, Liú Mǐnxíng, Fù Shènwēi, Liú Huàn, Gāo Chāngfú, Sūn Déyuān, Zhào Jiàn, Púchá Zhèngliú, Nǚxīliè Shǒuyú, Shímò Yuán, Zhāng Gòu, Zhào Chóngfú, Wǔdōu Gěshíliè Dé, Zhāng Tèlì, Wáng Hào.
From the time Jīn Mùzōng decreed that various tribes should not be called *Dōubójǐn*,
the tribes began to be listed under a unified administration.
Tàizǔ ordered three hundred households to form a *móukè*,
and ten *móukè* to form a *měng'ān*,
just like the system of appointing officials in commanderies and counties.
After Tàizōng conquered the Central Plains,
he demarcated the borders
and established governors and magistrates.
Xīzōng dispatched inspectors (*liánchá zhī shǐ*) to tour the four directions.
Shìzōng inherited the remnants after Hǎilíng's devastation,
and fostered recuperation and growth.
By the *Míngchāng* and *Chéng'ān* eras,
the population and resources flourished,
and model officials emerged one after another.
During the *Tàihé* military campaigns,
commanderies and counties faced many difficulties,
and official governance declined.
Xuānzōng favored bureaucratic practices
and strict assessment methods,
so capable officials were not lacking,
but benevolent governance was rarely praised.
The official administration of the Jīn dynasty for over a hundred years can be examined from beginning to end,
thus these biographies of model officials are compiled.
Lú Kèzhōng,
a native of Fèngjí, Guìdé Zhōu.
When Gāo Yǒngchāng occupied Liáoyáng,
Kèzhōng fled to the camp of Jīnyuán Jùnwáng Wòlǔ to surrender,
and was then sent out as a local guide with Sāwū.
Wòlǔ conquered Dōngjīng,
and Yǒngchāng fled to Chángsōng Dǎo.
Kèzhōng, along with the Bóhǎi man Tàbùyě, pursued and captured him.
In the second year of Shuōuò,
he was granted a hereditary *móukè* position.
Thereafter,
he rendered meritorious service in the pacification of Yān and the campaign against Sòng.
He was appointed *Dēngzhōu Cìshǐ* (Prefect of Dēngzhōu),
and later transferred to *Chánzhōu Cìshǐ*.
During the *Tiāndé* era,
he served as *Tóngzhī Bǎodà Jūnjiédùshǐ*.
Several soldiers from Suīdé Zhōu, passing through Fùchéng,
sought lodging in a civilian home.
That night, robbers plundered the owner's property and left.
The authorities arrested the soldiers who had sought lodging,
imprisoned them, and tortured them until they falsely confessed.
Kèzhōng discerned their injustice
and alone refused to sign the verdict.
Before long, the true culprits were found,
and the soldiers who had sought lodging were released.
In the second year of *Dàdìng*,
he was appointed *Běijīng Fùliúshǒu* (Deputy Resident Commander of Běijīng).
At that time, the people faced a food shortage.
Kèzhōng issued an order that anyone with stored grain should retain enough for one year,
and all remaining grain should be purchased at a fair price.
As a result, there was no suffering from starvation.
He was transferred to *Chénzhōu Fángyùshǐ* (Defense Commissioner of Chénzhōu),
and later retired as *Jìngnán Jūnjiédùshǐ*,
and died.
Niú Déchāng, courtesy name Yànqīn,
was from Dìng'ān, Wèizhōu.
His father, Duó,
was a *Liáo Jiāngzuò Dàjiān* (Grand Supervisor of Works in Liáo).
Déchāng was orphaned young.
His mother taught him to study.
When someone advised him to seek office through his father's influence,
his mother said:
"The Grand Supervisor's dying wish was not to let him become a *chéngfèng* (court attendant)."
He passed the *jìnshì* examination in the second year of *Huángtǒng*,
and was appointed *Fánshān Bù*.
He was promoted to *Wànquán Lìng* (Magistrate of Wànquán).
At that time, Pú and Shǎn suffered severe famine,
and bandits were rampant.
The city gates of prefectures and counties were closed during the day.
Upon arriving at his post, Déchāng
immediately opened the city gates, allowing the common people to enter and exit freely.
He posted a notice saying:
"The people are suffering from hunger and cold.
They plunder villages and towns to survive from day to day,
which is very pitiable.
Those who can reform themselves will not be questioned."
All the bandits were grateful and dispersed,
and the county became peaceful.
The *Fǔyǐn* Wáng Bólóng praised him
and treated him with great respect.
He successively held positions as *Xíngbù* and *Lìbù Shìláng* (Vice Ministers of Justice and Personnel),
*Zhōngdū Lù Dūzhuǎnyùnshǐ* (Chief Transport Commissioner of Zhōngdū Circuit),
and *Guǎngníng* and *Tàiyuán Yǐn* (Governors of Guǎngníng and Tàiyuán).
He died
and was posthumously granted the title of *Zhōngfèng Dàfū*.
Fàn Chéngjí, courtesy name Chǒngzhī.
He loved learning.
During the late Liáo dynasty, when bandits arose,
he never abandoned his books even while fleeing to safety.
In the eighth year of *Tiānqìng*, he passed the *jìnshì* examination (class C),
and was appointed *Mìshūshěng Jiàoshūláng* (Collator in the Imperial Library),
eventually becoming *Jīnyuán Lìng* (Magistrate of Jīnyuán) in Dàdìng Fǔ.
Upon returning to the imperial court, he served as *Yùqián Chéngyìng Wénzì* (Court Attendant for Literary Matters).
At the beginning of *Tiānhuì*,
he was promoted to *Diànzhōng Shàojiān* (Junior Supervisor of the Palace).
In the fourth year,
he followed in the attack on Tàiyuán,
and was promoted to *Shàofǔ Jiān* (Supervisor of the Lesser Treasury).
In the fifth year,
Zōnghán conquered Sòng.
Chéngjí was in charge of the incoming and outgoing gold and pearls that were obtained.
He did not cheat in the slightest.
When he returned,
he only had a calf-cart loaded with books and historical records.
Soon after, he was promoted to *Zhāowén Guǎn Zhíxuèshì* (Academician of the Zhāowén Academy)
and *Zhī Jiàngzhōu* (Prefect of Jiàngzhōu).
Before this,
when the army was raised,
there were civilians who had been plundered by generals and soldiers and then fled back home.
Chéngjí sent officials to inform everyone
to register themselves.
There were several thousand people in total.
He reported them all to the *Yuánshuàifǔ* (Grand Marshal's Office),
and they were allowed to redeem themselves and become free citizens.
For those who were poor and had no money, the government paid on their behalf.
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to *Hédōngběi Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ* (Transport Commissioner of Hédōngběi Circuit).
At that time, suffering from the abuses of the late Sòng,
the people's taxes were heavy and unfair.
Chéngjí then devised a plan,
establishing simple and convenient laws.
The revenue increased by tens of thousands of *hú*,
the government had enough, and the people had surplus.
He successively served as *Tóngzhī Píngyáng Yǐn* (Associate Governor of Píngyáng), *Xījīng Fùliúshǒu* (Deputy Resident Commander of Xījīng),
and was transferred to *Hédōngnán Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ* (Transport Commissioner of Hédōngnán Circuit),
and then changed to *Tóngqiān Yānjīng Liúshǒushì* (Associate Supervisor of Yānjīng Resident Commander's Affairs) and *Shùntiān Jūnjiédùshǐ* (Military Commissioner of Shùntiān Army).
At that time, an earthquake damaged civilian homes.
Some people wanted to compete to repair their houses first,
and craftsmen overcharged them.
Chéngjí ordered officials to oversee the work,
proceeding in sequence,
regardless of wealth,
and the people benefited from reduced expenses.

He successively served as *Zhènxī Jūnjiédùshǐ* (Military Commissioner of Zhènxī Army), *Xíngtái Lǐbù Shàngshū* (Minister of Rites in the Traveling Secretariat), *Tàiníng Jūnjiédùshǐ* (Military Commissioner of Tàiníng Army),
and then returned to govern Shùntiān.
Xī soldiers were scattered throughout the territory,
and thousands of them turned to banditry.
Chéngjí enforced the law without leniency,
and they became afraid and dared not commit offenses.
In the second year of *Zhēnyuán*, he retired as *Guānglù Dàfū* (Grand Master of Imperial Banquets)
and died at the age of sixty-six.
Wáng Zhèng,
was a native of Chénzhōu Xióngyuè.
His ancestors served the Bóhǎi and Liáo dynasties,
and all had prominent figures.
When Zhèng was in the chaos of the late Liáo,
he drifted in the prefectures and villages.
Gāo Yǒngchāng occupied Liáodōng,
knew of Zhèng's talent and strategy,
and wished to employ him.
Zhèng judged that he would not succeed,
and declined.
When Yǒngchāng was defeated,
the Bóhǎi people competed to capture Yǒngchāng to claim merit,
but Zhèng alone hesitated and withdrew.
Wúwáng Shēimǔ heard of this and found it extraordinary,
speaking of it to Tàizǔ,
who appointed him Móukè of the Bóhǎi Army in Lúzhōu.
He followed in the defeat of Báixī,
and the capture of Yān-Yún.
When the Jīn army attacked Sòng,
Huázhōu surrendered,
and Zhèng was left behind as Pacification Commissioner.
Before this,
several prefectures that had surrendered
had again killed their defending generals and rejoined Sòng.
At this point,
people worried for Zhèng,
but Zhèng said:
"If it benefits the state,
what death should I avoid?"
Sòngwáng Zōngwàng admired him,
saying:
"To die for royal service
benefits one's descendants;
your words are right."
Zhèng entered the prefecture with a few horsemen.
At this time,
many people had turned to banditry due to famine,
and were imprisoned.
Zhèng released them all,
opened the granaries to relieve the poor,
whereupon the prefectural people were all pleased,
and no longer rebelled.
Neighboring commanderies heard of this,
and many also surrendered.
Sòngwáng summoned Zhèng to the main tent,
patted his back and said:
"I thought you were dead,
but you have succeeded again!"
He comforted and encouraged him for a long time.
In Tiānhuì 4th year,
he served as co-supervisor of the Qūyuàn in Yānjīng Dū.
Not long after,
he was appointed Acting Jìedùshǐ of Jīnshèngjūn.
He was then transferred to be Acting Dūzhīhuīshǐ of the Imperial Guards, concurrently managing military supplies.
At this time,
the army was just being established,
and the regulations for warehouses and administration were not yet in place,
so all the clerks in charge took advantage to commit corruption.
Zhèng alone was clear in accounting,
and strictly locked the stores,
so that gold and silk piled up like mountains, yet there was no loss in even a fraction in disbursements and receipts.
Wúwáng Shēimǔ playfully asked him:
"You have been an official for a long time,
yet your poverty has not turned to wealth, why is that?"
He replied:
"Zhèng upholds the 'Four Knows' of Yáng Zhèn,
how could I not be poor?"
Wúwáng laughed and said:
"My earlier words were just a joke."
He presented him with one hundred taels of gold, five hundred taels of silver, and a horse to ride.
In the 6th year,
he was appointed Zuǒ Jiānmén Jiāngjūn,
and successively held the posts of Cìshǐ of Ānzhōu, Jūnzhōushì of Tánzhōu, and Hùlìfáng Zhǔshì.
In Tiānjuàn 1st year,
he was promoted to Jìedùshǐ of Bǎojìngjūn,
retired and died,
aged sixty-six.
Zhèng's original name was Nánsālǐ,
he once went on an embassy to Gāolì,
and subsequently changed his name to Zhèng.
His sons were Zūnrén, Zūnyì, and Zūngǔ.
Zūngǔ's son Tíngyún has a biography.
Zhāng Yì, courtesy name Yànwēi,
was a native of Zézhōu Gāopíng.
He entered officialdom through hereditary privilege,
and served the Qí dynasty as Tōngpàn of Guīdé Fǔ.
When the Qí state was abolished,
two thousand Qí soldiers in the commandery planned a rebellion,
agreeing to raise torches at midnight as a signal.
Yì knew of this,
selected strong men from the market and armed them,
formed a line to block the main alleyways,
and opened the small southern gate to show them a way out.
The rebellion could not start,
and by dawn, almost all the fugitives had disappeared,
and their ringleaders were captured and executed.
Five days later,
Dūtǒng Wányán Ālúbǔ arrived at Guīdé with an army,
intending to root out the remaining rebels.
Yì guaranteed that the people of the commandery were innocent,
and so he stopped.
The Xíngtái, acting on imperial authority, appointed him Co-Administrator of Guīdé Yǐn.
In Tiānjuàn 1st year,
as Hénán was ceded to Sòng,
he was transferred to be Co-Administrator of Yízhōu Fángyùshǐ.
In the 3rd year,
Zōngbì recaptured Hénán,
and summoned Yì to the Xíngshěng.
After Bìanjīng was pacified,
he was appointed Vice-Retainer of Bìanjīng.
He successively served as Fángyùshǐ of Chén and Qínzhōu,
and Co-Administrator of Tàiyuán Yǐn.
Jìnníng Jūn reported that the Xìa people had encroached on the border,
and an imperial edict ordered Yì to go and suppress them.
Yì arrived at the border,
and according to the registers, each returned the encroached land,
then returned and reported:
"The Zhé clan has for generations guarded Línfǔ,
to resist the Xìa people.
This dynasty acquired their land and then gave it to Xìa.
The Xìa people desecrated the Zhé clan's tombs and mutilated their corpses,
so the Zhé clan's resentment goes bone-deep and they cannot seek revenge.
Now they are again made to guard Jìnníng,
thus provoking the Xìa people to make minor incursions,
and then listing their crimes,
merely to instigate border conflicts to avenge private grudges.
It would be better to move the Zhé clan to another commandery,
then the Xìa people will be at peace."
The imperial court followed his advice,
and so the Zhé clan was moved to guard Qīngzhōu.
During the Zhènglóng reign,
he served as Co-Administrator of Xījīng Liúshǒushì,
and was promoted to Héběi Dōnglù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
In Dàdìng 2nd year,
he was summoned to be Hùbù Shàngshū,
but soon after taking office,
he fell ill and died.
Lǐ Zhān,
was a native of Jìzhōu Yùtián.
He passed the imperial examination in Liáo Tiānqìng 2nd year,
and became Wàngyún Lìng of Píngzhōu.
Zhāng Jué occupied Píngzhōu and rebelled,
making Zhān his aide.
When Zōngwàng recaptured Píngzhōu,
Jué fled,
and the city rebelled again.
Zhān scaled the city wall and surrendered,
but his son could not escape
and was harmed by the rebels.
Sòngwáng Zōngwàng commended him,
and by imperial decree, appointed him Pànguān of Xīngpíng Fǔ.
In Tiānhuì 3rd year,
he was promoted to Dàlǐ Shàoqīng,
and followed Zōngwàng in the southern campaign,
serving as supply commissioner for the Hàn army.
In the 4th year,
when the Jīn army besieged Biàn,
the Sòng people requested to cede the three prefectures north of the Hé.
Zhān, along with Lǐbù Shìláng Lǐ Tiānyì, pacified the eastern and western routes north of the Hé,
and generally stabilized Huái, Jùn, Wèi and other prefectures,
and Wèi, Tāngyīn and other counties.
In the 7th year,
he became Zhī Níngzhōu,
and was successively promoted to Dézhōu Fángyùshǐ.
His governance was lenient and fair,
and the people cherished his benevolence,
with several hundred thousand people spontaneously going to the capital to request his retention.
In Zhēnyuán 3rd year,
he was promoted to Jìzhōu Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and then transferred to Zhōngshùnjūn Jìedùshǐ.
At the end of Zhènglóng,
bandits arose everywhere,
so Zhān reinforced the city walls and ramparts as a precaution,
and the people of Wèi relied on this for safety.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he died in office.
Liú Mǐnháng,
was a native of Píngzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in Tiānhuì 3rd year.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Jiàoshūláng,
and successively promoted to Féixiāng Lìng.
In a year of great famine,
bandits plundered people for food.
The elderly and weak from various counties sought refuge in the commandery city,
not daring to cultivate,
so farming ceased,
and the fields became desolate.
Mǐnháng reported to the prefecture,
borrowed thirty soldiers to protect the county people going out to farm,
and displayed many flags to create the impression of a larger army.
Mǐnháng led patrols,
and at dusk, inspected the people returning to the city,
thus bandits dared not offend, and cultivation flourished.
He was transferred to be the Prefect of Gāopíng.
The county town had been dilapidated for a long time and was not repaired.
Big bandits ran rampant,
plundering the county town and could not be resisted.
Mǐn Háng spent his own salary
and led his subordinates and clerks to contribute money to hire laborers for repairs and maintenance.
The common people willingly followed him,
altogether using two thousand people,
and the rammed earth constructions were completed.
The villagers entered to protect themselves,
and when bandits arrived, they could not violate them.
After nine transfers,
he became the Transport Commissioner of Héběi Dōnglù.
He retired from office
and died.
Fù Shènwēi, courtesy name Jīxiān.
His ancestors were from Shāxī, Qínzhōu,
later moving to Jiànchāng.
Shènwēi moved to Cháng'ān.
At the end of the Sòng Dynasty, he passed the Jìnshì examination
and successively held the office of Jīngzhì Commissioner of Hédōng Lù.
After Zōnghàn had already conquered Biànjīng,
he sent Lóushì to pacify Shǎnxī.
Shènwēi led his troops to engage in battle,
but his army was defeated and he was captured,
then sent to the Marshal's Residence.
Marshal Zōnghàn admired his talent and learning,
and did not kill him,
but detained him in Guīhuà Zhōu.
Xīyǐn took him in as a subordinate.
When Zōngbì recaptured the land of Hénán,
Shènwēi was appointed as the Jīnglüè Commissioner of Shǎnxī,
and soon after, concurrently served as the Jìedùshǐ of Tóngzhōu.
The next year,
Shǎnxī experienced a severe drought,
and seventeen or eighteen out of ten people died of starvation.
Shènwēi was appointed as the Jīngjì Commissioner for the three circuits of Jīngzhào, Fūyán, and Huánqìng,
and was granted discretionary power.
Shènwēi recruited people to contribute grain,
obtaining over two hundred thousand shí.
He established relief shelters to feed the starving,
saving many lives.
He was changed to be the Deputy Prefect of Jīngzhào,
and concurrently served as the Transport Commissioner for all circuits of Shǎnxī.
He repaired the Sānbái, Lóngshǒu, and other canals to irrigate the fields.
He recruited people for military colonization and farming,
lending cattle and seeds to assist them,
and the people benefited greatly from this.
He was transferred to be the Vice Administrator of Zhōngjīng,
and for his integrity, was changed to be the Prefect of Xīnzhōu.
He was successively promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Qīng),
appointed Jìedùshǐ of Dìngwǔ Jūn,
and then transferred to Jìngnán Jūn.
He offended those in power,
but Sū Bǎohéng saved him from dismissal.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he was again appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies,
then promoted to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū),
and together with the Hanlin Lecturer (Hànlín Shìjiǎng Xuéshì) Túshān Zǐwēn and Hanlin Compiler (Hànlín Dàizhì) Yílà Xīzǎi, concurrently served as Co-compilers of the National History.
He died in office
at the age of seventy-six.
Shènwēi was learned and fond of writing,
and once presented the "Xīngwáng Jīnjìng Lù" in one hundred volumes.
His nature was pure and honest,
he was devoted to ancient studies and enjoyed discussing military strategy.
People at the time considered him quaint and impractical.
Liú Huàn, courtesy name Déwén,
was from Zhōngshān.
At the end of the Sòng Dynasty, when war broke out,
the city had been short of food for a long time.
Huàn was still young;
he cooked chaff and husks to eat.
He drank the clear liquid himself,
and offered the thick part to his mother.
The villagers considered him extraordinary.
As he grew older, he went to school,
and in cold weather, he huddled by a dung fire to read diligently.
He passed the Jìnshì examination in the first year of Tiāndé.
He was assigned as the Magistrate of Rènqiū.
The county magistrate was corrupt,
and Huàn always admonished him.
When his term expired,
the magistrate held a cup of wine and thanked him, saying,
"You, Magistrate, are honest and careful,
which enabled me to pass my performance review."
He was transferred to be the Prefect of Zhōngdū.
The Privy Councilor (Shūmìshǐ) Púshàn Hútǔ had tassel-making artisans in his household,
who profited in the market
but refused to comply with market regulations and service.
Huàn arrested them.
Hútǔ summoned Huàn,
but Huàn did not go.
He publicly announced the artisans' crimes and flogged them.
When Huàn was first appointed Prefect,
he visited to express gratitude to his fellow townsman, Shí Jū, a Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng).
Jū was displeased and said,
"The capital is vast and complex,
not like an outer prefecture.
To abandon simplicity for complexity
is something I don't understand."
By this time,
he began to respect Huàn.
For his integrity, he was promoted to Judicial Reviewer of Jīngzhào,
and then again promoted to Commissioner of Patrols for Běijīng.
He arrested two notorious young men and flogged them in the courtyard,
admonishing them:
"Be filial, fraternal, respectful, and cautious,
and you will be a gentleman.
Be violent, cruel, and secretive,
and you will be a scoundrel.
From now on,
do not cling to old habits.
The state has clear punishments,
and I cannot show favoritism."
From then on,
everyone feared and dreaded him,
and no one dared to offend.
He was summoned to be a Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
Several hundred elders either lay under his carriage
or pulled on his boots and stirrups,
saying,
"We wish to keep you, our lord, for another year,
but it cannot be."
He concurrently served as a Junior Director of the Board of Revenue (Hùbù Yuánwàiláng) with his original rank.
The Dàizhōu mint mixed bronze with pure copper to cast coins,
making the coins poor in color,
resembling iron coins.
Many common people committed illegal casting and were punished,
which the court worried about.
It was referred to the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) for deliberation.
Huàn submitted a memorial, saying,
"For currency, pure yellow copper should be used for refined casting,
with tin added in moderation.
If bronze could be used for casting,
there is no reason why previous dynasties would not have used it.
From Dàizhōu, they take two parts and mix it with four to six parts,
mixing bronze and yellow copper,
aiming to save copper and make the work easier.
Because of this,
many common people commit illegal casting
and are trapped in crime;
this is not the intention of the court.
If you truly wish to benefit the world,
it is appropriate to use pure yellow copper.
Though the quantity obtained will be less, the benefit will be long-term.
As for the new coins already in circulation,
they should be verified by count and submitted for exchange."
This was adopted.
He was again promoted to Prefect of Guǎnzhōu.
Several hundred elders listed eleven of his notable achievements
and went to the Military Governor (Jiézàng) to request that Huàn be retained,
saying,
"The Prefect adheres to his duties and upholds the law;
we beg that he be kept."
For his integrity, he was promoted to Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu,
then promoted one rank,
and transferred to be Deputy Administrator of Běijīng.
When Shìzōng visited Shàngjīng,
the prefectures and commanderies he passed through extensively mobilized laborers to build bridges and imperial roads
to curry favor and rewards.
However, Huàn's jurisdiction only ensured that the roads were flat and in good order.
The Emperor praised his intention
and promoted him to Transport Commissioner of Liáodōng Lù.
He died.
Gāo Chāngfú
was from Wǎnpíng, Zhōngdū.
His father, Lǚ,
was a Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) of Liáo who retired from office.
Tàizōng heard of his name and summoned him,
but he died before he could be received in audience.
A special imperial edict ordered Chāngfú to shed his mourning attire and participate in the examinations.
He passed the Jìnshì examination in the tenth year of Tiānhuì,
and was appointed as a Clerk in the Privy Council (Shūmìyuàn Lìshǐ).
The next year,
he was appointed as a Clerk in the Marshal's Residence.
At the beginning of Huángtǒng,
when Zōngbì recaptured Hénán,
the Marshal's Residence was set up in Biàn.
If anyone was suspected or captured,
they were all labeled as Sòng spies
and immediately killed.
Chāngfú investigated and ascertained the truth,
releasing many who had been unjustly imprisoned.
Xǔzhōu Dū Tǒng Hán Cháng's
enforcement of laws was strict. He enjoyed killing people.
He dispatched messengers to escort prisoners to Biàn,
but some died on the way.
The supervising official, fearing punishment for losing prisoners,
wished to kill all the remaining prisoners to silence them.
Chāngfú understood the official's intention
and thoroughly investigated the situation,
saving seventeen or eighteen people from death.
Consequently, the officials resented Chāngfú
and sought to frame him.
At that time, there was ongoing warfare.
Between Liáng and Chǔ, there were often overcast skies and rain at night.
The Yuánshuàifǔ selected men to scout the movements of Sòng troops,
and the officials sent Chāngfú.
Chāngfú departed without demur,
obtaining all the enemy's true and false information and reporting it to the Yuánshuàifǔ.
When the army returned,
he was appointed Zhènwǔjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ,
then transferred to Xíngtái Lǐbù Yuánwàiláng.
During the Tiāndé era,
the Xíngtái was abolished.
He was reassigned as Jiàngyángjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ,
then entered court as Bīngbù Yuánwàiláng,
and subsequently Hàjiān Shàoyǐn.
Upon Shìzōng's ascension,
he submitted a memorial outlining beneficial policies.
The emperor read it repeatedly
and then said to his attending ministers:
"Officials, both internal and external, all submit memorials on affairs.
This allows one to discern the quality of talent.
Otherwise,
how would I know?"
He was appointed Tóngzhī Dōngjīng Liúshǒu Shì three times.
His governance was exemplary,
and he was promoted to Shāndōng Xīlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ and Gōngbù Shàngshū,
then reassigned as Zhāng Déjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He submitted a memorial stating that taxes were too heavy.
The emperor asked Hànlín Xuéshì Zhāng Jǐngrén:
"The tax laws are lighter compared to recent times,
so why are they considered heavy?"
Jǐngrén replied:
"Today's taxes are indeed light.
If they were lightened further,
the national expenditure would be insufficient."
The matter was then dropped.
He was successively promoted to Hézhōng Yǐn,
retired from office,
and died.
His grandson, Sūn Déyuān, courtesy name Zīshēn,
was from Xìngzhōngfǔ.
He passed the imperial examination in the 16th year of Dàdìng (1176).
He was appointed Shízhōujūn Shì Pànguān and Láishuǐ Chéng.
After a rectitude investigation, he was promoted to Shāhé Lìng.
There was a thief who stole autumn mulberries.
The owner chased and apprehended him.
The thief stabbed himself in the instep with a fork
and said:
"It is customary not to prohibit picking autumn mulberries.
How dare you stab me?"
The owner was afraid
and offered a bribe to be spared.
The thief refused
and sued him at the county office.
Déyuān said:
"If you were injured while being chased and apprehended,
the wound would be at the back.
Since it is at the front,
you stabbed yourself."
The thief then confessed.
He was selected as Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
but did not accept.
He resigned due to his father's mourning,
and the people carved a stone tablet to commemorate him.
After a rectitude investigation, he was reinstated as Běijīng Zhuǎnyùnsī Dū Gōupànguān.
Through repeated recommendations, he was promoted to Zhōngdū Zuǒ Jǐngxúnshǐ, Jiānchá Yùshǐ, and Shāndōng Dōnglù Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ,
then successively to Dàlǐ Chéng and concurrently Zuǒ Shíyí.
The Shěnguānyuàn memorialized that Déyuān was upright, capable, and efficient,
fit for demanding duties,
and thus he was reappointed.
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period, he was specially promoted to Ēnzhōu Cìshǐ,
then entered court as Yòusī Lángzhōng,
then Téngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and subsequently Tóngzhī Héjiānfǔ Shì,
then successively Dàxīng Zhìzhōng and Tóngzhī Fǔshì.
At the beginning of Dà'ān,
he was promoted to Pán'ānjūn Jiédùshǐ,
then reassigned as Héběi Xīlù Ànchá Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and then as Zhāoyìjūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Lùzhōu fell, he was captured.
Soon after, some people prostrated themselves before him.
They were all former residents of Shāhé,
who secretly protected Déyuān,
allowing him to escape.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu (1214),
he was appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū,
concurrently acting as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
At this time,
Shāndōng lacked soldiers and provisions.
The relevant authorities requested to sell "grace examinations" to candidates,
even allowing those in mourning to pay money to take the test.
Déyuān memorialized that this would greatly harm moral education,
and the matter was thus dropped.
Soon after, he retired.
Jiānchá Yùshǐ Xǔ Gǔ discussed Déyuān, saying:
"He is loyal, honest, intelligent, and astute,
capable of great use.
Recently, he requested to retire due to old age,
which gentlemen secretly lamented.
We hope the court will reinstate him;
he will surely be able to propose clear plans to benefit the state."
Xuānzōng graciously accepted this,
but he died before he could be employed.
Zhào Jiàn, courtesy name Zéshàn,
was from Zhāngqiū, Jǐnán.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Sòng Jiànyán (1128).
He was appointed Lúzhōu Sīlǐ Cānjūn.
At that time, there was warfare in Jiāng and Huái.
Jiàn abandoned his office and returned to his hometown.
When Qí Guó was established,
he was appointed Lìchéng Chéng,
then transferred to Chángqīng Lìng.
Both were difficult and challenging districts to govern,
but Jiàn's administration was very effective.
Liú Yù summoned him for an audience,
promoting him to Zhí Mìgé, Tíjǔ Jīngyuánlù Gōngjiànshǒu, and concurrently Tídiǎn Běnlù Xíngyù Gōngshì.
He was admonished, saying:
"Border generals are often lawless;
you must strictly control them."
The commander of Yuánzhōu was fierce and self-willed,
and he underestimated Jiàn due to his youth.
Jiàn exposed his misdeeds,
and the commander was dismissed.
Counties and districts heard of this and dared not offend.
When Qí was abolished,
he was appointed Zhī Chéngyángjūn,
then reassigned as Shāndōng Dōnglù Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ,
concurrently acting as Xíngtái Zuǒsī Lángzhōng.
The Xíngtái Zǎixiàng wanted to appoint a former Sòng eunuch to oversee the Dūshuǐjiān.
Jiàn said:
"These eunuchs who have brought disaster to the nation
are regarded as enemies by the people of Biàn.
Entrusting them with a good office
will lose public support."
So he was not employed.
He was relieved of his post due to his mother's mourning.
At the beginning of Tiāndé,
he was reinstated as Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
then transferred to Zhuōzhōu.
Hǎilíng summoned Jiàn to court,
but he responded inappropriately,
and was sent back to his commandery.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhī Huǒshānjūn,
but was relieved due to illness.
At the beginning of Dàdìng,
he was reinstated as Zhī Nínghǎijūn.
As the autumn crops were ripe,
an insect plague erupted.
Jiàn went out of the city to inspect,
and the insects then died on their own.
He was successively promoted to Zhèn Xījūn Jiédùshǐ,
then reassigned as Héběi Xīlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
retired from office,
and died.
Púchá Zhèliú, courtesy name Wénshú,
was from Dōngjīnglù Wòdǐbìlà Méng'ān.
He passed the imperial examination in the 22nd year of Dàdìng (1182).
He was appointed Gāoyuàn Zhǔbù and Jùnzhōu Sīhòu,
then assigned as Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
then appointed Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
and successively promoted to Běijīng, Línhuáng Ànchá Fùshǐ, and Hùbù Shìláng.
The Yùshǐtái memorialized that Zhèliú had performed his duties commendably in his previous post at Běijīng.
He was promoted to Shǎnxīlù Àncháshǐ,
then reassigned as Shùnyìjūn Jiédùshǐ.
In Xījīng, Lǐ Ān and his brothers disputed over property.
The prefecture and county could not resolve it.
The Ànchásī referred the case to Zhèliú for fair resolution,
but he did not address it for over a month.
During a ceremony for Confucius at the temple,
Zhèliú invited Ān and his brothers to join the scholars,
seated them together for wine,
and recounted several stories of ancient fraternal harmony.
Ān and his brothers were enlightened and understood,
and they thanked him, saying:
"The Jiédùshǐ is like our parents.
We vow never to quarrel again."
They then yielded to each other and returned home.
Shōsūzhōu had many bandits.
Zhèliú prohibited vagrancy,
and the people kept many weapons.
He toured the region in spring, comforting and appeasing the people.
The banditry then declined,
and the prisons became empty.
He was bestowed money for a banquet as a commendation.
He was changed to Jìlìshè Jūnjié Dùshǐ.
An edict was issued to round up horses.
Zhèng Liú instructed the common people to raise them in preparation.
The Imperial Censor impeached him for this.
Later, when the campaign against Sòng was launched,
the horses rounded up from all routes were emaciated,
but only those from Lóngzhōu were fat.
Thus, Zhèng Liú was released.
In the early Dà'ān period,
he was transferred to Ānguó Jūn.
In the second year,
he became Zhī Qìngyáng Fǔshì.
In the third year,
the Xīxià people invaded the border,
and Zhèng Liú attacked and drove them away.
In the first year of Zhìníng,
he was changed to Zhī Píngliáng Fǔ.
At this time,
Píngliáng had just been ravaged by war,
and the Xīxià people came to attack again.
Zhèng Liú recruited scattered soldiers to devise a defensive strategy.
The Xīxià army retreated,
and he was promoted four ranks.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was changed to Dōngjīng Liúshǒu
and retired.
In the fourth year of Zhēnyòu,
he died.
Zhèng Liú was dignified, taciturn, and rarely smiled.
People could not discern his joy or anger.
Before his death, he took out all his memorials and burned them.
Nǚxīliè Shǒuyú, courtesy name Zhònghuì,
originally named Húlígǎimén,
was from the Wúzhíkè Měng'ān in Zhēndìng Fǔlù.
At six years old, he knew how to read.
Later,
someone said that eating meat clouded one's mind,
so he abstained from it.
He was extremely filial by nature.
When his father died, he was fifteen,
and he arranged the funeral according to ritual.
He managed his household methodically,
and the villagers praised him.
He passed the imperial examination in the second year of Míngchāng.
He was appointed Shēnzé Zhǔbù,
