and his administration was well-regarded.
He was promoted to Huáirén Lìng,
then changed to Hóngwén Jiàolǐ,
and after his term, he became Línyí Lìng.
There were five hundred unruly individuals
who formed a gang
and greatly disturbed the region.
When Shǒuyú took office,
the gang dispersed.
Locusts arose between Jǔ and Mì,
but did not enter Línyí territory.
Before this,
the imperial court had surveyed land in Héshuò and Shāndōng.
Those who concealed land had it confiscated by the government,
and informers were rewarded.
The Cìshǐ of Jǔzhōu instructed his slave to accuse the people of Línyí of illegally occupying land,
accumulating three million in reward money.
The official payment was first disbursed and then collected from the people,
which caused great suffering to the populace.
Shǒuyú reported their grievances to the prefecture.
When the prefecture did not address them,
he reported to the Hùbù, which had the collections reimbursed.
Displaced people returned to their livelihoods,
and the people of the county carved this event in stone.
He was changed to Mìshū Láng.
When his mother died,
he did not consume a single drop of liquid for three days.
Throughout the mourning period, he never entered his inner chambers.
The Tàicháng Sì and Quànnóng Sī both invited Shǒuyú,
but he accepted neither.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Tóngzhī Dēngwén Jiǎnyuàn,
then changed to Zhùzuò Láng and Yǒngdìng Jūnjiédù Fùshǐ.
When Tàihé attacked Sòng,
Shǒuyú served as Shāndōng Xíngliùbù Yuánwàiláng.
He was then changed to Dàxīng Dūzǒngguǎn Pànguān.
In the first year of Dà'ān,
he was appointed Xiū Qǐjūzhù,
then transferred to Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng, Hùbù Lángzhōng, and Tàizǐ Zuǒyùdé.
In the early Zhēnyòu period,
he was appointed Hùbù Shìláng.
After several months, he was made Jiànyì Dàfū and Tídiǎn Jìnsì Jú.
In the second year,
he was appointed Bǎodà Jūnjiédùshǐ,
then changed to Hànlín Xuéshì and Cānyì Shǎnxīlù Ānfǔsīshì.
The Ānfǔ Wányán Bì respected his character,
and consulted him before undertaking any matter.
Not long after,
he fell ill,
and an imperial edict bestowed him with imperial medicine.
In the third year,
he died.
Shǒuyú was a loyal and unadorned person,
diligent in public service;
this was his natural disposition.
Shímò Yuán, courtesy name Xīmíng,
was from the Hútǔhǔ Měng'ān in Yìzhōulù.
At seven years old, he lost his father and wailed without eating for several days.
At thirteen, he observed his mother's mourning as an adult would.
Once, while playing polo,
his horse stumbled.
He sighed, saying:
"I have no brothers in life,
and I often ride in such dangerous circumstances.
What if something unforeseen happens?"
From then on, he never played again for the rest of his life.
He was appointed Shūmìyuàn Shàngshūshěng Yìshǐ,
then transferred to Tóngzhī Ēnzhōu Jūnzhōushì,
promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
and became Tóngzhī Zīzhōu Jūnzhōushì.
The notorious bandit Liú Qí had long been a scourge to the people.
One day, he was captured.
Just as he was being interrogated,
word came that a general amnesty was approaching,
so Yuán immediately ordered him to be beaten to death.
The whole prefecture rejoiced.
He was changed to Dàxīng Fǔ Pànguān, Yíwángfǔ Sīmǎ, and Qìnnán Jūnjiédù Fùshǐ.
There were many families in Hénèi who grew beautiful oranges,
and annually reaped great profits.
An enemy family entered at night and destroyed them.
The owner caught them
and falsely accused them of robbery.
The enemy family confessed under coercion,
but no stolen goods could be found.
Yuán, acting as the prefectural official,
investigated and uncovered the truth.
Soon after, he was changed to Héběixīlù Zhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ,
and successively promoted to Shāndōngxīlù Ànchá Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
In the early Zhēnyòu period,
Huángguó Wúdiǎn was conscripting soldiers in Dōngpíng.
He amassed a crowd but did not advance,
instead greatly seizing people's wealth,
which caused widespread resentment.
The Deputy Commander Púsǎn Sǎohé killed Wúdiǎn in his seat,
took his tally and wore it,
becoming even more wanton.
Yuán secretly submitted a memorial impeaching Sǎohé for arbitrarily killing a high official,
which was disloyal and unrighteous.
Sǎohé was executed for this.
He was transferred to Zhī Jìnán Fǔ,
and died six months after arriving in office.
Throughout his life, Yuán was taciturn and rarely smiled.
He valued frugality,
maintained his integrity in office,
and did not associate with powerful figures.
People praised him for this.
Zhāng Gòu, courtesy name Bóyīng,
was from Línyǐng, Xǔzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination in the twenty-eighth year of Dàdìng,
and was appointed Nínglíng Xiàn Zhǔbù.
He was changed to Tàidìng Jūnjiédù Pànguān,
and led scholars in practicing the rural drinking ritual.
He was changed to Tóngzhōu Guānchá Pànguān.
At this time,
troops were dispatched to guard the border.
The prefecture demanded one hundred thousand arrows,
stipulating that they be made with eagle or wild goose feathers,
whose price soared, making them unobtainable.
Gòu said:
"Arrows are meant to be expended.
What feather cannot be used?"
The Jiédùshǐ said:
"We must await a report from the province."
Gòu said:
"The prefecture is two thousand *lǐ* from the capital.
What about the urgency of the people?
If, by any chance, there is blame,
this subordinate will bear the responsibility."
Within a single day,
the price decreased severalfold.
The Shàngshūshěng ultimately approved his request.
He was appointed Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
then made Tóngzhī Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ Shì,
and changed to Běijīng Yánshǐ.
He observed mourning for his father.
After the mourning period,
he was again promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
He participated in the campaign against Sòng,
and was promoted to Wǔníng Jūnjiédù Fùshǐ.
He observed mourning for his mother.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
he was changed to Huìmín Sī Lìng,
and successively served as Hénán Zhìzhōng, Xízhōu Cìshǐ, Xíngbù Lángzhōng, and Tóngzhī Hénán Fǔshì.
He was promoted to Hédōngnánlù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ, and provisionally held the titles of Xíngliùbù Shàngshū and Ānfǔshǐ.
In the first year of Xīngdìng,
he died of illness.
Gòu was naturally filial and fraternal.
He always provided for his nephews before his younger brothers,
and entrusted all his official salary and income to his younger brothers to manage,
never asking about their abundance or lack.
Zhào Chóngfú 字 Lǚxiáng,
a native of Fēngzhōu.
He was conversant with both the large and small scripts of the Nǚzhí language.
He was tested and appointed as a clerk in the Nǚzhí Edict Office.
He was transferred to the positions of Military Affairs Translator and Shǎnxī Judicial Commissioner.
He was promoted to Dūgōu Pànguān of Shǎnxī Dōnglù, Fùshǐ of Yòucángkù, and Tóngzhī Chénzhōu Fángyù Shì.
When the Sòng spy Sū Quán entered Hénán,
Chóngfú tracked him.
Reaching Yútái and about to cross the river,
he saw a boat ahead about to cross.
He ordered his attendants to shout Sū Quán’s name loudly.
Suddenly, someone in the boat ahead became flustered and lost his composure.
They seized him, and indeed it was Sū Quán.
He was changed to Cāngzhōu Yánfùshǐ.
During a famine,
the people boiled brine to make salt and sold it to sustain themselves.
Salt officials often beat them to death.
Chóngfú said,
"I would rather have the tax quota fall short
than endure killing people."
When his term was complete,
his quota was indeed short, so he was due for demotion.
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Wányán Kuāng and Sānsī Shǐ Ànchūhǔ knew of his situation,
so they lightened his punishment due to the famine,
and he was appointed Zhīrǎn Shǔlìng.
In Dà'ān third year (1211),
he assisted Hùbù Shàngshū Zhāng Wěi in mobilizing soldiers and provisions at Gǔběikǒu.
He was promoted to Dūshuǐ Shàojiān,
and acted as Liùbù Lángzhōng of Xīběilù.
He governed Mìyún Xiàn,
and shortly thereafter also served as Hùbù Yuánwàiláng.
In Zhēnyòu second year (1214),
for his meritorious defense of Mìyún, he was promoted to Tóngzhī Héjiānfǔ Shì,
acting as Liùbù Shìláng,
exercising authority as Qīngzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and temporarily serving as Héběi Dōnglù Bīngmǎ Dūzǒngguǎn.
In the third year (1215),
Héjiān was besieged.
A man named Liú Zhōng, who had previously worked with Chóngfú in Mìyún,
advised Chóngfú to surrender,
but Chóngfú did not listen.
At this time,
Héjiān had few soldiers,
many of whom were weak and ill, unfit for battle,
and wanted to flee.
Chóngfú encouraged the elders to lead their sons and younger brothers,
with the strong fighting and the weak defending.
Due to prolonged rain, the siege was lifted.
He was promoted to Hédōng Běilù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
and then retired.
In Yuánguāng second year (1223),
he died.
Wǔ Dū 字 Wénbó,
a native of Dōngshèngzhōu.
In Dàdìng twenty-second year (1182), he passed the jinshi examination.
He was appointed Yánggǔ Zhǔbù,
and promoted to Shāngshuǐ Lìng.
The county was notoriously full of bandits.
Wǔ Dū thoroughly investigated the names of all the wicked people who had set fires, committed robberies, murdered, or robbed graves,
and obtained their names.
He posted them on the public thoroughfare,
making a pact that they should not offend again,
and they all fled to other territories.
For his integrity and capability, he was promoted to Nánjīng Lù Zhuǎnyùn Zhīdù Pànguān.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngdū Lù Dūzhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ.
Due to his aging parents,
he and his younger brother, Inspector Yù, both requested leave to care for them.
Soon after, he observed mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Tàiyuán Zhìzhōng,
and again served as Dūzhuǎnyùn Fùshǐ.
He was promoted to Luánzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was appointed Xuānchāi Běijīng Lù Guīcuò Guān,
and recovered one million units of scattered and lost official funds.
He entered the central government as Hùbù Lángzhōng,
and temporarily held the position of Yòusī Lángzhōng.
His memorials were in accordance with the emperor's wishes.
He was ordered to transport grain from Liáodōng by sea to relieve Shāndōng.
Wǔ Dū raised the price to recruit people to bring grain,
and enlisted merchant ships for transportation.
He was thrice promoted to Zhōngdū and Xījīng Ànchá Fùshǐ.
In Dà'ān third year (1211),
he was appointed Xuānchāi Xíng Liùbù Shìláng.
For his efforts, he was promoted to Běnlù Àncháshǐ,
and acted as Xīnánlù Liùbù Shàngshū.
He assisted Marshal Mòlián Jìnzhōng in defending Xījīng.
For his services,
he was summoned to be Hùbù Shàngshū,
and was rewarded with two hundred taels of silver and one hundred rolls of silk.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
the demotion of Wèi Shàowáng was discussed.
The details are in the biography of Wèi Shàowáng.
Soon after,
martial law was declared in Zhōngdū.
Wǔ Dū was appointed Zhī Dàxīngfǔ,
granted a tiger tally and discretionary powers,
to control the military and civilians both inside and outside the capital.
Wǔ Dū, while drunk, met an imperial envoy in his informal attire,
and was dismissed from his post for this offense.
He was reinstated as Xíngbù Shàngshū.
After the siege of Zhōngdū was lifted,
he became Hédōng Lù Xuānfǔshǐ.
Shortly thereafter, Cānzhī Zhèngshì Xū Dǐng replaced him.
In Xīngdìng first year (1217),
he died of illness.
Gēsīliè Dé 字 Guǎngzhī,
a native of Shānchūn Měng'ān in Zhēndìng Lù.
In Míngchāng second year (1191), he passed the jinshi examination.
He was appointed Nánjīng Jiàoshòu.
For his integrity and ability, he was promoted to Yàncì Lìng,
appointed a clerk in the Shàngshū Shěng,
and served as Tóngzhī Sìzhōu Fángyù Shì, Jiānchá Yùshǐ, Dàmíng Zhìzhōng, and Cìshǐ of Ān, Cáo, and Yù three prefectures.
He successively held the positions of Tóngzhī Línhuáng and Dàxīngfǔ Shì.
In Zhēnyòu second year (1214),
he was promoted to Zhàozhōu Fángyùshǐ.
In that year,
Zhàozhōu was elevated to Wǔxīng Jūn Jiédù,
and Gēsīliè Dé became Jiédùshǐ Xuānfǔ Sī Shǔ Dū Tíkòng.
Zhàozhōu was under urgent siege,
and food was almost exhausted.
There were three hundred boats of grain on the Yāzi Hé,
five li from the prefecture, but unable to reach it.
Gēsīliè Dé then dredged the moat and raised the parapets,
and built a covered pathway to connect the moat water to the river.
He dug horse-trapping pits,
and ambushed soldiers beside them to resist the siege.
One day, the troops clashed several times,
and the soldiers fought desperately.
When the canal was completed,
the boats reached the city wall,
and the soldiers had enough food.
The siege was then lifted.
He was transferred to Liáodōng Lù Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
The military and civilians blocked the road to urge him to stay,
and he could only leave by night.
Púxiān Wànnú pressed on Shàngjīng.
Gēsīliè Dé and his subordinate general Liú Ziyuán fought and repelled him.
He was promoted to Dōngjīng Liúshǒu,
and successively served as Bǎojìng and Wǔshèng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In Xīngdìng second year (1218),
he held the position of Xíng Liùbù Shì with his original title.
In the third year (1219),
he was given authority as Jiédù Quán Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān,
and with Zuǒdūjiān Shànzhōu Jīnglüèshǐ Wányán Zhòngyuán, they jointly established the Yuánshuàifǔ in Sùzhōu.
In the fourth year (1220),
he was promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū.
The next year,
he was summoned back to Zhōngdū.
In that year,
he died.
Zhāng Tèlì 字 Wénjǔ,
a native of Dōngmíng, Cáozhōu.
In Tàihé third year (1203), he passed the jinshi examination.
He was appointed Xuāndézhōu Sīhòu.
The commandery had many imperial relatives and powerful families.
Zhāng Tèlì governed them strictly according to the law,
and the entire region became orderly.
He was appointed Láizhōu Jiédù Pànguān,
but did not accept the position.
He personally farmed in Yǔchéng of shí,
[一０] finding joy in classical studies.
In the early Zhèngdà period (1224-1232),
Zuǒchéng Hóu Zhì and Cānzhèng Shī Ānshí recommended his talent,
and he was appointed Luòyáng Lìng.
In the fourth year (1227),
he was appointed Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
He presented a memorial stating:
"The two imperial residences of Hào and Lì
have long been under strict confinement,
with thorny fences and warning drums,
as if guarding against bandits.
Recently, an amnesty was issued,
and those who plotted rebellion or high treason were all pardoned.
What crime, then, have they committed,
to be so imprisoned?
Is not the spirit of Shìzōng in heaven,
perhaps wounded by this?
The heir apparent has not yet been established,
which may not be unrelated to this."
He further stated:
"Currently, we are attacked on three sides,
the common people are destitute,
and the chief ministers are untalented.
I fear that the task of restoration cannot be achieved within a few years."
He also said:
"Shàngshū Yòuchéng Yánzhǎn Shìlǔ sent his slave to dispute land with commoners,
losing the dignity of a high minister.
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Túshàn Wùdiǎn flattered those close to the emperor,
and thus held his position.
Both should be dismissed."
Those in power envied his straightforwardness,
and secretly found a way to oust him.
They then impeached the provincial clerks, Gāo Zhēn and others, for accepting bribes
and drinking in brothels.
At that time, Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Bái Sā returned from rewarding the troops in Shǎnxī.
Gāo Zhēn and the others wept and complained to him on the road,
stating that Wáng Bīn, another provincial clerk, was also at the same banquet,
but Zhāng Tèlì did not impeach him because Wáng Bīn was a *jìnshì* (advanced scholar).
Bái Sā, considering this to be partial and untrue,
also punished Zhāng Tèlì and Wáng Bīn.
Zhāng Tèlì was demoted to Pīzhōu Military Judge,
〔一一〕received fifty strokes with a staff,
and Wáng Bīn was also dismissed.
Scholars generally lamented Zhāng Tèlì's departure.
He later died in the *Guǐchǒu* year,
at the age of seventy-five.
Wáng Hào,
rose from being a clerk,
and was first appointed magistrate of Jīngyáng.
He was known for his integrity and honesty, ranking first in Guānfǔ.
At that time, the Xītái (Western Tribunal) issued a directive to prefectures and counties to plant more jujube and fruit trees,
with strict and urgent supervision.
The people were greatly disturbed,
but Wáng Hào alone made no inquiries.
The presiding official was about to punish him,
but Wáng Hào said:
“This county has already planted the required number.
If we were to plant more,
we would have to steal from others,
taking from one place and putting it in another;
I see no benefit in that.”
His love for the people was often like this.
Wherever he served, he implemented good governance.
The people suffered not the slightest offense.
The people of Qín erected a living shrine for him,
and thought of him at all times of the year.
After the move south,
he became the magistrate of Fúgōu.
In the first month of the first year of Kāixīng,
the commoner Qián Dàhēng and others seized the county officials and presented themselves to the North.
Dàhēng, because Wáng Hào had been benevolent to the people,
could not bear to harm him with a weapon.
He daily sent those he knew to persuade him to surrender,
but Wáng Hào never listened.
Thereupon, they killed him,
without blood.
The Chief Clerk Liú Tǎn and the Captain Sòng Yǐ were also killed.
Their bodies were abandoned by the roadside.
From spring to summer,
only Wáng Hào's body remained as if alive,
his eyes not even closed.
Crows and dogs dared not approach,
as if protected by a deity.
Initially,
when the system of appointment by recommendation was implemented,

many worthy officials were appointed to counties, such as Zhāng Tiāngāng, magistrate of Xiánníng; Lǐ Xiànfǔ, magistrate of Cháng'ān; and Zhāng Tèlì, magistrate of Luòyáng, all of whom have biographies.

The others, such as Shī Kuí of Xīngpíng, Wǔ Tiānzhēn of Líntóng, Dǎng Jūnyù of Fànshuǐ, Wáng Dēngyōng of Yǎnshī, Sòng Jiǔjiā of Gāolíng, Xuē Jūzhōng of Dēngfēng, Lǐ Tiānyì of Chángshè, Sūn Dǐngchén of Héjīn, Lǐ Wúdǎng of Jiāchéng, Lǐ Guòtíng of Xíngyáng, Zhāng Yú of Wèishì, Zhāng Zǐyù of Chánggé, Ān Dézhāng of Yīshì, Xiāo Bāngjié of Sānyuán, Zhāng Dézhí of Lántián, and Liú Cóngyì of Yèxiàn, were all upright, cautious, talented, and astute,
the best selection of their time.
That they were able to uphold the hundred-year-old dynasty which was about to collapse
was also due to the right officials being in place.
Collation Notes
Cruel Officials: Gāo Lǘshān, Púchá Hézhù
Tàishǐgōng (Grand Historian) once said,
"Legalists are strict and show little mercy."
How true are these words!
The Jīn laws were strict and meticulous.
Although the legal texts were adapted from previous dynasties with additions and deletions,
they mostly conformed to harsh penalties.
Xīzōng repeatedly initiated major persecutions,
Hǎilíng eliminated the imperial clan,
and legal cases were fabricated and twisted.
Informers and those who reported treason were rewarded extraordinarily.
Consequently,
the customs both within and outside the court underwent a complete change.
Everyone esteemed cruelty and tyranny as achievements,
and slander and treachery arose.
The poisonous influence spread far and wide,
truly tragic.
The *Jīn Shǐ* (History of Jīn) has many omissions.
According to its old records, two individuals were found
to be included in the biographies of cruel officials.
Gāo Lǘshān,
a native of Xīmù, Chéngzhōu.
He was selected to serve as a guard,
then transferred to Vice Envoy of the Shùnyì Army Jìedùshǐ,
and then promoted to Cí Xiángwěn of the Tángkuò and Yílà Dū.
He was reassigned as Vice Envoy of the Zhènwǔ Army Jìedùshǐ, Wèi of Cáowáng Fǔ, and Zhìzhōng of Dàmíng.
He was promoted to Cǐshǐ of Rǔzhōu,
then reassigned to Dānzhōu.
When an edict was issued prohibiting the unlawful use of a staff to punish people,
Gāo Lǘshān saw it and laughed, saying:
"This will also be difficult to implement."
On that very day,
he deliberately used a large staff to beat to death a local resident, Yáng Xiān.
He was demoted one rank and
dismissed from office.
After a long time,
he was demoted to Zhìzhōng of Fèngxiáng,
and successively served as Cǐshǐ of Yuánzhōu, Jìzhōu, and Sìzhōu.
He was reassigned as Fángyùshǐ of Zhèngzhōu,
and promoted to Jìedùshǐ of Púyǔ Lù.
He was then transferred to Línhǎi Jūn,
Pán'ān Jūn, and Níngchāng Jūn.
In the second year of Zhēnyòu,
the city fell and he died.
Púchá Hézhù,
rose from being a clerk.
He was long trusted by Xuānzōng,
and his influence was immense.
He was also cruel and ruthless,
and although people knew he was harming the state, no one dared to speak.
His son, serving as a guard,
was expelled first.
Later, Púchá Hézhù became a Cǐshǐ of a prefecture,
awaiting appointment in a nearby county.
Later, a large army entered Shǎnxī,
and Guānzhōng was shaken.
Some said Púchá Hézhù went to the prefecture to plan an escape to the north.
The imperial court ordered Kāifēng to detain his relatives.
Púchá Hézhù made resentful remarks, saying:
"If you kill me, then there will be peace!"
Soon after, he was impeached by an Yùshǐ (Censor).
Initially, flogging and ransom were proposed,
but the Prime Minister deemed it unreasonable.
He was beheaded at the gate of the Kāifēng Fǔ.
Thus, at that time, there was a saying about the "three villains of Xuānzōng's court":
Wáng Ālǐ and Púchá Yǎozhù,
and Púchá Hézhù was one of them.
During the Xīngdìng period,
in the case of Fùmǎ Púshàn Āhǎi,
seventy or more investigations were conducted in the capital.
Wáng Ālǐ and his ilk seized the opportunity to act and unleash their cruelty.
Court officials were trembling and unable to protect themselves.
Only Jí Wénzhī, serving in the staff of the Kāifēng Fǔ,
clarified that Púshàn Āhǎi was not rebelling,
and ultimately did not sign the document.
When Púshàn Āhǎi was executed,
Jí Wénzhī was also not implicated.
Púchá Yǎozhù,
retired in the early Zhèngdà period,
and resided in Suīyáng.
When the defeated army revolted,
he and his family were all killed.
Originally,
Xuānzōng delighted in punishments.
Court officials were often flogged and beaten,
even to the point of using knives and staffs to kill those who spoke out.
Gāo Qí, when in power,
exercised his authority and cruelty wantonly.
After the southern migration, this became a pervasive custom,
even influencing scholars and officials.
For example, Túdān Yòuchéng Sīzhōng enjoyed striking people with a hemp hammer,
and was known as
"Hemp Hammer Xiànggōng (Chancellor)."
Lǐ Yùnshǐ Tèlì was known as
"Half-Sword,"
referring to his short but sharp and incisive nature.
Féng Nèihàn Bì was known as
"Féng Guì (Executioner Feng)."
Léi Yuān, as an Yùshǐ,
when he reached Càizhōu and found powerful ruffians,
beat five hundred people to death with a staff,
and was called
"Léi Bànqiān (Lei Half-Thousand)."
There was also Wányán Májīnchū,
all known for their cruelty.
As for Púchá Hézhù, Wáng Ālǐ, and Lǐ Huàn and their like,
they were particularly cunning and cruel among the minor officials.
Flatterers and Favorites: Xiāo Yì, Zhāng Zhòngkē, Lǐ Tōng, Mǎ Qīn, Gāo Huáizhēn, Xiāo Yù, Xū Chíguó
Those in the world who indulge in desires,
how can they not be harmed by them?
The dragon,
the most divine creature under heaven,
once it has desires, it becomes controlled by humans.
Thus, the same applies to rulers.
Desires are not only about being enamored with softness and beauty;
campaigns, hunting, construction, and pursuing immortality—
those who are flatterers always find a way to cater to these preferences.
Jīn rulers were inwardly infatuated with sensual pleasures
and outwardly fond of grand achievements and glory.
None were more so than Xīzōng and Hǎilíng,
followed by Zhāngzōng.
The *Jīn Shǐ* lists seven particularly treacherous ministers, from Xiāo Yì to Xū Chíguó,
all of whom were favored by these three rulers.
They brought about their own downfall,
and harmed their country.
Their misfortunes all began here.
How can one not be cautious?
Biographies of Flatterers and Favorites.
Xiāo Yì
was originally a man of the Xī.
He was favored by Xīzōng
and also flattered Dàohòu.
He successively rose to the office of Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
On the night of the *rénshēn* day in the fourth month of the ninth year of Huángtǒng (1149),
there was a great wind and rain,
and lightning and thunder struck and damaged the *chīwěi* of the sleeping chambers.
Fire entered from outside
and burned the curtains and drapes of the inner chambers.
The emperor moved to another palace to avoid it.
He intended to issue an edict blaming himself.
Hànlín Xuéshì Zhāng Jūn was drafting it.
Jūn's intention was to respond to the heavenly warning
by deeply demeaning himself.
His text contained phrases such as:
"Only if virtue is not of its kind,
it will offend the majesty of Heaven,"
and
"Consider this ignorant, obscure, and humble child that I am."
Yì interpreted and reported, saying:
"'Fú lèi' (弗類) means 'greatly unprincipled,'
'guǎ' (寡) means 'solitary and without kin,'
'mèi' (昧) means 'ignorant of human affairs,'
and 'miǎo' (眇) means 'blind, seeing nothing.'
'Xiǎozǐ' (小子) is a term for an infant or child.
These are the words of a Hàn person using text to curse the emperor."
The emperor was greatly enraged.
He ordered the imperial guards to drag Jūn down from the hall,
and flogged him several hundred times.
When he did not die,
they used a short sword
to cut open his mouth and mince him.
Yì was bestowed with a 'tōngtiān xīdài' (通天犀帶, rhinoceros horn belt).
Relying on his imperial favor and influence,
he acted arrogantly towards his peers
and thus incurred the enmity of Hǎilíng.
When Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
he promoted ministers and bestowed titles.
Yì was among those generally granted the rank of Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
A few days later,
Hǎilíng summoned Yì and questioned him, saying:
"What crime did Xuéshì Zhāng Jūn commit to be executed?
What merit did you have to receive a reward?"
Yì could not answer.
Hǎilíng said:
"It is not difficult for me to kill you,
but some people might say that I am seeking personal revenge."
Thereupon,
an edict was issued to strip him of his official title
and send him back to his hometown,
prohibiting him from leaving a hundred *lǐ* radius.
Zhāng Zhòngkē's childhood name was Niú'ér (牛兒).
He was a rogue from the marketplace,
who made a living telling fantastic stories
mixed with humorous and playful language.
Hǎilíng kept him close
for entertainment.
When Hǎilíng was enfeoffed as the King of Qí,
Zhòngkē wrote memorials for him.
Upon Hǎilíng's enthronement,
he became Mìshū Láng.
Hǎilíng often engaged in indecent acts with his concubines in front of Zhòngkē.
Zhòngkē merely acknowledged his death sentence,
not daring to look up.
He also once ordered Zhòngkē to strip naked for his viewing.
Attendant officials were often ordered to strip naked;
even Túshā Dānzhēn could not avoid this.
Bīngbù Shìláng Wányán Pǔlián and Dàxīng Shàoyǐn Lǐ Dūn both fell from power due to corruption,
yet Hǎilíng placed them in important and close positions.
The performer Yú Qìng'ér was a fifth-rank official.
Dà Shì's household slave Wáng Zhīzhāng became Mìshū Láng.
Zhīzhāng would place pearls in remote spots,
and Hǎilíng would personally observe them without finding it improper.
Tángkuò Biàn's household slave Héshàng, and Wūdài's household slaves Gé Wēn and Gé Lǔ,
were all placed in the imperial guard,
some even achieving the first rank through sheer luck.
Sometimes, individuals around him who held no official position,
or whom he called by name,
were immediately granted high ranks.
Hǎilíng would say to that person:
"Can you still call me by name now?"
He often placed gold in his bedding,
and those he favored were told to take it themselves.
His excessive generosity was like this.
When Sòng's Yú Tángbì came to congratulate him on ascending the throne,
and was about to return,
Hǎilíng attached a jade belt as a gift for the Sòng emperor,
and instructed him to tell the Sòng emperor:
"This belt was regularly worn by your father.
I now bestow it upon you
so that you may feel as if you see your father,
and should not forget my intentions."
After the envoy left,
Zhòngkē said:
"This is a rare treasure in the world,
it is a pity to bestow it lightly."
The emperor said:
"The land of Jiāngnán
will one day be mine.
This is but an item to be placed in an outer treasury."
From this, it was known that Hǎilíng had the intention of invading the south.
Soon, Zhòngkē was promoted to Mìshū Chéng,
then transferred to Shàojiān.
At this time,
when constructing palaces in Yānjīng,
officials took timber from the Tán Yuán of Zhēndìng Fǔ.
Zhòngkē seized the opportunity to say that the timber there was unusable.
Hǎilíng suspected Zhòngkē had received a bribe,
and dismissed him from office.
Not long after,
he was reinstated as Shàojiān.
Hǎilíng hunted at Túní Shān,
and stopped at Duówǎ.
He poured libations to Heaven and bowed,
saying to his ministers:
"When I was young, I practiced archery.
Upon reaching a certain gate,
I silently prayed, saying:
'If I am to become greatly honored in the future,
may an arrow be placed horizontally on the ridge of this gate.'
When I shot,
it indeed landed horizontally on the gate ridge.
Later, as the Grand Administrator of Zhōngjīng,
I once had a great hunt in this area.
Before the encirclement closed,
I prayed, saying:
'If I am to hold a high position,
I shall catch three deer within a hundred paces.
If I am merely a duke or prime minister,
I shall catch only one.'
Thereupon, I caught three deer within a hundred paces.
I further prayed, saying:
'If I am to unify all under Heaven,
I shall again catch a large deer.'
Thereupon, I indeed caught a large deer.
I once spoke of this matter with Xiāo Yù.
Now that I have returned to this place,
I therefore offer this libation and bow."
Hǎilíng intended to take Jiāngnán,
and therefore first established auspicious omens to subtly influence his ministers.
This is why Zhòngkē always anticipated his desires
and encouraged him to invade the south.
In the first month of the second year of Zhēnyuán (1154),
the Sòng envoy Shī Jù, who came to congratulate on New Year's Day, bid farewell.
Hǎilíng ordered Zuǒ Xuānhuīshǐ Jìng Sìhuī to ask Shī Jù:
"How many categories does the Sòng state have for selecting scholars?"
He replied:
"Poetry and rhapsodies, interpretations of the classics, and policy essays are all practiced concurrently."
He then asked:
"What office does Qín Huì hold,
and how old is he now?"
He replied:
"Huì is the Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè and Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì,
and he is sixty-five years old."
He further said to him:
"I heard that Qín Huì is wise,
that is why I asked."
In the second year of Zhènglóng
Zhòngkē became a Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū,
responsible for recording the emperor's daily activities.
However, he only received the salary of a Jiànyì,
and was not allowed to speak on matters of state.
In the first month of the third year,
Sòng envoy Sūn Dàofū, who was on a New Year's greetings mission, was granted an audience to bid farewell.
Hǎilíng ordered the Zuǒ Xuānhuī Shǐ Jìng Sìhuī to instruct him, saying:
“Go back and tell your emperor:
there have been many instances of insincerity in your dealings with our great country.
Today, I will briefly mention two matters. When your people flee into our territory,
our border officials immediately return them.
When our people flee into your territory,
your authorities often make excuses and fail to return them when requested. This is the first.
You are secretly buying saddles and horses along the border,
preparing for battle. This is the second.
Moreover, horses can only be used with people.
If there are no people,
what good are a million horses?
How can we not be prepared?
And if we don't take your country, so be it.
But if we want to take it,
it is certainly not difficult.
I hear that the harboring of fugitives and the secret purchase of saddles and horses
are all the doing of your country's Yáng Tàiwèi.
I often learn from captives that this person is incompetent.”
He also said:
“I hear Qín Huì is dead.
Is that true?”
Dàofū replied:
“Qín Huì is indeed dead.
This humble official was also recommended and employed by Qín Huì.”
He further asked:
“Why are your country's recent actions
so different from Qín Huì's time?”
Dàofū said:
“This humble official will return to his country
and report everything to the Sòng Emperor.”
Hǎilíng intended to launch a southern expedition,
so he first fabricated the two issues of harboring fugitives and secretly buying horses,
and interspersed them with other statements.
Hǎilíng summoned Zhòngkē, Yòu Bǔquē Mǎ Qīn, Jiàoshū Láng Tián Yǔxìn, and Zhícháng Xí Shī to the private palace to attend him.
Hǎilíng discussed the Hàn Shū with Zhòngkē,
and said to Zhòngkē:
“The territory of Hàn did not exceed seven or eight thousand *lǐ*.
Now our country's territory spans ten thousand *lǐ*;
it can be called vast.”
Zhòngkē said:
“Although the territory of our dynasty is vast,
the world has four rulers.
To the south, there is Sòng;
to the east, there is Gāolì;
to the west, there is Xià.
If we can unify them,
then it will truly be vast.”
Hǎilíng said:
“What crime have they committed that we should attack them?”
Zhòngkē said:
“Your subject hears that the Sòng people are buying horses, repairing weapons,
and harboring fugitives from Shāndōng.
How can they be considered guiltless?”
Hǎilíng was delighted and said:
“Earlier, Liáng Gū once told me
that Sòng has a Noble Consort Liú who is dazzlingly beautiful,
surpassing the Huárúi of Shǔ and the Xīshī of Wú.
Now, with one stroke, we can gain both.
This is what the proverb calls 'killing two birds with one stone' [literally: 'waving one's hand while on a journey'].
When Jiāngnán hears that I am raising an army,
they will surely flee far away.”
Mǎ Qīn and Tián Yǔxìn both replied:
“As for the island nations and the southern barbarians,
we all know the routes.
Where will they go?”
Mǎ Qīn added:
“When I was in Sòng,
I once led an army to conquer the barbarians,
which is why I know.”
Hǎilíng asked Xí Shī:
“Do you dare to fight?”
He replied:
“Having received your grace for so long,
what is there to avoid in death?”
Hǎilíng said:
“Do you expect them to dare to send out troops?
If they do send out troops,
can you truly fight to the death against the enemy?”
After a long pause, Xí Shī said:
“Although your subject is timid and weak,
I will still fight them as an enemy.”
Hǎilíng asked:
“Where will they send out their troops?”
He replied:
“No further than Huáinán.”
Hǎilíng said:
“Then Heaven is helping us!”
Soon after, he said:
“I will raise an army to destroy Sòng,
which will take no more than two or three years.
Then I will subjugate Gāolì and Xià Guó.
After unification,
I will assess merits and promote ranks,
and reward the generals and soldiers.
They will surely forget their toil.”
In the third month of the fourth year,
Zhòngkē died.
On the eve of the Winter Solstice,
Hǎilíng dreamt that Zhòngkē asked for wine.
Upon waking,
he sighed and lamented for a long time,
and sent an envoy to offer sacrifices at his tomb.
Lǐ Tōng,
gained favor with Hǎilíng through his obsequious and sycophantic behavior.
He was successively promoted to Yòu Sī Lángzhōng,
then transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
Requests for favors and bribes poured into his door.
On the *yǐyǒu* day of the first month of the second year of Zhènglóng,
an imperial decree ordered officials from the Zuǒ Sī Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng downwards to present memorials in the private palace.
Hǎilíng said:
“No one knows a son better than his father,
and no one knows a subject better than his sovereign.
I have tested this.
When I inquire about talented individuals,
if you do not recommend your own kind,
you will certainly recommend those with whom you are on good terms.
I hear that those of Nǚzhēn and Qìdān origin who seek official advancement
must rely on Xíngbù Shàngshū Wū Dài and Qiānshū Shūmì Yáoshè to introduce them,
with Zuǒ Sī Yuánwàiláng Ālǐgǔliè handling the matter.
Those of Bóhǎi and Hàn origin who seek official advancement
must rely on Lìbù Shàngshū Lǐ Tōng and Hùbù Shàngshū Xǔ Lín to introduce them,
with Zuǒ Sī Lángzhōng Wáng Wèi handling the matter.
Among those on the official roster,
I recognize few,
and do not recognize many.
Are they not all my subjects?
How can there be distinctions of distance, closeness, kinship, or estrangement?
If one performs one's duties without fault,
one can readily become a Shàngshū, Shìláng, or Jiédùshǐ.
If, by any chance, one commits a crime,
one will be punished without pardon.”
Shortly after,
he was appointed Cānzhī Zhèngshì.
Hǎilíng, relying on the dynasty's long-standing strength and prosperity,
desired to launch extensive military campaigns
to unify the realm,
and once said:
“Only when the world is one family
can there be legitimate succession.”
Lǐ Tōng, discerning his intentions,
then, along with Zhāng Zhòngkē, Mǎ Qīn, the eunuch Liáng Gū, and other close attendants and lesser figures,
extensively discussed the wealth of Jiāngnán,
its abundance of women, jade, and silk,
thus catering to his wishes and speaking of it first.
Hǎilíng believed their words
and regarded Lǐ Tōng as his chief strategist,
and so decided to raise an army to attack Jiāngnán.
In the second month of the fourth year,
Hǎilíng instructed his prime ministers, saying:
“Although the Sòng state is submissive,
it has vows but no sincerity.
Recently, I hear of them buying horses along the border and harboring fugitives,
which we cannot afford to disregard.”
He sent envoys to register the Měng'ān tribes of various circuits, and the Bóhǎi able-bodied men from prefectures and counties to serve as soldiers,
and also to confiscate civilian horses from all circuits.
Thus,

envoys were sent to Shàngjīng, Sùpín Lù, Húlígǎi Lù, Gélǎn Lù, Púyǔ Lù, Tàizhōu, Xiánpíng Fǔ, Dōngjīng, Pósù Lù, Gésūguǎn, Línhuáng Fǔ, Xīnán Zhāotǎo Sī, Xīběi Zhāotǎo Sī, Běijīng, Héjiān Fǔ, Zhēndìng Fǔ, Yìdū Fǔ, Dōngpíng Fǔ, Dàmíng Fǔ, and Xījīng Lù.
All men between twenty and fifty years of age were registered.
Even if a family had elderly parents and many able-bodied men,
a request to leave one son to attend to them
was not granted.
In the eleventh month of the fifth year,
he dispatched Yìdū Yǐn Jīng and thirty other officials to escort military equipment from various circuits to designated strategic gathering points
to be distributed when the army arrived.
Any surplus equipment and that which could not be repaired in time
were all gathered and burned.
In the first month of the sixth year,
Hǎilíng ordered Lǐ Tōng to convey an imperial decree to Sòng envoy Xú Dù and others, saying:
“When I was young, I once lived in Nánjīng with Prince Liáng,
and enjoyed its customs and climate.
It has been a practice since ancient times for emperors to make inspection tours.
Huáinán has many open spaces,
and I wish to hunt there,
with my escort troops not exceeding ten thousand men.
You all should return and inform your sovereign,
ordering your officials to proclaim my intention,
so that the people of Huáinán will not be filled with doubt and fear.”
In the second month,
Lǐ Tōng was promoted to Yòu Chéng.
An imperial decree stated:
“You, minister, have overseen the repair of military weapons,
and now the task is complete.
I commend your loyalty and diligence,
hence this appointment.
After the affairs of Jiāngnán are settled,
you will be separately commended and rewarded.”
At this time,
the waters of Liángshān Pò dried up.
The previously built warships could not advance.
Thus, Tōng was ordered to construct new warships.
The supervision was harsh and urgent,
and the generals and soldiers had no rest for seven or eight days and nights.
They destroyed the civilian houses in the city for timber,
and boiled fat from dead bodies for oil to use.
Then, a platform was built by the river.
Hǎilíng, clad in golden armor, ascended the platform,
slaughtered a black horse to sacrifice to Heaven,
and threw one sheep and one pig into the river.
He summoned Dūdū Āng and Fùdūdū Púlúhún and said to them:
"The boats are ready;
we can cross the river now."
Púlúhún replied:
"Your subject observes that the Sòng ships are very large,
while our ships are small and slow.
I fear we cannot cross."
Hǎilíng angrily said:
"You once followed Liáng Wáng in pursuing Zhào Gòu to the sea island;
were all those large ships?
Tomorrow, you and Āng will cross first."
When Āng heard the order for him to cross the river,
he was afraid and wanted to flee.
By evening,
Hǎilíng sent someone to tell Āng:
"What I said earlier was just a moment's anger;
there's no need for you to cross the river first."
The next day,
he dispatched Wǔpíngjūn Dūzǒngguǎn Ālín and Wǔjiéjūn Fùzǒngguǎn Āsā to lead the naval forces across first.
Sùzhíjīangjūn Wēndū Àolà, Guózǐ Sīyè Mǎ Qīn, and Wǔkù Zhícháng Xíshī all participated in the battle.
Hǎilíng placed yellow and red flags on the bank
to signal advance and halt.
When the red flag was raised, they advanced;
when the yellow flag was lowered, they retreated.
After crossing the river,
two boats first pressed towards the southern bank,
but the water was too shallow to advance.
They exchanged arrows with the Sòng soldiers for a long time,
until the arrows in both boats were exhausted.
They were then captured,
and one Měngān and over a hundred soldiers were lost.
Hǎilíng then returned to Hézhōu.
At this, Shàngshūshěng Shǐ Yòusī Lángzhōng Wúbǔkě and Yuánwàiláng Wáng Quán reported: Shìzōng has ascended the throne in Dōngjīng,
and the reign era has been changed to Dàdìng.
Hǎilíng had already sent Hùwèi Móuliánghǔ and Tèlíbǔ to Dōngjīng before this,
intending to harm Shìzōng.
When they reached Liáoshuǐ,
they met Shìzōng's imperial envoy Sābā,
captured and killed him,
then returned to the army.
Hǎilíng patted his thigh and sighed:
"I originally intended to pacify Jiāngnán and change the era to Dàdìng;
is this not fate?"
He then took out a previously written document detailing his ambition to unify the world in one campaign and change the era to Dàdìng,
and showed it to his assembled officials.
Then he summoned his generals to discuss returning north,
and also to divide the troops to cross the river.
After the discussion was settled,
Tōng again entered to report:
"Your Majesty personally leads the army deep into foreign territory.
To return without accomplishment,
if the multitudes scatter in front
and the enemy presses from behind,
is not a foolproof plan.
If troops are left to cross the river and
Your Majesty's carriage returns north,
the generals will also disband.
Currently, the armies north of Yān, especially those near Liáoyáng, may have disloyal intentions.
It is advisable to first dispatch troops to cross the river,
then gather and burn the boats,
cutting off any hope of return.
Then Your Majesty can return north,
and both north and south will be settled in no time."
Hǎilíng agreed with this,
and the next day hastened to Yángzhōu.
Passing through Wūjiāng Xiàn,
he visited Xiàng Yǔ's temple
and sighed:
"That such a hero could not gain the empire
is truly regrettable."
When Hǎilíng arrived at Yángzhōu,
he ordered Fúbǎo Yēlǜ Mòdáhù of Shénguǒ Jūn to guard the Huái River crossing.
Anyone returning from the army to the Huái River without a Dūdūfǔ document was killed.
He then took out an imperial arrow decorated with a golden dragon,
inscribed it "Imperial Arrow,"
and tied a silk letter to it.
He had someone shoot it across to the southern bank by boat.
The letter stated:
"The Sòng nation dispatched people to burn and destroy the palaces in Nánjīng,
and along the border bought horses and enticed soldiers and civilians.
Now, an army is raised to demand accountability.
Our righteous cause is to punish the wrongdoers.
Wherever the grand army reaches,
there shall be no slightest transgression."
With this, he sought to persuade the Sòng people.
At this,
Sòng general Wáng Quán also released three captured Jīn soldiers,
who carried a letter enumerating Hǎilíng's crimes.
Tōng submitted the letter,
and Hǎilíng immediately ordered it burned.
Hǎilíng was enraged
and urgently desired to cross the river.
Xiāoqí Gāo Sēng attempted to incite his faction to flee.
When the plot was discovered,
Hǎilíng ordered the crowd to hack him to pieces.
He then issued an order:
if a soldier fled, his Púlǐyǎn was killed;
if a Púlǐyǎn fled, his Móukè was killed;
if a Móukè fled, his Měngān was killed;
if a Měngān fled, his Zǒngguǎn was killed.
Because of this, the soldiers became even more fearful.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
an order was given for the army to transport Yāhú boats and grain boats to Guāzhōu Dù,
scheduled to cross the river the next day,
with death for anyone who lagged behind.
On the Yǐwèi day,
Wányán Yuányí and others attacked the imperial camp with troops.
Hǎilíng was assassinated.
The Dūdūfǔ regarded Tōng and others as having approved the southern campaign strategy;
Túdān Yǒngnián was his relative by marriage,
and Guō Ānguó was universally detested by the populace.
All were killed.
In the second year of Dàdìng,
an imperial edict stripped Tōng of his official titles and ranks,
and people's hearts finally rejoiced.
Mǎ Qīn,
whose infant name was Hángē,
once served in Jiāngnán,
thus he knew the roads of Jiāngnán.
In the third year of Zhènglóng,
when Hǎilíng was about to launch the southern campaign,
he summoned Qīn to serve,
appointing him from Guìdé Xiànlìng to Yòubǔquē.
Qīn was a frivolous and superficial person who lacked understanding of important matters.
Whenever Hǎilíng summoned him for a conversation,
Qīn would leave the palace and immediately tell others:
"The emperor discussed such-and-such a matter with me;
it will soon be implemented."
He regarded Hǎilíng as a peer.
He was successively promoted to Guózǐ Sīyè.
When Hǎilíng reached Hézhōu,
he wanted to send Púlúhún across the river.
Púlúhún said the boats were too small to cross.
Hǎilíng sent for Qīn,
first instructing his attendants:
"If Qīn says the boats are too small to cross the river,
immediately kill him."
When Qīn arrived,
Hǎilíng asked:
"Can these boats cross the river or not?"
Qīn replied:
"Your subject can also cross."
In the second year of Dàdìng,
he was dismissed from his post.
On that day,
the former Hànlín Dàizhì Dàyǐng was appointed Mìshū Chéng.
During the Zhènglóng era, Yǐng had spoken about the bandits in Shāndōng.
Hǎilíng disliked his words
and had him flogged and dismissed from office.
Shìzōng praised Yǐng's loyalty and honesty
and disliked Qīn's cunning flattery,
thus he re-employed Yǐng and dismissed Qīn.
Gāo Huáizhēn,
who was a Shàngshūshěng Lìshǐ,
had long been intimate with Hǎilíng.
Hǎilíng had harbored rebellious ambitions for a long time.
He once discussed his ambitions with Huáizhēn.
Hǎilíng said:
"I have three ambitions: all national affairs originating from me,
that is one.
Leading an army to conquer a nation,
capturing its ruler and interrogating him before me,
that is two.
Obtaining the most beautiful woman in the world and making her my wife,
that is three."
Because of this, all the petty and sycophantic men knew his ambitions
and competed to offer flattery.
Dàdìng Xiànchéng Zhāng Zhōngfǔ told Hǎilíng:
"I dreamt that you and the emperor were playing polo,
and you rode past him,
and the emperor fell from his horse."
Hǎilíng was greatly pleased to hear this.
At that time, Xīzōng had been on the throne for a long time,
delegating political power to his grand ministers.
Hǎilíng, as a close relative, became prime minister,
wielding exclusive power and influence.
Thus, he formed a plan to assassinate and usurp the throne.
It was all instigated and guided by petty men like Huáizhēn.
After Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
he appointed Huáizhēn as Xiū Qǐjūzhù,
and Huáizhēn's late father, the Bīnzhōu Cìshǐ, was posthumously honored as Zhōngfèng Dàfū.
Huáizhēn was successively promoted to Lǐbù Shìláng.
In Dàdìng (大定) second year (1162),
he was demoted to Fèngzhèng Dàfū (奉政大夫)
and sent back to his hometown.
Five years later,
he and Xǔ Lín (許霖) were both granted reinstatement.
Huáizhēn (懷貞) was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of the Dìngguó (定國) Army.
The Emperor [Shàng (上)] admonished them, saying:
"When you were serving during the ZhèngLóng (正隆) era,
you were treacherous, flattering, greedy, and selfish;
public opinion despised you.
I thought that if you were not given a chance to redeem yourselves, you would have no means to reform.
However, if you cling to your old ways and do not repent,
I will certainly not pardon you."
Xiāo Yù (蕭裕),
whose original name was Yáozhé (遙折),
was a Xī (奚) man.
He first served as a Měng'ān (猛安) in Zhōngjīng (中京).
Hǎilíng (海陵) was the Liúshǒu (留守) of Zhōngjīng (中京) at the time,
and he befriended Yù (裕),
often discussing state affairs with him.
Yù (裕) surmised that Hǎilíng (海陵) had covetous ambitions,
and secretly said to Hǎilíng (海陵):
"The Liúshǒu (留守) is the former Grand Preceptor [Xiān Tàishī (先太師)]
and the eldest son of Tàizǔ (太祖).
With such virtue and prestige,
the hearts of the people and the will of Heaven ought to belong to you.
If you truly intend to undertake a great enterprise,
I am willing to dedicate my full strength to follow you."
Hǎilíng (海陵) gladly accepted,
and so they began to plot together.
That Hǎilíng (海陵) ultimately succeeded in his regicidal plot [shì nì zhī móu (弒逆之謀)]
was initiated by Yù (裕).
When Hǎilíng (海陵) became Zuǒ Chéng (左丞),
Yù (裕) was appointed Bīngbù Shìláng (兵部侍郎),
then transferred to Tongzhī Nánjīng Liúshǒu Shì (同知南京留守事),
then to Běijīng (北京).
When Hǎilíng (海陵) was leading the Xíngtái Shàngshū Shěng Shì (行臺尚書省事),
he passed through Běijīng (北京)
and said to Yù (裕):
"I intend to establish my reign with the armies in Hénán (河南),
first pacify the two Hé (河) regions,
then lead an army north.
You must gather the Měng'ān (猛安) for me to respond to my call."
They made their pact and Hǎilíng (海陵) departed.
Although Hǎilíng (海陵) was recalled from Liángxiāng (良鄉),
he could not keep his promise.
He then assassinated Xīzōng (熙宗) and usurped the throne,
appointing Yù (裕) as Mìshū Jiān (祕書監).
Hǎilíng (海陵) was wary of Tàizōng's (太宗) sons
and wanted to eliminate them,
so he secretly plotted with Yù (裕).
Yù (裕) was treacherous, cunning, and deceitful,
and fabricated charges of rebellion against Tàifù Zōngběn (太傅宗本), Bǐngdé (秉德), and others.
Hǎilíng (海陵) killed Zōngběn (宗本).
Tángkuò Biàn (唐括辯) sent envoys to kill Bǐngdé (秉德), Zōngyì (宗懿), and over seventy descendants of Tàizōng (太宗), and over thirty descendants of Qín Wáng Zōnghàn (秦王宗翰).
After Zōngběn (宗本) had already died,
Yù (裕) then sought Zōngběn's (宗本) doorman Xiāo Yù (蕭玉),
instructing him to make a full confession of rebellion,
and ordered him to submit it under his own name.
When Hǎilíng (海陵) issued the imperial edict to the world,
the world felt injustice.
Hǎilíng (海iling) rewarded Yù (裕) for his service in executing Zōngběn (宗本),
making him Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng (尚書左丞),
adding the title Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
granting him the rank of Měng'ān (猛安),
and bestowing upon him twenty million coins, four hundred horses, four hundred oxen, and four thousand sheep.
After two more months,
he became Píngzhāng Zhèngshì (平章政事) and Jiānxiū Guóshǐ (監修國史).
According to old regulations,
the Prime Minister [Xiàng (相)] was the Jiānxiū Guóshǐ (監修國史).
Hǎilíng (海陵) appointed Yù (裕) to this position,
telling him:
"Tàizǔ (太祖) received the Mandate of Heaven with his divine military prowess.
His magnificent achievements and splendid virtues illuminated the four seas.
I fear that historians might overlook some,
hence I bestow this upon you,卿 [qīng]."
After some time,
Yù (裕) became Yòuchéngxiàng (右丞相) and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
When Yù (裕) was in the position of Prime Minister [Xiàng (相)],
he was quite arbitrary in his duties and exercise of power.
His authority and influence were his own;
his power swayed the court.
Hǎilíng (海陵) trusted him implicitly,
and other prime ministers merely deferred to him.
Yù (裕) was close to Gāo Yàoshī (高藥師),
and once told Yàoshī (藥師) a secret conversation with Hǎilíng (海陵).
Yàoshī (藥師) then reported Yù's (裕) words to Hǎilíng (海陵),
adding:
"Yù (裕) harbors resentment and discontent."
Hǎilíng (海陵) summoned Yù (裕) and admonished him,
but did not consider it a crime.
Some people accused Yù (裕) of abusing his power,
but Hǎilíng (海陵) thought that many people were jealous of Yù (裕)
and did not believe them.
He also thought that people saw Yù's (裕) younger brother, Xiāo Zuò (蕭祚), as Zuǒfù Diǎnjiǎn (左副點檢),
and his sister's husband, Yēlǜ Pìlílà (耶律闢离剌), as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍),
and that their positions of power depended on each other,
which led to jealousy.
So he sent Zuò (祚) out as Yìdū Yǐn (益都尹)
and Pìlílà (闢离剌) as Níngchāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ (寧昌軍節度使),
to dispel public suspicion.
Yù (裕) did not understand Hǎilíng's (海陵) intention.
Suddenly seeing his relatives [qīnbiǎo (親表)] sent out to provincial posts [bǔ wài (補外)]
without his knowledge,
he began to deeply worry that Hǎilíng (海陵) suspected him.
Hǎilíng's (海陵) younger brother, Tàishī Yǎn (太師兗), was in charge of the Sānshěng (三省).
Together in the position of prime minister,
Yǎn (兗) often restrained Yù (裕) because Yù (裕) was too self-willed.
Yù (裕) then thought that Hǎilíng (海陵) was using Yǎn (兗) to guard against him.
Moreover, Hǎilíng (海陵) was suspicious, cruel, and bloodthirsty.

Fearing disaster, Yù (裕) then conspired with former Zhēndìng Yǐn (真定尹) Xiāo Féngjiānú (蕭馮家奴), former Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Xiāo Zhāozhé (蕭招折), Bózhōu (博州) Tóngzhī (同知) Yáoshè (遙設), and Yù's (裕) daughter's husband Èlàbǔ (遏剌補) to enthrone the grandson of the deceased Liáo (遼) Yù Wáng Yánxǐ (豫王延禧).
Yù (裕) sent his trusted subordinate Xiāo Túnnà (蕭屯納) to contact the Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ (西北路招討使) Xiāo Hǎohú (蕭好胡),
who was also Huáizhōng (懷忠).
Huáizhōng (懷忠) was hesitant and undecided,
and said to Túnnà (屯納):
"This is a major undertaking.
You should go back and send an important person here."
Yù (裕) then sent Zhāozhé (招折).
Zhāozhé (招折) had previously been Zhōngchéng (中丞) but was dismissed due to a crime,
and thus was able to visit Huáizhōng (懷忠).
Huáizhōng (懷忠) asked Zhāozhé (招折) who else was involved in the conspiracy.
Zhāozhé (招折) replied:
"Yēlǜ Lǎng (耶律朗), the Wǔyuàn Jiédùshǐ (五院節度使), is also involved."
Huáizhōng (懷忠) had an old grudge with Lǎng (朗).
Moreover, Zhāozhé (招折) had previously reported Tàlǎndà (撻懶) incident,
so Huáizhōng (懷忠) suspected Zhāozhé (招折) of being duplicitous.
Therefore, he arrested Zhāozhé (招折)
and had Lǎng (朗) imprisoned,
and sent an envoy to report the treason.
Yáoshè (遙設) also wrote a letter to the Bǐyàn Lìshǐ (筆硯令史) Bái Dá (白荅),
asking Bái Dá (白荅) to assist Yù (裕) in gaining wealth and high position.
Bái Dá (白荅) submitted the letter to the throne.
Hǎilíng (海陵) trusted Yù (裕) without doubt,
believing that Bái Dá (白荅) was fabricating a slander,
and ordered Bái Dá (白荅) to be executed in the marketplace.
When Bái Dá (白荅) was led out through Xuānhuá Mén (宣華門),
Diǎnjiǎn Túdān Zhēn (點檢徒單貞) came in to report the treasonous activities of Xiāo Huáizhōng (蕭懷忠)
and encountered Bái Dá (白荅).
He asked the reason for his execution
and then stopped it.
After Túdān Zhēn (徒單貞) had reported the treason,
he pleaded for Bái Dá (白荅).
Hǎilíng (海陵) immediately ordered his release.
Hǎilíng (海陵) sent a chancellor to question Yù (裕).
Yù (裕) immediately confessed.
Hǎilíng (海陵) was greatly astonished,
still not entirely convinced,
so he summoned Yù (裕)
and questioned him personally.
Yù (裕) said:
"What a great man does,
when things have come to this, how can it be hidden?"
Hǎilíng (海陵) then asked:
"Why do you resent Us and do such a thing?"
Yù (裕) said:
"Your Majesty discussed everything with your servant,
but when it came to removing Zuò (祚) and others, you did not let your servant know.
The Prince who governs the province (領省國王) always tells your servant that I usurp power,
and has quite a lot of precautions,
I suspect this is with Your Majesty's instruction.
Your Majesty, Tangguō Biàn (唐括辯), and your servant swore to live and die together,
but Biàn (辯) was killed because of his stubbornness and boldness,
your servant knows all this,
and feared that I would not die a proper death,
hence this rebellion,
hoping merely to escape death.
All the innocent descendants of Tàizōng (太宗) died by your servant's hand,
your servant's death is also late."
Hǎilíng (海陵) then said to Yù (裕):
"We are the Son of Heaven,
if We had doubts about you,
even if your brothers were at court,
could We not carry it out?
To suspect Me based on this,
you are truly mistaken.
Tàizōng's (太宗) sons were not exclusively in your hands,
We acted for the sake of the country."
He also said to him:
"We have always been close to you,
though you have committed this crime,
We will spare your life,
but you may not be chancellor,
and We will let you guard your ancestors' tombs for the rest of your life."
Yù (裕) said:
"Since your servant has committed such a heinous crime,
what face do I have to meet the people of the world?
I only wish to be hanged,
to warn other disloyal ones."
Hǎilíng (海陵) then stabbed his left arm with a knife,
took the blood and smeared it on Yù's (裕) face,
saying to him:
"After your death,
you will know that We originally had no doubts about you."
Yù (裕) said:
"For a long time, I have received Your Majesty's extraordinary favor,
my longing is intense,
I know my mistakes,
Hǎilíng (海陵) wept as he sent Yù (裕) out the door,
and had him killed,
along with Yáoshè (遙設) and Féng Jiānú (馮家奴).
Féng Jiānú's (馮家奴) wife
was the daughter of Yù Wáng (豫王),
she and her son Gǔ (榖) were both involved in the rebellion,
and were also killed.
He sent the guard Pánggě (厖葛) to the Northwest Route Pacification Commissioner's office to execute Láng (朗) and Zhāozhé (招折).
Túnnà (屯納) and Èlābǔ (遏剌補) both fled.
Túnnà (屯納) was captured and executed in the marketplace.
Èlābǔ (遏剌補) hanged himself.
When Túnnà (屯納) fled,
he passed by Xiāo Zhīxiáng (蕭之詳), the Assistant Prefect of Héjiān (河間).
Zhīxiáng (之詳) initially knew nothing of Yù's (裕) affair,
and kept him for three days.
Túnnà (屯納) went to Zhīxiáng's (之詳) tea-house keeper, Cházhā (茶扎).
Cházhā (茶扎) sent someone to Zhīxiáng (之詳) to inform Gōng Yǐn (公引),
obtained him,
and handed Túnnà (屯納) over to be sent elsewhere.
Cházhā's (茶扎) household servant exposed the matter.
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Wāchǎn (窊產), interrogated him.
Zhīxiáng (之詳) said:
"Túnnà (屯納) stayed for two days and then left."
The jurists considered Zhīxiáng (之詳) to have concealed the matter,
deceiving the Department of State Affairs,
and his crime deserved redemption.
Hǎilíng (海陵) was enraged,
ordered him to be killed,
flogged Wāchǎn (窊產) and those who deliberated on the law,
and Cházhā (茶扎) was flogged four hundred times and died.
Pánggě (厖葛) killed Zhāozhé (招折) and others,
and also killed four innocent people.
Hǎilíng (海陵) did not question it,
but merely flogged him fifty times.
A decree announcing Yù's (裕) and others' crimes was issued to the whole realm.
For reporting the betrayal,
Huáizhōng (懷忠) was promoted to Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
and given Bái Dá (白荅) as a symbol (牌印云).
Gāo Yàoshī (高藥師) was promoted to Diarist of the Imperial Court,
and advanced to the rank of Xiǎnwǔ Jiāngjūn (顯武將軍).
Yàoshī (藥師) had once reported that Yù (裕) harbored resentment,
and was rewarded for it now.
Xū Chíguó (胥持國), courtesy name Bǐngjūn (秉鈞),
was a native of Fánzhì (繁畤) in Dàizhōu (代州).
He rose from a student of classics (經童),
and was repeatedly transferred to be Assistant Magistrate of Bóyě (博野) county.
A memorialist stated that commoners were illicitly occupying state land,
such as
"Tàizǐ Wù" (太子務)
and
"Dàwáng Zhuāng" (大王莊),
which should not belong to private families.
The Board commissioned Chíguó (持國) to investigate and verify it.
Chíguó (持國) returned and reported:
"This land has been privately owned by the people since previous dynasties,
and cannot be reclaimed."
The matter was then dropped.
Soon after, he was appointed Palace Storehouse Manager for the Crown Prince (太子司倉),
then transferred to Director of Imperial Beverages (掌飲令),
and concurrently Palace Storehouse Manager (司倉).
The Crown Prince recognized his abilities
and promoted him to Director of Imperial Attendants (祗應司令).
Upon Zhāngzōng's (章宗) accession,
he was appointed Assistant Superintendent of the Palace Registry (宮籍副監),
and bestowed 500,000 in cash from the Palace Registry Treasury and a residence.
Shortly after, he was made Associate Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (同簽宣徽院事) and Vice Minister of Works (工部侍郎),
and concurrently Superintendent of the Palace Registry (宮籍監).
After three months,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (工部尚書)
and dispatched as an envoy to Sòng (宋).
In the fourth year of Míngchāng (明昌)
he was appointed Grand Councilor (參知政事),
and bestowed with the title of the Jinshi (進士) degree from the Sūn Yòngkāng (孫用康) examination roll.
At that time, the river burst its banks at Yángwǔ (陽武),
Chíguó (持國) requested to supervise the work,
and thus acted as an official of the Department of State Affairs (尚書省事).
The following year,
he was promoted to Right Vice Grand Councilor (尚書右丞).
Chíguó (持國) was a flattering and intelligent person.
Initially,
Consort Lǐ (李妃) rose from humble origins
and gained favor with the emperor.
Chíguó (持國), having been in the Crown Prince's palace for a long time,
had long known the emperor's weakness for women.
He secretly used secret arts to gain her favor,
and also heavily bribed those around the consort who held influence.
The consort also felt her family background was humble,
and wished to rely on external court officials to increase her influence.
Thus, she frequently praised Chíguó's (持國) abilities,
and consequently, he was greatly trusted by the emperor.
He became the consort's external agent (表𩹉),
monopolizing and controlling court affairs.
The execution of Zhèng Wáng Yǒngdǎo (鄭王永蹈) and Hào Wáng Yǒngzhōng (鎬王永中),
and the dismissal of Wán Yán Shǒuzhēn (完顏守貞) and others,
all originated from Consort Lǐ (李妃) and Chíguó (持國).
Officials who were greedy and eager for promotion all flocked to his gate.
A saying circulated throughout the four quarters:
"A student of classics (經童) becomes chancellor,
a palace maid becomes consort."
This mocked their low and vulgar origins.
In the third year of Chéng'ān (承安),
the Censorate impeached and memorialized:

"The Right Remonstrance Official Zhāng Fùhēng (張復亨), the Right Corrector Zhāng Jiāzhēn (張嘉貞), the Co-Administrator of Ānfēng (安豐) Military Commissioner's Affairs Zhào Shū (趙樞), the Co-Administrator of Dìnghǎi (定海) Military Commissioner's Affairs Zhāng Guāngtíng (張光庭), the Revenue Bureau Secretary Gāo Yuánfǔ (高元甫), the Vice Director of the Board of Punishments Zhāng Yánsǒu (張巖叟), and the clerks of the Department of State Affairs Fù Rǔméi (傅汝梅), Zhāng Hàn (張翰), Péi Yuán (裴元), Guō Fú (郭郛),
all frequented the powerful household,
people jokingly called them the 'Ten Sages of Xū's (胥) Gate'.
Fùhēng (復亨) and Jiāzhēn (嘉貞) were especially servile and ingratiatingly sought advancement,
unbefitting their remonstrance duties.
They should all be dismissed."
The memorial was approved.
Thereupon, Chíguó (持國) retired with the title of Grand Master of Court (通奉大夫),
and Jiāzhēn (嘉貞) and others were all sent to provincial posts.
A little later,
he was appointed to govern Dàmíng Fǔ affairs.
Before he could depart,
he was reassigned as a Deputy Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
assisting the Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs in managing military affairs in Běijīng.
One day,
the Emperor summoned Hànlín Compiler Lù Duó to ask about other matters.
He then spoke of the relative merits of Dǒng Shīzhōng and Zhāng Wàngōng.
Duó said:
“Shīzhōng advanced by attaching himself to Xú Chígúo.
Chígúo is a treacherous villain,
unsuitable to command the military,
and in my estimation,
he not only fails to meet public expectations,
but will also surely fail to win the hearts of the troops.
If he were to return to a prime ministership,
he would surely bring chaos to the realm.”
The Emperor said:
“It is difficult for a subject to advance or retreat people,
but it is easy for a ruler to advance or retreat people.
How could I possibly appoint this man as prime minister again?
I merely promoted him two ranks,
allowing him to retire.”
He soon died in the army,
and was posthumously granted the谥
“Tōngmǐn.”
Later, the Emperor asked Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Zhāng Wàngōng:
“Chígúo is now dead.
What kind of person was he, after all?”
Wàngōng replied:
“Chígúo's conduct was always impure and not scrupulous,
as can be seen from the incident of selling wine at Pínglè Lóu.”
The Emperor said:
“This was not greed.
Someone like Mǎ Qí, who served as a Counselor,
privately selling wine from the provincial stores,
that is what constitutes greed.”
His son, Dǐng,
has a separate biography.
Collation Notes
Biographies

Volume 68: Notable Women Ālín Qī, Lǐ Bǎoxìn Qī, Hán Qìngmín Qī, Léi Fù Shī Shì, Kāng Zhùzhù, Lǐ Wén Qī, Lǐ Yīng Qī, Xiāng Qí Qī, Ālǔzhēn, Sāhéliǎn Qī, Xǔ Gǔ Qī, Féng Miàozhēn, Púchá Shì, Wūgǔlún Shì, Sùlán Qī, Mánggē Qī, Yǐn Shì, Bái Shì, Niè Xiàonǚ, Zhòng Dé Qī, Bǎofú Lǐ Shì (Zhāng Fèngnú attached)
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
Liú Xiàng first compiled accounts of virtuous empresses and noblewomen of the Three Dynasties,
as well as the causes of rise and fall, prosperity and decline due to extravagance and usurpation.
He categorized and classified them,
naming it the “Biographies of Notable Women,”
thereby using them for remonstrance.
Fàn Yè first included them in the History of Hàn.
In ancient times, when a girl was ten years old, she had a female teacher.
As she grew older, she engaged in tasks like hemp and silk production,
and assisted in sacrificial ceremonies.
After marriage, her duties were limited to the domestic sphere.
Therefore, being free from impropriety and disorder was considered virtuous.
However, living as a widow,
experiencing misfortune and hardship,
these were all misfortunes for women.
If one encounters misfortune
and can establish herself with extraordinary strength,
possessing the spirit of a resolute man,
then gentlemen consider her exceptional.
Ālín's wife, Shālǐzhì,
was the younger sister of Yínzhúkě, Prince of Jīnyuán Commandery.
In the sixth year of Tiānfǔ,
rebel soldiers from Huánglóng Fǔ attacked nearby tribes.
At that time,
Ālín was serving in the army.
Shālǐzhì gathered nearby residents, obtaining five hundred men and women,
and erected a camp and palisades for defense.
Over a thousand bandits came to attack.
Shālǐzhì used armor as her own,
and her skirt as a banner.
She gave armor to the men,
and the women raised a clamor.
Shālǐzhì wielded a sword, supervising the battle.
After three days, the bandits left.
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
for her meritorious service, she was enfeoffed as the Lady of Jīnyuán Commandery.
During the Dàdìng era,
her grandson Yàoshī was made a Móukè.
Lǐ Bǎoxìn's wife, Wáng Shì.
Bǎoxìn was the Magistrate of Yìfēng County.
When Zhāng Jué rebelled in Píngzhōu,
Wáng Shì was trapped among the rebels.
The rebels wanted to force her into their chambers.
Wáng Shì cursed the rebels.
The rebels, enraged, dismembered her.
In the twelfth year of Dàdìng,
she was posthumously granted the title
“Zhēnliè Xiànjūn.”
Hán Qìngmín's wife,
her origin is unknown,
nor is her surname known.
Qìngmín served Liáo as the Military Commissioner of Yízhōu.
During the Tiānhuì era,
Yízhōu was attacked and captured.
Qìngmín refused to yield and died.
His wife was to be given to soldiers.
His wife swore to die rather than comply
and subsequently committed suicide.
Emperor Shìzōng read the Veritable Records of Emperor Tàizōng
and saw the deeds of Qìngmín and his wife.
He sighed, saying:
“Such integrity and chastity
can be called difficult indeed.”
Léi Fù Shī Shì's
husband died,
and she dutifully cared for her parents-in-law.
When her mother-in-law fell ill,
she cut flesh from her arm to feed her,
and her mother-in-law immediately recovered.
After both parents-in-law had passed away,
her elder brother Shī Kuí and her husband's nephew Guī
coveted her property. They fabricated a marriage contract and brought her to the authorities,
intending to force her marriage.
The county official could not discern right from wrong.
Shī Shì, fearing coercion,
threw herself into a well in the county yamen and died.
An imperial edict ordered the officials to offer sacrifices at her tomb
and bestowed upon her the posthumous title
“Jié.”
Kāng Zhùzhù
was from Fūzhōu.
Her husband died young.
After the mourning period,
her father took her back home
and promised her in marriage to Yán Yí.
Kāng Shì swore to die rather than obey.
She wanted to return to her husband's family but could not,
so she threw herself off a cliff and died.
An imperial edict ordered the officials to offer sacrifices at her tomb.
Lǐ Wén's wife, Shǐ Shì,
was from Báishuǐ in Tóngzhōu.
Her husband died.
After the mourning period,
she swore to die rather than remarry.
Her father forcibly took her back home
and promised her in marriage to a townsman, Yáo Yǐ.
Shǐ Shì refused.
Yáo reported her to the authorities.
She was arrested
and subsequently hanged herself.
An imperial edict ordered the officials to offer sacrifices at her tomb.
Lǐ Yīng's wife, Zhāng Shì.
Yīng was initially a Censor,
residing in Zhōngdū,
while Zhāng resided in Wéizhōu.
In the winter of the first year of Zhēnyòu,
the Dàyuán army captured Wéizhōu
and entered her home.
Zhāng Shì gave them all her possessions.
Afterward,
they ordered Zhāng Shì to mount a horse.
Zhāng said:
“I have given you everything I own.
Am I still not redeemed?”
They replied:
“You are the wife of an official;
you should become a lady again.”
Zhāng said:
“I will die and become a ghost of the Lǐ family.”
She sat down abruptly and refused to get up,
and was then killed.
She was posthumously enfeoffed as the Lady of Lǒngxī Commandery,
and posthumously granted the title
“Zhuāngjié.”
Yīng rose to the position of Censor-in-Chief
and has a biography.
Xiāng Qí's wife, Luán Shì,
was beautiful.
Qí was a clerk in the Sī Lì office of Yè Xiàn, Láizhōu.
In the eighth month of the third year of Zhēnyòu,
the Red Turban bandits captured Yè Xiàn.
Qí, Luán Shì, and their son were all captured.
The bandits saw Luán and were pleased with her.
They killed Qí and their son and tried to entice Luán.
Luán bravely rose and struck her head against a bandit, causing him to fall.
She cursed, saying:
“How could I be defiled by dogs and swine!”
The bandits, enraged,
killed her.
She was posthumously enfeoffed as the Xiéhé Xiànjūn,
and posthumously granted the title
“Zhuāngjié.”
Ālǔzhēn
was the daughter of the imperial clan member Chéngchōng
and the wife of Húlígǎi myng'an Jiágǔ Húshān.
After her husband died, she remained a widow,
and had a following of over a thousand people.
In the first year of Xīngdìng (1212),
Chéngchōng was the commander of Shàngjīng.
Tàipíng, the acting governor of Shàngjīng Province, captured Chéngchōng and presented him to Púxiān Wànnú.
Ālǔzhēn repaired the dilapidated fortress,
mended weapons,
and accumulated fodder and grain to defend herself.
Wànnú sent someone to invite her to surrender,
but she refused.
Then he shot a letter from Chéngchōng into the city.
Ālǔzhēn got it and tore it up,
saying,
"This is a trick."
Wànnú's troops then attacked fiercely.
Ālǔzhēn dressed in men's clothing
and, with her son Púdài, led the people to fight vigorously,
killing several hundred people
and capturing over ten alive.
Wànnú's troops then withdrew.
Later, she again sent a general to attack Wànnú's troops
and captured one of his generals.
An imperial edict conferred upon her the title of Commandery Duchess,
and her son Púdài was promoted and rewarded according to his merits.
Chéngchōng had already been captured.
Taking advantage of an opportunity, he said to his two children, Hú and Púsùnǎi:
"I rose from being a palace guard
to a first-rank official.
I have no regrets about dying.
You all are also prominent.
You have not repaid the country for a single day.
You should consider how to conduct yourselves
for future plans."
The two children then risked their lives to escape south.
They arrived in Nánjīng in the fourth month of that year.
Dújíshì
was the daughter of the Grand Councilor Qiānjiānú
and the younger sister of the guard Yínzhúkě.
From a young age, her actions were always guided by ritual and law.
When she married her relative Sāhéniǎn,
her household was orderly and respectful.
Sāhéniǎn was the garrison commander of Zhōngjīng.
When a large army besieged it,
Sāhéniǎn suffered from a carbuncle on his back and could not lead the army.
Dújíshì realized the city would surely fall
and said to Sāhéniǎn:
"You originally had no special abilities,
but merely because you were of the imperial clan, you served close to the emperor,
rising to the position of Tián diǎn Jìnshì Jú
and co-supervisor of Mùqīnfǔ.
Now you are also the highest-ranking official in an outer province as garrison commander,
having received the deepest favors from the state.
Now a large army is at the city gates,
and unfortunately, you are ill
and cannot fight or defend.
Should the city fall,
you should lead your elite troops to force your way out of the gate
and take one son to the capital.
If you cannot, then go to the capital alone.
If that too is impossible,
to die in battle would still be to repay the country.
Please do not worry about me."
When Sāhéniǎn went out to inspect the city,
Dújíshì took out her everyday clothes, burial items, and favorite possessions and spread them on the couch.
She distributed all her wealth to her family members,
and dressed magnificently for burial, more so than usual.
She also instructed her maidservants, saying:
"When I die, place me on the couch,
cover my face with a quilt,
and set fire to it all around,
so that the soldiers do not see my face."
Having spoken,
she closed the door and hanged herself.
Her family followed her instructions,
laying her body on the couch
and covering it with a quilt.
When Sāhéniǎn returned from outside,
his family informed him of his wife's death.
Sāhéniǎn stroked the couch and said:
"My wife did not disgrace me.
How could I disgrace the imperial court?"
He then ordered her to be cremated.
She was thirty-six years old.
A short while later,
the city fell.
Sāhéniǎn led his sworn followers, intending to force his way out,
but failed.
He threw himself into the moat and died,
as reported.
Xǔ Gǔ's wife, Liúshì,
was the daughter of Liú Zhòngshū, the Military Commissioner of Dìnghǎi.
In the early years of Zhēnyòu (1213-1217),
Xǔ Gǔ took his family to reside temporarily in Púchéng.
Later, he left Liúshì and their children in Púchéng
and served at court.
Soon after,
troops besieged Púchéng.
Liúshì said to her two daughters:
"Your father is at court,
and the military situation is like this;
things cannot be guaranteed.
If the city falls and we are driven out, what if we are defiled?
It would be better for us all to die to preserve ourselves."
Immediately after,
the attack on the city intensified.
Thereupon, Liúshì and her two daughters successively committed suicide.
The officials reported this to the court.
In the fifth month of the fourth year (1216),
Liúshì was posthumously enfeoffed as a Commandery Lady
with the posthumous title
"Zhēnjié" (Chaste and Pure).
Her eldest daughter was given the posthumous title
"Dìngjiāng,"
and the second
"Sùjiāng."
Their deeds were entrusted to the Imperial Historiography Institute.
Féng Miàozhēn
was the daughter of Féng Yándēng, the Minister of Personnel.
At the age of eighteen,
she married the *jìnshì* Zhāng Zào.
In the fifth year of Xīngdìng (1216),
Zhāng Zào was the chief clerk of Luòchuān.
The Dàyuán army broke through Jiāzhōu and Suídé,
and then entered Fūyán.
The people of Fū were terrified and prepared defenses.
The defending official, seeing that the fodder and grain from the western route were not arriving on time,
dispatched Zhāng Zào to Píngliáng to oversee it.
At that time, Yándēng was a supernumerary department director in the Píngliáng Province.
Zhāng Zào wanted to take Miàozhēn with him,
but Miàozhēn declined, saying:
"My parents-in-law are old.
Although there are uncles and sisters-in-law, how can I be at ease?
You go,
and I will stay to care for them."
In the eleventh month,
Luòchuān fell.
Miàozhēn hid with her parents-in-law in a cave,
but the soldiers found them.
Miàozhēn wept as she bid farewell to her parents-in-law, saying:
"I, your daughter-in-law, was not born at a fortunate time.
I cannot continue to serve you.
It is my duty not to suffer disgrace."
She then took her three children and threw herself into a well to die.
Dozens of county residents followed her example and died.
In the spring of the following year,
Zhāng Zào retrieved their bodies from the well
and interred them outside the eastern wall of the county.
She was twenty-four years old at the time of her death.
Púchás Shì, courtesy name Míngxiù,
was the daughter of Nèshēn, the commander of Fūzhōu,
and the wife of Wányán Chánglè.
When Emperor Āizōng moved to Guīdé,
he appointed Chánglè as the supreme commander
to lead troops in escorting him.
As he was about to depart,
he instructed Púchás Shì, saying:
"Say nothing else,
my lady, be very careful not to disgrace yourself."
Míngxiù replied:
"You just devote yourself to serving the emperor;
do not worry about me.
I will certainly not be disgraced."
Chánglè had a young son
born to his former wife, Cháishì.
Míngxiù raised him as her own.
During the coup of Cuī Lì,
the wives and children of officials were driven into the provincial yamen,
where people selected them for themselves.
When Púchás Shì heard this,
she entrusted her young son to her maidservants,
and also gave them gold and silk.
She personally prepared her clothes, coffin, and sacrificial items,
and bid farewell to her family, saying:
"Cuī Lì is immoral,
forcing himself upon other men's wives and daughters.
The soldiers are below the city.
Where can I escape?
Only by death can I not betray my husband.
You all must take good care of the young son."
Then she hanged herself and died,
as if she did not find death difficult.
She was twenty-seven years old at the time.
Wūgǔlún Shì
was the younger sister of Bóxiáng
and the wife of Tuómǎn Hútúmén, the commander-in-chief of Líntáo.
Bóxiáng had a great reputation among the nobility at court,
and Hútúmén died in service to the state.
During Cuī Lì's coup,
many women from official families were defiled.
Wūgǔlún Shì said to her family:
"My husband did not disgrace the imperial court.
How dare I disgrace my brother and my husband?"
She immediately hanged herself.
One maidservant died with her.
The wife of Cānzhèng Wányán Sùlán,
her surname is lost.
When Cuī Lì's rebellion occurred,
she said to her close relatives:
"My husband holds a weighty reputation throughout the realm.
How can I be willing to fall into disgrace with the multitude, thereby shaming my husband?
Today, death is certainly fitting,
but I cannot die nameless,
nor can I die away from my home."
She then hanged herself in her chamber.
Wēntèhǎn Shì,
her husband was Wányán Mánggē,
the son of Huílǐbù, the Xuānchāi Tíkòng of Wǔyuánshān.
His lineage was from Xiāowáng.
Mánggē's uncle, Yìdū,
served as Jiédù in Qínzhōu.
When his territory was attacked by Dà Yuán forces,
he happened to be ill and unable to command the army.
Mánggē, acting as Tíkòng,
single-handedly defended a sector.
After the enemy retreated, Yìdū died.
Mánggē, for his meritorious defense of the city, inherited the rank of Móukè,
and was appointed Fèngyù.
When Cuī Lì's rebellion occurred,
Mánggē, righteously refusing to be disgraced,
bid farewell to his wife.
His wife said:
"If you can die for the nation,
can I not die for you?"
A maidservant said:
"If our master dies,
where shall this maidservant go?"
On that day,
the couple hanged themselves together with a single rope,
and the maidservant followed suit.
Yǐn Shì,
was the wife of Wányán Zhū'ér.
Zhū'ér's lineage was from Xiāowáng.
In the first month of the second year of Tiānxīng, he followed Āizōng as the Nánmiàn Yuánshuài,
and died in battle at Huánglínggāng.
His wife, Jīnyuán Jùnfūrén, upon hearing of Zhū'ér's death,
gathered her family possessions and burned them,
then hanged herself,
at the age of thirty-one.
Zhū'ér was posthumously granted an official title,
and his younger brother, Chángzhù, was immediately appointed to the imperial guard by imperial edict.
Bái Shì,
mother of Sū Sìzhī,
