was a native of Xǔzhōu,
and the wife of a fifth-generation grandson of Sòng Shàngshū Yòuchéng Zǐyóu.
Initially,
Dōngpō, Yǐngbīn, and Shúdǎng were all buried on Xiǎo'éméishān in Jiáchéng,
hence for five generations they all resided in Xǔchāng.
Bái Shì became a widow in her early twenties,
and after the mourning period,
her maternal family invited her to return home.
Her elder brother and sister-in-law secretly discussed remarrying her.
Bái Shì subtly overheard this,
and, pulling a cart, went straight home,
saying:
"I am the wife of the Sū Xuéshì family,
and I have a son. Are you then trying to make me lose my virtue?"
From then on,
she did not visit her maternal family unless there was a major event.
She once established a sacrificial chamber in the northeast of her residence,
where she painted portraits of the two gentlemen,
and depicted stories of Huángzhōu and Lóngchuān on the walls.
The incense and offerings were kept reverent and clean,
and she personally swept and cleaned it.
Gentlemen who sought to pay their respects often visited her home to offer sacrifices.
In the first month, Gēngxū day, of the first year of Tiānxīng,
Xǔzhōu was attacked by soldiers.
Sìzhī was a Xiāngguān in Biànjīng.
Bái Shì bowed and bid farewell before the two gentlemen's portraits, saying:
"My son is going to the capital.
This old woman will die without regret.
I dare to inform you of this."
She then hanged herself beside her chamber.
Her family burned the house along with her.
She was over seventy years old.
Sìzhī's original name was Zōngzhī,
but it was changed to avoid a taboo name.
Niè Xiàonǚ, courtesy name Shùnyīng,
was the eldest daughter of Shàngshū Zuǒyòusī Yuánwàiláng Tiānjì.
At twenty-three,
she married the Jìnshì Zhāng Bóháo.
After Bóháo died,
she returned to her parents' home.
When Āizōng moved to Guīdé,
Tiānjì remained in Biàn.
Cuī Lì kidnapped and killed the prime ministers,
and Tiānjì was severely wounded.
He wept bitterly day and night,
regretting that he did not die immediately.
Shùnyīng sought every possible medical treatment to save him,
even cutting flesh from her thigh to mix with other ingredients and offer it,
but Tiānjì eventually died.
At that time, the capital had been under siege for so long that food ran out.
Among the lanes and alleys, some married their wives for a full meal.
Compounding this was Cuī Lì's rebellion,
with plundering and brutal oppression,
leaving no human decency.
Shùnyīng, who had read extensively and understood moral principles,
considered that she was still young and beautiful,
her husband was gone,
and her father had died an unnatural death.
Rather than being defiled by soldiers,
how much better to follow her father to the underworld?
The day after her father's burial,
she cut her throat and died.
At that time, gentlemen and ladies alike esteemed her,
and some wept for her.
Her family buried Shùnyīng in Zhāng Bóháo's tomb.
The wife of Wányán Zhòngdé,
her clan name is unknown.
During Cuī Lì's rebellion,
the wife disfigured her own face and clothing,
and, taking her concubine and two sons, pretended to be gathering vegetables,
and fled from Biàn to Cài.
When Cài was besieged,
all able-bodied men manned the walls to defend.
She said to Zhòngdé:
"Given the situation,
if men can exert their strength for the nation,
can women not also?"
She then led the other noblewomen to form their own corps,
personally transporting arrows and stones below the city wall.
Women in the city vied to follow their example.
When the city fell, she committed suicide.
Āizōng Bǎofú Lǐ Shì,
after the fall of the state, she was relocated north with the empresses and concubines.
Upon reaching Xuāndézhōu,
she resided in Móhēyuàn,
sleeping day and night in the Buddha hall,
making banners.
When it was time to proceed to Lóngtíng,
just before departure,
she hanged herself before the Buddha statue,
and personally wrote on the door paper:
"Bǎofú Yùshì passed away here."
Later people who came to the place,
seeing her remains,
pitied and mourned her.
In the first year of Tiānxīng,
when Northern forces attacked the city,
amidst the arrows and stones, a woman was suddenly seen calling from below the city wall, saying:
"I am the singing girl Zhāng Fèngnú.
I was captured when Xǔzhōu fell and brought here.
Their army will leave in a few days.
Gentlemen, strive hard and hold firm for the country.
Do not be deceived!"
Having spoken,
she threw herself into the moat and died.
The imperial court dispatched an envoy to offer sacrifices at the West Gate.
During the Zhèngdà and Tiānxīng periods,
only a few women of integrity and righteousness are known.
The story of Fèngnú is recorded in other histories,
perhaps inspired by something.
Collations and Notes
Biographies, Chapter Sixty-nine: Eunuchs: Liáng Tōng, Sòng Guī (Pān Shǒu attached)
Eunuchs of ancient times all originated from those who had been castrated.
Those who had suffered castration could not be counted among scholars and commoners,
therefore they managed affairs of the imperial palace and temples,
and were called
"women's overseers."
Since the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
eunuchs adopted sons to continue their line.
In the Táng dynasty,
those who succeeded were all eunuchs.
When they first entered service,
their nature was often clever, astute, and ingratiating, adept at securing imperial favor.
When they achieved their ambitions,
their factions and conspiracies became uncontrollable.
The Eastern Hàn perished because of eunuchs,
and the Táng was even worse.
Scholars of later generations discussed the harm of eunuchs,
likening it to a poison or a fierce tiger from which there is no escape.
The Jīn legal system established the Jìnshì Jú,
which often participated in political affairs,
but eunuchs rarely partook in it.
Only during the reign of Hǎilíng did Liáng Tōng exist,
and during Zhāngzōng's reign, Liáng Dào and Lǐ Xīnxǐ interfered in governance.
These two rulers were greatly misled by them.
It is popularly believed that Liáng Dào encouraged Zhāngzōng to admit Concubine Lǐ to the imperial harem.
However, the Jīn Shǐ does not record the details of Liáng Dào,
so it cannot be discussed and arranged here.
Only Sòng Guī and Pān Shǒu were quite able to remonstrate with Xuānzōng and Āizōng,
providing timely benefits.
They were truly the outstanding ones among the ordinary, the resonant ones among the steadfast.
Therefore, the biographies of eunuchs are written.
Liáng Chéng,
originally a household slave of a powerful family,
entered the palace with Empress Yuánfēi.
As a eunuch, he served Hǎilíng.
Chéng was by nature obsequious and cunning,
skilled at flattery and ingratiation,
and particularly enjoyed trust and favor.
According to old regulations,
eunuchs were only in charge of matters concerning the inner palace and women's quarters.
In Tiāndé 3rd year (1151 CE),
Wáng Guāngdào was first appointed Commissioner of the Imperial Treasury.
Wèi Yù and Liáng Ānrén, also eunuchs, held positions in the Imperial Treasury.
Hǎilíng said to Guāngdào and others:
"People say eunuchs are not to be used,
but I think otherwise.
Later Táng Zhuāngzōng entrusted Zhāng Chéngyè with military affairs,
and he eventually performed great deeds.
How can there be no capable people among you?
You all should understand this intention.
The treasures in the treasury all come from the people's labor;
for every ten expended, only one is saved.
You must investigate corrupt practices,
and offenders will be punished without mercy."
Thus, eunuchs began to participate in government affairs,
and Chéng was entrusted with even greater responsibilities,
progressing to the position of Commissioner of the Bureau of Attendants.
When the palace in Nánjīng was being constructed,
Hǎilíng frequently sent Chéng to inspect the work.
At that time,
the cost of a single hall was already immeasurable.
If Chéng said it was not good,
it would be completely torn down.
Even Chancellor Zhāng Hào would defer to him,
treating him with equal courtesy.
When Hǎilíng wanted to attack Sòng,
Chéng seized the opportunity to greatly praise Sòng's Consort Liú Guìfēi, saying she was of peerless beauty, capable of overthrowing a nation.
Hǎilíng was greatly pleased.
When the southern campaign was about to commence,
he ordered Xiànjūn Gāo Shīgū'ér to prepare clean and fresh bedding, awaiting the capture of Consort Liú Guìfēi for her use.
Critics said that Chéng was conspiring with Sòng,
encouraging the emperor to attack Sòng
and exhaust Zhōngguó by conscripting all the soldiers in the realm.
When Hǎilíng reached Hézhōu,
he heard that Chéng had indeed been communicating with Sòng people.
He said to Chéng:
"I hear you have been communicating with the Sòng state,
leaking information.
You were originally a slave,
and I promoted you to this position.
How dare you do such a thing?
If, upon reaching Jiāngnán, the facts are confirmed,
it will not be too late to kill you."
He also said to Compiler Tián Yǔxìn:
"Your face also looks suspicious;
you must be conspiring with Chéng."
He ordered them both to be seized within the army.
When Hǎilíng was assassinated,
Chéng and Yǔxìn were both killed by the mutinous soldiers.
Sòng Guī's original name was Qǐnú,
and he was from Yān.
He was a Palace Attendant and Head of the Palace Guard.
Xuānzōng once wanted to watch lantern shows during the Yuánxī Festival,
and ordered Qǐnú to supervise the construction.
Qǐnú grumbled, saying:
"The state has been abandoned in Zhōngdū.
What is there to see in lantern shows in Nánjīng?"
Xuānzōng faintly heard this,
and had him flogged twenty times.
Later, he regretted it
and issued an edict to apologize.
Āizōng released a kite in the imperial garden,
but the kite flew away.
He ordered his close attendants to pursue and find it.
A farmer in the market had the kite on his arm.
The close attendants dared not say it was from the palace,
and tried every means to get it.
The farmer would not give it.
They offered him money for it,
and only then obtained it.
When the matter was reported,
Āizōng wanted to hand the man over to the authorities.
Qǐnú, from the side, advised:
"To value an animal and disparage a person,
how can this be proclaimed to the four directions?"
Āizōng disliked his bluntness
and flogged him again.
Soon after, he also regretted it
and gave him gifts to console and dismiss him.
When Āizōng arrived at Guīdé,
the Marshal of Cavalry, Púchá Guānnú, rebelled,
killing Left Chancellor Lǐ Qī, Privy Councilor Shízhǎn Nǚlǔhuān, and over three hundred other officials.
In a moment of panic,
Āizōng had no choice
but to provisionally appoint Guānnú as Provisional Administrator of Governmental Affairs.
Being controlled by him,
Āizōng harbored resentment and wished to execute him but could not.
When Guānnú went to Bózhōu,
Guī secretly plotted with Imperial Attendants Wúgǔsūn Àishí and Nàlán Yìdá,
and Imperial Guards Nǚxīliè Wánchū, Fàn Chénsēng, Wáng Shān'ér, and others to kill him.
When Guānnú returned from Bó,
Āizōng was at the Línyī Pavilion,
summoning Privy Councilor Zhāng Tiāngāng and Guānnú to discuss affairs.
As Guānnú entered to pay his respects,
Guī and the others immediately killed him from the side,
along with his associates Ālǐhé, Bái Jìn, and Xí Xiǎn.
When Cáichéng fell,
Āizōng hanged himself in the Yōulán Xuān.
Guī, Wányán Xiéliè, Jiāo Chūnhe, and others all died with him.
There was also a eunuch named Pān Shǒu,
who was known for his learning.
After the southern migration, he offered many beneficial suggestions.
When Āizōng fled from Púchéng to Guīdé,
he stopped at a commoner's house along the way.
Shǒu presented a comb,
saying:
"May Your Majesty, on the day of your return to the palace, not forget this thatched hut,
and become even more frugal
to accomplish the great undertaking."
The Emperor heard his words
and sighed sadly and emotionally for a long time.
Practitioners of Arts and Techniques: Liú Wánsù, Zhāng Cóngzhèng, Lǐ Qìngsì, Jì Tiānxī, Zhāng Yuánsù, Mǎ Guìzhōng, Wǔ Zhēn (Zǐkàng), Lǐ Mào, Hú Déxīn.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān, in his nine categories of scholars,
described those who divination by the sun, tortoise shells, milfoil, and included biographies of doctors like Biǎn Què and Cāng Gōng.
Liú Xīn, when cataloging the imperial library,
included "Mathematical Arts" and "Practitioners of Arts and Techniques" in his Qī Lǜe.
Later historians, when compiling biographies of practitioners of arts and techniques,
were following his intention.
Some say that the Sùwèn and Nèijīng discuss the waxing and waning of the celestial path, and the ebb and flow of qi and cosmic cycles.
They merely use the guise of medical arts,
attributing them to Qí Bó and Huáng Dì,
to transmit their profound secrets.
The people of Qín even listed the Zhōu Yì under divination.
How could this be easily dismissed?
However, in ancient times, practitioners used their arts to guide people towards good fortune and virtuous conduct.
Later generations of practitioners sometimes used omens to mislead people into wrongdoing.
Ancient physicians considered saving lives as their achievement.
Later physicians sometimes used medicine for personal gain, leading to accidental deaths.
Therefore, in governing the world,
even for matters of arts and techniques, it is essential to be cautious about their responsibilities and to diligently distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy.
During the Jīn dynasty,
people like Wǔ Zhēn and Wǔ Kàng were trustworthy and not deceitful.
Liú Wánsù and Zhāng Yuánsù were adept at adapting their treatments.
Those who learned their arts all respected them as teachers.
They must be recorded.
Liú Wánsù, courtesy name Shǒuzhēn,
was a native of Héjiān.
He once met an extraordinary person, Master Chén,
who gave Shǒuzhēn wine to drink.
He became extremely drunk, and upon waking, he had a thorough understanding of medical arts,
as if someone had imparted them to him.
Thereupon, he compiled the Yùnqì Yàozhǐ Lùn and Jīngyào Xuānmíng Lùn.
Fearing that incompetent physicians might spread erroneous theories,
he also authored the Sùwèn Xuánjī Yuánbìng Shì,
specifically elaborating on 288 characters
with over 20,000 words of commentary.
However, he preferred using cooling agents,
focusing on reducing heart fire and supplementing kidney water.
He styled himself
"Tōngyuán Chǔshì."
Zhāng Cóngzhèng, courtesy name Zǐhé,
was from Kǎochéng, Suīzhōu.
He was skilled in medicine,
thoroughly understanding the teachings of the Nánjīng and Sùwèn.
His methods followed Liú Shǒuzhēn,
often using cold and cooling medications.
However, he was often effective in curing illnesses and saving lives.
Ancient medical texts describe methods of sweating, purging, and vomiting,
but also state that sweating when inappropriate can lead to death,
purging when inappropriate can lead to death,
and vomiting when inappropriate can lead to death.
Each has its own meridians and pulse principles,
said to be the works of Huáng Dì and Qí Bó.
Cóngzhèng used these most skillfully,
earning the title
"Zhāng Zǐhé's Methods of Sweating, Purging, and Vomiting."
When ignorant and shallow practitioners adopted his prescriptions
without understanding how to examine the pulse and discern the origin of the illness,
they often caused deaths.
This is the fault of incompetent physicians who failed to properly transmit his teachings.
His written works include
the "Six Gates, Two Methods"
title,
which still exists in the world.
Lǐ Qìngsì,
a native of Míng.
As a young man, he attempted the imperial examination for jinshì but failed.
He abandoned it to study medicine,
reading the Sùwèn and other works,
and thoroughly understood their meaning.
During the Tiāndé period,
there was a great plague that year.
Guǎngpíng was especially severe,
and often the poor would fall ill behind closed doors.
Qìngsì distributed medicine and rice to them,
saving many lives.
Qìngsì died without illness at over eighty years old.
His writings, Shānghán Cuǎnlèi in four scrolls, Gǎizhèng Huórénshū in three scrolls, Shānghán Lùn in three scrolls, and Zhēnjīng in one scroll,
were passed down to later generations.
Jì Tiānxī, courtesy name Qíqīng,
a native of Tài'ān.
He early on abandoned the jinshì profession
to study medicine.
He became skilled in his craft,
and thus gained fame as a physician.
He compiled Jízhù Nánjīng in five scrolls.
In the fifteenth year of Dàdìng, he presented his book
and was appointed Imperial Medical Doctor.
Zhāng Yuánsù, courtesy name Jiégǔ,
a native of Yìzhōu.
At eight years old, he passed the examination for child prodigies.
At twenty-seven, he took the examination for jinshì in classical exegesis,
but failed due to infringing upon a temple taboo (miàohuì).
Thereupon, he left to study medicine.
He achieved no recognition,
but one night, he dreamt of someone using a large axe and a long chisel to carve open his heart and orifices,
inserting several scrolls of books into it.
From then on, he thoroughly mastered the art.
Liú Wánsù of Héjiān fell ill with shānghán for eight days,
suffering from headache and a tense pulse,
vomiting and inability to eat,
not knowing what to do.
Yuánsù went to visit him.
Wánsù faced the wall and did not look at him.
Yuánsù said,
"Why do you treat me with such disrespect?"
After taking his pulse,
he said to him,
"Your pulse and illness are so-and-so."
Wánsù said,
"Indeed."
"Did you initially take a certain medicine,
using a certain ingredient?"
Wánsù said,
"Indeed."
Yuánsù said,
"You are mistaken.
That ingredient is cold in nature,
descending to the tàiyīn,
causing the yáng to become deficient and preventing sweating.
Given your current pulse,
you should take a certain medicine, and it will be effective."
Wánsù was greatly convinced,
followed his advice, and recovered.
From then on, Yuánsù gained prominent fame.
He usually did not use ancient prescriptions when treating illnesses.
He explained,
"The movements of qi are not uniform,
and ancient and modern times follow different paths.
Ancient prescriptions are incompatible with new diseases."
He thus established his own medical principles.
Mǎ Guìzhōng,
during the Tiāndé period,
served as the Superintendent of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau (Sītiān Tídiǎn).
He and Gāo Shǒuyuán, Collator of the Imperial Library (Jiàoshū Láng), submitted a memorial regarding celestial phenomena and disasters, which displeased the emperor.
Hǎilíng flogged both of them
and demoted Guìzhōng to Assistant Administrator (Pàn guān) of Dàtóng Prefecture.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Director of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau (Sītiān Jiān).
On the xīn-sī day of the third month, the first day of the Zhènglóng third year,
there was to be a solar eclipse.
On that day,
they observed that there was no eclipse.
Hǎilíng said to Guìzhōng,
"From now on, whenever there is a solar eclipse, report it directly to me in person.
There is no need to announce it to the court or public."
When Hǎilíng was invading Sòng,
he asked,
"I wish to personally lead the invasion of Sòng.
What do the heavens portend?"
Guìzhōng replied,
"Last year, on the jiǎ-xū day of the tenth month,
Yínghuò (Mars) moved directly into Tàiwēi (Enclosure of the Supreme Palace),
reached Bǐng Xīng (Screen Star),
then stopped, retrograded, and exited to the west.
According to astrological texts,
Yínghuò usually enters the court of Tàiwēi in the tenth month
to be restrained and then emerges to spy on lawless nations.
In the twelfth month,
Tàibái (Venus) appeared in daylight, traversing the sky.
This portends war and death, disloyalty, or a change of ruler,
and also indicates that if there is war, it will cease; if there is no war, it will begin."
There was a great earthquake and strong wind in Zhènróng Jūn.
Hǎilíng asked about it,
and Guìzhōng replied,
"The encroaching yin forces the yang,
which is why there is an earthquake."
Hǎilíng then asked,
"If it is an earthquake,
why the great wind?"
Guìzhōng replied,
"If the earth loses its inherent nature, there is an earthquake.
Wind is a sign of command.
When the ruler's commands are severe and urgent, there will be disasters of fierce winds affecting things."
On the jiǎ-chén day of the second month, the first day of the sixth year,
the sun had a halo and an ear-like appendage on its back.
Hǎilíng asked,
"What do the heavens portend recently?"
Guìzhōng replied,
"Two years ago, on the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month,
Tàibái entered the Right Flank Gate of Tàiwēi.
On the second day of the ninth month,
it reached Duānmén (Upright Gate).
On the ninth day,
it exited through the Left Flank Gate,
passing through both the Left and Right Judicial Stars.
Tàiwēi represents the Emperor's Southern Palace,
and Tàibái is the image of a general or soldier.
This portends
soldiers entering the Emperor's court."
Hǎilíng said,
"Now I am about to launch a campaign, and soldiers are entering and exiting Tàiwēi.
This is precisely the meaning of the omen."
Guìzhōng further said,
"Exiting through Duānmén
portends being restrained.
Passing through the Left and Right Judicial Stars portends being subjected to duties.
This means there will be envoys,
or it could be soldiers,
or it could be bandits."
Hǎilíng said,
"At a time when an army is raised,
it is inevitable that there will be petty thieves."
Later, when he was assassinated in Yángzhōu,
Guìzhōng's words were all proven true.
In the eighth year of Dàdìng,
Shìzōng played polo at Chángwǔ Diàn.
Guìzhōng submitted a memorial admonishing him, saying,
"Your Majesty, as the ruler of the world,
you bear the heavy responsibility of preserving the ancestral temples and the state.
Hunting and playing polo are all dangerous activities.
A few days ago, the Crown Prince fell from his horse.
This can serve as a warning.
Your humble servant wishes that you would cease all such activities."
The Emperor said,
"Our ancestors established the empire through military might.
How can we immediately forget this during a period of peace?
Huángtǒng once abolished these activities,
and the people at that time all considered it wrong.
I personally witnessed this,
and therefore I show the world how to practice military skills."
In the eleventh month of the tenth year,
on the Crown Prince's birthday,
Shìzōng hosted a banquet for all officials at the Eastern Palace.
The Emperor drank with great joy.
Guìzhōng, affected by alcohol, knelt forward wanting to speak about an important matter,
but his words were confused and out of order.
The Emperor did not punish him,
but merely ordered him to be helped out.
Wǔ Zhēn,
a native of Línhuàn, Sùzhōu.
His grandfather was an official of the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ).
After Jìngkāng, his family became farmers,
and later, after the border was drawn, they belonged to Jīn.
Zhēn deeply studied mathematics.
During the Zhēnyòu period,
Púsàn Ānzhēn, acting Privy Council Administrator (Xíng Shūmìyuàn), heard of his reputation
and summoned him to Xúzhōu,
treating him with the courtesy befitting an honored guest.
Whenever an army was dispatched, he would consult Zhēn,
and his divinations were always accurate.
At the beginning of Zhèngdà,
he was summoned to Biànjīng
and appointed a scholar-in-waiting at Dōnghuá Mén.
His friend Wáng Xuàn asked Zhēn,
"If the imperial court were to ask about the longevity of the dynasty,
how would you respond?"
Zhēn replied,
"I would tell them the truth,
but also add that the Zhōu dynasty exceeded its allotted years,
while the Qín dynasty did not reach its term.
It also depends on cultivating virtue."
At that time, there was a prolonged drought and prayers for rain went unanswered.
The imperial court was worried.
Zhēn suddenly said to Xuàn:
“You should return home early today,
lest you be delayed by rain.”
Xuàn said:
“With ten thousand *lǐ* of cloudless sky,
and the scorching sun like this,
how could there be rain?”
Zhēn laughed and said:
“If that were the case,
then Heaven would be insincere.
How could Heaven ever be insincere?”
Soon after, there were clouds in the southeast,
which covered the sky in a moment.
Two *chǐ* of rain fell on the flat ground,
and everyone was astonished and marveled.
He was soon appointed as *Sītiāntái Guǎngōu*.
Zǐkàng
was a man of few words and little laughter,
and did not associate recklessly.
He once spent an entire day facing a student,
holding counting sticks and drawing diagrams.
His eyes were bright, as if he were planning something,
and those who saw him could not fathom it.
When Āizōng arrived in Càizhōu,
Right Chancellor Wányán Zhòngdé recommended his skills.
He was summoned,
and after dismissing others, spoke with the emperor,
who was greatly pleased.
He was appointed *Sītiān Chángxíng*
and rewarded generously.
He submitted a memorial saying:
“Recently, there has been a stellar anomaly in the division of Zhōu and Chǔ,
a comet rising west of Dàjiǎo,
sweeping the left axis of Zhěn.
This is an omen of removing the old and establishing the new.”
He also said:
“The three divisions of Zhèng, Chǔ, and Zhōu will experience a thousand *lǐ* of parched earth,
and great military calamities will arise.
The king cannot reside there.”
He further said:
“Cài City has omens of military disaster,
and Chǔ has signs of national collapse.
The three armies have been bitterly fighting around the western wall for days now.
The city walls are crumbling,
there is no visible grain inside,
and no relief troops from outside.
It is the year when the count of the ruler and his ministers runs out.”
Those who heard him were terror-stricken and lost courage.
Āizōng only sighed for a long time,
and did not consider it a crime.
He was quite arrogant by nature,
and court officials criticized him for this.
In the ninth month of Tiānxīng 2 (1233),
Càizhōu was besieged.
Kàng reported:
“The city will definitely be attacked on the third day of the twelfth month,”
and it happened as predicted.
Mòdì asked:
“On what day will the siege be lifted?”
He replied:
“On the thirteenth day of the first month of next year,
there will not be a single person or horse outside the city walls.”
The Emperor did not understand the reason,
but was happy that there was a date for the siege to be lifted.
He simply made secret plans for provisions to last until that day without shortage.
On the tenth day of the first month of Jiǎwǔ (1234),
Càizhōu was breached.
On the thirteenth day,
the Dàyuán army retreated.
On this day,
Kàng drowned himself, it is said.
Lǐ Mào’s
origin is unknown.
He possessed extraordinary skills.
During the Zhèngdà era,
he traveled to Jīngzhào.
The *Xíngshěng* Wányán Hédá admired his skills,
and brought him to Biànjīng,
recommending him to Āizōng.
The Emperor sent close attendants to secretly inquire about the fortunes of the state,
and he spoke without reservation.
He resided in Fántái Temple.
Court officials daily went to consult him,
and he could sometimes reveal hidden matters and changes in fortune,
leading people to believe him divine.
The Emperor disliked that his words were too revealing,
and sent an envoy to kill him.
The envoy then entered the temple with wine and food.
Mào came out to greet him,
and smiled, saying:
“This is it.”
The envoy asked:
“What do you mean?”
Mào said:
“My time is due to end today,
what more is there to say?”
Thereupon, he asked for wine,
drank heavily, and met his death.
Hú Déxīn
was a scholar family from Héběi.
He lived in Nányáng,
traveling between Wǎn and Yè,
addicted to wine, uninhibited and unconventional.
His predictions of misfortune and fortune were remarkably accurate.
In the summer of Zhèngdà 7 (1230),
he met Wáng Xuàn from Yān in a village in Yèxiàn.
He and Xuàn had not known each other before.
During their conversation, someone mistakenly introduced Xuàn as a military official.
Hú said:
“According to my method, this gentleman should pass the imperial examinations;
why call him a military official?”
Everyone was astonished,
and then told him the truth.
The two got along very well,
and Hú immediately ordered his family to prepare chicken and wine to host him.
As the wine flowed, he raised a large cup and said to Xuàn:
“Your future career is very distant;
there is no need to ask about it.
I have seen something
that I have long dared not tell anyone,
but now I wish to tell you.”
He then invited Xuàn to an open field,
and secretly told him:
“Since last year,
traveling on the roads between Wǎn and Yè,
I have seen that eight or nine out of ten passersby bear the aura of death.
This spring, I went to Chén and Xǔ,
and saw that more than half of the people there also ought to die.
If my eyes are to be trusted,
then the events of the time can be known.”
Xuàn asked in surprise about the speed of verification.
He said:
“It will be within a year or so.
I also will not escape this calamity.
Please record this secretly.”
The next year,
the Dàyuán army entered through Jīn and Fáng,
crossed the Hàn River at Qiàoshítān.
Wherever they passed, the houses were desolate.
Hú and his entire family also perished in the disaster,
such was the accuracy of his predictions.
Collation Notes

Biography 70: Rebellious Officials Bǐngdé (original name Yǐxīn), Tángkuò Biàn, Wūdài, Dàxìngguó, Túdān Ālǐchūhǔ, Púsàn Shīgōng (original name Hútǔ), Túdān Zhēn, Lǐ Lǎosēng, Wányán Yuányí, Hésīliè Zhízhōng (original name Húshāhǔ).
When Kǒngzǐ composed the *Chūnqiū*, chaotic ministers and wicked sons were struck with fear.
Its methods were five: subtle yet revealing,
meaningful yet obscure,
allusive yet clear,
exhaustive yet not disparaging,
punishing evil and encouraging good.
Indeed, punishing evil is how one encourages good.
Thus, the Biographies of Rebellious Officials are written.
Bǐngdé,
whose original name was Yǐxīn,
first served as *Xīnánlù Zhāotǎoshǐ*,
then was transferred to *Biànjīng Liúshǒu*.
After mourning his mother, he was reinstated as *Bīngbù Shàngshū*,
and then appointed *Cānzhī Zhèngshì*.
In Huángtǒng 8 (1148),
he, along with Wūlíndá Púlúhǔ and others, inspected the prefectures and counties.
Upon their return,
he was appointed *Píngzhāng Zhèngshì*.
The court debated relocating the Bóhǎi people from Liáoyáng to south of Yān.
Bǐngdé and *Zuǒsī Lángzhōng* Sānhé deliberated on the matter.
The close attendant Gāo Shòuxīng was among those to be relocated.
Shòuxīng complained to Dàohòu,
who informed the Emperor.
The Emperor was enraged,
flogged Bǐngdé, and executed Sānhé.
At this time,
Xīzōng had been on the throne for a long time,
Dàohòu meddled in politics,
and no heir had been established.
The Emperor was frustrated and discontent,
repeatedly executing imperial relatives
and flogging and humiliating high officials.
Bǐngdé, harboring resentment because of this,
then conspired with Tángkuò Biàn, Wūdài, and others to depose and enthrone a new ruler.
Wūdài informed Hǎilíng of his plan.
Hǎilíng then plotted with Bǐngdé to assassinate Xīzōng.
On the ninth day of the twelfth month of Huángtǒng 9 (1149),
they, along with Tángguō Biàn, Wūdài, Hūtǔ, Ālǐchūhǔ,
Dàxīngguó, Lǐ Lǎosēng, and Hǎilíng’s brother-in-law Tèsī,
assassinated Xīzōng in his sleeping quarters.
Bǐngdé’s initial intention was not for Hǎilíng.
After Xīzōng was assassinated,
there was no designated successor.
Hūtǔ supported Hǎilíng to sit,
and Bǐngdé and others all prostrated themselves, crying "Long live!"
They killed Cáo Guó Wáng Zōngmǐn and Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Zōngxián.
At that time, Bǐngdé’s rank was above Hǎilíng’s.
Because he had been beaten with a staff, he felt resentment and plotted to depose and enthrone.
Hǎilíng used this as an excuse to cause chaos.
After his enthronement,
Hǎilíng appointed Bǐngdé as Zuǒ Chéngxiàng,
concurrently Shìzhōng and Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài,
enfeoffing him as Xiāo Wáng,
bestowing an iron certificate,
along with twenty million cash, one thousand bolts of silk, three hundred horses and cattle each, and three thousand sheep.
After a long time,
he was slandered by Wūdài
and sent out to preside over the affairs of the Xíngtái Shàngshū Shěng.
At that time, Bǐngdé was on leave.
He was urgently summoned
and given ten days to depart.
Coincidentally, Hǎilíng wanted to eliminate Tàizōng’s sons,
and also eliminate Bǐngdé,
because Bǐngdé had been the prime plotter in the deposition and enthronement,
and after assassinating Xīzōng, had not immediately urged his ascension.
Hǎilíng bore a grudge against him.
Wūdài then said that Bǐngdé had plotted rebellion with Zōngběn, with evidence.
He said:
“Yesterday, Bǐngdé drank wine at Zōngběn’s house.
Hǎizhōu Cìshǐ Zǐzhōng said
that Bǐngdé had good fortune
and resembled Zhào Tàizǔ in appearance.
Bǐngdé leaned back, laughed, and accepted his words.
My wife said that Bǐngdé’s wife often pointed out and denounced the Emperor,
speaking disrespectful words.
And when Bǐngdé parted ways with Zōngběn,
the denunciation was even more severe,
and he even said that the mandate of heaven had shifted.
Bǐngdé summoned Xíngbù Shìláng Màndú and said,
‘Do you still remember that matter we spoke of before?’
Màndú replied,
‘How can one speak of matters concerning life and death casually in front of others?’
Such rebellious acts are very
clear.”
Hǎilíng sent an envoy to the Xíngtái to kill Bǐngdé,
and also killed the former Xíngtái Cānzhī Zhèngshì Wūlíndá Zànmóu.
Zànmóu’s wife
was Bǐngdé’s wet nurse.
Earlier,
Zànmóu and the former Xíngtái Zuǒ Chéng Wēndūn Sīzhōng were both in the Xíngtái.
Sīzhōng was insatiably greedy for bribes,
which Zànmóu disdained.
From this, a rift formed.
Thus, Sīzhōng took the opportunity to implicate and slander Zànmóu and his son,
killing them.
Zànmóu refused to kneel to receive his punishment.
The executioner stood and strangled him.
Hǎilíng bestowed all of Zànmóu’s family wealth and slaves upon Sīzhōng.
Bǐngdé and Wūdài incurred resentment through their words.
After his death, his younger brothers Tèlǐ and Cílǐ were also killed,
as were Zōnghàn’s descendants.
More than thirty people died.
Zōnghàn’s line thus ended.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he posthumously restored Bǐngdé’s official titles
and granted him the title Yítóng Sānsī.
Originally,
after Sākǎi died,
Zōnghàn inherited his Měng'ān Qīn Guǎn Móukè.
After Bǐngdé died,
Hǎilíng, as a reward to Wūdài,
transferred it to Wūdài’s son, Wùdábǔ.
In Dàdìng 6 (1166),
Shìzōng, pitying Zōnghàn for having no heirs,
decreed that the Měng'ān Móukè be returned to Sākǎi’s great-grandson, Pénmǎi.
He sent an envoy to rebury Sākǎi and Zōnghàn twenty *li* southwest of the imperial mausoleum.
All officials offered condolences,
and their family property was given to their close relatives to support the ancestral sacrifices.
After Bǐngdé died,
his residence in the Middle Capital
was occupied by Zuǒ Fù Yuánshuài Gǎo.
After Gǎo died,
Hǎilíng moved the capital,
and welcomed his legitimate mother, Túdān Shì, to live there.
After Túdān was killed,
Shìzōng, deeming it inauspicious,
converted it into a Buddhist temple.
Tángguō Biàn’s original name was Wògǔlà.
He married Xīzōng’s daughter, Dài Guó Gōngzhǔ,
and became Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
He successively held the posts of Cānzhī Zhèngshì and Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng.
He plotted with Yòu Chéngxiàng Bǐngdé to depose and enthrone.
Wūdài informed Hǎilíng of this.
Hǎilíng said to Biàn:
“We cannot rectify the situation;
disaster will befall us sooner or later.
If we undertake a great deed,
who can be enthroned?”
Biàn said:
“Perhaps Zhuówáng Chángshèng?”
Hǎilíng asked for the next best option.
Biàn said:
“Dèng Wángzǐ Āléng.”
Hǎilíng said:
“Āléng’s lineage is distant;
how can he be enthroned?”
Biàn said:
“Do you perhaps have aspirations yourself?”
Hǎilíng said:
“If it comes to it,
who else but me?”
Thereupon,
they plotted secretly day and night.
Hùwèi Jiàngjūn Tèsī suspected them
and reported to Dàohòu, saying:
“Biàn and others always whisper together whenever there is an opportunity,
I don’t know what they are discussing.”
Dàohòu reported this to Xīzōng.
Xīzōng was enraged.
He summoned Biàn and reprimanded him, saying:
“What are you plotting with Liàng?
What do you intend to do to me?”
He had him beaten with a staff and sent him away.
From then on, their plotting intensified.
On the ninth day of the twelfth month,
Dài Guó Gōngzhǔ was performing Buddhist rites for her mother, Dàohòu,
and stayed in the temple.
Therefore, Hǎilíng, Bǐngdé, and others all gathered at Biàn’s house.
That night,
Biàn and the others concealed knives under their clothes
and entered the palace together.
The gatekeepers, not suspecting Biàn, who was Fùmǎ,
let them all in.
Upon reaching the palace gate,
the guards on duty noticed them.
Biàn raised his knife and shouted at them to keep still.
After assassinating Xīzōng,
Hǎilíng was enthroned.
Biàn was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Chéngxiàng and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng,
enfeoffed as a king,
bestowed twenty million cash, one thousand bolts of silk, three hundred horses and cattle each, three thousand sheep, and an iron certificate.
He was later promoted to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
His father, Zhāngdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ Zhòngguó,
was transferred to Dōngpíng Yǐn.
Originally,
when Biàn plotted rebellion with Hǎilíng,
Biàn once said that many of his household servants could be used.
Hǎilíng already harbored suspicions about this.
On the night of the assassination, they gathered at Biàn’s house,
waiting for Xīngguó to leave the palace.
Biàn then prepared a meal.
Everyone was terrified and could not eat,
but Biàn alone ate heartily and showed no change.
Hǎilíng thus knew of his ruthlessness and cunning,
and feared him.
After ascending the throne,
he once viewed a portrait of Tàizǔ with Biàn.
Hǎilíng pointed to it and said to Biàn:
“These eyes resemble yours.”
Biàn’s expression changed.
Hǎilíng’s expression also changed.
From this, he suspected Biàn
and feared him even more.
When he conspired with Xiāo Yù to fabricate charges against Zōngběn,
he also fabricated that Biàn had plotted rebellion with Zōngběn,
and immediately killed him.
Zhòngguó was implicated and stripped of his office.
In Zhènglóng 2 (1157),
he was reinstated as Yízhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and later transferred to Qīngzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
In the early Dàdìng era,
Zhòngguó and Túdān Bágǎi were both renowned for their administrative achievements,
successively serving as Ànguó, Zhānghuà, and Hénghǎi Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Later, Biàn’s descendants submitted a memorial,
stating that Biàn died during the Tiāndé era,
and his grandfather Zhòngguó was also implicated and posthumously stripped of his rank.
In the early Zhènglóng era,
Zhòngguó had already been restored to his official posts.
They requested the posthumous restoration of Biàn’s official titles.
At this time,
Hǎilíng had already been demoted to a commoner.
Because Biàn was involved in the regicide,
the request was denied.
Yán was originally named Wūdài.
He was the son of Ālǔbǔ, the Right Chancellor of the Traveling Chancellery.
During Xīzōng’s reign,
he progressively rose to the rank of Dàlǐqīng.
In Xīzōng’s later years, his moods were unpredictable,
and ministers often felt fearful.
The Right Chancellor Bǐngdé and the Left Chancellor Tángkuò Biàn conspired to depose him and enthrone another.
Wūdài immediately went to Hǎilíng and informed him of this.
Thereupon, he joined with them to assassinate Xīzōng.
When Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
Wūdài was made Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
enfeoffed as the King of Xǔ,
and bestowed with money, silk, horses, cattle, sheep, and an iron certificate,
all similar to what his co-conspirators received.
Wūdài’s wife, Lady Tángkuò, was licentious;
she had previously had relations with Hǎilíng,
and also had an affair with her family slave, Yán Qǐ'ér.
Bǐngdé had once exposed this matter to Xīzōng,
and Wūdài had harbored a grudge but had not yet acted on it.
At that time, Hǎilíng was very suspicious,
and happened to fall ill.
After he recovered slightly,
Wūdài then falsely impeached,
saying, “Bǐngdé made critical remarks,
saying: 'The Emperor has not held court for several days.
If anything untoward should happen,
who would succeed him?'
I replied: 'The Emperor has a prince.'
Bǐngdé said: 'How can an infant bear the great responsibility of governing the world?
It must be Prince Gé!'"
Hǎilíng believed this to be true,
and thus dismissed Bǐngdé.
Later, he had him killed,
and bestowed Bǐngdé’s hereditary Měng'ān Móukè upon Wūdài.
He was promoted to Right Chancellor.
Wūdài was related to Zōngběn.
Because Hǎilíng had informed Wūdài of Bǐngdé’s affair,
Wūdài alone was spared from Zōngběn’s calamity.
Thus, Bǐngdé’s Qiānhù Móukè and all the family property of his son’s wife were bestowed upon Wūdài.
He was promoted to Sīkōng, Left Chancellor, and concurrently Shìzhōng.
After several months,
Wūdài attended early court.
Seeing that the day was overcast and looked like rain,
he assumed Hǎilíng would not hold court,
and so he hastened to leave court first.
All the officials followed him out.
Soon after, Hǎilíng presided over the court.
Learning that Wūdài had led the officials out,
he was displeased,
and thus stripped Wūdài of his Sīkōng title,
and sent him out as the Military Commissioner of Chóngyìjūn.
Later, Hǎilíng longed for Lady Tángkuò’s beauty.
When her maid came to inquire about his health,
Hǎilíng promised to establish her as empress
and ordered Wūdài’s assassination.
Hǎilíng feigned sorrow for Wūdài,
and sent his son Wùdábǔ with a golden tally by post to attend the funeral.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as a king,
and an imperial edict instructed the appropriate authorities to send his hearse,
and bestowed three hundred bolts of silk for travel expenses.
Lady Tángkuò was admitted into the palace
and enfeoffed as Guìfēi.
Wùdábǔ inherited the Měng'ān Móukè.
In the sixth year of Dàdìng,
the Měng'ān Móukè was returned to Sākǎi’s great-grandson,
and Ālǔbǔ’s Móukè was bestowed upon Wùdábǔ.
He eventually became Tóngzhī Dàxīng Yǐn.
His son, Táng,
originally named Wūyě'ābǔ,
due to his great-grandfather Ālǔbǔ’s merits,
served as a Bǐyàn Zhīhòu.
Dà Xīngguó
served Xīzōng as a Xǐndiàn Xiǎodǐ,
and provisionally as Zhícháng of the Jìnsìjú.
He was deeply trusted
and never left the Emperor’s side.
Every night,
when Xīzōng retired to bed,
Xīngguó would ask the attendant in charge for the keys and return home.
The attendant would immediately hand them over to him,
allowing him to enter and exit as was customary.
In the ninth year of Huángtǒng,
on Hǎilíng’s birthday,
Xīzōng sent Xīngguó with a portrait of Sīmǎ Guāng from the Sòng dynasty and other precious curiosities as gifts to Hǎilíng.
The Dowager Empress also attached items to be given.
Xīzōng was displeased
and had Xīngguó beaten with one hundred strokes.
When Hǎilíng planned the assassination,
he intended to first secure Xīngguó to find an opportune moment to enter the palace and carry out the great deed.
He also reasoned that Xīngguó, having been unjustly beaten, must harbor resentment,
which could be exploited to persuade him.
Thus, he used the monk Lǐ Lǎosēng to connect with Xīngguó.
Afterward,
knowing that Xīngguó had no disloyal intentions and could be part of the plot,
he summoned him to his private chamber,
ordered him to undress,
and intended to sleep with him,
implying a deeper relationship.
Xīngguó firmly declined, not daring to comply,
saying:
“Even if you have a command,
I will obey only Your Highness’s orders.”
Hǎilíng said:
“The Emperor unjustly killed Chángshèng,
and then killed the Empress.
Then he bestowed Chángshèng’s family property upon Āléng,
and then killed Āléng,
and thereupon bestowed it upon me.
I am deeply worried by this.
What should be done?”
Xīngguó said:
“That is indeed a cause for concern.”
Hǎilíng said:
“The court officials live in daily fear,
none feeling secure.
Previously, on my birthday,
because the Empress attached items for bestowal,
you were beaten,
and I also became suspected.
The Emperor once said he would eventually kill you.
You and I will both be unable to escape.
Would it not be better to undertake a great deed than to sit and await death?
I have already made plans with several ministers.
What do you think?”
Xīngguó said:
“As Your Highness says,
the matter cannot be delayed.”
They then agreed to act on the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month.
Xīngguó took the keys and opened the gate,
falsely summoning Hǎilíng to enter.
At the second watch of the night,
Hǎilíng, Bǐngdé, and others entered.
Xīzōng always kept a saber on his imperial couch.
That night, Xīngguó first took it and threw it under the couch.
When the chaos began,
Xīzōng searched for his saber but could not find it,
and was subsequently assassinated.
After Hǎilíng ascended,
he made Xīngguó the Grand Administrator of Guǎngníng,
bestowed upon him a hundred slaves, one rhinoceros horn belt and one jade belt each, money, silk, horses, cattle, and an iron certificate, like his co-conspirators,
and promoted him to the rank of Jīn Zǐ Guānglù Dàfū.

He again bestowed upon Xīngguó ten million cash, four hundred taels of gold, one thousand taels of silver, four fine horses, one camel carriage, three camels, a pearl headscarf, a jade belt hook, a jade-handled saber, and jade-ornamented saddle and reins.
In the fourth year of Tiāndé,
he was reassigned as Military Commissioner of Chóngyìjūn,
and given the name Bāngjī.
He was again appointed Military Commissioner of Jiàngyáng and Wǔníng,
and then reassigned as Grand Administrator of Héjiān.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Bāngjī was dismissed to his home,
and all that Hǎilíng had bestowed upon him was confiscated.
During the Dàdìng era,
Bāngjī’s elder brother, Bāngjié, returned from his post as Prefectural Judge of Jīngzhào.
Shìzōng said:
“Dà Bāngjié, having advanced due to his younger brother,
improperly joined the ranks of officials;
how can he be employed again?”
His sons and younger brothers, along with the official ranks conferred upon his father, were also dismissed.
When Hǎilíng was demoted to commoner,
an edict stated:
“Dà Bāngjī conspired with Hǎilíng in the regicidal rebellion,
and has escaped punishment until now,
which is already very fortunate.”
He was then flayed beside Sīlíng.
Túdān Ālǐchūhǔ was
a person from Gé Mǎhékūshēn in Huìníng,
who later moved to Yìzhōu.
His father, Bágǎi,
had military achievements during Tàizǔ’s time,
commanded a Móukè,
was the military commander of the Hésùguǎn.
In the fourth year of Huángtǒng, he became Bīngbù Shìláng,
and successively served as Military Commissioner of Tiāndéjūn,
and then Grand Administrator of Xīngzhōng.
He and Zōnggàn were in-laws for generations.
In the ninth year of Huángtǒng,
Ālǐchūhǔ and Púsàn Hūtǔ both served as commanders of ten guards.
When Hǎilíng was about to assassinate Xīzōng,
he wanted these two to be his internal agents,
and thus promised to give his daughter in marriage to Ālǐchūhǔ’s son,
and told them of his rebellious plot.
Ālǐchūhǔ was always fierce and violent.
Hearing his words, he was extremely pleased,
saying:
“My Lord, why did you speak of this so late?
The matter of deposition and enthronement is also a deed for men.
The Emperor cannot protect the realm.
The hope of the people rests only with My Lord.
Today’s plot is my long-cherished ambition!”
Thus, he and Hūtǔ both served in the forbidden palace on the ninth day of the twelfth month.
Hǎilíng deliberately entered the palace at the second watch that night.
Upon reaching the sleeping quarters,
Ālǐchūhǔ struck first with a blade,
followed by Hūtǔ.
Xīzōng collapsed.
Hǎilíng again struck him with a blade,
and blood splattered on his face and clothes.
Once Hǎilíng was established,
he appointed Ālǐchūhǔ as the Vice Commander of the Right Palace Guard.
He was bestowed with money, silk, horses, cattle, and sheep, matching his faction.
His son, ShúSīlà, married Princess Róngguó (who was Hégū's daughter),
and was promoted to Zhāoyì Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General of Resolute Valor) and Fùmǎ Dūwèi (Commander of the Imperial Son-in-Law).
In Tiāndé second year (1150),
he was left in charge of Dōngjīng (Eastern Capital).
He was promoted to Yítóng Sānsī.
In the eighth month,
he was transferred to be the Prefect of Héjiān.
He inherited the position of Xiélàāmēng'ān of Línhuáng Fǔlù, overseeing the Qīnguǎn Móukè.
He resigned due to mourning,
but was reinstated as the Prefect of Tàiyuán
and enfeoffed as a Prince.
Ālǐchūhǔ considered himself to have rendered meritorious service in the establishment of the new emperor,
and was granted an iron certificate (tiěquàn).
He became increasingly fierce and cruel,
treating his subordinates as slaves.
Any slight offense to his wishes would result in immediate flogging and humiliation without mercy.
He once inquired about his fortune from the diviner Gāo Dǐng,
and then used Dǐng's prediction to ask Zhāng Wángqǐ.
Wángqǐ believed that Ālǐchūhǔ would receive the mandate of Heaven.
Ālǐchūhǔ was pleased
and told Dǐng about Wángqǐ's words.
Dǐng reported his treason,
and Ālǐchūhǔ was executed,
along with his wife and Wángqǐ.
Hǎilíng ordered his son, ShúSīlà, to burn Ālǐchūhǔ's body
and throw the bones into the water.
Bágǎi served successively as the Western Capital’s Resident Administrator, Commander-in-Chief of the Southwest Circuit, and Military Commissioner of the Zhōngshùn Army.
He then entered the court as the Director of Agriculture,
then again became the Prefect of Héjiān,
then transferred to be the Prefect of Líntáo,
then entered the court as the Minister of Works,
then transferred to be the Military Commissioner of Xīngpíng Army and the Prefect of Jǐnán,
and then passed away.
Púsǎn Shīgōng's original name was Hūtǔ.
He was a native of Lǎohǎidágé in Shàngjīng.
Originally of humble origins,
Zōnggàn once extended aid to him
and promoted him to the palace guard as a leader of ten men.
When Hǎilíng plotted rebellion,
because Hūtǔ came from his household
and had received his grace,
he wanted Hūtǔ to be an insider.
He said to him:
"I have something I've wanted to tell you for a long time,
but I was afraid it would be leaked,
so I didn't dare."
Hūtǔ replied:
"Everything beyond my flesh and bones was bestowed by the late Grand Mentor.
If it can benefit the King,
I will not refuse even if it means death."
The late Grand Mentor
referred to Zōnggàn.
Hǎilíng said:
"The Emperor has lost the Dao.
I intend to carry out a dethronement and enthronement.
I must have your help to succeed."
Hūtǔ agreed.
On the ninth day of the twelfth month,
Hūtǔ was on night duty,
and Hǎilíng used this opportunity to enter the palace.
Upon reaching the sleeping quarters,
Xīzōng heard footsteps
and shouted at them.
Everyone retreated and dared not move.
Hūtǔ said:
"Things have come to this;
how can we not advance?"
Then they pushed open the door and entered together.
After assassinating Xīzōng,
Bǐngdé and others were still undecided.
Hūtǔ said:
"Initially, we discussed establishing the Píngzhāng.
What is there to doubt now?"
Then they escorted Hǎilíng to sit,
and the crowd acclaimed "Long live!"
Then Cáo Guówáng Zōngmǐn was summoned,
and Hūtǔ was immediately ordered to kill him.
After Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
Hūtǔ was appointed Vice Commander of the Left Palace Guard
and bestowed with money, silk, horses, cattle, sheep, and an iron certificate.
He was promoted to Commander of the Palace Guard
and his name was changed to Shīgōng.
He was transferred to be the Governor of Huìníng,
appointed Junior Tutor of the Crown Prince and Minister of Works,
and enfeoffed as a Prince.
After a short while,
he was relieved of his post due to mourning.
He was reinstated as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs
and then promoted to Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In Zhēnyuán third year (1155),
he became Right Chancellor.
In the early Zhènglóng period,
he was appointed Grand Commandant
and again served as Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Not long after,
he left due to mourning,
then was reinstated as Grand Commandant and Commissioner of Military Affairs.
When Hǎilíng arrived in Biànjīng,
he bestowed a mansion upon Hūtǔ,
neighboring Níngdé Palace.
The palace
was where Empress Dowager Túdān resided.
Hūtǔ frequently visited the Empress Dowager.
When the Khitan Sābā rebelled,
Hǎilíng ordered Hūtǔ and Xiāo Huáizhōng to campaign north.
Before departing,
Hūtǔ went to bid farewell at Níngdé,
and the Empress Dowager spoke with him for a long time.
Hǎilíng heard of this and disliked it,
suspecting him of having a different plot with the Empress Dowager.
At this time,
Xiāo Tūtālā and Wòlúbǔ had fought multiple battles against the Khitan Sābā without success,
and their provisions were running short.
They then retreated to Línhuáng.
However, Sābā heard that Shīgōng was approaching with a large army,
and thus planned to return to Dàshí,
moving west along the Lóngjū River.
Shīgōng reached Línhuáng but could not catch up.
Hǎilíng dispatched Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs Bái Yànjìng and others to suppress Sābā.
Shīgōng returned,
and Hǎilíng sent his son, Hūshāhǔ, by post-horse to intercept him.
Upon arrival,
Hūshāhǔ seized Shīgōng and executed him in the marketplace.
When Shīgōng was about to be executed,
his mouth was gagged with ropes, so he could not speak.
He merely raised his head to look at the sky and sun.
His clan was then exterminated,
and the families of Xiāo Tūtālā, Xiāo Zé, and Xiāo Huáizhōng were also purged.
In the early Dàdìng period,
all their official titles and ranks were restored.
However, when Hǎilíng was demoted to a commoner,
Shīgōng's status was again revoked for his involvement in the regicide.
When Shìzōng visited Shàngjīng,
he passed through Lǎohǎidágé.
Shīgōng's kinsmen, including Línhuáng Yǐn Shǒuzhōng and Dìngyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn Ālǐtú, were all stripped of their offices.
In the twenty-eighth year (of Dàdìng, 1188),
the Emperor said to his ministers:
"Hǎilíng dispatched Púsǎn Shīgōng, Xiāo Tūtālā, and Xiāo Huáizhōng to pursue Sābā, but they failed to catch him.
They were all executed and their clans exterminated,
which was truly excessive cruelty."
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Xiāng replied:
"At that time, I was in the army.
Hūtǔ and Zé had over thirteen thousand elite armored troops.
Although the rebel army was numerous, they were all coerced followers,
wearing felt and paper armor,
and easily defeated.
Hūtǔ and the others were timid and procrastinated,
allowing the rebels to escape."
The Emperor said:
"If that is truly the case,
then their execution was justified."
His elder brother was Húntǎn.
Túdān Zhēn,
whose original name was Tèsī,
was a native of Tèhēipìlà.
His grandfather, Chāo,
followed Tàizǔ in the campaign against Liáo and rendered meritorious service,
receiving a hereditary appointment as Mēng'ān.
His father, Pólúhuǒ,
accumulated official ranks up to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī through military achievements.
Zhēn married the daughter of Liáo Wáng Zōnggàn,
who was Hǎilíng's uterine sister.
In Huángtǒng ninth year (1149),
Zhēn and Hǎilíng together assassinated Xīzōng.
After Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhēn as Left Guard General
and enfeoffed Zhēn's wife as Píngyáng Chánggōngzhǔ.
Zhēn himself was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi and Vice Commander of the Left Palace Guard.
He was promoted to Commander of the Palace Guard,
concurrently serving as Junior Protector of the Crown Prince,
and enfeoffed as a Prince.
He was transferred to be the Prefect of Dàxīng,
with his position as Commander of the Palace Guard remaining unchanged.
Soon after,
he was appointed Hūnsīlǔ Mēng'ān of Línhuáng Fǔlù.
Two years later,
Hǎilíng summoned Zhēn and exhorted him, saying:
"You have been by my side since childhood,
and have rendered considerable minor service.
But recently, you have become negligent,
indulging in transgressions,
and forming private connections.
All who become rich and honored yet grow arrogant
bear the signs of impending death.
If you do not control your heart,
there will be nothing you won't do,
and what excuse could there be for granting you death?
I consider my brother Xiāng and the Princess to be my siblings,
which is why I am giving you a minor reprimand."
Zhēn only wept.
On that very day, he was relieved of his duties as Diǎnjiǎn,
but remained Dàxīng Yǐn.
Hǎilíng further warned him, saying:
"From now on, if you can motivate yourself to diligence,
I will consider it.
Otherwise,
I will dismiss you and send you back to your village."
More than a month later,
he was reinstated as Dūdiǎnjiǎn and Dàxīng Yǐn as before.
In Zhènglóng二年,
he was granted the customary title of Shěn.
He was promoted to Shūmì Fùshǐ,
bestowed a saber to carry into the palace,
and then transferred to Tóngpàn Dàzōngzhèng Shì.
When Hǎilíng was about to campaign against Sòng,
he decreed that court officials, except for envoys from the three kingdoms, should feast and drink;
those who drank otherwise would be put to death.
On the fourth day of the first month of the sixth year, the Lìchūn Festival,
Yìdū Yǐn Jīng, Ānwǔ Jiédùshǐ Shuǎng, and Jīnwú Shàngjiāngjūn Āsù drank at Zhēn's residence.
Hǎilíng sent Zhōu Fú'ér to deliver an earthen ox to Zhēn's residence;
he saw them and reported it.
Hǎilíng summoned Zhēn and questioned him, saying:
"Military affairs are pressing,
and all officials are forbidden to drink.
Do you gentlemen know this?"
Zhēn and the others prostrated themselves and begged for death.
Hǎilíng rebuked them, saying:
"If you think that executing someone for drinking is too severe,
you should indeed remonstrate.
The ancients, after three remonstrances were ignored, would still reluctantly follow the sovereign's command.
Wèi Wǔdì, while on a military campaign, issued an order: 'Those who trespass on the wheat fields shall die.'
Later, his own horse entered a wheat field,
and he cut his hair to punish himself.
Trespassing on wheat
is a minor matter,
yet he absolutely wished to show his trustworthiness.
I am the ruler of the empire,
can the law not be applied to the noble and close to me?
I consider that Empress Cíxiàn had four children,
and only I and the Princess remain.
As for Jīng and the others, they are all close relatives,
so I leniently spare you from the death penalty."
Thereupon, Zhēn was flogged seventy times,
and Jīng and the other three were each flogged one hundred times.
Zhēn was demoted to Ānwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ,
Jīng to Luánzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Shuǎng to Guīhuàzhōu Cìshǐ.
Before long,
Zhēn was appointed Yùshǐ Dàfū,
and with his original post, served as Zuǒjiānjūn,
following the campaign against Sòng.
Upon reaching Yángzhōu,
Hǎilíng died,
and they returned north.
He met Shìzōng in Zhōngdū,
who decreed that Zhēn's daughter be made the Crown Prince's consort.
Zhēn was appointed Tàiyuán Yǐn,
and then transferred to Xiánpíng.
While in Xiánpíng, Zhēn was corrupt and acted unlawfully,
accumulating a huge fortune from bribes.
He was transferred to Zhēndìng Yǐn,
and then the matter came to light.
Shìzōng sent Dàlǐ Qīng Lǐ Chāngtú to interrogate him.
Zhēn immediately confessed.
Chāngtú returned and reported,
and the Emperor asked him:
"Is Zhēn suspended from office?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
The Emperor was angry,
and punished Chāngtú.
He then dispatched Xíngbù Shàngshū Yílà Dào to Zhēndìng to question him,
and to reclaim the ill-gotten gains for their owners.
The authorities failed to return them in a timely manner,
so an edict was issued to first use official funds to return them to their owners,
and then order Zhēn to repay the treasury.
All returns of ill-gotten gains to their owners
were to follow this precedent.
Zhēn was demoted to Bózhōu Fángyùshǐ,
and Zhēn's wife was demoted to Qīngpíng Xiànzhǔ.
A short while later,
he was promoted to Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ.
An envoy was sent to warn and instruct him,
and the edict said:
"I consider you a distinguished relative,
and without waiting for the full term,
you are moved to a major garrison.
Such extraordinary grace is not often obtained.
You must not repeat your previous errors."
He was then transferred to Hézhōng Yǐn.
His wife was further enfeoffed as Rèn Guó Gōngzhǔ,
and bestowed one hundred liǎng of gold and twenty bolts of rich colorful silk.
Zhēn was bestowed two polo horses.
He was transferred to Dōngjīng Liúshǒu,
and bestowed a jade eagle and a bow and arrows.
Zhēn's wife was bestowed ten thousand strings of cash.
The officials reported,
"Hǎilíng has been demoted to a commoner;
Zōnggàn should no longer be referred to as 'Emperor'."
Thereupon,
because Zōnggàn had rendered service to the state,
an edict posthumously enfeoffed him as Liáo Wáng.
His sons, grandsons, and all his daughters were demoted.
Zhēn's wife was demoted to Yǒngpíng Xiànzhǔ.
Zhēn himself was demoted from Yítóng Sānsī to Tèjìn,
deprived of his Měng'ān,
and no longer called Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
He was again transferred to Línhuáng Yǐn.
Initially,
there were nine people involved in the assassination of Xīzōng.
Hǎilíng perished due to his own tyranny.
Bǐngdé, Biàn, Hū Tǔ, and Ālǐchūhǔ were killed on suspicion.
Yán died due to his wife.
Yù and Lǎo Sēng were executed for rebellion.
At this point, Zhēn and Dàxīngguó were still alive.
However, Xīngguó was discarded and not used.
Only Zhēn, through his marriage to a imperial relative, enjoyed favor.
Although he and his wife had their titles and ranks reduced,
Shìzōng, considering the long term,
ultimately did not protect him with private favor.
After a long time,
an edict was issued to execute Zhēn, his wife, and their two sons, Shènsī and Shíliù,
but to pardon their grandsons.
Shortly thereafter,
Xīngguó was also executed,
and thus all the rebel faction of Huángtǒng was eliminated.
Upon Zhāngzōng's ascension,
he honored his mother, the Crown Prince's consort, as Empress Dowager.
Zhēn was posthumously enfeoffed as Tàiwèi Liáng Guó Gōng.
Zhēn's grandfather, Chāo, was posthumously enfeoffed as Sīkōng Lǔ Guó Gōng;
his father, Pó Lú Huǒ, as Sītú Qí Guó Gōng;
Zhēn's wife as Liáng Guó Fūrén;
and his sons Bǔ Huǒ, Shènsī, and Shíliù all as Zhènguó Shàngjiāngjūn.
Not long after,
Zhēn was again posthumously granted the titles of Tàishī and Guǎngpíng Jùnwáng,
with the posthumous name Zhuāngjiǎn.
Zhēn's wife was promoted to Liáng Guó Gōngzhǔ.
Lǐ Lǎo Sēng,
formerly a clerk for a general,
was related to Dàxīngguó and had always been close to him.
When Hǎilíng assumed power,
Xīngguó recommended Lǎo Sēng to Hǎilíng,
and Hǎilíng made him a secretary in the secretariat (Shěng Lìshǐ).
When Hǎilíng was about to launch his coup,
he sent Lǎo Sēng to win over Xīngguó.
Xīngguó ultimately obtained the keys for Hǎilíng,
and let Hǎilíng into the palace to carry out the assassination;
Lǎo Sēng was responsible for this.
After Hǎilíng ascended the throne,
he made Lǎo Sēng Tóngzhī Guǎngníng Yǐn Shì,
and bestowed him ten million cash, five hundred bolts of silk, two hundred horses and cattle each, and two thousand sheep.
After a long time,
Hǎilíng became displeased with Hán Wáng Hēng
and planned to kill him.
He searched for his crimes but could not find any.
So he appointed Hēng as Guǎngníng Yǐn,
and again appointed Lǎo Sēng as Tóngzhī,
to observe and investigate Hēng,
and fabricate charges against him.
Hēng enjoyed gambling.
Upon arriving in Guǎngníng,
he often gambled with Lǎo Sēng
and treated him very well.
Because of this, Lǎo Sēng could not bear to condemn Hēng to death,
and hesitated for a long time.
Hǎilíng again sent Xiǎodǐ É Lùn to urge Lǎo Sēng.
Lǎo Sēng then conspired with Hēng's family servant Liù Jīn
to kill Hēng in prison.
The details are found in Hēng's biography.
When Yēlǜ Ānlǐ returned to court from Guǎngníng,
Hǎilíng said to him:
"Bódié has three crimes,
and admitting to one has already shown some disappointment.
You are a former subordinate of Liáng Wáng.
If Hēng were to confess his guilt,
the crime would surely extend to his relatives,
therefore he was flogged to death."
Hǎilíng, seeing that the old monk Yú Hēng had some hesitation,
demoted the old monk to Prefect of Yìzhōu.
After a long time,
he was promoted to concurrently serve as Dàxīng Yǐn,
given the name Wéizhōng,
and then reassigned as concurrent Prefect of Yán'ān Fǔ.
In the second year of Dàdìng (1162),
he conspired to rebel with the Minister of War Kěxǐ,
and was executed.
The commentary states: The Book of Documents says:
"The king's left and right have constant chiefs, constant officials, officials for special assignments, palace attendants, and tiger guards."
The Duke of Zhōu said: "Alas,
how rare are those who know to be solicitous and considerate!"
King Mù told Bó Jiǒng:
"Carefully choose your colleagues;
do not choose those who use clever words and pleasing looks, are obsequious and fawning.
Let them only be good gentlemen."
What the Jīn people called the palace attendants (寢殿小底) were like the Zhōu's palace attendants (綴衣),
and what they called the imperial guards (護衛) were like the Zhōu's tiger guards (虎賁).
Thus, they were all servants and attendants to the emperor.
Hǎilíng committed regicide,
and Dàxīngguó, Hūtǔ, and Ālǐchūhǔ were his close associates,
all coming from the ranks of palace attendants and imperial guards.
Xīzōng certainly did not know to be solicitous and considerate of them.
One day,
Xīzōng was drinking with his close attendants.
During the night,
the Jīggǔ Diàn caught fire.
The Emperor wanted to go see, but Dū Diǎnjiǎn Cíbùshī tugged on the Emperor's robes to stop him,
and memorialized:
"Your servant is here;
what does Your Majesty have to worry about?
Please do not go yourself."
Xīzōng thought Cíbùshī was drunk
and was very angry with him.
The next day,
he had him flogged and dismissed.
Later, he remembered his loyalty
and recalled him for re-employment.
Hǎilíng and Tángguō Biàn often privately whispered to each other, dismissing others.
The imperial guard Tèsī suspected something unusual.
Hǎilíng had him eliminated and killed.
In the last years of Huángtǒng,
the officials were disunited,
lacking respect for the monarch and diligence towards the emperor,
while a multitude of villains secretly emerged.
Among the servants and attendants, there were no longer any like Cíbùshī or Tèsī.
The Ode of Mián says:
"I say there are those who are attached,
I say there are those who lead and follow,
I say there are those who rush about,
I say there are those who ward off insult."
Alas,
how can officials who lead and follow, and ward off insult, be few?
Wányán Yuán yí,
originally named Āliè,
also named Yítèliǎn,
originally bore the surname Yēlǜ.
His father, Shènsī,
in the seventh year of Tiānfǔ (1123),
when Zōngwàng pursued the Liáo lord to Tiāndé,
Shènsī came to surrender,
and moreover said that the Xìa people were bringing troops to welcome the Liáo lord,
and would cross the river to leave.
Zōngwàng sent a letter to the Xìa people, explaining the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
and the Xìa people then stopped.
Shènsī was granted the surname Wányán
and rose to the office of Yítóng Sānsī.
Yuányí was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and good at polo.
In the first year of Huángtǒng (1141),
he was appointed imperial guard,
and progressively promoted to Qulièběn Qúnmù Shǐ,
then entered the court as Wǔkù Shǔlìng,
and transferred to Fúbǎo Láng.
When Hǎilíng usurped the throne,
he became Minister of War.
In the third year of Tiāndé (1151),
an edict ordered all those who had been granted surnames to revert to their original surnames.
Yuányí reverted to the surname Yēlǜ.
He successively served as Military Commissioner of Shùnyì and Zhāoyì,
and again became Minister of War and Quànnóng Shǐ.
When Hǎilíng attacked Sòng,
he was given his original office and also led the Shenwǔ Army as Dūzǒngguǎn,
with over ten thousand cavalry from Dàmíng Lù added to his command.
His vanguard crossed the Huái River,
captured Zhāoguān,
and encountered over ten thousand Sòng troops at Zhègāo.
They fought fiercely and repelled them.
Upon reaching Hézhōu,
one hundred thousand Sòng troops came to resist.
Yuányí waved his army and fought fiercely,
stopping only at dusk.
The Sòng people launched a night raid on the camp,
but Yuányí attacked and drove them away.
At dawn, he pursued the Sòng troops,
beheading tens of thousands.
For this achievement, he was promoted to Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
Hǎilíng then established the position of Zhéxīdào Dūwútǒngzhì,
making Yuányí lead it,
supervising all armies in crossing the Yangtze River,
wearing a golden plaque,
and bestowing a set of clothes.
At this time,
Shìzōng had already ascended the throne in Liáoyáng,
and many in the army were contemplating their allegiance.
Hǎilíng's military orders were cruel and urgent,
eagerly wanting to cross the river,
but the multitude wanted to flee north.
They decided to consult Yuányí.
Měng'ān Tángguō Wūyě said:
"Blocking the Huái crossing,
all will be captured.
We have heard that a new Son of Heaven has ascended in Liáoyáng;
it would be better to collectively carry out a great deed,
and then lead the army back north."
Yuányí said:
"Wait for Wáng Xiáng to arrive and then plan."
Wáng Xiáng was Yuányí's son,
serving as Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Agile Cavalry,
and was in a separate army.
Yuányí sent someone to secretly summon Wáng Xiáng.
When he arrived,
they agreed to act at dawn when the imperial guards changed shifts.
Yuányí first deceived his troops, saying:
"There is an order:
all of you dismount,
and cross the river at dawn."
All were afraid,
so he informed them of the planned uprising,
and all agreed.
At dawn on the Yǐwèi day of the tenth month,
Yuányí, Wáng Xiáng, along with the Wǔshèng Army Dūzǒngguǎn Túshàn Shǒusù, Měng'ān Tángguō Wūyě, Mòkè Wòlúbǎo, Lóuxuè, Wēndū Chángshòu, and others, led their forces to attack the imperial camp.
Hǎilíng heard the commotion,
thinking that Sòng troops had suddenly arrived.
He grabbed his clothes and quickly rose.
An arrow flew into his tent.
He picked it up to look at it,
and exclaimed in shock:
"It's our own soldiers!"
Dàqìngshān said:
"The situation is critical;
we should go out and avoid them."
Hǎilíng said:
"Where will I go if I run?"
As he was reaching for his bow,
he was already struck by an arrow and fell to the ground.
Yán'ān Shàoyǐn Nàhé Wòlúbǔ first stabbed him with a blade.
His hands and feet were still moving,
so they strangled him to death.
The Agile Cavalry Commander Dàpán gathered troops to rescue him.
Wáng Xiáng came out and told him:
"It's too late."
Dàpán then stopped.
The soldiers ransacked and took all the clothing and items from the traveling camp.
Then they took Dàpán's clothes and headscarf to wrap Hǎilíng's corpse
and burned it.

Then they arrested the Minister of the Right Lǐ Tōng, Vice Commander of Zhéxīdào Guō Ānguó, Supervisor of the Army Túshàn Yǒngnián, Director of the Imperial Attendants Bureau Liáng Qióng, and Vice Director Dàqìngshān,
and killed them all.
Yuányí acted as Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Left Lead Army,
and sent an envoy to kill Crown Prince Guāngyīng in Nánjīng.
The great army returned north.
In the spring of the second year of Dàdìng (1162),
he was granted an audience,
and appointed Censor-in-Chief.
The edict stated:
"Gāo Zhēn, as Censor-in-Chief,
was known for his uprightness,
but was somewhat overly fastidious,
even junior officials with improperly worn hats were impeached.
There are duties greater than this;
you should strive for them."
Not long after,
he was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì,
ennobled as Duke of Jìguó,
bestowed with a jade belt and a mansion,
and again granted the surname Wányán.
He went to Tàizhōu Lù to plan matters concerning the attack on the Qìdān.
Yuán Yí sent the loyal and brave captain Lǐ Róng to summon Wōwò.
Wōwò killed Róng.
An imperial edict posthumously granted Róng an advancement of four official ranks.
In the fifth month,
the Emperor, upon hearing that Yuán Yí was about to return,
sent an envoy to stop him.
After the Qìdān had been pacified,
Yuán Yí returned to court,
and memorialized to request an increase in armor for all the horse-breeding pastures.
The Emperor decreed to grant it,
adding twenty sets of armor to each pasture.
Yuán Yí again requested an increase in soldiers and horses for the garrison at Línhuáng.
An imperial edict granted six hundred horses.
After a long time,
he was dismissed and became the Grand Defender of Dōngjīng.
He requested to return the mansion that had been bestowed upon him.
The Emperor granted his request,
and bestowed upon him a set of robes, a Tǔhú falcon, a horse, and a Hǎidōngqīng falcon.
Not long after,
he retired from office
and passed away at home.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor
sent an envoy to offer sacrifices,
and granted a very generous funerary allowance.
In the eleventh year of Dàdìng,
the Shàngshū Shěng memorialized to propose a posthumous appointment for Nàhé Wòlǔ.
The Emperor said:
“When Hǎilíng was deposed,
this person was the first to enter and assassinate him.
There is no greater crime for a subject than this.
How can he be given an official position again?
However, his hereditary office of móukè may remain as before.”
In the eighteenth year of Dàdìng,
Zhālǐhǎi memorialized, saying:
“Any subject who can defend against disaster and resist insult and has made meritorious contributions
should be recorded and employed.
Now, those who assassinated Hǎilíng are considered to have performed meritorious service,
and are rewarded with high titles.
This is not the way to encourage loyal service to one's sovereign.
They should be stripped of their honors
to serve as a warning to subjects.
I, at that time, was also part of their faction.
If names are to be rectified and crimes defined,
I request that it begin with me.”
The Emperor said:
“Zhālǐhǎi requests to be punished for his own crime to encourage loyal service to the sovereign;
this is indeed something difficult for people to do.”
Thereupon, Zhālǐhǎi was appointed as a Zhīhòu Lángjūn in the household of Prince Zhào.
Yuán Yí’s son, Xíniè’ābǔ,
became a Fúbǎo Zhīhòu in the twenty-fifth year of Dàdìng.
He requested to be promoted according to the example of Nǚzhēn people.
The Emperor said:
“The bestowed surname was a temporary expedient.”
He ordered Xíniè’ābǔ to revert to his original surname.
A comment says: The Chūnqiū records:
“Qí Gōngzǐ Shāngrén assassinated his ruler Shè,”
and also says:
“The people of Qí assassinated their ruler Shāngrén.”
Alas,
the one who assassinated Shè was Shāngrén;
the ones who assassinated Shāngrén were Bǐng Chù and Yán Zhí.
Hǎilíng assassinated Xīzōng;
Wányán Yuán Yí assassinated Hǎilíng.
When Shāngrén assassinated,
Bǐng Chù and Yán Zhí removed him.
When Hǎilíng was assassinated,
Yuán Yí submitted to Shìzōng.
Bǐng and Yán were lowly servants;
Yuán Yí was a commander-in-chief,
who held the ruler's personal troops,
and looked for an opportunity to assassinate him for profit.
How could his crime be excused from punishment?
Shìzōng could only avoid promoting him greatly.
Zhālǐhǎi was like someone who kills a person and then surrenders himself.
In law,
there is no precedent for a murderer to be acquitted by self-surrender and then rewarded,
let alone for regicide.
Fifty-three years after Hǎilíng's assassination,
there was again the affair of Húshāhǔ.
Gēshíliè Zhízhōng,
whose original name was Húshāhǔ,
was a descendant of Āshū.
He moved to Dōngpíng Lù Měng'ān.
In the eighth year of Dàdìng,
he served as a bodyguard to the Crown Prince,
and was later appointed as Crown Prince's Stable Master,
then changed to Commander of the Falconry Bureau,
and again promoted to Director of the Falconry Bureau and Commander of the Imperial Guards.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng,
he was on an envoy mission and stayed in a remote area.
The wine official, Yílà Bǎo, greeted him late.
He offered him wine,
but the wine tasted poor.
Zhízhōng became angry
and beat and injured Yílà Bǎo.
An imperial edict ordered him to be flogged fifty times.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Right Vice Commander of the Imperial Guards.
He became arrogant and did not perform his duties,
and was demoted to Defense Commissioner of Zhàozhōu.
After more than a year,
he was promoted to Military Commissioner of Xīngpíng Jūn.
After his mother's mourning period,
he was reinstated as Military Commissioner of Guīdé Jūn,
then changed to Kaīyuǎn Jūn and Deputy Commander of Southwest Route Pacification.
Soon after, he was appointed to administer the affairs of Dàmíng Fǔ.
In the second year of Chéng'ān,
he was summoned to be a Grand Councilor of the Privy Council.
An imperial edict ordered him to assist Chancellor Xiāng in military expeditions.
Zhízhōng did not want to go
and memorialized, saying:
“I have a grudge against Xiāng,
and he will surely kill me.”
The Emperor was angry at his insolent words,
and the matter was submitted to the appropriate office.
Later, he was pardoned
and sent out as Military Commissioner of Yǒngdìng Jūn.
He was then made Pacification Commissioner of Northwest Route,
and again Yǒngdìng Jūn.
He was dismissed for seizing military horses.
In the first year of Tàihé,
he was reinstated to administer the affairs of Dàxīng Fǔ.
An imperial edict stated that Qìdān people who performed meritorious service should receive the same official rewards and favors as Nǚzhēn people,
that they were allowed to keep and raise horses,
and could serve as clerks and interpreters.
This was established as law.
Zhízhōng obstructed the edict from being implemented.
The Emperor rebuked him, saying:
“Although you may intend to prevent problems,
you do not know that the imperial court has its own established regulations.
From now on, do not again cause such trivial troubles.”
Thereupon, the edict was issued and implemented.
Wèi Tíngshí, from Láishuǐ, whose grandfather was Rèn'ér,
was formerly freed from the household of Jìn Wénzhāo.
In the third year of Tiāndé,
he was registered as a legitimate household,
and three generations had already passed.
Wénzhāo's grandson, Qíng, slandered Tíngshí as a slave,
and falsely accused him of assault and abuse.
The police investigation found no basis for the claims.
According to law, the complaint should be filed with his native district.
Qíng complained to the prefecture.
Zhízhōng ordered Tíngshí to pay five hundred strings of cash to Qíng.
Tíngshí did not comply
and returned to Láishuǐ.
Zhízhōng directly sent people to arrest Tíngshí with chains.
The Yùshǐ Tái requested to transfer the inquiry.
Zhízhōng, in turn, memorialized that the Yùshǐ Tái did not follow the regulations,
and that the prefecture had not concluded the case, ordering it to be transferred for investigation.
An imperial edict ordered Lǐ Bǐng, Assistant Minister of Personnel,
and Zhān'é Gédá, Assistant Minister of Revenue,
to conduct the investigation.
Bǐng and Gédá memorialized that the Yùshǐ Tái was in the right,
and the Emperor then severely reprimanded Zhízhōng.
Mèng Zhù, Censor-in-Chief, impeached Zhízhōng, saying:
“He is greedy, cruel, and arbitrary,
and does not obey laws and decrees.
After being pardoned,
he repeatedly errs and does not repent.
After receiving imperial grace and leniency,
he becomes even more overbearing.
For example, he falsely claimed horses in Xióngzhōu,
fraudulently drew salary in Píngzhōu,
destroyed Wèi Tíngshí's home,
and exhumed his ancestral tombs,
failed to attend when a memorial was presented,
gathered prostitutes during a prayer for rain,
and beat and insulted colleagues and arbitrarily ordered their suspension,
lacking the deportment of a military commander
and being unfit for the position of Metropolitan Prefect.”
The Emperor said:
“Zhízhōng is a coarse man,
and seems to be somewhat overbearing.”
Zhù replied:
“With an enlightened Emperor above,
how can there be overbearing subjects?”
The Emperor realized his error,
took out the memorial to read it,
and decreed the Shàngshū Shěng to interrogate him.
Because of this, he was changed to Commander-in-Chief of the Wǔwèi Army.
Púsǎn Kuí, Grand Councilor, pacified and announced imperial orders in Hénán.
Zhízhōng was appointed Commander of the Army for the Eastern and Western Circuits of Shāndōng.
Kuí, as head of the traveling provisional government in Biànjīng, attacked Sòng.
All the circuit military command offices were elevated to Metropolitan Headquarters of Soldiers and Horses.
Zhízhōng became Metropolitan Commander of Soldiers and Horses for the two Shāndōng circuits,
and Wányán Sálà, Military Commissioner of Dìnghǎi Jūn, served as his deputy.
Zhízhōng divided his troops to station them at Jīnchéng and Qúshān.
