He requested an additional deployment of troops from Dōngpíng Lù to station them in Mì, Yí, Nínghǎi, Dēng, and Lái to block military advances.
The Emperor granted his request.
This was in the fourth month of the sixth year of Tàihé.
In the fifth month,
Sòng troops invaded Jīnchéng.
Zhízhōng sent patrol commissioner Zhōu Nú with 300 cavalry to repel them.
At the same time, Sòng reinforced their troops and turned towards Shùyáng.
Móukè Sānhé ambushed 50 soldiers in the bamboo thicket.
Waiting for the Sòng troops to pass, they suddenly attacked them,
killing more than ten men.
They pursued them to the county seat.
The Sòng troops dared not come out.
At that time, Zhōu Nú entered the city with his troops.
The Sòng troops scaled the city walls and fled.
Sānhé had already burned their boats.
They jointly attacked and heavily defeated them,
beheading over 500 men,
killing Sòng commander Lǐ Zǎo,
and capturing Zhōngyì Jūn general Lǚ Zhāng.
In the tenth month,
Zhízhōng led an army of 20,000 out of Qīngkǒu.
The Sòng arrayed over 10,000 infantry and cavalry on the south bank,
and 100 warships blocked the upstream,
maintaining a standoff for several days.
Zhízhōng engaged in battle with 2,000 naval troops,
blocking the Sòng naval forces.
He sent deputy commander Yīlà Gǔyǔ Niè with 4,000 elite cavalry to cross directly from downstream.
The Sòng troops, seeing the cavalry land on the south bank,
collapsed both by land and water.
The number of those pursued, beheaded, and drowned was very large.
They captured all their warships and 300 warhorses,
then took Huái'yīn,
and advanced to besiege Chǔzhōu.
He was promoted to Marshal Zuǒ Jiānjūn.
Zhízhōng allowed his troops to plunder.
When the emperor heard of it,
he caned his staff official Ālǐ Bùsūn,
and ordered the return of the looted goods.
Not long after,
the Sòng requested peace,
and an imperial edict ordered the cessation of hostilities.
He was appointed Xīnán Lù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
then changed to Xīyīng Liúshǒu.
In the first year of Dà'ān,
he was granted a hereditary móukè title.
He was again made Zhī Dàxīngfǔshì,
then sent out as Zhī Tàiyuánfǔ,
and again became Xīyīng Liúshǒu,
acting Xūmì Yuàn,
and concurrently Ānfǔshǐ.
With 7,000 elite soldiers, he met the main army.
They battled north of Dìng'ān.
At dusk,
he first fled with his subordinates,
and the army then disintegrated.
When passing through Wèizhōu,
he illicitly took 5,000 liǎng of silver from the official treasury and various clothes and silks,
and seized horses from officials and commoners.
He entered Zǐjīngguān with his personal attendants,
and caned the Lái shuǐ magistrate to death.
Upon reaching Zhōngdū,
the imperial court did not question any of this.
He was then promoted to Yòu Fùyuánshuài,
acting Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
Zhízhōng became even more uninhibited.
He requested 20,000 infantry and cavalry to be stationed in Xuāndézhōu.
He was given 3,000,
and ordered to station them in Guīchuān.
In the first month of the first year of Chóngqìng,
Zhízhōng requested to move his encampment to Nánkǒu or Xīnzhuāng.
He sent a dispatch to the Shàngshū Shěng saying:
"If the main army comes, we will certainly not be able to hold out.
My own life is not worth regretting,
but 3,000 soldiers are cause for concern.
The Twelve Passes, Jiànchūn, and Wànníng Gōng will also not be preserved."
The court disapproved of his words,
and ordered the relevant authorities to investigate.
An imperial edict enumerated his fifteen crimes,
and he was dismissed and sent back to his hometown.
The following year,
he was again summoned to Zhōngdū
to participate in military discussions.
Left Jìanshì Dàfū Zhāng Xíngxìn submitted a memorial saying:
"Húshāhǔ acts solely on his private intentions,
deviating from public justice,
disregarding the ministries to show his tyranny,
and flattering close officials to gain praise.
He bends the law in his actions
and unjustly harms common people.
When acting in Shānxī,
his troops were undisciplined.
He retreated before fighting,
illegally took official property,
and caned a county magistrate to death.
Stationed in Guīchuān,
he requests to move inland;
his schemes are clear to see.
To expect him to change his past wrongs
and achieve future success,
is it not difficult?
If talent is truly commendable,
even if humble, it should be promoted.
Why must one be old and established to achieve merit?
The use of a general
is linked to safety and danger.
May the imperial court scrutinize this.
The world would be fortunate."
Chancellor Túdān Yì believed he was unusable.
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Wánwán Luòguì knelt and reported his wickedness,
and so the matter was dropped.
Zhízhōng was skilled at cultivating close favorites,
who all praised him.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict granted him half the salary of a liúshǒu,
and he participated in military discussions.
Zhāng Xíngxìn again remonstrated, saying:
"I humbly hear that Húshāhǔ, as an old minister,
is to be re-appointed.
Whether a person is capable or not
does not depend on whether they are new or old.
His past defeat
is already known to the court.
To re-employ him
is surely impermissible!"
So, it was stopped.
The emperor ultimately considered Zhízhōng usable.
He was granted a golden tablet,
and made acting Yòu Fùyuánshuài,
leading 5,000 Wǔwèi Jūn soldiers to garrison north of Zhōngdū city.
Zhízhōng then conspired with his associates, staff official Wénxiùjú Zhícháng Wányán Chǒunú, Tíkòng Sùzhí Jiāngjūn Púchá Liùjīn, and Wǔwèi Jūn Qiánxiá Wūgǔlún Duólà, to plot a rebellion.
At this time,
the great army of Dà Yuán was nearby.
The emperor sent an official to the army to reprimand Zhízhōng for only indulging in hunting
and neglecting military affairs.
Zhízhōng, who was feeding a hawk,
angrily threw and killed it.
He then falsely claimed that Zhī Dàxīngfǔ Túdān Nánpíng and his son Xíngbù Shìláng Fùmǎ Dōuwèi Mòliè were plotting rebellion,
and proclaimed that he had an imperial edict to suppress them.
Nánpíng's relative by marriage, Fúhǎi,
had another contingent of troops stationed north of the city.
Zhízhōng sent someone to invite him with kind words.
Fúhǎi, unaware of the plot,
was seized upon his arrival.
On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month, before the fifth watch,
he divided his army into three divisions.
One entered through Zhāngyì Mén.
He personally led another division through Tōngxuán Mén.
Fearing that troops in the city would come out to resist,
Zhízhōng sent a horseman to gallop ahead to Dōnghuá Mén and shout loudly:
"The main army has reached the North Pass,
and battle has already been joined!"
Soon after, he sent a second horseman to do the same.
He sent Túdān Jīnshòu to summon Zhī Dàxīngfǔ Túdān Nánpíng.
Nánpíng, unaware,
was riding to Fùyì Fāng, west of Guǎngyáng Mén,
when he met Zhízhōng on horseback.
Zhízhōng stabbed him with a spear, knocking him off his horse.
Jīnshòu then hacked him to death.
He sent Wūgǔlún Duólà to summon Mòliè,
and killed him.
Fúbǎo Zhǐhòu Shànyáng,
and Hùwèi Shírén Zhǎng Wányán Shígǔnǎi, hearing of the rebellion,
urgently summoned 500 Dàhàn Jūn soldiers to respond to the crisis.
They fought Zhízhōng but were defeated,
and all died.
Zhízhōng reached Dōnghuá Mén.
He ordered the gatekeepers, Qīnjūn Bǎihù Dōng'ér and Wǔshíhù Púchá Liùjīn,
but they did not respond.
He promised them hereditary mēng'ān and third-rank official positions,
but they still did not respond.
He then called Húdū Diǎnjiǎn Túdān Wèihé.
Wèihé was actually Túdān Háogāo.
Wèihé lowered himself from the city wall to meet Zhízhōng.
Zhízhōng ordered firewood to be gathered and Dōnghuá Mén burned,
and ladders erected to scale the wall.
Hùwèi Xiéliè, Qǐ'ér, and Qīnjūn Chūnshān together broke the locks and opened the gate, letting Zhízhōng in.
Zhízhōng entered the palace,
replaced all the palace guards with his followers,
and proclaimed himself Jiānguó Dūyuánshuài.
He resided in Dàxīngfǔ,
and arrayed troops for his defense.
He urgently summoned Dū Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Sūn Chūnnián to fetch silver and silks to reward Jīnshòu, Duólà, other military officers and soldiers, and the common laborers of Dàxīngfǔ.
That night,
he summoned courtesans and his close associates for a banquet.
The next day,
he used troops to force the emperor to reside in the Wèi residence.
He lured Zuǒchéng Wányán Gāng to the army camp,
and immediately killed him.
Zhízhōng's intentions were unfathomable.
Chancellor Túdān Yì persuaded Zhízhōng to enthrone Xuānzōng.
Zhízhōng assented.
At this time,
Zhuāngxiàn Tàizǐ was in Zhōngdū.
Zhíchōng used the imperial crown prince's ceremonial guard to welcome Zhuāngxiàn to reside in the Dōnggōng.
He summoned the Fúbǎoláng Túshàn Fúshòu to retrieve the imperial seals,
and displayed them on the open steps of the Dàxīng Fǔ.
He illicitly used the imperial seals to issue decrees,
appointing Wányán Chǒunú as Dèzhōu Fángyùshǐ,
Wūgǔlún Duólá as Shùntiānjūn Jiédùshǐ,
Púchá Liùjīn as Huánghǎijūn Jiédùshǐ,
and Túshàn Jīnshòu as Yǒngdìngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Although they were appointed to external posts,
he kept them all by his side.
The remaining appointments and promotions still numbered in the dozens.
At the same time, there were two Púchá Liùjīn;
one of them guarded the Dōnghuá Mén and refused to join the rebellion.
He summoned the Lǐbù Lìngshǐ Zhāng Hǎolǐ, intending to cast a seal for a Jiānguó Yuánshuài.
Hǎolǐ said:
"Since ancient times, there has been no regent of a different surname."
So he stopped.
He dispatched Fèngyù Wányán Hūshīlái and two others,
along with ten guards including Púxiān Bāndǐ and Wányán Chǒunú,
to welcome Xuānzōng in Zhāngdé.
He ordered the eunuch Lǐ Sīzhōng to assassinate the Emperor at the Wèi Dǐ.
He withdrew all border armies to Zhōngdū and Píngzhōu, and garrisoned cavalry in Jìzhōu to strengthen himself,
leaving the border defenses entirely unguarded.
In the ninth month, on the jiǎchén day,
Xuānzōng ascended the throne.
He appointed Zhíchōng as Tàishī, Shàngshūlìng, Dū Yuánshuài, and Jiānxiū Guóshǐ,
enfeoffed him as Zé Wáng,
and granted him the hereditary title of Méng'ān for Zhōngdū Lù Hélǔhūtǔ.
He made his younger brother Tèmòyě the Tóngzhī Hénán Fǔ and Dūdiǎnjiǎn,
concurrently Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
His son Zhūfèn was appointed Púwáng Fù and Bīngbù Shìláng.
Dūdiǎnjiǎn Túshàn Wèihé became Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Wūgǔlún Duólá was remotely appointed Zhī Zhēndìng Fǔ Shì.
Túshàn Jīnshòu was remotely appointed Zhī Dōngpíng Fǔ Shì.
Púchá Liùjīn was remotely appointed Zhī Píngyáng Fǔ Shì.
Wányán Chǒunú was Tóngzhī Hézhōng Fǔ Shì,
and provisionally Sùzhí Jiāngjūn.
An imperial edict granted Wūgǔlún Yì's residence to Zhíchōng.
The Yíluán Jú provided his furnishings.
His wife, née Wáng, was granted a purple-knotted silver-belled carriage.
On the wùshēn day,
Zhíchōng attended court.
Xuānzōng granted him a seat,
and Zhíchōng took it without declining.
Not long after,
Zhíchōng memorialized, requesting that Wèi Shàowáng be demoted to a commoner.
He submitted the memorial again.
An imperial edict ordered all officials to discuss it in the imperial court.
Tàizǐ Shàofù Àotún Zhōngxiào and Shìdú Xuéshì Púchá Sīzhōng supported Zhíchōng's proposal.
The others looked at each other, not daring to speak.
Only Wénxué Tián Tíngfāng boldly said:
"The former emperor had no known failures of virtue;
his honorific title should not be removed according to rites."
Those who agreed with him included Lǐbù Zhāng Jìngfǔ, Jiànyì Zhāng Xìnfǔ, Hùbù Wǔ Wénbó, Páng Cáiqīng, Shímò Jìnqīng, and twenty-four others.
Xuānzōng said:
"It's like asking for directions.
A hundred people say go east,
ten people say go west.
Will the traveler truly go east or go west?
Can one determine right and wrong simply by the number of one hundred or ten?"
Then he said:
"I will consider it slowly."
After several days,
an edict demoted him to Dōnghǎi Jùnhóu.
The scouting cavalry of Dà Yuán reached Gāoqiáo.
The prime minister reported it.
Xuānzōng sent someone to ask Zhíchōng.
Zhíchōng said:
"The plan is already set."
Afterwards, he reproached the prime ministers, saying:
"Since I am Shàngshūlìng,
how can I submit a memorial without first discussing it with you?"
The prime ministers merely humbly apologized.
Tídiǎn Jìnshì Jú Qìngshānnú, Fùshǐ Wéibì, and Fèngyù Wéikāng requested Zhíchōng's removal.
Xuānzōng, mindful of his merit in helping him ascend,
reluctantly refused.
Yuánshuài Yòu Jiānjūn Shúhǔ Gāoqí had repeatedly failed in battle.
Zhíchōng warned him, saying:
"If today's sortie proves fruitless,
you will be dealt with according to military law."
Gāoqí went out to battle and was defeated again.
Believing he could not escape punishment,
and having heard rumors of a plot by Qìngshānnú and others,
in the tenth month, on the xīnhài day,
Gāoqí consequently led his cavalry into Zhōngdū,
and surrounded Zhíchōng's residence.
Zhíchōng heard of the uprising,
drew his bow, notched an arrow, and shot outwards.
Unable to prevail,
he climbed the back wall, intending to flee,
but his clothes snagged, he fell, and injured his thigh.
The soldiers then cut him down.
Gāoqí took Zhíchōng's head to the palace gate to await punishment.
Xuānzōng pardoned him,
and appointed him Zuǒ Fùyuánshuài.
Zhíchōng's partisans shouted in the streets:
"The cavalry has rebelled!
Those who kill them will be rewarded!"
The townspeople followed them,
and many cavalrymen died.
The whole army was agitated.
Xuānzōng dispatched attendants to pacify them,
and issued an edict for the authorities to generously bestow funeral gifts.
Only then did the populace gradually calm down.
The next day,
Tèmòyě was appointed Tàiníngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Wūgǔlún Duólá was formally appointed Zhī Jìnán Fǔ Shì.
Túshàn Jīnshòu was formally appointed Zhī Guīdé Fǔ Shì.
Púchá Liùjīn was formally appointed Zhī Píngyáng Fǔ Shì.
On the jiǎyín day,
Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū Zhāng Xíngxìn submitted a sealed memorial, saying:
"According to the Spring and Autumn Annals,
if a ruler is established improperly,
but has once participated in covenants and meetings with the feudal lords,
he is still listed among the feudal lords.
The Prince of Donghai had been on the throne for six years.
Who among his subjects would dare to interfere with him?
Húshāhǔ took control of the troops and entered the city,
personally committing regicide and rebellion.
At that time, only Shànyáng and Shígǔnǎi led their forces to aid,
even fighting to the death.
Considering their loyalty and heroism,
all those who held office and received stipends in the court should be ashamed.
Your Majesty has just begun to personally handle all affairs of state,
and the realm looks to your transforming influence.
You should commend and honor these two,
extending favor to their descendants,
to perhaps slightly comfort their steadfast souls
and stir the righteous spirit of the world.
During the Sòng dynasty, Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, and Xiè Huì assassinated Yíngyáng Wáng and established Wéndì.
Wéndì executed them,
but because of their sincerity in welcoming him from Jiānglíng,
he spared their wives and children.
Húshāhǔ was a great bandit of the state,
universally detested.
Although he is dead, his crimes have not been formally settled.
It is fitting to expose his misdeeds,
announce them within and without the court,
strip him of his name and titles,
and punish his family by association.
Only then will there be satisfaction.
If Your Majesty cannot bear to overlook his effort in helping you ascend,
then following the precedent of Yuánjiā's story
would still be sufficient to demonstrate punishment and warning."
Xuānzōng then issued an edict exposing Zhíchōng's misdeeds,
and stripped him of his official titles and ranks.
Shànyáng and Shígǔnǎi were posthumously honored,
and their sons were granted additional favors.
Qìngshānnú, Wéibì, and Wéikāng were all promoted and rewarded.
From this point, the Jìnshì Jú became influential.
The commentary states: Among the nine rulers of Jīn,
three were assassinated,
and ten were involved in rebellious plots.
In the assassination of Xīzōng,
only Dà Xìngguó was publicly condemned by Shìzōng for his crime and dismembered beside the Sī Líng.
Although Túshàn Zhēn was executed,
his crimes were not publicly exposed.
Later, due to his powerful relatives, he was posthumously granted official titles and enfeoffments.
The other six, including Yú Bǐngdé and Tángkuò Biàn,
were all executed for other crimes.
In the assassination of Hǎilíng,
the principal culprit was Wányán Yuányí,
who then brought an end to it.
As for the assassination of Wèi Shàowáng, it was Húshāhǔ
who did not die by the execution of the Sībài,
but at the hands of Gāoqí.
What the ancients called "bandits who assassinate their lord, whom anyone may punish,"
meant requesting the public authorities to punish them,
as Kǒngzǐ requested the punishment of Chén.
How could there be someone like Gāoqí who unilaterally kills and takes it as a merit?
The governance and laws of Jīn were in such disorder.
If the state wished not to perish,
how could it achieve that?
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 71: Rebellious Officials: Zhāng Jué (whose son only spoke), Yēlǜ Yúdǔ, Wōwò.
In ancient texts,
"pàn" (畔)
is interchangeable with
"pàn" (叛).
The meaning of 畔 (pàn) is a boundary.
The Zuǒshì says,
"Governance is like
a farmer having boundaries."
This is it.
The established distinctions between ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
are like the clear-cut boundaries between this territory and that.
To violate this and turn to that
is to rebel.
Good and evil are decided in a single step,
and disaster can reach the utmost bounds of the world.
Alas,
how fearsome!
This chapter is titled "Biographies of Rebellious Officials."
Zhāng Jué 張覺 (also written as 瑴)
was a native of Yìfēng 義豐, Píngzhōu 平州.
During the Liáo 遼 dynasty, he passed the *jìnshì* 進士 examination
and rose to the position of Vice Military Commissioner of the Liáo Xīngjūn 遼興軍.
When Tàizǔ 太祖 subjugated Yānjīng 燕京,
Shí Lì'ài 時立愛 surrendered Píngzhōu.
At that time, the Sòng 宋 people, based on the Maritime Alliance, demanded Yānjīng and Xījīng 西京 territories.
Tàizǔ gave Yānjīng, Zhuó 涿, Yì 易, Tán 檀, Shùn 順, Jǐng 景, and Jì 薊 to them.
Píngzhōu had been separated and formed its own military prefecture since it came under the Khitans,
so it was not included.
Instead, Píngzhōu was made the Nánjīng 南京 (Southern Capital),
and Jué was appointed its Resident Commissioner.
Later, upon hearing that Jué had other intentions,
the Emperor dispatched emissaries Liú Yánzōng 劉彥宗 and Xiébō 斜鉢 to admonish him.
The imperial edict stated:
"The commandery of Píngshān 平山 is now Nánjīng;
the Military Commissioner is now the Resident Commissioner.
Our grace is already abundant.
Some say that you harbor treacherous designs.
Why, during this important farming season, do you stir up agitation?
This is not a plan to abandon danger and seek security.
Convey my intentions to them."
Whenever Tàizǔ captured cities,
he often relocated their populations to populate the capital,
causing widespread popular unrest.
Therefore, Shí Lì'ài had mentioned this in his memorial of surrender.
When Yānjīng was given to Sòng, its people were relocated,
and only an empty city was given to them.
Those who were relocated passed through Píngzhōu,
which Jué exploited to instigate rebellion.
In the fifth month of Tiānfǔ 天輔 seven years (1123),
Zuǒ Qǐgōng 左企弓, Yú Zhòngwén 虞仲文, Cáo Yǒngyì 曹勇義, and Kāng Gōngbì 康公弼 were en route to Guǎngníng 廣寧.
As they passed through Píngzhōu,
Jué ordered men to kill them beneath a chestnut forest.
He then occupied Nánjīng, rebelled, and submitted to Sòng.
The Sòng people accepted him.
Tàizǔ issued an edict to the officials and common people of Nánjīng.
The edict stated:
"When I first stationed my imperial carriage in Yānjīng,
I commended you, officials and common people, for being the first to surrender and pledge allegiance.
Therefore, I elevated your prefectural seat to Nánjīng,
reduced corvée labor,
and lightened taxes.
My grace has been extended to the utmost.
Why then endure such suffering to commit rebellion?
Now I intend to advance troops to attack and seize it,
but it is currently the farming season.
I cannot bear to harm the multitude for the sake of one evil person.
Moreover, the entire Liáo kingdom has become mine.
What can an isolated city accomplish by defending itself?
What will you ultimately achieve?
Now, only the chief culprit will be punished;
all others will be pardoned."
Jué's army of 50,000 was encamped in the vicinity of Rùnzhōu 潤州,
intending to threaten the four prefectures of Qiān 遷, Lái 來, Rùn, and Xí 隰.
Dújìmǔ 闍母 advanced from Jǐnzhōu 錦州 to suppress him.
He had already defeated Jué's army
and intended to press the advantage to attack Nánjīng.
However, due to the summer rains, he could not advance,
so he retreated to encamp by the seashore.
Not long after,
Dújìmǔ again defeated Jué's army
and fought him once more at Tù'ěrshān 兔耳山.
Dújìmǔ suffered a great defeat,
and Jué reported his victory to Sòng.
Sòng established Píngzhōu as the Tàiníngjūn 泰寧軍,
appointed Jué as its Military Commissioner,
and conferred titles like *Huīyóu Gédàizhì* 徽猶閣待制 upon Zhāng Dūngù 張敦固 and others.
Tens of thousands of *liǎng* 兩 of silver and bolts of silk were bestowed as rewards for the army.
Zōngwàng 宗望's army arrived east of Nánjīng city.
Jué's forces were utterly defeated and fled under the cover of night,
then escaped to Sòng,
entering Yānjīng.
Zōngwàng reproached the Sòng Xuānfǔ Sī 宣撫司 for harboring a rebel
and demanded Zhāng Jué.
The Xuānfǔ Wáng Ānzhōng 王安中 hid him in the armor treasury
and falsely claimed:
"He is not here."
As Zōngwàng's demands grew more urgent,
Ānzhōng then beheaded a person resembling Jué and presented him as such.
The Jīn 金 people identified him, saying:
"This is not Jué."
Having no other option, Ānzhōng
brought Jué out
and enumerated his crimes.
Jué cursed the Sòng people without ceasing.
Thereupon, Jué was killed, and his head was packed in a box and given to the Jīn people.
The surrendered generals and the Victorious Army (Chángshèngjūn 常勝軍) in Yānjīng all wept.
Guō Yàoshī 郭藥師 said to himself:
"What if they come to demand Yàoshī?"
From then on,
the surrendered generals and soldiers all lost morale.
When the Jīn people later attacked Sòng,
they indeed used the sheltering of the Píngzhōu rebel as a justification.
Only Zhāng Jǐnyán 張僅言 spoke.
Jǐnyán's childhood name was Yuánnú 元奴.
When Zōngwàng attacked and captured Píngshān,
Jǐnyán was in swaddling clothes.
Liú Chéngxuan 劉承宣 of the village found him
and raised him in his home.
His neighbor, Lady Hán 韓, loved him dearly.
At several years old,
he accompanied Lady Hán and had the opportunity to meet Empress Zhēnyì 貞懿皇后,
who kept him in the princely residence.
As he grew older,
he attended Shìzōng 世宗 in his studies.
Consequently, Jǐnyán was entrusted with managing the household affairs,
supervising the retainers and servants.
Everyone in the residence held him in awe.
When Shìzōng was Resident Commissioner of Dōngjīng 東京,
Hǎilíng 海陵 launched military campaigns along the Jiāng-Huái 江淮 region.
Generals and soldiers often deserted and returned
to Dōngjīng,
wishing to acclaim Shìzōng as Emperor.
Jǐnyán urged his enthronement.
Upon Shìzōng's ascension,
he was appointed Vice Commissioner of the Imperial Treasury and
concurrently acting Director of the Palace Archives.
When Hǎilíng died in Yángzhōu 揚州,

Jǐnyán, along with Minister of Rites Wū Jūfrén 烏居仁, Left General of the Imperial Guard Āhǔdài 阿虎帶, and Palace Courier Liú Qióng 劉珫, took charge of the Six Palaces, various departments, and the imperial libraries and treasuries located in Nánjīng.
Upon his return, he was appointed to his original post of Controller of the Imperial Provision Bureau,
then promoted to Assistant Director of the Imperial Manufactories,
still in charge of the Imperial Treasury.
Jǐnyán was capable in financial planning,
and Shìzōng relied heavily on him.
All palace construction, treasury disbursements and receipts, and arrangements for imperial travels and temporary lodgings were entrusted to him.
Shìzōng once said:
"Everything that passes through Jǐnyán's hands
never fails to please me."
In the sixth year (1166),
he was appointed Manager of Palace Renovation Projects.
The laborers dug up white gold and hid it.
When the matter was discovered,
by law, they should have been executed.
Jǐnyán demanded the return of the treasure to the government
and pardoned their crime.
Soon after, he concurrently managed the Imperial Service Bureau.
He was promoted to Director of the Imperial Manufactories,
still controlling the Palace Archives and Imperial Service Bureau as before.
He supervised the construction of Tàinínggōng 太寧宮,
diverting a stream on the left side of the palace to irrigate fields,
yielding ten thousand *hú* 斛 of rice annually.
In the seventeenth year (1177),
he was again appointed Supervisor of the Imperial Treasury,
oversaw the imperial tomb of Empress Zhāodé 昭德,
and was promoted to Commissioner for Agricultural Encouragement,
retaining all his previous positions.
Although Jǐnyán was an old official,
constantly at the emperor's side,
Shìzōng never truly granted him significant power.
In the twenty-first year (1181),
the Department of State Affairs reported
that Lǐ Lún 黎倫, the Director of the Palace Gardens Bureau, had served for sixteen years
and requested his promotion.
The Emperor said:
"This is my household minister,
an upright man,
who is now old.
Similarly, Commissioner for Agricultural Encouragement Zhāng Jǐnyán is also my old official,
honest and quite capable.
However, he has never been allowed to interfere
in court deliberations or appointments both inside and outside the court.
I observe that throughout history, many rulers have been misled by slanderers and sycophants.
Though I am not as wise as the ancients,
I have never let the deceitful words of close attendants enter my ears."
The Grand Counselor said:
"Truly as Your Majesty has instructed,
this is a blessing for the nation."
Shìzōng wanted to appoint him as Military Commissioner of the Hénghǎijūn 橫海軍,
but could not bear to part with him from his side,
so he dropped the idea.
Jǐnyán eventually fell ill,
but still used a cane to attend to his duties.
When his illness became critical,
an imperial edict summoned imperial physicians for diagnosis and treatment.
Close attendants inquired about his condition continuously.
When he passed away,
the Emperor deeply lamented his loss.
He dispatched officials to offer sacrifices
and bestowed 500 *liǎng* of silver, ten bolts of fine silk, and 200 bolts of plain silk.
The coffin, burial clothes, silver mercury, burial articles, and burial ground were all provided by the government.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand General Who Upholds the State.
Yēlǜ Yúdǔ
was a scion of the Liáo imperial clan.
He was a close relative of the Liáo emperor.
His father and grandfather served Liáo.
All are recorded in the History of Liáo.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ raised his army,
the Liáo people came to resist.
Yúdǔ offered to serve,
and for his merits, he was successively promoted to Jīn Wúwèi Dàjiāngjūn,
and appointed Eastern Route Dūtǒng.
In the first year of Tiānfǔ (1117 CE),
he and Dūtǒng Yēlǜ Mǎgē camped their army by the Húnhé River.
Yín Shùgē and Xīyǐn resisted them,
but Yúdǔ and others dared not fight.
By the time Yín Shùgē and others arrived,
Mǎgē and Yúdǔ had already fled.
Yín Shùgē and Xīyǐn were punished for their delay,
and Tàizǔ penalized them both.
The captives, livestock, and wealth they had acquired were confiscated by the government.
In the second year of Tiānfǔ (1118 CE),
Zhāng Yìnggǔ and others from Lónghuàzhōu surrendered,
but Yúdǔ recaptured it.
Liáo appointed Tàbùyě as Jiédùshǐ.
Not long after,
Yìnggǔ and others expelled Tàbùyě and offered their allegiance again.
Tàizǔ inquired of the Liáo emperor in an official letter,
"Lónghuàzhōu has already surrendered and pledged allegiance;
why inquire about their guilt and kill their leader?"
The Liáo emperor claimed that major bandits had risen en masse,
and sent Yúdǔ to suppress them.
Tàizǔ had already taken Línhuángfǔ,
and bestowed an edict upon Yúdǔ, saying:
"You command troops on the eastern route,
and in all battles, you have never not been defeated.
Now I hear you are rallying the scattered and lost
to resist my army.
On the fifteenth day of this month, I captured Shàngjīng,
and I am now going to capture the Liáo emperor.
If you wish to organize your troops for a decisive battle,
you may specify a place and date to report back.
If you know you are no match,
you should lead your forces to surrender,
so as not to cause future regret."
When Tàizǔ returned to the capital,
Shémǔ and others arrived back at the Liáohé River.
While crossing,
Yúdǔ attacked.
Wánpín Bèidá, Wūtǎ and others guarded the rear,
fought valiantly and repelled him,
capturing five hundred armored horses.
In the fifth year of Tiānfǔ (1121 CE),
Yúdǔ sent an offer of submission to the Xiánzhōu Road Dūtǒng,
offering to surrender with his forces,
and requesting assistance and reception at Sānglíndù.
The Dūtǒng Department reported this.
An edict said:
"When Yúdǔ arrives,
he shall come with his officials;
the rest of his troops shall be settled in a convenient location."
Before long,
Yúdǔ sent the edicts he had received from the Liáo state, as well as weapons, armor, flags, and banners,
and surrendered with his officers Hán Fúnú, Ābā, Xiè Lǎo, Tàishīnú, Xiāo Qìng, Chǒuhéshang, Gāo Fóliú, Pútá, Xièjiānú, Wǔgē, and others.
Yúdǔ wrote a letter,
fully explaining his reasons for surrendering,
stating generally:
"The Liáo emperor is addicted and lost in hunting and pleasure,
neglecting governance,
favoring sycophants,
alienating loyal and upright men,
inflicting harsh punishments and being stingy with rewards.
His government is burdensome, taxes are heavy,
and the people cannot make a living."
He also stated:
"The Shūmìshǐ Délǐdǐ has no talent or ability,
but only flatters to gain favor.
His son, Mógē, is put in charge of military affairs."
He also stated:
"Prince Jìn, the eldest son of Consort Wén, has always been the hope of the people,
and should be the heir apparent.
Délǐdǐ, because the sons of the primary consort were his own relatives,
made Prince Jìn adopted by Consort Wén."
He further stated:
"Prince Jìn and Fùmǎ Yǐxìn conspired to restore his Shūmìshǐ position,
and came to tell Yúdǔ to jointly decide on a grand plan,
but their plot failed."
He also stated:
"I have some experience in military matters,
and offered strategies to the Liáo emperor,
but Délǐdǐ concealed them,
and the Liáo emperor also failed to discern them."
He also said:
"The territory of Great Jīn is expanding daily,
and Yúdǔ clearly knows the mandate of heaven.
Thus, since last spring, he and Yēlǜ Shènsī and others decided
to surrender this summer.
Recently, hearing that Délǐdǐ and Gāo Shíniē and others were about to attack,
in the urgency of the moment, I could not rally forces from afar.
I only led three thousand households from nearby tribes, five thousand carts, and tens of thousands of livestock.
The Liáo Northern Army Dūtǒng pursued me with troops,
so I abandoned my baggage train,
and fought my way here.
As for the names of all officials and their positions, and the numbers of households and livestock,
I have sent Hán Fúnú to record them in detail and report."
Thereupon, he and his officers came to audience.
The Emperor comforted him,
granted him a seat,
placing him equal to the prime ministers.
A banquet was given, and they left when they were fully drunk.
The Emperor ordered Yúdǔ to command his forces with his old official title,
and instructed him, saying:
"If you can perform meritorious service for the state,
you shall be specially rewarded and employed."
From the time Yúdǔ surrendered,
the realities of the Liáo people became better known.
Yúdǔ repeatedly requested concubines and his son while in the army.
Tàizǔ was suspicious,
and issued an edict to the Xiánzhōu Road Dūtǒng Department, saying:
"Yúdǔ's family members,
guard them well."
He further decreed:
"When Yúdǔ surrendered,
many of his people were forcibly brought along.
Fearing they might cause trouble at the border,
they should be relocated to the interior."
When Dūtǒng Gǎo captured Zhōngjīng,
Yúdǔ served as a local guide,
and along with Xīyǐn and others, he pacified and won over the Xī tribes.
When Fèngshèngzhōu surrendered,
its officials all fled.
Yúdǔ recommended the former Jiānjiǔ Lǐ Shīkuí as Jiédùshǐ,
the Jìnshì Shěn Zhāng as Fùshǐ,
and the local official Péi Zé as Guānchá Pànguān.
Shěn Zhāng rallied over three thousand residents to return to their occupations,
and was promoted to Tàicháng Shàocīng.
After a long time,
Yēlǜ Mázhě accused Yúdǔ, Wú Shí, and Duólà of forming a faction and plotting rebellion,
suggesting that they should be arrested before they could act.
The Emperor summoned Yúdǔ and others and calmly told them:
"Now I hear you are plotting rebellion.
Is it true?
Each of you, hide nothing.
If you truly wish to leave,
all your saddles, horses, armor, weapons, and other equipment
shall be given to you.
I will not break my word.
If you are captured again,
do not beg for mercy.
If you wish to stay and serve me,
then harbor no dissenting thoughts,
and I will not doubt you."
Yúdǔ and the others trembled and could not reply.
Thereupon, Duólà was flogged seventy times,
while the others were not questioned.
In the third year of Tiānhuì (1125 CE),
a large-scale expedition was launched against Sòng.
Yúdǔ was Yuánshuài Yòudūjiān.
Forty thousand Sòng troops came to relieve Tàiyuán.
Yúdǔ and Wūlǐhǎi intercepted them north of the Fénhé River,
capturing their commanders Hǎo Zhònglián and Zhāng Guānsuǒ,
and the Tǒngzhì Mǎ Zhōng,
killing over ten thousand men.
When Zōnghán attacked Sòng,
Yúdǔ remained in Xījīng.
In the tenth year of Tiānhuì (1132 CE),
Yúdǔ plotted rebellion.
Yēlǜ Núgē, the Yúnnèi Jiédùshǐ, and others reported him.
Yúdǔ fled.
His associate, the Yānjīng Tǒngjūn Xiāo Gāoliù, was executed,
and the Wèizhōu Jiédùshǐ Xiāo Tèmóu committed suicide.
Frontier troops captured Yúdǔ and his sons,
beheading them and presenting their heads.
Yēlǜ Núgē was promoted to Shǒu Tàibǎo concurrent with Shìzhōng.
Zhào Gōngjiàn, Liú Rúxìn, Liú Jūnfǔ, and others were all granted remote Jiédùshǐ titles as rewards.
Yílào Wōwò
was from the Qìdān tribe of the Northwest Route.
He first joined Sābā in rebellion,
receiving his false appointments.
Later, he killed Sābā,
and thus acquired his followers.
Sābā,
initially served as an interpreter for the Commander’s Office (Zhāotǎo Sī).
In Zhènglóng Wǔnián (1160),
Hǎilíng (Wányán Liàng) levied troops from various circuits to attack the Sòng,
and sent Pái Yìn Zàohé and Yáng Gé to conscript all Qìdān men from the Northwest Circuit.
The Qìdān people said:
"The Northwest Circuit borders neighboring countries,
and we have fought wars for generations,
becoming sworn enemies.
If all our able-bodied men are conscripted into the army,
and they (the enemies) come with troops,
then our old and weak will surely all be captured and enslaved.
We hope the envoy will report this to the court."
Zàohé feared punishment and dared not speak,
while Yáng Gé deeply worried about being punished if something happened in the northwest later,
and thus died of distress.
Zàohé, together with Pái Yìn Yēlǜ Nà and the Shàngshū Shěng clerk Mòdá Nièhé, jointly supervised the raising of troops in the Northwest Circuit.
When the Qìdān heard that all their able-bodied men were to be conscripted,
Sābā and BóTèbǔ, with their followers, killed the Commander (Zhāotǎo Shǐ) Wányán Wòcè and Zàohé,
and seized Yēlǜ Nà and Mòdá Nièhé.
They took three thousand sets of armor stored in the Commander’s Office,
and revolted.
They debated establishing a descendant of Yùwáng Yánxǐ,
and the multitude acclaimed the Inspector (Dūjiān) Lǎohéshang as Commander (Zhāotǎo Shǐ).
The four groups of herdsmen in Shānhòu and all the herdsmen in Shānqián responded to him.
The Dīwò herdsmen’s commissioner (Qúnmù Shǐ) Túdān Sàilǐ and the Yēlǔwǎ herdsmen’s commissioner Hèshòu and others were all killed;
the details are in the biography of Hèshòu.
The people of the Wǔyuàn Office, Lǎohéshang Nàyě, also killed the Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) Shújiǎ Wùzhě in response to Sābā.
Eight Měng'ān from Huìníng were herding horses in Shānhòu;
when they reached Dīmóulǔ,
the rebels seized all their horses.
The Qiānhù of Pìshāhé, Shígē and others, along with the former Commander (Zhāotǎo Shǐ) Wányán Māpō, killed the Wūgǔdíliè Commander (Zhāotǎo Shǐ) Wūlíndá Púlúhǔ,
and led their subordinates towards the Northwest Circuit.
The Shìlǔ Department Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) Āsīliè pursued and defeated them;
Shígē escaped with a few horsemen,
and joined Sābā.
Kuòlǐ, a Mókè from Xiánpíng Fǔ,
fled back from Shānhòu with his subordinates.
The Xiánpíng Deputy Prefect (Shàoyǐn) Wányán Yúlǐyě wanted to arrest Kuòlǐ’s family,
so Kuòlǐ and his associates enticed wealthy families' slaves,
gathering two thousand men in a few days,
and consequently attacked and captured Hánzhōu and Liǔhé Xiàn,
then advanced towards Xiánpíng.
Yúlǐyě dispatched troops to intercept them,
but his army was defeated,
and the rebels then occupied Xiánpíng.
Thereupon, they repaired weapons and armor,
and took out treasures from the official storehouses to recruit soldiers,
thus increasing the rebel's power.
The acting Měng'ān of Cáojiā Shān, Chuòzhì,
gathered over a thousand soldiers,
and blocked the Gānyè Hé,
preventing the rebels from moving east.
Chuòzhì's army was defeated,
and Kuòlǐ then attacked Jìzhōu.
At that time, the Palace Duty General (Sùzhí Jiāngjūn) Bóshùlǔ Wúkuòlà was conscripting troops in Sùpín Lù;
he encountered Kuòlǐ in Xìnzhōu,
and with two thousand soldiers from Měng'ān Wūyán Chálà,
defeated Kuòlǐ.
Kuòlǐ gathered his remaining forces and headed towards Dōngjīng.
At this time, Shìzōng was the Administrator of Dōngjīng (Dōngjīng Liúshǒu),
and he resisted with four hundred soldiers.
When the rebels reached Cháng’ān Xiàn,
they heard the sound of drums beating in the air like thousands of drummers,
and then saw banners covering the fields.
Rumors spread that the Administrator (Liúshǒu) had arrived with one hundred thousand troops,
so they immediately retreated,
and also joined Sābā with their forces.
Hǎilíng sent the Privy Council Commissioner (Shūmì Shǐ) Púsàn Hūtǔ and the Xījīng Administrator (Xījīng Liúshǒu) Xiāo Huáizhōng with ten thousand troops,
along with the Right Guard General (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn) Xiāo Tūtúlà, to suppress them.
Tūtúlà confronted them for several days,
engaging in repeated battles without success,
and his provisions were insufficient,
so Tūtúlà retreated to Línhuáng.
Although Tūtúlà failed to defeat the enemy,
Sābā, estimating that large armies would surely arrive one after another,
and that his position would be untenable,
planned to defect to the Dàshí.
Thus, he led his forces west along the Lóngjū Hé.
When Púsàn Hūtǔ and Xiāo Huáizhōng's forces arrived,
they joined Tūtúlà's army and pursued them to the river,
but failed to catch them and returned.
Hūtǔ, Huáizhōng, and Tūtúlà were all executed for delaying and not immediately pursuing the rebels.
The Běijīng Administrator (Běijīng Liúshǒu) Xiāo Zé, unable to control his subordinates,
killed surrendered people and took their women,
and was also executed.
Thereupon,
Bái Yàngōng was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Army (Běimiàn Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng),
Hégélì Zhìníng was his deputy,
Wányán Gòuyīng was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Northwest Army (Xīběimiàn Bīngmǎ Dūtǒng),
and the Northwest Circuit Commander (Xīběi Lù Zhāotǎo Shǐ) Tángkuò Bóyīgǔdì was his deputy,
to suppress Sābā and others.
After Sābā had gone west,
those who previously resided in Shānqián all did not wish to go with him.
The self-proclaimed Military Governor of the Six Offices (Liùyuàn Jiédù Shǐ) Yílài Wōwò and the military officer Chénjiā killed Sābā,
and captured Lǎohéshang, BóTèbǔ, and others.
At this point,
Wōwò first declared himself Grand Marshal (Dū Yuánshuài),
with Chénjiā as Inspector (Dūjiān),
and led his forces back east,
reaching Xīnlúo Zhài southeast of Línhuáng Fǔ.
Shìzōng sent Yílài Zhābā, former Army Supervisor (Yājūn) Mókè Bōwò, former Pái Yìn Máhài, and Lìshè Jūn Judicial Officer (Jiédù Pànguān) Mǎnǎo, etc., to recruit them.
Zhābā and others met Wōwò,
and conveyed the emperor's wishes to him.
Wōwò had already agreed to surrender,
but then again said to Zhābā:
"If we surrender,
can you guarantee that we will be safe?"
Zhābā replied:
"I am only responsible for recruiting surrenders;
how can I guarantee anything else?"
Zhābā saw that Wōwò's forces were strong,
with tents covering the fields,
and felt that he might achieve something,
so he persuaded him, saying:
"When I first came,
it was because I thought you were incapable of achieving anything.
Now I see your military strength is so formidable.
Do you wish to be driven away like a flock of sheep,
or do you wish to await a propitious time?"
If you truly have great ambitions,
I will not return either."
A rebel general, Zhúwò, from the former BóTèbǔ tribe,
said:
"In the past, Chancellor Gǔshén,
a wise and capable man,
once said that one day, trouble would arise among the northwestern tribes.
Today, this saying is precisely fulfilled;
I fear we should not surrender."
Thereupon,
Wōwò then decided not to surrender.
Zhābā also remained among the rebels,
only Máhài and Bōwò returned.
Wōwò then led his army to attack Línhuáng Fǔ.
The Administrator (Zǒngguǎn) Yíshì Mǎn sallied out to fight,
but his troops were few and he was captured.
The rebels then besieged Línhuáng,
with a force of fifty thousand.
On the Jǐhài day of the twelfth month of Zhènglóng Liùnián (1161),
Wōwò then declared himself emperor,
and changed the era name to Tiānzhèng.
At this time,
the Northern Commander (Běimiàn Dūtǒng) Bái Yànjìng and Deputy Commander (Fùtǒng) Hégélì Zhìníng were in Běijīng.
Hearing that Shìzōng had ascended the throne,
they returned with their troops.
Shìzōng sent the Marshal Left Inspector (Yuánshuài Zuǒ Dūjiān) Wúzāhū and the Co-Administrator of Běijīng (Tóngzhī Běijīng Liúshǒu Shì) Wányán Gǔzhī to relieve Línhuáng,
marching day and night.
By the time they reached Línhuáng,
the rebels had already lifted the siege and gone to attack Tàizhōu.
Wúzāhū caught up with them at Wāliè.
The two armies had already arrayed for battle,
when the Army Supervisor Měng'ān Qìdān Hūlàshú, with his subordinate troops, sided with the rebels,
and Wúzāhū's army was consequently defeated.
The Tàizhōu Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) Wūlǐyǎ led over a thousand cavalry and encountered Wōwò.
Wūlǐyǎ's army was again defeated,
and he barely escaped with a few horsemen.
The rebel's power grew even stronger,
and the city was terrified,
no one daring to sally out to fight.
When the rebels scaled the city walls from all four sides,
the Army Supervisor Měng'ān Wūgǔsūn Ālǐbǔ led a few soldiers,
each holding a saber, personally taking the lead to patrol the walls and fiercely fight the rebels,
cutting down many.
The rebels then retreated,
and the city was saved.
The Tàizhōu clerk (Sīlì) Yánzhǎn Púchá reported the victory,
and was appointed Zhōngyì Xiàowèi,
and awarded fifty liǎng of silver and ten bolts of brocade.
In the first month of the second year (1162),
the Right Deputy Marshal (Yòu Fù Yuánshuài) Wányán Móuyǎn led all armies to campaign against Wōwò in the north.
On the Rénxū day of the second month, an imperial edict stated:
"All individuals who can escape from the Qìdān rebels and return,
regardless of whether they were originally leaders or followers, or were coerced,
their crimes, whether they are slaves or commoners, light or heavy, will all be pardoned and released.
Those who held official positions or organized people to return will still be granted official positions and rewards,
and be assigned duties according to their original rank and talent.
Their accompanying people will be settled according to their wishes,
and those with talent will also be recruited.
All officials, young masters, herdsmen, ordinary people's servants, and palace registry personnel (gōngjí jiānrén),
both inside and outside the court, will all be emancipated as commoners,
and also settled according to their wishes,
and exempted from three years of corvée labor.
If anyone can capture or kill a leader and return,
they will be rewarded according to the above regulations,
and their merits will be assessed for promotion and reward.
If Wōwò is captured,
a Měng'ān will be promoted by three ranks and appointed Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ),
a Mókè will be promoted by four ranks and appointed Defense Commissioner (Fángyù Shǐ),
and a commoner will be promoted by five ranks and appointed Prefect (Cǐshǐ)."
The edict also stated:
"To the Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū Shěng):
If a Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) or Defense Commissioner (Fángyù Shǐ) captures Wōwò, they will be granted a hereditary Měng'ān;
if a Prefect (Cǐshǐ) captures him, they will be granted a hereditary Mókè;
household slaves and palace registry personnel will receive the same as commoners."
Another edict instructed the Chancellors
to widely inform the generals and soldiers that
whoever could capture or kill Wōwò would be promoted to Tèjìn and appointed True Administrator (Zhēn Zǒngguǎn).
Thereupon,
Kuòlǐ was about to invade Hánzhōu,
but hearing that the Grand Marshal's army had arrived,
he fled without fighting,
intending to move towards Yìzhōu and Yízhōu.
Móuyǎn was stationed in Qìngyún County of Yìzhōu,
and also stationed in Wǔpíng County of Chuānzhōu.
He then submitted a memorial requesting that escorts be dispatched for grain transportation,
and that excellent weapons and armor be selected and provided to the troops.
An imperial edict ordered that soldiers who had fled and returned from the southern campaign be sent to garrison the area;
if insufficient,
they should conscript from wealthy families,
and conscript infantry from nearby areas,
providing them with weapons to escort grain transportation.
An imperial edict ordered Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Yílā Yuányí to go to Tàizhōu to plan border affairs.
Former Ānyuǎn Dàjiāngjūn Wòlǐniǎo, Méng'ān Qījīn, commoner Ālǐgé, Mógē, and others came to surrender from Wōwò's ranks.
Wòlǐniǎo and Qījīn were promoted to Zhāowǔ Dàjiāngjūn;
Ālǐgé to Wǔyì Jiāngjūn;
Mógē to Zhōngyǒng Xiàowèi.
Wōwò then went from Tàizhōu to attack Jìzhōu,
intending to intercept grain transports.
Grand Marshal Wányán Móuyǎn, together with Right Military Supervisor Wányán Fúshòu and Left Military Superintendent Wúzhāhū, combined their forces,
totaling thirteen thousand armored soldiers.
The Hélǎn Lù Zǒngguǎn Túdān Kèníng, Guǎngníng Yǐn Púsàn Húntǎn, Tóngzhī Guǎngníng Yǐn Wányán Yányǎ, and Zhàozhōu Fángyùshǐ Tángkuò Wūyě formed the left wing.
The Línhǎi JiéduShǐ Gēshíliè Zhìníng, Hésùguǎn JiéduShǐ Shéntǔmǎn, Tóngzhī Běijīng Liúshǒu Wányán Gǔzhī, and Zīzhōu Cìshǐ Nímánggǔ Chāowù formed the right wing.
Upon reaching Shùhǔyá,
they completely abandoned their baggage train,
and the soldiers carried several days' rations.
They launched a surprise attack with light cavalry.
Cíwǎn Qúnmù Rén Qìdān Cízhe,
along with his younger brothers Bódié and Ruólà,
all abandoned their homes and came to surrender from the rebels.
Cízhe said to Móuyǎn:
"The rebels' horses are fat and strong,
while the official army's horses are tired and weak.
It is eighty *lǐ* to the rebels from here;
by the time we encounter the rebels, our horses will already be exhausted.
The rebels' baggage train is not far from here;
if we attack it,
the rebels will surely rescue their stronghold.
When the rebels arrive, their horses will surely be tired,
while our horses will have had some rest.
This is what is called attacking what they are sure to defend,
and awaiting the tired with the rested."
Móuyǎn followed his advice and
set off urgently at night.
They encountered a strong wind, and the road was dark and indistinguishable.
At dawn, after marching about thirty *lǐ*,
they were close to the rebels' baggage train.
They arrayed their troops and rested briefly.
Wōwò, who was heading towards Jìzhōu,
learned that the main army was seizing his baggage train,
so he returned to rescue it,
and encountered them at Chángluò.
After forming their lines,
Móuyǎn set up an additional ambush on the side of the left wing.
Over four hundred rebel cavalry suddenly appeared between the left wing's ambushers.
Túdān Kèníng shot and repelled them.
On that day,
the other divisions of generals confronting the rebels
had not yet decided victory or defeat,
and stood about five *lǐ* apart.
The left wing's Wànhù Xiāngbié fought the rebels.
The rebel formation wavered,
and Xiāng waved his army to press on,
breaking through to their rear.
They were all out of reach of the main army.
Xiāng, with twenty skilled archers,
led his troops to attack from the rebels' rear.
The rebels could not resist.
Taking advantage of the situation, he waved his army to strike one flank,
and the rebels then retreated.
Xiāng then rejoined the main army,
and all the other divisional generals arrived.
They arrayed their forces and fought fiercely.
Suddenly, the wind reversed, blowing sand and stones.
The rebel formation was in disarray,
and the official army charged and attacked,
utterly defeating them.
They pursued the fleeing rebels for over ten *lǐ*,
slaughtering and capturing many.
An imperial edict made Cízhe Wǔyì Jiāngjūn,
Bódié Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi,
and Ruólà Zhōngyì Xiàowèi.
Cízhe was appointed Tóngzhī Jiànzhōu Shì,
but died before taking office.
Bódié went to retrieve his family from among the rebels
and was subsequently harmed.
The emperor pitied him,
and later appointed Ruólà as Rǔzhōu Dōuxúnjiǎn Shǐ.
Wōwò led his forces west,
and Móuyǎn pursued them to the Ménglì Hé.
The rebels had already crossed,
destroying the crossing point.
Gēshíliè Zhìníng's army arrived first
but could not cross.
They then created a feint across the river,
while ordering Jiágǔ Qīngchén and Túdān Hǎiluó, two Wànhù, to cross the river downstream.
The tributary's banks were steep cliffs and muddy,
so they ordered the soldiers to bundle willows to fill the stream and cross.
After pursuing for several *lǐ*,
they reached a flat area.
Just as they were eating,
the rebel forces suddenly arrived.
Zhìníng's army quickly formed their lines.
The rebels charged down from the southern ridge,
impacting the formation three times.
Zhìníng fought bravely,
an arrow striking his left arm,
but he fought on as if nothing had happened.
When the main army arrived,
the left wing cavalry engaged the rebels first.
The rebels, holding the windward position, set fire
and attacked the official army amidst the smoke.
The official army infantry also arrived,
joining forces and fighting together.
After more than ten engagements,
the soldiers, suffering from the wind and smoke, stood motionless as if dazed.
Just then, heaven sent down rain,
the wind stopped,
and the official army fiercely attacked,
greatly defeating them.
Túdān Kèníng pursued the fleeing rebels for fifteen *lǐ*.
The rebels were blocked by a stream ahead and could not cross quickly,
suffering many casualties.
After the rebels crossed,
the official army also crossed
and rested briefly.
The rebels turned back to attack.
Kèníng, seeing that the main army was not yet complete,
ordered his soldiers to dismount and shoot the rebels.
The rebels retreated south.
Kèníng was also about to retreat north.
Before the soldiers could remount,
the rebels charged again.
The official army retreated slightly
and recrossed to the north side of the stream.
When the main army arrived,
the rebels then withdrew.
In the fourth month,
an imperial edict was issued to the Marshal's office, saying:
"Regarding the Qìdān rebels,
those who surrender before fighting the main army
are not to be killed or injured,
and should be treated with leniency.
After their defeat and flight,
for those who are enticed to surrender,
excluding slaves who are to remain as captives,
their relatives are to be reunited,
and ransom will be paid by the government for them."
After Wōwò's defeat,
Móuyǎn did not pursue him further,
but garrisoned his troops at Báiluò.
Wōwò attacked Yìzhōu but could not capture it,
so he ravaged Chuānzhōu
and was about to flee to Shānxī,
but Běijīng also did not intercept him.
Thereupon,
two thousand elite cavalry and three thousand Hélǎn Lù troops garrisoned in the capital were dispatched,
totaling twenty thousand.
Six thousand troops from Huìníng and Jìzhōu also totaled twenty thousand.
Grand Marshal Left Military Superintendent Gāo Zhōngjiàn took command of all forces.
Wòzhōu Cìshǐ Wūgǔlùn Púchá was appointed Hélǎn Lù Yājūn Wànhù,
Pīzhōu Cìshǐ Wūlíndá Lāsà was appointed Jìzhōu Yājūn Wànhù,
Right Xiāoqí Fùdōuzhīhuǐshǐ Wūyán Chálà was appointed Xiāoqí Wànhù,
Qízhōu Cìshǐ Zōngníng was appointed Huìníng Lù Yājūn Wànhù,
Right Xuānhuīshǐ Zōnghēng was appointed Běijīng Lù Dōutǒng,
and Lìbù Lángzhōng Wányán Dájí was appointed Fùtǒng.
They were to join the Grand Marshal's office to suppress the rebels.
An imperial edict sent Púchá Púlúhún, Assistant Envoy of the Shàngjú, to Yìzhōu to admonish the generals.
The Emperor said:
"I entrusted you all with suppressing the rebels,
but I heard that instead of engaging the rebels promptly,
you garrisoned your troops idly and slowly,
which has lasted for several months.
Though you once pursued them,
you did not pass through areas with water and grass,
resulting in the horses becoming exhausted and unable to travel a hundred *lǐ* before returning.
Although the rebels were later defeated,
you allowed your various armies to loot and plunder,
only pursuing them north to the Mèngyēhé River several days later.
You also did not press your advantage,
but immediately retreated.
The rebels then entered the nearby territories,
and Běijīng and Yìzhōu consequently suffered military incursions.
I wished to severely punish you all,
but as you are currently entrusted with military affairs,
I shall await future merits.
You must exert yourselves with one accord,
and not be negligent and lax as before."
The Emperor said to Púlúhún:
"If you hear that rebels are nearby,
you must immediately supervise their suppression.
Record and report those who obey orders and fight bravely,
and I will determine their promotions and rewards.
Do not curry favor with superiors,
nor suppress the meritorious or indiscriminately assign credit to the undeserving.
Kindly restrain your soldiers,
and do not permit looting."
Héshíliè Zhìníng was made Yuánshuài Yòu Jiānjūn.
Yòu Fù Yuánshuài Wányán Móuyǎn and Yuánshuài Yòu Jiānjūn Wányán Fúshòu were recalled to the capital.
[一四]Xiánpínglù Zǒngguǎn Wányán Wùdài was reinstated to his former position.
Móuyǎn's son, Xiégē, behaved violently and arrogantly in the army,
so an imperial edict ordered him to be escorted back to his home jurisdiction.
Wōwò sent a trusted associate to entice the Jiédùshǐ Yílǐjīn Kūyù.
Kūyù seized the envoy and sent him to the authorities.
Kūyù fought continuously against Wōwò with distinction,
and was promoted to Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and awarded five hundred *liǎng* of silver and two sets of clothing.
Fifteen thousand bows and one and a half million arrows were transported from Zhōngdū to Yìzhōu.
Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Yílài Yuányí and Níngchāngjūn Jiédùshǐ Zōng came for an audience.
An imperial edict ordered them to return to the army from the middle of their journey,
and instructed Yuányí and Móuyǎn to focus on managing border affairs.
As the army had long achieved no success,
Shàngshū Yòu Chéng Púsàn Zhōngyì expressed his willingness to exert himself to the death to eliminate the border troubles.
Shìzōng praised him.
In the sixth month,
Zhōngyì was appointed Píngzhāng Zhèngshì concurrently with Yòu Fù Yuánshuài.
Zōng was made Bīngbù Shàngshū.
Each was awarded bows, arrows, and a saddled and bridled horse.
One hundred thousand *liǎng* of gold and silver were taken from the imperial treasury to support the military expenditure.
An imperial edict stated:
"For offenses committed by officers and soldiers in the army,
except for those involving high-ranking officials which must be reported,
all others shall be judged and punished according to military law,
and those who perform meritorious deeds shall be promoted and rewarded according to regulations."
Zōngyǐn, the Yǐn of Dàmíng, was appointed Hénánlù Tǒngjūnshǐ.
Púchá Shìjié, the Hénánlù Tǒngjūn Dūjiān, was appointed Xīběilù Fù Tǒng.
He was awarded bows, arrows, a saber, and a horse,
and was to accompany Zhōngyì on the campaign.
An imperial edict addressed to the officers and soldiers of the various armies stated:
"The army has been stationed on the frontier for a long time,
wasting resources without achieving success,
and the common people are unable to rest.
Now, I appoint Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Púsàn Zhōngyì concurrently as Yòu Fù Yuánshuài,
to work together with one heart to achieve pacification.
Yòu Fù Yuánshuài Móuyǎn has been dismissed to serve as Tóng Pàn Dàzōngzhèngshì."
An imperial edict ordered Jūyōngguān and Gǔběikǒu to inspect for Khitan spies,
and those captured would receive official ranks and rewards.
Wànhù Wēnhǎn Ālúdài garrisoned four thousand soldiers at Gǔběikǒu.
Jìzhōu and Shíménguān and other places were each guarded by five hundred men.
In the last years of Hǎilíng,
Ālúdài was a Měng'ān,
and Yílài Nuó was a Páiyìn Zhīhòu.
They were captured while raising Khitan tribal troops,
but now they came forward to surrender.
Shìzōng appointed Ālúdài as Jìzhōu Yājūn Wànhù,
and Yílài Nuó as Tóngzhī Luánzhōushì.
Xīnánlù Zhāotǎoshǐ Wányán Sījìng was made Dūtǒng.
He was awarded one gold plaque and two silver plaques.
Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ Tángkuò Bóyǐdǐ was his deputy.
They led five thousand soldiers to join the old garrison at Yànzǐchéng,
[一五]to observe the strategic terrain, and if necessary, to station troops at Gǒuluò,
to send out scouts far and wide,
and to engage the rebels immediately upon their arrival,
without regard for day or night.
An imperial edict to Sījìng stated:
"When the Khitan rebels are defeated, they will certainly flee to the region beyond the mountains.
You should select three thousand new horses,
and provide them with fodder to prepare for pursuit."
Púsàn Zhōngyì arrived at the army.
At this time,
Wōwò fled west to Huādào,
with eighty thousand troops remaining.
Zhōngyì and Gāo Zhōngjiàn's armies encountered the rebels.
Wànhù Zhālà and Púchá formed the left wing,
commanded by Zōng Hēng;
Zōng Níng and Lāsà formed the right wing,
commanded by Zōng;
Shìjié was also in the left wing.
They formed a battle line across the river from the rebels.
The rebels crossed the river,
and with over forty thousand troops, first attacked the left wing.
Zhālà, with six hundred cavalry, bravely counterattacked and defeated them.
Again, with forty thousand troops, they fought the left wing.
[一六]Zōng Hēng and Shìjié's seven *móukè*'s inadequate planning
led to the line breaking and defeat by the rebels.
Shìjié bravely fled into Zhālà's army.
The rebels surrounded Zhālà's army.
Zhālà fought valiantly.
Zōng came to their rescue with the right wing,
and the rebels then retreated.
An imperial edict stated:
"Since the Khitans rebelled,
for those who were misled by the rebels,
no matter how they joined the rebels,
as long as they can return to their former lives,
their original crimes will be pardoned.
If they can lead their followers to surrender,
or kill and capture their leaders and surrender,
or seize and deliver the people incited by the rebels to revolt,
they will all be given appropriate official ranks and titles.
I recall that during Zhènglóng's southern campaign,
the Měng'ān who were killed were recalled and executed,
but I have already ordered their sons and grandsons to inherit their positions.
You all should not be deterred by past events,
and thus hesitate.
Since the rebel army is now dispersed,
generals and soldiers have been ordered to block their escape routes in various places beyond the mountains.
Where will you go if you still refuse to surrender?
If you still waver,
you will all be utterly destroyed,
and it will be too late for regret."
Wōwò fled west from Huādào.
Púsàn Zhōngyì and Héshíliè Zhìníng pursued him with a large army and caught up at Xiànquán west of Niǎolǐng.
[一七]The next day,
three thousand rebel cavalry crossed the water to the east.
The main army first occupied the south ridge.
The left wing formed a line from the ridge,
extending northward,
followed by the infantry.
The right wing followed the infantry, extending northward and then eastward,
forming a crescent moon formation,
with the infantry in the center,
and cavalry at both ends,
so that the rebels could not see their front or rear.
That day,
there was a thick, dark fog.
After the formation was complete, the fog cleared.
A short while later, the sky was clear.
Seeing the left wing occupying the south ridge, the rebels dared not attack it.
They attacked the right wing.
Wūyán Zhālà fought valiantly,
and the rebels somewhat retreated.
Zhìníng, along with Jiágǔ Qīngchén, Wūlíndá Lāsà, and Duólà, fought together.
The rebels were greatly defeated.
They tried to cross the water to escape,
but the muddy ground prevented them from crossing quickly.
The main army pursued them northward.
Countless people and horses trampled each other to death.
The number was immeasurable.
Xiànquán was leveled.
The remaining rebels fled over the corpses,
or scattered and hid in the forests and thickets.
The main army pursued and attacked them.
Tens of thousands were captured and beheaded.
Wōwò's younger brother, the false Dàwáng of the Liùyuàn Division, Niǎo, was captured alive.
Wōwò escaped with only a few cavalry.
Chāowù and Qīngchén pursued him for over forty *lǐ* but did not catch him,
beheading over a thousand and capturing many chariots and tents.
His mother, Xúliǎn, led the entire camp to flee west from Luòguōgāng.
Zhìníng pursued them,
captured all their baggage,
and took over fifty thousand captives,
and countless livestock.
The false Jiédùshǐ Liù and his tribe all surrendered.
An imperial edict ordered Běijīng Fùtǒng Wányán Dájí to requisition horses from his department,
and to plan for fodder and provisions.
Dájí was also made a Jiānzhànguān,
to record meritorious deeds and report them.
An imperial edict ordered the selection of ten thousand new and old soldiers from the Zhōngdū and Xījīng routes for defense,
as Wōwò had been defeated and fled,
fearing he might still clash with them.
Pú-Sǎn Zhōng-Yì's envoy reported a victory.
The imperial edict roughly stated:
"The Grand Councilor and Right Vice Marshal, Zhōng-Yì's envoy, has come to report a great victory.
Those who were captured by the army,
or those who were able to surrender voluntarily,
or those who had no home and came to pledge allegiance,
or those who intended to surrender their entire lineage,
or those who led a portion of their families to surrender,
or those who had previously accepted a false command,
and those who had previously fought against the imperial army,
all their crimes are pardoned.
Among those who scattered and fled,
with the exception of Wō-Wò himself,
regardless of rank or title,
those who return to surrender,
will also be granted pardon.
Those who can execute or capture Wō-Wò,
or those who can capture from among the people who refused to be recruited and fled,
or those who can lead a multitude to surrender to the military commanders or local officials,
will all be granted official rewards.
Those who are brought in and settled by the various circuits
must not be arbitrarily harmed or deprived.
Those without means of support,
regardless of their origin,
shall be settled wherever there is grain
and shall be officially provided for."
Wō-Wò gathered more than ten thousand scattered soldiers
and then entered the Xī (奚) territory,
using the various Xī people to augment his forces.
From time to time, he dispatched troops to raid the area between Sù-Lǔ-Gǔ-Diàn (速魯古淀), Gǔ-Běi-Kǒu (古北口), and Xīng-Huà (興化).
Wēn-Dí-Hǎn Ā-Lǔ-Dài (溫迪罕阿魯帶) defended Gǔ-Běi-Kǒu (古北口),
but was defeated in battle there.
An imperial edict ordered Wán-Yán Móu-Yǎn (完顏謀衍), Pú-Chá Wū-Lǐ-Yǎ (蒲察烏里雅), and Pú-Chá Pú-Lú-Hún (蒲察蒲盧渾) to lead three thousand soldiers,
to combine with the five thousand permanently stationed troops,
to attack him.
An imperial edict ordered Wán-Yán Sī-Jìng (完顏思敬) to lead his subordinate troops into the Xī (奚) land
to join the main army to suppress Wō-Wò.
Pú-Sù-Yuè (蒲速越), a *méng'ān* (猛安) from the rebel faction's Měng-Mò (霿●) River, sent an envoy to the Marshal's office to negotiate surrender.
An imperial edict ordered the capture of Wō-Wò,
promising official rewards.
Many of the rebel generals surrendered.
Those who had scattered and fled, upon hearing the imperial edict offering clemency,
also mostly surrendered.
The rest mostly died of illness and plague,
no longer having the will to fight.
Wō-Wò, judging his situation to be desperate,
then planned to flee to the Xià (夏) Kingdom via the Yáng-Chéng (羊城) road to Xī-Jīng (西京).
The main army pursued him even more urgently,
and many of his followers again deserted.
Realizing he could not go west,
he then fled north into the Shā-Tuó (沙陀) region.
An imperial edict was issued to the Grand Secretariat (*Shàng-Shū-Shěng*) (尚書省),
stating, "All families coerced into joining the rebellion who were captured and dispersed
should be rectified.
Generals and soldiers often conceal these people;
the authorities should investigate and deliver them."
The Supervising General, Zhì-Níng (志寧), captured Shāo-Hé-Zhù (稍合住),
released him without killing him,
and let him return to the rebels,
instructing him to persuade his close associates to capture Wō-Wò to prove their loyalty,
promising official rewards.
On the *gēng-zǐ* (庚子) day of the ninth month,
Shāo-Hé-Zhù (稍合住) and Shén-Dú-Wò (神獨斡) captured Wō-Wò
and brought him to the Right Area Commander Wán-Yán Sī-Jìng (完顏思敬) to surrender.
[一八] They also captured his mother Xú-Niǎn (徐輦) and his wife, son, daughter-in-law, younger brother, and nephew,
and seized all his counterfeit gold and silver plaques and seals.
Táng-Kuò Bó-Gǔ-Dǐ (唐括孛古底) captured Shí-Wēn (什溫), the former *jìe-dù-shǐ* (節度使) of Hú-Lǐ-Gǎi (胡里改), and his family.
The Northwest Circuit Pacification Commissioner, Lǐ Jiā-Nú (李家奴), captured more than thirty people, including the counterfeit Privy Council Commissioner, Zhú-Wò (逐斡).
He then, along with *méng'ān* (猛安) Ní-Běn Pó-Guǒ (泥本婆果), pursued the counterfeit Supervising General, Nà-Yě (那也), to Tiān-Chéng (天成) County.
Nà-Yě (那也) then surrendered,
and they also captured the counterfeit Grand Marshal, Chǒu-Gē (醜哥), one gold plaque, and five silver plaques.
Zhì-Níng (志寧), along with Qīng-Chén (清臣), Zōng-Níng (宗寧), Sù-Gē (速哥), and others, pursued the remaining faction to Yàn-Zǐ-Chéng (燕子城),
capturing all their members.
They arrived at Mò-Bá-Lǐ-Dá (抹拔里達) land earlier
and captured everyone there.
The rebellious faction was thus pacified.
On the *jiǎ-chén* (甲辰) day,
the Crown Prince led all officials to submit a congratulatory memorial.
On the *yǐ-sì* (乙巳) day,
an imperial edict was issued to the whole empire.
On the *xīn-hài* (辛亥) day,
Wán-Yán Sī-Jìng (完顏思敬) presented the captives in the capital.
Wō-Wò's head was displayed in the marketplace,
his hands and feet were torn apart,
and distributed to be displayed in the various prefectures of the capital.
His mother, Xú-Niǎn (徐輦), and his wife and children were all executed.
The surrendered Qì-Dān (契丹) people had their weapons confiscated;
those who were too poor to support themselves were officially provided for.
Kuò-Lǐ (括里) and Zhā-Bā (扎八) led their followers south.
An imperial edict ordered the Left Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs (*Xuān-Huī-Shǐ*) (宣徽使), Zōng-Hēng (宗亨), to pursue them.
Zhā-Bā (扎八) falsely claimed to surrender,
and Zōng-Hēng (宗亨) believed him,
thus not engaging in battle.
Zhā-Bā (扎八) deceived him, saying:
"Kuò-Lǐ (括里) has fled in fright,
I wish to pursue him."
Zōng-Hēng (宗亨) allowed Zhā-Bā (扎八) to leave.
The *méng'ān* (猛安) of Yì-Dū (益都) wanted to pursue Kuò-Lǐ (括里) and Zhā-Bā (扎八) with his subordinates,
but Zōng-Hēng (宗亨) feared it would divide his achievements,
so he refused,
and instead allowed his soldiers to take the abandoned possessions, animals, and people of the rebels for themselves.
Kuò-Lǐ (括里) and Zhā-Bā (扎八) thus managed to escape
and fled to the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
Zōng-Hēng (宗亨) was demoted to the rank of Prefect of Níng-Zhōu (寧州).
Afterwards,
Lǐ Shì-Fǔ (李世輔) of Sòng (宋) employed Kuò-Lǐ (括里) and Zhā-Bā (扎八),
subsequently capturing Sù-Zhōu (宿州),
which became a significant border threat.
Shén-Dú-Wò (神獨斡) was appointed Assistant to the *Jìe-Dù-Shǐ* (節度使) of Ān-Huà (安化) Military Prefecture,
and Shāo-Hé-Zhù (稍合住) was appointed Assistant to the *Jìe-Dù-Shǐ* (節度使) of Zhèn-Wǔ (震武) Military Prefecture.
In the sixth year of Dà-Dìng (大定),
the Censorate (*Diǎn-Jiǎn-Sī*) (點檢司) memorialized that there were descendants of rebels among the imperial guards,
requesting that they all be dismissed.
The imperial edict stated:
"Those personally involved in the rebellion shall be dismissed;
the rest shall not be questioned."
A eulogy states:
The Jīn (金) people gave Yān-Shān (燕山) to Sòng (宋),
thus inciting Zhāng Jué (張覺) to act presumptuously.
How could Jué (覺) have been acting for Sòng (宋)?
He merely wished to take advantage of the times to seek profit.
Yé-Lǜ Yú-Dǔ (耶律余睹) followed Zōng-Wàng (宗望) in pursuing Tiān-Zuò (天祚),
sparing no effort,
but after achieving success, became arrogant and excessive,
bringing about his own demise.
Alas!
In the *Zhèng-Lóng* (正隆) era, with excellent troops,
the Qì-Dān (契丹) caused trouble.
It is said:
"Indeed, soldiers are like fire;
if not controlled, they will burn themselves."
How can one not be wary?
Collation Notes:
Biographies, Chapter 72, Foreign Nations (Part 1): Western Xià (西夏).
King Lǐ Gān-Shùn (李乾順) of Xià (夏) Kingdom.
His ancestor was named Tuò-Bá Sī-Gōng (托跋思恭).
During the reign of Emperor Xī-Zōng (僖宗) of Táng (唐) dynasty,
he was *jìe-dù-shǐ* (節度使) of Xià (夏), Suí (綏), Yín (銀), and Yòu (宥),
and with Lǐ Mào-Zhēn (李茂貞), Lǐ Kè-Yòng (李克用), and others, defeated Huáng Cháo (黃巢)
and recovered the capital.
He was bestowed the surname Lǐ (李).
Towards the end of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
the world fell into great chaos,
and regional governors waged continuous wars,
but Xià-Zhōu (夏州) never caused trouble for Táng (唐).
Through the Five Dynasties to the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
after several generations, it reached Yuán-Hào (元昊),
who first claimed the title of Emperor.
The Liáo (遼) people married their princesses into the Lǐ (李) clan,
and the tribute system was maintained uninterrupted for generations.
Details are found in the *Liáo Shǐ* (遼史).
In the sixth year of Tiān-Fǔ (天輔),
Jīn (金) defeated the Liáo (遼) army,
and the Liáo (遼) ruler fled to Yīn-Shān (陰山).
Xià (夏) general Lǐ Liáng-Fǔ (李良輔) led thirty thousand troops to rescue Liáo (遼),
arriving at the Wild Valley on the border of Tiān-Dé (天德).
Wò-Lǔ (斡魯) and Lóu-Shì (婁室) defeated them at Yí-Shuǐ (宜水),
pursuing them to the Wild Valley.
The mountain stream suddenly rose,
and countless numbers were swept away and drowned.
Zōng-Wàng (宗望) reached Yīn-Shān (陰山)
and, as a matter of expediency, negotiated peace with the Xià (夏) Kingdom.
His letter stated:
"It is stated in the imperial edict: The King of Xià (夏),
being of Liáo (遼) descent,
has been unwavering from beginning to end,
rescuing them in times of danger.
Now that the Liáo (遼) Kingdom has been conquered,
if he can render service and tribute as he did for Liáo (遼),
he shall be allowed to come,
without suspicion or wavering.
If the Liáo (遼) ruler arrives there,
he should be captured and sent."
In the second year of Tiān-Huì (天會),
they first submitted an oath memorial,
acknowledging vassalage with the same rituals as they used to serve Liáo (遼),
and requested to receive ceded and bestowed land.
Zōng-Hàn (宗翰) acted under imperial authority,
ceding the area north of Xià-Zhài (下寨), south of Yīn-Shān (陰山), and west of Tǔ-Lù-Luò (吐祿濼) in the Yǐ-Shì-Yé-Guā (乙室耶刮) tribe,
bestowing it upon them.
In the third month of Tiānhuì 2 (1124 CE),
Gānshùn sent Bǎlǐ Gōngliàng and others to present a sworn memorial,
which stated:
"Your subject, Gānshùn, states: On the fifteenth day of this month,
the Regional Commanders of the Southwest and Northwest Routes dispatched Wáng Jièrú, the Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left, and others, bearing dispatches, to promulgate a decree.
If the Xià kingdom repents of its past errors,
captures and delivers the Liáo ruler,
establishes an alliance and presents a memorial,
and continues to follow the old system of the Liáo kingdom and the granted sworn edict,
then in the future, should any unforeseen circumstances arise,
we shall assist each other.
Your subject has maintained marital and contractual relations with the Liáo kingdom for generations,
and is nominally a vassal state.
I rashly provided aid, thereby initiating hostilities,
and consequently incurred displeasure and formed enmity.
Thus, I quickly suffered the calamity of defying Heaven,
and indeed faced the sorrow of defeat.
I have received your benevolent decree, which pardons my former transgressions,
and furthermore bestows land to expand my domain.
I constantly remember this grace of toleration,
and forever cherish the hope of serving Heaven.
From now on,
regarding all matters such as seasonal court greetings, presentation of memorials, and exchange of envoys,
everything shall permanently follow the old precedents of your subject serving the Liáo kingdom.
The benighted ruler of the Qìdān is currently not within your subject's territory;
however, should he flee and arrive here,
he shall not be allowed to remain;
he will immediately be apprehended and presented.
If the Great Court knows his whereabouts,
and dispatches troops to pursue and capture him,
I shall not dare to provide him refuge or assist him as before.
Should conscription of troops be required,
I shall immediately comply.
Furthermore, should envoys from distant and foreign lands come to pay respects at the heavenly court,
and need to pass through my territory,
I shall not obstruct them.
Regarding all the matters enumerated above,
your subject swears to uphold this sincerity,
and pass it down through generations without change.
Should there be any violation,
Heaven and Earth shall bear witness,
the gods shall punish me,
calamity shall befall my descendants,
and they shall not enjoy the kingdom."
The so-called Regional Commander of the Northwest and Southwest Routes was Zōnghàn.
It is said that Zōngwàng, by Emperor Tàizǔ's (太祖) order, communicated with them,
while Zōnghàn, as he deemed appropriate, ceded land and negotiated peace.
Emperor Tàizōng sent Wáng Āhǎi and Yáng Tiānjí to bestow a sworn edict, which stated:
"On the Jiǎchén cyclical day of Tiānhuì 2,
the first day of the intercalary third month, Wùyín,
the Emperor bestows this sworn edict upon Gānshùn, King of the Xià kingdom.
The former emperor received the mandate of Heaven
and initiated a grand enterprise.
Your kingdom occupied Xiàtái and
its territory bordered Liáoyòu.
By exerting efforts for the benighted ruler,
you caused enmity with the royal army.
The former emperor believed that one should be loyal to what one serves,
and made it his business to extend grace and pardon transgressions.
When I, the humble one, inherited the succession,
I looked up to the ancestral instructions and followed them.
You have deeply reflected on your past errors,
and gladly submitted yourself internally.
You have dispatched envoys on chariots to present tribute,
and performed the duties of a subject to declare yourself a vassal.
Therefore, I bestow upon you glorious favor,
to manifest the renewed good relations.
All matters regarding ceded and bestowed lands, diplomatic protocols, and mutual assistance,
shall entirely conform to the edicts of the former court.
Regarding the request to comply with troop levies,
it shall be granted.
The Three Luminaries are above;
how could I break my word?
Should there be any change or violation,
it shall be as your oath.
May you heed this distant admonition,
and not fail in your sincerity."
Thereupon,
the Sòng people and the Xià people both received territory in Shānxī,
but the Sòng people encroached upon it.
Gānshùn sent an envoy to memorialize his gratitude for the sworn edict and to discuss the territory encroached upon by the Sòng.
The edict stated:
"We have read the memorial you presented,
and fully understood it.
We have already ordered the Regional Commanderates of the Southwest and Northwest Routes to make appropriate decisions."
At this time,
Zōnghàn had not yet returned from his audience at the capital.
The Xià kingdom's memorial was recorded and sent to the acting Regional Commander Wòlǔ.
The encroachment by the Sòng people on the newly received territory and the dispute over ceremonial objects with the envoy Wáng Āhǎi were to be decided expediently in communication with Xià.
Initially,
nine prefectures in Shānxī were given to the Sòng people.
However, Tiāndé was far away in a corner,
and could not be reached quickly in an emergency,
so it was ceded to Xià.
Later, after the Sòng capital was captured and the two emperors seized,
the Shǎnxī boundary was drawn,
starting from the east of Luòyánggōu in the Línfǔ Route to the west bank of the Yellow River, then west past Nuǎnquánbǎo;
from Mǐzhīgǔ in the Fūyán Route to Léishèngzhài;
from Wēibiānzhài in the Huánqìng Route across Jiǔxīngyuán to Wěibùgǔkǒu;
from Wēichuānzhài in the Jīngyuán Route, slightly past ancient Xiāoguān to Běigǔchuān;
from Tōnghuáibǎo in the Qínfèng Route to ancient Huìzhōu;
and from there directly to the Yellow River,
following the present course to the western edge of the Xīhé Route to demarcate the borders.
The northern frontier of Shǎnxī was again divided to exchange for Tiāndé and Yúnnèi,
with the Yellow River as the boundary.
When Lóushì pacified Shǎnxī,
Pólúhuǒ led his troops to first capture Wēiróngchéng.
When the army reached east of Wēiróng, they encountered the enemy,
defeated and drove them away.
They captured two men alive.
Upon questioning them,
they learned that it was Lǐ Yù, a Xià general, who was taking Wēiróng.
So they returned the men and communicated with Lǐ Yù.
Lǐ Yù's army was west of Wēiróng,
Púchá's army was east of Wēiróng,
and they sent an envoy to discuss matters with Lóushì.
Lóushì replied:
"The Marshal's Residence has given strict orders that
if troops approach the Xià border,
they should act in concert with the Xià people,
and not invade each other."
Lǐ Yù's envoy came and said:
"Since the Xià kingdom has returned Tiāndé and Yúnnèi to the Great Nation,
the Great Nation promised us the northern frontier of Shǎnxī,
which is why we are here."
Púchá and others then withdrew their troops.
After Ruìzōng pacified Shǎnxī,
the Marshal's Residence did not wish to give the northern frontier of Shǎnxī to the Xià kingdom.
The edict stated:
"You and others should carefully determine what is appropriate to do."
In Tiānjuàn 2 (1139 CE),
King Gānshùn died,
and his son Rénxiào succeeded him.
Envoys were sent to confer investiture,
and he was granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Shàngzhùguó.
In Huángtǒng 1 (1141 CE),
he requested the establishment of customs markets,
which was granted.
Initially,
when Wáng Āhǎi and others brought Emperor Tàizōng's sworn edict to the Xià kingdom,
Gānshùn received the envoys according to the old Qìdān ceremony.
Āhǎi refused, saying:
"The Qìdān and the Xià kingdom were nephew and uncle;
therefore, the king sat to receive,
and the envoy advanced with proper禮.
Now, the Great Jīn and the Xià kingdom are ruler and subject;
the Great Nation's envoy should be received according to ritual."
They debated for several days without resolution,
and it was then that he first stood up to receive it.
Subsequently, birthday envoys were not sent,
but from this point onward, envoys were dispatched to bestow gifts.
Initially,
Mù Wěi surrendered with Huánzhōu.
