When Shǎnxī and Hénán were ceded to the Sòng people,
Wěi fled to the Xià kingdom,
and the Xià people made him a leader of the Shān'é.
When Sālīhē again pacified Shǎnxī,
Wěi thought of returning.
The Xià people, knowing this,
executed Wěi's entire clan.
This was reported in a memorial,
and an imperial edict reproached them.
When Hǎilíng assassinated Xīzōng,
envoys were sent to report the situation to the border.
The Xià people asked:
"Why was Holy Virtuous Emperor deposed?"
They refused to accept it.
The imperial court then ordered the relevant authorities to issue an official document explaining the reasons for the deposition and succession.
In the seventh month of Tiāndé 2 (1150 CE),
the Xià envoy, Imperial Censor-in-chief Zálà Gōngjì and others, came to offer congratulations,
following the old ritual.
At the end of Zhènglóng's reign, the Sòng were attacked,
and Sòng people entered Qín and Lǒng.
Xià also took advantage of the opportunity to attack and capture the fortress cities of Dàngqiāng, Tōngxiá, Jiǔyáng, and Huìchuān.
The Sòng also invaded Xià territory.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
the Xià people again returned the fortress cities,
and also begged for troops to recover the territory invaded by the Sòng.
An imperial decree praised and commended them,
and also dispatched Wányán Dájí, a Lángzhōng of the Lìbù, to thoroughly investigate the advantages and disadvantages in Shǎnxī.
A border official reported,
"The Xià people have already returned the fortress cities,
but the population, property, and livestock they plundered have not yet been returned.
Please demand their return."
On the Jiǎshēn day of the second month of the fourth year of Dàdìng,
Xià dispatched their Wǔgōng Dàfū Niǔwò Wénzhōng and others to congratulate on Wànchūnjié.
They were granted an audience,
and submitted a memorial reporting,
which roughly stated:
"At the time when the armies devastated,
fortunately, those who escaped were one or two in ten.
Following that, many died from freezing and starvation.
How many are left?
Moreover, the Xià Kingdom engaged in battle with Sòng troops,
and many people and livestock were captured and slaughtered.
For consecutive years, we have toiled,
and our soldiers have been exposed to the elements,
their strength all exhausted.
Furthermore, we are constrained by the Sòng people,
making it impossible for our loyal and sincere intentions to be conveyed.
The entire world knows this.
We wish to stop the demand for restitution,
and listen to our humble words.
This would be an immense fortune for our humble state."
Thereafter, they repeatedly made this request,
and an imperial decree granted it.
After a long time,
their minister Rèn Déjìng seized control of the state government
and wished to partition the Xià Kingdom.
On the occasion of congratulating on the Yuándàn of the eighth year of Dàdìng,
he dispatched the memorial envoy, Diànqián Tàiwèi Bālǐ Chāngzǔ and others, with a Rénxiào chapter, to request a good physician to treat Déjìng's illness.
An imperial decree ordered Bǎoquán Láng Wáng Shīdào to wear a silver tablet and go there.
The decree instructed Shīdào, saying:
"If the illness is incurable,
then do not treat it.
If it can be cured,
return within one month."
Déjìng's illness improved,
and he dispatched the gratitude envoy, Rèn Décōng, to come.
Déjìng also attached a memorial presenting gifts.
The emperor said:
"Déjìng has his own fixed status.
The attached memorial and gifts cannot be accepted."
All were rejected.
Initially,
when Rénxiào succeeded to the throne,
his ministers repeatedly rebelled.
Rèn Déjìng had meritorious service in resisting them,
and thus served as prime minister of the Xià Kingdom for over twenty years.
He secretly harbored ulterior motives,
desiring to seize the Xià Kingdom,
and falsely accused and killed imperial relatives and high-ranking officials.
His power gradually became oppressive,
and Rénxiào could not control him.
In the tenth year of Dàdìng,
Rénxiào then ceded the Southwest Circuit and the territory of Língzhōu Luópánglǐng to Déjìng,
allowing him to establish his own state,
and also submitted a memorial requesting an enfeoffment for Déjìng.
Shìzōng asked his prime ministers about this.
Shàngshū Lìng Lǐ Shí and others said:
"This matter pertains to their country.
What concern is it of ours?
It would be better to permit it."
The emperor said:
"How could a ruler of a state willingly partition his country and give it to another without cause?
This must be due to a powerful minister coercing and seizing it,
not the original intention of the Xià King.
Moreover, the Xià Kingdom has been our vassal for many years.
If it is suddenly forced by a traitorous minister,
as the ruler of all under Heaven,
how can I tolerate this?
If they cannot rectify themselves,
then we should send troops to punish them.
It cannot be permitted."
Thereupon, their tribute was rejected,
and an imperial decree was bestowed upon Rénxiào, saying:
"Since our state pacified the Central Plains,
and brought peace to the Western regions,
we first drew boundaries for your father,
and subsequently granted a mandate to your person.
Our benevolence has been profound for your region,
spanning nearly three decades.
As a vassal minister, you should diligently uphold your duties,
and also firmly guard the ancestral inheritance.
This current request
is quite unusual.
We do not know the reason for this intention,
and will subsequently send an envoy to inquire of you.
All tribute items
have been ordered to be returned."
Déjìng secretly communicated with the Sòng people, seeking assistance.
The Sòng replied to Déjìng with a wax-sealed letter.
The Xià people obtained it.
Déjìng initially, under the pretense of seeking a physician, attached a memorial presenting gifts,
intending to test Shìzōng.
Since it was not feasible,
and the request for enfeoffment was also denied,
Rénxiào then plotted to execute him.
On the last day of the eighth month,
Rénxiào executed Déjìng and his confederates,
and submitted a memorial expressing gratitude,
and also sent the captured Sòng person and the wax-sealed letter.
His memorial of thanks stated:
"After Déjìng first received the partitioned territory,
he once dispatched an envoy to the Great Court to request enfeoffment.
We received an imperial decree that did not approve it.
This is the court's compassion and love,
and the Xià Kingdom is immensely grateful.
The Xià Kingdom presumptuously troubled the court
by daring to seek enfeoffment for a traitorous minister,
deeply violating protocol.
Now that the traitorous minister has been executed,
the Great Court need not send an envoy to inquire.
The land partitioned to Déjìng borders the Great Court's Xīqín Circuit.
Fearing that since the partition of the land, new troubles might arise,
we have already investigated and imposed prohibitions.
We beg the court to also impose prohibitions."
In the twelfth year,
the emperor said to his prime ministers:
"The Xià Kingdom exchanges pearls and jade for our silk and cloth.
This is exchanging useless things for our useful things."
Thereupon, the customs markets at Bǎo'ān and Lánzhōu were reduced and abolished.
Rénxiào deeply appreciated Shìzōng's profound kindness.
In the seventeenth year,
he presented a "hundred-headed tent" manufactured in his country.
The emperor said:
"The Xià Kingdom's tribute has its customary products.
This can be rejected."
Rénxiào again submitted a memorial, saying:
"The tent presented is not a rare or precious item.
The envoy has already reached the border.
If it is not accepted,
then our humble state's profound sincerity will have no means to be displayed,
and neighboring countries will believe that the Xià Kingdom is not among those favored by the Great Court.
How then shall we find peace?"
Thereupon, it was permitted to be presented along with the Yuándàn envoy.
Previously,
the Shàngshū had reported:
"Xià people and border residents of Shǎnxī privately cross the border,
stealing property and livestock.
Dishonest individuals use the pretext of customs market trade
to travel back and forth,
which could become a border concern.
Envoys entering the territory and exchanging goods with wealthy merchants
can also be prohibited."
Thus,
the Suídé customs market was again abolished,
leaving only Dōngshèng and Huánzhōu.
Rénxiào memorialized, requesting to re-establish the customs markets at Lánzhōu, Bǎo'ān, and Suídé as before,
and also begged for envoys to enter the border to exchange goods.
The imperial decree stated:
"Bǎo'ān and Lánzhōu lack silk and hemp.
Only Suídé has established customs markets to facilitate trade.
Envoys and deputies traveling back and forth
are permitted to trade at the post stations in the capital."
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
an imperial decree said:
"Trade within the Xià envoy's residence shall cease for now."
In the second year of Míngchāng,
it was restored.
After a short while,
Xià people grazed their livestock freely in the territory of Zhènjìng.
Patrol soldiers pursued them,
and the Xià people seized the patrol soldiers and left.
Border general Ālǔdài led troops to question them.
Xià canton officials Wú Míngqì, Xìnlíng Dū, Bǔ Xiáng, Xú YúLì, and others ambushed with three thousand soldiers in the valley.
Ālǔdài was struck by an arrow in the mouth and died,
and they took his bow and armor and left.
An imperial decree demanded the surrender of those who killed Ālǔdài.
The Xià people sentenced them to penal servitude.
The imperial decree repeatedly demanded their surrender.
Thereupon, the Xià people killed Míngqì and the others.
In the fourth year of Míngchāng (1193),
Rénxiào passed away.
His son Chúnyòu succeeded him.
In the second year of Chéng'ān (1197),
monopoly markets were re-established in Lánzhōu and Bǎo'ān.
In the fifth year of Chéng'ān (1200),
Chúnyòu's mother suffered from wind-illness and sought a physician.
An imperial edict ordered Grand Imperial Physician Panel Member Shí Déyuán and Wáng Lìzhēn to go,
and also bestowed imperial medicine.
In the eighth month,
medicine was again bestowed.
In the third month of the sixth year of Tàihé (1206),
Rénxiào's younger brother Rén'yǒu's son Ānquán
deposed Chúnyòu and enthroned himself.
He died at the place of his deposition after more than a month.
In the seventh month,
an envoy caused Chúnyòu's mother, Lady Luó, to present a memorial,
stating that Chúnyòu was unable to inherit and govern,
and that, with the deliberation of the high officials, Ānquán was established as king.
An envoy was dispatched to report this to the court.
The Xià envoy privately asked the reception official:
"Has the emperor approved the reported matter?"
The reception official said:
"This is not a matter to be asked about."
The Xià envoy said:
"Tomorrow I shall ask the Guest Office.
If there is still no answer,
then I will ascend to the palace hall and formally request it."
The Emperor heard of this,
and had the Guest Office convey the intention to grant what was prayed for.
Then an imperial edict was bestowed upon Lady Luó, inquiring about her intentions.
The Xià people again brought Lady Luó's memorial.
Thereupon, Ānquán was enfeoffed as the King of Xiàguó.
In the third year of Dà'ān (1211),
Ānquán passed away,
and his clan nephew Zūn Xù was enthroned.
Zūn Xù had previously achieved the top scholar degree in the imperial examination
and served as the head of the Grand Chief Military Governor's Office.
His enthronement occurred one month before Ānquán's death.
Wèi Shàowáng has no Veritable Records,
so the reason is unknown.
However, at this time, the Jīn army suffered a defeat at Huìhébǎo.
The Xià people took advantage of their military defeat to invade the border regions,
while diplomatic missions continued as before.
In the third month of the first year of Chóngqìng (1212),
Jiāzhōu was attacked.
In the sixth month of the first year of Zhìníng (1213),
Bǎo'ānzhōu was attacked.
In the eleventh month of the first year of Zhēnyòu (1213),
Huìzhōu was attacked,
and the Chief Military Commissioner Túdān Chǒu'ér repelled them.
In the twelfth month,
Jīngzhōu was captured.
In the eighth month of the second year (1214),
a returning person, Qiáo Chéng, brought a letter from Xiàguó,
which generally stated that Jīn border officials were encroaching
and requested that they be restrained.
An imperial edict ordered an official document in response.
The Chancellor stated:
"Since it is not an official dispatch,
if we now demand an explanation,
they will surely fabricate excuses,
making it a mere formality,
of no benefit to the matter."
Thus, it was stopped.
Not long after,
the Xià people attacked Qìngyuán, Yán'ān, and Jīshízhōu.
An imperial edict then ordered the relevant authorities to send a document demanding an explanation.
In the eleventh month,
Chéng Chénsēng, an interpreter from Lánzhōu, colluded with the Xià people to rebel with the prefecture.
The border general defeated their three thousand soldiers.
In the first month of the third year (1215),
the Xià army attacked Wǔyánchuān.
Xuānzōng said:
"This is not worth worrying about.
I fear they might enter through other routes."
Soon after, it was heard that border officials had invaded Xià territory,
whereupon the Xià people attacked Huánzhōu.
An imperial edict ordered the punishment of the border officials.
The Xià army attacked Jīshízhōu,
and Chief Military Commissioner Jiāng Bótōng defeated them.
The Xià army entered Ānxiāngguān,
and Chief Military Commissioner Cáojìsēng and Myriad Households Hū Sānshí repelled them.
In the second month,
they attacked Huánzhōu.
[一０]The prefect, Wūgǔlùn Yánshòu, defeated them at the border.
In the third month,
an imperial edict ordered a discussion on attacking Xià.
[一一]The Shǎnxī Pacification Commissioner's Office memorialized:
"Previously,
the Xià people invaded our Huán and Qìng,
and with their troops from Hé, Lán, and Jīshí,
they all fled,
hastily returning to their lairs,
which was our preparedness.
Now, the dispersed troops from Lánzhōu have not yet gathered,
and much military equipment is incomplete.
The border regions are cold,
and spring grass has just begun to grow,
so pasturage is not yet possible.
For over three hundred *lǐ* between the two territories, there are no smoke and fires (settlements),
so it is not advisable to act rashly."
This was followed.
In the fourth month,
an imperial edict ordered Tíkòng Cáo Jìsēng of Hézhōu and Jíedùshǐ Wányán Gǒu'ér of Tōngyuǎnjūn to attack Chéng Chénsēng.
The Xià people reinforced him.
In the ninth month,
they then broke Xīguānbǎo.
The Xià people again attacked Dìwǔjiàngchéng.
Myriad Households Yáng Zàixìng repelled them.
An imperial edict was issued to the Shǎnxī Pacification Commissioner's Office and the various border generals,
bestowing blank imperial decrees.
Those who established merits in battle,
from the fifth rank downwards, were all permitted to be promoted and appointed.
In the tenth month,
Bǎo'ān and Yán'ān were attacked,
and Chief Military Commissioner Wányán Guójiānú defeated them.
Thereupon, they penetrated deep into Líntáo,
and Grand Coordinator Tuómǎn Hútǔmén could not resist.
Shǎnxī Pacification Vice Commissioner Wányán Húshīlái went to rescue Líntáo,
suffering a great defeat at Wèiyuánbǎo.
The city was broken,
and Húshīlái was captured.
In the eleventh month,
the Xià army was defeated at Kèrǒngzhài,
and again defeated at Shúyángzhài.
The Chancellor entered to offer congratulations.
Xuānzōng said:
"This is due to the efforts of loyal and worthy officials."
The Xià army advanced to besiege Líntáo.
Tuómǎn Hútǔmén defeated them.
In the fourth month of the fourth year (1216),
Wāng Sānláng, the Grand Coordinator of the Xià Pā'é tribe, led his followers to surrender.
He presented a thousand sheep.
An imperial edict ordered them to be accepted
and their value generously compensated.
A spy was captured at Láiyuǎnzhèn,
who said that Sòng and Xià had allied to attack.
An imperial edict ordered the Shǎnxī Provincial Grand Secretariat to prepare.
Xià built a pontoon bridge at the border river of Láiqiāngchéng.
Marshal Right Supervisor Wányán Sàibù burned it,
and many were slain.
In the sixth month,
the Fūyán Circuit reported
that the Xià people had sent a dispatch using their country's Guāngdìng era name.
An imperial edict ordered the dispatch to be returned.
In the intercalary month,
Qìngshānnú, the Grand Coordinator of Qìngyáng, attacked Xià.
He set out from Huánzhōu.
The Shǎnxī Provincial Grand Secretariat requested that his army be divided into two,
ordering Qìngshānnú to exit from Huái'ānzhài of the Third Detachment,
and Wányán Húlǔ, the prefect of Huánzhōu, to exit from Huánzhōu.
Xuānzōng said:
"I hear that the Xià people have moved their army to defend their royal city.
I still fear they are deceiving us;
do not fall into their trap."
Tíkòng Wányán Gǒu'ér reached the Xīguānbǎo of Lánzhōu,
recruited nine former subordinates,
and ambushed the Xià army at Āmíwān,
killing over a hundred of their generals and soldiers.
In the eighth month,
Left Supervising Army Wūgǔlùn Qìngshòu defeated the Xià army at Ānsàibǎo.
[一二]Right Supervisor Sàibù repelled the Xià army at Jiéyězǐchuān,
and again defeated them at Chē'érbǎo.
In the eleventh month,
Tíkòng Shízhǎn Héxǐ and Yáng Wòliè lifted the siege of Dìngxī.
On the day Bingyin of the twelfth month,
Xuānzōng and the Crown Prince discussed attacking Xià.
Left Supervising Army Tuómǎn Hútǔmén and Yán'ān Grand Coordinator Gǔlǐjiǎ Shílún attacked Yán, Yòu, and Xiàzhōu.
Qìngyáng Grand Coordinator Qìngshānnú and the Prefect of Píngliángfǔ, Yílà Dábùyě, attacked Wēi, Líng, Ān, Huì, and other prefectures.
In the first month of the first year of Xīngdìng (1217),
three thousand Xià soldiers returned from Níngzhōu.
Qìngshānnú intercepted and attacked them with his troops,
defeating them.
An imperial edict ordered Xū Dǐng, the Provincial Grand Secretariat of Hédōng, to select thirty-five thousand soldiers
and hand them over to Tuómǎn Hútǔmén to attack Xià.
Dǐng hurriedly memorialized that this was not feasible,
so it was stopped.
The details are in Dǐng's biography.
Right Supervisor Wányán Zhòngyuán requested to test the troops against Western Xià,
believing that an unexpected attack would surely achieve a complete victory,
and once military might was established, the nation's strength would be further solidified.
An imperial edict was sent down to the Department of State Affairs and the Bureau of Military Affairs for deliberation.
Fúshān, a Xià person, surrendered with captured households.
He was appointed Associate Prefect of Zézhōujūnzhōu.
In the fifth month,
the Xià soldiers entered Dàběichà.
Dūtǒng Gēshíliè Zhūgǒu ambushed them
and defeated them.
Xuānzōng wished to negotiate peace with Xià,
but Yòudūjiān Qìngshānnú, stationed in Yán'ān,
reported:
"The Xià kingdom will certainly not agree to peace;
it will merely lead to our deception."
Later,
a captured spy stated
that Zūnxù had heard that Dàjīn intended to negotiate peace,
and had warned his generals and soldiers not to offend the western border.
The prime ministers reported:
"Even if this is the case,
border defenses should not be relaxed."
Xuānzōng agreed.
Yòudūjiān Wányán Lǘshān defeated Xià soldiers at Huánghèchà.
The Xià people besieged Yánghěnzài.
Dūtǒng Dǎng Shìchāng fought them.
Wányán Gǒu'ér sent Dūtǒng Jiágǔ Ruì to attack the Xià camp by night,
thus lifting the siege.
Still, they remained in the vicinity.
Zuǒdūjiān Báisā dispatched the elite troops from Dìngxī, and Kāngǔ Fùtǒng Bāo Xiàochéng's Fēihéyì army,
who jointly attacked and routed them.
In the eighth month,
the Āndìngbǎo Mǎjiāpíng Zǒngyā Lǐ Gōngzhí defeated three thousand Xià soldiers.
In the ninth month,
Dūtǒng Luó Shìhuī repelled Xià soldiers at Kèróngzhài.
In the third month of Xīngdìng second year,
Yòudūjiān Qìngshānnú reported:
"The Xià people show an inclination towards peace.
Baó'ān, Suídé, and Jiāzhōu have received written reports
requesting the resumption of mutual markets
to seek the old alliance.
In my opinion,
this comes from Zūnxù,
and is not something border officials would dare to decide on their own."
The court did not agree.
In the fifth month,
the Xià people entered Jiāzhōu.
Qìngshānnú defeated them at Mǎjífēng.
In the seventh month,
they attacked Kāngǔ.
Jiágǔ Ruì and Zhào Fáng defeated them,
pursuing them to Zhìgūbǎo.
In the intercalary month of the third year,
the Xià people captured Tōngqínzhài.
Tíkòng Nàhé Mǎizhù defeated them,
and they fled from Jiālúchuān.
Huázhōu Yuánshuài Wányán Hédá led his troops from Ānzhàibǎo to Lóngzhōu,
defeating two thousand of their soldiers.
He advanced to attack Lóngzhōu,
capturing its southwest,
and returned at dusk.
In the twelfth month,
an imperial edict instructed officials to send a diplomatic letter to the Xià kingdom.
In the second month of the fourth year,
the Xià people attacked Zhènrǒng.
The Jīn army was defeated.
The Xià people's official diplomatic letter was insolent.
An imperial edict ordered court scholars to draft a refuting dispatch.
In the fourth month,
Xià soldiers attacked the border.
Yuánshuài Shízhǎn Héxǐ met them at Lù'ér Yuán.
Tíkòng Wūgǔlún Shìxiǎn defeated them with a detachment,
and Dūtǒng Wáng Dìng again defeated their forces at Xīnquánchéng.
Yuánshuài Qìngshānnú attacked Yòuzhōu,
besieged Shénduīfǔ,
and breached its wall.
Some soldiers ascended it.
Reinforcements arrived
and drove them off,
beheading two thousand
and capturing over a hundred people,
and over three thousand miscellaneous animals.
In the eighth month,
the Xià people captured Huìzhōu.
Cìshǐ Wūgǔlún Shìxiǎn surrendered.
They again attacked Kāngǔ.
Jiágǔ Ruì repeatedly fought and defeated them.
The Xià people then left.
In this month,
an imperial edict instructed officials to send a diplomatic letter to negotiate peace,
but the matter ultimately failed.
Thirty thousand Xià people from Gāofēngzhèn besieged Dìngxī.
Cìshǐ Àishēn Āshīlà, Tíkòng Wūgǔlún Chángshòu, and Wēndūn Yǒngchāng attacked and routed them.
In the ninth month,
the Xià people besieged Suí píngzhài and Āndìngbǎo.
Soon after,
they captured Xīníngzhōu,
and then attacked Dìngxī.
Wūgǔlún Chángshòu attacked and repelled them.
They then raided Gǒngzhōu.
Shízhǎn Héxǐ counter-attacked,
fighting over ten battles in one day,
and then they withdrew.
In the first month of the fifth year,
an imperial edict instructed the Shūmìyuàn to discuss Xià affairs.
They reported:
"The Xià people are gathering troops on the border,
intending to enter via Huìzhōu.
We have already sent Xíngshěng Báisā to ambush them in strategic defiles.
The Fūyán Yuánshuàifǔ will watch for an opportunity to dispatch troops to harass their rear,
which should be sufficient to allay concerns."
In the second month,
Níngyuǎnjūn Jiédùshǐ Jiágǔ Hǎishòu defeated Xià soldiers at Sōuwéibǎo.
In the third month,
they recaptured Láiqiāngchéng.
In the tenth month,
they attacked Kāngǔ.
Báisā repeatedly defeated them.
In the first month of Yuánguāng first year,
the Xià people captured Dàtōngchéng,
but it was recaptured.
In the third month,
Tíkòng Lǐ Shīlín defeated Xià soldiers at Yǒngmùlǐng.
In the eighth month,
they attacked Níng'ānzhài.
In the tenth month,
they attacked Shénlínbǎo.
[一三]In the twelfth month,
they entered Zhìgūbǎo.
[一四]Tíkòng Tángkuò Fǎng defeated them.
In the second year,
Zūnxù sent his Crown Prince Dé Rèn to invade.
Dé Rèn remonstrated:
"Their military strength is still strong;
it would be better to make peace with them."
Zūnxù laughed and said:
"This is not something you understand.
They lost Lánzhōu and could not even recapture it;
how can they be strong?"
Dé Rèn insisted on his remonstrance, but it was not followed.
He requested to relinquish his position as Crown Prince
and wished to become a monk.
Zūnxù was angry
and imprisoned him in Língzhōu.
He sent someone to take his place as general,
but a drought occurred, and it did not materialize.
In this year,
the Dàyuán army attacked the Xià kingdom for its crimes.
The Yán'ān and Qìngyuán Yuánshuàifǔs wished to take advantage of the Xià people's exhaustion to attack them,
but Shǎnxī Xíngshěng Báisā and Hédá deemed it unfeasible,
and so they stopped.
Lǒng'ānjūn Jiédùshǐ Wányán Ālín daily feasted and drank with his generals and soldiers,
neglecting military affairs.
The Xià people took advantage of this,
plundering over five thousand people and tens of thousands of cattle, sheep, and other livestock before leaving.
Since the Tiānhuì peace treaty,
for over eighty years there had been no military conflicts with the Xià people.
However, at the beginning of Zhēnyòu,
there were minor incursions and plunder,
leading to a ten-year unresolved conflict.
With one victory and one defeat, all elite forces were exhausted,
and both nations were weakened.
In this year,
Zūnxù abdicated in favor of his son Déwàng.
In Zhèngdà first year,
peace negotiations were concluded,
and they referred to each other as brother states.
In the second month of the third year,
Zūnxù died.
In the seventh month,
Déwàng died.
The name of his successor is lost to history.
The following year,
the Xià kingdom fell.
Before this,
the Xià envoy, Jīngfāng Guǐxiá Shǐ Wáng Lìzhī, had come to offer tribute.
Before he could return with a reply, his kingdom had already fallen.
An imperial edict ordered him to be settled in Jīngzhào,
to serve as Xuānchāi Tányā,
and to manage the surrendered households of the Xià kingdom.
In the fifth month of the eighth year,
Lìzhī's wife and children, over thirty people, arrived in Huánzhōu.
An imperial edict ordered them to be returned to Lìzhī
and bestowed silk upon them.
Lìzhī memorialized,
stating that his ancestors were originally from Shēnzhōu,
and requested not to serve in office,
but to reside in Shēnzhōu.
An imperial edict granted his request,
allowing him to reside in Shēnzhōu with his original official title,
managing the surrendered households of the Xià kingdom in Táng, Dèng, Shēn, Yù, and other places,
subject to the control of the Táng and Dèng Zǒngshuàifǔ,
and granted him a thousand *mǔ* of prime land and farming implements.
An appreciation: The establishment of the Xià dynasty was ancient.
Its minister, Luó Shìchāng, in his genealogical record, states that
when the Yuán Wèi became weak,
those residing in Sōngzhōu consequently adopted the old surname Tuóbá.
According to the Táng Shū (History of the Táng Dynasty), among the eight tribes of the Dǎngxiàng, there was a Tuóbá tribe.
Those Dǎngxiàng who moved to reside between Yínzhōu and Xiàzhōu were called the Píngxià tribe.
Tuóbá Sīgōng was granted the surname Lǐ for his achievements in defeating Huáng Cháo.
His brothers successively served as jié dù shǐ (military governors),
residing in Xiàzhōu,
which was south of the Hé (Yellow River).
Jìqiān re-established the state,
and Yuánhào first made it great.
He then crossed the river to the north,
built Xīngzhōu as his capital.
Initially, its territory included Xiàzhōu, Suīzhōu, Yínzhōu, Yòuzhōu, Língzhōu, Yánzhōu, and other prefectures.
Later, it seized the lands of Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè, Jiǔquán, and Dūnhuáng commanderies.
Its southern border was the Héngshān Mountains,
and its eastern border was the Xīhé (Western River).
The land was suitable for three types of crops,
had good water and grass,
and was suitable for animal husbandry.
This is what was called "Líangzhōu's animal husbandry is the best under heaven."
The soil was firm and fertile,
the water clear and cold,
the climate vast and wide.
The people's customs were strong-willed, valuing spirit,
keeping their promises,
and daring to fight.
From the Hàn and Táng dynasties, water conservancy was used to accumulate grain to feed border soldiers.
Xīngzhōu had two canals from the Hàn and Táng dynasties.
Gānzhōu and Líangzhōu also each had irrigation.
Though its territory was small,
it could become rich and powerful;
such was its geographical advantage.
During the period of the Five Dynasties,
dynasties rose in the morning and fell in the evening,
institutions, rites, and music were reduced to ashes.
The Táng dynasty's jié dù shǐ had drum and wind ensembles,
hence the Xià state's music was clear, sharp, and punctuated,
still bearing traces of the drum and wind ensembles.
However, they were able to highly value Confucianism,
honoring Confucius with an imperial title.
Their writings and edicts are worth observing.
Having established the state for over two hundred years,
they vied for power with the three states of Líáo, Jīn, and Sòng,
their allegiance being inconsistent,
varying according to the strength or weakness of the three states.
Therefore, modern scholars who recorded the geography of the northwest
often spoke based on conjecture.
When a sage emperor arises,
the world unites.
Post roads will crisscross, and they will be seen as eastern and western prefectures.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 73, Foreign Nations (Part II): Gāolì
King of Gāolì,
Wáng Kǎi.
Its territory was
east of the Yālù Jiāng (Yalu River),
south of the Hélǎn Lù,
and its southeast reached the sea.
From the time of the Líáo dynasty,
they sent envoys annually to present tribute.
Details are found in the Líáo Shǐ (History of the Líáo Dynasty).
In the early Táng dynasty,
the Mòhé had two tribes, Sùmò and Hēishuǐ,
both subservient to Gāolì.
When the Táng destroyed Gāolì,
the Sùmò protected Dōngmóu Shān and gradually grew stronger,
calling themselves Bóhǎi.
Their surname was Dà,
and they possessed culture, rites, and music.
By the late Táng dynasty, they gradually declined,
and were not heard of again thereafter.
When the Jīn attacked the Líáo,
the Bóhǎi came to submit,
presumably their surviving descendants.
The Hēishuǐ Mòhé resided in the ancient Sùshèn land.
There was a mountain called Báishān,
which is Mount Chángbái,
where the Jīn state arose.
Although the Nǚzhí were formerly subject to Gāolì,
they had ceased communication for a long time.
When the Jīn destroyed the Líáo,
Gāolì, in accordance with its old rites of serving Líáo, submitted to the Jīn.
Initially,
there was a doctor skilled in treating illnesses.
He was originally from Gāolì,
his origins unknown,
and his name was also not recorded.
He resided in the Wányán tribe of the Nǚzhí.
During Mùzōng's time, a relative was ill.
This doctor examined him.
Mùzōng said to the doctor:
"If you can cure this person's illness,
then I will send someone to escort you back to your homeland."
The doctor said:
"Yes."
The person's illness indeed recovered.
Mùzōng then, as per his initial promise, sent him back.
The Bójǐn Hú Shílái of the Púsàn tribe at Yǐlígǔ Líng resided between Gāolì and the Nǚzhí.
Mùzōng sent his tribesman Sōu'ā to summon him,
and then sent Sōu'ā to escort the doctor,
returning him to the Gāolì border.
When the doctor returned to Gāolì,
he told the Gāolì people that
the Nǚzhí residing in the Hēishuǐ region had tribes that were growing stronger day by day,
their soldiers becoming more elite and fierce,
and their harvests repeatedly abundant.
The King of Gāolì heard of this
and then opened communication with the Nǚzhí.
Soon after,
Hú Shílái came to submit,
and consequently, all the tribes east of Yǐlígǔ Líng swore allegiance.
In the tenth year of Mùzōng, guǐwèi (1103 CE),
Āshū, sent by Líáo, sent his follower Dá Jì to instigate the Hélǎndiàn people.
The Hélǎndiàn people seized him.
Mùzōng sent Dá Jì to Gāolì,
saying to the King of Gāolì:
"Those who caused trouble in your borderlands before
were all these people."
When Xiāo Hǎilǐ was defeated,
Ōlǔhǎn was sent to Gāolì to report the victory,
and Gāolì also sent an envoy to congratulate.
Not long after,
Xié Gě and Ōlǔhǎn were again sent to visit.
The King of Gāolì said:
"Xié Gě is
the Nǚzhí clan's younger brother;
his courtesy is exceptional."
Then he presented a large silver plate as a thank you.
Thereafter,
all the tribes of Hélǎndiàn desired to come and submit.
Gāolì heard of this and did not want them to submit,
fearing it would be too close to them and thus disadvantageous.
They sent people to stop them.
Xié Gě, while in Gāolì and traveling to and from Hélǎn Dào,
knew all the details.
He then sent Shí Shìhuān to receive the Hélǎndiàn people.
Before he could depart, Mùzōng died.
Kāngzōng succeeded him.
He sent Shí Shìhuān with the army of Xīngxiǎn Tǒngmén to Yǐlígǔ Líng,
and further recruited soldiers to advance to Huóniè Shuǐ,
pacifying the Hélǎndiàn region,
recovering seven cities that had rebelled or been lost.
Gāolì sent a messenger to say:
"There are matters that need discussion."
The Hélǎndiàn officials and subordinates sent Xié Lè Xiángwěn and Yělà Bǎo Xiángwěn.
Shí Shìhuān also sent Bēilǔ.
Gāolì seized Yělà Bǎo and others,
and sent Bēilǔ back, saying:
"This has nothing to do with you."
At this,
the people of the Five Waters all submitted to Gāolì,
and fourteen tuán liàn shǐ (regimental commanders) were captured.
In the second year, jiǎshēn (1104 CE),
Gāolì came to attack.
Shí Shìhuān greatly defeated them,
killing and capturing many.
He pursued them into their territory,
burned and plundered their garrisons, and then returned.
In the fourth month,
Gāolì attacked again.
Shí Shìhuān, with five hundred men, defended at Pìdēng Shuǐ,
and again greatly defeated them,
pursuing them into Pìdēng Shuǐ,
chasing their remaining forces across the border.
At this,
the King of Gāolì said:
"Those who reported border conflicts were all officials like Xiángdān, Bāngdōulǐ, and Xībìhǎn."
The fourteen tuán liàn and six lù envoys who were in Gāolì
were all returned,
and an envoy was sent to request peace.
Then Xié Gě was sent to formally demarcate the border,
reaching Yǐlígǔ Shuǐ and Hélǎndiàn's Huóní Shuǐ.
He stayed there for two months.
Xié Gě was unable to handle legal disputes,
each matter becoming complicated,
which caused considerable distress to the people.
Kāngzōng recalled Xié Gě
and sent Shí Shìhuān instead.
Shí Shìhuān established his headquarters at Sānchán Shuǐ.
Those who had secretly colluded with Gāolì to cause trouble
were immediately punished,
while others were not questioned.
Kāngzōng considered him capable.
In the fourth year, *bǐngxū*,
a Gāolì envoy, Hēihuān Fāngshí, came to congratulate Kāngzōng on his succession.
Kāngzōng sent Bēilǔ to return the visit
and to reiterate the previous agreement
for the return of their runaway subjects.
Gāolì agreed,
saying:
"Send an envoy to the border to receive them."
Kāngzōng believed this to be true,
and sent Āguō of the Wányán部 and Shèngkūn of the Wūlíndá部 to the border to receive them.
Kāngzōng hunted at Mǎjìlǐng Yǐzhīcūn to await their return.
When Āguō and Shèngkūn reached the border,
Gāolì sent men to kill them,
and dispatched troops to Gélǎn Diān,
where they built nine cities.
Upon Kāngzōng's return,
the衆 all said:
"We cannot raise an army,
fearing that the Liáo people will blame us."
Tàizǔ alone said:
"If we do not raise an army,
it will not just be Gélǎn Diān that is lost;
all the tribes will no longer be ours."
Kāngzōng agreed,
and so sent Wòsài to lead troops to attack them,
greatly defeating the Gāolì forces.
In the sixth month,
Gāolì led their衆 to battle again;
Wòsài defeated them,
and advanced to besiege their city.
In the seventh month,
Gāolì again requested peace.
Kāngzōng said:
"If the terms are reasonable,
then we shall make peace."
Gāolì promised to return the runaway subjects,
withdraw the garrisons from the nine cities,
and restore the formerly encroached territory.
Thus, peace was made with them.
In the ninth month of the first year of Shōuguó,
Tàizǔ had already captured Huánglóng Fǔ
and ordered Jiāgǔ Sāhē to attack Bǎozhōu.
Bǎozhōu was near Gāolì,
having been established by Liáo after invading Gāolì.
Now,
Sāhē was ordered to take it.
It did not fall for a long time,
and Sāhē requested reinforcements,
also reporting that the King of Gāolì was about to send an envoy.
Tàizǔ sent Nàhé Wūchǔn with one hundred cavalry to reinforce him,
and issued an edict to Sāhē saying:
"You lead a detached force,
have repeatedly broken formidable enemies,
and captured many.
And I heard that Húshā achieved merit in several battles;
I greatly commend him.
If Bǎozhōu has not yet fallen,
just guard the border.
I have already captured Huánglóng Fǔ
and hear that the Liáo sovereign is about to arrive.
After defeating this major enemy, I will reinforce your troops again.
Regarding the matter of Gāolì sending an envoy,
it is uncertain whether it is true;
if they arrive, escort them here.
Be careful and do not neglect border affairs."
In the eleventh month,
fifteen people including the Liáo Jurchens Mámàn Tàiwān all surrendered.
Kāizhōu was attacked and captured,
and all the Jurchens in the Bǎozhōu region surrendered.
Tàizǔ appointed Sāhē as the Dūtǒng of Bǎozhōulù.
Tàizǔ had already routed the Liáo sovereign's army,
and Sāhē had captured Hézhǔ and Shùnhuà, two cities.
He again requested reinforcements to attack Bǎozhōu,
and Wòlǔ was sent with a thousand armored soldiers.
In the intercalary month of the second year,
Gāolì sent an envoy to congratulate on the victory,
and also said:
"Bǎozhōu is our former territory;
we wish for it to be returned to us."
Tàizǔ said to the envoy:
"You may take it yourselves."
An edict was issued to Sāhē, Wūchǔn, and others, saying:
"If Gāolì comes to take Bǎozhōu,
reinforce with the armies of Húlàgǔ and Xíxiǎn and other forces as a precaution.
If they wish to combine forces,
do not advance rashly;
just diligently guard the border garrisons."
When Sāhē and Āshílàilài attacked Bǎozhōu,
the Liáo defender fled,
and Gāolì troops were already in the city.
Afterward,
the King of Gāolì sent Púmǎ to request Bǎozhōu.
An edict was issued to the King of Gāolì, saying:
"Bǎozhōu is near your border;
you were allowed to take it yourselves,
but now you have troubled our army
to break the enemy in front of the city.
Furthermore, Púmǎ's request is merely verbal;
await a formal memorial,
then we shall discuss it separately."
In the twelfth month of the second year of Tiānfǔ,
an edict was issued to the King of Gāolì, saying:
"When I first raised an army to attack Liáo,
I had already announced it.
With the aid of August Heaven,
I have repeatedly defeated the enemy forces.
From Shàngjīng in the north
to the sea in the south,
all the prefectures, commanderies, counties, tribes, and people within that area have been pacified.
Now I send Bójǐn Shúbó to inform you,
and also bestow a horse,
which you may receive upon arrival."
In the third year,
Gāolì increased the height of its long wall by three *chǐ*.
The border officials dispatched troops to stop them,
but they did not comply,
reporting:
"We are repairing the old wall."
Húlàgǔ and Xíxiǎn, the Bójǐn of Gélǎn Diān, reported this,
and an edict said:
"Do not invade or create incidents,
but only strengthen your encampments
and extensively gather intelligence."
In the fourth year,
the Xiánzhōulù Dūtǒngsī deployed troops to garrison Bǎozhōu and Bìlǐwéi, two cities,
and requested more troops.
An edict said:
"It is very good
that you are arraying your garrisons
to strengthen the frontier defense.
Gāolì has served Liáo for generations;
they may have communications.
You can constantly send people to spy on them."
Xíxiǎn was sent to inform Gāolì about the captured Liáo prefectures and counties.
Their country was then executing rebels,
and an envoy said to Xíxiǎn:
"This is a letter for my late father, the King."
Xíxiǎn was lodged in the guesthouse.
After executing over seventy officials,
they received him according to the old rites,
and sent a memorial to congratulate
and present local products.
They were also informed about the Liáo emperor's escape into Xiàguó.
Gāo Suí and Xiéyě were sent as envoys to Gāolì.
Upon reaching the border,
the reception was not respectful,
and Suí and others dared not proceed.
Tàizōng said:
"Gāolì has been a vassal of Liáo for generations;
they should serve us with the same rites as they served Liáo.
However, our country has suffered a recent loss,
and the Liáo sovereign has not yet been captured.
Do not press them immediately."
He ordered Gāo Suí and others to return.
In the second year of Tiānhuì,
Gǔshídá, the Tóngzhī Nánlù Dūtǒng, reported that
Gāolì was harboring fugitives and increasing border defenses,
surely with other intentions.
An edict said:
"All communications
must not deviate from the usual form.
If they come to invade,
then array your ranks and engage them.
Whoever dares to attack them first,
even if victorious, will be punished."
An edict ordered Shémǔ to garrison the islands with a thousand armored soldiers
to prepare for them.
In the fourth year,
King Wáng Kǎi sent an envoy with a memorial declaring vassalage.
A generous edict was issued in reply.
The sovereign sent Gāo Bóshū and Wū Zhìzhōng as envoys to Gāolì,
stating that all diplomatic exchanges should follow the old Liáo customs,
and that all people from the Bǎozhōulù and borderlands who were in their territory
must be fully returned.
An imperial order to Bóshū said:
"If they agree to everything,
then grant them the territory of Bǎozhōu."
When Gāo Bóshū arrived in Gāolì,
King Kǎi attached a memorial expressing gratitude,
following entirely the old system of serving Liáo.
In the eighth year,
Kǎi submitted a memorial
begging for exemption from the demand for the runaway border households from Bǎozhōu.
That year,
ten Gāolì people were fishing,
and a strong wind blew their boat to the coast.
Hésūguǎn people captured them,
and an edict ordered their return to their country.
Later, Xù submitted a memorial requesting not to demand the Bǎozhōu households that had fled into Gāolì.
Tàizōng agreed,
and from then on, the border of Bǎozhōu was established.
In the second year of Huángtǒng,
an edict added the titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Shàngzhùguó to Kǎi.
In the sixth year,
Kǎi died,
and his son Xiàn succeeded him.
In Dàdìng fourth year,
the garrisons at Yālùjiāng Bǎo were frequently invaded, burned, and destroyed.
In the first month of the fifth year,
Shìzōng, when the New Year's Day envoy was leaving the court,
instructed him, saying:
"Regarding the minor unexpected incidents on the border,
was it your lord who caused them,
or were they perpetrated by border officials?
If indeed they were perpetrated by border officials,
your lord should also punish and admonish them."
Initially,
it was customary for Gāolí envoys to present private gifts.
That year, on Wànchūnjié,
the Emperor, considering that the envoys' private gifts were not in accordance with protocol,
issued an edict to abolish them.
In the tenth year,
Wáng Xiàn's younger brother, Yìyáng Gōng Hào, deposed Xiàn and enthroned himself.
In the tenth month,
when the birthday envoy and Dàzōngzhèng Cé Zhì arrived at the border,
Gāolí border officials claimed the former king had already abdicated,
and refused to receive the envoy.
In the third month of the eleventh year,
Wáng Hào sent a memorial reporting his abdication.
An edict was issued to Bàsùlù not to accept it,
and the relevant authorities were ordered to send a dispatch to inquire in detail.
Gāolí reported:
"The former king has been ill for a long time,
senile and unable to govern,
and has appointed his younger half-brother Hào to provisionally administer state affairs."
The Emperor said:
"Abdication is a major affair;
why was it not first submitted for approval?"
An edict was issued to the relevant authorities to inquire again in detail.
Gāolí then sent Wáng Xiàn's abdication memorial,
which generally stated that the late minister Jiē's dying wish was to pass the throne to his younger brother,
and also implied that his son had committed crimes and was unfit to be enthroned.
The Emperor was suspicious
and asked his prime ministers and executive officials.
Prime Minister Liángbì memorialized:
"This cannot be believed.
Xiàn only has one son,
who had a grandson born in previous years,
and he once sent a memorial to express his joy at having a grandson;
that is one point.
Hào once caused unrest,
and Xiàn imprisoned him;
that is two points.
Now Xiàn has not sent an envoy,
but Hào has sent one;
that is three points.
The court sent a birthday envoy to Xiàn,
but Hào did not forward it to Xiàn,
claiming he dared not accept it;
that is four points.
This is Hào usurping his brother and making a false plea to the Son of Heaven;
how can this be tolerated?"
Right Chancellor Mèng Hào said:
"We should inquire among the officials and common people of that country.
If they all truly accept him,
then an envoy should be sent to confer the patent of investiture."
The Emperor said:
"To confer a ruler of a country by inquiring among the common people,
how is this different from appointing a Měng'ān or Móukè?"
So he rejected their envoy,
and sent an edict to Wáng Xiàn for detailed inquiry.
Lìbù Shìláng Jìng was dispatched as the envoy to inquire with Wáng Xiàn.
Hào had indeed usurped the throne
and imprisoned Xiàn on an island.
When Jìng arrived in Gāolí,
Hào claimed Wáng Xiàn had already abdicated and moved to another place,
and his illness had worsened without improvement,
so he could not attend to receive the imperial decree,
and the journey was dangerous and distant,
not suitable for an envoy to undertake.
Jìng ultimately could not see Xiàn,
so he handed the edict to Hào,
who then submitted Xiàn's memorial,
the content of which was largely similar to the previous memorial.
When Jìng returned,
the Emperor consulted his ministers,
who all said:
"Since Xiàn's memorial is like this,
he can be formally invested."
Prime Minister Liángbì and Píngzhāng Zhèngshì Shǒudào said:
"It is not too late to wait for Hào to petition for it."
In the twelfth month,
Hào sent his Lǐbù Shìláng Zhāng Yìmíng and others to request investiture.
In the third month of the twelfth year,
the patent of investiture was conferred.
Hào's birthday was on the nineteenth day of the first month.
As the twelfth month of that year was almost over,
there was not enough time to send an envoy,
so the relevant authorities requested to hold it the following year.
In the fifteenth year,
Zhào Wèichǒng, the Xīyīng Liúshǒu of Gāolí, rebelled against Hào,
and sent Xú Yàn and ninety-five others to submit a memorial saying:
"The former king did not abdicate voluntarily;
Dàjiāngjūn Zhèng Chōngfū and Lángjiàng Lǐ Yìfāng actually assassinated him.
I, Wèichǒng, request that the forty-odd cities west of Cíbēilǐng up to the Yālù Jiāng be incorporated into the empire,
and I ask for military assistance."
The Emperor said:
"Wáng Hào has already been invested.
Wèichǒng dares to raise troops and cause rebellion,
and furthermore wishes to surrender territory.
I embrace and pacify all nations;
how could I assist a rebellious subject in tyranny?"
An edict was issued to arrest Xú Yàn and others and send them back to Gāolí.
Soon after,
Wáng Hào suppressed Zhào Wèichǒng's rebellion
and sent an envoy to report and express gratitude.
Since Wèichǒng's rebellion,
the envoys sent by Hào for birthday thanks, horizontal thanks, New Year's Day congratulations, tribute, and Wànchūnjié,
had all been obstructed and unable to pass.
At this point,
Hào memorialized them all at once.
An edict was issued in response to his intent,
stating that those who were supposed to send envoys should come to court in due order.
In the seventeenth year,
among the New Year's Day congratulatory gifts,
there was a jade belt made of stone resembling jade.
The relevant authorities requested to inquire about it,
but the Emperor said:
"That small country probably has no one who can recognize it;
they mistakenly took it for jade.
There is no need to inquire."
So it was dropped.
In the twelfth month,
the relevant authorities reported that the Gāolí Xiàjié Yāmǎguān Shùnchéng had exceptionally crossed the border three times with armor.
The Emperor, considering that the crime committed by the envoy was severe,
merely ordered him to be sent back to his own country.
In the twenty-third year,
Hào's mother, Rèn Shì, passed away.
Hào requested to be exempted from sending birthday gifts and congratulatory thanks.
An edict was issued to grant it.
When Zhāngzōng ascended the throne,
the imperial envoys were considerably delayed upon reaching the border.
An edict was issued to inquire,
and Gāolí humbly apologized.
In Míngchāng third year,
Xiàjié Jīn Tǐng, returning to Píngzhōu Fǔníng Xiàn,
beat to death an innkeeper named Hé Tiān'ér.
The relevant authorities requested,
"Whenever envoys travel back and forth,
we beg to set up guards as appropriate."
Cānzhī Zhèngshì Zhāng Wàngōng said:
"They can be patrolled and protected at their lodging places."
The Emperor approved his memorial.
An edict was issued that from now on, escorting and accompanying officials who fail in their duties of oversight would be punished.
According to precedent,
the New Year's Day congratulatory envoy would have an audience on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month.
In Míngchāng sixth year, Lìchūn fell on the *jǐmǎo* day of the twelfth month.
An edict was issued that the audience would be held on the *dīngchǒu* day, two days prior.
In Chéng'ān second year,
Hào submitted a memorial stating his infirmity,
and ceded the country to his younger brother Zhěn.
Zhěn provisionally administered state affairs.
That year,
Hào was deposed,
and Zhěn succeeded him.
On the *yǐchǒu* day, the first day of the first month of Tàihé fourth year,
a Gāolí retainer used a small dagger to cut pears under the gallery of the residence.
A Fèngzhí saw him and reprimanded him.
An edict was issued to the accompanying officials to send a notice in advance from now on to prohibit such acts.
That year,
Wáng Zhěn died,
and his son Yīng succeeded him.
In the first month of Tàihé seventh year,
at that time, troops were being used to attack Sòng,
and Xià also had issues.
Only Gāolí sent a New Year's Day envoy,
so an edict was issued not to grant a special banquet.
When Tiānshòujié arrived,
envoys from Xià and Gāolí were both present.
The relevant authorities memorialized:
"At the beginning of Dàdìng,
Sòng had not yet requested peace,
and envoys from Xià and Gāolí were granted special banquets.
Now we request to follow the precedent of Dàdìng."
An edict was issued to grant it.
In the eighth month of Zhìníng first year,
Wáng Zhěn died,
and his successor had not yet performed the funeral rites.
In the ninth month,
Xuānzōng ascended the throne.
Border officials reported:
"Gāolí's document states that
the successor has not yet performed the funeral rites,
so he cannot receive an auspicious imperial decree in mourning attire,
nor can he sign a memorial with a provisional title of 'straw and earth' [meaning an ordinary person]."
The ritual officials deliberated:
"A subject should not abandon public righteousness for private sentiment.
It is appropriate to temporarily use auspicious attire to receive the imperial decree,
and sign the memorial with the title of 'provisionally administering state affairs.'
After Gāolí's envoy reporting the mourning arrives at the imperial court,
then an envoy shall be sent to offer sacrifices, express condolences, and carry out the investiture."
This was approved.
The following year,
Xuānzōng (宣宗) moved to Biàn (汴).
The road to Liáodōng (遼東) was impassable.
In the third year of Xīngdìng (興定),
the Liáodōng (遼東) branch secretariat reported that Gāolì (高麗) again expressed its intention to present a memorial and pay tribute.
The chief ministers reported:
"The branch secretariat may be ordered to receive their memorial,
but the rituals of tribute should be deliberated later."
Xuānzōng (宣宗) agreed,
and thus sent envoys to pacify Gāolì (高麗).
Ultimately, due to impassable roads,
there was no time to welcome them.
An imperial edict instructed the branch secretariat to merely keep them in check and not sever good relations.
However, from then on, communication ceased.
A eulogy states: The Jīn (金) people originally came from the Mòhé (靺鞨) who were subject to Gāolì (高麗).
Initially, they maintained good relations as neighboring states,
but later became sovereign and subject.
After Zhēnyòu (貞祐), the roads became impassable,
and they met only once or twice.
Upon entering the sacred dynasty, they passed down governance as if they were descendants,
so it is not extensively discussed,
but rather only matters related to the Jīn (金) are discussed.
Collational Notes
The language of the extant Shàngshū (尚書) is often obscure and difficult,
probably a local dialect of that era.
The native languages recorded in the Jīn Shǐ (金史),
obtained through multiple translations,
and those that can be understood, how can they be omitted?
As for the informal names of their officials and subordinates,
some were given due to low status,
or due to illness,
still retaining the ancient custom of valuing simplicity;
they should not be embellished.
The imperial surname was so-and-so,
the Hàn (漢) surname was so-and-so,
a practice that has existed since Xiàowén (孝文) of the Later Wèi (魏).
These are preserved at the end of the chapter
for reference.
Official Titles
Dūbójíliè (都勃極烈):
a general official title,
like the Hàn (漢) term "zǒngzǎi (冢宰)."
Ānbǎnbójíliè (諳版勃極烈):
a respected and noble official.
Guólùnbójíliè (國論勃極烈):
one who is honored, privileged, and free.
Húlǔbójíliè (胡魯勃極烈):
a title for a commanding official.
Yílàibójíliè (移賚勃極烈):
ranks third, called
"yílàI (移賚)."
Āmàibójíliè (阿買勃極烈):
one who governs cities and towns.
Yǐshìbójíliè (乙室勃極烈):
an official for receiving guests.
Zhāshīhābójíliè (札失哈勃極烈):
a title for guarding official residences.
Zèbójíliè (昃勃極烈):
an official for yin and yang (astronomy/calendrical affairs).
Diébójíliè (迭勃極烈):
a deputy or assistant official.
Měng'ān (猛安):
a chiliarch (commander of a thousand).
Móukè (謀克):
a centurion (commander of a hundred).
Various Terms
"Xiángwěn (詳穩)":
an official of border garrisons.
Various
"Yílíjǐn (移里菫)":
leaders of tribes and fortified villages.
Xiángwěn (詳穩) and Yílíjǐn (移里菫)
were originally Qìdān (遼) terms,
adopted by the Jīn (金) people with slight variations.
Tūlǐ (禿里):
one who manages tribal lawsuits
and investigates wrongdoing.
Wūlǔgǔ (烏魯古):
an official for herding and stable management.
Wòlǐxīng (斡里𩽆):
a place where government offices conduct business.
Human Affairs
Bólúnchū (孛論出):
the name for an embryo.
Āhúdié (阿胡迭):
eldest son.
Gǔxīng (骨●):
youngest.
Púyángwēn (蒲陽溫):
means young son.
Yìdū (益都):
a general term for order or sequence.
The ninth is called
"Wūyě (烏也)."
The sixteenth is called
"Nǚlǔhuān (女魯歡)."
Àndáhǎi (按答海):
a general term for guests.
Shānzhīkūn (山只昆):
an attendant.
Sànyìbèi (散亦孛):
a remarkable man.
Sādá (撒答):
a term for an old person.
Shígǔnǎi (什古乃):
a thin person.
Sāhénián (撒合輦):
the name for dark-skinned.
Bǎohuólǐ (保活里):
a dwarf.
Ālǐsūn (阿里孫):
of unappealing appearance.
Ātúhǎn (阿徒罕):
son of a woodcutter.
Dábùyě (答不也):
one who weeds fields.
Ātǔgǔ (阿土古):
one skilled at gathering and hunting.
Ālǐxǐ (阿里喜):
a hunting encirclement.
Bálìsù (拔里速):
a wrestler.
Ālíhédá (阿离合懣):
one who carries a hawk or falcon on his arm.
Húlǔlà (胡魯剌):
head of a household.
Āhé (阿合):
a human slave.
Wùzhú (兀术):
means head.
Zhānhǎn (粘罕):
means heart.
Wèikě (畏可):
tooth,
also called Wúyìkě (吾亦可).
Pánlǐhé (盤里合):
refers to a finger.
Sānhé (三合):
a human dimple.
Yáwǔtǎ (牙吾塔):
a sore or ulcer.
Púlàdū (蒲剌都):
eyes red and blind.
Shígēlǐ (石哥里):
urinary disease.
Màndūgē (謾都謌):
means foolish or idiotic.
Móuliánghǔ (謀良虎):
the name for a scoundrel.
All are terms of ill repute.
To share blessings with others is called
"Hūdū (忽都)."
To help others with strength is called
"Āxībǎo (阿息保)."
Cíbùshī (辭不失):
to be sober from wine.
Núshēn (奴申):
means harmony.
Échūhǔ (訛出虎):
the name for tolerance.
Sàilǐ (賽里):
peace and joy.
Dígǔnǎi (迪古乃):
means to come.
Sābā (撒八):
means swiftness.
Wūgūchū (烏古出):
in dialect means "zài xiū (再休),"
which is like saying "never again."
Whatever is first is called
"Shílún (石倫)."
To have already given something to someone is called
"Ālíbái (阿里白)."
Wúlǐbǔ (吾里補):
the name for accumulated wealth.
Xíshī (習失):
like people say "chángchuān (常川)" (regularly).
When goods are already purchased is called
"Wùdài (兀帶),"
and those who take this name for their children
mean "acquired like an item."
Natural Objects
Wùdiǎn (兀典):
a bright star.
Ālín (阿鄰):
mountain.
Tàishén (太神):
high.
A sharp peak on a mountain is called
"Hādān (哈丹)."
A slope is called
"Ālán (阿懶)."
Large and steep is called
"Xiélǔ (斜魯)."
Tè lín
means sea.
Shāhū dài
means boat.
Pig iron is called
"Wòlún".
A cauldron is called
"Shēmǔ".
A blade is called
"Xiáliè".
Póluóhuǒ is a hammer.
Gold is called
"Ànchūn".
Yínshúkě
means pearl.
A cloth sack is called
"Púlúhún".
A basin is called
"Ālǐhǔ".
A jar is called
"Huónǚ".
Wūliè
means a grass sword.
Shālā
means lapel.
Huólàhú
means red color.
Húlà
means chimney.

Collation Notes
Memorial Presenting the History of Jīn
Ālútú, Minister with the Title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Shàngzhùguó, Lù Jūnguó Zhòngshì, Zhōngshū Yòuchéngxiàng, Jiānxiū Guóshǐ, Lǐng Jīngyánshì, Tídiào Tàiyīyuàn Guǎnghuìsīshì, states:
I humbly observe that when Emperor Gāo of Hàn entered the Pass,
he employed Xiāo Hé to collect the Qin records;
when Emperor Tàizōng of Táng ascended the throne,
he ordered Wèi Zhēng to compile the History of Suí.
Indeed, the mandate of heaven reverts to the court of the true ruler,
and the written records preserve the affairs of previous dynasties.
A state may perish, but history must not perish;
the good is our teacher, and the bad is also our teacher.
Furthermore, the origins and development of institutions and regulations,
and the evolution of systems and procedures,
if one does not examine past records,
how can one accumulate knowledge of the past?
This Jīnyuán (Jīn Dynasty),
arose from the edge of the sea,
with an army of ten thousand,
it swept across the world;
in less than ten years,
it dominated the realm.
Its use of troops was like a spreading fire driven by the wind;
its acquisition of the state was like setting up a relay post to transmit orders.
When it flourished with rites and music,
its fame and reputation shone brightly.
Having followed its beginning to its end,
we evaluate merits and discuss virtues.
Without Wǔyuán's (Emperor Tàizǔ's) brilliant strategy,
the foundation for nine emperors' reign could not have been established;
without Dàdìng's benevolent governance,
the hundred-year foundation could not have been solidified.
Tiānhuì had the potential to swallow the four seas,
but lacked a plan to unify them;
Míngchāng was able to establish a system for an era,
but also able to destroy the laws of an era.
Hǎilíng was without principle,
and brought about his own downfall;
Xuānzōng acted rashly,
how could he achieve a restoration?
By the time of the autumn when many fortifications lined the plains of Jùn,
and the day when smoke flew over the Ru River,
the hopes of heaven and man
had long been fixed;
the loyalty of monarch and subjects
was indeed commendable.
My Great Ancestor, Fǎtiān Qǐyùn Shèngwǔ Huángdì (法天啟運聖武皇帝),
with an army of renown,
released the grievances of generations;
with an invincible benevolence,
he captured the hearts of the common people.
His mighty troops stormed Jūyōng Guān (居庸關),
striking the enemy from the north;
his grand army marched out of Zǐjīng Kǒu (紫荊口),
blocking their throat from the south.
With a nod and a glance, he achieved splendid deeds,
his strategies in the ancestral temple were beyond comprehension.
He punished the cruelty of the conquest of Liáo (遼),
but permitted their crossing the river to relocate.
Tàizōng Yīngwén Huángdì (太宗英文皇帝) swept across Yún (雲) and Shuò (朔),
and seized territory in Bìng (幷) and Yíng (營);
he enveloped Zhào (趙) and Dài (代),
and sent dispatches to Qí (齊) and Lǔ (魯).
He annihilated the Xià (夏) Kingdom, conquering Qín (秦) and Gǒng (鞏);
he allied with the Sòng (宋) people to press against Hé (河) and Huái (淮).
Ruìzōng Rénshèng Jǐngxiāng Huángdì (睿宗仁聖景襄皇帝) braved myriad dangers,
emerging from Ráofēng (饒風),
and marched swiftly to Pínglù (平陸);
he fought at Sānfēng (三峯),
amidst heavy snow,
and thus pacified the Central Plains.
When the sun rises, the fireflies' light is extinguished;
when the proper music plays, all other sounds cease.
Eventually, Shìzǔ Shèngdé Shéngōng Wénwǔ Huángdì (世祖聖德神功文武皇帝)
expanded the utmost transformation,
and brought solace to the remaining populace.
He established the capital in Yān (燕) territory,
demolishing the old site of Wǔlíng (武靈);
he established a province in Liáoyáng (遼陽),
comforting the ancient ruins of Sùshèn (肅慎).
At that time, Zhāng Róu (張柔) submitted the history of Jīn (金) from his predecessors,
and Wáng È (王鶚) compiled the affairs of Jīn (金) thereafter.
Therefore, the mandate for compilation
was seen in the plans for widespread distribution.
The Yányòu (延祐) era renewed the effort but did not complete it;
the Tiānlì (天曆) era promoted it but it was not finished.
I, minister Ālǔtú (阿魯圖), with utmost reverence and trepidation,
bow my head repeatedly,
humbly observing that Your Majesty, the Emperor, illuminates sacred learning,
and carries on the traditions of your predecessors.
During a time of peace for the nation and the family,
you attend to the study and discussion of classics and history.
Recalling the events since Tàihé (泰和),
spanning the early years of our sacred dynasty.
Tàizǔ (太祖) received the imperial title in the year Bǐngyín (丙寅),
five years earlier, the vermilion phoenix appeared;
Shìhuáng (世皇) was born with a sacred nature in the year Yǐhài (乙亥),
one year earlier, the Yellow River ran clear.
Such auspicious signs
are clearly heavenly mandates.
However, due to many changes, the old histories are deficient;
as the elders passed away, new accounts became erroneous.
If not rectified by the great court,
it might lead to historical inaccuracies in the future.
Therefore, the Sacred Heart made an independent decision,
and grand deeds were carried out.

It was decreed that I, minister Ālǔtú (阿魯圖), as Grand Councillor of the Right of the Central Secretariat, and minister Bié'ěrqièbùhuā (別兒怯不花), as Grand Councillor of the Left of the Central Secretariat, should lead the compilation of the Three Histories.
Minister Tuōtuō (脫脫), former Grand Councillor of the Right of the Central Secretariat, was to remain the Chief Compiler.

Minister Tiēmù'ěrdáshì (帖睦爾達世), Censor-in-Chief; minister Hè Wéiyī (賀惟一), Administrator of Governmental Affairs of the Central Secretariat; minister Zhāng Qǐyán (張起巖), Hanlin Academician and Grand Academician Remonstrant; minister Ōuyáng Xuán (歐陽玄), Hanlin Academician; minister Lǐ Hǎowén (李好文), Investigating Censor; minister Wáng Yí (王沂), Minister of Rites; and minister Yáng Zōngruì (楊宗瑞), Supervisor of the Chongwen Academy, were appointed as Compiler-in-Chiefs.

Minister Shālābān (沙剌班), Surveillance Commissioner for Jiāngxī (江西) and Húdōng (湖東) Circuits; minister Wáng Lǐ (王理), Vice Surveillance Commissioner for Jiāngxī (江西) and Húdōng (湖東) Circuits; minister Báiyán (伯顏), Hanlin Attendant; minister Fèi Zhù (費著), Doctor of the Imperial Academy; minister Zhào Shímǐn (趙時敏), Writer in the Imperial Secretariat; and minister Shāng Qǐwēng (商企翁), Doctor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, were appointed as Historians.
Gathering all skills to produce the complete work,
I await the presentation of the chapters for your imperial review.
I, minister Ālǔtú (阿魯圖), reverently accept this weighty charge,
and humbly exert my meager efforts.
Though lacking the literary skill of Sīmǎ Qiān (司馬遷) in compiling the stone chamber records,
I present this Golden Mirror record, wishing to express the loyalty of Premier Zhāng (張).
I have respectfully compiled nineteen volumes of Imperial Annals, thirty-nine volumes of Treatises, four volumes of Tables, seventy-three volumes of Biographies, and two volumes of Catalogues,
bound into one hundred and thirty-seven fascicles.
I present this together with my memorial,
to trouble Your Majesty's celestial gaze,
overwhelmed by shame, trembling, and apprehension.
I, minister Ālǔtú (阿魯圖), with utmost reverence and trepidation,
bow my head repeatedly, respectfully stating.

Official Document on the History of Jīn (金)*
By Imperial Edict.
The Jiāngzhè (江浙) and other Provisional Central Secretariats received a communication from the Central Secretariat on the 26th day of the sixth month of the fifth year of Zhìzhèng (至正)
"On the 13th day of the fourth month of the fifth year of Zhìzhèng (至正),
the second day of Dúlian Tiēmù'ěrl Qièxī (篤怜帖木兒怯薛),
when Shālǐng Nàbò Wòtuō (沙嶺納鉢斡脫) was present,
Sùgǔ'ěrrchì Yǎpǔhuà (速古兒赤雅普化), Yúndūchì Sādílǐmíshī (云都赤撒迪里迷失), Diànzhōng Sāmǎ (殿中撒馬), Gěishìzhōng Yěxiānbùxiān (給事中也先不先), and others arrived.

Right Grand Councillor Ālǔtú (阿魯圖), Censor Tiēmù'ěrtǎshī (帖木兒塔失), Administrator Tàipíng (太平), Administrator Báiyán (伯顏), Right Vice Minister Dáshì Tiēmù'ěrl (達世帖睦爾), and others memorialized: 'Last year, an order was given to compile the histories of the three dynasties of Liáo (遼), Jīn (金), and Sòng (宋).
Currently, the histories of Liáo (遼) and Jīn (金) have been compiled.
Now, these histories are to be engraved and printed in the two provinces of Jiāngzhè (江浙) and Jiāngxī (江西).
The existing funds for schools there shall be used for this purpose.
Each is to print one hundred copies as quickly as possible.'
As it was memorialized,
this is by imperial edict.
Respect this.
We consult and request compliance and implementation,
and further instruct the Provisional Central Secretariat to appoint one high-ranking civil official and one leading official
to respectfully supervise
the swift printing, completion, and dispatch."
In accordance with this,
our province consults and appoints Councillor Qín Zhōngfèng (秦中奉) and Recorders Xú Pán Chéngdé (徐槃承德) of the Left and Right Bureaus
to respectfully supervise;
and instructs the Jiāngzhè (江浙) Confucian Directorate to appoint Director Bān Wéizhì Fèngzhèng (班惟志奉政) to proofread the characters.
The Hángzhōu (杭州) Circuit is instructed to appoint a high-ranking civil official
and a leading official to supervise the engraving, printing, and binding.
